## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who Flourished from the Apostolic Age down to the Times of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprinting of all the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that Have Survived through the First Twelve Centuries of the Church, Prepared from the Most Accurate Editions, Collated with One Another and with Several Manuscripts, Carefully Corrected; Continuously Illustrated with Dissertations, Commentaries, and Variant Readings; Enlarged with All Works Discovered after the Extensive Editions Owed to the Last Three Centuries, as well as with Other Writings; Furnished with Particular Analytical Indexes Following Each Volume and Each Author of Some Importance; Adorned with Chapters Properly Arranged within the Text Itself, and Also with Titles Distinguishing the Upper Margin of Each Page and Indicating the Subject Matter Below; Enlarged with Works Both Doubtful and Apocryphal, and with Others Possessing Some Authority in Relation to Ecclesiastical Tradition; Enriched with Two General Indexes: One of Matters, by Consulting Which Whatever Each Father Has Written on Any Topic May Be Seen at a Glance; the Other of Sacred Scripture, from Which It Is Easy for the Reader to Discover Which Fathers, and in What Places of Their Works, Commented on the Individual Texts of the Books of Scripture.**

**A Most Accurate Edition, and Easily Preferable to All Others, If One Takes into Consideration the Clarity of the Type, the Quality of the Paper, the Integrity of the Text, the Perfection of the Correction, the Variety and Number of the Reprinted Works, the Highly Convenient Format of the Volumes, Uniformly Consistent throughout the Entire Work, the Low Price, and Above All This Collection Itself—Unique, Methodical, and Chronological—which for the First Time Brings Together in Our Library the Six Hundred Fragments and Minor Works Previously Scattered Here and There, Gathered from Works Relating to Every Age, Place, Language, and Form.**

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## The Complete Works of Saint Eusebius Jerome, Priest of Stridon

After the recension of the monks of the Order of Saint Benedict from the Congregation of Saint Maur, but chiefly that of Jean Martianay of this Order, newly corrected against Roman, Ambrosian, Veronese, and many other manuscripts, as well as against all French and foreign editions; enlarged with very many monuments previously altogether unpublished and with other labors of the holy Doctor previously published only separately; illustrated with innumerable notes, observations, and corrections through the study and labor of Vallarsi and Maffei, priests of Verona, with the assistance of other learned men in that same city.

The latest Paris edition, revised after the second edition by the Veronese editors themselves through their later efforts, and so enriched from more recently discovered materials that the present edition, by its mere extent and apart from all omitted corrections, materially surpasses all preceding editions, even the Benedictine ones, by a third part, or one-third; prepared and finally revised by J. P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Jerome

[Column 0009]

## Preface

This volume is the fifth in the division of Jerome’s works. From the nature of its subject—namely, the commentaries on the remaining two major prophets, Ezekiel and Daniel—I had decided to join it into one volume with the fourth. I would indeed have done so, had not the enlarged material of that volume under the press grown into an abnormal mass, and had not the addition, which especially belongs to this volume and is by far the longer, namely the absolutely necessary addition of genuine writings lacking from the previously published editions, compelled us to divide the work into two volumes.

For this reason, however, I am far from thinking that I have caused any inconvenience to readers; rather, I have earned much gratitude from them, since, in order to serve their studies, a much greater labor had to be undertaken, and since I had to devote every amount of leisure and effort so that the most holy Father might not appear before the public still unfairly deprived in any part of his work.

For it is clear from the entire arrangement of this collection that we were no more concerned to embrace the whole circle, as it were, of Jerome’s labors in a single work than to prevent it from being burdened with alien materials—though materials that could be absent without any loss to the reading or dignity of his writings. The third volume itself, which abounds in writings of this kind, provides evidence. Yet from it we removed certain useless items that burdened the Paris edition: for example, that specimen of Origen’s *Hexapla*, which contributes almost nothing to Jerome and which later appeared, as an independent work, in two splendid folio volumes; and also one or two previously unpublished works concerning Hebrew Names, which we thought it better to leave hidden among our papers than to increase the mass of another’s miscellany.

The materials now added to this volume for the first time are thirty-two homilies which the holy Doctor translated from Origen’s Greek into Latin. They are the noblest portion of his explanations of the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel—not only because they were prepared for Roman ears through the labor of the greatest interpreter of Scripture and are praised by him in the catalogue of his own works, but also because, since the Greek text of Adamantius has now for the most part perished, these homilies alone almost sustain the glory of the original.

We have taken them partly from the edition of Huetius and partly from that of Genebrard. It is astonishing—especially in an editor whose learning we admire and whose talent we greatly enjoy—that we did not find in his publication of Jerome’s labors the diligence that would have preserved his reliability in other matters. The edition teems everywhere with so many faults that we have washed away an immense number of them, so that, now restored to their original integrity, these works may seem to enter the public domain for the first time.

We postponed them until the fifth volume, although the first fourteen, which explain certain chapters of Jeremiah in a disordered and confused sequence, properly belonged to the preceding fourth volume. The chief reason for postponing them is this: since they were joined by the holy interpreter himself under a single preface to Vincent the presbyter and in one distinct book, they could not properly be separated from one another, or from the fourteen following homilies, which interpret Ezekiel and properly belong to this volume.

Since the distinguished men Erasmus and Huetius paid no attention to this, and rashly divided this single book into two, they formed many opinions about the prologue—opinions far removed from the truth—by which the homilies on Jeremiah were supposedly mutilated.

In his criticism of Origen’s books, Erasmus first wonders why Jerome, who is otherwise frequent in his prefaces, prefaced nothing to the homilies on Isaiah—which we have consigned, among the spurious works, to the appendix of the preceding volume—and nothing to these homilies on Jeremiah. He then suspected that the prologue had been removed by those to whom Jerome had written after Origen’s name had become unpopular among the Romans, and that Jerome had probably praised Adamantius’s talent magnificently in it.

Huetius, on the other hand, does not deny that Jerome prefaced each of Origen’s works explained by him with prologues, since Gennadius asserts this in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*. But he thinks that the prologues prefixed to the treatises on Isaiah and Jeremiah were removed not deliberately but by accident and through the carelessness of scribes. Otherwise, he argues, other prologues would also have been removed, including those in which Jerome praises Origen warmly—for example, the prologue prefixed to Damasus and the homilies on the Song of Songs, and the other prologue to the homilies on Ezekiel.

Yet both men are splendidly deceived by their own opinions. Those prefaces did not perish deliberately, as the Bishop of Avranches maintains, nor accidentally through the carelessness of copyists, as Huetius supposes. The preface which they imagine to have been prefixed to the homilies on Isaiah never existed at all, much less was it composed by that translator whom we have proved to have been Rufinus, certainly not Jerome. Besides the arguments assembled in the preface to the preceding volume, we have demonstrated this from the very fact that those homilies are furnished with no prologue.

By contrast, a preface to the homilies on Jeremiah does exist, and it is precisely the one that they think was prefixed only to the homilies on Ezekiel. In truth, it is prefixed to both groups: to the earlier homilies on Jeremiah, joined together under the dedication of a single book, by the interpreter himself.

A careful reading of this preface teaches us this. So too does the mention, under a single recension, of twenty-eight homilies in the *Catalogue*, not to mention other weighty considerations. These leave no room for doubt and openly refute the judgment of learned men who hold the opposing view.

But to return to the point begun: the reason these homilies were postponed until this fifth volume was also the very character of the work. Jerome did not compose it from his own resources, but received it from another author—Adamantius—and had to adapt it for Latin ears by following another’s footsteps. Therefore this translation properly ought to follow, so to speak, the original labor of the holy Doctor on his commentaries on those prophets.

As for the Greek text of some of these homilies—only twelve of those on Jeremiah survive, while those explaining Ezekiel have entirely perished—I once intended to place it alongside the Latin translation. We had already noticed several points by which it might be presented either more accurately or more clearly. But when we came to undertake the work, we judged that what had seemed a sound plan ought rather to be abandoned.

For in these treatises Origen is only a small part of himself, and the Greek text increases the reader’s desire more than Jerome’s dignity. If the work had survived intact, or at least in substantial part, it would have contributed convenience and ornament to our edition; but I could not persuade myself to append it in its mutilated and incomplete state.

If I had included it, we would have had to reverse the order of the twelve homilies that alone survive in Greek. Origen had composed more than forty-five homilies on Jeremiah. From that immense heap Jerome selected fourteen to render into Latin. He did not begin with the first and proceed continuously, but translated them sporadically, as each presented itself, so that in translating he followed neither Origen’s plan nor even the order of Jeremiah himself, whom he was explaining.

From the homily that is first in Adamantius he moved to the last two, the thirteenth and fourteenth. You cannot know what place the second and third Jerome homilies held in the Greek original, since they are entirely missing there. The fourth, corresponding to Origen’s seventeenth, he translated after all the others.

After that, he explained the remaining homilies, from the fifth through the twelfth, in a straightforward sequence relative to one another, though not according to the order of the Greek exemplar, placing the eighth before the seventh.

This disordered sequence had to be preserved in our Latin edition. Although somewhat more confused, it is nevertheless Jerome’s sequence, as he himself openly admits in his preface; and it therefore had to be reproduced in the form in which he established it. For elsewhere, too, he often prefers, in accordance with his own judgment, to be heard not so much as a translator as the founder of a new work.

Finally, our purpose is not to present Adamantius but to revise Jerome, and, insofar as possible, to abstain from alien writings. Our nature is utterly opposed to the appetite that now torments certain people—the desire to become famous through cartloads of papers.

To note in order something about each of Jerome’s labors contained in this volume: the Commentary on Ezekiel, which occupies the first place, consists of fourteen books. Jerome spent nearly four years preparing them—not because the labor itself required so long a time from an astonishingly energetic mind, but because, interrupted and by no means continuous in his efforts, he dictated first one and then another section of the work at intervals.

He began the work scarcely after completing the Commentaries on Isaiah, namely in the eleventh year beyond four hundred. But at the very beginning of the dictation, as he himself explains in the prologue and in Letter 126 to Marcellinus and Anapsychia, he was so shattered and stunned by the sudden news of the deaths of Pammachius and Marcella, and by the devastation of the western provinces, especially the city of Rome, that he was compelled to abandon the work he had begun and remain silent for a long time.

Toward the end of that year, or at the beginning of the following one, he resumed the interrupted labor from the beginning and continued through the third book. Again, as he says in the letter to Marcellinus just mentioned:

> “This year a sudden onslaught of the barbarians swept across the frontier of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria like a torrent carrying everything away with it, so that scarcely could he himself escape their hands, much less turn his mind to writing—his mind, which had almost entirely despaired.”

Nevertheless, as his grief gradually diminished with time, and especially because Eustochium pressed him to complete the work, during the profitable—or rather stolen—hours of the nights of the year 413, as winter approached, he continued through the ninth book, as he himself states in the preface to the seventh book, although he was continually distracted by other occupations arising from the whole world’s flight to that place.

There is no doubt that the books following these, through the end of the work, belong to the succeeding year, 414. At the beginning of the ninth book he reports that Heraclian, the count of Africa, had **recently** paid the penalty for his treachery. This chronological indication clearly designates the earlier part of that year, when Heraclian was colleague in the consulship of Lucian, an illustrious man, and when, in the month of August, he lost honor and life after being held responsible for the new events in Africa, as Prosper says.

He declares in a letter to the virgin Demetrias that he preferred to interrupt the final two books, which explain the vision of the temple, when he had reached that part of the sanctuary in which the Holy of Holies and the Altar of Incense are described, so that, as he himself says, he might pass “from Altar to Altar.” That letter, which occupies number 130 in our recension, belongs to the year 414, as we have demonstrated in its proper place by certain arguments.

The individual book on Daniel, which follows in the sequence of Scripture, is seven years earlier than these commentaries. We assign it to the year 407.

When the holy Doctor turned his mind to writing it, he had already explained the twelve minor prophets—as he himself most clearly reveals in the preface to this book—and had therefore passed beyond the year 406. The final part of that year is certainly identified by the final explanation among those prophets, the one on Amos, through the explicit date of the sixth consulship of the Emperor Arcadius and of Anicius Probus.

The work also preceded the year 408, in August of which Stilicho was killed.

People jealous of Jerome’s glory accused him of attacking the barbarian commander of the Roman army. In explaining the mystery of the great statue seen by Nebuchadnezzar in a vision, whose feet were composed of iron and clay mixed with pottery, Jerome said that the Roman empire was signified:

> “For just as at the beginning nothing was stronger or harder than the Roman empire, so at the end of the world nothing will be weaker, since in civil wars and against various nations we need the assistance of other barbarian peoples.”

Later, clearing himself of the suspicion of malice in the preface to the eleventh book on Isaiah, he says:

> “One must not flatter rulers in such a way that the truth of the sacred Scriptures is neglected; nor is a general discussion an insult to one person—Stilicho. While it lacked the benevolent attention of my readers, he was suddenly removed by the judgment of God.”

Whenever, therefore, that accusation could have been printed, and especially after the Commentaries on Daniel had been made public, Stilicho was still alive and held the first place among the Roman forces. It is not reasonable to suppose that, as soon as that exposition reached the ears of the public, he was removed from the living. Rather, a considerable amount of time must have intervened, during which the holy Father could be watched by the wicked, maliciously misrepresented, and, on the other hand, kindly received by those devoted to him and interpreted favorably.

From this interval and sequence of events one can plainly infer that the work in question belongs to the year 407, though it could scarcely have reached the beginning of the following year.

The twenty-eight homilies now added for the first time, although—as we have said—they form one distinct book, do not all belong precisely to the same period, nor were they all rendered from Origen’s Greek text into Latin at one time and with one sustained effort.

Since the holy interpreter places them all under one recension in his catalogue of his own works—“Twenty-eight homilies of Origen on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which I translated from Greek into Latin”—the statement should, in my judgment, be understood as referring to the circulation of the edition, not to the fact that they were furnished with a single Latin style.

The first fourteen, those explaining Jeremiah, had been made Latin long before he applied his hand to the remaining homilies on Ezekiel. Jerome himself gives abundant testimony to this in the prologue to Vincent that he prefixed to this translation:

> “After the fourteen homilies on Jeremiah, which I translated long ago in disordered sequence, I dictated these fourteen on Ezekiel at intervals.”

We can understand when he joined and issued both groups together in one book from the place they occupy in the aforementioned catalogue. On one side stands the translation of the Eusebian Chronicle, and on the other Letter 18 in our recension, to Damasus, concerning the Seraphim; the two works lie between them.

Since the former of these two works most certainly belongs to the year 380, while the latter belongs to the middle of the following period, as has been proved in their proper places, there is no need to labor further to establish the period within which the homilies must be enclosed—though it should be placed nearer to 381.

You should never agree with the distinguished Tillemont, who postpones the fourteen later homilies on Ezekiel until the year 386. He was persuaded by a sufficiently weak argument: in the preface to this very book the holy Doctor calls Origen, according to the opinion of Didymus the Seer, “the second teacher of the churches after the apostles.” Tillemont supposed that Jerome could not have praised Didymus and called him “the Seer” before the year in which he came to know him personally in Alexandria.

But that conjecture was not worth so much. It is opposed both by the entire sequence of Jerome’s writings and—what is decisive—by the testimony of the holy interpreter himself, who consistently assigns the temporal precedence of his books in the catalogue.

[Column 0015]

# The Fourteen Books of the Commentaries of Saint Eusebius Jerome, Priest of Stridon, on the Prophet Ezekiel

[Note: We examined these Commentaries on Ezekiel and Daniel against the same manuscript codices as the commentaries in the preceding fourth volume. We also compared them, according to our usual practice, with Saint Gregory, surnamed the Great, who derived a large part of his homilies on Ezekiel from these commentaries of Jerome, and with Rabanus, who transcribed them in exactly the same words.]

## Book One

[Columns 0015A–0016A]

### Chapters 1–2

When the eighteen volumes of Explanations on Isaiah had been completed, I wished to pass on to Ezekiel—as I had often promised you, and your mother Paula of holy memory, O virgin of Christ, Eustochium—and to place, as they say, the final hand upon the prophetic work. But suddenly I received the news of the death of Pammachius and Marcella, of the siege of the city of Rome, and of the falling asleep of many brothers and sisters.

I was so shattered and stunned that day and night I thought of nothing except the salvation of all. I considered myself a captive among the captivity of the saints, and could not open my mouth before I learned something more certain, while I anxiously hung between hope and despair and tormented myself with the misfortunes of others.

But after the brightest light of all the earth had been extinguished—or rather, the head of the Roman empire had been severed—and, to speak more truly, when the whole world perished in one city, I fell silent, was humbled, and ceased from good words; my sorrow was renewed:

> “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire was kindled” (Psalm 38:4).

Nor did I think that the saying should be neglected:

> “Music in mourning is an ill-timed tale” (Sirach 22:6).

But because you continue to press me unceasingly, and because a scar is gradually forming over the great wound:

[Note: Rufinus died in Sicily.]

> “And the Scorpion is crushed beneath the soil of Trinacria between Enceladus and Porphyrion, and the many-headed Hydra has at last ceased to hiss against us; a time has been granted in which we must devote ourselves not to answering the plots of heretics but to explaining the Scriptures.”

[Note: On the basis of conjecture, though with a certain emendation, I substitute **Porphyrion** for the corrupt form **Porphyrium**, which has hitherto prevailed. The allusion is clearly to the myth of the Giants, of whom Enceladus was the greatest, while Porphyrion was more insolent and threatening in stature. They were struck down by Jupiter on the island of Sicily. See Claudian, *Gigantomachia*. Horace, Book III, Ode 4, writes most elegantly:

> “But what of Typhoeus and mighty Mimas,  
> or what of Porphyrion with his threatening stature,  
> what of Rhoecus and Enceladus,  
> the bold hurler of uprooted trees?” etc.

**Porphyrium**, the reading formerly found, is not the name of a giant but of a pagan philosopher, which has nothing to do with the passage. Everyone can see that Rufinus is sharply attacked here: he died in Sicily and is said to be joined with the two monsters, Enceladus and Porphyrion.]

I shall undertake the prophet Ezekiel, whose difficulty is confirmed by the tradition of the Hebrews. For unless someone among them has completed the age of priestly service—that is, the thirtieth year—he is not permitted to read either the beginning of Genesis, or the Song of Songs, or the beginning and end of this volume, so that he may approach perfect knowledge and mystical meanings only when the full period of human nature has been reached.

If, by the mercy of the Lord, I carry this work through to its conclusion, I shall pass on to Jeremiah, who in his Lamentations, under the figure of Jerusalem, mourns the four wounds of the world with an alphabet of fourfold structure.

[Column 0017B]

### Chapter 1, verse 1

> “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth, on the fifth of the month.”

The thirtieth year does not mean, as most people think, the age of the prophet, nor the year of the Jubilee, which is the year of remission. Rather, it is reckoned from the twelfth year of Josiah king of Judah, when the book of Deuteronomy was found in the temple of God, to the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, who was led into Babylon with his mother, Daniel, the three boys, and Ezekiel. This was the first captivity of the tribe of Judah, when the wrath of God fell upon Jerusalem (2 Kings 22; 2 Chronicles 34; 2 Kings 24).

According to the allegorical sense, however, the Lord and Savior is prefigured, who, being thirty years old, came to baptism (Luke 3), the age at which human maturity is complete.

Hence, in the Book of Numbers, according to the Hebrews, the priests begin to minister in the tabernacle not, as the Septuagint has it, from the twenty-fifth year of age, but from the thirtieth (Numbers 4).

[Note: Below, in chapter 26 of this same prophet, he says: “They approach the priestly office not after the twenty-fifth year of age but after the thirtieth.” In Numbers 4, where the Hebrew truth says that ministers in the tabernacle of the covenant are taken from the thirtieth year, the Septuagint translated “from the twenty-fifth.” Here, instead of “in the tabernacle,” Rabanus reads “in the temple.”]

Joseph also preceded him in this sign, when in Egypt he distributed grain to the starving people (Genesis 41), and John the Baptist came to the waters of the Jordan and preached a baptism of repentance (Luke 3).

The words “in the fourth,” with the sentence still incomplete, imply “month.” For immediately afterward it says, “on the fifth of the month.” To make this clearer, the Septuagint added the word above.

### Verse 2

> “When I was in the midst of the captives beside the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God on the fifth day of the month: it was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin.”

David prophesies in the Spirit that the captive people sat beside the rivers of Babylon:

> “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Psalm 137).

Chebar is either the name of a river or, according to the interpretation of its name, which is rendered “heavy,” signifies the Tigris and the Euphrates, and all the great and weighty rivers said to be in the land of the Chaldeans.

Understand “the heavens were opened” not as a division of the firmament but as the faith of the believer, because heavenly mysteries have been opened to him.

Thus, at the Savior’s baptism, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, we read that the heavens were opened (Matthew 3). When they are opened, the visions of God are displayed—not one vision but many, since the Lord says through the Prophet:

> “I will multiply visions, and I will be represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hosea 12:10).

[Note: The same authority preferred **“I multiplied”**, in accordance with the Greek, **ἐπλήθυνα**.]

These are the visions woven throughout the whole prophecy of Ezekiel.

More significantly, according to the Hebrews and the other interpreters, Jehoiachin’s departure is called a **transmigration**, not a captivity, as the Septuagint translated it. For he was not captured after the city had been conquered; rather, he surrendered himself voluntarily and was led into Babylon.

Therefore let Jehoiachin, that is, Jeconiah, be called the first transmigration, and let Zedekiah be called the second, or final, captivity.

### Verse 3

> “The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, son of Buzi, the priest, in the land of the Chaldeans, beside the river Chebar.”

To Daniel and Ezekiel, who were in Babylon beside the rivers, the mysteries of future things are revealed over the waters—or rather, in the purest waters—so that the power of baptism might be displayed.

Otherwise, the apostle Paul, too, when he was washed in the Lord by Ananias, after scales had first covered his eyes, was freed from blindness (Acts 9).

And in Genesis, the first living creatures came forth from the waters.

We must also understand that the Lord came to baptism in the thirtieth year of his age, in the fourth month, which among us is called January and is the first at the beginning of the year, apart from the month Nisan of new produce, in which Passover is celebrated.

Among the peoples of the East, October was the first month, after the gathering of the crops and the pressing of the wine, when the tithes were brought to the temple; January was the fourth month.

He adds the fifth day of the month to signify the baptism in which the heavens were opened to Christ. The day of the Epiphany remains venerable to this day—not, as some think, because it was the day of his birth in the flesh, for then he was hidden and did not appear.

This accords with that time, when it was said:

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

Now **Buzi** is translated into our language as “spurned” or “despised,” while **Ezekiel** means “strengthened by God.”

This can be applied to the Lord in such a way that we say that the Creator of the world, who is the Father of the Savior, is spurned and despised by all heretics who do not accept the Old Testament.

Nor is it surprising that the Lord is the strength of God, since he himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

> “And the hand of the Lord was there upon him.”

The Septuagint has:

> “And the hand of the Lord was there upon me.”

In order that we may behold the visions of God and understand them, we need the hand and strength of God upon us (1 Corinthians 1).

By that hand and arm the people of Israel were led out of Egypt. Even the magicians understood something of that strength when they said:

> “It is the finger of God” (Exodus 8).

And the Savior says in the Gospel:

> “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Matthew 12:28).

For this, another Gospel has:

> “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Luke 11:20).

### (Verse 4)

“And I saw, and behold, a whirlwind was coming from the north, and a great cloud, and fire enveloping it, and brightness around it. And from its midst there was something like the appearance of electrum—that is, from the midst of the fire.”

The Septuagint has: “And I saw, and behold, a spirit carrying away—or lifting up—was coming from the north, and a great cloud in it, and flashing fire, and brightness around it. And in its midst there was something like the appearance of electrum in the midst of the fire, and brightness in it.” The source marks the final phrase with an obelus and asterisks.

For the consolation of the people in exile and the revelation of God’s judgment, the prophet sees a very great vision. In interpreting it, all the synagogues of the Jews are silent, since they say that it surpasses human understanding; and concerning both this vision and the construction of the Temple, which is described at the end of this prophecy, they are unwilling to attempt any explanation.

We, however, entrust to kindly disposed and faithful readers [or, according to another reading, to kindly disposed readers as well] what we have received from our predecessors and, according to the measure of our modest ability, have attempted by comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. We can speculate about these matters more readily than we can explain them. We ask pardon, that they may favor rather than condemn our rashness—or rather, our faith that does not know its own measure.

First, it must be understood that the “spirit carrying away,” or “lifting up,” which we have translated according to Aquila as “a whirlwind,” and which Symmachus and Theodotion render as “a blast” or “spirit of tempest,” is understood by some in a favorable sense and by others in an unfavorable sense. The Hebrew word *ruaḥ*, according to the character of the context, can mean “spirit,” “soul,” or “wind.”

“Spirit,” as in: “Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created” (Psalm 103:30).

“Soul,” as in: “His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth” (Psalm 145:4).

“Wind,” as in: “With a violent wind you will break the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 48:8). The note in the source reads: “In a violent wind, breaking the ships,” and so forth.

And elsewhere: “Fire and brimstone and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup” (Psalm 11:7).

Those who read “wind” and “blast of tempest” understand the passage in this way: the anger and fury of God are coming from the north—that is, Nebuchadnezzar—and Jerusalem is to be captured six years after this vision. A note records the reading in Rabanus: “coming from Babylon, that is, Nebuchadnezzar,” and so forth. The vision is seen in the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin, which was also the fifth year of Zedekiah’s reign in Jerusalem. We read that after a similar period of six years—that is, in the eleventh year of his reign—he was led to Babylon after the city had been captured.

Thus, to those who lived near the river Chebar and had voluntarily surrendered themselves to the king, it is revealed that they had done well to obey God’s judgment. A note records that two manuscripts read “because of the river Chebar,” and adds, “We correct some less serious matters below.” For in a short time both the province of Judah and the city of Jerusalem would be captured. The great cloud that is described should be understood as carrying showers of devastation over Judah and rains of destruction. The enveloping fire indicates the punishments that were to come and the evils of captivity. The brightness around it signifies the manifest judgments of God.

Those, however, who understand the passage in the opposite sense—that is, in a favorable sense—understand the spirit carrying away or lifting up to be the Holy Spirit, who removes vices and sins from human beings, or lifts up those who lie prostrate to the heights. He causes them to withdraw from the north, the coldest wind, from which evils blaze over the whole earth (Ecclesiasticus 43); and in Jeremiah that dreadful pot is kindled from the face of the north (Jeremiah 1:13).

They also refer the great cloud to the person of Christ, who came into Egypt—that is, this world—upon a light cloud. It is called “great” specifically in comparison with the lesser clouds, namely the prophets, the apostles, and all the saints, concerning whom it is written: “And your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm 36:6); and: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon Israel” (Isaiah 5:6); and elsewhere: “The clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nahum 1:3); and again: “Cloud and darkness are around him” (Psalm 97:2).

They understand the flashing fire and the brightness around it in accordance with what is written: “God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24). The Savior says that he came to send this fire upon the earth, and he desires it to burn in us and in all who believe (Luke 11). Although it brings terror and punishment upon sinners, it nevertheless shines with brightness and is full of light and radiance. Therefore it purifies us by fire, so that, once made clean and purified, it may grant us more joyful things.

### (Verse 5)

“And in its midst there was the likeness of four living creatures, and this was their appearance: they had the likeness of a human being.”

The words “and brightness in it” should be marked with an obelus. If Scripture had not added the clarification, “that is, from the midst of the fire,” we might have gone astray because of the ambiguity of the wording and supposed that the appearance, or vision, of electrum was in the midst of the wind or spirit.

We should therefore understand that in the midst of the fire and torments of God there was the likeness of electrum, which is more precious than gold and silver. Thus, after the judgment and torments—which seem sad and harsh to those who endure them—the more precious radiance of electrum appears, since all things are governed by the providence of God, and what is thought to be punishment is medicine.

### (Verse 6)

“And in its midst there was the likeness of four living creatures, and this was their appearance: they had the likeness of a human being.”

“In its midst” implicitly means “in the midst of the electrum”; but it is better to understand it as referring to the fire, which is light for believers and punishment for unbelievers.

In the midst of this fire was the likeness of four living creatures: a likeness, not their nature. The four creatures, which are later called fourfold, had one likeness—that of a human being—so that all rational beings in the world might be represented. For he says: “Let us make a human being according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

The image and likeness of God is not the form of a body but of the mind, made according to the likeness of the true image of Christ, who is the image of the invisible God.

These rational creatures exist in four regions, either because of the four cardinal points by which the world is enclosed, or because of the four regions—celestial, terrestrial, infernal, and supercelestial—of which the Apostle Paul also speaks: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2:10). Paul’s testimony concerns three of these. Let us see also the fourth:

“Praise the Lord, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5).

Again, the Apostle says that some things are celestial and others supercelestial (1 Corinthians 15:40). The note reports that Victorius reads the verb in the plural: “and the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise,” and so forth, following the Greek.

### (Verse 7)

“Four faces for each one, and four wings for each one; their feet were straight feet, and the sole of their foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot, and there were sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze. Human hands were beneath their wings on their four sides.”

The Septuagint has: “Four faces for each one, and four wings for each one; their legs were straight, and their feet were winged. And the sparks were like flashing bronze, and their wings were light, and human hands were beneath their wings on their four sides.”

The four living creatures had the appearance of a human being, except that each had four faces and four wings, straight feet, and the sole of a foot like the imprint of a calf’s hoof—or, as Aquila translated it, rounded, a detail the Septuagint entirely omitted. Their sparks shone with the brightness of bronze. The Septuagint also adds that their wings were light, something not found in the Hebrew, and speaks of human hands beneath their wings on their four sides.

We shall attempt to explain what this seems to mean to us, after briefly summarizing the opinions of different interpreters.

Some think that the four creatures designate the four Gospels. We too followed this interpretation in the preface to our Commentary on Matthew. Matthew is represented by the human being, because he describes Christ as a human being: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.”

They refer the lion to Mark, because his Gospel begins: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight’” (Isaiah 40:3).

They refer the calf to Luke’s Gospel, because it begins with the priesthood of Zechariah.

They refer the eagle to the beginning of John’s Gospel, who, flying aloft, begins: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

We have stated what seemed to us concerning this in the work mentioned above. More fully, in the Apocalypse of John (chapter 4), the forms and names of these living creatures are referred to the four Gospels—or, according to another reading, the four Evangelists. In its proper place we shall attempt to explain how the description of all the creatures can be fitted to them.

Others, however, who follow the foolish wisdom of the philosophers, imagine the two hemispheres in the two cherubim of the Temple, and suppose that we and the Antipodes are represented as human beings lying on their backs and falling.

Many, following Plato, refer the rational, spirited, and appetitive parts of the soul—which he calls *logikon* (λογικόν), *thymikon* (θυμικόν), and *epithymētikon* (ἐπιθυμητικόν)—to the human being, the lion, and the calf.

They place reason, knowledge, intellect, and deliberation, together with virtue and wisdom, in the citadel of the brain. They place wildness, anger, and violence in the lion, which they locate in the gall. Lust, luxury, and the desire for every pleasure they place in the liver—that is, in the calf, which clings to earthly works.

They posit a fourth element, which is above and beyond these three. The Greeks call it *syntērēsis* (συντήρησις), “preservation” or “conscience.” This is the spark of conscience which, even in Cain’s breast after he was expelled from paradise, is not extinguished; through it, although overcome by pleasures or fury, and sometimes deceived by the apparent likeness of reason itself, we recognize that we are sinning. The note suggests that “Adam,” who was expelled from paradise, should perhaps be read instead of “Cain.” It also reports that in Rabanus the reading is “in the sinner” rather than “in the breast.”

Aquila assigns this fourth element specifically to the eagle. It does not mingle with the other three but corrects the three that have gone astray. In Scripture it is sometimes called the spirit, which intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (Romans 8:26). “No one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him” (1 Corinthians 2:11). Paul also speaks of it when he prays that the Thessalonians’ spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

Yet we see that even this conscience, in accordance with what is written in Proverbs—“When the wicked comes to the depths of sins, he despises them” (Proverbs 18:3)—is sometimes hurled down among certain people and loses its proper place. They do not even possess shame or modesty in their sins, and deserve to hear: “You have the face of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed” (Jeremiah 3:3). Another reading has: “You do not know how to be ashamed.”

God governs this fourfold team like a charioteer, restraining it when it runs with disordered steps, making it teachable, and compelling it to obey his command. We too shall touch upon this discussion of the parts of the soul—that is, of the human being, whom the same philosophers call a small world.

Some simply think that, according to the opinion of Hippocrates, the four living creatures display the four elements of the world, from which all things are composed: fire, air, water, and earth. How these elements are mixed with one another, and how, although each remains distinct, they appear joined together, touch one another, and possess four forms and shapes in a single living being, is not the concern of the present work.

They also understand the four wheels, rising from earthly things to heavenly things and joined to the individual fourfold creatures, either as the mixture of these elements or as the cycle of the four seasons. Each season consists of three months, and the revolving year received its name from the fact that it always turns and returns upon itself.

A poet beautifully expressed this in a single verse:

> Spring, summer, autumn, winter, month, and year.

And when it is said, “There was a wheel within a wheel,” they think that a year within a year is signified. Concerning this another poet says:

> And the year rolls back upon itself along its own tracks.

The likeness of the firmament, compared with crystal, they wish to be understood as this heaven which we see, beneath which the four creatures revolve and pass.

They maintain that the throne of sapphire color, and the human being seated above it under a human likeness, describe the dominion of the one who governs all things and has all things beneath his feet: the omnipotence of God. Finally, they believe that the words “This is the vision of the likeness of the glory of God” indicate, through something like a painting or image, the providence of God.

They also say that the creatures’ feet are called straight and that the sole of the foot resembles that of a calf—or is round—because earthly things fly upward toward heavenly things and, with all their angles cut away, follow roundness, which is the most beautiful of all figures.

The shining sparks indicate that all things are full of light. The human hands beneath the wings—whether of the human being, the lion, the calf, or the eagle—indicate that reason supports everything and raises it from earthly lowliness to heavenly things. We can refer these interpretations both to the Gospels and to all the matters we have set forth above.

I remember hearing that the four disturbances about which Cicero discusses at length in the *Tusculan Disputations*—joy, distress, desire, and fear—are signified by the four creatures. Two of these concern things present and two things future. Virgil briefly expresses this in the *Aeneid*:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.

These disturbances ought to be ruled by reason and by the power of God. Opposed to them, or rather imposed over them, are the four virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, so that the disturbances may be governed according to the judgment of these virtues. How these virtues are fitted to the faces of the human being, lion, calf, and eagle, they have left entirely unexplained. The same philosopher and orator discusses them in his three books *On Duties* addressed to his son.

I have also read a short treatise by a certain Catina, whom the Syrians call *leptos* (λεπτός), that is, “sharp” and “ingenious.” He thinks that the order of the army of the twelve tribes is described in the wilderness, toward the east and west, north and south. These tribes are joined to one another by affection and kinship, and this is the wheel within the wheel. They are led by the spirit, protected by the cloud in the wilderness, and illuminated by the pillar of fire at night. They do not return to Egypt but always hasten toward the promised land.

He interprets the likeness of electrum in the midst as the Holy of Holies. The human face represents all Israel; the lion represents the royal scepter of Judah; and the calf represents the priestly and Levitical tribe. Outside these is the face of the eagle, representing the vengeance and retribution of God, which looks down from heaven upon all things and is prepared to tear apart the sinner. Concerning it Hosea says: “Like an eagle over the house of God” (Hosea 8:1)—that is, over the Temple.

In this same prophet, a great eagle with great wings and claws, which had access to enter Lebanon, is understood to be Nebuchadnezzar (chapter 17 below). He is also understood here to signify that Nebuchadnezzar is to come, and that God sits like a charioteer upon this kind of fourfold team, commanding what must or must not be done.

This, he says, is spoken to the people living in Babylon: if they submit their necks to God and obey his reins, they will once again deserve his help and will recover the land they had lost.

### (Verses 8–9)

“And they had faces and wings on their four sides; their wings were joined, each to the other. They did not turn back as they went, but each one walked straight ahead.”

The Gospels are joined together and cling to one another. Flying throughout the whole world, they run here and there; their flight has no end. They are never overcome or withdrawn but always advance farther. Hence Paul says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians 3:13).

We can say the same about the virtues of the soul, the flight of time, and the mixture of the elements: leaving what is past behind, they always hasten toward what lies ahead.

That time slips away and flees is demonstrated in a brief verse:

> But meanwhile time flees, irretrievable time flees.

And in a lyric poem:

> Alas, alas, Postumus, Postumus,  
> the fleeting years slip away!

### (Verse 10)

“The likeness of their faces was the face of a human being; and the face of a lion was on the right side of all four; the face of an ox was on the left side of all four; and the face of an eagle was above all four.”

By “faces” he means the beginnings of the Gospels. The human being and the lion—that is, Christ’s birth and the prophet’s voice thundering in the wilderness—occupy the right-hand side.

The calf, that is, the sacrifices and the priesthood of the Jews, is on the left. This has passed away and been transferred to a spiritual priesthood, concerning which it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:2).

This is so arranged that all the parts cling to one another and are regarded as a single body. The note records that the earlier reading was “each individually,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts.

The eagle, however, which is above both the birth and the prophecy fulfilled by the Lord’s coming, and above the priesthood that has passed away, is also outside all these things. It speaks of the spiritual birth, of how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Concerning this it is rightly said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8).

These matters correspond to what we previously said concerning the Apocalypse (chapter 4): four living creatures full of eyes before and behind, one like a lion, the second like a calf, the third having a face like a human being, and the fourth like a flying eagle.

There they are said, after the manner of the Seraphim, to have six wings: with two they cover their faces, with two they cover their feet, and with two they fly. They never cease, day or night, saying:

> Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty,  
> who was, and who is, and who is to come (Revelation 4:8).

### (Verse 11)

“And their faces and their wings were extended upward; two wings of each were joined to one another, and two covered their bodies.”

We have already said that the Gospels, the ages, all rational creatures, and the four virtues are joined to one another, so that whoever lacks one lacks them all.

The fact that two wings are extended and rise upward signifies heavenly preaching and the tendency of all things toward the majesty of God.

The two wings by which their bodies are covered signify that human knowledge is excluded and that a complete vision is not granted, as the Apostle says: “We know in part and we prophesy in part. But when the perfect comes, what is in part will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 13:9–10).

### (Verse 12)

“And each one walked straight before its face. Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they walked; and they did not turn back as they went.”

Whoever holds the plow’s handle must not look back (Luke 9:62), nor imitate Lot’s wife (Genesis 19), lest he fall under the wound described in Deuteronomy (chapter 19) and perish by an incurable *opisthotonos* (ὀπισθότονος), the affliction by which Eli also fell, because he had offended God through the fault of his sons (IV Kings 4).

How much more must this be true of the four creatures, which were full of light and winged and followed the Holy Spirit who went before them? They fly throughout the world and lift themselves toward the heights in such a way that they protect their bodies with the wings of the historical sense and do not grant us a fuller vision.

The repetition of the statement, “They did not turn back as they went,” indicates the mystery of both Testaments: in these four living creatures, both the Law and the Gospel hasten toward what is to come and never turn backward.

### (Verses 13–14)

“And the likeness of the living creatures and their appearance was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps. This was the vision moving back and forth in the midst of the living creatures: the brightness of the fire, and lightning issuing from the fire. And the living creatures went and returned like the appearance of flashing lightning.”

The Septuagint has: “And in the midst of the living creatures there was a vision like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of lamps moving back and forth in the midst of the living creatures; and there was the brightness of fire, and from the fire something like lightning went forth.”

The words that follow—“And the living creatures ran and returned like the appearance of *bezec*”—have been added to the Septuagint from the edition of Theodotion. The earlier translators, so that the prophet would not appear to contradict the two preceding statements, thought it best to omit what seemed contrary, namely, “the living creatures ran and returned,” lest it cause scandal to the reader.

It is better in the divine books to translate what has been said, even if one does not understand why it has been said, than to remove what one does not understand. Otherwise many other things that are ineffable and beyond the capacity of the human mind would be erased by the same license.

We should therefore seek to understand why it is first said, “The living creatures did not turn back as they went,” and now, once, “The living creatures ran and returned.”

The question would remain unresolved if the text did not continue: “like the appearance of flashing lightning.” In Hebrew this is called *bezeq* [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source], and Symmachus translated it as “like the appearance of a ray of lightning.”

Just as the sky flashes with repeated fires, and in the blink of an eye and a moment the flashes of lightning dart about and return without losing their source—or, so to speak, the fountain and material of the fire—so these creatures, although they proceed with an unhindered step, hasten toward what lies ahead.

But if, in their attempt, they see that something has been covered over, they do not so much turn back as contract themselves, to be extended again and provide the light that they had briefly concealed. Thus they give the servants their food at the proper time, neither giving what is holy to dogs nor throwing pearls before swine (Matthew 7:6).

Hence Paul says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able to receive it” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

The election of Judah and the anointing of Saul do not demonstrate God’s ignorance of the future; they show him to be the judge of present circumstances (Matthew 10:26).

For this reason the Apostles are commanded that, if they find a house unworthy of their greeting, they should first shake the dust from their feet, and that the peace they had given the house should return to them.

The burning coals of fire and the lamps moving about in the midst of the living creatures are interpreted from the passage in Isaiah: “Fire shall consume the material like hay, and I will sanctify them in burning fire” (Isaiah 5:24).

Concerning these coals it is also written elsewhere: “Coals of fire shall fall upon them” (Psalm 140:11). And against deceitful lips another psalm says:

> What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?  
> The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of desolation (Psalm 120:3–4).

And elsewhere: “You have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them. They shall be your help” (Isaiah 47:14).

Whatever creature we contemplate flashes forth the knowledge of God, since the Creator is recognized through his creatures. From the midst of the living creatures the brightness of fire and the lightning proceed. If you bring the Gospels together, you will find, in the midst of the letter and the lowly historical narrative, the mysteries of the Holy Spirit.

### (Verses 15 and following)

“As I looked at the living creatures, behold, one wheel appeared upon the earth beside each of the living creatures that had four faces. The appearance of the wheels and their construction was like the appearance of the sea; the four had one likeness, and their appearance and construction were as though there were a wheel within a wheel. They went in their four directions and did not turn back as they went. The wheels had a height and an elevation, and their appearance was dreadful; and the whole body of all four of them was full of eyes all around.”

The Septuagint has: “And I saw, and behold, one wheel upon the earth following the four living creatures. The appearance of the wheels and their construction was like the appearance of *tharsis*. And there was one likeness in the four, and their construction was as a wheel within a wheel. They went in their four directions and did not turn back as they went. Their backs and their height were alike. And I saw them, and their backs were full of eyes all around, all four of them.”

Up to this point the form of the four living creatures, each of which had four faces, has been described. They followed the spirit and the cloud that was in the midst of the spirit. Now a single wheel is assigned to each individual creature. The wheels were not joined to the living creatures but followed them.

Alternatively, one wheel appeared upon the earth, divided into four parts, having as many faces as the creatures it followed. The likeness of the four wheels following the four living creatures was so great that they could truly be believed to be one wheel.

Their construction, or workmanship, was like the appearance of *tharsis*, which we have translated as “the sea.” Aquila rendered it “hyacinth,” the stone that resembles the color of the sky. The note observes that Symmachus, not Aquila, is said elsewhere to have translated the word as “hyacinth.” It suggests that the passage may have been corrupted by scribes or that the author’s memory may have slipped, since Aquila translated the word as “chrysolite,” not “hyacinth.”

The appearance was like a wheel within a wheel, so that one would not think there was merely one wheel but that one wheel was joined to another. They went in their four directions and were neither dragged nor turned backward. How could they have turned back, when they followed the living creatures, which were always reaching toward what lay ahead?

The size and height of the wheels were so great that they caused wonder in those who saw them. Their entire bodies and backs were full of light all around, so that one could see no limb that did not possess eyes of light. The poets’ stories describe Argus in this way: he had a hundred eyes, or many eyes, and Juno changed him into a peacock because he had guarded carelessly. Thus what is a marvel of the Creator God became a condemnation of an unavenged adultery.

All things celestial and terrestrial, and whatever falls within human understanding, are moved on the wheels of the sun. The moon traverses the sun’s annual circuit through the individual months. Lucifer, who is also the evening star, shines brightly toward the east and west and tempers the darkness of night with a small light; he completes the same course in two years. The other four stars called planets, and whatever shines in heaven, as well as the varieties of crops, trees, and plants, all run in their own wheels through the four seasons. We see nothing that was not there before.

“The spirit goes, moving in circles, and returns to its circuits. All the rivers go into the sea, and the sea is not filled” (Ecclesiastes 1:6–7). Why? Because they return to their own sources, to the womb of the abyss.

If someone considers the wheel and course of the Gospels—that is, of the four living creatures that breathe, live, and understand—he will see in a short time that the world has been filled with the apostolic message.

The wheel within the wheel is also either the joining of the two Testaments, which is indicated by Jacob’s ladder (Genesis 28), Isaiah’s tongs (Isaiah 6), and the two-edged sword; or it is the Gospels joined to one another. Their course and stature tend toward heaven, although they touch earth slightly, and, always hastening, they press toward the heights.

Concerning these things it is also said elsewhere: “The holy stones roll upon the earth” (Zechariah 9:16), and from them the heavenly Jerusalem is built.

I think the same meaning is conveyed by what is sung in the psalm: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Psalm 77:18), and elsewhere: “which sets the wheel of birth on fire” (James 3:6). What meaning these testimonies have in their own contexts is not a matter for the present occasion.

A note observes that the small word *quod* (“that”) was lacking, without which the sense was impaired, and that similar corrections are made from time to time without notifying the reader. The whole body and backs being full of eyes will be approved by anyone who sees that there is nothing in the Gospels that does not shine and illuminate the world with its radiance, so that even those things considered small and lowly shine with the majesty of the Holy Spirit.

### (Verses 19 and following)

“When the living creatures went, the wheels beside them went at the same time. When the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up with them. Wherever the spirit went, they went there also; wherever the spirit went, the wheels were lifted up with it, following it, for the spirit of life was in the wheels. When the creatures went, the wheels went; when they stood, the wheels stood; and when they were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up with them, following them, because the spirit of life was in the wheels.”

The four living creatures followed the spirit and the cloud that was in the spirit. Again, when the wheels followed the creatures as they lifted themselves from the earth, they did not follow the creatures so much as the spirit, in order to show that they possessed a will of their own, because the spirit of life was in the wheels.

Three things are indicated equally in the creatures and the wheels: standing, walking, and being lifted up. Both the creatures and the wheels performed these actions together.

When the creatures stood, the wheels could not walk; when the creatures walked upon the earth, the wheels could not lift themselves up. Their activity was one, and so were their rest, their movement, and their elevation.

The statement is repeated that “the spirit of life was in the wheels,” so that we should not think that the wheels were merely some sort of vessel like the wheels seen on carts, wagons, and chariots. Rather, they were living creatures—indeed, they were above the living creatures. A note records that the Vulgate had hitherto read *quasi in carpentis* (“as if on carts”) in place of *quas* (“which”). “The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

These wheels, therefore, in which the spirit of life was present, do everything in due order and measure. They possess harmony with the living creatures, following them and, through them, following the Holy Spirit—or rather, passing beyond the intervening stages, rejoicing in fellowship with the Holy Spirit.

According to the interpretation given earlier, the prudent reader will be able to adapt all these matters to the variety of possible meanings.

(Vv. 22 ff.) And above the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of a firmament, like the appearance of terrible crystal, stretched out above their heads. Beneath the firmament their wings were straight, each toward the other. Each covered its body with two wings, and the other was covered in the same way. And I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters, like the sound of the Most High God. When they moved, there was a sound like the sound of a multitude, like the sound of an army camp; and when they stood still, their wings were lowered. For when there came a voice from above the firmament that was over their heads, they stood and lowered their wings. And above the firmament that was over their heads there was something like the appearance of sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne; and above the likeness of the throne, a likeness like the appearance of a human being above it.

Where we have rendered “their wings were straight,” and “like the sound,” or “the voice of the Most High God,” the Septuagint translated “their wings were extended and flying,” and “like the voice of the Mighty One”—which in Hebrew is called *SADDAI* (). Many things both here and in other chapters were omitted by them, which, because of the length, I have refrained from setting down.

But what we have translated more clearly, “each toward the other: each covered his body with two wings, and the other was covered in the same way,” is written in Hebrew as “woman toward her sister”: “the man covered his body with two wings, and the man was covered in the same way.” Therefore, after “woman” he placed “man” in the same person, lest we should suppose that there is sex among heavenly beings; for, in one and the same being, according to the Hebrew idiom, the same one is called both man and woman.

It appears that above the four living creatures and the same number of wheels there was the likeness of the firmament, which we call heaven. It had the appearance of crystal, which is said to form from the purest substance, from clean and shining waters, through extreme cold [Note: Some manuscripts in Victorius read “to congeal” (*congelascere*)], to such an extent that water congealed into ice is also called *κρύσταλλος* (“crystal”) in Greek. Above them, therefore, there appropriately had to be an extraordinary purity that covers everything: that is, rational and wise powers, the course of the four seasons, the regions of the world, the order of all things, and the preaching of the Gospel, which is understood in part and in part veiled.

And the voice of flying wings is heard, like the voice of many waters, which, according to the Apocalypse of John (ch. XVII), signifies peoples. Progressively increasing, it is said to be like the voice of armies and like the voice of the Most High God, who in Hebrew is called *SADDAI*; and, according to the Septuagint, it is the voice of the Word, so that we may believe that everything preached in the world is the voice of the Son of God.

When the living creatures stood still, their wings were lowered. For they could not bear to carry the resounding voice of Almighty God in the heavens; rather, they stood and marveled, and by their silence displayed the power of God, who was seated above the firmament. This firmament had the appearance of crystal to those below, but to those above it appeared like sapphire stone. This likeness of sapphire was the throne of the one who sat in the likeness of a human being. From this we understand that the firmament, the crystal, the sapphire, and the human being are shown in likeness, not in reality.

Many testimonies teach that the human being is to be understood as God the Father. Among them is this passage in the Gospel: “A certain man planted a vineyard and leased it to tenants” (Matt. XXI, 33). And shortly afterward: “He sent servants, and, last of all, his son” (ibid., 37). Again: “A certain man made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. XXII, 2). This does not exclude the Son from the kingdom, concerning whom Isaiah wrote: “I saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. VI, 1). And John says: “Isaiah said these things because he saw the glory of the Son of God” (John XII, 41; *or*: “when he saw”). Rather, it means that the Son also reigns in the Father. For everything belongs to the Son of the Father, who is “the image of the invisible God the Father” (Col. I, 15).

For in Daniel also God the Father is introduced as seated (Dan. VII), and the Son of Man is brought before him to receive the kingdom. And in the Apocalypse of John the same things are written concerning the Son (Apoc. III, VII). At the contest of the first martyr, Stephen, he is seen standing at the right hand of the Father. Concerning him the Psalm sings: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1–2).

Just as the purest and most shining things are displayed in the heavens through crystal, illuminating our bodily eyes, so in sapphire—that is, in the throne of God—and above the firmament, which we understand as heaven, hidden, secret, and incomprehensible mysteries of God are revealed: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 12), and he is seen in cloud and darkness.

Hence it is also written in Exodus: “And beneath the feet of God there was something like a work of sapphire brickwork, and like the appearance of the firmament of the purest heaven” (Exod. XXIV, 10).

[Note: Victor says that this is the true and ancient reading, “according to the Hebrew and Greek exemplar.” In the Latin manuscripts we have *lapidis* (“of stone”) instead of *lateris* (“of brickwork”).]

Therefore the bride also describes the bridegroom’s beauty in the Song: “His belly is like an ivory tablet upon sapphire stone” (Song V, 14). And in the Apocalypse of John the first foundation is written as jasper and the second as sapphire (Apoc. XXI). And in the high priest’s breastpiece, in the verse and arrangement of the individual stones, the second row contains carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper (Exod. XXVIII). Concerning these stones, in part, we have spoken in the *Commentaries on Isaiah*.

(Vv. 27–28.) And I saw something like the appearance of electrum, like the appearance of fire within it all around, from his loins and upward. And from his loins downward I saw something like the appearance of shining fire all around, like the appearance of a rainbow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day. This was the appearance of the radiance all around. This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.

The likeness of the human being who sat above the likeness of the throne—whose throne had the likeness of sapphire stone—is compared, from the loins upward, to electrum. This electrum had, both within and without, something like the appearance of fire. From the loins downward there was radiant fire all around, to show that the things above the loins, where perception and reason operate, do not need fire or flames, but the most precious and purest metal. Those, however, that are below the loins, where intercourse, generation, and the incitements of vices occur, need purification by flames, so that, once purified, they may possess the likeness of a rainbow, commonly called *Iris*, when it appears in a cloud on a rainy day.

For the rainbow, which in Holy Scripture is called the bow, and in the Apocalypse of John is likewise called *Iris* (Apoc. IV), cannot appear except in rain and in a watery cloud. It has various and most beautiful colors, gradually passing into one another. Hence the poet says (Virgil, *Aeneid* IV):

> It snatches a thousand varied colors in the opposing light.

Following popular usage, the same poet also says:

> When it drinks, the rainbow—

By this he indicates that the rainbow never appears except in cloud and water.

This rainbow is a sign of mercy and of God’s covenant, which he made with human beings: when it appears in the cloud, we should know, according to the ancient example, that we shall by no means perish by a flood (Gen. IX). From this it is shown that after punishments and penalties, and after the purification of sins, mercy will come—at least to those who have been worthy to see God reigning.

Hence it says: “This was the appearance of the radiance all around,” all around God, or the throne, or all the things that were seen. And this was a vision of the likeness of God’s glory—not that he saw the glory of the Lord, but the likeness of his glory.

The whole vision was this: the Spirit lifting him up; a great cloud; four living creatures; and the same number of wheels following the living creatures and the Spirit, which had been found worthy to be beneath God’s firmament. After they had been lifted up and had heard a voice like that of many waters, like the voice of God’s exalted Word, and the voice of armies and an army, they lowered their wings and displayed their astonishment in silence. Then there appeared, seated above the likeness of sapphire, something like the likeness of a human being: from the loins upward he had the appearance of electrum, and from the loins downward the appearance of fire all around. After this terror, a sign of mercy was given: something like the appearance of a rainbow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day.

We have discussed this vision at greater length because it is obscure and is interpreted in various ways by many people. In what follows, as far as possible, we shall pursue brevity without damaging the meaning, because of the length of the work.

(Cap. II—v. 1.) And I saw, and I fell upon my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking.

He was not elated by the greatness of the visions; rather, conscious of human frailty, he fell upon his face. Hence the apostle Paul, after his ascent into heaven and paradise and his hearing of ineffable words, says that an angel of Satan was given to him to buffet him, lest he should be exalted (II Cor. XII). Abraham also fell upon his face after he had heard the words of God. Yet because he had fallen not through sin but through humility, he was raised up by the Lord and commanded to hear his words (Gen. XVII).

It should also be understood that falling upon one’s face is different from falling backward. Abraham, after he heard about the birth of Isaac, fell upon his face and laughed (I Reg. IV). Eli, however, because he had sinned, fell backward. And concerning Dan it is written in Genesis: “Let Dan be a serpent in the path, biting the horse’s heel, and the rider will fall backward, awaiting God’s salvation” (Gen. XLIX, 17–18). Because he had fallen from the horse at the serpent’s bite, he therefore awaits the coming of the Savior.

And in the Gospel according to John, those who had come to arrest the Lord, after he answered, “I am he,” fell backward to the ground (John XVIII, 6), unable to withstand the word of the one who had said to Moses: “Go, say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III, 14).

And he said to me: “Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I will speak to you” [Vulgate: “with you”].

Lying down, he could not hear the word of God, but he heard, with Moses: “You, however, stand here with me” (Exod. XXXIV, 2). Daniel also recalls that the same thing happened to him (Dan. X).

(V. 2.) And the spirit entered into me after he had spoken to me, and set me upon my feet. And I heard him speaking to me and saying: “Son of man.”

The Septuagint: “And the spirit came to me, and took me, and lifted me up, and set me upon my feet; and I heard him speaking to me, and he said to me: ‘Son of man.’”

The divine word had commanded the prophet: “Stand upon your feet” (Ps. XXXIX, 3), but without God’s assistance and the coming of the Holy Spirit he could not stand. Therefore the Spirit enters into him—or takes him and raises him up—so that he may stand with firm step and be able to say: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Eph. VI, 14).

We read of no sinner standing; rather, it is said to the saints: “Stand therefore, with your loins girded.” But the sinner deserves to hear the words of Deuteronomy: “There shall be no firm standing of your foot” (Deut. XXVIII, 56).

Ezekiel is frequently addressed as “Son of man” (Matt. VIII, 20), and Daniel rarely. Each of them, in the person of the one who had said, “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head,” consoles the captive people and recalls them to repentance.

(V. 3.) I am sending you to the children of Israel, to apostate nations that have departed from me. They and their fathers have transgressed my covenant to this very day.

He does not call them the people of God, Israel, but apostate nations: those who have departed from the Lord, not only their fathers but also their sons. The sons would not seem to be liable for the sin of their fathers; rather, the impiety of both fathers and sons is shown to be equal.

Moreover, what the Septuagint translated as “provoking me,” or “turning me into bitterness,” signifies that God, who is good and sweet by nature, is changed into bitterness by our vices. For just as it is said to the saints: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9), so sinners experience him as bitter. Hence the Apostle refers to the goodness and severity of God in relation to saints and sinners (Rom. XXI).

And concerning sinners who were lying down, it is written: “The Lord raises up those who are crushed; the Lord loves the righteous; the Lord looses those who are bound” (Ps. CXLV, 8). To the saints who stand, however, he promises rewards.

(V. 4.) And the sons are hard of face and stubborn of heart; to them I am sending you.

This is not found in the Septuagint. It is a sign of great clemency that God sends someone to such people and does not despair of their salvation; and it is a sign of prophetic confidence that he does not fear going even to such people.

By “stubborn of heart” and “hard of face,” we should understand what is said to the sinner: “Your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead bronze” (Isa. XLVIII, 6). In what follows they are also accused of having hearts of stone, which God says he will remove and replace with hearts of flesh, so that in their gentleness they may receive God’s commands.

(V. 5.) And you shall say to them: “Thus says the Lord God: Perhaps they will hear, and perhaps they will desist, for they are a provoking house; and they shall know that a prophet has been among them.”

Something similar is written in Jeremiah: “Perhaps they will hear and repent” (Jer. XXVI, 3). And in the Gospel: “Perhaps they will respect my son” (Matt. XXI, 37).

God speaks these words with the feeling of one who expresses uncertainty, in order to show human free will, lest foreknowledge of future good or evil make immutable what God knows will occur.

[Note: Compare Rabanus, who cites this passage from Jerome in his letter to Count Everard against the heresy of Gottschalk.]

For it is not because he knows what is to come that we must necessarily do what he has foreknown; rather, he knows as God what we are going to do by our own will.

(V. 6.) You, therefore, son of man, do not fear them, and do not fear their words [Vulgate: “lest you fear”], because they are unbelieving and subversive toward you.

The Septuagint: “And you, son of man, do not fear them, and do not be afraid before them, because they will rage and gather against you all around.”

Although they have a stiff neck and a stubborn heart, my commands are stronger than they are. Do not think that you have been deceived if you are sent to those who will not listen to you. Behold, I foretell to you that they will rage, gather against you, and surround you, leaving you no escape. They will do this because they are unbelieving and despise God’s commands.
