And you dwell with scorpions. Do not fear their words, and do not be afraid of their faces, because they are a provoking house. They can strike with a blow curved like a bow and with a hollow-tubed sting, so that the same wound both opens the skin and spreads poison.

Each person receives a name according to his character. To the scribes and Pharisees it is said: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. XXIII, 33). And concerning Herod, who was devious: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke XIII, 32). False prophets are compared to foxes in this same prophet. And now they are called scorpions because of their stubborn hearts.

Hence we also read in the Gospel: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not listen to them” (John X, 8). But how did the lost sheep of the house of Israel listen to their adversaries? From this it is shown that those who listened to thieves and robbers lost the name of sheep and assumed other names, so that they did not perish as sheep, but as vipers, foxes, and scorpions.

(Vv. 7–8.) And you shall speak my words to them: “Perhaps they will hear and fear, or perhaps they will desist, for they are provocateurs.” But you, son of man, hear what I speak [Vulgate: “whatever I speak”] to you.

Therefore we must not cease speaking, even though those to whom we speak are evil. Rather, according to the Apostle (II Tim. IV), in season and out of season we must preach the word of God, since it may happen that one who is hard may be corrected into gentleness, and that one who is obedient may, after changing his will, no longer listen.

Do not be provocative, as the provocative house is. We have already said that the Septuagint uses “bitterness” for provocation or irritation. What he says, therefore, is this: You must not imitate those to whose correction you have been sent, lest similar sin deserve similar punishment.

Open your mouth and eat what I give you. Make yourself worthy, he says, of my words, and receive spiritual food, so that just as it is said in the Gospel, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII, 8), so here it may be said: “Whoever has an open mouth for eating, let him eat.”

Hence the Lord speaks to the Psalmist: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX, 11). And he replies: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. CXVIII, 131). The apostle Paul, who possessed within himself the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and in whom Christ the Lord was speaking, writes to the Corinthians: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (II Cor. VI, 11). And Matthew reports concerning the Savior: “Opening his mouth, he taught them” (Matt. V, 2).

And I saw, and behold, a hand was extended toward me.

For “a hand was sent,” the Septuagint translated “an extended hand.” It is sent and extended toward those who receive benefits. It is withdrawn from those to whom he speaks through the prophet: “Is the hand of the Lord shortened and contracted?” (Isa. L, 2). And in the Psalm: “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom forever?” (Ps. LXXIII, 11).

Finally, in his Passion he extended his wings, received his disciples, and carried them upon his shoulders; and he said: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient people” (Isa. LXV, 2), so that he might gather the children of Israel as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings. And through the stretching out of Moses’ hands, Israel overcame Amalek (Exod. XVII).

(V. 9.) And in it was a scroll rolled up, and he spread it out before me; it was written inside and outside, and written upon it were lamentation, a song, and woe.

And he said to me: “Son of man, whatever you find, eat.”

For “a rolled-up scroll,” the Septuagint translated “a chapter of a book.” It was in the hand of the Lord seated upon the throne, which hand had been sent and extended. Concerning this it is also said in the Psalms: “In the chapter of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. XXXIX, 8).

We should understand “chapter” as the beginning. This scroll, rolled up, sealed, and written inside and outside, before and behind, was of such difficulty that no one could open and read it—neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth—except the lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David and Jesse, concerning whom John said in the Apocalypse that he himself had devoured it (Apoc. V): not the whole scroll, but the chapter, that is, the beginning. For it is impossible for human nature to devour all the treasures of this book.

He spread it out before the prophet and gave it to him to read and understand. In Isaiah it is said to be sealed for the unbelieving people (Isa. XXIX). To this day a veil has been placed over the Jews in the Old Testament.

It was written in front and behind: concerning future and past things. Or certainly, outside, in the letter of the historical account; inside, in the spiritual understanding, concerning which the Psalmist also says: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is inward” (Ps. XLIV, 14).

Written both inside and outside were lamentation, a song, and woe. Lamentation concerned those who are summoned to repentance, as Samuel and the apostle Paul mourned and grieved over Saul and the Corinthians, whom they desired to save (II Chron. XVI; II Cor. XII). A song concerned those who are worthy of God’s testimony, to whom the Psalmist commands: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. XCV and XCVII, 1). Woe concerned those who are utterly without hope and, when they have entered the depths of sins, despise them (Prov. XVIII).

(Cap. III—v. 1.) Eat this scroll, and go [Vulgate: “going”], speak to the children [Vulgate: “to the children”] of Israel.

Unless we have first eaten the opened scroll, we cannot teach the children of Israel. Thus David, after he himself had received mercy, says: “I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will turn back to you” (Ps. L, 15).

(V. 2.) And I opened my mouth, and he fed me that scroll. And he said to me: “Son of man.”

I opened my mouth, he says, because I was told: “Open your mouth and eat.” When my mouth was opened, the Lord bestowed food, so that the beginning of willing may be in us, while we receive the perfection of blessedness from the Lord. For it is “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16). Nevertheless, both willing and running belong to our free choice.

For “I opened,” the Septuagint translated “he opened,” so that God is understood: for he both opened the prophet’s mouth and fed him.

(V. 3.) Your belly shall eat, and your inward parts shall be filled with this scroll that I give you.

The Septuagint: “Your mouth shall eat, and your belly shall be filled with this chapter given to you.”

The eating of the scroll is the beginning of reading and of the simple historical account. But when, through constant meditation, we have stored the Lord’s book in the treasury of memory, our belly is filled spiritually and our inward parts are satisfied, so that with the apostle Paul we may possess “the inward parts of mercy” (Col. III), and that belly may be filled of which Jeremiah says: “My belly, my belly—I am in pain, and the senses of my heart trouble me” (Jer. IV, 19).

And I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey.

David also says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 103). And elsewhere: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. XVIII, 10–11).

And Samson found a honeycomb in the mouth of a lion (Judg. XIV); and after his resurrection the Lord ate a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb (Luke II).

And in Proverbs it is said concerning the bee, although the Hebrew copies do not contain this: “Go to the bee, and learn how it is a worker and makes its work pure; from its labors kings and ordinary people derive benefit for their health” (Prov. VI, 8, according to the Septuagint). This is what Moses, the prophets, the evangelists, and the apostles accomplished, so that whoever became a king, whose heart is in the hand of God, might enjoy sweet foods.

But whoever is simple and possesses the innocence of doves without the cunning of the serpent should believe with simple faith and be saved, because everywhere there are snares, and often the devil disguises himself as an angel of light (II Cor. II). Honey drips from the lips of the adulterous woman, promising sweetness so that she may insert poisons (Prov. V).

(V. 5.) And he said to me: “Son of man, go and enter the house of Israel, and speak my words to them” [the words “and enter” are absent from the Vulgate].

The one to whom it is said, “Go and enter the house of Israel,” is shown not to have been among the sinful people, although he appeared to dwell within the same borders beside the river Chebar. For it is written: “And I was in the midst of the captivity beside the river Chebar.”

The prophet’s way of life was separate, and he was offended by the sight of the wicked. Moses did the same (Exod. XXXIII), pitching the tabernacle far from the camp of the multitude; and when he entered it, the pillar of cloud descended and stood before the entrance of the tabernacle.

(Vv. 5–6.) For you are not being sent to a people of profound speech and difficult [Vulgate: “unknown”] language, to the house of Israel, nor to many peoples of unknown speech, whose speech you could not understand. And if I were to send you to them, they would listen to you.

Since they do not wish to come to you, you go to them. For “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke V, 31). Nor can you say: “I cannot speak to them, because they belong to another language, and we are barbarians to one another, unable to understand one another’s speech.”

What need is there to speak of one people? If I were sending you to different nations, still my authority and power would overcome every difficulty. Would that the time were at hand when I will send you to all nations, and give them the gift of languages, so that my apostles may preach and bring the whole world, despite its diversity of languages, under the yoke of one faith. Those who are of profound and lofty speech would more readily listen; they possess nothing of Jewish lightness, but proceed with a grave and solid step. Though their languages are unknown, their faith is known.

Hence it follows: “And if I were to send you to them, they would listen to you.” Indeed, afterward he sent him, and all believed together. Therefore Paul and Barnabas speak to the Jews [*or*: “to them”]: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you; but because you refused to receive the word, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46). And concerning the centurion it is said: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII, 10).

(V. 7.) But the house of Israel does not wish to listen to you, because it does not wish to listen to me. For the whole house of Israel has a worn forehead and a hard heart.

Do not be saddened, he says, if they refuse to listen to you. They will not listen to you for this reason: because they despise listening to me, in accordance with what the Savior also said: “Whoever does not receive you does not receive me” (ibid., X, 40).

Here free will is openly shown. Two reasons are given for their refusal to listen: because, he says, they are perverse in will and have a worn forehead—or, as the Septuagint translated, are contentious. It is implied that, although often summoned to salvation, they refused to listen.

(Vv. 8–9.) Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads. I have made your face like adamant and like flint. Do not fear them, and do not be afraid before them, because they are a provoking house.

And he said to me:

The house of Israel has a worn forehead, brazen audacity, and a heart so hard that it may be compared with scorpions. Therefore I have given you an exceedingly hard face and a forehead that no shame can overcome.

From this we learn that sometimes it is a gift of God to resist shamelessness and, when circumstances demand it, to strike forehead against forehead.

[Note: In Rabanus: “and when the occasion demands it.”]

This is granted so that our modesty and human sense of shame may not fear the ambushes of our rivals.

(V. 10.) Son of man, take into your heart all my words that I shall speak to you, and hear them with your ears.

This is the food of the scroll, and these are the words by which, according to the diversity of their hearers, he speaks either lamentation, or song, or woe to human beings [*or*: “we speak”].

Nevertheless, we should note that the words of God must first be stored in our heart, heard, and understood with the greatest care; only then are they to be brought forth before the people.

(V. 11.) Go, enter among the exiles [or: captivity], among the children of your people, and speak to them and say to them: “Thus says the Lord God: Perhaps they will listen and desist.”

And our Lord also came to the Jewish people, sent by the Father to preach release to captives, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. LXVII, 19).

(V. 12.) And the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great commotion: “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.”

The God of whom it is written, “The Lord takes up the meek” (Ps. CXLVI, 6), himself also took up the prophet. He was not in the flesh but in the spirit, and, walking in the spirit, he did not perform the works of the flesh, for the Spirit of God was in him.

Therefore, despising earthly things, he was carried away by the Spirit and heard behind him the sound of a great commotion, forgetting what lay behind and stretching toward the future, so that he might leave the plots of his enemies behind him.

We read something similar in Exodus (Exod. XXIV), when Pharaoh and his entire army were pursuing Israel. The angel in the pillar of cloud left the front of the camp, came behind it, and stood throughout the night between Israel and the Egyptians, so that, when their adversaries were terrified, Israel might hear: “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.”

The place of the Lord is all those in whom he finds lodging. Or certainly the Son is the place of the Father, just as the Father is the place of the Son, as the Lord and Savior says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 11).

Micah also signifies the same thing: “Behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and he will descend upon the high places of the earth; and the mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire, and like water carried down a steep place” (Mic. I, 3–4).

For when the Lord and Savior descended and went forth from the Father, the high places of the earth and the mountains were shaken, and the lower valleys melted.

The place may also be the glory of the Lord and the inaccessible light of which the Apostle speaks: “He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (I Tim. VI, 16).

When we turn over the Lord’s past judgments in our minds, we hear behind us the voice of a great commotion. When we meditate upon future things in our heart, a voice is heard from what lies ahead, from the things that are before us.

(V. 13.) And the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another, and the sound of the wheels following the living creatures, and the sound of a great commotion.

The words “I heard behind me the sound of a great commotion, and I heard the sound of the wings of the living creatures and the sound of the wheels” are understood jointly (*ἀπὸ κοινοῦ*) according to the Hebrew. The Septuagint added: “And I saw the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another,” and the rest, according to what is read in Exodus: “And all the people saw the voice of God” (Exod. XX, 18). Thus the prophet heard the voice that came from behind him, while he saw the voice that was before him.

But it is better and truer to understand that the voice was heard rather than seen: both the voice of the wings striking one another and that of the wheels, concerning which we spoke above, as well as the voice of the great commotion that showed God’s anger was going to come upon the people of Israel.

(V. 14.) The Spirit also lifted me up and took me, and I went away bitter in the indignation of my spirit.

The Septuagint: “And the Spirit lifted me up, and took me, and I went away exalted in the impulse of my spirit.”

After he had been lifted up by the Spirit and taken up by it, he went wherever he was carried in the indignation and bitterness of his spirit, understanding God’s anger and considering in his mind what the vision signified.

Or he was carried aloft by the very impulse of his spirit, desiring to go where the Lord commanded.

We should understand his spirit not as the Holy Spirit, but as the human spirit, concerning which it is said in many places, as in Isaiah: “From the night my spirit rises early toward you, O God” (Isa. XXVI, 9).

The prophet was transported—not, as some think, in spirit, but in his very body. We read the same concerning Habakkuk according to Theodotion (Dan. XIV).

(V. 15.) For the hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me. And I came to the exiles, to the mound of new grain, to those who lived beside the river Chebar. And I sat where they were sitting, and I remained there seven days, mourning in their midst.

The Septuagint: “And the hand of the Lord became strong upon me, and I entered into the captivity exalted. And I went around among the inhabitants beside the river Chebar who were there; and I sat there seven days, conversing in their midst.”

For what we translated “the mound of new grain,” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion retained the Hebrew words themselves, *THEL ABIB* (). The Septuagint translated “exalted” and “I went around,” believing it better to say something than to introduce a word that would raise a question for the reader.

We, however, learned from the Hebrews that *Thel abib* signifies the time when new wheat or barley is gathered and, after famine and scarcity, before it is threshed on the threshing floor, gives some promise of food.

Thus Israel, small and weak, dwelling on the banks of the river Chebar, as though coming back to life and rising from the earth, promised the seed of the Jewish people.

The hand of the Lord comes upon the prophet, strengthening him so that he may receive the name “watchman” and teach what he has learned. For seven days he first remains among them, observing everything they did, so that afterward he might know what to rebuke.

He mourns—or converses—in their midst, seeing their crimes and God’s just sentence because of the sinners’ iniquity.

For what we said, “mourning,” and what is written in Hebrew, *MASMIM* (), Theodotion translated “marveling,” expressing the prophet’s astonishment as he observed their iniquities.

Aquila’s second edition, which the Hebrews call *κατὰ ἀκρίβειαν* (“with exactness”), translated it as *ἠρεμάζων*, that is, “being quiet” and “set apart,” to show that although he was indeed in the midst of the captives, he was separated from them in mind.

(Vv. 16–17.) And when seven days had passed, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear a word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me.”

He who is to become a watchman and recount God’s words to the people must first remain quiet for a long time and grieve over what he sees, possessing none of those things in his conscience that he will rebuke in others.

(Verses 18–19.) “When I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you do not announce it to him, nor speak to turn him back from his wicked way so that he may live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but I shall require his blood at your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked, and he is not turned back from his iniquity and from his wicked way, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you have saved your own soul.”

[Note: Victor, following the Vulgate, reads “from his impiety,” and so forth, denying that “from iniquity” is Jerome’s reading; but the Septuagint has τῆς ἀνομίας αὐτοῦ, “from his lawlessness.”]

There are two wicked or sinful men, as the Septuagint translated it. One hears nothing from the watchman and dies in his wickedness; his blood is sought from the watchman’s hands. The other is warned by the watchman, but, scorning to listen, dies through his own fault—provided only that the watchman is free from blame. From this we understand why the Lord threatens the wicked and says, “You shall surely die”: so that he may turn back from his wicked way and live. The threat is directed not against persons but against sins [variant: sinners], and not against those who turn away from their vices, but against those who remain in sin.

There is a great distinction in keeping God’s words silent, for three reasons: fear, laziness, or flattery. Hence Isaiah also says: “Woe is me, miserable that I am, because I kept silent” (Isa. 6:5). What follows—“But you have saved your own soul”—echoes the apostolic saying: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:14). [Note: The same editor, following Victor, asks whether the external watchman is the cause of death of the one who perished, or whether he is guilty. So far as I know, no manuscripts support this reading.]

For the work of the teacher is the salvation of the disciple.

(Verses 20–21.) “But if a righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling-block before him. He shall die, because you did not announce it to him; he shall die in his sin, and his righteous deeds that he performed shall not be remembered. But I will require his blood at your hand. Yet if you announce to the righteous man that the righteous should not sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because you warned him, and you have saved your own soul.”

[Note: In accordance with the Vulgate, Victor rewrites the passage: “if he turns away from his righteousness and commits,” and so forth.]

Just as we read of two wicked or sinful men—one who did not listen and perished, and another who listened but persisted in wickedness—so there are two righteous men: one who did not listen and perished [Note: In Rabanus, with a negative particle inserted: “and did not perish.”], and another who listened, turned to repentance, and saved his soul. It should be noted that a righteous man can fall, and, if he has a teacher, can be converted to better things. Good works, therefore, also need a constant instructor, lest one who has fallen from the best course draw back his foot.

The wicked or sinful man, if he is not converted, will die in his wickedness and sin. But the righteous man, if he commits wickedness and sin, does not die immediately; rather, a stumbling-block is placed before him, or a torment; and, as Theodotion said, an infirmity, so that he may be tormented, fail to find a level path, and understand that he is sick. Of this the Apostle also says: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (ibid., 11:30).

It benefits the righteous man to understand his sin and the torment of his conscience, and to say with the Psalmist: “I turned back in my affliction, while the thorn was fixed in me” (Ps. 31:4). And just as iniquities do not confront the wicked if he turns away from his wicked way and lives, so former righteousness does not benefit the righteous man if he is overwhelmed by new crimes.

When it says, “He shall die, because you did not announce it to him,” the unstated meaning is that he could have lived if the watchman and teacher had instructed him.

[Col. 0041A] (Verse 22.) “And the hand of the Lord was there upon me, and he said to me: ‘Arise, go out into the plain, and there I shall speak with you.’”

The word “there,” which we translated from the Hebrew and which is absent from the Septuagint, is deliberately placed and certainly indicates a location. Earlier we read: “And I came to the exiles at the mound of new grain, to those who lived beside the river Chobar” (above, 3:15). It is fitting that the one to whom he had said, “I sat,” is commanded to arise. The one who had entered among the exiles hears, “Go out”—not into rugged valleys, nor among precipitous crags, but into the breadth of a plain capable of containing the glory of the Lord. Hence it is also said to the Corinthians: “Be enlarged” (1 Cor. 6:13).

When he enters among the captives, of whom it was said that they rage and persecute him, he needs a strong hand so that he may resist and endure the fury of his persecutors. But when he goes out into the plain, the hand of the Lord does indeed come upon him, because he could not go out without divine assistance; yet it is not called strong. He goes out to see the glory of God, not to fight. We should also observe that, while sitting among the seated captives, the prophet himself did not see the glory of the Lord.

(Verses 23.) “And I arose [the Vulgate: ‘rising’] and went out into the plain, and behold, the glory of the Lord stood there, like the glory that I had seen beside the river Chobar.”

At the Lord’s command he enters, and at his command he goes out; and he sits with those who are sitting, because the number of the captives could not hear him while he was standing. Having gone out into the breadth of the plain, he saw the glory of the Lord standing—the glory that he had previously seen walking, lifting itself up, and at times standing.

The glory was seen beside the Chobar, the river of this world, whose name may be interpreted as “most grievous.” This signifies that all the glory of this world flows past and has no fixed standing. But the glory of the Lord, standing and enduring, is seen with the standing prophet in the plain. Among the captives it could neither stand nor be seen.

(Verses 24.) “And I fell upon my face, and the spirit entered into me and set me upon my feet. And he spoke with me and said to me: ‘Enter and shut yourself up in the midst of your house.’”

Unable to endure the standing glory of the Lord, he fell upon his face so that the spirit entering him might raise him up. The spirit set him upon his feet and spoke to him, saying: “Enter and shut yourself up in the midst of your house.”

The meaning is this: Since you have been strengthened by the sight of the Lord’s majesty, fear no one and dread no one; return to your house—either for the necessities of the body, as some think, or as a sign of the future siege. Just as Isaiah, barefoot and naked (Isa. 20), announced the captivity lasting three years and the nakedness of the people, so you, shut up in your house, by the very act of it prophesy the approaching siege of the city of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0042A] (Verses 25–26.) “But you, son of man, behold, they have placed bonds upon you, and they shall bind you with them; you shall not go out from their midst [the Vulgate: ‘into their midst’]. And I shall make your tongue cleave to your palate—or throat—and you shall be mute, unable to rebuke them as a man who reproves them [the Vulgate omits ‘them’], because it is a house of provocation.”

That he is shut up in a house, bound with bonds, and does not go out to those among whom he lives, but suffers the solitude of imprisonment among a multitude of captives—as I said above—is a sign of the siege. Jerusalem, closed in and surrounded by the army of the Chaldeans, will permit none of its inhabitants to go outside. This is the pot of which Jeremiah speaks (Jer. 1), and which this prophet himself describes later, in which the flesh of the people is consumed.

The reason that the prophet’s tongue cleaves to his palate or throat and that he is rendered mute, without the authority to rebuke, is clear: “because,” he says, “it is a house of provocation.” The meaning is: They possess such bitterness and so much contention against God that they do not deserve to hear one who reproves them.

[Note: Following Victor and the Florentine manuscripts, we restore “of bitterness and contention,” which gives a more coherent sense; previously the text had “bitternesses and contentions.”]

From this it is evident that wherever there is a multitude of sins, sinners are unworthy of being corrected by the Lord.

(Verses 27.) “But when I speak with you, I shall open your mouth, and you shall say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God: He who hears, let him hear; and he who is quiet, let him be quiet, because it is a house of provocation.’”

What we read in Ecclesiastes—“A time to be silent, and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3)—is also confirmed in prophetic speech. It is the mark of the same wisdom both to be silent and to speak at the proper time, and to give one’s fellow servants their food at the proper time. Hence Isaiah also says to the unbelieving people: “I was silent; shall I always be silent? says the Lord” (Isa. 65).

The prophet, therefore, who had kept his mouth closed for a long time because of the multitude of sins, now saw that some might be converted—those of whom it was said, “He who hears, let him hear, and he who refrains from evil, let him be quiet and cease.” For this reason, once his mouth has been opened, he speaks to the people, not by his own will but at the Lord’s command.

The wording we have—“He who hears, let him hear; and he who is quiet, let him be quiet”—is rendered by the Septuagint: “He who hears, let him hear; and he who is unbelieving, let him be unbelieving.” The second edition of Aquila translated it: “He who hears shall be heard; and he who abandons shall be abandoned.”

The meaning is: “To him who has, more will be given; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Mark 4:25).

[Col. 0042D] (Chapter 4, verses 1–2.) “And you, son of man, take for yourself a brick, place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem. Arrange a siege against it, build fortifications, pile up a ramp, set camps against it, and place battering-rams all around.”

As we said earlier, “Enter and shut yourself up in the midst of your house,” and, “Behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they shall bind you, and you shall not go out,” signify that the prophet is a type of the future siege of the city of Jerusalem. So now he is commanded by a geometrical art to draw the city upon a brick, and the brick itself is to be placed before the prophet, so that after he has drawn Jerusalem in the dust, he may depict every aspect of the siege against it: fortifications, piled-up ramparts, the surrounding crown of the besieging army, and battering-rams, by all of which cities are usually captured.

Fortifications are structures by which a city is enclosed so that none of the besieged can escape. Ramps are piles of earth with which the ditch and trenches are filled. Camps are the guards of the soldiers stationed around it. Battering-rams shake the foundations of the walls and loosen the joints of the stones.

This is said to signify the approaching captivity of the city of Jerusalem under Zedekiah, in whose eleventh year both the king and the city were captured.

For “brick,” which in Greek is feminine, ἡ πλίνθος (*hē plinthos*), Symmachus translated more explicitly as πλίνθιον (*plinthion*), which we may call a small brick or tablet. On its dust geometers commonly draw γραμμαί (*grammai*), that is, lines and rays.

For this reason some think it is not absurd that the prophet should possess knowledge of this discipline as well. They repeat the examples that Jesus son of Nun sent scouts to survey the land (Josh. 2)—an activity properly called geometry—and that the angel in Zechariah possessed a geometric measuring cord with which to measure Jerusalem (Zech. 2).

Since the prophet is now commanded to draw Jerusalem in the dust—a practice which among them is properly called σκηνογραφία (*skēnographia*, “scene-drawing”)—we may also take the brick as a reproach against Israel, because Israel served Pharaoh in clay and brick (Exod. 1). Or the city, which they thought strong and impregnable, may be compared with a very fragile brick that immediately dissolves at the touch of water. Thus, concerning the city of which it was previously said, “Is the exceedingly hard rock, or the mountain of the wilderness, of the daughter of Zion,” it may be turned into a brick that will be destroyed by a Babylonian flood, according to what is written: “Therefore the Lord will bring upon you the mighty and abundant waters of the king of Assyria” (Isa. 8:7).

[Note: This is how the manuscript codices read; the printed books retain σκιογραφία (*skiographia*) instead of σκηνογραφία (*skēnographia*). According to Vitruvius, scenography is “the representation of the front and receding sides, with all the lines corresponding to the center of the compass,” which fits perfectly with the present passage, where Ezekiel draws Jerusalem in the dust. —MART.]

(Verses 3.) “And you, take for yourself an iron pan, place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city, set your face firmly against it, and it shall be for a siege; and you shall surround it. This is a sign for the house of Israel.”

What we said above—that both the prophet himself and the drawing of the brick, surrounded by fortifications, ramparts, and battering-rams, should go before as a sign of the siege of Jerusalem—is now stated more plainly after the intervening material: “It is a sign for the house of Israel.” The iron pan, placed like a wall between the prophet and the city, demonstrates the great anger of God, which will not be wearied by any prayers or bent toward mercy.

Just as iron subdues all metals and nothing is harder than it, so Jerusalem’s unbelievable crimes made God, who is naturally gentle, exceedingly hard through the people’s own fault. The pan is also called a wall set between the people and God, to show that the whole multitude will soon be broken and reduced to nothing.

The firmness of the face turned against the city is a sign of severity, according to what we read elsewhere: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33:17).

(Verses 4 and following.) “And you shall lie upon your left side, and place upon it the iniquities of the house of Israel, according to the number of the days during which you shall lie upon it; and you shall bear their iniquity. But I have assigned you the years of their iniquity according to the number of days—three hundred and ninety days—and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel. When you have completed these, you shall lie upon your right side a second time, and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days. I have assigned you one day for each year, one day, I say, for each year.”

Let us investigate what the three hundred and ninety years are which are reckoned as an equal number of days during which the prophet was to lie bound and constrained upon his left side, without turning to the other side, thereby displaying the captivity and miseries of the ten tribes, that is, of Israel.

As for the other forty years, during which he was to lie on his right side for Judah and its iniquities—or, as Holy Scripture relates, to sleep there—we must say the following about Israel. Under Pekah son of Remaliah, who reigned over Israel for twenty years and was its nineteenth king, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came and captured Aijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and the whole land of Naphtali, and carried them away into Assyria (2 Kings 15).

After him, Hoshea son of Elah reigned over Israel for nine years. He was captured with all Samaria by Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, and was carried away to Elam, and to the rivers of Gozan and Habor, in the cities of the Medes. In the sixth year of King Hezekiah, as the sacred history of Kings relates (ibid., 17), Hoshea was captured.

If we reckon from that point in sequence the years during which Israel was under distress and pressed beneath the yoke of captivity, we can arrive at the following calculation. From the sixth year to the twenty-ninth—so many years in all did Hezekiah reign—there are twenty-four years. Manasseh succeeded him and reigned for fifty-five years. After him Amon reigned for two years. Josiah followed and reigned for thirty-two years.

[Note: Victor says that Josiah reigned thirty-one years, not thirty-two, according to 2 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 34, as all manuscripts have it. Nevertheless, nothing has been altered, because the calculation of the numbers would not agree if one year were removed: after its removal there would be not 164 but 163, and not 135 but 134, leaving one year short of the prophetic number 390. Nor should you therefore think that the holy man’s memory failed. He treats an incomplete year as a complete one; for this reason in the total he counts not 390 years but 389 years and four months. Sacred Scripture, however, counts only complete years in the lives of kings, not incomplete ones. The holy man learned elsewhere that Josiah lived several months beyond the beginning of his thirty-first year.]

Joakim, also called Eliakim, succeeded Josiah and reigned for eleven years. After him came Joachin, called Jeconiah, who was immediately led into captivity. Zedekiah reigned in his place for eleven years, under whom Jerusalem was captured and the Temple destroyed.

Thus, from Israel’s first captivity, which occurred under King Pekah, until the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in which the Temple was desolated, there are 164 years [variant: 170]. From the second captivity, when Hoshea was captured and all Samaria was overthrown, there are 135 years [variant: 180]. The desolation of the Temple lasted seventy years; added to the first captivity, these make 234 years.

In the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, the Temple was rebuilt by Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak, while Haggai and Zechariah prophesied. Darius reigned for thirty-six years; with one year removed, thirty-five of his years are added. Xerxes son of Darius reigned after him for twenty years. After him came Artabanus, for seven months. Then Xerxes, who was called Μακρόχειρ (*Makrocheir*, “Long-handed”), reigned for forty years. After him came another Xerxes, for two months, and Sogdianus for seven months [variant: four].

Darius, called Νόθος (*Nothos*, “the Bastard”), succeeded him and reigned for nineteen years. After him Artaxerxes, called Μνήμων (*Mnēmōn*, “the Rememberer”) [variant: Memnon], son of Darius and Parysatis, reigned for forty years. He is called Ahasuerus by the Hebrews. Under him the story of Mordecai and Esther is related (Esther 8), when the entire Jewish people, delivered from the danger of death, recovered their former liberty.

From the second year of Darius to the final year of Ahasuerus there are 155 years and four months. Added to the preceding 234 years, these make 389 years and four months.

The forty years represented by the prophet’s lying on his right side are easily calculated. After Eliakim, who was called Joakim, his son Joachin, called Jeconiah, reigned for three months. During his reign:

> “The servants of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up against Jerusalem, and it was surrounded with fortifications. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against the city while his servants were attacking it. Joachin, king of Judah, went out to the king of Babylon, he, his mother, his servants, his princes, and his eunuchs; and the king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign and carried away from there all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal house.”

And shortly afterward:

> “He carried away all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the mighty men of the army—ten thousand into captivity—and every craftsman and smith. Nothing remained except the poor of the people of the land” (ibid.).

After Joachin was captured with an immense multitude of the people and all the wealth of Jerusalem, Zedekiah reigned for eleven years. Under him the city was captured and the Temple destroyed. Its desolation continued for seventy years, until the second year of Darius.

[Note: This figure is better known under the name Artaxerxes, by which Jerome himself calls him in his commentary on Daniel 7.]

In the thirtieth year of the Temple’s desolation, Cyrus reigned over the Persians after overthrowing Astyages, king of the Medes. In accordance with Isaiah’s prophecy (Isa. 45), he sent back to Jerusalem nearly fifty thousand people from the tribe of Judah, together with the Temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away and the other things recorded in the history of Ezra (1 Esdras 1).

Thus, in the case of Israel—that is, the ten tribes—we reckon 390 years from King Pekah of Israel, under whom Shalmaneser devastated much of the Israelite people, to the fortieth year of Ahasuerus, when the persecution of the entire Jewish people was mitigated. Similarly, from the first year of Jeconiah, when a large part of Jerusalem was carried away to Babylon, to the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians—the thirtieth year of the Temple’s desolation—we reckon forty years. Under Cyrus the captivity of the Jews was relaxed and liberty restored to the people.

Some, joining Israel’s 390 years to Judah’s forty, make 430 years and want these years to be fulfilled from the Savior’s baptism to the consummation of the world. Others, especially the Jews, wish the 430 years to be reckoned from the second year of Vespasian, when Jerusalem was captured by the Romans and the Temple overthrown, during which time the people were placed under tribulation, distress, and the yoke of captivity; they believe that afterward the people will return to their former condition.

Just as the children of Israel were in Egypt for 430 years, so, they say, the final captivity will end after the same number of years. It is written in Exodus: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in the land of Egypt, was 430 years.” And again: “After 430 years had passed, the whole army of the Lord went out by night.”

I am greatly astonished that the Vulgate copies contain 190 years, and that some have 150, although the Hebrew, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion plainly retain 390 years [Note: Rather, they have days, not years, according to the Hebrew text, although I do not deny that the days are to be understood as years. As for the Septuagint, the reading now found in their copies is ἐννενήκοντα καὶ ἑκατὸν ἡμέρας (*ennenēkonta kai hekaton hēmeras*), “ninety and one hundred days”; but in other manuscripts, especially the Complutensian, τριακοσίων (*triakosiōn*, “three hundred”) is placed before ἐννενήκοντα. Consult the notes in the Roman edition on this passage of the Septuagint.]

The same number is also found among the Septuagint, provided their copies have not been corrupted by scribal error.

We believe that we have explained this exceedingly difficult question—one which, not to speak arrogantly, no one has explained—not so much by our own knowledge as by the grace of the Lord, fulfilling what he himself promised: “Seek, and you shall find; ask, and you shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7).

Whoever wishes to reckon from the first captivity, which occurred under Menahem son of Gaddi, king of Israel, who reigned in Samaria for ten years (2 Kings 15), when Pul, king of the Assyrians, came into the land of Israel and received a thousand talents of silver, and then to add the two years of Pekah, who reigned in Israel after him, will find that the 390 years were completed in the twenty-eighth year of King Ahasuerus, when the story of Esther is said to have occurred. This is also more credible. Israel did not cast off the yoke of its most grievous servitude after Ahasuerus’s reign had ended, but while he was still reigning.

[Col. 0047A] (Verse 7.) “And you shall turn your face toward the siege of Jerusalem, and your arm shall be bared [the Vulgate: ‘outstretched’], and you shall prophesy against it.”

The Septuagint reads: “And you shall prepare your face for the confinement of Jerusalem, strengthen your arm, and prophesy over it.”

The prophet needs preparation of face, strength, and the firm positioning of an extended and uncovered arm, so that the siege of the city may be demonstrated not only by his voice but also by the gesture and appearance of the prophet.

(Verses 8.) “Behold, I have surrounded you with bonds, and you shall not turn from one side to the other until you complete the days of your siege” [or confinement].

The left side is assigned to Israel because Samaria had been without the Temple and knowledge of God; the right side to Judah, in which the worship and religion of God were present. It should be noted that in one case there is the punishment of sinners, and in the other the exercise of virtue.

He does not turn from one side to the other, signifying that there is no rest from the torments until the complete confinement of the aforementioned days has been fulfilled. What the days are for the prophet, the year is for those who suffer (Gen. 29). The years that Jacob thought long seemed to him only a few days.

There is not only variety in punishments according to the diversity of merits; there is also variety in the reward of the good: the lambs stand on the right, and the goats on the left. Hence it is written elsewhere: “The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, but the heart of the fool is at his left” (Eccl. 10:2).

There are the Lord’s bonds, by which we are bound for salvation, and there are the devil’s bonds, with which he had bound the woman in the Gospel for eighteen years (Luke 13). Hence also “each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. 5:22). The Lord loosens these bonds in the figure of Lazarus raised from the dead, who had lain bound in the tomb with bandages and wrappings (John 11).

(Verses 9 and following.) “And you, take for yourself wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and *vicia*; put them into one vessel, and make for yourself loaves according to the number of the days during which you shall lie upon your side: for 390 days you shall eat it. Your food, which you shall eat, shall be by weight—twenty shekels [staters] per day; from time to time you shall eat it. You shall drink water by measure, one-sixth of a *hin*; from time to time you shall drink it. You shall eat it like a barley cake baked under ashes, and you shall cover it with human excrement before their eyes.”

For the word which we translated as *vicia*, the Hebrew has CHASAMIM (). The Septuagint and Theodotion rendered it ὄλυρα (*olyra*), which some think means oats and others rye.

The first edition of Aquila and Symmachus translated it ζέας or ζείας (*zeas* or *zeias*), which we may call *far*—spelt—or, in the common speech of Italy and Pannonia, an ear of grain or spelt.

[Note: Other books have *secale* (“rye”); the ancient Sangerman manuscript has *sicala*. See the earlier volume on Isaiah 28:25. Compare also the ancient lexicons, especially Hesychius. Drusius, citing Rabbi David in the *Book of Roots*, gives spelt. In his commentary on this passage he says that the common term is “rye.”]

The Septuagint also added “earthen” to the vessel. The prophet is commanded to demonstrate by an action the future famine and deprivation of the people of Israel. For when there is scarcity of everything, one does not seek variety and delicacy in food, but only how the stomach may be filled. So now the prophet puts wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and oats into one vessel and makes 390 loaves, to eat one each day. Each loaf weighs twenty shekels, that is, staters.

A shekel, or stater, contains four drachmas. Eight drachmas make a Latin ounce, so that one loaf is said to contain ten ounces—more sufficient to drag out life than to sustain it.

[Note: Josephus agrees in Book 3, chapter 9, of the *Antiquities*. From this the especially notable rabbinic opinion about two shekels, the ordinary and the sacred—of which they think the latter was worth twice as much—collapses of its own accord. They insist that Jerome is speaking of that distinction here, but neither Jerome nor Josephus recognized it, nor can it be extracted with sufficient plausibility from Scripture itself.]

The barrenness of the food is increased by the barrenness of the water. He is commanded to drink each day one-sixth of the Hebrew measure called a *hin*. A *hin* makes two Attic χόες (*choes*), which we may call two Italian sextarii, so that the *hin* is the measure of a Jewish sextarius and of our military measure, one-sixth of which makes one-third of an Italian sextarius.

This food and drink, according to the famous Orator, gives no strength but prevents death.

When he says, “From time to time you shall eat or drink,” he means “from evening to evening,” although some wrongly think it means “from year to year.”

The loaves themselves are made like barley bread baked under ashes. He is told to cover them with human excrement—not without the knowledge of those who are to eat them, for ignorance commonly softens misery, but before their eyes, so that they may endure the horror of the sight before the nausea of the taste.

It should also be noted that, according to the number of days of the left side, 390 loaves baked under ashes are ordered to be made and eaten one per day, while the loaves for the forty days of the right side are not mentioned at all. Thus Holy Scripture secretly suggests that the punishment of the sinful people is not the same if they possess knowledge of God as it is for those who have entirely departed from the worship of the true God.

We may also say, according to the spiritual understanding, that the Jewish people, after offending God, continues to this day to eat loaves baked under ashes, mixed with wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and oats, of which some are human food and others the food of animals.

Insofar as they appear to believe in one God, they possess something of wheat. But because they deny the Son, they feed upon the barley of animals and upon beans, which inflate the stomach of those who eat them and are said to oppress the mind—so much so that this food is detestable even to the Pythagoreans. Esau lost his birthright because of lentils (Gen. 25). Millet is food for peasants, wild animals, and fattened creatures. Oats, or *vicia* and *olyra*, are eaten by brute animals.

Since it is written, according to the Septuagint, that Elijah, fleeing from Jezebel, found an ὀλυρίτης (*olurites*) loaf baked under ashes (3 Kings 19), this signifies persecution and poverty.

[Note: Compare the commentary on Isaiah 15, where he seems to deny that those ravens were birds, holding them instead to have been men who fed Elijah. See also what we noted there.]

Therefore he is fed by ravens: because he found no food in Israel, he was nourished by the provisions of the nations, which were unclean.

The Law itself, which they read but do not understand, is a loaf baked under ashes and covered with human excrement. For this reason the Apostle Paul says that he regarded the gains of the Law and the observance of his former ceremonies as dung, in order to gain Christ (Phil. 3).

(Verses 13 and following.) “And the Lord said: ‘Thus shall the children of Israel eat their polluted bread among the nations to which I shall drive them.’ And I said: ‘Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, my soul has not been polluted; from my childhood until now I have not eaten anything that died of itself or was torn by beasts, and no unclean flesh has entered my mouth.’ And he said to me: ‘Behold, I have given you cow dung instead of human excrement, and you shall make your bread upon it.’”

We read very frequently in many places that prophets are, according to Zechariah (Zech. 3), portentous men who signify future events by their actions, and concerning whom God says: “I have been represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hos. 12:10).

Therefore, just as Ezekiel ate bread in excrement, so the children of Israel—or the entire Jewish people, or, as others think, the ten tribes—will eat polluted bread among the nations. The threat does not apply to those who have already been expelled, but to those who are to be expelled from the promised land.

When the prophet learned this, he thrice expressed his disgust, according to Aquila: “Ah, ah, ah.” According to Symmachus and the Septuagint, he replied μηδαμῶς (*mēdamōs*), which in Latin means “by no means.” Theodotion rendered it: “O Lord God.”

We should not think that he was contradicting the Lord’s command; rather, he was giving the reasons—or indeed pleading—why he could not do this. Finally, he obtained what he requested, and the austerity of the sentence was tempered by a milder command.

It may be asked why Ezekiel refused things that were easier, whereas Hosea was immediately joined to a prostitute (ibid., 1) and did not contradict or even reply that he possessed a chaste body and ought not to be polluted by intercourse with a prostitute, when the Apostle says: “He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her” (1 Cor. 6:16).

From this it is shown that the event was a figure of the synagogue or the Church, and was not literally carried out as described. We have discussed this more fully in explaining the prophet.

Something that dies without the shedding of blood and in which the soul dies is called *morticinium*—an animal that has died of itself. Something torn by beasts is what the Greeks call θηριάλωτον (*thērialōton*).

The fact that cow dung is granted instead of human excrement signifies lighter evils: the prophet is indeed commanded to eat bread cooked in cow dung, but he is kept far from the uncleanness of human excrement. To this day this judgment is preserved among the Jewish people, so that they do not eat their bread in human excrement.

For they do not serve idols or worship various monstrous images of demons, but they live in cow dung, since they perform everything for the sake of the flesh, the belly, and the goods of this earth, according to what is said: “He who does these things shall live by them” (Lev. 18:5; Deut. 4).

But we despise earthly things. We not only trample underfoot the food of human excrement and regard earthly pleasures as worthless; we eat the bread that came down from heaven (John 6), and enjoy that food of which the Psalmist sings: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25), living not on Egyptian meats but on the lightness of manna.

**(Verses 16–17.)** And he said to me: “Son of man, behold, I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem, and they shall eat bread by weight, and with anxiety, and they shall drink water by measure and in distress, so that, when bread and water fail, each person shall collapse against his brother, and they shall waste away in their iniquities.”

The Hebrew word *MATE* [], Aquila’s first edition translated as “staff”; his second edition, and Symmachus and Theodotion, translated it as στερέωμα, that is, “firmament” or “support.” What he had shown would take place in action, he also demonstrates in words. The sleeping on the left and right sides, and the bread baked under ashes and mixed with six kinds of grain, signifying the evils of the world, all tend toward this: to proclaim the famine of food and the unbelievable scarcity of water in Jerusalem, so that each person collapses against his brother, hoping for help from another because he does not see it within himself [variant: “foresee it”]. For it is human nature that, when evils press upon us and the weight of distress bears down, we place our confidence more in our neighbor than in ourselves. And they waste away in their iniquities, while they suffer everything on account of their iniquities.

I fear that this breaking of bread may also be found in our Jerusalem, in which the vision of peace is perceived: the Lord breaks it when he is angry and judges us unworthy of his bread. Would that at least we might deserve to receive it by weight and with anxiety, and that the tip of Lazarus’s finger might moisten our tongue, parched by excessive dryness (Luke 16). But when bread and water fail in the Church, man will collapse against his brother, and everywhere there will be discord, as we tear apart Christ’s tunic—which even the soldiers did not dare to tear apart during the Savior’s Passion (John 19)—and waste away in our iniquities because we do not possess the righteousness of God.

It is written in Jeremiah that the little ones, that is, the common people of the Church, asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them (Lamentations 4:4). Paul, however, who was a man of the Church [Note: The word “Church” is absent from other books.], and who knew that Christ had broken the legal loaves and given them to the disciples for distribution, speaks confidently: “The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). Those who need the milk of infancy cannot eat the staff, or strength, of bread, nor are they able to receive solid food. Nothing strengthens the mind of one who eats so greatly as the bread of life, of which it is written: “And bread strengthens the human heart” (Psalm 183:15).

## BOOK TWO

[Column 0051]

[47] This is the beginning of the second volume of the *Commentaries on Ezekiel*, O virgin of Christ, Eustochium.

### (Chapter 5—Verses 1 and following.)

“And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, like a barber’s razor (or: one that shaves hair) [Note: In Jerome’s Vulgate version, the words “like a barber’s razor” are absent.], and draw it over your head and your beard; then take for yourself a weighing scale and divide them. Burn a third part in the midst of the city, at the completion of the days of the conclusion [Vulgate: ‘of the siege’], and cut a third part with the sword around it; but scatter the other third to the wind, and I will unsheathe the sword after them. Then take from them a small number and bind them on the edge of your cloak; and again take some of them and throw them into the midst of the fire, and burn them. From it fire will go out against the whole house of Israel.”

[Note: The Vulgate edition supplied by Victorius adds: “and you shall take them and draw,” etc. This reading is confirmed by the Hebrew and Greek manuscripts. Likewise, a little later, in the verse containing “and taking a third part,” the word “taking”; and in the phrase “and you shall bind them on the edge of your cloak,” the word “your”; these have been restored with the same support.]

In place of the three parts of the hair, one of which is burned in the midst of the city, another cut with the sword around it, and the third scattered to be carried here and there by the wind, from which a small amount is taken and bound at the edge of the cloak, and from which again a little is sent into the fire, from which a flame goes out against the whole house of Israel, the Septuagint translated four parts.

Although they had said: “You shall burn a fourth part in the midst of the city, and you shall cut a fourth part with the sword around it, and you shall scatter a fourth part to the wind,” since a fourth part still remained for them, they added on their own: “And you shall take a fourth part and burn it in the midst of the city,” as though this were not the same as the first part, and as though he had said one thing about the first and another about the added part.

Finally, in what follows, the Lord himself explains through the Prophet the riddle of the hair divided into three parts, saying: “A third of you shall die by pestilence and shall be consumed by famine in your midst,” signifying that famine and pestilence are the fire; “and a third of you shall fall by the sword around you,” describing slaughter and wars outside. “But I will scatter a third of you to every wind,” showing that these are those who are to be led into captivity.

After them he says that he will unsheathe or pour out his sword, so that captivity will not be the final evil. He will take some of those who have been scattered and captured and bind at the edge of his cloak those who are to return from captivity to Jerusalem. From them also he will take a portion and consume it with fire and flame, signifying the Macedonians, under whom the inhabitants of Judea, and especially Jerusalem, suffered harshly.

When he says “from it”—that is, from the Jewish people—or, according to the Septuagint, “from her,” with the city of Jerusalem understood—“fire will go out against the whole house of Israel,” the history of the Maccabees relates that a certain portion of the Jews surrendered to Antiochus Epiphanes and incited him to persecute the people, together with many other events recorded in that same history and in the works of Josephus, especially the conflict between Hyrcanus and Alexander. On their account Gnaeus [variant: “the consul”] Pompey captured Jerusalem and subjected it to Roman rule. Later, under Titus and Vespasian, the city was captured and the Temple overthrown. After fifty years, under Aelius Hadrian, the city was burned and destroyed to its foundations, so that it even lost its former name.

Just as the hair on the head and beard is an indication of beauty and manliness, and when it is shaved an ugly nakedness appears, and as the outermost and, so to speak, dead part of the whole body is found in the hair, so Jerusalem and its people, dead and separated from the living body of God, are handed over to famine, pestilence, slaughter, the sword, captivity, and dispersion. Concerning this dispersion, a portion is bound in the figure of the hair at the edge of the cloak, so that a little is again handed over to the fire; from it an immeasurable flame, devastating almost everything, goes out against the whole house of Israel.

### (Verses 5 and following.)

“Thus says the Lord God: This is Jerusalem. I placed her in the midst of the nations, with lands around her; but she despised my judgments, so that she was more impious than the nations, and my ordinances more than the lands that surround her. For they rejected my judgments and did not walk in my ordinances.”

That Jerusalem was situated in the middle of the world, this same Prophet testifies here, showing that she is the navel of the earth. And the Psalmist, expressing the Lord’s birth, says: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm 48:12). Then, concerning his Passion: “He worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 73:12).

On the eastern side she is surrounded by the region called Asia; on the western side, by what is called Europe; on the south, by Libya and Africa; and on the north, by the Scythians, Armenia, Persia, and all the peoples of Pontus. She was therefore placed in the midst of the nations so that the God who was known in Judea, and whose name was great in Israel (Psalm 75), might have all the surrounding nations follow its example. But Jerusalem followed the impiety of the nations situated around her and even surpassed them in her crime.

Symmachus translated the passage elegantly: “This Jerusalem, whom I placed in the midst of the nations, with regions around her, changed my judgments into the impieties which she learned from the nations, and my ordinances into those of the regions around her; for they rejected my statutes and did not walk in my judgments.”

But what the Septuagint said—“My judgments unjustly from the nations, and my statutes from the regions which surround her”—plainly lacks coherence, even without my saying so.

### (Verses 8–9.)

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you surpassed the nations that surround you, and did not walk in my ordinances, did not perform my judgments, and did not act according to the judgments of the nations that surround you, therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I myself will execute judgments in your midst before the eyes of the nations. And I will do in you what I have not done, and what I will never again do, because of all your abominations.”

For what we translated as “Because you surpassed the nations that surround you,” Symmachus translated: “Because your multitude was from the nations that surround you.” Aquila’s second edition has: “Because you were counted among the nations that surround you.” The Septuagint, moreover, has: “Because your occasion came from the nations that surround you.”

The meaning is either that Jerusalem surpassed all the surrounding nations in her crimes, or that her multitude should be understood not as the people of Israel but as a crowd of other nations; or, certainly, that they were transformed into the number of the other nations surrounding her; or that they derived every occasion from the nations whom they ought rather to have taught in a good direction.

“What excuse,” he says, “can you give for not walking in my ordinances and not performing my judgments, when you have even surpassed all the surrounding nations in your crime, and have not done what they often did according to the natural law written on their hearts?”

Therefore it is not through angels or any ministers, but “I myself will execute my judgments in you,” with all looking on—judgments which I have never before executed and will never again execute. By saying “judgments,” he shows the truth of the sentence, so that the anger may not appear to exceed the measure of the punishments. He did not do in any nation things such as he did in Jerusalem: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:48). “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6:7). And he says: “I will never again do the like.”

He rightly said, “I will not do the like.” For long afterward, following the killing of Christ, he would do harsher things. It is one thing occasionally to have worshiped idols, for which they had previously been punished; it is another thing to have slaughtered the Son of God.

### (Verse 10.)

“Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst, and sons shall eat their fathers. And I will execute judgments in you, and I will scatter all your remnant to every wind.”

To what he had said above—“Because you surpassed the nations that surround you,” or “because your occasion came from the nations that surround you, you did not walk in my ordinances and did not perform my judgments”—he referred three times with the word “therefore.”

First: “Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I myself will execute judgments in your midst.”

Second: “Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst.”

Third: “Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, unless it is because you profaned my sanctuary in all your offenses,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, it must be noted that wherever the things are honorable and good, and suited to the merit of those who endure them, God declares that he himself does them. But where the things are grievous and unworthy of God, he says that they occur, but not by him, as here: “Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst, and sons shall eat their fathers.” For he did not say: “I will cause fathers to eat their sons in your midst, and sons to eat their fathers.”

But what was honorable and did not seem unworthy of God’s majesty, he says that he himself does. For it follows: “And I will execute judgments in you, and I will scatter all your remnant to every wind.”

We can find something similar in the curses of Deuteronomy, especially in the passage: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be brought to nothing” (Deuteronomy 28). He himself glorifies those who glorify him. But those who despise him will not be despised or brought to nothing by the Lord—for that would be the expected continuation—but simply “shall be brought to nothing”: not by God, but according to their merits and sins.

We read in the Book of Kings that, when famine compelled her, a mother devoured her son (2 Kings 6). Josephus likewise records many such events during the siege of Jerusalem. But when fathers ate sons, or sons fathers, no history reports it, unless perhaps we should believe that this too occurred amid the many evils of necessity.

This same passage can also be referred to our Jerusalem, when teachers rise up against pupils—that is, fathers against sons—and pupils against teachers, that is, sons against fathers, in mutual sedition, and what the Apostle says is fulfilled: “But if you bite and accuse one another, beware lest you be consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15).

Hence the Prophet also sang in mystical language: “When those who afflict me approached against me, to eat my flesh” (Psalm 26:2). Job says something similar: “If my maidservants said: ‘Who will grant us some of his flesh, that we may eat?’” (Job 31). And concerning teachers who pursue profit from their pupils and show no concern for their salvation, it is said: “They devour my people as though eating bread” (Psalm 52:5).

Concerning them the Apostle also says: “And they devour widows’ houses” (Luke 20; Matthew 23). [Note: Marianus corrects Erasmus’s edition and has “Gospel” in place of “Apostle”; but since the manuscript codices read this way, we leave Jerome’s text untouched. For the holy man may have meant Matthew, not Paul, by the word “Apostle.” MART.]

We may understand the fathers who ate sons and the sons who ate fathers not only in the Babylonian siege but also in the Roman siege. But what is said—“And I will scatter all your remnant to every wind”—belongs more particularly to the Roman captivity, when they were scattered throughout the whole world. This is the scattering of the hair and beard to every wind.

### (Verse 11.)

“Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, unless it is because you profaned my sanctuary in all your offenses and in all your abominations, I too will break you [or, according to the Septuagint, ‘cast you away’], and my eye will not spare, and I will not show pity.”

This is said specifically to Jerusalem: because you profaned my sanctuary by abandoning me and worshiping idols in my Temple, I too will break all your idols, crush and cut them down; or I will cast you away, because you first cast me away. My eye will not spare you when I see you submit your necks to famine, the sword, and slavery, nor will I show pity, because you do not deserve my mercy. For it is written: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7).

The same must also be understood of the Church: God may say daily to teachers and priests who act negligently: “Because you profaned my sanctuaries in all your offenses and in all the abominations which you committed, I too will crush and break you, and I will repay through you what you perpetrated against my people.”

This same Prophet speaks more fully against shepherds below (chapter 34): they clothe themselves with the wool of the sheep, feed on their milk and cheese, and do not seek the broken or diseased sheep.

### (Verses 12–13.)

“A third of you shall die by pestilence and shall be consumed by famine in your midst; and a third of you shall fall by the sword around you. But I will scatter a third of you to every wind, and I will unsheathe the sword after them. And I will fulfill [Vulgate: ‘complete’] my fury, and I will make my indignation rest upon them, and I will be comforted, and they shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken in my zeal, when I have fulfilled my indignation upon them.”

Since above the Septuagint had set out four parts, although the prophetic speech showed that there were only three in the description of the fire, sword, and dispersion, so that one part of the fire had been divided unnecessarily into two, in this passage too they divided that same first part into two, saying: “A fourth part of you shall be crushed by death, and a fourth part of you shall be consumed by famine in your midst, and a fourth part of you shall fall around you, and I will scatter a fourth part of you to every wind.” Although the words “And a fourth part of you shall fall by the sword” have been added from Theodotion’s edition under asterisks.

It is clear, however, that, as the Hebrew truth contains it, there are three parts. Of the first it is said: “A third of you shall die by pestilence and shall be consumed by famine in your midst.” It would have been much better to translate what was written than to seek a defense for something badly translated.

Nor do we say that this was done by those to whom antiquity has given authority, but that it was corrupted through the fault of scribes and readers over many centuries. Nevertheless, Aristeas [Note: Aristeas, evidently, says only that the Scriptures of the Law were read before the king. Josephus, in the Preface to the *Antiquities*, states most explicitly that only the Law was communicated to him: “For he did not even succeed in receiving the whole inscription, but those who had been sent to Alexandria to interpret it delivered to him only the Law.” Our author has similar remarks in chapter 2 of his commentary on Micah and elsewhere. Thus, whenever he seems to assert that the entire work of Scripture was translated by the Septuagint, he speaks not from his own judgment but according to common usage.]

Josephus and the entire school of the Jews assert that only the five books of Moses were translated by the Septuagint. Since we discussed this matter above, it seems that it should now be omitted.

I will add only what is necessary concerning the statement: “And I will fulfill my fury, and I will make my indignation rest upon them, and I will be comforted, and they shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken in my zeal, when I have fulfilled my indignation upon them.” We have often explained how the fury, indignation, and zeal of God are to be understood: God speaks in terms of human emotions—not because he himself becomes angry, but because through punishments and torments we perceive God as angry.

“Zeal” is understood metaphorically through the relationship of husband and wife: so long as a man loves his wife, he is jealous; but if he neglects her, he says what we shall mention below: “My zeal will depart from you, and I will no longer be angry with you” (below, 61:42).

And when it is added, “They shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken in my zeal,” this does not refer to those who were consumed by famine and pestilence, nor to those who fell by the sword around the city, but to those who will be scattered to every wind. Through the deaths of the others and through their own miseries, they will perceive the God who is angry, whom they refused to perceive as merciful.

### (Verse 14.)

“And I will make you a desert.” The following words—“and a reproach among the nations that surround you”—are not found in the Septuagint; instead they added on their own: “and your daughters around you.” Again, according to both editions, the phrase continues: “in the sight of everyone who passes by.”

It is beneficial for all vices in Jerusalem to be laid waste, for her to be reduced to a desert, and for her to recognize her sins, so that she who ought to have been an example of virtues to the other nations may become an example of miseries.

We can understand her “daughters” as cities or villages, or as the Churches scattered throughout the world, so that whoever is a sojourner in this world and says with the Psalmist, “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Psalm 38:12), and of whom it is said, “Those who passed by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Psalm 128:8), may see her reproach and grieve.

### (Verse 15.)

“And you shall be a reproach and a blasphemy, an example and an astonishment among the nations that surround you.”

For this the Septuagint reads: “And it shall be στενακτή,” that is, “worthy of groaning.” Theodotion adds καὶ δηλαϊστή [Note: Through an error the form was δηλαίστη, and Drusius did not correctly restore it as δειλαϊστή for δηλαϊστή. The better manuscripts of Jerome, both ours and those cited by Montfaucon, prefer δηλαϊστή. A little farther below we likewise write Δηλαϊστήν or δηλαίαν in place of the corrupt forms Δηλαίστην and δαλαίαν.]

We do not know the meaning of this word. The other three interpreters translated it as “blasphemy,” which in Hebrew is called GEDDUPHA [].

It follows:

“When I execute judgments upon you in fury, indignation, and rebukes of wrath, which I, the Lord, have spoken.” [Note: Victorius deletes the word “which” and reads, with a punctuation mark before “I, the Lord,” etc., on the basis of the Hebrew manuscript, the Vulgate, and the Greek.]

That Jerusalem is worthy of groaning when she offended God, so that he might execute judgments upon her in fury and indignation, Paul also testifies, saying: “We were by nature children of wrath, as also the rest” (Ephesians 2:3). And again: “We who are in this tabernacle groan, being weighed down” (2 Corinthians 5). We also speak with Jerusalem: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him.”

Some wish Δηλαϊστήν or δηλαίαν to be understood as “unfortunate” and “wretched”; others, as “conspicuous” and “exposed to miseries.”

### (Verse 16.)

“When I send upon them the evil arrows of famine [Vulgate adds: ‘against them’], which will be deadly, and which I will send to destroy you; and I will gather famine against you, and I will break the support [or staff] of bread.”

It is evident that famine, pestilence, the most savage beasts, and whatever other evils we suffer in this world come upon us on account of our sins. Hence the famine recorded in Ruth (Ruth 1), and in the Book of Kings under Elijah (1 Kings 17), when the heavens were shut for three years and six months, and under Elisha (2 Kings 6), whose incredible scarcity was offset by sudden abundance, was sent by God’s judgment.

This did not happen only then in Jerusalem; it also happens in our Jerusalem, where, because of the greatness of our sins, famine is first sent upon us—the famine of hearing the word of God. Then death follows famine, so that those who did not hear, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9), may afterward experience: “The death of sinners is most evil” (Psalm 22).

We have spoken above concerning the support and staff of bread (above, chapter 4).

### (Verse 17.)

“And I will send upon you famine and the most savage beasts, unto destruction; and pestilence and blood shall pass through you, and I will bring the sword against you. I, the Lord, have spoken.”

The present times themselves show that the most savage beasts are brought against a desolate land laid waste by famine, sword, and pestilence: domestic animals—dogs [variant: “a domestic animal, a dog”]—are driven madly against their masters’ flesh [variant: “is driven”], and the earth is filled with bears, wolves, and every other kind of beast. Pestilence and blood passing through it signify disease and the sword.

The most savage beasts are also sent against our Jerusalem when we are handed over to dishonorable passions, to a depraved mind, and to the consciousness of sins that torment and tear our soul apart (Romans 1). Dissensions, heresies, schisms, rivalries, envies, griefs, slanders, evil desires, and avarice—which is the root of all evils (2 Corinthians 12)—are the most savage beasts.
