When these are within us, we deserve to hear: “Your apostasy shall rebuke you” (Jeremiah). And we pray and say: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you” (Psalm 73:19).

## (Chapter 6—Verses 1 and following.)

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them. And say: Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord God. Thus says the Lord God to the mountains and hills, to the cliffs and valleys.”

Because this Prophet frequently says *Adonai Dominus*, it seems necessary to explain briefly, for Greeks and Latins who do not know the Hebrew language. *ADONAI* is one of the ten names of God, and it signifies “Lord”; we often use it also of human beings. Thus Sarah, calling Abraham her lord, used this name (Genesis 18). And where “My lord the king” is said, *Adonai* is written (Exodus 28).

When, therefore, the two names “Lord” and “Lord” are joined, the first name is common, while the second properly belongs to God. It is called ἄῤῥητον [], that is, “ineffable,” and it was also written on the golden plate that was on the forehead of the high priest.

The mountains of Israel, which had been occupied by images of demons, hear and understand their Creator not with ears but through the command and power of the Creator. Thus: “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back” (Psalm 113)—certainly not with bodily eyes, which it did not possess. And it is said to the sea: “Be silent; be muzzled” (Mark 4:39). Commands are also given to the blasts of the winds, and the worm that struck Jonah’s shelter is ordered (Jonah 4). Of the same earth it is written: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Psalm 103:32).

The Prophet speaks to these mountains, indicating that the idols and altars must be destroyed, and that all the rites by which they had previously served idols must be crushed.

We can also understand the mountains of Israel as those who excelled in power, wisdom, knowledge, and wealth. We should also observe that the face is made firm and set against the mountains; yet he speaks not only to the mountains but also to the hills, cliffs, and valleys, in which lesser dignity and lower degrees of prudence and knowledge are recognized.

It seems to me, tropologically, that the mountains are those who have attained perfect knowledge; the hills those who are somewhat inferior; the cliffs those who possess no knowledge and rely only upon their way of life, yet presume to themselves some interpretation of the Scriptures, having, according to the Apostle, zeal for God but not according to knowledge (Romans 10; James 3). The valleys, however, are the lowest members of the Church, inferior in both life and knowledge, yet they do not withdraw from the assembly of the Lord’s household [Note: In Rabanus: “they do not withdraw from the Lord’s assembly.”]

All these are commanded to hear the word of God, so that each may understand, according to his measure and capacity, what the Lord commands.

### (Verses 4–5.)

“Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places. I will demolish your altars, and your images shall be broken, and I will cast your slain before your idols. And I will place the corpses of the children of Israel before your images, and I will scatter your bones around your altars in all your dwelling places.”

It is said [variant: “he says”] to the mountains of Israel that God will destroy their high places, where people worshiped gods they had fashioned; that he will break their altars and images; and that he will cause their worshipers to be slain in the sight of their shrines, so that the corpses of the dead may lie where the sacrifices had previously lain. The bones—not of the mountains, but of those who lay upon the mountains—will be scattered around the altars and throughout all the cities and villages of Israel.

This is the literal sense. Otherwise, a sword is also brought against those who are lifted up in pride and of whom the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1), so that all their images, which they fashioned from their own minds, may be crushed. They will lie slain and recognize themselves as dead when they perceive that their images and fabrications benefit them nothing.

When he says that he will scatter the bones of the mountains around the altars, he indicates that the strongest among them are to be separated from one another. For it is beneficial that the wicked be divided from wicked knowledge.

Just as those who, in an evil agreement, were building a tower were dispersed for their own good and their languages were divided (Genesis 11), lest their very bad agreement make them worse, so the bones of the mountains will be scattered [variant: “may be scattered”], so that they may understand the futility of their efforts.

The words we included—“And I will place the corpses of the children of Israel before your images”—are not found in the Septuagint.

### (Verses 6–7.)

“The cities shall be deserted, and the high places shall be demolished; your altars shall be shattered and perish, your images shall be broken and cease, your shrines shall be crushed, and your works shall be wiped out. And the slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

The reason why the cities of the mountains must be deserted is clear: so that the high places may be demolished, the altars and images destroyed, the shrines perish, and all worship of images cease; so that the slain may fall in the midst of the mountains and they may know that he is the Lord.

These things give us an occasion to follow a more spiritual interpretation: the cities of the heretics, which are interpreted as Churches, together with their high places of pride and the altars of their perverse doctrines, must be broken; the idols must perish, which they had fashioned for themselves from their own hearts; and the shrines—not temples—which had risen up against the Temple of the Lord must be crushed. In Greek they are called τεμένη, that is, “sacred precincts” and “shrines.” All the works of the mountains must be crushed, since they are not works of God but of teachers of false knowledge.

When the slain have fallen in the midst of the mountains, whether those whom the mountains themselves killed, or ecclesiastical men who killed them in their sinful way of life for the sake of their salvation, then the end of the proud mountains will come, so that they may know that he is the Lord.

It may also happen that, from one people of the mountains of Israel, after some have been slain, others may come to know. For when the pestilent man is scourged, the foolish man becomes wiser (Proverbs 19:25).

### (Verse 8.)

“And I will leave among you those who escape the sword among the nations, when I scatter you among the lands; and your survivors shall remember me among the nations to which they were led captive.”

What the Lord says to Elijah—“I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal” (1 Kings 19:18)—and what the Apostle Paul writes—“At the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5)—may be applied to this chapter.

For the Apostles, who were of the seed of Israel and had escaped the sword, were preserved for this purpose: that they might be scattered among the lands [variant: “in the lands”], preach the Gospel among the nations, and remember God among the nations in which they lived during the time of captivity.

It may also be said that some were preserved from Jewish captivity for this reason: that they might remember his name among the nations and proclaim his power.

This can also be understood of the peoples of the heretics: those who were able to escape the sword of their destruction and the most wicked faction that had been aroused against God, scattered here and there, will remember the name of God. They will repent and rejoice that they had been taken captive by ecclesiastical men.

### (Verses 9–10.)

“Because I have broken their adulterous heart, which turned away from me, and their eyes, which adulterously pursued their idols. They shall be displeased with themselves because of the evils which they committed in all their abominations. And they shall know that I am the Lord; I did not speak in vain when I said that I would do this evil to them.”

Much is omitted from this passage by the Septuagint, and the wording is changed to: “I swore to their adulterous heart,” whereas we have: “I have broken their adulterous heart.”

He swore and decreed that he would do what he demonstrated in action; or he broke the adulterous heart that had turned away from God—of those concerning whom the Lord speaks through Hosea: “They were seduced by a spirit of prostitution” (Hosea 4:12).

He also broke their eyes, which adulterously pursued idols, through whose windows death is said to have entered. For this reason, in Daniel, the two elders ordered Susanna to be exposed, so that they might enjoy the beauty of her naked body (Daniel 13).

Nor did the Lord speak in vain when he said that he would do evil or evils, since those subject to the sentence repent at his threat. But if the heart is hard and untamed, and does not perceive—even through punishments—the benefits of the one correcting it, it is said to them: “In vain I struck your children; you did not accept discipline” (Jeremiah 2:30).

It is also beneficial for heretics that their heart be crushed—the evil storehouse of perverse doctrines—because it turned away from the Lord, and their eyes adulterously pursued their inventions. When they remember the Lord, they will be displeased with themselves for all their abominations, and, understanding the truth of the true faith, they will know that he is the Lord.

For this reason he often brings tribulation upon them, which appears harmful and most grievous to those who suffer it, so that they may be converted to repentance.

### (Verse 11)

Thus says the Lord God: “Strike your hand and stamp your foot, and say: Alas! because of all the wicked abominations of the house of Israel.”

The prophet is commanded to display the magnitude of their sins with hands, feet, and speech, so that by the gesture of his body and the indignation of his voice he may show the demeanor of one who is astonished, amazed, and weeping. For just as, whenever we see something new and astonishing, we shudder in body and spirit, so that we clap our hands, stamp our feet upon the ground, and incline our voice toward weeping, so now the prophet, perceiving with the eyes of his spirit the punishments that are to come, speaks against all the wicked abominations of the house of Israel in what follows.

We strike spiritually with the hand when we separate ourselves from evil works. We stamp the foot when we do not walk along the path of sinners. We mourn and weep when the things being done displease us. This is expressed by the word “Alas!” Aquila translated it as ἂ ἂ, “Alas, alas!”; Symmachus as σχετλίασον, which means “lament” or “mourn.” The Septuagint and Theodotion have εὖγε, “well done,” which is more the language of one taunting than of one mourning.

[Note: Two of the manuscripts that we use, as well as several Brixian manuscripts examined by Victorius, have inclinatione here instead of indignatione.]

#### Those who are about to fall by sword, famine, and pestilence

This, then, is the reason for mourning: the inhabitants of the mountains and the worshipers of altars and idols are about to fall by sword, famine, and pestilence. Those who are led astray by various errors, who change their faith every day and are carried about by every wind of doctrine—these are cut down by the sword and divided into parts, abandoning the unity of ecclesiastical faith.

But whoever has no spiritual food dies of famine, not knowing him who said, “I am life” (John XIV, 6). Moreover, whoever is devoted to one or several vices and cannot be separated from them falls as though by the lethargy of pestilence [another reading: “by a certain uterine pestilence”].

[Note: Earlier, “he will die.” Victor says that the context of the passage shows the word to have been properly emended, since the same tense is consistently maintained.]

### (Verse 12)

“He who is far away shall die of pestilence; but he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who has been left and surrounded [the Vulgate: ‘and besieged’] shall die of famine, and I shall fulfill [the Vulgate: ‘complete’] my indignation against them.”

Whoever escapes the siege of the city and flees to the deserts shall die of pestilence; whoever is nearby shall fall by the sword of the enemy. Whoever is surrounded by the hostile army shall perish from famine and want. In all these things God’s indignation will be fulfilled, so that those who remain may know that he is the Lord.

Whoever also withdraws from the Church will immediately die of pestilence. Whoever seems wise and careful in his own eyes, unless he takes heed, will be struck by the sword of the enemy. Whoever is content with a simple faith and, like brute animals, remains indeed in the Church but makes no progress in any good work, and is not an imitator of the ant, which prepares and gathers food for itself in the harvest—that person will die of famine. In all these things the wrath of the Lord will be fulfilled.

### (Verse 13)

“And you shall know that I am the Lord, when your slain are among your idols, all around your altars, upon the high hill [the Vulgate: ‘upon every hill’], upon all the summits of the mountains, and beneath every leafy tree and beneath every spreading oak—the place where they burned fragrant incense to all their idols.”

The literal meaning is clear and requires no interpretation: in the mountains of Israel and upon the lofty hills, among the very altars of the idols and the sacred groves—for such trees are called “wooded trees”—the army of Israel was slaughtered, so that they might be punished in the very place where they had sinned.

Let us follow the proposed order according to the allegorical sense. When the teachers of the heretics have been crushed and defeated by ecclesiastical men who are instructed in the knowledge of the Scriptures, we see the slain of perverse doctrines lying among the images that they had fashioned. Those who exalted themselves against the knowledge of God lie prostrate upon the mountains and hills beneath every wooded tree. They possessed pompous words and the shade of leaves, but had no fruits of good works. They were beneath every spreading oak, which produces not the fruit of human beings but of swine, where they burned fragrant incense—not to God, but to their idols.

Nor could they say what is written concerning Noah: “The Lord smelled an odor of sweet fragrance” (Genesis VIII, 21), nor what Paul says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place” (II Corinthians II, 15). Just as the holy person pleases God by his odor, so the sinner, of whom that psalm is sung, “My wounds have become foul and festering because of my foolishness” (Psalm XXXVII, 6), burns foul-smelling incense to his idols.

What we have translated as “upon all the summits of the mountains” and, shortly afterward, “beneath every spreading oak,” the Septuagint omitted.

### (Verse 14)

“And I shall stretch out my hand over them, and I shall make the land desolate and deserted, from the wilderness of Deblatha, in all their dwelling places; and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

O mountains of Israel, when your slain have fallen among your altars and idols upon every high hill, upon all the summits of the mountains; when I have filled your sacred groves with the corpses of the dead, in which they once burned fragrant incense to their idols—then I shall stretch out my hand for vengeance, a hand that until now had been restrained, and I shall reduce the entire land of Israel to solitude, from the wilderness of Deblatha, which is in the land of Hamath and is today called Epiphania of Syria, throughout all their dwelling places. Thus it may be evident to all that between the desert and the Great Sea there is nothing that the enemy’s sword has not consumed.

Many think this is the same place of which it is written in Jeremiah: “They captured Zedekiah in the wilderness that is near Jericho, and all his company fled from him. When they had seized the king, they brought him to the king of Babylon at Reblatha, which is in the land of Hamath” (Jeremiah XXXIX, 5). Because of the similarity of the letters DALETH and RES in Hebrew, which are distinguished by only a small stroke, the place may be called either Deblatha or Reblatha.

According to the mystical interpretations, the Lord stretches out his hand over all who have been deceived by heretical error, so that he may make their land—which is interpreted as the Church—desolate, from the wilderness of Deblatha. In our language this name sounds like παλάθη, that is, “a mass of figs,” or dried figs pressed together. After they have encountered bitterness in a feigned sweetness—which was not that of cultivated soil but of the wilderness—then they will know that he is the Lord.

“For honey drips from the lips of the adulterous woman,” who for a time fattens the throats of those who eat, but afterward is found more bitter than gall (Proverbs V, 3–4). The same thing is signified by the two baskets of figs set before the face of the temple in Jeremiah (Jeremiah XXIV): one basket of very good figs and one of very bad figs. The former refers to the Church of Christ, the latter to the assembly of the wicked.

## Chapter VII

### (Verses 1–2)

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, thus says the Lord God of the land of Israel: The end—the end has come upon the four extremities of the land.”

[Note: Victorius reads, “The end has come, the end has come”; the word “has come” derives from the Vulgate edition and repeats the Hebrew.]

We have interpreted these as the four regions of the world: east and west, south and north. Isaiah also speaks of these extremities: “Lord, from the extremities, or ends, of the earth we have heard portents” (Isaiah XXIV, 16), those things that were accomplished throughout the whole world through the apostles.

Concerning the saints it is written: “If you sleep among the central divisions, the feathers of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of its back are in the pale gleam of gold” (Psalm LXVII, 14). Therefore, when the Lord drew near and saw Jerusalem, he wept and said: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matthew XXIII, 37). He is the one who, in the song of Deuteronomy, spread out his wings, received them, and carried them upon his shoulders (Deuteronomy XXXII).

One interprets the spiritual wings of the earth, by which we fly upward to heavenly things, as four classes of believers: the house of Aaron, the house of Levi, the house of Israel, and those who fear the Lord. Concerning them the Psalmist also sings: “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord” (Psalm CXXXIV, 19–21). In Aaron he understands the priesthood; in Levi, the doorkeepers and ministers; in Israel, the whole people; and in those who fear the Lord, proselytes.

We, however, think that the passage should be explained simply: after the threat against the mountains of Israel, the prophetic word is directed toward the whole land of Israel, whether the ten or the twelve tribes. The prophet is not announcing events still to come, but sees the captivity already descending upon them. For Ezekiel began to prophesy to the captives in Babylon in the fifth year of Zedekiah; in the ninth year Nebuchadnezzar came and besieged Jerusalem, and captured it in the eleventh year of Zedekiah.

From this it is clear that the end had come and was near—not upon the mountains, hills, crags, and valleys, but upon the four regions of the land, on every side of Israel; not “of the whole earth,” for had he said that, it could have been understood of the entire world, but simply “of the land,” which signifies Israel. Thus he had begun: “Thus says the Lord God of the land of Israel: The end—the end has come upon the four regions of the land.”

### (Verses 3–4)

“Now the end is upon you, and I shall send forth my fury against you, and I shall judge you according to your ways, and I shall set all your abominations against you. And my eye shall not spare you, and I shall not have pity; but I shall set your ways against you, and your abominations shall be in your midst; and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

In this chapter, according to the Septuagint interpreters, the order has been changed and confused, so that what comes first is last, and what comes last is either first or middle; the middle itself is transferred now to the end, now to the beginning. Therefore we have followed the Hebrew and the other translators and set out the order according to the truth.

The word, then, is directed to the land of Israel: the end and consummation have come upon it, and the Lord sends forth his fury against it—not an unjust fury arising merely from indignation, but one full of equity and reason—so that he may judge it according to its ways and show it all its abominations. Thus it may remember its deeds and understand what evil [another reading: “what evil things”] it has done.

When he says, “My eye shall not spare you, and I shall not have pity,” he speaks like the most compassionate physician who wishes to cut away putrid flesh and burn decayed wounds with a cautery. He does not spare in order to spare; he does not show pity in order to show greater pity, lest anything putrid remain in the body and corrupt the living flesh by its proximity. “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews XII, 6). To this understanding belongs the statement: “I wound, and I heal” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 39). Every medicine is bitter for a time, but afterward the fruit of the pain is revealed in health.

God says something similar through Amos: “Because I have known you from all the tribes of the earth, therefore I shall punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos III, 2). “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Timothy II, 19). And, he says, I shall set his ways [another reading: “his going forth”]—the course of his entire life—and his abominations and stains in his midst, so that the former sins may be placed before the eyes of the sinful woman who is being punished for her healing.

When the Lord has done this, those who have been afflicted will know that he is the Lord. The same is expressed by the testimony: “I shall punish Jacob according to his ways, and according to his inventions I shall repay him” (Hosea XII, 2).

### (Verses 5–6)

“Thus says the Lord God: One affliction—behold, an affliction comes; the end has come, the end has come. It has awakened against you; behold, it comes. Contraction [the Vulgate: ‘crushing’] has come upon you, inhabitant of the land.”

These words are not found in the Septuagint, but in their edition they have been added from the translation of Theodotion under asterisks. We shall follow the Hebrew.

Instead of “affliction,” which we have placed for clarity according to Symmachus, who translated it as κάκωσις, the Hebrew and the Greek have κακία or πονηρία—that is, “evil” or “wickedness.” It is said that the final period of the sins of the land of Israel has arrived, so that it may no longer escape the sentence of God, which it had long deserved. Because it had not yet completed its sins, the punishment was postponed, according to what is written: “For the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis XV, 16). Therefore the Lord also says to the Jews: “And you—fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matthew XXIII, 32).

Misery, then, has come upon you; affliction has come, and captivity has come. And lest you think that I am again threatening things still to come, I point them out and demonstrate them with my finger: “Behold, it comes; the end has come; the end has come.” What had seemed until now to slumber and rest has suddenly awakened against you and risen up.

“Contraction” is called SEPHPHIRA in Hebrew. Aquila translated it as προσκόπησιν, that is, “contemplation” or “watchful inspection”—the thing whose coming you had always feared in your anxiety. Theodotion translated it as πλοκὴν, that is, “the interweaving” or “connected sequence” of all evils.

As for the words “upon you who dwell in the land,” we should understand them according to the statement in the Apocalypse of John: “Woe to all who dwell upon the earth” (Apocalypse VIII, 13). The holy person is not an inhabitant of the earth but a resident alien and pilgrim; he says: “I am a resident alien and a sojourner, like all my fathers” (Psalm XXXVIII, 13). For this reason Abraham the Hebrew is also remembered as περάτης, “one who crosses over,” and as a pilgrim, hastening to pass from the present age to the future.

We can also interpret this passage spiritually against the Jewish people, upon whom the end and consummation came—from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar (Matthew XXIII). As long as they had not laid hands upon the Son of God, the Lord’s sentence against them seemed to slumber and was delayed. But when they killed the heir so that the inheritance might perish, then it awakened against them and rose up: the whole order and confusion of miseries came upon them, because they did not seek heavenly things but desired to cling to earthly ones.

### (Verse 7)

“The time has come; the day of slaughter is near, and not the glory of the mountains.”

The Hebrew word ADARIM, which we divided into two words—first AD, second ARIM—we interpreted according to Theodotion as “the glory of the mountains.” Symmachus translated it as “delay,” saying: “The time is near; the day of haste, and not of delay.” The Septuagint translated it: “The time has come, the day has drawn near—not with disturbance nor with pains.” Theodotion has: “The time has come; the day of famine is near, and not the glory of the mountains.”

The time of slaughter and famine is even now verified among the Jewish people, since they have neither prophets nor the word of God by which the souls of believers are nourished. Understand the mountains as teachers and as those who possess knowledge of the Scriptures. Concerning them it is said elsewhere: “You shine wonderfully from the everlasting mountains” (Psalm LXXV, 5).

The Septuagint, by saying “not with disturbance and not with pains,” signifies that they possess such ignorance of God and blindness of spirit that they are neither disturbed by their crimes nor tormented by the pains of repentance.

### (Verse 8)

“Now I shall pour out my wrath upon you shortly, and I shall complete [another reading: ‘repeat’] my fury against you, and I shall judge you according to your ways. And I shall impose upon you—or give you—all your abominations.”

[Note: From the exposition of Jerome that follows, where he says, “and now I shall complete my fury in you,” Victorius thinks that complebo should be read instead of replicabo, especially since Jerome’s Vulgate edition has the same reading and both the Hebrew text and the Greek συντελέσω agree with it.]

If we count from the fifth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin to the ninth year of the reign of Zedekiah, when Nebuchadnezzar came and besieged Jerusalem, there are three years in between. Hence it is rightly said: “Now I shall pour out my wrath upon you shortly.” I shall no longer announce to you things that are to come, nor threaten what will happen far off; now I shall complete my fury against you.

This fury and wrath are not without judgment, but are intended to return your ways upon your own head and make you feel all your abominations.

We can also speak of the final captivity: after the killing of Christ, when the end came upon them and sin awakened against them, what is written was fulfilled: “The wrath of God has come upon them to the end” (I Thessalonians II, 16). When Jerusalem was surrounded by Titus and Vespasian and its desolation came, the saying was fulfilled: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matthew XXIII, 38). Then they were judged according to their ways and the blasphemies by which they denied the Lord; they felt the fury of God, and all his indignation was poured out upon them. They received their crimes, so that the destruction of the temple might remain until the consummation.

### (Verse 9)

“My eye shall not spare, nor shall I have pity; but I shall impose upon you—or give you—your ways, and your abominations shall be in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord who strikes.”

He explains the reasons for God’s severity and harshness—or, as the heretics think, his cruelty—in saying that his eye does not spare and that he does not have pity: “I shall give you your ways, and your abominations shall be in your midst.” Thus you may feel what you have done, and, seeing your abominations either before your eyes or placed in the midst of all, may correct your error through repentance. When you withdraw from your former deeds and hate what you have done, then you will feel that he is the Lord (Hebrews XII), who strikes in order to correct and chastises every son whom he receives.

### (Verses 10–11)

“Behold the day, behold it comes; contraction has gone forth: the rod has blossomed, pride has budded.

[Note: This reading is to be retained: both the following exposition and the Hebrew, which means “circle,” support it. Jerome’s edition, however, reads “crushing.”] Iniquity has risen up upon the rod of impiety, not from them, and not from the people, nor from their clamor; and there shall be no rest for them.”

The Septuagint has: “Behold, the day gives birth; behold, the end has come; the complex has gone forth; the rod has blossomed, pride has budded, outrage has been raised up, and it shall crush the strength of the wicked, and not with disturbance nor with haste; they are not from themselves, nor is there beauty in them.”

The day, he says, has been contracted and shortened, and captivity is close at hand. The rod that had threatened you for a long time has blossomed, and from its blossom it has produced the fruit of blows [another reading: “is producing”]. Your pride has produced what you deserved, so that upon the rod of your impiety—the rod with which you wickedly struck those subjected to you—iniquity may arise.

This iniquity is not from the pitiable people, nor from those who, like brute animals, are led by their teachers, nor from their cry and clamor, with which they shouted in vain after being deceived by the priests and Pharisees, so that they might cry out with one voice and say: “Crucify, crucify such a one!” (John XIX, 6). Therefore there shall be no rest for them, but eternal captivity.

The Septuagint, according to the sense in which it is written, “You do not know what a day may bring forth” (Proverbs XXVII, 1), said: “Behold, the day gives birth”—that is, it brings forth what it conceived long before. The end has come, and the complex has gone forth, embracing and holding all your evils, or, as Symmachus translated it, “inspection,” so that God sees all the things you have done, considers your works, and repays each according to what he deserves.

In the fact that they likewise translated “the rod has blossomed,” we can use the testimony: “Do not take the rod away from your son” (Proverbs XIII, 13), and the Apostle’s words: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Corinthians IV, 21). God also speaks through the mouth of the Psalmist: “I shall visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but I shall not take my mercy away from them” [another reading: “I shall not scatter it from them”] (Psalm LXXXVIII, 33–34).

Therefore the Lord visits and strikes so that all the pride that had long been hidden and enclosed may arise and become manifest; so that outrage may be raised against the pride that has arisen and budded; and so that the strength of the wicked may be crushed—not with disturbance nor with haste. For the end of the blossoming rod is health and correction, which comes neither through the merit of those being corrected nor through any beauty that they possess, but through the mercy of the Lord.

This is a difficult passage, with considerable disagreement between the Hebrew and the Septuagint; much of what appears in the latter has been added from the edition of Theodotion so that it might have some coherence.

[Note: Our manuscripts, as well as the four manuscripts cited by Victorius, have this reading. Martianay, following Erasmus, has “because.”]

[Note: In the recension of Rabanus and in one Vatican manuscript, “that he may die” is found; some overly clever person inserted this on his own.]

### (Verse 12)

“The time has come; the day has drawn near.”

This is said not only concerning Jerusalem, that the time of its captivity has come and the day has drawn near on which it is to be surrounded by the Babylonian army. The Lord also speaks to the man who was rejoicing after constructing and enlarging his storehouses: “Fool, this night your soul shall be demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XI, 20).

Therefore the Apostle also says: “The time has been shortened” (I Corinthians VII, 29), and elsewhere: “For the form of this world is passing away” (ibid., 31).

[Note: In other books, with which Rabanus substantially agrees, the reading is: “But if all these things, which are in the world, continually pass away,” and so forth.]

It should be noted that he did not defer this to the future, but spoke of the present: “It is passing away.” The form of the world slips away and changes every day. It never remains in the same condition, but the form of things that grow and decline is always flying past and being transformed. Therefore the Lord also says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matthew XXIV, 35).

But if these things, which contain everything that exists in the world, pass away and disappear, what can be permanent in human affairs?

[Note: Since these testimonies are joined together, Victorius rewrote “in the same passage” for “elsewhere.” A similar procedure is adopted slightly below.]

### (Verse 13)

“Let the buyer not rejoice, and let the seller not mourn.”

It is natural to rejoice in the purchase of possessions and to mourn in their sale. But when slavery and captivity are imminent, both joy and sorrow in either case are vain. Therefore the Apostle says: “The time has been shortened; henceforth let those who have wives be as though they had none, and those who weep as though they did not weep, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, and those who buy as though they did not possess, and those who use this world as though they did not use it” (I Corinthians VII, 29–31).

The flood also overwhelmed those who were buying and selling, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Matthew XXIV).

#### Because wrath is upon all his people

This is not found in the Septuagint. Instead of “people,” one may understand “multitude” or “crowd” according to the Hebrew, for this is what AMONA signifies ().

The reason is evident: the buyer ought not to rejoice and the seller ought to cease mourning because God’s wrath is soon to come upon the entire multitude of the land of Judea, or of Jerusalem. This is understood from what precedes, where it is written: “Thus says the Lord God of the land of Israel,” and so forth.

### (Verse 13)

“Because he who sells shall not return to what he sold.”

He speaks according to Hebrew custom. Every purchase reverted to the seller in the fiftieth year of remission, which among them is called the jubilee. Before the year of remission arrives, when possessions return to their former owners, captivity will descend and remove every customary practice of the city.

As for what the Septuagint translated, “Because he who buys shall not return to the seller,” although it does not agree at all with the historical sense, it can have this meaning according to the allegorical interpretation: the person who had been deceived by heretical error, once he understands the fraud of his teacher, will by no means return to the seller—that is, to the teacher—but will despise and reject him.

### (Verse 13 continued)

“And while their life is still among the living, their vision shall not return to all its multitude.”

Just as possession does not return to its former owner when the overthrow of the city is imminent, so the prophetic vision and threat directed against the entire multitude of the city shall not return or prove vain, but shall be fulfilled in events while those to whom the prophetic word is addressed are still alive.

He says this to show that captivity is imminent, lest they say according to their custom: “This vision concerns distant days, and it will be fulfilled after a long time.”

We can also say that after prophetic vision departed from the Jews—for “the Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist” (Matthew XI, 13)—it did not return to them after the Savior’s killing, nor did they thereafter deserve to have prophets. Significantly he says, “The vision shall not return to all the multitude.” Therefore it will return to those among the Jews who believed in the Lord: namely, the apostles and the remnant of the Jewish people that was saved from Israel.

These two verses, however, are also not found in the Septuagint edition.

### (Verse 13 continued)

“And a man shall not be strengthened in the iniquity of his life.”

The Septuagint has: “And a man shall not prevail in the eyes of his life.”

According to the Hebrew, the sense is: A man’s iniquity will not profit him, nor will it provide him with any strength. According to the Septuagint: A man who desired what he thought precious in the world will not obtain it; but as freedom perishes, everything beautiful will be lost.

The ambiguity of the Hebrew letters IOD and VAU, which differ only in size, caused some translators to render the word as “iniquity” and others as “eyes.”

[Note: From the more correct manuscripts of Victorius, we have restored qui in place of quod.]

### (Verse 14)

“Blow the trumpet; let all prepare.”

The Septuagint has: “Sound the trumpet, and judge all things.”

We read in many places about the blast and sound of trumpets, as in: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah LVIII, 1); and elsewhere: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of our festival” (Psalm LXXX, 3); and in the Apostle: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (I Thessalonians IV, 16). In the Gospel also: “Do not sound a trumpet before you” (Matthew VI, 2).

The history in Numbers likewise speaks of hammered and silver trumpets (Numbers X and XXXI), which are compared with prophetic speech and apostolic teaching. The command is now given that all should prepare themselves at the signal of the blast and trumpet for battle.

As for what the Septuagint said, “and judge all things,” there can be no doubt that this belongs to the authority of the apostles. After the angels’ trumpet has sounded, they will judge the twelve tribes of Israel upon twelve thrones. Paul says concerning them: “We shall judge angels” (I Corinthians VI, 3), and elsewhere: “The world shall be judged among you” (ibid., 2).

According to the present sense, however, those who have been assigned to this duty are commanded ironically to sound the trumpet, so that all may prepare themselves against the Babylonian army.

[Note: Other printed editions, except that of Victorius, whom we follow, prefer vestrae to the reading given here.]

#### And there is no one who goes to battle

“For my wrath is upon all his multitude.”

These words are also not found in the Septuagint.

[Note: In Jerome’s Vulgate edition: “upon his entire people”; in the Hebrew, , which properly signifies crowds and a multitude of nations.]

God had commanded (Numbers X) that they sound the trumpet to prepare the army, which might resist the strength of the Babylonians. But it was useless to give the command when there was no one among the people who dared to go forth to war.

The people were therefore weakened and lacked the strength to fight because all God’s wrath was upon their entire multitude—that is, upon the city of Jerusalem or the land of Judea.

The same occurs in our land and Jerusalem when either public persecution or the incitements of various vices strive to overcome us. The teachers sound the trumpet in vain and hasten to prepare us for battle when the people possess no strength. That strength has been taken away because their present sins have deserved the wrath of God.

### (Verses 15–16)

“The sword is outside; pestilence and famine are within. He who is in the field shall die by the sword, and those who are in the city shall be devoured by pestilence and famine. And those who flee from them shall be saved; they shall be upon the mountains like all the frightened doves of the valleys, each one in his iniquity.”

The Septuagint entirely omitted “doves of the valleys,” or, as Theodotion translated it, “those who meditate.”

What we translated as “all the frightened ones, each in his iniquity,” Theodotion rendered: “all murmuring, each one in his iniquity.” Under the metaphor of meditating doves, this signifies that each person among the people mourns his own sin and understands and feels why he is suffering these things.

We read above about three groups: those who die in the city from pestilence and famine; those whom the sword kills outside; and those who escape captivity by flight. Of the last group, whoever is saved will pass to the mountains and, like murmuring doves, will mourn his sins in fear.

Tropologically, the passage should be understood as follows: whoever is in the field or countryside, outside the boundaries of the Lord’s city—which is interpreted as the Church—is struck by the sword of the adversary. Whoever behaves carelessly in the city and does not prepare food for himself, concerning which it is written in Proverbs, “He who works his land shall be filled [another reading: ‘satisfied’] with bread” (Proverbs XII, 11), will die of famine and pestilence.

But the few who escape either the sword of the heretics or the famine and death of their own sloth will not be saved unless they are upon the mountains, unless they take up the wings of a dove, fly away, and find rest.

As long as these doves are in the valleys, they tremble and fear every single thing. We are commanded to imitate their innocence. Concerning them it is written in the psalm: “If you sleep among the central divisions, the feathers of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of its back are in the pale gleam of gold” (Psalm LXVII, 14). In the form of this dove the Holy Spirit descended and remained upon the Lord Savior.

Beautifully, according to Theodotion, we may call “the meditating dove” the person who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, concerning whom it is written: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom” (Psalm XXXVI, 30).

### (Verse 17)

“All hands shall be weakened, and all knees shall flow with water. They shall gird themselves with sackcloth, and dread shall cover them.”

Instead of “knees shall flow with water,” the Septuagint translated: “The thighs shall be defiled with moisture.”

When all have trembled and fled to the mountains, everyone’s hands shall be weakened, and no one will be able to resist the enemy. Because of the magnitude of their fear, urine will soil their knees, nor will the bladder be able to restrain the flowing water. They shall gird themselves with sackcloth, and trembling shall possess everything.

This happened to that people not only under the Babylonians but also under the Romans, when the wrath of God reached them to the end.

Moreover, in our Judea, in which the Lord is confessed, when iniquities have multiplied and the charity of many has grown cold, all the hands of good works will be weakened. All the knees—or thighs—of those who sought illicit intercourse will flow with their fluids. Scripture calls such people γονοῤῥύεις, that is, “those suffering from a flux of semen,” and counts them unclean.

Therefore those who are such ought to gird themselves with the sackcloth of repentance and fear the judgment that is to come. Whoever does this will deserve to hear Isaiah say: “Strengthen the weakened hands, and make firm the feeble knees” (Isaiah XXXV, 3).

### (Verse 18)

“On every face there will be confusion, and on all heads baldness.” [Note: In Rabanus: “the chief points,” he says, in the *Summa*.]

The reddening of the face is an indication of shame, and consciousness of sins shines forth in the face; and there is hope of salvation when guilt is followed by shame. Hence it was said to her who gloried in her sins with a hard heart: “You have the face of a harlot; you do not know how to blush” (Jer. 3:3).

Baldness of the head also is a sign of mourning, when we lose the beauty of our hair and forfeit the loveliness of our locks. Finally, it is said even to Jerusalem: “Instead of the adornment of your head you shall have baldness, because of your deeds” (Isa. 3:17). And another prophet says: “Every head shall be shaved in every place, and every beard shall be cut off” (Jer. 48:37). Micah also says to the same Jerusalem: “Make yourself bald and shave yourself for the children of your delights; enlarge your baldness like an eagle” (Mic. 1:16).

And baldness is commanded to be made over the dead. Only the saints, that is, the Nazirites, and those who have been worthy to attain to the priesthood of the Lord, do not shave their heads (Num. 6). For they do not have the works of death, nor are they unclean, because they are Nazirites, that is, holy ones of the Lord. But if someone should die among them, all the preceding days will not be counted as part of their consecration.

Samuel was holy to God, and therefore he possessed an everlasting adornment of the head; he also heard the words from the Song of Songs: “Your locks are black like a raven” (Song 5:11). Samson, however, because he lost his hair, lost his strength (Judg. 16); and as his hair gradually grew back, his former strength returned, so that at his death he killed many more than he had killed during his life.

Elisha, although he had baldness of the body, nevertheless, because he was a Nazirite of the Lord, enjoyed the locks of his head. Therefore the little boys [alt. “young men”], because they were little boys and had not yet reached manhood, mocked his baldness, saying: “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!” (2 Kings 2:23), and they were torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, whose haunts are thickets and forests.

### (Verse 19)

“Their silver shall be thrown outside, and their gold shall be treated as refuse.”

The Septuagint: “Their silver shall be thrown into the streets, and their gold shall be held in contempt.”

Driven by flight and captivity, they will throw their wealth and the weight of their gold and silver into the streets, wishing only to preserve their lives, so that what had previously been an object of luxury will not become a burden. Otherwise, according to the allegorical sense, all the silver of those being captured and fleeing from Jerusalem will be thrown into the streets, upon the broad and spacious road that leads to death, because they abandoned the narrow path of salvation. And all the gold will be held in contempt, or reckoned as refuse and uncleanness. For no one outside the Church of the Lord can possess purity.

[Col. 0071D] “Their silver and their gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath.”

This is not found in the Septuagint. Yet there is no doubt that, in a time of siege and famine, gold and silver will not deliver the starving; and when their teeth are struck against the most precious metal, they will be blunted like teeth against an exceedingly hard stone. Finally, it follows:

“They will not satisfy their souls, and their bellies will not be filled.”

From present misfortunes we have learned that many wealthy people, surrounded by silk, jewels, and quantities of gold and silver, have been worn down by poverty and ended their lives as beggars.

But that the silver and gold of those who are outside the Church do not deliver the souls of their possessors [Col. 0072A] on the day of the Lord’s wrath, but that they suffer eternal hunger and are tormented with an empty belly, is shown by that testimony in which it is said: “A man’s wealth is the ransom of his life” (Prov. 13:8). The wealth in question is that which the truth of Christ has taught us [to regard as truly our own] (Luke 16): he commanded us to make friends for ourselves from unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive us into eternal dwellings.

“Because their gold was made an occasion of their iniquity.”

Therefore, he says, the souls of those who possess gold and silver will not be satisfied, nor will their bellies be filled, because this very gold and silver became an occasion of their crimes. He is referring to idols, which, fashioned from gold and silver, condemn [alt. “despise”] their craftsmen. For this the Septuagint translated: “because the punishment of their iniquities was,” so that in their unrighteous error they might be tormented and understand that they had wickedly turned God’s gifts into blasphemy.

### (Verse 20)

“And they made the ornament of their jewelry into pride, and from it they made images of their abominations and their idols.”

The Septuagint: “They set the chosen things of the world in pride, and from them they made images of their abominations and their stumbling-blocks.”

What I had given, he says, as adornment to those who possessed wealth, they turned into pride, so that from the very things by which they could have freed their souls through almsgiving and good works, they obtained material for arrogance. Finally, from gold and silver they made idols, turning my gifts into images of demons.

Moreover, what the Septuagint says, “They set the chosen things of the world in pride,” must be referred to gold and silver, than which nothing in the world is thought to be more precious. And the phrase that follows, “their stumbling-blocks,” should be understood as having been added from Theodotion.

According to the tropological sense, the meaning is readily understood: gold and silver—the understandings and utterances of the Scriptures, which are the chosen things of the world and were given to us as an adornment—the heretics have made into fuel and material for pride. From them they have fashioned images of their various doctrines, abominations, and stumbling-blocks, so that by the very things through which they could have worshiped and adored God, they have offended God.

### (Verse 21)

“Therefore I gave it to them for uncleanness; and I will give it into the hands of strangers for plunder, and to the wicked of the earth as spoil, and they will defile it.”

The Septuagint: “Therefore I gave them over to uncleanness; and I will deliver them into the hands of strangers, that they may plunder them, and to the pestilent ones of the earth as spoil, and they will pollute them.”

Because they made images of their abominations and idols for themselves from the gold and silver and the ornaments of jewelry that I had given them, therefore I gave these things to them for uncleanness and filth. In place of these words Symmachus interpreted “nausea,” wishing to express the foulness of the idols.

“And I will deliver them,” he says, “into the hands of enemies, that they may plunder everything.” I will not so much make them defiled as show that they have been defiled—things that previously appeared to be most holy.

We too are delivered into the hands of enemies and of those alienated from God [Col. 0073A] when we make our ornaments into images of demons, and all our glory is possessed by the impious, or by the pestilent ones of the earth, so that they may subject us to their power.

### (Verse 22)

“And I will turn my face away from them; and they will profane my secret place; and emissaries will enter into it”—or, as the Septuagint translated, “rashly”; or, as Symmachus and Theodotion have it, “bursting in,” and “pestilent”—“and they will defile it.”

When, he says, on account of the preceding causes—the abominations of the people—I turn my face away from them and judge them no longer worthy of my sight, then they will profane my secret place, which signifies the Holy of Holies. For this the Septuagint translated “visitation,” to show that the presence of God had been in the holy places. Then the impious and pestilent ones of the earth will burst into it, although no one except the priests and the high priest alone dared to enter there.

We know that this was done by the Babylonians, by King Antiochus, by Gnaeus Pompey, and finally under Vespasian and Titus, when the Temple was captured and destroyed, and everything was perpetrated that the prophet’s following discourse embraces.

[Note: Victorius could readily be agreed with when he emends by conjecture, reading “because of our” instead of “against our.” But the manuscripts do not support it.]

God also turns his face away from our evil works; and because his face has been turned away, God’s secret place is therefore profaned, so that, in place of priests and saints of God, pestilent men enter and contaminate everything. Thus the place that ought to have been a place of holiness becomes a place of uncleanness, according to the Gospel saying: “My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. 21:13).

### (Verse 23)

“Make a conclusion, because the land is full of judgment of bloodshed, and the city is full of iniquity.”

The Septuagint: “And I will bring disturbance, because the land is full of judgment of bloodshed, and the city is full of iniquities.”

The Hebrew word **ARETHIC** [Hebrew omitted in the supplied text], Aquila translated as “conclusion”; Symmachus and Theodotion translated it as **καθήλωσιν**, that is, “crucifixion” or “fixing in place.” In its place the Septuagint put **φυρμόν**, which we translate as “disturbance.”

Therefore, O prophet, sum up my wrath against the land of Judea and against the city of Jerusalem in a brief statement, so that, just as the land is full of the judgment of bloodshed—for all are judged in blood, since they shed innocent blood, as Scripture records that the Jews did in the case of Naboth [1 Kings 21]—so their own blood may also be shed, and the city may be shown to be full of iniquity.

For under Manasseh also the city of Jerusalem was filled with the blood of the prophets, from gate to gate (2 Kings 21). A conclusion, disturbance, and fixing in place will come upon them, so that no one will be able to escape the impending miseries.

### (Verse 24)

“And I will bring the worst of the nations, and they will possess their houses.”

This too is not found in the Septuagint.

In place of priests and prophets I will bring the worst of all the nations—the Babylonians—so that they may possess your houses and subject you to slavery. But they will also possess our houses, that is, our souls—for we are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in us (1 Cor. 6)—if our land is full of bloodshed and our dwelling full of iniquity.

“And I will cause the pride of the mighty to cease, and they will possess their sanctuaries.”

The Septuagint: “And I will turn away the tumult of their strength, and their holy things will be polluted.”

All pride offends God. Therefore the worst of the nations will possess the houses of the mighty and the proud, and they will seize their sanctuaries, because an unclean person enters a place of holiness and contaminates it with his uncleanness.

Significantly, because God’s sanctuaries had been polluted and his secret place profaned, he did not say, “They will possess my sanctuaries,” but “their sanctuaries,” because after the contamination they ceased to be mine.

“Distress is at hand.”

The Septuagint: “Propitiation will come.”

In accordance with the preceding order, Aquila and Theodotion correctly translated “distress is at hand,” and Symmachus likewise has “sorrow.” But the Septuagint, in the midst of all the grievous things, inserted a word of joy, so that the mourning spirit might be sustained and hope for better things amid adversity, and hope for a merciful Lord, of whom it is written: “The Lord raises up those who are bowed down” (Ps. 145:8).

We, however, following Symmachus, joined the earlier statement to the later one, so as to say:

### (Verse 25)

“When distress comes upon them, they will seek peace, and there will be none.”

According to the Septuagint this cannot stand at all. For if propitiation will come, how will they seek peace and not find it? But the one who heard from the apostles, “Peace to this house” (Matt. 10:12), and did not preserve it or make it rest in his mind, but drove it away through evil works, will seek peace and not find it.

This is the peace that surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4:7), and which the Savior, ascending victoriously to the Father, left to the apostles (John 14).

### (Verse 26)

“Disturbance will come upon disturbance, and report upon report.”

The Septuagint: “Woe will be upon woe, and messenger upon messenger.”

Just as it is said to the saints, “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4), and it is written of them, “They go from strength to strength” (Ps. 84:7), so that present blessings may be heaped upon future blessings, so upon those over whom distress has come, and who sought peace and did not find it, disturbance will come upon disturbance—or woe upon woe, according to what is also written in the Apocalypse: “One woe has passed; behold, another woe is coming quickly” (Rev. 9:12).

And report will come upon report, and messenger upon messenger, according to the words of blessed Job: “While he was still speaking, another messenger came” (Job 1:16), increasing evils with evils and describing the tumult and multitude of the approaching Babylonians.

“And they will seek a vision from the prophet; and the law will perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders.”

Each thing is properly sought from the proper person. A prophecy of future events is sought from a prophet. The interpretation of the Law is the priest’s task. A prudent counsel is sought from mature age, according to what is written: “In the council of the holy ones [alt. ‘righteous’] and in the assembly, the works of the Lord are great” (Ps. 111:1–2).

These things were sought not only at the time when the Babylonian army was coming against Jerusalem—from prophets, priests, and elders—but they are sought daily in the churches. If the churches have lost vision, law, and counsel, they boast in vain that they possess prophets, priests, and elders.

### (Verse 27)

“The king will mourn, and the prince will be clothed with sorrow”—or, according to the Septuagint, “with destruction.” I do not know what they intended by this, but they completely omitted the expression that we rendered from the Hebrew: “The king will mourn.”

That Zedekiah mourned, and that all the leaders of the Jewish people were consumed with sorrow, holy Scripture records.

We can also—although at first sight this may appear blasphemous—call the mourning king Christ, mourning our vices and sins, who speaks in the Psalms: “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down into corruption?” (Ps. 30:9). And as he approached Jerusalem, he wept over it and said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23:37).

The princes, too, may be the apostles in the good sense, who mourn sinners; or, in the contrary sense, those to whom it is said: “Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom” (Isa. 1:10).

“And he will be clothed,” according to the Septuagint, “with destruction”—the one who does not possess the armor of God and has not put on Christ. For as many as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ (Gal. 3:27).

[Col. 0076A] “And the hands of the people of the land will be disturbed,” or, according to the Septuagint, “will be dissolved.”

When there is no vision in the prophet, no knowledge of the Law in the priest, and no counsel among the elders; when the king has mourned and the prince is in sorrow or destruction, then consequently the hands of the people will also be disturbed, losing their proper order, or will be dissolved, no longer possessing their former strength.

And it is well that he does not call them the people of God, whose hands will be disturbed and whose citizenship is not in heaven, but “the people of the land,” of whom it is written: “Those who depart from you shall be written upon the earth” (Jer. 17:13).

“According to their ways I will deal with them, and according to their judgments I will judge them,” or, as the Septuagint translated, “I will punish them.”

God repays sinners according to their ways, so that the truth of judgment may be maintained. But in the saints he surpasses the measure of mercy. For “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). “The wages of sin is death” (ibid. 6:23), which the sinner receives according to his ways and his works.

The virtue of the righteous, however, enjoys the Lord’s generosity, of which Paul says: “The gift of God is eternal life.” And what he added, “and according to their judgments I will judge them,” echoes the Gospel: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7:1). It also echoes the apostle: “In the judgment by which you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2:1).

“And they will know that I am the Lord.”

This verse frequently occurs in this prophet: punishment and torments are followed by knowledge of God, so that those who did not understand him through benefits may come to know him through sufferings.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0075]

[Col. 0075C] 79–80 Nothing that possesses faith is long, and the entire succession of past times, once passed, is of no benefit—unless perhaps someone has prepared for himself a provision of good works, which always look toward the future, indeed toward the eternal, and are confined by no limits.

The saying is true: “All things that arise perish, and those that grow old decline.” And elsewhere: “There is nothing made by work and hand that old age does not finish and consume.”

Who would have believed that Rome, built up by the victories of the whole world, would collapse; that she herself would become both mother and tomb for her own peoples; that all the shores of the East, Egypt, and Africa, once subject to the ruling city, would be filled with the number of slaves and maidservants; that holy Bethlehem would daily receive as beggars people once noble in both sexes and overflowing with every wealth?

Since we cannot bring them aid, we share their grief and join tears to tears. Burdened with the labor of a holy work, and unable to bear seeing the crowds pour in without groaning, we have abandoned our explanations of Ezekiel and nearly all our other studies; we desire to turn the words of Scripture into deeds, and not merely to speak holy things, but to do them.

Therefore, again admonished by you, O virgin of Christ Eustochium, we resume our interrupted labor. We have undertaken the third volume and desire to satisfy your wish, entreating both you and the others who will read it to consider not our strength but our intention: the former belongs to human frailty, the latter to a holy will in the Lord.

### 81. (Chapter 8—Verse 1)

“And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, while I was sitting in my house and the elders of Judah were sitting before me.”

In the fifth year of the captivity of Jeconiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, we read that the preceding vision was given to the prophet. But the vision that we now wish to explain is recorded as having taken place in the sixth year of the same king, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month.

From this it is clear that what is written took place after a year and two months, and either that the prophecy was interrupted for a year and two months, or that the events described in the preceding discourse occupied the whole fourteen months.

No one will be surprised that the prophecy took place in the sixth year, the sixth month, and on the fifth day of the month—numbers that refer to the structure of the world and [alt. “to”] the carnal senses that look upon earthly things and do not yet contemplate heavenly things—if he understands that the discourse was directed to the elders of Judah.

Seventy of them held censers, and twenty-five worshiped the sun in the Temple. The prophet was sitting in his house, avoiding the crowds, while the elders of Judah sat before him, either desiring to hear the prophet’s words or lying in wait for what he said.

They are significantly called “the elders of Judah,” so that we may understand that this was addressed not to Israel—that is, to the ten tribes, which had previously been taken captive—but to those who had been led into captivity with Jeconiah from the tribe of Judah.

### (Verse 2)

“And the hand of the Lord God fell upon me. And I saw, and behold, a likeness, as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins downward there was fire, and from his loins upward there was something like the appearance of splendor, like the appearance of amber.”

The Septuagint: “And the hand of Adonai the Lord came upon me; and I saw, and behold, a likeness, as the appearance of a man: from his loins downward there was fire, and from his loins upward something like the appearance of a breeze, like the appearance of amber.”

The Hebrew text does not contain “man.” We have added “the appearance of a breeze,” which is not found in the Septuagint, from Theodotion. And in place of our rendering, “the hand of the Lord fell upon me,” Symmachus translated, “the hand of the Lord came upon me,” which in Hebrew is called **TEPHPHOL** [Hebrew omitted in the supplied text].

[Note: Previously the word was written TEPHPHOL, initially without aspiration. The oldest manuscript of Saint-Germain, cited by Montfaucon, has THEPPOL.]

The hand signifies **ἐνέργεια**, that is, “activity” or “operation,” so that he may understand the mysteries of the vision.

It must also be considered that he does not see the realities themselves, but a likeness of fire: from the loins downward fire appeared, and from the loins upward something like the appearance of splendor, like the appearance of amber.

For “splendor,” which in Hebrew is called **ZOR** [Hebrew omitted in the supplied text], Theodotion translated “breeze,” so as to indicate the refreshment of God in the higher regions. Thus, in the Book of Kings, blessed Elijah does not behold the Lord’s coming in storm or whirlwind, nor in the heat of fire, but in the appearance of a gentle and exceedingly mild breeze, thereby demonstrating the gentleness of Almighty God.

The works of intercourse, signified by the loins and extending downward, are purified by fire. The works of the virtues, which rise from the loins upward, possess splendor and radiance. Yet neither is the fire said to reach the feet, nor the splendor of amber to reach the head, but the text says “downward” and “upward,” so that, among sinners as well as among the holy, according to the diversity of their merits, one may reach one member or another, and another may reach other members.

And just as those who possess perfection of holiness are believed to reach as far as the crown of the head, so those who are in the depths of sins are believed to hold the soles of fiery feet.

### (Verse 3)

“And the likeness of a hand was extended and seized me by a lock of the hair of my head.”

The Septuagint: “And he extended the likeness of a hand and took me by the fringe of the crown of my head.”

Here too it is the likeness of a hand, not the hand itself, that is extended; for there is nothing corporeal in God. A hand is seen as a familiar member of the human body, so that the one who is taken up and grasped may not be terrified.

For if he had touched the prophet in the likeness of a serpent or of any other beast, the very dissimilarity of the limbs would have terrified the one who was taken up. A portion of the hair is grasped because human nature cannot endure the grasping of the entire head.

In place of “lock,” the Septuagint translated **κράσπεδον**, that is, “fringe”; one of these terms is ordinarily understood of the hair, the other of garments.

“And the spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven.”

First he is seized by the likeness of a hand; afterward he is lifted by the spirit. The spirit does not immediately raise him to heaven, but between earth and heaven, so that, leaving earthly things for the moment, he may hasten toward heaven.

We can also say that, on account of his good works, the prophet was seized by the likeness of God’s hand, and that, on account of his knowledge of spiritual things, he was lifted by the spirit.

### (Verse 4)

“And he brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God, beside the inner gate that faced north, where the idol of Jealousy was set up to provoke jealousy. And behold, there was the glory of the God of Israel, according to the vision that I had seen in the plain.”

The Septuagint: “And he brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God, to the vestibule of the gate that faces north, where there was the statue of the one who possesses. And behold, the glory of the Lord God of Israel was there, according to the vision that I saw in the plain.”

The phrase found in certain manuscripts, “and in the statue the image [of Jealousy],” [Note: Up to this point, the common printed books have manifestly preserved “of heaven” instead of “of jealousy.” We have not hesitated to correct it, compelled by the context of the explanation that follows and by Theodotion’s version itself, τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ ζήλου. In the Commentary on chapter 1 of Zephaniah also: “Judah and Benjamin,” he says, “had come to such impiety that in the Temple of the Lord, as Ezekiel writes and the Fourth Book of Kings shows, they had set up the statue of Baal, which the Lord calls the image of Jealousy, and in that same sanctuary they worshiped idols and the Lord together,” and so forth.] “of Jealousy” was added from Theodotion. The rest is similar.

When he says, “He brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God,” he shows that he was transferred not bodily but in spirit. In accordance with such a vision, we can contemplate the heavens, the depths of the sea, and the underworld, while embracing the principles of each in thought.

First he comes to the vestibule that faces north, so that there he may see the statue of the idol of Jealousy, to provoke jealousy; from that place he can penetrate into the interior and observe the other things that are described afterward.

History recounts that a statue of the idol Baal was placed in the Temple. It is fittingly called the idol of Jealousy, because it provokes the Lord to jealousy and rivalry, according to what is said in Deuteronomy: “They have provoked me to jealousy with what is not God, and I will provoke them to jealousy with a nation that is not a nation” (Deut. 32:21).

Since “jealousy” and “possession”—which in Hebrew is called **CENA** [Hebrew omitted in the supplied text]—are designated by the same name, the Septuagint translated “the statue of Jealousy” as “the statue of the one who possesses.”

[Note: Montfaucon also noted that Jerome says the word *cena*, by similarity of sound rather than of letters, means both “jealousy” and “possession”; for “possession” is otherwise expressed, and is derived from a different Hebrew root. There are other examples of this kind in Jerome, in which he attends only to sound and pronunciation, not to the letters.]

Thus, when Cain was born, his mother said, “I have possessed a man through God” (Gen. 4:1), alluding to the name Cain through the possession of a man.

And there was the glory of the God of Israel—not because it took pleasure in such proximity, but so that by its presence it might destroy the idol of Jealousy and the Temple. Hence the overthrow of the city and Temple follows shortly afterward.

And it is written in Isaiah that a narrow bed cannot contain two, and a short covering cannot cover both (Isa. 28:20), the Scripture signifying the apostolic saying: “What agreement has Christ with Belial? What has the temple of God with an idol?” (2 Cor. 6:15–16).

### (Verse 5)

“And he said to me: Son of man, lift up your eyes toward the way of the north. And I lifted up my eyes toward the way of the north; and behold, north of the gate of the altar was the idol of Jealousy at the very entrance.”

Instead of our reading, “North of the gate of the altar was the idol of Jealousy at the very entrance,” the Septuagint translated: “From the north toward the eastern gate,” which is not found in the Hebrew; they omitted the remaining words written here.

He said to me—either the glory of God, which I had seen in the plain, or the spirit that had lifted me between heaven and earth. After he had transferred me to Jerusalem and caused me to see either the city or the Temple, he spoke to me and commanded me to lift my eyes toward the way of the north.

For there the statue of Baal had been placed; he calls it the idol of Jealousy, at the very entrance of the gate.

Those who refer “the idol of Jealousy,” or “of the one who possesses,” to the glory of God or to the spirit are acting impiously, changing the person of the idol into the majesty of God.

### (Verse 6)

“And he said to me: Son of man, do you think you see what these people are doing—the great abominations that the house of Israel commits here, so that I may withdraw far from my sanctuary? And, turning again, you will see greater abominations.”

Do not think, he says, that I am abandoning the Temple unjustly and leaving the city to be destroyed. Look at what they are doing in the Temple. And when you have seen those things, do not think that the crimes have reached their end; you will see still greater things.

This can also be understood of our Jerusalem and our Temple, whenever we commit the crimes of idols in the tabernacle of God, after the example of Hophni and Phinehas (1 Sam. 2); whenever we commit fornication with those who have vowed themselves to military service and the ministry of God; whenever we tear away the firstfruits of his sacrifices, giving them for the use of clients and servants; and whenever we do everything for the sake of profit.

But if the things we see are so great, how much greater must those things be considered that escape human consciousness?

### (Verses 7ff.)

“And he brought me to the door of the court. And I saw, and behold, a single opening in the wall. And he said to me: Son of man, dig through the wall. And when I had dug through the wall, one door appeared. And he said to me: Enter and see the most wicked abominations that these people commit here.”

The words I translated, “And I saw, and behold, a single opening in the wall,” are not found in the Septuagint.

Because everything is shown as though in an image or painting, he says that he saw one opening in the wall, and he was ordered to dig through it and make it larger, so that, once the opening had been opened, he could enter more widely and see what, while outside, he could not see.

This shows that, both in the churches and in each of us individually, greater vices are revealed through small ones, and that through certain openings we arrive at the greatest abominations.

“For the tree is known by its fruit” (Matt. 12:33–34), and “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” The words that burst forth are signs of the inner person: a lustful person, because he carefully conceals his vices, is sometimes exposed by an obscene expression; and hidden greed is indicated by the desire for some small thing.

Greater things are revealed through lesser ones. Conscience cannot be concealed by the face and eyes, when a luxurious and wanton mind shines forth in the face; and the secrets of the heart are disclosed by bodily movement and gestures.

### (Verse 10)

“And I entered and saw; and behold, every likeness of creeping things and abominable animals, and all the idols of the house of Israel, were depicted upon the wall all around.”

Not only did the idol of Jealousy stand at the entrance of the north gate, but all the walls of the Temple were also painted with various images of idols, so that there was no beast whose form the painting on the wall did not display.

We see this to the present day in the shrines and temples of the pagans: foolish religion worships every kind of beast. Hence Virgil also says:

> “Monsters of gods of every kind, and barking Anubis,
> against Neptune and Venus, and against Minerva.”

As though those too were not monsters whom he praises.

We can also point out painted idols on the walls of our own temple [alt. “our temples”], whenever we are subject to every vice and paint in our heart the consciousness of sins and various images.

Concerning these it is also said in the Psalms: “Lord, in your city you will destroy their image” (Ps. 73:20). And in another place: “Nevertheless, man walks about in an image” (Ps. 39:6). That is, there is no human being who does not possess some image, whether of holiness or of sin.

Therefore it is said to the furious and wrathful: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers” (Ps. 58:4–5). And concerning wicked people: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. 3:7). Concerning the deceitful and fraudulent: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke 13:32). Concerning lovers of women: “They became for me like horses in heat for females; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. 5:8). Concerning the brutish and senseless: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.” And again: “With bit and bridle bind their jaws, those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 32:9). And many things of this kind.

The words we have inserted, “And behold, every likeness of creeping things and animals,” are not found in the Septuagint.

### (Verse 11)

“And seventy men from the elders of the house of Israel, with Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan standing in the midst of them, stood before the painted figures; each had a censer in his hand, and the smoke of the cloud rose from the incense.”

When he says that there were seventy men from the elders of the house of Israel, holding censers in their hands, he shows that there were many other elders who were not doing this, but were perhaps held by other sins.

One man, named Jaazaniah son of Shaphan, stood in their midst, as though the leader of their crime and sacrilege. Having abandoned the worship of God, they worshiped idols; and in the Temple, which belonged to God, they did not adore God but the paintings on the walls.
