It is fittingly said: “Jaazaniah son of Shaphan stood,” that is, in the midst of the elders who stood for their own judgment and condemnation, because both the leader and those over whom he presided stood firmly in their crimes. They did not waver in evil but persisted in it with the greatest strength.

The smoke of cloud, confusion, and storm that rose from the incense demonstrated the sacrilege of those who were offering it.

This happened at that time according to the literal sense. But we too must pray that the elders of the house of Israel, multiplying the sacred number seven by seven decades, may not stand in their errors and worship painted images of idols, and that the smoke of sacrilege may not ascend or rise up in resistance to God.

When we see an exceedingly wicked crowd gathered, of which it is written, “I hate the assembly of the wicked” (Ps. 26:5), and leaders worse than the crowd, with a more wicked ruler placed over the people and the elders, let us say that Jaazaniah is standing before the painted figures, and that each of them holds a censer in his hands.

They are worshiping not the majesty of God but their own opinions, and it is not the fragrance of a good odor that reaches God, but a stench that reaches the idols.

[Note: Rabanus reads “priests” in his copy; Jerome immediately contrasts the priests with the crowd.]

[Col. 0081D] **(Verse 12.)** And he said to me: “Surely you see, son of man, what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the darkness, each one in the hidden place of his chamber. For they say: ‘The Lord does not see us; the Lord has abandoned the land.’”

From what they do when assembled together in the temple, he says, it is shown what each one does in his chamber. But according to the allegorical sense, it may better be understood that certain leaders of the Churches do in darkness things that are shameful even to mention. This is the hidden man of the heart, of whom it is said: “Enter into your chamber” (Mic. VI, 4). And again: “He who sees in secret will repay you” [Note: [Col. 0081D] The same reading, *in absconso* (“in secret”), which was formerly found in Latin manuscripts, is shown by us in the commentaries at the relevant passage of Matthew.] Let each person examine his conscience and recall in the darkness the works of darkness, and let him know that it is written: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest he be reproved by the light” (John III, 20; I Thess. V). He will also recognize in himself the fulfillment of this saying: “He who is drunk is drunk at night” (Prov. II, 25).

This cannot stand according to the literal sense. For how many become drunk at the daytime meals and banquets? But because drunkenness of the heart, which offends God, belongs to darkness [Col. 0082B] and not to light, therefore whoever becomes drunk is drunk at night. When the elders of the house of Israel do evil in the darkness and in the secrecy of their chambers, and think that they can hide themselves from God, then they will consequently say: “The Lord does not see us; the Lord has abandoned the land.” There are also many sinners, walking according to their own thoughts, who do not believe that God concerns himself with mortal affairs, or that our vices have anything to do with him. Certainly, when we sin, if we considered that God sees and is present, we would never do what displeases him.

Moreover, what follows—“The Lord has abandoned the land”—is also the opinion of certain philosophers, who, from the courses and regularity of the stars, suppose that providence exists in heavenly things while earthly things are despised, since nothing upright or orderly is done on earth [Col. 0082C].

**(Verses 13, 14.)** And he said to me: “Still turning, you will see greater abominations that they [or: these women] are committing.” And he brought me through the entrance of the gate of the house of the Lord that looked toward the north; and behold, women were sitting there [the Vulgate: “there . . . were sitting”], mourning Tammuz.

The one whom we have interpreted as Adonis, both the Hebrew and the Syriac language call *Tammuz* (תַּמּוּז). [Note: [Col. 0081D] This is the commonly accepted opinion, which Jerome praises elsewhere, especially in Letter 58 to Paulinus, §3, and which other ecclesiastical interpreters, Greek and Latin, likewise confirm. Nevertheless, most recent writers explain this Egyptian worship as referring to Osiris and the bull Apis, concerning which Plutarch wrote an entire book. Tibullus also says, Book I, Elegy 8:

> “The barbarian woman, taught to mourn the Memphian bull.”

See Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 46; Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chapter 36; Pomponius Mela, Book I, chapter 9; and Strabo, Book XVII. It is certain, moreover, that at that time the Jews, servilely flattering the Egyptians, imitated their impious religious observances just as they imitated their civil customs.]

Since, according to the pagan myth, the lover of Venus and an exceptionally beautiful young man was killed in the month of June and is then said to have come back to life, they call that same month of June by his name and celebrate an annual festival for him. During it, he is mourned by women as though dead, and afterward, as though revived, is sung and praised.

[Col. 0082D] Consequently, after it has been shown what the leaders and elders of the house of Israel did in the temple, in the darkness, and in their chambers, the vices of the women are also described. They mourn because they have been deprived of the company of their lovers, and rejoice if they have been able to possess them. And [Col. 0083A] since paganism interprets such poets’ tales, which contain obscenity, with subtlety—following the death and resurrection of Adonis with mourning and rejoicing—it thinks that the one is represented in seeds that die in the earth, and the other in crops through which the dead seeds are reborn. We too, then, may call those who grieve or rejoice over the evils and goods of the world “women,” because of their soft and effeminate disposition; and we may say that they mourn Tammuz—that is, those things thought to be most beautiful among worldly possessions.

**(Verses 15, 16.)** And he said to me: “Surely you have seen, son of man; still turning, you will see greater abominations than these.” And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the Lord; and behold, at the entrance of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule [Col. 0083B] and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east; and they were worshiping toward the rising sun.

The word that we have translated “vestibule” according to Symmachus, who used *propylon* (πρόπυλον), is the word that the Septuagint and Theodotion translated from the Hebrew term [Note: [Col. 0083D] Aquila did not read *Ulam* in his copy of the Hebrew, but *Aelam*, with aleph and yod, which together form a diphthong, as Jerome himself indicates. From this one can see that no variant reading of the Hebrew text can be established on the basis of Erasmus and Marianus, who everywhere impose upon us Hebrew words distinguished by Masoretic points. Quite a few readings of this kind, however, will be found in our present new edition of Jerome. —MART.

In the Hebrew archetype *Ulam* is written with waw, not yod, so that one should render it in Latin letters as *Aelam*. Nevertheless, I would prefer that this word be omitted altogether here, as I see that Montfaucon also approves; thus the second edition’s *Aelam* would be written in Greek letters as αἰλὰμ. Nor is that reading free from difficulty, since Jerome says that the Septuagint agrees with Theodotion’s Hebrew exemplar, whereas Theodotion read οὐλάμ and the second edition αἰλάμ.] *AELAM* (אֵילָם). Aquila’s first edition translated it as *prostada* (προστάδα); his second as *AELAM* of the temple, which we may express as “the portico of the temple,” or the uncovered court that lay between the temple and the altar.

Since above we read, after the idol of Jealousy that appeared at the northern gate, “Still turning, you will see greater abominations,” and since the pictures of every kind of beast that the seventy elders worshiped had been displayed upon the wall, with Jezonias son of Saphan among them, holding censers in their hands, it is said a second time: “Still turning [Col. 0083C] you will see greater abominations that these people are committing,” because women were sitting and mourning Adonis. After the third sin also it is said: “Still turning, you will see greater abominations than these.”

What, then, is the greater abomination than the preceding three crimes? Clearly the fourth that follows: “Behold, at the entrance of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs toward the temple and their faces toward the east, and they were worshiping toward the rising sun.” [Note: [Col. 0084D] It had been read in the future tense, “and they will worship the rising sun,” although the manuscripts and the sacred text reject this.]

They did this because, having despised the Lord—that is, the Creator—they worshiped the sun, that is, a creature of the Lord. Yet the Lord himself had commanded through Moses (Deut. XII) that they should by no means worship God toward the east in the manner of the Gentiles; rather, wherever they might be in the world—whether toward the east, west, south, or north—they were to worship facing the temple, where the Lord was believed to dwell in the Holy of Holies. We read that Daniel did this in Babylon (Dan. VI): opening the windows of his upper room, he worshiped the Lord facing the temple that was in Jerusalem.

No one doubts that this was sacrilege according to the literal sense. According to the allegorical sense, all heretics are worse than the earlier offenders: worse than the idol of Jealousy, the figures of animals painted on the wall, and the mourning for Adonis, through which idolatry and pleasure are represented. He will understand this who understands the prophet’s words: “You have hated discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. XLIX, 17). And in another place: “They turned their back toward me as they went away” (Jer. II, 27).

Do we not know Marcion and the other heretics who tear apart the Old Testament and, having despised the Creator—that is, the just God—worship and adore some other good god whom they have fashioned from their own heart? And all the heretics of our own time, who preach that the Son of God is a creature and yet adore him, having abandoned the temple of his divinity and placed it behind their backs, by their own confession say that they worship a creature.

We, however, worship the Sun of righteousness in such a way that we worship God in the temple of the Old Testament, where the Law and the Prophets are, where the cherubim and the mercy seat are. The twenty-five men whom we have translated are rendered “twenty” by the Septuagint; in some copies, five have been added from Theodotion.

**91 (Verse 17.)** And he said to me: “Surely you have seen, son of man. Is it a small thing for the house of Judah to commit these abominations that they have committed here, filling the land with iniquity and turning to provoke me? And behold, they apply the branch to their noses.”

Where we said, “And behold, they apply the branch to their noses,” the Septuagint translated: “And behold, they themselves are like those mocking”; to this Theodotion added, “They stretch out the branch,” so that the whole reads: “And behold, they themselves stretch out the branch like those mocking.” Symmachus translated it: “as though sending forth a sound resembling a song through their nostrils.” [Note: [Col. 0084D] Here too the reading was corruptly given as “sending out,” although Symmachus translated ὡς ἀφιέντες, “as though sending forth,” in the plural.]

This signifies the twenty-five men, who are established in a solid square formation and, through the five senses multiplied by five, produce the figure of a quadrangle. They not only have the temple behind them but, like idols, apply a branch to their noses—without doubt a palm branch, which is called *baia* (βαΐα) in Greek—in order by this gesture to signify that they worship idols.

Finally, Job says that among his other virtues he also possessed this one: that, when he looked upon the sky, the sun, the moon, and the shining stars, he never kissed his hand (Job XXXI), that is, he never worshiped creatures. Symmachus’ interpretation signifies a foul and hoarse sound issuing from the nostrils in contempt of God. All heretics who have filled the land with iniquity and turned to the falsely named knowledge in order to provoke the Lord to anger should likewise be judged to do this: whenever they wish to praise God, they rather blaspheme with a shameful sound, or make light of, mock, and despise the God of the Old Testament.

**(Verse 18.)** “Therefore I also will act in fury: my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity. And when they cry out in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them.”

The clause that follows—“And when they cry out in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them”—is not found in the Septuagint. He says: “For all these things that they have done, I will act in fury, and my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity.”

When the ancient heretics hear this, they slander the Creator as cruel and bloodthirsty. Nor do they consider the Apostle Paul, who certainly is, as they wish to claim, the apostle of the good God, writing to the Corinthians: “When I come again, I will not spare” (II Cor. XV, 2), so that he may correct offenders with a rod and bring the erring back to salvation. For those who do not understand what benefits them, and who frequently ask for the opposite, it is advantageous that they not be heard by the Lord. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Your will be done” (Matt. VI, 10)—not our will, which is accustomed to err, but your will, which knows what is to come. Sometimes it is a great blessing not to deserve mercy in the present.

The Lord, therefore, will not spare these people who are of the house of Judah and have withdrawn from the confession of the Church. And when they cry out with a loud voice, of which the Lord said, “Their cry has come to me” (Gen. XVIII), nevertheless the Lord will not hear them, so that, compelled by their misfortunes, they may understand what they have done.

**(Chapter IX—Verse 1.)** And he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying: “The visitations of the city have drawn near.”

Instead of “visitations,” the Septuagint translated “vengeance”: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” says the Lord (Deut. XXXII, 35). Every vengeance is also a visitation, as of a sick person, as of one who has wounds, as of one awaiting the hands of a physician, according to what is written elsewhere: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 33–34). And rightly, as we said above, visitation or vengeance is said to be approaching, because captivity is near.

[Col. 0085D] “And each one has a vessel of slaughter in his hand.” He did not say “had,” as the Septuagint translated it. For he is not narrating past events but displaying present and future ones. Whoever strikes the wicked because they are wicked, and has vessels of slaughter in order to kill the worst offenders, is a minister of the Lord.

**(Verses 2, 3.)** And behold, six men were coming from the way of the upper gate that looks toward the north, each with his instrument of destruction in his hand. And one man among them was clothed in linen, with a writer’s inkwell at his loins. They entered and stood beside the bronze altar. And the glory of the God [the Vulgate: “of the Lord”] of Israel was lifted up from the cherub that was above him to the threshold of the house. And he called the man who was clothed in linen and had the writer’s inkwell at his loins.

Where we translated “linen,” following Symmachus, the Septuagint has *podere* (ποδήρη); Theodotion has the Hebrew word *baddim* (בַּדִּים); Aquila has *praecipua*. Again, where we said, “and the writer’s inkwell at his loins,” the Septuagint has: “and a sapphire belt around his loins”; Theodotion, “a *kasty* (κάστυ) of a scribe in his hand”; Aquila, “an inkwell (μελανοδοχεῖον) of a scribe at his loins”; Symmachus, “he had a writer’s tablets at his loins.” Where we translated “the threshold of the house,” the Septuagint and Theodotion have *the open court* (τὸ αἴθριον), that is, they placed “the vestibule under the open sky.” Instead of “the vessel of destruction,” which each man had in his hands, only the Septuagint translated “an axe.”

To erase the sins of human beings, who were made on the sixth day of the world’s creation, six men come and descend from the upper gate—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the lofty gate—toward the north. Each had an axe in his hands, of which John speaks: “For already the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III; Luke III, 9).

Among the six men was one, that is, the seventh, clothed in priestly garments, wearing linen vestments and having a writer’s inkwell at his loins. With it he was to record everyone’s sins and separate the number of the saints from the sinners; or else it was a sapphire-colored belt, the color of the sapphire stone used in the ornaments of the chief priest.

The six men went out and stood beside the bronze altar [Col. 0086C]. There were two altars: one for incense, golden and within the sanctuary; and another before the temple, bronze, for burnt offerings. They are said to stand beside the altar, prepared to obey the command of the one issuing orders, so that they might know that anyone whom they saw there not to have been forgiven his sins was subject to the Lord’s sentence and to death.

The glory of the God of Israel also ascended, or was lifted up, from one cherub and went to the threshold—or to the open-air court and vestibule of the house—which is not weighed down by a roof but enjoys the freedom of the air. This same glory of the Lord called the man who was in priestly attire and had the writer’s inkwell at his loins, and spoke the words that Scripture records.

Some interpret the six men as six angels who obey God’s will; and they understand the one who had the priestly garments as the Savior, in accordance with the fact that he is “the Priest and Angel of the Great Counsel,” and with what is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

*Podere* (ποδήρη), which the Septuagint translated, is one of the eight garments of the high priest. In Latin it is called *talaris*, and it received this name because it descends as far as the feet. Many years ago I know that I published a book on the high priest’s vestment; for its explanation I refer the reader to that work. I cannot say everything in every place.

As for what Aquila’s first edition and Theodotion called *kasty* (κάστυ), corresponding to the Hebrew *cesath* (כֶּסֶת), [Note: [Col. 0085] These are the very words of Origen cited by Drusius: “For I do not think that anything is signified among the Greeks by the word *kasty*; but a certain Hebrew said that *kasty* is what is called an inkwell.” Unless Jerome copied this from him, it is remarkable that both men were equally ignorant of the word and consulted a Hebrew teacher, receiving the same answer, which corresponded to the Greek. It is not implausible that the Septuagint, the Arabic, and the Syriac translate it as “belt,” nor that others prefer “ink.” In Jerome’s text we correct *in quo calami recondantur* (“in which pens are stored”) in place of the former corrupt reading *recordantur*.] when I asked a Hebrew what it meant, he replied that in Greek it was called *kalamárion* (καλαμάριον), because pens (*calami*) are stored in it.

We call it an *atramentarium*, an inkwell, because it contains ink. Many more precisely call such objects *thecae*, cases, because they are cases for writers’ pens.

Of the four cherubim, one cherub is sent by the glory of the Lord’s majesty to speak to the one clothed in priestly garments. Although many think that *the cherubim* (τὰ χερουβείμ) is neuter in gender and plural in number, we must know that *cherub* is singular and masculine, while *cherubim* is plural and of the same gender. This is not because there is sex among God’s ministers, but because each term is assigned different genders according to the usage of its language. Angels are called *malachim* in the plural, as are *cherubim* and *seraphim*, all of the same gender and number. But *Sabaoth*, interpreted as “armies,” “hosts,” or “powers,” is feminine and plural, ending in the final syllable *-oth* (אוֹת).

Those who wish the Savior to be understood under the figure of the high priest use an example from John’s Apocalypse, in which it is written: “And I turned and saw the voice that was speaking with me. And when I turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man” (Rev. II, 12–13), and so forth.

**(Verses 4 and following.)** And the Lord said to him: “Pass through the middle of the city, through the middle of Jerusalem, and mark a *tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in its midst.”

And to the others he said in my hearing: “Pass through the city after him and strike. Let not your eye spare, and have no pity. Kill the old man, the young man, the virgin, the little child, and the women, even to destruction. But do not kill anyone upon whom you see the *tau*. Begin from my sanctuary.”

It is commanded [Note: [Col. 0087C] Jerome also took this varying interpretation of the sign or letter *tau* from Origen. For comparison, we reproduce the Greek words themselves as they appear more fully in the Coislinian manuscript and in the Royal bombycine manuscript preserved by Montfaucon:

“The Septuagint say that the one clothed in the *podere* was commanded by the glory of the Lord to place a sign upon the foreheads of those who groaned and those who were in anguish. When the Hebrews were asked whether they possessed any ancestral knowledge concerning the *tau*, this is what we heard. One said that *tau* is one of the twenty-two elements among the Hebrews, the last according to the order of their letters. Therefore the last element was taken as an indication of the perfection of those who, because of the virtue within them, groaned and grieved over the sins committed among the people and fell together with the lawbreakers (that is, lest they fall).

Another said that *tau* is the symbol of those who have kept the Law, since the Law is called *Thora* among the Hebrews, and its first letter is *tau*. It is therefore the symbol of those who have lived according to the Law.

A third, one of those who also believed in the Savior, said that the ancient letters contain in *tau* a form resembling the sign of the cross, and that the sign made upon the forehead among Christians had been prophetically announced. All believers make this sign at the beginning of any undertaking, especially prayers and the reading of sacred writings, and so forth.”]

—namely, to the one clothed in the ankle-length or linen garment, who bore a priestly appearance—that he should place a sign upon the foreheads of the men groaning and grieving over all the abominations committed in the midst of Jerusalem.

Instead of “sign,” which the Septuagint, Aquila, and Symmachus translated, Theodotion retained the Hebrew word *tau* (תָּו), which is the final letter among the twenty-two Hebrew letters, so that it might signify the perfect knowledge of the men who groaned and grieved. Or, as the Hebrews maintain, since the Law is called *Thora* (תּוֹרָה) among them and begins with this letter of its name, those who had fulfilled the commandments of the Law received this mark.

And, to come to our own matters: in the ancient Hebrew letters still used by the Samaritans, the final letter, *tau*, resembles the cross that is painted on Christians’ foreheads and marked by the frequent inscription of the hand. [Note: [Col. 0088C] Scaliger and other learned men after him maintain that Origen misled Jerome when he wrote that the Samaritan *tau* resembled a cross, since Jerome transferred Origen almost word for word. They blame him for not having consulted the Samaritan alphabet and for following the testimony of one who had not himself seen it but had written from another’s report.

Yet on the most ancient surviving shekels, whose letters are the same as those found in Samaritan writings, and since there is therefore, they conclude, no reason to doubt that the Samaritan letters were other than those seen on the coins, they find no letter in that alphabet resembling the form of a cross. But on the very coins or shekels that they cite, the figure of the *tau* is so clearly shaped like the crossed form of the Greek letter X that those who appeal to their testimony should hardly be believed to have examined the coins themselves. The sign of *tau* in the form of X occurs three times on one coin of Simon, the Jewish ethnarch and high priest, cited by Rhenferd, on which the first year of the recovered freedom is marked. Rabbi Azariah, in *Me’or Enayim*, also records that this other *tau*, in the form of a crossed cross, formerly existed in the Samaritan alphabet; and I think that anyone who suspects it was fabricated by a Christian to agree with Jerome’s teaching is out of his mind. See also Morin’s *Exercitation* 2 on the Samaritan Pentateuch and Montfaucon’s *Palaeographia*, Book VI.]

Some think that, because this is the final letter according to the Hebrew alphabet, it demonstrates that among the multitude of sinners a remnant of saints remains.

Those who groan and grieve are therefore saved: they not only did not consent to evil deeds but also mourned the sins of others, just as Samuel mourned over Saul (III Kings XVI) and the Apostle Paul over those who did not repent after sinning. Hence he himself said: “We who are in this tabernacle groan” (II Cor. V, 2). And elsewhere: “There is great sorrow for me and unceasing pain in my heart” [variant: “to my heart”].

The six men are commanded to kill everyone except those who can say: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV, 7). They are to spare neither the old man, nor the young man, nor the virgin, nor the little child, nor the woman.

According to the mystical interpretations, the old men in the Church are those of whom it is said: “The gray hair of a human being is his wisdom” (Wis. IV, 8); the young are those most ready for the battles of faith; the virgins are those who preserve chastity with their whole mind; the little children are those nourished with the milk of infancy and not yet able to receive solid food; and the women are those who, through the weakness of their sex, testify to the weakness of the soul. None of these is spared if they believe themselves to be anything without the mark of Christ.

What follows—“Begin from my sanctuary,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “Begin from my holy ones”—either signifies the priests who were active in the temple and worshiped idols, or those who were called holy among the people because of the dignity of their priesthood and who, having been the cause of sin among the peoples, deserved to receive the punishments first. For it is time, as the Apostle says, “for judgment to begin from the house of God” (I Cor. VII).

**(Verse 7.)** Therefore they began with the older men who were before the face of the house. And he said to them: “Defile the house and fill the courts with the slain.”

“Fill the courts with the slain.” Instead of “courts,” which in Hebrew are called *aseroth* (עֲזָרוֹת), the Septuagint placed “streets.” The older men are killed, those of whom we read above that they had censers and burned incense to idols. There is no worship of the temple, because, when the God of worship has been offended [Note: [Col. 0090D] In Rabanus: “when God has been offended,” without the word “of worship.”], everything has been defiled, so that judgment comes from the place where sin arose.

The courts, not the streets, are filled with corpses in the temple; the streets were certainly outside, unless perhaps we may understand “streets” as the city’s public squares. Nor could the angels have dared to defile the temple with the blood of the dead, in which the glory of God had previously dwelt, unless the Lord of the departing [variant: “believing”] glory had commanded it.

Everyone who has died through sin defiles the courts of the temple and the streets of the Lord’s city, in which he lives; but when that person rises with Christ, he ceases to be dead.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] Victorius places this first and supplies from the Vulgate: “Go out,” and so forth. The Hebrew likewise has the corresponding expression.]

And they went out and struck those who were in the city. Or, as others translated it, “they struck the city,” calling the city itself “those who were in the city.”

**(Verse 8.)** And when the slaughter was complete, I remained; and I fell upon my face and cried out, saying: “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God! Will you then destroy all the remnant of Israel, pouring out your fury upon Jerusalem?”

When all who lacked the mark had been struck down in the slaughter, the prophet fell upon his face because of the multitude of the slain, supposing that no one except himself remained. Since this seemed contrary to the sentence by which the Lord had ordered that the men with marked foreheads not be killed, it was omitted in the Vulgate edition [98]. But we, following the Hebrew truth, have included: “I remained.”

It should be noted that he did not say “I alone.” If he had said that, it would have seemed contradictory. Rather, he said, “I remained,” with the others who had marked foreheads understood. To know how deliberate this wording—“I remained”—is, consider the Book of Kings, when Elijah says to God: “They have demolished your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my life” (III Kings XIX, 14). He used “alone” because he did not know that others had remained.

Some think that, spoken from the person of the Lord, in whose type Ezekiel preceded him, this can be understood of the Jewish people, when “all turned aside and together became useless” (Ps. XIII). The Prophet testifies: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Ps. II, 1). For the Lord alone was found who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (I Peter II).

When he added, “pouring out your fury upon Jerusalem,” the word “pouring out” shows the magnitude of the punishments, as we read elsewhere: “Contempt has been poured out upon princes” (Ps. CVI, 40). And again: “My steps had almost slipped” [literally, “my steps were almost poured out”] (Ps. LXXII, 2).

In a good sense: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. V, 5); and: “Grace has been poured upon your lips” (Ps. XLIV, 3). In the contrary sense: “Pour out your fury upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name” (Jer. X; Ps. LXXVIII, 6); and: “Draw out the sword and shut it against those who persecute me” [literally, “pour out the sword”] (Ps. XXXIV, 3).

**(Verses 9, 10.)** And he said to me: “The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is filled with blood, and the city is filled with apostasy. For they said: ‘The Lord has abandoned the land, and the Lord does not see.’ Therefore my eye also will not spare, nor will I have pity; I will repay their ways upon their heads.”

When the Lord sees his prophet weeping for the people and marveling at the magnitude of the indignation, he gives the reasons—not, as the prophet thought, for an unjust or excessive punishment, but for a deserved and just sentence.

“The iniquity,” he says, “of the ten tribes of Israel and the two tribes of Judah is great”—and not merely great, but exceedingly great. Nor was it enough to say this; he repeats “exceedingly,” so that the magnitude of the punishment may correspond to the magnitude of the iniquity. From this we learn that sins are not, as many think, especially the Stoics, all equal, but that some are great and others small, and that the judging punishment differs according to the quality and measure of the sinners.

“The land is filled,” he says, “with blood,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “with peoples”; and “the city is filled with apostasy,” or, as the Vulgate edition has it, “with iniquity and uncleanness.” Not a little blood has been shed, but from gate to gate; and the whole city has turned away from the worship of God and, in its place, is full of uncleanness, namely, the filth of idolatry.

The cause of such great crimes is that they thought there was no providence over the earth and that God did not concern himself with mortal affairs, in accordance with what we read elsewhere (Virgil, Book IV of the *Aeneid*):

> “Surely this is the labor that troubles the gods above;  
> this is the care that disturbs their quiet.”

Since they either thought that there was no providence, or that the providence formerly present among the peoples had at that time abandoned its own people, therefore God’s eye will not spare, nor will he have pity. Thus, while raging against vices, he is merciful toward virtues, and he repays their ways and sins upon their heads—either upon the ruling faculty (*hegemonikon*, ἡγεμονικόν) of the heart, or upon the leaders of the people, according to the Book of Numbers, in which the leaders are called the heads of the peoples.

**(Verse 11.)** And behold, the man who was clothed in linen and had the writer’s inkwell at his loins answered, saying: [Col. 0091C] “I have done as you commanded me.”

The Septuagint: “And behold, the man who was clothed in the *podere*—that is, the ankle-length garment—and had girded his loins with a belt, answered and said: ‘I have done as you commanded me.’” [Note: [Col. 0091D] Jerome’s version has “on his back,” and answers with the word: “I have done as you commanded me.”]

He is the man who was commanded to pass through the middle of Jerusalem and place a mark on the foreheads of the men who groaned and grieved over all their iniquities. He therefore says that he has fulfilled the Lord’s commands and marked—or armed—the foreheads of the mourners with the sign of the letter *tau*.

The six men whom the Lord had commanded, saying, “Pass through the city after him and strike; have pity on no one, even to destruction,” report nothing of the kind. For they fulfilled a sentence not of joy but of sorrow, which is proved not by words but by deeds.

Here too, instead of *podere*, that is, the ankle-length garment, which the Septuagint translated, Theodotion retained the Hebrew word *baddim* (בַּדִּים); Symmachus has “linen”; Aquila, “the principal garment,” or “stole.” [100] For “belt,” Symmachus has “tablets”; Aquila, “inkwell”; Theodotion, *kasty* (κάστυ).

## Chapter 10

### Verses 1–2

And I saw, and behold, upon the firmament that was above the head of the Cherubim there appeared something like a sapphire stone, like the appearance of the likeness of a throne above it [Vulgate: above him]. And he said to the man who was clothed in linen, and he said: “Enter into the midst of the wheels that are beneath the Cherub [Vulgate: Cherubim], and fill your hands with burning coals that are between the Cherubim, and scatter them over the city.” [Col. 0092A]

Concerning the firmament that was above the Cherubim, and the sapphire stone that bore the likeness of a throne, and the wheels that followed the living creatures, it is enough to have spoken above; let the reader be satisfied with the explanation of those matters.

But now, concerning the command given to the one who was clothed in linen—for whom the Septuagint here interpreted *stola* (“robe”)—to take burning coals from the midst of the Cherubim and pour or scatter them over the city, it seems to me to indicate that, after the slaughter and killing of many, and after the corpses of the dead have fallen in the streets, burning coals are taken up in order either to punish or to cleanse Jerusalem, according to what is written in Isaiah: “[Note: [Col. 0092D] Victor: ‘he will sanctify,’ from the Greek ἁγιάσει.] He sanctified him in burning fire, and it will devour the material like hay” (Isa. X, 17).

These are the coals which the Prophet, when questioned, desires as a remedy for the tongue and [Col. 0092B] for falsehood, destroying vices and sins:

> “What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you,  
> against a deceitful tongue?  
> The sharp arrows of the mighty one,  
> together with destructive coals” (Ps. CXIX, 3–4).

We shall be able to find many things of this kind in the sacred Scriptures, concerning which we have often spoken. This alone should be noted: in Isaiah, who had sinned only in speech and had said that he possessed unclean lips, one coal is taken with tongs for his cleansing. Here, however, because the city was full of iniquity and, after the punishments, full of the corpses of the dead, many coals are taken up—not with one hand but with both—so that all Jerusalem may be cleansed.

Yet it may also be understood that the burning coals are taken up not for cleansing but for punishments and torments, [Col. 0092C] and that they are scattered over Jerusalem.

### Verses 3ff.

And he entered in before me. Now the Cherubim were standing on the right side of the house when the man entered, and the cloud filled the inner court. And the glory of the Lord was lifted up from above the Cherub to the threshold of the house, and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the splendor of the glory of the Lord. And the sound of the wings of the Cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty speaking.

And when he had commanded the man who was clothed in linen, saying, “Take fire from the midst of the wheels that are between the Cherubim,” he entered and stood beside the wheel. And one Cherub extended his hand from the midst of the Cherubim toward the fire that was between the Cherubim, and took it and placed it into the hands of the one who was clothed in linen. And when he had received it, he went out, and there appeared among the Cherubim the likeness of a human hand beneath their wings.

While the prophet was watching, the man clothed in a long robe or in linen entered; and, as the Septuagint now changes its translation, he entered in a holy robe, although among the Hebrews there is one word, *BADDIM*, and the other interpreters persist in the translation they began. He enters, as it is said a second time, into the midst of the wheels that are beneath the Cherubim, so that he may fill his hands with fiery coals.

When he had entered, he merely stood beside the wheel; and, either because of sorrow at the punishment of Jerusalem or because he was struck with awe by the greatness of the glory, he did not himself stretch out his hand toward the fire. Rather, one of the Cherubim—that is, a Cherub—stretched out his hand, took the fire that was in the midst of the Cherubim, and placed it in the hand of the one who was clothed in linen garments. Having received it, he went out; yet Scripture does not say what he did after going out, so that it might leave the narration of this sorrowful event to our understanding rather than place it before our eyes.

When the man clothed in linen garments entered, the Cherubim stood on the right side of the house, so that the holy and heavenly powers might be understood to occupy the right side of the house of God, while those who are sent for punishments—concerning whom it is written, “a sending among evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 49)—might be believed to possess the left side.

And when the glory of the Lord had been lifted up from the Cherub who was about to hand over the burning coals to the man, and had passed to the threshold of the house, immediately the inner court was filled with cloud, darkness, [Col. 0093B] and gloom. For punishments are not carried out in the presence of the majesty of the Lord, and the glory of the Lord is seen in the court concerning which it is written: “The sound of the wings of the Cherubim was heard as far as the outer court.”

In Hebrew, instead of “sound,” the word “voice” is used; and this voice had the likeness of the voice of God [Col. 0093B] Almighty speaking. For this the Septuagint translated, “like the voice of God *Saddai*.” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it with *ἱκανόν* (*hikanon*), which signifies “strong” or “powerful.”

Observe, reader, in what respects the former Vision and this one agree or differ, so that by comparing the two, without our prompting, you may understand the divine mysteries—and also what I pointed out earlier: that in the firmament, the throne, and the hand of a man, it is not reality but likeness that is spoken of. For we do not contemplate the glory of the Lord face to face with unveiled countenance; rather, we see everything in likeness and image, as long as we are surrounded by a fragile, corruptible, and mortal body (I Cor. XIII).

### Verses 8ff.

And I saw, and behold, four wheels beside the Cherubim: one wheel beside one Cherub, and another wheel beside another Cherub. The appearance of the wheels was like the appearance of a chrysolite stone, and their appearance was one likeness among the four, as though one wheel were within another wheel.

And when they moved in the four directions, they proceeded and did not turn back as they went. Rather, toward the place to which the first one inclined to go, the others followed, and they did not turn.

And their entire body, their necks, their hands, their wings, and their rims were full of eyes all around the four wheels. And he called these wheels “rolling ones,” while I was listening. Now one had four faces: one face was the face of a Cherub, the second was the face of a man, the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle; and the Cherubim were lifted up [variant: the Cherub was lifted up].

Observe what the appearance of the wheels was previously, or how many kinds of wheels there were according to the Septuagint: previously, “like the appearance of *tharsis*”; now, according to the same translators, “like the appearance of a carbuncle.” This seems to display the likeness of the wings through the fire that is handed over by the Cherub. Yet in Hebrew both above and here *THARSIS* is written; Aquila translated it as “chrysolite,” and Symmachus as “hyacinth.”

Again, where we have translated, “And their entire body”—with “of the wheels” understood—in Hebrew it is written: “And all their flesh, and their necks, and their hands, and their wings, and their rims.”

Observe that flesh is attributed to the heavenly powers, so that when we read, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, nor corruption incorruption” (I Cor. XV), we may know that it is not the substance of flesh but its works that are condemned. For *BASAR*, which is written in this place, signifies not “body” but “flesh.”

As for the rims of the wheels, he called them iron bands [*cantos*, as printed], by which the roundness of wooden objects is tightened and bound. These wheels, however, possess not only flesh or body [Col. 0094B] or limbs, but also necks, hands, and wings, so that we should understand the effectiveness of things in each part, not images of bodily members.

The wheels themselves are also called in the Hebrew language *GELGEL*, which Symmachus translated as “rolling ones” and Aquila as “wheel.”

Furthermore, what follows—“while I was listening,” up to the place where it is written, “The Cherubim were lifted up” [variant: “the Cherub was lifted up”]—is not found in the Septuagint but has been added from the Hebrew. In this it should be observed that it is by no means as stated above: “the face of a man and the face of a lion” [Note: [Col. 0093D] “The words ‘on the right,’ which had previously been placed after the name of the eagle, have been restored here with Victor, and joined to the name of the lion, in accordance with the authority of the sacred text and with the earliest Greek text of the LXX in chapter 1 above.]—four on the right—and “the face of a calf” four on the left—and “the face of an eagle” four; so that some are thought to be on the left and others on the right. Rather, the same order of all of them is described, when Scripture says:

> “One had four faces: one face was the face of a Cherub,  
> the second face was the face of a man,  
> the third was the face of a lion,  
> and the fourth was the face of an eagle.”

Thus the first, second, third, and fourth faces are described not by a difference of place, right and left, but in a single order by stages.

He called the first face—that is, the first one—a Cherub, whereas above he had said “the face of a calf.” From this it is understood that the face of a Cherub is the face of a calf. The explanation of the preceding vision contains the meaning of all these things.

### Verses 15ff.

It was the same living creature that I had seen beside the river Chobar. And when the Cherubim moved, the wheels also went alongside them [variant: “alongside it”]. And when the Cherubim lifted up their wings so that they might rise from the earth, the wheels did not resist [Note: [Col. 0093D] It appears to have happened recently through a scribal error that “they resisted” is read instead of “they remained,” which is preferred by Jerome’s Vulgate and by the Hebrew text, and has been approved by Victor. But since the sense is nearly the same and the manuscripts do not support the change, we have decided to alter nothing.]; rather, they too were alongside them. When those stood, the wheels stood; and when the Cherubim were lifted up, the wheels were lifted up with them. For the spirit of life was in them.

All things live for God and perceive their Creator. For he is not the God of the dead but of the living (Matt. XXII, 32). Hence all the bodies of the wheels are full of eyes (above, chapter I). And in the psalm it is said:

> “The heavens declare the glory of God,  
> and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.  
> Day pours forth the word to day,  
> and night announces knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII, 1–2).

The sun and moon also, the sea and rivers, mountains and hills, praise God; and the elements roll through their own circuit year by year. We discern the order of the heavens upon the earth, so that, preserving the order of the ancient Law, they may roll and run, and we may see nothing new upon the earth.

But when it is said, “It was the same living creature that I had seen beside the river Chobar” (Eccles. I), Scripture shows that in explaining the living creature we ought to understand the same things that we understood above.

### Verses 18ff.

And the glory of the Lord went out from the threshold of the Temple and stood above the Cherubim. And as the Cherubim lifted up their wings, they were raised from the earth before me. And as they went out, the wheels also followed them. And it stood at the entrance of the gate of the house of the Lord that faces east, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them [variant: above it].

It was the same living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chobar, and I understood that they were Cherubim: four faces for each one, and four wings for each one, and the likeness of a human hand beneath their wings. The likeness of their faces was the very faces that I had seen beside the river Chobar; and their appearance and the movement of each one was directed forward before its face.

The glory of the Lord, or majesty, which had stood at the threshold of the Temple, stood above the Cherubim. As they lifted up their wings, or as their wings were lifted up [variant: “which lifted up and were raised”], they were raised while the prophet watched, with the wheels following alongside them. And it stood at the entrance of the gate of the house of the Lord that faces east. Gradually the protection of God departed from Israel.

At first it was in the Temple; then it stood in the court of the Temple, or at the threshold. When it withdrew from the Temple, cloud and darkness filled the inner chambers of the Temple. Again the same glory sat above the [Col. 0095C] Cherubim; and when they immediately flew away and went toward the exterior, the wheels followed. And the glory stood at the gate of the house of the Lord that faces east—not at the door of the Temple, but beyond the court and the threshold, at the entrance of the gate of the house of the Lord that faces east.

When the prophet saw this, he said: “It is the same living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chobar, and I understood that they were Cherubim.”

For what new thing had he seen that enabled him to understand that they were Cherubim, when previously he had not understood this? In our language, *Cherubim* means “a multitude of knowledge”: the knowledge of the mysteries of God, and his throne and resting place. Hence in the psalm it is said:

> “You who sit upon the Cherubim, reveal yourself” (Ps. LXXIX, 2).

For the glory of the Lord always sits in the multitude of knowledge; and it is manifested when all things are shown to be governed by providence, so that no one may say that anything happens by chance, or say: “The Lord has abandoned the earth, and the Lord does not see” (above, IX, 9).

Hence the gaze of the Cherubim and their desire consists in forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what is ahead (Philipp. III).

## Chapter 11

### Verse 1

And the spirit lifted me up and brought me to the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, which faces the rising of the sun.

Since the glory of the Lord had gone out from the threshold of the Temple and stood above the Cherubim, and afterward, when the Cherubim flew away, the glory itself stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, and since the prophet could not go there by himself, he was lifted up by the spirit and brought to that same eastern gate of the house of the Lord, which faces the sun of righteousness, concerning whom it is written: “Behold, a man: East is his name” (Zech. VI, 12). Thus he would not remain in the Temple, which had been clouded with ignorance, but, standing at the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, would come to know the mysteries that follow.

### Verses 2ff.

And behold, at the entrance of the gate were twenty-five men; and I saw in their midst Jezonias the son of Azur, and Phaltias the son of Banaiah, princes of the people.

And he said to me: “Son of man, these are the men who devise iniquity and deliberate an evil plan in this city, saying: ‘Have not houses been built recently? This is the cauldron, and we are the flesh.’ Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, son of man.”

And the spirit of the Lord fell upon me and said to me: “Speak. Thus says the Lord: So you have spoken, house of Israel, and I know the thoughts of your heart. You have killed many in this city and filled its streets with the slain.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Your slain whom you placed in its midst—they are the flesh, and it is the cauldron. But I will bring you out from its midst. You feared the sword, and I will bring the sword upon you, says the Lord God. And I will drive you out from its midst, and I will give you into the hand of enemies, and I will execute judgments upon you. By the sword you shall fall. In the borders of Israel I will judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord. This city shall not be a cauldron for you, and you shall not be the flesh in its midst. In the borders of Israel I will judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0095D] We have deleted from the manuscripts, with the help of the following verse, the sentence “Because you have not walked in my commandments,” etc., since here it was recited not only superfluously but also awkwardly in the sequence of the text, whereas it is soon placed in its proper location.]

The following is not found in the Septuagint, [Col. 0096C] but has been added from the Hebrew:

> “Because you have not walked in my commandments,  
> and you have not kept my judgments,  
> but you have acted according to the judgments of the nations  
> that are around you.”

The prophet is taken up according to what is written: “The Lord raises up the meek” (Ps. CXLVI, 6); or he is lifted up from the earth and brought to the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, so that he may come to know the mysteries of the twenty-five men who were at the entrance of the gate, and of Jezonias the son of Azur and Phaltias the son of Banaiah, the princes of the people.

These men, then, who were at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, despairing of salvation and prepared for destruction through consciousness of their crimes, and unwilling to correct their sins through repentance, say: “Although houses have recently been built after the first captivity, houses that had previously collapsed, nevertheless we know that this city is like a cauldron, and that we are the flesh, so that we may be consumed and burned up in it,” according to what is written in Isaiah: “If the storm should pass through, it will not take us away” (Isa. XXVIII, 15).

When they said these things, the spirit of the Lord fell upon the prophet; and a second time he commands him to prophesy and say: “Because you have said these things, and the secrets of your hearts do not deceive me, I shall interpret for you how the city is a cauldron and you are reckoned as flesh—not according to the meaning that you expressed, but according to another meaning that you do not fear.

“Indeed, the city is in the likeness of a cauldron, but it will not be filled with your flesh; rather, with the flesh of those whom you killed. But you, who suppose that you will die in this city, I will bring out from the midst of the city and deliver into the hands of enemies. And I will execute judgments upon you, so that when you have fallen by the sword, not in the city and not outside the borders of Israel, but within the borders of your own province, you may then know that I am the Lord.”

A second time it is said: “In the borders of Israel I will judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord.” You shall suffer all these things because you have not walked in my commandments and have not kept my judgments, but have committed the crimes of the other nations around you.

Although what is said is clear according to the literal sense, let us temporarily pass over the names of Jezonias and Azur, Phaltias and Banaiah, which [Col. 0097B] we reserve for another time. We should say this: even today in the Church, which is the house of the Lord, both before the gate and at the entrance—or on the road of the gate, which signifies the Savior, through whom we enter to the Father—there are twenty-five men who refer everything to the senses.

As far as my memory does not fail me, I have never been able to find this number in a favorable sense, although in [Note: [Col. 0097D] Instead of the book of Leviticus, Victor substitutes the book of Numbers: “For this testimony is in Numbers IV, where, according to the Hebrew truth, we read in the Vulgate edition: ‘Take the sum of the sons of Kohath from the midst of the Levites, by their houses and families, from thirty years and above up to fifty years.’ In this passage the Septuagint reads, ἀπὸ εἴκοσι καὶ πέντε, that is, ‘from twenty-five years.’”] Leviticus they are selected for priestly service from the age of twenty-five. For in Hebrew this number is not found, although it is stated in the Septuagint; rather, the Hebrew has thirty, the age that is contained at the beginning of this prophet’s book and in the Lord’s age, when he came to the waters of the Jordan and was baptized by John (Luke III).

But if in the Gospel five wise virgins and five foolish ones are found (Matt. XXV), let us know that this number, placed in the middle, can according to the character of those who use it be referred either to the good or to the bad.

These men, then, who refer everything to the senses and have two princes—about whom we spoke above—are contained in the number two, which divides unity and, according to the Hebrew truth, does not appear to have been regarded by the Lord on the second day. Hence in Noah’s ark unclean creatures are brought in two by two (Gen. VI).

But the Lord, compressing division into unity, made both one and destroyed the dividing wall, condemning hostility in his flesh (Eph. II). Hence he speaks in a more exalted and sublime manner: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 3), so that he might recall us from Jewish duality into the unity of Christian faith.

Finally, after the Jewish priesthood had been lost, the Lord suffers not under one ruler but under two, Annas and Caiaphas, in order to show the divided [variant: false] error of their religion.

There are many at the entrance of this gate before the eastern house of the Lord who are compared, through their vices, with the nations; through consciousness of their sins they despair of salvation, and say: “The city in which we live is a cauldron, and we are all the flesh; we shall be consumed by Babylonian fire, whose arrows are fiery.” They are unwilling to practice repentance and despair of salvation. Therefore they hear that they themselves are not the flesh of the former and ruined city, but those whom they have caused to stumble and whom they have killed.

For this reason the sword is brought upon them, so that, after they have been judged in the borders of Israel—not among the nations but among Christians—they may then know that he is the Lord, according to what is read in the Psalms: “When he slew them, they sought him” (Ps. LXXVII, 34). Thus they may recognize through torments the one whom they had not perceived through benefits.

### Verse 13

And it happened, while I was prophesying, that Phaltias the son of Banaiah died. And I fell upon my face, crying out with a loud voice, and I said: “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God! Are you making an end of the remnant of Israel?”

While the prophet was prophesying, one of the two princes, Phaltias the son of Banaiah, died. His name is interpreted as “turning away in ruin,” and he is the son of a builder or mason; for *οἰκοδόμος* (*oikodomos*) cannot be translated otherwise into our language.

The other prince, Jezonias the son of Azur, is preserved unharmed. *Jezonias* means “his ears,” with “of the soul” understood. *Azur*, however, means “support” or “assistance.”

Therefore the one who, by falling, had turned away from the Lord and had been of a most evil construction rightly falls while the one whom God strengthened is prophesying. But the one who obeyed God’s commandments and was sustained and supported by his help rightly remains in authority over the people.

We read in Exodus (chapter II) that, after Pharaoh the king of Egypt died, the children of Israel groaned under the works of clay, straw, and bricks, and cried out to the Lord, whom while Pharaoh was alive they could not invoke.

Isaiah also (chapter VI), after Uzziah the leprous king had died, saw the Lord seated upon a high and elevated throne, with Seraphim standing around him. And when he understood that he had unclean lips and lived among a people with unclean lips, he deserved that a coal be sent from the altar and cleanse his unclean lips.

Here, however, while the strength of God is prophesying, the prince who had turned away from the service of the Lord falls, so that he may be raised up by Christ. For if the Lord is resurrection, the devil is ruin.

Here it is asked how it can be said of the Savior: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke II, 34). He is for the fall of those who were standing in an evil manner, and for the resurrection of those who had fallen.

When the prophet saw this, he fell upon his face—not because he had sinned, but from the emotion of one who mourned. And with a loud voice, which arose from the great ardor of faith, he cried out three times and said: “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God! Are you making an end of the remnant of Israel?”

The meaning is: even those remnants that had seemed to remain among the people are, because you are indignant, being destroyed.

### Verses 14ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, your brothers, your brothers; the men of your kindred, and the whole house of Israel, all of them, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: ‘Go far away from the Lord; this land has been given to us as a possession.’

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because I have sent them far away among the nations, and because I have scattered them throughout the land [variant: ‘I have dispersed them throughout the lands,’] I shall be for them a little sanctuary in the lands to which they have gone” [Vulgate: “to which they went”].

The Septuagint has:

> “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:  
> ‘Son of man, your brothers and the men of your captivity,  
> and the whole house of Israel has been brought to an end,  
> to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said:  
> “You have gone far away from the Lord;  
> the land has been given to us as an inheritance.”’  
> Therefore he says:  
> ‘Thus says Adonai the Lord:  
> I will drive them away among the nations,  
> and I will scatter them throughout every land,  
> and I will be for them a little sanctuary  
> in the regions into which they have entered.’”

First, something must be said about the variation in translation. Where the Hebrew has “the men of your kindred”—for this is what *GOOLATHACH* signifies—the Septuagint translated “the men of your captivity.”

Then, where it follows, “all of them to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said,” instead of “all,” they have placed “has been brought to an end,” because of the ambiguity of the letters and the word. For *CHULLO*, which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as “all,” they translated as “has been brought to an end,” which according to the meaning does not correspond at all. [Note: [Col. 0099] One Vatican manuscript, together with the very ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain belonging to Montfaucon, has *CHOLLO*.]

The word of the Lord therefore came to Ezekiel, who had said: “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God! Are you making an end of the remnant of Israel?”—namely, in the death of Phaltias and of those who were killed with him. The remnants, he says, are not those whom the prophet thought were in Jerusalem, but those who appeared to be captives in Babylon.

The meaning is: “Son of man, your brothers, born from the same stock as you—your brothers, I say—to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: ‘You have gone away from the Lord because you are captives and surrendered yourselves with Jechoniah; but the land of Israel has been given to us as an eternal possession.’

“Tell them, therefore, that although I have indeed removed them far from the land of Israel, scattered them among the nations, and commanded them to live in foreign lands, yet because they have obeyed my command, I shall be present among them even in foreign and hostile places as a little sanctuary. For many of them will be found who do not bow their necks to idolatry, but remember the commandments of God, as Daniel and the three youths did; and it must be believed that the others did likewise, after the example of such great leaders as Scripture now recalls (Dan. III).”

From all these things we learn that we must not insult those who have been handed over to punishments by the judgment of God, nor reproach a person who has turned away from his sins, nor ever say to penitents and those who have departed from the Church: “You have gone far away from the Lord; the land has been given to us as a possession.”

For thus says the Lord: “Although I have separated them for a little while from my Church and scattered them among the nations, nevertheless I shall be for them a little sanctuary, while they remember their sins, so that those who withdrew from their place [variant: ‘from their land’] because of their vices may hasten, through repentance, to return to their former dwellings.”

### Verses 17ff.

“Therefore speak: Thus says the Lord God: I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you from the lands in which you have been scattered, and I will give you the soil of Israel. And they shall enter there and remove from it all offenses and all its abominations [Vulgate adds: ‘its’].

“And I will give them one heart [or: another heart], and I will put a new spirit within them. And I will take the heart of stone out of their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments, keep my judgments, and perform them; and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God.

“But as for those whose heart walks after their offenses and abominations, I will place their way upon their own head, says the Lord God.”

The divine word speaks to those who were captives in the land of Babylon, to the brothers of the prophet Ezekiel and to his kindred, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem [variant: “of Israel”] said: “You have gone far away from the Lord; the land has been given to us as a possession.”

It speaks the following words to them: “I will gather you from the peoples and return the land of Israel to you. And when you have entered it, you shall remove all the idols by which you offended God. And I will give you one heart of fear and service toward God, so that you may no longer serve different idols—or another heart than the one you previously possessed.”

“And I will give a new spirit within you,” according to what is written: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. L, 12).

“And I will take away from you the heart of stone,” that is, a hard heart, according to what Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, says: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart” (Acts VII, 51). Pharaoh’s heart is also hardened so that he will not release the people of Israel (Exod. VII).

“And I will give you,” he says, “a heart of flesh”—soft and tender, and able to receive the commandments of God, so that they may be written on tablets of fleshly hearts.

A soft heart is therefore given and a hard heart removed so that they may walk in the commandments of God, keep his judgments, and be among the people of God; and so that the Lord, who previously had been their adversary, may be their God.

But those who do not correct their former sins through repentance, but walk after their abominations, he says he will repay with what they deserve, so that their ways may be placed upon their heads.

Many believe that these things happened under Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, under Jeshua the son of Jehozadak the high priest, and under Ezra and Nehemiah, to the tribe of Judah and to those who returned with them.

They also believe that the inhabitants of Jerusalem who were captured under Zedekiah king of Judah, or who fled with Jeremiah into Egypt, were scattered throughout all the lands and never returned to the city of Jerusalem.

But the complete conversion of those who were captives, and of the remnant of Israel, is understood in Christ, when the remnants were saved, and three thousand believed in one day, and afterward five thousand (Acts II); and others concerning whom James says to the apostle Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands of believing Jews there are; they are all zealous for the Law” (Acts XXI, 20).

Even today the proud inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, whose heart walks after their offenses and abominations, deserve the offense of God. But those who were outside, when their heart of stone has been removed and they have received the softest heart, return to the Church through repentance; they walk in the commandments of the Lord, keep his judgments, become the people of the Lord, and the Lord, whom they had previously offended, becomes their God.

### Verses 22–23

And the Cherubim lifted up their wings, and the wheels with them, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them [variant: above it]. And the glory of the Lord ascended from the midst of the city and stood upon the mountain that is east of the city.

Gradually the glory of the Lord withdraws from Jerusalem. First, abandoning the Temple, it stands in the court or at the threshold of the house; afterward at the entrance of the eastern gate; finally, with its wings lifted up and the wheels following, it stands upon the mountain that is east of the city—clearly signifying the Mount of Olives, from which the Savior ascended to the Father.

The glory of the Lord, which had departed from the city of Jerusalem, stood upon the Mount of Olives as a sign of resurrection and light, so that from there it might look upon Jerusalem, which was destined to perish and burn.

And when he says, “The glory ascended from the midst of the city” (John XIV, 31), the Lord says the same thing to the disciples in other words: “Rise; let us go from here” (Luke XIII, 35). And to the Jews: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

Josephus also [Note: [Col. 0101] See what we have observed elsewhere on this matter, especially in volume I, on Epistle 18, section 9.] reports that a voice of angels and heavenly powers was heard in the Temple—those who had previously guarded the city—saying: “Let us depart from these places” (Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*).

And, remarkably, even to the present day the glory of the Lord, which abandoned the Temple, stands upon the Mount of Olives and, shining in the sign of the cross, looks upon the former Jewish Temple, dissolved into ashes and cinders.

### Verses 24–25

And the spirit lifted me up and brought me into Chaldea, to the captivity, in a vision, in the spirit of God; and the vision that I had seen was taken up from me. And I spoke to the captivity all the words of the Lord that he had shown me.

Where we translated from the Hebrew truth, “And the vision that I had seen was taken up from me,” the Septuagint translated, “And I ascended from the vision that I had seen.”

Both expressions signify that the prophet was not transferred bodily from Babylon to Jerusalem, but in spirit. When the vision that had led him in spirit to Jerusalem and had shown him all that the preceding discourse narrated was taken away, he returned to himself and spoke to the captivity everything that had been shown to him—namely, to those concerning whom it was written above: “I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting beside me, and there the hand of the Lord God fell upon me, and I saw” (above, VIII, 1).

In a remarkable manner, while those who had come to visit him were sitting beside him, the prophet beheld mystical visions: he was absent from those sitting before him in spirit, yet physically present.

Everything occurs so that those who were captives might receive consolation: they would be brought back to the land of Israel, walk in the commandments of the Lord, become his people, and he would become their God.

But those who were not converted to repentance, and instead walked after their abominations, receive what they have done. We have often pointed out that in the sacred Scriptures “words” are frequently spoken in place of realities.

## Chapter XII

### Verses 1ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, you dwell in the midst of a rebellious house, which has eyes to see and does not see, and ears to hear and does not hear, because it is a rebellious house.”

For what we translated as “You dwell in the midst of a rebellious house,” the Septuagint has: “You dwell in the midst of their iniquities.” But from what follows—“because it is a rebellious house”—we understand that the former sentence also suits this verse. We have often taught that “rebellion” may likewise be rendered “bitterness,” so that the sense is: “You dwell in the midst of a house that turns things toward bitterness,” a house that makes God, who is sweet and compassionate by nature, bitter and cruel through the bitterness of its vices.

Otherwise, we read of God: “Taste and see that the Lord is gracious,” or “sweet” (Psalm 33:9). The prophet dwells in the midst of a people who provoke God to bitterness, a people that has eyes and does not see and ears and does not hear—not through any defect of the senses, but through the obstinacy of its perversity. Hence the Lord also says to the Jews: “If you were blind, you would have no sin” (John 9:41), reproving and condemning their voluntary blindness.

Since, then, they have eyes to see and do not see, and ears to hear and do not hear, and despise your words, teach them through image and picture; display things by bodily representations, so that they may recognize the captivity that is to come not only by hearing but also with their eyes.

### Verse 3

“Therefore, son of man, prepare for yourself baggage for exile, and you shall go into exile [the Vulgate: ‘you shall be transported’] before their eyes. You shall go from your place to another place in their sight, if perhaps they will look, because it is a rebellious house.”

The Septuagint has: “And you, son of man, prepare for yourself baggage of captivity; and go into captivity by day before them; and go from your place to another place in their sight, so that they may see that it is a rebellious house.”

There is no doubt that the entire content of this passage indicates the future captivity of King Zedekiah of the tribe of Judah, who was captured together with Jerusalem. But since some wish Zedekiah’s captivity—his name is interpreted as “the Lord is righteous”—to precede typologically as a figure of the Savior, who descended from the heavenly realms to earthly things and assumed a human body, and since they take these things to be “baggage of captivity,” I think it necessary to warn the prudent and careful reader that we include these interpretations so that we may not appear to omit anything, but that we do not approve them.

For an impious king cannot precede as a figure of the one who is the example of all piety. Jeremiah the prophet and the history of Kings relate that Zedekiah was captured by the Babylonians and Chaldeans and led from one place to another (Jeremiah 39; 2 Kings 25)—that is, from Jerusalem to Babylon—as well as the other events that Ezekiel recounts in what follows. Those who refer this to the Lord Jesus Christ think that his captivity and migration from place to place signify his descent from the heavenly realms to earthly things.

### Verses 4ff.

“And you shall bring out your baggage by day, before their eyes, like the baggage of one going into exile. You yourself shall go out in the evening before them, as one goes out who is migrating before their eyes. Dig through the wall for yourself, and go out through it before their eyes. You shall carry [the Vulgate: ‘you shall be carried’] upon your shoulders; in darkness you shall escape [the Vulgate: ‘you shall be brought out’]. You shall cover your face and shall not see the land, because I have made you a portent for the house of Israel.”

The Septuagint has: “And you shall bring out your baggage of captivity by day before their eyes. And you shall go out in the evening before them, as a captive goes out. Dig through the wall for yourself, and you shall pass through it before their eyes. You shall be carried upon your shoulders, and you shall go out concealed. You shall cover your face and shall not see the land, because I have made you a portent for the house of Israel.”

The prophet is commanded to perform symbolically what Zedekiah will do in reality. “Gather your baggage,” he says—for this is the baggage of one going into exile—“while they watch. After they have seen what you will do, you shall go out in the evening in the likeness of one going into exile.”

We read that Zedekiah fled by night, after the wall had been broken through, toward the desert places of the Jordan, and was there seized by the Babylonians; this is signified by the wall being pierced. When he says, “You shall carry upon your shoulders,” the baggage is understood, together with whatever fugitives customarily carry as provisions for a journey. “In darkness you shall escape” [another reading: “you shall bring out”], so that you may not be seen by anyone.

“You shall cover your face”—either because of the blindness that befell him when Nebuchadnezzar tore out his eyes, or so that it might not be recognized that he himself was the king, thereby increasing the vigilance of those guarding him. What follows, “You shall not see the land,” signifies that he was led blind into Babylon and did not see it.

“Because I have made you a portent for the house of Israel,” he says; for the words and deeds of the prophets are both signs and figures. Hence in Zechariah men are called portentous because they portend future things (Zechariah 3). And in Hosea God says: “I have been represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hosea 12:10).

Those who wish Christ to be understood in the person of Ezekiel take the “baggage of captivity” as the human body; the pierced wall as the barrier of hell, which he shattered; and his being seen only by believers after rising again. He was carried upon shoulders when, victorious, he ascended to heaven with the angelic powers. He goes out concealed and covers his face so that the divine majesty may not be seen in mortal flesh; and he does not see the land so that it may not be illuminated by his eyes, since it does not deserve his gaze. For “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Psalm 33:16), and he turns his face away from the impious.

They say that he did all these things in order that, through the likeness of a human being, he might turn the hard hearts of the Israelite people toward faith. He is also given as a portent to the house of Israel, according to what is written: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many, and as a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2:24).

### Verses 7–8

“So I did as he had commanded me: I brought out my baggage by day, like the baggage of one migrating [the Vulgate: ‘of one going into exile’], and in the evening I dug through the wall with my hand. I went out in darkness, and I carried [the Vulgate: ‘was carried upon’] upon my shoulders before their eyes.”

The Septuagint has: “And I did according to everything he had commanded me. And I brought out my baggage by day, like baggage of captivity; and in the evening I dug through the wall with my hand, and I went out concealed. I was taken up upon my shoulders before their eyes.”

He testifies that he fulfilled by deed what he had previously been commanded to do. It requires no interpretation, according to either version, beyond what has already been explained.

This, however, should be noted: at one and the same time Jeremiah was prophesying in Jerusalem and Ezekiel in Babylon. Jeremiah’s prophecy was sent to the captives, while Ezekiel’s was sent to those who were living in Jerusalem, so that God’s providence might be shown to operate in different regions and those who heard might understand that whatever happened to the people came about not through the power of idols but by the command of the Lord.

### Verse 9
