And the word of the Lord came to me in the morning, saying: “Son of man, surely the house of Israel, the rebellious house, did not say to you, ‘What are you doing?’

Say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God.’”

If, he says, the rebellious house asks you, “Why are you doing these things?”—or, according to the Septuagint, even if they do not ask—go in, so that they may know why you have done these things. Say to them: “Thus says the Lord God.”

### Verses 10ff.

[Note: In conformity with the Vulgate edition, Victor prefers that “leader” (*ducem*) be read here; for he thinks that “prince” is derived from the Septuagint’s Greek ἄρχοντι. He likewise reads a little later, “But the leader who is in the midst,” etc.; he maintains this from Jerome’s repeated reading in the Commentary itself.]

“‘This burden is upon the prince who is in Jerusalem, and upon all the house of Israel that is in their midst.’ Say: ‘I am your portent. As I have done, so shall it be done to them. They shall go into exile and captivity. The prince who is in their midst shall be carried upon shoulders; he shall go out in darkness. They shall dig through the wall to bring him out. His face shall be covered so that he may not see the ground with his eyes [the Vulgate: ‘with his eye’]. I shall spread my net over him, and he shall be caught in my snare. I shall bring him to Babylon, to the land of the Chaldeans, but he shall not see it; there he shall die.

“‘All those who are around him, his protection and his troops, I shall scatter in every wind. I shall draw the sword after them, and they shall know that I am the Lord when I scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands [the Vulgate: ‘throughout the land’]. I shall leave a few men among them, spared from sword, famine, and pestilence, so that they may recount all their abominations among the nations to which they shall enter; and they shall know that I am the Lord.’”

First let us explain the historical meaning. “Say,” he says, “to them, son of man”—whether they ask or do not ask—“What are you doing? That burden and vision concern the prince who is in Jerusalem,” signifying Prince Zedekiah. And say: “I am your portent,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “I am the one who makes portents,” so that the future may be known from present events.

“As I have done, so shall it be done to them”—to the prince and to all who are in the prince’s company. They shall be led captive into Babylonian exile, and the prince who is in their midst shall be carried upon the shoulders either of animals or of those who had fled with him. He shall go out in darkness and in the night’s gloom; his companions shall dig through the wall to bring him out. His face shall be covered either through the fear of a fugitive or because of the injury of blindness, so that, being blind, he may not see the land of Babylon.

“I shall spread my net over him, and he shall be caught in my snare.” For by the Lord’s permission he was captured by the Babylonians, and he testifies that he himself caused the things inflicted upon him by his enemies. Led to Babylon, he shall not see the land of the Chaldeans, and there he shall die in captivity.

As for all his companions, helpers, and fellow fugitives, once he has been captured I shall scatter them here and there and not permit them to depart in safety. Rather, I shall draw my sword against them into the hands of their enemies, so that when they have been scattered among the nations they may understand that I am the Lord and that all these things have happened by my will.

“I shall leave,” he says, “a few of his companions who fled with him and were able to escape—those who escaped sword, famine, and pestilence—so that, when they have reached different regions either through flight or captivity, they may recount all their crimes, in word and by example, on account of which they deserved such great evils, and may understand that I am the Lord.”

But he who attempts to explain this tropologically, continuing the interpretation already begun concerning the Savior, interprets “the prince who is in the midst of Jerusalem” as the one who went beforehand as a portent and sign: both he and his companions are captives of this world, and, rising victoriously from the dead, he was carried upon the shoulders of angels. He went out in darkness, unknown to unbelievers; after destroying the dividing wall, he made the two one. His face was covered so that he would not look upon the land of the Jews (Ephesians 2).

Nor is it surprising that the Lord concealed his face, since to this day a veil lies before the face of Moses for the unbelieving people. The Lord spread his net over him, according to what the bride says of him in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, appearing through the lattice” (Song of Songs 2:9).

Of him Jeremiah also says: “The breath of our face, Christ the Lord, was captured in our sins” (Lamentations 4:20). And: “Although he had committed no sin, he was made sin for us” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

“And he shall be brought,” he says, “to Babylon”—the confusion of this world—and to the land of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as “demons,” so that he might draw those who had been enslaved to demons back to salvation and lead captive their former captivity. “He shall not see the land of the Chaldeans, and there he shall die,” so that by his death he might give life to us all.

He scattered all his helpers and companions—the apostles and apostolic men—throughout the whole world. He drew the sword after them so that they might be crowned with various martyrdoms. Then they themselves, or those who had come to believe through them, would understand that he is the Lord, and that he had therefore scattered them among the nations and dispersed them throughout the lands so that they might bear abundant fruit.

He left a few men among them, such as the apostle John and the others, who were spared from sword, famine, and pestilence and who avoided the violence of persecutions, so that they might recount the crimes of the Jews and the iniquities of all the nations to which they had gone; and so that, after repentance had been performed, they might know that he is the Lord.

We have said this while leaving the judgment to the reader’s discretion. In any case, there is no doubt that it is dangerous to compare the captivity and death of an impious king with the mystery of the Lord.

### Verses 17ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, eat your bread in agitation [the Vulgate adds: ‘but’], and drink your water in haste and sorrow. And say [the Vulgate: ‘you shall say’] to the people of the land: ‘Thus says the Lord God to those who dwell in Jerusalem, in the land of Israel: They shall eat their bread in anxiety, and they shall drink their water in desolation, so that the land may be desolated because of its abundance, on account of the iniquity of all who dwell in it. The cities that are now inhabited shall be desolate, and the land shall be deserted; and you shall know that I am the Lord.’”

The Septuagint has: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Son of man, you shall eat your bread with grief, and you shall drink your water with torment and anguish. And you shall say to the people of the land: Thus says Adonai the Lord to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, upon the land of Israel: They shall eat their bread in poverty, and they shall drink their water in devastation, so that the land and its fullness may be devastated. For all who dwell in it are in impiety, and their inhabited cities shall be desolate; the land shall be devastated, and you shall know that I am the Lord.’”

After the prophecy concerning the prince and his companions, which had been displayed through a bodily image, he comes to the people. Whatever is said to the prophet is reported through the prophet to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: in the calamity of the siege they will eat their bread in distress and poverty, and they will drink their water not in abundance but with torment and tribulation.

“These things,” he says, “are spoken to you, O prophet, so that you may speak to the people of your land and say: ‘Thus says the Lord to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, which is in the land of Israel: Besieged by Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, you will endure the evil of hunger and thirst, so that the whole land, with its fullness [another reading: ‘multitude’], may be destroyed,’” signifying the inhabitants through the land that is inhabited.

“And lest they think that this happens to them without cause, say to them that because of their crimes and impieties all the cities of Judea must be reduced to desolation, and the cultivation of the whole land must perish, so that they may recognize the God who rages, whom they were unwilling to recognize as merciful.”

According to the anagogical sense, we can speak of the inhabitants of Jerusalem as believers in Christ who dwell in the Church. If through their sins they have deserved his displeasure, let them eat bread in poverty and drink water with sorrow and anguish—not enduring the food of bread or the drink of water, but a famine of the word and teaching of God (Amos 8).

For whenever, either through the fault of rulers who are to be captured and handed over to the Babylonians, or through our own hardness, we lose the word of God and are no longer worthy to possess useful waters, then in sorrow and want we shall take our food. The earth will lose its multitude of believers, and the cities—understood as the Churches throughout the whole world—will be desolated. The land will be deserted, so that all may know that the Lord has been offended. We can understand this also in the time of persecution.

### Verses 21ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, what is this proverb that you have in the land of Israel, saying: ‘The days will be prolonged, and every vision will perish’?

“Therefore say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God: I shall put an end to this proverb, and it shall no longer be commonly spoken in Israel.’ And say to them that the days have drawn near, and the word of every vision. For there shall no longer be any empty vision, nor ambiguous divination in the midst of the children of Israel. For I am the Lord: I shall speak whatever word I speak, and it shall happen. It shall no longer be delayed; but in your days, rebellious house, I shall speak the word and perform it, says the Lord God.”

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, behold, the house of Israel is saying: ‘The vision that this man sees is for many days, and he prophesies for distant times.’

“Therefore say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God: None of my words shall be delayed any longer. The word that I speak shall be fulfilled,’ says the Lord God.”

What we called “proverb,” Symmachus and all the other interpreters translated as “parable,” which in Hebrew is called MASAL ().

Again, where we rendered, “Nor shall there be ambiguous divination,” the Septuagint translated: “Nor shall there be a diviner according to grace.” In place of this, all the others translated “slippery,” which we rendered “ambiguous,” so that we may understand that the words of the prophets deceive those who listen to them.

The sense of the entire chapter is this: above, he had prophesied against the prince who was in Jerusalem; then he had announced that famine and burning thirst were to come upon the people. Since the multitude did not believe this, it adopted an old and familiar proverb: “The threat of the prophets is deferred for a long time, and every vision will perish, since it is seen in vain”; or, according to Symmachus, διαπνεύσει, that is, “it will dissolve into wind and a thin breeze.”

“Say, therefore,” he says, “to them that my threat will by no means be delayed, nor will false and ambiguous divination be uttered to the peoples with an uncertain ending, so that it is spoken at one time and fulfilled at another. Rather, now—in the lifetime of you who speak and of those who hear—the word that I have spoken shall be fulfilled.”

He signifies the imminent captivity of the city of Jerusalem and the impending capture of Zedekiah together with the people of Judah.

Not only at that time, but even to this day, the unbelieving crowd and the hard hearts of mortals do not receive God’s prophecy. Everything that the prophets threaten, and everything that the Gospel proclaims, they think is to be deferred to another time.

We should understand here that the “parable” placed by the Septuagint is to be taken as a “proverb,” according to what we read in the psalm: “I became a parable to them” (Psalm 68:12). And in this same prophet: “What is this parable to you among the people of Israel, who say: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge’?” (below, 18:2).

We touch briefly upon what is clear, so that we may linger over what is obscure.

# Book Four

I would wish, Eustochium, if it were possible, to set out the explanations of Ezekiel in separate books according to the individual prophecies, and not to divide by exposition what is joined together in prophecy, so that the course might be easier both for the one dictating and for the one reading. I would also wish to separate the long and immense journey of interpretation by fixed intervals, so that, as it were, through titles and indexes—or, to speak more precisely, through summaries—I might show what each book contains.

But what shall I do, when some prophecies are short and others long, so that necessity often compels us both to compress several into one book and to divide one among many? Hence now, in the fourth book, we wish to include the material against the prophets and prophecies, also against the elders of the people of Israel, and against the land upon which four most grievous plagues are brought, as well as the passage about the vine-wood, which, once cut down, is useless among all the trees of the forests, and also a catalogue of the vices of Jerusalem.

Since the narrowness of a single volume does not permit this to be contained in one book, we reserve the second part for the fifth volume, warning the most discerning reader in advance so that he may know what we must explain in this volume and what he must read in the next.

## Chapter XIII

### Verses 1–2

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who prophesy, and say to those who prophesy from their own heart: Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God.”

The Septuagint omitted what we have placed—“who prophesy, and say to those who prophesy from their own heart”—and, in place of what is not found in the Hebrew, added: “And you shall prophesy, and say to them.”

The passage is directed against false prophets who deceived the people and, contrary to God’s commandments, prophesied something else. No one should be troubled that they are called prophets, for Holy Scripture has the custom of calling each person a prophet of his own prophecy and speech. Thus the prophets of Baal, the prophets of idols, and the prophets of confusion are so called.

Hence the apostle Paul also calls a Greek poet a prophet: “One of their own prophets said: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies” (Titus 1:12). And in Hosea we read: “Like a prophet, a man who is mad and carries the spirit” (Hosea 9:7).

Whatever was said at that time to the Israelite people is now referred to the Church, so that the holy prophets are the apostles and apostolic men. The lying and frenzied prophets, however, are all heretics, whose leaders fabricate doctrines from their own hearts, while those who have been led astray by them acquiesce in the lies of others.

### Verse 3

“Woe to the foolish prophets, who follow their own spirit and see nothing.”

The Septuagint has: “Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart and do not see at all,” omitting what we have set forth: “who follow their own spirit.”

Since, according to the rule of Scripture, the name “prophets” is shared by the good and the evil, they differ in this: the good prophets are called wise, while the evil are called foolish and senseless. The former refers to ecclesiastical men, the latter to all heretics, who abandon the Spirit of God and follow their own spirit, since they prophesy not through divine inspiration but from their own heart. Hence they see nothing.

The one who is wise follows not the thoughts of his own heart but the Spirit of God, according to what is said earlier (above, 1), where the living creatures and the wheels followed the Spirit of God. The prophet also says: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Psalm 26:11). And elsewhere: “Lead me in the right path” (Psalm 142:10). Again: “Your good Spirit shall lead me into a level land” (Psalm 59). For the people of God, the pillar of fire and the cloud were guides in the wilderness (Exodus 13). Jeremiah says: “I have not wearied in following you” (Jeremiah 17:16).

Which of the heretics who follows his own spirit does not stumble in darkness, and, being blind, lead the blind into a pit? Although they may seem to themselves to see more in their mysteries—or rather, in their orgies—than the teachers of the Church, nevertheless they see absolutely nothing, because they have lost the sun of righteousness.

In vain they imitate those who were formerly called “seers,” to whom it is said: “You who see, go away; withdraw into the land of Judah, and do not prophesy in Bethel” (Amos 7:12–13). Hence the visions of Isaiah and Obadiah are placed in titles. And the Lord commanded the apostles: “Lift up your eyes and see” (John 4:35). The prophet also prays: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118:18).

### Verses 4ff.

“Your prophets, Israel, shall be like foxes in the deserts [the Vulgate: ‘were’]. You did not go up to the breach, nor did you build a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord. They see vanity and divine falsehood, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although the Lord has not sent them; and they persist in confirming the word. Have you not seen an empty vision and spoken a lying divination? And you say, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although I have not spoken.”

The Septuagint has: “As foxes in the deserts, so are your prophets, Israel” [another reading adds: “were” or “shall be”]. “They did not stand in the firmament, and they gathered flocks against the house of Israel. They did not rise up, those who say, ‘On the day of the Lord,’ seeing lies and divining vanities, who say, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although the Lord did not send them; and they began to raise up a word. Have you not seen a false vision and spoken vain divinations? And you were saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although I have not spoken.”

Let us first discuss the Hebrew text. The prophets of Israel are like foxes, stealing domestic birds every day. According to Aquila and the Septuagint, they dwell in deserts; according to Symmachus and Theodotion, among walls and ruins. They cannot go up to the breach or set up a wall for the house of Israel.

We read that Aaron confronted the fire devouring the people of Israel, stood in the midst, and built a wall for the people’s salvation (Numbers 16). Jeremiah too is told not to confront the Lord or stand against his anger through persistent prayer (Jeremiah 7). Just as a wall is set against an enemy and an adversary is usually confronted face-to-face, so the sentence of God is broken by the prayers of the saints.

Hence Moses is told: “Let me alone, and I shall destroy this people.” For when someone is told, “Let me alone” (Exodus 32:10), it is shown that he has the power to restrain. These prophets cannot stand in battle on the day of the Lord, fighting and resisting God’s sentence on behalf of the people through their prayers and supplications.

Because they see vanity, divine falsehood, and claim to have been sent by the Lord when they have not been sent by him, and because they persist in their errors and desire to establish their own word, they are accused of making everything they proclaim empty, calling their own lie the word of the Lord.

According to the Septuagint, however, the sense is this: all heretics, because of their deceit and wickedness, are like foxes, of whom the Savior says: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests” (Matthew 8:20). And it is written concerning Herod: “Tell that fox” (Luke 13:32).

Concerning the same foxes, who deceive the little and simple and ravage Christ’s vineyard, Solomon says: “Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song of Songs 2:15). And in the psalm it is sung concerning those who are overthrown by their deceit: “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be handed over to the power of the sword; they shall become portions for foxes” (Psalm 62:10–11).

These prophets, who are like foxes, did not stand in the firmament. They were not worthy to hear with Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matthew 16:18). Nor are they like Moses, to whom it was said: “But you, stand here with me” (Deuteronomy 5:31). Nor are they like the one who says: “He set my feet upon a rock.” Rather, they were tossed about by every wind of doctrine.

They did not stand in the firmament, of which we read in the eighteenth psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.” They gathered every irrational person against the house of God; because of their excessive innocence, these people are like sheep.

Hence it now says: “And they gathered flocks against the house of Israel.” They themselves did not rise, nor could they raise up others. Whatever they did and do is full of lies.

What follows—“And they began to raise up a word”—signifies that they wish to rise and lift themselves toward lofty things, but cannot accomplish what they desire. They are told: “Have you not seen a false vision and spoken vain divinations?”

The final clause, “And you were saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although I have not spoken,” is not found in the Septuagint.

### Verses 8–9

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have spoken vanity and seen a lie, therefore, behold, I am against you,” says the Lord God. “And my hand shall be against the prophets who see vanity and divine falsehood. They shall not be in the council of my people, nor shall they be registered in the record of the house of Israel; nor shall they enter the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord God.”

The Septuagint has: “Therefore say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because your words are false and your divinations vain, therefore, behold, I am against you, says the Lord God. And I shall stretch out my hand against the prophets who see falsehood and speak vanities. They shall not be in the discipline of my people, nor shall they be registered in the record of the house of Israel, and they shall not enter the land of Israel; and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord.”

Under the person of the prophets, the discourse is directed against heretics who speak vanity, see falsehood, and persist in establishing their own doctrine. The Lord himself comes and rises against them, stretches out his hand against them to strike, and does not draw it back in order to spare them.

He threatens that they will not be in the council of the Lord’s people, nor in his Church, but in the synagogue of the devil; they will not be recorded in the house of Israel. Concerning them it is said elsewhere: “Let them be written upon the earth” (Jeremiah 17:13)—not in the land of Israel, which is the land of the living, of which it is now said, “They shall not enter the land of Israel,” but in the land of the dead and the shadow of death. After suffering these things, separated from the assembly of God’s people, they will understand that he is the Lord.

For what we translated as “They shall not be in the council of my people,” the Septuagint translated: “They shall not be in the discipline,” or “correction,” “of my people.” The correction of adversaries is one thing, and the correction of sons another. Hence Jeremiah says: “Correct us, Lord, but in judgment and not in anger, lest you make us few. Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name” (Jeremiah 10:24–25).

### (Verses 10 and following)

Because they have deceived my people, saying, “Peace,” when there is no peace. And he was building a wall, while they were plastering it with mud without straw. Say to those who plaster without proper mixture that it will fall. For there will be a flooding rain; and I will give very large hailstones falling upon it from above, and a tempestuous wind to scatter it. And behold, the wall has fallen. Will it not be said to you, “Where is the plaster with which you plastered it?”

Therefore thus says the Lord God: I will make a storm wind break forth in my indignation, and there will be a flooding rain in my fury, and great hailstones of wrath for destruction. I will destroy the wall that you plastered without proper mixture and level it with the ground; its foundation will be exposed, and it will fall and be consumed in its midst. And you shall know that I am the Lord. I will complete my indignation against the wall and against those who plaster it without proper mixture. I will say to you: “There is no wall, and there are none who plaster it”—the prophets of Israel who prophesy to Jerusalem and see for it a vision of peace, when there is no peace, says the Lord God.

**The Septuagint:** Because they deceived my people, saying, “Peace, peace,” when there was no peace; and he was building the wall, while they plaster it with folly.

[Note: The manuscripts and Rabanus read “he is building” in the present tense; indeed the Greek also has οἰκοδομεῖ. See the end of this chapter.] Say to those who plaster with folly: “It will fall.” There will be a flooding rain, and I will give great stones into their joints, and they will fall. And a sweeping wind will come, and it will be torn apart. And behold, the wall has fallen. And they will not say to you, “Where is your plaster with which you plastered it?”

[Note: Victorius, who was constantly eager to restore the readings of the versions to their respective archetypes, here removes the negative particle in accordance with the Greek manuscript he used, apparently the Aldine, where καὶ ἐροῦσι, “and they will say,” is written. But most other Greek copies, especially the Vatican manuscript, insert οὐκ: καὶ οὐκ ἐροῦσι, “and they will not say,” which must certainly be retained. We wished to alert the reader that the editor frequently makes similar alterations according to that standard, although they lack the support of the Hieronymian manuscripts and are by no means approved by us.]

Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: I will shatter the sweeping wind in my fury, and there will be a flooding rain in my anger; and I will bring great stones in my fury for destruction. I will undermine the wall that you plastered, and it will fall. I will set it upon the ground, and its foundations will be exposed, and it will fall. And you shall be consumed with rebukes, and you shall know that I am the Lord.

[Note: Again Victorius unwisely changes “you shall be consumed” because he read συντελεσθήσετε in the Aldine Greek copy, whereas other copies, especially the Vatican manuscript, quite properly have συντελεσθήσεσθε.] I will complete my fury against the wall and against those who plaster it; it will fall upon them. And I said to you: “There is no wall, nor are there those who plaster it—the prophets of Israel who prophesy concerning Jerusalem and see peace for it; there is no peace for them,” says the Lord God.

The prophets of Israel, who will not be in the council of God’s people, nor be written in the writing of the house of Israel, nor enter the land of promise, will suffer these things because they deceived my people, announcing peace and prosperity to them instead of the severity of repentance and conversion, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “Peace, peace, when there is no peace?” (Jeremiah 8:11).

God, therefore, metaphorically built for them a rampart. For this Hebrew word, printed as **HIS ()** [uncertain], signifies “rampart,” so that he might repel from them every attack of beasts and every hostile assault, while, converted to God, they would be enclosed as though by a very strong wall and rampart. But the false prophets repeatedly promised them peace; for this is what the repeated utterance of “peace” signifies. The false prophets plastered the wall—which is called **CIR** in what follows—without proper mixture, as Symmachus interpreted it, that is, with pure mud lacking straw, so that it could provide no strength.

But whereas the Septuagint and Theodotion say, “They plaster it with folly”—

[Note: This seems to be understood of the Hexaplaric Septuagint; for in one Complutensian manuscript the reading is ἀφροσύνη, “folly.”]

—Aquila interpreted the Hebrew word **THAPHEL** as ἀνάλῳ, “without salt”—

[Note: Other books have ἄναλον or ἄναλα.]

—passing from one translation into another. Just as food without salt has no flavor, so mud without the straw by which it is strengthened and bound can provide no strength to the wall.

“Say,” he says, “to those who promise them empty things and offer vain assistance, that this wall and this rampart will fall. I will send a most violent rain,” namely, the fiercest enemies. He means the Babylonians and Chaldeans. He likewise means the same hailstones falling upon it from above.

[Note: Victorius says that the Vulgate consistently reads “great” or “very great stones.” But because the Hebrew reads [term omitted in the supplied text], and the Hebrews explain the word as “hail,” understanding the very great stones here as hailstones, nothing has been changed. Jerome shows that he did not fail to know the force of the Hebrew word, although in the sacred text itself he translated only “great,” not “of hail.”]

Everything is expressed metaphorically, so that a sudden whirlwind may overturn and demolish the unstable rampart; and afterward it may be said to them, that is, to the false prophets: “Where is the plaster with which you plastered it, and where is the assistance you promised?”

Whatever we have said about the false prophets can also be applied to heretics: all their fabrications are dissolved by God’s wrath; the construction of their pernicious doctrines, which lacks the seasoning of the Holy Spirit, collapses and crumbles down to its foundations and dust; the rampart itself is leveled with the ground and falls; and the prophets who made the promises, together with the people to whom the promises were made, are consumed within it. After he has completed his indignation and said to them, “This is not a wall,” that is, “This is not your defense,” and “There are none who plaster it,” but everything is empty and comes to nothing, then by their experience they will know that he is the Lord.

To show who those are who plaster the wall, it follows: “The prophets of Israel,” that is, the false prophets, who prophesy concerning Jerusalem and see for it a vision of peace. These are the cause of sin, ruin, and foolish security. “There will be no peace,” says the Lord, because the Lord did not send them, nor did he speak to them.

What the Septuagint translated as “into their joints” is not found in the Hebrew. It signifies either the joints of the stones in the wall or the wooden supports by which walls are strengthened.

Nor is the phrase we read above—“he was building the wall”—

[Note: Rabanus adds “or he is building”; and we have already observed that the Greek presently has the same reading.]

—understood by most interpreters of anyone other than the people of Israel, who were promising themselves vain assistance either from the Egyptians or from peace.

### (Verses 17 and following)

And you, son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart. Prophesy against them and say: Thus says the Lord God:

Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand and make head-coverings beneath the head of persons of every age, to capture souls. When they captured the souls of my people, they kept their souls alive. And they profaned me before my people for a handful of barley and a piece of bread, killing souls that do not die and keeping alive souls that do not live, lying to my people who believe lies.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against your cushions, with which you capture the flying souls, and I will tear them from your arms. I will release the souls whom you capture, souls destined to fly. I will tear apart your head-coverings and deliver my people from your hand; they will no longer be in your hands as prey [the Vulgate has “to be preyed upon”]. And you shall know that I am the Lord.

Because you have falsely caused the heart of the righteous to grieve, whom I did not grieve, and have strengthened the hands of the wicked so that he would not turn back from his evil way and live, therefore you shall no longer see vanity, nor practice divinations any longer. I will rescue my people from your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord.

**The Septuagint:** And you, son of man, strengthen your face against the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart. Prophesy against them and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord:

Woe to those who sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hand and make coverings over every head of persons of every age, in order to pervert souls. The souls of my people have been subverted. And they saved souls, and they polluted me before my people for a handful of barley and a piece of bread, killing souls that ought not to die and saving souls that ought not to live, while speaking vain words to the people who listen.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against your cushions, over which you gather souls, and I will tear them from your arms. I will release the souls whom you pervert, their souls for dispersion. I will tear apart your coverings and deliver my people from your hands; they will no longer be in your hands for assembly. And you shall know that I am the Lord.

Because you were unjustly perverting the soul of the righteous, although I was not perverting him, and were strengthening the hands of the wicked so that he would not turn back completely from his most evil way and live, therefore you shall no longer see your lies, nor practice divinations any longer. I will deliver my people from your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord.

[Note: I would certainly prefer that the word “your” be removed here, since neither the Septuagint itself, nor the Hebrew text, nor the Latin translator knows it. Victorius adds that it is also absent from the Florentine and Brescia manuscripts. The manuscripts we use, however, consistently contain it.]

Above, the divine word was directed against the prophets who plastered a wall without proper mixture, without straw and therefore without any ability to give strength to the wall or rampart. Now the prophet is commanded to set, direct, or, as the Septuagint translated it, strengthen his face against the prophetesses, the daughters of his people.

Just as, in opposition to the prophets, other false prophets were inspired by a demonic spirit to overturn God’s commands, so against the prophetesses—such as Deborah (Judges 5), Huldah (2 Kings 22), and the four prophesying daughters of Philip the evangelist in the Acts of the Apostles—there were others inspired by a demonic spirit (Acts 21). There were also others of the same sex, among whom were Prisca and Maximilla, who overturned faith in the truth through lying prophecy.

The Hebrews say that these women were trained in magical arts through necromancy and the Pythian spirit, like the woman who appeared to have raised the soul of Samuel (1 Samuel 28). In the Acts of the Apostles there was also the woman whose divination brought considerable income to her masters, and from whom the unclean spirit was expelled at the command of the apostle Paul (Acts 16).

We, however, shall say that various heretics proclaim the power of their doctrines’ falsehoods. Among them were Pythagoras and Zeno, from whom the Stoics derive their name; the Brahmans of India; and the Gymnosophists of Ethiopia, who, because of their frugality in food, attribute to the nations a marvel concerning themselves. They are rightly said to plaster the wall and promise it some strength; but because they lack the seasoning of Christ, their labor is vain and their construction doomed to perish. “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

Others, teachers of pleasures and lust, are said to sew cushions and place them beneath every elbow of the hand: the Epicureans and Pyrrhonists, and among us Jovinianus and Eunomius, who say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.”

The prophet is therefore commanded to set or strengthen his face against the daughters of his people. First, we must explain what is meant by a face that is set, directed, and strengthened. It is surely what is written concerning the Lord: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psalm 33:17). For just as wax melts before the face of fire, so sinners perish before the face of God.

In this same sense it is said in this prophet: “Son of man, strengthen your face against Teman, Darom, and the Negeb” (below, 20:46). And again: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, strengthen your face against the children of Jerusalem” (below, 21:2). Shortly afterward: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, strengthen your face against the children of Ammon” (below, 25:2). Again: “Strengthen your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt” (below, 29:2). And again: “Son of man, strengthen your face against Gog and Magog.” Elsewhere: “I will set my face against that man, and I will make him an example and a proverb; I will remove him from the midst of the people, and you shall know that I am the Lord” (below, 14:8).

Woe, therefore, to these heresies and doctrines, which promise rest and deceive every age and sex in order to capture the souls of the wretched and pollute me before my people,

[Note: In Rabanus: “and pollute all my people.”]

while I am believed to love pleasure—not for a **cor** and a **hemicor** of barley, as we read in Hosea (Hosea 5), but for a handful of barley, with which brute animals feed, and a piece of bread.

It is not a whole loaf, nor solid testimonies of the Scriptures, but testimonies broken, mutilated, and diminished by heretical perversity, so that they may deceive even holy people, drag them to death, and attempt to give life to sinners through vain promises.

Therefore the merciful and compassionate God does not kill the prophetesses themselves, but tears apart their cushions, which, like nets, capture flying souls, so that, once torn, the souls may have freedom to fly. They will tear apart the coverings, or head-cushions, on which the soul’s ruling faculty reclined and with which the heads of the deceived were covered.

The Apostle teaches that men’s heads should not be veiled, but that, with unveiled face, they should contemplate the glory of the Lord (2 Corinthians 3). “For,” he says, “you were breaking the spirits of those who serve God with false terrors, and by fraudulent promises you kept the impious enclosed, lest, repenting, they should recover the life they had lost.”

Therefore you shall no longer see vain visions, nor shall I call your lies prophecies, but divinations, concerning which it is written: “There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel” (Numbers 23:23), so that I may rescue my people from your hands and, by your experience, you may know that I am the Lord, who have delivered the lost.

### (Chapter 14—Verses 1 and following)

And men came to me, the elders of Israel, and sat before me.

[Note: It seems that, with Victorius, “the elders” should be restored, corresponding to the Hebrew and the Greek ἄνδρες ἀπὸ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, “men from among the elders,” with which Jerome’s Vulgate translation and the truth of the context agree.]

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

Son of man, these men have placed their impurities in their hearts and have set the stumbling-block of their iniquity before their faces. Should I indeed answer them when questioned?

Therefore speak to them and say: Thus says the Lord God:

Any man, any man of the house of Israel, who places his impurities in his heart and sets the stumbling-block of his iniquity before his face, and then comes to the prophet to inquire of him through me—I, the Lord, will answer him according to the multitude of his impurities, so that the house of Israel may be caught in its own heart, by which they have departed from me in all their idols.

Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Turn back and depart from your idols, and turn your faces away from all your contaminations.

For any man, any man of the house of Israel, and of the proselytes—whoever is an immigrant in Israel—if he has become estranged from me in Israel, and has placed his idols in his heart and set the stumbling-block of his iniquity before his face, and then comes to the prophet to inquire of me through him, I, the Lord, will answer him through myself. I will set my face against that man, and I will make him an example and a proverb; I will destroy him from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the Lord.

And if the prophet has gone astray and spoken a word, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet. I will stretch out my hand against him and erase him from the midst of my people Israel. They shall bear their iniquity. As the iniquity of the one who inquires is, so shall the iniquity of the prophet be, so that the house of Israel may no longer go astray from me and may not be defiled by all its transgressions; but it may be my people, and I may be their God, says the Lord of hosts.

**The Septuagint:** And men came to me from among the elders of Israel and sat before my face. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

Son of man, these men have placed their thoughts in their hearts and have set the punishment of their iniquities before their face. If I answer them, shall I answer them?

Therefore speak to them and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord:

Any man, any man of the house of Israel, who has placed his thoughts in his heart and set the punishment of his iniquity before his face, and has come to the prophet to inquire of him through me, I, the Lord, will answer him in accordance with that by which his mind is held, so that I may turn the house of Israel according to their hearts, which have become estranged from me through their thoughts.

Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Turn back and depart from your inventions, and from all your impieties, and turn your faces toward me.

For any man, any man of the house of Israel, and of the resident foreigners who dwell in the land of Israel, who has become estranged from me, has placed his thoughts in his heart, and has set the punishment of his iniquity before his face, and has come to the prophet to inquire of me through him, I, the Lord, will answer him according to that by which he is held, and I will set my face against that man. I will make him desolate and destroy him; I will remove him from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the Lord.

And if the prophet goes astray and speaks a word, I, the Lord, have caused that prophet to go astray. I will stretch out my hand against him and destroy him from the midst of my people Israel. They shall receive their iniquity according to the iniquity of the one who inquires, and the prophet’s iniquity shall likewise be the same, so that the house of Israel may no longer go astray from me and may not again be polluted by all its sins. They shall be my people, and I shall be their God, says Adonai the Lord.

After he had spoken against the prophets who prophesied from their own hearts and plastered the wall without proper mixture, and against the prophetesses who sewed cushions and placed them beneath every elbow of the hand, making coverings and covering the heads of persons of every age—through which the doctrine of perverse teachings is represented—men came to the prophet. Not all the elders came, lest all should seem to have gone astray, but certain elders of Israel. They sat before the prophet, postponing in silence for what reason they had come. Immediately the word of God came to the prophet, revealing why they were present.

For it is not within human nature, even that of a holy person, to know the secrets of the heart. Hence it is said of the Savior alone: “But Jesus, seeing their thoughts, said: Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matthew 9:4).

The meaning is this: “Son of man, these men who sit before you have placed their impurities, or thoughts, in their hearts; and, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, idols and a stumbling-block—that is, the ruin and punishment of their iniquity—they have set before their face, and thus they have come to inquire into the Lord’s word.”

“Should I answer such men,” he asks, “who come to me with their former thoughts, not even at this time abandoning the crimes of their impiety, but believing in idols and fraudulent divinations, having the ruin of their iniquity and its punishment before their face, despairing of better things and prepared for punishment, and yet seeking through you to know my words?”

Because they have come to you with a perverse heart, answer them not from your own person, lest the authority of the response be slight, but by my command; and say to them: “Thus says the Lord God.”

To summarize the whole passage in a brief statement, its meaning is this: “Any man”—not one of the other nations, whose error may be forgiven, but one of the house of Israel—who comes to the prophet to inquire while retaining the former vices of which we spoke above, I will answer according to his heart and his impurities, so that he may hear according to what he wants and believes. For one who asks not with the intention of learning but of testing does not deserve correction.

They have departed from me and followed idols. This is a brief warning: let them depart from idols and perverse thoughts, and turn to me, abandoning their former crimes. One who asks deceitfully does not deserve to hear the truth; rather, he must be caught by his own heart. Accordingly, when the scribes and Pharisees questioned the Lord—or rather, tested him—they heard: “Why do you test me?” And again: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matthew 21:27).

When a person is such and asks in this way, God sets his face against him, or strengthens it, so that by the severity of his countenance the hardness of his brow may be softened; and he becomes an example and a proverb, or desolation and destruction. When that person has been destroyed from God’s people, the rest may know that he is the Lord, who knows the secrets of the heart and understands the perversity of the mind, considering not the words of those who speak but their hearts.

The following statement appears to raise a question: “If the prophet has gone astray and spoken a word, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet.” We should not think that this is spoken of a true prophet, but of a false prophet, who is called a prophet by a shared name. This can be explained from the passage of Scripture in which Ahab, king of Israel, goes to battle but refuses to listen to the prophet Micaiah and follows the counsels of the false prophets (1 Kings 22). Micaiah says that he saw the Lord seated on his throne and that a spirit of error voluntarily offered itself to deceive the king.

In the book of Job, the Devil is likewise said to roam through the earth and stand in God’s presence, receiving from the Lord power first over Job’s possessions and then over his body (Job 1–2). Balaam the diviner is also sent by the Lord to deceive Balak, son of Beor (Numbers 22).

All this is said so that the deception of the people may not be attributed to the strength of the false prophets, since the people preferred to hear a lie rather than lend an ear to the truth. Rather, it is the consequence of God’s wrath, that a perverse and unbelieving people should listen to false prophets more than to true ones.

Finally, he stretches out his hand against him—understand, against the prophet—and he is erased from the midst of his people, so that he may bear his iniquity. Since the error is alike, the punishment is alike: both the one who inquires and the one who is questioned bear their iniquity. Thus the house of Israel, consisting of those who wish to hear God’s words, will not be deceived by perverse prophecies, but will be God’s people and will merit having the Lord as its God.

In the statement, “I, the Lord, have deceived him,” Solomon’s words agree, for when discussing God he says: “He mocks the mockers” (Proverbs 3:34). The same is true of the testimony: “If they walk contrary to me, I too will walk against them in contrary fury” (Leviticus 26:27–28).

The fact that the phrase “any man, any man of the children of Israel and of the resident foreigners joined to them” is repeated shows in us, according to the Apostle, the twofold human being, exterior and interior (1 Corinthians 15).

Many possess the bodily appearance of a human being but assume the forms of various beasts. Wishing these forms to be dispersed, the prophet prays: “In your city you will disperse their image, O Lord” (Psalm 72:20). Those of whom it is written, “A man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm 49:21), are not human beings in the full sense, but human beings who are beasts.

Again, those who hear in the Gospel, “Serpents, offspring of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 23:33), are not human beings in the full sense, but human beings who are serpents.

[Note: The phrase “and serpents” was ineptly present, although Victorius had previously removed that conjunction with the help of the Brescia manuscripts. The material discussed here about the twofold human being is taken almost word for word from Origen’s third Homily on Ezekiel, among those that Jerome himself translated into Latin and that we have appended to this volume. Origen says: “All of us are born human beings, but not all of us are human beings in the full sense,” in accordance with what is written in Leviticus: “Any man, any man of the children of Israel,” and so forth.]

And those of whom it is written, “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven nests” (Matthew 8:20), as well as Herod, of whom it is said, “Tell that fox” (Luke 13:32), are not human beings, but human beings who are foxes.

Those who possess both uses of the word “human being,” if they go astray, are corrected through punishments so that they may understand that he is the Lord.

Moreover, the statement we rendered according to the Septuagint—“the man who has become estranged from me and has placed his thoughts in his heart, and the punishment of his iniquity before his face”—corresponds to the testimony written in Isaiah: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isaiah 50:11). Each person kindles the heat of his own flames and prepares punishments for himself by refusing to correct his errors through repentance and remaining in his errors, thereby deserving the burning of the flames.

(Verses 12, 13 and following.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, when a land sins against me by committing persistent transgression, I will stretch out my hand [Al. adds: ‘my’] against it, and I will break its staff of bread, and send famine upon it, and cut off from it man and beast [Note: In the singular, ‘beast,’ following the Hebrew and Vulgate edition, Victorius substitutes it here and below]. And if these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—are in its midst, they by their righteousness will deliver their own souls, says the Lord of hosts.

“But if I also bring the most savage beasts upon the land, so that I lay it waste and it becomes impassable, because no one can pass through it on account of the beasts, if these three men are in it, as I live, says the Lord [Vulg. adds: God], they will deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone will be delivered; the land, however, will be desolated.

“Or if I bring a sword upon that land [Col. 0120A] and say to the sword, ‘Pass through the land,’ and cut off from it man and beast, and these three men are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they will not deliver sons or daughters, but they alone will be delivered.

“But if I also send pestilence upon that land and pour out my indignation upon it in blood, to cut off from it man and beast, and Noah, Daniel, and Job are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they will deliver neither son nor daughter, but by their righteousness they will deliver their own souls.

“For thus says the Lord God: Even if I send my four most grievous judgments—sword, famine, savage beasts, and pestilence—against Jerusalem, to cut off from it man and beast, nevertheless a remnant shall be left in it: those who bring up sons and daughters. Behold, they themselves shall come out to you, and you will see their way and their deeds, and you will be comforted concerning the calamity that I have brought upon Jerusalem, concerning all that I have inflicted upon it. And they will comfort you when you see their way and their deeds; and you will know that I have not done all that I have done in it without cause, says the Lord God.”

Four scourges are brought upon the transgressing land—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the sinful land: famine, beast, sword, and pestilence. If these are brought separately, each upon its own region, and these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job, whose righteousness is proclaimed by the voices of Scripture—intercede on behalf of the sinful land, they will not be able to save it; nor will they even be able to save their sons and daughters if they have committed the deeds of the sinful land. They will be able to save only themselves.

It is asked: since Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as well as Moses and the other patriarchs and righteous prophets, were also righteous, why are only these three mentioned? The question is easily resolved. Noah, when the flood threatening the whole world was imminent, because the entire earth had corrupted the ways of the Lord, could not prevent it [Al. delay it] (Gen. 6–7); but he had his sons, who perhaps possessed the same virtue, reserved as the seed of the human race [Note: Following Victorius, we delete the word et (“and”) so that the sense may stand]. Daniel likewise did not mitigate the captivity threatening the Jewish people by any tears (Dan. 1). Job, too, did not deliver either his house or his children—not because of sins, but for the sake of testing (Job 1).

Others say that these three men alone saw prosperity and adversity, and prosperity again; therefore they are named together. This also secretly signifies that, just as they saw good things and evil things, and then joyful things again, so Israel too—having first enjoyed good things and afterward endured the yoke of captivity—may, if it does penance, return to its former happiness.

But if Noah, Daniel, and Job, gathered together and placed in one location, cannot withdraw the sinful land—that is, those who dwell on the land [Note: One Vatican manuscript inserts peccatrice, “sinful,” which is also found in the Brixia manuscripts, according to Victorius. “The sinful land,” he says, is spoken of in reference to those who are sinners on the land]—from the wrath of God, what should be said of those who think that sinful children can be delivered from the fires of Gehenna by the merit and virtues of their parents? Thus neither will a martyr [Al. righteous] father be able to deliver a sinful son [Al. a son of transgressors], nor will a mother of holy conduct give an immodest daughter the rewards of chastity. Conversely, the vices of parents will not harm their children; rather, the soul that sins will itself die (below, 17:4).

Lot lived in Sodom, yet was a stranger there both in spirit and in body. Because his wife looked behind her, he did not deliver her; he delivered only his daughters, who perhaps had not sinned (Gen. 19). And Josiah, a holy man, not only did not save the sinful people by his virtues, but he himself also died in their sins (4 Kings 13).

If at some time the Lord promises mercy to the descendants of Abraham and David on account of Abraham and David, it must be observed [Col. 0121B] that he does not spare those who persist in crimes, but those who repent, so that the conduct of the children may assist the merits of the fathers [Note: Other books, and Rabanus, read conversio, “conversion,” instead of conduct].

“When these things are so,” he says, “and the intercession of such great men does not save the sinful land from the individual scourges, thus says the Lord God: Because Jerusalem has sinned wickedly, I will bring four scourges upon it at once: the sword, by which it is slaughtered by enemies; famine, which it endures during the siege; beasts, by which fugitives are devoured in deserts and thickets; and pestilence, which always follows famine and scarcity.” In place of this, the Vulgate edition translated “death.”

“These things,” he says, “I will bring upon it, so that neither people nor beasts remain in it. Nevertheless, in my clemency, although four scourges threaten at once and devastate everything, I will leave some in it who will bring up their sons and daughters. Let them come here as captives—that is, to Babylon and Chaldaea—so that when you see them and examine their deeds, you may then understand that they were justly taken captive, and that my judgment was just; and let your captivity have consolation, while you understand that I delivered them from the sword, famine, beasts, and pestilence for this reason: so that from their perversity you may learn that Jerusalem was deservedly overthrown, the temple burned, and the people led captive, except those whom sword, famine, beasts, and pestilence consumed.”

These things have been said concerning that Jerusalem whose captivity was approaching while Ezekiel was prophesying among the Chaldaeans. But also upon our land, to which it is said, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19), and upon our Jerusalem and each of the faithful, if they despise God’s commandments and deserve to be called transgressors, famine will be brought—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God.

The sword will also be brought, concerning which we read: “They will be given into the hands of the sword; they will be portions of foxes” [Al. “They will be”] (Ps. 62:11). And to Mary: “A sword will also pierce your soul” (Luke 2:35). Beasts will also be brought, from which the righteous asks not to be delivered up: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. 73:19). Pestilence will also be brought—for which the Septuagint translated “death”—of which it is written: “The death of sinners is very grievous” (Ps. 33:22). And: “The soul that sins will itself die.” And: “If bitter death thus separates” (below, 18:4).

From all these things neither the teaching of spiritual parents, whom we understand as teachers (1 Kings 15), nor rulers will be able to deliver anyone, unless there is the assent of the children and they assist their parents’ entreaties by their own efforts. “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall remain upon him: each shall die by his own sin, and shall be saved by his own righteousness” (Deut. 24:16).

The Jews say in vain, “Abraham is our father” (John 8), when they do not have Abraham’s works. If there is trust in anyone, let us trust in the Lord alone. For “cursed is every man who places his hope in man” (Jer. 17:5), however holy they may be, however much they may be prophets. We read: “Do not put your trust in princes” (Ps. 145:2). And again: “It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in princes” (Ps. 117:6). Not only in the princes of this world, but also in the princes of the Churches, who, if they are righteous, will deliver only their own souls. But they will not be able to save the sons and daughters whom they have begotten in the Church if they are negligent. Yet the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work is burned, he himself will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:14, 15).

The hand is stretched out over the transgressing land so that the staff, or strength, of bread may be broken. When it is stretched out, it threatens scourges. The one who stretches it out does not wish to strike and destroy sinners, but to terrify them by its extension and preserve those who have been terrified.

(Cap. XV.—Verses 1 and following.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, what will happen to the wood of the vine among all the woods of the forest that are among the trees of the woodland? Will wood be taken from it to make some work? Or will a peg be fashioned from it, so that some vessel may hang upon it [Al. “upon it”]? Behold, it has been given to the fire as fuel: the fire has consumed both its ends, and its middle has been reduced to ashes. Will it be useful for any work? Even when it was whole, it was not suitable for work; how much less, when the fire has devoured and burned it, will anything made from it be useful?

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: As the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I gave to the fire to devour, so I will hand over [Al. “I handed over”] the inhabitants of Jerusalem. I will set my face against them. They will come out from the fire, and the fire will consume them. And you will know that I am the Lord when I set my face against them and make the land impassable and desolate, because they have proved to be transgressors, says the Lord God.”

In place of what we translated, “The fire has consumed both its ends, and its middle has been reduced to ashes,” the Septuagint translated: “The fire consumes its annual cleansing and leaves it for the end.” Again, where we said, “When I set my face against them,” they translated, “When I make it firm.” They also translated “transgression” as “sin.”

By various comparisons, which the Greeks call parables, the overthrow of the city of Jerusalem is foretold. Just as above (on chapter 4) the siege and famine of the same city were described in the frying pan in which the flesh of the people was fried, and on the side where the fortifications, siege embankments, battering rams, and vine-like siege engines were depicted—and we shall read the same thing later in this book—so also in Jeremiah it is written (Jer. 1:13) that the pot kindled from the face of the north signifies the city of Jerusalem. The cut-down forest of the Negeb, Teman, and Darom likewise foretells this very thing.

Thus, in the present passage, the same Jerusalem is compared to a vineyard and a fruitful vine. Concerning it, it is written elsewhere: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a strange vine?” (Jer. 2:21.) [Note: Vaticanus reads omne semen verum (“every true seed”), then aliena; Victorius supports alienae (“of a strange vine”) from the Septuagint, ἄμπελος ἀλλοτρία, “a strange vine.”]

And in Isaiah: “I planted,” he says, “a choice vine” (Isa. 5:2), which means one chosen and beautiful. And in the Psalms we read: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You were its guide before it” (Ps. 79:9). More plainly we learn this when Scripture says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7).

As long as this vine bears fruit, nothing among all the trees of the woodland is more precious than it. But if it ceases to have grapes, it will be useful for nothing except to be handed over to the fire, together with its root and branches.

The other trees of the forest—not to mention fruit-bearing trees, of which Scripture here makes no mention—although they do not bear fruit, provide great usefulness when cut down. They are useful for every kind of agriculture and for weapons: they are thinned into shields, shaved into spear shafts, fitted into doors, and used for cupboards [Note: Rabanus reads “for armoires, chests, and small boxes”], chests, and small boxes; indeed, they provide all the furniture of a house.

But if the vine once ceases to bear grapes, it is so useless that not even a peg can be made from it on which something might hang. When you cut off its branches, fire first seizes both ends of them, and then the flame consumes them. When it has been reduced to ashes, it is so entirely useless that even while whole, if it lacks fruit, it provides no usefulness.

There is an ambiguity in the Hebrew word SENE ([letters not printed]), which is written with three letters, SIN, NUN, and JOD. If it is read SENE, it signifies “two”; if SANE, “years.” Hence it happened that, in place of “its two ends,” which we translated “both its ends,” the Septuagint translated “its annual cleansing,” whereas Aquila said “its two extremities,” and Symmachus and Theodotion “its two ends.”

The order is as follows: Just as a fruitless vine is handed over to the fire for no use, so Jerusalem—or rather its inhabitants—will be handed over to flames, so that they may come out from the fire and the fire may consume them. That is, even if they escape from the city, they will be consumed outside by the enemy’s sword; and those who remain, oppressed by the very weight of their miseries, will recognize that I am the Lord, when I set—or make firm—my face against them and give them over to perpetual desolation.

For sinners are not like the other nations: they have proved to be transgressors. It is one thing to neglect what you do not know; another to despise what you have worshiped.

According to the spiritual understanding, we can also understand the vine and Jerusalem as the multitude of believers. If it is negligent, abandons the cultivation of its former religion, bears no fruits of virtue, and produces no wine that gladdens the human heart, it will be handed over to eternal fires and counted as nothing. “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47).

The Lord teaches something similar in the Gospel according to John: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator. Every branch that remains in me and does not bear fruit, the Father will take away. And everyone that bears fruit, he will cleanse, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2).

But if the Savior is the vine, we are the branches, and God is called the Father and cultivator, then as long as we keep God’s commandments, we are always cultivated, and our cultivation is cleansing. “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16).

If, when we bear fruit, we are cleansed by the Father so that we may bear more abundant fruit, it is shown that all our effort, with God’s assistance, reaches its completion and produces the fruit of fullness. But the branch that does not produce fruit will be taken away by the Father. And when it has been taken away, what the Father does with it Scripture does not say—unless perhaps separation from Christ’s body is perpetual punishment and destruction.

What we have understood through the image of the vineyard and vine, the Savior teaches in the Gospel under another figure: “Salt is good; but if salt has become tasteless, it is useful for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled by people” (Mark 9:49). And the eye that illuminates the whole body, if it has been blinded, hears from the Lord: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will that darkness be?” (Matt. 6:23, 13.)

By comparison with the transgressor, and with the one who first confessed and then denied God, the punishment of those who have never possessed knowledge of God is lighter. The trees of the woodland, or forest, according to the variety of believers, have some usefulness in the great house, in which there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthen vessels—some for honor, others for dishonor (2 Tim. 2).

(Cap. XVI.—Verses 1, 2.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations, and say: Thus says the Lord God to Jerusalem.”

The Septuagint: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, testify against Jerusalem concerning her iniquities, and say to her: Thus says Adonai the Lord.”

In the passages where the individual prophecies were briefly delimited, we have set down entire chapters and immediately added what seemed to us appropriate. Here, however, because a long discourse is directed against Jerusalem, as one testifying to it and teaching it the sins it has committed—and the prophecy extends almost to the number of two hundred verses, up to the place where it is written, “When I have been reconciled to you concerning all that you have done, says the Lord God” [Note: The whole, unbroken chapter in the Vulgate edition is divided into sixty-three verses; by that division it differs widely from the number assigned here by Jerome. Therefore, to see the ancient division, consult our edition of the Divine Library of St Jerome, or vol. I of our edition, cols. 673 ff., where in chapter XVI you will be able to find a total of almost two hundred verses. MART.]—we must present the whole prophecy in sections and attach suitable explanations to the passages we have proposed.

Under the person of a prostitute who was first joined to a husband, the origin, upbringing, puberty, marriage, adultery, repudiation, and renewed restoration of Jerusalem are woven together, so that both the husband’s mercy and judgment and the crimes of the adulteress and prostitute may be recognized, while, after all the punishments, he establishes an everlasting covenant with her, so that she may remember her iniquity and be ashamed, and no longer dare to open her mouth because of her shame, when he has been reconciled to her concerning all that she had done.

For it is very beneficial for sinners to know what they have done. Hence the penitent also says: “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:4).

Jerusalem can be understood in four ways: either as the Jerusalem that was burned by Babylonian and Roman fire; or as the heavenly Jerusalem of the firstborn; or as the Church, whose name means “vision of peace”; or as the souls of individuals who see God by faith.

The interpretation that many think must be applied to the heavenly Jerusalem is not accepted by the Church, lest we be compelled to apply everything woven together in the present prophecy to the downfall, sufferings, and restoration to their former state of the heavenly powers.

(Vers. 3.) “Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan [Vulg. Chananaea]. Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.”

Great is the faith and boldness of the prophets: one man dares to charge an entire city with ignobility. Daniel is remarkable: to the offending elder who had joined adultery to murder, he, though a boy, dared to say: “You offspring of Canaan, and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you” (Dan. 13:56).

Isaiah too is great, crying out to the rulers and people of the Jews: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the words of the Lord, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:10).

Ezekiel is no less great, speaking confidently to the whole city: “Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.”

Stephen, the first martyr of the Gospel, likewise spoke to the raging people: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).

Although we can understand Jerusalem’s root and origin as the land of Canaan according to the interpretation that the people were called in Egypt and lived there for a long time—for Ham, the father of Canaan, was the chief of the Egyptian nation—nevertheless, according to the similarity of their crimes, we shall say that the root of Jerusalem is the land of Egypt.

Hence her father is called an Amorite, which is interpreted as λαλούμενος, that is, “celebrated in much speech.” And her mother is a Hittite, that is, ἐξιστῶσα, “causing astonishment” or “driving into madness”—one who is herself insane or sends others into madness.

“For everyone who commits sin is born of the devil” (John 8:44). Hence throughout the whole world there is a famous name belonging to this ancient father, who turns many into madness.

Jerusalem, whether understood literally or spiritually, is therefore commanded to leave her ancient father, and it is said to her: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty” (Ps. 45:11).

And if, after sin, she wishes to return to her true father, this is promised to her: “I will restore you as you were when you were born.”

How great was the nobility of the city of Jerusalem, which descended from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and had God as its father! Yet because it sinned and abandoned its true parent, it deserved to hear: “Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.”

If Jerusalem heard this, what will become of us, who were called from the filth of the nations and lost every stain in the Savior’s washing, if we defile Christ’s garment and do not have a wedding garment at the banquet? Surely this: bound hand and foot, we shall be handed over to eternal fires, where there is weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 22).

(Verses 4, 5.) “And when you were born, on the day of your birth your umbilical cord was not cut, and you were not washed in water for cleansing, nor rubbed with salt, nor wrapped in cloths. No eye pitied you, to do one of these things for you, out of compassion for you; but you were thrown upon the face of the earth, to the rejection of your soul, on the day you were born.”

The Septuagint: “And your origin, on the day you were born, they did not bind your breasts; your umbilical cord was not cut, and you were not washed in water for cleansing, nor rubbed with salt, nor wrapped in cloths. No eye pitied you, to do one of all these things for you, or to suffer anything on your behalf; but you were thrown upon the face of the field because of the perversity [Note: Victorius reads pravitati, “perversity,” from the Septuagint, τῇ σκολιότητι.] of your soul, on the day you were born.”

Let us discuss each point according to the order of the reading.

When Jerusalem was born from an Amorite father and a Hittite mother, and was poured forth from the womb, her umbilical cord was not cut. By this cord fetuses are nourished in the womb, like trees and shrubs that are secretly nourished by the moisture of the earth through their roots.

And just as the seed of men is signified by the loins, so the female genital organs are called the umbilicus in the modest language customary in Scripture, as testified by Job, who speaks of the devil under the figure of a dragon: “His strength is in his loins, and his force in the umbilicus of his belly” (Job 40:11).

This ancient serpent, the dragon called the devil and Satan, who deceived the whole world, has strength against men in the loins and against women in the umbilicus.

This signifies concerning Jerusalem that she did not receive the law immediately, nor were the beginnings of her shameful birth cut away, but she first lived a Gentile life. In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “On the day you were born they did not bind your breasts” (Ezek. 7). Holy Scripture has the custom of naming the breast or little chest—and also the breasts—in place of the heart, as the context seems to require.

Priests, in whom teaching ought to reside and from whose mouths the law is sought, receive the breast. John reclines upon the breast of the Lord so that he may draw streams of wisdom from its most abundant spring (John 13).

In the Song of Songs the Virgin has two breasts, like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows are removed (Song 4).

A careful mother, as soon as a baby girl is born, binds her breasts so that they may cease their tender swelling and preserve virgin beauty [Note: Two manuscripts read tumore resistant; the reading is uncertain]. But when she reaches the age of puberty, it will be said of her: “Will a bride forget her adornment, or a virgin the band of her breast?” (Jer. 2:32.)

It follows: “And you were not washed in water for cleansing.”

The bloody bodies of infants are customarily washed as soon as they are brought forth from the womb; so spiritual birth also requires a saving washing. “No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life is but a single day” (Job 14:4, 5). And in the Psalms we read: “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50:6).

The second birth dissolves the first birth. For it is written: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

There are many washings that pagans promise in their mysteries, and heretics promise as well. They all wash, but they do not wash for salvation. Therefore it is added: “You were not washed in water for cleansing.”

This can be understood not only of heretics but also of members of the Church who do not receive saving baptism with complete faith. Of them it must be said that they received water but did not receive the Spirit, like that magician Simon, who wished to purchase the grace of God with money. He was indeed baptized in water, but he was by no means baptized for salvation (Acts 8).

Third, it is said: “Nor rubbed with salt.”

While infants’ tender bodies still retain the warmth of the womb and, by their first cry, bear witness to the beginnings of laborious life, midwives customarily touch them with salt, so that they may become drier and be tightened.

But Jerusalem, born from evil parents, acquired neither savor nor care. To those who are reborn in Christ it is said: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5:13). And the Apostle commands them: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Col. 4:6).

Hence, in common speech, wise people are called “salty,” and fools “insipid.” And the law is established in Leviticus: “Every sacrifice of yours shall be seasoned with salt. The salt of the covenant of the Lord shall not cease from your sacrifices; in all your offerings you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2:13).

Whoever has been seasoned with this salt, and by its admixture has dried out all corruption and harmful moisture, will no longer say: “My wounds have become foul and festering because of my foolishness” (Ps. 37:6).
