I know that I have read in a certain volume concerning the Lord Savior that he himself is heavenly salt, and that he has seasoned not only earthly and infernal things but also heavenly things with his savor, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Fourth: “Nor wrapped in cloths.”

The Savior too was wrapped in the cloths of infancy, and everyone who is born requires God’s protection through wrappings of cloth. It is natural—provided that the parents’ care is not lacking—that, when infants are born, first their umbilical cord is cut; second, they are washed with water to remove the blood; third, the moisture of their little bodies is dried by adding salt; fourth, their tender bodies are wrapped in cloths for two reasons: so that the body may be dried by the salt and, lest it flow away, be preserved and constricted by the cloths; and so that their most delicate limbs may not easily become deformed.

Hence the bodies of barbarians are straighter than Roman bodies. For until the second and third year they are always wrapped in cloths.

But Jerusalem was not like this. Her umbilical cord was not cut; her breasts were not bound; she was not washed in water for salvation; she was not rubbed with salt; nor was she wrapped and constricted in the cloths of infancy.

Why she deserved none of these things, the following Scripture testifies: “No eye pitied you, to do one of these things for you, out of compassion for you.”

In their place the Septuagint set: “Your eye did not pity you, to do one of all these things for you.” Since there are two editions, there must necessarily be two interpretations.

The first signifies: “No eye pitied you, to do one of these things for you, out of compassion for you.” The meaning is: No one pitied you, because God was offended; no one’s inward parts were moved over you, so as to do at least one of the four things mentioned above for you, since you did not deserve to receive them all together.

The other says: “Your eye did not pity you, to do one of these things for you, out of compassion for you.” Its meaning is: You acted in such a way, and were born in sins, and your mother conceived you in iniquities, that you did not even pity yourself. Since by your evil deeds you acted cruelly against yourself, what could I do for you, who did not deserve to receive even one of the things mentioned above?

Therefore, since none of the things normally done for infants was done for you—and this was not without cause or judgment, but because of your fault and sin, since you did not even pity yourself—you were thrown upon the face of the earth, or of the field, and were thrown there because of the perversity of your soul on the day you were born.

Let us pray that we may not be thrown because of the perversity of our soul upon the face of the field, where the way that leads to death is broad and spacious, and where the cavalry of the Chaldaeans rages.

At the same time, we must consider that no one can commit anything perverse on the day of his birth, except at the time of washing, when the wise generation of the believer is received through faith.

(Verses 6, 7.) “But passing by you, I saw you trampled in your blood. And I said to you, when you were in your blood: Live. I said to you, I repeat, when you were in your blood: Live. I made you numerous like the growth of a field, and you were multiplied and became great [Note: Through scribal carelessness, this verse has dropped out. Victorius supplies it from Jerome’s Vulgate edition and the Hebrew, indeed also from the Septuagint, whose Latin text reads: ‘and you were multiplied and magnified.’], and you entered and reached the adornment of a woman. Your breasts swelled, and your hair grew; but you were naked and full of shame.”

The Septuagint: “And I passed by you and saw you mixed in your blood, and I said to you, ‘From your blood, live and multiply.’ Like the growth of a field I made you; and you multiplied and grew great, and entered into cities of cities. Your breasts were raised, and your hair grew; but you were naked and full of dishonor.”

After you had been thrown upon the face of the field, or upon the face of the earth, because of the perversity of your soul, you no longer deserved my assistance. Nevertheless, passing by you, I saw you trampled—or mixed—in your blood, that is, guilty of mortal crimes; and I summoned you to repentance, saying to you: Although you are in blood, nevertheless live, having been converted.

Such abundance of all things was in you that you resembled a most fertile field, and possessed the blessing of Jacob with which his father blessed him, saying: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27).

You entered the Lord’s inner chambers and said with the bride: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:3). You reached the adornment of a woman. In place of this the Septuagint translated: “You entered into cities of cities,” so that, just as the Song of Songs and the age of ages are spoken of, cities may likewise be called cities of cities.

Concerning these it is said in the Gospel: “Have authority over ten cities,” or “over five cities” (Luke 19:17, 18), so that you may be called not merely a city but a metropolitan city, according to what is read in Isaiah: “Mother of cities is faithful Zion” (Isa. 1:26, 27).

What Symmachus translated as “you reached the adornment of women,” or what Theodotion rendered as “you entered into the adornment of adornments,” refers to the time of puberty. We, following the sense of the Hebrew, said: “You reached the adornment of a woman.” This indicates the time when girls are called marriageable and can be joined to the embraces of husbands.

Thus it follows: “Your breasts swelled, and your hair grew.” The maturity of young girls is decently indicated when their breasts swell, or are raised, and their hair grows.

When she was ready for marriage and possessed bodily beauty, however, she had no covering of clothing and was not protected by God’s assistance. Whoever does not have Christ’s garment is naked. Whoever is not clothed with compassion, goodness, humility, chastity, gentleness, and patience lies upon the face of the earth; and his beauty is disfigured by shame and nakedness [Note: Previously the text had turbatur, “is disturbed,” which gives an unsuitable sense; we have restored turpatur, “is disfigured.”].

### (Verse 8)

“And I passed by you and saw you; and behold, your time was the time of lovers. And I spread my garment over you and covered your shame.”

The Septuagint: “And I passed by you and saw you; and behold, your time was the time of those turning aside; and I spread my wings over you and covered your shame.”

What mercy! It had not been enough to see her once, trampled in blood, and summon her to repentance. He visits the sinner again; and because she was naked and full of shame, he comes and visits her again. “And behold, her time was the time of lovers,” or, according to the Septuagint, “of those turning aside”; or, according to Aquila’s second translation, συναλλαγῆς (*synallagēs*), that is, of betrothal and the time of marriage. According to that same translator’s first edition and Theodotion, it was the time of μαστῶν (*mastōn*), which means “of breasts”; for this Symmachus rendered ἀγαπῆς (*agapēs*), which signifies “of love.”

That, then, was the time when women can be joined to men and endure marital intercourse. Yet the merciful God spread his wings and received them, and carried them on his shoulders, according to what is written in the Gospel: “How often I desired to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Luke 13:34). Or he spread his garment in place of wings—for this is what πτερύγιον (*pterygion*) means, the garment with which Ruth was covered when she slept at Boaz’s feet (Ruth 3). And at the edge—that is, the πτερύγιον (*pterygion*)—of our garment, we are commanded to fasten violet-blue tassels.

He did these things in order to cover Jerusalem’s shame, indicating by this name the female genital body. For, according to the Apostle, “We clothe the dishonorable parts of our body with greater honor” (1 Corinthians 12:23). Hence the Psalmist also sings: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1). Because Ham did not cover these things in his father, he was marked with an eternal curse (Genesis 9).

What we have said about Jerusalem, let us apply to our own soul, which, so long as it remains in infancy, is free from sin. But when the time of its age arrives, there are many lovers of demons, heretics, and perverse doctrines who desire to turn toward it. They are driven away by God’s protection, so that the soul may receive not the devil’s attendants but the Savior’s ministers.

In place of “of those turning aside,” “of love,” and “of breasts,” the Hebrew has DODIM (דודים), which, according to the characteristic usage of their language, signifies all the things translated above. The time of love, and of breasts—or of God’s lovers—may be understood as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, when, after the Egyptian slavery, the Lord promised them that his people would be liberated.

“And I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you,” says the Lord God.

The Septuagint: “And I swore to you and entered into a testament with you,” says Adonai the Lord.

Because I spread my garment—or my wings—over you and covered your shame, therefore I swore to you and entered into a covenant, or testament, with you, so that you might be joined to me rather than to the others who wished to turn toward you, according to the saying: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 6).

For the end of every dispute is an oath. And: “As I live,” says the Lord, “I desire not the death of the sinner, but his repentance” (Ezekiel 18). At the time of marriage, therefore, Israel receives God’s oath in exchange for every bridal gift.

And because David had said of himself, “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness” (Psalm 132:1)—he who swore to the Lord and vowed a vow to the God of Jacob—the Lord himself also swears to him, as Scripture says: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him” (ibid., 11).

### (Verse 9)

“And you became mine, and I washed you with water, and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil.”

Because I spread my wings over you, covered your shame, swore to you, and entered into a covenant with you, therefore you became my possession: you who were alien when you appeared unclean began to be mine when I confirmed my covenant with you by an oath.

Or, according to the customary usage of the prophets, he says, “You became mine,” in place of, “You were joined to me in marriage.” And he says, “I washed you,” with the water of saving baptism. “Unless one is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). And elsewhere we read: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Mark 1:8).

Isaiah also speaks of this baptism, saying: “The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning” (Isaiah 4:4).

[Editorial note: Erasmus and Marianus thought that Jerome had called the woman with the hemorrhage holy; consequently, in place of the Latin particle *etiam* (“also”), they substituted the Greek word ἁγίαν (“holy”), contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts. MART.—For *sicut* (“just as”), preferred by our manuscripts and by Rabanus, Martianay reads *quo etiam* (“by which also”); older printed editions corruptly read *quo ἁγίαν*, that is, “which [the] holy [woman]”; αἱμοῤῥοῦσαν, etc.]

When he has washed and cleansed the blood—just as the αἱμοῤῥοῦσα (*haimorrhousa*), the woman who had been bleeding for twelve years, was healed by touching the fringe (Mark 5)—it is not enough for him to wash with water and cleanse with blood unless he also anoints with oil. In accordance with this, the Samaritan—whose name means “guardian”—first treated the half-dead man’s wounds by pouring on oil, and afterward restrained them with the harshness of wine (Luke 10).

Our Lord, however, was anointed with another oil, which did not relieve the pain of wounds but bestowed joy, as the Holy Spirit said to him: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:8).

The opposing powers also possess the apparent gentleness of counterfeit oil, promising sweet things through heretics; but these are turned into bitterness. The prophet condemns them when he says: “But the oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head” (Psalm 141:5).

But if, from anointing, the Anointed One is called “Christ,” see how greatly Jerusalem has advanced: she too, anointed with spiritual oil, has received the name of Christ. Accordingly, we read of Abraham in the Psalms: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.”

### (Verse 10)

“And I clothed you in garments of various colors.”

[Editorial note: This little verse, “And I clothed you in garments of various colors,” was absent. There can be no doubt that Jerome placed it here, since he also gives the Septuagint’s version and consistently places the Hebrew truth before it; below, moreover, he notes: “Jerusalem is not only clothed in garments of various colors and shod in hyacinth, but …” We supplied it from the manuscripts and Rabanus.]

The Septuagint: “And I clothed you in various garments.”

With the ceremonies of the Law, whose observance would occupy you so that you might abandon idols. These are the various garments in which Joseph was clothed; and his brothers could not sell him until they had first stripped him of his multicolored tunic (Genesis 37).

And concerning the bride it is said in the forty-fourth Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a golden garment and surrounded with variety” (Psalm 45:10). This is the garment of which the Apostle also speaks: “Put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his Creator” (Ephesians 4:24).

Do we wish to know what the various garments are? Let the same Apostle teach us, writing to believers: “Put on, therefore, compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (Colossians 3:12). What could be more beautiful than this variety? Job spoke of it also: “Who gave women wisdom in weaving, or skill in variety?” (Job 38, according to the Septuagint).

And the high priest, once a year, when he burned incense on behalf of the people and entered the Holy of Holies, used various garments (Exodus 39; Hebrews 9).

Certainly, if wealth—and not holiness and a diversity of virtues—created variety in clothing, Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar would be said to have possessed these garments, and not Joseph, who, having a foreigner and shepherd for a father, could not have had multicolored and royal garments.

“And I shod you with violet.”

The Septuagint: “And I shod you with hyacinth” [variant: “with hyacinth-colored material”].

Aquila and Symmachus translated it as “violet”; the Septuagint and Theodotion as “hyacinth-colored.” In Hebrew it is written THAS (תחש).

Since the discourse is fittingly directed toward Jerusalem, and all her adornment is expressed under the figure of a woman, shoes of hyacinth or violet are mentioned—shoes that do not suit a male figure. Indeed, those who were to make the Passover were commanded, without any variety of color, to have their loins girded and their feet shod.

These are the shoes of which the Apostle also writes: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace.” Philo, the most eloquent of the Jewish writers, compares the hyacinth material in the high priest’s garments to the air, through which he thinks the things above and heavenly things are signified.

Jerusalem is not shod in hyacinth until she has first been washed with water. Hence the Savior washes the feet of the Apostles, whom the Lord had previously commanded to shake the dust from their feet (Matthew 10). And the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song of Songs 5:3).

The divine word also testifies concerning Moses and Jesus (Exodus 3) that they should remove the strap of their sandal, because the place on which they stood was holy.

[Editorial note: In my opinion, *obtestatur* (“earnestly charges” or “adjures”) ought to be read, or something similar.] When their feet have been washed and cleansed from every impurity, they are shod in hyacinth or violet—both of which are aerial or sky-blue and κυάνεος (*kyaneos*, dark blue)—so that they may be snatched up to meet the Lord in the air and hasten toward the heavenly kingdoms.

“And I girded you with fine linen.”

Jerusalem is not only clothed in garments of various colors and shod in hyacinth; she is also girded with fine linen, from which the most delicate threads are woven into the high priest’s garment.

And the wife in Proverbs, who made two cloaks for her husband—one for the present age and one for the future—is said to have made garments for herself from fine linen and purple (Proverbs 31).

The loins are girded with this fine linen whenever the rich stimulants of lust must be weakened and no thick moisture is left in them [variant: “no thick Venus”]. Thus we fulfill the Apostle’s command: “Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth” (Ephesians 6:14), as though he were saying in other words, “with fine linen.”

And the Lord says to the Apostles: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). Unless we bind the flowing discharges of the loins, we cannot hold lamps in our hands. Hence God says to Job: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job 38:3).

Those who are about to eat the lamb, with shod feet, holding staffs, standing in the truth of the Gospel, and prepared for the blood of Christ, are also said to have their loins girded (Exodus 12). With this belt that mortifies the loins, Elijah and John the Baptist are likewise girded (2 Kings 1; Mark 1). Concerning them the repentant man groans sorrowfully, saying: “For my loins are filled with mockeries” (Psalm 38:8).

“And I clothed you with delicate material.”

The Septuagint: “And I surrounded you with a trichaptum.”

In place of this Aquila has “florid” or “tangible”; Symmachus, “garment”; Theodotion retained the Hebrew word itself, MESSE (מֶשֶׂה) [variant: “Messi,” as it is also read below].

When I carefully investigated what the word *trichaptum* meant—the word translated by the Septuagint—and could find neither its usage nor its etymology among any Greek writers, I finally learned that it had been coined by the Septuagint, since new things require new names. It referred to a garment of such delicacy that it was thought to possess the fineness of hairs and hair.

Therefore, wishing to express the garment’s delicacy, I translated *trichaptum* as “delicate material,” because it was woven with a fine warp and weft.

And appropriately, to those concerning whom he had earlier complained, saying, “The heart of this people has grown fat; Jacob ate and drank, was filled and grew fat, and the beloved kicked, and abandoned God his Maker” (Deuteronomy 32:15), the delicacy of garments is now granted.

In the Book of Wisdom, which some attribute to Solomon, the only-begotten and manifold spirit of wisdom is likewise called “thin” and “changeable” (Wisdom 7).

And manna, of which it is written, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 78:25), is described as extremely fine, resembling frost and coriander seed (Exodus 16).

According to Aquila’s second edition, in which he translated the word as “florid,” we may understand the garment metaphorically as the fertility of the land of Judea, or as the beauty of divine worship.

[Editorial note: Theodoret teaches that it was a braid made from hair, placed around women’s heads. A scholion in the Coislinian manuscript, preserved by Montfaucon, says: “A braid in which the hairs are woven together. But he calls *trichaptum* that which is fashioned from gold, as if he were saying, ‘made from golden thread.’ He speaks of a garment woven with figures of animals in gold.” *Plexus*, with which the hair is intertwined. He says *trichaptum* is something fashioned from gold, as though he meant “from gold thread.” He is speaking of a garment interwoven with animal figures in gold. Jerome himself considers a similar cloak, in Letter 107 to Laeta, to have been a sign of chastity.]

### (Verse 11)

“And I adorned you with adornment.”

He now speaks generally of the ornaments which he subsequently enumerates in detail: bracelets, a necklace, earrings, a crown, and the other ornaments that he granted to Jerusalem, and which Isaiah says she lost through her own fault.

For it is written: “Because the daughters of Jerusalem were lifted up”—that is, became proud—“and walked with an elevated neck” (Isaiah 3:16–17), and what follows: instead of a belt, they were girded with ropes; instead of head adornment, they were disfigured with baldness; and instead of beautiful and soft garments, they were wrapped in the roughness of sackcloth.

“And I gave bracelets upon your hands.”

The Septuagint: “And I surrounded your hands with bracelets.”

Whenever God gives us good works, he surrounds our hands with bracelets. Hence he says that he was likened to the hands of the prophets (Hosea 13), and we frequently read that the word came to the hand of Haggai, Jeremiah, and the others (Haggai 1).

In Job also, the lip of the dragon is pierced by a bracelet, and all his poisonous hissings—which are understood as perverse doctrines—are pierced by the circle of good works (Job 40).

“And a necklace around your neck.”

For “necklace,” which we have translated according to Aquila’s second edition and Symmachus, the Septuagint and Theodotion rendered κάθεμα (*kathema*). This word is written not only here but also in Isaiah: “The Lord will remove the glory of their clothing, the chains, the hair ornaments, the bracelets, and the *kathema*” (Isaiah 3:18).

I think they called *kathema* a necklace descending onto a woman’s breast, made from various gems; it too is a very beautiful ornament for women.

### (Verse 12)

“And I gave an earring upon your mouth—or your nostrils.”

Apart from Symmachus, who translated the Hebrew word NEZEM (נֶזֶם) as ἐπιρρίνιον (*epirrhinion*, “a nose ornament”), all the translators rendered it “earring.” This does not mean that earrings are placed in the nostrils—for they are called earrings because they hang from the ears—but that a circle made in the likeness of earrings was called by the same name. Even today, among women’s other ornaments, golden circles commonly hang from the face and extend over the nostrils.

We understand these ornaments according to their mystical meaning whenever, with the Apostle, we can say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to some, the fragrance of death unto death, and to others, the fragrance of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

When we live, and it can be said of us, “The dead shall not praise you, Lord, but we who live” (Psalm 115:17), then God smells the fragrance of our sacrifice, a good aroma, and we have in our nostrils a golden circle of divine thoughts and doctrines.

But when we are dead and lie in filth and the foulness of shameful things, we have that earring in our nostrils of which Solomon wrote: “As a golden earring in a pig’s snout, so is beauty in a badly behaved woman” (Proverbs 11:22).

“And rings in your ears.”

The Septuagint: “And little wheels over your ears.”

Whoever closes his ears so as not to hear judgment concerning bloodshed, and fences them with thorns so as not to become a participant with the envious and slanderers—of whom it is written, “Do not associate with slanderers, because their destruction will come suddenly; and who knows the ruin of both?” (Proverbs 24:21–22)—both of the slanderer and of the one who willingly listens: such a person has rings and little wheels in his ears.

These are not the wheels that follow the cherubim—for that belongs to the angelic powers—but little wheels, diminutively named, which correspond to human weakness. Therefore it is also said to God: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel” (Psalm 77:18).

Among those who pass through earthly things and scarcely touch the earth with slight footprints—of whom it is written, “The holy stones roll upon the earth” (Zechariah 9:16)—the voice of the Lord’s thunder and of exalted doctrines resounds.

But those who are led by human errors, who lack firm footsteps and are carried about by every wind of doctrine (Ephesians 4:14), and who, expelled from the paradise of stability, dwell in the region of Naid—which means “fluctuation”—deserve to bear the sentence of the lying tongue, which inflames the wheel of our birth (Genesis 4:24).

“And a crown of beauty upon your head.”

The Septuagint: “And a crown of boasting upon your head.”

We translated “beauty” according to Symmachus, on account of the elegance of the sense. Otherwise, in Hebrew THOPHERTH (תפארת), and in the other translators, the word is καύχησις (*kauchēsis*), “boasting.”

The remaining ornaments belong to individual limbs. The ornament of the head is the dignity of the whole body. By the crown he means the women’s diadem, by which the luxuriance of the hair is bound and adorned.

Do we wish to know what the crown of beauty is on Jerusalem’s head? Let us turn to Exodus, where it is written: “And he made a golden plate and wrote upon it letters engraved like a seal of holiness to the Lord, and placed it upon Aaron’s head” (Exodus 39:30).

The sign of the Lord’s holiness is the name of the almighty God, which is written with four Hebrew letters יהוה and among them is called ineffable, since his name cannot be pronounced.

Even the Gentiles are not ignorant of its majesty, as the altar of the Athenians testifies, inscribed: “To an unknown God.”

[Editorial note: If Oecumenius is to be believed, the inscription was: “To the gods of Asia, Europe, and Libya—to the unknown and foreign God.” Compare Jerome’s Commentary on Titus, chapter 1.] Hence the Apostle also says: “Whom you worship as unknown, him I proclaim to you” (Acts 17:23).

I think this is the crown of which the Psalmist also says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:6). And the Apostle said: “I have completed my course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the righteous judge will give me” (2 Timothy 4:7–8).

And elsewhere he says to believers: “My joy and my crown” (Philippians 4:1). For children are the glory of their fathers.

And in Solomon it is written: “Old age is a crown of glory” (Proverbs 16:31)—the old age, namely, of those who have destroyed the things belonging to children and, after reaching the age of a mature man, have come to old age and to the names of the fathers. To these John writes after the children and the young men (1 John 2). They can say: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, understood as a child, and reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of the child” (1 Corinthians 13:11).

### (Verse 13)

“And you were adorned with gold and silver.”

We have often said that gold refers to the mind and silver to speech. May the Lord grant us to be worthy to receive divine understanding and wisdom, and to express what we conceive in the mind with the beauty of speech; and may we never make an idol from these things, as the heretics do, of whom it is written: “I gave them silver and gold, but they made Baal from silver and gold” (Hosea 2:8).

This is especially appropriate to women’s adornment according to the spiritual interpretation. Otherwise, silver, being the cheaper material, is the ornament of rustic women, poor women, and maidservants; it does not suit Jerusalem, who is said to have advanced to queenship.

“And you were clothed in fine linen, embroidered work, and garments of various colors.”

The Septuagint: “And your garments were of fine linen, trichapta, and multicolored fabrics.”

The Hebrew word MESI (מֶשִׂי) is here also rendered by Theodotion as above; Aquila has ἄνθιμον (*anthimon*, “floral”); Symmachus, “embroidered work.”

[Editorial note: This is how the manuscripts read here, though above they retain *Messe* or *Mse*. Thus the Hebrew word could be read *Msse* or *Mesi* when it lacked vowel points. MART.—The Milanese manuscript of Archinto, which we now begin to use, reads *Msi*.]

What above we called “delicate,” here, following Symmachus, we have called “embroidered work.” The Septuagint translated it as τρίχαπτα (*trichapta*), preserving the earlier translation, so as to indicate garments delicate like hair.

All the adornment of women is described: she is washed, cleansed, anointed with oil, clothed in garments of various colors, shod with hyacinth, girded with fine linen, dressed in *trichapta* or delicate garments, given bracelets and a golden necklace, circles hanging before her face, little wheels in her ears, a diadem on her head, and adorned with gold and silver—although silver is the cheaper material and is introduced only afterward.

“And you were clothed in fine linen, embroidered work, and garments of various colors”; or, as the Septuagint translated it, “with a garment and cloaks.” For this is what περιβόλαια (*peribolaia*) signifies: she was adorned not only with bodily dress and possessed all the ornaments of women, but also showed marital concern for her bedding and couch, so that, after completing these things, she might proceed to the delights of food and not suffer anything to be lacking even there.

According to the explanation given above, we shall apply all these things to spiritual understanding: she is covered with fine linen and delicate garments, so that the delicate limbs of the wife may not be weighed down by the heavy burden of cloaks, but that the garments may provide both usefulness and beauty.

“You ate fine flour, honey, and oil, and you became exceedingly, exceedingly beautiful.”

After clothing, he takes care of food, so that Jerusalem may eat fine flour, honey, and oil—either separately, as most think, or combined into a sweeter bread, the bread that came down from heaven (John 6). Under these three names, as some think, he indicates the mystery of the Trinity—not that there is one substance here and another there, but that under the different names of fine flour, honey, and oil the one sweetness of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is displayed.

It should also be observed that fine flour, the marrow of grain and the purest part of it, is offered in many sacrifices. Of it it is written: “He satisfied them with the fat of wheat” (Psalm 81:17). It is not barley flour, nor ordinary flour, which is offered only when a husband is stirred by the spirit of jealousy.

In the Book of Judges we read of Deborah (Judges 4), whose name means “bee.” Her prophecy is exceedingly sweet honey, and it refers to the Holy Spirit, who among the Hebrews is called RUA (רוּחַ) in the feminine gender.

In the Gospel of the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes read, the Savior is introduced as saying: “Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, seized me.”

[Editorial note: Compare what we have said elsewhere, and especially in the prefatory admonition to the *Dialogues against the Pelagians*, concerning this Gospel of the Nazarenes.]

Fine flour, which is made from wheat, refers to the Lord, who says of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls and dies in the earth, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

Oil, however, which sustains and refreshes the limbs of the weary, nourishes light, and with which the perpetual lamp is kindled in God’s tabernacle, is said to correspond to the Father.

All these things bestow one grace upon believers, as the Apostle says: “There are divisions of graces, but one Spirit; divisions of ministries, but one Lord; and divisions of operations, but one God, who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6).

Whoever eats such food, and is nourished by this sweetest and most pleasant bread shining with the brightness of oil, will be transformed into beauty and become exceedingly beautiful—not once, but repeatedly: “exceedingly, exceedingly.” For the doubled adverb gives weight to the sentence, indicating that nothing further can be added to the greatness of the beauty.

“And you advanced into royalty.”

This is not found in the Septuagint. Perhaps, when they translated the Scriptures from the Hebrew truth into Greek at Alexandria, they feared publishing it, lest they seem to offend the king of Egypt by declaring that royalty belonged to Jerusalem from God—although learned men affirm that they translated only the five books of Moses [see above, chapter 5].

After her manifold adornment, her crown, the abundance of gold and silver, her beautiful garments and cloaks, and her incredible beauty, she advances to queenship, because she is the city of the great King, concerning whom it is written: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Psalm 72:1).

And in John’s Apocalypse Jerusalem is described as a bride adorned and prepared for her husband (Revelation 21). In the Psalms also it is said of her: “The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, surrounded with variety” (Psalm 45:10).

Everything that we say about Jerusalem—so that we do not dwell on each individual point and the length of the books does not weary the readers—we shall refer to the Church. For if Jerusalem, according to the Apostle (Galatians 4), is our mother, and our mother is the Church, then Jerusalem is consequently the Church, the mother of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.

### (Verse 14)

“And your name went out among the nations because of your beauty, for you were perfect in my beauty which I placed upon you,” says the Lord God.

The Septuagint: “And your name went out among the nations in your beauty, because it was completed in the beauty which I placed upon you,” says the Lord God.

Symmachus interpreted this passage more clearly: “And your name went out among the nations because it was perfected through my dignity, which I had placed upon you,” says the Lord God.

The sense is this: by my benefits and my incredible generosity you attained the name of queen, so that all the nations spoke of you; and you were perfected not through your own merits and virtues but through my generosity.

[Editorial note: The Vatican manuscript, followed by Rabanus, reads “which was,” followed by “not through your own merits … but through my generosity.”]

“For unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Psalm 127:1–2). “The one who plants and the one who waters is nothing, unless the Lord gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3), because it is “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16). Thus, after we have done everything, we should say: “We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke 17:10).

This does not mean that human free choice is removed because of God’s beneficence, but that freedom itself ought to have the Lord as its helper.

### (Verse 15)

“But trusting in your beauty, you committed fornication in your own name and exposed your fornication to every passerby, so that you might become his.”

There is great danger—not in trusting in God’s mercy, but in trusting in one’s own beauty. The higher anyone has risen, the more he ought to fear lest he fall and commit fornication in his own name.

For the hostile powers despise their customary food and desire foreign nourishment. Hence it is said of the devil: “His foods are choice” (Habakkuk 1:16). He does not wish to deceive just anyone. He hastens to overthrow King Saul, who was chosen by the Lord, and the Apostle Judas.

Let us not, therefore, trust in our own beauty, nor regard God’s generosity as our own virtue. Rather, let us hear: “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the day may bring forth” (Proverbs 27:1).

And elsewhere: “Brothers, if anyone is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

Nor should we expose—or pour out—our fornication to every passerby, so that we may become not the possession of the God in whom we believe but the possession of the one by whom we are polluted.

Whoever receives every vice, welcomes into his bosom the passing spirit of various sins, and spreads his legs before every passerby—such a person pours out his fornication and begins to endure the domination of the one whose guest he has become.

### (Verse 16)

“And taking some of your garments, you made for yourself high places sewn together here and there, and you committed fornication upon them, such as has not been done and will not be done.”

The Septuagint: “And you took some of your garments and made for yourself sewn idols, and you committed fornication upon them; and you will not enter, nor will it happen.”

Symmachus interpreted the passage in this way: “And when you had taken some of your garments, you made for yourself multicolored high places, and you committed fornication in them—things not made and not to be made.”

In place of “sewn,” “multicolored,” and “high places,” or “idols,” Aquila and Theodotion translated ἐμβολίσματα (*embolismata*), which signifies various pieces sewn together here and there, and an idol made in the manner of a plaster patch, like a πολυρράφον (*polyrrhaphon*), a garment of many patches.

“I clothed you,” he says, “with garments of various colors, and you were clothed in fine linen, embroidered work, and garments of many forms. But you took the garments with which you had been endowed through my generosity and made for yourself idols or high places, which in Hebrew are called BAMOTH (במות). Something such as this had never been done before, nor will it be done afterward: you turned what you had received for adornment into an insult against the giver.”

This may be understood literally concerning Jerusalem, since she assigned all the precepts of the Law, together with wealth and abundance of every kind, to idols—something no other nation had done or would do. For all the nations that had served idols from the beginning were not guilty of so great a crime.

Our Jerusalem, however, whose name means “vision of peace,” is torn apart by heretics when, plucking one or another testimony of Scripture from its proper setting, they attempt to sew it onto things with which it cannot be fitted.

Concerning them we read above in this same prophet: “Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow of the hand and make coverings over the head of people of every age” (Ezekiel 13:18). The Lord forbids this in the Gospel when he says: “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. Otherwise it takes away from its fullness, and the tear becomes worse; nor do they put new wine into old wineskins” (Matthew 9:16–17).

Such are the Nazarenes, who attempt to fit the observance of the old Law to the grace of the Gospel. Such also are all heretics, who strive to sew a testimony that agrees with one meaning in its proper place onto another meaning, even though the Lord’s tunic, woven from above throughout, cannot be torn at all; woven by the Holy Spirit, it admits no division.

As for the words according to the Septuagint, “You will not enter, nor will it happen,” they signify this: when you have made idols for yourself out of perverse doctrines, which you regard as high places, and have committed fornication upon them, believing in the things you yourself fashioned, you will not be able to enter the temple of God.

And your images will possess no substance and will not endure forever, as the Apostle says: “We know that an idol is nothing in the world” (1 Corinthians 8:4).

### (Verse 17)

“And you took the vessels of your adornment from my gold and my silver, which I gave you [the Vulgate: ‘which I gave you’], and you made for yourself male images, and you committed fornication in them.”

Literally, the Lord commanded through the Law that censers, bowls, the lampstand, the Ark of the Covenant, and everything made of gold or overlaid with gold should be constructed, together with other objects made of silver. Jerusalem melted all these things down and turned them into idols of Bel, or Baal, Chemosh, Astarte, and Milcom.

According to the spiritual interpretation, we make idols from the gold and silver of the Holy Scriptures when we corrupt, through heretical perversity, the grace of understanding and eloquence, and “set our mouth in heaven, while our tongue passes through the earth” (Psalm 73:9).

The images are called “male” because every heresy commits fornication with them, on the grounds that each person thinks he worships and possesses something extremely strong that he himself has fashioned, something that cannot be overthrown by any attack.

These are the images we have fashioned out of our own heart, and which must be destroyed in the heavenly Jerusalem. Concerning them the prophet declares: “Lord, in your city you will destroy their image” (Psalm 73:20).

For whoever is merely human and has lost the name of God is described in these words: “Nevertheless, man walks about in an image; nevertheless, he is troubled in vain” (Psalm 39:6).

We, however, have one man and venerate one image, which is the image of the invisible and almighty God.

### (Verse 18)

“And you took your multicolored garments and covered them”—that is, the male images—“so that you might turn all the worship you had received for use into blasphemy.”

We do this whenever we surround heretical perversity with prudence, temperance, courage, justice, and all the virtues, and under their pretext deceive the simple, so that, seeing the honey of the virtues, they do not beware of the poisons of the vices.

And my oil and my incense you set before them. And my bread (or, as the Septuagint translated it, “my loaves”), which I gave you—fine flour, oil, and honey, with which I nourished you—you set before them as a pleasing fragrance. The oil of which we spoke above, and the incense, concerning which the Psalmist proclaims, “Let my prayer be directed as incense before you” (Ps. 140:2); and the loaves of the Presence, which we are commanded to offer to God; likewise the fine flour, the purest meaning of the Scriptures; and the honey which Jonathan tasted, whereupon his eyes were opened and he was strengthened (1 Sam. 14)—wretched Jerusalem set all these before idols, or before the masculine images, so that they might be a pleasing fragrance to them. These things are sweet and exceedingly pleasant by nature; but when offered to idols and false doctrines, they are turned into bitterness.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0139]

[Col. 0139D] 163–164. So that the number of the books might not become confused, and the order of the volumes divided from one another over long periods of time might not be disrupted, I have prefixed brief prefaces to each book, so that from the beginning of the title the reader may immediately recognize which book he is to read and which prophecy we are to explain. In the preceding volume, therefore—that is, the fourth—I briefly discussed, as I was able, the portion of the prophecy against Jerusalem beginning, “Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan,” and extending to the passage where it is written, “Fine flour and oil and honey, with which I nourished you, you set before them as a pleasing fragrance.” Now the remaining portion of the same prophecy, together with what follows, is dedicated in this fifth volume to your name, Eustochium. In it you will find nothing from rhetorical technique, nothing from arrangement or verbal elegance; rather, you will find the care of simple and diligent application, so that this alone may be my praise: that through me you may understand the prophet’s words.

[Col. 0141B] (Verse 20 and following.) “And it came to pass,” says the Lord God, “that you took your sons and your daughters, whom you had borne [the Vulgate: begotten] for me, and sacrificed them to be devoured. Is your fornication a small matter, that you slaughter my sons?” [Note: From the Hebrew, and in the Vulgate edition Victorius restored “you slaughtered.”] “And you gave them over, consecrating them to them. And after all your abominations and your fornications, you did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and full of shame, trampled in your blood.”

The Septuagint: “And it came to pass after these things,” says Adonai the Lord, “that you took your sons and your daughters, whom you had borne, and sacrificed them to them for destruction, as though you had fornicated but little;” [Note: Victorius reconstructs the passage as follows: “and you gave them over to make atonement through them,” from the Septuagint, which reads καὶ ἔδωκας αὐτὰ ἐν τῷ ἀποτροπιάζεσθαι ἐν αὐτοῖς, “and you gave them over to make atonement,” or “to expiate,” and so forth. Jerome also supports this reading in his Commentary, where he says: “In that passage where we have placed ‘and you gave them over, consecrating them to them,’ the Septuagint translated ‘and you gave them over to make atonement,’ or ‘to expiate,’ and so forth.”] “and you killed your sons, and gave them over when you offered them to them—that is, above all your fornication and abominations—and you did not remember the day of your infancy, when you were naked and dishonored. You lived, mingled with your blood.”

That Jerusalem sacrificed her sons and daughters—concerning whom it is written, “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they despised me” (Isa. 1:2)—to idols, Holy Scripture records: “They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons” (Ps. 105:37). And again: “They poured out innocent blood” (ibid., 38), the blood of their sons and daughters, “whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan” (Exod. 4:22). He calls them “his own” according to the Hebrew. For he himself had said concerning them, “Israel is my firstborn son.” Or, according to the Septuagint, “your own,” whom you bore from fornication. In the passage where we have placed, “and you gave them over, consecrating them to them,” while the Septuagint translated, “and you gave them over to make atonement,” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion rendered it, “you transferred and led them across,” because the Gentiles either transfer their children through fire or compel adults to pass through it.

“When you have done these things,” he says, “you did not remember your infancy, when I took you, covered with blood, washed you, and, after the many things narrated by the prophetic word, joined you to myself.” Our Jerusalem also, if it has been overthrown by heretical deceit, takes her sons, who [Note: In the same source: “who are more discerning,” etc.] are stronger in faith, and her daughters, who do not possess such strength of faith. Or certainly, she takes sons who understand all that is mystical, and daughters who follow the simple historical sense; and she hands them over to demons to be devoured. When she kills them, she believes that she is giving them life and at the same time propitiating the images, whose slaughter satisfies them.

What is said according to the Septuagint—“above all your fornication and your abominations”—signifies that the doctrine of demons is worse than all sins and fornications; indeed, it kills those whom Jerusalem had either begotten for God with much labor or made her own sons, whom she bore in fornication.

(Verses 23 and following.) “And it came to pass after all your wickedness”—woe, woe to you, says the Lord God—“that you built yourself a brothel and made yourself a place of prostitution in every street. At the head of every road you built a sign of your prostitution, and you made your beauty abominable; you spread [variant: dismissed] your legs to every passerby and multiplied your fornications. And you fornicated with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, men of great flesh, and multiplied your fornication in order to provoke me.”

The Septuagint: “And it came to pass after all your wickedness—woe, woe to you,” says Adonai the Lord. “And you built yourself a dwelling-place of fornication and made yourself a place of prostitution in every street. At the beginning of every road you built your fornications; you corrupted your beauty, and spread your legs to every passerby, and multiplied your fornication. And you fornicated with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, who are men of great flesh, and fornicated in many ways in order to provoke me to anger.”

The Vulgate edition does not have the second “woe, woe to you”; it was added from Theodotion’s edition. Again, where we said, “And you built yourself a brothel,” while the Septuagint translated, “And you built yourself a dwelling-place of fornication,” Symmachus and Theodotion interpreted it as πορνεῖον, “brothel.” Aquila, wishing to express the etymology of the Hebrew word GOB (גוב), rendered it βάθυνον, which we may call a “pit,” so as to signify a tavern, a dug-out cavern, and a dark hollow in which the lust of prostitutes is exercised.

What follows—“And you made yourself a place of prostitution in every street”—for which the Septuagint translated ἔκθεμα, [Note: Polychronius says, ἔκθεμα λέγει οἷον τὸ προαγώγιον ἔνθα τὰς πόρνας τρέφειν εἰώθασι: “He calls it ecthema, like a brothel where they are accustomed to keep prostitutes.”] has RAMA in Hebrew; and both Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion interpreted it as “high” or “exalted.” Finally, in what follows, where it is written, “At the head of every road you built a sign of your prostitution,” the Hebrew again has RAMA (רמה) for “sign” and “fornication,” which we have interpreted either as “brothel” or “sign,” although among the Hebrews it is one word. It is placed in an elevated position so that the place of fornication may appear from afar to those wishing to fornicate, and there may be no need to search for it.

What we have said once, twice, and repeatedly may suffice as having been said forever: under the person of a woman who fornicates after receiving many benefits from her husband, the fornication of Jerusalem is described—how she departed from God and joined herself to idols, and was not content with hidden fornication, but built herself a brothel and set up a sign for passersby on every road, so that they might come to the prostitute and satisfy their lust—not so much their own as that of the woman who spread her legs to every passerby and disfigured the greatness of her beauty by the greatness of her fornication. Among other things, she also submitted herself to the Egyptians, her neighbors, out of love for great flesh.

And in order to display every kind of disgrace, she was disfigured by many forms of impurity. No one doubts that Palestine is near Egypt, since the Lord says to Abraham, “I will give you all the land from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates” (Gen. 15:18), so that on one side she would have the Egyptians and on the other the Assyrians, with whom she is also said to have fornicated later. Jerusalem’s fornication with the Egyptians is an imitation of their idolatry.

For our Jerusalem—whether the Church or the souls of believers—if they are negligent and open to every vice, a twofold word of curse is directed, so that they may hear, “Woe, woe to you,” says the Lord God, in accordance with what is written in the Apocalypse of John: “Woe to all the inhabitants of the earth” (Rev. 8:13). For if the holy man says, “I am a sojourner and a stranger, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:13), why should the sinner not be called an inhabitant of the earth?

He builds himself a brothel who sins with complete shamelessness, in accordance with what is written: “When the sinner comes into the depth of iniquity, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). He constructs a very high place in every street: “For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death.” And he builds at the beginning of every road, so that he may omit no kind of sin; but, imitating the prostitute of Proverbs, he openly invites foolish young men passing through the streets and street corners into her embraces and pollutes the beauty of the soul, which she received as a benefit from God the Creator (Prov. 5 and 7).

All her roads are full of disgrace. She opens her heart to every thought that supplies fuel for vices, spreads her legs, and fornicates with the Egyptians, her neighbors, whose examples she follows—namely, with the Gentiles, who glory in their own disgrace. She is so abominable that she surpasses even them in depravity. And she does all this to provoke God to anger.

The Egyptians are said to be “of great flesh,” either because of the greatness of their disgrace or because of the ugliness of their sins. Hence the holy man is said to be “of small flesh,” which daily diminishes in him and is attenuated through the virtues, so that it is no longer called flesh but spirit; and he says in the psalm: “My soul thirsted for you, O God; how manifoldly my flesh thirsted for you” (Ps. 62:2). Or, as certain copies have it: “How my flesh was consumed: in a barren, pathless, and waterless land, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary” (1 Cor. 5). For this reason also the Corinthian fornicator is handed over to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved.

Concerning this flesh it is written: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6–7). Concerning it the Apostle also said: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50). And in Genesis God says: “My spirit will not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). And it is said to believers: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Rom. 8:8–9).

There is, however, another flesh of the saints, concerning which it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. 40:5).

(Verses 27–29.) “Behold, I stretched out [the Vulgate: I will stretch out] my hand over you, and I will take away your ordinances [the Vulgate: your right], and I will give you over to the souls [the Vulgate: into the souls] of those who hate you, the daughters of the Philistines, who are ashamed [variant: burn] of your criminal way.”

The Septuagint: “But if I stretch out my hand over you, and take away your lawful observances, I will give you over to the souls of those who hate you, the daughters of foreigners, who made you turn aside from your way.” What follows, ἠσέβησας—that is, “you acted impiously”—is joined by the Septuagint to the following chapter, whereas according to the other interpreters it concludes the preceding one.

The Lord stretches out his hand over Jerusalem in order to correct the delinquent and to take away her ordinances. As long as she kept God’s commandments, they were called the Lord’s ordinances. But when she worshiped idols and changed religion into impiety, they were no longer called hers. This is to be understood not only of the law and its ceremonies, but also of Sabbaths, feast days, and new moons. For when he gives the law, he says, “My Sabbaths and my feast days.” But when they departed from God, it is said to them: “Your new moons and Sabbaths and great day I will not [Note: Victorius supplies “accept,” from the Septuagint οὐκ ἀνέχομαι.] accept. Your fast and rest and festivals my soul hates” (Exod. 31; Deut. 5; Isa. 1:14).

The same is written concerning the people (Deut. 7). For the people who were previously called God’s people, after departing from the Lord, are described to Moses in these words: “Your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt have sinned” (Exod. 32:7).

This stretching out of the hand is elsewhere called an uplifting or a visitation. For when God does not rebuke the sinner, he contracts his hand. But when someone has sinned and begins to languish under God’s law, visitation is sent to him, in accordance with what is sung in the psalm: “If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. 88:31–32).

It is also written in this prophet: “If the land sins against me by committing a transgression, I will stretch out my hand over it and destroy the support of its bread,” and so forth. Here we ask what difference there is between the stretching out of the hand and its sending forth. The devil says to the Lord: “Send your hand and touch all that he has; surely he will bless you to your face” (Job 2:5). It seems to me that the hand is sent forth for the testing of those to whom it is sent, but is stretched out for the punishments of those who deserve penalties.

Not only are the stretching out and sending forth mentioned; the spreading out of God’s hand is also spoken of, when Isaiah proclaims in the person of the Lord: “All day long I spread out my hands to a disobedient and contradicting people” (Isa. 65:2). The holy man too is said to raise his hands, as Scripture says: “The lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2).

Now that God’s ordinances have been taken away from the Jewish people, let us ask what observance of the law they possess. They cannot offer sacrifices after the Temple has been taken away and destroyed; nor can the stoning of adulteresses and the punishment of other crimes permitted by the law be carried out; nor can the land be left fallow in the year of remission, nor can the other practices of this kind be observed.

She is given over to the souls of the daughters of those who hate her—the daughters of Palestine—when she is handed over to the Palestinians, whom the Septuagint indiscriminately calls “foreigners.” By these we may understand the cities or towns of Palestine.

Our Jerusalem also, if we pass over God’s ceremonies, and his hand is stretched out over us, and all observance of the law is taken away, will be handed over to the daughters of Palestine [Col. 0145C] and not to the sons. For we are not first handed over to stronger punishments, but, according to the quality of our sins, to lesser ones, so that, chastised through what is minor, we may avoid greater torments of suffering.

Philistim—that is, Palestinians—with the first part of the word altered, is interpreted as “those who fall by the cup,” or “fracture” [perhaps “actura”]. By this is signified that we will be handed over to hostile powers that have drunk from Babylon’s cup and have fallen, and whose works are perverse. The correction and disgrace of wretched Jerusalem will be so great that even the hostile powers themselves will be ashamed at the magnitude of our sins.

What we interpreted according to Symmachus as “criminal,” Theodotion set down in the Hebrew word itself, ZEMMA (זמה). [Note: Martianaeus writes it with an intervening yod, זימּה; it is generally a thought directed toward evil.]

When God’s ceremonies are taken away from the Jewish people, priesthood and legislation pass over to us, as Scripture says: “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them” (Ps. 9:21). And in another place: “Teach me your law, O Lord, in your way” (Ps. 26:11).

(Verses 28–29.) “And you fornicated with the sons of the Assyrians, because you were not yet satisfied; and after you fornicated, you were still not satisfied. And you multiplied your fornication in the land of Canaan with the Chaldeans, and even then you were not satisfied.”

The Septuagint: “You acted impiously and fornicated with the sons of Assur; and even then you were not satisfied. You fornicated and were not filled; and you multiplied your covenants with the land of Canaan and with the Chaldeans, and even among these you were not filled.”

Above, Jerusalem was said to have fornicated with the sons of Egypt, her neighbors, who were men of great flesh; here another neighboring people, the Assyrians, is indicated. For this reason she is handed over to both nations: she worshiped the images of both, and, entering Chaldea—which is the land of Canaan—imitated the errors of those under whose rule she lived.

According to the tropological sense, we often pass from some sins to others. Since we do not repent of our earlier crimes, we add sins to sins and are satisfied by no error; rather, like a long rope and the strap of a stubborn heifer, we drag our sins along and multiply our covenant—or our fornication—in the land of Canaan, which is interpreted as something like “shaking” or “fluctuation,” and with the Chaldeans, who also sound with us like “demons” (Ps. 39:3). We always leave our footprints upon the sea and can never say, “He set my feet upon a rock.”

We are subjected to the perversities of heretics, who bear the likeness of demons, or to the demons themselves, concerning whom Paul writes: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

(Verses 30–31.) “How shall I cleanse your heart,” says the Lord God, “when you do all these works of a prostitute and shameless woman? For you built your brothel at the head of every road and made your high place in every street; and you did not become like a prostitute who, out of disdain, raises her price.”

The Septuagint: “What shall I do with your heart,” says Adonai the Lord, “when you have done all these works of a fornicating and shameless woman?—and you fornicated threefold with your daughters [the Hebrew does not contain this]—when you built your brothel at the beginning of every road and made your base in every street; and you were not like a prostitute collecting payments.”

What the Septuagint said, “And you fornicated threefold with your daughters,” is not found in the Hebrew, nor did any of the other interpreters include it.

Ἐπαπορητικῶς (“contentiously,” or “in perplexity”) God speaks all these words to Jerusalem, because he cannot find a remedy with which he might cure her, sick and half-dead, in accordance with what Isaiah writes: “What more was there that I ought to have done for my vineyard, and I did not do for it?” (Isa. 5:4). And Hosea says: “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like dew that passes away in the morning” (Hos. 6:4).

For your idolatry was committed not in secret but with complete shamelessness, so that you placed altars at the beginnings and crossroads of every road, and made your base—or your high place, about which we spoke above—in every street. Nor did you imitate the clever prostitutes who customarily increase the price of lust by making it difficult to obtain, and thereby provoke their lovers to greater madness.

Or, according to the Septuagint: “You were not like a prostitute collecting payments,” but you gave what you ought to have received, so that, even in the fact that you fornicated and followed demons, you were not protected by their aid; rather, being oppressed by various captivities, you experienced your calamities.

This can also be referred to every Christian soul which, having abandoned the worship of God, allowed itself to be polluted by vices [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, with which Rabanus agrees: “allowed itself to be polluted by luxury”], and, having followed a worldly life, did not even prosper in it. It lost the riches of religion and did not receive the riches of the world. Nor was there any difficulty in corrupting it; it thrust itself upon its lovers.

There is also another spiritual fornication, when we abandon the Church and join ourselves to heretics, and build our brothel at the head of every road. Against this the divine word commands us: “Stand in the roads and seek the everlasting paths of the Lord, and see which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jer. 6:16)—namely, in the books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, and Kings, and in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets.

He builds his brothel at the beginnings of all the roads who, in support of a perverse doctrine, abuses the testimonies of Scripture and says: “This is what Isaiah said; this is what Hosea says; this is what Moses spoke; this is what Daniel said.” And beautifully he does not place his brothel in the middle of the roads or at their ends, but at the beginning. For if he comes to the knowledge and depths of the divine books, he will not be able to err.

He also makes his high place—or his base—in every street, allowing himself to be corrupted by the revelry and vices of the Gentiles and the impious. Even among the heretics, after he has been defiled by them, he has no grace but is exposed to contempt, because he has too easily lost the chastity of his former faith.

This statement—“You fornicated threefold with your daughters”—which, as we said above, is not found in the Hebrew, may be understood according to the literal sense of Jerusalem, because she fornicated in every manner in her towns and villages, and no corner or street remained where she had not erected signs of idolatry.

Or it may be understood of the Church and of believers who have been deceived. They did not heed the Apostle’s words: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23); rather, they fornicated in every manner—in body, soul, and spirit.

We read in Proverbs: [Note: Variant: “But write them down for yourself threefold.”] “But write them down for yourself threefold, so that you may answer words of truth addressed to you” (Prov. 22:20–21). We are commanded to understand the utterances of truth—that is, the Holy Scriptures—in three ways: first, according to the letter; second, in the middle manner, through tropology; third, more sublimely, so that we may understand what is mystical.

According to the letter, this means: “Let us not fornicate, as some of them fornicated, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day” (1 Cor. 10:8). And: “Let us not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (1 Cor. 10:10).

The middle sense, according to tropology, occurs when we depart from the letter and ascend somewhat toward higher things, as the Apostle says: “It is written: You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain.” Immediately he adds: “Is it really for oxen that God is concerned? Or does he certainly say this for our sake?” (1 Cor. 9:9).

The final—that is, third, sublime, and sacred—understanding is found in the words of the same Apostle: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife. This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32).

The daughters of the fornicating Church are the souls of believers who were first deceived and later fell into heresy; their guilt is attributed to the mother.

(Verses 32 and following.) “But you are like an adulterous woman who brings strangers in upon her husband. All prostitutes receive payments; but you gave payments to all your lovers and gave them gifts so that they might enter you from every side and fornicate with you. What happened in you was contrary to the custom of women in your fornications, and after you there will be no fornication. For in that you gave payments and did not receive payments, the contrary happened in you.”

The Septuagint: “An adulterous woman—like you [the Hebrew does not contain this]—receiving payments from her husband: she gave payments to all who fornicated with her. But you gave payments to all your lovers and burdened them to come to you from every side in your fornication. And what happened in you was perverse, contrary to women in their fornication; and after you they did not fornicate. In that you gave payments and payments were not given to you, what happened in you was perverse.”

What is written in the Septuagint, “like you,” is not found in the Hebrew. It disrupts the order of the reading and creates no small difficulty: which woman is said to resemble whom, when Jerusalem herself is called the adulterous woman?

Jerusalem therefore took the abundance of all things with which she had been endowed through the generosity of her husband and gave it to strangers—namely, to demons and idols—in accordance with what is written in Hosea: “She did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied silver for her; but she made silver and gold into Baals” (Hos. 2:8). Therefore, in anger, he immediately adds: “For this reason I will return and take away my grain in its time and my wine in its time; and I will take away my clothing and my linen, so that I may no longer [Note: Victorius rewrites this as “cover,” from what he believes to be the meaning of the Greek text τοῦ μὴ καλύπτειν.] cover her shame. And now I will reveal her uncleanness before her lovers, and no one will rescue her from my hand.”

While all fornicating women ordinarily receive payments from their lovers, Jerusalem did the opposite, giving rather than receiving. To show the generosity of her payment, he says: “You burdened [variant: honored] them to come to you from every side,” so that there might be no neighbor who was not involved in her disgrace.

In this too Jerusalem surpassed the other prostitutes: she not only gave away her own possessions, which she had acquired through the labor appropriate to her shame, but also bestowed on her lovers and violators the gifts given by her husband. So great was the adulterous woman’s exposure to every degree of disgrace that she was placed ahead not only of present prostitutes but also of those yet to come. Hence, according to Symmachus, we translated: “And after you there will be no fornication.” In comparison with you, every subsequent fornication will be considered lighter.

Whatever we have said about Jerusalem refers to the Church and to the souls of believers. They give their lovers the gifts of marriage—gold in understanding, silver in speech, and garments by which our foulness and shame are covered—or they give them to opposing powers and teachers of perverse doctrines. Such teachers assert that luxury does no harm; that indiscriminate lust, in accordance with the body’s genital organs, demands intercourse by natural law; that all foods may be used without distinction, since they were made to be consumed; that prudence is necessary only insofar as it benefits oneself; and that justice has no place, since, if it prevailed, one would have to beg; and other doctrines of this kind.

Wretched Jerusalem, receiving these doctrines, though she ought to be the vision of peace, turns the sharpness of her intellect and the beauty of her speech into disgrace. She comes forth adorned against her husband for the sake of her lovers with the very ornaments with which she had been adorned by her husband for the service of good.

What follows—“And you gave them gifts so that they might enter you from every side and fornicate with you”—signifies every kind of sin: that she is not content with a single offense but endures a hunger for sin, and, defiled in every member contrary to the laws of nature, is polluted even to the crown of her head.

### (Verses 35 ff.)

Therefore, prostitute, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Because your bronze was poured out, and your shame was exposed in your fornication (Vulgate: “in your fornications”) with your lovers, and with the idols of your abominations, in the blood of your children whom you gave to them, behold, I shall gather all your lovers with whom you have mingled, and all those whom you loved together with all those whom you hated; and I shall gather them against you from every side, and I shall expose your shame before them, and they shall see all your disgrace. I shall judge you with the judgments passed upon adulteresses and those who shed blood; and I shall give you over to bloodshed in fury and jealousy. I shall give you into their hands, and they shall destroy your brothel and demolish your house of prostitution; they shall strip you of your garments and take away the vessels of your adornment, and leave you naked and filled with disgrace. They shall bring a mob against you, stone you with stones, and cut you down (another reading: “hack you to pieces”) with their swords. They shall burn your houses with fire and execute judgments against you in the sight of many women. You shall cease from prostituting yourself, and you shall no longer give payment. My indignation against you shall rest, and my jealousy shall be removed from you; I shall be at rest and shall no longer be angry, because you did not remember the days of your youth and provoked me in all these things. Therefore I too have repaid your ways upon your head, says the Lord God, and I have not acted according to your crimes in all your abominations.

The Septuagint: Therefore, prostitute, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because you poured out your bronze, your shame shall be exposed in your fornication toward your lovers, and in all the thoughts of your iniquities, and in the blood of your children whom you gave to them. Therefore, behold, I shall gather against you all your lovers with whom you have mingled, and all those whom you loved together with all those whom you hated. I shall gather them against you all around and reveal your wicked deeds to them, and they shall see all your shame. I shall take vengeance on you with the vengeance inflicted upon adulteresses and those who shed blood; I shall place you in bloodshed of fury and jealousy and hand you over to their power. They shall dig out your brothel and destroy your platform; they shall strip you of your garments and take away the vessels of your glory, and leave you naked and full of disgrace. They shall bring a mob against you, stone you with stones, and cut you down with their swords. They shall set your houses on fire and execute vengeance against you before many women. I shall turn you away from fornication, and you shall no longer give payment. I shall unleash my fury against you; my jealousy shall be removed from you, and I shall rest and no longer be anxious, because you did not remember the day of your childhood and grieved me in all these things. Behold, I shall place your ways upon your head, says Adonai the Lord, and thus you have committed iniquity upon all your iniquities.

First, let us lay the foundations of the historical interpretation. Because you have done these and those things encompassed by the preceding discourse, therefore hear, prostitute, what you have done and what you are to suffer. You poured out the bronze which you had received from me and gave your lovers the payment which you ought to have received; and you killed your children by offering them to idols, so that you proved to be not only an adulteress but also a murderer of your own children.

Therefore I shall gather against you all your lovers with whom you have prostituted yourself, both those whom you loved and those whom you hated, and I shall strip you according to the law concerning adulteresses, so that all may see your disgrace and the sexual organs for which they had previously been carried away by the madness of love. All these things, however, are said by way of metaphor concerning an adulterous and murderous woman who has not only prostituted herself against her husband but has also killed her children. They are said concerning Jerusalem, and concerning the fact that all the nations whose idols she worshiped, and whose service she turned all God’s gifts toward, are to be gathered against her; that the temple of Baal is to be destroyed; that all the city’s altars are to be overturned by fire; and that nothing is to remain in her.

Just as people customarily throw all the stones at an adulteress and slaughter a prostitute, so that she is killed by the wounds inflicted by each individual, and so that all women may see the punishment of the prostitute, so Jerusalem is to be abandoned in the sight of the other cities round about and of all the nations. This is done so that she may cease from prostituting herself, no longer give payments to her lovers, and so that God’s indignation may rest and he may no longer be angry with her, since he has ceased to love her.

From this we understand that it is a great offense not to be cared for by God at all, but to be abandoned to one’s own crimes and sins. “My jealousy shall be removed from you,” he says, “and I shall rest and no longer be angry,” as though she were alienated, had departed from him, and had been handed over by him to everlasting nakedness.

But if Jerusalem suffered this because she prostituted herself with idols, what do we suppose she will suffer when she has slaughtered the Son of God? “You have done all these things,” he says, having forgotten your former benefits, and you provoked me to anger—or grieved me, whom by good works you ought to have provoked to joy. Therefore I too repaid your deeds upon your head. And when I have overthrown you, adulteress, I shall nevertheless exercise less of my anger against you than you deserved, so that in this too divine clemency may be demonstrated: that the sins are greater than the punishments.

According to the tropological interpretation, every soul receives spiritual money from God, in accordance with what is said in the Gospel (Matthew 25; Luke 19) in the parables of the five, two, and one talents, and of the ten servants who each received a mina. When they have acted negligently, they become liable for fifty (another reading: ten) denarii and five hundred; and for this reason Jerusalem’s shame is revealed before her lovers, whom we understand as demons and hostile powers, either on the day of judgment or at the time of repentance, when sinners are reproved.

At first, the almighty God alone sees what is hidden, as the Gospel says: “And your Father who sees in secret” (Matthew 6:6). And elsewhere: “God, who searches hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7:10). Also in the Book of Kings: “You alone know the hearts of all the children of men” (4 Kings 8). But when this has been fulfilled—“Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, and nothing covered that will not be known” (Luke 12:2)—and elsewhere: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each person’s praise will come from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5)—when the time of correction has arrived, then the saying of Hosea will be fulfilled: “Now their thoughts have surrounded them” (Hosea 7:2). And elsewhere: “Their thoughts accusing or defending one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings” (Romans 2:15). And again: “Behold the man, and his deeds are before his face.”

All those who had previously prostituted themselves with her shall see her shame, and God shall give her over to the bloodshed of fury and jealousy. For a husband’s fury against an adulterous wife is intense, and she cannot be ransomed at any price.

The blood of the children may be understood in this way: we may call Jerusalem’s children λογισμοὶ καλοί, that is, “good thoughts,” which have been implanted in human beings by God.
