The adulteress kills them when she turns toward evil deeds. It is also beneficial for Jerusalem that her brothel be dug out and the seedbed of all her fornication destroyed. Once this has happened, she will no longer give payments, and God’s indignation will rest; he will no longer be jealous of her, being secure concerning her chastity—namely, according to those who interpret these words in a favorable sense.

Others, however, as we said above, refer them to the opposite sense: that it is a sign of God’s great anger not to be angry, when he has once despised the fornicator and despaired of her salvation.

But if heretics who do not accept the Old Testament, following the Septuagint version, object in this passage to the statement, “And you grieved me in all these things,” on the grounds that God is not only subject to anger but also to sorrow and grief, let us ask them how they accept what is certainly a command of the good God: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30). Whatever they say in defense of that testimony, we shall apply in explanation of the present passage.

### (Verse 44)

Behold, everyone who speaks a proverb commonly used among the people will take it up concerning you, saying: “As the mother, so also her daughter.” You are the daughter of your mother, who rejected her husband and her children; and you are the sister of your sisters, who rejected their husbands and their children.

The Septuagint: These are all the things which they have spoken against you in a parable, saying: “As the mother, so also the daughter.” You are the daughter of your mother, who rejected her husband and her children; and you are the sister of your sisters, who rejected their husbands and their children.

**Note:** With distinct wording and indeed a different sense, here and above Martianay reads, “you are a sister.” Nor do I deny, as Nobilius also noted, that ἀδελφή (“sister”) occurs in some Greek books and in Theodoret. But the text of the Septuagint in the greater number of manuscripts has καὶ ἀδελφαὶ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου, “and sisters of your sisters,” and the sequence of Jerome’s exposition which follows requires that reading.

After the catalogue of Jerusalem’s vices and the correction by which she is recalled to salvation, the common proverb is applied to her—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the parable: “As the mother, so also the daughter.” Jerusalem’s mother, as was written above and will be written below, is called Chethaea, interpreted as “the deranged woman” or “the one who turns toward madness.” By this are indicated the enticements of this world, which lead the captive soul to destruction and separate it from its husband—clearly, the Word of God and his teaching.

She is the sister of her sisters, as we shall read shortly—Sodom and Samaria. One signifies the life and luxury of the gentiles; the other, the deceptive snares of heretics.

But the Septuagint reading, “the sisters of your sisters, who rejected their husbands and their children,” makes no sense. What other sisters did Sodom and Samaria have, since they are Jerusalem’s sisters? And it must be asked which husbands Sodom and Samaria abandoned, and which children they rejected.

Unless perhaps we can say that the feet of those who are always wandering are unsteady, and that those who are opposed to the truth have no firm footsteps; instead, they run here and there and are carried about by every wind of doctrine, while they pass from one falsehood to another (Ephesians 4). When they realize that they have labored in vain over the first, they proceed to a second and a third.

**Note:** Two manuscripts read “which properly belong to the truth.”

### (Verses 45 ff.)

Your mother is a Hittite (another reading: Chethite), and your father an Amorite; your elder sister is Samaria, she and her daughters who dwell on your left. Your younger sister, who dwells on your right, is Sodom and her daughters. Yet you did not walk in their ways, nor did you act according to their crimes; you came very nearly to doing worse than they in all your ways.

The Septuagint: Your mother is Chethaea, and your father is an Amorite; your elder sister is Samaria, she and her daughters who dwell on your left; and your younger sister, who dwells on your right, is Sodom and her daughters. Yet not even so did you walk in her ways, nor did you act according to her iniquities; you came very nearly to them and surpassed them in all your ways.

Above he had said, “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother Chethaea”; here the order and number are changed: “Your mother is Chethaea, and your father is an Amorite.” For when crimes have multiplied, they are split into parts; and when unity has been abandoned, they advance into a crowd and multitude, which cannot ascend with Jesus into the mountains.

You will approve Samaria and Sodom as Jerusalem’s sisters—one on the left and the other on the right—even according to the physical interpretation, if you look eastward from the temple of Jerusalem.

**Note:** The Vatican manuscript, together with Rabanus, reads “you will approve,” adding the explanation that Samaria is called the elder because she is the greater, and so forth.

Samaria is called the elder because she sinned first and was led captive by the Assyrians; Sodom is called the lesser and younger because she refers to the multitude of the gentiles. Otherwise, Sodom did not exist at that time: before Jerusalem is mentioned in Scripture, Sodom, together with Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, had already been destroyed by divine fire (Genesis 19).

Jerusalem, which is called by the other name Judah and lies between the two sisters, was led by the Chaldeans into Babylon. Jerusalem sinned far more grievously than Samaria and Sodom, worshiping the idol of Jealousy in the temple and afterward killing the Son of God.

According to the tropological interpretation, Samaria and Sodom—that is, heretics and gentiles—often commit lesser offenses than those who are regarded as Jerusalem, that is, members of the Church. Hence it is said to the Corinthians, who did believe in Christ but were oppressed by evil deeds: “Fornication is actually reported among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife” (1 Corinthians 5:1), and so forth.

Heretics who nevertheless accept the Old Testament customarily understand three natures from this passage: the spiritual, the animal, and the earthly. They refer the spiritual nature to Jerusalem, the animal nature to Samaria, and the earthly nature to Sodom.

Let us briefly ask them how three natures—the spiritual, the animal, and the earthly—which are certainly different from one another, can be said to have one mother and one father. This does not fit their fiction. And how can the animal and earthly natures, according to this same prophet, be restored to their former state, that is, to the spiritual state? This too is contrary to their arguments.

That Samaria is understood as heresy is demonstrated both in the prophet Hosea and in many other passages, especially by the testimony: “Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria; they have harvested the firstfruits of the nations” (Amos 6:1). For all heretics despise Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower” and refers to the Church. They trust in the mountain of Samaria—in the pride of their perverse doctrines, which they consider lofty—and through these deceitful proclamations they harvest and plunder the firstfruits of the nations, drawing the powerful among the gentiles into heretical error by the marvel of their teachings.

### (Verses 48–49)

As I live, says the Lord, Sodom your sister herself and her daughters have not done as you and your daughters have done. Behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread, abundance, and ease for her and her daughters; yet they did not stretch out their hand to the needy and the poor. They became haughty and committed abominations before me, and I removed them, as you have seen (another reading: “as I saw”). Samaria did not commit even half your sins; but you surpassed her in crimes and justified your sisters by all your abominations which you committed.

**Note:** Victorius reads, “but you also surpassed them”—namely, your sisters, Sodom and Samaria. The plural is found in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin editions.

The Septuagint: As I live, says Adonai the Lord, this is what Sodom your sister and her daughters did, as you and your daughters have done. Nevertheless, the iniquity of Sodom your sister was pride, fullness of bread, and abundance. She and her daughters abounded in delights—this she and her daughters had—and they did not take the hand of the poor and needy. They behaved magnificently and committed iniquities in my sight, and I removed them, as you have seen. Samaria did not commit even half your sins; you multiplied your iniquities beyond theirs and justified your sisters by all your iniquities which you committed.

What the Septuagint added—“this she and her daughters had”—is not found in the Hebrew.

In the Old Testament God’s oath is, “As I live, says the Lord” (Numbers 14:21). In the New Testament it is, “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John 13:16). But if the expression “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob” is shared with others, and “he is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Mark 12:16, 27), and elsewhere, “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9), we ask why God specially claims for himself a common designation.

But just as one says “a good tree,” “a good man,” “a good shepherd,” and “a good servant” (Luke 18), while no one is absolutely good except God alone, so, although angels and the other powers, as well as patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, are living in comparison with the almighty God, they are called dead. For who is the human being who lives and will not see death? (Psalm 88:49). Hence the apostle Paul also says of God: “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Timothy 6:16). And concerning the fountain of the living: “Our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

This, then, is the one who swears and says, “As I live, says the Lord,” while describing the crimes of Sodom and her daughters. He placed pride first, the devil’s characteristic and the first sin. Hence the same Apostle says: “Lest, being puffed up with pride, he fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1 Timothy 3:6), because of which he fell from heaven.

For he had said: “By my strength I shall act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I shall remove the boundaries of nations; I shall lay waste their strength, shake inhabited cities, and grasp the whole world in my hand as though it were a nest; and as one gathers abandoned eggs, so shall I take it” (Isaiah 10:13–14). And: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

We also read elsewhere: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” And the Gospel recounts how the Pharisee’s pride was surpassed by the tax collector’s humility (Luke 18). The seedbed of this pride is fullness of bread, abundance of all things, and ease—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the wealth of pleasures and luxury.

The rich man dressed in purple in the Gospel (Luke 16) is reported to have had no other crime than that, overflowing with wealth and riches, he burst into such pride that he did not extend his hand to the needy and poor Lazarus. He so forgot his condition that he would not give even what ought simply to have been thrown away to this wretched man. For this reason it is also written elsewhere: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Pride, fullness of bread, abundance of all things, ease, and delights constitute the sin of Sodom. From these follows forgetfulness of God, which considers present goods permanent and never expects to lack what it needs. Therefore the Law also commands: “Take care lest, when you eat and drink and are full, having built fine houses and possessing sheep and cattle, silver and gold, you forget the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 8:11). And elsewhere it is written concerning Israel: “He ate and drank, became full and fat, and the beloved kicked” (Deuteronomy 32:15).

Knowing this, Solomon, wisest of all, prays in Proverbs: “Grant me what is necessary and sufficient, lest, when I am full, I become a liar and say, ‘Who will see me?’ or, having become poor, I steal and swear falsely by the name of my God” (Proverbs 30:8–9).

The statement that you “justified your sisters in all your abominations which you committed” does not simply declare Sodom and Samaria righteous, but righteous by comparison with those who are worse. Thus the tax collector mentioned above is not called righteous absolutely, but in comparison with one who is worse.

Yet although Sodom and Samaria are such as they are, they did not sin even half as much in comparison with Jerusalem. For “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47). And: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6:7).

As for the fact that the Hebrew contains “ease” in place of “delights” (another reading: “riches”), it should be understood as referring to the saying: “Every soul of the idle person is in desires.” This means that something must always be done, lest, when the hand ceases to work, the field of our breast be occupied by the thorns of evil thoughts.

### (Verse 52)

Therefore you too bear your shame, you who surpassed your sisters by your sins, acting more wickedly than they (another reading: “more wickedly than them”); for they have been justified by you.

The Septuagint: You too endure your punishment, because you corrupted your sisters by your sins, in which you acted wickedly against them, and you justified them over yourself.

The second plank after shipwreck is this: when you have sinned, to feel shame and not to be subject to the rebuke spoken against Jerusalem: “You have acquired the face of a prostitute; you do not know how to feel shame” (Jeremiah 3:3).

He bears his punishment who is tormented by his own conscience and, in this world, endures suffering by his own will, so that he may not endure eternal torments (Genesis 4). We corrupt our brothers or sisters by our sins when, through our sins, they are provoked to greater crimes.

What I mean will become clearer in this way. Imagine someone established at the summit of the priesthood who does not live well and disgraces his dignity by his deeds. Is not a lay brother corrupted by imitating his vices? For whoever causes one of the little ones to stumble is thrown into the depths with a millstone tied around his neck (Matthew 18:6).

Jerusalem’s sisters, Sodom and Samaria, are likewise justified—not because they are righteous in themselves, but, as we have said, by comparison with the worse.

Therefore, you too be ashamed and bear your disgrace, you who justified your sisters.

The Septuagint: You too be ashamed and receive your disgrace, because you justified your sisters.

Shame is followed by disgrace, disgrace by correction, correction by consolation, and consolation by salvation, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Tribulation produces endurance; endurance, testing; testing, hope; but hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5:3–5).

There is no doubt that this refers to the future, since in the present she has wiped away her sins through shame.

Something similar is also heard in the Gospel: “There is a shame that leads to death, and there is a shame that leads to life” (Ecclesiasticus 4:25).

**Note:** This sentence may perhaps have existed in some apocryphal Gospel or may have been added in copies of the ancient Vulgate, as were many other passages that are not now read among them. Martinus: “Something of this sort is also heard in the Gospel.” Victorius deletes the word “Gospel,” since nothing of the kind is found, at least in the present copies of the Gospels. The reference seems to be to the passage whose meaning is: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory and grace.” Also 2 Corinthians 7: “The sorrow that is according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, but the sorrow of the world produces death.”

The Holy Spirit also exhorts sinners in the Psalms: “Let all my enemies be ashamed and put to shame; let them turn back and be put to shame very quickly” (Psalm 39:15). It is written elsewhere: “You first declare your sins, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26, according to the Septuagint). And again: “The righteous is the first accuser of himself in his speech” (Proverbs 18:17).

It is therefore not surprising that Jerusalem is summoned to shame and disgrace, since she sinned so greatly that she justified her sisters. Thereafter it is said to her: “You and your daughters shall return to your former state.”

**Note:** Following Victorius, we read, in accordance with the sacred text, “you shall return,” instead of the reading “return.”

### (Verses 53–54)

And I shall turn them back, restoring them by the restoration of Sodom and her daughters and by the restoration of Samaria and her daughters; and I shall turn your return in their midst, so that you may bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all that you have done while consoling them.

The Septuagint: I shall turn back their restorations by the restoration of Sodom and her daughters; I shall turn back the restoration of Samaria and her daughters; and I shall turn back your restoration in their midst, so that you may bear your punishment and suffer disgrace for all that you have done in provoking me to anger.

Jerusalem has made great progress if, after the shame and disgrace which, when inflicted by God’s judgment, she willingly received and bore, saying, “I shall endure the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him,” she is promised restoration to her former state.

Yet because Sodom and Samaria have been justified in comparison with the magnitude of her crimes—one being on her right and the other on her left—the restoration proceeds first with the return, or captivity, of Sodom, as Aquila translated it; second with the captivity of Samaria, as Aquila and Symmachus likewise translated it; and finally Jerusalem will be restored, since she had been weighed down by greater iniquity and had shown her sinful sisters to be righteous in comparison with herself.

For who can doubt that among three sinners—or rather, three impious persons—a gentile, a heretic, and a church member, the one who possessed the greater dignity deserves far greater punishments? “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments,” as we have said (Wisdom 6:7). Whoever is lesser is worthy of mercy. And “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47).

Hence Peter also says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God” (1 Peter 4:17). And in this same prophet those holding axes are commanded: “Begin from my sanctuary” (above, 9:6), so that Jerusalem, the last of all, after her sisters have been converted and restored to their former state, may bear her disgrace, be ashamed, and blush over the sins she committed, and may console all her sisters while enduring more severe sufferings (Jeremiah 6).

Or certainly she is to be ashamed and blush because she provoked God to anger.

From this it is evident that God’s anger is not natural to him, but that our vices provoke the most merciful and gentle God to anger, as the Apostle says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that God’s goodness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself” (Romans 2:4–5)—wrath which God does not possess by nature.

Hence it is also written elsewhere: “You sent forth your anger, and it devoured them like stubble” (Exodus 15:7). For what is joined together and united in one body cannot be sent forth; only what is outside the body can be sent forth—for example, a spear, missile, arrow, or sword.

We also read in the Gospel (Matthew 10:15) that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for the one that did not receive the apostles.

### (Verse 55)

And your sister Sodom and her daughters shall return to their former state; and Samaria and her daughters shall return to their former state; and you and your daughters shall return (another reading: “return”) to your former state.

The Septuagint: Your sister Sodom and her daughters shall be restored as they were at the beginning; Samaria and her daughters shall be restored as they were at the beginning; and you and your daughters shall be restored as you were at the beginning.

Among their other fables, interminable genealogies, and fantasies, the Jews also dream that, at the coming of their Christ—whom we know to be the Antichrist—and during the thousand-year reign, Sodom will be restored to its former state, so that it will be like the paradise of God and like the land of Egypt; that Samaria will regain her former prosperity, so that the people may return from the Assyrians to the land of Judah (4 Kings 17–18).

For we read that the ten tribes were taken captive by the Assyrian kings Pul, Shalmaneser, and Tiglath-pileser, and that they remain captive there to this day.

They also say that Jerusalem will then be rebuilt, and that all her daughters—namely, the cities, villages, and fortified settlements that will be subject to her power—will flourish as they flourished before; and that Jerusalem herself will be constructed with gold, silver, and precious stones. Concerning her Isaiah prophesies: “I shall appoint your judges as at the first and your counselors as at the beginning; afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the mother of cities, faithful Zion” (Isaiah 1:26).

Our Apocalypse likewise speaks of this (Revelation 21), and David sings: “Do good, Lord, in your good pleasure toward Zion, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built” (Psalm 50:20). And elsewhere: “The cities of Judah shall be built, and they shall dwell and settle there, and their offspring shall be established forever” (Psalm 68:36).

Leaving the perfect knowledge of these matters to God’s judgment—or rather, confessing it plainly—we say that after the second coming of the Lord and Savior nothing humble and nothing earthly will exist in the future; there will instead be the heavenly kingdoms first promised in the Gospel. We say that all these things have been fulfilled, and are fulfilled daily, in the state of the Church.

Sodom returns to her former state when a soul formerly gentile and impious, restored to its own nature, understands the Creator. Samaria receives her ancient blessedness when, having rejected heretical error, she is joined to Christian teaching and faith. When those two have returned, Jerusalem too—the vision of peace, which is interpreted as “Church”—will return to her former state.

Concerning her it is written: “His place has become established in peace” (Psalm 75:2); and: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is in unity” (Psalm 121:3); and in the Apostle: “The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:25); and again: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and myriads of angels in assembly” (Hebrews 12:22).

She returns together with her daughters, which are dispersed throughout the whole world. We have discussed this more fully in our explanations of Isaiah.

### (Verses 56 ff.)

Was not Sodom your sister heard of in your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was revealed, as at this time, to the disgrace of the daughters of Syria and of all the daughters of the Philistines round about you, who surround you on every side? You have borne your crime and your disgrace, says the Lord God.

The Septuagint: If Sodom your sister had not been heard of in your mouth in the days of your pride, before your wicked deeds were revealed, as is now the case with the daughters of Syria—and if this had not happened, what would have become of you and of all the daughters of the foreigners around you, who surround you on every side? Bear your impieties and your iniquities.

Symmachus translated this passage as follows: “Because Sodom your sister was not heard of through your mouth in the day of your pride, before your disgrace was revealed, as in the time of the reproach of the daughters of Syria and of all the daughters of the Philistines who are around you and surround you on every side. You shall bear your crime and your outrage.”

Theodotion rendered it this way: “And Sodom your sister was not in the hearing of your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was revealed, as in the time of the reproach of the daughters of Syria and of all the daughters of the foreigners around it, who abhor you on every side. You have borne your fornication and your defilements, says Adonai the Lord.”

Our translation agrees with the edition of Aquila. I have set out all these versions so that, by comparing them, we may be able to discover some trace of the meaning. Meanwhile, without prejudicing the others, this seems to us the order in which the passage should be understood:

“In the days of your pride, when you were sinning, you did not remember the overthrow of your sister Sodom before your wickedness became manifest—wickedness which has now been revealed to such an extent that you have become a reproach to all the cities of Syria and Palestine that surround you. Because you surpassed your sister in crime and were not terrified by her example so as to avoid suffering similar things and restrain your foot, now that your disgrace has been revealed, hear the sentence of God.”

According to the Septuagint, one should understand “bear”; according to Aquila, “you have borne”; and according to Symmachus, “you are going to bear”—your crime and disgrace—so that, after suffering punishment for your sacrilege, you may obtain forgiveness not according to your covenant but from my clemency.

Syria is called in the Hebrew language אֲרָם (*Aram*), which is interpreted as “height” or “exaltation.” According to the explanation of that passage in the prophet Isaiah where Aram and Ephraim agree against Judah and Jerusalem, the clever wisdom of the gentiles—which promises itself the exaltation of knowledge—joined with the wickedness of heretics, attacks Judah, in whom there is true confession, but cannot prevail.

Here too the same arrogance of Syria—that is, of the philosophers—together with the daughters of the foreigners, in whom the manifold error of various doctrines among the nations is displayed, mocks Jerusalem and holds her up to reproach, having been overcome by her vices.

### (Verses 59 ff.)

“For thus says the Lord God: I will deal with you as you have despised the oath, so as to invalidate the covenant. And I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish with you an everlasting covenant. And you will remember your ways and be ashamed, when you receive your sisters, both those older than you and those younger than you; and I will give them to you as daughters, but not by your covenant. And I will establish my covenant with you, and you will know that I am the Lord, so that you may remember, be ashamed, and no longer have occasion to open your mouth because of your shame, when I have been reconciled to you concerning all that you have done,” says the Lord God.

**Note:** Victor, following the Vulgate edition and the Hebrew itself, reads: “and I myself will establish my covenant with you.” By the same reasoning, a little earlier he had emended “when you receive your sisters older than you” in place of “together with your older sisters.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says Adonai the Lord: I will deal with you as you have acted, as you have despised these things, so as to transgress my testament. And I will remember my testament that I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish for you an everlasting testament. And you will remember your ways and be despised, when you receive your sisters older than you together with your younger sisters; and I will give them to you as a test, and not by your testament. And I will establish my testament with you, and you will know that I am the Lord, so that you may remember, be ashamed, and no longer have occasion to open your mouth because of the face of your disgrace, when I have shown you mercy according to all that you have done,” says the Lord God.

Therefore I told you: “Bear your crime and your shame”—whether “you bear,” “you have borne,” or “you are going to bear” them—so that you may receive what you deserve, because you despised my oath and invalidated my covenant. But when it has been completed, “I kill and I make alive; I strike and I heal” (Deut. 32:39), then I will remember the covenant that I once had with you. And I will establish for you a covenant, no longer that of the Law, which has passed away, but the everlasting covenant of the Gospel. When you have remembered your ways and received your sisters, the older or the younger—Samaria and Sodom, together with their associates—I will grant them to you as daughters, or as a test (for “there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest,” 1 Cor. 11:19), not on account of your merit but through my mercy. Then you will know that I am the Lord; you will remember my benefits, be ashamed, and say with the Apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

And you will no longer have occasion to open your mouth because of your shame. For it belongs to the saints to open their mouth, according to the Apostle who says: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (2 Cor. 6:11), and to the Lord and Savior, who, opening his mouth, taught them (Matt. 5), saying also in the Psalm: “I will open my mouth,” he says, “in parables” (Ps. 77:2). But to the sinner it is said: “You have sinned; be quiet” (Gen. 4). And: “Why do you recite my testament with your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16). And: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9). But the holy person deserves to hear: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11).

From this we understand that even when, through God’s mercy, we have received our former glory—or rather, when we have received the everlasting covenant of the Gospel—after the Lord has been reconciled to us concerning all that we have done, we must retain the memory of our former sin and always keep our mouth closed, because we have been saved not by our works but by God’s grace.

### Chapter XVII—verses 1 ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, set forth a riddle; tell a parable to the house of Israel, and say: Thus says the Lord God: A great eagle, with great wings, long of limb, full of feathers and variegated, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar. He plucked off the topmost shoots of its foliage and carried it to the land of Canaan; he placed it in the city of merchants. And he took from the seed of the land and placed it in the ground as a seed, to establish its roots beside abundant waters; he placed it on the surface. When it had sprouted, it grew into a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches looked toward it, and whose roots were beneath it. Thus it became a vine, produced shoots, and sent out branches.”

The Septuagint: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, tell a narrative and speak a parable to the house of Israel, and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: A great eagle, with great wings, full of claws and of long reach, which has the reach to enter Lebanon, took the choice branches of the cedar. He plucked off the tops of the tender shoots and brought them to the land of Chanaan. He placed them in a walled city. And he took from the seed of the land and put it in a field as a plantation beside abundant waters; he placed it so that it might be seen. It sprouted and became a weak and small vine, so that only its branches appeared beneath it, and its roots were beneath it. And it became a great vine, produced branches, and extended its shoots.”

When the prophet is told, “Set forth a riddle; tell a parable,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “Tell a narrative and speak a parable,” it is shown that what is being said is obscure. For there is no doubt that a riddle and a parable express one thing in words while holding another in their meanings. The Savior too spoke to the people in parables, which he explained privately to the Apostles.

Thus we must understand “riddle” and “parable” as we understand a riddle and a parable. Two eagles, moreover, are set forth in the present prophecy of Ezekiel. We must now discuss the first; we shall treat the second in what follows. For the moment, let us follow the plain historical sense.

The great eagle with great wings, long of limb, full of feathers and variety—or, as the Septuagint translated it, full of claws—is Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, of whom Hosea also speaks: “Like an eagle over the house of God” (Hos. 8:1). He ruled many nations and was surrounded by an innumerable army. He came against the house of God, plainly meaning the temple—or, as Scripture now says, against Lebanon, concerning which Zechariah speaks: “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Howl, cypress, because the cedar has fallen, for the mighty have been laid waste” (Zech. 11:1–2).

And frequently the temple, which was renowned and exalted, is called Lebanon in the Holy Scriptures.

**Note:** This explanation is more appropriate as to why the name Lebanon is often attributed to the temple in the prophets. Just as Lebanon continually shone with snow and was higher than all the other mountains of Palestine, as Theodore notes on Psalm 71:16, so Josephus relates that the temple, seen from a distance, appeared like a very tall and snowy—or shining—mountain. Jerome cited the passage from Zechariah in this connection; Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai likewise applied it to the temple, when he saw its doors opened of their own accord. Josephus and Tacitus also report this portent, which foretold the time when the sacred building would be consumed by fire: “Open, O Lebanon, your doors, so that fire may consume your cedars.”

And he took the marrow of the cedar, plucked off the topmost shoots of its foliage, and carried it to the land of Canaan, placing it in the city of merchants. In place of “merchants,” or “commerce,” the Septuagint translated “walled city.” This indicates King Jeconiah of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar captured together with his mother, the leaders of the people, all the wealth of Jerusalem, and the vessels of the temple; he carried him to Babylon, which is in the land of Canaan, and there he grew old.

From his lineage, as the Scripture of Matthew the Evangelist testifies (Matt. 1), our Lord and Savior was later born through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. From that same seed of the land—that is, from the royal stock—he produced Mattaniah, Jeconiah’s uncle, changed his name, called him Zedekiah, and appointed him king in Jerusalem, placing many peoples under his authority.

Yet he placed him on the surface and did not establish his power with the deep root of sovereignty. He placed him so that he might be seen and might remain under Babylonian authority, or with low stature and his branches looking toward it, so that he might indeed rule the Jewish people but might look toward the command of Babylon, whose authority he obeyed.

This is what Scripture says: “Of low stature, with his branches looking toward it”—with “the eagle” understood. The Septuagint translated it more clearly: “It sprouted, and what had been planted became a weak and small vine,” so that only its branches appeared. It seemed indeed to possess a kingdom, but its kingdom was low and weak and was governed by the will of the Babylonian ruler.

Let this suffice for the present concerning the chapter; we shall add what follows.

### Verses 7 ff.

And another great eagle appeared, with great wings and many feathers. And behold, this vine sent its roots toward it and extended its branches toward it, so that it might irrigate it from the beds of its planting. It was planted in good soil, beside abundant waters **[Victor: “it was planted,” according to the Vulgate reading]**, so that it might produce foliage and bear fruit and become a great vine.

Say: “Thus says the Lord God: Will it prosper? Will he not pull up its roots, strip off its fruit, dry up all its budding branches, and make it wither? It will not require a mighty arm or many peoples **[Vulgate: ‘a numerous people’]** to pull it up by the roots. Behold, it has been planted; will it prosper? When the scorching wind touches it, will it not dry up and wither in the beds of its growth?”

The Septuagint: “And another great eagle appeared, with great wings and very many claws. And behold, this vine was entwined toward it, and its roots were directed toward it, and it extended its branches toward it, so that it might irrigate it with the clod of its planting. In a good field, beside abundant water, it was fattened, so that it might produce shoots, bear fruit, and become a great vine.

“Therefore say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Will it prosper? Will not the roots of its tenderness and its fruit rot, and will not all that has sprung from it wither? It will not require a great arm or a numerous people to pull it up from its roots. And behold, it is fattened. Will it prosper? As soon as the scorching wind touches it, will it not wither and dry up in drought, when the clod of its growth withers?”

The second, that is, the other eagle, itself great, full of feathers and many claws because of its rapacity and the devastation of very many nations, is the king of Egypt, Pharaoh. And this vine is understood to be King Zedekiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had appointed in Jerusalem. He began, it says, to send out his branches toward it—that is, to the king of the Egyptians—sending ambassadors and asking aid from him against the king to whom he was subject.

This is what Scripture now says: “So that it might irrigate it from the beds of its growth.” The vine had been planted by Nebuchadnezzar in good soil, so that it might produce foliage, bear fruit, and grow into a spreading vine. Therefore the prophet is commanded to speak to the vine that had been planted by Nebuchadnezzar and had sent its branches toward the Egyptian eagle: Will it prosper because it has attempted this, or will all its shoots and branches not immediately wither?

“And will it not,” he says, “require a mighty arm or a numerous people?” For Zedekiah, fleeing and deprived of the help of the Egyptian king, was captured by Nebuchadnezzar’s commanders in the wilderness of Jericho **[variant: Hierichuntis]**; and all his companions were scattered here and there, as is written in the Books of Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah (2 Kings 25; Jer. 39).

### Verses 11 ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Say to the rebellious house: Do you not know what these things mean? Say: Behold, the king of Babylon has come to Jerusalem, and he will take its king and its princes and bring them to himself in Babylon. He will take one from the seed of the kingdom, strike a covenant with him, and receive an oath from him. He will also take the mighty men of the land, so that the kingdom may be humble and not exalt itself, but may keep his covenant and observe it.

“But the one who departed from him sent messengers to Egypt, so that it might give him horses and a numerous people. Will he prosper? Will he obtain deliverance, the one who has done these things? And having broken the covenant, will he escape?

“As I live,” says the Lord God, “because he despised the oath and broke the covenant that he had with him, in the place of the king who appointed him king, he will die in the midst of Babylon. Pharaoh will not act against him with a great army or a numerous people in battle, by casting up a ramp and constructing siegeworks, in order to destroy many lives. For he despised the oath in order to break the covenant. And behold, he gave his hand; after doing all these things, he will not escape.”

**Note:** Previously this interpretation, as though different from the Hebrew, was enclosed and marked in a different typeface.

This is the riddle; this is the parable: under the two eagles and the vine, Scripture was showing the two kings, of Babylon and Egypt, and King Zedekiah, who, against his oath, abandoned his friendship with Nebuchadnezzar and transferred himself to the king of Egypt.

“He will strike a covenant with him,” it says, “and receive an oath from him, so that he may keep his covenant and observe it.” The one who breaks the covenant, it says, will he escape? From this we learn that fidelity must be kept even among enemies, and that one must not consider to whom one has sworn but through whom one has sworn. For the one who trusted you because of the name of God and was deceived proved far more faithful than you, who, by invoking divine majesty, plotted an ambush against your enemy—or rather, against one who had already become your friend.

“Because,” he says, “in the place of the king who appointed him king, whose oath he despised and whose covenant he broke, he will die in the midst of Babylon.” We read that Zedekiah was captured and brought to Riblah, where his sons were killed and he was blinded; then, like a wild beast shut in a cage, he was carried to Babylon (2 Kings 25).

Thus, although Scripture may appear to contradict itself, it is entirely truthful in both passages. For it had been said to Zedekiah: “You will enter Babylon, and you will not see it” (Jer. 34:4). He entered it because he was led to Babylon, and he did not see it because he had been blinded.

But what follows—“Pharaoh will not act against him with a great army or a numerous people in battle, by casting up a ramp and constructing siegeworks, in order to destroy many lives”—can be understood in two ways. Either the king of Egypt, coming against Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, will not be able to fight and will be unable, with a small army, to resist so great a multitude; or Zedekiah himself will be conquered by Pharaoh, from whom he had hoped for aid. This does not mean that Pharaoh conquered him, nor does Scripture testify to this anywhere; rather, Nebuchadnezzar’s conquest was brought about through the occasion provided by the king of Egypt. The one who besieged Jerusalem was not seen as the conqueror, but the one in whom Zedekiah had vainly placed his hope.

“Behold,” he says, “he gave his hand to the king of Egypt and surrendered himself,” and through perjury committed sacrilege against God. “Will it benefit him?” he asks. “After doing all these things, will he not escape?”

### Verses 19 ff.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: “As I live, because he despised the oath and transgressed the covenant, I will place it upon his head. I will spread my net over him **[Vulgate: ‘I will weigh it out over him’]**, and he will be caught in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon and judge him there for the transgression by which he despised me. And all his fugitives, together with his entire army **[the Vulgate adds: ‘his’]**, will fall by the sword, and the survivors will be scattered into every wind. And you will know that I, the Lord, have spoken.”

There is a secular saying:

> [lacuna] deceit or courage—who would seek these in an enemy?

This saying is commonly brought against us by those who claim that enemies should be deceived. Even if we accept it, Zedekiah did something much worse: he did not deceive an enemy but a friend, to whom he had been bound by the covenant of the Lord.

Therefore, so long as you have not sworn and have not entered into a covenant in the name of the Lord, it belongs to prudence and courage either to deceive or to overcome your adversary by whatever means you can. But once you have bound yourself by an oath, the person who trusted you is no longer an adversary but a friend; and he has been deceived under the pretext of the oath, that is, under the invocation of God.

Therefore Scripture now says: “The oath that he despised and the covenant that he transgressed, I will place upon his head.” And lest we suppose that the oath, covenant, and pact belonged to the Babylonian king—or to Zedekiah, who had made it—the text continues: “For the transgression by which he despised me.” Thus the one who despises an oath despises the one by whom he swore, and he wrongs the one whose name his adversary trusted.

“For this reason,” he says, “I will spread my net over him, and he will be caught in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon and judge him there.” Whatever, therefore, Nebuchadnezzar did against Zedekiah, he did not do by his own strength but by the anger of God, whose name had been invoked in the perjury.

According to the allegorical sense—although the interpretation may seem forced—we must understand that just as other living creatures are customarily referred both to the good and to the evil, so too are the eagle and the lion. In the good sense it is said: “A lion’s cub is Judah” (Gen. 49:9). In the contrary sense: “Our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion” (1 Pet. 5:8). And in the Psalm: “He lies in wait in secret places, like a lion in his lair; he lies in wait to seize the poor” (Ps. 9:9).

In the good sense, the eagle signifies the righteous person who, having become rich, makes wings for himself like an eagle’s, so that he may return to the house of his predecessor. And it is written in Isaiah that the righteous receive wings like eagles (Isa. 40): they run and do not grow weary; they walk and do not hunger.

Rightly, then, the one who had said, “By strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of nations and plunder their resources; I will shake inhabited cities, seize the whole world in my hand as though it were a nest, and as one gathers abandoned eggs” (ibid. 10:13–14), is now described under the figure of an eagle. He does not wish to strike at the small and humble shrubs of Lebanon—which is interpreted as “brightness” and is referred to incense—but at the tops of cedars, and at rulers and royal stock, in accordance with Habakkuk: “His food is choice” (Hab. 1:16).

He establishes a testament with those whom he has captured, so that they may submit their necks to the king of Babylon and fulfill what the Apostle says: “Those whom I have handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20). And elsewhere: “Those whom I have handed over,” he says, “to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Cor. 5:5).

Therefore, if perhaps on account of some sin we are expelled from the congregation of the brothers and from the house of God, we must not resist. Rather, with a calm spirit we should bear the sentence pronounced against us and say with the Prophet: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because [variant: “who”] I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause,” and the rest (Mic. 7:9).

It frequently happens that, having been subject to one person, we pass over to another who promises us his aid but does not allow us to remain in our former allegiance. This must be avoided by every means, lest our branches dry up and our shoots wither, and we be thought to act against the covenant of God.

### Verses 22 ff.

Thus says the Lord **[the Vulgate adds: “God”]**: “I myself will take from the marrow of the lofty cedar, and I will place it from the top of its branches. I will pluck off a tender shoot and plant it upon a high and eminent mountain. On Israel’s lofty mountain I will plant it. It will burst forth into a shoot, produce fruit, and become a great cedar. All the birds will dwell beneath it; every winged creature will nest in the shade of its foliage.

“And all the trees of the land will know that I am the Lord: I have humbled the lofty tree and exalted **[Vulgate: ‘raised up’]** the humble tree; I have dried up the green tree and caused the dry tree to put forth foliage. I, the Lord, have spoken and acted.”

The Septuagint: “For thus says Adonai the Lord: I will take from the choice branches of the cedar, from the top—**and I will give from the head of its branches; from their heart I will take**—and I will plant it upon a high mountain, and hang it upon Israel’s lofty mountain. And I will plant it, and it will produce a shoot and bear fruit, and it will become a great cedar. Every bird will rest beneath it, and every winged creature will rest in its shade. **And its branches will be restored.** And all the trees of the field will know that I am the Lord, who humbles the lofty tree and exalts the humble tree; who dries up the green tree and causes the dry tree to sprout. I, the Lord, have spoken and I act.”

What is read in the Septuagint, “And I will give from the head of its branches,” has been added from the edition of Theodotion. Again, what follows, “And its branches will be restored,” must be marked with an obelus, because it is not found in the Hebrew.

The true Nebuchadnezzar therefore takes from the marrow of the lofty cedar, from the top of its branches, so that his kingdom may be humble and not exalt itself. But the Lord God, the almighty Father, who spoke to Ezekiel, takes from the royal stock and from the lineage of David, and plants him upon the high and eminent mountain of which the Psalm speaks: “But I have been established as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6).

For the prince had failed from Judah and the ruler from Israel until he came to whom it had been reserved; and he himself would be the expectation of the nations (Gen. 49:10). He burst forth into a shoot, bore fruit, and surpassed all cedars by his height, so that all the birds of heaven might dwell beneath him and all winged creatures might be protected by his shade.

Concerning him Habakkuk says: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Hab. 3:4). He is the one who desired to gather the people like a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings (Matt. 23:37), so that all the trees of the land might know that he is the Lord.

Speaking allegorically of believers: this is the one who once humbled Israel, the lofty tree, and exalted the humble people of the nations; who dried up the green tree of the Jews, flourishing and sprouting in the Law and the Prophets, and caused the dry tree of the nations to put forth foliage, so that he might accomplish by his work what he had always spoken.

The words [variant: “word”] of Simeon in the Gospel signify the same thing: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke 2:34). So too the mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds, becomes, after it has grown, a dwelling place for birds (Matt. 13:32).

Some interpret the lofty tree humbled and the humble tree exalted differently, referring them to the passion of the Lord and Savior. Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). After the resurrection, that same tree was subsequently exalted: previously green, it was dried up by death and afterward came back to life, receiving again its former greenness.

Others interpret both statements in a Jewish sense, referring them to Israel: that at the first coming it was humbled and dried up, but at the second it will be restored to its former condition, when the saying of the Apostle Paul has been fulfilled: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Deut. 5:9–10).

## BOOK SIX

I had thought that, once the serpent had been pierced through the middle, the young shoots of the hydra would not come back to life; and, according to the poets’ fables, once Scylla was dead, the dogs of Scylla would no longer rage against me, though they never cease barking. And with the heretics struck down by the hand of God, so that, if possible, even God’s elect might not be tempted (Matt. 24:24), the heresy itself does not die. It leaves behind hereditary whelps of its hatred against us. They imitate what belongs to us but do not abandon the poisons of their ancient mother and of crafty Ulysses; they merely smear honey around their lips. According to the words of Scripture (Ps. 54:22), “They have softened their words more than oil,” but they themselves are arrows—fiery arrows—which must alike be repelled and extinguished by the shield of faith.

I have said this, daughter Eustochium, so that you may assist me with your prayers as I labor over prophetic work and resist the heretics, and so that the Lord may explain the sixth volume of the Explanations of Ezekiel through my mouth according to his own meaning. May the grace of the same Spirit, through whom the things we read written were revealed to the prophets, also be revealed to us as we discuss them, so that we may say: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118:131).

### Chapter XVIII—verses 1, 2

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “What is this proverb that you turn among yourselves into a byword in the land of Israel, saying: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge’ **[Vulgate: ‘are set on edge’]**?”

The Septuagint: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: **Son of man**—this is not found in the Hebrew—‘What is this parable among the children of Israel, who say: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge”?’”

This passage recalls what was said in Exodus: “I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who repay the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. 20:5–6; Deut. 5:9–10).

And again: “The Lord descended in a cloud and stood beside Moses; Moses invoked the name of the Lord, and the Lord passed before his face, and he invoked **him**, saying” **[the words “him, saying,” are absent from both the Septuagint and the Hebrew text. Victor, supported by his manuscripts, deleted them]**: “Lord God, merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy, and true, preserving justice and showing mercy for thousands, taking away iniquities, injustices, and sins; and he will not cleanse the iniquities of the fathers upon the children and upon the children’s children, to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 34:5 ff.).

These passages must be understood as a proverb and a parable, so that one thing sounds in the words and another is held in the meaning, as we said above concerning the parable of the two eagles. Therefore also in the seventy-seventh Psalm the Lord says: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning” (Ps. 77:2).

And in the Gospel he sets forth the parable of the seed, the darnel, and the mustard seed—which, although it is the smallest of all seeds, grows into a great tree (Matt. 13)—in such a way that it presents one thing in its words but holds another in its meaning.

Until the present day we had thought that the two testimonies from Exodus which we cited above (Isa. 29) were not parables but explained a straightforward meaning. Although we did not dare to say anything, nor to have the clay speak against the potter, asking, “Why have you made me this way or that?”, we nevertheless suffered a hidden scandal: it seemed unjust that one person should sin and another pay the penalty for the sins.

For if he repays the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one person should sin and another be punished. But the phrase that follows—“of those who hate me”—removes the difficulty, whether understood as a threat or as a command. They are not punished in the third and fourth generation merely because their fathers sinned, since the fathers who were sinners ought rather to have been punished; they are punished because they became imitators of their fathers, hated God with hereditary evil, and allowed impiety to grow out from the root into the branches as well.

At this point heretics who do not accept the Old Testament commonly say against the Creator: How good and just is the God of the Law and the Prophets, who, remaining quiet and silent concerning the sins of the fathers, repays them upon those who have not sinned? Indeed, how great is his cruelty, that he extends his anger to the third and fourth generation! We shall answer them that here too the clemency of God the Creator is demonstrated.

For it is not a matter of cruelty or severity to retain anger until the third and fourth generation; rather, it is a sign of mercy to defer the punishment of sin. When he says, “Lord God, merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy,” and adds, “repaying the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and the children’s children,” he indicates that his mercy is so great that he does not punish immediately but delays the sentence of punishment.

If, then, the vengeance due to sinners is deferred to the third and fourth generation, what more does he do for the just and holy? The text continues: “And preserving justice and mercy for many thousands, for those who keep his commandments and carry out his precepts.”

It is written in Proverbs: “As sour grapes are harmful to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so iniquity is harmful to those who practice it” (Prov. 10:26). From this it is clear that it is not the teeth of others that ache and are set on edge, but the teeth of those who have eaten the sour grapes.

The sense of this passage is therefore as follows: just as it would be ridiculous and altogether inconsistent for someone to say, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge,” so it is unjust and perverse for the fathers to sin while their children and grandchildren are tortured.

Some explain what is written in Exodus—“repaying the iniquities of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation”—by referring the statement to the human soul. They say that the father in us is a light point of sensation **[variant: “a gentle point”]** and the incitements of vices; the son is the thought, if it conceives sin; the grandchildren are the act, if one carries out in deed what one has thought and conceived; and the great-grandchild, that is, the fourth generation, is reached if one not only does what is evil and wicked but also glories in one’s crimes, according to what is written: “When the wicked comes to the depth of evils, he despises” **[variant: “will despise”]** (Prov. 18:3).

God therefore does not punish the first and second impulses of thoughts—which the Greeks call *propatheiai* (προπάθειαι, “prepassions”), without which no human being can exist—but only if someone decides to carry out what he has conceived in his mind, or refuses to correct by repentance what he has done.

Hence it is written: “No human being is without sin, not even if his life should last a single day. The years of his life are countable” (Prov. 20:9). And elsewhere: “Who can boast of having a pure heart?” And again: “Even the stars are not clean in his sight, and against his angels he has devised something perverse” (Job 25:5).

If that sublime nature is not free from sin, what should be said of human beings, who are surrounded by fragile flesh and must say with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

And they must also say, when they have done everything: “We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke 17:10). And: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 126:1–2).

To establish this point—that God does not punish the first impulse of thought, or rather the small stirring of the mind, but does punish one who consumes in action what he has conceived in his mind—we should bring forward the example from Genesis. Ham sinned by mocking his father’s nakedness, but the sentence was received not by the one who laughed, but by his son Canaan: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be the servant of his brothers” (Gen. 9:25).

What justice is there in this—that the father sinned but the sentence was pronounced against the son? Similarly, the Apostle’s statement in the opposite direction—that a woman will be saved if her children remain in faith, holiness, and chastity (1 Tim. 2:15)—seems not to possess justice, if good children and grandchildren bring salvation to their parents.

For how many holy parents have wicked children? And, conversely, how many sinful parents beget just and holy children? Therefore, according to this interpretation, everything we said above must be understood in this way: the sins of parents and progenitors are punished in the branches, not in the root.

For the present, let this suffice concerning the proverb or parable: the Law and the Prophets—that is, Exodus and Ezekiel, indeed the one God who spoke both here and there—do not appear to differ in their judgments, nor does one passage correct what the other supposedly stated wrongly.

If anyone can find either a better or another interpretation that removes the scandal of the apparently contrary testimonies, his judgment should rather be accepted.

[Col. 0169D] **(Verses 3–4.)** “As I live,” says the Lord, “if this proverb shall any longer be spoken as a proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine: the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins—it shall die.”

**The Septuagint:** “As I live,” says Adonai the Lord, “if this proverb shall any longer be spoken in Israel, since all souls are mine. As the soul of the father, so also is the soul of the son mine. The soul that sins—it shall die.”

[Col. 0170A] What is signified by “As I live, says the Lord,” and by “proverb,” or “saying,” we have explained more fully above. This proverb will by no means be spoken in Israel, but among those who have no knowledge of God and cannot perceive the truth.

“All souls,” he says, “are mine”—according to creation, not according to merit. Thus Moses was called “a man of God,” of whom it is written: “The prayer of Moses, the man of God” (Deut. 33:1). So too Elijah said to the commander of fifty soldiers: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven upon you and upon your fifty men” (4 Kings 1:12). [Note: Instead of “men,” says Victor, all witnesses have “your men,” and several manuscript codices read likewise.]

A man of sin and a son of iniquity, however, is not called a man of God, as those who are called servants and attendants of God are; for of such a man it cannot be said: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). And again: “By whatever a person is overcome, by that he is also enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:19).

Just as the sins of sons do not harm their fathers, so the sins of fathers do not pass over to their sons. Rather, “the soul that sins—it shall die,” not through the abolition of its substance, but through exclusion from the fellowship of him who says: “I am life” (John 14:6). Elsewhere he says: “Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die” (ibid. 11:26). And: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever keeps my word shall never see death” (ibid. 8:51).

“For your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3), because we shall live when Christ, our life, appears in glory. Then what is written will be fulfilled: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life” (John 5:24).

But what Balaam says—“Let my soul die among the souls of the righteous” (Num. 23:10)—has this meaning: he desires to die to the world and to sin, and to live with the souls of the righteous, whose life is Christ, and who can sing: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:9). For “God is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:32).

And if Balaam, as is likely, when translated into our language means “a vain people”—[Note: I would prefer to think this was written by Jerome rather than accept the reading that is actually found in the Vatican manuscript and approved by Victorius. For in Hebrew the name most truly signifies not “a vain people,” but “absorption” or “destruction.”]—it is clear that the formerly vain people of the nations desire to have fellowship with the souls of the righteous, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who are called εὐθεῖς—that is, upright and righteous.

Therefore the book of Genesis also received its name from them. [Note: He cleverly accommodates himself here to the opinion of the Jews, namely, that the book of Genesis is designated where the “Book of the Upright” is praised in Joshua 10:13 and 1 Samuel 28:18. He has a similar statement in his commentary on Isaiah 44. Hence the book of Genesis is called εὐθεῖς, that is, “of the righteous”—Abraham, Isaac, and Israel.]

[Col. 0170D] **(Verses 5 and following.)** “And if a man is righteous and practices judgment and righteousness; has not eaten upon the mountains; has not lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel; has not violated his neighbor’s wife; has not approached a menstruating woman; has not grieved anyone; has returned the pledge to the debtor; has taken nothing by force; has given his bread to the hungry; has covered the naked with clothing; has not lent at interest; has taken nothing extra; has turned his hand away from iniquity; has rendered true judgment between one man and another; has walked in my commandments and kept my judgments, so as to practice truth—he is righteous; he shall surely live,” says the Lord God.

**The Septuagint:** “But the man who is righteous, who practices judgment and righteousness; has not eaten upon the mountains; has not lifted up his eyes to the thoughts of the house of Israel; has not defiled his neighbor’s wife; has not approached a woman flowing with blood; has not oppressed anyone; has returned the pledge to the debtor; has not committed robbery; has given his bread to the hungry; has covered the naked with clothing; has not given his money at interest; has taken nothing extra; has turned his hand away from iniquity; has rendered just judgment between one man and his neighbor; has walked in my commandments and kept my ordinances, so as to perform them—he is righteous; he shall surely live,” says Adonai the Lord.

Do you wish, he says, to know that what is written—“I repay the sins of the fathers upon the third and fourth generation” (Deut. 5:9)—does not mean what most people think, nor is it equivalent to the statement: “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (Jer. 31:29)? Listen to what I am about to set forth.

Suppose a father is righteous, doing these things and avoiding those things, but has a very wicked son who, abandoning his father’s virtues, gives himself over to crimes. Will not the father live because he is righteous, and will the son die because he has committed everything by avoiding which the father became righteous?

Let us examine the father’s catalogue of virtues, which seems to me to be divided into seventeen parts. The first is to have practiced judgment; the second, similar to the first, to have joined righteousness to judgment; the third, not to have eaten upon the mountains; the fourth, not to have lifted up his eyes to idols—or, as the Septuagint translated it, to the thoughts of the house of Israel; the fifth, not to have violated his neighbor’s wife; the sixth, to have avoided intercourse with a menstruating wife; the seventh, not to have grieved anyone—or, as the Septuagint rendered it, not to have oppressed anyone through power; the eighth, to have returned the pledge to the debtor; the ninth, to have taken nothing by force—or, according to the Septuagint, not to have committed robbery; the tenth, to have given his bread to the hungry; the eleventh, to have covered the naked with clothing; the twelfth, not to have lent money at interest; the thirteenth, to have taken nothing extra from what he had given; the fourteenth, to have turned his hand away from iniquity; the fifteenth, which seems similar to the first but differs in some respect, to have rendered true judgment between one man and another, or between a man and his neighbor; the sixteenth, to have walked in the Lord’s commandments; the seventeenth, to have kept his judgments and ordinances.

What each of these means, we shall explain in what follows.

“If a man is righteous,” he says, “and practices judgment.” It is written in Proverbs: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. 12:5). Whoever possesses this virtue—so that he does nothing without reason and judgment—can say the prophetic words: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified altogether” (Ps. 18:10).

And when he has judged everything rightly, so that he does not show partiality to the poor in judgment, he will fulfill the Lord’s commandment: “You shall judge the small as well as the great” (Prov. 18). He will boldly say: “My soul has desired to desire your judgments at all times” (Ps. 118:10). And again: “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments” (v. 30). And in the same psalm: “I have known that your judgments are righteousness” [another reading: “righteous”] (v. 75).

He will advance to such great blessedness that he understands the judgments of the Lord, which are “a great deep,” and says with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). And in prayer he will recall: “For your judgments are delightful” (Ps. 118:39).

After judgment comes righteousness. Whoever possesses it will clearly possess Christ, who, according to the Apostle, “has become for us righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30), so that he may practice true righteousness and show no partiality [Note: Previously, with the same meaning, it read “regard persons in judgment.”] in judgment, but know that he himself is to be judged according to his righteousness in the judgment of others.

[Col. 0172B] The third is not to eat upon the mountains, which the Jews think pertains to the sin of idolatry. For we often read in the books of Kings and Chronicles: “Nevertheless he did not remove the high places. The people still sacrificed upon the high places and burned incense on the heights” (1 Kings 15:22; 2 Chronicles 20). Scripture thereby indicates that they sacrificed victims to idols upon mountains and in sacred groves, and burned incense.

We, however, shall say that the man who eats upon the mountains is the one who says with the Pharisee: “I thank you, God, that I am not like this tax collector; I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all my possessions” (Luke 18:12), and so forth.

Conversely, the tax collector, hearing him who had said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29), struck his breast with his hand—that is, the treasury of his evil thoughts—and did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven.

The statement made elsewhere, “Do not seek what is too great for you, and do not examine what is beyond your strength” (Sir. 3:22), also condemns all heretics who eat upon the mountains of pride, despise the simplicity of the Church, and do not know what is written about themselves: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6).

In the fourth place comes: “He has not lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel,” for which the Septuagint translated “thoughts.” Idols—that is, images which they have fashioned from their own heart—all heretics make. They lift up the eyes of their heart to them, believing their falsehood and deceit to be truth.

The images of the house of Israel are those which are found in the Church and, under the pretext of the falsely named “knowledge,” lead simple people astray, introducing the doctrines of philosophers into the house of Israel—that is, into the house of those who behold God with the mind.

In the fifth place comes: “He has not violated,” or “defiled,” his neighbor’s wife. This plainly prohibits adultery; but because “his neighbor” is added, unless every human being is understood as one’s neighbor, it would seem to command us to abstain from the wives of our friends while freely polluting the wives of enemies and strangers.

Therefore every human being is to be understood as the neighbor of every other, according to the Gospel parable which the Savior presents concerning a certain man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho [another reading: Hierichus] and was wounded by robbers. When the Pharisee asks who his neighbor was, the Lord teaches that the neighbor is the one who does good.

According to mystical interpretation, the wife may be understood as the wisdom of a holy man, as Solomon says: “Love her, and she will embrace you; cherish her, and she will guard you” (Prov. 4:6). Whoever criticizes the blessings of others, inflamed by the torches of envy, violates holy things, corrupts what is chaste, and defiles what is pure desires to contaminate her.

The sixth is: “He has not approached a menstruating woman,” or wife. Each month women’s heavy and sluggish bodies are relieved by the discharge of unclean blood. If a man has intercourse with a woman at that time, the fetuses are said to contract a defect in the seed, so that lepers and elephantiasis sufferers are born from such conception, and foul bodies in either sex arise, with corrupted matter degenerating through the smallness [another reading: deformity] or disproportion of the limbs. [Note: Compare here the statement of Aeneas of Gaza in the middle of his *Dialogue*, “since I also accept the law of the Hebrews,” etc., which reads in Latin: “For I also accept the law of the Hebrews, which condemned the father of a person foully impaired in body to stoning, because through intemperance he had not waited for his wife’s purification; whence an excess of matter and a most shameful disease of offspring resulted.” See Lev. 20:18.]

Men are therefore commanded to know definite times for intercourse—not only with other men’s wives, but also with their own, with whom they seem to be joined by the law, since Scripture says: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28)—knowing when intercourse is appropriate and when they should abstain from their wives.

The Apostle and Ecclesiastes likewise declare: “A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing” (Eccles. 3:5).

Let the wife also beware lest, overcome by desire for intercourse, she entice her husband, and let the husband beware lest he use force against his wife, supposing that the pleasure of marriage ought to be subject to him at all times. Hence Paul says: “Let each one know how to possess his vessel in holiness and chastity” (1 Thess. 4:4).

Beautifully it is said in the brief sayings of the Pythagorean Sextus: “Everyone who is an ardent lover of his own wife is an adulterer.” [Note: Concerning this book of Sextus, which Rufinus translated into Latin, recall what the holy teacher repeats in Letter 133, section 3, and in his Commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 22, as well as our notes there. This saying, praised here, appears under number 138 in this form: “Every unchaste person, or excessively ardent lover, is also an adulterer of his own wife.” Athenagoras, in his *Plea for the Christians*, and Clement of Alexandria, in *The Instructor*, book 2, chapter 10, have similar statements. So too the pagan Publius Syrus. The well-known saying about Otho is also relevant: “He had begun to be the adulterer of his own wife.”]

Someone translating this book into Latin wished to honor it with the name of the martyr Sixtus, without considering that throughout the entire volume—which he foolishly divided into two parts—the name of Christ and of the Apostles is wholly absent.

Nor is it surprising that he transformed a Gentile philosopher into a martyr and bishop of the city of Rome, since he also changed the first book of Eusebius of Caesarea written in defense of Origen by giving it the name of the martyr Pamphilus, so that through such a laudatory advocate he might more easily reconcile the impious books *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*) to Roman ears.

The seventh follows: “He has not grieved anyone,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “has not oppressed anyone through power.” I do not know who is free from this vice and sin. The Egyptians, too, oppressed the Hebrews through power. Hence Habakkuk complains: “Why does the wicked oppress the righteous?” (Hab. 1:3–4).

Would that this were said only of those who are outside, and not of those who are within! Even leaders of the Churches are accustomed to oppress the people through pride. Of them it is written: “They have made you a ruler; do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them” (Sir. 32:1). And the Savior commanded: “Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be the least of all” [another reading: “the last”] (Matt. 20:27).

But what is said according to the Hebrew—“He has not grieved anyone”—agrees with the Apostle’s testimony: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, who dwells in you” (Eph. 4:30). In the Gospel which the Nazarenes read according to the Hebrews, grieving one’s brother’s spirit is counted among the greatest crimes.

If another’s sadness kills the person who causes the grief, what should be said of iniquity and a tyrannical mind, to which the words apply: “Why does earth and ashes boast?” (Sir. 10:9)? Forgetting his condition—how he is full of phlegm, bile, and excrement, and shortly will be consumed by worms—such a man sets his mouth against heaven, and his tongue passes over the earth. He says with the true Nebuchadnezzar: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14).

The eighth is: “He has returned the pledge to the debtor.” Not to every debtor—for otherwise many would find in the recovery of pledges an opportunity for acquiring wealth—but to the debtor of whom the law says that he is poor, has given his own garment as a pledge, and must receive his covering back before sunset (Deut. 24:12–13), lest, tormented by the cold, he cry out to the Lord, who avenges his wrong.

If, according to what follows, we must give bread to the hungry and cover the naked with clothing (Exod. 22:26), how much more must we return his own pledge, provided that the debtor’s poverty is beyond doubt?

We may also return a pledge to a debtor when, to someone joined to us by love and who owes us reciprocal affection, we return his pledge, retaining nothing further of his debt with us.

The ninth place belongs to: “He has taken nothing by force,” or, according to the Septuagint, “has not committed robbery.” The Apostle also speaks of robbers, saying that among other sinners one must not even eat with a person of this kind (1 Cor. 5:11); and every robbery involves violence. For unless force has been applied, robbery achieves nothing.
