There is also a holy violence, and a desirable robbery, of which the Gospel writes: “From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). Jude, the brother of James, speaks of this as well: “Save others by snatching them from the fire; on others have mercy with fear” (Jude 23).

Conversely, hostile powers hasten to seize prey for the destruction of those whom they carry off. Jacob signifies this when he says: “An evil beast has devoured him; an evil beast has seized Joseph” (Gen. 37:33).

Hence the Lord’s sheep that follow him are not snatched from his hands. He himself says: “The Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from the Father’s hand” [another reading adds: “from my hand”] (John 10:29).

From this it is evident that the Father and Son possess one power, strength, and substance. For if no one can snatch from the Son’s hand what the Father has given, and these same things are in the Father’s hand and are not snatched from him, it is plainly proved that all things belong equally to the Father and the Son, and that the Father holds in the Son’s hand what is held in the Father’s hand.

The tenth is: “He has given his bread to the hungry.” By this we are taught that alms are to be given not to those who are full, but to the hungry; bread is not to be given to those who belch from fullness, but to those who are tortured by emptiness.

Every kind of food is contained in “bread.” And it is meaningfully said, “his own,” so that we do not turn into an act of mercy bread obtained through robbery, usury, or another person’s misfortune. For “the redemption of a man’s soul is his wealth” (Prov. 13:8).

We see many doing this: clients, poor people, and farmers—not to mention the violence of soldiers and judges, who oppress through power or commit theft, so that they may give a little of much to the poor and glory in their own crimes.

And in the churches the deacon publicly recites the names of those making offerings: “So much has this person offered; so much has that person promised.” They delight in the applause of the people while their conscience torments them. We provide wretched people with an occasion to rejoice over what they give and not mourn over what they have stolen. [Note: Jerome is criticizing here the practice of reciting the names of those making offerings. At nearly the same time Innocent I also disapproved of it in his letter to Decentius, section 5, ordering that the offerings of the faithful be commended to God—not to the people, nor by public recitation of the deacon, but by the priest’s silent prayer. The Council of Frankfurt in 794 renewed his command by decreeing that names should not be recited before the offering was presented.]

It is better, however, to understand the bread of the righteous as the one who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51), and whom we ask to be given to us in prayer: “Give us our substantial bread,” or “our future bread” (Matt. 6:11). [Note: Here he calls it “substantial” and “future” bread, which elsewhere he understands as supersubstantial, special, pre-eminent, and belonging to the morrow. See the learned commentary on the sixth chapter of Matthew concerning this matter.] Thus, although we shall always receive him afterward, we may deserve to receive him daily in the present age.

The righteous gives this bread to the hungry, of whom it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst” (Matt. 5:6). For the righteous person makes the common bread of all his own particular bread—a bread which had failed in Judea, as the prophet says: “I will take away from them strength,” or “the staff of bread.”

What we are speaking of, if indeed we belong to Christ—or rather, what the prophet recalls—is the bread of believers and of the hungry. It must by no means be given to those who have eaten and drunk, have been filled, have grown fat, and have kicked back. Of them it is said: “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry” (Luke 6:25), lest they vomit it out, as Solomon says: “For he will vomit and defile your good words” (Prov. 23:8).

The Savior expresses the same thing in other words: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs” (Matt. 7:6).

The eleventh place is: “He has covered the naked with clothing.” In accordance with the explanation of the preceding verse, this statement is to be discussed in two ways: first, that we give covering to the physically naked, as the Savior says: “I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. 25:36); and second, that we give the naked in faith and virtues the clothing of Christ, concerning which it is written: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

The person who had no wedding garment was naked in this respect and was thrown out of the banquet. Of this nakedness the Lord also speaks to Jerusalem: “You were naked and full of shame” (Ezek. 16:7).

The twelfth place is held by: “He has not lent at interest,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “has not given his money at interest.” In Hebrew, usury of every kind is prohibited; in the Septuagint, only monetary interest.

The same appears in the fourteenth psalm: “He has not given his money at interest” (Ps. 14:5). But how, then, is it said: “You shall lend at interest to your brother, but to a foreigner you shall lend at interest” (Deut. 15:6; 23:20)?

Observe the progress. At the beginning of the Law, interest is taken only from brothers; in the prophet, usury is prohibited from everyone, as Ezekiel says: “He has not given his money at interest.” In the Gospel, however, there is an increase in virtue, when the Lord commands: “Lend to those from whom you do not hope to receive” (Luke 6:35).

The thirteenth place follows: “He has taken nothing extra.” Some think that usury exists only in money. Divine Scripture, foreseeing this, removes excess from every kind of thing, so that you may not receive more than you gave.

People commonly demand interest in grain, millet, wine, oil, and other commodities; or, as the divine word calls it, “abundance.” For example, they give ten measures in winter and receive fifteen at harvest—that is, half as much extra.

Someone who considers himself especially just will take an additional quarter, and they commonly argue: “I gave one measure, and the seed produced ten. Is it not just that I receive half a measure more of my own, since through my generosity he has nine and a half measures of what belongs to me?”

“Do not be deceived,” says the Apostle; “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7).

Let the compassionate moneylender answer us briefly: did he give to someone who had, or to someone who did not have? If to one who had, he ought not to have given; but he gave as though to one who did not have. Why, then, does he demand more as though from someone who had?

Others customarily receive small gifts of various kinds in place of money lent at interest, and do not understand that usury is called “excess,” whatever it may be, if they receive more from the person to whom they gave than they themselves gave. [Note: Usury is therefore considered wicked because someone receives more than he gave. This most truthful judgment of the holy teacher, supported by so many examples and arguments above and below, completely overturns the recent doctrine granting permission for free lending through bills of exchange—commonly called “commercial” or “exchange” letters—and all the frivolous calculations alien to Christian charity which, with the greatest sorrow, recent Christian moneylenders put forward to defend their greed. In order cunningly to exempt themselves from the penalties of the laws through simulated contracts, they should hear Jerome, speaking from the Apostle: “God is not mocked.” Usury is called “excess,” whatever it may be, if they receive more than they gave. Let those who daily increase their fortunes through lending at interest also hear a similar testimony of Jerome from Saint Leo the Great’s Sermon 16: “Unjust and shameless greed, which says that it offers a benefit while it deceives, does not truly believe God who promises, but believes the man who makes a trembling agreement. While it considers present things more certain than future ones, it frequently meets this result: that the desire for unjust profit becomes the cause of unjust loss. Whatever the outcome, the moneylender’s calculation is always evil: it is a sin for him either to diminish or to increase his money, so that he is wretched in losing what he gave or still more wretched in receiving what he did not give. The wickedness of interest must be wholly avoided, and profit devoid of all humanity must be shunned. Interest on money is the funeral of the soul.”]

The fourteenth step is: “He has turned his hand away from iniquity,” so that he flees iniquity in every work. Iniquity is committed not only with the hand but also with other members, as Solomon says: “Put far away from you a crooked mouth” (Prov. 4:24). And in the Psalms: “They have spoken iniquity on high” (Ps. 72:8).

The foot, too, runs toward iniquity, and so does the eye if it desires another man’s wife. Let him not imitate the one of whom it is said: “He committed no iniquity, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (Isa. 53:9).

Hence, concerning unrighteous mammon, we are commanded to make friends for ourselves, so that they may receive us into eternal dwellings.

The fifteenth is: “He has rendered true judgment between one man and another,” or between himself and his neighbor. This seems to mean the same as the first, where it is written: “If he is righteous and practices judgment,” but the addition of “true judgment,” which he renders between one man and another, or between a man and his neighbor, appears to intensify the virtues.

Therefore at the beginning of Proverbs, after many commandments, an instruction concerning judgment is added: “To know wisdom and discipline, to understand words of prudence, to receive the subtleties of discourse, to know true righteousness, and, after all things, to correct judgment” (Prov. 1:2–3).

For this reason the Apostle also reproves those established in the Church (1 Cor. 6), because they have lawsuits among themselves. The least and despised person is chosen, who according to the Gospel is first, to judge between one man and another: he who has destroyed the things belonging to childhood and reached the mature man. Yet he still needs a more authoritative judgment in order to arrive at the truth of judgment.

The sixteenth place follows: “He has walked in my commandments.” And the seventeenth: “He has kept my judgments and ordinances, so as to perform them,” and, having performed them, to preserve them.

Both expressions have many possible meanings if we wish to review all the commandments of the Law, in which the Lord’s commandments and ordinances are said to be found.

The hundred-eighteenth psalm is full of commandments and ordinances, as is, in part, the eighteenth psalm, in which it is written: “The ordinances of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart, and the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9).

Here one asks how the same prophet can have said: “I gave them ordinances that were not good, in which they shall not live” (Ezek. 20:25). The answer is easy and will be fuller in what follows: the Jews, following the killing letter, do not live, whereas Christians, understanding the life-giving Spirit, do live.

It would take too long to prove by testimonies where the Lord’s commandments and where his ordinances are mentioned, and by what differences or obscurities each of them is surrounded.

Therefore in the present passage it is added: “He is righteous; he shall surely live,” says the Lord God. Whoever does these things and avoids those things will not be punished for his father’s sins, but will live by his own virtues.

[Col. 0178A] **(Verses 10 and following.)** “But if he begets a son who is a robber, shedding blood, and commits one of these things” [or, as the Septuagint translated it, “and commits sins”; “he has not walked in the way of his righteous father”], “and does not do all these things, but eats upon the mountains; pollutes his neighbor’s wife; grieves the needy and the poor” [or, “oppresses them”]; “commits robbery; does not return the pledge; lifts up his eyes to idols; commits abomination; lends at interest and takes something extra—shall he live?” [Note: The Vulgate adds, according to the Hebrew: “He shall not live.” This is also what Rabanus formerly read, and Victorius, as usual, considers sufficient.]

“When he has done all these detestable things, he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him.”

For “robber,” the Hebrew has *PHARIS* [the supplied text leaves the Hebrew term uncertain or blank]. The second edition of Aquila translated it “sinner”; Symmachus, “transgressor”; the Septuagint and Theodotion, “pestilent.”

Just as pestilence creates diseases and commonly devastates the regions in which it has settled, so a pestilent person lays waste to everything.

Let us speak first according to the historical meaning, so that you may know that the iniquities of fathers do not pass over to their sons. If a righteous man does what the preceding passage set forth in order, he shall surely live. But if he begets a son who departs from the service of the Lord and exchanges his father’s virtues for vices, doing what his father did not do and failing to do what his father accomplished, will he be able to live? Certainly he will not live, but will be guilty of his own blood.

According to the spiritual interpretation, however, suppose a righteous ecclesiastical man has preached the faith of the Gospel, but his son and disciple has been deceived by heretical error. He will be called pestilent. Of him it is written in the first psalm: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1:1). In Proverbs, too, the confident, shameless, and proud man is called pestilent (Prov. 21:24).

This man has shed the blood of those whom he deceived and heaps all sins upon himself: eating upon the mountains of pride; polluting his neighbor’s Church; grieving, oppressing, and overthrowing the needy and poor in knowledge of the Scriptures; committing robbery by seizing those whom he has led astray from the Church; not returning the pledge he received from his teacher, so as to fulfill what is written: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. 10:8); lifting his eyes to idols and images which he fashioned from his own heart; committing every abomination; lending money at interest so that the diligence of his disciples may increase the error of his teacher [Note: Previously, with less appropriate meaning and against the testimony of the manuscripts, it read: “and of the disciples.”]; and demanding back from those to whom he gave more than he had given. Certainly he will not be able to live, but will die in his own blood.

[Col. 0179B] **(Verses 14 and following.)** “But if he begets a son who sees all the sins of his father which he committed, and fears, and does not do likewise” [the Vulgate: “anything like them”]; “does not eat upon the mountains; does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel; does not violate his neighbor’s wife; does not grieve anyone; does not retain the pledge; does not commit robbery; gives his bread to the hungry; covers the naked with clothing; turns his hand away from injuring the poor; does not take interest or excess; practices my judgments; walks in my commandments—he shall not die in his father’s iniquity, but shall surely live.

“His father, because he slandered, used force against his brother, and did evil in the midst of his people—he is dead in his own iniquity.”

Do not be surprised, he says, if the son of a righteous man, turning toward vices and sins, dies the death of the wicked. Conversely, if the son of a sinful and impious man sees the perversity of his father’s ways and turns away so as not to do evil but to do good, he is not held guilty of his father’s crimes.

This may also be understood of us, to whom it is said in the Psalms: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:11). We, who were born from the stock of the nations, are to leave behind the crimes of our parents, practice judgment and righteousness, and live in them.

He repeats, therefore, what we discussed more fully above. For that reason we pass briefly over everything, wishing to move on to what is more obscure and new.

[Col. 0179D] **(Verses 19–20.)** “And you say: ‘Why has the son not borne the iniquity of the father?’ Clearly because the son practiced judgment and righteousness, kept all my commandments, and performed them; he shall surely live. The soul that sins—it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the impiety of the impious shall be upon him.”

He resolves the question which the hearer could raise in opposition. “You are accustomed,” he says, “to ask: ‘Why has the righteous son not borne the iniquity of his father?’” To this he himself replies: “Clearly because the son acted well and did not commit his father’s sins.”

It is just that, just as the sinner dies in his own crime, so the righteous should live in his own virtues; that the soul which has sinned should die, and that the soul which has kept God’s commandments should live.

### (Verses 21–22)

“But if the wicked man repents of all his sins that he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, and practices judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live; he shall not die. None of all his iniquities that he has committed will be remembered.”

He says that the sins of fathers do not overflow onto their children, nor does a guilty father burden a righteous son; nor are some punished for the crimes of others. Thus the very same person who was previously wicked and sinful, if afterward he repents, turns to better things, and wipes away his former sins, is not judged according to the oldness of his sin, but is received into my flock through the renewal of virtue. At the same time, we must consider what sort of wicked and sinful person he receives when repentant. “If,” he says, “he turns away from all his sins that he has committed, and keeps all the Lord’s commandments”—that is, if he abandons every crime and follows every virtue; if he does everything good and forsakes every evil—“then I also will forget all his iniquities that he has committed.”

### (Verse 23)

“He shall live by his righteousness which he has practiced.” He will live not so much by my righteousness as by his own, although it belongs to my righteousness to repay good things to the good and evil things to the evil.

“Is the death of the wicked truly my will,” says the Lord God, “and not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?” (1 Tim. II). Therefore it is the Lord’s will that all should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. Wherever God’s judgment appears severe and savage, it condemns not human beings but sins.

### (Verse 24)

“But if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity according to all the abominations that the wicked habitually commits, will he live? None of all his righteousnesses that he practiced will be remembered [the Vulgate reads: ‘will be remembered’]. In the transgression by which he transgressed, and in the sin by which he sinned [the Vulgate reads: ‘in the sin that he sinned’], in these he shall die.”

Just as former sins do not weigh down the person who was previously sinful and is now righteous, so former righteousnesses do not help the sinner who was previously righteous. For each person will be judged in whatever condition he is found.

### (Verse 25)

“And you said: ‘The way of the Lord is not fair.’ Hear, then [the Vulgate adds “then”], house of Israel: Is my way not fair? Are your ways not rather crooked?”

He gives the reasons why the Lord’s judgment is just. “You think me,” he says, “unjust, as though I return the sins of fathers to their children” (Deut. XXIV), and as though, while some eat the sour grape, the teeth of others are set on edge (Jer. XXXI). Behold, each person dies in his own sin and is brought to life in his own righteousness; in both cases he is judged not according to the past but according to the present [“is judged”].

[Note: [Col. 0180D] Victorius supplies the word *judicantur* (“are judged”), without which the sentence appeared incomplete, taking it from Jerome himself in chapter XXXV below, where it is said: “God judges in both cases not the past but the present.”]

Rather, your judgment is unjust, since you think that the parable is not a parable but receive it as though it were historical fact, so that the crimes of some are punished in others.

### (Verse 26)

“For when the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he will die in them. In the iniquity [the Vulgate reads: ‘injustice’] that he has committed he will die.”

This may also be understood as referring to the people of Israel, who were previously righteous but turned away from their righteousness because they abandoned the author of righteousness and committed iniquity by denying the Son of God. In the sin and crime that they committed they will die—not in many sins, but in one: killing the heir in order to destroy the inheritance.

### (Verses 27–28)

“And when the wicked man turns away from his wickedness that he has committed and practices judgment and righteousness, he will preserve his own life. For when he considers and turns away from all his iniquities that he has committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die.”

On the contrary, he says, the people of the nations, who have no knowledge of God and are wicked, if they turn away from their former wickedness, which they practiced in idolatry, and do the things commanded by the law to Israel, will themselves, though previously dead, bring their souls to life. Seeing that they have perished in the iniquities they committed, they will believe in him who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). They shall surely live; they shall not die.

### (Verse 29)

“And the children of Israel say: ‘The way of the Lord is not fair.’ Are my ways not fair, house of Israel? Are your ways not rather crooked?”

To this day Israel blasphemes God, asking why he has abandoned his own people and taken up the multitude of the nations. The Lord rebukes them because their ways are crooked, while the Lord’s judgment is just: when the former tenants have been destroyed, he sends other husbandmen into his vineyard. Understanding this in the parable of the Gospel, the Jews said: “It must not happen” (Luke XX, 16).

### (Verse 30)

“Therefore I will judge each one according to his ways, house of Israel,” says the Lord God.

Whether those who are judged belong to the multitude of the nations or to the people of Israel, “there is no partiality with God” (Col. III, 25); each person will be crowned according to his own faith and condemned for his wickedness and unbelief.

### (Verse 31)

“Turn and repent of all your iniquities, and iniquity will not be a ruin to you. Cast away from yourselves all your transgressions by which you have transgressed.”

This statement is directed specifically to Israel, so that they may repent and abandon their iniquities, or transgressions, by which they transgressed against God. It can also be understood as applying to both peoples, so that Israel and the multitude of the nations alike may abandon their vices and turn to him who can heal their brokenness.

“And make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit,” so that, abandoning the oldness of the letter, you may live in the newness of the spirit. Israel’s new heart is to believe in him whom it had previously denied. The new heart of the nations is to abandon idols and, rejecting the worship of the dead, to believe in him who is the God of the living.

“And why will you die, house of Israel?”

As we said above, it is better to understand this exhortation—“Turn and repent”—as referring to the persons of the Jews, whom he does not wish to die and to whom he now says: “Why will you die, house of Israel?” You have Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as fathers, concerning whom it is written: “He is the God of the living and not of the dead” (Mark XII, 27). Why will you die through your own fault, although through the merit of your fathers and through my mercy you ought to live?

### (Verse 32)

“For I do not desire the death of the one who dies [variant: ‘of the sinner’], says the Lord God. Return and live.”

“I do not wish you to die,” he says, “you whom I brought forth for salvation. For I brought forth children and exalted them, but they themselves despised me” (Isa. I, 2). Return, therefore, and live. “Return” is said only to those who were previously with God and afterward abandoned his company. And live through repentance, you who died through sin. Israel, therefore, because it does not return to its former state, must be considered dead.

### (Chapter XIX, verses 1ff.)

“And you, take up a lament over the princes of Israel, and say:

‘Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions? In the midst of young lions she raised her cubs. She brought up one of her cubs, and he became a lion; he learned to seize prey and to devour human beings. The nations heard about him, and they caught him in their pit and brought him in chains to the land of Egypt.

When she saw that she had become weak and that her expectation had perished, she took one of her cubs and made him a lion. He walked among lions and became a lion. He learned to seize prey and to devour human beings. He learned to make widows and to reduce their cities to a wilderness. The land and its fullness were laid waste at the sound of his roar.

The nations gathered against him from every side and from the provinces, and they spread their net over him. He was caught in their traps. They put him in a cage, brought him in chains to the king of Babylon, and put him in prison, so that his voice would no longer be heard upon the mountains of Israel.’

The Septuagint reads:

‘And you, take up a lament over the prince of Israel, and say: “What became of your mother? A cub in the midst of lions? In the midst of lions she multiplied her cubs. One of her cubs sprang forth; he became a lion and learned to seize prey. He devoured human beings, and the nations heard against him. In their corruption he was caught, and they brought him in a muzzle to the land of Egypt.

“And she saw that he had been taken away from her and that her substance had perished. So she took another of her cubs and made him a lion, and he lived among lions. He became a lion and learned to seize prey. He devoured human beings and fed upon his boldness. He reduced their cities to a wilderness and laid waste the land and its fullness at the sound of his roar.

“And the nations round about, from the regions, rose against him and spread their nets over him. In their corruption he was caught. They put him in a muzzle, and he came into a cage to the king of Babylon; they brought him into prison, so that his voice would no longer be heard upon the mountains of Israel.”’

I know that in this passage I have read a lengthy interpretation, entangled in such great obscurities that it opened up the reading less than it enveloped it, since it refers everything written here to hostile powers and describes lions and wars in the heavenly Jerusalem. It explains how one of them was captured and another was appointed in his place, and adduces many testimonies that the devil and his companions are customarily called lions, as in the statement of the apostle Peter: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking how he may enter” (1 Pet. V, 8); and in the Psalms: “Do not give the soul that confesses you to beasts” (Ps. LXXIII, 19).

Certainly, when it comes to the historical meaning, the interpreter says that Johanan son of Kareah was taken to Egypt. But how he could have been called a lion when he fled with a few companions, I cannot understand. He identifies the other lion as Zedekiah, who was likewise taken to Babylon.

Leaving such interpretations to the judgment of the reader, we shall say that, since the captivity was near, the prophet is not so much prophesying the future as recounting the past. For after Zedekiah’s sixth year—since immediately afterward we read, “And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month”—a lament is taken up over the princes, or the prince, of Israel, and it is said: “Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions?”

The lament over the princes therefore concerns all those who were born from the stock of Josiah. Jerusalem, the mother of the princes, is called a lioness; she bore and nourished young lions. She brought up one of her cubs and made him a lion, signifying Joahaz, the son of Josiah, whom Pharaoh Neco took to Egypt and in whose place he appointed Jehoiakim. After Jehoiakim’s death, his son Jeconiah was made king, but he was taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar together with his mother and the leading men of the city; from him was born Shealtiel, the father of Zerubbabel, who received his name from the fact that he was born in Babylon (2 Kings XXIII).

It is clear that under the metaphor of the lioness, the cubs, the lion, and again the other lion, the events that had already happened at the time when the prophet spoke are being described. After Jerusalem brought Joahaz, the son of Josiah, from the royal line and made him king, he became so cruel in a short time that, figuratively, he is said to have seized prey and devoured human beings. When the Egyptian came against him, he seized him—not without wounds, or, more precisely, in a pit, as the Hebrew contains—so that the figurative capture of lions might be preserved, since lions are always caught in pits. He brought him in a muzzle, or in chains, to the land of Egypt, where he died.

When his mother Jerusalem saw this—she who had borne him, nourished him, and established him as king—and saw that her expectation had perished, she took one of the other kings, Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim, and made him king. He too, imitating the cruelty of his predecessor, is described under the savagery of a lion: he devoured human beings, made many widows, reduced cities to a wilderness, and terrified the whole province with the sound of his roar. Thus the nations gathered against him, spread their net over him, caught him in a pit, put him into a cage and chains.

This was not literally done to Jeconiah, for he surrendered himself to the king of Babylon and was carried away to Chaldea; rather, the image of the lion is preserved, since a lion is caught in pits, bound in chains, and kept in cages. Otherwise, according to the historical account, we read that this happened to Zedekiah, who was made king of Jerusalem after Jeconiah. This circumstance led many people, because chains and cages are mentioned and a prison is named, to understand Zedekiah rather than Jeconiah.

He was therefore kept in prison and not killed, merely removed from the kingdom. But history relates that Zedekiah was led blind to Babylon and immediately killed there.

### (Verses 10ff.)

“Your mother was like a vine, planted in your blood beside the water; its fruit and its foliage grew because of abundant waters. Its branches became strong rods for the scepters of rulers, and its height was exalted among the foliage. It saw its height in the multitude of its branches; it was uprooted in anger and thrown to the ground, and a scorching wind dried up its fruit. They withered, and its strong branches dried up; fire consumed it. And now it has been transplanted into the wilderness, into a dry and waterless land. Fire went out from the rod of its branches and consumed its fruit, and there was no strong rod in it, no scepter for rulers. It is a lament, and it shall be a lament.”

[Note: [Col. 0183] In place of *in*, Victorius writes *inter* (“among”), following the Hebrew, the Vulgate, and the Greek ἐν μέσῳ (“in the midst”). Shortly afterward he reads *siccavit* (“dried”) instead of *siccabit* (“will dry”), as does Rabanus.]

The Septuagint reads:

“Your mother was like a vine, like a flower among pomegranates, planted in water. Its fruit and its shoot came from abundant water. It became a rod of strength for a tribe of rulers, and its stature was exalted in the midst of its branches. It saw its stature in the multitude of its branches, and it was broken in fury. It was thrown to the ground, and a scorching wind dried up its choice branches. They were avenged, and its rod of strength dried up. Fire consumed it, and now they have planted it in the wilderness, in a waterless land. Fire came out from the rod of its chosen branches and consumed it, and there was no rod of strength in it. It is a tribe for a parable of lamentation, and it shall be a lament.”

The same reality is expressed in different words. Just as above we read that Jerusalem was compared with a beautiful woman, and again with a lioness that raised lions in her lair, so now it is compared with a very beautiful vine planted beside abundant waters. Therefore, nourished by moisture, its branches grew so greatly that one branch—which Scripture calls a very solid or very strong rod—developed into scepters for rulers. For this the Septuagint translated “into a tribe of rulers,” so that kings might have arisen from it.

The vine itself was of such great beauty that the splendor of its greenery equaled the flowers of the pomegranate. In Hebrew it says “like a vine in your blood,” comparing the redness of the flowers with blood. The vine was therefore exalted and stood upright. But “God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6): it was uprooted in the Lord’s fury and thrown to the ground, so that the elegant image of the vine might preserve the ruins of Jerusalem.

Although the vine is beautiful and extends through long branches, if you remove its supports and poles, it lies upon the ground and dries up in the heat, especially if a scorching wind—called by the Greeks *kaúsōma* (καῦσωμα)—dries up its fruit, so that it withers and is burned as though by fire.

As for what has been added in the Septuagint, “They were avenged,” instead of what is written in Hebrew, “they withered,” I cannot understand what logical connection it could have.

How, then, has that vine of such fertility, such fruits, and such beauty now been transplanted into the wilderness, into a dry and waterless land? It signifies the land of Babylon, to which they were carried; or Egypt, to which they fled; or the land of Judea itself, in which a few poor people remained, with Gedaliah [variant: Gotholias] appointed over them to gather and govern the remnants of the people (2 Kings XXV).

Against him rose Ishmael, from the royal stock and from the rod of the vine’s branches. He killed him at Mizpah [variant: Masepha] and consumed all the fruit of the vine. From that time there was no strong rod in the vine, no scepter of rulers (Jer. XL–XLI). For no king remained to govern the people; instead, they fled with Johanan son of Kareah to Egypt.

Therefore it is a lament and a parable of lamentation, so that the royal line—which thereafter ceased in Judea—might be mourned, until he should come “for whom it has been reserved,” and “he himself was the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

It is therefore clear that both the preceding passage, in which it says, “Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions?” and this passage, in which it is written, “Your mother was like a vine in your blood, planted beside the water,” refer to Jerusalem. It lost its lions and its branches, and there remained in it no rod that could rise up into a tribe or into scepters of rulers.

The passage begins with a lament and ends with a lament: “Take up a lament over the princes of Israel.” That is, both at the beginning and now at the end there is a lament, and the royal stock must be followed with mourning and with the lament of the parable.

According to the anagogical interpretation, which others refer to the heavenly Jerusalem, they say that many fell from it into this valley of tears, ceased to be kings, and that a once most beautiful vine was dried up by a scorching wind, so that no green branch remained in it. Jeremiah afterward mourns it under the figure of the city. We, however, understand this as referring to the Church (Matt. XXIV), because in the last time, when iniquity has multiplied, “the love of many will grow cold” [variant: “will grow cold”], so that even God’s elect, if it were possible, might be tested, and its princes might be captured in the devil’s nets. The devil is not content with capturing one king but hastens every day to capture kings and princes, according to what is written: “His food is choice” (Hab. I, 16).

The branches of the Church, which once equaled flowers and the redness of blood, will afterward be dried up by the wind.

[Note: [Col. 0185D] The Vatican manuscript, together with Rabanus, adds *urente* (“scorching”).]

The parable of the Gospel also sounds this interpretation: when the sun rose, what had germinated was scorched by the heat and suddenly dried up (Mark IV). Thus scarcely one of the branches remains that might rise into a rod and become a worthy prince of the people.

Amos expresses the same thing in other words: “I will bring a famine and a thirst upon the land—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of God” (Amos VIII, 11). Therefore we ought to mourn and lament over the princes of Israel, through whose vice and pride Judea was deserted and Jerusalem captured.

### (Chapter XX, verse 1)

“And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, that men from the elders of Israel came to inquire of the Lord, and they sat before me.”

[Note: [Col. 0185D] Victorius restores, according to the Vulgate text, *sederunt* (“they sat”). The Hebrew has [Hebrew term].]

After eleven months and five days from the preceding vision, the word again comes to the prophet, after men from the elders of the house of Israel came to inquire of the Lord and sat before him.

Many examples testify that this was the custom of the people of Israel: whatever they wished to know from the Lord, they sought through the prophets. Saul, searching for his donkeys, went to Samuel and received advice from a servant to offer the prophet a quarter of a shekel. When Jeroboam’s son was sick, his wife was sent to Shiloh to Ahijah [variant: Abijah] the prophet, carrying gifts—loaves, *colliridae*, grapes, and a flask of honey—in order to learn about her son’s illness (1 Kings IX; 3 Kings XIV). David also asked the prophet Nathan whether he ought to build a temple for the Lord (2 Kings VII). Ahab inquired whether he should go up to Ramoth-gilead or not (3 Kings XXII). In Isaiah (Isa. XXXVII) and in the Book of Kings (2 Kings XIX), it is announced what things are to come upon Sennacherib.

Nor is it surprising that in the Old Testament prophets announce to individuals the things that are to come, since we read that Agabus prophesied what would happen to Paul (Acts XXI).

It is written in Deuteronomy: “The nations whom the Lord is going to destroy before you will listen to dreams and divinations; but the Lord your God has not given you this” (Deut. XVIII, 14).

[Note: [Col. 0186D] Victorius restores *omnia* (“all things”) in place of *somnia* (“dreams”), following the Greek κλῃδονισμῶν; the Hebrew likewise has “diviners and enchanters.”]

It belongs to the nations to approach Chaldeans, *harioli*, soothsayers, diviners, lots, and the oracles of demons, by which their error is mocked. Thus now the elders of Israel approach the prophet in order to inquire of the Lord through him, yet they say nothing about their question. The one who was to be questioned already knew what they were asking, so that there might be a miracle both in knowing why they had come and in answering what their silent speech held within their hearts.

### (Verses 2–3)

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Have you come to inquire of me? As I live, I will not answer you, says the Lord God.’”

To holy people who ask fitting questions the promise is given: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am.’” But to sinners such as the elders of Israel were—whose crimes the prophet describes afterward—no answer is given, but a rebuke for their sins. He adds an oath, “As I live,” so that the sentence of refusal may be firmer.

As for the Septuagint reading, “If I answer you,” Symmachus translated it more clearly: “I will not answer you.”

### (Verse 4)

“If you judge them—if you judge them, son of man.”

The Septuagint reads: “If I have taken vengeance upon them with vengeance, son of man.”

They came to inquire of me, wishing to learn about matters of uncertainty and about the future; but you, son of man, judge them, so that the prophet’s response may not be an answer but the sentence of one judging their iniquities and the crimes of their fathers, which they followed.

Or certainly, according to the reading “If I have taken vengeance upon them with vengeance,” the sense is this: They are so covered with iniquity that they are not even worthy of correction and chastisement, according to what is said in the prophet: “I will no longer visit your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your daughters-in-law when they have committed adultery” (Hos. IV).

For this reason sinners who have entered into the depths of sin are abandoned to carry out the desires of their hearts (Prov. XVIII).

“Show them the abominations of their fathers, and say to them.”

The Septuagint reads: “Bear witness to them concerning the iniquities of their fathers, and say to them.”

If the sins of fathers do not overflow onto children, why are the abominations and iniquities of the fathers now laid before the elders? The reason is that they may be shown to be acting like their parents and dragging along, through inherited evil, a very long rope of sins, so that they may fear the punishments of those whose vices they imitate.

### (Verses 5–6)

“Thus says the Lord God: On the day when I chose Israel, and raised my hand over the offspring of the house of Jacob, and appeared to them in the land of Egypt, and raised my hand over them, saying: ‘I am the Lord your God’—on that day I raised my hand over them to bring them out of the land of Egypt into the land that I had foreseen for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is distinguished among all lands.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Thus says the Lord God: From the day when I chose the house of Israel and became known to the offspring of the house of Jacob, and was made known to them in the land of Egypt, I took them up, saying: ‘I am the Lord your God.’ On that day I took them by my hand, saying that I would bring them out of the land of Egypt into the land that I had prepared for them, a land flowing with milk and honey; it is a honeycomb beyond every land.”

For the Septuagint’s “it is a honeycomb beyond all lands,” where we have translated “it is distinguished among all lands,” the first edition of Aquila has “foundation”; the second, “renowned”; Symmachus, “region”; Theodotion, “strength.”

[Note: [Col. 0187D] In Greek Symmachus has στάσιν, a word that properly means “station” or “standing-place.”]

The meaning is evidently that this land is the foundation of all lands, because it contains the worship of God, the temple, the rites, and knowledge of God. The people of Israel, while settled in Egypt, were so ignorant of God that Moses, when sent to them, said: “If they ask me, ‘Who sent you?’ what shall I say to them?” He replied: “Say to them, ‘He who is has sent me’” (Exod. III, 13–14).

In Egypt, therefore, he became known to the people and to the offspring of the house of Jacob, when he raised his hand against the Egyptians on their behalf and said: “I am the Lord your God.” He chose them in order to bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land flowing with milk and honey.

For they were not yet able to receive solid food. Like little children and infants, they needed the honey and milk of infancy.

According to the literal sense, no one who has considered the whole land from Rhinocorura to Mount Taurus and the Euphrates River can doubt that the land of Judah is renowned and more fertile than all lands. He will consider the power of its cities and the pleasantness of its regions—Palestine, Phoenicia, Arabia, Coele-Syria, Cilicia, and the other regions that the Lord promised to Israel if it kept his commandments.

Because Israel did not receive these lands, the fault lay in its unbelief. For even in Palestine and the province of Judea many nations remained and were not expelled. The guarantor is not at fault if the one to whom the promise is made makes himself unworthy of the promise, especially when the promiser’s choice is set forth: “If you are willing and obey me, you will eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling, the sword will devour you.”

The present circumstances are therefore chosen. The one who is chosen cannot immediately be considered incapable of being tested or of perishing, since Saul, chosen as king, and Judas, chosen as an apostle, later fell through their own fault.

The raising of the hand, or its extension, shows the posture of one striking: he was to strike the Egyptians on their behalf and free the people of Israel from Egypt.

### (Verse 7)

“And I said to them: ‘Let each person cast away the offenses of his eyes, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.’”

The Septuagint reads:

“And I said to them: ‘Let each person cast away the abominations of his eyes, and let him not be defiled by the inventions of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.’”

For “offenses,” which in Hebrew are called *sekuse* [Hebrew term], Symmachus translated “nauseas”; the second edition of Aquila, “cuttings-off,” so that he might indicate that the eye-disorders—or, as it were, nauseas—must be cast away from the eyes. They not only obstruct sight but also provoke vomiting in those who look at them.

There is also the Hebrew word *gelule* [Hebrew term], which the Septuagint translated “inventions”; the first edition of Aquila, “defilements”; and the second edition, together with Symmachus and Theodotion, “idols.” We too have followed them for the present.

He commands those who are first leaving Egypt to forget the idols to which they had long been enslaved—or rather, to cast them away from their eyes, so that they should consider them unworthy even of being looked upon, and no longer consent to what had long defiled them.

“I,” he says, “am the Lord your God”—not the Egyptian monsters, not the inventions of various creatures.

The same command is given to us when we leave Egypt: we must cast away the offenses of our eyes, so that we do not delight in the things in which we once delighted in the world, and so that we are not defiled by the images of Egypt—that is, by the inventions of philosophers and heretics, which are rightly called idols.

We should also remove our eyes from the spectacles—or rather, from the offenses—of Egypt: the arena, the circus, the theaters, and everything that contaminates the soul’s purity and enters the mind through the senses. Thus what is written is fulfilled: “Death entered through your windows” (Jer. IX, 21).

### (Verse 8)

“And they provoked me.”

The Septuagint reads: “And they withdrew from me,” or, as Symmachus translated it: “They did not obey me.”

Immediately after being called, they withdraw from God, so that there is no interval between the calling and the withdrawal. We must also note that no one withdraws from God unless he has previously been with him. Hence in the Book of Job the dragon is called an apostate, a transgressor, and one who withdraws (Job XXXIV).

“They were unwilling to listen to me. Each person did not cast away the abominations of his eyes, and they did not abandon the idols of Egypt.”

The Septuagint reads:

“And they were unwilling to listen to me. They did not cast away the abominations of their eyes, and they did not abandon the inventions of Egypt.”

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Victorius adds *suorum* (“of their own”) from the Greek ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν (“of their eyes”).]

“Therefore,” he says, “they provoked me and withdrew from me, because they were unwilling to listen to me.” Human freedom of choice is preserved: they did everything that I commanded by the law that they should not do. Immediately despairing of salvation, they murmured against Moses and distrusted God’s promises.

Therefore it follows:

“And I said that I would pour out my indignation upon them and fulfill my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt.”

As soon as I commanded them to abandon or cast away the offenses of their eyes and not to defile themselves with the idols of Egypt, they provoked me. They were unwilling to listen to what I said; instead, they did what I had commanded them not to do. Therefore I had determined to pour out fury and indignation upon them and to fulfill the anger that I had conceived in my mind in the midst of Egypt, since they had not yet gone out from Egypt.

For the passage continues below: “Therefore I cast them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness.” This shows that they had not yet left Egypt when he wished to pour out his indignation, fulfill his anger against them, and strike them in the midst of the land of Egypt.

### (Verse 9)

“And I acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations in whose midst they were and among whom I had appeared to them in order to bring them out of the land of Egypt.”

What I had planned to do on account of justice, I did not do because of the greatness of my mercy, lest my name be defiled and I appear unable to fulfill what I had promised Israel. I therefore spared my name, so that the nations among whom I had become known to them in the land of Egypt would not have an opportunity to blaspheme.

Up to this point the prophet describes what he had promised them while they were settled in the land of Egypt, how they immediately offended him, and what the Lord had contemplated doing against them but nevertheless did not do. What follows he spoke to them after they had gone out from Egypt.

### (Verses 10ff.)

Therefore I cast them out of the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness. I gave them my commandments and showed them my judgments, which a person does and by which he lives. Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, so that they might be a sign between me and them, and they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them.

But the house of Israel provoked me in the wilderness: they did not walk in my commandments, and they rejected my judgments, which a person does and by which he lives [Vulgate: “doing them, a person shall live”]; and they grievously violated my Sabbaths. Therefore I said that I would pour out my fury upon them in the wilderness and consume them. But I acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from whom I had brought them out in their sight.

These words are spoken about those who were led out of Egypt into the wilderness, so that, freed from the vices of the Egyptians, they might more readily fulfill God’s commandments in the solitude, carry out his judgments, and keep his Sabbaths. These were given as a sign between the one who gave them and those to whom they were given, as Scripture says:

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: And you, command the children of Israel, saying: See that you keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, so that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you. Keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Whoever violates it shall surely die. Whoever does work on it—that person shall be cut off from the midst of his people” (Exod. 31:13–14).

Thus the Sabbath and circumcision were given as signs of the true Sabbath and the true circumcision, so that we may know that, in the perfect and eternal Sabbath, we must rest from the works of the age, and that we must circumcise not the foreskin but the heart. Hence, after working for six days, we rest on the seventh, so that day and night we may do nothing other than recognize that everything by which we live is owed to the Lord. When the week returns, we are to consecrate ourselves wholly to his name, so that through the sanctification of the day we may remember the Lord who sanctifies us.

The Lord gave these commandments, ordinances, and observance of the Sabbath in the wilderness so that those who did them might live by them—not that they should pass from them to greater things, as was promised in the Gospel. They violated them, not once or slightly, but vehemently, so that the ἐπίτασις [intensification] of the violation might be shown.

Therefore he said and determined in his mind that he would pour out his fury upon them in the wilderness and consume them, when he said to Moses: “Let me alone, and, enraged with fury against them, I will destroy them” (Exod. 32:10). But he did not wish to do this, sparing them for the sake of the Egyptians and the other nations, so that they would not be scandalized, and also sparing those whom he pitied while awaiting the repentance of the converted.

It should be noted that, when he was speaking after the offense to those who were still established in Egypt, he said: “I acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from whom I brought them out in their sight.”

At that time they were still among them, because they had not yet departed. But now, after they had gone out, it says: “from whom I brought them out in their sight.”

[Note: [Col. 0189D] With the Vatican manuscript we read *constitutis* after *Victor.*, where previously *constitutus* had stood.]

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Victorius, aided by a manuscript, supplies *ut ait*—“as he says”—and adds *in quarum medio erant* (“among whom they were”). These words, however, are absent from our manuscripts and from other printed books.]

### (Verse 15)

[Note: [Col. 0191] That is, that I should lead them hence into the land, etc.; nor was there any reason for Victorius to change *educerem* to *inducerem*.]

“Therefore I also raised my hand against them in the wilderness, so that I would not lead them into the land that I had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the choicest of all lands, because they had rejected my judgments, had not walked in my commandments, and had violated my Sabbaths. For their heart went after idols, but my eye spared them, so that I would not kill them, and I did not consume them in the wilderness.”

**The Septuagint:** “And I raised my hand against them in the wilderness, so that I would absolutely not bring them into the land that I had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey; it is a honeycomb beyond every land, because they rejected my ordinances, did not walk in my commandments, violated my Sabbaths, and walked after the thoughts of their hearts. Yet my eye spared them, so that I would not destroy them, and I did not kill them to the point of destruction in the wilderness.”

I had indeed determined to pour out all my fury upon them and destroy and consume them. But I acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned among the nations—namely, the Amalekites and the others (Exod. 17; Num. 14) who fought against them in the wilderness. Thus I would not bring them into the land that I had promised them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the choicest of all lands—or, as the word may mean, a honeycomb.

The cause of this punishment and sentence is that they had rejected my judgments, had not walked in my commandments, and had violated my Sabbaths. The cause behind that cause was that they did not do these things because their heart followed the idols of Egypt.

“But my eye spared them,” he says, “so that I would not kill them or destroy them, nor consume them altogether.”

Here it is asked how he spared those whose corpses fell in the wilderness, and of whom, except Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, no one entered the promised land. From this we understand that they live, that they were not reserved for eternal punishments, that they were not erased from the book of the living, and that they were not consumed before the face of the Lord.

For if, because they were not brought into the promised land, they are to be considered lost, then Moses also perished, since he saw the promised land but did not enter it. Concerning him the Lord says in the Book of Joshua: “Moses my servant is dead” (Deut. 34:5). And in Malachi: “Remember the law of Moses my servant” (Mal. 4:4). In Jeremiah, moreover, God speaks of him as a friend and intimate of his: “If Moses and Samuel stood before me” (Jer. 15:1).

Otherwise, we must also believe that Moses’ prayers were heard when, interceding for the people, he said: “If you forgive their sin, forgive it; but if you do not wish to, erase me from the book that you have written” (Exod. 32:32–33).

To understand that God’s sentence against sons and servants is imposed not for destruction but for correction, let us hear the testimonies of Scripture:

“My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not faint when you are reproved by him” (Prov. 3:11).

“For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

And elsewhere: “When he killed them, then they sought him” (Ps. 77:34).

And in the Song of Deuteronomy: “I kill and I make alive” (Deut. 32:39).

We can also say, according to the literal sense, that he did not destroy them together with their stock and offspring, but that, after killing the fathers, he spared the sons, whom he brought into the promised land.

### (Verses 18ff.)

“But I said to their sons in the wilderness: Do not walk in the commandments [or: ordinances] of your fathers, and do not keep their judgments, and do not defile yourselves with their idols [or: thoughts]. I am the Lord your God. Walk in my commandments, keep my judgments, and perform them; and sanctify my Sabbaths, so that they may be a sign between me and you, and it may be known [or: so that you may know] that I am the Lord your God.”

After the death of the fathers who fell in the wilderness, he gives commandments to their sons, whom he spared in the salvation of their fathers. “My eye spared them,” he says, “so that I would not kill them utterly or destroy them, but might preserve the fathers in their sons.”

He testifies to the same things that he spoke to the fathers: after they have walked in his commandments, kept his judgments, and preserved the sanctification of the Sabbath, which was given as a sign, then they will know that he is their Lord and God.

The commandments and ordinances of the fathers, and their judgments, signify an ingrained error: they must not imitate the sins of those whose punishments they behold.

### (Verses 21–22)

“But the sons provoked me. They did not walk in my commandments, and they did not keep my judgments, to do them—things which, when a person does them, he will live by them—and they violated my Sabbaths. I threatened to pour out my fury upon them and fulfill my anger against them in the wilderness. But I withdrew my hand and acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from whom I had brought them out in their sight.”

But the sons, he says, followed the crimes of their parents and did everything that the parents had done. Therefore they also deserved a similar sentence. Yet they were preserved by the same abundance of my mercy by which their fathers were preserved, and for the same reasons for which I had pitied their fathers: so that, as the one and same Creator of both, I might likewise mitigate my anger by patience.

We pass quickly over what is clear and move on to what is more obscure.

### (Verses 23–24ff.)

“Again I raised my hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations [Vulgate: ‘the nations’] and to disperse them throughout the lands, because they had not done my judgments, had rejected my commandments, had violated my Sabbaths, and their eyes had been fixed upon the idols [or: thoughts] of their fathers.

Therefore I also gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live. I defiled them in their gifts, when they offered [or: passed through] everything that opens the womb because of their sins” [for this the Septuagint translated, “so that I might destroy them,” which they omitted], “and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

Where in the Old Testament the Lord raised his hand against their sons who fell in the wilderness, wishing to scatter them among the nations, Scripture does not say. But from what is reported here, we must believe that it happened.

Alternatively, this may mean that, after they entered the promised land, they were handed over at various times to different nations and kings because of their many sins. At that time, commandments of the Lord that were good by nature, and judgments by which believers could live, became for them “not good,” since in captivity they were in no way able to keep the commandments of the law or do what the divine word had commanded.

He did not say, “I gave them evil commandments,” but “not good” ones. For it does not immediately follow that what is not good is evil. Thus the Apostle also teaches that it is good for a person not to touch a wife or woman, but, because of lack of self-control, for each person to possess his own vessel in sanctification and chastity (1 Cor. 7).

If he does not do this, it is neither good nor evil.

[Note: [Col. 0193C] Rabanus inserts: “It is good for each person to have his own wife.”]

Therefore God gave them, when they had been scattered among the nations, commandments that were not good—that is, he abandoned them to their own thoughts and desires, so that they would do things that were unfitting.

“And I defiled them in their gifts,” just as a priest separates lepers from the people and declares them defiled, while they offer to idols what they ought to offer to God.

“And they pass through everything that opens the womb through fire to Baal,” that is, the firstborn. Thus, after they had been abandoned by God and handed over to the worship of idols, they might understand that he is the Lord whom, through their own fault, they had provoked to anger.

[Note: [Col. 0193C–D] In one Vatican manuscript we read *Bachalim*. From this we suspected that *Bachurim* should be restored, since Jerome seemed to interpret this word immediately as “firstborn,” and in Hebrew *Bachurim* does indeed mean “firstborn.” But since the word *Baali*, or the idol Baal, is more suitably connected with the fire, nothing has been altered.]

Symmachus interpreted this passage more clearly, using the future instead of the past:

“Therefore I will also give them commandments that are not good, and judgments by which they will not live, and I will defile them because of their gifts, since they consecrate and pass through everything that opens the womb, so that I may destroy them; and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

The sense is this: Because I saw that the sons had become equal to the crimes of their fathers and were doing the same things by which their fathers had offended God, I wished to divide them among the nations, scatter them throughout the whole world, and give them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live, so that I might defile them in their gifts, because they consecrated all the firstborn to idols, and destroy them forever, and they might know that I was the Lord.

By this he shows that he did not give commandments that were not good to those who were living in the wilderness, but that he had thought of giving them to those whom he wished to scatter among the nations and make strangers throughout the world—commandments that he did not give—so that there, by their own fault, they would make God’s good commandments not good, offering to idols what God had commanded them to offer to him.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Previously the less clear wording was: “he shows them that he did not give commandments,” etc. We have silently corrected other matters of this kind below.]

[Note: [Col. 0193D–194D] “I thought of giving them commandments that were not good, but I did not.” Martianaeus, following Erasmus, retained *coegisse* (“had compelled”) instead of *cogitasse* (“had thought”), although Victorius had earlier called it an error to be rejected with a hiss and corrected it through the support of three Florentine codices. The true reading is certainly *cogitasse*: “I thought of giving them commandments that were not good, but I did not.” This is also established by the immediately preceding words: “I wished to divide them among the nations, scatter them throughout the whole world, and give them commandments that were not good,” etc. We have restored *cogitasse*.]

It is also possible to say that, before the offense, they received only the Decalogue; but after idolatry and blasphemy, they received the many ceremonies of the law, so that they might offer to God the victims that they had been offering to demons. By comparison with sacrilege, something that was not in itself good—and yet not evil, because it was offered to God—would become less serious, though still not good, because they had offended the author of goodness.

[Note: [Col. 0193D–194D] “I do not know how this can be reconciled with the statement in Exodus, chapter 3, where the Hebrews are commanded to be sent out so that they may sacrifice to God. Certainly, after the calf had been cast, God may have bound the obstinate people with more numerous and harsher obligations of observance. Yet the whole context of Scripture proves that, even before the worship of the calf, sacrifices and victims—and many legal rites—were prescribed to the people, especially sacrifices and offerings. Nevertheless, I know that Jerome believed not only here but also in Jeremiah, chapter 7, column 895, that the Israelites were permitted to slaughter victims to God only after the worship of the calf. ‘It is clearly understood,’ he says, ‘that he first gave the Decalogue, written on stone tablets by the finger of God; and after the offense of idolatry and the making of the calf, he commanded these things to be done more for himself than for demons, removing the pure religion of God’s commandments and permitting the blood of victims and the desire for flesh.’ I am also aware that this was the opinion of some of the earlier Fathers, such as Lactantius, book 4, chapter 10, and Chrysostom, *Oration 2 Against the Jews* and *Homily 17 on the Acts of the Apostles*, an opinion later accepted by Anastasius the abbot, published by Canisius.]

### (Verses 27, 29ff.)

“Therefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Even in this your fathers blasphemed me, when they despised and scorned me, and I brought them into the land over which I had raised my hand to give it to them [Vulgate adds: ‘it’]. They saw every high hill and every leafy tree, and there they sacrificed their victims, there they presented the provocation of their offering, there they set the fragrance of their offering, and there they poured out their libations. And I said to them: What is this high place to which you are entering? And its name was called ‘high place’ to this day.”

**The Septuagint:** “Therefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Even to this point your fathers provoked me to anger in their offenses by which they fell away from me, and I brought them into the land over which I had raised my hand to hand it over to them. They saw every high hill and every leafy tree, and there they sacrificed to their gods, there they placed the fury of their gifts, there they placed the fragrance of them, and there they poured out their libations. And I said to them: What is *abbana*, because you enter there? And they called its name *abbana* to this present day.”

He says: I wished, while they were sinning in the wilderness, to scatter them throughout all the nations and give them commandments that were not good, so that they would sacrifice to idols what they ought to have offered to me, and consecrate every firstling [another reading: firstborn] to them through fire, so that I might kill and destroy them.

When he says “I wished,” he shows that he did not do what he wished. The statement that follows—“And they shall know that I am the Lord”—is absent from the Septuagint. For it did not seem logically consistent to them that, after being killed, they should know that he is the Lord.

But you, son of man, speak to them again—that is, to the elders of the house of Israel who came to question you:

“Your fathers, from whose stock you descended, also blasphemed me in this matter and considered me worthless. After I brought them into the land that they possessed by my strength, the land that I had given them to possess, they turned to provoking me. For when they saw every high hill and every leafy tree, they sacrificed on the mountains, in groves and wooded places; they sacrificed victims to idols and poured out libations. When I saw this, I said to them: What is this, *BAMA*? For this is interpreted as ‘high place.’ Or why do you enter such a place, which you have chosen among all the hills, so that even to this day such places are called *BAMOTH*, while the ancient error retains its former name?”

In place of *BAMA*, which we translate as “high place,” an error entered the Septuagint edition, so that it is written *ἀββανὰ* (*abbana*), a word that has no meaning in Hebrew.

*BAMA* (במה), if the two syllables are divided into two words, might mean “in which,” but this sense does not fit the present passage. Wherever it is written in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, “The people continued to burn incense and sacrifice on the high place,” *BAMA* in the singular and *BAMOTH* (במות) in the plural mean “high places.”

[Note: [Col. 0195D] The text now has *ἀβαμὰ*. Nobilius also found *ἀβανὰ* in many Greek copies, and an old scholion reads: “*Ἀββανὰ, λίθος ἑρμηνεύεται*—‘Abbana’ is interpreted as ‘stone.’”]

### (Verses 30–31)

“Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God [Vulgate places ‘Certainly’ first]: You defile yourselves in the way of your fathers, and you commit fornication after their stumbling-blocks. In the offering of your gifts, when you pass your sons through fire, you defile yourselves with all your idols to this day. And shall I answer you, house of Israel? As I live, says the Lord God, I will not answer you.”

You imitate the vices of your fathers and walk in the same paths, so that similar offenses may deserve a similar punishment. You have advanced so far in wickedness that you consecrate your sons through fire to demons. Nor has it been enough for you to do this once; you continue to do the same things even at the present time.

This does not mean that these things are being done by the elders in captivity, but by those who were living in Jerusalem and upon whom captivity was impending, and who did not cease doing all these things.

“And when you are bound by such great crimes,” he says, “you seek my answer? As I live, says the Lord God, and I swear by myself, I will not answer you.”

And what follows is:

### (Verses 32–33)

“Nor shall the thought of your mind come to pass, when you say: ‘We will be like the nations, like the families of the lands, to worship wood and stone.’ As I live, says the Lord God, I will reign over you with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and poured-out fury.”

This is the sense: Do not think that your thoughts, by which you blaspheme against me, can be fulfilled. For you say: “We do not wish to be under the Lord, nor to be called his people. But just as there are nations throughout the whole world, each living according to its own will, worshipping wood and stone and serving idols, so we too shall be one nation among many.”

To this God responds and swears by himself, saying: “I will not abandon or despise you, as negligent masters are accustomed to despise runaway slaves. Rather, I will draw you back under my rule, and with an outstretched arm, a striking hand, and poured-out fury, I will restore you to your former servitude and reign over you, so that, whether you wish it or not, you will have me as king and will experience the anger of the king whose mercy you neglected.”

### (Verse 34)

“And I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands in which you have been scattered; with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and poured-out fury I will reign over you.”

“I will not allow you,” he says, “to remain among the nations or to be held in eternal captivity. I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands to which hostile necessity scattered you here and there for service. I will do this not to destroy and erase you, but to be your king.”

From this we understand that even what heretics call the Creator’s cruelty expresses mercy: he becomes angry and rages and pours out all his fury for this purpose—that he may draw back to his kingdom those who chose the tyranny of demons in order to serve them.

### (Verses 35–36ff.)

“And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. As I entered into judgment against your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, says the Lord. I will subject you to my rod, and bring you into the bonds of the covenant. I will select from you the transgressors and the wicked. I will bring them out from the land of their sojourn, but they shall not enter the land of Israel; and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0196D] Victorius adds *vestros*—“your”—and, at the end of the verse, *Deus*, following the Vulgate and Hebrew.]

I will do for you who are in Babylon and now serve idols what I did for your fathers in Egypt: I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face, just as I contended in judgment against them when they went out from Egypt.

After I have judged you, I will subject you to my rod and authority, enter into a covenant with you, and bring you into your land in the bonds of love, so that, bound by my love, you may in no way be able to depart from me.

But the transgressors and wicked—those who persist in evil works through hardness of heart—I will select from among you, not for possession but for rejection. I will indeed bring them out from the land of their sojourn, but, once brought out, they shall not enter the land of Israel; instead they shall perish in different regions. Through the distinction between the good and the wicked, you shall know that I am the Lord, who does all things in judgment.

The discourse hastens toward what follows, and we pass briefly through each item, so as to provide readers only with the sense.

### (Verse 39)

“And you, house of Israel, thus says the Lord God: Let each of you walk after your idols and serve them. But if even in this you will not listen to me, and you continue to profane my holy name with your gifts and your idols.”

**The Septuagint:** “And you, house of Israel, thus says Adonai the Lord: Let each person remove his inventions; and afterward, if you listen to me, you shall no longer profane my holy name with your gifts and your pursuits.”

Symmachus translated the passage more clearly:

“Go, serve your idols, because you were unwilling to listen to me. But do not profane my holy name any longer through your gifts and images. In my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there the whole house of Israel shall serve me.”

The translation of Symmachus has this sense: Because you do not wish to serve me, go and serve idols, and tread in the tracks of your images. You do not wish to listen to me, so that you may no longer sacrifice victims to me, burn incense, or be called my people. For my worshippers will not serve me in groves, shrines, and places of idols, as you do, but on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel.

The Septuagint, however, explains its own sense: Abandon your former thoughts and remove the sins of your evil inventions. If after this you listen to me and do not profane my name through your gifts and images, then on my holy mountain you shall offer victims to me and serve me, O whole house of Israel.

Aquila agrees partly with Symmachus and partly differs:

“Go after your idols and serve them, because you are unworthy of my rule, and your worship does not please me. But if even in this you do not listen to me, and you profane my holy name by pretending to offer to me what you offer to idols, committing such blasphemy against my name that, although you are worshippers of idols, you call yourselves mine, know this: on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, the whole house of Israel shall serve me—not you, who serve idols, but the whole house of Israel that will believe afterward.”

### (Verses 40–41)

“But on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there the whole house of Israel shall serve me—all of them, I say, in the land in which they will please me. There I will seek your firstfruits and the beginning of your tithes. In all your sanctifications I will receive you as a pleasing fragrance, when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you before the nations, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

Concerning this mountain on which the whole house of Israel will serve God, Isaiah and Micah sang with one voice:

“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be manifest on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house [another reading: mountain] of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths. For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2ff.; Mic. 4:1–2).

And again Isaiah says: “Go up onto a high mountain, you who announce good news to Zion; raise and exalt your voice, you who evangelize Jerusalem” (Isa. 40).

We understand this mountain as either Mount Zion or the Church, whose name means “watchtower” and which is established in the height of holy doctrines; or as the Lord and Savior himself, in whom the firstfruits, the tithes, and every act of worship are turned into a pleasing fragrance.

Thus all the surrounding nations, seeing that the Lord’s people have been saved, may glorify God and know, once they have been saved, that he is the Lord.

### (Verse 42)
