“When I bring you into the land of Israel, into the land over which I raised my hand to give it to your fathers, then you shall know that I am the Lord.”

You will know, he says, that I am the Lord when I bring you into the land of Israel, over which I raised my hand in order to bring your fathers into it—land which they lost through their own fault, and which you have regained not so much through your own merit as through my mercy.

### (Verses 43–44)

“And you shall remember your ways and all your crimes by which you defiled yourselves in them. You shall become displeasing to yourselves in your own sight because of all your evils that you committed, and you shall know that I am the Lord when I do good to you for the sake of my name—not according to your evil ways and your most wicked crimes, O house of Israel, says the Lord God.”

We cannot remember our crimes and vices unless we have been brought into the land of Israel and, established there, say with the Apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

“And you shall be displeasing,” he says, “to yourselves in your own sight because of all the evils that you committed.”

Or, as Symmachus translated it: “You shall seem small to yourselves because of all the evils that you have done” (cf. Jas. 4), so that, after they have been exalted, they may believe themselves humble, because the Lord gives grace to the humble.

And elsewhere it is written: “Before destruction the heart of a man is exalted, and before exaltation it is humbled” (Prov. 18:12).

[Note: [Col. 0197] Victorius reads *exaltatur* (“is exalted”) for *in instanti* (“in an instant”), following the Greek ὑψοῦται; shortly afterward the Vatican manuscript reads *exaltationem* (“exaltation”) for *altitudinem* (“height”).]

Destruction follows pride, and exaltation follows humility.

“And you shall know that I am the Lord when I do good to you.” We know the Lord and Savior more fully when he did good to us, suffered for our sins, bore our iniquities, and grieved on our behalf—not because of any merit in those who are saved, but for the sake of his name. Otherwise our ways and our most wicked crimes deserved not mercy but punishment.

Whatever we have said about the people of Israel, who, after being freed from Egypt, committed many sins in the wilderness and offended God, and afterward, having been brought into the promised land, worshipped idols and served wood and stone, but were later preserved by God’s mercy—let us apply to those who were freed from the Egypt of this age by the Lord’s exalted hand and brought into the wilderness of vices, who again longed for Egypt and did things for which they ought to have been punished, but nevertheless were preserved through repentance, not by their own merit but by the Lord’s mercy.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0199]

### 239–240

Long ago we read, when we were children: “Nothing is so easy that it does not become difficult when you do it unwillingly.”

[Note: [Col. 0199D] In the Archinteus manuscript we read *Olim*, without the word *pueri*.]

I confess that I promised the explanations of Ezekiel long ago, but because of the occupations caused by people coming here from the whole world, I cannot fulfill my promise. There is no hour, no moment, in which we are not confronted by crowds of brothers, and we exchange the solitude of the monastery for the continual arrival of guests—so much so that either we must close the door, or abandon the study of the Scriptures through which the doors are to be opened.

Therefore, during the profitable—or rather stolen—hours of the night, which have begun to grow longer as winter approaches, we try to dictate these words, whatever they may be, by the light of a little lamp, and to relieve the weariness of an overheated mind through interpretation.

We do not boast of receiving the brothers, as some perhaps suspect; we simply acknowledge the causes of our delays, especially since the flight of the Westerners and the congestion of the holy places, filled with needy people suffering from nakedness and wounds, display the rage of the barbarians.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] Previously this was enclosed in parentheses: “whom,” etc.]

We cannot see this without tears and groaning: that former power and that ignorance of riches have fallen into such great poverty that they need shelter, food, and clothing.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] All our manuscript codices read this way. Erasmus retains *ignorantiam divitiarum* in the text, while adding *arrogantiam* in the margin. This is a false and uninformed conjecture. Jerome calls it “ignorance of riches” in order to show the magnitude of the wealth of the Romans, because they were unaware of the treasures and possessions belonging to their own masters. Martianaeus. The Florentine manuscript likewise prefers *ignorationem*, according to Victorius.]

[Note: [Col. 0200D] It is clear that “ignorance of riches” is used because the riches were so numerous and so great that their magnitude was unknown even to their own owners. Previously the reading was *ignorantiam*, for which Erasmus preferred *arrogantiam*.]

And yet the hard and cruel hearts of certain people are not softened, while they search through the rags and little bundles of these sufferers for gold during their captivity.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] He is referring to Heraclianus, count of Africa, who, after Alaric’s capture of Rome, brutally persecuted Romans who had escaped to him from the swords of the barbarians, driven by infamous greed, so that he might seize from the wretched whatever small possessions they had carried away in their flight. See Letter 130 to Demetrias, section 7, where he magnifies and condemns that man’s greed and cruelty.]

Another difficulty in dictating this work is that, with our eyes dimmed by old age and suffering something like blessed Isaac endured (Gen. 27), we are utterly unable, by the light of night, to reread the volumes of the Hebrews; even in the brightness of the sun and day, the smallness of their letters blinds us.

We know the commentaries of the Greeks only through the voice of the brothers. And there can be no doubt that food ground by another person’s teeth causes nausea to those who eat it.

Therefore I beg you, daughter Eustochium, to begin revising these things that we are hammering out with the stylus of secretaries and for whose correction we scarcely have time—that is, to begin the seventh book. As I have already said, if the books are unequal in their shortness or length, attribute this to the brevity or length of the visions, or rather of the ὑποθέσεις [outlines, subjects], since we do not wish to separate things that belong together or compress discordant matters into a single heap.

(Verses 45 and following.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, set your face toward the way of the South, drip words against the South, and prophesy against the forest of the southern country. And you shall say to the southern forest: Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall kindle a fire against you, and it shall consume in you every green tree and every dry tree. The flame of the burning shall not be extinguished, and every face from South to North shall be burned by it. And all flesh shall see that I, the Lord, have kindled it, and it shall not be extinguished.” And I said: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! They say of me: ‘Surely this man speaks in parables?’”

The Septuagint: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face firmly toward Theman, look toward Darom, prophesy against the forest, the leader of Mageb, and say to the forest of Nageb: Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall kindle a fire against you, and it shall devour in you every green tree and every dry tree. The kindled flame shall not be extinguished, and every face from South to North shall burn in it. And all flesh shall know that I, the Lord, have kindled it; it shall not be extinguished.” And I said: “By no means, Lord, Lord!” They say to me: “Is this not a parable that is being spoken?”

Above we have fully explained what is meant by “set your face” or “set your face firmly.” For firmness of countenance and hardness of forehead are required, so that the Prophet may speak fearlessly what is commanded, especially when grievous things have been announced against the whole multitude of the people. Theman, Darom, and Nageb—and again Nageb, which the Septuagint translated as “eastern” (ἀπηλιώτην)—what these words mean in Hebrew has been expressed in our translation. And where they said “the leader of Nageb,” the Hebrew more correctly has “of the southern country” or “region.” For it is not SARE (), as the Septuagint supposed—a word meaning “leader” and “prince”—but SADE that is written, which properly signifies “field” or “region.” Because of the similarity of the letters DALETH and RES, the error became established.

The divine word speaks metaphorically of a forest against Jerusalem, which is the dwelling place of beasts and savage men: it says that it will set it on fire [another reading: “him”] and that all its trees will be consumed. It does not call them trees lacking fruit, but “wood,” as though prepared for burning. First it burns the green wood, according to what we read in this same Prophet: “Begin with my sanctuary”; and afterward the dry wood, which could contain nothing living within itself: that is, both the holy and the sinners, so that some may escape the evils of captivity through death, while others may be handed over to eternal punishments.

And where it says, “From the South to the North,” this indicates from Jerusalem to Babylon, so that the entire journey of those going into captivity, falling by sword, famine, and pestilence, may be completed. For those who are in Babylon, Jerusalem lies to the South; just as, conversely, the pot in Jeremiah, which signifies Jerusalem, is kindled from the face of the North, that is, from Babylon (Jer. I). And beautifully at the beginning he says, “Drip words against the South,” so that God’s entire anger may not seem to have been poured out, but only a kind of drop and portion. But if such a great savagery is contained in a drop, what must be expected in the full rains? Thus all flesh that will see the salvation of God may recognize, through the forest’s burning and the flame that no help can extinguish, that he himself is the Lord.

Understanding this, the Prophet replied: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God!”—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “By no means, Lord, Lord!” And he adds: “And they themselves say to me: ‘Surely this man speaks in parables?’” Or: “Is this a parable that is being spoken?” The sense is: “Speak more plainly; we do not understand from your parable what you are saying. Reveal the meaning of God’s words to us in direct speech.”

In the tropological sense, Theman, Nageb, and Darom may be understood as Egypt.

[Note: Rabanus inserts what the Septuagint have set down.] For we frequently read in Daniel that “the South” signifies Egypt (Dan. XI), while Egypt refers to the afflictions of this present world. Ezekiel therefore prophesies what evils are to come upon the world, which he calls a forest lacking fruit-bearing trees but serving as a dwelling place for beasts. Of this it is also said in the twenty-eighth Psalm: “The voice of the Lord makes the deer give birth, and he will uncover the dense forests” (verse 9). These are the forests and woodland places that consumed more of Absalom’s army in battle than the sword killed (II Sam. XVIII).

In the forests the green wood is first set on fire, and then the dry: those who live in evil, and those who are dead to righteousness. And where it says, “Every face shall be burned in it from South to North,” this means: from those who seemed to burn with fervent spirit to those who, as iniquity increased and the love of many grew cold, lost their former warmth, so that all flesh might perceive that the Lord’s flame is not extinguished.

The Prophet prays that what the Lord threatened may not happen: that is, that the forest may not be set on fire and all the wood consumed; that they may either still be granted a place for repentance, or that he may not be forced to announce grievous things—especially since the people do not understand them and, through the obscurity of the words, are provoked still more toward madness.

(Cap. XXI.—Verses 1 and following.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, drip words against the sanctuaries, prophesy against the land of Israel, and say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I shall draw my sword from its sheath, and cut off from you the righteous and the wicked. But because I have cut off from you the righteous and the wicked, therefore my sword shall go out from its sheath against all flesh, from South to North. And all flesh shall know [the Vulgate: ‘so that you may know’] that I, the Lord, have drawn my sword [some copies omit ‘my’] from its sheath; it shall not return.”

The Septuagint: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Therefore prophesy, son of man, set your face firmly against Jerusalem, look toward their holy places, prophesy against the land of Israel, and say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I shall draw my sword from its sheath, and destroy from you the lawless and the unjust. Thus my sword shall go out from its sheath against all flesh, from the South to the North, and all flesh shall know that I, the Lord, have drawn my sword from its sheath; it shall not return again.”

Because above he had said, “They say of me, ‘Surely this man speaks in parables?’” and the people were demanding a clear statement, therefore what the Lord had spoken metaphorically—or, as others translated it, as a proverb—he now expresses more plainly: that the forest of Nageb, Darom, and Theman is Jerusalem, its temple, the Holy of Holies, and the entire land of Judea; and that the flame which will burn the forest signifies the devouring sword drawn from its sheath in order to kill the righteous and the wicked. For this is the green wood and the dry wood.

Hence the Lord also says: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will they do in the dry?” (Luke XXIII, 31). Instead of this, the Septuagint—whether for some reason of their own or otherwise—translated “the lawless and the unjust,” as though the two expressions did not signify the same thing.

And where he had said, “All flesh shall see that I, the Lord, have kindled it,” meaning the forest or flame, “and it shall not be extinguished,” here he speaks in other words: “So that all flesh may know that I, the Lord, have drawn my sword from its sheath; it shall not be recalled.” Truly, against Jerusalem the flame was not quieted, the fire was not extinguished, and the sword was not recalled, because after a short interval Jerusalem and its temple were burned by the Babylonian fire.

(Verses 6–7.) “And you, son of man, groan with breaking of your loins, and groan in bitterness before them. And when they say to you, ‘Why are you groaning?’ you shall say: ‘Because of the report, for it has come; every heart shall languish, all hands shall be weakened, every spirit shall faint, and water shall flow down through all knees. Behold, it has come, and it shall happen,’ says the Lord” [the Vulgate adds “God”].

The Septuagint: “And you, son of man, groan with the breaking of your loins, and moan in pain before them. And if they say to you, ‘Why are you groaning?’ you shall say: ‘Because of the message, for it has come; every heart shall be seized by fear, all hands shall be loosened, every flesh and every spirit shall lose breath, and all thighs shall be stained with moisture. Behold, it has come and shall be,’ says the Lord God.”

First he had said: “Prophesy,” or “Drip words against the South, the South, and the Meridional region, and against the southern forest.” Because this seemed obscure, and the people did not understand the Prophet’s words, it is stated a second time more plainly that the southern forest is Jerusalem, and that all the fruitless trees at whose roots the axe has been laid (Matt. III; Luke III) signify its inhabitants; and that the sword is to be interpreted as the fire.

Third, the Prophet is commanded, while they remain silent and do not ask why he has prophesied these things, to perform actions by which they will be led to question him, and to answer with what the Lord has spoken. “Groan,” he says; “wail”—not with a light voice or restrained grief, but with the breaking of your loins, so that your groaning may come forth from your inmost organs and from the bitterness of your soul.

You shall do this before them, so that when they ask why you are crushed by such great groaning, and what evil has happened to you that you lament in this way, you may answer them in my words: “For this reason I weep, and I cannot conceal the pain of my heart, because the report that has always sounded in my ears is being fulfilled in action and has arrived”—namely, the approach of the raging Babylonian army.

When it comes and surrounds Jerusalem, then every heart shall languish and all hands shall be weakened, so that, when the minds of men are seized by fear, no one will dare to resist. The spirit of all the warriors will fail, and such trembling and terror will seize everyone that, compelled by fear, their limbs and internal organs will relax, and the bladder will be unable to retain its fluid, so that urine will stain the knees.

It is natural for the bladder to relax under the compulsion of fear, and for fluid to flow against a person’s will. This also occurs in severe illnesses, so that after the strength of the sick has failed, not only their knees but even their beds are stained.

“Behold,” he says, “it has come”—what I have often foretold—and what not I but the Lord has spoken is being fulfilled and will happen.

I know someone who, in connection with the breaking of the loins and the flowing of waters, rehearsed many testimonies, so that the chastity of the Prophet might be fulfilled, and so that the bitterness of the soul and the inward pain of the mind might be understood as referring to waters of emission staining the knees. But this interpretation does not pertain to the present passage.

(Verses 8 and following.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God: Speak: A sword, a sword is sharpened and polished, sharpened to slaughter victims and polished so that it may shine. You who move the scepter of my son, you have cut down every tree. And I gave it to be polished, so that it might be held in the hand. This is the sharpened sword; this is the polished sword, so that it may be in the hand of the slayer.

Cry out and howl, son of man, because this has come upon my people; this has come upon all the leaders of Israel. Those who had fled were delivered to the sword together with my people. Therefore strike your thigh, because it has been tested—and this when it has overthrown the scepter, and it shall no longer be, says the Lord God.

You, therefore, son of man, prophesy, and strike hand against hand, and let the sword of those who are slain be doubled and tripled. This is the sword of the great slaughter, which makes them stunned, makes their hearts languish, and multiplies ruins. At all their gates I have given the confusion of a sharp sword, polished to shine, equipped for slaughter. Sharpen yourself; go to the right or to the left, wherever the desire of your face directs you. Indeed, I myself shall strike hand against hand and shall fill my indignation. I, the Lord, have spoken.”

It would be excessive to set out both editions, and the length of the books would be increased, especially where there is either no difference or only a small one. I shall therefore set down some passages that differ.

Where we said, “You who move the scepter of my son, you have cut down every tree,” they translated: “Kill, despise, drive away every tree.”

Again, where we said, “Those who had fled were delivered to the sword,” they and others translated: “My guests,” or “inhabitants.”

Where we said, “Strike your thigh,” they wrote: “Strike with your hand.”

Where we translated, “And this when it has overthrown the scepter,” their edition has: “The tribe has been rejected.”

He speaks to the sword of Nebuchadnezzar, ordering it to come against Jerusalem, to be sharpened and polished, since many are to be slaughtered; and he addresses the sword itself directly. “You are the one who moves and overturns the scepter of my son”—that is, the rule of the people of Israel—“and you cut down every tree,” the entire multitude of the people.

“I gave,” he says, “this sword so that it might be held in the hand of Nebuchadnezzar and be in the hand of the mightiest man.” Therefore, O Prophet, cry out and howl, and testify by the lamentation of your voice to the evils that are pressing upon you.

This sword spared no one and left no one untouched by the impending evils. It came upon the people, it came upon the leaders of Israel, it came upon my guests and priests who lived in my temple. Therefore strike your thigh—or your hand—and assume the posture of one who mourns.

For this sword was tested by me, and this occurred when it overthrew my scepter and kingdom, which shall exist no longer and shall end with King Zedekiah.

Again I command you, O Prophet, that you who struck your thigh because of astonishment and wonder should strike your hands, so that the sword may come not only once but a second and a third time to kill.

First Nebuchadnezzar had come when he carried away Jeconiah; second, when Jehoiakim was reigning; third, when Zedekiah was reigning. This is the tripled sword, when the great slaughter took place and it multiplied ruins so greatly that they were stunned in mind, their hearts languished, and it brought confusion to all their gates.

He is therefore commanded—that is, the sharp sword, polished to shine, equipped and prepared for slaughter—to go either to the right or, if it wishes, to the left. “Wherever,” he says, “the desire of your face pleases you, enter boldly, with me as your guide and helper. I shall strike hand against hand, so that, as your patron and encourager, I may urge you on while you rage against my adversaries. Do not hesitate, do not fear, and do not be afraid to suffer what Sennacherib suffered. I, the Lord, have spoken. You are the minister of my will; fulfill my sentence” (IV Kings XIX).

According to the anagogical interpretation, we may understand the sharp sword prepared for slaughter as the devil, concerning whom the Apostle says: “To deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (I Cor. V, 5). And elsewhere: “Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I delivered to Satan, so that they might learn not to blaspheme” (I Tim. I, 20). And it is written in the Psalms: “He sent upon them fury, anger, and distress, a mission through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 49).

Some think that this was the sword in the hand of the angel when Jerusalem was struck under David (II Sam. XXIV). Others also suspect that the saying refers to that sword of which it is written in the Gospel: “I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. X, 34), and to dividing among themselves every affection of kinship, so that the wicked may fall and the holy rise again.

But it is impious to believe this about the Savior’s sword, rather than about the devil, who overturns the Lord’s scepters in the Church, who kills all among the people—leaders and guests of God alike—and who is then approved by the Lord when he has overthrown Judas the betrayer and those like him (John XIII). After Judas had eaten the morsel, Satan entered into him.

And the sword of those who are slain is doubled and tripled, so that Jerusalem’s sin may be paid for, because it received double punishment for its sins from the hand of the Lord. But the Lord rejoices and exults, and is the sword’s encourager, so that it may go either to the right or to the left, wherever the desire of its face carries it, so that, once the wicked have been slain, the good may remain, and what is written may be fulfilled: “What has straw in common with grain?” says the Lord (Jer. XXIII, 32).

(Verses 18 and following.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “And you, son of man, set before yourself two ways, so that the sword of the king of Babylon may come. From one land they shall both go out [the Vulgate: ‘both ways’], and by hand he shall cast a lot; at the head of the road he shall cast it for the city.

You shall establish the way for the sword to come to Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, and to Judah, and to Jerusalem [the Vulgate: ‘in Jerusalem’], the most strongly fortified city. For the king of Babylon stood at the fork of the road, at the head of the two ways, seeking divination and mixing arrows. He consulted idols; he examined entrails.

At his right hand the divination was made concerning Jerusalem: to set up battering rams, to open his mouth for slaughter, to raise his voice in a howl, to set battering rams against the gates, to heap up a rampart, and to build fortifications.

It will be like consulting an oracle in vain in their eyes, and like imitating the Sabbath rest; but he himself will remember iniquity in order to capture them.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have recalled your iniquities [the Vulgate: ‘remembered your iniquity’], and have exposed your transgressions, and your sins have appeared in all your thoughts—because, I say, you have recalled them [the Vulgate: ‘remembered them’], you shall be seized by the hand.”

I know that in this passage, according to the Septuagint interpreters, I once read a lengthy exposition by someone who referred Rabbah of the sons of Ammon to the people of the nations, but Judah and Jerusalem to those who gather under Christ’s name and, by their deeds, give dignity to that name. He understood the king of confusion—the devil—to stand at the head of every road and lie in ambush secretly, so that the verse might be fulfilled: “Beside the path they placed a stumbling block for me” (Ps. CXXXIX).

He understood him to stand at the fork, either desiring to hold those who belong to him or seeking to acquire a new service for himself [Note: With the help of three manuscripts, Victorius emended this. Previously it read tenere, a reading also followed by Martianaeus.]; always going to the right, that is, toward those placed on the right, to attack them, rejoice in slaughter, and capture wretched Jerusalem through battering rams and the accumulation of earthly works. At first, indeed, he appears to be doing nothing and striving in vain. But when he recalls the iniquities of those who dwell in the Church—or rather, who by evil works bring hostile powers to remember their former crimes—all the sins and thoughts of the people are exposed. For this reason they are captured: because they have heaped old offenses upon new ones.

Let another give this interpretation; we must pursue the truth of the history we have begun.

When, he says, the divine word had said to me, “Prophesy, son of man, and speak to the sword and say: ‘Sword, sword,’” and the rest contained in the prophecy of the sword, a second time the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Do you wish, son of man, to know what this sword is, and to learn more clearly the person of the raging sword? Listen to what I say.

Set up two ways, so that by them the sword of the king of Babylon may come. It will indeed leave by one road from the land of the Chaldeans, but when it comes through the desert and wilderness to the fork of the land of Arabia called the land of the sons of Ammon—one of whose roads leads to Jerusalem on the right, while the left leads to Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, a metropolitan city now called Philadelphia—he will remember the slaughter that befell the king of Assyria, when one hundred eighty-five thousand were killed in a single night. He will fear turning to the right and going against strongly fortified Jerusalem.

Instead, he will stand at the crossroads itself and consult an oracle according to the custom of his nation: he will put his arrows into the quiver and mix them, inscribed or marked with the names of individuals, to see whose arrow comes out and which city he ought to attack first. The Greeks call this arrow-divination (βελομαντεία), or rod-divination (ῥαβδομαντεία).”

Therefore he consulted idols and examined entrails. His divination was made at the right hand, so that he might proceed against Jerusalem and attack it, carry up ramparts, set up battering rams, build fortifications, surround the city, open his mouth for slaughter, and stir up the roar of an exultant and howling army.

“By doing this,” he says, “he will seem to the inhabitants of Jerusalem to be consulting an oracle in vain and, as it were, wasting the Sabbath rest”—that is, playing and accomplishing no work. But the king of Babylon will rely not on his own strength but on the iniquity of the people, knowing that they have offended God and heaped [another reading: “to heap”] the sins of their fathers upon new offenses, and that their transgressions have become evident to all. Therefore he will not doubt victory, because he will trust in Jerusalem’s iniquity.

This follows the Hebrew, from which the Septuagint differs in many places not so much in sense as in wording.

(Verses 25 and following.) “But you, profane and wicked leader of Israel, whose day has come at the appointed time of iniquity. Thus says the Lord God: Remove the turban; take away the crown. Is this not what exalted the humble and humbled the exalted? Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity—I shall make it so; and this shall not happen [Note: From the Vulgate edition Victorius restored ‘it happened.’ In the Hebrew and Greek likewise, ‘it did not happen.’] until he comes whose judgment it is, and I shall give it to him.”

The Septuagint: “And you, profane and wicked leader of Israel, whose day has come, at the end of the time of iniquity. Thus says the Lord God: You removed the turban and placed the crown. This shall not be the same. You humbled the exalted and raised up the humble. Iniquity, iniquity—I shall make it so; nor shall this remain as it is until he comes to whom it is due, and I shall give it to him.”

Symmachus interpreted this passage as follows: “But you, profane and wicked leader of Israel, whose day has come at the appointed time of iniquity. Thus says the Lord God: He removed the turban and took away the crown; neither this nor that. He shall raise up the humble and humble the exalted. Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity—I shall make it. And this was not he whose judgment it is, whom I shall give.”

After the overthrow of Jerusalem and the captivity of the people, the word is directed to the leader of Israel, whom no one doubts to be Zedekiah, in whom the rule of the kings of Israel from the line of David came to an end.

“Your day has come,” he says, a day long ago appointed for you; and because of you the priesthood and kingdom of the Jewish people have perished. For the turban is the insignia of the high priest; the crown, that is, the diadem, is the sign of the king.

Is this not the turban and the crown that exercised no judgment, but, imitating the king of Babylon, exalted whom it wished and humbled whom it wished? Therefore, not once, and not twice as in the Septuagint, but a third time, I shall place iniquity upon you forever—an iniquity not immediately reckoned against you, but until Christ comes, whose judgment it is, and the Father gives him the kingdom and priesthood, or the Church gathered from the nations.

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22). And elsewhere: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXI, 1). He is the one for whom the rule has been reserved, and the everlasting priesthood, of whom Jacob also spoke: “The prince shall not fail from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes for whom it has been reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

Where we translated, “Is this not what it is?”, Symmachus rendered it beautifully: “Neither this nor that.” Because he had said, “Remove the turban; take away the crown,” he added, “Neither this nor that”—that is, both kingdom and priesthood shall cease.

Hence those who afterward, until Christ’s coming, were simultaneously kings and priests—one of whom, Hyrcanus the high priest, placed a diadem upon his head—vainly attempted to claim both this and that for themselves, since the kingdom was not owed to him after Zedekiah, but to the one for whom it had been reserved and who was the expectation of the nations.

Malachi also speaks of them: “You priests who pollute my name” (Mal. I, 6). And shortly afterward: “I have no pleasure in you, nor will I accept an offering from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place an offering is sacrificed and presented to my name, a pure offering.”

This pure offering, without the blood of goats, rams, and bulls (Ps. XLIX), is fulfilled at Christ’s coming, when he came who was desired by the nations, and the sun of righteousness rose, in whose wings there is healing (Hag. II).

[Col. 0208A] (Verses 28 and following.) “And you, son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God concerning the sons of Ammon and concerning their reproach. And you shall say: Sword, sword, draw yourself from your sheath to slaughter; polish yourself so that you may kill and shine.

While vain visions were seen for you and lies were divined for you, you were to be placed upon the necks of the wounded wicked, whose day has come at the appointed time of iniquity. Return to your sheath, to the place in which you were created; in the land of your birth I shall judge you.

And I shall pour out my indignation upon you; in the fire of my wrath I shall blow upon you. And I shall deliver you into the hands of foolish men and craftsmen of corruption [the Vulgate: ‘destruction’]. You shall be food for fire; your blood shall be in the midst of the land. You shall be handed over to oblivion, because I, the Lord, have spoken.”

We have read above that the sword of the king of Babylon stood at the head of the two roads, at the crossroads of the right and left, one of which led to Jerusalem and the other to Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, and that the lot went out so that he would proceed first against Jerusalem.

Once Jerusalem had been attacked and captured, he foretells that its kingdom and priesthood had also perished forever. What remained was for the sons of Ammon, and the order of the division itself demanded that we learn what had happened to the left-hand road.

Therefore the Prophet is commanded to speak to the sons of Ammon and concerning their reproach: they too are to be captured. He directs his speech to the same sword: “O sword, sword, you who are prepared for slaughter, polished so that you may shine and kill! Although the idols may have answered you, and everything answered by demons is vain—so that you might threaten the necks of the wounded and what the Lord had long threatened might be fulfilled—nevertheless, once you have completed your work, what you carried out against the sons of Ammon, return to your sheath, that is, to Babylon, to the place where you were made and created.

Thus I may judge you in the land of your birth, pour out my indignation upon you, and cause you to be captured by the power of the Medes and Persians.”

This is stated more fully in the book of Isaiah, in the vision against Babylon: “Behold, I shall stir up the Medes against them.” And shortly afterward: “And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; it shall not be inhabited forever” (Isa. XIII, 17 and following).

And because he had once spoken under the figure of the sword about the king—or rather, the kingdom—of Babylon, he preserves the metaphor (μεταφοράν). “In the fire,” he says, “of my wrath I shall blow upon you,” so that I may cause you to be consumed by fire and deliver you into the hands of foolish and unskilled men who have no art of forging swords or sharpening them. Thus you shall no longer be sharpened, polished, and made to shine for slaughter; instead, you shall be food for fire, and your blood, which you shed while all looked on, shall rather recoil upon you.

You shall be handed over to eternal oblivion and perish forever, because I, the Lord, have spoken; and for the one whose word is deed, to speak is to accomplish.

## Chapter XXII

### Verses 1 ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“And you, son of man, will you not judge the city of bloodshed [the Vulgate has ‘will you not judge’ twice]—and declare to her all her abominations? And you shall say: Thus says the Lord God:

‘City that sheds blood in her midst, so that her time may come, and that has made idols against herself, so that she might be defiled: in your blood which has been shed by you, you have sinned; and by your idols which you made, you have been defiled. You have brought your days near and brought on the time of your years. Therefore I have given you as a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all lands. Those near you and those far from you shall triumph over you—or mock you—filthy, illustrious, great in destruction.

Behold, the princes of Israel, each relying on his own arm, were in you to shed blood. They dishonored father and mother in you—or cursed father and mother. They slandered the resident alien in your midst. They grieved—or oppressed—the orphan and widow among you. You despised my sanctuaries [the Vulgate: “you despised and polluted”]; you polluted my Sabbaths.

There were slanderers—or robbers—in you, intent on shedding blood, and upon the mountains they ate in you. They committed wickedness—or, as the Hebrew more significantly has it, *zemmāh* (זִמָּה), that is, incest—in your midst. They uncovered their father’s nakedness in you; they humbled the uncleanness of a menstruating woman in you; each man committed an abomination with his neighbor’s wife; and the father-in-law polluted his daughter-in-law disgracefully. A brother violated—or humbled—his sister, his father’s daughter, in you.

They accepted gifts among you in order to shed blood. You accepted interest and increase, and you slandered your neighbors greedily—or, “I will complete the consummation of your wickedness in your oppression.” And you forgot me, declares the Lord God.

Behold, I have clapped my hands over your greed which you practiced, and over the blood which was shed in your midst. Will your heart endure, or will your hands prevail, in the days which I shall bring upon you? I, the Lord, have spoken, and I will act.

I will destroy you among the nations and scatter you among the lands [Note: Victorius says that ‘I will scatter’ is the correct reading, not ‘I will destroy’; Jerome accordingly repeats it in the explanation below on the force of the Hebrew verb. In Greek: διασκορπιῶ σε, ‘I will scatter you’]; I will cause your uncleanness to depart from you, and I will possess you in the sight of the nations—or, according to Aquila’s first edition and Theodotion, ‘I will defile you’; or, according to Symmachus, ‘I will wound you in the sight of the nations.’ And you shall know that I am the Lord.’”

And you, he says, son of man—for I shall use the customary address to you—judge the city of bloodshed and declare to her all her abominations, so that she may know that she deservedly suffers the captivity which threatens her and that, through many bloodshed, she has brought about the time of her own ruin.

First of all crimes, you worshiped idols in place of God; you adored the works of your hands and brought near the time of your years—that is, the time which had long been foretold and delayed, so that you might do penance. But according to your impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath (Rom. II).

Therefore I have given you as a reproach to the nations and as a mockery to all the lands around you, both near and far. They shall triumph over you, or mock you:

“Filthy, illustrious, great in destruction.”

Filthy, because you ceased to be clean. Illustrious in evil, since formerly you surpassed all cities in distinction for good. Great in destruction: the higher you were, the more forcefully you would fall.

Meanwhile, leaving the rest aside, I shall enumerate a few of the things that have occurred in you. Your princes, judging not by justice but by the strength of power and the arm, shed innocent blood in you. Some dishonored their father and mother, or cursed their parents, as Scripture says: “Whoever curses his father and mother shall surely be put to death” (Exod. XXI, 17).

They oppressed the resident alien and sojourner in your midst, as though the sojourning and exile from their homeland were not sufficient for every kind of hardship. They grieved—or oppressed—the orphan and widow among you, so that those whose entire possession is in the justice of the laws might not merely be grieved but oppressed by you.

You despised my sanctuaries, or holy places, and polluted my Sabbaths, so that you did not distinguish between the holy and the polluted, between the day decreed for religion and the Sabbath rest devoted to the worship of God, and the other days on which the Law permits one to work and serve the necessities of the flesh.

There were slanderers—or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, deceitful men—in you. In Hebrew this is called *rākîl* (רָכִיל). They were also murderers, so that they might blaspheme God, or else might conduct everything deceitfully or violently. “They ate upon the high mountains,” having become wise—or exalted—in pride against God; and they committed wickedness, or incest, in your midst. What is rarely done even in corners and secrecy, because evil men avoid the awareness of others, you did openly.

What incest means, the following statement indicates: they uncovered their father’s nakedness in you, having joined themselves to their stepmother against right and law; and they humbled the uncleanness of a menstruating woman in you, neither sparing nature nor granting any respite to shame; and they neighed after the wife of their neighbor.

And what is more criminal, the father-in-law burned with desire for his daughter-in-law, and the brother did not recognize the rights of a sister, so that he violated not a uterine sister but a sister by the same father.

They accepted gifts in order to shed innocent blood. They turned the needs of the poor into profit, accepting interest and increase; and through greed they slandered their friends.

“But this,” he says, “you did, O Jerusalem, because you forgot me.” For remembrance of God excludes every form of wickedness. Therefore I assumed the posture of an angry Lord and clapped my hands against your greed and against the blood that was shed in your midst, so that you might understand and recognize in your mind whether you could endure my anger either in spirit or by your hands.

For I am the Lord who has spoken, and I will act. And after you have been captured, Jerusalem, I will scatter you among the nations and disperse you into the air like useless straw to be carried here and there. I am so merciful that my severity is turned into mercy. I shall do everything so that your uncleanness may depart from you and you may recover your former purity.

When you have recovered it, I shall possess you in the sight of all the nations, so that, once you have been possessed by me, you may understand that I myself am the Lord.

But if we follow the interpretation of Symmachus and Theodotion—one of whom says, “I will wound you,” or “I will pierce you,” and the other, “I will defile you in the sight of the nations”—everything must be referred to the negative sense, although the statement made above is contrary to this interpretation: “I will cause your uncleanness to depart from you.” For the departure of uncleanness is the restoration of purity. I have discussed both editions equally, so as to avoid excessive length in the books.

### Verses 17 ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, the house of Israel has become dross to me. All these are bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace; they have become the dross of silver.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have all become dross, behold, I shall gather you in the midst of Jerusalem, in the gathering of silver, bronze, iron, tin, and lead, into the midst of the furnace, in order to kindle a fire in it for melting.

So I shall gather you in my fury and in my anger; I shall rest and melt you [Note: Victorius inserts, ‘and I will gather you,’ from the Vulgate, Hebrew, and Greek texts], and I shall kindle you in the fire of my fury, and you shall be melted in its midst, as silver is melted in the midst of the furnace. So you shall be in its midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have poured out my indignation upon you” [the Vulgate adds: “when”].

The Hebrew word is *SIG* [the Hebrew characters are not legible in the supplied text; Note: a Masoretic note says that *Sig* should be restored in modern Hebrew exemplars, whose printed reading is likewise not legible here]. Symmachus translated it as “dross”; Aquila’s first edition has *stémphylon* (στέμφυλον) and *gígarton* (γίγαρτον), both of which signify a grape seed or grape refuse. His second translation, and the Septuagint, rendered it “mixture.”

Now *dross* means the dirt and refuse of metals, so that, with the captivity near—or rather already threatening—the city’s destruction, fire is applied. Under the image of melting, the pure silver remains, which had been mixed with and corrupted by bronze, tin, iron, and lead. Three of these—bronze, tin, and lead—are materials that can be cast and are dissolved by fire. Iron, however, becomes soft and thin between an anvil and hammer and receives various forms according to the craftsman’s will.

Therefore, just as silver corrupted by the metals mentioned above is put into a furnace so that, once the dirt and adulterating materials have been removed, it may remain pure, so, he says, I shall gather you in the midst of Jerusalem and surround you with the Babylonian siege, so that I may kindle in you a fire for melting.

What the immense heat of flames accomplishes there, hunger and pestilence will accomplish here. After I have gathered you and kindled you in the fire of my fury, then I shall rest and restrain the pain of contempt through vengeance upon your punishments.

I shall do all this so that, after I have poured out my indignation upon you, the end of your torment may be knowledge of me, and you may know that I am the Lord, judge of all and giver of recompense.

That God is called a smelter we read in many other places, but especially in Malachi and Isaiah. One of them says:

“Behold, the Lord comes like a smelting fire and like the herb of those who wash, and he shall sit melting” [Victor supplies from the Greek text: “melting and cleansing like silver and gold, and he shall cleanse the sons of Levi”] “like gold and silver, and he shall melt the sons of Levi” (Mal. III, 1, 3).

The other says:

“And the Lord shall wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and shall cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning” (Isa. IV, 4).

And I think that this is what is expressed in the Psalms:

“Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. XXV, 2).

After this comes:

“Burn my kidneys and my heart,”

so that all the offenses of the loins, the phlegm of harmful bodily fluid within me, and the covering that has been placed there may be dried up.

What we have understood concerning Jerusalem, let us understand concerning the condition of souls, which were created pure by God. They received gold in understanding and wisdom, and silver in speech and eloquence, so that what they conceived in the mind they might express in words.

Concerning silver we read:

“The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI, 5).

Similarly, the sixty-seventh Psalm contains a passage concerning gold and silver, in which it is written:

“If you sleep among the middle parts of the inheritance, the wings of a dove covered with silver, and the hinder parts—or inner parts—of its back in the green or pale color of gold” (Ps. LXVII, 14).

“For all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV, 14), and she says in the Song of Songs:

“The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs I, 3).

Whoever sleeps and rests between the two Testaments immediately takes up silver-covered dove’s wings, and gold will shine with radiance in the treasure-house of his heart.

I think that the following too should be referred to this meaning: for sinners and those who have deserved God’s offense, heaven is bronze and the earth iron; especially the land of Egypt, from which the Lord brings Israel out as from an iron furnace.

In Zechariah also, wickedness sits upon a talent of lead (Zech. V). And in the Song of Exodus it is said:

“They sank like lead in the mighty waters” (Exod. XV, 10).

For they were weighed down by the heavy burden of sins, and could say:

“Like a heavy burden, they weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. XXXVII, 6).

And just as the likeness of bronze falsely imitates the appearance of gold, so tin simulates the whiteness of silver, which a simple and rustic person cannot easily distinguish.

It often happens that gold and silver, mixed with heretical perversity, are separated by the fire of the Holy Spirit and the judgment of the Lord, and that pure gold and silver remain. Of this the prophet says:

“I gave them silver and gold; but they made Baal from them” (Hos. II, 8).

A similar statement is:

“I brought them out with silver and gold, and there was no feeble person among their tribes” (Ps. CIV, 37).

And the end of all punishments is to know that he himself is the Lord.

We also read in Zechariah about a stone of tin, or a mass of tin (Zech. IV); what this signifies, we have interpreted in its proper place.

### Verses 23 ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, say to her:

‘You are an unclean land, and not rained upon on the day of fury. There is a conspiracy of prophets in her midst, like a roaring lion tearing prey: they have devoured souls, taken wealth and payment, and multiplied her widows in her midst.

Her priests have despised my law and polluted my sanctuaries. They have made no distinction between the holy and the profane; they have not understood the difference between the polluted and the clean; they have turned their eyes away from my Sabbaths, and I was polluted in their midst.

Her princes in her midst are like wolves tearing prey, to shed blood, to destroy souls, and greedily to pursue profits. Her prophets plastered them without tempering, seeing empty visions and divining lies for them, saying, “Thus says the Lord God,” when the Lord had not spoken.

They slandered the people of the land [the Vulgate: “the peoples” and “slander”] and violently robbed them. They afflicted the needy and the poor and oppressed the resident alien with slander, without judgment.

I sought among them a man who would interpose a wall and stand opposed before me on behalf of the land, so that I would not destroy it, but I found none.

Therefore I poured out my indignation upon them; in the fire of my wrath I consumed them. I returned their way upon their own heads,’ declares the Lord God.”

A diligent reader might ask what the dross was that corrupted the purity of silver and mixed it with bronze, lead, tin, and iron. What is expressed there under the figure of the city and the furnace is here proclaimed under the image of a land that has not been watered and has not received rain.

We should understand those rains as the ones about which it is written:

“I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. V, 6).

We await this rain when seasonal and latter rain is given to us, of which it is written:

“You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Ps. LXVII, 10).

The day of fury is the day which each person brings upon himself by the multitude of his sins.

We wish to know what the dross of the city is, and what is the squalor of the hardest earth, full of thorns and briars. “There is,” he says, “a conspiracy of prophets”—or, according to the Septuagint, “of rulers”—in her midst, having the likeness of a lion, concerning which Peter also writes:

“Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around” (I Pet. V, 8).

This lion and all his companions do not seek to devour bodies but souls; they receive payments and decide everything by money.

That this happened at that time to the Jewish people no one doubts. For on account of the priests, princes, and prophets, the Lord brought evil upon them.

But we often see this in our Jerusalem also: according to the Septuagint, they devour souls by their power and accept payment, making many widows—women who have lost the Lord as their bridegroom.

Their faction and conspiracy as prophets consists in this: they support one another and do everything for the sake of shameful profit.

The priests, who ought to be overseers of the temple and from whose mouth knowledge of the Law is sought, violate the sanctuaries and recognize no distinction between the holy and the profane except that of money.

They turn their eyes away from the Sabbaths and do not recall the rest of God, which consists in knowledge of the Scriptures. Nor do they say with the prophet:

“Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII, 18).

Nor do they heed the Apostle’s words:

“But we all, with unveiled face, contemplate the glory of the Lord” (I Cor. III, 12).

Among such prophets and priests, the Lord standing in the middle is defiled, of whom it is written:

“But there stands one in your midst whom you do not know” (John I, 26).

The prophets, or rulers, are therefore compared with lions.

The princes, whom we understand as men of lower rank, imitate the rapacity of wolves, so that they shed not the blood of bodies but of souls, and greedily pursue profits. They are by no means content with the principle that “those who serve the altar should live from the altar” (I Cor. IX, 13); after approaching the ministry of God, they gather the riches of Croesus.

Those prophets who announce future events also plastered them without tempering. We spoke above about such prophesying prophets, who plastered the wall without mixing in straw, and the wall was destroyed by the rains.

Such men see empty visions and do not so much prophesy as divine lies, saying to the wretched land:

“Thus says the Lord; the Lord promises these things,”

although the Lord had not spoken to them.

The people of the land, being not an imitator of God but an imitator of earthly works, princes, and priests, did everything through slander and power. They oppressed not the rich but the poor, concerning whom it is written:

“But the poor does not endure threats.”

And:

“A man’s own riches are the ransom of his soul” (Prov. XIII, 8).

They also oppressed the resident alien and sojourner who had not yet become a citizen of the Church but was merely a hearer and possessed only the beginnings of faith. After traversing sea and dry land, they made one proselyte and made him a son of Gehenna [Note: two manuscripts read, “so that they might make one proselyte, they might make him,” etc.].

Amid so many vices and such a multitude of crimes, I sought among them a man who could resist my anger and, like Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, oppose himself to my fire and conflagration; but I could not find one.

Hence he said to Moses:

“Let me alone, and I shall destroy this people” (Exod. XXXII, 10).

And because I could not find anyone who resisted me and held me back, therefore I poured out all my indignation upon them and consumed them—not without measure and judgment, but so that I might return their ways upon their own heads. This means either attributing to the leaders the sins they themselves had committed, or, certainly, placing them upon the heads of the people’s ruler, prince, and prophets, none of whom dared resist the Lord when he was angry. Because of them, the land became squalid and desolate and was not worthy to receive the Lord’s rain.

## Chapter XXIII

### Verses 1 ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, there were two women, daughters of one mother, and they prostituted themselves in Egypt; in their youth they prostituted themselves. There their breasts were pressed, and there the breasts of their puberty were broken [or, as the Septuagint has it, ‘there their breasts fell, and there they were deflowered’].

Their names were Oholah, the elder—or older—and Oholibah, her sister. I took them—or, ‘they became mine’—and they bore sons and daughters. Their names are: Samaria is Oholah, and Jerusalem is Oholibah.

Oholah prostituted herself against me and went mad—or departed—to her lovers, the Assyrians, who were approaching her, clothed in hyacinth-colored garments [the Vulgate: “clothed in hyacinth”], princes and magistrates, all young men of desire—or chosen men—horsemen, riders of horses.

She gave her prostitutions to all the chosen sons of Assyria, and she defiled herself with all those over whom she had gone mad, in their uncleannesses—or devices. Moreover, she did not abandon the prostitutions which she had practiced in Egypt. For they too had lain with her in her youth, and they had broken the breasts of her puberty [or, ‘they too had deflowered her’]; and they poured out their prostitution upon her.

Therefore I handed her over to the hands of her lovers, into the hands of the sons of Asshur, over whose lust she had gone mad. They uncovered her shame; they took her sons and daughters; and they killed her with the sword.

And she became famous among women—or, ‘she became a subject of women’s speech’; and they executed judgments—or acts of vengeance—upon her.”

The Scripture of Kings and Chronicles testifies that the twelve tribes of Israel, which had been united in Egypt, were afterward divided into two parts, ten tribes and two, and were called Judah and Israel.

Over Judah, from the line of David, Rehoboam, son of Solomon, reigned in Jerusalem, where the temple and the priests were located, together with a large part of the tribe of Levi.

Over the ten tribes in Samaria, Jeroboam son of Nebat [or Nabadi], from the tribe of Ephraim and Joseph, ruled. Samaria is now called Oholah, which in our language means “her tent”; Jerusalem, however, is Oholibah, that is, “my tent is in her.”

For among the ten tribes also there was a tent—not of God but of idols. To turn the people away from the worship of God, Jeroboam had placed golden calves in Dan and Bethel.

Let us therefore speak of each separately.

These two women, Samaria and Jerusalem, were daughters of one mother, born from the stock of Israel, and they prostituted themselves in Egypt in their youth. For they would not have received the Law when they were brought out of Egypt at Mount Sinai—a Law forbidding them to worship idols—unless in Egypt they had worshiped the monsters of Egypt.

The mother of both may also be the Hittite woman, of whom we read above:

“Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (above, XVI, 3).

And when it is said:

“Let each person remove the abominations of Egypt from his eyes,”

this signifies that Israel served idols in Egypt and that there her breasts fell, or were broken—that is, the breasts of her virginity.

Samaria is called the elder and older either because of the multitude of the ten tribes or because, after the death of Moses, Jesus son of Nun ruled the people from the tribe of Ephraim. Hence we also read that Jeroboam, who divided them, was from the house of David (III Kings XII).

God took them, or they became his, when they groaned over the works of Egypt, having previously served clay and brickmaking. Later they bore sons and daughters to him, either in the wilderness or in the land of promise.

Oholah—that is, Samaria—first prostituted herself against God when she went mad after the Assyrians, who were clothed in hyacinth-colored garments. They were not ordinary men from the people but leaders and magistrates, nor were they worn out by age; they were all young, chosen horsemen. She followed their idols and, contrary to God’s command, sought help from them.

They came and polluted her, so that she did not abandon whatever she had done in her youth in Egypt. For the Egyptians too had intercourse with her in her youth, and she worshiped their images. There she was deflowered and her breasts were broken; and so great was the abundance of her prostitution that they are said not merely to have prostituted themselves with her but to have poured out their prostitution upon her.

Therefore she was handed over to her lovers, Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Shalmaneser, over whose lust she had gone mad. They uncovered her shame, in a figurative or tropological sense, as though she were a prostitute (IV Kings XVII and XVIII; I Chronicles V).

The revelation of a city means captivity: they led her sons and daughters captive and slaughtered her herself with the sword, so that she was killed as an example to all women and was spoken of infamously among all.

They executed judgments and acts of vengeance upon her, leaving nothing of salvation in her. To this day the ten tribes remain captive in the mountains and cities of the Medes, to which they were transferred.

According to the allegorical sense, what Joseph, Ephraim, Samaria, Jezreel, and Israel signify, and how they are opposed to the house of David and Jerusalem, which signifies the Church, we have discussed more fully in the prophet Hosea.

Concerning these also the seventy-seventh Psalm says:

“The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. LXXVII, 9).

And again:

“He rejected the tent of Joseph and chose the tribe of Judah” (ibid., 67).

For God chose the house of confession, the Church, and rejected the tent of Joseph, whose name is interpreted as “increase.” Having abandoned the Law of God, they added golden calves to their worship and are called Oholah—that is, “tent”—not of God but of error and demons.

The elder and older sister, because of her multitude and captivity by the Assyrians, prostituted herself against God. She abandoned the truth of faith and went mad after her lovers, the leaders of the heretics, who were clothed in hyacinth-colored garments, promising her lofty and heavenly things.

They were riders, of whom it is said:

“Some trust in chariots and some in horses” (Ps. XIX, 8),

the chosen sons of Assyria, leaders, and magistrates, who promise themselves knowledge and eloquence.

She did this because she practiced in heresy the same prostitutions she had practiced in Egypt—that is, before she believed, while she still lived in the world.

She was deflowered by Assyrian men who persist in wickedness, or by avengers. For our adversary the devil is himself both enemy and avenger (I Pet. V).

They broke the breasts of Samaria and destroyed the virginity she had possessed in the Church.

Therefore she was handed over to her lovers, in accordance with the Apostle who writes:

“I handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (I Tim. I, 20).

And:

“I handed them over to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (I Cor. V, 5).

They uncovered the shame of wretched Samaria and displayed all her depravity. They led away captive her sons and daughters—those born from her, endowed with knowledge as well as simple and untrained people—and they killed her herself with a spiritual sword.

She is spoken of infamously by the whole world and becomes notorious among all the doctrines of the age, so that the shame of her may be punished as an example to all women.

### Verses 11 ff.

“When her sister Oholibah saw this, she went mad with lust more than she did, and she offered her prostitution to the sons of Assyria even more shamelessly than her sister’s prostitution: to leaders and magistrates who came to her, dressed in variegated—or costly—garments; to horsemen who rode horses; and to young men, all of outstanding appearance.

And I saw that both followed the same path of pollution, and she increased her prostitutions. When she saw men depicted on the wall, images of Chaldeans portrayed in colors, their loins girded with belts and their heads wearing dyed turbans, having the appearance—or form—of all the leaders [the Vulgate: ‘the form and likeness’], resembling all the sons of Babylon and of the land of the Chaldeans where they were born, she went mad with the desire of her eyes for them and sent messengers to them in Chaldea.

When the sons of Babylon came to her, to the bed—or lodging place—of breasts, they polluted her with their acts of prostitution. She was polluted by them, and her soul was sated—or withdrew—from them.

She exposed her prostitutions and uncovered her shame, and my soul withdrew from her as my soul had withdrawn from her sister.

For she multiplied her prostitutions, remembering the days of her youth, when she prostituted herself in the land of Egypt. She went mad with desire for their intercourse, whose flesh is like the flesh of donkeys and whose emission is like the emission of horses—or, ‘their male members were like the male members of horses.’

And you revisited the wickedness of your youth, when your breasts were pressed in Egypt and the breasts of your puberty were broken.”

According to the literal sense, the interpretation is straightforward: when Oholibah—that is, Jerusalem, in which God’s tent was—saw the wounds of her sister, she was not instructed by the example to withdraw her foot from error; instead, she increased her sister’s prostitution.

The former made idols only once and outside, in Dan and Bethel. The latter, however, repeatedly worshiped the statue of Baal in the high places and in the temple, and she prostituted herself with the Assyrians.

The idol Baal, or Bel—or, to speak more explicitly, Belus—is the religion of the Assyrians, consecrated by Ninus, son of Belus, in honor of his father.

And she offered her prostitution shamelessly to the Assyrians, to leaders and magistrates dressed in variegated and multicolored garments, to horsemen, and to young men of outstanding appearance, so that the prostitution of the two sisters became one.

Jerusalem increased her prostitutions in this respect: seeing images of the Chaldeans on the walls, she went mad with lust, and, deceived by their appearance and clothing, sent messengers to them, seeking help. They came and polluted her.

And because pleasure is not perpetual but quickly brings satiety, once polluted and sated with them she withdrew from their alliance.

Therefore I, seeing her shame and prostitutions made public to all, withdrew from her, so that she who had surpassed her sister in wickedness might also surpass her sister in the magnitude of her punishments.

She was so shameless that she committed all the errors of her youth at an already more advanced age, and she pursued the vices of Egypt in the lust of the Chaldeans.

For formerly she had gone mad with the intercourse of the Egyptians, whose flesh was like that of donkeys, and whose emission was so abundant—or whose male members were so large—that they surpassed the deformity of horses.

Nor did her youthful wickedness cease. Rather, after she had become mine, she returned to it, so that both in the wilderness and in the land of promise she might surpass her former lust [Note: Rabanus reads, “might sigh,” for “might surpass”], in which she had been deflowered, her breasts broken, and all the beauty of her virginity destroyed.

According to the tropological sense, the meaning is difficult: how does the Church surpass heretical lust, unless perhaps we can say this—that “the servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke XII, 47), and that heretics commit unspeakable things outside and perish in shipwreck outside Noah’s ark?

But if ecclesiastical people, while following the true faith, imitate the vices of Assyria and Chaldea and follow the variegated images of sinners, they deserve greater torments.

Do we not send messengers to the Chaldeans, whose name is interpreted as meaning “demons,” when we expose to them and offer to them breasts to be broken—breasts in which the dwelling place of the mind is located—and, once sated with pleasures, pass from one person to another?

Do we not desire, not so much prostitution as the number of prostitutes, and come to such madness that, after many years of service to the Lord, we return to Egypt and do the things we did in the world before we received the name of faith?

(Verses 22 ff.) Therefore, Oholibah, thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall stir up against you all your lovers, from whom your soul was satiated, and I shall gather them against you all around: the sons of Babylon and all the Chaldeans, nobles, tyrants, and princes, all the sons of Assyria, young men of outstanding beauty, commanders and magistrates, all the chief princes, and renowned riders of horses. And they shall come against you equipped with chariots and wheels, a multitude of peoples; they shall arm themselves against you on every side with breastplate, shield, and helmet. And I shall give them judgment, and they shall judge you by their judgments, and I shall place my jealousy against you, which they will exercise against you in fury. [Col. 0218D] They shall cut off your nose and your ears, and what remains they shall cut down with the sword. They themselves shall seize your sons and daughters, and your remnant shall be devoured by fire; they shall strip you of your garments and take away your vessels of glory. And they shall cause your crime and your fornication with the land of Egypt to cease from you, and you shall not raise your eyes toward them, nor remember Egypt any longer.

[Note: Again Victor reads “I shall cause,” on the basis of the Hebrew and Jerome’s Latin edition.]

[Note: Victor preferred “before them,” as it stands in the Hebrew, Greek, and Vulgate.]

**The Septuagint:** Therefore, Oholibah, thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall stir up your lovers against you, from whom your soul has withdrawn, and I shall bring them against you all around—the sons of Babylon and all the Chaldeans, Phacuth [φακοὺθ], Sue [συὲ], and Cue [κοὺθ], and with them all the sons of Assyria, young men, chosen men, commanders and magistrates, all the tristatae, and renowned riders on horses. All shall come against you from the north, chariots and wheels, with a multitude of peoples, shields and bucklers; and they shall set a guard over you all around. And I shall set judgment before their face, and they shall judge you by their judgments; and I shall set my jealousy against you, and they shall deal with you in the anger of fury. They shall remove your nose and your ears, and your survivors they shall cast down with the sword. They themselves shall take your sons and daughters, and fire shall devour your remnant; they shall strip you of your clothing and take up the vessels of your glory; they shall turn your impieties away from you, and your fornication from the land of Egypt; you shall not lift your eyes toward them, and you shall not remember Egypt any longer. For you remembered the flesh of the Egyptians and imitated the indecency of the unclean nation that venerates images of all animals together. Therefore I shall bring against you your lovers, with whose embrace you were satiated and from whose covenant you withdrew, so that the love formerly felt would be turned into such hatred. I mean the sons of Babylon and all the Chaldeans, nobles, tyrants, and princes; in Hebrew there are Phacud (פחוד), Sue (סוע), and Cue (קוע), which the peoples of the East understand as names of various nations, although names of this kind are found neither in the Book of Kings, nor in Chronicles, nor even in Jeremiah, who describes the captivity of Jerusalem, nor anywhere else in Holy Scripture. Nor is it surprising that the Septuagint retained the Hebrew names, since Symmachus and Theodotion likewise agree in the same wording.

“All,” he says, “the Assyrians, horsemen, and young men of outstanding beauty, commanders and magistrates”—or tristatae, whom we have interpreted as “chief princes.” Concerning them we also read in Exodus (Exod. XV, 4): “Chosen tristatae riders” (τριστάτας), for which the Latin simplicity translated “three-ranked statores.”

[Note: Even after Victor’s correction, Martianay retained *stratores* through error; this is not the name of an office second in rank after royal dignity, but rather of a very low office, derived from saddling a horse. Our manuscripts likewise prefer *statores*.]

Among the Greeks, however, *tristatae* is the name for the second rank after royal dignity. Concerning them it is written: “Yet he did not attain to the three first, who were commanders of cavalry, infantry, and tribute” [or “tribunes”] (I Par. XII; II Reg. XXIII). We call these magistrates of both branches of the army and prefects of the grain-supply office.

“All,” he says, “in chariots and on horses, armed with breastplate, helmet, and shield, besieged you all around; and I shall give them judgment, so that you may be judged by those whom you had left behind and whose covenant you had annulled; and they shall judge you according to their judgments, as an adulteress.” “And I shall place,” he says, “my jealousy against you, which they exercise against you in fury.” For my jealousy is among the enemies, because faith also was not kept.

“They shall cut off,” he says, “your nose and your ears,” as from an adulteress caught in adultery, so that, disfigured, you may cease to please. For just as all facial beauty consists in the grace of the nose, and in the ears from which, among women, pearls and precious stones hang, so the dignity of kings and judges, signified in the mouth and ears, shall be cut off by their sword.

“They themselves shall seize your sons and daughters.” He says “your sons” and “your daughters,” not “my sons” and “my daughters,” because they were begotten through adultery; and the rest shall be devoured by fire. “And they shall strip you,” he says, “of the garments with which I had adorned you, and of your vessels of glory,” which I had granted you for the rites of the Temple, vessels of gold and silver, concerning which it is written: “I gave them gold and silver, and they made them for Baal” (Hos. II, 8).

I shall do all these things so that, once your beauty has been destroyed and your deceitful face disfigured, your crime and the fornication that you learned and practiced in Egypt may at last cease; so that, after your nose and ears have been lost, you may no longer dare to raise your eyes toward the Chaldeans or display your ugliness to your former lovers, nor remember any longer the lust of the Egyptians, whose abundance of flesh delighted you.

All these things are spoken under the figure of an adulteress, disfigured because of adultery, so that she may no longer glory in her beauty but may blush at the ugliness she deserved because of the greatness of her pleasures. Whatever is said figuratively (τροπικῶς) about Jerusalem can also be referred to the soul, which, joined in the embrace of God through virtues, afterward committed adultery with vices, withdrew from him, and, once all its crimes had been exposed, was stripped, disgraced, and displayed to everyone, so that it might cease from its crime to some extent. Let it not glory in the dignity of its name, but, because of consciousness of evil and remembrance of Egypt, let it no longer dare to raise its eyes toward heaven.

Therefore its nose is also cut off and its ears are amputated, because it had changed the fragrance of a good odor into stench and had heard the judgment of blood. We understand this not only from smell and hearing but also from sight, of which Samson and Zedekiah were deprived because they had misused it. “The Lord made the deaf and the mute” as well (Exod. IV, 11), so that their tongue might not cross over to the earth; and every sense shall be taken away from those who have utterly lost life. These things shall happen so that all may be cleansed by fire and Egypt’s fornication may perish, and so that she may no longer be able to raise her eyes toward evil.

(Verses 28 ff.) For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall deliver you into the hands of those whom you hate, into the hands of those from whom your soul was satiated. And they shall deal with you in hatred, and they shall take away all your labors, and they shall leave you naked and full of disgrace, [Note: We supplied the second part of this verse, “and the disgrace of your fornications shall be revealed,” which was missing, from manuscripts and Rabanus. Victor had earlier supplied it, as usual, from the Hebrew, Latin, and Greek versions.] and the disgrace of your fornications shall be revealed. Your crime and your fornications have done these things to you, because you fornicated after the nations among whom you were polluted by their idols. You walked in the way of your sister; therefore I shall place her cup in your hand.

Thus says the Lord God: You shall drink the cup of your sister, deep and broad. You shall be made a laughingstock and a mockery, since it is exceedingly capacious; you shall be filled with drunkenness and grief, with the cup of mourning and sadness, the cup of your sister Samaria. You shall drink it and drain it to the dregs; you shall devour its fragments, and you shall tear your breasts [or, as the Septuagint translated: “I shall take away its festivals and new moons”], because I have spoken, says the Lord [the Vulgate adds “God”]. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have forgotten me and cast me behind your body, you too shall bear your crime and your fornications.

It is beneficial for Jerusalem to have hostility against the Assyrians and Chaldeans and no longer remember Egypt, but to be delivered into the hands of those who hated her for punishment. She is not delivered to them beforehand, unless her soul has first been satiated with them, so that, after she has repented of her former sins, she may then be cleansed by punishments and lose all the labors she acquired by the craft of prostitution. Let her see her nakedness and disgrace; and let her know that the Lord has not done all these things to her, but that her fornications have done so—those by which she fornicated with the nations listed above, in order to worship their images.

“You walked,” he says, “in the ways of your sister Samaria”; therefore you must drink her cup, whose sins you followed. The cup is often understood as punishments and torments. There are many examples, among them this one: “A cup of unmixed wine is in the hand of the Lord, full of mixture; and he inclined it from this side to that; nevertheless its dregs were not emptied: all the sinners of the earth shall drink from it” (Ps. LXXIV, 9–10). In Isaiah it is called “the cup of ruin” and “the cup of fury” (Isa. LI, 17).
