And God says to Jeremiah: “Take from my hand the cup of unmixed wine, and you shall give it to all the nations to which I send you; they shall drink, vomit, and go mad” (Jer. XXV, 15).

For just as certain purgatives are administered so that the harmful humor within bodies may be expelled, so the Lord gives a very pure cup of torments, in order to remove from sinners whatever there is of gall and bitterness and restore them to their former health. That cup shall also be deep and broad: deep because of the magnitude of the punishments, broad because of the duration of the captivity.

But when, he says, you have become drunk and been seized by grief, and have drunk the cup to the dregs and drained it so thoroughly that you even devour fragments of the cup itself, then you will become weary of your former fornication and tear the breasts that had been broken in Egypt and subdued and bruised by your lovers. Or: “I shall take away all your festivals and new moons,” so that instead of solemnity and joy you may have perpetual lamentation and sorrow.

Since, therefore, you have done these things, forgotten me, and cast me behind your body—or behind you, because of the vices of the body, or behind the genitals, by which the shamefulness of indecency is indicated—you shall therefore bear your crime and impiety, namely, the punishments that you have deserved because of your impiety and crimes.

What is said—“You shall drink to the dregs, and devour its fragments”—can aptly be understood of Jerusalem, which drank last the cup of her sister Samaria and, as it were, drained the dregs of her torments to the bottom.

(Verses 36, 37 ff.) And the Lord said to me: Son of man, will you judge Oholah and Oholibah and declare to them their crimes [or iniquities]? For they are adulteresses, and blood is on their hands; they fornicated with their idols [or devices]. Moreover, they offered to them for devouring [or caused to pass through the fire] their sons whom they had borne to me.

They did this also to me: they polluted my sanctuary on that day, and they profaned my Sabbaths. And when they sacrificed their sons to their idols and entered my sanctuary on that day to pollute it, they also did these things in the midst of my house.

They sent to men coming from afar, to whom they had sent a messenger. And behold, they came, for whom you washed yourself [or: “when they came, you immediately washed yourself”]; you painted your eyes [the Vulgate adds “with stibium”], and adorned yourself with women’s finery. You sat upon a beautiful couch, and a table was prepared [the Vulgate: “arranged”] before you. You placed my incense and my ointment upon it, [Note: For the single word *meum*, which we substituted on the authority of the manuscripts and Rabanus, Martianay, following Erasmus, retained two words, “and oil.” The reading restored by us is also supported by the Hebrew text and by the Latin version, whose evidence Victor especially praises. Nor can it reasonably be otherwise in Hebrew, as Jerome’s own exposition shows, where he says: “My incense and my ointment, which I had specially commanded to be made,” etc. I therefore suppose that, since the Septuagint translated “oil” for “ointment,” both readings had been noted in the familiar manner: “You placed my ointment (or oil),” etc.] and there was the sound of a celebrating multitude within it [or: “and she danced about with an ordered cry”].

[Note: Victor reads *quidem e multitudine* (“indeed, from the multitude”); and shortly afterward, “adulteries” for “adultery,” from the Hebrew and Greek sources.]

And among the men were brought multitudes of people, and they came from the desert [or: “drunk from the desert”]. They placed bracelets on their arms and splendid crowns on their heads. And I said to her who was worn out by adultery: “Now she will fornicate in her fornication as well.”

And they entered to her; just as one enters a prostitute, so they entered to Oholah and Oholibah, wicked women [or: “to commit iniquity”]. Therefore they are just men [the Vulgate inserts “these”]; they shall judge them with the judgment of adulteresses and with the judgment of women who shed blood, because they are adulteresses and blood is on their hands.

For thus says the Lord God: Bring a multitude against them, and deliver them to tumult and plunder; let them be stoned with the stones of the peoples and pierced with their swords. They shall kill their sons and daughters, burn their houses with fire, and I shall remove crime [or impiety] from the land. All women shall learn not to act according to their crime [or impiety]. And they shall place your crime [or impiety] upon you, and you shall bear the sins of your idols; and you shall know that I am the Lord God.

As I have often warned, I have placed alongside the Hebrew the small points in which the Septuagint edition differs from it, anticipating the reader’s weariness. It followed, however, that the one who had separately described the adulteries of Samaria and Jerusalem should announce their punishments together.

[Col. 0222D] Everything is spoken as though to adulteresses; and, after a summary, their crimes are briefly set forth, so that, in accordance with the command of the Law, the stoning of the adulteresses [or adulterers] should rightly follow at the hands of the people. Since they are adulteresses, pronounce a just sentence.

They committed adultery with idols, and blood is on their hands—namely, the blood of those whom they sacrificed to idols—for they consecrated to demons the sons whom they had borne to me. Nor did they do this outside, on mountains, or in sacred groves, as they had often been accustomed to do; rather, at last they polluted my Temple by setting up a statue of Baal in it.

And they profaned my Sabbaths, so that among them neither the holiness of place nor that of time was preserved. Nor were they satisfied with their present adulteries alone, nor was it enough for them that they sacrificed my sons to their idols or demons; but, indulging in foreign pleasures, they also worshiped the images of the Assyrians and Chaldeans.

When these men came, Oholibah—Jerusalem—fulfilled upon them every behavior of an adulteress: you washed your body, painted your eyes with stibium, assumed women’s finery, sat on a couch prepared for lust [or: “prepared for lust”], and set out banquets by which you might restore the strength of your lovers, exhausted by desire.

You offered to idols my incense and ointment, which I had specially commanded to be made (Exod. XXX) and which I had commanded that the person who wished to make it for private use should be cut off from the people. You did this in order to gather a crowd of peoples, or to sing with every kind of music, so that you might please your lovers not only by sight but also by hearing, smell, and every sense. They came to you drunk—not displaying the refinement of some city, but bearing the appearance of countrymen and robbers from the desert and wilderness.

And you burned with such madness for pleasures, worst of sisters, that you put your bracelets and head ornaments on the hands and heads of your lovers—or on yourselves, so that, filled with adornment, you might be made shameful.

Therefore I said to her—whether Jerusalem, Samaria, or both: “You have so worn away your forehead that you are no longer polluted secretly, nor do you avoid husbands or the gaze of men; rather, like prostitutes, you publicly offer yourselves to those who enter you as to prostitutes, eager to defile you in rivalry.”

Therefore I shall hand you over for punishment to those to whom you willingly handed yourselves over for disfigurement. For they are just men, insofar as, at my command, they torture an adulteress and a murderess.

For thus says the Lord God: At the prompting of your voice, O prophet, gather a multitude of peoples against them; first let all their property be plundered; then let them be stoned and pierced with swords, and let their sons and daughters be slaughtered and their houses burned.

All these things shall happen so that impiety may be removed from the land, and all women and all the distant provinces may learn to avoid similar things through fear of their punishments. After you have received what you deserve and borne the crimes of your idols, then you shall know that I am the Lord.

All these things are spoken figuratively and under the type of adulteresses against Samaria and Jerusalem: they were handed over to the Assyrians and Chaldeans and led into captivity; their cities were burned with fire, and their peoples were killed [Note: We removed the word “your,” which the manuscripts lack and which the context rejects], those who had worshiped images of demons instead of God.

These things may also be understood after Christ’s coming: righteous men from the nations themselves judge Samaritans and Jews by comparison with themselves and hand them over to those who will devour them, concerning whom the Lord had said: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 38); and, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, know that its desolation is near” (Luke XXI, 22).

To this day they are adulteresses, and they are crushed by the stones of the whole world. For they sent messengers to those who were far away and could not say: “I am God who draws near, and not a God from afar,” says the Lord (Jer. XXIII, 23). They prepared themselves for their lovers, the demons, and changed all the worship and adornment that they had received from God as a natural good into the worship of demons. They offered to their adulterous lovers their deeds and beauty, which we understand by the bracelets and diadems. Their punishment is a warning to the nations, indeed to those from the nations who have believed, lest they suffer similar things if they do what Samaria and Jerusalem did.

Their impieties will then be taken away when they have received their crimes and removed from their eyes the veil placed before Moses’ face (Exod. XXXIV), so that they may know that he is the Lord Jesus Christ, whom they denied to be the Son of God (II Cor. III).

**(Chapter XXIV, verses 1 ff.)** And the word of the Lord came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, saying: Son of man, write for yourself the name of this day, on which the king of Babylon established himself against Jerusalem—this very day. And speak a parable to the rebellious house, and say to them:

Thus says the Lord God: Set up a pot—set it up, I say—and pour water into it. Gather its pieces into it, every good piece, the thigh and the shoulder, the choice pieces full of bones. Take the fattest animal. Arrange also a pile of bones beneath it. Let its cooking boil, and let its bones be cooked in its midst.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Woe to the city of blood, to the pot in which there is rust, and whose rust has not gone out of it. Bring it out piece by piece and by its pieces; no lot has fallen upon it. For its blood is in its midst; she poured it upon the smoothest rock and did not pour it upon the ground, so that it might be covered with dust. In order that I might bring upon it my indignation and take vengeance in punishment, I placed its blood upon the smoothest rock, so that it might not be covered.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Woe to the city of blood, whose great pyre I shall make. Heap up the bones that I shall burn with fire; the flesh shall be consumed, the whole preparation shall be cooked, and the bones shall melt away. Place it also empty upon the coals, so that its bronze may grow hot and melt, its uncleanness may be melted in its midst, and its rust may be consumed.

It has been sweated over through much labor, yet its excessive rust has not gone out of it, not even through fire. Your impurity is abominable, because I wished to cleanse you, and you have not been cleansed from your filth; nor shall you be cleansed any longer, until I cause my indignation to rest upon you.

I, the Lord, have spoken: it is coming, and I shall act; I shall not pass over [the Vulgate: “pass by”], nor spare, nor be appeased. According to your ways and according to your devices I judged you, says the Lord.

[Note: In Hebrew it says “they judged you,” which Victor considers corrupt; he freely substituted “I shall judge” for “I judged,” on the basis of the Latin and Greek versions.]

**The Septuagint:** And the word of the Lord came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, saying: Son of man, write for yourself the day from this day, on which the king of Babylon was strengthened against Jerusalem, from this day; and speak a parable to the provoking house, and say to them:

Thus says the Lord God: Set up a cauldron and pour water into it; put divisions into it. Take every good cut, the thigh and the shoulder, with the flesh separated from the bones, taken from choice animals, and kindle the bones beneath them. It boiled, and its bones were cooked in the midst of it.

Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: O city of blood, cauldron in which there is rust, and whose rust has not gone out of it: bring it out by its pieces; no lot has fallen upon it, because its blood is in its midst. I placed it upon a very smooth rock; I did not pour it upon the ground, so that the earth might cover it, so that fury might rise for the vengeance of punishment. I placed its blood upon a very smooth rock, so that it might not be covered.

Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Woe, city of blood! I shall magnify terror, multiply the wood, and kindle the fire, so that the flesh may melt, the broth diminish, the bones burn, and it may stand upon its coals. It was kindled so that its bronze might be burned and heated, its uncleanness might burn within it, and its rust might fail.

Its rust shall be humbled, and much of its rust shall not go out of it; its rust shall be confounded. Your impurity is *zemma* (זִמָּה), because you have been polluted and have not been cleansed from your impurity. And what will happen if you are not cleansed further, until I fulfill my fury against you? I, the Lord, have spoken, and it shall come, and I shall act; I shall not delay, nor pity, nor be entreated. According to your ways and according to your devices I shall judge you, says Adonai the Lord.

[The following is added from Theodotion, for the most part, including the Hebrew word *zemma* (זִמָּה), which we have translated as “abominable impurity.” The following has also been added by them, although it is not found in the Hebrew and ought to be marked beforehand with an obelus: “Therefore I shall judge you according to your blood, and according to your thoughts I shall judge you, unclean and notorious, and exceedingly provoking.”]

Let us therefore speak about each point.

In the ninth year of the captivity of King Jehoiakim—for he had begun to prophesy in the fifth year—and in the tenth month of that same ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the word of the Lord came to the prophet Ezekiel, who was settled in the region of Babylon. He said to him: Son of man, write down this very day for yourself, and know that today the king of Babylon has begun in the region of Judea to besiege Jerusalem and surround it with an army. Describe this siege by a parable and proverb, which in the present passage signifies a metaphor and transference.

“Set up,” he says, “a bronze pot,” that is, a cauldron, and pour water into it. Cut into pieces the whole body of the fattest animals, both thigh, leg, and shoulder, and carefully separate the flesh from the bones. Put the flesh into the cauldron; place or arrange the bones beneath the cauldron, making piles and heaps of bones, so that the cooking of the cauldron may boil not once but repeatedly, that the flesh within may be thoroughly cooked and the bones beneath may burn in the fire.

Do you wish to know, prophet, what this cauldron is, or what the flesh and bones are? Speak these words, says the Lord God: Woe to the city of blood, that is, Jerusalem, the cauldron whose rust—that is, its excessive wickedness—is great. Although fire has been placed beneath it, its rust has not gone out. For even when captured and tortured, they persevered in their former crime.

“Consume it piece by piece and individually”; let no one remain for safety. No lot fell upon it, so that some might perish and others be saved; rather, a common destruction came upon all. For its blood—that is, murders and the slaughter of children—is in its midst. It poured out this blood upon the smoothest rock, so that it might be evident to everyone and the earth might not cover it with soil or dust. Thus my indignation would not pass over it, but vengeance would hasten upon the exposed blood.

It is natural that if blood is poured upon the earth, the soil absorbs the moisture of the blood, or the earth is gradually covered with soil and dust. But when blood has been poured upon the smoothest rock, having no hollow, it runs down and occupies a broad surface. This signifies that she committed not hidden but public murders, in accordance with what is said to Cain: “The blood of your brother cries out to me” (Gen. IV, 10).

Therefore say to the city—not of one blood, but of many bloods: Behold, I shall make a great pyre in you, or bring forth a log, which the common people call a firebrand; and I shall burn not only the soft and tender flesh in you but also the hardest bones, so that nothing may remain in you that is not consumed by fire.

When both flesh and bones have been consumed and burned, place the empty cauldron itself upon the coals, so that its bronze too may grow hot and be consumed; and when the bronze has been consumed, let its rust also perish—that is, when the city has been burned with fire, let wickedness perish together with the city.

But what benefit is there in having done what was commanded? Not even through fire could the rust and wickedness of the cauldron and city be removed; rather, criminal and abominable impurity remains in it. For this is what *zemma* signifies. He turns in apostrophe to the cauldron itself, that is, to the city itself: “I wished to cleanse you, and you have not been cleansed from your filth, nor will you be able to be cleansed any longer until I fulfill my indignation against you.”

I, the Lord, have spoken, and my sentence cannot pass away. The siege of the city has already come; I shall do what I threatened. I shall not pass over your crimes, as I often did; I shall no longer spare you, nor be appeased by you, even if you multiply your prayers. Rather, I shall repay you according to your ways and devices—or, rather, judge you according to your works and thoughts—so that in this also I may show my mercy, like a physician who does not spare rotten flesh so that healthy members may be saved. He does not spare in order to spare; he is cruel in order to show mercy; he does not consider the patient’s pain but the health of the wound, in accordance with the Gospel saying that he would rather allow one member to perish than let the whole body be destroyed (Matt. V).

[Note: The reading had been corrupted by an erroneous addition, contrary to the sense, context, and Jerome’s meaning, so that it said “so that the healthy members may not be saved.” We deleted the negative particle in accordance with the manuscripts; the matter itself plainly demanded this.]

It should also be noted how, from the beginning of the prophecy up to the present day, when Jerusalem began to be besieged, the captivity proceeds in order. First the sword is provoked; then two roads are set forth, Ammon and Jerusalem, at whose right-hand side the lot falls to Nebuchadnezzar. Silver is smelted in the city, along with bronze, tin, lead, and iron; the land too is not watered by rain but is occupied by thorns. Afterward, under the name of the two sisters Oholah and Oholibah—Samaria and Jerusalem—their sins are recounted: how the former was captured and the latter was to be captured.

Finally, in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, while Ezekiel and those with him were in captivity and had surrendered themselves with King Jeconiah, the day on which the city began to be besieged is shown, and the image of the cauldron is presented. Just as flesh and bones heaped into the cauldron are consumed by fire, so the entire city with its citizens will perish, and none of those who are besieged will remain unconsumed by famine, sword, or pestilence; the surviving portion will be led captive to Babylon.

This same prophecy can also refer to the time of the Lord’s Passion, on account of which Jerusalem was surrounded by an army and her children were killed. When Titus, the son of Vespasian, besieged it, no one escaped to safety, and the Temple was overthrown; afterward, fifty years later, under Hadrian, the city was consumed by everlasting fire.

Jeremiah also sets forth this present captivity, which Ezekiel was witnessing in Babylon, at the beginning of his book: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” He answered: “A burning cauldron, with its face turned from the face of the north” (Jer. I, 13).

There are those who, according to the moral sense, transfer this entire passage to the consummation of the world [or age] and temper the number nine—which in Holy Scripture signifies punishments and sorrows and always follows justice—with the mercy of the tenth month and the tenth day. Punishments are applied to the sick for this reason: so that health may follow pain.

The world, therefore, which lies in wickedness (I John V, 19), is kindled with divine fire on the day of judgment; and the city of blood is placed upon burning coals, so that what is written in Isaiah may be fulfilled: “You have coals of fire; sit upon them. They shall be a help to you” (Isa. XLVII, 14).

It is difficult, however, to understand how, when the coals and bones with which even the Pharisees are filled are consumed—for the Lord says to them in the Gospel, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who are like whitewashed tombs, which inside are full of uncleanness and the bones of the dead” (Matt. XXIII, 27)—it can now be said that the rust and filth of the world are not consumed, but that wickedness remains even after the severity of judgment.

This is easily resolved if we understand the Apostle’s statement: “God shut up all things under sin, so that he might have mercy on all” (Gal. III, 22). For creation has been subjected to vanity (Rom. VIII, 28). The blood that has been poured out in the open is set before the whole creation, so that the crimes of all may be exposed.

We can understand the smoothest rock also as the Lord and Savior, who followed the people of Israel in the wilderness. Of it it is written: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). Everything is revealed in him, and what is written is fulfilled: “There is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed.”

The Lord says that he will not have mercy, nor pass over the sins of the world; he will neither spare the impious nor be appeased, so that the ways of the impious may perish, in accordance with what is written at the end of the first Psalm: “And the way of the impious shall perish.”

### (Verses 15ff.)

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, behold, I am taking from you the delight of your eyes by a blow; yet you shall not mourn, nor shall you weep, nor shall your tears flow. Groan silently; you shall not observe the mourning for the dead. Let your crown be bound upon you, and your sandals shall be on your feet; you shall not cover your face with a garment, nor shall you eat the food of mourners.”

So I spoke to the people in the morning, and my wife died in the evening; and in the morning I did [Vulg.: he did] as he had commanded me. And the people said to me: “Will you not explain to us what these things mean that you are doing?” And I said to them: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Speak to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am profaning my sanctuary, the pride of your dominion, the delight of your eyes, and that upon which your soul trembles; and your sons and daughters whom you have left behind shall fall by the sword. And you shall do as I have done: you shall not cover your faces with a garment, and you shall not eat the food of mourners. You shall have crowns upon your heads and sandals on your feet. You shall not mourn, nor shall you weep; rather, you shall waste away in your iniquities, and each one shall groan toward his brother.

“And Ezekiel shall be a portent to you. According to everything that he has done, you shall do when this comes to pass, and you shall know that I am the Lord God. And you, son of man, behold, on the day when I take from them their strength, the joy of their dignity, and the desire of their eyes, upon which their souls rest—their sons and daughters—on that day, when the fugitive comes to you to announce it, on that day your mouth shall be opened together with that of the fugitive, and you shall speak and shall no longer be silent; and you shall be a portent to them, and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

**The Septuagint:** “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold, I am taking from you the desirable things of your eyes in battle (or, in preparation); you shall not mourn, nor shall you weep, nor shall tears come to you. A bloody groan: the mourning of the loins. Your hair shall be bound upon you, and your sandals shall be on your feet; you shall not be comforted on their lips, and you shall not eat the bread of men.

“I spoke to the people in the morning, as he had commanded me; and my wife died in the evening, and in the morning I did as I had been commanded. And the people said to me: ‘Will you not announce to us what these things are that you are doing?’ And I said to them: ‘The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say to the house of Israel: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am profaning my holy places, the pride of your strength, the desirable things of your eyes, and those things which your souls spare. Your sons and your daughters whom you have left behind shall fall by the sword, and you shall do as I have done. You shall not be comforted by their mouths, and you shall not eat the bread of men. Your hair shall be upon your heads, and your sandals upon your feet. You shall not mourn, nor shall you weep; you shall be consumed in your iniquities, and each one shall comfort his brother, and Ezekiel shall be a portent to you.

“‘According to everything that he has done, you shall do. And when these things come, you shall know that I am Adonai the Lord. And you, son of man, is it not so that on the day when I take away their strength from them, the exaltation of their glory, the desirable things of their eyes, and the exaltation of their souls—their sons and daughters—on that day the one who has been saved shall come to you, to announce it in your ears. On that day your mouth shall be opened to the one who has escaped, and you shall speak and shall no longer be silent; and you shall be a portent to them, and they shall know that I am the Lord.’”

Above, the heating of the pot and the cauldron had signified the siege of the city; now the prophetic word testifies that it has been captured and destroyed, and that the entire people have either been killed by the sword or led into captivity. And first, according to our custom, let us lay the foundations of the historical interpretation.

“Son,” he says, “of man, behold, I shall take from before your eyes whatever is desirable for you, and I shall take it away by a blow—or, as the Septuagint translated it, ‘in preparation’—so that you may prepare yourself not to do the things that are customarily done in mourning. You shall not mourn, nor shall you weep, nor shall flowing tears show the grief of your heart. But if perhaps you are overcome by excessive sorrow, keep your groan silent, and do not let it break into words.

“You shall not observe the mourning for the dead”—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “a bloody groan: the mourning of the loins.” By this he shows that his wife was to die. For immediately it follows: “And my wife died in the evening” (Proverbs 19), which properly pertains to the joining of the loins. Nothing is more precious to a husband than a good and loving wife, who is provided for a man by God, joined to him by the Lord’s law, and made one body with him.

And what follows—“Let your crown be bound upon you, and your sandals shall be on your feet”—means this: You shall have hair, which is cut in mourning, and sandals on your feet, which mourners ordinarily cast off. Hence David, fleeing from his son Absalom, and repenting over the death of Uriah, walked barefoot (1 Kings 12, 15, 18).

The Hebrews say that, down to the present day, the Babylonian teachers, observing the precepts of the Law, bind the Decalogue, written on little parchment strips, around their heads. They say that these are the things commanded to be before the eyes and upon the forehead, so that they may always see the commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] The same material occurs at the beginning of the fourth book on Matthew, chapter 23, concerning the commandment of Deuteronomy, “You shall bind them on your hand,” and so forth. “The Pharisees,” he says, “misinterpreting this, used to write the Decalogue of Moses—that is, the ten words of the Law—on strips of parchment, folding them and binding them upon the forehead, and making them almost like a crown for the head, so that they might always move before their eyes. This is what the Indians, Persians, and Babylonians do even today, and whoever possesses such an object is judged religious among the peoples.” Nevertheless, it must be admitted—if the rabbis deserve any credibility when recounting their own practices, and if the custom that prevails among them today has any authority—that the Hebrews customarily write not the Decalogue, as Jerome reports, but several passages of Scripture on parchment, namely two from Exodus and as many from Deuteronomy, and bind them to the forehead like a diadem, with ribbons flowing down on either side. Such is the superstition of this foolish people. They call them *frontals*; one especially elegant specimen, and perhaps the oldest anywhere, is in my possession.]

Since Ezekiel was a priest, they say that he ought never to remove the crown of glory, but should keep it bound upon his head. That is what they say. We, however, following the Septuagint, should understand a crown of hair, a head of hair, although their interpretation likewise has not fully expressed the force of the Hebrew wording.

“Nor shall you cover your face with a garment,” he says, “nor shall you take the food of mourners”—the things customarily done in mourning: covering the face and receiving from those who offer consolation what the Greeks call *perideipna* (περίδειπνα), “funeral meals.”

“I spoke,” he says, “to the people in the morning what the Lord had commanded me, and in the evening my wife died—the delight of my eyes, and the mourning of my loins and blood. Immediately, on the following morning, I did everything that had been commanded me; and the people asked me why I had acted contrary to the custom of all.”

When they sought the reasons for such endurance, I replied: “The word of the Lord that came to me, so that I might speak to the people of Israel, commanded this: ‘Behold I’—that is, ‘now at once’—‘shall profane my sanctuary,’ so that the temple may be burned and exposed to all foreigners and profane persons; and that in which you possessed pride—that is, confidence, hope, and the desire of your salvation—and at whose siege your souls trembled, and your sons and daughters whom famine and pestilence had left to you, I shall consume by the sword.

“Whatever I have done, you also shall do. When custom is observed in mourning, grief is moderated; but when such a necessity of evils presses upon people that it surpasses all weeping, each person, anxious about his own necessity, does not groan over the miseries of others, however close they may be.

“You shall do nothing,” he says, “of what is customarily done in mourning. Rather, when the city and temple have been burned, you shall be stupefied at the magnitude of your evils. You shall not cut your hair, nor shall you walk barefoot; you shall not mourn, nor shall you cover your faces with garments, nor shall you receive food from those who offer consolation. Rather, you shall waste away and be consumed in your iniquities, and scarcely shall you have a free groan, lest you offend the arrogance of the victors if you appear to weep publicly. Thus the prophet Ezekiel shall be a portent to you, and everything that he did not do at the death of his wife you shall not do at the overthrow of the city and temple.

“And still more plainly: ‘O son of man,’ he says, ‘at the time when I take away from them their strength—the temple, as we have said, their confidence and the joy of their dignity, and that in which they had their only hope, the object upon which their souls rested—and, moreover, their sons and daughters, as is understood from what precedes—at that time, when a fugitive comes to you from Jerusalem, or one who has escaped, saying that the city has been overthrown, then you, who had previously been silent and had no free groan, and who had shown such endurance that at the death of your wife and in the pain of your loins you shed no tear, shall open your mouth and speak—not to the one who has come, but together with him. Thus whatever you had foretold as about to happen, he shall announce as already accomplished, and you shall no longer be silent; rather, you shall rebuke them and say that all these things have deservedly befallen them. Thus you shall be a portent to them, according to what is written in Zechariah: “Prophets are men who signify portents” (Zechariah 3:8). And the Lord says elsewhere: “I have been represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hosea 12:10).’

Let this suffice as the historical interpretation. Let us come to the allegorical interpretation—provided, at least, that it does not appear forced to the prudence of a cautious reader.

That the Son of Man is called the Lord and Savior is beyond doubt. At the world’s final hour—that is, toward the evening of this world—he lost his former wife; he neither mourned her nor covered his face with a garment, nor received any human consolation. In the morning he foretold these things that were to come, and they were completed in the evening. Then again, in the morning of his second coming, he proved by events what he had foretold: that the sanctuary of the Jews, what they had held desirable in their eyes and over which their souls had trembled, had been profaned, and that their sons and daughters had been cut down by the Roman sword.

As for what is said—“You shall have crowns upon your heads, and sandals shall be on your feet”—we shall refer it to the point that they must by no means mourn or assume the signs of mourning after they have received the truth in place of the shadow, and after some of them have become Nazarenes, and each one has comforted his brother. Thus Ezekiel, whom God the Father strengthened, shall be a portent to them, announcing what is to come. After Jerusalem has been overthrown, the temple burned, the whole world has heard of it, and the dispersion of Israel—which inhabits the ends of the earth—has taken place, then, when the words of the Lord have been fulfilled in deed, they shall have freedom. Once his sanctuary has been profaned, and the Law has been fulfilled—or destroyed according to the letter that kills—the glory of the Gospel shall be opened, and Israel shall know that he himself is the Lord and God who foretold these things in the morning, and proved by his coming that they had been completed in the evening and at the consummation of the world.

## BOOK EIGHT

**283–284.** What benefit our writing about the prophets brings to others belongs to the judgment of God and to the consciences of those who, setting aside declamations, applause, and verbal ornamentation, desire to know whether the prophet’s speech recounts the past, reproves the present, or foretells what is to come.

For the moment it benefits us [Note: Col. 0231D. In Rabanus: “For the moment it benefits us first.”]: while we do this and think of nothing else, we undertake these explanations as though by stealth, and compensate for the miseries of the days through the labor of the nights. The mind is nourished and forgets the calamities of the age, which, already placed at its final end, groans and labors in childbirth (2 Thessalonians 2), until the one who now restrains is removed from the midst, and the feet of the once iron statue are crushed by the weakness of its clay toes.

The world is falling, yet its stiff neck is not bent. Wealth is perishing, yet greed does not cease. People hasten to gather what others will again seize. Tears have dried up; all compassion has been taken away. There are many who ask, but few who give. Nor are we ashamed, preferring poverty in a cheap little cloak while reclining upon the wealth of Croesus;

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Victorius preferred, from the Brixian manuscripts: “and to preserve our treasures for the hunger and destruction of many.”]

preserving our treasures for the hunger and destruction of many, like that rich man dressed in purple who—whatever else he may have done, for Scripture does not testify to his robberies and injustices (Luke 16)—was nevertheless without limit in cruelty and arrogance. Lazarus lay at his gate, half dead, and he did not order even those things to be given him that are thrown to dogs.

How many Lazaruses now lie about, and how many are covered by purple garments of various colors,

[Note: [Col. 0232D] The same editor prefers, from the same manuscripts: “and how many purple-clad men … turning into their own uses even those things which they preserve for destruction.”]

even without turning to their own uses what they preserve for destruction!

Let these words, O virgin of Christ, Eustochium, have been spoken from the abundance of the heart, and let us have spoken somewhat more freely than suits our humility. In any case, the eighth book on Ezekiel, which contains the rebuke of the Ammonites and the other nations, together with the prophecy of future events, shall have the following beginning.

### (Chapter 25)

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, set—or, strengthen—your face against the sons of Ammon, and prophesy against them, and say to the sons of Ammon: Hear the word of the Lord God. Thus says the Lord God: Because you said, ‘Bravo, bravo!’ over my sanctuary—or, ‘Because you rejoiced over my sanctuary’—because it was profaned, and over the land of Israel, because it was desolated, and over the house of Judah, because they were led into captivity; therefore, behold, I shall deliver you to the sons of the East—or, *CEDEM*—as a possession, and they shall place their sheepfolds in you and set up their tents in you. They themselves shall eat your crops, and they themselves shall drink your milk [another reading adds: ‘your’]—or, your abundance. And I shall make Rabbah a dwelling place for camels—or, the city of Ammon a pasture for camels—and the sons of Ammon a resting place for flocks; and you shall know that I am the Lord.

“Because thus says the Lord God: Because you clapped your hands, stamped your feet, and rejoiced with all your affection—or, insulted with all your heart—over the land of Israel; therefore I [Vulg.: behold, I] shall stretch out my hand against you and deliver you for plunder to the nations. I shall cut you off from among the peoples, destroy you among the lands, and crush you; and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

Jerusalem had been captured or besieged. After one who could escape [another reading: had been able to escape] had come to Babylon and announced that the city was on the point of being captured—or that it had been overthrown together with the temple—the prophetic speech, according to the custom of all the prophets, turns against the other nations surrounding Israel that had mocked the ruin of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple. It begins with the sons of Ammon, who possessed a metropolis named Rabbah. Today it is called Philadelphia, after Ptolemy, king of Egypt, surnamed Philadelphus, who ruled Arabia together with Judaea.

“Son,” he says, “of man, set—or strengthen—your face against the sons of Ammon, who were born from the stock of Lot, and say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God’”—for these are not the prophet’s words but the Lord’s. We have discussed the strengthening of the face more fully in this same prophet—“because you said, ‘Bravo, bravo!’ or insulted and rejoiced because my temple and sanctuary had been profaned by the entry of hostile nations, and over the land of Israel because it had been desolated, and especially over the house of Judah—that is, the two tribes—which have now been led into captivity [another reading: may have been led into captivity]. Therefore I shall also deliver you to the sons of *CEDEM* [another reading: *Edem*], whom we have interpreted as the Easterners.

“There is no doubt that the Midianites, and the whole wilderness adjoining the land of Arabia, possess herds of camels and great numbers of sheep and goats, and live from these resources. History relates that the same thing happened to the land of Israel in the Book of Judges (Judges 6), when the Midianites came and consumed all their territories as far as Gaza.

“Therefore, metaphorically, through the Midianites, Ishmaelites, and Hagarenes—who are now called Saracens, falsely assuming the name of Sarah, so that [another reading: because] they may appear to have been born from a free woman and a mistress—Scripture signifies the following. It is said of King Nebuchadnezzar and his entire army that he would come and capture the city of Rabbah, whether that name is proper to it or is given because of its greatness; for *Rabbah* means ‘very great.’

“And lest we doubt that Nebuchadnezzar overthrew Arabia after Jerusalem was captured, Scripture testifies above: ‘And you, son of man, set before yourself two roads, one for Ammon and one for Jerusalem, and the sword of the king of Babylon shall come.’ And again: ‘At the head of the road of the city he shall cast lots, and you shall appoint a road for the sword to come to Rabbah of the sons of Ammon and to Judah, to fortified Jerusalem’ (above, chapter 21:19–20). And again: ‘Thus says the Lord God concerning the sons of Ammon and concerning their reproach’ (verse 28).

“The sons of *CEDEM* will therefore come and set up their sheepfolds, like shepherds, and fix their tents. They themselves will ravage your crops and drink your milk and abundance, sending in herds of camels and animals of every kind, so that the sons of Ammon will become a resting place for flocks. Through the necessity of these evils they will understand that he is the Lord who both foretold future events and commanded that they come to pass.

“This was not enough for the sons of Ammon: they insulted and said, ‘Bravo, bravo!’ over the temple and sanctuary of the Lord, which had been profaned by the entry of various nations. Their insolence in mocking was so great that the whole people clapped with their hands and stamped with their feet, crying out with all the feeling of their hearts because the land of Israel had been desolated.

“Therefore, not through angels or other ministries, but the Lord himself, stretching out his hand to strike, will deliver them for plunder—not to camels and flocks of sheep, but more manifestly to the nations—so that they may be utterly uprooted from the number of the peoples, perish, and be reduced to nothing. After they have been crushed, they will understand that he is the Lord who judges all things and has power over every land.”

According to the tropological interpretation, we may understand the sons of Ammon as all heretics who were generated from Lot’s seed in a cave, and generated in drunkenness and incest. Of them Scripture says, and the apostle John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

They arose from inclination—for this is how *Lot* is translated into our language: “For all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13:3). Against these the prophetic face is set or strengthened, so that it may crush them by its severity. He says to them: “Because you insulted my Church in the time of persecution,

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Victor: “and because the sanctuary was polluted by various vices,” which is also how Rabanus formerly read it.]

because my sanctuary was polluted by various vices—or by the vice of those who served me,

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Victor: “and because the house of Israel, that is, those who see God in understanding, was desolated of its choir of virtues, and because the sons of the house of Judah …”]

or by the cruelty of the enemies who persecuted my people—and because the land of Israel, those who see God in understanding, was desolated of its choir of virtues; and because the sons of the house of Judah—that is, of the one who confesses God, in whom there is true faith and right confession—were led into captivity [another reading: may have been led into captivity] and ceased to serve the Lord [another reading: may have ceased]: 

“therefore, O you who insult, you shall be delivered to the sons of the East, who have proceeded from the true light, and you shall be delivered to them as a possession, so that you too may learn to confess the Lord.

“By way of metaphor it is said that the sons of the East shall place their sheepfolds upon them, fix their tents, drink their milk, and eat their crops. The city that was once proud shall become a dwelling place for camels, which, having laid aside the burden of sins, may enter through the eye of a needle (Matthew 19), and it shall become a resting place for flocks governed by the good shepherd (John 10). When they have done this, mixed with and delivered to the shepherds of the East, they will understand that he is the Lord.

“Again he reproaches them because they insulted, with excessive feeling of heart, the ruins of God’s people and thought the land of Israel completely deserted. For this they deserve the hand of the avenging God: those who had exceeded the proper measure of exultation and rejoicing over the ruin of the house of Judah shall not be delivered to the sons of the East, but shall be plunder for all the nations. They shall be killed from among the peoples, perish, and be crushed; and they are to be believed to belong not to the stock of Abraham but to all the nations. Then, through the magnitude of their evils, their crushing, and the slaughter of the people, they shall know that he is the Lord.

“What we have understood generally of the Church can also be understood of each of the saints. Worldly people and hostile powers rejoice at their ruin if they have long lost their chastity, since evil people think their own crimes are consoled if they have more companions in crime and punishment. Let no one do this unless he is a son of Ammon—that is, a son of the people generated in turning aside.”

### (Verses 8ff.)

Thus says the Lord God: “Because Moab and Seir said, ‘Behold, the house of Judah is like all the nations,’ therefore, behold, I shall open the shoulder of Moab from its cities”—or, “from its cities, I say”—“and from its borders the renowned land, Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim, to the sons of the East together with the sons of Ammon. And I shall give it as a possession, so that there may no longer be any remembrance of the sons of Ammon among the nations; and I shall execute judgments in Moab, and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Victor, on the basis of the Hebrew and Jerome’s edition, repeats *de civitatibus* (“from the cities”) twice, and shortly afterward reads *inclytas* (“renowned,” plural) instead of *inclyta* (“renowned,” singular), in agreement with the exposition of Jerome that follows. Referring the word to the cities, he says: “So that the victorious Babylonian may enter those places as well, and the cities may cease to exist in Moab, and the renowned cities in its borders and territories may be destroyed.”]

**The Septuagint:** “Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because Moab said—and Seir—‘Behold, the house of Judah is like all the nations,’ therefore, behold, I shall dissolve the shoulder of Moab from its cities, from its heights; the choice land, the house of Beth-jeshimoth, above the spring of the maritime city. I have given the sons of the East to the sons of Ammon as a possession, so that there may be no remembrance of the sons of Ammon among the nations; and in Moab I shall execute vengeance, and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

What we have translated as “and Seir” is not found in the Septuagint, but has been added from the edition of Theodotion.

The Hebrews tell a ridiculous story concerning this passage. After the city had been opened and the temple unlocked, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Seir entered the temple and saw the cherubim protecting the mercy seat. They said: “Just as all the nations worship images, so Judah too has idols belonging to its religion. Therefore,” they said, “the Lord was angry and delivered them into captivity.”

We, however, shall say that these people also insulted the house of Judah when it was captured by the Chaldeans, thinking that, as among the other nations, the power of God was not present there, and that therefore the kingdom of Judah and Jerusalem, deprived of God’s protection, had been exposed to Babylonian power.

Therefore, not long afterward but immediately, the Lord threatens that he will dissolve—or open—the shoulder of Moab, namely its strength and power, from its cities, so that the Babylonian victor may enter those places as well, and the cities may cease to exist in Moab, and the renowned cities in its borders and territories may be destroyed. He lists their names: Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim.

In place of these names, I do not know what the Septuagint intended when it translated “the house of Beth-jeshimoth,” since this name signifies “a deserted village.” To this day, Baal-meon is also a very large village in Moab; they translated it as “above the spring.” And Kiriathaim they translated as “the maritime city.” It too is delivered, together with the sons of Ammon, to the sons of the East—that is, to the Babylonians—according to the interpretation that we gave concerning the sons of Ammon.

“And I shall give Moab,” he says, “as a possession, so that just as there is no longer any remembrance of the sons of Ammon among the nations, so I shall execute vengeance and judgments in Moab. Thus they may know that I am the Lord, who delivered Judah because of its sin and will appear as avenger against the sons of Ammon and Moab.”

Even to the present day, Moab—which is interpreted as “from the father”—and Seir, which means “hairy” and “shaggy,” despise and hold in contempt the house of Judah, in which there is true confession, and think that it can be overthrown as easily as the fortifications of other cities are overthrown.

Therefore the Lord threatens to open or dissolve all the strength of the Moabites, so that they may cease to possess cities and no longer place confidence in dialectical skill [another reading: to place confidence]. Let all their boundaries, which they call promontories because they break the waves, be destroyed; and let Beth-jeshimoth, the renowned and chosen land—which is interpreted as “the house of solitude” and “deserted”—and Baal-meon, which likewise means “having a spring,” or “above the spring,”

[Note: [Col. 0236D] With the help of the Brixian manuscripts, Victorius restored *super* (“above”) in place of *per* (“through”), which Martianus, following Erasmus, wrongly retained. For the word itself, from which the name Baal-meon is formed, does not mean “through” but “above.”]

and Kiriathaim, which the Septuagint translated as “the maritime city,” perish.

Although they may possess the strength of warriors and advance to battle with renowned skill in warfare, and although they may march surrounded and fortified on every side, nevertheless their renowned land is not a house of habitation but a house of solitude.

And although they think that they possess a fountain of knowledge and a maritime city capable of enduring all the storms of the age, promising themselves endurance and strength, nevertheless they shall be transformed so that they too may be delivered to the sons of the East, the true light in Christ, just as the sons of Ammon were delivered, who trusted in their heretical multitude.

Let us consider God’s progress and mercy in the very midst of his threat: they are delivered together with the sons of Ammon to the sons of the East as a possession, and no heresy whatsoever is named among the nations. Once judgments and vengeance have been executed in Moab because of its arrogance, they shall learn from the end of events that the Lord is he who orders all things.

To demonstrate that Moab in the present passage is understood as the pride of the philosophers, of whom it is said, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Corinthians 1:19), a few examples from the prophets should be repeated.

Amos says: “Thus says the Lord: For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I shall not turn away from him, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes” (Amos 2:1). Truly, whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever belongs to earthly knowledge and is thought to be strong, is overturned by dialectical skill and dissolved like a fire into ashes and embers, so that what was thought most powerful may be shown to be nothing.

Isaiah, however, rebukes the pride of Moab, saying: “We have heard of the insult of Moab; he is exceedingly insolent. I have taken away his pride” (Isaiah 16).

Jeremiah too, prophesying against all the nations, speaks specifically to Moab: “Because you trusted in your fortifications” (Jeremiah 48:7). And shortly afterward: “You shall have confidence in your glory.” And again: “How do you say, ‘We are mighty’?” Then: “The day of Moab is near, that it may come, and his evil is exceedingly swift” (ibid. 14, 10). And more plainly: “Say, How has the glorious staff, the rod of magnificence, been broken?” (ibid. 20). And again: “The horn of Moab has been broken.”

These things are said so that, under the name of Moab, the foolish pride of the age, lifting itself to heaven, may be crushed.

### (Verses 12, 13ff.)

Thus says the Lord God: “Because Edom executed vengeance, seeking to avenge itself upon the sons of Judah, and sinned by committing offense, and sought vengeance against them; therefore thus says the Lord God: I shall stretch out my hand against Edom and remove from it human being and beast. And I shall make it desolate from the South, and those in Dedan [printed reading: “those who are absent”; Vulg.: “those who are”] shall fall by the sword. And I shall execute my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall act in Edom according to my anger and my fury; and they shall know my indignation, says the Lord God.”

[Note: [Col. 0237D] Victor reads *facient* (“they shall act”), in accordance with the Vulgate edition and the Hebrew *וְעָשׂוּ*, as well as the Greek *ποιήσουσιν*. Shortly afterward, following the sense of these manuscripts, he likewise substitutes *vindictam* (“vengeance”) for *indignationem* (“indignation”).]

**The Septuagint:** “Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because Edom acted to execute vengeance against the house of Judah, and they retained the memory of evil, and executed vengeance, therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: I shall stretch out my hand against Edom and kill from it human being and animal, and I shall make it desolate. And from Teman those who flee shall be struck down by the sword. And I shall execute my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall act in Edom according to my anger and my fury, and they shall know my vengeance, says Adonai the Lord.”

Above, two matters were proposed: “Because Moab and Seir said”; afterward, remaining silent about Seir, he spoke only against Moab. Now he resumes the problem that he began: what Seir—that is, Edom—had done.

That Esau, Seir, Edom, Idumaea, and Duma are all names for one nation will not be doubted by anyone who possesses knowledge of the Scriptures. To say nothing of the other prophets—Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Amos, who prophesied against Idumaea, Duma, and Edom—the prophet Obadiah directs his entire prophecy against this nation; we discussed him long ago as best we could.

Seir is therefore reproved. Because he was hairy, he received the name “Hairy”; Edom is “blood-colored,” because he lost his birthright over the cooking of the red lentil dish and received his name from the food (Genesis 25); and the deeds of Esau are likewise interpreted.

It should also be known that in Hebrew “Idumaea” is never written, but always *Edom*; the Greek translation rendered it as *Idumaea*.

Therefore Idumaea—or Edom—did not speak as Moab did, but executed vengeance against the sons of Judah. It sinned—or retained the memory of its former pain—so that it might take vengeance on those by whom it had been supplanted in the womb.

Therefore the Lord himself, not through angels or anyone else, stretched out his hand against Idumaea, removed from it human being and beast, and reduced its cities to a desert—that is, to Theman, which we have translated as “the South.” From there, and from another city, Dedan, those killed by the sword shall fall.

When they had taken vengeance upon Judah, I shall execute vengeance upon the Edomites by the hand—or in the hand—of my people Israel, so that they may be oppressed by those against whom they had exercised vengeance. They shall act against Edom, or Idumaea, according to my anger and fury, to fulfill my indignation; and through the hands of my people Israel my anger shall rage against the hostile nation. They shall understand that, against the unjust vengeance of Idumaea, my vengeance was just, says Adonai the Lord.

According to the tropological interpretation, this seems to me to be the meaning. Idumaea is called “earthly” and “fleshly”; it rises up against the spirit so that we may not do the things of the spirit, and it hastens to drag back to itself the soul placed in the midst. It wishes to repay vengeance to the sons of Judah, to whom it had formerly been subject, and remembers the ancient pain of not having been master of itself. Therefore it sought vengeance against those who, departing from the flesh, followed the spirit.

For this reason the Lord himself, as the avenger of the sons of Judah, stretches out his hand against Idumaea and removes from it human being and beast—whatever appears to possess either reason or simple faith—in order to reduce it to solitude.

From Theman, which means “failing,” and Dedan, which likewise signifies kinship, he kills all by the sword. He placed that sword in the hand of his people Israel, so that Edom might be overthrown, feel the Lord’s anger and fury, and understand that his vengeance had served the purpose of making it subject to the house of Judah.

This is what the Apostle also discusses when he writes: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9:13). He loves Jacob because he supplants and overcomes what is fleshly and earthly, and deserves to receive its blessings.

For first we live according to the flesh, and afterward according to the spirit; first in vices, then in virtues by which vices are overthrown, because the inclination of the human heart toward evil from childhood, and the errors of adolescence, are condemned by mature age (Genesis 8). Hence David also says: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Psalm 24:7).

Nevertheless, it must be known that Jacob received the first blessing, and Esau the second. And what is finally said concerning him—“You shall serve your brother” (Genesis 27:40)—signifies that after the flesh has been subjected to the spirit and joined to it, it ceases to be flesh, and Idumaea passes over into Judaea.

(Vv. 15–16.) Thus says the Lord God: Because the Philistines acted in vengeance [Vulgate: “vengeance”], and took revenge with all their heart, killing and fulfilling ancient enmities, therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will stretch out my hand over the Philistines, and kill the killers, and destroy the remnant of the maritime region; and I will execute great acts of vengeance upon them, reproving them in fury, and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have executed my vengeance upon them.

The Septuagint: Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Because the foreigners executed vengeance and stirred up revenge, insulting from the heart, so as to destroy forever, therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I will stretch out my hand over the foreigners, and destroy—or kill—the Cretans, and destroy the remnant of the maritime shore; and I will execute great acts of vengeance upon them in the vengeance of fury, and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord, when I have executed my vengeance upon them.

After the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Seir, who are themselves Edomites and are related by Lot and Esau to the people of Israel and the house of Judah, the prophecy comes to the Philistines, whom the Septuagint translated as *allophyles* (ἀλλόφυλοι), that is, “foreigners”—not by the general name for all nations that are not of Jewish descent, but by the specific name of their own nation, which is now called Palestine. The Hebrew letter *phe* was changed, according to Greek usage, into *pi* (π), just as among us the Hebrew *Phase* () is celebrated in Greek and Latin as *Pascha*.

*Philistines* is interpreted as “those falling by the cup.” They too were intoxicated by Babylon’s golden cup, and they rage, insulting with all their heart as they remember the ancient enmities by which they were separated from the people of God. Although the Lord says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32:35), they themselves take revenge, killing and fulfilling their ancient hatreds. For this they will feel the Lord’s hand stretched out against them, and it will kill the killers.

For this reason the Septuagint, I do not know with what intention, translated *Cretans*, whereas Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated the very Hebrew word *CHORETHIM* (), either as “killers” or “slaughter,” not only in the present passage but also in Zephaniah, where the following is said against the Philistines:

“Gaza shall be plundered, and Ashkelon shall become desolation, and Ashdod [Note: [Col. 0239D] Victorius supplies the following from the Septuagint text itself: ‘and Ashdod shall be expelled at noon, and Ekron [Col. 0240D] shall be uprooted.’] and Ekron shall be uprooted. Woe to the inhabitants of the seacoast, inhabitants of Crete: the word of the Lord is against you, Canaan, land of the foreigners; and I will destroy you from your habitation. And Crete shall become pasture for shepherds and a fold for sheep” (Zeph. 2:4ff.).

Here too, although the Septuagint translated *Crete*, the other translators rendered it as *olethron* (ὄλεθρον) [al. *karron* (κάῤῥον)], that is, “slaughter” or “destruction.” Concerning this, in the prophet mentioned above, God willing, we have said what seemed appropriate to us.

Hence, of David’s two legions, one called *Phelethi* and the other *Cerethi* (2 Sam. 15), the latter received from the fact that they killed and slaughtered the name *Choretim* [al. *Cherethim*], that is, “the killers.”

The Lord destroys all the remnant of the maritime region, which is beaten by salt waves, and he will execute not small but great acts of vengeance in fury, so that his fury may have mercy as its end. After he has executed vengeance, reproving them with fury, then the Philistines will know that he himself is the Lord.

[Col. 0240A] (Cap. XXVI.) And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first [or: one] month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, because Tyre [or: Sor] said concerning Jerusalem, “Aha! The gates of the peoples [or: nations] are broken; she has turned toward me; I shall be filled, for she has been laid waste [or: she that was full has been laid waste],” therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Tyre [or: Sor], and I will bring up against you many nations, as the sea brings up its waves. And they shall destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish its towers, and I will scrape away its dust from it [Vulgate: “from her”], and make her a perfectly clear [or: brilliantly shining] rock. She shall be a place for drying nets in the midst of the sea, for I have spoken, says the Lord God; and she shall become plunder for the nations. Her daughters also who are in the countryside [or: in the field] shall be killed by the sword, and they shall know that I am the Lord.

The order of the prophecy is fittingly continued. He had spoken against the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Seir, who are themselves Edomites, and against the Philistines, who inhabit the coast and occupy the same boundary along the seacoast. After the Philistines comes the region of Phoenicia, whose metropolis is the city of Tyre, called *SOR* () in Hebrew and Syriac.

When Jerusalem was captured, Tyre too rejoiced and insulted her, saying: “The gates of the peoples are broken; I have the safest harbor. Since that city has been overthrown, the whole multitude that was governed by its authority has turned toward me; and because she has been laid waste, I shall be filled”—or, “she that was formerly full shall be reduced to solitude.”

Because you have said this and insulted the ruins of Jerusalem, which was overthrown by God’s judgment on account of its sins, therefore I myself—not messengers or any others—will be against you, Tyre. I will bring up against you, like the waves of the sea, the Babylonians with very many nations. By their assault your walls and towers will be destroyed, so completely that they will fall to the ground; her dust will be scraped away or scattered in various directions by the wind. Thus she will be humbled until she resembles a most brilliant rock. Such solitude will exist in the city, once thronged with people, that fishermen’s nets will be spread out and dried in its midst.

For I, the Lord, have spoken; my words cannot be rendered void. I will give her over to the nations for plunder. Her daughters also, which are in the countryside or in the field—that is, the cities, towns, villages, and fortresses along the Phoenician coast—will be killed by the sword. Metaphorically, because he called them “daughters,” he speaks of their killing by the sword, so that through the outcome of these events they may know that I am the Lord, who commanded them to occur.

According to the tropological interpretation, since the Hebrew name *SOR* is translated as “anguish,” every soul occupied by disturbances may be called *Sor*. When such a soul sees Jerusalem overthrown by God’s judgment on account of its vices and sins—Jerusalem, in which there was the temple and the vision of peace—it rejoices and thinks that the government of the once-famous city is to be transferred to itself.

This may also be understood of contrary doctrines and of worldly people, when they see a holy man fall through negligence: they rejoice and exult, as though another’s ruin were their resurrection. Therefore the Lord threatens that he himself will fight against such people, and will bring up against them, like maritime waves, very many nations that will destroy whatever in them seems most fortified and firm. He will overturn all their arguments so completely that they will be reduced to dust.

He will also cause the nets and seines with which they previously fished for the deceived multitude to cease, and will have them spread out and dried on the ground of the deserted city, so that other fishermen may take their place—those whom the Lord sent out to fish. Her daughters too, which were formerly kept as though in a bridal chamber and were not easily entrusted to anyone because of their mystical and more secret doctrines, will be brought forth and dragged into public view and cut down by the ecclesiastical sword, so that they may understand that he himself is the Lord, who for a short time abandoned Jerusalem on account of its sins and destroyed Tyre’s defenses because of its insult and rejoicing.

296 (Vv. 6ff.) For thus says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0241] Victorius adds “God,” from the Vulgate and Hebrew text]: Behold, I will bring against Tyre [or: against you, SOR] Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, from the north, king of kings, with horses, chariots, and cavalry, and a gathering and a great people. He shall kill your daughters who are in the countryside with the sword, and he shall surround you with fortifications, and pile up a siege-mound around you, and raise a shield against you; and he shall prepare siegeworks and battering rams [or: lances] against your walls, and destroy your towers with his armor. At the flood of his horses he shall cover you with their dust; at the sound of the cavalry, wheels, and chariots your walls shall shake, when he enters your gates as one enters a devastated city [or: as one entering a city from the countryside]. With the hooves of his horses he shall trample all your streets; he shall strike your people with the sword, and your noble statues shall fall to the ground [or: he shall bring the substance of your strength down to the ground]. They shall devastate [or: he shall devastate] your wealth, plunder your merchandise [or: he shall plunder your substance], and destroy [or: he shall destroy] your walls; they shall overthrow [or: he shall overthrow] your splendid [or: desirable] houses; and they shall cast your stones, timber, and dust into the midst of the waters [or: he shall cast them into the midst of the sea]. And I will make the multitude of your singers [Vulgate: “songs”] rest [or: I will destroy the multitude of your musicians], and the sound of your harps [or: the voice of your instruments] shall be heard no more. And I will make you a perfectly clear [or: brilliantly shining] rock. You shall be a place for drying nets, and you shall never be rebuilt, for I have spoken, says the Lord God.

As is my custom, I have combined both editions, placing their differences alongside one another, so as to take account of the brevity of the volumes. Therefore, what he had said—“I will bring up against you many nations, as the sea brings up its waves”—and, “Tyre shall become plunder for the nations,” he now states more explicitly: the Lord will bring Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, from the north, king of kings, with horses and chariots and an innumerable multitude of soldiers.

First he will overthrow the cities and fortresses subject to Tyre along the coast; afterward he will cause Tyre to be besieged, surround it with an army, a siege-mound, and fortifications, and attack and destroy its walls with siegeworks [al. shields] and battering rams. His cavalry will be so numerous that the dust of the horsemen, the sound of the shouting army, the rumbling of wheels, and the neighing of horses will shake the foundations of the city. He will enter the city through its broken walls as though entering the countryside without opposition.

Such confidence will characterize the victorious army that the hooves of the horses will trample the streets of Tyre, the whole population will fall in the midst of the city, and the once-noble statues—or the entire substance of the city—will collapse to the ground. None of its former wealth will remain in the conquered city. Its noble houses too will be destroyed along with its walls, and the cruelty of the victors will be so great that the timber and stones left over from the fire will be thrown into the middle of the sea.

Either Nebuchadnezzar or the Lord himself will make all the city’s rejoicing cease—the rejoicing that had previously resounded in songs and psalteries. Overthrown down to the ground, it will become a place for drying nets.

The following statement—“You shall never be rebuilt”—seems to raise a question: how has it not been rebuilt, when today we see a most famous and beautiful city of Phoenicia? For this reason some wish to interpret these words as referring to Tyre’s suffering at the end of time, after which it will not be rebuilt.

But how will they be able to preserve the role of Nebuchadnezzar, especially since we read in what follows that Nebuchadnezzar attacked Tyre but did not receive the reward for his labor, and that Egypt was therefore given to him because he had served God’s judgment in the attack on Tyre?

They say that they have read Greek and Phoenician histories—especially those of Nicolaus of Damascus—and other histories of the barbarians that contradict this account, but that they found nothing concerning the Chaldeans’ attack on the city of Tyre. Yet we can demonstrate that Scripture often reports events that are not found in Greek books; nor should we submit to the authority of those whose faithlessness and lies we detest.

The statement “You shall never be rebuilt” may therefore be understood to mean that she will never again be queen of peoples or possess her own sovereignty, as she did under Hiram and the other kings. Instead, she will serve Chaldean, Macedonian, Ptolemaic, and finally Roman kings.

No one, however, who follows the allegorical interpretation doubts that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who comes from the north, signifies the devil. Although he is a harsh and baleful wind, he is called by the name “right hand,” arrogating to himself the dignity of that name. He is the king of kings and of all the kingdoms that he showed to the Lord, saying to him: “All these things have been delivered to me, and I will give them to you if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

He has horses and chariots, concerning which it is written: “The horse is a false hope for salvation” (Ps. 32:17); and, “All who mounted horses fell asleep” (Ps. 75). Elsewhere: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. 15:1).

He kills the daughters of Tyre—souls placed in anguish and in a kind of prison of sins—in the broadest field and countryside. He surrounds Tyre with his fortifications so as to hold her shut, so that no one can escape from her the authority of the Babylonian king.

He will destroy her walls and overthrow her towers. Whatever strength she possessed in her doctrines will tremble at the flood of his horses, the sound of his cavalry, and the noise of wheels and chariots. He will enter her gates without anyone preventing him, and the streets of the city—because “broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. 7:13)—will be trampled by his horses’ hooves.

He will cast down to the ground the whole substance of the city, or the noble statues by which they had fashioned images of falsehood for themselves, concerning which it is written: “Lord, in your city you will destroy their images” (Ps. 72:20). When the walls have been destroyed, the noble houses too, which she had prepared for herself and in which she rejoiced, will be overthrown.

She will come into such desolation that her stones and timbers, with which she had built her walls and constructed her masonry, will be cast into the depths. Her songs and music, in which she trusted because of the wisdom of this age, and every sound of her harps, will no longer be heard. Her fishing will cease, and she will be humbled, becoming a place for drying nets and never being rebuilt again, because, delivered over to the judgment of the Lord, she has been utterly overthrown. Hence the Apostle says: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20).

These are difficult passages, and a prudent and diligent reader should pardon my labor. Or, if someone can discover something better, I too will adopt his judgment—provided that he understands that the forgiveness he grants me he will receive from others.

(Vv. 15ff.) Thus says the Lord God to Tyre: Will not the islands be shaken at the sound of your downfall and the groaning of your slain, when those killed have fallen in your midst? And all the princes of the sea shall descend from their thrones; they shall remove their robes of office and cast off their variegated garments, and they shall clothe themselves with astonishment. They shall sit on the ground, and, stunned, shall marvel at your sudden collapse. They shall take up a lament over you and say to you: How have you perished, you who dwell in the sea, famous city, which were strong in the sea with your inhabitants, whom everyone feared? Now the ships shall be stunned on the day of your terror, and the islands in the sea shall be troubled, because no one is coming out of you.

The Septuagint: For thus says the Lord God to Sor: Will not the islands be shaken at the sound of your downfall, when your wounded groan, when the sword has been drawn in your midst? And all the princes of the sea shall descend from their thrones, and they shall remove their crowns and strip off their variegated garments. They shall rage in fury; they shall sit on the ground and fear their destruction. They shall groan over you and take up a lament over you, and say to you: How have you perished and been destroyed in the sea, celebrated city, which were strong in the sea, you and your inhabitants, who inspired fear in all your inhabitants? The islands shall fear on the day of your downfall, and the islands in the sea shall be troubled at your departure.

First let us set forth the words of the history in a very brief *metaphrase* (μετάφρασις), explaining the meaning of what has been said.

Thus says Adonai the Lord to Tyre, which is called *SOR* () in Hebrew: On the day of your downfall, when you collapse under Nebuchadnezzar’s attack, and amid the groaning of the wounded or slain who will be killed in your midst, will not the islands be shaken?

All the kings and princes of the sea, who rule over various islands, will descend from their seats or thrones. They will remove the diadems from their heads, laying aside all the glory of kingship, and cast away from themselves their most precious garments, resplendent with incredible variety. Overcome by the magnitude of their astonishment, they will become almost insane. Cast down in humility, they will sit on the ground, and when they see you fallen, they will fear a similar fate for themselves. They will think that nothing among earthly goods is everlasting.

Instead, they will take up a lament over you and recall a mournful song, saying: “How have you perished, you who dwell [al. dwelt] in the sea, famous or celebrated city?”

We read in Greek, Latin, and barbarian histories that Tyre was once an island and had no entrance from the mainland. Later, however, either Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, or, as some assert, Alexander, king of the Macedonians, cast up embankments by means of siegeworks and battering rams, preparing a passage to the island and making a peninsula out of it.

You, therefore, O Sor, O Tyre, who were once the strongest of all islands—or celebrated by everyone among all cities—together with your inhabitants, whom all feared, how have you suddenly fallen?
