Now the islands shall be astonished or afraid on your account, and, as it is better expressed in the Hebrew, the ships shall be astonished on the day of your terror and downfall; and the islands in the sea shall be troubled. Hence it is more coherent to read “ships” above, so that “islands” is not repeated twice. This is because no one will come out of you—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “on the day of your departure,” when you have been led captive.

Let these things meanwhile serve as foundations laid for the historical interpretation. Now let us strive to place upon them a spiritual summit.

Imagine someone who, having preserved his chastity for a long time and flourished in many virtues, afterward falls into some grave and mortal sin. Will not all the islands be shaken at the sound of his downfall and of the virtues he has killed—namely, those who are battered by the salty and bitter waves of this age?

All who seemed to be princes amid the saltiness of this world will descend from the throne of their pride. Cast down in humility, they will remove from their heads the diadems that they seemed to possess through good works, cast away their variegated garments—the varied forms of virtue—and clothe themselves with astonishment. Because of the magnitude of their fear, they will appear almost insane.

They will sit on the ground and, stunned by his sudden fall, will marvel at it, so that all take up weeping and lamentation over the one who has fallen and say: “How have you perished, you who were formerly safe? How have you fallen, you who stood for so long, who in the sea of this age were considered famous among all, who in everyone’s judgment were strong?”

And your inhabitants—that is, the strongest thoughts resisting all the fiery darts of the devil, which formerly inspired fear in all adversaries—have been turned into astonishment.

The ships too, namely all the saints who cross the waves of this age, will be stunned when they see you collapse. On the day of your terror and downfall the islands will be troubled, lest they themselves suffer similar things.

The fall of others serves as an example to the righteous, while we all remain in this age with a frail and weak condition and an unsteady step; our victory is never certain and secure. This is true when those who formerly stood go out from you—or “at your departure,” at your end and completion. For we are judged not by what is past but by what is present. We must beware and always fear lest the storm of a single hour overthrow ancient glory and solid firmness.

(Vv. 19ff.) For thus says the Lord [Vulgate adds: “God”]: When I make you a desolate city, like cities that are not inhabited, and bring the abyss over you, and many waters cover you, and drag you down with those who descend into the pit [or: to those who descend into the pit], to the everlasting people, and place you in the farthest land [or: in the depths of the earth], like ancient solitudes, with those who are led down into the pit [or: descend into the pit], so that you may not be inhabited, and when I give glory in the land of the living [or: so that you may not rise again in the land of the living], I will reduce you to nothing [or: give you over to destruction], and you shall not exist, and you shall not be found when sought [Vulgate adds: “any longer”] forever, says the Lord God.

Join these words with what was said above. When I make you, O Tyre, a city desolate forever, like other cities that are not inhabited at all; when I bring the abyss over you and many waters cover you—whether these mean the immeasurable multitude of enemies, or, more literally, since he is speaking to an island and to a city established on an island, when he compares the multitude of adversaries to the waves of the abyss—and when I drag you down with those who descend into the pit, or into the place of the dead, to those who are in hell, concerning whom we also read in the Psalms:

“They shall enter the lower parts of the earth; they shall be handed over to the power of the sword; they shall become a portion for foxes” (Ps. 62:10–11),

to the everlasting people, where there is weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth; and when I place you in the farthest land, where the ancient dragon has been established, like ancient solitudes and deserts, where there is no remembrance of good things but everlasting punishments; and when I do not raise you up in the land of the living, of which it is written, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4), and elsewhere, “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:9)—then you shall be reduced to nothing, or perish forever, and shall exist no longer, according to what is written in another psalm: “Let me recover, before I depart and exist no longer” (Ps. 38:14).

This does not mean that the one who is in everlasting punishments ceases to exist; rather, Scripture says that the one who does not live for God does not subsist. Hence Esther too, speaking against idols, says: “Do not hand over your scepter to those who are not” (Esther 14). Certainly those for whom she begs not to have it handed over did exist; but they were not for God, since they had ceased to exist in virtue and for the living God.

It should also be noted that Tyre is sought by the one who came to seek and save what had perished, and who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains, seeks the one wandering sheep (Luke 19). The woman too who had lost one drachma seeks it, finds it, and calls her neighbors to share her joy (ibid., 15).

But if Tyre, when sought, is not found, the fault is not in the one who seeks, but in the one who has fled the hand of the good shepherd. “And you shall exist no longer,” he says, “forever”—or, as it is written in Hebrew, *LOLAM*, and in Greek, αἰών, which signifies one age, according to Isaiah, who says that after seventy years Tyre will be restored to its former condition (Isa. 23).

They say that one age—that is, the span of human life—is reckoned by the number seventy, as the Psalmist says: “The days of our years are seventy; and if, because of strength, eighty years, yet what exceeds this is labor and sorrow” (Ps. 89:10).

We have said this briefly, in *metaphrase*, about Tyre. It may also be referred to those who, established in the anguish of this age, are led down to hell, covered by the abysses and waves of punishments, dragged into the lower regions of the earth, joined to those who are in the ancient solitude, and led down into the everlasting pit or ditch, so that they may no longer be inhabited by the Holy Spirit.

Concerning them it is written: “When the wicked falls into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). They will no longer be in the land of the living, but will perish, be reduced to nothing, and cease to exist for God.

Those who say that the punishments of the wicked, but not of sinners, are everlasting misuse these testimonies. [Note: [Col. 0245D] We have discussed this matter at greater length at the end of the commentaries on Isaiah and in *Dialogue 1 Against the Pelagians*, no. 28. In Jerome’s view, two classes of the condemned must be distinguished: some, whom he calls “the wicked,” are assigned to eternal punishments; others, whom he calls “sinners”—either those who will repent of their sins or those burdened by lesser crimes—are assigned to punishments that will one day end. The confused and inconvenient reading formerly said: “who say that the punishments of the wicked and sinners are not everlasting.” The Vatican manuscripts and Rabanus assisted us in restoring the true reading.] Those who were sought by God were not found and ceased to exist forever, because by their own fault they lost the one who says: “I am life” (John 14:6).

(Cap. XXVII.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: You therefore, son of man, raise a lament over Tyre, and say to Tyre, which dwells at the entrance of the sea and conducts the commerce of the peoples with many islands [or: from many islands]: Thus says the Lord God.

If I wished to encompass the whole prophecy against Tyre, or the lamentation over Tyre, in a single discourse, I would make it long and obscure the reader’s understanding, since the mind cannot retain everything at once—especially because in this passage the Septuagint differs from the Hebrew edition in what it adds and what it omits.

Therefore we shall be content with our own translation, and wherever the versions differ we shall place them alongside one another, leaving the perfect knowledge of all things to God [Note: [Col. 0247D] This is also how our manuscripts read after Victorius. Martianay, following Erasmus, gives the sentence in this form.]. We shall briefly indicate what seems to us to be the meaning of each point.

The one who is mourned is still cared for by the one who mourns him. Thus Samuel wept and lamented over Saul (2 Sam. 15), and the Apostle Paul laments and grieves over those who committed fornication and did not repent (2 Cor. 12). Jeremiah too writes four alphabetic Lamentations over the destruction of Jerusalem.

Literally, therefore, Tyre or Sor dwells at the entrance of the sea—either because it was formerly an island or because, with its very safe harbor, it receives ships coming from the open sea—and it conducts the commerce of the peoples with many islands or from many islands. This commerce continues to the present day, so that the trade of almost all nations is carried on there.

Following the interpretation already begun, let us refer everything said about Tyre to *synochē* (συνοχή), that is, to the anguish of this world, which lies in wickedness and is constricted and battered by various disturbances as by waves. Of such merchants the mystical language of the Psalm also speaks:

“Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business on many waters, these have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. 106:23–24).

(V. 3.) O Tyre, you have said, “I am of perfect beauty” [or: “You have said, ‘I have surrounded myself with beauty’”], and you are situated in the heart of the sea.

Tyre’s first crime is that, if she seems to possess anything good, she does not regard it as God’s but as her own, and considers all the beauty that comes to her from various regions to be the result of her own diligence and virtue. For she said, “I am of perfect beauty,” or, “I have surrounded myself with beauty,” although she is situated in the heart—that is, in the midst—of the sea, and, like an island, is tossed about and fluctuates and is broken by the battering of the waves.

That “the heart of the sea” signifies the middle is also demonstrated by the prophetic utterance:

“Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is troubled and the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea. Its waters roared and were troubled” (Ps. 45:2–3).

Our Lord too is said to have descended into the heart of the earth—that is, into the middle of it—and to the underworld.

True and perfect beauty is found in no human being except in the body of Christ, which is interpreted as the Church, and is gathered together in the virtues of many saints. Hence he himself speaks to the bride: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4:7).

[Col. 0248A] (Vv. 4–5.) Your neighbors who built you have filled your beauty. With fir trees from Sanir they built you, with all the planks of the sea. They took cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] The verse that follows in its proper place from the Septuagint interpretation had here also been inserted, improperly and inconveniently with respect to the sequence of the discourse. We have deleted it in accordance with the manuscripts and will discuss it once in its proper place.]

For this the Septuagint, I do not know with what intention, translated as follows: “Beelim, your sons, surrounded you with beauty; a cedar from Sanir was built for you; they brought thin cypress boards from Lebanon to make fir-wood masts for you.”

The word *Beelim* is not found at all in this passage among the Hebrews. Instead of *Beelim*, *GEBULAIC* is written, meaning “your boundaries.” In saying “your sons” as well, they were deceived by the ambiguity of the word and by the similarity of the writing: with different pronunciation, the same letters are read as *BONAICH* and *BENAICH* (), meaning “your masons” [or: “your builders”] and “your sons.”

O Tyre, therefore, who said in your pride, “I am of perfect beauty,” or, “I have surrounded myself with beauty,” although you are situated in the middle of the sea, hear how much has been bestowed upon you by God’s generosity. Your neighbors and those who share your borders—those who come not from distant but from nearby regions—have filled your beauty, and you think that what belongs to another is yours.

He speaks metaphorically, as though to a ship, signifying the beauty of the city and its abundance in all things. After describing all its equipment—the mast, yards, oars, sails, prow, keel, ropes, coverings, skins, and everything else required by well-equipped ships—he then announces that a storm and a south wind will come upon it, by which the greatest waves will be stirred, and that it will be exposed to shipwreck.

Through these things he signifies the overthrow of the city of Tyre by King Nebuchadnezzar or, as many think, by Alexander, king of the Macedonians, who is said to have besieged and captured the city after defeating Darius in Lycia, and to have besieged it for six months.

According to the mystical interpretation, the planks of the Tyrian ship are cut from fir trees or cedars of Sanir; with these the ship is covered and fitted together. Its mast is made of cedar or cypress from Lebanon [Note: [Col. 0248D] Victorius supplies, with the help of certain manuscripts, the word “is raised.”]

The fir trees are used because of the smoothness [al. lightness] and the joints of the planks, which hold and grip one another more gently; or cedars are used because that wood is imperishable.

Sanir, they say, is interpreted as “the way of the lamp,” or, as we more correctly think, “the tooth of the watches,” because the entire prosperity and illumination of the ship has come from the true light.

Literally, Sanir is the mountain that is also called Hermon, which others call Sanior. Read the history.

Lebanon is interpreted as “brightness” or “whitening,” which likewise pertains to grace coming from elsewhere.

### (Verse 6.) The oaks of Bashan fashioned your oars; they made your benches for you of Indian ivory, and your cabins from the islands of Italy.

The Septuagint: “From Bashan they made your oars, your temples, and they made for you, from the ivory of the wooded regions of the islands of Chettiim, houses.”

How great was the beauty of the ship and its equipment, that it should have cedar oars—not from just anywhere, but from Bashan—ivory benches, and cabins, or storerooms in which the most precious merchandise is kept, from the islands of Chettiim, which we translate as Italy, understanding by it the region nearer to Greece and all the islands of the western peoples.

Let us therefore speak according to the allegorical sense. The oars of the Tyrian ship are made from Bashan, concerning which it is also written in the Psalms: “The Lord said, ‘From Bashan I will turn them back, I will turn them back from the depths of the sea’” (Ps. 67:23). Bashan in our language is interpreted as “shame.” God therefore turns back those who were in the depths of the sea and in the shame of sins, and turns them into oars, so that, sailing with the Apostles, they may reach the land and the shores. Benches are made of ivory when they have put their bodies to death, or when they have devoted the use of their teeth to the praises of God. Cabins, or storerooms, are made from the islands of Chettiim, which, according to the etymology of the Hebrew language, is translated as “struck,” so that the person is not so much killed by the blows of the devil as tested by them.

We can also understand the ivory houses and the wooded houses to be from the islands of Chettiim, which heretics try to build not in the house of God but in the Tyrian ship. They possess the ivory of their speech and, building temples with their tongues, construct buildings opposed to the temple of God, as well as wooded houses—habitations of beasts—although Scripture says that groves, forests, and sacred woods are not to be planted in the house of God (Deut. 12).

[Col. 0249C] (Verse 7.) “Fine linen, woven with variegated work from Egypt, was made for you as a sail, to be placed on the mast; violet and purple from the islands of Elisa became your covering.”

The Septuagint: “Fine linen with variegated work from Egypt was made for you as a bedding, to surround your glory and cover you. Violet and purple from the islands of Elissa became your coverings.”

Because Tyre had said, “I am perfect in beauty,” or, “I myself have surrounded myself with beauty,” she is reproved for what she received from each region, according to that saying of Scripture: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

It is therefore described what each province sends, according to Virgil’s words (Georgics, Book 1):

> India sends ivory; the soft Sabaeans their fragrant incense;  
> But the harsh Chalybes send iron, and Pontus sends  
> Its poisonous castoreum, and so forth.

Fine linen grows especially abundantly in Egypt. From it the sail of the Tyrian ship is woven, suspended from the mast. Its covering, which in the heat of the sun and in calm weather provides shade for the sailors and passengers, is made of violet and purple. These are from the islands of Elisa, the name by which he calls the islands of the Ionian Sea.

According to the Septuagint, however, coverings are woven from fine linen as a bed and resting place for the Tyrian ship, so that, covered with them, it may be more glorious and, wrapped in them, may have a more beautiful garment.

We have often pointed out that fine linen refers to the earth, because it arises from the earth; violet to the air; and purple to the sea, from which it is produced. Scarlet, twice dyed, is added to these, and from them the vestments of the High Priest are woven. They signify the four elements: earth, fire, air, and water, from which everything consists. Tyre takes these to herself so that she may not use God’s creatures with thanksgiving, but say, “I am perfect in beauty,” or, “I myself have surrounded myself with beauty.”

[Col. 0250B] (Verses 8, 9.) “The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad were your rowers. Your wise men, Tyre, became your pilots. The elders of Byblos and its wise men provided sailors for you to serve your varied equipment. All the ships of the sea and their sailors were among your people in your commerce.”

The Septuagint: “Your princes dwelt in Sidon, and those of Arvad were your rowers. Your wise men, Tyre, who were in you, these were your pilots. The elders of Byblos and its wise men were in you; these strengthened your counsel. All the ships of the sea and their rowers became yours, toward the West of the West.”

Above he had said: “Your neighbors who built you filled your beauty.” Before coming to those who live far away, he describes the assistance of the neighboring provinces.

“Your inhabitants,” he says—or your princes—of Sidon and Arvad, which is a neighboring island, were your rowers. Your wise men, O Tyre, became your pilots. Governance properly belongs to the wise, as Scripture says: “Where there is no guidance, they fall like leaves” (Prov. 11, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Col. 0249D. Consult Scaliger in the Appendix to his book *On the Correction of Times*. Victorius also wishes *Biblii* to be read above and below in accordance with the Hebrew [reading lost in the supplied text], and holds that the Septuagint’s Βιβλίων arose through scribal error for Γιβλίων. Jerome, however, settles the whole question in Eusebius’s *Book of Places*, under the letter B, from the books of Kings: “Byblos,” he says, “is a Phoenician city mentioned by Ezekiel, for which the Hebrew has GOBEL.” Thus the Biblii and the Giblii are the same. See 3 Kings 5, at the end.]

The elders, or seniors, of Byblos and its prudent men provided sailors for your service, or strengthened the counsel of Tyre and provided varied equipment. All the ships of the sea and their sailors belonged to the people of Tyre’s commerce, or “to the West of the West.”

This is according to the literal sense for the moment. According to the mystical interpretations, however, since Sidonians are interpreted as “hunters” and Arvadites as “those who bring down,” we shall say that Tyre, the glorious and most arrogant city, which, when the wind blows, is afterward to be crushed, has citizens or princes who are hunters, of whom it is written: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters.”

Where we read “of the hunters,” the Hebrew has “of the Sidonians.”

[Note: Cols. 0249D–0251D. In citing this testimony from the Psalm to prove that Sidonians is rendered “hunters,” the holy Doctor seems to have relied on memory and neglected to consult the Hebrew exemplar. In all manuscripts the Hebrew here reads *Jocesim*, not *Sidonim*, as he says; *Joces* means “fowler,” while “hunter” is properly *Saiad*. Hence, more correctly, in the *Book of Names*, Sidon is interpreted “hunter of sorrow.” Yet, says Victor, Jerome asserts this so constantly that I am inclined to believe not that his memory slipped, but that the Hebrew text has since been altered. Below, in chapter 28: “Sidonians,” he says, “are interpreted ‘hunters,’ of whom it is also written in the Psalms: ‘Our soul, like a sparrow,’ etc.” And in chapter 32: “In the Hebrew it is more correctly written, ‘all the Sidonians,’ whom we render ‘hunters,’ according to what is written: ‘Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of hunters’; whereas in the Hebrew ‘of the Sidonians’ is written.”]

These people hunt unwary souls set in high places, in order to drag them down to earthly things, and they become rowers, so as to lead them to shipwreck. The wise men of Tyre, who are understood in the evil sense—through whom the children of darkness are wiser than the children of light—they themselves pilot Tyre, which has been prepared for shipwreck (Luke 16).

The elders of Byblos and its prudent men provided sailors for Tyre’s service, or strengthened its counsel. Sacred history relates that many elders were rejected by the Lord and younger men chosen, as a type of the Synagogue and the Church. The elder Cain is rejected and the younger Abel chosen (Gen. 4); Ishmael, Abraham’s son, is alienated from his father, while the younger Isaac receives the inheritance (Gen. 21). Among Isaac’s sons also, the elder Esau is a hunter and wanders in the forests, while the younger Jacob dwells simply at home (Gen. 25). Hence it is written in Malachi as well: “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau” (Mal. 1:2).

And rightly, according to the Apostle (Rom. 9:13), while they were in their mother’s womb they had done nothing good or evil, nor had they any merit or offense, so that one might be chosen and the other rejected. Rather, as we have said, in the type of the Synagogue and the Church, the elder is rejected and the younger taken up.

“All the ships of the sea,” he says, “and their sailors were among the people of Tyre’s commerce, or toward the West of the West.” Just as one says “Song of Songs,” “age of ages,” and “work of works,” so that one song is greater than other songs, one age longer than other ages, and one work more useful than other works, so “West of the West” is named to signify the magnitude of the western regions.

And beautifully, the ships of the sea, their sailors, and the rowers who assist the Tyrian ship do not proceed toward the East, nor toward the rising of the light where the Sun of righteousness is born, but toward the West of the West, where the light sets and where the beginning of darkness is.

(Verses 10.) “Persians, Lydians, and Libyans were in your army, your warrior men; they hung shield and helmet on you for your adornment”—or, “They hung bucklers and helmets on you; they themselves gave you your glory.”

Both sacred and secular history relate that the Persians were very powerful, and that their king Cyrus, as Isaiah’s prophecy foretells (Isa. 45), overthrew Astyages, king of the Medes, and captured Babylon. Xenophon writes in great detail that the Lydians also were then considered among the strongest nations, and that their king Croesus was captured by the same Cyrus. We read in the book of Chronicles that the Libyans came against Jerusalem with the Troglodytes and Ethiopians (2 Chron. 12). Because they were then flourishing and famous warriors in battle, they are remembered as defenders of the city of Tyre, who hung shields and helmets between the battlements of the walls to terrify their enemies.

The spiritual meaning, however, is that the Persians, who are interpreted as “those who test” or “those who are tested”; the Lydians, whom we understand as “those who are begotten”; and the Libyans, who in Hebrew are called PHUT () and are translated as “mouth” (from the mouth, not from the bone), strive in vain to defend Tyre, since they are overcome by temptation and serve generation and lust, multiplying only empty words. They do not possess the helmet of salvation or the shield of faith (Eph. 6), but display only the glory and clamor of words as her adornment.

(Verses 11.) “The sons of Arvad, with your army—or, with his army—were upon your walls all around. The Pygmies who were in your towers also hung their quivers upon your walls all around; they themselves completed your beauty.”

[Note: Cols. 0251D–0252D. Following the manuscripts, and after Victorius, we restore “towers,” in accordance with the Hebrew and Jerome’s Latin translation. Martianus, with Erasmus, retained “cities.”]

The Septuagint: “The sons of the Arvadites and your strength were upon your walls; guards were all around in your towers. They hung their quivers upon your battlements all around. They themselves perfected your beauty.”

The word GAMADIM (), in the first edition of Aquila, is translated “Pygmies”; Symmachus, “Medes”; the Septuagint, “guards”; Theodotion, “Gomadim,” retaining the Hebrew word.

[Note: Col. 0252D. Symmachus easily read two words, *Gam madim*, “but also Medes,” instead of the one word *Gamadim*. The Archinto manuscript reads: “Theodotion, Gomodim itself,” etc.—Theodotion read *Gomadim*, not *Gammadim*, as was wrongly printed in earlier books. Martianus.]

The island of Arvad, which is entirely a city and has the town of Antaradus opposite it, is near Tyre and extends toward the Phoenician coast of the mainland. We see it to this day. Its inhabitants are in the army of the city of Tyre and are guardians of its towers. They hung their quivers all around and complete its beauty, so that they may be shown to be archers. Or perhaps they are Pygmies—that is, warriors and men most ready for battle—ἀπὸ τῆς πυγμῆς, a Greek expression referring to combat.

But if Arvadites means “those who bring down,” anyone who displays knowledge bearing a false name and carries in the quiver of his breast the flaming arrows of the devil, with which he wounds and inflames the hearts of the deceived, should be called an Arvadite. He wants to bring down those who strive to climb to lofty things, and he completes the beauty of Tyre, concerning whom it is written in Proverbs: “Do not let desire for beauty deceive you, lest you be captured by your eyes” (Prov. 6:25). And again: “Like a gold ornament in a pig’s snout, so is beauty in a woman of bad character” (ibid. 11:22).

(Verses 12.) “The Carthaginians were your merchants; because of the abundance of all kinds of wealth, with silver, iron, tin, and lead they filled your markets.”

Not only in the present passage, but also in Isaiah, where it is written, “Wail, ships of Carthage” (Isa. 23:14), the other interpreters translated the Hebrew word THARSIS (), which is undoubtedly a colony of the Tyrians. From the regions of the West they filled the markets of Tyre with silver, iron, tin, and lead.

Tarsis in our language means “an exploration of joy.” Here, however, we must understand “explorers” not in the good sense, like those whom Moses sent to explore the promised land (Num. 13), but in the opposite sense, like those whom the Apostle says he avoids: “Because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who came in to spy out our freedom which we have in Christ” (Gal. 2:4); and those of whom Joseph says: “You are spies; you have come to observe the tracks of the land” (Gen. 42:9). His brothers, recognizing that it was no small crime to spy out another’s affairs by treachery, replied: “Your servants are not spies.”

These people therefore multiply the markets of Tyre not with gold or precious stones, but with silver, iron, tin, and lead. They possess elegance of speech and weapons for assault; tin represents the likeness of eloquence, which falsely imitates silver; and lead represents the gravest impiety, according to Zechariah (Zech. 5), in which a woman sits upon a talent of lead, and the Egyptians are submerged in the depths like lead.

A lengthy discussion of the individual metals would be required, but we must pursue brevity.

(Verses 13, 14.) “Greece, Tubal, and Meshech were your merchants; they brought slaves and bronze vessels to your people. From the house of Togarmah they brought horses, horsemen, and mules to your marketplace.”

The Septuagint: “All Greece and its neighboring regions were your merchants in human lives, and they gave bronze vessels to your market. From the house of Thorgama they gave horses, horsemen, and mules to your markets.”

The Ionians, who in Hebrew are called Javan, and Tubal—that is, the eastern Iberians, or the Spaniards from the western regions, who are called by this name from the river Iberus—and Meshech, whom we understand as the Cappadocians, whose capital, later called Caesarea by the Emperor Augustus, is still called Mazaca in their language: these people made Tyre’s commerce valuable, bringing slaves and bronze vessels from Corinth to Tyre. From the house of Togarmah—that is, from Phrygia—they brought horses, horsemen, and mules, of which that province once possessed a very great supply.

The Hebrews say that Greece, that is, Javan, is interpreted as “is” and “is not.”

[Note: Col. 0253D. Concerning this Hieronymian etymology and interpretation of the word Javan, I had said something in vol. II, col. 338; I could not please John Clericus in his Plautine wisdom. Yet it does not matter to me that such an adversary was displeased, provided I please learned and kindly readers. Martianus.]

[Note: Cols. 0253D–0254D. He says, therefore, that the name Javan is expounded thus not in his own view but according to the Hebrews. The Hebrews, a people born for devising etymologies, somehow forced it out of the terms for “is,” “and,” and “not,” as Martianus observed. One should note, however, that this etymology is forced and false, and that Javan derives its name from a supplied Hebrew term [lost in the supplied text], whose root [lost in the supplied text] signifies “beautiful.”]

This properly refers to secular wisdom: when it discovers something correctly, it is called “is”; when it proceeds in the opposite direction, it is called “is not.” For they discuss many matters in accordance with the good of nature, concerning duties, self-control, and contempt for riches. The Stoics especially claim these matters for themselves, and they seem to profit by the souls of those whom they have deceived. They have bronze vessels with which they counterfeit the appearance of gold, and they thrust these upon the people of Tyre in order to overthrow them through belief in false doctrine.

From the house of Togarmah as well, which is interpreted as “foreigner” and “newcomer,” horses, horsemen, and mules will be brought to its marketplace and markets. Concerning these it is written: “The horse is deceptive for salvation” (Ps. 32:17); and elsewhere: “All who mounted horses slumbered” (Ps. 75:7); and in the Psalms: “Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

Therefore Doeg, the accuser and murderer of the priests, was also chief over many (2 Sam. 22), and these are from the house of the foreigner and newcomer, who do not eat the flesh of the lamb, concerning whom it is written: “The foreigner and the hired servant shall not eat of it” (Exod. 12:43). Thus all the markets of Tyre are filled with these commodities.

“The sons of Dadan were your merchants.”

For this the Septuagint, wishing perhaps to say something else, translated “sons of the Rhodians”—unless perhaps, because of the similarity of the first letters ( and ), they read Radan instead of Dadan. Radan itself is the largest of the Cyclades and was once a most powerful city in the Ionian Sea, renowned for naval combat and, because of its very safe harbor, a refuge for all merchants.

Since the Rhodians are translated in our language as “those who see judgment,” the passage may now be understood tropologically of those who perceive the truth of judgment but do not practice it, as the Apostle says: “Therefore you are without excuse, O man, everyone who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2:1).

But it is better to take DADAN as the name of another place, as it is found both in the Hebrew and among the other interpreters.

[Col. 0254C] (Verses 15, 16.) “Many islands were the commerce of your hand; they exchanged ivory tusks and ebony for your merchandise. Syria was your merchant because of the abundance of your works; they offered stacte, purple, embroidered cloth, fine linen, silk, and Chodchod—or, according to the Vulgate, scarlet—in your market.”

[Note: Col. 0254D. Victorius prefers, in keeping with the character of the Vulgate, that “a gem” be read. The Hebrew below, in chapter 28, is rendered “carbuncle,” and so elsewhere.]

The Septuagint: “From the islands they multiplied your commerce; ivory tusks, and to those who were brought in you gave your wages. Men carried on your commerce because of the abundance of your market. In Aphec, stacte, and figured cloth from Tharsis, Ramoth, and Chodchod they gave [goods] to your markets.”

The Septuagint differs greatly from the Hebrew in this passage. Therefore a few things must be said according to both versions, lest, occupied with the merchandise of Tyre, we proceed too slowly to the remaining prophecies.

The sons of Dadan, merchants of Tyre, multiplied its commerce from many islands, so that they gave elephant tusks to those who came to trade with it, and had men in its markets because of the abundance of its commerce.

They had goods in Aphec, which was added to the Septuagint from Theodotion’s edition; Symmachus translated it as “figured cloth.”

[Note: Cols. 0254D–0255D. Theodotion in fact translated ἐν Ναφέχ, “in Naphech.” For the Latin *in Aphech* and Greek ἐν Ἀφέχ should be read *Naphech* in accordance with the Hebrew: the error arose from the concurrence of two N’s, one of which scribes mistakenly omitted.] They also had stacte, for which all the others interpreted “purple,” called ARGAMAN () in Hebrew; and variegated cloth from Tharsis, for which the Hebrew has BUS (), translated by everyone as “fine linen.” Tharsis itself is not found at all in the present passage.

“And Ramoth,” they say, “and Chodchod they gave in your markets.” This is how it stands in the Hebrew, except that Aquila translated Ramoth as “silk” or “fine fabrics.” Chodchod, however, all the interpreters translated exactly as it is written in the Hebrew ().

According to the Septuagint, therefore, the sons of the Rhodians, merchants of Tyre, multiplied its commerce from many islands. According to the Hebrew, after the sons of Dadan, its merchants, the islands of various peoples also increased its trade, bringing ivory tusks from India and ebony wood, which is extremely precious because of its black color, and exchanging them for other Tyrian goods.

Syria was also a merchant of Tyre. The Hebrew has ARAM (), but the Septuagint translated it as “men,” reading ADAM instead of ARAM because of the similarity between the letters RES and DALETH, as above.

To this day the innate passion for commerce persists among the Syrians. They travel throughout the whole world in their desire for profit and pursue trade with such madness that, now that they have occupied the Roman world, they seek wealth amid swords and the deaths of wretched people, and flee poverty through dangers.

Such people are merchants of Tyre. They trade in figured cloth, purple, and embroidered fabrics; they offer fine linen, silk, and Chodchod in its market. In place of purple, which all the others translated, the Septuagint rendered stacte—that is, “a drop.” What Chodchod signifies I have not yet been able to discover.

[Note: Cols. 0255D–0256D. Jerome himself translated it “jasper” in Isaiah 54:12, saying in his commentary: “Where we, following the Septuagint, said ‘jasper,’ the Hebrew has Chodchod, which Symmachus alone translated καρχηδόνιον.” Most later interpreters indeed hold that it denotes a precious stone. Victorius, who translates it “sapphire,” is more approving.]

The Hebrews say that all the most precious merchandise is signified by this name, or that it is a certain kind of precious merchandise for which the Roman language has no equivalent, or a common term used by sellers of miscellaneous goods.

From many islands—so that we may pass to the allegorical sense, for these islands are battered by the salty or bitter waves of this age—the merchants of Dadan bring ivory tusks, promising the whiteness of eloquence. Concerning them it is written: “From ivory houses, out of which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor” (Ps. 45:9).

But they are not white, nor do they imitate the bride of whom it is said: “Who is this who comes up whitened, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5). Rather, they are black like ebony and cannot change their blackness, as Jeremiah says: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?” (Jer. 13:23).

Syria also—that is, Aram, which is interpreted as “exalted” and swells with pride—is a merchant of Tyre. In the abundance of Tyre’s works it carries false-named knowledge, many varieties, and promises stacte of excellent fragrance, purple of royal dignity, embroidered cloth produced by the art of dialectic, and fine linen, for which the Septuagint interpreted Tharsis, devoted to works of the earth.

It also carries silk, for which the Hebrew has RAMOTH (), interpreted as “vision of death.” For all earthly works hasten toward destruction. And it offers Chodchod—whatever it may be understood to mean—in the markets of Tyre.

Dadan, from the merchandise said to be brought by its merchants and islands, may be understood either as the region of India or, as some judge, as the Idumeans and the vast wilderness. Its name sounds like “kinship,” so that in heretics we may recognize a likeness of divine doctrines.

[Col. 0256B] (Verse 17.) “Judah and the land of Israel were your merchants, offering first-quality grain; they set balm, honey, oil, and resin in your markets.”

The Septuagint: “Judah and the sons of Israel were your merchants in the trade of grain and ointments. They first gave honey, oil, and resin in your markets.”

The Hebrew word PHANAG (), Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated just as it is found among the Hebrews; for it the Septuagint has “ointments,” while we translate “balm.”

It is said that the land of Judah, which is now called Palestine, abounds in supplies of grain, balm, honey, oil, and resin, which Judah and Israel bring to the markets of Tyre.

Since the literal sense is clear, according to the spiritual sense we shall say that the land of confession, and the understanding that sees God—which is referred to the Church—ought not to bring to Tyre first-quality wheat, which, falling into the earth, is multiplied and is understood as the word of God: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Deut. 8:3).

Next it must not bring balm, which grows in the vineyards of Engaddi, or ointment, concerning which it is written: “Like ointment on the head, which runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 133:2).

Nor must it bring honey, concerning which Solomon says: “You have found honey; eat as much as is sufficient. For if you eat more, you will vomit it” (Prov. 25:16), since through excessive satiety honey is turned into wormwood.

It must not bring oil either, with which the lamp is lit in the tabernacle of God, lest that prophetic saying be applied to us: “You sold oil in Egypt” (Hos. 12:1). If it is found in Egypt and in Tyre, it will be turned into the opposite, and it will be said of it: “But may the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Ps. 141:5).

Resin too is soft—or light—and suitable for bodies, and it is received as medicine. Hence it is written in Jeremiah: “Is there no resin in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why has healing not risen for the daughter of my people?” (Jer. 8:22).

Jacob also had this resin, which he sent to his son Joseph together with honey, terebinth, nuts, incense, and stacte (Gen. 43). The Ishmaelites who bought Joseph from the land of Israel also carried these things into Egypt: incense, resin from Gilead, and stacte (ibid. 37).

And so that we may understand more clearly what grain, balm, honey, oil, and resin are when they are carried to the market of Tyre, let us hear the words of the Lord: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6).

To the Canaanite woman who pleaded for her daughter, saying, “My daughter is grievously tormented by a demon,” the Lord replied: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs” (Matt. 15:22, 26). But because she had come out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon and was drawing near to the land of Israel, she obtained what she had asked.

(Verses 18.) “Damascus was your merchant because of the abundance of your works, in the abundance of your various riches, in rich wine and wool of excellent quality.”

The Septuagint: “Damascus was your merchant in the abundance of your works, from the abundance of all your strength; wine from Chelbon and wool from Miletus.”

[Note: Col. 0257D. This reading, restored by Victorius—“rich wine, or shining wool”—is more elegant; Martianus, after Erasmus, has “rich wine, or shining wool.” It means wine from Chelbon.]

For “rich wine,” as Symmachus translated it—and as Aquila, Theodotion, and the Hebrew itself have it—the text reads “wine of HELBON ().” Again, where we have “wool of excellent quality,” or “shining wool,” Aquila and Theodotion translated “wool of Soor.”

The meaning is that, among Tyre’s other commerce, the finest wine and excellent wool were brought to its markets from Damascus. We see this to the present day.

But if Damascus is interpreted as “drinking blood,” and the true tradition of the Hebrews is that the field in which Abel was killed by his fratricidal brother Cain was in Damascus (Gen. 4), and that the place received its name from this event, then it was fitting that Paul, after the killing of Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, should go to Damascus in order to lead those who believed in Christ in chains to Jerusalem.

By God’s mercy—God who makes the seeing blind and the blind seeing—Paul lost the eyes of the flesh so that he might receive those of the mind. The scales of the dragon fell from his eyes, through which he had lost the light of truth, so that he went to the village called Straight and found Ananias, whose name in our language means “obedient” (Acts 9).

From this land, therefore, to which it was said, “Cursed is the earth which opened its mouth and drank the blood of your brother” (Gen. 4:11), the markets of Tyre are supplied with rich wine and shining wool—or wine from Chelbon, which is interpreted as “milky.”

The Septuagint understood “wool of Miletus,” or Soor, in place of “wool of excellent quality.” Miletus is not found in the Hebrew; but because the finest wool is brought from there, they translated Miletus for SOOR.

From this it is clear that Tyre feeds on the milk of infancy and has no clothing of its own, but gathers it from elsewhere and from various provinces.

The interpretation of Damascus as “blood of sackcloth” and “blood of a kiss” does not suit the present passage. Hebrew names are frequently interpreted in different ways according to differences of accent, changes in the letters and vowels, and especially according to the peculiar properties they possess among the Hebrews.

(Verses 19.) “Dan, Greece, and Uzal placed—or, according to the Vulgate, offered—worked iron in your markets; stacte and reed were in your commerce.”

The Septuagint adds: “Dan and Javan and Uzal in your markets,” words added to their edition from Theodotion. “Iron worked by craft, and a wheel, are in your mixture.”

The tribe of Dan, the place where the tribe dwelt, and the name of the patriarch Dan all gave their name to the region where Paneas is now situated, once called Caesarea Philippi. Hence the river Jordan also received its name: Jor, meaning “stream,” and Dan, which flows from Lebanon.

[Note: Cols. 0257D–0258D. Josephus, *Antiquities* III.11, is cited in support of this view, though I do not know with what accuracy. Several later Greeks agree—Philostorgius and John of Antioch in his *Archaeology*—but compare the observations at Epistle 78, on the Stations, station 41, at the end.]

Javan means Greece, which, as we have said, is interpreted as “is and is not.” Symmachus translated Uzal as “bringing,” so that the sense is: “Dan and Greece brought worked iron and the rest to your markets.” Aquila, however, rendered Uzal as “from Uzal.”

We must believe that iron, stacte, and reed were carried to the markets of Tyre from these regions.

Let us say that Greece—that is, Javan—possesses worked iron, most ready for battle, constructed by the art of dialectic, boasting that it presents everything by judgment and reason. It also promises vocal sound, which is signified by “reed,” and stacte of excellent fragrance; or it possesses worked iron and a wheel which rolls through the arrangement of words and has the course of speech.

[Col. 0258C] (Verse 20.) “Dadan, your merchants, dealt in carpets for sitting.”

The Septuagint: “Dedan, your merchants, with chosen beasts for chariots.”

The Hebrew and the Septuagint differ greatly in the present passage, apart from the name of the region, which is close in form: Dedan and Dadan. There is an immense difference between “carpets for sitting” and “chosen beasts for chariots.”

There can be no doubt that four-horse chariots, chariots, and horses are understood in the evil sense if they are earthly. Otherwise, Elijah too is carried up to heavenly things in a chariot, and Elisha calls him “father, father, chariot and horseman of Israel” (2 Kings 2:12).

Gehazi’s eyes also are opened so that he sees chariots on the mountain and horses without riders, prepared for the Lord’s seating (ibid. 6).

In the carpets, however, the beauty of words is displayed. In them the merchants of Dedan are carried and rest, seated in orderly fashion as they come to the markets of Tyre.

(Vers. 21.) Arabia and all the princes of Kedar—these were your merchants—came to you with lambs, rams, and goats. [Note: [Col. 0258D] Victor supplies, in accordance with the Vulgate, “your merchants.” In place of “came,” however, the Hebrew has [the text is absent], and the Greek has ἐν οἷς (“among which”).] Instead of “lambs, rams, and goats,” the Septuagint translated “camels, rams, and lambs.” Arabia and the princes of Kedar—which is now the region of the Saracens, as has been demonstrated most fully in the passage of Jeremiah written against Kedar [Col. 0259A] [Note: [Col. 0259D] It should read “is demonstrated” or “will be demonstrated,” not “has been demonstrated,” since Jerome wrote his commentary on Jeremiah after completing all his commentaries on Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, as he himself informed us in the preface to his commentaries on Jeremiah; and, forestalled by death, he was unable to complete even the passage against Kedar, which is read in chapter XLIX, verse 28. MARTIAN.---Suppose that this refers to Jeremiah himself, not to Jerome’s commentaries on that prophet, which he worked on much later; indeed, he did not reach even that passage against Kedar, chapter XLIX, verse 28, because of his intervening death.] abound in these animals—namely, lambs, rams, and goats—and by this importation they multiply the markets of Tyre (Jeremiah XLIX). It is also an exceedingly fertile region for camels, because of the breadth of the desert’s pastures [Alternative: pasturelands] and the temperateness of the air, which this animal enjoys.

Arabia is interpreted as “evening,” and Kedar as “darkness.” Concerning it the Psalms also say: “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Psalm CXIX, 5). These regions bring Tyre camels weighed down by the heaviest burdens of sins, or lambs, rams, and goats, which they sacrifice on their altars—altars which they have feigned from an evil and rebellious heart. In this same prophet, too, in the vision of the shepherds, we read of rams disturbing the purest waters, striking the sheep with their sides, and fighting with their horns (below, XXXIV); and of goats, which customarily stand on the left, and of lambs that counterfeit the Lamb (Matthew XXV), concerning whom it is written: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29).

Isaiah, however, writes of camels in a favorable sense (Isaiah LX): they come to Jerusalem from Midian—which is interpreted as “the judgment of the Lord”—and from Ephah; and rams come from Nabaioth, while Sheba brings gold and frankincense. The last two are also offered to the Lord by the Magi (Matthew II). These camels, having laid down the burden of sins, can enter the narrow and constricted way that leads to life (Matthew VII and XIX).

(Vers. 22.) The merchants of Sheba and Raamah [Alternative: Remaah], these were your merchants, with all the finest spices, [Col. 0259C] precious stone [Vulgate: precious], and gold that they displayed in your market. In the Psalms, where it is written: “The kings of Arabia and Sheba shall offer gifts to you” (Psalm LXXI, 10), the Hebrew has: “The kings of Sheba and Sheba shall offer gifts to you.” One of these Shebas is written with the letter SIN, the other with SAMEKH, which resembles our own letter.

Since Sheba is therefore interpreted as “conversion,” it must be said that in the present passage it signifies not conversion but aversion, from which gifts are brought to Tyre together with every kind of spice, the finest fragrances, precious stone, and gold—all of which are displayed in the markets of Tyre. For these people too counterfeit the finest fragrance, and the precious stone with which they endeavor to build the churches of their perversity, and the gold which they promise in their understanding; and everything is perverse. They accept nothing gratuitously, nor do they give anything freely, but buy and sell everything, whereas the kings of Arabia and Sheba freely offer gifts to Christ.

These are the people who do everything for the sake of shameful profit, and who received these gifts from him who says in the Gospel: “For these things have been delivered to me; I will give them to you if, falling down, you worship me” (Matthew IV, 9). Raamah—or, according to the Septuagint, Rhegma—I have been unable to find in any other place in Scripture [Col. 0260A], nor have I discovered what region it is or what it signifies, except that it is clear from the context that Sheba is a region neighboring this province.

(Vers. 23, 24.) Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, your merchants; Sheba, Asshur, and Chelmad, your sellers: these were your merchants in garments of various kinds, in violet-colored wrappings, and in embroidered goods and precious treasures, which were wrapped and bound with cords.

The Septuagint: “Harran, and Chana, and Edne, these were your merchants; Sheba, Asshur, and Chalman, your traders, bringing merchandise in Machalim and in Galima, [in] violet cloth, and [in] embroidered goods, and selected treasures bound with cords.” These are the names of nations belonging to different regions. What has been added to the Septuagint from Theodotion—“in Machalim and in Galima”—Symmachus translated as “in precious wrappings” [Col. 0260B]. We have also added “embroidered goods,” which Theodotion translated variously, from Aquila and Symmachus. So precious were the merchants’ garments that they were carried in wrappings and fastened with violet-colored cords.

Haran—or, as the Septuagint said, Charran—means “openings” in our language; Canneh means “preparation”; Eden means “delights.” In its place the Septuagint has Edne, which is not found in the Hebrew; we do not know what it means, and we should not seek the etymology of a fabricated name. In the commerce of Tyre, therefore, through the carnal senses signified by the openings, there is the entire preparation of the people of the world, who think that their only delights consist in increasing the commercial activity of the city of Tyre.

We have spoken above about Sheba. Asshur is interpreted as “directing”; Chelmad—or, as it appears in certain copies, Cherma—is translated as “vineyards.” There can be no doubt that these are the Sodomites who come to the market of Tyre in order to direct what is perverse—or rather, to condemn it by punishments and correct what had been corrupted—in accordance with what is said in the Psalms: “That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger” (Psalm VIII, 3).

They possess household goods of many kinds, distinguished by incredible variety, which are fastened in violet-colored wrappings; or their treasures are bound with cords, treasures that they have stored up for themselves on earth, according to what is written: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Proverbs V, 22). They have not conducted free commerce, but have entangled everything in the bonds of sins. Because of the similarity of their color, let us refer the violet wrappings to the aerial powers, which distribute their treasures in the markets of the world.

[Col. 0260D] They also had cedars in your commerce. The ships of the sea—or, as it is contained in the Hebrew, of Tarshish—were your princes in your commerce. In place of “cedars,” the Septuagint translated “cypresses.” Since we have spoken above about both, it would be superfluous to increase the reader’s weariness.

(Vers. 25.) You were filled and glorified—or, weighed down—exceedingly in the heart of the sea. “Nothing,” he says, “was lacking to you that belongs to the riches of the islands.” Yet this glorification was a burden to the possessor, since you cannot bear riches in moderation, although poverty too is often a temptation [Note: [Col. 0261D] In the Vatican manuscript: “although poverty too is often,” etc.] (Proverbs XXX). Hence Solomon asks only for what is necessary; and he detests riches and poverty equally, lest in the one case pride, and in the other impatience and falsehood, steal in.

(Vers. 26.) Your rowers brought you into many waters. Above we read that the rowers of the city of Tyre were Sidonians and Aradians, one of whom is interpreted as “hunters,” the other as “those who remove.” For they hunt the souls of those whom, amid the waves of this world, they lead according to their own will; they do not raise them to high places but plunge them into the depths. Nor do they imitate those who, sailing until the morning watch, broke the mad waves of the sea [Col. 0261B] and were worthy to receive the Lord and Savior; immediately, with such a passenger and companion, they reached the harbor of rest. This is written about more fully in the Gospel.

The south wind shattered you in the heart of the sea (Matthew XIV). All the riches of Tyre perish when the south wind blows. This wind is more significantly called CADIM in Hebrew [the Hebrew term is absent], and in Greek καύσων, which we can translate as “burning wind.” Concerning it holy David said: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Psalm CXX, 6). Jacob was scorched by this wind, yet not shattered, when he says: “By day I was scorched by heat, and by frost at night” (Genesis XXXI, 40). Those too who were hired at the first hour endured the heat and burning of the entire day, yet they received the denarius, because they were scorched but not shattered.

Hence the bride also says in the Song: “I am black but beautiful, because the sun has looked upon me” (Song of Songs I, 4); or, as it is better contained in the Hebrew: “The sun has discolored me.”

Your riches and your treasures, and your equipment of every kind. Many read it this way: “In the heart of the sea are your riches and your treasures, and your equipment of every kind,” so that all the riches and treasures of Tyre, and her entire substance, are placed in the heart of the sea and overwhelmed by the waves of the world, and her inhabitants have nothing stable or lasting, in fulfillment of the Gospel saying: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20). And also the apostolic saying: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and many snares, and are dragged into the depths” (1 Timothy VI, 9).

The historical meaning is clear; and for that reason we attach brief statements to nearly every verse [Col. 0261D]. For the discourse is already hastening toward the end of the book.

(Vers. 27.) Your sailors—or rowers—and your pilots, who held your equipment and presided over your people; and your warriors who were in you, together with all your multitude that is in your midst, will fall into the heart of the sea on the day of your ruin. We read that the rowers or sailors of the city of Tyre were Sidonians and Aradians, about whom we have already spoken; and, according to the edition of the Septuagint, the counselors were from Byblos, which in Hebrew is called GEBAL [Hebrew term absent]. Its warriors were Persians, Lydians, and Libyans. All these will fall and be shown to be nothing when Tyre falls and all her glory reaches the end of its ruins.

The multitude, which the Septuagint translated as “mixture,” signifies the common people, apart from the rulers; without the names of dignities, they will be crushed under the same judgment. The prophecy is interwoven between the city and the ship, so that from one you may understand the other; nevertheless, both pertain to the consummation of the world and to shipwreck.

(Vers. 28, 29.) At the sound of the cry of your pilots the fleets will be thrown into confusion, and all who held the oar will descend from their ships. The sailors, and all the pilots of the sea [Note: [Col. 0261D] The words “passengers” and “prowsmen,” which we have enclosed in parentheses, are not found in the Hebrew or in Jerome’s version; they seem to have been noted from the Septuagint interpretation, ἐπιβάται καὶ οἱ πρωρεῖς (“passengers and those at the prow”). Accordingly, following the usual practice, the disjunctive particle “or” should be placed before them.]—or, passengers and those at the prow—will stand on the land and lament over you with a loud voice; they will cry out bitterly and cast dust upon their heads, and they will be sprinkled with ashes—or, they will spread ashes beneath themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0262D] The verse that follows, “And they will deliver,” was also placed here, against the testimony of the manuscripts, in an inconvenient order of the discourse.]

The following words—“They will shave their heads because of you and gird themselves with sackcloth; they will mourn for you in the bitterness of their soul with most bitter mourning; they will take up a lamentation over you and lament you”—are not found in the Septuagint but have been added from the edition of Theodotion.

When Tyre has fallen, her pilots will be thrown into confusion and will descend from the fleets; the rowers, passengers, those at the prow—or sailors—and all the pilots of the sea, having been tossed by the waves, will at last stand on firm ground [Col. 0262C]. They will lament over her with a loud voice, with which previously they had enriched themselves through their merchandise, and they will express the bitterness of their minds by their cries. They will also throw dust or earth upon their heads, performing repentance for earthly works. They will be sprinkled with ashes, or with the ashes of the heifer, according to the Law (Numbers XX), so that they may be purified; or certainly they will spread ashes beneath themselves, according to what is said to Jerusalem: “Scatter earth upon your head, spread ashes beneath you, and make mourning” (Jeremiah VI, 26).

It is also written in the Gospel: “If these signs had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Luke X, 13). The Psalmist says: “I ate ashes like bread” (Psalm CI, 10). They will shave their heads over Tyre and make themselves bald, as is customary in mourning, at the time when the magnitude of grief has excluded all joy [Col. 0262D]. The hairs of the apostles, however, were numbered, because they had consecrated their hair to the Lord like the Nazirite men (Matthew X; Luke VI). Samson, too, as long as he had his hair, possessed strength; but when his hair was cut off, he was captured by the Philistines (Judges XVI).

When it is said, “They will gird themselves with sackcloth,” the ancient lust of the loins is condemned, so that those who had lived in luxury may afterward, in repentance, live in austerity and hardship. The Ninevites wore sackcloth (Jonah III). And again it is said to Jerusalem: “Mourn before me like a bride girded with sackcloth for her virgin husband” (Joel I, 8).

“And they will mourn for you,” he says, “in the bitterness of their soul with most bitter mourning.” For it is better to enter the house of mourning than the house of feasting (Ecclesiasticus VII), so that they may mourn for Tyre and repeat a lamentation, which the following Scripture adds.

To make clear that those who mourn the downfall, those who previously moved about in the heart and midst of the sea, have made progress, let the example of the prophet teach us: he too is commanded to mourn for Tyre so that, when the period of repentance has been completed, she may be restored to her former state and, taking up the lyre, make music to the Lord. Read Isaiah.

Some interpret the pilots, absurdly—but what we have read must nevertheless be stated—as bishops of the heretics; the counselors as presbyters; those at the prow as archdeacons; the rowers and sailors as deacons; and they refer the passengers to the entire people. If they had added the shipmaster as the devil, they would have completed the tragedy.

All these will lament and weep most bitterly together, and will repent after they have experienced the shipwreck of their vessel and stood on land, losing all the splendor of their falsely named knowledge; instead of joy and gladness, they will mark their repentance with sorrow in the bitterness of their hearts.

(Vers. 33 and following.) What city is like Tyre, which has fallen silent—or become mute—in the midst of the sea? (This is not found in the Septuagint.) When your merchandise went out—or, “the profit that you found”—from the sea, you satisfied many peoples [Col. 0263C]. With the abundance of your riches and of peoples [Note: [Col. 0263D] Rabanus and Victor add “your.” Here, instead of “many,” he reads “of the earth,” from the Vulgate, Hebrew, and Greek texts; he says that several manuscript codices and Jerome’s exposition below agree with these.] you enriched many kings. Now you have been shattered by the sea—or, in the sea; in the depths of the waters your riches—or, your merchandise—and all your multitude that was in your midst have fallen. All the inhabitants of the islands have been astonished—or, shattered—over you, and all their kings, struck by the storm—or, turned to madness—have changed their faces—or wept. The merchants [Note: [Col. 0264D] Victor reverses the order: “merchants of peoples,” or “of nations.” For, he says, the Hebrew [term absent] Jerome translated as “of peoples,” while the Septuagint has ἐθνῶν, “of nations.” Jerome’s version should therefore precede.] of the nations—or peoples—have hissed at you: you have been reduced to nothing—or, become a ruin—and you will not be anymore [Vulgate omits “anymore”] forever—or, for eternity.

The pilots, rowers, those at the prow, and passengers will recall these things in the mourning of Tyre: how no other city became so silent that it had no confidence to speak, and heard the Gospel saying: “Be silent and be muzzled” (Mark IV, 39). And from the Psalms: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my ordinances and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Psalm XLIX, 16).

With how many wares, O Tyre, have you been enriched? And what did you seek with such great labor, that day and night you might gather together what was destined to perish in shipwreck? You indeed satisfied many peoples and enriched kings with your wealth, concerning whom it is written: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm II, 2).

But now you have been shattered in the sea and in the depths of the waters, in accordance with what is written concerning Pharaoh: “He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea” (Exodus XV, 4). He was sunk into the deep like a stone and could say: “I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed me” (Psalm LXVIII, 3).

All the islands, or the inhabitants of the islands, which are battered by the waves of this world, will be astonished over you. Their kings, struck by the storm, will perceive their own destruction; and, imitating the voice of the serpent, they will hiss and say: “You have been reduced to nothing,” or, “You have become a ruin,” so that you have not possessed the nature of ruin but its will.

“And you will not be.” If he had stopped here, a major question would arise: how could she not exist, when we now see her built up? But from what follows—“forever”—he indicates the duration of a single age, which, according to the lifespan of a human being, is reckoned as a cycle of seventy years. Or: “You will not be” before God, who, as the Apostle says, “calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans IV, 17). And the prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, all your adversaries will be confounded and ashamed; they will be as though they do not exist” (Isaiah XLI, 11). And Esther, according to the Septuagint translators: “Do not deliver your scepter to those who do not exist” (Esther XIV, 11). And in the Psalm: “Let me recover before I depart and exist no more” (Psalm XXXVIII, 14). We have explained above in what sense these testimonies are to be understood.

All these things can be referred to the person of the heretics. In the ruin and shipwreck of Tyre they will perceive their error; placed in the midst of the sea, they will desire to save their souls, and they will mourn the riches they wrongly gathered, by which they had enriched many kings—namely, their patriarchs—and the ignoble multitude, whose wealth will collapse into the midst of the sea.

The inhabitants of all the islands also—if we wish to refer what has been said to the favorable sense—will be astonished at the ruin of Tyre; and all the kings of the islands, either themselves struck as if by a storm, will change their faces, or will reveal the sorrow of their hearts through weeping and tears. By the greatness of their astonishment they will testify, through wonder and hissing, how she has been reduced to nothing and perished, although she had promised salvation to many nations. And she will no longer exist—not merely for a definite period, so that we interpret αἰών as “an age,” but forever, because the same expression signifies both.

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0265]

[Col. 0265A] 325–326 It was appropriate, daughter Eustochium, that I should encompass in one volume the prophecy concerning Tyre and the prince of Tyre, and not separate by the order of the books subjects joined both by place and by prophecy. But because there are many things to be said, exceeding the measure of length, the exposition has therefore been postponed to the ninth book. We believe that, through your prayers and those of all the saints, it will reach its conclusion, so that we may also discuss what has been written in Ezekiel against Pharaoh and all Egypt. These matters too, because of their length, must be divided into a tenth book, both so that the proportion between the volumes may be maintained and so that the labor of dictating, writing, and reading may breathe again when distributed into sections.

[Col. 0265B] (Chapter XXVIII.—Vers. 1 and following.) “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been lifted up and you have said, ‘I am God, and I have sat [Vulgate: I sit] in the seat of God, in the heart of the sea,’ although you are a man and not God, and you have set your heart as though it were the heart of God: behold, you are wiser than Daniel? No secret is hidden from you. By your wisdom and understanding you made strength for yourself and acquired gold and silver in your treasuries. By the abundance of your wisdom and in your commerce you multiplied strength for yourself, and your heart was lifted up in your strength.

“Therefore thus says the Lord [Vulgate adds: God]: Because your heart was lifted up as though it were the heart of God, therefore behold, I will bring foreigners against you, the strongest of the nations, and they will draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and profane your splendor. They will kill and [Note: [Col. 0265D] Victor reads “and they will bring you down,” for the Vulgate edition also reads this, and it corresponds to the Hebrew [term absent] and the Greek καταβιβάσουσί σε.] hand you over, and you will die by the death of those slain in the heart of the sea. Will you still say, as you speak, ‘I am God,’ before those who kill you, although you are a man and not God, in the hand of those who slay you? You will die the death of the uncircumcised at the hand of foreigners, because I have spoken, says the Lord God.

“The Septuagint: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been exalted and you have said, ‘I am God; I have dwelt in the dwelling-place of God in the heart of the sea,’ although you are a man and not [Col. 0265D] God, and you have set your heart as though it were the heart of God: are you wiser than Daniel? The wise have not instructed you with their discipline. By your instruction or prudence, have you made strength for yourself and made gold and silver in your treasuries? By your abundant instruction [and] commerce, have you multiplied your strength? Your heart has been lifted up in your strength.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have set your heart as though it were the heart of God, therefore behold, I will bring against you pestilential foreigners from the nations, and they will unsheathe their swords against you, against the beauty of your teaching, and they will humble your beauty in destruction; they will lead you away and dispose of you, and you will die the death of the wounded in the heart of the sea. Will you, while speaking, say, ‘I am God,’ in the presence of those who kill you [Col. 0266B]? But you are a man and not God, in the multitude of those who wound you. You will die the deaths of the uncircumcised at the hands of foreigners, because I have spoken, says Adonai the Lord.”

Wherever, according to the Septuagint, “Lord, Lord” is placed a second time, the first [Note: [Col. 0265D] Rather, the second, or the latter, is the tetragrammaton, while the first is the ordinary name; nor do I doubt that this is a scribal error attributable to the carelessness of ancient copyists, who rashly changed the numerical signs. Jerome himself guarantees the correctness of his writing in this very Commentary, shortly above, at the beginning of chapter VI: “When the two names ‘Lord, Lord’ are joined, the first is ordinary, while the second properly belongs to God; it is called ἄρρητον, that is, ineffable, and it was written on the golden plate that was on the forehead of the high priest.” This practice certainly holds throughout Ezekiel’s prophecy; but we know that in other books, especially in the Psalms, the tetragrammaton is often placed before τῷ Adonai. This is why we change nothing in the proposed text of Jerome. See the notes below on Origen’s Homilies 4 and 12 on this same prophet.] name is the tetragrammaton [the Hebrew form is absent], which properly pertains to God and is called ineffable; the second is the ordinary name [the Hebrew form is absent], which is often found among human beings.

Just as the riches of the city of Tyre were first described under the figure of a ship, and afterward its ruin and mourning, so now a prophetic word is first spoken concerning the prince of Tyre: that he has been raised up by pride and has not used well the riches he possessed; afterward come mourning and lamentation, describing how he passed from such great blessings to such great evils.

The first matters must therefore be discussed first. It is written in Isaiah (Isaiah XIV) concerning the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, that he equated himself with the power of God and was raised to such arrogance that he dared to say: “I will ascend above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High.” Having been hurled down from his throne, he deserved to hear: “How has Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning?” And concerning Pharaoh, in this same prophet: “My rivers are mine, and I made them” (below, XXIX, 9).

And concerning the prince of Tyre, that with an exalted heart he arrogantly said: “I am God, and I have sat in the seat of God,” or, “I have dwelt in the dwelling-place of God,” although he is a man and not God. Although these words seem to exceed the capacities of human frailty, and to be not so much the words of human beings as of raving demons, we must nevertheless understand them as hyperbole: they swelled up so greatly and did not know their own measure [Col. 0266D], so that, elated by worldly prosperity and royal power, while they thought present goods perpetual, they failed to recognize themselves as human beings and claimed an eternal empire for themselves.

It is possible that under the type of princes, kings, and individual cities or provinces, hostile powers are also indicated. Concerning these the Apostle Paul writes: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against princes and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI, 12). And in another passage: “We speak wisdom among the mature; yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed” (1 Corinthians II, 6). Again, discussing wisdom, he says that none of the rulers of this world knew it: “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians II, 8).

In Daniel’s prophecy too we read clearly of Michael, prince of the people of Israel, and of the prince of Greece and the prince of Persia (Daniel X). Moses writes even more openly in the Song of Deuteronomy: “When the Most High divided the nations and scattered the children of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 8); or, as it is better found in the Hebrew: “according to the number of the children of Israel.” “And the Lord’s portion became his people Jacob, the measuring line of his inheritance Israel.”

Nor will we be surprised that, on the opposing side, the worst kings precede in type the apostate princes, since we teach that the best kings—David, Solomon, and Josiah—and the patriarchs and prophets preceded in the figure of the Lord Savior. Let us therefore discuss what has been written according to both interpretations: of proud kings and of apostate princes.

He says, then [Alternative: “Although he is a man, he says”]: Even though you are held amid the constrictions of the sea and of an island, I will say more: although you are a man, surrounded by the frailty of human flesh, and lifted up by the swelling of your heart, you imagined that you dwelt on the throne of God, in the heavens.

And because you boast of wisdom, to such an extent that the people of your kingdom challenged Solomon with riddles: are you wiser than Daniel, who by the grace of God conquered all the magicians and diviners [329], and is now the wisest man in Babylon?

Or it should be understood this way: Even if you are wiser than Daniel, who by everyone’s confession is the wisest of all, and by the greatness of your riches and power wish to equate yourself with the power of God, nevertheless you will be captured by adversaries; your city will be destroyed, you will be pierced by many wounds, and you will no longer say, “I am God.” Taught by destruction, you will recognize that you are a man, not God.

But if we wish to say that the prince of Tyre is the same power to which the city or province itself was entrusted by God, let us take up this testimony: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High. But you will die like men, and like one of the princes you will fall” (Psalm LXXXI, 7).

The provinces were entrusted to them to govern, as to judges appointed by the Emperor. Forgetting that their honor depended upon another’s command, they—like Heraclianus recently in Africa [Alternative: Heradianus]—were raised in a tyrannical spirit against their king and lord, so that, scattered throughout the whole world, under the names of idolatry they assumed for themselves the names of gods; puffed up by pride, they fell into the judgment and snare of the devil.

Concerning this the Savior also spoke in the Gospel: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke X, 18).

(Vv. 11 ff.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, raise a lament over the king of Tyre, and say to him: Thus says the Lord God:

You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in the delights of the paradise of God. Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald. Gold was the work of your adornment, and your sockets were prepared on the day when you were created. You were the outstretched and protecting Cherub, and I placed you on God’s holy mountain. You walked in the midst of fiery stones. You were perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you. In the abundance of your commerce your inner parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned. Therefore I cast you out from the mountain of God and destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones.
