Your heart was lifted up in your beauty; you lost your wisdom in your beauty [the Vulgate: “your wisdom in your beauty”]. I cast you to the ground; I set you before kings, that they might gaze upon you. By the multitude of your iniquities and by the iniquity of your commerce you profaned your sanctuary. Therefore I will bring forth a fire from within you, which shall devour you, and I will reduce you to ashes upon the earth before the eyes of all who see you. All who see you among the nations shall be astonished at you. You have become nothing, and you shall not exist forever.

The Septuagint: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over the ruler of Tyre, and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and a crown of beauty. You were in the delights of the paradise of God. You were surrounded with every good stone: sardius and topaz, emerald and carbuncle, sapphire and jasper, silver and gold, ligure and agate, amethyst and chrysolite, beryl and onyx; and with gold you filled your treasures, and your storehouses within you were prepared from the day when you were created, together with the Cherub anointed by God [Note: Victor says that the words “by God” are superfluous, since they occur neither in Hebrew nor in Greek. Likewise, the words “anointed” and “dwelling in the tabernacle” are absent from the Greek text as it now stands; but that they once existed may be inferred from the Hebrew and from Jerome’s Commentary.] and dwelling in the tabernacle. I placed you on God’s holy mountain; you were made in the midst of the fiery stones. You were blameless in your days, from the day when you were created, until iniquities were found in you. From the abundance of your commerce you filled your storerooms with iniquity, and you sinned; and you were wounded by the mountain of God, and the Cherub who overshadows brought you out from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty; your discipline was corrupted along with your beauty. Because of the multitude of your sins I cast you to the ground; I set you before kings, that you might be disgraced. Because of the multitude of your sins and the iniquities of your commerce I polluted your holy things. And I will bring out a fire from within you [Note: Victor reads “from within you”; the Greek has ἐκ μέσου σου, “from within you”.]. It shall devour you. And I will reduce you to ashes upon the earth before the eyes of all who see you, and all who have known you among the nations shall mourn over you. You have become destruction, and you shall not exist any longer.

Since we have explained who the ruler of Tyre is and how he fell through pride, let us understand his lamentations over his former glory. First he is reminded what he was, so that he may grieve over having lost what he possessed. “You are,” he says, “the seal of likeness”—in accordance with what John the Evangelist says specifically of the Savior: “For this one the Father, God, has sealed” (John 6:27). And concerning human beings: “He has sealed that God is true” (John 3:33). And in the Psalms: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4:7). And elsewhere: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). Hence it is also said to God: “Who shall be like you?” (Ps. 34:10).

For likeness is one thing, equality another. Hence that is an exceedingly savage heresy which confesses in Christ only a likeness to the Father and removes his nature. We, however, say that in the Son there is not only likeness but equality. For this reason the Jews were persecuting him: because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but also was making himself equal to God (John 5). Where there is equality, there is the same nature and one substance.

This is what the Apostle also says concerning likeness: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19), so that you may receive, namely, his likeness, which through your own fault you lost. And because Latin manuscripts read resignaculum, “an unsealing,” instead of signaculum, “a seal,” the translator, slavishly rendering word for word (κακοζήλως), set down the Septuagint’s ἀποσφράγισμα—that is, resignaculum, “an unsealing.”

Hence some understand the passage in this way: the king of Tyre had unsealed and lost God’s seal and figure, impressed as though in the softest wax; so that instead of being a signaculum he became a resignaculum, no longer possessing the image and likeness of God, according to which the first human being was created, when God said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). And it should be noted that the image was made then, whereas the likeness is completed in Christ’s baptism.

Accordingly, to the one addressed as “the seal of likeness” are joined the words “full of wisdom, perfect in beauty,” or “a crown of beauty.” For where there is the likeness of God, there are also the fullness of wisdom and perfect beauty—or, as though adorned and arranged with various flowers, a crown of virtues, which the diligent person increases by his own effort while nourishing nature’s good through industry, and which the negligent diminishes, in accordance with what is said in Proverbs under the figure of a beautiful but ill-behaved woman: “Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout, so is beauty in an ill-behaved woman” (Prov. 11:22).

It follows: “You were in the delights of the paradise of God.” In Hebrew the word is EDEN (עֵדֶן), which is also related in the narrative of Genesis. Eden is translated as “delights.” And he appropriately calls it “the paradise of God,” in order to show that there is also a contrary paradise, not God’s, among those who exchange truth for falsehood (Rom. 1) and boast that they possess paradise [Col. 0270A] 332. By this language he demonstrates that the one of whom these things are written is not a human being at all, but an opposing power that once dwelt in God’s paradise—although the Jews judge that this was prophetically spoken of Hiram, king of Tyre, by τρόπος, that is, by the figure called ὑπερβολή, “hyperbole.”

When it is said to him, “You were in the delights of the paradise of God,” or “you became so,” it shows what he had possessed and what he lost. Moreover, the fact that “every precious stone was your covering,” or “your setting” and “your encirclement”—sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald—or, as in the Septuagint, with different order and different names, twelve stones in all—must be understood as follows: the king of Tyre was not surrounded, covered, or, as Symmachus translated, bound and fastened, with every precious stone; rather, every stone that the ruler of Tyre possessed was precious.

Otherwise there are many precious stones that Scripture does not name in the present passage: chalcedony, sardonyx, chrysoprase, hyacinth, crystal, and the most precious pearl. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion also differ greatly from one another and from the Septuagint interpreters in this passage—not only in order, but also in number and names.

In John’s Apocalypse also, where Jerusalem is described as constructed of living stones, the same stones are placed in its foundations, with their order slightly altered toward the end, so that its gates are said to have been built with the radiance of crystal (Rev. 21). The same stones are also described on the breast of the high priest, in four rows on the Rational [the breastpiece] (Exod. 28); and on his shoulders are two onyx stones, on which the names of the twelve patriarchs are written. The true high priest, of whom it is written, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4), carries them on his breast and carries them on his shoulders, so that in the twelve stones he may display the number of the apostles, and in the two the mysteries of the two Testaments. One of these, John the Evangelist, reclined upon his breast, so that he might draw up the streams of wisdom and be able to say: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2).

These are the living stones of which the Church is built, and concerning which the Apostle Peter writes: “If you have believed that the Lord is gracious, coming to him as a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves also, as living stones, are being built into spiritual houses, into a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices pleasing to God through Jesus Christ. For Scripture says” (Isa. 28:16): “Behold, I place in Zion a cornerstone, chosen and precious, and the one who believes in him shall not be put to shame” (1 Pet. 2:3 ff.).

Concerning this the chosen vessel [the Apostle Paul] also agrees in the same words, saying: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus our Lord himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple [Note: Victor reads, “a holy temple in the Lord”] of God” (Eph. 2:10).

These are the stones of which we also read elsewhere: “Holy stones roll upon the earth like wheels” (Zech. 9:16), touching the ground only slightly and hastening toward heavenly things by their rolling. Concerning them Scripture also says: “Behold, I prepare your carbuncle as a stone, and your foundations as sapphire; I will make your battlements jasper, and your gates stones of crystal [Note: The same translator reads, “crystal stones,” and “your walls stones chosen,” following the text of the Septuagint, so that the Latin expression may be more harmonious], and your walls stones chosen; and all your children shall be taught by God, and your children shall enjoy abundant peace, and you shall be built in righteousness” (Isa. 54:11–13). What seemed to us concerning this we have explained in the expositions of the same prophet.

Of such stones the twentieth Psalm also sings: “O Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength, and in your salvation he shall exult greatly. You have granted him the desire of his soul, and you have not denied him the request of his lips. For you anticipated him with blessings of sweetness; you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone” (Ps. 20:1 ff.).

These are the pearls of the prophets and apostles, all of which are sold in comparison with Christ in the Gospel (Matt. 14), so that the most precious pearl may be purchased, and the stone of which Zechariah writes that it has seven eyes—that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit (Zech. 3 and 4). Read Isaiah. Paul also places this stone in the foundation of the Church, upon which gold, silver, and precious stones are built (1 Cor. 3). To discuss the colors, natures, and effects of each of these is not appropriate at present; they require a volume of their own. Thus, in Ezekiel, Exodus, the Apocalypse, and Isaiah, when all the stones and the orders of the stones are compared with one another, they create a great difficulty both for the reader and for the interpreter. Concerning these matters the holy bishop Epiphanius himself has also given me a volume of his own. And Book 37 of Pliny the Elder’s Natural History, after treating of a multitude of all kinds of subjects, discusses gems and stones. A diligent reader must be directed by us to these works for knowledge of them.

Symmachus’s translation, moreover, describes this ruler of Tyre as though he were a most precious necklace distinguished by stones. Finally, he calls it a golden drum, in which the stones are set. Hence, in accordance with the Hebrew, it follows: “Gold was the work of your adornment, and your sockets were prepared on the day when you were created.”

Instead of this, the Septuagint interpreters placed: “With gold you filled your treasures and your storehouses,” conveying the sense and thought that his mind had been open to divine mysteries and that he had gathered spiritual riches for himself, concerning which the Lord commanded: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart is also” (Matt. 6:21).

This is the hidden treasure of which the Gospel also speaks: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field; when someone finds it, he hides it, and for joy over it he goes and sells everything that he has and buys that field” (ibid., 13:44). The storehouses, or granaries, are those of which it is written elsewhere: “Blessed shall be your storehouses and your remnants” (Deut. 28:5). [Note: In the Vatican manuscript: “Moreover, what is said …”]

After this, according to the Hebrew, it says: “You were the outstretched and protecting Cherub”—with “the ark of God and the mercy seat” understood; or, according to the Septuagint, that he himself was anointed and created together with the Cherub. From this it is shown that the passage cannot refer to a human ruler of the city of Tyre, but to a formerly holy and preeminent power who had been appointed ruler of the city of Tyre.

“And I placed you,” he says, “on the holy mountain of God”—without doubt signifying paradise, to which the Apostle Paul says that he was caught up after the third heaven (1 Cor. 12). Cherub is masculine and singular; in the plural they are called Cherubim, interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge.” Upon them God rests and sits, and he uses this as his chariot, as the prophet says to him: “You who sit upon the Cherubim, reveal yourself” (Ps. 79:2). And elsewhere: “He mounted upon the Cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 17:11).

This Cherub, or the one created together with the Cherub, stretched out and protecting the mysteries, was placed on God’s holy mountain, about which we have often spoken. The Apostle Paul says—if one accepts the Epistle to the Hebrews: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and myriads of angels” (Heb. 12:22). Or certainly God’s holy mountain is to be understood as paradise, as we have said.

He also walked in the midst of fiery stones, concerning which it is written: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4). Not only does God, who is called a consuming fire, consume hay, wood, and straw (Deut. 4), but angels also are called fiery stones, fervent in spirit. Hence the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled!” (Luke 12).

What follows—“Perfect in your ways from the day of your creation,” for which the Septuagint placed, “You were blameless in your days, from the day when you were created”—shows that every creature was created good by God and possessed perfect virtue. Therefore the ruler of Tyre also was blameless, so that what followed might be understood as a blemish not of nature but of will.

“Until iniquity was found in you.” It was found by God, although it had been kept hidden in the treasuries of your heart through pride and the abuse of the power you had received. “In the abundance of his commerce his inner parts,” or his storerooms, “were filled with iniquity.” For while he acquired much and was not content with the knowledge he had received or with the power over which he had been appointed, he filled the storerooms and inner chambers of his heart, so that, once sated and fattened, he might kick against his Creator.

“For Jacob ate and was satisfied, and the beloved kicked; he grew fat and thick and broad, and he abandoned the God who had made him” (Deut. 32:15). And “from the heart proceed evil thoughts” (Matt. 15:19). On account of these God says: “You sinned, and I cast you out from the mountain of God”—or “you were wounded by the mountain of God”—which compels us who read this to fear.

For if the outstretched and protecting Cherub, placed on God’s holy mountain and perfect and blameless in the midst of the fiery stones, filled his inner parts with iniquity because of the abundance of his commerce, and sinned, and was cast out from the mountain of God—that is, from the dwelling of paradise—or was wounded by the mountain of God, which is plainly understood as Christ; or, if he was established and dwelling on God’s mountain, was wounded by himself and pierced by the evil of his conscience when he understood himself to be unworthy of dwelling on the mountain—what should we think about ourselves?

Therefore it is said to him: “And I destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones,” so that you would no longer stand among the fiery stones but perish. O Cherub—or Cherubim [Note: Victor corrects this to “who were protecting,” for the Cherubim protected the ark and the mercy seat]—who protected you, I brought you out from the midst of the fiery stones, in accordance with what is also written concerning Adam: “He cast Adam out and stationed him” [another reading: “the Cherubim”] “opposite the paradise of delights” (Gen. 3:24).

He gives the reasons why he was brought out, or cast, from the midst of the fiery stones. “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty,” while you thought that what belongs to God was yours. Hence the Apostle says that he received a thorn in the flesh and an angel of Satan to buffet him, lest he become proud because of the greatness of his revelations and fall into the judgment of the devil (2 Cor. 12).

“And therefore,” he says, “your doctrine was corrupted along with your beauty,” or “you lost your wisdom in your beauty,” so that, while you wished to be more than you had been created and to know more than you had received from God, you lost even what you possessed; and in place of beauty and instruction, deformity and folly took possession of you. Hence you were cast to the ground, although previously you had dwelt on God’s mountain.

Concerning this Isaiah also writes: “How Lucifer has fallen, who used to rise in the morning!” (Isa. 14:12). And the Savior says in the Gospel: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). Jeremiah likewise speaks to Jerusalem: “How the Lord in his anger has darkened the daughter of Zion; he has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth” (Lam. 2:1).

You were cast down before all kings, so that they might be terrified by your example—whether good kings, whose heart is in the hand of God (Prov. 21), or evil ones, whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Savior (Matt. 4). They met the king of Babylon, saying: “You also have been captured as we were, and you have been counted among us.”

For this reason he also polluted the sanctuary that he had possessed when he dwelt on the mountain and moved about in the midst of the fiery stones. It follows: “I will bring forth a fire in the midst of you, which shall devour you.”

That fire had been kindled in the heart of the king of Tyre by the one whose arrows are fiery and concerning whom it is written: “All of them commit adultery; their hearts are like an oven” (Hosea). Isaiah also speaks of this fire: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isa. 50), so that, coming out, it may devour the one who possesses it, in accordance with what is written in the same Isaiah: “It devoured the material like hay” (Isa. 5). “On that day the mountains, hills, and forests shall be consumed, and it shall devour from soul to flesh.”

Nadab and Abihu had offered this fire, which is called alien fire, upon the Lord’s altar, and therefore they were consumed by divine fire (Lev. 10). Hence Moses says: “This is the word that the Lord spoke: ‘Among those who draw near to me I shall be sanctified.’” The sanctification of God is the punishment of sinners.

After this it says: “And I will reduce you to ashes,” so that the fire may consume everything you built above the foundation of your evil conscience. When you should have rested on the Sabbath and done no servile work, you gathered wood on the Sabbath, so that the blaze might have something in your breast to devour. [Note: Rabanus has: “It is also useful for all evil works to be turned into ashes …”]

It will also destroy all evil works, turning them to ashes, so that the harmful fire may be completely extinguished, and so that all may see and marvel that the king of Tyre has perished and become nothing—not after many ages, but in one; or certainly forever, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “I will not spare you, and I will not have pity.”

Among their other fables, genealogies, and endless questions, the Hebrews customarily understand these words as spoken against Hiram, king of Tyre, although from Solomon to Ezekiel there were many years, and it is obvious that human beings do not live for that length of time. Thus they pronounce the passage as though the prophet were speaking to him ironically: “Are you really the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty? Are you adorned with every stone? Are you the Cherub, or created together with the Cherub?—when, on the contrary, you have sinned and are to be dissolved into ashes?”

They add a marvel to their fable, saying, contrary to Scripture—or rather without the authority of Scripture—that Hiram lived for a thousand years. But how violent this interpretation is, the prudent reader understands without our judgment.

(Vv. 20 ff.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set [or “strengthen”] your face against Sidon, and you shall prophesy against her, and say: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Sidon, and I shall be glorified in you [or “in your midst”] [Note: Victor reads: “I shall be glorified in the midst of you (or in you), and they shall know,” etc.; and shortly afterward, “when I have been sanctified in her (or in you).” For the Septuagint has “in you,” ἐν σοὶ, and Jerome’s translation accordingly follows it.]; and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I execute judgments in her [or “in you”], and I am sanctified in you [or “in her”]. And I shall send pestilence into her [or “into you”], and blood in her streets [or “in your streets”]; and the slain [or “the wounded”] shall fall in her midst by the sword [or “by swords”] all around, and they shall know that I am the Lord.

And there shall no longer be for the house of Israel an obstacle of bitterness or a thorn causing pain on every side, around those who oppose them [or “who have insulted them”]; and they shall know that I am the Lord God.

Thus says the Lord God: When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples [or “from the nations”] among whom they have been scattered, I shall be sanctified in them before the nations. And they shall dwell in their own land, which I gave to my servant Jacob. And they shall dwell in it securely [or “in hope”]; they shall build houses and plant vineyards, and they shall dwell confidently [or “in hope”], when I execute judgments upon all who oppose them [the Vulgate adds: “them”] on every side [or “who have insulted them”]. And they shall know that I am the Lord their God.

What follows according to the Septuagint—“And you are the God of their fathers”—is not found in the Hebrew.

After Tyre, therefore, which is itself situated on the Phoenician coast, the word is addressed to Sidon; for both cities belong to one province. In the Gospel also Tyre and Sidon are mentioned together: “If the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon” (Matt. 11:21). Hence the Canaanite woman, whose daughter was tormented by a demon, because she came out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, obtained what she requested (ibid., 15).

The divine word foretells that Sidon too is to be captured by the Babylonians and, under the weight of its evils, is to learn that he is the Lord: when he judges it and is sanctified in it, and consumes it with famine, pestilence, and the sword, so that its people fall in its streets and it may no longer be an obstacle to God’s people or attack them continually.

When this has happened, the people of Israel, whom he had scattered among various nations, will return to their land. He will be sanctified in them—not, as in Sidon, in an evil sense, but in a good one, when he has had mercy on them; and they will dwell in the land that he gave to their father Jacob. They will dwell securely and trusting in the Lord, build houses, and plant vineyards, when he has fulfilled his promises. Then they will know that he is the Lord, whose promises are utterly firm.

Many refer this to the time of Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, when the people of Israel returned and dwelt in the land of Judea. Others hope that it will be fulfilled at the end of time and in the thousand years.

According to the spiritual interpretation, this seems to us to be the meaning. The Sidonians are interpreted as “hunters,” concerning whom it is also written in the Psalms: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. 123:7). And in Proverbs: “The eye of a prostitute is the sinner’s snare” (Prov. 23:27).

There are also hunters opposed to these in a good sense, concerning whom Jeremiah writes: “Behold, I will send fishermen and hunters, and they shall hunt you from every hill and mountain” (Jer. 16:16). The Lord sends these to fish and makes them, from fishermen of fish, fishers of human beings (Matt. 4). Hence the village of Peter and Andrew is called by this name: Bethsaida, for in our language it is interpreted as “house of hunters.”

Against these most evil hunters, therefore, the word of God is directed, and the prophet is commanded to set, or strengthen, his face against Sidon, so that he may not be tossed about by every wind of doctrine, but stand firm in the truth and slay his hunters.

What, then, are the things that the Lord threatens Sidon? “Behold, I myself shall come against you, and I shall be glorified in you when I have slain you. And all who survive shall know that I am the Lord, when I repay you what you deserve. I shall send pestilence and blood into your streets.”

The streets of Sidon are rightly called streets: “Wide and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. 7). And the slain shall fall—those who had stood wrongly—by the sword all around, by the sword that the Lord came to send upon the earth, so that it might separate what had been joined wrongly. Those who remain shall know that he is the Lord.

When these things have ceased, there shall no longer be an obstacle of bitterness or a thorn of pain that pricks and wounds God’s people. All this is spoken against the opposing powers, which at the end of time are to be destroyed, and there shall be eternal security when the Lord gathers the house of Israel—those who behold God with understanding. He will be sanctified in them, and what is written will be fulfilled: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 19:2).

And they shall dwell in their own land, concerning which we also read elsewhere: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). He had given it to Jacob, who had previously supplanted his brother and deserved to receive his birthright.

“And they shall dwell in it securely,” or “in hope”; “they shall build houses and plant vineyards, and they shall dwell again in hope,” in accordance with what is read in Isaiah: “You who have been weaned from milk, you who have been taken away from the breast, expect affliction upon affliction and hope upon hope” (Isa. 60).

They will build houses, as the one builds in the Gospel who establishes his foundations not upon sand but upon rock (Matt. 7). Concerning these it is written: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126:1). And in Exodus, according to the Septuagint: “Because the midwives feared the Lord, they made houses for themselves” (Exod. 1:21), and many similar passages.

When the Lord executes judgment against those who oppose or insult Israel on every side, then every creature will know that he is the Lord, whose judgments are true and justified in themselves.

(Cap. 29—Vv. 1–2.) In the tenth year [or, according to the Septuagint, “the twelfth”], in the tenth month [or, according to the Hebrew, “the twelfth”] [Note: The Hebrew has בֶּעָשׂוֹר, “on the tenth,” בִּשְׁנֵים עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ, “on the twelfth day of the month.” Compare the commentary below, chapter 30], on the first [or “one”] day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set [or “strengthen”] your face against Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and you shall prophesy against him, and speak concerning all Egypt, and say: Thus says the Lord God.

After Sidon, which is also situated on the Phoenician coast, the word is addressed to the prophet in the tenth year of the captivity of King Jehoiakim, in the twelfth month and on the first day of the month, so that he may set, or strengthen, his face against Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and speak concerning him and concerning all Egypt, or against all Egypt. For the province of Egypt is situated on the same coast, on the opposite side of Judea, and he prophesies what is to come upon it.

But if it is necessary to say something about the numbers, what position does one occupy among ten days? Hence at the beginning of Genesis it does not say, “There was evening and morning, the first day,” but “one day” (Gen. 1), to teach that the same day continually revolves. The tenth number occupies the same order among ten decades—that is, among the number one hundred—as the lamb is taken for sacrifice so that it may be slaughtered on the fourteenth day. In this way the order of numbers proceeds through its decades up to one thousand, ten thousand, one hundred thousand, and beyond.

After the tenth year, the twelfth month is placed, so that the perfect number of the twelve apostles and prophets—who are contained in one volume—may be indicated.

According to the Septuagint, however, the tenth month, which in Hebrew is called TEBETH (טֵבֵת), among the Egyptians τυβί, and among the Romans January, is so called because among them it is the gate of the year: with all heat removed, it holds the primacy of winter’s cold. Let this suffice concerning the numbers.

But above all, this must be investigated: is this the same Pharaoh who is named in Exodus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and many other places, and in the Song of Songs: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song 1:9)—or is he one and another?

It seems to me that there was not one Pharaoh, but that among the Egyptians this name indicated royal dignity, just as among the Romans their kings are called Caesars and Augusti after the first Gaius Caesar and his adopted successor Octavian, who was later called Augustus; among the Syrians, Antiochi; among the Persians, Arsacids; among the Philistines, Abimelech; and after Alexander, in Egypt, Ptolemies down to Cleopatra, who was defeated at Actium, after which Egypt became a Roman province.

Therefore at present the word of the Lord is spoken against any one of the kings of Egypt, whose name is interpreted as διασκεδαστής, “scatterer”—that is, destroyer and tearer, cutting and dividing everything with the sword. According to the mystical interpretations, this must be referred to the power to which Egypt is subject.

For no human being would dare to say, “My rivers are mine, and I made them,” nor would he be called a great dragon, sitting in the midst of his rivers. Egypt, however, is called in Hebrew MESRAIM (מִצְרַיִם), and is translated into our language as ἐχθλίβουσα, “the one that constrains,” namely, oppressing and afflicting those subject to it, and not allowing them to raise their eyes toward heaven, but, in accordance with the Gospel and the example of the woman whom the devil had bent over for eighteen years, always forcing them downward toward earthly things (Luke 13).

Let us therefore see what threat is made against Pharaoh and all Egypt.

### (Verses 3ff.)

“Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, the great dragon who lies (or: sits) in the midst of your rivers and says: ‘The river is mine, and I made myself’ (or: ‘I made them’). I will put a bridle (or: a hook) in your jaws, and I will make the fish of your rivers cling to your scales (or: fins), and I will draw you out from the midst of your rivers; and all your fish will cling to your scales. I will cast you (or: put you down) into the wilderness (or: swiftly), and all the fish of your river will fall upon the face of the earth (or: your plain). You will neither be gathered up nor collected; I have given you to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky as food.

“And all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the Lord, because you became (or: were) a reed-staff (or: reed-rod) to the house of Israel. When they grasped you with their hand (the Vulgate omits *their*), you broke, and you tore their whole shoulder; and when they leaned upon you, you were crushed, and you dislocated (or: broke) all their loins.”

For the sake of brevity, we combine the two editions wherever they do not differ greatly from one another.[^c0028-1] Where there is substantial variation, we present both.

He speaks against Pharaoh, the prince of Egypt, and under his figure he speaks to that great power to which Egypt was entrusted for governance; nevertheless, it grows arrogant against its Creator, claiming dominion over the earth for itself and offering itself to the Egyptian peoples for worship. He speaks according to the situation of the province, as though addressing a king who trusts in the flooding of the Nile and does not greatly desire rain from heaven, and who considers himself his own author—or boasts that he himself made the rivers, that is, the *διωρυχαί* (*diōrychai*, “canals”), and the channels of the Nile.

“‘I will not send an angel,’ he says, ‘but, O great dragon, who lie and recline in the midst of your rivers, I myself will come against you to punish you. You have dared to say: “The Nile is mine, and I am my own creator”; or, “I myself made the river by which all Egypt is irrigated.” When I come, I will put a bridle in your jaws—or bind your mouth with hooks, the mouth with which you spoke so proudly—and I will make all your companions and commanders, whom he calls fish, cling to your fins or scales, so that, when you have been drawn out of the river, you may be cast down or deposited. For you had lifted yourself excessively in the wilderness. You will fall upon the face of your plain or land, because Egypt is a level province. Your corpse will neither be gathered up nor collected—that is, you will in no way be buried—but I will give you to the beasts and the birds of the sky to devour. When the inhabitants of Egypt see these judgments of mine accomplished against you,[^c0028-2] they will know that I myself am the Lord.’

“These things will happen to you because you deceived my people Israel by your assistance, so that they would put their trust not in God their Creator but in you. You were for them a reed-staff, according to Isaiah (Isa. XXX), or an empty rod and an exceedingly fragile reed, upon which they leaned and discovered their support to be futile. Thus, when they rested upon you, you broke and tore their shoulder and the hand by which you were held; and while they were secure in you, all their loins were crushed as they fell to the ground and received wounds instead of assistance.

“These things are said metaphorically, as though to the king of Egypt, because that province itself was not hostile to Israel; but, while making great promises, it separated them from the assistance of God.

“We often read of the dragon, in the anagogical sense, as the opposing power. Hence Pharaoh is called *διασκεδαστής* (*diaskedastēs*, ‘the one who scatters’), because he separates and sunders from God; and Egypt, that is, *MESRAIM* (מצרים), is rendered as ‘those who trouble and afflict,’ namely, those whom it can subject to itself.

“This dragon is the transgressor of whom Job speaks at length (Job XL, 41). In the Psalms it is written: ‘You crushed the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia’ (Ps. LXXIII, 14). He is called ‘the great dragon’ in comparison with the lesser dragons of whom the Psalm sings: ‘You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters’ (ibid.). And elsewhere:

> This is the great sea, broad in extent.  
> There are creeping things without number,  
> small animals with great ones.  
> There ships pass through:  
> this dragon whom you formed to mock him.  
> (ibid., CIII, 25ff.)

“Of him it is also said elsewhere: ‘He is the king of all that are in the waters, and the beginning of the Lord’s creation, made so that he might be mocked by his angels’ (Job XLI, 24, according to the Septuagint).

“He sits or lies in the midst of his rivers—not in one river but in many, which we understand as the various heresies through which he has flowed into the Egypt of this present age and watered the souls of the deceived, not with rains coming from heaven but with muddy waters from the earth. Jeremiah does not forbid drinking them when he says: ‘What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Geon?’ (Jerem. XI, 18). In Hebrew, *SIOR* (שיחור) is written instead; the word is rendered ‘turbid and muddy waters.’

“To understand what the rivers of the Egyptian dragon are, we can learn from their opposites. The Lord speaks of his own rivers: ‘Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly’ (John VII, 37). And to the Samaritan woman: ‘Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst; but the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life’ (ibid. IV, 13–14). These are the rivers coming from heaven, of which David sings: ‘The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God’ (Ps. XLV, 4)—there is no doubt that he means the Church.

“Let us therefore consider what punishment and penalty belong to the dragon. It follows: ‘I will put a bridle or a hook in your jaws.’ The following passage in Job is similar:

> Will you draw out the dragon with a hook  
> and put a halter around his nostrils?  
> He trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth;  
> with his eyes he will receive it.  
> You will pierce his nostrils with a ring,  
> and his lips likewise.  
> (Job XL, 19)

“The Lord places a bridle in the jaws of this dragon and pierces his lips, constricting them with the circle of a ring, when through ecclesiastical men trained in the holy Scriptures he imposes silence upon him and all the doctrines of perversity are dissolved.

“He makes the fish of his rivers cling to his fins or scales. By these the heretics, through their pride, hasten toward high things, so that they too, bound together with the dragon, become one body with him and are joined to him either in sharing his error or in resembling his punishment—just as ‘the one who is joined to the Lord is one spirit’ (1 Cor. VI, 17).

“The Egyptian dragon does not have one river but many, with which he waters Egypt, lowly and prostrate, possessing no mountains within itself; nor does he have the waters of Siloam, which flow quietly, but turbid and muddy waters (Isa. VIII). Hence the Lord draws him out from the midst of his rivers, so that he may no longer lie upon or sit in them. All the fish cling to his scales according to the nature of their vices, clinging throughout the dragon’s body—to his head, belly, tail, and extremities—so that, when the dragon is drawn out, the fish that cling to him may also be drawn out with him.

“‘I will cast you,’ he says, ‘into the wilderness, so that you may find no one whom you can deceive.’ Or certainly, ‘I will bring you down from the summit of your pride, and I will bring you down swiftly,’ according to the Apostle: ‘May the God of peace crush Satan under your feet swiftly’ (Rom. XVI, 20). Thus, when the dragon has been crushed and cast down, the fish of that river will also be cast down, and the author of crimes, who previously thought himself able to stand and roam throughout the whole world, will fall.

“He will fall upon the face of his own land, to which he was hurled down from heaven, so that he may no longer be gathered or collected in the churches of the heretics, nor be gathered together or buried among those who have believed him, once they have been freed from him. Instead, he will be given to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky to devour.

“The beasts are those of whom it is written: ‘Do not deliver the soul that confesses you to the beasts’ (Ps. LXXIII, 19). The birds of the sky are those that eat the seed beside the road and are interpreted by the Savior as the devils (Matt. XIII). For not only is the prince of wickedness called the devil, but so are his disciples, according to what is said of Judas: ‘Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?’ (John VI, 71).

“The birds are called ‘of the sky’ because they promise themselves lofty things. After the dragon and his fish have been cast down and thrown away, and he has been handed over to the beasts of the earth for devouring—beasts that possess no gentleness within themselves—and to those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV), then all the inhabitants of this age will understand that he himself is the Lord.

“The whole cause of the punishments is that he falsely promised assistance to the house of Israel and was for it an empty and vain reed-staff, possessing no fullness within himself, because he could not say: ‘But we have all received from his fullness’ (John I, 16), whereas Scripture commanded: ‘You shall not appear before the Lord your God empty or in vain’ (Exod. XXIII, 15).

“That we should not seek assistance from Egypt is also attested elsewhere in Scripture: ‘Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help’ (Isa. XXXI, 1). Concerning this reed-staff, the Rabshakeh also falsely reproaches Hezekiah, king of Judah, saying:

> Behold, you trust in this broken reed-staff, in Egypt;  
> upon which, if anyone leans, it enters his hand.  
> Such is Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to all [or: all those]  
> who trust in him.  
> (Isa. XXXVI, 6)

“He was lying when he said these things about the righteous king, whose name is interpreted as ‘abundant in the cup.’ For he was drunk from Babylon’s golden cup, and therefore he thrust upon the people confessing the Lord the things that belonged to himself.

“Here, however, Pharaoh is reproached because he was for the house of Israel a reed-staff or reed-rod, promising them a vain, fragile, and quickly crumbling assistance.

“To understand what the reed-staff is in which the house of Israel ought not to trust, we can understand it from the opposite rod and staff of the Lord, of which it is said to the Lord: ‘Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me’ (Ps. XXII, 4). Aaron also had this rod, which devoured the Egyptian dragons; and when he struck the embankments of the Nile, gnats were produced throughout all Egypt (Exod. VII–VIII).

“Moses also, according to the Septuagint, extended this rod and lifted it toward heaven, and the Lord brought a south wind over the land throughout that day and night. In the morning the wind lifted and brought locusts over all the land of Egypt.

“I think that this is the rod of which it is also written in the book of Numbers that it blossomed and brought forth nuts or almonds (Num. XVII). The Apostle had this rod when he said: ‘What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?’ (1 Cor. IV, 21). Those who celebrated Passover also held staffs in their hands; without these staffs, which supported the weakness of the human body, they could not eat the flesh of the lamb.

“This is the rod from the root of Jesse, upon which the seven spirits rested. But Pharaoh is not such, nor is the rod and reed-staff of Egypt like it—the reed-staff that deceives those who grasp it and tears their shoulders, that is, their strength. Whoever leans upon it has his loins dislocated and cannot stand, nor can he celebrate Passover girded about the loins. This applies to those whose hearts and loins God searches.”

[^c0028-1]: Victorinus: “you into the wilderness (or: swiftly), and all the fish, etc.” That is, “swiftly” is the rendering of the Septuagint, which translated *ἐν τάχει*; Jerome’s “into the wilderness” is from the Hebrew and is therefore to be preferred. By the same reasoning he shortly afterward reads: “because you were (or: were made) a reed-staff (or: reed-rod) to the house,” etc.

[^c0028-2]: In Rabanus: “accomplished, in my judgment.”

---

### (Verses 8ff.)

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will bring a sword against you and destroy man and beast from among you. The land of Egypt shall become a wilderness (or: destruction) and desolation; and they shall know that I am the Lord, because he said (or: you said), ‘The river is mine, and I made it’ (or: ‘The rivers are mine, and I made them’).

“Therefore, behold, I am against you and against your rivers. I will make the land of Egypt into desolate places, laid waste by the sword (or: destroyed), from the tower of Syene (or: from Migdol and Syene) to the boundary of Ethiopia. No human foot shall pass through it, nor shall the foot of a beast travel through it, and it shall not be inhabited for forty years.

“I will make the land of Egypt desolate in the midst of desolate lands, and its cities shall be desolate in the midst of overthrown cities for forty years (the Vulgate adds: ‘and they shall be’). I will scatter (or: sow) the Egyptians among the nations, and I will winnow them among the lands.

“For thus says the Lord God: At the end of forty years I will gather Egypt (or: the Egyptians) from the peoples (or: nations) among whom they had been scattered. I will restore the captivity of Egypt and settle them in the land of Pathros, in the land of their birth (or: in the land from which they were taken).

“They shall be there a humble kingdom (or: principality); among the other kingdoms it shall be the humblest (or: the most humble). It shall no longer exalt itself over the nations, and I will diminish them, so that they may not rule over the nations (or: so that they may not be numerous among the nations). Nor shall they any longer be a source of confidence (or: hope) to the house of Israel, teaching iniquity, so that they flee and follow them (or: recalling their iniquity to them, so that they follow them). And they shall know that I am the Lord God.”

Join what follows to the preceding passage. Because you were a reed-staff to the house of Israel, and not only were you broken in its hand, but, according to Isaiah (Isa. XXXVI), you pierced its hand; and now you tore its shoulder, and you yourself were crushed, and you dislocated the loins of those who leaned upon you—therefore I will bring against you the sword of the enemy, and together with human beings I will destroy the beasts. The land of Egypt shall be reduced to desolate places, and the Egyptians shall know a second time that I am the Lord.

Nor will I be content with this alone. Because it burst into such great blasphemy that it called its rivers its own and claimed all Egypt’s abundance for itself, I will therefore remove the one who had called himself the Creator, together with the rivers he boasted of having created, and I will reduce the land of Egypt to a very long desolation, laid waste by the sword, from the tower of Syene to the boundaries of Ethiopia.

In place of the tower called *MAGDAL* (מגדל) in Hebrew, the Septuagint set the name of the place, writing *Μαγδαλόν* (*Magdalon*).[^c0028-3] The tower of Syene still exists to this day: it is a fortress subject to Roman rule, where the cataracts of the Nile are located, and as far as that place the Nile is navigable from our sea.

He therefore says that all Egypt is to be depopulated as far as the boundaries of Ethiopia, where the outermost region of Egypt joins them, so that no human foot crosses Egypt, no beasts are found there, and it is not inhabited for forty years.

Egypt is spared, and because the Egyptians were once hosts to Israel, the period of condemnation is shorter. Tyre kept its Sabbaths for seventy years and was then restored to its former condition. The captivity of Judah and the destruction of the Temple likewise lasted seventy years, until Cyrus, king of the Persians. “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI, 7).

When he says, “I will make the land of Egypt desolate in the midst of desolate lands,” he signifies the Philistines, Idumeans, Moabites, and all the other regions against which the prophet’s earlier oracle was directed. Then he will scatter or sow the Egyptians among the nations and winnow them among the lands.

And because the Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and rich in mercies, after forty years Egypt is restored. All the captivity will be brought back to its former soil and settled in the metropolitan city called Pathros, where it arose and from which it departed—yet only so that, for its own benefit, it may lose its ancient pride and become a humble kingdom, indeed the humblest of all nations. It will no longer exalt itself over the nations or exercise dominion over them; reduced to a small number, it will no longer deceive the house of Israel by its confidence, nor teach it iniquity—or recall its iniquity to it—because, having abandoned God’s assistance, Israel sought help from Egypt.

All these things will happen so that, for the third time, the Egyptians may know that he is the Lord. We have touched on these matters briefly, laying the foundations of the historical sense. Now the clouded matter of the allegory must be expounded, and with the same brevity we shall try to avoid making this explanation too long.

The passage concerns the dragon who had said: “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (above, in the same passage). The Lord himself will bring a sword against him, of which it is written in Isaiah: “My sword is drunk in heaven”; now it will descend to earth to destroy from it man and beast (Isa. XXXIV, 5)—whatever appears to possess either reason or simplicity. He will destroy it, not absolutely, but for the dragon, so that it may perish for the dragon and live for God. The land of Egypt will become a destruction, according to the earlier sense: whatever belongs to the dragon will perish, and after its destruction it will be reduced to desolation, ceasing to have so evil a guest.

Then human beings, beasts, and the desolated land will know that he is the Lord, in the sense in which it is written in the seventy-seventh Psalm: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Ps. LXXVII, 34). For everyone who seeks will find.

It is indeed an act of God’s mercy that the abundance of this world should perish, that the streams of Egypt should dry up—indeed, that their land should become desolate places—and that the Lord’s sentence should be dispersed from the tower of Syene, which is interpreted as “a circuit,” so that it possesses nothing upright within itself, as far as the land of the Ethiopians, who are called “the humble.” Thus all the pride that had raised itself against the knowledge of God is destroyed and humbled for its own salvation.

Nor should the foot of man—that is, anything rational—pass through Egypt; nor should the foot of a beast walk in it. This is so that it may not retain the simple, whom Pharaoh wanted to keep in Egypt after the human beings had been released, while Moses opposed him and wanted the beasts also to be freed from Egypt’s captivity.

“And it shall not be inhabited,” he says, “for forty years.” This number is always associated with affliction and punishment. Thus Moses, Elijah, and the Savior himself fasted for forty days and nights; and the people remained in the wilderness for forty years, so that afterward, circumcised at Gilgal, they might be freed from the reproach and disgrace of Egypt (Exod. XXXIV; 1 Kings IX; Matt. IV; Num. XIV).

In the sacramental meaning of this number, the same prophet also sleeps for forty days on his right side for the tribe of Judah, and it is announced that the people will serve in Egypt for four hundred years (Gen. VII). These make forty decades, or four *ἑκατοντάδες* (*hekatontades*, “hundreds”).

The rains of the Flood likewise bring shipwreck upon the world for forty days. For it was just that one who offended God while loving and cherishing the four elements of the world, by which everything is said to consist, should be punished through that same number. Israel, which had sinned against the Sabbath, likewise endured a punishment of seven decades, that is, seventy years.

The land of Egypt is given over to desolation, and its cities are placed in the midst of desolate lands and overthrown cities. These cities were not built of stones but of brick and straw, so that Egypt, which had been wrongly joined to itself, might be scattered and winnowed among the lands—namely, so that the grain might be separated from the straw.

When the forty years have been completed, Egypt will be restored, its captivity will be brought back, and it will be settled in the land of Pathros, which is interpreted as “trampled bread.” There the bread that said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 5), has been trampled by heretical perversity. Thus, when they come to the Church, they will dwell in trampled bread and will no longer be lifted up in pride, but will exist as a humble kingdom.

Even after they have been restored to their former condition, they will humble themselves through humility because they lived in Egypt and built brick cities. Among the many kingdoms of the Church they will be humble, and they will know against whom they sinned. Egypt will no longer exalt itself over the Churches divided throughout the world; instead, it will be reduced to a small number, and only a few will remain in it among the nations, according to what is written:

> Give them, Lord.  
> What will you give them?  
> Give them a barren womb  
> and dry breasts.  
> (Hos. IX, 4)

Thus they will not rejoice and exalt themselves in the multitude of those whom they have deceived, but will be reduced to a few. “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX).

They will no longer deceive the house of Israel—that is, the Church—nor promise it a vain hope and confidence, teaching iniquity so that people flee ecclesiastical discipline and follow Egyptian pleasures.

All these things will happen so that, for the third time, the Egyptians may know that he is the Lord. It seems to me that this is said because the first knowledge of the Egyptians is in the flesh, the second in the soul, and the third in the spirit: first upon the earth, second after the life of this world has ended, and third after the resurrection.

---

### (Verses 17ff.)

“And it came to pass in the twenty-seventh year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, made his army perform great service against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder stripped bare, yet no payment was made to him or to his army from Tyre for the service with which he served me against it.”[^c0028-4]

Therefore thus says the Lord God: “Behold, I will give Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, the land of Egypt, and he will take away its multitude, plunder its booty, and seize its spoils. It shall be payment for his army and for the work by which he served me against it. I have given him the land of Egypt in return for the labor by which they served me,” says the Lord God.[^c0028-5]

“On that day a horn will sprout for the house of Israel, and I will give you an open mouth among them; and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

The question arises how, after the tenth year in the preceding passage, the twenty-seventh year is immediately placed here, while in what follows the tenth and twelfth years occur, and in the final description of the Temple the twenty-fifth year appears.

The solution is easy. Since both the preceding prophecy and the one now being spoken concern Egypt, although they were made at different times, they have been joined together because they prophesy about one province. We often read the same thing in Jeremiah, where the times are described in an inverted order. First, certain events concerning Zedekiah are reported, and afterward those concerning Jehoiakim, who preceded him. In the Psalms, however, because the poem is lyrical, no historical order is required.

Let us therefore speak first according to the literal sense. When Nebuchadnezzar attacked Tyre, he could not bring up battering rams, siege engines, and vineae against it because it was surrounded by the sea and could not attach them to the walls. He ordered the immense multitude of his army to carry stones and earthworks, and, after filling in the intervening sea—or rather the very narrow strait—he made the neighboring shore continuous with the island.[^c0028-6]

When the Tyrians saw that this was now almost complete and that the foundations of the walls were being shaken by the blows of the battering rams, they loaded onto ships whatever the nobility possessed that was precious in gold, silver, clothing, and varied furnishings, and carried it away to the islands.[^c0028-7] Thus, when the city had been captured, Nebuchadnezzar found nothing worthy of his labor.

And because in this matter he had obeyed God’s will, after several years of Tyrian captivity Egypt was given to him—Tyre being much more savage than Egypt. Tyre had attacked Jerusalem; Egypt had promised vain assistance. For it is one thing to deceive weakness through hope, and another to fight against the people of God.

This, then, is what he says: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, made his army serve me in the siege of Tyre, so that I might fulfill my will. “Every head was made bald and every shoulder stripped bare,” as they carried baskets of earth and stones, by which the shoulders were rubbed and the head made bald. Yet neither he nor his army found anything worthy in Tyre.

Because he had served me in this and fulfilled my will against Tyre, I will therefore give him the land of Egypt. Some say that this was fulfilled under Nebuchadnezzar; others under Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, who devastated Egypt as far as Ethiopia, killing Apis and destroying all their images at once.

For this reason they think that he was driven mad through an accident involving a horse and stabbed himself with his own dagger. Herodotus recounts this history at length. He describes all Egypt by its districts, fortresses, and villages, as well as the origin of the Nile and of that people, and he sets out the measurement of the land in its circuit as far as the desert of Ethiopia, the shores of the Great Sea, and the borders of Libya and Arabia.

The reason for the Lord’s anger against Egypt is that it deceived God’s people with its assistance, so that they would not hope in God and would provoke him to anger.

“On that day,” he says, “when Egypt is captured, a horn will sprout for the house of Israel.” There is no doubt that this signifies the royal line. Some refer it to Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, who was descended from David’s line through Jeconiah; others refer it to the final age, when they think Elijah also will come.

We, however, understanding the Lord’s horn as referring to Christ, take up the present history. “When,” he says, “this has first been fulfilled, then your mouth, O prophet, will be opened, and your prophecy will no longer hang upon a doubtful promise; rather, it will be seen accomplished in deed, so that all who hear will know that I am the Lord, whose speaking is doing.”

These things have been said according to the literal sense, indeed according to the truth of the prophecy. But from the fact that Nebuchadnezzar received payment for a good work, we understand also that, if the Gentiles do anything good, it does not pass without reward in God’s judgment.

Hence Nebuchadnezzar is called God’s dove through Jeremiah, because he served God’s will against the sinful people. “I will bring,” he says, “my servant Nebuchadnezzar” (Jerem. XXV). From this it is clear that we are condemned by comparison with the Gentiles if they act according to the natural law while we neglect even the written law. The Apostle Paul discusses this fully in his letter to the Romans.

And, so that we may not seem to pass over anything according to the spiritual understanding, let us ask where we have read this number, the twenty-seventh. In the book of Genesis Scripture testifies that, in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the waters of the Flood were brought upon the face of the earth; afterward, in the seventh month of that same year, which is close to the Sabbath, on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, the waters of the Flood ceased and Noah’s ark rested upon the mountains of Ararat, which are interpreted as Armenia.

From this we understand that the number is intermediate and can be applied in both directions: in it God’s anger begins with the Flood, and in the seventh month his mercy is displayed through the same number of days.

Among the Hebrews, the month—which among us proceeds according to Kalends, Nones, and Ides—is calculated according to the course of the moon. Hence the moon, by the Greek term *μήνη* (*mēnē*), derived its name from the month. This is why it is said that on the twenty-seventh day of the moon only a little light remained, so that his anger might not be entirely without mercy.

When the entire circle of the moon is filled, Passover and all the greatest solemnities are celebrated. We have set this down briefly so that we may know that this number contains both good and evil alike: good for Nebuchadnezzar, whose labor receives payment; evil for the Egyptians, whose devastation is announced.

[^c0028-3]: Elsewhere the form is *μαγδωλόν*. Drusius says that Jerome may have written *magdol* instead of *magdal*, since the word is also used appellatively for “tower.”

[^c0028-4]: Victorinus: “from Tyre,” according to the Vulgate edition and the Hebrew, since the Septuagint reads *ἐπὶ Τύρου* (“against Tyre”).

[^c0028-5]: Victorinus: “and it shall be the payment of his army and the work by which he served against it; I have given him the land of Egypt.” In the Vulgate edition and Hebrew, the additional words “and to me” are found in place of “for me”; they are also absent from the Greek.

[^c0028-6]: Variant: “contiguous” rather than “continuous.”

[^c0028-7]: Marsham argues that the text should read “to the island,” in the singular. Nevertheless, all manuscripts and printed books preserve the reading “to the islands,” and the truth of the historical account ultimately supports it.

### (Chapter 30—verse 1 and following)

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God:

“Wail: Alas, alas for the day! For the day is near, and the day of the Lord approaches; it will be a day of cloud, a time of the nations. And a sword will come upon Egypt, and there will be terror in Ethiopia when the slain fall in Egypt, its multitude is taken away, and its foundations are destroyed. Ethiopia and Libya, the Lydians, and all the remaining populace, and Cub, and the sons of the land of the covenant, will fall by the sword with them.

“Thus says the Lord God: Those who support Egypt will fall, and the pride of its dominion will be destroyed; from the tower of Syene [variant: Soene] they will fall by the sword within it, says the Lord of hosts.

**Note:** Victor reads *God* instead of *Lord of hosts*, following the Hebrew [Hebrew text omitted in the source]. Jerome’s own version, however, gives both: “the God of hosts.”

“And they will be scattered in the midst of desolated lands, and its cities will be in the midst of deserted cities. And they will know that I am the Lord, when I set fire to Egypt and all its helpers are crushed.

“On that day messengers will go forth from my presence in ships to shatter Ethiopia’s confidence, and there will be terror among them on the day of Egypt, for it will surely come.

“Thus says the Lord God: I will make the multitude of Egypt cease at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He and his people with him, the strongest of the nations, will be brought to devastate the land. They will draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain. And I will make the channels of the rivers dry, and I will deliver the land into the hand of the worst men; I will scatter the land and its fullness into the hand of foreigners. I, the Lord, have spoken.

“Thus says the Lord God: I will destroy the idols, and I will make the images cease from Memphis; and there will no longer be a ruler [or: prince] in the land of Egypt. **Note:** The same editor reads “from the land,” following the Hebrew, with the agreement of the Greek *ἐκ γῆς* (“from the land”) and the Vulgate. And I will bring terror upon the land of Egypt. I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire to Taphnis, and I will execute judgments in Alexandria. I will pour out my indignation upon Pelusium, the stronghold of Egypt, and I will kill the multitude of Alexandria, and I will set fire to Egypt.

“Pelusium will suffer like a woman in labor, and Alexandria will be scattered, while daily distress will be in Memphis. The young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis [variant: Bugastis] will fall by the sword, and the cities themselves will be led captive. In Taphnis the day will grow dark when I crush there the scepters of Egypt and its proud strength fails. A cloud will cover it, and its daughters will be led into captivity. And I will execute judgments in Egypt, and they will know that I am the Lord.”

#### The Septuagint

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord:

“Ah, ah, for the day! For the day is near, and the way of the Lord is near; it will be a day of cloud, the end of the nations.

“And a sword will come upon the Egyptians, and there will be confusion in Ethiopia. The slain will fall in Egypt, its multitude will be taken away, and its foundations will be cut down. Persians, Cretans, Lydians, Libyans, and all the mixed peoples, and the sons of my covenant, will fall by the sword.

“Thus says Adonai the Lord: The supports of Egypt will fall, and the disgrace of its strength will descend from Magdolus to Syene; they will fall by the sword within it, says Adonai the Lord.

“And it will be desolated in the midst of desolated lands, and its cities will be in the midst of deserted cities. And they will know that I am the Lord when I set fire to Egypt and all those who help it are crushed.

“On that day messengers will go forth from my presence, hastening to destroy Ethiopia’s hope, and there will be confusion among them on the day of Egypt, because—behold—it will come.

“Thus says the Lord God: I will destroy the multitude of the Egyptians by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—himself and his people with him, pestilential men sent from the nations to destroy the land. They will draw all their swords against Egypt, and the land will be filled with the wounded.

“And I will make their rivers desolate, and I will deliver the land into the hand of the worst men; I will destroy the land and its fullness into the hands of foreigners. I, the Lord, have spoken.

“For thus says the Lord God: I will destroy the abominations, and I will make the nobles of Memphis cease, as well as the rulers of the land of Egypt, and they will no longer exist. I will bring terror upon the land of Egypt; I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire to Taphnis. I will execute vengeance in Diospolis, and I will pour out my fury upon Sais, the stronghold of Egypt. I will destroy the multitude of Memphis.

“And I will set fire to Egypt; Sais will be thrown into confusion, and there will be a rupture in Diospolis, and the waters will be poured out. The young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis will fall by the sword, and the women will be led captive. In Taphnis the day will grow dark when I crush there the scepters of Egypt; there its disgraceful strength will perish, and a cloud will cover it, and its daughters will be led away. And I will execute judgments in Egypt, and they will know that I am the Lord.”

After the twenty-seventh year of the captivity of King Jehoiakim, he returns to the present occasion, when he had begun to prophesy against Egypt—that is, to the tenth year, the tenth month, and the eleventh day of the month—and says that he was commanded by the Lord to speak to all the nations, and especially, together with all of them, to Egypt.

What, then, are the things he says? “Wail: Alas, alas for the day! For the day is near, and the day of the Lord approaches”—not shining with the bright sun, but covered with clouds and bringing the storm of Babylon.

When the sword begins to ravage Egypt, there will be terror in Ethiopia, which is near Egypt, lest the Babylonian blade reach it as well. For the slain will fall in Egypt, its multitude will be taken away, and everything will be destroyed down to its foundations, so that if anyone from Ethiopia, Libya, Lydia, or the various peoples in general, and Cub—which Symmachus translated as Arabia [the Greek phrase is *καὶ πᾶσα ἡ Ἀραβία*, “and all Arabia”]—and from the sons of the land of the covenant, that is, from the Jewish people, is found in Egypt, he too will fall by the sword with them.

**Note:** Some think that Jerome is mistaken here when he says that Symmachus translated the word *Cub* as “Arabia,” [Col. 0288D] since it is much more credible that his translation, *καὶ πᾶσα ἡ Ἀραβία* (“and all Arabia”), refers to the two immediately preceding words [Hebrew text omitted], which properly mean “and all the populace,” though it does not concern the root of the name “Arabia.” Nevertheless, Jerome repeats the same point a little farther on: “and Cub, that is, the Arabs.”

In place of these nations the Septuagint set “Persians, Cretans, Lydians, Libyans, all the mixed peoples, and the sons of my covenant”; they too will fall by the sword with Egypt itself.

And so that we might know that all these nations had been assisting Egypt, the following statement shows it: “Those who support Egypt will fall,” or “the supports of Egypt”—that is, its allies—and all the pride of its empire, or the disgrace of its strength, will be destroyed and brought down “from the tower of Syene,” which, as we have said, is situated at the extreme borders of Egypt; or, as the Septuagint translated, “from Magdolus to Syene.”

All the cities of Egypt will be deserted, so that they may know the Lord when the fire of the Chaldeans has ravaged everything, all its helpers have been crushed, and messengers will arrive in *SIIM*, according to Aquila and Theodotion; Symmachus translated it as “hastening,” while we translated it as “in triremes,” for thus we received it from the Hebrews: so that all Ethiopia’s confidence might be crushed, and, when the neighboring province has been desolated, terror might seize the one next to it.

But so that we might know what sword would ravage Egypt and terrify Ethiopia, the text continues more clearly: “I will make the multitude of Egypt cease at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.” He will not merely come, but will come accompanied by many nations, so that all Egypt will be filled with the blood of the slain. Such will be the Lord’s anger that the channels of the rivers—that is, the Nile’s *διώρυχες* (“canals” or “channels”)—will be dried up to the ground, and the fullness of Egypt will be desolated into the hand of pestilential men, or of the worst men.

For my words cannot be frustrated. His indignation will advance to the point that the idols of Egypt will be destroyed, and the images of Memphis will cease—Memphis, which remains to this day the capital of Egyptian superstition—or the nobles and rulers of Memphis and of the land of Egypt.

Such terror, however, will possess all Egypt that the whole land of Pathros will perish, and fire will ravage Taphnis—or, as the Septuagint translated it, Tanis. “I will execute judgments,” he says, “in Alexandria,” which is so called today. Its former name, however, was **No**, which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as it stands in the Hebrew.

In its place, I do not know with what intention, the Septuagint said “Diospolis,” which is a small city of Egypt. We, however, rendered *No* as “Alexandria,” by anticipation—a figure called in Greek *πρόληψις* (*prolēpsis*)—following Virgil’s line:

> “He came to the Lavinian shores.”

This does not mean that, at the time when Aeneas came into Latium, they were called Lavinian; rather, they were later given the name Lavinian, so that the passage might be clearer to the reader’s understanding.

“And I will pour out,” he says, “my indignation upon Sais,” which we rendered as Pelusium. It is called the “stronghold of Egypt” because it has an extremely secure harbor and because maritime commerce is conducted there above all.

Hence the poet also calls the lentil “Pelusian” (*Georgics* I), not because this type of legume grows there especially, but because it is brought there in great quantity from the Thebaid and from all Egypt by way of a branch of the Nile.

“And I will kill,” he says, “the multitude of Alexandria,” which is again given as *No* in the Hebrew. In its place the Septuagint did not, as above, translate “Diospolis,” but “Memphis.” And to show that the city was already populous at that time, he says: “I will destroy the multitude of No” [Hebrew text omitted]. “And I will set fire” means that the king of Babylon will be in Egypt, ravaging everything like a fire.

“Pelusium will suffer like a woman in labor,” that is, Sais; or, “it will be thrown into confusion.” And in Alexandria—that is, in No—there will be a rupture, and the waters will be poured out; in its place the Septuagint again translated “Diospolis.”

It is the custom of the Egyptians, because of the inundation of the Nile, to construct high embankments along the banks of the Nile. If these are breached through the negligence of their guardians or the excessive volume of the waters, the waters do not merely irrigate the fields below, but overwhelm and ravage them. This signifies that the army of the Chaldeans will occupy Egypt in the same way that fields are accustomed to be covered and ruined when the waters of the Nile overflow and rise beyond measure.

For the inundation of the waters and the bursting and rupture of the embankments, the Hebrew has: “And there will be daily distress in Memphis”—so that where the Nile divides, and where the temple of Apis stands and oracles give their answers, daily distress may arise.

The young men of Heliopolis, which in Hebrew is called **On** [variant: Aven] [Hebrew text omitted], and of Bubastis, another city, will also fall by the sword, so that the cities themselves—that is, their inhabitants—or their women, will be led into captivity; this sex is subject to such violation.

In Taphnis, however, which is a royal city, the scepters of Egypt—that is, the entire royal line—will be crushed. When its power has failed through the killing of its rulers, then the day will grow dark, and everything will be filled with gloom and darkness, so that the city itself will be covered by a cloud of grief and mourning, and its daughters—that is, the remaining towns—will be led into captivity.

After I have executed judgments in Egypt and shown myself to all as judge, then the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord.

We have described these matters as elementary lessons for children, so that through letters, syllables, names, and the arrangement of words they may advance to the reading of prose or verse. Now let us approach the tropological interpretation and, as though on a small painted tablet, display the broad sea of discussion in brief.

The word of the Lord, which was always in the Father, came to the prophet. He calls him not by his own name but “son of man.” In the sacred Scriptures this is always understood in a favorable sense, at least when the number is singular, as in this same prophet, in Daniel, and in the Gospel. Otherwise, in the plural number, it is read in the opposite sense, as in: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5). And again: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:3).

“For the lion will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord has spoken, and who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3:8).

“Wail,” he says, “alas, alas for the day, because the day is near and approaches,” says the Lord. “It will be a day of cloud, a time—or an end—of the nations.”

There are two kinds of consummation: one general, when the end arrives, and one particular, when the time of each person’s death approaches. It is called “near” because, compared with eternity, all time is brief. Hence Jacob, speaking of the one hundred and thirty years he had lived, said: “Few and evil are the days of my life” (Genesis 47:9). And the Psalmist, discussing the frailty of the whole human race, says: “Our days have passed away like a shadow” (Psalm 143:4).

Considering this, we will neither be elated by power, nor cling to riches, nor rejoice in prosperity, knowing that everything will soon be taken away. Beautifully, then, it is called the Lord’s day, when the entire conduct of this world will be destroyed, error will be removed, and one truth will appear—the day of cloud and mist.

No person who is fearless and uncertain of the sentence can await the Judge without fear. And it will be “a time,” or “an end,” “of the nations,” not merely of the one Egyptian nation but of all nations, so that it may become clear that the prophecy concerns every nation.

It follows: “A sword will come upon Egypt.” This is the revolving, fiery sword: the divine word, which separates the good from the wicked and consumes the worst with its fire.

It comes upon the Egypt of this world, so that there is terror in Ethiopia—those who dwell beyond Egypt in the night of error and in darkness, whose blackness is converted into whiteness either with difficulty or not at all.

The wounded will fall in Egypt, those who had stood wickedly in evil. “The multitude of Egypt will be taken away.” For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death (Matthew 7:13).

“And its foundations will be destroyed,” so that nothing of Egypt’s former stability may remain; but when the worst foundations have been abandoned, the foundation of Christ may be laid, upon which the Church is built. For every planting that the heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted (Matthew 7). Hence Jeremiah is also commanded to destroy what had been built, so that he may build better things (Jeremiah 1).

The Ethiopians, Libyans, and Lydians will also perish in Egypt—or, according to the Septuagint, Persians, Cretans, Lydians, Libyans, and Cub, that is, Arabs—and all the remaining populace, whom the Septuagint translated as “hybrids” and “mixed peoples.”

According to the diversity of their vices and the interpretation of their names, which we set forth in the vision concerning Tyre, we can understand all these as different nations. Hence the Apostle says: “You Gentiles in the flesh, who are called the Uncircumcision” (Ephesians 2:11).
