He would never have said “Gentiles in the flesh” unless there were others in the spirit, as in another passage: “Behold Israel according to the flesh.”

Therefore, we must take the greatest care not to return in our hearts to Egypt, from which we once departed, and be found among the other nations, and perish by the sword. Of this sword it is said later: “The young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis will fall by the sword,” especially since the text adds: “and the sons of the land of the covenant,” or “of my Testament,” will be struck down by the same blade.

Of these it is written: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots” (Isaiah 31:1). But if the people of the other nations are slaughtered in Egypt, how much more will the sons of the land of the covenant and of God’s Testament suffer—those who, scorning the bread of angels, remembered the melons, onions, garlic, and cucumbers of Egypt (Numbers 11).

Then the supports and props of Egypt will fall—those that sustained it in wickedness: the subtleties of dialecticians and the tricks of philosophers. Its insulting and arrogant dominion will also be destroyed: those who speak everything through arrogance and regard ecclesiastical simplicity as worthless.

“For from the tower of Syene they will fall in it.” Syene lies at the extreme boundaries of Egypt, bordering Ethiopia and the land of the Blemmyes. There the Nile is unnavigable; there is the crash of cataracts, and everything is inaccessible and full of serpents and venomous creatures.

But if, as we said above, Magdolus signifies magnificence and Syene signifies a circuit, it is clear that the wealth of Egypt, its insulting strength and magnificence—that is, its boasting and exaltation—will perish by force as far as the circuit of Egypt, where nothing is stable, but everything turns in an uncertain fall and reaches ruin.

Then the cities of Egypt will be scattered, the land will be desolate, and no assembly possessing any stability will remain, so that, at the end of all things, they may know that he is the Lord, when he sends into Egypt a fire which the Lord desires to burn, so that the hay, wood, and stubble built upon the foundation of Christ may be consumed—and all the helpers of perverse doctrines are crushed. **Note:** Rabanus reads, with which the Vatican manuscript nearly agrees: “the exaltations may be censured, which pertain to the circuit of Egypt, where, etc.”

From this we should understand that the knowledge falsely so called, and those of whom it is written, “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Psalm 67:32), are called the companions and helpers of Egypt.

“On that day,” he says, “messengers will go forth from the presence of God.” Of these it is written in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:20). And in the parable of the seed, the reapers—that is, the angels who are messengers—are sent to gather all scandals and cast them into the furnace of fire, where there is weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth (ibid., 13).

They will hasten to fulfill the command, to terrify—or crush—Ethiopia’s confidence. They had reached the summit of wickedness, so that when Egypt is overthrown, Ethiopia may be crushed and may tremble because the day of the Lord is a day of vengeance and retribution, by which the darkness of sins is driven away and the light of virtues remains.

“And I will make the multitude of Egypt cease,” he says, “at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon,” to whom they have been handed over for punishment. For he is the enemy and avenger who also received a reward because he served in the conquest of Tyre.

He will cause the multitude of Egypt to cease—that is, many will cease to be in Egypt who are always present there. But if someone objects: how can this be said in Deuteronomy—“Your fathers went down into Egypt with seventy souls, but now you have become as numerous as the stars of heaven” (Deuteronomy 10:22)—the answer is easy.

For he did not set forth an example of earthly multitude, but of heavenly multitude, which shines with virtues and is full of lights. Against this multitude of Egypt the strongest of the nations are brought in order to destroy the land; the Septuagint translated these as “pestilential men.”

I do not know how this can fit those who are brought by the Lord, unless perhaps it is understood according to the example of “the sending of evil angels” (Psalm 77:49). These will draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain or wounded, so that the dead and wounded may perceive themselves to be such. Egypt will be so destroyed and brought to nothing that all the rivers of eloquence by which Egyptian errors were irrigated—reeds and papyrus—will dry up, and they will be delivered into the hand of the worst men, who will torment them. The fullness of the land of Egypt, which had grown wickedly, will be destroyed by the hand of foreigners [Col. 0293A] from God.

For it is not good angels but evil angels who have been appointed over torments. They must know these things because the Lord has spoken. This statement is frequently repeated so that those who hear may know that these are not the prophet’s words but the Lord’s, whose commands cannot be frustrated.

It follows: “And I will destroy the images,” which are abominations. The Septuagint translated it: “I will make the idols—or the nobles—of Memphis cease, and the ruler, or prince, in the land of Egypt will no longer exist.”

It belongs to the most merciful Lord to overthrow things falsely fashioned, so that no likeness that pretends to represent truth may remain in Egypt. The nobles of Memphis must also perish. Memphis is interpreted as “from the mouth,” from which they fashioned all the idols. When the heads and teachers of idols have been cut off, there will be no ruler in Egypt, and the whole of Egypt will be filled with terror and destruction.

Of its cities it is said: “I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire to Taphnis,” or Tanis, “and I will execute judgments in No,” which the Septuagint translated as Diospolis, “and I will pour out my indignation upon Sais, the stronghold of Egypt.”

Pathros is interpreted as “the trampling of bread”; Taphnis as “a humble command”; Diospolis—which corresponds to No in the Hebrew—as “rest”; and Sais as “temptation.”

By these names are signified the various gatherings of heretics and of all falsehoods: those who trample upon and despise ecclesiastical bread, follow a humble command that does not lead to heavenly things, devote themselves to pleasures, and remain in repose—such as the rich man clothed in purple whom we read of in the Gospel (Luke 16)—and serve tempters [variant: temptations]. One of them asks the Lord for the power to tempt Job.

The Lord will destroy and burn all these things, pour out his indignation upon them, and scatter the strength of Egypt, so that, reduced to nothing, they may no longer trouble God’s people or make them hope in their help. Having abandoned the truth, they would seek falsehood and be wounded by their own support as though by a reed-staff.

After this it is said: “And I will kill,” or “destroy,” “the multitude of Memphis.” In the Hebrew it has *No*, which the same Septuagint above translated as Diospolis; it is interpreted as “rest.”

For many seek rest and wish to lie upon ivory couches and eat suckling lambs. Or, according to the Septuagint, which translated the word as “Memphis,” there are many who say to others: “Let me remove the splinter from your eye,” while they themselves have beams in their own.

And fire is given to Egypt, to consume with its heat its verbosity and pleasures. All temptation will suffer, and in Diospolis—which again corresponds to *No* in the Hebrew—there will be a rupture, so that the waters and every worst assembly may be poured out and scattered, disappearing in every direction.

Or, according to the Hebrew, “in Memphis there will be daily distress,” so that they may render an account for every idle word and understand that none of their words will escape the Lord’s judgment.

The young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis will also fall by the sword. Heliopolis is called **On** in Hebrew, which is interpreted as “pain.” Bubastis, according to the Egyptian language, means “an experiment of the mouth.”

All those who could not endure the pain of this world but pursued the pleasures of Diospolis, trusted in the instability of their speech, and argued against other doctrines, having tested their victory, will be cut down by the sword of God’s word. Those who are not called young men but, because of weakness of mind, are called women will be led captive. Or the cities themselves—pain and boastfulness of the mouth—will be led into captivity.

“And in Taphnis,” he says, “the day will grow dark.” Taphnis is interpreted as “yielding to the mouth,” with “of the devil” understood. Those who yield to him will lose the light of truth, turn day into night, and discover that the scepters of Egypt and its entire dominion have been crushed in Taphnis.

Thus its insulting strength—or the pride of its power—will fail; the rays of the Sun of justice will be darkened by the cloud; and not women but daughters will be led into captivity. The Lord will execute not one judgment but many judgments in Egypt.

For just as there are diverse dwelling places of the good with the Father, so there are diverse judgments of punishment for Egypt. When all these things have happened, the Egyptians will know that he is the Lord, whose judgments are true and justified in themselves.

### (Verse 20 and following)

And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first [the Vulgate adds: “month”], on the seventh day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and behold, it has not been wrapped so that it might be restored to health, bound with bandages, and [Note: Victor corrects this to “that it might be mended,” which is closer to the Vulgate reading, “that it might be bandaged,” and corresponds sufficiently well to the Hebrew word [Hebrew text omitted]. For it means “to bind,” as in Exodus 27 and Isaiah 30. Thus, in the exposition that follows, Jerome says: “He says that he has broken his arm, and that it has not been wrapped, bound, or mended with strips of linen.” Shortly afterward, Victor replaced “received” with “restored,” following the Vulgate.] mended with strips of linen [or: so that it might receive a poultice], and, having received strength, might be able to hold a sword.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and I will shatter his strong arm, though it is already broken [or: his strong and prepared arms]; and I will cast the sword from his hand. I will scatter Egypt among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands [the Vulgate: “through the lands”].

And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and I will give my sword into his hand; and I will break the arms of Pharaoh, and they will groan with the groans of one slain before his face [or, as the Septuagint has it: “And he will bring the sword upon Egypt, and he will ravage its spoil and plunder its booty.” It continues:] And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and Pharaoh’s arms will fall. And they will know that I am the Lord when I give my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he stretches it out over the land of Egypt; and I will destroy [the Vulgate: “scatter”] Egypt among the nations, and I will disperse them throughout the lands, and they will know that I am the Lord.

He returns to the sequence of the prophecy. For after the twenty-seventh year, he now sets down the eleventh. The same question is also found in the preceding passages. Although the word of the Lord against Tyre occurred in the eleventh year, as was previously stated, he subsequently speaks to Pharaoh in the tenth year; then, as we have said, he sets down the twenty-seventh year, and now the eleventh.

To pass over other examples contained in the sequence of the Psalms: how is the third psalm placed before those psalms in which David “changed his face” before Abimelech, and before the psalms concerning Doeg the Edomite and the time when he was found in the cave, and before the penitential Psalm 50, whose title shows that he went in to Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, when these psalms are earlier than the third psalm, in which he is noted as fleeing from the face of his son Absalom?

In the Psalms the answer is easy: the work is lyric poetry, and in such a composition the historical order is not sought, but rather the songs of individual events. In history, however, one must say that things spoken at different times about one subject should not be divided in the exposition, but enclosed within the narrative of a single place. For example, matters spoken about Egypt at one time and another should be understood in a single order of reading.

Even after saying this, the question nevertheless remains: Why, in this same place, was the word of the Lord first directed to Pharaoh in the eleventh year, then in the twenty-seventh, and afterward in the tenth, when, according to the proper order, the tenth, eleventh, and twenty-seventh years ought to have been placed before the individual prophecies in that sequence?

To this we can respond: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). And in another passage: “Who will search out the abyss and wisdom?” (Ecclesiasticus 1:2–3).

We can also say that even in the Prophets the order of history is not always preserved—at least not everywhere, but in certain passages—for they do not narrate past events but foretell future ones according to the will of the Holy Spirit.

In historical works, however, such as the five books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Esther, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and the book of Ezra together with Nehemiah, no inverted narrative is found.

Let what we have said about the order of the years suffice. Now let us see what prophecy is spoken against Pharaoh, or concerning Pharaoh.

He says that he has broken his arm, and that it has not been wrapped, bound, or mended with strips of linen, nor received a poultice, in accordance with what is written: “It is not to apply a poultice, nor oil, nor bandages” (Isaiah 1, according to the Septuagint).

If this had been done, then, having recovered his strength, he would certainly have been able to hold a sword and go forth to war. Therefore the merciful and compassionate God again shatters his arm—or arms—so that the sword may completely fall from his hand, Egypt may be scattered among the nations, and it may be dispersed throughout the lands.

By “arm” understand strength and power, as Scripture says: “Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked” (Psalm 9:15). This is broken in our adversaries when they persecute us but cannot crush us.

For the sake of the salvation of God’s servants, the king of Babylon frequently rises against Pharaoh, so that the stronger may crush the powerful, and the wicked may be handed over to worse men, while God strengthens the arms of the worst men, so that the one who has been delivered may know that he is the Lord. It is a sign of spiritual progress to know that he is the Lord.

Conversely, we can say: “The sons of Eli, sons of pestilence, did not know the Lord” (1 Samuel 2:12). On the other hand, of kings who did what was right in God’s sight it is written, in a favorable sense, that they knew the Lord.

But the phrase in the Septuagint, “I will shatter his strong and arranged arms,” where the Greek word is *τεταγμένα* (*tetagmena*), has been corrupted through scribal error. They translated not *τεταγμένα* but *τεταμένα* (*tetamena*), that is, not “arranged” but “extended.” [Note: The printed editions read the invented form *τετειμένα*, while the manuscripts retain *tetamena* in Latin characters, meaning “extended,” from the verb *τείνω* (“to stretch”). —MART.] In accordance with their usual practice, the other translators rendered this as “exalted.”

## Book Ten

As I said earlier, I would like to explain the prophecies against a single province or a single king in the same books, and not divide the reader’s understanding. But what am I to do about the length? Unless it is divided into parts, it exceeds the size of a volume, and the endless accumulation is burdensome both to the one dictating and to the one reading.

Therefore, after the discourse against Egypt and its lamentation, and after what we said in the final part of the ninth book about the king of Egypt, whose arm had not been wrapped or restored to its former health, we pass to the beginning of the tenth book, concerning that same Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He is compared with the king of Assyria; after a very long prophecy, a lamentation over the same king is taken up, and afterward a prophecy against all Egypt.

In explaining these matters, O virgin of Christ, Eustochium, lift up your hands with Moses, so that our victory may be the fruit of your prayers. For it depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy (Romans 9:16), who speaks to the prophet: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11).

The prophet responds to the Lord: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Psalm 118:131). The Spirit breathes where he wills. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (John 3:8; 2 Corinthians 3:17), and with this liberty the Lord has set us free.

How vainly the Jews boasted that they possessed this liberty when they said: “We are Abraham’s seed and have never been enslaved to anyone” (John 8:33), while they were subject to many vices and sins and did not understand the statement: “By whatever a person is overcome, by that he is also enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

[Col. 0297A] **(Chapter XXXI.)** And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and to his people: Whom have you become like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was like a cedar (or cypress) in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches, thick with foliage, and lofty in height; its crown was raised high among the dense foliage (or in the midst of the clouds). The waters nourished it; the abyss exalted [Vulgate: raised] it; its rivers flowed around its roots, and it sent out its channels to all the trees of the region.

“Therefore its height was raised above all the trees of the region (or plain), and its thickets (or branches) multiplied, and [Note: These words, ‘and its branches were raised,’ we supplied from a Vatican manuscript and from Rabanus after Victor, who had supplied only the testimony of Scripture. Martianay, with Erasmus, omitted them.] its branches were lifted up because of the many waters. When it spread its shade, all the birds of heaven made their nests in its branches, [Col. 0297B] and beneath its foliage all the beasts of the forest gave birth, and beneath its shade [Vulgate: shelter] dwelt an assembly of all the nations.

[Note: Victor has “of very many nations,” in accordance with the Vulgate; the Hebrew and Jerome’s exposition appended to it agree. For *universarum* properly represents the Septuagint, πᾶν πλῆθος ἐθνῶν, ‘the whole multitude of nations,’ unless Jerome set down both readings: ‘of very many nations (or of all).’]

“It was exceedingly beautiful in its greatness and in the spreading (or multitude) of its thickets (or branches); [Note: Here too Victor follows the Vulgate and the Hebrew text: ‘for its root was beside many waters.’ Rabanus likewise agrees with the reading in which the word ‘many’ has been supplied.] for its roots were beside the waters. The cedars (or cypresses) in the paradise of God were not taller than it; the firs (or pines) did not equal its summit; and the plane trees (or firs) were not equal (or comparable) to its foliage (or branches). No tree in the paradise of God (or in God’s paradise) was like it or equal to its beauty, for I had made it beautiful, with many thick branches, and all the trees of delight (or pleasure) that were in paradise [Vulgate adds: of God] envied it.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because it was raised up to great height, and it gave its crown, green and thick (or in the midst of the clouds), and its heart was lifted up in its height, I delivered it (or him) into the hand of the mightiest (or prince) of the nations. He shall deal with it; he shall surely deal with it (or: and I shall bring about its destruction). According to its wickedness I cast it out. [Note: After Victor we restore *succident*, ‘they shall cut it down.’ Previously *succedent*, ‘they shall succeed,’ had been read through an obvious and shameful error; for *succident* is found in the Hebrew, Greek, Vulgate, and Jerome’s own commentary.]

“And strangers and the most cruel of the nations (or the pestilent among the nations) shall cut it down, and cast it upon the mountains; its branches shall fall in all the valleys, and its thickets shall be broken on all the crags (or plains) of the earth. All the peoples of the earth shall withdraw from its shelter and leave it. In its ruin all the birds of heaven dwelt (or rested), and all the beasts of the region were in its branches.

“Therefore all the trees of the waters shall no longer exalt themselves in their height, nor set their loftiness among the wooded and leafy places (or in the clouds), nor shall all that is watered by the waters stand in its height [Vulgate: their height], because they have all been handed over to death, to the lowest earth, in the midst of the sons of men, among those who descend into the pit.

“Thus says the Lord God: On the day when it descended to the underworld, I proclaimed mourning (or: the abyss mourned for it); I covered it with the abyss, and I restrained its rivers and checked the many waters. [Col. 0297D] Lebanon was darkened (or grieved) over it, and all the trees of the field were shaken (or withered). [Note: Victor replaces *contritus*, ‘crushed,’ with ‘mourned,’ following the Vulgate and the Hebrew, which can mean either ‘to grow dark’ or ‘to grieve.’ The Septuagint translated the other reading, *contritus*, ‘crushed.’]

“‘At the sound of its fall I shook the nations (or: the nations were shaken), when I brought it down (or her) to the underworld with those who descended (or descend) into the pit.’ [Note: Previously the reading was *deducerent*, ‘they were bringing down.’ Here we agree with Victor, who produces Brixian manuscript copies in support of the reading.] And all the excellent and splendid trees of delight (or pleasure) in Lebanon were comforted in the lower earth, and all were watered by the waters. For they too shall descend (or descended) with it (or him) to the underworld, to those slain (or wounded) by the sword; and the arm (or seed) of each one [Note: In place of *habitantium*, ‘of those dwelling,’ Rabanus and Victor, following the Vulgate, read *sedebit*, ‘shall sit.’ Shortly afterward he reads ‘or in the midst of his life they perished,’ retaining the verb *perierunt*, ‘they perished,’ as a Septuagint reading within the text, and supplying the words ‘in the midst’ from their interpretation. For there is nothing in the Hebrew corresponding to the Greek verb ἀπώλοντο, ‘they perished.’] dwelling beneath its shelter, in the midst of the nations (or of its life), perished.

“To whom are you like, O illustrious and exalted one, among the trees of delight? Behold, you have been brought down with the trees of delight to the lowest earth; in the midst of the uncircumcised you shall sleep, with those who have been slain by the sword.” [Note: Here again Victor agrees with Rabanus: “He himself is Pharaoh.” Jerome’s exposition appended below strongly supports this reading, since the holy Father combines his own translation with that of the Septuagint.]

“Thus shall Pharaoh be, and all his multitude,” says the Lord God.

I have mixed the two editions together according to my custom wherever they differed substantially, lest presenting both versions increase the size of the books. First, it must be understood that whatever is said of the future king of the Assyrians is recorded by the Septuagint as already accomplished; and thus he addresses either the tree or the prince of the Assyrians, so that the same person is understood in both the masculine and feminine genders: the tree refers to the Assyrian, and the Assyrian is named in the tree.

There is no mention here of the king of Babylon, lest the passage appear to provoke the anger of the rulers and kings against the captive people situated in Chaldea. Rather, it speaks of the king of the Assyrians, who by that time had already been captured by the Chaldeans, and all the strength of Assyria was subject to Babylonian rule. Thus the Assyrians captured the ten tribes, that is, Israel, while the Chaldeans overcame the two, that is, Judah and Benjamin, and destroyed the city of Jerusalem.

Since the divine word was about to speak against Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and his people, it used this opening against him: “To whom have you become like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon,” and what follows. The meaning is: Do not be surprised if you are to be conquered and destroyed by the Babylonians, and are to lose your empire, and if all the wealth of Egypt is to be destroyed, since Assyria, much stronger than you, was itself destroyed when the same Chaldean prevailed.

He describes the power of the Assyrian king under the figure of a cedar—according to the Hebrew—or a cypress—according to the Septuagint—standing on Mount Lebanon, beautiful in its branches, thick with foliage, and raised up to the clouds. It grew so greatly because it was watered not by ordinary waters but by abysses, that is, by waters in immense abundance. For the abyss is a multitude of the sound of waters, so that all the birds made nests in its branches, and all the beasts of the forest gave birth beneath its foliage.

And lest we be uncertain which birds of heaven and beasts of the forest were meant, he states more openly: “And beneath its shelter dwelt an assembly of very many nations.” “The cedars,” he says, [Note: Victor argues that the reading should be “or cypresses,” since Jerome always translates the Hebrew word as “cedars,” while the Septuagint has “cypresses.”] “and cypresses, firs or pines, and plane trees or cypresses, were not equal to its branches.”

And lest he speak individually of all the trees, he says: “No tree in the paradise of God was like it or equal to its beauty.” Through these words some understand that the passage does not concern the king of Assyria but the opposing power, which in the oracle concerning Tyre is said to have been created among the cherubim, adorned with precious stones, and afterward to have fallen to earthly things through its own fault. In Isaiah, when it falls, it is called Lucifer (Isa. XIV), and in the Gospel the Lord points to it: “I was watching Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X, 12).

For the present, however, let us follow the historical sense and understand all these things as expressed hyperbolically, namely, that the Assyrian had possessed such great power and had oppressed all the nations so completely that he compared himself with the strength of the angels. Everything is said metaphorically of the Assyrian under the image of the highest cedar or cypress, and his killing is called its cutting down.

What follows—“I delivered it into the hand of the mightiest of the nations”—calls the Babylonian king to mind, so that the destruction of Assyria may be understood as resulting not from his own strength but from divine power. “According to its wickedness,” he says, “I cast it out,” secretly warning the Babylonian that he ought not to be cruel or oppress the people of God, who had been delivered into his power, lest he suffer similar things at the hands of the Assyrian, who had been cruel and wicked.

“And strangers and the most cruel of the nations shall cut it down”—or, according to the Septuagint, “the pestilent”—which he would never have said [or: intended to say] while situated in Chaldea, lest he stir him up against his own people. It is also cast upon the mountains; its branches fall in all the valleys; they are broken on the crags; and it is abandoned by all the peoples—that is, by the birds of heaven and the beasts of the field. It will come to such destruction that all the trees that were thought lofty in comparison with the Assyrian tree will, following its example, cease to raise themselves and lift themselves on high, nor will they stand in their height. Once it has been cut down, all will likewise be cut down through fear.

What had been expressed figuratively becomes clearer. “All,” he says, “have been handed over”—with “kings” understood—“to death, to the lowest earth,” that is, to the underworld, “in the midst of the sons of men,” not among trees, “among those who descend into the pit.” There is no doubt that this signifies the regions below.

After the cutting down of the Assyrian tree—or on the day when the Assyrian descended to the underworld and the Lord brought in (or proclaimed) mourning—he again speaks of him figuratively: he was covered by the abyss, according to the words written elsewhere, “I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm submerged me” (Ps. LXVIII, 3). All the rivers—that is, all the nations—ceased to water him, and Lebanon was grieved or darkened over it, that is, over the tree, or over him, that is, the Assyrian.

And lest we think that the passage concerns a tree, he adds: “At the sound of its fall I shook the nations.” For what fall of a single tree could be so great that all the nations would be shaken at its sound? “When I brought it down,” he says, “to the underworld.” Literally, a tree cannot be brought down to the underworld with the others who were descending into the pit, that is, to the underworld.

“And all the trees of delight were comforted in the lower earth,” that is, in the heart of the earth. In Hebrew this is called *EDEN* (), signifying wooded groves and forests, excellent and splendid, which were in Lebanon and were watered by the waters. For those trees too, with him—that is, with the Assyrian—will descend into the underworld, to those slain or wounded by the sword.

Trees are not wounded by swords but cut down, nor do they descend into the underworld. “And the arm,” he says, “or the seed”—since among the Hebrews the word *ZARA* () signifies both—[Note: This is evidently due to a difference of reading; for the vowels, which formerly were absent, have no bearing here. See below the Commentary on Daniel XI, 31, where the various interpretations of this word among the ancients are also noted. What is commonly read, “And the arms from him shall stand,” was interpreted by another as, “And the seeds from him shall stand.”] “shall rest beneath its shelter in the midst of the nations,” not of the forests but of the peoples.

Finally, an apostrophe is addressed to the Assyrian himself, or to Pharaoh: “To whom are you like, O illustrious and exalted one, among the trees of delight?” No one, he says, was your equal, but you surpassed all kings in power; nevertheless, with the other kings who accompanied you, you have been brought down to the lowest lands, that is, to the underworld. Scripture says: “They shall enter into the farthest parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII, 10–11).

“In the midst of the uncircumcised,” he says, “you shall sleep with those who have been slain by the sword.” He shows what the trees were—the cedar or cypress wounded by swords and lying with the uncircumcised. And, to join the conclusion to what came before, since he had said above, “To whom have you become like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in branches and foliage,” and what follows, he now adds: “Thus shall Pharaoh be, and all his multitude,” says the Lord.

Just as the Assyrian, the cedar and cypress, was felled by the Babylonian, so Pharaoh and his people—that is, the tree itself and its branches—will be cut down by the Babylonian.

Let these things meanwhile be understood according to the historical sense. Many understand them as things that will occur at the consummation of the world: Pharaoh, that is, the power to which Egypt is subject, is compared with the most powerful king of the Assyrians, namely, the Antichrist. If he falls, then surely the other rulers of these darknesses and the princes of the world will fall more easily as well.

Let us therefore speak about each point, briefly touching on everything, so that we may seem not so much to discuss and explain obscure matters as to provide material for those who wish to explain them.

First we must examine why, in the eleventh year, the third month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, saying: “Son of man, speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and to his multitude.” As he is about to speak to Pharaoh, the word of the Lord comes in the eleventh year, for the twelfth had not yet arrived; and twelve is the number of complete and consummated strength.

Thus there are twelve sons of Jacob (Gen. XXXV), from whom afterward the twelve names of the Prophets are contained in one volume. There are also twelve Apostles (Luke VI); and because one of them, Judas, was a traitor, Matthias was chosen in his place. The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue [or: of the synagogue ruler] is also raised by the Lord when she is twelve years old (Mark V). Likewise the woman with the hemorrhage receives healing in the twelfth year.

But because Pharaoh is rebuked and afterward lamented, the third month and the first day are joined to the number eleven. Therefore, in what follows, in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord comes to Ezekiel, saying: “Son of man, take up a lamentation over Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and speak to him.” For one who is lamented is lamented so that he may understand how many good things he has lost.

Nevertheless, because he was Pharaoh, and his arm had not yet been bound up nor recovered its former strength, twenty-nine days still remained in the twelfth year, so that the number of twelve years might be completed. Thus, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord comes to the Prophet, and he is commanded to speak to the king of Egypt and his multitude.

Here it is remarkable that the four translators did not say “people” but “multitude.” For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII, 14). And in the Law it is written: “You shall not be with the multitude in evil.”

And it is said to the king of Egypt: “To whom have you become like in your greatness,” or in your height? He exalted himself and is subject to the sentence: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV, 11). Yet his height is not equal to that of the one who was like a cedar or cypress in Lebanon, beautiful in branches, thick with foliage, lofty in height, and who raised his head even to the clouds. According to David (Ps. XXXV), God’s truth reaches to the clouds, and they are commanded not to rain upon Israel.

His beauty too is praised, though by a perverse will it was changed into ugliness (Ps. LXXVII), so that it is said of him: “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII, 5). And he himself, established high upon the highest mountains of Lebanon, fell all the more violently the higher he had been raised.

Holy Scripture, wishing to demonstrate his height, calls him a great cedar nourished by waters—not the waters of Shiloah that go silently (Isa. VIII), but the waters of Rezin and the waters of Egypt, concerning which it is written: “What have you to do with drinking the waters of Gihon” (Jer. II, 18), or of Sihor? The name signifies turbid waters.

The abyss also exalted him—the abyss over which darkness was borne at the beginning of the world (Gen. I), and into which the demons in the Gospel beg not to be sent (Luke VIII). The rivers of that same abyss were around his roots, concerning which it is said: “What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the waters of the rivers?” (Jer. II, 18). And elsewhere: “Behold, the Lord will bring upon you the waters of the river, strong and abundant: the king of Assyria and all his glory” (Isa. VIII, 7).

The abyss also sent out its channels to all the trees of the region, so that it might water not only the prince of this world but also his companions. Therefore he was exalted and grew above all the tallest trees, his thickets multiplied, and he possessed the empire of the whole world, saying: “All these things have been delivered to me” (Matt. IV, 9). His branches were raised because they had been watered by the waters of the abyss.

He spread or enlarged his shelter in order to subject all things to his dominion. “All the birds of heaven made their nests in his branches.” For everyone who commits sin (John VIII, 34) is born from the devil and is counted among the number of his branches.

Those birds made nests in his branches which, according to the Gospel parable, devour the seed along the road (Matt. XIII); or because all have sinned and lack the mercy of God (Rom. III), concerning whom it is said: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless” (Ps. XIII, 3), therefore they made nests in his branches.

It follows: “And beneath his foliage all the beasts of the forest gave birth.” These are those who have lost the gentleness of Christ. “And beneath his shelter dwelt an assembly of very many nations,” so that no one would exist who was not covered by his shelter [Note: With Victor we read *regeretur*, “was governed,” from the Brixian manuscripts. Martianay, with Erasmus, reads *tangeretur*, “was touched.”], except the one who said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

For through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death (Rom. V, 12); and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom we all sinned. In Adam we all die, and all have sinned and lack the glory of God (1 Cor. XV).

Yet even within that dwelling there are different conditions. Some dwell in his branches like birds, promising themselves knowledge in philosophy and in the doctrines of heretics. Others are like wild beasts, savage and cruel. Others are like a multitude of very many nations, signifying those mingled with various vices and sins.

Assyria was exceedingly beautiful in its greatness and in the spreading of its thickets, because its root had been watered by many waters. So great was this that in the paradise of God no cedar or cypress was taller, nor did the firs and pines equal its height; or the plane trees were not equal to its foliage.

Therefore none of the trees planted in paradise had been made equal to it, because no tree in the paradise of God was like it or equal to its beauty. They were not raised up through pride, but knew their own humility, nor did they attempt with sacrilegious mind to claim equality with God.

What follows—“And all the trees of delight that were in paradise envied it”—we explain in this way: the trees of paradise envied the multitude of its branches. For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16), and “broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (ibid. VII, 13). It desires to have as many for salvation as Assyria had for destruction.

Therefore, because Assyria was exalted in height, gave its height green and thick foliage, or raised its crown up to the clouds, and its heart was lifted up so that it might say, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14), it was delivered into the hand of the mightiest of the nations.

We understand this as another detestable power to which it is delivered for punishment. He is the enemy and avenger: Assyria is understood as the Antichrist, and the mighty one of the nations to whom it is delivered is Satan, according to the Apostle’s words: “Whom I delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. I, 20).

He will do for it whatever the Lord commands him.

This cypress, however, was cast out of the paradise of God because of its wickedness; and strangers and cruel ones—or pestilent ones among the nations—shall cut it down, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser” (Prov. XIX, 25). And again: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the trees” (Matt. III, 10). They shall cut it down [Note: Victor preferred “they shall cast it down,” drawing the reading, in his view, from the preceding and following context.] upon the mountains, so that it may fall in its pride.

Its branches shall fall in all the valleys, so that all who were in its company may be brought down to Tartarus, withdraw from its shelter, and leave it. Thus the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, which had previously been beneath it and covered by its shelter, will afterward share in its punishment.

When the other trees of the forests or of paradise see that Assyria, the cypress, has fallen by God’s judgment, they will no longer raise themselves in pride, nor think themselves to be something, nor regard the watering of their waters as their own riches. For all the branches, birds of heaven, and beasts of the earth that were under Assyria’s dominion will be brought down in death to the lowest earth.

Concerning them it is written: “All who go down into the earth shall fall before him” (Ps. XXI, 30). And elsewhere: “They shall enter into the farthest parts of the earth” (Ps. LXII, 10). They shall be not with the angels but with the sons of men, who descend into the pit, or into the everlasting ditch.

When he has descended to the lowest parts of the earth and has become a portion for foxes, by whom he is to be torn apart, then there will be mourning either for all his companions or for the holy powers, who will grieve that he has descended to the underworld.

Therefore the Lord says: “I covered him with the abyss,” whose waters had previously nourished him; “and I restrained its rivers,” that is, those of the abyss, “and checked the many waters,” so that they would not water him but rather overwhelm him.

Lebanon, in which he had been exalted, grieved over him, and all the trees of the field were shaken, fearing a similar cutting down. “At the sound of his fall I shook the nations,” so that no one would be unaware of his destruction and his descent to the underworld with his other companions.

All the trees of delight, that is, of paradise, received consolation [Col. 0304B] when they saw evil restored to the evil and good to the good. These trees of Lebanon were watered by the rivers of the Lord, and that tree which fell had also been watered by them.

Or all the trees that had once been good, that were watered by the waters and dwelt in the height of Lebanon, will receive consolation when they see their prince suffering torments like theirs. For they too will descend into the underworld, to those slain by the sword of the Lord, and all the strength of the trees will dwell beneath its shelter, that is, in punishment, in the midst of all the nations that will be held in the prison of the underworld.

After this the speech turns to Pharaoh himself. At the beginning it had been said to him, “To whom have you become like in your greatness?” Now it is said to him: “To whom are you like, O illustrious and exalted one, among the trees of delight?” Surely to the Assyrian who fell.

You too were illustrious and exalted among the trees of Eden, that is, of delight and paradise; and behold, you have been brought down like the Assyrian, with all the trees that once existed in delight, to the lowest earth and to the underworld. You will sleep not in rest but in punishments, in the midst of the uncircumcised, that is, the unclean, and with those who fell by the sword of the Lord.

And so that we may know who is meant by the one to whom he says, “O illustrious and exalted one among the trees of delight,” he states it more clearly: “He himself is Pharaoh, and all his multitude.” Or, according to the Septuagint: “Thus shall Pharaoh be, and all his multitude”—just as the Assyrian was cut down and fell above, so the Egyptian too shall be overthrown.

### (Chapter 32—verse 1 and following)

And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month (or the tenth), on one day of the month [the Vulgate omits “day”], that the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, raise a lament over Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and say to him: You have been compared to a lion among the nations and to a dragon that is in the sea; you thrashed your horn in your rivers, troubled their waters with your feet, and trampled their rivers” [the Vulgate has “their,” rather than “its”; or, “your”].

Therefore thus says the Lord God: “I will spread my net over you among a multitude of many peoples, and I will draw you out in my seine” (or, “I will draw you out with a hook”). “And I will cast you onto the earth—or, I will draw you out—and upon the surface of the field [Col. 0305A] I will throw you” (or, “your fields will be filled”). “And I will make all the birds of the sky settle” (or, “sit”) “upon you, and I will satisfy the beasts of the whole earth with you. I will place your flesh upon the mountains and fill the hills [the Vulgate adds ‘your’]” (or, “the valleys”) “with your corruption” (or, “your blood”). “And I will water the land” (or, “the land will be watered”) “with the stench [the Vulgate has ‘stench’; another reading, ‘foulness’] of your blood” (or, “with your dung”) “upon the mountains, and the valleys will be filled from you.

“And when you have been extinguished, I will cover the sky and make its stars dark. I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light. I will cause all the lights of heaven to mourn” (or, “they will grow dark”) “over you, and I will bring darkness over your land,” says the Lord God.

“And I will trouble the hearts of many peoples when I bring your collapse” (or, “your captivity”) “among the nations, over lands” (or, “over the land”) “that you do not know. And I will make many peoples” (or, “many nations”) “stare in astonishment at you [Col. 0305D]” [Victor., following chiefly the Vulgate text, has “many peoples” or “many nations”; Rabanus differs from this only by reading *multas* rather than *multae*, scarcely by a single word]. “And their kings will fear you with immense terror, when my sword begins to fly over their faces; and each of them will suddenly be stupefied for his life on the day of your ruin” (or, “awaiting their ruin from the day of your ruin”).

“For thus says the Lord God: The sword of the king of Babylon will come against you. With the swords of the mighty” (or, “of giants”) “I will overthrow your multitude” (or, “your strength”); “all these are unconquerable nations” (or, “pestilential ones from all the nations”). “And they will lay waste” (or, “destroy”) “the pride” (or, “the injury”) “of Egypt, and its multitude will be dispersed” (or, “all its strength will be crushed”).

“And I will destroy all its cattle that were beside abundant waters” (or, “away from many waters”), “and no human foot will trouble them any longer, [Col. 0305C] nor will the hoof of cattle trouble” (or, “trample”) “them. Then I will make their waters utterly pure” (or, “so that their waters may at last rest”), “and I will lead their rivers along like oil” (or, “so that they will flow like oil”), says the Lord God, “when I make the land of Egypt desolate” (or, “ruined”).

“But the land will be deserted of its fullness” (or, “together with its fullness”) “when I strike” (or, “scatter”) “all its inhabitants; and they will know that I am the Lord. There is a lament, and the daughters of the nations will lament over it” [Col. 0306D] “over Egypt and over its multitude” (or, “over all its strength”), “they will lament over it,” says the Lord God.

We combine both editions, but only where they differ. Otherwise, wherever there is one sense, we follow the Hebrew. In many copies, according to the Septuagint, the twelfth year and the tenth month are given; according to the other interpreters, however, the tenth year and the twelfth month are given, so that either Jerusalem had already been captured and Pharaoh’s joy was taken away by the evils impending over him, or else it was about to be captured, and he grieved more over his own miseries than he rejoiced over the captivity of others.

Meanwhile, briefly laying certain foundations of the history, let us pass over what the Hebrews understand concerning this passage. Pharaoh is compared to a lion, not of one nation but of many nations; or to a dragon in the sea, so that he possesses both land and waters. He was lifted up in pride by the irrigation of the rivers, which is called a horn, and, by the multitude of his army, he could trouble all the waters as he crossed them. Therefore he says that he will spread his net over his multitude and draw him out with his seine or hook, and cast him down—or stretch him out—upon the earth. He had been entwined like a serpent in many coils, so that he might be devoured by all the birds of heaven.

And when not only the birds but all the beasts of the earth have torn him apart, his remaining flesh will fill the mountains, valleys, and fields, so that everything will swarm with worms. He speaks metaphorically: after the birds of heaven and the beasts have been glutted with his flesh—that is, with his army and the whole of his multitude—the rest will be changed into worms and corruption.

Then, he says, the heavens will be enveloped in darkness; the sun, moon, [Col. 0306B] and the remaining lights will not give their light, but everything will grow dark over you. Nothing joyful will remain for you, and all peoples and all their kings will fear with immense terror at your destruction, seeing my sword flying here and there and sparing no one; and at your ruin they will dread a similar ruin for themselves.

But so that you may know what this sword is, hear more clearly: “The sword of the king of Babylon will come against you; with the swords of the mighty, or giants, I will overthrow all your multitude.” These giants are unconquerable nations that were held by the army of the king of Babylon. They will lay waste, or destroy, the pride of Egypt and all its multitude. Nothing will remain in Egypt; rather, human beings, cattle, and brute animals alike will be carried away.

And such solitude will there be in Egypt that neither the foot of a human being nor the hoof of an animal will trouble its waters, [Col. 0306C] but everything will be quiet; its river waters will flow like oil, utterly pure and shining, with no one passing through them or disturbing their streams. This will happen because of Egypt’s desolation: it will be reduced to a wilderness, stripped of all its multitude, when the Lord strikes down its inhabitants, so that those who remain may understand that he is the Lord.

Therefore there is a lament over Pharaoh, and the daughters of the nations around will lament him—not only over him, but also over his multitude, which, as the Lord lays waste, has been destroyed. Let it suffice to have said these things briefly concerning the literal sense; let us come to the spiritual understanding.

Nor do I think we must labor greatly to learn who Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is, since above we explained more fully that he is the power to which Egypt has been entrusted—whether one province, or Egypt as a figure of the whole world—which was not created a lion but, through its own fault, was made like a lion among the nations. For “when a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm XLVIII, 13).

Peter also speaks of this lion: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking whom he may devour” (I Peter V, 8). And in the ninth psalm (verse 9) it is written: “He lies in wait secretly like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor.” And in Jeremiah [Col. 0307A] the Holy Spirit says: “The lion from the forest has struck them” (Jeremiah V, 6).

I have demonstrated through many testimonies, in accordance with the foregoing explanation, that the dragon is also called the devil—Aquila translated it as *Leviathan*, explaining the name as “dragon”—the one who had said: “The rivers are mine, and I made them.” This dragon, therefore, thrashed many nations with his rivers as with horns. We may understand these as referring to Marcion, Valentinus, Arius, Eunomius, and the other leaders of heresies, who imitate ecclesiastical men and say to the Lord and Savior: “In you we will toss our enemies with the horn” (Psalm XLIII, 6). They do not toss them toward salvation, so as to lift them from earth to heaven, but so as to cast them into the depths.

Accordingly, what follows is: “And you troubled the waters with your feet,” in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “But the one who troubles you will bear the judgment” (Galatians V, 10). For he does not wish to drink the waters of Shiloah, which go silently (Isaiah VIII), but the turbid and muddy waters of Egypt. Before they were trampled by the dragon’s feet, these waters were pure and flowed in their proper order; but after they were troubled by his feet, they lost the order of their course. For heretics do not use the testimonies of Scripture in ways that cohere with one another; rather, they trouble everything.

And because he himself is the enemy and avenger, the Egyptian dragon not only troubles alien waters with his feet but tramples his own rivers, showing no mercy to those whom he has once reduced to his power. Wishing to avoid this, the righteous man prays: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Psalm XXXV, 12). And elsewhere, having been trampled, he asks not to be trampled again: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for man has trampled me” (Psalm LV, 1).

The hostile man is the devil, of whom another psalm also speaks: “So that man may no longer be exalted over the earth.” Therefore thus says the Lord God: “I will spread my net over you among a multitude of many peoples” (Psalm IX, 18). The net of the Lord, woven from the reasoning of the Old and New Testaments, is cast over the dragon who dwells among the multitude of peoples and always delights in crowds and in the multitude of peoples, so that he may draw him out in his seine or his hook.

This is the seine cast into the sea of this age, which draws out many fish, some to be chosen and others to be rejected (Matthew XIII). Or this is the hook of which it is written in Job: “You will draw out the dragon with a hook and put a halter around his nostrils” (Job XL, 19). Aquila translated it: “You will draw out Leviathan with a hook and bind his tongue with ropes.”

The dragon, or Leviathan, is drawn out of the sea by the Lord’s hook or seine, so that he may be cast down, or stretched out, upon the earth; all his coils, with which he concealed his ambushes, may be opened and brought into public view; he may be cast upon the earth; and he who had set his mouth in heaven and boasted that he was like the Most High may lie prostrate.

Hence what follows: “And I will make all the birds of heaven settle, or sit, upon you, and I will satisfy the beasts of the whole earth with you,” in accordance with what is written: “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm LXXIII, 14). These are called either birds [Col. 0308A] or beasts of the earth (Matthew XIII; Luke VIII): birds, which, as we have said, snatch away the seed beside the road; beasts of the earth, made savage by vices. This may refer to heretics and gentiles.

But what follows—“And I will place your flesh upon the mountains and fill your hills with your corruption; or, I will fill the valleys with your blood”—has this meaning: we are to understand the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth as the peoples of the deceived; the cruelty of the gentiles; the mountains as the leaders of heresies, such as Valentinus and Marcion; and the hills as their successors, who are filled with the dragon’s corruption; or the valleys, which are filled with the dragon’s blood, as the lowliest of the believers.

Alternatively, the mountains are the hostile powers that roam through the air, and the valleys are those that penetrate the underworld [382] and have been consigned to eternal punishments.

Moreover, when it says, “And I will water the land with the stench [another reading: foulness] of your blood upon the mountains,” or, “the land will be watered with your dung upon the mountains, and the valleys will be filled from you,” it signifies that all the pride and arrogant swelling of heretics is filled not with blood that is living and pure, but with blood that is putrid and foul, in accordance with what is written: “Place them like dung upon the earth” (Psalm LXXXII, 11).

From this the saint is delivered by the Lord: “He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to set him with princes, with the princes of his people” (Psalm CXII, 7–8). The valleys, depressed into the lowest places, signify either the underworld, as we said above, or the lowly understanding of heretics, who do everything for pleasure and earthly riches.

But what is added—“And when you have been extinguished, I will cover the sky, and I will make its stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light; I will make all the lights of heaven mourn, or grow dark, over you, and I will bring darkness over your land,” says the Lord God—cannot be understood at all if we follow the literal sense.

For when Pharaoh, or the dragon, was killed, when did the sun, moon, and stars not give their light, and when was the sky covered with darkness, in accordance with that poetic passage (Virgil, *Georgics* I):

> “And the impious ages feared eternal night”?

Therefore this must be said: when Pharaoh, who transformed himself into an angel of light, has been extinguished—concerning whom it is written elsewhere, “The light of the wicked will be extinguished” [Col. 0308D] (Job XVIII)—the sky, or the heavens, will be covered with darkness. Paul also speaks of these: “The spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI, 12).

And the Lord will make its stars—whether the dragon’s or the sky’s—dark. Concerning this the Apostle Jude also writes: “Wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been reserved forever” (Jude XIII).

The sun also will be covered with a cloud: the sun of iniquity, which is opposed to the sun of righteousness, will be covered either by a cloud, or by the Lord and Savior himself, who descended into Egypt upon a light cloud (Isaiah XIX), unburdened by any weight of sins; or by the prophets and apostles, concerning whom we read: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isaiah V, 6). And in the Psalms: “Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm XXXV, 6).

But when the sun of iniquity has been darkened, the moon—which we understand as the Church of the heretics, and which was thought to receive its light from the sun of iniquity—will not give its light, nor will it deceive believers with knowledge falsely so called.

All the lights also, and whatever doctrine appears to exist among heretics, will dry up when the dragon has been extinguished, or they will mourn when their prince has been destroyed. Thus the Lord himself will cover the land of the heretics with darkness, namely, ignorance of the truth, so that the blind may lead the blind into the pit, and the inhabitants of the earth may be cast into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.

After this it is said: “And I will trouble the heart of many peoples when I bring your collapse, or captivity, among the nations over a land that you do not know.” Those who had previously served Pharaoh will grow angry against him when they see his captivity brought to another land, one that the dragon did not know existed.

Nor should we doubt that the lands unknown to Pharaoh are good lands—namely, when Pharaoh’s captivity is exchanged for another captivity, concerning which it is said to the Savior: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he received” (or, according to the Apostle [Ephesians IV, 8], “gave”) “gifts to human beings” (Psalm LXVII, 19).

“And I will make many peoples stare in astonishment at you,” he says, so that those who had previously admired Pharaoh’s power may afterward marvel at his fall from his height. The kings of the peoples will also fear him with immense terror—their kingdoms having been shown by the devil to the Lord, and concerning whom it is said in the psalm: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together” (Psalm II, 2).

This will happen when the sword of the Lord begins to fly over their faces [Col. 0309C], with “kings” or “peoples” understood. The sword of the Lord is to be understood as the living, effective word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword. It flies and moves about, grazes the eyes of those who see, and terrifies their faces, so that, astonished at Pharaoh’s ruin, they may see themselves overthrown in him.

The Lord’s sword, concerning which it is written, “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising again of many” (Luke II, 34), raises those who lie prostrate and changes those who stand wrongly erect through humility.

But the sword of the king of Babylon will come against the Egyptian dragon, so that, with the swords of the mighty, or giants, the Lord may overthrow his multitude, which followed the king of Egypt. “All these,” he says, “are unconquerable,” or “pestilential,” from among the nations, so that evil people may be handed over for punishment to worse ones, concerning whom it is written: “A sending through evil angels” (Psalm LXXVII, 49). And the Apostle says: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme,” or “for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (I Timothy I, 20).

When the pride of Egypt has been cast down through such ministers, and its multitude dispersed, all its cattle [Col. 0310A], which were beside abundant waters, will be destroyed, and no human foot will trouble them any longer.

For if blessed is the one who sows beside the waters, where the ox and donkey trample (Isaiah XXXII), then, conversely, unhappy is the one who will still be able to hold the simple in his error, so that no human foot may tread upon them; thus the Egyptian waters appear to possess not even a sign of wisdom and reason.

Nor will the hoof of cattle trouble them, making what was clear and shining turbid and muddy. Then the waters that had been troubled by the dragon’s domination will be restored—not by someone else, but by the Lord himself—to complete purity, so that their rivers may flow like oil and become nourishment for the true light.

This will happen when the Lord makes the land of Egypt desolate, destroys its multitude, and all its inhabitants are struck down, so that through this improvement they may know that he is the Lord.

But what is added—“There is a lament, and the daughters of the nations will lament him over Egypt, and over its multitude they will lament him,” says the Lord God—is clear: the souls of all the nations that had previously been oppressed, or of those nations that did not dwell in Egypt at all but in the land of the living, lament the dragon who has been killed, and all his multitude—not in hope of salvation, but because, through his own fault and pride, he has been cast down from such great power into eternal punishments.

### Verses 17 and following

“And it came to pass in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, sing a mournful song [Col. 0310C] over the multitude of Egypt, and bring it down, together with the daughters of mighty nations, to the farthest land, with those who descend into the pit. Whom do you surpass in beauty? Descend, and sleep with the uncircumcised.

“In the midst of those slain by the sword they will fall. The sword has been given; they have dragged her away, her and all her peoples. The most powerful of the mighty will speak to it from the midst of hell, those who descended with its helpers” [another reading: “with their helpers”] “and slept” [385]

[Note: According to his custom, Victor, together with the Vulgate and the Hebrew, reads: “They slept uncircumcised, slain by the sword.” His meaning, he says, is that the most powerful of the mighty themselves descended and slept uncircumcised, having been slain, rather than that they slept with the uncircumcised and slain. For since he had already said above, “Sleep with the uncircumcised,” there was no need to repeat it at greater length; rather, it was more fitting that he should explain afterward who these uncircumcised were with whom he was to sleep, saying that they were the most powerful of the mighty, who slept uncircumcised and were slain. The printed reading, however, is more that of the Septuagint than of Jerome.]

“with the uncircumcised, and slain by the sword. There is Asshur and all his multitude; around him are his graves, all of them slain and those who fell by the sword, whose graves were placed in the farthest parts of the pit. And his multitude was made around his grave—all of them slain and fallen by the sword, who had once given terror in the land of the living.

“There is Elam and all his multitude around his grave [the Vulgate has ‘his own’]: all these were slain and fell by the sword; they descended uncircumcised to the farthest land; they placed their terror in the land of the living; and they bore their disgrace with those who descend into the pit.

“In the midst of the slain they placed his bed among all his peoples; around him is his grave. All these are uncircumcised and slain by the sword. For they had given terror [the Vulgate has ‘their terror’] in the land of the living, and they bore their disgrace with those who descend into the pit; they were placed in the midst of the slain.

“There are Meshech and Tubal, and all his multitude; around him are his graves. All these are uncircumcised and slain, falling by the sword, [Col. 0311D] who gave their terror in the land of the living” [the same editor preferred *qui* (“who”) to *quia* (“because”), following the Hebrew].

“And they will not sleep with the mighty who have fallen and the uncircumcised, who descended to hell with their weapons and placed their swords beneath their heads; and their iniquities were upon their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living.

“And you too will be shattered in the midst of the uncircumcised, and you will sleep with those slain by the sword. There are Edom and its kings and all its leaders, who were given over with their army to those slain by the sword, and who slept with the uncircumcised and with those who descend [the Vulgate has ‘who descended’] into the pit.

“There are all the princes of the north, and all the Sidonians” (or, “hunters”), “who were led away with those slain, terrified, and in their strength” [Col. 0311D] [we have restored, following Victor, “in their strength” in place of the reading “in terror”; apart from the Vulgate and Hebrew text, Rabanus formerly read this way as well, and Jerome testifies that he himself placed it thus in the exposition appended below] “confounded, because” [the Vulgate has “who”] “they slept uncircumcised with those slain by the sword, and bore their confusion with those who descend into the pit.

“Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude, which was slain by the sword—Pharaoh and all his army,” says the Lord God. “For I have given” [another reading: “he gave”] “my terror” [Col. 0311C] [although the Hebrew word is ambiguous, the Vulgate has “my”; Victor preferred “his,” from the Greek αὐτοῦ (*autou*)] “in the land of the living, and Pharaoh and all his multitude slept in the midst of the uncircumcised with those slain by the sword,” says the Lord God.”

The edition of the Septuagint interpreters differs greatly in this passage, both in order and in translation, and certain things have been added to it from Theodotion. Therefore we deemed it necessary to include it as well, sparing no length and serving the diligence of the attentive reader.

### LXX

“And it came to pass in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

‘Son of man, lament over the multitude of Egypt, and bring down its daughters, the nations of the dead, to the depths of the earth, to those who go down into the pit.’

(Additionally, under asterisks, the following has been added: “Go down from the fairest water; and sleep with the uncircumcised.” Again the order follows.)

‘In the midst of those pierced by the sword they shall fall with him, and all his strength shall sleep. And the giants shall say to you, “Go down into the depths of the pit. In what are you better? Go down and sleep with the uncircumcised in the midst of those pierced by the sword.”’

There is Assur, and all his assembly.

(The following passage—“All the wounded are given there, and his grave is in the depths of the pit, and his assembly has been made”—is not found in the Hebrew, but was added by the Septuagint. It is again said:)

‘Around his grave are all the wounded who had fallen by the sword.’

[Col. 0312A]

(Again, from Theodotion’s edition, the following was added under asterisks: “Those who gave his graves on the sides of the pit; and an assembly was made around his grave; all these wounded and fallen by the sword.” After this the Septuagint placed:)

‘Those who gave their terror in the land of the living.

There is Elam, and all his strength around his grave, all wounded and falling by the sword; and those who go down uncircumcised into the depths of the earth, who gave their terror in the land of the living, and received their punishment with those who go down into the pit in the midst of the wounded.

There they have been given over—Meshech, Tubal, and all their strength—around his grave, all his wounded, all the uncircumcised and pierced by the sword, who gave their terror upon the land of the living. They did not sleep with the giants who fell from of old, who went down to the underworld with the weapons they used for war. They placed their swords beneath their heads, and their iniquities were in their bones, because they had terrified the giants during their life.

And you shall be broken in the midst of the uncircumcised, and shall sleep with those pierced by the sword.

There is Edom, and its kings, and all the princes of Assur, who gave his strength over to the wound of the sword. These slept with the wounded, with those who went down into the pit.

There are all the princes of the North, all the magistrates of Assur, who went down wounded with their terror, and slept uncircumcised with those pierced by the sword, and took away their punishment with those who descend into the pit.

Pharaoh shall see them, and shall be comforted over all their strength: Pharaoh, pierced by the sword, and all his strength, says the Lord God. For I have given his fear over the land of the living; and he shall sleep in the midst of the uncircumcised with those pierced by the sword—Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God.’”

I am not unaware that so great a discrepancy between the two editions will seem wearisome to a refined reader. But what am I to do with my critics? If I omit anything from the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, they cry out that I am sacrilegious and without fear of the Lord—especially those who, while they disagree concerning the truth of the faith and follow the errors of the Manichaeans, stir up the souls of the uninstructed if they can point to anything in the Old Testament that has been altered from customary usage. They prefer to err rather than to learn something true from a rival.

Meanwhile, according to the historical interpretation, the meaning is clear. For in the same twelfth year, and, as we think, in the same month—but not on the first day of the month, as above, rather on the fifteenth day—a lamentation is taken up, not over Pharaoh but over the strength, or multitude, of Egypt. It is brought down from its pride, together with all its daughters, that is, with the nations of the mighty, to the furthest land, namely, to the depths of hell. And it is said to the king of Egypt: “In what respect are you better, that you should deserve to escape death?”

For since Assur, and Elam—that is, the Persians—and Meshech, who are interpreted as the Cappadocians, and Tubal, whom some wish to understand as the Iberians and others as the Italians; and likewise the Idumaeans, the princes of the North, and the Sidonians, together with all their armies, by whose aid they brought dread upon all the nations, have died and been slain by the sword, and have placed their swords beneath their heads—a statement to be understood more emphatically [Greek: emphatikōteron]—will you alone be able not to suffer the same things?

Rather, when you see so great a multitude sleeping with you among the dead, and your grave surrounded by the memorials of once-mighty princes, you will have consolation, judging your punishments lighter because of the company of so many. For the present, it is enough to have said these things briefly according to the simple sense.

Now, with the same brevity, let us gather the chief points of the spiritual interpretation, insofar as the difficulty of the explanation permits.

Above, the word of the Lord came to the Prophet on the first day of the month; here, on the fifteenth. On the first day, that is, at the new moon, the beginning of the month occurs; on the fifteenth, when the whole circle of the moon is full—and if it is the first month, it is the first day of Unleavened Bread; but if it is the seventh, it is the feast of Tabernacles, when the booths are erected. These are especially important festivals among the Hebrews.

A lamentation is made over the strength of Egypt, so that it may cease to be strong in evil and receive weakness; and when it has become weaker, then it will be stronger. Instead of “the strength of Egypt,” the Hebrew has “the multitude.” For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many enter through it (Matt. 7:13). Conversely, it is said to Israel: “You are few among all the nations” (Deut. 28). For virtue is always rare, and the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted, and few are those who enter through it.

When Egypt is lamented, and its dead daughters, according to the Septuagint, or the mighty nations, are brought down to the furthest land, into the lake or deepest pit, souls are signified that dwell in the Egypt of this age and have lost the one who says: “I am life” (John 14:6). Dead through sins, they are dragged down to hell by the weight of them, as the sinner says: “For my iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me” (Ps. 37:5).

These are the ones of whom it is written elsewhere: “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be given over to the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. 62:10). “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (Ecclus. 27:29; Ps. 7:16). Hence we also read: “He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit that he made.”

What follows—“Go down, you who are more beautiful, and sleep with the uncircumcised”—is addressed specifically to Pharaoh, king of Egypt; or, as was added in the Septuagint from Theodotion, to Egypt itself: “Go down from the fairest water, and sleep with the uncircumcised.”

This applies especially to one who, reborn in Christ’s baptism and hearing with the Church, “Who is this who comes up whitened, leaning upon her cousin (fratruelem)?” (Song 8:5), is afterward defiled by fornication or other vices, is cast out of the Church, and is told: “Go down from the fairest water, and sleep with the uncircumcised”—that is, with the unclean—according to the sense expressed by the Apostle: “We are the circumcision” (Phil. 3:3), that is, those who serve God in the Spirit, glory in the Lord, and do not trust in the flesh.

All these shall fall in the midst of the wounded, or slain, with Pharaoh, by that sword which the Lord came to cast upon the earth. For just as Christ’s sword separates the good from the wicked, saying, “I came not to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34), so the sword of heretics cuts down all peoples and leads the wounded to hell.

These are the exceedingly powerful giants, rebellious and lifting their mouth on high. The more they raise themselves up to lofty things through pride, the more they are dragged down into the depths of the pit and the furthest reaches of hell. All of them have been slain by the sword.

And so that Pharaoh—or all the strength of Egypt that has been dragged down to the underworld—might know whom it would have as companions in punishment, the following speech shows: “There is Assur, and all his multitude,” or his synagogue. For the prince of heretics is the devil, whose assembly is truly a synagogue, concerning which it is said in the Apocalypse: “Those who are the synagogue of Satan” (Rev. 2:9).

[Note: Rabanus reads: “which among the Septuagint [is marked] by an obelus,” etc.]

I think that the following verses, which are marked beforehand by an obelus, should be passed over, and that what is found in the Hebrew should be said: “Around him are their graves,” namely, the graves of those deceived by him.

All these were wounded or slain by the sword, and therefore they fell; their graves were placed in the furthest parts of the pit. That the pit is called hell is clearly demonstrated by that psalm in which the penitent says: “I have become like those who descend into the pit” (Ps. 27:1).

We must not understand it according to the proper usage of the Latin word as the place called in Greek [Greek: limnē], such as Lake Tiberias, Lake Larius, Lake Benacus, and many others, but as those which we are not accustomed to call cisterns. Because these pits cool waters and remove all the heat of the spirit from them, sinners and all heretics dig them. As far as my memory serves, Scripture testifies that no saint ever dug a pit—that is, a cistern—but that all sinners did so. Among them was King Uzziah, the leper, who fell through his pride. It is written of him that he was a man occupied with the works of the earth, built many towers of pride at the corners, and dug pits (2 Chron. 26).

Conversely, it is said to the righteous: “Drink water from your own vessels, and from the springs of your wells” (Prov. 5:15). And again: “Let the fountain of your water be your own.” Hence the Lord also says: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns”—that is, pits—“that cannot hold water” (Jer. 2:13).

It follows: “And his multitude was made around his grave.” All these surround the Assyrian, and their multitude is very great; they are all wounded, slain, and falling by the sword. None of them can stand with Moses or hear: “You who stand in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 134:2).
