Rather, all are wounded and slain, falling—those who once gave terror in the land of the living: terror to those who had been placed over the Churches, lest they make peoples of the dead in the land of the living and deceive the simple.

Hence Paul also said: “But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:3). Yet this fear is mitigated by hope in the Lord, as the ecclesiastical man says: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (Ps. 26:1–2).

After this it is said: “There is Elam [another reading: Assur], and all his multitude around his grave”—without doubt, the Assyrians. Elam is translated in our language as “their ascent.” For all who, despising Christ’s humility, have climbed into the devil’s pride and have judged themselves to be something in a knowledge falsely so called are to be called Elamites. They surround the grave of the king of the Assyrians, and have been slain and wounded by the sword.

Although they placed their mouth on high, nevertheless they descended, unclean and uncircumcised, to the furthest land, so that the more loftily they had been raised, the more violently they might fall. These gave their terror not once but twice in the land of the living. For what ecclesiastical person is safe from the terror of such Elamites and has not lost someone from his flock?

The Church of Christ is beautifully called the land of the living, so that, conversely, the gatherings of heretics may be believed to be the land of the dead. “And they carried,” he says, “their disgrace,” or punishment, “with those whom they dragged down with them into the pit and into the depths of hell.” Their dwelling is in the midst of the slain—namely, those whom they slaughtered with their sword and among whom they are surrounded.

These peoples are the peoples of the king of Assur. Although they boast that they are circumcised, they have been slain by the sword as uncircumcised, and for the third time they gave terror and dread in the land of the living. Therefore they carried their punishment and penalty in the midst of those whom they deceived by their frauds.

There also, that is, beside the Assyrian, are Meshech, Tubal, and all his multitude around his grave: all uncircumcised, slain, and falling by the sword, who had given their terror in the land of the living.

Instead of Meshech and Tubal, Symmachus and Theodotion translated “their dwelling-place.”

[Note: The reading apparently intended is one word in place of the omitted or corrupt form.]

They wished to show that the dwellings of heretics—or rather, their eternal pits—are the punishments of the king of Assur. Meshech is interpreted as “madness”; Tubal as “conversion,” not conversion from evil to good, but from good to evil; or “all things,” so that it may show that all heretics are mad and turn with equal zeal toward worse things (Rom. 12).

Nor is it surprising that, being mad and heaped together for evil, they have a multitude, since they are companions of the king of Egypt, who rejoices in a multitude. All these were slain by the sword, those who gave their terror—not once, nor twice, but three times—in the land of the living. We have spoken more fully of them above.

It follows: “And they shall not sleep with the mighty,” or giants, “falling and uncircumcised, who went down to hell with their weapons. They placed their swords beneath their heads, and their iniquities were upon their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living.”

These, he says, who had been princes among the heretics reached such a height and torment of wickedness that they did not even deserve to suffer punishments like those of the mighty and the giants who fell from the beginning. Without ever repenting of the deeds of their error, they went down to hell with their weapons, rebels against God and his Church, carrying with them the weapons of which it is written: “The teeth of the sons of men are their weapons and arrows” (Ps. 56:5).

“And they placed,” he says, “their swords beneath their heads,” resting in the disposition of a rebel mind and, as though for supreme victory, embracing the darts of their doctrines. Their iniquities were in their bones—that is, they possessed the strongest fabrications and doctrines of their error.

“For they became the terror of the mighty during their life,” or “in the land of the living.” This is said a fourth time, so that by their perversity they might terrify the strongest, those possessing knowledge of the Scriptures and belonging to the region of the living, while they descend to hell with their weapons, place their swords beneath their heads, and their iniquities reach even to their bones.

After this it is written: “And you, therefore, shall be broken in the midst of the uncircumcised” (Rom. 16:20). This is said either to Pharaoh or to the strength, or multitude, of Egypt; and that it itself is broken, according to what is written: “But God will crush Satan under your feet speedily.”

“And you shall sleep,” he says, “with those slain by the sword,” in perpetual sleep. There, together with the Assyrian and the multitude of Egypt, will be Idumaea and its kings—all who served earthly works or took pleasure in blood. For Idumaea signifies both “earthly” and “bloodthirsty.”

All the kings and all the princes of whom the Apostle frequently speaks (Phil. 3), who devote themselves to earthly works and daily pour out the blood of those whom they have deceived by their fraud, slept with the uncircumcised and unclean, and with those who went down into the pit, of whom we have spoken above.

In that same company will be the princes of the North, from which evils blaze forth upon the earth, and from which both in Jeremiah (Jer. 1) and in this same Prophet (above, chap. 22) that pot full of flesh and bones is kindled.

And not only the princes of the North, but all the magistrates of Assur—or, as it is more correctly written in the Hebrew, all the Sidonians, whom we translate as “hunters,” according to what is written: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. 123:7), whereas the Hebrew has “of the Sidonians.”

Those Sidonians, or hunters, shall be led trembling to the underworld, having once trusted in their strength, and shall sleep unclean. They shall carry their disgrace, or punishment, bearing the everlasting remorse of an evil conscience, so that “their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66) and “their worm shall not die” (Mark 9).

[Note: To conform to the sacred text, “confounded” (confusi) seems to be the required reading, as Victorius restores; compare the preceding annotation on this passage.]

When Pharaoh sees all these, he will be comforted—either because he still possesses his former wickedness and sees that he has many companions in punishment, or because he was comforted when he saw them also confounded in their punishments and terrors—over all his multitude that was slain by the sword: namely, Pharaoh’s multitude, or that of all his companions, especially the king of Assur, Meshech and Tubal, the Idumaeans, the princes of the North, and the Sidonians.

For these had given their terror in the land of the living. This is said a fifth time, so that we may beware of and flee from all nations of this kind, which have deceived us through all our senses, and know that they are terrible and cannot easily be avoided unless we guard our heart with every care.

“He himself also slept,” he says, “with his companions, slain by the sword.” These companions are his multitude, proceeding along the broad and spacious way toward everlasting punishments.

### Chapter 33 — verses 1 and following

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

‘Son of man, speak to the children of your people, and say to them:

When I bring a sword upon a land, and the people of the land take one man from among their last ones—or, one man from among them—and appoint him as a watchman over themselves, and he sees the sword coming upon the land, and blows the trumpet and announces it to the people; then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet, whoever he may be, and does not take heed, and the sword comes and takes him—or seizes him—his blood shall be upon his own head.

He heard the sound, or voice, of the trumpet and did not take heed; his blood shall be upon him. But if he had taken heed, he would have saved his life.

But if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, and the people do not take heed, and the sword comes and takes from them—or, takes away—their life, he indeed has been seized in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from the hand of the watchman.

And you, son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Therefore, hearing the word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me.

If, when I say to the wicked, “Wicked one, you shall surely die,” you have not spoken so that the wicked man may guard himself from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from your hand.

But if, when you announce to the wicked man that he should turn from his ways, he does not turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your life.’”

Again the word of the Lord comes to the Prophet, who had been silent for some time, because neither a prophet nor human frailty can sustain continual and uninterrupted prophecy. He speaks the same things that are contained above:

“Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. You shall hear the word from my mouth, and you shall threaten them from me, in what I say to the wicked man: ‘You shall die by death.’ If you have not announced it to him, nor spoken so as to warn the wicked man, that he might turn from his ways and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, and I will require his blood from your hand.

But if you have announced to the wicked man, and he has not turned from his iniquity and from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your life [another reading: shall deliver it].”

If you examine these things carefully, you understand that they are similar but not identical, since they differ in many respects. We must observe this throughout all the Holy Scriptures: when a statement appears to have a similar meaning, the same thing is not said in every respect, but much is either withdrawn or added; and we must take account of the individual words that differ from one another.

For the present, before we come to higher matters, a brief explanation of the meaning must be given.

If a watchman has been appointed among the peoples to announce the sword of the Lord and the coming wrath, and the people refuse to listen when he announces it, the watchman will be free, while the one overwhelmed by the sword will bear the guilt of his own blood. But if he listens, he will save his life.

If, however, the watchman does not sound the trumpet, and the people, unaware that the sword is coming, do not take heed, the people will indeed die in their own iniquity; nevertheless, I will require the blood of the one who dies from the hand of the watchman.

And so that the Prophet Ezekiel might know that this general discussion applied especially to him, he says:

“And you, son of man, you have not been appointed watchman by the land and by the people of the land, as I said above, but by me you have been appointed watchman for the house of Israel.

Therefore, if, when I say to the wicked man, ‘Wicked one, you shall die by death,’ you have not spoken to him so that he may take heed and be delivered from destruction, he indeed will die in his iniquity, which he had previously committed and from which he could have been delivered if you had announced it; but I will require his blood from your hand.

But if you announce and command the wicked man to turn from his evil ways, and he is unwilling to do so, he indeed will die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your soul from the destruction caused by negligence.”

From these words we learn that a person, however iniquitous and wicked, can be saved from his wickedness if he listens to the words of his teacher and performs repentance. No less does the teacher incur danger if he is unwilling to teach, whether from fear of danger or from despair concerning the sinner, since he is guilty of the blood of one who could have been delivered and rescued from death had he not fallen through the teacher’s silence.

In both cases free choice is preserved: it lies in the teacher’s will either to remain silent or to speak, and in the hearer’s choice either to listen, act, and be saved, or to despise and perish through his own contempt.

Nor does it immediately follow that, because the Prophet foretells something, what he foretells must come to pass. He does not prophesy it so that it may come, but so that it may not come. Nor, because God speaks, is it necessary that what he threatens must occur. He threatens for this reason: so that the one threatened may turn to repentance, and so that what will happen if the words of the Lord are despised may not happen.

We can explain this passage in three ways.

The land that appointed a watchman for itself may, according to the literal sense, be the land of Judaea; or, according to the spiritual interpretation, the Church, which often chooses a watchman from among the last of its people—namely, the one whom the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, appoints as judge (1 Cor. 15); or certainly the soul of the believer, which places mind and reason over the people and crowd of its thoughts, so that it does not accept every incitement of thought but judges and distinguishes what it ought to pursue and what it ought to avoid.

The watchman of the land of Judaea may be understood as a king or a prophet. The watchman of the Church may be a bishop or a presbyter, since he has been chosen by the people and, knowing the Scriptures through reading them and foreseeing what is to come, announces it to the people and corrects the sinner.

Hence we must greatly fear approaching this office unworthily and, having been appointed by the people, giving ourselves over to negligence and laziness. Worse still, we must not serve pleasures, the belly, and leisure and imagine that we have received an honor rather than a ministry.

For the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve (Matt. 20:28), and he washed the disciples’ feet (John 13), showing that all filth and vices must be washed away and purged by teachers from their disciples.

Let us not immediately answer: “What benefit is there in teaching if the hearer is unwilling to do what you have taught?” Each person is judged according to his own mind and office: you according to whether you have spoken, and he according to whether he has scorned to listen.

Concerning negligent teachers Solomon says: “Wisdom hidden and treasure concealed—what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20:32). Something similar is signified in the Gospel (Mark 9): whoever causes one of the least of the Church to stumble, it would be better for him to have a millstone tied around his neck and to be cast into the depths than, having been placed as a watchman, to harm many.

### Verses 10 and following

“Therefore you, son of man, say to the house of Israel:

‘Thus you have spoken, saying: “Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and in them we waste away; how then can we live?”’

Say to them:

‘As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn, turn from your exceedingly evil ways. And why will you die, O house of Israel?’

[Note: Victorius repeats the word “turn,” which is also read twice in the Hebrew: “turn, turn.”]

Therefore you, son of man, say to the children of your people:

‘The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins; and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness; nor will the righteous be able to live by his righteousness on whatever day he sins.

Even if I say to the righteous man that he shall live by life, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be consigned to oblivion, and in the iniquity that he has committed—in that he shall die.

But if I say to the wicked man, “You shall surely die,” and he repents of his sin, and performs judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge [the Vulgate adds: “that wicked man”], returns what he has seized, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, he shall surely live and shall not die.

None of all the sins that he committed [the Vulgate adds: “of his”] shall be charged against him. He has performed judgment and righteousness; he shall surely live.’

And the children of your people said: ‘The way of the Lord is not balanced, and their own way is unjust.’

For when the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquities, he shall die in them. And when the wicked turns away from his wickedness and performs judgment and righteousness, he shall live by them.

And you say: ‘The way of the Lord is not straight.’

I will judge each one of you according to his ways, O house of Israel.”

If we read carelessly, this prophecy appears to us to be the same as the one above, in which it is said: “Do I desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord, rather than that he should turn from his evil way and live?” (above, chap. 18). And at the end of that same prophecy: “Turn and return from all your iniquities, and your iniquities shall not be a torment to you” (ibid. 18:30).

[Note: I would prefer, with Victorius, “of iniquity” in the genitive, following the Greek ἀδικίας (“of iniquity”).]

There the word is addressed to those who wish to repent and erase their sins through righteousness, so that they may turn with confidence and practice repentance with a full heart.

Here, however, he speaks to those who despair of salvation because of the magnitude of their sins—indeed, of their wickedness—and say: “Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and in them we waste away; how then can we live?”

The meaning is: “Since death has once been set before us, and no medicine can restore health to our wounds, why should we labor and be consumed in vain, and pass our present life without hope, so that at least we may enjoy it, since we have lost the future life?”

God answers them that he does not desire the death of the wicked, but that he should turn and live. He turns his address directly to despairing sinners: “Turn from your exceedingly evil ways.”

And so that we may know who the wicked are to whom he speaks, the following statement shows: “Why will you die, O house of Israel?”

Life and death in this passage do not signify the life by which we all live, or the death by which, under the common law of nature shared with the beasts, we are dissolved. They signify the life of which it is written: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:9), and: “The soul that sins, it shall die.”

From this particular admonition, since he was speaking to the house of Israel, he passes to a general discussion: the righteous person’s former righteousness will not save him if he is seized by new crimes, nor will ancient sins destroy a sinner or wicked person if he has corrected his former errors by works of righteousness. God judges neither person according to the past, but according to the present.

“If I say,” he says, “to the righteous man, ‘You shall live by life,’ and promise him the rewards of righteousness, and he, trusting in himself, sins, all his former righteousnesses will be consigned to oblivion, and he will die in his present iniquity.”

My judgment has not changed, since I cannot render to the same sinful person what I had promised to him as righteous.

Conversely, if I threaten the sinner and the wicked man and say: “Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,” and he repents and corrects his former error by good works, so that he performs judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, returns what he has seized, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust—ought he not to live the life that is Christ, and in no way die, since the sinner’s threat ought not to punish the righteous?

The divine word says something similar to Jeremiah when he went down to the potter’s house and heard either God’s promises or his threats. God acts in this way either to summon people to salvation or to deter them from sin (Jer. 18).

Therefore those who say, “The way of the Lord is not equitable,” are reproved because their own judgment is unjust: they have an evil eye and judge not new things but old ones.

Through all these statements it is shown that a sinner must not despair of salvation if he repents, nor should a righteous person trust in his righteousness if through negligence he loses what he had acquired with great labor.

We pass quickly over the obvious, so that we may dwell on the more obscure matters. In what respects the present prophecy differs from the preceding one, and in what respects it speaks similarly, a comparison of the two will be able to show. As for what it means to perform judgment and righteousness, restore a pledge, return what has been seized, walk in the commandments of life, and the rest, we have spoken above in this same Prophet.

### Verses 21–22

“And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the tenth month [the Vulgate omits ‘month’], on the fifth day of our captivity, or transmigration, that there came to me one who had escaped, or one who had been saved, from Jerusalem, saying:

‘The city has been devastated, or captured.’

Now the hand of the Lord had come upon me in the evening before the one who had escaped arrived. He opened my mouth until he came to me in the morning; and when my mouth had been opened, I was silent no longer.”

In the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah, in the fifth month, the city of Jerusalem was captured.

This prophecy, however, belongs to the twelfth year, the tenth month, and the fifth day of the captivity or transmigration, when Jeconiah was captured [another reading: “with Jeconiah”]. From this it is shown that one year, four months, and twenty-five days after Jerusalem was captured, one of the citizens of Jerusalem came to Babylon to announce that the city had been captured and devastated.

One day before the arrival of the one who was to report these things, the hand of the Lord came in the evening upon Ezekiel the Prophet. It opened his mouth, which had long been closed, and whatever the messenger was going to say, Ezekiel had already proclaimed beforehand as accomplished. He was silent no longer, seeing his prophecy fulfilled in fact, and so that the people who were in Babylon—or those who had been taken captive—would no longer doubt the prophetic prediction.

The Prophet’s mouth is opened when he has shown by events that what he had previously announced has come to pass. Then he proclaims with complete freedom, demonstrating not future events but either present or completed ones.

This is according to the literal sense.

According to the allegorical interpretation, however, if Ezekiel means “strength of God,” while Christ is the power and wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24), this is to be understood as follows: once Jerusalem has been captured and overthrown, whoever is able to escape the unbelief of the Jews—such as the Apostles and the remnant that was saved—announces to Christ that all the ceremonies of the Jews have been overthrown. Some people still think that these must be observed even today, not listening to the Apostle’s words: “You have fallen away from grace, you who are justified in the Law” (Gal. 5:4).

I marvel at the stubbornness of people who wish to defend in words what they do not dare to fulfill in deeds—unless perhaps Jewish wolves are hiding under sheep’s clothing, that is, under the appearance of Christians. Why does a defender of the synagogue resound in the Churches of Christ?

Therefore, once Jerusalem has been captured and overthrown, the mouth of the Lord is opened through the Apostles and apostolic men, who can say: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (2 Cor. 6:11); and: “A great and effective door has been opened to me.”

And also: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118:131). It will never be able to remain silent, nor will it hear with Israel: “Hear, O Israel, and be silent.” Rather, it will resound throughout the whole world and open Christ’s Gospel to the nations.

According to this interpretation, therefore, the twelfth year refers to the twelve tribes; the tenth month refers to the time of Jewish propitiation, which in Greek is called [Greek: hilasmos, “propitiation”]; and the fifth day of the month refers to the carnal senses. We have shown that all these things were destroyed and passed away when Jerusalem was captured and the Gospel succeeded it.

And in the evening—that is, at the consummation of the world—the hand of the Lord came upon the true Ezekiel, who had proclaimed through the Prophets the future ruins of the city, and showed them to have been fulfilled in the morning.”

(Vv. 23 ff.) And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, those who dwell in these ruins upon the land of Israel and speak say: “Abraham was one, and he possessed the land as an inheritance; but we are many” [the Vulgate omits “we are”; Note: at Col. 0321D Victor supplies “as an inheritance” from the Hebrew text; Rabanus too formerly read this word here, and Jerome indicates it in the following exposition]. “The land has been given to us as a possession.” Therefore say to them:

“Thus says the Lord God: You who eat blood, lift up your eyes to your impurities, and shed blood—will you possess the land as an inheritance?” You have stood upon your swords, you have committed abominations, and each of you has defiled his neighbor’s wife; yet will you possess the land as an inheritance?

Say this to them:

“Thus says the Lord God: As I live, those who dwell in the ruins shall fall by the sword; whoever is in the open country shall be handed over to the beasts to be devoured; but those who are in fortifications and caves shall die of pestilence. I will make the land desolate and a wilderness; its proud strength shall fail, and the mountains of Israel shall be laid waste, because there is no one passing through them. And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I make their land desolate and deserted because of all their abominations that they have committed.”

And you, son of man, your people’s sons [the Vulgate adds “who”] speak about you beside the walls and at the doors of the houses, saying to one another, each man to his neighbor: “Come, and let us hear what word is going forth from the Lord.” And they come to you as though the people were entering—or as the people ordinarily gather—and my people sit before you, and they hear your words, but they do not do them, because they turn them into a song for their mouths; and their heart follows their greed.

[Or, as it is contained in the Septuagint: “Because they themselves practice falsehood in their mouth, and their heart walks after their abominations.” The passage continues:] And you are to them like a musical song sung with a pleasant and sweet sound; they will hear your words but will not do them. Yet when what has been foretold comes—for behold, it is coming—then they will know that a prophet has been in their midst. [Note: Rabanus and the Vulgate read, “a prophet,” or “a prophet has been,” among them. Drusius is mistaken in maintaining that, instead of the eight verses Jerome says are lacking in the Septuagint, “two” should be restored to match the present division; he fails to observe that verses in Jerome’s age were formerly extremely short, so that those eight roughly correspond to two divisions in the Vulgate.]

First, it must be understood [Note: Consult the Divine Library of St. Jerome, that is, vol. I of our edition, where the eight verses whose number this eminent doctor indicates are printed. Our Vulgate counts only two. Martianaeus.] that approximately eight verses, more or fewer, from the place we have quoted—“You who eat blood and lift your eyes to your impurities”—up to the place where it is written, “Say this to them: Thus says the Lord God,” are not found in the Septuagint. Along with many other passages, these too were omitted by them, or, after being translated by them, were gradually removed from the copies through scribal error.

And our Latins—or rather, the envious Christians, or, to speak more plainly, the heirs of the Grunnian faction [the disciples of Rufinus are indicated]—bark against us, asking why we expound according to the Hebrew, as though food should be forced upon those unwilling to receive it, rather than banquets prepared for those who accept them with thanksgiving.

Certainly, if they do not trust us, let them read the other editions, those of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. Let them consult Hebrews not from one locality only—lest they boast that I have bought them off—but from different provinces. When they see that all agree with what they call my error or ignorance, let them recognize that they are excessively wise and prefer to sleep rather than learn. Let them dwell in the seventy chambers of the Alexandrian Pharos, lest they lose sails from their ships and sigh over the loss of their ropes.

This against the envious. Now let us discuss what we have proposed.

When Jerusalem had been captured and the Temple overturned, the poor of the land, about whom Jeremiah writes (Jer. XXXIX), had been left alone in Jerusalem to cultivate the vineyards and fields and to live amid the ruins of the burned city. Although they ought to have repented of the things because of which the captivity had come, they deceived themselves with empty hope and said:

“Our father Abraham was one, and yet he possessed this land as an inheritance”—not because he himself possessed it, but because his offspring received the land of promise. “If, then, that one man multiplied into so many peoples, surely we, who are far more numerous and have been left in the land of Judah, dwelling in deserted and ruined cities, will multiply much more abundantly, so that we may possess more than that one man possessed.”

The Lord answered them that Abraham possessed the land of promise through faith. For Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. XV, 8). But these men, occupied by unbelief and crimes—even though they may be more numerous—cannot possess it.

At the same time, he lists the things by which they offend God: namely, six kinds of sin. “You who eat blood and lift your eyes to impurities,” that is, to your idols, “and shed blood,” that is, commit murder—can you, while doing these things, retain the land as an inheritance?

Nor are you content with this limit of your crimes. Rather, you stand daily upon your swords, ready to kill, and, imitating Esau, who stood and lived by his sword, you commit unbelievable abominations, namely, shameful acts of lust. Each of you defiles his neighbor’s wife, becoming all the more criminal because he has defiled the wife of a friend and neighbor.

“And when you do these things,” he says, “do you suppose that you will retain the land as an inheritance?”

Answer them, therefore, O prophet, and pronounce this sentence against them in my words. “I swear by myself that those who dwell in ruins and among fallen walls shall fall by the sword; those who are in the fields, or in the open country, shall be devoured by beasts; and those who are in walled places, that is, in fortifications and caves, shall not be able to escape God’s anger, but shall die of hunger and pestilence.”

“And I will make the land of Judah a wilderness,” he says, “and its proud strength, which once had been its strength, shall fail.” But God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James IV, 6). The mountains also, and everything else, shall be abandoned and become so desolate that no one will pass through them. Then the few who had remained will no longer trust in their multitude; rather, through the magnitude of the desolation they will recognize that I am the Lord, who made the land a wilderness because of all the abominations they committed.

These things have been said against those who, after Jerusalem had been captured and the entire region of the Jews devastated, lived as a small remnant among ruins and in deserted cities and villages.

Now let us come to the tropology, and, according to our custom, let us condense a lengthy discussion rather than expound it at length.

Every heretic dwells among ruins and in deserted places, yet thinks that he possesses the land of Israel. He says:

“If Abraham, one man, came through his faith to such blessedness that his offspring was multiplied like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven, how much more shall we, who are more numerous, possess the land of Israel—that is, the land of those who see God—and Judea, that is, the confession of the Lord?”

The Lord answered them:

“He possessed the land through the merit of faith; but your unbelief—or rather, your blasphemy—will not be able to possess the land of Israel, that is, the Church.

“For first, you eat in blood, shedding the blood of those whom you scandalize. Then you lift your eyes to your impurities or abominations, which you have fastened into your own soul, when you ought to imitate the churchman and say: ‘To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven’ (Ps. CXXII, 1).

“Third, you shed blood—not giving life to those whom you have led astray, but killing them.

“Nor is it enough for you to have done these three things. You stand upon your swords—that is, you persist in the perversity of your opinion and are ready for slaughter. You have committed abominations, doing in your bedchambers what is shameful to speak of, and you have defiled your neighbor’s wife—that is, the ecclesiastical way of life—hastening daily to snatch the deceived from Christ’s embrace.

“And when you have done these things, do you think that you will retain the land of Israel as an inheritance?”

God says to them that whoever dwells among the ruins—that is, in the heretics’ assemblies—shall fall by the ecclesiastical sword, of which it is written: “Two-edged swords are in their hands” (Ps. CXLIX, 6). And in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). And the servant who gives himself over to luxury and idleness shall be divided, that is, struck by the blade, and his portion shall be placed with the unbelievers (Luke XII).

Whoever is in the field or open country shall be handed over to beasts to be devoured. Wishing to avoid them, the prophet prays: “Do not deliver the soul that confesses you to the beasts” (Ps. LXXIII, 19).

But whoever is in fortifications and walled places, concerning which it is written, “The righteous man ascends fortified cities and destroys their defenses in which the wicked trusted” (Prov. XXI, 22), and who dwells in caves, of which it is said, “It is written: My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a cave of robbers” (Matt. XXI, 33), shall die of hunger for the Lord’s word and of pestilence.

And the whole land of the heretics shall be made a wilderness, so that their pride may be broken and the mountains reduced to desolation—those mountains that promised themselves the height of knowledge. They are called the mountains of Israel because, under the name of Christ, they overthrow those whom they have deceived. No one will pass through them, nor will anyone be able to say what Moses said: “Passing by, I will see this great vision” (Exod. III, 1). For they are inhabitants of perverse mountains, not travelers and sojourners.

When they have suffered these things, then they will know that he is the Lord who has made their land a wilderness because of the abominations they committed.

It follows:

On the same day and at the same time—that is, in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth day of the month—when the man who had escaped from Jerusalem came, and when the prophet spoke to those who were in the land of Judah and promised themselves hope of eternal possession, he commands the prophet to speak to the people who were living in Babylon and dwelling there with him, and to rebuke them concerning their flattering snares. They desired to hear the prophet’s words not for the salvation of their souls but for the pleasure of their ears.

These people sat beside the walls and at the doors of their houses, not at all wishing to enter into the prophet’s meaning. Rather, they encouraged one another and said: “Come, and let us hear what word is going forth from the Lord.” Thus they come as a people entering the Church of God and sit before you—my people, who claim to be mine—but they do not wish to do what they have heard.

Such people seem to me like those who are entertained by theatrical songs, whether they listen to tragedians or comedians, and are there delighted and flattered with pleasure, so that when they have gone out from you, they repeat and chant the things they heard and deceive themselves with sweet sounds. “They will hear your words,” he says, “but will not do them.”

Even today there are many such people in the Churches who say: “Come, let us hear this or that man, rolling out the words of his preaching with wondrous eloquence.” They stir up applause, shout, wave their hands, and, although they had neglected these things in their actions, once they recognize that the foretold event has come—for what the prophet declares in God’s word must necessarily happen—then they will begin to approve and to know that all they had heard were not human words, but the words of the Lord, who spoke through the prophet and the churchman.

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0325]

[Col. 0325C] 405–406

The eleventh book of explanations on Ezekiel will contain, in its final part, the prophecy against Gog and Magog, and will extend as far as the beginning of the city set upon the mountain and of the Temple situated in it [Martianaeus, following Erasmus, adds “Jerusalem.” Victor rightly deleted the word, supported by two manuscripts at Brescia and by a third printed edition. For, he says, apart from the fact that Jerusalem is described below only in chapter XL, the passage is not interpreted as referring to the earthly Jerusalem. If the name were to be included, it ought not to stand here but above, in this form: “And it will extend as far as the beginning of the city of Jerusalem set upon the mountain and of the Temple situated in it.”]

If, with the Lord’s help and with him disclosing his mysteries, I am able to bring this book to its conclusion, I shall have to deliberate long and anxiously whether I ought to lay hands upon the spiritual Temple or openly confess my ignorance—especially since there is profound silence among both the Jews and ourselves concerning its interpretation. Some think that it is to be built in the future; others, indeed with good intentions but without adequate knowledge, understand that the things spoken are spiritual, yet do not know how those spiritual realities ought to be expounded.

Meanwhile, so that the care of the present work may hold our attention, know, O virgin of Christ, Eustochium, that you ought to pray for us.

In this exceedingly difficult prophecy I briefly point out that [St. Ambrose, Book II of *On the Faith* to the Emperor Gratian, chapter 16] a man of no little distinction in our own age, writing to the Emperor, said concerning this nation: “This Gog is a Goth.”

How all the things written about it can be fitted to this interpretation is not for me, but for those who hold this view, to explain.

## (Chapter XXXIV)

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, prophesy concerning the shepherds (or: to the shepherds) of Israel; prophesy, and say to the shepherds: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who were feeding themselves. (Or: O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds perhaps feed themselves?) Are not flocks fed by shepherds? (Or: do sheep perhaps feed shepherds?) You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and slaughtered what was fat; but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen (or: comfort) the weak; you did not heal the sick; you did not bind up the broken; you did not bring back what had been cast away (or: what had gone astray); you did not seek what had perished. Instead, you ruled them with harshness and power (or: you afflicted what was strong with labor). And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd (or: no shepherds), and they became food for all the beasts of the field, and they were scattered. My flocks (or: my sheep) had wandered over all the mountains and every high hill, and my flocks (or: my sheep) were scattered over the whole face of the earth, and there was no one who sought them—there was, I say, no one who sought (or: brought back) them.

“Therefore, O shepherds, hear the word of the Lord: As I live, says the Lord God, because my flocks (or: my sheep) became a prey, and my sheep became food for every beast of the field because there was no shepherd (or: shepherds)—for the shepherds did not seek my flock [the Vulgate adds: ‘my’], but fed themselves, and did not feed my flocks—therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will require my flock at their hand, and I will make them cease from feeding my flock [the Vulgate omits: ‘my’], so that the shepherds will no longer feed themselves (or: the sheep); and I will deliver my flock (or: my sheep) from their mouths, and they will no longer be food for them.

“For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will seek my sheep, and I will visit them as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep (or: when darkness and cloud are in the midst of his separated sheep). So I will visit my sheep, and I will deliver them from all the places in which they were scattered on the day of cloud and darkness. And I will lead them out from the peoples (or: nations), and gather them from the lands (or: regions), and bring them into their own land, and feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the streams and in all the habitations of the land. I will feed them in the most fertile pastures, and on the high mountains of Israel their pastures (or: their sheepfolds) will be. There they will rest in green grass, and they will feed in rich pastures on the mountains of Israel. I will feed my sheep, and I myself will make them lie down (or: rest), says the Lord God. What had perished I will seek; what had been cast away (or: had gone astray) I will bring back; what had been broken I will bind up; what had been weak I will strengthen (or: comfort); but what was fat and strong I will guard, and I will feed them with judgment (or: according to judgment).

“But you, my flocks (or: my sheep), thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will judge between animal and animal, between rams and goats. Was it not enough for you to feed on good pasture? Moreover, you trampled [another reading: ‘will trample’] the remains of your pastures with your feet; and when you drank the purest water, you muddied what remained with your feet (another reading: ‘you muddied it’). And my sheep fed on what had been trampled by your feet, and they drank what your feet had muddied.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God to them [the Vulgate: ‘to you’]: Behold, I myself will judge between the fat animal and the lean (or: between the strong animal and the weak), because you thrust with your sides and shoulders [Note: ‘your’ is added here; it occurs only in the Septuagint, and Victorius removed it.], and with your horns you butted all the weak animals until you scattered them outside. I will save my flock, and it will no longer be a prey; and I will judge between animal and animal (or: between ram and ram).

“And I will raise up over them [the Vulgate has ‘over it’ here and below] one shepherd who will feed them (or: feed it), my servant David; he will feed them (or: it), and he himself will be their shepherd. And I, the Lord, will be their God, and my servant David will be ruler in their midst. I, the Lord, have spoken.

“And I will make with them a covenant (or: testament) of peace, and I will cause the most evil beasts to cease from the land; and those who lived [the Vulgate: ‘live’] in the wilderness will sleep safely in the forests. And I will place them around my hill as a blessing, and I will send (or: give) rain in its season; they will be rains of blessing. And the tree of the field (or: the trees of the countryside) will give its fruit, and the land will give its growth (or: strength); and they will be (or: dwell) in their land without fear (or: in the hope of peace). And they will know that I am the Lord, when I have broken the chains (or: the collar) of their yoke and delivered them from the hand of those who ruled them (or: those who made them serve). They will no longer be a prey to the nations, nor will the beasts of the earth devour them; but they will dwell securely (or: in hope), without any terror.

“And I will raise up for them a renowned shoot (or: a planting of peace); and they will no longer be diminished (or: perish) by hunger in the land, nor will they bear the reproaches of the nations any longer. And they will know that I am the Lord their God, with them, and that they are my people, the house of Israel, says the Lord God.

“But you, my flocks, the flock [the Vulgate: ‘flocks’] of my pasture (or: sheep), you are human beings, and I am the Lord your God, says the Lord God.”

I have often pointed out that I combine both editions in order to avoid the excessive length of books, but only in passages where the translations do not differ greatly from one another. After Jerusalem had been captured, after he had announced in Babylon the arrival of the man who had escaped, he spoke about those who were living amid the ruins of Jerusalem; and afterward he addressed those who, although placed in captivity, nevertheless persisted in wickedness and refused to hear the prophet’s words. Now he directs his speech to the shepherds—that is, to the rulers—through whose fault the sheep, that is, the peoples, have been scattered.

It should also be noted that from the twelfth year, the tenth month, and the fifth day of the month of Jeconiah’s migration (or: captivity), and of those who had been taken captive with him, up to the twenty-fifth year, when the temple is built upon the mountain of the city that has been rebuilt and the incredible mysteries of the Church are disclosed, no intervening year or period of time is given. Rather, it is simply said: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to them and to them,” so that we should understand that everything we read was spoken over thirteen years, at different times, and yet that no definite intervals of time are established between them.

The word is directed to the shepherds of Israel, whom we should understand either as kings or rulers, scribes and Pharisees, and teachers of the Jewish people; or, certainly, among the evangelical people, as bishops, presbyters, and deacons; or, according to mystical interpretations, as the angels of the individual churches, to whom John wrote in his Apocalypse (Revelation I), and whose angels continually see the face of God (Matthew XVIII).

The first statement is: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel,” who, although they ought to feed the Lord’s flock and provide for its salvation, hasten instead toward their own luxury. Hence one must take the greatest care to observe those commandments: “Do not seek to become a judge, lest you be unable to remove iniquities” (Ecclesiasticus VII, 6). And again: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find grace in the sight of the Lord” (ibid. III, 29). And once more: “They appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus XXXII, 1). Hence the Apostle says that he is like a little child, still nursing, among the disciples (I Corinthians III).

What follows—“You ate the milk, and clothed yourselves with the wool”—speaks metaphorically of shepherds to rulers, concerning whom it is also written elsewhere: “They devour my people as though eating bread” (Psalm LII, 5). By “milk,” understand every kind of food; by “wool,” the varied abundance of clothing.

When it says, “And what was fat you slaughtered,” it speaks of the wealthy among the people, whom wicked rulers are said to slaughter in the churches, when they praise them [another reading: ‘preach to them’] and do not dare to rebuke their vices. Of such people the prophet also says: “My people, those who call you blessed, deceive you and pervert the path of your feet” (Isaiah III, 12). James also speaks of them (James II, 3): when people enter them dressed in splendid garments and wearing a gold ring, they are honored by them, while the holy poor man is told: “You sit here on a footstool,” or “on the ground,” or “stand.”

These rulers do not strengthen or consolidate what is weak. Hence Paul says: “Receive the weak” (Romans XIV, 1); and: “Receive the one who is weak in faith”; and: “Many among you are weak and sick.” To such people the divine word is sent, concerning which it is written in the Psalms: “He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions” (Psalm CV, 10).

“And what is broken,” he says, “they do not bind up,” because they pay no attention to the mortal wounds among the people—such as those of the adulterer, murderer, or sacrilegious person. “And what has been cast away,” or what they see wandering, “they do not bring back,” allowing such people to be deceived by heretics. “And what has perished they do not seek”: they do not wish so much to save those who are lost as to devour those who are in the churches. Instead, “they rule them with harshness and power,” which pertains especially to the haughtiness of bishops—those, namely, who disgrace the dignity of their title by their deeds and assume pride in place of humility, imagining that they have acquired an honor rather than a burden. Whenever they see people in the Church who are powerful and possess the word of God, they try to oppress them.

Hence, according to the Septuagint, it is written: “And what was strong you afflicted with labor.”

And God’s people were scattered, either through vices or through the error of heretics, because there was no good shepherd who would lay down his life for the sheep. Instead, all were hirelings, who looked only to profit from their flocks and fled when they saw the wolf. Through their negligence the Lord’s flock is devoured by the beasts of the field, concerning which it is written: “You appointed darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the field will pass through, the young lions roaring to seize prey and seek their food from God” (Psalm CIII, 20–21).

And they are scattered and wander over all the mountains, which rise up against the knowledge of God, and over every high hill, which in heretical pride despises the simplicity of the Church. They are scattered over the whole face of the earth, seeking earthly things rather than heavenly ones. And there was no one who sought them, nor anyone who brought them back, because those occupied with pleasures do not care about the losses of the Lord’s flock [another reading: ‘the Lord’s flock’].

Therefore the word of the Lord is spoken against the wicked shepherds: “Because you have done these things and those things which I explained above, and which he enumerates a second time: Behold, I myself will come to the shepherds and require my flock from their hand.” It is better for them that a millstone be fastened around their neck (Matthew XVIII) than that they scandalize even the least of my people.

And this will be their greatest punishment: that they will no longer feed my flock, lest under the pretext of caring for the sheep they feed themselves and gather wealth. “And I will deliver my people from their mouth.” He says, “I will require them from their hand, and I will deliver them from their mouth”—from the greedy jaws by which they are devoured.

When he has sought the sheep, he visits them as sick and emaciated, scattered through the negligence of the shepherds; and he will deliver them from every place on the day of cloud and darkness, of which Joel also speaks: “The day of the Lord is at hand, and the day of darkness and gloom is near, a day of cloud and mist” (Joel II, 1–2).

Then they will be led out from the lands so that they may be brought into their own land, which is the land of the living. He himself will feed them on the mountains of Israel, concerning which David says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me” (Psalm CXX, 1). And not only on the mountains, but by the streams and in all the habitations of the land, in the most fertile pastures and on the high mountain, about which Isaiah and Micah prophesy more fully (Isaiah II; Micah IV, VII)—or, in the high mountains of Israel.

There they will rest in green grass and say: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing. He has placed me there in a pasture; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Psalm XXII, 1–2). And they will feed in the richest pastures upon the mountains of Israel.

There is an immeasurable promise and hope of blessedness, when the Lord himself promises, saying: “I will feed my sheep”; he will not hand them over to wicked shepherds, but will himself make them lie down, says the Lord God, so that they may rest in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Then what had perished among the peoples will be sought; what had gone astray through the persuasion of heretics will be brought back; what had been broken will be bound up; and what had been crushed and weakened will be consolidated, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “He heals their infirmities and binds up their bruises” (Psalm CII, 3). “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm L, 19). Hence the saint also says: “Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled” (Psalm VI, 2). And in the thirty-seventh Psalm the penitent says: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins” (verse 4).

“And what is fat,” he says, “and strong, I will guard,” so that it may not be devoured by beasts. And he will feed his sheep with judgment, knowing which pasture is owed to which sheep. For “there are different dwelling places with the Father” (John XIV), and: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid. V).

These words have been spoken against the shepherds. Now he speaks to the sheep, that is, to the people, and to the flock of both kinds of animals, sheep and goats; and not only to sheep and goats, but also to rams and he-goats, who are the rulers among the flocks. To them he says: “Was it not enough for you to feed upon the good pastures of the Scriptures? Yet you also trampled the remains of your pastures under your feet. And when you drank the purest water of God’s utterances, you muddied the remaining waters with your feet, so that my people ate the pasture trampled by you and drank the muddy waters, and through your fault received as corrupted and violated what was good in itself.”

All heretics do this: they gnaw at the utterances of the Scriptures and, as far as they can, stain them. But ecclesiastical men also who do not preserve the truth of doctrines, but invent things from their own hearts and make their own presumption their teacher, are held by the same error. Once they have persuaded the people that what they invent is true, and have stirred up applause and shouting in theatrical fashion, they forget their own ignorance. With raised brows and carefully balanced and weighed words, they assume for themselves the authority of teachers.

Let us therefore see what judgment exists between animal and animal, and by what judgment the good and true shepherd judges them—the one who received all judgment from the Father.

“Behold,” he says, “I myself judge between the fat and the lean animal,” or between the strong and the weak. For the strong thrust and collide with their sides and shoulders against the weak animals, and butt them with their horns, not knowing that according to the Law a horned ox must be punished (Exodus XXI). They thrust with their sides and butt with their horns until they scatter and drive the sheep outside.

Through the pride of the great and the wickedness of rulers, people are frequently expelled from the Church, so that those whom the Lord himself saved may be scattered. But the Lord will no longer abandon them as prey. He will judge between animal and animal—not between the names of dignities with which rulers swell, but between one human being and another, according to the fact that both are servants of the Lord.

Then he will raise up one shepherd who says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” (John X, 11); his servant David, inasmuch as he deigned to assume the form of a servant (Philippians II). “David” is interpreted as “strong of hand.” He himself will feed them, and the Lord will be their God—either the Son and the Father, or certainly the shepherd according to the flesh he assumed; but the Lord and God according to the Word who was in the beginning with God.

When this David’s animals progress into rational creatures, he will no longer be called a shepherd, but ruler in their midst, concerning whom it is written: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John I, 26).

Then he will establish with them a covenant of peace, not of wars and discord, “because his place has become peace” (Psalm LXXV), but the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding (Philippians IV), who says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27).

And he will cause the most evil beasts to cease from the land: vices and disturbances by which human souls are tormented, or hostile powers by which they are attacked. “And those who dwell in the wilderness will sleep securely in the forests.” For the Lord will reveal the dense places of the forests, and in his temple all will speak of glory (Psalm XXVIII, 9). Once the beasts have been driven out and the land reduced to solitude, they will sleep securely, safe from such creatures, and will say: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm XXVI, 1).

And he will place those who sleep securely around his mountain or hill, and they will be a blessing. Then he will give rain in its season, and the rains will be rains of blessing, which he promises in the blessings of Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy XXVIII).

“And he will give,” he says, “the tree of life,” concerning which it is written in Genesis (Genesis II), and “the tree of wisdom,” of which it is said: “She is a tree of life to all who take hold of her” (Proverbs III, 18). He will give its fruit when the land also gives its fruit; or, the trees of the regions, that is, the immense multitude of the saints. And the land will give its growth, for “truth has arisen from the earth” (Psalm LXXXIV, 12).

And they will be in their land without fear, or in the hope of peace, in the land of the living and the land of the gentle, concerning which it is written: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew V, 4). Thus, amid the happiness of all things, they will know that he is the Lord, when he has broken the chains or iron band of their yoke, by which they were oppressed as by the heaviest domination, and has delivered them from the hand of those who ruled them or afflicted them with servitude. For each person is the servant of the one by whom he is conquered.

And they will no longer be a prey to demonic nations, nor will the beasts of the earth devour them—those of whom we have spoken. Instead, they will dwell securely, without any terror, according to the preceding interpretation.

“And I will raise up for them,” he says, “a renowned shoot,” or “a planting of peace,” which speaks in the Gospel: “I am the true vine” (John XV, 1). And they will no longer be diminished by hunger in the land. Therefore hunger belongs to earthly things; but the hunger to hear the word of God will no longer exist in the land under the good shepherd, the renowned shoot celebrated in everyone’s speech, and the planting of peace. Nor will they any longer be subject to the reproaches of the nations, who say: “Where is their Lord God?” (Psalm CXIII, 10).

And after all these things they will know that he is not merely the Lord, as he had also said above, but that, with this addition, the Lord of all is specifically their God, who is with them. He says to the Apostles in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, 20).

When the Lord himself is their God, then they too will be his people—not just any people, but those who have deserved to be called the house of Israel.

And lest we think that all these things refer to shepherds, sheep, goats, and rams, he solves the riddle—or rather, the metaphor—and states it more plainly: “But you, my sheep, the sheep of my pasture, are human beings.” Thus all the divine discourse concerns human beings, to whom he says: “I am the Lord your God,” says the Lord God.

## (Chapter XXXV)

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, set (or: turn) your face against Mount Seir, and prophesy concerning it (or: to it), and say to it: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir, and I will stretch out my hand over you, and I will make you desolate and deserted. I will demolish your cities (or: I will make desolation in your cities); and you will be deserted, and you will know that I am the Lord [the Vulgate omits ‘I am’], because you have been an everlasting enemy and have shut up the children of Israel in the hand of the sword (or: have deceitfully besieged the house of Israel with the sword), in the time of their affliction, in the time of their final iniquity.

“Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, I will hand you over to bloodshed (or: because you have sinned in blood), and blood will pursue you; and because you have hated blood, blood will pursue you. And I will make Mount Seir desolate and deserted, and I will remove from it the one who goes out and the one who returns (or: human beings and beasts). And I will fill its mountains with those slain upon it (or: with the wounded). On your hills, in your valleys, and in your streams, those killed by the sword will fall. I will hand you over to everlasting desolations, and your cities will not be inhabited. And you will know (or: he will know) that I am the Lord [the Vulgate adds ‘God’], because you said: ‘The two nations and the two lands (or: regions) will be mine, and I will possess them as an inheritance,’ although the Lord was there.

“Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, I will act according to your anger (or: hostility) and according to your jealousy, which you displayed, hating them; and I will make myself known to you when I judge you, and you will know that I am the Lord. I have heard all your reproaches (or: the sound of your blasphemies) which you spoke (or: because you spoke) against the mountains of Israel, saying: ‘They have been given to us as desolate places to devour’; and you rose up [the Vulgate: ‘rose’] against me with your mouth (or: you spoke grandly against me with your mouth), and you uttered your words against me (or: shouted against me). I heard them.

“Thus says the Lord God: While the whole earth rejoices, I will reduce you to desolation. Just as you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel because it had been scattered, so I will do to you. You will be scattered (or: deserted), Mount Seir, and all Idumea, and they will know that I am the Lord.”

The words added in the Septuagint—“and they will be consumed”—are not found in the Hebrew.

If the word of God were always present in the prophets and continually had a dwelling in their hearts, Ezekiel would never so frequently write: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying.” But because, on account of human weakness and the necessities of this life, it sometimes withdrew from them, John the Baptist therefore says: “The one who sent me to baptize, he said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one’” (John I, 33). For the phrase “and remaining upon him” would never have been added as something distinctive of Christ unless the Spirit sometimes withdrew from others.

Otherwise God also says to Moses: “I will take from the spirit that is in you” (Numbers XI, 17). Moses would certainly not have had that spirit unless it had descended upon him from the Lord.

The whole prophecy of this chapter is directed against Mount Seir, that is, against the sons of Esau and Edom, who in Greek and in our language are called Idumeans. At the time of necessity and distress, when Judah was being captured by the Babylonians, they insulted the Jews, and, after the Jewish people had been expelled, thought that the land had been handed over to them for possession. They not only failed to receive their brothers, namely the sons of Jacob, but also persecuted them and shut them up in the hands of the sword.

[Note: We follow Victorius, on the authority of manuscripts and older editions. Martianay, with Erasmus, reads, in an unsuitable sense, “receive the sons,” namely those of his brother Jacob, but so forth. For, as the aforementioned Victorius says, the discourse concerns the sons of Esau, not Esau himself, whose brother was Jacob. Those brothers were the sons of Jacob, since they had been born from two full brothers.]

Hence Symmachus translated the passage more plainly: “You hated your blood, and blood will pursue you.”

It is prophesied that Seir itself too will be captured and reduced to everlasting desolations, and that at the end of all things it will recognize God as judge, because it said: “The two nations and the two regions are mine.” This may refer either to Idumea and Judea, or certainly to Judah and Israel, namely the two tribes and the ten tribes.

And you spoke about the mountains of Israel, saying: “They have been given to us as desolate places to devour,” without considering that this blasphemy would rebound against God. Hence what follows: “While the whole earth rejoices, I will reduce you to desolation.” The meaning is: when the whole land of Judea has recovered its former condition, you will remain in everlasting desolation.

The statement that follows—“Just as you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel because it had been scattered, so I will do to you”—is not found in the Septuagint, but has been added under asterisks from the edition of Theodotion.

The whole purpose of God’s anger against Mount Seir is that, once it and all Idumea have been scattered, they may recognize that he is the Lord.

These things I have stated briefly according to the historical account and the sense rather than the precise wording. I shall now pass to the allegorical interpretation and touch upon only a few points for the sake of brevity.

“Set,” he says, “or turn your face against Mount Seir.” Significantly he says “turn,” that is, turn from one prophecy to another prophecy. The face is not the face of the body, but of the soul, concerning which the Apostle also says: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord” (II Corinthians III, 18).

Mount Seir, whose name is interpreted as “rough” and “hairy,” must be understood as a hostile power that ruled over the nation of the sons of Esau and had raised itself against the people of Judah—that is, against confession and true faith.

If a prudent reader objects that in this passage Seir, meaning “rough” and “hairy,” is understood in a negative sense, whereas Elijah too is called a hairy man (IV Kings I), I shall answer briefly: Esau is described as red and as being like a hairy skin (Genesis XXV), whereas Elijah is described simply as a hairy man. In Esau, who was bloodthirsty and murderous, the comparison with a hairy skin is an indication of mortal deeds and of death itself; in Elijah it is an indication of manly strength. Therefore his dwelling in the wilderness and the austerity of his way of life demonstrated not merely a man, but a very strong man.

Jacob, on the other hand, who had supplanted Esau and received his birthright (Genesis XXV), lived simply at home and was not a hunter like the giant Nimrod; therefore he is called light and smooth.

Let us therefore see what God commands to be said to Mount Seir, or against Mount Seir.

“Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir.” I will not send angels or employ other ministers, but I myself will come against you, stretch out my hand over you, and assume the posture of one striking. I will make you desolate and deserted. You who were badly inhabited and had many companions in your impiety, so many that you even built cities and claimed a kingdom of your own, will now be desolate together with your cities—which Jeremiah too is commanded to destroy and dig up (Jeremiah I, LI), so that good cities may be built in their place. In this way you will advance toward knowing that I am the Lord, whom you could not know before your desolation.

The whole cause of your sin is that you have been an everlasting enemy. Hence the Psalm also says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm IV, 5), so that we may quickly be reconciled with our enemies and change hatred into love.

But Mount Seir was not like this. It maintained everlasting enmities and deceitfully shut up—or besieged—the children of Israel with the sword. From this we understand that whoever takes up the sword against the children of God, acts deceitfully, and besieges them will be handed over to the hands of the sword, as Mount Seir was in the time of final iniquity, when the days are evil, the world lies in the power of the Evil One (I John V), and, because iniquity has multiplied, the love of many grows cold.

There is also another sin of Mount Seir: because it hated the blood of the righteous, which it desired to shed in every persecution, it will itself suffer persecution from that blood. Hence the souls of the saints cry out beneath the altar and ask the Lord for vengeance for their blood (Revelation VI).

“And the one who goes out and the one who returns” are removed from Mount Seir—that is, every inhabitant, or human beings and beasts that are saved in the Church, concerning whom it is written: “You will save human beings and beasts, Lord” (Psalm XXXV, 5). In Mount Seir both are destroyed, so that both those who seem to possess some reason and those who are content with simple faith may, by God’s command, perish.

And its mountains are filled with the wounded and the slain—not only the mountains that have reached the summit of impiety, but also the hills, that is, the lower disciples of Mount Seir; and the valleys, which are sunk in the depths; and the streams, which have turbid waters gathered from various directions and flowing down from pride—or, according to the Septuagint, the plains [another reading: ‘the fields’], which lie between the hills and the valleys.

All these, slain by the sword of the Lord and struck by his outstretched hand, will fall, so that they may be reduced to everlasting desolations. And if there were cities—that is, assemblies of wicked habitation—they too will perish and cease to maintain an evil agreement. Their languages will be divided (Genesis XI), so that they will be unable to build a tower of blasphemy against God; and, reduced to desolation and desert, they will know that he is the Lord.

Nor was it enough for Mount Seir to have said all the things recounted in the preceding discourse. In its pride it also said: “The two nations and the two lands,” or regions, “are mine”—namely Idumea and Judea—and “I will possess both the heretics and the ecclesiastics.” And this, he says, you said while the Lord was there, ruling over his people.

Therefore the Lord swears and says: “As I live, says the Lord God, just as your anger raged against the people of God, and your jealousy pursued the household of Christ, hating those whom you desired to possess, so, when I have struck and judged you, I will make myself known to you. Then you will know that I learned of your reproaches and blasphemies not from another reporter, but because I myself heard what you spoke against the mountains of Israel, saying: ‘They have been given to us as desolate places to devour.’”

We should understand the mountains of Israel as Moses, the prophets, and the apostles, whom heretics—and the devil, the prince of heretics—imagine have been handed over to them for devouring. This occurs when scarcely anyone, or no one at all, is found in the Church who can fight for the Lord’s mountains and defend their mutilation with his voice.

“And you rose up,” he says, “against me with your mouth,” or “you spoke grandly”—not, as you suppose, against the mountains, but through them against me—and “you uttered against me,” or “shouted against me.”

For all your prayers, O Mount Seir and companions of Mount Seir, of whom it was said above—“I will fill its mountains, hills, valleys, and plains,” or streams—were against me. They were not prayers and supplications directed to God, as you suppose, but cries, shouting, and blasphemies.

Hence the Lord also threatens and says: “Just as you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel, when it was scattered, torn apart, and dispersed throughout the whole world by your persecutions, so I will do to you.”

For while the whole land of the living and the land of the saints rejoices, and all have been converted to the service of God, you will be scattered, rough mountain, hairy mountain, and all Idumea—that is, earthly works devoted to gore and blood—so that then you may know that I am the Lord, who elsewhere have said: “I am the Lord your God.”

(Cap. XXXVI—Verses 1 ff.) “But you, son of man, prophesy concerning the mountains of Israel and say: Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Because the enemy has said of you, ‘Aha! The ancient heights [or: solitudes] have been given to us as a possession [Vulgate: inheritance]’—therefore prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God: Because you have been desolated and trampled on every side [or: because you have been scattered by those who surround you], and have become an inheritance [or: possession] for the remaining nations, and have risen upon the lips of tongues, and have become a reproach to the peoples [Vulgate: people] [or: nations]—therefore, mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord God.

[Col. 0336D] “Thus says the Lord God to the mountains and hills, the ravines, valleys, and deserted ruins [or: scattered places], and the abandoned cities that have been depopulated and mocked [or: trampled] by the remaining nations round about. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because I have spoken in the fire of my zeal against the remaining nations and against all Idumea, who have given my land to themselves as an inheritance with joy [variant: with the sword], with all their heart and soul, and have driven it out in order to lay it waste [or: despising its inhabitants with hatred, in order to overthrow them in destruction]—therefore, he says [Vulgate omits “he says”], prophesy concerning the land of Israel and say to the mountains and hills, the ridges and valleys: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I have spoken in my zeal and fury, because you have endured the shame [or: reproaches] of the nations.

[Col. 0337A] “Therefore thus says the Lord God [or: Adonai the Lord]: I have raised [or: will raise] my hand, so that the nations that surround you may themselves bear their shame [or: disgrace]. But you, mountains of Israel, put forth your branches [or: your grapes] and yield your fruit for my people Israel, for it is near, ready to come. For behold, I am coming to you, and I will turn toward you [or: regard you], and you shall be tilled and receive seed. I will multiply people upon you, the whole house of Israel; the cities shall be inhabited, and the ruins restored [or: the deserted places shall be rebuilt]. And I will fill you with people and cattle; they shall multiply and increase. I will make you inhabited as at the beginning, and I will bestow greater blessings upon you than you had at the start; and you shall know that I am the Lord.

[Col. 0337C] “And I will bring [or: beget] people upon you, my people Israel, and they shall possess you as an inheritance [or: possess you], and you shall be a possession [Vulgate: inheritance], and you shall no longer add that you are without them [or: you shall no longer be made childless]. Thus says the Lord God: Because they have said of you [or: to you], ‘You devour people and strangle your nation,’ therefore you shall no longer devour people, and you shall no longer kill your nation, says the Lord God. I will no longer make you hear [or: bear] the shame [or: disgrace] of the nations, and you shall no longer bear the reproaches of the peoples [or: you shall not bear them], and you shall no longer lose your nation [or: your nation shall no longer be without children], says the Lord God.”

[Note: In accordance with the Vulgate and the Hebrew text, Victor says that *constituit* (“he established”) should be read here; he thinks that *dixerunt* (“they said”) arose from the Septuagint’s εἶπαν.]

Above, the prophet’s face is turned, or directed, against Mount Seir; here the son of man speaks to, or concerning, the mountains of Israel, which are commanded to hear the word of God. And, for the moment setting aside the allegorical interpretation, this is briefly the meaning of the whole prophecy concerning the mountains of Israel: Because the enemy—that is, Mount Seir—insulted you and thought that he would possess you forever, and that the ancient heights of the Lord, now deserted, had passed into his inheritance—and because he not only said this but also possessed you for some time, to such an extent that he spoke proudly against you, saying that you were a reproach to all the nations—therefore thus says the Lord God, not only to Mount Seir but also to its mountains and hills, ravines, valleys, deserts, devastations, and abandoned cities:

[Col. 0338A] Because he has spoken in the fire of his zeal against all the nations, but especially against Idumea, which, he says, held my land as a possession together with the other nations and possessed it by the sword, possessing it with all its heart in order to expel its inhabitants and lay the land waste. Therefore, he says [Vulgate omits “he says”], prophesy concerning the land of Israel and speak to the mountains, hills, and ridges—for which the Septuagint translated *ταῖς νάπαις* (*tais napais*), by which we understand wooded places—and to the valleys.

[Col. 0338B] Thus says the Lord God: In my zeal and fury I shall become the avenger of your reproach, and I shall raise my hand so that the nations surrounding you may bear their disgrace and shame. But you, mountains of Israel, according to your former condition, shall put forth shrubs and send out branches; or, according to the Septuagint, you shall yield grapes with which my people Israel may be satisfied.
