Do not think that this will happen after a long time: it is near, it is at hand, and the time will come. And lest this seem difficult to you, I myself shall come to you; I who had withdrawn from you shall turn toward you, so that you may recover your former cultivation and be filled with seed, so that many people may be in you and the cities that had previously been destroyed may be inhabited.

And I shall multiply not only people, but cattle also shall likewise multiply and increase. I shall make you inhabited as at the beginning, when, under the leadership of Moses, two and a half tribes received their possession beyond the Jordan (Num. XXXII), and, under Joshua son of Nun, the other nine and a half tribes possessed the land of Judah (Josh. I and XIII). I shall bestow blessings upon you far greater than those you had at the beginning, before you experienced your various captivities. And when I have done this for you, then you shall know that I am the Lord.

“And you shall be filled,” he says, “O land of Israel, with my people, who shall possess you as an inheritance; and you shall be their possession, and you shall no longer be without children.” When your inhabitants have multiplied, O mountains of Israel, then your enemies shall no longer say against you that you devour people and that your possession is childless. On the contrary, you shall multiply people, and your descendants shall put forth a very abundant offspring.

“You shall no longer hear,” he says, “or endure the shame of the nations; nor shall you lose your nation, so as ever again to suffer captivity, because the Lord has spoken.”

We have stated these things *παραφραστικῶς*—“paraphrastically”—in the Jewish manner. The Jews expect them in the kingdom of a thousand years, when they assert that the city of Jerusalem will be built, together with the temple described at the end of this volume, and that all things will enjoy prosperity. Some of them think that these promises were fulfilled under Zerubbabel.

But how can this statement stand: “I will make you inhabited as at the beginning, and I will bestow greater blessings upon you than you had at the start”? Under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, only a few of the people were brought back. They were subject first to the Medes and Persians, and thereafter served the Macedonian, Egyptian, and Roman rulers of various nations, down to Titus and Vespasian—and they continue to serve to this day. Thus the final statement of the prophecy cannot possibly stand: “You shall no longer bear the reproach of the peoples, and you shall no longer lose your nation.”

And because it would take too long now to argue against the Jewish doctrine and against the blessedness that serves the Jewish belly and throat—since they desire everything earthly and say, “Let us eat and drink,” concerning whom the Apostle also says, “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both one and the other” (1 Cor. VI, 13)—let us pass briefly to the spiritual understanding, according to which we have also interpreted the final portions of Isaiah.

For we do not expect, according to the Jewish fables that they call *δευτερώσεις* (“second traditions”), a Jerusalem set with gems and gold to descend from heaven. Nor shall we again suffer the injury of circumcision, nor offer sacrifices of bulls and rams, nor sleep in the leisure of the Sabbath. This is promised also by many of our own writers, especially Tertullian’s book entitled *On the Hope of the Faithful*, the seventh volume of Lactantius’s *Institutes*, and the frequent expositions of Victorinus, bishop of Petovium, as well as our recent Severus in the dialogue to which he gave the name *Gallus*. And, to name Greeks and join the first with the last: Irenaeus and Apollinarius.

[Note: Compare the book *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 74. Tertullian’s book *On the Hope of the Faithful* has been lost. See our notes on the Preface to Book XVIII on Isaiah.]

We shall therefore say that the mountains of Israel are the prophets and apostles, who hear the word of God and whom the devil, their enemy, insulted, saying: “Aha! You once-exalted mountains, of whom it is written, ‘The mountains surround him, and the Lord surrounds his people’” (Ps. CXXIV, 2)—you have been given to me as a possession when you were desolated by the constraints of persecution, trampled on every side, made an inheritance for the remaining nations, and blasphemed by everyone.

Therefore the Lord speaks to the trampled and desolated mountains, and not only to the mountains but also to the lower places, and to those established at every level in the land of Judah—that is, on the mountain of the Church, concerning which it is written, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V, 14)—and to the hills and ravines, whose faith is increased by the winter of persecutions and the storm of affliction.

He speaks also to the valleys that have been depressed in humility, to the deserted churches, the ruins, and the abandoned meeting-places of the churches throughout the world. Such was the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian throughout the world, when the churches were proscribed and devastated, and when all the nations of the pagans and heretics round about mocked the Church.

He spoke in the fire of his zeal and fury, particularly against Idumea, which by earthly works wanted everyone, after laying aside the heavenly image, to bear the image of the earthly (1 Cor. XV). For they gave the land of God to themselves as an inheritance, and persecuted the Lord’s Church with all their heart and soul; they drove it from its dwelling places and laid it waste.

But what did it benefit the nations, what advantage did the nations of heretics gain by insulting the land of the Lord, when the Lord speaks to it—to its mountains, hills, and ridges, or wooded places that flourished with the beauty of paradise—and when he has spoken to its hills, of which we spoke above, in his zeal and fury? He raises his hand against the adversaries who persecuted the Church, so that they may bear their shame and disgrace.

Then, when the persecutors have been killed and peace has been restored to the Church, the mountains of Israel—that is, the apostles and apostolic men—shall make their trees flourish, extend their branches, and bring grapes to be trodden in the Lord’s winepress. From these grapes new wine is poured out, wine that intoxicates the peoples of believers; and wine is pressed out that gladdens the human heart (Ps. CIII), so that all the fruit of the mountains, from which the bread descending from heaven is made, may be eaten by God’s people Israel.

And lest we perhaps despair amid persecutions, it is added: “The time is near when it shall come.” “Coming, it shall come, and it shall not delay” (Hab. II, 3). Therefore he promises his coming to the mountains and to those who have persevered in tribulations, and promises that after the heat of persecution the land, previously cut by Christ’s plough, shall be cultivated and receive every seed of virtue, from which people and the whole house of Israel shall be born and multiply.

And when the cities—that is, the churches of believers—have been inhabited by the returning crowds, then not only people who were strong in knowledge of the Scriptures, but also cattle—that is, all the simple among believers—shall multiply and increase. The churches shall be inhabited as at the beginning, that is, before persecution existed; and they shall flourish with greater blessings than they had at first, crowned with the victories of the martyrs.

Then they shall know that he is the Lord, who restored his people to their former condition, so that they might possess the churches, and themselves be the inheritance of the churches, and no longer be without the children whom they had lost during the persecution.

Therefore the prophet is commanded to speak to the land of the meek, the land of the living, or to the mountains of Israel, and to say: “You shall no longer suffer the reproach of persecutors, nor shall they insult your slaughtered people, like sheep destined for slaughter.” When peace has been restored, all reproaches shall cease. You shall no longer endure shame and disgrace among the various nations round about, but you shall have your nation and people, because the truth of the promise has been confirmed by the Lord’s word.

## Verses 16 ff.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Son of man, the house of Israel dwelt [or: dwelled] in their land, and they polluted it by their ways and their pursuits [or: idols]. Their way before me became like the uncleanness of a menstruating woman. And I poured out my indignation [or: fury] upon them because of the blood which they had shed upon the land. They polluted it with their idols, and I scattered them among the nations; they were scattered [or: I scattered them] through the lands [or: regions]. According to their ways and their deeds [or: sins] I judged them.

[Col. 0341A] “And they entered among the nations to which they went, and they profaned my holy name, when it was said of them, ‘This is the people of the Lord, and they have gone out from his land.’ But I spared my holy name [or: I spared them for the sake of my holy name], which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations to which they went.

“Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: It is not for your sake that I shall act, O house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you entered. And I shall sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, which you profaned in their midst, so that they may know [Vulgate adds “the nations”] that I am the Lord, says the Lord of hosts, when I have been sanctified in you before their eyes.

[Col. 0341B] “For I shall take you from the nations, gather [Vulgate adds “you”] you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land. And I shall pour clean water over you [or: sprinkle you with clean water], and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities; and I shall cleanse you from all your idols. And I shall give you a new heart, and I shall place a new spirit within you [or: I shall give it to you]. I shall take the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.

“And I shall place my spirit within you [or: give it to you], and I shall make you walk in my commandments [or: ordinances], keep my judgments, and perform [or: do] them [Vulgate omits ‘them’]. And you shall dwell in the land which I gave to your fathers, and you shall be my people, and I shall be your God. And I shall save you from all your impurities [or: uncleannesses], and I shall call for grain and multiply it [Note: We have restored *grain*, following Victor, who relied on the Vulgate and Hebrew text, but also in response to the Vatican manuscript and Rabanus. It was moreover clear from the holy Father’s exposition that he had written this. ‘Grain will be multiplied for them,’ he says, ‘from which the heavenly bread is made, and they will no longer suffer hunger for the word of God.’ Nevertheless, the Manuscript of Martin and Erasmus retained *fruit*.]. I shall not impose famine upon you [or: I shall give you no famine], and I shall multiply the fruit of the tree and the produce of the field, so that you shall no longer bear the reproach of famine among the nations.

“And you shall remember your most evil ways and your pursuits that were not good, and your iniquities and crimes shall displease you. It is not for your sake that I shall act, says the Lord God; let this be known to you. Be ashamed and confounded because of your ways, O house of Israel.

[Col. 0341D] “Thus says the Lord God: On the day when I have cleansed you from all your iniquities, have caused the cities to be inhabited, and have restored the ruins, and when the desolate land has been cultivated—though it was formerly laid waste in the sight of every passerby—they shall say: ‘That land which was uncultivated [or: deserted] has become like a garden of delight, and the deserted, abandoned, and excavated cities [Vulgate: all the cities] have been fortified and inhabited.’

“And the nations that remain round about you shall know that I, the Lord, have built what was destroyed and planted what was uncultivated. I, the Lord, have spoken and acted.

“Thus says the Lord God: In this also the house of Israel shall find me [or: I shall be sought by the house of Israel], so that I may act for them [Vulgate: in them]. I shall multiply them like a flock of people [or: like human sheep], like a holy flock [or: holy sheep], like the flock [or: sheep] of Jerusalem during its solemn feasts. Thus the deserted cities shall be filled with flocks of people [or: sheep], and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

What is said is clear, and the entire meaning concerning the mountains of Israel, which had first been deserted and afterward restored, is now set forth more plainly. God gives the reasons why he handed the people of Israel over to captivity, and in his clemency promises that he will bring them back to the land of Judah and give them much more than he had taken away.

Some Jews refer this to the time of Zerubbabel, when Cyrus, king of the Persians, released them from captivity and many from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin were brought back to Judea. Others refer it to the kingdom of a thousand years, when, under Christ—whom they think is yet to come—the city of Jerusalem will be built and the temple constructed, concerning which we shall speak in the final part of this prophecy.

Meanwhile, leaving aside the Jewish fables and their endless genealogies, let us briefly run through the *περικοπή* (“section”) of this chapter according to our custom and discuss what seems appropriate to us according to ecclesiastical understanding.

The house of Israel—that is, the Jewish people—once dwelt in its own land, that is, in the land of Judea, when it had been brought out of Egypt. But they polluted it by their ways and pursuits, or by their idols, and became so polluted that they were compared with the uncleanness of a menstruating woman.

For this reason God poured out his indignation upon them because of the blood of the prophets and righteous people which they had shed upon the land, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you” (Matt. XXIII, 37). And again: “Truly, truly, I say to you, all the blood that has been shed, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom they killed between the altar and the temple, shall be required of this generation” (v. 35).

They not only shed blood but also polluted the land with their crimes (2 Chron. XXIV). Therefore he scattered them, either in the Babylonian captivity or under the Romans, when they truly shed the blood of Christ. They were scattered through the lands as chaff is scattered, and according to their ways and their most evil deeds they were judged, so that even among the nations to which they had been led captive they polluted the holy name of God.

For all the nations mocked them, saying: “Behold, this is that people of God, who boasted that they alone knew the worship of God.” When I saw this, he says, I spared them—not for their sake, but for the sake of my holy name, for I am the Creator of all things. I spared them, sanctified them, and restored them to their former glory, so that I might pour clean water, the water of saving Baptism, upon believers and those converted from error, cleanse them from their abominations and from all the errors with which they had been occupied, and give them a new heart, so that they might believe in the Son of God, and a new spirit, concerning which David says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me” (Ps. L, 21).

It must also be considered that the new heart and new spirit are given through the pouring and sprinkling of water. When the new heart and new spirit have been given, then all hardness shall be taken away from the Jewish heart, hardness compared with stone, so that in place of a heart of stone there may be a heart of flesh—soft and tender, able to receive the Spirit of God within itself and to be inscribed with saving letters.

Then they shall walk in the commandments of the Lord, keep his judgments, and dwell in the land of confession which he had given to their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to all the saints and prophets. They shall be a people for God, and the Lord shall be their God; this is demonstrated in the present time.

When they have been saved, the Lord will call for grain and multiply it. “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John XII, 24). And they shall no longer suffer famine (Amos VIII, 11)—not famine of bread or thirst for water, but famine of hearing the word of God. This was suffered by the one who departed from the Father and squandered all the substance he had received, when, compelled by the necessity of hunger, he fed on the pods of pigs (Luke XV).

Then the fruit of the tree—that is, wisdom—shall multiply, concerning which it is written: “She is a tree of life to all who seek her” (Prov. III, 18). And the produce of the field shall multiply in the likeness of Jacob, whose fragrance was like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord had blessed (Gen. XXVII, 27).

They shall no longer bear the reproach of famine among the nations, which the unbelief of the Jews suffers even today. But after they have attained blessedness, they shall imitate the Apostle who says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. XV, 9). They shall remember their evil ways and pursuits that were not good, by which they had offended God; their iniquities and crimes, by which they had previously gone astray, shall displease them.

The Lord will grant all these things not because of those who perished through their own error, but for the sake of his holy name. Therefore he summons the house of Israel to be confounded and ashamed because of its former vices and to understand its Creator.

After he has cleansed the people of believers from among the Jews from their iniquities, caused the cities of the Church to be inhabited, restored the ruins that had fallen in the synagogues, and cultivated the land of confession with the ceremonies of God—land that once seemed desolate to all the saints who passed by the works of earthly conduct—then all shall say:

“How is it that the land of Judea, which was once uncultivated, now resembles the paradise of God? And how are the cities of Judea, which had been deserted and abandoned and undermined by their unbelief, now raised up and fortified in confession and in the name of the Lord Savior?”

Thus every creature shall know, as shall the multitudes of angels that surround the land of Israel, that the Lord has built the cities that were destroyed and planted the regions that were uncultivated, and that he has fulfilled by his work what he had promised through the prophets.

Nor will he be content with giving this gift of his generosity to the people whom he has saved; he will provide much greater things. He will be found by the house of Israel, though he had been sought for a long time and not found. And after they have found him, he will multiply them like sheep—not irrational animals, but human sheep, full of reason and confession, like holy sheep and the flocks of Jerusalem, in which the worship of God and the vision of peace are especially found.

This will occur during its solemn feasts, when we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. V), feed on the flesh of the Lamb and drink his blood, and celebrate the Lord’s festivals during the seven weeks and in the tabernacles of this age. Thus the cities that were once deserted shall be filled with flocks of people, and in this way they shall know that he is the Lord who has provided all things.

These remarks, according to the truth of history—or rather, according to the faithfulness of the prophecy—briefly suffice concerning how the people of Israel are restored to their complete condition, and how the remnant of the Jewish people, as the Apostle Paul teaches (Rom. IX, 11), is saved in the Apostle and in all who believed from among the Jews at the beginning and who continue to return to the Church even to this day.

Now the same meaning must be disclosed with equal brevity according to the allegorical interpretation.

Whoever belongs to the house of Israel and perceives the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, dwells in his own land—that is, the Church—or in the lodging of the flesh that has been entrusted to him by God.

But if he pollutes either land by his most evil ways and becomes like the uncleanness of a menstruating woman, God pours out his indignation upon him because of the blood—whether his own blood or that of those whom he has scandalized and caused to be shed upon the earth—and because of the perverse thoughts by which he has polluted it.

Then he shall be scattered among the nations, so as to be made like unbelievers, and shall be scattered through the earth like chaff, so that he may be separated from the grain of the Church and judged according to his ways.

And if even then he does not recognize his sin but pollutes God’s holy name, everyone among whom he dwells shall say: “Behold the people of God; behold the one who has gone out from his land—or rather, has been cast out.”

But if they repent, and I am sanctified in their midst, then every multitude of the nations shall know that I shall take them from the lands into which they had been scattered and bring them back to the land of the Church. I shall pour over them not the waters of saving Baptism, but the waters of doctrine and of the word of God. I shall cleanse them from all their impurities and from all the idols and errors that they had fashioned in their hearts.

“And I shall give them,” he says, “a new heart,” which they had lost through sin, “and I shall renew a steadfast spirit in their hearts.” I shall remove the heart of stone—that is, the unbelieving heart—and give them a heart of flesh, soft and tender, which receives the commandments of God.

Thus they shall walk in my commandments and carry out the judgments which they had previously neglected. They shall dwell in the land that I had given to their fathers—that is, to their teachers and instructors—and once again they shall be God’s people. The Lord shall become their God, whom they had previously offended.

Then they shall be saved from all their impurities, and grain shall be multiplied for them, grain from which the heavenly bread is made. They shall no longer suffer hunger for the word of God. The tree of wisdom shall multiply in them, and the produce of the field shall be brought to completion in their hearts.

They shall no longer be a reproach among the nations. But after God has had mercy on them, they shall remember their evil ways, know where they had been, and be displeased with their iniquities. The Lord says that he does this not because of them, but because of his own clemency.

Therefore he exhorts those who have gone astray to be confounded and ashamed because of their ways, to be restored to the cities of the Church so that they may again inhabit them, and to have all that had fallen within them rebuilt. They shall return to their former ceremonies, and the land that had once been deserted—which had appeared desolate to inhabitants, strangers, and all who passed beyond the conduct of this world—shall return to its former condition.

All shall marvel and say: “That uncultivated land, that deserted land in which all virtues once perished, has now become like a garden of delight and the paradise of God. And the cities that were once deserted, that did not have God as their guest, that had been abandoned by the Holy Spirit, and that had been undermined by credulity (*credulitate*), shall be fortified by the faith of Christ.”

Thus all those round about shall know that the Lord has built the scattered souls and planted and sown in them the trees of every virtue, and that he himself has accomplished in reality what he promised in word.

Again the prophetic word exhorts penitents that, even after they have returned to the Church, they should continually seek the Lord and find him, so that the Lord’s flocks may be multiplied by the crowds of those returning—not flocks of cattle and irrational animals, but flocks of people full of faith and reason, holy flocks, the flocks of the city of Jerusalem, at all the solemn feasts which they have received through the clemency of God.

After the cities of the Lord have been filled with such a multitude of flocks, then all shall know that he is the Lord.

### (Chapter XXXVII—verses 1 ff.) 431

“The hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me out in the spirit of the Lord and set me down in the midst of a plain that was full of bones, and he led me around among them in a circle [Vulgate: ‘around’]. There were very many upon the face of the plain, and they were exceedingly dry. And he said to me: ‘Son of man, do you think that these bones will live?’ And I said: ‘Lord God, you know.’ And he said to me: ‘Prophesy concerning these bones, and say to them: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring spirit into you, and you shall live; and I will place sinews upon you, and cause flesh to grow upon you, and stretch skin over you, and give you spirit, and you shall live and know that I am the Lord.’

“And I prophesied as he had commanded me. And as I prophesied there was a sound, and behold, a commotion; and the bones came together, each one to its joint. And I saw, and behold, sinews were upon them, and flesh grew up, and skin was stretched over them from above; but they had no spirit. And he said to me: ‘Prophesy to the spirit; prophesy, son of man, and say to the spirit: Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.’

“And I prophesied as he had commanded me, and the spirit entered them, and they lived; and they stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great army. And he said to me: ‘Son of man, all these bones are the whole house of Israel. They say: “Our bones have dried up, and our hope has perished, and we have been cut off.” Therefore prophesy, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will open your tombs and bring you out of your graves, my people, and lead you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have opened your graves and brought you out of your tombs, my people; and I shall give my spirit to you, and you shall live; and I shall cause you to rest upon your own soil, and you shall know that I am the Lord. I have spoken and I will act, says the Lord God.’”

#### The Septuagint

“And the hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me out in the spirit of the Lord and set me in the midst of a plain; and it was full of human bones. And he led me around over them in a circle, and behold, there were very many upon the face of the plain, and they were exceedingly dry. And he said to me: ‘Son of man, will these bones live?’ And I said: ‘From where, Lord, Lord? You know these things.’

“And he said to me: ‘Son of man, prophesy over these bones and say to them: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring upon you the spirit of life; and I will place sinews upon you, and bring flesh upon you, and stretch skin over you, and give my spirit upon you, and you shall live; and you shall know that I am the Lord.’

“And I prophesied as he commanded me. And there was a sound while I was prophesying, and behold, a commotion; and bones approached bone, each to its joint. And I saw, and behold, sinews were upon them, and flesh was arising, and skins were ascending over them from above; but there was no spirit in them.

“And he said to me: ‘Prophesy, son of man, prophesy over the spirit, and say to the spirit: Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four spirits, O spirit, and breathe upon these dead, and let them live.’

“And I prophesied as he had commanded me, and the spirit entered them, and they lived, and stood upon their feet: an exceedingly great multitude. And the Lord spoke to me, saying: ‘Son of man, all these bones are the whole house of Israel. They say: “Our bones have become dry; our hope has perished; we have despaired.” Therefore prophesy, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will open your memorials, and bring you up from your graves, my people, and lead you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have opened your graves in order to bring you out of your graves, my people; and I will give my spirit to you, and you shall live; and I will place you upon your own land, and you shall know that I am the Lord. I have spoken, and I will act, says the Lord God.’”

This vision is famous and celebrated in the reading of all the Churches of Christ. For this reason above all I have set out both editions in full, lest the Hebrews bring any accusation against us if they should find even some discrepancy in the wording. They are accustomed to laugh at us, to raise their eyebrows, and, with puffed-out cheeks, to belch forth their knowledge of the Scriptures if they can demonstrate in our codices not, I will not say, a discrepancy of meanings—for that would rightly be censured—but a discordance of words.

Those, therefore, who think that this is the word of God concerning the resurrection believed in by all, both Jews and Christians, usually say the following: “The hand of the Lord came upon the prophet”—that is, the Lord and Savior, through whom the Father brought all things into being. “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” [Note: Jerome consistently reads this passage from John with this punctuation and sense whenever he cites it—and he cites it very often, although we have not previously warned the reader about the matter. There is, however, an ancient question, already debated in the age of the holy Father himself, whether the words “that was made” should be joined in the same sequence to “in him was life,” or whether another sense should begin with them. As you see, Jerome continually preferred the latter reading, which he clearly expressed from the ancient Latin translation. Other ancient Fathers agree with him, especially the Greeks; others, however, both Latins and Greeks, disagree, preferring to read: “That which was made, in him was life.” But the Arians and Macedonians twisted this reading into a heretical sense. When the words “that which was made, in him was life” were separated from what preceded, they made a separate assertion and understood it of the Word and the Holy Spirit; by this text they impiously numbered these divine Persons among created things. All the orthodox, as was fitting, opposed this impious interpretation, while retaining the reading each had previously used. Augustine gives the faithful this one warning: they should not punctuate with the Manichaeans, “That which was made in him was life,” but should read with the Church, “That which was made, in him was life.” For the rest, whichever punctuation—Greek: *stíxis* (στίξις), that is, division of the sentence—the heretics preferred, Saint Ambrose shows in Book III *On the Faith* that they adapted it falsely and rashly to their own meaning: “Therefore,” he says, “there is no need to fear that which the Arians are accustomed to construct by their savage interpretation, saying that the Word of God was made, because, they say, it is written: ‘That which was made in him is life,’ etc. … Furthermore, how can they prove that the evangelist pronounced it in this way? For many learned and faithful people pronounce it thus: ‘All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made.’”].

“And he brought me out,” he says, “in the spirit of the Lord,” with “hand of the Lord” understood. He brought him out in the spirit—not in the body, but outside the body—and set him, or rather let him down, in the midst of a plain that was full of human bones. He did not allow him to rest, but made him go around all the bones, which were not covered by earth but were lying upon the plain; and they were not merely numerous, but exceedingly numerous, and, because of the long passage of time, exceedingly dry and parched, possessing no moisture at all.

And when the divine word had asked him whether he thought that these bones could live, he replied: “Lord God, you know”—you who possess complete knowledge of future things. And the Lord said to him: “Prophesy concerning these bones,” or “over these bones,” and say to them: “Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord.” Here it is marvelous how he spoke to dry bones, which, before they had sinews, flesh, skin, and the life-giving spirit, could hear the word of God.

First the bones are joined to other bones by the bonds of sinews; then they are filled with flesh; and above them, for the sake of beauty, skin is stretched, covering the ugliness of the exposed flesh. Then they receive the spirit, which makes them live; and after they have lived, they know that he is the Lord.

When the prophet had said what had been commanded him, a commotion immediately occurred, and the bones were fitted into their proper framework, bound with sinews, filled with flesh, and covered with skin. Human bodies lay there, however, without spirit. Therefore the prophet prophesies to the spirit and says: “Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four winds, O spirit”—that is, from the four regions of the world—so that, just as at the first creation of humanity God breathed into its face, and it became a living soul (Genesis 2:7), so also the second creation, namely, the resurrection of the dead, may be given life through the breathing of the spirit.

The spirit entered the human bodies, and immediately they lived and stood upon their feet. Hence the resurrection of the dead is called a “multitude,” or the Church—a great multitude (Psalm 103:30)—and, as it is found in the Hebrew, a “great army.” At that time the words are fulfilled: “Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth.”

What follows—“And he said to me: Son of man, all these bones are the whole house of Israel”—appears to raise a question, because it seems to speak not of the general resurrection but specifically of the resurrection of the house of Israel, which says: “Our bones have dried up, and our hope has perished, and we have been cut off from our land,” or “we have utterly despaired.” When they have said this, Ezekiel is compelled a third time to prophesy and say to the dry bones: “Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will open your tombs.”

Here the question arises: If he opens the tombs, how can he earlier have said: “There were very many upon the face of the plain, and they were exceedingly dry”? “And I will bring you out,” he says, “from your tombs, my people,” according to what is written in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life” (John 5:2). And again: “Those who hear will live” (ibid.).

And if, as some think, the divine word speaks of the general resurrection, why was it necessary to say specifically: “And I will lead you into the land of Israel,” when throughout the whole world the dead must rise from the places in which they were buried? “And when,” he says, “I have brought you out from your tombs and given my spirit to you, and you have lived, then I will cause you to rest upon your own soil”; so that, after you have rested in the land of Israel, you may know that I am the Lord, who have fulfilled my promises by my work.

Those, therefore, who understand these words as referring to the general resurrection refer the statement that seems to raise the question—“These bones are the whole house of Israel”—to the resurrection of the saints, concerning which the apostle John also speaks in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; over such the second death has no power” (Revelation 20:6). This means, plainly, that there is one resurrection of the saints and another of sinners. Hence it is also said in the first psalm: “The impious do not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.”

The land of Israel that the Lord promises to those who rise, they affirm to be the land of which it is written: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matthew 5:4); and: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9).

This is the interpretation of those who, as we have said, maintain that Ezekiel wrote concerning the general resurrection. Those who interpret these things in this way should not begrudge us our different exposition of the passage, as though, by explaining it otherwise, we appeared to deny the resurrection. For we know that much stronger testimonies, in which there is no ambiguity, are found in the holy Scriptures. Such is the passage in Job: “He will raise up my skin, which bears these things” [Job 19; alternatively, “you will raise up my skin”]. And in Daniel: “Many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall rise: some to everlasting life, and others to reproach and everlasting shame” (Daniel 12:2). And in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28). And the apostle Paul says: “He will give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:11) [Note: Victorinus supplies the complete testimony thus: “He who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will give life to mortal things, etc.,” from the Florentine codices.], along with many other passages.

From this it is clear that we do not deny the resurrection; rather, we maintain that this particular passage is not written about the resurrection, and that through the parable of the resurrection a restoration of Israel is being prophesied—Israel, which at that time was captive in Babylon. Nor shall we immediately give the heretics an opportunity by denying that these words can be understood of the universal resurrection. For the likeness of resurrection would never have been set forth to signify the restoration of the Israelite people unless the resurrection itself stood firm and was believed to be future, since no one confirms an uncertain matter by reference to things that do not exist. [Note: Compare Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 30, where this twofold Hieronymian argument is especially found: “For although a representation of truth is in an image, the image itself exists in the truth of its own subject; it must necessarily exist prior to itself, by which another is fashioned,” etc.]

Our entire argument therefore tends toward this point: just as it seems incredible that a future resurrection should be promised to dry bones, worn away by great antiquity—and yet what is promised will happen—so also the restoration of the people of Israel, who were led into captivity and scattered throughout the whole world, seems indeed incredible to those who do not know God’s power; yet it will happen, because, he says, “I, the Lord, have spoken, and I will act as I have promised.”

Finally, in the earlier prophecy in which the ancient condition of the mountains of Israel is promised anew, the Lord says to them: “I will turn to you, and you shall be tilled, and you shall receive seed, and I will multiply human beings upon you, the whole house of Israel” (above, XXXVI, 9–10). Again, the statement that the house of Israel will dwell in its own land, which was once uncultivated and will afterward become like a garden of delight; that the deserted cities will be fortified; and that the house of Israel will be multiplied in them like a flock of sheep—along with the other things that follow—belongs to the same meaning that is now expressed allegorically and parabolically by the dry bones, entirely lacking the moisture of life. Thus is fulfilled what is written in the Gospel: “The things that seem impossible to human beings are possible with God” (Matthew 19:26).

They are brought out from their tombs—from the tombs of captivity and from the bonds by which they were held fast in Babylonian servitude.

The Jews affirm that all these things were fulfilled either under Zerubbabel, as I said earlier, when a great commotion occurred and the kingdom of the Chaldeans was transferred to the Medes and Persians; or in the present time of their Christ, whom they believe is yet to come.

We, however, understand them spiritually as having been fulfilled after the cross of the Lord and Savior. We see them occurring every day, especially in those who, like Lazarus, are bound in the bandages of their sins and are raised at the voice of the Lord (John 11). They truly are the house of Israel, once dry and possessing no hope of salvation; but when the spirit of grace enters them and the Lord extends his hand, they are freed from the depth of hell. And those who had formerly said, “Lord God, you know these things,” afterward hear, once they have been liberated: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:31).

### (Verses 15 ff.)

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘And you, son of man, take for yourself one piece of wood and write upon it, “Judah and the sons of Israel, his companions”; and take another piece of wood and write upon it, “Joseph, the wood of Ephraim, and the whole house of Israel, his companions.” And join them one to the other for yourself into one piece of wood; 437 and they shall be joined together in your hand.

“And when the sons of your people say to you, asking: “Will you not explain to us what you intend by these things?” you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will take the wood of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel that are joined to him; and I will place them together with the wood of Judah, and make them one wood, and they shall be one in his hand.

“And the pieces of wood upon which you have written shall be in your hand before their eyes. And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will take the sons of Israel from among the nations to which they have gone, and gather them from every side, and bring them to their own soil. And I will make them one nation in the land, upon the mountains of Israel, and one king shall rule over all of them.

“And they shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they ever again be divided into two kingdoms. Nor shall they defile themselves any longer with their idols, their abominations [Vulgate adds: ‘their abominations’], and all their iniquities. And I will save them from all their settlements in which they sinned, and cleanse them; and they shall be my people [Vulgate: ‘as a people for me’], and I shall be their God [Vulgate: ‘as God for them’].

“And my servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd for all of them. They shall walk in my judgments, and observe my commandments, and do them. And they shall dwell upon the land that I gave to my servant Jacob, in which your fathers dwelt; and they themselves and their sons, and their sons’ sons, shall dwell upon it forever. And David my servant shall be their prince forever.

“And I will make a covenant of peace with them; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them. I will establish them and multiply them [Vulgate omits ‘them’], and I will place my sanctuary in their midst forever. And my tabernacle shall be among them; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. And the nations shall know that I am the Lord who sanctifies Israel, when my sanctuary is in their midst forever.”

#### The Septuagint

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘And you, son of man, take for yourself one staff, and write upon it, “Judah and the sons of Israel who have been joined to him”; and take for yourself a second staff, and write upon it, “Joseph, the staff of Ephraim, and all the sons of Israel who have been joined to him.” And join them together for yourself into one staff, so that you may fasten them together; and they shall be in your hand.

“And it shall be that when the sons of Israel say to you: “Will you not tell us what these things mean to you?” you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will take [Note: Victorius deletes the word “in” in accordance with the Greek text, although the Vulgate and the Hebrew likewise support it.] the tribe of Joseph by the hand of Ephraim, the tribes of Israel that have been joined to him, and I will place them all upon the tribe of Judah; and they shall be one staff, and they shall be one in the hand of Judah.

“And the staffs upon which you have written shall be in your hand before them. And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will take the whole house of Israel from among the nations into which they have entered, and gather them from all the surrounding peoples, and bring them into the land of Israel. And I will make them one nation in my land, upon the mountains of Israel, and one prince shall be over all of them as king.

“And they shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they ever again be divided into two kingdoms, so that they may no longer defile themselves with their idols, their stumbling-blocks, and all their impieties. And I will rescue them from all their iniquities in which they sinned, and cleanse them; and they shall be my people [Col. 0351C], and I shall be their God.

“And my servant David shall be prince in their midst, and there shall be one shepherd for all of them, because they shall walk in my commandments, observe my judgments, and perform them. And they shall dwell in their own land, which I gave to my servant Jacob, where their fathers dwelt; and they themselves, their sons, and their sons’ sons shall dwell in it forever. And David my servant shall be their prince forever.

“And I will establish for them a covenant of peace; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them. And I will give them, multiply them, and set my holy things in their midst forever. And my tabernacle shall be among them; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. And the nations shall know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them, when my holy things are in their midst forever.”

History of the kingdoms relates (III Kings 12) that under Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, the twelve tribes were divided; and that two of them—Judah and Benjamin, together with the Levites and priests—followed Rehoboam, who reigned in Jerusalem. His kingdom was called Judah.

The other ten tribes, however, said: “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse,” and submitted their necks to Jeroboam son of Nebat, of the tribe of Ephraim, who was descended from Joseph, and served him. For the most part they were called by the ancient name of the people, Israel. For a long time the kingdoms of Judah and Israel fought against each other and obeyed their own kings (IV Kings 25).

First the ten tribes were captured by the Assyrians; after some time those called Judah were led captive to Babylon by the Chaldeans. The tribe of Judah was restored to its ancient land after seventy years. The ten tribes called Israel, however, remain to this day captive in the mountains and cities of the Medes (IV Kings 25).

The present prophecy therefore promises from the mouth of the Lord that the two kingdoms will be joined to one another—that is, the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel. The staff of Ephraim, who was descended from the stock of Joseph, together with the remaining tribes joined to him, will be taken up and joined to the staff of Judah, so that they will no longer be called Judah and Israel but will be called Judah by one name. And, under the figure of the prophet, who precedes as a type of the Lord and Savior, they will be held not in two hands but in the one hand of Christ.

For he says that he will take the sons of Israel from among the nations to which they were led captive and bring them back to the land and mountains of Israel, of which we read above. They will be called one nation and ruled under the authority of one king, so that they will no longer defile themselves with their idols and abominations. Rather, once they have been freed from the settlements of captivity in which they sinned, they will be cleansed of all their vices and become the people of God, so that the Lord will be their God.

“And my servant David,” he says, “shall be king over them” (Luke 1). Concerning him the angel also speaks in the Gospel, saying that he will reign over the house of Jacob and that there will be no end to his kingdom. His kindness will be so great that he will be called not only king but also shepherd, because by the title of shepherd he tempers the proud name of imperial power.

Once they have become one nation and have dwelt in the land and mountains of Israel, they will walk in all the judgments of the Lord and observe his commandments. They will dwell not in another land but in the one he gave to his servant Jacob, in which their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the other saints, dwelt. Not only will they themselves dwell there, but also their sons and descendants, according to the Virgilian line (*Aeneid*, Book IV):

> “And the children of children, and those who shall be born from them.”

And they shall dwell not for a short time but forever.

“But do you wish to know,” he says, “who this king and shepherd is?” He is the one of whom I spoke above: “My servant David.” Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized; rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6 ff.).

When they are under such a king, “I will make a covenant of peace with them”—not as in the Old Testament, with its conflicts and wars, but a covenant of peace that surpasses all understanding, concerning which the Savior says to the Apostles: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). And the prophet says: “His dwelling-place has become peace” (Psalm 75:2).

When he has established and strengthened them in the Church, so that they can say, “He has set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm 39:3), then they will be multiplied either in the number of believers or through an increase of virtues.

“And I will give,” he says, “my sanctification”—or “my sanctuary”—“in their midst forever.” The Jews interpret this as the Temple built under Zerubbabel. But how can the statement “forever” stand, when that Temple, built by Zerubbabel and later restored by many, was burned by Roman fire?

All these things must be referred to the Church and to the time of the Savior, when his tabernacle was placed in the Church, where he became our God and we became his people. The outcome of everything is that they may know that he is the Lord, and that he sanctifies Israel—not according to the flesh but according to the spirit—when his sanctification has been established forever in the midst of believers.

That the Lord rejected the tribe of Ephraim and chose the tribe of Judah we also read in the Psalms, where it is written: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim; but he chose the tribe of Judah” (Psalm 77:67–68). Concerning Judah it is written: “The prince shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10).

For truly, at the coming of the Lord and Savior, the two staffs—or, as it is written in the Hebrew, the two pieces of wood—were joined into one scepter; and in the baptism of Christ those who had long been separated were united, so that they might become one new human being and one nation. They would no longer defile themselves with idols and abominations; rather, washed clean in the baptismal bath, they would be the people of God. Christ would rule over them, and they would dwell upon the land of the meek, the land of the living, which he had given to his servant Jacob, who supplanted the people of Israel in his mother’s womb.

But if we wish to understand this according to the prophecy of Hosea—which is directed almost entirely to the ten tribes, that is, to Joseph, Ephraim, Samaria, and Israel—as referring to knowledge falsely so called and to the various throngs of heretics, we shall say the following: At the end of time, when the fullness of the nations has entered and all Israel has been saved (Romans 11), then the hostile people who fought against the house of Judah and the confession of the Church will also surrender themselves to the ecclesiastical faith. Having abandoned all their errors, the rulers of this world who are being destroyed [alternatively: “who are to be destroyed”], and their patriarchs who led them into the abyss of blasphemies, they will rise up and leave behind their idols and abominations, which they had fashioned from their own hearts. They will pass from all the settlements in which they sinned into the ecclesiastical faith, be cleansed, and become the people of Christ; and he himself will be their God. I know that I have set this out more fully in the prophet Hosea.

But if Jews and Judaizing Christians wish to refer these things to a thousand-year reign, they are compelled to accept that all who are to be saved will dwell in the land of Israel; that Jerusalem will be rebuilt; that the Temple will be erected; that all the ceremonies of the Law will be practiced; that the Sabbath will be observed; that the injury of circumcision will be accepted; and that people will eat and drink and regard an abundance of wealth as the highest blessedness and the sum of all goods—although the Apostle says: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians 6:13).

Just as the preceding prophetic discourse, in the figure of the resurrection, demonstrated the resurrection of the Jewish people—not a bodily resurrection but a spiritual one—so also this prophecy pertains not to the happiness of the flesh but to that of the soul, and to the faith of Christ, by which we are cleansed in baptism. His kingdom is everlasting, so that we should not await as future what has already passed and what we know is taking place every day.

[Col. 0354B] (Chapter XXXVIII.) “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Gog, the land of Magog, the prince of Rosh (or: the head), Meshech, and Tubal, and prophesy against him. And you shall say to him: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of Rosh (or: the head), Meshech, 442 and Tubal. I shall turn you about, put a bridle in your jaws, and bring you out (or: gather you), you and your whole army: horses and horsemen, all clothed in coats of mail, a great multitude carrying spear and shield and sword (or: bucklers and helmets and swords); Persians, Ethiopians, and Libyans with them, all equipped with shields and helmets; Gomer and all his troops; the house of Togarmah, the farthest parts of the North (or: from the remotest parts of the North), and all his forces, [Col. 0354C] and many peoples (or: nations) with you. Prepare and equip yourself, and all your multitude that has been assembled to you, and be a command for them (or: you will be my guard). After many days you will be visited: in the latter (or: last) years you will come to the land that has turned back (or: been turned away) from the sword; and it has been gathered from many peoples to the mountain (or: mountains) (or: land) of Israel, which had been continually desolate. This land was brought out from the peoples, and they will all dwell in it securely. You will advance like a storm; you will come like a cloud to cover the land, you and all your troops, and many peoples with you.

“Thus says the Lord God: On that day words will rise upon your heart, and you will devise an exceedingly evil plan. And you will say: ‘I shall go up against a land (or: over a land) without walls (or: abandoned); I shall come against those who rest and dwell securely (or: in peace). All of them dwell without walls; they have no bars or gates, in order that you may plunder spoil and seize prey, stretch out your hand against those who had been desolate and afterward restored, and against the people gathered from the nations, who have begun to possess and dwell at the center of the land.’

“Seba and Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish (or: the Carthaginians and all its villages’ lions) will say to you: ‘Have you come to take spoil? Have you assembled your multitude to plunder prey, to carry away silver and gold, to remove possessions and wealth, and to plunder countless booty?’

“Therefore prophesy, son of man, and say to Gog: Thus says the Lord God: Will you not know (or: will you rise up) on that day, when my people Israel dwells securely (or: in peace)? And you will come from your place, from the farthest parts (or: the remotest parts) of the North, you and many peoples with you, all riding horses, a great assembly and a powerful army. You will rise up against my people Israel like a cloud, to cover the land. In the latter [Col. 0355B] days you will be (or: it will be), and I shall bring you against my land, so that all the nations may know me, when I have been sanctified in you before their eyes, O Gog.

“Thus says the Lord God: Are you that one of whom I spoke in ancient days by the hand of my servants, the prophets of Israel, who prophesied in those days and times (or: years), that I might bring you against them? And it shall be on that day, on the day when Gog comes against the land of Israel, says the Lord God: My indignation will rise in my fury. And in my jealousy, in the fire of my wrath, I have spoken: On that day there will be a great commotion over the land of Israel, and the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts of the field (or: plain), [Col. 0355C] every creeping thing that moves upon the ground, and all human beings who are upon the face of the earth will be shaken before me and overthrown (or: the mountains will be split, the hedges—or: valleys—will fall), and every wall will collapse to the ground.

“And I shall summon against him throughout all my mountains a sword (or: every terror of the sword), says the Lord God. Each person’s (or: each man’s) sword will be directed against his brother. And I shall judge him with pestilence (or: death) and bloodshed, with a torrential rain and immense stones (or: hailstones). I shall rain fire and sulfur upon him, upon his army (or: upon all who are with him), and upon the many peoples who are with him. And I shall magnify myself, sanctify myself, and make myself known before the many nations, and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

First the foundations of the history must be laid, and it must be understood that this is the final word of the Lord to the prophet Ezekiel. For after this we cannot find anything similar, except what is written in the twenty-fifth year of Jehoiachin’s deportation: “The hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me there,” that is, into the land of Israel, when the construction of the Temple is described and the order of its ceremonies is recounted.

Next, it must be observed that the prophet’s face is said to be set, or fixed, against Gog the land, or against the land of Magog. For firmness and profound consideration of countenance are required if we are to understand what is said, according to the Apostle’s statement: “But we all, with unveiled face contemplating the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18).

Therefore the Jews and our Judaizers think that Gog consists of Scythian nations, savage and innumerable, extending beyond Mount Caucasus and Lake Maeotis, and near the Caspian Sea as far as India. They think that after the thousand-year kingdom these nations will be stirred up by the devil and come into the land of Israel to fight against the saints, having gathered many nations with them. First, Meshech, whom Josephus interprets as the Cappadocians; then Tubal, whom he likewise interprets as the Iberians or Spaniards, while the Hebrews suspect them to be Italians; and with them, in their army, Persians, Ethiopians, and Libyans. They also identify Gomer and Togarmah with the Galatians and Phrygians, and Seba and Dedan and the Carthaginians—or Tarshish—with those mentioned here. This is also what John sets forth in his Apocalypse:

“And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea. And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. And fire descended from God out of heaven and devoured them. And the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet were; and they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever” (Rev. 20:7ff.).

They do not understand that John’s entire book, which is prefaced by the title Revelation, is mystical and that we need revelation in order to be able to say with the prophet: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18).

Others, however, abandoning the earthly sense and the Jewish and old-womanish fables that are harmful (1 Tim. 4), and indulging themselves, descend into the depths and climb excessively to the heights. They invent things far worse, describing battles in the heavenly Jerusalem between the devil and his entire army, and under the *topologies* [Greek τοπολογίαις; alternatively: “etymologies”] of the individual nations they interpret the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

Leaving all these matters to the reader’s judgment, we shall strive not so much to condemn what belongs to others as to affirm an ecclesiastical explanation.

Gog is called by the Greek word δόμα (*doma*), “roof,” in Latin. Magog, moreover, is interpreted as “unroofed” or “exposed.” Thus every pride and false knowledge, which raises itself against knowledge of the truth, is indicated by these names. These are the roofs of which Isaiah also speaks in his vision against the valley of Zion: “What has happened to you now, that you have all climbed onto empty roofs?” (Isa. 22:1).

We shall interpret “roof” as the leaders of heretics, and “from the roof” as those who have received their doctrines. And beautifully, after the many mystical prophecies in this book, the final prophecy is against Gog and Magog. For if, according to Peter, it is the time for judgment to begin from the house of God, and according to this same Ezekiel, who says, “Begin with my sanctuaries” (above 9:6), and if death, the last enemy, will be destroyed (1 Pet. 4), then in Isaiah too the first word is against Judah, in which there is confession of the Lord, and the final word against the four-footed beasts that are in the wilderness (Isa. 2). It is rightly also here the final word against Gog and Magog, who attack the city of God, which the river’s stream makes glad (Ps. 45).

And Isaiah says of it: “I am the fortified city that is attacked” (Isa. 27:10).

Of it the Gospel says: “A city cannot be hidden when it is set upon a mountain” (Matt. 5:14). And more fully in the Psalm: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is in unity” (Ps. 121:3); “The mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Ps. 124:1).

As for the statement that in the army of Gog, or Magog—who according to the Septuagint, Symmachus, and Theodotion is the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal—the first nation, Rosh, is interpreted by Aquila as “head,” we have followed him, so that the sense is: “the prince of the head, Meshech and Tubal.” Indeed, neither in Genesis nor in any other place in Scripture, nor even in Josephus, who explains the names of all the Hebrew nations in the first book of the *Antiquities*, have we been able to find this nation.

From this it is evident that Rosh does not signify a nation but “head.”

This too should briefly be noted: in Ezekiel, Gog is called the prince of the land of Magog, whereas the Apocalypse mentions both Gog and Magog as nations (Rev. 20), which go out from the four corners of the earth. Just as from Jacob, who was afterward called Israel, the entire Hebrew people received the name Israel (Gen. 32), and from Aram came Syria, from Mizraim Egypt—whose names are written in Genesis (10)—so from the prince Gog all who are subject to him are called Magog.

Meshech is interpreted as “madness,” and Tubal as “all” or “everything.” Thus the prince and head of proud madness and of every evil, according to the statement “The world is set in wickedness” (1 John 5:19), are called Gog and Magog.

These nations, hostile and opposed to the saints, go out from the corners of the earth, abandoning the straight line and the arrangement of God’s camp, which is recounted in Numbers. They do not know the testimony: “Many will come from east and west and north and south, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 8:11).

And elsewhere: “I shall say to the North, ‘Give them up,’ and to the South, ‘Do not hinder.’ Bring my sons from the distant land and my daughters from the end of the earth, all who are called by my name” (Isa. 43:6).

But the corners of the earth from which Gog and Magog go out are not like those others. Near such corners stands the harlot in Proverbs (Prov. 23), who hastens to deceive foolish young men passing through the streets, that is, along the broad and spacious way that leads to death.

The scribes and Pharisees also pray at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by human beings; they have received their reward (Matt. 6).

What, then, is the threat against Gog? “I shall turn you about,” or “convert you,” “and put a bridle in your jaws.” First, “I shall make you waver from your own opinion and turn you about.” And I shall put a bridle in your jaws, concerning which it is written: “Restrain their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31:9), so that the untamed horse, behaving wantonly and falling over precipices, may be subdued by the Lord’s bridle. To him the prophet says: “Mount your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Hab. 3:8).

And to Job, through the cloud and whirlwind, it is said: “Did you clothe the horse with strength?” (Job 39:19). Such were the horses and horsemen whose multitude John saw in heaven (Rev. 6).

He therefore says to Gog: “I shall bring you out,” or “gather you,” and your whole army, or strength. Whoever is brought out and gathered from dispersion is drawn back to salvation, according to what is promised in the Law: “If your dispersion should be from the summit of heaven to its summit, from there I shall gather you” (Deut. 30:3).

His horses also and horsemen clothed in coats of mail—those who imitate the Apostle’s armor and boast that they possess breastplates of righteousness (Eph. 6)—constitute an immense multitude. All seize shield and sword against the Church, and they are exceedingly savage nations hostile to Israel: Persians, Ethiopians, and Libyans, whose wars against the people of God are recounted in the Holy Scriptures.

Gomer and the house of Togarmah also, who come from the remotest parts of the North—which is the coldest wind and is called “the Right”—and all the strength of Magog, and all the peoples subject to him, will come with him to battle.

He is addressed ironically: “Prepare yourself, equip yourself, and gather to yourself all your multitude that obeys your commands.” And know that after many days you will be visited, according to what is written:

[Col. 0359A]

[Col. 0359C] [This note appears at the foot of column 359, but the callout letter (a) has not been printed in the text.]

Erasmus wished this passage to be changed by the following conjecture: “Perhaps,” he says, “it should be read thus: If you write it with the letter [*chi*] in the first and last syllable, it is called ‘lion cub.’ But if without [*chi*], it is called ‘field’ and ‘village.’”

Marianus rashly transferred Erasmus’s marginal note into Jerome’s text itself, so that the simple reader might be deceived into thinking that Jerome had written what, after so many centuries, Erasmus—or someone else in his place—had devised. The error of these editors is therefore obvious: they did not understand that the name *Chaphir*, written with chi, signifies “lion cub,” whereas *caphir* or *capher*, written with *c*, signifies “field” or “village,” as *Capernaum* is written with the Greek Kappa. The Greek Kappa and the Latin C correspond to the Hebrew letter *coph*. MART. [Martianus.]

The experts in Hebrew know that both names begin with the same letter, *chaph*, or the Latin *c*, and that the only difference between them is the *yod*, which in *Chaphir*, that is, “little lion,” has a sound but is absent from *Chaphar*, that is, “village.”

This, then, seemed to be the one difference that required explanation. Hence Erasmus wrote in the margin of the book how the passage should be emended: “If you write it with the letter [*chi*] in the first and last syllable, it is called ‘lion cub.’ But if without [*chi*], it is called ‘field’ and ‘village.’”

Victorius not only approved this reading with his own judgment but inserted it into the text, rejecting the old printed reading. The evidence of the manuscript copies, however, stands against him. A great number of manuscripts were consulted for this passage, and an extraordinary agreement was found among all of them in this reading, which Martianus therefore rightly judged should be retained.

I do not deny that the word is never written with *coph*, and that almost nothing of the kind exists in the Hebrew language. I think that Jerome intended to note not a difference of letters but of sound or pronunciation, which may at that time have existed, so that one name, although written with the same letter, was pronounced with K or the Latin C—as in Καπερναοὺν—while the other was pronounced with X, or chi, as in Χερουβίμ, Χαναάν, and similar names.

[Col. 0359D] “I shall visit their iniquities with the rod and their sins with scourges” (Ps. 88:33).

“In the latter years,” he says, “you will come.” Hence John also says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

The people of the nations are brought in at the eleventh hour to work in the vineyard (Matt. 20). Against their land—that is, the land of the meek and the land of the saints, which bears fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold—Gog comes to attack it, the land that has turned back, or turned away, from the sword.

For he knows that it is written: “Scatter, O Lord, the nations that desire wars” (Ps. 67:30). It stands in peace and has been gathered from many peoples and nations, so that, having despised the error of the nations, it might come to the mountains of Israel—that is, to the patriarchs and prophets, who had once been continually desolate, without the law and commandments of God. To it is afterward said: “The children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1).

These are the deserted and waterless places in which the devil could find no place, because they had been called to salvation. Later, however, having taken seven other spirits more wicked than himself, he returned to his house (Matt. 12), namely, to the nation of Israel.

“This,” he says, “was brought out from the peoples,” with “land” understood; or, here, “he was brought out from the nations,” so that the people of believers may be understood, the people who dwelt in peace and trusted in the Lord.

But Gog, advancing with his entire army, will come like a storm and like a cloud to cover the land of believers. For what heretic, whose prince is the devil, does not come against the Church like a storm and hasten to crush and cover the simple among believers with the cloud of his words?

Therefore it is said to him: “As far as it lies within you, you will cover everything—you and all your troops and many peoples with you.”

And beautifully, when Gog advances, he does not have willing rain or an early or late shower to make the dry fields rejoice, but storm and darkness, so that he may confuse everything with darkness and error.

Therefore the Lord God says to him: “At that time,” that is, in the last days, “words will rise upon your heart, and you will devise an exceedingly evil plan.” Scripture says: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not abandon your place” (Eccl. 10:4).

By contrast, God rises into the heart of the saint, concerning which it is written: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. 83:6).

And Gog says: “I shall go up against a land without walls,” or “cast off,” that is, a land deprived of God’s help and not fortified by the arguments of dialecticians. “I shall come against those who rest and dwell securely,” or “in peace.” For our king is peaceful, and “his place is in peace” (Ps. 75).

“All,” he says, “dwell without walls; they have no bars or gates.” The devil, the prince of heretics, says this because the Church has no defenses. He intends to plunder its spoil and seize its prey, and to stretch out his hand against those who had been desolate when they did not possess knowledge of God, but were afterward restored through Christ and came to the Father, to whom Christ says in the Gospel: “Father, I have revealed your name to the human beings” (John 17:6).

[Col. 0360B] And so that we may know that the people who had been desolate and were afterward restored signify the Christian people, what follows says: “And against the people gathered from the nations” (Ps. 73:12). This people began to possess Christ’s inheritance and to dwell at the center of the earth, concerning which it is written: “He worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Truth has arisen from the earth” (Ps. 84:1). It says in the Gospel: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John 14:6).

While he is thinking and speaking these things and hastening to seize the Church’s possession, the nations that had been converted from their former error to salvation—Seba and Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish, of Carthage, or of the sea, who amid the waves of this world seek profits through good works—and all their villages, or lions, or lion cubs, as the Hebrew text contains, will speak to him as follows.

As for the fact that the Septuagint and Theodotion put “villages” for “lion cubs,” which in Hebrew are called *CAPHIR* (the Hebrew letters are omitted in the supplied text), the error is obvious. If you write it with the letter chi, it is called “lion cub”; but if with *c*, which in Hebrew is called *coph*, it is called “field” and “village.” Hence *Capernaum* is said to mean “beautiful field.”

Seba and Dedan, the merchants of Tarshish, and all the saints, who are now called lion cubs—or certainly the villages and dwellings of believers—will therefore say: “O Gog, are you coming for this reason, to plunder the Church’s spoil? Have you assembled this multitude so that Christ’s possession may become your inheritance? Or do you think that you will possess the silver and gold of the Church—understood as eloquence and understanding—in order to remove all its possessions and wealth and plunder the countless spoils gathered through Christ’s victories?”

Therefore, O prophet Ezekiel, who in the figure of Christ are called “son of man,” speak to Gog and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: When the error of the whole world has been removed and my people Israel, who perceive God with the mind, dwells securely in the Church, or in peace, then you will know—or you will rise up—and come from your place.

What the place of heretical depravity is, the following sentence shows: “From the remotest parts of the North,” which strives to cool all the warmth of believers.

Many peoples will come with him, all riding horses, concerning whom it is written: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. 15:1)—a great assembly and a powerful army. With them, he says, advancing against my people Israel like a cloud and darkness, you will cover the land, my land, of which it was said above: “In the latter days you will be,” when the evangelical preaching is proclaimed, “and I shall bring you against my land.”

For heresies must exist, so that those who are approved may become manifest (1 Cor. 11:19); and by God’s will the devil, the ἀγωνιστής [*agonistēs*, “combatant”; in the Vatican manuscript: ἀναγωνιστής, perhaps ἀνταγωνιστής should be restored], and all the doctrines of perversity have been left. Thus all the nations may know and understand me, when I have been sanctified in you before their eyes, O Gog—that is, when through your punishments they understand that I am the judge.

And he turns in apostrophe to Gog himself: “Are you not that one of whom I spoke in ancient days by the hands of my servants, the prophets of Israel?” Namely, Moses, who says in the Book of Numbers, at least according to the Septuagint: “A man will arise from his seed and will rule many nations; Gog’s kingdom will be exalted, and his kingdom will grow” (Num. 24:7).

According to the Hebrew text, however, I find it written thus: “Therefore Agag [the Vulgate has ‘Gog’], his king, will be taken away, and his kingdom will be removed,” because the kingdom of Israel under Saul was destroyed on account of Agag, king of Amalek.

And elsewhere: “He will cleanse the land of his people” (Joel 3). Joel too, in the valley of Jehoshaphat—that is, in the judgment of God—describes the nations being gathered. Isaiah and all the prophets likewise speak of those by whose hands and good works the word of the Lord is accomplished.

When, therefore, you come against the land of Israel, my indignation will rise in fury against you and in jealousy for my people. In the fire of my wrath I have spoken, and it will consume all the wood of your vices.

“At that time,” he says, “there will be a great commotion over the land of Israel.” For when the devil incites it, frequent persecution will arise against the Church. When this persecution has been calmed and conquered by God’s protection, then the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts of the field, every creeping thing that moves upon the earth, and all human beings upon the face of the earth will tremble before him.

This is plainly demonstrated concerning the inhabitants of the Church: some are like fish of the sea, others like birds of heaven, others like beasts of the field, and others like all the creeping things that move upon the earth; still others, retaining the dignity of human beings, dwell upon the face of the earth.
