That the diversity of conduct is marked by various names is also written by the Apostle to the Corinthians, who says that after the resurrection there are different heavenly bodies and different earthly bodies (1 Cor. 15), and that the body of a fish is one, that of a bird another, that of beasts another, that of creeping things another, and that of human beings another—those who have retained their former name.

In the Acts of the Apostles too, the sheet shown three times to the apostle Peter by its four corners (Acts 10) signifies the variety of believers, which is also contained in Noah’s Ark during the Flood.

Then, before the face and presence of the Lord’s majesty, the mountains that were raising themselves against the knowledge of God will be overturned. The hedges—or valleys—will fall, whether they have been sunk to the depths through humility of understanding or are fortifications that promise something while imitating the Church of God. Concerning the Church’s hedges it is said: “Whoever breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a serpent” (Eccl. 10:8).

And all the walls will collapse to the ground. For when the strength of ecclesiastical discourse has appeared, all the fortifications of the heretics will fall.

“And I shall summon against him,” he says—that is, against Gog, the prince of the heretics—“throughout all his mountains a sword,” so that the princes of his army may be destroyed by the Lord’s sword.

Then heresy will fight against heresy, and their mutual conflict will be our victory.

“And I shall judge him,” he says, “with death, or pestilence, and bloodshed, and a torrential rain, and immense stones, or hailstones” [alternatively: hail].

Gog is judged by his own death, by the blood that he shed, by the torrential rain—that is, by the words of the learned and perfect man—and by immense stones that crush him with testimonies of Scripture, or by hailstones that make his heat grow cold. “For all are adulterers, like an oven—their hearts” (Hos. 7:4).

“I shall rain fire and sulfur upon him,” he says, by which the punishment of eternal judgment is indicated. And not only upon him, who was the author of perversity, but also upon his entire army and multitude, and upon the many peoples who are with him.

For heretics have many companions; indeed, their prince, the devil, is surrounded by an innumerable multitude.

[Col. 0362D] When every error has been removed and the princes of the heretics have been punished and destroyed, the Lord is magnified and sanctified in believers. He becomes known in the eyes of the many nations that have believed in his faith. Both from his blessedness and from the punishments of his adversaries, they will know and recognize that he himself is the Lord.

We have interpreted these matters as best we could, obeying that command: “You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left, but you shall walk by the royal way” (Deut. 28:14).

If anyone criticizes our work, let him either bring forward better things for us to follow, or, if he wishes to say nothing, let him leave perfect knowledge to God—provided that he understands that it is not our strength but our intention that must be judged.

[Notes: Col. 0353D] Victorius supplies “and many peoples, or nations, etc.” from the Vulgate and the Hebrew.

[Note: Col. 0353D] The same editor reads *aversa* (“turned away”) for *perversa* (“perverse”), as is clear from Jerome’s exposition below: “Gog comes to attack their land …, which has turned back, or turned away, from the sword.” He likewise prefers *projectam* (“cast off”) to *abjectam* (“abandoned”) from the same exposition.

[Note: Col. 0355D] From the manuscripts, following Rabanus, we have substituted “hedges” (*sepes*); previously “walls” (*maceriae*) stood here, though with the same sense.

[Note: Col. 0355D] St Augustine also says in Book XX, chapter 11, of the *City of God*: “These nations, which he calls Gog and Magog, are not to be understood as though they were certain barbarian peoples established in some part of the world—whether those whom some suppose to be the Getae and Massagetae, because of the initial letters of these names, or certain other foreigners separated from Roman rule.” Consult the Preface to this book and the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.

[Note: Col. 0356D] The same writer, in the cited book *City of God*, says: “We have discovered that the interpretation of these names is: Gog, ‘a roof’; Magog, ‘from a roof,’ as though the former were a house and the latter one who proceeds from the house.”

[Note: Col. 0357D] Victorius restored *firma* (“fortified”) from the Greek ὀχυρά, “fortified.”

[Note: Col. 0357D–0358D] Bochart preferred “Hebrew [nations].” Nor did Jerome’s argument seem sufficiently firm to him for denying that Rhos was the name of a region or people. For Ezekiel has many other place-names found nowhere else: Chebar, Gammadim, Chelmad, Chub, Cheton, Sibraim, and the like. Indeed, he thinks Rhos properly denotes the river Araxes; while, as a people-name, besides the Septuagint’s ἄρχοντα Ῥῶς (“prince of Rhos”), Symmachus, Theodotion, and Bishop Proculus in Socrates, *History*, Book VII, chapter 43, accept it.

[Note: Col. 0358D] The missing word “place” (*loco*) has been supplied from the manuscripts after Victorius.

[Note: Col. 0358D] Victorius deleted the word *ejus* (“his”), which is absent from the biblical text, and shortly afterward supplied *quorum* (“whose”), that is, “whose multitude,” etc.

[Note: Col. 0362D] Victorius, more correctly perhaps, following the Vulgate, reads *propter* (“because of”) for *propterea* (“therefore”).

### Chapter XXXIX

**Verses 1 and following.** “But you, son of man, prophesy against Gog and say: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of Rosh [or: chief], Meshech, and Tubal. I will turn you about [or: gather you], and I will bring you back [or: lead you down]; I will make you come up from the remotest parts [or: the farthest ends] of the north, and I will bring you upon the mountains of Israel. I will strike your bow from [or: in] your left hand, and your arrows from your right hand; and I will cast you down upon the mountains of Israel. You shall fall, you and all your armies, and the peoples [or: nations] who are with you. I have given you to the wild beasts, the birds, every winged creature, and the beasts of the earth, to be devoured. You shall fall upon the face of the field [or: open country], because I have spoken, says the Lord God.

“And I will send fire upon Magog and upon those who dwell securely in the islands [or: and the islands shall be inhabited in peace]; and they shall know that I am the Lord. I will make my holy name known in the midst of my people Israel, and I will no longer profane my holy name [or: my holy name shall no longer be profaned]; and the nations shall know that I am the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.

“Behold, it comes, and it has happened [or: you shall know that it will be], says the Lord [the Vulgate adds: God]; this is the day of which I have spoken. The inhabitants of the cities [the Vulgate: of the cities] of Israel shall go out, and they shall kindle and burn the weapons: the shield and spears [or: bucklers and lances], the bow and arrows, staffs of the hands [the Vulgate: of the hand], and spears [or: lances]; they shall burn them in the fire for seven years. They shall not carry wood from the regions [or: fields], nor cut it from the forests, because they shall feed the fire with the weapons; and they shall plunder those by whom they had been plundered, and despoil their despoilers, says the Lord God.

“And it shall come to pass on that day that I will give Gog a recognized place for a tomb in Israel: the valley of travelers east of the sea, which causes passersby to be astonished [or: the *polyandrion* of those who have come to the sea, and they shall build around the entrance of the valley; and they shall bury Gog and all his multitude there; and the valley shall be called the valley [or: *Ge*] of the multitude of Gog]. The house of Israel shall bury them in order to cleanse the land [or: so that the land may be cleansed] for seven months. All the people of the land shall bury them [the Vulgate omits ‘them’], and the day shall be named for them on which I was glorified, says the Lord God.

“They shall appoint men continually to inspect [or: traverse] the land, to bury and search out those who have remained [the Vulgate: who had remained] upon the face of the land, in order to cleanse it; but after seven months they shall begin the search. They shall travel through the land; and when they see a human bone, they shall set up a marker beside it until the buriers bury it in the valley [or: *Ge*] of the multitude of Gog. The name of the city shall be Amona [or: *Polyandrion*]; and they shall cleanse the land [or: the land shall be cleansed].”

> **Editorial note:** In Rabanus: “I will bring out”; Victorius preferred “I will lead astray,” following the example of the Vulgate.

> **Editorial note:** Victorius again altered the text to agree with the Vulgate: “I will cast them down from your right hand.” “You shall fall upon the mountains of Israel, you and all your armies, and your peoples.” Shortly afterward, *I will send* occurs in place of *I will dispatch*. The explanation of the holy Doctor appended below also supports this reading.

The heirs of Jewish tradition and disciples of endless fables assert that these things are to happen after the thousand-year reign: that Gog, the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, is to be slain in the territories of Israel and devoured by all the birds and beasts; that the inhabitants of the cities of Israel will for seven years have no use for wood cut from the forests, but will use the weapons of Gog—namely, shields, spears, arrows, and staffs or lances; and that Gog himself will be buried in a valley called in Hebrew *Ge* (), and that his tomb will be called *polyandrion*—that is, a place where a multitude of people has been buried.

He is to be buried by the house of Israel for seven months, so that the land may be cleansed; and the day on which Gog was slain is to be celebrated as illustrious. Men are to be appointed who will diligently search for and bury the bones, so that nothing unburied remains in the land. After the months, or during seven months, they are to travel throughout the land; and wherever they see a human bone lying, they are to indicate it by placing a marker nearby, so that afterward those appointed to this work may bury it. The name of the city is to be called Amona, which in Greek is *polyandrion*—that is, a multitude of buried people—and thus the land is to be cleansed.

That is what they have said. But, holding to the sense of the explanation we began, let us discuss each of the points we set forth.

Gog himself also has his own trinity: Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal—namely, head, madness, and totality—so that there is no vice which does not reside in Gog’s possession. He will be brought out, or turned about, and handled [or: enticed], so that, hoping for victory, he may be led to battle in order to be killed. He will come up from the remotest parts, or the ends, of the north, from which evils blaze forth upon the whole earth (Jer. 1). And from that very place he will be brought upon the mountains of Israel. We should understand these as the apostles, apostolic men, and ecclesiastical men. Once he has been brought upon the mountains of Israel, the bow in his left hand and the arrows held in his right hand will then be struck.

For he too imitates those whom he has deceived in order to kill them, possessing weapons on the left and the right, through good and evil reputation. These are the arrows and darts of which the Psalmist also speaks: “For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. X, 2). These fiery darts of the devil must be extinguished with the shield of faith (Eph. VI).

Gog, who had mounted upon the mountains of Israel, will be cast down, or will fall, upon those very mountains, with all his army and all his forces; and he will become food for the wild beasts, the birds, all winged creatures, and the beasts of the earth—namely, for hostile powers that devour the seed beside the road, and for bloodthirsty beasts. For just as it is written of the dragon, “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Ps. LXXIII, 14), so all who have been deceived by heretics are food for demons.

Gog will fall either upon the broad expanse of the field or upon the cultivated ground that has been tilled by God’s farmers. For it cannot happen that the words of the Lord should be void.

Then fire will be sent upon Magog—that is, upon those who have received Gog’s teaching, and upon those who, like islands beaten by the waves of the world, are buffeted by its floods yet think that they ought to be secure. It is the fire of which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what I will is that it burn” (Luke XII, 49). Thus all shall know and understand that I am the Lord, and my holy name shall be made known in the midst of my people, who have not been led astray by Gog’s authority. Nor shall my name any longer be polluted among heretics through the pretext of a false name of knowledge. The nations around them shall know that I am the Lord.

What follows—“Behold, it comes, and it has happened”—is spoken of the judgment of Christ: “He who comes will come and will not delay” (Hab. II, 3). This is the day of punishments and vengeance of which the Lord has spoken through all the prophets.

The inhabitants of the cities of Israel shall go out: these are the peoples of believers. By the cities of Israel we understand the Churches of right faith. They shall kindle and burn the weapons of which it is written elsewhere: “He will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Ps. XLIII, 10). These weapons are shields and spears, bows and arrows, staffs of the hands with which they celebrated a perverse Passover, and lances or spears with which they inflicted the broad and incurable wounds of their doctrines. They are also the shields, bows, and arrows mentioned above.

The statement that they will burn these things in the fire for seven years is to be explained from Exodus and Leviticus (Exod. XXI; Lev. XXV). There the Law commands that in the seventh year of remission, when freedom is restored to Hebrew slaves, all debts are canceled, the ancient possession returns to its owners, rest is granted to the land, and all its produce is given to the poor, the weapons of the heretics may likewise be destroyed during the sacred and perfect number of seven years. Ecclesiastical men are not to cut wood from the fields and regions, from the forests and wooded places of the nations whom they desire to save rather than destroy, but from the shields, spears, arrows, staffs, lances, and other weapons of the heretics whom they have overcome.

For they too possess various weapons with which to attack the Church of Christ. Learned men must kindle these weapons with the fire of the Holy Spirit, namely, with ecclesiastical speech. Whoever possesses this speech can say: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV, 12).

Nor can we have complete peace and confidence of dwelling unless we plunder the entire equipment of our adversaries, so that everything may perish and be consumed into ashes; and unless we plunder those who previously plundered us and devastate those who first devastated the Church.

On that day—in the clear light of preaching—he says, “I will give Gog a recognized place for a tomb in Israel.” According to the Hebrew, it is a valley of travelers east of the sea, which causes passersby to be astonished. The sense of this passage is as follows: Gog’s tomb will not be in the mountains but in low valleys and rugged places, which in Hebrew are called *Ge* (). Although the heretics are in the West, they pretend that these are places of the East, in order to deceive travelers—those, namely, who pass through this present age and are not inhabitants but pilgrims, saying the prophetic words: “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. XXXVIII, 12).

Who among those passing by, of whom it is written, “Nor did those who passed by say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Ps. CXXVIII, 8), does not marvel and become astonished when he sees the valley of travelers, which appears as a valley to travelers but as a mountain to its inhabitants? This is according to the Hebrew.

The Septuagint, however, translated it as “their *polyandrion*, those who have come to the sea,” and “they shall build around the entrance of the valley.” The labor of those who go out from the cities of Israel is to close off and enclose every entrance and exit of heretical depravity—those who had come to the sea and delighted in its bitterness, its masses of waves, and the cruelty of shipwreck—and to bury them in the chasms of the earth, so that they may no longer be able to escape or deceive anyone through their fraud.

There, therefore, they will bury Gog and all his multitude, in which the heretics always delight. The name of the valley in which Gog has been buried will be called the valley of the multitude of *Ge*, or *polyandrion*—that is, the tomb of a very great multitude.

And just as we said above that the weapons of the adversaries would be burned for seven years, so for seven months the land will be cleansed of the filth of the heretics. From the first month, when we celebrate the Lord’s Passover and avoid the destroyer of Egypt through the blood of the Lamb on our doorposts, until the end of the year—that is, until the seventh month, when we set up the tabernacles and are protected, among the other branches, by palm branches—the victory against the enemies is shown to be complete.

We fulfill all the festivals among the peoples. Not only the teachers but the whole people will eagerly do this, in order to bury Gog and cover him with earth, and not allow him to breathe the open air. After the killing and destruction, or the burial, of Gog, ecclesiastical men will be chosen who will devote themselves to ensuring that no remnant of the former filth, no corpse, remains in the land of Israel. They will inspect the land, search out the dead, and bury them, so that the land of the Church may be cleansed.

But if, after seven months—when everything ought to have been purified—those who traverse and inspect the land see that somewhere a human bone, that is, the hardness of heretical depravity, or some remnant of former teaching, has remained, they will set up or build a marker beside it. Once such people have been marked out, they may either be cleansed or buried with Gog and shut away in his tomb [variant: in the multitude of his burial].

The name of the city where the servants of the Lord have won victory, where the adversaries lie and the whole multitude of his enemies has been struck down, will be called Amona, or *polyandrion*, so that the end of all things may be the restoration of purity.

Finally, it follows: “And they shall cleanse the land”—clearly, these are the people of whom it was written above: “They shall begin to search, and they shall travel throughout the land.”

### Verses 17 and following

“But you, son of man, thus says the Lord God: Say to every winged creature and to all the birds, and to all the beasts of the field [or: countryside]: Assemble and hasten; come together from every side [or: around] to my sacrifice, which I have sacrificed [the Vulgate: which I sacrifice] for you—a great sacrifice upon the mountains [the Vulgate: mountain] of Israel—so that you may eat flesh and drink blood.

“You shall eat the flesh of mighty men [or: giants], and drink the blood of the princes of the earth: of rams, lambs, and goats, and of fattened and well-fed bulls. You shall eat fat to satiety and drink blood to drunkenness, from the sacrifice which I have sacrificed [the Vulgate: which I will sacrifice] for you. You shall be filled at my table with horse and strong horseman [or: giant], and with all men of war, says the Lord God.

“I will place [or: give] my glory among the nations [or: among you], and all the nations shall see my judgment which I have executed and my hand which I have placed [or: brought] upon them. The house of Israel shall know that I am the Lord their God, from that day and thereafter.

“All the nations [the Vulgate omits ‘all’] shall know that the house of Israel was taken captive on account of its iniquities [or: because of their iniquities], because they abandoned me, and I hid [or: turned away] my face from them, and delivered them into the hands of their enemies [or: their foes], and they all fell by the sword. According to their uncleannesses and their crimes [or: iniquities] I dealt with them, and I hid [or: turned away] my face from them.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Now I will restore the captivity of Jacob and have mercy upon the whole house of Israel. I will be zealous for my holy name, and they shall bear their confusion [or: disgrace] and all their transgression with which they transgressed against me, when they dwell securely [or: in peace] in their own land, fearing no one; when I bring them back from the peoples [or: nations] and gather them from the lands of their enemies [or: from the regions of the nations], and I am sanctified in them in the sight [or: presence] of many nations.

“They shall know that I am the Lord their God when I have transferred them among the nations [or: when I have appeared to them among the nations]; and I shall gather them upon their own land, and I shall not leave any of them there. I shall no longer hide [or: turn away] my face from them, because I have poured out my spirit [or: fury] upon the whole house of Israel, says the Lord God.”

> **Editorial note:** This is the reading of the Septuagint: “on account of their sins” (*διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν*). The Hebrew has “in his iniquity.” Since the latter reading has been received into the text, Victorius customarily removes the former.

What we have translated according to the Hebrew—“I will gather them upon their own land, and I will not leave any of them there”—is not found in the Septuagint. Again, what according to the Hebrew is placed at the end as a blessing, “because I have poured out my spirit,” the Septuagint translated as “fury,” which pertains to anger, especially since the Hebrew has *RUHI* (), which properly means “my spirit,” and by no means “my fury.”

All the way to the place where the building of the temple begins, those Jews whom we mentioned above, as well as our Judaizers, refer these matters to the final age. They say that the flesh of Gog and his entire army will be offered to birds and beasts as exceedingly fat sacrifices, that Israel will be restored to its former condition, and that it will no longer be attacked by the nations, but that God will pour out his spirit upon them so that they may dwell in their own land—not upon all the nations, but specifically upon the house of Israel.

Following the tropological interpretation we began, however, we shall say that the Lord summons all the birds and every beast in order to hand over to them the leaders of the heretics for devouring, as though they were exceedingly fat sacrifices. They are called birds and beasts either because of their speed in rushing everywhere or because of their savagery and cruelty. To them the adversaries are delivered for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved and they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim. I).

They will eat a great and exceedingly fat sacrifice—not elsewhere, but upon the mountains of Israel, which we should understand as the prophets, apostles, and holy men. For upon these the teachers of contrary doctrines fall, and wounded by them they perish—upon those mountains upon which the Church is built. To speak more truly, this is upon the mountain of mountains of which Isaiah and Micah speak: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways” (Isa. II, 3; Mic. IV, 2).

These swift and savage birds and beasts will eat the flesh and drink the blood of those who cannot possess the kingdom of God: the flesh of mighty men, or giants, who rebelled against the knowledge of God; and the blood of princes—not of heaven, but of the earth, since they savored everything earthly. They will drink the blood of rams, lambs, and goats—or, according to the Septuagint, of rams, calves, and goats—so that the three animals signify those which are sacrificed in God’s offerings.

Heretics also imitate the gentleness of the Church, but their offering does not advance the worship of God; it serves as food for demons. This is their exceedingly fat sacrifice. They are filled with fat and drink the blood of the deceived to drunkenness. God offers this sacrifice through ecclesiastical men, so that the worst of banqueters may be filled with the multitude of the deceived and drink to vomiting and drunkenness.

When you see holy men, trained in the divine Scriptures, cutting down the horses and riders of the heretics, of whom it is written, “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. XV, 1), and striking down all rebels and giants with their sword, pouring out the blood of all the warriors of falsely named knowledge, then know that the Lord’s table has been prepared. He will place his glory among all the nations that believe in his name, and they will understand the judgment which the Church of his saints has executed upon the adversaries, and the strong hand with which it has struck them.

Then the house of Israel shall know and understand that he is the Lord their God, who said: “I am the Lord your God, from the day of the Lord’s victory and forever.” They shall reflect that the house of Israel was once taken captive by the heretics and scattered throughout the whole world of perverse doctrines because they abandoned him who for a little while hid or turned away his face from them, delivered them into the hand of the heretics, and they fell, pierced by their sword, on account of their uncleannesses and iniquities. These were the reasons why he hid and turned away his face from them.

After these explanations, in accordance with what is written—“There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. XI, 19)—the captivity of Israel, namely, of the Church in which those who see God dwell, is now promised restoration. Jacob, who had supplanted the Jewish people, and was afterward himself supplanted by the deceptions of the heretics, will be brought back into the Church. He will have mercy upon the whole house of Israel, not according to the flesh but according to the spirit.

“And I will take up my zeal,” he says, “for my holy name,” which was blasphemed among the nations because of the heretics. Once he has freed them, they will blush and be confounded because, abandoning the Church’s faith, they transgressed against him.

They will be very swiftly confounded and ashamed when they dwell in their own land, the land of the meek and the land of the saints, and dwell securely, or in peace, fearing no longer the snares of the heretics (Ps. VI). Then they will be brought back from the peoples and gathered from the lands of their enemies into their own land. The Lord will be sanctified in them in the sight of many nations, which themselves will also believe in the Lord.

The final blessedness will be to know and understand that he is their Lord God, because he has appeared to them among the nations—or has transferred them from the nations—and has gathered them upon their own land: the land of Judea, the land of confession, the land of the meek, and the land of the living. He will not have left even one of them to heretical depravity. He will no longer hide his face from them or turn away from them, because he has poured out the spirit of his grace, of which the prophet Joel also speaks: “In the last days I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II, 28). He will pour it out upon the whole house of Israel.

But if, according to the Septuagint, we read “fury” instead of “spirit”—a reading not found in the Hebrew—we should understand it in this way: he will no longer hide his face from those upon whom he had previously poured out his fury.

Thus far we have spoken on the prophet Ezekiel, with God’s help, as we hope and believe, opening our mouth. We have not destroyed the opinions of others, whether of those who have written or of those who may write hereafter; we have simply asserted whatever value our own views may possess.

But concerning the building of the temple, the order of the priests, the division of the holy land, the river flowing from the temple, the trees growing ever green on both banks and producing fruit each month, and the remaining matters contained in the prophetic book to its conclusion, we openly confess our ignorance. For the present we think it better to say nothing than to say too little.

## Book Twelve

[Col. 0369]

My hesitation in explaining Ezekiel’s temple—or rather, my perseverance in remaining silent—has been overcome by your prayers, daughter Eustochium, and by the Lord’s promises, who says: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. VII, 7).

The excuse we used at the end of the preceding volume, when we said that it is better to say nothing than too little, you have turned in the opposite direction, so that you think it preferable to report at least a little rather than say nothing. In the one case there is a ready will; in the other, despair of the entire work.

You also recall that it is characteristic of such people that they feel no gratitude proportionate to what you have given them, but feel pain over what you have denied them. We praise virtues with less enthusiasm than we criticize vices; and although bodies may be beautiful, the deformity of a single limb makes them more conspicuous.

I shall therefore obey your wishes and, with the Holy Spirit breathing, raise the sails, not knowing at what shores I shall arrive, and crying out with this same prophet: “Come from the four winds, O spirit.” To the fastidious reader—or rather, to the hostile mind that will read what we have written—I declare with complete freedom, in explaining the temple, that if he desires the truth, he should seek it from others.

For our part, we openly acknowledge and set down whatever we are able to conjecture in this most difficult work. We shall give thanks to the Lord if he opens to us the doors of knowledge—not in everything, which is impossible, but in most things. For, as the lofty orator says:

> “For one who pursues each thing, it is honorable to come to a standstill even at the second or third place.”

### Chapter XL

#### Verses 1 ff.

> “In the twenty-fifth year of our transmigration (or captivity), at the beginning of the year (or in the first month), on the tenth day of the month, fourteen years after the city had been struck (or captured), on that very day (or on that day) the hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me there. In visions (or in a vision) of God he brought me into the land of Israel and set me upon a very high mountain, on which there was something like a city building, facing toward the South (or opposite it). And he brought me there; and behold, there was a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze (or shining bronze), with a linen cord (or a builders’ cord) in his hand and a measuring reed in his hand. Now he was standing in the gate, and that same man spoke to me: ‘Son of man, see with your eyes and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon everything that I shall show you (or set in your heart everything that I shall show you), because you have been brought (or have entered) here in order that everything may be shown to you; and announce (or show) everything that you see to the house of Israel.’”

If in the fifth year of the captivity, or transmigration, of King Jehoiachin, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, the heavens were opened to the prophet Ezekiel beside the river Chebar, and he saw visions of God, here, however, it is said that in the twenty-fifth year of the transmigration of that same Jehoiachin, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and that he was brought into the land of Israel and set upon a very high mountain so that he might see a city building facing toward the South. There is no doubt that his entire prophecy was composed after nineteen years, nine months, and five days of the twentieth year had been completed.

[Note: The printed editions retain Joachim instead of the name Jechoniah; but this Joachim was a man with two names, whom the princes of Nebuchadnezzar led captive into Babylon. Therefore, let readers beware of scribal errors: in place of Jechoniah they often write Joachim, and the printed editions have Joakim. MART.]

But if, following Theodotion, who at the place where we have put “at the beginning of the year” translated “in the new year,” the tenth day of the month is understood in this way—the new year among the Hebrews is called the seventh month, which among them bears the name *Thesri* [Hebrew: תשרי], so that on the first day of the seventh month there is the blast of trumpets, on the tenth day of that same month the day of fasting and propitiation, and on the fifteenth day, when the whole circle of the moon is full, the Feast of Booths—it may be understood that on the tenth day of the Lord’s day of propitiation the building of the city was shown to Ezekiel.

And just as he demonstrated the restoration of the people, or rather their revivification, in the bones of the field under the image of resurrection, so now the Lord promises the rebuilding of the city that had been destroyed by Babylonian fire fourteen years earlier, under a description of it. Just as the captivity and overthrow had been shown by the image of the burning pot from the face of the North, and the truth of the prophecy had been confirmed by the event, so, on the basis of faith in past events, the truth of the future building might be established by prophecy.

Nor is this said of that period which some ignorant Jews claim, when the Temple was built under Zerubbabel and under Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, while Haggai and Zechariah were prophesying. For this Temple that is now being described, together with its priestly order, the division of the land, and its fertility, is far more magnificent than the one Solomon had built. But the one built under Zerubbabel was so small and so insignificant in comparison with the former that those who had seen the first Temple and afterward looked upon this one wailed and testified to their grief with tears; and the cry of the wailers was much louder than the sound of the trumpets. Read the Book of Ezra.

Moreover, what is added—“fourteen years after the city had been struck (or captured)” (3 Esdras 5)—in accordance with mystical interpretations signifies fourteen generations. When these had been completed, from David to the birth of Christ, restoration of the city is promised by him of whom it is written: “He himself shall build my city and bring back the captivity of my people” (Isaiah 45:13). And again: “He has come to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, saying to those who were in bonds, ‘Come out,’ and to those who were in darkness, ‘Be revealed’” (ibid. 61:1).

The hand of the Lord comes upon him so that, although he was in Babylon according to the flesh, in the spirit he might come to the land of Israel; and he is set not merely in a vision, but in the visions of God, upon a very high mountain, concerning which Isaiah and Micah prophesy: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isaiah 2:3; Micah 4:2).

This mountain is exceedingly high in comparison with the other mountains of which the prophet testifies, saying: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me” (Psalm 120:1). And in another place: “The mountains are around him, and the Lord is around his people” (Psalm 125:2). Concerning it Isaiah also says: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion” (Isaiah 40:9).

Upon this mountain the building of the city is shown, according to the Septuagint and Aquila, “opposite,” and “facing the North,” from which the prophet was coming to the land of Israel; but according to Theodotion and Symmachus, “facing toward the South,” where there is full light and where the sun of righteousness is placed at the summit of heaven. Hence it is also said in the Song of Songs: “Rise up, North Wind, and come, South Wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song of Songs 4:16).

For the North Wind, exceedingly harsh, is driven away from the Lord’s garden, lest the heat of love grow cold and the flowers wither. When it is said, “something like a city building,” it is not truly a city that is shown, but the likeness of a city, concerning which it is written: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 86:2)—the Jerusalem built as a city, whose participation is in unity, and in which the great and exceedingly praiseworthy Lord is present, in the city of our God, upon his holy mountain (Psalm 48).

And in the towers of this city God is known when he receives it. Of it another passage says: “The river’s rushing waters make glad the city of God” (Psalm 45:4). And: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14), which speaks in Isaiah: “I am a fortified city, a city under attack” (Isaiah 23). He did not say “a city that is conquered,” but “a city under attack”: a city built upon a rock and shaken by no storm.

It follows: “And he brought me there”—the hand of God is understood. “There,” that is, to something like a city building, so that he might show me everything that was within it.

“And behold,” he says, “a man whose appearance—or vision—was like the appearance of shining bronze,” namely the one of whom it is written: “Behold, a man; his name is Rising” (Zechariah 6:12). His appearance was not like electrum, as is said at the beginning of this book, nor was he girded with a golden belt, as is contained in John’s Apocalypse (Revelation 1); rather, according to the Hebrew, he had an appearance like bronze.

This material is more resonant than all other metals and carries its ringing sound far away. Hence in Daniel, in the image composed of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, the kingdom of Alexander and of the Greeks is represented by the likeness of bronze (Daniel 2), so that the eloquence of the Greek language might be signified. From this it is clear that those who have not yet fully understood the mysteries of the spiritual building of the Temple still require instruction.

There was also a linen cord, or a builders’ cord, in his hand. Of this it is written in Zechariah 2 that he had a geometric cord for measuring the breadth and length of the city. “A builders’ cord” may refer either to angels who minister at God’s command, or to Moses and all the prophets and apostles who build the city of God and are helpers or ministers of the Lord’s will. Hence the apostle Paul said: “We are God’s cultivated field, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What follows—“And a measuring reed in his hand”—signifies prophetic grace, of which it is written in the forty-fourth Psalm: “My tongue is the reed of a swift-writing scribe” (Psalm 44:2). And concerning John the prophet and baptizer: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind?” (Matthew 11:7).

[Note: Victorius: “shaken,” especially from the Greek text, σαλευόμενον.]

Those who write iniquity imitate this reed; against them the prophet invokes: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed” (Psalm 67:31).

He was standing in the gate because through him we enter to the Father, and without him we cannot enter the city of God: he receives the worthy and casts out the unworthy. Judgment is also in the gate. Hence the prophet says: “They hate the one who reproves in the gate” (Isaiah 29:21). And in another place: “He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Psalm 126:5).

This man spoke to the prophet—the man in whose hand was the cord, whose appearance was like bronze, and who held the reed in his hand. The true architect spoke to Ezekiel, the one whom the apostle Paul imitated when he said: “As a wise architect I laid a foundation” (1 Corinthians 3:10). He calls him a wise architect in distinction from the one who is foolish, who in Zechariah is called the foolish shepherd.

He spoke the words that follow: “Son of man, see with your eyes and hear with your ears” (Zechariah 11). Not with the eyes of the flesh, but of the spirit; not with the ears of the body, but of the soul. “Lift up,” he says, “your eyes, and see that the fields are already white for harvesting” (John 4:35). And: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8).

The building of the city is seen, and the order of its ceremonies and priests, together with the description of the land, is heard. Nor was it enough to command him to see with his eyes and hear with his ears; he added: “And set your heart upon everything,” or, “Set in your heart everything that I shall show you.” For it is of no benefit to have seen and heard unless you store in the treasury of memory the things you have seen and heard.

When he says, “everything that I shall show you,” he makes the hearer attentive and prepares him with the eyes of his heart, so that he may retain in memory the things that are to be shown him; for “you have been brought here in order that everything may be shown to you.”

By these words he specifically shows that nothing is sweeter than contemplation and knowledge, which the prophet desires when he says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the delight of the Lord and visit his temple” (Psalm 26:4–5). Hence he adds and says: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells.”

“Announce,” he says, “everything that you see to the house of Israel,” so that those who cannot see for themselves may learn through you what is shown to you by the Lord. The house of Israel means those who contemplate God with the mind; among them was Nathanael, who sought Christ with the greatest devotion and deserved to hear: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

#### Verses 5 ff.

> “And behold, a wall outside the house all around, on every side; and in the man’s hand was a measuring reed six cubits and a handbreadth long. And he measured the width of the building with one reed, and its height with one reed. And he came to the gate that faced the eastern road, and went up its steps, and measured the threshold of the gate: one reed in width, that is, one threshold one reed in width; and one chamber one reed in length and one reed in width; and between the chambers five cubits; and the threshold of the gate beside the vestibule of the gate, on the inside, one reed. And he measured the vestibule of the gate: eight cubits, and its front two cubits. The vestibule of the gate was on the inside. Moreover, the chambers of the gate facing the eastern road were three on this side and three on that side, all of one measure, and the fronts on both sides were of one measure. And he measured the width of the threshold of the gate: ten cubits; and the length of the gate: thirteen cubits. And a border before the chambers, one cubit, and one cubit at each end; and the chambers were six cubits on this side and on that. And he measured the gate from the roof of one chamber to the roof of the other: a width of twenty-five cubits, doorway opposite doorway.

> “The Septuagint: ‘And behold, a wall outside the house all around, and in the man’s hand a measuring reed of six cubits and a handbreadth; and he measured the wall, its width equal to a reed, and its height of the same measure. And he entered the gate that faced the East by seven steps, and he measured the *thee* ÷: six on this side and six on that side **; the *aelam* of the gate equal to a reed in length and equal to a reed in width; and the *aelam* in the middle, the *theelath*, six cubits; and the *thee* next, equal to a reed in width and equal to a reed in length; and the *aelam*, five cubits. And the third *thee*, equal to a reed in width, three, and equal to a reed in length, three; and the *aelam* of the gate beside the *aelam* of the gate, eight cubits, and an *aelam* of two cubits, and the *aelam* of the gate on the inside; and the *thee* of the gate opposite, three on this side and three on that, and one measure of three; one measure for the *aelam* on this side and on that. He measured the width of the entrance of the gate, ten cubits, and the width of the gate, thirteen cubits; and one cubit was drawn back before the *theeri*, one cubit, and one cubit at each end; and the *thee* was six cubits on this side and six cubits on that. And he measured the gate from the wall of the *thee* to the wall of the *thee*, a width of twenty-five cubits. This gate was opposite that gate.’”

When I was a boy in Rome and was being educated in the liberal studies, I used, with others of the same age and inclination, to go around on Sundays to the tombs of the apostles and martyrs. I often entered the crypts, which are dug deep into the earth and have on both sides, along the walls of those entering, the bodies of the buried. Everything there is so dark that the prophetic saying is almost fulfilled: “Let them go down alive into hell” (Psalm 54:16). Rarely does light admitted from above temper the horror of the darkness, so that you would think it not a window but an opening through which a little light has been lowered.

Then, as one proceeds gradually, surrounded by blind night, Virgil’s words are brought to mind (Aeneid, Book II):

> “Horror everywhere terrifies their hearts;  
> even the very silences terrify.”

I have said this so that the prudent reader may understand what view I hold concerning the explanation of God’s Temple in Ezekiel, of which it is written: “Cloud and darkness are beneath his feet” (Psalm 96:2). And again: “Darkness is his hiding place” (Psalm 17:12).

Hence Moses also entered the cloud and darkness so that he might contemplate the mysteries of the Lord, which the people, remaining at a distance and below, could not see (Exodus 24 and 34). Finally, after forty days, the common and uncultivated crowd could not look upon Moses’ face with its dimmed eyes, because Moses’ face had been glorified—or, as it is contained in the Hebrew, horned.

So it happens to me when I read the description of the mystical Temple—which the Jews, understanding it according to the letter, think will be built at the coming of their Christ, whom we demonstrate to be the Antichrist, while we refer it to the Church of Christ and see it being built every day in his saints. Whenever the eye of my heart is opened and I think that I see something and grasp the Bridegroom, and rejoice and say, “I have found him whom my soul sought; I shall hold him and not let him go” (Song of Songs 3:4), once again the divine discourse leaves me, and the Bridegroom flees from my hands. My eyes are closed in blindness, so that I am compelled to say: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33).

And there is also what is written elsewhere: “The judgments of the Lord are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). And: “From the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice” (Psalm 129:1). And the words of Elisha, who followed with the eyes of his heart the master snatched away from him, saying: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” (2 Kings 2:12).

Therefore, I must simply confess that I do not wish to discuss the Temple of blessed Ezekiel—which all the ages have kept silent about—with rashness, but with faith and fear of God; I wish to display to readers the conjecture of my mind. If I offer to God’s tabernacle the skins of goats and their hair, to protect against the thorns and prickles of sins and to ward off rains and storms, let another who is rich offer, according to the quality of his merits, iron, bronze, silver, gold, and the most precious stones; and let him not despise our offerings because they are smaller, but rejoice in his own riches. For unless the lowest things exist, the highest cannot exist; and the greater are praised in comparison with the lesser, by which they grow.

Let us therefore see what Ezekiel first saw when he entered the city building facing toward the South, and afterward what he heard.

“And behold,” he says, “a wall outside all around the house.” In place of “wall,” which Aquila and Theodotion translated, Symmachus and the Septuagint put *peribolos* (περίβολος), that is, an enclosure.

Therefore a wall, or *peribolos*, surrounded the house—that is, the Temple of the Lord—on every side. The man whose appearance was like bronze held in his hand not only the geometric and builders’ cord but also a reed. Its measure was previously left unspoken; now it is given as six cubits and a handbreadth, which is more correctly called in Greek *palaistē* (παλαιστή), and is one-sixth of a cubit.

Otherwise, *palmos* (παλμός), or *spithamē* (σπιθαμή), means a handbreadth, which some call a palm for purposes of distinction; but they customarily call the *palaistē* a palm. With this reed, therefore, he measured the width and height of the wall, and both—the width and the height—were one reed, that is, six cubits and one handbreadth.

[Note: Martianaeus has σπιθαμήν here and elsewhere. Eustathius derives the origin of the term from παρὰ τὸ θαμὰ σπίζεσθαι τοὺς δακτύλους, that is, “from the frequent spreading apart of the fingers.” The Hebrews also report that in some parts of the Temple cubits of five handbreadths were used, and in others of six.]

Although there were many gates, he did not wish to enter through the others, but through the one that faced toward the eastern region. Since the ground was not level—the wall surrounded the area, and the house of God itself had been built in higher places—he entered, or rather ascended, by steps. Only the Septuagint names the number as seven; in the Hebrew and in the other translators we read merely “steps,” without a number.

After entering the gate, he immediately measured the threshold of the gate, which the Septuagint calls *thee* (θεὲ); for this the Hebrew has *seph*.

I think the diligent and devoted reader should be admonished—provided that he is guided by knowledge of the Scriptures and not by the empty declamations of orators—to know that nearly all the Hebrew words and names placed in the Greek and Latin translations have been corrupted by extreme antiquity and distorted through scribal error. While they are copied from uncorrected texts into texts even less corrected, Hebrew words have become Sarmatian—or rather words belonging to no nation—since they have ceased to be Hebrew without yet becoming foreign.

The threshold of the gate, therefore, whether called *thee*, or rather *seph*, was translated by Symmachus as *oudon* (οὐδόν), and by Aquila and Theodotion as *prothyron* (πρόθυρον). It had one reed, that is, six cubits and a handbreadth, in width. In its place, I do not know with what intention, the Septuagint added from their own text: “six on this side and six on that.”

After the threshold of the gate, according to the Hebrew, he measured a chamber, or room—as Symmachus translated it, *parastades* (παραστάδες), that is, doorposts—on either side, one reed both in length and in width. The Septuagint also translated this as *aelam* (αἰλὰμ), which Symmachus later interpreted as “the space before the threshold.”

Between the two chambers, or rooms, and *parastades* there were five cubits; and there was another threshold of the gate beside the vestibule on the inside, one reed.

The third vestibule of the gate also had eight cubits, and on its front, or along its borders, two cubits. Lest anyone think that this vestibule was the same as the one mentioned above, he added: “The vestibule was of the inner gate.” For this the Septuagint translated “the first, second, and third vestibule.”

The chambers, that is, the rooms, which had been built after the eastern gate in the vestibules, faced toward the eastern road. And so that we may know how many chambers there were, it is added: “three on this side and three on that”—namely, facing North and South, and facing the eastern road. The fronts on both sides were of one measure.

He also measured the width of the threshold of the gate and found it to be ten cubits, and its length thirteen cubits. The ends of the chambers were narrowed by one cubit; or, as Symmachus translated it, the ends of the *parastades* were narrowed by one cubit, and each front had one cubit. The chambers, or *parastades*, which the Septuagint on their own authority called *theelath*, had six cubits on either side.

[Note: In Rabanus, “the chambers” is rendered *thalamum*, and shortly afterward, “that there be five cubits.”]

He measured the gate from the roof of one chamber, or *parastades*, to the roof, or wall, of the other, and found the space between roof and roof to be twenty-five cubits in width. That much space lay between doorway and doorway, or between gate and gate.

We have said these things briefly, more in the spirit of one making conjectures than of one explaining, wishing to sketch an outline of the obscure and almost invisible literal sense. For the rest, we shall set down the few things we can conjecture, briefly and with hesitation [Vulgate: “doubtingly”].

The apostle Paul, wishing the Ephesians to know more sacred things (chapter 3), prays for them to be filled with the wisdom and love of the Lord, so that, rooted and founded, they may be able to know and comprehend what is the breadth, length, height, and depth of his riches. And he speaks to those same people:

> “Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone; in him the whole building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you also are built up [or are built together] into a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 3:2 ff.).

The apostle Peter also speaks in nearly the same words, because he speaks by the same Spirit, in his Epistle:

> “If indeed you have believed that the Lord is good, approaching him, a living stone rejected by human beings but chosen and honored by God,” you yourselves, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:3 ff.).

From this it is clear that the Lord and Savior, who is the true architect, tests which stones can be placed in the foundations of the Temple, which in the middle, which in the upper places, and which of inferior measure or of less solid strength can be placed in the wall and around the outside of the Temple, in the *peribolos* (τοῦ περιβόλου).

For it is no small strength and no slight firmness to sustain stones placed above. Hence the Apostle writes to believers: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2). And in another place it is written that we ought not to take upon ourselves a weight that we cannot bear.

The measuring reed, which had six cubits and one handbreadth, signifies that our manner of life is known to God, being contained in the six days in which the world was made; and that the account of each person’s works is known, so that one thing pertains to works and another to the mind. Hence the width is equal to the height: the width, as we have said, refers to works; the height refers to the mind, which hastens toward lofty things.

Let it be enough to have warned once that I know *cubitum* and *cubita* to be neuter in gender, but that, for simplicity and ease of understanding and in accordance with popular usage, I use them in the masculine gender. For it is not our concern to avoid defects of language, but to explain the obscurity of Holy Scripture in whatever words we can.

The man whose name is “Rising” enters through the eastern gate, so that he may illuminate those whom he finds at the front of the vestibule, or at the very entrance of the gate. He does not enter by one step but by several, whose number is left unspoken, so that the difficulty of the ascent may become evident; and however many steps you propose to yourself, you should know that they are fewer than what is left uncertain.

I think this is the gate of which the Psalms also sing: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm 117:20). He measured the threshold of the gate so that we might know that everything is open to the knowledge of God. The threshold is said to be one reed in width, while its height and length are left unmentioned. For it is both a road and an entrance, and through it one must proceed to the inner parts—although in this passage the Septuagint unnecessarily gives “length,” or, as it is contained in many manuscripts, “height.”

[Note: In Rabanus: “the chambers,” but they render it *thalamum*; and shortly afterward, “that there be five cubits.”]

The rooms, that is, the chambers and *parastades*, have one reed both in length and width; but between room and room there are only five cubits, so that the inner parts of the rooms have the full measure of a reed, namely six cubits and one handbreadth, while works and reason agree together.

But the things that are outside—that is, between chamber and chamber—are five cubits. For they have not yet penetrated the mysteries of Christ and cannot say: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 1:3). Nor can they yet say: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44:14). But those who are outside cannot hear his mysteries while the disciples remain at home with Christ; instead, they desire the word of God to go out to them. For this reason the measure of five cubits is assigned to them, so that they may be taught to refer everything to the five senses.

The threshold of the other gate—or, as it is contained in the Septuagint, of the second and third vestibule—is likewise one reed in measure. After this vestibule, that is, after the threshold of the gate, eight cubits are placed at the entrance, so that the inner parts of the vestibule may possess not the number seven, nor six cubits and one handbreadth, but the number eight, which pertains to the mystery of the resurrection and of the Lord’s Day.

“And on its front,” he says, “there were two cubits,” which may pertain either to both Testaments, or to the letter and the spirit, or to the mystery of the tongs by which, in Isaiah, a coal is taken from the altar and carried to cleanse the prophet’s lips.

And so that we may know which vestibule this is, one bounded by eight and two cubits, he states more clearly: “The vestibule of the gate was on the inside,” through which we reach the Temple of God.

The chambers and rooms that were beside the road of the eastern gate—for which the Septuagint writes *Elau*—

[Note: Previously it was written in Greek letters as ἐλεῦ; but in Greek copies you also find ἐλεοῦ. The manuscripts prefer *Elau* in Latin here. Likewise, shortly afterward, instead of αἰλὰμ there was ἐλὰμ; elsewhere we correct scribal errors without consulting the reader.]

—were three on this side and three on that, of one measure, that is, one reed, which contained six cubits and one handbreadth, as was said above: “And *aelam*, one reed in length and one reed in width, and between the chambers five cubits.”

Lest we think that there were only two chambers, he placed three on each side, thereby indicating the number six. This number is also indicated in the Gospel’s water jars (John 8), in which water was changed into wine; and every day the Jewish waters are changed into wine that gladdens the human heart and becomes sweeter through Christ’s blood.

He also measured the width [alternative reading: boundary] of the gate: ten cubits. This is a perfect number, contained either in the Decalogue or in the mystery of the four Gospels. Beginning with one, it reaches four in such a way that it completes the number ten.

[Note: Victorius explains that ten is produced by counting the four numbers individually: since among the four there are 1, 2, 3, and 4, if these numbers are added together, ten results.]

Its length was thirteen cubits. In place of this, the Septuagint again gives “width,” which seems to me to have been corrupted through scribal negligence. For Scripture would not say “width” in one place and again “width” of ten or thirteen cubits in another.

The gate of the threshold, in which the sacred number of the Old and New Testaments is found, may be understood either as the Lord himself, who says, “I am the door” (John 10:9), or certainly as all the saints, through whom we enter into the knowledge of God. Of these the apostle Paul said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians,” and: “You also be enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6:11).

The thirteen cubits, following the number eight, contain the mystery of the books of Moses, which are also represented by the five loaves (Matthew 14) and by the Samaritan woman in the Gospel (John 4), who is accused of having had five husbands and of not having the sixth whom she thought she had. Yet the number eight and the number five are completed by one cubit, that is, by the fourteenth [alternative reading: thirteenth], because all things are recapitulated in Christ.

Hence it is said: “And one cubit was the end at both sides,” since the Old and New Testaments are embraced by one measure of Christ, and one cubit encompasses the height of Noah’s ark, thirty cubits.

But the chambers, he says—or, as the Septuagint put it, *thau* or *thee*, translating and changing the Hebrew names in each place as they wished—were six cubits on each side, which is expressed by “on this side and on that.” They had neither a handbreadth nor a further measure added above, which would summon the present manner of life to future blessedness; they had only six cubits.

Hence it follows: “And he measured the gate from the roof of the chamber to the roof, or wall, of it, and found its width to be twenty-five cubits.” Although this number is itself square, it nevertheless refers to the senses. For if you arrange five cubits opposite one another five times, you produce the number twenty-five. This is the space between the roof of one set of chambers and the roof of the other; yet, with both set opposite one another, each has at its upper ends a doorway opposite a doorway.

Let these things not seem frivolous to the reader, even though they displease me myself as I say them, since I feel that I am knocking at a closed door. They should be read with indulgence; otherwise I could simply have confessed my ignorance and cut off every desire of diligent readers. For just as we are far from perfect knowledge, we consider it at least a lesser fault to say something rather than to say nothing at all.

(Vv. 14 ff.) “And he made projections sixty cubits long, and the projection of the gateway-court all around. And before the face of the gate, which extended as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits; and slanting windows in the chambers, and in their projections that were within the gate all around. Likewise there were windows in the vestibules round about on the inside; and before the projections, representations of palms.

“The Septuagint: ‘And in the open air, an *aelam* of the gate, sixty cubits; and a *theim* of the court of the gate all around. And in the open air of the court outside, an *aelam* of the inner gate, fifty cubits; and hidden windows above the *theim*, and above the *aelam* within the gate of the court all around. Likewise *elamoth*, and windows all around on the inside, and above the *aelam*, palms on both sides.’”

Symmachus interpreted this passage as follows: “And he made περιστάσεις [peristaseis], which we may call circumstantial structures;” for these the Hebrew has *elim*, which Aquila interpreted as κρίωμα (*kriōma*), and which we render “projections.” Again, where the Septuagint placed “theim of the court,” the Hebrew has *el* in the singular, which Symmachus translated “near the court,” and Aquila as κρίωμα, that is, “the projection of the court.” Likewise, “in the open air, the vestibule of the gate”: Aquila translated this “before the face of the doors of the gate,” and Symmachus “opposite the face of the vestibule of the gate.”

The hidden windows, which in Hebrew are called *atemoth*, Symmachus translated τοξικάς (*toxikas*), “arched” or “bow-shaped.” And where the Septuagint said “above theim and above aelam,” that same Symmachus placed “doors” and “circumstantial structures”; Aquila, “chambers and their projections.” In Hebrew these are written *theim* and *ele*. Moreover, *elamoth*, which the Septuagint and Theodotion translated in the same way, Symmachus rendered “circumstantial structures,” and Aquila “projections.” But *aelam*, for which the Hebrew has *el* [the manuscripts read *ul*], is called a door or portico. In place of “palms,” the Hebrew has *thamarim* in the plural, because the singular is *thamar*, “a palm.”

I know that these matters will be troublesome to a reader who is impatient: but I wished briefly to show how greatly, through the passage of time—or rather through the fault of copyists, and, to speak more plainly, through ignorance—the ancient translation differs from the Hebrew truth, especially in Hebrew names. In rendering these into Latin from the editions of others, we have indicated not so much an explanation of the words as simply our conjecture.

I think, then, that between the wall of the temple on the outside, all around, and the building itself in the court—that is, in the middle—there were certain structures placed for ornament, which Symmachus interprets as “circumstantial structures,” that is, certain things standing there, raised upward from the ground; and these occupied a space of sixty cubits. Again, as one went out from the inner gate toward the face of the vestibule that looked toward the outer gate, this area occupied fifty cubits. In it were slanting windows, which the Septuagint calls “hidden,” while Symmachus calls them τοξικαί (*toxikai*).

These windows were in the chambers—that is, in each individual room—and in the porticoes extending before the rooms, occupying fifty cubits. These slanting or τοξικαί windows received their name from arrows because, like arrows, they admit a narrow light into the buildings but widen inwardly. Everything all around was full of windows of this kind.

“And before the projections,” he says, “of the porticoes, a representation or carving of palms.” By this it is shown that at the entrance of the gate, and immediately upon entering the wall, sixty cubits met the entrant, together with various ornaments. These are referred to the creation of the world, so that the Creator may be understood from the creatures; and so that all things proceeding in order and according to reason may display the variety of the world. Among the Greeks, the world is called κόσμος (*kosmos*), taking its name from adornment; and it was made in six days, so that ten-cubit units may be counted for each day. We spoke above of this as a perfect number.

After this, when we enter the inner court, chambers with slanting windows meet us before the vestibule itself of the inner gate. They occupy a space of fifty cubits, and this too is a sacred number. After seven complete weeks of festivity and joy, the first day of the Ogdoad begins—the day of resurrection—and leads us toward the vicinity of the temple. For when we have done everything, repenting of our former error, then we become near and close to God. In the outer court, the order and steadfastness of created things teach us the knowledge of the Creator; and in the inner court, the true jubilee, in which all our debts are forgiven, instructs us in θεολογία (*theologia*) and leads us into the Holy of Holies.

It should also be noted that the inner court has many windows, not straight and equal, but slanting and narrow on the outside, widening inwardly. Thus, through certain small openings, we may penetrate to the interior and reach the fullness of the brightest light that exists in the temple.

Finally, after the sixty and fifty cubits, the chambers, the porticoes, the projections of the porticoes, and the many windows all around, a carving or representation of palms is shown to us, so that, possessing victory over the world, we may be made worthy to see the palms of the virtues.

(Vv. 17 ff.) “And he led me out to the outer court, and behold, storerooms and a pavement laid with stone in the court round about: thirty storerooms around the pavement. And the pavement in front of the gates, corresponding to the length of the gates, was lower. And he measured the width from the face of the lower gate to the projection of the inner court on the outside: one hundred cubits toward the east and toward the north.

“The Septuagint: ‘And he brought me into the inner court, and behold, chambers and colonnades of the court round about, thirty chambers by the columns, and a portico behind the doors, along the length of the doors, before the columns, lower down. And he measured the width of the court from the place that was beneath the open air of the outer gate to the interior, beneath the open air of the inner gate that faced outward, one hundred cubits, and it inclined toward the east.’”

In place of the thirty chambers, which the Septuagint translated, or the storerooms and cells, as Aquila interpreted them, Symmachus placed ἐξέδραι (*exedrai*), “recessed chambers.” In place of the one hundred cubits of the outer space, which extended as far as the eastern gate, the Hebrew likewise gives the same number of cubits, and says that it extended toward the north also; but in the Septuagint the word “north” has been removed.

That man, therefore, who held the measuring cord of the builders in his hand, together with the measuring reed, and stood at the gate, after showing the prophet, among other things, the court of sixty cubits and another vestibule of the inner gate that occupied fifty cubits, led the prophet to the outer court—or, as the Septuagint has it, brought him into the inner court.

I am greatly puzzled, according to the literal sense and according to the Septuagint, how, after the outer parts of the court occupying sixty and fifty cubits, there can be an inner court extending across a width of one hundred cubits—unless perhaps, according to mystical meanings and the progress of those who enter, the things that are interior in teaching are broader.

When he had been brought into the inner court, or led to the outer court, as the Hebrew text contains, he immediately saw thirty chambers or storerooms, or, as Symmachus interpreted them, *exedrae*. These had been prepared as dwellings for Levites and priests. He also saw a pavement laid with living stones, or colonnades [variant: columns], so that it might be shown that the inner or outer court had before its doors a row of columns, and a pavement in front of the gates—or porticoes behind the doors.

In these porticoes, I think, columns had been arranged in order, so that porticoes stood before the storerooms, and columns supporting the porticoes stood at the fronts of the porticoes. The pavement laid with stones, which extended before the porticoes of the court, was lower at the ascent to the porticoes, and had the same length as the building of the chambers.

The same man, in whose hand were the cord and the reed, measured from the face of the lower gate—or, as the Septuagint wishes, the outer gate—to the projection of the court or inner gate, one hundred cubits toward the east, and, as the Hebrew says, also toward the north.

From these things we understand that the Gospel saying narrated by the Savior (Matt. 15)—the seed sown in the field, in good earth that multiplies its crops according to the variety of virtues thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold—agrees with the prophecy of this passage. Here too the thirtieth, sixtieth, and hundredth numbers are set down, so that by these as by steps we may be able to reach perfect knowledge; provided only that the number fifty leads us into the interior of the Church. That number, when the sabbath of seven complete weeks has ended, bursts forth into the day of resurrection.

Storerooms are so called because they are full of spiritual riches, concerning which it is written: “The redemption of a man is his own riches” (Prov. 13:8). Paul the apostle also rejoices over his disciples because they are “full of every word and of all knowledge” (Phil. 1).

[Note: Hesychius writes that among the Persians this word signifies Βασίλειον ἢ τοὺς ἐκ τῶν πολλῶν φερομένους φόρους, “a royal treasury, or the tribute brought from the many.” Eustathius, in his commentary on verse 910 of Dionysius Periegetes, writes: Γάζαν ἢ Ἄζαν, Καλοῦσι δὲ οὕτως οἱ Πέρσαι τὰ χρήματα, “They call Gaza, or Aza, the possessions in this way among the Persians.”]

For *gaza* in the language of the Persians means “riches.” Or, alternatively, the chambers, which in Greek are called παστοφόρια (*pastophoria*), signify rooms prepared for the bridegroom’s arrival. They numbered thirty, to demonstrate the mature age of their inhabitants.

The pavement was laid with stone, so that the footsteps of the inhabitants might not be polluted by mud, earth, and the dust of sins, but that they might walk upon living stones, by which the temple of God is built. Or the colonnades stood before the doors of the chambers, supporting the building placed above them.

These are the columns of which the apostle Paul also writes: “Peter and John, who seemed to be columns, gave me and Barnabas the right hand” (Gal. 2:9). And elsewhere: “The column and foundation of truth” (1 Tim. 3:15). In the Apocalypse of John we read: “The one who conquers, I will make him a column in the temple of my God, and he shall never go out again” (Rev. 3:12).

The pavement, therefore, that was in front of the gates, of which we have already spoken, or the porticoes behind the doors, which protected the inhabitants of the chambers from the rains, was lower. For what is lower is always placed in what is higher, so that by ascent and steps we may reach mystical and secret things, full of spiritual riches.

The full and perfect number is in the number of ten decades, which also multiplies Isaac’s seed a hundredfold (Gen. 26). But because he was on earth and could still say, “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:13), he is said to have sown barley and reaped a hundredfold harvest. For the grain of wheat had not yet died in the earth, so as to produce many crops (Matt. 13; John 12), and satisfy the hunger of the Jewish people for hearing the word of God with that bread which descended from heaven (Amos 8; John 6). How the one hundred cubits applied not only to the eastern gate but also to the northern gate, the following testimony will show.

(Vv. 20–21.) “He also measured the gate that faced the way of the north of the outer court, both in length and in width, and its chambers, three on this side and three on that, and its projection and its vestibule, according to the measure of the former gate: fifty cubits its length and twenty-five cubits its width. Its windows, its vestibule, and its carvings were according to the measure of the gate that faced east. Its ascent had seven steps, and a vestibule before it. And the gate of the inner court was opposite the northern gate and the eastern gate. And he measured from gate to gate one hundred cubits.

“The Septuagint: ‘And he brought me toward the north, and behold, a gate facing the outer court. And he measured it in length and in width, and its theim, three on this side and three on that, and its elau and elamoth—which are not found in the Hebrew—and its palm. And it was made according to the measure of the gate that faces east: its length was fifty cubits and its width twenty-five cubits. And its windows, its elamoth, and its palms were like those of the gate that faced east; and by seven steps one went up to it, and elamoth were within; and the gate of the inner court faced the northern gate—and what is not found in the Hebrew, ‘like the gate that faces east.’ And he measured the court from gate to gate, one hundred cubits.’”

We have explained above more fully what the Hebrew words *thee*, *elau*, and *elamoth* signify; but our translation will also make their meaning clear here by comparing them with one another.

The man whose measuring cord was in his hand measured the northern gate of the outer court also—or, as the Septuagint says, he led the prophet through the northern gate to the outer court. Here we must observe that he is first led through the northern gate, second through the southern gate, and third through the eastern gate.

“For from the north evils are kindled against all the inhabitants of the land” (Jer. 1:14). And rightly, whoever is an inhabitant of the earth, and not a sojourner and pilgrim, lies open to the arrows of the one who comes from the north, whose fiery arrows are extinguished, according to the apostle, by the shield of faith (Eph. 6).

The outer court is named in relation to the north; but in relation to the south, that is, the south wind, it is not called outer but inner. Scripture says: “And he brought me to the inner court, to the southern gate,” which is likewise written concerning the eastern court.

The first entrance into virtue is to trample the north beneath our feet, and, through the number fifty and the number twenty-five, to arrive at the summit of the hundred. Then we are brought into the southern region and drive away the cold of the north; and then we come to perfect virtue, that is, to the eastern gate, where the sun of righteousness rises and through which the high priest alone enters.

It should also be observed that although there are four regions, the western gate is passed over in silence. Concerning it, at the beginning of the sixty-seventh Psalm, it is written: “Make a way for him who ascends over the west; the Lord is his name” (Ps. 67:5). Thus, after we have prepared a way for the Lord and fulfilled what John the Baptist cries in the wilderness—“Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Matt. 3:3)—we may hear what is said at the end of that same psalm: “Sing to God, sing praises to the Lord, who ascends over the heaven of heaven toward the east” (Ps. 67:33).

When it is said, “three chambers on this side and three on that,” this teaches that both letter and spirit, both forms of understanding, history and tropology, pertain to the mystery of the Trinity.

And what is said—“its projection and its vestibule according to the measure of the former gate”—signifies the eastern gate, which is called “former” not in order but in merit.
