“And it had,” he says, “fifty cubits in length and twenty-five in width,” so that in the fifty, after seven weeks, eternal rest may be indicated, extending through the day of resurrection to the kingdoms of heaven, in which true rest exists.

[Note: Rabanus: “on the fiftieth day, namely.”]

In the twenty-five, concerning which we have already spoken, the measure of the five senses is preserved through five rows of the quadrangle, one of which is applied to length and the other to width. Thus, in length, rest and the delight of more sacred knowledge are indicated; in width, the reasoning of present things, which pertains to the senses.

And when it follows: “Its windows, vestibules, and carvings—or, as the Septuagint added, palms—were according to the measure of the gate that faced east,” this subtly indicates that whoever, placed at the entrance of the virtues, has entered three chambers on each side and has recognized the projection and vestibule according to the measure of the former gate, reaches and beholds those things which he will also receive most fully at the eastern gate.

Moreover, what follows—“Its ascent had seven steps, and a vestibule before it,” or “within”—has this meaning: through the seven steps of the week, and through the pot that is kindled before the face of the north, and through the ceremonies of the Jews, to which God gave commandments that were not good, and statutes in which they would not live, we climb to higher things and to its vestibule, that is, the vestibule of the gate, for which the Septuagint translated *elamoth*.

The vestibule is before the gate, or within it. There is not only one northern gate, which above is called the outer gate, but also another inner gate, which resembles the eastern gate, as the Septuagint expressed more clearly: “And the gate of the inner court faced the northern gate, as did the gate that faced east.”

He measured from the outer northern gate to the inner northern gate one hundred cubits, so that by these steps and measurements, withdrawing from the outer gate, we may be able to reach the inner one. The sacramental meaning of this number has been discussed above.

(Vv. 24 ff.) “And he led me toward the southern way, and behold, a gate that faced south. And he measured its projection and its vestibule according to the former measurements, and its windows and vestibules all around, like the other windows. [Note: Victorius reads: ‘the other windows, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width.’] Its length was fifty cubits and its width twenty-five; and by seven steps one went up to it, and there was a vestibule before its doors, and carved palms, one on this side and one on that, on its projection.

“And the gate of the inner court was on the southern way, and he measured from gate to gate on the southern way one hundred cubits. And he brought me into the inner court to the southern gate, and he measured the gate according to the former measurements—its chamber, its projection, and its vestibule, with the same measurements—and the windows [Note: The same authority reads: ‘its windows and its vestibule all around,’ etc., according to the Vulgate edition.] of the vestibules all around, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width. And the vestibule all around was twenty-five cubits in length and five cubits in width. And its vestibule was toward the outer court, and its palms were on the projection, and it had eight steps by which one went up to it.”

The Septuagint agrees in the same words, except for *thee*, *elau*, *elamoth*, and *elam*, in place of which the Hebrew has *ulam*.

*Thee* means “threshold” or “projection”; *elau*, “around it” or “supports”; *elamoth*, “propyla” or “vestibules”; *ulam*, πρόπυλον (*propylon*), that is, “before the doors.”

What we have placed according to the Hebrew—“and the vestibule, or πρόπυλον, all around, twenty-five cubits in length and five cubits in width”—is not found in the Septuagint.

It should also be noted that in the southern gate the Septuagint does not say “the way,” but simply: “And he led me toward the south, and behold, a gate that faced south.”

Accordingly, through each entrance Ezekiel, whom God strengthened—for this is what his name means—is led. He passes from the northern gate to the southern gate, whose projections, thresholds, τροπύλαια (*tropylaia*), or vestibules, and windows all around had similar measurements: fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width. By seven steps one went up to it, that is, to the southern gate, and to its vestibule, that is, its *elamoth*, before its doors. There were also two carved palms, concerning which we spoke in connection with the gate of the northern region.

It is enough to have pointed out this much: whatever is set down there, according to the lower interpretation—that is, according to the letter—we understand in the southern gate according to the spiritual sense. History and tropology proceed along the same lines, but the former is lower and the latter higher; the former clings to the earth, while the latter flies upward to heavenly things.

Everything around was filled with light through the windows. For each προβλήματα (*problemata*) has its own boundaries, and through them a particular light enters the soul of the believer—especially if the length of his life has been extended through the mystery of the fiftieth year, that is, the jubilee, and he has been able to reach the breadth of the more divine sense.

In that breadth and in the public squares, Wisdom acts confidently, and with a lofty voice cries out. She enters by seven steps, so that she may reach the vestibule and, by the palms of her purpose and effort, attain everlasting victory.

And lest we should think that there was only one court on the southern side, a second court is mentioned: “And the gate of the inner court was on the southern way, and he measured from gate to gate on the southern way one hundred cubits.” Thus, after the mysteries of the weeks and of the Old Testament, he might reach the good land and the grace of the Gospel.

Nor is there only a second court at the southern gate; there is also a third, concerning which it now says: “And he brought me into the inner court to the southern gate, and he measured the gate according to the former measurements,” and so forth.

Each court has its own measurements and arrangements, and within the same measurements there is a different grace, since we recognize the same things differently at the beginning, in progress, and at the end.

What is not found in the Septuagint—“and the vestibule, or πρόπυλον, all around, twenty-five cubits in length and five cubits in width”—seems to raise a difficulty, since it was not included in the ancient translation: how, after the progress of the third step, are twenty-five cubits and five cubits introduced?

But the following removes the ambiguity: “And its vestibule was toward the outer court, and its palms were on the projection.” Thus this court, which had twenty-five cubits in length and five in width, belongs not to the inner but to the outer court. The length of the outer court possessed the width of the former court—that is, twenty-five cubits—and it held five cubits in width.

We refer these measurements, twenty-five and five, to the same senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. If we ascend to higher things, we double them five times and turn bodily senses into spiritual ones, as in the saying: “Lift up your eyes and see, for the fields are already white for harvest” (John 4:35); and: “The one who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8); and: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:8); and: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who believe” (2 Cor. 2:15). And in the Letter of John it is said: “What we have heard and seen, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1).

Finally, the seven steps alone do not suffice, as in the northern region; rather, after the seven, the number eight is placed, so that we may pass from the Synagogue to the Church, from the Old Testament to the New, and from earthly things to heavenly ones.

(Vv. 28 ff.) “And he brought me into the inner court by the eastern way, and he measured the gate according to the former measurements: its chamber, its projection, and its vestibule [Note: Victorius, following the Vulgate reading, has ‘and its vestibule all around, fifty cubits in length,’ and shortly afterward ‘on the projection’ in place of ‘toward the projection.’] as above, and its windows and its vestibules all around, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width.

“And its vestibule, that is, of the outer court” [in place of which the Septuagint and Symmachus have “the inner court”], “and carved palms on its projection, on this side and on that, and its ascent had eight steps.”

From the northern region, in whose court there was an ascent of only seven steps, he passes to the southern gate and the court of that same region, to which one ascends not only by seven steps, as above, but by eight. This signifies that we pass from the old to the new—or, to speak more plainly, that through the patriarchs and prophets we come to the apostles, so that in the one place there may be a hebdomad and in the other an ogdoad.

Now he comes to the last—or rather, the highest—place and leads the prophet through the way of the inner gate, or through the court reached by the eastern way.

According to the Septuagint, “way” is found only in this passage. In the northern and southern regions it is entirely omitted, so that we may understand that only at the eastern gate is that way to be understood which says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Through him we come to the Father, and concerning him it is written: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way” (Ps. 118:1)—those who think nothing sinister about Christ, but whose faith is pure and in no way polluted by the filth of heretics.

The same number of chambers, projections, vestibules, windows, and lights in the windows is maintained, together with the same measure of length and width—namely, the sacred measures of fifty and twenty-five cubits. Its vestibule, belonging to the gate or inner court, is placed outside according to the Hebrew, so that everything may be enclosed in eastern light, in accordance with what is written: “There is nothing hidden from its heat” (Ps. 18:7).

But if we take the court as both outer and inner, it is to be understood in this way: God is both surrounding and indwelling, as the prophet says: “He holds the heavens in his palm and the earth in his fist” (Isa. 40:12). Thus everything is seen to be enclosed by him.

And again: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the stool for my feet” (Isa. 66:1), so that he is believed to be within all things, in accordance with the words of Virgil (*Aeneid* VI):

> In the beginning, heaven and earth, and the liquid plains,  
> And the shining globe of the moon, and the Titanian stars,  
> An inward spirit nourishes; and, infused through its limbs,  
> Mind moves the whole mass and mingles with the great body.

When, through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and disgrace, through good report and bad report, through praise and reproach, we have gained victory over this age (2 Cor. 6), then palms are given to us on both sides. These are people whom neither joys have changed nor sorrow, neither prosperity nor adversity has overcome.

And we ascend to the highest things not through seven [variant: eight] steps, as in the northern region, nor through seven and eight, as is contained in the southern region, but through eight [variant: seven] steps alone. The number eight—that is, the mystery of the Gospel—is sufficient for us, so that we may say with the apostle: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (2 Cor. 5:16), with “according to the flesh” understood.

(Vv. 35 ff.) “And he brought me to the gate that faced north, and he measured according to the former measurements: its chamber, its projection, its vestibule, and its windows all around—fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width. Its vestibule faced the outer court, and there was a carving of palms on its projection, on this side and on that, and its ascent had eight steps.

“And at each storeroom there was a doorway in the doors (Vulgate: ‘fronts’) of the gates; there they shall wash the burnt offering. And in the vestibule of the gate, two tables on this side and two tables on that, upon which the burnt offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering shall be slaughtered. And on the outer side, which rises toward the doorway of the gate that goes north, two tables; and on the other side, before the vestibule of the gate, two tables.

“Four tables on this side and four tables on that: on the sides of the gate there were eight tables, upon which they shall slaughter [Vulgate: ‘slaughtered’]. But four tables for the burnt offering were constructed of squared stones, one and a half cubits in length, one and a half cubits in width, and one cubit in height. Upon them they shall place the vessels in which the burnt offering and the sacrifices are slaughtered. Their rims were one palm wide, turned inward all around. [Col. 0390A] Upon the tables were the flesh of the offering.”

In this passage the Hebrew truth differs greatly from the edition of the Septuagint interpreters. The words that we rendered, “There they shall wash the burnt offering,” and “In the vestibule of the gate, two tables on this side,” and again, “so that the burnt offering and the sin offering may be slaughtered upon them,” are not found in the Septuagint; but in many copies they have been added from Theodotion.

Again, where we said, “And their rims were one palm wide, turned inward all around,” the Septuagint translated: “and *gisum*, having rims of one palm, carved inward all around.”

[Note: Concerning the word γεῖσος (*geisos*), that is, *giso*, we said a little in the *Book of Hebrew Names*. But there it is written γησσός (*gēssos*) or γαισός (*gaisos*), and it means a shield or a weapon of war, not the rim of a table, as the Septuagint wished. Although γεισίον (*geision*) can also mean an enclosure or breastplate; γεῖσος (*geisos*) is also used for a farmer; and γεῖσα (*geisa*), or γεῖσοι (*geisoi*), are the projecting parts of a roof by which rainwater is kept away from the walls. It is surprising that this work of ours was not anticipated by the critic—or rather, the slanderous cleric—against Jerome. But it is enough for him to exult in commonplaces and to pass over those matters that can raise a question. —MART.]

Whether this word is Hebrew,

[Note: It is rather an ancient Gallic word. For this is how the Gauls called a javelin, and it is easy to suppose that the Greeks and Romans received the word from them. Statius, *Thebaid* IV, by an anticipation, attributes it to the most ancient Greeks:

> This band, three thousand in number, followed Adrastus.  
> Some brandished *gesa* in their hands; others carried clubs  
> Hardened for a long time in the flames, etc.

With the same license Silius, Book II, attributes the word to the Carthaginians:

> All the Carthaginian  
> [Col. 0390C] Herdsmen follow the watchman of the herd according to their ancestral custom,]

Gesa and barking Sidon, etc. [Col. 0390D] Nonius: *gessa*, a weapon of the Gauls; he also describes the Gauls, on Varro’s authority, as carrying two *gessa* each. Servius gives the same information in his commentary on *Aeneid* VII, where *alpina gessa* (“Alpine gessa”) are mentioned; so too Caesar, *Gallic War* III, and Propertius, concerning Virdomarus, king of the Gauls, in Book IV. Finally, Claudian likewise mentions them in Book II against Eutropius and again in Book II against Stilicho. But now let us hear Saint Augustine on Joshua:

“Why it says *gessa*,” he remarks, “is not easily understood. The translator Symmachus is said to have called this a shield. But the translators of the Septuagint, whose version we are discussing, who rendered it *gesson*,—I wonder whether in the Greek language they wished *gesson* to be understood as a spear or lance (a Gallic one); for such weapons are called *gessa*.”

There is little agreement among the Greeks concerning the spelling of the word: they write γαισός, γαῖσος, γεσός, and γαῖσον; among the Latins, too, *gaesum*, *gaessum*, *gesum*, and *gessum* are all accepted.

Whether it is Greek, we cannot know; we know only that, in place of *giso*, Symmachus and Theodotion translated “lips”; Aquila’s first edition has ἐπιστάσεις (“projections,” plural), while his second has “lips.” In Hebrew the word is **ASEPHATHAIM** (אספתים). [Note: The printed books omit the article, or A, a letter retained by all manuscript codices. MART.] And where we said, “but upon the tables were the flesh of the offering,” the Septuagint added on its own authority, “and upon the tables above were coverings, so that they might be protected from rain and drought.”

As for what they rendered by the Hebrew names *Thee*, *Elau*, *Elalamoth*, and *Aelam*, we have already indicated its meaning above, and our translation can show it in the corresponding place. There is no need to remind the reader of this repeatedly or to distrust his intelligence and diligence.

He is therefore brought again to the gate that looked toward the north—but not, as above, to the outer court, rather to the inner court. For in what follows, “Its vestibule looked toward the outer court,” it is shown that this court was situated within. Through these details the progress of the one entering is indicated: each place has its own names and measurements, and the windows all around, filled with the light of knowledge, reveal everything. Through the fifty and twenty-five cubits are placed the mysteries of the remission of divine meanings, so that, standing in the vestibule of the inner court, we may see the outer things; contemplating knowledge of past and present, we may come to the double palms and victories, and understand the mysteries of the eight steps; entering the treasuries in which the riches of the temple are contained, we may have our prayers washed clean of every stain of sin. Two tables are placed on either side, so that first the whole burnt offering may be sacrificed,

“the watchman of the herd follows according to the ancestral custom,

and the *gessa* and barking Sidon,” etc.

[Col. 0391A] so that sacred fire may consume all of it; then an offering for sin; and finally one for ignorance—what we have committed knowingly or unknowingly.

On the outer side also, according to the Septuagint, there was a constructed channel that carried outside the ashes of the whole burnt offerings and the foulness of the meat (another reading: *juiciness*). Alternatively, there were two tables, and on the other side of the vestibule of that same gate two tables—that is, four on each side, four here and four there—and behind them, or beside them, another eight tables, making sixteen tables altogether. By this number the mysteries of the prophets are signified, so that whatever we offer through the gracious dispensation of the Gospel, we may confirm as foretold by their prophecies.

And because four tables are brought in, constructed from square stones, and these same tables are for sacrifice and whole burnt offering (another reading: “whole burnt offerings,”), these are the living stones that roll upon the earth and have with them the cornerstone by which the walls of the Old and New Testament are held together.

The number four signifies the mysteries of the Gospel. In length and breadth each table has one and a half cubits—that is, a square whose sides, joined together, make three cubits. These three cubits have one cubit in height, so that the mysteries of the one Trinity may preserve the measure of one cubit, that is, of the divine majesty, as the Lord says to the disciples: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

The name of God is, as it were, a cubit of one height, embracing three properties; and it always receives the whole burnt offerings of our oblations.

Upon these four tables of whole burnt offerings, constructed of living stones, whose length, breadth, and height have been described, vessels are placed in which the sacrifice of the martyrs is offered. Of them it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:5). So too are offered the victims of those who, through self-restraint and purity of body, sacrifice their souls to the Lord.

By the name of these tables, I think, Matthew, Luke, Mark, and John the apostles are signified. A crown bent inward from above surrounded their edges all around, so that it might contain the whole burnt offerings within and prevent them from flowing about indiscriminately; it held the flesh of the offering. Or, as the Septuagint translated: “And the tables themselves were covered above, because of the violence of the rains [Col. 0391D] and the excessive dryness of the summer sun,” so that the flesh placed upon them might say with the prophet: “The sun shall not burn us by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120:6). The one of these—the excessive rains and storms of tribulations—dissolves the offerings; the other, the fierce heat of persecutions, dries out whatever has been offered.

Forgive the difficulty of these passages, reader; or, if you can find something better, teach me. We gladly learn what we do not know.

*(Verses 44 and following.)* “And outside the front gate were the treasuries of the singers in the inner court, which was beside the gate looking toward the north, and their fronts were toward the southern road; one was beside the eastern gate, which looked toward the northern road. [Col. 0392A] And he said to me: This is the treasury that looks toward the southern road; it shall belong to the priests [the Vulgate adds: ‘it shall be’] who keep watch in the temple’s guard duties. But the treasury that looks toward the northern road shall belong to the priests who keep watch over the ministry of the altar. These are the sons of Zadok, who approach from the sons of Levi to the Lord, to minister to him. And he measured the court: its length was one hundred cubits, and its breadth one hundred cubits, square; and the altar was before the face of the temple. And he brought me into the vestibule of the temple, and measured the vestibule: five cubits on this side and five cubits on that side; and the breadth of the gate was three cubits on this side and three cubits on that side. The length of the vestibule was twenty cubits, and its breadth eleven [Col. 0392B] cubits; and it was ascended by eight steps, and its columns [thus in the manuscripts; the Vulgate has: ‘were’] were at the front, one on this side and another on that side.” 490

In place of “treasuries,” the Septuagint translated “chambers.” They omitted what we said, “the chambers or treasuries of the singers.” Again, after “the vestibule five cubits on this side and five cubits on that side,” they added on their own authority, “and the breadth of the gate was fourteen cubits,” whereas the Hebrew has only, “and the breadth of the gate was three cubits on this side and three cubits on that side.”

I have warned the reader of this so that he may not be disturbed by the diversity of the translations, but may remain content with the Hebrew truth in the present passage, especially in the measurements of the temple.

Accordingly, after the wall, which the Septuagint translated as περίβολος (*peribolos*, an enclosure), and which surrounded the entire temple on every side in a square circuit, we read that the prophet was brought into the inner court, then to the north, to the south, to the eastern gate, and again to the north. We have discussed these matters as best we could; and the preceding discussion has shown what we think about their differences, whether of names or of measurements. Their meaning is briefly indicated by the Savior’s testimony: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2).

When these things have been completed, he enters the temple—that is, the Holy of Holies—of which the text now speaks, and within the inner gate are the treasuries, or chambers, of the singers. To them this command applies: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. 95:1). With the angels they cry out: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

This inner court was situated beside the gate that looked toward the north, the south, and the east, so that the singers of the Lord and those devoted to the service of the angels might always remember by what steps they had reached the heights, and might diligently recognize the mysteries of each place.

Finally, the man whose measuring cord and measuring reed were in his hand, after bringing the prophet into the inner court that looked toward the southern road, said: “This is the treasury,” or chamber; and as Theodotion rendered it, “the bridal chamber,” which had been set apart as the dwelling of the priests who keep watch in the temple.

But the treasury that looks toward the northern road shall belong to the priests who keep watch over the ministry of the altar. Here it must be noted that the priests to whom the guarding of the temple has been entrusted dwell in the treasury that looks toward the southern road, where the light is fullest. Those who keep watch over the ministry of the altar, on which victims for sin are offered, are to be in the treasury that looks toward the northern road, wishing to receive and save those who come from the north and offer victims for their sins.

Both groups, serving the Lord according to their duties, are called sons of Zadok, which is interpreted “just” or “justifying”—namely, the almighty God, of whom it is written: “The Lord is just, and he has loved justice; his face has seen equity” (Ps. 10:8).

These sons of Zadok are from the sons of Levi, whose name is interpreted “taken up”; and they too are taken up by the Lord, so that they may approach him. The statement is not to be applied only to Moses—“Moses approached the Lord; the others did not approach” (Exod. 19)—but all who serve and minister to him are said to draw near to the Lord.

This man, then, who brought Ezekiel into the inner court, or, so to speak, into the Holy of Holies, measured the court itself. In it were two chambers, or treasuries, assigned either to the guardians of the temple or as dwellings for those serving at the altar. He found that it was one hundred cubits in length and one hundred cubits in breadth, square, so that the priests who serve in God’s ministry, having entered by the narrow and confined way, might possess very broad walkways and dwell in the perfect and complete number of virtues.

In that court there was also an altar before the face of the temple, so that prayer of the saints to God might never cease.

The aforesaid man also brought Ezekiel into the vestibule, or πρόπυλον (*propylon*), of the temple. He measured it as five cubits on this side and five cubits on that, because the one who had been brought in had been instructed in divine meanings, knew neither right nor left, but entered by the royal way.

The breadth of the gate through which there was entry into the temple vestibule was three cubits on this side and three on that. Here one should observe the elegance of Holy Scripture: it did not say “on the right and on the left,” lest it appear to name anything left-handed in the Holy of Holies, but “on this side and on that,” that is, on both sides.

At once the prudent reader understands that the number three pertains to the mystery of the Trinity, which is the gate of those entering to God: the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. This threefold number is one gate for those who, after the baptism of the Trinity, reach salvation.

What follows—“The length of the vestibule was twenty cubits, and its breadth eleven cubits”—seems to pose a question: how can the dual number, which refers to two tens, and the eleventh, which appears to have one less than the sacred number twelve, be said to be in the vestibule of the temple?

Most explain it as follows. Although the priests are holy, appointed to the ministries of the temple, and daily offer victims to Christ, nevertheless, because they dwell in this mortal and fragile body, subject to sicknesses and defects, they possess the number twenty and the number eleven. Hence the Apostle also said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

We do not say this because we believe, according to the most savage heresy, that bodies must be abolished; rather, our desire is to be clothed over, not stripped, and for this mortal body to receive immortality and this corruptible body to put on incorruption.

But what follows—“And it was ascended to it by eight steps” (1 Cor. 15)—that is, to the inner gate, creates great difficulty for those who know the Hebrew language. Symmachus, whom we have followed in this passage, gives eight steps; the Septuagint gives ten; Theodotion and Aquila’s second edition give eleven. The first edition, however, gives no number, but says simply: “and by steps by which one ascended to it.” Thus either, according to the custom of the earlier gates, we should understand eight steps, as Symmachus did, [Col. 0394C] or else the inner gate had whatever number of steps it possessed, which Scripture did not state.

[Note: Earlier printed books falsely read here “*positum est verohab*,” and so on, whereas Jerome reads in the manuscript codices *UROB* according to the ancient custom, not according to modern punctuation. Likewise, in manuscript copies I find written *sed pro nomen sermonis*, and elsewhere *sed pro nomen quibus Hebraei*, and so forth. These are corruptions by ancient copyists, who themselves were also ignorant of the Hebrew language. MART.]

[Note: Victorius deletes these four lines enclosed in brackets, relying, as he says, on the judgment of learned men, who supposedly could neither grasp the meaning of the holy man nor determine what the true diversity of translation was. For my part, I judge that the words *Urob*, *Aste*, and *Esre* in Hebrew are not placed for the number of the steps by which one ascended, as Jerome explains them, but belong to the first part of that verse itself, which says that the breadth of the chamber was eleven cubits. They therefore have nothing to do with the difficulty under discussion. Yet this inserted passage should not be considered rashly fabricated and falsely attributed to Jerome; rather, it is probably mutilated and deformed by the errors of ancient scribes. The words themselves faithfully reflect the style of the holy Doctor, and especially the sequence of the discourse that follows strongly suggests that something of this kind had previously been observed from the Hebrew. A verse may easily have dropped out; I could supply it by conjecture, but I do not wish to do so without the support of the manuscripts.]

In Hebrew the words are **UROB** (אורב), that is, “and the breadth,” **ASTE** (אסת), **ESRE** (עשרה). If it is read in this way, it signifies eleven. But if instead of **ESRE**, that is, “ten,” we read **ESER** (אשר), it does not signify “ten,” but “which,” a pronoun.

These things may seem like ravings to those ignorant of the Hebrew language. But we are not now writing controversies or speeches, in which one may play with the arrangement of words; we are writing explanations and commentaries on Hebrew books.

But let us return to what we began. By eight or ten steps—the perfect number—or by eleven, about which we have already spoken, one ascends to the gate of the holy places. At its front were columns, one on this side and another on that. He did not say “two,” lest he should fall into the dual number, but “one and one,” which is a perfect number and, through its unity, imitates God.

These were the two columns of which Revelation also says: “The one who conquers, I will make him a column in the temple of my God, and he shall never go out” (Rev. 3:12). Peter and John too are called columns of the Church (Gal. 2); through them we enter the Holy of Holies, and through their teaching comes our entrance to Christ.

*(Chapter XLI—verses 1 and following.)* “And he brought me into the temple and measured the fronts: six cubits in breadth on this side and six cubits in breadth on that side—the breadth of the tabernacle. And the breadth of the gate was ten cubits, and the sides (or shoulders) of the gate were five cubits on this side and five cubits on that side. And he measured its length as forty cubits, [Col. 0395B] and its breadth as twenty cubits.”

After many mysteries, various entrances, and the particular features of each place, at last the man whose hand held the builders’ cord and measuring reed brings Ezekiel the prophet into the temple and measures the front of the temple. For this the Septuagint has *aelam*, Theodotion *aelim*, and Symmachus “around” or “on every side.”

On either side the breadth of the tabernacle was six cubits, containing the mystery of all creatures. For the world was completed in six days. Through knowledge of these days, and of the causes and order of creation, we enter the temple of God; from the order and stability of created things we recognize the Creator.

The breadth of the temple gate was ten cubits, a sacred and perfect number, on the tenth day of the seventh month being observed the fast and propitiation. On the tenth day of the first month, called Nisan, the lamb is taken for sacrifice and preparation of the Passover. In the seventh month, therefore, tithes are offered into God’s storehouses, or, as Scripture commonly calls them, winepresses.

Hence the Apostle says: “Make room for us also” (2 Cor. 6:11), so that after someone has entered the temple through its ten-cubit gate, the sides of that gate—or, as it is properly said in Hebrew, its shoulders—may be measured on either side, since shoulders always refer to works.

Thus Issachar desired the good (Gen. 49), resting between the allotments, seeing that the resting-place was good and the land fertile; he placed his shoulder under the burden of labor and became a husbandman. In the priest’s vestment, too, the shoulder-piece is fastened to the breastpiece, so that works may be joined to reason, and the churchly man may say: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 119:104).

These shoulders of the gate had five porticoes on either side, so that through earthly and divine senses—concerning whose distinction we have often written—we might enter the inner chambers of the temple. The man who guided the prophet measured its length as forty cubits and its breadth as twenty cubits—or, more properly, the length and breadth of the gate, since previously he had spoken only of its breadth and shoulders.

There is no doubt that twenty times forty makes eight hundred, a number close to eight. Hence Ecclesiastes commands: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. 11:2). I know that I have often discussed the mystery of this number. Since we enter the Lord’s sanctuary through the tribulations and narrow straits of this age, the length of the gate was forty cubits, for this number is always associated with labor.

Thus Moses and Elijah neither eat bread nor drink water for forty days (Deut. 9; 1 Kings 19; Deut. 29); for forty years the people of Israel are harassed and tested in the wilderness and, through many labors, enter the promised land; and the Lord and Savior, in the frailty of the body he assumed, is tempted in the wilderness for forty days, so that after his victory angels come and minister to him (Matt. 4).

But when through tribulations and narrow straits we can say the Apostle’s words, “In everything afflicted, but not crushed” (2 Cor. 4:8), and the prophet’s, “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4:1), then a very broad entrance is opened to us, having a breadth of twenty cubits. Having overcome the struggles of the world and earthly things—for twenty is itself a dual number—we enter the inner chambers of the temple and hear the Lord commanding his disciples: “Take courage: I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

[Col. 0396C] *(Verses 3–4.)* “And entering within (or into the inner court), he measured at the front (or *aelam*) of the gate two cubits, and the gate six [another reading: ten] cubits, and the breadth of the gate seven cubits (or: and the shoulders of the gate seven cubits on this side and seven cubits on that side). And he measured its length (or the length of the doors) as twenty cubits and its breadth as twenty cubits before the face of the temple. And he said to me: This is the Holy of Holies.”

[Note: The passage is printed in a thoroughly corrupt form in Erasmus and Marianus, who read as follows: “At whose front, or αἰλάμ (*aelam*)” (Erasmus has *elau*), “for which Symmachus has περὶ τὴν θύραν, that is, ‘around the gate’; Theodotion has the Hebrew [term] *el*; Aquila has ‘door’; we have translated it ‘front.’” I find nothing of Jerome’s own words here: the manuscripts have substituted αἰλάμ or *elau* for **AEL**, added Symmachus’s Greek words, and replaced Theodotion’s reading *aelam* and the Hebrew **UL** (אול) with the modern Hebrew **EL**, “he says” or “or *el*.” MART.]

However far we advance, a greater progress is always opened before us. Thus, after entering the temple, we again enter within—or, as the Septuagint translated it, into the inner court. At its front, or **AEL**, for which Symmachus has “around the gate,” Theodotion **AELAM**, the Hebrew **UL** (אול), Aquila “door,” and we “front,” there were two cubits. Thus, according to the interpretation given above, through the dual number we enter the place where the Holy of Holies is.

The gate itself was six cubits, through which, once entered, we possess eternal rest, signified by the number seven. In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “and the breadth of the gate was seven cubits on this side and seven cubits on that side”; in Hebrew and the other editions, only a single seven cubits is given for the breadth of the gate.

What follows—“And he measured its length,” or, as the Septuagint translated, “the length of the doors, twenty cubits,” whereas in most manuscripts, according to the Septuagint, forty is found, “and its breadth twenty cubits before the face of the temple”—signifies that before the face of the temple and its entrance, the measure of former labor and struggle always confronts us.

The same significance that the dual number possesses in individual numbers is possessed by two decades. We should also consider that the prophet is taught what that place is and by what name it is called: he enters within through a gate having two cubits at the front, six cubits, seven in breadth on either side, and twenty cubits in length, with the same number in the doors of the temple itself. For he says: “He said to me, ‘This is the Holy of Holies.’”

But if the Holy of Holies is before the temple—or, as Scripture calls it, before the face of the temple—how great a blessedness should we suppose to exist in the temple’s inner chambers and interior spaces! Concerning this the prophet says: “This is labor in my sight, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny” (Ps. 73:16–17).

It should also be noted that in the description of the tabernacle the expression is “Holy things of holies,” plural; here, however, it is “Holy thing of holies,” singular, so that after the holy things we may come to the Holy Thing, just as after many songs we come to the Song of Songs, which is the song of all songs; and, while singing it, we are joined to the embraces of the bridegroom.

[Col. 0397C] *(Verses 5 and following.)* “And he measured the wall of the house: six cubits; and the breadth of the side-chamber four cubits, all around the house. And the side-chambers were side by side, thirty-three [the Vulgate: three] of them; and there were projections that extended through the wall of the house into the side-chambers all around, to support them without touching the wall of the temple. And there was a circular passage rising upward by a spiral staircase, and it led around into the upper chamber of the temple. Therefore the temple was broader above, and from the lower parts one ascended to the upper parts, to the middle, and from the middle to the third story and Thrael.”

What is placed in the Septuagint—“and from the middle to the third story,” that is, “to the three upper chambers,” and *Thrael*—is not found in the Hebrew. In place of *Thrael* (which I do not know what it means, [Col. 0397D] for it is not found in the Hebrew), they have **URAITHI** (וראיתי), which we and the other translators rendered “and I saw,” so that the sequence of the testimony may continue.

[Note: To Victorius, however, this reading appeared so difficult to understand and so corrupt that he did not hesitate to rewrite it on his own authority: “I do not know what it means among them”; in Hebrew one reads *Uraithi*, which means, etc. It is perfectly clear from Jerome that, deceived by the similarity of Hebrew letters, the Septuagint read the words differently and joined them together as *Vethrael*, or *et Thrael*, “the house,” although this word is neither Hebrew nor found in the Hebrew text. In its place one reads *Uraithi*, “And I saw,” etc.]

*(Verses 8 and following.)* “And I saw in the house a height all around, the side-chambers being founded according to the measure of a reed, with a space of six cubits; and the breadth along the outer wall of the side-chamber five cubits; and the interior of the house, and the side-chambers of the house, and between the treasuries, a breadth of twenty cubits around the house on every side. And the doorway of the side-chamber was toward the place of prayer” (which is not found in the Septuagint), “one doorway toward the northern road and one doorway toward the southern road, [Col. 0398A] and the breadth of the place of prayer” (which likewise the Septuagint did not translate), “five cubits all around. And the building that was set apart and turned toward the road facing the sea was seventy cubits in breadth; but the wall of the building was five cubits broad all around, and its length was ninety cubits.”

After reaching the Holy of Holies, about which we have spoken above, that venerable man measured the wall of the Holy of Holies. Because of the structure of the world and of all visible creation, which was created in six days, it had six cubits; and the breadth of one side-chamber was four cubits—not on one side only, but all around.

The breadth around the house was four cubits, to indicate the four elements from which everything is composed, especially human bodies. Against these the saints fight, subjecting themselves to the power of the soul; thus they deserve to enter the interior places and learn the Lord’s secrets.

The side-chambers that were around the house, separated from the walls of the temple by a space of four cubits, were joined to one another, so that one side-chamber touched another, and they had in length not thirty-three cubits but twice thirty-three, that is, sixty-six.

The Old Testament says in Leviticus that after the birth of a male child, the woman who gave birth and the one who was born complete thirty-three days before they come for purification (Lev. 12). But if she gives birth to a female, a double number is observed—that is, sixty-six days.

And because, in order to come to the Holy of Holies, we need not only a first birth but also a second, so that, born in the flesh, we may be reborn in the spirit, the number is not simply sixty-six but twice thirty-three. Thus both births are owed to God as their author and to his mercy, and the side-chambers that support the temple’s structure are surrounded by a double wall.

What follows according to the Hebrew—“And there were certain projections that extended through the wall of the house into the side-chambers all around, to support them without touching the wall of the temple”—signifies that holy men, in the multitude of believers, burst through the temple wall on every side, supporting the foundations of the Church, yet do not touch the temple wall: content merely to have seen and from afar to have adored mysteries that cannot be expressed. For now we see “through a mirror in an enigma,” and we cannot touch or comprehend the truth in its fullness.

As for the circular passage that rose upward by a spiral staircase and led around into the upper chamber of the temple, and the fact that the temple was broader above, so that from the lower parts one ascended to the upper and middle parts: I think it is clear to the reader that the things below are always narrower, in fasts, χαμευνίαι (*lying on the ground*), and restraint of food; and that, as we gradually climb toward the heights, a broader way is opened to us, fulfilling what is written: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4:1).

We ascend by a circular route and a spiral staircase to the upper chamber of the temple. Of all the σχῆματα (*figures*), this form is also judged by the philosophers of this age to be the most beautiful: heaven, the sun, the moon, and the other stars; the point of the earth; and, in human bodies, the eyes, like twin stars, the shape of the head, which receives all the senses, the rounded fingers, the thighs, and the arms—all display this circular form.

As for the upper chamber of the temple, to which we climb from narrower places toward higher ones, I think it is what Elijah and Elisha possessed in the Book of Kings, and what Tabitha possessed in the Acts of the Apostles—Tabitha, that is, δόρκας (*dorkas*, “gazelle”), our doe, who had climbed to the heights through good works (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 4; Acts 9; Acts 10).

The Apostle Peter, upon whom the Lord solidified the foundations of the Church, went beyond the upper chamber and came to the roof, which is more significantly called in Greek δῶμα (*dōma*), that is, the roof terrace. There he came to know the mysteries of the Church, previously unknown to the world.

The Savior too celebrated the Passover of the human race in an upper chamber—in a large and spacious upper chamber, purified and swept clean of every impurity, furnished and prepared for a spiritual banquet. There he gave his disciples the mystery of his body and blood and left us the everlasting feast of the spotless Lamb.

What he added—“And from the middle to the third story, and Thrael”—seems to me to require an obelus. Why should we discuss doubtful things that are not written, when we ought to devote ourselves to what is preserved in the books of the Hebrews?

The text continues: “And I saw in the house a height all around, the side-chambers being founded [Col. 0399C] according to the measure of a reed, with a space of six cubits; and the breadth along the outer wall of the side-chamber was five cubits, and between the treasuries”—which Symmachus calls ἐξέδραι (*exedrae*, “chambers”)—“a breadth of twenty cubits around the house.”

By these numbers it is shown that, from this world, from earthly senses, and from the dual number of two decades, which refers to twenty, we may deserve to ascend not only into the Holy of Holies but also into their upper chambers. We must always keep in mind that through the six days of our creation, the five senses, and the twenty cubits of breadth, we have ascended to the upper chamber of the temple; and, leaving behind earthly lowliness and the sense of the letter, have passed to the summit of the Church and rejoiced in fellowship with the Holy Spirit.

“And the doorway,” he says, “of the side-chamber was toward the place of prayer, facing the northern road” (Jer. 1:14), from which evils blaze out over the whole earth, and which the Lord promises to drive away from us, saying: “And I will drive away from you the one who comes from the north” (Joel 2:20).

It is fitting that the place of prayer should be at the doorway facing north, so that, according to the Apostle (1 Thess. 5), we may pray without ceasing and say with Jeremiah: “Let not the pupil of my eye be silent” (Lam. 2:18), whether we desire to escape present evils or give thanks for those that have passed.

As long as we are in the tabernacle of this body, we groan and say: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

There was also a doorway toward the southern road, likewise having, according to the Hebrew, a place of prayer and extending five cubits all around. After the cold of the north we pass to the warmth of the south, yet again seek a place of prayer: at the northern doorway, so that we may escape dangers; at the southern, so that we may give thanks for past things and possess the victory securely.

The five cubits here too indicate the divine senses, through which we climb from earthly things to higher realities.

“And the building,” he says, “that was set apart and turned toward the road facing the sea was seventy cubits in breadth.” Thus, after the labors, dangers, waves, and shipwrecks of this age, and after the seventy years about which Jeremiah, Daniel, and Zechariah write (Jer. 25 and 29; Dan. 9; Zech. 9), we may attain the true and legitimate sabbath of seven decades, so that eternal rest may be ours.

Through the breadth of five cubits we come to a length of ninety cubits. This is the age in which Sarah, who was ninety years old—that is, possessed of nine decades—bore Isaac according to the promise, with Abraham, who was one hundred years old, that is, possessed of the mystery of ten decades (Gen. 21). What this number signifies, the following Scripture will show.

[Col. 0400C] “(Verses 13 ff.) And he measured the length of the house: one hundred cubits. And the building that was separate, and its walls, one hundred cubits in length. The breadth before the face of the house, and of that which was separate opposite the east, was one hundred cubits. And he measured the length of the building opposite the face of that which was separate, behind it. [Note: [Col. 0399] In the Latin of Jerome, *ecthetas*; in other books, *ethecas*, a derivative word from the Hebrew [term omitted], which has the same meaning.] *ΕΚΘΕΤΑΣ* (that is, projections), on both sides, one hundred cubits. And the inner temple and the vestibules of the court. Thresholds and slanting windows, *ΕΚΘΕΤΑΣ*, around, opposite each threshold, and covered with wood all around in a circuit. The ground extended up to the windows. And [Col. 0400D] the windows were closed. Above the doors, and up to the inner house; and outwardly, along the entire wall all around, within; and outwardly, according to the measure. And carved cherubim and palm trees; and a palm tree between one cherub and another. Each cherub had two faces: the face of a human being beside the palm on one side, and the face of a lion beside the palm on the other side; represented throughout the entire house all around. From the ground up to the upper parts of the gate, cherubim and carved palm trees were on the wall of the temple. The threshold was square. And the appearance of the sanctuary was opposite the appearance of the wooden altar: its height was three cubits, and its length [Col. 0401A] two cubits; and its corners, its length, and its walls were wooden.

The Septuagint: ‘And he measured opposite the house—[the text has a mark of omission or corruption]—the length, one hundred cubits; and the remainder, and the separate structures, and its walls, one hundred cubits in length; and the breadth opposite the face of the temple, and the remainder opposite, one hundred cubits. And he measured the length of the separation opposite the face of the remainder that was behind the house, and the remainder on either side, one hundred cubits in length. And the temple, and the corners, and the outer *Aelam* were covered with wood, and the windows were made in the form of a lattice, threefold, for giving light, so that one could look through them. And the house, and the things adjacent to it, were covered with wood all around; and the pavement, [p. 501] and from the pavement up to the windows. And the windows [Col. 0401B] were opened in three ways, so that one could look through them; and up to the inner and outer house, and along every wall all around, within and without, according to measure; and carved cherubim and palm trees between cherub and cherub. The cherubim had two faces: the face of a human being toward the palm on this side, and the face of a lion toward the palm on that side. Every wall was carved all around, from the pavement up to the ceiling, with cherubim and carved palm trees. And the sanctuary and the temple opened toward the four corners opposite the face of the holy places. There was the appearance, as it were, of a wooden altar: its height was three cubits, its length two cubits, and its breadth two cubits; and it had horns, as well as bases and wooden walls.’”

The word “opposite,” which the Septuagint translated [Col. 0401C] at the beginning of the passage, where it is written, “And he measured opposite the house,” is not found in the Hebrew. It should therefore be marked beforehand with an obelus, so that the text may be more correctly and accurately read: “And he measured the house, one hundred cubits in length,” and so forth.

The holy of holies and the inner temple are described. After the ninety cubits, it is said to have one hundred cubits on three sides, [Note: [Col. 0401D] I have already discussed this corruption in the annotations on this chapter of Ezekiel, vol. I, cols. 713 and 714. Consult the passage, and you will see the false restoration of Marianus. MART.] namely, the complete number of ten decades: so that we may serve the Lord in mind, word, and works, remembering that apostolic example in which he says: “that we may be able to comprehend what is the breadth and length and depth and height” (Ephesians III, 18).

But where the Hebrew says “the separate building and its walls,” the Septuagint interprets “the remainder and the separate structures,” which do not adjoin the walls of the temple but have walls of their own nearby. The temple itself, too, with its corners and its *Aelam*, that is, its *πρόπυλον* (*propylon*), or vestibule, was outwardly covered with wood—clearly signifying wisdom, since Scripture recalls that the tree of life was planted in paradise (Genesis II).

The windows, too, were made in the form of a lattice, like grilles, so that they might be closed not with transparent stone or glass but with wood cut through and patterned. In their place, the Hebrew has “slanting windows,” which were found only on three sides of the temple: on the right and left, and at the rear—that is, toward the south, north, and west. The eastern [Col. 0402A] side had no windows, because the entrance itself admitted bright light within, and all the inner parts of the temple were filled with the light of the doors, [p. 502] so that through each window and opening of the grilles one could look inside.

And not only were the outer parts covered with wood, but there was such an abundance of wood all around that both the pavement and everything from the pavement up to the windows were joined together with wood. According to the Septuagint, these windows were opened in three ways, so that when they were opened a threefold understanding might be displayed in the temple of God, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “But you describe these things three times” (Proverbs XXII, 20).

One looks through them not only inwardly but also outwardly, so that we may understand that the inner things are invisible and the outer things visible; so that one window may reveal the mind, another the flesh; one a spiritual understanding, another the simple historical sense. Along all the walls around, both within and without, there were their proper measurements. For nothing in the temple of God—and especially in the holy of holies [variant: *sancta*]—was made by God without reason and measure.

There were also carved cherubim, without doubt in the wood extending from the pavement up to the windows. The carvings were so skilfully fashioned that they appeared not to have been sculpted but attached. Cherubim is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge.” Therefore, within, in the inner parts of the temple, after the multitude of knowledge, palm trees are carved, in which there is a sign of victory, as the Apostle says: “I pursue the appointed prize of the upward calling of God in Christ Jesus” [Col. 0402C] (Philippians III, 14).

These palm trees were between one cherub and another, so that one cherub was enclosed by the sides of two palm trees. This cherub did not, as we read at the beginning of this prophet, have four faces—of a human being, a lion, a calf, and an eagle—but only two, namely those of a human being and a lion. The first pertains to reason; the second to anger, which in Greek is more precisely called *θυμός* (*thymos*).

By “anger” we do not mean that which is close to disturbance and vice, but that which strengthens the softness of the mind and makes the spirit of the combatant more courageous. At the beginning, we are subject to desire, which is represented by the calf because of earthly works. Some things are carnal and others spiritual, the latter being assigned to the eagle.

But when we have entered the holy of holies and possessed the inner parts of the temple, we need nothing else except reason and strength. The one refers to understanding and prudence, the other to the perseverance of the spirit. [Col. 0402D] [p. 503]

Thus every wall around the temple, from the pavement up to the ceiling, had cherubim and palm trees carved with marvelous skill. After these, the sanctuary and the temple opened toward the four corners opposite the face of the holy places.

First we possess the multitude of knowledge, through which we gain victory over the enemy; afterward the sanctuary and the temple are opened to us. It has four corners, a most stable position, and does not slope more toward one side than another. For this is the nature of the square: that it stands upon a stable base and, in the mystical number apparent to the prudent reader, possesses solid and everlasting the four elements from which all things consist.

Everything looked toward the face of the sanctuary. Before the sanctuary—or in the sanctuary—there was the appearance of a wooden altar three cubits high, two cubits long, and two cubits wide; together these dimensions make seven cubits. That altar had horns, and both its bases and its walls—that is, its sides—were wooden.

In this the mysteries of Holy Scripture contain something that human speech cannot explain: how the altar on which fire was to be kindled, namely the table of incense, suffers nothing from the fire, [Col. 0403B] but, so to speak, becomes purer through fire. For just as the works of the saints, about which the Apostle writes, “The fire will test what sort of work each one has done” (I Corinthians III, 13), do not perish but are shown to be purer through fire, so also the wood of the altar, which is from the woods of paradise, is not consumed by the nearby fire but is made purer.

Nor is it surprising that we should believe this of the sanctuary, the inner parts of the temple, and the altar of incense, since even [Note: [Col. 0403D] *Amiantus*, a stone found in Cyprus, resembling cleavable alum, from which, because it is flexible, they make fabrics. When thrown into fire, these do indeed ignite and produce flames, but, losing none of their substance, they emerge more shining. This is reported by R. Constantine from Dioscorides, book V, chapter 148; and Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 19. I have preserved a piece of this stone, or linen-like material, out of curiosity, when stones of asbestos had been brought to us from the Pyrenees mountains. MART.] *ἀμίαντον* (*amianton*), which is a kind of linen or has the appearance of linen, is found to become cleaner the more it has burned.

Forgive, reader, the difficulty, and grant pardon to my poor understanding. Through the slanting windows made in the form of a lattice, which are always closed, we can scarcely bring the eye of our heart as far as the inner house, so that everything we see we see in shadow and in an image. And with the Apostle we cry out: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways” (Romans XI, 13)! And: “Who has known the mind of God” (Isaiah XL, 13), except the one who is the angel of great counsel and is able to disclose his mysteries to those worthy of them?

[Note: [Col. 0403D] Elsewhere, *Ethecas*: *ἐκθέτας*, which appears to have been expressed from the Hebrew word [term omitted] found here and signifying “its corners.” Concerning the *meniana*, recall what we observed in Letter 106, to Sunnia and Fretella, p. 661. Finally, Victorius reads *ἐξώστοας* instead of *ἐξώστρας*.]

But at Rome they call *ἐκθέτας* the projecting terraces extending from the walls of upper rooms, or *meniana*, after the person who first devised them. Some Greeks call them [Note: [Col. 0403D] Whoever wishes to read Marianus’s notes on this and the preceding passage will find much that is false and insufficiently learned, which we have not wished to criticize out of regard for his name and for the fastidious reader. Moreover, Marianus should have learned what *meniana* are from Jerome himself, who says in his letter to Sunnia and Fretella: ‘*Doma* in the eastern provinces is the word used for what we call a roof; for in Palestine and Egypt … they do not have peaked roofs, but *domata*, which at Rome they call either terraces or *meniana*, that is, flat roofs supported by transverse beams … And when we are commanded to make a crown for our *domus*, this means that on the roof we are to make projections around it, so that a person may not easily fall headlong. Thus *meniana*, named after the censor Menius, were *ἐκθέται* and *ἐξῶστραι*, terraces projecting from the walls of upper rooms. Do not read *Mediana* in the letter to Sunnia and Fretella, but *meniana*. MART.] *ἐξώστρας* (*exostras*).

“(Verses 23 ff.) And he said to me: ‘This is the table before the Lord.’ And there were two doors in the temple and in the sanctuary; and in each of the two doors, on either side, there were two little doors, which folded inward upon one another. For there were two doors on either side of the doors, and cherubim and carved palm trees were represented on those doors, [Col. 0404A] just as they were also represented on the walls.

Therefore the timbers at the front of the vestibule were also thicker [Vulgate: coarser] on the outside. Above them were slanting windows, and on either side there was the likeness of palm trees on the projecting shoulders of the vestibule, along the sides of the house and the breadth of the walls.’

In this passage the Septuagint version differs greatly from the Hebrew truth. I shall therefore point out only that, instead of “thicker timbers,” they translated *σπουδαῖα*—that is, “necessary” or “worthy of care”—and instead of “slanting windows,” “hidden windows.” At the end of the passage they placed: “And he measured on either side the ceiling of the lintel, or vestibule, and [variant: ‘through’] the sides of the house, fitted together,” or “joined together,” which they rendered *ἐζυγωμένα*. For this we may translate “of equal weight.”

The man who had brought the prophet into the hidden parts of the temple and, among other things, had shown him the wooden altar, which according to the Septuagint had corners and horns and wooden walls, said to him: “This altar that you see is itself the table before the Lord,” which burns in the likeness of the bush and is not consumed. Concerning it the holy man says to God: “You have prepared a table before me, against those who trouble me” (Psalm XXII, 5).

There were also two doors in the temple and in the sanctuary itself, through which the mysteries of both instruments are displayed. In each of the two doors, on either side, there were two little doors folding inward upon one another, so that in the historical sense you may possess a spiritual understanding, and in the tropological (moral) sense the truth of the history; each of these depends upon the other, and if one is lacking, complete knowledge is absent. What follows—“There were two doors on either side of the doors”—is clear according to the literal sense.

In larger dining rooms, two doors are commonly attached and joined together, so that a larger entrance is closed or opened not by two enormous doors but by four smaller ones. On these doors of the temple, or of the holy of holies, cherubim were carved, concerning which we have spoken above, as well as carvings of palm trees, so that after the multitude of knowledge victory might be offered to those entering.

This carving of palm trees was also on all the walls of the temple. He gives the reasons why cherubim were carved [variant: *caelata*] on the doors themselves and likenesses of palm trees were represented. Therefore the timbers at the vestibule of the gate were thicker [variant: coarser], so that they might possess both strength and the capacity to receive carving.

Beautifully, according to the spiritual understanding, the doors are stronger and carved, so that they have both strength and beauty, lest anyone like Uzziah should be able to burst into the holy of holies and claim the priesthood for himself (II Chronicles XXVI). Above these doors were slanting, or hidden, windows, so that even the light admitted within would not possess perfect knowledge or a clear light open to everyone, but would be hidden from many in part. For now “we see in a mirror dimly” (I Corinthians XIII, 12), and we do not yet know as we ought to know. But when that which is perfect has come, then that which was partial will be destroyed.

And there was a likeness of palm trees on either side. Elegantly, in the inner parts of the temple and in the holy of holies, he did not say “on the right and on the left,” lest anything left-handed or sinister should seem to be spoken of in things that are great and mysterious. Instead he says “on either side,” in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew V, 39). Could he not have said “the left” as well? But when the right cheek is struck, another right cheek is offered, because in a holy person both sides are right, and both are perfect.

“And on the projecting shoulders of the vestibule, along the sides of the house and the breadth of the walls.” For this the Septuagint translated “on the ceilings of the *Aelam*,” that is, of the *propyli* [variant: *προπύλου*], and “the sides of the house, of equal weight or measure.” Through this it is secretly shown that the doorposts and lintel of the vestibule—for this is what the projecting shoulders seem to signify—as well as the sides of the house and the breadth of the walls, are all full of reason and measure. Nothing is found in the temple of the Lord that has been established without measure and wisdom.

## BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405B] 505–506

The thirteenth book of the Explanations on Ezekiel is the second book of the exposition of the temple. With the help of our Savior, I wish to dictate it through to the end, and also the fourteenth book, singing with David, in the fourteenth psalm and with the same number: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm XIV, 1).

We should understand this as referring both to what is difficult and to what is impossible. Therefore, elsewhere, like a man of desires, he prays with greater earnestness and says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the Lord’s delight and visit his holy temple” (Psalm XXVI, 4–5).

And again: “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm LXXXIII, 1). [Note: [Col. 0405] Victor preferred *in atria*, from the Greek *τῶν LXX* and several manuscripts of Jerome.]

I anticipate the curses of my rivals, [Col. 0405C] 507–508 who consider not what they themselves are capable of but what I am incapable of; and while they judge our work, they do not offer their own to be judged. They never fight in the contest, but judge those who fight with an idle—indeed, arrogant—spirit.

It is easy to issue written exercises from the crowd, to criticize every blow, to laugh at another’s blood, and, like an inexperienced trainer, to explain where the wound ought to have been inflicted. In my exposition of the temple of Ezekiel, and of the other matters belonging to the end of the book itself, I confess that, in view of the greatness of the subject, I shall write nothing worthy of it; and if I should nevertheless have been granted the ability to grasp anything, I shall give thanks to the Savior.

For it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah VI). And elsewhere: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed and say to this mountain, ‘Move from here and be transplanted into the sea,’ it will happen” (Matthew XVII, 19). And how the Apostle shows that the grain of mustard seed means not a small portion of faith but faith in its entirety, when he says: “And if I have all faith, so that I remove mountains” (I Corinthians [Col. 0406B] XIII, 2).

Therefore this grain of mustard seed, even if it is small, grows into a great tree, and the birds of heaven dwell in its branches (Luke XIII). For this reason, daughter Eustochium, who gladly receive whatever our writings may be, I want you to know—and I briefly remind you of the statement of the rhetorician Victorinus—that you should understand the obscurity of books to arise from three causes: the greatness of the subject, the incompetence of the teacher, or the dullness of the hearer.

Of the first and second I shall plainly confess myself guilty in this work. The third, however, your keen intelligence and desire for the Scriptures readily rejects; for by the privilege of virginity and the continence of your way of life, you possess God not merely as a frequent guest but as a continual guest.

Therefore let us undertake the thirteenth book on Ezekiel, whose beginning is as follows:

### (Chapter 42—Verses 1 ff.)

“And he led me into the outer court by the way leading toward the north, and brought me into the treasury that was opposite the detached building and opposite the structure extending toward the north. On the front, along the length, there were one hundred cubits of the northern entrance, and in width fifty cubits, opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court and opposite the pavement laid with stone in the outer court, where there was a portico joined to a triple portico.

“And before the treasuries there was a passageway ten cubits wide, facing inward, with a way one cubit wide; and their entrances were toward the north. There the treasuries in the upper stories were lower, because they bore [Vulgate: “supported”] the porticoes that projected from them, from the lower and middle levels of the building. For they were three-storied and had no columns such as the columns of the courts; therefore they projected from the lower and middle levels [variant adds: “courts”], fifty cubits from the ground.

“And the outer enclosing wall was alongside the treasuries that were on the way of the outer court, in front of the treasuries; its length was fifty cubits. For the length of the treasuries of the outer court was fifty cubits, while the length in front of the temple was one hundred cubits.

“And beneath these treasuries there was an entrance from the east for those entering them from the outer court, across the width of the enclosure of the court that was opposite the eastern way, in front of the detached building. And in front of the building there were treasuries, with a way in front of them, corresponding to the treasuries that were on the northern way, according to their length and width.

“And all their entrances, their corresponding arrangements, and their doors were like the doors of the treasuries that were on the way facing south [the Vulgate reads *Notum*, “south”], with one door at the head of the way [the Vulgate adds “way”] that was in front of the detached vestibule, for those entering by the eastern way.”

### The Septuagint

“And he led me into the outer court toward the east ÷ ** opposite the northern gate; and he brought me in, and behold, five chambers [Note: Victorius rewrites the passage as ‘five chambers belonging to the remaining building and near it,’ etc., in accordance with the Greek text; Jerome does not disagree in his Commentary.] beside part of the building and near the detached building toward the north. And opposite them, one hundred cubits in length toward the north, and fifty cubits in width, they were laid out like the gates of the inner court and like the columns of the outer court, in order, opposite the front of the triple porticoes.

“And opposite the chambers there was a passageway ten cubits wide and one hundred cubits long, leading inward by a way one cubit wide, and their doors were toward the north. And the passageways of the upper chambers were likewise, because the columns projected above the lower columns, and the space was similar. They were triple porticoes, and they had no columns like the columns in the outer structures; therefore they projected above those below and in the middle, fifty cubits from the ground.

“And there was an outer light like that of the chambers of the outer court, which faced the northern chambers, fifty cubits in length. For the length of the chambers facing the outer court was fifty cubits. These were opposite their front, all one hundred cubits long, and the doors of these chambers opened toward the eastern entrance, so that one might enter the outer court by them, according to the light that was at the beginning of the passageway toward the south, opposite the southern side and the front of the remaining building and of the detached building.

“And the chambers and the passageway opposite them corresponded to the measurements of the chambers and the way toward the north, according to their length and width and all their exits, entrances, lights, and doors. The doors of the chambers were toward the south, and the entrance was from the beginning of the passageway toward the light, a reed’s distance; and by these one proceeded toward the east.”

What the Septuagint translated as “toward the east” is not found in the Hebrew, and it is plainly superfluous. For how is he led to the outer gate toward the east when what follows says “opposite the northern gate”?

The wording that we placed both above and in this passage—“And [Note: Victorius likewise inserts “brought me in,” in accordance with the Greek εἰσήγαγε, “he brought [me] in.”] he led me into the treasury that will be opposite the detached building and opposite the structure extending toward the north”—is rendered by the Septuagint: “And he led me, and behold, five chambers belonging to the remaining building and beside the detached building toward the north.” For “detached,” Aquila and Symmachus gave translations; Aquila’s second edition and Theodotion retained the very word *GAZERA*, expressing it similarly in all passages.

Many other features of the present passage differ between the Hebrew and the Septuagint, not only in order but also in number and in the interpretation of words. If we linger over each item, investigating and explaining the reason for their differences, we shall stray far from our purpose. I had intended, because of the difficulty and magnitude of the subject, to pass over the present testimony in silence; but I judged it better to say something—whatever it might be—than to say nothing at all, adopting that Socratic maxim: “I know that I do not know” [variant: “that I may not know”]. For it is part of knowledge to know what one does not know.

After the prophet had carefully examined what was within, the man whose hand held the measuring cord and reed led him into the outer court by the way leading toward the north, which he had already seen above before penetrating into the interior. Yet those who possess perfect knowledge see one thing differently from those who are at the beginning of instruction. And it is necessary that whoever has looked upon the interior should also see the exterior according to the same form and measurements and in accordance with the hidden mysteries.

He was led into the treasury—or, as Symmachus and the Septuagint translated it, the chamber, or, as Theodotion has it, *pastophorion* (παστοφόριον), which is translated as “bedchamber”—which was opposite the detached building. What the Septuagint added in place of “treasury,” namely “five chambers,” is not found in the Hebrew. The treasury was opposite the detached building, about which we have already spoken: *GAZERA*. The detached building received those who came from the north and was opposite the structure extending toward the north—that is, it faced the northern region but was not situated in the north—so that the passage might be easier for those leaving the cold of the north, from which evils blaze forth over the earth (Jer. 1).

We read in the Book of Numbers that the tribes of Dan, Naphtali, and Asher, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, the maidservants of Rachel and Leah, encamped in the northern regions. Now too, on the front, the length of the northern entrance was one hundred cubits and its width fifty: so that through ten decades the quadrangular and perfect number might be displayed, and through seven weeks—the number of remission, which breaks forth into the beginning of unity, that is, the ogdoad—the spaces of the temple of God might be signified.

That which, according to the Hebrew, is joined to the text—“opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court”—is translated by the Septuagint, “laid out like the gates of the inner court.” Its meaning is this: the number one hundred and fifty belonging to the outer court has the same force as the twenty belonging to the inner court. For if you count four times five, you will find both Testaments in the number twenty: the Law being held within the Gospel, and the Gospel springing from the root of the Law. In place of this number, the Septuagint interpreted “the likeness of the inner court,” perhaps fearing to place the number twenty—the number in which Esau’s gifts are offered—in the inner court.

It follows: “And opposite the pavement laid with stone in the outer court, where there was a portico joined to a triple portico.” The Septuagint translated this: “And like the columns of the outer court, set in order opposite the front of the triple porticoes.”

This signifies that the pavement of the outer court was laid with living stone, so that neither the dust of summer nor the mud of winter might defile the footsteps of the priests. Therefore, too, when the Lord was about to ascend to the Father, he washed the feet of the Apostles (John 13), so that, with their footsteps cleansed and purified, they might ascend the kingdoms of heaven.
