He also commands the Apostles that, if they enter any city and its inhabitants do not receive them, they should shake the dust from their feet (Matt. 10; Mark 6), so that they might permit no earthly gifts to remain among them.

Nor was the pavement merely laid with stone; a portico was also joined to a triple portico. One portico, protecting the priests from rain and heat and joined to a triple portico, demonstrates the mystery of the Trinity: although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished by name, they are nevertheless joined by one divinity.

There was also before the treasuries—or chambers or bedchambers—a passageway ten cubits wide, facing inward, with a way one cubit wide. What the Septuagint added, “one hundred cubits in length,” is superfluous, because it is not found in the Hebrew. By adding it, they removed what is found in the Hebrew, namely, “facing inward, with a way one cubit wide,” which we translated from the Hebrew truth.

This signifies that before all the doors of the treasuries, chambers, or bedchambers there was a passageway ten cubits wide, a perfect number either because of the Decalogue or because of the mystery of the Gospel. For if one proceeds from one through two and three to the fourth number, the number ten [variant: “the denary number”] of the Gospels is produced. In its breadth the priests walk, proceeding before each treasury, provided that they always face inward toward the way that leads to one cubit—that is, toward the worship of the one divinity—for the Son says to the Father: “I have revealed your name to the men” (John 17:6). This is the way that faces inward, of which the Gospel says: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John 14:6), because no one comes to knowledge of the Father except through the Son.

It follows: “And their doors were toward the north, where the treasuries in the upper stories were lower, because they supported the porticoes that projected from them, from the lower and middle levels of the building. For they were three-storied and had no columns such as the columns of the courts; therefore they projected from the lower and middle levels, fifty cubits from the ground.”

The words “their doors” refer implicitly to the chambers or treasuries of which the preceding discussion spoke. These treasuries were in the upper levels—that is, in the upper chambers—but were lower. Elijah and Elisha ascended such upper chambers (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 4), as did the Lord when he was about to celebrate the Passover with his disciples (Mark 14), and Tabitha, who was raised because of the faith of the Apostle and the merit of her virtues (Acts 9).

These are the upper chambers of which it is written in the psalm: “He waters the mountains from his upper chambers” [variant: “from his higher places”] (Ps. 103:13). Unless someone has become a mountain and risen to higher things, he will not be watered by the Lord’s rains; according to the diversity of merits, one is watered from the first, second, and third upper chamber.

These treasuries too—that is, the treasuries of the Lord’s riches—are lower in the upper places (Eph. 3). For the higher someone is, the more he is cast down in humility with the Apostle, saying: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

The treasuries themselves were lower in the upper chambers because they supported the porticoes that projected from them, from the lower and middle levels of the building. He gives the reason why the treasuries placed in the upper chambers were lower: “Because,” he says, “they supported the porticoes,” which enjoyed the open air and projected from the lower and middle levels of the building. Thus the second upper chamber was higher than the pavement of the lower house, and the third upper chamber was higher than the second. The higher one ascended, the loftier was the upper chamber he used; yet it grew through humility, as the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him become the least of all” (Mark 9:34).

They were not supported by other columns, as we read of the columns of the courts; rather, they projected from the lower and middle levels, fifty cubits from the ground—the number of the remission of all debts. These, then, are the three-storied structures of which the instruction is given: “Describe them three times, with counsel and knowledge, so that you may answer words of truth to those proposed to you” (Prov. 22:20–21).

The lower and exterior structures require columns; the higher and interior ones, however, do not need columns—that is, the assistance of another.

After this it is said: “And the outer enclosure was alongside the treasuries that were on the way of the outer court, in front of the treasuries; its length was fifty cubits, because the length of the treasuries of the outer court was fifty cubits, while the length in front of the temple was one hundred cubits.”

The *peribolos* signifies the outer wall that enclosed the treasuries on the way of the outer court, having a length of fifty cubits. We have often spoken of the mystery of this number. The length in front of the temple, however, was not fifty cubits, as it was before the treasuries, but one hundred cubits, so that after the remission of all sins we might await perfect rewards in the number one hundred (Lev. 12).

In place of *peribolos*, or wall—the Hebrew word is *GADER*—the Septuagint translated “light,” which comes from outside and illuminates the eyes of our heart. The natural light within us, which operates in sensation, is not sufficient to possess the perfect radiance of knowledge unless it enters from outside through the grace of God. This first illuminates the eyes of our heart and makes bright the entire outer court, which extends fifty cubits in width. Afterwards, when we come before the front of the temple, we shall receive perfect rewards in the number one hundred.

Beneath the treasuries there was an entrance from the east for those entering them from the outer court. We must possess the riches of God, find an entrance from the outer court beneath the eastern treasuries, and come, across the width of the enclosure facing the eastern way, to the building separated for the saints, before which are the treasuries, and on that way the likeness of the treasuries that were on the northern way.

Although we reach the eastern entrance, the likeness of greater things is nevertheless present in lesser things. We cannot reach the eastern light except by the northern way—that is, by progressing through lesser and humbler things toward greater and higher things.

At this entrance the length was like the width, that is, the same measure in both dimensions. Every entrance, corresponding arrangement, and door had the same measure and likeness as the treasuries that were on the way facing south. Through the east, driving away the cold of the north, we arrive at the south, where the Bridegroom reclines at noon and dwells in full light.

At the head of the same way—the eastern way, which is open to those entering—there is a door. Unless it is opened by him who says, “I am the door” (John 10:9), and who possesses the key of David, we cannot reach the vestibule of the saints, separated by virtues, which receives those coming from the north (Isa. 22).

It is superfluous, following the Septuagint, to discuss each word of this passage, since both the things already explained are not free from obscurity and those we omit are nearly similar to those we have discussed.

### (Verses 13–14)

“And he said to me: ‘The northern treasuries and the southern treasuries that are before the detached building—these are the holy treasuries, in which the priests who approach the Lord in the Holy of Holies eat. There they shall place the holiest things, and the offering for sin and for guilt, for the place is holy. When the priests enter, they shall not go out from the holy place into the outer court; there they shall put down the garments in which they minister, because they are holy. They shall put on other garments, and then they shall go forth to the people.’”

The man who was the prophet’s guide, after leading him into the outer court and showing him everything narrated in the preceding passage, including the treasuries or chambers in which he had remained for a very long time, said to him: “These are the treasuries, chambers, and bedchambers toward the north and south, which are before the detached building. They are called holy treasuries, in which the priests who approach the Lord in the Holy of Holies eat.”

From this we learn that there are many varieties of food which priests may or may not eat; and even among those foods that may be eaten, they are not all consumed in every place, by everyone, or at every time.

I think that the northern and southern treasuries are those which contain either the simplicity of history or the mysteries of spiritual understanding, so that through the north we may come to the south. The letter and the foundations of history must not be read in such a way that we never come to the heights; nor should the roof of a beautiful building be set in place so that its foundations are not solid.

The priests who eat in the storerooms in which many riches are contained are those who approach the Lord. Scripture testifies concerning them (Exod. 24) that Moses approached the Lord, while the others were unable to draw near.

In the construction of the mystical temple and in the mystery of the Church there are many priests and apostolic men who approach the Lord—not in just any place, but in the Holy of Holies. What is said according to the Septuagint, “the sons of Zadok,” whose name means “just,” is not found in the Hebrew.

“There,” he says, “the priests shall place the holiest things and the offering”—that is, the victim of the burnt offering—“for sin and for ignorance.” Thus they should know not only to offer a continual sacrifice but also, according to the variation of times and the nature of sin and ignorance, to appease the Lord, because the place itself is holy and priestly dignity dwells there, able to pray on behalf of the others.

When they must go out to those who cannot penetrate the innermost parts of the temple or know the secrets of divine knowledge, “let the priests,” he says, “go forth to them outside into the outer court.” They should not go forth wearing the garments with which they were clothed within—namely, the bowels of mercy and the Lord and Savior, concerning which it is written: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14)—nor should they use the words about which God says: “My mystery is for me and for my own.” Otherwise they may fall into what the Savior forbids when he says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6).

Rather, they shall put down inside the garments with which they are clothed when they minister in the innermost parts of the temple. For these garments are holy and ought not to be brought before those who do not possess perfect holiness. They shall take other garments and then go forth to the people.

Thus, he says, they shall speak to the people in a manner that the people can hear. Therefore the Apostle also spoke to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 5), among whom fornication was heard of—a fornication such as did not even occur among the Gentiles: “I gave you milk to drink, not food,” that is, solid nourishment, “for you were not yet able to receive it” (1 Cor. 3:2). Again he says to them: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

For solid food not only does not benefit little ones and infants; it kills them, although it is appropriate for people of mature age.

The addition made by the Septuagint—“Therefore the priests shall not go out into the outer court, so that those who offer may always be holy”—we mark with an obelus, because it is not found in the Hebrew.

### (Verses 15 ff.)

“When he had completed the measurements of the inner house, he led me by the way of the gate that faced toward the eastern way, and he measured it on every side around [or: the likeness of the house around, in order]. [Note: Victorius deletes, on the authority of the Vulgate edition and the Hebrew codex, the words “on every side around,” which, he says, are also shown to be superfluous because “all around” is immediately added.] He measured toward the eastern wind [or: “and I stood behind the gate facing east”] with the measuring reed: five hundred reeds around, with the measuring reed, all around [the Vulgate: “the circuit”]. And he measured toward the northern wind five hundred reeds, with the measuring reed, around. And toward the southern wind he measured five hundred reeds, with the measuring reed, around. And toward the western wind he measured five hundred reeds, with the measuring reed. By the four winds he measured [the Vulgate adds “this”] its wall on every side around, five hundred in length and five hundred in width, separating between the sanctuary and the place of the common people.”

It should be known that after the eastern and northern winds, the Septuagint has the order reversed for the southern and western winds. They first placed the western wind—that is, the sea—and afterwards the southern wind, whereas in the Hebrew the southern wind is placed first and the western wind afterwards.

When Scripture now says, “When he had completed the measurements of the inner house, he led me by the way of the gate that faced toward the eastern way,” it shows that all the things mentioned above, both outside and inside and in the inner parts of the temple—that is, the Holy of Holies—properly pertain to the structure of the temple and of the inner temple.

Hence what follows: “He led me by the way of the gate that faced toward the eastern way, and he measured it on every side around,” or “the likeness of the house.” This demonstrates that what is seen is not the house itself but the likeness of the house, because now “we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13:12, 10).

Therefore Moses in the tabernacle and Solomon in the building made not the reality of the tabernacle or temple but its likeness and figure, so that through these lesser and earthly things we might understand the things that are heavenly and belong to the spiritual building.

The man who had led the prophet out did not first measure him in the outer court but by the way of the gate that faced toward the eastern way. First he measured toward the eastern wind, that is, toward the eastern region, five hundred reeds around; second, toward the north; third, toward the south; fourth, toward the sea, that is, toward the west. Thus, by the four winds, there was a wall around, both in length and in width—that is, in a square—which wall altogether measured two thousand reeds.

But if a reed was six cubits and one *palastē* (παλαιστή) [Note: Victorius prefers the more regular form, *palastē*, one *palastē*, etc.]—a *palastē* being the sixth part of a cubit—it is clear that the outer wall had two thousand reeds around, which make twelve thousand three hundred thirty-three and one-third cubits.

Let the prudent and diligent reader read the Book of Joshua, and he will find how this measurement is maintained in the surrounding suburbs. Therefore the legion of demons chose this number in the drowning of the swine (Luke 8), so that what had been set apart by the Lord’s command for those who serve God might be directed in the contrary direction toward the destruction of those who pursue a life worthy of filth and uncleanness.

The entire outer wall, which has an extremely broad length and width in the form of a square, contains the number of the Apostles, namely twelve thousand, so that a thousand may be assigned to each Apostle. Yet it does not reach the measure of the fullness of Christ and of the perfect man unless the *palastē* is added to it—three hundred thirty-three cubits and one-third—through which the mystery of the holy and venerable Trinity is demonstrated. It surrounds and fortifies everything and makes the inhabitants of its temple completely secure.

Therefore Noah’s ark has a length of three hundred cubits and a height of thirty cubits, which is completed in one cubit (Gen. 6). The fifty cubits added there in width signify, as we have often said, the mystery of remission. Hence the Lord came to baptism at the age of thirty, and this same prophet at the beginning of his book gives the thirtieth year. This number of three hundred and thirty is completed by the addition of three and one-third.

That which, through the simplicity of interpretation, we included both in the Septuagint and in our translation because we paid little attention amid the speed of dictation—“its wall on every side around, five hundred cubits in length and five hundred cubits in width”—is not contained in the Hebrew text. It simply has “five hundred in length and five hundred in width,” with “reeds” understood, just as it was said above: toward the eastern wind, toward the north, toward the south, and toward the sea, the wall of each side was measured by the man holding the reed with five hundred reeds.

The five-hundredth number, which is close to fifty, and which pertains to the remission of all sins, is demonstrated not only by the Old Scripture (Lev. 25) but also by the words of the Savior in the Gospel, when he says: “Two debtors owed money to a certain creditor: one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty” (Luke 7:41).

“And the wall separates between the sanctuary and the place of the common people.”

From this we understand that the entire description of the temple above was assigned to the ministries of the priests, who are the sons of Zadok. This wall, however, extending over so great a space and surrounding everything, separates the sanctuary from the place of the common people.

## Chapter XLIII

### Verses 1 and following

“And he led me [the Vulgate has *led*] to the gate that faced toward the eastern road; and behold, the glory of the God of Israel was entering by the eastern road. Its voice was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his majesty. And I saw a vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to destroy the city; and the appearance was according to what I had seen beside the river Chebar, and I fell upon my face. And the majesty of the Lord entered the Temple by the way of the gate that faced eastward. And the spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord. And I heard him speaking to me from the house. And the man who stood beside me said to me: ‘Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I dwell in the midst of the children of Israel forever. The house of Israel and their kings shall no longer defile my holy name with their fornications, with the ruins of their kings, with their fornications, with the ruins of their kings, and with the high places. They set their threshold beside my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, and there was a wall between me and them. They defiled my holy name by the abominations that they committed; therefore I consumed them in my anger. Now therefore let them put their fornication far from me, and the ruins of their kings; and I shall dwell in their midst forever.’

The Septuagint reads:

“And he brought me to the gate that faced toward the east ÷ and he led me out ** and behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming by the eastern road. The voice of the encampments was like the voice of many people repeating their cry, and the earth shone like lightning from the glory all around. [Victor: “brightness” (*fulgor*) instead of “lightning” (*fulgur*), from the Greek φέγγος, “radiance.”] And the vision that I saw was according to the vision that I had seen when I entered to anoint the city ÷ and the vision of the chariot that I saw ** according to the vision that I had seen above the river Chebar; and I fell upon my face. And the glory of the Lord entered the house by the way of the gate that faced toward the east. And the spirit took me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the house was full of the glory of the Lord. And I stood, and behold, there was a voice speaking to me from the house; and the man stood beside me and said to me: ‘You have seen, son of man, the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, in which my name shall dwell in the midst of the house of Israel forever. The house of Israel shall no longer defile my holy name, they and their rulers, by their fornication and by the murders of their rulers in their midst, when they set my threshold within their thresholds and my doorposts beside their doorposts. And they made my wall, as it were, a connecting partition between me and themselves; and they defiled my holy name by the iniquities that they committed. And I crushed them in my fury and in slaughter. And now let them cast their fornication and the murders of their rulers away from me; and I shall dwell in their midst forever.’”

First, we must speak about the variation among the translations. What the Septuagint has, “And he led me out,” is not found in the Hebrew. For if he had been brought to the gate that faced eastward, why was it necessary for him to be led out, since he had been brought in precisely to see what would happen at the eastern gate?

Next, where it says, “There was a voice belonging to him”—clearly referring to God—“like the voice of many waters,” which John also confirms in his Apocalypse, the Septuagint has: “And the voice of the encampments was like the voice of many people repeating their cry” (Revelation XIV).

Third, the Hebrew has: “I saw a vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to destroy the city.” The one who came was he who, at the beginning of this prophet’s book, was clothed in linen and had an inkwell at his loins, together with six others, in order to destroy the city—not to anoint it, as the Septuagint translated. Fourth, the Septuagint says: “And the vision of the chariot that I had seen,” which is not found in the Hebrew.

Let us speak briefly about each point, insofar as the difficulty permits explanation, lest, while striving for brevity, the veil remain upon us—not only the veil of Moses, but also that of the prophet Ezekiel—although we desire to contemplate the Lord’s truth with unveiled face (Exodus XXXIV; 2 Corinthians III).

The glory of the God of Israel therefore enters by the eastern road, by which it had also departed when the city of the Lord was struck in anger. It enters—or rather, returns—to it because he had shown that the Temple of the Lord was built upon the mountain. Yet much more is expressed in what follows: “The spirit lifted me up and brought me into the outer court, and behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord.” Here only the glory of the God of Israel enters; there, however, it is said that the fullness of the Lord’s glory was in the Temple. Isaiah also writes of this: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his house was full of his glory” (Isaiah VI, 1). When, with unveiled face, we contemplate the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the image of the Creator.

The voice also was God’s voice, like the voice of many waters—that is, of all the peoples throughout the world, as John the Evangelist interprets it (Revelation XIV)—or like the voice of encampments and like the voice of many people repeating their cry, so that the army might recognize the mysteries of God. Understanding this, Jacob called the name of that place “Encampments” (Genesis XXXII). Of these encampments it is also written: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing ones” (Psalm LXVII, 18). The voice of the encampments and of the multitude is called one voice because of their single agreement in the praise of God. The voice of those singing to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is repeated: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isaiah VI, 3).

It follows: “And the earth shone with his majesty” (Psalm XVIII). This was fulfilled especially at Christ’s coming, when “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Romans XVIII); and it is fulfilled daily in believers, and will be fulfilled perfectly when “this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality” (1 Corinthians XV).

As for what follows—“And I saw a vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to destroy the city,” for which the Septuagint translated, “when I entered to anoint the city”—the Hebrew is clear, whereas the Septuagint is extremely obscure. How did Ezekiel enter to anoint the city, and why did he fall at the prophecy and threat against it? Unless perhaps we say that the prophet’s correction is the city’s anointing, and that the anointing is the priestly and royal oil of gladness. Those who willingly receive it and wish to hear it become the Lord’s anointed, concerning whom it is written: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Psalm CIV, 15).

According to the anagogical interpretation, he can anoint the city of which it is written: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm LXXXVI, 2)—he who saw the vision of the chariot and of the mysteries of God, which Ezekiel beheld above the river Chebar, whose name signifies burden and weight.

For what is heavier than the Babylonian rivers, beside which David sat and wept when he remembered Zion? Of these it is written: “For the form of this world is passing away” (Psalm CXXXVI). I think that nothing in the confusion of this age is permanent; everything passes away and flows onward (1 Corinthians VII, 31). Whoever considers these things will fall upon his face, understanding how far he is from the majesty of God, and will bend his knees before the Father in the name of Jesus Christ.

“And when,” he says, “I had fallen, the majesty of the Lord entered the Temple by way of the gate that faced eastward. Immediately the spirit lifted me up—for while lying there I could not proceed—and brought me into the inner court, since I had fallen outside. And I, who had previously seen the glory of the God of Israel coming by the eastern road, saw his house filled with the glory of the Lord, and I heard a voice speaking to me from the inner house.”

What this voice said, Scripture does not relate, unless perhaps it was what the Apostle says: “I heard ineffable words which it is not permitted to a human being to speak” (2 Corinthians XII, 4).

But the man, he says, who stood beside the prophet said to him—by whom we clearly understand the Lord. For to whom else could what follows apply: “Son of man, the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I dwell in the midst of the children of Israel forever,” except to him who dwells in the Church amid the children of Israel who see God, and dwells forever, not temporarily as in Solomon’s Temple?

His place is that of which it is written: “His place has become peace” (Psalm LXXV, 2), which surpasses all understanding. And the place of the soles of his feet is indicated by the words of the Apostles: “Let us worship in the place where his feet have stood” (Psalm XXXI, 7). Beautifully he says, “have stood”: in the Church the Lord’s feet stand; in the synagogue they walk and pass by.

To show that this is spoken of the Church, it is added: “The house of Israel shall no longer defile my holy name”—which applies particularly to those who dwell in the Church in holy conduct.

He then makes clearer who previously defiled God’s holy name: “They and their kings”—both people and priests—“in their fornications,” by which they fornicated against God, “and in the ruins of their kings,” who vainly assume the royal name through pride. Finally it follows: “And in the high places.” An arrogant mind offends God; a humble one calls forth mercy.

After their pride—or rather, through their pride—they built their threshold beside God’s threshold and their doorposts beside his. Let women weighed down with sins hear this in its literal sense—women who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never attaining knowledge of the truth. A mind joined to God—not proximity to churches or a nearby dwelling—calls forth God’s clemency; rather, the Lord’s indignation is aroused when an unworthy inhabitant occupies places consecrated to God.

“They built,” he says, “their threshold beside my threshold,” so that there would be nothing between the sacred and the profane, “and their doorposts beside my doorposts,” so that laypeople and priests would have one and the same entrance. Hence the Apostle also says: “Let a person examine himself, and so let him approach the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Corinthians XI, 28).

And to make his statement more serious, he joins the following verse: “And there was a wall between me and them”—so that priestly sacrifices and the places containing the mysteries of Christ’s body and blood would be separated by only a very short wall.

“And they defiled,” he says, “my holy name by the abominations that they committed.” What benefit is there in living nearby, or in having a wall between our cell and the Lord’s altar, when in the things we do secretly—and which it is shameful even to mention—the Lord’s name is contaminated and defiled?

I think that no one defiles the Lord’s name except one who appears to believe in his name and is reckoned by his title. Just as the one who previously believed in Christ takes Christ’s members and makes them members of a prostitute, so the one who first received faith in God’s name defiles the name of God.

Otherwise, although the pagan and the Jew are defiled and contaminated—indeed, are themselves defilement and contamination—they cannot defile or contaminate God’s name. Those defile it to whom it is said: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans II, 24).

For these reasons, therefore, I consumed them in my anger, because they did what we have described. Yet the merciful Lord again commands the prophet to order them to remove their former fornications far from him, to abandon the ruins of their kings and rulers, and to cast them away not so much from himself as from God. He immediately promises the rewards of good works, saying: “And I shall dwell in their midst.” Of this the Gospel says: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John I, 26). He will dwell not for a short time, as in the synagogue, but forever, as is demonstrated in the Church of Christ.

### Verses 10 and following

“But you, son of man, show the house of Israel the Temple, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities, measure its construction, and be embarrassed by all that they have done. Show them the form of the house and its construction, its exits and entrances, its entire description, all its ordinances, its whole arrangement [the Vulgate adds *of it*], and all its laws; and write them before their eyes, so that they may keep all its arrangements [the Vulgate has *descriptions*] and its ordinances, and perform them.

“This is the law of the house: upon the summit of the mountain, all its boundaries around it shall be the Holy of Holies [the Vulgate has *is* the Holy of Holies]. This, therefore, is the law of the house.”

The Septuagint reads:

“And you, son of man, show the house of Israel the house, and they shall cease from their sins, and its vision and its arrangement; and they shall endure their punishment for all that they have done. And you shall describe the house and its preparation, its exits and entrances, its substance and all its ordinances, all its lawful requirements and all its laws; you shall show them and describe them before them. And they shall keep all my judgments and all my ordinances, and they shall perform them. And the description of the house upon the summit of the mountain: all its boundaries around it are the Holy of Holies. This is the law of the house.”

It is no small task to demonstrate to those who hear what you have seen with the eyes of the flesh or perceived in the mind, so that they themselves may seem to have seen it with you. For this reason Josephus also writes that those who were sent by Jesus son of Nave to survey the land were *geometers* (*γεωμέτραι*), and that they possessed the art now regarded as belonging to philosophers—geometry. [The land to be surveyed was Jericho, not the Holy Land, as others note; the latter explorers were sent by Moses, not Joshua, and Joshua himself was one of them (Numbers XIII). Nor, in this passage, does Josephus (*Antiquities*, V.1) state that those sent by Joshua were skilled in geometry.]

The house is therefore shown to the house of Israel, that is, to those who contemplate God in their minds. It is the Temple that Ezekiel saw situated upon the mountain, and not merely upon the mountain but, as it is now said, upon the summit of the mountain. We must not suppose that this is the Temple narrated as having been built by Solomon in the books of Kings and Chronicles.

That Temple belongs to another order and has different measurements in every part. It is so much inferior to the Temple now shown to Ezekiel that not only its worshipers and custodians but even its builder, Solomon himself, sinned and offended God, although afterward he performed repentance, writing Proverbs, in which he says: “At the end I repented, and I looked to choose discipline” (Proverbs XXIV, 2).

But what is shown to Ezekiel, and through Ezekiel to the house of Israel, is such that whoever sees it with the mind will cease from his iniquities—not from some, but from all—or, as the Hebrew contains it, will be ashamed and endure his punishment for all that he has done.

He endures the punishment of his iniquities who ceases to commit former sins. It greatly benefits the one who has sinned previously to see the house of God and understand the arrangement of all its construction, so that he may cease to sin and, possessing desire for it, say to the Lord: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm XXV, 8). And again: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm XXVI, 4)—when I shall begin to live and to be with Christ, who is the life of believers.

It follows: “Its exits and entrances,” with “of the house” understood. The exits are those of people who go out to those who are outside; the entrances are those of people who penetrate inward through the discipline of teachers.

“And its entire description,” he says—or “its substance,” as the Septuagint translated—which refers not so much to the nature of the house as to its furnishings and riches.

“And all its ordinances, its whole arrangement, and all the laws of the Temple you shall show them,” to those who have endured the punishment of their iniquities and ceased—or have been ashamed—of what they previously did. He shows it to them for this reason: so that they may keep everything that has been commanded.

For it is of no benefit to know the description of the house and all its arrangements, concerning which it is written, “There are many dwelling places with my Father” (John XIV, 2), and again, “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the children of Israel,” or of the angels of God (Deuteronomy XXXII), unless you do what has been commanded.

The house, the law of all God’s ordinances, and the city established upon the summit of the mountain must be understood as that of which it is written: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew I, 14). And: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm XLV, 4). This clearly refers to the Church, which is situated upon that mountain that is at the summit of all mountains and from which the prince of Tyre was wounded.

All the boundaries and limits of this house are the Holy of Holies. In that house—that is, in the tabernacle built by Moses and in the Temple constructed by Solomon—only the inner parts, where the cherubim, the mercy seat, the ark of the covenant, and the table of incense were located, were called the Holy of Holies.

But in this house shown to Ezekiel, which is established upon the summit of the mountain, all its boundaries are reckoned as the Holy of Holies. What follows—“This is the law of the house”—either refers to the preceding matters, which have already been discussed, or to those that will be discussed later.

### Verses 13 and following

“These are the measurements of the altar, in the true cubit, which had a cubit and a palm [or *παλαιστήν*, a handbreadth]. Its hollow was a cubit; and its width was a cubit; and its rim, from its edge around it, was one palm [the Vulgate has *one palm*]. This also was the trench of the altar.

“And from the hollow of the ground to the lowest ledge were two cubits, and its width was one cubit; and from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge were four cubits, and its width was one cubit. The *ariel* itself was four cubits, and from the *ariel* upward were four horns.

“And the *ariel* was twelve cubits in length, by twelve cubits in width, square, with equal sides. And the ledge was fourteen cubits long, by fourteen cubits wide at its four corners [Victor likewise supplies the word “cubits” here from the Hebrew and Vulgate]; and its rim around it was half a cubit, and its hollow was one cubit around. Its steps faced toward the east.”

The Septuagint reads:

“And these are the measurements of the altar, in a perfect cubit: a cubit and a *παλαιστής* [handbreadth]. The height of its hollow around it was a cubit, and its width a cubit; and its *gisus* [rim] by its edge around it was one palm.

“And this is the height of the altar, from the depth of its foundation in its hollow to the great mercy seat, which was beneath: two cubits, and its width one cubit. And from the smaller mercy seat to the larger mercy seat, four cubits; and its width one cubit. And the *ariel* was four cubits, and from the *ariel* to the upper parts of the horns was one cubit.

“The *ariel* itself was twelve cubits in length and twelve cubits in width, with four corners on each of its sides. And the mercy seat was fourteen cubits in width, along its four sides; and its *gisus*, turning around it, was half a cubit; and its circumference was one cubit around. Its steps faced toward the east.”

It is written: “Who shall investigate the abyss and wisdom?” (Ecclesiastes I, 2). And: “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans XI, 33). Who can discover its profound depths?

It would be a considerable undertaking to compare Solomon’s Temple with this Temple, and all its parts and tabernacles with it. Since this is extremely difficult, let us for the present compare, in a small measure, the altar shown to Ezekiel with the altar that we read about in Exodus (Exodus XXXVIII).

There the altar is described as five cubits in length and five cubits in width—that is, square—and three cubits in height. Here, however, departing from the five senses, it extends toward unity, in which the perfect or true cubit is placed, to which the palm is joined—that is, the *παλαιστή*, which, as we said above, contains a sixth part of a cubit.

In its hollow—that is, in the altar—was a cubit, which received the things consumed by fire; and another cubit was in its width, so that the interior parts, the hidden places and spaces of the altar indicated by its width, would be bounded by one cubit.

What follows—“And its rim as far as its edge”—for which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion rendered “boundary,” the Septuagint again translated *gisus*. As I said earlier, I cannot know the reason for this word, nor can I confidently say what language it belongs to. I can only alert the reader that where I have here translated it as “boundary,” I translated it above as “crown.” [Victor: “Rather below”; for a little later Jerome renders the Hebrew word itself, which here he translates “boundary,” as “crown.”]

Victor notes: “Recall what we annotated a little earlier, column 497.”

It is briefly shown that around the altar itself—that is, at its margin and circular edge—there was a projecting lip, like a crown in the form of a lily, possessing great beauty in appearance. This rim, or *gisus*, extended around it to the width of one palm, or *παλαιστής*.

The trench of the altar—or its depth and height, for which the Hebrew has *GAB*—was two cubits from the hollow of the ground to the lowest ledge, or to the greatest mercy seat, and its width was one cubit.

The lower and deeper parts, joined to the earth, are contained by the number two, which is also assigned to unclean animals (Genesis VII). But the upper parts, which reach the ledge or mercy seat—which Theodotion called by the Hebrew name *AZARA*—have a width of one cubit, so that the number two may pass into the solitary number, and the good of marriage, which is below, may reach the blessedness of unity.

Victor notes: “Elsewhere, *azera*. The Greek of Theodotion has ἀζαρά.”

What follows—“And from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge, four cubits, and its width one cubit,” for which the Septuagint has, “And from the smaller mercy seat to the larger mercy seat,” and for which Theodotion translated *AZARA* in both places—is to be understood as follows.

The smaller mercy seat is the stone cut from the mountain without hands; the larger mercy seat is the stone that grew into a great mountain and filled the whole world (Daniel II).

Or, according to another interpretation, the smaller mercy seat is when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians II); the larger mercy seat is when he received the glory that he had with the Father before the world existed (John XVII).

First we recognize Christ’s humility, and thus we reach the height of his divinity. Yet the mercy seat of both natures—the lesser and the greater—belongs to the mystery of one altar.

Between the two mercy seats, the smaller and the larger, there were four cubits, signifying the four elements of the world, which themselves reach the height of one cubit.

It must also be observed that in the measurement of the altar the first cubit in width is joined to nothing else but is perfected by its own unity. The second cubit of width, after two cubits, rises to the summit; and the third cubit, after the smaller and larger mercy seats, through the four elements, extends toward the mystery of one cubit. The first, second, and third cubits in the Lord’s altar are therefore not to be called first, second, and third, but one, one, and one.

The *ariel* itself was four cubits, and it had four horns upward from the *ariel*; or, as the Septuagint says, one cubit extended from the *ariel* to the upper parts of the horns.

*Ariel* (the Hebrew form is absent in the supplied text), according to many, is interpreted as “God is my light.” We have discussed this more fully in the prophet Isaiah, where it is written: “Woe to you, city of Ariel, which David besieged,” or “surrounded” (Isaiah XXIX, 2).

But in my opinion it means “lion” or “strong one of God.” This name properly refers to the altar, in which there is either God’s illumination or his lion and strength. Jacob says to Judah: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son. Having rested, you lay down like a lion, and like a lioness—who will rouse him?” (Genesis XLIX, 9).

It is four cubits, and it has four horns; or the four upper parts of the horns end in one cubit. Thus the measure of the Gospels and the strength extending throughout the whole world are shown under God’s illumination and the strength of the lion, and the divine confession reaches one cubit.

To make the obscurity of the present passage gradually clearer, it follows:

“And the *ariel* was twelve cubits in length, by twelve cubits in width, square, with equal sides.”

No one doubts that this refers to the twelve tribes written about in John’s Apocalypse, and to the number of the Apostles, concerning whose mystery I remember having spoken above (Revelation VII).

Through the four sides of the world, twelve cubits on each side together make forty-eight cubits—the number of the priestly cities—so that, with these foundations distributed throughout the whole world, the strength of the Church may be made firm.

Moreover, the ledge—for which the Septuagint has “mercy seat,” Theodotion, as above, *AZARA*, and Symmachus *περιδρομή* (*peridromē*, “circuit”)—was fourteen cubits long by fourteen cubits wide, at its four corners, and its rim around it was half a cubit. For this the Septuagint again translated *gisus*, while “its hollow,” or, according to Symmachus, “its completion and perfection,” was one cubit around.

This secretly indicates that our Lord, who is truly called the mercy seat not only for our sins but for the whole world, came through fourteen generations from Abraham to David, and again through another fourteen to the captivity of Jechoniah, and by the mystery of the same number descended to earthly things. Thus, in the third *τεσσαρακαιδεκάς*—the third group of fourteen—and by the mystery of the divine number [another reading: *gift*], he saved the four corners of the world, concerning which it is written: “Many shall come from east and west, and from north and south, and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VIII, 11).

What follows—“And the crown,” or *gisus*, “around it”—with “the mercy seat” understood, had half a cubit; and the hollow of that mercy seat, or its completion and perfection, which Symmachus translated as *περιδρομή* (*peridromē*), had one cubit around it.

This signifies that both sinners and the righteous are saved by the Lord’s mercy, as the Apostle Paul says: “We have been reconciled to God through the blood of his Son” (Romans V, 10).

Of sinners it is said that they have a measure of half a cubit around them; nevertheless, they are saved by the mercy of the Creator, according to what is written in the Psalm: “For nothingness you will save them” (Psalm LV, 8).

Of the righteous: they are saved in the solitary and perfect number one, and they imitate the one divinity, as the same Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians V, 19).

As for what is placed at the end of this testimony—“And its steps faced toward the east”—the steps of this mercy seat must be understood either as the twenty-four books of the Old Testament, which had harps in John’s Apocalypse (Chapter V) and crowns upon their heads, or as the mystery of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in which true propitiation is given to us.

Editorial note: “I think this passage, formerly corrupted by ignorant critics, should be left unchanged, since no manuscripts provide assistance. For what Rabanus reads, ‘seventy-four books . . .,’ must be accepted neither as a satisfactory restoration nor as helpful for recovering the reading, and it lies in a still graver error. It is clear that Jerome compares the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse with the twenty-four books of the Old Testament; likewise, in the prologue to the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, he says that writings not found among the Hebrews, and not belonging to the twenty-four elders, must be cast far away. But what could be equally discordant with this as the idea that books have harps and crowns upon their heads? The elders must certainly be mentioned, to whom these things refer. Thus, where Rabanus has ‘seventy-four,’ I would read ‘twenty-four elders’; and I conjecture that the passage should be restored as follows: ‘or the twenty-four elders in the books of the Old Testament,’ and so forth.”

To put it more plainly, the number of the steps is left uncertain so that, however earnestly we may be able to climb toward higher things, we may still consider ourselves placed among the lower, and may bear in mind the Psalmist’s words: “They shall go from strength to strength” (Psalm LXXXIII, 8).

### (Verses 18ff.)

And he said to me: “Son of man, thus says the Lord God: These are the rites of the altar on whatever day it is constructed, so that a burnt offering may be offered upon it and blood poured out. You shall give to the priests, the Levites who are from the seed of Zadok, who approach me,” says the Lord God, “a bull from the herd as a sin offering. You shall take some of its blood and place it on the four horns [the Vulgate adds: “of it”], on the four corners of the ledge, and on the rim all around; and you shall cleanse and make atonement for it. You shall take the bull that was offered for sin and burn it in a separate place of the house outside the sanctuary. On the second day you shall offer an unblemished he-goat as a sin offering, and they shall make atonement for the altar as they made atonement with the bull.”

**LXX:** And he said to me: “Son of man, thus says the Lord God: These are the ordinances of the altar on the day when it is made, so that burnt offerings may be offered upon it and blood poured upon it. You shall give to the Levitical priests who are from the seed of Zadok and approach me,” says the Lord God, “a bull from the cattle as a sin offering. They shall take some of its blood and place it on the four horns of the altar, on its base all around, and they shall cleanse and make atonement for it. They shall take the bull for sin, and it shall be burned in a separate place of the house outside the holy place. On the second day they shall take two unblemished kids from the goats as a sin offering, and they shall make atonement for the altar as they made atonement with the bull.”

After he had shown the prophet the altar, its one-cubit measurement, then two cubits, and again one cubit and four cubits, and, thirdly, one cubit; also twelve cubits by twelve cubits, and the altar’s four horns; likewise the Ariel, twelve cubits by twelve cubits, and the ledge—that is, the mercy seat—fourteen cubits by fourteen cubits; also its rim and its recess, half a cubit [Note: [Col. 0424D] The Vatican Codex omits “and one cubit”] and one cubit all around; and the steps toward the east, whose number is uncertain—the man whose staff and cord were in his hand spoke and taught him how, once the altar had been completed, the altar ought to be atoned for [Col. 0424D] and consecrated.

First a victim is offered and given to the priests from the tribe of Levi, who are from the seed of Zadok. Why the Septuagint calls him “Sadduc,” I do not know. Now Zadok is interpreted as “just”; and, according to the Septuagint and Theodotion, a calf is offered; according to Symmachus, a bull, which in Hebrew is called **PHAR**. [Col. 0425A]

The bull that was sacrificed for us is named by many passages of Scripture, and especially by the Epistle of Barnabas, which is counted among the apocryphal writings. The he-goat is offered on the second day. Hence, when they are about to celebrate Passover, they take from the flock a lamb and a kid; and those who could not celebrate the first Passover celebrate it in the second month. One of these pertains to the righteous, the other to penitents.

But if we prefer the translation of the Septuagint, who said, “On the second day they shall take two unblemished kids as a sin offering,” what we are about to say is indeed bold; nevertheless, the opinion of others must be stated plainly. They say that, after the Lord’s Passion, two unblemished kids were offered upon the Lord’s altar: James and Stephen. One of them was from the number of the apostles, [Col. 0425B] the other was chief among the seven chosen for the Lord’s ministry (Acts XXII).

This is the James who saw the Savior transfigured on the mountain (ibid., VII), who witnessed the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter rising with the Lord, Peter, and John (Matt. XVII), and who, in the list of the apostles in which the names are paired, is placed before his brother (Mark IX). Herod killed him (Matt. IX), and, like an unblemished kid, sacrificed him on the second day after the Savior’s Passion (Mark III).

The Jews also overwhelmed Stephen with stones—Stephen, against whose wisdom and teaching no one could prevail (Acts XIV), and who saw the Son standing at the right hand of the Father and said (Acts XIV, 7): “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Just as the Apostle calls certain believers the firstfruits of Achaia and Asia, [Col. 0425C] so these too were the firstfruits of the martyrs (1 Cor. XVI), whom the confession of Christ afterward crowned.

This also should be noted: the whole bull is offered as a burnt offering, and the fat of its body is consumed by divine fire. For although we once knew Christ [Note: [Col. 0425D] In the Vatican Codex the words “according to the flesh” are absent] according to the flesh, nevertheless we now know him no longer according to the flesh (2 Cor. V, 16). But James and Stephen, who were offered on the second day—or the he-goat, which according to the Hebrew is reported as having been offered—is indeed offered as a victim, while the burnt offering is reserved for the presence of the Lord.

The blood that is taken, of which Peter speaks, “You were redeemed [Note: [Col. 0426D] Victorius reads “we were redeemed,” in accordance with the Greek text] from your vain manner of life inherited from your fathers by the precious blood of Christ” (1 Pet. I), and which the Apostle Paul teaches: “You were bought at a price” (1 Cor. VII, 23); and elsewhere: “Making peace through the blood of his cross, whether on earth or in the heavens” (Col. I, 20)—this signifies that by the Savior’s blood the four horns of the altar, that is, the four regions of the world, are purified. The rim of the mercy seat, or its bases, is sprinkled all around, so that everything may be cleansed and the atonement may be firm.

The reason, moreover, that on the second day either the two kids of which we spoke above or a he-goat is taken is that this animal is always hastening toward the heights, suffers no danger on precipices, and finds a path where other animals meet destruction. Hence in Greek the herd of goats and he-goats is called the life of those who dwell on high: **αἰπόλιον**, as though **αἰποπόλιον**, since **αἴπος** means “high place,” and **πόλιον** [manuscripts: **πολεῖν**] means “way of life” or “conduct.”

Moreover, Christ’s altar is cleansed by blood, so that the prayers of the saints may pass pure to God.

This also should be noted: according to the Hebrew, Ezekiel himself, like a priest, is commanded to take the bull, make a burnt offering, and sprinkle its blood all around, both on the altar and on its corners and rim, or base. The Septuagint translators, however, indicate that other priests are to do this—those of whom it is said: “You shall give it to the Levitical priests who are from the seed of Zadok and approach me.”

### (Verses 23ff.)

“And when you have finished making atonement for it, you shall offer an unblemished bull from the herd and an unblemished ram from the flock. You shall offer them in [Col. 0426B] the presence of the Lord, and the priests shall sprinkle salt upon them; and they shall offer them as a burnt offering to the Lord. For seven days you shall make a he-goat as a sin offering each day, and they shall offer an unblemished bull from the herd and an unblemished ram from the flock. For seven days they shall make atonement for the altar and cleanse it, and they shall fill its hand. When the days have been completed, on the eighth day and thereafter the priests shall offer upon the altar your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, and I shall be reconciled to you,” says the Lord God.

**LXX:** And when you have completed the atonement, they shall offer an unblemished bull from the cattle and an unblemished ram from the sheep; and you shall offer them before the Lord, and the priests shall sprinkle salt upon them; and they shall offer them as burnt offerings to the Lord. For seven days you shall make a kid as a sin offering each day, and for seven days they shall make an unblemished bull from the cattle and a ram from the sheep. They shall make atonement for the altar, cleanse it, fill their hands, and complete the days. From the eighth day onward the priests shall offer upon the altar your burnt offerings and those for your well-being, and I shall receive you, says the Lord God.

After the altar and its measurements had been shown on the summit of the mountain, and its atonement and consecration had again been displayed to the prophet through one unblemished bull and a he-goat—or two kids, the first of which we referred to the Lord Savior, and the two that followed to the apostles and ministers—so that, in the consecration of the spiritual altar properly belonging to the Church, the Law and the Prophets might not appear to have been excluded, therefore, once the altar has been consecrated, an unblemished bull [Col. 0426D] and a ram are taken and offered in the presence of the Lord. The sons of Zadok—that is, the priests of the righteous—sprinkle salt upon their heads, so that both the Law and the Prophets may be seasoned with the flavor of the Gospel.

There is no sacrifice, according to the command of the Law and the Apostle’s interpretation, which says (Col. IV, 6), “Let your speech be seasoned with salt,” that lacks salt.

Both are offered as burnt offerings to the Lord, so that the body of the fat letter, signified in the Law, and the clouded substance of prophecy may, by the fire of the Lord—that is, by the Holy Spirit, of whom Paul says, “fervent in spirit” (Rom. XII, 11)—be changed into a spiritual and subtle substance.

We wish to know more clearly who the unblemished bull from the herd and the ram with the purest fleece from the sheep are. Let us understand them as Moses and Elijah (Num. XII; 1 Kings XIX): the former was the meekest of all the human beings who lived upon the earth; the latter resembled Moses in the ardor of his faith. Hence he dared to say, “I alone am left.”

There should be no difficulty because what is written in the Hebrew is, “You shall offer the bull,” whereas in the Septuagint it is, “The priests shall offer it.” Ezekiel himself, to whom these things are said, belongs to the priestly number, being of full and mature age; and grace added a priestly rank to his prophecy.

Moses and Elijah also appear on the mountain with the Lord—that is, the Law and the Prophets, who announced to him what he was to suffer at Jerusalem.

Once the altar has been cleansed, for seven days a he-goat or kid [Col. 0427B] is offered daily as a sin offering, together with an unblemished bull from the herd and a ram from the flock, so that through these seven days of sacrifices the altar may be cleansed completely.

In the seven days the sabbath rest is revealed, which, according to the Apostle (Hebr. IV), is reserved for the people of God. In it we hope for eternal and true rest, and will by no means perform the servile work of sins [another reading: “will perform”].

In the he-goat, the bull, and the ram, three general kinds of sin are indicated, to which the entire human race is subject. For we sin either in thought, in speech, or in deed. Thought is referred to the ram, since it is the first of all sins and from it the other two sins arise. The kid or he-goat refers to utterance or speech, which always debates matters of higher things. Deeds, however, are properly assigned to the bull, [Col. 0427C] because it is devoted to the plow, labor, and earthly works.

These unblemished offerings, therefore, we ought to offer to God for seven days of the true and perfect Sabbath, and cleanse the altar, so that our prayer may reach God pure.

What follows—“And they shall cleanse it and fill its hand,” which both the Hebrew and the other interpreters have translated—means that the gifts of the altar itself, for whose cleansing the sacrifice is offered, must also be completed, just as an offering is made for the priests, the people, and the high priest, so that nothing may appear to have stood empty in the presence of the Lord.

For this reason the Septuagint rendered it, “They shall cleanse it and fill their hands,” with “the priests” understood. When they have been filled with good works—for this is what “hands filled” signifies—after the Sabbath has passed, let them come to the eighth day of resurrection and say with the Apostle, “We have risen with Christ” (Rom. VI; Col. III). Let them extend beyond the eighth day toward the heavenly things, and offer on our behalf burnt offerings, or things that are for the peace of our sins and for our salvation, so that through the fire of the Holy Spirit everything we think, say, and do may be changed into a spiritual substance; and that the Lord, pleased by sacrifices of this kind, may become propitious toward us.

### Chapter XLIV—(Verses 1ff.)

And he turned me toward the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary, which faced east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: “This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered [Col. 0428A] through it (or: will enter through it); and it shall remain closed for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord. He shall go out by way of the vestibule—that is, the **Aelam**—of the gate, and he shall go out by way of it.”

For what is written in the Hebrew, “It shall remain closed for the prince,” the Septuagint translated, “It shall remain closed, because the ruler himself shall sit in it.”

There are many gates that Scripture mentions in the description of Ezekiel’s temple, both within and outside. The preceding discourse also passed through the figure of the altar, its consecration, and its sacrifices. Once that was completed, it came to the gate of the outer sanctuary, which faced east and was closed. Immediately the man who was guiding the prophet and showing him everything spoke to him: “This gate that you see closed shall always remain closed; it shall not be opened, [Col. 0428B] and no man shall pass through it.”

He gives the reason why it is always closed: “Because the Lord God of Israel has entered—or will enter—through it.” According to the Hebrew it shall remain closed “for the prince,” whom the Septuagint translated as “the ruler.”

This prince and ruler—that is, the **NASI**—shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord; and he shall enter by way of the gate’s vestibule and go out by way of the same gate.

What is this gate that is always closed, through which only the Lord God of Israel enters? Surely it is the one of which the Savior speaks in the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, and woe to you, lawyers, who take away the key of knowledge: you yourselves do not enter, and you prevent those who are entering” (Matt. XXIII, 23).

Under the name of a book Isaiah also writes about this gate: “The words of this book shall be like the words of a sealed book. When it is given to a person who does not know letters and one says to him, ‘Read,’ he will answer, ‘I do not know letters.’ And they will give it to a person who knows letters, saying, ‘Read’; and he will say, ‘I cannot read, because it is sealed’” (Isa. XXIX, 11).

This is the book whose seals no one can loose and open, neither in heaven nor on earth nor under the earth, except the one of whom it is said in the Apocalypse of John: “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root and Offspring of David, has conquered, so that he may open the book and loose its seals” (Rev. V, 5).

Before the Savior assumed a human body and humbled himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II), the Law and the Prophets were closed, as was all knowledge of the Scriptures; paradise was closed. But after he hung upon the cross and said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43), immediately the veil of the temple was torn, and everything was opened. Once the veil had been removed, we say: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory” (2 Cor. III, 18).

But if everything has been unveiled—for in Christ, according to Paul’s statement, everything is revealed (ibid., XIII)—how will the gate be closed and not be opened, and no man pass through it? From this we learn that, although we may have attained the highest knowledge, in comparison with divine knowledge we now know and understand only in part. But when the perfect comes, then what is partial will be destroyed.

Hence in another passage the Apostle speaks of himself as imperfect, and again as perfect. If this is not interpreted, it appears contradictory. For he says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect” [Note: [Col. 0429D] Victor supplies the remainder of the verse: “but I pursue, if I may apprehend that for which I was apprehended by Christ Jesus,” which more suitably supports what Jerome intends]. “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God” (Phil. III, 12, 14).

When we thought that, according to his own profession, he was not yet perfect and was seeking rather than having found the truth, he says not only that he himself but also that others are perfect: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this” [Phil. III, 15].

The meaning of this passage is as follows: In comparison with other people, who do not care about knowledge of the Scriptures or the mysteries of God, I confess that I am perfect. But insofar as concerns knowledge of the divine majesty, I now see in a riddle, through cloud and darkness, and I say with the prophet: “Your knowledge is wonderful beyond me; it is strengthened, and I cannot attain it” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 6).

This gate, therefore, which is closed to everyone—for no man will pass through it—shall be closed for the prince or ruler. At his coming it will be opened: he will sit in it to eat bread before the Lord. Of him he himself confesses in the Gospel, saying: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work” (John IV, 34).

He is the prince and high priest according to the order of Melchizedek, the victim and the priest, who in the presence of the Father eats the heavenly bread with us and drinks the wine of which he speaks in the Gospel: “I shall not drink of the fruit of this vine until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. XXVI, 29)—in that kingdom of which he also says elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21).

The gate shall remain closed. No one can, in view of the majesty of the matter, understand the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion and of his body and blood.

Our prince is of such goodness and mercy that, although he alone sits in the closed gate and eats bread before the Lord, he wishes to have many companions at his table and banquet, and says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III, 20).

He alone eats bread before the Lord because his substance and divine nature are separated from the substances of all creatures. He enters and goes out through the same vestibule gate, because [Note: [Col. 0430D] Victor substitutes “is” for “and”] he is both within and without—that is, infused into and surrounding all things. He enters through the gate in order to bring in with him those who cannot enter without his teaching and help; and he goes out in order again to bring others in and to speak to those who cannot grasp more difficult matters.

That the eastern gate outside the boundaries of the world is always closed and is in no way accessible to human sight is proved by John’s Gospel, which says: “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known” (John I, 18).

It is as though he had said in other words: “It shall remain closed for the prince.” The prince alone shall sit in it, to eat the bread of perfect and consummated knowledge. “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27).

Some people aptly understand the closed gate through which only the Lord God of Israel enters, and the ruler for whom the gate is closed, as the Virgin Mary, who remained a virgin both before and after childbirth. For when the angel was saying, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35), and when he was born, she remained forever a virgin. This confounds those who suppose that after the Savior’s birth she had sons by Joseph, on account of the brothers of his who are named in the Gospel (Mark III). Concerning this small question, I know that in Rome, during my youth, I wrote a not very large book against Helvidius, a heretic of that time.

### (Verses 4ff.)

And he brought me by way of the northern gate, before the house; and I saw, and behold, the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord [the Vulgate reads: “filled the house of the Lord”], and I fell [Note: [Col. 0430D] “Instead of ‘before,’ Victor restored ‘upon my face’ in accordance with the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin codices] upon my face.

And the Lord said to me: “Son of man, set your heart, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears everything that I shall say to you concerning all the ceremonies of the house of the Lord and all its laws; and set your heart upon the ways of the temple through all the exits of the sanctuary.”

The man who guides the prophet, by whose showing him everything in the temple he comes to know it all, after showing him the gate that was closed and was never to be reopened, yet open to the one who entered through closed doors, leads the prophet to the way of the northern gate, which was itself also in view of the house—without doubt signifying the temple.

When the prophet saw opposite him the house of the Lord filled with the glory of the Lord—that same house, namely, which, positioned in the northern region, he was looking toward—he immediately fell upon his face, unable to bear the majesty of the Lord’s glory. Therefore, since he had been cast down in humility, the one who speaks to him is not merely a man but the Lord: “Son of man, set your heart,” and so forth.

At the completion of the tabernacle and of the temple building constructed by Solomon, the glory of the Lord appeared; afterward it was destroyed in comparison with the glory of the Gospel, as the Apostle says: “Indeed, what was glorified was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory. For if what is destroyed came through glory, much more will what remains be in glory” (2 Cor. III, 10).

We must take care not to understand the destruction of the former glory as its abolition. Rather, we should think that, when the perfect has come, what was partial will be destroyed—just as one compares a lamp with the rays of the sun, or the light of a lamp with a lantern [another reading: “a small lantern”]. Hence it is also said concerning John the Baptist: “He was the lamp burning in the house” (John V, 35). But after the sun of righteousness came, the light of the lamp was hidden, as that same prophet and Baptist says: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John III, 30).

The prophet fell upon his face lest, while desiring to see more than human frailty can behold, he should also lose the very light of his eyes. Therefore the Lord addresses him more familiarly as “son of man,” and commands him to set his heart, to see with his eyes, and to hear with his ears.

First, the mind must be opened to understand what is said. Second, one must understand with the eyes of the heart, concerning which it is said to Abraham: “Lift up your eyes and see the stars of heaven” (Gen. XV, 5). Third, one must hear with those ears of which the Savior says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII, 8). Thus he may understand all the ceremonies of the temple and its ordinances, and finally set his heart upon the ways of the temple, because there are various entrances to God. Or, “the ways of the temple” signifies the order of the ceremonies and the exits of the sanctuary.

This is therefore a preface and preparation of the prophet for understanding what he would afterward come to know concerning the order of the temple. This too should be noted: in the region of this world, which lies in wickedness and is established in the cold of the north, the heavenly order of the ceremonies is shown to us.

### (Verses 6ff.)

And you shall say to the house of Israel that provokes me: Thus says the Lord God: “Let all your crimes suffice you, house of Israel,” because you bring in foreign sons—or foreigners—uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, so that they may be in my sanctuary and pollute [Col. 0431C] my house; and you offer my bread, the fat and the blood, and you have dissolved—or transgressed—my covenant in all your abominations; and you have not kept the ordinances of my sanctuary, but you have appointed guardians of my observances in my sanctuary for yourselves.”

When he says, “Let all your abominations,” or “iniquities,” suffice you, he urges repentance for former sins, lest we add sins to sins and prepare fuel for a future fire. But let us hear what Isaiah says: “Woe to those who draw sins as with a long cord, and iniquities as with a cart rope” (Isa. V, 18).

The first sin is that they bring in foreign sons, or foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, so that they may be in God’s sanctuary and pollute God’s house. “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. V, 6); and in certain copies of Proverbs it is found: “Do not bring the wicked into the tents of the righteous.”

Here the Jews and Ebionites press us, since they accept circumcision of the flesh: How can we explain the present passage, “uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh”? Apparently, after spiritual understanding, we too ought to receive circumcision of the flesh.

But we read Paul saying: “I testify again to every man who receives circumcision that Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. V, 2). And Jeremiah says: “Behold, your ears are uncircumcised, and you were unwilling [Note: [Col. 0431] Victor preferred “and they cannot hear,” according to the received reading] to hear” (Jer. VI, 10).

And in Exodus Moses spoke before the Lord, saying: “Behold, the children of Israel have not listened to me; how then will Pharaoh listen to me? For I am slow of speech” (Exod. VI, 12). For this the Septuagint said: **ἐγὼ δὲ ἄλογός εἰμι**, “But I am without speech,” which is better rendered in the Hebrew: “But I am uncircumcised of lips.”

Let us question them—indeed, compel them—to circumcise their ears and cut away their lips, so that they may appear to fulfill Scripture. But if they begin to interpret circumcision of the ears as applying when we tolerate nothing shameful or dishonorable to hear, and circumcision of the lips as applying when we say nothing indecent, let us tell them that they must preserve the same interpretation with respect to the heart and the flesh.

We circumcise the heart with God’s knife, and the foreskin is removed from our heart when shameful thoughts do not at all emerge from it, nor is it said of us: “The heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears” (Acts XXVIII, 27).

The flesh likewise is circumcised, so that we no longer perform earthly works, which we are compelled by bodily necessity to perform—taking food and drink, sleeping, and using clothing. We circumcise these things when we do everything not for pleasure, luxury, and idleness, but for the necessity of nature and the support of this body.

He who drinks a little wine because of his stomach and frequent illnesses, and hates drunkenness, circumcises his flesh (1 Tim. V). He who sleeps as much as nature permits will hear from Solomon: “When you sit, you will be without fear; when you sleep, you will sleep sweetly, and you will not fear sudden terror or the attacks of the wicked that come upon you” (Prov. III, 24).

And he who flees fornication and, returning to the same, renders the due to his wife, lest Satan tempt him (1 Cor. VII), will hear with the people of Israel: “On this day I have taken away from you the reproach of Egypt” (Josh. V).

He will also wear clothing that repels the cold, not clothing which, because of its thinness, displays naked bodies. Flesh attenuated by fasting and circumcised by continence (Josh. V) flees the reproach of the Egyptians, who are large in flesh, and can say what is read in many copies according to the Septuagint edition: “How my flesh wasted away in a desert land, pathless and waterless; so I appeared to you in the holy place” (Ps. LXII, 3).

Therefore, whenever we wish to introduce foreigners into the temple of God, let us circumcise their ears, lips, and heart, and their entire flesh, as well as their eyes, taste, and smell, so that we may do everything with the fear of God and with reason.

Let bishops, priests, and the entire ecclesiastical order hear this, so that they do not introduce foreign sons uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, allowing them to be in God’s sanctuary and pollute his house. For if they do this, what follows will be applicable to them: “And you offer my bread”—namely, the bread of the presence in all the churches and throughout the world, springing from one bread—and not only bread, but also fat, of which it is written: “He satisfied them with the fat of wheat” (Ps. LXXX, 17), and blood, which was poured out in Christ’s Passion.

The passage should be read and its order restored as follows: “When you bring foreign sons, uncircumcised in heart and body, into my sanctuary and pollute my house, do you dare to offer breads, fat, and blood—the mystical sacraments—and do you not understand that you have dissolved and transgressed my covenant in all your abominations and impieties, and that you have not kept the ordinances of my sanctuary, nor appointed guardians of my ceremonies in my sanctuary?”

The whole threat is directed against those who have not heeded the Apostle’s warning: “Do not be hasty in laying hands on anyone, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Tim. V, 22).

Or it may certainly be understood in this way: “You have dissolved my covenant in all your abominations, and you have not kept the ordinances of my sanctuary, and you dare to appoint unworthy foreigners as guardians over the observance of my sanctuary for yourselves”—with “for yourselves,” rather than “for me,” understood.

The meaning is: those who may serve and minister to you in carnal matters, and on account of your comforts pollute my sanctuary.

(Verses 9 and following.) Thus says the Lord God: “No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter my sanctuary: every foreign son who is among the sons of Israel. Likewise the Levites who have gone far from me in the error of the sons of Israel and have strayed from me after their idols shall bear their iniquity [Vulgate: ‘and they bore their iniquity, they shall be in,’ etc.].
