They were in my sanctuary as attendants and gatekeepers of the gates of the house, and as ministers of the house; they themselves slaughtered the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the people, and stood there before them to minister on their behalf. Because they ministered on their behalf [Vulgate: ‘they themselves shall slaughter, shall stand before them to minister to them, because they ministered to them in,’ etc.] in the presence of their idols, and became for the house of Israel a stumbling-block of iniquity, therefore I raised my hand against them, says the Lord God, and they bore [Vulgate: shall bear] their iniquity. They shall not approach me to serve me as priests, nor shall they draw near to any of my sanctuary, to the holy of holies; but they shall bear their disgrace and the crimes that they committed. And I shall make them gatekeepers of the house in all its service, 543 and in everything that is done [Vulgate: shall be done] in it.

“But the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept the regulations of my sanctuary when the sons of Israel strayed from me, they shall approach me to minister to me; and they shall stand before me to offer me the fat and the blood,” says the Lord God. “They shall enter my sanctuary, and they shall approach my table to minister to me and to keep my regulations.”

**The Septuagint:** “Therefore thus says the Lord: Every foreign son, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall not enter my holy places, among all the foreign sons who are in the midst of the house of Israel. But the Levites who went far from me when Israel strayed from me after its thoughts shall receive their iniquity, and they shall be in my holy places serving, gatekeepers at the gates of the house and ministers of the house. These shall slaughter the burnt offerings and sacrifices for the people, and these shall stand before the people to minister to them. Because they ministered to them before their idols and became a torment of iniquity to the house of Israel, therefore I raised my hand against them, says the Lord God, and they shall receive their iniquity. They shall not approach me to serve me as priests, nor to offer anything among all the holy things of the sons of Israel, nor at my holy of holies; and they shall receive their disgrace in the error in which they strayed. And they shall appoint them to keep the watches of the house, for all its works and for everything that they did in it.

“The Levitical priests, the sons of Sadduc, who kept the watches of my holy places when the house of Israel strayed from me, these shall approach me to minister to me, and they shall stand before my face to offer me sacrifice, fat and blood,” says the Lord God. “These shall enter my holy places, and these shall approach my table to minister to me and to observe my watches.”

I have placed the testimony according to both editions, so that by comparing them we may know what the Septuagint understood and what the Hebrew text contains. The Septuagint signifies that foreigners uncircumcised in heart and flesh, who dwell among the sons of Israel, must not enter the sanctuary of God; but the Levites—that is, the priestly order—who went far from the Lord in the error of the sons of Israel and strayed after their idols, after receiving their iniquity, should remain in the Lord’s sanctuary as attendants, gatekeepers, and ministers of the house, and should slaughter the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the people. They are to stand before them to minister to them what they ministered to them in the presence of their idols, and they became a torment of iniquity to the house of Israel. Therefore the Lord God says that he raised his hand against them, so that they should not approach him and serve him as priests, nor offer to him in the holy of holies, but should bear their disgrace in the error in which they strayed, and should be assigned to the keeping of the watches of the house, for all its works and everything done in the house.

But if this is so, how can it stand that the Levites who went far from God in the error of the sons of Israel and strayed from him after their idols should themselves minister in the house, slaughter the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the people, and stand before them to minister to them? What more, then, will the priests, the sons of Zadok, do, who kept the regulations of God’s sanctuary, of whom he says: “They shall approach me to minister to me, and shall stand before me to offer me the fat,” and the rest?

The Hebrew text, however, has this sense: Every foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh shall not enter my sanctuary, even if he appears to be among the people of Israel. But the Levites—that is, the priestly order—who went far from me in the error of the sons of Israel and followed idols shall bear their iniquity, because they were in my sanctuary ministering in the office of the gates of the house and as its ministers. For they themselves offered the burnt offering and the sacrifices of the people, and they themselves stood before them to minister on their behalf. Since, therefore, they ministered on their behalf in the presence of their idols and became a stumbling-block of iniquity to the house of Israel, therefore I raised my hand against them, says the Lord God; and they bore their iniquity and shall not approach me to serve me as priests, nor shall they draw near to any of my sanctuary, to the holy of holies. Instead, they shall bear their disgrace and the crimes that they committed.

In place of the priestly office—for they had been accustomed to offer the burnt offering, the sacrifices, and every offering—they shall be reduced to the lowest rank and shall be gatekeepers of the house, to everlasting disgrace, so that they may be seen by the whole people as they enter and leave, and so that it may be evident from what lofty dignity they have fallen to what lowest rank. “But the priests,” he says, “that is, the Levites who are the sons of Zadok”—that is, of the righteous, or of the Righteous One of God—“and who, during the time of the error of all Israel, kept the regulations of my sanctuary, they shall approach me to minister to me, stand before me, and offer me the fat,” that is, the richest sacrifice, and the blood, namely, the living and pleasing sacrifice to God. They shall enter my sanctuary and approach my table to burn incense to me and to keep every rite of sacrifice.

But if this is so—if those who, in the time of error and persecution, followed idols that they had devised from their own heart, and who asserted not only with their voice but also by the subscription of their hand that the Son of God was a creature, and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever—how do they claim for themselves priestly and episcopal eminence, and dare to offer sacrifices to God, though they were once worshipers of idols?

But, as the most fervent poet testifies:

> Whatever is committed by many goes unpunished:  
> The multitude of sinners has made pardon more attainable for the wicked,

so that those who, after being reduced to the lay state, ought to have lamented [variant: ought to lament] the former crimes of their sacrilege, now recline on the episcopal throne and belch forth upon us the nauseas of feigned faith—or rather the open expedients of concealed perfidy.

[Note: We wrote, after Victorinus, “the concealed treachery,” because it answers the other isocolon, “of pretended faith,” more harmoniously. Martianaeus nevertheless retained “the manifest.”]

Let them hear, then, at least belatedly, and observe the commands of almighty God: “Every foreigner uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh shall not enter my sanctuary.” Even if he is a son, even if he is related by kinship, even if an ancient bond unites him to us: if he is uncircumcised in heart or flesh, let him not be brought into the sanctuary of God, lest we make the ministers of Christ our own ministers and pollute the altars of the Lord for the sake of carnal comforts.

As for the wording I have placed: “And I shall make them gatekeepers of the house in all its service and in everything that is done in it”—namely, the Levites who went far from God in the error of the sons of Israel and followed the idols to which they sacrificed victims—Symmachus, considering the order and sense of the reading, translated it more correctly, saying: “For I had appointed them guardians of the doors of the house, of all its service and of everything that is done in it,” so that it refers not to those who will be in the temple, but to those who were there. 546

(Verses 17 and following.) “When they enter the gates of the inner court, they shall be clothed in linen garments [or robes]; no woolen garment shall be upon them [or: they shall not clothe themselves in woolen fabrics] when they minister at the gates [or: from the gates] of the inner court and within. Linen turbans shall be upon their heads [or: they shall have linen turbans upon their heads], and linen undergarments shall be upon their loins; and they shall not gird themselves violently [or: in sweat]. When they go out to the outer court among the people, they shall remove their garments [or robes] in which they ministered and shall place them [or: place the garments] in the treasuries [Vulgate: treasury] [or chambers] of the sanctuary [or holy places], and they shall put on other garments [or robes], and they shall not sanctify the people with their garments [or robes]. They shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long, but they shall clip their heads by cutting [or: they shall not shave their heads and shall not cut their hair close; they shall cover, yes cover, their heads]. And no priest shall drink wine when he is about to enter the inner court.”

First, the words of the historical account must be set forth. Among the other things that the divine command prescribes for priests, it also orders this to be observed: at the very gates of the inner court they are to be clothed in garments—that is, linen robes. They are not to use woolen clothing either at the gates of the inner court or within it, that is, in the sanctuary and the holy of holies. Linen bands or turbans are to be upon their heads, and linen undergarments upon their loins.

What follows according to the Septuagint—“and they shall not gird themselves violently”—Aquila and Symmachus translated “in sweat.” Theodotion, expressing the Hebrew word itself, rendered it *JEZE* [Hebrew term as printed: ]. The second edition of Aquila has *BUSA* [variant: *BUZA*] [Hebrew term as printed: ], by which it signifies that they are not to be girded violently, tightly, or constrictively, like men in bonds, lest they become incapable in priestly and Levitical services, unable to hold and cut up the victims, or to draw them along and move about.

And because he had once prescribed what garments the priests ought to use when they were within, engaged in their ministry, he again orders that when they go out they remove their former garments in the treasuries, or chambers, of the holy places, and put on others. Otherwise, if they retained the holy garments, they would sanctify the people standing outside, who had not yet been sanctified or prepared for the sanctification of the temple, so as to become the Lord’s Nazirite.

From this we learn that we must not enter the holy of holies in ordinary garments, or in whatever garments have been polluted by common use in daily life, but with a clean conscience and clean garments, holding the mysteries of the Lord.

[Note: If I see correctly, the text that follows has been interpolated and displaced for nearly fifty subsequent lines—from this point, namely, to Paul’s testimony at 1 Timothy 5. I am indeed troubled by the interrupted and disjointed sequence of the explanation: after suddenly breaking off the discussion of garments, it introduces some material concerning the care of the hair, which belongs to the following verse, then a little concerning abstinence from wine, and finally abruptly falls back into the earlier discussion of garments. After its clear exposition of those garments, it again discusses the avoidance of luxurious hair and drunkenness. I have no doubt that anyone who carefully considers the whole exposition of this chapter will reach the same conclusion.

How the material can be restored to its original and proper order, Rabanus indicates clearly. First, the entire subsequent patch of thirty-nine verses should be removed from here, and in its place the following should be continued immediately and in one sequence: “Egyptian priests use linen garments,” and so forth, to nearly the middle of column 550, after the second passage from Proverbs 20:25. Then the patch itself should be divided, as it were, into two parts. The first, which discusses the care of the hair, should be inserted there through the words following the verse of Virgil: “But this is a forced interpretation.” The second, which praises temperance in wine, should be appended to the end of the chapter. Rabanus reads it in this order. But when the authority of manuscripts is not also available, it is enough to warn the reader about the displacement without altering the printed reading in any way.]

What follows—“They shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long, but they shall clip their heads by cutting”—plainly demonstrates that we ought not to have shaven heads, like priests and worshipers of Isis and Serapis.

[Note: Formerly “Serapis.” Saint Ambrose, Letter to Sabinus: “They shave their heads and eyebrows when they undertake the rites of Isis.”]

Nor, again, should we let our hair hang loose, which is characteristic of luxury, barbarians, and soldiers; rather, the appearance of the priests should display an honorable bearing.

[Note: The modern custom of letting the hair grow long belonged to barbarians, luxurious men, and soldiers, not to honorable men and Christians, who are commanded not to let their hair grow long. —Martianaeus.]

For this reason the Septuagint said: “They shall not shave their heads, and they shall not cut their hair close, but they shall thoroughly cover their heads.” From this we learn that neither should the head be made bald with a razor, nor should it be cut so close that we appear like shaven men; rather, the hair should be allowed to grow enough for the skin to be covered.

Or certainly priests ought always to cover their heads, in accordance with the Virgilian line (*Aeneid* 3):

> To veil the hair, covered with a purple cloak.

But this is a forced interpretation.

As for wine, priests and Levites are not only forbidden to drink it while ministering; they may not even drink it when about to enter the holy of holies, lest the mind be oppressed and the understanding become dull. Hence the Apostle also says: “It is good not to drink wine and not to eat meat” (Romans 14:21). And elsewhere: “Wine, in which there is wantonness” (Ephesians 5:18). “The people ate and drank, and rose up to play.” And the permission he gives Timothy to drink a little wine plainly shows why he granted it: “For your stomach,” he says, “and your frequent illnesses” (1 Timothy 5).

Egyptian priests use linen garments not only within but also outside. Divine religion, however, has one form of dress for ministry and another for ordinary life and daily use.

[Note: In the first centuries of the Church, the garments of laymen and clergy were in fact common; but clergy used, in sacred functions, the garments they wore in daily life, though cleaner and of the finest quality. Saint Jerome has a similar statement in Book 1 against Pelagius, rejecting the ornamentation of clothing: “What hostility toward God is there, I ask, if I have a cleaner tunic? If a bishop, presbyter, deacon, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order appear in white garments when administering the sacrifices?” See what we noted on this passage in volume 2, column 713.]

Undergarments are rightly worn so that modesty and decorum may be preserved, lest, as they ascend the steps of the altar and move about in their ministry, they reveal what is shameful.

Shaven heads belong to pagan superstition. As far as my knowledge is concerned, I do not think any pagan abstains from wine.

[Variant: “as far as my information is concerned.”]

What all these things signify according to the spiritual sense, the words that follow will show. The Apostle also teaches that there are holy and spiritual garments, saying: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14). And elsewhere: “Put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (Colossians 3:12). And again: “Having stripped off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, which is renewed in knowledge according to the image of its Creator” (1 Corinthians 15:54). I think this also signifies the saying: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. But when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass,” and what follows.

The priestly garments are described more fully in Exodus 28; and long ago we published a book on the subject, the *Letter 64 to Fabiola*, to whose interpretation the diligent reader should be referred. We cannot encompass so broad a subject in a brief discourse.

We make these garments for ourselves by our own labor. They are woven from above, like the tunic that the Lord also had, which could not be torn (John 18). We put them on when we come to know the Lord’s secrets and mysteries and possess the Spirit who searches even the deep things of God—things that ought not to be displayed to the crowd or brought forth before the people, who have not been sanctified or prepared for the Lord’s holiness. Otherwise, if they hear things too great for them, they may be unable to bear the majesty of knowledge and may be choked, as it were, by solid food, when they still need to be nourished on the milk of infancy. 549

That, on the other hand, there are very bad garments, divine Scripture teaches, as in the saying sung in the Psalms concerning Judas the betrayer: “He clothed himself with cursing as with a garment” (Psalm 108:29). And shortly afterward: “Let it be to him as the garment with which he wraps himself, and as the belt with which he is always girded.”

Therefore the Lord, who suffered for us and bore our sins, is said in Zechariah to have filthy garments, concerning which it is written: “And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments” (Zechariah 3:4). He later removes them, as Scripture says: “Take the filthy garments away from him, and clothe him with a long robe,” and what follows.

What follows—“Linen bands or turbans shall be upon their heads”—I think signifies the crown of graces, concerning which it is written: “For he will receive a crown of graces upon your head” (Proverbs 4:9).

Nor should the matter of the covered and uncovered head trouble us because of what the Apostle says: “A woman ought to have a veil on her head, because of the angels. For if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be covered. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man” (2 Corinthians 11:10).

If it belongs to men not to cover their heads, this seems contrary to the command that priests now cover their heads with bands or turbans. But if we read more carefully, what is present will be resolved by what precedes. Above it says: “When they minister at the gates of the inner court and within.” If we enter the holy places and stand in the presence of the Lord, we ought to cover our heads, because “no living person will be justified in the sight of the Lord” (Psalm 142:2). And: “From childhood the human heart is inclined toward evil.”

Finally, we also use undergarments within, so that no shameful exposure of a polluted conscience or of marital acts may appear in the sight of God. The Savior wishes the Apostles to be girded with these undergarments when he says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 13:35). And the Apostle says to believers: “Stand therefore, having your loins girded with truth” (Ephesians 6:1). The imitators of Christ also hear what is written of him: “He shall be girded with righteousness at the loins, and shall be wrapped about the sides with truth” (Isaiah 11:5).

With this very belt, the one who is holy and has risen to the summit of virtue is by no means bound violently, lest he appear unwillingly to observe continence and to eat bread in the sweat of his face, rather than to perform the Lord’s command willingly.

Finally, when he goes outside and mixes with the people, the priest removes his priestly garments in the treasury where the Lord’s riches are preserved, and the priests use other garments and another kind of teaching for the lowly crowd, lest the people be sanctified by their robes.

It is burdensome for the multitude to take upon itself a load beyond its strength, as Solomon says: “It is a snare for a man rashly to sanctify something of his own; for when he has made a vow, repentance follows” (Proverbs 20:25, according to the Septuagint). Finally, Nazirites also offer themselves voluntarily; and whoever makes a vow and does not fulfill it is guilty concerning the vow.

Thus it is said of widows: “When they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have rejected their first faith” (1 Timothy 5:11–12). For it is better not to promise than to promise and not to do.

Hannah offered Samuel, who remained in perpetual holiness (1 Samuel 1). Manoah offered his son Samson, but Delilah’s lust brought disgrace upon the sanctification of his hair (Judges 13). Finally, the Lord departed from him, and he was condemned to blindness, except that afterward, when his hair grew again, he recovered his former strength and, as a type of Christ, killed far more foreigners in his death than he had killed while alive.

The Lord wishes his priests to have the hair of sanctification perpetually and their heads covered, not by some external covering but by their own natural hair—not for ornament or luxury, but for decency.

Hence the hairs of the head are numbered, as the Savior says: “But your head-hairs are numbered” (Matthew 10:30). This concerns the head of which it is written in Ecclesiastes: “The wise man’s eyes are in his head” (Ecclesiastes 2:14).

The head of the man is Christ. The sinner tramples upon and despises him and, so to speak, shaves him with a razor and removes his beauty. The sons of Ammon did this also to those whom David had sent as messengers (2 Samuel 10).

But if transgression of the law dishonors God, then consequently whoever preserves the commandments of the law honors him, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:13).

What follows—“So that every priest, when he is about to enter the inner court, shall not drink wine”—plainly shows that in drunkenness and strong drink the state of the mind is overturned, and that we do not think with full understanding when the mind is occupied by an excess of wine [variant: by wine and excess].

Drunkenness, however, is displayed not only in drinking wine but in all things by which, in contracts and worldly business, in losses and profits, love and hatred intoxicate and agitate the mind, so that it cannot maintain its proper state.

And because we are surrounded by fragile flesh and compelled, for food, clothing, and necessities relating to the body, to do certain things that we ought not to do, at least this is required of us: when we return to ourselves and know why we were born and enter the inner chambers and sanctuary of the temple, we must withdraw from the vices of the world and commit not even the smallest sins.

From this it is also shown that we commit light sins for the sake of the necessities of the flesh, and that there is likewise a time when, entering the inner court, we must be free from every drunkenness of the world and of what is foreign to God.

[Col. 0440C] (Verses 22 and following.) “They shall not take a widow or a divorced—that is, rejected—woman as a wife, but a virgin [Vulgate: virgins] from the seed of the house of Israel. But they may take a widow who was the widow of a priest. And they shall teach my people what is holy and what is polluted, and show them the difference between clean and unclean. When there is a dispute [the Septuagint adds: concerning blood], they shall stand in my judgments, and they shall judge my laws and keep commandments [Vulgate adds: “my”] at all my solemn feasts.”

This whole passage contains commandments for priests. After the many matters we have explained above, they are ordered not to take a widow or a divorced—that is, rejected—woman as a wife.

The widow and the divorced woman are the synagogue—that is, the congregation of the Jews—which did not receive the Lord. Hence it is rightly called rejected, or the widow synagogue. Rejected also is the multitude of heretics who went out from us because they were not of us.

“But a virgin,” he says, “from the seed of the house of Israel,” who was brought up in the house of God, in the Law and the Prophets. Of her the Apostle also speaks: “I wish to present you all as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

This is the virgin of whom the divine word also says elsewhere: “Love her, and she will keep you; embrace her, and she will exalt you; honor her, so that she may embrace you” (Proverbs 4:8). Who this virgin is, whom one ought to love and who preserves her own lover, will be known by whoever reads: “I loved her and sought her from my youth, and I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wisdom 8:2). And again: “The Lord of all loved her.”

Priests ought to take not only a virgin but also a widow, provided that she had been the wife of another priest—that is, knowledge discovered by another worshiper of God. For we must not be content only with new teaching, but must also cultivate the old and join it to our own company, provided that it has been instructed in sacred worship.

It is also the duty of a priest to teach the people what is holy and what is polluted, what is clean and what is unclean, referring the first to doctrines and the second to works accomplished through the flesh. “Who understands his offenses?” (Psalm VIII, 13).

And when there is a dispute about anything—or, as the Septuagint translated it, about blood, that is, concerning a crime bearing the penalty of death—the priests shall stand in God’s judgments, so that they may not judge according to rank or show partiality to the poor or the rich in judgment. Rather, they should stand in the judgments of God and remember that psalm: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Psalm 82:1), calling gods those who have authority to judge human beings, and by the judgment with which they judge, judgment will be rendered concerning them (Matthew 7).

“They shall keep my laws,” he says, “and my commandments at all my solemn feasts,” so that they may know how Christ was sacrificed for us as the Passover; how we ought to complete seven weeks in joy and gladness and humble our souls in fasting; and how to understand the sound of the trumpets and the spiritual festivals of booths, in which we say: “I am a stranger and a sojourner, like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12).

These are the true solemn feasts of God, which someone will interpret more appropriately when expounding the Pentateuch. The first virtue of a priest is not merely to teach what he knows, but to keep all God’s festivals, so that he can command others to keep what he himself has observed.

That it is the duty of priests to possess knowledge of the law, we also learn from Malachi, who says: “The lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7).

(Verses 25 and following.) “And they shall sanctify my Sabbaths, and they shall not enter upon a dead man, lest they be polluted” [the Septuagint translates: “and they shall not enter upon a human soul, lest they be polluted”], “except for a father,” he says, “and mother, son and daughter, brother and sister who has not had a husband; they shall be polluted by them. And after he has been cleansed, seven days shall be counted for him. On the day of his entering the sanctuary and the inner court, to minister to me in the sanctuary, he shall offer for his sin to the Lord God” [or: “he shall offer an expiation]. “They shall have no inheritance; I am their inheritance. You shall give them no possession in Israel; I am their possession.”

[Note: The Vulgate reads, “who has not had another husband.” Nevertheless, Jerome says in the following exposition: “if the sister has remained a virgin and has not been defiled by the embrace of any man.” Rabanus likewise says, “in which they were contaminated.” Shortly afterward Victorinus, following the Vulgate reading, has “for his sin,” says the Lord God.]

The command is still being given to priests. We should observe here that he did not say absolutely, “They shall sanctify the Sabbaths,” or, according to Isaiah, “Your new moons and Sabbaths my soul hates” (Isaiah 1:13), but, with a distinction, “my Sabbaths.”

Hence it is also written in the Gospel: “The priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are without guilt” (Matthew 12:5)—not God’s Sabbath, but the Sabbath of the letter, the Sabbath of the Jews, which those who are a chosen, royal, and priestly race rightly profane.

As for the Sabbath that has been sanctified, let us understand it as the Sabbath that the Apostle also teaches has been left for the people of God, concerning which it is said: “If they shall enter into my rest” (Psalm 95:11). This is called *sabbath* in Hebrew.

[Note: Victorinus says: “In Hebrew it is [Hebrew term as printed: ], not ‘Sabbath.’” Jerome, however, alludes to the word for “rest,” which also signifies Sabbath, rather than to the word “Sabbath” itself.]

The one who does not carry the burden of sin on the Sabbath sanctifies God’s Sabbath, and does not say: “Like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me” (Psalm 38:4). Such a person does not gather wood on the Sabbath, nor build upon the foundation of Jesus Christ wood, hay, and straw (1 Corinthians 3). He does not kindle a fire that consumes useless material, and on the Sabbath he remains in one place; he does not go outside, but, placed like a pillar in the temple of God, he remains there. Concerning him John writes in the Apocalypse: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall never go out again” (Revelation 3:12).

What follows—“They shall not enter upon a dead man, lest they be polluted”—properly belongs to the priestly office: they must not touch corpses, so that the one who intercedes for the sins of others may himself approach the altar clean.

The Savior speaks of these dead in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22). Such people are polluted by a dead father when they abandon their Creator, and by a dead mother when they depart from the Church. They are also polluted by a son and daughter, one referring to thoughts and the other to deeds, which in Greek are more significantly called *τὰ νοητὰ καὶ αἰσθητά*—“the intelligible and the perceptible.”

A brother and sister, likewise, who have been reborn in the same Spirit: if someone considers them dead, he is polluted by them—provided only that the sister has remained a virgin and has not been defiled by the embrace of any man.

From this we understand the privilege of virginity: contact with any man removes perfect purity. Whether this has been said rightly or wrongly, we leave to the reader’s judgment.

Nature’s affection is also proved in this matter, so that, in the order of love, according to what is written, “Set love in order within me” (Song of Songs 2:4), after God, the parent of all things, one should love one’s father and mother according to the flesh, son and daughter, brother and sister—provided only that the sister has not left the household and passed into another’s power.

After the priest has been cleansed according to the order of purification prescribed in the Mosaic Law, seven days shall be counted for him: either the perfect number of repentance, or the period after the consummation of the world, when we pass into the true octave, so that he may enter the holy of holies—that is, the inner court—and may minister in the sanctuary and always offer a sacrifice for the sin of his conscience. There should be no time when he does not remember that he was polluted through father and mother, son and daughter, brother and sister.

For we are compelled to do many things while placed in the straits of this world, either by the condition of the flesh or by the fragility of nature. But whoever has become such that he ministers in the sanctuary, enters the inner court, and continually offers sacrifice to God, so that he is a true priest—or rather an imitator of the one concerning whom it is written, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4)—will have no inheritance except God, who is his inheritance. He will receive no possession in Israel, that is, among the ignoble multitude, but a priestly possession, so that the Lord may say of him: “I am their inheritance, and I am their possession.” When they have found him, they will speak and say: “I will hold him and will not let him go,” and they will sing with the prophet: “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm II, 26).

[Col. 0443B] (Verses 29–30.) “They shall eat the offering both for sin and for guilt (or, for ignorance), and every vow (or, separation) in Israel shall belong to them. And the firstfruits of all the firstborn, and all the offerings from everything that is offered, shall belong to the priests; and you shall give the firstfruits of your foods to the priest, so that he may store up a blessing for his house [Vulgate: your house] (or, so that he may place blessings upon your houses).”

For “offering” and “sacrifice,” which in Hebrew is called *MANAA* (), Aquila and Symmachus translated “gift.” Again, for “vow,” which the Septuagint translated as ἀφόρισμα, that is, “separation,” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated ἀνάθημα, which in Hebrew is called *HEREM* ().

It must be considered that everything the Lord now speaks through the prophet He had already said earlier through Moses. And one must ask why He repeats the same things that had been said: namely, so that what has been erased from people’s minds through negligence in reading, or contempt and forgetfulness in listening, may be renewed by the living voice—a voice not written with pen and ink, but with the Spirit and word of God. Hence the Savior likewise left no book belonging specifically to His teaching, although in many apocryphal ravings such a book is fabricated; rather, through the Spirit of the Father and His own Spirit He speaks daily in the hearts of believers. This will also be our response to those who slander the prophets, asking why they repeat in their own books what is contained in the Pentateuch.

Let the priests, therefore, eat the offering both for sin and for guilt, or ignorance—those of whom it is written: “They shall eat the sins of my people” (Hosea 4:8). We must not rejoice so much in the offering of gifts as fear the condemnation attached to honor, if we abuse it unworthily.

In the literal sense, the firstfruits are of living creatures and things without life that are born first, and of what the earth produces first. The firstfruits of our foods are also offered to the priests, so that we taste none of the new crops unless the priest has tasted them first. We do this so that the priest may store up the blessing and our offering in his house—or so that, in response to his imprecation, the Lord may bless our houses. [556] Great is the dignity of priests, but great also is their downfall if they sin. Let us rejoice at the ascent, but fear the fall. It is not as great a source of joy to have held lofty places as it is a cause of grief to have fallen from higher ones. For we shall render an account not only for our own sins, but also for those of everyone whose gifts we abuse and whose salvation we are in no way concerned about.

(Verse 31.) “The priests shall not eat any carcass or anything torn by beasts, whether of birds or of livestock.”

[Note: Consult the interpreters of this passage; I have no wish to rehash their very familiar teachings.]

In the literal sense, these commands apply to every chosen people, royal and priestly, which properly refers to Christians, who have been anointed with spiritual oil, of which it is written: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8). They must not eat a carcass, whether of birds or of livestock, whose blood was not poured out—what is called “strangled” in the Acts of the Apostles—and these things must necessarily be observed, as the apostles’ letter from Jerusalem commands (Acts 15). Nor may they eat anything torn by a beast, since it too has likewise been strangled. He condemns priests who, through greed of appetite, fail to observe this rule with thrushes, fig-peckers, dormice, and other creatures of this kind.

We may also understand “carcass” allegorically as one in whom the soul’s blood has died, who imitates Nabal the Carmelite—Nabal being interpreted as “fool.” When he heard of David’s anger, he trembled with fear, and his heart died within him (1 Samuel 25). But “something torn by beasts,” lest it be mangled by their bites—as the prophet sighs, saying, “Do not give the soul confessing you to the beasts” (Psalm 73:19)—is one who is devoured by the bites of the adversary: the lion, the leopard that does not change its spots, the bear that rages after its stolen cubs, the wolves of Arabia [variant: of rage], and the remaining beasts, which we understand as demons in their various forms. [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, “whose variety we understand as demons.”]

By “birds,” meanwhile, we understand those that set their mouths against heaven; and by “livestock,” those that bend down toward the earth and serve only their belly and the things beneath the belly.

(Cap. XLV—verses 1 ff.) “When you begin to divide the land as a possession [Vulgate: by lot], set apart as sacred to the Lord a firstfruits offering from the land, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth; it shall be holy throughout all its boundary on every side. And from this sacred portion there shall be a square, five hundred by five hundred, on every side, with fifty cubits of open land around its suburbs. [Col. 0444D] From this measure you shall measure a length of twenty-five thousand and a breadth of ten thousand; and within it shall be the temple (or, the sanctuary) and the holy of holies. The sacred portion of the land shall belong to the priests, the ministers of the sanctuary, who draw near to the service of the Lord; and it shall be a place for their houses and for the sanctuary of holiness. Its length shall be twenty-five thousand and its breadth ten thousand.

“But the Levites who minister in the temple shall possess twenty chambers [The Septuagint translated: ‘They shall hold the city in which they shall dwell’]. And you shall give the city as a possession, five thousand in breadth and twenty-five thousand in length, corresponding to the sacred portion, for the whole house of Israel. The prince also shall receive, on either side [Note: Victorius reads, ‘on either side for the sacred portion, or firstfruits, of the sanctuary, and for the possession,’ in accordance with the Vulgate, Hebrew, and Greek texts], a possession from the sacred portion (or, the firstfruits) of the sanctuary and from the city’s possession, opposite the face of the sacred portion of the sanctuary and opposite the face of the city’s possession, from the sea-side to the sea-side, and from the eastern side to the east; but in length, alongside each portion, from the western boundary to the eastern boundary, the land shall be his possession in Israel [Vulgate: ‘from the land’]. The princes shall no longer oppress (or, devastate) my people; but they shall give the land to the house of Israel according to their tribes.”

After the ceremonies of the priests, their worship, and the food they ought to eat and avoid, the prophet now describes the holy land. Before dividing it among all the tribes, he commands that a place be selected from all the tribes, having a length of twenty-five thousand and a breadth of ten thousand. Since no unit—cubits, feet, or ells—is specified, it is understood to signify the measuring reed that was in the man’s hand. It had six cubits and a sixth of a cubit, that is, a παλαιστή. Let the diligent reader calculate how many thousand paces the reeds make, and how many thousands there were in length and breadth.

After this description, he again commands that, from the sacred land selected from all the tribes of Israel—that is, twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in breadth—another portion of land be selected within it for building the sanctuary, that is, the temple of the Lord: a square of five hundred reeds on every side, [558] that is, two thousand in total. And lest other buildings perhaps be joined to the temple structure, he commands that the land be empty for fifty cubits around it, as open ground in the suburbs—or, as Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Septuagint translated, “as a boundary,” “separation,” and “open space.”

When this description has been completed, another measure of sacred ground to be set apart is prescribed in its entirety: a length of twenty-five thousand reeds and a breadth of ten thousand. Beyond the preceding measure, another tract of land is to be measured, in which there is not a temple—that is, a sanctuary—but the holy place and the holy of holies; and the priests who draw near to the service of the Lord are to dwell there. They are to dwell there at the time when they are performing their priestly office, and the possession itself is, as we said, twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in breadth.

The Levites, however, who serve the priests and have their own ministries, shall receive a place for building twenty chambers: according to Aquila, *exedrae*; according to Symmachus, “bedrooms”; according to Theodotion, *gazerae*; or, as the Septuagint translated, “a city.” By this we understand that a certain separate place for the dwelling of the Levites is called by the name “city,” having five thousand reeds in breadth and twenty-five thousand in length.

All these things—that is, the sanctuary, the other sanctuary, the holy of holies, the dwellings of the priests, and the houses of the Levites who minister to the priests—are called [Col. 0446A] separate and consecrated places for service and sanctification for the house of Israel. [The transmitted text reads *luca separata*; the sense appears to require “separate places.”]

After the fourfold description of the holy land, a fifth division is introduced. The prince, or leader of the people, shall receive on either side—that is, from both sides of the sanctuary—a possession for himself and shall dwell in the city. His possession shall face the place separated for the temple and the face of the city; it shall extend from the sea-side, that is, from the west, to the other sea-side, with the breadth that the prophet describes below in the division of the individual tribes. Finally, it follows: “In length, alongside each portion” [559] that the individual tribes receive, “from the western boundary,” that is, the sea, “to the eastern boundary,” whose endpoint we shall learn from the division among the tribes. This shall be the possession of the leader, or prince, in the land of Israel.

Let these remarks suffice for the present, so that the simple historical meaning may be understood. But if we wish to compare spiritual things with spiritual things and, following certain interpreters, ascend to higher matters—those who assert that present realities are figures of things to come, and that everything said here pertains to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, and to the Church of the firstborn—it would not indeed be difficult to repeat what others have said. But we fear that a prudent reader may not accept such an interpretation.

Accordingly, everything should for the present be referred to the present time, to the Church that now struggles in the world and hastens toward heaven, so that from the whole world some may be chosen as God’s possession, to possess the holy place, and others, who have advanced to greater things, may possess the holy of holies. There is also a distinction of rank among the ministers, priests and Levites: some offer sacrifices to God daily through their prayers and virtues; others occupy a second and lower rank, serving them; and finally there is a leader or prince who possesses such power that he receives a possession corresponding to one tribe, so that the merit of one compensates for the merits of many. At first, while he remains in this world, he possesses breadth from sea to sea; thereafter, from the west, or sea, to the east, abandoning present things and hastening toward those to come. He has a fixed possession of his own, and the princes must not desire what belongs to others; each tribe must hold its own portion.

This may properly be referred to bishops and presbyters, who are commanded not to ravage and plunder the people of God any longer, nor to possess the land of Israel as an inheritance, but for each to hold the possession assigned to his rank.

The twenty-five thousand are referred to the senses, since the number is given four times. The ten thousand, moreover, refer to perfect knowledge: in one case only the simple historical meaning is retained, while in the other theology and heavenly virtues are also discussed, because ten is a perfect number.

It must also be considered that the priests, who are established in the higher rank, possess twenty-five thousand in length [Col. 0447A] and ten thousand in breadth. The Levites, however—that is, the lower rank—have the same number in length, namely twenty-five thousand, but their breadth ends with the number five. Hence they hold only twenty chambers. In this number the gifts of Esau are offered.

The prince, however, who is truly prince among the people and deserves to receive the name of leader, receives a possession on either side of the sanctuary—from all, that is, who are willingly subject to him—and is an inhabitant of the city. He makes the salvation of many his reward.

In the former temple, which is called the sanctuary, five hundred reeds are described on each side, and again fifty cubits, by which the entire possession of the priests is separated. In the second sanctuary, where the holy of holies is located, the breadth and extent of the temple are not described, but the number is indefinite. We find the same in the prince’s possession: he has a possession among the people of Israel without any number being assigned, since the progress of all redounds to the prince, and the salvation of the disciples is the reward of the teachers.

(Verse 9.) “Thus says the Lord God: Let it be enough for you, princes of Israel! Cease from violence and plunder, and practice judgment and righteousness, and separate your boundaries from my people, says the Lord God.”

For “plunder,” the Septuagint translated “misery”; for “boundaries,” “oppression.” The sense is this: Since you have received your portion, O princes—for Scripture says, “The prince shall receive on either side, for the sacred portion of the sanctuary, a possession of the city,” with “you shall give” understood—and since your power is so great that your possession has received the portion of one tribe, I command and admonish you: let it be enough, up to this point, to have practiced violence and plunder, while you invade and seize what belongs to others.

And since it is written, “Turn away from evil and do good,” conversely, “practice judgment and righteousness” (Psalm 36:27), judging for the orphan and justifying the widow. Separate your boundaries from my people, so that you do not move the boundaries. Since proximity itself injures the weaker person, who cannot endure the arrogance of one greater and more powerful, [Note: The words “From this point Isaiah says, ‘Woe to those who join house to house and attach field to field, even to the boundary of the place’” were first supplied by us in order to complete the sense, which previously gaped without them. It is clear—for it is remarkable that none of Jerome’s interpreters has hitherto noticed this—that where the conjunction “because” required a corresponding connective, the other connective was missing. We supplied it not from our own ingenuity but on the authority of the reading of Rabanus, although he additionally appends a long passage from his commentaries on the cited place in Isaiah, which was entirely irrelevant to our purpose. It was also easy to suppose that an old scribe, deceived by the similarity of the words *hinc* and *hoc*—the former placed by us in the preceding passage and the latter beginning the following sentence—had omitted the earlier words with the customary lapse of hurried eyes.] Isaiah therefore says here: “Woe to you who join house to house and attach field to field, even to the boundary of the place.”

Let this be said for the present concerning the people of that time. But the command may also be applied to our own princes, who, after the manner of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, oppress the children of Israel by their power and do not remember what is written: “They have appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1).

And there is also what the Lord says in the Gospel according to Luke: “But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, to eat and drink and become drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know; he will cut him in two and appoint his portion with the unbelievers” (Luke 12:45–46).

He also instructs His disciples in the Gospel according to Matthew with these commands: “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who are great exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you; but whoever wishes to be first, let him be servant of all. The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:25 ff.). [Note: According to Rabanus, as also in the sacred text, one should supply: “Whoever wishes to be great among you, let him be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first,” etc.]

There are many passages I could review from the sacred Scriptures in which the pride of the great is restrained and all are summoned to humility by the Lord, who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

## BOOK FOURTEEN

[Col. 0447]

[Col. 0447D] 561–562 What I ought to have said at the beginning of Ezekiel’s temple, I shall now say at the end, in inverted order, remembering that verse of Virgil (Aeneid 6):

> This was that toil of the house, and the inextricable wandering.

The same poet sings elsewhere (Aeneid 5):

> As once the labyrinth in lofty Crete is said to have had
>
> A path woven with blind walls, and a twofold contrivance
>
> Of a thousand ways, by which the marks of following
>
> Might deceive, untraced, in an inescapable wandering.

Thus I too, having entered the ocean of these Scriptures and, so to speak, the labyrinth of God’s mysteries, of which it is written, “He made darkness his hiding place,” and, “Clouds surround him” (Psalm 17:12), do not dare claim for myself a perfect knowledge of the truth. But to those who desire knowledge I have offered some indications of teaching—not by my own strength, but through the mercy of Christ, who, while we were wandering, Himself unravels the hidden traps and winding passages, guiding our blind footsteps by the Holy Spirit. Following Him, we shall be able to reach the harbor of the explanations of the prophet Ezekiel, into which this fourteenth and final book carries us.

If, through your prayers, virgin of Christ Eustochium, I bring it to its conclusion, and the Lord grants me time in this life, I shall pass on to Jeremiah, who remains for us the one surviving prophet; his interpretation will belong to my labor and to your prayers, but properly to the mercy of Christ.

563 (Chapter XLV—verses 10 ff.) “You shall have a just balance, a just ephah, and a just bath. The ephah and the bath shall be equal [Vulgate: equal in quantity] and of one measure, so that the bath may contain a tenth part of a kor, and the ephah a tenth part of a kor; according to the measure of the kor their quantities shall be equal. The shekel shall contain twenty obols [Vulgate: let it contain]. Twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, and fifteen shekels shall make a mina [Vulgate: shall make].”

The Septuagint: “You shall have a just balance, a just measure, and a just *choenix* for a measure; the choenix shall likewise be one measure for receiving. A tenth part of a *gomor* shall be a choenix, and a tenth part of a gomor shall be an ephah. The gomor shall be equal in weight [Note: Victorius substituted “and an appendage” for “by weight,” following the Greek, since Jerome also reports that the Septuagint translated *shekel* as “appendage.”] to twenty obols. Twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, and fifteen shekels shall be your mina.”

This passage, according to the Septuagint, does not cohere and cannot be understood at all, since they have changed not only the numbers of the measures but also their names. For instead of *ephah* they translated “measure,” a general term for a specific one; instead of *bath*, *choenix*; and instead of the Hebrew *homer*, which in Greek is called *koros*, they translated *gomor*. Again, instead of *bath*, they used *choenix*.

Let us therefore speak according to the Hebrew and the literal sense, explaining more clearly what seems to us to be intended in each case.

The balance, called in Hebrew *MOZENE* (), is understood as referring to things that are weighed. The ephah, which in Greek is corruptly called ἔφι, belongs to the measurement of various crops—for example, wheat, barley, and legumes. The bath, which in Hebrew is *BATH* (), is the same measure as the ephah, but is used for liquid substances only, such as wine, oil, and things of that kind.

The kor contains thirty *modii* and serves as the basic measure for both kinds of substance, dry and liquid. A tenth of a kor among things measured by the *modius* is called an ephah, that is, three *modii*. A tenth of a kor among liquid substances is called a bath, or vadus, so that the ephah and the bath are the same measure.

The shekel, which in Greek is called στατήρ, contains twenty obols. The mina, called *mna*, contains sixty shekels, which amount to twelve hundred obols.

What is said—“twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, and fifteen shekels make a mina”—should not trouble the reader. Difficulty is deliberately introduced into the numbers so that it may command the hearer’s attention. Hence many things are spoken in parables and riddles, so that “whoever has ears to hear may hear” (Luke 8:8). Every prophecy contains the truth in obscurity, so that the disciples may hear inwardly while the ignoble multitude outside does not know what is being said.

Divine Scripture therefore commands that the weights be just, saying: “There shall not be in your bag a greater and a lesser measure; a true and just balance shall be yours, and a true and just measure shall be yours” [variant: “for itself”] (Leviticus 19:36). And in Proverbs it says: “A greater and a lesser balance, both are abominable in the sight of God” (Proverbs 11:1).

This must be observed not only in commerce and the ordinary conduct of life, but justice must be preserved in everything, as Scripture says: “You shall make a balance and a counterweight for your words” (Ecclesiasticus 28:23), so that in words, deeds, and thoughts alike we may do everything with weight and reason.

We read elsewhere that an obol, that is, a twentieth part of a shekel or *stater*, is the smallest portion: [Note: See what we have said about this sentence in Letter 53, toward the end.] “The whole world is rich to the one who is faithful, but to the unbeliever there is not even an obol” (Proverbs 17:6 according to the Septuagint). It is as though he had said in other words: The unbeliever possesses nothing in the world, but lacks even the smallest portion.

Elsewhere in the Gospel it is said of him: “He will not leave there until he has paid the last quadrans” (Matthew 5:26), that is, even the last and smallest coin.

We read that ten minas were given to individual servants for trading (Luke 19), and in another parable talents were distributed among servants; that there was a debtor of five hundred denarii and another of fifty (Matthew 25); that the laborers in the vineyard each received a denarius (Luke 7); and that the widow lost a drachma and scarcely found it again by lighting a lamp (Matthew 20; Luke 15). What meaning all these things have is not for us to discuss at this time.

(Verses 13–14.) “These are the firstfruits that you shall take: a sixth part of an ephah from a kor of wheat, and a sixth part of an ephah from a kor of barley. The measure of oil shall be this: a bath of oil is a tenth part of a kor; and ten baths make a kor, because ten baths fill a kor.”

The Septuagint: “These are the firstfruits that you shall set apart: a sixth part of a measure from a gomor of wheat, and a sixth part of an ephah from a kor of barley, and a prescribed offering of oil, a *cotyle*, that is, a cup; ten cotyles of oil, because ten cotyles are a gomor.” [Note: Victorius reads “a *cotyle*, that is, a cup of oil from ten cotyles,” in accordance with the Greek exemplar.]

[565] Here too, because the Septuagint has changed the names of the measures, everything is confused, so that what is being said cannot be understood. For above they had translated *ephah* as “measure,” *bath* as *choenix*, *kor* as *gomor*, and *shekel* as “appendage”; here they use “measure” for *ephah*, now *gomor* for *kor*, now the word *kor* itself, and for the measure of oil they use κοτύλη, that is, a cup, instead of *bath*.

Let us therefore first speak according to the literal sense. The *dekada* [variant: *dekadas*], that is, the tenth part of all crops, the people owed to the tribe of Levi according to the Law. Again, from these tithes the Levites—that is, the lower rank of ministers—gave tithes to the priests; this is what is called the δευτεροδεκάδη, the “second tithe.”

There were also other tithes, which each person among the people of Israel set aside in his storehouses, so that he might eat them when he went to the temple in the city of Jerusalem, in the vestibule of the temple, and invite the priests and Levites to the feasts.

There were still other tithes which they stored up for the poor; in Greek these are called πτωχοδέκαδαι, “tithes for the poor.” But the firstfruits that they offered from their crops were not fixed by a specific amount; they were left to the discretion of the offerers. We have received the tradition of the Hebrews—not commanded by the Law, but established by the custom of the teachers—that the one who had much gave a fortieth part to the priests, while the one who had little gave a sixtieth; between a fortieth and a sixtieth, one was permitted to offer whatever one wished.

What was therefore left uncertain in the Pentateuch is here specifically defined on account of the priests’ greed, lest they demand more from the people when they bring the firstfruits: namely, that they offer a sixtieth part of what the earth produces.

For if the kor, which in Hebrew is called *HOMER* () and by the Septuagint *gomor*, contains thirty *modii*, both for dry substances and for liquids; and if the ephah and bath, as we said above, are a tenth part of a kor; and if it is commanded that a sixth part of both the ephah and the bath be given to the priests as firstfruits, which plainly amounts to half a *modius* from three *modii*, it can plainly be calculated that the priests ought to receive a sixtieth part as firstfruits.

Let this suffice for the present, both as to the literal sense and as to what we have understood and heard according to the Hebrew truth. Now let us return to the spiritual meaning, [566] in which we must first ask how it is said: “Honor the Lord from your righteous labors, and give him from the fruits of your righteousness, so that your storehouses may be filled with grain and your winepresses may overflow” (Proverbs 3:9). After you have offered the firstfruits of your labors and virtues and said, “Behold, now I have brought you the firstfruits of the fruits of the earth that you gave me, O Lord,” may you deserve to hear: “Blessed are you in the city, and blessed are you in the field; blessed are the fruit of your womb, and the produce of your land, and the offspring of your cattle” (Deuteronomy 28:3 ff.), and the rest; and may you possess, according to the Apostle, “every blessing of the spiritual things in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1), since whatever you have you do not consider to be the result of your own virtue but of the mercy of Him who gave the crops.

If we have enough knowledge of the Scriptures to open up their mysteries and teach human beings, that is, rational creatures, then we give the firstfruits of our wheat. But if, after the allegorical sense, we follow only the pure history, which can nourish the simple, according to what is written, “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Psalm 35:7), then we give the firstfruits of our barley—the barley that Isaac sowed in the land of foreigners and that yielded him a hundredfold (Genesis 26).

Whoever gives the firstfruits of barley can say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has settled me in a place of pasture; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Psalm 22:1–2). But whoever feeds rational creatures changes the sentence and says: “You have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me.”

And after offering the firstfruits of oil and wine, he adds and says: “You have anointed my head with oil, and your intoxicating cup, how glorious it is”—with that oil which, free from sediment and most pure, is prepared for the lamp of the Lord. Whoever prepares it has his face brightened by oil: the oil of gladness with which Christ was anointed above His companions. He becomes an olive tree, and with the prophet he will sing: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Psalm 51:10).

And there is also that wine which overflows from the true vine in the winepresses of the Savior, as the Lord says: “I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the cultivator” (John 15:5). We read three psalms concerning these winepresses: the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-third; all of them refer to the mysteries of the Church.

In the old Law the firstfruits were without measure or number, for God did not give the Spirit according to measure. [567] But in the second construction of the temple, which the prophecy of Ezekiel contains, there is a fixed measure, namely the number sixty, by which the world is completed, as it is said to us: “With the measure by which you measure, it shall be measured back to you” (Matthew 7:2).

(Verses 15 ff.) “And one ram from the flock of two hundred, from those which Israel raises, for sacrifice, for a burnt offering, and for a peace offering, to make atonement for them, says the Lord God. All the people of the land shall be bound to these firstfruits for the prince in Israel. And upon the prince shall be the burnt offerings, the sacrifice, and the drink offerings at the feasts, at the new moons, on the Sabbaths, and at all the appointed feasts of the house of Israel. He shall offer the sacrifice for sin, the burnt offering, and the peace offerings, to make atonement for the house of Israel.”

Above he said what portion of things weighed and what measure of both dry and liquid substances ought to be offered to the prince. Now he maintains the same order regarding the firstfruits of living creatures: he commands that one from a flock of two hundred rams, which Israel raises, be offered as a sacrifice, a burnt offering, and a peace offering, to make atonement for the people of Israel, says the Lord God.

What we translated as “from those which Israel raises” is written in Hebrew as *MEMMASCE* (), which Aquila and Symmachus translate as ἀπὸ τῶν ὑδάτων, “from the waters”; the Septuagint and Theodotion translate it as ἀπὸ τῶν ποτιστηρίων, “from the watering places.” The former means irrigated places, the latter channels or pools. Thus the prince’s firstfruits are to be raised nowhere except in irrigated places. [Note: We supplied here the preposition ἀπό, which was missing; then we corrected the earlier Greek reading, which had *ποτηρίων*, substituting *ποτιστηρίων*. This reading was suggested first by the conjecture of Drusius, then by the Sangermanensis manuscript cited by Montfaucon, and finally by the reading found in Rabanus.]

Just as above we read that a sixtieth part should be offered to the prince from things that are weighed and things subject to measurement, so now a two-hundredth part of the animals is commanded to be offered. The whole people are subject to this kind of legal command, so that they offer to the leader or prince what, through him, will be offered for the people as burnt offerings, sacrifices, and drink offerings at each of the appointed feasts, and the house of God will be purified.

From this we should observe that, just as the people are obligated to offer firstfruits to the prince, so the prince is obligated to offer sacrifices for the people. In the tropological sense, we can understand no one else as the prince except the Lord Savior.

He is the one who receives from two hundred animals a ram—or, as the Hebrew expression more significantly indicates, a *boskema*, which may refer to every kind of animal and not specifically to a ram. He receives an animal or ram that has been raised in irrigated places, namely, in the holy Scriptures, and can say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has settled me; beside waters of refreshment he has led me” (Psalm 22:1–2).

These were the irrigated places—or rather, these were the channels to which Jacob led his flocks, so that they might drink and conceive there and, according to the color of the rods, produce offspring for the Lord (Genesis 30).

For “sacrifice,” that is, θυσία, Aquila and Symmachus translate “gift,” which in Hebrew is called *MANAA* (), and properly does not refer to a victim but to offerings made from fine flour, meal, and oil.

A burnt offering is what is offered entirely to God and consumed by sacred fire. A peace offering is made when we are reconciled to God; and the Apostle speaks for us: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). And elsewhere: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (ibid. 5:19). [Note: Victorius rewrites this as “And in the same passage,” since the testimonies are joined there.]

This prince, to whom the firstfruits from the animals are offered, is also king, as is shown in the title of the cross by Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters. When the Jews pressed for the triumphant title to be removed, the crowd of the Gentiles answered through Pilate: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:22).

“Under the prince,” he says, “they shall be.” The priestly dignity is beautifully reminded of the office to which it is subject, so that it may know that it must offer the sacrifice and the drink offerings made from wine [variant: earth] for the people at all the appointed feasts: both at the new moons, that is, the *neomeniae*, when darkness covers everything and the beginning of lunar light appears, and on the Sabbaths, in the rest of the Sabbaths. Thus it is to offer for sin, to make atonement for the house of Israel, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth.

For this is the house of the living God, and the house of Israel, which needs purification from its sins.

(Verses 18ff.) Thus says the Lord God: “In the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall take an unblemished bull-calf from the herd, and you shall make atonement for the sanctuary. And the priest shall take some of the blood that will be for the sin-offering and shall place it on the doorposts of the temple, on the four corners of the ledge of the altar, and on the doorposts of the gate of the inner court. And so you shall do on the seventh day of the month for each person who was ignorant [Variant: was ignorant] and was led astray through error; and you shall make atonement [Vulgate: you shall make atonement] for the house.

“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall have the solemnity of Passover; for seven days they shall eat unleavened bread [Col. 0454A] [Note: [Col. 0454D] He preferred *comedentur*, ‘they shall eat,’ from the Vulgate and the Brixian manuscripts. In Hebrew it is ]. And on that day the prince shall offer for himself and for all the people of the land a bull-calf as a sin-offering. And during the seven-day solemnity he shall offer a burnt-offering to the Lord: seven unblemished bull-calves and seven unblemished rams each day for seven days, and a male goat as a sin-offering each day. And he shall make a grain-offering of an ephah [Manuscripts: *oephi*] for each bull-calf and an ephah for each ram, and a hin of oil for each ephah.

“In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the solemnity, he shall do the same for seven days as was said above, both for the sin-offering and for the burnt-offering, and for the grain-offering and for the oil.”

I have set down the whole chapter, lest its division point by point disturb the reader’s mind. First, we must speak about the variety of the translations. Where we translated, “on the four corners of the ledge of the altar,” the Septuagint translated, “and on the four corners of the temple” [Col. 0454B] “and on the altar.” And where we said, “for each person who was ignorant and was led astray through error,” they rendered, “for the ignorant person and for the child.” Likewise, where we said, “he shall make a grain-offering of an ephah for the bull-calf, and an ephah for the ram, and a hin of oil for each ephah,” their edition reads: “and you shall give a grain-offering and a cooking to the bull-calf, and a cooking to the ram, and a hin of oil for the cooking.” In the final verse also, where we said, “in the grain-offering and in the oil,” they said, “as in the *manaa*, as in the oil.”

“In the first month,” he says, “and on the first day of the month”—there is no doubt that he means Nisan—“you shall take a bull-calf from the herd”: not one that has been raised at home, but one that is in the herd, that is, from the herd and from among many animals. On the seventh day of that same month also—which two solemnities, namely, the first day of the first month and its seventh day, are not found in the Mosaic Law. The fourteenth day of the month, however, on which Passover is celebrated and which Moses commanded to be observed, is the day on which we eat unleavened bread for seven days.

The fourth solemnity, of which he says, “In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the solemnity” (Exodus XII), and so forth, seems to me to signify the Feast of Booths, which he has here mentioned without naming it. Let us therefore proceed through the individual points and briefly explain what seems to us appropriate.

That there are spiritual solemnities the Apostle also teaches: “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in a part of a solemnity, or of a new moon, or of sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Colossians II, 16). And through Isaiah God speaks as follows: “Your new moons and your sabbaths and the great day I do not accept; fasting, and festivals, and new moons, and your solemnities my soul hates” (Isaiah I, 13). It is evident that whoever hates the solemnities of the Jews loves his own: namely, the sabbath that has been left for the people of God, so that we may see what things have been given to us by God and speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

In the present age, which lies in wickedness, we cannot see good days, but in the new age we shall see them. Concerning those days the Holy Spirit sings in the Mosaic Song: “Remember the days of old; understand the years of generation upon generation” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 7). Concerning them the holy man also spoke in the psalm: “At night I meditated in my heart” (Psalm LXXVI, 7). And again: “I remembered the eternal years in my mind, and I meditated” (ibid., 6).

Let the person who does not accept this understanding answer how he can explain what Isaiah prophesies concerning the future and the new age: “There shall be month after month and sabbath after sabbath, and all flesh shall come to worship before the Lord” (Isaiah LXVI, 23). Then true worshipers will worship neither on Mount Garizim nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth (John IV); then there will be a new heaven and a new earth, and every creature will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the children of God, and the sun will receive sevenfold light, and the moon will be made comparable to the sun (Romans VIII; Isaiah LXV).

For we have approached Mount Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and thousands of angels, solemn assemblies [Col. 0455A]. Concerning this solemnity another prophet also speaks: “What will you do on the days of assembly and on the days of the solemnity of the Lord?” (Hosea IX, 5). This is what is also said elsewhere: “Celebrate, Judah, your festivals; fulfill your vows” (Numbers I, 15).

If, then, we have learned about spiritual solemnities, we shall consequently also be taught about spiritual victims. A bull-calf is taken from the herd—or a bull, as Symmachus interpreted it—free and pressed by no yoke, that is, burdened by no load of sins, and unblemished: one who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found; a young bull-calf, bearing horns and hooves, so that in him the sanctuary may be cleansed and atoned for.

“And the priest shall take,” he says, “some of his blood, which will be for the sin of all” [Col. 0455C]. In other words, he is called the Lamb in Exodus and in the Gospel, when John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29). That blood itself is precious: in it we are redeemed through the passion of the Lord and Savior; by his flesh we are nourished and by his blood we drink. With it the four corners of the ledge of the altar are touched. Theodotion retained the Hebrew word itself, *AZARA* (), or “of the temple,” as the Septuagint translated it, so that the house and the altar may be sanctified.

For all the elements of the world are sanctified by this blood, so that, once someone has been atoned for and cleansed, he may enter the gate of the inner court, be able to know the Lord’s mysteries, and consequently come to the seventh day of the first month, attain rest, and offer sacrifice to the Lord both for ignorance, concerning which David says, “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Psalm XXIV, 7), and for the child, who, when he reaches the measure of a mature man, will destroy the things that belong to childhood and will speak confidently: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child” (I Corinthians XIII, 11). Or it is for the one who has been deceived by error and has sinned not so much deliberately as through a mistaken conception of what is good.

When the two solemnities of the first month have been completed—that is, of its first and its seventh day—he comes to the fourteenth day of the month, on which the solemnity of Passover occurs [Col. 0456A]. Of it it is written: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Corinthians V, 7). Then we eat unleavened bread for seven days in rest and security from all things, when, destroying the leaven of malice and wickedness, we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, while our prince offers all these things for us, and first for himself.

For he assumed a human body and, through sin, destroyed sin; he grieves for us and bears our infirmities. Then [Vulgate: therefore] he offers for his house, which is written in the Septuagint but is absent from the Hebrew—that is, for the Church—and for all the people of the land, namely, for the whole human race. For he is the Savior of all human beings, and especially of believers, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not only for ours but for the whole world.

After the bull-calf has been offered for all the people of the land, during the remaining seven days of the Lord’s passion seven bull-calves and seven unblemished rams are offered each day, to be consumed as a burnt-offering by the Lord’s fire [Col. 0456B]. The seven bull-calves and seven rams are those who are conformed to the Lord’s passion, so that they may imitate the true bull-calf and the true ram; through the blood of the martyrs, the sins of the whole world are cleansed throughout the seven days.

A male goat is also offered daily as a sin-offering, namely, for seven days. We must attend more carefully to the fact that in the grain-offering of an ephah for the bull-calf and an ephah for the ram, and in the hin of oil, the things prescribed by the Law are offered. In the offering of the goat, however, neither an ephah nor—as the Septuagint translated it—a cooking is mentioned; for *ephah* they interpreted πέμμα, that is, “cooking” [Col. 0456C]. The hin, which is a fixed measure of oil, about which we have already spoken, is taken in the sacrifice of the bull-calf and the ram, so that after the appeasement of sins we may receive the nourishment of eternal light, rest from labor, and healing from weariness.

In the seventh month also, on the fifteenth day of the month, that is, at the Feast of Booths [Note: [Col. 0455] Thus we emend after Victorius; Martianus, following Erasmus, incorrectly retained *id est*], the same order of offerings and sacrifices is to be observed, both for the sin-offering and for the burnt-offering, and in the grain-offering and in the oil, so that, darkness having been driven away and the light of oil having arisen, we may attain the Lord’s festival and possess more radiant solemnities, in which all sins are forgiven.

## Chapter XLVI—Verses 1ff.

Thus says the Lord God: “The gate of the inner court that faces east [Col. 0456D] shall be shut for the six days on which work is done; but on the sabbath day it shall be opened, and on the day of the new moons it shall be opened.
