And the prince shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the outer gate and shall stand on the threshold of the gate; and the priests shall make his burnt-offering and his peace-offerings, and he shall worship on the threshold of the gate, and he shall go out. But the gate shall not be shut until evening.

“And the people of the land shall worship at the entrance of that gate on sabbaths and on new moons before the Lord. The burnt-offering that the prince shall offer to the Lord on the sabbath day shall be six unblemished lambs and an unblemished ram, and a grain-offering of an ephah for the ram; for the lambs, a grain-offering as much as his hand shall give, and a hin of oil for each ephah [Col. 0457A].

“On the day of the new moons there shall be an unblemished bull-calf from the herd, and six lambs and unblemished rams. He shall make a grain-offering of an ephah for the bull-calf and an ephah for the ram; for the lambs, as much as his hand shall find, and a hin of oil for each ephah.”

Where we translated *ephah*, which is a tenth part of a *cor*, the Septuagint translated πέμμα, which in our language means “cooking.” And where we said “grain-offering,” they set down the Hebrew word itself, *MANAA* (), which Aquila translated as “gift” or “offering,” and Theodotion as “sacrifice.”

Before we discuss what these things signify, the words of Scripture themselves must be unfolded παραφραστικῶς, that is, in paraphrase. “The gate,” he says, “of the inner court shall be shut for six days,” of which it is written, “For six days you shall labor, and do all your work” (Exodus XXIII, 12) [Col. 0457B]. It will not be just any gate, but the one that faces east, from which the sun of righteousness rises.

On the sabbath day, however—that is, the seventh day, on which there is rest—it shall be opened every week. And again, when thirty days have been completed, when one month ends and another begins, that is, on the day of the new moon, it shall be opened, so that the beginning of the month may have the same privilege that the seventh day has in the week.

Why the gate of the inner court that faces east is opened on the seventh day and on the day of the new moons, the following discourse will show. “And the prince,” he says, “shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the outer gate” [Note: [Col. 0457] Again, with Victorius, we supply the word *vestibule* from the manuscripts], namely, of the outer court; “and he shall stand on the threshold of the gate of the inner court that faces east” [Col. 0457C]. He shall not enter the inner court, but, while he stands there, the other priests shall make the burnt-offering for him, which Symmachus interpreted as “offering,” and the peace-offerings, or the offerings that pertain to salvation.

After the prince’s victim has been consumed by the sacred fire and the leader has been reconciled to God, he may then worship on the threshold of the gate of the inner court where he has stood, and he shall go out. What follows? Will the gate immediately be shut after the prince’s departure? By no means. Rather, it shall remain open until evening, so that after the prince the whole people of the land may worship opposite the entrance of that gate. They shall worship on sabbaths and on new moons, when the gate is opened [Col. 0457D].

Since he had said above, “The priests shall make his burnt-offering and his peace-offerings,” but had not indicated the number of the burnt-offerings, he now adds: “The burnt-offering that the prince shall offer to the Lord on the sabbath day.” He shall offer it not by himself but through the priests, concerning whom it is written: “The priests shall make his burnt-offering and his peace-offerings.” He shall offer six unblemished lambs and an unblemished ram, so that the ram’s grain-offering shall be an ephah in measure, which in Hebrew is called *EPHA* ().

For the six lambs, the grain-offering shall be whatever the hand of the one who offers is able to provide; and for each ephah there shall be a measure of oil called a hin. The day of the new moons, that is, the day of the new moons, shall have this additional privilege over the sabbath day: an unblemished bull-calf—or bull—from the herd shall be sacrificed.

The remaining offerings—that is, the six unblemished lambs, the unblemished ram, and their grain-offerings—shall follow the rite of the sabbath, with this provision: just as an ephah of grain-offering, that is, of fine flour, and a hin of oil are offered with the ram, so they shall also be offered with the bull-calf [Col. 0458A].

Let these remarks suffice for clarity. Now, with the Lord granting it, let us disclose the spiritual meaning.

For the six days during which we labor in the world, the eastern gate of the inner court is closed to us. But when we have come to the seventh day, that is, to the sabbath day, on which there is eternal rest, or to the day of the new moons, when after blind night and dreadful darkness the beginning of light appears, the eastern gate is opened to us.

And if one of us, through the merits of virtues, has attained the name and dignity of prince, he will enter by the way of the vestibule of the outer gate, that is, through the labors of this world [Col. 0458B], and he will enter through the gate of the Church, which is still situated within earthly boundaries. He will not enter the inner court—for this is what is written in the present passage—but he will come to the threshold of the inner gate and stand there.

If, then, the prince in the present Scripture does not enter the inner court but stands on its threshold, there is no doubt that we now see in part and know in part, and that we do not yet contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face (I Corinthians XIII). Accordingly, while the prince stands on the threshold of the gate of the inner court, the other priests to whom this office has been assigned—whom we may understand as the angelic powers—will make the burnt-offering and peace-offerings for him [Col. 0458C].

For we need God’s mercy, and every creature is unclean in comparison with the Creator and must be purified by divine fire, by which the lips of the prophet Isaiah were also purified. Once he has received peace through the sacrifice, then, standing on the threshold, he will worship the omnipotence of God and confess himself unworthy to enter the inner court; and immediately he will enter (Isaiah VI).

After the one who is first has gone out, the gate of the inner court will not be shut until the evening of this age, but will remain open, so that the people of the land also may stand at the entrance and worship him—not at every time, but when they have rested from sins and, darkness having been driven away, have received the light of knowledge through faith [Col. 0458D].

This same burnt-offering that the prince offers through the priests on the sabbath day is completed in the number of six unblemished lambs, corresponding to the six days during which we labor in the world, and an unblemished ram, who is the leader of the flock. Thus, for each ram an ephah is offered as a grain-offering, that is, a tenth part of a *cor*.

For the sacrifice of the six lambs no fixed measure is prescribed; rather, whatever the hand of the one who offers gives is accepted, that is, according to the quality and measure of his works (Matthew XXV). He shall offer a hin of oil for each ephah, that is, the oil which the five virgins prepared for themselves, so that he may anoint or mix the fine flour, and every offering of God may be full of the light of truth, and the face of the one who offers may be made joyful by oil.

On the day of the new moons, that is, on the thirtieth day, when the firstborn and the Levites are numbered in the Law, apart from all Israel, about whom we spoke above, an unblemished bull-calf from the herd is offered [Col. 0459A]. We discussed it more fully in the preceding chapter, as well as six lambs, unblemished rams, and the other things offered on sabbaths, so that we may attain eternal rest and deserve to hear: “Well done, good servant, because you were faithful in a little, I will set you over much; enter into the rest of your lord” (Matthew XXV, 21; Luke XIX, 17).

Then may we not only reach the gate of the inner court but also enter its inner chambers and possess it in deed: “Those planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of our God” (Psalm XCI, 14).

## Verses 8ff.

And when the prince enters [Vulgate: has entered], he shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate and shall go out by the same way. And when the people of the land enter before the Lord at the solemnities [Col. 0459B], whoever enters through the northern gate to worship shall go out by the way of the southern gate; and whoever enters by the way of the southern gate shall go out by the way of the northern gate. He shall not return by the way of the gate through which he entered, but shall go out opposite it. The prince shall be in their midst: when they enter, he shall enter with those entering; and when they go out, he shall go out with those going out.

And at the markets and at the solemnities there shall be a grain-offering of an ephah for the bull-calf and an ephah for the ram. [Note: [Col. 0459D] The Vulgate, Victorius, and other books read, “for the lambs.”] For the lambs there shall be a grain-offering as much as his hand shall find, and a hin of oil for each ephah.

That prince of whom it was said above, “The prince shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the outer gate, and by the same gate he shall enter and by the same he shall go out” (John X), is free in will and has power to lay down his soul and to take it up again. Both when coming to us and when ascending to the heavenly things, he exercises the same liberty of his majesty [Col. 0459C].

Accordingly, he does not seek markets, solemnities, or any distinction among days, because every time is a festival for him. The people, however, enter and depart only at markets and solemnities, and not by the same way, but by one way and then another.

For it is written: “When the people of the land enter before the Lord at the solemnities, whoever enters through the northern gate to worship shall go out by the way of the southern gate; and whoever enters by the way of the southern gate shall go out by the way of the northern gate. He shall not return by the way of the gate through which he entered, but shall go out opposite it.”

This is commanded not only to those who are leaving Sodom, to whom it is said, “Do not look back” (Genesis XIX, 17) [Col. 0459D], nor only to those who put their hand to the plow, so that they should not look back at what lies behind them. It is also commanded to those established in the house of the Lord: they must not look behind them and return to the poor and weak elements, and, having begun in the spirit, be consumed in the flesh [Variant: be consumed], but must advance from spiritual things also to greater things and say with the Apostle: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians III, 13).

Thus they must not know in part and prophesy in part, but come to perfection—yet according to the perfection that human nature can receive [Col. 0460A]—so that we may understand the Gospel saying: “When you have done everything, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were bound to do’” (Luke XVII, 10).

Therefore the Apostle speaks in the same Epistle of two kinds of perfection. As though imperfect, he writes: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if I may apprehend that for which I was apprehended by Christ” (Philippians III, 13). Immediately, as though perfect, he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to the goal I pursue toward the prize of the heavenly calling. Let all of us, then, who are perfect, think this” (ibid., 14). [Note: [Col. 0459D] Previously *quo* stood for *quomodo*, “how.”]

How can the statement stand, then, that the one who had said, “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect,” should dare to say, “Let all of us, then, who are perfect, think this”? From this it is clear that every human being, and every creature, although it may have come to perfection, nevertheless needs God’s mercy and possesses complete perfection by grace, not by merit. [Note: [Col. 0460D] Here too *tunc*, “then,” had been written incorrectly for *tamen*, “nevertheless.” The Vatican manuscript corrects both passages.]

The people of the land are therefore commanded that, if they enter through the northern gate to worship, they should go out by the way of the southern gate. Who are these people to whom this is commanded? Clearly, the Gentiles. Having abandoned the northern gate, from which evils blaze forth over the earth, the one who has entered the temple must go out only by the way of the southern gate: to the gate of light, to the gate of heat, to the gate in which the bridegroom rests at noon (Jeremiah I).

Accordingly, it is said in the same Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song of Songs IV, 16). But whoever enters by the way of the southern gate shall go out by the way of the northern gate. Who is that people? Clearly, the Jews, who, abandoning the gate of the way of light, go to the northern gate, concerning which it is said: “A most harsh wind is the north wind” (Jeremiah I). For Jeremiah’s pot also is kindled from the face of the north [Col. 0460C].

Let us state the matter in another way. The one who abandons sins enters through the northern gate and goes out through the southern gate, because he follows virtues. Conversely, if a righteous person falls into sins, he enters through the southern gate but goes out by the way of the northern gate.

“But the prince,” he says, “shall be in their midst,” namely, in the midst of those entering and those going out, in accordance with what is written: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John I, 26). And the Apostle says: “Do you not know that Christ is in you?” (II Corinthians XIII, 5). If it is said to those who do not know that Christ stands among them, how much more is this true of those who do know!

But when Christ stands among those who know, then the body will be dead because of sin, while the spirit will be alive because of righteousness. The prince enters with those entering and goes out with those going out, standing as witness to the virtue and sin of both groups [Col. 0460D].

At the markets, therefore, and at the solemnities—namely, of the sabbaths, the new moons, and every festival of which we spoke earlier—an ephah of grain-offering shall be offered both for the bull-calf and for the ram. For the lambs there shall be no fixed number, nor shall it be left to arbitrary choice; rather, each person shall use his strength and the goodness of his conscience, so that he offers as much as he can, not as much as he wishes. Above all, there shall be a hin of oil for each ephah, so that the fine flour may be anointed and the lamp kindled before the Lord; and the one who uses it may say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Psalm LI, 10).

## Verses 12ff.

But when the prince makes a voluntary burnt-offering or voluntary peace-offerings to the Lord, the gate that faces east shall be opened for him, and he shall make his burnt-offering and his peace-offerings, as is usually done on the sabbath day. Then he shall go out, and the gate shall be shut after he has gone out.

And he shall make an unblemished year-old lamb a burnt-offering to the Lord every day [Vulgate adds: always]; morning by morning he shall make it. And he shall make a grain-offering [or *manaa*] upon it [Note: The Vulgate and Rabanus, here and in the following verse, where “morning” occurs twice, place the first expression *kata mane*, “according to the morning,” before it]—morning by morning—a sixth part of an ephah [or of the measure], and a third part of a hin of oil, so that the fine-flour offering [or *manaa*] may be mixed [or, according to Symmachus, sprinkled], as an ordinance for the Lord, continual and perpetual. [Note: He preferred *faciet*, “you shall make,” as Victor did, from the Vulgate.]

“You shall make the lamb and the offering and the oil morning by morning, an everlasting burnt-offering.”

Where we read “unblemished,” and in Hebrew it is written *THAMIM* (), Aquila translates “perfect.” And where the Septuagint has *MANAA* (), Theodotion translates “sacrifice,” while Aquila and Symmachus translate “gift.” For what we said as “voluntary,” the Septuagint translated ὁμολογίαν, that is, “confession.” And for “prince” they used “leader,” for this is what *NASI* () signifies.

The discourse still concerns the prince, of whom Isaiah speaks: “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the nations, a prince and commander of the nations” (Isaiah LV, 4). And Ezekiel says: “And I, the Lord, will be their God, and David will be prince in their midst” (Ezekiel XXXIV, 24).

When, therefore, this prince makes a voluntary offering and says, “Make acceptable, Lord, the willing offerings of my mouth” (Psalm CXVIII, 108), the voluntary burnt-offering means that he offers his whole self to God. The voluntary peace-offerings are not found in the earlier passage, for it is written there: “The priests shall make his burnt-offering and his peace-offerings”; but concerning the spontaneous and voluntary offerings mentioned here, nothing at all is said. Thus they are not to offer by necessity but by willingness. After the burnt-offering, he offers peace-offerings and is reconciled to God.

Hence virginity is greater than marriage (I Corinthians VII), because it is neither demanded nor repaid, but offered. For the peace-offerings, which in Hebrew are called *SELAMIM* (), the Septuagint translates “salutary offerings,” so that the reconciliation represented by the peace-offerings may itself be the salvation of the one who offers.

When the prince has done this, the gate shall be opened for him—or, according to the Septuagint, he shall open for himself the gate that faces east: that gate concerning which it is written, “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm CXVII, 20), and from which the sun of righteousness rises.

“And he shall make,” he says, “his burnt-offering and his peace-offerings,” about which we have now spoken. He shall make them because the sacrifice is voluntary, and the priests will not make them for him, as is usually done on the sabbath day.

Therefore, at every time, the gate of the Lord is open for the burnt-offering and peace-offering that is offered voluntarily. He does not observe the sabbath, but all days are counted for him as rest. Accordingly, after he has offered the burnt-offering and the peace-offerings, he immediately goes out, and the door is shut behind him—or he himself shuts the door—so that the prince’s privilege may be preserved and his sacrifices not mixed with those of the people.

Since he had said generally, “a voluntary burnt-offering or voluntary peace-offerings to the Lord,” without adding whether it was a bull or bull-calf, a ram or sheep, or a goat for sin, he now teaches what the burnt-offering itself is: “He shall make an unblemished year-old lamb a burnt-offering,” and not on fixed days but every day, and not at any hour but morning by morning, he shall make it. That is, at each morning, when the sun has risen and the beginning of light has appeared.

Concerning this morning David speaks in the psalm: “In the morning you shall hear my voice; in the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Psalm V, 4). And elsewhere: “In the evening weeping will lodge, and in the morning joy” (Psalm XXIX, 6). And again: “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn” (Psalm LXII, 1).

Isaiah teaches more fully who this unblemished—or perfect—and year-old lamb is, saying: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent and did not open his mouth” (Isaiah LIII, 7). And Jeremiah says: “But I was like an innocent lamb led to the slaughter, and I did not know” (Jeremiah XI, 19). And John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29).

This is the lamb that is sacrificed in Egypt, by whose blood the doorposts of the faithful are armed and the destroyer is kept out (Exodus XII) [Col. 0462C]. He is year-old because he proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution.

Let the reader not be surprised if the same person is both prince and priest, bull-calf and ram, and lamb, since in the Holy Scriptures, according to the variety of circumstances, we read of him as Lord, God, human being, prophet, rod, root, flower, prince, judge, king, righteous one, righteousness, apostle, bishop, arm, servant, ointment, shepherd, son, child, only-begotten, firstborn, door, way, angel, arrow, and wisdom, together with many other names. If I wished to cite the testimonies for all of them, they would require a book of their own.

In the burnt-offering of this unblemished year-old lamb, which is always offered in the morning, the prince himself shall make the grain-offering, or *MANAA*, and, morning by morning, a sixth part of an ephah of fine flour, understood as a sixth part of an ephah of fine flour [Col. 0462D]. A sixth part of an ephah is half a *modius*. For if an ephah is a tenth part of a *cor*, that is, three *modii*, there is no doubt that a sixth part of an ephah makes half a *modius*.

Of the measure of a hin of oil, a third part is also offered, so that the fine-flour offering may be mixed—or sprinkled—with oil, a legitimate, continual, and perpetual offering to God. It is not interrupted on any day but is offered continually, whenever the sun has risen, so that what is stated at the end of this chapter may be fulfilled [Col. 0463A]: “He shall make the lamb for the offering, and the oil morning by morning, an everlasting burnt-offering.”

## Verses 16–17ff.

Thus says the Lord God: “If the prince [or leader] gives a gift to one of his sons, it shall be his sons’ inheritance; they shall possess it as an inheritance. But if he gives a bequest from his inheritance to one of his servants, it shall belong to him until the year of remission—for which Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, *DEROR*—but it shall return to the prince; his inheritance, however, shall belong to his sons.

“And the prince shall not take from the inheritance of the people by violence, or from their possession. Rather, from his own possession he shall give an inheritance to his sons, so that my people may not be scattered, each one from his possession.”

Up to this point the discourse has concerned the prince. Now instructions are given concerning his heirs—or rather, concerning the gifts, inheritances, and bequests that he ought to give, and concerning whose possession is temporary or eternal.

“If,” he says, “he gives his sons either a gift or an inheritance, they shall possess it,” because it is owed to them by right of succession, and possession cannot pass from one to another. But if he gives something to one of his servants as a bequest, he shall possess it only until the seventh year of remission, which is called *DEROR* (), or the jubilee, that is, the fiftieth year, arrives [Col. 0463B]. Then every purchase and gift returns to the former owners, so that the servant has the use of the possession for a time, while ownership belongs to the prince’s son.

What follows—“And the prince shall not take from the inheritance of the people by violence” (Leviticus XXIII), or, as the Septuagint translated it, “so as to oppress them,” or, as Aquila and Symmachus have it, “so as to afflict and distress them,” but “from his own possession he shall give an inheritance to his sons”—rebukes not only the priests and princes of that time but also ours, who become richer through the dignity of the priesthood and, apart from what is owed to them by the Lord’s dispensation, take things from the poor by violence [Col. 0463C].

Or, under the pretext of honor, they strip the rich, so that they have nothing to leave even to their own sons, to whom the paternal inheritance is owed, except what was left to them by their parents. Therefore, a priest who is richer than he was when he came to the priesthood must not give whatever he has acquired beyond that to his sons, but to the poor, to the holy brothers, and to the members of the household of faith, whose merits surpass those of children, so that he may return to his Lord the things that belong to the Lord, who speaks in the Gospel: “Whatever you did for one of these, you did for me” (Matthew XXV, 40) [Col. 0463D].

For he is received as a guest in the poor; he is visited in prison; naked, he is clothed; thirsty, he drinks; hungry, he is fed.

“So that my people,” he says, “may not be scattered from their possession.” For if the prince has permission either to receive, seize, or retain under the guise of honor things that are not his, and to leave them to his children, the people who had been gathered in the name of God will be scattered into parts and torn apart [Col. 0464A].

Or, according to the Law, this is so that another person’s inheritance may not gradually pass to someone else and the boundary line of the division may not perish—the line by which the inheritance perhaps came to each individual. Therefore, the one who leaves alien gifts or property to his sons and brothers and relatives, whether by theft, flattery, cajolery, or under the pretext of religion, disperses the people of God and takes away from them the everlasting possession of faith.

### (Verses 19 ff.)

And he brought me through the entrance that was at the side—or behind—the gate, into the treasury chambers of the sanctuary for the priests—or into the side rooms and chambers—which faced north. And behold, there was a place extending toward the west—or toward the sea; and, as the Septuagint translated it, “separated.” And he said to me: “This is the place where the priests will cook the offering for guilt and for sin—or for ignorance, and consequently—where they will cook the sacrifice—or *manna* and offering—so that they may not carry it out into the outer court and sanctify the people.”

And he brought me out into the outer court and led me around the four corners of the court. And behold, there was a small court in a corner of the court, with one small court at each corner of the court. In the four corners of the court small courts had been arranged, forty cubits in length and thirty in width. The four were of one measure. And there was a wall surrounding the four small courts on every side, and kitchens had been constructed beneath the porticoes all around—or beside the dining couches, which Aquila translated as *στιβάδας*; Symmachus as *περιφράγματα*; Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself: **TUROTH**.

**[Note: Jerome did not read *Tiroth* with the Masoretes in his Hebrew copy, but *Thuroth*, with *schourec*, that is, with *vav*, the vowel. MART. Martianaeus aspirates *THUROTH* and insists that it should therefore be retained; but, apart from the fact that the manuscripts—especially the most ancient Sangermanensis manuscript in Montfaucon—read otherwise, the Hebrew is not written with [the indicated letter], but with [the other indicated letter]: although the second is a *yod*, not the letter *vav*; and Theodotion’s Greek has *τειρώθ*.]**

And he said, he tells me: “This is the house of the kitchens, in which the ministers of the house will cook the sacrifices of the people.” The Vulgate adds: “for the Lord”—or “the sacrifice.” For this is what **ZEBA** signifies in Hebrew: [Hebrew term].

The man who held the reed in his hand, together with the builder’s cord by which he was to measure the building, brought me, he says, through the entrance that was at the side of the gate, or behind the gate. He did not specify which gate—eastern, southern, or that of some other region—but left the matter uncertain, so that I might go to the place of the sanctuary and to the treasury chambers, or the priests’ rooms, which faced north and the sea—that is, north and west. Sacred Scripture has this custom: according to the position of the land of Judea, it always calls the west “the sea.”

It should be considered that the place of the priests, where sacrifices are cooked for guilt—or ignorance—and for sin, so that they may not be offered raw, was situated toward the outer court, to the north and west: from the north arises the coldest wind, and in the west the light of the sun sets. From this it is shown that whatever pertains to food is either for error or for sin. But if a sacrifice is offered even for ignorance, how much more for consciousness of guilt! Hence Job also offered a sacrifice every morning for his sons (Job 1), fearing that they might have sinned through ignorance.

What follows—“so that they may not offer it in the outer court and sanctify the people,” who had not been prepared for sanctification—means that we should not lightly give holy things to those who have not been sanctified; nor, according to the Gospel, cast pearls before swine, nor give what is holy to dogs (Matt. 7). Finally, Moses wishes the people to be sanctified for three days from every impurity and from intercourse with their wives, so that they may approach Mount Sinai and, having been sanctified, receive holy things (Exod. 19).

But if those who are about to hear and receive the words of God are commanded to be sanctified by abstaining from their wives, it is clear that the apostolic statement is contained in the Law: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5); that is, they should abstain from their wives by mutual consent so that they may devote themselves to prayer.

After this it is written:

“And he brought me out into the outer court and led me around the four corners of the court. And behold, there was a small court in a corner of the court, with one small court at each corner of the court; in the four corners of the court small courts had been arranged.”

The man whom he so often mentions brought him out from the priests’ place, which extended toward the north—or which was separated—where the priests cook offerings for guilt and for sin, or for ignorance. He brought him out into the outer court.

**[Note: Victorius supplies, from the Sacred Codex in conjunction with the Septuagint, “where there was a place extending toward the west”; for the words, “or which was separated,” indicate that another translation had preceded, namely Jerome’s, “extending toward the west.”]**

From this we understand that the court from which he departed had been an inner court, and that there are many courts in the holy Scriptures, of which we read: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. 134:2). And in John: “I have other sheep that are not of this court; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one court and one shepherd” (John 10:16). For the Greek word is *αὐλή*, which Latin simplicity has rendered as “fold.”

When he says, “of this court,” he shows that there is another as well: either among the multitude of the nations, in distinction from Israel, or in heaven, in separation from the earthly court. According to the quality of their merits, a court is assigned to each office; this was discussed more fully above.

This court of which we are now speaking had, at each of its four corners, a small court. The Septuagint calls them “smaller ones,” and, for ease of understanding, we have rendered the diminutive form as “small courts.” They were forty cubits long and thirty wide.

I remember discussing these numbers in this same prophet, explaining that one number refers to tribulations and narrowness, and the other to perfect maturity. Hence Moses, Elijah, and the Lord and Savior fasted in the wilderness for forty days (Exod. 34; 1 Kings 19; Matt. 4; Luke 3). And for priestly service they do not approach before the twenty-fifth year of age—

**[Note: Jerome observes this because of the Septuagint translation. In the fourth chapter of Numbers, the Septuagint reads “from the twenty-fifth year,” whereas according to the Hebrew truth one should read “from the thirtieth year.” MART. Certainly, where the Vulgate, according to the Hebrew, says in Numbers 4 that ministers in the tabernacle of the covenant are to be taken from the thirtieth year, the Septuagint translated it as from the twenty-fifth year. This was noted both by Victorius and by Martianaeus.]**

—but after the thirtieth. For this reason the Lord was thirty years old when he came to baptism; and in this same prophet the thirtieth year is placed at the beginning.

Where there is food, therefore, there are also constraint and temptation, through which food is prepared. But when we have reached the age of a mature man, everything of this kind must be trampled underfoot, and we must say: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6:8). And: “If the Lord gives me food to eat and clothing to wear” (Gen. 28:20). Or certainly: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both the one and the other” (1 Cor. 6:13).

For in the future we shall neither eat nor drink, but shall feed upon that bread which descended from heaven, concerning which it is sung in the Psalter: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 76:25). And: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).

That the four small courts, which occupied the corners of the larger court, were of one measure signifies the four regions of the world (Gen. 3): that in the sweat of our face we eat bread, and that all labor serves the belly and excrement. One wall surrounded these four small courts, and kitchens had been constructed beneath the porticoes all around—or they had nearby dining couches—so that where there is food, there is also preparation for measuring it.

And lest the prophet perhaps not know what the things he saw were, he said to him: “This is the house of the kitchens, in which the ministers of the Lord will cook the sacrifices of the people.” The sacrifices of the people, which will be offered for guilt—or ignorance—and for sin, are the food and refreshment of the priests, so that they may remember that they ought to desire nothing else, since even in the temple meats have been prepared for their refreshment.

**[Note: Victorius prefers to invert the words in this way: “for guilt, or ignorance, and for sin,” as it is also written above: “It should be considered that the place of the priests, where sacrifices are cooked for guilt, or ignorance, and for sin,” etc. Moreover, the Hebrew word, although it certainly signifies “guilt,” is nevertheless used for guilt committed through ignorance, and ignorance is sometimes called by that name.]**

### Chapter 47 — Verses 1 ff.

And he turned me—or, according to the Vulgate, “he turned”—to the gate of the house, and behold, waters were coming out from beneath the threshold of the house toward the east. For the front of the house faced east. The waters descended along the right side of the temple, south of the altar.

And he brought me out by way of the northern gate and turned me toward the way outside the outer gate, the way that faced east. And behold, waters were overflowing from the right side. When the man went out toward the east, he had a cord in his hand; and he measured a thousand cubits and led me through the water up to the ankles—or, “he passed into the water, the water of remission.” Again he measured a thousand and led me through the water up to the knees—or, “he passed into the water up to the thighs.” And he measured a thousand and led me through the water up to the loins—or, “he passed through the water up to the hips.” And he measured a thousand: it was a torrent that I could not cross, because the waters of the deep torrent had swollen—or, in the alternative reading, “the deep waters of the torrent”—which could not be forded; the Vulgate reads, “which cannot be forded.” The Septuagint translated this as: “And he measured a thousand, and he could not cross, because the water was carried along like a rushing torrent that cannot be crossed.”

These waters that came out from beneath the threshold of the house—that is, of the temple—were carried not toward the north and west, but toward the east and along the right side of the temple, that is, toward the south; and not merely toward the south of any place, but toward the south of the altar. From this it is evident that the waters are sacred and signify the teaching of our Savior, according to what is written: “The law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). And in another passage: “The earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant waters cover the sea” (Isa. 11:9).

The prophet Zechariah also prophesied concerning these waters, saying: “On that day living water shall go forth from Jerusalem, half of it toward the eastern sea and half of it toward the western sea” (Zech. 14:8).

Concerning these waters the Lord also spoke to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10). And again: “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst” (ibid. 13).

And in the temple he cried out and said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this concerning the Spirit whom those who believed in him were about to receive (John 7:37–38).

These are the waters of which the prophet spoke in the psalm: “He led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. 22:2). And Ezekiel: “I will take you from the nations—

**[Note: Victorius completes the citation: “and I will gather you from all lands and bring you into your land, and I will sprinkle,” etc.]**

—and from the lands, and I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities” (Ezek. 36:24–25).

For the springs of the waters appeared. And in Psalm 92 it is sung: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voices”—

**[Note: For the same reason Victorius here supplies: “the rivers have lifted up their waves.”]**

—above the voices of many waters. “The uprisings of the sea are wonderful” (Ps. 92:2–3).

These are the waters of Siloam, which go quietly, concerning which Isaiah speaks: “You shall draw waters from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. 12:3). And the Psalmist: “Bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. 67).

And the same Isaiah says concerning the Lord and Savior: “This one shall dwell in a lofty cave of a very strong rock. Bread shall be given him, and his water shall be sure” (Isa. 33:16).

For water burst forth in the wilderness, and a valley in a thirsty land. And it is said to believers: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; you are mine. And if you pass through water, I am with you” (Isa. 43:1–2). And again: “You who thirst, go to the water” (Isa. 55:1).

And through Jeremiah God says—although the citation is given as Isaiah 55:1—: “My people have committed two evils. They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. 2:13).

Therefore, just as we read in a favorable sense about the waters that come forth from the threshold of the temple and are referred to the teaching of the Church, so there are bitter and very bad waters, to which the prophet Jeremiah forbids us to draw near, saying: “What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Gihon?” (ibid. 18). In Hebrew these are called **SIOR**—[Hebrew term]—that is, “turbid and muddy.”

Concerning these God speaks in anger against heretics: “Behold, I will feed them with distress, and give them water of gall to drink” (Jer. 9:15). In this water the Egyptian dragon reigns, the one who says: “My rivers are mine, and I made them”; the one who sees every lofty thing and is king over all those who are in the waters.

Hence the ecclesiastical man implores the Lord and says: “Save me, O Lord, for the waters have come in even to my soul. I am sunk in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold”—

**[Note: Victorius again supplies: “I have come into the depth of the sea.”]**

—and the storm has submerged me (Ps. 68:1–2). And again: “Deliver me from those who hate me, and from the depths of the waters. Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me up, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (ibid. 15–16).

And in another psalm: “If the Lord had not been with us, let Israel now say: if the Lord had not been with us, when people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. When their anger was kindled against us, perhaps the water would have engulfed us” (Ps. 123:1–3).

And the Bride in the Song of Songs: “Many waters cannot extinguish love, nor can rivers overwhelm it” (Song 8:7).

This is the water of which Hosea says: “Gilead despised me, a city that works vanity, troubling the water; and its strength is the man of the pirate” (Hos. 6:7–8).

This water is also called by another name, **MARA**, that is, “bitterness”; into it the wood of the Cross is cast, and bitter things are changed into sweet.

Consider the Law of Moses: if it is understood according to the fleshly understanding of the Jews, how bitter it is, digging out an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Exod. 21). See the fornication in Tamar (2 Sam. 13), and Hosea joined to a prostitute (Hos. 1), Jeremiah’s *περίζωμα*—“waistband” (Jer. 13)—, Moses’ Ethiopian wife, and the killing of the Egyptian, and a thousand other things. If we understand these according to the western letter, and not according to the life-giving Spirit, they are bitter and build up their reader no more than they destroy him (Num. 12; Exod. 2).

**[Note: For “see,” there was formerly the reading “Judam”; Victorius preferred “Judae,” so that the phrase might depend on what precedes, namely, on the verb “consider,” and so on.]**

These, then, are the waters that come forth from the temple of the Lord, go toward the east, and descend along the right side of the temple, south of the altar, where the bridegroom feeds his guests and reclines.

What follows—“And he brought me out by way of the northern gate, and turned me toward the way outside the outer gate, the way that faced east”—shows secretly that we cannot reach the eastern gate immediately, unless we come to it by a long circuit through the way of the northern gate.

For unless we overcome the coldest wind with the warmth of faith and trample its regions beneath our feet, so that the apostolic saying may be fulfilled in us, “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Rom. 16:20), we will not be able to enter the gate through which the waters go out and which is on the right side.

And note that these waters, which enter through the eastern gate, flee the left-hand regions so completely that they are described as proceeding from the right side of the altar toward the south.

But the man, he says, who had the cord in his hand, after leading me through the northern gate outside to the way that faced east—and after he too had reached that same place—measured a thousand cubits of the same water and led me through the water up to the ankles. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated “ankles” as *ἀστράγαλοι*. In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “and he passed into the water, the water of remission.” The alternative reading is: “and he will pass.”

We can understand this as signifying the first sins of human beings, which are forgiven when we enter the waters of the Lord; they display the saving grace of baptism and are the beginnings of progress, though they themselves reach to the heights.

Finally, they extend as far as the ankles, which are close to the sole and heel and are exposed to the serpent’s bites, as the Lord says: “You shall watch his head, and he shall watch your heel” (Gen. 3:15, according to the Septuagint).

**[Note: Victorius reads “so that it may refer to the heel.”]**

And in the Psalter it is said concerning Judas the traitor: “He who ate my bread magnified his supplanting over me” (Ps. 40:10), or “his heel”; for this is what the Greek word *πτέρνη*—in the manuscripts, *πτέρνα*—signifies.

After the thousand cubits that reached to the ankle, he measured another thousand cubits in the water and led me up to the knees.

After the remission of sins and the path of progress, when we attempt to ascend a little from earthly things to higher realities, we bend our knees before the Lord, as the Apostle says: “So that every knee should bow”—the alternative reading is “should cause every knee to bow”—“of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:10).

A third time he measured another thousand cubits and led me, he says, through the water up to the loins. By these steps we reach the heights; yet even those heights reach only to the hips and loins, so that every ignoble desire may be cut away in us and we may possess holiness of body, without which no one sees God.

Hence in this same prophet (above, chapter 8) God is seen as fiery from the feet to the loins. The works of the loins require fire and purification, as the righteous man says: “For my loins are filled with illusions” (Ps. 37:8), through which the enemy mocks us both by day and in the fantasies of the night.

But from the loins up to the head and crown, he shines with the radiance of electrum, the most precious metal, so that there is nothing sordid or base in him.

Hence now, for the fourth time, it is said: “And he measured a thousand”—understand, cubits—“of the torrent,” a word the Septuagint did not translate, “which I could not cross.” This is much better than the Septuagint, which said: “and he could not cross,” or, according to another reading, “which he could not cross.”

For the prophet and the whole of human nature cannot cross the torrent after the loins: the torrent of thoughts and the impulses of vices in the heart. But that man who was clothed in *BADDIM* and was the prophet’s guide crossed it clearly; he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 56).

He gives the reasons why the prophet could not cross the fourth thousand cubits—the alternative reading has “at the fourth”: “because,” he says, “the waters of the deep torrent had swollen, which cannot be forded”; the alternative reading has “could not be forded.”

But how is it written, with the prophet rejoicing, “Our soul has crossed the torrent” (Ps. 123:5)? The difficulty is easily resolved if we know that the Hebrew reads: “The torrent crossed my soul.”

Isaiah also speaks of this torrent: “Behold, I will incline toward them like a river of peace and like an overflowing torrent of glory” (Isa. 66:12).

**[Note: Victorius, following the Greek, supplies: “like a river of peace and like an overflowing torrent.”]**

And in Psalm 35 it is said of the saints: “They will hope in the shelter of your wings. They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delights; for with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:8–9).

And in Psalm 125: “Restore our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south” (Ps. 125:5). And concerning the Savior: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109:7).

For what human being can boast that he has a pure heart (Prov. 20)? Or into whose mind, through the windows of the eyes, will the death of desire not enter—

**[Note: The alternative reading is *introivit*, “entered.”]**

—or, to say little, the tickling of the soul? “The world is set in the evil one” (1 John 5:19); and from childhood the human heart is inclined toward evil, so that no human condition is without sin, even for a single day from the beginning of its birth (Job 15).

Hence David also confesses in the psalm: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50:7). Not in the iniquities of my mother, nor indeed in my own, but in the iniquities of the human condition.

Therefore the Apostle also says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. 5:14).

As for why we say *cubitos* in the masculine gender rather than the neuter *cubita*, I have explained above, according to the rule of grammarians: we do this not through ignorance, but by customary usage, for the sake of the simple and uneducated, whose number is greater in the assembly of the Church.

### (Verses 6 ff.)

And he said to me: “Surely you have seen, son of man.” And he led me out and turned me back toward the bank of the torrent (or river). When I had turned back (or when he had turned me back), behold, on the bank of the torrent (or river) were very many trees (or exceedingly numerous trees), on both sides. And he said to me:

“These waters that go out toward the sand-dunes of the East [Vulgate: eastern], and descend to the level places of the wilderness (or: this water that goes out toward Galilee, which turns toward the East, and descends to Arabia), will enter the sea and flow out, and the waters will be healed. Every living creature (or: every living animal) that crawls (or: every creeping thing), wherever the torrent (or river) comes, will live. There will be very many fish after these waters have come there; they will be healed, and everything to which the torrent (or river) comes will live. Fishermen will stand above them, from Engaddi to Engallim; it will be a place for drying nets. There will be very many kinds of its fish, like the fish of the great sea, exceedingly numerous.”

[Note: Victor places another reading before this verse, proving from the exposition that follows that it is Jerome’s. He reads it as follows: “But on its banks and in the marshes,” or, “But in those places,” and so forth. The former reading is also found in the Vulgate; yet he maintains that both readings are reported by Jerome, since both are his, and neither belongs to the Septuagint, which translated the passage differently.]

“But in those places that go out beyond the banks and are marshy, the waters will not be healed, but [Vulgate: because] they will be given over to salt-pits. Above the torrent (or river), on its banks, on both sides, every fruit-bearing tree (or: every productive tree) will grow. Its leaf will not fall from it (or: it will not wither), and its fruit will not fail. Each month it will produce firstfruits (or: everything will be renewed), because its waters go out from the sanctuary. Its fruit will be for food, and its leaves for healing (or: its growth will be for health).”

Although the whole chapter is lengthy, I wanted to set it down all at once, so that I would not interrupt the reader’s meaning and so that the order of the reading, divided into sections, would not confuse the listener’s understanding.

First, it must be said that where the Hebrew has “torrent,” it says NEHEL (), which in Greek is called χειμάρρους, while the Septuagint translated it as “river.” Next, in place of “Galilee,” which in Hebrew is called GALILA (), Aquila translated θίνας, meaning “sand-dunes”; Symmachus translated μεθόριον, which we can render “boundary.” For “Arabia,” Symmachus translated “uninhabitable”; Aquila, “low-lying” or “level”; and Theodotion, “Araba.”

[Note: θεινὰς stood corruptly for θίνας, and shortly afterward μετόριον for μεθόριον. The Sangermanensis manuscript corrects it. Compare the Commentaries on Hosea 12:11.]

[Note: Up to this point *Arabas* was incorrectly read for *Araba*, or ἀραβὰ, by which word Theodotion rendered “the plain,” or “level places.” See volume III, the book *On Places*, under the names *Araboth Moab* and *Araba*, etc.]

Let us therefore say what seems to us concerning each point.

The man who was Ezekiel’s guide urges the prophet to look more attentively, to see, and to direct the eyes of his mind toward hidden mysteries. He calls him “son of man,” either as a figure of the Lord and Savior—for Ezekiel is interpreted as “strength” or “command of God”—or certainly to remind him of human frailty, lest he forget his condition while great things are being shown to him. Having admonished him, he leads him and turns him toward the bank of the torrent, so that, since he had not been able [variant: was not able] to cross through the middle of its depth, he might at least recognize what was on the banks.

“And when I had turned back,” he says—or when the guide and admonisher had turned me back—“behold, on the bank of the torrent,” or river, “were very many trees, or exceedingly numerous trees, on both sides.”

This torrent, which because of the abundance of its waters flows like a torrent and receives rains from heaven, of which we spoke in the preceding lecture, is called “river” by the Septuagint, because it has perpetual waters—not waters gathered here and there from rain, but waters flowing from a living and perpetual spring. Concerning this river we read much in the Holy Scriptures, but for the present only a few passages should be mentioned, beginning with this:

“The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45:4).

And elsewhere:

“The river of God is filled with waters; you have prepared their food, because such is your preparation” (Psalm 64:10).

[Note: Victor reads “his” for “your,” following the Vulgate exemplar. In Greek the neuter is read. See the letter to Sunia and Fretela.]

Again, in the plural:

“The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices,”

[Note: Victor again supplies the text by completing it: “The rivers have lifted up their waves.”]

“at the voices of many waters. The liftings of the sea are wondrous” (Psalm 92:2–4).

And in Isaiah:

“I will make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the trackless land” (Isaiah 43:19).

And elsewhere in the same prophet, more explicitly:

“A glorious river flowing through the thirsty land will appear in Zion” (Isaiah 44:3).

Above this river were exceedingly numerous trees on both sides of the bank, so that, between the two Testaments, the old and the new, the river might run enclosed. By the many trees, or exceedingly numerous and very many trees, I understand those that Scripture mentions in paradise as abounding in various fruits.

The preceding guide and teacher instructs the prophet and says:

“These waters that go out either toward Galilee of the nations, according to the Septuagint, or—as is more accurately contained in the Hebrew—toward the sand-dunes of the East, and descend to the level places of the wilderness, or to Arabia, will enter the sea, or flow out toward the sea, and the waters will be healed.”

We said earlier that the waters signify either the grace of baptism or evangelical teaching. If they go out from the threshold of the Lord’s temple and hold to apostolic discipline, they make sand-dunes, previously sterile and unproductive, fruitful; and all level and deserted places are so irrigated that they display within themselves the mystery of the river of Jericho (2 Kings 2). Elisha healed that river with evangelical and apostolic salt, so thoroughly that where previously there had been sterility and death, there were abundance and life.

Nor did they heal only the wilderness. They enter the eastern sea—namely, the Dead Sea, in which nothing living could exist—and the exceedingly bitter sea, which in Greek they call λίμνην ἀσφαλτῖτιν, that is, “the bitumen lake.”

[Note: Previously it read ἀσφάλιτην instead of ἀσφαλτῖτιν. To this testimony of Jerome, concerning the lake’s excessive bitterness, add the very clear account of Galen, *On the Powers of Simple Drugs*, book 5, chapter 19. And when the holy Doctor says that not even little snails can live in its waters, know that Maundrell, praised by Reland, reports that some such creatures are found along its shore.]

In a remarkable way, the evangelical waters heal dead waters, which have received the name of death because they contain nothing living. For they did not know him who says: “I am life and truth” (John 14:6).

And indeed, literally speaking, up to the present nothing that breathes and can move can be found in this sea because of its excessive bitterness—not even little snails, tiny worms, eels, or the other kinds of animals or creeping things, whose little bodies we can more readily know than their names. Finally, if the Jordan, swollen by rains, carries fish into it as it flows in, they immediately die and float upon its thick waters.

Since these waters therefore possess no usefulness, as the plain sense testifies—even if these things should take place, as the foolish superstition of the Jews believes—according to the spiritual understanding, once healed by the Lord’s torrent, they will have very many fish, and everything to which this torrent comes will live. Thus fishermen will stand on the banks from Engaddi to Engallim. The former name means “the spring,” or “eye,” of the kid; the latter means “the spring” or “eye” of calves. Engallim is at the beginning of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan enters; Engaddi is where it ends and is consumed.

I think that the Dead Sea is the one of which Zechariah speaks:

“On that day living water will go out from Jerusalem, and half of it into the first sea” (Zechariah 14:8).

Daniel likewise agrees with this in the following words:

“I saw, and behold, the four winds of heaven were striving upon the great sea” (Daniel 7:2).

And David:

“The liftings of the sea are wondrous” (Psalm 92:4).

And in the person of the Savior, in the psalm:

“I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed me” (Psalm 68:2).

The king of Egypt is also called a dragon by the same Ezekiel (Ezekiel 32), dwelling in the sea and agitating the rivers as though they were his horns. And again:

“This sea, great and spacious” (Psalm 103:25).

As long as it has not received into itself the waters of the river or torrent, it kills everything that it contains. But the Lord, of whom it is said, “He will strike, and he will heal after two days, and on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight” (Hosea 6:23), himself speaks through the same prophet Hosea:

“I bound Ephraim, I took him in my arm, and they did not know that I healed them in the corruption of man” (Hosea 11:9).

[Note: With Rabanus and Victor, we read “in corruption” instead of the former reading, “in correction.” The Greek text has ἐν διαφθορᾷ, “in corruption,” and there it also reads ἀνθρώπων, “of men,” rather than ἀνθρώπου, “of man.”]

He was wounded because of our sins and weakened for our iniquities. “The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

He healed this sea, which is extremely salty and dead from excessive bitterness, by his death—he who says through Isaiah:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me; he sent me to evangelize the poor, to heal those who are brokenhearted” (Isaiah 61:1).

Therefore through Jeremiah also he cries out:

“Turn back, rebellious children, and I will heal your rebellions” (Jeremiah 3:22).

For the impatient people, unable to endure the pain of their wounds any longer, said:

“The summer has passed, the harvest has ended, and we have not been saved.”

Therefore the Lord answered them:

“Is there no resin in Gilead, or are there no physicians there? Why has the healing of the daughter of my people not risen up?” (Jeremiah 8:22).

Jeremiah himself cries aloud and says:

“Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved” (Jeremiah 27:14).

Finally, the angels who were guardians of the Jewish people at the time when the foolish crowd cried out, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25), and when “the veil of the temple was torn” and all the mysteries of the Hebrews were opened, answered the commanding Lord and said:

“We have healed Babylon, and she is not healed; let us abandon her” (Jeremiah 51:9),

namely, the city of confusion and vices.

Josephus likewise relates in his *History* that after the Lord had been crucified and the veil of the temple had been torn—or the temple’s lintel had been broken and had collapsed—a voice was heard in the innermost sanctuary of the temple among the heavenly powers:

“Let us pass from these dwellings.”

[Note: Josephus, book 7 of *The Jewish War*, chapter 12, reports that this voice was heard, but he does not speak of the Lord’s Passion. Jerome’s words should therefore be understood charitably, not dissected literally. —Mart.]

All this has been said not superfluously but necessarily, because the Dead Sea is said to have been healed when the Lord’s river flows into it.

Above this sea, from Engaddi—the eye and spring of the kid, which is always offered for sin—to Engallim, the spring of calves, which are slaughtered for the Lord and imitate the calf lifting up its horns and hooves, the calf slaughtered on the altar as a type of the Savior—there will be fishermen. To them the Lord Jesus says:

“Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19).

Jeremiah also speaks of them:

“Behold, I will send fishermen” (Jeremiah 16:16).

There will be very many species, or rather genera, of fish in the sea that was formerly dead. These are the fish that Peter, at the Lord’s command, drew out on the right side. There were one hundred and fifty-three, so that the nets burst because of their multitude (John 21).

Those who have written about the nature and properties of animals, and who have learned the *Halieutica* (ἁλιευτικά) in both Latin and Greek, say that among them is Oppianus the Cilician, a most learned poet.

[Note: Manuscript copies read as follows: “among whom Oppianus the Cilician is a most learned poet.” Others have “Appianus,” and so forth. Oppianus was by origin from Anazarbus, a city of Cilicia, and wrote the *Halieutica* in highly elegant verse, which he presented to the emperor Antoninus, the son of Severus, with the greatest distinction for his learning. —Mart. All manuscripts call him Oppianus or Appianus. In common usage he is known as Oppianus of Anazarbus, a Cilician, and a well-known poet. Jerome’s learning is particularly remarkable in applying the various kinds of fish to the account in John 21:11 of the one hundred and fifty-three fish caught by the apostles and brought ashore by Peter. By that number Saint Augustine also teaches that the election of every kind, rank, and condition of human beings into the heavenly homeland is signified.]

There are one hundred and fifty-three kinds of fish, all of which were caught by the apostles; nothing remained uncaught, since noble and ignoble, rich and poor, and every kind of human being is drawn out of the sea of this world for salvation.

But what follows—“On its banks and in the marshes,” or “in those places that extend beyond the banks, the waters will not be healed”—quietly indicates that whoever was not in Noah’s ark would perish while the flood reigned; and those whom this river did not reach would not receive healing. Rather, it says, they would be given over to salt-pits, in accordance with what is written:

“When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser” (Proverbs 19:25).

The examples of the worse instruct the good.

Or they will be given over to salt-pits, according to what is written in the Gospel:

“Salt is good; but if the salt has become tasteless, it is useful for nothing” (Matthew 5:13),

so that they may forever lack crops and greenery. A city sprinkled with salt after its ruin demonstrates this as well.

Above the torrent, or river, on its banks and on both sides, every fruit-bearing tree will grow, or—as all the translators unanimously rendered it—βρώσιμον [variant: βρῶμα], “that which provides food and nourishment” and can be eaten. In Hebrew it is called MACHAL ().

[Note: In other books, and perhaps more correctly, MAACHAL.]

According to the Septuagint, nothing in it will grow old; rather, its fruits will be renewed daily. Or, “its leaf will not fall from it, and its fruit will not fail,” in accordance with what is written in the first psalm:

“He will be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall” (Psalm 1:3).

“Each month,” he says, “it will produce firstfruits,” or, as it is written in the Septuagint:

“Its fruit will give its firstfruits in its renewal.”

Thus all the fruits of believers may be firstfruits, and each month may be assigned to a particular apostle.

This will happen because its waters will go out from the sanctuary. Lest we suppose that the abundance of such fruits belongs to the banks, the trees, or the months, he gives the reason for their fruitfulness and adds:

“Because its waters will go out from the sanctuary.”

Therefore it depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy (Romans 9:16).

Among all these trees, the chief place belongs to the tree of life, which is understood as wisdom, concerning which it is written:

“She is a tree of life to all who believe in her” (Proverbs 3).

And what is said—“Its fruits will be for food, and its leaves for healing”—demonstrates the mysteries of the divine books. One of these pertains to the letter, the other to the spirit: we understand simple words in the leaves, but in the fruits a hidden meaning.

Just as knowledge of the Scriptures leads to the kingdoms of heaven and gives us the bread that says, “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41), so its leaves contain moral teaching and provide healing, curing the wounds of sinners.

In place of “leaves,” which in Hebrew are called ALE (), because of the similarity of the word and sound, the Septuagint translated “ascent.” This too can be explained in such a way that after the food of fruits, we ascend toward heavenly things through the admonitions of words.

### (Verses 13–14)

Thus says the Lord God:

“This is the boundary within which you shall possess the land among the twelve tribes of Israel, because Joseph has a double portion. You shall possess it, each one equally with his brother, the land over which I raised my hand to give it to your fathers; and this land shall fall to you as a possession.”

[Note: Victor reads “over which,” following the Vulgate exemplar; he maintains that “into which” is the reading of the Septuagint.]

In place of our reading, “because Joseph has a double portion,” the Septuagint translated, “the increase of the portion.” For Joseph is interpreted as “increase.” They understood the thing in place of the name and confused the mind of the reader.

When the tribe of Levi, assigned to the sacrifices of the temple, had been removed, eleven tribes remained. The tribe of Joseph was divided into two, Ephraim and Manasseh, who said to Joshua son of Nun:

“Why have you given me the possession of one lot and one portion, when I am so numerous and the Lord has blessed me?”

Joshua answered them:

“If you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and cut out spaces for yourself in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, because the possession of Mount Ephraim is too narrow for you” (Joshua 17:14–15).

And again:

“Joshua said to the house of Ephraim and Manasseh: You are a numerous people and possess great strength; you shall not have one lot, but you shall go up to the mountain and cut down and clear spaces for yourselves to inhabit. You will be able to go farther when you have overthrown the Canaanite, whom you say has iron chariots and is exceedingly strong” (ibid., 27).

I have said this because Scripture now mentions Joseph—that is, Ephraim and Manasseh—as having a double portion.

Each tribe receives equal areas of land according to its population, not by the discretion of the one who divides, but by lot, which remains in the power of the Lord. Finally, Joshua himself, who was the divider of the land, did not set apart land for himself, lest he seem to have chosen the best. Instead, he received Thamnath-sareh in Mount Ephraim from the leaders of all the tribes.

### (Verses 15 ff.)

This is the boundary of the land on the northern side: from the Great Sea, by way of Ethalon, as one comes to Sadada, Emath, Berotha, Sabarim, which is between the middle of Damascus and the boundary of Emath; the court of Thicon

[Note: Victor reads “between the boundary of Damascus,” etc., from the Hebrew Vulgate and Jerome’s own Commentary.]

 [Vulgate: the house of Atthicon], which is beside the borders of Auran (or Auranitis). The boundary will be from the sea to the court of Enon (or Seraranan), the boundary of Damascus; and from the north to the north, the boundary of Emath, the northern side [Vulgate: “and the boundary of Emath; the side, however”].

Between the description of the Holy Land allotted among the twelve tribes by Joshua son of Nun and the distribution now commanded through Ezekiel, there is this difference: there the land is divided among the tribes by lot, whereas here it is assigned by the command of the Lord.

In the book of Numbers (Numbers 34), where the whole Promised Land is divided in a brief account according to its four sides, this description is given for the north, that is, the northern side:

“On the northern side [Vulgate: region], the boundaries will begin from the Great Sea and proceed as far as the highest mountain. From there you will come to Emath, as far as the borders of Sadada. The boundaries will continue as far as Zephrona and the village of Enam, or Aser Enon.”

The Hebrews say that the northern side begins at the Great Sea, which extends along the coasts of Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria—which is called Coele Syria—and Cilicia, and stretches through Egypt toward Libya.

But when it says, “The boundaries will reach the highest mountain” (Numbers 34:7), those same Hebrews think that either Mount Amanus or Taurus is meant.

[Note: The Hebrews extend the boundaries of this side to understand either Amanus or Taurus by “the highest mountain,” which many more correctly interpret as Lebanon, although Jerome here has a different view.]

From there, he says, “you will come to Emath,” which is now called Epiphania, its name having been changed after Antiochus, the most savage of tyrants; for his surname was Ἐπιφανής, “Epiphanes.”

“As far as the borders of Sadada,” he says. This place also occurs in the present reading of Ezekiel. “The boundaries will continue as far as Zephrona,” the city now called Zephyrium, a town of Cilicia.

[Note: We read this passage corrupted in Marianus, who incompetently corrected the Erasmian edition with the following note. In Hebrew it is written Haser Enan, and the present passage contains the ancient reading, or Enan. He understands nothing. —Mart.]

What follows is “and the village of Enam,” for which the Hebrew has ASER ENON (), or Enan, and the present passage contains it.

For the present, it is enough to have briefly summarized the historical account and to have set the description in Numbers alongside that of Ezekiel, so that the prudent reader may understand where they mention the same, neighboring, or different things.

Now, having interpreted the names of each place, let us follow the allegorical interpretation and, with the Lord providing, discuss what seems to us concerning each.

Ethalon is interpreted as “the cradle of sorrow.” Sadada means “his side”—understand “from the side,” not “from breadth.” Emath means “fury,” which in Greek is called χόλος, “anger.” Berotha means “wells.” Sabarim means “a circuit of mountains.” Damascus means “blood of sackcloth and of a kiss,” or “of a cup.”

Symmachus interprets “the house,” or “court,” of Thicon as “the middle court,” which extends toward the borders of Auran. Thicon therefore means “middle.” Auran, which the Septuagint rendered in Greek as Auranitis, means “anger.” Aser Enon, which is the boundary of Damascus, is called in our language “the court of the spring.”

The northern side therefore begins at the Great Sea by way of Ethalon, which is interpreted as “the cradle of sorrow,” and through repentance comes to Sadada, where there is a turning to the side. For we understand Emath, that is, the indignation of God, to be hanging over us.

Or Emath may mean that, once the truth has been discovered, the wells of Berotha are opened to us—wells dug by the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. By a long circuit we reach the mountains of Sabarim, which are situated between Damascus—that is, “the blood of sackcloth”—and the boundary of Emath, which, as we have said above, signifies truth.

Just as through sorrow we turn aside from the evils hanging over us and avoid them by turning to the side, so after blood and sackcloth, after a bloodstained life, before we come to the borders of Emath, we go around and reach the mountains of which it is written:

“Mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Psalm 124:2).

The place is called the court of Thicon, that is, the middle court, as Symmachus interpreted it, beside the borders of Auran, which signifies anger. With the prophet, let us say:

“I will bear the anger of the Lord, because I have sinned against him” (Micah 7:9).

And from the sea to the boundaries of Damascus—in that place the apostle Paul (Acts 9), from the fury of the Jews and the shedding of ecclesiastical blood, saw light amid blindness. Taking upon himself the sackcloth of his former persecution, he preached the Gospel, so that he might reach the court of the eternal spring and, having once been placed in the north, seize the boundary of truth.

### (Verse 18)

But the eastern side, from the middle of Auran, from the middle of Damascus, and from the middle of Gilead, and from the middle of the land of Israel, with the Jordan as divider, you shall measure the eastern side as far as the eastern sea [Vulgate adds: “also”].

In the book of Numbers I find the following written in its place:

“From there they shall measure the boundaries toward the eastern side, from the village of Enan—that is, Aser Enon—to Sephama. From Sephama the boundaries shall descend opposite Rebla, toward the spring. From there they shall reach eastward to the sea of Chenereth, and extend as far as the Jordan, and finally end at the sea.”

Earlier it had said:

“The boundary will be from the sea to Aser Enon, the boundary of Damascus” (Numbers 34:10–11).

From the end of the northern side, therefore—that is, from the court of Enan—the boundaries extend, according to the book of Numbers, as far as Sephama, which the Hebrews call Apamia. From Apamia the boundaries descend to Rebla, now called Antioch in Syria.

And so that you may know that this Rebla signifies the city that is now most famous in Coele Syria, it follows: “opposite the spring,” by which it is plainly understood that Daphne is meant. From this spring the aforementioned city receives its abundant waters.

This place was planted by the military hand of Gnaeus Pompey, who first subjected Judaea to Roman rule; according to the poets’ story, it received the name Daphne from him because of the laurels and cypresses, trees that are especially abundant there.

[Note: Testimonies of the ancients can prove that the place was neither first established by Pompey nor named by him Daphne; it had been called that long before.]

“From there,” he says, “the boundaries shall reach eastward to the sea of Chenereth,” as far as the lake of Tiberias.

It is called a sea although it has fresh waters, according to the idiom of Scripture, by which collections of waters are called seas.

“And the boundaries,” he says, “shall extend as far as the Jordan, and finally end at the sea”—either the Dead Sea, or, as some think, the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Ahila is situated, where the Legion and the Roman garrison are now stationed.

This has been said according to the book of Numbers.

According to Ezekiel, however, the eastern side begins from the middle of Auran, which is a town of Damascus in the wilderness, and from the middle of Gilead. This mountain, joined to the hills of Lebanon, fell to the lot of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. It lies behind Phoenicia and Arabia. Jacob reached this mountain after setting out from Charris, and Laban overtook him there (Genesis 31). Jeremiah also speaks of it:

“Gilead, you are to me the beginning of Lebanon” (Jeremiah 22:6).

Gilead was taken from the territory of the Amorites by Gilead son of Machir, son of Manasseh. The boundary of this side is the Jordan, which divides it, and the eastern sea. In this passage they understand “the Dead Sea,” not the tongue of the Red Sea.

Let us speak according to the moral interpretation.

After the boundaries of the north, by a long circuit through Ethalon, Sadada, Berotha, Sabarim, Thicon, Auran, Damascus, and the court of Enon, it reaches as far as Emath; the eastern side proceeds from the middle of the anger of Auran, from the middle of Damascus—that is, through the blood of repentance—and from the middle of Gilead, which is interpreted as “revelation” or “the mound of testimony,” so that after anger and repentance it may show the hope of salvation.

From the middle of the land of Israel, which contains the vision of peace, it reaches the sweetest streams of the Jordan. These, with the sea set far apart, attain the light of the East, so that it ends at the Jordan, whose name means “the stream of judgment,” and at the boundary of the East.

The word φοινικῶνος in the Septuagint, that is, “palm-grove,” is not found in the Hebrew. In its place we translated “you shall measure.” The error is obvious: deceived by the similarity of the letters, they read THAMORRU () instead of THAMODDU (), confusing daleth and resh.

[Note: The printed editions incorrectly read Thamaroth instead of Thamorru, which the manuscript codices retain. The error was not in the name but in changing the letter resh for daleth; hence Thamorru instead of Thamoddu. —Mart. Other books have Thomurru.]

### (Verse 19)

The southern side, the meridional side, extends from Thamar to the waters of contradiction (or to the waters of Mariboth—for this means “contradiction,” or διαδικασμός, that is, “disputes”). It includes Kadesh and the torrent, as far as the Great Sea [Vulgate: “the side”]. This is the southern side toward the south.

In its place the book of Numbers has the following:

“It will begin from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and its boundaries will have the sea [variant: “the most salt sea”] toward the east. They will surround the southern side by the ascent of the Scorpion, cross Senna, and reach southward as far as Kadesh-barnea. From there the boundary will go out to a village called Addar and extend as far as Asemona. The boundary will turn around from Asemona as far as the torrent of Egypt and will end at the shore of the Great Sea” (Numbers 34:3–5).
