This briefly means—and let us not, taking the opportunity of Ezekiel, seem to have passed over to an excessively broad exposition of Numbers—that the boundary begins at the wilderness of Sin beside Edom and the Red Sea, circles around through the ascent of the Scorpion, Senna, and Kadesh-barnea, reaches the court of Addar, and from Asemona continues as far as the torrent of Egypt, which flows into the sea beside the city of Rhinocorura.

Here, however, the boundary of the southern, meridional side begins at Thamar, a city in the wilderness that Solomon built with marvelous works and which is now called Palmyra. In Hebrew it is called THAMAR (), which in our language means “palm,” and extends as far as the waters of contradiction at Kadesh, which is unquestionably in the wilderness, and the torrent flowing into the Great Sea—the sea that stretches along the shores of Egypt and Palestine. This is the southern side toward the south.

After the northern and eastern sides, when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, we receive the southern side, when their light is poured down upon us from above, and with Abraham we enter the banquet (Genesis 19) and are made drunk with the wine that gladdens the human heart (Psalm 103), together with Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 43).

This possession and these boundaries begin at Thamar, that is, at the palm and victory over vices, and extend as far as the waters of contradiction. Virtues are always opposed.

Thus the Jews, arguing against Paul, assert that evangelical preaching is opposed throughout the whole world (Acts 15). And in the Gospel we read Simeon saying:

“This one will be for the fall and resurrection of many, and for a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2:34).

Every contradiction is a matter of holiness, which is what Kadesh signifies, as the Psalmist says:

“The Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh” (Psalm 28:8).

That wilderness originally did not possess the holiness of the Lord; but it was shaken and moved so that it might receive as a guest the God who says:

“Upon whom will my spirit rest [variant: will rest], except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

After the wilderness of Kadesh, as far as the Great Sea in the south, is the torrent of the southern side, of which we spoke above. It has rains collected from heaven, not from the earth, with a variety of different virtues.

### (Verse 20)

The western side is the Great Sea, extending directly from the boundary until you come to Emath. This is the western side.

The book of Numbers writes of it more clearly and briefly:

“The western side will begin from the Great Sea and end at the same boundary,” that is, from sea to sea—namely, from the torrent [variant: from the torrent] of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, as far as the place opposite Emath, the city of Syria, of which we spoke above.

According to the laws of the moral interpretation, the west is always in the sea—always in salt and waves, where shipwrecks arise daily, and the deaths of wretched people, and the loss of riches and merchandise. Yet when we have overcome all these things through patience, we come directly to Emath, that is, to the truth of the Lord, who, after persecutions have been conquered, has promised us eternal rewards.

### (Verses 21 ff.)

“You shall divide this land among yourselves according to the tribes of Israel, and you shall assign it [variant: measure it] to yourselves as an inheritance, and to the resident foreigners who have joined [Vulgate: shall join] you, who have begotten children among you. They shall be to you like natives among the children of Israel; with you they shall divide the inheritance in the midst of the tribes of Israel. In whatever tribe the foreign resident is residing, there you shall give him his possession,” says the Lord God.

From this chapter we learn—and the brow of the Jews is struck down—that nothing is divided between Israel and the people of the nations. For if the land is divided between resident foreigners and strangers together with those who belong to the people of Israel, that is, the natives, no one can doubt that the inheritance of the people of the nations and of the Jewish people is the same—provided that they have turned to the worship of the God of Israel, a designation that properly belongs to the Christian.

The Jews have the letter of the Law, while we have its spirit; they hold the parchment, while we hold the one who is written upon the parchment.

With Moses, the land is divided by lot; here, however, as we have said, it is assigned by the judgment of the Lord. There is one possession for the resident foreigner and the Israelite, and in each tribe an inheritance is given at the command of the Lord God.

## (Chapter XLVIII.—Verses 1 ff.) “And these are the names of the tribes, from the northern boundaries, along the road to Ethalon, as one goes toward Hamath, the court of Enon, the boundary of Damascus to the north, beside Hamath; and its eastern side shall be the sea: one portion for Dan. And from the boundary of Dan, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Asher. And over the boundary of Asher, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Naphtali. And over the boundary of Naphtali, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Manasseh. And over the boundary of Manasseh, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Ephraim. And over the boundary of Ephraim, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Reuben. And over the boundary of Reuben, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Judah.”

[Note: Victorius reads “along the road to Hamath,” and shortly afterward, “and over the boundary of Dan,” from the Hebrew and the Vulgate. The printed reading of the Septuagint is ἀπὸ ὁρίων τοῦ Δάν, “from the boundaries of Dan.”]

After the possession of the Holy Land has been described, both according to the present prophecy of Ezekiel and according to the Book of Numbers, the possession of each tribe is now described, from the eastern side to the western side, that is, to the sea. First, their boundaries begin in the north, along the road to Ethalon, as one goes toward Hamath, the court, or Aser-Enon, the boundary of Damascus to the north beside Hamath, concerning which we have already spoken above.

The first tribe is Dan; the second, Asher; the third, Naphtali; the fourth, Manasseh; the fifth, Ephraim; the sixth, Reuben; the seventh, Judah—that is, on the left side—and the number seven is completed. Then come the first-fruits of the priests and of the Levites, with the sanctuary of the Lord in the middle, and the Holy of Holies. The city itself is also described, square on each side, having four thousand five hundred reeds. The suburbs of the priests and Levites are likewise described in order, as is the prince’s possession.

Again, on the right side, five tribes follow, likewise from the eastern side to the western side. The first is Benjamin; the second, Simeon, having its own distinct possession and no longer, as previously, mixed with Judah; the third, Issachar; the fourth, Zebulun; the fifth, Gad. There are also three gates on each side, and the name of the city, which is inscribed on the golden plate on the forehead of the High Priest. We shall discuss all these matters in their proper places.

It should also be noted that the names of the forty-eight cities given in the Book of Numbers to the Levitical tribe for habitation, together with their suburbs, are omitted here, as are the cities of refuge. Three of these were given beyond the Jordan in the two and a half tribes: namely, Bosor, Ramoth, and Gaulon; and three within the Jordan: namely, Kadesh, Shechem, and Kiriath-arba. For in a mystical description, in the dwelling-place of the saints and in perfected conduct, there was no need to describe the refuges required by Israel while still placed upon the earth and hastening through many labors and dangers to reach this city, with every saint saying: “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:13). And elsewhere: “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long sojourner” (Ps. 119:5).

### (Verses 8–9.) “And over the boundary of Judah, from the eastern side to the western side, shall be the first-fruits that you shall set apart, twenty-five thousand in breadth and length, like the several portions from the eastern side to the western side; and the sanctuary shall be in its midst. The first-fruits that you shall set apart for the Lord shall be twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth.”

It is superfluous to discuss matters already discussed, and to labor again over matters on which we have worked above as though they had not been said. After the boundaries of the seven tribes have been described from east to west, the first-fruits are described. Their breadth is to be twenty-five thousand reeds, while their length is to be the same as that of the individual tribes from the east to the sea, the number of whose length is uncertain. For no measurement was given in the description of the individual tribes.

But if the breadth is twenty-five thousand reeds, it may be inferred that the length is considerably greater, since it is always greater than the breadth. In the midst, however, the sanctuary is placed beside the first-fruits set apart for the Lord: twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in breadth. When I read this, I can say nothing other than the Apostle’s words: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). And elsewhere: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Eph. 3:18–19).

We briefly touched upon this above and shall recall it here in part: the number twenty-five refers to the senses, concerning which it is said, “You shall possess divine understanding,” while ten thousand refers to perfect and consummated virtue, which proceeds from the Decalogue of the Old Testament to the mystery of the Gospel. For if, adding one number at a time, you reach four, you will complete the number ten. Thus the Old Testament is joined together in the New, and the New is unfolded in the Old.

### (Verses 10 ff.) “And these shall be the first-fruits of the sanctuary for the priests: toward the north, twenty-five thousand in length; toward the sea, ten thousand in breadth; toward the east, ten thousand in breadth; and toward the south, twenty-five thousand in length. The sanctuary of the Lord shall be in its midst. It shall be for the priests—the sanctuary for the sons of Zadok, who kept my ordinances and did not go astray when the sons of Israel went astray, as the Levites went astray. And the first-fruits of the first-fruits of the land shall be theirs, a Holy of Holies, beside the boundary of the Levites.”

Four sides of the priestly sanctuary’s first-fruits are described: north, west, east, and south. They do not belong to the people, to the common crowd, or to the Levites, who hold the lower rank, but specifically to the worship of the priests. The order of spiritual progress is narrated in stages: leaving behind the cold of the north, we come to the west, so that vices may set and perish for us; from there we pass to the east, and when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, we come to the south, where the light is brightest and complete.

Thus, both from the north to the sea and from the east to the south, the length is twenty-five thousand and the breadth ten thousand, so that the same measure of length and breadth may be preserved everywhere. The sanctuary, that is, the Temple of the Lord, will be in the midst of the priestly first-fruits and will be enclosed on every side by equal dimensions.

And when he had said, “These shall be the first-fruits of the sanctuary for the priests,” lest all priests claim possession of this place by the common designation, he adds specifically: “The sanctuary shall be for the priests, for the sons of Zadok”—a name interpreted as “just,” concerning whom it is said: “The Lord is just and has loved justice; his face has seen equity” (Ps. 11:7). In place of Zadok, the Septuagint write Saddouk.

This Zadok speaks in the Gospel: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). Concerning him, under the name of Solomon, the Prophet sings mystically: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 72:1).

Those priests, then, shall possess the sanctuary of the Lord and shall keep his ordinances who did not go astray when the sons of Israel and the Levites went astray, as was discussed above. They do not offer sacrifices, but, content with the privilege of their name and the humility of their error, they continually say in their heart: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 51:3).

Let the priestly order hear this—even that order overcome by the heat of the Arian persecution and afterward bowing its neck to the power of the true faith lest it be deprived of its wealth—thinking it sufficient if it is not expelled from the temple, if it retains some shadow and image of its former name, and not, lying on its back and belching out pleasures as though immaculate and pure, spew upon us from its lofty throne the nausea of its ignorance and barbarous chatter.

“They shall have,” he says, “the first-fruits from the first-fruits of the land,” that is, the priests, “who did not go astray when the sons of Israel and the Levites went astray.” The first-fruits from the first-fruits are like the tithe of tithes, and the Holy of Holies, beside the boundary of the Levites. Thus the Levites have the priests’ borders, but they cannot possess the center—that is, the middle—and the possession itself.

### (Verses 13 ff.) “And likewise for the Levites, beside the boundaries of the priests, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth; the whole length shall be twenty-five thousand and the breadth ten thousand. They shall not sell any of it, nor exchange it—or measure it—nor shall the first-fruits of the land be transferred—or taken away—which have been sanctified to the Lord. But the five thousand that remain in the breadth, along the twenty-five thousand, shall be common land for the city, for dwelling and for suburbs; and the city shall be in its midst.”

What we have translated as “profane,” Aquila renders βέβηλον; Symmachus and Theodotion, λαϊκόν; and the Septuagint, προτείχισμα, which we may call an “outer wall.” For “profane” is also “lay,” that is, common, which the whole people may freely inhabit.

As for the Septuagint’s reading, “It shall neither be measured nor taken away,” instead of our “It shall not be exchanged nor transferred,” it is plainly evident that the sense is defective. The Levites’ possession is also described. It is close to the boundaries of the priests and has the same dimensions in length and breadth because of the multitude of the Levites, whereas the priests are few.

[Note: Victorius rejects the words “and in breadth.”] Nevertheless, it uses its own boundaries and understands that it is separated from the priestly rank.

This is intended to humble the pride of ministers who, ignorant of the humility proper to their station, swell beyond priests—that is, presbyters—and think that they possess dignity not by merit but by wealth.

[Note: On this point refer to Letter 146, to Evangelus, especially the following: if someone is ordained presbyter from the diaconate, he should know that he is inferior in wealth but superior in priesthood. It should also be observed that here, contrary to the customary usage of the ancients, the term “priests” signifies presbyters, not bishops. Innocent I uses the word in this sense in his letter to Alexander, bishop of Antioch, section 1, where he mentions “the priests and ministers who are in the city.” Elsewhere, however, he calls presbyters “second priests.”]

Certainly, the one who is first among the ministers, because he—or, according to another reading, “who”—addresses the people one by one and never leaves the High Priest’s side, considers it an insult if he is ordained presbyter. He does not remember that, as a minister of tables and widows, he has been appointed to the service and ministry not only of priests but also of widows and the poor.

[Note: I do not see why Victor removes the words “and of widows” here.]

“They shall not sell any of it,” he says, “nor exchange it,” so that the possession of the Levitical distribution may remain eternal, that the merit of dignity may not be overcome by money, and that we may not transfer it from one person to another, because what has been sanctified to the Lord belongs not to those to whom it has been given but to the one in whose name it is possessed.

The five thousand that remain in breadth, along the twenty-five thousand—“of length” is understood—shall be common land for the city, so that all Israelites and everyone from the people may inhabit it. This does not mean that they are unclean, or that anything in the habitation of the Holy Land is thought contaminated, rotten, or filthy, but that everyone except the priests is permitted to dwell there.

By these things we understand that everything related to the senses—that is, to bodily pleasures, which we receive through sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste—is common and does not possess the sanctity of the temple. It is not a priestly privilege, but belongs to lay lowliness.

The city, however, shall be in the midst. Concerning it, it is written: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 46:4), and: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14). We shall speak of it in what follows.

Προτείχισμα, that is, “outer wall,” and διάστημα, that is, “space,” which the Septuagint translated here for “suburbs”: what meaning they have in this passage, we do not know.

### (Verse 16.) “And these shall be its measurements: on the northern side, four thousand five hundred; on the southern side, four thousand five hundred; on the eastern side, four thousand five hundred; and on the western side, four thousand five hundred.”

When he says, “These shall be its measurements,” “of the city” must be understood. At the end of the preceding chapter it was stated: “And the city shall be in its midst,” that is, in the midst of the land.

He begins with the northern side and places the southern side opposite it. Again, he matches one side with its counterpart, placing the west—that is, the sea—opposite the east. Each side of the city shall have four thousand five hundred reeds, which, calculated, amount to nearly eleven thousand eighty-five paces. Thus the entire city, as is written at the end of this book, shall have eighteen thousand reeds around it, amounting to forty-four thousand three hundred forty paces.

Accordingly, Psalm 45, entitled “For the end, for those who shall be changed,” and referring to Idida—that is, “the beloved of the Lord”—or, as Aquila translated it, “for the lilies,” and Symmachus, “for the flowers,” contains the mysteries of the Church, which is the city of the Lord. Concerning it, the same psalm says: “The queen stood at your right hand in golden garments, surrounded with variety” (Ps. 45:9). And again: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 45:13), so that she may not resemble tombs whitewashed on the outside, but may wash everything within and without, even the inside of the dish (Matt. 23:26).

When we have withdrawn from the north, the coldest wind, we pass to the south. After the light of knowledge has risen within us, we fear the setting of our strength, considering not the past but the future and possessing no secure hold on virtue, but saying daily in prayer: “Do not lead us into temptation which we cannot bear” (Matt. 6:13).

[Note: From this passage it is clear to us that this clause was added from ancient times to the Lord’s Prayer: “which we cannot bear,” in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “God will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able.” Other manuscripts read “which we may not be able to bear.” Moreover, that these words belonged to the text of the Lord’s Prayer, and were not, as Clericus thinks, added by Jerome for explanatory purposes, is established by the testimony of other Fathers, such as Hilary in Psalm 118, letter 1; Ambrose, On the Sacraments, book 5; and the author who copied him, Sermon 84 in the Appendix to the works of Saint Augustine. Saint Ambrose says very clearly: “See what he says: ‘And do not permit us to be led into temptation which we cannot bear.’ He does not say, ‘Do not lead us into temptation,’ but, like an athlete, he wishes for such temptation as human nature can bear.” Add that these words could not have been cited immediately in identical language unless they formed part of the petition in some books. They are also found elsewhere in Saint Jerome, for example in the commentary on Matthew, chapter 26.]

### (Verse 17.) “The suburbs of the city shall be two hundred fifty on the north, two hundred fifty on the south, two hundred fifty on the east, and two hundred fifty toward the sea.”

For “suburbs,” which in Hebrew are called MAGRAS, the Septuagint again translated διάστημα, that is, “space.” When it says two hundred fifty on each side, reeds are understood, each having six cubits and one handbreadth. Along each side they amount to slightly fewer than six hundred seventeen paces, and together to one thousand reeds, containing two thousand four hundred sixty-eight paces. These spaces surround the walls of the city, separating the city from the remaining land.

From this it is shown that no one has permission to use these spaces for the city’s work or for gathering its produce, but that they are to remain free from human use and labor, so that the areas around the city walls may possess the beauty of naturally growing shrubs, grasses, and the other things produced by the earth.

Whatever remains in length beside the first-fruits of the sanctuary—ten thousand toward the east and ten thousand toward the west—shall be like the first-fruits of the sanctuary, and its produce shall be food, or bread, for those who serve, or work for, the city. Those who serve, or work, for the city shall serve, or work, from all the tribes of Israel.

All the first-fruits, twenty-five thousand by twenty-five thousand, in a square, shall be set apart as the first-fruits of the sanctuary and as the possession of the city.

After the description of the holy city and its suburbs, he wishes the remaining part of the sanctuary’s first-fruits—ten thousand reeds extending eastward and another ten thousand extending westward—to be assigned to those who perform the city’s work for its various needs. They are to sow it and eat the produce growing in this portion of land: the workers who either build the city’s walls or restore what is broken and ruined, so that the city may have its proper cultivation and, whenever necessity demands, its damaged structures may be repaired.

This is contained spiritually not only in Israel, or in the possession of the Holy Land through the mystery of the Church; we also know it happens in the Roman Empire, where certain estates belong to the rights of cities, whether through royal munificence, inheritance, or the gifts of many people, lest buildings gradually collapse and public structures, which are an ornament to the city, suffer from prolonged neglect.

The workers, he says, or those who serve in the city’s works, shall come from all the tribes of Israel, so that no one may consider himself exempt from the city’s work, but all may eagerly build the Church.

We read that this also happened in the tabernacle: according to the diversity of their abilities, some offered gold, silver, scarlet, fine linen, purple, and various and different woven materials; others offered skins and goats’ hair. Although the gifts differed according to the nature of their resources, the reward of the donors was one—or rather, greater was the reward of those who offered little but gave more in proportion to their means. The poor widow is an example: she put two small coins into the treasury and was praised by the Lord’s judgment, which said: “Truly I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For all these out of their abundance have put gifts into the offerings of God, but she out of her poverty has put in all the living that she had” (Luke 21:3–4).

As we have said concerning the city’s works, so this too should be briefly noted: all the first-fruits of the sanctuary and the possession of the city, calculated together as a square, contain two hundred and forty-six thousand and one third [Roman paces]. For if twenty-five thousand reeds, each six cubits and one handbreadth, make sixty-one thousand six hundred sixty-seven of our Roman paces, there is no doubt that, calculated fourfold, they produce the number given above.

From this we perceive that everything must be understood spiritually: the possession of the Church is far broader than it once was in Judaea. For the Levites did not even receive portions of the Holy Land, but received forty-eight cities from the individual tribes—not full possession, but habitation and lodging—so that even those who appear to be laymen and have not reached the priestly or Levitical rank may nevertheless, if they work in the Lord’s city, eat from the holy land, the land of the meek and the land of believers. One of them said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 27:13).

### (Verses 21–22.) “Whatever remains shall belong to the prince on every side, both on this side and on that side” [the Vulgate omits “both on this side and on that side”] “of the first-fruits of the sanctuary and of the possession of the city, opposite the twenty-five thousand of the first-fruits as far as the eastern boundary, and also from the sea” [the Vulgate reads “to the sea”] “opposite the twenty-five thousand as far as the boundary of the sea. Likewise, it shall belong to the prince in his portions; and the first-fruits of the sanctuary and the sanctuary of the temple shall be in its midst. The possession of the Levites and the possession of the city shall likewise be in the midst of the prince’s portions, between the boundary of Judah and the boundary of Benjamin; it shall belong to the prince.”

The prince was discussed more fully above, including the fact that he alone would receive as much as one tribe. Now we learn something else: whatever remains from all the tribes shall be received by him alone, so that there may be no tribe that does not offer gifts to the prince—not from elsewhere, but from the first-fruits that serve the temple, the sanctuary, and the portions assigned to the city.

For this is what he says: “Opposite the twenty-five thousand of the first-fruits as far as the eastern boundary,” or “as far as the boundary of the sea,” so that the first-fruits may lie between the seven and the five tribes, and within those first-fruits may be the city, its suburbs, and, in the midst of the city, the sanctuary of the temple.

Likewise, whatever remains of the possession of the Levites and of the possession of the city shall be assigned to the prince. The outermost portion of the seven tribes, in the tribe of Judah, shall be adjacent to the first-fruits, the city, and the temple; and the outermost portion of the five tribes, under the same arrangement as above in the tribe of Benjamin, shall belong to the prince.

The mysteries of Holy Scripture are therefore marvelous and must be pondered more than expressed in words (Deut. 32:29).

In the earlier division of the lands beyond the Jordan by Moses, land was divided among the two tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh (Josh. 13). Within the Jordan, Judah possessed the south (Josh. 15), while Ephraim and the half-tribe of Manasseh possessed the north (Josh. 18).

Later, after scouts had been sent from Shiloh through the individual tribes and a description of the land had been brought to Joshua and Eleazar, Benjamin received its possession beside Judah to the south and beside Ephraim and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The second tribe, Simeon, received its inheritance within the tribe of Judah, so that what was written concerning Levi and Simeon might be fulfilled: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Gen. 49:7).

The third, Zebulun, received Galilee, where Mount Tabor is located. The fourth, Issachar, received the region containing Jezreel, as far as the Jordan. The fifth, Asher, extended to Mount Carmel, which overlooks the Great Sea, and to Tyre and Sidon. The sixth, Naphtali, extended through Galilee to the Jordan, where Tiberias is situated, formerly called Chinnereth. The seventh, Dan, extended to Joppa, where there are [or, according to Relandus’ conjecture, “three cities instead of towers”] the towers of Aijalon, Selebi, and Emmaus, now called Nicopolis.

Although afterward we read that, having crossed beyond the other tribes, they took for themselves the city of Leshem in the tribe of Dan, which is now called Paneas.

Since these things are so, and there is such great diversity between the earlier description of the tribes and the one now presented, let us consider how, both in the present description and in the earlier one, the city and the Temple are placed between the tribe of Judah and Benjamin.

In the earlier description, Judah was to the south and Benjamin to the north. Here, on the contrary, Judah is to the north and Benjamin to the south. After Benjamin comes Simeon second, Issachar third, Zebulun fourth, and Gad fifth—five tribes, as is stated in what follows. For it is written:

### (Verses 23 ff.) “And for the remaining tribes, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Benjamin. And opposite the boundary of Benjamin, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Simeon. And over the boundary of Simeon, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Issachar. And over the boundary of Issachar, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Zebulun. And over the boundary of Zebulun, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, one portion for Gad. And over the boundary of Gad, toward the south, in the direction of the Negeb, its boundary shall extend from Tamar to the waters of contradiction at Kadesh; its inheritance shall be toward the Great Sea. This is the land that you shall measure” [the Vulgate reads “that you shall cast by lot”] “for the tribes of Israel, and these are their divisions, says the Lord God.”

Whenever “one” is placed at the end of the five and seven tribes, either portion, possession, or inheritance is understood, although Aquila and Symmachus translate the word with the neuter τὸ ὅριον, meaning “the boundary.”

It should briefly be observed that among the last five tribes, the tribe of Gad—which in the earlier description was beyond the Jordan—is placed in the region previously held by Judah, namely, toward the south, in the direction of the Negeb. Its boundary extends from Tamar to the waters of contradiction at Kadesh, and its inheritance is toward the Great Sea.

This is Tamar, about which we have already spoken, now called Palmyra, formerly built by Solomon. For “palm” is called תמר, Thamar, in the Hebrew language, and some think it received this name because there are many palm groves there.

As for what follows, “as far as the waters of contradiction at Kadesh, an inheritance toward the Great Sea,” for which the Septuagint translated “from Theman and the water of Mariboth, Kadesh, an inheritance as far as the Great Sea,” it should be noted that in Hebrew the same word, NEHELA (the Hebrew form is uncertain or absent in the supplied text), is ambiguous and can mean both “inheritance” and “torrent.” Here “torrent” should be understood rather than “inheritance.”

For this is the torrent that enters the Great Sea at Rhinocorura, as we have already said. Kadesh, which in the Book of Joshua is called Kadesh-barnea, is in the wilderness extending as far as the city of Petra. Mariboth, interpreted as “contradiction,” is not, as many think, the name of the place, but of the waters in which the people contradicted the Lord and Moses offended God. The Psalm says: “They provoked him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses suffered because of them” (Ps. 106:32).

The entire inheritance of the Holy Land ends on the southern side, along the boundaries of Egypt, at Rhinocorura and the torrent.

Since Gad is interpreted as “temptation,” in his possession we pass from the palm groves to the waters of contradiction as far as Kadesh, which is interpreted as “holy.” Thus we understand that even after the world has been conquered we must remain vigilant and always live in fear, remembering the verse: “Temptation is the life of human beings upon the earth” (Job 7:1). We must reach holiness while adversaries attack, and obtain victory in such a way that from nearby we behold the torrent full of rains.

### (Verses 30 ff.) “And the city’s exits on the northern side shall be measured at four thousand five hundred. The gates of the city shall bear the names of the tribes of Israel; three gates on the north: one gate of Reuben, one gate of Judah, one gate of Levi. On the eastern side, four thousand five hundred, and three gates: one gate of Joseph, one gate of Benjamin, one gate of Dan. On the southern side, you shall measure four thousand five hundred, and three gates: one gate of Simeon, one gate of Issachar, one gate of Zebulun. On the western side, four thousand five hundred, and their three gates: one gate of Gad, one gate of Asher, one gate of Naphtali. Around the city, eighteen thousand; and the name of the city from that day shall be ‘The Lord Is There.’”

The preceding discussion stated that the city had four thousand five hundred reeds on each side, forming a square. These amount to eighteen thousand reeds, as is also stated in the present chapter: forty-four thousand three hundred forty paces.

Now it is written that on each side—namely, over eleven thousand eighty-five paces—there were three gates. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion call them διεξόδους, “passages,” while the Septuagint calls them διεκβολάς, “outlets.” We translated them as the city’s exits and departures.

First, it should briefly be noted that the same tribes were encamped around the tabernacle in this arrangement: Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, the sons of Leah, were to the east; Reuben, Simeon, and Gad—two sons of Leah and a third son of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant—were to the south.

To the west were Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin, two sons of Rachel. Joseph, in place of the tribe of Levi, which was assigned to the sacrifices, was divided into the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.

To the north were Dan, Asher, and Naphtali. The first and third were sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant; the second was a son of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant. They were placed to the north because they were born from the offspring of maidservants who were hostile to one another. This is according to the Book of Numbers and the description of the tabernacle dictated by God through the mouth of Moses (Num. 34).

Our city, however, which is “the city of the great King,” whose architect and maker is God, concerning which the Psalmist also sings, “Shall a man say, Sion? And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 87:5), has a different arrangement of the tribes in the Holy Land, a different measurement of the city and order of its possession, and different sides for the individual tribes.

First, three gates, or exits, of the city face the north: Reuben, the firstborn; Judah, the founder of the royal line; and Levi, concerning whose name nothing was said in the tabernacle or in the description of the sacred rites. Thus, possessing the rights of the firstborn, as a royal and priestly race, let us despise the cold of the north.

Second, to the east are Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan: two sons of Rachel and one of her maidservant Bilhah. To the south are Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun, three sons of Leah. To the west are Gad, Asher, and Naphtali: the first two sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, and the third a son of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant.

“Who is wise and understands these things? Who is discerning and knows them? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them, but transgressors shall fall in them” (Hos. 14:10).

I believe that these twelve gates, or exits, have been assigned to the individual tribes according to the quality of their merits and virtues, under the names of the Apostles and Patriarchs. They are described more openly in the Apocalypse of John, and many mysteries of the divine Scriptures bear witness to them (Rev. 21).

It is necessary that such a city contain eighteen thousand reeds around its circuit. Under this number, the natural law is written in Psalm 19, and the grace of the Gospel is described. By these the Church, that is, the city of the Savior, has been built.

The name of the city itself will no longer be Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” but ADONAI SAMA [also ADONAISAN and ADONAISAMIA] (the supplied Hebrew form is incomplete or uncertain), which is translated into Latin as “The Lord Is There.” He will never depart from it, as he departed from the former people when he said to the disciples: “Rise, let us go from here” (John 14:31). And to the Jews: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38). Rather, it shall possess an eternal possession, and he himself shall be its possession, promising the same disciples: “Behold, I am with you always, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

---

[Col. 0491]

# Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, One Book of Commentaries on the Prophet Daniel, to Pammachius and Marcella (C)

[Note: Cassiodorus, Institutes, chapter 3, praises this exposition on Daniel, which is arranged in one continuous sequence in a single book, as divided into three books. We have collated and revised it against very ancient manuscripts: one Vatican manuscript, numbered 333, and another Palatine-Vatican manuscript, numbered 173.]

## Prologue
[Col. 0491A] 617–618 Porphyry wrote twelve books against the prophet Daniel, refusing to believe that it had been composed by the person whose name it bears, and claiming instead that it was written by someone who lived in Judaea during the time of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes. He maintained that Daniel had not so much foretold future events as narrated the past. In short, whatever he had said up to Antiochus contained true history; but if he had gone beyond that, since he did not know the future, he had lied.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, answered him most skillfully in three volumes—that is, the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth books. Apollinarius likewise responded in one substantial book, the twenty-sixth; before them, in part, Methodius had done so. [Note: The Palatine manuscript does not recognize the words *before these*.]

But since our purpose is not to answer the calumnies of an adversary, which would require a lengthy discourse, but to explain for our fellow Christians what was said by the prophet, I wish to point out in this preface that none of the prophets spoke about Christ so openly. 619–620 For Daniel does not merely write that Christ will come, which he shares with the other prophets; he also teaches at what time he will come, sets out the kings in sequence, counts the years, and announces the clearest signs beforehand.

Because Porphyry saw that all these things had been fulfilled and could not deny that they had already taken place, overcome by the truth of history he burst into this calumny: he asserted that the things said to occur at the consummation of the world concerning the Antichrist had been fulfilled under Antiochus Epiphanes, because of the similarity between some of their deeds. His attack is itself a testimony to the truth. So great was the credibility of the prophet’s words that, to unbelieving people, he seems not to have foretold the future but to have narrated the past.

Nevertheless, whenever an opportunity presents itself in the exposition of this same book, I shall attempt briefly to answer his calumny and to oppose, by a straightforward explanation, the philosophical arts—or rather, the worldly malice—by which he tries to overthrow the truth and, through certain tricks, to deprive clear eyes of their light.

Therefore I beg you, most devoted lover of learning, Pammachius, and you, Marcella, unique model of Roman holiness, united by faith and by blood, to support my efforts with your prayers, so that the Lord and Savior may answer on behalf of his own cause, with his own understanding, through my mouth—he who says to the prophet: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX, 11).

For if, when we are seized and brought before judges and tribunals, he warns us not to consider what we ought to answer (Luke XII), how much more will he himself wage his battles against blaspheming adversaries and conquer in his servants? Hence many psalms contain the Hebrew expression placed in their titles, **LAMANASSE** (), for which the Seventy translated “for the end”; but it means rather “for victory.” Aquila translated it τῷ νικοποιῷ, that is, “to him who grants victory.” Symmachus translated it ἐπινίκιον, which properly signifies a triumph and a victory-palm. [Note: The Vatican manuscript seems to prefer ἐπινίκην.]

Among other things, we must also know that Porphyry objects to us concerning the book of Daniel that it appears to have been fabricated and is not found among the Hebrews, but is a composition in the Greek language, because in the story of Susanna Daniel says to the elders, ἀπὸ τοῦ σχίνου σχίσαι, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ πρίνου πρίσαι—“to split you from the terebinth, and to saw you from the holm-oak”—and this etymology is more appropriate to the Greek language than to Hebrew. [Note: The excellent and very ancient Corbie manuscript reads “the name of God”; thus it has ϹΧΙϹΗϹΕϹΙ ΘΕΟϹ, etc., instead of σχίσας σε, σχίσει σε Θεός.]

Eusebius and Apollinarius answered him with one accord: the stories of Susanna, Bel, and the Dragon are not contained in the Hebrew text but form part of the prophecy of Habakkuk, son of Jesus, of the tribe of Levi. Thus, according to the translators of the Seventy, the title of the story of Bel reads: “There was a certain priest named Daniel, son of Abda, a guest of the king of Babylon.” Yet Holy Scripture testifies that Daniel and the three boys were from the tribe of Judah.

[Col. 0493A] Accordingly, many years ago, when we translated Daniel, we marked these visions with an obelus, indicating that they are not found in the Hebrew text. I am astonished that certain fault-finders complain to me as though I had abridged the book, when Origen, Eusebius, Apollinarius, and other ecclesiastical men and teachers of Greece acknowledge, as I have said, that these visions are not found among the Hebrews, and that they ought not to answer Porphyry on behalf of passages that provide no authority for Holy Scripture.

I also wish to warn the reader that the Churches read Daniel not according to the translators of the Seventy but according to Theodotion, who, in any case, was an unbeliever after the coming of Christ—although some say that he was an Ebionite, a person who was a Jew in another sense.

But Origen, in his edition of Theodotion’s work in the Vulgate, placed asterisks over the passages that had been lacking and had been added, and marked certain verses with obeli, indicating whatever was superfluous. [Note: Hieronymus seems somewhat inconsistent here to Montfaucon. Having just said that the Churches read Daniel not according to the Seventy but according to Theodotion, he immediately adds that all the Churches of Christ—Greek, Latin, Syrian, and Egyptian—read the Vulgate edition, which is plainly understood as that of the Seventy, augmented and corrected by Origen from Theodotion’s edition with asterisks and obeli. If this is understood of its use in the public assemblies of the Church, it is exceedingly difficult to believe: how could two editions of the same prophet have been read indiscriminately in all the Churches? Moreover, Hieronymus himself states again in his Commentary, chapter IV, verse 5, that by the judgment of the teachers of the Church the edition of the Seventy was rejected in this book and Theodotion’s was commonly read, since it agrees both with the Hebrew and with the other translators. Montfaucon therefore thinks that the contradiction should be reconciled as follows: when Hieronymus says that the Vulgate revised by Origen was read by all the Churches of Christ, both Greek and Latin, and so forth, this should be understood to mean that it was in everyone’s hands privately, but not in the public assemblies, where only Theodotion’s edition prevailed—at least among the Greeks, as the Greek Fathers, especially Chrysostom and Theodoret, may testify, since they cite no other edition.

I maintain, however, that this was not Hieronymus’s meaning and that there is therefore no difficulty in the passage. He is not speaking here of a special Vulgate edition of the book of Daniel, which, although the Vulgate was entirely based on the Septuagint in the other books, was taken in this one book from Theodotion’s translation. Thus, when Daniel is under discussion, his Vulgate edition and Theodotion’s version are precisely the same thing. I believe that no one—not even the distinguished Montfaucon—would deny this. For it is evident both from the testimonies just cited and from this entire preface, as well as from another preface to Daniel translated into Latin by Hieronymus, that the Vulgate edition adopted all the other books of Scripture from the Seventy but Daniel from Theodotion; consequently, the Vulgate Daniel itself is Theodotion’s edition.

Therefore, when the holy Doctor says in the passage under discussion that Origen placed asterisks and obeli from Theodotion’s work in the Vulgate edition, he cannot possibly mean this particular book of Daniel. How could that have happened, and what extraordinary redundancy would it have been for Origen to place obeli and asterisks in Theodotion’s edition against Theodotion’s edition—for there was no other Vulgate edition of that book?

It is therefore perfectly clear that he is speaking here of the whole work of Scripture. Adamantius devoted this labor to its Vulgate edition; Hieronymus testifies that this revision was the Hexaplaric edition, and no one now is unaware that it was approved and read in the Churches of the Greeks, Latins, Syrians, and Egyptians, each in its own language. The context that follows also plainly proves that Scripture as a whole, not the single book of Daniel, is being praised.

Hieronymus takes the opportunity provided by Theodotion’s unbelief to commend his own labor more forcefully to students or to defend it against rivals. For if the diligence of that heretic earned such favor among the Churches that, with Origen’s support, it was judged useful not only in Daniel but also in the remaining books, how much more ought Hieronymus himself, a Christian, to be welcomed, since he imitated Origen and wished to provide his own people with what the Greeks read in the editions of Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus.]

And since all the Churches of Christ, both Greek and Latin, Syrian and Egyptian, read this edition with its asterisks and obeli, let the envious forgive my labor: I wished to provide our people with what the Greeks read in the editions of Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus. If they, amid such great riches of learning, do not despise the studies of Jewish men, why should Latin poverty despise a Christian? If his work displeases, at least his intention ought to be accepted.

But now it is time for us to set forth the words of the prophet himself—not, as is our custom, presenting everything and explaining everything, as we did in the Twelve Prophets, but briefly explaining at intervals only what is obscure, lest the vastness of innumerable books weary the reader.

For understanding the final parts of Daniel, a wide range of Greek history is necessary: namely, the histories of Sutorius Callinicus, Diodorus, Hieronymus, Polybius, Posidonius, Claudius, Theon, and Andronicus surnamed Alipius, whom Porphyry also says he followed. Likewise the works of Josephus and those whom Josephus cites, especially our Livy, Pompeius Trogus, and Justin, who recount the whole history of the final vision and describe, after Alexander down to Caesar Augustus, the wars of Syria and Egypt—that is, of Seleucus, Antiochus, and the Ptolemies. [Note: Previously *Suctorium*. It was also incorrect to distinguish Sutorius from Callinicus as though they were two authors. This is Callinicus the Syrian, or Arab sophist, who flourished under Gallienus and wrote, among other works, a ten-book history of Alexandria addressed to Cleopatra, which Hieronymus refers to here. As Suidas notes, he was surnamed Σουτώριος.]

And whenever we are compelled to recall secular writings and to say something from them that we formerly omitted, this is not by our choice but, so to speak, from the gravest necessity: namely, to prove that the things foretold many ages earlier by the holy prophets are contained in the writings of Greeks, Latins, and other peoples.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0495]

[Col. 0495A] 623 (Chapter I, verse 1.) “In the third year of the reign of Joacim, king of Judah, Nabuchodonosor, king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem and besieged it.”

Joacim, the son of Josiah, under whose reign Jeremiah began to prophesy in his thirteenth year, and under whom the woman Huldah also prophesied, is the same person who is otherwise called Eliakim. He reigned over the tribe of Judah and Jerusalem for eleven years. His son Joachim, surnamed Jeconiah, succeeded him; in the third month of his reign, on the tenth day, he was captured by the commanders of Nabuchodonosor and led away to Babylon. In his place, Sedecias, the son of Josiah and his uncle, was appointed king. In the eleventh year of Sedecias, Jerusalem was captured and destroyed.

Therefore no one should suppose that the Joacim at the beginning of Daniel is the same as the Joachin written at the beginning of Ezekiel. The latter has the final syllable *chin*, whereas the former has *cim*. For this reason one generation appears to be missing in the Gospel according to Matthew, because the second τεσσαραδέκας—“fourteen”—ends with Joacim, the son of Josiah, while the third begins with Joachin, the son of Joacim. [Note: The Palatine manuscript has *τεσσαρακαιδέκας*. Victor has noted that Matthew calls Jeconiah both Joachim, in whom the second group of fourteen generations ends at the Babylonian deportation, and Joachim his son, in whom the third group begins after that deportation; thus both are called Joacim by the Seventy in 4 Kings XXIII. Porphyry failed to notice this and, taking Jeconiah in Matthew as only one man, said that one generation was missing and therefore tried to accuse the Evangelist of falsehood.]

Porphyry, ignorant of this, constructs a calumny against the Church, displaying his own incompetence while attempting to charge the Evangelist Matthew with falsehood.

(Vers. 2.) [Note: Our manuscripts pass over this verse and continue the Hieronymian exposition.] “And the Lord delivered Joacim, king of Judah, into his hand.” The fact that Joacim is said to have been delivered shows that the victory belonged not to the strength of the adversaries but to the will of the Lord.

“And part of the vessels of the house of God, and he carried them away into the land of Sennaar, into the house of his god; and he brought the vessels into the treasury of his god” (Gen. XI). [Note: Victor reads “into the house of the god of his god,” not only according to the Vulgate but also according to the testimony of the three manuscripts that he cites.]

The land of Sennaar is the region of Babylon, where there was the plain of Dura and the tower which those who had moved from the East attempted to build up to heaven. Hence, from the confusion of languages, the place received the name Babylon, which is translated into our language as “confusion.”

At the same time, according to the anagogical interpretation, we should observe that the king of Babylon could not transfer all the vessels of God and place them in the idol he had fashioned, but only part of the vessels of the house of God, which are to be understood as the doctrines of truth. For if you examine all the books of the philosophers, you must find in them some part of God’s vessels: for example, in Plato, God as the maker of the world; in Zeno, the founder of the Stoics, the underworld, immortal souls, and the one good, namely moral virtue. But because they join falsehood to truth and destroy the good of nature with many evils, they are therefore said to have seized part of the vessels of the house of God, not all the vessels whole and complete.

(Vers. 3.) “And the king said to Asphanez, the chief of his eunuchs” [the Vulgate omits “his”], [Note: Our manuscripts complete the remaining text of Daniel, which is necessary for the exposition that follows. The Vatican has ΑΒΗΙϹΔΡΙ; the Palatine, together with the Sangerman manuscript cited by Montfaucon, has *Abiesdri* in Latin letters. Likewise, the Vatican soon has ΠΟΡΘΟΜΙΜ, and the Palatine, together with the Sangerman manuscript, *Porthommim*.]

“that he should bring in some of the children of Israel and of the royal seed and of the tyrants, boys in whom there was no blemish.”

For *Asphanez*, I found ἀβριεσδρὶ written in the Vulgate edition. In place of φορθομμὶν, which Theodotion used, the Seventy and Aquila translated “chosen,” while Symmachus translated “Parthians,” understanding it as the name of a nation. We, following the Hebrew edition, which is read κατ’ ἀκρίβειαν—“with exactness”—translate it “tyrants,” especially because “of royal seed” precedes.

[Col. 0496B] Hence the Hebrews suppose that Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah were eunuchs, fulfilling the prophecy spoken to Hezekiah through the prophet Isaiah: “And they shall take of your seed, and they shall make them eunuchs in the house of the king of Babylon” (Isa. XXXVII, 7). [Note: Our codices do not contain the name “Babylon.”]

But if they were of royal seed, there is no doubt that they were of David’s lineage. Unless perhaps the following statement contradicts this interpretation: “boys,” or “young men,” “in whom there was no blemish, and to teach them the letters and language of the Chaldeans.”

Philo believes that the language of the Hebrews itself was Chaldaic, because Abraham came from the Chaldeans. If we accept this, we must ask how the Hebrew boys are now ordered to be taught the language that they already knew—unless perhaps, according to the opinion of some, we say that Abraham knew two languages, both Hebrew and Chaldaic.

(Vers. 7.) “And the chief of the eunuchs gave them names: to Daniel, Belthasar; and to Hananiah, Sidrach; to Mishael, Misach; and to Azariah, Abdenago.”

The chief of the eunuchs—or teacher, or, as others have translated it, ὁ ἀρχιευνοῦχος—does not merely change the names of the holy youths. Pharaoh also gave Joseph a name in Egypt (Gen. 41), [Note: The printed editions incorrectly read *sapharatphaneb* according to the Hebrew, whereas Hieronymus here has taken the form *samtonphanech* from the edition of the Seventy. MART. Two manuscripts have ϹΟΜΤΟΦΑΝΗϹ.]

“Somtonphanech,” because they did not want them to retain Jewish names in the land of their captivity [or “names of Judaea”]. Hence the prophet says in the Psalm: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI, 4).

The Lord, however, changes ancient names for the better and assigns names of virtues according to their meanings, as when he changed Abram into Abraham and Sarai into Sarah (Gen. XVII). In the Gospel also, the former Simon received the name Peter (Mark III), and the sons of Zebedee were called “sons of thunder.” This is not, as most people think, *Boanerges*, but is more correctly read [Note: The Vatican has *baneraem*; the Palatine, *banarehem*.] *benereem*.

(Vers. 8.) “Daniel resolved in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s table or with the wine that he drank, and he asked the chief of the eunuchs not to be defiled.”

If he who refuses to eat from the king’s table and drink his wine does so lest he be defiled, then, if he had known that the wisdom and teaching of the Babylonians themselves were sinful, he would never have agreed to say that they were permissible. They learn these things not in order to follow them but to judge and refute them. If someone wished to write against mathematicians while ignorant of μαθήματα—“mathematical learning”—he would be exposed to ridicule; likewise, anyone disputing against philosophers would be ridiculous if he did not know the doctrines of philosophers. Thus they learn the teaching of the Chaldeans with the same purpose with which Moses learned all the wisdom of the Egyptians. [Note: The Palatine manuscript has “the wisdom of Ham and of the Egyptians,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 9.) “And God gave Daniel grace and mercy in the sight of the chief of the eunuchs,” and so forth.

He who had been led into captivity because of the sins of his ancestors immediately received a reward because of the greatness of his virtues. He had resolved in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s table and had preferred humble food to royal banquets. Therefore, by the Lord’s generosity, he received grace and mercy in the sight of the chief of the eunuchs. From this we understand that whenever, because of circumstances, the saints are loved by unbelievers, this is due to God’s mercy [or “the mercy of God”], not to the goodness of wicked men.

(Vers. 12.) “Test your servants, I beg you, for ten days, and let vegetables be given us for food and water for drink.” [Note: Here again our manuscripts supply the remainder of the verse.]

The magnitude of their incredible faith is shown not only in their promising themselves bodily health from eating cheaper food but also in setting a definite period of time. Their action was therefore not presumption but faith, on account of which they rejected the royal dishes.

(Vers. 17.) “But God gave these boys knowledge and discipline in every book and wisdom; and to Daniel he gave understanding of every vision and dream.”

Observe that God gave the holy boys knowledge and discipline in secular literature, in every book and in wisdom. Symmachus translated this as “grammatical art,” so that they understood everything they read and, by the Spirit of God, judged the learning of the Chaldeans.

Daniel possessed this distinction beyond the three boys: visions and dreams, through which future events are shown by means of symbols and riddles, he perceived with a discerning mind. What others saw in imagination, he saw with the eyes of his heart.

(Vers. 18.) “When the days were completed, after which the king had said that they should be brought in, the chief of the eunuchs brought them before Nabuchodonosor.”

By “the completed days,” understand the period of three years which the king had established, so that, after being nourished for three years, they might then stand before the king.

(Vers. 20.) “And in every word of wisdom and understanding about which the king questioned them, he found them ten times better than all the diviners and magicians who were in his entire kingdom.”

In place of “diviners and magicians,” the Vulgate edition translated “sophists and philosophers”—not according to the philosophy and sophistical discipline promised by Greek learning, but according to the teaching of the barbarian nation in which the Chaldeans philosophize even to the present day.

“Daniel continued until the first year of King Cyrus.”

We shall explain later how the one who is here said to have remained until the first year of King Cyrus is afterward said to have been present in the third year of the same King Cyrus and in the first year of Darius.

(Cap. II, verse 1.) “In the second year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor, Nabuchodonosor saw a dream, and his spirit was terrified, and his dream fled from him.”

If the boys entered his presence after three years, as he himself had ordered, how is it now reported that he saw a dream in the second year of his reign? The Hebrews solve the problem by understanding “the second year” here as the second year of his rule over all the barbarian nations—not only Judah and the Chaldeans, but also the Assyrians, Egyptians, Moabites, and the remaining nations that, with the Lord’s permission, he had conquered.

Thus Josephus writes in the tenth book of the *Antiquities*: “After the second year of the devastation of Egypt, King Nabuchodonosor saw a marvelous dream, and his spirit was terrified, and his dream fled from him.”

The impious king saw a dream concerning future events, so that, when a holy man interpreted what he had seen, God might be glorified and the captives who served God in captivity might receive great consolation. We read the same thing concerning Pharaoh—not because Pharaoh and Nabuchodonosor deserved to see these things, but because Joseph and Daniel were found worthy to surpass everyone in interpreting them.

(Vers. 2.) “Therefore the king commanded that the diviners, magicians, enchanters, and Chaldeans should be summoned, to declare his dreams to the king. When they had come, they stood before the king.”

What we call “diviners,” others translated as ἐπαοιδούς, that is, “incantators.” It seems to me, then, that incantators are those who accomplish a matter by means of words. Magicians are those who philosophize about individual matters. [Note: From the Brescian manuscripts and older printed books, Victor prefers “concerning signs” in place of “concerning individual matters.”] Enchanters are those who use blood and sacrifices and often touch the bodies of the dead. In the Chaldeans, I think γενεθλιαλόγους [or γενεθλιολόγους] are meant—those whom the common people call mathematicians.

Common usage and speech, however, call magicians “enchanters,” although among their own people they are regarded differently, because they are the philosophers of the Chaldeans; and the kings and rulers of that nation devote themselves entirely to knowledge of this art. Hence, at the birth of the Lord and Savior, they were the first to understand his birth, and they came to holy Bethlehem and worshiped the child, with a star showing the way from above (Matt. II).

(Vers. 3.) “And the king said to them: I saw a dream, and I am confused in mind; I do not know what I saw.”

A kind of shadow—or, so to speak, the atmosphere and trace of the dream—remained in the king’s heart, so that when others recounted it he could remember what he had seen and they could not deceive him by lying.

(Vers. 4.) “The Chaldeans answered the king in Aramaic.”

[Note: We have removed from this point, on the authority of our manuscripts, the following verses of the sacred text: “O king, live forever. Tell the dream to your servants, and we shall declare its interpretation to you.” And the king answered the Chaldeans: “The word has departed from me.” These verses were improperly appended and contrary to the holy Doctor’s intention, since they themselves are written in Aramaic and therefore must be excluded.]

Up to this point, what has been read is narrated in the Hebrew language. From here up to the vision of the third year of King Belshazzar, which Daniel saw at Susa, the text is written in Hebrew letters but in the Chaldaic language, which is here called Aramaic.

[Col. 0499B] (Vers. 5.) “Unless you make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you shall perish, and your houses shall be confiscated,” and so forth.

He threatens punishment and also offers rewards: if they can recount the dream, he will consequently believe what is uncertain as well—that is, what the dream signifies. But if they cannot recount the things of which the king, though confused, could remember something, they will also lose credibility concerning the interpretation of the future. Thus the text continues:

(Vers. 9–10.) “Therefore tell me the dream, so that I may know that you will also speak its true interpretation.”

[Note: In place of these words, our manuscripts substitute the following other text of the sacred passage: “The word that you, O king, seek is difficult, and no one will be found who can declare it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with human beings.”]

“Then the Chaldeans answered before the king and said: There is not a man upon the earth who can fulfill your word, O king,” and so forth.

The magicians confess it; the diviners confess it; and all secular literary knowledge confesses that foreknowledge of future events belongs not to human beings but to God. From this it is proved that the prophets spoke by the Spirit of God, since they proclaimed future events.

(Vers. 12–13.) “When the king heard this, he was angry and very furious, and he commanded that all the wise men of Babylon should be destroyed. And the sentence went forth, and the wise men were being killed,” and so forth.

[Note: Our manuscripts add: “And Daniel and his companions were sought so that they might perish.”]

The Hebrews ask why Daniel and the three boys did not enter before the king with the other wise men, yet, when the sentence was issued, they were ordered to perish with the rest. They explain it as follows: at the time when the king was promising rewards, gifts, and the highest honor, they refused to go, lest they should seem shamelessly to desire Chaldean wealth and dignity. Or perhaps the Chaldeans, jealous of their glory and knowledge, entered alone, as though they alone were to receive the rewards, and afterward, when danger arose, wanted as companions those whom they had rejected when glory was in prospect.

(Vers. 15.) “And he asked the man who had received authority from the king why such a cruel sentence had gone forth from the king’s presence.”

[Col. 0499D] The Chaldeans knew that Daniel and the three boys were ten times wiser and more discerning than all the diviners and magicians throughout Chaldea. They concealed the king’s question from them, lest they should surpass them in interpreting the dream. For this reason Daniel asked about the cruelty of the sentence, since he did not know the cause of his own danger.

(Vers. 16–17.) “When Arioch had explained the matter to Daniel, Daniel entered and asked the king to give him time to declare the interpretation to the king. And he entered his house and informed Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions, of the matter,” and so forth.

[Note: Our manuscripts do not contain the opening words, “When he had explained the matter to Daniel,” nor the complete following verse, “And he entered his house,” and so forth.]

Daniel asks for time—not in order to investigate hidden things by deliberation and intellectual ingenuity, but in order to pray to the Lord of hidden things. Therefore he joins Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah to his prayers, lest he appear to rely solely on his own merit; so that, since their danger was shared, their prayer might also be shared.

(Vers. 19.) “Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision by night.”

He learns the king’s dream through his own dream—or rather, he learns both the dream and its interpretation through God’s revelation. What demons did not know, and worldly wisdom could not know, he learns. Thus the apostles also came to know, by the Lord’s revelation, the mystery that had been unknown to all former generations.

(Vers. 20.) “And Daniel blessed the God of heaven and spoke, saying,” and so forth.

To distinguish God from those who dwell upon the earth and deceive earthly beings through demonic arts and tricks, Daniel blessed the God of heaven. For the gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish.

[Col. 0500C] (Vers. 21.) “He changes times and seasons, and transfers kingdoms and establishes them.”

Therefore we should not be surprised when we see kings succeeding kings and kingdoms succeeding kingdoms. They are governed, changed, and brought to an end according to God’s judgment. He who is the creator of all knows the causes of each individual event, and he often permits wicked kings to arise so that the wicked may punish the wicked. At the same time, he hints at and prepares the reader, through a general discussion, for the dream that Daniel saw, which concerned the change and succession of kingdoms.

“He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who possess understanding.”

This accords with what is written: “The wise man will hear and will add to his wisdom” (Prov. I, 5), and “To the one who has, it shall be given” (Matt. XXV, 29). The Spirit of God is willingly poured into the soul that burns with love of wisdom. “Wisdom will not enter a perverse soul” (Wis. III).

(Vers. 22.) “He reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is established in darkness, and light is with him.”

To the person to whom God reveals deep things, and who has the Spirit dwelling within him, it is possible to say: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. XI, 33). Such a person searches even the deep things of God and digs the deepest wells in the depths of his soul, removing all the earth that commonly covers the deep waters. He keeps God’s command, saying: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the spring of your wells” (Prov. V, 15).

What follows—“He knows what is established in darkness, and light is with him”—means that darkness signifies ignorance, while light signifies knowledge and teaching. Thus, just as corrupt things do not conceal God, so upright things encompass and surround him.

Or it should be interpreted as signifying every dark and profound mystery, according to what we read in Proverbs: “He also understands a parable and a dark saying.” The same meaning is found in the Psalms: “Dark water is in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII, 12).

For the person who climbs to lofty places, abandoning earthly things and desiring, like the birds, the thinnest air and all things ethereal, becomes a cloud to which God’s truth comes and which habitually rains upon the saints. Filled with an abundance of knowledge, he has many waters in his heart, dark and wrapped in obscurity, into which Moses alone enters (Exod. XXXIII) and speaks with God face to face. Of him it is written: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 12).

(Vers. 23.) “To you, God of my fathers,” I confess, “and I praise you, because you have given me wisdom and strength.”

[Note: This is how the Vatican and Palatine manuscripts read, and Victor formerly restored it according to the Vulgate and Chaldaic text, judging—although I do not know how soundly—that the reading found in our manuscripts, which Erasmus retained and Martianaeus preserved, belonged to Theodotion’s version.]

So that he may not appear to have obtained what he requested through his own merit, he refers it to the righteousness of his fathers and to the truth of God, who even in captivity shows mercy to their descendants.

“And now you have shown me what we asked of you,” and so forth.

What four men request is shown to one, both so that he may avoid arrogance and not appear to have obtained it alone, and so that he may give thanks because he alone has heard the mystery of the dream.

(Vers. 24.) “Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon. Bring me into the presence of the king” [the Vulgate has “before the king”], “and I shall declare the interpretation to the king,” and so forth.

He imitates the mercy of God, who pleads even for his persecutors and does not wish those to perish for whose sake he himself was about to perish.

(Vers. 25.) “I have found a man among the sons of the captivity of Judah who will announce the interpretation to the king.”

He attributes God’s favor to his own diligence and says that he found Daniel, although Daniel had voluntarily offered himself in order to be brought before the king. Here the character of messengers is displayed: when they bring good news, they want it to appear to be their own achievement. [Note: In place of ἦθος, the Vatican has the Latin *mos*; the Palatine has *typus*.]

And whoever promises to interpret the dream must, of course, first recount the dream. Observe also that Daniel is from the descendants of Judah, not a priest, as the conclusion of the story of Bel contains.

(Vers. 26.) “Can you truly make known to me the dream that I saw?” and so forth.

He preserves the order of the question: first he asks about the dream, which the magicians had replied that they did not know, and afterward he asks for its interpretation. Once he has heard the dream and recognized what he had seen, he may then believe the interpretation as well, since the interpretation admits of various conjectures.

### (Verse 27)

“The mystery about which the king asks the wise men, magicians, soothsayers, and haruspices cannot be declared to the king.” In place of *haruspices*, as we have translated, the Hebrew has **GAZARENOS**, which only Symmachus translated as **θύτας** (*sacrificers*), whom the Greeks commonly call **ἡπατοσκόπους** (*inspectors of entrails*): they examine the entrails and from them predict the future.

[Note: Previously **θυὰς** was printed erroneously; our manuscripts correct it, although they unanimously prefer **ΘΙΤΑϹ** instead of **θύτας**, which is less accurate orthography. Montfaucon likewise advised restoring this from the Roman edition’s scholion on the Septuagint in chapter IV, verse 4: “They translated the Gazarenes as those who perform the sacrifices, for Theodotion gave *sacrificers* instead of Gazarenes.” There you should understand that Theodotion’s name has been put in place of Symmachus’ by Jerome. The Sangerman manuscript has **EAS**, incorrectly. Shortly afterward, with the help of the same manuscripts, we correct *praedicent* to *praedicant*, since the former had previously been corrupt.]

By calling it a “mystery”—that is, the order of the revealed dream—he shows that whatever is hidden and unknown to human beings can be called a mystery. He also removes the king’s mistaken suspicion, lest he think that human ingenuity can discover what has been reserved for the knowledge of God alone.

### (Verse 28)

“But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.” Therefore you seek in vain from human beings on earth what God alone knows in heaven. He also secretly draws him away from the worship of many gods and directs him toward knowledge of the one God.

He has shown you, King Nebuchadnezzar, what is to come in the last times. Joined with truth without the fault of flattery, he speaks courteously to the king: mysteries have been revealed to him by God concerning what is to come in the last times. The last days, however, are either to be counted from the time when the dream was revealed to Daniel up to the consummation of the world, or certainly this should be understood: that the entire interpretation of the dream points toward the end, at which the image and statue that are seen are to be crushed.

[Note: The same manuscripts have “the image of the statue that is seen,” and so forth.]

“Your dream and the visions of your head upon your bed are as follows.” He did not say “the visions of your eyes,” lest we think that something bodily was intended, but “of your head”: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Ecclesiasticus 2:14)—that is, in the governing faculty of the heart, according to what we read in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). And: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (ibid., 9:4).

[Note: Victor supplies “evil” from the Fesulan manuscript and the Vulgate.]

Others, however, taking their cue from this passage, suppose that **τὸ ἡγεμονικόν**—the ruling faculty—is located not in the heart but, following Plato, in the brain.

### (Verse 29)

“You, O king, began to think upon your bed what would happen after these things.” In place of “after these things,” the Septuagint alone translated “the last days.” If this is how it is read, let us inquire more carefully where “the last days” are written, and refute those who do not believe that the world will perish. For they would never be called “the last days” if the world were eternal.

And when it says, “You, O king, began to think,” it indicates the causes of the dream: God revealed to him the mysteries of the future because the king himself wanted to know what was to come. And so, in order that Nebuchadnezzar might marvel at the grace of divine inspiration, he explains not only what the king had seen in the dream, but also what he had silently thought before the dream.

[Col. 0503A]

“And he who reveals mysteries has shown you what is to come.” We understand that what we read in the Gospel—“He makes his sun rise upon the evil and the good” (Matthew 5:45)—was fulfilled even in Nebuchadnezzar. So great is the mercy of almighty God that he revealed to Nebuchadnezzar also the mysteries of his providence, by which he governs the world.

Let us ask those who assert that there are different natures: of what nature do they consider Nebuchadnezzar to be, good or evil? If good, why is he called wicked? If evil—as is certain—why did God display his sacred mysteries to one who was evil and earthly, that is, **χοϊκός**?

### (Verse 30)

“But as for me, this mystery has not been revealed to me through wisdom that is in me more than in all the living, but so that the interpretation might be made clear to the king and you might know the thoughts of your mind.”

The king had thought that knowledge of the future could be grasped by human mental ingenuity, and for that reason he had ordered the wise men of Babylon to be killed. Daniel therefore excuses those who had been unable to give an answer, and he himself avoids envy, lest anyone think that he is about to speak from his own wisdom.

The reason for the prophetic revelation, however, is the king’s desire: he wanted to know what was to come. Daniel therefore honors the king when he says that the mysteries were revealed to him by God because of the king’s desire for knowledge.

This too must be considered: dreams in which future events are indicated, and truth is shown as though through a cloud, are not open to interpreters or to the judgment of the human mind, but only to the knowledge of God.

### (Verse 31)

“You, O king, were looking, and behold, something like a single great statue.”

[Note: Six other complete verses of the sacred text are appended in our manuscripts. In place of **ἀνδριάντι**, from the noun **ἀνδριάς**, **ἀνδριάντη** had previously been read. The Sangerman manuscript has **ἀνδριάντε**; as Montfaucon says, if this is the true reading, Jerome evidently gave the Greek word a Latin termination so that it would fit with the preposition *pro*. The Palatine manuscript, having undergone later correction, prefers *andriante* in Latin letters.]

In place of “statue”—that is, **ἀνδριάντι**, which Symmachus alone translated in this way—the others translated “image,” wishing by this term to indicate a likeness of future events.
