Let us follow the prophetic interpretation and, while interpreting Daniel’s words—spoken briefly by him—explain them at greater length.

### (Verse 38)

“You are therefore the head of gold.” He says: “You, O king, are the golden head.” By this he shows that the first kingdom, the Babylonian kingdom, is compared with the most precious gold.

[Col. 0503D]

### (Verse 39)

“And after you there shall arise another kingdom, inferior to you, of silver” [the Vulgate omits “of silver”]. This refers to the Medes and Persians, which resembles silver, inferior to the preceding kingdom and greater than the one that follows.

“And a third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over the whole earth.” He signifies Alexander and the kingdom of the Macedonians, together with Alexander’s successors. It is rightly called bronze: among all metals, bronze is the more resonant; it rings more clearly, and its sound spreads far and wide. Thus it indicates not only the fame and power of the kingdom but also the eloquence of the Greek language.

[Col. 0504A]

### (Verse 40)

“And there shall be a fourth kingdom, like iron: just as iron crushes and subdues everything, so it shall crush and shatter all these things,” and so forth.

The fourth kingdom, which plainly refers to the Romans, is the iron that crushes and subdues everything. But its feet and toes are partly iron and partly clay; this is demonstrated most clearly in our own time. For just as at the beginning nothing was stronger or harder than the Roman empire, so at the end of affairs nothing will be weaker, when in both civil wars and conflicts against various nations we need the assistance of other barbarian peoples.

[Note: Compare the Preface to Book XI on Ezekiel.]

At the end of all these kingdoms of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, a stone is cut out—the Lord and Savior—without hands, that is, without sexual intercourse and human seed, from the virgin’s womb. When all the kingdoms have been crushed, it becomes a great mountain and fills the whole earth.

The Jews and the impious Porphyry wrongly refer this to the people of Israel, whom they want to be strongest at the end of the ages, to crush all kingdoms and reign forever.

### (Verse 45)

“The great God has shown the king what is to come afterward; the dream is true, and its interpretation is faithful.”

Again, he says that the revelation of the dream is not due to his own merit, but so that the interpretation might be made clear to the king and might teach the king that God alone should be worshiped.

### (Verse 46)

“Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face and worshiped Daniel, and he commanded that sacrifices and incense be offered to him.”

[Note: More correctly, the Vatican and Palatine manuscripts lack the words “Then the king, speaking, said to Daniel.”]

Then the king, speaking, said to Daniel. Porphyry attacks this passage, claiming that the exceedingly proud king would never have worshiped a captive—as though the Lycaonians, because of the greatness of the signs, had not wanted to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas.

The error of the pagans, who consider everything superior to themselves to be gods, should not be attributed to Scripture (Acts 14), which simply reports everything that happened. We can also say that the king himself explained the reasons for worship, sacrifices, incense, and offerings when he said to Daniel:

[Col. 0504D]

### (Verse 47)

“Truly, your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, and a revealer of mysteries, since you were able to disclose this mystery.”

Therefore he worships not so much Daniel as God in Daniel—the God who revealed the mysteries. We also read that Alexander the Great, king of the Macedonians, did the same with the high priest Joiada.

[Note: The account of this deed is again especially worthy of being read in Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XI, chapter 8, section 5, particularly Alexander’s reply to Parmenion: “I did not worship him, but God, whose high priesthood has honored him.”]

If this explanation is displeasing, we must say that Nebuchadnezzar, overcome by the greatness of the signs and by astonishment, did not know what he was doing: understanding that the true God was Lord and Lord of kings, he worshiped his servant and burned incense to him.

### (Verse 48)

“Then the king exalted Daniel to a high position and gave him great and many gifts, and appointed him ruler over all the provinces of Babylon,” and so forth.

[Note: Our manuscripts supply the remainder of the verse.]

Here too the enemy of the Church attempts to criticize the prophet: why did he not refuse the gifts, and why did he willingly accept Babylonian honor? He does not consider that the king had the dream, and that the mysteries of its interpretation were revealed through the young man, so that Daniel might rise and, in the place of his captivity, become ruler over all the Chaldeans, and so that the omnipotence of God might be recognized.

We likewise read that this happened with Joseph in the presence of Pharaoh and Egypt (Genesis 41), and with Mordecai in the presence of Ahasuerus (Esther 8), so that in both nations captive and resident Jews might have consolations when they saw a man of their own people made ruler of the Egyptians or of the Chaldeans.

[Note: The same manuscripts have “resident Jews.”]

### (Verse 49)

“Daniel, however, made a request of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon. Daniel himself was at the king’s gate.”

He does not forget those with whom he had entreated the Lord and who had shared his danger. Therefore he makes them administrators of the province; he himself, however, does not withdraw from the king’s side [some manuscripts: “did not withdraw”].

## Chapter III

### (Verse 1)

“King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue sixty cubits high and six cubits wide.”

How quickly truth is forgotten! The man who shortly before had worshiped God’s servant as though he were God now orders a statue to be made for himself, so that he himself may be worshiped in the statue. The reason it is golden and of immense weight is that it may create astonishment in those who see it, and that an inanimate object may be worshiped as God, while each person consecrates his own greed.

An opportunity for salvation is also given, through the captives, to the barbarian nations (Colossians 3): those who had first learned through Daniel’s revelation the power of the one God may now, through the courage of the three young men, learn to despise death and not to worship idols.

[Note: Victor’s manuscripts read “it is made,” supported by three Florentine manuscripts.]

### (Verse 1)

“And he set it up in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.”

In place of *Dura*, Theodotion has **Deira**, Symmachus **Durau**, and the Septuagint translated it as **περίβολον**, which we may call an enclosure or enclosed place.

[Note: Previously *Duraum* was printed, and one of our manuscripts indeed preferred that form. Montfaucon’s opinion was accepted: he thinks that the *m* arose from a small stroke placed above the word in the very ancient Sangerman manuscript, where it actually indicates an accent, not an *m*. Symmachus translated it **Δουραῦ**, Theodotion **Δειρᾶ**; the Vatican manuscripts have Theodotion’s **ΔΕΙΡΑ** and Symmachus’ **ΔΥΡΥΜ**.]

### (Verse 2)

“Therefore King Nebuchadnezzar sent to assemble the satraps, magistrates and judges, commanders and tyrants, prefects, and all the princes of the regions.”

[Note: The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts supply the words “and all the princes of the regions.”]

Things that stand high stand more dangerously and fall more quickly. The princes are assembled to worship the statue, so that through the princes the peoples too may be led astray. Those who are rich and powerful, because they fear losing their wealth and power, are more easily overthrown. Once the magistrates have been led astray, the subject peoples perish by the example of their superiors.

### (Verses 4–5)

“And the herald cried out loudly: ‘To you it is commanded, peoples, tribes, and languages: at the hour when you hear the sound of the trumpet,’” and so forth.

This does not mean that all the peoples of every nation could have been assembled in the plain of Dura and worshiped the golden statue, but that, in the princes of all the nations, all nations and peoples are understood to have worshiped.

Reviewing the whole of Holy Scripture in my mind—unless forgetfulness deceives me—I nowhere find that any saint worshiped God by falling down. But whoever worships idols, demons, and unlawful things is said to worship by falling down, as repeatedly in the present passage.

In the Gospel, the devil says to the Lord: “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9). We must also say that all heretics who compose false doctrine through the splendor of worldly eloquence make a golden statue and, as far as they can, compel people by persuasion to fall down and worship the idol of falsehood.

### (Verse 7)

“Therefore, immediately after all the peoples heard the sound of the trumpet, pipe,” and so forth.

This must be understood in the same sense as above, so that we understand all the peoples through their princes. For all the nations could not have been present at once.

### (Verse 8)

“And at that very time Chaldean men came forward and accused the Jews,” and so forth.

They envied those who had been placed in charge of the king’s affairs in Babylon, and they were offended by their foreign religious practice and their rejection of idols. Having found an opportunity, they brought an accusation against them before the king. Finally, the text continues:

### (Verse 12)

“There are Jewish men whom you appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men have despised your decree” [the Vulgate reads: “These men have despised your decree, O king”].

In a way they speak as follows: “Those whom you preferred to us, and whom you made rulers—captives and slaves—have been lifted up in pride. They despise your commands, do not worship your gods, and do not worship the golden statue that you erected.”

What we said at the beginning of this vision is demonstrated more clearly here: Nebuchadnezzar has other gods, and there is another golden statue that he ordered to be erected for his own worship. For in what follows the king himself says:

“Do you not worship my gods, and do you not worship the golden statue that I established?” and so forth.

Others say that this is a customary feature of Holy Scripture: to refer to a single idol in the plural, as in Exodus concerning the calf: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 32:4). And in the Book of Kings, when Jeroboam placed a golden calf at Bethel, he is said to have made idols (1 Kings 12).

Conversely, many demons are referred to in the singular, as in Isaiah: “He bows down and worships it, and, praying to it, says: ‘You are my god’” (Isaiah 44:17).

### (Verse 14)

“Fall down and worship the statue that I have made.”

Although in his anger he ordered the young men to be brought before him, he nevertheless gives them time for repentance, so that if they fall down and worship, their earlier offense may receive pardon; but if they refuse to worship, the punishment of the burning furnace will immediately follow.

### (Verse 15)

“And who is the god who will rescue you from my hand?” and so forth.

That is, the one whose servant you worshiped shortly before, whom you declared truly to be God of gods and Lord of kings.

### (Verse 16)

“King Nebuchadnezzar, we do not need to answer you concerning this matter.”

[Note: Our manuscripts do not recognize the words “King,” as in the Septuagint.]

In Hebrew the word *king* is absent, lest they appear to flatter the wicked man or call him king when he was compelling them to commit wickedness. If someone stubbornly insists on reading *king* as well, we shall say that they are not insolently provoking the king to shed their blood, but are rendering the king his due honor in such a way that the worship of God is not harmed.

When they say, “We do not need to answer you concerning this matter,” the sense is: “You should not need to hear words whose strength and steadfastness you will soon prove by the deeds themselves.”

### (Verse 17)

“For behold, our God whom we worship is able to rescue us from the furnace of blazing fire and to deliver us from your hands, O king.”

From the very thing by which he had thought to terrify the young men, he sees in them the material of courage. They do not delay their assurance but promise themselves help immediately, saying: “Behold, our God whom we worship is able to deliver us both from the fire with which you threaten us and from your hands.”

### (Verse 18)

“But if he does not wish to do so…”

Beautifully, in response to what they had said—“He is able to rescue us”—they do not add the opposite, “if he is unable,” but “if he does not wish to,” so that, if they perish, it may be attributed not to God’s inability but to his will.

“Let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods, and that we do not worship the golden statue that you have erected.”

Whether we choose to read “statue,” as Symmachus translated it, or “golden image,” as the others translated it, worshipers of God ought not to worship it. Therefore the judges and rulers of this age who worship the statues and images of emperors should understand that they are doing what the three young men refused to do, and that refusal pleased God.

The precision of their wording should also be noted: they say that gods are worshiped, but that an image is adored; neither practice is fitting for servants of God.

### (Verse 19)

“Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the appearance of his face was changed.”

[Note: Our manuscripts supply: “and the appearance of his face was changed.”]

Some psalms have headings prefixed to them: “For those who shall be changed.” The language of change is therefore ambiguous, referring both from good to evil and from evil to good. The change of Nebuchadnezzar’s face cannot be applied to the good side.

Some also refer the heading of the Psalms from good to evil: those who by nature ought to have understood God were changed against Christ and his saints through mental disturbance and fury.

### (Verse 20)

“And he commanded that the furnace be heated seven times more than it was accustomed to be heated.”

[Note: Our manuscripts do not contain the passage of the sacred text that follows from this point, nor does the exposition appended here require it.]

“And he commanded the strongest men in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego by their feet and throw them into the furnace of blazing fire.”

It was as though ordinary and customary fire could not have consumed the bodies of the three young men. But fury and anger, which are close to madness, cannot keep within bounds. He wants to terrify those whom he saw prepared for death by threatening them with a punishment multiplied many times over.

### (Verse 21)

“And immediately those men, bound in their trousers” [the same manuscripts and the Vulgate add “with their trousers”], “their turbans, their shoes, and their garments, were thrown into the midst of the furnace of blazing fire,” and so forth.

In place of *trousers*—which Symmachus translated as **ἀναξυρίδας**—Aquila and Theodotion used *saraballa*. The word should not be read, as it is corruptly printed, *sarabara*.

[Note: The form **Σαράβαρα** in the Septuagint is corrupt, as are the forms found in Pollux, Hesychius, Photius, and others. The correct form is **σαράβαλα**, used by Aquila, Theodotion, and the Arabs. There is no reason to pursue further the origin of the word, which most derive from the Persian language. Drusius rightly observed that Jerome’s *Saraballa*, with a double *l*, is less correctly written, since the Chaldean script has only one. Compare what we noted in the first letter to Innocent, section 9. The various ways of writing this word have also produced various interpretations. Isidore, Book XIX, chapter 23, reports that for some it means head coverings, while for others it means loose and flowing garments; he himself approves the latter.]

In the language of the Chaldeans, *saraballa* means the legs and shins of human beings; by homonymy it also means the trousers by which their legs and shins are covered, as though they were called coverings for the legs and shins.

*Tiara* is a Greek word that has passed into Latin usage. Virgil also uses it (*Aeneid* 7):

> “The scepter and sacred tiara.”

It is a kind of small cap used by the Persian and Chaldean peoples.

### (Verse 22)

“Moreover, the men who had thrown Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego into the furnace were killed by the flame of the fire.”

These are the men of whom he had said above: “He commanded the strongest men in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego by their feet and throw them into the burning furnace.”

Nebuchadnezzar therefore did not accidentally lose some random servants, but strong men from his entire army, men most ready for battle, so that he would not merely fear the miracle but also experience the losses suffered by his army.

### (Verse 23)

“But these three men—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—fell into the midst of the burning furnace, bound. And they walked in the midst of the flame, praising God and blessing the Lord.”

Then Azariah, standing, prayed as follows. Opening his mouth in the midst of the fire, he said:

A great miracle! Bound men are thrown into the furnace and fall headlong into the midst of the fire. The bonds with which they were tied burn, but the flame, fearing the bodies of the prisoners, does not touch them.

Up to this point the Hebrews read. The material that follows, up to the end of the Song of the Three Young Men, is not found in Hebrew. Concerning it, so that we may not seem to have passed over it entirely, a few things must be said.

### (Verse 26)

“Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers, and your name is praiseworthy” [some manuscripts: “praiseworthy”] “and glorious forever, because you are righteous in all the things that you have done to us” [the Vulgate: “in us”], and so forth.

[Note: Our manuscripts add: “And all your works are true, and your ways are straight, and all your judgments are true. You have made true judgments according to all that you have brought upon us.”]

Whenever we are oppressed by various afflictions, let us speak this from the whole affection of our hearts, and whatever happens to us, let us confess that we endure it justly, so that what is written may be fulfilled in us: “The daughters of Judah rejoiced and were glad in all your judgments, O Lord” (Psalm 96:8).

### (Verse 29)

“For we have sinned and acted unjustly by departing from you, and we have offended in all things.”

Yet the three young men had not sinned, nor were they of an age at which they could have been led into Babylon and punished for their own faults. How, then, do they speak here in the person of the people?

In the same way, the Apostle’s words should be read: “For I do not do what I want, but what I do not want, that I perform” (Romans 7:19), together with the other words written in that passage.

### (Verse 37)

“For, Lord, we have been diminished more than all the nations, and today we are humbled throughout the whole earth because of our sins, and at this time there is no prince, or prophet, or leader,” and so forth.

[Note: They also add: “Neither burnt offering, nor sacrifice, nor offering, nor incense, nor a place of firstfruits before you, so that we may find mercy.”]

These verses may be used whenever the churches, because of the sins of the people, suffer a shortage of holy men and teachers who are highly learned in God’s law, and whenever sacrifice and offering are not presented during persecutions.

Some refer this passage also to the heavenly Jerusalem: souls that have fallen to earthly things and have been placed in a place of tears and confusion lament their former sins and the other matters contained in the prophetic speech. But the Church of God does not accept this interpretation.

### (Verse 39)

“But with a contrite soul and a spirit of humility may we be received, as though with the burnt offerings of rams and bulls,” and so forth.

From the present passage and from what follows—“Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous”—and from the Psalms—“A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50:19)—there are some who wish to posit in a human being another spirit, apart from the Holy Spirit, and another soul.

[Note: Plotinus and, after him, Apollinarius, a bishop, uttered this foolish opinion: that a human being was composed of three substances—flesh, soul, and spirit—or, as Nemesius reports in *On the Nature of Man*, chapter 1, soul, body, and intellect. Saint Augustine also censures Didymus in *On the Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 20, because he thought that the spirit was a third component in the substance of a human being. Recall our Jerome’s letter to Hedibia, question 12. What is added here, “apart from the Holy Spirit,” conveys Catholic teaching: that in righteous human beings, besides the soul, the Holy Spirit dwells.]

But they will have to struggle to explain how, without flesh and the grace of the Holy Spirit, two substances and two interior human beings can be said to exist in one human being.

### (Verse 46)

“And those who had thrown them in—the king’s ministers—did not cease heating the furnace with naphtha and tow.”

Sallustius writes in his histories that naphtha is a kind of fuel found among the Persians, by which fires are especially nourished.

[Note: Our manuscripts, I think less correctly, read *Napta* or *Naphtha*. As for the statement that Sallust’s histories discuss this kind of fuel, no mention of it survives today, either in the collection of fragments or elsewhere. Other authors may repair the loss, among them Ammianus Marcellinus, who most fully describes it. In Book XXIII he calls it “medicinal oil”: “In this region medicinal oil is prepared. If a weapon smeared with it, after being shot more slowly from a looser bow—for it is extinguished by a rapid stroke—sticks anywhere, it burns tenaciously. If anyone tries to wash it away with water, it produces more intense heat and flame, and no remedy puts it out except throwing on dust. It is prepared as follows: experts in such matters preserve ordinary oil after treating it with a certain herb, keeping it for long use; it thickens and hardens from a material resembling a natural vein of thicker oil. This substance is produced among the Persians, who, as we have said, call it naphtha in their native language.” He adds in the same book: “Naphtha is also produced here, sticky in appearance like pitch and itself likewise resembling bitumen. If even a small bird alights upon it, its flight impeded, it sinks entirely and disappears. Once this kind of liquid begins to burn, the human mind can devise no way of extinguishing it except with dust.” Pliny too, in Book II, chapter 195, after speaking of the mud called *maltha*, adds: “Naphtha has a similar nature. It is so called around Babylon and in the Parthian region of the Astaceni, flowing like liquid bitumen. It has a great affinity with fire, and flames immediately leap toward it from wherever they see it. Thus they say that Medea’s rival was burned after she approached the altar to sacrifice, when the fire seized her crown.” Add to these the Greek authors: Strabo, Book XVI, who, drawing on Eratosthenes, says that one form of asphalt is called naphtha and describes its marvelous fiery power; Plutarch in his *Alexander*; Xiphilinus, drawing on Dio; Dioscorides, Book I; Procopius, Book V of *The Vandalic War*; Suidas in more than one place; and others who speak of naphtha, whom there is no time to enumerate.]

Others think that the dried olive pits thrown away with the lees are called *naphtha*, which is why in Greek it is called **πυρίνη**, from **πῦρ**, meaning “fire,” because it nourishes fire.

### (Verse 49)

“But the angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace and drove the flame of the fire out of the furnace,” and so forth.

When the soul, oppressed by disturbances and occupied by various troubles, has despaired of human assistance and turned its whole mind toward the Lord, the angel of the Lord descends to it—that is, the divine word—and drives away the burning heat of the flame, so that the fiery darts of the enemy may not penetrate the secret places of our heart, nor may we be enclosed in his furnace.

### (Verses 57–58)

“Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord; praise and exalt him above all forever. Bless the Lord, angels of the Lord; praise and exalt him,” and so forth.

After first presenting a general summons to praise—that every creature ought to praise the Lord—he then exhorts each part individually: the angels and heavens, the waters and powers, the sun and moon, rain and dew, spirit, fire and heat, cold and burning heat, and the other things that would take too long to list.

He summons springs and seas, sea monsters, birds, wild animals, and cattle to the praise of the Lord; then the sons of men; and after the whole human race, Israel; and from Israel, the priests and servants of the Lord; the spirits and souls of the righteous; the holy and humble in heart. Finally, he calls Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, who are summoned to praise the Lord by the benefit presently bestowed upon them.

Every creature praises the Lord not with its voice but by its works, because from creatures the Creator is consequently understood, and God’s magnificence is displayed in each of his works and effects.

### (Verse 87)

“Bless the Lord, holy and humble in heart,” and so forth.

This verse teaches us to have humility of heart, as does what is said in the Gospel: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

The humility of heart is what elsewhere is called poverty of spirit: we must not be lifted up by pride, nor seek glory through a pretended humility, but bend ourselves with our whole heart.

Up to this point we have briefly touched upon the edition of Theodotion, concerning the confession and praises of the three young men, which are not found in Hebrew. From here onward, let us follow the Hebrew truth.

### (Verse 91)

“Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished, and rose up hastily, and said to his nobles: ‘Did we not throw three men into the midst of the fire, bound by their feet?’”

After the princes have been punished, the king is corrected, so that while still alive he may glorify God. He asks his nobles—the men whose accusation and advice had caused the three young men to be thrown into the furnace—so that, when they answer that they had thrown three young men into the furnace, he may announce and show it to them.

[Note: Victor inserts a fourth man here, or says that the king announces a fourth man to them, but the manuscripts do not support this.]

### (Verse 92)

“Those who answered the king said: ‘Truly, O king.’ The king answered and said: ‘Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire; there is no corruption in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of God.’”

[Note: Victor adds “like the Son of God,” following the reading of the Vulgate; the exposition that follows does not entirely reject this.]

Again I say: O how wise is the fire, how indescribable the power of God! The bodies are bound with chains; the chains burn, but the bodies do not burn.

As for the appearance of the fourth, whom he says is like a son of God, we must either understand him as an angel, as the Septuagint translated it, or certainly, as many think, as the Lord and Savior. But I do not know how an impious king could deserve to see the Son of God.

Therefore, according to Symmachus, who translated it, “The appearance of the fourth is like the sons of gods,” we should understand angels, who are very often called both gods and sons of gods or of God.

This is the historical interpretation. In the typological sense, however, this angel or Son of God prefigures our Lord Jesus Christ, who descended into the furnace of hell, where the souls both of sinners and of the righteous were held captive, in order to free those enclosed there from the bonds of death without burning or harming them.

### (Verse 93)

“Then Nebuchadnezzar approached the door of the burning furnace and said: ‘Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out and come here.’ Immediately Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out from the midst of the fire.”

Terrified with fear, he does not inquire about the young men through messengers but calls them by name himself, calling them servants of the Most High God and asking them to come out to him—those whom he had thrown bound into the furnace.

### (Verse 95)

“Blessed be the God of Shadrach” [the Vulgate adds “their God”], “Meshach, and Abednego” [the Vulgate adds “that is”], “who sent his angel and rescued his servants who believed in him,” and so forth.

The one whom he earlier called the Son of God he now calls an angel, although in the preceding passage he was called “the likeness of the Son of God,” not the Son himself.

Again, therefore, Nebuchadnezzar accepts a confession of God. Having condemned the idols, he praises the three young men, who refused to serve and worship any god except their own God, and he marvels that the fire could not touch God’s holy servants.

But when he says—
(Vers. 96.) “Therefore this decree is set forth [Vulgate: ‘placed’] by me: that every people, tribe, and tongue that speaks blasphemy against the God of Sedrach, Misac, and Abdenago shall perish, and its house shall be laid waste. For there is no other God who can save in this way.” Some people very wrongly refer this to the devil, supposing that at the consummation and end of the world he too will acknowledge God, exhort everyone to repentance, and that he is the king of Nineveh who finally descended from the throne of pride and obtained the rewards of humility.

(Vers. 97.) Then the king promoted Sedrach, Misac, and Abdenago in the province of Babylon. Those who above say that the three youths were not governors of provinces but overseers of individual works in Babylon, here nevertheless wish them to have been appointed governors of provinces.

(Vers. 98 ff.) “King Nabuchodonosor to all peoples, nations, and languages who dwell throughout the whole earth: may your peace be multiplied. The Most High God has performed signs and wonders with me. Therefore it has pleased me to proclaim his signs, because they are great, and his wonders, because they are mighty, and his kingdom [Vulgate omits ‘because’], because it is an everlasting kingdom, and his power endures from generation to generation.” Nabuchodonosor’s letter is placed in the prophet’s book, so that it may be believed to be Daniel’s own, rather than a fictitious book later composed by another person, as the impostor Porphyry lies.

(Cap. IV.—Vers. 1.) “I, Nabuchodonosor, was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace.” The historical meaning is plain and requires no extensive interpretation: Nabuchodonosor, turned to madness because of his offense against God, lived for seven years among the beasts, fed on the roots of grasses, and afterward, restored to his kingdom by God’s mercy, praised and glorified the King of heaven, because all his works are true, his ways are judgments, and he is able to humble those who walk in pride.

But those who wish to understand Nabuchodonosor as the opposing power of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel—“I was watching Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18)—and of which John says in the Apocalypse that the dragon, falling to earth, dragged down with him a third of the stars (Rev. 12), and Isaiah: “How has Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14:22), assert that it could in no way have happened that a man who had been raised amid luxuries should eat hay for seven years and live among beasts for seven years without any tearing of his body. They ask how an empire could have been preserved for seven years for a madman, and how so powerful a kingdom could have remained without a king for so long; or, if another succeeded him in the kingdom, how great his folly must have been, that he should yield the empire he had possessed for so long—especially since the histories of the Chaldaeans contain nothing of the sort, and it could not have happened that those who wrote about lesser matters would have concealed greater ones. [Col. 0513A]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts we use, and Victorinus, prefer this reading from older printed editions. Martianay, with Erasmus, has: ‘they ask and repeat.’]

They ask and repeat all these objections so that, since the historical account does not stand, the devil may be signified through Nabuchodonosor. We absolutely do not accept this, lest everything we read appear to be shadow and fable. For who does not see madmen living like brute animals in fields and wooded places? And, to pass over everything else, since both Greek and Roman histories have reported that much more incredible things happened to human beings, and since their fables tell of Scylla and Chimaera, the Hydra and Centaurs, birds and wild beasts, flowers and trees, stars and stones being made from human beings, what is surprising if, to display God’s power and humble the pride of kings, this was accomplished by God’s judgment? [Col. 0513C]

“I was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace,” or “on my throne,” as Theodotion interpreted it. Those who follow the contrary understanding take the devil’s house to mean this world. Concerning it he himself also says to the Savior in the Gospel: “All these things have been handed over to me” (Matt. 4:9). And the Apostle says: “The world is established in evil” (1 John 5).

(Vers. 2.) “I saw a dream that terrified me, and my thoughts on my bed,” etc. Let those who hold the contrary interpretation answer what sort of dream the opposing power saw—unless perhaps everything it seems to possess in this world is shadow and dream.

“And the visions of my head troubled me.” Note that Nabuchodonosor also knew that the visions were not of his eyes or heart, but of his head: for, on account of the glory of God’s future servants, mysteries are revealed to him.

(Vers. 6.) “Until my colleague Daniel entered before me,” whose name was Balthasar according to the name of my god. Except for the translators of the Septuagint, who for some reason omitted all this, the other three translated the word as “colleague.” [Col. 0513D]

[Note: The Palatine manuscript, omitting the remainder of the verse, immediately adds: “The others likewise, except the Seventy, who for some reason omitted all these things. Hence, by the judgment…”]

[Note: The ancient translators read not “colleague” but “another,” that is, not ἑταῖρον but ἕτερον; Chrysostom and Theodoret expressly do so. That interpretation—which prefers “friend” or “colleague”—is farther from the Chaldaean truth. For this reason learned men thought Jerome had used insufficiently corrected manuscripts, accepting colleague for another, or reading ἑταῖρον for ἕτερον in the Greek. Yet Nabuchodonosor may have wished to call Daniel “colleague” because Daniel was another self, and second after the king. The well-known saying of Clement of Alexandria also applies: “The colleague is another me” (ὁ δὲ ἑταῖρος ἕτερος ἐγώ). Finally, Origen, in Homily 18 on Numbers, wrote in Greek: “Let us reread what is written in Daniel about Daniel himself and his three friends,” using ἑταίροις, “friends.”]

Therefore, by the judgment of the teachers of the Church, their edition was rejected in this book, and Theodotion’s edition is commonly read, since it agrees with both the Hebrew and the other translators. Hence Origen also asserts in the ninth book of the *Stromata* that from this point onward, in the prophet Daniel, he will discuss what follows not according to the Septuagint translators, who differ greatly from the Hebrew truth, but according to Theodotion’s edition.

“He who has the spirit of the holy gods within himself: and I told the dream before him,” etc. In place of the expression used here, “of the holy gods,” we read in the Chaldaean language, in which Daniel was written, **ELAIN CADISIN** (), which means “holy gods,” and not “holy God,” as Theodotion translated it. It is not surprising if Nabuchodonosor errs and considers whatever he sees above himself to be not one God but gods. Indeed, later also he says: “Balthasar, chief of the diviners, whom I know to have the spirit of the holy gods within you.” “Balthasar, chief of the diviners,” or “of the enchanters,” as others have translated it. It is not surprising that he was appointed chief of all the diviners, since, at the king’s command, he had learned the wisdom of the Chaldaeans and had been found ten times wiser than all the others. Let us ask those who do not accept the historical meaning in this vision who this Nabuchodonosor is who saw the dream, and who this Daniel is who explains his dream and foretells future events; and how this same Daniel—who, according to them, must signify the holy power—is appointed by Nabuchodonosor chief of his diviners and called his colleague.

(Vers. 7.) “I saw, and behold, a tree in the midst of the earth, and its height was immense,” etc. The prophet speaks not only about Nabuchodonosor, king of the Chaldaeans, but about all the impious: “I saw the impious man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. 36:35). They are elevated not by the greatness of their virtues but by their own pride, and therefore they are cut down and fall. Hence it is good to pursue what the Lord teaches in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29).

As for what Theodotion says, τὸ κῦτος, that is, “its height,” or ἡ κυρεία, as he himself later interpreted it, namely, “dominion”—for which we translated “its appearance”—the same despisers of the historical meaning criticize us, saying that the dominion of King Nabuchodonosor never possessed the whole world. For he did not rule over the Greeks and Barbarians, or all the nations of the north and west, but held only the provinces of the East, that is, Asia, not Europe and Libya. From this they wish it to be understood that everything must be referred to the devil, although we should take all these expressions as hyperbole, on account of the pride of the impious king, who boasts so greatly in Isaiah (chap. 14) that he holds heaven and regards the world as a nest and the eggs of birds. [Col. 0515A]

[Note: The Palatine manuscript has ΚΥΡΙΩΤΕϹ. From this I would certainly prefer that κυριότης be restored in the text in place of κυρεία, a less proper and less elegant word for expressing dominion.]

(Vers. 10–11.) “And behold, a watcher and a holy one descended from heaven, and he cried out forcefully and said: Cut down the tree and cut off its branches,” etc. In place of “watcher,” Theodotion used the very Chaldaean word **HIR**, written with the three letters AIN, IOD, and RES. It signifies angels, because they are always watchful and ready for God’s command. Hence by frequent vigils through the night we imitate the angels’ duties. It is also said of the Lord: “He who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. 120:4). Finally, in what follows we read: “By the decree of the watchers,” that is, of the angels, “the decision, and the word of the holy ones, and the petition.”

It is customary in Greek and Latin speech to call this word ἶρις, “iris,” which is said to descend to the earth in the form of a many-colored bow.

[Note: It is as though the Chaldaean word were written with aleph rather than with *hain* (ayin). The ancients interpreted the word as “splendor” or “light.” Chrysostom, commenting on this passage, says: ὅρα, φησὶν εἶρ φῶς μέγα, καὶ λαμπήδονα, “See, he calls Ir a great light and radiance.” The Suda likewise has εἶρ λαμπηδών, “Ir, radiance.” Nazianzenus therefore, although he teaches that angels are signified, does not explain the word, as Jerome does, from their perpetual watchfulness, but from their shining. Finally, the Septuagint translate Job 36:30, at least in the older Alexandrian manuscript, as τόξον, “bow,” which interpreters of that passage commonly understand as the heavenly bow, or rainbow. In the present passage of Daniel, Origen likewise read Ir as Iris, that is, Ἶρις.]

(Vers. 16.) “Then Daniel, whose name was Balthasar, began silently to think within himself for about an hour, and his thoughts troubled him. And the king answered and said: Balthasar, let not the dream and its interpretation trouble you. Balthasar answered and said…”

Daniel silently understood that the dream concerned the king. He showed the fear in his heart by the pallor of his face, and he grieved for one who had shown him great honor. And, lest he appear to insult or rejoice against the hostile king, he finally, detesting what he understood, addressed him.

“My lord”— [Col. 0516D]

[Note: On the authority of the Vatican and Palatine manuscripts, we removed the added word “king,” which Victor had also noted was absent from the Vulgate, Chaldaean, and Greek manuscripts.]

“May this dream and its interpretation be for those who hate you and for your enemies.” When Nabuchodonosor saw that Daniel was afraid, lest he seem to be saying something sinister and hostile against the king, he urged him to speak plainly and truthfully what he understood and not to fear anything.

(Vers. 17.) “The tree that you saw, lofty and strong, whose height reaches to heaven,” etc. He explains the truth without insulting the king, so that he appears to charge him not with pride but with power.

(Vers. 20.) “And let him be bound with iron and bronze among the grass outdoors, and let him be sprinkled with the dew of heaven, and let his food be with the wild beasts, until seven times pass over him.” The same thing was written above. Those who contradict the historical meaning therefore ask us how Nabuchodonosor was in an iron and bronze bond, or who bound him and fastened him with fetters, when it is obvious that all madmen are bound with chains so that they may not throw themselves down or attack others with iron.

(Vers. 21–22.) “This is the interpretation of the sentence of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king: They will drive you away from human beings, and your dwelling will be with wild and savage beasts,” etc. He tempers the severity of the sentence with words of flattery, so that, after harsh things have preceded [another reading: ‘and’], he may lift [another reading: ‘lifts’] the mind of the terrified man with gentler promises. Finally, he adds:

(Vers. 23.) “Your kingdom shall remain yours after you have recognized that heavenly power rules.” Hence those who contradict the historical meaning and wish the devil to receive his former dignity make sails for themselves at this passage: after torments, after becoming savage, after eating grasses and hay, and after the cycle of seven years, he confesses the Lord and becomes what he previously was. They should answer how it is fitting that the angelic powers who had never fallen should again have as their prince one who returned through repentance.

(Vers. 24.) “Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you, and redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by mercies toward the poor; perhaps God will forgive your offenses.” If he foretold God’s sentence, which cannot be changed, how does he urge almsgiving and mercy toward the poor so that God’s sentence might be changed? This is easily resolved by the example of King Hezekiah, whom Isaiah had said would die (Isa. 38), and by that of the Ninevites, to whom it was said: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jonah 3). Nevertheless, at Hezekiah’s prayer and at Nineveh’s repentance, God’s sentence was changed—not through any fickleness of judgment, but through the conversion of those who deserved pardon.

Otherwise, in Jeremiah also God says that he threatens evil against a nation (Jer. 18), and that, if it does good, he changes his threats through mercy. Again, he declares that he promises good to one who does good, and that, if he does evil, he changes his sentence—not with respect to human beings, but with respect to the works that have changed. For God is angry not with human beings but with vices; and when those vices are no longer in a person, he does not punish what has been changed.

Let us explain it in another way. Nabuchodonosor did indeed, according to Daniel’s counsel, show mercy to the poor, and for this reason the sentence against him was postponed until the twelfth month. But afterward, as he walked in the court of Babylon, he boasted and said: “Is this not Babylon, which I have built as a royal residence, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my name?” [Note: For ‘great,’ which the sacred text does not contain, Victorinus substituted ‘city.’] He lost the benefit of mercy through the evil of pride. [Col. 0517A]

“Perhaps God will forgive your offenses.” When blessed Daniel, who knew the future, expresses doubt concerning God’s sentence, those who boldly promise sinners pardon are acting rashly. Yet it should be understood that if forgiveness is promised to Nabuchodonosor when he performs good works, it is promised all the more to others who have committed lesser sins. We also read in Jeremiah that the Jewish people were commanded to pray for the Babylonians, because in their peace there would be peace for the captives.

(Vers. 28.) “While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: To you it is said, Nabuchodonosor the king: Your kingdom shall pass [another reading: ‘has passed’] from you, and they shall drive you away from human beings.” The arrogant boast is immediately punished by the Lord. Therefore the sentence is not delayed, lest mercy toward the poor appear to have accomplished nothing. As soon as he spoke in pride, he lost the kingdom that had been preserved for him on account of his almsgiving.

(Vers. 29.) “Until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of human beings.” What a great consolation in misery, when a person placed amid torments knows that prosperity will follow! Yet Nabuchodonosor is so possessed by rage and madness that, in the time of his evils, he did not remember the good things God had promised him.

[Col. 0517C] (Vers. 31.) “I, Nabuchodonosor, lifted my eyes toward heaven, and my understanding was restored to me.” If he had not lifted his eyes toward heaven, he would not have recovered his former understanding. When he says that his understanding was restored to him, he shows that he had not lost his physical form but his mind.

“And his kingdom is from generation to generation.” If we take the expression used in Scripture, “from generation to generation,” simply as meaning “through all future times,” there is no difficulty. But if—as we have often said—“generation and generation” signifies two generations, that of the Law and that of the Gospel, we must ask how Nabuchodonosor came to know God’s mysteries. Unless perhaps we say that, after he lifted his eyes toward heaven and recovered his former state, and exalted and blessed the living God forever, he also came to know this.

(Vers. 32.) “For according to his will he acts both among the powers of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth,” etc. Here he speaks like a worldly man. For God does not do whatever he wills; rather, God wills what is good. Nabuchodonosor, however, spoke in such a way that, while proclaiming God’s power, he appears to criticize his justice, as though he had suffered punishment undeservedly.

(Vers. 33.) “And my nobles and my magistrates sought me, and I was restored to my kingdom, and greater magnificence was added to me.” Thus, according to those who contradict the historical meaning, all the angelic powers will seek the devil, and he will grow to such great power that the one who once became proud against God will be greater than he was before his sin.

(Vers. 34.) “Now therefore I, Nabuchodonosor, praise, magnify, and glorify the King of heaven, because all his works are true, his ways are judgments, and he is able to humble those who walk in pride.” Nabuchodonosor understood why he had endured seven years of punishment, and therefore that he had been humbled because he had become proud against God.

(Cap. V.—Vers. 1.) “King Balthasar made a great banquet for his one thousand nobles, and each one drank according to his age.” It should be understood that this man was not the son of Nabuchodonosor, as readers commonly suppose. According to Berosus, who wrote the history of Chaldaea, and Josephus, who follows Berosus, after Nabuchodonosor, who reigned forty-three years, his son Evilmerodach succeeded to the kingdom. Jeremiah writes of him that in the first year of his reign he lifted up the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and brought him out of the prison house (Jer. 52). Josephus likewise reports that after the death of Evilmerodach, his son Neglisar succeeded to his father’s kingdom, and after him his son Labosordach. When the latter died, his son Balthasar held the kingdom; he is the one whom Scripture now mentions. After Balthasar was killed by Darius, king of the Medes, who was the uncle of Cyrus, king of the Persians, and by Cyrus the Persian—these two kingdoms being called by Isaiah “the rider of the chariot, the camel, and the ass” (chap. 21)—the empire of the Chaldaeans was destroyed.

Xenophon also writes this in his account of the early life of Cyrus the Great, as do Pompeius Trogus and many others who wrote barbarian histories. In Greek books some consider this Darius to have been Astyages [variant: Astyagea], others the son of Astyages, and they say that he was called by another name among them.

[Note: Compare the passage of Berosus preserved in Josephus, Book 1 *Against Apion*, chapter 20. Berosus calls this last king Nabonidus, whereas Jerome calls him Balthasar and makes him the son of Labosordach; Berosus calls him a certain man from Babylon, of the same nation. There is also a greater disagreement below between the two accounts: the holy Doctor says that this man was killed by Darius, king of the Medes, who was the uncle of Cyrus, king of the Persians. Berosus, however, says that in the seventeenth year of Nabonidus, Cyrus attacked Babylonia; Nabonidus was driven out and shut up in the city of Borsippa, and, after being expelled from there, obtained from the clemency of the victorious Cyrus a dwelling in Carmania (*οἰκητήριον Καρμανίαν*). There he spent the remainder of his life in that region (*τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ χρόνου διαγενόμενος ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ χώρᾳ*) and died in the province.]

“Each of the nobles drank according to his age,” or, as the other translators rendered it: “The king himself drank wine before all the nobles whom he had summoned.”

(Vers. 2.) “Therefore, already intoxicated, he ordered the golden and silver vessels to be brought, which Nabuchodonosor his father had carried away from the temple that was in Jerusalem, so that the king might drink from them,” etc. The Hebrews transmit the following story: Believing that God’s promise was void and false—namely, the promise through which Jeremiah had said that the captivity of the Jewish people would be ended in the seventieth year, concerning which Zechariah also speaks at the beginning of his book—Balthasar, overcome by joy, held a great banquet, in a certain sense mocking the hope of the Jews and the vessels of God’s temple. But vengeance immediately followed.

When Balthasar calls Nabuchodonosor his father, he does not err in the eyes of those who know the customary usage of sacred Scripture, by which fathers are also called all ancestors and forefathers. It should also be considered that a sober man would not do these things, but an intoxicated one, who had forgotten the punishment that had overtaken his great-grandfather Nabuchodonosor.

(Vers. 4.) “They drank wine and praised their gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.” What utter folly! Drinking from golden vessels, they praised wooden and stone gods. As long as the vessels remained in the Babylonian temple, the Lord was not angry: they seemed, according to their perverse belief, to have consecrated God’s property to divine worship. But once they contaminated divine things with human uses, punishment immediately followed sacrilege.

They praised their gods while insulting the God of the Jews, since, attributing victory to those gods, they drank from his vessels. According to the tropological interpretation, this should be said: all heretics, and every teaching opposed to the truth that takes up the words of the prophets, abuses the testimonies of divine Scripture for its own meaning, and gives drink to those whom it deceives and with whom it has committed fornication—such teaching takes away the vessels of God’s temple and becomes drunk from them. It praises not the God whose vessels they are, but golden, silver, bronze, iron, wooden, and stone gods.

The golden gods seem to me to be those composed according to worldly reasoning. The silver ones are those who possess elegance of speech and are constructed by rhetorical art. Those who introduce the fables of poets and use ancient traditions, possessing among themselves great differences either of elegance or of folly, are called bronze and iron. Those who put forward utterly foolish ideas are called wooden and stone. Deuteronomy divides all of them into two categories, saying: “Cursed is the one who makes a carved or cast image, the work of an artisan’s hands, and sets it up in secret” (Deut. 27:15). For all heretics hide and cover the doctrines of their lies, so that they may shoot at the upright in heart from darkness. [Col. 0519D]

(Vers. 5.) “At that same hour the fingers appeared, as of a human hand writing opposite the lampstand on the surface of the wall of the royal hall. And the king was watching the joints of the writing hand.” He appropriately says, “At that same hour,” just as above we read concerning Nabuchodonosor: “While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven,” so that he might know that the punishments had been brought upon him for no other reason than blasphemy.

The fingers appear to write on the wall opposite the lampstand, so that both the hand and what was written might not be hidden by being too far from the light. They write on the wall of the royal hall so that the king might understand that what was written concerned him.

(Vers. 6.) “Then the king’s face was changed,” etc. Here also it should be noted, for the sake of those psalms that bear the title “For those who will be changed,” that change belongs not only to the saint but also to the sinner. For later we read: “King Balthasar was greatly troubled, and his face was changed.”

(Vers. 7.) “Therefore the king cried out loudly that they should bring in the magicians, Chaldaeans, and diviners,” etc. Forgetting what had happened to Nabuchodonosor, he follows the ancient and ingrained error of his nation, calling not God’s prophet but magicians, Chaldaeans, and diviners.

“He shall be clothed in purple and shall have a golden necklace around his neck.” I am making the matter seem ridiculous by arguing as though I were a grammarian about kinds of words in an exposition of the prophets. But because I have been criticized by someone who knows nothing yet promises everything, I shall briefly note why I translated *torques* with the feminine gender: Cicero and Vergil used *torques* as feminine, while Titus Livius used it as masculine.

[Note: Conversely, one can find examples even in Cicero, as in the famous passage in *De Officiis* 3.31 concerning Manlius, who, after removing the *torques*, acquired the name Torquatus.]

“And he shall be third in my kingdom,” etc. Either “third after me,” or “one of the three princes,” whom elsewhere we read called τριστάται.

But the queen, because of what had happened to the king and his nobles, entered the banquet hall, etc. Josephus writes that she was Balthasar’s grandmother, while Origen says she was his mother; hence she knew the past, which the king did not know. Let Porphyry therefore keep awake: he dreams that she was Balthasar’s wife and mocks her for knowing more than her husband.

(Vers. 10.) “There is a man in your kingdom who has the spirit of the holy gods within him.” Apart from Symmachus, who followed the Chaldaean truth, the others translated this as “the spirit of God.”

“And in the days of your father, wisdom and knowledge were found in him,” etc. He calls Nabuchodonosor his father, as we said above, because he was his great-grandfather, according to the custom of Scripture. The conduct of the holy man among barbarians should be imitated, since he is praised so highly by the king’s grandmother or mother on account of the greatness of his virtues.

[Col. 0520D] (Vers. 11.) To this Daniel answered before the king: “Let your gifts be for yourself, and give the presents of your house to another,” etc. Let us imitate Daniel, who despised the king’s dignity and gifts, and who, speaking the truth without payment, was already at that time following the Gospel command: “You received without payment; give without payment.” Besides, it was unbecoming for someone announcing sad news to accept gifts gladly.

(Vers. 19.) “Whomever he wished, he killed; whomever he wished, he struck; whomever he wished, he exalted; and whomever he wished, he humbled.” He sets forth the example of Nabuchodonosor, his great-grandfather, both to teach God’s justice and to show that, because of pride, even his great-grandson would suffer similar things.

But if Nabuchodonosor killed whomever he wished, struck whomever he wished, exalted whomever he wished, and humbled whomever he wished, then in such honors and punishments, exaltations and humiliations, there is neither God’s providence nor his command. Rather, they strike, exalt, and do the rest according to their own will. Since this is so, we must ask in what sense we read: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; wherever he wills, he will turn it” (Prov. 21:1). Unless perhaps we call a holy person a king, one whose sin does not reign in his mortal body, and whose heart is therefore preserved because it is in God’s hand (Rom. 6). Whatever is in the hand of God the Father, according to the Gospel, no one can snatch from it; and whoever is snatched away is understood not to have been in God’s hand.

(Vers. 22.) “You also, his son Balthasar, did not humble your heart, although you knew all these things, but you raised yourself against the ruler of heaven,” etc. “Because your great-grandfather’s heart was raised up and his spirit was hardened in pride, he was deposed from the throne of his kingdom, and his glory was taken away,” and the rest (Jer. 4). Therefore, since you knew these things about your ancestor and knew that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, you should not have raised your heart against the ruler of heaven, insulted his majesty, or done the things you did.

Some refer this passage to the Antichrist, saying that, imitating the pride of his father the devil, he rises up against God. But we should ask them who Daniel is who interprets God’s Scripture for them, and who are the Medes and Persians who kill him and succeed to his kingdom. For no one doubts that after the Antichrist the saints will reign.

(Vers. 25.) “This is the writing that was inscribed: MANE, THECEL, PHARES. And this is the interpretation of the words: MANE, God has numbered your kingdom and brought it to an end. THECEL, it has been weighed on the balance and found wanting [Vulgate: ‘you have been weighed and found’]. PHARES, your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians.”

[Note: Thus Victorinus restored the reading from the Brixian manuscripts. Martianay retained *scripta* with Erasmus.]

Only three words had been marked on the wall: *Mane, Thecel, Phares*. The first signifies numbering, the second weighing, and the third division. Therefore not only reading was required, but also the interpretation of what he had read, so that he might understand what these words foretold: namely, that God had numbered and completed his kingdom, had seized him on the balance of his judgment, and that the sword would slaughter him before nature dissolved him, and his empire would be divided between the Medes and the Persians. For Cyrus, king of the Persians, as we said earlier, joined with Darius his uncle, overthrew the empire of the Chaldaeans.

[Col. 0522A] (Vers. 29.) Then, at the king’s command, Daniel was clothed in purple, a golden necklace was placed around his neck, and it was proclaimed concerning him that he would have third authority in the kingdom—that is, perhaps, a third part of the kingdom. He received the royal insignia, the necklace and purple, so that he would be better known to Darius, who was to succeed to the kingdom, and through that recognition would be more honored.

It is not surprising that, upon hearing the sad news, Balthasar granted the reward he had promised. Either he believed that the things Daniel had foretold would occur only after a long time, or, while honoring God’s prophet, he hoped to obtain forgiveness for himself. If he did not obtain it, we must believe that his sacrilege against God was greater than his honor toward a human being.

(Vers. 30.) “That same night Balthasar, king of the Chaldaeans, was killed, and Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom, being sixty-two years old.” Josephus writes in the tenth book of the *Jewish Antiquities* that, when Babylon was besieged by the Medes and Persians—namely, Darius and Cyrus—Balthasar, king of Babylon, became so oblivious to himself that he held a famous banquet, drank from the vessels of the temple, and, while under siege, devoted himself to feasting.

Thus the historical account can stand: he was captured and slaughtered that same night, while everyone was either terrified by the interpretation of the vision or occupied with the celebration and drunkenness of the banquet. As for the statement that, when Cyrus king of the Persians and Darius king of the Medes had conquered, Darius alone succeeded to the kingdom, this is explained by the order of age, kinship, and kingdom. Darius was sixty-two years old; we read that the kingdom of the Medes was greater than that of the Persians; and the uncle, who was older according to the law of nature, ought to be counted as the successor to the kingdom.

Hence in Isaiah’s vision against Babylon, after many things too lengthy to set out here, the following future events are announced: “Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, who will not seek silver and will not desire gold, but will kill the children with arrows and will not spare the infants at the breast.” [Col. 0521D]

[Note: Victor has *lactentibus uteri*, “infants of the womb.” He says that the text calls nursing infants *infantulos uteri*. In Hebrew it is “fruit of the womb,” and the reference is not to mothers who provide milk but to the little ones who suck it.]

And Jeremiah says: “Consecrate nations against her, the kings of Media, her leaders, and all her magistrates, and the whole land under her authority” (Jer. 51:28). And later: “Daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor; it is the time of her threshing. In a little while the time of her harvest will come” (ibid., 33).

That Babylon was captured during a banquet, although Isaiah urges it to battle, he writes more clearly: “Babylon, my beloved, has become a wonder to me. Set the table, watch from the lookout; eat and drink. Rise, princes, seize the shield” (Isa. 21:4–5).

## Chapter VI—Verses 1 ff.

**(Verse 1.)** It pleased Darius, and he appointed over the kingdom one hundred and twenty satraps, so that they might be throughout his whole kingdom; and over them three officials, one of whom was Daniel.

Josephus, whose history of this passage we mentioned above, speaks as follows:

“Darius, who destroyed the empire of the Babylonians with the assistance and joint participation of Cyrus, his kinsman, was sixty-two years old when he captured Babylon. He was the son of Astyages, though among the Greeks he was called by another name. He took the prophet Daniel with him and brought him into Media, granting him every honor; he kept him with himself, for Daniel was one of the three satraps whom he appointed over the three hundred and sixty satrapies.”

[Note: The Greek of Josephus, *Antiquities*, book X, chapter 11, reads as follows: “Darius, who overthrew the rule of the Babylonians together with Cyrus his kinsman, was sixty-two years old when he captured Babylon. He was the son of Astyages, though he was called by another name among the Greeks. He took Daniel the prophet and brought him to Media, sharing every honor with him; for he was one of the three satraps whom he appointed over the three hundred and sixty satrapies.”]

From this we understand that, after Babylon had been overthrown, Darius returned to his own kingdom in Media and brought Daniel with him, retaining him in the same honor in which he had received him after Balthasar had advanced [variant: sent] him. It is not doubtful that he had heard of the sign and portent that had occurred to Balthasar, of the interpretation that Daniel had given, and of how he had foretold the kingdom of the Medes and Persians.

Therefore let no one be perplexed that Daniel is now said to have been in the kingdom of Darius and now in the kingdom of Cyrus. In place of Darius, the Septuagint translators rendered *Artaxerxes*. As for the reversed order—that the history is narrated first under Darius and afterward under Balthasar, whom we shall read was killed by Darius—it seems to me that the reason is that he immediately joined one history to another. At the end of the preceding vision he had said: “And Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom, being sixty-two years old.” Therefore, under this Darius, who killed Balthasar, the events we are about to relate took place.

**(Verse 4.)** Moreover, the king was considering appointing him over the whole kingdom; therefore the officials and satraps sought an occasion so that they might find something against Daniel on the king’s side, and so forth.

In place of “officials,” Symmachus translated **τακτικούς** (*taktikous*, “orderly” or “administrative officials”), while Aquila translated **συνεκτικούς** (*synektikous*, “those who hold together” or “supervisors”). When I asked who these **τακτικοί** or **συνεκτικοί** were, I found the matter stated more clearly in the Septuagint edition, which says: “and two men whom he appointed with him, and one hundred and twenty satraps.” Since the king was considering making Daniel first among the two officials, while a third stood between them, an opportunity for envy and plotting arose.

[Note: Victor places first: “Therefore the officials and satraps sought an occasion,” and so forth.]

“They sought an occasion so that they might find something against Daniel on the king’s side.” At this point the Hebrews speculate—I scarcely know what—that “the king’s side” means the queen, or his concubines and other wives, who sleep at his side. They therefore sought an opportunity in matters of this kind, to see whether they could accuse Daniel through speech, touch, gesture, or an intermediary.

But, they say, they could find no cause or suspicion against him, because he was a eunuch and they could not accuse him of sexual misconduct. Let those say this who, because of the opportunity afforded by a single word, habitually weave lengthy tales. Let us interpret it simply: they found no occasion against him by which he might be guilty before the king, because he was faithful and no suspicion of any fault could be found in him.

In place of “suspicion,” Theodotion and Aquila translated **ἀμπλάκημα** (*amplakēma*, “fault” or “offense”), which in Chaldean is called **ESSAITHA**.

[Note: In Chaldean one now reads *Uschehhitha*, “and corruption.” The published editions read *schehhithah* in the margin, not understanding that Jerome did not cite the Chaldean text itself, but said that “suspicion” is called in the Chaldean language *Essaitha*, which truly signifies “corruption” and “perversity.” Perhaps Jerome was reading this in his own copy.]

When I asked a Hebrew what it meant, he replied that the force of the word corresponds to **δέλεαρ** (*deleár*), “bait” or “enticement,” which we may call an *illecebra* (“allurement”) or **σφάλμα** (*sphalma*), that is, “an error.” Moreover, Euripides in the *Medea* calls **ἀμπλακίαι** (*amplakiai*), with *p* rather than *b*, **ἁμαρτίαι** (*hamartiai*), that is, “sins.”

**(Verse 5.)** Then those men said: “We shall find no occasion against Daniel unless it concerns the law of his God.”

Blessed is the conduct in which enemies find no occasion except in the commandments of God.

**(Verse 6.)** Then the officials and satraps approached the king secretly and spoke to him in this manner.

He aptly said “approached secretly.” For they did not tell him what they were planning to do; under the pretext of honoring the king, they plotted against their enemy.

**(Verse 8.)** “Now therefore, O king, confirm the sentence and write the decree, so that what has been established by the Medes and Persians may not be changed.”

It becomes clear from this what we said above: that under Darius and Cyrus there was one kingdom of the Medes and Persians.

**(Verse 10.)** When Daniel learned of this—that is, of the law that had been established—he entered his house and, with the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, knelt three times a day and worshiped; and he confessed before his God as he had been accustomed to do before.

A rapid survey of the whole of sacred Scripture should gather the passages in which we read of **δώματα** (*dōmata*), which in Latin are called *menia* (or *meniana*), *tecta* (“roofs”), or *solaria* (“terraces”), and of **ἀνώγαια** (*anōgaia*), that is, “upper rooms.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscript not inappropriately has **ἀνάβατα** (*anabata*), that is, “places accessible by ascent.”]

For our Lord also celebrates the Passover in an upper room (Matthew XIV); and in the Acts of the Apostles the Holy Spirit descended upon the one hundred and twenty souls of the believers in an upper room (Acts I). Now too Daniel, disregarding the king’s commands and placing his trust in God, does not pray in a low place but in an elevated one; and he opens the windows toward Jerusalem, where the vision of peace was located.

He prays according to God’s command and the words of Solomon, who instructed that one should pray toward the temple. There are three times at which the knees are to be bent before God; ecclesiastical tradition understands them as the third, sixth, and ninth hours. Accordingly, at the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles (Acts III). At the sixth hour, Peter, wishing to eat, went up to the upper room for prayer (Acts X). At the ninth hour, Peter and John were going up to the temple (Acts III).

[Note: The manuscripts read *menia*; Erasmus, *meniana*. See our annotations above on Ezekiel XLI.]

[Note: The manuscripts of our copies also have *maenia*, with the diphthong. Nevertheless, following Victor after Erasmus, I would prefer *meniana*, supported by one manuscript at Brescia and another formerly published book. See what we observed above in Ezekiel XLI and in the letter to Sunnia and Fretela.]

**(Verse 11.)** Those men, therefore, investigating more carefully, found Daniel praying and beseeching his God.

From this passage we learn that we should not rashly expose ourselves to dangers, but, as far as lies within us, avoid ambushes. Thus Daniel did not act against the king’s command in the marketplace or in the streets, but in a hidden place, so that he might not neglect the commands of the true Lord, God almighty.

**(Verse 12.)** “O king, did you not establish that anyone who should make a petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to you, O king, should be thrown into the lions’ den?”

The king replied to them. They keep silent about Daniel’s name so that, when the king has answered generally that he gave the command, he may be bound by his own word and not act differently toward Daniel from what he had declared.

**660** “The statement is true, according to the decree of the Medes and Persians, which may not be violated.”

We frequently note this wherever the kingdom of the Medes and Persians is mentioned, in order to resolve the very difficult question of why Daniel is remembered now under Darius and now under Cyrus.

**(Verse 13.)** Then they answered and said before the king: “Daniel, one of the children of the captivity of Judah, has paid no attention to your law,” and so forth.

So that the indignity of the one who despised the king might be greater, they say that the man who disregards the king’s commands is a captive.

[Note: Victor restores the reading “so that the indignation might be greater,” partly from a manuscript and partly from a published book. Namely, in order to stir the king to greater indignation, they despise the man who despises the king’s commands, saying that he is a captive and, as it were, a slave.]

**(Verse 14.)** When the king heard this statement, he was deeply grieved, and he set his heart on Daniel in order to deliver him. He understood that he had been deceived by his own answer and that envy was the cause of the plot.

Therefore, so that he would not appear to act against his own law, he sought to free Daniel from danger not by royal authority but by reason and deliberation. He struggled and labored so intensely that the most powerful king took no food until sunset; yet those men were so stubborn in evil that they were moved neither by the king’s will nor by the injustice of the act.

**(Verse 15.)** Those men, understanding the king, said to him: “Know, O king, that it is the law of the Medes and Persians that no decree which the king establishes may be changed.”

Just as the king understood that the officials were accusing Daniel out of envy, so they understood the king’s mind—that he wished to rescue Daniel from the death immediately before him. Therefore, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, they say that the king’s commands cannot be annulled.

**(Verse 16.)** Then the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den. The king said to Daniel: “Your God, whom you serve continually, will himself deliver you.”

He yields to the multitude and, with his adversaries in agreement, does not dare deny them the death of his friend [variant: enemy]. What he himself could not obtain, he entrusted to God’s power. He does not speak ambiguously, saying, “if he is able to deliver you,” but boldly and confidently: “Your God,” he says, “whom you serve continually, will himself deliver you.”

For he had heard that the three youths, who were inferior to Daniel in rank, had overcome the Babylonian flames; and many mysteries had been revealed to Daniel. Therefore he loved him and held the captive man in the highest honor.

A single stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his ring, and so forth. He sealed with his ring the stone by which the mouth of the den was closed, lest the enemies plot anything against Daniel. For he trusted him to God’s power, while the man who was secure against lions feared human beings. He also sealed it with the rings of his nobles, lest he appear to harbor any suspicion against them.

**(Verse 18.)** Then the king went to his house and spent the night without eating, and so forth.

How great was the king’s benevolence: he took no food by day or night and allowed no sleep to his eyes, but remained anxious with the endangered prophet. If a king who did not know God did this for another whom he wished to rescue from danger, how much more ought we, for our own sins, to incline God toward mercy by fasting and vigils.

**(Verse 19.)** Then the king rose at first light and hurried to the lions’ den.

He calls it a den—a deep pit sunk into the ground, or a dry cistern in which lions were kept. At first light he hastens to the den, believing that Daniel was alive.

In Latin, *lacus* means a gathering of fresh waters, as in Lake Benacus [variant: Venacus], Lake Larius, and others; the Greeks call such a place **λίμνη** (*limnē*), that is, “a pond” or “lake.”

**(Verse 20.)** As he approached the den, he called to Daniel in a tearful voice and addressed him.

He shows the emotion of his heart through tears. Forgetting his royal dignity, the victor runs to the captive, the master to the servant.

“Daniel, servant of the living God.”

He calls him “living” to distinguish him from the gods of the gentiles, which are images of dead men.

“Your God, whom you serve continually—has he been able to deliver you from the lions?”

He does not doubt God’s power, of whom he had said above, “Your God, whom you serve continually, will himself deliver you.” Rather, he moderates his statement with ambiguity, so that, when Daniel appears unharmed, the more incredible the event is, the more just the indignation against the officials may be.

**(Verse 21.)** “O king, live forever.”

He honors the one who honors him and invokes eternal life upon him.

**(Verse 22.)** “My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths, and they did me no harm,” and so forth.

The ferocity of the lions was not changed; rather, their jaws and fury were shut by the angel. They were shut because the prophet’s good works had gone before him, so that this was not so much a favor of deliverance as a repayment of righteousness.

Let every holy man who has been rescued from the mouth of invisible lions and from the pit of hell utter these words, because he believed in his God.

**(Verse 25.)** Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, tribes, and languages dwelling throughout the whole earth:

“May peace be multiplied among you. I have established a decree that throughout my entire empire and kingdom they should tremble and fear the God of Daniel. For he is the living God, and he endures forever; his kingdom shall not be destroyed, and his power shall endure forever. He is the deliverer and savior, performing signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, who delivered Daniel from the lions’ den.”

Just as someone interpreted Nebuchadnezzar’s writing to the languages and nations as referring to opposing powers, so he also interprets Darius as summoning everyone to repentance. And the question is raised whether this is to happen in this world, or in the other, or perhaps after other worlds.

We, considering such matters delirious and empty stories, say only this: signs are performed through God’s servants among barbarian nations so that the worship and religion of the one God may be proclaimed.

[Note: The words of the sacred text that follow from this point are neither necessary for the exposition that follows nor found in our manuscripts. Whenever such passages occur above or below—passages about which it was of little importance to warn the reader—we shall silently conform the presentation of the Scriptural passages to the more harmonious rule of the manuscripts.]
