**(Verse 28.)** Daniel continued until the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

Therefore, when we read above at the end of the first vision, “Daniel continued until the first year of Cyrus the king,” this should not be understood as referring to the duration of his life. For in the final vision we read: “In the third year of Cyrus king of the Persians, a word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar.” Rather, it signifies that until the first year of Cyrus the king, who destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans, Daniel was powerful in Chaldea; afterward he was transferred by Darius to the Medes.

## Chapter VII—Verse 1

In the first year of Balthasar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream. The vision of his head was upon his bed. And, writing down the dream, he contained it in a brief account, summarizing it, and said:

This section, which we are now attempting to explain, and the following one, about which we shall speak, precede the two earlier ones according to the historical order. For this section and the next are said to have occurred in the first and third years of King Balthasar (Jeremiah XXXIX). The passage read before the preceding one is written as belonging to the last year, indeed the last day, of Balthasar’s reign.

We read this not only in Daniel but also in Jeremiah and Ezekiel (Ezekiel XVII), as we shall be able to demonstrate in those passages themselves, if life permits. In the earlier passages, however, the historical order is followed: what marvelous signs occurred under Nebuchadnezzar, Balthasar, Darius, or Cyrus. Here, by contrast, the dreams seen at the various times are narrated. The prophet alone is aware of them, and among the barbarian nations they possess no significance or revelatory magnitude; they are written only so that the memory of what was seen may endure among later generations.

**(Verses 2, 3.)** “I was seeing in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were fighting upon the great sea, and four great beasts were coming up from the sea, differing from one another.”

I think that the four winds of heaven are the four angelic powers to whom the principal kingdoms have been entrusted, according to what we read in Deuteronomy: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God. But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the measuring-line of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 8).

The sea signifies this world and this age, overflowing with salty and bitter waves, just as the Lord interprets the net cast into the sea in the parable (Matthew XIII). Hence the dragon is also called king of all that is in the waters, and according to David its heads are broken in the sea (Psalm LXXIII). And in Amos we read: “If he descends into the depth of the sea, there I will command the dragon, and it shall bite him” (Amos IX, 3).

Let us learn from the angel’s explanation what the four beasts that rose from the sea and differed from one another mean. “These,” he says, “are four great beasts; four kingdoms shall arise from the earth.”

The four winds that were fighting upon the great sea are called the winds of heaven for this reason: each angel acts on behalf of the kingdom entrusted to him. We should also note that the ferocity and cruelty of kingdoms are indicated by the name “beasts.”

[Note: Victor inserts the name “Israel” from the Greek text, maintaining that without it the sense is certainly incomplete.]

**(Verse 4.)** “The first was like a lioness, and it had the wings of an eagle. I watched until its wings were torn out; it was lifted from the earth, made to stand upon two feet like a human being [variant: stood], and a human heart was given to it.”

The Babylonian kingdom is called not a lion but a lioness because of its savagery and cruelty, or because of its luxury and life devoted to lust. Those who have written about the natures of animals say that lionesses are more ferocious, especially when they are nursing cubs, and that they are always eager for mating.

That it had the wings of an eagle signifies the pride of the most powerful kingdom, whose prince speaks through Isaiah: “I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV). Therefore it is said to him: “Though you soar high like an eagle, from there I will bring you down” (Obadiah).

Otherwise, just as the lion holds the kingdom among beasts, so the eagle holds it among birds. It must also be said that an eagle lives for a very long time, and that the Assyrian kingdom ruled for many generations.

As for its wings being torn out—that is, the wings of the lioness or eagle—this signifies the other kingdoms over which it had previously ruled and with which it had flown through the world. “And it was lifted up from the earth,” he says—that is, when the empire of the Chaldeans was overthrown.

As for what follows, “It was made to stand upon its feet like a human being, and a human heart was given to it,” if we understand this of Nebuchadnezzar, the meaning is clear: after he lost his kingdom and his power was taken away, he was restored again to his former condition, learned that he was a human being rather than a lioness, and received back the heart he had lost.

But if this is to be understood generally of the kingdom of the Chaldeans, then, after Balthasar was killed and the empire passed to the Medes and Persians, the Babylonians understood that they were human beings of humble, fragile nature.

Note the order: what is called the golden head in the image is here called a lioness.

[Note: What was previously read as *impio* (“impious”) was erroneous; the manuscript corrects it.]

**(Verse 5.)** “And behold, another beast, like a bear, stood on one side, and there were three rows in its mouth and in its teeth; and thus they said to it: ‘Rise, devour much flesh.’”

The second beast, like a bear, is the same kingdom about which we read in the vision of the statue above (II, 32): “Its chest and arms were of silver.” Because of its hardness and ferocity it is compared to a bear.

The kingdom of the Persians was rigid and accustomed to a frugal diet, after the manner of the Lacedaemonians, so that it used salt and cardamom in its broth. Let us read the account of the childhood of Cyrus the Great—his education or upbringing.

As for the statement “it stood on one side,” the Hebrews interpret it as meaning that they had done nothing cruel against Israel. Hence, in the prophet Zechariah, they are also represented as white horses (Zechariah I).

Some have interpreted the three rows, or lines, that were in its mouth and teeth as meaning that the Persian kingdom had been divided among three rulers, just as in the section concerning Balthasar and Darius we read that there were three officials over the one hundred and twenty satraps.

Others maintain that there were three Persian kings after Cyrus, but they do not state their names.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript entirely omits which men they were.]

We, however, know that after Cyrus, who reigned thirty years, the Persians were ruled by Cambyses, his son; by the Magian brothers; and afterward by Darius, in whose second year the temple in Jerusalem began to be built.

The fifth was Xerxes, the son of Darius; the sixth, Artabanus; the seventh, Artaxerxes, who was surnamed **μακρόχειρ** (*makrocheir*), that is, “long-handed”; the eighth, Xerxes; the ninth, Sogdianus; the tenth, Darius surnamed **νόθος** (*nothos*), “the Bastard”; the eleventh, Artaxerxes, who was called **μνήμων** (*mnēmōn*), that is, “the Remembering” or “Memor”; the twelfth, another Artaxerxes, also surnamed Ochus; the thirteenth, Arsenes, son of Ochus; the fourteenth, Darius, son of Arsames, who was defeated by Alexander, king of the Macedonians.

How, then, can we say that there were three Persian kings? Perhaps only if we choose certain exceptionally savage rulers whom we cannot find in the histories.

Therefore, the three rows in the mouth of the Persian kingdom and in its teeth must be understood as the three kingdoms—the Babylonian, Median, and Persian—which were brought together into one kingdom.

What follows—“And thus they said to it: ‘Devour many fleshly bodies’”—signifies the time when, under Ahasuerus, whom the Septuagint calls Artaxerxes, at the prompting of Haman the Agagite, all the Jews were ordered to be slaughtered on a single day (Esther III).

And he aptly does not say, “It devoured them,” but, “Thus they said to it,” so that the attempt alone is indicated and the outcome of the deed is shown not to have followed.

**(Verse 6.)** “After this I watched, and behold, another beast, like a leopard, and it had four wings of a bird upon it, and the beast had four heads, and authority was given to it.”

[Note: Victor inserts “like” as though from the Vulgate and Hebrew.]

The third kingdom is that of the Macedonians, of which we read in the statue: “Its belly and thighs were of bronze.” It is compared to the leopard, an exceedingly swift and **ὁρμητική** (*hormētikē*, “impetuous”) beast, which rushes headlong toward blood and plunges by leaps into death.

“And it had four wings.” Nothing was swifter than the victory of Alexander, who traversed the region from Illyria and the Adriatic Sea to the Indian Ocean and the river Ganges, not so much through battles as through victories, and within six years subjected to himself part of Europe and all Asia.

By the four heads he means his same commanders, who afterward became successors to the kingdom: Ptolemy, Seleucus, Philip, and Antigonus.

The addition “and authority was given to it” shows that this was not the work of Alexander’s strength but of the Lord’s will.

**(Verse 7.)** “After this I watched in the night vision, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and wondrous, and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth; it was devouring and crushing, and trampling the remainder with its feet.”

The fourth kingdom, which now holds the world, is the Roman Empire, of which it is said in the statue: “Its legs were of iron; part of its feet was iron and part clay.” Yet here he recalls the iron specifically, testifying that its teeth were iron and great.

I am sufficiently astonished that, after assigning the lioness, bear, and leopard to three kingdoms, he compared the Roman kingdom to no beast—unless perhaps, in order to make the beast more frightening, he deliberately omitted its name, so that whatever is most savage among beasts we should understand as applying to the Romans.

The Hebrews think that what is left unspoken here is said in the Psalms: “The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it” (Psalm LXXIX, 14). The Hebrew, however, has: “All the beasts of the field have torn it,” since within the single Roman Empire we recognize all the kingdoms together that had previously been divided.

What follows—“devouring and crushing, and trampling the remainder with its feet”—signifies all the nations, either killed by them or subjected to tribute and slavery.

It was different from all the other beasts that I had seen before [Vulgate: “before it”]. In the earlier beasts there were individual signs of terror; in this one they are all present.

**667** “And it had ten horns.”

Porphyry places the two final beasts, the Macedonian and Roman, within a single Macedonian kingdom and divides them. He wants the leopard to be understood as Alexander himself; but by the beast different from the other beasts he understands the four successors of Alexander, and then, down to Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, he counts ten exceptionally savage kings.

He does not assign these kings to one kingdom—for example, Macedonia, Syria, Asia, or Egypt—but constructs one kingdom from various kingdoms, arranged in a series, so that the words “a mouth speaking great things” may be thought to refer not to the Antichrist but to Antiochus.

**(Verse 8.)** “I was considering the horns, and behold, another little horn arose in their midst; and three of the first horns were torn out before it. And behold, there were eyes like human eyes in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things.”

Porphyry foolishly supposes that the little horn, which arose after the ten horns, was Antiochus Epiphanes, and that the three horns torn out from the ten horns were Ptolemy VI Philometor, Ptolemy VII Evergetes, and Artaxias, king of Armenia. The first two died long before Antiochus was born.

[Note: Ptolemy Philometor had been omitted, and Ptolemy Evergetes had previously been listed as the sixth rather than the seventh. The Palatine and Vatican manuscripts, in agreement, supply and correct the text; we have expressed the name of Ptolemy in the words between the two occurrences of the name. The repeated word apparently misled the copyist, so that his hurried eye skipped the intervening material, as commonly happens.]

We know that Antiochus did indeed fight against Artaxias, but Artaxias remained in his former kingdom. Therefore let us say what all ecclesiastical writers have handed down: at the consummation of the world, when the Roman kingdom is to be destroyed, there will be ten kings who will divide the Roman world among themselves, and an eleventh, a little king, will arise, who will overcome three of the ten kings—that is, the king of Egypt, the king of Africa, and the king of Ethiopia—as we shall explain more clearly below.

After these have been killed, seven other kings will also submit their necks to the victor.

“And behold,” he says, “there were eyes like human eyes in this horn.” Let us not suppose, according to the opinion of some, that he is either the devil or a demon, but one of human beings, in whom Satan in his entirety will dwell bodily.

“And a mouth speaking great things” (II Thessalonians II). For he is the man of sin, the son of perdition, so that he dares to sit in the temple of God, making himself as though he were God.

**(Verse 9.)** “I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat. His clothing was white like snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was flames of fire; its wheels were burning fire. A stream of fire, swift and rushing, came forth from before him.”

We read something similar in the Apocalypse of John (Apocalypse IV, 2 ff.). “After this I was immediately in the spirit, and behold, a throne had been set in heaven, and one was seated upon the throne. The one seated had the appearance of a jasper and sardius stone, and around the throne was a rainbow resembling an emerald in appearance. Around the throne were other thrones, twenty-four of them, and upon the twenty-four thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, and upon their heads were golden crowns. From the throne proceeded flashes of lightning, voices, and thunderclaps. And seven lamps of burning fire were before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God. And before the throne was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal.”

The many thrones seen by Daniel therefore seem to me to be those whom John calls the twenty-four thrones.

[Note: Victor substitutes the plural “crowns” from the Brixian manuscripts.]

[Note: Our manuscripts and Victor’s all more correctly have this reading. Previously it was *Vetus* (“old”).]

The Ancient of Days is the one who alone sits upon the throne in John. The Son of Man, who comes to the Ancient of Days, is himself the one who in John is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Apocalypse V), the Root of David, and other expressions of the same kind.

I think these are the thrones of which the apostle Paul speaks: “whether thrones or dominions” (Colossians I, 16). And in the Gospel we read: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew X, 28).

He is called God, seated and Ancient of Days, so that the dignity of the eternal judge may be demonstrated. His clothing is white like snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. The Savior too, when transformed upon the mountain and assuming the glory of divine majesty, is seen in white garments (Matthew XVII).

The comparison of his hair with the purest wool indicates a pure and sincere judgment that accepts no person in judging. He is also described as old, so that the maturity of his decision may be established.

His throne is flames of fire, so that sinners may fear the magnitude of their torments and the righteous may be saved, though as through fire. His wheels are burning fire, or his chariot. In Ezekiel God is also presented as seated upon a chariot drawn by four creatures (Ezekiel I), and everything belonging to God is fiery.

Of him it is said elsewhere: “God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy IV, 24), so that we may understand wood, hay, and stubble to be burned on the day of judgment. And in the Psalms we read: “Fire shall go before him and shall burn up his enemies round about” (Psalm XCVI, 3).

A stream of fire, swift and rushing, came forth from before him, in order to drag sinners into Gehenna.

**(Verse 10.)** “Thousands upon thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.”

This does not mean that the number of God’s ministers is fixed, but that human speech cannot express a greater multitude. These are the thousands and myriads of whom we read in the Psalms: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands upon thousands of rejoicing; the Lord is among them” (Psalm LXVII, 18). And elsewhere: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm CIII, 4).

The service of the angels is twofold: some bestow rewards upon the righteous, while others preside over punishments.

[Note: Instead of *cruciatibus* (“torments”), some wish to restore *civitatibus* (“cities”), as the published and manuscript books retain the former reading. The authority of Thomas Aquinas in his commentary on this prophet supports the reading *civitatibus*. Yet, although Jerome elsewhere mentions angels as rulers of cities, here he is certainly speaking of others—namely, ministers of rewards and punishments. In this sense he says in the ninth book, chapter XXX, of his earlier Commentary on Ezekiel: “It is not good angels but evil angels who have been appointed over torments,” which should be understood of the torments of hell. Saint Ambrose also says in book V of his letters, formerly letter 38: “Do we believe that even those angels who, as we read in the Apocalypse of John, perform various ministries amid the labors of this world do not groan when they are employed as ministers of punishments and destructions? Although they possess eternal life, they would surely prefer to continue it in that former state of their tranquility rather than be summoned to the avenging punishments of our sins.” And the ancient author of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, among the works attributed to Ambrose, says on chapter I, verse 7: “It may be said that when they are sent to announce gentle things, they are called angels; when they are sent for vengeance, they are ministers—that is, burning fire.”]

Judgment sat, and the books were opened.

The consciences and deeds of individuals, whether good or evil, are revealed to everyone. The good book is the one we often read of, the book of the living. The evil book is held in the hand of the accuser, who is the enemy and avenger, of whom we also read in the Apocalypse: “the accuser of our brothers” (Apocalypse XII, 10). This book is earthly, of which the prophet also says: “Let them be written in the earth” (Jeremiah XVII, 13).

**(Verse 11.)** “I watched because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking.”

God’s judgment came to humble pride. Therefore the Roman Empire will be destroyed, because that horn spoke great things.

“And I saw that the beast was killed and its body perished.”

Within the single Roman Empire, because of the blaspheming Antichrist, all kingdoms must be destroyed together; there will no longer be an earthly empire, but the way of life of the saints and the advent of the triumphant Son of God, of whom it is said:

**(Verse 13.)** “And behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven.”

The one who in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream is described as a stone cut out without hands, growing into a great mountain and crushing the clay, iron, bronze, silver, and gold, is now introduced under the figure of the Son of Man, so that the assumption of human flesh in the Son of God may be signified, according to what we read in the Acts of the Apostles:

“Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I, 11).

(Vers. 14.) And he reached the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him, and he gave him authority, [Col. 0533C] and honor, and kingship. Everything that is said here—namely, that he was presented to almighty God and received authority, honor, and kingship—is to be understood according to the Apostle’s statement: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians II, 6–8). If the heresy of the Arians would attend to all these things with a pious understanding, it would by no means bring against the Son of God the charge of inequality.

“And all peoples [Al. all of the people], tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His authority is an everlasting authority, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed,” etc. [Col. 0533D] Let Porphyry answer to whom this can apply among human beings—or who this person can be, so powerful that he has broken and crushed the little horn whom Porphyry interprets as Antiochus. If he answers that Antiochus’s commanders were defeated by Judas Maccabaeus, he must explain how this person comes with the clouds of heaven like a son of man, is presented to the Ancient of Days, receives authority and kingship, and how all peoples, tribes, and tongues serve him, while his authority is everlasting and enclosed by no limit.

[Col. 0534A] (Vers. 17.) “These four great beasts are four kingdoms that shall arise [Vulg. four kingdoms shall arise] from the earth. But the saints of the Most High God shall receive the kingdom.” The four kingdoms of which we spoke above were earthly. For everything that is from the earth shall return to the earth (Ecclesiastes III, 20); but the saints shall by no means possess an earthly kingdom, but a heavenly one. Let the fable of a thousand years therefore cease.

“And they shall possess the kingdom forever, and forever and ever,” etc. If this is understood of the Maccabees, let the person who argues this point explain how their kingdom is everlasting.

(Vers. 25.) “And he shall speak words against the Most High” [Al. he speaks]. Or, as Symmachus translated it: “He speaks words as God,” since the one who assumes God’s power also claims for himself words belonging to the divine majesty.

“And he shall crush the saints of the Most High, and shall think that he can change times and laws.” For Antichrist will fight against the saints and overcome them; and he will be raised up in such great arrogance that he will attempt to change the laws and ceremonies of God, and will exalt himself above everything that is called God, subjecting the whole of religion to his own power.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “And he will be raised up in such arrogance that …” And somewhat more correctly below: “above everything that is called God and religion, subjecting all things to his own …”]

“And they shall be delivered into his hand until a time, and times, and half a time.” “A time” signifies one year. “Times,” according to the characteristic usage of the Hebrew language, which also has a dual number, prefigures two years. “Half a time” means six months. During this period the saints are to be handed over to the power of Antichrist, so that the Jews may be condemned, since, by refusing to believe the truth, they accepted a lie.

[Col. 0534C] Concerning this period the Savior also speaks in the Gospel: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matthew XXIV, 22). In the final vision we shall say that these periods do not fit Antiochus.

(Vers. 6.) “And judgment shall sit, so that his power may be taken away, crushed, and destroyed unto the end.” This concerns Antichrist—that is, the little horn that spoke great things—because his kingdom is to be destroyed forever.

672 (Vers. 27.) “But the kingdom and authority and greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings shall serve and obey him.” [Col. 0534D] This speaks of Christ’s dominion, which is everlasting.

“Thus far is the end of the word.” This is the end of the word and discourse that the Lord revealed to me in the present vision.

(Vers. 28.) “I, Daniel, was greatly troubled by my thoughts [Note: We have supplied the remainder to the end of the verse from our manuscripts: [Col. 0534D] so that it might be perfectly clear how far the Chaldaic wording extended; in previously published editions it seemed to end with the word ‘I was troubled,’ according to Jerome’s interpretation.], and my appearance was changed within me; but I kept the matter in my heart.” Up to this point the Book of Daniel has been written in the Chaldaic and Syriac language. The remaining passages that follow up to the end of the book we read in Hebrew.

[Col. 0535A] (Chapter VIII.—Vers. 1.) “In the third year of the reign of Belshazzar the king, a vision appeared to me. I, Daniel, after what I had seen at the beginning.” This vision occurred two years after the preceding revelation. The former was in the first year of Belshazzar; this one is seen in the third. Hence he adds: “After what I had seen at the beginning.”

(Vers. 2.) “I saw in my vision, when I was in Susa the citadel, which is in the region of Elam” [Vulg. city]. Or, as Symmachus translated it, “in the city,” from which the region also received its name, just as from Babylon come the Babylonians, and from Elam the Elamites. The Septuagint translated it as the region of Elymais. Susa, however, is the metropolis of the region of the Elamites. There, according to Josephus’s account, Daniel built a lofty tower constructed of squared marble, of such size and beauty that it still appears new. In it are buried the remains of the Persian and Median kings, and the guardian, or caretaker, and priest of that place is a Jew.

[Note: This is copied almost word for word from Josephus; see Book X of the Antiquities, at the end of the chapter.]

“When I was in Susa the citadel.” This does not mean that the citadel itself was the city—which, as we said, was a metropolis and extremely powerful—but that it was built with such strength that it appeared to be a citadel.

“I saw in the vision that I was above the gate of Ulai.” For this Aquila translated “above Ubal Ulai”; Theodotion, “above Ubal”; Symmachus, “above the marsh of Ulai”; and the Septuagint, “above the gate of Ulai.”

[Note: Palatine manuscript: “near the gate,” etc.]

It should be understood that Ulai is the name of a place, or of a gate, as at Troy there is the Scaean Gate (σκαιὰ porta), and among the Romans it is called the Carmental Gate, each deriving the origin of its name from particular circumstances.

[Col. 0535C] “And I lifted up my eyes and saw.” Although in dreams things are seen in shadow and, so to speak, in an image, nevertheless we cannot even see such things without eyes.

[Note: Two manuscripts add: “without lifted-up eyes.”]

(Vers. 3.) “And behold, one ram stood before the marsh” (or “before the gate,” which in Hebrew is called UBAL), “having lofty horns, one higher than the other and growing up.” By the ram he means Darius, the maternal uncle of Cyrus, who reigned over the Medes after Astyages, Cyrus’s father. The horn that was higher than the other and growing up signifies Cyrus himself, who, after Astyages his maternal grandfather, ruled over the Medes and Persians together with his maternal uncle Darius, whom the Greeks call Κυαξάρης (Cyaxares).

(Vers. 4.) “Afterward I saw the ram pushing with his horns toward the west” [Note: Vatican manuscript: “toward the east and toward the west.” The Palatine has “the east” alone instead of “the west.”], and toward the north, and toward the south, etc. This does not mean the ram himself—namely, Cyrus or Darius—but the ram of that same kingdom, that is, the second Darius, who was the last king of Persian power and whom Alexander, son of Philip, king of the Macedonians, defeated. That this Darius was an extremely powerful and wealthy king is related by Greek, Latin, and barbarian histories alike.

“And I understood.” From the preceding visions, in which the second kingdom was signified by the ram and the he-goat, he now likewise understands that he is seeing the empire of the Medes and Persians.

(Vers. 5.) “And behold, a he-goat was coming from the west over the face of the whole earth, and he did not touch the ground,” etc. So that no one may think that I am putting forward my own interpretation, let us give the words of Gabriel, who explained the prophet’s vision: “The ram,” he says, “which you saw with two horns is the king of the Medes and Persians”—namely, Darius son of Arsames, in whose time the kingdom of the Medes and Persians was destroyed.

“But the he-goat that came from the west and, because of its excessive speed, did not appear to touch the ground is Alexander, king of the Greeks. After overthrowing Thebes, he took up arms against the Persians, defeated the commanders of Darius in battle at the Granicus River, and at last struck the ram himself and broke his two horns, the Medes and Persians. He cast him beneath his feet and brought each horn under his own rule.

“But the great horn is the first king himself, Alexander. When he died in Babylon in the thirty-second year of his life, four of his commanders arose in his place and divided the empire among themselves. Ptolemy, son of Lagus, held Egypt; Philip, who was also called Aridaeus [Al. Arius], the brother of Alexander, held Macedonia; Seleucus Nicator held Syria, Babylon, and all the kingdoms of the East; and Antigonus ruled Asia.

“But,” he says, “not in his strength.” For no one could equal Alexander’s greatness. “And after many times a king of Syria, shameless in appearance and understanding riddles, will arise”—Antiochus Ἐπιφανής, son of Seleucus, who was also called Philopator. When he had been a hostage at Rome and, without the Senate’s knowledge, had seized power by deceit, he fought against Ptolemy Philometor—that is, against the south and against the Egyptians. Again he fought toward the east, against those who were stirring up revolts in Persia; and finally, fighting against the Jews, he captured Judaea and entered Jerusalem. In the temple of God he set up an image of Jupiter Olympius. He raised his magnificence even to the host of heaven—that is, to the children of Israel, who were protected by the aid of angels—so that he subjected many of the saints to idolatry and trampled them under his feet like the stars of heaven.

“Thus it happened that he held the south and the east—that is, Egypt and Persia—under his power. And when it says, ‘He was magnified even against the prince of the host,’ this signifies that he rose up against God and persecuted his saints; that he removed the ἐνδελεχισμός, that is, the continual sacrifice, which was offered morning and evening; and that he polluted and cast down the place of his sanctuary. This happened not through his own strength, but because of the sins of the people. Thus it came about that truth was thrown down upon the earth, and, while the worship of idols flourished, the religion of God lay dormant.”

(Vers. 13.) “And I heard one of the saints speaking; and one saint said to another—I do not know to whom he was speaking.” Instead of “to another, I do not know whom,” Symmachus translated [Col. 0537A] τινί ποτε (“to some one or other”), which we too have followed. Aquila, Theodotion, and the Septuagint placed the Hebrew word itself, φελμονί (pelmoni) [Note: Vatican manuscript, as also the Sangallensis in Montfaucon: in Latin letters PHELMONI; other books have pelmoni or pelimoni.]. Thus, without stating the angel’s name, he generally indicated one of the angels.

[Col. 0537C] “How long will the vision last, and the continual sacrifice, and the sin of desolation that has occurred, and the sanctuary and the host be trampled?” One angel asks another angel how long, by God’s judgment under Antiochus king of Syria, the temple will remain desolate and the image of Jupiter stand in the temple of God, in accordance with what he adds when he says: “And the sanctuary and the host shall be trampled.”

(Vers. 14.) “And he said to him: Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days [Note: Victor says that the word ‘days’ is absent both from the Hebrew and from the Brixian manuscripts. It was added either from Theodotion or as a word understood and transferred here from the margin.], and the sanctuary shall be cleansed.”

Let us read the Books of the Maccabees and the history of Josephus. There we shall find it written that in the 143rd year from Seleucus—who first reigned in Syria after Alexander—Antiochus entered Jerusalem and laid everything waste. Returning in the third year, he placed a statue of Jupiter in the temple. Until Judas Maccabaeus—that is, until the 148th year—six years of Jerusalem’s devastation and three years of the temple’s defilement had been completed, totaling 2,300 days and three months; after this period the temple was cleansed.

Some read 2,200 instead of 2,300, so that the six years and three months may not seem to remain.

Most of our writers refer this passage to Antichrist, saying that what was done figuratively under Antiochus will be fulfilled literally under him. When it adds, “The sanctuary shall be cleansed,” it signifies the time of Judas Maccabaeus, who, with his brothers and relatives supporting him, and with many of the Jewish people, defeated the commanders of Antiochus near Emmaus, which is now called Nicopolis.

[Note: Two manuscripts and the older printed books read “sons” instead of “brothers,” a reading which Victor long ago corrected with the help of Florentine manuscripts, since the history itself of I Maccabees II and II Maccabees 8 requires it. The brothers of Judas Maccabaeus were Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan. Josephus, Antiquities, Book XII, chapter 9, should also be compared.]

When Antiochus heard this—he who had risen up against the Prince of princes, that is, the Lord of lords and King of kings—he was in Elymais, a region of Persia, wishing to plunder the temple of Diana, which contained valuable offerings. There too he lost his army, and he was crushed without hands, that is, he perished from an illness of grief. “Evening and morning” signifies the succession of day and night.

(Vers. 15.) “And it happened, when I, Daniel, saw the vision and sought understanding.” He saw the vision through a picture and an image, but he did not know its meaning. Not everyone who sees therefore understands—just as when we read Holy Scripture with our eyes but do not understand it with our heart.

[Col. 0538A] “And behold, there stood before me something resembling the appearance of a man.” Angels are not men, but they appear in the form of men. Thus, at the oak of Mamre, three men appeared to Abraham (Genesis VIII), though they were certainly not men; one of them is worshiped as the Lord. Hence the Savior also says in the Gospel: “Abraham saw my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII, 56).

(Vers. 16 and 17.) “And I heard the voice of a man between Ulai; and he cried out and said: Gabriel, make this vision understood” [Vulg. “make him understood”]. “And he came and stood near where I was standing. And when he came, I fell trembling upon my face.”

The Jews maintain that the man who commanded Gabriel to make Daniel understand the vision was Michael. Since the vision concerned battles, however, and conflicts between kings, indeed the succession of kingdoms, Gabriel—who is placed in charge of battles—is assigned to this duty. For Gabriel is translated into our language as “strength” or “the strong one of God.” Thus, at the time when the Lord was about to be born, to declare war on the demons, and to triumph over the world, Gabriel came to Zechariah and to Mary (Luke I). Later we read in the Psalms concerning the triumphant Lord: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle; he is the King of glory” (Psalm XXIII, 8).

Wherever medicine and healing are needed, Raphael is sent; his name means “healing” or “the medicine of God” [Note: The Palatine manuscript transfers here the words “signifying by the interpretation of this name that true medicine is in God,” approximately as in the editions of Erasmus and Victor, which Martianus more correctly placed at the end of the chapter.], provided one is willing to accept the Book of Tobit. But wherever prosperity is promised to the people, and ἰλασμός (hilasmos)—which we can call “propitiation” or “expiation”—is necessary, Michael is sent, whose name means “Who is like God?”

[Col. 0538C] [Note: The same wording is found in the ancient editions: “It is necessary that Michael be sent, whose name means ‘Who is like God?’—so that it may be understood that no one can grant propitiation or expiation except God.”]

This interpretation of the name signifies that true medicine is in God.

“And he said to me: Understand, son of man, that the vision will be fulfilled at the time of the end,” etc. Ezekiel, Daniel, and Zechariah—because they often see themselves among angels—are warned, lest they be lifted up in pride and believe themselves to belong to the angelic nature or dignity, of their own frailty; they are called sons of men so that they may know themselves to be human beings.

(Vers. 18.) “And he touched me and set me upon my feet. And he said to me,” etc. The prophet, who had fallen in fear and lay face down upon the ground, is raised at the angel’s touch, so that he may hear and understand what is said without fear.

(Vers. 26.) “Therefore, seal up the vision, for it shall be after many days.” After the angel Gabriel had explained the vision, which we have discussed above as best we could, he concludes: “Therefore, seal up the vision, for it shall be after many days.” By the expression “seal up,” he shows that what was being said was obscure, not open to the hearing of many, and impossible to understand beforehand unless it is fulfilled by events and deeds.

(Vers. 27.) “And I, Daniel, languished and was sick for days. And when I had risen, I performed the king’s business.” This is like what we read in Genesis concerning Abraham: after hearing the Lord speak to him, he said that he was dust and ashes (Genesis XVIII). Daniel therefore says that he languished and was sick at the horror of the vision; and when he had risen, he performed the tasks that had been commanded him by the king, rendering to everyone what was due, and knowing that Gospel saying: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke XX, 25).

“And I was astonished at the vision, and there was no one to interpret it.” If there was no one to interpret it, how did the angel interpret it above? What he means is that he had heard of the kings but did not know their names; he had learned what was to come but hesitated uncertainly about the time when it would come. Thus, the only thing he could do was to be astonished at the vision and leave everything to the knowledge of God.

(Cap. IX.—Vers. 1.) “In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans, in the first year of his reign.” This is the Darius who, together with Cyrus, conquered the Chaldeans and Babylonians. We must not suppose that he was the Darius in whose second year the temple was built—which Porphyry conjectures in order to extend the years of Daniel—or the one who was defeated by Alexander, king of the Macedonians. He therefore adds the father’s name and also the victory, since this Darius, the first of Median descent, overthrew the kingdom of the Chaldeans, thereby removing the possibility of a reading error caused by the similarity of the names.

(Vers. 2.) “I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years concerning which the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet, that the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolations might be fulfilled.” Jeremiah had foretold seventy years of the temple’s desolation (Jeremiah LII, 29), after which the people would again return to Judaea and the temple and Jerusalem would be rebuilt. This does not make Daniel negligent but rather prompts him to pray, so that what God had promised through his mercy might be fulfilled through his [Al. their] prayers, lest negligence produce arrogance and arrogance produce offense.

In Genesis we read that 120 years of repentance were appointed before the Flood (Genesis IX). Because the people did not wish to repent for so long a time—that is, for a hundred years—God did not wait for the remaining twenty years to be completed, but brought beforehand what he had later threatened. Hence it is also said to Jeremiah, because of the hardness of the Jewish people’s heart: “Do not pray for this people, for I will not hear you” (Jeremiah VII, 16). And to Samuel: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him?” (I Samuel XVI, 1).

Thus, in ashes and sackcloth, Daniel asks that what God had promised be fulfilled—not because he doubted the future, but so that security might not produce negligence, and negligence offense.

“I beseech you, Lord God, great and terrible.” He speaks against those who despise your commandments.

(Vers. 4.) “Keeping the covenant and mercy with those who love you and keep your commandments.” What God promises does not therefore happen immediately; rather, he fulfills his promises in those who keep his commandments.

(Vers. 5.) “We have sinned, we have acted unjustly [Note: One Palatine manuscript reads “we have acted impiously, polluted by sins.” Since he is one of the people, etc. The Vatican reads “we have acted impiously.” “The sins of the people,” etc. To avoid tautology, Victor wrote “we have committed iniquity, we have acted impiously” in the Vulgate edition.], we have acted impiously, and we have turned away,” etc. Because he is one of the people, he enumerates the people’s sins in his own person, just as we also read that the Apostle does this in his Epistle to the Romans.

[Col. 0540B] (Vers. 7.) “To you, Lord, belongs righteousness; but to us confusion of face,” etc. For we justly suffer what we deserve.

(Vers. 8.) “To you, Lord our God, belong mercy and propitiation,” etc. Above he had said: “To you, Lord, belongs righteousness.” Now, because the Lord is not only just but also merciful, he says: “To you, Lord, belongs mercy,” so that after the sentence of the judge he may move him to clemency.

(Vers. 11.) “And it has dripped upon us.” You have not poured out upon us the whole of your wrath, which we could not bear, but only a drop of your fury, so that, corrected by the blow, we might return to you.

“The curse and the denunciation that is written in the book of Moses, servant of God,” etc. In Deuteronomy we read the curses and blessings of God (Deuteronomy XXVII), which were later pronounced on Mounts Gerizim and Ebal, over the righteous and sinners.

(Vers. 13.) “All this evil has come upon us, and we have not entreated the face of you, Lord our God, that we might turn back from our iniquities and consider your truth.” Great is their hardness, that, placed amid afflictions, they did not entreat God—or, if they did entreat him, they did so ineffectively because they had not turned back from their iniquities. To turn back from iniquity is to consider the truth of God.

(Vers. 14.) “And the Lord watched over the evil and brought it upon us,” etc. When we are chastised because of our sins, God watches over us and visits us. But when we are abandoned by God and are not judged, when we are unworthy of the Lord’s correction, then he is said to sleep. Hence we read in the Psalms: “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, and as one intoxicated with wine” (Psalm LXXVII).

[Note: Victor adds “powerful,” following the text of the Psalm.]

For our evil and iniquity intoxicate God. When these are corrected in us, he is said to awaken and rise from his drunkenness, so that he may make us, who are drunk with sin, awaken to righteousness.

(Vers. 15.) “And now, Lord our God,” etc. He recalls the ancient benefit, so that he may move God to show similar clemency.

(Vers. 17.) “And show your face upon your sanctuary, which is desolate.” Fulfill by deed what you promised by word; the approaching time of desolation is being fulfilled.

(Vers. 18.) “For your own sake incline your ear, my God, and hear; open your eyes and see our desolation,” etc. He speaks these things ἀνθρωποπάθως (“anthropopathically,” in human terms), so that when we are heard, God may appear to incline his ear; when God deigns to look upon us, to open his eyes; and when he turns away his face, we may seem unworthy both of his eyes and of his ears.

(Vers. 20.) “And while I was still speaking and praying and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and [Vulg. ‘and that I might’] presenting my prayers before my God for the holy mountain of my God.” Thus, as we said above, he repeats not only the people’s sins but also his own, because he is one of the people. Or, humbly, although he himself had not sinned, he joins himself to the sinful people so that he may obtain forgiveness through humility.

Note that he says here, “confessing my sins.” In many passages of Holy Scripture, confession signifies not repentance but praise.

(Vers. 21.) “While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man Gabriel whom I had seen [Note: Palatine manuscript: “in the vision at the beginning”; Vatican: “at the beginning” alone.] at the beginning of the vision.” He calls “the beginning” the earlier vision, which this one follows. Great also is the effect of prayer, and the Lord’s promise is fulfilled: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isaiah LVIII, 9). Gabriel appears not as an angel or archangel but as a man, so that he might indicate not sex but the name of power.

“Swiftly flying, he touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice.” He is said to fly because he appeared in the form of a man [Al. “who appeared as a man”], and at the time of the evening sacrifice because the prophet’s prayer had continued from the morning sacrifice until the evening sacrifice; therefore he bent God’s mercy toward himself.

(Vers. 22.) “And he instructed me and spoke with me, and said.” The vision is so obscure that the prophet requires the angel’s instruction.

“Daniel, I have now come forth so that I might instruct you and you might understand.” “Now I have been sent to you and have come forth”—not from God’s presence so as to depart from him, but to come to you.

[Note: The Vatican reads: “And I have come forth from the presence of God, not in order to …” In the Palatine manuscript the words “and I have come forth” are entirely absent.]

(Vers. 23.) “At the beginning of your prayers the word went forth; and I have come to show you, because you are a man of desires.” As soon as you began to pray, you immediately obtained God’s mercy; the decree went forth, and for this reason I was sent, to explain to you what you do not know, because you are a man of desires—or “beloved” and worthy of God’s love, as Solomon was called Jedidiah [Al. Jedida]—or “a man of desires,” because, on account of your desire, you have deserved to hear God’s secrets and to be aware of future things.

681 “Therefore, pay attention to the word and understand the vision.” If Daniel is told to attend carefully so that he may hear and understand what he sees, what ought we to do, whose eyes are blinded by the darkness of ignorance and the fog of vices?

### (Verse 24)

[Note: Col. 0541D. The entire following pericope of the sacred text is blank in our manuscripts.]

“Seventy weeks have been decreed for your people and for your holy city, to finish transgression, to bring sin to an end, to erase iniquity, to bring everlasting righteousness, to fulfill vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Holy of Holies.

“Know, therefore, and understand: from the issuing of the word that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt until Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and the street and the walls shall again be built, though in troubled times. And after the sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed, and there shall not be for him (the words enclosed in parentheses—“the people who will deny him”—are not in the Hebrew) a people who will deny him; and the people, together with the coming leader, shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end shall be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation is decreed. He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week; and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease. And there shall be in the Temple the abomination of desolation, and desolation shall continue until the consummation and the end.

“Because the Prophet had said, ‘You led forth your people, and your name was invoked over your city and over your people,’ therefore Gabriel speaks in the person of God: ‘It is not at all God’s people, but your people; nor God’s holy city, but holy—as you call it [or, ‘as you may learn’]—for yourself.’ We read something similar in Exodus, when God says to Moses: ‘Go down, for your people has sinned’ (Exodus 32:7), that is, ‘not my people,’ because it abandoned me.

“Since, therefore, you plead for Jerusalem and pray for the Jewish people, hear what will happen to your people and to your city during the seventy weeks of years that follow.”

I know that the most learned men have discussed this question in various ways, and that each has expressed what he thought according to the capacity of his understanding. Since it is dangerous to judge the opinions of the teachers of the Church and to prefer one to another, I shall report what each one thought, leaving it to the reader’s judgment which exposition he ought to follow.

Africanus, in the fifth book of his *Chronology*, spoke as follows, literally:

[Note: Col. 0542D. This fragment from Africanus’s work survives in Greek in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book VIII, chapter 1.]

> “The passage that we read in Daniel concerning the seventy weeks contains many remarkable and wonderful things, which it would now take too long to discuss. Therefore, as far as the present work is concerned, we must speak about the chronology. No one doubts that the prophecy concerns the coming of Christ, who appeared in the world after the seventy weeks; after him transgressions were completed, sin came to an end, iniquity was erased, and everlasting righteousness was proclaimed, a righteousness that would surpass the righteousness of the Law. Vision and prophecy were fulfilled, because the Law and the Prophets lasted until John the Baptist (Luke 16:16) [in the Vatican manuscript: “until John’s baptism”]. The Holy of Holies was anointed. Before Christ assumed a human body, all these things were hoped for rather than possessed.

“But the angel himself says that the seventy weeks are seventy weeks of years, that is, four hundred and ninety years, beginning from the issuing of the word that the answer should be given and Jerusalem rebuilt. Their beginning, he says, is to be reckoned from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians. Nehemiah, his cupbearer, as we read in the book of Ezra, asked the king and received permission that Jerusalem should be rebuilt. This was the word that went forth granting permission to construct the city and enclose it with walls, which until that time had been exposed to the incursions of neighboring peoples.

“For although, at the command of Cyrus the king, who had granted permission to those wishing to return to Jerusalem, Jesus the high priest and Zerubbabel, and afterward Ezra the priest and the others who wished to depart with them, had attempted to build the Temple, the city, and its walls, the surrounding nations prevented the work from being completed, claiming that the king had not ordered it. Thus the work remained unfinished until Nehemiah and the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes.

“[Therefore the captivity preceded the Persian kingdom by seventy years.]

“At that time 115 years of the Persian kingdom had passed, while it was the 185th year of Jerusalem’s captivity. Then, for the first time, Artaxerxes ordered the walls of Jerusalem to be built. Nehemiah supervised the work, and the street was built and the walls enclosed. From that time, if you wish to count, you can find the seventy weeks of years extending to Christ.

“But if we choose another time as their beginning [two manuscripts: “if we should not wish to take the beginning from that time”], the chronological periods will not coincide, and we shall discover many contradictions. For if the seventy weeks are counted from Cyrus and his first act of clemency, by which the captivity of the Jews was relaxed, we shall find more than a hundred years, exceeding the number fixed by the seventy weeks—and many more if you wish to make the beginning of the weeks the captivity itself. For the Persian kingdom lasted 230 years, until the beginning of the Macedonians; the Macedonians themselves reigned 300 years; and from then until the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Christ suffered, sixty years are counted [the Greek printed here reads *ekkkaidekaton*, “sixteenth,” whereas the Latin says “fifteenth”]. Together these make 590 years, leaving a surplus of 100 years.

“But from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king until Christ, seventy weeks are completed according to the lunar reckoning of the Hebrews, who count their months not by the course of the sun but by that of the moon. For from the 115th year of the Persian kingdom, when Artaxerxes, king of that empire, was in the twentieth year of his reign—the fourth year of the 83rd Olympiad—until the 202nd Olympiad and its second year, the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, 475 years are reckoned. These make 490 Hebrew years according to lunar months, as we have said.

“According to their reckoning, the months may consist of twenty-nine and a half days [another reading: twenty-eight and a half]. Thus, in 490 years, the solar cycle has 365 days and a quarter more than the lunar reckoning; and in twelve months of each year there are eleven days and a quarter more. For this reason the Greeks and Jews insert three intercalary months every eight years.

“If you calculate eleven and a quarter multiplied by eight, you will produce ninety days, that is, three months. In 475 years [another reading: forty-five] there are fifty-nine eight-year periods and three months; together they amount, more or less, to fifteen years. If you add these to the 475 years, you obtain seventy weeks of years, that is, altogether 490 years.”

This is what Africanus said in the very words we have reproduced.

Let us pass to Eusebius Pamphilus, who in the eighth book of the *Evangelical Demonstration* conjectures something of the following kind:

> “It does not seem to me that the division of the seventy weeks was made without purpose: first seven are mentioned, then sixty-two, and finally one week is added, which itself is divided into two parts. For it is written: ‘You shall know and understand: from the issuing of the word that the answer should be given and Jerusalem rebuilt until Christ the prince, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.’ Then, after recounting other matters in the middle, he places at the end: ‘He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week.’

> “It is evident that the angel did not answer these things without purpose and without divine inspiration. This arrangement seems to require a careful and attentive explanation, so that the reader may observe closely and investigate the reason for the division [another reading: ‘vision’].

> “But if it is necessary for us to say what we think, according to another interpretation that is present in the reading before us, when the angel says, ‘From the issuing of the word that the answer should be given and Jerusalem rebuilt until Christ the prince,’ we think that he means not others but the rulers who governed the Jewish people after this prophecy and their return from Babylon—that is, the high priests, the *archiereis* and pontiffs whom Scripture calls ‘Christs’ because they were anointed. Their first was Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest, and those who followed him until the coming of the Lord and Savior.

“These are signified by the prophetic oracle when it says: ‘From the issuing of the word that the answer should be given and Jerusalem rebuilt until Christ the prince, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks’—that is, seven weeks and afterward sixty-two, which together make 483 years, counted from Cyrus.

“And lest we seem merely to assert an impudent opinion without proving what we say, let us count those who governed the people after Jesus son of Josedec until the coming of the Lord—those ‘Christs,’ that is, those anointed to the high priesthood.

“First, therefore, as we have already said, after Daniel’s prophecy, which was given under King Cyrus, after the people had returned from Babylon, there was Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who laid the foundations of the Temple. When the work was hindered by the Samaritans and the other surrounding nations, the years of seven weeks were completed—that is, forty-nine years, during which the work of the Temple remained unfinished—and prophecy separates these years from the remaining sixty-two weeks.

“Indeed, the Jews in the Gospel speak to the Lord from this understanding: ‘This Temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?’ (John 2:20). These are the years from the first year of King Cyrus, who granted freedom to the Jews wishing to return to their homeland, until the sixth year of King Darius, under whom the entire work of the Temple was completed. Josephus, moreover, added three years in which the *periboloi* of the Temple and certain other remaining works were completed. Added to the forty-six years, these make forty-nine years, that is, seven weeks of years.

“They count the remaining sixty-two weeks from the seventh year of that same Darius. At that time Jesus son of Josedec and Zerubbabel, now advanced in age, governed the people. Haggai and Zechariah prophesied under them. After them Ezra and Nehemiah came from Babylon and built the walls of the city, while Joachim, son of Jesus, surnamed Josedec, held the high priesthood. After him Eliasib succeeded to the priesthood, then Joiada, afterward John, and after John Jaddua. In Jaddua’s time Alexander, king of the Macedonians, founded Alexandria,

> as Josephus relates in his *Antiquities*: he came to Jerusalem and sacrificed victims in the Temple.”

[Note: Cols. 0545D–0546D. Josephus does indeed state in Book XI, chapter 8, that Alexander came to Jerusalem and sacrificed in the Temple “to God according to the high priest’s direction” (*tō Theō kata tēn tou Archiereōs hyphēgēsin*); but Josephus by no means says that he founded Alexandria at that time, that is, in Jaddua’s age.]

“After Alexander died, in the 113th Olympiad, in the 236th year of the Persian kingdom—which had begun in the first year of the 55th Olympiad, when Cyrus, king of the Persians, conquered the Babylonians and Chaldeans—after the death of Jaddua the priest, who presided over the Temple under Alexander, Onias assumed the high priesthood. At that time Seleucus, having subdued Babylon, placed the diadem of all Syria and Asia upon his head, in the twelfth year after Alexander’s death. From Cyrus’s reign, all the years up to that time total 248. From this period Scripture begins to count the kingdom of the Greeks in the books of the Maccabees.

“After Onias, Eleazar the high priest governed the Jews. At that time the Seventy Interpreters are said to have translated the sacred Scriptures into Greek at Alexandria. After him came another Onias, whom Simon succeeded. While Simon governed the people, Jesus son of Sirach wrote the book called in Greek *panaretos* (‘completely virtuous’), which many falsely attribute to Solomon. He was succeeded in the high priesthood by another Onias, during whose time Antiochus compelled the Jews to sacrifice to the gods of the nations. After he died, Judas Maccabee purified the Temple and shattered the images of the idols.

“His brother Jonathan succeeded him, and after Jonathan his brother Simon ruled the people. At Simon’s death the 277th year of the kingdom of Syria was completed; and the first book of the Maccabees contains the history down to this point. From the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, until the end of the first volume of the Maccabees and the death of Simon the high priest, 425 years are counted.

“After him John held the high priesthood for twenty-nine years. When he died, Aristobulus governed the people for one year. He was the first, having returned from Babylon, to assume the distinguished diadem of royal power together with the honor of the high priesthood. His successor was Alexander, both king and high priest, who ruled the people for twenty-seven years. Up to this point, from the first year of King Cyrus and the return of the captives who wished to come to Judea, 483 years are counted; these are formed by seven and sixty-two weeks, that is, sixty-nine weeks altogether.

“Throughout this entire period high priests governed the Jewish people; I now think that these are called ‘Christs the princes.’ After the last of them, Alexander, died, the Jewish nation was harassed by seditions, without any leader, and was divided in various directions, to such an extent that Alexandra, also called Salina, the wife of that Alexander, obtained the authority. She reserved the high priesthood for her son Hyrcanus, but gave the kingdom to her other son Aristobulus, who held it for ten years.

“When the brothers fought one another in civil strife and drew the Jewish nation into opposing factions, Gnaeus Pompey, commander of the Roman army, arrived. After capturing Jerusalem, he entered as far as the inner chambers of the Temple, which were called the Holy of Holies. He bound Aristobulus [another reading: defeated him] and sent him to Rome, reserving him for his triumph, and handed the high priesthood to his brother Hyrcanus. Then, for the first time, the Jewish nation became tributary to the Romans.

“After him Herod, son of Antipater, having killed Hyrcanus, received the kingdom of the Jews by decree of the Senate and was the first foreigner to rule the Jews. He did not, in accordance with the law of Moses, hand the high priesthood to children after their parents’ deaths, but to outsiders, and not even to them for long, except for favor and payment, disregarding the commands of the divine Law.”

[Note: Col. 0546D. This passage is absent from all but our manuscripts; consult the Greek text.]

Eusebius also presents another explanation. If we wished to translate it into Latin, we would lengthen the book excessively. This, therefore, is the substance of his interpretation:

From the sixth year of Darius, who reigned over Persia after Cyrus and his son Cambyses, when the work of the Temple was completed, until Herod and Caesar Augustus, he counts seven and sixty-two weeks, which make 483 years. At that time Christ—that is, Hyrcanus, the last high priest of the Maccabean line—was slaughtered by Herod, and the succession of high priests ceased in accordance with the law of God. The city and the sanctuary themselves were devastated by the Roman army under a Roman leader—or by Herod himself, who through the Romans seized an unlawful power over the Jews.

As for the statement, “He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week” [another reading: “for weeks”], and “in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease,” he interprets it as follows: while Herod ruled Judea and Augustus ruled the Romans, Christ was born. According to the Evangelist John, he preached the Gospel for three years and six months and confirmed the worship of the true God for many—undoubtedly together with the apostles and believers. After the Lord’s Passion, in the middle of the week, sacrifice and offering ceased again. Whatever was later done in the Temple was not God’s sacrifice but the worship of the devil, while all together cried out: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25), and, “We have no king but Caesar.”

A careful reader will be able to find this passage explained more fully in the *Chronicle* of the same Eusebius, which many years ago we translated into Latin.

That from the completion of the Temple until the tenth year of the emperor Augustus, when Herod obtained Judea after killing Hyrcanus, seven and sixty-two weeks—that is, 483 years—should be counted, can be demonstrated as follows: the construction of the Temple was completed in the first year of the 66th Olympiad, that is, the sixth year of Darius; and in the third year of the 186th Olympiad, that is, the tenth year of Augustus, Herod began his rule over the Jews. These periods make 483 years, counting four years for each Olympiad.

The same Eusebius gives another opinion, which I do not entirely reject [Vatican manuscript: “which I do not reject”; Palatine manuscript: “which is not in every respect rejected”]:

[Note: Col. 0547D. The Vatican manuscript continues, “then, because he more fully [explains] the weeks of years into seventy, etc.”] many extend one week of years over seventy years, reckoning ten years for each year of the week. They hold that from the Lord’s Passion until Nero’s reign there were thirty-five years, when Roman arms were first raised against the Jews, and that this constitutes half of the week of seventy years. Then, from Vespasian and Titus, and thereafter, when Jerusalem and the Temple were burned, until Trajan, there were another thirty-five years; this, they say, is the week of which the angel speaks to Daniel: “He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week.”

For throughout the whole world the Gospel was preached by the apostles, who continued until that time; ecclesiastical histories report that John the Evangelist lived almost until the times of Trajan. But I do not know how we can take the earlier seven and sixty-two weeks as periods of seven years each, and this one as periods of ten years, that is, seventy years.

This is what Eusebius says.

Hippolytus, however, formed the following opinion concerning the same weeks [Note: Col. 0548D. In his *Commentaries on Daniel*, or in the work on the history of Susanna]:

> “He reckons seven weeks before the return of the people, and sixty-two after the return, until the birth of Christ; but the chronological periods do not at all agree. For the Persian kingdom is reckoned as lasting 230 years, the Macedonians 300, and after them until the birth of the Lord thirty years. Thus, from the beginning of Cyrus, king of the Persians, until the coming of the Savior, there are 560 years.

> “He places the final week at the consummation of the world and divides it between the time of Elijah and that of the Antichrist, so that during three and a half years of the final week the knowledge of God may be confirmed. Concerning this it was said: ‘He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week’ (Daniel 9:27). During the other three years, under the Antichrist, sacrifice and offering shall cease. When Christ comes and kills the wicked one with the breath of his mouth, desolation shall continue until the consummation and the end.”

Apollinarius of Laodicea, freeing himself from every question concerning past times, extends his expectations into the future and rashly gives an opinion about uncertain matters. If those who live after us should not see these things completed at the appointed time, they will be compelled to seek another solution and to accuse their teacher of error.

He says, then—and I shall translate him literally, lest I seem to misrepresent what he says—that during 490 years sins and all vices arising from sins must be restrained; after these things good events will come, and the world will be reconciled to God at the coming of Christ his Son.

“For from the issuing of the Word, when Christ was generated from the Virgin Mary, until the forty-ninth year, that is, the end of the seven weeks, the repentance awaited from Israel. Then, from the eighth year of Claudius Caesar, Roman arms were taken up against the Jews. For in the thirtieth year of his age, according to the Evangelist Luke, the Lord began to preach the Gospel in the flesh (Luke 3:23). According to John the Evangelist (John 2 and 11), after three Passovers he completed two years; from that point six years of Tiberius are counted, together with four years of Gaius Caesar, surnamed Caligula, and eight of Claudius—that is, forty-nine years altogether, which make seven weeks of years.

“When 434 years have passed after this, that is, sixty-two weeks, then Elijah, who is to come according to the word of the Lord and Savior (Luke 1:17), will restore the heart of the fathers to the children. In the final week Jerusalem and the Temple will be rebuilt for three and a half years. The Antichrist will come and, according to the Apostle, sit in the Temple of God (2 Thessalonians 2:4), and he will be killed by the breath of the Lord and Savior after he has fought against the saints. Thus it will happen that the middle of the week will confirm God’s covenant with the saints, while the other half of the week will announce the cessation of sacrifices under the Antichrist, who will place the abomination of desolation—that is, an idol and a statue of his own god—in the Temple. There will then be utter devastation and condemnation of the Jewish people, who, having rejected the truth of Christ, accepted the falsehood of the Antichrist.”

The same Apollinarius asserts that he adopts this reckoning of the times because Africanus, the chronological writer whose exposition I set out above, testifies that the final week belongs to the end of the world. He says that it is impossible for joined periods to be divided, but that all the times must be connected with one another according to Daniel’s prophecy.

Clement, the very learned presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, disregarding the number of years, says that from King Cyrus of the Persians until the Roman emperors Vespasian and Titus the seventy weeks of years were completed—that is, 490 years—adding to that number the 2,300 days of which we spoke above. He attempts to count within these weeks the periods of the Persians, Macedonians, and Caesars, although, according to the most careful reckoning, from the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians and Medes, in which Darius also ruled, until Vespasian and the destruction of the Temple, 630 years are counted.

Origen, after this same passage had benefited him, urged us to seek what we do not understand. Since there was no room here for allegory, in which discussion is free, but he was confined by the truth of history, he briefly noted the following in the tenth book of the *Stromata*:

> “The chronology from the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus until the coming of Christ must be investigated more carefully: how many years there were, what events are said to have taken place in them, and whether we can adapt those events to the coming of the Lord.”

What Tertullian said we may learn from the book he wrote *Against the Jews*. His words should be briefly set down:

> “How, then, shall we show that Christ came within sixty-two weeks?” [Note: In Tertullian: “within seventy-two and a half weeks.”]

> “Let us count from the first year of Darius, since it was at that time that this very vision was shown to Daniel. For he says to him: ‘Understand, and reckon that I answer you concerning the prophecy of this word.’ [Note: Pomerius, cited by Pamelius, reads: “Understand the prophecies of this word”; Pamelius nevertheless prefers the received reading, “from the issuing of the word,” etc.] Therefore we must calculate from the first year of Darius, when Daniel saw this vision.

> “Let us see, then, how the years are fulfilled until the coming of Christ. Darius reigned nineteen years; Artaxerxes forty; Ochus, who was also called Cyrus, twenty-four; Argus [whom nearly everyone calls Arses; the *Mathematical Canon* calls him Arogus] one year; another Darius, also called Melas, twenty-one years; Alexander of Macedon twelve years.

> “Then, after Alexander—who had ruled the Medes and Persians whom he had conquered and had established his kingdom in Alexandria, naming the city after himself—[Note: Our manuscripts and the printed codices of Tertullian add, “After him”; Victorius deleted these words as redundant after the preceding parenthesis.] Soter reigned there in Alexandria for thirty-five years. Philadelphus succeeded him and reigned thirty-eight years. [Note: The received text of Tertullian assigns him one further year, or thirty-nine years; Pomerius and the Gloss agree. Pamelius therefore judges that this number of years must be corrected here also in Jerome.] After him Evergetes reigned twenty-five years; then Philopator seventeen; after him Epiphanes twenty-four; then another Evergetes twenty-nine [our manuscripts count only twenty-seven, as does Pomerius]; Soter thirty-eight; Ptolemy thirty-seven [Pamelius restores thirty-eight, maintaining that this correction is needed here and in Jerome and Pomerius, to make the total 436 years; he observes that Eusebius assigns eight years to Ptolemy, Cleopatra’s son—if the manuscript is not corrupt—and thirty to Ptolemy Dionysius, whom others count as one and the same person]; Cleopatra twenty years and five months [Pamelius restores six months here and below from the Ordinary Gloss, and restores Augustus’s post-Cleopatra reign as forty-three rather than forty-eight years: thirteen years with Cleopatra plus forty-three after her make fifty-six].

> “Cleopatra also reigned jointly with Augustus for thirteen years. After Cleopatra, Augustus ruled for another forty-three years. For all the years of Augustus’s reign amounted to fifty-six.

> “Let us see, then: in the forty-first year of Augustus’s reign, who ruled after Cleopatra’s death, Christ was born, and Augustus himself lived fifteen years after Christ was born. [Note: Pamelius says that the repeated phrase “after Cleopatra’s death,” here and shortly below, is certainly due to a lapse of memory, though genuine. He notes the consequent inconsistency: the ensuing computation includes Cleopatra’s thirteen years with Augustus and a further forty-one years, although only twenty-nine post-Cleopatra years should have been counted; it also says Augustus survived Christ’s birth by fifteen years, though on the earlier reckoning he could have survived only two. Pomerius, Jerome, and the Ordinary Gloss read “the remaining periods of years to the day of Christ’s birth, in Augustus’s forty-first year after Cleopatra’s death: 437 years, six months,” rather than the received wording. Pamelius also prefers “sins are remitted” to “granted,” and “he himself is the seal” to “that one is the seal.”] From the death of Cleopatra until the day of Christ’s birth, in the forty-first year of Augustus, there were 437 years and five months.

> “Thus the sixty-two and a half weeks are fulfilled, making 437 years and six months up to the day of Christ’s birth. Everlasting righteousness was manifested, and the Holy of Holies was anointed, that is, Christ; vision and prophecy were sealed; and sins were forgiven, which are granted [another reading: ‘remitted’] through faith in the name of Christ to all who believe in him.

“But what does it mean that the vision and prophecy are said to be sealed? All the prophets announced concerning him that he would come and suffer. Since prophecy was fulfilled through his coming, he therefore said that the vision and prophecy were sealed, because he himself is the seal of all the prophets, fulfilling everything that the prophets had previously announced concerning him. After his coming and his Passion, there is no longer a vision or prophecy announcing that Christ is to come.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let us see what the other seven and a half weeks, which are subdivided at the cutting off of the earlier weeks, have accomplished. After Augustus, who lived fifteen years after Christ’s birth, there are fifteen years. [Note: Pamelius deletes something as superfluous. The Palatine manuscript reads “whom he outlived”; Vatican and other manuscripts support “fifteen years” in place of “years fifteen,” with corrected punctuation. Pamelius thinks the text should perhaps read “the first [year] of Augustus” rather than “after Augustus,” since these fifteen years belong to Augustus himself.] Tiberius Caesar succeeded him and held the empire for twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. [Note: Tertullian has only twenty years; although Jerome, Pomerius, and the Ordinary Gloss read twenty-eight, Pamelius prefers the received text, especially since the author does not count days. The Consular Fasti give Tiberius’s death on 17 March, A.U.C. 789; from Augustus’s death in A.U.C. 766 to March 789 are only twenty-two years and seven months.]

> “In the fifteenth year of this reign Christ suffered, being about thirty-three years old when he suffered. [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “was baptized” for “suffered,” much as the Ordinary Gloss does, and omits the subsequent “when he suffered.” In combination with the Palatine manuscript and Tertullian’s own codices it counts not thirty-three but only thirty years for Christ. The allusion is evidently to the Gospel testimony that Christ was baptized in Tiberius’s fifteenth year, being about thirty years old.]

> “Then came Gaius Caesar, also called Caligula, for three years, eight months, and thirteen days; Nero for nine years, nine months, and thirteen days; Galba for seven months and twenty-eight days [Pamelius prefers six days rather than twenty-eight, since Galba ruled only seven months and a few days, from 10 June to 15 January]; Otho for three months and five days; Vitellius for eight months and twenty-eight days [Tertullian instead reads ten days, which Pamelius supports from Vitellius’s rule from 20 April to 24 December, when he was killed].

> “In the first year of his reign Vespasian conquered the Jews. Thus the total is fifty-two years and six months. For he reigned eleven years; and so, up to the day of his conquest, the Jews completed the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel.”

I shall briefly touch upon what the Hebrews think about this passage, leaving to those from whom these statements came the responsibility for their truth. Let us therefore speak *paraphrastically* (*paraphrastikōs*), so that the meaning may become clearer.
