“O Daniel, know that from this day on which I am now speaking to you—it was the first year of Darius, who killed Belshazzar and transferred the kingdom of the Chaldeans to the Persians and Medes—until the seventieth week of years, that is, 490 years, these things will happen to your people in stages.

“First, God, whom you are now earnestly entreating, will be propitiated toward you; sin will be erased, and transgression will come to an end. For now, with the city deserted and the Temple destroyed down to its foundations, the people are in mourning; but after no great length of time it will be restored.

“And not only will it happen during these seventy weeks that the city will be built and the Temple restored, but Christ will be born, that is, everlasting righteousness.

“Vision and prophecy will be sealed, so that no prophet will be found in Israel; and the Holy of Holies will be anointed. Concerning him we read in the Psalter: ‘Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions’ (Psalm 44:8). In another passage he says of himself: ‘Be holy, because I also am holy’ (Leviticus 19:2).

“Know, therefore, that from this day on which I speak this to you and promise it by the word of God, that the people will return and Jerusalem will be restored, until Christ the prince and the perpetual desolation of the Temple, sixty-two weeks are to be counted, together with another seven weeks, in ...”
in which, according to their proper sequence, two events will take place—events I have already mentioned: that the people will return and that the street will be rebuilt by Nehemiah and Ezra. At the end of the weeks, therefore, God’s [Col. 0552B] sentence will be fulfilled amid the distress of the times, when the Temple will again be destroyed and the city captured. For after sixty-two weeks Christ will be slain, and his people—which will deny him—will no longer be his, or, as they say, his dominion will no longer exist, which they had thought they would retain.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] Thus corrected in the Vatican manuscript. Previously it read: “which he thought he would redeem.”]

And why should I speak of Christ’s being slain and the people being wholly deprived of God’s aid, when the Roman people, under the leadership of the future Vespasian, will destroy the city and the sanctuary? After his death, when seven weeks—that is, forty-nine years—had passed, Aelius Hadrianus overcame the rebelling Jews while Timo Rufus was fighting as commander of the army; afterward, from the ruins of Jerusalem, the city Aelia was founded.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] Perhaps “will overcome.” Immediately afterward the Vatican manuscript has *defecit* instead of *deficiet* (“will fail”).]

Then sacrifice and offering will cease, and desolation will continue until the consummation of the world and its [Col. 0552C] end.

Nor should it trouble us, they say, that seven weeks are counted first, then sixty-two, and again one, which is divided into two parts. For this is a characteristic of Hebrew speech and of the speech of the ancient Latins: they count the smaller number first and the larger afterward. For example, contrary to the normal usage of our language, we do not now say, “Abraham lived for years one hundred seventy-five”; they, conversely, speak as follows: “Abraham lived for five, and seventy, and one hundred years.” The fulfillment, therefore, does not occur according to the way it is read, but it reaches its conclusion when the whole is counted together.

Nor are we unaware that some of them say that the one week of which it is written, “696 He will confirm the covenant with many [Col. 0553A] for one week,” is divided between Vespasian and Hadrian. For, according to the history of Josephus, Vespasian and Titus made peace with the Jews for three years and six months. The three years and six months are then reckoned under Hadrian, when Jerusalem was completely overthrown and the Jewish people were slaughtered in great numbers, so that they were also driven from the borders of Judaea.

This is what the Hebrews say, without paying much attention to the fact that, from the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, to the final destruction of Jerusalem, which befell them under Hadrian, one hundred seventy-four Olympiads—that is, six hundred ninety-six years—are reckoned. These amount to ninety-nine Hebrew weeks and three years, when Cochebas, the leader of the Jews, was crushed and Jerusalem was razed to the ground.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] Consult my fellow countryman, Cardinal Noris, *[Col. 0553D] Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*, Dissertation III, chapter 4, who brings together further material from coins to illuminate this passage of Jerome. Some ancient inscriptions of this kind of reckoning have also survived.]

[Col. 0553B] **(Chapter X.—Verse 1.)** In the third year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, a word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar; and the word was true, and the strength was great. And he understood the word. For understanding is required in a vision. But how do we read at the end of the first vision, “Daniel continued until the first year of Cyrus the king”? We therefore understand that he remained among the Chaldeans in his former dignity, clothed in purple and fine linen, until the first year of Cyrus the king, when he overthrew the Chaldeans; and afterward he began to be with Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who ruled over the Chaldean kingdom. Or certainly, Darius having already died—in whose first year he had learned the mystery of the seventy weeks—he is now said to have seen these things in the third year of King Cyrus. “And the word was true, and the strength was great”: either that of God, who was to do these things, or that of the prophet, who was to understand them.

**(Verse 2.)** In those days I, Daniel, mourned for three weeks of days. I ate no desirable bread, and neither meat nor wine entered my mouth; nor did I anoint myself with oil, until the three weeks of days were completed. By this example we are taught, during a time of fasting, to abstain from more delicate foods—which, I think, is what is now meant by “desirable bread”—and neither to eat meat nor drink wine, [Note: [Col. 0553D] Thus in Letter C, or Theophilus’s Paschal Letter III, no. 6: “By no means, during the days of Lent, as luxurious rich men are accustomed to do, should we gulp down a cup of wine.” And in no. 8: “During the time of fasts one must abstain from wine and meats.” See our observations on that passage. Shortly afterward the Palatine manuscript reads: “and not anoint oneself with oil.”] and, moreover, not to seek perfumes. This custom is still observed among the Persians and Indians, so that they use perfumes in place of baths.

He joins three weeks together while afflicting his soul, so that his prayer might not appear transient and accidental. According to the spiritual interpretation, however, this should be understood as follows: He who is in mourning, and mourns the bridegroom’s absence, does not eat desirable bread, which descended from heaven; nor does he take solid food, which is understood in relation to the flesh; nor does he drink wine, which gladdens the heart of man; nor does he cheer his face with oil, according to what we read in the Psalms: “That he may gladden his face with oil” (Ps. CIII, 15). By this fasting the bride makes her tears effective, when the bridegroom has been taken away from her. Daniel also rightly dares to beseech the Lord, since the captivity of the Jews had already been partly loosened in the first year of Cyrus the king.

**(Verse 4.)** On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, I was beside the great river, which is the Tigris. Ezekiel also saw a great vision beside the river Chebar (Ezek. I). And for the Lord and Savior, and for John the Baptist, the heavens are opened over the streams of the Jordan (Matt. III). [Note: [Col. 0553D] The entire following sentence—“Therefore let their ravings fall silent,” etc.—is absent from our manuscripts and is directed against the Origenists.] Therefore let the ravings of those men fall silent who, seeking shadows and images in the truth, attempt to overturn truth itself, thinking that rivers, trees, and paradise must be destroyed according to the laws of allegory.

**(Verse 5.)** And I lifted up my eyes, and I saw. An elevation of the eyes is necessary, so that we may be able to behold the mystical vision.

“And behold, one man clothed in linen.” In place of “linen,” which Aquila translated, Theodotion put **BADDIM**; the Septuagint, “clothed in fine linen”; Symmachus, **ἐξαίρετα**, that is, “choice” or “excellent.” In place of what we have translated according to the Hebrew, “behold, a man,” Symmachus put “as though a man”; for he was not a man, but had the appearance of a man.

[Col. 0554C] “And his loins were girded with refined gold.” In Hebrew one reads [Note: [Col. 0554D] The Palatine manuscript, together with the manuscript at Saint-Germain in Montfaucon, has *Opaz*; and for the Greek **ὠφάζ**, which follows, they read in Latin letters *ophaz*.] **OPHAZ**, which Aquila translated in this way: “And his loins were girded with the color **ὠφάζ** [ophaz].”

**698 (Verse 6.)** “And his body was like chrysolite.” [Note: [Col. 0554D] After these words the printed books add: “Concerning these things we have interpreted more fully in the explanation of Ezekiel; now let us say a little about chrysolite.” We recognize this most inept commentary, which none of our manuscript copies contains, as false and spurious, because Jerome had not yet written on Ezekiel when he illuminated Daniel with his commentary. MART.] In place of “chrysolite,” which is one of the twelve stones set in the breastplate of the high priest, the Hebrew has **THARSIS**, which Theodotion and Symmachus translated by the same word. The Septuagint, however, called it “the sea,” in accordance with what we read in the Psalm: “With a violent wind you will break the ships of Tharsis” (Ps. XLVII, 8), that is, “of the sea.”

And Jonah desired to flee not to the city of Tarsus in Cilicia, as most people think, substituting one letter for another, nor to the region of India, as Josephus believes, [Note: [Col. 0554D] “It is useless,” says Drusius, “that he cites Josephus.” For in Book IX, chapter 2 of the *Antiquities*, Josephus expressly says that the prophet Jonah intended to sail to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia. And in Book I, chapter 2, he says: “Tharsis is Tarsus. Thus Cilicia was called in ancient times.” Hence even today Tarsus retains among them the ancient name as the greatest of all the cities of the province, with theta changed into tau. Jerome himself, when explaining the passage concerning Jonah, likewise says: “Thus Cain, stirred up and departing from the face of the Lord, wished to flee to Tharsis, which Josephus interprets as Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, with only the first letter changed.” Accordingly, he suspects that this passage is corrupt, and that it should perhaps be restored as follows: “Not to Tarsus of Cilicia, as Josephus thinks, substituting one letter for another, nor to the region of India, as most people suppose.”] but simply into the open sea (Jon. I).

[Col. 0555A] **(Verse 7.)** “But I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; the men who were with me did not see it, but a very great terror fell upon them, and they fled into hiding.” The apostle Paul likewise suffered something similar in the Acts of the Apostles, so that, while the others did not see it, he alone beheld the vision (Acts XXII).

**(Verse 10.)** “And behold, a hand touched me and raised me upon my knees,” etc. The angel appears in human form and extends a human hand to the prophet lying prostrate, so that, seeing a body of his own kind, he would not be terrified.

**(Verse 11.)** “And he said to me: Daniel, man of desires,” etc. He is appropriately called “man of desires,” because through persistent prayers, bodily affliction, and the severity of fasts he wishes to know what is to come and to understand the secrets of God. In place of “man of desires,” Symmachus translated “desirable man.” For every saint who possesses beauty of soul within himself is loved by the Lord.

**(Verse 12.)** “And he said to me: Do not be afraid, Daniel, for from the first day on which you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself before the presence of the Lord [or: your God], your words were heard, and I have come because of your words [Vulgate: ‘I came because of your words’].” On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, that is, Nisan, after the completion of three weeks—that is, twenty-one days—he sees this vision and hears from the angel that from the first day on which he began to pray and afflict himself before God, his words had been heard.

The question arises: if he was heard immediately, why was the angel not sent to him immediately? The delay gave him an opportunity to beseech God more earnestly, so that, by desiring more, he might deserve to hear more through labor. What he says, “And I entered because of your words,” has this meaning: After you began to invoke God’s mercy through good works, tears, and fasting, I too received the opportunity to enter before God and pray for you.

**(Verse 13.)** “But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days.” It seems to me that this is the angel to whom Persia was entrusted, in accordance with what we read in Deuteronomy: “When the Most High divided the nations and scattered the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. XXXII, 8). These are the princes of whom the apostle Paul also speaks: “We speak wisdom among the mature, which none of the princes of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 6).

The prince resisted—that is, the angel of the Persians—acting on behalf of the province entrusted to him, so that the entire people of the captives would not be released. And perhaps, although the prophet was heard by God from the first day on which he set his heart to understand, the angel who was to announce God’s pardon was not sent immediately for this reason: the prince of the Persians resisted him for twenty-one days, enumerating the sins of the Jewish people, arguing that they were being held captive justly and ought not to be released.

“And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me [Vulgate: ‘to help me’].” While the angel of the Persians resisted your prayers and my embassy—for I was presenting your prayers to God—the angel Michael, who presides over the people of Israel, came to my assistance. By “chief princes” we understand the archangels.

“And I remained there beside the king of Persia.” He calls the angel, that is, the prince, “the king of Persia,” and shows that he lingered for a while beside Michael, who was speaking against the prince of Persia.

**(Verse 14.)** “I have come to teach you what will happen to your people in the latter days.” Because Daniel had asked this, he deserved to hear from God what would happen to the people of Israel—not in the near future, but in the latter days, that is, at the consummation of the age.

**(Verse 16.)** [Note: [Col. 0556D] Our manuscripts read: “Lord, in your vision my inward parts were turned within me.”] “My lord, in your vision my joints were loosened,” etc. Thus Theodotion translated it, in accordance with what we read in the hundred-and-second Psalm: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name.” Before we are worthy to see the vision of God, our inward parts look outward; but when we have seen God’s vision, our inward parts will be turned within us. We are wholly in those inward parts, concerning which it is also written in another Psalm: “All the glory of the daughter of kings is within, in golden borders” (Ps. XLIV, 41). [Note: [Col. 0556D] The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts have “within” and omit what follows, “in golden borders.” Victor, following the Vulgate edition and the Greek, has “the daughter of the king from within.” Shortly before the word “Psalm,” which was missing, has been supplied from the manuscripts.]

**(Verse 19.)** And while he spoke with me, I recovered my strength and said: “Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me.” And he said: Unless the touch, which was like that of a son of man, had strengthened him and fear had withdrawn from his heart, he could not hear the mysteries of God. Therefore he now says: “Because you have strengthened me, speak, Lord.” You have made me able both to hear and to perceive what you say.

**(Verse 20.)** “Do you know why I have come to you? And now I will return to fight against the prince of Persia.” What he says is this: “I have indeed come to teach you that your prayers have been heard; but I will return again to fight against the prince of Persia before God, who does not wish your people to be released from captivity.”

“When I was going out, behold, the prince of the Greeks entered [Vulgate: ‘was coming’].” I was leaving, he says, the presence of God to announce to you what will happen to your people in the latter days, although I am not yet secure, since the prince of Persia remains and opposes your prayers and my embassy. And behold, the prince of the Greeks—that is, of the Macedonians—was coming and entered before God, to accuse the prince of the Persians and Medes, so that the kingdom of the Macedonians might succeed to their place.

And truly, the mysteries of God are wondrous: when the Jewish people had been released from captivity, Alexander, king of the Macedonians, killed Darius and overthrew the kingdom of the Persians and Medes; and the prince of the Greeks conquered the prince of the Persians.

“Nevertheless, I will announce to you what has been expressed in the writing of truth.” The order of the reading is this: The matter is still uncertain. While you are beseeching the Lord and I am presenting your prayers, the prince of Persia stands opposed and does not wish your people to be released from captivity. But because the prince of the Greeks has come and is meanwhile fighting against the prince of Persia, with Michael there to help me, I will tell you what God has foretold to me concerning the future and commanded me to recount to you.

Let no one be troubled that, instead of “the prince of the Macedonians,” he has said “the prince of the Greeks,” that is, **Ἑλλήνων** (*Hellēnōn*). For Alexander, king of the Macedonians, first overthrew Greece and brought it under his power, and then took up arms against the Persians.

“And no one is my helper in all these things except Michael, your prince.” I am, he says, that angel who offers your prayers to God, and there is no other who is my helper in entreating God for you except the archangel Michael, to whom the Jewish people have been entrusted. Meanwhile, at this time, the prince of the Greeks and I are fighting the prince of Persia through a common effort.

The ancient histories must be reviewed, and one must consider whether that time perhaps signifies the period when the Persians were defeated by the Greeks. According to the Vulgate edition, the vision that appeared to Daniel in the third year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, is thought to be one continuous vision through the end of the book. According to the Hebrew truth, however, what follows is separated and written in reversed order. We have spoken above about the reasons for this. For these things are not related as having occurred in the third year of Cyrus, but in the first year of Darius, who overthrew Belshazzar.

[Col. 0557D] **(Chapter XI.—Verse 1.)** “But I, from the first year of Darius the Mede, stood so that he might be strengthened and fortified.” I, Daniel, he says, from the first year of King Darius, who overthrew the Chaldeans and, so far as lay in his power, freed me from the hands of my enemies—also sealing the lions’ den with his ring, because of my guardianship, so that my adversaries would not kill me—stood in God’s presence and sought his mercy on behalf of the one who loved me, so that either he himself or his kingdom might be strengthened and fortified.

While I persisted in prayer, I learned these things, the Lord answering. It is the custom of the prophets suddenly to introduce speakers without any verbal preface, as in the thirty-first Psalm. For when the prophet had entreated the Lord and said, “You are my refuge from my tribulation, which surrounded me; you are my rejoicing; deliver me from those who surround me” [Note: [Col. 0557D] Our manuscripts omit *mea* (“my”), and that word is not in the Greek text either.], the person of God is suddenly introduced as answering: “I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk; I will fix my eyes upon you” (vv. 7–8).

So now also, while the prophet says, “From the first year of Darius the Mede I stood and entreated that his rule might be strengthened and fortified,” God suddenly answered:

**(Verse 2.)** “And now I will announce the truth to you.” The meaning is: “Since you wish to know what will happen concerning the kings of Persia, hear the order of events and listen to what you ask.”

“And behold, three more kings will arise in Persia, and the fourth will become exceedingly rich, richer than all the others; and when he has grown strong through his riches, he will stir everyone up against the kingdom of Greece.” He says that four kings will arise in Persia after Cyrus: Cambyses, the son of Cyrus; and Smerdis the Magus, who married Pantaptes, the daughter of Cambyses. When Smerdis had been killed by the seven Magi and Darius had assumed the empire in his place, that same Pantaptes married Darius and bore him a son, Xerxes. He was a most powerful and wealthy king, led an innumerable army against Greece, and did what the histories of the Greeks relate.

For he burned Athens under the leadership of Callias; and at that time the battle was fought at Thermopylae and the naval engagement at Salamis. Sophocles and Euripides were then famous, and Themistocles, fleeing to the Persians, died after drinking bull’s blood.

It is therefore futile for some person to write that Darius, who was defeated by Alexander, was the fourth king. He was not the fourth, but the fourteenth Persian king after Cyrus; Alexander defeated and killed him in the seventh year of his reign.

It should also be noted that, after enumerating four Persian kings following Cyrus, he passed over and skipped nine [Note: [Col. 0558D] Namely, Artaxerxes Longimanus, Xerxes, Sogdianus, Darius Nothus, Artaxerxes Mnemon, Artaxerxes Ochus, Arses, and Darius Codomanus, who was defeated by Alexander.] and moved on to Alexander. For the prophetic spirit was not concerned to follow the order of history, but to touch briefly upon the most important events.

**703 (Verse 3.)** “But a mighty king will arise and rule with great power, and do whatever he pleases. And when he has arisen, his kingdom will be broken.” He plainly speaks of the great Alexander, king of the Macedonians, who was the son of Philip. After conquering the Illyrians and Thracians, defeating Greece and destroying Thebes, he crossed into Asia. Having routed the commanders of Darius, he captured the city of Sardis. Afterward, when he had conquered India and founded the city of Alexandria, at the age of thirty-two and in the twelfth year of his reign, he died from poison at Babylon.

**(Verse 4.)** “And it will be divided toward the four winds of heaven, but not among his descendants, nor according to the power with which he ruled.” After Alexander, his kingdom was divided toward the four winds of heaven: east, west, south, and north.

In Egypt Ptolemy, son of Lagus, ruled first—that is, toward the south. In Macedonia, Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, Alexander’s brother—that is, toward the west. Over Syria, Babylon, and the upper regions, Seleucus Nicator—that is, toward the east. Over Asia, Pontus, and the remaining provinces in that quarter, Antigonus—that is, toward the north.

We speak of these according to the regions of the whole world. In relation to the land of Judea, however, Syria lies to the north and Egypt to the south. What he says, “but not among his descendants,” signifies that he had no children, but that his kingdom was torn apart among strangers, except for his brother Philip, who held Macedonia. Nor was it according to the power with which he ruled. For the kingdom, divided into four parts, was weaker, while they fought against one another and raged with internal fury.

“For his kingdom will also be torn apart among outsiders, besides these.” In addition to the four kingdoms—Macedonia, Asia, Syria, and Egypt—the kingdom of the Macedonians was torn apart among other, more obscure and lesser kings. He means Perdiccas, Craterus, and Lysimachus. For Cappadocia, Armenia, Bithynia, Heraclea, the Bosporus, and other provinces, withdrawing from Macedonian power, established kings of their own.

**(Verse 5.)** “And the king of the South will grow strong.” He indicates Ptolemy, son of Lagus, who first ruled in Egypt and was a most prudent, powerful, and wealthy man, [704] so influential that he restored Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, after his expulsion, to his kingdom; gained possession of Cyprus and Phoenicia; and, after defeating Demetrius, son of Antigonus, restored to Seleucus the portion of his kingdom that had been taken from him by Antigonus. He also gained possession of Caria and many islands, cities, and regions, which it is not appropriate to discuss at this time.

He leaves aside the remaining kingdoms, namely Macedonia and Asia, and speaks only of the kings of Egypt and Syria because Judea lay between them and was held now by one set of kings, now by the other. The purpose of Holy Scripture is not to weave an external history unrelated to the Jews, but one connected with the people of Israel.

[Col. 0559D] “And one of his princes will prevail over him and rule with authority. For his dominion will be extensive.” This is Ptolemy Philadelphus, the second king of Egypt, son of the earlier Ptolemy. Under him the Seventy interpreters are said to have translated Holy Scripture at Alexandria into the Greek language. He also sent many gifts and vessels to Jerusalem for Eleazar the high priest and for the temple treasury. Demetrius Phalereus, who was both an orator and philosopher among the Greeks, was in charge of his library. Ptolemy Philadelphus is said to have possessed such power that he surpassed his father.

For the histories relate that he had two hundred thousand infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, two thousand chariots, and four hundred elephants, which he was the first to bring out of Ethiopia. He had fifteen hundred long ships, now called Liburnians, and another thousand for transporting provisions for the soldiers; also a great quantity of gold and silver, so that each year he received from Egypt fourteen thousand eight hundred talents of silver, and fifteen million *artabae* of grain, each measure containing three *modii* and one-third of a *modius*.

**(Verse 6.)** “And after the end of the years they will form an alliance” (or, as Theodotion translated it: “And after his years they will mingle”). “And the daughter of the king of the South will come to the king of the North to make an alliance; but she will not retain the strength of the arm, nor will her offspring stand; and she herself will be handed over, as will those who brought her, her young men [Vulgate: ‘adolescents’], who strengthened her in those times.”

As we have said, Seleucus, surnamed Nicator, was the first to rule Syria. The second was Antiochus, called Soter. The third was another Antiochus, [705] who was called **Θεός**, that is, “God.” He waged very many wars against Ptolemy Philadelphus, who was the second ruler of the Egyptians, and fought with all the strength of Babylon and the East.

Ptolemy Philadelphus therefore wished, after many years, to end the troublesome conflict. He gave his daughter, Berenice, in marriage to Antiochus. Antiochus had two sons by his former wife, Laodice: Seleucus, surnamed Callinicus, and another Antiochus. Ptolemy escorted Berenice as far as Pelusium and gave an immeasurable amount of gold and silver as her dowry. Hence he was called **φορνοφόρος**, that is, “the dowry-bearer.”

Antiochus said that he would have Berenice as his consort in the kingdom and Laodice in the place of a concubine. But after a long time, overcome by affection, he brought Laodice back into the palace with her children. Fearing her husband’s uncertain disposition and that he might restore Berenice, Laodice had her husband killed by servants with poison. She handed Berenice and the son born from Antiochus over to Icadion and Gennaeus, leading men of Antioch, to be killed. She established her elder son, Seleucus Callinicus, as king in his father’s place.

This is what is now meant: After many years Ptolemy Philadelphus and Antiochus **Θεός** would make an alliance; and the daughter of the king of the South—that is, of Ptolemy—would come to the king of the North—that is, to Antiochus—in order to establish friendship between her father and her husband. “But she will not be able,” he says, “to prevail, nor will her offspring stand in the kingdom of Syria; rather, Berenice herself and those who brought her will be killed.” King Antiochus, who strengthened her—that is, through whom she might have prevailed—was also killed by his wife with poison.

**(Verses 7–9.)** “And a plant from the shoot of her roots will stand; and he will come with an army, enter the province of the king of the North, deal with them, and prevail. Moreover, he will carry their gods, their molten images, and their precious vessels of gold and silver into Egypt as captives; and he will prevail against the king of the North. And the king of the South will enter the kingdom and return to his own land.”

After Berenice had been killed and her father Ptolemy Philadelphus had died in Egypt, her brother, also named Ptolemy and surnamed Euergetes, succeeded to the kingdom as the third ruler. He was “from the plant and shoot of her root,” because he was her brother. He came with a great army and entered the province of the king of the North—that is, of Seleucus, surnamed Callinicus, who ruled Syria with his mother Laodice.

He dealt with them and prevailed, to such an extent that he captured Syria and Cilicia, the upper regions beyond the Euphrates, and almost all Asia. When he heard that a revolt was being stirred up in Egypt, he plundered Seleucus’s kingdom and carried away forty thousand talents of silver and two thousand five hundred precious vessels and images of the gods, among which were those that Cambyses had taken from Egypt and carried into Persia.

Finally, because after many years he had brought back their gods, the Egyptian people, devoted to idolatry, called him Euergetes. He himself retained Syria, but entrusted Cilicia to his friend Antiochus and the provinces beyond the Euphrates to another commander, Xanthippus.

**(Verse 10.)** “But his sons will be provoked; and they will gather a multitude of very great armies; and he will come hastening, overflowing, and returning, and will be stirred up; and he will engage with his strength.”

After the flight and death of Seleucus Callinicus, his two sons, Seleucus surnamed Ceraunus and Antiochus who was called the Great, provoked by the hope of victory and by revenge for their father, took up arms after gathering an army against Ptolemy Philopator.

When Seleucus, the elder brother, was treacherously killed in Phrygia in the third year of his reign by Nicanor and Apaturius, the army stationed in Syria summoned his brother Antiochus the Great from Babylon to the kingship. Hence the passage now says that the two sons were provoked and gathered a multitude of very great armies.

But because Antiochus the Great came from Babylon into Syria—which at that time was held by Ptolemy Philopator, son of Euergetes, who was the fourth ruler of Egypt—and, after fighting against his commanders, or rather obtaining Syria through the treachery of Theodotus, which had already been held successively by the kings of Egypt, he became so audacious that, despising Philopator’s luxury and the magical arts to which he was said to devote himself, he attempted voluntarily to make war upon the Egyptians.

**(Verses 11–12.)** “And the king of the South, provoked, will go out and fight against the king of the North; and he will prepare a very great multitude, and the multitude will be given into his hand. And he will capture the multitude, and his heart will be exalted, because [Vulgate: ‘and’] he will overthrow many thousands; but he will not prevail.”

Ptolemy, surnamed Philopator, after losing Syria through the treachery of Theodotus, gathered a very large force and marched against Antiochus the Great, whom he now calls the king of the North, according to the position of Egypt and the province of Judea. The same place is situated toward the South for one and toward the North for the other, according to the character of the region. For example, if we speak from the perspective of Judea, Egypt lies to the north and Syria to the south.

Thus, when battle was joined near the town of Raphia, which lies at the gates of Egypt, Antiochus lost his entire army and, fleeing through the deserts, was nearly captured. When he had yielded Syria, the conflict was finally ended by a treaty and certain conditions. This is what Scripture now says: Ptolemy Philopator will overthrow many thousands, but he will not prevail. For he could not capture his adversary.

**(Verses 13–14.)** “And the king of the North will return and prepare a multitude much greater than before; and at the end of times and years he will come hastening with a great army and immense riches. And in those times many will rise against the king of the South.”

He signifies Antiochus the Great, who, despising the indolence of Ptolemy Philopator—because Ptolemy was infatuated with Agathoclea [or: Agathoclida], the harp-player, and with her brother, and had made Agathocles himself his concubine, later appointing him commander of Egypt—gathered an incredible army from the upper regions of Babylon.

After Ptolemy Philopator died, Antiochus broke the treaty and led an army against his son, who was then four years old and was called Ptolemy **Ἐπιφανής** (*Epiphanes*). Agathocles was so dissolute and arrogant that the provinces previously subject to Egypt rebelled, and Egypt itself was harassed by seditions.

King Philip of the Macedonians and Antiochus the Great also made peace and fought against Agathocles and Ptolemy Epiphanes, on the condition that each should add to his own kingdom the neighboring cities taken from Ptolemy’s realm. This is what the passage now says: many would rise against the king of the South, namely Ptolemy Epiphanes, who was still a child.

“And the sons of the transgressors of your people will exalt themselves, to fulfill the vision, and they will fall [Vulgate: ‘will fall’].”

While Antiochus the Great and Ptolemy’s commanders were fighting against one another, Judea, lying between them, was divided into opposing factions: some favored Antiochus, others Ptolemy. Finally, Onias the priest fled to Egypt with a great number of Jews. Ptolemy received him honorably, [Note: [Col. 0561D] This entire history of Onias’s temple has been translated from Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book VII, chapter 10. Josephus describes the region that Onias received from Ptolemy at greater length. He says: “He gave him a region one hundred and eighty stades distant from Memphis; this district is called the nome of Heliopolis. There Onias built a fortress and constructed a temple, not like the one in Jerusalem, but resembling a tower.” Here you see that Josephus disagrees with Jerome, who says that it was built like the Jewish temple, since Josephus says that it was unlike it.] and gave him the region called Heliopolis. With the king’s permission, he built a temple in Egypt resembling the temple of the Jews. It remained until the reign of Vespasian, for two hundred and fifty years. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Josephus, rather, counts three hundred and forty-three years: “The time from its construction until the closing of the temple had been three hundred and forty-three years” (**χρόνος ἦν εἰς τὴν ἀπόκλεισιν τοῦ ναοῦ γεγονὼς ἀπὸ τῆς κατασκευῆς ἔτη τρία καὶ τεσσαράκοντα καὶ τριακόσια**). Rufinus translates this as 333; but a recent editor of Josephus advises that 233 should be read, since that temple was closed by order of Vespasian shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem, around the year 824 of the City. See Selden, Book I, *On the Succession in the Hebrew Priesthood*, chapter VIII.] The city itself, which was called [Col. 0563A] Onias, was later utterly destroyed when the Jews fought against the Romans; and no trace remains of either the city or the temple. On the occasion of the high priest Onias, therefore, innumerable swarms of Jews fled to Egypt. At that time it too was filled with a multitude of Cyrenians.

For Onias asserted that he was fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah, who wrote: “There will be an altar of the Lord in Egypt, and a monument to the Lord at its borders” (Isa. XIX, 19). [Note: [Col. 0563D] Elsewhere the holy Doctor attacks Onias on the basis of this prophecy of Isaiah in his Commentary on that passage. For Isaiah, describing the spiritual kingdom of Christ, had said that it would be extended even into Egypt.]

This is what the passage now says: “The sons of the transgressors of your people,” who abandoned the law of the Lord and wished to sacrifice victims to God in another place, contrary to what had been commanded, “will exalt themselves in pride and boast that they are fulfilling the vision,” that is, the Lord’s command. But they will fall, because both the temple and the city will later be destroyed.

While Antiochus held Judea, Scopas was sent against him. [Note: [Col. 0563D] Our manuscripts read “Aethiolus,” or “son of Eptolius.” See Polybius, Book IV, chapter 26, and following.] He was the commander of Ptolemy’s faction. He fought Antiochus bravely, captured Judea, and, taking with him the leading men of Ptolemy’s faction, returned to Egypt.

709 (Verses 15–16.) “And the king of the North shall come, and shall cast up a rampart, and shall capture the most strongly fortified cities; and the arms of the South shall not withstand him. His chosen troops shall rise up to resist, but there shall be no strength. And when he comes, he shall act against him according to his pleasure, and there shall be no one who can stand before him. And he shall stand in the glorious land, and it shall be consumed by his hand.”

For Antiochus, wishing to recover Judaea and many cities of Syria, routed Scopas, Ptolemy’s commander, near the sources of the Jordan, where Paneas has now been founded. After engaging him in battle, he shut him up with ten thousand armed men in Sidon. To free him, Ptolemy sent the distinguished commanders Eropus, Menocles, and Damoxenus [Variant: Damoxeum]. But they could not lift the siege. At last, overcome by hunger, Scopas surrendered, and was released naked, together with his companions.

By the statement, “He shall cast up a rampart,” he indicates that Antiochus besieged Scopas’s garrison in the citadel of Jerusalem for a long time, with the Jews supporting him; and that he captured other cities which had previously been held by Ptolemy’s forces—cities of Syria, Cilicia, and Lycia [Variant: Lydia]. At that time Aphrodisias, Soli, Zephyrion, Mallus, Anemurium [Variant: Anemurum], Selenus, Coracesium, Corycus, Andriace, Limyra, Patara [Variant: Patra], Xanthus, and finally Ephesus were captured. Greek and Roman history both relate these events. 

As for what follows—“And he shall stand in the glorious land, and it shall be consumed,” or “be completed,” “by his hand”—the glorious land, or, as the Seventy translated it, “the land of desire,” that is, the land pleasing to God, signifies Judaea, and specifically Jerusalem, where he honorably [Note: Victorius conjectures *susceptus*, either from the sequence of the preceding context—namely, “Antiochus was received”—or because *persecutus* follows shortly afterward in place of *prosecutus*.] received those who belonged to Scopas’s faction and pursued them.

In place of “glorious land,” Aquila translated the expression as we have followed him here; Theodotion retained the Hebrew word itself, writing σαβὶν, for which Symmachus translated “land of strength.” [Note: More correctly, it seems, the Palatine manuscripts and the Sangermanensis cited by Montfaucon read *Sabir*, with r and Latin letters. Thus Theodoret: “Some of those who translated the Hebrew language into Greek have called it the land of Sabeir.” Theodotion nevertheless seems to have written Σαβεὶ or Σαβαεὶμ.]

(Verses 17.) “And he shall set his face to come and seize his whole kingdom, and he shall make an agreement with him. And he shall give him the daughter of women, to overthrow him” [Vulgate: “it”]. “To overthrow him,” that is, Ptolemy; or “it,” that is, his kingdom.

Antiochus wished not only to possess Syria, Cilicia, Lycia, and the other provinces belonging to Ptolemy’s faction, but also to extend his kingdom into Egypt. Through Eucleides of Rhodes, in the seventh year of the young Ptolemy’s reign, he betrothed his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemy, and gave her to him in the thirteenth year, granting him all Coele-Syria and Judaea as her dowry.

He calls her “the daughter of women” by πλεονασμός [pleonasm], as in the poetic expressions:

> . . . . . . . . . . . . Thus she spoke with her mouth.
>
> . . . . . . . . And with these ears I drank in her voice.

(Verses 18–19.) “And he shall not stand, nor shall it be his. And he shall turn his face toward the islands, and shall capture many; and he shall cause the prince of his disgrace to cease, and his disgrace shall turn back upon him. And he shall turn his face toward the dominion of his own land, and shall stumble, and fall, and shall not be found.”

For he could not gain possession of Egypt, because Ptolemy Epiphanes and his commanders, perceiving the deception, acted more cautiously, while Cleopatra favored her husband’s cause more than that of her father. Therefore he went into Asia and, fighting naval battles against very many islands, captured Rhodes [Variant: Hrodus], Samos, Colophon [Variants: Colophoniam and Boclam], Phocaea, and many other islands.

But L. Scipio Nasica came against him with his brother Publius Scipio Africanus, who had defeated Hannibal. Since the consul Nasica, Africanus’ brother, was the less capable in judgment, and the Senate was unwilling to entrust him with a war against so powerful a king, Africanus offered himself for this voluntary embassy, on account of the insult to his brother.

Thus defeated, Antiochus was ordered to reign only within the Taurus Mountains. From there he fled to Apamea, then reached Susa and the furthest cities of his kingdom. When he fought against the Elymaeans, he was destroyed together with his entire army.

This is what Scripture now says: he captured many islands; when the Roman prevailed, he lost the kingdom of Asia; his disgrace was turned back upon his own head; and finally, fleeing from Asia, he returned to the dominion of his own land, stumbled and fell, and his place was no longer found.

(Verses 20.) “And in his place shall stand one most contemptible and unworthy of royal honor; and within a few days he shall be crushed, neither in anger nor in battle.”

He means Seleucus, surnamed Philopator, the son of Antiochus the Great, who accomplished nothing worthy of the rule of Syria or of his father and perished ingloriously without any battles.

Porphyry, however, does not wish this to refer to Seleucus, but to Ptolemy Epiphanes, who plotted against Seleucus, prepared an army against him, and was therefore killed by his commanders with poison. When someone asked him, as he was undertaking such great enterprises, where he had his money, he replied that his friends were his wealth. When this answer became known among the people, the commanders feared that he would take away their property, and so they killed him by criminal arts.

But how can Ptolemy stand in the place of Antiochus the Great, when he did none of this at all—especially since the Seventy translated the passage: “And a plant shall stand from his root,” that is, from his offspring and seed, “striking at the dignity of the kingdom; and within a few days he shall be crushed, without anger and without battle”?

The Hebrews wish “the most contemptible and unworthy of royal honor” to be understood as Tryphon, who, having been guardian of the boy, seized the tyranny.

(Verses 21 and following.) “And in his place shall stand one who is despised, and royal honor shall not be given to him; and he shall come secretly and obtain the kingdom by deceit. And the arms of the warrior shall be broken before him; they shall be utterly crushed, together with the leader of the covenant. And after forming friendships with him, he shall act deceitfully; he shall rise and prevail with a small people. And he shall enter rich and fertile cities; and he shall do what his fathers and his fathers’ fathers did not do: he shall scatter their plunder, spoil, and wealth; and he shall devise plans against the firmest counsels—and this for a time.”

Up to this point the sequence of history is followed, and there is no disagreement between Porphyry and our interpreters. The remainder, however, through the end of the book, Porphyry interprets as referring to Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, the brother of Seleucus and son of Antiochus the Great. He reigned in Syria for eleven years after Seleucus and gained possession of Judaea. Under him the persecution of God’s Law and the wars of the Maccabees are related.

Our interpreters, however, believe that all these things are prophesied about the Antichrist, who will come at the end of time. When it is objected to them, “Why has the prophetic discourse left so many events in the middle untouched, from Seleucus to the consummation of the world?”, they reply that in the earlier history, where the Persian kings were discussed, Scripture likewise named only four kings after Cyrus of Persia, and, leaping over many intervening events, suddenly came to Alexander, king of the Macedonians. This, they say, is the custom of Holy Scripture: not to narrate everything, but to explain those things that appear more important.

Since many of the events that we shall later read and explain fit the person of Antiochus, they wish him to possess the type of the Antichrist: what occurred partially beforehand in Antiochus will be completely fulfilled in the Antichrist. This too, they say, is the custom of Holy Scripture: to anticipate the truth of future events in types, according to what is said of the Lord and Savior in the seventy-first Psalm, which bears the superscription “of Solomon.” Everything said there cannot apply to Solomon:

> For he did not remain with the sun and before the moon, throughout all generations (Psalm 71);
>
> nor did he rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth;
>
> nor did all nations serve him;
>
> nor did his name endure before the sun;
>
> nor were all the tribes of the earth blessed in him;
>
> nor did all nations magnify him.

These things were anticipated in Solomon in part, as though in a shadow and image of the truth, so that they might be fulfilled more perfectly in the Lord and Savior. Therefore, just as the Savior has Solomon and the other saints as types of his coming, so the Antichrist must rightly be believed to have had as his type the most wicked king Antiochus, who persecuted the saints and violated the temple.

Let us therefore follow the order of the exposition and, in accordance with both explanations, briefly record what our opponents and what our own interpreters think.

“He shall stand,” they say, “in the place of Seleucus: his brother Antiochus Epiphanes, to whom royal honor was not initially granted by those in Syria who favored Ptolemy, but who later obtained the kingdom of Syria through a pretended clemency. The arms of Ptolemy, who was fighting and devastating everything, were defeated and crushed before Antiochus.”

By “arms” he means strength; hence “hand” also denotes a multitude of soldiers. He says that Antiochus not only conquered Ptolemy by deceit, but also overcame the leader of the covenant—namely, Judas Maccabaeus—by trickery. Or the meaning may be this: after Antiochus himself had offered peace to Ptolemy and had become the leader of the covenant, he later plotted against him.

Here “Ptolemy” does not signify Ptolemy Epiphanes, who was the fifth to reign in Egypt, but Ptolemy Philometor, the son of Cleopatra, Antiochus’ sister, whose uncle he was. After Cleopatra’s death, when the eunuch Eulaeus, Philometor’s tutor, and Leneus governed Egypt and demanded back Syria, which Antiochus had seized by deception, war arose between the uncle and the boy Ptolemy.

When they engaged in battle between Pelusium and Mount Casius, Ptolemy’s commanders were defeated. Antiochus, sparing the boy and pretending friendship, went up to Memphis. There, receiving the kingdom according to Egyptian custom and claiming that he was acting for the boy’s benefit, he subdued all Egypt with a small force and entered its rich and exceedingly fertile cities.

He did what his fathers and his fathers’ fathers had not done. No one had ever devastated Egypt in this way while ruling the kingdom of Syria. He scattered all their wealth and was sufficiently crafty to overturn by his deceit the prudent plans of those who were the boy’s commanders.

Porphyry, following Sutorium [Note: Previously *Suctorium*, in other books *Suturium*; then *latissimo* rather than *laciniosissimo*. See above, in the Prologue to this Commentary, near the end, note b.], has related these matters in a very elaborate discourse, whereas we have stated them in brief.

Our interpreters, however, give both the better and the more accurate interpretation: that at the end of the world the Antichrist will do these things. He will arise from a small nation—that is, from the Jewish people—and will be so humble and despised that royal honor will not be given him. Through plots and deceit he will obtain power; the arms of the fighting Roman people will be defeated and crushed by him. He will do this because he will pretend to be the leader of the covenant—that is, of God’s Law and Testament.

He will enter the richest cities and do what his fathers and his fathers’ fathers did not do. For no Jew ever ruled the whole world without the Antichrist. He will devise plans against the firmest counsels of the saints and will do all these things for a time, until God’s will permits him to do them.

(Verses 25–26.) “And his strength and his heart shall be stirred up against the king of the South with a great army. And the king of the South shall be provoked to war with very many and exceedingly strong auxiliaries; but they shall not stand, because they shall devise plans against him. And those who eat bread with him shall crush him, and his army shall be overwhelmed, and many slain shall fall.”

Porphyry interprets this of Antiochus, who marched against Ptolemy, the son of his sister, with a great army. The king of the South—that is, Ptolemy’s commanders—was likewise provoked to war with numerous and exceedingly strong auxiliaries, but they could not withstand Antiochus’ deceitful plans. He pretended peace with his sister’s son, ate bread with him, and afterward seized Egypt.

Our interpreters, however, according to the preceding sense, interpret everything of the Antichrist, who will be born from the Jewish people and will come from Babylon. He will first overcome the king of Egypt, who is one of the three horns about which we spoke earlier.

(Verses 27–28.) “And the hearts of the two kings shall be set on doing evil, and at one table they shall speak lies, but they shall not succeed, because the end is still for another time. And he shall return to his land with great wealth.”

There is no doubt that Antiochus made peace with Ptolemy, dined with him, plotted against him, and accomplished nothing, because he was unable to obtain his kingdom and was driven out by Ptolemy’s soldiers.

Yet, because Scripture now says that there were two kings whose hearts were deceitful, so that they might harm one another, this cannot be demonstrated from the historical account. Ptolemy was young in years; deceived by Antiochus’ fraud, what harm could he have planned against him? Therefore our interpreters wish all these things to be referred to the Antichrist and to the king of Egypt, whom he will first overcome. [Note: Victorius, from the Brixian manuscripts, supplies *referri*; shortly afterward, *superaturus est*.]

(Verses 29–30.) “And his heart shall be against the holy Covenant, and he shall act, and shall return to his land. At the appointed time he shall return and come toward the South; but the latter expedition shall not be like the former. And ships shall come against him, together with the Romans, and he shall be struck down.” Or, as another translated it: “And they shall threaten him.”

Greek and Roman history relate that after Antiochus had returned, expelled by the Egyptians, he came into Judaea—that is, against the holy Covenant—plundered the temple, carried away a very large quantity of gold, placed a Macedonian garrison in the citadel, and returned to his own land.

Two years later he again assembled an army against Ptolemy and came toward the South. When Ptolemy’s two brothers, the sons of Cleopatra and Antiochus’ nephews, were being besieged in Alexandria, Roman envoys arrived. One of them, Marcus Popilius Laenas [Note: Our manuscripts read *Pompilius*. These names are commonly confused; hence also *Pompilia lex* and *Popilia*, and *Pompilius Rufus* and *Popilius Rufus*.], found Antiochus standing on the shore and handed him a decree of the Senate ordering him to withdraw from the friends of the Roman people and be content with his own authority.

When Antiochus postponed his reply in order to consult with his friends, Popilius is said to have drawn a circle in the sand with the staff he held in his hand, surrounded the king with it, and said: “The Senate and the Roman people command you to answer here what you intend to do.” Terrified by these words, Antiochus replied: “If this pleases the Senate and the Roman people, I must withdraw,” and immediately moved his army.

He is said to have been “struck down,” not because he died, but because he lost all the grandeur of his arrogance.

No one doubts that the Antichrist will fight against the holy Covenant and that, first fighting against the king of Egypt, he will be terrified at once by the aid of the Romans. [Note: This is the more coherent reading of the Vatican manuscript: “immediately by the aid of the Romans,” etc. The Palatine manuscript also reads well, “through fear of the Romans,” in place of “by his aid.” Previously, “of the Romans” in place of “by his aid” made no sense.] These events occurred beforehand under Antiochus Epiphanes as an image, so that the most criminal king, who persecuted God’s people, might prefigure the Antichrist, who will persecute Christ’s people.

Therefore many of our interpreters think that, on account of the magnitude of his savagery and depravity, Domitius Nero will be the Antichrist. [Note: Victorinus, in his commentary on the Apocalypse, held this view, to name one example. Lactantius refutes it thoroughly in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 2, at the end; so also Augustine, *City of God*, book 20, chapter 19; Ambrosiaster, on 1 Corinthians 4:9; Sulpicius Severus, *History*, book 2, chapter 29, and *Dialogue* 2, final chapter; and, among the Greeks, Chrysostom, Homily 4 on 2 Thessalonians. See also Letter 121 to Algasia, final question. The manuscripts read *Domitianum* for *Domitium*; the Vatican manuscript has *Domitianum vel Neronem*.]

“And he shall return and be angry against the Covenant of the sanctuary, and he shall act, and shall return, and shall devise plans concerning those who have abandoned the Covenant of the sanctuary” [Vulgate: “against them”].

We read a fuller account of these events in the deeds of the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 1): after the Romans had driven him out of Egypt, he came in anger against the Covenant of the sanctuary, and was invited by those who had abandoned God’s Law and mingled themselves with the rites of the pagans.

This will be fulfilled more fully under the Antichrist, who will be angry against God’s Covenant and will devise plans against those whom he wishes to make abandon God’s Law. Hence Aquila translated the passage more expressively:

> And he shall devise that the covenant of the sanctuary be abandoned.

(Verses 31.) “And arms shall arise from him, and shall pollute the sanctuary of strength” [Vulgate: “and shall pollute”], “and shall remove the continual sacrifice, and shall give the abomination of desolation.”

In place of “arms,” another translator rendered “seeds,” signifying offspring and descendants. [Note: Victorius would have preferred Aquila’s reading, *semina*, as found in the two manuscripts he cites.]

They wish those sent by Antiochus to be understood here: two years after he had plundered the temple, they were sent to exact tribute from the Jews, abolish the worship of God, and place in the temple at Jerusalem an image of Olympian Jupiter and statues of Antiochus. These are what Scripture now calls “the abomination of desolation,” when the burnt offering and continual sacrifice were removed.

Our interpreters contend that all these events occurred beforehand as a type of the Antichrist, who will sit in the temple of God and make himself out to be God.

The Jews, however, wish this to be understood neither of Antiochus Epiphanes nor of the Antichrist, but of the Romans, about whom it was said above: “And ships shall come,” that is, the Italians and Romans, “and he shall be humbled.”

“After many years,” he says, “from those same Romans who came to Ptolemy’s aid and threatened Antiochus, King Vespasian shall arise. His arms, his seed—his son Titus with the army—shall arise; they shall pollute the sanctuary, remove the continual sacrifice, and deliver the temple to eternal desolation.”

SIIM () and CHETHIM (), which we have translated “ships” and “Romans,” the Hebrews wish to be understood as the Italians and Romans.

(Verses 32.) “And the impious shall act deceitfully against the covenant. But the people who know their God shall prevail and act.”

We read this also in the Maccabees: some pretended to be guardians of God’s Law, but afterward made a covenant with the Gentiles; others, however, remained steadfast in their religion. I believe the same will happen in the time of the Antichrist, when the love of many will grow cold. Of these the Lord speaks in the Gospel:

> Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on the earth? (Luke 18:8)

“And the learned among the people shall teach many, and shall fall by the sword, by flame, by captivity, and by the plundering of days.”

The books of the Maccabees relate how much the Jews suffered under Antiochus, and their triumphs bear witness to it. For the preservation of God’s Law they endured flames, swords, slavery, plunder, and the ultimate punishments.

No one should doubt that these things will occur under the Antichrist, when many will resist his power and flee in various directions.

Some of the Hebrews interpret this of the final destruction of the temple, which occurred under Vespasian and Titus. They say that many among the people knew their Lord and were killed [Variant: “may be killed”] for the preservation of his Law.

[Col. 0569D] (Verses 34–35.) “And when they fall, they shall be helped with a little help, and many shall join themselves to them deceitfully. And some of the learned shall fall, so that they may be refined, chosen, and made white until the appointed time, because there shall still be another time.”

Porphyry thinks that “a little help” signifies Mattathias from the village [Variant: mountain] of Modin, who rebelled against Antiochus’ commanders and attempted to preserve the worship of the true God (1 Maccabees 2).

He calls it “a little help,” he says, because Mattathias was killed in battle; afterward his son Judas, who was called Maccabaeus, fell fighting; and the rest of his brothers were deceived by the fraud of their adversaries. Read the books of the Maccabees.

“All these things,” he says, “were done so that the saints might be tested, chosen, and made white until the appointed time, because the victory had been postponed to another time.”

Our interpreters wish “a little help” under the Antichrist to be understood as follows: the saints will assemble and resist him, using a little help; afterward many of the learned will fall. This will happen so that they may be refined as though in a furnace, made white, and chosen until the appointed time arrives, because the true victory will come at Christ’s advent.

Some of the Hebrews understand these things of the emperors Severus and Antoninus, who greatly loved the Jews. Others understand them of the emperor Julian: when the Jews had been oppressed by Gaius Caesar and had suffered much in the hardships of captivity, Julian would arise, pretending to love the Jews and promising that he would sacrifice in their temple. In him they would have a small hope of help, and many Gentiles would join them, not in truth but in falsehood. For the worship of idols, they would pretend friendship with him.

They would do this so that those who had been tested might be revealed. For they think that the time of their true salvation and help will be Christ, whom they falsely believe is to come, although they will receive the Antichrist (1 Corinthians 11). [Note: The Palatine and Vatican manuscripts read: “whom they falsely hope will be,” and so on.]

(Verses 36.) “And the king shall act according to his will, and shall be exalted and magnified against every god, and shall speak magnificent things against the God of gods; and he shall direct” [Vulgate: “shall be directed”] “until wrath is completed” [Vulgate: “indignation”], “for the determination has been carried out.” [Note: Victorius, following the Vulgate, reads *loquetur* and, shortly afterward, *dirigetur*.] Or, as another translated it: “For the consummation shall be in him.”

From this point the Jews think that the passage speaks of the Antichrist. After Julian’s little help, they say, a king will arise who will act according to his will, exalt himself against everything called god, and speak magnificent things against the God of gods, so that he will sit in the temple of God, make himself God, and prosper in his will until God’s wrath is completed, because the consummation will be in him.

We too understand this of the Antichrist. Porphyry, however, and those who follow him believe that the passage speaks of Antiochus Epiphanes, who rose up against the worship of God and became so arrogant that he ordered his image to be placed in the temple at Jerusalem.

As for what follows—“and he shall be directed until wrath is completed, for the consummation shall be in him”—they understand it to mean that Antiochus would have power only until God became angry with him and ordered him to be killed.

Polybius and Diodorus, who write the histories of the Libraries [Note: Some strongly wish this to be emended to *Bibliothecas*, “Libraries,” as in the title of Diodorus’ work and in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 1, chapter 6: “having brought the whole historical Library together into one work.”], relate that he not only acted against God in Judaea, but, inflamed by the torches of greed, also attempted to plunder the temple of Diana in Elymais, which was exceedingly wealthy. [Note: Compare also 1 Maccabees, book 1, chapter 7, and Appian, *Syrian Affairs*, who calls this temple not Diana’s but Venus’s; Josephus, besides Polybius and Diodorus, calls it Diana’s.] They say that he was overwhelmed by the temple guards and the surrounding peoples, driven mad by certain apparitions and terrors, and finally died of disease. They report that this happened to him because he had attempted to violate the temple of Diana.

We, however, say that even if this happened to him, it happened because he had exercised great cruelty against God’s saints and polluted his temple. He must not be thought to have been punished for what he attempted and then ceased to complete after repenting, but for what he actually did.

(Verses 37 and following.) “And he shall not regard the God of his fathers, and he shall be in the desires of women; nor shall he care for any god, because he shall rise up against all things. But in his place he shall worship the god MAOZIM; and he shall honor with gold, silver, precious stones, and costly objects a god whom his fathers did not know. And he shall act so as to fortify MAOZIM with a foreign god whom he knew; and he shall multiply glory, give them power over many things, and divide the land for nothing.”

For what we translated as “and he shall be in the desires of women,” the Seventy translated: “and he shall not submit to the desires of women.”

Again, for the Hebrew term MAOZIM (), Aquila translated “the God of strongholds,” and the Seventy “the strongest God.”

Since the Hebrew wording corresponding to what we rendered “and he shall be in the desires of women” is ambiguous, Aquila, who translated word for word, gives:

> καὶ ἐπὶ Θεὸν πατέρων αὐτοῦ οὐ συνήσει, καὶ ἐπὶ ἐπιθυμίαν γυναικῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ πάντα θεὸν οὐ συνήσει,

that is:

> “And he shall not understand concerning the God of his fathers, nor concerning the desire of women, nor concerning any god shall he understand.”

[Note: We have supplied the word ἐπὶ here from the Vatican manuscript. It had previously been omitted because the same letters recur in the following word.]

From these words it can be understood both that he will have a desire for women and that he will not have one. If we read and understand the phrase ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (“in common”)—“and concerning the desire of women he shall not understand”—the interpretation concerning the Antichrist is easier: he will pretend to chastity in order to deceive many.

But if we read it as “and concerning the desire of women,” with “he shall be” understood, it will fit the person of Antiochus better. He is said to have been exceedingly lustful and to have fallen into such disgrace through sexual misconduct and seductions that he publicly consorted with actors and prostitutes and satisfied his lust in the presence of the people.

Porphyry ridiculously interpreted the god MAOZIM as referring to the village of Modin, from which Mattathias and his sons came. [Note: Here and below, wherever this passage recurs, the Palatine manuscript includes a negative particle: “a foreign god whom he did not know.”] He said that Antiochus’ commanders set up a statue of Jupiter there and compelled the Jews to sacrifice to it—that is, to the god of Modin.

What follows, “and he shall honor a god whom his fathers did not know,” fits the Antichrist more than Antiochus. For we read that Antiochus worshiped the idols of Greece and compelled the Jews and Samaritans to venerate his gods.

The further statement—“and he shall act so as to fortify MAOZIM with a foreign god whom he knew; and he shall multiply glory, give them power over many things, and divide the land for nothing”—Theodotion translated as follows:

> “And he shall do these things to fortify strongholds with a foreign god; and when he has shown him to them, he shall multiply honor, make them rule over many things, and divide the land freely.”

In place of “strongholds,” Symmachus translated “refuges.”

Porphyry explains the passage in this way: Antiochus will do all these things to fortify the citadel of Jerusalem and place garrisons in the other cities, and to teach the Jews to worship a foreign god—without doubt Jupiter. When he has shown him to them and persuaded them to worship him, he will then give the deceived great honor and glory, appointing them to rule over the others who are in Judaea; and for their transgression he will divide possessions and distribute gifts.

The Antichrist, too, will bestow many gifts upon the deceived and divide the land among his army. Those whom he cannot subjugate by terror he will overcome by greed.

[Col. 0572B] (Verses 40–41.) “And at the appointed time the king of the South shall fight against him; and the king of the North shall come against him like a storm, with chariots, horsemen, and a great fleet. He shall enter the lands, crush them, and pass through. And he shall enter the glorious land, and many shall fall.”

In place of this, Symmachus translated: “and many thousands shall fall”; Theodotion: “and many shall become weak.”

Following Aquila, understand “many” who fall to mean either cities, regions, or provinces.

Porphyry refers these events to Antiochus: in the eleventh year of his reign he again fought against his sister’s son, Ptolemy Philometor. When Ptolemy heard that Antiochus was coming, he gathered many thousands from among the peoples.

But Antiochus, like a powerful storm, with chariots, horsemen, and a great fleet, entered many lands and devastated everything as he passed through. He came to the glorious land—that is, Judaea—which Symmachus translated as “the land of strength.” Theodotion retained the Hebrew word itself, SABAI [Variants: SABAM and SABA] (). Antiochus fortified the citadel with the ruins of the city walls and then proceeded into Egypt.

Our interpreters, referring these events also to the Antichrist, say that he will first fight against the king of the South—that is, Egypt—and afterward overcome the Libyans and Ethiopians. These are the three horns that we read above would be crushed from among the ten horns. They also say that he will come into the land of Israel, and that many cities or provinces will surrender to him.

“But these alone shall be saved from his hands: Edom, Moab, and the beginning of the sons of Ammon.”

They say that Antiochus, hastening against Ptolemy, the king of the South, did not touch the Idumaeans, Moabites, or Ammonites, who were situated alongside Judaea [Variant: Idumaea], lest, being occupied in another war, he make Ptolemy stronger.

The Antichrist likewise will leave Idumaea, Moab, and the sons of Ammon—that is, Arabia—untouched, because the saints will flee there into the deserts.

(Verses 42–43.) “And he shall stretch out his hand over the lands, and the land of Egypt shall not escape. He shall rule over the treasures of gold and silver and over all the precious things of Egypt. He shall also pass through the Libyans” [Vulgate: “Libya and Ethiopia”] “and the Ethiopians.”

We read that Antiochus fulfilled part of this. But what follows—“he shall pass through the Libyans and Ethiopians”—our interpreters assert fits the Antichrist better.

For Antiochus did not possess Libya, which most understand as Africa, or Ethiopia, unless perhaps because these provinces lie within the same climate as Egypt and are nearby across the deserts; once the Egyptians had been captured, these provinces too were thrown into confusion.

Therefore Scripture does not say that he captured them, but that he passed through the Libyans and Ethiopians.

(Verses 44–45.) “And a report will trouble him from the East and from the North. And he will come with a great multitude, to crush and kill many. And he will pitch his tent at Apedno, between the two seas, upon the illustrious and holy mountain; and he will come even to its summit, and no one will help him.”

[Note: Victorius removes “the two,” although the expression is implied in the exposition; nevertheless, it occurs in no edition of the sacred text.]

And in this passage Porphyry dreams up something of this sort concerning Antiochus:

“Fighting against the Egyptians and passing through Libya and Ethiopia, he will hear that battles are being stirred up against him from the North and from the East. Therefore, returning, he will capture the resisting Aradians and lay waste the whole province along the Phoenician coast. 722 Immediately he will proceed against Artaxias, king of Armenia, who will move from the regions of the East; and after killing many of his army, he will pitch his tent at a place called Apedno, situated between the two broadest rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. When he has advanced this far, he cannot say upon what illustrious and holy mountain he will have sat; nor can he prove that he sat between two seas, and it is foolish to interpret the two rivers of Mesopotamia as two seas. He passed over the illustrious mountain because he followed the interpretation of Theodotion, who says: ‘between the midst of the seas, upon the holy mountain of Saba.’ Since he supposes Saba to be the name of a mountain either in Armenia or in Mesopotamia, he cannot say why it is holy. Even with this license for lying, we can add what he left unsaid: that the mountain is called holy because, according to the error of the Armenians, it has been consecrated to idols.

“‘And he will come,’ he says, ‘to the summit of that mountain, in the province of Elymais, which is the easternmost region of the Persians. There, wishing to plunder the temple of Diana, which possessed innumerable offerings, he was driven away by the barbarians, who regarded that shrine with extraordinary reverence, and died, consumed by grief, at Tabes, a town of Persia.’”

He composed these words with the most elaborate rhetoric to mock us. Even if he could prove these things, what does it matter to us if they were spoken not about Antichrist but about Antiochus? Suppose that these statements are about Antiochus: how does that harm our religion? In the preceding Vision also, where the prophecy was fulfilled in Antiochus, is anything said about Antichrist? Let him abandon doubtful matters and cling to what is manifest. Let him say who that stone is which was cut from the mountain without hands, grew into a great mountain, filled the world, and shattered the fourfold image; who that Son of Man is who will come with the clouds, stand before the Ancient of Days, and receive a kingdom that will have no end; and to whom all peoples, tribes, and languages will serve. 723

He passes over these manifest things and asserts that the prophecy concerns the Jews, whom we know to be serving to this day. He says that the man who wrote the book under Daniel’s name lied in order to revive the hope of his people—not that he could have known the whole future history, but that he was remembering events already accomplished. He dwells upon the allegations against the final Vision, putting rivers in place of the sea, and Apedno in place of the illustrious and holy mountain.

[Note: Here Victor adds to the preceding context the words “calling it Sabin.”]

But when he reads this, he cannot produce any historical account. Our writers, however, explain the final chapter of this Vision concerning Antichrist as follows: while fighting against the Egyptians, Libyans, and Ethiopians, and crushing three horns from among the ten horns, he will hear that wars are rising against him from the northern and eastern regions. Coming with a great multitude to crush and kill many, he will pitch his tent at Apedno, near Nicopolis, which was formerly called Emmaus, where the highlands of the province of Judaea begin to rise.

Then, rising from there as far as the Mount of Olives, one ascends toward the region of Jerusalem. This is what Scripture now says: “And when he has pitched his tent at the roots of the mountainous province, between two seas”—namely, the sea now called the Dead Sea to the east, and the Great Sea, on whose shore Caesarea, Joppa, Ascalon, and Gaza are situated.

[Note: Two manuscripts have “Gaza,” in the singular. But since the holy Doctor seems to say “Gazas” in the plural, he appears to understand both cities, namely Maiuma and Gaza proper, although the latter lay some distance from the sea. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.21, also calls that place Gaza by its proper name and says that it was maritime: Ἐν Γάζῃ πρὸς θάλασσαν, ὅπερ καὶ Μαϊουμᾶν ὀνομάζουσιν, “At Gaza by the sea, which they also call Maiuma.”]

Then he will come to the summit of its mountain—that is, of the mountainous province, the peak of the Mount of Olives, which is called illustrious because from it the Lord and Savior ascended to the Father—and no one will be able to help Antichrist, while the Lord rages against him. They assert that Antichrist will perish there, at the place from which the Lord ascended into heaven.

“Apedno” is a compound word which, if divided, may be understood as θρόνου αὐτοῦ, that is, “of his throne.” The sense is: “And he will pitch his tent and his throne between the seas, upon the illustrious and holy mountain.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscript has “the tent of his throne”; these final words are entirely absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

Symmachus interpreted this passage as follows: καὶ ἐκτενεῖ τὰς σκηνὰς τοῦ ἱπποστασίου αὐτοῦ μεταξὺ τῶν θαλασσῶν εἰς τὸ ὄρος τῆς δυνάμεως τὸ ἅγιον, καὶ ἥξει ἕως ἄκρου αὐτοῦ.

In Latin this means: “And he will extend the pavilions of his cavalry between the seas, upon the holy mountain of strength, and he will come as far as the summit of the mountain.”

Theodotion: “And he will pitch his tent at Aphedano, between the seas, upon the holy mountain of Saba, and he will come as far as its part.”

Aquila: “And he will plant the tent of his praetorium at Ἀφαδανῷ, between the seas, upon the glorious and holy mountain, and he will come as far as its end.”

Only the Septuagint, freeing itself from every difficulty concerning the name, translated: “And he will then establish his tent between the seas and the holy mountain of desire, and the hour of his consummation will come.” Apollinarius followed them and was entirely silent about the name Apedno.

I have set this out at greater length in order both to expose Porphyry’s slander—for he either did not know all these things or pretended not to know them—and to display the difficulty of the sacred Scripture, whose meaning the most ignorant people especially claim for themselves without God’s grace and the instruction of their predecessors.

It should be noted, however, that the Hebrew language does not have the letter P, but uses *phe* in its place, whose force is represented by the Greek φ. In this one place, among the Hebrews, *phe* is indeed written, but pronounced P.

[Note: Most manuscripts consistently have *phe* without aspiration.]

As for Antichrist’s coming to the summit of the holy and illustrious mountain and perishing there, Isaiah speaks more fully: “The Lord will hurl down upon the holy mountain the face of the ruler of darkness over all the nations, and him who rules all peoples, and the anointing which has been anointed against all the nations.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscript has “and the anointing,” with the conjunction joined to the preceding phrase.]

## Chapter XII—Verses 1 ff.

“At that time Michael will arise, the great prince who stands for the sons of your people, and there will come a time such as has not been since the nations began to exist, until that time. And at that time your people will be saved, everyone who is found written in the book.
