And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake: some to everlasting life, and others to reproach, 725 that they may see forever. But those who have been instructed will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars for everlasting eternities.”

Thus far Porphyry held himself together to some extent and imposed upon the ignorant among our people and the poorly instructed among his own. But what will he say about this chapter, in which the resurrection of the dead is described—some raised to everlasting life and others to everlasting reproach? He cannot say who under Antiochus shone like the brightness of the firmament, or who were like the stars for everlasting eternities.

But what will obstinacy not do? Like a crushed serpent, he raises his head and, as he is about to die, pours out his venom upon those who are destined to die.

“This too,” he says, “was written about Antiochus. When he went into Persia, he left his army with Lysias, who was in charge of Antioch and Phoenicia, so that he might fight against the Jews and overthrow their city, Jerusalem. Josephus, the author of the Hebrew history, recounts all these things: that such a tribulation occurred as had never been, and that a time came such as had not existed since the nations began until that time.

“After victory had been restored, the commanders of Antiochus had been slain, and Antiochus himself had died in Persia, the people of Israel were saved—all who were written in God’s book, that is, those who had defended the Law with the greatest courage. Conversely, those erased from the book were those who had become transgressors of the Law and had taken Antiochus’s side.

“Then,” he says, “those who had been sleeping as though in the dust of the earth, covered and buried as it were in tombs of misery under the weight of evils, rose from the dust of the earth for an unexpected victory and lifted their heads from the ground: the guardians of the Law rising to everlasting life, and the transgressors to everlasting reproach.

“The teachers and instructors who possessed knowledge of the Law will shine like heaven, and those who exhorted the lower classes to observe God’s ceremonies will shine like the stars for everlasting eternities.”

He also introduces the history of the Maccabees, in which it is said that many Jews under Mattathias and Judas Maccabaeus fled to the wilderness, hid in caves and clefts of rocks, and came forth after the victory (1 Maccabees 2). These things, he says, were predicted μεταφορικῶς—figuratively—as though concerning the resurrection of the dead.

But it is more truly understood that at the time of Antichrist there will be a tribulation such as has never been since the nations began to exist. Let us suppose that Lysias, who was defeated, had conquered, and that the Jews, who were victorious, had been completely crushed: was there ever a tribulation like that when Jerusalem was captured by the Babylonians, the Temple overthrown, and the entire people led into captivity?

When Antichrist has therefore been crushed and destroyed by the Savior’s spirit, the people who are found written in God’s book will be saved. According to the diversity of their merits, some will rise to everlasting life and others to everlasting reproach. The teachers will have the likeness of heaven, and those who instructed others will be compared to the brightness of the stars.

For it is not enough to know wisdom unless one also instructs others. Silent discourse of teaching, when it does not edify another, cannot receive the reward of labor.

Theodotion and the Vulgate edition expressed this passage as follows: “And those who understand will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and many of the righteous like the stars forever and beyond.”

Some people commonly ask whether an instructed saint and a simple saint receive the same reward and have one dwelling in heaven. Hence, according to Theodotion, it is now said that the instructed possess the likeness of heaven, while the righteous without instruction are compared to the brightness of the stars. The difference between learned holiness and holy simplicity is therefore as great as the distance between heaven and the stars.

### Verse 4

“But you, Daniel, close up the words and seal the book until the appointed time. Many will pass through, and knowledge will be multiplied.”

He who had revealed multifaceted truth to Daniel, signifying that the things he had spoken were hidden, commanded him to wrap up the words and seal the book, so that many might read it, seek the truth of the history, and, because of the greatness of its obscurity, form different opinions.

When he says, “They will pass through”—that is, “many will run through it”—he signifies the reading of many people. For we commonly say, “I ran through a book,” or, “I passed through a history.”

Isaiah likewise speaks about the obscurity of his own volume: “And the words of this book will be like the words of a sealed volume. If they give it to a man who does not know letters, saying to him, ‘Read,’ he will answer, ‘I do not know letters.’ But if they give it to a man who knows letters and say, ‘Read the book,’ he will answer, ‘I cannot read, for it is sealed’” (Isaiah 29:11).

In the Apocalypse of John also, the book appears sealed with seven seals, inside and out. When no one could open its seals, John said: “I was weeping greatly.” And a voice came to me, saying: “Do not weep. Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, to open the book and loose its seals” (Revelation 5:4).

Only he can open that book who knows the mysteries of the Scriptures, understands riddles and dark sayings because of the greatness of their mysteries, interprets parables, and transfers the letter that kills into the Spirit that gives life.

### Verses 5–6

“And I, Daniel, looked, and behold, two others were standing: one here upon the bank of the river, and the other there upon the opposite bank of the river. And I said to the man clothed in linen, who stood above the waters of the river: ‘How long until the end of these wonders?’”

Daniel saw two angels standing on opposite banks of the Babylonian river. Since the river is mentioned here without a name, I think, on the basis of the preceding Vision, that it is the Tigris, which in Hebrew is called *Eddecel* (עדקל).

Yet he does not question those who stood upon the two banks, but the one whom he had seen at the beginning, who was clothed in linen or byssus garments, which in Hebrew is called *baddim* (בדים). This same Angel stood above the waters of the Babylonian river, treading upon them with his foot.

From this we understand that the two earlier angels whom he saw standing upon the bank, and whom he does not question or consider worthy of questioning, are the angels of the Persians and the Greeks. But this one is the most merciful angel, who had presented Daniel’s prayers before God.

[Alternative: “who had presented” may be read “who presented.”]

The angel of the Persians had resisted him for twenty-one days. Daniel asked him about the wonders spoken of in the present Vision, namely, at what time they would be fulfilled. Porphyry interprets this, as usual, of Antiochus, while we interpret it of Antichrist.

### Verse 7

“And I heard the man clothed in linen, who stood above the waters of the river. When he had raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven, he swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, times, and half a time.”

Porphyry interprets “a time, times, and half a time” as three and a half years, and we do not deny this according to the idiom of the sacred Scriptures.

For above we also read that seven times passed over Nebuchadnezzar—that is, seven years of his becoming beastlike. In the Vision of the four beasts it is written of the lion, the bear, the leopard, and the other beast whose name is not given, which signifies the kingdom of the Romans. Then, concerning Antichrist, it says that he will humble kings, speak words against the Most High, crush the saints of the Most High, and think that he can change times and laws.

“And they will be given into his hand for a time, times, and half a time. Then judgment will sit, so that his power may be taken away, crushed, and destroyed to the end.”

And it plainly speaks of the coming of Christ and the saints: “But the kingdom, power, and greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings will serve and obey him.”

If Porphyry refers the preceding statements, which are clearly written about Antichrist, to Antiochus and to the three and a half years during which he says the Temple was desolate, then he must also prove this following statement concerning Antiochus—or, as he thinks, concerning the Jewish people: “His kingdom is everlasting, and all kings will serve and obey him.” It is plainly evident that this cannot stand.

We read in the books of the Maccabees, and Josephus agrees with the same view (Josephus, book XI, chapter 10), that the Temple was polluted in Jerusalem for three years, and that an idol of Jupiter stood in it under Antiochus Epiphanes, in the 145th year of the Macedonian kingdom, from the ninth month, Casleu, of that same year until the ninth month of the 148th year—which makes three years.

[Note: Victorius has “and in that place an idol,” and so forth.]

From this it is clear that the three and a half years are spoken of the time of Antichrist, who for three and a half years—that is, 1,290 days—will persecute the saints, and afterward will fall upon the illustrious and holy mountain.

Therefore, from the time when the *endeulectismos* (ἐνδελεχισμός), which we have translated “the continual sacrifice,” is removed—when Antichrist, having gained possession of the world [alternative: “the city”], forbids the worship of God—until his death, three and a half years, that is, 1,290 days, will be completed.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “when he has forbidden the worship of God, until his killing.”]

### Verse 12

“Blessed is he who waits and reaches the 1,335 days.”

“Blessed,” he says, “is he who, after Antichrist has been killed, waits forty-five days beyond the appointed number; during those days the Lord and Savior will come in his majesty.”

Why there should be a silence of forty-five days after the killing of Antichrist belongs to divine knowledge—unless perhaps we say that the delay of the kingdom of the saints is a testing of patience.

Porphyry explains this passage as meaning that the forty-five days beyond the 1,290 signify the period of victory over the commanders of Antiochus, when Judas Maccabaeus fought bravely, cleansed the Temple, destroyed the idol, and offered sacrifices in God’s Temple.

He would be right to say this if the book of the Maccabees stated that the Temple had been polluted for three and a half years, and not for three years (1 Maccabees 4).

### Verse 13

“But you, Daniel, go to the appointed end, and rest, and you will stand in your lot at the end of the days.”

[Note: Victorius removes the name “Daniel,” since it is not present in the sacred text.]

Theodotion translated it as follows: “But you, go and rest, and you will rise in your appointed order at the consummation of the days.”

By this expression it is shown that the whole prophecy is close to the resurrection of all the dead, when the prophet also will rise.

[Alternative: “close to the resurrection” may be read “close to resurrection.”]

Porphyry is therefore wasting his effort when he wishes to refer everything said in the type of Antiochus about Antichrist to Antiochus himself. As I have said, Eusebius of Caesarea, Apollinarius of Laodicea, and, in part, the most eloquent martyr Methodius have answered his slander more fully. Anyone who wishes to know these things can find them in their books.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript does not contain the following final sentence or the verse from chapter XIII that follows it. In the Vatican manuscript, their place is occupied by this red heading: “Here begins the history of Susanna according to blessed Jerome.”]

Thus far we have read Daniel in the Hebrew volume. The rest, which follows to the end of the book, has been translated from Theodotion’s edition.

## Chapter XIII—Verses 1–2

“There was a man living in Babylon, and his name was Joacim. He took a wife named Susanna, the daughter of Helcias, exceedingly beautiful and fearing the Lord.”

Having explained, as I was able, what is contained in the book of Daniel according to the Hebrew, I shall briefly set down what Origen said in the tenth book of his *Stromata* about the stories of Susanna and Bel.

These are his words, which you will note in their proper places.

[Note: Our manuscripts do not know these words, which you will note in their proper places. Moreover, Jerome does not seem to have rendered Origen in Latin with exactly the same words.]

### Verse 3

“And her parents were righteous [the Vulgate: ‘Since they were righteous, they instructed’], and they taught their daughter according to the Law of Moses.”

This testimony should be used to exhort parents to teach according to the Law of God and to impart the divine word not only to their sons but also to their daughters.

### Verse 4

“And …”

[Note: In place of this verse, which our manuscripts supply, another was proposed: “Now Joacim was exceedingly rich, and he had an orchard adjoining his house.” This has no connection with the exposition that follows. The same words are found almost exactly in Origen’s letter to Africanus concerning the history of Susanna, section 7:

Μέμνημαι μέν τοί γε φιλομαθεῖ Ἑβραίῳ, καὶ χρηματίζοντι παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς Σοφοῦ υἱῷ . . . . συμμίξας περὶ πλειόνων· ἀφ᾽ οὗ ὡς μὴ ἀθετουμένης τῆς περὶ Σωσάννης ἱστορίας, ἐμάνθανον καὶ τὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ὀνόματα, ὡς παρὰ τῷ Ἰερεμίᾳ κείμενα τοῦτον ἔχοντα τὸν τρόπον· ποιήσαι σε Κύριος etc.

“I certainly remember that, after conversing with a learned Hebrew, who among them was known as the son of a wise man … and discussing several matters with him, I learned from him, as though the history of Susanna were not rejected, also the names of the elders, as they are found in Jeremiah, and are given in this form: ‘May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom, etc.’”]

“Two elders from the people had been appointed judges in that year.”

[The Vulgate omits “from the people.”]

The Hebrew said that these were Ahab and Zedekiah [alternative: Alchiah and Zedekiah], concerning whom Jeremiah writes: “May the Lord make you like Ahab and Zedekiah, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire because of the wickedness they had committed in Israel and because they had committed adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens” (Jeremiah 29).

### Verse 5

“Concerning them the Lord said: ‘Iniquity has gone forth from Babylon, from the elder judges who seemed to govern the people.’ These men frequented Joacim’s house,” and so forth.

He rightly does not say of the sinful elders, “who governed the people,” but “who seemed to govern.” Those who preside well over a people govern the people. But those who possess only the name of judges and preside unjustly over the people seem to govern rather than actually governing.

### Verse 8

“And they burned with desire for her, overturned their understanding, and turned their eyes away so that they would not see heaven or remember the judgments of the righteous.”

[Note: Here again, as often elsewhere, we supply from the manuscripts the proposed scriptural text needed for the exposition that follows.]

What the Greeks call πάθος, we more correctly translate as *perturbatio*, “disturbance,” rather than “passion.” This disturbance and lust therefore titillated—or rather struck—the hearts of the elders.

But in order that it might lay a foundation in their minds and that they might think of fulfilling their desires, they themselves overturned their understanding. Once it had been subverted, their eyes were turned downward, so that they did not see heavenly things or remember the judgments of the righteous—whether of God, of morality, or of nature, which has been implanted in everyone for the good.

“And behold, Susanna was walking about, as was her custom.”

It has already been said that Susanna would walk about early in the morning. It is not inappropriate, for the benefit of those who seek examples in the sacred Scriptures for everything we do, to adopt this passage about walking, since it is proper to walk in order to invigorate the body.

“This passage,” he says, “I have now taken from the Septuagint edition.” By saying this, Origen shows that he did not discuss the rest according to the Septuagint translators.

### Verse 19

“Then Susanna groaned and said: ‘I am in distress on every side.’”

He who has reached the summit of perfect virtue never says that he is in danger if he has not escaped the hands of adulterers who say: “Consent to us and lie with us. Otherwise, if you refuse, we will testify against you that a young man was with you, and that for this reason you dismissed the girls from you.”

It belongs to human weakness to fear death when it is inflicted for righteousness—unless perhaps we interpret “distress” as referring not to the impending death but to the disgrace and dishonor with which she was to be covered by those accusing her and saying: “A young man was with her, and for that reason she dismissed the girls.”

### Verse 22

“For if I do this, it is death for me; but if I do not …”

She calls sin death. Just as adultery is death for the person who commits adultery, so every sin that leads to death should be called death. We are believed to die as often as we sin unto death. Conversely, we rise and are made alive as often as we perform works worthy of life.

### Verse 23

“But it is better for me to fall into your hands without doing the deed than to sin in the sight of the Lord.”

In Greek the text does not have αἱρετώτερον, meaning “better,” but αἱρετόν, which we can interpret as “good.” Therefore she elegantly did not say: “It is better for me to fall into the hands of wicked elders than to sin in the sight of the Lord,” lest, by comparison with sin, she seem to call something that was not good “better.”

“But,” she says, “it is good for me not to do evil and to fall into your hands, so that I may not sin in the sight of the Lord.” 733

Thus the passage should not be read comparatively: “It is better for me to fall into your hands than to sin in the sight of the Lord.” Rather, it should be read absolutely: “It is good for me not to do evil and to fall into your hands, so that I may not sin in the sight of the Lord.”

### Verse 24

“And Susanna cried out with a loud voice,” and so forth.

Her loud voice did not arise from the striking of bronze or from the shouting of her throat, but from the greatness of her chastity, by which she cried out to the Lord. Hence, in the cry of the elders, holy Scripture did not add “a loud voice.” For it continues: “And the elders cried out against her.”

### Verse 42

“But Susanna cried out with a loud voice,” and so forth.

The feeling of her heart, the pure confession of her mind, and the goodness of her conscience had made her voice clearer. Her cry was therefore loud before God, although it was not heard by human beings.

### Verse 44

“And as she was being led to death, the Lord stirred up the Holy Spirit of a young boy.”

This expression shows that the Holy Spirit did not enter Daniel, but that the Spirit who was in him and had been resting because of the weakness of his age, unable to display its works through him, was stirred up by the Lord when an opportunity arose on behalf of the holy woman.

### Verse 46

“And he cried out with a loud voice: ‘I am pure from the blood of this woman,’” and so forth.

After the Holy Spirit had been stirred up in him and had suggested what the boy ought to say, his voice was loud. It should also be noted whenever, in the sacred Scriptures, the voice of a sinner is called loud.

[Alternative: “is said to be called loud.”]

### Verses 58–59

“Tell me, under what tree did you see them speaking with each other?”

He answered, “Under the mastic tree.” Daniel said to him: “You have rightly lied against your own head; for behold, the Angel of God, having received the sentence from him, will cut you in two.”

A little later the other elder said, “Under the holm-oak.” Daniel said to him: “You too have rightly lied against your own head. Behold, the Angel of God remains, holding a sword with which to cut you in two.”

Because the Hebrews reject the history of Susanna, saying that it is not contained in Daniel’s book, we must carefully investigate the names σχίνου and πρίνου, which the Latins translate as *ilex* and *lentiscus*—holm-oak and mastic tree—and determine whether they exist among the Hebrews and what etymology they possess, so that in their language “splitting” may be derived from σχίνῳ and “cutting,” or “sawing,” from πρίνῳ.

If this is not found, we too will necessarily be compelled to agree with those who wish this passage to be a Greek verbal division only, possessing a Greek etymology but no Hebrew one. If someone can show that the etymology of the cutting and slicing of these two trees stands in Hebrew, then we shall also be able to accept this Scripture.

[Note: In the letter to Africanus cited above, sections 6 and 7, he draws a much more correct conclusion. There he responds to the objection in such a way that, although the Hebrew text that had been destroyed could not display the etymology of the two trees from “cutting” and “slicing,” he nevertheless wishes no doubt to remain that such an etymology could have existed, since other examples of this kind of play on words occur in the Scriptures. It is useful to transcribe at least part of his response from the Latin translation:

“Let us examine what you allege in the argument itself. Let us begin with what might deter us from accepting the history, namely, the derivation by which πρῖνος has πρῖσις from πρίνου and σχῖνος has σχίσις from σχίνου. You have pronounced upon this as though you had established how these forms agree in Greek but differ entirely in Hebrew. I, however, still remain uncertain.

“For I too, being concerned about this passage and myself hesitating in doubt, consulted not a few Hebrews, asking how πρῖνος is named among them and how they say πρίζειν, and likewise by what word they render σχῖνος, the tree, and how they say σχίζειν. They said that they did not know the Greek words πρίνου and σχίνου and asked that the trees themselves be shown to them, so that they might know what names to give them.

“I did not hesitate to bring the actual pieces of wood before them—for truth is my friend. One of them said that he could not affirm how things that had nowhere been named in the Scriptures were called in Hebrew; but, he added, it was readily possible for anyone in doubt to use the Syriac word in place of the Hebrew. He also said that even the wisest sometimes inquire after words.

“‘Therefore,’ he said, ‘if somewhere you can show that the *prinus* or *schinus* is named in a Scripture, there certainly the word we seek and the derivation arising from those names will be found. But if they have nowhere been named, that too remains unknown to us.’

“Since these things were said by Hebrews with whom I was accustomed to associate, who nevertheless did not acknowledge the history, I hesitate to declare whether a similar derivation of the names is preserved among the Hebrews. But perhaps you know why you do not affirm that it exists.”]

(Vers. 60.) But the whole assembly [Vulgate: congregation] cried out with a loud voice, and blessed God, who saves those hoping in him, etc. If the whole assembly killed them, the opinion we mentioned above seems to be refuted [Note: Jerome presses this difficulty much more strongly on the basis of the Hebrews’ understanding in his Commentaries on Jeremiah, chapter 29, at the Prophet’s words, “May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab,” etc. “The Hebrews say,” he writes, “that these were the elders who committed folly in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens. To one of them Daniel says: ‘You have grown old in evil days’; and to the other: ‘Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah, appearance has deceived you, and desire has perverted your heart’ . . . . But what is said here at present—‘whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire’—seems to contradict Daniel’s account. For Daniel asserts that they were stoned by the people in accordance with his judgment; whereas here it is written that the king of Babylon roasted them in the fire. Hence, by many, indeed almost all, of the Hebrews, this story itself is not accepted or read in their synagogues. ‘For how,’ they ask, ‘could it have happened that captive rulers and prophets had the power to stone their elders?’ They maintain instead that the following is true: what Jeremiah writes, namely, that the elders were indeed convicted by Daniel, but that the sentence against them was pronounced by the king of Babylon, who, as victor and lord, exercised authority over the captives.”], about which we spoke above, according to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 29), namely, that they were the elders Ahab and Zedekiah—unless perhaps we interpret the statement “They killed them” as meaning that they handed them over to the king of Babylon to be killed. 735 Just as we also say that the Jews killed the Savior—not because they themselves struck him, but because they handed him over to be killed and cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him” (John 19:15).

(Vers. 63.) But Helcias and his wife praised God on behalf of their daughter Susanna, etc. Worthily [variant: Worthily, plural], as holy people, they praise God—not because Susanna was delivered from the hands of the elders, for this is not sufficiently praiseworthy, nor would it have been a great danger if she had not been delivered, but because no shameful matter was found in her.

(Cap. XIV.—Vers. 1.) And immediately, when he had opened the doors, the king, looking upon the table [Vulgate: the king, having looked at the doorway, saw the table], cried out with a loud voice: “Great are you, Bel, and there is no deceit in you.” What Scripture now says, “He cried out with a loud voice,” since it is spoken of an idolater who does not know God, seems to overturn our interpretation, in which we recently maintained that a loud voice is found only among holy people. The one who says that this story is not found in the Book of Daniel among the Hebrews will easily resolve the matter. But if anyone should be able to establish that it belongs to the canon [Note: Recall the Letter to Africanus, nos. 4 and 5], then we must inquire what answer we ought to give him.

[Col. 0583]

TRANSLATION OF THE HOMILIES OF ORIGEN ON JEREMIAH AND EZEKIEL BY SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, TO THE PRESBYTER VINCENTIUS. (C)

Prologue.

[Col. 0583B] 741–742. It is indeed a great undertaking, my friend, that you ask of me: to make Origen Latin, and to present to Roman ears a man who, in the judgment of Didymus the Seer, is another teacher of the Churches after the Apostle [variant: after the apostles]. But, as you yourself know, I am tormented by pain in my eyes, which I contracted through excessive and impatient reading, and by the lack of copyists, since poverty has taken away even this assistance. Therefore I cannot fulfill what you rightly desire, and desire so ardently. Accordingly, after the fourteen homilies on Jeremiah, which I translated long ago in confused order, I dictated these fourteen on Ezekiel at intervals, taking great care that the idiom of the aforesaid man should be preserved in translation with the simplicity of expression that alone benefits the Churches, while rejecting all the splendor of rhetorical art. For we wish to praise the substance, not the words. I add this brief reminder so that you may know that Origen’s works on the whole of Scripture are of three kinds. His first work consists of Excerpts, which in Greek are called σχόλια (*scholia*), in which he briefly and summarily touched upon those matters that seemed obscure to him or to contain some difficulty. [Col. 0586A] The second is the homiletic genre, to which the present translation also belongs. The third he entitled Τόμοι (*Tomoi*), which we may call volumes; in this work he spread all the sails of his intellect before the blowing winds and, leaving the shore, fled into the open sea. I know that you want me to translate every kind of discourse; I have explained beforehand why I cannot do so. This, however, I promise: if, at your prayer, Jesus restores my health, I shall translate many works—not all, for it would be rash to say that—but very many, according to the arrangement I have often made with you: I shall provide the voice, and you the copyist.

HERE BEGIN THE FOURTEEN HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH.

FIRST HOMILY. “The word of God that came to Jeremiah the son of Chelcias,” etc. (Jeremiah 1:1).

[Col. 0585B]

743 God is ready to bestow benefits; but in punishing those who deserve punishment, he delays. Although he can punish in silence and without announcing what is to come those whom he has once judged worthy of punishment, he never does so. Even if he has condemned them, he tells them what he has always resolved to say, so that those who were condemned on account of their offense may be freed from condemnation through repentance [Note: Huetius has it: “he foretells to him what he has resolved,” whereas the Greek is προλέγει αὐτῷ τὸ προκείμενον, “he declares beforehand to him what has been determined.”]. Although we can gather many examples of this from Scripture, the examples that arise in the present passage are sufficient for us to proceed to the contemplation of what has been read.

The Ninevites were sinners condemned by God: “Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4). God did not wish to punish the condemned in silence; rather, giving them an opportunity for repentance and conversion, he sent to the Gentiles a prophet of the Hebrews, so that, when he said, “Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown,” those who had been condemned might not perish but, by practicing repentance, might obtain the mercy of God. The people of Sodom and Gomorrah had already been destined for destruction, 744 as is clear from the words of God spoken to Abraham. Nevertheless, the angels did what was proper to them, wishing to save those who had judged themselves unworthy of salvation, when they said to Lot: “Do you have anyone here—a son-in-law, or sons, or daughters?” (Genesis 19:12). For they did not fail to know that these people would not follow Lot; rather, they displayed both their own kindness toward human beings and the love of the one who had sent them. We find something similar written in Jeremiah also: the time of his prophecy has been recorded, when he began to prophesy and for how long.

Therefore, whoever reads the Scriptures, if he attends carefully to his reading and investigates the intention of what has been written, can say from the heading of the history when Jeremiah began and when he completed his prophecy. What, then, does the historical chronology have to do with me? By reading I learned that he began to prophesy in the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah, until the thirteenth year of his reign; thereafter he prophesied in the days of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the completion of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, son of Josiah, king of Judah. And by reading I learned that for three kings his prophecy was despised, until the captivity of Jerusalem [Col. 0586C] in the fifth month. What, then, are we taught by this if we attend to our reading? God had condemned Jerusalem because of the sins it had committed, and this was the final sentence: that it should be handed over to captivity [Note: The royal manuscripts in Huetius read “that they should be left,” that is, “handed over.”] Nevertheless, since he loves human beings and does not wish anyone to perish, before the time of devastation arrived he sent this prophet also, so that through his words the people might be converted to repentance [Note: One manuscript, R., in the same editor’s collection, reads “might be converted.”]. He sent him again under the second king after the first, and he also sent him under the third.

What more need be said? Captivity was already impending, and God was still exhorting them, granting—as I may put it—even a single day’s opportunity for repentance. Hence it is written that Jeremiah prophesied until the captivity of Jerusalem and until the fifth month. The fetters of the enemy had already bound their hands, and nevertheless God was, in a manner, saying this: “Behold, you have become captives; repent, even though late; pray to me, and I will spare you. I can rescue from captivity those whom I handed over.” Thus we have something necessary from this heading, which contains the times of the prophecy: in accordance with his clemency, God always exhorts human beings to salvation, so that, when sin ceases, captivity too may come to rest.

We can understand these things about ourselves also: if we sin, we too shall become captives. For to hand the sinner over to Satan (1 Corinthians 5:5) differs in no way from the fact that the Jews were handed over to Nebuchadnezzar. And just as God gave them over to the adversary because of their repeated impieties, so we, because of the sins we have committed, are handed over to a spiritual Nebuchadnezzar. “And those whom I have handed over,” he says, “to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:20)—the Apostle is speaking about other sinners. Consider how great an evil it is to sin, so that we may be handed over to Satan, who takes captive the minds of those whom God abandons [Col. 0587B] [Note: Again the same manuscript reads “that I may be handed over”; another reading has “that he may hand over.”].

God does not abandon those whom he forsakes without cause or judgment [Note: Manuscript R. reads “of God who abandons”; another reading has “God abandoning.”]. For when he has sent rain upon a vineyard, and the vineyard has produced thorns instead of grapes, what will he do except command the clouds not to rain upon it? Therefore it is close at hand, because of our sins of which we are conscious, that we too should be taken captive. For we shall be handed over, if we do not repent, to Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians, who will torment us visibly.

With these events already near, the words of the prophets, the words of the Law, the words of the Apostles, and also the words of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ urge us to repentance and summon us to salvation. But if we listen, we believe him who said: “And I too will repent of all the evils that I have spoken of doing to them” (Jeremiah 18:8).

These matters, then, belong to the Prologue. After the prologue it is written as follows: “The word of the Lord came to him”—it is certain that this means Jeremiah. What does the word of the Lord say to him? It says something preeminent among all that was spoken to the other prophets. For we never find this said to any other prophet. Abraham was called a prophet in the statement: “He is a prophet, and he will pray for you” (Genesis 20:7); yet God did not say to him: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5). Abraham was sanctified only later, at the end of his life, when he went out from his land, from his kindred, and from his father’s house (Genesis 12:1). Isaac was born from the promise, and yet we do not find this word spoken to him either. And why must I go through each one individually? Jeremiah received a gift preeminent among all others, when the Lord said: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you.”

Nor are we unaware that there are some who refer these words—as though they were greater than Jeremiah—to our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ. We should know that many of these statements can apply to the Savior, and we too shall insert them. But a few of the things spoken to Jeremiah constrain the interpretation, as though they could not, in the opinion of many, be referred to the Lord. What, then, are the statements that can apply to the Lord?

“To all those to whom I send you, you shall go; and everything that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their presence, because I am with you to deliver you,” says the Lord (Jeremiah 1:7–8). These words do not yet seem improperly to be referred to the Savior. But the words that follow make the interpretation difficult when applied to Jeremiah: “The Lord stretched out his hand to me, and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to destroy” (Jeremiah 1:9–10) [Note: Rabanus inserts something resembling Jerome’s words: “Unless perhaps we understand it in the manner mentioned above, namely, that he received in his hand a cup full of unmixed wine and was ordered to offer it to all the nations round about; but these words do not occur in the Greek.”]. For what nations did Jeremiah uproot? What kingdoms did he overthrow, so that it could rightly be said to him: “Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to dig up”? What power did he have to destroy, so that he should hear: “and to destroy”? And whom did he build up, so that “to build” should subsequently be added? Jeremiah said: “I have not profited, nor has anyone profited me”; so how was building and planting given to him?

As we have said, when these statements are referred to the Savior, they do not constrain the interpreter. For in these matters Jeremiah is a figure of the Savior. But the statements that follow also bring difficulty of interpretation to a learned man: how can they apply to the Lord? “And I said: Who are you, O ruler, Lord? Behold, I do not know how to speak” (Jeremiah 1:6) [Note: The same editor retained “who are you”; but he advised restoring “who you are,” as Rabanus also does.]. How can this be applied to him who is Wisdom, who is the power of God, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9): “I do not know how to speak”? There is also the statement: “For I am young.” He is interrupted [Note: Previously the reading was “for he is forbidden,” as though the passage continued “for he…” We read “to him” with the royal manuscripts and Rabanus. Rabanus also has “who” for “as though,” and the Greek has ὡς λέγοντα, “as though he were saying.”], as though he had not given a proper answer. For if the Lord says to him, “Do not say, ‘I am young,’” it is evident that he was reproved as one who had spoken improperly.

These are the statements that do not seem to apply to the Savior. The preceding ones, however, are easily referred to him. To say that some things should be interpreted of Jeremiah and other things of the Savior is not altogether wrong. But whoever strives to know the Scriptures well will insist forcefully at this point, seeing that under a single textual discourse the interpretation is divided and it is said: “These things, because they are lesser, do not apply to the Savior but to Jeremiah; those things, because they are greater, do not apply to Jeremiah but to Christ.”

For this reason we shall attempt to refer everything to Jeremiah—that is, even those matters which, because they are greater, seem to exceed his condition. Whoever receives words from God, receiving the grace of heavenly speech, receives them for this reason: so that he may uproot and overthrow kingdoms and nations. But when nations and kingdoms are mentioned, I do not want anyone who receives divine words to understand kingdoms and nations in a bodily sense. Rather, considering the souls of human beings ruled by sin [Note: Rabanus reads “governed” instead of “ruled”; the Greek has βασιλευομένας, “ruled”], in accordance with what is written in the Apostle, “Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6:12), and also seeing many forms of sin, let him allegorize kingdoms and nations according to the various sins that have taken possession of human souls [Note: Huetius rightly advises that the Greek should read κατὰ τὰ φαῦλα, “according to evil things,” as Jerome had read it, rather than καὶ τὰ φαῦλα, “and evil things,” which is a scribal error]. These, then, are what will be uprooted and dug up by the words of God, which were given either to Jeremiah or to the other saints.

Thus it will come about that the first statements, which did not seem to apply to the Savior, will be assigned to Jeremiah; and the second statements will be assigned to Jeremiah by the one who knows how to give a figurative interpretation to the words that were spoken [Note: Manuscript R. in Huetius reads: “who knows how to give a figurative interpretation to the words that were spoken.”].

Someone among the hearers will say to me: “Explain another passage as well, and establish that everything written about the Savior was written as though it concerned him.” Do not be anxious about the secondary matters. For it is evident that the Savior uprooted the kingdoms of the devil and overthrew the nations, destroying the pagan way of life.

What makes the interpretation difficult here is this: how can the Savior say, “I do not know how to speak, because I am young,” and so forth? In this interpretation we are constrained. We know Jesus Christ to be God; we are seeking words that can be explained in accordance with the dignity of his person. Therefore it is necessary for us to call upon the holy Scriptures as witnesses. Our understandings and expositions have no credibility without these witnesses; indeed, the statement “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII, 16) applies more to the proof of an interpretation than to any arbitrary number of people. Thus, to confirm the meaning of my interpretation, I take two witnesses from the New and Old Testaments, or three witnesses from the Gospel, the Prophet, and the Apostle. In this way every word will stand.

How, then, shall we connect these statements with the Savior? Let the Old Testament testify for me: “Before the child knows good or evil” (Isa. VII, 16), and so forth. Let Isaiah also testify: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb, and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14). There too it is added: “Before the child knows.” If testimony must also be taken from the Gospel, Jesus, not yet a man but still an infant, because he had emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, “was advancing” (Luke II, 32). No one who is perfect advances; rather, the one who needs advancement does so. Therefore he advanced in age, advanced in wisdom, advanced in grace, both with God and with human beings.

For if, in descending to us, he had emptied himself, and by emptying himself had again taken up what he had previously emptied himself of, what is improper about his having advanced in wisdom, advanced in age, advanced in grace with God and with human beings—and about these statements being true of him: “Before the child knows good or evil” (Isa. VII, 16), together with the other words we have introduced concerning him?

But someone will say to me: “Even if the statement that he did not know can be understood of the Savior, as well as similar statements that are greater, and even if you accept him as a child, do you not offend by thinking such things about the Only-begotten and Firstborn of all creation—about him who, before he was conceived, was announced by Gabriel, who said: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you’ (Luke I, 37)? And do you dare to say that he did not know how to speak?”

Therefore I shall see whether I can bring forward here something worthy of the Savior: something by which, if he did not know certain things, he might be greater than if he had known them. Let us use his own words to show how there are certain things he does not know. He answered those who said to him: “Did we not eat in your name, and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works?”—“Depart from me; I do not know you” (Matt. VII, 22).

Do you suppose that his saying “I do not know you” proves his power to be lesser, or rather greater and more wonderful, because he does not know the wicked and those destined for destruction? For he knows what is pre-eminent and better; the Lord knows those who are his; and if anyone does not know, he is not known.

Thus, as is clear, the sinner is not known by God.

Someone among the hearers will say to me: “You have shown that God does not know sinners; you have shown that he does not know those who practice iniquity, for they are not worthy of being known by him. How, then, will you prove that what he said—‘I do not know how to speak’—is something great and glorious?”

Speaking is a human activity, and we always make use of speech—for example, in the language of the Hebrews, or of the Greeks, or in the speech of other peoples. Therefore, if you ascend to the Savior and know that he was in the beginning the Word with God, observe that he does not know how to speak, since what is called speaking is human, if he does not know it because he knows greater things.

If you compare the languages of angels with human languages, and know that he is greater than the angels—as the Apostle testified concerning him in the Epistle he wrote to the Hebrews (Hebr. I, 4–5), understanding that he was greater even than the languages of the angels when he was only the Word of God with the Father—then he speaks and, in a certain sense, receives instruction in things not great but lower and lesser.

It is like me: I learn to stammer, forcing myself to do so when I speak with little children. I do not know, so to speak, how to speak like a child, or how, already an old man, to converse with children in broken words. In the same way, the Savior, while dwelling in the magnificence of God’s glory and in the Father, does not speak humanly; he does not know how to address those below.

But when he came in a human body, he said at the beginning: “I do not know how to speak, because I am young” (Col. I, 15). He is young because of the dispensation; old according to the fact that he is the Firstborn of all creation; young because he came at the consummation of the ages and at the final period of this life.

He therefore says: “I do not know how to speak.” For I know how to speak certain greater things; I know certain things greater than this mortal speech. Do you want me to speak to earthly beings? I have not yet assumed human frailty. I have your speech; I am your Word. I know how to speak to you; I do not know how to speak to human beings. I am young.

Do not say: “I am young,” because “you shall go to all those to whom I send you.” Then he moved his hand to touch his mouth, so that he might give him words with which to uproot kingdoms.

The Savior did not need words in order to receive them, since, when he was in the Father, there was nothing in heaven worthy of being overthrown. But now he receives small things, temporarily setting aside greater ones.

Thus this is confirmed, just as elsewhere he said gloriously: “I do not know you, because you are workers of iniquity” (Luke XIII, 27). Now too he has gloriously received words, although he is God, and in accordance with the magnificence of his glory has said: “I do not know how to speak”—that is, “I do not know human speech.”

Whether the statement “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. I, 5) is spoken of Jeremiah or of the Savior, read Genesis and observe what is written there concerning the creation of the world. You will find that divine Scripture, very careful in its wording, did not say, “Before I made you in the womb, I knew you.” For when the creation is according to the image, God says: “Let us make a human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26), and he does not say, “Let us form” one.

But when he took clay from the earth, it is not written, “He made the human being,” but “He formed the human being” (Gen. II, 7), and he placed in paradise the human being whom he had formed, to work it and guard it.

If you can understand the difference between making and forming, then observe that, whether he is speaking to Jeremiah or to the Savior, he did not say: “Before I made you in the womb.” For what is made is not made in the womb; rather, what is created from the dust of the earth is formed in the womb. “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.”

If God knows everyone, why does he say to Jeremiah, as though he were distinguished from the others, “I knew you”? Or does God know only those who are worthy of his knowledge, and recognize those who are his, while he does not know the unworthy—not the Father nor the Son, who says: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII, 23)?

We human beings, when endowed with some distinction, judge some people worthy of our acquaintance and others unworthy. Those whom we do not wish to know or hear, we do not know. What, then, do you suppose about the God of the universe? He wishes to know Pharaoh; he wishes to know the Egyptians, but they are unworthy of his knowledge. They themselves make it so that they are not known. He knows Moses, he knows the prophets, and anyone who resembles them.

You must labor greatly in order to begin to be known by the Lord. He knew Jeremiah before he formed him in the womb; another of the prophets he began to know at the age of thirty, another at forty.

The sayings concerning the Savior are ineffable and need not be pursued in detail. But concerning Jeremiah we need the ears of those who possess knowledge of the Scriptures, so that we may understand how he says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from your mother’s womb, I sanctified you.” God sanctifies some people for himself. He does not wait for this one to be born in order to sanctify him; rather, he sanctifies him before he comes forth from the womb.

If you refer the passage to the Savior, as I said, it is not wrong to say that he was sanctified before he was born. Understand it of the Lord in this way: he was sanctified before he came forth from the womb, although he had always been holy from eternity; but this one was sanctified before he came forth from the womb.

“I have appointed you as a prophet to the nations.”

If you are asking about Jeremiah, consider the subsequent passage, when he is commanded to prophesy to all nations. For this is the form of the writing: “Jeremiah prophesied concerning all the nations—Elam, Damascus, Moab”—and you will see that he prophesied to all nations, in accordance with the statement: “I have appointed you as a prophet to the nations,” if indeed you wish to understand these words as spoken of Jeremiah.

But if you transfer the interpretation to God, then he truly preached to all nations. For just as he is, among many other things, the prince of the prophets, so also he is a prophet. He is the high priest; he is the Savior; he is the physician; likewise, he is also a prophet.

Moses, announcing him, called him not merely a prophet but a prophet wondrous among all others, saying: “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall hear him. And it shall be that whoever does not hear that prophet shall perish from his people” (Deut. XVIII, 15).

He is the prophet appointed among the nations. He received from God grace poured upon his lips, so that, not only when he was bodily present but also now, when he is present in power and in spirit, he might prophesy to all nations and by his prophecy draw people from the whole world toward salvation.

And he said: “Who is the ruler, Lord? Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am young” (Jer. I, 6).

And the Lord said to him: “Do not say, ‘I am young,’ because you shall go to all those to whom I send you” (Jer. I, 6).

We have often said that someone may be a child according to the inner human being, even if he is advanced in bodily age; conversely, someone may be a child according to the outward human being and yet be inwardly a mature man.

Such was Jeremiah. He already possessed grace granted to him by God, although he was still a child in bodily age. Therefore the Lord said to him: “Do not say, ‘I am young.’”

He shows that this is a sign that Jeremiah is not young but a mature man when he says: “For you shall go to all those to whom I send you; and according to everything I command you, you shall speak. Do not fear their presence.”

The word of God knows that those who serve as ambassadors of the Word encounter danger from those who disdain to hear. Those who are reproved hate the reprovers; those who are convicted pursue those who convict them.

The prophets always suffer every kind of evil: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house” (Mark VI, 4). We recently made mention of this as well.

Thus God, who sends the prophet, knows what dangers he will have to endure. Therefore he encourages him, saying: “Do not fear their presence, because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord” (Jer. I, 8).

Everything Jeremiah suffered is written down. He was thrown into a pit of mud; he remained there, eating the bread of the day and drinking only water; and many other things that he endured are contained in his book.

“Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” the Lord says to the Jews (Acts VII, 52).

Those who desire to live religiously in Christ must necessarily suffer persecution in every form from opposing powers, through the instruments by which those powers act. Therefore nothing new or strange should appear to those who are afflicted by tribulations. Let them do everything that has been commanded, but let them pray only that Christ may be the cause of their persecution—not injustice, not sins, not greed.

If anyone is harassed on account of righteousness, let him hear: “Blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you and say every evil thing against you for my sake.” Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you” (Matt. V, 11).

“Because I am with you to deliver you,” says the Lord. And the Lord extended his hand toward me, touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me (Jer. I, 8–9).

Observe the differences between Jeremiah and Isaiah. Isaiah says: “I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips; yet I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes” (Isa. VI, 5).

Because he confessed that his deeds were not unclean but only his words—for up to that point he had committed sins—the Lord did not extend his hand, nor did one of the Seraphim touch his lips with his hand. Rather, touching them only with tongs, he said: “Behold, I have taken away your iniquities.”

But because Jeremiah had been sanctified in the womb, neither tongs nor a coal kindled from the altar was sent to him. He had nothing worthy of fire; instead, the hand of the Lord itself touched him. Therefore he says: “The Lord extended his hand toward me and touched my mouth.”

And the Lord said to me: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot” (Jer. I, 9–10).

He is so blessed that he uproots the many kingdoms which the devil showed Christ: the kingdoms of demons and the kingdoms of sin. For this he needs the words given to him by God.

For it is written: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot” (Jer. I, 10).

Just as there are many kingdoms, so likewise there are many nations. A kingdom cannot be called a kingdom unless it contains nations beneath it. For example, let it be said that fornication reigns in a sinful person; necessarily, the kingdom of fornication has its own nations.

That general sin of greed and deceit, from which scarcely anyone is free, has its own kingdom, and under one kingdom it possesses many nations—namely, the many forms of greed. Therefore the words of God are necessary, so that kingdoms of this kind, together with their nations, may be uprooted.

The Savior shows this in the Gospel, saying: “Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matt. XV, 13).

There are certain things planted inwardly in your souls—or, according to another reading, “in our souls”—which the heavenly Father did not plant. All the worst thoughts—murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies—are plantings which the heavenly Father did not plant.

If you wish to know whose planting such thoughts are, hear that “the enemy did this,” the one who sowed weeds among the wheat (Matt. XIII, 25).

Behold, God is at work, and the devil is also at work, each possessing his own seeds. If we give the devil room, the enemy will sow the planting which the heavenly Father did not plant, and which must therefore be uprooted. But if, having driven back the devil, we give room to God, God, rejoicing over the ruling faculty of our heart, will scatter his seed.

No one should suppose that Jeremiah received some gloomy command, because he was appointed to uproot kingdoms and nations. This is an indication of God’s goodness: to uproot vices by his words, to destroy kingdoms hostile to the heavenly kingdom, and to overthrow the nations that wage war together with their own people—to uproot and subvert them.

There is an edifice of the devil, and there is an edifice of God. Whatever is built upon sand belongs to the devil, for it is not founded upon anything stable and solid. But whatever is built upon rock belongs to God. Hence it is said to those who belong to him: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (I Cor. III, 9).

“Over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, to overthrow, and to destroy.” If something is uprooted and the uprooting itself does not perish, what has been torn out still remains. If a house is thrown down and its stones remain intact in the ruin, the house has been destroyed but not lost.

Therefore God’s goodness is needed, so that the uprooting itself and the entire overthrow may perish.

Read more carefully how uprooted things are destroyed: “He will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire”; and: “Bind the bundles of weeds and hand them over to the fire” (Matt. III, 12; XIII, 30). In this way what has been uprooted perishes.

If you wish to know how the destruction is reduced to nothing, how the worst material of a building is crushed into dust, consider the house which is ordered to be destroyed on account of leprosy (Lev. XIV). When it has become dust, it is thrown outside the city, so that not even a stone from it remains, according to what is written: “Likewise I will wipe them away like the mud of the streets” (Ps. XVII, 43).

For evil must perish completely. Something has been overthrown; the stones themselves that have been destroyed must also be crushed, so that they may not be used for some other building which the devil might construct.

Something has been uprooted; the adversary finds even among the things that have been uprooted some seed which he may sow again. Therefore the Lord commands, saying: “Gather them and burn them with fire”—that is, so that the devil’s uprooting itself and the overthrow itself may also be consumed.

But the divine word does not stop at this point, merely uprooting, destroying, and annihilating. Suppose that every evil in me has been uprooted, and that the worst things have been destroyed and annihilated: what benefit is that to me if better things are not planted and built within me in place of what has been uprooted and torn out?

For this reason the words of God first do what is necessary: they uproot, destroy, and annihilate; afterward they build and plant.

We have always observed in the holy Scriptures that things which appear grievous are named first, and then those which are more joyful are mentioned second: “I kill, and I make alive” (Deut. XXXII, 39).

He did not say first, “I will make alive,” and afterward, “I will kill.”

For it is impossible that one whom God has once made alive should be killed either by God himself or by another. Rather: “I kill, and I make alive. Whom shall I kill? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor; and I will make alive, so that Paul may become the apostle of Christ Jesus.”

If the wretched heretics understood this, they would never bring these statements against us, repeatedly saying: “Do you see the God of the Law and the Prophets? How savage and inhuman he is! How he says, ‘I kill, and I make alive’?”

They do not notice that the Scriptures announce the raising of the dead, nor do they consider that the resurrection has already begun in individuals: “We were buried with Christ through baptism, and we shall rise with him” (Rom. VI, 4; Col. II, 12).

God always begins with things that are grievous but necessary, as in: “I kill, and I make alive”; “I strike, and I heal.”

“For whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6); and afterward he heals. He himself causes grief and again restores joy.

Likewise, in the present passage the Lord says: “Today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, to tear down, to destroy, to build, and to plant.”

Nevertheless, the first thing is that evils be taken away from us. God cannot build in the place of an evil building: “What partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” (II Cor. VI, 14).

Evil must be uprooted from its deepest foundations; the worst building must also be entirely removed from our souls—or, according to another reading, from our minds—so that afterward the words of God may build and plant.

We can also understand the written words in another way: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.” And he explains what the words are to do: “To uproot, to tear down, and to destroy.”

“Over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, to overthrow, and to destroy.” But these are not those kingdoms of flesh and of this age: they are worthy of destruction and uprooting by words.

Consider what has been uprooted and overturned. Do you suppose that, in what we are now saying, there is no power which the Lord grants, according to what is written: “The Lord will give words to those who evangelize with great power” (Ps. LXVII, 12)?

Is there no power uprooting and tearing down any unbelief, any falsehood, any wickedness, any lust, any discord?

Just as an idol has been built in the heart, once it has been removed let the temple of God be built in its place; let his glory be found in it; let it become not a barren place or a place rising up merely in appearance, but a planting of paradise, where the temple of God may be in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## Alternative Readings

- **[Col. 0590C]** An alternative reads *quomodo* (“how”) in place of *quod* (“that”).
- **[Col. 0591A]** An alternative reads *sed* (“but”) for *si* (“if”); another reads *Dei Verbum* (“the Word of God”) for *Deus Verbum* (“God the Word”).
- **[Col. 0592A–B]** Alternatives read *animis nostris* (“our minds”) for *animabus vestris* (“your souls”); *praecipuum* for *praecipuo* in the description of Jeremiah as distinguished; and *judicavimus* (“we judged”) for *judicamus* (“we judge”).
- **[Col. 0592D]** An alternative reads *superscriptio est quae* (“this is the heading which”) for *scriptio est, quod* (“this is the form of the writing: that”).
- **[Col. 0595A–B]** Alternatives read *animis nostris* (“our minds”) for *animabus vestris* (“your souls”); *quoniam* (“because”) for *quam* (“which”); and *sub principali* (“under the ruling faculty”) for *super principale* (“over the ruling faculty”).
- **[Col. 0596A–B]** Alternatives read *pessimae* (“of the worst [building]”) for *pessima* (“the worst”), and *aliam* (“another”) for *aliquam* (“some”).

## Editorial and Variorum Notes

- **[Col. 0589D]** The same manuscripts read: “as though they were written concerning God.”
- **[Col. 0589D]** In Rabanus: “the discourse of the interpreter is constrained,” more closely corresponding to the Greek *ho logos stenochōreitai* (“the discourse is cramped/constrained”).
- **[Col. 0589D]** Rabanus reads: “even if you can understand that passage of the Savior”; shortly afterward, “the lesser things.”
- **[Col. 0590D]** The Greek reads: *egnō gar ta diapheronta kai kreittona* (“for he knew the things that differ and are better”). Here Jerome slipped: “He knows distinctions from them; he knows better things; the Lord knows those who are his.” Translate instead: “For he knows what is pre-eminent and better.” —Huetius.
- **[Col. 0590D]** For *loqui* (“to speak”), which has been restored from Rabanus in accordance with the Greek *to lalein*, the text had *quod* (“that”), and frequently *semper* (“always”) for it. The following clause too—“or in the speech of other peoples”—is farther from the Greek than Rabanus’s reading: “Therefore, whatever speech you ascend by,” etc.
- **[Col. 0591D]** Rabanus: “he is greater even than the angels.”
- **[Col. 0591D]** Rabanus: “better things.” Jerome’s text had long been badly disordered: “I know certain things scarcely expressible to earthly beings in this mortal speech,” etc.; Huetius restored: “I know certain things greater than this mortal speech.”
- **[Col. 0591D]** “To all to whom I send you,” etc., has been restored in place of “to everything, to whatever I send you,” etc. Rabanus, the manuscript cited by Huetius, the Greek text (*pros pantas, hous ean exaposteilō se*), and the Latin text repeatedly cited above support it.
- **[Col. 0592D]** The cited manuscript and Rabanus read “setting aside”; another reading is “differing.”
- **[Col. 0592D]** “Today” was missing; Rabanus and the Greek *sēmeron* supply it.
- **[Col. 0592D]** The words “he needs” are unknown to Rabanus and are absent from the Greek text; nor, as Huetius supposes, was there reason for Jerome to supply them from Greek.
- **[Col. 0592D]** In Rabanus: “needing,” corresponding to Greek *deomenoi*.
- **[Col. 0592D]** The same source reads: “Understand this of the Lord not only before he came forth from the womb.”
- **[Col. 0592D]** Earlier the text read, “If you ask about Jeremiah.” Rabanus corrects it.
- **[Col. 0592D]** The royal manuscript, according to Huetius: “For, just as he is the prince of prophets, so he is also a prophet.” Rabanus: “many other similar things” for “many.”
- **[Col. 0593D]** We have deleted *dixit* (“said”) here, and supplied “God” after “our”; we have supplied “and it shall be, whoever,” in accordance with the Greek text and Rabanus’s reading.
- **[Col. 0593D]** The Greek should apparently be restored: *kai eipa, Ho ōn* (“And I said, ‘Who are you?’”). The Hebrew has: “And I said, Ah, ah, Lord God,” etc.
- **[Col. 0593D]** The royal manuscripts cited by Huetius read “he shows: For.”
- **[Col. 0593D]** The Greek has only *kai prōēn emnēmoneuomen* (“and we mentioned recently”); Jerome read *hou kai prōēn emnēmoneuomen* (“of which we also mentioned recently”), which is correct. One might reasonably think that Origen’s *Commentary on Matthew* is meant, for in book 40 of that work the passage at Matthew XIII, 57 is extensively explained. Although Origen began composing his volumes on Matthew when over sixty, he had not previously delivered those homilies to the people; they belong to the class of homilies which, when he delivered them extemporaneously after his sixtieth year, he allowed stenographers to commit to writing, though he had always forbidden this before. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 36. The word *prōēn* also supports this conjecture: it means “recently,” not “not long ago,” as Corderius translated it. Jerome’s “recently” is thus correct, since he wrote on Matthew and allowed his spoken homilies to be recorded at about the same time. —Huetius.
- **[Col. 0594D]** The royal manuscript reads “by these tribulations”; another, “who by these,” etc.
- **[Col. 0594D]** Greek: *to de hen tōn seraphim* (“but one of the seraphim”). Jerome read *mēde hen* (“nor one”), which is correct and is plainly supported by Isaiah VI, 6.
- **[Col. 0594D]** The word “today” was missing; Rabanus and the Greek *sēmeron* supply it.
- **[Col. 0594D]** Rabanus does not recognize the words “he needs”; they are absent from the Greek text, and Huetius’s supposition that Jerome supplied them from Greek is unwarranted.
- **[Col. 0595C]** Rabanus reads: “Let no one suppose that God gave Jeremiah a gloomy command, when he was appointed,” etc.; the Greek text opposes this reading.
- **[Col. 0595C–D]** The earlier text was corrupt: “for it is founded on nothing, abortively it is not made firm.” The royal manuscripts cited by Huetius read “it is made firm by this one,” or “by this which is made firm.” Rabanus rightly indicated that the reading should be restored: “for it is not founded upon anything stable and solid.” The Greek likewise has: *ep’ oudeni gar estērikai hedraiō kai bebaiō kai hēnōmenō* (“for it has not been founded on anything firm, secure, and united”).
- **[Col. 0595D]** The Greek inserts: “Therefore the words of God,” which Jerome either omitted or, as Huetius thinks, the passage of time erased from his translation. We supplied “and kingdoms” from Rabanus and Greek *kai basileias*.
- **[Col. 0595D]** Read with Rabanus “perishes,” corresponding to Greek *apolētai*; the royal manuscript has “perishes” for the formerly prevailing “is scattered.”
- **[Col. 0595D]** The text wrongly had “streets” for “chaff.”
- **[Col. 0595D]** Rabanus reads “perish,” and then “how the overthrow too is reduced,” etc.; both are more correct in relation to the Greek.
- **[Col. 0595D]** “Likewise” has been supplied from Rabanus and Greek *homoiōs*.
- **[Col. 0596C–D]** Jerome’s statement, “it is impossible for one whom God has once made alive to be killed either by God himself or by another,” is interpreted as follows: one made by God a participant in eternal life is sustained by such firm divine aids that he cannot lose it. What follows, where these statements are referred to the resurrection of the dead, confirms this interpretation. Origen explains how the blessed are kept from falling in the future life in book V on Romans: “The Apostle briefly teaches us what will preserve freedom of choice in the ages to come, so that it does not again fall into sin, when he says: ‘Love never falls.’ Love is therefore called greater than faith and hope because it alone will remain, and through it sin will no longer be possible. For if the soul rises to such perfection as to love God with its whole heart, whole soul, and all its strength, and its neighbor as itself, where will there be a place for sin?” And shortly afterward: “Therefore love, which alone is greatest of all, will deservedly preserve every creature from falling, when God is all in all.” —Huetius.
- **[Col. 0596D–0597D]** The entire passage, “Whom shall I kill? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor; and I will make alive,” was missing, with serious loss of sense; we first supplied it from Rabanus. As the preceding note shows, the Greek has the same words: *tina apoktenō? Paulon ton prodotēn, Paulon ton diōktēn, kai zēn poiēsō* (“Whom shall I kill? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor; and I will make alive”). Since Huetius did not find them in Jerome’s Latin manuscripts, he said that Jerome had wandered too far from Origen’s exemplar.
- **[Col. 0597D–0598C]** This attacks Basilidians, Valentinians, Cerdonians, Marcionites, and others of that stamp. Origen, on Matthew XIX: “You will ask how even the things which are not understood by those who, so far as lies in them, slander and accuse the God of the Law nevertheless breathe his goodness—things which it would perhaps not be easy to say even about a human being. For I am persuaded that ‘I will kill’ breathes God’s goodness no less than ‘and I will make alive’; likewise ‘I will strike’ no less than ‘and I will heal.’” In Homily XVII on Luke: “For the Valentinians say: ‘Look at what the God of the Law and Prophets is like: “I will kill and make alive; I will strike and I will heal; and none shall deliver from my hands.”’ They hear ‘I will kill’ and do not hear ‘I will make alive’; they hear ‘I will strike’ and refuse to hear ‘and I will heal.’ On such grounds they slander the Creator.” —Huetius.
- **[Col. 0598D]** The word “God” was wrongly absent; we supplied it from Rabanus and the Greek: *hoi logoi tou Theou oikodomēthōsin* (“that the words of God may be built up”).
- **[Col. 0598D]** The royal manuscripts cited by Huetius read: “worthy of being destroyed, worthy of being uprooted.”

## SECOND HOMILY

Concerning what is written: “Flee from the midst of Babylon” (Jer. LI, 6).

759 Just as our body exists in some place on earth, so also the soul, according to its condition, is in some figurative place on earth. [Note: This term is also used shortly afterward. Therefore, what we said in the preface to the fourth volume—that it is nowhere found in Jerome’s writings in the interpreter of the homilies on Isaiah—we now wish to retract on the basis of one or two examples.] What I am saying will become clearer in this way. Our body is either in Egypt, or in Babylon, or in Palestine, or in Syria, or certainly somewhere else. Similarly, the soul too is in some place bearing the same name as one of these lands [Note: More elegantly in Rabanus: “bearing the same name as the land.”]: one in Babylon, another in Egypt, another in the region of the Ammonites; and thus, according to the judgment of the Scriptures, it is distinguished separately [Alternative: consecrated], in accordance with the quality of its life, by the diversity of places. [Note: Previously: “the diversities of places are distinguished.” The reading we restore from Rabanus is better: “it is distinguished by diversity”; that is, the reference is plainly to the soul.]

It is in Babylon when it is confused, when it is troubled, when, with peace abandoned, it endures [Alternative: “they endure”] the wars of the passions, when the tumult of wickedness roars around it. Then, as we have said, it is in Babylon. To this soul the prophetic word is addressed, saying: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own soul again.” For as long as someone is in Babylon, he cannot be saved. Even if he remembers Jerusalem there [Note: In Rabanus: “Even if he remembers where Jerusalem was.”], he groans and says: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI). And because it is impossible for those situated in Babylon to sing to God with instruments—the instruments of God’s hymns are useless there—therefore the Prophet says: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, O Zion; on the willows in its midst we hung our instruments.”

Our instruments remain hung upon the willows of the rivers of Babylon for as long as we are in Babylon. But if we come to Jerusalem, the place of vision and peace, then the instruments that previously hung idle are taken up in our hands; then we continually play the lyre; and there is no time when we do not praise God with the instruments we hold in our hands. [Note: Likewise: “then we sing psalms continually, then we play the lyre without interruption.”]

Thus, as we had begun to say, the soul is always in some figurative place on earth. And just as sinners are in Babylon, so conversely the righteous are in Judaea. Nevertheless, according to the quality of life and faith, even in Judaea they are separated from one another by various places. One may be in Dan, which is at the extremity of Judaea; another in places somewhat higher and better than Dan; another in the central territories of Judaea; another around Jerusalem. The most blessed of all is the one who dwells in the middle of the city of Jerusalem.

But whoever is a sinner, weighed down by exceedingly great crimes, is in Babylon. One who is somewhat less wicked and has not yet risen to the highest summit of sins dwells in Egypt and in the regions of Egypt. And just as not all who are in Judaea possess equal places—for one is in Jerusalem, another in Dan, another in Naphtali, another in the territory of Gad—so all who are in Egypt do not inhabit equal regions of Egypt. One lives in Taphnis, another in Memphis, another in Syene, another in Bubastis.

The prophet Ezekiel bears witness in a voice full of mysteries to these places, explaining also the names of the regions of Egypt. If any reader is spiritual, discerning all things and himself judged by no one, he will allegorize not only the greater regions—Judaea, Egypt, and Babylon—but also the smaller parts of the earth. Just as, when reading of Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and the other cities in Judaea, so in Egypt, when he reads of Diospolis, Bubastis, Taphnis, Memphis, and Syene, he will form figures according to the meaning of the things.

761 Who is wise and understands these things? Or who is understanding and knows them? Who, even if established in the more superficial sense, will be able to know the intention that the Holy Spirit has invested in the letter?

But our present subject is different: what is commanded by the word of God to those who are in Babylon? “Flee from the midst of Babylon.” Do not flee gradually or step by step, but with speed and haste; for this is what fleeing means: “Flee from the midst of Babylon.”

All of you who have a confused soul because of the various passions of vices, this word is directed to you. And I too am commanded to do the same, if I am still aged in confusion [Note: Rabanus: “I am in confusion of mind”], and therefore am in Babylon.

What, then, does God command? He did not say, “Come out from the midst of Babylon,” for that could be done gradually; rather: “Flee from the midst of Babylon.” I seek the reason for the expression “from the midst.” It can happen that someone is in Babylon but, because he dwells at its outermost boundaries, seems in a certain sense to be outside Babylon. But it is one thing to stand in the middle of Babylon, so that the distance is equal on every side, and to dwell at its navel, as it were in the middle of an animal’s heart.

For just as the heart is the middle of an animal, and in the Gospel according to Luke “the heart of the earth” is called the middle of the earth (Luke XVII), so it seems to me that Tyre is said in Ezekiel to be placed “in the heart of the sea” (Ezek. XXVI). And now sinners must flee from the midst of Babylon—that is, from its heart.

“Flee, therefore, from the midst of Babylon,” so that, abandoning the middle of Babylon, you may begin to be at its boundaries, not in its center. [Note: Rabanus: “so that, abandoning the middle of Babylon,” and so forth—that is, so that you may be there.]

If this seems obscure to anyone, it will become clearer in this way: the person who is deeply submerged in vices is an inhabitant of the middle. But the one who gradually abandons evil and turns his nature toward better things—who has begun not so much to possess virtues as to desire them—although he has fled from the midst of Babylon, has not yet departed from Babylon.
