According to interpretations of this kind, it is fitting to believe that the sacred Scriptures do not contain even one letter devoid of the wisdom of God. For he who commands me, a human being, saying, “You shall not appear before my presence empty-handed” (Deut. XVI; Exod. XXIII), himself does this much more thoroughly, so that nothing may be spoken by him empty of meaning.

The prophets received from his fullness the things they sang, which had been taken from that fullness; and therefore the sacred volumes breathe the fullness of the Spirit. [Note: Likewise: “therefore the sacred books always breathe the spirit of fullness.”] There is nothing—whether in the Prophets, the Law, the Gospel, or the Apostle—that does not descend from the fullness of the divine majesty.

Therefore the words of fullness in the Holy Scriptures breathe even today. [Note: Likewise: “Therefore the words found in the Holy Scriptures breathe fullness even today.”] They breathe for those who have eyes for seeing heavenly things, ears for hearing divine things, and nostrils for sensing what belongs to fullness.

I have said this because the text does not simply say, “Flee from Babylon,” but adds what is necessary: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own soul again.” First one must flee from the midst of Babylon; then, after fleeing, each must save his own soul again.

Nor did it say, “Save,” but “Save again.” The addition of the syllable signifies a sacrament. Those who once tasted salvation and afterward fell away from it because of sins came into Babylon. For this reason each person must save his soul again, so that he may begin to recover what he lost, according to the Apostle Peter, who says: “We shall receive as the end of our faith the salvation of our souls,” concerning which salvation the prophets searched and investigated, prophesying on account of our grace (1 Pet. I). [Note: The reading “saying” was faulty. We have restored this to the end, and so forth.]

Nevertheless, it is in our power to flee from Babylon, and it depends on us whether we wish to raise up again what has fallen.

The third commandment is: “And do not be cast into its iniquity.” When someone has fled from the injustice of Babylon but has not repented, it follows that he is cast away. [Note: Rabanus: “When someone has been in Babylonian injustice,” and so forth.]

Observe how Scripture, although translated from the Hebrew language into Greek, has nevertheless expressed its distinctions of words clearly, insofar as the language can bear them. It says elsewhere: “I have chosen to be rejected in the house of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII), and it does not say “cast away.” Here, however, it does not say, “Lest you be rejected into its injustice,” but, “Lest you be cast into its injustice.”

For it is one thing to be cast away and another to be rejected. What is treated with contempt and neglect is not cast away but rejected. What is outside salvation and alien to blessedness is cast away. Divine Scripture makes this clear elsewhere, saying: “The leaders of my people shall be cast out from the house of their delights because of their most evil desires. Their lots will not profit them” (Mic. II, 9). [Note: Restored from the same source and the Greek text: ἐκ τῶν οἰκιῶν τρυφῆς αὐτῶν, “from the houses of their delights.” Previously it was corruptly read: “from the dwelling-place of their possessions.”]

You too can gather together wherever you find in the Scriptures the words “casting away” and “rejection,” so that by comparing the words you may pronounce your judgment with greater confidence. For although the dispensation of providence did not take particular care, in translating into Greek, to follow the eloquence praised in the Greek language, it did take care to present what is significant and to explain their difference clearly to those who examine the Scriptures most diligently.

“Lest you be cast into the iniquity of Babylon, for the time of her vengeance is from the Lord.” With remarkable meaning, he says that punishments are inflicted for the sake of vengeance upon the one who suffers them. When someone is not avenged and is left unpunished, I remember having often said what is written in the Twelve Prophets: “I will not visit upon your daughters when they commit fornication, nor upon your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery” [Alternative: “when they commit adultery”] (Hos. IV).

God therefore does not, as some think, punish sinners in anger. But, if it is permissible to speak in this way, it is a great anger not to undergo torments from God. For the one who is punished, even if he is corrected by what is called the anger of God, is punished in order to be amended.

“Lord,” David says, “do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Ps. IX). But even if you rebuke, Jeremiah said, rebuke us in judgment and not in fury.

You will also find, from God’s promise, that correction is given to some. Therefore, when punishment is promised to the sinful children of Christ, mercy is not denied [Alternative: “so that mercy may not be denied”], as it is written: “If his children forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their crimes with a rod and their iniquities with scourges, but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

Considering this, see how one who continues to commit crimes up to the present time without being punished is not yet worthy of punishment. For God’s visitation is demonstrated through the torments by which he visits; but as for the sinner who is corrected, I do not know what may be accruing to him in place of punishment.

This has been said because of the statement, “For the time of her vengeance is from the Lord.”

It follows: “He himself will repay her with repayment.” God will not repay Babylon through ministers, but he himself will repay her what she deserves.

I wish to say something about the addition of the pronoun in the phrase “he himself,” for it says: “He himself will repay her with repayment.” God himself will not repay all people what they deserve. There are some to whom he restores through others, whether by punishing or by healing through pain, as is contained in the Psalms: “He sent upon them the anger of his indignation, fury, anger, and distress, a sending through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII).

To these he did not himself repay, but used evil angels as ministers for their repayment. Perhaps to others he repays not through evil beings but through good ones, as happens in those who are punished for crimes. If you examine the Scriptures, you will find many similar examples. [Note: Previously: “You will find many similar things of this kind throughout the Scriptures, if you examine them,” and so forth.]

Sometimes, however, after rejecting the service of ministers, God himself restores repayment, as now to Babylon. [Note: It previously read: “the office of ministers is rejected.”]

I fear introducing something obscure into an evident passage, something that seems to me to lie hidden if I remain silent. Nevertheless, it is at least worth touching briefly upon a few points.

When wounds are easy and treatment is straightforward, the physician sends his servant or his disciple to heal the sick person through him, for the wounds are not serious. Sometimes, too, the person being healed requires incision and iron; nevertheless, the physician himself does not go to him, but chooses one of his disciples who is able to treat him and uses him as a minister.

But when the wounds are incurable, when decay has consumed even the dead flesh, and the illness is so severe that it requires not servants or disciples—who have already approached him in the near possession of medical skill—but the hands of the master himself, then the great physician, girded about the loins, hastens to the cutting of the most dreadful wound. [Note: Rabanus: “the physician himself with his hands.”]

In the same way, then, when the sins are lesser, God himself does not repay sinners but uses other ministers. But when, because of his deserts, a person is seized by an immense illness—as Babylon now is, pierced by the grievous wounds of its own wickedness [Note: Previously it was corruptly read “confused”]—then God himself hastens to repayment.

If you seek similar examples, you will find some concerning Jerusalem as well, things that happened to it after the prophets because it plotted against Christ.

Thus ends the contents of the first chapter. Let us examine what follows:

“A golden cup is Babylon in the hand of God, making the whole earth drunk. The nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations were shaken, and suddenly Babylon fell and was crushed.”

Nebuchadnezzar, wishing to deceive human beings through Babylon’s treacherous cup, did not mix the drink he was preparing in an earthen vessel, nor in a somewhat better vessel of bronze or tin, nor in the silver vessel superior to these. Instead, choosing a golden vessel, he prepared the drink in it, so that anyone seeing the beauty of gold, delighting in the radiance of the shining metal and fixing his eyes entirely upon its appearance, would not consider what lay hidden within, and, taking the cup, would drink without knowing that it was Nebuchadnezzar’s cup.

[Note: The following period, badly corrupted in many places and defective in sense, has been restored in accordance with the Rabanian reading.] You will understand the golden cup named here if you observe what kind of arrangement of words, what beauty of eloquence, and what organization of ideas the deadly words of the worst doctrines possess. You will recognize how each of the poets who are thought among you to be most eloquent has mixed a golden cup and poured into it the poison of idolatry, the poison of shameful speech, the poison of doctrines that kill the human soul, and the poison of falsely named knowledge.

But my Jesus acted otherwise. Knowing the golden cup of the Devil, and taking care lest anyone who came to his faith should suppose that Christ too had a cup like that one and, because of the similarity of the material, fear the error, he took care that we should have this treasure in earthen vessels. [Note: In Rabanus the reading is “what kind he left,” but neither reading is altogether satisfactory.]

I have often seen a golden cup in beautiful verbal adornment, and, considering the poisons of its doctrines, I have detected the cup of Babylon.

“A golden cup is Babylon in the hand of God.” Babylon is not always a golden cup. But when the time of vengeance comes and it is placed in the hand of God, then it becomes the earth that was once touched in Jobath [Alternative: Job]. Nor is it continually held in the hand of God, but only at the time of vengeance, when the Lord begins to repay it what it deserves. Then, in his hand, this golden cup of Babylon will make the whole earth drunk. [Note: More fully in Rabanus: “In his hand this golden cup of Babylon will become one that makes the whole earth drunk.”]

How it will make the whole earth drunk, you will easily understand if you consider that all human beings are drunk. We are drunk with anger; we are drunk with grief; we are drunk in mind; we lose our minds through love, lusts, and empty glory. How many cups this cup has mixed, how many intoxicating cups it has offered—what need is there to say?

“A golden cup is Babylon, making the whole earth drunk.” Observe that the whole earth is full of sins, and you will not ask how Babylon has made the whole earth drunk.

But if perhaps you see a righteous person who is not drunk from the cup of sins, do not suppose that Scripture has lied when it says, “making the whole earth drunk,” because this person is not made drunk by Babylon and nevertheless remains on earth. Hear [Note: The vulgate editions wrongly add “you.”] that the righteous person is not earth [Alternative: “is not in the earth”]:

“This golden cup makes the whole earth drunk.” But although the righteous person is above the earth, his manner of life is in heaven. Therefore it is no longer fitting to say to the righteous person, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). But [Note: Rabanus has the word “if.” There are many restorations of this kind which we have made without separately alerting the reader.], if it is necessary to speak boldly, God says to the righteous person who still remains above the earth: “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go.” For he bears the image of the heavenly one.

To conclude, the golden cup makes the whole earth drunk—that is, we are all made drunk by it for as long as we are earth.

“Of her wine the nations drank; therefore they were shaken.” Just as, among those who drink the ordinary liquid of wine, if they drink beyond their thirst and beyond the proper measure, we see the movement of a drunken body [Note: Previously read: “movement of body.”], unsteady feet, a head and temples weighed down, a slack mouth, a tongue expressing drunken speech, and words broken off by clinging lips, so one may see those who have drunk from Babylon’s golden cup: how they are moved, how unsteady their steps are, how, with their minds weakened and their thoughts [Alternative: efforts] wavering, they hold nothing firmly but are always driven about in uncertainty and confusion.

Therefore divine Scripture says of such people elsewhere: “For this reason they were shaken.”

Let us insert something concerning the mystery: what is said about the sinner Cain? “When he went out from the presence of God, he dwelt in the land of Naid, opposite Eden” (Gen. IV). In the Greek language, Naid is interpreted as “shaking.” Whoever abandons God, whoever deserts the understanding that comes from continually thinking about him, dwells even today in the land of Naid—that is, he remains in the tribulation of an evil heart and the agitation of the mind.

“The nations drank; therefore they were shaken, and suddenly Babylon fell and was crushed” (Luke XVII). When he says, “Suddenly Babylon fell,” it seems to me that he is prophesying the sudden coming of the end of the world. For just as in the days of the Flood they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, until the Flood came and swept them all away, and the inundation suddenly arrived, so also, in the days of Lot, and likewise at the end of the world, everything will not happen in stages but suddenly.

Consider this comparable to what is written in Joshua [Jesus son of Nun] (Josh. VII), when Jericho, a city collapsing at the mere sound of the trumpet, suddenly perished. In accordance with this likeness, Babylon too will fall at the consummation of the age, be suddenly crushed. These things have been said concerning the consummation.

But if you turn to the coming of my Lord Jesus Christ and observe his great work—how he overturned all the doctrines of the nations concerning idols, so that he might free believers from the yoke of error—you will understand that, at the time of his Passion, Babylon immediately fell and was crushed.

Let each one of us examine himself and observe whether Babylon has fallen in his own breast. If the city of confusion has not fallen in someone’s heart, Christ has not yet come to him. For when he comes, Babylon customarily falls.

Therefore, fleeing to the protection of prayers, ask that Jesus come into your hearts, crush Babylon, make all its wickedness fall, and rebuild in place of what has been overturned—and in place of Babylon, which had previously been constructed—the holy city of God, Jerusalem, in the very principal part of your heart [Alternative: our heart].

“Mourn over her, and take resin for her correction, if somehow she may be healed.” “Mourn,” he says, “over Babylon.” Furthermore, because every soul can receive salvation and not one is incurable before God, he gives counsel to those who can migrate to Jerusalem to have balm, as a testimony [Alternative: “and as testimony”], for making poultices, so that they may take medicines and, with all the zeal they possess, restore Babylon to health.

Let us try to do this ourselves also, beseeching God that we may learn to apply to it rational resin from ourselves [Alternative: “reasonable resin”], and, from rational resin, a poultice, oil, and bandages; and, applying them, let us bind Babylon’s wounds, imitating the Samaritan, so that the wretched city may be healed and, once cured, cease to be what it was.

This is what he means by: “Take the resin of her correction, if somehow she may be healed” [Alternative: “Take the resin of her correction…”].

Where are the heretics? Where are those who introduce certain natures and assert that there is a nature [Alternative: matter] destined for destruction, which cannot receive salvation at all? If any nature is destined to perish, what other nature will be like Babylon? Yet God does not despise even this one. For God commands the physicians to take resin for Babylon, if somehow it may be healed.

Some of those who had received the command took the resin for the correction [Alternative: corruption] of Babylon, to see whether it might be healed. They did what had been ordered and found [Alternative: received] resin for its correction [Alternative: corruption], hearing that it might be possible for Babylon to regain health.

But because they did not accomplish what they had hoped [Alternative: “did not find what they had hoped”], Babylon, persisting in its former [Alternative: intended] wickedness, refused to be healed. The good physicians therefore offer their defense and say: “We have healed Babylon, and she has not been healed. Let us abandon her.”

But consider, human being, lest God someday command the angels to prepare medicinal poultices for the illness of your soul, to see whether you might be healed from your sickness, and the angels reply: “We have healed Babylon”—pointing to a soul confused by its passions [Alternative: “your soul”]—“and she has not been healed.”

They do not accuse their medical skill or the power of the resin; rather, they accuse you, who refused to obey their commands, saying: “We have healed Babylon, and she has not been healed. Let us abandon her.”

The physicians, the angels of God, stood under the great physician, wishing to heal our weaknesses and free the soul from vices, but we ourselves drive them away by refusing to heed their counsels.

They see that they are wasting their labor as they speak to one another and say: “Let us abandon her, and let each of us go to his own land.” This means: “The medicine was entrusted to us by God so that we might heal the human soul. We applied assistance; we imposed medicine [Alternative: medicines]. She is exceedingly stubborn; she does not wish to observe what we say; our efforts are not followed by success. Let us abandon her, and let each of us go to his own land”—that is, to his domestic and personal place. [Note: Rabanus: “to his domestic and personal concern.” Take care.]

Beware, human being, lest the physician abandon you—whether he is an angel of God or any human being entrusted with the care of conveying the word as medicine for salvation [Alternative: “medicines for salvation”]. For if they abandon you and say, “Let each of us go to his own land, because his judgment has drawn near to heaven,” it is clear that their departure is your condemnation, since you are beyond remedy and unwilling to be healed.

When they have abandoned you, what else will happen to you except what usually happens to those whom physicians despair of—namely, that they follow the inclination of their disease and sink into worse things? [Note: Previously: “So similar things also happen in this life,” and so forth.]

Similar things occur in ordinary life among experienced physicians. One of them approaches a sick person as far as his skill permits, and his medical diligence does not cease. But if either the illness is so great that it resists treatment, or the patient himself, through impatience of pain, acts contrary to what he is ordered, the physician leaves such a person in despair [Alternative: “despairs of such a person”] and withdraws, lest the patient expire in his hands and the cause of his death be attributed to him.

Therefore, if we too are in danger of dying in the hands of the holy angels whom the Lord has sent to heal us, they abandon us in despair of our soul and say: “There is no time to apply a poultice, oil, or bandages, because his judgment has drawn near to heaven and has been raised up to the stars.”

The one whose sin is small does not raise his judgment to heaven and the stars [Alternative: “his judgment is not brought up”]. For it is small and lowly. But the one who grows in crime grows also in judgment, and as his vices increase, so does his punishment. Because he sins to such an extent [Alternative: “errs to such an extent”] that his judgment is raised to the heavenly places, and through his impiety, resisting God, he climbs to higher things, God brings forth his judgment for the humiliation of the judgment that had been hidden from the sinner. [Note: In Rabanus: “in the humiliation of his judgment, which was exalted by sin; and, bearing his judgment, he humbles sin indeed, but renders to the righteous what is worthy of his life,” and so forth.] In bringing forth his judgment, he humbles the sinner, but he repays the righteous with what is fitting for his life in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## THIRD HOMILY

On the passage that is written: “And the hammer of the whole earth has been crushed” (Jer. L, 23).

### 769

“How,” he says, “has the hammer of the whole earth been broken and crushed? How has Babylon become a desolation?” [Note: With Rabanus: “We must therefore inquire who spiritually is the hammer of the whole earth, and what its prophesied crushing is.”]

We must inquire who spiritually is the hammer of the whole earth, and what its crushing is—hence the prophet says that it was first broken before it was crushed—so that, when we have gathered together whatever has been written about the hammer in various places and have found its name, we may also investigate the significance of that name from the examples we shall present.

Once the house of God was being constructed, according to the Third Book of Kings (III Kings 6), and Solomon was building and erecting it. Everywhere, as though in praise of the house of God, it is said that neither hammer nor axe was heard in the house of God. Therefore, just as the hammer is not heard in the house of God, so—because the house of God is the Church—the hammer is not heard in the Church.

Who is this hammer that wishes, so far as it can, to prevent the stones of the temple’s construction from coming together, once crushed, with its foundations? [Note: We emend *now* from Rabanus; the earlier reading was “to me.”]

See now whether the Devil is not himself the hammer of the whole earth.

I shall speak confidently, however, of someone who does not greatly concern himself with the hammer of the whole earth. [Note: For *taken*, which Rabanus reads, an obvious copyist’s error in the old printed books had substituted three words: “to the Holy Spirit.”]

And since the example has been taken from a material hammer, I ask for a material stronger than the hammer, one that suffers nothing when struck by it. In seeking such a thing, I found [variant: “to be found”] it in what is written: “Behold, a man standing upon adamantine walls, and in his hand an adamant.” History relates of adamant that it is stronger than every hammer striking it, remaining unbroken and unconquerable [variant: “remaining steadfast”].

Although the Devil’s hammer stands above it, and the dragon—which is like an unconquerable anvil—is placed beneath it, nevertheless the adamant standing in the hand of God and in his sight suffers nothing. Thus two things are opposed to this adamant: the hammer and the unyielding anvil.

There is also a proverb already common among the nations, so that people say of those who are oppressed by anxieties and great evils: “They are between the hammer and the anvil.” You, however, apply this to the Devil and the dragon, who are always designated in Scripture by such names according to the variety of circumstances; and you say that the holy man, who is like an adamantine wall or is an adamant in the Lord’s hand, cares neither about the hammer nor about the anvil, but that the more he is struck, the more his strength shines forth.

They say that those who deal in precious stones, when they wish to test an adamant but do not know whether it is truly an adamant, do not know how to establish this until they have found a hammer and an anvil. They then become convinced that it is the genuine adamant if the stone remains unconquered and endures between the anvil and the hammer [delete the printed words “alter si”]; that is, when the hammer strikes from above and the anvil is placed beneath, its harder nature holds firm.

[Note: These words have been grievously disordered; the Greek text that might provide assistance is also lacking here. You may repair the passage as follows: “Such a man, before the trials, is unknown to those who test stones,” and so forth.]

Before the trials, such a man is unknown to those who test stones. But God alone knows with absolute certainty the nature of the adamantine stones, which is unknown to very many. I myself still do not know whether, when the hammer comes and strikes me, I shall be broken and crushed, thereby convicted that I am not an adamant, or whether I shall be shown to be a true adamant, if, when persecutions, dangers, and temptations assail me, I am crushed by the hammer’s blows as one who has been tested.

And you yourself run through the Scriptures and ask whether you can find any indication that God rightly promises that the hammer will strike what must be struck. For example—and examples are used to clarify more obscure matters—if there were no hammer, there would be no drawn-out trumpet, which according to the Law is to be sounded at the solemnities of God, and which kindles the minds of its hearers to battle with its blast. The hammer is necessary for the drawn-out trumpet to be made.

This hammer greatly assisted Paul’s drawn-out trumpet, bringing him forth and proving him through various trials, so that, unharmed, he might be fashioned and take on the form of a loud-sounding trumpet, giving a clear voice to his hearers, so that they might prepare themselves for the battle of the service.

And since the hammer is found to be an opposing power, while the dragon is a ductile or malleable anvil, I shall continue my discourse concerning the hammer, or whatever other material takes a name compounded in this fashion.

Cain begot sons, and from Cain came a worker in bronze and iron. Therefore, just as the Devil, who is the author of all temptations, is called the hammer, so the one who serves him is the hammerer, the son of Cain. Whenever you fall into temptation, know that the hammer is the Devil, and that the hammerer is the one through whom the Devil pursues you.

Thus, in the betrayal of the Savior, the Devil was the hammer and Judas the hammerer. There were also many hammerers at the time when the Lord suffered, crying out, “Take such a man from the earth; crucify him, crucify him.” Everything is full of hammerers. For all who, in their actions, look to the Devil and serve him in testing the righteous and convicting the unjust are hammerers.

Therefore, if yesterday you were a hammerer and held a hammer in your hand, learn now that hammerers come from Cain the fratricide, throw the hammer from your hand, and pass over to the spiritual generation of the hammerers, such as Enos and the others who are praised in the Scriptures.

Nevertheless, the end is breaking and crushing.

We must understand that the hammer now prophesied is the Devil: not the hammer of some part of the earth, but of the whole earth, because his wickedness is dispersed throughout the whole earth, and everywhere this hammer works evil.

It must also be said that the Devil is the hammer of the whole earth, not the hammer of heaven. For a hammer does not belong to a subtler substance, but to a coarser one. If you bear the image of the earthly, the hammer strikes you because you are earthly; if you sin and are earth, and will return to earth, you will experience the hammer of the whole earth working in you.

According to this interpretation, we must also observe that the hammer of the whole earth is the Devil because he exercises his power against everything earthly. Yet a lesser hammer may also be understood: not the hammer of the whole earth, but, so to speak, the hammer of this or that part of the earth.

If some one opposing power resists and struggles with me, unable—as the Devil is—to engage all human beings at once, then there is indeed a hammer in me, but not the hammer of the whole earth; rather, so to speak, it is the hammer only of my earth.

But once the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and crushed, what need is there to consider the hammer of particular parts of the earth? At the same time, I think it worthy of wonder that the hammer of the whole earth has been shattered. For what great thing would it be if the hammer of a part of the earth had been broken and crushed? But what is truly astonishing now is that the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and crushed.

After this I ask who it is that has broken and crushed the hammer of the whole earth. I shall say that Moses could not break and crush the hammer of the whole earth, nor Abraham before him, nor Joshua after him, nor any other of the prophets.

[Note: Rabanus restores: “such and so great a hammer of the whole earth”; the earlier printed text read “such and so great a man, and [the] hammer of the whole earth …”]

Who, then, could break and crush such a great hammer, the hammer of the whole earth? Who is this? Jesus Christ broke and crushed the hammer of the whole earth.

And, wondering at this in the Holy Spirit, the prophet says: “How has the hammer of the whole earth been broken and crushed?” First it was broken, and afterward it was crushed.

[Note: Formerly it was read: “First it was broken, and then it was crushed.”]

Since I have found that the Savior is the one who broke and crushed the hammer of the whole earth, I shall come to the Gospel, to see the first temptation, when the Devil said to him: “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me,” and what follows. I shall say that at that time Jesus did not crush [variant: “had not crushed”] the hammer of the whole earth, but only broke it.

But when the Devil withdrew [variant: “departed”] from him “until an appointed time,” and afterward came when that time had arrived, then the hammer of the whole earth was crushed—not merely broken, as it was at first.

And because the hammer of the whole earth, which had previously been broken, was crushed, it is therefore broken in each one of us when we are introduced into the Church and advance in [variant: “to”] faith. It is crushed and shattered, however, when we come to spiritual progress [Note: In Rabanus, “when we attain perfection.”].

If you doubt that the Devil is crushed when we advance, hear the Apostle blessing the righteous with a kind of benediction and saying: “But God will crush Satan under your feet swiftly” (Romans 16:20).

This hammer is an animate one. Perhaps it is now raging against us and seeking to crush us because we disclose these things about it—for it is not merely broken, but also crushed by us. It seeks, on the contrary, to break and crush us. Indeed, it has crushed many who do not attend to themselves and have not guarded their hearts with vigilance.

But we, trusting in God and believing in Christ of God, should not fear the Devil. The fear of God makes us not fear the Devil, and makes us suffer nothing from him, but also enables us to say—not merely in general, but about ourselves: “How has the hammer of the whole earth been broken and crushed?”

Once it has been broken and shattered, Babylon becomes a desolation. The city of confusion is not destroyed before the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and crushed.

Therefore the prophet used a marvelous and excellent order when he said: “How has the hammer of the whole earth been broken and crushed? How has Babylon become a desolation?” He first narrated what happened first, and then explained what happened second. We must observe this same principle throughout the individual statements of Scripture.

When, then, does Babylon become a desolation? When all confusions are destroyed from my soul, and death no longer confuses me through the death of a son or the death of a wife; when there is no one who provokes and incites me to sadness, anger, desire, or pleasure; when I remain unconfounded, adopting reason, which confirms and strengthens me—then what was said happens to me: “Babylon has become a desolation,” that is, every confusion.

These things—that is, the breaking and crushing of the hammer of the whole earth and the destruction of Babylon—take place when the nations are placed upon the hammer and upon Babylon.

For it is written: “Upon the nations they shall be placed upon you”—that is, those who are from the nations shall be placed upon you, O Babylon; they shall be placed upon you, O hammer, so that you may be broken and crushed.

When did these things happen? At the coming of my Lord Jesus Christ, when the Gospel was preached to all the nations. Then the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were placed upon Babylon and upon the hammer of the whole earth, and this that is written was fulfilled: “Upon the nations they shall be placed upon you, and you shall be captured, Babylon, and you shall not know.”

Would that Babylon were captured in each one of us as well.

From what precedes, the captivity of Babylon can be understood as occurring when, after being captured, it is dug up, overturned, and laid waste, so that no remnant of confusion remains in us.

“And you shall be captured, Babylon, and you shall not know; you have been found and seized, because you resisted the Lord.”

Did Babylon alone resist the Lord, and not rather all the nations, when, having abandoned the Creator, they worshiped idols and resisted the Lord? Or does he figuratively call every soul opposed to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace—Babylon?

Hence the saints were in Jerusalem, while sinners were in Babylon. Even when the inhabitants of Jerusalem sinned, they were sent into Babylon and thus converted to repentance while remaining in Babylon. The saints, however, returned to Jerusalem.

Babylon, therefore, is captured, and does not know it. Babylon is not subject to the Law; indeed, Babylon could not be found and seized if it had not been found. But it was seized when it was found, because it resisted the Lord.

### The beginning of another chapter

“The Lord has opened his treasury and brought forth the vessels of his wrath, because the work of the Lord of hosts is in the land of the Chaldeans. Since her times have come, open her storehouses; search her out like a cave and destroy her, so that none of her remnants may remain. Dry up all her fruits, and let her descend to slaughter. Woe to them, for their day has come, the time of their vengeance” (Jeremiah 50).

Wishing to understand what is meant by “The Lord has opened his treasury and brought forth the vessels of his wrath,” I ask about the vessels of God’s wrath elsewhere in Scripture. For a fuller comparison with this passage, I find the apostolic Scripture, and there I find the Apostle setting out for me what the vessels of God’s wrath are.

He says: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—those whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the nations” (Romans 9:22–24).

In general, the Apostle divided all human beings into two classes, saying that some are vessels of mercy and others vessels of wrath. For example, he called Pharaoh and the Egyptians vessels of wrath; then he called himself, who first obtained mercy, and those who in due course believed from the Jews and the nations, vessels of mercy.

There are therefore vessels of wrath in God’s treasury. For it is written: “The Lord has opened his treasury and brought forth the vessels of his wrath.”

What is this treasury of the Lord in which vessels of wrath are found? Perhaps someone will ask whether only vessels of wrath are in the Lord’s treasury, and whether God’s treasury—which is the treasury of all things—does not contain vessels of mercy; or whether something else must be understood by God’s treasury, from which his vessels of wrath are brought forth.

Confidently, then, I shall say that the Lord’s treasury is his Church, and that in this treasury—that is, in the Church—there are often people hiding who are vessels of wrath.

The time will come when the Lord opens the treasury of the Church. For now the Church is closed, and the vessels of wrath dwell together with the vessels of mercy; the chaff is with the grain, and the fish destined to perish and be thrown away are enclosed together with the good fish that had fallen into the nets.

When he opens it at the time of judgment and brings forth from it the vessels of his wrath, the one who is a vessel of mercy will perhaps say concerning the vessels of wrath that are going out: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us. But they went out so that it might be shown that they were not all of us” (1 John 2:19).

The discourse wishes to break out into another subject; but what we dare to say is of this kind: there are vessels of wrath in God’s treasury. Outside the treasury, however, sinful vessels are not vessels of wrath, but are lesser than vessels of wrath.

For they are servants who do not know the will of their lord and do not do his will. But whoever enters the Church is either a vessel of wrath or a vessel of mercy. Whoever is outside the Church is neither a vessel of mercy nor a vessel of wrath.

I seek another name for the one who dwells outside the Church. And just as I confidently decide that he is not a vessel of mercy, so, strengthened by the truth of reason, I openly advance the judgment that he cannot conversely be called a vessel of wrath either, but is a vessel reserved for something else.

Can I then prove from the Scriptures that he is neither a vessel of mercy nor a vessel of wrath, so that this second exposition may also contribute something useful to us in the present passage, and that the discourse may once again dare to break out into what it has been attempting for some time?

The Apostle says: “But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some indeed for honor, but others for dishonor” (2 Timothy 2:20). “If anyone therefore cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.”

Do you think that the great house exists in the present age, and that in it there are vessels for honor and others for dishonor? Or will vessels of gold and silver, which are for honor and are vessels of mercy, be found in that future house, while the rest—ordinary people who are outside the treasury—are neither vessels of wrath nor vessels of mercy? Could these, according to some profound dispensation of God, be vessels in the great house that have not been cleansed, but are earthen vessels for dishonor, nevertheless necessary to the house?

See whether I may also establish this very example from another testimony of Scripture. “Jeconiah,” it says, “is dishonored, like a vessel of which there is no use” (Jeremiah 22:28).

It does not say, “There is indeed a use for it, but its use is for dishonor”; rather, because he was from the house of God and sinned, he is altogether without use.

I have another Scripture in which it is said of another sinner: “He will be like a potsherd in which you draw up a little water and in which you carry a coal.” Again it affirms that he is wholly and entirely an unnecessary vessel.

When the Lord begins to open his treasury, will we, who are in this house of God, not also begin to be cleansed, if only we are vessels of mercy and the vessels of wrath are cast out from among us? Or is it already the beginning of our duty to take care not merely that we ourselves are not vessels of wrath, but that those who are such are cast out from among us?

For something of this sort is what the Apostle Paul says to the Corinthians: “Fornication is actually heard of among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the nations, namely, that someone should have his father’s wife—and you have not rather mourned, so that the one who committed this deed might be removed from your midst” (1 Corinthians 5:1–2). It is as though he were saying: “When God’s treasury has been opened, let his vessels of wrath go out.”

The Lord has indeed opened his treasury and brought forth the vessels of his wrath.

I have read somewhere, as though the Savior were saying it, and I ask whether someone has represented the Savior’s person, or recalled this to memory, or whether the statement is true: “The Savior said to him: ‘Whoever is near me is near the fire; whoever is far from me is far from the kingdom’” (Mark 7).

For just as the one who is near me is near salvation, so he is also near the fire. And whoever hears me but transgresses what he has heard becomes a vessel of wrath prepared for destruction; although he is near me, he is near the fire.

But if someone takes care, because the one who is near me is near the fire, to become far from me so that he may not be near the fire, such a person will indeed be far from the kingdom as well.

As an athlete who has not been enrolled in the contest neither fears the lashes nor awaits the crown, whereas one who has once registered his name, if he is defeated, is beaten and cast out, but if he wins, is crowned—so, in the same way, you who have entered the Church, catechumen, listen: whoever has approached the word of God has done nothing other than enroll in the contest of piety. And once enrolled, if he does not contend lawfully, he is beaten with the lashes with which those who were not enrolled at the beginning are not beaten.

But if he contends bravely in order to avoid the blows and insults, he will not merely be freed from injury, but will receive an incorruptible crown of glory.

“The work of the Lord of hosts is in the land of the Chaldeans. Since her times have come, open her storehouses.”

According to differing meanings, an earthly place is called by many names. Just as the Savior, while one in underlying subject [Note: Rabanus reads *notion* rather than the earlier, less correct *reason*; “underlying” is also explained as “subject” or “substrate”], has many names according to different meanings—he is physician, because “the healthy have no need of a physician, but the sick do”; shepherd, because he rules irrational creatures; king, because he governs rational ones; the true vine, because those grafted into him bear very abundant fruit and, cultivated by the Father who is the farmer, receive the richness of the true vine through fellowship in one root; and, in other meanings, wisdom, truth, and justice—while the underlying subject is one: so too earthly affairs are one in underlying subject but many in their meanings.

We have often said, in allegorizing, that Babylon means earthly affairs, which are always confusions [the transmitted reading after this is uncertain], and Egypt likewise afflictions. We have said that the land of the Chaldeans signifies those who devote themselves to such superstitions, because very many consecrate what occurs on earth to the stars and assert that the causes either of our sins or of the things that happen to us, whether favorable or adverse, arise from their movements [Note: Rabanus reads substantially: “because very many consecrate to the stars what is done on earth, and maintain that whatever happens to us, whether from our sins or our virtues, comes about through their nods”; he reads *persuasions* for *superstitions*]. Everyone, therefore, who believes these things is in the land of the Chaldeans. If any of you follows the ravings of astrologers, he is in the land of the Chaldeans. If anyone calculates a birthday and, trusting in various calculations of hours and moments [variant: “methods”], accepts the doctrine that stars configured in this or that way make people lustful, adulterous, chaste, or anything else of the kind, he is in the land of the Chaldeans. Some now even suppose that Christians are made from the courses of the stars. All of you who think or believe such things are in the land of the Chaldeans.

Therefore God spiritually threatens those in the land of the Chaldeans—those who have devoted themselves to genealogies and fate, maintaining that everything occurring among mortals depends either on the movements of the stars or on the necessity of fate. But, leading Abraham onward to better things, God said to him: “I am he who brings you out of the land of the Chaldeans” (Genesis 15). God is able also to grant us to leave the land of the Chaldeans, so that we may believe that there is no other besides him who orders all things and, according to the quality of merits, governs our life and regulates the diverse events that befall us. No twinkling star—whether that of Phaethon, as they call it, or the star of the corrupted catamite [Note: Rabanus calls him by the name Ganymede]—holds the cause of our affairs. In one sense, then, the person who believes the calculations already mentioned is in the land of the Chaldeans; in another, the person who goes up onto roofs and worships the host of heaven is so. In Jeremiah we find a severe threat also against those who pour libations to the host of heaven.

It is clear that this concerns the land of the Chaldeans.

[Note: Rabanus likewise reads: “It is clear who those in the land of the Chaldeans are.”]

[Note: Likewise: “It is clear who those in the land of the Chaldeans are.”]

The storehouses of the Chaldeans are the teachings concerning nativities. “Search her out like a cave and destroy her.”

Whoever rejects the calculation of birth-times, whoever uses the word of truth against it, whoever shows that none of the things the astrologers say is true, whoever teaches that the judgments of God are inscrutable and cannot be comprehended by human beings, whoever asserts that the stars are not the causes of what happens on earth—and still less of what happens to us Christians—fulfills the Lord’s command: “Destroy her.”

What, then, must we seek in the statement that follows: “Let none of her remnants remain”?

“Do not,” he says, “cut away some things of the Chaldeans while preserving others.” For this reason he commands that not even a little be left in her.

“Dry up all her fruits.” Who is so blessed that he can dry up all the fruits of the land of the Chaldeans and make them descend to slaughter?

“Woe to them, for their day has come, and the time of their vengeance.”

### The continuation of another chapter

“The voice of those fleeing and of those who have been rescued from the land of Babylon, to proclaim in Zion the vengeance of our Lord.”

He now prophesies concerning those who, abandoning the customs of their fathers, [Note: Rabanus inserts “and the nations”] the laws of the nations, and the unbelief of earlier times, come to the word of God.

For something of this sort is signified in the statement: “The voice of those fleeing and of those who have been rescued from the land of Babylon.”

Would that your voice too, catechumens, were the voice of those fleeing from Babylon—fleeing vices and fleeing sins.

For it is the voice of those fleeing and of those who have been rescued. It is not enough to flee from the land of Babylon; one must also be rescued from the land of Babylon in order to proclaim in Zion the vengeance of the Lord our God. Thus, fleeing from the land of Babylon, you must come to Zion, the watchtower [variant: “of the watchmen”], the Church of God.

To proclaim in Zion—that is, in the Church—the vengeance of the Lord our God.

“Declare in Babylon the vengeance of his people to many, to everyone who bends the bow.”

The word “many” has been significantly placed. Many are those who are in Babylon, while few are in Jerusalem.

He does not say that the Lord your God loved you because you were many; for you are few in comparison with all the nations. And rightly it was said to those who belonged in part to God: “You are few among all the nations.”

Understand this also: few are those who are saved. And likewise: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate.” But “many walk in the broad and spacious way” (Matthew 7:11).

[Note: We supplied the words “many walk” from Rabanus. Previously the printed books had a defective and incomplete sense, incorrectly joining the words in this way: “But in the broad and spacious way proclaim in Babylon,” as though there were a single testimony of Scripture.]

“Declare in Babylon to many, to everyone who bends the bow. Let none of them be saved; destroy and kill everything belonging to Babylon.”

[Note: Rabanus corrects this to “little ones” (*parvulis*); some printed books had “parables.”]

Recently we spoke of the little Babylonians, of the Babylonian men, and of Babylonian seed. Let there be no one from Babylon’s seed who is rescued. Repay her according to her works, according to all that she has done, and do this to her because she resisted the Lord, and against the Lord, the holy God of Israel.

[Alternative: “the holy God of Israel.”]

As long as you have within you wicked thoughts resisting piety and true faith, you have Babylonians within you. But execute vengeance and kill all the sinners of the earth that is within you—that is, all the Babylonians—so that, once cleansed, you may cross over into Jerusalem, the city of God, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY FOUR

On the passage that is written: “The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not hatch, making its riches without judgment. In the middle of its days they will abandon it, and at its end it will be foolish” (Jeremiah 17:11).

781 The throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, is the place of our sanctification, the support of Israel. Lord, all who have forsaken you shall be put to shame; those departing from you shall be written upon the earth, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living water. Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise. Behold, they say to me: “Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.” But I have not wearied, following after you, nor have I desired the day of man: you know.

We have come to the famous question: what is the partridge of which Scripture now speaks—“The partridge cried out, gathered what it did not hatch, making its wealth not with judgment. In the midst of its days they will abandon it, and at its end it will be foolish” (Jer. XVII, 12 ff.)? From the nature of the bird it seems worthwhile to recount a certain account, so that, by knowing the animal, we may determine whether the interpretation of the partridge now mentioned should be referred to the good or the evil sense.

[Note: Origen, in the Greek Catena which Ghislerius appended to his Commentaries on Jeremiah, says: “In the natural history of animals it is said that the partridge is exceedingly vicious. For, twisting about the feet of the hunter and giving the impression that it may be caught, it draws itself away from the nest; and when it supposes that the young have escaped, it too suddenly flies away. It is also impure (variant: “impure”), so that the males—or, in the variant reading, the widowed birds—fight one another in single combat over intercourse, and after victory a male mounts a male.” It is uncertain whether the compiler of the Catena took this passage from the homily of Origen that we are discussing and reheated it according to the usual practice of such patchwork compilers, or whether he translated it whole from elsewhere. It is taken from Aristotle, *History of Animals*, book IX, chapter 8: “When someone hunts and comes upon the brood, the partridge rolls itself before the hunter, as though it were an easy prey, and draws him toward itself, as if it were to be caught, until each of the young has escaped; then it flies up and calls them back.” And shortly afterward: “As has been said, the bird is vicious and thoroughly crafty.” The same material was taken from there by Pliny, book X, chapter 33; by Solinus from Pliny, chapter 7; by Aelian, book IX *On Animals*, chapter 16; by Athenaeus, book IX; by the Commentary on the *Hexaemeron* attributed to Eustathius; by Phile in the *Iambi*; and by the Scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Birds.” H.]]

It is said that this animal is wicked, deceitful, cunning, and greatly skilled at deceiving hunters. For it often rolls about before the fowler’s feet and, in the midst of its maneuver, slips away as though it were already about to be caught. It offers the promise of capturing it because it is nearby; and it does this so that the hunter may not quickly reach the nest of its young. When it has perceived that its chicks have escaped, it too withdraws, having mocked its enemy.

But its impurity surpasses its wickedness.

[Note: Aristotle himself, in the passage cited, says: “When it has escaped and is brooding, the males cry out and gather to fight one another. They call these birds widowed. The one defeated in the fight follows the victor, being mounted by him alone. But if someone is defeated by a second or by any other, he too is secretly mounted by the victor.” And in book VI, chapter 8: “The male mounts the chicks also when he first brings them out.” Antigonus of Carystus, *Paradoxa*, chapter 110, says of partridges: “When they first bring out the young, they mount them, and they also fight with one another”—that is, they subdue the young and at the same time fight among themselves. Xylander did not understand this passage. The same things are found in Pliny, Solinus, Aelian, Athenaeus, and Phile, in the passages cited above; and, following Origen, in Jerome on this same passage of Jeremiah; as well as in Isidore, book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 7. Yet not only partridges, but roosters also practice this shameful lust among themselves; for the victor subdues not only the wives of the defeated bird but the cock himself as well. The same author.] 

There can be no doubt about what we are going to say, since truth confirms it from those birds that are raised tame in houses: the male rises upon the male; impetuous lust forgets its sex; they fight for intercourse; and the victor’s sole triumph is to defile the one whom he has defeated.

If, therefore, this animal is wicked, impure, and deceitful, it will seem impious to refer its name to the better meaning and adapt it to the interpretation of our Savior Jesus Christ. It is more fitting to associate it with evil, with the devil, and to understand the present reading as referring to the adversary—provided that the interpretation of the whole chapter follows us.

Let us therefore begin with what is written: “The partridge cried out, gathered what it did not hatch.” [Note: This concerns another property of the partridge, nowhere mentioned by Origen in this passage. It is reported that it steals, incubates, and broods over the eggs of others. So Hippolytus the Martyr in the Catena on Jeremiah; Epiphanius, *Physiologus*, ch. 9; Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, VI.3, and Epistle 49; Philastrius, preface to *On Heresies*; Phile in his *Iambics*; Jerome on this passage of Jeremiah; Augustine, *Against Faustus*, XIII.12; Isidore, *Etymologies*, XII.7; and Abbot Rupert, *On Deuteronomy*, I.14. So too the Chaldee Paraphrast, Jeremiah XVII.11.

Since these claims do not occur among pagan authors who treat natural history, they probably arose from this passage of Jeremiah, where the Septuagint rendered the bird “partridge,” and the others followed them. Having no name for that bird, unknown to Europeans, they adopted the name of a highly similar and closely related bird: not the partridge properly so called, but the bird called the rustic, or little rustic, partridge, also “wild” (*agria*, ἄγρια), and by Aristotle *skolopax* (σκολόπαξ). Authoritative Hebrew and Arab writers say that the former bird has a very long bill, short legs, a green colour, is edible and mountainous, is smaller than a dove, and foretells rain. Almost all these features are common to both birds. Moreover, both derive their names from the length of their bills: just as *skolopax* is derived from *skolops* (σκόλοψ), because it bears a stake-like bill, so too the Hebrew name is derived from “stake” [the term is absent in the supplied text].

But it differs from the rustic partridge not only in the greenness of its colour, but also in brooding over foreign eggs—a thing no one has reported of the little rustic partridge. I acknowledge my debt for this and many other matters to Samuel Bochart, a man most richly endowed with exceptional learning; he discusses the question at length in his distinguished work on the animals of Scripture. I add that nearly everything which Hebrew and Arab writers report agrees with the woodpecker (*picus*), which the Greeks call *dryokolaptes* (δρυοκολάπτης): it has a rather long bill, of remarkable strength, with which it strikes and hollows out trees; it has short legs, is green, smaller than a dove, mountainous and edible, and pre-eminently foretells rain. Most noteworthy is that one might plausibly derive *picus* either from [a term absent in the supplied text], “it digs, excavates,” or from [a term absent in the supplied text], “beam, stake, trunk, wood,” because it pierces tree-trunks with its bill; hence the Greek name *dryokolaptes*. If any author had ascribed the care and incubation of others’ eggs to the woodpecker, I should not doubt that this is the bird denoted by the word. The same author.]

The devil does not gather his own creatures; he does not collect what he himself generated. Rather, by crying out and gathering alien creatures, he makes them his own.

[Note: Epiphanius, nevertheless, in the *Physiologus*, chapter 9, compared a pious person to the partridge. The same author.]

The partridge cried out through Valentinus, cried out through Basilides, through Marcion, and through all who were carried away by the desire for glory alien to God.

[Note: Jerome interpreted this most badly: “through all who were carried away by desire for glory belonging to God.” Among ecclesiastical writers, *heterodoxos* (ἑτερόδοξος) is opposed to *orthodoxos* (ὀρθόδοξος), and he ought to have translated it: “through all who cling to perverse opinions.” The same author.] 

For none of them could utter the voice of the Lord Jesus: “My sheep hear my voice” (John X, 27). But Christ’s voice was in Paul; it was in Peter. Therefore Paul said: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

The voice of the partridge gathering what it did not hatch is found in those who entangle the simple among the faithful in the snare of a heretical faction. Thus the partridge cried out, gathered what it did not hatch, made its riches without judgment, and became rich.

Behold how many thousands belong to it, what an immense crowd, how many peoples of captives there are. And it makes its wealth without considering judgment, without possessing justice in its heart, conducting everything lawlessly; rightly it is accused of having made its wealth without judgment.

But my Jesus makes his wealth with judgment.

[Note: The reading “Its wealth has been emptied and destroyed,” which is surprisingly found even in Huet, was corrupt. The Greek text in the adjacent column, where it reads “and its wealth has been judged and selected” (καὶ κεκριμένος ἐστιν ὁ πλοῦτος καὶ ἐκλελεγμένος), ought to have warned him of the error. Following Rabanus, we have corrected the passage against the Greek exemplar, restoring: “Its wealth has been examined and chosen.”]

“In the midst [or: middle] of its days they will abandon it” (Jer. XVII, 11).

We all who were once under the power of the partridge that cried out—for it cried out not only through those whom we mentioned above, but generally through all who, as though calling people to piety and religion, cried out under a doctrine contrary to the truth—we, I say, all of us abandoned it in the middle of its days.

[Note: The word “who,” necessary to the context, is supplied by Rabanus.]

Its days are indeed all the days of this age; but because the Lord Jesus delivered us from the present evil age, therefore we abandoned it in the midst [or: middle] of its days.

“And its end will be foolish” (Jer. XVII, 11).

But when was it wise, so that its end should rightly become foolish? Let us nevertheless say that it was wise. For “the serpent was wiser than all the beasts upon the earth which the Lord God had made” (Gen. III, 1).

It was wise according to what is written: “I will bring upon the understanding a great prince of the Assyrians.” He said: “By my strength I shall act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I shall remove the boundaries of the nations, consume their powers, and shake inhabited cities” (Isa. X, 12–13). [Rabanus reads: “I shall feed upon their strength.”]

If anyone can, let him understand how its end will be foolish. What it was—wise, since it was wiser than all the beasts upon the earth—it becomes, on the contrary, wickedly foolish because it was wise.

You will understand what “its end will be foolish” means if you know how the Apostle also commands you, for your salvation, to accept foolishness: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age,” he says, “let him become foolish” (I Cor. III, 18).

[Note: In place of “He who cried out earlier has been released,” Rabanus reads: “Pay attention, because he not only did not cry out,” and so forth.]

He undoes what he cried out before: “Become foolish and stupid, so that you may become wise” [variant: “so that he may become wise”].

If, therefore, there is a certain blameworthy wisdom, according to which “the children of this age are wiser than the children of light in their generation,” God is good, overturning different things by means of opposites, so that what was said may be fulfilled: “Its end will be foolish.”

When its end will be foolish, Christ must reign until God places all his enemies beneath his feet. When he has subjected all things to him, the last enemy, death, will be destroyed. When death has been destroyed, then the partridge’s last things will come to pass, and its end will become foolish.

This is what concerns the partridge.

But the beginning of the chapter—

[Note: Shortly afterward occurs the phrase, “Here the second division also ended” (ἐνθάδε ἔληξε καὶ ἡ δευτέρα περικοπή), which Jerome rendered: “Thus the circumscription of the second chapter also ended.” In the *Homily on Jeremiah*, according to the Latin arrangement, it is the third homily: “Then the beginning of another chapter: ‘The Lord has opened his treasury,’” and so forth.

Likewise, on Isaiah XXXII, 2, Jerome says: “The Hebrews call the preceding chapter, in which it reads, ‘Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered?’ and the rest to the end, and so forth,” calling that a chapter.

Here, certainly, while interpreting Origen, Jerome renders the *pericope* which Origen called it by the word *chapter*; it contains verses 13 and 14 of Jeremiah XVII. We observed in the *Homilies on I Kings* that Origen called *pericopae* passages which, in the present and accepted division, are treated as chapters; and in Homily 18 on Jeremiah he calls everything from verse 7 through verse 12 “one *pericope*.”

But to make these matters clearer, we shall go back further.

It is known to scholars that the sacred books of the Bible were not divided and marked out in former times as they are now, whether one considers the Jewish copies, the Greek copies of the Seventy, or the Vulgate edition.

First, then, concerning the Jewish books. Elias Levita writes that the whole Law was once a single verse. Jerome testifies in his prefaces to Joshua, Chronicles, and Isaiah that he distinguished his translations by a new manner of writing. From this it is an easy inference that such a division was absent from the Hebrew codices; Jerome himself bears witness that the division into cola and commas was introduced to avoid confusion and barbarity of expression.

For use in the synagogues, however, the books of Moses were distributed, and not in only one manner. Since on each Sabbath some portion of the Law and the Prophets had to be read aloud to the people, the Law was divided, according to the number of Sabbaths, into readings called [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text]; some attribute these to Moses, others to Ezra.

This seems to have been what Luke calls “the section of Scripture” (περιοχὴ τῆς γραφῆς) in Acts VIII, 32. In addition, they introduced certain distinctions which they called “Open” and “Closed” [the Hebrew terms are absent in the supplied text], and they mark the margins of their books with these letters and signs.

Finally, the Law was divided into [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text], that is, verses, from ancient times: according to some, by Moses himself; according to others, by Ezra; according to the rest, by the Masoretes. The Talmudists mention these verses. They recorded, and still record, the total number of all these divisions and even of the individual letters at the end. What labor they undertook for themselves!

The Prophets too were formerly divided into [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text] and verses. They refer the invention of the *haphtarot* to the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, and that of the verses to an age earlier than Christ, but on slight evidence.

It should also be added that Eusebius reports from Origen, book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 25, that among the Hebrews the books of Kings I and II constituted one volume; likewise Kings III and IV constituted one; the two books of Chronicles constituted one; Ezra I and II constituted one; and the prophecy of Jeremiah, together with the Lamentations and the Epistle, constituted one.

As for the translation of the Seventy Elders, since it was read in the synagogues of the Jewish Hellenists, it is probable that they distributed it for their own purposes, though in such a way that these divisions prevailed only in the synagogues.

The two most ancient copies of the edition of the Seventy Interpreters—one of which is kept at Rome, while the other, apparently corrected by Hesychius and transferred from Alexandria to Constantinople by Cyril Lucaris, patriarch of Constantinople, was later sent to Charles, king of Britain, and is preserved in England—were both written more than twelve hundred years ago. Neither displays any division into chapters or verses, indeed not even into words, except in the books written in *stichoi*, which were probably composed in verses by their authors themselves: Job, I mean, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song.

Since most of the Greek Fathers used this translation while elucidating Holy Scripture in their commentaries, each one divided the sacred text, which they called *edaphos* (ἔδαφος), according to his own judgment and capacity. It is therefore clear that no division was then approved and commonly received above the others.

Those ancient Fathers distributed Scripture not only into chapters but also into verses, according to their own judgment. Origen had divided his *Hexapla* into cola, as Eusebius reports in book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 16. Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem, testifies that he did this in the Twelve Prophets and that he maintained this custom, deriving it from ancient times.

Origen appears, nevertheless, to have observed in the prologue to the *Song of Songs* some division already received and established in the very title of the Song. But I fear that Rufinus, an interpreter of unreliable fidelity, added this from his own resources. If the passage is genuine, it must be said that Origen used some ancient codex equipped with its own divisions, perhaps taken from the library of Symmachus.

According to Hilary of Poitiers, the order in which we possess the Psalms is due to the diligence of the Seventy Elders. He writes that the Psalms, first scattered and disordered, were afterward collected by Ezra into one volume and finally arranged into number and order by the Seventy Interpreters.

If this is so, the Psalter must have been divided into five books by the Hebrews after the time of Ezra, as Epiphanius reports in his book *On Weights and Measures*, chapter 5.

Jerome refutes this opinion in his preface to the Psalms according to the Hebrew truth, addressed to Sophronius: “Following,” he says, “the authority of the Hebrews, and especially that of the Apostles, who always name the book of Psalms in the New Testament, we assert that there is one volume of Psalms.”

The two accounts can be reconciled if we say that this division prevailed in some Hebrew codices but not in others. Nor does Jerome’s argument prove anything against the claim that there is one volume of Psalms: Epiphanius will admit that there is one volume, though divided into five books.

That some division existed in the Latin Psalter in Jerome’s own time is sufficiently indicated by the beginning of his twenty-fourth letter to Marcella; what sort it was, however, is uncertain.

This statement of Jerome in the preface to his Commentary on the Psalms should be noted: “The Psalms which do not appear to bear titles are regarded among the Hebrews as one Psalm.”

In addition to this fivefold division of the Psalter, the ancient Greek Liturgies and Euchologia present it divided into twenty sections. These sections are called *kathismata* (καθίσματα), as though one were to say “sessions.”

Nor did the Latin edition of the Old Testament have a fixed division. The distinction now used, by verses, is extremely recent, born only yesterday—or today. The older division was by chapters. The former was first introduced into Latin books and then spread among the Hebrew and Greek books; whether the latter originated with the Latins or the Greeks is unclear.

Among the ancient Fathers, no one, when citing passages of Scripture, noted the number of the verses or chapters now received. Augustine does seem to have divided the verses of the Bible in such a way that each verse contained six words, but this appears to have been peculiar to Augustine’s codex and not common to all.

Jerome divided most, and perhaps all, of the books of Scripture by verses, but there are no traces in him of the division now used.

If one asks when the recent division by chapters, which has taken root throughout the Bible, was devised, I would answer that it was discovered six hundred years ago. Theophylact certainly used it; he flourished before the end of the eleventh century, as the *ektheseis* (ἐκθέσεις) that he prefixed to the Gospels demonstrate. Ancient manuscripts from this period also prefer it.

We nevertheless think it more recent than Jerome.

The Syrians, Samaritans, and Copts followed almost the same method as the Hebrews in dividing the Old Testament, but each possesses a particular division of its own. The Hebrews distribute Genesis into 1,534 verses; the Syrians into 4,509. Kircher noted the division of the Samaritans and Copts in his *Prodromus Coptus*.

I have spoken of the Old Testament; let us proceed to the New.

The most ancient division of the Greek New Testament appears to me to be that by Titles, which are also called *epigraphai* (ἐπιγραφαί) and *lemmata* (λήμματα). Titles were divided into *kephalaia* (κεφάλαια), or *pericopae* (περικοπαί); *pericopae* into *stichoi* (στίχοι), or commas, or cola, which are also called sections and cuttings.

The *stichoi*, or verses, were generally defined by sense, so that some were shorter and others longer. At the end of the book the total number of *stichoi* was finally collected and noted, just as the *ekthesis of the lemmata* (ἔκθεσις τῶν λημμάτων) was noted at the beginning.

The fact that the *stichometriai* (στιχομετρίαι) vary in different codices results from the fact that scribes, according to their own judgment, divided sentences more or less extensively and marked them off with strokes.

A Title embraced a complete subject; a *kephalaion* a particular part of that subject; a *stichos* a period or a distinct and determinate sentence.

Many are mistaken who suppose that whenever the Fathers designate a *pericope*, they were referring to the division commonly received at that time. Very often they called *tmemata*—sections separated from the remaining context at will and according to circumstances—by this name.

In the common codices there were fixed Titles distributed into a number of chapters, and these chapters presented a determinate number of verses. An example will clarify the matter.

The Gospel of Matthew is divided into sixty-eight Titles. These Titles are also called *kephalaia* by Euthymius, Oecumenius, and others; they survive in their proper order in manuscripts and in certain printed books. The first is “Concerning the Magi” (περὶ τῶν μάγων); the second, “Concerning the Slaughtered Children” (περὶ τῶν ἀναιρεθέντων παιδίων); and so on.

The *kephalaia*, however, numbered 355, according to Ammonius, Eusebius, and Tatian. Suidas says: “Matthew has 68 Titles and 358 chapters” (Ματθαῖος ἔχει τίτλους ξηʹ, κεφάλαια τνηʹ). Different manuscripts present different numbers of *stichoi*: some 502, others 562.

Casaubon therefore must not be listened to when he teaches that among the ancients a *kephalaion* was almost the same thing as what we today call a little verse. For although *kephalaion*, and *capitulum*, are sometimes taken for a single verse—or, if one wishes to speak precisely, encompass a single verse—Casaubon does not here mean such *kephalaia*, but those into which the Titles of the New Testament were divided.

The number of our little verses, however, is approximately three times greater than the number of the ancient *kephalaia*. Yet the ancient *stichoi* were shorter than those used today.

Eustathius of Antioch, in his book *On the Ventriloquist*, counts 135 *stichoi* from John VIII, 59, through X, 31, whereas the more recent division has only 72. Origen, as Eusebius reports, writes that the last two Epistles of John scarcely fill one hundred verses, although the present division contains only 29 verses. The *stichometriai* of the New Testament, however, assign thirty to the Second Epistle and thirty-four to the Third.

The more recent division eventually passed from Latin codices to the Greeks.

Certainly this entire method of division depended on the judgment of authors and scribes. Certain books present us with a distinctive division of the Gospels. Euthymius divides Luke’s Gospel into 83 chapters; Ammonius into 343 chapters; the old Latin division into 107 chapters; the present division into 24; Ambrose into 164 Titles; Bede into 193 chapters.

Nevertheless, the most widely received and most ancient division was that introduced by Ammonius and expressed by Suidas, for it is recognized by Caesarius, brother of Gregory Nazianzen, and by Epiphanius. The same variety is also found in the division of the remaining books of the New Testament.

The Latin division appears to be contemporary with that of the New Testament. It was customary among the Latins to distribute the longer chapters of the New Testament into seven parts and the shorter into four, marking these parts with alphabetic letters. This practice is often preserved even in printed books of the New Testament.

I have said that the *stichometriai* of the books of the New Testament were customarily collected and written down. The same was done in the Old Testament by the Syrians, Samaritans, Jews, Greeks, and Latins.

This practice was used not only in sacred books but also in Greek and Latin works of profane literature. Salmasius proves this learnedly in his *Prolegomena to Solinus*. The headings prefixed to the commentaries of Asconius Pedianus on the Cornelian oration and other speeches of Cicero also demonstrate it; so do the prefaces to Justinian’s *Digest*.

It is known from Laertius that the books of Aristotle, Zeno, Chrysippus, and others were divided into verses.

The Arabs too retained the method of dividing and counting verses handed down to them by the Jews. The Qur’an is divided into chapters and verses; the number of verses and letters is collected and written at the end. The former number, however, varies, and the codices do not always present the same total.

Although you can see that they generally observed the practice of ending each verse with *homoioptota* (ὁμοιόπτωτα), without regard to equality among them, I cannot at all agree here with the great Salmasius. Following Henry Stephanus and Casaubon, he writes that the Hebrews and Arabs determined their verses by sense and counted the number of such verses at the end; but that the Latins and Greeks divided a single sentence into more or fewer lines according to the narrowness of the codex, called these lines *stichoi* or verses, and designated not the whole sentence but the individual lines. He consequently adds that he does not know what benefit the Greeks and Latins derived from this counting of lines, since the lines varied according to the narrowness of the codex.

It would indeed be astonishing if this were so; but it certainly is not. For although I admit that *verse* can sometimes signify a line, those totals of verses certainly comprised not individual lines, strokes, or furrows of the books, but complete sentences. Salmasius himself eventually acknowledged this in his letter to Sarravius, whether he had changed his earlier opinion or simply forgotten it:

“Sometimes,” he says, “each verse occupied two lines, sometimes three or more. The Greeks call these *stichoi*. Works themselves were counted by verses, and their total was noted at the end of the book. Hence the expression *polystichon biblion* [πολύστιχον βιβλίον], and so forth.”

I mention these matters not because I wish to diminish anything of the reputation of a man learned beyond belief, and one who formerly deserved exceedingly well of me, for—
For other noble men this reproach is thrust aside.

There was therefore almost one and the same method among the Hebrews, Arabs, Greeks, and Latins—both in sacred and in secular books—for counting and marking verses. Since, however, not everyone followed this practice, and since they sometimes wrote their books in a single continuous series, such books were later divided into sections by ignorant scribes, with the result that monstrous errors and dense obscurities were often introduced into the finest authors. They even went so far as to attach the most foolish headings to the sections. This blemish has spread through a very large part of good literature. But that belongs elsewhere. Let us now return to our subject.
