From what has been said above it is clear that one searches in vain in the present division of Scripture for Origen’s *pericopes* and Jerome’s chapters. Adamantius called a *pericope* a definite passage of Scripture, determined and bounded according to one’s discretion. Jerome used “chapter” in the same sense, namely for what we call in French *un passage*, “a passage.” Thus the term is understood in hundreds of places in Rufinus, as when he says in his interpretation of Pamphilus’s *Apology*:

“Especially in your books, in which he sets out several interpretations of a single chapter.”

And shortly afterward:

“We shall give an example corresponding to the preceding one, from the book which he wrote on the Epistle of the Apostle Paul to Titus, concerning the chapter in which the Apostle says: ‘Avoid a heretical man after the third admonition, knowing that he is perverse and sins, being self-condemned.’”

Philastrius speaks similarly, *Heresy* 45:

“What the Scriptures say as though about a man, he receives as chapters.”

And *Heresy* 50:

“These men use those chapters of Scripture which teach about Christ as though about a man.”

[HUETIUS.]

According to this reading, the following passage was read:

“Throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, place of our sanctuary, support of Israel. Lord, all who have forsaken you shall be put to shame; those who depart shall be written upon the earth, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of life” (Jeremiah 17:13).

Isaiah says (chapter 6), the blessed prophet who saw the Lord and his kingdom:

“I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” [Col. 0621A].

Jeremiah also saw how God reigns, and therefore, glorifying him, said:

“Throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, place of our sanctuary.”

Whether you wish to understand these words of Christ or of the Father, you will not err. For he is a lofty throne of glory [alternative: “of brightness”], and from the beginning he is Savior. He is a throne of glory because his kingdom is exalted [Col. 0622A].

[Note: We read with Rabanus: “because his kingdom is exalted, and our sanctification is Christ.” In other printed editions, with different punctuation and meaning, it read: “because his kingdom and our sanctification are Christ.” For he is...]

Christ is our sanctification:

“For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one” (Hebrews 2:11).

“Support of Israel.” Just as Christ himself is righteousness, truth, and sanctification, so also he himself is support. And there is nothing righteous without Christ, nothing holy without him, nor anything enduring which does not have Christ in itself: for he is the support of Israel.

[Note: These words—“without Christ, nor anything holy without him”—were lacking. We supplied them from Rabanus, compelled to do so by the Greek text: χωρὶς Χριστοῦ, οὔτε ἅγιον χωρὶς αὐτοῦ, “without Christ, nor anything holy without him.”]

If you refer this also to the Father, you do not understand it impiously.

“Lord, all who forsake you shall be put to shame; those who depart...” (Jeremiah 17:13).

Whenever any one of us sins, by the things in which he sins he forsakes Christ. But in forsaking the Son, he has also forsaken the Father. The unjust person is far from righteousness; the polluted person from holiness; the warrior from peace; the one who begins to be under the power of the enemy becomes alienated from redemption; and the one who is outside the wisdom of God forsakes the wisdom of God.

[Note: Rabanus does not acknowledge the words “of God” here.]

Thus, teaching us what will happen to all who abandon the Lord, the prophet says:

“All who forsake you shall be put to shame as they depart”—that is, to the extent that they forsake him, to that extent they shall be put to shame as they depart.

“Let them be written upon the earth.” All human beings are recorded: the holy in heaven, sinners upon the earth. Jesus says to the disciples:

“Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

Therefore one ought to rejoice if one is such that one’s name is written in heaven. And just as the names of the righteous are recorded above, so, conversely, the names of those who live in an earthly manner—who do not pass beyond the land of Edom, but possess the fields and vineyards of the land of Edom—are written upon the earth, as belonging to those who abandon God.

“Let them be put to shame as they depart; let them be written upon the earth. For by the measure with which they have measured, it shall be measured back to them” (Matthew 7:2).

[Note: Rabanus has the slightly more polished version: “Each person is his own cause.”]

Each person is his own cause for being written upon the earth, if he does not seek heavenly things while on earth, if his soul is always agitated by the affairs of this world which appear good to the age. But if, hearing Jesus say,

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves upon earth, where moths and worms destroy, and where thieves break in and steal; but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matthew 6:19),

he stores up treasure for himself in heaven, he himself is the cause of his being written in heaven [Col. 0624A].

This has been said because it is written, “Let them be written upon the earth”; and he adds the reason:

“Because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of life” (Jeremiah 17:13).

At the beginning the prophet himself, speaking in the person of the Lord, says:

“They have forsaken me, the fountain of life.”

[Note: The words “and now, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of life” are lacking in Genebrard’s edition.]

And now:

“Because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of life.”

Let us therefore also say, if we do not wish to forsake the Lord, the fountain of life, in the words of the disciples of Jesus Christ, who spoke to their master when he said to them:

“Do you also wish to depart?”

What then shall we say?

“Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68).

Thus the delimitation of the second chapter has also ended.

The following discourse contains this passage:

“Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my boast. Behold, they themselves say to me: ‘Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.’ But I have not labored by following after you, and I have not desired the day of man; you know” (Jeremiah 17:14–16).

To the physician who came for the sake of the sick and says,

“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but the sick do” (Matthew 9:12),

the one who wishes his sick soul to be saved ought confidently to say:

“Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed.”

For that woman in the Gospel who suffered from a flow of blood spent all her property on physicians (Luke 8:43), yet could not be healed by any of them. To none of them could it fittingly be said, “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed,” except to him alone for whom it is enough merely to touch the fringe of his garment. To him alone I shall say:

“Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed.”

Then, indeed, health follows the remedy, if Christ deigns to heal:

“Save me, and I shall be saved.”

“A false horse is for salvation” (Psalm 32:17).

Therefore I shall say to him:

“Save me, and I shall be saved.”

And I shall rejoice to speak this if, renouncing all worldly glory, I can also say the rest:

“For you are my glory” [alternative: “my praise”];

or when I have fulfilled the commandment in which it is prescribed:

“Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows that I am the Lord” (Jeremiah 9:23).

Blessed, then, is the person who renounces every glory that is below—glory based on noble birth, beauty, bodily advantages, riches, and ostentation [Col. 0625A].

Blessed is the one who, having despised vain glory, says to the Lord:

“For you are my glory” [alternative: “my praise”].

[Note: The Greek has ἀρκούμενος, “being content.” Jerome translated it, “having despised vain glory”; the same reading is found in one manuscript of the Royal Library. Another has, “despising vain glory.” What if we should read, “being content with one glory”? The Greek wording certainly requires this, and the Vulgate reading could easily have been distorted from it. HUETIUS.]

“Behold, they themselves say to me: ‘Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.’ But I have not labored by following after you, and I have not desired the day of man” (Jeremiah 17:15–16).

Jesus said to you:

“Take up your cross and come, follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

And:

“Whoever does not leave father or mother and follow me is not worthy to be my disciple” (Luke 14:26).

If, then, you are such that you always follow Christ, the more closely you follow, the less you will labor. For there will be no weariness in Jacob, nor will pain appear in Israel. Therefore he said that we should labor no longer, since we labored before we began to follow him:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

If we come to Jesus while laboring, and follow him, then we shall be able to say:

“But I have not labored by following after you, and I have not desired the day of man.”

There is a day of man, and there is a day of the Lord—that is, the day of resurrection, which every holy person desires. It is not the day of which it is written:

“Woe to those who desire the day of man. For that day is darkness and not light” (Amos 5:18).

Who can say:

“I have not desired the day of man”?

The explanation of the word exposes us, because we do desire the day of man. Often, when we are sick, when we have begun to exist in the feverish realm of delusion and are pressed upon the threshold of death, we raise our weary hands to the brothers who visit us, asking them to pray to the Lord for us, and saying:

“Ask for some extension of my life; ask that I may remain for a little while in this light.”

When we remember such things, we desire not the holy day of the Lord but the day of man. Therefore, laying aside our love of long life and our desire for the human day, let us seek to see that day on which we shall become participants in the blessedness that is in Christ, to whom belong glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.

## FIFTH HOMILY

Concerning what is written: “He who made the earth by his strength” (Jeremiah 10:12).

The prophet, taking up in a certain sense three virtues—strength, wisdom, and prudence—assigned to each its proper work: the earth to strength, the inhabited world to wisdom, and heaven to prudence. Hear the order of Scripture:

“The Lord, who made the earth by his strength, established the inhabited world by his wisdom, and by his prudence stretched out heaven.”

We too, in our earth—for it was said to Adam, “You are earth” (Genesis 3:19)—need the strength of God, since without it we cannot carry out what resists the flesh. But when the members upon the earth have been put to death, then the spirits obey the will. For, according to the Apostle, “by the spirit the deeds of the flesh are put to death” (Colossians 3; Romans 8).

“The Lord, then, who made the earth by his strength.”

But if you also come to this earth and consider what is written in Job (26:7), according to the most carefully corrected manuscripts—how he established it upon nothing—you will find the strength of God sustaining the balance of the earth at the center of the world.

I shall now come to the inhabited world, which in Greek is called οἰκουμένη (*oikoumenē*), that is, “the inhabited [world].”

[Note: The Vulgate has “inhabited.” Rabanus, however, in a later usage, follows the Greek, as will become clear below when both Origen and Jerome are seen to have understood the word continuously in this way.]

I know that my soul is inhabited; I know that my soul is desolate. For if it does not have the Son saying,

“I and my Father will come to him [alternative: “to her”] and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23),

if it does not have the Holy Spirit, the soul is desolate. It is inhabited when it is full of God, when it has Christ and the Holy Spirit.

Yet Scripture speaks in different and varied ways of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit dwelling in the human soul. David too, in the psalm of confession, asks for three spirits, saying:

“Establish me with a principal spirit. Renew a right spirit within me. Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 50).

What are these three spirits? The principal Spirit is the Father; the right Spirit is Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit.

We have said this to establish that the inhabited world was fashioned in the wisdom of the one who fashioned it.

[Note: Rabanus has: “that the inhabited world, that is, the earth, was fashioned in the wisdom of God.” The Royal manuscripts known to Huetius differ little: “that the inhabited world was fashioned in the wisdom of God.” The Greek agrees especially with Rabanus’s reading: τὴν οἰκουμένην οὐκ ἄλλως γινομένην ἤ ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the inhabited world does not come into being otherwise than in the wisdom of God.”]

“For wisdom will assist the righteous person who has authority over ten cities” (Ecclesiastes 7:20).

[Note: Rabanus has, more closely following the Greek: “who have authority over ten persons in the city,” corresponding to ὑπὲρ δέκα ἐξουσιάζοντας, τοὺς ὄντας ἐν τῇ πόλει, “over ten who exercise authority, those who are in the city.”]

“Unhappy is the one who rejects wisdom and discipline; his hope is vain, his labors senseless, and his works useless,” says Wisdom, which bears the title of Solomon (Wisdom 3:11).

Therefore, as far as we can, let us strive and labor so that our inhabited world may be raised up by the wisdom of God.

[Note: Here we have deleted the word *anima* (“soul”), which the common editions inserted contrary to the author’s meaning. Origen calls our *habitata* (“inhabited world”) our world. I do not deny that soul or mind ought properly to be understood, but I say that neither does the Greek contain ψυχή (“soul”), nor did Rabanus read *animam* (“soul”) in Jerome’s Latin translation.]

For it fell and collapsed from a height when we came into this place of misery. Our inhabited world fell after we sinned, acted wickedly, behaved unjustly, and conducted ourselves impiously; and after its fall it needs to be raised up.

[Note: Again we have removed the word *anima* (“soul”), which neither Origen nor Jerome has according to Rabanus’s purer reading. We have stated what our *habitata* means according to Origen’s sense.]

But if you do not wish to accept this interpretation, let us seek the common fall of the whole world, so that after its fall God may consequently be proclaimed as the one who raises it up. Whoever is in this world fell before being raised. But if he fell, he consequently had to be raised; no one is lifted up without a fall. If he has been raised, let us see what fall preceded it.

We all fell through sin into the inhabited world [alternative: “on the inhabited earth”]. And the Lord, who raises up those who are cast down, lifted us as we lay prostrate (Psalm 144). In Adam we all die; and thus the inhabited world fell and needs to be raised, so that in Christ we may all be made alive.

We have therefore presented a twofold interpretation of the inhabited world: one, how individual souls are either inhabited or desolate; the other, how the whole world fell together.

“And by his prudence he stretched out heaven.”

It was not by chance that wisdom was introduced in connection with the stretching out of heaven. In Proverbs too you will find:

“The Lord founded the earth by wisdom; he prepared the heavens by prudence” (Proverbs 3:19).

There is therefore a prudence of God which I do not want you to seek apart from Christ. For everything that belongs to God is Christ: he is his wisdom, his strength, his sanctification, his righteousness, his holiness and redemption—and, to come to the present point, his prudence.

Although he is one in substance, he is called by different names according to the variety of meanings. Wisdom signifies one thing, righteousness another. When he is called wisdom, the instruction and formation in divine and human matters is signified; when righteousness, he is understood as distributor and judge of merits. When holiness is described, it is that virtue which makes believers holy to God.

Thus I also understand his prudence as the teaching and demonstration of good, evil, and neutral matters. In this manner heaven is now said to have been stretched out in prudence.

But how is heaven stretched out by the one who stretches it out? Hear:

“I stretched out my words, and you did not heed them” [alternative: “attend to them”] (Proverbs 1:24).

He asserts that there is a certain stretching out of words, just as there is now said to be a stretching out of heaven. Likewise it is written elsewhere:

“He stretches out heaven like a skin” (Psalm 103:2).

Our soul, which had previously been contracted, is also stretched out, so that it may be capable of the wisdom of God.

But to return to our subject: we said that heaven was made by his prudence.

[Note: Previously this had been read in an inappropriate sense contrary to the author’s meaning: “that the prudence of this age is evil.” The reading we have restored—“that heaven was made by his prudence”—was supplied by Rabanus and is supported by one Royal manuscript known to Huetius. The other differs slightly: “that the age was made by the prudence [of God].” The Greek text of Origen decisively requires this correction: ἐλέγομεν περὶ τοῦ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἐν φρονήσει γεγονέναι, “we were speaking of heaven’s having been made in prudence.”]

And now we affirm that those who bear the heavenly man are heavens.

[Note: Thus Rabanus, and Origen himself: καὶ αὐτοί εἰσιν οὐρανός, “and they themselves are heaven.” Previously it was falsely read, “heavenly.”]

For if it is said to sinners, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” why should it not be said to the righteous, whose kingdom is heaven, “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go”?

[Note: These words—“or on account of the earthly man”—which had been lacking in the printed editions up to now, have been supplied from Rabanus, compelled by Adamantius’s Greek text: ἢ διὰ μὲν τὸν χοϊκόν, “or on account of the earthly man.” Shortly afterward the gloss “that is, earthly” should more properly be relegated to the margin. The remaining words of the sentence have also been emended from Rabanus and the Greek. Instead of “why on account of the heavenly man to him,” there was “therefore to the heavenly”; and “let it be fitting” is correct instead of “let it not be fitting,” under the interrogative mark.]

Or, if on account of the earthly man it is said to one who bears the image of the earthly man, that is, of the one made from earth:

“You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19),

why, on account of the heavenly man, should it not fittingly be said to the one who bears the image of the heavenly man:

“You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go”?

Each one of us has either heavenly things or earthly things as his product. If earthly things have been produced, they lead the person who stores up those things on earth to the earth related to them. But those things which are done according to virtue carry their treasurer upward to the heavenly regions related to them.

And he added:

“Bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth” (Psalm 134:7).

A similar discussion recently arose in the Psalm, and we explained how God brings forth clouds from the end of the earth. We are now compelled to review the matter again, so that those who heard may fully remember what they know, and those who were not present, or who have forgotten, may recognize the text of the discourse which we then presented as best we could.

We said that the saints are clouds. For what is written,

“Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm 35:6),

cannot refer to inanimate clouds. The truth of God reaches those clouds which hear the command of the Lord and know where they should bring the rains and from whom they should withhold them.

It is concerning these clouds that it is said:

“I shall command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6).

For concerning those clouds which are said to consist of dense air: if there is no rain, God does not command them not to rain upon the vineyard or upon any region; rather, they do not appear at all, as we read in the Third Book of Kings (1 Kings 18), when no cloud appeared during the time of drought, and afterward, according to the prophecy of Elijah, a sign of the coming rain was shown in the imprint of a man; then, after the cloud had gathered, rain descended upon the earth.

But these clouds, as though they subsisted [alternative: “these mists”], are commanded to hold back the rain when the soul is unworthy of heavenly rain, and it is said:

“I shall command the clouds not to rain upon it.”

Thus each of the saints is a cloud. Moses was a cloud, and as a cloud he spoke:

“Give ear, O heaven, and I shall speak; let the earth hear the words from my mouth. Let my words be expected like rain” (Deuteronomy 32:1–2).

If he had not been a cloud, he would never have said:

“Let my words be expected like rain, and let my speech descend like dew.”

As a cloud he said:

“Like showers upon the grass, like frost [alternative: “rain”] upon the hay, because I have called upon the name of the Lord.”

Isaiah likewise spoke as a cloud:

“Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah 1:2).

And because he himself was a cloud and knew that other clouds were prophesying together with him, he therefore foretold:

“I shall command my clouds not to rain upon it.”

But if we have now learned who the clouds are, let us see how God brings forth clouds from the end of the earth.

The Savior says:

“Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be last of all” (Matthew 9:35).

Paul kept this commandment and was last in this world, saying:

“I think God has displayed us apostles as the last, as though sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to this world, to angels and to men” (1 Corinthians 4:9).

Therefore, if any holy person, keeping the Savior’s commandment, becomes last in this life, let him be a cloud. And the Lord brings forth clouds not from the first men of the earth—not from consuls, not from commanders, not from the rich.

“For blessed are the poor, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

You see how God brings forth and forms clouds from the ends of the earth.

[Note: The printed editions had falsely and incongruously preferred “these bodily mists” instead of “and forms clouds,” which we have supplied on Rabanus’s testimony, supported by Adamantius’s Greek καὶ σωματοποιεῖ, “and makes corporeal,” or “gives bodily form to.”]

Therefore, if we wish to become clouds to which the truth of God may reach, let us become last of all, and let us say in both feeling and deed:

“I think God has displayed us apostles as the last.”

And even if I am not an apostle, I may nevertheless become last, so that, as God brings forth clouds from the end of the earth, he may bring me forth also.

“And he made lightning into rain” (Psalm 134:7).

Those who investigate natural causes say that lightning is generated by the collision of clouds, like the harder flints which, when struck together, release fire from between them. Thus thunder roars together with lightning: thunder indicates the sound of the collision, and lightning the brightness of the light struck out.

[Note: Obviously, “of the concussion,” or “collision.” Rabanus reads *concursus*, “meeting” or “collision”; previously it had been *concussum*, “struck.” I would prefer *sonitu*, “by the sound,” instead of *sonitum*, “the sound.”]

If you have understood the example, now consider rational clouds. Moses was a cloud; Jesus son of Nun was a cloud. If these men speak with one another [alternative: “converse with one another”], lightning flashes from their words. Jeremiah and Baruch were clouds; let them converse with one another, and you will see lightning gleaming.

You too can find in the holy Scriptures, in this manner, collisions from which fire may be emitted.

[Note: Rabanus not inappropriately inserts “of clouds.” The Greek has a different meaning.]

To come to the New Testament: Paul and Silvanus came together as two clouds, and behold, they illuminate the whole world with the brilliance of their Epistle:

“He made lightning into rain, and brought forth winds from his treasuries” (Psalm 134:7).

Are, then, these winds which blow over the earth in the treasuries of God? Are they not of a nature whose existence and manner of subsistence are manifest?

But there are certain treasuries of winds, treasuries of spirits: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of God, of fortitude, love, and charity.

You too can gather these winds from the Scriptures and discover the treasuries of these spirits.

Where are these treasuries? Certainly in him in whom the treasures of knowledge are hidden.

[Note: Rabanus has: “Certainly in him in whom the treasures of knowledge are hidden.”]

They have their seat in Christ. From there these spirits arise, so that one person may be wise, another faithful, another learned, and another possess some other gift of God.

“To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:8–9).

He therefore brought forth clouds from the end of the earth, made lightning into rain, and brought forth winds from his treasuries. We hope [alternative: “we think”], by the mercy of God, that we shall come to these treasuries.

And because there are many treasuries, perhaps the repose of those who rise will also correspond to an order among the treasuries of God.

What I mean is this: the resurrection of the dead will take place according to certain orders. The Apostle says:

“Each person will rise in his own order” (1 Corinthians 15:23).

The orders of those who rise are not mixed together indiscriminately. There will be one order in this treasury and that treasury of God, and another order in another and another treasury of God.

All these treasuries have one treasury, in which are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).

And just as I possess one precious pearl by means of several other pearls, so I come to the treasure of treasures, the Lord of lords, and the King of kings, when I have become worthy to dwell among the spirits residing in the treasuries of God.

“For he brought forth winds from his treasuries” (Psalm 134:7).

“Every human being has been made foolish by knowledge” (Jeremiah 20:14).

If every human being has been made foolish by knowledge, and Paul is a human being, Paul has been made foolish by knowledge.

“We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9).

Made foolish by knowledge, he sees through a mirror, sees in an enigma, sees only a small portion; and, if it is appropriate to say so, he recognizes only the smallest part of that small portion itself.

Conversely, you will understand what is meant by:

“Every human being has been made foolish by knowledge.”

[Note: Huetius’s Royal manuscripts read *intelligeret* (“would understand”); he himself reads *intelliges* (“you will understand”).]

In comparison with the sins of Jerusalem, the sin of Sodom is righteousness. For he says:

“Sodom was justified in comparison with you” (cf. Matthew 10:15).

Thus, just as the sins of Sodom do not possess righteousness in themselves but are justified by comparison with greater crimes, so conversely the knowledge of Paul, compared with that heavenly knowledge and that consummate understanding of reason [alternative: “of reading”], is regarded as folly.

Therefore:

“Every human being has been made foolish by knowledge.”

Ecclesiastes, I think, detected something of this kind and declared:

“I said, ‘I shall become wise,’ and it withdrew farther from me than it was; and the depth is deep—who will find it?” (Ecclesiastes 7:23–24).

[Note: Rabanus has “I shall become wise.” The Greek is σοφισθήσομαι, “I shall become wise.”]

We wish, if permitted, to say something boldly: that what descended into the world emptied itself, so that by its emptying the world might be filled.

But if what descended into the world emptied itself, the emptying itself is wisdom, because:

“What is foolish of God is wiser than men” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

If I had said “the foolishness of God,” how the hunters of words would seize upon my expressions, and those always devoted to accusation would brandish their poisoned tongues against me! But Paul, as a wise man possessing apostolic authority, dared to say that all earthly wisdom—whatever wisdom was in himself, in Peter, and in the other apostles, whatever wisdom had descended into this world—was the foolishness of God.

For compared with that wisdom which no earthly place can contain, with that wisdom which is heavenly and exceeds the limits of the world, what descended to human beings is the foolishness of God.

Yet that very foolishness of God is wiser than human beings. Which human beings? Certainly not fools, but the wise. You may call them the wise men of this age, whether rulers or prophets of these wise men of the age:

“The foolishness of God is wiser than men.”

[Note: Besides Rabanus, the Royal manuscripts known to Huetius also read: “even if you call them the wise men of this age, whether rulers or prophets,” though he retained the common reading, “the wise men of this age, whether rulers or those vain men,” which, although otherwise acceptable, is certainly false in reading *vain men* instead of *prophets*. The Greek text is entirely correct: κἂν τοὺς σοφοὺς εἴπῃς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, εἴτε ἄρχοντας εἴτε προφήτας, τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου τὸ μωρὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, “even if you call them the wise men of this age, whether rulers or prophets, the foolishness of God is wiser than the rulers of this age.”]

We wish to insert something remarkable: that the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God, and that God has made the wisdom of the world foolish (1 Corinthians 1:25).

[Note: This passage—“For in his wisdom he made the wisdom of the world foolish”—was lacking in the editions printed up to now. It is easy to suppose that, because of the repetition of the word “world,” with which the sentence ends, it was omitted by the copyist through a customary scribal error. Not only does Rabanus plainly read it, but so do the Royal manuscripts known to Huetius, although these err more seriously in what follows. Origen expressly wrote the essential point in Greek: ἄρα ἐν σοφίᾳ ἐμώρανε τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ κόσμου, καὶ οὐ δύναται χωρῆσαι τὴν σοφίαν, ἵν’ ἐλεγχθῇ μωρὰ εἶναι ἡ τοῦ κόσμου σοφία. This may be rendered in Latin: “Therefore in wisdom he made the wisdom of the world foolish, and the wisdom of the world cannot contain wisdom [supply: ‘the wisdom of God’], so that the wisdom of the world may be proved to be foolish.” For this reason we shortly afterward supplied from the same Rabanus the words “the wisdom of God,” which were lacking and produced an inconvenient and disjointed sense. The sequence of the discourse itself now also confirms the restored passage, in addition to Rabanus’s testimony and the authority of the Greek text.]

For in his wisdom he made the wisdom of the world foolish; the wisdom of the world cannot contain the wisdom of God, so that it may be proved to be foolish.

For the wisdom of God did not deign to descend in its entirety to refute the wisdom of the world.

[Note: The printed editions corruptly had *commiscendam* (“to be mingled”) instead of *convincendam* (“to be refuted”), which we restored from Rabanus, as the Greek text ἵνα ἐλεγχθῇ requires.]

But rather it descended in the small measure that was necessary—the thing that was the foolishness of God—so that by this small and foolish thing of God the wisdom of the age might be made foolish.

[Note: Huetius’s Royal manuscripts read: “but rather a little, that is, the mystery of the Incarnation. What was necessary.”]

[Note: These words, which were lacking in the earlier editions and produced an incomplete or meaningless sense, are supplied here. For the wisdom of the age was not sufficient; after Rabanus, the Royal manuscripts known to Huetius also read this, with the Greek text itself in agreement.]

For the wisdom of the age was unable, in itself powerless, to sustain the greatness of the wisdom that came into it.

But let us insert an example, so that it may be clearly understood how the foolishness of God made the wisdom of the world foolish. Let me imagine for a moment that I, who am thought to know something, am engaged in conversation with some foolish and uneducated person who understands nothing and asks nothing concerning subtle argument.

[Note: Previously *esse* (“to be”) was read, against the Greek εἰδέναι (“to know”). Rabanus corrects it to *nosse*, “to know.”]

Do I need to bring to bear dialectical skill and profundity of meaning in order to expose his foolishness? Will I not, by the utterance of a single short and insignificant statement, which nevertheless appears extremely sharp to his understanding, prove him to be foolish and ignorant?

[Note: Rabanus has: “in order to refute his foolishness, do I need dialectical skill and profundity...”]

Thus, in order to make the wisdom of the world foolish, it is not necessary for the wisdom of God to descend and wrestle with the wisdom that is below. The foolishness of God is sufficient, because:

“The foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.”

My Savior and Lord assumed all the opposites, so that he might dissolve opposites by opposites; so that we might be strengthened by his weakness [alternative: “by Jesus”], made wise by his foolishness, and, having been introduced through this, be able to ascend to the wisdom and power of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.

## SIXTH HOMILY

“The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear the words of this covenant” (Jeremiah 11:1), up to the passage where it says:

“They have turned back to the iniquities of their fathers” (Jeremiah 11:10).

[Col. 0632B]

801 According to the literal truth of the history, we do not deny that the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ took place bodily and that he shone upon the whole world when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). We must, however, understand that even before he assumed a body he descended also to the saints; and after this bodily presence, ascending victoriously into heaven, he will come to us again. If you wish to grasp the proof of this, listen to what is said: “The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear,” and the rest. For what is this word that came from the Lord, whether to Jeremiah, Isaiah, or [Col. 0632C] any of the prophets? Is it the one who was in the beginning with God? I know no other word of the Lord besides him, of whom the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word [Al. sermon], and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

We must understand this: the benefit for believers is that the word should come to each individual. For what does it profit me if he descends into the world and I do not possess him? Conversely, even if he does not come to the whole world, but I become like the prophets, I possess him. I will say, then, that the same word came to Moses, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and each one of the saints; [Col. 0633A] and what was said by the Lord to the disciples—“Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20)—was fulfilled in deed before his advent, which he made manifest to all. For he was with Moses, with Isaiah, and with all the saints.

For how could they have spoken the word [Note: [Col. 0633D] Up to this point the commonly printed editions had an incomplete and defective meaning, reading “words,” without the coming of God himself. We have restored “the words of God,” without the coming of the Word himself, with the Greek text before us: πῶς δύνανται ἐκεῖνοι λόγον Θεοῦ λελαληκέναι, τοῦ λόγου τοῦ Θεοῦ μὴ ἐπιδημήσαντος αὐτοῖς?—“How could they have spoken the word of God, when the Word of God had not come to them?” Rabanus likewise approves the restored reading, reproduced in exactly the same words.] of God without the coming of the Word himself?

But we who belong to the Church ought to pay particular attention to this, since we wish the God of the Law and of the Gospel to be the same God, the same God in ancient times, now, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen. There are some who, according to their own opinion, divide the ancient divinity from the one proclaimed in Christ. We know one God, both in the past and in the present; one Christ, likewise then and now; and one Holy Spirit, eternal with the Father and the Son.

This has been said because it is written: “The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying.” Let us therefore hear what he says: “Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants [Al. inhabitatores, inhabitants] of Jerusalem.”

We are the men of Judah on account of Christ, and there is no doubt that our Lord arose from Judah. If I prove from the Scriptures that the name “Judah” itself refers to Christ, [Note: [Col. 0633D] We supplied the word “men,” which was missing, both from Rabanus’s reading and from the Greek ἄνδρες Ἰούδα, “men of Judah,” and from Huet’s own conjecture.] the men of Judah will not be unbelieving Jews, but we who believe in Christ.

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands are upon the backs of your enemies” (Genesis 49:8). “They praise you.” The brothers of Jacob’s son Judah did not praise that Judah; rather, his brothers now praise Judah. For this Judah says: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing to you” (Psalm 22:22). [Note: [Col. 0633D] In Rabanus, instead of “I will sing to you,” read “I will sacrifice you” in the hymn; perhaps the one-word form hymnificabo, “I will hymn,” should be read, corresponding to the Greek ὑμνήσω.]

It is said to that Judah: “Your hands are upon the backs of your enemies.” Where is it found that that Judah placed his hands upon the backs of his enemies? History records nothing of the sort about him. But if you consider the advent of my [Al. our] Lord Jesus Christ, who destroyed the Devil, stripped the principalities and powers, displayed them openly, and triumphed over them on the wood (1 Corinthians 15:24), you will see how the prophecy was fulfilled concerning this Judah: “Your hands are upon the backs of your enemies.”

And now, when the word is addressed to the men of Judah, no one doubts that it is addressed to Christians, on account of Christ, who was born from the tribe of Judah. The word is also addressed to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, namely, to those [Col. 0634A] who dwell in the Church. This is the city of the great King; this is the vision of peace. For peace is multiplied and made visible in us—provided that we are sons of peace.

“Hear, therefore, the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this covenant, which God commanded your fathers” (Jeremiah 11:2–3). [Note: [Col. 0633D] The name “God,” missing here, is supplied by Rabanus and the Greek. We have often elsewhere restored minor omissions of this kind.] Who hears the words of the covenant that God commanded the fathers more truly: we who believe in Christ, or those who did not even believe Moses because they do not believe in Christ? To them the Savior says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5:46–47).

Therefore they did not believe Moses; but we, truly believing in Christ, believe the covenant handed down through Moses. To us it is said, lest we become accursed: “Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this covenant, which he commanded your fathers.” Thus they are accursed, for they did not hear the covenant that God commanded the fathers: “On the day,” he says, “when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace.” [Note: [Col. 0633D] The words “And God brought us out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace,” which were absent from the previously printed editions, had been fused with the preceding words into a single sentence, leaving no coherent meaning. The recurrence of the word “iron,” which caused the copyist, through a common scribal error, to skip the words between the two occurrences, was responsible. Without discussing the other editors, Huet should at least have been alerted by the Greek text, which he printed in the facing column: Καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐξήγαγεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐκ τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ἐκ τῆς καμίνου τῆς σιδηρᾶς, μάλιστα κατά … These words mean exactly in Latin: “And God brought us out,” and so forth. We have also supplied the words from Rabanus, and restored above the scriptural testimony to its original completeness.]

“And God brought us out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace”—especially if one understands what is written in John’s Apocalypse: that the place where the Lord was crucified is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt. For if someone is called Egypt spiritually, and is not Egypt according to bodily or literal understanding, there is no doubt that, if you understand the spiritual Egypt and come out of it, you are one who is coming out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, and the following is said to you: “Hear my voice, and do according to all these things.”

Then God’s promise is made to those who hear, if they do whatever the Lord commands: “You shall be my people, and I shall be your God” (Jeremiah 11:4). Not everyone who says that he is God’s people is God’s people. The Jewish people, proclaiming themselves to be God’s people, deserved to hear: “You are not my people”; and it was said to them: “Not my people.” Again, this people was called “not a people.” [Note: [Col. 0634D] In view of the sense of the passage and the Holy Doctor’s intention, we did not doubt that Origen himself supplies here the missing negative particle in the Greek, οὐ λαός, “not a people,” although we have not found it in the Latin manuscripts.] “They have made me jealous,” he says, “with what is not God” (Deuteronomy 32:21). Concerning them he says: “They provoked me with their idols, and I will make them jealous with what is not a nation; with a foolish nation I will provoke them.”

We, therefore, have been made God’s people, and righteousness is proclaimed to the people [Col. 0635A] that will be born from the Gentiles. For this people is born suddenly, and it is written in the prophet: “If a nation was born all at once.” When the Savior ascended into heaven, and five thousand believed in one day (Acts 4:4), while on another day three thousand were added, then truly one could see a people born all at once through the word of God, and suddenly the barren woman giving birth, to whom it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman, who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1).

The Church was desolate, abandoned by the Law and abandoned by God. But the synagogue, having a husband, possessed the Law and God. What, then, does God promise? “You shall be my people, and I shall be your God.” God is not the God of everyone, but only of those to whom he has given himself, as to that patriarch to whom he says: “I am your God” (Genesis 17:7); and again to another: “I will be God; I will be your God” (Exodus 29:45); and concerning others: “I will be their God,” he says.

Do we perhaps at some point attain what I express individually, so that the God of all may become our God? But if you wish to learn more fully whose God he is, and to whom he grants the title of his name, he says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). Explaining this very saying, the Savior says: “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Luke 20:38).

Who is dead? Certainly the sinner, who does not have one saying: “I am life” (John 11:25); who has dead works; who has not yet repented of dead works. Of him [Al. them] the Apostle says: “Not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works” (Hebrews 6:1).

If, therefore, God is not the God of the dead but of the living; and we know that the one who lives in Christ, so as to become a participant in him, is living; and if we wish God also to be our God, let us renounce dead works, so that he may fulfill his promise in us, saying: “I will be your God,” in order that I may establish [Al. raise up a testimony, etc.] my oath, which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey (Jeremiah 11:4).

Observe what he says: “I will establish the oath that I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey.” This is not, however, the land concerning which the Savior taught: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew 5:5).

Then, in response to these words spoken by God—namely, to the statement, “Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this covenant” (Jeremiah 11:3)—the prophet answered and said: “Let it be, Lord.” What does “Let it be, Lord” mean? Certainly it means what God pronounced: “Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this covenant.”

And the Lord said to me: “Read these words in the city of Judah and outside Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 11:6). [Note: [Col. 0635D] Previously the text was read continuously, as though it were a scriptural testimony: “and to those who are outside, hear the divine words calling us to salvation”; or, “We read the divine words calling them to salvation.” The Greek text strongly contradicts that reading: Καὶ τοῖς ἔξω ἀναγινώσκομεν τοὺς λόγους τοῦ Θεοῦ, προσκαλούμενοι αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ σωτηρίαν, τοὺς λόγους τῆς διαθήκης etc.—“And to those who are outside we read the words of God, calling them to salvation, the words of the covenant,” and so forth. A manuscript designated R by Huet supports this reading and agrees with the Greek: “Also to those who are outside we read the divine words, calling them to salvation: ‘The words of this covenant,’ and so forth.” Elsewhere the text was also incorrectly printed, according to Huet: “Also and to those who are outside. Hear the divine words calling you to salvation, the words of this covenant,” and so forth.] “And to those who are outside we read the divine words, calling them to salvation: ‘The words of this covenant, and do them.’”

And the Lord said to me: “A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” If we sin, we who are called Christians on account of Christ [Note: [Col. 0636D] Huet’s Royal manuscripts read: “we are called men of Judah, and knots of sins are found in us”; the Greek text is somewhat closer to this reading.], and if we are found among the number of sinners, then it is said concerning us: “A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 11:9). When there are such people in the Church of God, people in whom the snare of iniquity and the bonds of sin are found, so much so that what is said concerning a sinner can apply to them—“Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Proverbs 5:22)—then God says: “A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah.”

But no conspiracy will be found in us. How, however, will no conspiracy be found in us if, even to this hour, a conspiracy exists in some? Rather: “Loosen every bond of iniquity; undo the obligations of violent exchanges; scatter every unjust contract; break your bread for the hungry” (Isaiah 58:6–7).

Thus a conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

“They have returned to the iniquities of their former fathers” (Jeremiah 11:10). [Note: [Col. 0636D] What follows from here to the end has wrongly been appended to the ninth homily on Isaiah, which falsely claims Jerome as translator; we published it in the Appendix to Volume IV to supply that homily’s mutilation.] “They have returned to iniquities.” Whose? He does not simply say “of their fathers,” but adds “of their former fathers.” We have said that this is spoken concerning us and concerning those who are sinners among us.

How, then, have the sinners among us returned to the iniquities of their fathers, and of their former fathers? We have two kinds of fathers, and one kind consists of the worst fathers. For before we believed, the Devil was our father, as the Gospel saying shows: “You are born from your father the Devil” (John 8:44). But when we believe, we become sons of God.

If, therefore, after this we sin, we return to the iniquities not simply of our fathers, but of our former fathers. As proof of this, that we have two kinds of fathers, we also use the testimony of David, who says in the forty-fourth Psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and the house of your father” (Psalm 45:10). For he begins as though speaking of a father: “Hear, daughter.” Therefore our fathers are of two kinds. But he says: “Forget the house of your former father.”

If, therefore, after forgetting the house of your former father, you again turn toward sins, you have fallen into what is now called sin: “They have returned to the iniquities of their former fathers.”

We said earlier that the Devil was our father before God became our Father—if indeed we do not now also have the Devil as our father. This too we establish from the Epistle of John, where it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is born from the Devil” (1 John 3:8). As often as we sin, we are born from the Devil. Unhappy is the person who is continually begotten by the Devil; and exceedingly blessed, in turn, is the one who is continually born from God.

For I will not say that the righteous is born from God only once; rather, through each individual work of virtue the righteous is continually born from God. This can be proved more fully if we also speak about the daily birth of our Savior, clearly establishing in the righteous what preceded in the Lord.

Our Savior is the radiance of glory. Radiance is not born only once and then ceases to be born; whenever the light from which the radiance arises comes forth, the radiance of glory likewise comes forth. [Note: [Col. 0637D] Huet notes that Origen uses the same comparison in his second book against the Origenists, section 24; Tertullian also uses it in his Apology, chapter 21: “Even when a ray is extended from the sun, it is a portion from the whole. Yet the sun is in the ray, because the ray belongs to the sun; the substance is not separated but extended. Thus there is spirit from Spirit and God from God, as light kindled from light. The original substance remains complete and undiminished, even if several offshoots borrow from it their quality. Thus what proceeds from God is God, and the Son of God; both are one.” Similar statements occur in Against Praxeas, chapter 9: “The Father is the whole substance, but the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole,” as he himself declares: “Because the Father is greater than I.” From this it is clear in what sense he said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance, one state, and one power, and that the Son derives himself from nowhere other than the substance of the Father. Augustine himself explains the generation of the Word by the same comparison at the very beginning of Book VI of On the Trinity, although he does not draw the same conclusions from it: “Arius himself is said to have argued: If he is Son, he was born; if he was born, there was a time when the Son did not exist—without understanding that for God being born is eternal, so that the Son is co-eternal with the Father, just as radiance, which is generated by fire and diffused from it, is coeval with it, and would be co-eternal if the fire were eternal.”]

Thus, as often as the light has arisen, the radiance [Col. 0637B] also arises. Our Savior is the wisdom of God; and wisdom is the radiance of eternal light. Therefore the Savior is always being born, and for that reason he says: “Before all the hills he begets me,” not, as some incorrectly read, “he begot me.”

If the Lord is always born from the Father, then you too, having only the scriptural status of adoption in his likeness, are always begotten by God through each individual understanding and each individual work, and you become a son of God in Christ Jesus, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY SEVEN

Concerning what is written: “The whole land has been utterly devastated”; and concerning this passage: “The loincloth” (Jeremiah 12:11 and 13:1).

[Col. 0637C]

807 Who is the one who says: “Because of me the whole land has been utterly devastated”? Christ speaks these words. For before his advent there were indeed many sins among the people of Israel, but when the Lord came he prevented such things, so that they would be abandoned altogether and the people would be handed over to a long captivity.

But when they had filled up the measure of their fathers, and added to the killing of the prophets, the persecution of the righteous, and the killing of the Savior, then this was fulfilled: “Your house shall be left to you desolate.” And because he suffered from them what is written in the Gospel, therefore it is now said: “The whole land has been utterly devastated.”

808 If you wish to understand this more subtly—“Because of me the whole land has been utterly devastated”—consider how the earth that is in you has been devastated; then you will see that, after the advent of Jesus Christ, what was said has been fulfilled through the mortification of our members that are upon the earth. The earth no longer performs its works; among the righteous there no longer occur the things by which the flesh was formerly nourished: neither fornication, nor uncleanness, nor [Note: [Col. 0638D] Instead of “luxury of adultery,” which appeared corruptly in the printed editions, we have restored “luxury” from Rabanus. The Greek likewise differed, reading οὐκ ἀσέλγεια, “not licentiousness,” and the sequence of the argument is more harmonious.] excessive luxury, nor the service of idols, nor benefits.

The Lord says: “What do you think? I have come to send peace upon the earth? I have not come to send peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34). Truly, before he descended, there was no sword upon the earth; nor did the flesh desire against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. But when he came, and we were taught what belongs to the flesh and what belongs to the spirit, his teaching, like a sword inserted between them, divided the flesh—that is, the earth—from the spirit, and devastated it (2 Corinthians 4:10), because we carry the mortification of Jesus Christ in our body. We no longer live according to the flesh; the spirit lives, and we sow not in the flesh but in the spirit, so that we may not reap corruption from the flesh but eternal life from the spirit (Galatians 6:8).

It is said to sinners: “You have sown wheat and reaped thorns” (Jeremiah 12:13). Whoever produces the words of God neither according to the intention of the Scriptures nor according to the truth of faith sows wheat and reaps thorns. Heretics do this: they read the Scriptures, but they reap thorns not from the holy books, but from their own opinions.

“Their clergy will not benefit them.” Others before me have explained this, and since I do not reject their interpretation, I offer the same interpretation in agreement with them—not as though I myself had discovered it, but repeating what has already been discovered, so that it may benefit me and you alike, provided that an attentive mind receives what must be said.

We who are thought to be something—that is, we who preside over you in the order of the clergy—so much so that some wish to pass from a lower rank to this position, must understand that we are not automatically saved because we are clergy. For many presbyters perish, while laypeople are found to be supremely blessed; rather, we must both deserve and possess the clerical order.

Because there are certain clergy who do not live in such a way that they themselves receive the fruit of their order and are an ornament to their dignity, those who have explained the prophet say that he now declares: “Their clergy will not benefit them” (Jeremiah 12:13). [Note: [Col. 0638D] Huet’s royal manuscripts read: “those who explained the things that the prophet has now said.” Rabanus reads: “those who explained this prophet has said.”]

The benefit of the clerical office does not consist in someone sitting in the ranks of presbyters, but in his walking worthily according to his station and according to the Lord’s commandments.

But, beloved, [Col. 0639A] do not think that this has been said only about us. The divine majesty admonishes both us and you to live according to the commandments of the Scriptures. And, if it is appropriate to say so: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” [Al. “will suffer,” rather than “suffer”]. More is required of me than of a deacon, and more of a deacon than of a layperson.

Whoever holds the citadel of the entire Church [Note: [Col. 0639C] Huet considers it appropriate to reproduce the following words concerning this passage. Origen seems, he says, to have indicated the bishop or metropolitan at the place where he was preaching. It is likely that these homilies were delivered at Caesarea in Palestine. Thus he may have meant either Theoctistus, bishop of Caesarea, or certainly Babylas, patriarch of Antioch. I am not certain, however, whether he had already gone to Tyre. It is likely that Jerome understood this as referring to the Roman pontiff, as his words indicate. He calls him the chief priest in the preface to the Gospel addressed to Damasus and discusses his authority at length in the letter to the same man: “Although your greatness terrifies me, your kindness nonetheless invites me. I ask protection from a shepherd for a sheep. Let envy stand aside; let the ambition of the Roman summit withdraw. I speak with the successor of the fisherman and the disciple of the cross. Following no one as first except Christ, I am joined in communion with your blessedness—that is, with the chair of Peter. I know that the Church is built upon that rock. Whoever eats the Lamb outside this house is profane. If anyone is not in Noah’s ark, he will perish when the flood reigns.” Ambrosiaster says something similar in his commentary on 1 Timothy 3: “Although the whole world belongs to God, the Church is nevertheless called his house, whose ruler today is Damasus.” It is likewise probable that Rufinus means the Roman pontiff when he says, in his interpretation of Origen’s seventeenth homily on Genesis: “A ruler will not fail from Judah”—that is, the one who is appointed ruler of the Churches after Christ’s resurrection.] will render an account for the whole Church.

For this reason the Apostle Paul—since much had been entrusted to him—said: “Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here, moreover, it is required among stewards that one be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:1–2).

It is so rare to find a good steward that Jesus, who knew beforehand what would happen before those future events arose, said: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise steward whom the Lord will set over his household, to give his fellow servants their food at the proper time?” (Luke 12:42). And shortly afterward, having spoken against certain stewards, he continued: “But if that evil servant begins to say: ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat, drink, and become drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in two and appoint his portion with the unbelievers” (Luke 12:45–46).

This concerns what is written: “Their clergy will not benefit them.”

Let us consider also the correction that follows and that, as it seems to me, ought to be understood in a moral sense: “Be ashamed of your boasting, from the reproach before the Lord” (Jeremiah 12:13).

There are many things in which, while boasting, we display our foolishness. For example, if some boast in extensive possessions, it is said to them: “Be ashamed of your boasting.” If some boast in the nobility of their lineage, it is said to them: “Be ashamed of your boasting.” If some walk about boastfully in the most costly garments or in a house richly adorned with wealth—for this boasting is alien [Note: [Col. 0640D] We supplied the words “this boasting” from Rabanus, in agreement with the Greek text: ἀλλοτρία ἐστὶν ἡ καύχησις καυχήσεως ἁγίων, “this boasting is alien to the boasting of the saints.” We likewise supplied “it is said to them” instead of “he says,” from the same source. Rabanus also consistently reads “them” instead of “him.”] to the boasting of the saints—it is said to them: “Be ashamed of your boasting.”

But this is little. Hear what the divine word speaks in Jeremiah, commanding us not to boast even in our own wisdom: “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let the one who boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows that I am the Lord” (Jeremiah 9:23–24).

Do you wish to boast and not hear the command, “Be ashamed of your boasting”? Boast as the Apostle [Al. “Paul” is added] does, and say: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through [Al. “because of”] whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

Do you wish to boast and not hear “Be ashamed of your boasting”? Hear Paul boasting, and learn what he says: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.” Hear what his boasts are, in which the holy man exalts himself: “In labors abundantly; in prisons beyond measure; in deaths often; from the Jews five times I received forty lashes minus one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck” (2 Corinthians 11:23–25). [Note: [Col. 0640D] The royal manuscripts in Huet read: “in which the holy man used to exalt himself.”]

Let us learn the differences among boasts. There are some who boast in things deserving shame, whose glory is in their disgrace. For they boast in things that, when they do them, they seek concealment and secrecy (Philippians 3:19).

After this, let us consider what command was given concerning the loincloth.

Thus says the Lord: “Go and take for yourself a linen loincloth, and put it around your loins, and you shall not pass through water with it.” And I took the loincloth according to the word of the Lord, who said to me: “Take the loincloth that is around your loins, and go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a cleft of the rock” (Jeremiah 13:1–4).

After some days the prophet came and took the loincloth from the place where he had buried it, and behold, it had rotted and was fit for no use. And lest anyone presume to derive from this passage an interpretation according to his own inclination, the Lord, giving occasion for the interpretation, added: “For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I attached to myself the house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, so that they might become for me a people of renown, praise, and glory; but they did not obey me” (Jeremiah 13:11).

Therefore, in this passage the prophet should be understood as representing God, surrounding his loins with a linen loincloth—that is, God surrounds himself with the people. “I attached,” he says, “the house of Israel to myself,” and in a certain sense a righteous person becomes God’s loincloth.

You may ask for what reason. Read Ezekiel and understand how God appears in a body, why fire is seen from his loins down to his feet, and amber from his loins up to his head (Ezekiel 1:27). Then you will also be able to discover the meaning of the present Scripture: why the lower parts of God are fiery. The kidneys are considered generative, and the loins are regarded as fire. For everything that proceeds from intercourse and pleasure requires purification, and purification itself is mingled with punishment.

But the things that rise upward from the kidneys transcend the works of lust by their virtue; like a purer substance, they are compared to amber. Amber is said to be more precious than gold. Why, then, does Scripture use examples to show that the upper part of God’s body is magnificent and the lower part inferior? For this reason it now introduces the Lord as subsisting of fire and amber. [Note: [Col. 0641D] The royal manuscripts read: “It introduced the Lord’s body as consisting of fire and amber.”]

Thus each of us, according to the beginning of our birth, is compared to fire; but according to our zeal and progress we become that upper body of God, that which is of amber, as we depart from fire, punishments, and torment.

Therefore put a linen loincloth around your loins. Why? So that it may be shown that the people are God’s kingdom. For it resists and protects the works of its God against those who wish to accuse God’s providence, and it does not allow anything indecent to be said about his majesty.

But when we sin, just as the prophet removed that loincloth and cast it into the Euphrates so that it might rot there, so God will cast us away from his loins and leave us abandoned by the Euphrates River of Mesopotamia, where the Assyrians who are enemies of Israel dwell, where the Babylonians dwell; and there we shall rot.

For why, with so many rivers throughout the whole world left aside, does the prophet send the loincloth from Judea to the Euphrates, unless he intends, according to the force of the name, to teach a sacramental meaning?

After this we ask why it is called a linen loincloth. [Note: [Col. 0641D] Rabanus incorrectly has: “Flax feeds upon the earth.” Shortly afterward he also has “from the harvest” instead of “harvested.”]

Flax grows from the earth. When its seed has been cast into the soil, it first sprouts as grass; then, to pass over countless intermediate stages, once harvested it is carried home, combed, washed, beaten, pounded, and, so to speak, stripped by immense labor, so that it may become something from which a loincloth [Note: [Col. 0641D] The royal manuscripts read: “from which a loincloth may be made, or something else adapted to necessary uses”; for the final verb, Rabanus has comparari, “be prepared.”] or something else may be fashioned for necessary use.

We too, therefore—all of us who have our origin from the earth, who are woven into God’s loincloth [Note: [Col. 0641D] We have restored from Rabanus the reading found also in ancient manuscripts: “who are woven into God’s loincloth,” as more consonant with Origen’s Greek text and more suitable: καὶ ἡμεῖς οὖν πάντες τὴν γένεσιν ἔχομεν, ὡς περίζωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ, “and so we all have our origin as God’s loincloth.” Previously the text read: “or flax, which is combed into God’s loincloth”; one manuscript in Huet reads: “as flax which …”]—require much care, so that we may be combed, washed, and cast off the color of the earth.

For flax has one color in its natural state and another when it has been cleansed by labor [Al. “cleansed through work”]. The color of its natural state is darker and blacker [Al. “and we call it black”], while that produced by work is brighter. [Note: [Col. 0642D] Here too it would have been preferable to reproduce Rabanus. For instead of these words—“I do not know what and in us”—the printed editions had a single word, “something.” The Greek text clearly reads τοιοῦτόν οὖν τι καὶ ἐπὶ ἡμᾶς, “something of this kind also occurs in us.”]

Something of this kind also happens to us at the beginning: we are black when we are regenerated, when we believe, when we say in the Song of Songs: “I am black and beautiful” (Song of Songs 1:5). We have a soul like that of the Ethiopians, disgraceful [Note: [Col. 0642D] The word “disgraceful” should more properly be removed here, for neither Rabanus knows it nor does it occur in the Greek text. Instead of the following word “we are washed,” Rabanus reads “then why are we washed?” The Greek nearly agrees: εἶτα ἀποσμηχόμεθα, “then we are scrubbed clean.”]

We are washed so that we may become white, so that through diligence we may attain the radiance that was not implanted in us by nature, according to what is written in the same passage: “Who is this that comes up whitened?” And we become pure, white linen [Note: [Col. 0642D] Previously the text read: “and pure with water. Thus, when …” We have removed the word “water” according to Rabanus, since it is superfluous and absent from the Greek, and begin: “And so, when …” Likewise, Origen’s Greek has εἶτα καί, “and then.”].

And so, when we have become worthy of fellowship with God, we are folded [Al. “woven”] into his loincloth, nor are we ever removed from him, provided that we always retain the whiteness he has granted us.

When, therefore, the Jews and the whole house of Israel proved unworthy of God and were cast away by him, he girded himself with us in their place. For we must not think that, after casting away the loincloth, he remained ungirded. As soon as he cast them away, he wove another loincloth for himself.

This loincloth is the Church gathered from the Gentiles. It must understand that, if God did not spare the former people, neither will he spare it if it abandons him, if it is not worthy of his loins, if, cleaving to the Lord, it is not one spirit in Christ Jesus, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY EIGHT

Concerning what is written: “Make known to me, Lord, and I shall know” (Jeremiah 11:18), up to the passage where he says: “Go, gather all the beasts of the field” (Jeremiah 12:9).

[Col. 0642C]

813 If the divine utterances are found in the Law and the Prophets, the Gospels and the Apostles, the disciple of God ought to ascribe the role of teacher of divine discourse to God. For, according to the Psalmist, God is the one “who teaches man knowledge” (Ps. 93:10). The Savior likewise bears witness that no one ought to be called teacher upon earth, saying: “And do not call anyone your teacher upon earth. For one is your teacher, the Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:8). The Father, then, who is in heaven, will instruct [or: instructs] human beings either through himself, or through the Son, or through the Holy Spirit; and, to come down to lesser matters, he instructs through Paul, through Peter, or through any other of the saints—provided only that the Spirit of God [or: the God-Spirit] and the word of God descend and teach.

Why have we said this? Clearly because the prophet says: “Make known to me, Lord, and I shall know.” For I cannot know unless you reveal it to me. But if, when you demonstrate it, 814 I am able [or: shall be able] to know what I do not know, then I shall see the thoughts of each person, and I shall know what each one is doing and what his will is [or: what each one’s will is]. Thus far the prophet.

Let us then see what the Savior says in the prophet: “I was led like an innocent lamb to be slaughtered, and I did not know. They plotted a scheme against me, saying: Come, let us put wood into his bread, and let us destroy him from the land of the living, and his name shall no longer be remembered” (Jer. 11:19). Isaiah likewise declares that Christ was led like a sheep to the slaughter and, like a lamb before its shearer, was silent and did not open his mouth. There, however, the prophet speaks about Christ; here Christ himself speaks about himself: “I,” he says, “was led like an innocent lamb to be slaughtered, and I did not know” (Isa. 53:7).

Nor does he add what it was that he did not know. For he did not say, “I did not know evils; I did not know good things; I did not know sin or injustice,” 815 but simply, “I did not know.” He has therefore left it to you to ask what he did not know. Read the Apostle: “He made him who did not know sin to be sin for us” (2 Cor. 5:21). For to know sin is to sin, just as to know righteousness is to act righteously. From this it is clear that the one who preaches righteousness but does not act righteously does not know righteousness.

“They plotted a scheme against me, saying: Come, let us put wood into his bread.” That the Lord was crucified by the Jews is beyond doubt, and we proclaim this with complete freedom. But how shall we apply to him what is said—“They plotted a scheme against me, saying”—when what follows, “Come, let us put wood into his bread,” presents an extreme difficulty? The bread of Jesus, by which we are nourished, is interpreted as his word. Since, then, certain people wished, while he was teaching, to place a stumbling block in his doctrine, when they crucified him they said: “Come, let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11:19). For when the crucifixion of the teacher is joined to the word and teaching of Jesus, wood is put into his bread.

[Note: [Col. 0643D] We have emended the text in this manner on the basis of Rabanus’s reading, “let those plotting say,” since up to now it stood with the rather disgraceful error, “unless those giving say.” The Greek archetype likewise indicated that it should be restored in this way; for it has: “Let those who have plotted a conspiracy out of treachery say” (ἐκεῖνοι μὲν ἐξ ἐπιβουλῆς βουλευσάμενοι λεγέτωσαν), and so forth.]

And let those plotting treachery say: “Come, let us put wood into his bread.” But I shall add something marvelous: the wood put into his bread made the bread better. Take an example from the Law of Moses. Just as the wood thrown into the bitter water made it sweet, so the wood of Christ’s passion, thrown into his teaching, made his bread sweeter.

Before wood was put into his bread—when there was only bread and no wood—his sound had not gone out into the whole earth. But after he acquired strength through the wood, then the word of his passion was spread throughout the entire world. This was prefigured also when the water in the Old Testament was made sweet by the touch of wood.

For I say that the Law, when it is not understood, is bitter water. But when the wood of Jesus Christ comes, and the word of my Savior descends into it, then it is sweetened and becomes of the most pleasing taste: the Law of Moses is understood as well as read.

Those who say, “Come, let us put wood into his bread,” add this also: “And let us destroy him from the land of the living, and his name shall no longer be remembered” (Jer. 11:19). Thus they killed him as though they would utterly erase [or: erase] his name. But Jesus knows why and how he dies. Therefore he says: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, has died, it remains alone; but if it has died, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

[Note: [Col. 0643D] These words of the sacred text had previously been missing: “it remains alone; but if it has died.” Previously it read: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, has died,” followed immediately by “it bears not much fruit.” We restored the text from Rabanus and from the Greek text itself, as Origen cites it: “it remains alone; but if it dies, [it bears] much fruit” (αὐτὸς μόνος μένει· ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ, πολλὴν etc.).]

816 Therefore the death of Jesus Christ became a head of grain, returning sevenfold and much more than what had been sown. Let us suppose for a moment that he had not been crucified and had not descended after his death to the underworld: it follows that the grain of wheat would remain alone, and many would not be born from it.

Pay close attention to the divine utterances and what they intend to be understood as saying. “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, has died, it bears not much fruit” (John 12:24). The death of Jesus made all these people fruitful. But if his death brought forth such abundant crops, what abundance will his resurrection have?

“Lord of hosts, judging justly, testing kidneys and hearts, let me see your vengeance upon them” (Jer. 11:20). Prophetically he prays that he may see vengeance upon them with the Father. For Jerusalem was surrounded by an army, its overthrow had drawn near, and what had been said to it—“Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38)—was fulfilled.

“Let me see, then, the vengeance upon them that comes from you, because to you I have revealed my justification.” Therefore the Lord says this concerning the men who are in Anathoth, who seek my life and say: “You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, or else you shall die by our hands.” “Behold, I shall visit them: their young men shall fall by the sword, and their sons and daughters shall die of famine, and there shall be no remnant of them. For I shall bring evils upon the inhabitants of Anathoth in the year of their visitation” (Jer. 11:21–23).

Figuratively, the name Anathoth is now assumed [the transmitted text repeats “now”]. The whole Jewish mystery is contained in it. Anathoth is interpreted as “obedience.” Since, therefore, obedience to God was in that people, as was his kingdom, what we know had been foretold concerning the kingdom came to pass: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21:43).

[Note: [Col. 0644D] We supplied from Rabanus and from the Greek archetype the word “people,” which had previously been absent: “in that people” (ἐν ἐκείνῳ ἦν τῷ λαῷ). Below we have also corrected several less important matters.]

Now, too, the men who are in Anathoth—that is, in obedience—817 seek the life not of Jeremiah; for no history records this, that the men of Anathoth sought [or: seek] his life. We have the Books of Kings: Scripture mentions Jeremiah there, but nothing of this sort is written. We have Chronicles as well, and in the very volume of the Prophet that is now being interpreted, the men of Anathoth said nothing. Rather, they seek the life of Christ, my Lord, saying: “You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord.” We read this [or: here] also: the Jews forbade Christ to teach, saying, “Otherwise you shall die by our hands.”

“Behold, I shall visit them: their young men shall fall by the sword, and their sons and daughters shall die of hunger” (Amos 8:11). They did not fall by the sword in Jeremiah’s time, but after the Lord’s coming. Then famine also came upon them—not famine of bread or thirst for water, but famine of hearing the word of God.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] More correctly, together with the Greek text, the word “God” is absent here; Rabanus does not have it in this place.]

For now it is no longer said among them: “Thus says the Lord God Almighty.” This is the famine of prophecy, when the prophetic voice has ceased among them.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] In Rabanus: “This is the famine of the prophetic voice that has ceased,” and so forth.]

But why should I speak of prophets? No teachers or instructors at all have remained in Judaea.
