And although there are countless people who lay claim to wisdom for themselves, the word of God is no longer among them. For that prophecy has been fulfilled: “The Lord will remove from Judaea and Jerusalem the mighty man and the mighty woman, the strength of bread and the strength of water, the giant and the strong man, and the warrior, and the judge, and the prophet, and the counselor, and the elder, and the captain of fifty, and the marvelous counselor, and the wise architect, and the intelligent hearer” (Isa. 3:1).

[Note: [Col. 0645D] Rabanus likewise has this reading, as does the Greek text itself cited by Origen: “the giant and the strong man and the warrior” (γίγαντα καὶ ἰσχύοντα καὶ ἄνθρωπον πολεμιστήν).]

Now there is no one among them who can say: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (1 Cor. 3:10). The architects have migrated from them and come to the Church; they have laid Jesus Christ as the foundation. All who believed after them build upon it.

That people, therefore, has been abandoned in famine: “For I shall bring evils upon the inhabitants of Anathoth in the year of their visitation” (Jer. 11:23).

818 “Righteous are you, Lord, for I shall plead my case before you. Nevertheless, I shall speak judgments to you. Why does the way of sinners prosper? All who scorn contemptuously have flourished” (Jer. 12:1).

Let us ask whether God is good, since he gave the Law and the prophets, while we see the way of the ungodly prospering and observe that they suffer nothing from him in proportion to their deserts. For “all who scorn contemptuously” have flourished.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] “I cannot at all devise the reasoning behind this interpretation,” says Huetius, “for the Greek has: ‘all who reject rejections’ (πάντες οἱ ἀθετοῦντες ἀθετήματα).” Corderius correctly has: “All who transgress transgressions.”]

These are the people who bark against the Creator with rabid jaws and accuse him with blasphemous words: “They have flourished”—they have been planted and have taken root; they have begotten children and produced fruits. How many fruits did Marcion produce by begetting children of unbelief? How many Basilides? How many Valentinus? Concerning these, indeed, the prophet says: “They have begotten children and produced fruit.”

“Near are you to their mouth, but far from their kidneys” (Jer. 12:2). They name Jesus, but do not possess him; for they do not confess him as Christ.

“And you, Lord, have known me and tested my heart in your presence. Sanctify them on the day of their slaughter” (Jer. 12:3).

[Note: [Col. 0645D–0646D] Origen adds “me” (μὲ), and then “you saw me” (εἶδές με), as in Rabanus and the Vulgate: “you have known me, you have seen me, and you have tested,” and so forth.] What shall I do to explain this? He calls the torments of those who are tormented their sanctification. “Sanctify them,” he says, “on the day of their slaughter”—that is, sanctify them by the very fact that you kill them. “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

“How long shall the earth mourn, and all the grass of the field wither because of the wickedness of those who dwell upon the earth?” (Jer. 12:4.)

[Note: [Col. 0646D] Since Origen here defines the earth as inanimate, but says that it can be called animate only through an angel, as through an attending rather than informing form, it is sufficiently demonstrated from this that he did not adhere entirely to the error which Jerome, in his letters to Avitus and Pammachius, and Justinian, in his letter to Menas, attribute to him—namely, that the stars are not only animate but can also sin and await salvation.]

As though the earth were an animal, the prophet now speaks in this way, saying that it mourns when wicked inhabitants dwell in it. For in each one of us the earth either rejoices in the virtues of its inhabitants or mourns in their vices.

But if the earth does so, then consequently the other elements do so as well, including the water—that is, the angel who has been set over the waters. For I cannot otherwise explain the earth as mourning or rejoicing; nor does reason allow us to believe that an insensible body feels, unless we understand that angels preside over all things: over earth and water, air and fire—that is, that they rule the elements—and in this order extend to all animals, every plant, and even the heavenly stars.

One angel has been appointed over the lands. Thus all those angels with whom we live upon the earth rejoice when we act justly, and mourn when we sin.

819 “The earth shall mourn because of all who dwell upon it.” The angel of the earth is called by the same name by which the earth itself is named. For just as, when something made by hand is cursed, the one who made it is also said to be cursed—not because the thing is cursed, since it lacks soul and sensation, but because the one who attends the insensible image is called by the same name as the object that was made—so now the angel appointed over the earth is also called “earth.”

Do not understand this only of the earth. The angel of the waters is likewise called by the name of the waters, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “The waters saw you and were afraid; the abysses were troubled. The multitude of the sound of the waters uttered their voice; indeed, your arrows passed through. I have abandoned my house; I have left my inheritance” (Ps. 76:17).

“I have given my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies” (Jer. 12:7). See him who existed in the form of God in the heavens. See his house: the Thrones and all the exalted Powers. But if you wish to understand something still higher because he says, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” see his house as God the Father.

He leaves his heavenly Father and his heavenly mother, Jerusalem, and comes to this earthly place, saying: “I have abandoned my house; I have left my inheritance.” His inheritance was the angelic possessions and the order of the holy virtues.

“I have given my beloved soul into the hands of my enemies.” He handed his soul into the hands of his enemies: into the hands of the Jews who killed him, into the hands of the rulers gathered against him, into the hands of kings, since “the kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2:1).

“My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest” (Jer. 12:8). This inheritance of his that was upon the earth, which he had chosen for his possession and which had been his portion, 820 became savage against him and became for him—namely, the Jews—like a lion in the forest.

Nor is it surprising that it was compared with so savage a beast. To the present day there are [or: then were] lions in the forest, anathematizing the Lord Jesus, blaspheming him, and plotting against those who believe [or: believers] in his name.

“My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest. It raised its voice against me; therefore I hated it. Is my inheritance for me like a hyena’s cave?” (Jer. 12:8.) He foretells concerning his inheritance that it will become a hyena’s cave, the lair of a rabid and savage beast that lives on the corpses of the dead and always haunts tombs and bones.

“Is my inheritance for me a hyena’s cave, or a cave surrounding it?” (Jer. 12:9.) Since they are such people, I command you, angels: “Go and gather the beasts, and hand them over to be torn apart. Go, gather all the beasts of the field; let them come and devour them.” The beasts of the field came and devoured the Jewish people.

See how the hearts of all have been consumed by opposing powers. If God did not spare them, but said, “Go, gather the beasts,” how much more will he not spare us? If we do not keep his law, if we neglect the word of the Gospel, he will again say: “Go, gather the beasts and hand her over.”

[Note: [Col. 0647D] Previously the text read, “and hand them over,” contrary to Rabanus and the Greek text, which has: “and hand her over” (καὶ παράδοτε αὐτήν).]

But let us trust in the Lord and say in prayer: “Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. 73). Let us repent of our sins and confess the offenses we have committed, and we shall not be handed over to the beasts. Rather, angels will come, carry us in their bosom, transfer us from earthly places to heavenly ones, and establish us from the present age in everlasting eternity, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY NINE

On the passage that is written: “Every wineskin shall be filled with wine” (Jer. 13:12), up to the passage: “And your eyes shall shed tears, because the Lord’s flock has been broken” (Jer. 13:17).

[Col. 0647D]

[Col. 0648A] What the prophet is commanded by God to say ought to be worthy of God’s command. But it does not appear worthy if we remain with the literal sense and seek nothing higher—821 so much so that if an inexperienced hearer were present, he might say that it is foolish to lend an ear to the Scriptures and to understand what is repeatedly read in them. This is the statement of the animal person: “For the animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him” (1 Cor. 2:14).

Let us therefore consider what the word of God commands: “And you shall say to the people this word: Thus says the Lord God of Israel.” What the Lord God of Israel says ought, I ask, to be worthy of the Lord God of Israel: “Every wineskin shall be filled with wine.”

“And it shall be, if they say to you: Surely, knowing, we do not know [or: shall we not know] that every wineskin shall be filled with wine?” If they answer in this way, following only the literal sense and saying that they know [or: shall know] every wineskin shall be filled with wine, they are mistaken. For it does not necessarily follow that all wineskins are filled with wine. Some wineskins are full of oil; others are empty or not full of some liquid substance.

But the Lord says that every wineskin shall be filled with wine, and the people answer: “Surely, knowing, we do not know [or: shall we not know] that every wineskin shall be filled with wine?” This may be interpreted, according to the poverty of my understanding, if we first discern [or: foresee] the differences among wines, so that then we may consequently treat the matter and establish the truth of the statement that every wineskin shall be filled with wine.

[Note: [Col. 0647D] Rabanus inserts “concerning the wineskins”; this is also more faithful, at least to the Greek archetype: “consequently we shall consider them concerning the wineskins, that it is true,” and so forth (ἀκολούθως αὐτοῖς περὶ τῶν ἀσκῶν ὀψόμεθα, ὅτι ἀληθές etc.).]

For whether someone is good, if I may speak in this way, among the wineskins, the wineskin shall be filled with the wine of its goodness; or whether he is evil, according to what he is, the wineskin shall be filled with evil wine.

How, then, can we understand from the Scriptures the differences among wines? Concerning evil wine it is written: “From the vine of Sodom, their vine, and their branch from Gomorrha; their grape [or: grapes] is a grape [or: grapes] of gall, a cluster of bitterness among them; their wine is the poison of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32:32).

[Note: [Col. 0647D] We supplied from Rabanus the words “their vine and their branch,” which completed the previously defective text and which Origen also cites in the Greek: “their vine and their branch” (ἡ ἄμπελος αὐτῶν, καὶ ἡ κληματίς αὐτῶν).]

The following is said of good wine: “Your cup that intoxicates—how excellent it is!” (Ps. 22:5). And Wisdom summons people to her mixing bowl, saying: “Come, eat my breads, 822 and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Prov. 9:5).

There is therefore wine from Sodom, and there is the wine that Wisdom has mixed.

[Note: [Col. 0648D] This second occurrence of the word “wine,” which Rabanus and the Greek text also have, was missing.]

Again: “A vineyard was planted for the beloved [or: love] on a horn, in a fertile place, planted by God.” It is called the vineyard of Sorec, “a certain chosen and remarkable vineyard among all vineyards.”

[Note: [Col. 0648D] Previously the text read: “chosen indeed among all vineyards; but another is remarkable,” contrary to the much more coherent reading of Rabanus and the Greek: “being a certain chosen and remarkable one; but there is also another vineyard,” so that “remarkable” should by no means be applied to the Egyptian vineyard, refe— [source boundary].]

There is also another vineyard of the Egyptians, which God strikes, according to what is written: “He struck their vineyards with hail, and their sycamores with frost” (Ps. 77:47).

Let us therefore consider all human beings, figuratively, to be capable of wine. We can give them no other name than “wineskins,” since they are capable of wine. We may say that the wicked person is full of wine from the vineyard of Sodom and Egypt, full of the wine of Israel’s enemies; but the holy person and the one who advances in virtue is full of wine from the vineyard of Sorec, the wine of which it is written: “Your cup that intoxicates—how excellent it is!” (Ps. 22:5), the wine that Wisdom has mixed.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Instead of “for me,” the text had been corruptly read there; the Greek rejects that reading: “Let it be understood by me according to…” (νοείσθω μοι κατὰ τὴν), as does the older reading of Rabanus. A little later the sense was also incomplete because a particle was missing, which Rabanus supplied, as did the Greek ἵνα.]

Let these things, then, be understood by me according to wickedness and virtue, so that we may recognize how every wineskin shall be filled with wine.

But if wineskins are filled with wickedness or virtues, it follows that they are filled with punishments on account of wickedness and with blessings on account of virtue. Let the sacred Scriptures provide testimony as to how torments or promises are called [or: are called] “wine.”

“Take this cup of unmixed wine and give it to drink to all the nations to which I am sending you” (Jer. 25:15). Jeremiah says this, and then adds: “They shall drink, vomit, rage, and fall.”

Thus in the present passage he has called punishments “unmixed wine.” Some drink unmixed wines—that is, they are worthy of unmixed torments. Others drink punishments that are wines not wholly unmixed but tempered to some degree.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] In the manuscripts of the Royal Library consulted by Huetius: “They shall drink unmixed wines”; and in one manuscript a little later: “punishments not entirely unmixed.”]

“For a cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine that is mixed; he inclined it from this to that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied: all the sinners of the earth shall drink from it” (Ps. 74:9).

823 If you wish also to behold the cup of blessing that the righteous drink, although the testimony of Wisdom is sufficient, where it says, “Drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Prov. 9:5), nevertheless see the Savior ascending on the day of Passover, a large upper room furnished and cleansed, celebrating the feast with his disciples and offering them the cup concerning which it is written in the Gospel (Luke 22:12).

[Note: [Col. 0650D] The sense absolutely requires the opposite reading, with the following supplied: “concerning which it is written, not that he mixed it.” The Greek text compels this: “concerning which it is written, not that he mixed it” (περὶ οὗ γέγραπται, οὐχ ὅτι ἐκέρασεν). In Rabanus, however, the next three complete lines are absent; he reads instead: “concerning which it is written in the Gospel: Take and drink,” and so forth.]

Jesus, bringing joy to the disciples, offers them an unmixed cup and says: “Take and drink: this is my blood, which will be poured out for you for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26:27). “Do this whenever you drink, in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11:24). And: “Amen, I say to you, I shall not drink it from now on until I drink it with you anew in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 26:28).

Do you see the cup of the New Testament? Do you see that the cup of punishments which we explained above is full of unmixed wine? There is also another cup which, in recompense for good or evil deeds, is mixed and handed to you.

Understand [or: you understand], then, that those who entirely depart from piety and oppose religion [or: turn away from religion] in every respect, living by chance and like beasts, drink the cup of unmixed wine that we brought forth from the Book of Jeremiah. But those who have not entirely departed, who are sinners yet are judged unworthy of the cup of the New Testament, and who sometimes perform good works and sometimes their opposites, drink a cup mixed with unmixed wine.

For God “inclined it from this to that.” What does he mean by saying, “from this to that”? I see two cups. “He inclined it from this to that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied” (Ps. 74:9).

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Thus both Rabanus and the manuscripts—Reg. in Huet’s possession—read it: previously, however, it stood, “Now observe.” The Greek is νοεῖ (“consider”). Shortly afterward we likewise added “of your own,” which was missing in those copies.]

Consider the cup of your good works in the Lord’s one hand. But if you will allow me to say something rather boldly, let the cup of virtues be in his right hand and that of vices in his left. When, therefore, you begin to be tormented on account of your sins—for you have also done good works—the cup in the Lord’s hand is full of unmixed wine mixed with something else, and he has inclined it from this one into that: that is, from the cup which was in the right hand into the one held in the left. For you cannot drink only the cup of good works, as though you had done nothing but good; nor, conversely, only that of sins, since you have at times done good as well. Therefore he has inclined it from this one into that, so that, in accordance with the balance of your works, a more watery or a purer punishment is mixed for you, and according to your merits either the sting of divine anger is blunted or sharpened.

If, however, you are good and have kept God’s commandments, attend to what you say: “I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXV, 13).

Every vessel, therefore, whether good or bad, will be filled with wine of its own quality; nor will oil, or anything else liquid, be poured into it, but only the wine of Sodom or of Sorec.

Next, while for the moment following the literal sense, he teaches what sort of wine such vessels must be filled with, on account of those who sinned in Jerusalem and were then living in Judaea. For he continues:

“If they say to you: ‘Do we not know, knowing full well, that every vessel will be filled with wine?’ you shall say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am filling all the inhabitants of this land, the kings, the sons of David who sit upon his throne, and the priests, with drunkenness’” (Jer. XIII, 12).

He spares no one whom he is going to punish for sins. A person will not be freed from punishment merely because he has been called a prophet or a priest. These things, however, are recalled concerning them, as the Apostle says: “They were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X, 11).

If, then, anyone among these priests—I mean among us presbyters—or among those Levites who attend upon the people, that is, the deacons [Ms. “Zaconibus”], has sinned, he will endure the punishment which the Lord now threatens through the prophet. Conversely, there are certain priestly blessings, concerning which, with God’s help, we shall discuss after explaining this passage, when we come to the Book of Numbers; for there certain things are written about priests.

God therefore testifies that priests and prophets, Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem will be made drunk with wine, and that he will scatter man from his brother, and fathers from their sons (Jer. XIII, 11, 19). These words, as it seems to me, are to be understood as follows: God gathers the righteous, but separates sinners.

Thus, so long as the people had not been moved from the east, they were not scattered [Al. dispersed]. But when they had moved from the east, and a man said to his neighbor, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top may reach to heaven” (Gen. XI, 4), God spoke, saying, “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages there” (Gen. XI, 7, 9).

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Rabanus has: “whose top may reach as far as heaven,” etc. The Greek is οὗ ἔσται ἡ κεφαλὴ ἕως τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, “whose top will be as far as heaven.”]

Shortly afterward Scripture adds: “And God scattered them from there over the face of all the earth.”

The people of Israel likewise, before they sinned, were in Judaea; after their sins they were scattered throughout the whole world.

Understand something similar concerning all of us.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Previously it was corruptly read, “and understand concerning good men,” instead of “and understand concerning all of us.” We restored the reading from Rabanus, in agreement with the Greek text: νόει καὶ περὶ πάντων ἡμῶν, “understand also concerning all of us.”]

There is a Church of the firstborn—that is, of those who are enrolled in heaven—where there are Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. Blessed are those who will be gathered there.

Sinners, however, will be separated from one another, so that they may likewise be tormented together in this very punishment. I know that certain kings have been accustomed to deport those who plotted against their rule to deserted islands, and, as a great punishment, to order this—not allowing them to endure the misery of exile in one place, but having their wives banished to one part of the world and their children to another, so that even in their calamities they could not enjoy the comfort of one another: neither father that of son, nor mother that of daughter, nor brother that of brother.

In a similar way, through a certain providence of God, the sinner suffers the bitterer torments of solitude if he is sent alone into exile, so that, once corrected, he may return to his former condition.

And just as you seek to lead your relatives or children back from the error into which they had fallen—not through a sudden or irrational anger, but through words—

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Earlier printed books read, “not in a strong and irrational blow, etc.” Rabanus and the manuscripts of R. in Huet’s possession correct this to “not through a sudden or irrational [act], etc.” Rabanus then reads, “but you seek to lead them back from error through blows,” instead of “you seek to lead them back from error through words.” Although the Greek agrees in sense, it differs somewhat in wording.]

so God brings back through pain and torments those who could not be converted by speech to what they had been, according to Scripture’s saying: “Through every pain and scourge you shall correct Jerusalem.”

To increase the pain of the punishing correction, those who are corrected are separated from one another. For punishment somehow becomes lighter if several people, situated in the same place, console one another with mutual conversation. If it is necessary to introduce another explanation for the separation of the wicked, we shall offer this one as well.

When the wicked are together, they think about wicked things and, persisting in their former depravity, add sins to sins; just as, conversely, when the good are together, they speak about honorable things. Thus wicked thought is dissolved and reduced to nothing when it does not have the conversation of another who is still more wicked.

Therefore, by God’s providence, the worst are separated from the worst,

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Rabanus reads, in closer agreement with the Greek text: “It is also just and advantageous that …” Previously it stood: “It was nevertheless just and advantageous that …”]

also for their own benefit, so that through solitude itself and the lack of companionship they may eventually desist from their former crimes.

This concerns what was said: “And I will scatter them, man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons together, says the Lord; I will not seek them out, I will not spare, and I will not have mercy on their destruction” (Jer. XIII, 14).

On the basis of these and similar statements, heretics rise up and say: “Do you see what the Creator—the God of the prophets and of the Law—says? ‘I will not spare, and I will not have mercy on their destruction.’ How can he be good?”

[Note: [Col. 0651D] The reading “what the error of the prophets is” has prevailed until now and ought to be rejected. The reading is “what the Creator, the God of the prophets and of the Law, is saying,” and so forth. It was well known that this was the blasphemous doctrine of Valentinus and Basilides: that the Creator and God of the Old Testament was evil. This is what Origen is now discussing. Rabanus therefore most correctly restored “Creator” in place of “error”; the Greek likewise has δημιουργόν, “Creator.”]

I shall therefore take the example of a good judge who, for the sake of the common welfare, shows no mercy to certain people, so that we may understand how God, sparing the many, does not spare one. I shall also take the example of a physician, showing that he does not spare one bodily member in order to spare all the members.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Rabanus prefers “murderer” to “robber”; Origen likewise wrote φονεύς, “murderer,” in Greek. Then he has “of fairly sound age” instead of “sound.”]

For example, let us suppose that a judge has resolved to provide quiet for the city and peace for the people over whom he presides. If a handsome and physically sound robber is brought before him, while on one side the man’s mother pleads with disheveled hair that he have compassion on her old age, and on the other side his wife laments in a tearful voice that he not kill her husband, while little children stand around, soon to be orphaned, what will the judge do? Will he have pity on the robber, or not? What is advantageous to the city as a whole?

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Rabanus reads: “He will carry out what is advantageous to the city as a whole.”]

If he has pity, the murderer will return to his former crime. But if he remains firm in judicial severity, one man will perish and the whole population will be protected.

In the same way, if God spares the sinner and, having compassion on him, does not wish to punish him for his crime, who would not take license for wickedness?

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Previously it stood: “Who would not take license? Who among the wicked, who are now at least restrained by fear of punishment, would not invade the time to accomplish whatever he wished, and rush headlong into vices?”]

Would not the person who is restrained at least by fear of punishment seize the opportunity to accomplish whatever he wished and rush headlong into vices?

We can often observe such things happening in the Church. Someone has sinned, and after his sin asks for communion. If what he requests is granted, pardon proceeds to the detriment of all, and, when the reins are loosened, a way is opened to crimes.

But if, after rational deliberation—not as an unmerciful person, nor again as a cruel judge, but as one who is concerned for one person while considering the salvation of all—he recognizes the harm done to the people by pardon granted to one person, there is no doubt that he will have one expelled from the Church in order to save many unharmed.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] The previously printed books had, “not as a merciful person.” The old reading of Rabanus, and especially the Greek, has the contrary: ἀνελεήμων, “unmerciful.”]

Now consider a physician as well. If he ceases cutting a wound that must be cut, if he does not cauterize what requires the cautery because of the pains that result from such remedies, how the illness grows and the lethargy grows worse.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] The words previously read “old humor”; from Rabanus and the Royal manuscripts in Huet’s possession we restored “lethargy” (veternus).]

But if a rash surgeon approaches the wound and cauterizes the lesion,

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Here too “cultus” had previously been read corruptly instead of “vulnus,” “wound,” which Rabanus corrects.]

he cures the person being cut and cauterized because he has assumed a little severity, although he may seem for the moment not to have compassion on the sick person.

So too God cares not for one human being alone but for the whole world—for heavenly and earthly things—and orders everything everywhere. When he takes into consideration what is advantageous to one person, he much more carefully considers what benefits the whole world and all human beings. He also provides for what benefits one person, but in such a way that the advantage of one does not become the harm of all.

Therefore eternal fire has been prepared, and Gehenna, and the outer darkness. All these things have been established not so much for the one who is to be punished as for the sake of all human beings.

If you wish to take Scripture as a witness to this matter—that even sinners who are already hopeless and wholly beyond healing are tormented for the instruction of others—listen to Solomon saying in Proverbs: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the simple will become wiser” (Prov. XIX, 25).

He did not say that the one who is scourged would become more clever and wiser because of his own correction, but that the foolish person is turned from folly to prudence because of the punishment of the pestilent man. This is indicated by the very meaning of “cleverness”: he is turned away from cleverness when he sees others being tortured on account of the very sins to which he himself is liable.

It therefore benefits us—provided that we are worthy of salvation—that others are tormented for our advantage.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] The Greek reads: ἐάν γε σωτηρίας ἄξιον γενόμεθα δι’ ἄλλων κολαζομένων, “provided that through the punishment of others we become worthy of salvation.” Huetius, a faithful translator, renders it thus; the Hieronymian version is rejected.]

And just as Israel’s sin was useful for the salvation of the nations, so the punishment of some is useful for the salvation of others.

Therefore God is good and compassionate: “I will not spare,” he says, “and I will not have mercy on their destruction.”

Having brought this chapter to a close, let us see what the following passage of Scripture teaches:

“Hear and perceive with your ears, and do not be exalted, for the Lord has spoken. Give glory to the Lord your God before he grows dark, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains; then you will await the light, and there will be the shadow of death, and they will be placed in darkness. If you do not hear secretly, your soul will weep because of insult, and your eyes will shed tears, because the Lord’s flock has been crushed” (Jer. XIII, 13, 16, 17).

He wishes the same people to hear and to perceive with their ears, not content with hearing alone or with the perception of the ears alone. Hence he says, “Hear and perceive with your ears,” and, what is greater than these, “Do not be exalted,” followed by the rest.

Let us consider from the very words what it means to hear and what it means to perceive with the ears. To perceive with the ears is, as it seems to me, to hear with the ears what is said. But if the preceding command, “Hear,” is stated in distinction from the command that follows, “Perceive with your ears,” it orders them to receive what is said into their mind and understanding.

This is not found only in this passage but throughout Scripture. Some things are easy and readily understood; as soon as they are read, they confer benefit upon those who read them. Other things are more hidden [Note: Rabanus reads “more sacred”; perhaps “more holy.” The Greek is μυστηκώτερα, “more mysterious” or “more hidden.”] and ineffable, and, so to speak, wrapped in certain obscurities.

Concerning these hidden matters, therefore, which require exposition, I think it is now said, “Hear.” But concerning those matters which, without any difficulty for the interpreter, are beneficial to the hearer, it says, “Perceive with your ears.”

Let us pass through all the Scriptures and, having become tested money-changers, let us say: “This we ought to hear; this we ought to perceive with our ears.”

When we have heard and perceived with our ears what is said, let us not be exalted. For “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII, 14). Our Savior also teaches us not to be exalted when he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI, 29).

Although the human race is afflicted by many vices, it is oppressed above all by this sin. Pride does not have only one form. One person is irrationally exalted, in the manner of fools, in matters more deserving of shame, or at least exceeds the proper measure of exaltation. Another, as though led astray by plausible reasoning,

[Note: [Col. 0654D] The printed books read, “as though deceived by a semblance of truth.” Rabanus more aptly has, “as though deceived by plausible reasoning,” and the Greek has μετὰ πιθανότητος, “with plausibility.”]

is lifted up over things he considers worthy of glory, although even in such matters it is dangerous to boast.

Let me give an example to make this clearer. Some people boast that they are sons of leaders and were born into a noble family.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] In place of “sons of kings,” which had previously been printed, we substituted “sons of leaders” from Rabanus, against the Greek archetype, which has υἱοὶ ἡγεμόνων, “sons of leaders.”]

Such people cannot display even the shadow or image of their exaltation. Others are lifted up because they have the power to kill people and, as they themselves think, possess such authority that they may cut off the heads of whomever they wish. Their glory is in their disgrace.

Others applaud themselves over their wealth—not true wealth, but the wealth that is below. Others are proud of a splendid house or of many possessions; yet in none of these things is there any real ground for boasting.

But what some consider plausible and worthy of glory is this: when someone is lifted up on account of his wisdom, or is conscious that for ten years he has not touched sexual relations,

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Rabanus reads “women” instead of “sexual matters”; the Greek specifically has οὐχ’ ἥψατο ἀφροδισίων, “he has not touched sexual matters,” that is, “he has abstained from sexual intercourse.”]

or has remained pure and chaste from childhood. Another is raised up because he has borne chains for Christ.

All these things appear right and

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Previously the text read less correctly, “subject to a certain persuasion.” Conversely, the force of the Greek text—πιθανότης μέν ἐστιν ἐνταῦθα ὑποβάλλουσα, ὅτι εὐλόγως τις ἐπαίρεται, “there is here a plausibility inducing the thought that someone is reasonably exalted”—is best conveyed by the reading we substituted from Rabanus: “subject to a certain persuasion toward boasting,” and so forth. The same statement recurs shortly afterward.]

subject to a certain persuasion toward boasting. Yet even in these things, if we follow the truth, no one is reasonably exalted, because even boasting in good things is not without danger.

Paul had grounds for exaltation: he possessed visions, revelations, signs, and powers; he had suffered hardships for Christ’s sake; he had established churches; and he strove to lay a foundation where Christ had not been named. All these were grounds for boasting, or, if one may put it so, plausible reasons that could give rise to honorable self-confidence.

But because even in such matters being exalted is not without danger, the gracious and provident Father, just as he granted Paul revelations and various graces, so also, for the protection of his gifts, gave him an angel of Satan (II Cor. XII, 7), so that the angel might buffet him [Al. “buffet”], lest he be exalted. For this reason he thrice entreated the Lord that the angel of Satan might depart from him—the angel who, according to the divine dispensation, had been assigned to him.

But the Lord answered him—and Paul was worthy of the Lord’s answer—and said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you; for power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9).

Nothing, therefore, is to be a matter of boasting. For boasting is followed by ruin, as Scripture says: “Before destruction the heart of a man is exalted, and before glory he is humbled” (Prov. XVIII, 12).

These things have been said concerning the words: “Hear and perceive with your ears, and do not be exalted, for the Lord has spoken” (Jer. XII, 15, 16).

Let us now look at what follows:

“Give glory to the Lord our God before he grows dark, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains, and you await the light.”

He wishes the one who is going to give glory to God to give it in the light, as though he could no longer proclaim glory once darkness had arisen.

When does it grow dark, and when is there no darkness? “Work while you have the light.” The light is in you if you have within you the one who says: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII, 12). As long as this light rises for you, glorify God, knowing that darkness will come.

It is not advantageous for you to wait for it; rather, before it comes, give glory to God.

Perhaps you will understand this passage if you take an example from the Gospel, where it is joined together in this way: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work” (John IX, 4).

There he called this present age “day,” and I have necessarily added that point there. For I know that in other passages things differing from the present one are signified by the word “day.” Here, therefore, he called this age “day,” but darkness and night the consummation of the world, on account of the punishments that are to come.

For why should we desire the day of the Lord? “Is not that day darkness and not light?” the prophet Amos says (Amos V, 18).

If you consider, after the consummation of the world, that mournful event which nearly the whole human race will suffer because of the things it has sinned, you will see how darkness will seize everything and no one will be able at that time to glorify [Al. “illuminate”] God.

Indeed, even to the righteous it is commanded in Isaiah: “Go, my people, enter your chambers, shut your door, and hide yourself for a little while, until the anger of God has passed” (Isa. XXVI, 20).

At the same time, whoever is able should observe why he said “for a little while”:

[Note: [Col. 0656D] One Royal manuscript in Huet’s possession reads: “For how little this little while is! This little while of the Lord is not little to human beings.” Another reads: “How little is this little while? It is not little to a human being.”]

for this “little while,” which is little, is not little to human beings. We ought to consider how for each individual something may be little or great.

We may also use an example to prove this. For each animal, according to the nature and proportion of its body, food is either small or great; what is little for one is equally much for another.

Why speak of animals? Even in the human being there are differences among things. What is little for an adult is excessive for an infant.

In this way, the whole span of human life—even if it exceeds a hundred years—is brief in comparison with eternity. Thus God’s little while is much for us, while all the ages, when referred to God, are exceedingly brief.

Thus it is said: “Go, my people, enter your chambers, shut your door, hide yourself for a little while.”

That “little while” does not refer to the nature of the one who is commanded to enter his chambers, but to the one who commands, for whom everything that is great is little.

If, then, until God’s anger passes, some must enter their chambers, while there are others whose sins are not to be forgiven—not only in the present age but also in the age to come—it is clear that “little” must be understood in relation to what we have said.

“Give glory, then, to the Lord your God” (Jer. XIII, 16).

How do we give glory to the Lord our God? The Lord is not to be glorified merely with words and voices. Glorify him in chastity, justice, and beneficence; glorify him in courage, patience, piety, wisdom, and the other virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Huetius suspects that the conjunction “if” should be placed at the beginning, so that this may be joined to the following sentence; and indeed it is found in the Greek: εἰ δὲ ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει, καὶ οὕτω δοξάζει τις τὸν Θεὸν, ἐὰν εἴπω τὰ ἐναντία, “But if these things are so, and if someone glorifies God in this way, if I say the opposite …” Rabanus divides the passage differently and reads: “Thus God is to be glorified. If I bring forward contrary examples, do not suppose that I am glorifying but blaspheming. For I shall produce Scripture …”]

Thus God is to be glorified. If I bring forward contrary examples, do not suppose that I am blaspheming. For I shall produce Scripture as a witness to my meaning, showing how a chaste person glorifies God and how a licentious person dishonors him.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Here we removed the word “who,” which was plainly awkward in the remaining context, and reconstructed the whole sentence according to the reading of Rabanus, especially where we read, “through transgression of the Law he dishonors God,” whereas previously it stood, “he transgresses and dishonors God.” The Royal manuscripts mentioned by Huetius are also available after the testimony of Rabanus; they differ from Rabanus only in that they do not recognize the word “Law.” But the Greek text agrees above all: τὸν γὰρ ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ὡς Ναβουχοδονόσορ καταστρέφει, καὶ φθείρει … καὶ διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως τοῦ νόμου τὸν Θεὸν ἀτιμάζει; λέξις ἐστὶ καὶ αὕτη ἀποστολική, “For he destroys and corrupts his temple like Nebuchadnezzar … and through transgression of the Law he dishonors God; this too is an apostolic expression.”]

“For he destroys and corrupts his temple like Nebuchadnezzar, and, according to the Apostle, through transgression of the Law he dishonors God” (Rom. II, 23).

The righteous, therefore, glorifies God, while every sinner insults him.

Even the matter about which some doubt—whether there is a providence of God—arises from no other cause than vices. Remove them, and you have simultaneously removed and destroyed the reasons for denying providence, both above and below.

Those who argue against providence say: “Why are there so many adulterers? Why so many effeminate men? Why so many sacrilegious people? Why so many irreligious people?”

In this way sinners generate insults against providence, offenses against God, and accusations against the Creator. From these things it clearly appears that some give glory to God, while others heap abuse upon him by serving passions and vices.

“Give glory to the Lord your God before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains” (Jer. XIII, 16).

Some mountains are dark, others radiant. Yet because both kinds of mountains are great, the radiant mountains are God’s angels and prophets: Moses, his servant, and the apostles of Jesus Christ. Concerning these, I think it is said: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1).

The dark mountains are those raised up against the knowledge of God (II Cor. X, 5). The devil is a dark mountain. The rulers of this age, who are being destroyed, are dark mountains.

The demon of the lunatic was a mountain, and a dark one. It was the mountain concerning which the Savior said: “If you say to this mountain” (Matt. XVII, 19). The question had arisen concerning the lunatic demon: when the disciples said, “We were unable to cast it out,” the Savior replied: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain”—the mountain about which you asked, which you proposed for consideration—“say to this mountain: ‘Move from here,’ and it will move,” that is, from the human being to the place appointed for it.

Those who stumble, therefore, do not stumble upon radiant mountains but upon dark mountains, if they are with the devil and his angels, who are dark mountains.

“And you will await the light.”

This saying, “And you will await the light,” can certainly be applied to what has just been said: “Give glory to the Lord your God” (Jer. XIII, 16). If you give glory to the Lord your God before it grows dark and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains, there is no doubt that, even if darkness comes and you await the light, he will receive you.

Another person may say—I do not know whether rightly or wrongly—that even those who stumble upon the dark mountains at some time await the light of mercy. For this seems to be shown by the words: “And you will await the light.”

But if someone comes to the dark mountains, see what he finds there. There is the shadow of death; there are the dark mountains; there is the shadow of death produced by those very mountains.

“And they will be placed in darkness.”

“And if you do not hear secretly, your soul will weep because of insult” (Jer. XIII, 17).

Some of those who hear, hear secretly; others, when they hear, do not hear secretly.

What, then, is it to hear secretly? It is this: “We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory” (I Cor. II, 7).

And elsewhere it is said that many of God’s works are hidden (Eccl. XVI, 22).

If I hear the Law, I either hear it secretly or not secretly. The Jew, because he does not hear the Law secretly, is circumcised openly, not knowing that the one who is circumcised openly is not a Jew, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh.

But the one who is a hearer of hidden circumcision is circumcised inwardly. Whoever hears the Law secretly concerning the mysteries of Passover feeds on the sheep, Christ, for “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V, 7). Knowing that the flesh of the Word of God is truly food, he eats it. He has heard secretly concerning Passover.

But the wretched Jew killed the Lord Jesus and remains guilty of his death to the present day because he did not hear the Law and the prophets secretly.

If, when you read about unleavened bread, you can hear secretly, you can also hear openly. Whoever among you celebrates unleavened bread—for Passover is near—that is, these bodily unleavened breads,

[Note: [Col. 0658D] Previously it was corruptly read “bodies.” The Greek is σωματικά, “bodily” or “material.”]

has not heard the command that says: “Unless you hear secretly, your soul will weep.”

Concerning the Sabbath also, certain little women, because they do not hear the prophet, do not hear secretly but openly: on the Sabbath they wash themselves and then return again to the poor and weak elements, as though Christ had not yet descended and washed us with his baptism from the beginnings of the Law into evangelical perfection.

Therefore let us pay closer attention whenever we read the Law and the prophets, lest we fall under the curse now expressed: “Unless you hear secretly, your soul will weep because of insult.”

Whoever among you observes the Jews’ fast—as though ignorant of the day of redemption after the coming of Jesus Christ—does not hear redemption secretly but only openly.

The hidden hearing of propitiation consists in knowing how God appointed Jesus as a propitiation for our sins, and that he himself is the propitiation not only for our sins but also for those of the whole world (I John II, 2).

When parables are read in the Gospel, an outsider who is listening cannot hear them secretly. But if the hearer is an apostle, one of those who enter Jesus’ house, he approaches him and asks about the obscurity of the parable. If Jesus interprets for him what he has heard, then, understanding the Gospel, he hears it secretly, so that his soul may not weep.

For the souls of those who do not hear secretly will weep.

[Note: [Col. 0659D] Rabanus adds: “And it should be noted how remarkable it is that he does not say, ‘You will weep,’ unless you hear secretly, but rather, ‘Your soul will weep.’”]

How remarkable it is that he does not say, “You will weep,” unless you hear secretly, but rather: “Your soul will weep.” There is indeed a weeping of the soul alone, and perhaps this is the weeping of which the Savior says: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VI, 25).

That threat also, by which he announces mourning and tears to those who laugh, concerns this weeping which the prophet now mentions,

[Note: [Col. 0659D] The words “now,” which are also present in the Greek and in Rabanus, were missing from the earlier printed books.]

saying: “Unless you hear secretly, your soul will weep because of insult” (Jer. XIII, 17).

For when you have suffered insult, then you will weep, and your eyes will shed tears, because the Lord’s flock has been crushed.

If we consider the state in which the Jews now are and compare it with their former happiness, we shall see how the Lord’s flock has been crushed.

[Note: [Col. 0659D] Previously it read, “how the Jews are.” We judged Rabanus’s reading, which we restored, to be more correct and closer to the Greek: ἐὰν ἴδῃ νῦν τις τὰ Ἰουδαϊκά, “if someone now sees the Jewish condition,” and so forth.]

For this flock of the Lord once existed, and because they judged themselves unworthy of salvation, the word of the Lord turned to the Gentiles.

If that flock has been crushed, are we—the wild olive tree grafted contrary to nature into the good olive tree of the patriarchs (Rom. XI, 24)—not even more bound to fear that this flock of the Lord may also be crushed?

For it will happen at some time that this flock too will be crushed, according to what the Savior said: “When iniquities have multiplied, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12).

Of whom is it said that the love of many will grow cold? Is it not of those who are called Christians? Is it not of us, concerning whom this statement is made: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke XVIII, 3).

Therefore let us take more careful thought, so that each day this flock of the Lord may become better, grow strong, and remain whole, so that, with every crushing removed from our souls,

[Note: [Col. 0659D] We restored from Rabanus “that we may be made perfect,” compelled by the Greek archetype’s word τελειωθῶμεν. The common text previously read “we become the Lord’s flock.” Huetius noted these two words in the Royal manuscripts, which, he says, are entirely absent; instead, the passage is read continuously as “that we may be made perfect in Christ,” and so forth.]

we may be made perfect in Christ Jesus, to whom are glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.

## TENTH HOMILY

“Who will spare you, Jerusalem?” etc. (Jer. XV, 5 and following).

### 835

We wish to understand the things said to Jerusalem with immense threat as follows:

“Who will spare you, Jerusalem? Or who will grieve over you? Who will turn aside to ask for the things that concern your peace? You have turned away from me, says the Lord. You shall walk backward, and I shall stretch out my hand over you, and I shall destroy you, and I shall no longer spare you, and I shall scatter them in dispersion.

“I said: ‘I have been left without children; deprivation has seized me.’”

I shall give an example. Some enemy [Note: Rabanus punctuates: “rebel.”] and rebel against the emperor of this land has been judged [variant: adjudged] guilty. All mercy is withdrawn from him, lest, while someone pities the condemned man, he begin to offend the one who has condemned him. There are also some who add to the severity, so that they do not even grieve over him, carefully avoiding showing by the sorrow on their faces [Note: In Rabanus: “lest by an error of the face they should be thought to offend the king’s judgments.” One Royal manuscript, according to Huet, reads: “lest by grief they should offend the king’s judgment.”] that they are displeased with the king’s sentence.

If you have understood this, [Note: Rabanus adds, “the example”; it then reads, “consider then, on account of sins,” etc.] consider for me the sinner condemned by God on account of his many sins, and see how, although countless angels preside over the human race, he is judged worthy of mercy by not even one of them. For each of the angels [Note: The printed editions read: “each indeed of the angels, looking on.” Shortly afterward they have adversatur for aversatur.] perceiving that it is God who has condemned him, that it is the Creator who has turned away, and that the sin is of such a kind that God [Note: Rabanus and the Greek text restore the missing word Deus, “God.”], merciful and compassionate, was in a certain sense compelled to pronounce a sentence against him [variant: “to pronounce judgment upon him”], neither spares him, nor grieves, nor has pity, nor turns back to ask for peace on his behalf.

Therefore, Jerusalem, which added this also to its former crimes: that it crucified my Lord Jesus—and its crime rose to such a height that the Savior said of it:

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children, just as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling? Behold, your house shall be left to you deserted” (Matt. XXIII, 37; Luke XIII, 34).

For this reason it was abandoned, and remains desolate even to the present time. The angels who had always assisted it—and through whom the Law of Moses was also given, “arranged through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. III, 19)—abandoned it and said: “It has been crushed beneath many crimes; it killed Jesus, and laid hands upon our Lord.”

As long as it sinned in lesser matters, we could pray for it, we could entreat the Lord, we could spare it. [Note: The earlier printed editions incorrectly read, “who [will spare] concerning these things,” etc. Rabanus corrects this, and the Greek has ἐπὶ τούτῳ, “in this matter.” They also supplied the missing word peccans, “sinning,” from these same sources.] But in this matter, who will spare it? If a man sins against a man, prayer may be made for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him? Jerusalem committed a great sacrilege and perpetrated a great outrage; therefore it has become an object of agitation [or: has been shaken with terror] (Lam. I, 8). And it is said to it:

“Who will spare you, Jerusalem, or who will grieve over you?” [Note: This verse was missing from previously published editions: “Who will spare you, Jerusalem, or who will grieve over you?” We have supplied it from Rabanus and from the Greek of Origen, since it is especially necessary to the context.]

We do not grieve [variant: we shall not grieve] over Jerusalem, nor over its calamities, nor over all that people. Through their offense salvation has come to us, in order to provoke them to jealousy.

And because it sinned in such a way that the Lord’s voice said, “Who will spare you, Jerusalem?”, I too say to the slayer of my Lord: “Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will grieve over you?”

I shall now pass to the spiritual interpretation, rising above the lowliness of the letter, with reason opening a way for me, so that I may see how every soul worthy of God’s peace is called Jerusalem.

After divine instruction you became Jerusalem, although previously you had been Jebus. [Note: Rabanus reads: “he became Jerusalem who had previously been Jebus.” History relates that the name, etc.] History relates that the name of this place was Jebus and that afterward, when its name was changed, it was called Jerusalem. The descendants of the Hebrews report that Jebus means “trampled.”

Thus our soul, trampled by hostile powers, was transformed and became Jerusalem, “Vision of Peace.” If, therefore, after your transformation from Jebus into Jerusalem you sin, and, like certain people, regard the blood of the covenant as common, it will also be said of you:

“Who will spare you, Jerusalem, and who will grieve over you?”

For who will grieve if you are such a person as betrays Jesus? Each one of us, whenever he sins—and especially whenever anyone commits grave sins—sins against Jesus. [Note: The previously published books had read, with almost no intelligible meaning, or at least with extreme obscurity: “Each one of us sometimes sins, especially when he sins greatly, he sins against Jesus.” Rabanus restored the true reading, as did the Greek text of Adamantius: “Each one of us, when sinning, and especially if he commits greater sins, sins against Jesus.”]

But if he also departs from the faith, he does spiritually to Christ what Jerusalem did bodily. Therefore, how much worse punishment do you think is deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as common the blood of the covenant [variant: of the New Covenant] by which he was sanctified [variant: in which he has been sanctified], and insulted the Spirit of grace (Heb. X, 29)?

If you have trampled underfoot Jesus, the Son of God [Note: Rabanus places “if” first; the Greek has καί, “and,” etc.], and insulted the Spirit of grace, who will spare you? Who will grieve over you? Who will turn back to ask for the things that concern your peace?

The sinful soul betrayed that very Jesus who both prayed for and granted the things that concerned your peace. Who can thereafter turn back to ask for the things that concern your peace? [Note: Previously the text incorrectly read “destroyed”; Rabanus corrected it to “betrayed,” as does the Greek, προέδωκεν, and Huet himself had finally conjectured that it should be so. Shortly afterward Rabanus also more correctly reads: “turning back to ask for the things that concern your peace,” etc.]

Knowing, therefore, that it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who also tasted the heavenly gift, became participants in the Holy Spirit, tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then fell away, to be renewed again to repentance—since they crucify the Son of God in themselves again and expose him to contempt (Heb. VI, 4)—let us strive with every effort lest it also be said of us:

“Who will spare you, Jerusalem? Or who will grieve over you? Or who will turn back to ask for the things that concern your peace?”

As for the remaining interpretation, what follows is appropriate:

“You have turned away from me, says the Lord; you shall walk backward” (Jer. XV, 6).

Because you have turned away from the Son of God, and through this have also withdrawn from God the Father, you shall walk backward.

What need is there to repeat what is obvious? Jerusalem, which once existed in Judea—and through which all the Jews are figuratively understood—walks backward because it turned away from Christ. There was a time when they did not walk backward; now, however, they do, and in their hearts they have turned back toward Egypt, so that they walk backward [variant: so that they are walking backward].

Consider what it means to walk backward, or to stretch oneself toward what lies ahead. “Forgetting what lies behind, the righteous stretches toward what lies ahead” (Phil. III, 13). The sinner remembers what lies behind and does not desire what lies ahead.

But the person who remembers what lies behind transgresses the law of Jesus, who says: “Let him not turn back to take up his garment” (Mark XIII, 26). He is disobedient to his command: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVII, 32). [Note: Here we have removed a superfluous conjunction, in accordance with the text of Rabanus and the Greek. We also correct above and below several other matters of lesser importance.] He disregards the Savior’s injunction: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 62).

We also find it written in the Law that the angels said to Lot as he was leaving Sodom:

“Do not look back, and do not stand anywhere in the whole region; save yourself on the mountain, lest you be caught” (Gen. XIX, 17).

You also have an interpretation worthy of the Spirit of God: “Do not,” he says, “look back”—that is, stretch toward what lies ahead. You have left Sodom; do not return to Sodom. You have left vices and sins; do not go back to them.

“Do not stand anywhere in the whole region.” Even if you have kept the preceding command, concerning which it says, “Do not look back,” that is not sufficient for your salvation unless you also observe what follows: “Do not stand anywhere in the whole region.” For it is not beneficial for one who is beginning to make progress to stand in the regions of Sodom.

And if you have crossed beyond Sodom, and, departing from Satan’s region, are beginning to be free from punishments, it is beneficial for you to be saved on the mountain.

“Do not look back, and do not stand anywhere in the whole region; save yourself on the mountain, lest you be caught.”

If you do not wish to be caught in the ruin of Sodom, do not turn back, do not stand in their region, and do not proceed to other places. Rather, when you have departed from there, ascend the mountain, on which alone there is salvation: the name of Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

### ELEVENTH HOMILY

From the passage where it is written: “Alas for me, my mother” (Jer. XV, 10), to the passage where he says: “If you return, I will restore you” (Jer. XV, 19).

839 Physicians of the body, attending the sick and wishing, according to the discipline of their art, to cure those who are afflicted, see sorrowful and unpleasant things, and are themselves consumed by grief at the misfortunes of others. Their whole life is always amid groaning, always amid anxieties; they never associate with the cheerful. With the wounded, with those whose flesh is weakened by various disorders, with those burning with fevers and tortured by pain, they persist in continual service. And if one of them wishes to fulfill his medical duty, he does not grow indignant or forget the purpose of his art after he has been among those whom I have described.

[Note: One Royal manuscript cited by Huet reads: “seeing them afflicted, they grieve, [and find the matter] unpleasant,” etc.]

We have said this in the preface because the prophets too are, in a certain sense, physicians of souls, and are always commanded to go where the sick are: “For it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill” (Luke 9:31). What the physicians suffer from luxurious patients, the prophets and teachers suffer from those who do not wish to be cured. For they are hated as though they were issuing commands contrary to the desires of the sick, because they forbid those who are ill—and who do not wish to eat the food of the sick—to indulge in luxuries and various foods. The disobedient and sick therefore flee from the physicians and drive them away with curses and insults, doing to them precisely what one might do to enemies and adversaries. They detest them as though they came as enemies, as though they desired only this: that pains and restriction of food should arise from their prescriptions; as though they were cutting bodies with the sharpest knife. They curse them as the authors of such great tortures, and not of the health that is restored through suffering.

The people, then, were sick with various ailments, and God sent them the prophets as physicians. One of these physicians was Jeremiah, reproving sinners and wishing to turn them from vices to virtues.

[Note: From the Greek text, which has βουλόμενος (“wishing”), we have not hesitated to restore *volens* (“wishing”) in Latin, in place of the former, quite incongruous *videns* (“seeing”). I also advise you to compare the preface of this homily with that placed before the spurious Abridgment which we printed in the Appendix to the fourth volume from a Veronese manuscript.]

Yet although they ought to have listened to what was said, they instead accused the prophet before judges like themselves. Thus it came about that Jeremiah was always amid accusations and sorrows, caring for them, so far as lay in him, because of their perversity.

[Note: One Royal manuscript cited by Huet reads: “because of their perversity, who, so far as concerned them, had been cured, but according to their own unbelief were still sick.” Another reads: “because of their perversity, who, so far as concerned him, cared for them; but according to their own unbelief, while they were still sick, such things,” etc.]

To such people, still sick because of their own unbelief, he says at one point: “And I said, ‘I will not speak, nor will I mention the name of the Lord.’ And it became like a burning fire in my bones; I was undone on every side, and I cannot endure it.” At another point, seeing that he was constantly attacked with curses, outcries, and insults, he says: “Alas for me, my mother! Why did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and distinguished by all the earth?” And because the sick had despised listening to one who gave good counsel according to the discipline of medicine, he says: “I have been of no benefit.” Again, because, when he lent them spiritual money, his hearers did not wish to receive it in order to gain benefit and return profit from what they had received, he says: “Nor has anyone been of benefit to me.”

I have anticipated these words before explaining, “I have been of no benefit, nor has anyone been of benefit to me” (Jer. 20:9). There are in fact two textual forms. Many copies contain: “I have been of no benefit, nor has anyone been of benefit to me.” But in the copies that are more reliable and agree with the Hebrews, the reading is: “I was not indebted, nor was anyone indebted to me.” We must therefore explain both what is in common use and read in the churches, and also not pass over what is found in the Hebrew books.

Jeremiah preached the divine commandments; no one paid attention to what was preached. Therefore, like a physician willingly and readily administering medicines to the sick, while they acted not according to the skill of the healer but according to their own wishes, he says: “I have been of no benefit, nor has anyone been of benefit to me.” In a certain sense, the one who heals himself receives a benefit if he sees the fruit of his labor in the sick person; through the joy of his mind he too gains an advantage, according to what is said elsewhere: “Blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of those who hear.”

[Note: According to Rabanus, the teacher receives this benefit from his hearers if they advance by listening, inasmuch as he somehow reaps the fruit of their salvation. Jeremiah says that he did not have this benefit among the Jews. Therefore he says, “No one was of benefit,” etc.]

This, then, is the benefit that a teacher receives from his hearers if they advance by listening, while he gains the fruit of their salvation. Seeing that he did not have it from the Jews, Jeremiah says: “No one has been of benefit to me.” For if what I say ought to benefit the hearers, but the hearers reject what is said, I too say: “I have been of no benefit, nor has anyone been of benefit to me,” because I have not obtained the benefit obtained by the one who becomes blessed while speaking into the ears of those who hear.

It can also be understood in another way. Whoever gives commands to disciples, if he has intelligent hearers of an attentive nature, profits the more he commands: they ask questions and repeatedly inquire about what he says—what meaning the statement has, what its order is, and what the intention of the text is. Hence, conversely, he says: “I have been of no benefit, nor has anyone been of benefit to me.”

Since we still have another interpretation on account of the more reliable copies, in which it reads, “I was not indebted, nor was anyone indebted to me,” let us also consider this passage. The one who restores all things to everyone—“taxes to whom taxes, fear to whom fear, tribute to whom tribute, honor to whom honor” (Rom. 13:7)—and renders everything to everyone, owing no one any duty: honoring parents as parents, brothers as brothers, children as children, bishops as bishops, presbyters as presbyters, deacons as deacons, the faithful as the faithful, catechumens as catechumens—if he renders everything to everyone, owes no one a duty. If, however, he ought to render something and does not render it, he cannot say, “I was not indebted”; for when he was indebted, he did not pay.

What follows, “No one was indebted to me,” is to be understood in this way: “I wished to lend at interest and to lend spiritual money, but they turned their ears away from what was said and did not wish to make themselves teachable, so that they would owe me what they heard. Therefore no one was indebted to me.” For if anyone wishes to hear the words that are spoken, he becomes their debtor, and as a debtor he is also required to repay interest. It is therefore much more advantageous for hearers to receive the words of instruction with interest and become debtors than not to receive them and owe nothing. Such people are accused when the prophet says: “No one was indebted to me.”

What he says—“Alas for me, my mother! Why did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and distinguished by all the earth?” (Jer. 15:10)—does not, in my judgment, apply to the other prophets as it does to Jeremiah. Many of the prophets began to prophesy after some interval: at first they were evil, and then, having turned from their sins, they began to prophesy. Jeremiah, however, took the beginning of his prophetic calling from childhood. We can receive testimony to this from the Scriptures.

Isaiah did not hear: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you and appointed you as a prophet among the nations.” Nor did he say, “I do not know how to speak, for I am young.” Rather, when a vision had been revealed to him, he said: “Woe is me, for I am pierced through, because I have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips; and I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes. And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and he touched my lips and said: ‘Behold, I have taken away your iniquities and cleansed your sins’” (Isa. 5:5).

[Note: The Royal manuscripts cited by Huet add: “Thus, after his former sins, he was made worthy of the Holy Spirit.”]

Isaiah’s former sins, then, were cleansed, and, having been made worthy of the Holy Spirit, he prophesied. If you seek similar examples concerning the others, you will find them. Jeremiah, however, was not like this; from his very cradle he began to prophesy, full of the Holy Spirit. Therefore he says—and we ought first to explain the common meaning:

“Alas for me, mother! Why did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and distinguished from all the earth?”

One interpreter of this passage says that the prophet did not speak these words to his bodily mother, but to the one who gives birth to prophets; and that the prophets have no other mother than the Wisdom of God, to whom he says: “Alas for me, my mother,” as though he were saying: “Why did you give birth to me, O Wisdom?” We also read elsewhere of the children of Wisdom, Scripture saying: “Wisdom casts away her children.”

[Note: One Royal manuscript cited by the same Huet reads: “the prophets, the Wisdom of God, and no other,” etc.]

“Alas for me,” he says, “my mother, Wisdom,” as though he were saying: “Why did you give birth to me, a man who is judged? Who am I, who was born for this purpose—that I should be judged and distinguished because of reproaches, correction, and teaching, while I strive to correct those who dwell upon the earth?”

If Jeremiah says, “Why did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and distinguished by the earth?”, we cannot explain what “by all the earth” means. For Jeremiah is not distinguished from all the earth, unless perhaps, by violently forcing the Scripture, we say that “all the earth” has been put for “all Judaea.” At that time his prophecy had not yet reached the whole earth.

Unless perhaps, just as we have shown in many other passages that Jeremiah represents our Lord Jesus Christ, we interpret the present passage in the same way. At the beginning of this book we noted the statement: “I appointed you as a prophet among the nations, to uproot kingdoms, to overthrow, to destroy, to build, and to plant.” Jeremiah did not do these things, but my Lord Jesus, who uprooted the kingdoms of sin and, when the structure of wickedness had been overthrown, caused justice and truth to reign in our souls.

How, then, do those words apply more to Christ than to Jeremiah? In my opinion, so do many others, including these words now under discussion, which must be referred to the Lord. First, we must see whether what appears incongruous and blasphemous if referred to the Lord can be understood in that way: “Alas for me, mother”—that is, our Savior saying this in compassion for others.

To prove this, we must produce testimonies that plainly suit no one but the Savior: how, seeing Jerusalem, he wept over it because he said, “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children” (Matt. 23:37), and the rest. Likewise there are those words that are plainly spoken by the Savior:

“Alas for me, for I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest and like one who gathers grapes at the vintage, when not a single cluster of first-ripe grapes remains to eat. Alas for me, soul, for the reverent one has perished from the earth, and there is no one who corrects among human beings. All are judged in blood” (Mic. 7:1).

He came to harvest fruits and, finding something like straw in the grain because of the great number of sinners, said: “Alas for me, for I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest.” He came to gather clusters of grapes from human beings and, finding a harvest of crimes, said: “And like one who gathers grapes at the vintage, when not a single cluster of first-ripe grapes remains to eat.”

Elsewhere he speaks similarly to the Father, saying: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption? What benefit have I brought to so many people, since they have not profited even from my blood, which I poured out for their salvation? What profit is there in my blood, when I descend from heaven, when I come to earth, when I suffer insults, when I bear a human body? What worthy thing has been accomplished among human beings by all this? What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption? Will dust confess to you, or announce your truth?”

Such, then, is the meaning of what is said in Jeremiah: “Alas for me, my mother, why did you give birth to me, a man?” He does not say, “Alas for me, mother,” insofar as he is God and Savior, but insofar as he is human, as in another prophet: “Alas for me,” he says, “my soul, for the reverent one has perished from the earth.” It is the soul of a human being that is troubled and sorrowful unto death—not the Word who was in the beginning with God, who never mourns, is never troubled, and never said, “Alas for me.” For the Word does not suffer death; rather, it is the human being who undergoes these experiences, as we have often explained:

“Why did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and distinguished by all the earth?” (Mic. 7:2.)

[Note: Formerly *utique* (“certainly”) was read incorrectly. Rabanus corrects it to *ubique* (“everywhere”), in agreement with the Greek text πάντοῦ (“everywhere”). Shortly afterward the name *Christus* (“Christ”) was also missing.]

If you consider the martyrs everywhere condemned and brought from the individual churches before the tribunal, you will see how Jesus Christ is condemned in each martyr. For it is he who is judged in those who bear witness to the truth.

[Note: Here too we have restored *veritati* (“to the truth”), compelled by the Greek archetype τῇ ἀληθείᾳ (“to the truth”); the published books formerly read *divinitati* (“to divinity”).]

You will faithfully accept this: he does not say that you are in prison when you are in prison, nor that you hunger when you hunger—when you thirst; he says instead of himself: “I was in prison, and you came to me; I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25:36).

[Note: The words “when you thirst,” missing from the text, have been supplied from Rabanus, with Origen’s Greek supporting them: ὅταν σὺ πεινᾷς (“when you hunger”).]

Therefore, if a Christian is also condemned, yet not for any other reason or for his crimes, but solely because he is a Christian, it is Christ who is condemned. Thus Jesus is condemned throughout the whole earth whenever one who is condemned for his sake is condemned.

Christ is not condemned only before the judges and authorities of the world’s tribunals. If someone brings a false accusation against Christians and challenges them to a lawsuit, Christ is then also judged unjustly:

“As though whom did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and distinguished by all the earth?”

[Note: In place of *Christus*, the published books had incorrectly supplied *justus* (“just”), in order to create an antithesis. The Greek has Χριστός (“Christ”), as does Rabanus, which we have restored; the sequence of the discourse also requires “Christ.”]

We can also understand in another way how Jesus is condemned and judged throughout the whole earth. What wicked person does not condemn the Christian religion? What Gentile, at least in passing, does not examine it? What Jew does not speak about Christians? What philosopher? What ignorant person?

[Note: Again we have restored *ubique* (“everywhere”) from Rabanus and the Greek πάντοῦ, in place of *utique* (“certainly”) in the published books. It is clear that the author’s meaning is to prove, from Jeremiah’s text, that Christ is judged and condemned everywhere, that is, throughout the whole earth.]

Christ is condemned and distinguished everywhere. Some condemn him; others do not condemn him. If he is not condemned, he is welcomed: you open the door to him, and he enters to you; you believe in him, and he eats with you. But if, on hearing about the Christian religion, you do not accept it, you do nothing other than condemn Jesus as a liar, as a deceiver, as one who leads the world into error.

[Note: We have supplied the word *hominum* (“of human beings”) from Rabanus and Origen’s own text, ὡς πλανήσαντα τοὺς ἀνθρώπους (“as one who led human beings astray”). We have likewise supplied the second *ut* (“as one who”) from the same witnesses.]

“As though whom did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and distinguished by all the earth?” Whoever does not believe in him completely condemns him. Those who believe but still doubt judge him. Christ therefore suffers two things among human beings: he is condemned by unbelievers and distinguished by those who doubt.

If you bear the image of the heavenly, having laid aside the image of the earthly, you are not the earth that condemns him, nor the earth in which he is judged and distinguished (1 Cor. 15:49).
