[Note: The published books formerly had *neque in terra tua judicatur* (“nor is he judged in your earth”) instead of *neque terra in qua judicatur* (“nor the earth in which he is judged”), which Rabanus restored and which Origen formerly wrote in Greek: οὐδὲ εἶ γῆ ἐν ᾗ καταδικάζεται (“nor are you the earth in which he is condemned”).]

“My strength has failed among those who curse me” (Jer. 15:10). The Apostle speaks about our Savior, that he was crucified in weakness. The prophet bears similar witness, saying:

“Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has your arm been revealed? He will be announced before him like a child, like a root in thirsty ground. He has no appearance or glory; we saw him, and he had neither appearance nor form, but his appearance was dishonored and diminished among the children of human beings. A man in affliction and pain, knowing how to bear weakness; because his face was turned away, he was despised and not reckoned. He bears our sins and suffers for us; and we considered him to be in pains, in affliction, and in distress. But he himself was wounded and weakened because of our iniquities. The discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed” (Isa. 53:1ff.).

Therefore he took upon himself the weaknesses of our sins, bore us—

[Note: We have restored *nos* (“us”) from the Greek ἡμᾶς and from the Royal manuscripts cited by Huet; the former reading was *eas* (“them”).]

—and came to those who cursed him; and his strength failed among those who cursed the one who had descended from heaven. For he also took the form of a servant; the Word became flesh and emptied himself. In accordance with the Apostle’s statement, “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7), he now too says: “My strength has failed among those who curse me.”

Let us see whether, with the Word himself granting us meaning and discourse, we can say something else more clearly from what has been said.

[Note: The Greek has exactly these words: ἴδωμεν εἰ αὐτοῦ διδόντος τοῦ λόγου δυνάμεθα καὶ ἄλλο σαφέστερόν τι (“let us see whether, with the Word himself granting us [understanding], we can say something else more clearly”), etc. Rabanus likewise read the Latin in a convenient and straightforward form. Here understand *sensum*, or “meaning,” as referring to *sermo*, “discourse,” that is, the Word, to which he immediately refers his interpretation. The published books formerly read: “Let us see whether, with him granting us meaning, we can say something else from this discourse,” and one Royal manuscript cited by Huet had the still more corrupt reading: “with him granting us meaning, speech, if we can say something else more clearly,” etc.]

“There was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). The true light is the Son of God, who enlightens every human being coming into this world. Whoever is rational becomes a participant in the true light. Every human being is rational, or *rationalis*; another reading has *rationabilis* (“capable of reason”).

Since all human beings are rational, rational power increases in some and decreases in others. If you see a soul full of vices and enslaved to disturbances, you will see how the power of the Word fails in it. If you see a holy and just soul, you will see that the power of God advances and grows in it day by day, and you will apply to it what is written about Jesus.

[Note: The word *plena* (“full”), which is not known to Rabanus or to Origen himself, was inserted here.]

For Jesus did not advance only in himself—in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings (Luke 2:52)—

[Note: We have supplied the words *in se* (“in himself”) from Rabanus; they are necessary to the context and derive from Origen himself: οὐ γὰρ καθ’ ἑαυτὸν μόνον ὁ Ἰησοῦς (“for Jesus did not advance only in himself”), etc.]

—but in each of those who receive an increase of wisdom, age, and grace, Jesus advances in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings.

The Word, therefore—the Son of God who was God the Word, who dwells in the one saying, “Alas for me, my mother,” and the rest—speaks according to the nature of his majesty: “My strength has failed among those who curse me.” If someone curses the Word, he immediately receives the corresponding return and suffers torments. For the strength of Jesus has failed in him when reason is diminished. If, conversely, someone blesses and receives Jesus, his strength undergoes the opposite of what it suffers among those who curse him: just as it had failed among those who curse him, so it grows among those who bless him.

“May it be done, Lord, to those who direct them, if I have not stood by you in the time of their troubles” (Jer. 15:11).

Anyone who can consider the words themselves may ask what this means: “May it be done, Lord, to those who direct them.” To those themselves, Lord, who were cursing me: may the strength that was failing in them be made present in them when, after their curses with which they persecuted me, they turn to repentance and begin to walk in the right way.

“May it be done, Lord, to those who direct them, if I have not stood by you.” He gives the reason why, for those who cursed him, he asks for direction and strength, saying: “If I have not stood by you in the time of their troubles.” He stood by the Father as a propitiation for our sins and pleaded with him in the time of our troubles. For he did not stand by him after the time of our affliction; rather, while we were still sinners, Jesus Christ died for us.

“If I have not stood by you in the time of their troubles, and in the time of their tribulation, let the enemy arise: I stood by you for them” (1 John 2:2). And who is our enemy except the devil, who afflicted us and oppressed us under the yoke of slavery? Against him the Savior stood by the Father, and, freeing us from captivity, restored us to liberty.

The Lord said these things prophetically. It is also possible that the prophet said the same thing for the people: “in the time of their troubles.” God responds concerning him and speaks to the people who had been accused by the Savior or by the prophet, saying:

“Your strength is iron and a bronze covering, hard and indomitable, which does not seek to be softened and is scarcely brought forth” (Jer. 15:12).

“Your strength is iron and a bronze covering”—that is, a cursing strength, cutting and dividing, disturbing what has been well joined.

“I will give your riches and your treasures for plunder freely” (Jer. 15:13).

[Note: Between the words “freely” and “he grants,” two or more words seem to have fallen out of the Hieronymian manuscripts—something like “in exchange for all your sins”—which should be read as a question. “What treasures of sinners does God grant for plunder,” and “does he give them as a ransom,” etc.? These words occur in the Greek archetype: ἀντάλλαγμα διὰ πάσας τὰς ἁμαρτίας σου (“as a ransom for all your sins”). “What treasures of those who sin does God give for plunder, and does he give them as a ransom,” etc. From the very appearance of the Greek text, however, I would conclude that, because the same words—ἀντάλλαγμα διὰ πάσας—recur at the end of the sentence, they were omitted in the Greek copy used by Jerome through the ordinary scribal error of repetition. Such verbal similarity could not have misled the copyists in the Latin text to the same extent.]

God grants and gives them as a ransom for all their sins. Is this referring to the treasures that they have stored up for themselves on earth? For every human being stores up treasure for himself: if he is a sinner, on earth; if he is righteous, in heaven, as the Gospel teaches us.

Or does he mean something like this? Behold, Jeremiah is one treasure; Isaiah is another treasure. Moses was also a treasure, as were the others. God took these treasures away from the people and, through Christ, who said, “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits,” bestowed them upon us.

“I will therefore give your treasures for plunder on account of your sins.” The Lord gave us the treasures of that people, because the oracles of God were first entrusted to them and afterward assigned to us. We have already asserted that what is written—“The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21:42)—has been fulfilled.

It is not that Scripture was taken away from them: they have the Law and the Prophets; they have the volumes of the divine writings. Rather, they do not understand them. Thus the kingdom of God has been taken away from them when the meaning of Scripture is removed. Interpretation of the Law and the Prophets has ceased among them: they read everything but do not understand.

That prophecy has been fulfilled after the coming of the Lord: “Tell this people: ‘You will hear by hearing and will not understand; and seeing, you will see and will not know, for the heart of this people has grown dull’” (Matt. 13:14).

Likewise, what is said by Isaiah has been fulfilled: “The Lord will take away from Judaea and from Jerusalem the strong man and the strong woman, the giant and the warrior, the judge, the prophet, the arbiter, the wise architect, and the wise hearer” (Isa. 3:1).

[Note: The word *prudentem* (“wise”) had fallen out. Rabanus and Origen himself supply it: καὶ σοφὸν ἀρχιτέκτονα (“and the wise architect”).]

God took all these away from them and, if we are willing to receive them, handed them over to us who come from the nations.

“And I will give your treasures for plunder, a ransom for all your sins throughout all your borders.” What he says means this: all these things have been given to you because of your sins, which have extended throughout all your borders.

[Note: Rabanus likewise prefers *propter peccata* (“because of sins”), and Origen’s Greek has διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας (“because of sins”); the sound sense requires this. The published books had the rather corrupt reading, “all these sins,” etc. We have also repaired the following context, which was slightly defective in several places.]

There is no border of that people that has not been filled with their sins. Nor could every border of that people fail to be filled with sins, since, as far as lay in them, they killed righteousness, if Christ is righteousness; they killed wisdom, if Christ is wisdom; they killed truth, if Christ is truth.

Therefore, because of their cruel outcries against the Son of God, they lost all these things. And when my Lord Jesus Christ rose again, he no longer appeared to his killers, but was shown victorious over death only to those who believed in him.

“And I will give you into slavery to your enemies, in a land that you did not know” (Jer. 15:14). The Jewish people served their enemies and were scattered in a land that they did not know.

“For a fire has been kindled in my wrath; it will burn over you.”

After the words of threat to the people that we have explained, the one who had prayed above completes his prayer and joins to the preceding words what follows:

“You know, Lord; remember me and visit me. Make me innocent of my persecutors; ‘not in patience’” (Jer. 15:15; the printed text is incomplete at this point).

The prophet can say this, having suffered persecution from those whom he rebuked and who did not wish to hear the truth; for by speaking the truth he became their enemy. The Savior too can say this, having suffered persecution from the people up to the cross: “‘Not in patience.’”

What does he mean by saying, “‘Not in patience’”? 

[Note: The gloss “that is, in patience,” which had been wrongly inserted in the published books, has been removed here. It is absent from the Greek archetype and was unknown to Rabanus in the Latin interpretation; moreover, it is unsuitable to the context of the discourse.]

You have always been patient with this sinful people; but because they also raised their insolence against me, do not be patient with them.

[Note: The previous reading, obscure and incomplete, was *sed per hoc etiam* (“but also through this”). The former integrity has been restored from Rabanus’s reading, *sed super hoc quod etiam* (“but because they also”), which is confirmed by the Greek text of Adamantius: ἐπὶ δὲ τοῖς κατ’ ἐμοῦ τετολμημένοις (“but because of the things they dared against me”), etc.]

And in fact God was not patient. If you consider the times of the Lord’s Passion and of Jerusalem’s ruin, when it was destroyed, you will see how God did not refrain from them in patience. From the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar until the destruction of the Temple, forty-two years are counted.

[Note: These words, essential to the context, had been entirely missing; consequently the following argument was also defective. We have restored the text according to Rabanus and the Greek archetype: τεσσαράκοντα καὶ δύο πεπλήρωται ἔτη (“forty-two years have been completed”). Huet also adds a passage from Origen’s fourth book *Against Celsus*: “For, I think, forty-two years elapsed from the time when they crucified Jesus until the destruction of Jerusalem.” In this he followed his teacher Clement of Alexandria, who writes in Book I of the *Stromata*: “From the time when the Lord suffered until the destruction of Jerusalem, forty-two years and three months passed.” This was the calculation of those who believed that Christ suffered in the fifteenth year of Tiberius and preached for approximately one year. Origen, in Book IV of *On First Principles*, chapter 1, says that Christ taught for a year and some months; and in Homily 32 on Luke: “According to the simple interpretation, they say that the Savior preached the Gospel in Judaea for one year, and that this is what is meant by ‘Proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.’” Eusebius, however, places his death in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, teaching in Book III, chapter 7 of his *History*, that Jerusalem was destroyed after forty years. Both opinions are supported by distinguished authorities. The opinion of Phlegon of Tralles cannot at all be maintained: Origen reports that, in his Olympiads or *Chronicles*, Phlegon wrote that forty years intervened between the fifteenth year of Tiberius and the capture of Jerusalem.]

For it was necessary that a small interval of time should intervene, so that they might be left for repentance, on account of those who were going to believe through the signs and wonders of the apostles.

“Know how I received reproach because of you from those who despise your words.” The prophet may say this, despised by the sinful people because of the things he preached; for elsewhere he says: “I have completed my days in mockery” (Jer. 20:7). He therefore suffers reproach from those who despise hearing the words of God, and he asks to have God’s help, saying: “Know how I received reproach because of you from those who despise your words.”

“Consume them” (Jer. 15:16). The prophet can say this, but it suits the Savior more, after whose Passion came the destruction of Jerusalem and the slaughter of the Jewish people.

After this, since the prophets suffered many things because of the commission of the Word and the rebukes of God that they conveyed to the people,

[Note: The Royal manuscripts cited by Huet read: “because of their mission and the rebukes of the Word of God.”]

the hearers must be briefly admonished concerning their life and promises, and concerning our own desire, so that, insofar as our strength permits, if we wish to attain rest with the prophets, we may also strive to perform their works.

What I say is this: I frequently say in prayer, “Almighty God, grant us a portion with the prophets; grant us a portion with the apostles of your Christ; grant that we may be found following the footsteps of your Only-Begotten.”

When we say these things, we do not perceive what we are asking. In reality we are saying: “Make us hated in the way the prophets were hated, and give us such words that we may suffer persecution because of them; grant that we may fall into the calamities that the apostles endured.”

For someone to say, “Grant me a portion with the prophets,” while unwilling to suffer what the prophets suffered, is utterly unjust. To say, “Grant me a portion with the apostles,” while unwilling to speak sincerely from Paul’s own spirit—“in labors most abundant, in beatings beyond measure, in prisons exceedingly, in deaths often” (2 Cor. 11:23), and all the rest—is most iniquitous.

If, then, we wish to rest with the prophets, let us consider the lives of the prophets: how, because they rebuked and reproved sinners, they were judged and condemned:

“Stoned, sawn apart, they died by the slaughter of the sword; they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, in poverty, in tribulation, and in misery, wandering through deserts” (Job 12:37).

At the time when there were very many synagogues in Israel, they nevertheless hid in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the rocks.

[Note: The manuscripts cited by Huet read: “sawn apart, cut to pieces,” etc.]

What follows? If anyone wishes to imitate the lives of the prophets and rebuke and reprove sinners, he will immediately earn hatred, immediately be slandered, and immediately suffer plots against him. We often see this happening even now in the churches. If someone commits any sin, the one who presides over the people and governs ecclesiastical discipline expels him from the congregation of the saints. At once that person goes around the city, tearing apart the one who, as far as lay in him, defended the Church. But

[Additional variants and conjectures: At “when I suffer insults,” the text offers *Forte afficior* (“perhaps, ‘I am afflicted’”). At “the Word does not suffer death,” an alternative reads *sermo* (“discourse”) for *Verbum* (“Word”). At “you will faithfully accept,” an alternative reads *suspiciens* (“looking up”); at “if someone brings a false accusation … and challenges them to a lawsuit,” the alternative is *patitur et provocatur* (“suffers [a false accusation] and is summoned to litigation”). In the subsequent reception-of-Christ passage, the alternatives are future forms: *excipietur*, *aperies*, *ingredietur*, *coeperis*, *facies*, and *condemnabis* (“will be welcomed,” “you will open,” “will enter,” “you begin,” “you will do,” and “you will condemn”). The true light alternatively *illuminavit* (“enlightened”); “you will see that” alternatively has *ut* (“so that”). “The Gospel teaches” alternatively reads *docet* (“teaches”); “Or” has the alternative *an*; “we have asserted” alternatively *asserimus* (“we assert”); and “has been fulfilled” alternatively *jam* (“already”). At “they killed righteousness,” the corrupt alternative is *eo interfecit* (“he killed it”); “if you consider” alternatively reads *consideras*. Finally, *Forte et propheta* means “perhaps the prophet also [said these things].”]
we should not lend an ear to those who, because they have been excommunicated, rend with mad speech both their superiors and the entire assembly of the Church. But the blessed apostles, worthy of all admiration, spoke while suffering innumerable insults for the sake of the truth:

> “Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, [Col. 0673C] in persecutions and distresses for Christ” (II Cor. XII, 10).

We ought to labor only to this extent: that we endure insult for no other reason than Christ, and that Christ be the cause of our necessity. Let us desire that, having suffered curses, we may know that we are cursed for the truth, since we defend it and proclaim it with complete confidence in accordance with the will of the Scriptures.

Therefore, as far as we can, let us devote ourselves to imitating the life and conduct of the prophets and apostles, avoiding neither troubles nor dangers. For if an athlete flees the difficulty of the contest, he is not crowned with joy and does not attain the glory of praise.

> “And your word shall become for me a joy.”

He does not say, “It is,” but “It shall become”; for at the present time prisons, exiles, insults, and labors bring me suffering, but the end of all these things shall be joy. “And your word shall become for me a joy, and the gladness of my heart, because your name has been invoked over me, O Lord, [Note: [Col. 0673D] In the Greek, and in Rabanus, *pater* (‘Father’) is not present.] almighty Father” (Jer. XV, 17).

Even if Christ says this, it does not conflict with the meaning: for the name of the Father has been invoked over him. [Col. 0674A]

> “I did not sit in the assembly of those who play.”

Whenever the prophet saw an assembly not of the concerned but of those who played, he fled from it. Hence we ought to understand the distinctions between assemblies: that of the concerned and that of those who play.

If this assembly of ours is concerned; if it seeks everything with ecclesiastical diligence; if its speech is disciplined; if its life is watchful; if its affairs are conducted with caution—then it is an assembly not of those who play, but of those who are concerned.

But if it abandons the pursuit of religion and devotes itself to the amusements of this world, which arise from wickedness, it becomes an assembly of those who play. Thus the prophet says:

> “I did not sit in the assembly of those who play, but I was afraid before the face of your hand.”

When two alternatives were set before me—either to sit in the assembly of those who play and offend your majesty, or at least to rise from it and do what pleased you—I chose rather to rise from the gathering of those who play, [Note: [Col. 0673D] One manuscript, the *Regius* cited by Huet, reads: “and to be your friend.”] so that I might be your friend, than, by doing what was contrary, to be counted among those who are your enemies.

> “I did not sit in the assembly of those who play, but I was afraid before the face of your hand.”

Our Savior also did not sit in the assembly of those who play. Teaching that he had risen from it, he said:

> “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII).

For the divine Word left the assembly of the Jews and gathered for himself another assembly from among the nations. [Col. 0674C]

> “I sat alone.”

This statement by itself, without explanation, greatly edifies those who hear it, when there is a multitude of sinners that does not tolerate a righteous person living piously alongside it [alternative reading: “a righteous, pious person”]. [Note: [Col. 0673D] Thus literally the Greek text of Origen: “as it is in no way strange to flee the council,” etc. Rabanus too formerly read in his manuscripts, very correctly, as we restore it: “it is not unfitting to flee,” etc. The corrupt and false reading in the previously printed books was: “then he is needy to flee,” etc.]

It is not unfitting to flee their assembly and imitate the prophet who says, “I sat alone”; to imitate Elijah, who laments miserably:

> “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug up your altars, and I alone have been left, and they are seeking to take my life” (III Kings XIX, 14). [Note: [Col. 0674D] In place of *Eliam*, which is found in the Greek, in Rabanus, and is required by the sense of the passage, *etiam* (“also”) was read through a laughable error.]

But if we wish to receive something more sacred in the statement, “I sat alone,” perhaps we shall find an interpretation worthy of the Holy Spirit.

When we imitate the life of the multitude, when our conduct is no better than that of the people, and when, having disregarded God the judge, we do not separate ourselves from human wickedness, we cannot say, “I sat alone”; for we sit with very many.

But when our life is such that no one is equal to us in thought, speech, or deeds, then we can say, “I sat alone.” Even one who is not a priest, bishop, deacon, or adorned with any other ecclesiastical dignity may say, if he lives well, “I sat alone,” [Col. 0674D] “because I am full of bitterness” (Matthew VII, 14).

If the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted, it is beneficial for you, withdrawing from every sweetness, to be filled with bitterness in the present age. Or do you not know that God’s feast is celebrated with accompanying bitternesses? [Col. 0675A]

For the divine Word says:

> “When you keep a feast day, you shall eat unleavened bread with bitterness” (Exodus XII, 8). [Note: [Col. 0675D] Huet says: “The Septuagint rendered μετὰ πικρίδων, ‘with bitter herbs’; the Hebrew is [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text]. Jonathan: ‘with parthenium and iatybes.’ Jerome: ‘with wild lettuces’; Cyprian: ‘with picrides’; Ambrose: ‘with bitterness,’ as do most interpreters. Rufinus, in his interpretation of Origen’s twenty-third homily on Numbers, has: ‘For you shall eat unleavened bread with bitterness, or with picrides.’ *Picrides* is a general term containing all bitter things, and, when eating is mentioned, all bitter foods. In these passages, however, the Septuagint restricted the term to a particular species, namely πικρίδες, which is an inferior kind of lettuce. Jerome followed the Septuagint.”]

At the same time, I think we ought to consider what this command means: it orders the person celebrating God’s Passover to eat unleavened bread with bitter things. As for the unleavened bread, the Apostle Paul explained my interpretation. But concerning the bitterness that follows, it is necessary to offer something resembling the Apostle’s argument. [Note: [Col. 0676D] Again, one *Regius* manuscript cited by Huet reads *simile reperiatur*, “something similar may be found.”]

Concerning the unleavened bread, then, the Apostle says:

> “Let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Cor. V, 8).

Concerning the bitter things, an explanation must be given that teaches that they are to be celebrated in the same way as the unleavened bread is eaten. Have sincerity and truth, and bitterness will follow you; and you will eat unleavened bread with sincerity and truth.

Because Paul ate this kind of unleavened bread, bitterness followed him, as he says:

> “I have become your enemy by telling you the truth” (Gal. IV, 16).

He ate bitter things in pain, in labor, in frequent vigils, in hunger and thirst (II Cor. XI, 27), besides all the other things that he disclosed for the salvation of the whole world—things that made him, as a leader of the truth, eat unleavened bread with bitter things.

The Law indeed says: “Eat unleavened bread with bitter things and be filled,” just as elsewhere it is said of certain people: “Eat and fill yourselves.” But the prophet does not say, “I ate bitterness”; rather, “I am filled with bitterness”—that is, so great a burden of the persecutions of the age has weighed upon me [alternative reading: “weighs upon me”] that I have become full of bitterness.

> “Why are those who distress me strengthened against me?”

Jeremiah suffered much from those who did not wish to hear the truth, and they were stronger than he in this world, because the kingdom of God is not of this world but of another region of the living, as the Savior says:

> “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would labor so that I would not be handed over to the Jews” (John XVIII, 36).

Therefore they are strengthened against him in this world. And that the righteous person is weaker than those who persecute him, consider the sufferings of the martyrs.

The judge sits in lofty tribunals, pronouncing sentences; [Note: [Col. 0676D] In place of these two words, we have substituted from Rabanus *sententias promens* (“pronouncing sentences”), compelled by the correct sense and by Origen himself, who writes in Greek: ὁ δικαστὴς καθέζεται δικάζων, καὶ τρυφῶν ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, “the judge sits judging and indulging himself in the tribunal.” In the previously printed books the reading was meaningless, or at least incongruous: *prominens*.] the Christian, in whom Christ dwells, is judged, full of bitterness, and subjected even to death, while his enemies are strengthened against him.

> “My wound is firm.”

Those who are strengthened against me inflict wounds upon me; and my wound is firm. Whether you wish to understand this as spoken of the Lord’s cross, of the righteous, or specifically of Jeremiah, it will not conflict with the meaning.

> “My wound is firm; from where shall I be healed?”

The Savior too can say, “From where shall I be healed?” as he announces his resurrection after the wounds of the nails; and so can the righteous person who receives healing after his wounds.

> “It has become for me”—with “wound” understood—“like deceptive water that cannot be trusted” (Jer. XV, 18–19).

For my wound does not remain, but passes over me. Therefore the Lord says:

> “If you return, I shall restore you.”

God speaks these words to all whom he wishes to return to salvation. Yet he seems to signify some mystery in saying, “I shall restore you.” For no one can be restored except to the place from which he had previously departed.

For example, if a member of my body has been separated from its joints, the physician tries to restore it to its former place. If someone is separated from his homeland and sent into exile, and afterward, through the indulgence of those who can release exiles, is returned to freedom, he returns from the place from which he had been expelled. A soldier who has been cast out of his rank is likewise restored to his rank if he receives pardon.

So now it is said to the mortal race—that is, to us human beings—who had turned away from God:

> “If you return, I shall restore you.”

For the end of the promise is restoration, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Until the time of the restoration of all things that God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, in Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.”

# TWELFTH HOMILY  
## On the passage written: “Behold, I am sending many fishermen, says the Lord,” etc. (Jeremiah 16:16)

**855** In the Gospel according to Matthew it is written that our Savior came near the Sea of Galilee [Col. 0676C] and there saw Simon and his brother Andrew casting nets into the sea. For they were fishermen. And there is added: “When Jesus saw them, he said to them, ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers of human beings.’ And they left their nets and followed him” (Matt. 4:18). Thus the Savior made them, from fishermen of fish, fishers of human beings.

The Lord also found two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and his brother John, in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets (Matt. 4:21). When he likewise called them to the ministry of the Gospel, he made them fishers of human beings.

Therefore, if anyone considers the Savior’s disciples in accordance with this narrative—so that they possess not only the grace of speech, but also a structure of Scripture woven together like nets, which can be spread over human souls in the circle of a skilled craftsman—and considers this same matter with the fullest reasoning of faith, he will see how the Savior was not sending out fishers of human beings only then, **856** but continues to send them even to the present day, appointing them to rescue souls from the sea and to lead them from the most bitter waves [Col. 0677A] into freer air.

Yet when those fish have been drawn from the water with seines, nets, and hooks, they die. Among us, however, when someone has been caught by the net of speech and brought out of the sea of this world, he too dies—but to sin and to the world—so that, rising with Christ, he may live for God.

If, then, you can bring yourself to understand the meaning we are attempting to explain—namely, that fish drawn from the sea assume another life and put on another body—you will know how the example benefits us. Let no one blaspheme; let no one maliciously tear this apart; let no one call a crime what has been drawn from another person’s understanding.

You too, therefore, when you have been drawn out by the Lord’s disciples from the waves of this world, change the vices of your body; change the disposition of your soul. [Col. 0677B] Do not be that fish which moved about in salty waves, but, pulled from the deep whirlpool, turn toward better things, in accordance with the apostolic statement: “But we all, with unveiled face, contemplating the glory [Alt. *brightness*, here and below] of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18).

And when you have been freed by the apostles and disciples of Jesus from the waves of the sea, do not seek the deep; let your dwelling be in the mountains. Then you will no longer need fishermen to draw you out of the waves again, but rather certain others whom Scripture calls hunters, who will later hunt you from the mountain, from the hill, from higher places. Let your walking be there, your mind be there, your steps and your standing. Forget the sea; forget the valleys and the depths. Come to the mountains—[Col. 0677C] the prophets. Come to the hills—the righteous [Alt. *there]. Let your dwelling be among them, so that when the day of death arrives, hunters may be sent—others, different from the fishermen—who have been appointed to receive souls [Note: The word *souls* was missing from previously published books. We have supplied it, following Rabanus’s reading and the text of Origen himself, *οἱ ἐπιτεταγμένοι ἐπὶ τοῦ παραλαμβάνειν τὰς ψυχάς* (“those appointed to receive souls”), in order to restore the sense, which had been mutilated.] and may receive you with the other saints from hill and mountain, from a higher place.

See whether the Prophet does not agree with this in the same sentence, speaking with sacred voice: “Behold, I am sending many fishermen, says the Lord, and they will fish for them. And after this I will send many hunters, and they will hunt them upon every mountain and hill” (Jer. 16:16).

If you too wish to be caught by these hunters, take care not to move about in the valleys or stand in some other lowly region. Seek the hills; seek the mountain onto which the Lord ascended when he saw the people, and his disciples followed him. From there he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, [Col. 0677D] for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5), and the remaining seven beatitudes. Nor should you think that these hunters are permitted to catch people from elsewhere except from mountains and hills, and—what follows—from the caves of rocks [Note: In Rabanus we find *nor indeed can it be permitted*. The Greek has only *οὐκ ἔξεστί γε*, and so forth. For the word which shortly afterward we read as *to capture*, the reading *to seek* was formerly printed less correctly; following Rabanus and Origen himself in Greek, *συλλαβεῖν*, we have restored *to capture*.]

How can I understand rocks? Where can I find caves of rocks? I turn to Exodus; I seek some opportunity for interpretation, and there I find Moses wishing to see the Lord, and the Lord promising him this and saying: “Behold, I am placing you in a cleft of the rock, and you shall see my back, but my face you shall not see” (Exod. 33:22).

If you consider what is called the rock there, and the opening of the rock [Note: Here we have supplied approximately the next three lines, which, because of the customary scribal error arising from the repetition of the words *opening of the rock*, had dropped out of previously printed books. Because of their absence, the sense of the present sentence was either lacking altogether or did not fit the subject. The text had read: “If you consider what the rock and the opening of the rock are there, you understand also the other rocks,” etc. Rabanus first alerted us to the mutilation of the passage; we have faithfully transcribed his reading and inserted it here. Origen himself also confirms it, for these are his very words: *ἐὰν νοήσῃς ἐκεῖ τὴν πέτραν, καὶ ἴδῃς ἐκεῖ τὴν ὀπὴν τῆς πέτρας, τινὰ τρόπον ἐπὶ τῆς πέτρας ἱστὰς καὶ τὴν ὀπὴν τὴν ἐν τῇ πέτρᾳ ἰδὼν βλέπει τὸν Θεὸν διὰ τῆς ὀπῆς τῆς πέτρας, ὄψει τε καὶ τὰς πολλὰς πέτρας* etc. Literally in Latin these words are: “If you consider the rock there, and see the opening of the rock there, how, standing upon the rock, and seeing the opening that was in the rock, he sees God through the opening of the rock: you will understand also the many rocks,” etc.]—how Moses, standing upon the rock and looking from the cave of the rock, sees God through the opening of the rock—you will understand also the other rocks and the openings of the rocks.

What, then, is the rock? [Col. 0678B] The Lord Jesus Christ: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (1 Cor. 10:4). And in the thirty-ninth Psalm it is said: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. 39:3).

What is the opening of the rock? If you see God with God the Father, the Word who is God, you will see the entire rock. If you see the dispensation of the body assumed, you will see the opening of the rock, through which the human gaze, according to the capacity of its weakness, beholds the back of God. For this is what he says: “You shall see my back” (Exod. 33:23).

I have found one cave of one rock; I seek other rocks and other caves. I come to the chorus of prophets and apostles, and of the transcendent holy angels, and I say that all imitators of Christ are rocks [Alt. *are*], just as that one is the rock who taught. And just as he has an opening through which the back of God is seen, so each one of us [Note: Rabanus has *each one of the righteous*; in Greek alone it is simply *each one*, *ἕκαστος*] who opens through his words a way to understanding God also makes himself [Alt. *has made himself*] an opening of the rock.

But if you wish to understand the rock and the opening of the rock in another way, see the Law through Moses, prophecy through Isaiah, and other divine utterances through Jeremiah. If, however, it is an angel who speaks in a human being, in accordance with the prophetic statement, “The angel who was speaking in me” (Zech. 2:3), I stand in the angel, and through his opening I see God in an angelic manner.

I have a necessary example, by which I may teach how someone standing in an angel can see God. It is written in Exodus: “The angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from a bush”; Moses saw that the bush was burning and was not consumed (Exod. 3:1). **859** And Scripture did not continue in the same manner in which it had begun when it said, “The angel of the Lord appeared,” as though it would then say, “I am the angel of the Lord.” Rather, it says: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6). God was therefore visible there in the angel, and through the angel’s opening his back appeared.

Because you do not know at what time the hunters will be sent, take care never to descend from the mountain, never to leave the hills, never to come out of the caves of the rocks. For if you are found outside, the things that those who are outside deserve to hear will be said to you: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20) [Note: In agreement with the Greek text quoted by Origen, we have restored from Rabanus’s reading *they will demand your soul from you*: *ἀπαιτοῦσι τὴν ψυχήν σου ἀπὸ σοῦ*. This passage recurs here and shortly afterward. Previously published editions had *your soul will suddenly be taken from you*.]

These things will be said to you if you say: “I will tear down my storehouses and build larger ones, and I will say to my soul: ‘Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, rejoice.’”

Do you see him descending from the mountains and hills? Do you see him standing outside the opening of the rock? How he goes astray and thinks that things which are nothing are good, saying: “I will say to my soul: ‘Soul, you have many good things stored up’”? He considered grain and the abundance [Alt. *usefulness*] of earthly produce to be good things, not knowing that true goods are not born in the accursed earth but in the heavenly regions. He stored up treasures for himself on earth because he thought that treasures were located on earth.

But if anyone, taking up the cross, follows the Lord Jesus and stores up treasure for himself in heaven, it is not said to him, “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you.” Instead, the hunters will come, seeking creatures from the mountains, hills, and caves of the rocks; they will take that person also with them from their exalted hunt and carry him to the higher realms of blessedness.

“For my eyes are upon all their ways” (Jer. 16:17). God has his eyes upon all the ways of such people who dwell in the mountains, walk in the hills, and live in the caves of the rocks. “They have not been hidden from my face.”

Those who are holy do not hide themselves from the face of God; the unjust, however, hide themselves from his face. After the transgression of the commanded precept, Adam heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the afternoon, and he hid himself (Gen. 3:8). A holy person does not do this, but through the testimony of his deeds possesses confidence before God: “If our conscience does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him” (1 John 3:21).

Yet although Adam had sinned, his mind had not fallen into complete wickedness [Alt. *had not fallen completely*]; therefore he hid [Alt. *was hidden*] himself from the face of God. [Note: Rabanus’s reading seems more harmonious: “But when the most wicked fratricide perceived what he had done, he went out,” etc. In the manuscripts, however, Rabanus has: “But you, most wicked parricide, observe what he did,” which is erroneous.]

But when the most wicked fratricide sinned, observe what he did: “He went out from the face of God, and dwelt in the land of Nod” (Gen. 41:16). If you compare evils, it is better to hide oneself from the face of God than to flee from him. In the one case, a wound inflicted [Alt. *fixed*] in the conscience seeks darkness and secrecy and does not allow a person to raise his eyes to heaven. In the other, an obstinacy born of despair disregards the Lord.

“They have not hidden themselves from my face, nor have their iniquities been hidden [Alt. *have not hidden themselves*] from my eyes.” The righteous—over what injustices have they not hidden themselves from the face of God? At some time they were in sins, when they were in the sea from which they were drawn by the fishermen.

Therefore, lest they suppose that they came from the deep to the mountains not through God’s mercy but through their own merit, the divine word admonishes them [Alt. *admonishes*]—and in them us—of their former offense [Note: Here we have again supplied from Rabanus’s reading the words *of their former offense*, which Origen also wrote in Greek: *τῶν προτέρων ἁμαρτημάτων*]. And therefore, after favorable and happy things, it introduces sorrow, saying: “Nor have their iniquities been hidden from my eyes.”

What follows presents difficulty for our interpretation. For whether we understand it as connected with what precedes, we nevertheless fear the punishments that are to be repaid; or whether it seems not to fit what precedes—what we have said about fishermen and hunters—it still generates no small perplexity:

“And I will first repay them double for their iniquities and their sins, by which they polluted my land, with the corpses of their abominations and their iniquities, with which they filled my inheritance” (Jer. 16:18).

When he says “first,” either because some did not understand what was written, they removed it, [Col. 0680C] or the translators of the Septuagint, as with other passages, wished to remove it according to their own editorial procedure—God knows [Note: Here Jerome is being rather unfair to the translators of the Septuagint. What is more surprising is that, while he complains that they mutilate everything at will and recklessly, he himself attributed foreign and spurious words to Origen, namely, *as with the other passages*. Huetius].

We, comparing this passage with the other editions, found the following wording: “And I will first repay them double for their iniquities.” This shows that although they have been made worthy of God’s blessedness by their subsequent deeds, nevertheless, because they once sinned and were not free from human faults, they must first receive what belongs to their offenses.

And consider whether the reasoning is not true: who does not receive punishment for sins? Surely it is the one who, after faith and baptism, hears the Lord saying, “Your sins are forgiven” (Matt. 9:2; John 8:11), and does not sin again [Alt. *who does not sin again*].

But if after washing and forgiveness of sins we return again to our former filth, and, while our understanding is still imperfect, withdraw from the footsteps of the apostles, or commit some injustice, or if indeed in our very righteousness some sins are mixed [Alt. *have arisen*], let us consider what happens to us: whether, when we depart from the present world, if we possess either vices or virtues, we shall receive rewards for our virtues and the sins we knowingly committed will be forgiven; or whether we shall be punished for our offenses and receive no rewards for our virtues.

Neither alternative is true. We shall be tortured both for our sins and shall receive for our righteousness the rewards we deserve. For if, after the foundation of Jesus Christ, you have built upon it not only gold, silver, and precious stone in your heart—if indeed you possess any gold or silver—but also wood, hay, and straw, what do you wish to happen to you when your soul has been separated [Alt. *led astray*] from the body?

Will you enter the holy places with your wood, hay, and straw, so as to defile the kingdom of God? Or will you remain outside because of the wood, hay, and straw, and receive no reward for the gold, silver, and precious stone? But this too would not be just.

What, then, follows, except that first, because of the wood, fire must be given to you, which will consume the wood, hay, or straw? For our God, among those who are able to understand divine things, is said to be a consuming fire. And when the prophet says, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29), he did not specify what it consumes, leaving you to infer the clearer meaning.

For this fire does not consume what remains according to his image and likeness, nor does it consume God’s own creatures, but the wood, hay, and straw that have been built upon them. **862** This is a difficult passage, requiring very great labor for interpretation, so that the latter statements may agree with the former. We read promises, and suddenly after favorable things sorrow is proclaimed: “And I will first repay them double for their iniquities.” The word “first” has necessarily been added [Note: Origen is chiefly branded with this error on the basis of this passage, because he seems to have assigned human crimes to purifying rather than eternal punishments. Yet it is an article of faith that after the resurrection and judgment no hope of correction remains. On this matter compare Bellarmine, Book II *On Purgatory*, chapter 9, and Huet, *Origenianorum*, Book II, question 11, section 17.]

First, then, we endure torments because of injustice; afterward we are crowned because of righteousness. For, conversely, the rewards of righteousness must not be bestowed first and sins repaid afterward, so that, once the good have ceased, the vices remain eternal. Rather, we shall first receive what is evil, and afterward what is good, so that, once the vices have been removed, the virtues may remain forever.

Observe the entire treasury of Scripture, and you will always find God first threatening the things that are sorrowful and afterward bringing about the things that offer joy to those who hear: “He kills, and he makes alive; he strikes, and he heals; he himself causes grief, and again restores; he has struck, and his hands have healed” (Deut. 32:39).

Therefore, when he who is righteous considers these things with devout understanding, let him sigh and say: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” He says: “The one who walks without blemish and practices righteousness, who speaks truth in his heart, who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue, who has not done evil to his neighbor, and who has not accepted reproach against his neighbors” (Ps. 14:1–3).

Let us also not reproach those who turn from sins to repentance, since Scripture says: “Do not reproach a man who turns from sins” (Eccles. 8:6). “He has not accepted reproach against his neighbors”; “the wicked has been reduced to nothing in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord” (Ps. 14:3–4).

All of us, therefore, whoever possess within us material for that fire, shall first receive our offenses. But someone among the hearers will say to me: Explain also what follows, “double for their iniquities.” Suppose that I receive my sins [Alt. *suppose that I am to receive my sins*], so that what the Apostle said may be fulfilled: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:15). Why, then, do I receive sins twice?

The answer must be that “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47). It is appropriate for those who are from the Gentiles [Alt. *the Gentiles*] to receive single sins, but for us to receive double sins, as the Apostle says: “If we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sin, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and the fury of fire that will consume the adversaries” (Heb. 10:26–27).

It was prophesied concerning those who had been drawn by fishermen and hunters from the deep into the mountains, and how they would first receive their sins doubly. After this, the calling of the Gentiles was prophesied—not of those who had not yet known Christ, but of those who have already been called, so that they might know to give thanks for grace and, standing in the Church, confess and worship his name:

“Lord, my strength, and my help [Col. 0682C] [Alt. *power*, *fortress*], and my refuge in the day of troubles, to you the Gentiles will come from the ends of the earth, and they will say: ‘For our fathers possessed false idols, and there is no benefit in them’” (Jer. 16:19).

How did the Gentiles come to the Lord from the ends of the earth and say, “For our fathers possessed false idols, and there is no benefit in them”? Who are those who come from the ends? Some are the first of the earth, and others are the last. Who are the first? The wise of this world, the noble, the rich, the eminent. Who are the last? “God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the strong, and the things that were not, to destroy the things that are.”

“The Gentiles will come from the ends of the earth”—as though he had said: From all those who are last upon the earth, from the foolish, the ignoble, and the despised.

And they will say: “For our fathers possessed false idols, and there is no benefit in them” [Col. 0682D]—not because the idols are true beings, in contrast to which they are now called false, but because the idols are false by nature, and there is no benefit in them. “If a human being makes gods for himself, these are not gods.”

People make gods for themselves not only from bodily images, but also fabricate them from the heart. For those who can imagine another creator besides the God of the universe, another Holy Spirit, another Christ, other ages beyond those that we see—those people have made gods for themselves **864** and have worshiped the works of their own hands.

All philosophers who have handed down various doctrines, and all heretics who have become for wretched mortals authors of believing differently about God, have made idols for themselves. They thought the pleasure of the mind [Alt. *soul*] to be God, and, turning toward it, they worshiped the work of their own hands, thinking that what they had fashioned was true.

All, therefore, who fashion gods for themselves either from visible matter or from false doctrines, the divine word now rebukes, saying: “If a human being makes gods for himself, and these are not gods, therefore at this time I will reveal to them the work of my hands; I will show them my power” (Jer. 16:20). At what time, except at this time, when our Savior assumed a human body? [Col. 0683B]

“And they shall know that I am the Lord.”

Then another prophecy follows—which I do not know why we did not find it among the Septuagint, but discovered it in the other editions that agree with the Hebrew wording. It is full of necessary matters and so useful that, if the reader’s mind is attentive, it can call him back from vices. It follows in this way:

“The sin of Judah has been written with an iron stylus, with a diamond claw, engraved upon the breast of their heart” (Jer. 17:1).

Because it is difficult for anyone to confess himself evil, the Jews [Note: Compare Jerome, *Commentary on this passage*, vol. IV, col. 156, and what we have annotated there] who falsified certain copies also altered this passage, replacing “the sin of Judah” with “their sin.”

But if you consider the matter figuratively—as we have often shown—so that Christ is called Judah, perhaps “the sin of Judah” is our sin, since we believe in Christ who is from the tribe of Judah and descended from his lineage according to the flesh.

But if you wish to understand this more sacredly as spoken of Judas the betrayer—“The sin of Judas has been written with an iron stylus, with a diamond claw, engraved upon the breast of their heart”—the word “their” will oppose you.

Therefore, as we said above, these words apply to us who sin. Our sins are not written somewhere outside us, but in the conscience of the heart, inscribed with an iron stylus and engraved with a diamond claw.

Understand that our sins are written upon the breast from what follows. Before I commit sin, no image of sin is present in my heart. But when my conscience has received the image of sin, I possess its form, and the pageant of my offense is continually painted before the eyes of my heart.

And if my sin were written with ink, perhaps I could erase it. But now it is written with an iron stylus and a diamond claw; it is written [Alt. *engraved*] upon the breast of my heart, so that it may come with me to the tribunal and that what Christ prophesied may be fulfilled: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, and nothing is concealed that will not become known” (Matt. 10:26).

The conscience of my breast will be laid bare, and, when the heart has been opened, the letters of my sins will be seen, engraved with an iron stylus and a diamond claw. And thus the entire multitude of spectators [Alt. *sinners*] will read upon my breast the images of my sins marked there.

“For nothing is hidden [Alt. *concealed*] that will not be revealed.” And: “The thoughts mutually accusing or else defending one another” (Rom. 2:15). And: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the purposes of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5).

To whom will he reveal them [Alt. *to whom will it be revealed*]? Certainly not to himself, who knows all things before they happen, but to those who will come with him and, because of the purity of mind and body, will follow the Lamb. He will show them the offenses impressed upon the sinner’s heart, so that the righteous may rise to glory, but sinners to eternal reproach and confusion.

From these things may God free us, as we rise with Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# THIRTEENTH HOMILY  
## On the passage written: “How have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jeremiah 2:21–22), up to the place where he says: “You have been defiled in my sight by your iniquities, says the Lord.”

865. God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living. For he created all things that they might exist, and the generations of the world are wholesome [Note: The manuscripts of the Royal Library cited by Huetius read: “he made the generations wholesome”]; there is no poison of death in them, nor the kingdom of Hades upon the earth (Wis. 1:13). Proceeding a little farther, I find the source from which death comes: “But through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. 2:24).

God therefore created all good things in us and for our sake, but we ourselves, by our own will, drew wickedness and our own sins into ourselves. Hence, in the present reading, God now complains through the prophet and, as it were, asks in perplexity how the soul in certain people has become bitter, although he himself had created it sweet; and he says: “How have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?”

What he says amounts to this: “I made feet with which the human race might walk; why is it, then, that so many limp? I made all the limbs strong and sound; how do I see them weak and useless in so many?” Thus not only was the soul of the first human being made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1:26), but the image that belongs to God is also older than the image of the Devil, which afterward we put on through sin. Therefore we must labor with the utmost diligence so that, just as while sinning we bore the image of the earthly, so, having turned to repentance, we may bear the image of the heavenly, after which every creature was originally formed. Because of the turning of this creation toward evil, the rebuking word now says to sinners: “How have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?”

“I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true.” We have said this before, and now we repeat it more fully so that you may understand: God planted the human soul as good, but it was corrupted by its own fault against the will of its Creator. “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true”: I did not plant you true in part and false in part, but wholly true. “How, contrary to my planting, have you been turned into bitterness and become a foreign vine?”

After this comes: “Even if you wash yourself with natron and multiply for yourself the herb”—[Note: Jerome: “and multiply for yourself the herb poam.” Throughout this homily he renders πόαν as poam in the same way. The Hebrew has [Hebrew term], which the Septuagint rendered πόαν and Jerome, “the herb borith.” Thus, in Malachi 3:2, the Septuagint translates “the herb of those who wash” as πόα πλυνόντων, while Jerome has “the herb of fullers.” What the Hebrew term means is debated in many ways. Some wish it to be smegma, and anything possessing cleansing power, from the verb meaning “to purge”; the Syriac explains it as sulfur; others, soap; others, στρουθίον, a plant called by the Latins lanaria, or a root; others, the herb called soapwort, which fullers use to cleanse and wash cloth. This last opinion is the most probable, and Jerome supports it in Jeremiah 2:22: “For the herb borith,” he says, “which we have translated as it stands in the Hebrew, the Septuagint rendered πόαν, so as to indicate the herb of fullers, which, according to the custom of the region of Palestine, grows in green and moist places and has the same power for washing away dirt as natron.” Matthew Sylvaticus, in the Pandects, under “Fullers,” says: “Soapwort is called the herb of fullers, because fullers wash and clean cloth with it; borith, burith; likewise borich and guaisdo; so also Rabbi Jonah.” There is therefore no doubt that, when the Septuagint rendered πόαν as “herb,” they understood the soapwort plant; since they could not name it by its proper term, they called it by the general word πόα, because its use in cleaning clothes was extremely common and well known, leaving no room for doubt. Theodoret, commenting on this passage, says that πόαν names “the things growing from the earth that possess cleansing power.” He calls it an herb that springs from the earth endowed with the power to cleanse. Further, from πόα came the rabbinic term [Hebrew term], which signifies madder. The Arabs also use it; the Greeks render it ἐρυθρόδανον. Hence Philo, in the book *Who Is the Heir of Divine Things?*, says: “φουὰ δὲ ἔρυθρον ἑρμηνεύεται,” “phoua is interpreted as red.” Origen, *Homily 2 on Exodus*: “Phua, which among us may be called Red or Bashful.” Jerome, *On Hebrew Names*, in Exodus: “Phua, red.” Huetius.]

“—you are stained before me by your iniquities, says the Lord.”

Is it therefore to be supposed that the sinful soul has attempted to cleanse its stains with natron and, taking the poam that grows from the earth, has tried to wash the uncleanness of its sins from itself? Hence the divine word now speaks to it: “Even if you wash yourself with natron and multiply for yourself the poam, you are stained before me by your iniquities, says the Lord.”

Or should we regard this as more truly intended: just as the sacred books are full of every virtue, so God’s word is full of every virtue and possesses a power of this kind, able to cleanse vices and, when the filth has been scrubbed away, restore the soul to its original color? For “the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12), and so forth. From this we said that the word contains remedies for the passions of the soul: it contains natron, and it contains poam, by which stains may be washed away.

Yet not every sin can be cleansed by the natron of the word and by poam. There are certain offenses that do not require an easy cure and that do not depart merely after being washed with natron and poam. Thus it is now said: “If you wash yourself with natron and multiply for yourself the poam, you are stained before me by your iniquities, says the Lord.”

Just as some wounds are restored to their former health by poultices, oil, and bandages, while others are of such a kind that it is said of them: “There is no poultice to apply, nor oil, nor bandages; but your land is desolate, your cities have been burned with fire” (Isa. 1:6–7), so there are certain sins that soil the soul and require a person who possesses poam and the word of natron. Others, however, are such that they cannot be healed by the power of the word mentioned above, for they are not comparable to stains.

Therefore, knowing the differences among sins, the Lord says through Isaiah: “The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons of Zion” [in blood]. “He will cleanse from their midst the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, the filth and the blood” (Isa. 4:4). The filth by the spirit of judgment, the blood by the spirit of burning. If you have sinned and have been polluted by the filth of sins, the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion and will cleanse the blood from their midst.

But if it is a mortal sin, we cannot be cleansed by natron and poam; rather, we are cleansed by the spirit of judgment, the spirit of burning, and punishment. Perhaps Jesus also baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire (Luke 3:16)—not because he baptizes the same person with the Holy Spirit and with fire, but so that the holy person may be baptized with the Holy Spirit, while the one who, after faith and instruction [Note: The Royal manuscripts cited by Huetius read “the mystery”] in God, has turned back again to crimes may be purified by the torment of fire [Col. 0686B]. [Note: Origen, however, teaches the contrary in Homily 24 on Luke: only those baptized with water and Spirit who need purification will be baptized by Christ in a river of fire. But in Homily 6 on Exodus, Homily 25 on Numbers, and Homily 3 on Psalm XXXVI, he declares that everyone is to be purified by fire, as is explained more fully in the Origeniana. The same.]

Blessed is the one who has received the washing of the Holy Spirit and does not need the washing of fire. Wretched, however, and deserving of every tear is the one who, after the washing of the Spirit, must be baptized with fire.

Jesus possesses both baptisms: “A rod has gone forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower has risen from his root” (Isa. 11:1)—the rod for sinners, the flower for the righteous. Thus Scripture calls God both “a consuming fire” and “light” (Heb. 12:20; 1 John 3:5): fire for sinners, light for the holy. And: “Blessed is the one who has a share in the first resurrection.” If anyone preserves the washing of the Holy Spirit, that person shares in the portion of the first resurrection. But if anyone is preserved for the second resurrection, that person is a sinner who needs the baptism of fire and is purified by burning, so that whatever wood, hay, and straw he possesses, the fire may consume.

Therefore, since we see that such things remain for us after death, let us read the Scriptures carefully together, lay them up in our hearts, and strive to live according to their commands, so that, if possible, before the day of our departure we may be cleansed from the filth of our sins and be taken up with the saints, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY FOURTEEN

On the passage written: “And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah” (Jer. 3:6), up to the place where he says: “Israel justified her soul rather than sinful Judah” (Jer. 3:11).

[Col. 0686C]

869 We must first examine the very opening discourse of the reading, which is exceedingly obscure, and afterward, if the Lord grants us a path to understanding, proceed to the higher sense.

In the Books of Kings there is a history that teaches that, after Solomon’s death, in the days of Rehoboam, the twelve tribes were divided: that is, Jeroboam ruled over ten tribes, and they were called Israel; Rehoboam ruled over two, and they were called Judah. This division of the people, according to the testimony of the book, continues to the present day. [Note: One Royal manuscript cited by Huetius reads: “which separation.”] For no book is found in which Israel and Judah are again brought under one rule.

Israel therefore first sinned under Jeroboam and his other successors, and sinned so greatly that it was handed over by God to captivity and has remained subject to the Assyrians to the present day. Judah also sinned and was handed over to the Babylonians—not to the present day, but, as Scripture attests, for seventy years, about which Jeremiah and Daniel prophesied.

If you have understood the history written in the Books of Kings, consider the prophet’s words, and you will see that the same meaning is expressed. Israel is accused, and it is said: The assembly of Judah heard that Israel had been handed over to captivity on account of its sins, but did not repent or turn back to me. Rather, it heaped sins upon sins to such an extent that, in comparison with its vices, Israel is found to be more righteous.

Then the prophet is commanded to preach to Israel, so that, because Judah had become worse than it, both Israel and Judah might turn to the Lord, be under one rule, and return to their former concord.

To make this clearer, the words of Scripture itself must be set down:

“And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah: Have you seen what the habitation of the house of Israel did to me?” (Jer. 3:6–8). He did not say Judah, but first Israel. “She went beneath every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree, and there she committed fornication. And I said, after she had committed all these acts: Return to me; but she did not return.”

“And her treachery was heard,” that is, the treachery of the people Israel, “by faithless Judah. And they saw”—that is, those who belonged to Judah—“that, because of all the things in which the habitation of Israel was committing adultery, I had dismissed her and given her a bill of divorce.” I dismissed the people Israel and cast them out among the Assyrians. “And I gave her a bill of divorce into her hand, yet faithless Judah, her sister, did not fear” (Jer. 3:9).

After all that Israel had suffered, after being dismissed by God and receiving the bill of divorce into its own hands, Judah ought to have turned away from its vices and, corrected by another’s sins, guarded against similar ones. But it not only did not cease from sinning; it doubled its former crimes, so that, in comparison with it, the assembly of Israel, which had previously itself been condemned, was more righteous.

“And I gave her a bill of divorce into her hand, yet faithless Judah, her sister, did not fear. She went away and committed fornication herself, and her fornication was made nothing, and she committed adultery with wood and stone. Yet in all these things faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood” (Jer. 3:10). She did not fear because of what Israel had done, so as to turn to me with her whole heart and, laying aside the falsehood in which she persisted, truly repent.

“And the Lord said to me: Israel justified her soul rather than faithless Judah” (Jer. 3:11). Israel’s sins, when compared with Judah’s vices, somehow justify its soul. “Go and proclaim these words toward the north” (Jer. 3:12).

If you have understood the history, let us see what the mystical meaning signifies in these things. The calling of the nations and the expectation of Israel had their beginning, as the apostles testify, after the proclamation that they preached in the synagogues of the Jews: “It was necessary that the word be spoken to you; but since you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Paul likewise speaks with sacred authority: “Because of their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make them jealous” (Rom. 11:11).

Thus the many sins of that people caused it to be abandoned by the Lord and enabled us to come to the hope of salvation, though we were strangers to the covenants and the promise. For how could I, born somewhere—I do not know where—outside the holy land, now discuss the promises and believe in the God of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and in Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed by the voices of all the prophets?

[Note: Jerome: “If you have understood the two peoples, Israel and the Gentiles,” he brought back the sense but departed from the words. Origen, a little farther below: “Then you are Judah, and Judah because of the Savior who has risen from the tribe of Judah”; and in Homily 9: “We are men of Judah because of Christ, for it is clear that our Lord has risen from Judah”; and in Homily 16: “But if you understand Christ figuratively, perhaps the sin of Judah is ours—the sin of us who believe in Christ from the tribe of Judah.”” Huetius.]

If you have understood the two peoples, Israel and the Gentiles, understand the migration of Israel from the people of the Jews, and understand that it is written concerning it: “I dismissed her and gave her a bill of divorce.” For God truly dismissed the people Israel and gave it a bill of divorce, as the following example confirms. [Note: In Rabanus: “as the following example, leaving her, confirms.”]

The law of Moses commands that a woman who displeases her husband be given a bill of divorce and dismissed, and then permits the husband to take another wife. According to this meaning, understand that the Jews received the bill of divorce and were wholly abandoned by the Lord. For where are the prophets among them now? Where are the signs of mighty works? Where is the manifestation of God? There is no temple, no sacrifices, no other form of worship expressed in the books of the Law. They have been expelled from their territories, and thus the Lord gave Israel a bill of divorce.

After them, we who are called Jews in the Scriptures—for we are Jews because of the tribe of Judah, from whose stock the Savior descended—have turned [Al. “may turn”] to the Lord. And our final condition—which I wish at least would not be fulfilled in our own time—will be like Judah’s sins, or rather worse.

And so that you may believe that, at the consummation of the age, worse things will happen to us than happened to the Jews, hear the Savior proclaiming in the Gospel: “When iniquities have multiplied, the love of many will grow cold. But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:12–13). And elsewhere: “There will be signs and wonders in heaven and on earth to deceive, if possible, even the elect” (Matt. 24:24).

872 Such unbelief will exist throughout the entire human race that our Savior—who knew all the things that were to come—said: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

Indeed, if we judge faith [Note: Rabanus reads “our faith,” and not “the multitude”] and truth rather than numbers, and consider human intention rather than the assembly, we see that among so great a number of churches it is difficult to find one who is faithful [Note: It was formerly read “faith”; Rabanus, following the Greek, substituted “faithful,” and shortly afterward reads “they became” for “they were struck.” The Greek likewise has ἐγίνοντο].

They were truly faithful when the victims of the martyrs were being slain, when we followed bloody funerals and returned sorrowfully to the church [Note: Rabanus and the Greek have ἠρχόμεθα, “we were coming”; formerly the printed editions had “they were returning”], when the entire multitude was mourning, when catechumens, immediately upon their first reception of the faith [Note: Rabanus has: “At the very first reception of faith they were taught about postponing martyrdom.” We did not hesitate to restore this final expression in the text, since previously it had been less satisfactorily printed as “they were led.” The Greek word κατηχοῦντο also compelled this correction], were taught to endure martyrdom, and when women and the weaker sex remained fearless even unto death [Al. “continued fearless.”]

Then there were truly signs from heaven; then wonders occurred upon the earth. They were few, certainly, but truly faithful, entering by the narrow and constricted way that leads to life.

Now, however, when we have become more numerous—for it is difficult for the good to be numerous, and Jesus does not lie when he says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16)—among so many who profess the Christian faith, few indeed [Al. “enough”] are found who possess faith and truth and are worthy of blessedness [Note: Rabanus: “and worthy of true blessedness.”]

Therefore, if he says: “First, because of its sins I dismissed Israel and left it in migration” [Al. “in threat”], but Judah, hearing what had happened to Israel, did not wish to turn to me, he is speaking about our sins. We read what the Jewish people suffered, yet we are not afraid, nor do we say: “If he did not spare the natural branches, neither will God spare us.”

If Christ, the most merciful God [Note: Rabanus inserts: “who is gracious,” etc.], uprooted them—though they boasted that they were a good olive tree and came from the root [Al. “were the root”] of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—because of their merit, how much less will he spare us if we do similar things?

Observe the kindness and severity of God. He is not kind only and not severe; nor is he severe only and not also kind. If he were kind alone, we would despise his goodness; if severe alone, despair of salvation would plunge us into vices because of the sins we have committed.

But now, as God [Note: We read with Rabanus and one Royal manuscript preserved by Huetius: “as God has both”; for the reading requires: “we human beings need kindness,” and the Greek text agrees: νῦν δὲ ὡς Θεὸς ἀμφότερον ἒχει, χρήζομεν γὰρ οἱ ἄνθρωποι μετανοοῦντες, “but now, as God has both, for we human beings who repent need…” From the same Greek I would further prefer to supply the passage as follows: “as God has both, we need…” Nevertheless, this reading is preferable to the one previously printed, which contains more than one error: “as giving what is necessary, for we all have need of his goodness because of repentance,” etc.], has both, we human beings need his goodness because of repentance and his severity because of offenses. Thus he is both kind and severe, and he speaks to us through the prophet:

“Have you seen what the habitation of the house of Israel did to me?” Understand Israel here as representing the Jewish people in the present passage. “She went upon every high mountain and went beneath every leafy tree.”

If you consider the Pharisee ascending to the temple with pride, not beating his breast and not recognizing his own evils, saying: “I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke 18:11–12), you see how he ascends upon every high mountain and, inflamed with this arrogance, presumes upon himself.

There are others who ascend upon the hills and place themselves beneath every tree—not a fruitful tree, but a leafy one. For one kind of tree is fruitful through its abundance, while another merely abounds in foliage. In groves and sacred woods no one plants a fig tree, no one a vine, no one fruitful trees, but only leafy trees that delight the eyes.

Such are the heretics, who compose their prayer with verbal elegance, not to turn their hearers away from vices, but to please them. Therefore the person persuaded by this sort of seduction has gone beneath every tree.

At the same time, observe why he did not say “every tree” and remain silent, nor again add “every fruitful tree,” but significantly added: “beneath every leafy tree.” Therefore, if you understand why the Law commands: “You shall not plant any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God, nor make a grove” (Deut. 16:21)—for it explicitly forbids the planting of a grove in the temple—observe carefully why it is said: “She committed fornication there, and I said, after she had committed all these acts: Return to me; but she did not return. And faithless Judah saw the treachery of faithless Israel.”

Understand this as spoken about us. We have abandoned the covenant that we made with God and do not keep it; nor do we consider that the former people, the covenant, the promises, and the nobility of their lineage were lost through a similar sin.

“If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham your father,” the Lord says to them (John 8:39). And in another place John the Baptist says: “Do not begin to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Luke 3:8). He signifies that we are stones, because by hardening our hearts like stones we rejected the truth.

And truly, almighty God will raise up children for Abraham from stones if we remain in his adoption and preserve within us the Spirit through whom we were adopted.
