Thus faithless Judah saw the treachery of Israel, which had not kept the covenant it had made with God: “And she saw that, because of all the things in which that habitation had committed adultery, the entire generation had been caught” [Note: The sense was mutilated—or rather, there was no sense—in the earlier printed books: “because of all the things in which the habitation committed adultery,” etc., with the words supplied here omitted. We have substituted the reading from Rabanus: “had been caught,” “in which it committed adultery,” etc. The restored reading is confirmed by the original Greek text: ὅτι περὶ πάντων ὦν κατελήφθη ἡ κατοικία τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ, ἐν οἷς ἐμοιχᾶτο.]

Everything that Israel suffered, we who are Judah, reading in the sacred books, discover: because of all the things in which the habitation of Israel had been caught committing adultery, the Lord dismissed it and gave it a bill of divorce.

And although, from what they suffered, we ought to turn ourselves toward better things and observe that they were handed over to captivity and killed by their enemies because of their sins, and that their cities were burned with fire—although, as we have said, we ought to take these things into account [Al. “ought to have taken them into account”], remembering that, if God did not spare the natural branches, he will certainly not spare us; if he dismissed those who descended from the race of the patriarchs because of their sins, what must we, who were called from the Gentiles, expect to suffer?—we take none of this into account.

Therefore, although we were called so that they might be moved to jealousy, when they see that those who were once slaves are now free, and those who were once ignoble are now children of God, nevertheless, if they suffered so much, how much worse will we suffer if we sin?

“In the things in which the habitation of Israel committed adultery I dismissed her and gave her a bill of divorce into her hand, yet faithless Judah did not fear these things that the habitation of Israel had done, because I dismissed her and gave her a bill of divorce” (Jer. 3:8–9). Faithless Judah did not fear lest, because of its own sins, it too should suffer similar things.

If someone newly purchased enters the house of the buyer and master, he asks one of his fellow servants which of the former servants offended the master and what punishment he received. If he wishes to remain in the master’s house, he takes care not to do what he hears those did who proved worthy of blows, tortures, and exile.

Then, diligently inquiring what those did who earned freedom from their master, he strives with every effort to do what he knows they did.

So we, who were not servants of God but of idols and demons, and afterward, gathered from the Gentiles, believed in Christ, should read the Scriptures and see who was justified and who offended God. With the utmost vigilance, let us strive to do what we read the righteous did, and let us beware of falling into the things into which those fell who were handed over to captivity and expelled from God’s inheritance.

“And faithless Judah did not fear, but went away and committed fornication herself.” After the fornication in which Israel first [Al. “the first”] fell, Judah also committed fornication.

“And her fornication was made nothing, and she committed adultery with wood” [Al. “with a tree”] “and stone” [Al. “with a stone”]. When we sin against God with a hardened heart, we do nothing other than commit adultery with a stone. When we sin in pleasure [Note: Rabanus has “by the will,” a reading also preferred by the Royal manuscripts preserved by Huetius; the text formerly had “when we sinned” instead of “when we sin.” The Greek has ὅταν ἁμαρτάνωμεν], we commit adultery beneath every leafy tree.

“And in all these things faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood.” We too have turned to the Lord, but because we have not turned with our whole heart, it is said: “Faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood.”

He did not say: “Faithless Judah did not turn to me,” and stop there. Rather, he says: “Faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood,” to show that those who turn, if they do not turn with their whole heart, turn in falsehood and not in truth.

Therefore let us read the histories of the Old Testament and the prophets, and if we find anyone justified, let us imitate the things by which they were justified. Let us read the Gospels and the whole New Testament. Let us read all the Epistles of the apostle Paul, and let us write them upon our hearts, living according to the heavenly commands, so that a bill of divorce may not also be given to us, but so that we may become co-heirs [Al. “heirs”] with Christ Jesus.

And we shall see that, when the fullness of the Gentiles enters the Church of God, Israel will at last be saved, according to the saying: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (Rom. 11:25; John 10:10), teaching his people together to magnify almighty God with Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HERE BEGIN THE FOURTEEN HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL

[Col. 0691]

## HOMILY ONE

On the first vision of Ezekiel (chap. 1).

[Col. 0691D]

877. Not everyone who is captive is enduring captivity because of sins. For when the whole multitude of the Jews, on account of sin, had been abandoned by God, and, enduring captivity, had been seized by Nebuchadnezzar, [Col. 0692D] expelled from the holy land, and led all the way to Babylon, nevertheless a few righteous people who were among the people endured captivity not on account of their own guilt, but so that the sinners who had been crushed beneath the yoke of captivity would not be left entirely without assistance. For let us suppose that, once the sinners had been led away to Babylon, the righteous had remained in their ancient territories: the result would have been [Col. 0693A] that the sinners would never have obtained a remedy. Therefore the merciful, benevolent, and human-loving God arranged to mingle the kindness of his visitation even among the punishments by which he chastises sinners, and not to crush the wretched with immoderate punishment. Our God is always like this: he torments the guilty, but, like a compassionate father, joins mercy to the punishments.

If, however, you wish to recognize that what we are saying is true, consider what happened in Egypt during the famine. If he had wished merely to kill the Egyptians and punish them by torment throughout the seven-year famine, he would certainly have done what he wished; and Joseph would not have descended into Egypt, nor would Pharaoh have seen the dream concerning what was going to happen to Egypt, nor would the king have been told by the chief cupbearer that there was someone who could interpret the king’s dream. [Col. 0693B] But as you see, God chastises like a father, yet spares not only Israel but also the Egyptians, although they are alien to him, on account of his own gentleness.

And it is evident that the work of the good God was being carried out among them: Joseph descended into Egypt; Pharaoh was warned by dreams; the chief of the wine-stewards pointed out the interpreter; the interpreter explained the vessels; and thus, when crops had been gathered in the time of abundance, the scarcity of the subsequent famine was overcome. From all this it is clear that the anger which the heretics criticize in the Creator is not immoderate.

We could indeed recount many stories to prove what I have said, but, lest I seem to depart from my purpose, I shall make my discourse brief. My purpose is to explain how the people of Israel were led away captive on account of their sins. And lest someone perhaps suppose that those delivered over by God as sinners are no longer governed by him, and that, once reduced to captivity, they no longer deserve his dispensation and mercy, let us examine the present passage more carefully.

Daniel did not sin; Ananias, Azarias, and Misael were free from sin; nevertheless they became captives, so that, placed there, they might console the captive people and, through the exhortation of their voice, restore the repentant, chastened for a time, to Jerusalem. For they paid the penalties of servitude for seventy years, and thereafter returned to their own settlements, because the holy speech of the prophets had lifted up their dejected spirits.

Yet not only those four were prophets in captivity, [Col. 0693D] but Ezekiel was one of them, and Zechariah son of Barachiah sang during the captivity under King Darius. We also find Haggai and many other prophets prophesying in those same times. From this it is shown that God not only punishes those who sin but also mingles mercy with punishments.

And if you doubt this, listen to the voices of those suffering torments, how, even in their sufferings, they speak of God’s clemency in sacred language:

“You will feed us with the bread of tears, and you will give us drink in tears and according to measure.”

He does not say simply, “in tears,” but “in tears and according to measure.” For God’s mercy is measured out.

If it were not useful for the conversion of sinners to apply torments to those who sin, the merciful and benevolent God would never punish crimes with penalties. Rather, like the most indulgent father, he corrects his son for the purpose of educating him; like the most provident teacher, he chastises a wanton pupil with sternness of countenance, lest, feeling himself loved, the pupil perish.

Consider Solomon, wisest of all, and what he thinks concerning God’s corrections:

“My son, do not be fainthearted under the discipline of God, nor faint when you are corrected by him” (Eccl. VII).

“For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives.” For, as the Apostle says, “there is no son who, when he sins, is not scourged by his father.” And he wonderfully adds:

“Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as to sons” (Hebr. XII).

For what son is there whom his father does not correct? “But if you are without discipline, of which all have become participants,” [Col. 0694B] “then you are illegitimate and not sons.”

[Note: [Col. 0693] “Adulteri” was corruptly read instead of “adulterini,” and shortly afterward “si” instead of “sit.”]

But perhaps someone, offended by the very name “anger,” may accuse God on that account. We shall answer that God’s anger is not so much anger as a necessary dispensation. Listen to what the work of God’s anger is: to rebuke, to correct, and to amend:

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Ps. VI).

The person who speaks these words knows that God’s fury is not useless for healing, but is applied in order to cure the sick and amend those who have disdained to hear his word. Therefore he does not pray that he may not be amended by such remedies, lest, when he receives healing through punishment, he recover his former health—just as a servant already placed beneath the rod might pray to his master, promising that he will do what has been commanded, and say:

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

Everything that belongs to God is good, and we deserve to be corrected. Listen to what he says:

“I will rebuke them when they are in the hearing of their distress.”

For this reason we have heard the things concerning tribulation: so that we may be amended. In the curses of Leviticus also it is written:

“If after these things they do not obey, nor turn back to me, I will add sevenfold blows against their sins. But if after this they do not turn back, I will correct them” (Levit. XXXVI).

Everything belonging to God that appears bitter contributes to education and healing. God is a physician; God is a father; he is lord—not a harsh lord, but a gentle one.

If you come to those who have been punished according to the declarations of Scripture, “join Scriptures to Scriptures,” as the Apostle also teaches you, and you will see that what is sweetest is found precisely where things are thought to be most bitter.

It is written in the prophet:

“He does not take vengeance twice for the same thing in judgment” (Num. I).

He took vengeance once in judgment through the Flood (Gen. VII, 19); he took vengeance once in judgment upon Sodom and Gomorrah; he took vengeance once in judgment upon Egypt and the six hundred thousand Israelites (Exod. XIV). Do not suppose that this vengeance was merely punishment for sinners, as though after death they were to be punished again by further punishments. They were punished in the present, so that they would not be punished perpetually in the future.

Observe the poor man in the Gospel: he is oppressed by squalor and poverty, and afterward rests in Abraham’s bosom. “He received his evil things during his life” (Luke XVI).

How do you know whether those who were killed in the Flood received their evil things during their life? How do you know whether Sodom and Gomorrah received their evil things during their life? Listen to the testimony of Scripture. Do you wish to learn the testimony of the Old Testament? Do you wish to be instructed by that of the New?

“Sodom will be restored to its former state.” And do you still doubt whether the Lord is good when he punishes the Sodomites?

“It will be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrhaeans on the day of judgment,” says the Lord, taking pity on the Sodomites (Mark VI).

God, therefore, is benevolent; God is merciful. He truly makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and truly sends rain upon the just and the unjust—not only upon this sun that we see with our eyes, but also upon that sun which is perceived by the eyes of the mind.

I was wicked, and the sun of righteousness rose upon me. I was wicked, and the rain of righteousness came upon me (Matt. V).

The goodness of God is present even in those things that are thought bitter.

Therefore the Prophet was established in the city, and observe what he sees, so that he might not suffer the pains of captivity (Ezek. I). He sees the troubles below, but, raising his eyes upward, he looks upon the heavens opened; he sees the heavenly things opened for him; he sees the likeness of the glory of God; he sees the four living creatures, concerning whom there is much discourse and difficult interpretation. He sees the charioteer of the four living creatures. He sees wheels enclosing one another.

The charioteer of the four living creatures is not entirely fiery, but from the feet to the loins, and from there to the top, he shines with the radiance of electrum. For God does not possess punishments alone; there are also refreshments in him. He punishes sinners, but through those mysteries [Col. 0695C] that are below. For the Prophet did not see fire in the head, nor in those members that rise from the boundary of the loins to the highest parts.

The Lord is fiery, but from the loins to the feet, to show that those who are engaged in generation require fire. For the loins signify intercourse. Levi was still in the loins of Abraham his father when Melchizedek met him (Hebr. VII). And in the psalm it is said:

“From the fruit of your loins I will set upon my throne” (Ps. CXXXII).

The Lord is fiery from the loins downward. For the works of generation and lust are chastised by the punishments of Gehenna.

God is fiery, but he is not entirely fiery: his upper parts are electrum. Electrum is more precious not only than silver but also than gold. Scripture used electrum as an example of radiance, [Col. 0696A] not because God is truly electrum. And just as God is not such electrum as he appeared to be, so the fire is not such a fire as appeared from the loins to the end of the feet.

This fire consumes, but it is not stated what it consumes, so that you may seek and discover what it is that is consumed by God’s fire.

“Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV).

What does this fire consume?

[Note: [Col. 0695D] The first book, On First Principles, chapter 1, has a parallel passage which it is worthwhile to quote here: “For what,” he says, “will God consume according to the fact that he is fire? Will he be thought to consume bodily matter, such as wood or hay or straw? And what worthy thing concerning God’s praises is said in this, if God is such a fire as consumes these materials? But if we consider that God consumes what he exterminates—if he consumes evil thoughts of the mind, consumes shameful deeds, consumes desires of sin, when he inserts himself into the minds of believers, and, dwelling together with his Son in those souls which are made capable of his word and wisdom, according to what has been said, ‘I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him,’ consumes all their vices and passions, and makes them worthy of himself as a temple—so also in Homily 2 on the Song of Songs: ‘Finally, for this reason our God is said to be a consuming fire, [Col. 0696D] and nevertheless a light in which there are no darknesses, unquestionably light for the righteous and fire for sinners, so that it may consume in them whatever it finds in their soul that belongs to corruption or weakness.’”]

Not the wood that we see, not visible hay, not the straw that appears; but if you build upon the foundation of Jesus Christ the wood of sinful works, the hay of sinful works, and, lower down, the straw of sinful works, the fire comes and tests all these things (1 Cor. III).

What is this fire which the Law proclaims and the Gospel does not keep silent about? “The quality of each person’s work—the fire will prove it.”

What is this fire, Apostle, which tests our works? What is this fire so wise that it preserves my gold, displays my silver more splendidly, leaves unharmed the precious stone that is in me, and consumes only the evil things I have done—the wood, hay, and straw that I have built upon? What is this fire?

“I came to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled!” (Luke XII).

[Note: [Col. 0696D] Compare the observations cited below in Homily 5 on this Gospel passage.]

Jesus Christ says, “How I wish that it were already kindled.” For he is good, and he knows that if this fire is kindled, wickedness will be consumed.

It is written in the Prophets:

“He sanctified him in burning fire, and devoured the forest like hay” (Zech. XIII).

And again:

“The Lord Sabaoth sends an insult to your honor, and a burning fire is kindled for your glory”—that is, fire is sent into your sinful works so that you may be glorified.

Do you still wish to learn from the Prophet that the torments of the good God have been established for the benefit of those who endure them? Listen to the same prophet saying:

“You have coals of fire; you will sit upon them. They will be a help to you” (Isa. LVII).

These things ought to have been hidden and not brought into public view, but [Note: [Col. 0696D] Consider here the followers of Simon, Valentinus, Cerdo, and other heretics of that kind, who posited two principles, or two gods: one evil, although just, the creator of the world and maker of the Law; the other good, the Father of Christ and author of the New Testament. Against their madness, many of the Fathers—including Tertullian and Irenaeus, but especially Origen—fight everywhere, so that he may be heard as particularly diligent in condemning and refuting it by the author of the Dialogue on the Right Faith in God.]

the heretics compel us to bring into public what ought to be concealed, because these things are profitably hidden from those who are still little ones in respect of the age of their soul—those who require fear, and who must be corrected by the threats and terrors of their teachers—so that they may attain goodness and, through bitter remedies, eventually cease from the wounds of their sins.

883. For the mysteries of God are always covered with certain veils for the sake of immature hearers.

“How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you.”

The God of the Law and the Prophets has hidden the multitude of his goodness from those who do not love him, but fear him. For they are little ones and cannot, for their own benefit, learn that they are loved by the Father, lest they become lax and despise the goodness of God.

Therefore, when you hear about the captivity of the people, believe that it truly occurred according to the historical account, but also that it preceded as a sign of another reality and signified a mystery that followed.

You too, who are called faithful and who behold peace—for Christ is our peace—are dwelling in Jerusalem. But if you sin, God’s visitation will abandon you, and you will be delivered captive to Nebuchadnezzar and led away into Babylon. For when your soul has been confused by vices and disturbances, you will be led away into Babylon, since Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.”

And if you again repent and, through the conversion of a true heart, obtain the mercy of God, Ezra will be sent to you to bring you back and make you build Jerusalem. For Ezra is interpreted as “helper,” and the assisting word is sent to you so that you may return to your homeland.

There is also a mystery in what is spoken in an enigmatic manner by Daniel and narrated by the Apostle, who at once conceals and reveals it:

“In Adam we all die, and in Christ we are all made alive” (1 Cor. XV).

Adam was indeed in paradise, but the serpent was the cause of his captivity and caused him to be expelled either from Jerusalem or from paradise and to come into this place of tears. The serpent is an enemy opposed to the truth. But the one who is opposed was not created opposed from the beginning; he did not immediately walk upon his breast and belly, nor was he cursed from the beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] It would be better to remove one of the two particles of negation here, so that the sense may be coherent.]

Just as Adam and Eve did not sin immediately when they were made, so the serpent was once not a serpent, when it dwelt in the paradise of delights. Thus, afterward, when it fell because of its sins, it deserved to hear:

“You were the seal of likeness, the crown of beauty; you were born in the paradise of God. Until iniquity was found in you, you walked undefiled in all your ways” (Ezek. XXVIII).

Job also mentions him, saying that he became proud in the presence of the almighty God:

“Lucifer, who rose in the morning, fell from heaven and was crushed upon the earth” (Job XI).

Observe the harmony between the prophetic and Gospel word. The Prophet says:

“Lucifer fell from heaven, who rose in the morning; he was crushed upon the earth” (Isa. XIV).

Jesus says:

“I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning” (Luke XVIII).

What difference is there, as far as the matter is concerned, between saying that lightning or Lucifer fell from heaven? The essential point is that both agree concerning one who falls.

God did not make death, nor did he work evil. He permitted free will to both human beings and angels in all things. Here we must understand how, through the freedom of their will, some rose to the highest things that are good, while others fell into the depths of wickedness.

But you, human being, why do you not wish to be left to your own will? Why do you find it burdensome to strive, labor, and contend, and to make yourself, through good works, the cause of your own salvation?

Or would you rather enjoy resting in eternal prosperity while sleeping and remaining idle?

“My Father,” says the Lord Jesus Christ, “is working until now, and I am working” (John XV).

And you dislike working, although you were born for works? Do you not wish your work to become righteousness, wisdom, and chastity? Do you not wish fortitude and the other virtues to be your work?

Therefore those who, on account of their sins, have deserved the penalties of servitude are led into captivity. And Jesus Christ comes to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind (Luke IV).

He cries out to those who are in chains: “Come out!” and to those who are in darkness: “See!”

We too were once in the chains of sins, and we too once lived in darkness, contending against the rulers of the darkness of this world. Jesus came, proclaimed by the voices of all the prophets, saying to those who were bound, “Come out,” and to those established in darkness, “Look!”

But if you wish to hear Ezekiel, son of man, preaching in captivity—and he too was a type of Christ—he says:

“Therefore it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, and I was in the midst of the captivity beside the river Chobar, and the heavens were opened.”

Thus, beside the river Chobar, Ezekiel, when he was thirty years old, saw the heavens opened. And the Lord Jesus Christ, when he was beginning to be about thirty years old, was beside the river Jordan, and the heavens were opened (John I; Luke III).

Throughout the whole prophecy Ezekiel is called “son of man.” But who is the son of man except my Lord Jesus Christ?

[Note: [Col. 0697D] Hear Origen himself explaining the reason for this title, by which Christ is called, par excellence, “Son of man,” in his Commentary on Matthew, chapter XXII, from the Latin translation:

“We can find the reason why the Savior so often calls himself ‘son of man’ (υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ‘Son of man’) or ‘son of man’ (υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ‘Son of man’): just as God, caring for human beings, is called ‘man’ in parables and perhaps in some way becomes one, so the Savior, who is first and chiefly the Son of God, is also God, and the Son of his love, and the image of the invisible God; but in what he first and chiefly is, he does not remain. Rather, according to the administration of the one who is called ‘man’ in parables but is truly God, he becomes the Son of man, imitating God when he rules human beings—he who is called ‘man’ in parables and in some way becomes one. Nor should one seek some human being and call the Savior his son; rather, by adhering to this divine rationale and following the parables that indicate him to be man, one must understand wisely and cautiously what he means when he calls himself ‘Son of man.’”]

Let the heretics answer me:

[Note: [Col. 0698D] Since Origen so often attacks and refutes the heresy of the Docetists with most forceful arguments, it is quite astonishing that this very charge was brought against him: that he believed Christ’s body to have been fabricated and merely apparent, rather than real. “The fourth accusation,” says Pamphilus in his Apology, “after the foregoing ones, is opposed to them all (for malice is blind): they say that he maintains that everything done by the Savior was done δοκήσει, that is, only ostensibly and allegorically, and not also according to the historical events recorded.” For elsewhere he does not depart from the truth. It is worthwhile to hear him himself as guarantor of his position, in countless other places, but especially in Homily 14 on Luke, in the translation of Jerome: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments.” This also tells against those who deny that our Lord had a human body, maintaining instead that it was composed of heavenly and spiritual substances. For if his body was of heavenly things—or, as they falsely assert, of stars—and of some other higher spiritual nature, let them answer why a spiritual body could be filthy, or how they interpret the words we have cited: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments.” Parallel testimonies occur in Book II of On First Principles, chapter 6; Book V on the Epistle to the Romans; and Against Celsus, chapter 2, as Huetius notes.]

Why is Christ called the Son of man, if they elude his birth as a phantom?

I affirm that he was the Son of man. For one who assumed human sufferings necessarily received birth before suffering. He could not have received human emotions, words, customs, the cross, and death if he had not received the beginning of humanity. And it followed that those who remove his birth would also remove his passion and simply say, “Jesus was not crucified.”

Yet now you confess the cross and are not ashamed. You proclaim to the Jews a crucified Christ as a stumbling block and to the Gentiles as foolishness (1 Cor. I), and, though you are less offended by his passion or death, you are ashamed to confess his birth. Surely it is less a stumbling block that Jesus was born than that he died—or, if the Christian faith is not afraid of the scandal, why are you afraid to speak of the lesser things when you have dared to confess the greater?

Especially since his birth is believed not to have been from the seed of a man and the ordinary intercourse of a woman, but according to the prophetic declaration:

“Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII).

The word “Emmanuel” does not merely sound like one name; it signifies a reality. For when Jesus comes, we say, “The Lord is with us.”

It is not without reason, therefore, that Ezekiel prophesies in the thirtieth year. For his name too is a figure of Christ. Ezekiel is interpreted as “the dominion of God”; and there is no dominion of God except Christ Jesus.

886. He is also written as the son of Buzi, which is interpreted as “despised.” If you come to the heretics and hear them despising and regarding the Creator as nothing, and even accusing him, you will see that, according to them, our Lord Jesus Christ is the Son of the most despised Creator.

But if someone resists and does not wish to receive as prophecy what we have explained, I shall ask him why it is written that, in the thirtieth year of Ezekiel’s life, the heavens were opened and he saw the visions contained in his book. What benefit is there for me in the number of years, unless it is so that I may learn that in the thirtieth year the heavens were opened both to the Savior and to the prophet, and, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, recognize that everything written consists of the words of the same God?

“For the words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep,” because they were given by one shepherd to those who contend with one another (Eccl. XII).

I also investigate, as far as my understanding permits, what is meant by the words “in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month,” and I pray to God that I may be able to understand that same meaning which accords with the intention of his Scriptures.

The new year is now approaching for the Jews, and among them the first month is counted from the beginning of the new year. Passover is celebrated according to the numbering of the new year.

“This month shall be for you the beginning of the months of the year” (Exod. XII).

Count the fourth month for me from this year, and understand Jesus to have been baptized in the fourth month of the new year. For we know that the Lord’s baptism occurred in the month which the Romans call January, which is the fourth month from the new year according to the reckoning of the Hebrews.

And because he had assumed a body constituted from the four elements of the world, also receiving human senses, perhaps for this reason he saw the vision in the fourth month and [887] on the fifth day of the month.

“And I was in the midst of the captivity.”

It seems to me that this was said ironically: “And I was in the midst of the captivity.” It is as though the prophet were saying, according to the historical sense, “I too, who was not held in the sins of the people, was in the midst of the captivity”; but according to the allegorical sense, Christ says, “I too came into the place of captivity; I came to those regions where slaves and captives were held.”

You have similar words of our Savior in the Prophets, expressing indignation because we do not do things worthy of his dispensation—and especially we who are thought to believe in him. For he says to his Father:

“What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption? Will dust confess to you, or will it announce your truth?” (Ps. XXIX).

I also find another such saying spoken through the prophet from the person of our Savior, who seeks souls full of righteousness, full of divine understanding, and full of holy fruits; who seeks true clusters of truth, but finds many sinners, unproductive of good things, and therefore says:

“Alas for me, for I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest, and like one who gathers grapes at the vintage, when there is not even a cluster of firstfruits to eat. Alas for me!” (Mic. VII).

The words “Alas for me!” are not the voice of the firstborn of all creation; they are not the voice of divinity, but of the human soul which he assumed. Hence he continues:

“Alas for me, my soul, for the righteous has perished from the earth, and there is no one among human beings who corrects. They all judge in blood; each one oppresses his neighbor.”

These things have been recalled because the Prophet says:

“And I was in the midst of the captivity beside the river Chobar.”

Chobar is interpreted as “heaviness.” The river of this age is heavy, just as it is also spoken of elsewhere in sacred language. According to the simple historical sense, he explains matters; but to those who hear the Scriptures spiritually, he signifies the soul that has fallen into the storms of this life.

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments, because there those who had taken us captive asked us for the words of songs” (Ps. CXXXVI).

These are the rivers of Babylon. Beside them they sit, remembering their heavenly homeland, mourning and lamenting; there they hang up their instruments upon the willows of the Law and the mysteries of God.

It is written in a certain book that all believers receive a willow crown. And in Isaiah it is said:

“Grass will spring up as in the midst of water, and a willow beside flowing water” (Isa. XLIV).

And at God’s festival, when his tabernacles are assembled, they set willow branches in place for the construction of the tabernacles.

“Beside the river Chobar”—beside this most heavy river of the age.

“And the heavens were opened.”

The heavens had been closed, and at Christ’s coming they were opened, so that, once they had been unsealed, the Holy Spirit might descend upon him in the form of a dove. For he could not come among us unless he had first descended to the one who shared his nature.

“He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he received gifts among human beings. He who descended is the one who also ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things. And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as shepherds and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints” (Eph. IV).

The heavens were opened. It is not enough for one heaven to be opened; many are opened, so that angels may descend from all the heavens, not from one alone, to those who are to be saved.

[Note: [Col. 0701D] In other books it reads “from many.” Origen seems, both there and especially in the following context, to assign a guardian angel not to every single person indiscriminately, but only to the saints who profess the faith of Christ. Shortly afterward he says, “He distributes guardians to those who believe in his name. Yesterday you were under a demon; today you are under an angel.” And somewhat later, in fuller form. See what Huetius has collected on this subject in Origeniana, book II, question 5, no. 18. It should also be noted that the Hebrew language does not at all tolerate this distinction between the plural and singular numbers.]

The angels who ascended and descended upon the Son of man approached him and ministered to him. The angels descended because Christ had descended first. They feared descending before the Lord of all powers and things had commanded it; but when they saw the commander of the heavenly army dwelling in earthly places, then they entered by the opened way, following their Lord and obeying his will.

He distributed them as guardians of those who believe in his name. Yesterday you were under a demon; today you are under an angel.

“Do not despise,” says the Lord, “one of these little ones who are in the Church. For I say to you truly, their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

The angels serve your salvation; they have been granted for the ministry of the Son of God, and they say among themselves:

“If he descended—and descended into a body; if he clothed himself in mortal flesh, endured the cross, and died for human beings, why do we remain at rest? Why do we spare ourselves? Come, let us all descend from heaven!”

For this reason the multitude of the heavenly host was praising and glorifying God when Christ was born.

Everything is full of angels. Come, angel, receive the one who has been converted by the word from his former error, from the teaching of demons, from iniquity speaking arrogantly; and, receiving him like a good physician, cherish him and instruct him. He is a little one: today an old man is born again as a child. Receive him, giving him the baptism of a second regeneration, and call other companions of your ministry to yourself, so that all of you together may instruct in the faith those who were once deceived.

“For there is greater joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke XV).

Every creature rejoices, is glad, and applauds those who are to be saved. For “the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God” (Rom. VIII).

And although those who have interpolated the Apostolic Scriptures do not wish such statements to be present in their books—statements by which Christ the Creator could be established—nevertheless all creation awaits the sons of God: when they are freed from guilt, when they are removed from the hand of the Devil, when they are regenerated by Christ.

But now it is time to touch upon certain matters from the present passage.

The Prophet saw not one vision but visions of God. Why did he not see one vision but many? Listen to the Lord promising and saying:

“I multiplied visions” (Hos. XII).

“The fifth day of the month.”

This is the fifth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin. In the thirtieth year of Ezekiel’s age and the fifth year of Jehoiachin’s captivity, the Prophet is sent to the Jews. The most merciful Father did not despise them, nor did he abandon the people without warning for a long time.

It is the fifth year. How much time had passed? Five years had elapsed since they had been serving as captives. Immediately the Holy Spirit descended and opened the heavens, so that those who were oppressed by the yoke of captivity might see what had been seen by the Prophet.

For when he said, “The heavens were opened,” they too, in a certain way, looked with the eyes of the heart upon what he had seen with the eyes of the flesh.

890. “And the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, son of Buzi, the priest.”

The word of the Lord, which in the beginning was with God the Father, God the Word; the word which makes believers gods. For if he called those to whom the word of God came “gods,” and Scripture cannot be annulled, then all to whom the word of God came were made gods.

Ezekiel too was a god, because the word of God came to him:

“I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High. But you will die like human beings, and like one of the rulers you will fall” (Ps. LXXXII).

Where do you have a promise of this kind in the New Testament? If it is necessary to distinguish the instruments and to say that the gods differ among themselves—a thing which it is impious even to suspect, although we say it according to an abuse of language—I shall certainly say that far greater humanity was displayed in the Old Testament than in the New:

“I said, You are gods and all of you are sons of the Most High.”

He does not say, “Some of you are gods and some are not”; rather, “All of you are gods.”

But if you sin, listen to what follows:

“But you will die like human beings.”

The fault does not lie with the one who calls to salvation; nor is the one who invites to divinity and adoption into the heavenly nature himself the cause of death. Rather, it lies in our sin and in our crime when it is said:

“But you, like human beings, will die, and like one of the rulers you will fall.”

There were many rulers, and one of them fell. Concerning him it is also written in Genesis:

“Behold, Adam has become as one, not as one of us, but as one of us” (Gen. III).

Therefore, when Adam sinned, he became “as one.”

“And the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, son of Buzi.”

Even if you wish to understand these words as referring to the Savior, do not be afraid; the allegory also has its meaning in this way. The word of the Lord came to him who was being born from the Virgin, that is, to the human being—the word who always remained in the Father—so that the two might become one, and so that the human being whom, for the sake of the mystery and salvation of the whole human race, he would assume might be joined to his divinity and to the nature of the only-begotten God.

“The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, son of Buzi, the priest, in the land of the Chaldeans.”

The Chaldeans discuss heavenly matters; the Chaldeans calculate human nativities. “In the land of the Chaldeans,” as though he were saying: in the land of those who assert fate, of those who claim that the causes of everything lie in the circuit of the stars. Thus this error and this perversity of mind are now figuratively signified by the land of the Chaldeans.

“In the land of the Chaldeans, beside the river Chebar. And there the hand of the Lord came upon me.” And the word of the Lord came to the prophet, and the hand also, so that he might be adorned both by deeds and by words.

“And I saw visions.” I shall touch upon some matters briefly; and although, given the pressure of time, what I have said might suffice, nevertheless I shall also taste a little of the chief points from the entire body of the vision.

“And I saw, and behold, a spirit rising—or, ‘taking away’—was coming from the north.” Carefully consider the number of the things that are said: “a spirit rising,” or “taking away,” was coming from the north—there is one thing. “And there was a great cloud in it”—there are two. “And radiance all around it”—there are three. “And a flashing fire”—there are four. “And in its midst, something like the appearance of amber in the midst of the fire”—there are five. “And light in it”—there are six. After this come the likeness of four living creatures, their appearance, and the account of the vision—there are seven. “And in the midst of the living creatures, something like burning coals”—there are eight.

Who can explain these things in detail? Who is so capable of the Spirit of God as to illuminate these mysteries? The accusers of the Creator and of the God of the prophets ought first to understand what is said by the prophets, and only afterward to bring accusations. For one who truly accuses must accuse what he knows. But if heretics are not even close to divine understanding, how can they reasonably bring accusations concerning matters which we prove that they do not know? Let them learn what the meaning of this vision is.

First there appears a spirit that takes away; second, a great cloud in the spirit that takes away; third, radiance around the spirit that takes away; fourth, a flashing fire; fifth, in its midst, something like the appearance of amber—without doubt in the midst of the fire; sixth, radiance in that same amber.

I willingly acknowledge the statement made by a wise and faithful man, a statement that I often accept: speaking truth about God is dangerous. For it is not only false things said about him that are dangerous; even true things, when spoken at an inappropriate time, create danger for the one who speaks them. A pearl is genuine, but if [cast] perversely, its peril lies in the words “... their feet.” [The wording is corrupt or incomplete.]

[Note: Thus also the older editions of Genebrard and Basel read. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that the passage is corrupt or mutilated; but when the ancient books provide no assistance, I do not wish to emend it by conjecture.]

And, to offer an example close to us, these collections—not only in Aelia, not merely in Rome, not in Alexandria, but once throughout the entire world—bear the likeness of a dragnet that catches fish of every kind. Everything that falls into it cannot be good. For the Savior says: “When they have drawn it out and sat down beside the shore, they will put the good into their vessels, but they will throw the bad outside.” Therefore, in the dragnet of the whole Church there must be both good and bad. If everything is already clean, what do we leave for the judgment of God?

And, according to another parable, both grain and chaff are contained on the threshing floor, although only the grain is to be gathered into Christ’s granaries; the chaff is separated from it by him “whose winnowing-fan is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor, and gather the grain into the barn, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Luke 3). For I do not assert that the threshing floor is the whole world; rather, I understand the threshing floor to be the assembly of the Christian people. Just as each threshing floor is enclosed and is full either of grain or of chaff, yet is neither wholly grain nor wholly chaff, so in the earthly churches one person is grain and another is chaff.

Yet there they are chaff neither through their own fault nor by their own will—for grain too is not such by its own choice—whereas here it has been placed in your power whether you are chaff or grain.

These things ought to teach us that, if at some point someone sees a sinner in our assemblies, he should not be scandalized or say: “Look, there is a sinner in the holy assembly. If this is permitted, if this is allowed, why should I not sin as well?” While we are in the present age—that is, on the threshing floor and in the dragnet—both good and bad are contained in it. But when Christ comes, there will be a separation, and what the Apostle says will be fulfilled: “We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 4).

These words were spoken in the preface by a mind feverishly occupied with interpreting the visions, uncertain what to pass over in silence, what to bring forth, what to leave after touching upon it lightly, and which matters among these should be explained more clearly or more obscurely—if indeed we are able to fulfill what we desire.

First, then, there appears a spirit that takes away. What we said shortly before—that our Lord is a consuming fire—we repeat now, and say that this testimony agrees with it.

How is a spirit that takes away presented? “God is spirit” (John 4), and a spirit that takes away is seen. What does it take away from me and from my soul, so that it may rightly be called “taking away”? Certainly, evils. And then I perceive his goodness, if he has removed from me every kind of wickedness.

Nor should it be thought that freedom from evils is the end of blessedness; it is the beginning of happiness to be without sin. And it is written in Jeremiah—for I attribute everything written in the Prophets to the most merciful God—“Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, to dig under, to destroy, to build, and to plant” (Jeremiah 1).

God is benevolent, giving words for uprooting. But what is it that must be uprooted and overturned? If there is some evil planting in the soul, if there is some wicked sect, prophetic speech uproots and overturns it. Would that it might happen that such speech were granted to me—speech that would uproot the seeds of the heretics and the teaching flowing from the source of the Devil, and that would remove from the soul of the one who is now entering the Church for the first time the planting of idolatry.

“I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, I have appointed you to uproot and to dig under”—that is, so that if there is some utterly evil structure, it may be destroyed. How I too would like to dig under, uproot, overturn, and destroy whatever Marcion has built in the ears of the deceived, just as Jacob destroyed the idols!

To this very day there is both destruction and building. The heretics have heard only of destroying and overturning, but they have turned deaf ears to the word of building and planting. For they do not wish to consider that the painful things are mentioned first, and the joyful things second.

Why do we now recall these matters? Clearly, so that God’s word may be shown to overturn evils and build what is best, to uproot vices like a good farmer, so that, once the field has been cleansed, a most abundant harvest of virtues may arise.

This has been said concerning the spirit that takes away. For he first saw the spirit that takes away, and afterward the great cloud in it. When you have been cleansed by the spirit that takes away—provided that every evil has been removed from you, and everything wicked that moves about in your soul—then you will begin also to enjoy the great cloud that rests in the spirit that takes away.

This cloud is close to that cloud which we read about in the Gospel, from which the voice came: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3).

But first there is the spirit that takes away, then the great cloud in it, and afterward the most splendid light around it. Evil has been removed from you. A great cloud has been given to you, so that it may rain upon your vineyard. According to what is said elsewhere: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isaiah 5)—namely, upon the utterly wicked vineyard. But if this is commanded concerning a bad vineyard, there is no doubt that, conversely, if you are a good vineyard, the cloud will rain upon you.

“And radiance all around it.” Then: “A flashing fire, and in its midst something like the appearance of amber.” God removes evils from us in two ways: by spirit and by fire. If we are good and attentive to God’s commandments and are instructed by his words, he removes our evils by the Spirit, according to what is written: “But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” But if the Spirit has not removed our evils, we need purification by fire (Romans 8).

Therefore observe carefully each conjunction. The first conjunction is of spirit and cloud; the second, of fire and light; the third, of amber and radiance. Each thing that appears to be sorrowful is balanced by the proximity of something more joyful. For whether the spirit arises, the cloud immediately follows; whether fire appears, light is joined to it; whether amber comes first, radiance is around it.

For we must be melted like gold in a furnace, and like amber in the fiercest fire. And in this prophet whom we are now explaining, you have the Lord sitting in the midst of Jerusalem and melting those who are mixed with silver, tin, bronze, and lead, complaining in a lamenting voice about those who contain within themselves a mixture of inferior material. “You have become mixed silver,” he says, “and you have become like a grape-berry, rejected silver” (Ezekiel 16) [the printed wording is uncertain]. For when we impose upon God’s creature—which is good from the beginning—the vices and passions arising from our evils, then we mix bronze, tin, and lead with silver and gold, and fire is necessary for purification.

Therefore we must carefully ensure that, when we come to this fire, we pass through it safely, like gold, silver, and precious stone, which are adulterated without fire—or like those who are adulterated without fire: may we not so much be consumed by the blaze as be tested by it.

“Behold, a spirit that takes away was coming from the north.” The fact that the spirit that takes away came from the north and afterward returns also has a meaning. For from the north evils blaze up against those who inhabit the earth. The north wind is a most violent wind, which we call by another name the “right-hand wind”; among the four quarters of heaven, from which the winds are said to blow, it is colder and more powerful.

The matter written in Numbers concerning the order of the camps of Israel (Numbers 1) also represents this. For the final camp is placed toward the north: Dan; the first camp, Judah, toward the east; then behind him Reuben; afterward, toward the sea, Ephraim; and at the extreme point, as we said, toward the north, Dan. And the pot described as being kindled is lit from the face of the north.

Figuratively, the north is called the opposing power—that is, the Devil, who is truly a most harsh wind. A spirit that takes away came from the north, and a great cloud in it: we have explained that the vices come from it. “And radiance all around it, and a flashing fire.” He could have said “a consuming fire,” but Scripture was reluctant to name sorrow and attribute its work to it; therefore, in place of a punitive force, it added only radiance.

“And in its midst, something like the likeness of four living creatures.” This is their vision. “The likeness of a man was in them. And each had four faces, and each had four wings, and their legs were straight, and their feet were winged.”

You see what sort of beings are governed by God, as in the words: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear.” “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” and whoever is full of knowledge becomes a cherub, governed by God.

But what do the four faces signify? Those who are to be saved bow the knee before the Lord Jesus, and they are named threefold by the Apostle: “so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2). Those who bow the knee before the Lord Jesus are subject to him. And those who are subject say: “Is not my soul subject to God? From him comes my salvation” (Psalm 61). And: “He must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15).

What, then, is the fourth? There are only three: heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those under the earth.

Certainly, it is that which says: “Praise the Lord, heavens of heavens, and the water that is above the heavens, let it praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148). All these things are governed by God and led by his majesty.

“Wherever the spirit went, the living creatures went also.” These same living creatures have above them the likeness of a man, although they possess four faces. It is not said at the beginning that they have four faces; rather, because among the four faces one stands out and holds the chief place—the human face—it is described, as are the human face, the lion’s face on the right of the four parts, the calf’s face on the left of the four, and the eagle’s face on the four sides.

Let us therefore see whether this signifies the tripartite soul, about which we must also dispute with the opinions of others, so that a fourth power, courage, presides over the tripartite soul.

What is the tripartition of the soul? Its rational element is indicated by the man, anger by the lion, and desire by the calf. But the spirit that presides in order to assist is not on the right, like the man or the lion; nor is it on the left, like the calf; rather, it stands above all three faces. For the eagle is named in another passage, so that by the eagle he may signify the spirit presiding over the soul. By “spirit” I mean the spirit of the human being, which is in him.

And thus all things are led by God’s command: heavenly, earthly, and infernal things, and those that are above the heavens. And we all become cherubim, who are beneath God’s feet; wheels are joined to them, and we follow them. We are not beneath the wheel, nor do we move about under the dominion of the age and its affairs, since through Christ’s passion we have already been freed from the business of the world.

“And a wheel within a wheel.” If you consider how the totality of things is saved through contrary events—whether in those who are thought to be in error or in those who are said to be free from error—you will see how there is a wheel within a wheel.

But this governs all things, and the God of the whole universe turns it wherever he wills, in Christ Jesus; to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# SECOND HOMILY

On the passage: “Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who prophesy from their own heart,” through: “I will stretch out my hand against the prophets who see vanity and divine lies” (Chapter XIII).

897 Scripture passes over no form of sin without instructing its readers concerning it. For the word of God, sent to heal those who heard it, had to touch upon every sinful spirit and speak to all human beings, so that no one might be deprived of saving remedies or of medicines capable of benefiting the healing of wounds.

How, then, are some things said concerning the people, others concerning the chief priests, some concerning presbyters, and others concerning stewards—and indeed praise is assigned to good stewards, but blame to the wicked—so that some may receive exhortation toward better things while others may not fall into worse things? In the same way, divine teaching concerning false and true prophets must be given, so that those who serve with the words of God may finally be recognized as prophets, while by “false prophets” may be designated the teachers of the churches who do not rightly correspond, either in speech or in life, to the discipline they preach.

Let us therefore rejoice if Scripture admonishes us, teaching us to withdraw from vices; but even more so if the word of God touches upon some members of our own order, when we desire to be healed and converted from our sins.

The word of the Lord came to the prophet Ezekiel, saying to him: “Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel.” There were indeed prophets of Israel in name rather than in truth. And even today, in the true Israel—that is, in the Church—there are certain false prophets and false teachers, against whom this word gives warning.

If the word of God rebukes me, I shall try to be converted; nor, because certain things are said against me—who appear to be a teacher of the Church—ought I to remain silent. Rather, sparing no one, least of all myself, I shall disclose everything that has been said, so that I may turn away from vices and become not one of those whom Scripture now rebukes, but one of those who, preaching the word of God most truly, have arisen as teachers in the Church.

“Prophesy against the prophets of Israel who prophesy, and say to the prophets.”  

898 [Note: Rabanus appears to have read this as meaning that it was the work of the prophets to proclaim spiritually those things that they were commanded to proclaim; likewise, by the same Spirit, etc.]

Just as it was the work of the prophets to proclaim spiritually those things that were seen, so it is the work of one who wishes to explain those things that have been secretly signified to show—

[Note: He has virtually the opposite sense: “to show” that prophecy is now directed against those who prophesy contrary to God’s will “from their own heart.”]

—that prophecy is directed against the one who teaches contrary to the will of God, who prophesies from his own heart.

According to the simple meaning, some of the prophets, speaking by the divine Spirit, did not speak from their own heart but from the understanding of God. Others, however, pretending to be prophets and saying, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord was not speaking in them, became false prophets.

The present passage may also apply to those who teach in the churches if they teach otherwise than truth demands. For if someone teaches exactly what the Lord Jesus Christ spoke, he speaks the words of God’s Son, Jesus, not from his own heart but from the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Again, Rabanus has: “the very things which the Lord Jesus Christ spoke, he himself who taught not from his own heart but from the Holy Spirit.”] If the Holy Spirit consents to the will of the one who spoke in the apostles, he does not speak from his own heart but from the heart of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in Paul, who spoke in Peter, and who spoke in the other apostles.

But if someone, while reading the Gospel, adapts his own meaning to the Gospel, not understanding it as the Lord spoke, he is a false prophet, speaking from his own heart in the Gospel.

There is nothing absurd in understanding these words also of heretics. They dispute as though in the Gospels and as though concerning the apostles, expounding from their own heart the myths of their own αἰῶνες [aeons], rather than from the heart of the Holy Spirit. For they cannot say: “But we have the mind of Christ, so that we may see the things given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 12).

But when this also comes upon me—who am called an ecclesiastical teacher, who take up the holy book and strive to interpret it—I ask you who are listening to pay close attention and to receive the grace of the Spirit of which it is said: “The discernment of spirits,” so that, having become tested money-changers, you may carefully observe when I am a false teacher and when I proclaim what belongs to piety and truth.

If, then, I find the mind of Christ in Moses and in the Prophets, I speak not from my own heart but from the Holy Spirit. But if, finding nothing appropriate, I invent for myself what I am to say, wavering in speeches that are alien to God, I speak from my own heart rather than from the thoughts of God: “Prophesy, and say to the prophets who prophesy from their own heart.”

He does not simply say, “from the heart,” but “from their own heart.” And: “You shall prophesy and say to them: Hear the word of the Lord.”

These words are spoken to me and to the one who professes to be a teacher, so that a greater fear of God may arise in us, lest we endanger ourselves by presenting a discourse as though it had been written not by human beings but by the angels of God.

For I know that when that tribunal sits of which Daniel prophesied (Daniel 7), and the books are opened, all my efforts and all my interpretations will be brought into the midst, either for my justification or for my condemnation. For my justification will be those things that have been blessed; for my condemnation, those things explained otherwise than truth demands.

“For by your words,” he says, “you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12)—as though one possessed neither all the words by which he might be justified nor, conversely, all the words by which he might be condemned. If someone is free from alien words and from words that can be reproved, he will be justified by his words and will not be condemned. But if he has never spoken rightly and has always uttered perverse things, he will be condemned by his words and will not be justified.

But because we, who are not perfect in every respect, neither speak in such a way that we are always justified nor, conversely, are such sinners that we are always condemned—and because we have some words by which we may be justified and others by which we may be condemned—God places both upon his scales, weighs them carefully, and judges in what respects I am just and in what words I must be condemned.

What he does with words, he does likewise with deeds. For there must be some deeds by which we are justified and others by which we are condemned. I am not so perfect that all my deeds are such that I may be considered just; nor am I so sinful that I have done only things that condemn me in every respect.

That there are also deeds of one kind and deeds of another is clear from what is said: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but those of others follow after” (1 Timothy 5:24). Likewise, good deeds are manifest, and deeds of another sort cannot remain hidden.

The same is true of understandings. Therefore, the judgment of accusing or defending thoughts against one another awaits me concerning everything I do, understand, and say, and I wait uncertainly to see what will happen to me in that judgment.

The more the fear of God is impressed upon me at the prospect of answering for all that I have done, the more I must guard myself. If only I could be free from all sins; but if I cannot, at least may I be free from the greatest.

These things have been said concerning the matter we proposed about the prophets who prophesy from their own heart, to whom it is said: “Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says Adonai the Lord: Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart, who walk after their own spirit.”

There are two sins: one of the heart, the other of the spirit. Let us first consider the better part, so that we may also consider the things opposed to it.

The Apostle says: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the understanding. I will sing psalms with the spirit; I will sing psalms also with the understanding” (1 Corinthians 14). Thus there is both spirit and understanding in us. And just as the holy person prays with the spirit and prays also with the understanding, sings psalms with the spirit and sings psalms also with the understanding, so this false prophet prophesies from his own heart and walks not after the Spirit of God but after his own spirit.

There is indeed a certain spirit of a human being that operates within him. Far be it from me to walk after it; rather, understanding the Holy Spirit of God, may I walk after my Lord Jesus.

Therefore, the prophets who prophesy from their own heart and walk after a spirit that is not so much God’s as their own do not see at all what is expressed in Greek as [lacuna], and the meaning of the sentence is ambiguous.

For either they do not see the general things [lacuna]—that is, they do not see what is general, although in some respect they perceive it—or else, as I think better, they do not see at all, although they seem to themselves to see in some respect.

There are other eyes in us, better than those that we possess in the body. These eyes either see the Lord Jesus, who created them to behold him, or else they are blind. If I am a sinner, I see nothing and cannot behold the light of truth. For he says: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

But if I am just, I receive grace from God, and it is said of me also that I see. For formerly the prophets were called “seers.” And: “You who see,” he says, “go, descend into the land of Judah, and dwell there; there you shall prophesy. But at Bethel you shall no longer prophesy” (Amos 7). And again elsewhere: “The vision which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw” (Isaiah 1).

Blessed is the one to whom the Lord will reveal his eyes, so that he may see the wonders of God’s law, according to the prophet’s entreaty: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118 [119]).

Let us also examine another statement by which false prophets and false teachers are rebuked. I ask that, while you pray, I may be found pure from it.

What, then, is this rebuke? “Like foxes in the deserts are your prophets, Israel.”

The fox is a wicked animal: cunning, untamable, and wild. “Say,” the Savior says, “to that fox: Behold, I accomplish healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Ezekiel 13; Luke 13).

Samson needed such foxes against the foreigners; having tied fire to their tails—for he had captured three hundred—he sent them to destroy the crops of his enemies.

[Note: Rabanus reads “with a rope” instead of “with fire”; see Judges 15:4 ff.]

Such are false teachers: cunning, malicious, and like beasts. If I am such, I am a fox—not simply a fox, but a fox in the deserts, a fox among the ruins, a fox in the rocky places; for these expressions are understood in different senses.

[Note: He has “in different seditions”; the cunning ones are contained in them. “These cunning ones,” etc.]

These cunning and wicked creatures always dwell in deserts, always in solitudes. For wherever the soul is inhabited by God and filled with the Holy Spirit, the teaching of heretics cannot penetrate there, nor can their word break through. But where there is the solitude of Christ, where there is the desert of righteousness, there the poisons of the most wicked discipline are found.

Therefore he says: “Like foxes in the deserts are your prophets, Israel.”

“They did not stand in the firmament.” If you wish to consider the teachers—

[Note: With Rabanus, I would prefer to insert “false”: “If you wish to consider false teachers”; for the discourse specifically concerns them.]

—you will see that they are weak, unstable, and unable to say: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Psalm 73). Since they are not such as have stood, founded upon a strong root, therefore they did not stand in the firmament but loved to move their feet.

Yet it is also a great sin to move one’s feet even slightly, as the psalmist David sings: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart; but as for me, my feet were almost moved.”

Blessed and exceedingly fortunate is the one who, standing most firmly, has been granted firm feet of soul and who is worthy to hear God say: “But you, stand with me.”

902 But the false prophets were not such, nor were the false teachers such; for they did not stand in the firmament.

“And they gathered flocks of the children of Israel,” whom they teach and instruct—whether heretics preaching an impious doctrine or false teachers deceiving those whose ears itch. They gather flocks of schisms against the Church of God and against the house of Israel.

“They did not rise up to say, ‘On the day of the Lord.’” Those who see false things did not rise up. But these, when they rise, say: “We were buried with Christ through baptism, and we rose with him” (Romans 6).

For we have, as a pledge, the Holy Spirit, whom we shall receive in fullness after “that which is perfect” has come. Likewise we have the pledge of the resurrection, since in the perfect resurrection none of us has yet risen.

Nevertheless, we have risen, as Paul says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism, and we rose with him.”

Therefore the false prophets and false teachers who, seeing false things, could never behold the truth, have not yet risen—that is, they have not yet attained the baptism of the resurrection—to say, “On the day of the Lord.”

[Note: In Rabanus: “What they say, seeing from the Lord, is false, nor …”]

Take an example. Whoever reads Scripture and receives it otherwise than it is written sees Scripture falsely. But whoever hears Scripture according to the understanding of the truth and interprets it accordingly sees the truth.

[Note: In the same author: “and as the understanding of truth has it, so he interprets it.”]

The holy, however, do not divine. For there is no divination in Jacob. But sinners divine false things, saying: “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord has not sent them.

Hear how heretics claim to possess the tradition of the apostles. Hear how false teachers assert that their doctrine is the Lord’s doctrine, that their understanding agrees with that of the prophets, and they say: “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord has not sent them.

[Note: The word “understanding” is to be supplied: as Rabanus also has it, “that their own understanding agrees with the understanding of the prophets.”]

“And they began to raise up a saying: ‘Have you not seen a false vision?’” (Numbers 23). For these too wish to raise up some saying in their own defense; but the Lord rebukes them and says: “Have you not seen a false vision, and spoken empty divinations, and said, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although I have not spoken?”

Therefore say: “Thus says the Lord,” because your words are false. Pray for us, that our words may not be false.

Although some people, through ignorance of judgment, may assert that our words are false, while the Lord does not say so, we shall be dealt with rightly. But if a thousand people say that they are true, while by God’s judgment they are false, what benefit will that bring me?

The Marcionite teachers also say that the words of their master are true; and the Valentinians, who accept the inventions of his myths, say that their sect is exceedingly strong. What benefit is there in this? The fact that many, deceived by heretical perversity, have agreed with their opinion is precisely what is at issue: what is sought is that the Lord himself should stand as witness to my words, that he himself should approve what is said through the testimony of the holy Scriptures.

Therefore Adonai the Lord says to us concerning these things: “I will stretch out my hand against the prophets who see lies.”

These are threats against false teachers and against those who speak lies. Let us see what he threatens them with: “They shall not be among the discipline of my people.”

Sinners are not rebuked by the Lord in only one way. The Lord’s people are reproved in one manner, and one who is alien from him in another: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him. For whom the Lord loves he chastens; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Proverbs 3).

“Reprove us, Lord, but in judgment and not in anger.” This is the correction of the people. The correction of the sinner and of one who is alien is that which the righteous person rejects, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Psalm 6).

Therefore it is said concerning false teachers and false prophets: “They shall not be among the discipline of my people, nor shall they be written in the register of the house of Israel.”

As it is also said elsewhere: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous.”

And now Scripture says: “They shall not be written in the house of Israel, and they shall not enter the land of Israel.”

Heretics will remain outside the land of promise, which is a very good land and into which we pray to be brought, having first been inscribed in the book of the living by Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# THIRD HOMILY

On the passage that is written: “Son of man, set your face firmly against the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart,” through: “Set my face firmly against that man, and I will make him desolate” (Chapter XIII).

[Column 0712D]

903 First, we must inquire into what is meant by the words, “Strengthen your face.” Then, if the Lord grants it, we must investigate the daughters of the people who prophesy from their own heart, and who do those things for which the word of God reproves them. That there is another face besides this bodily face of ours is evident from many passages; it is also indicated by what the Apostle says: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III). We all have this bodily face unveiled, unless perhaps we are oppressed by calamities and hardships. But that countenance of which the Apostle speaks is veiled in many and unveiled in few. For whoever has confidence in an undefiled life, in sound understanding, and in true faith has no veil of confession, fraud, or sin; rather, because of a pure conscience, he contemplates the glory of the Lord with unveiled face.

Far be it from us, however, that we should have this face veiled. These few remarks concerning the face enable us to understand what follows: “Strengthen your face against the daughters of your people.” This face—that is, the governing faculty (ἡγεμονικόν) [Col. 0713B] of our heart—unless it has been strengthened and fixed upon what is to be understood, so that it may announce to the nations what it sees in the manner in which it sees it, cannot see what ought to be seen. It is impossible for anyone whose countenance is not strengthened and fixed—wandering, unstable, and carried about by every wind of doctrine—to see what he ought to see, or to see as he ought.

For anyone who wishes to understand must have his face fixed upon that which he strives to understand. For this reason those who are about to prophesy are first commanded to strengthen their face. We too can strengthen our face in the Gospel, in the Law, in the Prophets, and in the Apostles: fix it upon Christ, and not upon the affairs of the world. But while our soul is occupied with worldly cares, while it constantly burns with the hunger to possess, we do not fix our face upon what God has commanded, but upon what is opposed to God’s commandments. Who, I ask, among us is not impure because he has fixed his face upon forbidden things? Who is so diligent and watchful that day and night he fixes the face of his heart upon what is commanded?

Now, if we are to understand the present Scripture, how the prophet is told, “Strengthen your face against the daughters of your people,” so that he may see the things he is about to declare, we must strengthen our understanding and devote ourselves fully to the meditation of the heart: we must determine what is signified here, so that at last, overcome by reason, we may withdraw from the letter.

According to the common interpretation, certain daughters of the people appear to have committed the sin described in what follows. They sewed together cushions; when they had sewn them, they did not place them beneath the heads of those listening, but beneath their elbows, and they covered the heads of people of every age with certain veils. These are the acts counted as grave sins against the daughters of the people who prophesied. But who could maintain, on the basis of the literal wording, that if someone sews cushions and places the sewn cushions beneath another person’s elbow, he sins and is reproved by God? Who could assert that if someone makes veils to cover the head of people of every age, he is acting impiously?

Against our will, Scripture itself imposes upon us the necessity of withdrawing from the mere letters and seeking its word, wisdom, and will: we must uncover sins that are closed and illuminate what is dark, so that we may become strangers to the curse [Col. 0714A] concerning every elbow of the hands—or, perhaps, of the hand. Those who are occupied with bodily nourishment, and who cannot see even in dreams the spiritual delights that the divine word wishes us to possess—“Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart”—and who do not know the will of the blessed, of whom it is written, “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight,” seek, like lovers of luxury rather than lovers of God, to remain perpetually amid bodily pleasures.

The cushion sewn beneath the elbow of the hands seems to me a sign of carnal pleasure. For when we recline at table for the sake of bodily benefits, we seem to use certain sewn and embroidered things beneath the elbow of our hands.
