Perhaps, therefore, through this figure and image the divine word censures those teachers who, through empty talk and every kind of blessed promise, surrender the multitude of their hearers to lust, vices, and pleasure. The word of God—and God the Word himself—ought to utter those things that lead to the hearer’s salvation, encouraging him to self-restraint, to a way of life composed of sound actions, and to all the pursuits to which a diligent person, devoted to labor rather than lust, ought to apply himself, so that he may attain what God has promised.

When, therefore, someone adapts his conduct to the people in order to please those whose ears itch, and says what they gladly receive—what is akin to pleasure—such a teacher sews cushions beneath every elbow of the hands. Along with this sin, he proceeds to make coverings for veiling the head of people of every age. We must consider more carefully what the veil also signifies.

[Col. 0714C] Whoever has confidence and is truly a man does not have a veil upon his head, but prays to the Lord with uncovered head and prophesies with uncovered head. Through the sign of a bodily matter he secretly displays a spiritual reality: just as he has no veil over the head of his flesh, so he should have no veil over the governing faculty of his heart. But if someone wears a veil of shame and sin, he has, as it were, feminine veils upon his head.

Thus, when someone teaches things that flatter the people’s ear and provoke the applause of admirers rather than the groaning of repentance—when he touches wounds like a flattering enemy rather than cutting them—such a man weaves a covering upon the head. When a speaker’s discourse pours itself out into luxurious speech and leaps into wanton eloquence, he weaves a veil over the head of people of every age, not only of boys and young men but also of old men.

For just as the false Christ and the false prophet perform signs and wonders, if possible, to deceive even the elect, so those who present carefully prepared material for pleasure, always seeking what will delight their hearers rather than turn them away from their vices, make veils over the heads not only of boys and young men but, if possible, of old men and fathers as well. They deceive even those who, through the labor of the soul, have advanced to spiritual maturity and old age.

907 The prophet could indeed have said, “Upon the sons of your people who prophesy,” but because those who weave coverings and sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hands are like women, and because no one among them is considered worthy of the name of man, the prophet says: “Upon the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart,” and who do the things that follow.

For the souls and wills of those teachers are effeminate: they constantly compose things that ring and sound melodiously. And—to speak the truth—there is nothing manly, nothing strong, nothing worthy of God in those who preach according to the favor and desire of their hearers. Therefore he speaks of daughters rather than sons sewing cushions.

Observe also the precision of the word: he says “sewing together,” not “weaving.” Do you not know that the tunic of your Lord Jesus has no seam in it, but is woven throughout? These women, therefore, deceitfully and cunningly sew word to word, sewing together rather than weaving. They make cushions not for resting the head upon, but for resting the elbow upon—that is, so that their hands may not be engaged in labor or grow weary in work, but may remain at rest, at leisure, occupied with actions that serve pleasures.

That what we have said is understood in this way is shown more clearly by the prophet’s subsequent words: “Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am against your cushions, upon which you turn souls there toward dissolution.” He has plainly disclosed the hidden riddle, showing that the sewn cushions are made for the dissolution of souls. Who, hearing the passage that is read, can fail to understand God as threatening that he himself will tear apart such a fabric and such cushions? For he says: “Behold, I”—not that I command it, but that I myself tear apart the sewn cushions [Col. 0715C] beneath every elbow of the hands.

It is God’s work to rebuke every such fabric and dissolve the entire wicked fabrication that harms those who do not wish to work with their hands, but to use them in idleness. “And I will tear them from your arms”—that is, the cushions—“so that you may no longer have them placed beneath your elbows. And I will release the souls that you are overthrowing, their souls.”

What, then, is the overthrow involved in sewing cushions and placing them beneath the elbows? But if you understand the mystery of the passage, you will see that it is a great overthrow to make a person delicate with respect to the body. Such are the words of heretics, where there is no strictness of life. You will find the disciples of Valentinus lax in their conduct, striving toward nothing strong and nothing manly, and likewise the followers of Basilides. They even teach people shamelessly to deny, as though it were commanded in connection with their martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0715D] This was indeed the wicked doctrine of Basilides: that during a persecution it was permissible to worship idols, provided that one did so outwardly and not from the heart. Origen himself notes this more explicitly in a fragment of one of his Homilies on Psalm LXXXII, translated into Latin by Henri Valois. “He also teaches,” he says, “that it is an indifferent matter to deny Christ, and that the person who understands will deny him with his mouth, in the very crisis itself, but not according to the intention of his heart” [Col. 0716D]. See also Saint Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 19.1, and Saint Augustine, who later refutes the adoption of this kind of infidelity by the Priscillianists in *On Heresies*, condemning it by the example of Saint Peter. Although Peter denied Christ with his mouth and not from his heart, he was nevertheless guilty of a more serious sin, which he washed away with bitter tears.]

—. They do not teach what churchmen show: that one must be ready to take up the cross and follow the Savior. The Word, the Son of God, who makes this threat, therefore tears apart these most wicked seams.

Grant me, Christ, that I may tear apart the cushions sewn together for the luxury of souls. But what follows? “And I will tear apart the veils.” What does he testify that he will tear apart? Not only the cushions but also the veils. He will tear them apart so that the head may become bare, and so that, having received confidence and having both face and head unveiled, the ecclesiastical man may pray boldly.

“I will tear apart your veils and deliver my people from your hand.” Although you overthrow souls through cushions and veils, I will tear these things apart and deliver my people. God delivers his people through a strict way of life that withdraws from pleasures. “And they will no longer be in your hands for overthrowing.” In your hands—that is, in the hands of those who deceive their hearers—these cushions will no longer remain for their overthrow. “And you will know that I am the Lord.”

If the cushions are not torn apart, if I do not tear apart the veils, you will not know that I am the Lord [Col. 0716B]. Pleasures, leisure, and dissolution prevent the recognition of the one who says, “I am the Lord.”

“Because you overturned the heart of the righteous unjustly.” Just as it was said in the passage concerning signs that they might deceive even God’s elect, so it often happens that heretics also trip up the righteous. For people love pleasure: as soon as it appears, it is tranquil, wanton, pleasing to the senses, and enticing us to make use of it. We flee what is bitter, even when it is beneficial, and, lulled by pleasures, we do not wish to labor, unaware that it is impossible to be both a lover of God and a lover of pleasure. Therefore the Apostle says of the worst people that they are “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God” (II Tim. III).

“And I did not turn aside to strengthen the hands of the wicked.” I did not turn aside, but distributed all that served for edification. But these effeminate prophetesses turned aside to strengthen the hands of the wicked—that is, so that the hand of wickedness might become stronger, so that the wicked person would not turn away at all from his evil way and be given life; that is, so that no one would turn completely from his most evil way and be given life.

“Therefore you shall no longer see falsehood, you who teach falsehood.” I will no longer allow you to proceed with prosperous success, so that you may insinuate what you say; and you shall no longer prophesy divinations. “And I will deliver my people from your hand.” Let us pray that God may also deliver us from the hand of such teachers, who, wherever they are, speak to the pleasures of their hearers and tear apart and divide the Church, because there are more who love pleasures than who love God.

“And you shall know that I am the Lord.” If I overturn your divinations, if I silence your lies, then you shall know that I am the Lord.

This was the first prophecy. Another follows, which is connected in this way: “And men from the elders of Israel came to me and sat before my face” (Ezek. XIV). The word of God surveys everything and leaves untouched no order established in the Church. Passing through them all, it desires to heal everyone, and now speaks in a particular way to presbyters. The preceding words concerned teachers. Let us therefore consider what is said about presbyters as well, examining ourselves lest any presbyter among us should be like the one described below.

“And men from the elders of Israel came to me and sat before my face. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man.” Let us examine the accusation, so that we may know whether we discover it in ourselves. “Have not these men placed their thoughts in their hearts and set the punishment of their iniquities before their face?” Shall I answer them by saying, “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. V)?

For those who have a pure heart do not place their thoughts in their hearts, but rather have them in the word of God. Those who labor amid worldly cares and seek nothing else but how to pass through the present life place their thoughts in their hearts. For example, if you see a person thinking of nothing except the affairs of the world, bodily profits, and an abundance of food—if he seeks with distress only the future sustenance he will need, and is anxious and sighing over these matters—he has placed the punishment of his thoughts in his heart.

The divine word, therefore, reproving certain presbyters of this kind, says to the prophet: “These men”—that is, the presbyters mentioned above—“have placed their thoughts in their hearts and set the punishment of their iniquities before their face.”

Let none of you suppose that our torments are inflicted by anyone other than ourselves. God does not create the punishments; we ourselves prepare what we suffer. Therefore let us now appropriately use the testimony that we have often employed: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled.” There is no other fire than your own—the fire for which you have gathered wood, straw, and fuel for the future conflagration.

He therefore speaks about the presbyters—though far be it from us: “These men have placed their thoughts in their hearts and set the punishment of their iniquities before their face.”

“But shall I answer them at all?” Is it fitting for me to answer those who have come to you, the prophet, wishing to learn my words? “Therefore speak to them and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Man, man, from the house of Israel.” All [Col. 0717D]

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Here should be added what Jerome comments in almost the same words in his exposition of Ezekiel chapter XIV, and what appears to have been taken from this passage of Origen: “Many,” he says, “while possessing the bodily face of a man, assume the forms of various beasts. Wishing these forms to be scattered, the prophet prays: ‘Lord, in his own city you will scatter their image.’ Those of whom it is written, ‘Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them,’ are not human beings, but human beasts. Again, those who hear in the Gospel, ‘Serpents, brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?’ are not human beings, but human serpents. And those of whom it is written, ‘Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests,’ and concerning Herod, ‘Go and tell that fox,’ are not human beings, but human foxes.”]

All of us are born human beings, but not all of us are human beings in the full sense, as I have very often observed concerning what is written in Leviticus: “Man, man, of the sons of Israel, or of the resident aliens who have joined themselves to us.” Be human beings—human beings, that is, because not all human beings are human beings.

Let us show from the Scriptures how certain human beings are not human beings. “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. XLIX). This person is not a human being in the full sense, but a human beast. “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III). Such a person is not a human being in the full sense, but a human serpent. “They became frenzied stallions in their lust for women; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife.” This person too is not a human being in the full sense, but a human horse.

Far be it from us, therefore, that we should be such people as to deserve to hear that we are not human beings in the full sense, but something other than human beings. For if we are good and gentle, we double the name of human being, so that what is in us is not simply “human,” but “human human.”

Consider whether we can discover what it is that doubles the name “human.” When this human being who is outward becomes human, while the inward human being is a serpent, there is not in us “human human,” but merely “human.” But when the inward human being perseveres according to the image of the Creator, then a human being is born and becomes such both according to the outward and the inward human being: twice human, “human human.”

If, however, someone who has been called to become “human human” places his thoughts in his heart and his punishment before his face, and comes to the prophet, the Lord says: “I will answer him in the things by which his mind is held captive.”

The present passage teaches us how he could answer individuals without applying unsuitable medicines, but by offering remedies appropriate to the nature of their diseases. Pay attention to what we are saying. Ten people go to a doctor, each suffering from a different kind of illness. He does not treat them all in the same way, but one with this remedy and another with that: for example, he heals one with a plaster, gives another a different medicine, applies to some what is called a cautery, tempers one with a bitter potion and another with a sweet one, and soothes the wounds of yet another with a thicker ointment.

So too the word of God speaks according to the qualities of human beings, and does not indiscriminately thrust the mysteries of its wisdom upon them. Thus it says: “I will answer him in the things by which his mind is held captive”—namely, in order to heal the things by which his mind is held captive, so that he may not cause the house of Israel to turn aside.

Whoever does not offer himself as an example of a good life but walks perversely, by his perversity causes even God’s people to turn aside. For he inclines toward those things toward which he ought not to incline, and thus causes God’s people to turn aside according to their hearts, which have been alienated from me. Whoever does this acts according to a heart alienated from God, in his thoughts.

Therefore the answer is given to them in the things by which their hearts are held captive, and it is said: “Say to the house of Israel: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Turn back, and turn away from your pursuits.”

Because he had promised that he would speak to them in the things by which their hearts were held captive, he now speaks to them as sinners, saying: “Turn back, and turn away from your pursuits, and turn away your faces.” Does this not seem to you to be what they should do? Your faces have been fixed upon things upon which they ought not to be fixed; turn them and fix them upon those things that are for your benefit.

“Therefore, man, man, from the house of Israel, and from the proselytes who come into Israel, whoever has been alienated...” It can happen that a “human human”—that is, a human being created or perfected as a “human human”—may become alienated. For, according to this same Ezekiel, even the righteous sometimes turn away from their righteousness and sin.

If, therefore, such a person places his thoughts in his heart and the punishment of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of me, the Lord says: “I will answer him in the very thing by which he is held captive; and I will set my face against that man.”

Consider how at first he promises mercifully that he will answer, and then how, if the person comes again, still not healed, he says in the former words: “I will set my face against that man and make him desolate.” For if he does not obey the words of admonition but persists in his offense, I will make him desolate and bring him to destruction, and I will remove him from the midst of my people.

Do not remove us, almighty God, from the midst of your people; rather, preserve us within your people. The one who does things worthy of rejection is justly cast out, removed from God’s people, uprooted from them, and handed over to Satan.

In the present life, someone who goes out from the people of God can return again through repentance. But if he has been uprooted from that people of which a certain parable says that someone came, reclined, and entered without having a wedding garment, and the master of the house said to him, “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. XXII), and then commanded the attendants to bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness, he will return to his former place only with great difficulty.

But may we not be uprooted. Rather, both in the present age and in the age to come, may we be planted in our Lord Jesus Christ and bear abundant fruit in him, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY FOUR

On the passage that is written: “When the land sins against me by committing a transgression, and I stretch out my hand against it,” up to the words: “And if there are three men in its midst—Noah, Daniel, and Job—they will deliver their souls by their righteousness” (Chapter XIV).

913 The word of the Lord that came to the prophet speaks of the sinful earth, how, because of its transgressions, it has been tormented by various punishments—famine, evil beasts, the sword, and death; death, moreover, a sudden death, whether caused by the corruption of the air or arising from whatever circumstance. And it says: “Even if I send my four punishments upon the sinful land, and if these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—are in the sinful land, they alone shall be saved.” In the first threat, in which he disclosed the punishment of famine among the other punishments, he omitted the names of sons and daughters. But in the speech in which he threatened the land with evil beasts, he says: “If their sons and daughters are saved, they themselves alone shall be saved.” But as for “the earth”—and, after he had been silent for a little while, he added—“And it shall be at the entrance.” [The transmitted wording is syntactically uncertain.] Again, in the threat of the sword he says: “They shall not deliver sons or daughters.” And he spoke similarly concerning death: “Their sons or daughters shall not be spared, but Noah, Daniel, and Job themselves alone shall deliver their souls.”

A great burden of interpretation therefore rests upon us. For this reason we must pay close attention, and we beg our hearers—gathering as though for some great spectacle—to turn the face of their minds toward it, lest the obscurity slip away when their faculties relax. He did not say here that, if the inhabitants of some city or place sinned, but that if the earth sinned. And I know that, when the simpler hearer hears “if the earth sins,” he is immediately carried toward an easy interpretation, so that he says “earth” is named for those who dwell upon the earth. But what follows in Scripture at once removes that interpretation.

914 For when the earth has sinned and fallen into its sins, the hand is extended not over the inhabitants of the earth but over the earth itself. By the first correction it is crushed, so that the support of bread is taken away from it—that is, the earth is punished when famine prevails in it and crops are denied to the seed. For just as the sinful and barren human being, without offspring, is punished among the accursed, according to what is written in one passage—for contrary things are understood from contrary things—and it is said of the righteous, “There shall be no one without offspring or barren among you,” while sinners are condemned to perpetual infertility, without children and descendants, as happened in the house of Abimelech (Gen. XX) and to those whose womb God closed because of the sin committed against Isaac: so the earth too, in a certain sense, is left without offspring and barren when famine is sent upon it.

Do you think that what the speech seems to foreshadow is true—that this is said not of the inhabitants of the earth but of the earth itself? I can ascend for a little while to higher things and demonstrate from the testimonies of Scripture how the sinner is called “earth.” For it is said to Adam: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). We can say that even now the earth, when it sins, is a sinner.

But, on the other hand, as I review the broad forest of Scripture, I am constrained to suspect that this earth which we see is an animate being. If we wish to understand according to the written text what is said, “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. CIII), we understand that earthquakes are stirred up at God’s gaze—not those tremors which the Jews suppose. For they assert that the trembling of the earth is its agitation, which is far removed from the truth. We too are anxious and trembling because of our sins while on earth, yet our trembling does not shake our body so that it trembles visibly. Thus it is said elsewhere: “Upon whom shall I look,” says the Lord, “if not upon the humble and quiet one, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. ult.) From this it is clear that one who serves God gently and humbly trembles at his words in mind rather than in body.

These things have been said incidentally, in satisfaction of the testimony we introduced: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble.” Receive, however, other statements concerning the earth. “The earth is offended by those who sit upon it.” How is the earth offended, and when does it turn away from those who dwell upon it? When they become sinners. Receive another example: “The earth shall please itself in its Sabbaths.” For, conversely, certain Sabbaths of the earth are named in which it pleases and rejoices.

I do not yet say: “Attend, heaven, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (Isa. I). Nor another passage: “Hear, heaven, and listen with your ears, earth.” Nor yet Jeremiah’s prophecy: “Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord; write this man down as rejected” (Jer. XXII).

Much remains hidden from us because of the poverty of our memory and the slowness of our intellect. God has created many rational beings capable of understanding—not only “principalities and powers and rulers of this darkness,” but also, on the better side, thrones, dominions, and the others whom the Apostle left to our understanding when he said: “And above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come” (Eph. I).

The air too is full of living beings, according to the testimony of the same Apostle, who proclaims: “Among whom you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience” (Eph. II).

There is therefore an earth, and all living beings, and varieties corresponding to the parts of living beings. When the earth is offended and again pleases itself in its Sabbaths, it is not the whole earth that is offended, nor does the whole earth rejoice. In a certain sense it has been instructed together with its inhabitants, and has learned to keep Sabbaths either in shadow or in truth, according to the quality of its nature. Hence, with a more sacred understanding, a sabbatical rest is practiced after seven years for the holy land, until it pleases God to dwell in it. But if there are sinners in it, the earth keeps Sabbath not merely for weeks of years but for seventy years.

We have the statement concerning the seventy years recorded in sacred writings both in Jeremiah (Jer. XXV) and in Daniel (Dan. IX). And it will come to pass that on the day of judgment not only the human being but also the whole created order will be judged.

For “every creature groans together and suffers labor pains” (Rom. VIII). If every creature groans together and suffers, and if among creatures there is the earth, heaven, and all the other things beneath heaven and above the heavens, and if every creature will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, who knows whether the earth too, according to its nature, is held liable in some sin?

For if it is an animate being, if it is rational, if it needs to hear the prophetic word that says, “Attend, heaven, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth,” and again, “Hear, heaven, and listen with your ears, earth,” why should we not say that, just as among human beings one person hears and does the words he is commanded to do, while another hears but does not fulfill what is commanded, so also there is an angel who transgresses?

For God “will keep the angels who did not preserve their principality but abandoned their proper dwelling under darkness, bound with everlasting chains for the judgment of the great day” (Jude I). When, therefore, angels transgress, while others keep God’s commandments and await judgment—not only of human beings but also of God, as we have frequently said both concerning the things written in the Apocalypse and from countless other passages—why, I ask, should there not also be a judgment of the earth and of the air?

917 But if you do not think that this argument should be accepted, by which we assert that every creature will be judged, hear another testimony concerning the earth. God questions Cain, who killed his brother Abel. After the many words that we read in Genesis, he finally says concerning the earth: “Cursed is the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand” (Gen. IV).

I do not pass over that other statement either: “Cursed is the earth in your works”; and, conversely, whenever it is blessed. We read that the earth is both cursed and blessed by God’s words.

You see, therefore, that it is rightly said: “Every creature groans together.” And, to return to the preceding example, the earth is offended by those who sit upon it. I think that the earth, supporting us like a mother, both rejoices over good children and grieves over sinners. For an unwise son is a grief to his father, and likewise to the mother who bore him—not only to this father and mother from whose seed we arise, but also to that mother who is truly our mother.

God took dust from the earth and fashioned the human being. Therefore the earth is our mother. It rejoices when it supports a righteous son. The earth rejoiced when it bore Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The earth rejoiced at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, seeing itself worthy to support the Son of God.

What need is there to speak of the Apostles and the prophets, when it is written concerning the Lord’s coming: “The whole earth cries out with joy”? The wretched Jews too confess that these words are proclaimed concerning Christ’s presence, but in their foolishness they fail to recognize the person in whom they see the things spoken fulfilled. For when did the land of Britain, before Christ’s coming, agree in the worship of the one God? When did the land of the Moors? When did the whole world at once? But now, because of the churches that occupy the boundaries of the world, the whole earth cries out with joy to the Lord of Israel and is capable of good things within its borders.

“He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the children of Israel, and the Lord’s people Jacob became his portion, Israel the lot of his inheritance” (Deut. XXXII). The earth is capable, I say, as an animate being, according to the qualities of its parts and of the good and evil actions by which it may deserve either praise or punishment.

When, therefore, it is said, “The earth that sins against me, committing transgression,” a certain mystery is signified. For the statement is made in one way about the inhabitants and in another way about that which is inhabited: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. XXIV). Why does heaven pass beyond, and why does the earth pass away, unless they have done certain things worthy of their passing away? And elsewhere he says: “The whole earth was corrupted” (Gen. VI). When was it corrupted? Before the Flood—not in the sense that it was corrupted by the Flood’s inundation.

He therefore says: “The earth that sins against me by committing transgression—I will stretch out my hand, and I will crush its support of bread.” Stretching out his hand over the sinful earth, God sends famine upon it.

I can also interpret the passage differently, because the earth sometimes sins. For our soul is earth, as is signified in the Gospel parable (Matt. XIII). The soul is rock; the soul is good and fertile earth through great endurance. This earth, therefore, often sins and often does not sin. And if it has sinned, he stretches out his hand over it and crushes all its support of bread.

Do not crush, almighty God, the support of bread from this earth of ours; rather, grant us your seed, so that it may produce in us a hundredfold harvest. “And I will send famine upon it, and I will remove from it human being and beast.”

How can I bring such hidden matters into public view? How can I explain why famine, fertility, abundance, and poverty befall the earth? “O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” Who can count the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? Who can investigate the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of wisdom (Eccl. I)?

Famine is therefore sent in various ways upon the sinful earth. “And I will remove,” he says, “human being and beast from it.” The earth is one thing, and the human being another.

918 He does not now name the inhabitants of the earth by the term “earth,” as some think. If he wished the inhabitants of the earth to be understood by “earth,” it would have been superfluous to say: “I will remove human being and beast from it.” The earth rejoices when it is full of inhabitants; it mourns when what is said comes to pass: “I will remove human being and beast from it.”

Concerning these matters, if the Lord grants us understanding while you pray—provided that we have become capable of the Lord’s understanding—we wish to say a few things. Just as it is a punishment for a mother destined for exile to be deprived of her children, or at least to see her children sent away to another province, so in a certain sense our mother earth is scourged by God for her sins when human being and beast are removed from her. She rejoices when she has human beings, and more especially when she has the best human beings, those who live in devotion to God, as we explained above.

Thus, when it is said that the earth has sinned, it is as though it were said: “If the mother should ever sin, I will remove her son from her house.” So now he says: “I will remove human being from it.” The earth does not rejoice over beasts and savage wild animals, but over domestic animals, because it loves creatures that are peaceful and tame.

“And I will remove human being and beast from it. And if these three men are in its midst.”

How can the number of these three dwell together in a sinful earth? How can the lives of people who lived in such different periods be joined together? In the present passage we read that they stand together in the sinful earth—namely, Noah, who lived at the Flood; Daniel, who lived in the Babylonian captivity; and Job, who is said to have lived in the times of the patriarchs and Moses.

For this is the period we find assigned to Job’s life. What, then, can we say? We must remember—as we have already often said—that just as one human being begets another human being, and Israel begets Israel, so also Israel, when it was Jacob, begot the people Israel. We find in Scripture that the name Israel is used both for one person and for the whole people.

Thus not only does Israel beget Israel, but Reuben begets Reuben, Simeon Simeon, Levi Levi, and Judah Judah. All the others who belong to the tribe of Judah and descend from his stock are called Judah. The Scriptures are repeated in the tribe of Judah among people named Judah.

The things spoken by Moses in Jacob’s blessings concerning Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah (Gen. XLIX), and concerning the others, do not apply to the patriarchs themselves in the same way as to those who, because of the root of their family, became their namesakes.

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours, and in the evening he gives food.” That Benjamin was never a ravenous wolf. That Benjamin never gave food in the evening. Rather, the one born from the tribe of Benjamin—“a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee,” circumcised on the eighth day—was proclaimed a ravenous wolf devouring in the morning when he was a young man, and giving food in the evening when, after believing, he provided spiritual nourishment to the churches he established.

Therefore Benjamin begets Benjamin. Just as one human being is born from another human being, Benjamin from Benjamin, and Judah from Judah, and Reuben from Reuben, so let Reuben live and not die, and let him be numerous.

The subject was not the patriarch, but the people who were to descend from the patriarch. Why has this been said? Clearly, so that I might explain the present passage concerning Noah, Daniel, and Job. For just as Israel begets Israel, and Job Job, and Reuben Reuben, and the others their counterparts, so Noah begets Noah.

I will say that, among Noah’s sons, Shem was Noah, but Ham was not Noah, for he did not possess the likeness of his father. And just as not all who are Abraham’s children—although they are descended from his seed—are his children, because they are sinners, so those who possess the likeness of Daniel’s deeds are Daniel, and those who imitate Job’s patience become Job.

Do not say, therefore: “Blessed is Noah, because he was found worthy to be chosen by the Lord alone in the Flood, while the others perished in the inundation and he was preserved unharmed with his own.” Consider instead that, if you do what Noah did, you will be Noah.

Hear the Savior saying: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do Abraham’s works” (John VIII). Therefore, if anyone is Abraham’s child, he performs Abraham’s deeds; if anyone is Noah’s child, he performs Noah’s work; if anyone is Daniel’s child, he does what Daniel did.

If anyone follows the conduct by which a person became glorious—for example, anyone who loses his possessions and patiently endures both the loss of his household goods and the deaths of his children, saying: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord forever” (Job I)—and who is consumed by bodily afflictions and scourged by the varied pain of his sufferings, yet glorifies the Lord even amid those punishments, and can give a divine answer and utter amid torments the prophetic voice that Job uttered, that person is an imitator of Job.

In this way, therefore, Noah, Daniel, and Job can all be found at the same time.

But because Ezekiel is not now speaking of those whom we read about in Scripture—those whom either translation or death has removed from the present life—we shall try to establish this from another passage as well. Daniel, who was handed over with Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael to the chief of the eunuchs, was himself a eunuch. And it is said here: “Noah, Daniel, and Job shall not deliver sons and daughters” (Dan. I), and the rest.

Let us suppose that Noah had sons. But how will Daniel be shown to have had sons, when the Jews report that he was a eunuch? Yet because his soul was fertile and holy, and he produced many children through prophetic and divine words, it is therefore said: “If at that time, or at this time, there are Noah, Daniel, and Job, they alone shall be saved.”

And we too can become Daniel. And, not to enumerate all the saints, I can be Paul if I become an imitator of him, who says: “Be imitators of me” (I Cor. XI); if I possess the same branding by which Paul was marked; if I possess the same form by which he was formed in Christ, by which, as a good father, he said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

But if I am convicted by the dissimilarity of the mark, because Paul had one form while I have another in my soul, I deceive myself by saying: “You are my son, the seed of Paul.” Do not be surprised that you may become an Apostle’s child. Possess the virtues, and you will be Christ’s child. “Little children,” he says, “I am with you only a little while” (John XIII). When you become Christ’s, you will also be the child of the almighty Father, because they are one and their natures are united.

For this the righteous labors; toward this he directs all his effort: to show himself the child of Daniel, Job, Noah, and Abraham, adopted by God, and no longer to be called by human names but by the names of God’s children.

“If these three men are there.” The Holy Spirit does not need even now to point out Noah, Daniel, and Job. “These three men are in its midst.”

An educated hearer says to me: “Three are named in the present passage, but your speech asserts that there are many—Daniel, Job, and Noah.” We shall answer him as follows: Every multitude of similar people is one, not many, when they are alike. We are not many bodies but one body, according to what is written: “You are the body of Christ, and individually members of it” (I Cor. XII).

Our Savior came to seek and save what had perished, represented in the mystery of the ninety-nine sheep that did not go astray and the one that was lost. For the Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished.

Just as one body consists of many members and one sheep can represent many sheep that have perished, so all the Noahs, Daniels, and Jobs are reduced to one Noah, one Job, and one Daniel.

“They shall be saved by their righteousness,” says the Lord Adonai.

First, the four-letter name of God is the one that naturally signifies God.

923 Famine is therefore sent because of the sins of the earth. But concerning the earth, according to all the meanings we have given above, and according to whatever other interpretations we leave to the intelligence of our hearers, so that from our words they may discover further meanings for themselves, let us examine another work of divine wrath: the sending of evil beasts upon the sinful earth.

The Jews too say that whenever wolves have devoured human beings, rushing into houses, and when other beasts have done likewise—as history relates that lions were once sent against the human race, and at another time bears—such devourings proceed from God’s indignation. For the moment, following the prophet according to the literal sense and departing from the higher understanding, we see him following this meaning.

But the spiritual person, judging all things and judged by no one, confidently says that there are many beasts whom God sends upon the sinful earth, if our earth has sinned: “Our adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V).

That historical episode, which presents itself plainly to those who carefully observe the Scriptures, has the following meaning: when two bears were sent against the children who mocked the prophet, saying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” Those bears were signs of other beasts that truly are wild and truly savage, which are sent upon this sinful earth.

But far be it from us that beasts should be sent against us as God’s punishment. Rather, let us say in prayer: “Do not deliver the soul that confesses you to the beasts.”

I know righteous people who persevered in faith, were handed over to wild beasts, and completed their martyrdom while being torn apart by them, yet did not cease to be blessed. For they had not been handed over to spiritual and invisible beasts that tear the souls of sinners and drive their teeth into the hearts of the ungodly.

Just as a shepherd might snatch from a lion’s mouth two legs of a sheep, or the tip of an ear, so the children of Israel will be snatched away (Amos III). The earth is therefore sometimes handed over to beasts for destruction, so that human being and beast may be removed from it.

Observe carefully the differences among the threats. In the first threat, concerning famine, he says: “They alone shall be saved”—Noah, Daniel, and Job. In the second, where he testifies that he will send beasts, sons and daughters are named: “Nevertheless, they alone shall be saved,” says the Lord Adonai.

924 This passage is understood in two ways. First, let us explain it according to the common sense, because of certain foolish people who assert that the thought of their own mind is the truth of God. They frequently say: “It will happen that each one of us, by his prayers, will rescue from Gehenna whomever he wishes.” Thus they introduce iniquity before the Lord, failing to see that “the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the iniquity of the wicked shall be upon him; each one shall die in his own sin and live in his own righteousness.”

A martyr-father is of no benefit to me if I do not live well and adorn the nobility of my family—that is, his testimony and confession by which he was glorified in Christ.

It is of no benefit to the Jews who say: “We were not born of fornication; we have one father, God” (John VIII), and shortly afterward: “Abraham is our father.” Whatever they may say, whatever they may wish to claim for themselves, if they do not possess Abraham’s faith, they boast in vain. Nor will they be saved simply because they are Abraham’s children.

Since some people therefore hold an incorrect opinion, we necessarily inserted the literal sense, which says: “Noah, Daniel, and Job shall not deliver sons and daughters, but they alone shall be saved.”

Let none of us place confidence in a righteous father, a holy mother, or chaste brothers. Blessed is the person who has hope in himself and in the right way. To those who place their confidence in holy people we appropriately offer the example: “Cursed is the person who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. XVII). And this: “Do not put your trust in human beings.” And also: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in princes” (Ps. CXLV, CXVIII).

If it is necessary to hope in someone, then, abandoning everyone else, let us hope in the Lord, saying: “Though armies encamp against me, my heart shall not fear.”

Since these things stand thus, another question also arises for us, which we must carefully examine so that the truth of Scripture may shine forth: Why, when there are so many righteous people, are only three now named—Noah, Daniel, and Job?

925 I once heard a certain Hebrew explain this passage and say that these men were named because each of them experienced three periods: a joyful one, a sorrowful one, and again a joyful one.

Consider Noah before the Flood. Consider the world intact, and then Noah alone, with his sons and the animals, preserved in the ark amid the shipwreck of the whole world. Consider how he came out after the Flood and planted a vineyard, becoming in a certain sense the creator of the world a second time.

Such is the righteous person. He saw the world before the Flood—that is, before the consummation. He saw the world in the Flood, in the corruption and destruction of sinners that will occur on the day of judgment. Again he will see the world in the resurrection of all sinners.

Someone says to me: “I grant in Noah’s case that he saw three periods. What will you answer me concerning Daniel?” He too flourished in his homeland’s nobility before the captivity; afterward, when he was transferred to Babylon, he was made a eunuch, as can clearly be understood from his book. He also saw the return to Jerusalem.

To prove that he was in Jerusalem before the captivity and became a eunuch after the captivity, let us take up what was said to Hezekiah: “They will take some of your sons and make them eunuchs in the king’s house” (Isa. XXXIX). Then, after seventy years, he is found praying to God that, when the time of the captivity had been completed, he might enter Jerusalem again. We have his prayer written in his own book (Dan. IX), yet we cannot find where he died.

926 He therefore saw three periods: before the captivity, in the captivity, and after the captivity.

Such is the righteous person. Let us see whether Job too had three periods. He was indeed wealthy: he had seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, very many possessions, seven sons, and three daughters. Then the devil received power against him. Observe the changed circumstances. A father rich in children suddenly becomes childless; a master rich in property is brought to the utmost poverty. These are two periods.

After this, the Lord appears to him and speaks to him from the cloud, and Job himself answers the things written in his book (Job I). Thus in the first period he is praised in the Lord’s praises; in the second he is handed over to temptation and, struck with a most grievous ulcer from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, suffers sorrowful and harsh afflictions.

Finally, he receives fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, a thousand she-asses grazing, and seven sons and daughters are born to him (Job ult.). Thus in Job too we discover three periods, such as we find in righteous people.

The righteous see three periods: the present one; the period of change, when God will judge; and the future period after the resurrection of the dead—that is, the perpetuity of heavenly life in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY FIVE

On the fact that four exceedingly evil punishments—namely, the sword, famine, evil beasts, and pestilence—are brought upon the sinful earth; and on the parable that says: “Son of man, what will happen to the vine wood?” (Chapters XIV and XV).

---

### Editorial notes

**[Col. 0721D]** Origen—Adamantius, that is—had apparently attributed to the stars themselves and to the elements the power of acting well or badly. See Huet, *Origenianorum*, book II, question 10.

**[Col. 0721D]** This is a solemn error of Adamantius: that angels, whether appointed to govern us or assigned to the administration of churches, receive reward for the good conduct of the human beings entrusted to them, or condemnation and blame for their sins. The occasion for this error appears to have been supplied by a faulty understanding of the passage in the Apocalypse where the angels of the churches of Asia—who are none other than the bishops placed over those same churches—are addressed with praise or reproof according to their merits. Likewise the passage in I Cor. VI, 3: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” And the similar passages in Scripture, including II Pet. II, 4: “He did not spare the angels when they sinned.”

Saint Thomas attempts to excuse him, *Summa*, part I, question 113, article 7, as does Genebrardus in his *Collectanea*, as though Origen intended that angels would be brought to judgment for human sins not as guilty parties but as witnesses, to convict human beings of their negligence.

Yet, as Huet observes, it is permissible to believe that Christ merited by his death the first grace for all angels and obtained by his blood that benefit for those who persevered in integrity through the Church. Cyril, book IX, *On Adoration*; Augustine, book I, chapter 35, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*; and other Fathers seem to have held this view. See the same Huet, *Origenianorum*, book II, question 5, numbers 14 and following, and 21 and following.

**[Col. 0723]** Here we removed a second negative particle, improperly inserted.

**[Col. 0725C–D]** This is properly a Hebrew opinion, which they also zealously promote, so that for this reason they exclude Daniel from the number of the prophets, following Moses, who ordered eunuchs to be expelled from the assemblies of the Israelites.

Rabbi Eliezer, in *Pirke*, chapter 52: “These were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who were made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon and did not beget sons.”

A little farther below Origenes says that this is clear from Daniel’s own book: “What will you answer me concerning Daniel? He too flourished in his homeland before the captivity in nobility, and afterward, when he was transferred to Babylon, was made a eunuch, as can plainly be understood from his book.”

He explains this again very fully from Hebrew traditions in his *Commentary on Matthew*. Jerome too, our own author, agrees in book I *Against Jovinianus*: “It is superfluous to speak of Daniel, since the Hebrews even to the present day maintain that he and the three boys were eunuchs, on the basis of that divine sentence which Isaiah spoke to Hezekiah: ‘And from the sons who shall be born from you, they will take and make eunuchs in the king’s house.’ Again in Daniel we read: ‘And the king said to Ashpenaz, chief of the eunuchs, that he should bring in from the children of the captivity of Israel and from the royal seed and from the *phortommim* young men in whom there was no blemish, beautiful in appearance and understanding in wisdom.’ He argues that, if Daniel and the three boys were chosen from the royal seed, and Scripture foretold that the royal seed would become eunuchs, these are the ones who were made eunuchs.”

Moreover, in *Commentary on Daniel* I, 5: “Hence the Hebrews also believe that Daniel, Hananiah, and Azariah were eunuchs, fulfilling the prophecy spoken to Hezekiah through the prophet Isaiah: ‘And from your seed they will take and make eunuchs in the king’s house.’”

This also seems to have been the opinion of other Fathers, derived from the cited prophecy of Isaiah. Saint Epiphanius, however, in his *Life of Daniel*, thinks that Daniel was regarded as a eunuch only because of the chastity and integrity of his conduct; many others later adopted this view. Josephus does not report that Daniel himself was castrated by name, but that some of those whom Nebuchadnezzar had selected for himself as boys were castrated at his command.

**[Col. 0727D–0728D]** Jerome appears to have fallen into the same error, or to have copied it from Origen with a hasty pen, in his *Commentaries on Ezekiel*, book IX, chapter 28: “Wherever,” he says, “according to the Septuagint, *Lord, Lord* is written twice, the first name is the Tetragrammaton, which properly belongs to God and is called ineffable; the second is the common name, which is often found among human beings.”

But we said in our discussion of that passage that, since it is perfectly clear that in Ezekiel’s prophecy—the one under discussion—the opposite usage is consistently maintained, so that the first is the common name and the second the proper name of God, it appears that this was not the error of the holy Doctor but of ancient scribes, who rashly exchanged the numerical marks 1 and 2 there. Elsewhere, for example in chapter 6, he teaches the opposite quite correctly. Yet I do not see how this remedy can properly be applied to Origen’s testimony, for here he is mistaken not only in explicit words but also farther below, in Homily 12, where he asserts the same thing clearly.

**[Col. 0728D]** This passage strongly recalls that opinion of Origen which so often occurs in his writings: that an end will be imposed upon the punishments of the damned, and then a complete restoration of all things (*apokatastasis*, ἀποκατάστασις) and perfect happiness will come about when God is all in all. We shall discuss this matter at greater length below, in connection with a very similar passage in Homily 10.

925 The famine brought in on account of the sinful land has been examined in accordance with the limits of our powers, and after the famine we spoke of the most evil beasts that God will send against sinners. For at the beginning we proposed four punishments, of which the remaining two are the sword and death. In the first, only the names of sons and daughters are mentioned; but in the second and third, which we are now attempting to explain, the names of sons and daughters are appended—that is, in the sword, by which those who have done things deserving of its slaughter fall.

What, then, is this sword—that is, the *romphaea*—which we ought to fear, lest at some time it be sent against our land, against the land 927 which we have explained figuratively, so that we too may have to pass through a sword possessing something doubled in its punishment? For the very form of the sword divides and cuts the one against whom it is brought. But if the very contact with the sharp edge of its blade is also punitive, the one who must be punished by this sword is tortured in two ways.

For it is written: “He established the flaming sword, and the Cherubim to guard the way of the tree of life” (Gen. III). And just as, if a sharp, cutting sword is driven into the body, it inflicts a double torment of burning and cutting, so also the *romphaea*, which is said to have been appointed for the guarding of Paradise—and which we have now adopted for the exposition of the present sword—inflicts a double torture while it burns and divides.

But, in order to insert here something useful from the things by which God illumines our understanding, receive an example. Those devoted to the medical discipline say that for certain bodily cures not only the cutting of iron but also burning is necessary. For those whose bodies are consumed by the chronic decay of cancer, they apply either a glowing blade or razor, or some other kind of extremely sharp iron, so that through fire the roots of the cancer may be torn out, while through incision the rotten flesh is cut away and a path is opened for medicines to be introduced.

Who, do you suppose, among us has a sin resembling cancer, so to speak, such that either the simple sharpness of iron or the burning of fire alone is not sufficient for him, but both must be applied, so that he may be burned and cut? Hear the Savior signifying the principle of fire and iron in two places. In one place he says: “I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. X). In another: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and would that it were already burning” (Luke XII).

[Note: Origen wrote, as in his commentaries on Exodus, where he praises this very passage from Luke, πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ εἴτε ἤδη ἐκάη—“I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and would that it had already burned.” If the text of Luke itself was not then formulated in precisely this way, this at least was the sense he faithfully retained when he recited the passage from memory. The very wording that is written in present-day manuscripts, καὶ τί θέλω, εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη, Grotius, praised by Huet, punctuates as follows: καὶ τί θέλω; εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη—“But what is it that I desire? Would that it had already been kindled!” He shows with sufficient learning that εἰ with the indicative can signify “would that” among Hellenists.]

Thus the Savior brings both—the sword and the fire—and baptizes what could not be cleansed by the purification of the Holy Spirit. The divine mysteries are ineffable and known to God alone; nevertheless, they consist more in the bestowal of graces than in varieties of torments. For physicians, in accordance with the rational principles of their art, do not irrationally cut, burn, administer a potion of the bitterest mixture, and perform many other procedures as the case requires for those whom they treat. Rather, God, the Lord of the universe, does not inflict punishments on sinners without a certain rational wisdom and without an administration worthy of his majesty.

For he does not, as some suppose, apply punishments merely in order to torture. Rather, like a father, he knows the wounds of all of us: he knows for what reason each ulcer has arisen, from what beginning the putrefaction of the unhappy soul has been drawn, what form of pain comes from what sin. He knows the forms, modes, and numbers of sins: who has sinned once, twice, or three times; who has often fallen into one kind of offense; who has erred only once in each of various kinds of vices.

We ought to investigate all these things according to the wisdom of God, in accordance with what is written: “God searches hearts and reins.” He wants us to understand the punishments inflicted by him as things worthy of God and appropriate to his administration, rather than merely to torment us. For he created all things so that they might exist, and made the generations of the world wholesome, and there is no medicine of destruction in them. But because, by despising what he willed, we did not do it, and because he did not exercise in us what he had desired, the discussion compelled us to say something about the nature of the punishments inflicted upon the earth.

We must know, however, that famine does not immediately bring death after it. It can happen that someone who endures famine remains alive, although he is tormented by starvation, squalor, and emaciation. It can happen that, when evil beasts have been sent in, not everyone immediately perishes, those being preserved through the aid of flight. It can happen that, when the *romphaea* withdraws, destruction ceases. Some are now wounded and cut, and, so to speak, pierced through by repeated blows, yet they do not perish.

[Note: It must certainly be read: *confodiuntur*—“are pierced through.”]

For this reason death, the final punishment, is now introduced in the enumeration of punishments. The most sacred Apostle, sensing something of this kind, was saying: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (I Cor. V). I will dare to say it: death is the last enemy to be destroyed. There was an enemy before death, namely the *romphaea*; there was an enemy before death, namely the most evil beasts; there was an enemy before the most evil beasts, namely famine. All these are enemies of those who are enemies of religion.

For if you do not wish to become a friend of God, who invites you to reconciliation and says through the Apostle, “I beseech you, be reconciled to God through Christ” (II Cor. V), why do you complain against God when you have chosen to be under the authority of enemies in matters involving your own causes? Or do you not know that God therefore sent fury and wrath, distress, and an irruption through evil angels upon Egypt, because they were his enemies and were ruled by his adversary?

But far from us be the punishments of these four penalties: famine, the most evil beasts, the sword, and death. Whatever of these is inflicted comes upon those who are enemies of God; it passes by his friends and does not dare to touch those who glory in their intimacy with him.

And just as it has rightly been believed concerning fire, with the Scriptures bearing witness that the righteous pass through it and are not burned—“For the fire will test what sort each person’s work is”—so also among these punishments let there be found some Daniel, Noah, or Job who will suffer none of the penalties.

We have explained these matters individually according to each punishment; but in the final part the prophet joins them together and says: “Thus says the Lord Adonai: If I send my four most evil punishments—the *romphaea*, famine, the most evil beasts, and death.” Where? Not upon the earth, but upon Jerusalem. For if the earth is punished, one correction is sufficient for it. But if Jerusalem is corrected—upon which the name of God has been invoked (II Pet. II)—four torments are inflicted upon it together.

It would have been much more beneficial for us not to have believed the divine word than, after believing, to turn back again to the sins we previously committed. Consider how Scripture says that the punishments are inflicted individually upon “the earth,” without specifying which earth. But when it comes to Jerusalem, it says: “And if I send my four most evil punishments—the *romphaea*, famine, the most evil beasts, and death—upon Jerusalem.” It thereby indicates us as Jerusalem: when we sin, we are the Jerusalem that is destroyed; but when we remain in the commandments, Jerusalem is said to be the one that is saved.

All the lamentations that we read concerning Jerusalem, all the complaints with which God mourns over it, pertain to us, who have tasted the word of God and afterward acted contrary to his commandments. The one who despises the laws of Solomon is not punished; the one who abandons the statutes of Lycurgus is not punished in the same way. One punishment belongs to the person who tramples upon and scorns the law of God handed down through Moses; the greatest punishment of all belongs to the one who has considered the commandments of the Son of God worthless.

“For anyone who nullifies the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Heb. X); how much worse punishments, do you think, does the one deserve who has trampled upon the Son of God?

He says, therefore, that those whom we have enumerated did not trample upon the Son of God but merely entered into the law of God—especially those who lived before the Lord’s coming. Nor are those who crucified my Savior guilty of as great a punishment as those to whom the Apostle says: “Trampling upon the Son of God and treating the Spirit of grace with contempt” (ibid.), and whatever else is signified in that passage where he recalls the sins of those who sinned after faith in God.

These things have been said concerning the four most evil punishments that are brought upon Jerusalem. And all of us who have learned the divine Scriptures, whether we live well or badly, are Jerusalem. If we live badly, we are that Jerusalem which is punished with torments and suffers the four punishments; if well, that Jerusalem which rests in the bosom of God.

There is a great difference in the rest of the earth, and likewise within Jerusalem itself. For all who are sinners in the Church, who have tasted the word of God and transgress it, certainly deserve punishments; yet each will be tormented according to the measure of his rank. The one who presides over the Church and commits an offense receives a greater punishment. Does he not deserve greater mercy by comparison with the faithful catechumen? Is not a layman more worthy of pardon when compared with a deacon? And again, in comparison with a presbyter, does not a deacon deserve more pardon? You know, without my saying it, what follows.

Therefore, fearing the judgment of God and setting before my eyes that order of judgment which is contained in the Scriptures, I remember that saying: “Do not lift a burden beyond your strength.” And also this: “Do not seek to become a judge, lest you be unable to remove iniquities.”

What does it profit me that I sit first, reclining in the chair, and receive the honor of a greater rank, if I cannot have works corresponding to my dignity? Shall I not be tormented by a greater punishment because everyone pays me the honor due to the righteous, although I am a sinner (Eccl. VII)?

As I more carefully reconsidered what was being said concerning the four punishments of the earth, it was necessary to add that Jerusalem belonged to the tribe of Benjamin; the priests of the temple and the Levites who served in the ministries of God, together with the other orders included in the language of Scripture, lived there. This Jerusalem receives the four most evil punishments, which are not alike for those who dwell in it.

For the threat is not directed in the same way against the people and against the Levites. A sinful Israelite falls into an Israelite offense. But whoever is greater than an Israelite—the more exalted he is in rank, whether Levite or priest—the greater punishments he will endure. If the high priest should sin, his fellow priest Heli says to him: “If a man sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” (I Reg. II).

These things have been said in explanation of that passage in which punishments were threatened both individually against the sinful earth and collectively against unhappy Jerusalem.

Let us examine also what follows in Scripture. When the prophet hears it in a parable, we ought to explain only its meaning, leaving aside the actual sequence of the testimony and sending the hearer to the book:

“As the wood of the vine is more honorable in its fruit than all other woods, especially those that bear fruit in the forest, so in relation to other works it is more useless than all woods” (Ezek. XV).

Certain vessels can be made, and they can be useful for various works and necessary services; but from the branches of the vine not only can no vessel or useful object be made, but not even a peg is useful. The divine word therefore says that just as the branch of the vine becomes more honorable than other woods if it bears fruit, so it should be judged inferior to all if it does not possess that by which it excels.

In this way it speaks of those who have been imbued with the utterances of God as being more honorable than all others, and as having been placed, in whatever manner, in a position of dignity within the vineyard, when they bear fruit—the clusters of salvation, concerning which it is written: “But I planted you as a wholly true, fruitful vine” (Jer. II). And elsewhere: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V). And again: “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Ps. LXXIX), and what follows.

But if they do not bear fruit, so that God can say, “How have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” then they are found to be far worse than those woods which, although they are of lesser value, nevertheless bear their own fruit. For just as the woods of the forests surpass unfruitful vines, so, within a certain dispensation of divine wisdom, some things are fashioned from inferior woods that are necessary for a household.

Do not be disturbed, thinking that we are asserting outside the Scriptures what we say will happen: that something useful may be made from the woods of the forest—that is, from me myself, if I do not bear the proper fruits of my nature. For the Apostle also takes up a certain image of those vessels that exist in human society, saying: “But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthen ones” (note that he has called them wooden vessels); “some indeed for honor, others for dishonor” (II Tim. II).

These wooden vessels, which the Apostle declares to exist in the great house, are not made from vines, nor from the branches of vineyards, but from other woods that have borne fruit in the groves in a lower order. How great, then, is the evil, and what a danger, that once-inferior woods should be found in the great house of the master of the household, while the branch of my vine is useless in the house and is thrown into the fire? For it is written that the fire consumes its annual pruning.

These things concern Ezekiel. But the Savior briefly set forth the meaning of this parable in the Gospel, saying: “I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the cultivator. Every branch that remains in me and bears fruit, my Father prunes, so that it may bear greater fruit. But the branch that remains in me and does not bear fruit, my Father cuts away and throws into the fire” (John XV).

Do you see the similarity of the two sayings? Do you see how the Father cuts away and casts into the fire? We foolish people, as though Scripture ought indeed to be neglected, unwilling to learn those things that instill fear in us but desiring to hear those that bring pleasure to itching ears, gladly heard the things that overturn and deceive us.

The person who says to his neighbor, “God forgives our sins,” if indeed we play at such mysteries, promises in turn that God will send us a cloth. And because he is good and dissolves everyone’s sins, we ought to sit and say with an anxious heart: “If we sinned yesterday, let us repent today.”

But to this branch—for it is an animal—that says, “God is powerful and a good cultivator, who will not cut me away and throw me into the fire,” the cultivator will reply: “But if the branch is such that it is useless on the vine, can it really be left there? If it is left, will it not hinder the vine from producing green branches rich in fruit, in place of the dry branch?”

For just as it belongs to a good cultivator to cut away and prune what is dry and to consign unfruitful branches as fuel to the fire, so it belongs to the good God to cut away the unfruitful branches from all vines and consign them to the fire for destruction.

But we deceive ourselves, and, deceived as well as deceiving, we prefer to continue in error with the multitude rather than turn away from error. We ought instead to seek what builds up, increases the fear of God, recalls us to repentance, leads us to confess our crime, and makes us think day and night about how we may please the Lord, so that we may become fruitful branches in the true vine, Christ Jesus, clinging to his root—to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY SIX

On the passage: “Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations,” up to: “You poured out your fornication at every passage” (chap. XVI).

933 As I consider the steadfastness of the prophets, [Col. 0735A] I am struck with wonder at how those who truly believed God more than human beings despised death, dangers, insults, and everything they suffered at the hands of those whom they reproved while they served God’s will in prophesying. I once admired Isaiah before comparing him with Ezekiel, and I was astonished at how he said: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; attend to the law of God, people of Gomorrah. What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?” says the Lord (Isa. I). For he said these things when he could have spoken—or remained silent. The prophets were not, as some suppose, out of their minds and speaking under compulsion of the Spirit. “If something is revealed to another who is seated,” says the Apostle, “let the first be silent” (I Cor. XIV). From this it is shown that the one who speaks has the power to speak when he wishes and to be silent when he wishes. And to Balaam it is said: “Nevertheless, observe to speak the word that I put into your mouth” (Num. XXII), as though he had the power, after receiving God’s word, either to speak or to remain silent.

What, then, is it that I admire in Ezekiel? When he had been commanded to testify and make known Jerusalem’s iniquities, he did not set before his eyes the danger that was to follow from his preaching; but, in order to keep only God’s commands, he spoke whatever he had been ordered to speak. Granted that this is a mystery, a revelation of sacred understanding concerning Jerusalem and all that is said about her; nevertheless, while prophesying, he also reproves her for fornication, because she spread her legs to every passerby, and with a condemnatory voice bears witness against her, rebuking the city for its crimes. But because he trusted that he was doing God’s will, ready both to die and to see the outcome, he spoke without fear.

Let us therefore examine the prophecy itself, and first consider how it was placed within the prophet’s power whether he should speak or not. “The word of the Lord came to him, saying: Son of man, testify against Jerusalem concerning her iniquities, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord.” The Lord did not place this command upon him through the necessity of an impulse, but in accordance with the will of the speaker, so that he might testify against Jerusalem concerning her iniquities; and he said, “You shall say.” What shall you say? The words that follow. In the prophet who heard “You shall say,” it remained a matter of choice whether he would say it or not, just as it was placed in Jonah’s power. For it was within the power of the one who heard, “Say: In three days Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jon. III), either to speak or to remain silent. And because it had been left to his discretion and he did not wish to speak, see what later consequences followed for him: the ship was endangered because of him; he was found hiding by lot; the whale swallowed him after he had been cast out.

Those prophets, then, whoever came after Jonah, perhaps considering what had happened to him or to other prophets, saw that distress threatened them on every side: persecution according to the world if they spoke the truth, and offense against the Lord if, fearing human beings, they put forward falsehoods in place of the truth. Therefore Ezekiel testified and made known Jerusalem’s iniquities, and said:

“Thus says the Lord: Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite.” What city was ever so exalted and so highly esteemed in the world as the city of God? Yet this very city, promising herself great things—as though she were near to God and his city—is rebuked by the Holy Spirit as degenerate and alien because she sinned. For her father was an Amorite, and therefore no longer God. As long as she did not sin, God was her father; but when she sinned, her father became an Amorite. As long as she did not sin, the Holy Spirit was her father; when she sinned, her mother became a Hittite. As long as she did not sin, she had Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as her root; when she sinned, her root became Canaanite.

I have often marveled at what Daniel said to the sinful presbyter, giving him a name that corresponded to his sin: “Seed of Canaan,” he said, “and not Judah.” Great indeed was Daniel, who most steadfastly called the sinful presbyter “seed of Canaan” [Col. 0736B] and not Judah (Dan. III). Yet Ezekiel was greater in comparison with him: he did not charge one presbyter, nor two individuals, with an insulting origin, but said, “Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan. Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.”

Because Jerusalem had committed many sins, the prophet rebuked her and marked her not with one or two names, but with three. Seven nations are enumerated by God in Genesis in the passage concerning the land he gave to the children of Israel. These seven are: “Into the land,” he says, “of the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, Girgashites, and Jebusites.” If it had been possible to gather these seven together in order, through them, to reproach sinful Jerusalem for her ignobility, the prophet surely would have done so. But what did he do? From the seven he selected the Amorite and the Canaanite, and said that sinful Jerusalem shared in them: she was related to the Canaanite in respect of her root and origin, specifically to the Amorite in respect of her father, and specifically to the Hittite in respect of her mother.

If such things are said about Jerusalem, concerning whom such great and wondrous promises were written, what will become of wretched me if I sin? Who will be my father, or who will be my mother? Of such greatness and such a character was Jerusalem, yet her root and origin are called Canaanite, her father Amorite, and her mother Hittite. If I sin, I who believe in Christ Jesus and have entrusted myself to so great a teacher, who will be my father? Certainly not merely an Amorite, but some worse father. Who is he? Whoever commits sin is born from the devil: “You are from your father the devil” (I John). If, then, Jerusalem is said to be from the root and origin of the land of Canaan, what will be said of us?

Fathers are also found for us, who beget us in sins. For just as, if I am good and established in excellent conduct, Jesus says to me, “Son, your sins are forgiven” (Matt. IX), and Paul, the disciple of Jesus, says to me, “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel,” so, if I become a sinner, the devil, begetting me in sins and taking to himself the words with which God the Father spoke to the Savior, says to me, “You are my son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. IV). And many other fathers will be mine, to whom I shall go. Each person goes to his own fathers.

If someone is from Abraham, it is said to him: “But you shall go to your fathers, brought out in peace, nourished in a good old age.” But if someone departs from the world not in peace but amid the warfare of sins, in an old age that is not good, grown old in days of evil, it is surely said to him: “But you shall go to your fathers, nourished in warfare, in an evil old age” (Gen. XV).

God teaches us under other names what we ought to do. “On the day when you were born, they did not bind your hands,” or, as the Hebrew has it: “Your umbilical cord was not cut.” Allegorically, he presents Jerusalem as a girl begotten from infancy. Let us understand that what is said concerning Jerusalem applies to all human beings who are in the Church. Her first period is such as it is described; but far be it from us that we should have a third period such as is attributed to Jerusalem. For all of us who were initially sinners are called Jerusalem by God, and we possess the things first mentioned.

The second period concerns us if, after God’s visitation and our knowledge of him, we persist in sins. The third consists of the evils that we utterly detest; we shall pursue them in their order.

To return now to the first period, it is written as though concerning Jerusalem: “On the day when you were born, your umbilical cord was not cut.” We need God’s help in order either to discover the uncut umbilical cord of sinful Jerusalem or, alternatively, to explain the cut umbilical cord of the woman who did not sin.

Whether, then, I seek the umbilical cord of Jerusalem or of anyone else in another passage of Scripture, I compare spiritual things with spiritual things in order to find how Jerusalem’s umbilical cord was not cut.
