It is written in Job concerning the dragon: “His strength is in his navel, and his power is upon the navel of his belly” (Job XL). From what divine grace has granted me, I know that when I was expounding the present passage I said that the dragon is the opposing power. For this is the dragon, the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole inhabited world. His strength is in the navel.

There is no doubt about this, for the beginning of all evils lies in the loins. Therefore the one who was to be born is said to have been still in his father’s loins, because human seeds are gathered in the loins. Wherever the seeds are, the opposing power therefore attempts to display there the force of its ambushes. Against males its power is in the loins; against females its power is in the navel of the belly. Observe also how Scripture, under veiled names, has honorably named the male and female genitals, so as not to signify indecency through terms that are openly used.

If the example we brought forward from Job has been understood, understand that just as the foreskin is circumcised in a man, [Col. 0738A] so in a woman the navel is cut off.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] He is alluding to female circumcision, which was practiced especially in those regions where Adamantius himself lived, that is, in Egypt. Saint Ambrose also mentions it in Book II of *On Abraham*, chapter 11: “The Egyptians circumcise males in their fourteenth year, and they report that females are circumcised in the same year, since from that year the male passion begins to burn and the menstrual periods of women begin.” Strabo, Book XVII, likewise reports of the Egyptians that they “cut out the females” (*τὰ θήλεα ἐκτέμνειν*, “excise the females”). The distinguished physicians whom Huetius cites should be consulted: Paul of Aegina, Book VI, chapter 70; Aetius, *Tetrabiblos* IV, sermon 4, chapter 103; and those who report that this custom is still retained not only by Egyptians but also by Persians and Copts: Bellonius, Book III of *Observations*, chapter 28, and Leo Africanus, Book XXVIII.]

When a woman has been chaste and has undergone clean menstrual changes, that is, when she does not fall into filthy things and the shamefulness of sins, then her navel has been cut off. But if she has sinned, her navel has not been cut off. Thus he rebukes Jerusalem as a woman whose navel has not been cut off.

The Seventy translated the passage as: “They did not bind your breasts,” expressing the sense of the wording more than rendering the word literally. The breasts are taken in the Song of Songs in place of your thoughts and mind: “For your breasts are better than wine” (Song I). And, “He reclined upon the breast of Jesus” (John XIII), where your breasts are found—that is, the one who was to have communion in his understanding.

When the understanding is rigid and knowledge is constricted and solid, and speech does not flow, it is clear that “your breasts are bound.” But when the things that are said are loosened and flow, “your breasts are not bound.”

“You were not washed with water for salvation.” Let us examine the things said concerning Jerusalem, lest perhaps they also be found in us. For example, let it be said: “There is a certain woman who has now been washed”; but it is asked whether she has also been washed for salvation, so that we too may fear because of the words “for salvation.” Not all who are washed are washed for salvation.

We who have received the grace of baptism in the name of Christ have been washed; but I do not know who has been washed for salvation. Simon was washed and received baptism, and he continued in the company of Philip; but because he had not been washed for salvation, he was condemned by the one who spoke to him in the Holy Spirit: “May your money be with you for perdition” (Acts VIII). It is exceedingly difficult for one who is washed to be washed for salvation.

Pay attention, catechumens; listen, and from what is said prepare yourselves while you are catechumens, while you have not yet been baptized, so that you may come to the washing and be washed for salvation. Do not be washed like certain people who have been washed but not for salvation—like one who receives water but does not receive the Holy Spirit. Whoever is washed for salvation receives both water and the Holy Spirit.

Because Simon was not washed for salvation, he received water but did not receive the Holy Spirit. Thinking that the gift of the Spirit could be purchased with money, he was not washed [F. *lotus*, “washed”] for salvation.

These words that we now read as spoken to Jerusalem are addressed to every sinful soul that appears to believe, so that I may not ascend to greater things and seek what lies beyond my strength and ability.

“Nor were you salted with salt.” This too is a crime of Jerusalem: she was not worthy of the salt of God. If I believe in my Lord Jesus Christ, he will make me salt and say to me: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. V). If I believe in the Spirit who spoke through the Apostle, I am seasoned with salt and can keep the command: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Col. IV).

To be salted is a great work. Whoever is seasoned with salt is full of grace. For even in common speech a person is called “salty” when he is gracious, and conversely “insipid” when he lacks grace. If, then, grace comes to us from God and we are filled with his gift, we are salted with salt.

Again, sinful Jerusalem is not wrapped in cloths. Observe what we are saying: the soul that is reborn and first brought forth in the washing is wrapped in cloths. My Lord Jesus himself was wrapped in cloths, as the Gospel according to Luke reports (Luke II). Therefore the one who is reborn—reborn, certainly, in Christ—ought to desire rational and pure milk; and before desiring rational and guileless milk, he must be salted with salt and bound in wrappings of cloth, lest it be said to him: “You were not salted with salt, and you were not wrapped in cloths.”

That these things are crimes of Jerusalem—her not having her navel circumcised, not being salted with salt, not being wrapped in cloths, and not being washed for salvation—the remaining speech indicates, for it continues as follows: “Nor did your eye spare you, to do one of all these things for you. Therefore I did none of these things for you, so that I might suffer something on your account,” says the Lord.

I shall take an example from human beings; then, if the Holy Spirit grants it, I shall pass on to Jesus Christ and God the Father. When I speak to a person and entreat him concerning some matter, asking him to have mercy on me, if he is without mercy, he suffers nothing from what I say. But if he is gentle in spirit, and no hardness of heart has become rigid within him, he hears me and has mercy on me; his inward parts are softened by my prayers.

Understand something similar concerning the Savior. He descended to earth in pity for the human race, and he suffered our passions before he endured the cross and deigned to assume our flesh. For if he had not suffered, he would not have entered into the conditions of human life. First he suffered; then he descended and was seen.

What is this suffering that he endured for us? It is love that is suffering.

The Father himself, too, God of the universe, long-suffering, greatly merciful, and compassionate—is he not in a certain sense suffering? [Note: [Col. 0739D] To this should be referred what is found in Book II of *On First Principles*, chapter 4: “But if, because of the things said in the Old Testament—that God becomes angry, or repents, or that some other passion of human feeling is attributed to him—they think they have material for refuting us, asserting that God is altogether impassible and free from all such emotions, it must also be shown to them that similar things are found in the evangelical parables, and so forth.” Likewise, in the *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter XXII: “We have a very great abundance of examples from the Gospels, in which, according to certain parables, God is likened to a human being. In defense, then, of those parables which, taken literally, establish that God the Father of Christ is subject to the emotions of human condition, we shall use those in which God is called a human being; and we shall address the heretics who, because they have failed to notice similar passages of the Old Testament, fall into offense against the law of God, the prophets, and the Creator of the world, as follows: If, according to the evangelical parables, God is compared with a human being, why, consistently with these parables, do you not also wish the anger, fury, repentance, turning away of the face, sitting, standing, and walking of God to be a parable?”]

Do you not know that, when he administers human affairs, he suffers human suffering? For “the Lord your God bore your conduct,” just as someone might bear his son. God therefore bears our conduct, just as the Son of God bears our sufferings.

The Father himself is not impassible. If he is entreated, he has mercy and suffers something through love; he comes to be in those things in which, according to the greatness of his nature, he cannot be, and for our sake he endures human sufferings.

“Your eye did not spare you,” he says, “to do one of all these things for you, so that I might suffer something on your account.”

And because you became such, “you were cast out upon the face of the field.” O God, do not allow us to be such that we are cast away by you and by your Church upon the face of the field; rather, let us pass from the narrowness of our understandings into the open field.

“And you were cast out upon the face of the field.” Why? “Because of the perversity of your soul on the day when you were born.” Can someone possess perversity of soul on the very day on which he was born? He is describing our passions, human vices, and customary perversities. Because of our perversity, if the heart has not been made straight, we are cast upon the field on the day when we are born.

If, after the regeneration of the washing, after the word of God, we sin again, we are cast out on the day when we are born. Such people are very often found washed with the washing of the second regeneration, yet not producing worthy fruits of repentance; they do not enliven the mystery of baptism with the greater fear they possessed while they were catechumens, nor with the greater love they practiced while they were hearers of the word, nor with holier conduct than they displayed before.

Such people encounter what is said here: “You were cast out upon the face of the field because of the perversity of your soul on the day when you were born.”

But observe the mercy of God; observe his singular clemency. Although Jerusalem has been cast out upon the face of the field, he does not despise her as though she were to remain cast out forever. He does not abandon her so completely to her perversity that he forgets her altogether or never again raises her who lies fallen.

Attend to what follows: “And I passed by you.” You were cast out, yet I came to you again; my visitation did not fail you after your fall. “And I saw you sprinkled with your blood.” It is as though he said: I saw you guilty of murder, guilty of blood and deadly sins. “And I said to you: Live from your blood and be filled with life.” Suck from your blood and be filled with life.

“I gave you as a garden of the field.” I had mercy on you after you had been cast out; I saw you sprinkled with blood and sins; I made you like a garden of the field, and you multiplied. Because I came to you and visited you after you had been cast out, I became the cause of your multiplication.

“And you multiplied and grew great.” I gave you increase in number and greatness: that is, I made you grow and multiply. For we grow and multiply through this.

“And you entered into cities of cities.” Again he explains the errors of Jerusalem as she enters into cities of cities. Let us consider how she entered criminally into cities of cities. If some ecclesiastical person enters into individual cities in which there are heresies and doctrines alien to God, and becomes a participant in such cities, he hears: “You entered into cities of cities.”

“Your breasts were raised.” After so many crimes you flourished again; your time came, and the time of those who turn aside.

I am told: “Do not allegorize; do not explain by a figure.” Let those who say this answer me, please: Does Jerusalem have breasts? Is there a time when they are not gathered together and a time when they are raised? Does she have a navel, and is she reproved because it was not cut off? How can these things be understood without allegorical interpretation?

“Your breasts were raised, and your hair grew.” With complete propriety, the divine word describes what ordinarily occurs in the bodies of virgins. “And your hair grew, but you were naked and dishonored.”

Whoever has not put on Jesus Christ is naked. Whoever has not put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, so as to bear with his neighbor, is dishonored.

“But you were naked and dishonored, and I passed by you.” A second time he came to her, saw her sinning, and again departed because of her sins; yet once more the merciful and kind God returns and visits her.

“And I came to you, and I saw you, and behold, your time and the time of those who turn aside.” What does he mean by “your time”? It signifies the time of adolescents, when, by reason of age, they are already capable of fornication.

And again: “The time,” he says, “of those who turn aside.” Who are these people who turn aside? While we are little ones, those who do not wish to turn aside to those who strive to overthrow us—such as wicked Christians, unclean demons, and the angels of the devil—have no place in us and cannot turn aside to us.

But when we have reached a greater age and are already able to sin, they seek access to us in order to turn aside to us—and this applies both to the angels of God and to the angels of Satan. It is impossible for both groups to turn aside to us in the same way. If we sin, the angels of the devil turn aside to us; if we stand with firm resolve, the angels of God turn aside to us.

“Your time therefore came, and the time of those who turn aside.” Because the time of those who turn aside had come, our Lord Jesus Christ, our God, again visits wretched Jerusalem—that is, our sinful soul.

“I spread my wings over you.” Scripture commonly calls the edges of garments “wings” [Al. “penalties”], as in Ruth, who came secretly, uncovered the garment at Boaz’s feet, and slept beneath the edge of his clothing (Ruth III).

God, then, speaks as though clothed in a garment: “I spread my wings over you, and I covered [Al. opened] your shame.” Blessed is the one whose shame God covers with his wings—provided that he perseveres in the blessedness in which Jerusalem did not persevere.

“And I swore an oath to you in the covenant, and I entered into a covenant with you.” After all these things, because of which he returns and again departs, after such frequent visitations, he now enters into a covenant with her for the first time.

“And you became mine, and I washed you with water.” After all these things I took you to myself, and I washed you for salvation and cleansed your blood from you. Understanding these things, let us pray that God’s mercy may come upon us and wash the blood from our souls. For if we have done anything deserving of death, this is our blood.

“I cleansed your blood from you, and I anointed you with oil.” God wishes to make us *Christoi*—anointed ones.

“And I clothed you in variegated garments.” How great is God’s kindness toward each of the souls of Jerusalem! He grants believers not a tunic of one color, but one of great variety. Jacob had already made this variegated tunic as a sign when he clothed his son Joseph and dressed him in variegated garments (Gen. XXXVII).

If you consider the varieties of understanding and good works, you will truly see the many-colored tunic that God’s visitation grants to those who have been called to salvation. I understand the Law, I comprehend the prophets, I recognize the Gospels, and the Apostle is not hidden from me. I am prudent, I am just, I am merciful—and do you still seek another variegated tunic with which the Lord clothes Jerusalem, saying: “I clothed you in variegated garments, and I shod you with hyacinth”?

He wishes our shoes to be flourishing and well-dyed. What are the shoes? Hear Paul preaching more plainly: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace” (Eph. V).

“And I girded you with fine linen.” The Apostle speaks more clearly about this girdle: “Stand with your loins girded in truth” (ibid.). Truth is understood as the fine linen.

“And I covered you with *trichapton*.” Since I found neither what *trichapton* was nor any explanation of it, I found in one edition the reading *florens*, “flourishing,” and in another, “garment.” Thus, after the variegated garment, God clothes us also with a flourishing tunic.

“And I adorned you with adornment, and I put bracelets upon your hands.” When he gives me opportunities for good works, he places bracelets around my hands.

“And a chain around your neck.” If, after my deeds of justice, he adorns me with the understanding of truth, then a nuptial ornament, a beautiful chain, is placed around my neck.

“And I gave you an earring for your nostril.” When I am able to receive the mysteries of true sweetness and good fragrance, then God adorns my nostril with earrings.

“And rings for your ears.” Thus not only may your ears have earrings, but a great golden wheel may also be placed around your hearing. The golden wheel is that which turns around sacred understandings.

“And a crown of glorification upon your head.” Almighty God, grant also to us that we may become worthy of a crown of glorification upon our heads.

“And you were adorned with gold”—that is, with divine meanings—“and silver”—that is, with sacred words.

“And your coverings were of fine linen.” The depth of meanings is a linen covering.

“And with flourishing garments”—for which word the Seventy used *trichapta* (*τρίχαπτα*), signifying an exceedingly delicate covering and a garment thinned almost to resemble hair.

“And with variegated garments.” Behold, all Jerusalem is protected by wings, clothed in many colors, and adorned with jewels.

What does the great and human-loving God do after these things? He nourishes her with delicate foods. “You ate fine flour, honey, and oil.” He does not simply say flour, nor barley bread. What we are speaking to you now is fine flour.

But wretched Jerusalem, after the fine flour, after the honey, after the oil, is again rebuked as a prostitute. Therefore let us take greater care, lest perhaps, after the pure words of fine flour, after the exceedingly sweet sayings of the prophets, after the oil that gladdens the face and with which we wish to anoint our head so that our fasting may become acceptable, we sin again. We are not only anointed with this oil; we also eat it.

“And you became exceedingly, very beautiful.” He praises her beauty, praises her appearance, and proclaims her form.

“And you were directed toward kingship.” What great progress—that she should even be directed toward kingship!

“And your name went out among the nations.” These things are fitting for one who, after beginning to be free from the world, progresses in conduct toward the blessed life and also obtains a glorious name in the world.

But far be from us what follows; for this has been written to instill fear in those who hear. After her beauty and her great name, wretched Jerusalem commits fornication. Therefore do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bring.

And elsewhere: “Brothers, even if a person should be overtaken in some sin, you who are spiritual support such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI). And again: “Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.”

“And your name went out among the nations because of your appearance, because the beauty of the appearance that I established in you had been perfected,” says Adonai the Lord.

“And you trusted in your beauty.” She became proud, and her consciousness of her beauty caused beautiful Jerusalem to become exalted. And because she became high-minded, neither humbled herself nor glorified God, hear what is said to her:

“And you fornicated in your own name, and you poured out your fornication upon every passerby.” What does he mean by: “You poured out your fornication upon every passerby”?

The opposing power surrounds our souls, traversing them in various ways and seeking a place through which it may break in. Anger wishes to fornicate with me in its own name. Sorrow, joined to my character, seeks in its own name to make me mourn. Avarice, for its part, introduces the desire for gold and silver and for everything similar. If I do not guard myself and close my door, but receive every assault of the enemy, it is said to me: “You poured out your fornication upon every passerby, and you took your garments and made yourself sewn idols.”

From the things with which I adorned you, through which you became beautiful, you made yourself sewn idols. I wish to explain further what these sewn idols are, since they are sewn from garments.

The garments are the divine Scriptures, and their meaning is what is contained in them. The heretics cut these garments apart and sewed them together, joining saying to saying and words to words, but not with suitable and fitting connection. By sewing them together, they made impious images for themselves, with which they enticed certain people to believe and consent to their worship and to accept their fabricated discipline.

But may God free us all from these and every other image, so that we may be glorified in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY SEVENTH

Concerning the passage: “Taking some of my garments, you made for yourself sewn high places here and there,” up to: “And even after this you were not satisfied” (Chapter XVI).

945 The catalog of the sins of Jerusalem, however it may be understood, edifies the hearer. For just as, if in his own house the master should reprimand one of his household and set forth his sins, another who has recently been purchased as a slave, seeing the discipline of the head of the household—what he censures and what he praises—is instructed not to do what his fellow servants did before him, and hastens with every effort to do those things by which the others earned honor and freedom from their master: so we too, when we hear the sins for which God censures either Jerusalem, or all Judea, or any one of the tribes in particular, gain no small benefit, lest we also fall into the things into which the others fell.

The beginning of today’s reading is that Jerusalem received garments from God and made from them certain stitched images for herself, and committed fornication upon them. I discussed these matters, as far as I was able, in the preceding discourse, teaching that those who tear apart the Scriptures, breaking words away from words and sewing them together, and composing fabricated doctrines, serve the idols which they have clothed in those garments.

“You shall not enter my tabernacle; you are outside, and outside you shall remain.” Scripture knows that the holy are within, and sinners outside. Therefore, since Jerusalem committed such sins that she was not worthy to enter the promises of God, and it is said to her, “And you shall not enter,” let us beware lest this also be said to us: “And you shall not enter.”

“Nor shall it be.” What is said—“nor shall it be”—is not complete, and therefore something must be understood after it, so that the sense may be fulfilled: the good things that were promised to you and that you were going to receive shall not come to pass.

Another offense follows:

“And you took the vessels of your glory from your silver and your gold, which I had given you, and you made for yourself male images.”

According to the ordinary sense, this may be understood as follows: you took the vessels of glory about which Moses wrote in Numbers—the censers, bowls, the golden lampstand, the ark gilded within and without (Num. VIII), and the other things—and melted them down and made male figures, and committed fornication with them.

According to the allegory, however, it will be explained in this way: we have golden and silver vessels—that is, censers, bowls, and things of this kind—in the sacred writings. Therefore, when we twist the meanings of Scripture into another meaning contrary to the truth, we melt down the divine words and transform the things of God into other forms. By doing this we fall into the sin that Jerusalem has now committed.

The vessels of our glory are the Law and the Prophets; over these we rejoice, and in these we are exalted. When we interpret them otherwise than the truth requires, we turn the vessels of our glory, made of rational silver and perceptible gold, which God gave us, into something else; we make for ourselves male images and commit fornication with them.

It follows:

“And you took garments of various colors and covered them.”

A garment of various colors is also this passage from Scripture, by which we are clothed when we “put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, bearing with one another.” If we tear apart these varied garments and beautiful coverings that God has bestowed upon us, and wrap them around false doctrine for the deception of human beings, there is no doubt that we cover idols with garments of various colors.

You will understand what is said if we describe the matter itself more clearly. Consider for me some Marcionite, or a disciple of Valentinus, or certainly a defender of any heresy, and observe how he clothes his idols—that is, the inventions he himself has composed—with gentleness and chastity, so that an eloquent discourse adorned by the goodness of his life may more easily insinuate itself into the ears of his hearers. When he has done this, understand that he has assumed a garment of varied morals and excellent conduct and has placed it upon the idols he himself constructed.

And, according to my own judgment, a heretic of good conduct is far more harmful and has greater authority in his teaching than one who soils his teaching by his conduct. For someone of utterly bad conduct does not easily entice people toward a false doctrine, nor can he deceive the simplicity of his hearers by the shadow of holiness. But one who is perverse in speech and opposed to saving discipline, while having composed and adorned morals, does nothing other than take the varied garments of good practice and quiet conduct and place them around his idols, so that he may deceive his hearers more effectively.

Therefore let us carefully beware of heretics who have excellent conduct, whose life perhaps has been fashioned not by God but by the devil. For just as bird-catchers set out certain enticing morsels of food so that they may more easily capture birds through the pleasure of the appetite, so—if I may speak more boldly—there is a certain chastity of the devil, that is, a snare for the human soul, so that through this kind of chastity, gentleness, and justice he may more easily seize and entangle it with false words.

The devil fights with diverse ambushes to destroy the wretched human being. He attributes a good life to evil people in order to deceive those who see them, and he impresses a bad conscience upon good people. He often lays snares even for me, who preach in the Church, so that through my conduct he may bring shame upon the whole Church. Therefore those who stand in the midst are attacked more fiercely by the enemy, so that through the fall of one person—which cannot be concealed—scandal may be caused to all, and faith may be impeded by the very bad conduct of clerics.

As we have said, the devil brings about everything: both those things that appear good but are not, and those that are evil by their nature; everything he contrives against the human soul. Therefore the person who takes care of his life is neither captured by the gentleness of heretics so as to consent to their doctrine, nor scandalized by my sins, since I appear to preach in the Church. Rather, considering the doctrine itself and examining the faith of the Church, he will turn away from me but respect the teaching, in accordance with the Lord’s command, who says:

“The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore whatever they tell you, hear and do; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matt. XXIII).

This saying concerns me: I teach good things, but act contrary to what I teach, and sit upon Moses’ seat like a scribe and Pharisee. The command is given to you, O people: if you find no accusation against my teaching—no extremely bad doctrine or beliefs alien to the Church—but see my blameworthy life and sins, do not order your life according to the life of the one who speaks; instead, do the things that I say.

Let us imitate no one. And if we wish to imitate someone, Christ Jesus has been set before us for imitation. The deeds of the apostles have been recorded, and from the sacred volumes we recognize the achievements of the prophets. That exemplar is firm; that model is solid. Whoever wishes to follow it proceeds securely. But if we seek out blameworthy persons to imitate, so that we say, “He teaches, yet he himself does the opposite of what he teaches,” we act contrary to the Lord’s command, who ordered that the doctrines of teachers be considered more than their lives.

These things we have said concerning what is written:

“You took your variegated garment and covered with it”—that is, the vessels of glory that you transformed into idols.

It follows:

949 “And you placed my oil and my incense before their faces” (Apoc. VIII).

Through the teaching of Scripture we have learned that the prayer of the saints is incense. For it says: “The incense is the prayers of the saints.” Therefore, if we have been instructed to pray, and ought to offer prayer to God—that is, to the God of the Law and the Prophets, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, and the Father of Jesus Christ—but instead offer to idols the things that we ourselves have fabricated, even to the point of setting God’s incense before idols, we do what is said here:

“You placed my oil and my incense before their faces.”

Let this be understood concerning incense. What shall we say about the oil? Oil is that with which the holy person is anointed: the oil of Christ, the oil of holy doctrine. Therefore, when someone receives this oil with which the holy person is anointed—that is, Holy Scripture, which teaches how one ought to be baptized, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”—and, changing a few things, anoints someone and in a certain sense says, “You are no longer a catechumen; you have obtained the washing of the second birth,” such a person takes God’s oil and incense and places them before the faces of idols.

“And my bread, which I gave you, I fed you with fine flour, honey, and oil.”

Behold our breads: the purest fine flour in the Scriptures, and the honey of the bees, the Prophets. God gave us all these things and fed us with the breads of the Prophets, with the fine flour of the Law, and with the honey of the Gospel. Having been fed by these, we place the very same things before idols.

For when, wishing to obtain a defense from false doctrines, we say, “It is written in the prophet,” “Moses testifies,” or “the Apostle speaks,” what else are we doing than taking the breads of truth and setting them before images that we ourselves have fashioned? Marcion made an idol and set before it the breads of Scripture. Valentinus, Basilides, and the other heretics did likewise.

“And you placed them before their faces as a pleasing fragrance.”

By nature these things that God has bestowed upon us are of the sweetest fragrance. Whoever either acts or understands contrary to the authority of the Scriptures places this most pleasing fragrance before idols.

“And it came to pass,” says Adonai the Lord, “that you took your sons and your daughters, whom you had borne, and sacrificed them for destruction.”

When sinful Jerusalem has borne sons and daughters, the end of those who are born is slaughter. For salvation is not the end of the worst people. Therefore it is written: “You sacrificed them for destruction.”

“Was your fornication a small thing? You killed my children and gave them over.” He says specifically, “You took your sons,” and significantly adds, “You killed my children.” Whoever is born within the doctrines of heretics and there receives the beginnings of his faith—these are the children of the harlot and sinful Jerusalem. But one who was born in the Church and was later deceived by heretical falsehood, although he is a son of God, has been seized by sinful Jerusalem and set up as a victim for her idols.

“This is beyond all your fornication and your abominations.” To take the children of the Church and sacrifice them to idols is beyond all your sins.

“And you did not remember the days of your infancy, when you were naked and acting shamefully.”

He had already spoken of the nakedness and shamefulness of Jerusalem. Therefore, in her iniquity, she ought to have remembered how I spread my wings over you, took you from your blood, and washed you. But you forgot all these things—things appropriate to one who was naked, acting shamefully, and immersed in her blood.

“And it came to pass after all your wickedness: Woe, woe to you, says Adonai the Lord. And you built yourself a house of prostitution and made yourself a place of display in every street.”

If you consider the soul exposed to its lovers, you will see how it makes a house of prostitution and receives all those lovers whom we have mentioned. Understand what we are saying from what follows—that is, who the lovers of Jerusalem are.

The human soul is exceedingly beautiful and possesses wondrous loveliness. For when its Maker first fashioned it, he said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I). What is more beautiful than this beauty and likeness?

Certain adulterous and filthy lovers, enticed by its beauty, desire to corrupt it and commit fornication upon it. For this reason the wise man Paul says: “But I fear lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve in his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted” (II Cor. XI). Our minds are corrupted in bodily fornication; but in spiritual adulteries the mind is corrupted and the soul itself is wounded.

“And you polluted your beauty.”

Even if someone is not established in the greatest sins, nevertheless, since the beauty of the soul is immense, it is defiled even by the company of lesser sins. Consider the virtues implanted in the soul by God; see its beauty, its inventiveness, arrangement, expression, memory, and articulation; consider what kind of intelligence it possesses, how it first understands and then judges what it has understood, so that it is stirred toward perceptions and brings its perceptions to the mind; consider what impulses and thoughts it has concerning God.

Possessing these things, it is of great beauty; but it is corrupted by the sects of heretics and by an alien religious discipline.

“And your legs passed through every passage, and you multiplied your fornication.”

There is a fornication different from fornication. Just as in bodily fornication someone may not be greatly promiscuous and yet be polluted by fornication, while another multiplies his fornication, so in that fornication which stains the soul and its mind, one person is overwhelmed by the multitude of his fornications, while another is not so deeply seduced by fornication. Therefore, by whatever measure we have measured, it shall be measured back to us.

“And you committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors.”

The sons of Egypt are opposing powers. Nor is it surprising if our neighbors are called Egyptians. The neighbors of Egypt and Jerusalem are situated in their own city; they are those who are “of great flesh.” This does not mean that these Egyptians possess enormous flesh—for it appears that their private parts are indicated by an altered expression, namely, “great flesh”—but because carnal interpretations make us people of great flesh. By contrast, there is a certain deficient flesh, concerning which it is said: “As in a desert and trackless and waterless land, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary.”

Thus Jerusalem commits fornication with the sons of Egypt, her neighbors, those of great flesh. “And you committed fornication in many ways,” he says, “to provoke me.” You committed many forms of fornication in order to incite me.

“But if I stretch out my hand against you, I shall take away your ordinances and deliver you into the souls of those who hate you, the sons of foreigners.”

You see that she is delivered into the souls of foreigners because she is unworthy of the use of the Law and the words of God.

“Those who turned you away from your way: you acted impiously and committed fornication with the sons of Assyria.”

First with the sons of Egypt, then with the sons of Assyria. These are forms of sin. For when the Assyrians took the children of Israel captive, the event reported by Scripture is indeed sacred; yet it was written because of our frequent captivity, which is perpetrated by spiritual Assyrians. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. VI).

“And even then you were not satisfied: you committed fornication, and you shall not be satisfied.”

When someone is not filled while sinning, but continually joins new sins to earlier sins, binding them together “like a long rope” and “like the strap of a heifer’s yoke,” never turning toward better things and never repenting of his evils, it is said to him: “And you shall not be satisfied.”

“And you multiplied your covenants with the land of Chanaan.”

When God makes covenants with us and we consent to him, we are blessed. But when we commit fornication with spiritual forces of wickedness (Eph. VI), we turn God’s covenants toward the land of Chanaan and establish a pact—or, according to another reading, a deed—with it.

Understand this also concerning the Chaldeans and the other nations, whenever we are convicted of any particular sin: “And covenants with the Chaldeans, and even then you were not satisfied.”

After the catalog of sins, he speaks to sinful Jerusalem:

“What shall I establish in you,” says Adonai the Lord, “when you do all these works of a shameless harlot?”

Let us rise somewhat in our discourse, since it is not always useful to speak about fornication; and far be it from us that there should be anyone in the Church who needs discourses warning him away from fornication. For if someone needs to hear, “You shall not commit fornication” (Exod. XX), rather than, “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III), he is like those of whom the Apostle says: “The Law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and the disobedient, the ungodly and sinners.”

Just as the Law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous and disobedient, so the teaching that warns one to withdraw from fornication is not laid down for the chaste, but for the unrighteous, fornicators, and disobedient. Therefore we do not need to learn how to withdraw from fornication; rather, we should strive toward more perfect things, advancing beyond the beginnings of the elements of Christ (Rom. XIII).

“For although by this time you ought to be teachers,” he says, “you again need someone to teach you what are the elements of the beginning of the words of God; and you have become those who need milk, not solid food” (Heb. V). Every discourse that commands, “You shall not commit fornication, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal,” is not solid food but is offered like milk to infants.

The food of athletes comes from the Almighty God: to perceive his mysteries, which are hidden and signified secretly in the Scriptures. See how Paul speaks to the Corinthians: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able—and even now you are not able” (I Cor. III). And because they still needed milk and were learning what little children ordinarily learn—“It is good for a man not to touch a woman, but because of fornication …” (I Cor. VII)—and the rest, they were again instructed not to eat sacrificial offerings.

All this teaching is milk for little ones and for those who are still infants in Christ. But how solid food is provided for the Ephesians is shown by the fact that fornication is not heard of in Ephesus, nor idolatry, nor the eating of sacrificial offerings. From these things we learn what solid food is: rational and guileless milk is the moral passage, while mystical understanding is solid food.

It is therefore blessed if we hasten toward these things, passing beyond the less perfect beginnings. And that a moral passage is milk, the Apostle teaches when, after having already said certain things about milk, he adds: “Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works” (Hebr. VI). All such people are still fed with milk; the perfect person, however, needs other disciplines.

Let these things have been said in passing, because I had risen in my discourse, lest, immediately after one discussion of fornication, I should fall into another fornication, which I shall now explain.

For it is said to Jerusalem:

“And you committed fornication threefold in your daughters.”

What does it mean that Jerusalem committed fornication threefold in her daughters? We need God’s help, so that he himself may explain the obscurity of this passage to us. Just as Moses heard God and then brought before the people the things he had heard from God, so we need the Holy Spirit speaking the mysteries within us, so that through our prayers we may be able to hear Scripture and then make known to the peoples what we have heard.

What, then, is, “You committed fornication threefold in your daughters”? If you understand fornication of the flesh, of the soul, and of the spirit, and see someone fornicating in all these realms, you will see Jerusalem fornicating threefold. But whoever is chaste in all three ways deserves to hear from the Apostle:

“May the God of peace sanctify us completely, so that our spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Tim., final chapter),

to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY EIGHT

On what is written: “In what shall I establish your heart, says the Lord God, when you do all these works of a shameless harlot?” up to: “You gave wages to all your lovers.”

953 We have explained today what was read first. Let us begin from what is written:

“In what shall I establish your heart, says Adonai the Lord, when you do all these works of a shameless harlot? And you committed fornication threefold in your daughters.”

Up to this point we have already spoken. It follows:

“When you built your brothel at the head of every road, and made your platform in every street, and did not become like a harlot gathering wages. The woman who commits adultery, like you, receives wages from her husband; but you gave wages. She gave wages to all her lovers, and you gave wages to all your lovers, and you honored them so that they might come to you from all around, on account of your fornication.”

One human being can establish another human being: an evil person in evil, a good person in good. For bad conversations corrupt good morals. There is no doubt that the speech of the person speaking urges the hearer toward worse things, when a heretic, by speaking, establishes his hearer in heretical perversity.

And to come to better things: if the speaker can be beneficial, and his life agrees with his speech, he establishes his hearer in good things. We who occupy the lowest place, if we hear a word that commands chastity, try to establish our hearers in it. If we ourselves speak about modesty, we establish our hearers in modesty. If we preach about justice, we impel them toward justice. If about faith, we instill faith, so that we may worthily obey the divine majesty in the Lord.

Therefore, if we human beings, although evil, usually establish the heart of the hearer either in good things, if we are good, or in evil things, if we act badly, do you suppose that God does not have the power to establish someone in better things? Or, if he abandons that person, to become for him an occasion for being established in the worst things?

The wretched Jerusalem has certainly sinned greatly according to the present discourse. God very often wished, through his prophets, to establish her in better things; but because she did not wish to hear his counsels or receive God’s commands, God hesitates and says that he does not know what to do:

“In what shall I establish your heart,” says Adonai the Lord? “What shall I do? In what shall I establish it?”

You are bound by many chains of sins; your offenses prevent your life from being established by my words. I myself often wished to establish you, speaking to you through my holy ones, but you did not listen. Now I do not know what to do, and I say to you:

“In what shall I establish your heart,” says Adonai the Lord, “when you do all these works of a shameless and brazen harlot?”

We have often said that opposing powers love the beauties of the human soul, and when the human soul receives the seeds of its lovers, it commits fornication with them in a certain sense. But because in ordinary life also there are certain harlots who commit fornication while wishing to conceal their shame, and others who not only do not hide their sins out of shame but prostitute themselves with complete shamelessness, he therefore used the example of a shameless harlot for this sinful Jerusalem and said that in her fornication she had become like a brazen prostitute.

We often commit such things. Those who have not entirely withdrawn from religion, but are overcome by sin and wish to hide their sins, do things like a harlot who is ashamed. But those who turn away from religion completely, to the point that they do not care about the bishop, presbyters, deacons, or brethren, and sin with complete shamelessness, become like a prostitute displaying herself with confidence.

Therefore, in the present passage God complains about sinful Jerusalem because she performs the works of an immodest prostitute, and says to her:

“And you committed fornication threefold in your daughters.”

We explained this when the words were spoken to us:

“You built your brothel at the head of every road and made your platform in every street.”

But now we also wish to interpret what it means to build a brothel—not simply on every road, but at the head of every road—so that it may not appear sufficient merely to have built a brothel at the head of every road, but that she additionally placed her platform in every street.

Thus Jerusalem committed two general sins: when she built her brothel at the head of every road, and when the harlot made a platform and set it in every street.

What, then, are these roads?

“Stand in the roads and ask about the eternal paths of the Lord, and see which is the good way, and walk in it.”

There are many eternal roads, if you retain the interpretation that I have often offered. You know that Moses is also a road, and each of the prophets is a road. And just as there are many pearls, which the person coming to the one precious pearl must possess, so the person coming to him who says, “I am the way,” must enter the many roads of Moses and of all the prophets.

But someone may say to me: “What relevance does what you have said have to the subject?” I shall answer him as follows: Jerusalem built her brothel on every road. If you consider all the heretics alien to the truth, building a house from the words that are read in Moses, from those they found in Isaiah and Jeremiah and the remaining prophets, you understand that the new doctrines are the fornication of Jerusalem, who builds her brothel on every road, but at the head of every road.

For if someone has been anticipated beyond the beginning of Moses, the opening of the prophets, and has reached their depth and the knowledge of all things, this harlot who builds a brothel at the head of every road can do nothing to him. She seeks the one who first enters the Church, who receives the elementary principles of faith, who is inexperienced in the mysteries—the one established at the beginning of faith. She wishes to lead him into her brothel, building a house for the prostitute.

And because fornication is frequently mentioned in the Scriptures, I wish to explain the reason for this discourse. Ecclesiastical teachers who are in the Church purify both their own morals and those of their people, and through this diligence build the house of God, the Church; their work is the building of God.

Heretics build a brothel on every road: for example, a teacher from the workshop of Valentinus, a teacher from the assembly of Basilides, a teacher from the tabernacle of Marcion, and teachers of the other heretics build a house for the harlot. For the assembly of all the wicked is a brothel.

But what does Scripture say?

“My son, do not attend to an evil woman; for honey drips from the lips of a harlot” (Prov. V).

From where does honey drip for her? Honey indeed drips from the lips of the harlot. She entered Moses, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, and gathered honey for herself from their Scriptures.

Go to the heretics when they speak: “This is what Moses says; this is what Isaiah says; this is what Jeremiah says.” And you will see how it is not honey that flows from their lips, but the very few words plucked from the Scriptures that drip from them.

And therefore, “Honey drips from the lips of a harlot” (Prov. V). Thus she builds a brothel at the head of every road.

Granted that the brothel has been understood; let us interpret also the platform that the harlot Jerusalem placed in all the streets. It is written elsewhere how the harlot openly calls passersby in the streets. For sin eagerly strives to draw us to itself in various ways, whether through heresy or through pagan conduct. Through heresy, when it builds a brothel at the head of every road; through pagan conduct, when it places a platform in all the streets.

“For broad and open is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. VII). Therefore, when the things she says and by which she tries to instruct her hearers are supported by Scripture, she builds a brothel at the head of every road. But when the moral passage has been dissolved, and by teaching luxury she makes the hearer wanton, what else has she done than place a platform in every street?

“She did not become like a harlot gathering wages.”

Let us examine the harlot who gathers wages, and another who does not gather them. For the present passage concerns a harlot who does not gather wages. When I see that she is a harlot who does not gather wages, and read that it is said of her that she became like a harlot who does not gather wages, I shall say that gathering wages means becoming rich through sinning, and acquiring glory in worldly matters through sinning, and prospering in the world through sinning.

When, as I said, these things arise through sin, the soul commits fornication and gathers the wages of its fornication—glory, riches, and the other things that it has sought for the destruction of its soul. But when it commits fornication and does not prosper in worldly affairs, but because it has sinned even lives unhappily in the world, it is a harlot who does not gather wages and does the opposite: it gives wages freely to fornicators.

“And you gave wages to all your lovers.”

Sometimes the soul makes its lovers rich, and they rejoice that they have received wages from it.

But the hearer says to me: “Explain more clearly how the soul commits fornication, giving wages from the possessions of its husband.”

For both here and frequently elsewhere the divine discourse says that the harlot Jerusalem took what belonged to her husband and gave it to her lovers. What is this that her husband bestowed upon her, which, after she became an adulteress, she gives entirely to her lovers?

The husband of the soul is the Word of God, the true lover and bridegroom, who gave it chastity, gave it justice, and gave it the other good things. Therefore, when the soul wishes to follow opposing powers—that is, to put it more plainly, when someone who has lived chastely for ten years finally commits fornication—it takes the good things of its husband, which it had acquired through long labor, and gives them to its lovers.

Those bloodthirsty lovers seize for themselves the virtues of the wretched soul, strut boastfully upon its riches, and say:

“I have taken away from her ten years of chastity; I have wrested from her five years of justice; I have claimed her powers for myself. God has forgotten all her good deeds, whatever she once did, because she has been caught in sin. And you have forgotten her, because she confessed to us, her friends, the secrets she had heard, and handed over all her good things to us, her lovers.”

Learning these things, let us guard our hearts with all vigilance and beware lest at any time the things that belong to the husband be handed over to his lovers. Rather, let us invite the bridegroom, the Word and the Truth, to make for us golden ornaments marked with varied designs through varied commandments, so that, having been adorned, we may be prepared for our husband Jesus Christ,

to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY NINE

On Ezekiel, concerning what is said: “Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite,” up to: “And she did not stretch out her hand to the needy and poor” (Chap. XVI).

[Col. 0753B] 959 Whoever reads at the beginning of the prophecy about Jerusalem how she is rebuked as having her root and origin from the land of Canaan, with an Amorite father and a Hittite mother—if he also reads these passages, which we are now attempting to interpret—will think that the same things are being repeated and that one discourse is being proclaimed twice. But whoever is a careful reader, concerned with the significance of divine Scripture, and compares what came before with what is present, setting word beside word, will see that the difference is not accidental. For there it says, “Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan,” whereas this is not said here; and there it says, “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite,” whereas this is not signified here. Again, there the first statement is, “Your father was an Amorite,” and the second, “Your mother a Hittite”; here, however, it says, “Your mother was a Hittite, and your father an Amorite.” There the discourse is addressed as though to one person; here, as though to several. For it does not say, as it did above, “your mother,” but “your mother,” addressed to “you” in the plural.

When, therefore, sin spreads, wickedness advances farther, and sinners tear apart among themselves the sins that belong to them, then there is not merely one sinner, but many within one; just as at the beginning, when sinning had begun, there were not yet such multitudes as there are now. Hence it seems useful to me, withdrawing for a little from the present discourse, to consider the nature of sins and virtues.

Where sins are, there is multitude; there are schisms, heresies, and dissensions. But where virtue is, there is singleness and unity, in accordance with the fact that the heart and soul of all believers were one. To put it more plainly, the beginning of all evils is multiplicity; the beginning of good things is being narrowed together and being reduced from crowds to singleness—namely, that all of us, if we are to be saved, may be brought into unity, so that we may be made perfect in the same understanding and the same judgment, and may be one body and one spirit.

But if we are such that unity does not encompass us, and it can be said of us, “I indeed belong to Paul, but I to Apollo, and I to Cephas” (1 Cor. I), and we are still divided and torn apart by wickedness, we shall not be where those are who are brought into unity. For just as the Father and the Son are one, so those who have one spirit are constrained into unity. The Savior says, “I and the Father are one.” And: “Holy Father, I ask that, just as I and you are one, so they also may be one in you” [or: “in us”] (John XVII). And it is read in the Apostle: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, and to the measure of the fullness of maturity, into the unity of Christ” (Eph. IV). And again: “Until we all reach the unity of the body and spirit of Christ.”

This signifies that virtue makes one out of many, and that we must become one through it and flee multiplicity. These things have been said because in the previous reading it was written: “Your father, and your mother, and the root of your origin”; but in the present passage: “Your mother and your father.” There we did not learn—although the discourse concerned an Amorite father and a Hittite mother—that Jerusalem had sisters. Here, however, he adds: “Your mother was a Hittite, your father an Amorite; and your elder sister was Samaria, she and her daughters, who dwells on your left, and your younger sister, who dwells on your right, was Sodom.”

Just as virtue makes me a son of Abraham if I live according to it—for whoever does the works of Abraham is Abraham’s son—so vices make me a son of the devil. “Everyone who commits sin is born of the devil” (John III). Virtue also makes me have Christ as my brother, so that when I have become good and well-conducted, he may say to his Father, “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing to you” (Ps. XXII). And he speaks to the woman who could proclaim his words: “Go and tell my brothers.”

But just as virtue makes the Lord Jesus my brother, so wickedness acquires many brothers for me—and these are sinners—and it generates these as my brothers when it has grown. For when sinful Jerusalem was at her beginning, she did not yet have Samaria as a sister, nor was Sodom yet her kinswoman. But when she advanced in crime, as the previous discourse showed, she became the middle one of two sisters: Samaria the elder and Sodom the younger.

What are these two sisters of sinful Jerusalem? Schism and separation of the people made Samaria. For when the ten tribes withdrew, saying, “We have no part in David, nor any inheritance in the son of Jesse” (1 Kings XII), two golden calves were then set up by Jeroboam, and Samaria became a division. This division grew still more after the captivity of the ten tribes, when [Note: [Col. 0753D] The twenty-sixth volume on John contains the same material, expressed in Latin as follows: The Hebrews say that *Somer* means “keeper,” and therefore maintain that the Samaritans were first so called because they had been sent by the king of the Assyrians to guard the land of Israel after the captivity of Israel, which was distinct from Judah, and so forth. Jerome himself, both elsewhere and especially from Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, says: “Sennacherib, king of the Chaldeans, sent Assyrians who lived nearby to guard the region of Judea; having become imitators of the law of Judea, they were called Samaritans.” Yet it is established that they were sent not to guard but to repopulate Judea, and not merely colonies of Assyrians but also of various nations. Therefore Origen, and most who subsequently followed him, wrongly derive the etymology of the name “Samaritans” from “guarding.” The passage in 1 Kings XVI:24 also refutes them: “And Omri, king of Israel, bought the mountain of Samaria from Somer for two talents of silver, and built upon it, and called the city which he had built by the name of Somer, the lord of the mountain: Samaria.”]

[Col. 0755A] guards were sent by the Assyrians to the land of Israel, who are called Samaritans. For *Somer* is interpreted in the language of the Hebrews as “keeper.” Therefore, as I had begun to say, Samaria is not yet my sister so long as I remain far from sins; but when I sin, two sisters grow for me: Samaria the elder and Sodom the younger.

Let us consider what figure each of them represents. Whoever makes promises concerning the divine words but does not possess within himself the truth of the preaching in the manner he promises—in Scripture such people are figuratively called “Samaria.” “Woe,” he says, “to those who despise Zion and trust in Mount Samaria” (Amos VI): “You have harvested the dominions of the nations.” It is as though he had said: Woe to those who despise the Church and trust in the arrogance and swollen words of heretics. For this is to despise Zion and trust in Mount Samaria.

If, then, we who are of the Church also sin, heretics are not strangers to us in the perversity of their doctrines. Whoever sins believes wrongly. If we have an evil manner of life, Sodom is our sister. For Sodom represents the Gentiles. Thus we are brothers of heretics and Gentiles when we sin, because Samaria is understood as heresy and Sodom as paganism.

Samaria dwells on the left of sinful Jerusalem, and Sodom on her right. For the sin committed in deed is more highly honored by her, and therefore Sodom is on her right. Yet Samaria is not far away either, since she dwells on her left; and Jerusalem is rebuked because she walked with Samaria’s daughters and sisters in all their iniquities, and walked so far in them that the comparison of her sins made their iniquities appear as righteousness.

Therefore we ought to recognize the iniquities of the Sodomites, so that, having been instructed, I may guard myself against them and not be caught through ignorance of what the iniquities of the Sodomites are. Nevertheless, these are “the iniquities of Sodom your sister.” What iniquity? Pride. “In the fullness of bread and in abundance she herself and her daughters overflowed, and they did not look upon the hand of the poor and needy.”

No one who uses the Scriptures doubts that sins are unequal. Some are said to be great, others lesser. But when they are unequal—that is, small or very great—someone may inquire which among all sins is the greater. It is readily accepted that the greatest of all sins is fornication, or impurity, or whatever contamination of lust. These things are indeed abominable and polluted, but not like the sin which Scripture now condemns as greater than all and from which we must guard ourselves.

What, then, is the sin greater than all sins? Surely the sin on account of which the devil also fell. What is this sin into which such loftiness fell, so that, being lifted up, he fell into the judgment of the devil? The Apostle says: “Inflation, pride, and arrogance are the devil’s sin” (2 Tim. III); and because of these offenses he migrated from heaven to earth.

Therefore, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” And why should earth and ashes be proud, so that a human being is lifted up by arrogance, forgetting what he will be, how fragile a vessel contains him, in what filth he is immersed, and what kinds of refuse he continually expels from his flesh? What does Scripture say? “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Eccl. X); and “in his life he cast out his entrails”? Pride is greater than all sins, and it is the devil’s chief sin.

Whenever Scripture describes the devil’s sins, you will find them flowing from the fountain of pride. For he says: “By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of the nations; and I will feed upon their strength. I will shake the inhabited cities and grasp the whole world like a nest, and like abandoned eggs I will take them away” (Isa. X). Observe his words: how proud they are, how arrogant, and how they count everything as nothing. Such are all who are puffed up with boastfulness and pride.

The material of pride is wealth, rank, and worldly glory. Frequently the cause of pride for one who does not know how to possess ecclesiastical dignity is the priestly order and the Levitical rank. How many priests, having been appointed, have forgotten humility—and for what reason they were ordained, as though to cease being humble! Rather, they ought to have followed humility because they had attained dignity, as Scripture says: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself.” And: “He makes you beloved of the Synagogue; submit your head more nobly. They appointed you a leader; do not exalt yourself, do not become one of them, as though you were one of them.” One must be humble, one must be downcast, one must flee pride, the head of all evils.

Consider the Gospel, in which the pride and boastfulness of the Pharisee are struck as though by condemnation. The Pharisee stood and prayed such things within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or like this tax collector. I fast twice a week” (Luke XVI). But the tax collector, standing at a distance humbly and gently, did not dare even to raise his eyes, and said: “Be merciful, God, to me a sinner.” And the tax collector went down to his house justified.

He was not simply justified, but justified in comparison with the Pharisee. For every word, order, and connection of Scripture must be observed with the greatest care. It is one thing to be justified, another to be justified in comparison with someone else. It is similar to saying that the tax collector was justified by the Pharisee: Sodom and Samaria were justified in comparison with sinful Jerusalem.

And we must know this, because each of us will be justified by one person and condemned by another on the day of judgment. [Col. 0756D] Even when we have been justified in comparison with someone else, that righteousness is counted not so much to our praise as to our indictment. For example, if I am found to have Sodomite sins, and another is brought forward who has committed crimes twice as great, I am indeed justified—but I am justified not as righteous, but because, in comparison with the one who committed more, I am judged righteous, although I am far from righteousness.

Woe to the person who is justified by many sinners; conversely, greatly blessed is the one who is shown to be righteous in comparison with the righteous. We find it included among the praises of Scripture that the good are better: for example, “No one did what was right before the Lord as he did,” and “no one celebrated Passover as Josiah did.” This shows that comparisons are made among the righteous, and that the one who deserves to be justified in this way is truly righteous.

Would that I, when compared with the wise, might be found wise, and might be judged righteous in comparison with the righteous! I do not wish to be justified by the wicked, because such righteousness is criminal.

I have said these things in advance because in the passage that has been read it says: “You justified your sisters in all your iniquities which you committed” (2 Chron. XXV). Samaria and Sodom were justified by Jerusalem’s iniquities: “In all your iniquities which you committed beyond them.” Therefore let us attend more carefully, so that we may recognize that on the day of judgment all of us will be justified by those worse than we are, and that others in turn will be justified by us.

There is one alone who is justified by everyone, and he justifies no one. For example, Sodom is justified by Jerusalem because Jerusalem committed more heinous crimes than Sodom; and perhaps Jerusalem is justified by some other city worse than herself. Thus someone will be justified by the Antichrist, when compared with him and found less wicked because of his iniquity and crimes. But the worst demon is—and, as they say, pitiable—the one who is justified by him; perhaps even his father is not justified by him, being found much more criminal than he.

My Lord Jesus Christ, however, is justified according to the dispensation of the flesh which he bore for our salvation—by Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the remaining prophets. For whenever all the righteous, prophets, and blessed people are found, when compared with him, to be the opposite of what is said concerning Sodom and Jerusalem, I glorify our Savior all the more.

What I mean is of this kind, and, with God’s generosity, while you pray, I shall offer an explanation from the Scriptures. Sodom committed sin; Samaria also sinned; Jerusalem was overwhelmed by iniquities. Yet lesser sins are justified by greater ones, according to the example in which Sodom is justified by her sister Jerusalem.

Just as iniquity therefore justifies, so righteousness sometimes condemns. But please wait a little, until you are taught how righteousness is said to condemn. My iniquity is righteousness in comparison with a greater iniquity. Likewise, my righteousness is counted as iniquity in comparison with multiplied righteousness. Therefore it is said to God: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L).

If God wishes to save me, he does not bring his own light into judgment; if he wishes me to be safe, he does not bring forward the light of his Christ. Otherwise he will punish me. Instead, he brings forward the light of lesser ones, comparing me with those who are inferior. The greater and better those whom he sets before me, the more righteous I shall be if they are found by me to be inferior.

The following saying is to be understood in the same way: “One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness—so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. XV, 41). For example, that shining heavenly body shines not in the presence of a brighter star, but of a dimmer one.

Who among us can shine like the moon? Who can flash with the light of the brighter stars, according to what is written in Daniel: “They will shine like a star forever” (Dan. XII)? We necessarily discuss these matters so that we may withdraw far from pride. For the iniquity of the proud is a Sodomite sin.

He adds where the pride of “Sodom your sister” arises and what roots it has: “They overflowed in the fullness of bread and in abundance” (Gen. XIII). If you attend only to the letter, there was great abundance in ancient Sodom. Their land was like the paradise of God and like the land of Egypt. But if you rise from the carnal understanding to the spiritual, so that you may see how the pride of Sodom overflowed in the fullness of bread and abundance, you will gain a lesson useful both for the conduct of life and for correcting other greater matters by greater examples.

Let us first set before us what was read many days ago: a rich man clothed in linen and purple, rejoicing every day in luxury and indulgence, while Lazarus, wasted by the corruption of wounds and the stench of worms, sought as relief for his hunger the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table (Luke XVI).

This example has appropriately come into the present passage, so that it may become clear what the rich man’s iniquity was. He was wealthy and abounded in luxuries. Scripture did not accuse him of possessing riches unjustly; the divine word did not charge him with giving his wealth to prostitutes; nor did it call him a murderer or accuse him of any other crime. But if you consider what is written here and what is said in the Gospel, you will see that his greatest sin among all his sins was also pride: overflowing in the fullness of bread and abundance, he had no compassion for the one who lay before his gates, covered with sores. He was lifted up into such pride, despising poverty, that he took no account either of the punishments of the underworld or of the common laws of humanity—for a human being ought to think humanely and, because of the likeness of his own condition, to show some compassion in the calamities of others.

That rich man, then, is also a Sodomite. For if Sodom’s sins were such that she existed in the fullness of bread and abundance, and if the rich man described in the Gospel was such, there can be no doubt that the rich man was a Sodomite.

Just as Sodom and the daughters of Sodom were proud, so are arrogant souls and the daughters of Sodom—all who do not know the saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII). This was true of her and her daughters.

Next follows another offense of Sodom, which we must discuss so that we may not be found in a similar crime: “She did not take hold of the hand of the poor and needy.” Carefully consider the enumeration of Sodom’s sins. If I myself, according to my strength, do not assist the hand of the poor and needy, I have a Sodomite sin.

Another accusation follows: “And she proudly boasted.” Boastful glory is also a Sodomite crime. There are Egyptian sins, Sodomite sins; there are Babylonian sins, Assyrian sins, Moabite sins, and Ammonite sins. “Who is wise and understands these things, or intelligent and recognizes them?” (Hos. XXIV, 10).

Whenever we read what has been written about the overthrow of Sodom, let us not say, “Miserable Sodomites, whose land no longer produces fruit; miserable and greatly deserving of lamentation, who suffered such mournful and terrible things.” Rather, let us turn this discourse into our own hearts, search our inner parts and thoughts, and then we shall see that those whom we lament are contained within us inwardly, and that the Sodomite, Egyptian, Assyrian, and every other sin which Scripture enumerates while rebuking them are active within us.

Above we promised to say something more profound from Scripture. To Sodom, sinning in the fullness of bread, abundance, luxury, and such things, the Law speaks: “Take heed to yourself, lest, when you have eaten and drunk and are filled, and have built good houses, and your sheep and cattle have multiplied for you, and silver and gold have multiplied for you, you forget the Lord your God.” And in another place: “He ate and drank, was filled and grew fat, and the beloved kicked” (Deut. XXXII).

Solomon says similar things in Proverbs: “Give me what is necessary and sufficient, lest, when I am filled, I become a liar and say, ‘Who sees me?’ Or, being needy, I steal and swear by the name of God.” In short, it must be said that nothing so lifts a person into arrogance as riches, satiety, and the abundance of great resources, along with rank and power.

It is also possible to move to higher matters and see that I frequently nourish pride if I understand the divine word, if I am wiser than others. “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. VIII)—I do not say this, but the Apostle. And therefore I fear that I too may be lifted up.

Gifts are given for what is beneficial. If they are given for what is beneficial, who is the person for whom they are not beneficial? Listen to why they may not be beneficial. A lesser gift is enough to produce inflation and a certain self-satisfaction, when one thinks that one excels among others.

Thus fullness of bread and abundance are often the material of arrogance. Often, too, the crime of pride arises from spiritual gifts, and there is no difference between the two cases. The Apostle Paul, so great a man, needed Satan’s angel to buffet him, lest he be excessively exalted (2 Cor. XII). For by praying and beseeching God he had often obtained for many people what he asked; but when he had also asked for this and had not obtained what he had requested, it was said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.”

Therefore, whoever still lives within the human race and in this present light must fear—not only those things that are considered good in the world, but even those that are truly good, because we cannot bear great things.

As proof of this present statement, I offer the history of David, in which it is recorded that he committed sin in the matter of Uriah. Before Uriah, no offense is found in David; he was a blessed man and blameless in the sight of God. But because, conscious of his spotless life, he said what he ought not to have said: “Hear, O Lord, my righteousness; attend to my supplication; give ear to my prayer, which is not from deceitful lips. Let my judgment come forth from your face; let your eyes see equity. You have tested my heart and visited me by night; you examined me with fire, and in me no iniquity was found” (Ps. XVI)—and he said these things because God’s visitation, on account of his conscience and blessed life, was being granted to him—he was tested and deprived of assistance, so that he might see what human weakness is capable of.

When God’s protection withdrew, that most chaste and admirable man in purity, who had heard, “If the young men are pure, especially from a woman” (1 Sam.), and had received the Eucharist as one who was pure, could not persevere. He was found in the very crime in which he had been applauding himself as though he were continent.

If, then, someone conscious of his purity glorifies himself, failing to remember the saying, “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. IV), he is abandoned, and in his abandonment learns by experience that in the good things of which he was conscious, he was not so much their cause himself as God, who is the fountain of every virtue.

From this it is evident that both fullness of bread and spiritual gifts generate pride in the person who cannot bear them. Therefore let us flee from Sodom and her sins; let us flee from Samaria and the crimes with which wretched Jerusalem is chastised, so that, with God supplying us strength in all things, we may attain humility and righteousness in Christ Jesus, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY TEN

On Ezekiel, concerning what is written: “Therefore you also be ashamed, and bear your disgrace,” up to: “And I will establish my covenant with you” (Chapter XVI).

969 First of all, the point is to do nothing that brings shame, but to do everything of such a kind that one can look upon God with an untroubled face. Since, however, we often sin—as human beings do—we must understand that the second, so to speak, vessel after works of shame is to feel shame, to cast down our eyes in embarrassment for our crimes, and not to go about with an impudent face as though one had committed no sin at all. For it is good to feel shame after works of shame, because the artificer of evil often works even this effect: preventing the sinner from returning to repentance, so that he acts as though he were still persevering in righteousness.

We can see, and learn from daily life, that many people, after their sins, not only do not mourn what they have done, but even [Col. 0761B] defend their own ruin with an impudent face. A great benefit, therefore, is preserved for Jerusalem—provided that she believes the Lord who says: “And you shall feel shame.” Nor should you think that these words were spoken only to Jerusalem and not to each one of us, who are held liable for our offenses.
