Let each person consider himself: what he has done that deserves shame; what disgraceful thing he has said, about which he ought not to have the boldness—as though it were a good saying; what he has thought that appears worthy of embarrassment before him who examines the hidden things of heart and kidneys. And when he has carefully examined his thoughts, deeds, 970 and words, then let him hear the prophet saying: “And you shall feel shame.”

After this the Prophet adds: “And bear your disgrace because you justified your sisters.” Shame is followed by disgrace, and God gives disgrace also to the one [Col. 0761C] who has done things deserving of shame. He says to him: “And bear your disgrace.”

You will be able to understand what is said if you consider what happens daily in cities. For a citizen, dishonor is exile from his homeland; for a member of the municipal council, infamy is being erased from the register of the curia; and for a person of any other status, it is to be left alive but with disgrace—whether to live in public works or on some island of solitude. Imagine, then, a just judge saying to one who has done something deserving of infamy: “You who are liable to punishment, do not accept your exile with grief. You will not deserve mercy if you become angry at your punishment. Rather, understand that you are suffering deservedly what you suffer. And when you have humbled yourself and said that judgment has rightly been passed against you, perhaps you will obtain mercy [Col. 0761D] from him who can restore a person to his former condition after condemnation.”

For just as a great ruler is permitted to free someone from an island, from exile, and from public imprisonment, so much more is the God of the universe permitted to restore to his former honor the one who has been dishonored—provided that, recognizing his offense, he confesses that he has deservedly endured what he suffered. 971

I shall give another example from ecclesiastical custom. It is infamy to be separated from the people of God and from the Church. It is disgrace in the Church to rise from the presbyters’ assembly and to be expelled from the rank of the diaconate. Among those who are expelled, some stir up rebellions, while others accept the judgment passed against them with complete humility.

Therefore, all who are removed and, in the grief [Col. 0762A] of their deposition, gather peoples together to cause a schism and agitate a multitude of wicked persons do not accept their dishonor in the present, but store up for themselves a treasure on the day of wrath. Those, however, who are deposed with complete humility—whether justly or unjustly—leave the judgment to God and patiently endure what has been judged concerning them: these will obtain mercy from God, and often they are even restored by human beings to their former rank and to the glory they had lost.

The teaching, then, is excellent: both what is said, “And you shall feel shame,” and what follows, “And bear your disgrace.” I say this also so that I may introduce a deeper sense concerning the dishonor of the future. For there too there will be disgrace for those who have done a deed deserving [Col. 0762B] disgrace. “Some will rise to everlasting life, and others to reproach and everlasting confusion” (Dan. XII). What else is this but to endure the punishment of infamy?

While it is still permitted us, therefore, we ought patiently to bear our humiliation, so that, having bravely endured sorrow here, we may—in a manner of speaking—move the bowels of God’s mercy in the age to come, and his kindness, so that he may restore us from disgrace and confusion to our former condition. Conversely, it is impossible for someone with a heart of stone, who feels his offense not at all and proudly stands before the face of almighty God, to obtain mercy.

For we see that some good people willingly accept the sentence pronounced against them and, for the sake of their salvation, justify God’s judgment; but evil people [Col. 0762C] blaspheme against God’s providence and say: “I was not deservedly condemned to this infamy; I suffer these things unjustly.” If we justify providence, we dissolve our infamy. But if we do not accept God’s judgments, we multiply our infamy. And just as with infamy, so also with punishments, and with the rest. For these are the things that ordinarily befall those who have been condemned by God for their own offenses.

“And you shall feel shame, and bear your disgrace because you justified your sisters.” We deserve greater disgrace when we do things by which other sinners are justified, so that, in comparison with my offenses, mercy may free those whose crimes were condemned in former times, because I, coming afterward, have committed worse things.

Thus it is said to sinful Jerusalem: [Col. 0762D] “Bear your disgrace because you justified your sisters.” Then, if someone has fulfilled what is written, “Feel shame”; if someone has followed the succeeding sentence of God, “Bear your disgrace because you justified your sisters,” let him also see the grace by which, in exchange for shame, clemency is restored, because he has not despised God’s judgment but has accepted with complete humility what had been judged concerning him.

What, then, is promised? “I shall turn back their turning away, the turning away of Sodom and of her sisters, because you justified your sisters, Sodom and Samaria.” Sodom the younger, and Samaria the elder, as we said earlier. “I shall turn back their turning away”—that is, he turns the turning [Col. 0763A] away of the three, whose turning away he had turned back, toward better things: first that of Sodom, then that of Samaria, and third that of Jerusalem.

But when, he says, I have turned back the turning away of Sodom, Samaria, and Jerusalem, then they will be restored to their former condition: first Sodom, whose earlier turning away he will have turned back; second Samaria, which he will have turned back a second time; third Jerusalem, to whom a third turning away is attributed.

Thus the healings of those who sin occur in the turning away of Sodom and her daughters, and in the turning away of Jerusalem herself; and they are granted more slowly to those who are loved more by God. For Sodom, justified by Jerusalem, first obtains mercy—that is, the Gentiles. Samaria, that is, the [Col. 0763B] heretics, receive healing in the second place. In the third place, as though unworthy of swifter treatment, those who came from Jerusalem are restored to their former condition.

Before us, therefore, the Gentiles—and after them the heretics—will consequently receive clemency, if we are impious, and if sins have also weighed us down. For the nearer we have been to God, and the closer to blessedness, the farther we shall be from it when we sin, and the nearer to terrible and very great punishments. For God’s judgment is just, and “the mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI). The one who is least, however, deserves mercy more quickly.

Sodom is the least. After it, in comparison with Jerusalem, Samaria is the lesser, though not as Sodom is; and therefore he first turns back the turning away of those two, and afterward that of Jerusalem, saying: “I shall also turn back your turning away.” For this is said to Jerusalem at the third degree.

There is one occasion when he turns back my turning away: if I am found to be Jerusalem, and a sinner in the midst of my sisters, [Col. 0763C] when I hear: “So that you may bear your punishment.” Therefore he says in the third place: “I shall turn back your turning away,” and afterward: “So that you may bear your punishment and be dishonored for all that you have done.”

There is a certain measure of sin, which each person will receive according to what he has sinned. If I have fifty sins, I shall have fifty disgraces; if a hundred, my punishment will be doubled for my deeds, and disgrace will be assigned to me according to the greatness of my offenses. Great torment is joined to great sins. God alone, the true Judge, can discern the magnitude of sins, the kinds of disgrace, and the number of sins.

Therefore it is said to Jerusalem: “So that you may bear your punishment and be dishonored for all that you have done by provoking me.” Conversely, observe God making satisfaction, so to speak, by these words, testifying that he himself does not possess anger, but that the sinner [Col. 0763D] provokes God to anger. Hence the Apostle also says: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that God’s goodness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment” (Rom. I).

This statement separates anger from God. Indeed, anger is something other than God, nor is it joined to him as something inherent in him. Hence it is said of sinners: [Col. 0764A] “You sent forth your anger, and it consumed them” (Ps. LXXVII). No one can send forth what is his companion and kindred; rather, what is sent forth is something different from the one who sends it. Thus by sinning we provoke God to send forth anger, which he himself does not possess.

After these things—that is, after the turning away—it is said: “Sodom, your sister and her daughters, shall be restored as they were at the beginning.” I come to images and figures, and I see after how long a time Sodom will be restored to its former state. But if what has been said figuratively is so, what will happen to the one who is truly Sodom?

Immediately after the Flood, in the tenth generation, Sodom suffered the events that are read in Genesis (Gen. XIII). For previously it was like the paradise of God and like the land of Egypt; nevertheless, what happened to Sodom is something that can still be perceived today from the traces of its region [Col. 0764B]. Behold how many cycles of time have already passed; behold, three thousand years have elapsed, and Sodom has not yet been restored—not that Sodom which is presented in sign and riddle, but that which is perceived according to the reality of the matter.

The Hebrews say that Sodom is to be restored to the same condition in which it previously stood, so that it may again be compared with the paradise of God and the land of Egypt.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] A warning worth noting, lest one overlook how often Adamantius repeats the false doctrine derived from the filthy sources of the Hebrews, concerning the eventual ending of the punishments of the condemned. Although he may appear uncertain and wavering in this opinion from what he adds—“If this is so, and whether it is to happen or not; for such matters will be investigated among those who are most learned”—and although he says somewhat more explicitly shortly afterward, “provided that you restore it,” there are nevertheless scattered throughout his writings many other passages of this kind, which Huetius quotes in Origen, testimonies concerning such ἀποκατάστασις (apokatastasis), that is, restoration to the former condition; on account of these he was continually criticized by the Fathers of the Church.]

If this is so, and whether it is to happen or not—for such matters will be investigated among those who are most learned—then, for what is said to occur to be fulfilled, my three thousand years will be completed, and then Sodom, tormented [variant reading: “is tormented”] for three thousand years, will be restored—that is, my soul: Sodom, punished for my sins. A great interval of time has been placed between restoration and ruin.

Even if you are restored [Col. 0764C] to the condition in which you formerly were, observe how many evils you must exhaust, and by how many calamities you must first be overwhelmed. What we have said about Sodom must also be understood about Samaria. For she too has not yet been restored; rather, from the time when the ten tribes were expelled from Judea and Samaria, she endured captivity and received her name, having none of her former inhabitants. She too will be restored as she was at the beginning, when the ten tribes have returned, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The people were led captive into Assyria, even to this day” (IV Kings XVII).

But if what preceded as a sign will be restored only after so long a time, when will you be restored—if indeed you are restored—you Samaritan and heretical soul, which believed in idols, false festivals, and inventions arising from Jeroboam’s heart? When will you be restored, [Col. 0764D] unhappy soul, when the example of you is restored after so many ages?

But if this happens to Sodom and Samaria, which were justified by Jerusalem, what must be said about Jerusalem herself, who justified the crimes [variant reading: “crime”] of those mentioned above? “And you shall be restored as you were at the beginning. You and your daughters shall be restored as you were in the beginning.”

He knows what he says—“As you were in the beginning”—and Isaiah likewise says [Col. 0765A]: “I shall appoint your judges as at first, and your counselors as at the beginning” (Isa. I).

“And if your sister Sodom had not been mentioned in your hearing and in your mouth in the days of your pride, just as now you are a reproach to the daughters of Syria and to all the daughters of foreign peoples who surround you on every side: bear your impieties yourself.”

O most merciful God, making satisfaction concerning restoration and saying: “Bear your impieties and your iniquities”! I do not say “you will be restored” without reason; rather, when you have exhausted your impieties and iniquities, then you will be restored to your former place.

Just as wounds that are on the body often arise in a short time, while remedies for wounds are applied amid great suffering—not according to the length of time in which they were inflicted, but according to the requirements [Col. 0765B] of the cure—for example, a fracture [Note: [Col. 0765D] It was previously incorrectly read as “factura.”] of the hand and a crushing of the foot occur in a moment of time, yet what happened in a brief instant is scarcely healed in about three months and after a long period: so pleasure, which cuts down the sinews of the soul, and luxury, and all sins together, when they have enticed the unhappy soul in a short time and drawn it toward vices, afterward deserve a long period of punishments and tortures.

Therefore the Lord says this: “And I shall do to you as you have done, as you have despised these things by transgressing my covenant; and I shall remember.” First, “As you have done, so I shall do to you”; then, “I shall remember my covenant, which I made with you in the days of your youth.”

For he made a covenant in her days of youth. We explained above how he made a covenant with her. “And I shall establish my covenant with you forever.”

“I kill and I make alive,” he says [Col. 0765C]. When he makes these promises, he inflicts pains, and then restores. “He has struck, and his hands will heal.”

It is said in Micah: “I shall bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause” (Mic. VII). How is my cause justified? When I have borne the wrath of the Lord, whose riches of goodness, patience, and forbearance I despised, and according to my hardness and impenitent heart stored up wrath for myself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment.

“And you shall be dishonored because you received your elder sisters with their daughters, and I shall give them to you for your edification.” Above he called one sister Sodom and the other Samaria. Now he repeats this and says, “your elder sisters with their daughters,” although only Samaria is elder and Sodom younger. But because their [Col. 0765D] daughters are counted together with them, he says that they all belong to one category. And as many as are Sodom’s daughters, so many are Samaria’s.

“And I shall give them to you for your edification, and not according to your covenant; and I shall establish my covenant with you.”

Consider the end of the promise, and you will recognize that I am the Lord, so that you may remember and feel shame—that is, when you have received your sins and remembered them, then you will feel shame. “And you shall no longer have the freedom to open your mouth.”

When I have received my sins and have been restored, when a covenant has been made with me, then I understand my evils [Col. 0766A] more fully, feel shame, and, conscious of them, willingly punish myself. But observe what happens to me: “So that you may no longer have the freedom to open your mouth because of disgrace,” and when this occurs, “when he is reconciled to you.”

Even then, when he is reconciled to me, who have sinned greatly, I cannot open my mouth. Nor, when he forgives my crimes, am I free from disgrace; rather, conscious of my crimes, I am continually tormented by the fire of my conscience.

Therefore, because eternal disgrace and shame have been reserved for us if we sin, let us pray to God with our whole heart that he grant us to contend for the truth, with the exertion of both soul and body, to the very end; so that, even if a period should arise that tests our faith—for just as gold is tested in a furnace, so our faith is examined in danger and persecutions—even if persecution [Col. 0766B] should break out, it may find us prepared; so that our house may not collapse in winter, and our building, constructed as though upon sand, may not be scattered by storms.

Thus, when the winds of the devil blow—that is, the evil spirits—our works may remain, as they have remained to this day, provided that they have not secretly been undermined; and, girded for action, we may make manifest our love for God in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## ELEVENTH HOMILY

Concerning what was said: “Son of man, propose a riddle and speak a parable to the house of Israel, and say: An eagle with great wings,” and so forth (Chapter XVII).

977 Exercise of the body, and strength in general, is acquired by those who train, and it makes each limb and the senses of the limbs more vigorous for enduring something or for perceiving it. For example, the sharpness of the eyes, if exercised in sight, becomes keener for seeing; the ears, if they hear more frequently, can better distinguish discordant sounds. The same may be observed in the other limbs, though we have shown it in only a few cases.

But what does it profit me for blessedness and eternal life if the body is strengthened by exercise? What advantage is it to me even if I become extremely strong in body, even if I move about vigorous in all my limbs? On the other hand, if I have the senses of my soul trained to perceive, if I spend days and nights learning, this benefits me not only in the present life, but will also accompany me when I depart from the body. Therefore God has spoken in parables and enigmas, so that our mind might extend itself—or rather, gathering together the things said into one, might contemplate their subtleties—and, withdrawing from bodily vices, might direct the course of its life according to the truth when it understands it.

We said this in the preface because the word of God came to Ezekiel, saying: “Son of man, tell a tale and speak a parable to the house of Israel.” In place of “tell a tale,” as the translators of the Septuagint rendered it, another translator rendered it, “propose a problem”; another, “present a problem”; another, “signify an enigma.”

[Note: In the collection of the Hexapla this passage is missing. Nevertheless, from the annotations on the Septuagint in the Roman edition it can be gathered that Aquila read αἴνιγμα (*aínigma*, “enigma”), while Symmachus and Theodotion read πρόβλημα (*próblēma*, “problem”).]

Thus what has been read is both a problem, an enigma, and a parable. Whenever we need illumination for the knowledge of God, now above all and necessarily we need it, so that it may be not so much I as the grace of God in me—through your prayers—that explains the solution of the problem, the enigma, or the parable.

What, then, is the parable of the eagle which the Holy Spirit now sets before us? It is written not merely as an eagle, but, in comparison with other eagles, as a great eagle, with immense wings, long in its extension, and full of claws—or, as one translator rendered it, full of feathers. It is greater than the other eagles not only in the respects we have mentioned, but is especially distinguished by the fact that it has a way of entering Lebanon. For, entering there, it plucked from the cedar tree that stood in Lebanon its tender shoots and all its highest branches, brought them into the land of Canaan, into a city described as belonging to merchants, or as merchantly, or as a city of those who transfer things, or certainly—as the Septuagint translated it—as fortified, and placed there what it had taken from the cedar of Lebanon, so that it might be planted and grow in the land of Canaan.

After this, the same eagle took from the seed of the land from which it had taken the tops of the cedar, and obtained seed for itself from outside, and planted it in a leafy field above abundant water. But this very thing that had been taken from the land of Canaan, from what had been plucked from the highest branches of Lebanon—that is, what it had received on the second occasion—became a vine, not strong but weak, and also small in stature. The branches of this weak vine bent toward what had been taken from Lebanon and the cedar, so far that it had its roots planted beneath its own trunk.

Indeed, the vine came into being, put forth shoots, and extended its branches. After this another eagle came, itself also great, with great wings and many feathers—or claws; and, behold, this vine of which we have just spoken, when the second eagle came, turned its covenant toward it, scorning the covenant that it had previously made with the tree against which the vine had leaned, after putting forth its shoots and spreading its branches more widely. It embraced the second eagle and transferred its roots from the former to the latter. Then it sent out its branches toward the second eagle, so that the latter might water it with the clod of its planting, in a good field and with abundant water.

This vine was indeed watered and transferred to the second eagle so that it might grow, bear fruit, and become a great vine. Therefore the prophet is commanded to say that the vine, having transgressed the covenant it had made with the former eagle and established it with the second, will not prosper, nor will the tender roots of it blossom. Rather, because of its transgression, its fruit will rot; everything that sprang from it will wither; and it will no longer have a large arm or a numerous people. It will be uprooted completely, and, although it has been watered, it will not endure or prosper into fruitfulness. As soon as the scorching wind touches it, it will wither and dry up together with the clod of its planting.

This is what the presentation of the history itself demands: that we explain more clearly, by adding certain words, what has been said more obscurely. And if it is such a great labor merely to understand what is being said, what need is there to say how much obscurity the question itself contains—who the former eagle is, what Lebanon is, what the cedar is, what the top of the cedar is, who the second eagle is, and what the transfer of the vine from the former to the latter means?

If ever we have needed God’s help, and if we always need the Holy Spirit for understanding the Scriptures, now surely is the time for him to grant us assistance and himself to unfold what he has said. Just as our Savior in the Gospels himself interprets certain parables, so now the prophet, in the second prophecy that follows in the reading, signifies that the first eagle is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who entered Lebanon—that is, Jerusalem—and took from the top of the cedar—that is, the king of Jerusalem and his nobles—and brought them into the land of the Chaldeans, namely Babylon.

For, taking the children of Israel into captivity, he planted them there; and from the royal seed and from the stock of the nobles he established them in that same land. After this, and after the royal lineage, another multitude was also captured by him, and it became a vine—not as strong as it had been when it was in the vineyard of God and in the holy land where God’s sacrifices are celebrated, but a weak vine transferred to Babylon.

After these events, war arose between Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Therefore the people who, together with their kings and the stock of their nobles, had been afflicted by the Assyrians, finding an opportunity to cast off Nebuchadnezzar’s yoke and free themselves from his rule, went over to the second great eagle with great wings—that is, to Pharaoh (IV Kings 25).

Then, as events proceeded in their order, because God had not handed them over to Pharaoh but to Nebuchadnezzar, and because they had not endured his judgment and rule but had shaken Nebuchadnezzar’s yoke from their necks and defected to Pharaoh, God’s anger fell upon them, and the outcome was contrary to what they had thought.

For one who has been condemned by God ought not to flee his sentence or wish to change the will of the judge, but to endure it with the greatest patience until God himself, who condemned him, sets him free. Therefore, because the people transferred themselves to Pharaoh, they were abandoned by God’s help and suffered worse things than they had previously suffered from Nebuchadnezzar.

We have explained the solution of the parable according to the literal sense and according to what is written. A more difficult interpretation now follows, hard to understand, concerning the true Nebuchadnezzar, the true Pharaoh, and the words that were spoken about the eagles. Before inserting the following reading, we therefore gave this exposition briefly and summarily, so that the present passage might be understood more easily, while the fuller exposition might nevertheless be preserved in its proper place and the ensuing parable might also be discussed at length according to its allegorical meaning.

For the present, however, we must take up a few matters and, as though with a kind of armament, prepare the way for the interpretation to come from what God’s grace grants us, knowing what we shall explain more fully in the following passage. First, we must consider why Nebuchadnezzar and Pharaoh are called eagles.

Perhaps someone who does not read the Scriptures casually or superficially may ask: Nebuchadnezzar is a great eagle, with great wings, and this Pharaoh is another great eagle, likewise with immense wings; yet in the Law the eagle is placed among the unclean animals. Why, then, does the righteous man, having become rich, prepare for himself the wings of an eagle, so that he may be changed into the house of his prince? Why also is there a promise in the prophet Isaiah, who says: “The righteous shall receive wings like eagles; they shall run and not grow weary, they shall walk and not hunger”?

For if the eagle is unclean, we ought not, when we have become righteous, to receive wings like an eagle; nor, when riches have increased for us, ought we to prepare for ourselves the wings of an eagle.

First, then, we must answer that certain names of animals in Scripture are used in both senses, that is, in the evil and the good sense. For example, “lion” is understood in both a good and an evil sense. In the good sense:

> “A lion’s cub is Judah; from a sprout, my son, you have risen. Lying down, you have slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who will rouse him?” (Genesis 49)

But in the evil sense:

> “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour,”

and it is beneficial for us to resist him, firm in faith. The malicious one, too, desiring to deceive, lies in wait secretly, “like a lion lying in wait in his cave to seize the poor.”

Therefore, just as “lion” is used in both an evil and a good sense, it is not inappropriate for “eagle” also to be understood in both senses. And, as I suspect, the righteous man is not an eagle, but is like an eagle; he imitates the eagle. Just as the bronze serpent was a type of the Savior—for it was not truly a serpent but imitated a serpent, when the Lord said, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3)—so in the same way the righteous man is not so much an eagle as similar to an eagle, because it is useful for him to follow the image of the eagle.

According to this understanding, the righteous man also received a command elsewhere to be wise as a serpent—not to become a serpent, but so that he might not be caught by the craftiness of the true serpent.

But if the word of God, carefully examining the Scriptures, and the Spirit of whom it is written, “The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God” (1 Corinthians 2), enters someone’s soul, it will show most clearly from the Scriptures that both the eagle and the lion have been placed among the clean animals.

The cherubim of God have the face of a man, and on the right the face of a lion, fourfold; and the face of a calf, and on the left the face of an eagle, fourfold. These things seen in the cherubim—that is, the eagle and the lion—are clean. Nothing unclean exists in God’s chariot.

And just as you, believing from the Gentiles, have become clean—“What God has cleansed, you must not call common”—this is said concerning all the things hanging from heaven that were shown to Peter; so the lion and the eagle that appeared in the cherubim have been cleansed.

There is also another matter that is foretold as destined to occur at Christ’s coming: it recognizes as clean the lion and the eagle that is now called unclean.

> “The wolf and the lamb shall feed together” (Isaiah 11).

For the wolf that feeds harmlessly with the sheep is no longer to be feared. I am not speaking of such a wolf when I say:

> “Beware of those who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7).

He spoke pointedly when he said, “but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.” There are, in fact, others who are not ravenous, when wolves and lambs feed together, and calf and bull and lion eat together.

When a fellowship of natures so diverse from one another has been formed in the faith of Christ, the lion will no longer be unclean. Rather, it will forget its ferocity, and all the animals that are called unclean in the Law will recover the purity of their original condition. This has already been accomplished in part and will be completed most fully at the second coming.

Thus the mystery shown in the cherubim anticipated the reality of the matter. Indeed, the faces of the lion and the eagle are so closely related to the other faces that what appeared in the cherubim seems greater to us than the calf, bull, and lion feeding together. For Isaiah makes no promise concerning the things foretold that is coherent with them or mutually connected. In the cherubim, however, each animal is related to another: the face of the calf to the face of the lion, and the face of the man to the face of the eagle.

Therefore do not be greatly surprised when Pharaoh and the Nebuchadnezzar who preceded him are called eagles, while the righteous man is said to take wings like an eagle, and one who has become rich in God’s cause prepares for himself the wings of an eagle in order to fly.

But to return to the subject: something particular is signified concerning Nebuchadnezzar, because he is great, with great wings and an extremely long extension, so much so that he dared to say:

> “By my strength I will act; by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of nations, consume their strength, shake the inhabited cities, and grasp the whole world in my hand like a nest; and like broken eggs I will take it away” (Isaiah 10).

Behold, this is the extension of his wings. Nor is this enough for him: he is full of claws and many feathers, and he has a way of entering Lebanon in order to pluck off its highest branches.

As long as those who dwelt in Lebanon had not sinned—that is, as long as, established in Jerusalem, they had not been found in crimes—this great eagle had not received the power to enter Lebanon, nor had it taken for itself the chosen things, the royal seed of the cedar, and the stock of the nobles. These are its tender shoots, which for a certain time had not been hard of heart. Nevertheless, it seized them because they sinned against the Lord.

This great eagle and so forth transferred the tops of the entire tree into Canaan, because, figuratively, the land of the Babylonians is called the accursed land of Canaan. Concerning this Noah says:

> “Cursed be the boy Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Genesis 9).

In the city of merchants, or of a merchant, or of those who transfer things, or certainly in a fortified city, it placed what it had taken from the cedar. It took for itself some of the seed of the land, no longer only from the higher branches but also from the lower ones and from the people of the Jews, and placed it in a leafy field, establishing it above abundant water to be watched over. It sprang up and became a strong vine.

In Babylon the people of God truly became weak, and therefore could not sing the Lord’s song, saying:

> “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm 136)

It truly could not fail to be weak, since it had been planted in Babylon. How could it preserve its former strength once it had begun to be a Babylonian vine? Since it had not borne fruit in the holy land, it was therefore transferred by the eagle and, when placed in the land of Canaan, became a weak vine and small in stature.

As long as it was in the holy land, it was a great vine; but when it was transferred into the territory of sinners, it became both weak and small. And you, therefore, vine that hear me: if you wish to be great, do not leave the boundaries of the Church; remain in the holy land, Jerusalem.

But if, because of your sins, you fall into worse things, you will be transferred to another land and become a small vine. Your branches will fall and your roots will dry up, so that afterward you will desire to rest upon another eagle, as it is now said, with great wings and many claws.

It is better for one who has been condemned to remain under the sentence of condemnation as long as the one who condemned him so wills. Let us not run willingly to Pharaoh. For if we run to him, we act against God, who said:

> “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery” (Deuteronomy).

We do not hasten to Nebuchadnezzar so much of our own accord as we are condemned and dragged to him.

It follows:

> “And another great eagle came, with great wings and many claws; and behold, this vine embraced it,”

that is, the second eagle.

It often happens that we are transferred from one opposing power to another. God had commanded the people of Israel to submit their necks to Nebuchadnezzar’s yoke, as we read in Jeremiah, so much so that he threatened the one who withdrew from his service. At the time when we expounded Jeremiah, we discussed the matters that God’s grace, through your prayers, granted us—or at least attempted, as best we could, to explain them.

The people did not wish to do what had been commanded. Instead, they extended their branches toward Pharaoh in the clod of his planting; they were established by him in a field above abundant water, so as to bear very rich fruit. Having abandoned Egypt, they again desired Egypt, thinking that they would recover their former abundance. Above all, it considered that if Nebuchadnezzar crossed over to Pharaoh, it would strengthen its roots, restore its stature, and bear fruit.

But everything turned out contrary to what they had thought. All their fruit rotted, and the shoots that had at least come forth in Babylon withered through the change of region, so completely that the vine was uprooted, lest it ever again grow strong with a large arm or a numerous people.

What great or such mysteries do these things contain? What does each expression signify? We can, if we have listeners, ascend to another Jerusalem and show there how the great eagle made its way and carried the tops of the tree into this Babylon that we now possess.

We can speak of certain more secret matters concerning Pharaoh. But because time presses us, and perhaps we are making a bold promise that we cannot fulfill, let us return to lesser matters and explain them according to the measure of our understanding.

This great and true eagle, Nebuchadnezzar—that is, the devil—came to this Lebanon, namely the Church, where God’s sacrifices are offered and the incense of its prayers is celebrated, and he seized it. May it never happen in our times that he transfers from the tops of the cedar—that is, from the leaders and the royal seed—into Canaan.

Let us pray that what has often happened may not occur. Certain people who were leaders in the Church have been taken up and transferred into Babylon, removed from the height of Lebanon because of their sin. Concerning them it must be said that the great eagle, with great claws and extended feathers, took them from the tops of the cedar and stripped them from Lebanon—that is, from Jerusalem—and planted them in the land of Canaan.

But this eagle does not claim only the top of the cedar—that is, those of the nobility—for itself; it also seizes the seed of the land and transfers it into the land of Canaan whenever someone from the people sins and someone from God’s people is ensnared by the devil’s traps.

Therefore, day and night, let us implore God’s help both for ourselves and for our brothers, lest anyone be transferred from Jerusalem into Canaan; lest, abandoning his sentence, we turn from his will toward another eagle; lest a greater anger come upon us, and the entire planting rot, and its fruit wither together with its roots.

The planting of Jerusalem cannot bear fruit in another land; it does not produce branches in foreign territories. Rather, as soon as it fails to persevere in the will of God and in his Church—that is, in the deeds, words, and knowledge of the truth of Christ Jesus—it dries up together with its clod.

To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY TWELVE

On what is written: “Son of man, say to the exasperating house: Do you not know what these things signify?” (Chapter 17).

**985** What I have already mentioned above concerning the two great eagles, with great wings and great talons, as well as what the first and second eagle did, divine speech now wishes to explain in part, as though in prophecy—that is, figuratively—leaving us to understand what it has itself left untouched. And first, although I have often said this already, I shall nevertheless now try to introduce something not new, which may bring salvation to our soul, in the passage addressed to the prophet: “Say to the bitter-making house,” or “to the exasperating house.” For he did not add, “to the house that has exasperated me.” And if we wish to see what sort of sin exasperation is, let us hear how sweet God’s words are to the one who understands, when he says: “How sweet are your words to my throat” (Ps. 118 [119]). When believers receive these words, naturally sweet, they either live well or do the exact opposite. If they walk according to the divine rule, they preserve God’s words in the sweetness in which they were born. As far as the movement of my own mind is concerned, I think that by the goodness of their conduct they even increase the sweetness of God’s words, mingling the sweetness of life with the sweetness of speech.

But if someone sins and walks perversely outside God’s commandments, then, receiving the supremely sweet words of God, he turns all their sweetness into a bitter taste through the nature of his exceedingly bitter sin—for sin is bitter, since it destroys the sweetness of speech. You will notice more fully what I mean if you take an example. The herb called wormwood is naturally bitter. If you put it into honey in proportion to the quality and quantity of the honey, its bitterness overcomes the honey’s sweetness and forces what is sweet to become bitter. Sin has the power of this herb. If I commit more sins, I put more bitterness into the sweetness of God’s words. If what I do wrong is great, I turn all the sweetness of the honey into a harsh taste. And therefore God, who avenges the trampling of his word by sinners, returns to each person a bitterness of punishments and penalties corresponding to the quality of his love of life and the measure of his purpose.

And if we who say these things and once believed in God should sin, we try to exasperate his word. But those who have entirely departed from faith in him and have not entered the Church do not make God’s words bitter. How can those who have not yet believed in his words exasperate their sweetness? Therefore different torments are reserved for us, who seem to believe and yet sin within that very belief, from the punishment of those who have had not even the beginning of faith.

And lest we think only that we exasperate the Lord’s word when we sin, our offense reaches even to an insult against God himself. For it is written that the one who sins dishonors God through transgressing the law. It would have been a small matter if he had said, “He dishonors an angel”; but now he says, “Through transgressing the law he dishonors God.” Whenever we transgress God’s law, we dishonor God; and the greater the sins we commit, the greater the insults with which we treat God. The more we sin, the more we dishonor the Father and his Christ, as it is written: “How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, considered the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified profane, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Heb. 10:29).

Therefore everyone who sins exasperates, insults, and dishonors both the words of God that he has received and the one who taught them. Say now to the exasperated house: “Do you not know what these things are?”—that is, what was spoken in the parable of the eagles. Say: “When the king of Babylon comes to Jerusalem and takes its king and its princes.” As far as the prophet’s historical account is concerned, this has been explained: that Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem and led away captive Zedekiah, king of Judah, together with the princes who were with him and part of the Jewish people (4 Kings 25 [2 Kings 25]). We shall also add how he planted them in the land of Babylon.

But let us not remain with the letter or cling to the historical account. Rather, you who make progress in God’s Scriptures and know that all these things happened to them figuratively, but were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, should understand. Behold, the true Nebuchadnezzar is at hand, seeking to capture some of us. First, if possible, he desires to lead away captive some of the rulers of the Church. But as long as Hezekiah, Josiah, or certainly any righteous king reigns among the people, this Nebuchadnezzar cannot carry away the rulers or the people from Judea in chains.

But if we who seem to preside over the Church sin, giving place to the devil, contrary to Paul’s command, which says, “Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4:27), then, in a certain sense, through the sins we have committed in Jerusalem, we give Nebuchadnezzar an opportunity to enter the holy city and carry away whomever he wishes. The one who does not sin, however, shuts out Nebuchadnezzar, so that he cannot enter the land of God.

Therefore let us shut out Nebuchadnezzar with all our strength, so that he may not approach the blessed assembly of this Church. Let us shut him out by taking up the key of knowledge; let us shut him out by our conduct and good works, so that he may not seize the king of Jerusalem and his princes, or lead them away into Babylon as a triumph of his captivity.

But if the savage enemy is able to overcome one of us, he leads him into Babylon—not into a spacious region of some land, but into the Babylon of the soul, that is, into confusion. We have often said that Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” Whoever is overcome by him and led away is transferred into the confusion of his own mind, into Babylon.

Let us look to daily life. Whenever we see a soul confused by sins, vices, sadness, anger, desires, or greed, let us know that this is the soul whom the devil is leading away into Babylon. But if, in the ruling part of the heart, tranquility, serenity, and peace produce fruit, let us know that Jerusalem is present in it, for Jerusalem is inwardly the vision of peace.

“And he leads them to himself into Babylon, and takes from the seed of the kingdom, and establishes a covenant with him.” All of us who have received the word of God are royal seed. For we are called “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2:9). If, therefore, one of us who has been placed among the royal seed is led away captive by the devil through his sin, there is no doubt that he has been taken from the royal lineage into Babylon, and that he makes a covenant with Nebuchadnezzar, because he has already rejected God’s covenant.

For it is impossible for a human being to exist without a covenant. If you have God’s covenant within you, Nebuchadnezzar cannot make a covenant with you. But if, by transgressing his commandments, you have rejected God’s covenant, you have accepted Nebuchadnezzar’s covenant. For it is written: “He establishes his covenant with him and brings him under a curse.” God makes a covenant with us in blessing; Nebuchadnezzar, however, establishes his covenant in a curse. The one who has made a pact with Nebuchadnezzar cannot be in blessing.

But someone learned in the divine Scriptures says to me: “I find curses established in the law of Moses against the sinner. If, then, a curse has been established by God’s command against sinners, why should there not conversely be some blessing with the devil, so that some are blessed by him and others are under a curse?”

I shall try to answer this acute and exceedingly sharp question in this way: there is indeed a certain blessing from Nebuchadnezzar, which God utterly rejects from us, and there is also the curse of which we must now speak, which rightly comes upon sinners.

What, then, is Nebuchadnezzar’s blessing? When someone is wealthy in this world, prospers, and everything flows for him in a favorable course, so that what is written can be applied to him—“His ox will not miscarry”—and when he possesses all the prosperity of the age, Nebuchadnezzar’s blessing is upon him.

His curse, however, is present when someone departs from God and, although established on the devil’s side, is tormented by miseries and punishments.

God therefore wishes, as Scripture now recalls, for the covenant with Israel to be a curse under Nebuchadnezzar. And because the king of Jerusalem wished to reject Nebuchadnezzar’s covenant and, sending his messengers to Egypt, attempted to make a covenant with Pharaoh, divine speech says: “He shall not prosper; he shall not be saved.”

Accordingly, we ought to endure patiently when we are handed over by God for punishment. The Apostle handed a certain member of the Church over to the devil for the destruction of the flesh; and he handed him over for the destruction of the flesh not in order to destroy the one handed over, but to preserve his spirit. Hence Scripture says: “To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus” (1 Cor. 5:5).

The sinner is handed over to torments so that, in the present, he may receive punishment and sufferings for his sins, and in the future attain refreshment; and it may be said of him: “He received his evil things during his life.”

If, therefore, someone tormented by punishments according to the curse under which God has placed sinners should prefer to flee his penalties and send to Egypt to obtain help from Pharaoh—from whom God delivered his people—“he shall not prosper; he shall not be saved.”

But if someone patiently endures the curse, the punishments of Nebuchadnezzar, and the time of his sins in suffering, then, like the one who according to Paul’s Letters was tormented so that his spirit might be saved on the day of judgment, he will attain an excellent end.

“He brings him under a curse, and will take the rulers of his land, so that they may become a weak kingdom.” The kingdom that is transferred from the holy land into Babylon becomes weak. No one is strong in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of his own mind. A confused person cannot at all be exalted “to keep my covenant, to uphold it, and to depart from it, and to send his messengers to Egypt.”

Because this man suffers torments from Nebuchadnezzar on account of his sins and sends his messengers to Egypt, unable to endure the surrender by which he has been handed over to the enemy by God, he has done what is forbidden in that passage. For Scripture says, “You shall not multiply horses for yourself” (Deut. 17:16).

“Shall he prosper? Shall he be saved?”—the one who acts perversely and transgresses the covenant. The one who had been handed over to Nebuchadnezzar’s covenant ought to have endured the punishment. But he does not endure it, and therefore it is said of him, “He shall not be saved.”

“As I live,” says the Lord Adonai, “unless in the place of the king who appointed him, who despised my curse and transgressed my covenant.”

There is one who dishonors God’s curse, and there is another who honors it. There is no doubt that here God is speaking about the one who has dishonored his curse. For when someone is handed over to punishments in order to be disciplined and does not endure what has been commanded, he dishonors God’s curse. But if he endures it with complete gentleness, blessing, and thanksgiving toward God, he honors the curse. And when he has honored the curse, it is necessary that he also attain God’s blessing.

“And he transgressed my covenant; with him, in the midst of Babylon, he shall die, and Pharaoh shall not wage war for him with great strength or a numerous army.” Pharaoh cannot provide help to the one who has transgressed and dishonored God’s curse; rather, he will die in the midst of Babylon on account of his transgression.

Then the text continues and relates what sinners will suffer. After this it recalls more favorable things, saying: “I shall take from the chosen branches of the cedar, and from the top of their heart I shall pluck it out, and I shall plant it on a high mountain.”

After the curses mentioned above, the promise of blessedness and the sweetest assurance are brought forth at the end of the speech, since those who required punishments had already endured torments for their sins.

**991** Considering this within myself and carefully examining the meaning of the passage, I think that it is a prophecy concerning the apostles. These are the chosen branches of the cedar, from its summit and topmost point, whom God gave as the greenness of the age, stripping their hearts and planting them on the high mountain, Jesus Christ our Lord.

“And I shall hang it upon the high mountain of Israel; I shall plant it, and it shall produce a shoot and bear fruit.” They produced shoots and brought forth fruits. “And it shall become a great cedar.”

Consider the greatness and sublimity of Christ’s Church, so that you may understand that, according to God’s promise, what is said has come to pass: “And it shall become a great cedar, and every bird shall rest upon it, and every winged creature shall rest under its shade.”

Take for yourself the wings of God’s word, and you will be able to rest beneath this tree, which has been planted on the high mountain. “And it shall rest, and its shoots shall be restored.” See how the prophecy ends in a good sense.

For it follows: “And all the trees of the field shall know that I am the Lord, who humble the tall tree.” The tall tree is the Jewish people, now humbled and paying the penalty for its crime, because it dared to lay hands upon our God, Jesus Christ.

“And I exalt the lowly tree.” You were a lowly tree, a fallen tree, a tree clinging to the earth; but God exalted you.

“And I dry up the green tree.” The green tree is the people of circumcision, who once sprouted and flourished but have now withered through excessive drought. For where among them is there now a living word? Where is the chorus of virtues?

“And I make the dry tree grow green again.” You were a dry tree, but the advent of Christ made you green again.

“I, the Lord, have spoken, and I shall act.”

With these words, let us pray more earnestly to Jesus Christ our Lord together with his Father, so that we too may grow green again, so that we may be able to bear fruit, so that we may become a tree that sprouts and not one that is dry, and so that the axe proclaimed in the Gospel may never be placed at our roots. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

**HOMILY THIRTEEN**

Concerning the passage: “Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre, and set your face against Sidon” (Chapter 27).

[Col. 0777B] 991 The bishops instruct us to examine the speech concerning the prince of Tyre, so that we may declare his praises and his faults; and we have likewise been commanded to reconsider certain matters concerning Pharaoh, king of Egypt. The prince of Tyre, then, is mourned—but we must not think that this is a human being. For no human being was created in the midst of the cherubim, and, if we follow the literal sense simply, no human being was nourished in the paradise of God. Yet, although—as we have said—no one was in the paradise of delights, the prince of Tyre is now said to have been born and nourished in the paradise of delights.

Who is this prince of Tyre? Let us turn to Daniel, and, finding there an opportunity for understanding, let us say that the princes now under discussion are not corporeal rulers. After Daniel, let us seek an example from the Apostle. Then let us again call upon the testimonies of the prophets. To all these we must also join the passage which Moses does not leave unmentioned in Deuteronomy.

Let us now review the examples, beginning with Daniel. “The prince,” he says, “is Michael” (Dan. X); and again, “the prince of Israel”; and subsequently: “Michael was helping the prince of the kingdom of the nations.” To this the Apostle adds: “But glory and honor and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and to the Greek.” Perhaps the prince of the Israelites has already helped the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks. For at the coming of my Lord Jesus Christ, the prince of Israel helped the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks, so that the nations might attain salvation and, by believing, be saved.

In this way, then, a certain prince of the kingdom of Persia is mentioned, just as Michael is called the prince of the Israelites and another is called the prince of the Greeks. These, therefore, are not human beings, nor are they named according to the names of the places in which they rule. Hence the Apostle, as though he were not speaking about human beings, says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the princes of this age, who are being brought to nothing; but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, hidden, which God ordained before the ages for our glory, which none of the princes of this age knew. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. II).

And that the princes of this age crucified the Savior and Lord, prophecy bears witness, saying: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.” Hence it is also written elsewhere in the Psalms: “I said, You are gods, and all sons of the Most High; but you shall die like human beings, and like one of the princes you shall fall” (Ps. LXXXI). There the discussion is certainly not about any corporeal prince.

If, then, there is a certain prince of the kingdom of Persia, and Michael is the prince of the Israelites, consequently there is also a prince of Tyre; and it is concerning these princes that the prophetic word now speaks.

Since we also promised a testimony from Moses, listen to what follows: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God”—or, as the better reading has it, “according to the number of the sons of Israel”—“and the Lord’s portion became his people Jacob” (Deut. XXXII). Tyre became the portion of one prince, Babylon of another, and other nations of others; and in this way princes possessed all the boundaries of the nations.

But if anyone, reading the Scriptures, thinks that these things are spoken as though about human beings, let him understand them in a higher, spiritual sense, a sense judged by no one. For certain things are discerned concerning Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, which do not suit his person. He said: “By strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of the nations; I will shake inhabited cities, and I will encompass the whole world; I will ascend above the stars of heaven and the clouds,” and the rest, “and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. X). This is said of Nebuchadnezzar. The same applies to the prince of Tyre and to Pharaoh.

For the true, corporeal Pharaoh was not so driven by madness that he would say, “The rivers are mine, and I made them.” This, however, was read earlier in the prophecy against Pharaoh. Nor would that prince—that is, the corporeal Pharaoh—ever have been called a dragon, when it says: “Behold, I am against Pharaoh, the dragon who sits in the midst of the rivers of Egypt, who says, The rivers are mine; I made them” (Ezek. XXIX). Let what has been said here be reserved for its proper place; we have introduced it now so that, through our knowledge of the Scriptures, what appeared obscure might become clearer.

Our struggle is against these princes. The blessed apostles, who had been sent to preach, suffered ambushes from those who possessed the boundaries of the nations when they were leading human beings away from them. Let this serve as an example: the apostles entered Tyre, and the prince of Tyre persecuted them; they went up to Antioch, and the prince of the kingdom of Syria attacked them. It was he who fought against them, not all those who appeared to do so, such as the betrayer Judas.

For just as Judas must be regarded as having betrayed the Savior under the primary influence of another, so also, in the case of all the apostles who suffered persecution, there was another who was the prince of the persecution. It is written concerning Judas: “After the morsel, Satan entered into him” (John XIII).

“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood,” even though those who persecute us may appear to be flesh and blood. We should not hate them; rather, we should love them, even though they wish to remain our enemies. Let us have pity on them: they have a demon and are suffering madness. Those who persecute us are not so much against us as the one who has filled their hearts. Let us pray for the Lord’s help, therefore, so that the efforts of so great an adversary, fighting against the human soul, may prove weak, and let us say: “If the Lord had not been with us, when people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

There is, then, a certain prince of Tyre, and the prophecy does not teach us about Hiram—for this name is written in the Third Book of Kings (3 Kgs. V)—nor about another prince of Tyre, nor about any human being. Human words do not teach us these things, but divine words, and certain ineffable and sacred realities under the persons of human beings.

Pharaoh is a human being, but the more learned person understands something else by Pharaoh. Nabal of Carmel is a human being, and Hiram is a human being (1 Kgs. XXV), but under their likeness I am taught something else. Who is so great and of such character that, rising above corporeal things, he contemplates invisible realities through visible ones, and can understand each of these according to God’s will?

Who, then, is this prince? Let us learn, so that, recognizing the lamentation, we may also avoid what is now said concerning him. The prince of Tyre is mourned. How good God is, who even mourns those who have denied him! This too proceeds from the affection of love. No one mourns one whom he hates; and the one who is mourned is indeed mourned as dead, yet, as though still sought and desired among the living, is loved.

When Jerusalem is mourned, it is written: “And it came to pass, after Israel had been taken captive and Jerusalem had been laid waste, Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented this lamentation over Jerusalem, and said: How the city that abounded in peoples sits alone! She has become like a widow, who was multiplied among the nations; the princess among the regions has become tributary” (Lam. I).

Nebuchadnezzar too is mourned. Where are the heresies? Where are those who say that these beings were created for destruction? They accuse the Creator in order to absolve themselves from their own accusations. “Receive this lamentation over the king of Babylon, and say: How has he who demanded ceased? How has he who exacted rested?” These things are said concerning the king of Babylon: “How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, he who arose in the morning? He has been crushed to the earth” (Isa. XIV).

Both he fell from heaven, and this one—the prince of Tyre—was the seal of likeness, the crown of beauty, nourished in the paradise of delights. Behold, all are said to have fallen from heaven, not to have descended. But my Lord descended from heaven, and the one who descended is the Son of Man.

Yet it was not so with Satan. He did not descend from heaven; nor would any evil have happened to him if he had descended. Hear Jesus saying: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke X)—not descending. But the Savior alone did not descend from heaven: daily a multitude descends and ascends upon the Son of Man (John I). “For you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.”

You too should await your ascent. Only rise from your fall, and hear: “Arise, Jerusalem, from your fall.” Hope, because you know that you will ascend into heaven; and beware lest this also be said to you: “Shall the one who falls not rise again? Or shall the one who turns away not return?” (Jer. VIII). “Woe to those who turn with a most evil turning,” says the Lord.

This one, therefore, is also among those who fell, and the prince is mourned by a human being, although the prince ought to have mourned the human being. Ezekiel is a human being, and a son of man; but the one who is mourned is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Receive your own lamentation over the king of Babylon, and say: “How has he who demanded rested?” and the rest.

Consider to what great hope you have been called, O human being, who, clothed in flesh, say: “You milked me like milk, and curdled me like cheese; you clothed me with skin and flesh, and joined me together with bones and sinews” (Job X). You, then, who were grieving over your condition, behold, you mourn; and the one who is not clothed in flesh is mourned by you. For you have been called to the hope from which he fell.

Through Israel’s sin, salvation entered among the nations. I shall dare to say something more sacred: you are going to ascend into the place of the angels who fell, and you will be entrusted with the mystery once entrusted to them. Concerning it is said: “How has Lucifer fallen, he who arose in the morning?”

You, however, have become the light of the world; you have become Lucifer in his place. Lucifer was one of the stars who fell from heaven, while you—provided you are truly of the seed of Abraham—will be counted among the stars of heaven. For God led Abraham outside and said to him: “Look; so shall your seed be” (Gen. XV).

This will occur when the stars fall from heaven like leaves, and there is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead (1 Cor. XV).

But do not boast against such branches, which fell through unbelief and were broken off (Rom. XI). Since you stand in faith, by faith you will also ascend.

And through the fact that you mourn the prince of Tyre and lament with mourning the things we inserted above, learn not to begin falling among those good things that the prince of Tyre possessed, should you become slightly boastful and fail to guard your heart with every vigilance.

See what he says to the prince of Tyre: “You are the seal of likeness.” I want to know what he was, so that he was called the seal of likeness. When you have made progress, you receive the seal, because God is truly the Father of the one whom he sealed and sent; therefore all who believe are sealed by the Lord.

A common expression has now also arisen, so that we say: “This person and that person did not receive the seal,” or, “That person has the seal.” Who has the seal? The one whom God has sealed.

I shall dare to say that the one marked with this seal is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire, the one who bestows the image of the heavenly, who forms you for things above, so that you may no longer bear the image of the earthly.

Beware, O human being, lest, as you depart from this age, you be stamped with the seal of the devil. For he has a seal. “As we have borne the image of the earthly”—where, when, or by whom was it signified that we should bear the image of the earthly with this sign?

The devil goes around and surveys everything, wishing also to seal those subject to him. He seals the hearts of individuals, observing them, and impresses upon them the form of the earthly through sins and vices, so that they may bear the image of the earthly.

Hear what Jesus answers when the image and inscription of Caesar are requested: “Let the one who has ears to hear hear” (Matt. XI). Since he himself did not possess the image that was being sought, nor did his disciple, he teaches where the image in question may be found.

“Go,” he says, “to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it for me and for you” (Matt. XVII).

Neither I nor you possess this image and inscription, provided you are truly my disciple and the gates of hell do not prevail against you. Thus Jesus gives an image for himself in another way, taking from the sea the image that had been enclosed in a fish, like those fish of which we read today, which cling to the scales of the dragon who sits upon the rivers of Egypt.

Such fish truly cling there. How many fish there are even today whose king is the one who reigns in many waters! For it is written concerning the invisible dragon that he himself is king of all who are in the waters. But you are not in the waters; you are in the land that has been promised to you.

These things have been said so that we may examine more carefully what the seal of likeness is. How blessed he was at that time when he was the seal of likeness! You still lack becoming the likeness of the seal, and you are far from such a gift.

God did indeed say: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I); nevertheless, you have not yet attained the likeness. “God made the human being; according to the image of God he made him.” Where is the likeness of God? “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III).

I understand what the prophet says, “O God, who is like you?” (Ps. XXXIV), in this sense—as though it meant: “Who, do you suppose, is a faithful and wise steward?”—just as it also means: “When he appears, we shall be like him.”

Who is the one who is made like him? Very few have received likeness, such as the apostles. “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.” The one who is now mourned, then, was the seal, full of wisdom, and you too will mourn him if you have become an Ezekiel.

I do not know whether you too will be full of wisdom. For the present, the one who is mourned was full of wisdom and was a crown of beauty. Consider what kind of being he was who was a crown of beauty. Beauty was not merely present in him, nor was it merely glory; he was a crown of glory.

Do not seek this beauty outside yourself, but in the religious life of the soul, in the mind—the place where the intellectual faculty resides, where true beauty is found. If you wish to seek beauty where there are flesh and blood, moisture and veins, where there is corporeal matter, you will not be able to find it.

True beauty is in the Savior, and from him, according to his generosity and mercy, it has been divided among all souls. “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one, in your appearance and in your beauty and in your loveliness” (Ps. XLIV, 3).

There is therefore a certain beauty in the ruling faculty of our heart and in the soul. And that such beauty also reaches the human soul, let the prophet teach you, saying: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, forget your people and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty” (ibid., 11)—that is, the bridegroom.

Who possesses a soul so beautiful? Who possesses such beauty? Who is so free from every foulness that it can be said to him: “The king has desired your beauty”? You are still seeking this beauty and striving to please; but he, from the beauty that he possessed, fell into ugliness.

And just as we often see this happen in bodies—that a woman beautiful and fair of face loses her beauty through illness and through old age loses the radiance of her countenance—in the same way, a soul that was beautiful loses its beauty through weakness and becomes deformed through old age.

For when it has taken on the old human being with his deeds, it loses its former beauty through old age. Jesus came to transfer us from the old human being and from the marks of old age. A wrinkle is indeed an indication of old age, as the Apostle says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind, but that it might be holy and without blemish” (Eph. V).

It is therefore possible to pass from old age and wrinkles to youth. Here is the remarkable thing: the body proceeds from adolescence toward old age, but the soul, if it reaches perfection, is carried from old age into adolescence. Hence, although our outward human being is being corrupted, the inward human being is renewed from day to day.

You ought to know the beauty that the king desires; you ought to know the one who was once a crown of beauty. And when you have attained this glory, beware lest you fall. For the one who fell was also the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and a crown of beauty.

“In the delights of the paradise of your God you were defiled.” He does not say simply “in paradise,” but “in the paradise of delights.” I ask whether there are various distinctions among paradises, and whether someone may be in the paradise of God without being in the paradise of delights.

The thief entered paradise with Jesus at the first hour. If I ask you whether he entered paradise or not, surely you will answer that he did. Then, if I ask you again: Since he entered paradise, was he immediately received into the place of delights? Perhaps you will say that, although he entered paradise at the first hour, he was not made to be in the paradise of God’s delights.

But if you now see him receiving from the tree of life and from all the trees which God did not forbid, so that he eats from every tree of paradise; if you see him eating the fruit of that tree and of all those which are not now forbidden; and if I ask you whether he has not only been placed in paradise but also in the paradise of God’s delights, what else will you answer me except that he has been established in the delights of paradise?

You are hastening toward this blessedness, you who appear to mourn. But the one who is mourned was once in the delights of God. He was clothed with every precious stone: sardius and carbuncle, sapphire and beryl, hyacinth and jasper, and the remaining twelve stones.

The difficulty of this passage and the nature of the subject raise the exposition beyond our powers. For who can explain the nature of each stone and describe either its color or its power, so as to discover why these stones were chosen?

Nevertheless, although we are not such people as can understand everything, let us observe briefly how he was clothed with those twelve stones. If anyone cares for the divine Scriptures—a matter concerning which we often exhort young people, although, as I see, we accomplish nothing and merely consume our time, for we have not been able to bring any of them to devote themselves to the sacred volumes—and if he seeks those twelve stones and the other things in the Scriptures, he will find them named in the Apocalypse in the same manner and order.

The one placed first there is also placed first here; the second, second; the third, third; the fourth, fourth; and so the order is preserved through the twelfth stone.

Why, then, and upon what, are these stones named in the Apocalypse? Clearly, upon the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem. There it is said that the first gate is topaz, the second emerald, the third carbuncle, and the fourth sapphire; and in this way individual stones are distributed among the individual gates.

If you understand the gates of Jerusalem and the gates of the daughter of Zion, where it is also fitting for you to sing to God—for he says, “I shall sing all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. IX, 15)—if you observe how someone is clothed with twelve stones and enters Jerusalem through its various gates, you will behold twelve virgins.

In the Book of the Shepherd, [Note: [Col. 0783D] You have these passages in Book III, Similitude 9, chapters 2 and 16. Origen often praises this book of the Shepherd, or Hermas, yet never imposes it as canonical. Indeed, in Homily 9 on Numbers he says: “In the little book of the Shepherd—if, at least, that writing seems acceptable to anyone—similar things are indicated.”] in which the angel teaches repentance, the twelve virgins have their own names: Faith, Continence, and so forth. You can read them if you wish.

Then, when the tower is built, once you have taken the strengths of the virgins, you will likewise receive what is said about the gates. Each virtue is an ornament for you, and in this way they are built upon Christ’s foundation—not only gold and silver, but also precious stones. It is forbidden to build wood, hay, or straw (1 Cor. III).

This, then, is the twelfth stone within. We are still commanded to speak about Tyre and Sidon and Pharaoh. The pressure of time has not allowed us to complete what we began above, and the things we wish to explain must be touched upon briefly, as is customary in a commentary.

There is a threat against Sidon, which is interpreted as “hunters.” [Note: [Col. 0783D] This very passage of Origen seems to have misled Jerome when he wrote in his commentary on Ezekiel, ch. XXVII, about this testimony from the Psalm: “Where we read ‘of hunters,’ in Hebrew is written ‘of Sidonians.’” We have pointed out in our note on that passage that the Hebrew reads *Jocesim*, not *Sidonim*, and that *Joces* means “fowler,” whereas “hunter” is properly *Sajad*. See what Victorius has assembled to excuse Jerome’s lapse of memory, and our notes on the cited chapter of Ezekiel above, p. 307, note.] “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. CXXIII). If you read it in Hebrew, you have: “from the snare of the Sidonians.”

The Sidonians, therefore, are hunters, and the threat made against them is made on your account, because they wish to capture you and carefully watch how they may tear hearers of the Scriptures away from the Church, and transfer them from the borders of Judea to the borders of Sidon. But guard your heart with every vigilance, and learn that the threat against the hunters is made for your sake.

As for Pharaoh, the discussion has already said something, affirming that he is a dragon sitting in the midst of the rivers and saying: “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezek. XXIX).

I know the differences among rivers, and I know the rivers upon which the dragon sits. Upon those rivers the people who had been taken captive from Israel sat and wept, because they could not sing the song of Zion, according to what is written in the Psalms: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. CXXXVI, 1).

And I know another river whose streams make the city of God glad, according to the Psalmist’s words: “The river’s streams make glad the city of God.” Do you wish to hear what river this is, whose streams make the city of God glad? It is Jesus Christ our Lord, the river whose streams make the city of God glad.

He is the one who says through Isaiah: “Behold, I shall incline toward you like a river of peace” (Isa. LXVI). I know that there are certain promised rivers which flow from this river.

For everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but “whoever drinks of the water that I shall give,” says Jesus, “will never thirst, but the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life, and rivers shall flow from his belly” (John IV).

You therefore have holy rivers, from which the dragon is far removed. For just as three things are impossible for me to understand—the way of the serpent upon a rock, and the Rock was Christ, and there is no way of the serpent where Jesus is—so I cannot find the dragon’s tracks in these rivers.

There is, however, a certain river which the dragon made. For the dragon says, and God threatens both the dragon and the rivers in which the dragon is: “The rivers are mine, and I made them.”

Hear the heretic preaching with every cunning and skill that Jesus Christ has not yet come. These are the rivers in which the dragon moves; he himself made them, and the dragon says: “The rivers are mine, and I made them.”

Therefore pay careful attention when you drink water, lest perhaps you drink from the river in which the dragon sits. Drink instead from living water, and from the river in which the word of God is found, in which is our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# FOURTEENTH HOMILY

Concerning the passage: “This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, because the Lord God shall pass through it” (Chapter XLIV).

1001 And the Lord said to him: “This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel shall pass through it, and he shall go out. And it shall remain closed.”
