Ezekiel, the son of man, describes several gates of the temple, and what he described concerning each of the gates he now explains again to those who have ears to hear: the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faces east and is to remain always closed.

And the Lord said to him: “This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel shall enter through it and go out, and it shall remain closed.”

He adds another reason why the gate is closed—not only because the Lord God shall pass through it, but also because the prince shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord, according to the way of Eloam, which is interpreted as “the vestibule of the gate.” He shall enter by its way and shall go out.

The Lord God, creator of the universe, enters and goes out through a gate made of sensible material, and it remains perpetually closed. For the sake of the one who founded heaven and earth, as he enters and goes out, the gate is nowhere opened.

But the outer gate and the way of the saints have another meaning. What, then, is the reason that it remains closed? The prince mentioned above sits there, so that no one may see him sitting [Read: eating] bread in the presence of the Lord.

Anyone who reads these things attentively—does he not somehow hear Scripture saying: “Rise, you who sleep”? Is he not urged to rise from the dead and seek the things that are closed?

I shall boldly say that the more secret things are closed, while the more manifest things are opened and are not closed. We are the ones who open the things that are closed; but the Gospels testify: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, and woe to you, lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and you prevented those who were entering” (Luke XI).

There is therefore a certain key of knowledge with which the things that are closed may be opened. And there are many who neither enter themselves nor permit those who wish to enter.

Elsewhere the meaning of the Scriptures is said to be sealed: “And the words of this book shall be like the words of a sealed book. If they give it to a person who does not know letters, saying to him, ‘Read,’ he will say, ‘I do not know letters’; and they will give it to a person who knows letters, saying, ‘Read,’ and he will say, ‘I cannot read, for it is sealed’” (Isa. XXVIII).

The Apocalypse of John contains the meaning of this example more clearly, saying: “An angel went around saying, ‘Who is worthy to open the seals, and to release them, and to read what is written?’ And no one was found in heaven or on earth or under the earth who could open the seals and read what was written in the book. But I was weeping. And someone came to me and said: ‘Do not weep. Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root and Offspring of David, has conquered, to open the book and release its seals.’ And the one who was from the tribe of Judah opened it and revealed what had been written” (Rev. V).

As long as my God had not come, the Law was closed, the prophetic word was closed, and the reading of the Old Testament was veiled. Even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon the heart of the Jews.

There are some who love the veil and hate those who interpret what lies beneath the veil. But let us turn to the Lord, so that, when the veil has been removed, we may say: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (2 Cor. III).

There is a certain gate—one gate—which is closed, and through which no one has passed. There are realities unknown to the whole creation and known only to one. For whatever the Son knows, he has not disclosed to the world. The creature cannot contain what God contains.

And, to come to greater things, beings do not possess knowledge equally. There was more in Paul than in Timothy when Paul was a vessel of election. Yet Timothy, a great vessel in the house, again contains things that I cannot contain. Perhaps there is also someone who contains less than I do.

There are certain things which Christ alone contains, and therefore the door of God’s temple is closed.

What door is this, I ask? The outer door, which opens realities beyond worldly things, incorporeal things, and, so to speak, immaterial things. For it was not placed without reason that the outer door should always be closed.

What is this outer door? The door of the sanctuary. Why is it closed? Because the Lord God of Israel alone enters and goes out through it.

Why does he enter? So that he may be known. By whom? By the prince.

Who is this prince at the closed gate? He is the Savior, who eats bread, who closes the gate with the Father, who is nourished by spiritual food. “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work” (John IV).

The door is therefore closed so that no one may see the great priest eating bread in the Holy of Holies.

To prove what we are saying, anyone who reads Leviticus (Lev. VII), after removing the veil from his heart, will be able to recognize the mystery of the priests. There it speaks of sacrifices and foods which only the priests eat.

There are certain priestly foods which the priest does not eat in his house, nor with his children, although they are priestly, nor with his wife, although she is lawfully married to him; but he eats them in a holy place, and there he eats food in the Holy of Holies [Variant: “in the holy places”].

Just as the priest does not eat food in his house or anywhere else, but in the Holy of Holies, so my Savior alone eats bread, with no one able to eat with him.

There is, however, a certain place in which, when he eats, he draws me with him to eat: “Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I shall enter to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III). From this it is clear that another can also dine with him.

Yet there is a certain food of which he alone eats. For his nature, exalted above the whole creation and separated from all, causes him to eat as daily bread that which proceeds from the Father’s nature.

Each of us asks for daily bread; and when we ask for daily bread, we do not all receive the same bread, nor bread of the same measure. Rather, in pure prayers, with a clean conscience and in works of righteousness, we eat our daily bread.

If someone is less pure, he eats daily bread in another manner. But may the Lord, who is judge of all, give us living bread, so that, nourished and strengthened by it, we may make our journey into heaven, glorifying almighty God through Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# APPENDIX

## [ON THE LAMENTATIONS OF JEREMIAH]

[Col. 0787]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING TREATISE

The Appendix to the third volume of the Vallarsian edition, besides the following treatise on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, also contained Commentaries on Job of doubtful authenticity. But just as the Italian editor had placed those commentaries there in order to avoid making the volume too thin, so we, taking precautions against the inconvenience of an excessively large volume, have deferred them to the following volume. In every respect the transposition will be reasonable.

As for the little commentary on the Lamentations, let the editor speak:

“Moreover,” he says, “Erasmus had included the treatise on the Lamentations of Jeremiah in his earlier edition among the genuine works, together with the other three books. It was later learned that this work either belonged to Bede or at least appeared to belong to him, whose principal practice was to weave together from the books of the ancients a kind of cento of his own commentaries, in which one finds certain passages copied word for word from the writings of others.”

[Col. 0787]

# ON THE LAMENTATIONS OF JEREMIAH (C, G, S)

[Col. 0787A] And it came to pass, after Israel had been led into captivity and Jerusalem had been laid waste, that Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented this lamentation over Jerusalem, and said:

**Aleph.** How the city that is full of people sits alone!

Just as, among all the songs of the Old and New Testaments, the Song that Solomon sang in the person of Christ and the Church holds first place—to such an extent that, because of its greatness, it is called the Song of Songs—so among all the laments of the Old and New Testaments the Lamentations of Jeremiah possess first place, to such an extent that they may rightly be called the Lamentation of Lamentations.

Finally, it should be known that these Lamentations, which the Greeks call *Threnoi*, were composed among the Hebrews according to the requirements of meter. At the beginning of every sentence, the series of the alphabet is marked in order. But the translator who rendered them from Hebrew into Latin did not wish to insert delays in order to preserve this feature; instead, he placed only the letters of the alphabet at the beginning, because the meaning of the sentence depends upon the interpretation of the letter.

This too should be known: these laments can be referred historically to the people of Israel; spiritually, also according to the letter, to the holy Church, which is the city and people of God; and morally, to each individual soul.

### Aleph

Aleph is interpreted as “doctrine.” True doctrine is knowledge of the holy Trinity, and the knowledge by which a person recognizes his own growth and increase—that is, in what matters he can grow and in what matters he can diminish. But because the Jews, although they possessed this knowledge, did not observe it, that people then sat, and now sits, alone.

How, then, did the city sit alone if it was full of people? This can be explained in two ways: it sat alone because it had once been full of people in the time of David and Solomon; or the city itself sat full of people—that is, that people—because there was a very large number of inhabitants there, but it was alone without God’s help.

This is to be understood metonymically, so that by “city” the people placed in captivity are meant. She became “as a widow, mistress of nations”—that is, Jerusalem, [Col. 0787C] which had once ruled over many nations when she had as her husband the Lord Almighty; when led into captivity, she was like a widow. But she was not [Col. 0788A] entirely a widow, only “as a widow,” because her husband had compassion on her and, after seventy years, joined her to himself.

“Prince of the provinces” means, by implication, prince of those provinces that the kings of Israel had subdued. She was made tributary to the Chaldeans.

Similarly, the holy Church and every soul, often because of their vices, sit alone, deprived of God’s help. They are led by the devil into the confusion of sins and become desolate of their husband, though they had been mistress of many nations. She who had been the ruler of many provinces through the apostles—of whom the Psalmist says, “You will appoint them rulers over all the earth”—is reduced to the devil’s tribute by serving vices.

### Beth

Beth is interpreted as “house.” It signifies that house, namely the Israelite people, whom the prophet Isaiah addresses, saying: “House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.”

This house of the Israelite people wept bitterly in the night while it was being led into captivity, and its tears were upon its cheeks. Literally, it wept at night [Col. 0788B] because it dared not weep by day on account of its masters, but consoled itself by weeping at night. In the higher sense, it wept “in the night,” that is, in captivity and tribulation.

The repetition of the verb—“weeping, she wept”—provides an intensification. “Her tears were upon her cheeks,” that is, upon her rulers. Although everyone wept, those who possessed knowledge wept most of all. Rulers and wiser persons are understood by “cheeks” because, just as food is conveyed from the cheeks into the body, so doctrine ought to have descended from them into the people.

“There is none among all her beloved to comfort her”: namely, none among the prophets, kings, and priests after the Lord’s ascension. These words properly concern the final devastation, after which they had no ruler at all. In the Babylonian captivity, however, they had Daniel and his companions, Ezekiel, and many others.

“All her friends”—that is, the kings of the nations—despised her, or counted her as nothing, and became her [Col. 0788C] enemies. If we refer this to the Church, all the holy angels, her friends, counted her as nothing when they saw that she had been cast down by her Creator; and they seem to be [Col. 0789A] her enemies when they withdraw from her their customary help.

### Gimel

Gimel is interpreted as “fullness.” This is the fullness of sins of which the Lord said to the Jews: “Fill up the measure of your fathers”—that is, what they left incomplete by sinning, complete yourselves. And in Genesis: “For the sins of the Amorites have not yet been filled up.”

Because Judah possessed this fullness of sins, she migrated from her land on account of the affliction with which she was then afflicted by the Chaldeans and afterward by the Romans. Because of the abundance of servitude by which she served the devil, she lived among the nations and found no rest.

All her persecutors—the Chaldeans, that is, and the Romans—seized her amid her distress.

The same may be referred to the holy Church, which is often afflicted because of its sins by pagans and heretics, and is frequently taken captive both by enemies and by demons.

### Deleth

Deleth sounds in Latin like *tabulatum*, “a boarded ceiling.” [Note: [Col. 0789] Through similarity of sound, the author was misled by *tabularum* and *tabulatum*. See the note on Jerome, Letter 30, no. 5.]

And whose boarded ceiling is meant? The house of the Lord; for the house [Col. 0789B] of the Lord has ceilings made of imperishable wood.

“The roads of Zion mourn because there is no one who comes to the solemn assembly.” How can roads mourn? This is said figuratively. “The roads of Zion,” he says, mourn—that is, those who once customarily directed their steps along the roads of Jerusalem at the principal festivals toward the house of the Lord constructed with boarded ceilings, now placed in captivity, mourn. That is, among those passing by, no one will come to the Lord’s solemn assembly.

Or otherwise: “The roads of Zion mourn,” that is, those who pass along them provoke mourning.

Spiritually, by the roads of Zion we should understand the rulers who are later represented by the gates and priests. The rulers and priests who ought to have provided guidance to the people and opened the gates of their life through preaching were placed in captivity and mourned because they had been destroyed and desolated.

“Her virgins are squalid, and Zion herself is oppressed by bitterness.” Not only were the virgins squalid—that is, made dirty in body, although previously they had been exceedingly beautiful—but also [Col. 0789C] virgins in mind, who possessed the integrity of faith. Daniel and his companions, for example, were squalid because of their excessive captivity. Or those who ought to have been virgins by possessing the integrity of faith became squalid with the filth of sins.

All these things can likewise be referred to the Church, whose roads and gates are its prelates and preachers.

### He

He is interpreted as “this,” and the meaning is: These things written here were foretold by the Lord in Deuteronomy, when he commanded Moses to write the curses and blessings: “If you do not keep my commandments,” he said, “I will hand you over to your enemies, and you will be at the tail, while your enemies will be at the head.”

Yet these things did not happen because they had been foretold by the Lord; rather, because they were going to happen, they were foretold by him. And because the people had sinned, these things came upon them.

“Her enemies became the head; her adversaries grew rich,” that is, they became wealthy through her riches. For the Lord had spoken against her, as we said a little above. She who had previously been at the head, mistress of other nations, became a maidservant [Col. 0789D] and tributary.

The remaining matters that relate to the meaning of this letter are sufficiently evident.

### Vau

Vau is interpreted as “and,” which is a conjunction joining what precedes to what follows. It is as though he said in other words: “And because they sinned, all her beauty departed from the daughter of Zion.”

What was her beauty? Her kings and rulers, her priests and prophets, the golden altar, the magnificent temple, the city, and all its ornaments.

All these things departed from the daughter of Zion when Zedekiah was blinded and led to Babylon in a cage like a lion, when her rulers were killed, her altar broken, her temple burned, her city destroyed, and her gold and silver vessels carried to Babylon.

“Her rulers became like rams finding no pasture” when they were oppressed by the Chaldeans’ siege for a year and a half. [Col. 0790A] “And they went away without strength before the face of the pursuer”—namely, the enemy—because none of them was able to resist the Chaldeans.

The same things may be referred to the final captivity and to the Church, both historically and spiritually. Its rulers often seek the pasture of God’s word but do not find it, because the Lord has sent famine upon the land.

### Zai

Zai is interpreted as “these,” and the meaning is: This is the vengeance of almighty God upon Jerusalem, that she should fall into the hand of the enemy.

The sentence is therefore constructed in this way: When Jerusalem fell, and her people into the enemy’s hand, she remembered the days of her affliction, by which she had been afflicted. She remembered her transgression—namely, of God’s commandments—recognizing that she suffered such things because of her sins. She remembered all her desirable things, that is, all the good things she had possessed from ancient days, from the time when she came out of Egypt.

The Chaldean enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths, which she wished to observe in captivity, just as Jews are now mocked by Christians. [Col. 0790B]

Jerusalem, whose name is interpreted as “vision of peace,” signifies the holy Church. When it is handed over into the hands of heretics and pagans, it remembers the transgression of God’s commandments. Its Sabbaths—that is, rest from all works—are mocked by its enemies, namely, the evil spirits, because after they deceive us by their suggestion and make us cease from good works, they insult and mock us.

### Heth

Heth is interpreted as “life.” The interpretation of this element relates to what is said at the end of the sentence: “But she herself groaned and turned backward.”

Here I understand “turned backward” in a good sense. God brings affliction upon every person so that the person may turn from error and live; and whoever has fallen into death through sin may turn from vices to virtues and return to eternal life through lamentation and groaning.

### Teth

Teth is interpreted as “good.” The interpretation of this word likewise relates spiritually to the end of the sentence, where it says: [Col. 0790C] “See, Lord, my affliction.”

For it is good whenever either the holy Church in general, or every soul spiritually, recognizing its guilt, turns toward God’s mercy and says: “See, Lord, my affliction, and have mercy on me, for my enemy”—the devil—“has risen up in pride against me.”

“The filth of Jerusalem is upon her feet,” that is, upon those by whom she ought to have been carried. “She did not remember her end,” that is, those evils that could befall her when the end of death was approaching, or even when Christ came into the world. She did not remember Christ, who is the beginning and the end.

“She was brought down exceedingly,” from the throne of kingdom and priesthood, “having no comforter”—the Holy Spirit, who is called *Paraclete*, that is, Comforter.

### Ioth

Ioth means “beginning” in Latin. What follows are the beginnings of evils, whether for Jerusalem, the Church, or every individual soul.

The beginning of Jerusalem’s ruin was this: the enemy, [Col. 0790D] Nebuchadnezzar—or the Roman army—sent out his hand and took all her desirable things, namely, her kingdom, priesthood, temple, and city.

Spiritually, our enemy is the devil. When he sends out his hand—that is, his activity and evil suggestion—he removes the virtues and good works signified by Jerusalem’s desirable things. Moreover, he leads us into Babylon, that is, into confusion. Israel suffered this then; the Church, or every soul, suffers it daily.

### Caph

Caph is interpreted as “hand.” The hand is the activity of God, rendering to her what she deserves.

“All her people groan and seek bread.” Because the Lord’s hand struck the people, they therefore groaned and mourned while being led into captivity.

### Lamed

Lamed is interpreted as “discipline [Col. 0791A] of the heart.” Discipline of the heart occurs when a person understands his evil, turns from evil to good, and proclaims the just judgment of almighty God to others.

Thus Jerusalem said: “O all you who pass along the road, pay attention and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow.” He had harvested me through the Chaldeans and Romans, leading me into captivity—the one who had once planted me in the promised land.

“And he did this as he had spoken,” through his servants the prophets, “on the day of his wrath,” that is, on the day of vengeance.

### Mem

Mem is interpreted as “from them.” From whom? From those Jews who had perished through unbelief came the apostles, whom the Church now calls “bones,” because they were exceedingly strong in enduring adversity. Just as the body is supported by bones, so the Church is supported by their examples, faith, and teaching.

“Upon them he sent fire from heaven” when, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended upon them in fiery tongues.

“He spread the net of his commandments over my feet.” He turned me backward—that is, from vices to virtues—so that I would not proceed [Col. 0791B] according to the works of the flesh. He left me desolate, deprived of temporal goods [Al. “times”], or of his help and presence, exhausted by sorrow all day long—that is, throughout the whole time.

We have explained this according to the spiritual understanding, first because of the interpretation of the letter, which properly relates to the same meaning. Let us also examine it literally.

Jerusalem says: “From his lofty throne he sent fire”—the fire of tribulation and captivity—“into my bones; and he disciplined me” through tribulation, although I had refused to be disciplined through peace and gentleness.

The remaining matters are clear from the sense.

### Nun

Nun is interpreted as “everlasting.” It should be noted that the things said in this sentence properly concern the time of the final captivity, namely, the day of judgment, when all the reprobate will be handed over to everlasting punishments.

“The yoke”—or condemnation—“of my iniquities has kept watch”: the time of vengeance has arrived. In his hand, that is, in the power of almighty God, all my iniquities have been gathered together and placed upon my neck.

Who [Col. 0791C] has ever seen a yoke keeping watch? By “yoke,” as we have said, vengeance and condemnation are understood. It is said to keep watch when it punishes the guilty, and to sleep when it ceases from scourging.

### Samech

Samech is interpreted as “help.” Because almighty God’s help withdrew from Jerusalem, the Lord himself removed all her magnificent persons from her midst.

### Ain

Ain is interpreted as “fountain” or “eye.” The eye, then, is a fountain of tears. Because the Lord was the winepress of tribulation for the daughter of Zion, the prophet wept and his eye poured forth a stream of tears.

### Fe

Fe is interpreted as “of the mouth,” with “demonstration” understood.

“Zion spread out her hands.” By the spreading out of the hands we should understand the greatest tribulation, which is often shown by the extension of the hands. Women in labor, placed in extreme tribulation and anxiety, customarily extend their hands, fearing death, because they wish to give birth but cannot, [Col. 0791D] and because of the excessive pain that they cannot express with their mouths, they show it by extending their hands.

So Jerusalem, placed in the greatest distress, spread out her hands, but there was no one to comfort her.

### Sade

Sade signifies “justice.” It is just—or justice itself—that a person placed in tribulation should confess that he suffers such things by God’s just judgment and is worthy of greater [Col. 0792A] punishments, because he has transgressed God’s commandments.

Thus he says with Jerusalem: “The Lord is just, because I provoked his mouth to anger.”

### Coph

Coph is interpreted as “calling.” The prophet therefore alluded to the interpretation of the letter and said: “I called my friends, and they deceived me, promising me peace.”

### Res

Res is interpreted as “of the head,” with “understanding” implied.

By the head, therefore, we should understand the mind’s chief faculty, where understanding resides. Just as the limbs are governed by the head, so the will and thoughts are directed by the mind.

“See, Lord, for I am in tribulation; my belly is troubled.” What we should understand by “belly” the same prophet shows elsewhere when he says: “My belly, my belly, I grieve”—that is, the senses of my heart have been troubled.

### Sen

Sen is interpreted as “of the teeth.” What should we understand by teeth? Teeth break and grind food, and through them food is conveyed into the body. We should understand by them the teachers and preachers who ruminate upon God’s [Col. 0792B] commandments and lament their own guilt and falls as well as those of others.

The prophet speaks in their person, saying: “My enemies heard that I groaned, and they rejoiced, because you did this”—that is, you permitted me to groan and them to exult.

What he adds—“You have brought the day of consolation, and those who afflicted me will become like me”—must be referred to the final time, and the past is put for the future. “You will bring,” he says, “the day of my consolation,” and the rest that follows.

“They will become like me,” not in glory, but they will receive things corresponding to what they did to me. In this respect they will become like me: just as I was mourning and grieving while they afflicted me, so they will be grieving and groaning when placed in punishments.

### Tau

Tau is interpreted in the plural as “signs.” Just as the Jews have twenty-two letters, the last of which in their order is tau, so they have twenty-two books in which the complete knowledge of the holy Trinity is contained, since it consists in twenty-two books.

Because they observed the commandments of almighty [Col. 0792C] God narrated in those books, the prophet says: “Let all their evil come before you, and harvest them as you harvested me because of my iniquities.”

We can also speak differently about the interpretation of this letter. I want you to know that among the Samaritans, even to this day, the letter tau has the shape of a cross, although among the Hebrews it has been corrupted. Therefore, by tau, which is interpreted as “signs,” those are understood who bear the sign of Christ’s cross on their forehead and in their heart and believe that they can be saved through faith in Christ’s passion.

After explaining the order of one alphabet, the remaining three that follow are to be understood in the same way. We therefore judged it unnecessary to repeat the same explanation for each one individually.

But I admonish you, reader, that although you may find another interpretation of these letters in other places, you should not therefore reject this one. They require their own exposition and meaning in their respective places, so that they may be joined to what follows, just as in the Psalms one finds [Col. 0792D] that different authors have expounded them differently. Jeremiah therefore composed his Lamentations with a fourfold alphabet because he was lamenting those who, being composed of the four elements, had aroused almighty God’s anger against themselves by transgressing his commands and following the pleasure of the flesh.

[Col. 0793]

# [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF JEROME]

## [Col. 0809]

## PREFACE

This volume, sixth in the division of Jerome’s works, contains the twenty books of commentaries on the twelve minor prophets—that is, as many as Jerome worked out. The sole exception to this recension is the specimen of a commentary on Obadiah, which, in his youth, when he was about to make a trial of his learning, stirred by ardor and study of the Scriptures, he sketched; afterward, when age had more subdued his talent, he himself erased it, and it has long since perished in accordance with his own judgment.

As for what learned men—Tillemont and, following him, Martianay—claim: that there once existed shorter commentaries on the twelve prophets, which either the holy Doctor himself later rejected when he pursued the same work with a fuller pen, or which a later age willingly allowed to perish—concerning this, in the second part of our general preface, where we discussed those writings of Jerome that learned opinion believes to have been destroyed by the injury of time, while we are persuaded, on the contrary, that they never existed, we have argued that this view is contrary to every appearance of truth and have demonstrated it, I think, with good arguments, so decisively that no room for doubt ought to remain.

We said that the error arose from the fact that learned men thought that whenever the holy Doctor says that he had written a commentary on the twelve prophets, each individual prophet must be understood as one on whom he had bestowed his labor in interpretation. On the contrary, simply naming “the twelve prophets” (*duodecim prophetas*), he understood the book properly so entitled. In addition to the testimonies and examples brought forward there on this subject, let this especially clear corollary be added from the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, no. 5. There, when the holy Father is about to cite this distinctive passage from chapter 9 of Hosea—“Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning: all who eat them shall be defiled”—he says that this is found “in the TWELVE PROPHETS” [Note: [Col. 0809] See also the preface to the interpretation from the Hebrew.].

As for the rest, so that I may not repeat what has already been done, if it is worth the trouble, I would prefer you to consult the cited general preface, no. 29.

Now, to speak of the commentaries presented in this volume, which the holy Doctor alone composed and completed, one is first moved to wonder that, although they were all produced by a single author and are filled in the same manner with the most splendid judgments drawn from all antiquity for the investigation of Scripture’s native meaning, some nevertheless seem to surpass others and enjoy greater favor among readers.

Some would have it that those interpreting Haggai excel the rest. Others call the exposition of Nahum more elegant—the very exposition praised by the author himself in the prologues to Obadiah, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah. For the same reason, others prefer the explanation of Hosea, since he commends it in Joel and Amos. If I were to enter upon this debate and argue for the superiority of one over another, I do not know whether I would be doing anything worthwhile; and even if I knew, I would not dare say so. For I see that they all stand with the highest dignity, and I would rather direct the minds of readers earnestly toward the very matters contained in them: the teachings of divine Scripture and true wisdom.

Nevertheless, one point should not be passed over in silence: Saint Augustine thought that the commentaries on Jonah deserved so much esteem that he not only embraced them with great eagerness but also confidently set them against the recently arisen heresy of the Pelagians as strongholds and walls of the most secure faith. He repeatedly professed, in letters that we too have included among Jerome’s, that the Catholic doctrine of original sin was remarkably confirmed by testimonies drawn from that work.

He states this much more clearly in book 3 of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, no. 12:

> “This I know: Saint Jerome, who even today is engaged in ecclesiastical letters with a reputation for outstanding learning and labor, uses this most certain proof, without any debate, to resolve certain questions in his books. For in the commentary he wrote on the prophet Jonah, when he came to the passage where even the little children are mentioned as being chastened by fasting, he says: ‘The older age begins and reaches down to the younger. For no one is without sin, not even if his life should have lasted only a single day, and his years of life are numbered. For if the stars are not clean in the sight of God, how much more the worm and corruption, and those who are held liable through the sin of Adam, who offended.’”

If we could easily ask this most learned man how many interpreters of the divine Scriptures in both languages, and how many writers of Christian disputations, he would recall who, from the time the Church of Christ was established, held no other opinion, received no other teaching from their ancestors, and handed no other teaching on to their descendants, the following words from book 1 *Against Julian*, chapter 7, are closely parallel:

> “Nor should you think Saint Jerome, who was a presbyter, deserving of contempt. He was learned in Greek, Latin, and also Hebrew speech; he passed from the Western Church to the Eastern Church; he lived in the holy places and in sacred letters into extreme old age; and he read all, or nearly all, who before him had written anything about ecclesiastical doctrine in either part of the world. He neither held nor expressed any other opinion on this matter. When he was explaining the prophet Jonah, he said most plainly that even the little children were held liable through the sin of Adam, who offended.”

It seemed worthwhile to set forth testimonies of such authority, so that if other rivals of Jerome’s glory—both ancient and recent—should grumble, you may regard it as of no consequence and pass it by with deaf ears.

Certainly Rufinus—to mention him here for the moment by name—or, more truly, the uncertain author of the book on Hosea appended to Rufinus, when he says that in these commentaries on the minor prophets Jerome’s entire aim was to heap together the interpretations of others, especially those of Origen, and the traditions of the Hebrews, without troubling himself to investigate coherence, condemned himself more by the charge of envy than he harmed the holy Doctor by his criticism.

For what, in truth, was more dear to Jerome than ensuring that the allegories themselves were linked together in a single continuous sequence and flowed spontaneously toward the truth of the history? Indeed, one may see him rejecting the expositions of others in six hundred passages for no other reason than that they were not sufficiently well joined either to what preceded or to what followed. He does this so often that to want merely to touch briefly upon the more illustrious passages would be the act of someone abusing his leisure.

It is better that you understand this from the writings themselves than by any other method. To enable you more easily to obtain the proper fruit from your reading of them, I shall first explain, as it were, their historical setting and chronology in the customary manner. I shall ask this as the reward for my labor: that what I shall explain later you may first learn from the author himself, who, in the preface to the third book on Amos, explained the whole matter to Pammachius in its several parts as follows:

> We began, and, with Christ’s help, shall complete, the work on the Twelve Prophets in an inverted and confused order. For we did not discuss them from the first to the last according to the order in which they are read; rather, we discussed them as we were able and as we were asked. First I addressed Naum, Micah, Zephaniah, and Haggai to the most industrious Paula and her daughter Eustochium; second, I dedicated two books on Habakkuk to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia; third, after a long silence, I expounded Obadiah and Jonah for you, who had commanded me to do so. In the present year—which was named in the consular records of the sixth consulship of Augustus Arcadius and of Anicius Probus—I interpreted the prophet Malachi for Exuperius, bishop of the Church of Toulouse, and for Minervius and Alexander, monks of that same city. Immediately returning to the beginning of the volume, I could not refuse you Hosea, Joel, and Amos. Now that this order has been established, it is easy to assign each book to its proper time.

The four whom he names first—Naum, Micah, Zephaniah, and Haggai—must accordingly be assigned to the year 392, as must the fifth, Habakkuk. This is confirmed by the place they occupy at the end of the Catalogue, which was certainly drawn up by the holy Doctor in that very year. In the passage addressed to Paula, it is worth noting, they are listed here in an order different from that in which he discussed them above:

> I wrote two books of Explanations on Micah. One book on Zephaniah. One book on Naum. Two books on Habakkuk. One book on Haggai. And I now have many other works on the prophetic writings in hand, which are not yet completed.

For almost three years thereafter he refrained from the undertaking, being occupied with other affairs. He did not set his hand to the Commentaries on Jonah—whom he mentions third—before the year 397. He himself provides especially weighty testimony to this in the prologue:

> About three years have passed since I interpreted the five prophets Micah, Naum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai; and, being detained by another work, I could not complete what I had begun.

A little later he adds:

> Therefore, after so long a time, as though by a kind of restoration to my former status, I take up the interpretation beginning with Jonah.

He confirms the same point when, among the works he wrote in the interval, he also mentions the Epitaph of Nepotianus—or the Letter numbered 60 in our recension—which, as we have demonstrated in its proper place, certainly belongs to the earlier part of the preceding year.

We need not linger over Tillemont, who presses this testimony and insists that “four years” should be written instead of “three,” despite the unanimous opposition of the manuscripts and printed books—and, more importantly, of the actual chronological sequence. We have sufficiently refuted this conjecture of an otherwise most learned man, to whom we attribute the highest distinction, in the Chronological Notes on Letters 57 and 60 of our recension.

I cannot, however, pass over another matter, which I see led him into error through a preconceived opinion. He maintains that when Jerome praises the Commentaries on Jonah in connection with the third chapter of Zephaniah, those Commentaries must already have existed. Since he does not doubt that they are later than the work on Zephaniah, and argues this at excessive length, he attempts to escape the difficulty by claiming that shorter Commentaries, which we have shown nowhere to have existed, are indicated there as though by a finger. He thinks he has found in this a decisive means of establishing his thesis, with the author himself, as he believes, guaranteeing it.

Yet none of what he imagines can be found in that passage or anywhere else. On the contrary, although the holy Father frequently cites testimonies from Jonah there as occasion requires, he makes not the slightest mention of any Commentary on that prophet composed by himself. This very silence is most useful for blowing away that opinion.

To return, however, to the genuine Explanation of Jonah under discussion: another testimony of the same holy Father, in the Commentaries on the twelfth chapter of Matthew, does not permit us to date it later than the year 397:

> Concerning this [namely, the sign of Jonah], we have discussed more fully in the Commentaries on the prophet Jonah.

There is therefore no doubt—and we shall prove it in its proper place by the most certain arguments—that the holy Doctor expounded Matthew with a very rapidly moving pen by the middle of the following year, 398.

The Explanation of Obadiah is also assigned by learned scholars to this same year, as are the Commentaries on Jonah; indeed, they assert that it preceded the latter in order and chronological priority. Their apparently most certain argument is drawn from Jerome’s own testimony, which we have just quoted from the preface to the Commentaries on Amos:

> Third, after a long silence, I expounded Obadiah and Jonah for you, who had commanded me to do so.

Nevertheless, I am persuaded of something quite different; and, with due respect to the commonly accepted opinion, I am so far from considering these works contemporary that I would rather place the work on Obadiah a full five years later.

I shall explain why that testimony should not be accepted—or at least how it should be understood. Jerome joins this pair of prophets in a single enumeration, not because he expounded both in the same year, but because he wished to indicate the order, or place, which they occupied in relation to the explanations of the others. He places them in the third series, or, as it were, class; and this was both entirely accurate and fully sufficient for his purpose. He had not set out to define the number of years covered by the class itself.

When he says that, after a long silence, he set his hand to interpreting these two prophets, he leaves the matter of the interval open to the reader. Indeed, if I understand him correctly, he subtly indicates that the long period—although its precise duration is uncertain—should be placed not before the prophets whom he lists in the second class, but between the interpretations of Jonah and Obadiah themselves.

Certainly, a period enclosed within three years cannot properly be called “long” in Jerome’s mind. It can rightly be so called if, as we have proposed, the five-year interval between Jonah and Obadiah is included in the reckoning. Therefore the holy Father ought not to have divided the two works into separate classes according to their dates. Although they are widely separated in time, and although the interval from Jonah to Obadiah is greater than that between the preceding class and Jonah, they were deliberately included in a single series, since throughout that entire period he interpreted no other prophets and dedicated these two works to one and the same Pammachius.

Once this has been established—the sole purpose of the discussion—Jerome placed Obadiah first for no other reason than that he recalled the prophets in the more obvious order of Scripture, as they follow one another. Otherwise, it is impossible to suppose that he first devoted his labor to Obadiah, given the contrary evidence.

What, indeed, could be clearer than these words in the prologue to Jonah itself?

> After so long a time I take up the interpretation beginning with Jonah.

There is therefore nothing on which the common opinion rested. The reason why we extend these Commentaries over five years, or to the year 403, must now be explained.

The preface to this very book supplies the principal argument, through the sequence of events it recounts. Jerome says that, from the time when he had attempted a specimen of this Commentary in his youth, he had already labored for thirty years in God’s service and work. He explains below what that period was:

> When, my Pammachius, we had left the school of the rhetoricians and were being carried along by different pursuits; when Heliodorus, dearest to me, and I were striving to live together in the solitude of Chalcis.

This is a clear indication of the year 373, which we have established quite plainly from the evidence of Jerome’s travels and of his earlier writings, as may be seen from the chronological arguments attached to Letters 1 through 12.

If thirty further years are added to the year 373—the years that, as he himself says, elapsed between the exercise of his youthful talent and this work of mature old age—we arrive at the year 403, to which we have assigned the book. We attach so much importance to this calculation that, if it is preserved, everything remains sound; but if one adopts another calculation, one must overturn both the traces of Jerome’s life and the order and dates of many of his writings.

The matter is straightforward concerning the remaining Commentaries: those on Zechariah and Malachi, and the three others on Hosea, Joel, and Amos. The testimony of the holy Father, quoted so often, leaves nothing for critical observation to add, and binds them all quite clearly to the same year—the year named in the consular records of the sixth consulship of Augustus Arcadius and of Anicius Probus. This is the year 406, not 408, as Martianaeus mistakenly concluded after Victorius. All the records of antiquity agree on this date.

[Col. 0815]

# Three Books of Commentaries on the Prophet Hosea by Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Priest of Stridon, Addressed to Pammachius

[Note: We read Jerome’s Commentaries on all twelve prophets contained in this volume against two most ancient Palatine-Vatican manuscripts, numbered 173 and 174. We also consulted, for the six later prophets, manuscript no. 93 belonging to the Queen of Sweden, a very old and carefully corrected codex. In part we consulted now one, now another, together with other manuscripts of the highest quality, which we shall cite in their respective places.]

## Prologue

[Col. 0815A] If, in explaining all the prophets, we need the coming of the Holy Spirit, so that the writings composed under his inspiration may be disclosed by his revelation; and if we read in Isaiah and in the Apocalypse that a book was sealed—one which the scribes and Pharisees, who boast that they know the letters of the Law, cannot read because it is sealed—and that no one could be found except the Lion from the tribe of Judah, whom God the Father sealed and who alone could open its mysteries: how much more must the Lord be entreated in explaining the prophet Hosea, and how much more must we say with Peter, “Explain this parable to us” (Matt. XIII, 16).

This is especially so since the author himself testifies at the end to the obscurity of the book:

> “Who is wise and shall understand these things, intelligent and shall know them?” (Hosea XIV, 10.)

We must take this not as referring to impossibility but to difficulty, in accordance with the saying of the Gospel:

> “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the master appointed over his household?” (Matt. XXIV, 65.)

For who would not immediately be scandalized at the beginning of the book and say: Hosea, the first of all the prophets, is ordered to take a prostitute as his wife—and he does not object? He does not even pretend to be unwilling, so that he may appear to undertake a shameful act reluctantly; rather, he carries out the command gladly, as though he had desired it, as though he regretted having devoted himself to chastity for so long. Yet we read that holy men refused more honorable commands, and commands involving no sin, when the Lord ordered them.

[Note: The word “ordering” (*jubente*) is absent from the Palatine manuscripts and from Victor’s edition.]

Moses is sent to Pharaoh and appointed leader of the Israelite people; yet he answers not from weakness but from humility:

> “Provide someone else whom you may send” (Exodus IV, 13).

Jeremiah says that he is a child, lest he rebuke Jerusalem when it sins (Jeremiah I).

Ezekiel is ordered to make from every kind of legume and seed a single cake and bake it in human dung; and he says:

> “By no means, Lord, for nothing unclean has ever entered my mouth” (Ezekiel IV, 14).

But Hosea, hearing the Lord say to him, “Take a wife of prostitution” (Hosea I, 2), neither wrinkles his brow, nor shows grief by pallor, nor displays shame by changing the redness of his cheeks [Alternative: “shame by changing the color of his cheeks”]; rather, he goes to the brothel and takes a prostitute to his bed. He does not initiate her into the chastity of a married woman; instead, he proves himself lustful and debauched. For “he who clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her” (I Corinthians VI).

What, then, can we answer when we hear these things except the prophetic saying:

> “Who is wise and shall understand these things, intelligent and shall know them?” (Hosea XIV, 10.)

Therefore we too must say with David:

> “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm CXVIII, 18);

so that the King may bring us into his chamber (Song of Songs I), and remove from us the veil that was placed before Moses’ eyes in the reading of the Old Testament (Exodus XXXIV; II Corinthians III).

For as soon as the Lord said, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,” and, having said this, expired (Luke XXIII, 46), the veil of the Temple was torn and all the secrets of the Jews were laid open.

The fountain that went out from the house of David [Alternative: “of the Lord”] entered the sea of the wilderness; and the true Elisha seasoned sterile and deadly waters with the salt of his wisdom and made them life-giving (IV Kings IV). The Marah of the Law, whose name means “bitterness,” was sweetened by the wood of the gallows (Exodus XV).

[Note: Erasmus and Marianus corrupt this passage while trying to correct it: disregarding the authority of the manuscripts and relying excessively on their own conjectures, they change whatever they please. They read, “Marah, or Marath, the waters of the Law, which means bitterness,” etc. Following the context and the authority of the manuscripts, we restore “and the Marah of the Law,” as the manuscript of Saint-Cyran reads, although others retain *myrrh* for *Marah*. Martianaeus.—The older printed editions read, “Marah (or Marath), the water of the Law,” etc.]

We understand who Judah was, the patriarch chosen as king, and are not surprised that the holy man entered in to Tamar as though she were a prostitute (Genesis XXXVIII); why Samson, whose name means “sun,” loved Delilah, whose name is rendered “poor,” and, having been mocked and killed because of her, slaughtered thousands of his enemies (Judges XVI); why Salmon, a righteous man, fathered Boaz by Rahab the prostitute, and why Boaz, covering Ruth the Moabite with the corner of his cloak, brought her—lying at his feet—to the beginning of the Gospel (Ruth I–III).

What is the reason that, although David had so many wives, he made no one else his successor to the kingdom except the one born from Bathsheba (III Kings I), so that not only prostitutes but also adulteresses seem to please God?

Accordingly, in this very prophet we read that the man who was first joined to a prostitute is afterward joined to an adulteress, when the Lord says to him:

> “Go again, love a woman beloved by a friend” (Hosea III, 1),

or, alternatively, “one who loves evil” [Alternative: “evil”], “and an adulteress.”

This is the prostitute and adulteress who washed the Lord’s feet with her tears in the Gospel, wiped them with her hair, and honored them with the ointment of her confession. When the disciples, and especially the traitor, expressed indignation that the ointment had not been sold and its price distributed as food to the poor, the Lord answered:

> “Why do you trouble the woman? She has performed a good work upon me. For you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me” (Matthew XXVI, 10–11). [Alternative: “you have” for “you will have.”]

And lest we think that what she had done was insignificant, or that pure nard—that is, the most faithful ointment—should be referred to something else rather than to the Church, he gives us an occasion for understanding and promises great rewards for great faith, saying:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her” [Alternative: “of me”].

This is the prostitute of whom the Lord speaks to the Jews:

> “Amen, I say to you, prostitutes and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matthew XXI, 31).

For you refused to receive the Son sent to you by the father of the household, the Lord of the vineyard who planted it.

This prostitute received my two exceedingly brave spies with kindness, hid them carefully, lifted them onto the roof, and covered them with stalks of flax (Joshua II)—one of whom I sent to the circumcision and the other to the nations. Cut down by persecutions and washed in baptism, she changes her color and is transformed from black to white.

Nor is it surprising that we should recall these events as figures of the Lord Savior and of the Church gathered from sinners, since in this same prophet he says:

> “I shall speak to the prophets; I multiplied visions, and I was represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hosea XII, 10),

so that whatever the prophets are commanded to do may be referred to my likeness.

His wife is an Ethiopian woman, against whom Aaron and Miriam—the carnal priesthood of the Jews and the prophecy enslaved to the letter—murmur and offend God (Numbers XII). She says in the Song of Songs:

> “I am dark and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song of Songs I, 4).

Otherwise, if we maintain that everything commanded is actually performed for the sake of being made a likeness, then Jeremiah too, girded with a loincloth—a woman’s garment—went among countless nations, including the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the bitterest enemies of the Jews, to the Euphrates, in order to hide his loincloth there; and after a long time he returned and found it rotten and useless (Jeremiah XIII).

How could he have left and traveled so far when Jerusalem was under siege, with fortifications, ditches, ramparts, and citadels built all around it? When he once wished to leave for his village of Anathoth, situated three miles from the city, he was seized at the gate, brought back to the rulers, beaten as a traitor, and thrown into prison.

If that event occurred figuratively because it could not have happened literally, then this one too occurred figuratively because, if performed literally, it would be most shameful.

But you will answer: “When God commands, nothing is shameful.” We reply that God commands nothing except what is honorable, and that by commanding shameful things he does not make shameful things honorable. Since we know that God wills nothing except what is honorable, he commanded what is honorable.

I have spoken at such length at the beginning in order first to resolve the most difficult question and, with God’s help, pass beyond the obstacle at the very end to secure ground.

[Note: Thus reads the manuscript of the monastery of Cluny, which we have followed. Another copy, from Saint-Martin-des-Champs, preserves a different reading, namely, “and the opposite stumbling-block at the very end.” The same reading occurs in the manuscripts of Saint-Albin of Angers and Saint-Cyran, except that they read “obstacle” instead of “stumbling-block.” Erasmus preferred to supply on his own: “the hidden obstacle at the very end,” and Marianus follows him. Our manuscripts read *obpositum* or *oppositum*, as do some of those used by Martianaeus.]

I am not unaware, dearest Pammachius, that many churchmen have passed over this matter. Among those who attempted to explain it, I found among the Greeks Apollinaris of Laodicea. In his youth he left brief little commentaries on this and other prophets, touching their meaning rather than explaining it. Later, when asked to write more fully on Hosea, he did so; the book came into our hands, but even it, because of its excessive brevity, cannot lead the reader to complete understanding.

Origen wrote a small book on this prophet, to which he gave the title *Περὶ τοῦ πῶς ὠνομάσθη ἐν τῷ Ὠσηὲ Ἐφραΐμ*—that is, “Why Ephraim is called Ephraim in Hosea”—wishing to show that everything said against Ephraim must be referred to the person of the heretics. He also wrote another volume, *ἀκέφαλον καὶ ἀτέλεστον*, “without a head and unfinished,” lacking both beginning and end.

I also read an extremely long treatise by Pierius, which he delivered at the beginning of this prophet in an impromptu and eloquent discourse on the day of vigil for the Lord’s Passion.

Eusebius of Caesarea, in the eighteenth book of the *Εὐαγγελικὴ ἀπόδειξις*—the *Evangelical Demonstration*—also discusses certain matters concerning the prophet Hosea.

About twenty-two years ago, when I was in Alexandria at the request of your holy and venerable mother-in-law—or rather, your mother—Paula (for the former name belongs to the flesh, the latter to the spirit; she has always burned with love for monasteries and the Scriptures), I saw Didymus and frequently listened to him, the most learned man of his age. I asked him to complete what Origen had not done and to write Commentaries on Hosea. At my request he dictated three books, and five more on Zechariah.

Origen himself wrote only two volumes on Zechariah, scarcely explaining a third of the book, from its beginning to the vision of the chariots.

[Note: Understand this as denying that Origen wrote a complete Commentary on Hosea, not as denying that he wrote short books on certain parts of the prophet. See Huet, *Origenian*, p. 251, no. 11.]

[Note: Didymus also dedicated the books to himself, as Jerome himself reports in the Catalogue and in his final Apology against Rufinus. The same is attested by the scribe of the Palatine codex, who reads: “three books addressed to me, when I was able,” etc. Damascus quotes some fragments from Didymus’ work in the *Parallels*.]

I say these things so that you may know which predecessors I had in the field of this prophet. Yet, to confess candidly and without arrogance—as one of my friends is always whispering—I did not follow them in everything. I preferred to be a judge of their work rather than merely its interpreter, stating what seemed to me correct in each matter and what I had scarcely received from one or two teachers among the Hebrews.

Among the Hebrews themselves such a teacher is now a rare bird, since they all pursue luxuries and money, care more for the belly than the heart, and consider themselves learned if, in the shops of physicians, they disparage the works of everyone else.

But it is now time, after setting out the prophet’s words, to explain what has been written.

# Book One

[Col. 0819]

## 1. Chapter I, verse 1

> “The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri.”

The Septuagint has the same wording.

The Word of the Lord, which in the beginning was with God the Father, and the Word was God, came to Hosea son of Beeri, so that it might also make the prophet a god, as the Savior says:

> “If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be annulled—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John X, 35–36.)

Thus, just as God makes gods and stands in the assembly of gods, judging among the gods (Psalm LXXXI); and just as he himself is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John I), and says to the apostles, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew V, 14), so the Savior himself makes his prophet a savior.

For Hosea means “savior” in our language. This was also the name of Joshua son of Nun (Numbers XIV), before God changed his name. For he was not called Ause—as the Greek and Latin manuscripts incorrectly read, a name that has no meaning at all—but Hosea, that is, “savior.” The name “Lord” was added to it, so that he might be called “the salvation of the Lord.”

This savior, then, is the son of Beeri, that is, “of my well”—the wells that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob dug, and which the Philistines were always trying to fill in (Genesis XVI, XXI, XXVI, XLVI).

There is this difference between a well and a pool—that is, a cistern: a well contains perpetual waters flowing from a living spring, whereas a cistern, which provides cooling, possesses waters that are foreign and brought in from elsewhere.

Therefore God says through the prophet Jeremiah:

> “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah II, 13).

Of this fountain the psalmist cries out to God:

> “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm XXXV, 10).

Some therefore think that *Beeri* means “my light,” but the translation given above is the correct one.

> “In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.”

The Septuagint has the same wording.

Azariah, also called Uzziah, of the line of David, reigned in Jerusalem over the two tribes called Judah for fifty-two years. His son Jotham succeeded him and reigned for sixteen years; after him his son Ahaz likewise reigned for sixteen years.

[Note: I restored this entire passage from the manuscript of Saint-Albin of Angers, since it is most corrupt in the other manuscript copies and in the edition of Erasmus. Martianaeus. Instead of “sixteen,” the Palatine manuscripts prefer “fifteen” here and in the preceding verse. They also continue the formerly printed reading in the following manner: “In his eleventh year the ten tribes called Israel were captured by Shalmaneser, king of the Chaldeans, and settled in the mountains of the Medes. After Ahaz, his son Hezekiah reigned for twenty-eight years.” Victorius had previously restored the passage to its present form. His judgment concerning the ancient reading was as follows: “No one will doubt that it is false and erroneous. Two errors are evident in it. First, it asserts that the ten tribes were captured during the reign of Ahaz, and that this occurred in his eleventh year, whereas they went into captivity under Hezekiah, in his sixth year, as is clearly established in IV Kings XVIII: ‘In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria, besieged it, and captured it.’ For three years later, in the sixth year of Hezekiah—that is, the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel—Samaria was captured, and the king of Assyria transferred Israel to Assyria and settled them in Halah and Habor, by the river of Gozan, in the cities of the Medes. The second error is that it says Hezekiah reigned for twenty-eight years, whereas he reigned for twenty-nine, as stated in IV Kings XVIII and II Chronicles XXIX.” The errors have been removed with the aid of the sacred manuscripts in the following manner: “After him his son Ahaz reigned for sixteen years. After Ahaz his son Hezekiah reigned for twenty-nine years; in his sixth year the ten tribes called Israel were captured by Shalmaneser, king of the Chaldeans,” and so forth. The first error was easily removed by restoring to its proper place the verse that had been lying below. Martianaeus likewise appealed to the manuscript of Saint-Albin of Angers. See the *Chronicle*, no. 1272.]

After Ahaz, his son Hezekiah reigned for twenty-nine years. In his sixth year the ten tribes called Israel were captured by Shalmaneser, king of the Chaldeans, and settled in the mountains of the Medes.

It is therefore clear that, while Hosea, Isaiah, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah—who were his contemporaries—were prophesying, the kingdom of the ten tribes came to an end. That kingdom had lasted 250 years, from the first king, Jeroboam, to the last, Hosea.

[Note: The manuscript of the monastery of Cluny reads without a number of years; I do not hesitate to prefer it to the others, both because of its antiquity and because of its elegant script and careful hand. Others read, “was reigning over Israel in the twelfth year,” which Marianus showed to be false against Erasmus; see their editions. Martianaeus.—Again the Palatine manuscripts, together with the old printed books, insert “the twelfth year,” words which Martianaeus deleted on the authority of the Cluny manuscript. Victorius was content to observe in his Notes: “This ancient reading too is false; for instead of ‘twelfth’ one must read ‘twenty-seventh,’ according to IV Kings XV: ‘In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah began to reign.’ No one will doubt that Uzziah and Azariah are the same person if he reads IV Kings XV and II Chronicles XX.”]

At the time when Uzziah began to reign over Judah, Jeroboam, great-grandson of Jehu, was reigning over Israel. The Lord had promised that Jehu’s descendants would reign to the fourth generation, because he had struck down two wicked kings, one of Judah and one of Israel.

[Note: The word “saw” is found neither in our manuscripts nor in Victorius.]

We say this briefly to show you that the prophet Hosea prophesied both before and after Israel’s captivity; that he saw and announced what was near, what was present, and what was past; that he foretold what was to come, mourned what was approaching, and reworked the past for Judah’s correction. We shall attempt to establish this according to the historical sense in the prophet himself.

Uzziah means “strength of the Lord”; Jotham, “the Lord’s consummation and perfection”; Ahaz, “strength”; Hezekiah, “the rule of the Lord.” These kings ruled over the people of Judah, whose name means “confession.”

In Israel, however, which had made idols for itself and had been separated from the people of God, Jeroboam was reigning.

[Note: Drusius has noted very learnedly and, in my opinion, most correctly that the name Joash has fallen out of Jerome’s text through the error of scribes and should be restored as follows: “Jeroboam, son of Joash, who is interpreted as *χρονισμός*.” Yet Jeroboam cannot mean *χρονισμός*, that is, “temporality” or “delay,” nor did the ancients ever possess this etymology of his name; rather, it belonged specifically to Joash. Jeroboam, by contrast, is commonly interpreted as *δικασμὸς λαοῦ*, “judgment of the people.” Jerome himself writes in Amos I, 1: “Jeroboam, *δικασμὸς λαοῦ*, that is, judgment or cause of the people; Joash, *Κυρίου χρόνισμα*, that is, the Lord’s delay or temporality.” The sacred text of Hosea itself requires that the two words be restored: “In the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel,” and so forth.]

Jeroboam is interpreted as *χρονισμός*, that is, “temporality” or “delay,” because he loved the world and thought that to linger in it for a long time was life, delighting not in future things but in present ones.

## Verse 2

> “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea.”  
> Septuagint: “The beginning of the word of the Lord to Hosea.”

As we said above, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah are placed in the title before the other prophets because they prophesied during their reigns. Therefore he now says that, among all these kings, the Lord first spoke in Hosea and afterward to the others.

There is, however, a difference between saying that the Lord speaks “in Hosea” and that he speaks “to Hosea.” When he speaks “in Hosea,” he does not speak to Hosea himself but, through Hosea, to others. When he speaks “to Hosea,” he is understood to direct the speech to Hosea himself.

Others do not think that Hosea was the first of all the prophets on the basis of the words, “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea”; rather, they understand them to show that the Lord first spoke to Hosea the things that follow.

> “And the Lord said to Hosea: Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution.”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord said to Hosea: Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution.”

The Hebrew word *ZANUNIM* [Note: One Palatine manuscript has *ZANNIN*.] does not mean “a prostitute” or “prostitution,” as most think, but signifies “many prostitutions.” From this it is shown that the woman whom the prophet takes as his wife had prostituted herself not once but repeatedly, so that the more sordid she was, the more patient the prophet might be in taking such a wife.

And what is added is:

And [Vulgate: “Make for yourself”] children of fornication; for the land, by fornicating, will fornicate away from the Lord. LXX: And children of fornication, for the land, by fornicating, will fornicate after the Lord. By the shared construction—*ἀπὸ κοινοῦ*—the following is understood: “Take for yourself a wife of fornication, and take for yourself children of fornication.” Both possibilities can be understood: either that he receives the children whom the prostitute had previously conceived from fornication, or that he himself fathers children by the prostitute, who are therefore called children of fornication because they were born of a prostitute. Nor should the prophet be blamed—so long as we follow the historical sense—if he converted a prostitute to chastity; rather, he should be praised for making a good woman out of a bad one. For one who remains good is not himself polluted if he associates with evil; rather, the evil person is turned toward good if he follows the examples of the good. From this we understand that the prophet did not lose his chastity by being joined to a prostitute; instead, the prostitute acquired the chastity that she previously lacked—especially since blessed Hosea did this neither for the sake of lust, nor of sexual desire, nor by his own will, but obeyed God’s command, so that what we read as having happened carnally in this man, we might recognize as having happened spiritually in God. He took to himself the Synagogue, that is, the Jewish people, enslaved to fornication and lust. To her the Lord speaks through Ezekiel: “And you, prostitute, hear the word of the Lord: for her breasts were broken in Egypt” (Ezek. 23:3); she wallowed in blood and had been polluted to the crown of her head, so that no part of her body or limbs was free from the stain of disgrace. The Lord covered such a woman with a cloak, joined her to his embraces, gave her honey, oil, and fine flour to eat, clothed her in the most precious garments, placed jeweled ornaments around her neck, adorned her ears with gold and the most precious stone, and also gave bracelets to her arms, so that she might perform good works. Nevertheless, scorning this generosity and goodness of her husband and forgetting her former shame, she followed Chaldean, Assyrian, and Egyptian lovers, who are “great of flesh.”

[Col. 0823C] We have spoken in the preface about the type of the Savior and the Church: that he took for himself a prostitute as wife, one who had previously served idols. But if some contentious person, especially one of the gentiles, refuses to accept this as spoken figuratively and mocks the prophet for being joined to a prostitute, we may confront him with what Greece is accustomed to praise and the schools of philosophers applaud. Why do they praise the highly learned Xenocrates, who made Polemo—a most dissolute young man, drunk among female harpists, flute players, and immodest women, and crowned with ivy [Note: The Palatine manuscripts do not recognize the word “ivy.”]—obey wisdom, and transformed the most depraved youth into the wisest of philosophers? Why do they raise Socrates to heaven, because he transferred Phaedo—the title of Plato’s book comes from his name—from a brothel, where, because of his master’s cruelty and greed, he served the lust of many, into the Academy? Whatever they may answer concerning those teachers of philosophy, we apply it to the defense of the Prophet.

We have said these things against the pagans and those who resemble pagans. To our own people, however—those who nevertheless wish to accept the truth—we should briefly show that, from the statement, “For the land, by fornicating, will fornicate against the Lord,” it is not so much the prophet who is joined to a prostitute as the entire human race that has withdrawn from fellowship with the Lord. Since the phrase “the whole land” has not been added, it can now be understood as referring to Judea, or specifically to Samaria and Israel—that is, the ten tribes—which at the time when these things were spoken had withdrawn from the Lord.

### (Verses 3–4)

And he went and took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived and bore [Vulgate adds: “to him”] a son. And the Lord said to him: Call his name Jezreel, for in a little while I will visit the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will bring the kingdom of the house of Israel to an end. LXX: And he went and took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to him: Call his name Jezreel, for in a little while I will avenge the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Judah, and I will bring the kingdom of the house of Israel to an end.

The prophets promise, many centuries in advance, the coming of Christ and the calling of the gentiles in such a way that they do not neglect the present time, lest they seem to address an assembly convened for another purpose without teaching about what is at hand [Variant: “what stands before them”], and instead amuse themselves with uncertain and future matters. Accordingly, this Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, who is taken by Hosea as his wife, conceives by him and bears him a son named Jezreel—whose name means “seed of God”—and for whose blood Jehu overthrows the kingdom—or, as an erroneous tradition has it, Judah. All this must be referred to the calling of the nations in such a way that it corresponds to the time under which she is said to have borne a son.

So that I do not delay the reader’s eagerness with a lengthy treatment: these two women—one called Gomer, who is a prostitute and bears three children, first Jezreel, second a girl called “Without Mercy,” and third a boy who is himself called “Not My People”; and the other woman, who is purchased for fifteen silver pieces, a *kor*, and half a *kor* of barley, and is called an adulteress—refer to Israel and Judah: that is, to the ten tribes that were in Samaria under King Jeroboam, who was from Ephraim, and to Judah, which ruled in Jerusalem from the line of David.

These are the two women who, in Zechariah, are said to have the wings of a hoopoe, or a kite, or a heron, and to go to the land of Shinar, where Babylon was founded. Under the name of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah signify these women; they are represented by the two staffs that Ezekiel joins into one staff. Since we are writing commentaries, not extensive volumes, reserving separate explanations for each chapter in its proper place, let us now discuss only the present chapter.

Gomer is interpreted as *τετελεσμένη*—that is, “completed” or “perfected”; others think it signifies *θώρακες*—that is, “breastplates.” Some conjecture that it means “measure” or “bitterness,” which they would say correctly if the word did not contain the letter *gimel*. *Diblaim* means *παλάτας*, “fig-cakes,” of which there is a very abundant supply in Palestine and which the prophet Isaiah commands to be applied to the ulcer of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 2; Isa. 38). It is a mass of fat figs, which they shape like bricks, then press and pack together so that they may remain unspoiled for a long time.

Thus Israel, completed and perfected in fornication—the daughter of pleasure, who seems sweet and pleasant to those who enjoy her—is taken by Hosea as a wife in the type of the Lord and Savior. And the first son born from her is the son of God, namely Jezreel. Jezreel is the metropolitan city of the ten tribes, in which Naboth [Variant: Nabutha] was killed; on account of his blood Jehu was raised up, and he destroyed the house of Ahab and Jezebel.

But because Jehu himself, the avenger of righteous blood, entered upon the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to fornicate and set up golden calves in Dan and Bethel (1 Kings 12), his kingdom too is said to be destined for overthrow. Under his great-grandson Jeroboam, Hosea began to prophesy; after Jeroboam’s death, his son Zechariah succeeded him in the kingdom, and in the sixth month of his reign Shallum, born from another line, killed him (2 Kings 15). For this reason it is now said: “In a little while I will visit the bloodshed of Jezreel”—that is, the slaughter of my people—upon the royal house of Jehu, which at that time ruled Israel.

Nor is it surprising that the house of Jehu should be overthrown, since even the kingdom of the house of Israel—that is, the ten tribes—was to be completely destroyed after not many years. From Zechariah son of Jeroboam, whose great-grandfather was Jehu, until the ninth year of Hosea, under whom the ten tribes were led into captivity, forty-nine years are reckoned. After Zechariah was killed—the last of the line of Jehu—the Assyrian kings immediately captured Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, which were beyond the Jordan; then many cities of Samaria; then all Naphtali; and finally all the remaining tribes.

In place of Jehu, the Vulgate edition reads Judah. But this seems to me to have arisen not through any fault of the Septuagint translators, but through the ignorance of scribes who, not knowing Jehu and finding Judah the more familiar name, wrote “Judah.” The type of the seed of God and the vengeance for his bloodshed refer to the Lord’s Passion, on account of which both the house of Judah and the kingdom of all Israel are said to be destined for overthrow.

### (Verse 5)

And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel. The LXX is the same.

When I have avenged the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read “the house of Judah” instead of “Jehu”], and have destroyed the kingdom of Israel through the victory of the Assyrians, then, on that day and at that time, I will break all the strength of the army of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.

We said above that Jezreel, which is now near Maximianopolis, was the metropolis of the kingdom of Samaria [Note: The same manuscripts have “on account of which,” instead of “near which.”], near which there are extremely broad plains and a valley of immense extent, stretching for more than ten thousand paces. In the battle fought there, Israel—that is, the ten tribes—was struck down by the Assyrians. Because of Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim, who first caused the schism in the people, they were called Ephraim. At times, because of Joseph, who was Ephraim’s father, they are called Joseph; sometimes they are called Samaria, which was itself another metropolitan city of the ten tribes and was later called Augusta by Caesar Augustus—that is, *Σεβαστή*—where the bones of John the Baptist were buried.

After the division of the two and the ten tribes, because of the great majority of the population that followed Jeroboam, the former name “Israel” remained with the ten tribes. Because of the tribe of Judah, which ruled in Jerusalem, the other tribes were called Judah. At the same time, the truth of the type is made clear.
