Just as the house of Ahab was destroyed because of the blood of Naboth [Variant: Nabutha], which was shed in Jezreel, so that Elijah’s prophecy might be fulfilled, so the kingdom of the Jews was destroyed because of the blood of the true Jezreel—that is, the seed of God.

In all the prophets, but especially in Hosea, the ten tribes refer to heretics, whose multitude is very great; the two tribes called Judah possess the person of the Church, which ruled [Variant: “rules”] under the line of David. Therefore the bow of the heretics, of whom it is written, “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. 77:9), will be broken in the valley of the seed of God, concerning whom they formed lowly and earthly opinions.

### (Verses 6–7)

And she conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said to her: Call her name “Without Mercy,” for I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them. And I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the Lord their God; I will not save them by bow, or sword, or war, or horses, or horsemen.

LXX: And she conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said to her: Call her name “Without Mercy,” for I will never again continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will oppose them and utterly oppose them. But I will have mercy on the sons of Judah, and I will save them by the Lord their God; I will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by war, nor by horses, nor by horsemen. [Note: Victor prefers to transpose “by bow and sword,” in accordance with the Hebrew and the Greek-Latin context.]

After Israel’s bow had been crushed and broken in the valley of Jezreel, and the kingdom of the ten tribes had been abandoned so that they were led into captivity, Jezreel—that is, “seed of God”—is no longer born as a son, a male child. Instead there is a daughter, a female of fragile sex, exposed to the insults of her conquerors, and she is called “Without Mercy.” She was led into captivity because she had not obtained the mercy of God.

The Lord’s indignation must also be considered: he says that he will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but will erase them from his memory in eternal oblivion, because to this day they serve the kings of Persia and their captivity has never been released. To the house of Judah, however, he promises mercy and says that he will save them in the Lord their God—either in himself, who is speaking, or the Father will save them in the Son, in accordance with what is written: “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Gen. 19:24).

For he saved them even when Israel was handed over to the Assyrians, from the hand of Sennacherib—not by bow, sword, war, or a multitude of horsemen, but by his own strength, when he sent an angel and struck down 185,000 of the army of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, in one night (2 Kings 19).

In accordance with the type, we say that those who, because of the blood of the seed of God, are called “Without Mercy,” and who dared to say, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25), have continued to serve the Romans to this day. But the house of Judah—that is, those Jews who confessed the Lord—were saved not by the strength of armies but by the preaching of the Gospel.

What we have interpreted concerning Israel and Judah both historically and typologically, let us apply to the gatherings of heretics and to the Church of the Lord and Savior: when those others had been abandoned “Without Mercy” and had lost their kingdom, the Church overcame by the power of her God.

### (Verses 8–9)

And she weaned her who was “Without Mercy”; and she conceived and bore a son, and he said: Call his name “Not My People,” for you are not my people, and I will not be yours. The LXX is the same.

He who had been called the seed of God, changed into a female because of weakness of strength and because he had offended God, and led into captivity because he did not have the Lord’s mercy, is not said to have been weaned, but to have been weaned as a girl [Variant: “as a female”]; for he had already lost the strength of a man. One who is weaned withdraws from the mother and no longer feeds on the parent’s milk but is sustained by external nourishment.

So Israel, cast off by the Lord, surrounded by the constraints of captivity, and sustained in Babylon by unclean foods, is called “not the people of God.” It is struck by the eternal sentence of a foreign nation, so that it is called “Not My People” and rejected [Variant: “renounced”] forever. We may rightly understand this both of the entire Jewish people, which, because it offended the seed of God, was handed over to captivity, lost its kingdom and province, and is called “not the people of God,” and of heretics.

But if some contentious interpreter refuses to accept what we have said and understands the prostitute named Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, to have borne first and third sons and the second child, the middle one, a daughter, wishing Scripture to convey precisely what is read, let him explain how he interprets the passage in Ezekiel where the Lord commands him to bear the iniquities of the house of Israel—that is, of the ten tribes—and to sleep continually on his left side for 390 days, although in the LXX 190 days are written, sleeping in such a way that he never wakes and does not change sides, unless perhaps, satisfied with sleep, he opens his eyes for a little while to eat the most filthy food of a cake baked under ashes, made from wheat, barley, beans, lentils, and millet, cooked in human dung.

Nature does not permit this: that any human being should sleep for 390 days always on one side. And again, he says: “You shall bear the iniquities of the house of Judah, and for forty days you shall sleep on your right side.” These days are reckoned as years [Variant: “were reckoned as years”], during which Israel and Judah are held under siege and in an exceedingly long captivity [Note: Again, two Palatine manuscripts have “will be pressed down,” instead of “are held”], so that, bound and immobile, they cannot turn from one side to the other.

If he cannot prove that these things and others like them, which we read in the Holy Scriptures, actually happened, but insists that they signify something else, then this prostitute and the other adulterous woman, who were either joined to the prophet or kept by the prophet, likewise indicate not a shameful union of fornication but mysteries of things to come.

### (Verse 10)

And the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured, and it shall not be counted. And in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” it shall be said to them, “Children of the living God.” And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head, and they shall go up from the earth, for great is the day of Jezreel.

LXX: And the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted. And in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” they shall be called children of the living God. And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one ruler, and they shall go up from the earth, for great is the day of Jezreel.

We have read of the rejection of the ten tribes and of Israel, which cannot be measured [Note: “Measurable” has been restored from the same manuscripts, as required by the sacred text itself, which had previously declared Israel to be without measure; the earlier reading was “pitiful”], condemned by perpetual indignation and no longer the people of God. Now we learn how the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, appoint for themselves one head or principality [Variant: “beginning”], go up from the earth, and, in the place where it was formerly said, “You are not my people,” be called children of the living God. This will happen because the day of Jezreel is great.

To one who is uncertain and wavering among various interpretations, the words of the apostle Paul in his letter to the Romans come to mind: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, so that he might show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—those whom he also called, us not only from the Jews but also from the gentiles—as he says in Hosea: ‘I will call the one who was not my people, my people; and her who had not obtained mercy, one who had obtained mercy.’ And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people’; there they shall be called children of the living God.”

Isaiah, however, cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved. For he will complete and cut short the word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.” And as Isaiah foretold (Isa. 1:9): “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.”

What then shall we say? “That the gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness—the righteousness that is from faith; but Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness” (Rom. 9:22 ff.).

Therefore the blessed apostle, taking up the testimony of the prophet Hosea and explaining it concerning the calling of the gentiles and the faith of those Jews who wished to believe, has cut away every difficulty of interpretation for us. He asserts that in the time of Christ this was fulfilled: namely, that in Israel the twelve tribes would be chosen—that is, the entire Jewish people—and in Judah those from the gentiles who confess Jesus as Lord. [Note: In place of “Jesus the Lord,” the Palatine manuscripts prefer “the dominion of the Lord.”]

But if someone alien to the faith of Christ and unwilling to accept the authority of the New Testament, yet belonging to the number of the circumcised, answers that “the children of Judah and the children of Israel” refer to the two and the ten tribes, about which we have often spoken, we shall concede this without showing any harm to our faith.

After the number of the children of Israel has become like the sand of the sea, scattered throughout the whole world, and the multitude of the people has surpassed every reckoning, then Israel—which even today remains captive and was formerly called “Without Mercy” and “Not My People”—will have the opportunity to enter into concord with the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, a great part of whom has believed in Christ. Thus faith will join together those separated in body, and they will appoint for themselves one head and prince, concerning whom Ezekiel wrote: “And there shall be one prince in their midst, David my servant, and they shall rise again like the dead from the underworld” (Ezek. 34:24)—namely, Judah and Israel, who had died in unbelief.

All these things will happen because great is the day of the seed of God, which is interpreted as Christ. From this it is clear that the blood of Naboth [Variant: Nabutha] the Jezreelite preceded as a type so that the truth might be fulfilled in Christ. For the day of Jezreel is great not in Naboth but in Christ, of whom it is said: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:24).

The sense of the third interpretation that we have adopted—understanding Israel as heretics and Judah as the people of the Church—is this: after the Lord has come to reign in his glory, those who were formerly called “not his people” will be called children of the living God, when they have been joined to Judah, that is, to the Church of God, have Christ as their one head, and have gone up from the earth—that is, from earthly ways of thinking and from the lowliness of the letter—and have received the great day of the seed of God.

In place of *οὐκ ἠλεημένη*, “Without Mercy,” some copies are reported to read *οὐκ ἠγαπημένη*, “Not Loved.” [Note: Saint Jerome prefers the other reading—“and not loved, loved”—in Letter 120 to Hedibia, question 10. The Vulgate retains both readings.] But the copies that have “Without Mercy” are more reliable, especially because, by way of distinguishing Israel, on whom he does not have mercy, God adds: “But I will have mercy on the house of Judah.”

### Chapter 2—Verse 1

Say to your brothers, “My People,” and to your sister, “She Who Has Obtained Mercy” [Variant: plural, “Those Who Have Obtained Mercy”]. LXX: Say to your brother, “My People,” and to your sister, “She Who Has Obtained Mercy.”

Because the day of Jezreel is great, on which Judah and Israel will have one ruler, and Israel will no longer be called “Not My People” but, on the contrary, will be called children of the living God, therefore, O men of the tribe of Judah, do not despair of the salvation of the ten tribes. Instead, summon them daily, by speech, prayer, and letters, to repentance, because they are called your brother and sister: brother, because it is said, “My People”; sister, because she is called “She Who Has Obtained Mercy.”

Alternatively: You who believe in Christ and are from both Jews and gentiles, say to the broken branches and the former people who have been cast off, “My People,” because he is your brother, and “She Who Has Obtained Mercy,” because she is your sister. For when the fullness of the gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11:25). The same command is given to us: not to despair completely of heretics, but to summon them to repentance and desire their salvation with the affection of kinship.

### (Verses 2–3)

Judge your mother, judge her, for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband. Let her remove her fornications from her face and her adulteries from between her breasts, lest perhaps I strip her naked and set her up as on the day of her birth.

LXX: Be judged together with your mother, be judged, for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband. I will remove her fornication from my face and her adulteries from between her breasts, so that I may strip her naked and restore her according to the day of her birth.

Up to this point the speech has been directed to the people of Israel, that is, the ten tribes. Now another section begins, and the children—that is, the people—are commanded to enter into judgment against their mother, who gave birth to them. Having been made a wife from a prostitute, she did not abandon her former ways and again fornicated with her lovers.

Observe the husband’s clemency. She has already been repudiated; she has already been cast off; he has already said to her, “She is not my wife, and I am not her husband.” Nevertheless, he commands the children not to speak to the wife whom their father dismissed [Note: Thus the Palatine manuscripts; the earlier reading was “whom he dismissed”], but to their mother, who gave birth to them. They are to speak to her in order to summon her to repentance, so that she may remove her fornications from her face and her adulteries from between her breasts.

A prostitute is one who is joined to many. An adulteress is one who abandons one husband and joins herself to another. Both descriptions apply to the Synagogue. If she persists in fornication and adultery, God will remove from her the clothing and ornaments that he had given her. Concerning these Ezekiel writes: “On the day when you were born, they did not bind your breasts, nor were you salted; and I passed by you and saw you naked, defiled, and sprinkled with blood” (Ezek. 16:4–5). And shortly afterward: “I clothed you with fine linen and delicate fabrics, surrounded you with ornaments, gave bracelets for your hands, and a necklace around your neck.”

The most generous husband gave these things to her when he found her in Egypt, defiled by the lust of idolatry and spreading her legs to everyone. And now he threatens that, if she is unwilling to return to her husband, she will become without God [Note: Some books corruptly read “without the true and eternal God”] and without a husband, just as she had previously been in Egypt.

So that we do not continually extend our volumes with a threefold interpretation, it should be enough to have noted this rarely: these statements apply both to Jews who deny Christ and to heretics who abandon faith in the Lord. Their fornication is properly “between the breasts,” and in their hearts they turn over the craft of idols and various doctrines; they will return to the day of their birth, so that, if they do not repent, they may be compared with the gentiles.

And I will make her like a wilderness, and I will set her like an impassable land, and I will kill her with thirst [Vulgate: “in thirst”].

LXX: And I will make her like a desert, and I will set her like a waterless land, and I will kill her with thirst.

If she is unwilling to turn toward better things, I will do to her what I did in the wilderness: those led into captivity will fall in a foreign land, suffering thirst for every good thing, and they will be unable to return to their homeland. Or certainly let them hear in the Gospel: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23). And the Lord will send her not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord (Amos 8). Isaiah likewise speaks of this: “They shall be like a garden that has no water” (Isa. 1:30). Heretics who have been cast off by the Lord, if they do not return to their former house, will suffer such poverty in all things that even what they seem to possess falsely will be reduced to nothing.

### (Verses 4–5)

And I will not have mercy on her children, for they are children of fornication, because their mother has fornicated. She who conceived them has been put to shame, for she said: “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread, my water, my wool, my flax, my oil, and my drink.”

LXX: And I will not have mercy on her children, for they are children of fornication, because their mother has fornicated. She who bore them has been put to shame, for she said: “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my clothing and my linen, my oil, and everything that I need.”

This is what I will do further to her to whom I said, “She is not my wife, and I am not her husband,” and whom I will make like a wilderness and set like an impassable land. For when I brought her out of Egypt, after killing her parents, their children entered the promised land. Now, however, the children of the prostitute mother will perish with their adulterous mother, because they are children of fornication, and evil offspring born from evil.

To them it is said in the Gospel: “Generation of vipers” (Matt. 3:7). She has reached such shamelessness that she hears through Jeremiah: “You have acquired the face of a prostitute; you have become shameless” (Jer. 3:3). Is this not hard-faced and prostitute-like shamelessness: to glory in her crime and say, “I will follow my lovers; I will go to the idols that supplied me with everything necessary for food and clothing”?

Everything that the prophetic word describes, the Jews received spiritually from the Lord. And because they denied the Son of God, choosing for themselves Barabbas, the author of robbery and sedition, and crucifying the Son of God (John 18), they continue to follow demons to this day and attribute God’s benefits to those who destroyed the souls of their worshipers.

Heretics too have bread and water: their bread is mourning, and their waters are muddy, suffocating and killing those who have been baptized. They have wool from scabby sheep, and flax that persists in blackness, and oil concerning which the prophet says: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Ps. 140:5), and the drink of the waters of Egypt, concerning which Jeremiah cries: “What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of the Gihon?” (Jer. 2:18). And: “What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the waters of the rivers?” We have briefly run through everything, so that we may proceed to what remains.

### (Verses 6–7)

Therefore, behold, I will fence in your way with thorns, and I will fence her in with a wall, and she will not find her paths. She will pursue her lovers but will not overtake them; she will seek them but will not find them; and she will say: “I will go and return to my former husband, because it was better for me then than now.”

LXX: Therefore, behold, I will fence in her way with stakes and block her paths, and she will not find her path. She will pursue her lovers but will not overtake them; she will seek them but will not find them; and she will say: “I will go and return to my former husband, because it was better for me then than it is now.”

The prostitute had said: “I will go after my lovers, who have provided me with an abundance of everything.” The Lord replied: “I will fence your way with thorns,” or stakes, so that you cannot go where you desire. I will place between you a wall—or rampart—and you will not find your paths, which you had often worn down with your feet, so that you cannot overtake those whom you followed with such devotion. Compelled by necessity, you will return to your husband and say what is found in the Gospel: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread, while I perish here from hunger! I will arise and go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.”

From this we understand that, by God’s providence, evils often befall us so that we may not obtain the things we desire, and that, oppressed by various calamities and miseries of this world, we may be compelled to return to God’s service.

As the lovers of Jerusalem and the Jewish nation, in accordance with the history of that time, we should understand the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Egyptians, and the other nations whose idols she fornicated with, from whom, in times of war and under the pressure of evils, she vainly hoped for help. In the spiritual sense, heretics follow these lovers; often abandoned by them, they return, under the weight of their evils, to the bosom of the mother Church. For Israel is instructed through every scourge and torment.

### (Verse 8)

And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied silver for her; and they made these things for Baal.

LXX: And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied silver for her; but she made these silver and gold things for Baal himself.

He responds to what came before. She had said: “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread, my water, my wool, my flax, my oil, and my drink”—all of which she had received in order to turn them toward the worship of God.

But she turned into idols the bread and wine that strengthen and gladden the human heart (Ps. 103), the oil that illuminates every person coming into this world (John 1), the silver concerning which we have often spoken: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11:7); and the gold of which we read: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the backs of her wings are green with gold” (Ps. 67:14). She turned these things into idols and made Baal, whose name means “the higher one” and “devouring”: either because she thinks that she has doctrines higher than those of the Church, or because she is devoured in the very knowledge of her false opinion.

As for the fact that Jerusalem, in the literal sense, abounded in gold, silver, and every kind of wealth, and made idols for Baal, the demon of the Sidonians—or, as some more correctly judge, the Babylonian demon, from whom he is also called Bel—Ezekiel sets it out more fully in his own book, and the entire chorus of the prophets relates it.

### (Verse 9)

Therefore I shall return [Vulgate: “I shall turn”] and take away my grain at its proper time, and my wine at its proper time, and I shall reclaim my wool and my flax, which covered her shame.

**LXX:** Therefore I shall return and take away my wheat at its proper time, and my wine at its proper time, and I shall remove my garments and my linens, so that they may no longer cover her shame.

The punishment is more severe when, at the time of the expected harvest and vintage, the crops and wine are taken away, and, so to speak, what has been grasped is snatched from one’s hands. But if at the time of the threshing floor and the winepress, when the earth makes up for its former barrenness by bringing forth new crops, there is scarcity of everything, what should we suppose about the rest of the year, when the old stores are preserved?

The wool and flax—or the garments and linens—are reclaimed so that they may no longer cover the harlot’s shame; that is, so that she may be stripped of God’s protection and the guardianship of all the angels appointed by him may depart. Hence the Apostle also says that creation will be liberated from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. VIII).

[Note: The reading *olim, erat liberatam* (“formerly, she had been liberated”) stood in the text; Victor preferred *liberandam* (“to be liberated”), corresponding to the Greek ἐλευθερωθήσεται.]

Many have received the gold and silver of wisdom and eloquence, from which they made a seven-branched lampstand of purest gold, a golden table of the Presence, an expiation-cover, and Cherubim radiant with the splendor of gold; silver bases for the columns; the grain of God’s word; and the wine that is the joy of the Holy Spirit. They also received garments and linens with which believers would be clothed in Christ. But they turned all these things to the worship of idolatry, composing various doctrines of error; and, deceived, they deceived others. God will take all these things away, so that those who had not recognized the giver in their abundance may recognize him in their poverty.

### (Verses 10–12)

“And now I shall reveal her foolishness in the eyes of her lovers, and no man [variant: *and no one*] shall rescue her from my hand. I shall bring all her joy to an end—her solemn feast, her new moon, her sabbath, and all her festival seasons. I shall ruin her vine and her fig tree, of which she said, ‘These are my wages, which my lovers have given me’; and I shall make her into a forest, and the beast of the field shall devour her.”

**LXX:** “And now I shall reveal her uncleanness in the sight of her lovers, and no one shall rescue her from my hand. I shall turn away all her joys, her solemn feasts, her new moons, her sabbaths, and all her festivals. I shall destroy her vine and her fig trees, of which she said, ‘These are my wages, which my lovers have given me’; and I shall make her a testimony, and the beasts of the field shall eat her.”

[Note: In accordance with the manuscript evidence, we have removed the words “the birds of heaven and the reptiles of the earth,” which had previously been placed here in advance, since they recur immediately afterward in their proper place.]

What follows—“the birds of heaven and the reptiles of the earth”—should be marked beforehand with an obelus (÷). Instead of “forest,” which is *JAR* in Hebrew [note: the Palatine manuscripts read *JAIR*], whence *CARIATH JARIM* [Hebrew], “village of forests,” the LXX translated “testimony,” because of the similarity between the letters RES and DALETH. For if DALETH is read in place of RES, the word means “testimony,” provided only that the letter JOD does not precede it.

When, therefore, the garment and linen have been removed so that they may no longer cover the shame of the fornicator, all the disgrace of Jerusalem—or her foolishness, through which she committed her disgrace—will be revealed in the sight of her lovers, so that those who desired her while veiled may despise her when she is exposed. And when she has been handed over to her lovers, the Assyrians—or the demons, whom both she and the Assyrians serve—“no one,” he says, will be able to rescue her from my hand. Thus the weakness of the demons will be demonstrated: those who had received her when she abounded in every possession cannot free her when she is overwhelmed by evils.

Once she has been handed over to Babylonian captivity, she will no longer be able to celebrate the three solemn feasts of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles. She will not be able to rejoice in the new moons, that is, the kalends, nor in the sabbaths, nor in all the festivals that he gathers under one name. Her vine and fig tree, too, and the abundance of all things will be ruined. In the vine understand joy; in the fig tree, pleasantness and sweetness—things removed by the evils of the most grievous slavery. They will be removed for this reason: she regarded them not as gifts bestowed by God, as by a husband, but as things assigned by her lovers to a harlot as payment for her lust.

Then she will no longer have fruit-bearing trees; everything will be turned into a forest. And because he had once begun the metaphor with forests, he brings it to its conclusion, calling the enemies by whom everything is to be devoured “beasts.”

Unhappy Judaea suffered these things both according to the historical sense and according to the moral interpretation. All her disgrace was revealed in the eyes of the nations, and no one could rescue her from the hands of God. All her ceremonies ceased; her festival was turned into mourning. She now recognizes that everything she thought was given to her by demons has been taken away because of God’s displeasure. First the Assyrians and Chaldaeans devoured her, then the Medes, Persians, and Macedonians; finally the fiercest beast tore her apart—the empire of the Romans, whose name is suppressed in Daniel so that the terror of those who are to be devoured may be increased.

What we have said about Judaea should be referred to heretics. At first appearance they promise doctrine and knowledge; but, having gone out from the Church, they are abandoned by God, and all their shame is displayed before the eyes of those whom they had previously deceived. Handed over to the beasts whom the prophet avoids naming, they will be abandoned to their bites, as he says: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. LXXIII, 19).

### (Verse 13)

“And I shall punish her for the days of the Baals, when she burned incense to them and adorned herself with her earrings and her necklace; and she went after her lovers, while she forgot me, says the Lord.”

**LXX:** “And I shall take vengeance upon her for the days of the Baals, when she sacrificed to them; and she put on her earrings and necklaces, and went after her lovers; but she forgot me, says the Lord.”

He preserves the character of a harlot, who adorns herself with gold and jewels in order to please her lovers, acquiring by art whatever beauty she does not possess by nature. These earrings, with which her ears had been adorned by God’s teaching, and these pearls hanging preciously from her neck, so that the bridegroom and husband had said to her, “Your neck is like necklaces” (Song I, 9), she cast before swine’s feet and gave what was holy to dogs (Matt. VII). And what we read in Proverbs was fulfilled: “As a golden earring in a pig’s snout, so is beauty in a wicked woman” (Prov. XI, 12).

She did all these things in order to follow her lovers and abandon her husband. So great was her desire for pleasure and lust that she lost every memory of her marriage and forgot that she had been a wife. Therefore, during the very solemn feasts on which she burned incense to the demons, she will be visited with blows and chastised with punishments.

“Baal,” in the singular, and “Baalim,” in the plural, designate the same idols, in the masculine gender. Wherever in the Hebrew language we find the syllable *-im* at the end of a word, it is plural and masculine; where we find *-oth*, it is plural and feminine. Thus we understand *Seraphim* and *Cherubim* to be plural in number and masculine in gender. *Sabaoth*, however, translated “of the armies,” “of hosts,” or “of powers,” is plural in number and feminine in gender. Thus *Baalim* is masculine and plural.

[Note: Earlier editions omit the Greek articles τῇ and ταῖς, which the manuscript codices retain; without them the sense is unclear. MART.]

Nevertheless, some incorrectly read τῇ Βαάλ and ταῖς Βααλεὶμ [variant: βαλὶμ] in the feminine gender. How heretical teachers deceive their lovers, how they adorn themselves with the beauty of eloquence and the arrangement of words in order to make lies resemble truth, how they abandon marital chastity and burn incense to the Baals—that is, to idols they have fashioned from their own hearts—we see every day. They do not care about rustic simplicity, which seeks no harlot’s adornments, but about the elegance and artistry of falsehood, so that they may please their lovers, the devils and demons.

[Note: Our manuscripts read *mendacio* (“falsehood”), which is equally satisfactory; shortly afterward they read *simplicis rusticitatis* (“of simple rusticity”) instead of *rusticae simplicitatis* (“of rustic simplicity”).]

### (Verse 14)

“Therefore, behold, I shall allure her; I shall lead her into the wilderness, and I shall speak to her heart.”

[Note: From the same manuscripts we have supplied here the remainder of the verse: “and I shall give her vinedressers from that place, and the Valley of Achor for opening hope.” In agreement with the LXX: “and I shall give her possessions from there, and the Valley of Achor for opening her understanding.” In the books generally published until now, these words had been separated into another chapter, contrary to the sequence of the exposition that follows and to the mind of the holy Doctor.]

“And I shall give her vinedressers from that place, and the Valley of Achor for opening hope.”

**LXX:** “Therefore, behold, I shall seduce her and place her as a wilderness; and I shall speak to her heart, and I shall give her possessions from there, and the Valley of Achor for opening her understanding.”

For our “for opening hope,” which the LXX translated “for opening her understanding,” Symmachus interpreted εἰς θύραν ἐλπίδος, that is, “into a door of hope.” Theodotion has ἀνεῴξασθαι τὴν ὑπομονὴν αὐτῆς, that is, “to open her patience,” or “her expectation.”

[Note: Instead of ἀνεῴξασθαι, our manuscripts prefer ΑΙΑΝΟΙΞΑΙ, that is, διανοῖξαι, “to open completely,” the verb also used by the LXX.]

After the shame of Jerusalem—or of Judaea, the harlot—has been revealed in the eyes of her lovers; after every solemn feast has ceased; after the vine and fig tree have been ruined by drought or hail and, reduced to forests and fruitless trees, have been devoured by beasts; and after the Lord has repaid her with afflictions and torments because she burned incense to the Baals and thought that she could never rise again from ashes and embers—then, that is, at the coming of Christ his Son, he will open the hope of salvation, grant a place for repentance, and speak tenderly to her. For this is what “I shall allure her” signifies: after the greatness of her punishments, he softens her former pains by promising prosperity.

“And I shall lead her,” he says, “into the wilderness,” that is, I shall bring her out from evils, just as formerly I brought her out of Egyptian slavery. “And I shall speak to her heart”—gentle words, words of consolation—so that I may temper sadness with joy, according to the idiom of the Scriptures. With such words Shechem also spoke to Dinah’s heart (Gen. XXXIV), and Joseph spoke in Egypt to his sorrowful and fearful brothers (Gen. XL), so that grief might be changed into joy.

What follows:

### (Verse 15)

“And I shall give her vinedressers from that place.”

[Note: Here too, compelled by the correct sequence of the discourse, we have restored the text in accordance with the Palatine manuscripts.]

Because he had previously mentioned tenderness and the wilderness in the likeness of those who went out from Egypt, where Moses and Aaron became leaders of that same Jewish people, he now likewise promises that he will give her vinedressers from that same place.

That Israel is to be understood as the vine is attested by all the Scripture of both the Old and the New Testament: “The vine of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V, 7); and, “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Ps. LXXIX, 9). In the Gospel also (Matt. XXI), a householder leased his vineyard and received no fruit. After killing his son, he finally leased it to other vinedressers.

This, therefore, is what the prophetic word promises: that the leaders of this vineyard, coming forth from the nations and from captivity to enemies—or to vices—will be of that very race of Jews, namely, the apostles. The place of tumult and valley of disturbances—for this is what Achor means—will be changed into a door of hope, or into a place for opening hope and patience. She suffered punishments and torments for this reason: so that through them she might reach prosperity.

As for the fact that the Valley of Achor, where Achan was killed for stealing what had been consecrated to God, is interpreted as “disturbance” and “tumult,” some do not think it means διαστροφή, that is, “perversity.” Jesus himself explains it when speaking to Achan: “Because you have troubled us, may the Lord trouble you on this day” (Josh. VII, 23). Hence that place was called [Hebrew] *EMEC ACHOR*, that is, “the valley of disturbance.”

[Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read *ANEC*; read *AMEC*. Shortly afterward, *prope fluenta* (“near the streams”) was printed; the manuscripts have *propter* (“because of” or “alongside”).]

At the same time, we understand here that, at the beginning of the Holy Land, near Jericho, when the people had come out of the wilderness, sorrow was changed into joy beside the streams of the Jordan, in Israel’s first victory. Hope was opened there where despair had existed: those who had sinned against Christ and committed sacrilege were punished, while those among them who had detested the blaspheming Jews and, so far as it lay within them, had killed them, were saved.

The Circumcision and our Judaizers refer this to the thousand-year reign. Yet we see that it was fulfilled already at the beginning through the apostolic vinedressers and the many thousands of believers from Israel, and that it is fulfilled daily in those who are willing to believe.

[Note: Marianus, following his usual practice and most ineptly, changes the word *circumcision* into *concision* and *pericope*, not understanding that Jerome calls the Jews “the Circumcision,” in accordance with the usage of the Apostle Paul. MART.—For Victor’s reading *concisio*, as if the text had περικοπήν, one of our manuscripts, written by a second hand, agrees. It is clear, however, that here “circumcision” denotes the Jewish people.]

What we said, “I shall allure her,” and what the LXX translated, “I shall seduce her,” they refer to the time of Antichrist: those who did not receive Christ’s truth will receive his falsehood, and afterward, when Christ comes, they will be saved.

“And she shall sing there according to the days of her youth and according to the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt.”

**LXX:** “And she shall be humbled according to the days of her infancy and according to the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt.”

Where we placed “she shall sing,” and the LXX translated “she shall be humbled,” the Hebrew has written *ANATHA* [Hebrew]. Symmachus interpreted it as “she shall be afflicted”; Theodotion rendered it “she shall answer”; Aquila, “she shall obey,” that is, ὑπακούσει. We accept it more literally from the Hebrew, κατὰ λέξιν, that is, “she shall lead the singing,” because, having once mentioned the throwing out and leading into the wilderness, the vineyards from that place, and the Valley of Achor, and having briefly touched upon the whole history of those who went out from Egypt and proceeded toward the Holy Land, he now likewise preserves the likeness of that history.

Just as at that time, when they were going out from the land of Egypt, after Pharaoh had been drowned in the Red Sea, Miriam took a tambourine and, leading the singing before the others, rejoiced and said, “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. XV, 1), so now also, according to the days of her youth—or her adolescence—when she went out from the land of Egypt, let her sing and rejoice, and let her proclaim the reign of Christ and her salvation amid the choirs of the Church.

Observe also that when we come out of Egypt and pass to better things, we are said to ascend, because Jerusalem is situated in the mountains. From it, whoever wished to descend to Jericho was wounded (Luke X). But to those who seek the aid of Egypt, that is, of this world, it is said: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help” (Isa. XXXI, 1).

Aquila’s and Theodotion’s interpretations—of whom one wrote ὑπακούσει, that is, “she shall hear,” and the other ἀποκριθήσεται, that is, “she shall answer”—agree with ours: when some lead the singing, others respond by singing along.

But “she shall be humbled” and “she shall be afflicted,” as the LXX and Symmachus translated it, does not suit a time of joy, unless perhaps she will imitate Paul, who, after being called as an apostle, mourns his former sins and says that he is unworthy of the apostolic calling because he persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor. XV). Thus the humiliation and affliction should be understood as arising from consciousness of a former wound, not from sorrow over present evils.

[Note: The text incorrectly had “those who lead the singing”; the manuscript reading is “when others lead the singing.”]

### 24 (Verses 16–17)

“And it shall be on that day, says the Lord: She shall call me, ‘My husband,’ and she shall no longer call me ‘My Baal.’ I shall remove the names of the Baals from her mouth, and she shall no longer remember their name.”

The LXX likewise.

All Greek and barbarian histories relate that Ninus, son of Belus, first ruled over all Asia. Among the Assyrians he founded a city called Nineveh after himself, which the Hebrews call Nineveh. His wife Semiramis, concerning whom many remarkable things are reported, built the walls of Babylon. The distinguished poet bears witness to this, saying:

> Semiramis is said once to have surrounded  
> the city with baked bricks.

[Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, 58.]

He fought a great and vigorous war against Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, and attained such glory that he made his father Belus into a god. In Hebrew he is called *BEL* [Hebrew], and in many prophets, especially in Daniel according to Theodotion, this is the name used for the Babylonian idol.

The Sidonians and Phoenicians call him *BAAL* [Hebrew].

[Note: Our manuscripts consistently aspirate the form, *Bahal*.]

For the vowel letter AIN is placed between the consonantal letters BETH and LAMED; according to the usage of that language, the name is now read *Beel*, now *Baal*. Thus Dido, a Sidonian woman of royal lineage, when she had received Aeneas as a guest, poured wine to Jupiter from this cup:

[Note: Virgil, near the end of the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> Here the queen called for a cup heavy with gems and gold,  
> and filled it with unmixed wine, a cup  
> which Belus and all those descended from Belus were accustomed to use.]

We have learned the origin of a demon—or rather, of a human being consecrated into a demon; for all idols arose from the error concerning the dead.

Let us hear the rest. In the Hebrew and Syriac languages, *BAAL* means ἔχων, that is, “having.” If we wish to say “having me,” we say *BAALI* [Hebrew]. Among both peoples, wives call their husbands *Baali*, that is, “my husband,” which means “the one who has me”; the sense is, “the one who possesses me in marriage.”

In that same Hebrew language, a husband is called *IS* [Hebrew]. Hence the wife, who was taken from a man, is called *ISSA* [Hebrew] in Genesis (Gen. II, 1), as if from *is*, “man”: “woman.”

What the Lord therefore says is this: although “my husband” or “my spouse” may be called by both expressions, *ISSI* and *BAALI*, I hate the names of idols so deeply that, because of the ambiguity and similarity of the word, I do not wish even what may properly be said to be spoken. Instead, let me be called *ISSI* rather than *BAALI*, lest, while one thing is being said, another be remembered, and while the husband is named, an idol be imagined.

Forgive the obscurity, which arises in three ways: from the difficulty of the subject, from the teacher’s lack of skill, or from the learner’s excessive slowness. In explaining a Hebrew prophet, I ought not to amuse myself with little rhetorical declamations, nor sing in the Asiatic manner through narratives and epilogues, but, with the help of your prayers and your extraordinary zeal for learning, to open what has been closed.

Finally, Aquila, a careful and inquisitive interpreter, says: “She shall call me, ‘My husband,’ and she shall no longer call me, ‘My possessor,’” that is, *BAAL*.

### (Verse 18)

“And on that day I shall establish a covenant for them with the beast of the field, with the bird of heaven, and with the reptile of the earth. I shall shatter bow, sword, and war from the land, and I shall make them sleep securely.”

**LXX:** “And on that day I shall establish a testament for them with the beasts of the field, with the birds of heaven, and with the reptiles of the earth. I shall shatter bow, sword, and war from the land, and I shall make them dwell in hope.”

When all the names belonging to an opposing religion have been removed from the people who confess the Lord, and, he says, she has called me “my husband,” and no longer “my Baal,” that is, “my idol,” then I shall establish for them a covenant and concord with the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the reptiles of the earth.

Isaiah also speaks of this time: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid. The calf, the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together, and a little boy shall lead them. The calf and the bear shall feed, and their young shall rest together; and the lion shall eat straw like an ox” (Isa. XI, 6–7). The lion will no longer desire flesh and blood, but will feed on clean and simple foods.

When Peter was commanded by revelation to receive Cornelius from the nations (Acts X, 15), he was ordered to eat all the beasts and to recognize that nothing was unclean if it was received with thanksgiving. Concerning these things he later hears: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Eph. II, 1).

Therefore, at the coming of the Lord and Savior, after the triumphs of his resurrection and his ascent to the Father, two walls were joined by him through the cornerstone, he who made both [variant: *utraque*] one.

He called the one who had been called “without mercy” one who had obtained mercy, and the one who had been called “not my people” his people. When all things had been pacified, bow, sword, and war would be shattered. The instruments of combat will not be necessary, since those who fight will no longer exist.

Israel will be joined to the nations, and the word of Deuteronomy will be fulfilled: “Rejoice, nations, with his people” (Deut. XXXII, 43). For “God is known in Judaea; his name is great in Israel.” And: “His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV)—that is, in the Church, in which he has broken the powers of bows, shield, sword, and war.

When these things have been broken and crushed, believers will sleep securely and rest under one shepherd—or will hope for those things “which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. I).

### (Verse 19)

“And I shall betroth you to myself forever; I shall betroth you to myself in righteousness and judgment, in mercy and in compassion [Vulgate: without *in*]; I shall betroth you to myself in faith, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

The LXX likewise.

O how great is God’s clemency! The harlot who had fornicated with many lovers and, because of her crime, had been handed over to beasts, after returning to her husband is not merely said to be reconciled to him, but to be betrothed.

And observe the difference between God’s union and that of human beings. When a man takes a wife, he makes a woman from a virgin—that is, he makes her no longer a virgin. But God, when joined to harlots, changes them into virgins, according to what is said to the adulteress through Jeremiah: “Have you not called me as lord, or father, or leader of your virginity?” (Jer. III, 4).

Hence, after fornication and the worship of idols, the Apostle says to the believing Corinthians: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. XI, 1).

We ask why he repeats the word “betrothal” three times. First he says, “I shall betroth you to myself forever.” Second: “I shall betroth you to myself in righteousness and judgment, in mercy and compassion.” Not satisfied even with this, he adds a third: “I shall betroth you to myself in faith, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

First he betrothed her in Abraham, or in Egypt, so that she might have an everlasting husband. Second, at Mount Sinai, giving her as betrothal gifts the righteousness and judgment of the Law, and joining mercy to the Law, so that whenever she sinned she would be handed over to captivity, and whenever she repented she would be recalled to her homeland and obtain mercy.

The psalmist sings of these betrothals in various places: “I shall sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. CII, 2). And: “Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed one another” (Ps. LXXXIV, 11).

We read of these two cups in Psalm LXXIV: “In the hand of the Lord is a cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, and he has poured from this into that”—from the cup of righteousness into the cup of mercy, and again from the cup of mercy into the cup of righteousness. “If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who will endure? For with you there is forgiveness” (Ps. CXXIX, 3–4).

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts read *in exteros fuerat* (“she had been [joined] to strangers”), etc., and a little later *per legitima assumitur* (“she is taken up again through lawful [means]”).]

This harlot, therefore, who had first been joined by the promise of the bridegroom in an everlasting embrace, so that she might never withdraw from the marital bond, because she withdrew and fornicated even in Egypt, is taken up again through the Law. But because she transgressed it, and killed the prophets—like companions of the bridegroom—who had been sent to her, at last the Son of God, the Lord Jesus, came. After he was crucified and rose from the dead, she is betrothed no longer in the righteousness of the Law, but in the faith and grace of the Gospel, so that when she knows the Only-Begotten, she may also know the Father.

For he himself says to Philip: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father also. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John XIV, 10–11).

Whoever has been betrothed in faith and has believed the Gospel will immediately know that he himself is God, believing in the one whom he had previously denied.

### (Verses 20ff.)

“And it shall be on that day: I shall answer, says the Lord; I shall answer the heavens, and they shall answer the earth, and the earth shall answer the grain, the wine, and the oil, and these shall answer Jezrael. I shall sow her for myself in the land; I shall have mercy on her who was without mercy; and I shall say to the one who was not my people, ‘You are my people,’ and he shall say, ‘You are my God.’”

**LXX:** “And it shall be on that day, says the Lord: I shall answer heaven, and heaven shall answer the earth, and the earth shall answer the grain, the wine, and the oil, and these shall answer Jezrael. I shall sow her for myself upon the earth.”

[Note: In place of “and I shall have mercy on her who was without mercy,” which is the reading of the Alexandrian and Aldine codices, our manuscripts substitute “and I shall love the one who was not loved,” which is the reading of nearly all Greek manuscripts: καὶ ἀγαπήσω τὴν οὐκ ἠγαπημένην.]

“And I shall have mercy on her who was without mercy, and I shall say to the one who was not my people, ‘You are my people,’ and he shall say, ‘Lord, you are my God.’”

On that day and at that time, when I have betrothed you to myself in faith and you have recognized that I am the Lord, I shall answer the heavens, which declare the glory of God (Ps. XVIII), and the heavens shall answer the earth, watering it with heavenly rain. The earth, from which truth has sprung (Ps. LXXXIV), and into whose field the householder goes to sow his seed (Matt. XIII, 3), shall answer the grain, wine, and oil, of which we spoke above. And all these shall answer Jezrael, that is, “the seed of God,” so that it may be understood that abundance and fertility in all things are bestowed because of the seed of God, who [variant: *quod*, “which”] is Christ.

The seed of God is sown in the earth so that it may produce manifold fruits: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold (ibid., 8).

And let that harlot who had been joined to God, and had borne three children—two males and one female, the first Jezrael, the second “without mercy,” and the third “not my people”—see that, because of the seed of God, the names of things have been changed, and that in the faith of Christ the one who was without mercy has obtained mercy, while the one formerly called “not a people” has been called God’s people.

From this we perceive that all these things can be referred both to the ten tribes called Israel, who, under the name of the harlot, bore three children, and to the whole people bearing the name of Jew.

Concerning the answering of heaven and earth, and of the grain, wine, oil, and Jezrael, some think that after Christ has come all things will proceed in their proper order, and that every creature will serve human benefit, just as it was created from the beginning. The Jews and our Judaizers await all these things bodily after Antichrist, at the end of the world.

### Chapter III

#### (Verse 1)

“And the Lord said to me: ‘Go again; love a woman who is loved by a friend and is an adulteress, just as the Lord loves the children of Israel, while they look toward foreign gods and love raisin cakes.’”

**LXX:** “And the Lord said to me: ‘Go again and love a woman who loves evil things and is an adulteress, just as the Lord loves the children of Israel; while they look toward foreign gods and love baked goods with raisin cakes.’”

The prophet, having been joined to the earlier woman as a type of the ten tribes or of the entire fornicating Jewish people, finally received the rejected and afflicted children into salvation. Here he is commanded still to love an adulterous woman.

When “again” is said, it shows that he had previously loved a fornicator. She may be called adulterous because she loves those evils, or because she is loved by the friend and neighbor. For the Hebrew word *RE* [Hebrew] can mean either “evil” or “friend.”

And lest we think that the prophet’s love for the adulteress signifies something other than God’s love for the children of Israel, he adds: “just as the Lord loves the children of Israel.”

Therefore, because the prophet loves the adulteress but is not joined to her in marriage or united with her in fornication, but merely loves the transgressor, he is a type of God. God loves the worst of the children of Israel, who, although they are loved by the Lord, look toward foreign gods and idols, and love raisin cakes that contain no wine and have lost their former grace. So too are demons: having fallen from their proper dignity and possessing none of their former grace, they are dry and withered by ancient aridity.

Hence, for “raisin cakes,” which is *ASISE* in Hebrew [Hebrew], Aquila translated παλαιά, that is, “old.” Symmachus translated ἀκάρπους, that is, “fruitless.” They are not merely raisin cakes, but old raisin cakes, testifying to ancient sins.

It should be noted that this adulteress signifies the present condition of the Jews. Although they are without God, without knowledge of the Scriptures, and without the grace of the Holy Spirit, they are loved by the Lord, who awaits the salvation of all, opens the door to those who repent, and yet they love useless things, cherishing human traditions and the dreams of δευτερώσεις, “secondary interpretations.” They possess neither grapes, wine, nor wine-filled winepresses, but old raisin cakes that have been cast away.

For the *pemmatia* that the LXX translated—and which are eaten with dried grapes or raisin cakes—we may say in Latin “cakes” or “little pastries.” They are offered to idols and are called in Greek πόπανα.

At the present point the children of Israel are called the twelve tribes; above, however, the reference was to the ten tribes that were in Samaria and possessed the metropolis Jezrael.

### (Verse 2)

“And I dug her out for myself for fifteen pieces of silver, and a *cor* of barley, and half a *cor* of barley, and I said to her.”

**LXX:** “And I hired her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver, a *gomor* of barley, and a *nebel* of wine, and I said to her.”

In place of *gomor*, the Hebrew has *OMER* [Hebrew], which all the interpreters except the LXX translated as *cor*, using a Greek and especially Palestinian term that contains thirty *modii*.

In place of “a *nebel* of wine,” the Hebrew reads *LETHECH SEORIM* [Hebrew]. [Note: In the Hebrew archetype the form is printed without *waw*.] The other interpreters translated it as ἡμίκορον of barley, that is, half a *cor*, amounting to fifteen *modii*.

The addition in the Vulgate edition, “nor shall you be with another man,” does not have “another” in the Hebrew; it simply says, “you shall not be with a man.” For if “another” is supplied, it implies that she is possessed by her own husband. But when it says absolutely, “you shall not be with a man,” we understand that she is to be joined to no one at all and is to remain without marital intercourse.

We read of the measure of a *cor* in Ezekiel (Ezek. XLV) and in the Gospel (Luke XXVI).

He therefore dug her out for himself—that is, the adulteress—or hired her, for fifteen pieces of silver. When he says “I dug her out,” he indicates the vineyard planted by the Lord, which is mentioned in many places in Scripture and signifies the Jewish people.

But if we read “I hired,” the payment is the price for the adulteress, not so that she may sleep with the prophet, but so that, content with her payment, she may cease to commit adultery and no longer join herself indiscriminately to others.

The *cor* of barley and the half-*cor* of barley are likewise dug out or hired—that is, forty-five *modii*. Having received this payment, she heard from the Lord:

*[The supplied source ends here.]*
### (Verse 3)

You shall wait for me many days: you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a husband; but I too shall wait for you.

The Septuagint: You shall sit for me many days; and you shall not commit fornication, nor belong to another husband, and I shall be for you.

That is: you shall neither shamefully prostitute yourself to other lovers, nor lawfully join yourself to me, the husband by whom you were hired. And lest you think that an injustice has been done to you because I said, “You shall wait,” I shall render like for like: I too shall wait for you.

At dawn on the fifteenth day of the month of Nisan, the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck, and the people of Israel was led out of Egypt [Col. 0843C] and hired into the service of God for a price (Exod. XII). Accordingly, for the firstborn of Israel who did not experience the common plague, accept five shekels of silver each (Num. III), which are contributed to the temple treasury.

Most of our writers refer the fifteen to the week of the Law, and the forty-five to the octave of the Gospel—that is, to the Sabbath and the day of resurrection, on which spiritual circumcision is practiced. But they cannot explain how an adulterous woman who is fed with barley and is estranged from her husband should receive both Testaments as her payment.

On the forty-fifth day the people reached Mount Sinai, and immediately on the following day it was commanded that they sanctify themselves from intercourse with women for three days and prepare themselves to receive the law of God (Exod. XIX). After the three days had passed, on the fiftieth day Moses ascended the mountain and received the Decalogue.

Thus the Jewish people, once hired for fifteen pieces of silver and forty-five measures of barley, after the coming of the Lord the Savior sits and awaits the coming of her husband. When he says, “You shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a husband,” he shows that in the meantime she is neither to serve idols nor yet to possess God; rather, she has been deprived both of her lovers and of her husband.

And because she has no husband, she does not eat human food—wheat and legumes—but the barley of irrational animals, chewing the baseness of the letter, which kills, and lacking the life-giving spirit. [Col. 0844A] Hence also in the Law the woman accused of adultery by her husband, in the drink of testing—*ἐλεγμός*, that is, of conviction—when she is accused of sin, receives barley flour (Num. V). For she who has imitated horses and mules, which have no understanding (Ps. XXXI), is sustained by the food of horses and mules.

In place of half a *cor* of barley, the seventy translators rendered “a *nebel* of wine,” which is entirely absent from the Hebrew. We may say that by “a *nebel* of wine”—that is, by a full and perfect measure—the adulterous woman has been intoxicated and afflicted with full punishments. Hence Jeremiah also offers the nations and Jerusalem a cup of unmixed wine (Jer. XV).

The husband too sits—or rather, waits for the adulterous woman’s repentance, so that after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered (Rom. XI), and Israel at the end has believed, so that [Col. 0844B] what had been the head may be turned into the tail (Deut. XXVIII), and the tail into the head, then there may be one flock and one shepherd.

### (Verses 4–5)

For the children of Israel shall sit many days without a king and without a prince, without sacrifice and without an altar, without an ephod and without teraphim. And afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days.

The Septuagint: For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, without manifestations—called *δῆλοι* in Greek. And afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; 32 and they shall be astonished before the Lord and at his good things in the latter day.

In place of “ephod” [Col. 0844C] and “teraphim” (), the Septuagint translated *ἱερατεία*, that is, “priesthood,” and *δῆλοι*, that is, “manifestations.” It should be known—as we have often said—that *ephod* signifies the priestly garment, which in Exodus and Leviticus is called by the Septuagint *ἐπωμίς*, that is, “shoulder garment,” and by Aquila *ἐπένδυμα*, that is, “outer garment.”

The *teraphim* properly signify *μορφώματα*, that is, figures and images. In the present passage, however, we can understand them as the Cherubim and Seraphim, or the other things that were commanded to be made as ornaments of the temple.

But because the Septuagint translated the term as *δῆλοι*, for which Aquila rendered *φωτισμοί*, and because these are found in the *λογεῖον*, that is, in the Rational, we understand this to mean that in the breast and heart of the high priest there ought to be *ἀλήθεια* and *φωτισμοί*, that is, truth and instruction, so that he may not only know the right faith but also be able to express orally what he knows.

The apostle Paul likewise writes to Titus, teaching what sort of bishop should be ordained:

> For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward; not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain; but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast the faithful word according to [Note: [Col. 0843] Our manuscripts do not insert “sound,” and the Greek text likewise lacks the word here.] sound doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort with sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it (Tit. I, 7–9).

We also read of the ephod and teraphim in the book of Judges (Judg. XVII and [Col. 0845A] XVIII), which a Levite had made for himself and who afterward set out with six hundred armed men from the tribe of Dan.

From the passion of the Lord the Savior until the present day, [Note: [Col. 0845D] Only twenty-five or twenty-seven years were lacking for the completion of four hundred years; hence he says “almost,” and so forth.] almost four hundred years have been completed. How much time remains until the day of judgment, neither the angels nor the Son know. He says that he does not know for the reason that it is not profitable for us to learn [variant: “to know”].

These, then, are the many days during which the unhappy Synagogue, the adulterous woman, is fed with barley and sits bent over, because she cannot stand with Christ: without a king, of whom the Father says, “I have raised up a king with righteousness” (Isa. XLV, 13); and he himself says in the Psalm, “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. II, 6).

Without a prince: either the Lord the Savior himself, or certainly the high priest, concerning whom it is written: [Col. 0845B] “You shall not curse the prince of your people” (Exod. XXII).

And without sacrifice and without an altar. For once the temple had been overturned and Jerusalem burned, the Jewish people could practice neither sacrifice nor priesthood. And without ephod and without teraphim, that is, without the instruments of priestly attire.

Jacob also speaks of this king in the blessing of the patriarch Judah:

> The prince shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations (Gen. XLIX, 10).

Therefore, after the prince departed from Judah and the ruler from his loins, and the foreigner and proselyte Herod assumed the power, we understand that he had come to whom the kingdom had been reserved, and that he was himself the expectation of the nations.

This is the blindness that has happened to Israel in part, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter and then all Israel might be saved (Rom. XI). And after a very long time they shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king, who was born from David’s line and whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand.” For he released his people from captivity and granted release to those in bonds.

And when the children of Israel see him—him whom his own brothers rejected—reigning in the majesty of the Father and of himself, they shall fear and be astonished before the Lord and at his goodness. This good Son was born from a good Father; or, alternatively, they shall be astonished at the Lord’s good things, of which the holy man says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13). For this land in which we sinners dwell is the land of the dead.

Others interpret the present chapter as referring to the Babylonian captivity, when the Temple was desolate for seventy years, and there were neither altar, victims, nor priesthood; afterward, under Zerubbabel, they returned to their former dwellings.

Others, like us, defer it to the future, and cannot discover any other cause for so great an offense—so that they have been abandoned for so long a time—especially since they do not worship idols, apart from the killing of the Savior.

## Chapter IV

### (Verses 1–2)

Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a lawsuit with the inhabitants [Col. 0846A] of the land. For there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and 34 adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.

The Septuagint: Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a lawsuit with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God upon the earth. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have been poured out over the land, and they have mingled blood with blood.

From the beginning of the prophet up to this passage, under the description of a prostitute and an adulterous woman—after their most severe punishments and their long abandonment, followed afterward by restoration to their former or a better condition—the sins of the ten tribes, or of the two, and collectively of all, are enumerated.

Now [Col. 0846B] the discourse turns again to Israel, that is, to the ten tribes, explaining that God does not threaten and inflict such severe punishments without reason, lest the sentence against those who have not sinned appear to have been imposed unjustly, not according to the truth of judgment but by God’s power [Note: [Col. 0845D] We have deleted the words “the voice of prophecy,” which had been added here, since they are superfluous and are not found in our manuscripts or in those consulted by Victorius, thirteen in number.].

“Hear,” says the prophet, “the word of the Lord, O children of Israel,” for the Lord wishes to be judged with his people and to set forth the reasons for his indignation.

“There is no truth, and there is no mercy, and there is no knowledge of God in the land.” For truth cannot be maintained without mercy, nor does mercy without truth produce anything but negligence. Therefore one is mingled with the other; and whoever does not possess them will consequently not possess knowledge of God either.

But, conversely, in place of truth there is lying, and in place of mercy there are cursing, murder, theft, [Col. 0846C] and adultery. He did not say “there is,” but, to demonstrate the abundance of their crimes, he added, “they have overflowed” [variant: “they have abounded”]. And in place of the knowledge of God, which is not in the land, “blood has touched blood,” or, “they have mingled blood with blood,” so that they might add sins to sins and heap old offenses upon new ones.

It is rightly the inhabitants of the land, not its temporary residents, who are summoned to judgment, because “from the face of the North evil shall blaze upon the inhabitants of the land” (Jer. I). And in the Apocalypse of John, “Woe, woe, woe” is pronounced upon the inhabitants of the earth (Apoc. VI).

But whoever can say with the prophet, “I am a sojourner with you and a stranger, like all my fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII, 1), and passes through this world as a resident alien and a pilgrim, follows truth and mercy, 35 and the knowledge [Col. 0846D] of God, lest he be overwhelmed by an inundation of cursing and lying, murder, theft, adultery, and blood.

### (Verse 3)

Therefore the land shall mourn, and everyone who dwells in it shall languish, together with the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven; even the fish of the sea shall be gathered up.

The Septuagint: Therefore the land shall mourn, and it shall be diminished together with all who dwell in it, together with the beasts of the field, [Note: [Col. 0846D] The words “with the serpents of the earth” are absent from another Palatine manuscript, and are also lacking in the Greek Complutensian text.] with the serpents of the earth, with the birds of heaven; and the fish of the sea shall perish.

Because there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God upon the land, but instead cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood, therefore the land shall mourn with its inhabitants and shall languish, so that it will have neither beasts of the field nor birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea will perish.

For when the captivity of the ten tribes comes and the inhabitants have been removed, the beasts also, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea will perish; even the mute elements will feel the Lord’s anger.

If anyone does not believe that this happened to the people of Israel, let him look at Illyricum, look at Thrace, Macedonia, and the Pannonias, and the entire land extending from the Propontis and the Bosphorus to the Julian Alps. He will find that, together with human beings, all the animals also have perished, [Col. 0847B] animals which the Creator had formerly nourished for human use.

But if we wish, as some think, to interpret the wild men as “beasts,” and as “birds of heaven” those who are lifted up in pride and despise everything human, and as “fish of the sea” those who are irrational and so brutish that they understand absolutely nothing and do not see the free air or the sky, this is the action not so much of an angry as of a merciful Lord, so that evil things may be removed from the earth.

### (Verses 4–5)

Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be reproved; for your people are like those who contradict the priest. You shall fall today, and the prophet also shall fall with you.

The Septuagint: So that no one may be judged, nor anyone reproved; but my people are like a priest with whom opposition is made, and they shall become weak by day, and the prophet also shall become weak with you.

According to the Septuagint translators, the words we have rendered, “so that no one may be judged, nor anyone reproved,” should be joined to the preceding chapter; but we follow the Hebrews. 36

The children of Israel, summoned to God’s judgment, who lived in the land in order to hear the causes of the Lord’s indignation and learn the past sins for which they would be handed over to their enemies, now, because they persist in their crimes and shamelessly despise God, hear this:

“It is not necessary for you to come to judgment, to be convicted of your offenses, because you are so shameless that even when convicted you have no shame or modesty; instead, you contradict me, as a little populace without priestly dignity might contradict a teacher or priest.”

And because you are such, therefore today you shall fall [variant: “you are falling, and are being led away, and are perishing”], that is, you shall be led into captivity and shall lose the kingdom of Israel.

What he says—“today”—either signifies the present time, or means that you will be led into captivity in broad daylight, not through fraud and ambush. And your weakness will be so great that even the prophets who used to prophesy falsehood to you will fall with you and experience captivity.

Here we should understand either the prophets as false prophets, or certainly the entire prophetic grace. For as long as the ten tribes had not been captured, they had the prophet Elijah and Elisha, and the other sons of the prophets who prophesied in Samaria. Hence even the prophet Amos, who was from the tribe of Judah and from the village of Tekoa, is compelled to return to his homeland, lest he prophesy in a foreign kingdom, in Samaria.

### (Verse 6)

I have silenced your mother in the night; my people have become silent because they had no knowledge. Because you rejected knowledge, I too shall reject you, so that you may not serve as my priest; and because you have forgotten the law of your God, I too shall forget your children.

The Septuagint: I have likened your mother to night, and my people has become like one who has no knowledge. Because you rejected knowledge, I too shall reject you, so that you may not serve as my priest. You have forgotten the law of your God, and I too shall forget your children.

He does not call one person the mother and others the children, as though the mother were different and the children different. Rather, the Lord speaks to the Jewish people as he said:

> Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling (Matt. XXIII, 5).

This does not mean that Jerusalem is one thing and its people another; for he was not speaking, apart from the people, to the cement, wood, and stones of the city.

Thus the multitude of the people and the entire Hebrew nation is called the mother, to whom he speaks; the children are either the individual members of the people or those scattered through towns and villages.

Israel, therefore, is handed over to the night and darkness of captivity, mourning, and oppressive distress, and its people fall silent in eternal silence, because they did not possess knowledge of the law and did not keep God’s commandments; and they receive what they had done.

For she herself rejected the law of God, and therefore lost the priesthood forever, worshiping golden calves in Dan and Bethel. And because she forgot the law of God and surrendered herself entirely to Egyptian idols, therefore the Lord also will forget her children, handing them over to eternal captivity.

“For whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (I Cor. XIV), and in the Psalms we read: “They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness” (Ps. LXXXI, 5).

Everything said concerning the ten tribes can be referred to heretics, who abandoned the kingdom of David and Jerusalem—that is, Christ and the Church. Therefore they are covered by eternal night, possess no knowledge of God, and are rejected by the Lord so that they may not serve him as priests; and he never remembers the children whom they have begotten, because they have become children of another.

### (Verses 7 and following)

According to their multitude, so they sinned against me; I shall change their glory into disgrace. They shall eat the sins of my people, and they shall lift up their souls toward their iniquity. And as the people is, so shall be the priest; and I shall visit his ways upon him, and I shall repay him for his thoughts.

The Septuagint: According to their multitude, so they sinned against me; I shall turn their glory into disgrace [variant: “I shall reveal it”]. They shall eat the sins of my people, and in their iniquities others shall receive their souls [Note: [Col. 0847] The Palatine manuscripts do not have the word “others,” nor does the Greek text, except in the Aldine codex. In one Barberinian manuscript, instead of *ἄλλοι*, there is *λαοί*.]. And as the people is, so also shall be the priest; and I shall punish his ways upon him, and I shall repay him for his thoughts.
