As many people as Israel had, so many altars it built for demons, and in their sacrifices it sinned against me. Therefore I shall change their glory—in which they gloried and preferred idols to God—into disgrace, so that both priests and people may be captured.

For the priests eat the sins of my people, concerning whom it is written: “They devour my people as they eat bread” (Ps. XIII, 8). They eat the sins of my people because they consent to the crimes of those who sin. When they see them sinning, they not only fail to reprove them but praise and exalt them and proclaim them blessed.

Isaiah speaks of such men: “My people, those who call you blessed, deceive you and overthrow the paths of your feet” (Isa. III, 12). Concerning them the Psalmist also cries: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed” (Ps. IX, 24).

Therefore people and priest alike shall endure the judgment of the indignant God, because he will visit not only their deeds, which are called “ways,” in which they walk, but also the thoughts by which they planned to do such things. For not only the deed but also the thought of the evil deed shall pay the penalty.

The meaning concerning heretics is clear: the more numerous they become, the more they sin against God and glory in their numbers. Therefore they deceive the wretched, so that they may eat the sins of the people and, through flattering words, devour widows’ houses (Luke XX).

When they see some people sinning, [Note: [Col. 0849D] “How aptly,” says Victorius, “he portrays the innovators of our age, who with a brazenly shameless face bark that faith alone is necessary and works not at all. St. James refuted this heresy from the beginning and, as it were, explained Paul when misunderstood, affirming in such learned words that faith without works is altogether empty and dead. Yet the evil weed, however often uprooted, always sprouts again, since anyone especially approves the opinion that says a person is carried to heaven from idleness and pleasures, and that a soldier is crowned without any contest.”] they say: “God seeks nothing else but the truth of faith; if you preserve that, he does not care what you do.” By saying this, they lift up their souls in their iniquities, so that they not only do not repent or humble themselves but rejoice in their crimes and walk with their necks held high.

Therefore people and priest alike—both those who have been taught and those who have taught—shall be bound by an equal judgment.

### (Verses 10 and following)

They shall eat and not be satisfied; they have committed fornication and have not ceased, because they abandoned the Lord by failing to keep him. Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart.

My people asked of their wooden image, and their staff announced it to them. For the spirit of fornication deceived them, and they committed fornication against their God.

The Septuagint: They shall eat and not be filled; they committed fornication and shall not be directed, because they abandoned the Lord so as not to keep his commandments. The heart of my people received fornication, wine, and drunkenness. They asked in divinations, 39 and their rods announced it to them, because they were led astray by the spirit of fornication [Note: [Col. 0850D] The words “and they committed fornication,” absent from the manuscripts, have been supplied from ours, with the support of the following exposition and also of the Greek text, *ἐπλανήθησαν καὶ ἐξεπόρνευσαν*. The careless scribes were deceived by the repeated word *sunt*, passing from the first occurrence to the second.] and committed fornication against their God.

Pleasure is insatiable, and the more it is indulged, the greater hunger it creates in those who use it. Conversely, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V). Just as righteousness satisfies, so iniquity, having no substance, deceives those who consume vain things by fraud and leaves the bellies of those who devour it empty. [Note: [Col. 0850D] In one Palatine manuscript: “consuming good things by fraud,” and so forth.]

“They committed fornication and did not cease.” Strength fails in fornication, but the desire for fornication does not rest. The ten tribes also fornicated with the idols of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and they abandoned the Lord their God by failing to keep what he had commanded when he said: “You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone” (Deut. VI, 13).

The words should be read emphatically: “Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart.” Just as wine and drunkenness render the one who drinks incapable of controlling his mind, so fornication and pleasure pervert the understanding and weaken the soul; they turn a rational human being into a brute animal, so that he pursues banqueting halls, brothels, and haunts of lust.

And when the heart has thus been moved from its proper place, it considers wood and stones to be gods and worships the works of its hands. Hence the prophet, as though astonished and amazed, declares: “My people, who were once called by my name, asked wood and rods.” The Greeks call this kind of divination *ῥαβδομαντεία*.

Accordingly, we read in Ezekiel that Nebuchadnezzar mixed his rods against Ammon and Jerusalem, and that the rod came out against Jerusalem (Ezek. XXV). The cause of this madness is the spirit of fornication, which deceived them so that they fornicated against their God.

[Note: [Col. 0850D] Our manuscripts read: “but fornication signifies idolatry,” in accordance with, etc.] He calls idolatry “fornication,” in accordance with what we read in Jeremiah:

> They committed adultery with wood and stone, and I said: “After they fornicated with all these things, return to me”; but she did not return with her whole heart, but in falsehood.

And again:

> You abandoned me and said: “I shall go up upon every high hill and spread myself in my fornication beneath every leafy tree” (Jer. III, 5–6).

And in the Psalm it is said: “You destroyed all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. LXXII, 27). For the beginning of fornication is the invention of idols.

Heretics are never satisfied with their error, nor do they cease from the shamefulness of fornication. Every day, by failing to keep the Law and the holy Scriptures, they abandon the Lord; they rave and become drunk, and, having lost the judgment of their mind, worship the idols they have fashioned from their own heart. They are possessed by the spirit of fornication.

### (Verse 13)

They sacrificed upon the peaks of the mountains and burned incense upon the hills; beneath the oak, the poplar, and the terebinth, because its shade was good.

The Septuagint: They sacrificed upon the summit of the mountains and offered sacrifices upon the hills, beneath the oak, the poplar, and the wooded trees, because the shelter was good.

The Law commanded that sacrifice be offered to the Lord only in the place that the Lord God had chosen; and that a grove or trees should not be planted beside the altar, lest a passion-ridden and pleasure-seeking religion overturn the austerity of the one true religion.

Israel, by contrast, sacrificed on the mountains and burned incense on the hills, loving the high places of the earth because it had abandoned the exalted God; and, seeking shade, it lost the truth.

This is what we read concerning individual kings: “Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places; the people still sacrificed and offered sacrifice upon the high places” (III Kings XXII, 44), which in Hebrew is called *BAMA* ().

Heretics promise themselves the sublimity of doctrines and sacrifice beneath the oak, the poplar, and the terebinth—fruitless trees that have neither fig nor vine—beneath which the Holy One is said to rest. At times they also take the terebinth for themselves, [Note: [Col. 0851D] Victorius noted that this alludes to Genesis XVIII. Where it says that the Lord appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre, the Hebrew has “in the terebinth,” whereas the Septuagint translated it “oak,” and others “terebinth,” since *terebinth* is the word used, as is clear from Genesis XXXV, and likewise I Kings XVII and III Kings XIII. Although in I Chronicles X it may be understood as “oak.” The word is derived from .] which according to Isaiah has no leaves, so that they may seem to imitate Abraham’s example (Isa. VI).

### (Verse 14)

Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication, and your brides shall commit adultery. I shall not punish your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery, because they themselves consorted with prostitutes [Vulgate: “associated with them”] and sacrificed with effeminate men; and the people without understanding shall be beaten.

The Septuagint: Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication, and your brides shall commit adultery; and I shall not punish your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery, because they themselves mingled with prostitutes; and they sacrificed with the initiated, and the people [Note: [Col. 0851D] The negative particle is absent from the Palatine manuscripts, and is also rejected by the Greek text itself; the name of Symmachus and the Greek interpretation are likewise lacking. Moreover, in place of Aquila’s word *ἐνηλλαγμένων*, these manuscripts, both here and below where the same word recurs, seem to prefer *ἐνδιηλαγμένων*, which is also more agreeable.] without understanding adhered to the prostitute.

The word *CADESOTH* (), which Aquila translated *ἐνηλλαγμένων*, Symmachus *ἑταιρίδων*, the Septuagint *τετελεσμένων*, and Theodotion *κεχωρισμένων*, we have rendered “effeminate,” so as to disclose the meaning of the word to the ears of our people.

These are the people whom today at Rome they call *Galli*, serving not the mother of gods but of demons. They are so called because the Romans, having mutilated men of this nation through lust, made them priests in honor of Attis, whom the prostitute goddess had made a eunuch.

Therefore men of the Gallic nation are feminized, so that [Note: [Col. 0851D] Jerome apparently confuses the Gallic people, by whom Rome was once captured, with the Galli, the priests of Cybele, who were named after the river Gallus in Phrygia. The error arises from homonymy, as Ovid so elegantly sings in Book IV of the *Fasti*, lines 315–316:

> Why then do we call those “Galli” whom we say have castrated themselves,  
> when the Phrygian land is so far removed from Gaul?  
> Between green Cybele and lofty Celaenae,  
> the Gallus flows in its madly named waters.

Pliny also mentions this river in Phrygia, from which the Galli priests received their name, in Book V, at the end.] those who had captured the city of Rome might be punished with this disgrace.

Such idolatry existed in Israel, especially among women worshiping Beelphegor because of its obscene size [Note: [Col. 0852D] See *Against Jovinian*, Book I, chapter 12.] [Col. 0852A], whom we may call Priapus. Hence King Asa removed the high places from the people and such priests, and deposed his mother from her august office, as Scripture testifies:

> Asa did what was right in the sight of the Lord, like David his father, and he removed the effeminate men from the land and cleansed all the filth of the idols that his fathers had made. Moreover, he removed Maacah his mother, so that she would not be chief in the rites of Priapus and in the grove that she had consecrated; he overturned her cavern, broke the most shameful image, and burned it at the brook Kidron. But he did not remove the high places. Nevertheless, Asa’s heart was perfect before God all his days (III Kings XV, 11 and following).

It should be known that in the present passage *CADESOTH*, prostitutes, are called *ἱερείας*, that is, [Col. 0852B] “priests,” dedicated to Priapus. In other passages we read of men mutilated through lust, *CADESIM* (), as Isaiah says:

> And mockers shall rule over them.

In Hebrew it is written:

> And *CADESIM* shall rule over them,

which we have rendered “effeminate men.”

[Note: [Col. 0852D] I do not know why our manuscripts place the Greek text here: *καὶ ἐμπαῖκται κυριεύσουσιν αὐτῶν* (“and mockers shall rule over them”).]

Aquila, interpreting the word as *ἐνηλλαγμένους* [Note: [Col. 0852D] Our manuscripts, as noted above, prefer *ἐνδιηλλαγμένους*.], that is, “changed,” wished to show that they had changed their nature and had become women from men.

Symmachus properly called them *ἑταιρίδας*, “prostitutes.” The Septuagint used *τετελεσμένους*, that is, “consecrated” or “initiated,” to show that they were worshipers of idols. Theodotion used *κεχωρισμένους*, that is, “separated from the people,” because they seemed to themselves to possess something beyond the common people.

We have discussed the word briefly; let us now return to the meaning of the chapter.

It is a great offense, after having sinned, not to deserve the anger of the Lord. Israel had fornicated against the Lord its God and had been led astray by the spirit of fornication. Therefore its daughters and brides also commit fornication and are left in their crime without any punishment, so that they may experience in their children and wives what children and wife had done to the true Father and Husband, and may understand through their own pain the pain of God, who is so angry that he does not strike the offenders at all.

The apostle also testifies to this in mystical language when he writes to the Romans:

> Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents (Rom. X, 22 and following).

And because they had fornicated with idols, they are struck by this sentence:

> Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves—those who exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

But so that we may know that visitation is imposed by God upon the wounded and sick so that, as by cautery and the bitterest medicines, they may recover health and be rid of their diseases, let us hear the Lord speaking through the prophet:

> I shall visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows; but I shall not remove my mercy from him (Ps. LXXXVIII, 33–34).

Therefore the one who is loved is corrected; the one who is neglected is abandoned to his own sins.

And the number of Israel’s fornicators was so great [Note: [Col. 0853D] Two Palatine manuscripts read: “the number of those fornicating in Israel,” so that punishment despairs of correction.] that punishment ceased, despairing of their reform. 43 For what is more shameful than men joining themselves to the worship of prostitutes and sacrificing, with effeminate men, the victims of their own lust?

As for what he adds, “and the people without understanding shall be beaten,” for which the Septuagint translated, “and the people without understanding adhered to the prostitute,” this signifies that they will be beaten in captivity and afflicted with various blows, so that through pain they may receive instruction.

The meaning concerning heretics is clear: their children commit fornication, and their brides—that is, the souls whom they have begotten in error and betrothed to their doctrines—do likewise. Such people are unworthy of God’s correction, because all their worship is fornication, and the shameful mingle with the shameful. Therefore they will be beaten, so that eventually through their wounds they may understand which God they should seek.

When you see a sinner overflowing with wealth, boasting of his power, rejoicing in health, delighting in his wife, surrounded by a crown of children, and fulfilling what is written—“They are not in the labor of mortals, nor are they scourged with human beings” (Ps. LXXII, 5)—say that the Prophet’s threat has been fulfilled in him:

> I shall not punish your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery.

### (Verses 15–16)

“If you commit fornication, Israel, let Judah at least not offend; and do not enter Gilgal, nor go up to Beth-aven, nor swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’ for Israel has turned aside like a wanton heifer. Now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place.”

The Septuagint: “But you, Israel, do not be ignorant, and Judah, do not enter Gilgal; do not go up to the house of ὢν, and do not swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’ for Israel, struck by the gadfly, has gone mad like a heifer. Now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in an open space.”

In some copies, and especially in Theodotion, instead of “house of ὢν” one reads “house of iniquity,” which Aquila and Symmachus rendered as “house of ἀνωφελοῦς,” that is, “of the useless one”—something that gives no benefit—and which by another word is called an idol. This is Bethel. Although it was formerly called “house of God,” after the calves had been placed in it, it was called Beth-aven, that is, “house of uselessness” and “house of the idol.” We have rendered it as it is read in the Hebrew.

It seems to me that this is also why the people of Israel made for themselves in the wilderness the head of a calf to worship, and why Jeroboam son of Nebat fashioned golden calves: so that what they had learned in Egypt—that Apis (ἄπις) and Mnevis (μνεῦις), which are worshiped under the form of oxen, are gods—might be preserved in their own superstition.

Let us state the meaning of the passage. If once, Israel, you were deceived by error and mingled with prostitutes, so that anyone who filled his own hand or the king’s by offering and giving him gifts became a priest of the high places, then at least you, Judah, who possess Jerusalem, have the Levites from the Law, and perform the temple ceremonies, ought not to follow the example of your former sister Oholah in her fornication, nor worship idols with her.

Do not enter Gilgal, concerning which we read in this same prophet: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal” (Hosea 9:15); in Gilgal Saul was anointed king, and there, after leaving the wilderness, the people first encamped and were purified by a second circumcision. From that time, in a place famous for the opposing religion, error took root.

And do not go up to Beth-aven, that is, to what was once called Bethel, because after the golden calves were placed there by Jeroboam son of Nebat, it is called not the house of God but the house of the idol.

In regard to this, I wonder why the Septuagint rendered it “house of ὢν.”

[Note: Here Jerome is plainly mistaken, as all editors and critics maintain, when he says that the Septuagint are at fault because they correctly read *vau* as the middle letter of the word. Victorius, in order to come to the saint’s aid, alters the text of Jerome into the opposite sense, unless they supposed *yod* rather than *vau* to be the middle letter—a letter differing only in size—which is enclosed on either side by *aleph* and *nun*. Yet this reading is supported neither by good witnesses nor by a lesser difficulty: if the Septuagint supposed the middle letter to be *yod*, how could they pronounce it not as *on* or *en*, but as *ōn*? It is moreover clear that in Hebrew the word is written not, as Jerome here supposes, with *yod*, but with *vau*. The word can be read *Aven*, *Aun*, or *On*, and so it was rendered at the discretion of the ancient translators. Indeed, Jerome himself in this very passage reads it with *vau*, Beth-aven; and this is all the more certain because he interprets it as “house of the idol,” or “house of vanity.” It is therefore more surprising that he could say that the Septuagint rendered it Ὢν by taking *vau* for *yod*. Otherwise, I know that the Greeks also read Bethaim, as Bonfrerius notes in his commentary on the Book of the Places of Eusebius, or of Jerome.]

Unless, perhaps, through their customary error they thought that *vau* was in place of the middle letter *yod*, which is enclosed on either side by the letters *aleph* and *nun* and differs from *vau* only in size.

“And do not swear, ‘As the Lord lives.’” For I do not wish the mention of my name to be made through your mouths, since it has been polluted by the remembrance of idols.

For just as a wanton heifer casts off the yoke, so Israel—that is, the ten tribes—turned aside from the service of the Lord. Instead of “a wanton heifer,” the Septuagint rendered παροιστρῶσαν, “one struck by the gadfly or the asilus,” which is commonly called the *tabanus*.

Concerning this Virgil also writes in the third book of the *Georgics*:

> … whose name is *asilus*,  
> the Romans call it so; the Greeks called it *oistros*,  
> a harsh, sharp sound; terrified by it,  
> the herds flee scattered through the woods: the air rages,  
> shaken by their bellowing, and the woods, and the bank  
> of the dry Tanagrus.

Therefore, because Israel went mad and, struck by the spirit of fornication, raged with unbelievable frenzy, not long afterward—while the prophet still speaks, while the Spirit still governs these limbs—the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place.

Because he had begun with the metaphor of the wanton heifer, or of the heifer struck by the gadfly, he preserves it in what follows: he calls Israel’s captivity among the Assyrians and the people’s dispersion through the broadest land of the Medes the pasture of a flock and of lambs in a very broad field and spacious land.

The meaning concerning heretics is obvious. To them, or about them, it is said: “If you once commit fornication, heretic, let you at least, ecclesiastical man, not offend; nor enter Gilgal,” the gatherings of heretics, where everyone’s sins are exposed—or, according to another reading, “rolled about”—like pigs in the mire.

Do not think that you are ascending to the proud and arrogant fabrications of false doctrines. There is not the house of God there, but the house of the idol. Nor swear by the name of Christ, whose majesty you have polluted by mingling it with idols.

For just as a heifer struck by the asilus is driven mad, so heretics are struck by the burning arrows of the devil and have abandoned knowledge of the Law. Therefore they will be pastured on the broad and spacious road that leads to death, and the Lord’s patience and the good Shepherd will nourish them toward destruction.

### (Verses 17 and following)

“Ephraim is a partner with idols; let him alone. Their feast is separated. They have committed fornication utterly; his protectors loved to bring disgrace. The spirit bound him in its wings, and they will be put to shame because of their sacrifices.”

The Septuagint: “Ephraim is a partner with idols; he set up stumbling-blocks for himself; he provoked the Canaanites. They committed fornication utterly; they loved disgrace because of his snorting. The spirit will hiss in his wings, and they will be put to shame because of their altars.”

Ephraim, from whose tribe came Jeroboam son of Nebat, who first established golden calves at Bethel and Dan, is the king of the ten tribes.

Therefore, Judah, to whom I said above, “If Israel commits fornication, let Judah at least not offend,” hear my counsel and do not disregard the prophet’s words. Since Ephraim has once become a friend and partner of idols, leave him; do not follow his impiety. His worship, religion, and food have been separated from your feast.

They serve idols once and for all, sacrifice to demons, and commit fornication every day; they love their fornication. Indeed, their rulers and protectors—that is, their kings—loved to bring disgrace upon the people. Through the vice of their rulers, the unhappy people accepted the worship of idols, whose unclean spirit bound Israel in its wings and does not permit him to fly freely.

Therefore they will be put to shame in their sacrifices, and in their confusion they will receive the disgrace of their rulers.

Instead of “the spirit bound him in its wings,” Symmachus rendered it in Greek as though someone were “binding the wind in the wings of the wind,” thereby asserting that rulers and people, indeed demons and Israel, were joined—vain things to vain, empty things to empty things. For among the Hebrews “wind” and “spirit” are called by one word, *ruaḥ* (רוּחַ).

What the Septuagint rendered “he provoked the Canaanites” is not found in the Hebrew. Nevertheless, it can be interpreted as follows: Israel showed such zeal in the worship of idols that he did not imitate the Canaanites, that is, the pagans, but provoked them to imitate his error.

This too can be referred to heretics. It is said to Judah, that is, to the ecclesiastical man: since Ephraim, whose name means καρποφόρος, “fruit-bearing,” promises himself a false abundance of doctrine and fruitful dogmas, and has once become a friend of demons, leave him and despise him—especially since their sacrifices have been separated from your sacrifices.

This is what is meant by “their feast is separated.” They committed fornication once and for all, and their rulers deceived the unhappy people; instead of the worship of God, they imbued them with the disgrace of idols. The spirit of the devil bound them in its wings; they are carried about by every wind of doctrine and cannot stand firm in the Church.

They will truly be put to shame in their sacrifices, because their bread is the bread of mourning.

What is said—“he provoked the Canaanites”—can likewise be applied to heretics, because many heretics have fabricated things so filthy and impious, and possess such unclean sacrifices, that idolatry is less wicked by comparison.

Or else, because “Canaanite” means “merchant,” or μετάβολος, that is, “transferrer,” all who make the Father’s house a house of commerce (John 2), seek profits from the peoples, and transfer the truth of the Church into falsehood, ought to be called Canaanites.

## Book Two

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859C] 51–52 Whoever often sails eventually suffers a storm; whoever frequently travels a road either endures the attacks of robbers or at least fears them. In every art, both glory and abuse arise from favorable and adverse winds, when friends praise beyond what is deserved or enemies disparage beyond what is just. You will rarely find someone who is guided in either direction neither by favor nor hatred, but by fairness toward the facts.

I see this happening to me as I labor in the explanation of the Scriptures. Some despise them as trifles and, whatever we may say, look down on it with a wrinkled nose. Others, out of hatred for our name, consider not the facts but the persons, and approve the silence of others more than our diligence.

There are those who boldly assert that we are undertaking a task which no Latin before us has dared to attempt. Some think themselves eloquent and learned if they disparage another’s work, judging not what they themselves can do but what we cannot do.

But you, Pammachius, who commanded us to do this, must support your own command, and with an evangelical foot kick the Amafinii and Rabirii of our time, who make poor Latin from good Greek and render the most eloquent men speechless.

You must burn the hydra—and, according to another reading, the viper—and crush the scorpion with the cautery and with the sole, according to the tales of the poets. You must pass with deaf ears by the Scyllaean dogs and the deadly songs of the Sirens, so that together we may hear and know what the prophet Hosea foretells, whose explanation we shall set forth in this second book.

Although I rejoice in your assistance, and in the first city of the world I am glad to have as my defender a man distinguished both by nobility and by religion, I would nevertheless prefer that what happened to Titus Livy concerning Cato should happen to me. Livy writes that no one benefited that man’s glory by praising him, nor harmed it by criticizing him.

[Note: The printed books again add “anyone,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]

Both things were done by men endowed with the highest talents. He means Marcus Cicero and Gaius Caesar, one of whom wrote the praises and the other the criticisms of the aforementioned man.

For while we live and are contained in a fragile vessel, the efforts of friends seem to help and the insults of rivals to harm us. But after the earth has returned to its own earth, and pale death has taken away both us who write and those who judge us, and another generation has come, and, with the first leaves falling, a green forest has grown up, then talents alone are judged, without regard to the distinction of names.

The future reader does not consider whose work he is about to read, but what kind of work it is—whether its author is a bishop or a layman, emperor or master, soldier or servant, whether he lies in purple and silk or in the cheapest cloth. He will be judged not by differences of rank but by the merit of his works.

### (Verses 8–9)

“Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; howl in Beth-aven, behind you, Benjamin. Ephraim will be desolate on the day of correction; among the tribes of Israel I have shown faithfulness.”

The Septuagint: “Blow the trumpet upon the hills, sound upon the high places; proclaim in the house of ὢν. Benjamin has lost his mind. Ephraim has become desolate in the days of correction; among the tribes of Israel I have shown faithful things.”

Ephraim, Israel, and Judah will be devoured month by month—or by rust—with their possessions. Therefore I command you who hear: do not sound with a raised voice, but blow loudly on the clear trumpet. A clear sound is needed, so that all who are nearby may hear.

“Blow the horn in Gibeah,” whose etymology the Septuagint rendered as “hills”; “and the trumpet in Ramah,” which means “high.” These are two cities in the tribe of Benjamin, neighboring one another: Gibeah, where Saul was born, and Ramah, which lies near Gibeah, seven milestones from Jerusalem. The king of Israel attempted to occupy it in order to close the way in and out for the tribe of Judah.

Therefore sound a clear horn and trumpet in Gibeah and Ramah. The horn is pastoral and is made with a curved shape; hence it is properly called in Hebrew *sophar* (שופר), and in Greek κερατίνη, “horn-shaped.”

The trumpet, however, is made of bronze or silver; with it they sounded in wars and at solemn occasions.

Over Beth-aven, which was once called Bethel and lies in the tribe of Ephraim, where the golden calf stood, there is need not of a blast or sound but of a howl, because captivity is near.

He beautifully says that Beth-aven lies behind Benjamin. For where the tribe of Benjamin ends, not far away, in the tribe of Ephraim, this city was founded.

Therefore I say and command: “Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah, and howl in Beth-aven,” because the royal house of Ephraim, or Ephraim himself—that is, the kingdom of Israel—will already be desolate, and nearby captivity is imminent.

On the day of correction and punishment of the ten tribes of Israel, I showed the truthfulness of my words, which I had announced through the prophets, so that what I had foretold in speech I might confirm by deed.

Some, following the Septuagint, who rendered “house of ὢν,” have interpreted Beth-aven as “city of the sun.” Calling Christ the Sun of Justice, they wanted the city to be his Church. This displeases me. For the house of the idol, which Aquila interpreted as “the useless house,” cannot, according to the allegorical sense, be referred to the Church.

Let us say instead that the heretics who in Gibeah and Ramah promise themselves lofty knowledge are ordered to howl—or, according to another reading, “to rejoice”—in the house of the idol. They are not to be before the face of Benjamin, whose name means “son of the right hand,” but behind him, where he has no eyes.

For all the boasting of Ephraim, whose name means “abundance,” will soon be desolate. And when, he says, the day of judgment and the time of correction arrive, I will show by events that my words were not empty.

Instead of what we rendered “behind you, Benjamin,” the Septuagint translated “Benjamin was moved in his mind.” They consistently apply ἔκστασις, that is, “mental ecstasy” or “a going out of the mind,” to Benjamin, the ecclesiastical man.

Hence in the sixty-seventh Psalm also it is said: “There is Benjamin, the young one, in a state of mental ecstasy” (Psalm 67:28). And in Jacob’s blessings, under the person of Benjamin—from whose tribe the apostle Paul came—we read: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will distribute food” (Genesis 49:27).

For the one who at first persecuted the Church later supplied nourishment throughout the world to those who believed in the Gospel. Hence Saul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin, prophesied all day until evening in a state of mental ecstasy among the company of the prophets (1 Samuel 10).

### (Verse 10)

“The princes of Judah became like those who remove a boundary; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water.”

The Septuagint: “The princes of Judah became like those who transfer boundaries; upon them I will pour out my onslaught like water.”

After Ephraim and Israel had been led into captivity and their land reduced to solitude, the princes of Judah, who ought to have wept and exhorted their people to withdraw from idolatry lest they too suffer the same things, began to rejoice and celebrate that their land was open for them to possess and enlarge their territory.

They became like those who remove Israel’s boundaries, crossing their borders and desiring to extend their kingdom and possessions into the places that had once belonged to Israel.

Therefore the Lord says: “The Babylonians will come upon the princes of Judah, and like a rushing flood they will overwhelm them”—not by their own strength but by my indignation.

He also speaks to the princes of Judah—that is, to the Church—and says that they ought not to rejoice or consider the destruction of heretics their own salvation, but rather mourn that the heretics have perished.

Therefore the apostle Paul teaches ecclesiastical men not to boast over the breaking off of the Jewish branches, but rather to fear lest they themselves also be broken off (Romans 11). And elsewhere he says: “Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

Otherwise, upon such princes—who glory in the misfortunes of others and think that they themselves stand if others fall—the Lord will pour out his wrath like water.

Instead of “wrath,” the Septuagint translated ὅρημα, that is, “onslaught.” Some think it should be understood as a blessing, according to what we read elsewhere: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45:4).

But it is more correctly understood as wrath, as all translators except the Septuagint rendered it—especially since the noun agrees with an outpouring of wrath, as the prophet says to the Lord: “Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your anger overtake them” (Psalm 68:25).

The princes of Judah transfer the boundaries established by their fathers when they change truth into falsehood and preach something different from what they received from the apostles.

### (Verse 11)

“Ephraim suffers oppression; he is broken by judgment, because he began to go after filth.”

The Septuagint: “Ephraim oppressed his adversary; he trampled upon judgment, because he began to go after vanities.”

If Ephraim is impious and, because of his impiety, will become desolate, how is it now said that “Ephraim suffers oppression and is broken by judgment”? For whoever suffers oppression and is broken has his judgment unjustly suppressed, especially when a just reason is given for why he was handed over to captivity.

It follows: “because he began to go after filth,” that is, after idols, which are compared to filth.

The meaning, therefore, is this: Ephraim is oppressed by the Assyrians—first by Pul, then by Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 15), and afterward by Shalmaneser—not because those who oppressed him were righteous, or because he was handed over to them for that reason, but because those who had once been my people, when I abandoned them, were handed over to punishment.

In this there appears to be oppression—not on God’s part, who delivers a just sentence, but on the part of those who endure torments while being surrendered to adversaries worse than themselves.

The Lord gives the reason why they suffer oppression in this respect, why they are handed over to worse men, and why judgment is not observed toward them: because Ephraim—that is, Jeroboam—began to go after idols and abandon God. For he himself fashioned the golden calves.

According to the Septuagint interpretation, “Ephraim,” that is, Jeroboam, oppressed his adversary Rehoboam—that is, the tribe of Judah—and oppressed him because, having abandoned Jerusalem and the temple, he pursued images of Egyptian filth.

[The meaning concerning heretics is clear: by their false sophistries and dialectical skill they often oppress ecclesiastical men. But when they have done this, they follow not the purity of true faith but the filth of falsehood. Handed over to the devil and his angels, they seem to themselves to suffer oppression and to have the truth of judgment broken against them.]

Thus Israel is laid waste, and all his labors are plundered when the Assyrian prevails. He has lost God as his ruler, and therefore he is broken by judgment, because he followed idols.

### (Verse 12)

“And I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like rottenness to the house of Judah.”

The Septuagint: “And I am like confusion to Ephraim, and like a goad to the house of Judah.”

In Hebrew, *ash* (עש) means “moth”; *raqab* (רקב) means “rottenness” or “decay.” One consumes clothing, the other wood. In their place the Septuagint translated ταραχή, that is, “tumult” or “confusion,” and “goad.”

It should be noted that the moth is referred to Ephraim and rottenness to the house of Judah.

Therefore, just as a moth consumes garments and rottenness or decay consumes wood—and both processes occur over a long period—so God, giving both the ten tribes and afterward the two tribes a long period for repentance and calling them toward salvation, becomes for them like a moth and rottenness as they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath.

This does not mean that God is a moth or rottenness, confusion or a goad, but that all these things appear so to those who suffer punishment.

Ephraim and Israel were therefore consumed first; afterward the house of Judah followed—not Judah himself, but his house. Otherwise, one was preserved from the stock of Judah, concerning whom it had been ordained: “He himself was the expectation of the nations.”

When the heretics, who are understood as Ephraim, have been punished, Judah also—that is, those who remain with the Church yet are entangled in the errors or vices of heretics—will be subjected to a similar sentence.

Textual and editorial apparatus:

- At 14:16, another reading has “now the Lord pastures them”; at the discussion of priesthood, “has filled” replaces “filled,” and “bringing” replaces “offering.” A Palatine manuscript reads: “and worship idols with God.”
- In the heretical application, another reading has “nor enter,” and another has “their sins are disclosed” for “are revealed.”
- At 14:17, the Vulgate reads feminine “her” for “him.” A note records that Palatine manuscripts read “you are” rather than “will hiss,” as do most Greek manuscripts, which have σὺ εἶ rather than συριεῖ. Another reading has “they placed” for “they rendered.”
- At 5:1, the Vulgate has “this” for “these,” and, in the phrase concerning the royal house, “be silent, ears.” Manuscripts give *Itabyrium* for Ἰταβύριον; another reading has singular “sounds” for “they sounded.”
- At 5:3, an alternative reading has “of the Lord” for “the Lord.” At 5:6, Palatine manuscripts read “that they may seek,” agreeing with Greek τοῦ ἐκζητῆσαι; the Vulgate has “the Lord” in place of “in the Lord.” A Palatine reading says that ecclesiastical persons suppose that they redeem sins in which they remain “by almsgiving.”
- The omitted Joel citation reads: “Rust will eat the remains of the locust” (Joel 1:4), that is, *hasil*.
- At 5:10, one reading has “name” in place of “the noun.” At 5:11, manuscripts read “thus” rather than “in this way.”
- In the preface, an alternative has “has happened” for “I see happening.” The editorial note explains that the printed reading *contrectare* (“to handle”) is corrupt; manuscripts require the two words *contracta nare*, “with wrinkled nostril.” Another reading has “to your command” for “of your command.”
- The note on *Amafinii* states that the manuscripts restore this historically correct name in place of the corrupt *Amasinii*; Victorius's proposed *Amasii* is less correct. Jerome alludes to Cicero's testimony concerning Amafinius and Rabirius (*Academicae Quaestiones* 1.2; *Tusculanae Disputationes* 4.3, with notes by Lambinus, Gruter, and others), and to Terence's prologue to the *Andria*: “From good Greek works they make poor Latin ones.” Another reading has “viper” for “hydra,” and “we dictate” for “we shall dictate.” Printed books again add “anyone” after “nor harmed it by criticizing,” though the manuscripts lack it.
- In the Virgil quotation, the printed lacuna before “whose name is *asilus*” remains a lacuna; no words are supplied. At the conclusion of the preface, the alternative “goods” is printed for “goods,” without a substantive difference.

[Col. 0864C] (Verse 13.) “Ephraim saw his sickness and Judah his bond, and Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king; but he will not be able to heal you, nor will he be able to release the bond from you.” The Septuagint reads: “Ephraim saw his weakness and Judah his pain, and Ephraim went to the Assyrians and sent [messengers] to King Jarib; but he could not [variant: will not be able] deliver you, nor will he make the pain cease from you.” “Messengers” is not found in the Hebrew. Where the Septuagint has “Jarib,” we, following Symmachus, have translated it “avenger”; for Aquila and Theodotion interpreted it as “judge.” That JARIB () signifies “avenger” and “judge” is shown by the name of Gideon (Judg. VI). When the worshipers of Baal sought to put him to death because he had destroyed the grove and altars of Baal, his father replied: “Let Baal avenge himself,” or, “Let Baal judge him”; and, he says, he was called Jerubbaal, that is, “Let Baal avenge himself.”

Thus Ephraim, understanding his weakness, and Judah, understanding his bond—by which he had been bound in sin together with the ten tribes—sought help not from God, who could have released them, but from the king of the Assyrians. We read that under King Menahem, who ruled the ten tribes (IV Kings XV), Israel sent gifts to the Assyrians; and that Judah, under King Ahaz, demanded the protection of Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians. Yet these kings could not deliver them, because God opposed them, nor could they release the bond of captivity.

We can also refer the “bond,” for which MEZUR () is written in the Hebrew [Note: The same manuscripts read MEZOR.], and which Aquila translated as ἐπίδεσιν or σύνδεσμον, that is, “binding” or “conspiracy,” to the time when Rezin and Pekah son of Remaliah devastated many thousands of men from the tribe of Judah (ibid. XVI), when Judah vainly demanded the aid of the two kings—not God’s aid, but that of the Assyrians.

Some, following the tropological interpretation, refer Ephraim and Judah to heretics and ecclesiastical men, since both they and Judah, bound by the cords of sins, in accordance with what is written, “Everyone is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V, 22), sent to Assur and to the avenging king—that is, to the devil, of whom we read: “That you may destroy the enemy and avenger” (Ps. VIII, 3). And because they did not appeal to the true helper or judge, he made them remain in the pain of sickness and in the bonds of sins.

I have read in someone’s commentaries that King Jarib is interpreted as Christ. Since it follows, “He will not be able to heal you,” he used this argument: Christ cannot heal heretics or ecclesiastical sinners at the time of judgment, when there is no mercy, in accordance with what is written: “But in hell, who will confess to you?” (Ps. VI). And that he cannot heal or deliver them is not due to any weakness of his, but to the merit of those who sought help too late. In the same way the Lord is said to have been unable to perform signs in his own country; and he explains the reason why he could not: “Because,” he says, “they did not believe in him.”

That is what he said. We, however, shall interpret the king in a negative sense, as the avenging king. In place of what we have rendered Jarib, that is, “avenger,” others wrongly read JARIM, with the letter MEM, which is translated “woods”; hence also KIRIATH-JEARIM is interpreted as “village of woods.”

(Verses 14.) “For I am like a lioness [variant: lioness] to Ephraim and like a lion’s cub to the house of Judah.” The Septuagint reads: “For I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion in the house of Judah.”

When they go to Assyria and send to the king who will vindicate or avenge them, but who will not be able to heal them or release the bond with which they are bound, I shall show that, when I oppose them, all human help is vain. For I shall be like a lioness to Ephraim and like a lion’s cub to the house of Judah.

Instead of “lioness,” which in Hebrew is called SOHEL [Note: Our manuscripts read SOHOL.], the Septuagint translated “panther,” which is similarly named in Greek and Latin; and the word may signify both the name of the animal and any beast generally, so that you may understand that whatever is savage among beasts is present in God’s indignation. Nothing is swifter than a panther, nothing stronger than a lion. In the panther, the swift destruction of the kingdom of Samaria through the Assyrians is signified; in the lion, the very strong kingdom of the Chaldeans against Jerusalem and Judah is shown, at a somewhat later time. Since he had said that he was a lioness or panther and a lion, he preserves the metaphor and says:

(Verses 15.) “I, I shall seize and go away; I shall take away, and there is no one who can rescue. Going away, I shall return to my place [Col. 0866A] until you fail and seek my face.” The Septuagint reads: “I shall tear away, and I shall go and take away, and there will be no one who rescues. I shall go and return to my place until they perish and seek my face.”

It is asked how, if God seizes, takes away, and holds, no one can snatch anything from his hands, according to what is written, “No one can snatch anything from the hand of my Father” (John X, 29), Judas could be snatched from God’s hand by betrayal. We shall answer briefly that no one can snatch anything from God’s hand, but that the one who is held can, by his own will, fall away from God’s hand.

What follows—“Going away, I shall return to my place”—must be understood as referring to God’s place, his magnificence and majesty. Thus, by no dispensation does he descend to human beings, become angry, show mercy, forget, become like a panther, turn into a lion, or change into beasts; rather, he despises human affairs and permits those whom he had previously protected to fall under the power of enemies, so that they waste away, fail, and perish, and afterward seek the face of the Lord and say: “Make your face shine, and we shall be saved” (Ps. LXXIX, 4); and, “Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation” (Ps. LXXXIV, 8).

To heretics also and to the negligent Church, God becomes a panther and a lion. He will take away from them the prey which they had previously snatched from the Church, so that those who had perished while free may be saved after being captured. He will in no way dwell in the gatherings of the wicked, but will return to his place, concerning which he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 1). He will despise and reject them until they fail in impiety and seek him through repentance, the one by whom they had been abandoned.

Others think that God’s place is heaven: offended by those who dwell on earth, God returns there and makes those perish who, by the magnitude of their sins, have transformed the most merciful Lord into the fury of wild beasts.

(Cap. VI.—Verses 1, 2.) “In their tribulation they will rise early to me: ‘Come, let us return to the Lord, for he has seized us and will heal us; he will strike us and will cure us. After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence. We shall know, and we shall follow on, that we may know the Lord.’”

The Septuagint reads: “In their tribulation they will keep watch for me in the morning, saying: ‘Let us go and return to the Lord our God, for he has scourged us and will heal us; he will strike us and will cure us. He will make us well after two days; on the third we shall rise and live before him. We shall know, and we shall pursue, that we may know the Lord.’”

For this reason God handed Ephraim and Judah over to captivity, and no one can rescue them from his hand. He will return to his place until they fail and seek his face, so that they may seek him as angry and absent, whom they had not experienced as present and propitious. In their tribulation, when the light of repentance has dawned upon them, they will rise early to him, in accordance with what we read in Isaiah: “In tribulation I remembered the Lord” (Isa. XXVI, according to the Septuagint). And in the first of the Gradual Psalms: “To the Lord, when I was in tribulation, I cried, and he heard me” (Ps. CXIX, 1).

When they have risen early to the Lord, what will they say? “Come, let us return to the Lord.” They are not content with their own salvation, but encourage one another to return to the Lord whom they had abandoned, whom they had deserted because of their sins, and by whom they had been abandoned.

“For he has seized us, and he will heal us”: he who had said above, “I, I shall seize and go away,” will strike us and cure us. Instead of what we have rendered “cure,” all the translators similarly rendered μοτώσει; properly, however, μότα are the linen cloths inserted [variant: brought in] into wounds so that they may consume the putrid flesh and draw out the pus. It is the art of physicians to heal great wounds over a long period and to restore health through pain. The Lord therefore strikes and cures us, because “the Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). He not only cures us, but also revives us after two days and, rising from the dead on the third day, raises the whole human race with himself.

When he has cured those who were struck, revived those who were cured, and raised those who were revived, then we shall live in his presence—we who, while he was absent, lay dead. We shall live [variant: living] in his presence; we shall know him and follow him with every effort, so that we may know the Lord, he having risen on the third day, when we rose with him.

These words explain what we have often already pointed out: that Israel and Judah—that is, the ten and the two tribes—will then have one shepherd and one king, David, when they believe in the Lord who rises again. The Jews vainly promise themselves dreams of a thousand years, since the salvation of all was promised for the third day on which the Lord rose from the dead.

The Hebrews interpret the second day as the advent of their Christ and the third day as the judgment, when those who are to be saved will be saved. Even if we grant them this, let them answer us what the first day is—that is, the first advent of the Savior. When they cannot answer, let us infer that, according to their own view, the first day is the advent of the Savior in humility, the second in glory, and the third in the appearance of the judge. Those who accept the second and third thereby testify that they have lost the first, since the second and third cannot be called such without the first.

(Verses 3.) “His going forth is prepared like the dawn, and he will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain and the autumn rain upon the earth.” The Septuagint reads: “We shall find him prepared like morning, and he will come to us like the spring rain and the autumn rain upon the earth.”

“Come,” he says, “and let us return to the Lord, for he who seized us and will heal us, who will strike and cure us, who will revive us after two days and raise us up on the third day—he and no other—is prepared for us like morning and dawn.” Hence also the title of the twenty-first Psalm: “For the taking up of the morning,” although in Hebrew it is written, “For the morning hind,” because, having conquered death and the ancient crooked serpent, he desires to ascend to the mountains; and, when the darkness has been scattered, the sun of righteousness rises for us, to illuminate our blindness.

And beautifully he says, “His going forth is prepared.” Concerning him, we read in the eighteenth Psalm according to the tropological interpretation: “And he himself goes forth like a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII, 5). He is called not only morning, dawn, and daybreak; he will also come to us like the spring rain and the autumn rain upon the earth.

We receive Christ as the spring rain when the foundations of faith have been laid in us, and we shall receive him as the autumn rain when, with the crops mature, we shall gather eternal fruits and be stored in the Lord’s granaries. Therefore the Jews, who did not receive the spring rains and sowed without rain, will not receive the fruit of the crops at the end of time. This is the rain concerning which the Lord promises, saying: “I will give you the spring rain and the autumn rain” (Deut. XI, 14).

According to the allegorical interpretation, the spring rain is given when we know in part; the autumn rain is given when that which is perfect has come. The Lord is always prepared for those who rise early, who can say: “I shall rise at dawn” (Ps. LVI, 1); and, “God, my God, to you I keep watch from the light; my soul thirsts for you” (Ps. LXII).

(Verses 4, 5.) “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like dew that passes away early. Therefore I carved them through the prophets, and I killed them by the words of my mouth, and your judgments shall go forth like light.”

The Septuagint reads: “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah? Your mercy, however, is like a morning cloud and like dew that passes away early. Therefore I cut down your prophets; I killed them by the words [variant: word] of my mouth, and your judgment [Note: “Your” is absent from two Palatine manuscripts. Most Greek manuscripts, however, have μου, that is, “my.”] shall go forth like light.”

When he says, “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah?” he shows the affection of a parent toward lost children, in accordance with what we read in Isaiah: “What more ought I to have done for my vineyard that I did not do for it?” (Isa. V, 4). And in Micah: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what way have I wearied you? Answer me. For I brought you up from the land of Egypt, I freed you from the house of slavery, and I sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam before you” (Mic. VI, 2, 4).

“What, then, shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah?” Your mercy, by which I have always had mercy on you, has passed away like a morning cloud and like dew that rises in the morning and is dried up when the sun rises. For captivity is already near; already I see you being led in chains to the Assyrians and the Babylonians. I carved you through the prophets and threatened you with terrifying words; I brought out the knife, fires, and cauteries, so that you who despised the merciful one might fear him when offended. I killed the negligent by the words of my mouth, so that I might punish sinners first by the terror of words, before captivity threatened.

I did all these things so that the truth of the judgment by which I shall judge you might appear, and no one might doubt that you had justly suffered what you were suffering.

For “I carved them through the prophets,” the Septuagint translated, “I cut down your prophets,” understanding the prophets themselves as false prophets killed by the Lord. Since they had been the cause of error by promising prosperity, once killed they became an occasion of salvation. The meaning is: “Lest you should say, ‘We believed the prophets,’ I also killed them, so that every occasion for you to sin might be removed.”

We read in the Book of Kings [Note: The same manuscripts read, “three hundred prophets only.”] that four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal were killed under Elijah (III Kings XVIII), and another innumerable multitude under Jehu (IV Kings X), who overthrew the house of Ahab.

We understand these same things as spoken both to heretics and to the true [variant: upright] Judah, who will undergo similar experiences: the Lord summons them to mercy and desires them to return to salvation. But they pursue the delights and refreshments of this age as though they were a cloud and dew that quickly pass away. To them it is said in the Gospel: “Fool, this night they are demanding your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20). And that rich man dressed in purple, who despised Lazarus lying before his doors (Luke XVI), learned that everything he had enjoyed had passed away like a cloud and dew.

God, moreover, continually kills the prophets of heretics by threatening them with eternal punishments, taking them away from true life, and abandoning them to the death of their crimes.

Let us, however, love that cloud which is everlasting and protects us from the heat of this world—the cloud upon which the Lord sat when he came into Egypt and shattered all the images of the Egyptians. Let us love that dew of which Moses speaks: “Let my words descend like dew” (Deut. XXXII, 2). And of which Isaiah says: “The dead will rise, and those who are in the tombs will be raised; for the dew that is from you is their healing” (Isa. XXVI, 19, according to the Septuagint).

There are some who think that the prophets were truly [variant: righteous men] killed, since, because of the sinning people, the prophets too were killed and delivered over to their enemies.

(Verses 6, 7.) “For I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. But they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant; there they transgressed against me.”

The Septuagint reads: “For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. But they are like a man passing beyond the covenant.” [Note: We removed from this passage the words “There he despised me,” which had been inserted twice without reason and contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts, since Jerome immediately repeats them once in their proper place.]

The following words in the Septuagint—“There Galaad, a city that practices vanity, despised me,” and the rest—belong with the following chapter [variant: ought to be joined to it]. Let us discuss what we have proposed:

“I carved them through the prophets; I killed them by the words of my mouth. I threatened them with severe things so that I might have mercy on the penitent, so that I might extend my hand to those who had fallen and were rising again.” For I am not delighted by sacrifices and victims or by the multitude of burnt offerings. My victims and burnt offerings are the salvation of believers and the conversion of sinners.

But they imitated Adam, so that what he had done in paradise—passing beyond my covenant and law—they might do on earth. And there, that is, in paradise, they all transgressed against me in imitation of Adam’s transgression. It is not surprising if what preceded in the parent is also condemned in the children.

Every day God summons both those who are outside the Church and those who sin while remaining in the Church to repentance, saying to them: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” But they offer sacrilegious bread, give alms, and appear to pursue humility. If these things are truly done, I interpret them as burnt offerings. But when they have abandoned knowledge of God, they boast in vain that they possess the remaining members after cutting off the head of faith. For they have transgressed God’s covenant in the Church, just as Adam transgressed in paradise, and they show themselves imitators of their ancient parent, so that just as he was expelled from paradise, they too may be expelled from the Church.

(Verses 8.) “Galaad is a city of those who work an idol, undermined by blood, and like the throat of men who are robbers [or: of a robber].” [Note: We have restored this context from the manuscripts in accordance with Jerome’s intended meaning. Previously the words “Both readings are possible” were placed after the Septuagint interpretation itself, which also lacked the words “There Galaad despised me.” The Father himself had already taught that these words must be joined to this chapter above.]

The Septuagint reads: “There Galaad despised me, a city that practices vanity and troubles the water, and your strength is like that of a pirate.”

We read that Jehu was anointed king at Ramoth-gilead (IV Kings IX). He mixed blood with blood, overthrew the house of Ahab, and ordered heaps of the heads of his sons to be set up before sunrise. In this city, across the Jordan in the territory of the tribe of Gad, an idol was consecrated; and it was inhabited by priests, since it was itself also a city of refuge.

Therefore, the more celebrated and authoritative it was because it had been assigned to the portion of the priests, the more it became, across the Jordan, the beginning of idolatry and of every evil for Israel dwelling there, so that those who had sinned first were the first to be captured by the Assyrians.

Since that province itself is full of robberies, he compares them to robbers, so that just as robbers lie in wait for travelers, so the priests lay snares for the simplicity of the people.

According to the tropological interpretation, however, Galaad is interpreted as “migration of testimony.” It despises God when it distorts the testimonies of Scripture into perverse doctrines. All its works are vain; it troubles the waters of the Church and turns streams from the purest springs into muddy and filthy channels, which defile rather than cleanse the baptized.

All the strength of this city is like that of a pirate, since it imitates the devil, who in the sea of this age—through which ships pass—lies in wait for those striving to reach the harbor. Symmachus therefore translated the passage more plainly, saying: “And your throat is like that of a man who lies in wait.”

We read concerning such pirates in Job: “There is no delay for pirates” (Job XXV, 3, according to the Septuagint). [Note: Victorius noted that this testimony is found in the Septuagint of Job XXV, in these words: μὴ γάρ τις ὑπολάβοι ὅτι ἐστὶ παρέλκυσις πειραταῖς. In this passage our edition reads: “Is there a number of his troops?” παρέλκυσις signifies delay, from ἕλκειν, “to draw”; Suidas likewise explains it by ὑπέρθεσις, “postponement.”]

Although in the present age they may boast, trouble the waters, practice vanity, and exercise piracy, nevertheless there is no delay in the punishments that will swiftly overtake them.

(Verses 9.) “A band of priests kills those journeying on the way to Shechem, for they have practiced wickedness.”

The Septuagint reads: “The priests hid the way of the Lord; they killed at Shechem, because they practiced iniquity.” [Note: Our manuscripts have only “on the way,” without the addition “of the Lord.” That word is found only in the Alexandrian and Aldine copies, contrary to the Hebrew archetype. Symmachus’ interpretation, which follows, likewise omits the name Shechem.]

Symmachus interpreted the passage in this way: “The company of priests were killing Shechem on the road.” Theodotion: “The priests hid the way; they were killing on the back.” Aquila: “The participation of priests on the road; they were killing shoulders.”

When we sought the meaning of these readings according to the historical interpretation from the Hebrew, the passage was explained to us as follows:

The priests of Bethel—or rather, the fanatics of Bethaven—at the times of Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Booths, when it was necessary to go through Shechem, which is today called Neapolis, to Jerusalem, where alone it was permitted to sacrifice victims, placed robbers along the road to lie in wait for travelers. Their purpose was that people should worship the golden calves in Dan and Bethaven rather than God in Jerusalem and in the Temple.

What he calls “the participation and company of priests” signifies their conspiracy and their sinful agreement. But if we read it as we have translated it—“the companion of priests”—it must, he says, refer to Galaad, which practices idolatry and is also trampled down by blood, since it followed the priests’ impiety and occupied itself with robbery and bloodshed.

That is what they may say. We, however, shall say that heretics block the way, so that we may not go from Shechem—that is, from good works—to Jerusalem—that is, to the Church. They are like the throats of men who are robbers, and they kill those who desire to proceed through the way of this world to the truth.

Shechem is interpreted as ὦμοι, that is, “shoulders.” [Note: The same manuscripts prefer ΩΜΗΑΣΙΣ in this form of letters. Moreover, Ωμίας, “broad-shouldered,” is the term used.] By “shoulders” we understand work, and all false priests hide the way and kill human beings by evil works, so that they may not reach Jerusalem.

That “shoulder” signifies work is shown by the words: “Give your heart to your shoulder” (Gen. IV, 9, 15)—that is, turn what you understand into works. And we read concerning Issachar that he placed his shoulder under labor and became a husbandman.

(Verses 10, 11.) “In the house of Israel I saw a horrible thing: there is the fornication of Ephraim; Israel has been defiled. And Judah, prepare a harvest for yourself, when I restore the captivity of my people.”

The Septuagint reads: “In the house of Israel I saw horrible things; there is the fornication of Ephraim; Israel and Judah have been defiled. Begin your vintage when I restore the captivity of my people.”

Jeremiah spoke [variant: speaks] of this crime and terrible horror: “The heavens were astonished at this, and the earth shuddered exceedingly” (Jer. II). For what could be more horrible than the ten tribes suddenly turning to the worship of idols?

Therefore it is said to their capital: “Take away your calf, Samaria, in which Ephraim first fornicated”—that is, Jeroboam, from the tribe of Ephraim—and when he fornicated, Israel was defiled: namely, the people of Samaria, which obtained, in large part, the common name of Israel.

Thus the word is also turned to Judah: “You too, Judah, prepare a harvest for yourself.” The meaning is: “Do not think yourself secure because Israel is being led into captivity. You too, prepare fields to be harvested, for not much later you will be led captive to Babylon, and the time of your harvest will come.”

When the Chaldeans have harvested you, I will again restore the captivity of my people; under Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Artaxerxes I will bring my people back.

Observe how significantly Judah’s captivity and return are prophesied together. Concerning Israel—that is, the ten tribes—nothing is said here, and whenever anything prosperous is mentioned, it is deferred to the advent of Christ.

In the house of heretics we see horrible things every day: first the teachers fornicate, and the people who are led by them are defiled. Judah also—that is, the Church—is commanded to prepare a harvest, or vintage, for itself because of its sins when the time of judgment arrives. Yet the Lord pardons it and promises forgiveness, because “whom the Lord loves he chastises, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII), so that, once tested and purified, he may place it among his treasures.

Some refer the words “Judah, begin your vintage,” or “prepare a harvest for yourself,” to a favorable meaning: once Israel has been punished, Judah will receive the fruit of its works, in accordance with what is written: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV, 6). We prefer the interpretation given above.

(Cap. VII.—Verse 1.) “When I would heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim and the wickedness of Samaria was revealed, because they practiced falsehood; the thief entered, and the robber plundered outside.” [Note: After Victorius we removed the unnecessary conjunction et, in accordance with the testimony of all editions.] [Note: Here we supplied the words “The Septuagint likewise,” which had been absent from earlier printed editions, from our manuscripts.]

The Septuagint is the same.

Israel has often received many wounds from idolatry, and especially that wound when they cast the calf in the wilderness and said: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XXXII, 4). Therefore I, who desire the sinner’s repentance rather than his death (Ezek. XVIII, XXXIII), and who afterward say in the Gospel, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke V, 31), attempted to heal the wounds of my people.

When I was treating these wounds with every skill so that the miserable people might be cured, Jeroboam suddenly arose from the tribe of Ephraim, making golden calves; and the wickedness of Samaria was revealed when it followed the impious king. For both king and people practiced falsehood—that is, an idol. Just as an image is opposed to God, so falsehood is opposed to truth.

The king himself entered the people of Israel like a thief, and like a robber stripped the unhappy people of God of their protection. The meaning is: “When I wished to erase the ancient sins of my people, Ephraim and Samaria devised new idols because of their ancient idolatry.”

It may also be said that, when the Lord and Savior wished, after the shedding of his blood, to heal the sins of the people and gather his Church from both Jews and Gentiles and bring them back to repentance, Ephraim—those who promise an abundance of false doctrines—and the people of Samaria, who claim to observe God’s commandments, suddenly rose up and fashioned an idol of false doctrines. Through them the thief and robber, the devil, entered the Church; or rather, the doctrine of heretics entered like a thief and robber. Concerning them the Savior says in the Gospel: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John X, 8).

Thieves lie in wait and deceive by hidden fraud; robbers openly seize what belongs to others. Those who steal, steal at night and in darkness. Therefore he says significantly that the thief entered secretly, while the robber plundered outside. For they cannot strip those whom they have taught of the garment of Christ unless they first lead them outside the Church and make them walk in the perverse way of their doctrines.

The thieves and robbers who came before the Lord must not be understood as Moses and the prophets, who are always praised by the Savior’s mouth, but as the false prophets, and afterward the heretics, who were not sent by the Lord but came of their own will.

(Verses 2.) “And lest they should perhaps say in their hearts, ‘He has remembered all their wickedness,’ now their inventions have surrounded them; they have been done before my face.” [Note: We inserted the word “perhaps” in accordance with our manuscripts and the Vulgate edition.]

The Septuagint reads: “So that, singing together as though they were singing in their hearts, ‘I have remembered all their wickedness,’ their thoughts now surrounded them; they were done against my face.”

“Lest,” he says, “they should perhaps say in their hearts: ‘God has brought back upon us our ancient sins, and we are paying for the offenses of our fathers; they ate the sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’” (Jer. XXXI); therefore I shall now relate in the following discourse the things that they have done and continue to do in the present, before my eyes each day. I shall show them their inventions, or thoughts, by which they diligently pursued evil and acted in my presence without fearing my face.

As for what we read in the Septuagint, “so that they may sing together as though singing in their hearts,” it refers to the reason why the thief entered, or the robber stripped them outside: lest, remaining in their former riches and garments, they should reject the thief’s and robber’s agreement. But once stripped, they sing together with them and become of one heart (Dist. 4, On Penance, chap. “Cum ita”). Therefore they shall receive what they have done, and none of their thoughts or works will deserve my regard.

Heretics likewise cannot lay the sins of the past against God, since every day they add new impiety to their ancient works. They perish with the lost, are bound by their own errors, and, although they think they can conceal themselves from God, cannot escape his eyes.

(Verses 3.) “In their wickedness they made the king glad, and in their falsehoods, the princes.”

The Septuagint reads: “In their wickedness they made the kings glad, and in their falsehoods, the princes.”

He explains what they did before his face: “In their wickedness they made King Jeroboam glad, and in their falsehoods, the princes who ruled the people under Jeroboam.”

Heretics also, in the wickedness of their deeds, have made the king—the devil—glad; and in the falsehoods of their perverse doctrines, the princes, unquestionably of this world, whose false wisdom God destroys.

Among heretics, we can call the king the one who first devised heresy, and the princes those who, placed over heretical peoples, claim for themselves a false priesthood. At the same time, it must be observed that in our sins the opposing powers, rulers, and princes of this darkness rejoice.

(Verses 4.) “All are adulterers, like a furnace heated by the baker; the city rested for a little while from the mixing of the leaven, until the whole was leavened.”

The Septuagint reads: “All are adulterers, like a burning furnace for baking, for the burning of the flame, from the mixing of the leaven, until the whole was leavened.”

Those who in their wickedness made the king glad and in their falsehoods the princes are all adulterers. They were kindled by Jeroboam with the fire of idolatry like a furnace, to bake the bread of impiety. When the fire of error had set their souls ablaze, the furnace and oven, first kindled with fire, rested for a little while, so as not to force the people but to leave them to their own will, until all falsehood was leavened.

For whatever is done under compulsion is quickly dissolved; what is undertaken willingly persists. Therefore, since he had taken the metaphor from the furnace that is kindled for baking bread, he preserves it in what follows, showing by the mixing of all the leaven the consent of the whole people, so that king and people alike fell through an equal ardor for idolatry.

No one doubts that the hearts of heretics are kindled by the devil’s fire, so that the loaves of Antichrist may be baked in them. For this reason they first remain quiet in the Church, speak secretly, and promise everything peaceful [Note: Martianus, following Erasmus, reads “promise to make everything peaceful.” Victorius says this is a mistake in punctuation. Four Florentine manuscripts preserve the true reading: “And they promise everything peaceful.” He is speaking of heretics, who always promise prosperity and happiness and claim the kingdom of heaven for themselves without labors or works; this plague spreads through the Church in a remarkable way in our own time.] so that, like a cancer, they may gradually spread among the peoples.

When the leaven of their teaching—which the Lord also understands when he says, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matt. XVI, 6)—has swollen in the hearts of the deceived, then they burst forth into open madness, and what is said by the Apostle John is fulfilled in them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (I John II, 19).

(Vers. 5 and following.) The day of our king: the princes began to rage from wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers, [Note: [Col. 0874D] Victorius preferred *quia* instead of *qui*, on the basis of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin editions. No manuscript, however, supports this.] who applied their heart like an oven when he was plotting against them. All night he slept while baking them; in the morning he himself was inflamed like a flame of fire. They all grew hot like an oven and devoured their judges; all their kings fell; there was no one among them who cried out to me. [Vulgate: *among them*.]

The Septuagint: The days of your kings. The princes began to rage from wine; he stretched out his hand with pestilent men, because their hearts were inflamed like an oven when they were being hurled headlong throughout the night. Ephraim [another reading: Israel] was filled with sleep; morning came; he was kindled like a flame of fire [another reading: *flame*]. They all grew hot like an oven, a burning fire, and fire devoured their judges. All their kings fell; there is no one among them who calls upon me. [Note: [Col. 0875D] Two Palatine manuscripts give a reading closer to the Greek: “They all grew hot like an oven and ate their princes; all their kings fell before them; there is no one,” and so forth. The Greek is: “They all grew hot like an oven, and devoured their judges; all their kings fell.” [Col. 0876D] The printed reading adheres more closely to the Alexandrian or Aldine manuscripts.]

This is an obscure passage and requires the attentive reader’s understanding, so that we may first learn the history. For a little while Israel and the city of Samaria were quiet, having received into themselves the heat of error, until the whole mass became like leaven, grew, and burst forth, and the swelling people cried out at the doors of King Jeroboam, saying: “This is the day of Jeroboam our king; this is the festival day that our ruler has appointed for us. We celebrate it, we sing it, we rejoice and play on it; on it we worship the golden calves.”

When the people cried out, the princes were not angry, as some think; rather, they too began to rage from wine, losing the understanding of their minds, forgetting God, and stumbling against the wood of idols. When the king saw this—namely, the people crying out and saying, “This day belongs to our king,” while the princes, like drunkards and fanatics, did not know what they were saying—he stretched out his hand to the mockers, giving his approval to those who mocked him with empty praises. When these mockers’ own king was plotting against them and drawing them away from their God, they presented their heart to him like an oven, so that he might set them ablaze and make them burn with the flames of idolatry.
