For this reason he gave his approval to the people: he understood that they had turned their whole mind toward error.

What follows—“All night he slept while baking them; in the morning he himself was inflamed like a flame of fire”—means this: after he had placed fire in the oven of their hearts and seen them rage, with no one able to resist his will, he slept throughout the night, that is, he was secure. He moved about in darkness while they were being baked and made into the bread of impiety. Therefore he later rose in the morning and openly displayed the flame of his crimes in madness, so that they might leap not by stealth but shamelessly from the worship of God to the rites of idols.

What more need be said? They all, heated like an oven by the fire of idolatry, devoured their judges, so that even someone who by nature might have been good and remembered the Lord’s religion, seeing both princes and people subjected to the calves and believing them to be gods, would himself also be devoured by the crime. Finally, all the kings of Israel fell and walked in the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin; and no one was found who, abandoning the idols, would return to God.

[73] We have spoken these things according to the tradition of the Hebrews, more boldly than learnedly, leaving the credibility of what we have said to its authors. Now let us pass to the spiritual interpretation.

Unhappy are the peoples who are led astray by the devil as king and by his princes; or those who, led by the prince of heresy and its leaders, have accepted other solemnities, abandoning the Church and trampling upon the truth of the faith. They commonly cry out and say, “This is the day of our king”—for example, of Valentinus, Marcion, Arius, or Eunomius.

When those appointed over them hear this, they do not merely become drunk with wine, lest the sin be thought trivial; they go mad from the wine of which Moses wrote in the Song of Deuteronomy: “The fury of dragons is their wine, and the fury of asps is incurable” (Deut. 32:33). For these people eat the food of impiety and become drunk with the wine of iniquity. Of this the Apostle also says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18). And in Proverbs we read: “Let princes not drink wine, lest they forget wisdom and be unable to judge rightly” (Prov. 31:5).

Thus, when both peoples and leaders have been deceived, the prince stretches out his hand either to mockers or to pestilent men, such as the sons of Eli, and those of whom we read in the first Psalm: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilent men” (Ps. 1:1). Of them it is said: “Drive out the pestilent man from the council, and strife will go out with him” (Prov. 22:10). Their hearts have been inflamed so that they may strike down those whom they have deceived. For this is what, according to the Septuagint, the cataracts signify: they do not raise up, but strike down.

When he says, “All night Ephraim was filled with sleep,” he shows that heretics, sleeping, do not see the light of the sun of righteousness. Those who sleep, sleep at night, because their understanding has been overwhelmed. Of them we read in the Psalms: “They slept their sleep, and found nothing” (Ps. 75:6). Their hearts grow warm with various disturbances—anger, love, greed—and they devour their judges, whether whatever virtues they might possess in their minds, or the faculties by which they distinguish evil from good.

Or this may be understood to mean that the leaders of the heretics are devoured by their own peoples: just as they devour the households of others for the sake of shameful gain, so they themselves are devoured by the approval of those people.

All the princes of the heretics have fallen. Although they cry out to the Lord, no one calls upon his name: “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Rom. 10). “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name: they called upon the Lord, and he answered them” (Ps. 98). He does not answer the kings and princes of the heretics, because there is no one among them who cries out to the Lord.

(Vers. 8–10.) Ephraim mingled himself among the peoples; Ephraim became a cake of bread baked under ashes [Note: [Col. 0876D] The Hebrew text has only [the corresponding Hebrew word] and does not add “bread.” The ancient author of the commentary on Hosea, once thought to have been Rufinus, who professed to follow Jerome’s edition, likewise reads only “baked under ashes,” omitting the word “bread.]. He does not turn back. Foreigners have devoured his strength, and he did not know it; moreover, gray hairs were scattered upon him, and he did not know it. The pride of Israel will be humbled before his face; they did not return to the Lord their God, and they did not seek him in all these things.

The Septuagint: Ephraim mingled himself with his peoples; Ephraim became a cake baked under ashes that does not turn back. Foreigners devoured his strength, but he did not know it; gray hairs blossomed for him, and he forgave. The disgrace of Israel will be humbled before his face; they did not return to the Lord their God, and they did not seek him in all these things.

The kingdom of the ten tribes became like all the nations, because they withdrew from the Lord. And, like a cake baked under ashes that does not turn back—that is, that does not repent—the Assyrians and Chaldeans devoured its strength and consumed whatever power it could possess. It was so mindless that it did not know it had been devoured; or at least it did not understand the reason why it had been handed over to those who devoured it. Finally, it remained in its begun error until old age, that is, until the final captivity.

Therefore the pride of Israel will be humbled—not after a long time, but now and in the present. For this is what he says: “before his face.” It will be humbled because it had raised itself up and trusted not in God but in the multitude of its army. And because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4), instead of “pride,” that is, *GAON* [Hebrew term], the Septuagint, according to its custom, translated *hybris* (ὕβρις), that is, “injury” or “insult.”

Since he had said above, “Ephraim became a cake of bread baked under ashes that does not turn back,” and this seemed obscure and insufficiently clear, he now states it more plainly: “They did not return to the Lord their God, and they did not seek him in all these things.” If they had returned to the Lord their God, they would certainly have heard God speaking through Jeremiah: “Return to me, and I will return to you.”

Although they did all these things, they did not seek him whom they had lost through their own fault.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] For “ought,” the Palatine manuscripts read “seems” or “may see.” Further, for “let us pass” and the following “draw,” Martianus, with Erasmus, retained “let us transfer” and “withdraw”; Victorius had already corrected these readings from four Florentine and three Brescian codices.]

But since Ephraim ought—if we pass to another interpretation—to teach the peoples and draw them after his own likeness, he himself mingles with the peoples and becomes like them, according to what was said above: “As the people, so the priest.” Or Ephraim mingles with peoples and nations, so that all heretics differ in nothing from the error of the Gentiles.

He who was once a prince in the Church became a cake baked under ashes, surrounded on every side by filthy ash and the heat of fire, so that he would not return to the Lord but remain in his begun error. Demons devoured his strength: they are the foreigners and enemies of all Christians. He did not know it, considering his adversaries friends and supposing that his devourers were his table-companions. Moreover, gray hairs were scattered upon him—or rather, they blossomed, that is, he wandered for a long time—and nevertheless he did not recognize his old age and decrepitude, of which it is written: “What grows old and becomes aged is near disappearance” (Heb. 8:13).

And if it is said of a righteous man and a churchman, “The gray hairs of a person are his wisdom” (Wis. 4:8), why should it not be said of an unrighteous man and a heretic, “The gray hairs of a person are his folly”? Daniel spoke of this old age when he said to the elder: “You who are grown old in evil days” (Dan. 13:52).

Hence also in the book of the Shepherd—if anyone is willing to accept that book’s authority—Hermas first seems to see the Church with gray hair, then as a young woman, [Note: [Col. 0878D] Cotelerius preferred “as a bride.” The holy Doctor refers to the vision of Hermas’s book, Vision 1, chapter 2, and Vision 4, also chapter 2.] and as a bride adorned with hair.

When the pride of the heretics is humbled, or the disgrace that they daily inflict upon churchmen, they do not return to the Lord; in all these things they do not seek him at all, because they have been heated like an oven and have not sought him. They devoured their judges, and their kings likewise fell; there is no one who cries out to the Lord. They suffered all these things so that they might seek the Lord whom they were unwilling to seek.

(Vers. 11–12.) Ephraim became like a dove, deceived and without understanding. They called upon Egypt; they went to the Assyrians. When they have departed, I will spread my net over them; like a bird of the sky I will bring them down; I will strike them according to the report [Note: [Col. 0878D] The Palatine manuscripts read “according to the discovery of the assembly,” and so forth.] of their assembly.

The Septuagint: Ephraim was like a foolish dove without understanding. He called upon Egypt [another reading: *will call upon Egypt*], and they went to the Assyrians, as they will go. I will send my net over them; like birds [another reading: *a bird*] of the sky I will bring them down; I will chastise them at the hearing [another reading: *arrival*] of their affliction.

The Lord commanded in the Gospel (Matt. 10) that we should be “simple as doves and wise as serpents,” so that, imitating the simplicity of doves and the cunning of the serpent, we might neither be able to harm others nor suffer ambushes from others, but might display a balanced human character through simplicity and prudence. For prudence without goodness is wickedness, while simplicity without reason is called foolishness.

Ephraim therefore became like a deceived dove, which in Hebrew is *PHOTHA* [Hebrew term]. Aquila and Symmachus render it θελγομένη or ἀπατωμένη, that is, “charmed” or “deceived”; the Septuagint renders it “foolish” or “senseless.” For ἄνους can express both meanings.

He is beautifully called a deceived or foolish dove because there is also a wise dove, which says in the Psalms: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I will fly away and rest?” (Ps. 54:7). Its wings are silvered, and the rear parts of its back are the green of gold.

Ephraim, however, is shown to be a foolish dove without understanding, so brutish in mind that, while calling upon Egypt, he went to the Assyrians. For he who sought the aid of the Egyptians is led away captive by the Assyrians.

Egypt is a staff of reed; whoever leans upon it, it immediately breaks, and, once broken and shattered, pierces the hand of the one leaning upon it. To show that, even when we change our location, we cannot escape God’s eyes and are always governed by his power, God says: “When they have gone to the Assyrians, even there I will spread my net, and if they are lifted up like birds, from there I will bring them down.”

“I will bring them down,” however, does not mean for destruction, but so that I may strike them like sons; and I will strike them not with the severity of punishments but through fear, so that, hearing of future [another reading: *former*] punishments, they may be corrected by terror alone.

The question arises why Ephraim is compared not to other birds but to a dove. Other birds hasten to protect their young even at the risk of their own lives. When they see a hawk, serpent, raven, or crow approaching their nest, they fly here and there, attack with their beaks, tear with their claws, and express the parent’s grief with plaintive cries. The dove alone does not grieve for or seek its stolen young. Ephraim is therefore rightly compared to it, because he does not perceive that his people have been devastated piecemeal but is negligent of his own salvation.

When he says, “I will strike them according to the report of their assembly,” this may signify: just as they all fashioned the idols by common counsel, so, when I am angry, they will all likewise be devastated.

We may rightly call the teachers of contrary doctrines, who have abandoned Christ the Wisdom and gone out from the Church, a foolish and heartless dove. Desiring earthly things, they have been handed over to the Assyrians. When they departed from the Church, the Lord spread his net over them, woven from the testimonies of Scripture and the carefully constructed language of wisdom, so that, raising themselves against the wisdom of God and flying like a bird toward high places, he might bring them down to lowliness and correct them by threats and by hearing of punishments, so that, once corrected, they might not perish eternally.

(Vers. 13.) Woe to them, because they have departed from me; they will be devastated, because they have transgressed against me. I redeemed them, and they spoke lies against me [Vulgate: “And I redeemed them”]. They did not cry out to me in their heart, but they howled upon their beds.

The Septuagint: Woe to them, because they have departed from me; they have been exposed, because they have acted impiously against me. But I redeemed them; yet they spoke falsehood against me. Their hearts did not cry out to me, but they howled upon their beds.

When I spread my net to seize them, and, like a bird of the sky, to bring them down from their pride and strike them when they heard of distress, they departed and sprang back from me. For this is what the Septuagint’s ἀπεπήδησαν means. Therefore they will be devastated, because they have transgressed against me.

Instead of what we said, “they will be devastated,” the Hebrew has written *SOD LAEM* [Hebrew term], that is, “devastation for them.” Symmachus translated it “destruction”; Theodotion, “misery.” Moreover, in the Vulgate edition we read it in two ways. Some manuscripts have δῆλοί εἰσιν, that is, “they are manifest”; others have δειλαῖοί εἰσιν, that is, “they are fearful” or “miserable.” They will therefore be devastated and miserable, always afraid and trembling, because they have transgressed against God, worshipping golden calves and abandoning him who redeemed them from Egyptian slavery and led them out with an exalted arm.

They spoke lies against the Lord, saying of the idols: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. 32). They did not cry out to the Lord in their heart, but wallowed in the fornications of idolatry. Or, because the worship of demons is followed by lust and luxury, those who worshipped demons consequently wallowed like pigs in the mire of lust.

Beautifully, he calls the songs of those serving idols not songs to God but howling. The interpretation concerning heretics is straightforward: they will have eternal woe because they have departed from God, and they are miserable because they abandoned their Creator, who redeemed them by his blood. They speak lies against him, constructing impious doctrines of falsehood; they do not cry out in their hearts but continually howl in their little assemblies, which he aptly calls beds and lairs of wild beasts.

Such people cannot say: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch” (Ps. 6:7). Instead, they wallow in the filth of lust, devote themselves to fornication, and whatever they say or think they are saying to the praise of God is the howling of wolves and the sound of raging *bacchae*.

Rarely does a heretic love chastity. Whoever pretends to love purity—such as Manichaeus, Marcion, Arius, and Tatian, and the restorers of the ancient heresy—promises honey with a poisoned mouth. But, according to the Apostle, “it is shameful even to speak of the things they secretly do” (Eph. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0879D] In the Palatine manuscripts, “of cows” appears. This seems not to result merely from the commonly encountered similarity between the letters *b* and *v* in pronunciation, but to have been deliberately made according to the pattern of the preceding context.]

[Note: [Col. 0879D] Do not refer anything similar here to the conduct and heresy of Arius. The passage fits Aerius very well, who, in the Encratite sect—to which Tatian also belonged—was either a disciple or a leader (ἐξάρχων). I would therefore have this passage corrected to “Aerius,” which I have additionally confirmed from the testimony of Philastrius, who says: “The followers of Aerius were so called from a certain Aerius. In the province of Pamphylia very many people live who devote themselves to abstinence and are called Encratites, that is, abstainers. They possess nothing and reject the foods that God has bestowed with blessing upon the human race.”]

(Vers. 14 and following.) They ruminated over grain and wine; they departed from me, and I instructed [Note: [Col. 0880D] Victorius adds the word “them,” on the basis of the Vulgate edition and the Hebrew. Jerome’s edition, however—the one which the author of the commentary on Hosea praises under the name of Rufinus—does not recognize it.] and strengthened their arms; they devised wickedness against me. They turned back so as to be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow. Their princes will fall by the sword because of the rage of their tongue. This is their mockery in the land of Egypt.

The Septuagint: They were cut to pieces over grain and wine [Note: [Col. 0880D] The Palatine manuscripts read “they were slaughtered”; shortly afterward they read “this is the mockery” instead of “so is,” and so forth.]. They were instructed in me, and I strengthened their arms; they devised evil against me. They turned into nothing; they became like a drawn bow. Their princes will fall by the sword because of the incompetence of their tongue. Such is their mockery in the land of Egypt.

“Because of abundance,” he says, “of all things, they fell.” Ezekiel likewise recalls that this happened in Sodom and Gomorrah (Ezek. 19), so that they ruminated upon nothing but food and luxury. Instead of this, the Septuagint translated, “They were cut to pieces over grain and wine,” after the example of the prophets of Baal, who, in Elijah’s presence, prayed for rain by cutting their limbs (1 Kings 18).

At the same time, to show that they were like beasts, he did not say “they ate” but “they ruminated.” Therefore they departed from the Lord, who says, “I instructed them; I gave them strength,” and they raised their necks against him—not because they could do anything against or harm their Creator, but because the only thing they were able to do was to devise evil against him.

Just as they were at the beginning, before I called them through Abraham and later through Moses and Aaron, when they were without a yoke and knowledge of the Law and mingled with all the nations, so now they have returned to their former state: without a yoke or reins, they are carried over precipices and changed into a deceitful bow. [Note: [Col. 0881D] Victorius corrected the text from four Florentine codices as “which God,” with “bow” understood; Martianus, following Erasmus, retained “whom.”] Thus the bow which God had drawn against his adversaries they themselves might turn against their Lord and shoot at him arrows of blasphemies.

Therefore their princes, who deceived the unhappy people, will fall by the sword because of the fury of their tongue, since they dared to call the golden calves gods. Thus they did in the land of promise what they had learned in Egypt, worshipping the Egyptian Apis and venerating all their monstrous objects of worship.

For in the wilderness too, when they had gone out from Egypt, they mocked the Lord, saying: “These are your gods, Israel” (Exod. 32:4), and: “Would that we had been in the land of Egypt, where we sat by pots of meat” (Exod. 16:3), and so forth.

[80] [Note: [Col. 0881D] One Palatine manuscript reads “the false mystery”; in another, the word “false” is deleted.]

Over grain and wine, and over the false mysteries of the body and blood of Christ, who says in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24); and elsewhere: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1); and: “Unless you drink my blood” (John 6:54). Over this grain and wine, therefore, the heretics are cut to pieces, and they construct various tabernacles for themselves. Or they are cut off from the body of the Church, while they pretend to meditate upon and ruminate over the Law of God.

But in doing this they depart from the Lord, who instructed them in the Church and gave them the strength with which to fight against adversaries. They, however, devised wickedness against the Lord, constructing most impious heresies. They returned to the state of the Gentiles, so as to be without knowledge of God and without a yoke. Or they returned to nothing—not that they ceased to exist, but because, in comparison with him who says to Moses, “Go, say to the people of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me’” (Exod. 3:14), all who think against the Lord are said not to exist [another reading: “are said to be non-existent”].

This agrees with what we read in Esther, only in the Septuagint: “Do not hand over your scepter to those who are not” (Esth. 14:11, according to the Septuagint). [Note: [Col. 0881D–0882D] Victorius also noted that this is said only according to the Septuagint, since chapter fourteen, where it occurs, is absent from the Hebrew, as are the preceding three chapters. From the middle of chapter ten onward, the material subsequently read in Esther derives from the Septuagint’s Vulgate edition; it is absent among the Hebrews.] There is no doubt that this signifies idols. For if God is truth, whatever is contrary to truth is falsehood and is called nothing.

This applies to heretics, who, instructed in the Holy Scriptures, turn the words of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel against the Lord. They are like a deceitful or perverse bow. A deceitful and perverse bow is one that strikes the person directing it and wounds its own master.

Or they became like a drawn bow, always ready for battle and disputes, to the overthrow of their hearers. Therefore their princes—that is, the founders of heresies—are struck by the Lord’s sword because of the madness of their tongue, with which they blasphemed the Lord. They do the same thing in the church bearing a false name that they did when they lived in Egypt, that is, when they were Gentiles. For all the questions of heretics and Gentiles are the same, because they follow not the authority of the Scriptures but the judgment of human reason.

(Cap. 8—Vers. 1 and following.) Let there be a trumpet in your throat, like an eagle over the house of the Lord, because they have transgressed my covenant and violated my Law. They will call upon me: “My God, we have known you, Israel.” Israel has rejected the good; an enemy will pursue him. They themselves reigned, but not from me; princes arose, and I did not know them. They made idols for themselves from their silver and gold, so that they might perish.

The Septuagint: In their bosom, as earth, like an eagle over the house of the Lord, because they have transgressed my covenant and acted impiously against my Law. They called upon me: “God, we have known you,” because Israel rejected the good. They pursued an enemy; they reigned by themselves and not through me; princes arose, and they did not declare it to me. They made idols for themselves from their silver and gold, so that they might perish.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] Our manuscripts, together with Victorius, read “rejected”; Martianus, with Erasmus, reads “rejected” in the feminine form. The hand of an ignorant glossator seems evident here, since the same manuscripts immediately add “they followed the wicked thing” instead of “they pursued an enemy.” The Greek is ἐχθρὸν κατεδίωξαν, “they pursued an enemy.”]

What we have translated as “Let there be a trumpet in your throat,” for which the Hebrew has *ALECHCHAC SOPHAR* [Hebrew term], Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated in the same way. Only the Septuagint said, “In their bosom, as earth,” the meaning of which is uncertain.

Some think that “bosom” is to be understood in two ways: as the lower part of a garment, from the genitals to the feet, and as a sea gulf—that is, a bay, such as the Adriatic, Ionian, or Propontis. They interpret the false teachers who followed the blasphemy of Egypt as retaining in their bosom everything earthly and serving lust; or else, in the harbor and refuge of their voyage, as seeking not precious merchandise but earthly things.

We, however, following the Hebrew truth, shall continue the sequence of the explanation already begun.

The prophet is commanded, and it is said to him: “Let there be a trumpet in your throat,” that is, raise your voice so that it may resemble a trumpet, so that many may hear, because many have sinned. When you have raised your voice, say this with a cry: “Like an eagle over the house of the Lord.” The meaning is: Nebuchadnezzar will come with his whole army so swiftly and rapidly that he will imitate the flight of an eagle hastening toward its prey. He will come not to another place but to Jerusalem, in which the temple of God is situated, in order to destroy and overthrow it.

Ezekiel speaks more fully of this eagle (Ezek. 17), “with great wings, feathers, and claws,” which has a course entering Lebanon, that is, the temple of God. This agrees with the prophet Zechariah, in whose book it is written: “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars” (Zech. 11:1).

This command that I give you, O prophet—“Let there be a trumpet in your throat,” so that you may cry out and say that, like an eagle over the house of the Lord, the king of the Chaldeans is coming—I give for no other reason than that they have transgressed my covenant and abandoned my rites.

Therefore, in the time of necessity and distress, when captivity comes, they will call upon me and say: “My God, we have known you, Israel.” We who are called Israel know and recognize you, and we preserve the ancient name of Jacob, which pleased you, so that we may be called Israel.

The Lord answered them: How can you be called Israel, when Israel has rejected the good—that is, the Lord his God, from whom Israel received its name? Because Israel rejected the good, an enemy—that is, the Assyrian—will pursue and seize him.

When I had been abandoned as king, they asked for a king for themselves, like the other nations, and acted against God’s will [another reading: *my will*]. Therefore Samuel set before them the harsh commands of a king, and said that their sons and daughters would serve kings, so that they might turn to the Lord, the most merciful king (1 Sam. 8). But they established princes without God’s will.

Nor was this crime enough for them; they had to double their offense through greater impiety, turning the silver and gold they had received for wealth and adornment into idols.

Saul therefore became king not by God’s will but through the people’s error. And because he had no root of piety, as soon as he began to reign he was inflamed by impiety.

What he says—“They themselves reigned, but not from me; princes arose, and I did not know them”—may also be understood of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the other princes who succeeded him in the kingdom. Nor, merely because God, being angry with Solomon, wished his kingdom to be divided, did Israel therefore rightly accept a king. It ought first, according to the precepts of the Law, to have asked the Lord whether he wished this to happen.

For it is said concerning the Savior that the Son of Man must indeed be handed over, but woe to the one through whom he is to be handed over (Matt. 26).

We frequently read of the devil, who wishes to place his nest above the stars of heaven, under the image of an eagle: “If you are exalted like an eagle, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord” (Obad. 1:4). The eye that mocks its father and despises its mother’s old age will be dug out by ravens, and the young of eagles will devour it (Prov. 30), as it loses the clear light of its vision through the devil and demons. Hence the Law commands that we must not eat the eagle (Lev. 11).

This eagle therefore comes upon the little assemblies of the heretics, which were once houses of the Lord. It comes because they have transgressed his covenant and abandoned the Law of God. They call upon him without reason and say: “You are my God, and we have known you”—we who are called Israel, who see God and are called by the Christian name.

In vain, he says, do they do these things, since they themselves have appointed kings over themselves, acted against my will, and have as their princes my adversaries, whom I do not know because they have not deserved knowledge of me.

They have also turned their silver and gold, and whatever they could naturally possess, into idols—that is, into words and notions they fashioned from their own hearts. They turned them into idols not in order to perish; rather, because they turned them into idols, they perished. For they did not act for the purpose of perishing; but because they acted in this way, they perished.

### (Verses 5–6)

“Your calf has been rejected, Samaria. My anger has been kindled against them: how long will they be unable to become clean? For it too is from Israel: an artisan made it, and it is not God; for the calf of Samaria will be [like] threads of spiders.”

[Col. 0883] **Note:** Victorius, following the Vulgate edition together with the Hebrew, reads “against them.” Likewise, “an artisan made it,” that is, the calf discussed in the preceding passage. No manuscripts, however, support these readings.

**Septuagint:** “Cast away your calf, Samaria; my anger has been aroused against them. How long will they be unable to become clean in Israel? An artisan made this also, and it is not God, because your calf, Samaria, was deceiving.”

In the place where we have put “threads of spiders,” the Hebrew has *SABABIM*, with the penultimate letter written as *yod*—not, as some falsely suppose, *SABABUM*, with *vav*. The Septuagint and Theodotion translated this as *planōn* (πλανῶν), that is, “deceiving” and “misleading”; Aquila has “wandering” or “turned aside”; Symmachus, “inconstant” or “unstable,” that is, *akatastatōn* (ἀκαταστατῶν); the Fifth Edition, *rhembeuōn* (ῥεμβεύων), “wandering and fluctuating.”

From the Hebrew we have learned that *SABABIM* properly denotes spider-threads flying through the air, which, while they are seen, perish and dissolve into atoms and into nothingness. The calf of Samaria is rightly compared to these, since at that time the people worshiped it because of its great value, as it was made of gold.

What he had said above—“They made silver and gold for themselves as idols, in order that they might perish”—he now explains more clearly: “Your calf has been rejected, Samaria; my anger has been kindled against them.” “Against them” may mean against the calves, since they had made two; or against the inhabitants of Samaria, who worshiped them.

Moreover, where we read in the Septuagint, “Cast away your calf, Samaria,” he exhorts its inhabitants—not those of one city, but of all ten tribes, which are called Samaria—to cast away the calves against which God is angry. Otherwise, there were no calves in the city of Samaria, but in Dan and Bethel. Or the Septuagint’s *apotripsētai* (ἀποτρίψεται), “let him rub away,” may be understood: let them gradually rub away and cleanse from themselves those whom they had worshiped for a long time.

When they do not listen, he turns to others and speaks, as it were, in the third person: “How long will they be unable to become clean?” What kind of madness is this, he says, that, while I am granting [alternative: mediating] an opportunity for repentance, they do not wish to turn back to health?

And because he had said, “Cast away your calf, Samaria,” he explains what this calf is: “For it too is from Israel.” He does not say that you received the calf from other nations—as Baal and Astaroth from the Sidonians, Chamos from the Moabites, and Moloch from the Ammonites (IV Kings 23)—but that you yourselves, and your king Jeroboam, made in Israel what you had learned in Egypt.

Or what sort of god is one who is shaped by the hand of an artisan? Finally, just as spider-threads are dissolved by the wind, so the calf of Samaria will be reduced to nothing.

The Lord rejects the calves of the heretics and of Samaria—those who claim to observe the precepts of the Law. These calves cling to the ground and work upon the earth; they are not spiritual and do not raise their eyes toward heaven. Therefore the Lord’s anger is kindled against them, and he wonders at such great perversity: that they do not wish to abandon the idols they have fashioned for themselves, but may love [alternative: “love”] heretical filth instead of the purity of the Church.

Israel did not receive these calves from the other nations, although it pretends to see the Lord; rather, it forged for itself from the holy Scriptures a perverse understanding. It is the artisan of its own god, which will quickly perish and resemble spider-threads, which are torn by the slightest touch.

[Col. 0885C] **(Verse 7.)** “For they will sow the wind, and reap the whirlwind; the standing stalk has no bud and will not produce flour; and even if it does, strangers will eat it.”

**Septuagint:** “For they sowed things corrupted by the wind, and their overthrow will receive them; a sheaf without strength, unable to produce flour; and even if it does, strangers will eat it.”

He compares the calf of Samaria to spider-threads. Therefore he preserves the metaphor in what follows, comparing those whom he had called spider-threads to wind, to a whirlwind, and to stalks that do not stand; and, if they stand, to stalks that have no flour; and if, he says, they produce flour, it will be devoured by others.

Since the meaning is common both to the heretics and to those who fashioned idols in Samaria, they must be discussed together.

These people sow the wind—or seeds corrupted by the wind, seeds that lack the marrow which the Greeks call *enteriōnē* (ἐντεριώνη). Therefore, by sowing empty things, they receive empty and vain things. Indeed, they sow in the flesh and reap corruption from the flesh, being carried about by every wind of doctrine.

When they have sown the wind, they will reap whirlwinds and storms. First, the stalk—that is, the straw—will not arise from these seeds, nor will they be able to possess any appearance of a fruitful crop. And if it should rarely happen that they seem to possess something resembling an ecclesiastical doctrine, the very bud and ear will not produce flour.

It is into this flour that the Gospel woman puts leaven in three measures (Matthew 13), so that the spirit by which we perceive, the soul by which we live, and the body by which we walk may be brought together into one Holy Spirit, according to the Apostle: “In him we live and move and exist” (Acts 17:18).

And if it should rarely happen among the heretics that the flour of their seed is produced, from this flour there will be made a hearth-cake that does not rise, and which strangers will eat. Hence he now says: “And even if it produces flour, strangers will eat it.”

We must understand those strangers to be the ones of whom it is written: “The sons of strangers have lied to me” (Psalm 17:46). And in the eighteenth Psalm: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, Lord, and spare your servant from strangers.” If they do not rule over the righteous man, then he will be blameless and will be cleansed from the greatest offense.

[Col. 0885D] **Note:** Victorius inserts the Greek word *anemophthera* (ἀνεμόφθερα), which our manuscripts do not contain. Concerning *enteriōnē*, see Jerome elsewhere, where he attacks Origen’s opinion in *Against John of Jerusalem*, no. 26: “For just as the roots, stalk, leaves, ears, and chaff are not dissolved in a grain of wheat, so also in the constitution of human bodies certain ancient principles of rising remain, and something like an *enteriōnē*, that is, a seedbed of the dead, is cherished in the bosom of the earth.” Later, drawing on his own understanding, he says: “Why do you slander the power of God? He can draw from your marrow and from your seedbed, your *enteriōnē*, not merely flesh from flesh, but a body, and make one thing from another,” and so forth.

[Col. 0885D] **Note:** The words “from themselves” are unknown to our manuscripts.

**(Verse 8.)** “Israel has been devoured; now he has become among the nations like an unclean vessel.”

For “unclean,” the Septuagint translated “useless”; the rest is similar.

[Col. 0886D] **Note:** From our manuscripts we have supplied the words “the rest is similar,” which had been absent from the books published hitherto.

The Hebrews call an unclean or useless vessel a *matula*, which we commonly use for receiving and throwing away excrement. He compares idolaters and heretics to this impurity: they mingle with the nations because they do not preserve God’s truth, and, though made a vessel for honor, they have been changed into vessels [alternative: “a vessel”] of dishonor.

For what is more unclean than the demonic spirit and the doctrines of the heretics, which have mingled them with the pagans? Such was Jeconiah, enslaved to idols, concerning whom God speaks through Jeremiah: “Jeconiah is dishonored, like a vessel for which there is no use” (Jeremiah 22:18).

By contrast, Paul, who could say, “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Corinthians 13), is called a chosen vessel, golden and silver, because he possessed wisdom and eloquence with which he preached the Gospel of Christ.

When he says “has been devoured,” or “absorbed,” this signifies that, having been mixed with idols and nations, Israel has lost its distinctive name as Israel and as Christian.

**(Verses 9–10.)** “For they themselves have gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by itself; Ephraim has given gifts to lovers, and they have hired nations with payment. Now I will gather them, and they will rest for a little while from the burden of the king and princes.”

**Septuagint:** “For they themselves have gone up to the Assyrians; Ephraim has germinated by itself. They loved gifts; therefore they will be handed over among the nations. Now I will receive them, and they will rest a little while, so that they may anoint kings and princes.”

“Israel has been devoured,” he says, and has become like a useless or unclean vessel, of which no shard remains from which water or even a small amount of ember might be drawn. And because it has become an unclean vessel, they went up to the Assyrians, imitating a solitary wild ass—not, like sheep, fed by the Lord, but abusing their freedom. They were led into captivity, and the prophet laments them, saying:

“Ephraim has given gifts to the Assyrians and hired his lovers with payment.” Ezekiel writes concerning these lovers: “Gifts are given to all prostitutes; but you gave gifts to all your lovers” (Ezekiel 16:33)—and the opposite has happened in your case.

When they have given gifts to the nations and hired nations with payment to aid them, they will be gathered for battle and led away together in chains. And because they love offering gifts to their adversaries, they will therefore obtain a benefit for a little while: they will not pay tribute to the king and princes until they reach Assyria, where they will no longer pay taxes and wages as free men, but will be reduced to the most extreme slavery.

There is no doubt that the same applies to heretics. According to the error of their mind, they go to the Assyrians and think that they are ascending rather than descending. Hence Isaiah says to them: “What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up onto empty roofs?” (Isaiah 22:1). Their Assyrian prince is the great intellect.

Thus Ephraim germinated within himself, presuming that he had grown through his own self-confidence. Or he became a solitary wild ass, so that he might penetrate not the planted fields of the Church but the deserts of the devil.

He loved gifts for his error, promising rewards to himself; or he did everything for the sake of shameful profit. Or certainly he gave gifts and payments to his lovers, the demons, and, when he has done this, he will be handed over to the nations.

For just as the nations worship physical images, so these people regard as gods the idols they have fashioned from their own hearts. Therefore they will be counted among the nations.

But if, he says, they repent now, in the present age, and I receive them, they will cease to set up over themselves a little king and his princes. We should understand the little king to be the devil, in contrast with the great King, who cannot have fellowship with Belial. As soon as he has been received, he drives the little king and his princes from the hearts of believers.

According to the Hebrew, however, those who had previously been scattered and had hired nations for themselves will be gathered into the Church of God, and they will rest from the burden of the king—concerning whom the Apostle rebukes those who have been divided from the Church, saying: “Without us you reign; and I wish that you did reign” (I Corinthians 4:8)—and from the princes whom they have established in the synagogues of the devil.

[Col. 0888A] **(Verse 11.)** “Because Ephraim multiplied altars for sinning, the altars became for him occasions of guilt.”

**Septuagint:** “Because Ephraim multiplied altars, the beloved altars became for him occasions of sin.”

[Col. 0887D] **Note:** This is another absurd gloss by an inept annotator in the Palatine manuscripts: “the altars became offenses for him,” instead of “beloved,” contrary to the Greek text, *eis hamartias egenonto autō thysiastēria ēgapēmena* (εἰς ἁμαρτίας ἐγένοντο αὐτῷ θυσιαστήρια ἠγαπημένα), “the altars became for him beloved things toward sins.”

He says that, after being led into captivity, they will rest for a little while from the burden of king and prince. And they will suffer this because Ephraim, their prince, multiplied altars—not altars on which he might sacrifice to the Lord, but altars on which he might join sins to sins. These altars, that is, the shrines, will become for him a transgression, so that the more numerous they are, the more his crimes will multiply.

Then, just as he had said above, “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah?”—as though hesitating and seeking with what medicine he might heal the sick person and by what counsels he might recall the sinner to salvation—

**(Verse 12.)** “I shall write for him my many laws, which are reckoned as foreign [Vulgate: ‘computed’].” They will offer [Vulgate: ‘bring’] sacrifices, slaughter meat, and eat it, but the Lord will not receive them.

**Septuagint:** “I will write for them a multitude of laws; his ordinances were regarded as foreign altars.”

[Col. 0887D] **Note:** The Palatine manuscripts also insert here “altars of transgression” instead of what should be restored from the Greek, “beloved altars,” *thysiastēria ta ēgapēmena* (θυσιαστήρια τὰ ἠγαπημένα). Moreover, they join this verse to the preceding one both in the Hebrew and in the Septuagint, and after the words “recall the sinner to salvation” continue Jerome’s exposition as follows: “I will write for them again the laws which I first gave through Moses. But…” and so forth.

For if they sacrifice offerings and eat meat, the Lord will not receive them—the offerings that I formerly gave through Moses. But what benefit is there in writing other laws, when they have despised those which they previously received?

Is it not contempt for God when, although I commanded that there should be one altar in Jerusalem, they made idols on every mountain and hill, by which they provoked the Lord? They also made altars not to please me, but to eat the meat of the animals after sacrificing many victims, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Truly, truly, I say to you, you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled” (John 6:16).

Their entire concern with sacrifices is that they may devour the victims, not that through them they may please God. Nor will the Lord receive the offerings which they sacrificed not to him but to their belly and throat.

The Apostle teaches that there is one altar in the Church, one faith, and one baptism (Ephesians 4). The heretics have abandoned this and constructed many altars for themselves—not to appease God, but to multiply their offenses.

Therefore they do not deserve to receive the laws of God, since they previously despised the laws they had received. And if they say anything from the Scriptures, it must be compared not with divine words but with pagan ideas.

[Col. 0887D] **Note:** The text was corruptly printed as “but also with pagan ideas.” Victorius says: “I have thought it worthwhile to place these words before the eyes of readers, so that anyone may learn from them how aptly the innovators of our time are described by Jerome in those ancient heretics. Yet our own are so much worse than those men in that they remove from the Church the sacrifice which the whole world has never lacked, and assert that Christ’s unbloody victim is to be contemplated only in the mind, not also offered in reality—contrary to what Christ himself commanded us through the Apostles when he said: ‘Whenever you do these things, do them in remembrance of me.’ You hear also that we receive Christ’s true flesh in the sacrament of the Eucharist, not its shadow or figure, as these men blasphemously claim.”

These people sacrifice and eat many victims, abandoning the one sacrifice of Christ. Nor do they eat the flesh of him whose flesh is the food of believers.

Whatever they do, whether they imitate the order and rite of sacrifices, give alms, promise chastity, pretend humility, or deceive simple people with feigned flatteries, the Lord will receive nothing from such sacrifices.

**(Verses 13–14.)** “Now he will remember their iniquities [Vulgate: ‘iniquity’] and visit their sins; they themselves will return into [Vulgate: ‘to’] Egypt. Israel has forgotten his Maker, and has built shrines; Judah has multiplied fortified cities. I will send fire upon his city, and it will devour his houses.”

**Septuagint:** “Now he will remember their iniquities and avenge their injustices. They themselves have turned to Egypt. Israel has forgotten the one who made him, and they have built shrines. Judah has multiplied fortified cities, and I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour his foundations.”

The difference between *anomia* (ἀνομία), “iniquity,” and sin is this: iniquity occurs before the Law, while sin occurs after the Law. The Lord will remember the iniquities of those who remain in offenses—the iniquities they committed before the Law—but he will not remember their sins; he will exact vengeance.

He will remember the iniquity of former times and visit their previous sins because they have returned to Egypt, either seeking its aid or worshiping the same gods in which they formerly went astray: Apis and Mnevis (*āpin et mneuin*).

For Israel has forgotten his Maker and, having despised the Creator, has fashioned another lord for himself. He built shrines on high places—whole hills and mountains and shady trees—consecrating them to Baal, Astaroth, and other idols.

Judah likewise understood that Israel had withdrawn from the love of God and that their sins had been visited, yet did not turn back to the Lord. Instead, he trusted in the fortification of cities, which the Lord says he will destroy and devour down to their foundations.

[Col. 0889D] **Note:** In one Palatine manuscript: “which he says he will destroy, devouring its houses down to the foundation.” In another: “and devouring them down to their foundations,” and so forth. There is no doubt that “its” refers to Judah, although some read “their foundations,” referring to the cities.

According to the allegorical interpretation, the iniquities—*anomia* (ἀνομία) and *adikia* (ἀδικία)—are the sins we committed before baptism and which were forgiven for us in baptism. The sins, however, are those we committed after baptism, concerning which it is also written in the Psalm: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31).

All these things will be charged against the heretics, so that both their former iniquities and their new sins may be repaid to them. Those who had gone out from Egypt through confession of Christ have returned to Egypt through faithlessness.

Israel has forgotten his Maker, and, having despised the Creator, has fashioned another lord for himself. Judah too—that is, the ecclesiastical man—has built fortified cities for himself through evil works or through a perverse interpretation of the holy Scriptures, relying not on God’s help but on an artful falsehood [alternative: ‘an artisan’s falsehood’].

The Lord says that he will set these cities on fire with the fire of his Spirit and devour their *baris* (βάρις), that is, their great houses built in the form of towers. He will overthrow their badly laid foundations, so that they may no longer be able to construct sacrilegious shrines against God.

[Col. 0889D] **Note:** Earlier printed editions corruptly have *bareis* (βαρεῖς), which denotes something heavy rather than large houses. The term is derived not from *barus* (βαρύς), “heavy,” but from *baris* (βάρις). Jerome himself teaches this in Letter 65 to Principia, no. 14, on Psalm 44: “For what we translated as ‘from ivory houses,’ since the Greek reads *apo bareōn elephantinōn* (ἀπὸ βαρέων ἐλεφάντινων), some Latins, because of the ambiguity of the word, translated ‘from heavy things’; but *baris* is a local Palestinian word, and even today enclosed houses, built in the form of towers and public fortifications, are called *bareis*. See what we have noted more fully on this passage.”

Some understand the fortified cities built by Judah in a favorable sense. They attempt to soften the statement that seemed contrary to this interpretation—“I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour his houses”—by saying that, after what is perfect has come, what is partial will be destroyed.

What we read according to the Septuagint—“and in Assyria they ate unclean things”—is not found in the Hebrew and should therefore be marked with an obelus.

We can say, however, that the Israelites, longing for Egypt and having been captured by the Assyrians, ate unclean things there, in accordance with Ezekiel, who describes them as eating sacrifices offered to idols in Chaldea (Ezekiel 4), and as being so polluted by the filth of idols that they are compared to human excrement.

Heretics likewise, whose princes are the Assyrians, as we have often said, eat unclean things among them while they are defiled by their filth.

### Chapter 9 — Verses 1–2

“Do not rejoice, Israel; do not exult like the peoples, for you have prostituted yourself away from your God. You have loved the prostitute’s payment above every threshing floor of wheat. The threshing floor and winepress will not feed them, and the wine will deceive them.”

**Septuagint:** “Do not rejoice, Israel, and do not exult like the peoples, for you have prostituted yourself away from your God. You have loved gifts above every threshing floor of wheat. The threshing floor and winepress did not know them, and the wine deceived them.”

Those who have withdrawn from God, when they have entered the depths of sins and despaired of their salvation, will despise everything (Proverbs 18).

Thus Israel, withdrawing from the Law of God and worshiping idols, says that it is one nation among many nations, rejoicing and congratulating itself that it has withdrawn from knowledge of God, that it is a people mixed with the others. Therefore he now rebukes them and says: “Do not rejoice; do not exult; do not think that you are like the other nations.”

For one who does not know God is punished differently from one who withdraws from God, because “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten much” (Luke 12).

You considered many threshing floors and winepresses the payment for your prostitution, so that you might enjoy abundance of all things. Therefore the threshing floor and winepress will produce neither wheat nor wine, and the winepress will deceive them—or will deny them the wine with which they thought they would be made drunk.

We read that under Ahab, king of Israel, and Elijah the prophet, there was a very severe famine in Samaria, so severe that mothers ate the corpses of their own children (III Kings 6). At that time, literally, the threshing floor and winepress did not feed them; the wine deceived them, and they wasted away in poverty.

The same is said to the heretics: they should not exult or rejoice or think themselves like the other nations. The nations did not believe in God; these, however, worship idols under the name of God and prostitute themselves away from their God.

They multiply many threshing floors and countless winepresses for themselves. They eat wheat from which the bread of mourning is made, and drink the wine of Sodom, which is crushed with the gall of asps.

And because they have prepared many winepresses and numerous threshing floors for themselves, they will therefore neither eat nor drink from the true and one threshing floor and from the winepress that the Lord Jesus trod. Whatever they think they possess will be corrupted by falsehood.

**(Verses 3–4.)** “They will not dwell in the Lord’s land. Ephraim has returned to Egypt, and in Assyria he has eaten what is unclean. They will not pour wine for the Lord, and their sacrifices will not please him. Like the bread of mourners, all who eat [Vulgate: ‘will eat’] it will be defiled, because their bread is for their own souls and will not enter the house of the Lord.”

**Septuagint:** “They did not dwell in the Lord’s land. Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, and in Assyria he ate what is unclean. They did not pour wine for the Lord, nor did their sacrifices please him. They were like the bread of his mourning; all who eat them will be defiled, because the bread of their souls will not enter the house of the Lord.”

[Col. 0891D] **Note:** Victorius, following four Florentine manuscripts and the Vulgate, substituted the singular *intrabit*, “will enter,” for *intrabunt*, “will enter,” in the plural. Understand it, he says, of the bread. Hence Jerome: “Their bread”—that is, the food they offer—“will not enter the house of the Lord,” which has been destroyed. In the Septuagint, however, it reads “they will not enter,” because they translated “bread” in the plural.

Not only did the threshing floor and winepress fail to feed them, and did wine deceive them in the land of Israel when everything perished for three years and six months, but the inhabitants themselves will also depart from the Lord’s land and be led into a foreign land, so that they will not dwell in the holy land which they polluted by their fornications.

“Ephraim has returned to Egypt,” he says, “and in Assyria he has eaten what is unclean.” Some have added above, “and in Assyria he ate what is unclean,” although it is not found in the Hebrew, as we have already said.

When they are in Chaldea, without a temple and without an altar, they will not pour wine for the Lord but for demons, nor will they please him who pour libations to foreign gods, who are held in captivity, and who eat sacrifices offered to idols in Assyria, becoming like the bread of mourners.

For it is not permitted to eat from the sacrifices of mourners; and if someone eats, what was lawfully offered will become unclean. The Greeks call the meals of mourners *nekrodeipna* (νεκρόδειπνα); we may call them *parentalia*, because they are offered to deceased parents.

[Col. 0891D] **Note:** I have not altered what all the published books present. Yet I think what our manuscripts have is more correct: *perideipna* (περίδειπνα), the term by which the Greeks call funeral meals or funeral banquets; the Latins call them *parentalia*. Conversely, I doubt whether *nekrodeipna* was ever used in this sense by any good writer, or whether it is even a Greek word. Certainly Jerome elsewhere continually uses the word *perideipnon*. In his Commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 16, he says: “It is customary to bring food to mourners and prepare a banquet, which the Greeks call *perideipna* and which our people commonly call *parentalia*, because rites are performed for parents.”

Not only the one who offers such food but also the one who eats it will be unclean. For their bread—that is, the food they offer—will not enter the house of the Lord, which has been destroyed and burned by Babylonian fire. Rather, it will belong to their soul—that is, to their appetite and their concern for pleasure. As for me, I do not approve of polluted things.

Those who have withdrawn from the Church will not dwell in the Lord’s land. In their minds they have returned to Egypt, and they eat [alternative: ‘have eaten’] the sacrifices of the Assyrians—that is, of demons. Nor do they pour out for the Lord the wine by which they have been made drunk for debauchery; neither what they offer nor those who offer it please him.

The sacrifices of the heretics are bread of mourning and tears, for everything they do will be turned into weeping. They will not be able to hear, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:5), but instead they will hear: “Woe to those who laugh, for they will mourn” (Luke 6:25).

Whatever they offer, they offer not to God but to the dead—namely, to those who devised criminal heresies. Whoever eats from their sacrifices will be defiled. “The blind will be led into the pit by the blind.” Whatever they do, they do for the sake of pleasures: to deceive the people and devour the houses of widows.

We may call the bread of mourning deadly words, by which they speak iniquity against the Lord. This bread does not enter the house of God. For the assemblies of the heretics are not called houses of God but dens of thieves.

**(Verses 5–6.)** “What will you do on the solemn day, on the day of the Lord’s festival? For behold, they have gone away from devastation. Egypt will gather them; Memphis will bury them. Their desirable silver will be inherited by the nettle; the burdock will be in their tents.”

**Septuagint:** “What will you do on the day of assembly and on the day of the Lord’s festival? Therefore, behold, they will go away from the misery of Egypt, and Memphis will receive them and bury them. Machmas will possess their silver; thorns will be in their tents.”

When the day of captivity comes and the fiercest enemy presses in, he says, what is my festival? What sacrifice do I have that is acceptable to me, since it avenges me upon my enemies, imposes a limit on injury, and scourges impious children?

What, then, will you do on the day of the Lord’s festival? Answer.

When they remain silent, he answers for himself—or rather, he sees with divine eyes what they are going to do: “Behold,” he says, “while misery and devastation oppress them, and the Assyrian and Chaldean seek to bind them as captives, they fled to Egypt.”

There Memphis will bury them. At that time Memphis was the capital of Egypt, before Alexandria—which was previously called *No*—received both the size and the name of its city from Alexander the Macedonian.

[Col. 0892D] **Note:** The name Mamach or Mamachas has been restored in the text of the Septuagint and in St. Jerome’s Commentary, where I found it corrupted because of ignorance of Hebrew. Unless we read it in this way, St. Jerome’s observation will be foolish and contrary to the truth: he teaches us that the Septuagint translators were deceived by the similarity of the letters *daleth* and *kaph*. Therefore, instead of *Mamad*, they read *Mamach*, and not *Machmas* with *shin* at the end, since that letter has no similarity to *daleth*.

In the book of Hebrew Place Names, the same name is written in Greek as *Machō* (Μαχώ), and in Latin as *Machaas*. Thus it is certain to us that this word was corrupted everywhere in the Septuagint, since it is correctly read in St. Jerome’s book of Hebrew Names and here in chapter 9 of Hosea.

Martianus, although no manuscript supports him, consistently inserted *Mamachas* here and above instead of *Machmas* or *Magmas*. His sole reason for changing the name is the one he elaborates in several notes: unless we read it this way, St. Jerome’s observation would be foolish and contrary to the truth, since Jerome teaches that the Septuagint was deceived by the similarity of *daleth* and *kaph*, and therefore read *Mamach* instead of *Mamad*. He should consequently have written *Mamach* himself, not *Mamachas*.

Indeed, if one may alter an author’s text according to a preconceived opinion, nothing will remain that cannot be reshaped according to human judgment. We have restored the ancient reading, which is also found in all the manuscripts, especially since the Greek archetype consistently has *Machmas* (Μαχμᾶς). Moreover, Jerome would not have said that, if the Septuagint had taken one letter for *daleth*, they had placed it in the first position but not in the second syllable.

The Septuagint’s statement, “Machmas will bury them,” is not found in the Hebrew. Instead, the Hebrew has *MAMAD*, which means “desirable.”

From this it is clear that they were deceived by the similarity of the letters *DALETH* and *CHAPH*, and that, instead of *Mamad*, which all translated as “desirable,” they thought that Machmas was a city of Egypt.

We may also understand the words, “Behold, they have gone away from devastation; Egypt will gather them; Memphis will bury them,” as referring to the tribe of Judah: when Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had appointed over the land, was killed by Ishmael, the remnant of the people fled with the prophet Jeremiah to Egypt. There, later pursued by the Chaldeans, they were either captured or buried (IV Kings 25).

Their desirable silver may be understood as the estates and all the ornaments of their estates, which are purchased with silver. What follows—“the burdock in their tents”—signifies a long desolation: where their houses once stood, burdock, nettles, and thorns will grow.

[Col. 0894D] **Note:** Our manuscripts restore after Victorius the word “all,” which Martianus rashly deleted. In the same manuscripts, shortly afterward: “but the desirable things of silver.”

The same is said to the heretics: when the solemn day comes, what will you do? Instead of “solemn day,” Aquila translated “time.” From this it is clear that the phrase does not refer to a feast day but to the time of retribution, for it immediately continues: “The days of vengeance have come; the days of your retribution have come.”

Behold, you have been devastated by many enemies. The Assyrians and Chaldeans have slaughtered you; you have fled to the world and have been compared with the other nations.

There Memphis will bury you. Memphis is interpreted as “from the mouth,” and the meaning is: according to your blasphemies, you will receive what you deserve; what you have spoken, you will experience in punishments.

The desirable things—that is, the doctrines you had artificially composed for yourselves with eloquence, which is interpreted as silver—will be possessed by the nettle, which will consume you with eternal burning.

And there will be burdock or a thorn in your tents, for thorns will arise in the hands of those who have been drunk from the Babylonian cup (Jeremiah 51).

In the Gospel also we read that shameful thoughts, the cares of this world, and clinging vices are called thorns, which, springing up among the plants, choke the growing grain (Matthew 13).

### (Verse 7)

“The days of visitation have come; the days of retribution have come. Know, Israel, the foolish prophet, the spiritual man mad because of the multitude of your iniquity and the multitude of your madness.”

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The same manuscripts: “Know, Israel, that you are foolish”; and a little later, “the multitude of your madness.”]

The Septuagint: “The days of vengeance have come; the days of your retribution have come, and Israel will be afflicted like a prophet gone mad, a man who possessed the Spirit, because of the multitude of your iniquities; your madness has increased.”

Here too there is the customary error. Where we have translated, “Know, Israel”—that is, “Israelites”—the Hebrew reads *JADAU* ( ), but the Septuagint translated it “will be afflicted,” taking the letter *YOD* for *VAU* and reading *RES* instead of *DALETH*. The one reading signifies knowledge, the other affliction or wickedness.

The days of visitation have therefore come, of which he had said above (verse 5): “What will you do on the solemn day, and on the day of the Lord’s festival?” The days of retribution have come. O Israel, now recognize your own words: you called the prophet who spoke the truth to you and prophesied by the Holy Spirit foolish and mad, in accordance with what the princes said to Jehu at Ramoth-gilead: “Why has this madman come to you?” (IV Kings IX, 11).

Therefore, because of the multitude of your iniquities, in which you raged for a long time in crime, recognize that it is not my prophet but you who are mad—you who labored for the purpose of trampling upon my words. In place of “madness,” Aquila translated *ἐγκότησιν* (*enkotēsin*), which in Latin we may call either anger or the remembrance of pain.

Some interpret the day of vengeance and retribution as the day of judgment, when Israel will be afflicted—Israel, who now boasts that he sees God, although he is not guided by the Holy Spirit but is driven in various directions by a demonic spirit, not knowing what he says: calling the Son of God a creature, denying that the Holy Spirit is God, and again asserting that one God is good and another is the creator of the world. Their madness is manifold, because their iniquities too have been exceedingly numerous.

The one whom we called “the foolish prophet,” the Seventy translated “the false prophet.” And lest, by repeating the same things too often, we seem to distrust the reader’s intelligence, we briefly remind him that whatever is said in this prophet about Israel and Ephraim is to be referred to heretics, who, truly mad, speak lies against God.

### (Verses 8 and 9)

“Ephraim is a watchman with my God; the prophet is a snare of ruin over all his ways; madness is in the house of his God. They have sinned profoundly. As in the days of Gibeah, he will remember their iniquities and visit their sins.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts insert, according to the Vulgate, “he has become.” In place of *iniquitates*, Victorius rewrites *iniquitatis*, in the genitive, following the same Vulgate reading and the Hebrew. We correct certain lesser matters below.]

The Septuagint: “Ephraim is a watchman with God, a prophet; a crooked snare is over all his ways. They devised madness in the house of God. They were corrupted according to the days of the hill. He will remember their iniquities; he will avenge their sins.”

For this reason God gave rulers, so that they might correct a people who were sinning and bring them back to the right path. Hence he also says to Ezekiel: “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. V, 17).

Jeroboam, therefore, was appointed as a watchman among the people and as a prophet with my God—that is, with the God who speaks these things through Hosea. But, according to what was written above, “You became a snare to the watchman, and a net spread over Tabor, and you turned aside victims into the depths,” he is even now called a snare of the people of Israel, because all fall into his snare—especially since he placed, or devised, madness in the house of God: that is, he made the golden calf at Bethel. For this is what “house of God” means. And he sinned so profoundly in his crime, and was so sunk in the abyss of impiety, that he surpassed the crime once committed at Gibeah, when they killed the Levite’s wife, who was returning from Bethlehem, by an illicit act of intercourse (Judg. XIX).

We may understand “the days of Gibeah” also as referring to the time when they chose a king for themselves instead of God from the city of Gibeah—that is, Saul. And he says that they have now sinned much more grievously by choosing Jeroboam and worshiping idols than at the time when they chose Saul. For here idolatry was joined to schism; there, the worship of God remained among the people.

Therefore he will remember their iniquities—he who now seems, because of his patience, to have forgotten them—and he will visit their sins and wounds, which have festered for a long time.

Searching the ancient histories, I cannot find that anyone divided the Church and led a people astray from the house of the Lord except those who had been appointed by God as priests and prophets, that is, as watchmen. These men, therefore, are turned into a crooked snare, placing an obstacle everywhere, so that whoever enters by their ways may fall and be unable to stand in Christ; he is led away into various errors and carried along crooked paths to destruction.

These are the watchmen of Ephraim, who devised madness in the house of the Lord—that is, in the Church or in the Holy Scriptures—by interpreting them perversely; or certainly in each individual believer, who is most rightly called the house of God.

Therefore they were corrupted and perished according to the days of the hill, when they spoke iniquity on the high places and climbed upon empty rooftops. God will remember their iniquity, by which they acted wickedly toward their neighbor, leading him out of the Church, and he will visit their sins, by which they sinned against their own souls.

This is what we read in the psalm: “Beside the path they placed a stumbling-block for me” (Ps. CXXXIX, 6). For unless someone sees the path of God—that is, hears the name of Christ—he will not enter through him. Hence heretics also, under the name of Christ, place snares beside the path, so that the one who believes he is walking upon Christ—of whom we read that he himself is the way—may tread upon the snares of those who devised madness in the house of God.

### (Verses 10 and 11)

“Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel; like the first fruits of the fig tree at its top I saw their fathers. But they themselves went in to Baal-peor, and were alienated into confusion, and became abominable, like the things they loved.”

The Septuagint: “As a grape in the wilderness I found Israel, and as a fig on a fig tree in its season I saw their fathers. But they entered Baal-peor, and were alienated into confusion, and became abominable like those beloved.”

In other copies we read: “And they became beloved, like the abominable”—which agrees better with the truth.

When the whole world was a wilderness and had no knowledge of God, he says, “I found the people of Israel like a grape in the solitude.” And he explains how he found them: “Like the first fruits of the fig tree at its top I saw their fathers.” Therefore the people were found in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Observe the propriety of the expression: the ancestors are seen, while the people are found; and in both cases there is a vine and a fig tree, beneath which the one who trusts in the Lord is said to rest.

But they themselves, after being brought out of Egypt, fornicated with the Midianites (Num. XXV), and entered—elsewhere, “went out”—to Baal-peor, the idol of the Moabites, whom we may call Priapus.

[Note: The older editions corrupt everything wherever a difficulty of reading occurs. Here, despite the protest of the manuscript codices, they retain a shameful and false reading. Finally, Baal-peor is interpreted as “an idol having lust in its mouth,” that is, at its summit, a skin. How absurdly this has been placed is clearly shown both by the etymology of the name Baal-peor and by the commentary that follows, where it is said that they entered the idol Baal-peor, which has a skin in its mouth. Therefore Baal-peor does not mean “having lust in its mouth”; rather, it was an idol of lust, which, because of the name Baal-peor, is interpreted as “having a skin in its mouth.” MART. — Our manuscripts: “that is, an idol of lust.”]

Finally, Baal-peor is interpreted as “an idol of lust,” having in its mouth—that is, at its summit—a skin, so that it might display the obscenity of the male member.

And because they entered Baal-peor, they were therefore alienated from God and enslaved to their own confusion—that is, to the idol—so that they worshiped the very thing on account of which they had withdrawn from God. As it is written: “By whatever anyone is overcome, by this he is also enslaved” (II Pet. II, 19). And just as those who serve their appetite have their belly as their god (Phil. III), so those who serve lust have Baal-peor as their god.

“And they became,” he says, “abominable, like the things they loved,” in accordance with what is written in the Psalms: “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Ps. CXXXIV, 18), so that they may be called not only idolaters but idols.

But when the Lord said in his passion, “I alone have trodden the winepress, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. LXIII, 3), and in the psalm, “Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed” (Ps. II, 1), when the whole world was held in sin, the nations did not know God, and Israel had rejected the one whom it had previously known, then the Lord found the people of Christian Israel first in the apostles and in apostolic men, a people seeing God in understanding; and he was satisfied with their sweetest fruits, the grape and the fig. If they are found in the wilderness and before their season has ripened, they are all the more precious because of their rarity.

But they themselves—that is, Israel, who assume the Christian name, for this is not to be understood of the ancestors—entered the idol Baal-peor, which has a skin in its mouth. For whatever the heretic says is deadly and separated from the living word of God.

Or we may understand “they entered into lust.” For it is difficult to find a heretic who loves chastity—not that he ceases to commend it with his lips, but he does not preserve it in his conscience, saying one thing and doing another. Hence they were alienated from God, had glory in their confusion, and became abominable—those who had previously been loved in their ancestors.

But if we wish to read, “They became abominable, like the beloved,” although this is not found in the Hebrew, we shall say that the Gentiles became abominable in the same way as the heretics who had previously been loved in their ancestors: that both alike became abominable and guilty of sin.

### (Verse 12)

“Ephraim, like a bird, flew away; their glory has departed from childbirth, from the womb, and from conception. Even if they raise their children, I will make them without children among men. But woe to them also when I depart from them.

“Ephraim, as I saw, was Tyre, founded in beauty; and Ephraim will bring his children out to the slayer.”

The Septuagint: “Ephraim, like a bird, flew away; their glory was in childbirth, in labor, and in conception. For even if they raise their children, they will be without children among men, because woe is also to them: my flesh is from them. Ephraim, as I saw, offered his children for capture; and Ephraim, to bring his children out to slaughter.”

The interpreters disagree greatly in this passage. Where we said, “Woe to them when I depart from them,” the Septuagint and Theodotion translated, “Woe to them; my flesh is from them.” Seeking the cause of such great variation, I think I have found it.

“My flesh” in the Hebrew language is called *BASARI* ( ); while, if we say “my departure” or “my turning aside,” it is called *BASORI* ( ). Thus the Septuagint and Theodotion translated “my flesh” in place of “my departure” and “my turning aside.”

Again, where we placed, “Ephraim, as I saw, was Tyre,” the Septuagint translated *θήραν* (*thēran*), that is, “hunting” or “capture.” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it as “a very hard rock,” that is, flint, which in Hebrew is called *SUR* ( ). If we read *SOR*, it means Tyre.

But the Septuagint interpreters, thinking that because of the similarity of the letters *RES* and *DALETH* the letter was not *RES* but *DALETH*, read *SUD*, that is, “hunting” or “capture.” Hence *Bethsaida* ( ) is said to mean “house of hunters.”

We have discussed the diversity of the interpreters; let us return to the meaning.

Ephraim—that is, the ten tribes—flew away like a bird into captivity and departed from its own place. He called it a bird to show the speed of its passage into Babylon.

But if we read, “Like a bird, their glory flew away,” we shall understand this to mean that God’s help departed from them and flew away.

What follows—“from childbirth, from the womb, and from conception”—may be understood in two ways: either that the glory which flew away from Ephraim also departs from their childbirth, womb, and conception—that is, that it abandons their children and leaves their descendants—or else we may say that all Israel’s glory consisted in its multitude, and that it considered itself greater than its brother Judah, because Ephraim ruled ten tribes while Judah ruled two.

Therefore the Lord says that even if they raise children and gather a multitude of offspring, they will be handed over to slaughter. And now a true woe weighs upon them, when God has departed from them.

Then he explains what Ephraim once was, though it has now been abandoned: “It was so beautiful,” he says, “and so surrounded by God’s protection that it was like Tyre, encircled by the sea, or like an exceedingly hard cliff, fixed in the earth, which despises all storms and cares nothing for whirlwinds and winds.”

But Ephraim itself—or Tyre, which was founded in the beauty—elsewhere, “fullness”—of the sea, will bring its children out to captivity.

Many refer this chapter to the time of Hazael, who besieged Samaria and afflicted it with famine for a long time, so that those under siege considered death by the sword easier than death by starvation (IV Kings VI, VII, and VIII).

We, however, shall understand it tropologically: Ephraim—that is, the heretics—has departed from the Church like a bird and has all its glory in childbirth, in the womb, and in conception. If they have begotten many children, the Lord threatens that even if they raise them, they will be punished—not by someone else but by the Lord himself—because they have generated children of fornication. And a true woe will be theirs when God has departed from them.
