At the same time he repeats what Ephraim had been. “When it was in the Church,” he says, “it was battered by the temptations of this world like Tyre by the waves of the sea; yet no adversity could overcome it, because it had the foundation of Christ, upon which the house was built and could not be overthrown” (Matt. VII).

But now it brings its children out to the slayer—that is, to the devil. And he beautifully says “brings out,” meaning that it makes them go out from the Church.

We may call the children of Ephraim its worst thoughts and doctrines opposed to the truth. The Lord kills these with the breath of his mouth and does not allow them to possess such children; rather, he abandons them to eternal destruction.

But where we read in the Septuagint, “My flesh is from them,” and, “Ephraim, as I saw, offered his children for capture,” we understand it as follows:

If Christ is the head of the body, that is, of the Church, then all of us are members of Christ and of the Church. Whoever therefore departs from the Church tears the body of Christ. Ephraim, then, was flesh and a member of the Lord and Savior.

But he offered his children for capture—for the capture of those concerning whom it is written: “Our soul, like a sparrow, has been rescued from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. CXXIII, 7).

And he led his children out from the Church to slaughter, or to wounding, so that they might be wounded by those who shoot burning arrows, striking and consuming them at once.

### (Verse 14)

“Give them, Lord. What will you give them? Give them a womb without children and dry breasts.”

[Note: The Septuagint has the same wording. The words that were missing have been supplied from our manuscripts.]

The Septuagint likewise.

If we misuse the things God has given as blessings and turn them into the opposite of what he intended, it is expedient that they be taken away from us.

Thus the tongue was given for praising the Lord God and speaking what is good. If someone abuses it for blasphemy, the Psalmist prays against him: “Let deceitful lips that speak iniquity against the righteous with pride and abuse become mute” (Ps. XXX, 19). And elsewhere: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Ps. XI, 4).

Therefore, since Ephraim gloried in the womb, conception, childbirth, and multitude of peoples, the prophet prays to the Lord and says: “Give them, Lord.” And he answers himself: “What will you give them?” He immediately adds: “Give them a barren womb and dry breasts,” so that they may have no grounds for pride and may be confounded precisely in what they customarily boast about.

It is clear that this may also be understood of teachers of doctrines opposed to the truth, who glory in the multitude of peoples and in the children whom they have nourished for destruction, leading them out of the Church and bringing them to the slayer. The devil slaughters as many as the heretics have begotten as children in error.

Of such a soul it is said: “Blessed is the sterile and undefiled woman who has not known a bed in sin” (Wis. III, 12). For blessed is the ecclesiastical man who, in comparison with the heretic, has not procreated children in error.

And elsewhere we read: “It is better to be childless with virtue. For from an unlawful union the seed will perish” (Wis. IV and III, according to the Septuagint). “And even when they have lived long, they will be counted as nothing, and their old age will be without honor at the end. For the multitude of the ungodly, though fertile, is of no use.” Nor should we think that he prayed bodily for a barren womb and dry breasts.

### (Verse 15)

“All their wickedness is in Gilgal, for there I hated them.”

[Note: The same words are again supplied by our manuscripts; the Septuagint likewise has them.]

In Gilgal Saul was anointed king, while Samuel announced God’s anger to the people (I Kings X). “There,” he says, “I hated them; and, asking for a human king, they withdrew from my rule.” Or this may be because Gilgal is a place of idolatry, where they committed all their crimes.

But because Gilgal is interpreted as “revelation,” or as *κυλισμοί* (*kylismoi*), that is, “rollings,” he says that all the evils of the heretics will be revealed at the time when God gives them a barren womb and dry breasts, and they see their own disgrace. Those who boasted in pride that they had climbed to lofty places will be rolled down to the earth or dragged to the underworld.

Truly heretics are worthy of God’s hatred, for they speak lies against the Lord. Of them he says in what follows:

“Because of the wickedness of their inventions I will drive them out of my house. I will no longer love them. All their princes are departing,” or “disobedient.”

[Note: We have again and for the third time supplied from our manuscripts the words that were missing; the Septuagint has the same wording.]

There is no doubt that this also applies to the heretics: they have been cast out of the house of God, and he will not continue to love them as long as they remain in error. All their princes have departed from God, or are disobedient, such as Valentinus, Marcion, and the others.

We may call the demons the princes of the heretics. They truly have departed from God and are called princes, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “The prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). And the Apostle says that we fight against powers, principalities, and the rulers of this darkness (Eph. VI).

But according to the historical sense it is asked how he cast them out of his house—that is, the ten tribes—when they had not been in the house of God.

We may call the house of God either the Holy Land, into which they had been brought, or the false name of Israel, or the fact that prophets were sent to them as to the people of God.

That he would not continue to love them, and that all the kings of Israel had departed from God, is clear: even to this day they remain in captivity.

Others think that the statement, “I will drive them out of my house,” refers to the kingdom of Judah, which too would be led into captivity. But how could “I will not continue to love them” apply to them, since afterward they were brought back to Jerusalem? And how could all their princes be described as departing, when we read that David, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah were righteous kings?

Therefore we must pass to the time of Christ, at whose coming they were cast out of the house of God and were no longer saved as Israel but as the Christian people.

Hence the Lord also made himself a whip of cords and drove them out of the temple, because they had made his Father’s house “a house of commerce” (John II).

### (Verses 16 and 17)

“Ephraim has been struck; their root has dried up; they will never bear fruit. Even if they should beget children, I will kill the beloved offspring of their womb. My God will reject them, because they did not listen to him, and they will be wanderers among the nations.”

The Septuagint: “Ephraim has suffered in his roots; he has dried up; he bears no fruit. For even if they should beget children, I will kill the desirable things of their womb. God will repel them, because they did not listen to him, and they will be wanderers among the nations.”

He takes the metaphor from a tree whose roots, if they have dried up, cannot produce fruit; and even if it produces a little, it will immediately dry up in the flower itself.

He speaks of Ephraim, whose root dried up because it lost God, in whom it had been founded; or because it did not deserve to have its fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—in whom it had planted its root. Therefore it does not produce the fruit of righteousness.

“And even if it does,” he says, “I will kill the beloved offspring of its womb,” in accordance with what he had said above: “If they raise their children, I will make them without children among men.” Hence God also rejected them and made them go into captivity.

“And they will be wanderers among the nations.”

We may say the same thing about all the Jews. Because their leaders departed from God and stirred up the people to seek Christ’s death, he therefore cast them out of his house and will not continue to love them. He struck their root and dried it up, and they will no longer produce fruit. Even if they do and seem to meditate upon Holy Scripture and the Law, and as though they were producing beloved children bring forth some knowledge and doctrine from their own heart, it will be cut down, with the Lord opposing it.

[Note: Martian, following Erasmus, reads *amantissimi filii*, “most beloved sons,” in the nominative, contrary to the manuscripts. A little later, for *succidetur*, the manuscripts of Florence, cited by Victor, read *succidentur*, “they will be cut down,” which may appropriately refer to those who will have brought them forth.]

For the God of all the prophets has rejected them, because they did not listen to him. They will be wanderers among the nations, having neither an altar, nor a seat, nor a city of their own.

Hence David also says in the psalm: “Do not kill them, lest my people forget; scatter them by your power” (Ps. LVIII, 12). And elsewhere: “According to the multitude of their impieties, drive them out, for they have provoked you, Lord” (Ps. V, 12).

Of this tree we also read in the Gospel: “The axe has already been laid to the roots of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10).

No one should doubt that heretics cannot produce the fruit of virtues, because they have lost the Lord, in whom, according to the Apostle, they ought to have been rooted and founded (Eph. III). Even if they do produce fruit and generate some children through the fertility of their womb, they will die, with the Lord opposing them.

Or, because their fruits are all the things they invent and generate from their own heart, they will dry up and perish. It will become clear to everyone that a dry root cannot produce crops.

These men will be rejected—or rather, they have been rejected—by God because they did not listen to him when he said: “Do not move the boundaries which your fathers established” (Deut. XIX, 14).

Therefore they will be wanderers among the nations, now passing to these opinions and now to those, since they are not satisfied with what they have once discovered but continually exchange old things for new and imitate the errors of the pagans.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0903]

[Col. 0903D] 109–110 I am not unaware, Pammachius, that it is exceedingly difficult for me to produce [Al. “a little work”] a Latin translation of the work of the Twelve Prophets—certainly [Note: I would certainly prefer *ininterpretatum* to be reprinted as a single word. Yet Victorius says that *certe interpretatum* means the same as the Greek ἀκριβῶς ἡρμηνευμένον, “translated accurately.” But Hieronymus himself writes most clearly in the preface above to the book addressed to Pammachius: “There are some who assert that we have acted rashly in undertaking a work which no Latin before us has dared to attempt.”]—and, what might more strongly accuse our rashness than display our learning. But since we can refuse nothing to you when you urge us—indeed, command us—and since, according to the means of those who offer, the two small coins of the poor woman surpassed the riches of many in the treasury of God (Luke 21), whatever we can do we repay first to God, and then to you, who belong to God [Note: Two manuscripts read: “to you, who are God’s pontiff”]. We always remember that little verse:

> Pollio himself is composing new songs.

And although I rejoice that you are openly favorable to me by right of friendship, I fear the silent judgment of your learning; I fear you praising me more than I fear adversaries disparaging me. Rivalry takes credibility away from them, and they should be called not so much judges as accusers. But you, who love [Al. “who”] not persons at all but things, freely express your judgment—although love too allows error, and that saying of Theophrastus is beautiful [Note: The same manuscripts read: “that Theophrastean saying,” equally well], which Tullius translated more by sense than word for word:

> τυφλὸν τὸ φιλοῦν περὶ τὸ φιλούμενον,

that is, “the judgments of those who love are blind.” Nevertheless, in this respect [Note: “The Brixian copies,” says Victorius, “read: ‘Nevertheless, in this respect you should err more, so that you may go astray not through hatred but through love’; this reading is not displeasing.” The sense is: Since, when judging the writings of others, one is generally more likely to err through hatred or love, may you, in judging mine, err in this direction, going astray not through hatred but through love.] I ask you rather to go astray—not through hatred, but through love.

We are dictating the third book on the prophet Hosea, and have reached the heifers of Bethaven. As we spread the sails of our translation, you must utter that prophetic saying:

> “Come, spirit, from the four winds of heaven,”

so that, passing swiftly among the various [Note: Our manuscripts more correctly read *avaros*, “greedy,” instead of *varios*, “various”] reefs of those lying in wait, we may carry the Lord’s merchandise to the safest harbors, while shipwreck rages on every side.

[Col. 0905B] (Verses 5 and 6.) “The inhabitants of Samaria worshiped the heifers of Bethaven, because its people mourned for it; and its priests exulted over it, over its glory, because it had departed from it. Indeed, it itself was carried away to Assyria as a gift to the avenging king; shame will seize Ephraim, and Israel will be ashamed of its [Al. “the”] will.”

The Septuagint: “Those who dwell in Samaria will remain beside the calf of the house of Ὦν, because its people mourned over it. And just as they provoked him, they will rejoice over his glory, because it has been removed from him; and they carried it, binding it among the Assyrians, and brought gifts to King Jarib in the house. Ephraim will receive shame; Israel will be ashamed of its counsel.”

What Bethaven is, for which the Septuagint translated “house of Ὦν,” and who King Jarib is—whose name is interpreted as “avenger”—we discussed more fully above. In Bethaven, therefore, that is, Bethel, the inhabitants of Samaria worshiped golden heifers, which he mockingly called not male calves but heifers, that is, females, so that Israel might be understood to worship not only calf-gods but also cow-goddesses.

And to show that by “the heifers of Bethaven” one heifer in Bethel was meant, he did not say that the people mourned over *them*, but “over it,” that is, over the golden calf. But if the people mourned, why did its priests exult over it? The Hebrews relate that the golden calves were secretly stolen by the priests and that bronze and gilded replacements were put in their place. Thus, when the people mourned in a time of need and distress, the priests rejoiced because the golden calves themselves had been sent among the other gifts to the Assyrian kings, and especially to King Sennacherib, by the king of Israel, and their fraud could neither be exposed nor detected. [Col. 0905D]

This is what he means by “its priests”—that is, the calves—“exulted over it in its glory,” that is, in the calf which they possessed as their glory, because it had departed from it, that is, from the people, and had been transferred to the Assyrians. And, they say, the following verse plainly shows that this is the meaning:

> “Indeed, it itself was carried away to Assyria as a gift to the avenging king.”

Immediately it follows:

> “Shame will seize Ephraim, and Israel will be ashamed of its will,”

or “of its counsel.” For the fraud of the gilders of the calves was reported by letter to the king of Israel, and they were most deeply shamed by the very thing through which they had thought to please those to whom they had sent the gifts, since the recipients judged that this had been accomplished not through the theft of the priests but through the fraud and counsel of the kings.

We read in the Book of Kings that King Menahem of Israel sent a thousand talents of silver to Pul, king of the Assyrians, “so that his hand might be with him,” that is, so that he might provide him assistance. Some think that the golden calves too were sent among these gifts [Note: Other manuscripts prefer “carried away,” while others read “left behind”]. In the present passage Symmachus translated *Jarib* as [Col. 0906B] ὑπερμάχοντι, that is, “champion” and “defender” [Note: Although the sense is the same, the reading of the Palatine manuscripts is preferable: ὑπερμαχητῇ].

According to the spiritual understanding, we must labor to adapt everything to the heretics. The heretics who boasted that they dwelt in the keeping of God’s commandments—that is, in Samaria—worshiped the heifers of Bethaven, or the house of Ὦν, which is interpreted as “labor.” On the day of judgment, when judgment sprouts like bitterness upon the furrows of the field, the people will mourn over it, that is, over the calf and over the perverse doctrine which it thought to be God.

But of the priests he did not say “they will exult”; he said “they exulted,” referring to the past, over their former glory, which they had once magnificently fashioned, because the people had departed from God, or because the very glory of God had departed from the people by whom it had been abandoned.

Whatever the heretics say and compose in elegant language, they send as gifts to their own king, the devil, referring everything to him. Therefore shame will seize them forever, and they will be confounded in their own desires. Someone left it written in his commentaries, both above and in the present passage, that King Jarib, that is, “the avenger,” should be understood as Christ. We reject this entirely. For it is impious to refer to Christ, according to the tropological sense, what according to the historical sense is understood of the Assyrian king.

(Verses 7 and 8.) “Samaria has caused its king to pass away like foam upon the surface of the water, and the high places of the idol, the sin of Israel, will be destroyed.”

The Septuagint: “Samaria has cast away its king like kindling upon the surface of the water, and the altars of Ὦν, the sins of Israel, will be removed.”

For “foam,” which the Septuagint and Theodotion translated as φρύγανον, that is, “kindling,” Symmachus used ἐπίζεμα, meaning the upper waters of a boiling pot, rising into foam and bubbles, which the Greeks call πομφόλυγες. [Col. 0906D] The former term means dry grasses [Note: So read the manuscripts and Victorius; previously this word was missing. Minor corrections are made below], namely, dried herbs and brushwood prepared for a furnace and burning.

Just as foam upon water is quickly dissolved, so the kingdom of the ten tribes will quickly come to an end, and the high places—that is, *BAMOTH* (), concerning which it is written, “Nevertheless the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places” (1 Kings 22:44)—will perish. These very high places are ὢν, or *AVEN* (), that is, “idols,” a word interpreted as “useless.” The idol, and the uselessness, is the sin of Israel. Once the idol and its high places have been destroyed—

(Verses 9.) “The thistle and thorn will rise upon their altars, and they will say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us.’”

The Septuagint: “Thorns and thistles will rise upon their altars, and they will say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us.’”

This is a sign of the final desolation, so that not even walls or the last traces of buildings will remain. At that time they will say to the mountains, “Cover us,” and to the hills, “Fall upon us”—which the Lord says will be fulfilled at the final time of the Jewish captivity.

Whatever is now said against the ten tribes, or against all Israel, we should understand can figuratively (*τυπικῶς*) also be transferred to the whole people: when the Romans have captured Jerusalem and overthrown the Temple, or when the day of judgment has come, as some suppose, they will say in great terror and fear, “Mountains, cover us, and hills, fall upon us,” preferring to die rather than see what brings death.

Samaria of spiritual wickedness, which had separated itself from the people of God, likewise caused its king to pass swiftly away—namely, the word and doctrine of the heretics—like foam or kindling upon the surface of the water. One of these dissolves suddenly while it is being seen; the other is easily lifted from the surface of the waters and thrown into the fire.

Such are the heretics: swelling with foaming words, and mixing burning precepts with the baptism of Christ and with his teachings. All these things will pass away, and the grand words in which they labored—which is what ὢν signifies—will immediately be scattered. In them Israel sinned, and so great will be the desolation of the worst doctrine that thorns and thistles will rise upon their altars.

Everyone knows that thorns and thistles grow where there is no cultivation of the fields. These are the thorns which choke the seed and do not allow what grows in a drunkard’s hand to grow; Israel produced these instead of grapes. For the Lord expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns, or a wild vine resembling grapes, whose bitter taste twists the mouths of those who eat.

Therefore, when the time of judgment has arrived and everything has been overthrown, they will say to the mountains—which they formerly considered high—and to their former teachers, “Cover us”; and to the hills, “Fall upon us.”

But because he placed “Cover us” with the mountains and “Fall upon us” with the hills, something more sacred must be explained. To the mountains, that is, to the saints who possess a true, not feigned, loftiness, they will say, “Cover us.” Blessed are those whose iniquities are covered (Psalm 32). But to the hills, which do not possess natural height and which they formerly thought had some summit, they will say, “Fall upon us.” The mountains will cover them, and the hills will fall; these things will happen because of terror and incredible fear, by which both mountains and hills will be humbled.

(Verses 9 and 10.) “From the days of Gibeah Israel sinned; there they stood. The battle against the sons of iniquity will not overtake them at Gibeah. According to my desire I will chastise them; peoples will gather against them when they are chastised for their two iniquities.” [Note: Instead of *super*, Victorius reads *propter*, following the Vulgate.]

The Septuagint: “From the time when the hills existed Israel sinned; there they stood. The battle against the sons of iniquity did not overtake them on the hill. He came to chastise [Al. “destroy”] them, and peoples will gather against them when they are chastised for their two iniquities.”

From the day when Benjamin shamefully and cruelly killed the Levite’s wife in the city of Gibeah, all Israel sinned against me (Judges 19)—not because it avenged the injury and punished the crime with blood, but because it rushed into battle out of marital grief and refused to avenge the sacrilege against its God, since they had neglected the ephod and teraphim in Micah’s house, which were worshiped as idols [Note: The same manuscript tradition addressed to the Brixian copies omits *neglexerit*; the sense is the same].

There, therefore, Israel stood; there it restrained its step, so that it would no longer walk in the ways of the Lord. Therefore the battle—or captivity—will not overtake them on account of Gibeah, as they themselves think. For there they acted well in pursuing the sons of iniquity. But “I will chastise them,” he says, “and instruct them with the full desire of my heart; and I will gather against them a multitude of peoples,” because they committed two iniquities: avenging a man while neglecting the injury done to their God.

Or, two iniquities because they first sinned in the idols of Micah and afterward in the calves of Jeroboam; or certainly we can call the two calves of Samaria, in Dan and Bethel, two iniquities [Note: One Palatine manuscript reads more explicitly: “or certainly the two iniquities, the two calves, etc.”]. Jeremiah also speaks of these:

> “My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

These two iniquities burst forth against the two commandments of the Decalogue, in which it is said:

> “I am the Lord your God; you shall have no other gods besides me” (Exodus 20:2–3).

The Septuagint translated Gibeah as “hills.” Therefore, “From the days of the hills Israel sinned,” when it abandoned the mountains of the Church and descended to the hills, or slopes, of the heretics, thinking itself more learned than the Church and that it had discovered something more sublime. “There they stood,” that is, they persevered in error.

As for what follows—“The battle will not overtake them on the hill”—some have interpreted it as follows: Because they begot sons of iniquity and, withdrawing from the Church, began to be on the hills, when persecution comes the battle will not overtake them, since the devil does not wish to attack his own.

Others interpret it this way: Since Israel sinned from the days of the hills, and stood there and could go no farther, ought it not to be overtaken by battle on the hills? Should not ecclesiastical men fight against it in order to destroy them, “against the sons of iniquity”? If they are overtaken and conquered, they will no longer be able to beget.

At the same time the Lord promises that he will chastise and instruct them, so that when the teachers have been conquered, their disciples—whom they had previously deceived—will gather against them and recognize that they are being chastised because of two iniquities: they abandoned the Church, the Lord’s fountain, and dug for themselves broken cisterns, namely, the caverns of the heretics, which cannot contain waters—that is, the Savior’s teaching and the sacrament of baptism.

(Verses 11.) “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing; and I passed over the beauty of its neck, and I will mount Ephraim. Judah will plow; Jacob will break up his furrows.”

The Septuagint: “Ephraim is a heifer”—or “cow,” for the Hebrew word *EGLA* (), that is, μόσχος and δάμαλις, signifies both—“Ephraim, then, is a heifer trained to love contention. But I will come upon the beauty of its neck; I will place [Note: We read in our manuscripts *superponam*, in accordance with the Greek ἐπιβήσω or ἐπιθήσω, and with Hieronymus himself below, where he repeats this passage. Previously it read *supponam*] Ephraim upon it, and I will keep silent concerning Judah; Jacob will become strong for himself.”

This passage—or rather, everything that follows in this chapter—is enveloped in great obscurity. Therefore both we, who attempt to explain it, and the prudent reader should pay close attention, so that, if we cannot discover the truth, which is exceedingly difficult, we may at least investigate what appears plausible.

Divine speech has this customary manner: through tropology and metaphor it expresses the truth of history. Ephraim, therefore, is like a cow or heifer which from its youth learned to tread the threshing floor and to drag iron rollers over heaps of grain, so that the straw might be separated from the wheat. And it not only learned this, but through excessive habit began to love what it had been taught.

“And I,” he says, “passed over the beauty of its neck.” The Hebrew word *ABARTHI* (), that is, “I passed over” [Note: The same manuscripts read *aspirant*, “they aspirate,” *Habarthi*], whenever it is said of God, always signifies blows and adversity. Thus the destroyer is said to have passed through Egypt.

Since Ephraim, therefore, a cow or heifer, loved to tread the threshing floor, “I,” he says, “passed over the beauty of its neck,” and by placing a yoke upon it I subdued the swelling muscles of its neck. Why should I mention the yoke of the Law? I myself mounted upon it; and while I was laboring in this way, Judah—that is, the two tribes—began to cut the fields with a plow and turn the earth into furrows.

While Ephraim carried the yoke and Judah plowed, Jacob broke up his furrows. Here we should understand Jacob, in distinction from Israel and Judah, as the twelve tribes: they began to break the clods with plows [Al. “rakes”] and crumble the earth, so that, softened, it might receive the seed and shortly produce a fertile crop.

Instead of “threshing” or “threshing floor,” the Septuagint translated “contention,” and the sense is this: Because Ephraim does not wish to receive the yoke of the Law, “I will pass over and mount the beauty of its neck,” so that the contentious and wanton heifer may learn to labor at what it does not wish to do.

But Judah will plow voluntarily, because it has the Temple and dwells in the Law, so that all twelve tribes, vying with one another, may prepare the fields for sowing.

As for what follows according to the same Septuagint—“I will place Ephraim upon it; I will keep silent concerning Judah; Jacob will become strong for himself”—the sense may be this: Ephraim, who is contentious and does not wish to bear the burdens of the Law, I will impose captivity upon. Judah I will leave for a little while and say nothing concerning it. But whoever, whether of Ephraim or Judah, keeps my commandments will become strong for himself and will be called Jacob.

According to the *anagoge*, this may be said: Ephraim, who was instructed in the Law of God to tread the threshing floor of Scripture and meditate upon it day and night, began to love contention, cast off the yoke of the Law, and contend against ecclesiastical men for the ruin of those who hear them.

Therefore the Lord will either press down with a yoke the neck which they have raised and which promises itself lofty things, or, passing over it, will trample it under his feet and mount upon it, so that it may know that it has a Lord.

But Judah—that is, the ecclesiastical man—will plow, persevering in the work he has begun. Or: “I will retain Judah,” he says. For “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke 5).

Jacob, however, whose name means “supplanter,” who daily supplants vices and sins, receives the birthright of his brother, is heir to his father’s possession, and sleeps at Bethel, which is interpreted as “house of God”—this Jacob will break up the furrows and clods, so that the earth may receive the seed cast into its soft bosom and produce a hundred measures of barley, or, as it is found in the Hebrew, a hundredfold.

For we should not believe that the patriarch Isaac devoted himself to barley rather than grain. To this day the ecclesiastical man Jacob breaks apart the clods of history and the harshness of the letter, dividing them spiritually so that they may yield spiritual fruits.

We read that the Lord did this as well: he broke into pieces the five loaves of the Law, which the people could not eat whole, so that through the hands of the apostles he might give them to believers to eat (Luke 9). And when he says, according to the Septuagint, “Jacob will become strong for himself,” he shows that everyone who labors must labor for himself, in order to receive everlasting fruits.

(Verses 12.) “Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap in the mouth of mercy. Break up for yourselves a fallow field. It is time to seek the Lord, when he comes who will teach you righteousness.”

The Septuagint: “Sow for yourselves in righteousness; harvest [Note: The Palatine manuscripts insert *for yourselves* here and below, where this passage recurs; it is indeed also found in the Alexandrian Greek manuscript, ἑαυτοῖς] the fruit of life. Illuminate for yourselves the light of knowledge, for it is time. Seek the Lord until the fruits of righteousness come to you.”

He preserves the agricultural metaphor once begun. He had said that Ephraim was a heifer trained to love and desire the threshing floor, that he had mounted upon its neck, plowed Judah, and broken up the furrows or clods of Jacob.

Now he commands them to sow for themselves through repentance, to sow in righteousness—that is, in the Law—and to reap in mercy—that is, in the grace of the Gospel. For there we read:

> “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exodus 21);

here we read:

> “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5:39).

When you have sown in righteousness and reaped in mercy, break up for yourselves joyful fallow fields.

He also gives the reasons why they should sow, reap, and break up joyful fallow fields. “It is time,” he says, “to seek the Lord, when Christ and the Savior will come, who will teach you the righteousness which you now await in the Law.” For:

> “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who does good” (Romans 10).

Instead of what we said, “Reap in the mouth of mercy,” the Septuagint translated, “Harvest the fruit of life.” Harvesting suits seed better than vintage; and the fruit of life is itself also the tree of life.

Instead of what we rendered, “Break up for yourselves a fallow field,” they translated, “Illuminate for yourselves the light of knowledge,” so that from the works and commandments of the Law we may deserve to possess knowledge, according to what we read in a certain book:

> “You desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will give it to you” (Sirach 1:33).

For whoever turns the commandments into deeds sows in righteousness and reaps from it the fruits of life. Hence elsewhere we read:

> “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 19:8).

And Isaiah says to the Lord:

> “Your commandments are light upon the earth.”

And in another passage:

> “From your commandments I gained understanding” (Psalm 119).

Those who have separated themselves from the Church and assumed for themselves the false name of Christians are also commanded to repent and receive both Testaments: in the Old, let them sow righteousness; in the New, let them reap mercy; let them illuminate for themselves the light of knowledge, or break up for themselves fallow fields; and let them seek the Lord, who can teach them true righteousness, and destroy the false teachers from whom they learn not righteousness but iniquity.

(Verses 13.) “You plowed impiety; you reaped iniquity; you ate the fruit of deceit.”

The Septuagint: “Why are you silent about impieties, and have you harvested its iniquities? You ate a deceitful fruit.”

Against my will I am repeatedly compelled to discuss the peculiarities of the Hebrew language. For we do not, after the manner of rhetoricians, repeat sentences, construct phrases, and arouse our hearers or readers through declamations to praise us. Rather, we strive to explain what is obscure, especially to people who do not know the foreign language.

Above, where we translated “Judah will plow,” the Hebrew reads *JEROS* (), with Jod as its first letter. The Septuagint, thinking it was Vau (), translated it as “I will keep silent.” Here too the Hebrew has *ARASTHEM* (), which we translated “you plowed”; the Septuagint rendered it “Why are you silent,” through the same error as above, interpreting silence instead of plowing.

The sense of these statements is as follows: I passed over the neck of the contentious Ephraim, the heifer that loves threshing, and I mounted upon it, so that while Judah plowed and broke up the furrows, Jacob might thresh the floor and endure the heat of the sun.

I instructed them to sow in righteousness, reap in mercy, and break up for themselves fallow fields; and I told them to recognize that the time of seeking the Lord was that time when he would come who would teach us righteousness.

While I commanded these things and wished to receive from joyful fallow fields the fruits of righteousness and mercy, they plowed impiety: they acted impiously against the Lord, abandoning the Creator and worshiping idols. They reaped iniquity, receiving evil fruits from evil seed, from which they made not merely bread baked beneath ashes but fraudulent and deceitful bread, which would deceive the eater with a false hope.

Such are the heretics, who plow with carefully composed speech and conceal or silence impiety, so that it may not appear to be impiety but may be believed to be piety. Therefore, because they said in their heart, “There is no God” (Psalm 14), they were corrupted and became abominable, and they reaped—or harvested—iniquities.

For just as avarice is the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6), so impiety is the root of all sins and crimes. Whoever plows or sows it will reap iniquities.

Therefore those who plowed impiety and reaped iniquities ate the fruit of deceit: proclaiming everything false to deceived peoples, so that they would not seek the true bread which descended from heaven, but the bread of deceit, which chokes and kills those who devour it.

(Verses 14 and 15.) “Because you trusted in your ways, a tumult will arise among your people through the multitude of your warriors, and all your fortifications will be devastated, just as Salmana was devastated by the house of him who avenged [Vulg. “judged”] Baal on the day of battle, when a mother was dashed to pieces upon her children. So Bethel has done to you because of the evil of your wickedness.”

The Septuagint: “Because you hoped in your chariots and in the multitude of your strength, destruction will arise among your people, and all your fortified cities will depart; just as the princes of Salmana from the house of Jerobaal did in the days of battle, when they dashed a mother upon her children, so I will do to you, house of Israel, because of the face of your wickedness.”

Therefore [Note: The manuscripts read, somewhat more elegantly, “you will eat”; previously it read “you will eat” in a different form] you ate the fruit of deceit, and in everything you undertook, vain hope deceived you, because you trusted, O Ephraim, in your ways of idolatry. For these are your ways. You trusted in the multitude of your warriors, placing your hope not in God but in the strength of your armies.

Therefore a tumult will arise among your people. In Hebrew this is called *SAON* (), that is, the sound and roar of a howling army. When they cry out, all your fortifications will be devastated, and what you thought fortified and secure will lie open to the enemy. They will be devastated just as Salmana, prince of the Midianites, was devastated and crushed, being killed by the house of Jerobaal (Judges 8).

There is no doubt that Gideon is meant: because he destroyed the shrine of Baal and cut down its grove, and Baal could not avenge himself, Gideon received the name Jerobaal, that is, “Let Baal avenge himself.”

Just as Salmana killed sons in the presence of their mothers and afterward killed the mothers themselves, so your sons, O Ephraim, will be killed in your presence, and you yourself will also be slaughtered.

We ask where it is written that Salmana killed a mother upon her sons. In the Book of Judges we read Gideon speaking to the prince of Midian [Note: Victorius says: “These are not Gideon’s words to Salmana but Samuel’s to Agag, as is clear from 1 Samuel 15. The history of Gideon and Salmana is written in Judges 8, where it is reported only that Salmana killed Gideon’s maternal brothers at Tabor, and that Gideon therefore said to him: ‘As the Lord lives, if you had spared them, I would not kill you.’ Yet the history reported by Hieronymus cannot be denied as true, since the prophet Hosea here affirms it when he says: ‘Just as Salmana was devastated by the house of him who avenged Baal on the day of battle, when a mother was dashed upon her children.’ For just as the Book of Judges records the killing of Gideon’s maternal brothers, so here it records that their mother too was killed by Salmana. It makes no difference that such words are not recorded in the Book of Judges, since Hieronymus elsewhere gathers what was said from both passages, following the example of Samuel. He often joins testimonies and weaves one history from different places. This is clear in Zechariah 11, where he interprets the Prophet’s words, ‘I will not feed you,’ as though spoken to Moses, writing: ‘Therefore, angered, I said to Moses: I will not feed you; let me go, and I will destroy them.’ A little farther on he presents words written by Isaiah as though spoken to the people in the wilderness: ‘To whom I also spoke in the wilderness: If you obey me, you will eat the good things of the land.’ These words are found only in Isaiah 1. Likewise the Apostle Paul in Romans 9, joining the testimony from Genesis and Malachi as though it belonged to one passage, says: ‘The elder will serve the younger, as it is written: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’ Similarly Mark, in chapter 1, joining testimonies from Malachi and Isaiah, gives the name of Isaiah alone, not of Malachi. Therefore those are entirely mistaken who think that the blessed Hieronymus suffered a lapse of memory here.”]:

> “How has your sword made many mothers childless? So your mother will be childless among women” (Judges 8).

Therefore, just as Salmana was devastated by Jerobaal—whom some wrongly think was Jeroboam son of Nebat, who ruled the ten tribes—and was devastated, as the Hebrew contains, by *ARBEL* (), which signifies the same thing as Jerobaal but in a shorter and more elegant expression, so Bethel has done to you, O Israel, because of your wickedness: Bethel, in which you placed the golden calf and worshiped Egyptian gods.

Instead of Bethel, which is interpreted as “house of God,” the Septuagint translated “house of Israel,” a phrase entirely absent from the Hebrew.

We have somehow escaped the rugged places; now, spreading our sails into the deep, let us cross the sea of allegory.

Because you trusted, O Ephraim, in your ways—or in your chariots—of which it is written:

> “Some trust in chariots and some in horses,  
> but we will glory in the name of the Lord our God” (Psalm 19:8);

and because you trusted in the multitude of your warriors, whom you strengthened with false knowledge, therefore a tumult and a sound will arise among your people.

Whatever the heretics say, they do not possess a voice that explains their judgments, but only tumult, shouting, and noise. And all your fortifications, or all that is fortified, will be devastated—for they are not protected and built by testimonies from Scripture but by dialectical art and the arguments of philosophers—just as Salmana was once devastated by Gideon, with a mother killed upon her sons.

The history of this event is also recalled by Psalm 82, where, among the other leaders of Midian, Salmana is mentioned:

> “Do to them, Lord”—there is no doubt that he means those who entered into a pact or covenant against the Lord—“as to Midian and Sisera” (Psalm 82:12–13).

And afterward:

> “Make their princes like Oreb and Zeeb, and like Zebah and Salmana, all their princes who said: ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’

In this same psalm the leaders of the heretics are described, those who attempted to claim the altar of God for themselves.

What follows—“So Bethel has done to you because of the evil of your wickedness”—is properly applied to the leaders of the heretics: Bethel, which they themselves call Bethel, that is, “house of God,” has done this to them, namely, the false Church.

The sense is: “So your Church, which you call the house of God, will do to you.” But from the time it has been held by you, it must be called Bethaven, that is, “house of the idol,” because of the multitude of your wickedness.

[Col. 0914A] (Chapter XI.—Verses 1 and 2.) “As morning passed away, the king of Israel passes away”—for Israel was a child, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son. They called to them; thus they departed from their presence. They sacrificed to the Baals and burned offerings to images.

[Note: [Col. 0914D] Victor omits “passed away,” following the Vulgate and the appended exposition of Jerome. But “and he passed away immediately” should also have been read from the same Vulgate, as two Palatine manuscripts prefer.]

The Septuagint reads: “At dawn they were cast away; the king of Israel was cast away, because Israel was little. I loved him, and from Egypt I called his sons. As I called them, so they departed from my presence. They sacrificed to the Baals and burned offerings to carved images.”

[Note: [Col. 0914D] Two Palatine manuscripts add “incense.”]

He explains the same meaning through different figures. Above he had said: “Samaria caused its king to pass away like foam upon the surface of the water,” because foam and bubbles floating on the surface of water quickly dissolve. Now he presents the same matter under another comparison. For just as sunrise, dawn, and the beginning of day—which is called “morning”—quickly pass between night and the sun, so that night ends and day grows bright, so the king of Israel, that is, the ten tribes, will quickly pass away.

He then explains the benefits that God had bestowed upon him. “While he was a child and little, and was held captive in Egypt, I loved him so greatly that I sent my servant Moses and called my son from Egypt,” concerning whom I said elsewhere: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4). Since “Israel” is grammatically singular but understood as plural—as are “the people,” “Ephraim,” and “Judah”—for a multitude is contained within the singular number, he recalls the ancient history: that he did indeed call them through Moses and Aaron, who called them to depart from [Col. 0914C] Egypt. But they, summoned by them, withdrew from their presence, turning their backs upon him and indicating the hardness of their minds by the gesture of their bodies.

Nor was it enough for them to despise those who called them, unless they sacrificed to Baal and burned incense to their carved images or idols. We read that they first worshiped Baal under Ahab, king of Israel, who married Jezebel, the daughter of the king of Sidon, and brought the Babylonian and Phoenician idol into Samaria.

Thus he joins together sins separated in time within a single statement: how they were first called from Egypt and named sons; then, in the wilderness, withdrew from God, worshiping Beelphegor rather than God; and afterward, in the Holy Land, served the Baals, Astaroth, and the other idols.

We may also understand the passing away of heretics as resembling dawn, and their king as the devil or the heresiarch. When they were in infancy—when they believed in the Church, were little ones, and were counted by the name of Christ—God loved them and called 123 them from the tribulation and darkness of Egypt. He called them through the apostles and teachers of the Church.

“And when they had been called by my leaders,” he says, “they withdrew from their presence and worshiped Beelphegor,” that is, they served their own vices and lust; afterward they sacrificed to the Baals and to the images they had fabricated for themselves. For each of the heretics has his own gods, and whatever he invents he worships as a carved or cast image.

For what we have said, “From Egypt I called my son” (Matt. 2), the Septuagint translated, “From Egypt I called his sons,” a reading not found in the Hebrew. There is no doubt that Matthew took his testimony from [Col. 0915B] this passage according to the Hebrew truth.

Therefore, let those who disparage our translation produce the Scripture from which the Evangelist took this testimony and interpreted it with reference to the Lord and Savior, when he was brought back from Egypt into the land of Israel.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] Up to this point the text has been transmitted corruptly. Let them examine the Scripture: Jerome himself neither indicates the passage nor urges them to search the Scriptures; rather, he challenges his opponents, if they know it, to identify the passage precisely. This formula of challenging opponents is frequent in the holy Doctor: “Let them produce the Scripture; let them indicate the passage.” We have corrected the text according to the manuscripts. One Palatine manuscript also reads, instead of “from which the Evangelist repeats,” “from which the Evangelist took.” Shortly afterward we likewise restored “let it be” in place of “it is.”]

When they cannot find it, let them cease wrinkling their foreheads, raising their brows, flaring their nostrils, and snapping their fingers.

In the seventh book which Julian Augustus spewed forth against us—that is, against Christians—he attacks this passage and says that what was written about Israel the Evangelist Matthew transferred to Christ in order to mock the simplicity of those who had believed from the nations.

To him we shall briefly reply. First, Matthew published the Gospel in Hebrew letters, which could be read only by those who were Hebrews.

[Note: [Col. 0916D] It is nevertheless closer to the truth that the Evangelist himself composed it in Greek letters. See what we have noted concerning this matter in the *Catalogus*, chapter 3.]

Therefore he did not do this in order to mock the Gentiles. But if he wished to mock the Hebrews, he was either foolish or ignorant: foolish if he deliberately fabricated an obvious falsehood; ignorant if he did not understand of whom these words were spoken. The book itself acquits him of folly, since it is composed prudently and orderly. Nor can we call him ignorant, for we know from other testimonies of Scripture that he possessed knowledge of the Law.

It remains for us to say that things which precede typologically (*τυπικῶς*) in others are referred to Christ according to truth and fulfillment. We know that the Apostle did this with the two mountains, Sinai and Zion, and with Sarah and Hagar. For Sinai is indeed a mountain, and Zion is a mountain; Sarah existed, and Hagar existed. Yet the Apostle referred these things to the two Testaments (Gal. 4). Thus what is written here—“Israel was little, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son”—is indeed spoken of the people of Israel, who were called from Egypt, who were loved, and who, at that time, after the error of idolatry, were called as an infant and a little child; but it is perfectly referred to Christ.

Isaac too was a type of Christ, because he himself carried the wood of his future death (Gen. 22); and so did Jacob, because he had Leah, whose eyes were dim, and Rachel, who was beautiful, as his wives (Gen. 29). In Leah, who was older, we understand the blindness of the Synagogue; in Rachel, the beauty of the Church. Yet those who were types of the Lord and Savior in certain respects are not to be thought to have done everything that is narrated about them as a type of him. A type indicates a part. If the whole event should precede in type, it must no longer be called a type but the truth of history. These matters we have briefly stated, as in the *Commentaries*; let us now return to what follows.

(Verses 3 and 4.) “Yet I was like a nurse to Ephraim; I carried them in my arms, and they did not know that I was caring for them. In the cords of Adam I will draw them, in the bonds of love. And I shall be to them like one lifting a yoke over their jaws, and I bent down to him so that he might eat.”

The Septuagint reads: “And I bound Ephraim; I took him upon my arm, and they did not know that I was healing them in the corruption of men. I stretched them out in the bonds of my love. And I shall be to them like a man giving slaps upon his cheeks; and I shall look upon him, prevailing over him.”

The Hebrew and the edition of the Septuagint translators differ greatly from one another. Let us therefore attempt to weave the history according to the Hebrews and the spiritual interpretation (*ἀναγωγή*) according to the Septuagint.

Above he had said: “Israel was little, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son.” Then he added what crime Israel had committed: “They sacrificed to the Baals and burned offerings to images.” Now he recounts with what love he loved Israel, in accordance with what is read in Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God carried you, as a man is accustomed to carry his little son, along the whole way on which you walked, until you came to this place” (Deut. 1:31). 125

And elsewhere: “He spread out his wings and took him up, and carried him upon his shoulders” (ibid. 32:11). “I,” he says, “who was a father, became a nurse, and I myself carried my little one in my arms, lest he be injured in the wilderness or be frightened by heat or darkness. By day I was a cloud; by night, a pillar of fire” (Exod. 13), so that those whom I had protected I might enlighten and heal with my light.

When they sinned and made for themselves the head of a calf, I gave them an opportunity for repentance; but they did not know that I was healing them. I closed the wound of idolatry over a period of forty years and restored them to their former health. I healed them because of the cords and bonds of love by which I had bound Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to myself.

For “Adam,” Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translated “men”:

[Note: [Col. 0916D] Two Palatine manuscripts read “all human beings.”]

thus they read, “In the cords of men I will draw them, in the bonds of love.”

As for what follows, “I shall be to them like one lifting a yoke,” which Symmachus translated, “They thought that I was placing a yoke upon their jaws,” it may be understood in two ways: either I removed from them the yoke of all the surrounding nations, or they regarded my Law as the heaviest burden of a yoke.

And I gave them manna as food in the wilderness (Exod. 16), so that they might eat. This is what he says: “I bent down to him so that he might eat.” Symmachus translated this, “And I bent down to him with food.” God did not bend down toward him, but caused the food of manna to be brought down toward him.

Alternatively: I loved them so greatly, and was such a compassionate shepherd, that I myself carried the sick sheep upon my shoulders (Luke 15). But they did not understand that I was healing them through my passion. As the lover of all human beings, I would draw them to faith through the bonds of love, according to what is written in the Gospel: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

They thought my yoke, which was light, to be extremely heavy. I bent down to them, abandoning the kingdoms of heaven, so that I might eat with them [Col. 0917B], having assumed the form of a human being—or, “I gave them the food of my Body”: both food and fellow diner.

Let us pass to the spiritual interpretation, according to the Septuagint translators alone, lest, if we wish to expound both the historical and the spiritual meaning, we prolong the length of the book.

While they were sacrificing to the Baals which they had invented from their own hearts, and fleeing from my presence when I called them—for this is what the Septuagint contains—I, the most merciful Lord, bound Ephraim’s feet so that they would not flee farther from me. For this is what *συνεπόδισα* signifies.

I bound them with the testimonies of Scripture and the disputation of the teachers of the Church, so that, bound by patience, they might be held within my arms, though they did not understand that the patience of God was the occasion of their salvation.

Therefore, in the corruption of men—that is, of the teachers who had deceived them—I extended the warmth of faith over them, contracted by the cold of unbelief, and, as though they were resisting, I bound them with the bonds of my love.

Since they did not run of their own accord but were dragged, bound by cords, I struck their jaws lightly with slaps—not punishing, but correcting and reforming. A judge tears flesh, tortures with cords, and torments with whips and fire. But a father strikes a disorderly son with the palm of his hand.

Beautifully, therefore, he did not say, “I shall strike them with slaps,” but, “I shall be like a man striking cheeks with his hand.” God strikes erring children with threats of punishment, the reading of the Gospel, and the testimonies of the prophets.

When he has struck the cheek so as to shake the bread and teaching of the heretics from their polluted mouth, then he looks upon him, while the chastened son says to him: “Look upon me, and have mercy on me” (Ps. 85:16). And again: “Look upon me and hear me, Lord my God” (Ps. 12:4).

When he has looked upon him, he will prevail—or, as it may be understood, he will benefit them: he will overcome their adversaries and make servants out of fugitives. Alternatively, he will give them true and sweet food, since previously they had devoured the lies and most bitter foods of the heretics.

[Col. 0918A] (Verses 5, 6, and 7.) “He shall not return to the land of Egypt, and Assyria itself shall be his king” [the Vulgate adds “is”], “because they refused to convert. The sword began in his cities and will consume his chosen ones; it will devour their heads, and my people will long for my return. A yoke will likewise be placed upon them, which will not be removed.”

The Septuagint reads: “Ephraim shall dwell in Egypt, and Assyria itself shall be his king, because he refused to convert. The sword has grown weak in his cities and has ceased in his hands, and they shall eat from their own counsels. His people are suspended from their dwelling, and God will be angry over his precious things and will not exalt him.”

When he says, “He shall not return to the land of Egypt,” he shows that Israel desires to return but cannot go. Israel desired to return by imploring aid from the Egyptians, but he was seized by the Assyrian, who captured him and ruled him by the right of a conqueror. He suffered this because he refused to convert and would not practice repentance.

Or certainly we may say that he returned to the land of Egypt when, in the Holy Land, he worshiped the gods of the Egyptians. Alternatively, it must be understood in the sense in which it was said above: “They called upon Egypt; they went to the Assyrians.”

Therefore the sword began in his cities—or “will fall upon them,” as Aquila translated it, or “will wound,” as Symmachus rendered it. Consider the weight of the miseries: it is not fields, possessions, and rural estates that are laid waste; the enemy enters the very midst of the cities and consumes his chosen ones, or “his arms,” as Symmachus translated it, corresponding to the Hebrew word *BADDAU* [Hebrew form not displayed in the source].

When the sword has consumed his chosen ones and leaders, or the strength of his army, and has devoured either their heads or their counsels, so that they cannot find any means of defense, then the wretched populace that refused to return to me will await my return to them. It will repent too late, after the enemies have laid everything waste.

Therefore, because great sins must be punished by great penalties, they will impose upon those left from the people—after their king and leaders have been cut down by the Assyrian sword—the heaviest yoke of servitude. They will impose it upon them together, and it will not be removed according to the literal sense unless it is spiritually taken away in Christ.

According to the Septuagint [Col. 0918D], Ephraim will dwell in Egypt, claiming to possess the Holy Land and the Church of the Lord and Savior; yet because of vices, sins, and perversity of faith, he has always remained in Egypt.

Since he dwelled in Egypt, the great Assyrian intelligence will be his king. For he refused to return to the Church, and, having lost his strength—that is, Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God—he was always in a state of weakness and was infirm, subject to all demons and disturbances.

Therefore the sword—that is, spiritual knowledge or the discourse of a man of the Church—will continually remain in his cities, laying waste and defeating them, cities which he impiously built against the Lord. The sword itself will rest in his hands, so that, having been slain by another, he cannot slay another or raise his hand against his adversary.

Finally, they will receive and devour according to their own counsels. But the unhappy people and uneducated multitude will sigh for their ancient homeland and will realize that they have been captured; or they will remain suspended in their dwelling, not knowing what to do or where to turn.

God, however, will be angry over their precious things—namely, the gold and silver they had received from him, concerning which we have often spoken—and will by no means free the one who has fallen through his own fault.

This is according to the Septuagint; we shall also apply the same meaning to the Hebrew.

[Note: [Col. 0918D] Victor again corrects the text from the Florentine manuscripts to “dwelt,” according to the Greek *κατῴκησεν*. He also introduces the conjunction “and,” giving the sense: “He claims to possess the Holy Land and the Church of the Lord and Savior.”]

(Verses 8 and 9.) “How shall I give you up, Ephraim? Shall I protect you, Israel? How shall I give you up like Admah? Shall I make you like Zeboiim? My heart is changed within me; at once my compassion is stirred. I will not act according to the fury of my anger; I will not turn to destroy Ephraim, because I am God” [the Vulgate omits “I am”], “and not a human being; the Holy One is in your midst, and I will not enter the city.”

The Septuagint reads: “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? Shall I protect you, Israel? What shall I do for you? I shall make you like Admah and like Zeboiim. My heart is changed within me [Note: [Col. 0919] The Palatine manuscripts omit the words “within me,” both here and at the end of the following verse.] and at once my compassion is stirred. I will not act according to the anger of my fury. I will not abandon Ephraim to be destroyed, because I am God and not a human being; the Holy One is in you, and I will not enter the city.”

In the place where we and the Septuagint translated, “Shall I protect you, Israel?” the Hebrew has *AMAGGENACH* [Hebrew form not displayed in the source], which Aquila translated, *ὅπλῳ κυκλώσω σε*, that is, “I shall surround you with a shield.”

Although we thought this should be understood positively and should signify protection, the edition of Symmachus presents a meaning contrary to ours, saying, *ἐκδώσω σε*, that is, “I shall hand you over.” The translation of Theodotion likewise indicates not prosperity but adversity: *ἀφοπλίσω σε*, which means, “I shall disarm you,” and “I shall take away from you the weapon”—that is, the shield—with which I had previously protected you. This meaning is more appropriate to the Lord as he threatens.

What he says, therefore, is this: Since they refused to convert, and Assyria became their king, the sword will devour cities, leaders, and people, and a yoke will be imposed upon them which will not be removed from them. Since the sentence appeared harsh, leaving them no opportunity for repentance, God now speaks to Israel with a parent’s affection:

“What shall I do for you, Ephraim? How shall I strip you of my assistance? What shall I do for you? By what means can I correct you? With what remedy can I heal you?”

“I shall make you like Admah and Zeboiim.” These are two of the five cities, as we read in Genesis: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela, which is Zoar and is called Zoara in the Syrian language. Thus I shall make you desolate and turn you into a wasteland; I shall destroy you even to ashes and cinders, as I destroyed Admah and Zeboiim.

When he had pronounced this harsh, indeed cruel, sentence, once again, out of a parent’s affection, mercy overcame him, and he softened the severity of judgment with a father’s compassion. For he says: “My heart is changed within me; at once my compassion is stirred.”

As soon as I said that I would make Ephraim and Israel like Admah and Zeboiim, my inward parts were moved. I regretted destroying my former people forever. Therefore I will not act according to the fury of my wrath, nor will I change my clemency so as to destroy Ephraim. I do not strike in order to destroy forever, but in order to correct.

My severity is an occasion for repentance and compassion. For I am God, and not a human being. A human being punishes in order to destroy; God disciplines in order to correct.

“The Holy One is in your midst, and I will not enter the city.” That is: I am not one of those who dwell in cities, who live according to human laws, who consider cruelty justice, for whom the highest right is the highest wickedness. My law and my justice, however, are to save those who have been corrected.

We may also say otherwise: the first murderer, Cain, built a city in the name of his son Enoch. The Lord does not enter such a city, which was constructed from crime, blood, and murder.

But if we wish to read, “How shall I give you up, Ephraim? Shall I protect you, Israel?” the meaning should be understood thus: “What shall I do for you? Are you worthy of protection, after having done such things?”

It should also be noted that when the word is spoken against Judah—that is, against the people of God—Admah and Zeboiim are not mentioned, but Sodom and Gomorrah. For we read in Isaiah: “Hear the law of God, rulers of Sodom; attend to the word of the Lord, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:10).

In the Gospel also, concerning the city that did not receive the apostles, when they shake the dust from their feet, it is said that on the day of judgment it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that city (Matt. 10).

And the prophetic word is directed to Jerusalem: “Sodom was justified by you” (Ezek. 16). We are therefore given reason to suspect that Sodom and Gomorrah were leaders in sin, while Admah and Zeboiim followed their example; that the powerful will suffer powerful torments (Wis. 6); and that the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it will be beaten with many blows (Luke 12).

Hence ecclesiastical men, if they are held by the same crimes as the heretics, will not be subjected to the torments of Admah and Zeboiim, which are lesser, but to those of Sodom and Gomorrah, which are said to represent greater crimes.

To the heretics and to the people deceived by them the Lord also says that unless they repent, they will be made like Admah and Zeboiim, so that they will have no hope of salvation. Again, as the most merciful Father, he says that he will change his sentence and repent of having spoken such things, in order thereby to summon them to conversion and repentance.

“I will not act,” he says, “in my fury; I will not destroy Ephraim. Insofar as it lies with me, insofar as I desire it, if he corrects his error with truth, if he loves me more than the leaders of heresy—for I am God and not a human being—I will extend my hand to the fallen and call the erring to salvation.

And because I am holy, I will not enter the city,” that is, the councils and cities of the heretics. When they come out of their cities, I gladly receive them; I will not enter their cities.

Some have interpreted what he said, “I will not enter the city,” together with what follows in the Septuagint, “I will follow after the Lord,” as though the people had answered the Lord, giving the following sense:

“Because your heart has been changed within you, and you have not dealt with us according to our sins; because you imitate your own clemency, do not punish our transgressions, and promise that you, holy and merciful, will dwell in our midst, therefore I too will not enter the city of wicked men, nor will I belong to the number of sinners; rather, I will walk after the Lord my God.”

The Hebrews, however, explain the passage as spoken by God:

131 “I will not abandon you; I will not go to another nation; I will not enter another city.”

[Col. 0921B] (Verses 10 and 11.) “They shall walk after the Lord. He will roar like a lion, for he himself will roar, and the sons of the sea will fear. They will fly like a bird from Egypt and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians; and I will settle them in their houses, says the Lord.”

The Septuagint reads: “I will walk after the Lord. He will roar like a lion, for he himself will roar, and the sons of the waters will fear [Note: [Col. 0921D] For the remainder of the verse, the Palatine manuscripts read, “the rest similarly”; the text is in fact the same in both places.] They will fly like a bird from Egypt and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians; and I will settle them in their houses, says the Lord.”

When the Lord promises prosperity, the people will be converted to him and will walk after the Lord, because the Lord will roar like a lion. The prophet Amos also mentions this: “The Lord will roar from Zion and from Jerusalem will give his voice” (Amos 1:2).

He will roar when he says: “I shall make you like Admah and set you like Zeboiim.”

When he has roared, then the sons of the sea—or of the waters, as the Septuagint translated—will fear. The word *MAIM* [Hebrew form not displayed in the source] is written with three letters, MEM, YOD, MEM. If it is read *MAIM*, it signifies “waters”; if *MEJAM*, it is understood as “from the sea.”

The Hebrews refer these things to the coming of Christ, whom they expect to come. We demonstrate that they have already been accomplished, because from Egypt and from Assyria—that is, from the East and the West, from the North and the South—those have come, and daily come, who recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matt. 8).

We may call the sons of the sea or of the waters those who have been caught in the Lord’s net and drawn out from the sea of this world (Matt. 13:47). When they have been captured from death to life, they will be settled in their houses. The Gospel calls these houses storehouses (Matt. 13), in which the selected grain, separated from the chaff, is stored.

Lions are said to be of such a nature that, when they growl and roar, all living creatures tremble and cannot move from their fixed position; such is the terror and fear they inspire.

Thus, when the Lord roars like a lion, thunders, and gives his voice, all birds and flying creatures will shudder and go to their nests—that is, to their houses, in which the Lord will dwell with them.

Let us speak in another way. When the true lion has growled, the false lion, who according to the apostle Peter is our adversary (1 Par. 5), will immediately fall silent, and no perverse doctrine will be able to open its mouth. Those who had previously been captured by him will be released by the lion’s roar and by the terrible threat, and will follow the Lord their God.

Then the sons of the sea or waters will fear—those who had been begotten in the bitterness and [Col. 0922A] salty waters of the heretics [Note: [Col. 0922D] Martianus retained “false,” although Victor had long before pointed out the obvious error.]. Having taken wings, they will fly like birds from Egypt and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians, and they will say: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I will fly and rest?” (Ps. 54:7).

Those who had labored among the heretics will rest in the Church and dwell in their own houses, from which they had been led astray by error.

We know that Egypt, that is, *MESRAIM* [Hebrew form not displayed in the source], is interpreted as “tribulation” and “distress.” The Assyrians likewise signify “those who direct,” or, as we think better, “those who reprove.”

From these, therefore, the heretics will be freed when they begin to dwell in their own houses and say to their evil parents: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23).

(Verses 12.) “Ephraim has surrounded me with his denial” [the Vulgate omits “his”], “and the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah descended as a faithful witness with God and with the holy ones.”

The Septuagint reads: “Ephraim has surrounded me with falsehood, and the house of Israel and Judah with impiety. Now God has known them, and the holy people will be called God’s people.”

The Hebrews transmit the following story. When Israel departed from Egypt, with a mountain on one side, the Red Sea on another, and Pharaoh’s army surrounding them on the third, the enclosed people were trapped. While the other tribes despaired of salvation and wished either to return to Egypt or to fight, Judah alone faithfully entered the sea. For this reason he deserved to receive the kingdom. This, they say, is what is now meant: Judah, the witness of God’s words, his supporter and avenger, descended with God into the sea and was most faithful among the holy ones, believing the words of God who commanded him.

This is what they say. Let us follow the order of the explanation we have begun: Ephraim, the royal tribe, and the house of Israel, the people who served the royal tribe, surrounded him in denial or falsehood, while they denied the Lord and confessed idols.

But Judah—that is, the two tribes which possessed the Temple, the Law, and the Prophets and observed the legal commandments—were witnesses, walking with God and faithful with the holy ones.

We may understand the holy ones as angels, patriarchs, prophets, and others who served at God’s command. For, in comparison with the time when these things were spoken, while Ephraim had completely gone astray and Israel had been deceived in the worship of idols, Judah alone remained engaged in the worship and testimonies of God. He could descend with him, or “be strong with the Strong One,” for *RAD* [Hebrew form not displayed in the source] signifies both “descent” and “strength.” Aquila translated it *ἐπικράτειαν*.

[Note: [Col. 0922D] The Palatine manuscripts correctly read, together with Victor’s edition, *ἐπικράτειαν*, although they write it somewhat corruptly as *ἐπικράτειαον*. Martianus retained the faulty reading *ἐπικράτων*.]

According to the spiritual interpretation, the heretics surround the Lord in falsehood, indeed in denial. Whatever they say is denial, indeed falsehood. They surround him with deceit or with the impiety of the house of Israel, composing everything they pretend through artful speech and uttering impiety against the Lord.

Judah, however—that is, the ecclesiastical man—is not proud or puffed up with heretical arrogance. He is humbled with God and is faithful and strong with the choir of the holy ones, building his house upon the rock, which no storm can shake (Matt. 7).

The Septuagint translated the passage very differently: Ephraim, the house of Israel, and Judah have surrounded God with falsehood and impiety, yet God is so merciful that he does not cut off their hope of salvation. He acknowledges them and is ready to call a people holy and a people of God those who are now perverted by impiety.

According to the tropological interpretation, God desires both heretics and ecclesiastical sinners to be saved and all to be called by his name. But the one who is truly holy does not surround God with falsehood but with truth, as the Psalmist says: “You are powerful, Lord, and your truth is round about you” (Ps. 88:9).

(Cap. XII.—Verse 1.) “Ephraim feeds on wind and pursues the scorching heat; all day long he multiplies falsehood and desolation. He made a covenant with the Assyrians and carried oil into Egypt.”

The Septuagint reads: “But Ephraim is an evil spirit; he pursued the scorching heat. All day long he multiplied empty and vain things. He made a covenant with the Assyrians, and he traded oil in Egypt.”

Sacred history relates that Menahem, king of Israel, after making peace with Assyria, sought help from the Egyptians (2 Kings 15). This is what is now meant: Ephraim feeds on wind, that is, deceives himself with vain hope; he pursues *καύσωνα*, that is, “scorching heat,” and goes toward the South, doing nothing all day except mock himself.

As he runs here and there, he prepares desolation and ruin for his cities. Is it not desolation and falsehood to make a covenant with the Assyrians and carry oil into Egypt? This is a synecdoche, in which the whole is signified by a part, namely, that he sent gifts to the Egyptians.

Some, however, think that oil does not grow in Egypt at all, but that the most precious oil was sent by Ephraim, whose land—Samaria—is exceedingly fertile in oil.

According to the tropological interpretation, all heretics are held by the most evil spirit of the demons, concerning which it is also written in the Apostle: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:10). And when the unclean spirit has gone out from a person and found no rest, it joins to itself seven other spirits more wicked than itself and returns to its former house (Luke 12).

Therefore, under the influence of an exceedingly evil spirit, they pursue *καύσωνα*, that is, aridity or a burning wind, which is hostile to flowers and destroys everything that grows. All day long they pursue empty and vain things, nor are they content with their own error; instead, they multiply many disciples, indeed companions of their vanity and error.

They also make a covenant with the Assyrians, whose prince is the great intellect, so that whatever they invent may appear to have been wisely fabricated—by that wisdom which is destroyed by God and which the Apostle commands us to avoid, saying: “See that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world” (Col. 2:8).

They also carry oil into Egypt, or purchase the wisdom of Egypt, desiring to mix with ecclesiastical doctrines the oil of anointing with which prophets and priests were anointed, and with which kings were also anointed.

The saints possess this oil, concerning whom it is said: “Your children are like olive shoots around your table” (Ps. 127:4). And the good olive tree is the one into which our wild olive has been grafted.

Although the heretics attempt to mix falsehood with truth, oil cannot be joined to water or to other moist and liquid substances. Truth is always above, while falsehood is below.

All the other kinds—that is, the heresies—which, as we have said, do not possess the oil of truth, can be mixed with one another and made into a single body from many parts.

But the prophet detests the oil of these heresies, which is carried into Egypt and descends from the Holy Land to the kingdoms of Pharaoh, saying: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Ps. 140:5).

### (Verses 2, 3 and following)

“Therefore the judgment of the Lord [Alternatively: of God] is with Judah, and visitation is upon Jacob. According to his ways and according to his deeds he will repay him. In the womb he supplanted his brother; and in his strength he contended with the angel, prevailed against the angel, and was strengthened. He wept and entreated him; at Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us. The Lord is God of hosts; the Lord is his memorial. Therefore you shall return to your God: keep mercy and judgment, and hope in your God always.”

The Septuagint reads: “And the judgment of the Lord [Alternatively: of the Lord] is with Judah, so that he may avenge Jacob; according to his ways and according to his deeds he will repay him. In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his labor he prevailed with God; he was strengthened with the angel and prevailed.
