They wept and entreated me; in the house of ὢν they found me, and there it was said to them: ‘The Lord God Almighty will be his memorial. And you shall return in your God; keep mercy and judgment, and draw near to your God always.’”

Ephraim, having once fed on winds and followed falsehood, came into such madness that he wavered uncertainly between two hostile nations, making peace with the Assyrians and carrying oil into Egypt. Now, he says, “my entire judgment is with Judah, and visitation is upon Jacob.”

By “visitation” he means scourges and punishments: just as he repaid Ephraim what he deserved, so he will repay Judah also, who was born from Jacob’s seed, according to his ways and according to his deeds. Judah was not merely deceived by an accidental error or overcome by human frailty; rather, he sought out and devised the things through which he would sin and fall.

He then explains what great blessings Judah—that is, Jacob—received. The son is called by the name of his father, and the ancient history is recalled, so that both God’s mercy toward Jacob and Jacob’s stubbornness against the Lord may be recognized.

While he was still in Rebecca’s womb, he supplanted his brother Esau (Genesis 25)—not, certainly, by his own strength, since he could not yet perceive anything, but by the mercy of God, who knows and loves those whom he has predestined.

Nor did he supplant his brother only in the womb; he was also made upright with the angel in his strength, when Jacob wrestled throughout the night against the angel at the stream (Genesis 32). And because he was made upright with the angel, he consequently received the name εὐθυτάτου [Alternatively: εὐθύτατον], which in Hebrew is said to be ISAR (), that is, “of one who directs,” or “of one directed.”

“And he prevailed,” he says, “against the angel”; and he was strengthened by the blessing of the one whom he had conquered. He also wept and entreated him—that is, the angel—saying: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (ibid., verse 26).

When he fled to Mesopotamia at the advice of his father and mother, he found the same angel at Bethel. The angel spoke to him, and spoke with us—that is, he spoke in the father and in the sons; and in Jacob he loved Judah also. From that time until the present, the memory of the name imposed upon him by the angel and by God has endured.

Since these things are so, you too, O Judah, imitate your ancestor. Weep and entreat the Lord of hosts, and return to him. Keep both mercy and judgment; and when you have done both, hope in your God always, advancing through good works toward greater things.

For the Hebrew wording, “He wept and entreated him; at Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us,” we read in the Vulgate edition: “They wept and entreated me; in the house of ὢν they found me, and there it was said to them.” ὢν is interpreted as “pain.”

If, therefore, someone weeps, repents, and entreats the Lord, he will find him in the pain of his heart; and when he has called upon him, he will hear him answer.

We can understand Judah as the ecclesiastical man, who is rebuked by the Lord because he does not remember in himself the Lord’s former benefits, but daily joins sin to sin. The passage explains what those benefits are:

“When the Church, in faith, was giving birth to you as you emerged, you supplanted your brother, whether Jew or Gentile; you received his birthright; and in your strength you contended with the angel—either overcoming hostile powers, or strengthened by the blessings of the angel, who is himself God. You prevailed figuratively against the angel, so that you might prevail against human beings, and you were strengthened.

“When you had gained the victory, you wept and entreated the angel of the Lord; and, remembering your former sins, you found him at Bethel, that is, in the house of God, which is the Church, or in the house of ὢν, the house of pain, tears, and repentance.

“And so that we might know who this Judah is, the passage says: ‘There he spoke with us,’ that is, with us Christians. From that time until the present day, we are reckoned by the name of Christ, and by him who directs us we are corrected.

“Therefore, O ecclesiastical man, who are called Judah, that is, ‘confessing,’ return daily through repentance to the Lord your God. And if you should perhaps sin, imitate the prophet who says: ‘I have labored in my groaning; every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears’ (Psalm 6:7).

“Nor is it enough to have said this. Keep God’s commandments; show mercy to others, so that you too may obtain mercy. Judge with true judgment, so that in whatever judgment you pronounce, judgment may be pronounced upon you. And hope in your God always—or, ‘draw near to your God continually’—so that, advancing in strength at every moment, you may draw near to your God.”

### (Verses 7, 8)

“Canaan has a deceitful balance in his hand; he loved extortion, and Ephraim said: ‘Nevertheless I have become rich; I have found an idol for myself. All my labors will not find in me the iniquity that I have committed.’”

The Septuagint reads: “Canaan has a balance of iniquity in his hand; he loved to oppress by force. And Ephraim said: ‘Nevertheless I have become rich; I have found rest for myself. None of his labors will be found in him, because of the iniquities in which he sinned.’”

He had warned Judah to return to the Lord his God, to preserve mercy and judgment, and to hope in the Lord always, or continually to draw near to him. Now the discourse turns to Ephraim, that is, to the ten tribes, whom he calls “Canaan,” in accordance with what Daniel says to the elder, who was certainly of the tribe of Judah: “The seed of Canaan, and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you” (Daniel 13:56).

And in Ezekiel we read that it was said to Jerusalem: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezekiel 16:3). In Isaiah it is said to the tribe of Judah: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1:10). We also read in the final verse of Zechariah: “And there shall no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the Lord” [Alternatively: “in the city”] (Zechariah 14:21).

He says that Canaan—that is, Ephraim—has a deceitful or wicked balance in his hand, although Scripture commands: “You shall have equal weights” (Leviticus 19). He not only has an unjust and deceitful balance; he also loves oppression and overpowers people by force.

And lest we think that some other person is meant by Canaan, he makes clearer who this Canaan is. Ephraim said: “Nevertheless I have become rich.” The meaning is: “It does not matter how I possess, provided that I possess.” Many suffer from this disease, concerning whom it is written: “Riches gathered unjustly will be vomited out” (Job 20:15), for “a man’s ransom is his own riches” (Proverbs 13:8).

Therefore we are commanded to make friends for ourselves from unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive us into eternal dwellings (Luke 16). But Ephraim, who boasts and says, “Nevertheless I have become rich; I have found an idol for myself,” or ἀνωφελές, that is, AVEN (), which is of no benefit to its possessor, has sweated in vain labor.

Just as the belly is a god for gluttonous and lustful people, so the miser worships the idol of gold and says in his heart: “I have found what I was seeking.” But he will hear: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

When his eyes have been seized—not, I should say, by the splendor of riches but by their blindness—he says: “All my labors will not find the iniquity in which I have sinned.” The meaning is: “Whatever I may have done wrong, if I possess riches from those who need my assistance, it cannot be counted against me,” in accordance with what is written: “And the one who acts wickedly is blessed” (Psalm 9); for “the friends of the rich are many.”

This same interpretation may also be applied to heretics. Canaan can indeed be interpreted as “those who move.” Observe, however, that he says “as those who move” [Alternatively: “as one who moves”], not simply “those who move.” They are “those who move” those whom they have deceived—“as those who move” those whom they have tested.

But because the latter are founded upon the rock (Matthew 7), they cannot be shaken by any storm, nor can they alter the footprint of their feet.

In the hand of this kind of Canaan—that is, in his works—there is a deceitful and wicked balance. Whatever a heretic says does not possess the justice of God; it is full of deceit and fraud. Hence they love oppression, while they depress the innocent or overpower them by force.

The poor ecclesiastical man is oppressed by the wordiness and sophistries of heretics. After they have deceived some people, they are accustomed to say: “We have become rich; we have a very large multitude; a crowd of disciples follows us. We have found an idol or refreshment for ourselves.”

For this reason above all, heresies are formed: to devour the houses of widows, who are always learning and never arrive at knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 3:7). And it is beautifully said: “I have found an idol for myself.” All the fabrications of heretics are idols and images of the gentiles. They do not differ greatly in impiety, although they may appear to differ in name.

They are accustomed to say: “Whatever I do, whatever I undertake, cannot be counted against me. I possess my riches—the arguments of the philosophers; I possess a multitude of people, and whoever has seen it will not think that I am sinning.”

### (Verses 9 and 10)

“And I, the Lord your God” [Note: The words “who brought you out” are wholly unknown to the Hebrew and Vulgate edition. They read: “I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt,” etc.] “who brought you out from the land of Egypt, will still make you dwell in tents as in the days of the feast. I spoke through the prophets, and I multiplied visions; and in the hand of the prophets I was represented.”

The Septuagint reads: “But I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt. I will still make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the feast; I will speak to the prophets; I multiplied visions, and in the hands of the prophets I was represented.”

You have indeed sinned so greatly that you rejoiced in wickedness, considered the multitude of your sins to be riches, and said: “I have become rich; I have found an idol for myself. All my labors will not be able to discover my sins.”

But I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt (Exodus 5), when you were serving Pharaoh and building cities from mud and straw. I still grant you a place for repentance, and by the greatness of my promises I urge you to return to me. For I will still make you dwell in tents as in the days of the feast.

He calls the feast “the day of the Festival of Booths” [Scenopegia], in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, when the children of Israel came out of Egypt.

“Just as,” he says, “at that time I freed you from Egypt, and you dwelt in tents in the holy land, hastening to go to the place of the temple, so now also I will bring you out of tribulation and distress, and from the captivity that threatens—provided, however, that you do what I have commanded.”

For I am the one who, through all the prophets and through various kinds of visions, was represented in human form and summoned you to repentance.

Is it not an instance of human likeness when Moses, raising his hands on high, prays that Jesus may conquer Amalek (Exodus 17), and the mysteries of the cross are displayed in him?

Is not God represented in the hands of the prophets when Jonah is in the depths for three days and nights, signifying the Lord rising from the dead on the third day?

We read of visions multiplied among all the prophets when Ezekiel sees the Lord seated upon the cherubim in the likeness of a charioteer (Ezekiel 17).

And Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne, and two Seraphim around him crying out to one another: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of Sabaoth’” (Isaiah 6:1–2).

Habakkuk stood in his watchtower [Alternatively: “cave”], so that he might see horns in the hands of the Savior, in which his strength is hidden (Habakkuk 3).

Hence the Psalmist also cries out: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me” (Psalm 84:9).

To show that every prophecy in the Holy Scriptures is called a vision, Scripture says: “And all the people saw the voice of the Lord” (Exodus 28:18). For this reason the prophets were formerly called “seers.”

To those also who have been led astray by heretics it is said that they should return to the Lord, who prefers the repentance of a sinner to his death (Ezekiel 18). For he is the one who brought them out of the land of Egypt—that is, from the darkness and error of the gentiles.

And lest, perhaps, remembering their sin, they should return too slowly, he says: “I will still make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the feast.” What baptism accomplishes, repentance should accomplish also: let them dwell in the tents of the Savior, that is, in the Churches, concerning which it is said: “Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 91:14).

And lest they should think that the heresiarchs and leaders of their error spoke by the Spirit of God, he says: “I am the one who spoke to the prophets, and not to your teachers. I multiplied visions, and in the hand of my prophets, who have been established in the Church, I was represented.”

### (Verse 11)

“If Gilead is an idol, then those sacrificing oxen in Gilgal were acting in vain; and their altars are like heaps upon the furrows of the field.”

The Septuagint reads: “If Gilead is not so, then the rulers sacrificing in Gilgal were false, and their altars were like tortoises upon the wilderness of the field.”

For what we translated as “oxen,” which in Hebrew are called SURIM (), the Septuagint translators rendered “rulers,” which are called SARIM (), being misled by the similarity and ambiguity of the words.

Again, where we placed “heaps,” which in Hebrew are called GALLIM () and properly signify θῖνες—that is, mounds gathered from sand—the Septuagint translated “tortoises” (χελῶνας).

For this term Symmachus translated “heaps of stones.” Theodotion translated it “hills.”

[Note: The manuscripts prefer θῖνας to θεῖνας, although many manuscripts have θεῖνας; Martianay’s θινὰς is incorrect. Consult the Commentary on Ezekiel 47:8 and below on Joel 3:4.]

[Note: From one Palatine manuscript, which reads “for which Symmachus interpreted ‘heaps,’ ‘heaps of stones,’ Theodotion, etc.,” one may easily infer that a name has fallen out, perhaps to be restored as follows: “Symmachus, heaps; Aquila, heaps of stones,” etc. Another Palatine manuscript likewise leaves space after the name of Symmachus for restoring the reading. The Barberinian Hexaplaric codex cited by Montfaucon, however, differs considerably: there Theodotion is said to have translated “frogs,” and Aquila “foxes.” There is no doubt that in Ezekiel 47:8 Aquila rendered the word by θῖνες.]

Indeed, if one considers θῖνες, they resemble large tortoises in a desert field or on banks and shores, rising slightly above the soil.

The meaning, therefore, is this: If in Gilead—of which it is written, “Gilead is a city of those who work idols, trampled down by blood”—the gods are false and the religion perverted, and if it lies beyond the Jordan, where the two tribes, Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh dwell, then Gilgal too—of which we read in this same prophet, “All their wickedness is in Gilgal, which is behind Bethaven”—is false.

Whoever worships idols does not sacrifice oxen to the gods; rather, he offers sacrifices to oxen, imitating the error of Samaria.

At the time when these things were prophesied, Gilead belonged to the kingdom of the ten tribes, while Gilgal was under the rule of the two tribes called Judah. Thus both the ten tribes and the two tribes were deceived by the same error of idolatry.

Their altars, therefore, are like heaps and mounds gathered from stones or sand. And when both peoples have been led into captivity, their former altars, without worshipers, will have the appearance of tortoises or mounds.

Since Gilead is interpreted as “translation of testimony,” and Gilgal as “rolling,” we can say that this means that the leaders of heretics transfer the testimonies of truth into falsehood. Whatever they worship is an idol, and their sacrifices resemble either heaps gathered from stones or tortoises.

For just as θῖνες [Alternatively: θεῖναι], heaps, are gathered here and there from stones and sand, so heretics construct images from secular wisdom and human sophistries, through fraud and falsehood.

When they have done this, they move slowly in one place and cannot occupy the whole world. A tortoise, slow-footed and burdened—or rather, weighed down—by its own weight, does not so much walk as move, signifying the exceedingly grave sins of heretics, who sacrifice in their own mire and muddy rolling-place, worshiping the works of their hands and, like oxen, laboring at everything for earthly crops.

### (Verses 12 and 13)

“Jacob fled to the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch. But through a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved.”

The Septuagint reads: “Jacob withdrew to the plain [Alternatively: plains] of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch. And through a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved.”

It seems unreasonable and contrary to the prophetic order that, after the idol of Gilead and Gilgal and the altars resembling heaps of stones, he should suddenly wish to narrate the history of Genesis concerning Jacob. But the difficulty is immediately resolved by one who remembers that he had previously read concerning Jacob:

“In the womb he supplanted his brother; in his strength he contended with the angel, and prevailed against the angel, and was strengthened; he wept and entreated him; at Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us.”

This Jacob, therefore, was not strengthened by the angel without reason. Rather, because he wrestled throughout the night and conquered his adversary, he learned from this not to fear his brother, out of fear of whom he fled to Syria, to Laban his uncle (Genesis 27).

He served for Rachel, the wife, for seven years; and for Leah he kept watch over the sheep of his father-in-law Laban for the same number of years.

And because Jacob had once been called Israel, he joins father and sons together and recalls the later history, when, through the prophet Moses, the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt. The twelve tribes that were generated from Israel were preserved while the prophet led them out.

He will not err who says that Jacob the supplanter and Israel, the one who sees God, preceded in a type the Lord; that Rachel, at first barren and beautiful, whom Jacob loved exceedingly, signifies the Church; and that Leah, with dim eyes yet fruitful, displays the mysteries of the Synagogue. He may also say that the Lord himself led the people of believers out of the darkness of this age and brought them to the sweetest streams of the Jordan—that is, to the waters of baptism.

### (Verse 14)

“Ephraim provoked me to anger by his bitterness; his blood will come upon him, and his Lord will repay him for his reproach.”

[Note: Here too we added from the manuscripts the words “the Septuagint likewise,” which were lacking in the Vulgate books.]

The Septuagint likewise.

Since I had done such great things for Ephraim—bringing him back, naked, exiled, and alone, as a rich and powerful master, and making him the father of many children—Ephraim abandoned me, or rather provoked me to anger. By his bitterness he made bitter the one who is sweet.

Therefore his blood will come upon him; that is, he himself will be the cause of his own death, according to what David says to the man who reported Saul’s death and claimed that he himself had struck down the king of Israel: “Your blood be upon your head” (2 Samuel 1:16).

Not by my judgment, but because of Saul’s blood, your blood will be poured out.

What follows—“And his Lord will repay him for his reproach”—agrees with the meaning of what Nathan said to David: “Because you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme the name of the Lord, because of this thing” (2 Samuel 12). That is, because of the sin by which you killed Uriah, the very blasphemy and reproach by which the Lord was blasphemed through you will be turned back upon your head.

Heretics always provoke the merciful Lord to anger. By the hardness of their hearts they compel him to punish the one who prefers the sinner’s repentance to his death. Their blood—the blood by which they have shed both their own blood and that of many others—will come upon their heads. The reproaches by which they blasphemed the Lord, their Lord will repay them—not because he is now their Lord, but because he was once their Lord.

### (Chapter 13, verses 1 and 2)

“When Ephraim spoke, terror seized Israel, and he sinned in Baal; he died. And now they added to their sin: they made for themselves a cast image from their silver, as though it were the likeness of idols. It is entirely the work of craftsmen. To these they say: ‘Sacrifice human beings, worshiping calves.’”

The Septuagint reads: “According to the word of Ephraim, he himself received ordinances in Israel; and he set them against [Alternatively: without] Baal, and he died. And now he continued to sin. They made for themselves a cast image from their gold and silver, according to the image of idols, completely finished work of craftsmen. To these they themselves say: ‘Sacrifice human beings, for the calves have failed.’”

Where the Septuagint translated, “Sacrifice human beings, for the calves have failed,” we translated, “Sacrifice human beings, worshiping calves.”

Symmachus translated: “Sacrifice; let human beings worship calves.” The meaning is: “Sacrifice”—that is, “offer sacrifice to idols”—and let this be followed by the punctuation: “Let rational creatures, human beings, worship calves, mute animals.”

When Ephraim spoke—that is, Jeroboam son of Nebat, from the tribe of Ephraim—terror seized Israel, that is, the ten tribes.

In place of the terror called RATHATH () in Hebrew, which Symmachus and Theodotion translated as “trembling,” the Septuagint, for some reason, rendered the term δικαιώματα, that is, “justifications.”

Such terror seized Israel that it sinned and offended God in Baal, and died, losing the one who says: “I am life” (John 14:6). “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18). And the Apostle says: “The widow who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:6).

He did not merely die in Baal; he added sins to sins, so that from the silver the Lord had given him he might fashion idols, the work of human hands.

To these they themselves—that is, the priests and leaders who ought to have taught the people what is good—say: “Sacrifice human beings, worshiping calves.” This is also said in the Psalms: “They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons” (Psalm 105:37).

In place of “worshiping,” which we translated according to Symmachus and Theodotion, Aquila translated καταφιλοῦντες, that is, “kissing.” Those who worship are accustomed to kiss their hand. Job denies that he did this, saying: “If I have kissed my hand, placing it upon my mouth, may this also be counted to me as the greatest iniquity” (Job 31:27–28).

But if, as some wish, the demons are speaking to the people—“Sacrifice human beings, for the calves have failed”—their greed is shown: they are nourished by the blood of victims and the smoke of holocausts. When the victims fail, they desire human beings to be sacrificed to them, and they rejoice not only in their death but also in their blood.

When heretics—or rather, the leaders of heretics, that is, Ephraim—speak, terror and trembling seize the unhappy people. They sin [Alternatively: will sin] in the idols that they have fabricated from their own heart, and they die with the people whom they have deceived.

Nor is it enough for them to have fallen, unless they turn the tongue that they received for singing to God toward images of idols and construct, through an artificial eloquence, a doctrine resembling the truth. This is nothing other than a product of human perversity.

They command their disciples also to sacrifice human beings—that is, to steal them from the Church of God, introduce them among the heretics, and kill those whom they have deceived.

What follows—“For the calves have failed”—has this meaning: “Do not seek those whom you may seduce from the gentiles, who are called brute animals; seize and sacrifice those who have been established in the Church and are reckoned by the name of Christ, and who are called human beings.”

[Note: Our manuscripts immediately add, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “But the chosen food …”]

### (Verse 3)

“Therefore they shall be like a morning cloud, and like the morning dew that passes away [Vulgate: ‘passes by’], like dust snatched from the threshing floor by a whirlwind, and like smoke from a chimney.”

The Septuagint likewise, changing only the final expression: “and like vapor from locusts,” or “from tears,” since in many manuscripts we find ἀκρίδων, “of locusts,” and in others δακρύων, “of tears.”

Because, he says, they sacrificed human beings instead of calves and worshiped calves, therefore they shall be like a morning cloud, and like dew passing away in the morning, like dust snatched from the threshing floor by a whirlwind, and like smoke from a chimney.

All these things appear for a time and suddenly disappear, in accordance with what he had said: “He made the king of Samaria pass away like foam upon the face of the water.” And again: “As morning passes, so the king of Israel passes away” [Alternatively: “will pass away”].

No one doubts that a cloud or dew passes quickly, as do dust from the threshing floor and smoke from a chimney, in accordance with what is written: “As smoke fails, so may they fail” (Psalm 67:2).

We ask, however, why the Septuagint translated “locusts” in place of “chimney,” which Theodotion rendered καπνοδόχην [the printed editions read καπνοδόχον].

Among the Hebrews, “locust” and “chimney” are written with the same letters: ALEPH, RES, BETH, HE. If it is read ARBE (), it means “locust”; if OROBBA [Alternatively: arobba], it means “chimney.” In place of this, Aquila translated καταράκτην, and Symmachus “opening.”

A cataract properly means an opening made in a wall through which smoke escapes.

If someone contentious, unwilling to accept the Hebrew truth, should seek the meaning “locust,” let him hear that Ephraim is compared to ἀτμός, that is, vapor, breath, or spirit. It is so thin when it comes out of a locust’s mouth that it cannot be perceived.

But if he should object: “Why was Ephraim not compared with other things that are smaller and destined to perish—for example, a flea, which has all its limbs, a head, eyes, feet, belly, and the rest? Although we do not see these things with our eyes, we nevertheless perceive them by sensation, so much so that, although we do not see the flea’s mouth and teeth, we feel them in its bites”—the answer should be that the glory of those who are destined to perish is compared to the vapor or thinnest breath of a locust because the locust is harmful and so hostile to mortals that it brings famine and lays waste cultivated crops. It even strips trees and vineyards of their bark, as we read more fully in the prophet Joel (Joel 1 and 2).

Heretics are compared with this locust, with the morning cloud, with dew, and with dust. Concerning them the Catholic Epistle says: “These are clouds without water” (Jude 12).

They have the appearance of prophets and of the apostolic clouds to which the truth of God came, but they do not have water—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The evangelist adds: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:38–39).

As for “tears,” which in Greek have some resemblance to “locusts”—δακρύων καὶ ἀκρίδων—this is an obvious error: certain manuscripts take the word “tears” in place of “locusts.”

### (Verse 4)

“But I am the Lord your God” [Note: The words “who brought you out,” as above and again where this same verse recurs below, are absent here from the Hebrew and Vulgate editions; even the Palatine manuscripts derived from Jerome’s manuscripts omit them.] “who brought you out from the land of Egypt.”

In the Septuagint the following is read: “But I am the Lord your God, who establishes heaven and creates the earth, whose hand created the whole host of heaven; and I did not show them to you, so that you might walk after them … And I brought you out from the land of Egypt.”

Since these words are found neither in the Hebrew nor in any of the translators, and since they are also absent from the ancient edition of the Septuagint, they should be marked with an obelus, especially since their meaning is clear.

Let us therefore proceed to what follows, joining it to the preceding chapter together with the material that follows.

### (Verses 5 and 6)

“But I am the Lord your God” [Note: The Vulgate, or Hieronymian, translation itself omits the words “who brought you out,” although they occur differently in the exposition that follows. See the preceding note.] “who brought you out from the land of Egypt. You shall know no God besides me, and there is no savior except me. I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of solitude. According to their pastures they were filled and satisfied; they lifted up their heart and forgot me.”

The Septuagint reads: “But I am the Lord your God, and I brought you out from the land of Egypt. You shall know no God besides me, and there is no savior apart from me. I fed you in the wilderness, in an uninhabited land, according to their pastures. They were filled with satiety, their hearts were lifted up; therefore they forgot me.”

Since he had said above: “Jacob fled to the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch; through a prophet the Lord God brought Israel out of Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved,” he now also recounts what he did for them:

“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt, who commanded you through Moses: Take care lest you eat and be filled and forget your God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt. For there is no other God besides me, and there is no other who can save.

“I am the one who is the creator of all things. I knew you—or fed you—in the wilderness and in an uninhabited land, where there was a lack of everything and no water. I gave you manna from heaven and brought forth springs of water from the hardest rock.”

In accordance with what is written elsewhere—“The beloved grew fat, grew thick, grew broad, and kicked” (Deuteronomy 32:15)—they too ate and were satisfied, lifted up their heart, and forgot the one whose benefits they ought to have remembered.

For throughout such a vast wilderness, where not only crops, trees, and vineyards but even grass fails to grow, and where no waters temper the sun’s heat, Israel could not have reached the land of the Jordan in forty years unless the Lord had provided everything.

The Lord also brought heretics out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery and from the iron furnace. At first they served Pharaoh and his commanders. In the Church he commanded them to know no other God than the one who is the creator of all things and knows how to save those whom he made.

He himself knew them and fed them in the land of solitude, so that they could say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. He placed me in a place of pasture; he led me beside the water of refreshment” (Psalm 22:1–2).

He gave them the bread of angels, manna from heaven, which they had never eaten in Egypt, and water from the rock that followed them.

The rock, according to the Apostle, is Christ (1 Corinthians 10). They ate, were filled, and could not bear the Lord’s food. To them the same Apostle says: “Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you reign without us—and would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you” (1 Corinthians 4:8).

They ate in the Holy Scriptures the bread that descended from heaven, and with David they said: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Psalm 50:8).

When they had been filled and satisfied, they lifted their heart against the Creator and fabricated another god for themselves, attributing whatever they had drunk and eaten to their own merits rather than to God’s mercy.

Therefore they forgot God, who had commanded them to bind the words of the Law between their eyes, upon their hands, and upon the fringes of their garments, so that they might never forget their God.

(Verses 7, 8.) “And I shall be to them like a lioness, like a leopard on the road of the Assyrians; I shall confront them like a bear deprived of her cubs, and I shall tear open the inward parts of their liver; there I shall consume them like a lion; the beast of the field shall rend them.”

[Note: [Col. 0934D] We have inserted here the word “I,” which, apart from the Hebrew and the Vulgate editions, is rejected by the Palatine manuscripts of Jerome.]

The Septuagint: “And I shall be to them like a panther, and like a leopard on the road of the Assyrians; I shall confront them like a bear in need of food, and I shall tear open the inward parts of their heart, and the whelps of the forests shall devour them there; the beasts of the field shall rend them.”

“They were filled and satisfied; they lifted up their hearts, and forgot me.” But, he says, I shall be to them like a lioness, or a panther, concerning which we have spoken more fully above; and like a leopard on the road of the Assyrians, when they are led captive by the Assyrians; and I shall confront them like a bear deprived of her cubs, or one in need of food; and I shall tear apart all their vital organs. Those who have written about the natures of beasts say that among all wild animals nothing is more savage than a bear when it has lost its cubs or is in need of food. He threatens not only the ferocity of the panther, leopard, and bear, but also that of the lion and of all the beasts born in the forests; and he says that he will be transformed into all these when they have gone to the Assyrians, lest, after suffering harsh things there, they should attribute their miseries not to the power and indignation of the Lord but to the strength of their enemies.

Let us also consider that he who speaks to believers in the Gospel—“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you; for my yoke is easy and my burden light” (Matt. 11:28–29)—now becomes, through the prophet, a panther, leopard, bear, and lion to unbelievers and to those unwilling to repent: not only to the Israelites, because they have been settled in the cities or mountains of the Medes on account of idolatry, but also to heretics, because through the pride of their minds and the vanity of false doctrines they have forgotten their God, fashioned idols, and followed foreign gods.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Two manuscripts read “and fashioned,” “and followed,” and so forth.]

(Verses 9, 10, and 11.) “Your destruction, Israel; only in me is your help.” Where is your king? Let him now save you in all your cities; and your judges, of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and princes.’ I shall give you a king in my wrath, and I shall take him away in my indignation.”

The Septuagint: “Israel, who will help you in your destruction? Where is this king of yours? Let him save you in all your cities. Let him judge you, of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and a prince.’ I gave you a king and a prince; I gave you a king and a prince in my anger, and I took him away in my fury.”

[Note: [Col. 0935D] The whole of this passage—“and a prince,” “and I gave you a king,” “and a prince,” and “I gave you a king”—which had been omitted in the Benedictine edition through the customary error caused by the repetition of the same word “king,” has been restored with the help of our manuscripts. [Col. 0936D]]

In place of what the Septuagint translated as “I possessed,” all others have translated “I took away.”

Unhappy Israel, and worthy of perpetual condemnation, who descended into such a depth of impiety that he can be saved only by God’s mercy. In Hebrew, however, it can be read with this meaning: “May you perish, Israel, because nothing remains for you except that you be preserved by my clemency alone.”

In the Septuagint there is another meaning: “Who will help you in your destruction, Israel?”—that is, in your captivity and ultimate servitude, who will be able to bring help from those whom you considered your rulers? Where is your king, about whom you said to Samuel, “Set a king over us, to judge us, as all the other nations have” (1 Sam. 8:5)? And when he objected, you answered: “No, but there shall be a king over us, and we too shall be like all the nations, and our king shall judge us, and shall go out before us, and shall fight for us.” Since you had promised yourself, then, that he would wage your wars, let him now come to your aid in your necessity and free all your cities from servitude.

Where are your judges? Where are your kings? For you said: “Give me a king and princes.” Therefore I gave you Saul as king in my wrath, to such an extent that on the days of harvest I displayed rain contrary to the nature of the province of Judea. “And I took away,” he says, “the king in my indignation”—namely, Zedekiah—so that the one whom I had given in wrath I might take away in indignation.

Others think that the king given in wrath was Jeroboam son of Nebat, and that Hosea, the last king of the ten tribes, was taken away in indignation. What we have explained—“I gave you a king, and I took away a king in my indignation”—the Hebrews refer to a future time. At that time, he says, when you were saying, “Give me a king and princes,” I answered you through Samuel that I would give you one in my wrath and take him away in my indignation.

Every heretic is lost and handed over to destruction: for “he who destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him.” He has no help in anything except in God’s mercy alone, which he obtains through repentance. The king and judges of such a person are the devil and demons, or all the princes of perverse doctrines; these will not be able to free them in the time of necessity and distress. They were given in wrath and will be taken away in indignation—not because the Lord wished them to have such kings, since otherwise he would not take away those whom he had willingly given, but because he abandoned them to their own desires, so that, eating and becoming fat in flesh, they might grow disgusted and vomit them out through their nostrils, and begin to hate those whom they had followed with such zeal.

(Verses 12 and 13.) “The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is hidden. The pains of a woman in labor shall come upon him; he is an unwise son, for now he shall not stand in the destruction of his children.”

The Septuagint: “The gathering of Ephraim’s iniquity; his sin has been hidden. Pains like those of a woman in labor shall come upon him. This is your wise son, for now he shall not endure in the destruction of his children.”

[Col. 0936C]

Just as, when something is tied up in a pouch, it is preserved and does not perish for the one to whom it has been bound, so every iniquity with which Ephraim sinned against God has been bound to him and hidden, as though stored up in a purse. Finally, when the day of vengeance and the final captivity arrives, pains like those of a woman in labor shall come upon him, or shall seize him.

A woman in labor knows long before she gives birth—ever since she conceived—that she must give birth, and every day she awaits the final torments and sufferings that are to come. So too Ephraim, the foolish son, of whom he had said above, “Ephraim is a foolish dove, without understanding,” shall have neither the strength to stand nor the ability to endure when the day of childbirth and captivity arrives, amid the destruction of his children and his people.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] We have deleted, following Victorius and in accordance with the manuscripts, the particle “in,” which the Benedictine edition had inserted at the cost of good Latin usage.]

In the Septuagint, instead of “foolish son,” the phrase “this wise son” is read ironically—that is, “the one whom you thought wise,” so that he may be understood in the contrary sense as foolish.

All heretics have an iniquity bound up within them, which they have spoken on high; their sin is hidden while they imagine that they conceal the poisons of their hearts and keep them secret. But when the day of childbirth arrives, these things will be revealed in pain and lamentation. This Ephraim is a foolish son because he abandoned the wisdom of God. Of him it is written in Jeremiah: “His end shall be foolish” (Jer. 17). In the destruction of his children, whom he killed and slaughtered, he will not be able to endure the wrath of God.

(Verses 14.) “From the hand of death I shall free them; from death I shall redeem them. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O underworld. Consolation is hidden from my eyes, for he himself shall divide among the brothers.”

The Septuagint: “From the hand of Hades I shall free them; from death I shall redeem them. Where is your cause, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades? Consolation is hidden from my eyes, for he himself shall divide among the brothers.”

According to both interpretations—Ephraim meaning both the ten tribes and heretics, who will not be able to endure in the destruction of their children when the pains like those of a woman in labor arrive—the Lord promises that he will free them from the hand of death and redeem them from death.

He calls the works by which death kills “the hand of death,” in accordance with what is written: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21). The Lord freed and redeemed everyone in the passion of the cross and the shedding of his blood, when his soul descended into hell, while his flesh did not see corruption; and he spoke to death itself and to hell: “I shall be your death, O death.” For I died for this reason: so that you might die through my death. “I shall be your bite, O hell,” which used to devour everyone in your jaws.

And when he sees the harsh necessity of death, and that there is no human being who lives and does not see death (Ps. 88), the most merciful Father recalls the ancient sentence: “In Adam we all die” (1 Cor. 15:22).

Or the prophet, understanding his own frailty and the condition of human flesh, says: “Consolation is hidden from my eyes.” The meaning is: “I cannot be consoled; whatever I conceive in my mind cannot ease my grief, as I see the most beloved names among themselves separated by death.” For hell itself divides brothers.

Whatever, therefore, separates brothers must be called hell—and especially the harlot woman who, calling the foolish man to herself, says in the riches of wisdom: “Freely touch hidden breads, and drink the sweetness of stolen waters.” The foolish man does not know that “earthborn ones perish beside her and fall into the depths of hell.” For whatever is forbidden is desired more strongly, and what is sweet because of its rarity is turned into bitterness through continual use.

Honey also drips from the lips of the harlot woman, who for a time fattens the throat of the foolish man, but in the end it is found more bitter than gall and sharper than a two-edged sword (Prov. 5). Whoever is earthborn and is not born from heaven is killed by her embraces and bound by the cords of her bed; and folly leads down to death and to hell the feet of those who make use of her.

There is this difference between death and hell: death is that by which the soul is separated from the body; hell is the place in which souls are shut away, either in refreshment or in punishments, according to the quality of their merits.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] Victorius discusses at length, on the basis of this passage from Jerome, the place of purgatory after this life. He does so appropriately and very clearly, but nevertheless abuses his leisure if he wishes to introduce here what theologians have discussed in works of their own and in enormous volumes. But what if there is no mention of purgatory here? I think that when Jerome says “in refreshment,” he means the dwelling of the blessed, which he contrasts with the punishments of the condemned. No one is unaware that the name “hell” is common to the designation of rewards and punishments, and that originally it means nothing other than what the holy Doctor himself notes: the place of separated souls.]

We have said this to show that death does what the harlot woman does. Death divides brothers, and the woman does the same. By “brothers,” understand every form of affection: a mother being separated from her daughter, a father from his son, and a brother from his brother.

The psalmist also demonstrates that death is one thing and hell another, saying: “There is no one in death who remembers you; but in hell who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6). And in another place: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell” (Ps. 54:16).

In place of what we have translated, “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell,” the Septuagint translated: “Where is your cause, O death? Where is your sting, O hell?” The Apostle rendered it: “Death has been swallowed up in contention; where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. 15:54ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0937D] This was how the old Latin translation read. Victorius writes: “It is clear from this passage that in 1 Cor. 15 Jerome read νεῖκος (*neikos*, contention), not νῖκος (*nikos*, victory), as it appears in the Vulgate edition. He cites the passage in the same way in the second exposition of Isaiah, chapter 13, writing these words: ‘Hence the Apostle Paul, after death had been killed—the death to which the prophetic word through Hosea was speaking, “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell”—speaks to it: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?”’ Tertullian likewise cites the passage in this manner. Cyprian too writes in *To Quirinius*: ‘Then will be fulfilled the word that is written: “Death has been swallowed up in contention. Where is your sting, O death? Where is your contention, O death?”’ The most ancient Greek codex of the Vatican Library has retained this reading: it has εἰς νεῖκος (*eis neikos*), where we have εἰς νῖκος (*eis nikos*). *Neikos* means “battle, contention”; λοιδορία means “quarrel,” as in Homer’s *Odyssey*.]

In explaining the power of the testimony, he added: “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law; but thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Therefore, since he interpreted that passage as referring to the Lord’s resurrection, we can neither interpret it nor dare to interpret it otherwise.

Death, hell, and the devil may also be understood here: the devil was slaughtered by Christ’s death. Of him Isaiah also speaks: “He will swallow up death when he prevails” (Isa. 25:8, according to the Septuagint). And afterward it follows: “The Lord will remove every tear from every face.”

According to the history of that time, some understand the two brothers divided from one another by death to be Israel and Judah, so that what was then represented in part might now be understood in the whole, and Israel and Judah might be liberated and redeemed together with the entire human race.

In the passage where the Septuagint translated, “Where is your cause?” and we said, “I shall be your death,” Symmachus translated, “I shall be your plague”; the Fifth Edition and Aquila: “Where are your words?”

[Note: [Col. 0938D] Jerome read the form *Dabarach* in the Chaldean manner, not *Devarecha* according to the present pointing of the Masoretes. MART. Perhaps the holy Doctor wrote *Dabarich*, since our manuscripts also read *Dabari*, and the current Hebrew text likewise prefers this form.]

This is written in Hebrew as DABARACH (). They read DABAR, that is, “word,” instead of DEBER, which means “death,” in accordance with what we read in Isaiah: “The Lord sent death upon Jacob, and it came upon Israel” (Isa. 9)—that is, *deber*, in place of which we translated, “The Lord sent the Word upon Jacob, and it came upon Israel,” namely *dabar*.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] “Lord” was lacking here and has been supplied by the manuscripts. In place of “it came,” the Jerome manuscript tradition itself had fallen away.]

In place of the sting, which we translated as “bite,” Symmachus translated ἀπάντημα (*apantēma*), that is, “encounter”; Theodotion and the Fifth Edition translated it as “plague” and “conclusion.”

(Verses 15.) The Lord shall bring a scorching wind, rising from the desert; he shall dry up its veins and desolate its spring, and he himself shall plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel.

The Septuagint: “The Lord shall bring a scorching wind from the desert upon them; he shall dry up its veins and desolate its springs. This one shall dry up its land and all its desirable vessels.”

I read in the commentaries of a certain person that the scorching wind which the Lord will bring from the desert is the wind that struck Job’s house at its four corners and caused it to fall upon his feasting children (Job 1), and that it is one of the winds which we read in the Gospel blow and come with a storm, rains, and rivers, so as to overthrow the house built either upon the rock or upon the sand (Matt. 7). This does not seem right to me. For it is not written in Job that the Lord brought a wind from the desert; rather, the name of the Lord is left unmentioned, so that the wind from the wilderness, which came against the holy man by its own will, may be understood as a hostile power. Nor can the winds that overthrow the foundations of houses be referred to the good side.

It remains, then, that we understand the scorching wind which the Lord will bring, rising from the desert, to be the one of which we also read in Habakkuk: “God shall come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran” (Hab. 3:3)—a place situated in the wilderness and in the south. And in the Song we read: “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at noon?” (Song 1:6).

This scorching wind, then, which dries up the veins of death and makes its springs arid, the Lord shall bring, rising from the desert. By “desert” we may understand the human race, in which the devil, seeking rest, was unable to find it.

Or we may understand the desert as the virginal womb of holy Mary, which, without human seed, put forth no growth from any plant, but, as a simple and most pure branch, fruitful in its union, produced the flower—

[Note: [Col. 0939D] That is, through its uniqueness or unity, without intercourse with a man. See what we have noted in Letter 22 to Eustochium, *On Virginity*, no. 19, on the words: “The Branch is the Mother of the Lord, simple, pure, sincere, joined to no external shoot, and, in the likeness of God, fruitful through a second UNION.”]

—who says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:2).

And beautifully, both in Isaiah and in the present passage, the flower and the wind are said to rise: for he ascended from the lowliness of the flesh to exalted things and drew us with him to the Father, saying in the Gospel: “When I have been lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

He himself shall rise like a root from uninhabitable earth. Death did not come upon him; rather, he came upon death. For death found no path in him by which to exercise its power. This is what is said in Proverbs: “It is impossible for the serpent to find tracks upon a rock” (Prov. 30). And he himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30).

He shall dry up the veins of death and desolate its springs. The veins and springs of death, and its sting, are called sins by the Apostle. When these have been dried up, death itself too will be dried up.

What follows—“He himself shall plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel”—is understood in two ways: either that these things are desirable to those who dwell in death, or that by the desirable vessels formerly kept in the treasure of hell we should understand the saints, whom the Lord, once bound, perhaps rescued and took from hell and led with himself into paradise.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] Much that is obscure in Jerome is to be explained from this passage, for he expressly asserts that souls bound in hell were freed by Christ’s death. [Col. 0940D] MART. The manuscripts read this way; previously the text had “he rescued,” “he seized,” and “he took.”]

In place of “treasure,” the Septuagint translated “land.” There can be no doubt that “land” signifies death. We read in the Psalms: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). And according to the Gospel: “The meek shall possess the land” (Matt. 5).

Conversely, we must understand the land of hell not to be the land of the living but of the dead. It is plundered and laid waste when the souls bound in hell are liberated through Christ’s death.

According to the allegorical interpretation, in the same commentaries of which we spoke above, we read that the scorching wind is understood as the devil and the individual founders of heresies. We do not approve this. For the devil cannot dry up the veins of death and the springs of error, since he himself is the source and beginning of the dead.

Therefore, in ecclesiastical language, the scorching wind is to be understood as the wind that dries up all the doctrines of heretics and reduces them to nothing, and that plunders and disperses those who had been gathered together in death by the teaching of heretics.

(Chapter 14, verse 1.) “Let Samaria perish, because she has provoked her God to bitterness. Let them perish by the sword; let their little ones be dashed to pieces, and let their pregnant women be ripped open.”

The Septuagint: “Samaria shall be destroyed because she resisted her God. They shall fall by the sword; their sucklings shall be dashed against the ground, and those who are pregnant shall be ripped open.”

[Note: [Col. 0940D] Victorius corrects “against the ground” in place of “against the rock,” on the basis of Jerome’s exposition that follows and of nine manuscript copies, five from Brescia, and four from Florence. The Greek word is ἐδαφισθήσεται (*edaphisthēsetai*); it means “I cast down” or “I dash against the ground,” since ἔδαφος (*edaphos*) denotes ground or pavement, not rock. Suidas likewise explains ἔδαφος as “ground,” not “rock.”]

We have often said that the ten tribes are called Samaria after the metropolitan city Samaria, which, from the name of Augustus, is now called Augusta, that is, Sebaste. Why the city was called Samaria is found in the Book of Kings.

The prophet therefore gives an order—or, to speak more accurately, he speaks in the optative mood—that Samaria should perish. Although God had prepared such great blessings for her, she acts against God and instead follows the images of demons.

Symmachus, however, did not say “let her perish,” but μεταμελήσει (*metamelēsei*), that is, “she shall repent,” and she shall repent of her error because she has turned the sweetest God into bitterness. Thus her warriors shall perish by the sword, her little ones and sucklings shall be dashed against the ground, and her pregnant and expectant women shall be torn apart unto death.

All this must be believed to have happened to her at the time of captivity and distress, when they lost their homeland and those who escaped the sword were led away into perpetual servitude.

The meaning concerning heretics is readily apparent: they are called Samaria because they boast that they preserve God’s commandments—not because they are guardians of his Law, but because they claim to be so, in the likeness of the schism of the Novatians, who likewise call themselves καθαρούς (*katharous*), that is, “pure,” although they are the most impure of all, denying repentance, by which sins are cleansed, in accordance with what is written: “You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. 50). And in Isaiah: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1:16).

By “washing,” he does not mean baptism, but every kind of repentance that washes away the filth of sins.

Let such a Samaria therefore perish, because whatever she says opposes her God and turns his clemency into cruelty, to such an extent that the men among her who have reached the full age of wickedness—

[Al. “of military service”]

—are cut down by a spiritual sword.

Those who are little ones and sucklings, however, are dashed against the rock. Of them we also read in the psalm: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136:9).

Her pregnant and expectant women, who conceived from an evil seed, shall likewise be ripped open, so that they may not produce the worst offspring. Something similar is also proposed to us in the Gospel: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Luke 21:23)—namely, in the days of tribulation and distress.

The warriors of Samaria are killed by the sword, the sucklings are dashed to pieces, and the pregnant women are ripped open so that, once the evil seed has perished and its weeds have been burned, only the wheat may remain, to be stored in the Lord’s barns.

[Col. 0941D] (Verses 2, 3, and 4.) “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have fallen through your iniquity. Take words with you and return to the Lord. Say to him: ‘Take away all iniquity, and receive what is good, and we shall repay the calves of our lips. Assyria shall not save us; we shall not mount a horse, nor shall we say any longer, “Our gods are the work of our hands,” because you will have mercy on the orphan who is in you.”

[Al. “on the people”]

The Septuagint: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have become weak through your iniquities. Take words with you and return to the Lord. Say to him: ‘Do not take away iniquity, but take what is good, and we shall repay the fruit of our lips. Assyria shall not save us; we shall not mount a horse. We shall never again say, “Our gods are the works of our hands,” because he who is in you will have mercy on the orphan.’”

With Samaria perishing, and its men, children, and pregnant women killed, dashed to pieces, and ripped apart, all Israel is summoned to repentance. The one who has become weak—or has fallen—in his iniquities is to return to the physician and receive healing, or the one who had fallen is to begin to stand. He is taught how he ought to repent.

“Take,” he says, “words with you”—that is, prayers and confession of sins—and return to the Lord in words as well as in deeds. Say to him: “Take away all iniquity; leave in us nothing of our sickness and former ruin, lest the living shoots of an evil seed sprout again. And,” he says, “receive what is good.” For unless you take away our evils, we cannot have anything good to offer you, in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “Turn away from evil and do good.” And, he says, “we shall repay the calves of our lips” (Ps. 36:27).

In place of the calves, which in Hebrew are called PHARIM (), the Septuagint translated “fruit,” which is called PHERI (), because of the similarity of the words.

The calves of the lips are praises of God and thanksgiving. For “the sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19). Thus, even at that time, when carnal victims had already been rejected, the sacrifice pleasing to God was pure confession.

Those who say that they will repay the calves of their lips and sing God’s praises continually with their voice also promise that they will place no hope in the Assyrians, nor mount the horses of Egypt, since “a horse is deceptive for salvation” (Ps. 32). They also promise that they will no longer worship the works of their hands—the golden calves that they cast at Dan and Bethel.

Therefore, they say: “We shall never again say to the work of our hands, ‘Our gods,’ because you will have mercy on the orphan who is in you”—that is, on the people of Israel, of whom you had said: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4:22); and, “I have begotten and raised children, but they have rejected me” (Isa. 1:2); and elsewhere: “Foreign children have lied to me” (Ps. 17:46).

He is called an orphan because he lost God as his father.

Someone else explained the orphan as one who has withdrawn from the evil father, the devil, and is therefore lifted up by God’s mercy.

The prophet also speaks daily against every perverse doctrine and summons its followers to repentance, saying: “Return to the Lord your God, you who have fallen—or grown faint—after losing the Lord’s health. Take words with you, a true confession of faith, and say: ‘Take away the iniquity that moves in our heart, and receive the good of faith,’ for faith is believed with the heart unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

The calves and sacrifices, or the fruit of the lips, consist in believing in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and in the passion and resurrection of the Lord. Whoever offers this to him will place no hope in the Assyrian king, about whom we have often spoken. Nor will he mount the horse which the Lord commanded should never be multiplied (Deut. 17), and which Pharaoh possessed, together with whose cavalry he was drowned (Exod. 14).

Every heretic mounts horses through pride, horses that he himself has generated in his error. They will no longer say to the works of their hands—which they have fashioned by an artificer’s eloquence—“Our gods.”

The glutton’s god is his belly; the miser worships Mammon; the heretic worships the doctrine he has fashioned. Whoever abandons all these—the Assyrian, the horse, and the works of his hands—will return to the Lord and appease his Father, from whom he had been cast away.

(Vers. 5 ff.) “I will heal their breaches; I will love them freely, because my anger has turned away from him [Vulgate: them]. I will be like dew. [Note: [Col. 0943D] It should be read and joined as follows: ‘I will be like dew to Israel: he will germinate,’ etc. Consult what we have observed in *Pseudo-Rufinus*.] Israel will germinate like a lily, and its root will burst forth like Lebanon. Its branches will go out, and its glory will be like an olive tree, and its fragrance like Lebanon. They will return, sitting in his shade; they will live on grain, and will germinate like a vine. His memorial will be like the wine of Lebanon. Ephraim, what have I to do with idols any longer? I will hear him and guide him. I am like a flourishing fir tree; from me your fruit has been found.”

The Septuagint: “I will heal their inhabitants; I will love them openly, because my anger has turned away from them. I will be like dew. [Col. 0943B] Israel will blossom like a lily and will send out its roots like Lebanon. Its branches will go out, and it will be like a fruitful olive tree, and its fragrance like Lebanon. They will return and sit under its shade; they will drink and [Note: [Col. 0943D] Martianus reads *inebriantur* (‘they are made drunk’), contrary to the manuscripts and the Greek text, μεθυσθήσονται (‘they will be made drunk’).] be made drunk with grain, and its memorial will blossom like a vine, like the wine of Lebanon. Ephraim, what has he to do any longer with idols? I have humbled him, and I will strengthen him; I am like a dense juniper. From me your fruit has been found.”

When those who have turned to repentance, and who recognize as a father the one whom they had abandoned, have returned, God answers: “I will heal their breaches”—or their dwellings, in which they had been wounded or broken, or in which they had dwelt so wickedly. “I will love them freely”—which the Septuagint translated ὁμολογουμένως, “plainly and openly,” [Note: [Col. 0943D] The Palatine manuscripts read ὁμολόγως, which is the same thing.] [Col. 0943C] or “without any doubt.” But the Lord loves those who love him, concerning whom he also says elsewhere: “I love those who love me” (Prov. 8:17).

For previously I was angry with them because of the sins they had committed; now I will have mercy because of my clemency. And I will be to them like dew: I will extinguish with my dew the Babylonian furnace and the kiln of blazing fire. Through the patriarch Isaac I also spoke to my servant Jacob: “Your dwelling shall be from the dew of heaven.” For just as the Lord becomes for believers light, way, truth, bread, vine, fire, shepherd, lamb, gate, worm, and so forth, so for us, who need his mercy and burn with the fevers of our sins, he is changed into dew. To him Isaiah says: “For the dew that is from you is their healing” (Isa. 26:19, according to the Septuagint). And Moses speaks in the Song of Deuteronomy: “Let my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32:2).

When the Lord has sprinkled us with his dew and watered the dryness of our breast with his rains, we will germinate—indeed, we will blossom—like a lily, imitating the Lord and Savior, who says in the *Song of Songs*: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1). He speaks to his bride, who has neither wrinkle nor blemish: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.”

And when we have grown in the Lord, we will send down our roots like the trees of Lebanon. As far as they rise into the air with their crowns, so far do they plunge their roots into the depths, so that they are shaken by no storm but stand firm in their stable mass. The branches of these trees extend in every direction, so that the birds of heaven may come and dwell in them.

And lest we perhaps think that, when he said “its root will burst forth,” or “it will send out its roots like Lebanon,” he was speaking of cedars and unfruitful trees, he compares the holy man who has turned to the Lord with a fruitful olive tree. He says elsewhere: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51:1). Its fruit the five wise virgins prepared for themselves (Matt. 25); from it the swelling of wounds is soothed, the limbs of the sick find rest, light is kindled in darkness, and those contending in the arena are anointed.

This olive tree will have a fragrance like Lebanon, or frankincense, which is a kind of incense: ὁμωνύμως, “under the same name,” [Note: [Col. 0943D] Among the Hebrews, Lebanon signifies both frankincense and the mountain of Lebanon; similarly, among the Greeks, *Libanos* is both a mountain and incense. Hence Jerome says that the mountain and the incense are called by one name. MART.—More correctly, in the *Commentaries on Habakkuk*, chapter 2, he said, according to the Greek expression alone, that *Libanos* is homonymous with frankincense. Although it is by no means certain whether Lebanon was so called from frankincense—or rather, it seems more likely that it took its name from whiteness, namely, from the snows with which it is covered, just as the Alps were called from *alpus*, or “white”—it is nevertheless certain that in Greek *Libanon* means frankincense. In Hebrew there is also a certain similarity of sound, for incense is called [Hebrew text omitted in the supplied text], while that mountain is [Hebrew text omitted in the supplied text].]

Among Greeks and Hebrews it is called both a mountain and frankincense, or it may refer to the frankincense of Mount Lebanon, which is exceedingly fertile and green and is protected by the densest foliage of trees. Thus the olive tree may say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Cor. 2:16).

Those who have turned to the Lord will receive the reward of their conversion, so that they may sit in his shade and say: “I rested and sat beneath his shade, and his fruit is sweet in my mouth” (Song 2:3). When they have sat in his shade, those who had previously been dead will live; or, according to the Septuagint, they will drink and be made drunk with wheat—that is, with an abundance of all things.

That drunkenness here signifies not the overthrow of the mind but an abundance of all things is shown by the verse that says: “You visited the earth and made it drunk” (Ps. 64:10). So too Joseph’s banquet, at which he is said to have made his brothers drunk (Gen. 43), and the Lord speaking to the apostles: “Eat, my friends, and drink; drink deeply, brothers” (Song 5:1). Or, because our Lord himself is grain and vine, whoever believes in him is said to be made drunk.

Finally it follows: “And his memorial will blossom like a vine, like the wine of Lebanon.” We may call the wine of Lebanon wine mixed and seasoned with incense, so that it has a most sweet fragrance; or the wine of Lebanon may be the wine poured out to the Lord in the Temple, concerning which we read in Zechariah under the name of Lebanon: “Open, Lebanon, your gates” (Zech. 11:1).

[Note: [Col. 0944D] Victorius says that he understands this of the wine which, in the mysteries of the Mass, having become the blood of Christ, is poured out and offered to the Lord. On this subject Malachi, in the first chapter, explicitly declares in these words: the offering is not to be made in only one province of the world, Judea, nor in only one city of Judea, Jerusalem, but “in every place an offering shall be made,” by no means unclean as among the people of Israel, but clean, as in the ceremonies of Christians. Likewise, in Ezekiel 46: “A lawful, perpetual, and continuous sacrifice,” which is interrupted on no day but is always offered at every time after sunrise, so that what is set down at the end of this chapter may be fulfilled: “He shall make a lamb for a sacrifice, and oil, morning by morning, for a perpetual burnt offering.” Everyone can see how strongly these words convict the innovators of our time, who remove from the Church the sacrifice which the whole world has never been without.] 

Since such an abundance of things is to come, O whole Ephraim, who are practicing repentance and have begun to be mine, abandon idols and despise images. For I am the one who humbled you, and I will exalt you—or, “I will hear and guide you”—and I will make him like a flourishing fir tree, so that concerning him, according to the Hebrews, it may be said in the psalm: “His house is a fir tree” (Ps. 103:18).

[Note: [Col. 0946D] Victorius says: “In Psalm 103, where according to the Septuagint we read, ‘The houses of the heron are their leader,’ the Hebrew has [Hebrew text omitted], which signifies a fir tree, as in 3 Kings 5 and 2 Chronicles 3. Likewise in Isaiah 41 and 60. I do not overlook the fact that the Septuagint, in 2 Chronicles 2, translated it as ἄρκευθος, that is, juniper.”]

Or certainly: “I will be like a dense juniper,” so that he may rest beneath my shade. Concerning the ἀρκεύθοι, that is, junipers, according to the Septuagint translators, Solomon is remembered to have made the doors of the Temple, because Christ, through whom we approach the Father, has this nature: he always blossoms, always brings forth new fruits, and never lays aside his greenness.

This juniper gives fruit to those resting beneath its shade, so that they are not struck by the heat of this world and the heat does not strike their heads, just as it once struck Jonah’s (Jonah 4). It provides not only rest to those sleeping and sitting, but also satiety to those who eat.

Whatever we have interpreted according to ἀναγωγήν, the higher or spiritual sense, concerning the coming of the Lord and Savior and the conversion of true Israel, can equally be referred to heretics and Jews, to the nations, and to every perverse doctrine, so that when they practice repentance they may obtain pardon.

If, therefore, the fullness of the promise was accomplished in the coming of the Savior, and is accomplished daily in the Church, we must believe that it will be fulfilled more completely when, with perfection coming, what now exists in part will be destroyed.

It should be noted—as we have often already said—that the salvation of Israel, its return to the Lord, and its redemption from captivity are not to be understood carnally, as the Jews think, but spiritually, as is most truly demonstrated.

(Vers. 10.) “Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is discerning and will know them? For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them, but transgressors will fall in them.”

The Septuagint: “Who is wise and will understand these things, or discerning and will know them? For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk [Al. walk] in them; but the impious will become weak in them.”

When he says, “Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is discerning and will know them?” he shows the obscurity of the book and the difficulty of its explanation. But if the very author confesses that it is difficult, or impossible, to understand, what can we do, whose eyes are bleary and darkened by the filth of sins, so that we cannot gaze upon the clearest radiance of the sun, except to say what is written: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways past finding out!” (Rom. 11:33).

For who, without Christ as teacher, can know what Jezreel signifies; who is meant by his sister who did not obtain mercy; who is the third brother, “not my people”; who is the adulteress who will sit for so long without the law of God; what is the covenant with the beasts of the earth and with the birds of heaven; who is the David to whom the people will return; whose is the resurrection on the third day and whose going forth is compared with the dawn; what is the early and latter rain; who is the one whom the prophet says will come and show us righteousness; or in whose figure Israel is brought out of Egypt, carried in arms, and led with cords of love; who is the one who kills death, dries up its veins and makes its springs dry, and plunders the vessels stored in the treasury—and all the other matters that would take too long to unfold?

Therefore, whoever is holy and righteous will recognize that the ways of the Lord are straight. We understand the ways of the Lord to be the reading of the Old and New Testaments and the understanding of the holy Scriptures. Whoever walks in these ways will not be able to find the straight path unless he turns to the Lord and the veil that had been before Moses’ eyes is removed from him.

But if he says with David, “Uncover my eyes, and I will contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18), he will walk in them and find Christ. He will also perceive that the Jews and heretics, whom Scripture now calls either transgressors or impious, stumble in them, become weak, and fall, according to what is written: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34).

[Col. 0947]

# The One Book of the Commentaries of Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, on the Prophet Joel, to Pammachius. (C)

## Prologue

[Col. 0947A] 165–166 The order of the twelve prophets among the seventy translators is not the same as that retained in the Hebrew text. The former place Amos second, Micah third, Joel fourth, Obadiah fifth, Jonah sixth, Nahum seventh, Habakkuk eighth, Zephaniah ninth, Haggai tenth, Zechariah eleventh, and Malachi twelfth. The Hebrews, however, after Hosea—who is first among both groups—read Joel second, Amos third, Obadiah fourth, Jonah fifth, Micah sixth, Nahum seventh, Habakkuk eighth, Zephaniah ninth, Haggai tenth, Zechariah eleventh, and Malachi twelfth and last.

And since we have once enumerated all the prophets of the single volume, it seems useful briefly to note the etymologies of each, both in Greek and in Latin. Hosea is interpreted as σώζων, “saving,” which we may call “savior.” Joel is ἀρχόμενος, “beginning.” Amos is βαστάζων, “bearing,” which among Latins is called “carrying.” Obadiah is δοῦλος Κυρίου, “servant of the Lord.” Jonah is περιστερά, “dove.” Micah is τίς ὡς [Al. ὀστισοῦν], a name composed of two parts of speech, which among us sounds like “who as?” or “who is like?”

Nahum is παράκλησις, “consolation.” Habakkuk is περιλαμβάνων, “embracing” or “wrestling” [Al. “embracing”]. Zephaniah is κεκρυμμένος Κυρίου, “hidden of the Lord,” or “the Lord’s secret.” Haggai is ἑορτάζόν, whom we may call “festive” or “solemn.” Zechariah is μνήμη Κυρίου, “memory of the Lord.” Malachi is ἄγγελός μου, “my messenger.” In what sense all these names are to be understood will be discussed in their respective books.

The other four prophets, so that the number sixteen may be complete—I mean Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Daniel—have the following meanings: Isaiah is called σωτηρία Κυρίου, “salvation of the Lord”; Ezekiel is κράτος Κυρίου, which we may call “the strength” or “rule of the Lord”; Jeremiah is ὐψηλὸς Κυρίου, “the exalted one of the Lord”; Daniel is ἔκρινε με Κύριος, “the Lord judged me.”

Since these things are so, I beg you, my Pammachius, who fight against the devil with every art [Note: [Col. 0947B] Two manuscripts lack the word *pugnandi* (“of fighting”). It alludes to the name Pammachius.] of fighting, so that, while we fight against Amalek, you may lift your hands with Moses to the Lord and overcome the adversaries of Israel by your prayers.

We have recently come out of Egypt and, with Pharaoh drowned in Hosea, crossed the Red Sea (Exod. 14–15). Now, after the broad wasteland of the desert, we must sweat with great labor if we are to be able to reach the seventy palms and the apostolic springs.

Though a scorpion may rise up and attempt to strike with a curved wound, you, our companion on the journey and charmer of poisonous bites, [Note: [Col. 0947B] The extent of the corruption of this word and sentence will scarcely be comprehensible to anyone who has seen it in the ancient editions of Erasmus and Marianus. Those editions show Saint Jerome absurdly being read as Ψηφιστὴν, “one who gives a vote” or “calculator,” rather than ψυλλέα, that is, a Psyllus, in accordance with the evidence of all the manuscript codices. The Psylli were peoples of Libya in Africa, named after King Psyllus. They possessed an inborn poison deadly to serpents, and by its odor could put them to sleep. See Pliny, book 7, chapter 2. Plutarch also writes in his *Life of Cato* that Cato, traveling through the deserts of Libya, took Psylli with him to cure snakebites, drawing out the poison with their mouths and calming the snakes themselves with songs. Saint Jerome’s entire passage refers to this: he wishes to have in Pammachius a spiritual Psyllus for overcoming the poison and venom of rivals and heretics, as is clear to the prudent reader.
