MART.—He alludes to the history that Plutarch relates concerning Cato, who, when he was about to penetrate the deserts of Libya, had Psylli as companions and charmers of poisonous bites. The Psylli, men who formerly inhabited the region of Cyrene, were well known among ancient writers for their innate power against snakes and wild beasts: not only were they themselves unharmed by them, but they also rendered others harmless. On this subject, above all, see Strabo, book 17, and Dio Cassius in his account of Caesar Octavianus, where he says that Psylli were brought to Cleopatra’s body to restore her to life. Pliny also writes of them in book 7, chapter 2, as does Lucan in book 9:

> One race alone throughout the lands  
> Dwells unharmed by the deadly bite of serpents,  
> The Marmaric Psylli, whose tongue matches powerful herbs;  
> Their own blood is safe and can admit no poison,  
> Even when the chant has ceased. The nature of the region  
> Has ordained that they should be immune, mingled with serpents.

Here, in place of ψυλλέα or ψύλλον, Erasmus and Victorius had read ψηφιστὴν, “one who gives a vote,” whom Martianus rebukes above with excessive severity, himself copying his annotation from Calepinus.] present us with a spiritual ψυλλέα, and, as a pious heir, receive what we promised to your holy and venerable mother Paula. Whatever we can do, whether by talent or learning, below your expectation, support with a friend’s favor. Do not consider our strength but our willingness.

## The Book Begins

[Col. 0949]

[Col. 0949A] 167 (Chapter 1.—Verse 1.) “The word of the Lord that came to Joel son of [Note: [Col. 0949D] Beware of a false understanding of these words, lest you find Saint Jerome ignorant of the Hebrew language. In his own *Book of Hebrew Names* he says that the name Bathuel signifies and sounds like “virgin” or “daughter of God.” Understand, therefore, that in this passage the name Bathuel does not have that meaning: no suitable sense would result if Joel were called the son of Bathuel, that is, “of the father of the virgin of God.” MART.—Our manuscripts consistently read Patuel and Batuel without aspiration. What Saint Jerome says, that Bathuel has no meaning among the Hebrews, should be understood to mean that he does not intend the Hebrew etymology of Bathuel here, according to which Bathuel is interpreted as “daughter of God.” It would therefore be equivalent to saying “Joel, son of the daughter of God,” as Martianus also observes.] Phatuel.”

The Septuagint translators rendered PHATUEL () as Bathuel, which among the Hebrews has no meaning at all. Phatuel, however, is translated into our language as “the breadth of God” or “God opening,” just as in Mark we read of the Savior [Note: [Col. 0950D] The printed editions read the Hebrew form *Hippathehh*, but it should be read with an initial aleph as *Eppethahh*, or *Ephphetha*, according to the ancient witnesses and the Evangelist Mark, chapter 7, verse 34: Ἐφφαθὰ, ὅ ἐστι, Διανοίχθητι, “which is, Be opened.” From the Syriac passive [Syriac text omitted], *Etphethahh*, “he was opened,” comes the imperative *Eppethahh*, or *Epphetha*, “open.” MART.] saying to a deaf and mute man: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened” (Mark 7).

For he could say with the Apostle: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11), and he heard from the Lord: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11). The opening of the mouth itself, therefore, lies not in human but in divine power, since Paul says: “A great and evident door has been opened to me; but there are many adversaries” (1 Cor. 16:9). For this reason God is called “the one who opens.”

And since the saint is always progressing, knowing in part and prophesying in part until what is perfect comes, he is called Joel, generated from breadth and opening. Joel () sounds among us as “beginning,” or “the Lord is God,” the Apostle saying: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have grasped it” (Phil. 3:13). Through this humility, as he grows together with Moses, he deserves to hear: “He who is” sent me (Exod. 3).

For the distinction of those who are not, concerning whom we also read in Esther, “Do not hand over your scepter to those who are not” (Esth. 14:11), God and his saints are shown to be. [Note: [Col. 0950D] Victorius prefers *memorantur*, “are mentioned”; this is the reading of the Florentine codices.]

Let this brief treatment of the name Joel and of his father suffice, so that the word of God, which was in the beginning with God, may rightly be said to have come to be. John the Baptist bears witness: “He who is to come after me has come before me, because he was before me” (John 1:30).

Moreover, the statement that the word came to be refers to the merit of the one to whom it comes, not to the condition of the one who is said to come to be, just as we read elsewhere: “The Lord has become my salvation” (Ps. 117:21).

Just as in the prophet Hosea, whom we explained at the beginning of the Twelve Prophets before this book, prophecy is directed under the name of Ephraim to the ten tribes, often called Samaria or Israel, [Col. 0949D] 169 so in Joel, who according to the Hebrews is second, everything that is said must be understood to pertain to the tribe of Judah and to Jerusalem; no mention at all of Israel—that is, of the ten tribes—is made here.

We should also understand the times in which he prophesied to be the same as those we read about in Hosea: “In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.”

(Vers. 2, 3.) “Hear this, elders, and perceive with your ears, all inhabitants of the land: has such a thing happened in your days or in the days of your fathers? Tell it to your children, and your children to their children, and their children to another generation.”

The Septuagint: “Hear these things, elders, and perceive with your ears, all inhabitants of the land: have such things happened in your days or in the days of your fathers? Because of these things, tell your children, and your children to their children, and their children to another generation.”

The elders are commanded to hear; the inhabitants of the land are told to perceive with their ears. The elders are not told, “Hear, all”; to the inhabitants of the land is added, “Perceive with your ears, all.”

For hearing in the holy Scriptures is not merely that which resounds in the ear, but that which is grasped by the heart, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13:9). What we have translated as “perceive with your ears” is expressed by one word among both the Greeks and the Hebrews: among the Greeks, ἐνωτίσασθε; among the Hebrews, [Note: [Col. 0950D] One Palatine manuscript has *Hiezina*, which is properly perceived not by the heart but by the ear.] EEZINU (). It properly means “perceive,” not with the heart but with the ear.

And so that we may know that hearing is more sacred than what merely resounds in the ears, let us learn from Isaiah, who says: “Hear, O heaven, and perceive with your ears, O earth” (Isa. 1:2). Those who are elders and heavenly hear spiritually; those who dwell on earth and are called earthly perceive with their ears. This should be noted throughout the Scriptures wherever these two words are placed together.

We read the same in the case of Lamech the sinner, who spoke to his wives Adah and Zillah: “Hear my words, wives of Lamech; perceive with your ears my words, because I have killed a man to my wound and a young man to my bruise” (Gen. 4:23). He knew that what he was saying was obscure, and therefore he summoned his wives not merely to the simple sound of the words but also to the hidden meaning of what he said.

If anyone, then, is an elder, mature in age and chosen in the Lord—[Al. “and joyful,”] as we read below according to the Septuagint translators—and has left behind the infancy of little ones, let him hear what is said. But whoever still dwells on earth and cannot say, “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:14), let him perceive with his ears.

“If it has happened,” he says, “in your days or in the days of your fathers.” By rhetorical art he makes the hearer attentive through the magnitude of the events. “No age,” he says, “remembers what I am about to say; it happened neither in your time nor in the time of your fathers and ancestors.”

Understand “fathers” as grandfathers and great-grandfathers, and “children of children” as every succeeding offspring, according to Virgil’s line (*Aeneid* 3):

> And the children of children, and those who will be born from them.

Therefore let both the elders and the inhabitants of the land tell their children and descendants. Let the elder teach his children the mysteries; let the inhabitant of the land tell the simple history.

Thus even to this day we who believe in Christ, from whose eyes the veil has been removed together with Moses, and of whom it is said, “The wisdom of a man is his gray hair” (Wis. 4:8), tell our children secret and wondrous things.

But the Jews, who dwell on earth, speak earthly things and cling to the ground, concerning whom it is written: “He who is of the earth is earthly and speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3:31).

(Vers. 4.) “What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust ate; what the swarming locust left, the consuming locust ate; and what the consuming locust left, the stripping locust ate.”

The Septuagint likewise.

The narrative follows the beginning. There he promised, in order to make the hearer attentive, that he would speak of great and incredible things, such as neither ancient history knew nor the present age had witnessed. Here he introduces the cutting locust, the swarming locust, the consuming locust, and the stripping locust, so that things which rarely occur individually may be remembered as having all happened together, and may therefore be wondrous.

The cutting locust, called in Hebrew GEZEM (), and in Greek κάμπη, the Hebrews interpret as the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Chaldeans. Proceeding from one region of the world, they devastated everything belonging both to the ten tribes and to the two—that is, to the Israelite people.

They interpret the swarming locust as the Medes and Persians, who, after overthrowing the Chaldean empire, held the Jews captive.

The consuming locust they refer to the Macedonians and all Alexander’s successors, especially King Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, who sat in Judea like a consuming locust and devoured all the remnants of the former kings. Under him the wars of the Maccabees are recorded.

They refer the stripping locust to the empire of the Romans, who, as the fourth and last power, oppressed the Jews so completely that they expelled them from their own borders.

Josephus writes about this more fully in seven books, recounting the triumphs of Vespasian and Titus. We also read of Hadrian’s campaign against the Jews, in which he so thoroughly overthrew Jerusalem and its walls that from the remains and ashes of the city he founded a city called Aelia, after his own name.

These four kingdoms that overthrew Judea are what Zechariah writes that he saw in four horns, when the angel said to him: “These are the horns that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem” (Zech. 1:19).

And again: “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses; in the second chariot, black horses; in the third chariot, white horses; and in the fourth chariot, dappled, strong horses” (Zech. 6:1).

When the prophet said to the angel who spoke in him, “What are these, my lord?” the angel replied: “These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand before the Ruler of the whole earth.” The meaning is: these are those who go forth from the presence of the Lord to fulfill his will.

With the inhabitants of the earth we have perceived with our ears what the cutting locust, the swarming locust, the consuming locust, and the stripping locust signify. Now, with the elders, let us hear what has been said.

All the schools of philosophers proclaim that there are four disturbances by which the health of souls is overturned: two present and mutually opposed, and two future and mutually conflicting.

The present ones are grief and joy. We speak of grief of soul; otherwise, bodily grief is not called grief but illness. Either, then, we are sad and consumed by sorrow, and the condition of our mind is overturned. Hence the Apostle warns that a brother not be swallowed up by excessive sorrow (1 Cor. 2).

Or, conversely, we rejoice and exult in happiness and cannot bear our good fortune with moderation. Yet it belongs to a just and courageous man neither to be broken by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity, but to be moderate in both.

We have spoken of the disturbances of the present; let us speak also of those of the future, in which there are fear and hope. We fear adversity and await prosperity. What grief and joy produce in the present, fear and hope produce concerning the future, when we either fear more than is fitting that adversity is about to come, or the prosperity we hope for causes us to exult so greatly that we do not keep within bounds—especially in matters that are [Note: [Col. 0951] A Palatine manuscript, with the opposite meaning, reads “in matters that are certain”; perhaps this is the more correct reading.] uncertain, because future things are hoped for rather than possessed.

The illustrious poet has comprehended these four disturbances in a single, though not complete, verse (*Aeneid* 6):

> These fear and desire—this concerns the future—  
> They grieve and rejoice—this concerns the present—  
> Nor do they look back upon the open air, he says,  
> Shut up in darkness and a blind prison.

Those who are wrapped in the darkness of disturbances cannot behold the clear light of wisdom.

We must therefore take care lest grief, like the cutting locust, consume us; lest the swarming locust lay waste in joy, flying here and there and hurling itself in different directions through exultant happiness; lest the consuming locust—that is, dread and fear of future things—devour the roots of wisdom; lest the stripping locust and desire for future things long for useless objects and carry us to ruin.

Rather, in all things let us govern with the reins of wisdom the four chariots, the four horns, and the four horses—red, dappled, white, and black—that is, adversity, prosperity, or what is compounded of both.

I think the cutting locust is a passion beginning in the soul, one that is slow and unable to move rapidly and that, by its very delay and persistence, drinks up and sucks out all greenness. If we do not kill it, it grows within us and takes flight. Sometimes it devours whatever it touches; sometimes, leaving things only half-eaten, it moves on to others. Returning to its former seat, it becomes the consuming locust, so that through its slowness it devours not only crops, leaves, and bark but even the marrow itself.

But if it should happen—though this is rare—that some vital breath still remains in us even after the consuming locust, the stripping locust ravages everything, turning even straw and worthless hay black, so that they are useless not only for food but even for manure.

Concerning these four disturbances we will also speak at the beginning of Amos, if life accompanies us, where it is written: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, of Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the children of Ammon, Moab, Judah, and Israel, I will not revoke it, says the Lord” (Amos 1:3 ff.).

The disturbances we have interpreted are called by the Greeks πάθη. If we render this as *passiones*, “passions,” in a misguided fashion, we will have expressed the word more than its meaning.

(Vers. 5.) “Awake, drunkards, and weep and howl, all who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.”

The Septuagint: “Awake, you who are drunk with your wine; weep and lament, all who drink wine in drunkenness, because it has been taken away from your mouth.”

As elders and presbyters, we must understand that nothing so intoxicates as the disturbance of the mind. There is a sorrow that leads to death; this is the detestable drunkenness.

There is anger that does not produce the righteousness of God and that comes close to madness, making a person powerless over his own mind, so that his lips tremble, his teeth gnash, and his face changes color with pallor.

The saying of Archytas of Tarentum is rightly praised. When he was angry with his steward, he said: “I would have killed you by now, if I were not angry.”

What should I say about joy and pleasure, and especially love, which blinds the eyes of the heart and permits the lover to think of nothing except what he loves? [Note: [Col. 0953D] Two Palatine manuscripts read, “what he loves and thinks about,” which it permits him to see.] Is this not rightly called drunkenness, when, because of a worthless prostitute and a dishonorable part of the body, the soul’s freedom is bent toward servile flatteries; when one makes another’s labor into his own pleasures; when by theft, crime, and perjuries one prepares wealth for future pleasure; and when, though seen by everyone, one thinks oneself unseen, provided only that one obtains what one desires?

Avarice also blinds the mind of the person for whom nothing is enough, as do womanish fear and the desire for sweet vices.

Hence it is said to them: “Awake and rouse yourselves, you who are drunk”—not with wine, as is contained only in the Septuagint, but with every disturbance of vices. “Weep, lament, and practice repentance; take up the sorrow that leads to life, and howl, all who drink wine in sweetness” (Prov. 3), or “in drunkenness.”

For vices are sweet, because “honey drips from the lips of a prostitute.” Therefore wine is not offered in the sacrifices of God, because the wine—or drunkenness and sweetness—that had deceived you has perished, or been taken away, from your mouth.

Often God’s providence operates so that those who did not know God in prosperity may know him in adversity, and those who misused riches may be corrected toward virtue by poverty.

According to this meaning, let the elders hear. Let the inhabitants of the earth perceive with their ears that the command is now given concerning that wine in which there is debauchery, and by which those who are drunk cannot possess the kingdom of God (Eph. 5).

Whoever has been lulled to sleep by drunkenness from wine should awaken, weep that he was drunk, and howl, so that afterward his howling and weeping may be changed into laughter, and he may rejoice that he no longer has the material of drunkenness which, through abundance, had made him drunk and mad.

### (Verses 6–7)

“For a nation has come up upon my land, strong and innumerable; its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of a lion’s cub. It has made my vine a wilderness and stripped the bark from my fig tree; stripping it bare, it has utterly despoiled it and cast it away; its branches have become white.”

The Septuagint: “For a nation has come up upon the land, strong and innumerable; its teeth are those of a lion, and its molars like those of a lion’s cub. It has made my vine a desolation and my fig trees a breaking; searching, it has searched it out and cast it away; it has whitened its branches.”

[Note: [Col. 0953D] The word “my” was missing; it is present both in the Greek text and in our manuscripts.]

The Jews think that in Joel’s time such an innumerable multitude of locusts came upon Judea that they covered everything; and I will not say merely the crops, but that they left behind even the bark and branches of the vines and trees, so that, after all their greenery had been consumed, the branches of the trees remained dry and the shoots of the vines withered.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] One Palatine manuscript reads “whitish”; Jerome below follows the same sense: “after all their greenery has been consumed, it leaves the branches of the trees white and dry.”]

Whether this actually happened or not, we cannot affirm with certainty. For the history in Kings and Chronicles does not relate it (1 Kings 17). If it had happened, how could Scripture have remained silent about the famine under Elijah, which we read lasted three years and six months?

We say only that, under the metaphor of locusts, the coming of enemies is described: whether the Assyrians and Babylonians, who were then threatening; or the Medes and Persians, who were to come afterward; or the Macedonians, whom we know came much later; or finally the Romans, about whom we spoke above. At present, however, it seems to us that the passage speaks more particularly of the Babylonians and Chaldaeans, whose cruelty and savagery toward the people of God are described. And, if I am not mistaken, I seem to have discovered something in this Prophet.

The impiety of the enemies is narrated under the figure of locusts; and then the locusts themselves are described as though they were compared with enemies, so that when you read of locusts, you should think of enemies, and when you have thought of enemies, you should return to the locusts.

Thus a nation of locusts has come up from the wilderness—or the army of the Chaldaeans upon God’s land—strong and innumerable. For what is more innumerable and stronger than locusts, against which human effort cannot prevail?

Its teeth—the teeth, that is, of the nation of locusts (understand everything typologically, τυπικῶς)—are like the teeth of a lion; and its molars are like those of a lion’s cub. Thus those who equal locusts in strength and multitude are compared with lions in ferocity and cruelty.

[Note: [Col. 0955D] In place of “nation,” the Palatine manuscripts read “teeth”; and in place of τυπικῶς they perhaps more correctly prefer τροπικῶς, “tropologically.”]

“This nation,” he says, “has made my vine a wilderness”—the vine which I brought out of Egypt and planted—and has stripped the bark from my fig tree, that is, the Jewish people, to whom the Savior came to eat its fruit and found none. He cursed it, and it withered forever (Matt. XI).

Let us recognize that all these things are spoken under the metaphor of locusts. They devastate everything so completely that they gnaw away the bark of trees, strip them, cast the bark aside, and, after consuming all the greenery, leave the branches white and dry.

We have spoken according to the historical sense. Let us pass to the spiritual understanding, so that with the elders we may hear: “A nation has come up upon the land of God,” namely, the human soul. For all souls belong to God: the soul of the father no less than the soul of the son.

And the nation of the rulers of this world and of darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, against whom we struggle and contend, has come up. Concerning them it is said: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4). The teeth of this nation are like the teeth of the lion, concerning which the Apostle Peter says: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

And its molars are like those of a lion’s cub. By the lion’s cub understand either the one who exalts himself against everything that is called God and religion, or certainly every perverse doctrine. Concerning the crushing of its molars, which lie hidden within and are not seen, so that they may not easily be avoided, the Psalmist also rejoices, saying: “The Lord will break the molars of the lions” (Ps. 57:7).

If, therefore, we give this nation a place so that it may rise up within us, it will immediately make our vine a wilderness—the vine from which we used to make wine that gladdens the human heart (Ps. 104:15)—and strip the bark from our fig trees, or break them, so that we may not possess within us the sweetest gifts of the Holy Spirit, and so that the holy man may not rest beneath our vine and fig tree. When he is beneath them, he will not fear the assault of his adversaries.

Nor is it enough for this nation to destroy the vine and break the fig tree, unless, searching, it searches them out and kills whatever life may be in them, so that, after all their greenery has been consumed, only white and lifeless twigs remain, and what is written may be fulfilled: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will they do in the dry?” (Luke 23:31).

### (Verse 8)

“Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of your youth” [the Vulgate: “for her husband”].

The Septuagint: “Lament to me for the bride girded with sackcloth, for her virginal husband.”

The “husband of youth,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, παρθενικός (*parthenikos*), commonly called “virginal,” because he was the first to take away the flower of virginity, is understood to be none other than God, who in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob betrothed to himself a virgin bride undefiled by any stain of idolatry.

To her he also speaks through Jeremiah: “Did you not call me ‘my lord,’ and ‘father,’ and ‘prince of your virginity’?” (Jer. 3:4). Hence the Apostle also says to believers: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Cor. 11:2).

As long as the bridegroom is with this bride, she cannot fast (Matt. 9), nor lament, nor express her longing for the absent bridegroom with tears. But when the bridegroom has been taken away from her, she laments and weeps, girds herself with sackcloth and haircloth, and wraps a rope around herself instead of a belt.

[Col. 0956B] We have understood who the virginal bridegroom is. But since this bridegroom, or husband, not only took a virgin as his bride but also, in Hosea, takes a prostitute as his wife, for this reason it is written in Deuteronomy:

“If you go out against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hand, and you take them captive, and among the captives you see a beautiful woman, and desire her, and wish to have her as your wife, you shall bring her into your house. She shall shave her head, trim her nails, and remove the garment in which she was captured. Sitting in your house, she shall mourn her father and mother for one month; afterward you shall go in to her, sleep with her, and she shall be your wife” (Deut. 21:10ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Victorius maintains that it should be corrected to *hujuscemodi*: [Col. 0956D] according to the Florentine manuscripts, “Such a woman does not have the virginal lord as her husband.”]

He is not the husband—that is, the virginal lord—of such a woman; rather, he took a prostitute as his wife from the filth of the nations.

We can say the same concerning every believing soul. If it believed in the Lord from early childhood, it has the Lord as its virginal bridegroom. But if it came to the truth of faith from the Jews, or from the Gentiles and the most filthy refuse of heretics, and passed from darkness into light, it will indeed have a bridegroom, but not a virginal one. Of such people it is said: “In Egypt your breasts were broken, and there you were deflowered” (Ezek. 23:3).

### (Verses 9ff.)

“The sacrifice and the libation have perished from the house of the Lord; and the priests, the ministers of the Lord, have mourned. The land has been devastated; the soil has mourned, because the grain has been destroyed. The wine has been ruined, the oil has languished, and the farmers have been confounded. The vinedressers have howled over the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine has been ruined, and the fig tree has languished; the pomegranate, the palm, and the apple tree, and all the trees of the field, have withered, because joy has been confounded among the children of men.”

The Septuagint: “The sacrifice and the libation have been taken away from the house of the Lord. Mourn, priests, ministers of the Lord, because the fields have been desolated. Let the land mourn, because the wheat has been afflicted [variant: ‘struck’]. The wine has dried up; the oil has been diminished [variant: ‘changed’]. The farmers have dried up [variant: ‘the trees’]. Mourn, estates, over the wheat and barley, because the vintage has perished from the field.”

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Palatine manuscripts read: “The fig tree has dried up, and the vines have been changed.”]

“The vine has dried up, and the fig trees have been diminished. The pomegranate, the palm, the apple tree, and all the trees of the field have been dried up, because they have confounded the joy of the children of men.”

As far as the historical sense is concerned, because of the multitude of locusts—or of enemies, who are described under their appearance—everything having been devastated and consumed, the sacrifice and the libation have perished from the house of the Lord. One of these they were accustomed to offer from fine flour, the other from wine.

For this reason the priests, who are the ministers of the Lord, have mourned: neither sacrifices nor libations were properly celebrated, especially since the tithes that they were accustomed to receive were not offered at all. For the whole land was devastated.

The soil mourned, by metonymy (μετωνυμικῶς), for those who work the soil.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Victorius again restores, on the authority of the Florentine manuscripts, *versabantur* (“were engaged”); for, he says, both the preceding and following passages refer to past time.]

The wheat, wine, and oil languished. The farmers and vinedressers themselves were also confounded and howled, because not only the grain but also the barley, which is cheaper and more productive, had dried up. I think that legumes too are signified by the phrase “the harvest of the field has perished,” that is, everything that the soil usually produces.

Why speak of wheat, wine, oil, and barley, when even the fruits of the trees have dried up? The fig tree has languished, and the pomegranate, palm, apple tree, and all the trees, whether fruit-bearing or barren, have been consumed by the ravaging locust. All this happened so that joy would be removed—or confounded—from the children of men.

We can also say that these same things happened to the Jewish people after the coming of the Savior, when they cried out with equal fury: “Crucify, crucify such a one! We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:9, 15). Jerusalem was then surrounded by an army, and they fell into such a state of famine and pestilence that they ate the bodies of children not yet mature.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] One Palatine manuscript reads: “and the sacrifices were taken away in reverse order.”]

All the sacrifices were taken away, and joy was confounded among the children of men, because they refused to receive the joy of which the angel speaks to the shepherds: “I announce to you great joy” (Luke 2:10).

According to the anagogical sense, this seems to be the meaning: after the bride, who had received the teaching of God, has been separated from the bridegroom through sins, and instead of linen and fine garments has been wrapped in sackcloth—that is, has assumed the clothing of mourning—then the sacrifice will perish, concerning which it is written: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit” (Ps. L, 19), and the libation of wine, which gladdens the human heart, will perish from the house of God, which is the Church. The Apostle says to Timothy: “So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God” (1 Tim. 3:15).

The sacrifice and libation will be taken away from the house of the Lord when, because iniquity has multiplied, the love of many has grown cold (Matt. 24:12), and the leaders of the people and the ministers of the altar see that the fields and open plains of believers produce no fruits of virtue but bristle everywhere with vices.

This will happen when the wheat, barley, vines, and oil have been consumed by the caterpillar, locust, beetle, and mildew, and we no longer possess the cup of which it is written: “Your intoxicating cup, how glorious it is!” (Ps. 23:5).

The oil will also have perished, concerning which we read in Ecclesiastes: “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccl. 9:8). With this oil the face is brightened and the head of one who fasts is anointed.

Then the farmers will be confounded when they see that in their possessions there is no wheat, by which human beings are nourished, nor barley, by which irrational animals are sustained, and that the vine has been ruined. Concerning it is written: “Israel was a leafy vine, abundant in fruit” (Isa. 5:2), yet when the Lord expected it to produce grapes, it produced thorns.

The fig tree also languished, beneath which Nathanael was before he believed (John 1). So did the pomegranate, to whose rind the cheeks of the bride are compared in the Song of Songs (Song 6); and the palm, which, having lost its greenery, dried up, although once it was said: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. XCI, 13); and the apple tree, concerning which we read in the same Song: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men” (Song 2:3).

Why is it necessary to go through all the trees, when everything has withered, and instead of joy and gladness sorrow and confusion have overwhelmed the children of men?

### (Verses 13–14)

“Gird yourselves and lament, priests; howl, ministers of the altar. Enter, lie down in sackcloth, ministers of my God, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God. Sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the elders, all the inhabitants of the land, into the house of your God, and cry out to the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “Gird yourselves and lament, priests; mourn, you who minister at the altar. Enter, sleep in sackcloth, ministers of God, because sacrifice and libation have failed from the house of your God. Sanctify a fast, proclaim a healing [variant: ‘take care of a proclamation’]. Gather the elders, all the inhabitants of the land, into the house of your God, and cry out to the Lord vehemently.”

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Victorius inserts “of the Lord,” saying that this word is found in the Hebrew. Thirteen very ancient copies from Monte Cassino also have it, as do some Bolognese manuscripts; and, something I value greatly, the manuscript of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, given to that church by Charlemagne. I omit the many printed copies and several Florentine manuscripts.]

Whoever is a holy priest and eats the Lord’s Passover should gird himself with the belt of chastity and hear the words spoken to the apostles: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35).

But whoever is a sinner and is stung by his own conscience should gird himself with sackcloth and lament either his own sins or those of the people. He should enter the Church, from which he had gone out because of his sins, and lie down, or sleep, in sackcloth, so that through the austerity of his life he may compensate for the former pleasures by which he had offended God.

“For those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (Matt. XV).

The priests should gird themselves, lament, howl, and sleep in sackcloth, as the Prophet exhorts them to repentance when he says: “Ministers of my God, how have sacrifice and libation perished from the house of your God?” (Joel 2), concerning whom it was said above.

[Note: [Col. 0958D] One Palatine manuscript reads: “He says, ‘Lie down in sackcloth, ministers of God: how has sacrifice perished,’ and so forth.”]

It is not enough to weep or lament and assume the clothing of mourning unless they also sanctify a fast and call an assembly.

If every fast pleased God, he would never say: “Sanctify a fast,” nor: “I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord” (Isa. 58). In the Gospel those who disfigure their faces so that they may appear to fast before men are condemned (Matt. 6). And in the days of your fasts, he says, you strike with your fists and oppress the poor.

Therefore he now says: “Sanctify a fast.”

A Manichaean fasts, and many heretics—especially the Encratites, whose leader is Tatian—but this fast is worse than fullness and drunkenness.

And “call an assembly,” or “a healing,” so that through repentance we may heal our sins.

In place of “assembly,” the Hebrew reads ASARA (אסרה), which Symmachus translated as “synod,” and Aquila as “day of assembly.”

Gather the elders, whose age is close to death and whose judgment is mature, and who therefore receive the fear and worship of God more readily.

Also gather all the inhabitants of the land, concerning whom he had said above: “Hear this, elders, and give ear, all inhabitants of the land,” so that both the elders and the inhabitants of the land may be gathered into the house of God, which is the Church.

When they have come into the Church, and from the diverse flock of priests and people, elders and inhabitants of the land, one flock has been formed, he says: Cry out to the Lord in your hearts and say:

### (Verse 15)

“Ah, ah, ah, for the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and like devastation [variant: ‘storm’] it will come from the Almighty.”

The Septuagint: “Woe is me, woe is me, woe is me on the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and like misery upon misery it will come.”

For what we translated “from the Almighty,” the Hebrew has SADDAI. We have said several times that this is one of the ten names of God. The Septuagint translated it as “misery,” reading SOD instead of SADDAI.

The voice of the priests and the people crying out to the Lord is therefore introduced, so that they may say “Woe is me” three times—presumably because, through the sins they had committed, they had offended the holy Trinity.

The day of retribution for all sins is that day about which all the prophets write, and especially Isaiah cries out: “Behold, the day of the Lord comes, incurable, with fury and wrath, to make the whole world desolate and destroy sinners from it” (Isa. 13:9).

This day is rightly called incurable, because when the day of judgment has come, there will be no place for repentance. Compared with eternity, it is near and not far away.

What follows—“And misery will come as misery,” or “devastation will come from the Almighty”—means that evils will follow evils and that every affliction will be dispensed by God as judge, who is powerful enough to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna (Matt. 10:28).

What we have said generally about the day of judgment, let us apply specifically to the time of the Jewish captivity, when Jerusalem was captured and the Temple destroyed. Not long afterward, the captivity of the ten and two tribes also came upon them from the Assyrians and Chaldaeans.

This captivity is foretold as future, so that when it comes it may not seem to have happened by chance or through the strength of the enemies, but through the wrath and threat of God—or, if the people should repent, so that what is destined to come may not come.

### (Verse 16)

“Have not provisions perished before our eyes, and joy and exultation from the house of our God?”

The Septuagint: “Before your eyes provisions have perished; from the house of our God, joy and gladness.”

Before their eyes the provisions of sinners perish when the crops already hoped for are taken from their hands, and the locust overtakes the reaper, so that what has been stored in the granaries in hope [variant: “often”] is consumed by the beetle and mildew.

For those also who dwell in the Church, according to the quality of their merits, the wheat of the spirit and the barley of the letter are taken away if they sin, so that they suffer hunger for the word of God.

When the provisions have been taken away, joy and gladness are consequently removed from the house of God, so that those who had previously heard the Apostle say, “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4), may afterward hear the Lord calling them to repentance: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

### (Verses 17–18)

“The beasts have rotted in their dung; the granaries have been demolished, the storehouses have been destroyed, because the grain has been ruined. Why has the animal groaned? The herds of cattle have lowed, because there is no pasture for them; and the flocks of sheep have also perished.”

The Septuagint: “The calves have leaped about in their stalls; the treasuries have been scattered, the winepresses have been dug up, because the wheat has dried up. What shall we store up for ourselves? The herds of cattle have wept, because there were no pastures for them, and the flocks of sheep have perished.”

After provisions had perished and joy and gladness had been taken away from the house of God, the beasts also rotted in their dung; or, according to the spiritual understanding, they became wanton in their stalls and kicked against their Creator, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “If they are not filled, they will murmur” (Ps. 59:15).

He rots in his dung whose god is his belly and who says: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. 22:16).

For him the granaries of future happiness have been demolished, and the storehouses of eternal abundance have been destroyed—or the winepresses have been overturned—because if there are no grains and wines, granaries and winepresses are prepared in vain.

[Note: [Col. 0960D] The words “of future happiness” and “of eternal abundance” are acknowledged neither by Victorius nor by our manuscripts.]

When everything has dried up, then they will complain in a mournful voice and say: “What shall we store up for ourselves?”

What follows according to the Septuagint—“The herds of cattle have wept, because there are no pastures for them”—compels us not to understand these words as referring to oxen and cattle, but to those who, because of their simplicity, are called oxen and sheep.

Concerning their pastures the Savior says: “He will enter and go out, and will find pasture” (John 10:9).

Understand all these things under the metaphor of the caterpillar, locust, beetle, and mildew: when the crops had been removed and devastated, famine and pestilence seized everything.

### (Verses 19–20)

“To you, Lord, I will cry, because fire has devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness, and flame has set fire to all the trees of the land. The beasts of the field, like a thirsty plot of ground longing for rain, have looked to you, because the springs of water have dried up, and fire has devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness.”

The Septuagint: “To you, Lord, I will cry, because fire has consumed the beautiful places of the wilderness, and flame has set fire to all the trees of the field. The beasts of the plain have looked to you, because the channels of water have dried up, and fire has devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness.”

The Prophet—or the people through the Prophet—cries out to the Lord because fire has devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness and flame has set fire to all the trees of the land. The beasts and animals of the field, or plain, have looked to the Lord like a thirsty plot of ground longing for rain.

Aquila signifies this in a single word, ἐπρασιώθη.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] One Palatine manuscript reads ἐπρασώθη. Aquila’s verb πρασιάω means “to thirst for rain”; he also uses it in Psalm 42:1, where we have: “As the deer longs for springs of water.”]

They have looked to him because the springs, or channels, of water have dried up, and fire has devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness. This means, of course, that the caterpillar, locust, beetle, and mildew have done what fire does in stubble and flame in thorns.

The beautiful places of the wilderness, called in Hebrew NAOTH (נאוה), may be understood either as the level places of the fields, the flowering meadows, or green places covered with grass that supplied pastures for the animals.

The fire that devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness and the flame that set fire to all the trees of the land caused the beasts to cry out to the Lord through the Prophet and to look to him, so that both crops and fruits might perish together. Since the springs of water had dried up, the greedy flame consumed whatever could be found in the wilderness.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] Victorius inserts the conjunction “and” on the authority of the Florentine manuscripts. The earlier reading was *poterant invenire* (“could find”), instead of *poterat inveniri* (“could be found”).]

Let us also consider that, unless it were because of distress and the removal of their pleasures, neither the Prophet nor the beasts would have cried out to the Lord or looked to him.

This can also be applied to the righteous man of former times: when he turns aside and does evil, his former virtues will not benefit him at all, but the Lord will judge him according to what is found in him.

We can call “the beautiful places of the wilderness” those concerning which it is written: “The children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1).

The flame that sets fire to all the trees of the land should be understood as the flame sent through the devil’s burning arrows, so that no good fruit may remain in us, but everything may be consumed by fire.

“All adulterers are like an oven—their hearts” [variant: “the whole seed of the adulterer”]. Not only the Prophet, or the people through the Prophet—for the human being is a rational animal (Hos. 7)—but also the beasts, concerning which it is said: “You save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 36:6), and elsewhere: “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. 73:22), and again: “I will sow them with the seed of human beings and of beasts” (Jer. 31:27), have looked to the Lord and demanded the dew of his mercy.

For the springs of water have dried up, those springs which the deer longs for, and concerning which the Lord speaks through Jeremiah: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. 2:13).

When the springs of water have dried up—springs that irrigate and refresh all that is dry—then consequently whatever was beautiful in us has been consumed by the heat of the fire, concerning which the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

## (Chapter II.—Verse 1 ff.)

Sound the trumpet in Zion; howl on my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the land be thrown into confusion, because the day of the Lord is coming, because the day of darkness and gloom is near, a day of cloud and storm; like dawn spread over the mountains, a numerous and mighty people, such as has not existed from the beginning, nor will exist after it throughout the years of generation after generation.

Before its face is a devouring fire, and behind it a flame consuming; the land before it is like a garden of delight, and behind it like a desolate wilderness. There is no one who can escape it. Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like horsemen so they will run. Like the sound of chariots they will leap upon the mountaintops; like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble, like a mighty people prepared for battle. Before its face the peoples will be tormented; every face will be reduced to the appearance of a cooking pot. Like strong men they will run; like warriors they will climb the wall. The men will proceed along their own ways, and will not turn aside from their paths. No one will crowd his brother; each will walk in his own lane. Yet they will fall through the windows and will not be destroyed; they will enter the city, run upon the wall, climb into the houses, and enter through the windows like a thief.

Before its face the earth trembled, the heavens were shaken; the sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness. And the Lord gave his voice before the face of his army, because his camps are exceedingly many, because they are mighty and carry out his word. For great is the day of the Lord and exceedingly terrible; and who will endure it?

**The Septuagint:** Sound the trumpet in Zion; proclaim upon my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the earth be thrown into confusion, because the day of the Lord is present, because the day of darkness and gloom is near, a day of cloud and frost; as dawn will be poured out upon the mountains, a numerous and mighty people, such as did not exist from the beginning, nor will exist after it throughout the years of generations.

Before it is a consuming fire, and behind it a kindled flame. The land before its face is like a paradise of delight; and what lies behind it is like a field of desolation, and there will be no one who can be saved from it. Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like horsemen they will pursue. Like the sound of chariots they will leap upon the summits of the mountains; like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble; like a numerous and mighty people prepared for battle. Before its face the peoples will be crushed; every face will be like the scorching of a cooking pot. Like fighters they will run, and like warriors they will climb upon the walls. Each will walk along his own way, and they will not turn aside from their paths; each will not withdraw from his neighbor. Laden with their weapons they will go; they will fall upon their spears and will not be consumed. They will seize the city and run upon the walls; they will climb over the houses and enter through the windows like thieves. Before its face the earth will be confounded, and the heaven will be shaken; the sun and moon will be darkened, and the stars will remove their light. And the Lord will give his voice before the face of his strength, because his camps are exceedingly many, because the works of his words are mighty; for great is the day of the Lord, great and exceedingly glorious, and who will be sufficient for it?

**Note:** Victor wishes to read *confundantur* (“let them be confounded”) instead of *conturbentur* (“let them be thrown into confusion”), believing that the Greek is συγχυθήτωσαν (*synchythētōsan*). But in other copies, and especially in the Alexandrian, it is συναχθήτωσαν (*synachthētōsan*), while in the Complutensian it is συνταραχθήτωσαν (*syntarachthētōsan*), which properly means “let them be confounded.”

**Note:** One Palatine manuscript has *similis ei non erit, nec fuit*, “there will be none like it, nor has there been,” and elsewhere too improperly departs from the Greek archetype.

Again, through the metaphor of locusts, the assault of the Chaldeans is described. The prophet—or rather, through the prophet, all who are able to hear God’s word—is commanded to raise his voice like a trumpet, proclaim in Zion, and sound upon his holy mountain, so that at the noise of the cry and trumpet blast all the people of Jerusalem may tremble.

“When,” he says, “you have sounded the trumpet, say this: The day of the Lord will by no means be delayed any longer”—that is, the day of vengeance and retribution. Captivity is near at hand; the army of the Babylonians has already departed from its own place; the day of darkness is near, and of distress, a day of gloom, cloud, and storm, in which every light of joy [another reading: *justice*] will be taken away, and all things will be overwhelmed by darkness.

“As,” he says, “morning and dawn suddenly drive away the darkness, and the sunrise illuminates all the mountains, so the army of the Babylonians will be poured over all your land.” Do not suppose that the multitude is weak: it is a numerous and mighty people, whose like no other nation could be found either in the past or in the future. Whatever it touches, it will consume like a devouring flame, leaving nothing intact behind it. Whatever land it has not touched is like a garden and paradise of delight; whatever it has plundered is like solitude and wilderness, and no one will be found who can escape its hands.

Their appearance is like that of savage horses, and like horsemen they will run here and there. They are not compared with Babylonian horsemen; rather, because through the metaphor of enemies the locusts are said to run here and there like horsemen. “As the sound,” he says, “of chariots and wagons, so will be the sound of the locusts.” They will leap upon the mountaintops in order to climb every elevated place; and as flame quickly consumes stubble, so the sound and terror of their voice will ravage everything.

When he adds, “like a mighty people prepared for battle,” he again refers to the locusts, so that he appears to be speaking not of enemies but of locusts; yet while we read of locusts, we are to think of the Babylonians. So great will be the terror that all the surrounding nations will shudder in mind and body—or rather, will be tormented. From the magnitude of their fear, everyone’s faces will be changed into the likeness of a cooking pot, which, burned by fire, displays a foul appearance of blackness and soot.

“They will run,” he says, “like strong men”—plainly meaning the locusts; “and like warriors they will climb the wall,” so that the height of the walls cannot prevent the assault of the strong, and so that they will enter not through the gates but over the walls. “They will proceed along their own ways, and will not turn aside from their paths.”

We recently saw this in this province.

**Note:** Our manuscripts have *audivimus* (“we heard”). For *venirent et occuparent* (“were coming and occupying”), Victor, from Florentine manuscripts, reads *venerint et occuparint* (“have come and occupied”).

When swarms of locusts were coming and occupying the air between heaven and earth, they flew in such order, according to the arrangement commanded by God, that, like little tiles fixed by an artisan’s hand in a pavement, each kept its own place and did not deviate toward another even by a point—or, so to speak, by the width of a fingernail.

And to make the metaphor plain, he says, “They will fall through the windows and will not be destroyed.” Nothing is impassable to locusts, since they penetrate fields, crops, trees, cities, houses, and the hidden chambers of bedrooms. But this is said about locusts so that it may be understood about enemies.

What we translated as “they will fall through the windows and will not be destroyed,” the Septuagint rendered: “They will go, weighed down by their armor; they will fall upon their spears and will not be consumed.” This seems to me not at all to fit the order of the interpretation. Rather, the error arose because the Hebrew word **SALA** () they understood as “spears,” while we understood it as “windows.”

The narrative preserves its beginning by saying that they enter the city, run upon the walls, climb into the houses, and enter through the windows like thieves—not because those who are victorious fear thieves, but because, just as thieves customarily enter through windows and secretly carry things away, so they, with the doors closed, will burst in everywhere through the windows with complete boldness, so that there may be no delay.

Before the face of such locusts the earth trembled and the heavens were shaken. We should understand these statements hyperbolically: not that the force of locusts or enemies is so great that it can move the heavens and shake the earth, but that, for those suffering adversity, because of the magnitude of their terror, heaven seems to fall and the earth to waver.

Finally, because of the multitude of locusts covering the sky, the sun and moon will be turned into darkness, and the stars will withdraw their brightness: the cloud of locusts placed in between will not allow the light to reach the earth.

The Lord also will give his voice before the face of so powerful an army, because its camps are numerous, and the greatness of his strength is shown even in these tiny creatures. These camps are very numerous and innumerably strong, and they carry out his word. By this statement it is shown that the Babylonians will come by God’s will and obey his command.

“Great,” he says, “is the day of the Lord,” on which Jerusalem must be captured, “and exceedingly terrible”; no one will be able to endure it and escape the necessity of captivity or death.

I did not wish to divide a passage joined and coherent with itself, lest what was one in meaning should be torn apart among different chapters. Let us pass to its spiritual understanding, repeating each point in turn.

We read not only in Leviticus and the Book of Numbers (Num. X) about the sound of trumpets and clarions, where Moses is commanded to make two silver trumpets, with which those assigned to this office are to sound both at the new moons, and in the seventh month on the first day of the month, and at the jubilee, and at the other festivals, and when they go forth to war; but it is also written that the walls of Jericho fell at the sound of trumpets (Josh. VI). The Lord likewise says that he will send an angel with the sound of a trumpet (Matt. XXIV), and the Apostle proclaims that the resurrection of the dead takes place at the sound of the trumpet (I Cor. XV). In the Apocalypse of John also we read that seven angels received seven trumpets, and that, when they sounded them in order, the events described by Scripture took place (Rev. VIII).

Therefore priests and teachers are now commanded to raise their voice like a trumpet and fulfill what is written: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; raise your voice, you who announce to Jerusalem” (Isa. XLVIII, 9), so that the trumpet may sound in Zion—that is, in the Church, which is interpreted as “watchtower” and “elevation.” And on the holy mountain of God, which is Christ, all the inhabitants of the earth are to be thrown into confusion, or confounded, so that their confusion may draw them to salvation.

Understand the day of the Lord as the day of judgment, or as the day when each person departs from the body. For what will happen to all on the day of judgment is fulfilled in each individual on the day of death. It is a day of darkness and distress, a day of cloud and storm, because everything is full of punishments and torments.

A numerous and mighty host of angels will come to render to each according to his works. And just as morning and dawn, rising, first occupy the mountains, so judgment will begin with the exalted and powerful, so that the powerful may suffer powerful torments.

“Such as has not existed from the beginning, nor will exist after it throughout the years of generation after generation” (Wis. VI). All the evils contained in ancient histories—whether caused by the inundation of the sea, the overflowing of rivers, pestilence, diseases, famine, wild beasts, the devastation of enemies, or human beings—cannot be compared with the punishments that will be inflicted on the day of judgment.

Before the face of this people, which is strong and numerous, there will be a devouring or consuming fire, so that it may consume everything in us that is hay, wood, and stubble. Hence it is also said of God: “God is a consuming fire,” and “after him, a burning flame” (Deut. IV, 24), so that he may leave nothing without punishment.

Whoever this people does not touch, and in whom it does not find material for burning, will be likened to the garden and paradise of God’s delight, which in Hebrew is called **EDEN** (). But whoever it burns, it will reduce, like a wilderness, to ash and embers; and no one can escape its fury. Its cruel appearance will resemble that of neighing horses, and they will run about to torment those whom they have taken under their power, like horsemen flying here and there.

Their sound will be terrible, like chariots running down steep slopes. They will leap upon the mountaintops, desiring to torment all who are elevated and established at the summit of the Church. And because before their face there is a devouring and consuming fire, they will lay waste to everything as flame consumes stubble. Thus they will come to punish; thus swift and prepared will they be, like a mighty people ready for battle.

So great will be everyone’s fear, and so great the conscience of sins, that nothing will shine and no one will possess the radiance of joy; rather, each person’s face will be turned into darkness like that of a burned cooking pot.

“They will climb the wall” and every fortification; and, fulfilling the work assigned to them, they will not turn aside to another part. Rather, they will gape hungrily at the punishments of the wretched and will not be satisfied with their torments; each will pursue the punishment entrusted to him against sinners.

**Note:** One Palatine manuscript reads: “but they will cling to punishments.”

They will also enter through the windows, or will fall; or they will walk weighed down by their armor, and those whom they have taken to be consumed will fall upon their spears.

These are the windows of which Jeremiah also says: “Death will enter through our windows” (Jer. VI, 21). For enemies desire to enter all our senses, seize the city of a good conscience, run through our fortifications, and destroy the houses that we have built for ourselves by good works. They do everything by entering through the windows, like a thief; for they do not enter openly, “to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart” (Ps. X).

Before the face of this people, which is numerous and strong, the earth trembled and the heavens were shaken. For “heaven and earth will pass away, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Matt. XXIV). The sun and moon also will not be able to look upon such great punishments of the wretched, and they will mourn.

**Note:** The same manuscript rejects the negative particle.

They will not possess the justice of their office, and instead of clear light they will be covered with dreadful darkness. The stars too will withdraw their radiance, since even those who are holy will not see the presence of the Lord without fear.

In all these things the Lord will give his voice before the face of his army. For just as the Babylonians, when they punish Jerusalem, are called God’s army, so the evil angels—of whom it is written, “fury and wrath and distress, a sending through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 49)—are called God’s army and named his camps, since they carry out the Lord’s will.

Great is the day of the Lord and terrible, of which it is written elsewhere: “Why do you desire the day of the Lord?” (Amos V). “It is darkness and not light”; it is exceedingly terrible, and scarcely anyone—or no one—will be able to endure it without providing in himself material for its violence.

## (Verses 12 ff.)

Now therefore, says the Lord: Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning; and tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, because he is gracious and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy, and relenting over evil. Who knows whether he may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing, sacrifice, and libation for the Lord our God [the Vulgate: “your God”]?

**Note:** Again the same manuscript reads, “and abundant in mercy, and supplicable”; the latter word, in the Canon of Hebrew Truth, as Martianus calls it, is placed in the Sangerman manuscript in the margin as a variant reading, while the Carcassonian manuscript has it in the text itself.

**The Septuagint:** And now, says the Lord our God: Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, in sackcloth, in weeping, and in mourning; and tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and repentant over evils. Who knows whether he may return and repent, and leave behind him a blessing, sacrifice, and libation for the Lord our God?

**Note:** Our manuscripts do not know the words “in sackcloth”; only the Aldine edition recognizes them among the Greek copies of the Septuagint.

The preceding chapter, from the place where it is written, “Sound the trumpet in Zion; howl on my holy mountain; let all the inhabitants of the earth be thrown into confusion,” to the place where we read, “Great is the day of the Lord and exceedingly terrible; who will endure it?”, announces, through the metaphor of locusts, the coming of the Chaldeans and the evils that were going to befall the people.

Now he calls them to repentance and exhorts them to return to the Lord, so that, corrected with their whole mind, they may not suffer what the Lord threatens. The meaning is this:

“All the things contained in my preceding speech I spoke for this reason: to terrify you by my threat. Therefore return to me with all your heart, and show by fasting, weeping, and mourning the repentance of your soul, so that, having fasted now, you may later be filled; having wept now, you may later laugh; having mourned now, you may later be comforted.”

And because it is customary, in sorrowful and adverse circumstances, for you to tear your garments—a thing which the high priest is remembered to have done in the Gospel to intensify the charge against the Lord and Savior (Matt. XXVI), and which Paul and Barnabas also did when they heard words of blasphemy (Acts XIV)—therefore I command you not to tear your garments, but your hearts, which are full of sins and which, like wineskins, will burst of their own accord unless they are torn.

When you have done this, return to the Lord your God, whom your former sins had made alien to you. Do not despair of forgiveness because of the magnitude of your crimes: great sins will be erased by great mercy.

For he is gracious and merciful, preferring the repentance of sinners to their death (Ezek. XXXIII); patient and abundant in mercy, not imitating human impatience, but awaiting our repentance for a long time; and relenting, or repenting, over evils, so that if we repent over our sins, he too may repent of his threat, and not inflict upon us the evils he threatened, and, when our judgment changes, he himself may also be changed.

In this place, however, we must not understand “evil” as opposed to virtue, but as affliction, according to what we read elsewhere: “Sufficient for the day is its evil” (Matt. VI, 34). And: “If there is evil in a city which the Lord has not made” (Amos III, 6).

Likewise, because above he had said, “gracious and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy, and relenting, or repenting, over evils,” lest perhaps the greatness of his clemency make us negligent, he joins and says in the person of the prophet: “Who knows whether he may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?”

“I,” he says, “exhort you to repentance; this is what is mine to do. I know that God is ineffably merciful, as David says: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity’” (Ps. L, 1–2).

But because we cannot know the depth of God’s riches, wisdom, and knowledge, I moderate the sentence and express a hope rather than a presumption, saying: “Who knows whether he may turn and forgive?”

What he says by “who” should be understood as indicating either an impossibility or a difficulty:

“Sacrifice and libation for the Lord our God,” so that, after he has given a blessing and forgiven us our sins, we may be able to offer sacrifices to God.

## (Verses 15 ff.)

Sound the trumpet in Zion; sanctify a fast; call an assembly; gather the people; sanctify the Church; assemble the elders; gather the children and those nursing at the breast. Let the bridegroom come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room. Between the vestibule and the altar the priests, the ministers of the Lord, will weep and say: Spare, O Lord [the Vulgate adds “spare”], your people, and do not give your inheritance to reproach, so that nations may rule over them. Why should they say among the peoples, “Where is their God?”

**The Septuagint:** Sound the trumpet in Zion; sanctify a fast; proclaim a healing; gather the people; sanctify the Church; choose the elders; gather the children and those nursing at the breast. Let the bridegroom come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room. Between the pavement and the altar the priests, the ministers of the Lord, will weep and say: Spare, O Lord, your people, and do not give your inheritance to reproach, so that nations may rule over them, lest they say among the nations, “Where is their God?”

He still exhorts them to repentance before the hostile army arrives. “Above,” he says, “I had said: Sound the trumpet in Zion; howl on my holy mountain, and the rest, because the day of the Lord is coming, because the day of darkness and gloom is near, a day of cloud and storm; announcing to you that a numerous and mighty people was going to come and overthrow your possessions and cities.

“Now, because I am gracious and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy, I again command and say: Sound the trumpet in Zion, and proclaim repentance among the peoples. Sanctify a fast; proclaim a healing, or an assembly, concerning which we have already spoken. Gather the people, so that those who sinned while scattered may cease from sinning when gathered together.

“Sanctify the Church, so that no one in the Church may be unholy, lest perhaps your prayers be hindered, and a little leaven corrupt the whole lump” (I Cor. V). Assemble, or choose, the elders, so that what is chosen in them may be not age but holiness. Gather the children and those nursing at the breast, so that no age may be excluded from turning to the Lord.”

Of the children and infants we read in the Psalms and in the Gospel: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. VIII, 3; Matt. XXI, 16). Peter says that they are nourished with rational and guileless milk (I Pet. II); Paul speaks to them: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III, 2); and the Savior also remembers them: “Do not despise one of these little ones” (Matt. XVIII, 10).

Let the bridegroom also come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room, so that at the time of fasting, calling and assembly, the sanctification of the Church, the selection of the elders, and the gathering of the children and nursing infants, the bridegroom and bride may not serve the work of marriage—those to whom the Law also permitted that they should not go forth to war.

Hence the Apostle also commanded that they withdraw for a time from intercourse, so that they might devote themselves to prayer (I Cor. VII). Therefore whoever says that he is doing penance through austerity of food, fasting, and almsgiving promises this in vain unless he comes forth from his chamber and completes a holy and pure fast with chaste repentance.

What follows—“Between the vestibule and the altar the priests will weep”—the Septuagint interpreted “vestibule” as *crepidinem* (“pavement”); Symmachus, προπύλαιον (*propylon*, “forecourt”);

**Note:** The Palatine manuscripts have πρόπυλον, which means the same.

Aquila has πρόδομον (*prodromon*, “front building”); Theodotion placed the Hebrew word itself, **ULAM** (), which we can render “before the doors” or “portico of the temple.”

Observe what he commands the priests, who are the ministers of the Lord: that they should weep between the temple and the altar, and say with the Apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (II Cor. XI, 29). And: “Weep with those who weep.”

The place suitable for repentance and confession is the temple and altar. He teaches what the priests ought to say—indeed, how they ought to entreat the Lord: “Spare, O Lord, your people.” When the people were sinning, they were called “not your people”; now, after they have withdrawn from their vices, they are called “your people.”

“And do not give your inheritance to reproach, so that nations may rule over them.” The hidden riddle is now clear. That numerous and mighty people which was earlier described under the names of the caterpillar, locust, grub, and mildew is now shown more plainly to be what it is: “so that nations,” he says, “may rule over them.”

The Lord’s inheritance is given to reproach when they serve enemies, and the nations say: “Where is their God,” whom they used to boast of as their ruler and defender?

We can interpret “nations” also as hostile powers, which, as long as we do not repent, rule over us, reproach us, and say: “Where is their God?”

The Jews refer this passage to Gog and Magog, exceedingly savage nations which, they say, will come against Israel at the end of time; more fully concerning them is written in Ezekiel.

## (Verses 18 ff.)

The Lord was jealous for his land and spared his people. And the Lord answered and said to his people: Behold, I will send you grain and wine and oil, and you will be filled with them; and I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations. And I will drive far from you the one who is from the north, and expel him into a land impassable and desolate. His face will be toward the eastern sea, and his rear toward the western sea; and his stench will rise, and his decay will rise, he who has acted arrogantly [the Vulgate: “because he has acted arrogantly”].

**The Septuagint:** And the Lord was jealous for his land and spared his people. And the Lord answered and said to his people: Behold, I will send you grain and wine and oil, and you will be filled with them; and I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations. And I will drive away from you the one who is from the north, and lead him into a land without water. I will destroy his face in the first sea and his rear in the western sea. And his stench will rise, and his decay will rise, because his works have been magnified.

After the priests had entreated the Lord for the people and said, “Spare, O Lord, your people, and do not give your inheritance to reproach,” and the people had done what was commanded—sanctifying a fast, proclaiming a healing, gathering [another reading: compelling] the multitude, sanctifying the Church, choosing elders, gathering children and nursing infants, and having the bridegroom come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room, so that they might serve not the flesh and pleasure but the soul and tears—the Lord was jealous for his land, which he had previously despised as though it were alien, and had allowed the locust to ravage.

He showed such mercy to those who repented that he deemed them worthy of his answer, saying: “Because the locust, the caterpillar, and the mildew have ravaged all your crops, therefore I will give you grain,” and the rest that the prophet describes, “and I will no longer deliver you into captivity.”

And the Assyrian and Chaldean who is from the north [another reading: “from Babylon”] I will drive far from you—he of whom it was written above: “A numerous and mighty people, before whose face is a devouring fire and behind whom is a consuming flame, whose appearance is like the appearance of horses.”

“And I will expel him,” he says, “into a land of solitude; his front parts will fall into the eastern sea and his rear parts into the western sea. His stench will rise”—that is, the one who is from the north—and his decay, because he acted arrogantly.

I have often pointed out that, under the metaphor of locusts, the assault of the Chaldeans by which Judea was devastated is described. Therefore he preserves the metaphor in what follows and, in accordance with the position of the province, speaks as though he were referring not to enemies but to locusts.

Even in our own time we saw swarms of locusts cover the land of Judea. Later, through the mercy of the Lord, when priests and peoples entreated the Lord between the vestibule and the altar—that is, between the place of the cross and the resurrection—and said, “Spare your people,” they were driven by a rising wind into the first and last sea.

Understand the first sea, which lies near the wilderness and extends toward the East, as the sea where Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim once were, which is now called the Dead Sea because no living creatures live there.

**Note:** He elaborates on this in his *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter XLVII, column 593: “Thus far nothing that breathes and can move can be found in this sea because of its excessive bitterness—not even little snails, or tiny worms, or eels, or any other kinds of animals or reptiles, whose small bodies we may know better than their names. See what we have observed concerning this passage.”

The last sea is the one toward the West, which leads to Egypt, on whose shore Gaza, Ascalon, Azotus, Joppa, Caesarea, and the other coastal cities are situated.

When the shores of both seas were filled with heaps of dead locusts vomited forth by the waters, their decay and stench were so harmful that they corrupted the air as well, and a pestilence arose among both animals and human beings.

Let the learned reader ask where this literally happened in the case of the Chaldeans. Not long after these things were prophesied, we read in Isaiah that one hundred and eighty-five thousand Chaldeans under King Hezekiah were struck down in a single night while an angel raged (Isa. XXXVII).

This is what we may say according to the historical sense. But according to the tropological sense, every soul is the Lord’s land, in which the head of the household sows his seed. When that soul produces weeds instead of wheat—that is, oats and darnel—and offends its Lord, and later repents, weeping and saying, “Spare, O Lord, your people,” the Lord is jealous for his land and spares the one whom he had previously despised. He deigns to address it and says:

“I will send you grain,” concerning which it is written: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII).

And he will send wine, which gladdens the heart of man, and oil, which makes the face shine, so that the old sadness of sins may be tempered by the joy of grain, wine, and oil—that is, by the joy of virtues. They will possess such abundance of all good things that they will be filled and satisfied with them.

When they have attained this, they will no longer be given as a reproach to the nations, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 12).

“The one who is from the north”—of whom Jeremiah speaks: “From the north evils will blaze forth upon all the inhabitants of the land” (Jer. I, 14), and of whom Solomon writes: “The north wind is an exceedingly harsh wind”—“I will drive far from you,” he says, “and expel him into an impassable and desolate land,” which has no knowledge of God and in which the Holy Spirit does not dwell.

His face will be toward the first sea and the last sea, toward those who have opened the door of sins to him and among whom they have remained until the end of life. His stench and decay rise even into those who make great promises to themselves and fall through pride, because human weakness is never secure. The more we grow in virtues, the more we must fear falling from exalted places.
