According to the literal sense, swarms of locusts are accustomed to be brought more by the south wind than by the north; that is, they do not come from cold but from heat. But because he was speaking of the Assyrians while using the comparison of locusts, he inserted the north, so that we might understand not the true locust, which usually comes from the south, but the Assyrians and Chaldeans under the locust.

(Vv. 22ff.) Do not fear, O land; rejoice and be glad, for the Lord has done great things. Do not fear, animals of the region, for the pastures of the wilderness have sprouted; for the tree has borne its fruit, the fig tree and the vine have yielded their strength. And you, children of Zion, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, for he has given you a teacher of righteousness, and he will bring down for you the early and the late rain at the beginning [Note: See the commentaries of Rufinus, or of the person called Rufinus, on this passage.], and the threshing floors will be filled with grain, and the winepresses will overflow with wine and oil. And I will restore to you the years that the locust, the young locust, the mildew, and the caterpillar have eaten. My great strength, which I sent against you: you shall eat, eating your fill, and be satisfied, and you shall praise the name of your God [the Vulgate adds “of the Lord”], who has done wonders with us [the Vulgate: “with you”]; and my people shall not be put to shame forever. And you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and there is no other; and my people shall not be put to shame forever.

The Septuagint: Take courage, O land; rejoice and be glad, for the Lord has done great things. Take courage, beasts of the field, for the fields of the wilderness have sprouted; for the tree has borne its fruit, the fig tree and the vine have yielded their strength. And you, children of Zion, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, for he has given you the food of righteousness, and has rained upon you the seasonal and late rain, as at the beginning. The threshing floors will be filled with wheat, and the winepresses will overflow with wine and oil. And I will repay you for the years in which the locust, the young locust, the mildew, and the caterpillar have eaten. My great strength, which I sent against you; you shall eat and be nourished, and be satisfied; and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders with you. My people shall not be put to shame forever, and you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and there is no other besides me; and my people shall not be put to shame forever.

For all the things with which he had earlier threatened them, he now promises their opposites. Above he had said: “Fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and flame has consumed all the trees of the region, and the beasts of the field have looked to you as a thirsty land looks for rain, because the springs of water have dried up, and fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness.” Now he mitigates sorrow with joys and turns tears into laughter. “Do not fear,” he says, “animals of the region, for the pastures of the wilderness have sprouted; for the tree has borne its fruit, the fig tree and the vine have yielded their strength.” And such will be the abundance of all things that you will in no way lack grain, wine, and oil with which to satisfy yourselves; rather, the threshing floors will be filled with grain and the winepresses will overflow with wine and oil, so that you may not only eat yourselves but also be able to provide for others.

He also speaks particularly to the children of Zion, so that they may rejoice and be glad—not in some trivial matter, but in the Lord their God, who has given them the nourishment of righteousness; and, as the Seventy translated it, the seasonal and late rain, so that they may eat, rejoice, and praise the name of the Lord their God, who has done wonders with them, and may never be put to shame. Let them know that the Lord God of Israel dwells in their midst and that there is no other besides him, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father; and his people [variant: “my people”] shall not be put to shame forever.

According to the literal sense, because these things were promised by the Lord, we believe that they happened, and that the past barrenness was compensated by new crops, so that whatever the locust, the young locust, the mildew, and the caterpillar had consumed would be restored in the following years. [Note: Palatinus inserts the Greek word τροπικῶς (“figuratively”).]

We ask why the caterpillar is called the Lord’s strength or power, and not merely power but great power. Just as the power of God was displayed in the plagues of Egypt through small creatures, especially the gnats, which are so tiny that they can scarcely be seen by the eyes, so now, in a small and sluggish worm which can scarcely move and is crushed by the lightest touch, the power of God and human weakness are demonstrated. This does not mean that God, according to his will and the majesty of his power, is unable to overturn the earth, cover everything with a flood, or burn it up with lightning; rather, through small things, or, so to speak, points of bodies, he displays human frailty.

Hence we also customarily respond to Marcion and the other heretics who tear apart the Old Testament that God made fleas, gnats, bedbugs, and creatures of this kind for this reason: to show the frailty and weakness of our flesh, which is so utterly insignificant that it is wounded by things that are small. But if the caterpillar, a sluggish and tiny worm, is stronger than a human being, why does earth and ash boast and, lifted up by pride—although it comes from the soil, from which the human being is named—despise human beings?

Some interpret this passage as follows. We read of God’s powers and strengths on the right and on the left, which the Greeks call δυνάμεις (“powers”). On the right are the Seraphim and Cherubim and all the angelic powers; on the left are opposing powers, of which it is written: “He sent against them the fury of his indignation, wrath and anger and tribulation, a sending of evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 49). Of these also Micah speaks in the Book of Kings: “I saw the Lord God of Israel sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven stood beside him, on his right and on his left” (III Kings XXIII).

I think that the spirit on the left was the one who went out, stood before the Lord, and said: “I will deceive Ahab, and I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” To this left-hand and opposing power, which was suited to deception, practiced in destruction, and had deceived many before, God says: “You shall deceive and prevail; go out and do so.” That spirit also which strangled Saul, concerning which his servants said to him, “Behold, an evil spirit of God makes you faint” (I Sam. XVI, 15), belonged to the regions on the left and ministers to the Lord in punishing those who deserved to be tormented because of their sins.

For human beings alone are not his ministers and avengers against those who do evil, and do not carry the sword without cause; there are also opposing powers, which are called the fury and wrath of God, concerning which the prophet, turning away from them, says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. VI, 1). The Apostle handed over the sinner to such “questioners” and torturers, so to speak, for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved (I Cor. V); among them is Satan, to whom he handed others over so that they might learn not to blaspheme (I Tim. I).

So much concerning why the caterpillar is called the power of God. Let us pass to the order of the spiritual understanding.

“Do not fear, O land”—indeed, take courage and rejoice—you who previously lost the Lord’s seed through your barrenness, because the Lord has magnified his mercy toward you, so greatly that even the animals of the region and of the deserted wilderness might be filled with joyful new fields; that the tree of the cross might bear its fruit; and that the sweetest gifts of the Holy Spirit might bestow their abundance upon all.

You also, whom after repentance I rightly call children of Zion and of the Church, rejoice and be glad, because God the Father has given you a teacher of righteousness, or has granted you the nourishment of righteousness, and has caused seasonal and late rains to descend upon you (Isa. XXX). The early rain is when we first receive the teaching; the late rain is when we receive the fruit of our labor and arrive at perfect knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. The seasonal and late rain can also be understood as the Old and New Testaments.

“And not only this,” he says, “has he given you; he has also caused you to abound in the new fruits of the virtues, and to be satisfied and made drunk with grain, wine, and oil,” about which we have often spoken. And the years which you had previously lost amid reigning disturbances, when your works had been consumed by the locust, the young locust, the mildew, and the caterpillar, God did not allow to perish for you. Then you will eat the fruits of righteousness, be satisfied, and praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders with you.

But if after repentance God promises such great abundance of all things, what will Novatian reply, denying repentance and denying that sinners can be restored to their former state if they perform worthy works of repentance? God receives penitents to such an extent that he calls them his people, declares that they will in no way be put to shame, and promises that he will dwell in their midst; nor will they have any other God, but will trust with their whole heart in him who remains in them forever.

(Vv. 28ff.) “And it shall come to pass afterward that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Moreover, upon my servants and handmaids in those days I will pour out my spirit, and I will give wonders in heaven and on earth, blood and fire and columns of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

The Septuagint: “And it shall come to pass afterward that I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. And upon my servants and upon my handmaids in those days I will pour out of my spirit, and I will give wonders in heaven and upon the earth: blood, fire, and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes. And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

The blessed apostle Peter explained this passage as fulfilled at the time of the Lord’s passion, when the Holy Spirit descended upon the believers on the day of Pentecost and they all spoke as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance. Those present were amazed and said: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how do we hear each of us in our own language in which we were born? Parthians, Medes, and Elamites” (Acts II), and the others. But others said, “What does this mean?” While still others mocked and said, “They are full of new wine,” Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and said:

“Men of Judea, and all you who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. These men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day; but this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘And it shall come to pass afterward, says the Lord, that I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy,’” and so forth, up to the passage which we have set out in this chapter.

[Note: See the commentaries of the ancient writer who is called Rufinus, who dares to accuse Jerome of audacious rashness and ignorance.]

Since Peter records that Joel’s prophecy was fulfilled at the time when the Lord suffered, we ask only how the preceding, middle, and following passages, all the way to the end of the book, can cohere with one another, lest under a single text and continuous sequence of speech there appear an explanation that is diverse and discordant with itself.

From the beginning up to the passage where it is written, “The day of the Lord is great and exceedingly terrible; and who can endure it?” there is a threat and description of what the Lord will bring upon the sinful people. From the passage where we read, “Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning,” up to the place where he says, “Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’” there is the Lord’s exhortation, calling them to repentance after punishments and penalties.

Again, from the passage that follows, “The Lord was jealous for his land and spared his people,” and “The Lord answered and said,” up to the place where it is written, “My people shall not be put to shame forever,” there is a promise of future things which they should expect after they had practiced repentance.

And after many matters which it would now take too long to recount, these things also are spoken in the promise which we are attempting to explain at present: “I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy,” and so forth. It seems to me that from the beginning up to this passage I have preserved the continuity of the discourse. It is a matter of the greatest difficulty to determine how what follows should be fitted to what we are now discussing.

One person says that the things generally promised for the end time have now been fulfilled in part. Because the apostles perceived the reward of future things in the Lord’s first coming, they record that certain foretaste offerings and first fruits of the wonders were fulfilled, so that until what is perfect comes, we might experience what had preceded in part.

[Note: One Palatinus manuscript reads: “and because the reward of future things,” etc. From the same source, after Victorius, we have removed the conjunction that was prefixed to the word “foretaste offerings” (*libamenta*).]

Another asserts that this is the apostolic custom, according to what is written concerning the holy man: “He will distribute his words in judgment” (Ps. CXI, 5). Whatever they saw to be useful to their hearers and not contrary to present circumstances, they strengthened with testimonies from another period—not that they abused the simplicity and ignorance of their hearers, as the impious Porphyry falsely alleges, but that, following the apostle Paul, they preached “in season and out of season” (II Tim. IV).

Following the rule of the prophets, they declared spiritually fulfilled, at the first coming of the Lord and Savior, whatever the Jews promise themselves carnally for the last time. This is especially so since both they and we say that the promises are to be fulfilled in Christ; we differ only in this: they maintain that these things are still future, while we prove that they have already happened. More must be said about this in what follows.

All flesh upon which the Lord promises that he will pour out his spirit is that of which Isaiah speaks: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. XL, 5). Therefore the salvation of God cannot be seen unless the Holy Spirit is poured out. Whoever says that he believes in Christ but does not believe in the Holy Spirit will not have the eyes of perfect faith.

Hence also in the Acts of the Apostles, those who had been baptized with John’s baptism into the one who was to come—that is, in the name of the Lord Jesus—were baptized again. For when Paul asked them, they replied: “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit” (Acts XIX). Indeed, they received true baptism, because without the Holy Spirit and the mystery of the Trinity, whatever is received with reference to one or another Person is imperfect.

Nor will everyone who has received the Holy Spirit immediately possess spiritual grace; rather, through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit he will receive various graces (I Cor. XII). Some receive prophecy, like the sons and daughters who possess greater merit; others receive dreams, like the old, already advanced in age; others receive visions, like the young who have conquered the evil one.

But servants and handmaids who still possess the spirit of fear and not of love—for perfect love casts out fear—will not have prophecy, dreams, or visions. Content with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, they will possess only the grace of faith and salvation.

Then the Lord will give wonders in heaven and on earth: in heaven, because the sun was turned into darkness and the moon into blood; on earth, because the earth trembled with so violent and unusual a movement that the tombs were opened and the rocks split apart.

What he calls blood and columns of smoke, or vapor of smoke, refers to the blood of which we read in the Psalms: “That your foot may be dipped in the blood” (Ps. XLVII, 24), and in Isaiah: “How red are your garments!” (Isa. XCIII, 2), and to the blood which the Roman soldier poured out, mixed with water, after piercing the Savior’s side (John XIX).

The fire is the fire of the Holy Spirit which descended from heaven, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts II, 3ff.). This is the fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth and which, before he suffered, he desired to burn in his disciples (Luke XII).

Fire has a twofold nature: it has light for believers, but darkness and punishments for unbelievers; these are called vapors of smoke. This smoke is exceedingly bitter; it blinded the eyes of the Jews. Concerning it we read in Proverbs: “As smoke is harmful to the eyes and an unripe grape to the teeth, so is iniquity to those who practice it” (Prov. X, 26).

Isaiah also speaks of this smoke in the great vision in which the blindness of the Jews was foretold: “And the lintel was shaken, and the house was filled with smoke.” Hence what follows: “Go and say to this people: Hearing you shall hear and shall not understand; and seeing you shall look and shall not see. For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have heard heavily” (Isa. VI, 9–10).

The sun was also turned into darkness when it did not dare to look upon its Lord hanging upon the cross; and the moon into blood. We may believe either that this happened according to the historical sense but was passed over in silence by the evangelists—for not everything Jesus did is recorded in writing, since, if each deed were written down separately, I do not think that even the world itself could contain the books that would have to be written (John XXI)—or else we may understand how the sun was turned into darkness not as meaning that it itself was changed into darkness, but that it brought darkness upon the world.

Similarly, the moon was not turned into blood; rather, it condemned the Jews, covered with the horror of blasphemy and denial of Christ, by the eternal blood of its testimony, since they had said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25).

All these things, he says, will occur before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. The great and terrible day of the Lord must be understood either as the day of the resurrection or, certainly, as the day of judgment after many ages, which is truly great and terrible.

[Note: Here the Erasmian edition adds the following words: “It is better understood of the day of Christ’s passion or resurrection. But the invocation in which salvation consists is established not by speech alone, but by heart and deed. Therefore, because of the grace of this threefold invocation, it must be believed to belong not to the foolish but to the perfect: for what the heart believes and loves, the mouth confesses and the hand accomplishes in action. Conversely, this is said to those who invoke the Lord by speech alone and do not fulfill the word of faith by deed: ‘Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” shall enter the kingdom of heaven; but he who does the will of my Father shall enter the kingdom of heaven.’” I have been unable to find this addition in any manuscript codex, nor do I know from where Erasmus derived it. MART.] 

But since it follows, “And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved,” and the apostle Paul refers this to the time of the Lord’s passion, it is better understood of the day of the resurrection. For, writing to the Romans, he says: “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek. For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. How, then, shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. X, 12ff.).

Let us not think lightly of the statement, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” Although the same apostle writes, “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 3), we must nevertheless weigh this saying itself as referring not merely to speech but to the affection of the heart. “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

Hence Paul and Sosthenes also write to the Church of God which is at Corinth: “Sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. I), according to what we read in the Psalms: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name. They called upon the Lord, and he answered them; he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud” (Ps. XCVIII, 9).

If, then, it is written of the believers at Corinth, and of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, that they called upon the name of the Lord, let us believe that this grace belongs not to beginners but to the perfect.

The word “outpouring,” which in Hebrew is called ESPHOCH (אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ), and which all the translators rendered similarly, displays the generosity of the gift: the gifts of the Holy Spirit descended not, as formerly in the Old Testament, upon a few prophets, but upon all who believe in the Savior’s name—not upon this person or that, but upon all flesh.

For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, because we are all one in Christ (Rom. X). Hence Agabus prophesied at Caesarea (Acts XXI), and in Antioch there were many prophets; and the Apostle commands that if something is revealed to another while one is prophesying, the first should be silent (I Cor. XIV). We also read that the four daughters of Philip the evangelist prophesied (Acts XXI).

The old men likewise saw dreams, when Paul, already old, heard a Macedonian man saying to him: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts XVI, 9). And all the young men who were exceedingly strong in Christ and fought the Lord’s battles saw visions, with the Lord fulfilling his promises: “I multiply visions, and I was represented in the hands of the prophets” [variant: “I will multiply visions”] (Hos. X, 12).

[Note: Martianus retained the reading “and they fought in the Lord,” contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts. We have restored the reading from the Palatinus manuscripts; Victorius had earlier restored it from the Florentine codices: “and they fought the battles of the Lord,” and he showed that St. Jerome often used this manner of expression.]

(V. 32.) “For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call.”

The Septuagint: “For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be one who is saved, as the Lord has said, and one proclaiming those whom the Lord has called.”

In the place where we have put “salvation,” or “one who is saved,” the Hebrew has PHALETA (פְּלֵיטָה); Symmachus translated it, “the one who flees.” Again, where we said “among the remnant,” and the Septuagint translated “proclaiming,” the Hebrew reads SARIDIM [variant: SARADIM] (שְׂרִידִים), which the Jews consider to be the name of a place.

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts do not contain the words “in Mount Zion,” etc.]

After the great and terrible day of the Lord had come, and everyone who invoked his name after the Lord’s resurrection had been saved, everyone who was in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem was saved. For “the law went forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II), concerning which it is written: “It is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII, 33).

The beginning, therefore, of those who were saved was in Zion and Jerusalem—in the watchtower and in the vision of peace—and among those who remained, whom the Lord called.

We should understand as the remnant those who believed from the people of the Jews, concerning whom Isaiah speaks: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. I, 9). The Lord called these remnants, or evangelized those whom he called; for this is how the Septuagint interpreted it.

This passage is extremely difficult and admits of multiple interpretations, so that under the tropological sense we may refer everything that has been said to those times to which the apostles Peter and Paul referred it—that is, to the time when the Lord suffered and rose again. For it cannot be that we understand the preceding matters as referring to the time of the passion and what follows as referring to the day of judgment, especially since the next verse says: “For behold, in those days and at that time,” connecting what follows with what precedes and declaring that everything occurred at one time.

(Chapter III—Vv. 1ff.) “For behold, in those days and at that time, when I restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat. And I will contend with them there on behalf of my people and my inheritance Israel, whom they scattered among the nations; and they divided my land and cast lots over my people. They placed a boy in a brothel and sold a girl for wine, so that they might drink.”

The Septuagint: “For behold, I am in those days and at that time, when I restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem. I will gather all the nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will contend with them there on behalf of my people and my inheritance Israel, who were scattered among the nations. They divided my land and cast lots over my people. They placed a boy in a brothel, and they sold girls for wine, and they drank.”

Let us speak as we promised. [Note: Victorius wishes the passage to be restored, with a full stop placed here and the conjunction immediately following removed.] First, joining the later passages to the earlier according to the spiritual sense, we shall attempt, if possible, to refer the same things to the day of judgment.

After the believers have been saved on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and the remnants of the Jewish people have been called—those who believed with and through the apostles—at that time, after the Lord restores the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, he who came to preach sight to the blind and release to captives, and who freed those who confess the Lord and who dwell in the Church, in which there is a vision of peace, will gather all the nations that refused to believe. And he will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, which, more significantly, according to the Hebrew truth, is expressed in Greek by κατάξω, that is, “I will bring down,” and “I will drag down from lofty places to lower ones.”

At the same time, consider that when the Lord summons all unbelievers, or opposing powers, to judgment and contends with them on behalf of his people, he says: “I will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat.” But when he urges believers to battle, he says: “Stir up the strong; let all the warriors draw near and go up; let the nations arise and go up into the valley of Jehoshaphat.” They are urged not to descend but to ascend.

For everyone who is judged because of his sins [Note: Victorius’s edition lacks the words “because of his sins.”] is situated in the valley called Jehoshaphat, that is, “the judgment of the Lord.” Whoever believes in the Lord will not be judged.

There he will dispute with them—not by the power of his majesty, but by convicting them through the truth of reason—those who divided God’s people and dispersed his inheritance among the nations, so that they might compel God’s servants to serve them. They divided his land, separating it among themselves through many errors, so that some worshiped Jupiter, others Juno and Minerva, and others fever, mildew, Anubis, the crocodile, the ibis, owls, hawks, and storks.

Under these names God’s people were once divided. The hostile nations—that is, the rulers of this world and the governors of darkness—not only divided God’s people among themselves but also placed boys in a brothel, compelling them to alter their masculine nature. Of these the Apostle speaks: “Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions. Their women exchanged the natural use” [variant: “their natural nature”] “for that which is contrary to nature. Likewise the men, abandoning the natural use of the woman, burned with desire for one another, men committing shameful acts with men and receiving in themselves the recompense which was due for their error.”

Not content with having done this, they sold a girl for wine, so that they might drink and put gluttony before lust. The Jews assert that all these things were fulfilled according to the literal sense in the times of Vespasian and Titus, and especially under Hadrian.

But if we wish to refer what is written to the day of judgment, we say that everyone who is saved is saved in the Church, or in the heavenly Jerusalem. And after the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem has been restored, then all will be gathered and brought down into the valley of Jehoshaphat. There the Lord will contend with those who persecuted his people, divided the Lord’s inheritance among themselves, scattered them among the nations, and cast lots over his land.

We should understand this not only of heretics, who divided God’s people among themselves and make them into Gentiles, but also of every harsh and proud teacher who, under the name of doctrine and priesthood, lords it over the clergy and oppresses those who are subject to him.

When such men are negligent and cause one of the least to stumble, they also place boys in a brothel, or hand them over to prostitutes. And for the sake of their own pleasure—of those whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame (Phil. III)—they sell girls so that they may drink wine.

He hands over young men to prostitutes and sells girls to lust who, for the sake of sordid gain, does not rebuke those who sin.

(Verses 4–6.) “But what have you to do with me, Tyre and Sidon, and all the territory of the Philistines? Will you render me vengeance [variant: are you rendering vengeance to me]? And if you take vengeance against me [variant: will take vengeance], I will swiftly and speedily return your retaliation upon your own heads. For you have taken my silver and my gold [Vulgate omits *my*], and you have brought my desirable and most beautiful possessions into your shrines; and you have sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, in order to remove them far from their borders.”

The Septuagint reads: “What have I to do with you, Tyre and Sidon, and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you rendering me repayment, or are you retaining anger in your heart against me?” For this is what the Greek word μνησικακεῖτε signifies. “Swiftly and speedily I will return your repayment upon your heads, in return for your having taken my silver and my gold, and brought my chosen and finest possessions into your temples, and sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, in order to drive them out of their borders.”

The Jews understand this to refer against Tyre and Sidon and the territories of the Philistines—or, as the Septuagint has it, Galilee of the foreigners—because at the time of the Jewish captivity, when they were defeated by the Romans, these peoples persecuted God’s people; indeed, they persecuted God himself, who presided over his people, according to what is written: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40). Therefore, conversely, whoever persecutes God’s people persecutes God himself, whose people they are. “I will return to you,” he says, “what you have done to my people,” because you have taken my silver and gold—that is, the vessels of the Temple and everything in it that was most precious and splendid: the golden lampstand, the golden table of the Presence, the two golden cherubim, the mercy seat, and the golden bowls and censers—and you have consecrated them to your idols (2 Kings 25).

History, however, relates that the Chaldeans did these things more particularly: they placed the vessels of the Lord’s Temple in the temple of Bel; later, Belshazzar drank from the bowls, and immediately his kingdom was transferred to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5). But since these things are said to be future after the great and dreadful day of the Lord—which the apostles interpret as the resurrection of the Lord, while the Hebrews defer them to the future time of judgment—they are better understood as referring to the Romans: Vespasian and Titus, after building the Temple of Peace at Rome, consecrated the vessels of the Temple and all its offerings in that shrine, as Greek and Roman history relates.

At that time the sons of Judah and Jerusalem—not Israel, nor the ten tribes, which to this day dwell in the cities and mountains of the Medes—were sold to the sons of the Greeks, so that they might be expelled from their borders, and the whole world was filled with Jewish captivity. They relate this in order to establish that the vengeance for Christ’s blood and the overthrow of Jerusalem, which occurred by God’s judgment, happened in their own right against Tyre and Sidon [Note: Victor does not recognize the vowels independently.].

We, however, following the interpretation begun above, should understand Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistines as those who constrict, afflict, and persecute God’s people—for this is what *Tyre* signifies in our language—and hunt him to death, which the name *Sidon* indicates; and who, drinking blood, fall or wallow in filth, which *Philistines* and *Galilee* signify. Swiftly and speedily the Lord will restore to them what they deserve, because they persecuted him. And they have enslaved his silver and gold—that is, the sayings of the Scriptures and their νοήματα, namely, their meanings—and everything beautiful that existed in the Church, to their own errors.

Whenever a heretic deceives someone and makes him worship his own images, he sells the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the Greeks, or Gentiles, and makes them pagans instead of Christians, so that he may expel them from the borders in which they had been begotten in Christ; and they may live no longer in Judea and the confession of the truth, but in the error of the nations. All these things can also be referred to the day of judgment, with no difference in the vengeance, although they may appear to differ in time from the events mentioned above.

In place of “Galilee,” the Hebrew has GALILOTH (), which Aquila translated as Θῖνας [Note: The manuscript codices read Θεῖνας, not Θινὰς. Jerome cites this name in his commentary on Ezekiel 47, saying: “Then, in place of GALILEE, which in Hebrew is called GALILA, Aquila translated Θηνὰς, which signifies ‘sand-hills.’” Thus Aquila’s Greek word is written in three ways in Jerome’s printed and manuscript books: Θινὰς, Θεῖνας, and θηνὰς. Whether we read Θῖνας or θῆνας, I would prefer, with Scapula’s Greek lexicon, to write the circumflex accent on the penultimate syllable rather than the grave accent on the final syllable. MART.—Martianus: θεῖνας. Consult the Commentary on Ezekiel 47.]. Symmachus translated it as “boundaries.” Θῖνας, however, that is, “sand-hills,” should be referred to the shores of Palestine, not to the Galilee of the Philistines, which does not exist at all.

(Verses 7–8.) “Behold, I will raise them up from the place where you sold them, and I will turn your repayment upon your own heads; and I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant nation, because the Lord has spoken.”

The Septuagint reads: “Behold, I will raise them up from the place where you sold them, and I will return your repayment upon your heads; and I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them into captivity to a nation that is far away, because the Lord has spoken.”

The Hebrew word SABAIM (), which Aquila and Symmachus translated exactly as it is written, the Septuagint translated as “captivity,” though it more properly signifies “captives.” The Sabaeans are said to be a nation beyond India; from them came the queen of Sheba, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 10). Isaiah also speaks of them: “And the Sabaeans, men of stature, shall pass over to you” (Isaiah 43:14). Hence incense is also said to come from them, as Virgil says (*Aeneid* 1):

> … and a hundred altars glow  
> With Sabaean incense …

Although some suspect that the Sabaeans were Arabs.

The Jews therefore promise themselves—or rather, dream—that at the end of time they will be gathered and brought back by the Lord to Jerusalem. Not content with this happiness, they even assert that God himself will deliver into their hands the sons and daughters of the Romans, so that the Jews may sell them—not to the Persians, Ethiopians, and other neighboring nations, but to the Sabaeans, the most distant of peoples—because the Lord has spoken and will avenge the injury done to his people.

This is what they and our Judaizers assert: they promise themselves a thousand-year kingdom within the borders of Judea, a golden Jerusalem, the blood of sacrifices, sons and grandsons, unimaginable delights, and gates distinguished by a variety of gems.

We, however, should say that the Lord both raised up after his coming, raises up daily, and will raise up those whom varied error had led out of their borders. “I will raise up,” he says, fittingly, as though they were lying prostrate and falling, so that those who had been lying in heresy might stand in the Church [Note: One Palatine manuscript not incongruously adds: “because he will raise up as if …”]. He will return to the heretics what they had done: he will deliver their sons and daughters—those whom they had instructed both in mystical and in carnal matters—into the hands of the sons of Judah, into the hands of those who have become leaders of the Churches, who have been equipped with the armor of the Apostle and possess the shield and spear of the Old and New Testament. When they have captured them, they will sell their sons and daughters to the Sabaeans and make them captives, so that they may be far from their former borders; and, converted to better things, they will begin to be subject to the teachings of the Church.

(Verses 9 and following.) “Proclaim this [variant: these things] among the nations: consecrate war; rouse the strong. Let all the men of war draw near and come up. Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruning hooks into spears. Let the weak man say, ‘I am strong.’ Break forth and come, all nations from every side, and gather yourselves there. The Lord will cause your strong men [variant: his strong men] to fall.”

The Septuagint reads: “Proclaim this [variant: these things] among the nations: consecrate war; rouse the fighters; bring forth and lead up all the men of war. Beat your plowshares into swords and your sickles into spears. Let the strong man say, ‘I prevail.’ Gather yourselves and enter, all nations round about; gather yourselves there. Let the fighter be gentle.”

This passage is understood in two ways. Some think that these things are proclaimed to holy nations so that they may prepare for war and fight on behalf of God’s people; that they may turn all instruments of agriculture into swords and spears; that the weak man may say he is strong; and that all may come from every side and gather for the Lord’s battle. This is especially so because, according to the Septuagint, what follows is: “Let the fighter be gentle and mild,” in accordance with what is written in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 5:18): “And across the Jordan, of the Reubenites and Gadites and half the tribe of Manasseh, there were one hundred and twenty thousand with every kind of weapon of war; all these were men of war, ready for battle, with peaceful minds” [Note: Martianus incorrectly wants this to read *hoc esse volunt*. One Palatine manuscript has: *nos esse volunt imitatores David*, “they want us to be imitators of David,” without *veri*, “of the true [David].”].

They wish these men to be imitators of the true David, of whom we read: “Remember, Lord, David, and all his gentleness” (Psalm 131:1). He himself also says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am humble and gentle” (Matthew 11:29), or “meek.” They also wish the men to be understood as those who, destroying the beginnings of childhood, have advanced to the strength of mature age, and who have directed all the zeal with which they formerly cultivated the fields of their souls toward the requirements of battle.

To us, however, who follow the opinion of the Hebrews, this interpretation seems contrary to the text. The hostile nations are therefore prepared for battle against Israel; they change their plowshares and mattocks, or sickles, into swords and spears (Isaiah 2); the weak man declares himself strong; they break forth and come from every side and gather against the Lord’s army, so that the Lord may cause their strong men to fall and they may understand that they have been conquered because God opposed them. This is what wretched Israel promises itself according to the literal sense.

We, following the interpretation begun above, can understand by the nations the demons, those who fight daily against the Church, and, at the end, those who under Antichrist will fight against the Lord’s saints. They gather for this reason: that they may perish.

(Verses 12 and following.) “Let the nations arise and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, because there I will sit to judge all the nations round about. Send forth the sickles, because the harvest has ripened. Come and descend, because the winepress is full; the winepresses overflow, because their wickedness has multiplied.”

The Septuagint reads: “Let all the nations arise and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, because there I will sit to judge all the nations round about. Send forth the sickles, because the vintage is present. Enter and tread, because the winepress is full, and the winepresses overflow, because their evils are filled up.”

These words too are interpreted in two ways according to the preceding sense. Some understand the nations’ ascent into the valley of Jehoshaphat—which is interpreted as “the Lord’s judgment”—and God’s sitting there to judge all the nations that come from every side, in a favorable sense: namely, that the saints will gather against God’s adversaries, send forth their sickles to reap the ripe harvest of their enemies, and come and descend and tread the winepresses, because the vintage is present, and the must will overflow so greatly that the winepresses cannot contain it.

And so that we might know what the vintage and the full winepress are, he added [variant: “added that”]: “Their wickedness has multiplied”—clearly signifying those who have gathered against the Lord.

Others, however, assert that the nations arise and gather in the valley of Jehoshaphat, and that the Lord sits there to judge all the nations, for this reason: that they may arm themselves and take up all the weapons of combatants, and in the valley of Jehoshaphat be cut down by the Lord’s sickles. The time of judgment has come against them, they say, and their evils have grown so great that they have overcome God’s patience. The Amorites too were expelled only when their sins had been completed.

The Jews refer this passage to the nations Gog and Magog, the most savage peoples, of whom we spoke above. They believe that at the end of time, when Jerusalem has been restored, these nations will come against God’s people under the rule of a thousand years and will fall [variant: rage] in the valley of Jehoshaphat, which lies on the eastern side of the Temple. The time of their slaughter will have arrived, they say, and the vintage of shedding their blood will be at hand.

(Verses 14–15.) “Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of slaughter, because the day of the Lord is near in the valley of slaughter. The sun and moon have been darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their brightness.”

The Septuagint reads: “Sounds have been heard in the valley of judgment, because the day of the Lord is near in the valley of judgment. The sun and moon will be darkened, and the stars will cause their brightness to fall.”

Where we have “multitudes, multitudes,” the Septuagint translated “sounds have been heard.” In Hebrew it is written AMONIM, AMONIM (), which certainly signifies a multitude and crowds of those who are to be judged, as well as a din and tumult.

Again, where we said “in the valley of slaughter,” following the translation of Aquila, Symmachus, and the fifth edition, the Septuagint and Theodotion translated τῆς δίκης καὶ τῆς κρίσεως, that is, “of the case and of judgment.” In Hebrew it is written HARUS (), which the Hebrews think signifies not only “slaughter” but also “gold,” so that in the valley of judgment—which they suspect to be Gehenna—the impurities of sins may be smelted away and pure gold remain.

For this reason the nations of whom we spoke above gather in the valley of judgment, or slaughter: so that they may be killed and fall and be judged by the Lord. Not even the sun, moon, and other stars will be able to look upon the sorrow of that day and the torments of those who perish; instead, they will withdraw their radiance and will not dare to behold the severity of the one who judges and repays each person’s deeds upon his own head. This is not because they are more merciful than God’s judgments, but because every creature fears, in the torments of others, the judgment awaiting itself.

(Verses 16–17.) “And the Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice; the heavens and the earth will be shaken. And the Lord is the hope of his people and the strength of the sons of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion [Vulgate adds: ‘in’] my holy mountain; and Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall no longer pass through it.”

The Septuagint reads: “But the Lord will cry out from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice; heaven and earth will be shaken. And the Lord will spare his people and strengthen the sons of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion, in my holy mountain; and Jerusalem shall be holy, and the foreigner shall no longer pass through it.”

When the brightness of the sun, moon, and all the stars has been changed into darkness, the Lord will roar or cry out from Zion like a lion, and his voice will be so lofty and terrifying that the hinges of the heavens and the foundations of the earth will be shaken. Although he will be so severe toward those who are to be punished, he will be merciful toward his own people and will give strength to those who are called the sons of Israel—that is, to the mind that sees God—or εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ, which we may call “the most upright of God”: those who have not walked along crooked paths, but have advanced in the way of Christ and done all things uprightly.

Then both those who are punished and those who are received into glory will know that the Lord dwells in his watchtower, Zion, and in his holy mountain, Christ—or in the one who has prepared himself as worthy to be God’s dwelling place. Then Jerusalem will be holy, the vision of peace, from which Solomon also received his name, and strangers will no longer pass through it.

Understand by “strangers” either demons, who are alien to God, or all the worst thoughts and sins, concerning which the prophet says: “Spare your servant from strangers” (Psalm 18:24). They would never again find a path in us if we possessed the peace of God and our heart were not open to adversaries.

The Jews and our Judaizers, as we have said, refer these things to their fable of a thousand years. They think that Christ will dwell in Zion and in a golden and jeweled Jerusalem, and that the peoples of the saints will be gathered there, so that those who were oppressed in this age by all the nations may in that same age rule over all nations.

(Verses 18.) And it shall be in that day: the mountains will drip sweetness, and the hills will flow with milk, and waters will run through all the streams of Judah.

The Septuagint reads: “And it shall be in that day: the mountains will drip sweetness, and the hills will flow with milk, and all the outlets of Judah will flow with waters.”

When the Lord dwells in Zion and in his holy mountain, and no one attempts to pass through holy Jerusalem, whoever is a mountain in it and has attained the heights of the virtues will sweat sweetness and honey, and spiritual graces will drip from him, concerning which the prophet says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 119:103).

But whoever is lower than the mountains and has not yet climbed to the summit of perfection will be called a hill, and streams of milk will flow from him. By these the infancy that is still immature in Christ is nourished, together with rivers of water, which the Lord testified would flow from his belly (John 7). For all the streams, or outlets, of Judah will be filled with waters, and nothing in them will be dry, since all will overflow with spiritual grace.

And a spring will go out from the house of the Lord and water the torrent [variant: spring] of thorns.

In place of “torrent of thorns,” the Septuagint translated “torrent of cords,” that is, σχοίνων [Note: Our manuscripts have χοινίων, as does the Greek Complutensian edition. One Palatine manuscript has it corruptly. That the word signifies “cord,” and, among the Egyptians, a measure of a definite journey, we have learned from the Psalmist, who says …].

This word either signifies “cords” or, according to the Egyptians, a measure of a definite journey, as the Psalmist says: “You have investigated my path and my cord” (Psalm 139:2). On the river Nile, or on its channels, they customarily draw boats by ropes, with fixed intervals which they call “cords,” so that when those who are worn out by the labor have become exhausted, fresh necks may take over the pulling.

Nor is it surprising that each nation calls fixed distances along roads by its own names, since the Latins call them a thousand paces, the Gauls leagues, the Persians parasangs, and the whole of Germany rastas [Note: Glossary of German by Georg Wachter, Leipzig 1717: “Rost, rest; Rast, mile. Rasta is used in the Gothic Gospel for a mile; in the Runic Lexicon Rost is used for a measure of a road. See our Jerome, Preface to Book II of the Commentary on Galatians.”], with a different measure corresponding to each name.

This explanation is given because the Hebrew word SATTIM () was translated by the Septuagint as “cords.” Otherwise, no one doubts that everything we read in the tabernacle of God was made from wood of the *settim* tree, which the Septuagint translated as “incorruptible wood.”

This is a species of tree in the wilderness, resembling white thorn in color and leaves, though not in size. Otherwise, the trees are so large that boards of great width can be cut from them, and the wood is extremely strong, yet extraordinarily light and beautiful. Thus even the vessels of winepresses—which they call ἄρσενας and θηλύας—are made from it by the richest and most skilled craftsmen. Such wood is not found in cultivated regions or in Roman territory, except in the solitude of Arabia.

In place of “torrent of cords,” or “of thorns,” Symmachus translated “valley of thorns.” There is a place near Liviada, across the Dead Sea, six miles distant from it, where Israel once fornicated with the Midianites. The prophet Micah mentions this place in the person of God, saying: “My people, remember, I ask, what Balak the king of Moab planned, and what Balaam son of Beor answered, from Shittim to Gilgal” (Micah 6:5). In that passage too the Septuagint translated the phrase as ἀπὸ τῶν σχοίνων, that is, “from the cords” or “from Shittim” to Gilgal.

Therefore the spring will go out from the house of the Lord, which is interpreted as the Church. Ezekiel and Zechariah also place this spring at the end of their books (Ezekiel 47; Zechariah 13), so that it may transform our thorns and our vices and sins, which have produced no fruit of righteousness, into the Lord’s cultivated fields; water our aridity with the most abundant waters; and cause us to produce, instead of thorns and brambles, a profusion of flowers of virtue.

And in that place where Israel once fornicated and was initiated into the worship of Beelphegor, lilies of chastity, roses of modesty, and the abundance of virginity will flourish.

(Verses 19.) Egypt will be a desolation [Vulgate: “will become desolate”], and Edom a wilderness of destruction, because they acted wickedly [Vulgate: “will have acted wickedly”] against the sons of Judah and shed [Vulgate: “will have shed”] innocent blood in their land.

The Septuagint reads: “Egypt will be in destruction, and Edom will be a plain of desolation, because of the iniquities of the sons of Judah, because they shed righteous blood in their land.”

Here too the Jews sleep in the deepest slumber. They fabricate, with utterly vain hope, a vengeance at the end of time—when they will receive not Christ but Antichrist—against the Egyptians, who are their neighbors, and against the Romans, whom they interpret as Edomites. Just as Pharaoh and his entire army, which held God’s people captive for four hundred and thirty years, were submerged in the Red Sea, so too, they say, the Romans, who will possess the Jews for the same number of years, will be destroyed by the Lord’s vengeance.

Let them promise themselves this in their empty hope. For they cannot explain why, when there are so many nations in the world, only two peoples, the Egyptians and Edomites, are singled out for punishment; or why the Romans should be understood as Edomites, since, by the same license of invention, we could conversely assert that under the name Edomites the Persians, Elamites, Franks, Alemanni, and other peoples are signified.

We, however, should say that at the time of the Lord’s resurrection, or on the day of judgment—for we accept both interpretations—both Egypt and Edom will be destroyed insofar as they are Egypt and Edom. Egypt is called MESRAIM (), which is interpreted as ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, “persecuting and afflicting the saints of God.” Edom means “earthly” or “bloody.”

Therefore whoever has persecuted God’s people, devoted himself to earthly works, and daily shed innocent blood through the multitude of his sins—that is, the blood of those whom he deceives [variant: “whom he will have deceived”]—will be destined for destruction. We know that the souls of the martyrs cry out beneath the altar: “How long, O holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell upon the earth?” (Revelation 6:10).

(Verses 20 and following.) “And Judah shall be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation; and I will cleanse their blood, which I had not cleansed, and the Lord will dwell in Zion.”

The Septuagint reads: “But Judah shall be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation; and I will seek their blood and will not permit it to remain unavenged. And the Lord will dwell in Zion.”

This is not the Judah that will be inhabited forever, for we see that it lies desolate; nor is it the Jerusalem whose ruins we behold. Rather, it is that Judah whose daughters rejoiced and were glad in all the judgments of the Lord. Concerning it we read at the end of the fifty-first Psalm: “Deal kindly, Lord, in your good pleasure with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.”

In this province of confession and glory, and in this city in which the Lord’s peace is seen, there will be an eternal habitation—not for one, three, or several generations, but “from generation to generation,” that is, in the two generations of those who believed from the Jews and from the Gentiles.

And the Lord will cleanse the blood of all sins, which he had not previously cleansed, so that in the Gospel he may cleanse those whom he had left unclean when they sinned under the Law. For this reason he confined all things under sin, so that he might have mercy on all (Romans 11). Or else he will avenge the blood of his servants, which they shed in martyrdom for the confession of his name.

And the Lord will dwell in Zion, concerning which it is written: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Psalm 87:1–2).

[Col. 0989]

THE THREE BOOKS OF THE COMMENTARIES OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS OF STRIDON, PRESBYTER, ON THE PROPHET AMOS. (C) [Note: Besides the Palatine codices already mentioned, henceforth we shall use one Nonantolan manuscript, now in the library of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme at Rome, numbered 90. Its age may be inferred from this inscription on the first page: “Acquired by Lord Abbot Anfrit.” For the ancient author of the Catalogue of the Abbots of Nonantola, published long ago by Hughellus, writes of him: “Anfrit sat for seventeen years. He was ordained in the year of the Lord 821. He was a religious and God-devoted man and lived most holily. He made a casket for the Gospels wholly of gold and adorned with precious stones; he made a large silver chalice and a paten, which he splendidly overlaid with gold and adorned with stones. He died on the third Ides of March” (that is, in 838). Eginhard mentions his embassy ten years earlier: “Halidgarius, bishop of Cambrai, and Ansfridus, abbot of the monastery of Nonantola, were sent to Constantinople and honorably received by the emperor Michael.” Nor should this be his last praise: he applied himself to collecting the books not only of other holy Fathers but especially of Jerome. With the help of those manuscripts—certainly very ancient and corrected—which the library of the Cistercians at Rome preserves and which the most reverend abbot of that monastery, Bessotius, most kindly made available to us, it is scarcely possible to say how much progress we have made in correcting many of Jerome’s writings.]

**PROLOGUE** [Note: This exposition is entitled “To Pammachius,” as is clear from the Preface to the third book on this prophet.]

[Col. 0989A] 219–220. The prophet Amos, who follows Joel and is the third of the Twelve Prophets, is not the same person whom we read of as the father of the prophet Isaiah. The latter is written with the first and last letters of his name, ALEPH and SADE, and is interpreted as “strong” or “powerful.” This one, however, is written with AIN and SAMECH, and is interpreted as “a people torn away.” The middle letters MEM and VAU are common to both.

Among us, however, who do not possess such a distinction among vowel letters, nor the distinction of the letter *s*, which among the Hebrews is threefold, these and other names appear to be identical, although among the Hebrews they are distinguished by the difference and individual properties of their letters.

This prophet whom we now have in hand was from the village of Tekoa, which lies six miles to the south of holy Bethlehem, which gave birth to the Savior of the world. Beyond it there is no village, [Note: I may be mistaken, but instead of “not even rustic huts,” one should read “unless there were certain rustic huts.” For what if there were none at all—not even rustic ones—and he calls them like furnaces and compares them with the African huts? Moreover, if everything was full of shepherds, and the multitude of livestock compensated for the sterility of the land, then there must also have been caves, folds, and huts in which the shepherds could at least spend the night. This is what I think; and, if some judgment may be entrusted to conjecture when the manuscripts refuse assistance, I would restore the printed corrupt reading in this way: the change of letters is slight, replacing *ne* (“not”) with *nisi* (“unless”), and *quidem* (“indeed”) with *quaedam* (“certain”). I shall now also cite the testimony of Cassianus, *Collation* 6.1—not merely because it corresponds closely to Jerome’s text, but so that I may correct one or another error:

“Near the village of Tekoa, in the regions of Palestine, which was privileged to produce the prophet Amos, there extends an immense wilderness as far as Arabia and the Dead Sea, where the streams of the Jordan disappear after entering it, and the ashes of the Sodomites, stretched out over a vast expanse.” First, instead of “the Dead Sea,” I think “the Red Sea” should be restored, since Jerome too states that the wilderness extends as far as the Red Sea; conversely, the Dead Sea was not very far away, indeed scarcely more than twelve miles from Tekoa. Next, the words “where the streams of the Jordan disappear after entering it, and the ashes of the Sodomites” seem to have been wrongly added.]

There were not even rustic huts resembling furnaces, which the Africans call *mapalia*. So vast is the wilderness, extending as far as the Red Sea and the borders of the Persians, Ethiopians, and Indians. And because no crops at all grow in the dry, sandy soil, everything is full of shepherds, so that the multitude of livestock may compensate for the sterility of the land.

Amos the prophet belonged to this class of shepherds. He was untrained in speech, but not in knowledge. For the same Spirit who spoke through all the prophets was speaking in him. Therefore we have translated from the Hebrew.

**BOOK ONE**

[Col. 0989A] (Chapter 1.—Verse 1.) 221. “The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel.”

The Septuagint, however, translating—I do not know with what intention—rendered it: “The words of Amos, which came to pass in Accarim, from Tekoa, which he saw concerning Jerusalem.”

It should be understood that this prophet did not prophesy concerning Jerusalem—for Jerusalem is entirely absent from the Hebrew—but concerning Israel, that is, …

[Col. 0990B] In the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam, [Col. 0991A] of the ten tribes called Israel, which were in Samaria, he prophesied. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion likewise translated this. Thus the first prophet, Hosea, speaks to the ten tribes called Ephraim, Samaria, the house of Joseph, and Israel. The second, Joel, delivers his prophecy to Jerusalem and the two tribes called Judah, Jerusalem, and Jacob, [Note: [Col. 0991D] These words, which make no mention whatever of Israel, are absent from our manuscripts. Two of those same manuscripts shortly afterward read “the tribe was reigning” instead of “the tribe was ruling.”] making no mention whatever of Israel. The third, Amos, preaches not at all to Jerusalem, which was ruled by the tribe of Judah, but to Israel in Samaria. This can be demonstrated from his entire book, and especially from what is written: “Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel” (Amos 7:10). Shortly afterward Amaziah said to Amos: “You who see, go away, flee into the land of Judah; eat bread there, and there you shall prophesy. But at Bethel you shall no longer continue to prophesy, for it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom.” Amos answered him: “I was not a prophet, nor a prophet’s son, but a shepherd stripping the berries of brambles: [222] and the Lord took me as I followed the flock, and the Lord said to me: Go, prophesy to my people Israel”—certainly not to Judah and Jerusalem, as it is wrongly found among the Greeks and Latins—but to Israel, that is, the ten tribes, which, because of the multitude of the people, had retained their former name.

In the passage where the Septuagint translated “in Accarim,” Theodotion set down the very Hebrew word *NOCEDIM* (), which Aquila translated as ἐν ποιμνιοτρόφοις, that is, “among shepherds”; Symmachus and the fifth edition have ἐν τοῖς ποιμέσιν, that is, “among the shepherds.” I think that here too they were deceived because of the similarity of the letters DALETH and RES, reading *NOCERIM* instead of *NOCEDIM*; hence they rendered it as *Accarim*, although at the beginning of the name the letter NUN leaves no room for excusing the error. I have never read that *Accarim* is Hebrew even to the present day. Those who translate “sterility,” that is, στείρωσις, represent rather the Philistine city Accaron than *Accarim*, which is nowhere found.

The words of Amos, therefore, who was from the town of Thecuah and belonged to the number of shepherds—for that region too is pastoral—are contained in this book. He saw them “over Israel,” not with the eyes of the flesh but with the contemplation of the mind, because the prophets were called “seers.” Otherwise, according to the literal sense, words are not seen but heard. Thus the people also “saw the voice of God,” and Moses, while silent, spoke to the Lord when he said to him: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exodus 14:15). In the New Testament also we read: “What we have seen and heard with our eyes, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life” (John 1:1). For the Word of God, which is invisible in itself, the apostles see and handle with their hands: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

He saw these words [Col. 0992A] in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. At that time Sardanapalus was reigning among the Assyrians and in the cities of Cilicia; of him a celebrated orator said: “More shameful in his vices than in his name.” Among the Latins, Procas Silvius was reigning, and Amulius succeeded him after expelling his brother Numitor from the kingdom. After killing him, Romulus gathered a band of shepherds and robbers and founded a city bearing his own name.

This Uzziah is the king of Judah, also called Azariah. When he attempted to seize for himself a priesthood that did not belong to him, he was struck with leprosy on the forehead (2 Chronicles 26). At that time the wrath of the Lord was shown not only by the punishment of the sacrilegious man but also by the earthquake, which the Hebrews record as having occurred then.

Jeroboam, however, is not the son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin (1 Kings 12), but the son of Joash, son of [Col. 0992B] Joathan [Another reading: Jehoahaz and Joachan], son of Jehu and great-grandson of that same Jehu, under whom Hosea, Joel, and Amos prophesied.

Thus Uzziah is interpreted as κράτος Κυρίου, that is, “the power” or “strength of the Lord.” Jeroboam means δικασμὸς λαοῦ, that is, “the judgment” or “case of the people,” although some, reading the Greek letter chi, suppose it to mean “division of the people.” Joash means Κυρίου χρόνισμα, that is, “the Lord’s delay” or “temporality.”

The words of Amos, then, at the time when the people of Israel had been torn away from the Lord and served golden calves—or had been torn away from the kingdom of David’s lineage—sang out in a clear voice like the blast of a trumpet, which is what Thecuah signifies. They sang against Israel, which had once been the most upright people of God, that is, εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ. This occurred in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, in whom, because of the Temple and the Holy of Holies, the strength of the Lord remained and ruled by its authority the confessing people.

The name Jeroboam, who had become the cause of the people’s division, signifies that Israel remained for a long time in the error of idolatry before the captivity as a whole shook it. That captivity, within two years, displayed a double distress, that of the ten tribes and that of the two, so that, if they wished to repent, they would no longer experience an earthquake.

Dearest Pammachius, since from the interpretation of your name you show, as though by a prophecy of future things, that you will fight the devil and the opposing powers with every art of warfare, [Note: [Col. 0992D] One Palatine manuscript has *debellare*, “to conquer.” The Greek Παμμαχὸς means, as Jerome notes, “a man skilled in every art of warfare.”] I have set forth at length, as though it were an argument and ὑπόθεσις, the subject of the prophet Amos. I mention briefly that I promised to explain this prophet, as well as Hosea and Zechariah, to other holy men, but especially to your parent Paula, of holy and venerable memory, while she was alive. Nor shall I be far from fulfilling my pledge if I give back to the son what I promised to his mother. But now it is time, as I set forth the words of the prophet himself, to explain in detail what I think of each passage.

**(Verse 2.)** “And he said: The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice. And the beautiful places of the shepherds will mourn, and the summit of Carmel will dry up.”

The Septuagint: “And he said: The Lord has spoken from Zion, and from Jerusalem he has given his voice; and the pastures of the shepherds have mourned, and the summit of Carmel has dried up.”

It is natural that all craftsmen speak by examples drawn from their craft, and that each person brings forward the likeness of the occupation in which he has spent his life. For example, a sailor and helmsman compares his sadness to a storm; he calls his loss a shipwreck and names his enemies adverse winds. Conversely, he calls prosperity and joy a most peaceful breeze and favorable winds, and compares calm seas and waters to fields.

A soldier, on the other hand, makes everything he says sound of shield, sword, cuirass, helmet, spear, bow, arrow, death, wound, and victory. In the mouths of philosophers Socrates and Plato, Xenophon and Theophrastus, Zeno and Aristotle, the Stoics and the Peripatetics are always present. Orators praise Lysias and Hyperides, Pericles and Demosthenes, the Gracchi, the Catos, the Tullii, and the Hortensii to the heavens. Poets, if they are epic poets, continually celebrate Homer and Virgil; if lyric poets, Pindar and [225] Flaccus.

Why have I said this? Clearly, to show that the prophet Amos too, who was a shepherd from among shepherds—and a shepherd not in cultivated places planted with trees and vineyards, or at least among green woods and meadows, but in the broad desolation of the wilderness, where the savagery of lions and the slaughter of flocks are found—used the vocabulary of his craft in his speech, calling the Lord’s terrifying and fear-inspiring voice the roar and growl of lions.

He compares the overthrow of the Israelite cities with the desolation [Another reading: “anxiety”] of the shepherds’ lands and the dryness of the mountains: “The Lord,” he says, “will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice.” [Note: [Col. 0993D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “roaring.”]

“Will roar” is said in Hebrew as *JESAG* (). Beautifully, therefore, he says that he will roar from Zion and give his voice from Jerusalem, where the Temple and the worship of God were, to teach that God was not to be found in the cities of Israel—that is, Bethel and Dan, where the golden calves were—nor in the capitals Samaria and Jezreel, but in the true religion that at that time was practiced in Zion and Jerusalem.

When he roars from Zion and gives his voice from Jerusalem—for “from Zion the law will go forth” (Isaiah 2), and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem—all the beautiful places of the shepherds and kings of Israel mourned, and the summit of Carmel, which had once abounded in happy pastures, dried up.

*Carmel* is called by the same name in Greek and Latin, but in Hebrew it is *CHERMEL*. There are two mountains called by this name. One is where Nabal the Carmelite, Abigail’s husband, lived, toward the south. The other is near Ptolemais, formerly called Acho, overlooking the sea; there the prophet Elijah obtained rain on bended knees (1 Kings 18).

If he is speaking of Chermel, where Nabal lived, the reference is more appropriate to the flocks of shepherds, because it is near the wilderness (1 Kings 18). But if he means the mountain near the shore, the reference concerns the kings and the pride of the kings of Israel, whom, with captivity impending, he says will be devastated like deserted mountains.

Alternatively: When the Lord gives his voice from Zion and Jerusalem—from the watchtower of the Church, which is set upon a mountain and cannot be hidden, and in which there is a vision of peace—through the Old and New Testament and through the teachers of the Church, and when he sounds forth like a clear trumpet, then all the beautiful places of the shepherds—that is, the teaching of heretics, which seemed to be composed in beautiful language—and the knowledge of circumcision (for this is what *CHERMEL* means []), by which they promise themselves knowledge of true circumcision, will mourn and dry up; and the thousands of peoples who, because of their simplicity, are called flocks will wither in sudden dryness.

**(Verse 3.)** “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they threshed Gilead with iron threshing carts.”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord said: For three impieties of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn them away, because they sawed pregnant women with iron saws in Gilead.”

For the threshing boards, which in Hebrew are called *ARSOTH* (), and which Theodotion translated as “iron wheels,” we translated “iron carts”; the Septuagint translated “iron saws.” There is a kind of cart that rolls on iron, toothed wheels beneath it, so that, after the grain has been beaten out, it crushes the straw on the threshing floors and, because hay is scarce, reduces the chaff to fodder for the animals.

Again, where the Hebrew has *BENADAD* (), which is one name, the Septuagint translated “sons of Ader,” because of the deceptive similarity between the letters RES and [Col. 0994C] DALETH. In the passage where we said “from the house of pleasure,” which in Hebrew is *MEBBETH EDEN* (), and which all the others translated similarly, the Septuagint translated “from the men of Charran,” taking the middle letter of the name, DALETH, for RES, and, according to its custom, placing the Greek chi (Χ) before the first Hebrew letter, AIN.

They also translated Cyrene, which in Hebrew is *CIRA* (), as ἐπίκλητον, that is, “called” or “named,” because of the similarity of the word, since *CARAE* (), can mean “calling” as well as a proper name; thus they understood a common noun instead of a proper name. [Note: [Col. 0993D] The same manuscript reads *care*, and also *ciru*, “calling”; from this reading I see that something useful may be extracted. The Septuagint read in the Hebrew .]

We have spoken briefly about the reasons for the divergent translations. Let us now proceed to the meaning of what has been said.

First, the word of God is directed against Damascus, where Hazael was reigning. At the time when Amos prophesied, Hazael was grievously oppressing Israel, that is, the ten tribes. After he had defeated Ahab, king of Israel, at Ramoth-gilead, he slaughtered and crushed the entire region called Gilead—which had fallen by inheritance to half the tribe of Manasseh—as though it were grain being threshed on the threshing floors.

The prophet Elisha speaks of this more fully in the Book of Kings, where we read: “He stood with him, and he was troubled even to the flushing of his face; and the man of God wept. Hazael said to him: Why does my lord weep? And he answered: Because I know what evil you will do to the children of Israel. You will burn their fortified cities with fire, kill their young men with the sword, dash their little ones to pieces, and divide their pregnant women. Hazael said: What is your servant, a dog, that I should do this great thing? And Elisha said: The Lord has shown me that you will be king of Syria” (2 Kings 8:11–13). But what follows in the prophet is this:

**(Verse 4.)** “And I will send fire into the house of Hazael, and it will devour the houses of Ben-hadad. And I will break the bars of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitants from the plain of the idol.”

The Septuagint: “And I will send fire into the house of Hazael, and it will devour the foundations of the son of Ader; and I will break the bars of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitants from the plain of ὢν.”

This makes clear that Hazael had already died in Syria while Uzziah and Jeroboam were reigning, and that his son Ben-hadad had succeeded him in the kingdom. Afterward all the kings of Aram—that is, of Syria and Damascus—possessed the name Ben-hadad. Thus the prophet aptly did not say, “I will send fire against Hazael,” but “into the house of Hazael,” that is, into his royal house, over which his son Ben-hadad was then ruling.

“And I will break,” he says, “the bars of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitants from the plain of the idol”—that is, the entire strength [Another reading: “multitude”] of the Syrians, which, like a kind of cart and bars, drove back the attacks of its enemies.

The plain of the idol, which in Hebrew is called *AVEN* (), was translated by the Septuagint and Theodotion as ὢν. Symmachus and the fifth edition rendered it “iniquity”; Aquila, ἀνωφελοῦς, that is, “useless,” in order to show the vain assistance of idols, when the people of Damascus would be captured as the Assyrian approached. For we read that Theglathphalasar, king of Assyria, after killing Rasin, king of Damascus, of whom Isaiah also speaks, transferred to Cyrene the whole population of Syria, called Aram; and for this reason it is said at this point (2 Kings 16).

**(Verse 5.)** [228] “The one holding the scepter from the house of pleasure [Note: [Col. 0995D] Three manuscripts unanimously add “and luxury.” Below, we have restored *leviores* in place of *ultimos*, and corrected other minor matters from the same manuscripts.], and the people of Syria will be transferred to Cyrene, says the Lord.”
