The Septuagint: “And I will cut off the tribe from the men of Charran, and the named people of Syria will be led captive, says the Lord.”

The sense is that one should supply: “I will crush and destroy,” and that the people of Syria will be transferred to the farthest borders of Egypt.

As for what is said at the beginning—“For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back,” and according to the Septuagint, “I will not turn him away,” that is, the people of Damascus, or Aram, that is, the Syrian people—this may have the following historical sense: If he had persecuted my people once or twice, I would grant pardon. But now, since he has become cruel a third and fourth time, crushing the multitude in captivity with iron carts, ought I not correct him with punishments? Ought I not turn away from him the face of my mercy?

According to the tropological interpretation, we can say this: The first sin is to have thought what is evil. The second is to have consented to perverse thoughts. The third is to have completed in deed what one has resolved in the mind. The fourth is, after sinning, not to repent but to take pleasure in one’s offense.

All heretics do this. They not only think and do evil, but by their teaching deceive the simple, and, in the manner of the Damascenes—whose name is interpreted as “drinkers of blood”—they drink the blood of those whom they have deceived. Concerning such sins the Lord says: Is it not right that I should correct them with punishments and turn my face away from them, so that those who do not see the truth of my doctrines may be overwhelmed by the darkness caused by the turning away of my face?

“For they crushed,” or “sawed,” pregnant women in Gilead with iron carts. These are the pregnant women of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Luke 21:23). The pregnant women are the souls of believers, who at the beginning of faith can say: “Because of fear of you, Lord, we conceived and gave birth” (Isaiah 26:17–18). If they have not been cut and mangled by iron carts and toothed wheels—of which the Psalmist says: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows” (Psalm 56:5)—they can also say what follows: “And we have given birth; we will make the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0995D] Victorius: “which we have made upon the earth.”]

At the same time, consider that they cannot cut men of mature age, but those who are still in the womb or who cannot yet take solid food and are still nourished with the milk of infancy. These pregnant women are from Gilead, which is interpreted as “transmission” or “migration of testimony.” For they migrated from the Church into heresy and transferred to foreign boundaries the testimonies of God that they had formerly received.

But the Lord will send fire into the house of Hazael, which they themselves call *AZAEL* (), that is, “vision of God”—fire that will consume the wood and straw in them and devour the foundations of the son of Ader. We must also speak according to the Septuagint, lest we seem to have proposed their reading without purpose: Ader is interpreted as εὐπρέπεια, which we can call “beauty,” because every speech of heretics, elegant and carefully composed and possessing the beauty of secular eloquence, more easily deceives its hearers.

The bars of Damascus, like very strong and firmly fixed bolts [Another reading: “most powerful”], should be understood as those trained in dialectical technique and the arguments of philosophers. For example, the “door” is the one who conceives and gives birth to a false doctrine, as Arius did in Alexandria. His bars and his very firm bolts are Euticius and Eunomius, who try to strengthen their position with syllogisms and enthymemes—or rather, with sophisms, false arguments, and sorites that others wrongly devised. [Note: [Col. 0995D] We have restored the received reading *Euticius*, which Martianus, without support from any manuscript, had altered to *Aetius*. Nor is it the mark of a learned man to suppose that, if one retains Euticius instead of Aetius, the statement would be inconsistent with ecclesiastical history. On the contrary, it is well known that Aetius departed from the Arians because they said that the Son was in every respect similar in nature to the Father, whereas he, maintaining that the very nature or essence of God consisted in being ἀγέννητος, or “unbegotten,” inferred that the Son, because he was begotten, was of a nature unlike the Father. From this arose the new heresy of the Anomoeans, whose two quasi-sects were those named after Eutychus and Eunomius. On this subject see Socrates, Book V, chapter 24, and Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 26.]

When the bars of Damascus have been crushed and broken, he will also destroy the inhabitants from the plain of Ὦν, which is interpreted as “labor” or “pain.” For all heretics have tried, through immense labor and the pain of seeking, to discover some order and coherence for their heresy.

“And I will cut off the tribe from the men of Charran,” which in our language means “holes.” They do not have windows through which the light of truth may enter them, but certain holes and hidden passages through which harmful and unclean creatures enter.

“And the people of Aram will be led captive”—Aram, the lofty and exalted people, which has been lifted up in pride and promises itself heavenly things—so that it may be captured for its own salvation and, according to the Hebrew, transferred to Cyrene, where the calling of God is.

**(Verses 6 ff.)** [Col. 0997B] “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn him back [Another reading: “them”], because he transferred a complete captivity to shut it up in Idumea; and I will send fire against the wall of Gaza, and it will devour its houses; and I will destroy the inhabitant from Azotus, and the one holding the scepter from Ascalon; and I will turn my hand against Accaron, and the remnant of the Philistines will perish [Note: [Col. 0997D] Victorius preferred: “the remnant of the Philistines, says the Lord God.” The final words are also supplied by the authority of the Brixian manuscripts.], says the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn them away, because they led captive the captivity of Solomon in order to shut it up in Idumea; and I will send fire against the walls of Gaza, and it will devour its foundations; and I will destroy the inhabitants of Azotus; and the tribe of Ascalon will be removed; and I will bring my hand against Accaron [Another reading: “after Accaron”], and the remnant of the foreigners will perish, says the Lord.”

In the third and fourth generation the Lord threatens in the Law to repay the sins of the fathers upon their children—not with equality of judgment, so that some sin and others are punished, but through the greatness of his mercy, since he always waits for repentance. What is done wrong in the first generation he does not immediately punish and correct until the third and fourth generation has come.

The apostle Paul speaks similarly to the Romans: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” [Another reading: “his work”] (Romans 2:4 ff.).

What he says, therefore, is this: I waited a long time for them to repent, and for that reason I did not wish to punish those who were sinning, so that at some point they might turn and recover health. But because they do the same things a third and fourth time, I am compelled to change my decision and correct the offenders with punishments.

Let us see, then, what the Philistines and their cities did to sin, since the Septuagint always translated the name as “foreigners.” Wherever in the Old Testament we read ἀλλοφύλους, that is, “foreigners,” we should understand not the common name of all external peoples, but specifically the Philistines, who are now called Palestinians.

What did Gaza do to provoke the Lord to anger and vengeance? It transferred the complete captivity of the Jewish people and shut it up in Idumea, so that it could sell to the Idumeans those whom it had taken captive from the Jews.

Instead of “complete captivity,” the Septuagint translated “the captivity of Solomon,” judging the Hebrew word *SALMA* (), which signifies “perfect” and “complete,” to be the name Solomon. Aquila translated it as ἀπηρτισμένην and ἀναπεπληρωμένην; Symmachus and Theodotion as τελείαν, which does not signify Solomon but “perfect” and “complete,” so that no captive remained who had not been handed over to the Idumeans. [Note: [Col. 0998D] Some manuscripts read *Salama*; others *Salomo*.]

Therefore he says that he will send fire against the walls and houses—or foundations—of Gaza, which will consume and swallow everything.

Since we read that the Philistines had five cities, which were struck with punishments because of the Ark’s mistreatment, after Gaza he proceeds to Azotus (1 Samuel 5), which is called *ESDOD* (), and then to Ascalon. In a terrifying voice he threatens to destroy the inhabitants of Azotus and the one holding the scepter of Ascalon—that is, its royal power or the tribe of Ascalon—so that no one will remain there, not even men of extreme old age who support their trembling limbs with a staff.

Again, he stretches out his hand to strike Accaron. After enumerating four cities, he includes the remaining cities of the Philistines in a single statement: “The remnant of the Philistines will perish.” We should understand these either as the city of Geth [Col. 0998C] or as all the villages subject to the cities mentioned above.

According to the tropological interpretation, this is how it seems we should explain it: Gaza, which in Hebrew is called *AZA* (), signifies “strength” or “imperium”; Solomon means “peaceful”; Idumean means “bloodthirsty” and “earthly”; Azotus, that is, Esdod, means “fire of the breast” or “fire of the uncle,” although some, wrongly reading *dor* for *dod*, think it means “fire of generation”; Ascalon is interpreted as “murderous fire,” or “weighed” and “measured”; Accaron means στείρωσις, that is, “sterility,” and ἐκρίζωσις [Another reading: ἐκρίσωσις], which means “uprooting.”

[232] Gaza, therefore, which promises itself the strength and dominion of its knowledge, is accused because it shut up the captives from Solomon’s family in Idumea. I think these are the teachers of the Jews and all who follow the letter that kills and refuse to receive the life-giving spirit. Whatever they interpret and understand, they wish to be earthly. They do not listen when the Lord explains the parables to the disciples and says to them: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11:15), especially since the Apostle understands the manifest history in the two Testaments (Galatians 4).

“One” is upon Mount Sinai, which is Hagar, and serves with her children; the other is the free Jerusalem above, which is our mother. [Note: [Col. 0998D] The Cistercian and Palatine manuscripts read: “One is upon Mount Sinai, which is Hagar, and serves with her children; the other is upon …”]

He therefore says that he will send fire against the walls of Gaza and all its arguments, by which it strives to surround and defend its lies. When he has sent fire against the walls, its houses or foundations will be devoured—whatever firm structure it may have or may have been able to construct by dialectical skill.

From Azotus too, which itself belongs to the foreigners, he will remove the inhabitant. Because it follows the letter, its breasts are filled not with milk but with fire; and because it falsely claims to have the fire of its uncle, its entire generation is to be assigned to the flames [Note: [Col. 0999D] Three manuscripts read: “or the whole of whose generation.”] (Hosea 9:14).

He will also remove the scepter, or tribe, from Ascalon, where there is murderous fire. For just as the fire of the Lord will save those whose hearts it penetrates, so this fire that fell from heaven like lightning and sets the devil’s arrows ablaze will kill all whom it touches.

He will also turn his hand against Accaron, where there is sterility and uprooting. For whoever has not received spiritual understanding will hear through Hosea: “Give them, Lord.” What will you give them? “Give them a barren womb and dry breasts.”

And so that he might include everything in one statement, he says that he will destroy all the remnant of the Philistines—either the city of Geth, in which there is the winepress of the devil, or all the remaining Philistines, whose name is interpreted as “those falling because of a cup.” For when they have become drunk, they will fall and wallow in their own vomit.

**(Verses 9–10.)** “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they shut up the complete captivity in Idumea and did not remember the covenant of the brothers; and I will send fire against the wall of Tyre, and it will devour its houses.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says [Col. 0999C] the Lord: For three impieties of Tyre and for four, I will not turn her away [Note: [Col. 0999D] This reading of the Cistercian manuscript, which we have restored, also agrees with the Greek text, οὐκ ὑποστραφήσομαι αὐτὴν, ἀνθ’ ὧν etc. Previously it read, “I will not turn them away, because …”], because they shut up the captivity of Solomon in Idumea and did not remember the covenant of the brothers. And I will send fire against the walls of Tyre, and it will devour its foundations.”

He charges Tyre with the same three and four impieties or crimes that he had imputed to Damascus, Gaza, Azotus, Ascalon, Accaron, and the remaining cities of the Philistines. He reproaches it for having shut up a captivity that was complete and perfect in Idumea, as we have discussed above, and for not remembering the covenant of its brothers.

We ask how the Tyrians could be brothers of the Jews. Here he calls friends and those joined by kinship “brothers,” because Hiram, the ruler of Tyre, had maintained friendship with David and Solomon. Their relationship was so close that Hiram transported cedar wood by rafts as far as Joppa for the construction of the Temple and palace, while they gave the Tyrians grain and oil and presented him with twenty cities in Bashan. Since these were full of grass, he refused to accept them (1 Kings 5; 2 Chronicles 2).

He therefore says that he will send fire against its walls and devour its houses or foundations—something that the prophet Ezekiel records Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, as having done in his vision concerning Tyre, where he says: “He will surround you with fortifications and bring up a mound all around” (Ezekiel 26:8). And again: “Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, made his army perform great service against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder stripped bare, yet neither he nor his army received wages from Tyre for the service with which he served against it” (ibid. 29:18), because his army carried up the mound for capturing Tyre, which had formerly been an island.

History also relates that Alexander of Macedon did the same, making a peninsula out of an island; the Greeks call this a χερρόνησος [Another reading: χερσόνησος].

Tyre is interpreted as “tribulation” or “the one constricting.” Every perverse teaching tries to seize the truth and shut it up within earthly meanings, and does not remember the covenant of its brothers: that we must rise from the letter to the spirit and from earthly things to heavenly things. We have also been commanded to write the sacred Scripture three times upon our heart.

But God will send fire against all the fortifications of Tyre, which will devour not only its walls but also its foundations. We have spoken above about the captivity of Solomon, for which the Hebrew has “complete and perfect.”

### (Verses 11ff.)

Thus says the Lord:

“Because of three crimes of Edom, and because of four, I will not revoke it: because he pursued his brother with the sword, violated his compassion, maintained his fury, and preserved his indignation to the end. I will send fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the houses of Bozrah.”

**The Septuagint likewise:** “Thus says the Lord: Because of three impieties of Idumea, and because of four, I will not turn away from them: because he pursued his brother with the sword, violated the womb upon the earth, seized his horror as a testimony, and guarded his impulse forever. I will send fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the foundations of its walls.”

Edom is the same as Esau, so called because of his cooking of red lentils, for whose eating he lost his birthright. He is also called by another name, Seir, meaning “hairy” and “shaggy.” Hence the mountains of the Idumeans are called the mountains of Seir, and Idumea is called by the Greek term derived from Edom.

He pursued his brother with the sword—that is, the sons of Jacob, concerning whom a fuller account is written in the blessings of Isaac, by which he first blessed Jacob and afterward Esau—so that hatred between the brothers might be preserved among their descendants. The Idumean nation persecuted its brothers so relentlessly that, when they were coming out of Egypt, it would not even grant them passage into the holy land [Note: Martianay reads *egredienti* (“to one coming out”), and, a little later, rather worse, *vulvam ejus* (“his womb”); it has *ut apertius*, etc., without the intervening *vel* (“or”), which our manuscripts and Victorius supply.]. He not only pursued his brother with the sword, but also violated his compassion—or his womb—or, as Symmachus interpreted it more explicitly, his own entrails—so that he might forget his kinship, harden the organs of compassion, fail to recognize that he was a brother, and despise Rebecca’s womb, which had borne twin infants in a single birth.

What follows—“He maintained his fury beyond measure, and preserved his indignation to the end”—shows an ancient hatred, since they were never joined to one another in peace [Alternatively: *may they not be joined*]. Therefore he threatens punishment for their crimes and says: “I will send fire upon Teman,” which is a region of the Idumeans and extends toward the southern part. This is what Teman means. The province is called not only Teman but also Daron and Negeb, because it faces east, south, and southwest.

When he says, “It shall devour the houses of Bozrah,” he does not mean, as some think, another city; rather, he signifies Idumea, which is fortified—ὀχυρωμένην, and [perhaps, that is] *fortified*—in accordance with what we read in Isaiah: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? This one is beautiful in his robe, advancing in the abundance of his strength” (Isaiah 63:2).

Whatever we have said about Esau and Jacob, let us apply to the Jews and the Christian people. Those earthly and bloodthirsty men persecuted their brother Jacob, who supplanted them and took away their birthright. They persecuted him with the sword, even to the point of confiscating the possessions and property of believers, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2:4) [Note: For *Jacob*, the Palatine manuscripts read *his own*; Victorius retained both readings. We pass over other minor matters of this kind.]. They violated compassion and the laws of nature, and forgot their mother Rebecca, whose name means “patience,” and who bore them together in Christ. Maintaining their ancient fury and anger, they still blaspheme the Christian people in their synagogues under the name of Nazarenes; and, provided only that they kill us, they wish us to be burned by fire.

But the Lord will send fire upon Teman, into the dry and desolate places of Judaea, which are in no way watered by the rains of the prophets, and it will devour all their fortifications, or the foundations of its walls, so that, when every meaning of the letter has collapsed, the Church of Christ the Lord may be built upon the foundations.

For “compassion,” the Septuagint translated “womb”; for “fury,” “horror”; and for “indignation,” “violence,” being led by the ambiguity of the words. For **REHEM** () signifies both “womb” and “compassion”; **APHPHO** () signifies both “his fury” and “his horror”; and **EBRATH** () is used for both “indignation” and “impulse.” Furthermore, **ARMANOTH** (), which we translated as “houses,” Aquila and Symmachus rendered as βάρεις, that is, “houses” [Note: Recall what we observed above on Hosea 8, column 9.]; Theodotion translated it as “inhabitants.” Only the Septuagint, both here and above, translated it as “foundations.”

### (Verses 14–15)

Thus says the Lord:

“Because of three crimes of the sons of Ammon, and because of four, I will not revoke it: because he ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge his territory. I will kindle fire upon the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour its houses amid howling on the day of battle and amid a whirlwind on the day of upheaval. And Milcom shall go into captivity, he and his princes together, says the Lord.”

**The Septuagint:** “Thus says the Lord: Because of three impieties of the sons of Ammon, and because of four, I will not turn away from them: because he ripped open the pregnant women of the Gileadites in order to enlarge his boundaries. I will kindle fire upon the walls of Rabbah, and it shall devour the foundations with shouting on the day of battle; and it shall be shaken on the day of its consummation. And the kings shall go into captivity, [division] their priests ** and their princes together, says the Lord.”

The divine word reproves the sons of Ammon, who were born from the stock of Lot and dwell in Arabia, where Philadelphia now stands, because Naash the Ammonite, their ruler, under Saul king of Judaea, devastated Jabesh-gilead and ripped open its pregnant women in order to enlarge his boundaries and bring all Gilead under his authority (1 Kings 11).

Therefore he threatens that he will kindle fire upon the walls of Rabbah, which was the metropolis of the Ammonites, so that its houses may be devoured amid the shouting and howling of the victorious army, on the day of upheaval and whirlwind, when its captives will be led away after Nebuchadnezzar’s victory. The idol of the Ammonites, called Milcom—that is, “their king”—will be carried off to the Assyrians, and its princes, that is, its priests, will be led away together.

“Priests” is not found in the Hebrew, but “princes” is. Thus the Septuagint added “priests,” so that, if you wish to know who those princes were, you may hear: “priests.”

There is this difference between the cruelty of Damascus and that of the sons of Ammon: the former crushed the pregnant women of Gilead with iron carts, or with iron saws [Note: Through a shameful error caused by the occurrence of the same word *Galaad* in Martianay’s edition, this passage—especially necessary for marking the distinction concerning the Ammonites—was omitted.]; the latter ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory.

In the Damascenes, who drink blood, we understand heretics, who not only plundered the people of God from the Church but also crushed and ground them with iron teeth, concerning which it is written: “Why do they devour my people as though they were eating bread?” (Psalm 52:5) [Note: Victorius says that *diripuerunt* should be read, as several manuscripts from Brescia have it; this word more properly concerns the tearing and cutting about which the prophet writes.].

In the sons of Ammon, whose name means “people of sorrow” or “my people,” we understand schismatics. They do separate a deceived multitude from the Church of God, and tear apart and divide the inexperienced souls that have recently conceived Christ’s word. Yet they do not do this with the cruelty by which heretics slaughter those whom they have deceived. Rather, while remaining within the same rule of faith, they desire to enlarge their boundaries and transmit a name of glory to posterity.

Therefore the Lord threatens that he will set fire to the walls of Rabbah—that is, of the multitude—on the day of howling and battle, upheaval and whirlwind; and that their king, the author of the schism, will go into captivity, while the princes of the Church submit their necks to the yoke.

### (Chapter 2—Verses 1ff.)

Thus says the Lord:

“Because of three crimes of Moab, and because of four, I will not revoke it: because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes. I will send fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the houses of Kerioth. Moab shall die amid tumult, with the sound of the trumpet. I will destroy the judge from its midst, and I will kill all its princes with him, says the Lord.”

**The Septuagint:** “Thus says the Lord: Because of three impieties of Moab, and because of four, I will not turn away from them [Alternatively: from him], because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes. I will send fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the foundations of its cities. Moab shall die in weakness, with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet. I will destroy the judge from it, and I will kill all its princes [Note: The Cistercian manuscript adds *with him*, words also found in most Greek manuscripts.], says the Lord.”

Not only the sons of Ammon but also Moab was born from Lot, who was the son of Abraham’s brother. To show that God is Lord of all and that every soul belongs to his rule, since he is their creator, he also avenges the injury done to the king of the Idumeans—indeed, the crime perpetrated against him by the Moabites, who burned his bones to ashes and did not end their savagery and rage even with his death.

The Hebrews relate that the bones of the king of Edom, already buried—the king who had gone up with Joram king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah against Moab—were later torn from the grave and burned by the Moabites as vengeance for their suffering (2 Kings 3).

Therefore, they say, God declares that he will send fire upon Moab, whether upon the metropolis of the Moabites, from which the whole province received its name, or upon the entire province, so that it may devour the houses of Kerioth, which is the name of a city. Although the Septuagint translated it as “its cities,” that is, Moab, it will perish amid the tumult and howling of the victorious army. In Hebrew, the first of these is called **SAON** (), and the second **THERUA** () [Note: Two manuscripts read *Thruah* and *Suphar.]. The sound of the trumpet, or horn, is what **SOPHAR** () signifies.

When Moab has perished, the counsel of its princes and judges will be useless, with its cities and leaders alike overthrown.

Just as we ought not to transfer the “completed captivity,” or Solomon, and confine it in Idumea, making the lofty and heavenly lowly and earthly—something Gaza and Tyre are said to have done—so we ought not to burn the bones of the king of Edom and reduce them to ash and dust.

The Jews transfer the spiritual meaning to the flesh of the Idumeans. They weaken and crush the royal meaning, which resides in the letter and is most solid and firm, with certain genealogies and superfluous traditions, reducing it to dust. Not only do they do this, but so do all heretics who wish God to sit in human form upon a high and elevated throne and place his feet upon the earth, lest they hang down; who wish him to have a nose with which he may smell a fragrant odor, eyes with which he may see, hands with which he may work, feet with which he may walk, ears with which he may hear, a mouth with which he may speak, and teeth with which he may crush food.

Whoever reads that Judah went in to Tamar the prostitute and fathered two sons by her (Genesis 38), if he follows the shamefulness of the letter and does not ascend to the beauty of the spiritual meaning, burns the bones of the king of Edom.

Whoever thinks that Hosea took a prostitute as his wife (Hosea 1) and understands nothing more in the statement than what is contained in the simple words burns the bones of the king of Edom.

Therefore the Lord will send fire upon Moab, whose name means “from the father,” because although he was born from God, he abandoned him. It shall devour his cities or towns, which is what Kerioth signifies. Hence Kiriath-jearim is translated into our language as “village of the woods.”

Moab will die in no other way than amid shouting, noise, howling, and the blast of the horn, so that elevated understandings—which in the sacred books are compared with the blasts of the horn—may be overthrown.

Then the divine word also destroys judges and princes, and all who preside over earthly works, and commands the teachers of the Church: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice, you who preach to Jerusalem” (Isaiah 40:9).

### (Verses 4–5)

Thus says the Lord:

“Because of three crimes of Judah, and because of four, I will not revoke it: because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments. For their idols, after which their fathers had gone, deceived them. I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the houses of Jerusalem.”

**The Septuagint:** “Thus says the Lord: Because of three impieties of the sons of Judah, and because of four, I will not turn away from them: because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments; and they were deceived by their vanities, which their fathers followed [Note: Again the Cistercian manuscript supplies *which they made and which they followed*. These words are also found in most Greek manuscripts; they are absent from the Aldine edition.]. I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the foundations of Jerusalem.”

The Lord does not reproach the other cities and nations mentioned above—Damascus, Azotus, Ascalon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remaining towns of the Philistines, as well as Tyre, Idumea, the sons of Ammon, and Moab—for rejecting God’s law and despising his commandments. For they did not possess the written law, but the natural law.

Therefore he says that they violated their own entrails and the entrails of compassion, crushed the pregnant women of Gilead with iron carts, transferred Solomon’s captivity, or the completed captivity, and confined it in Idumea; that they did not remember the covenant of their fathers; and that they pursued their brother with the sword. They advanced not merely into cruelty but into such madness that they burned the bones of the king of Edom and would not allow death to be the ultimate of all evils.

Judah, however—at the time when these things were being said, the place in which the worship of God, the temple, and the ceremonies existed, and which had received the law, precepts, judgments, testimonies, and commandments—was rebuked and convicted by the Lord, and would receive deserved punishments because it had rejected his law and failed to keep his commandments. The distinction among these terms is discussed more fully in the eighteenth and one-hundred-eighteenth psalms.

Because Judah rejected and despised them, its idols deceived it in due order and by a process of succession. It could not previously have been deceived by idols unless it had rejected the law of the Lord and failed to carry out his commandments.

These are the idols after which their fathers went in Egypt: they fashioned images of the Egyptian bull, worshiped Beelphegor, and revered Astarte and the Baals.

Therefore the Lord also threatens to send fire upon Judah, which will devour its houses and the foundations of Jerusalem—not of that Jerusalem in which the vision of peace dwells, but of those Jerusalems that arose under the name of Jerusalem in various cities.

Whatever we have said about Judah refers to the Church, in which there is true confession, the peace of the Lord, and the vision of truth. Thus each person is reproved because he has despised God’s law and failed to obey his commandments. Whoever worships his own vices and sins begins to regard as god the one by whom he has been conquered, as the apostle Peter says: “By whatever anyone is overcome, by this he is also enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

The miser worships gold; the glutton, his belly; the lustful man, his sexual organ, and Beelphegor. A wanton woman, who lives in luxury but is dead, worships the pleasures of Venus.

Therefore the Lord will send fire upon Judah, and it will devour the most wicked houses and corrupt foundations that have forfeited Jerusalem’s glory. At the same time we learn that the Creator of all is concerned not only with Judah and Israel but with all nations, and that, according to the Apostle, those who have sinned without the law will perish without the law, while those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law of the Lord (Romans 2).

### (Verses 6ff.)

Thus says the Lord:

“Because of three crimes of Israel, and because of four, I will not revoke it: because he sold the righteous for silver [Vulgate: *for money*], and the poor for a pair of sandals; they who crush the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble; and a son and his father went in to the same girl in order to profane my holy name. They reclined beside every altar upon garments taken in pledge, and drank the wine of the condemned in the house of their God” [Note: Victorius, following only the example of the Vulgate and wishing to preserve the same tense, changed *they were turning aside* to *they turn aside*. We now affirm this reading on the evidence of the Hieronymian manuscripts as well. In one Cistercian manuscript, a little later, *they would violate* is found where the Vulgate reads *they would pollute*.].

**The Septuagint:** “Thus says the Lord: Because of three impieties of Israel, and because of four, I will not turn away from them [Alternatively: from him]: because he sold the righteous for silver and the poor for sandals, which trample upon the dust of the earth; and they struck the heads of the poor with the fist [Note: The Cistercian manuscript does not recognize the word *fist*; in Greek, however, the word is ἐκονδύλιζον, meaning ‘they struck with fists’]; and they turned aside the way of the humble; and son and father went in to the same girl in order to defile the name of their God. They tied their garments with ropes and made coverings beside the altar, and drank wine obtained through accusations in the house of their God.”

He places Israel last—that is, the ten tribes—because we have already stated that nearly everything that follows was spoken concerning it, so that the prophetic discourse might preserve the order of the book within a single continuous text.

Their first crime, or impiety, is enumerated in three or four offenses: they sold a human being for money, and a righteous person, whose greater distinction is that he was not overcome by poverty so as to do anything unjust. If they had sold a poor righteous person for a price because hunger compelled them, there might have been some excuse for the crime. But they sold a human soul for the most worthless thing, sandals, with which one tramples dust and dung.

According to the Septuagint, they strike the poor man on the head; according to the Hebrew, they crush the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth. They rise to such arrogance that they do not wish to walk with human beings.

And lest this crime seem small, son and father went in to one girl in order to violate the holy name of God. Whatever is done shamefully is therefore referred to the injury of God, who says: “Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations” (2 Peter 2:2).

This is also what the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “It is commonly reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the nations, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst” (1 Corinthians 5:1–2).

It frequently happens that a son violates his father’s wife, or a father-in-law violates his daughter-in-law. Both are prohibited in the Law: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father,” and “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law” (Leviticus 18:7) [Note: The manuscripts we use insert *that is*, by which the sense is made somewhat intelligible. But what follows—that both are prohibited in the Law, or, as these manuscripts have it, *both of whom are prohibited in the Law*—must clearly be understood as referring to different persons, since the passage in Leviticus actually prefers this interpretation. Here, however, the reference is to one and the same person, if the father violates his son’s wife and the father-in-law violates his daughter-in-law. I therefore readily agree with Victorius, who corrects the text to read: “the son his father’s wife, the father-in-law,” and so forth.].

Thus even the literal sense has the greatest usefulness, if it is preserved.

Because every disgrace, once it has exceeded the limits of modesty, adds crimes to crimes and always proceeds toward worse things, the ten tribes also reclined beside every altar upon garments taken in pledge [Alternatively: *pawned garments*]. The Hebrews interpret this as follows: they reclined upon the garments of those who were unwilling to go to the idols, garments which they had extorted by force while feasting in the idol shrine.

According to the Septuagint, their contempt for God was so great that they stretched out their own garments—the garments in which they slept or in which they committed fornication—beside the altar with ropes, and made παραπετάσματα, that is, coverings, so that no one could see those committing fornication in the Temple.

Serving drunkenness and lust, they also purchased the wine they drank not from their own labor but through acts of accusation. They did this in the shrine of their god, so that they might pollute with shame and sexual vice those whom they imagined to be gods.

Those who follow the simple historical account speak and interpret these matters in this way. But since in Hosea we taught that Israel, Samaria, Ephraim, and the sons of Joseph signify heretics—and Jeroboam, who belonged to that tribe, separated the people from the kingdom of David, Jerusalem, and the temple of God (1 Kings 12)—let us now also understand that, after Judah and Jerusalem, whose name means “Church,” the prophetic discourse is directed toward heretics.

They sell a holy and righteous man, but one who is poor, for money. The poor and righteous man is the ecclesiastical person who does not possess knowledge of the Scriptures but is content with simplicity and carries out the commandments that have been given. Concerning him it is written: “The poor man does not endure reproach” (Proverbs 13:8). And in Galatians: “Only that we should remember the poor” (Galatians 2:10).

All heretics do these things for riches and for sandals, with which they trample the dust of the earth. Since they cannot stand barefoot upon the holy ground on which Moses and Jesus son of Nun stood (Exodus 3; Joshua 5)—and since the apostles were commanded to walk barefoot (Luke 10), lest they possess anything of death or of the skins that signify the flesh—they therefore strike the poor on the head.

The Savior commanded the disciples that, if perhaps, because they were still dwelling on earth, something mortal had clung to their works, they should shake the dust from their feet (Matthew 10; Mark 5).

Heretics strike the heads of the poor, although this is not read in the Hebrew [Alternatively: *is not to be read*], because they have turned aside from the way of the humble.

The way of the humble is the way that says: “I am the way, the life, and the truth” (John 14:6), which urges us to walk along it, and says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

All the leaders of the heretics swell with pride. Of them the Apostle says: “Lest, being puffed up, he fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1 Timothy 3:6). The devil says: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14).

Therefore God resists the proud heretics, but gives grace to the humble ecclesiastical people (James 4).

Son and father also went in to one girl in order to violate and defile the holy name of God.

We often read that the Jewish people are our father, as Paul says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1–2).

And elsewhere: “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you” (Deuteronomy 32:7).

Again: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Psalm 44:17).

Hence the Church of the Gentiles says: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song of Songs 1:5).

We are therefore the sons, and the Jewish people are the father. We sin and commit a crime when, together with our parent, we enter into observance of the Sabbath, the injury of circumcision, and the ceremonies of the abolished Law. Concerning these the Apostle says: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5:2, 4).

And again: “You who are justified by the law have fallen away from grace.” Whoever enters the Church in such a way as to keep the Law within the Gospel enters with his father to the girl, commits fornication, and violates the name of the Lord.

Therefore those who say that Jews do not suffer harm after the coming of Christ if they believe in the Lord in such a way that they also keep the commandments of the Law contaminate father and son in a single act of fornication.

They also tie their garments with ropes and make coverings beside the altar, claiming to display the faith of Christ. For “as many as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3). They place their garments, which they have tied with the cords of sins, before the eyes of those who see, so that their crimes may not be observed; thus the one who looks upon the altar does not suspect the fornication.

All heretics do this while committing fornication under the Christian name and covering their errors and lies with testimonies from the Scriptures.

Therefore the apostles spread their garments beneath the colt of the donkey, so that the Lord might sit more softly (Matthew 21), and so that he might tread upon a road spread from the Law and the Prophets.

Heretics, on the contrary, do not place their garments beneath the Savior’s feet. They tie them beside the altar and use them to conceal their sins, so that they may drink wine obtained through accusation, or the wine of the condemned, who have been condemned because they have gone out from the Church.

This is the wine of the Sodomites, the fury of dragons and of asps; whoever drinks it cannot be healed.

They drink wine not in the house of God, where the temple and Jerusalem are, but in the house of their own god, whom they have fabricated for themselves by skillful speech.

### (Verses 9ff.)

“But I destroyed the Amorite from before them, whose height was like the height of cedars, and who was strong like an oak. I crushed his fruit above and his roots below. I am the one who brought you up from the land of Egypt and led you through the wilderness for forty years, so that you might possess the land of the Amorite. I raised up prophets from your sons and Nazirites from your young men.”

**The Septuagint:** “But I removed the Amorite from before them. His stature was as high as the height of a cedar, and he was strong like an oak. I dried up his fruit above and his roots below. I brought you out of the land of Egypt and led you around in the wilderness for forty years, so that you might possess the land of the Amorites. I took from your sons for prophets and from your young men for sanctification.”

You sold the righteous for money and the poor for sandals, striking his head or crushing the heads of the poor in the dust. You turned aside from the way of the humble, to such an extent that father and son went in to one girl and violated or polluted my holy name. You tied garments polluted by brothels and fornication with the cords of sins, so that you committed adultery in a holy place, joined injustice to drunkenness, and drank another’s wine—and you did this in the house of your god.

But, in contrast, I gave you good things in return for the evils you rendered to me. When you came out of Egypt, I destroyed before your face Sihon, king of the Amorites, who was so tall and strong, like a cedar and an oak. I crushed his fruit above and his roots below.

I brought you out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 29) and, through a long circuit lasting forty years, brought you to the holy land, so that you might possess the land of the Amorite, about which we spoke above. Moses divided it among the sons of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 32).

After so many benefits, I added this also: from your sons I took prophets for myself, and from your young men—or chosen men—I made Nazirites, whom the Septuagint translated as “sanctified.”

Nor, when the praises of God are being recounted, must the order of history always be preserved. It frequently happens that events which occurred first are mentioned last, and those which occurred last are referred back to the beginning.

The seventy-seventh and one-hundred-fourth psalms can teach us this: in them the power of the signs, not their order, is described. The titles of the psalms can also teach it, and we shall offer only two examples: the title of the third psalm and that of the fifty-first. In them, what happened earlier is narrated last, while what we read as having happened last is referred to at the beginning.

For we read in the Book of Kings about Doeg the Idumean (1 Kings 21–22), which is the title of the fifty-first psalm, before Absalom rose up against his father (2 Samuel 15), which is announced in the title of the third psalm.

Thus the Amorite was destroyed, or blotted out, last, although this is mentioned first here; and the fact that he brought them up from the land of Egypt and led them back into the wilderness for forty years occurred at the beginning, although here it is mentioned last, the order having been altered.

Before God brought us out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, he destroyed before our face the Amorite, whose name means “bitter,” or λαλητὸς, that is, “speaking,” or “famous” and celebrated in frequent speech.

This Amorite is also called Sihon, king of the Amorites, meaning a fruitless and barren tree—not because it produces no fruit, but because it produces bad fruit. Concerning such trees it is said: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10; 7:19).

And concerning false prophets we read: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:15–16)—that is, by their bad fruits.

Whether, therefore, it produces no fruit or produces fruit that is not good, it is called a fruitless tree.

This Sihon, concerning whom it is written, “Now the axe has been laid at the roots of the trees” (Luke 3:9), was a fruitless tree. When the Lord struck it, it was cut down. Its height is compared with the height of cedars, concerning which we read: “I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; then I passed by, and behold, he was not there. I sought him, and his place was not found” (Psalm 36:35–36).

He fittingly says that he passed by, because for the one who passes from the world and can say, “As I pass by, I will see this great vision” (Exodus 3:3), the cedar is taken away, and the place of pride can no longer be found.

His strength also was like that of an oak, an exceedingly hard and powerful tree. From this name Philo, the most eloquent of the Hebrews, thinks that Esau was called δρύινον, that is, “oaken” and “stout,” although Esau may also be understood as ποίημα, that is, “a work” or “creation,” so that it may refer to evil deeds.

Concerning this strong and powerful one the Lord speaks in the Gospel [Note: Here, following Victorius, above where Psalm 36 is cited, we read the word *Lord*; throughout, we likewise restore from the manuscripts other readings necessary to the context.]: “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, everything that he possesses is in peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his armor in which he trusted and distribute his spoils” [Alternatively: *he takes away … he distributes*].

The Lord granted us that he might crush and remove the fruit of this Amorite, Sihon, whom we have said means “fruitless tree,” because his fruits were evil, lest anyone, thinking them good, eat and perish.

He also cut down and crushed his roots, so that nothing further from the evil tree might sprout.

The Lord himself caused us to leave the world and, through forty years—a number that always signifies affliction, fasting, mourning, and grief—to reach the holy land through tribulations and distress. Thus we might first possess the land of the Amorite, and his former territory might become our possession.

Afterward he raised up from our sons prophets, all holy men who received the prophetic spirit, concerning whom we read more fully in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 14).

And from our young men [Note: Martianay reads *your young men* instead of *our young men*; some manuscripts know neither reading.] or chosen men he took Nazirites and sanctified persons, who, offering their souls to God, do not touch wine that can intoxicate and overturn the state of the mind, so that they may have Samson’s hair, in whose head—because Christ is the head of a man—strength and victory resided (Judges 16).

### (Verse 12)

“Is it not so, children of Israel,” says the Lord, “that you gave the Nazirites wine to drink and commanded the prophets, saying: ‘Do not prophesy’?”  

[Note: The words “the Septuagint likewise” were absent; our manuscripts supply them.]

The Septuagint likewise.

I bestowed such great benefits upon you: I killed your adversaries, gave you their land, and from your sons and young men chose prophets and Nazirites, consecrating them to my worship. Can you say that I did not do these things, and deny my clemency toward you, through which you live? You have burst into such great madness that you made my Nazirites drunk with wine, although they are commanded by the Law not to drink anything that can intoxicate (Num. 6); and you commanded the prophets not to prophesy in my name.

This is also what Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, commanded the prophet Amos, whom we now have in hand. A similar command was given by the king to Jeremiah: he was not to speak the words of the Lord to the people, to such an extent that the king even burned his utterances in the fire.

Tatian, the leader of the Encratites, tries to construct his heresy from this passage, asserting that wine ought not to be drunk, since the Law commanded that Nazirites should not drink wine, and since the prophet now accuses those who give wine to Nazirites. But if they follow the letter in everything and introduce Jewish fables into the churches of Christ, then they ought also to let their hair grow, not eat dried or fresh grapes, and not approach either mother or father when dead. And if they should do these things and then be overcome either by human weakness or by necessity, they must shave their heads, and all the days of their consecration and labor must be nullified.

If they do not do these things—and they cannot, in the manner of Jewish tavernkeepers, mix water with wine, shadows with truth, the necessity of the Law with the grace of the Gospel—let them understand that intoxication as the state in which the soul’s vigor is made drunk and overwhelmed by worldly cares. And let them understand the command to the prophets, “Do not prophesy,” as referring to those who, overcome by envy, prevent learned men from bringing forth a discourse of instruction. When the Lord says, “Go and say to this people” (Isa. 6:9), they, on the contrary, command: “Do not speak in the name of the Lord,” especially when the teacher seeks not shameful profit, glory, or boasting, but the benefit of those who read and hear.

### (Verses 13 ff.)

“Behold, I will creak beneath you as a wagon creaks when loaded with hay, and flight shall perish from the swift; the strong man shall not retain his strength; the mighty man shall not save his life; the one holding the bow shall not stand; the swift-footed shall not be saved; the horseman shall not save his life; and the strong-hearted among the mighty shall flee naked on that day,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “Therefore, behold, I will overturn you as a wagon full of straw is overturned; flight shall perish from the runner; the strong man shall not retain his strength; the fighter shall not save his life; the archer shall not endure; the swift-footed shall not be able to save himself; the horseman shall not save his life; and the heart found among the mighty shall flee naked on that day,” says the Lord.

[Note: It is remarkable here how much the Greek copies themselves differ from one another. Although this rendering largely follows the Alexandrian text, the words “and his heart was found among the mighty” are absent from the Cistercian manuscript.]

Although I bestowed benefits upon you, led you out of the land of Egypt, and killed the Amorite before your face so that you might possess his land, and raised up prophets from your sons and Nazirites from your young men, you made my Nazirites drunk with wine and said to the prophets, “Do not prophesy.” Therefore, just as a wagon heavily burdened with straw or hay cries out from its creaking and noise, so I, no longer able to bear your sins and handing you over like straw to the fire, will cry out and say: “Flight shall perish from the swift.”

The Hebrews understand “the swift” as Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had previously fled into Egypt (1 Kings 11). Here, however, let us understand not the men themselves but their houses and descendants.

[Note: The author called Rufinus regards this entire Hebrew tradition as of no great weight.]

“And the strong man shall not retain his strength”: they interpret “the strong man” as Basan, who was extremely ready for war (1 Kings 15).

“And the mighty man shall not save his life”: here they understand Omri [variant: Amri].

“And the one holding the bow shall not stand,” or “endure”: they think this was said of Jehu son of Nimshi [variant: Nemshi], who struck Joram king of Israel with an arrow (2 Kings 9).

“And the swift-footed shall not be saved”: they understand Menahem, who, although he hurried in vain, sent gifts to the king of the Assyrians (2 Kings 15).

“And the horseman shall not save his life”: they interpret this as Pekah son of Remaliah, who, having joined himself to Aram—that is, Syria—devastated much of Judah under King Ahaz.

“And the strong-hearted among the mighty shall flee naked on that day,” says the Lord (ibid.). Only Hoshea, the last king of the ten tribes, who tried to bring the erring people back to the worship of God (2 Kings 18), will emerge [variant: “will go out”] from the fire as a naked man.

He calls him naked because under him the ten tribes were captured. This is what the Hebrews assert, and, as it was handed down to us by them, we have faithfully explained it to our own people.

Now let us return to our subject. God threatens to overturn beneath them a wagon burdened with hay or straw, because, since they have no grain to be stored in barns, their hay and straw will be burned in the fire. This is the hay of which the prophet says: “Let them become like the grass of the housetops, which withers before it is plucked up” (Ps. 128:6). And: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6).

That straw is the subject of the prophet’s mournful lament:

“Woe is me! For I have become like one who gathers straw in the harvest, and like gleanings at the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat as firstfruit. Woe is me! A devout person has perished from the earth, and there is no one who does right among humankind; all are judged for blood” (Mic. 7:1) [variant: “my soul” is added], and so forth.

This is the hay and straw of which the Apostle also speaks: “Wood, hay, straw—the work of each person will become manifest” (1 Cor. 3), “because on the day of the Lord it will be revealed in fire.”

And the wagon that is overturned is the one of which we read in Isaiah: “Moab shall be trampled, as the threshing floor is trampled in wagons” (Isa. 25:10).

[Note: In place of “the Moabites,” printed books had “Moab beneath it,” contrary to the manuscripts we use and to the Greek, καταπατηθήσεται ἡ Μωαβίτις ὃν τρόπον πατοῦσιν, “Moab shall be trampled as they trample,” and so forth. In Martianay’s edition it was also corrupt in the main text.]

And elsewhere: “I will make you like new wagon wheels with teeth like saws, and you shall thresh mountains and crush hills” (ibid. 41:15).

[Note: Our manuscripts read “after” where Martianay had “so that,” and shortly afterward read “may perish.”]

And after you have crushed the mountains and hills, “flight shall perish from the swift,” as Paul says: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize?” (1 Cor. 9:24). And elsewhere: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Gal. 5:7). Hence, fearing for himself, he says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I run in order to seize it, because I too have been seized by Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:12).

He did all these things so that “flight might not perish from the swift.” Therefore, when he had already reached the finish and received the prize of victory, he confidently said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

If we flee with rapid steps, sin will not be able to seize us. But if wickedness binds our feet, we shall say with the prophet to God: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 139:7).

The Apostle speaks of wicked runners: “It depends not on human willing or running, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16).

It follows: “And the strong man shall not retain his strength.” This does not mean one who truly is strong, but one who boasts that he is strong; or one who trusts in his strength and not in God’s mercy, according to what is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Cor. 1:19). This does not mean that true wisdom can perish or that the understanding of truth can be rejected, but that the wisdom of those who seem wise in their own eyes and trust in their own learning will perish.

The mighty man, or fighter, who will not save his life is one who does not possess the Apostle’s armor: he has a shield, but not of faith; he has his loins girded, but not in truth; he is clothed with a breastplate, but not of righteousness; he carries a sword, but not of salvation (Eph. 6). Such a fighter does not sanctify the battle and cannot wage the Lord’s wars, fighting against the truth on behalf of falsehood. Such a fighter cannot say: “Blessed be the Lord, my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war. He is my mercy and my refuge” (Ps. 144:1).

Heretics too have their archers. They draw their bow in vain and will not be able to withstand the Lord’s arrow, who speaks through Isaiah: “I was like a chosen arrow in the Lord’s quiver” (Isa. 49:2). These are the archers of whom David also sings: “Behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at those upright in heart” (Ps. 11:2).

“And the swift,” he says, “shall not be saved”—the person who, because of the sharpness of his intellect, runs through the testimonies of Scripture and tries to overwhelm the truth with the eloquence of orators or the sophisms of dialecticians. He is tripped up and falls because he trusts not in God but in his own feet.

The horseman too will not save his life, because he does not know what the prophet said: “The horse is deceptive for salvation” (Ps. 33:17). He does not know that it is written: “All those who mounted horses slumbered” (Ps. 75:7). He will not save his life, but when he perishes he will hear: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God. They were tripped up and fell, but we rose and stood upright” (Ps. 20:8–9).

The strong-hearted among the mighty will also flee naked. This passage can be explained in two ways: either he is able to escape because he has stripped off the old man and the skin garments of sins and has been burdened by no baggage; or, conversely, because he is naked and has lost Christ’s garment, concerning which the Apostle says: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14). And elsewhere: “If indeed we are clothed, we shall not be found naked” (2 Cor. 5:3). His strength will profit him nothing; but on the day of battle and struggle he will flee from his pursuers and, unable to resist without the Apostle’s armor, will turn his back to his enemies.

### (Chapter 3, verses 1–2)

“Hear the word that the Lord has spoken concerning you, children of Israel, concerning the whole family that I brought up from the land of Egypt, saying: You alone have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities.”

The Septuagint: “Hear this word that the Lord has spoken concerning you, house of Israel, and against every tribe that I brought up from the land of Egypt, saying: Nevertheless, I knew you from all the tribes of the earth; therefore I will avenge upon you all your wickednesses.”

The prophetic word is directed to the children of Israel, and the following verse shows who these children of Israel are: “Concerning the whole family,” he says, “that I brought up from the land of Egypt.” We should understand this not only of the ten tribes but of all twelve, adding Judah and Benjamin. For he brought them all out of the land of Egypt and said: “You alone”—or, as Symmachus translated it, “I knew only you from all the families of the earth.”

Because I knew only you, I who am the Creator of all things, and had you as my special people, therefore upon you alone will I restore all your sins. “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6); but the one who is least is worthy of mercy. And in Ezekiel we read: “Begin with my holy ones” (Ezek. 9:6). It is also said that God’s judgment begins with his own household (1 Pet. 4).

For the moment, let this be understood historically. But since in the holy Scriptures “hearing” does not mean only what we receive with the ears of the flesh, but also that of which the Lord says, “The one who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8), therefore the entire people “saw the voice of God” (Exod. 20). The Lord’s word is properly addressed to those who see God with the understanding: those whom he brought out of the land of Egypt and from Pharaoh’s power, so that they might no longer serve clay and straw while building Egyptian cities; and those whom he knew from all the tribes of the earth, as the Apostle says: “Now that you have come to know God—or rather, to be known by God” (Gal. 4:9).

And elsewhere: “If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). God therefore does not know everyone, but those who are worthy of his knowledge. In the Gospel he says: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke 13:27). Insofar as they are workers of iniquity, they are unknown to God. Therefore he says: “Because I knew only you and made you my own, I will visit upon you all your iniquities.”

“The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12). And beautifully he says, “I will visit,” rather than “I will strike,” because God’s blow is visitation and healing. “I will visit all your iniquities,” he says, or “your sins,” so that nothing may remain unstruck and nothing fail to receive healing.

### (Verses 3 ff.)

“Will two walk together unless they have agreed? Will the lion roar in the forest unless it has prey? Will the lion’s cub give voice from its den unless it has seized something? Will a bird fall into a snare on the ground without a bird-catcher? Will the snare be removed from the ground before it has caught something? If the trumpet sounds in the city, will the people not be afraid? If there is evil in the city, which the Lord has not made [the Vulgate has ‘will not have made,’ and ‘makes’]? For the Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets. The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?”

[Note: Victorius had restored the word “his” (*suum*) from twelve manuscripts, following the authority of the Vulgate, Hebrew, and Greek texts; Martianay nevertheless omitted it, while our manuscripts also support it.]

The Septuagint: “Will two walk together at all unless they know one another? Will the lion belch from his forest without having prey? Will the lion’s cub give its voice from its den at all unless it has carried something away? Will a bird fall upon the earth without a bird-catcher? Will the snare be placed upon the ground unless it has caught something? If the trumpet sounds in the city, will the people not be afraid? If there is wickedness in the city which the Lord has not made [variant: ‘will not have made’], because the Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his instruction to his servants the prophets? The lion will belch, and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy?”

I have read in the commentary of someone who tried to establish a difficult proposition: that the eight crimes, or acts of impiety and sins—first Damascus; second Gaza and the other cities of Palestine; third Tyre; fourth Idumea, that is, Edom; fifth the children of Ammon; sixth Moab; seventh Judah, that is, the two tribes; and eighth, the last, Israel, that is, the ten tribes—are now matched by an equal number of threats, the first corresponding to the first, namely Damascus, the second to the second, namely Gaza, and the rest to the rest. Whether this is true, let the author himself know.

[Note: Martianay corruptly reads “six examples” in place of “six,” and so forth.]

Another person thinks that six examples are proposed: two people walking together, a lion roaring in the forest, a lion’s cub giving its voice after seizing something, a bird caught by a bird-catcher, a snare fixed in the ground to capture prey, and a trumpet sounding in the city. A comparison is then supplied through these examples: just as the preceding things have causes and do not occur unless those causes have come first, so no evil occurs in the city which has not been done at the Lord’s command.

Some think that the first example contains a teaching, because two people cannot walk together unless they have first agreed with one another in him who made both one, destroyed the middle wall of the barrier, and created the two as one new man (Eph. 2). He made peace between them and joined them by the bond of charity, so that when the two are together they may ask the Father and obtain whatever they request.

These are the two staffs joined to one another in Ezekiel (Ezek. 7), and the two peoples, of circumcision and of the nations, concerning whom the Lord says to Elijah: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (1 Kings 19:18). And elsewhere God says: “I was found by those who did not seek me; I appeared to those who did not ask me” (Isa. 65:1).

When the two have been brought into one, they will cling to the Lord, and there will be one spirit: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). These two, therefore, who agree with one another and walk together on Christ’s path, need fear no attack from their adversaries.

But if they are separated by discord, the roaring lion will immediately attack them. Concerning him the Apostle Peter says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

That roaring lion does not inhabit sown fields, vineyards, or olive groves, nor does he live among fruit-bearing trees that praise God, but where there are forests, uncultivated ground, and wild beasts. They will not merely be exposed to the lion’s bites: the lion’s cub will also seize them and lead them to its den, fleeing the light and proceeding toward darkness. “Everyone who sins loves darkness and hates the light” (John 3).

Concerning these things we read in the psalm: “You appointed darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forests will pass through. The lion cubs roar, that they may seize prey and seek their food from God” (Ps. 104:20–21). The lion’s cub does not seek prey that it already possesses and that is under its power, but seeks to snatch it from the Church of Christ. Concerning this it is written in Habakkuk: “Its chosen food” (Hab. 1:16).

The third punishment is that of those whom discord has separated: they lose the wings by which they had previously been carried aloft, fall from heaven to earth, and are caught by the bird-catcher, who is more properly called ἰξευτής (*ixeutēs*), because he catches free birds that cling to birdlime and descend to earthly things by their own will.

Concerning them it is written in Proverbs: “Not unjustly are nets spread for birds” (Prov. 1:17; 29:5). Their ruin is just: although they had the wings of a dove and ought to have flown through the air, they have been weighed down to earthly things by the burden of their sins and, through their own fault, have adhered to the birdlime. Of this we read in the Apostle: “The one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her” (1 Cor. 6:16).

The fourth punishment of those who disagree is that they are caught in a snare, which is placed not in heaven but on earth. Concerning escape from it the saint exults and says: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare was broken, and we were set free” (Ps. 124:7). This is the broken snare of which the Apostle speaks to believers: “God will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Rom. 16:20).

Again we read in David: “They placed a stumbling block beside the path for me” (Ps. 136:6). They cannot deceive the simple among believers unless they put forward the name of Christ, so that, while we think we are finding Christ, we proceed to the Antichrist.

The fifth punishment is that of those who have abandoned the peace that surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4), which the Lord left to the Apostles when he was going to the Father, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). Thus, established in the city of the Lord, they are terrified by the sound of the trumpet.

Whatever is said in the holy Scriptures is a threatening trumpet, penetrating the ears of believers with a great sound. If we are righteous, through Christ’s trumpet we are summoned to blessedness; if we are sinners, we hear what torments we shall suffer.

The evil that the Lord makes in the city is not contrary to virtue, but is affliction and torment. Concerning this we read: “Sufficient for the day is its evil” (Matt. 6:34), that is, tribulation and distress. And in the prophet we read: “I am God who made light and darkness, who makes peace and creates evil” (Isa. 45:6–7).

Just as darkness is contrary to light and day, so war is contrary to peace. War is not evil in itself, but appears evil to those who endure it. And so that we may know that in the holy Scriptures “wickedness” is sometimes understood not as the opposite of virtue but as affliction, punishment, and distress, let us take one further example from Jonah: “God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil ways, and God repented of the evil that he had said he would do to them” (Jonah 3:10).

There “evil” means the overthrow of the Ninevites, which God had threatened through the prophet; it does not mean the evil opposed to virtue and belonging to sin, for which he was threatening torments against sinners.

It follows: “The Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his secret,” or “his correction,” “to his servants the prophets.” This does not mean that God reveals to the prophets everything he does in heaven or has already done, but what he is going to do on earth.

He revealed to his servant Noah that he would bring the flood (Gen. 6). He revealed to his servants Abraham and Lot that he would burn Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim (ibid. 18). He revealed to Joseph the interpretation of the dream concerning the seven years of famine in Egypt (ibid. 41), and to the prophet Jonah the overthrow of Nineveh (Jonah 3), so that those who heard of the coming punishments might either repent and avoid the torments, or, if they despised the warning, might be punished more justly.

So now also the Lord reveals through his servant and prophet Amos what he is going to do to the ten tribes, so that, if they turn to better things and abandon their idols, they may be freed from the impending danger. Observe that the merciful and benevolent God always announces future events beforehand, lest he be compelled to inflict punishments.

What heretics maliciously allege against the Creator—as though he were severe, harsh, cruel, and merely a judge, because there is no evil in a city that he does not do—we refer to the greatness of his mercy: he does not inflict punishments unless he has first foretold them. Whoever foretells does not wish to punish sinners.

And when he says, “The lion has roared, and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?” the word “who” is used here not of impossibility but of rarity. The one who will not fear, and the one who will not prophesy, is the person who, because of his hardness, has disdained to hear the Lord.

The historical sense is this: if everything trembles at a lion’s voice and the whole nature of living creatures is terrified, shall we not prophesy and speak when God commands us to speak and announce to the people the punishments that are coming?

I know that someone left in his commentary the view that the roaring lion should be understood as the devil, roaring at those who are going to perish; but that God, who speaks through the prophets, should be referred to the Lord the Savior. Thus, just as they hear the lion’s roar in an evil sense and are captured for death, so the saints hear the Lord’s command in a good sense and are saved.

### (Verses 9–10)

“Make it heard in the houses of Ashdod and in the houses of the land of Egypt, and say: Gather upon the mountains of Samaria and see the many insanities in its midst, and those suffering oppression [the Vulgate has ‘oppression’] within its inner chambers; they do not know how to do what is right,” says the Lord, “those who store up iniquity and plunder in their houses.”

The Septuagint: “Announce to the regions in Assyria and in the regions of the land of Egypt, and say: Gather upon the mountain of Samaria and see many wonderful things in its midst, and oppression in it, and it did not know what things would occur before it,” says the Lord, “those who store up iniquity and misery in their regions.”

We said above that the prophet Amos prophesies especially to the ten tribes, which are called Israel, Ephraim, and Samaria—indeed, that this occupies a large part of his book. Therefore now also he is commanded to announce what follows to Ashdod and to the land of Egypt.

In place of Ashdod, the Septuagint, for some reason unknown to me, has “Assyrians,” although Ashdod is called *Esdod* in the language of the Hebrews, whereas the Assyrians are called *Assur*. In place of the houses, which are called *armanoth*, they also translated “regions,” which are called *sadoth*; the words have no similarity at all.

“Say,” he says, “that all the neighboring nations should gather and see Israel’s crimes, lest they think God’s judgment unjust.” It is as though he were saying: “First see what they do, and then approve my sentence.”

He beautifully adds: “Upon the mountains of Samaria,” whether this means the city that is now called Sebaste and was then called Samaria, or the whole province situated in mountainous country. “And see the many insanities in its midst”: they worship calves instead of God and sacrifice their sons. Not content with this crime, they oppress the poor within their inner chambers and altogether do not know how to act rightly, storing up in their houses not gold and money—which are sometimes acquired by labor—but iniquities and plunder.

Because they abandoned the worship of God and worshiped idols, God gives them over to a debased mind (Rom. 1), so that they do what ought not to be done.

And because, according to the laws of allegorical interpretation, Samaria is once again referred to heretics, who pretend that they are guardians of God’s commandments, the divine word commands that they proclaim among the nations—who have no knowledge of God and whose teaching is a consuming fire, tribulation, and distress—that they should consider false Samaria, ascend the mountains of her pride, and see the many insanities in the midst of the city. Each person fabricates whatever he wishes and worships his own invention:

Marcion invents a good and inactive god;

Valentinus invents thirty *aeons* (*αἰῶνες*) and the final Christ, whom he calls *ektrōma* (*ἐκτρῶμα*), that is, “abortive”;

Basilides, who calls the omnipotent God by the monstrous name *Abraxas* (*Ἀβράξας*) and says that this name, according to the Greek letters and the number of the solar year, is contained in the circle of the sun—the pagans, using the same number of other letters, call him *Meithras* (*Μείθραν*).

[Note: The name was written in Latin letters as *Abraxas*, and shortly afterward as *Mythran*, so that there was no conformity among these names and no equal numerical calculation. The same error is made by those who write Μύθραν with upsilon or Μίθραν with iota. Either this name too, when its letters are converted into numbers, must yield the total of 365 days in the whole year; or one should write Μείθρας or Μήθρης. We discuss the numerical equivalence of the letters elsewhere. Compare *Against the Luciferians*, no. 23, where Basilides is discussed—he devised the supreme God Abraxas with 365 editions; see also Letter 75 to Theodora, no. 3; Letter 107 to Laeta, no. 2; and the preface to the Pentateuch addressed to Desiderius.]

And they marvel at the Iberian absurdities concerning Balsamus and Barbelo.

Are these not insanities—many insanities—with each person inventing whatever enters his mind?
