They also suffer oppression within its inner chambers, or the simple among believers are oppressed, while under the name of truth they worship falsehood. They altogether do not know how to act rightly because they have lost the path of truth and do not believe in the one who says, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). They store up for themselves doctrines of iniquity and seize and imprison in their houses those whom they are able to deceive by false error.

But if it should please us to read “Assyrians”—although this is not found in the Hebrew—let us say that these are those of whom it is written: “I will bring upon the proud mind the great prince of the Assyrians, who said, ‘By my strength I will act,’” and so forth. Thus heretics may be captured by the Assyrian and held in the land of Egypt, from which they had already come to the Church and been liberated.

### (Verse 11)

“Therefore, thus says the Lord God: The land shall be afflicted and surrounded; your strength shall be taken away from you, and your houses shall be plundered.”

The Septuagint: “Therefore, thus says the Lord God: Tyre, and your land round about, shall be desolate; he shall take away your strength from you, and your regions shall be plundered.”

In place of “Tyre,” which in Hebrew is written with two letters, *ṣade* () and *resh* (), and is called *ṣor* (), both Aquila and the Septuagint translated similarly. The Hebrew teacher who instructed me in the holy Scriptures interpreted it as “tribulation,” and we do not reject his opinion, since Symmachus—who ordinarily follows not a slavish verbal rendering but the order of the meaning—says “siege and encirclement of the land.”

[Note: We have removed here the word “land,” which Victorius had long ago deleted on the evidence of seven Florentine manuscripts, with which all our manuscripts agree; I can scarcely believe that Martianay, who retained it, could have found it in manuscripts.]

In place of “siege,” which he renders as πολιορκία, Theodotion supplied “strength.” He thought that one should read not *sar* () and *ṣor* (, meaning “tribulation” or “Tyre”), but *sur*, which properly refers to an extremely hard rock, called in Greek ἀκρότομος and which we can call in Latin *silex*, “flint.”

Let us therefore discuss each point separately. The Septuagint said: “Tyre and your land round about.” The sentence seemed incomplete, so they added from themselves, “shall be desolate.” Nor is the translators’ error surprising, since, because of the ambiguity of the word, it can mean both “tribulation” and “Tyre.”

The sense is this: On the mountains of Samaria my people committed many insanities, practicing oppression, utterly ignoring what was right, and storing up iniquity and plunder for themselves. Therefore it will be afflicted, or crushed; their land will be surrounded by the Assyrian army; and, he says, your strength will be taken away from you, O Samaria, O ten tribes, O my former people. Your houses will be plundered—the houses in which you gathered wealth through oppression and from the tears of the miserable.

Heretics too will either be afflicted on the day of judgment, all their strength will be weakened, and the things they acquired by plunder will be taken away so that the peoples whom they deceived may be freed; or else they will daily be afflicted through ecclesiastical men, surrounded by testimonies of the Scriptures, and stripped of the strength of their syllogisms and of the verbal subtleties by which they had established their doctrine.

And their houses will be plundered, so that those who had been carried away from the Church may return to the Church.

### (Verses 12–13)

Thus says the Lord: “Just as a shepherd rescues from the lion’s mouth two legs or the tip of an ear, so shall the children of Israel who dwell in Samaria be rescued, upon the corner of a couch and on a bed in Damascus.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord: Just as a shepherd tears two legs or the tip of an ear from the lion’s mouth, so shall the children of Israel who dwell in Samaria be torn away, opposite the tribe and in Damascus.”

At the beginning of Amos, where we discussed those verses—“The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice; and the beautiful places of the shepherds will mourn, and the summit of Carmel will dry up”—we said that he employed the language of his profession: since a shepherd of flocks knew nothing more terrifying than a lion, he compared the Lord’s anger with lions. In keeping with this meaning, therefore, he now too takes his example from something he had often seen, and says that the small remnants of the ten tribes will be rescued from the hands of the Assyrians: just as, after all the limbs have been devoured, a shepherd snatches two legs or the tip of an ear from the lion’s jaws.

After setting forth the example of the comparison, he says: “Thus shall the children of Israel be rescued”—that is, the ten tribes that dwell in Samaria—“upon the corner of a couch and on a bed in Damascus.” This seems to me to be explained as follows. We read in Isaiah that Rezin, king of Aram—that is, of the Syrians—who ruled in Damascus, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, made an alliance and came against Judah to fight (Isa. 7). Concerning them, the Lord commands Ahaz, king of Judah and Jerusalem, not to fear two smoking firebrands, when, as a sign of complete freedom, the Virgin’s conception and birth are shown to him. [Col. 1020C]

The children of Samaria therefore dwell in the region and upon the corner of a couch, resting on the aid of the Syrians and promising themselves victory on a bed in Damascus: so that, just as someone who is tired is refreshed on a couch, they might strengthen their broken forces through the assistance of the neighboring nation.

Hence, in the same Isaiah, by a type of things to come, it is said that a child will be born who, before he knows how to call his father and mother, will receive the spoils of Samaria and the strength of Damascus—those forces, namely, that were fighting against Jerusalem with their strength joined together (ibid.).

Instead of “upon the corner of a couch and on a bed in Damascus,” the Septuagint translated “opposite the tribe and in Damascus,” so that, according to the tropological interpretation, we may refer the tribe to Judah and Damascus to the calling of the nations. From these a single flock of the Lord was made; its sheep are often torn by the ferocity of lions, and from their jaws scarcely two legs or the tip of an ear is carried away.

In the leg is shown the way of doctrines; in the ear are the mysteries of utterances. Hence the apostles are commanded [another reading: “were commanded”] to walk without sandals and without any covering of dead animal skin, with bare feet (Matt. 10). And to believers it is said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8). In the Apocalypse of John we likewise read: “Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. 2:7). And more plainly through the prophet: “Set,” he says, “your words in the ears of your heart.”

Both the heretics and their teachers, the demons, hasten to obstruct this path and to weave nets in it, so that we may fall on the way that is Christ. But if an ecclesiastical man, a man of God, should come—and Samson, whose name is interpreted as “sun”—he kills the lion. Descending into the lake of hell, which cools the waters in the time of snow, storm, and winter, he suffocates the lion, so that we may follow the Lord with a secure foot and hear his words with ears kept safe.

### (Verses 14–15)

“Hear and bear witness in the house of Jacob,” says the Lord God of hosts, “for on the day when I begin to visit the transgressions of Israel upon him, I will also visit the altars of Bethel. The horns of the altar shall be cut off and fall to the ground. I will strike the winter house together with the summer house, and the ivory houses shall perish; and the many houses shall be destroyed,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “Priests, hear! Bear witness against the house of Jacob,” says the Lord God Almighty, “for on the day when I avenge the iniquities of Israel upon him, I will also avenge them upon the altars of Bethel. The horns of the altar shall be dug out and fall upon the ground. I will confuse and strike the winged house together with the summer house, and the ivory houses shall perish, and other many houses shall be added,” says the Lord.

The word “priests,” which is placed at the beginning of the chapter according to the Septuagint, is not found in the Hebrew. Instead, the word ARES () is read; Aquila interpreted it as “bed.” I think that the Septuagint retained the Hebrew word itself, but that certain people who did not understand it read ἱερεῖς—that is, “priests”—in place of ARES.

The prophetic word commands them first to hear and then to bear witness in the house of Jacob—that is, among the ten tribes—what the Lord has said. “When I begin,” he says, “to visit the transgressions, or impieties, of the house of Israel and repay it what it deserves, and the time of captivity arrives, then the altars of Bethel, where the golden calves were, will be destroyed. The horns of the altar, which was broken when Jeroboam also stretched out his hand (1 Kings 13), will be cut off and will fall to the ground, shattered by the Assyrian devastator.”

“And I will strike,” he says, “the winter house together with the summer house.” We may understand this simply according to the literal sense: they possessed such great wealth that they had two kinds of houses, winter houses and summer houses, some turned toward the north and others toward the south, so that they could provide for changes in the seasons, cold and heat, and the temperateness of the sky.

We may call the winter house the kingdom of Israel, in which there was the coldness of religion and the worship of God, various blasts of wind, and savage storm; and the summer house Judah and Jerusalem, in which there was a temple, burnt offerings were made morning and evening, and the warmth of religion flourished.

“And the ivory houses shall perish,” he says. This too can stand according to history. For we read that Ahab, king of Israel, gave himself over to such great luxury that he made himself an ivory house (1 Kings 22). In place of “ivory houses,” we find in Hebrew “houses of tooth,” that is, elephantine houses. Concerning these it is also written in the forty-fourth Psalm: “From houses of ivory; the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.”

When the Lord begins to visit the transgressions of Israel—the people who formerly perceived God with the mind—he will also visit the altars of Bethel: not the one altar possessed by the Church, but the many altars of the heretics. They have as many altars as they have schisms.

He will also cut off the horns of the altar, which they boast in their pride that they alone possess. Their horns—that is, their arrogance—will fall to the ground. He will strike the winter house: those heretics who labor in continence and fasting, in dry foods and foods taken without cooking, among whom are Tatian and Mani­chaeus.

And he will strike the summer house: the Nicolaitans and Eunomians, and the new followers of an old heresy, who, because of their greed for the belly, admit every pleasure.

“And the ivory houses shall perish”—those composed with an artificial tooth and the brilliance of rhetorical polish. “And the many houses shall be destroyed”—those scattered throughout the whole world. For when the one truth rises, many falsehoods will be destroyed.

Instead of “winter house,” the Septuagint translated οἶκον τὸν περίπτερον, “the winged house.” We translated this as “winged,” because it has little doors by the windows, as though wings for repelling the severity of the cold.

## Book Two

I read in a certain controversy: “The weakness of the body carries away with it the powers of the mind.” To the contrary, the apostle Paul says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10); and: “Power is perfected in weakness” (ibid., 9). “The spirit wars against the flesh, and the flesh against the spirit” (Gal. 5); these oppose one another, so that we do not do the things we wish. Hence it is also said in the Gospel: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41).

[Note: Two manuscripts omit “Paul,” and shortly afterward read fortis, “strong,” instead of fortior, “stronger.”]

Old age brings many good things and many evils with it. Its good things are these: it frees us from the pleasures of the most shameless masters; it places a limit on the appetite; it breaks the impulses of lust; it increases wisdom; it gives more mature counsel. And, as the body grows cold, it sleeps with the perpetual virgin Shunammite; and, scorning luxury with Barzillai, it delegates it to the young man Chamaam [another reading: Maacha], and does not wish to cross the Jordan or leave its own boundaries—that is, its own regions—entering foreign territory (2 Sam. 19).

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript and two Palatine codices read: “to leave its own regions for foreign territory.”]

The things that are thought to be the evils of old age are these: frequent illnesses; the most troublesome catarrh, which some Greeks call κόρυζα (“coryza”) and others φλέγμα (“phlegm”); dimming eyes; food becoming sour; an occasionally trembling hand; teeth bare at the gums and falling out during meals. In addition, it is often tormented by colic, stomach cramps, and the pains of gout and arthritis, so that it cannot even hold a stylus or pen; [another reading adds: “and”] it cannot walk on its own feet; a large part of life seems to have been cut away from it, and it is half-dead in many of its members.

When these things are so, I shall endure illnesses more tolerably in comparison with other evils, provided that I am free from that one and very grave mistress, lust.

[Note: One Palatine manuscript reads: “When these things are so, it will be useful for me, in comparison with other evils, to endure illnesses more tolerably.”]

Old age too sometimes suffers the incitements of vices; and, according to the holy martyr Cyprian, no one who is near danger is safe for long. But to be tickled is one thing; to be overwhelmed by pleasures is another.

There, youth speaks with the apostle—youth that knows the needs of a flourishing body: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I do not wish” (Rom. 7:15); and: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid., 24).

Here, however, among dead ashes, a rarely glowing spark strives to come back to life, but it cannot kindle a blaze.

Therefore, Pammachius, with hair already gray upon my head, obtain for me from the Lord that I may deserve to have wisdom as my companion. Of her it is written: “Love her, and she will preserve you; honor her, and she will embrace you” (Prov. 4:8). With her as my helper and companion, may I complete the work begun on Amos, and may the second book begin with the cows of Bashan, so that, having discussed at length in the prophet Hosea the cows or calves of Beth-aven, I may now also be able to expound upon the fattest cows.

[Note: Another of our manuscripts omits this “for me.”]

[Note: A Palatine manuscript reads: “May I discuss the cows of Bashan.”]

### (Chapter 4, verse 1 and following)

“Hear this word, you fat cows who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the needy and crush the poor, who say to your lords, ‘Bring it, and we shall drink.’ The Lord God has sworn by his holiness: Behold, days are coming upon you, and they will lift you up on poles, and your remnants in boiling pots. You will go out through the breaches, one opposite another, and you will be cast into Armon,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “Hear this word, cows of Bashan [another reading: Bashanite cows], who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor and trample the needy, who say to your lords, ‘Give us, so that we may drink.’ The Lord swears by his holy ones: Behold, days are coming upon you, and they will carry you on weapons, and those who are with you in pots—pestilential merchants—and you will be cast out naked, one opposite another, and you will be cast upon Mount Remman,” says the Lord.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript adds Deus, “God,” as do some Greek copies: Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς, “the Lord God.” In place of Basanidis, which we restored from the manuscripts and the Greek, Basanitides had consistently appeared both above and below.]

In place of “fat cows,” the Septuagint put “of Bashan.” Aquila and Theodotion retained the Hebrew word itself, BASAN (). Following Symmachus, who says αἱ βόες εὔτροφοι—that is, “well-fed cattle”—we translated it as “fat cows.”

He speaks to the leaders of Israel and to all the nobles of the ten tribes, who were occupied with luxuries and plunder, so that they might hear God’s word and know that they were not working oxen but fat cows from the herd—or cows nourished in the pastures of Bashan, places exceedingly rich in grasses. Thus he signifies that they were prepared not for agriculture but for sacrifice and eating.

“You are fat cows on the mountain of Samaria, and you crush all the humble, and you say to your lords”—that is, to the shepherds, by whom we understand the kings—“Give us, and we shall drink,” that is, “Command only, and we shall lay everything waste.”

Because he says, “Give us, and we shall drink,” and does not say, “Give us, and we shall eat,” he signifies their drunkenness in wine and luxury, which overturn the condition of the mind.

Therefore the Lord God swore by his holiness—or by himself, or by the Son, or by the Temple, or by everyone who is holy and is called the temple of God—that a day would come, not far off after many ages but already impending: the day of captivity and distress, in which the cows would be lifted upon poles and their remnants in boiling pots. For this reason, in Hebrew and in Aquila, it is written “in fish kettles.”

In place of “poles,” which in Hebrew are called SANNOTH (), Aquila translated “shields”; Symmachus and the Septuagint, “weapons”; only Theodotion has δόρατα, “spears.” Following him, we translated it as “poles” or “lances.”

This signifies that they are captured in battle and carried away as the right of victory, while preserving the metaphor of the cows already begun: those whom he had called fat cows, he now says have their flesh carried on poles or shields.

And just as a boiling kettle envelops small fish all together, so the cows of Bashan will be oppressed by the miseries of captivity without any order.

What follows—“You will go out through the breaches, one opposite another”—can be explained as follows: The way of captivity is open to you; and when your kettles have been burned, you will go out one opposite another, according to the idiom of the Hebrews, who, where we say “mutually” or “in turn,” say “woman and woman,” that is, “one opposite another.”

[Note: Victorius supplies “we say,” from seven Florentine manuscripts.]

“And you will be cast,” he says, “into the places of Armenia called Armona ().” Accordingly, Symmachus translated: “You will be cast into Armenia.” In place of this, the Septuagint has “Mount Remman”; Aquila, “Mount Armona”; Theodotion, “Mount Mona”; and the fifth edition translated “a lofty mountain.”

[Note: In the work On Places, under the entry Remma, Aquila is said to have translated it differently: according to Eusebius, ὄρος ἐν Ῥεμμωνᾷ, “a mountain in Remmon”; but according to Jerome, “Mount Emmona.”]

According to the tropological interpretation begun above, the word of the Lord that the cows of Bashan are commanded to hear gives an order to the heretics. Since they serve the belly and the appetite, they are rightly called the fattest cows, or shameful cows—for this is what Bashan means, namely αἰσχύνη, “shame.” If we wish to call it “confusion,” we shall interpret Babylon more readily than Bashan.

These fat cows, or shameful and dry cows—for Bashan also conveys this meaning—are on the mountain of Samaria. Concerning it, Hosea too says: “Take away your calf, Samaria.” And again in the same prophet: “For your calf was leading you astray, Samaria” (Hos. 8:5–6). Therefore they are on the mountain of Samaria because they are always lifted up in pride and promise themselves lofty things.

Samaria is also interpreted as “watch,” not because they keep the Lord’s words, but because they boast that they are guardians of his commandments.

They oppress the needy and crush the poor. Understand the needy and the poor as the ecclesiastical man who, content with the simplicity of truth, does not seek the furnishings of the heretics, the brilliance of eloquence, or the riches of arguments.

These cows say to their lords: “Bring it, and we shall drink.”

We can call their lords the princes of perverse doctrines—Valentinus, Marcion, Arius, and Eunomius—or those who reinforce, through many books, the wicked inventions of others. To these the cows of Bashan say: “Bring it to us, and we shall drink.” For unless they give it, the others have nothing to devour—or rather, nothing to drink so that they may become drunk.

To know that waters and cups signify doctrine, the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman: “Everyone who drinks [another reading: ‘has drunk’] from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst” (John 4:13). Therefore those who drink from the waters of the Samaritan—that is, of the heretics—will always thirst and will not be able to cool the burning of their parched throats.

Isaiah cries out concerning this very matter: “As the thirsty man dreams that he is drinking, and when he rises he is still thirsty, while his soul has hoped in vain, so shall all the nations be that fight against Jerusalem” (Isa. 29:8). Truly, whoever drinks from the waters of the heretics and fights against Jerusalem, the Church of God, drinks in a dream, and his soul is mocked by empty images. When he thinks he has been satisfied, then his thirst will begin.

Hence it is also said to the ecclesiastical man: “Drink water from your own vessels, and water from your own wells, and let them be yours alone” (Prov. 5:15).

Your Lord God swears by his holiness against the cows of fattening and feasting—or he swears by his holy ones—that days will come upon them: days of judgment and punishment, so that they may carry them on their weapons and send those who are with them into kettles, or carry them away.

Either the cows themselves are pestilential merchants, or those who come to carry them are; and they will be cast out naked, seeing one another, and thrown upon Mount Remman, says the Lord God.

We ought also to speak according to the Septuagint, lest we seem to have proposed them without reason. When the days of judgment and vengeance come against the heretics, they will be carried away on weapons—that is, with the weapons with which they had fought against the Church—or, defeated by the armor of God and overcome by his warriors, they will be thrown into kettles, so that those who were previously pestilential merchants may be burned and boiled. For they traded [another reading: “will trade”] in order to hand over to death those whom they had deceived.

These are the ones of whom it is said: “The sons of Eli, sons of pestilence” (1 Sam. 2), who sat in the seat of pestilence [another reading: “of the pestilential ones”].

When they have been boiled and burned, they will come out naked, possessing none of the things on which they had formerly presumed. They will see their shame and will be cast upon Mount Remman, which is interpreted as “loftiness,” so that they may be crushed in their pride.

Some interpret Remman as “the vision of someone,” that is, ὅρασίν τινος. They were not able to see everything; rather, they promised themselves knowledge of some part, so that they might be cast down in the very thing [another reading: “in it”] they believed they knew.

According to the literal sense, when the days of captivity come upon the cows of Samaria, we can understand that their enemies will overcome them in battle, crush them with their weapons, and, after defeating them in the encounter, drive them into fortified cities that are compared with boiling pots.

Just as Jerusalem, with its people shut in and besieged, is compared to a boiling pot full of meat, so the cities of Samaria may be compared to boiling pots. They compel the people enclosed within them by famine and pestilence to go out, to go into captivity while seeing one another, and to be transferred to the mountains of Armon in Armenia, which border the Medes and Persians.

### (Verses 4 and following)

“Come to Bethel, and act impiously; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression; bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days. And sacrifice a thanksgiving offering of leaven [Vulgate: “leavened”], and proclaim voluntary offerings, and announce them. For this is what you desired, children of Israel,” says the Lord God.

“Therefore I also gave you paralysis of teeth in all your cities and lack of bread in all your places; yet you did not return to me,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “You entered Bethel and acted wickedly; in Gilgal you multiplied wickedness. You brought your sacrifices in the morning and your tithes on the third day. They read the law outside and invoked confessions. Announce that the children of Israel loved these things,” says the Lord God. “And I shall give you paralysis of teeth in all your cities and lack of bread in all your places; yet you did not return to me,” says the Lord.

[Note: Victorius says: “The Hebrew word , means ‘to bring’; the Septuagint also rendered this sense when they translated ἠνέγκατε, ‘you brought.’ The Vulgate edition consistently reads offerte, ‘offer,’ in all manuscripts and printed copies. Jerome acknowledges both readings in his Commentary. We wished to give advance notice of this, since nothing has been changed by us. The meaning is the same with either word.”]

First let us lay down the foundations of the history. O miserable Israel, captivity is already near you; the Assyrian army is already pressing upon you. Do what you wish; act impiously; fornicate freely with idols, so that the more shameless you are, the more just my sentence concerning your torments may appear.

“Come,” he says, “to Bethel,” where you set up the golden calf, “and act impiously against God. Come to Gilgal,” a place of idolatry, concerning which I spoke through Hosea: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal” (Hos. 9:15). And again in the same prophet: “They were useless at Gilgal, sacrificing oxen” (ibid. 12:11).

And when you have come to Gilgal, “multiply transgression.” For whatever you do there is transgression against God, to whom you preferred idols.

“And bring your sacrifices every morning,” so that there may be no delay in your crime. “Your tithes every three days,” or, as Symmachus translated, “your tithes on the third day.”

The explanation of this passage seems to us to be as follows. In Leviticus it is commanded that certain sacrifices not be kept until the next day, and that others not remain until the third day; if they remain, they are unclean (Lev. 7). The meaning is therefore: “Every day slaughter unclean sacrifices, offer polluted offerings, and sacrifice a thanksgiving offering of leaven,” which according to the precepts of Moses is never offered to God.

For “thanksgiving,” Aquila interpreted εὐχαριστίαν, that is, “giving of thanks,” which in Hebrew is called THODA ().

“And proclaim,” he says, “voluntary offerings,” which the Hebrews call NADABOTH (), that is, “spontaneous offerings.” A voluntary [another reading: “free”] sacrifice pertains to joy; in Latin we can call it an epulum, a feast.

And when you have done this, announce your impiety to everyone, so that you may seem not only to have committed these acts but also to have taught them to others.

I command these things, and speak in the imperative, in order to satisfy your desire, because this is how you acted and this is what you desired, children of Israel, says the Lord God.

Therefore I also gave you paralysis of teeth, as the Septuagint translated it; because of the simplicity of the word, we have followed them here. Or it may mean “cleanliness of teeth,” as Aquila and Symmachus translated it, so that through clean teeth the magnitude of the famine might be demonstrated.

And I caused a lack of bread, not in one city but in all your cities, and not in one place but in all your places. When I had done this—not punishing, but giving an opportunity for repentance—you did not even then return to me, says the Lord.

We have said these things according to the Hebrew. Let us pass to the Septuagint interpreters and briefly discuss what seems to us according to the anagogical interpretation in each point; for if we wished to say everything in both editions, the size of the books would not allow it.

“You entered Bethel,” that is, the house of God, which is understood as the Church, “and acted impiously against the Lord,” trampling upon his commandments.

But in Gilgal, which is interpreted as “revelation” or “rolling place,” you multiplied impieties, claiming for yourselves knowledge of the holy Scriptures; and, while you lift yourselves up in pride, you have rolled down to the lowest depths of mud.

You also brought your sacrifices in the morning and your tithes on the third day, transformed into an angel of light, and compressing the threefold understanding of the Scriptures—concerning which we have been commanded to inscribe it three times upon our hearts—into the meaning of a single day.

For we ought first to understand Holy Scripture according to the letter, carrying out whatever has been commanded in ethical matters. Second, according to allegory, that is, spiritual understanding. Third, according to the blessedness of things to come.

But you, he says, despising the first and second day, compose certain spiritual fantasies for yourselves without a foundation, placing a roof upon walls from above.

Nor are the heretics content with this end of impiety. They read the law outside, withdrawing from the Church, and attempt to join confessions and testimonies to each of their doctrines, which they have fashioned with a perverse heart.

Or they sacrificed from leaven, concerning which it is said in the Gospel: “Beware of the leaven—that is, the teaching—of the Pharisees” (Matt. 16:6).

And they did these things not through error but deliberately, not by chance desire but with the fullest love [or: affection] for evils.

[Note: Victorius again says: “By a new manner of speaking he called the love of evils, instead of the love of evil, that is, affection for evil, ‘charity.’ He did this so that he might respond word for word to the Septuagint version, which he is explaining here. The Greek text is: ‘These things the children of Israel ἠγάπησαν, loved,’ or in the Vulgate: ‘For this is what you desired, children of Israel.’ Otherwise charity is directed only toward the good.”]

Therefore the Lord threatens vengeance against these things: “I shall give you,” he says, “paralysis of teeth,” which in Greek is called γομφιασμὸς, “numbness of the teeth.”

For if someone, according to Ezekiel, eats a sour grape, his teeth will be set on edge (Ezek. 18). Thus those who misuse the testimonies of the holy Scriptures and eat them while they are unripe and without their sweetness will lose the strength of their teeth, so that they cannot grind hard food and pass it into the stomach for the benefit of the whole body.

I shall give this paralysis of teeth and scarcity of food in all the cities and all your places, so that you may suffer a famine of the word of God and of that bread which descended from heaven (John 6), concerning which it is written in the Psalms: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:15).

I did all these things not because of cruelty and savagery, as the heretics slander, calling the judgment fierce and grim, but so that you might be converted to me. As it is written: “In vain I struck your children; you did not accept correction” (Jer. 2:30).

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript and two Palatine manuscripts read: “and of a grim judge,” rather than “and grim judgment,” followed by “but so that I might convert you,” and so forth.]

### (Verses 7 and following)

“I also withheld rain from you, when there were still three months until the harvest. I rained upon one city, but upon another city I did not rain. One part was watered, but the part upon which I did not rain dried up. Two or three cities came to one city to drink water, but they were not satisfied; yet you did not return to me,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “I also held back rain from you before the three months of the grape harvest. I shall rain upon one city, but upon another city I shall not rain. One part shall be watered, but the part upon which I do not rain shall dry up. Two or three cities shall gather into one city to drink water, but they shall not be satisfied; yet you did not return to me,” says the Lord.

Not only did I give you paralysis of teeth in all your cities and lack of bread in all your places, but I also withheld rain from you when there were still three months until the harvest. This is called the latter rain, and it is especially necessary for the fields and farms of Palestine, so that, when the grass swells toward the harvest and the wheat begins to form, it may not dry up through excessive drought.

[Note: Three of the same manuscripts read “wither.”]

This indicates the spring season at the end of April, from which three months remain until the wheat harvest: May, June, and July.

In place of “harvest,” the Septuagint, in its customary manner, translated “grape harvest.” If we accept this, it is entirely strange and impossible in all the regions of the East. For we have never seen rain in these provinces, especially in Judea, at the end of June or during July.

Indeed, in the books of Kings, as a great sign and portent, rain was brought forth during the days of summer and harvest when Samuel prayed (1 Kings 12). It would therefore have been superfluous to threaten July with drought, since he had never given rain in that month.

He withheld the rain so that they would suffer not only lack of bread but also the burning of thirst and scarcity of drinking water. In these regions where we now live, apart from small springs, all water is in cisterns; and if divine anger withholds the rains, the danger from thirst is greater than that from famine. Scripture records that this happened in the days of Elijah the prophet for three years and six months (1 Kings 17).

And lest they perhaps think that this happened to cities and peoples through the law of nature, the course of the stars, or the variation of the seasons, he says that he rained upon one city and its fields and withheld rain from another, so that two or three cities might go to another city and yet not be satisfied with drinking water.

When he has done these things—not as punishment but as medicine—he rebukes those who persist in crime: “Even then you did not return to me,” says the Lord.

The Lord also prevents or restrains spiritual rains and every dew of divine wisdom from the heretics, and commands his clouds not to rain upon them before the three months of harvest or grape harvest, so that they cannot reach the fruits of the mystery of the Trinity.

Just as this sun, which we see, completes its annual course in twelve months, each month turning through thirty days until it returns to its former goal; and as the moon, which in Hebrew is called JARE () and in Greek μήνη, gave the months their name from its own name in both languages, and is illuminated by the rays of the sun on the side nearer to it, receiving more or less light according to the variation of the seasons; so also the Church, adorned with the splendor of the true Sun, completes the number of the twelve apostles.

Hence the twelve are also called tribes in Israel. And as a testimony to eternal remembrance, twelve stones are taken from the bed of the Jordan to be placed at the site of the second circumcision (Josh. 4).

The Lord rains upon one city, the Church of true confession, and does not rain upon another, which exists in the assemblies of the heretics. While the former receives everlasting rain, the latter is dried up by continual aridity, so that those who thirst, compelled by their need, come to the city of the Lord, from which a most abundant fountain flows and waters the torrent of thorns.

This is the fountain that speaks through Jeremiah: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. 2:13).

This fountain, proceeding from one source, flows in a threefold unity. The Psalmist longs for these fountains of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the manner of a thirsty deer, saying: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41:1).

When two or three cities have gone to one city in which the waters are abundant—waters of hope, faith, and love—they will not be satisfied, because they have come to seek divine grace not willingly but from necessity.

(Vers. 9.) I struck you with scorching wind and with jaundice. The abundance of your gardens and your vineyards, your olive trees and your fig trees, the locust devoured; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.

**LXX:** I struck you with heat and with jaundice. You multiplied your gardens, your vineyards, your fig trees, and your olive trees the locust devoured; and not even then did you turn back to me, says the Lord.

I did not merely do the things mentioned earlier in order to correct you; but whatever remained after the drought, I struck with scorching wind and jaundice.

[Note: The earlier Palatine manuscripts read “from which we corrected shortly afterward, joining the Cistercian manuscript and seven Florentine manuscripts in Victor’s possession, ‘whatever remained after the drought, I struck with scorching wind.’ For in Martianay’s edition, following Erasmus, it read: ‘whatever remained, in drought, with wind,’ and so forth. The reading restored by us is itself supported by the context of the holy Doctor, which Victor explained as follows: “Above he says that God struck everything with drought, raining upon one city and not raining upon another; then he added: ‘I struck you with scorching wind and jaundice.’ All the interpreters here rendered jaundice (ἴκτερος, ikteros); this disease is nothing other than a diffusion of bile throughout the body. It is called ‘royal disease’ (regius) by Celsus because of the royal apparatus by which it is treated, and ‘jaundice’ (icterus) from a bird of the same color, which our people of Rieti call raulum. Theodotion rendered it ὠχρίασις (ōchriasis), that is, pallor. It is called aurugo, ‘jaundice,’ from gold (aurum), since the disease has that color; and it is a different word from aerugo, ‘verdigris,’ which signifies the corrosion of bronze.”]

For “scorching wind,” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated ἀνεμοφθορία (anemophthoria); the Septuagint rendered it πύρωσις (pyrōsis), which we may call “burning.” As for “jaundice,” all alike translated it ἴκτερος (ikteros), except Theodotion, who alone rendered it ὠχρίασις (ōchriasis), which signifies pallor. And when, in opposition to the Lord’s anger, they multiplied gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees, the locust consumed everything; concerning this the book of Joel speaks more fully (Joel I).

And not even through the blows and the weight of their misfortunes did they wish to come to God. By these words let the heretics be put to shame, who interpret the discipline of the Creator—and, so to speak, his medicine—as cruelty.

The Lord strikes heretics spiritually with that burning of which the apostle Paul says: “It is better to marry than to burn” (I Cor. VII, 9). And the chief of the apostles says: “Beloved, do not be astonished at the burning which comes upon you for your testing” (I Pet. IV, 12). He strikes them also with jaundice, which, when bile is diffused, changes the redness of the blood into pallor [Al. “with pallor”] and permits nothing healthy to remain in the body, to such an extent that even the sweetest honey seems bitter.

Those who earlier heard in the Church, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet,” and themselves said, “How sweet are your sayings to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII), should be called παραπικραίνοντες (*parapikrainontes*, “those who make bitter”), and their waters and rains should not drip sweetness. Let them not belong to the land of promise, which we read flows with milk and honey; rather, let them be called Mara, that is, “bitterness.”

These people multiplied gardens for themselves, into which Naboth preferred to die rather than have his vineyard turned (III Kings XXI). [Al. Nabutha] “Let the weak person eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV). And because heretics are always swollen with pride, falling into the condemnation of the devil, promising themselves great things, and fabricating images of good things in order to mix poisons with honey, they boast that they possess vineyards, olive groves, and fig gardens. But their vineyard is the vineyard of Sodom; their olive trees are not good olives but wild olives, which the Apostle commands to be grafted into the roots of good olive trees (Rom. XI). They also have fig gardens of such a kind that they fill a basket with the worst figs, figs which Jeremiah testifies cannot be eaten because of their bitterness (Jerem. XXIX).

When the Lord comes upon them, he curses them with eternal dryness (Mark XI), so that they never bear fruit and cannot deceive passersby with the greenness of their leaves. And so that we may understand that the gardens, vineyards, olive groves, and fig gardens of the heretics are referred to in an evil sense, he added the word “your” to each expression, showing that they belong not to God but to the heretics: “your gardens, your vineyards, your olive trees, and your fig trees.” The locust laid waste to all these, the final form of every punishment. It does not fly away like a grasshopper, leaving things half-eaten as it runs here and there; rather, it remains with the crops destined to perish and, moving slowly and biting sluggishly, consumes everything.

After suffering these things, they still did not wish to return to the Lord.

(Vers. 10.) “I sent death upon you by the way of Egypt; I struck your young men with the sword, together with the captivity of your horses. And I caused the stench of your camps to rise into your nostrils; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

**LXX:** “I sent [Al. “sent forth”] death upon you by the way of Egypt, and I killed your young men with the sword, together with the captivity of your horses. And I brought out your camps in fire, in my anger; and not even then did you return to me, says the Lord.”

Through every scourge and torment Israel is instructed. Therefore, at the time when they were seeking aid from the Egyptians, death is sent against them; their young men are struck with the sword; and the horses they had multiplied for themselves against God’s command are enclosed by savage captivity, so that the stench of the camps and the odor of the dying army may fill the nostrils of the living. And when he had done these things also, in order to rebuke the sinners and correct the erring, even then they did not return to him, says the Lord.

He sends death not only at that time but every day by the way of Egypt, so that whoever has trodden the Egyptian path may, dying, hear the Apostle teaching: “For in that I died, I died to sin; but in that I live, I live to God” (Gal. II). And elsewhere: “If we have died with Christ, we shall also live with him” (Rom. VI, 8). And again: “Always carrying in my body the dying of Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 10). And once more: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20).

By this death the Lord wishes to give us life, so that, dying to sin, we may live to God. We die to sin when we put to death our earthly members: fornication, impurity, lust, idolatry, and the rest.

We read in Isaiah—at least according to the Septuagint translators; for in Hebrew the passage is different—“I sent death upon Jacob, and it came upon Israel” (Isa. IX). Jacob is the name of the body at birth; Israel is the name of blessing. Because he wrestled all night and prevailed in the struggle (Gen. XXXII), and at the rising of the morning star was able to say with the Apostle, “The night is far gone, the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII, 12), he therefore received the name Israel, “one who sees God.”

Death is therefore first sent upon Jacob, so that we may put to death our earthly members and, through the mortification of bodily members, come to the death of Israel, so that all the incentives to disturbance within us may die. God strikes whatever is strong in evil; the perverse youth is cut off so that it may not reach old age; and he hands over the horses to captivity so that they may not plunge headlong into hell. He causes the stench of the camps to rise into their nostrils so that they may recognize their sins and sense their foulness, saying with David: “My wounds have become foul and festering because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6).

When he had done these things with the purpose of healing, even then they did not return to him, says the Lord.

(Vers. 11.) “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

**LXX:** “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand plucked from the fire; and not even then did you turn back to me, says the Lord.”

This is the final remedy for the ten tribes, for heretics, and for all sinners: after he has sent death upon them by the way of Egypt, struck their young men with the sword, consumed their horses, caused the stench of their camps to rise into their nostrils, and they still have not returned to him, he overthrows them as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. Once they have been overthrown, because of the likeness of their crimes to those of Sodom and Gomorrah, and once the divine fire has burned up the worst structures within them, they themselves are saved like a brand snatched from the fire.

As Lot was saved while Sodom perished, losing his possessions and a part of his body, which we understand to mean his wife (Gen. XIX), so all these people, losing the riches of the Sodomites, may escape naked, according to what we read in the Apostle: “If anyone’s work which he built upon the foundation remains, he will receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (I Cor. III, 14–15). Whoever is saved through fire is snatched like a brand from the fire.

To such people, whom the Savior rebuked in the Gospel, saying, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John VIII, 39), John the Baptist says: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Produce, therefore, fruit worthy of repentance, and do not presume to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III, 7–9).

Thus Israel and all heretics, because they possessed the works of Sodom and Gomorrah, are overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, so that they may be freed like a brand snatched from the fire. This is what we read in the prophet: “Sodom shall be restored to its former state” (Ezek. XVI, 55), so that the person who is a Sodomite through his own vice, after the works of Sodom have burned within him, may be restored to his former condition.

(Vers. 12, 13.) “Therefore I shall do these things to you, Israel; but after I have done these things to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel, for behold, he forms the mountains, creates the wind, announces his word to humanity, makes the morning mist, and treads upon the heights of the earth: the Lord God of hosts is his name.”

**LXX:** “Therefore I shall do this [Vulg. “these things”] to you, Israel; nevertheless, because I shall do this to you, prepare to call upon your God, Israel. For behold, he makes firm the thunder, creates the spirit, announces his Christ to humanity, makes morning and mist, and ascends upon the heights of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name.”

In place of what we translated “afterward,” the Hebrew has ECEB (), which Aquila rendered ὕστερον (*hysteron*), that is, “afterward,” and Theodotion “at the very end,” while the Septuagint has “nevertheless.” In Hebrew the passage may be read as follows: “Therefore I shall do these things to you, Israel, afterward”—that is, after a very long time and in the last ages—so that the sentence begins again from another starting point: “And when I am about to do this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel.”

Again, where the Septuagint translated “prepare to call upon your God,” and where we have placed, following Theodotion, “prepare to meet your God,” Symmachus and the Fifth Edition translated, “prepare to oppose your God.” In Hebrew this is said as HECHIN LACERATH ELOICA ().

[Note: The present-day Hebrew copies have *vav* in place of *yod*.]

For “mountains,” which in Hebrew are called ARIM (), the Septuagint alone rendered βροντή (*brontē*), that is, “thunder.” Why they called the Hebrew word RUA (), which we translated “wind,” “spirit,” is clear: the same word means both wind and spirit.

What follows, “announcing his word to humanity,” all the translators rendered as we did. The Septuagint alone translated it, “announcing his Christ to humanity,” deceived by the similarity and ambiguity of the word. If we read “his Christ,” which in Hebrew is called MESSIO (), it is written with the letters MEM, SIN, IOB, HETH, and VAU, as the Septuagint thought.

[Note: A reading in the Cistercian manuscript suggests that Aquila’s translation could most correctly be restored as τίς ἡ ὁμιλία αὐτοῦ or ἑαυτοῦ, “what is his—or your—conversation?” Other books have τίς ὁμιλίας αὐτοῦ or ἑαυτοῦ. Indeed, the Roman edition of the Septuagint quotes Aquila’s words in this passage better than Jerome does.]

But if, as it stands in Hebrew, we read it according to Aquila as τὴν ὁμιλίαν αὐτοῦ, according to Symmachus as τὸ φώνημα αὐτοῦ, according to Theodotion as τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ, and according to the Fifth Edition as τὴν ἀδολεσχίαν αὐτοῦ, all of these interpret it as “his word.” It is written with the letters MEM and HE, which give MA (), that is, “what” or “which.” Then come SIN, IOD, and HETH, which we read as SIA (), that is, “word.” The O, written with the single letter VAU, signifies αὐτοῦ, “his”; and, joined together, it is read MASIO (), having from the preceding word HE as an additional second letter.

We have spoken about the variety of interpretation, which will be burdensome to the careless but pleasing to the diligent. Let us now pass to the meaning of what has been written.

“I gave you dulness of teeth, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. I withheld rain from you, and I rained upon one city and did not rain upon another; and two or three cities came to one city to drink water, but were not satisfied. Yet even then you did not return to me, says the Lord.

“I struck you with scorching wind and jaundice, your gardens, vineyards, olive groves, and fig gardens; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.

“I sent death upon you by the way of Egypt, struck your young men with the sword, and caused the stench of your camps to rise into your nostrils; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.

“I overthrew you as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

Therefore I shall do these things to you, O Israel, so that you who have despised what has passed may at least be corrected by what I am about to bring upon you. When he says, “I shall do these things to you,” he does not say what he is going to do,

[Note: Compare the man who follows Rufinus and disparages the exposition of the holy Father.]

so that while Israel remains uncertain about the individual kinds of punishment—for this reason they are more terrifying, since they suspect everything—it may repent, lest God inflict what he threatens.

“After I have done to you what I testify that I shall do, prepare to call upon the Lord your God.” For “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel II). Or else, “prepare to meet your God,” so that you may receive the Lord who comes to you with complete eagerness.

He is the one who makes the thunder firm—or confirms the mountains.

[Note: Two manuscripts insert *argue* here.]

At his voice the hinges of heaven and the foundations of the earth are shaken (Ecclus. XVI). He is the one who creates the spirit. In this passage we do not understand “the Holy Spirit,” as the heretics suppose, but wind, or the human spirit: “No one knows what is in a person except the spirit that is in him,” and this spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. VIII). Or certainly we should understand “spirit” as the soul, according to what is written: “You take away their spirit, and they fail and return to their dust” (Ps. CIII, 19); and, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,” and, saying this, he expired (Luke XXIII, 46).

When he has created the spirit, he announces his word to human beings, or he announces to a person that person's word, since he knows the secrets of thoughts and understands what the hidden mind considers in silent speech, according to what we read in Jeremiah in Hebrew: “The heart of humanity is small and inscrutable; who will know it? I, the Lord, search the heart and test the kidneys” (Jerem. XVII, 9–10).

Scripture also bears witness to this in the hundred and thirty-eighth Psalm: “Your eyes saw my unfinished state.” The sense is: before I was formed, before I was shaped into limbs, while I was still contained in the seed, your eyes saw me. And Jeremiah hears from the Lord: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet to the nations” (Jerem. I, 5). And the evangelist says: “The Lord, seeing their thoughts” (Luke XI, 17).

But if we read “announcing his word to humanity,” it must be understood according to the earlier statement in which he says: “The Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets” (above, III, 7).

The one who announces the thoughts of humanity and its word—or his own—is also the one who makes the dawn and the morning light, fills everything with clouds, and walks upon the heights of the earth. His name is the Lord God Almighty.

[Note: In place of “in the Septuagint,” the manuscripts prefer “in the Church.”]

In place of this, the Septuagint reads: “announcing his Christ to humanity.” On this occasion the heretics wish to assert that the Holy Spirit was created, following the sequence: “creating the spirit and announcing his Christ to humanity,” as though the former had been created and the latter announced among the peoples.

We shall answer them according to their own sense and according to the Vulgate edition: the one who is Creator of all things and makes the thunder firm—or forms the mountains—then brings forth the winds from his treasuries and, as the Creator of the universe, promises his Son Christ to humanity.

After Christ has been announced, the light of truth is then opened to us, not perfectly—for now “we see in part and we know in part,” and through a mirror and image we contemplate the things that are to come (I Cor. XIII). Hence the passage continues: “making morning and mist, and ascending upon the heights of the earth.”

For the Lord is exalted in the heights and, being exalted, does not dwell among lowly things. But the Creator of the mountains ascends upon the mountains, among those who possess citizenship in heaven; and those who walk in the flesh do not live according to the flesh but according to the spirit.

But if, according to Symmachus and Aquila, we read, “I shall do these things to you, Israel, afterward,” and, “When I have done these things to you, prepare yourself to oppose your God” [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads *prepare*; the Palatine manuscripts, *opposing* for *to oppose*], it must be understood as follows:

“I did what the preceding passage described in order to correct you. Since you did not wish to return to me, I shall do to you what is contained in my secret counsel. You killed the servants whom I had sent to you; at last I shall send my Son. But according to your custom, by which you have always resisted the Lord’s will, prepare yourself to contradict and oppose your God,” according to what is written: “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed” (Luke II, 34).

He says this not as a command concerning what Israel ought to do, but as a prediction of what it will voluntarily do, rebuking and reproving it, so that, at least when corrected, it may not do what has been foretold.

[Col. 1036A] (Cap. V.—Vers. 1, 2.) “Hear this word, which [Al. “whereby”] I raise over you as a lamentation. The house of Israel has fallen; it shall not rise again. The virgin of Israel has been cast upon her land; there is no one to raise her up.”

**LXX:** “Hear this word, which I shall take up over you as a lamentation. The house of Israel has fallen; it shall not rise again. The virgin of Israel has been cast upon her land; there is no one to raise her up.”

As far as the order of the text and the truth of the history already begun are concerned, the ten tribes called Israel, once led into captivity, never afterward returned to their land. The people of Israel is called a virgin, not because it remained in the purity of virginity, but because it was once joined to the Lord like a virgin.

Therefore the prophet is commanded to take up a lamentation over it, since it will not be restored to its former condition.

As for the spiritual understanding, the prophet takes up a lamentation over all Israel—that is, over the one who perceived God with the mind but afterward ceased to serve him—according to the command given to Ezekiel (Ezek. II) to eat the book written within and without, in which were lamentation, song, and woe.

Within, understand the Song of Solomon that follows, where he says: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song I, 3), and the forty-fourth Psalm, in which it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” Outside is whatever is read in the letter and seen in the outer shell but is not grasped in the marrow of the spirit.

Thus, both according to the letter and according to allegorical interpretation, all the books of the prophets contain lamentation over those who repent after sins, song over those who are stained by no defilement of sins and are worthy of song and praise, and woe over those who do not repent but store up wrath for themselves according to the hardness of their heart on the day of wrath.

But if, as we have said, the lamentation is over those who repent, and repentance restores the health of a wound, how can the Septuagint say, “The house of Israel has fallen; it shall rise no more. The virgin of Israel has gone astray upon her land; there is no one to raise her up”?

This can be resolved as follows: after the house of Israel has fallen by its own will, it will not recover its former dignity; after the virgin of Israel has gone astray in her own land, she will no longer be able to find one who raises her up.

Consider also the precise force of the words. One who is a house and is counted among the multitude is said to fall. But one who belongs to the number of virgins, if she goes astray, cannot be raised up even after a slight—or indeed any—sin. This does not mean that she will not be raised at all, but that the virgin of Israel will not be raised, and the Lord of Israel will not rise again in her. For the glory of one who has always followed the Lord is not the same as that of one who has wandered from the flock and afterward has been carried back on the shoulders of the good shepherd (Luke XV).

Therefore, through another prophet, the Lord says: “I desire the repentance of the sinner rather than his death” (Ezek. XVIII, 32). Repentance is considered better when compared with death and hell, not with the purest holiness and the Church of Christ, which has neither wrinkle nor stain.

We say this not to abolish, with Novatian, the hope of repentance, but to make those more fearful and therefore more watchful who, because the door of repentance stands open, lose the present while hoping for the future; and those who could have remained without a wound carelessly receive one, so that afterward they may be tormented by pain.

“There are many dwelling places with my Father” (John XIV), and “star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV): the saints shining like the sun and moon, the evening star and the morning star. Those who have repented after sin will, according to the diversity of their merits, be made equal to other stars.

[Note: Two Palatine manuscripts, as also one manuscript of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, read “according to the diversity of the heretics.” Martianay found this reading.]

(Vers. 3.) “For thus says the Lord God: From the city from which a thousand went forth, a hundred shall be left in it; and from the one from which a hundred went forth, ten shall be left in it, in the house of Israel.”

**LXX:** Likewise.

The divine word gives the reasons why the house of Israel, having fallen, does not rise again, and why the virgin of Israel, having gone astray or having been cast upon the land, has no one to raise her up: “The city,” it says, “from which a thousand went forth, a hundred shall be left in it; and from the one from which a hundred went forth, ten shall be left in it, in the house of Israel.” Thus, where there had once been a multitude, because of the immense devastation scarcely a tenth will remain.

[Note: The words “the LXX likewise,” absent from the common editions, are supplied by our manuscripts.]

And lest, while clinging to the letter, we leave untouched the mysteries of the numbers, let us observe that the number seven is holy, as the Sabbath also proves, on which God rested from all his works (Gen. II). He commands that no servile work be done on it except what pertains to the soul, and that we carry no burdens on it (Num. XV).

Therefore the man who gathered wood in the wilderness on the Sabbath, wood destined to burn, was condemned by the Lord’s sentence. Seven weeks also complete the number of holy Pentecost; and the Jubilee year of remission and the sound of the trumpets is framed by this number. In the seventh month booths are set up, and the Hebrew, after serving six years, is freed [Note: Victor preferred “is set free,” on the evidence of the Florentine manuscripts] in the seventh year.

Secular philosophy also knows this, as do the books of physicians. Galen, most eloquent and learned, wrote three books περὶ κρίσεων καὶ τῶν κρισίμων ἡμερῶν (*peri kriseōn kai tōn krisimōn hēmerōn*), “On crises and critical days.”

[Note: The preposition περὶ seems preferable here, as in Victor’s edition, and the title of the book itself supports it. In other books, instead of κριτικῶν, there is κρισίμων.]

In these books, showing the power of the number seven, he says that the most violent fevers are resolved on the seventh day. Or, if the quantity of harmful fluid and phlegm is so great that it has not been consumed by the fever of the first week, the final day of the second week is awaited, that is, the fourteenth day. If the νόσος (*nosos*, “disease”), to speak according to Hippocrates, overcomes this day, they pass to the twenty-first day, that is, the end of the third week.

Thus, from the beginning of the world, days were established in such a way that all labors and troubles should come to rest at the number seven. Finally, the captivity of the people of Israel and the destruction of the Temple were completed in the seventieth year of desolation, and seven stars are said to wander according to the number of the days.

[Note: Petrus Petitus, in Book III, chapter 3, of his *Miscellaneous Observations*, argues that *hebdomada* should be read here instead of *errantia*.]

Cicero tells more fully of the mysteries of this number in the Dream of Scipio. Plato’s *Timaeus* is exceedingly obscure, a book which not even Cicero’s golden eloquence makes clearer.

[Note: He wishes the passage to be read: “and Plato’s exceedingly obscure *Timaeus*, a book which not even Cicero’s…”]

[Note: So also in the Preface to Book XII on Isaiah: “Finally, while discussing the harmony of the world, the course of the stars, and numbers in the *Timaeus*, Cicero himself, who translated it, confesses that he does not understand it. Indeed, Cicero himself says in Book VII, Letter 13 to Atticus: ‘I did not fully understand the riddle of the Oppii from Velia; for it is more obscure in number than Plato.’”]

Just as the number seven has its mystery, so the sanctified and perfect number—and, so to speak, the true number—is the one held together by unity and enclosed within the majesty of the one God.

Therefore the Son says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 11). And, wishing all to be one with the Father, he says to him: “Father, grant that just as you and I are one, so they also may be one in us” (ibid. XVII, 21).

The first blessedness, therefore, is to be in the first number, which is one and true; the second is in the second, that is, in the number ten; the third is in the third, that is, in the number one hundred. For just as the decad is completed by a tenth unity, so the hundred is constructed from ten decads. The fourth number, which is contained in the thousand, consists of ten hundreds.

When someone has repented, therefore, he scarcely returns from the thousand, the fourth number, to the hundred, the third number. Again, one who is in the hundred scarcely returns to the second number of the first decad. Thus it happens that the house of Israel, which had fallen, cannot rise, and that the virgin of Israel, which had gone astray, has no one on earth to raise her up.

The reason is that one who has once departed from unity and lost the glory of that purest virginity—of which the Apostle says, “I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI), a virgin in whom there is neither stain nor wrinkle—will not be able to recover the former state and blessedness of unity. Scarcely will it be granted him to return from a thousand to a hundred and from a hundred to ten.

I have spoken briefly of these matters, lest I seem to have entirely avoided allegorical interpretation in this chapter because of the difficulty of the numbers.

(Vers. 4, 5.) “For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me, and you shall live. And do not seek Bethel, and do not enter Galgal, and do not cross over to Beersheba; for [Vulg.: “you shall not cross over, because”] Galgal shall surely be led captive, and Bethel shall become useless.”

**LXX:** “For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me, and you shall live; and do not seek Bethel, and do not enter Galgal, and do not cross over the Well of the Oath, because Galgal shall be led captive, and Bethel shall be as though it did not exist.”

It is the custom of Scripture always to join joyful things to adverse ones. After God has threatened sad things, he summons those whom he has terrified to repentance, according to what we read in Isaiah: “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, evil seed, lawless children” (Isa. I, 4).

After he had said, “Your land is desolate; your cities are consumed by fire; strangers shall eat your regions before your eyes [Al. “in your sight”],” he speaks to them with better promises: “Wash yourselves; be clean. Remove your evils from your souls. Learn to do good [Al. “to do what is good”]; seek judgment; judge the orphan; justify the widow; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord” (ibid. I, 16–17).

Just as in Isaiah he supports with gentle speech those whom he had terrified with a severe voice, so in this prophet, after saying, “The house of Israel has fallen; it shall not rise again; the virgin of Israel has gone astray upon the land; there is no one to raise her up,” he speaks to them and says:

“House of Israel”—that is, the ten tribes—“seek me and you shall live,” because in not seeking me you are dead. When you seek, you will find; and when you have found, you will live.

“Do not seek Bethel,” where there was the golden calf; nor Galgal, a place of idolatry, concerning which I also spoke above: “All their wickedness is in Galgal” (Hosea IX, 15). “And you shall not cross over into Beersheba.”

He appropriately says, “You shall not cross over into Beersheba,” that is, to the Well of the Oath, where, whenever the tribe of Judah went astray, it was accustomed to worship idols. Israel was so inflamed with the worship of images that, not content with its own idols, it crossed over to foreign ones.

“Galgal,” he says, “shall be led captive, and Bethel shall become useless,” or entirely cease to exist, when the idols within it have been overturned.

He says nothing at all about Beersheba, because once the ten tribes had been defeated, the city called Beersheba, which at that time lay in the tribe of Judah, was neither captured nor destroyed.

We must also observe that in the present passage the Septuagint translated the name Beersheba, saying “Well of the Oath,” while later they retained the name itself: “Your God lives, Dan; and the way of Beersheba lives.” They called it “the way of Beersheba” because people from Israel traveled a long distance to the farthest boundaries of Judah, which were at Gerar and bordered the Egyptian wilderness, in order to worship idols.

This is the place where Abraham lived. Because he and Abimelech swore a mutual covenant after giving seven sheep, it was called the Well of the Oath, or the Well of the Seven, because of the number of the seven sheep (Gen. XXV). For SABE () signifies both.

According to the laws of allegory, he commands the house of Israel—that is, those who claim for themselves knowledge of God—not to seek Bethel, not to enter Galgal, and not to cross over or ascend to the Well of the Oath, but rather to seek God and live in him.

They seek Bethel, which is interpreted as “house of God,” who say, “The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord,” and trust in buildings concerning which the Lord spoke to his disciples: “The days will come when not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed” (Luke XXI, 6).

They enter Galgal who, after the coming of Christ, again desire to be circumcised. For the people were circumcised a second time at Galgal. Hence the place received its name because the Lord removed from them the reproach of Egypt (Josh. V).

“And you shall not cross over into Beersheba,” he says, “or to the Well of the Oath.” Do not think that these are the boundaries of Judea which, according to the literal sense, Scripture once promised from Dan to Beersheba; and do not say any longer with the prophet, “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV, 1). Rather, hear the apostles: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 4).

For Galgal—that is, circumcision of the flesh—will be led captive by the true circumcision of the heart; and Bethel, which you think to be the house of God, will not subsist—or, as I think better, will become useless, that is, AVEN (). It will no longer be called the house of God but will be called the useless house, or the house of an idol.

Alternatively: He seeks Bethel who follows only the letter that kills and does not seek the meaning, which is God, in the words. He enters Galgal who strives toward greater revelations and promises himself knowledge of heavenly things; and he crosses over, or ascends, to the well from which the Samaritan woman, desiring to draw water that could not quench thirst, did not know the one from whose belly flow rivers of living water springing up into eternal life (John IV).

### (Verse 6)

Seek the Lord and live, lest he perhaps burn like fire the house of Joseph; he will devour it, and there will be no one to extinguish Bethel. The Septuagint reads: “Seek the Lord and live, lest the house of Joseph be kindled like fire; let it devour it, and let there be no one to extinguish the house of Israel.”

Just as it is said in the person of God, “Seek me, and you shall live,” so the prophet speaks concerning the Lord, that they should seek him and live. For in seeking the Lord they begin to live; but if they do not seek him, and therefore do not live, the house of Joseph will immediately be kindled like fire. Because of Jeroboam, who was from the tribe of Ephraim and the house of Joseph, we must understand this as referring to the ten tribes, which were called Israel and retained their former name because they constituted the greater part of the people. The two tribes ruled by the line of David, who was from the tribe of Judah, were called Judah and possessed Jerusalem, where the temple of God was.

When the house of Joseph has been kindled, it will devour and consume Bethel, concerning which I said above: “Do not seek Bethel”; and there will be no one to extinguish it when it has been burned by its kings. For “Bethel,” the Septuagint reads “house of Israel,” interpreting the sense rather than the word, so that, under King Jeroboam and all the kings who subsequently succeeded him in power, the ten tribes called Israel may burn.

This is the fire that is kindled—or rather, that shines forth and inflames—the house of Joseph, so that Bethel may be consumed. Concerning it another passage says: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isaiah 50:11).

Since we have often referred the house of Joseph—because of Jeroboam, who separated God’s people from the line of David, made golden calves in Dan and Bethel, and said, “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (1 Kings 22:36)—to the person of heretics, who, with carefully composed speech, have fashioned and worship images that are attractive, beautiful, and, so to speak, golden, and who worship the works of their hands and promise themselves an image of agriculture under the form of cows, the following is said to them:

“Seek the Lord and live”—him who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:16)—so that, after walking in him and finding the truth, those who were previously dead may then begin to live. And unless they do this, they will be consumed by the fires of the devil. No one among their leaders, who themselves have been inflamed by heretical fire, will be found capable of extinguishing the flame that devours all things, especially Bethel, which assumes for itself the false name “house of God.”

### (Verses 8 and following)

“Those who turn justice into wormwood and abandon righteousness on the earth, who make Arcturus and Orion, who turn darkness into morning and change day into night, who call for the waters of the sea and pour them out upon the face of the earth—the Lord is his name, who smiles destruction upon the strong and brings devastation upon the powerful.”

The Septuagint reads: “He who makes judgment on high and has established righteousness on earth, who makes all things, transforms and turns the shadow of death into morning, and darkens day into night; who calls the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth—the Lord God Almighty is his name; who divides ruin upon strength and brings misery upon a fortress.”

[Note: The words “the Lord Almighty” are absent from the Cistercian manuscript and are also lacking in some Greek copies, especially the Roman one. Shortly afterward, the words “upon strength,” which had been absent from all previously published books, have been supplied from the same Cistercian manuscript as genuine and necessary. They are also found in the Greek text, with no manuscript, so far as I know, disagreeing: Ὁ διαιρῶν συντριμμὸν ἐπὶ ἰσχὺν, καὶ ταλαιπωρίαν ἐπὶ ὀχύρωμα ἐπάγων—“who divides ruin upon strength and brings misery upon a fortress.”]

The Vulgate edition differs greatly from the Hebrew truth in this passage, as a prudent reader immediately understands from what we have set forth, even without our warning. Let us therefore first explain it according to the Hebrews, and afterward, with Christ revealing it if we are worthy, say what seems to us to be intended in the translation of the Septuagint.

The house of Joseph—that is, the house of Ephraim, and therefore the royal house—and Bethel, or, as the Septuagint translated it, the house of Israel—that is, kings and peoples, worshipers and idols together—will be overthrown, because by unjust judgment they provoked God to anger. They turned the sweetness of judgment into the bitterness of wormwood, a kind of exceedingly bitter herb, taking up iniquity and abandoning righteousness.

What this righteousness is, the following verse shows: “He who makes Arcturus and Orion, who turns darkness into morning and changes day into night.” Concerning him he had said above: “Forming the mountains, creating the wind, and declaring his word to human beings, making the morning mist and treading upon the heights of the earth: the Lord God of hosts is his name.” He is the Creator of Arcturus, which in Hebrew is called *CHIMA* (), and which Symmachus and Theodotion translate as εἰς πλειάδα, “into the Pleiad,” and which people commonly call Boötes. The following constellation, Orion, is called *CHASIL* () in Hebrew. Symmachus translated it simply as “stars,” while Theodotion interpreted it as “evening.” The Hebrew teacher who instructed us in the sacred Scriptures thinks that *CHASIL* should be interpreted as “splendor” and understood generally as shining stars.

When we hear “Arcturus and Orion,” we must not follow the fables of the poets and their ridiculous and monstrous lies, by which they even attempt to defame heaven and place the reward of sexual immorality among the constellations, saying (Aeneid, books 1 and 3):

> Arcturus, the rain-bringing Hyades, and the twin Triones;  
> And he looks upon armed Orion, surrounded with gold.

But we must know that Hebrew names, which are called something else among the Hebrews, have been translated into our language by the names of pagan fables. We cannot understand what is being said except through those terms that we have learned by usage and absorbed along with error.

Thus, in the Book of Kings, the Greek translators rendered the Hebrew *RAPHAIM* () as “Titans,” although among the pagans this is a very famous myth. From it they compose praises of the gods in their *gigantomachies* (γιγαντομαχίαι), recounting the weapons of Typhoeus and the mountain Etna placed upon Enceladus, whose movement causes Trinacria to tremble.

[Note: Claudian left us a work on the *Gigantomachia*, which has reached us incomplete. See Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book 1, chapter 20. MART.—Claudian gave his poem this title; a substantial portion of it is missing.
