Jerome praises him in his commentary on Isaiah 27: “A certain poet played finely with Enceladus in the *Gigantomachia*: ‘Where are you fleeing, Enceladus? Wherever you approach, you will always be beneath Jupiter.’”]

This God, however, the Creator of all things, who makes Arcturus and Orion, changes night into day and day into night, and purifies and filters the exceedingly bitter waters of the sea, suspended by ethereal heat, into the sweet taste of rain, like a medicinal gourd that draws moisture and blood upward by the heat of its upper circuit. From this we learn the origin of the rains.

As for what follows—“who smiles destruction upon the strong”—it returns to the present subject, and the order is: He who is the Creator of all things also threatens captivity upon Samaria and brings devastation upon the powerful, because they have turned judgment into wormwood and abandoned righteousness on the earth.

Where we said “who smiles,” Aquila translated ὁ μειδιῶν, “the one who smiles.” Properly speaking, *meidíama* means what we may call a “smile” or “smirking,” when someone is angry and pretends to smile with his lips slightly parted, thereby displaying the magnitude of his anger.

Let us also interpret the passage according to the Septuagint. God makes judgment on high when he judges the truth and repays each person according to his work. Anyone who desires to be his imitator and son, and to be perfect just as his Father is perfect, who dwells in heaven (Matthew 5), makes judgment on high. He does not imitate that judge who neither feared God nor respected human beings and who, through the perversity of his judgment, did not raise his sentence toward heaven but dragged it down toward low things (Luke 18).

What follows—“and established righteousness on the earth”—we should understand in relation to the fact that he has given us Christ as his righteousness and has not cast it away, but has placed it upon the earth, so that, after every iniquity has been overcome, he might make us heavenly beings out of earthly ones.

I think that a pagan poet also stole this idea from this passage. Speaking of the simplicity and blessedness of country people, he wrote:

> Through them  
> Justice, departing from the earth, left her final footprints.

When they say, “making all things and transforming them,” they encompass Arcturus and Orion in a single expression, neglecting to transfer the proper names into the Greek language. God transforms all things when he makes heavenly beings out of earthly ones and grants human beings the likeness of angels; when the moon will shine with the sun’s radiance and the sun will possess sevenfold light; when the animal, weak, and corruptible human being is transformed into one who is spiritual, strong, and incorruptible—changing the glory, not the nature; when the wise will shine like the splendor of the firmament; and when what is written is fulfilled: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41). This occurs when every creature is freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

This God, who transforms all things, also changes the shadow of death into light (Luke 1), when those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death saw a great light, and those who were sons of night and darkness became sons of light and sons of day.

This is the God who also turns day into darkness: the day of those who said, “Crucify him, crucify him; take such a man away from the earth” (John 19:6). From the sixth hour onward, as a symbol of Jewish blindness, day was turned into night. And not only according to the literal sense, but also according to a higher understanding, the light that arose for them in the Law and the Prophets was turned into darkness because they did not understand what they were reading or hearing, so that what is written concerning them might be fulfilled: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually” (Psalm 68:24).

This God calls the water of the sea to himself and pours it out upon the face of the earth, making the righteous out of sinners. To explain this, let us give only one example for the sake of brevity.

The apostle Paul, like a violent whirlwind, a savage storm, and the surge of a swelling sea, persecuted the Church of God and sought to overwhelm it. When he was called by the Lord, he was poured out upon the face of the whole earth, preaching the Gospel from Jerusalem to Illyricum. He built not upon another’s foundation, where Christ had already been preached (Romans 15), but extended his course as far as Spain; and from the Red Sea—or rather, from Ocean to Ocean—he ran, imitating his Lord and the sun of righteousness, concerning whom we read: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course reaches to its highest point” (Psalm 18:7). The earth would fail before his zeal for preaching.

This God also divides ruin upon strength, making those who are wickedly strong weak, so that they may imitate the Apostle, who said: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12). For “the children of this age are wiser than the children of light in their own generation” (Luke 16:8). Bodily strength is weakness of the soul; conversely, strength of the soul is weakness of the body.

Therefore, the Lord, who orders all things rationally and accomplishes everything with true judgment, divides ruin upon the strong enemy, so that he may bring misery upon the fortress that raises itself against the knowledge of God. Concerning this we also read in Proverbs: “The wise man entered fortified cities and destroyed the fortress in which the impious trusted” (Proverbs 21:22).

This applies to every worldly power, but especially against heretics, who attempt to strengthen the falsehood of their doctrines through arguments, sophistries, and dialectical skill. The wise man, aided by God, destroys this power and shows every fortress to be utterly vain, so that he may bring misery upon it; and, with pride humbled, he may say with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24).

### (Verse 10)

“They hated the one who rebuked in the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke with integrity.”

The Septuagint reads: “They hated the one who reproved in the gates, and they abhorred the holy word.”

These are the people upon whom God smiles destruction and brings devastation, who are strong in evil and hate the one who rebukes them in the gate—that is, in judgment—whether myself or other prophets who were sent to them. They abhorred the one who spoke with integrity, or, as Symmachus translated it, “the undefiled word,” or, as Theodotion and the Septuagint translated it, “the holy word.”

According to the ancient Jewish custom, judgments were held at the gate of the people, as we often read and have frequently explained. Thus neither a farmer coming to court would be frightened by the crowds and unfamiliar appearance of the city, nor would an inhabitant of the city have to travel far from the city and seek transportation by animals. This is what we say according to the literal sense.

But it is a great sin to hate the one who rebukes, especially if he rebukes you not out of hatred but out of love; if he speaks privately to you, then with one other brother present, and afterward in the presence of the Church, so that it may be clear that he brings the accusation not from a desire to slander but for your correction (Matthew 18).

We often read in Scripture of two kinds of gates, the gates of death and life, of vices and virtues. Thus we read in the Psalms: “You who raise me up from the gates of death, that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Isaiah 9:16). There is no doubt that this signifies the exalted mountain of Zion, the Church, and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, the multitude of angels, and the Church of the firstborn who are written in heaven.

Whoever has been exalted in the gates of Zion will not be able to fear the gates of death, concerning which the Lord said to Peter: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

We plainly learn of the gates of virtue in another psalm: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; I will enter them and give thanks to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm 17:19).

Finally, Wisdom also spoke confidently in the gates of the city:

> As long as the innocent possess righteousness, they will not be put to shame.

[Note: Martianus reads “sitting” (*considens*), contrary to the manuscripts and the Greek θαρροῦσα, “speaking confidently.”]

I think that the gates of the city—that is, of the soul believing in Christ—are the virtues through which Christ enters those who believe. Since it is not written in which gates they hated the one who rebuked them, whether in evil or in good gates, let us apply the statement to both.

Standing in the gates of vices, the prophet rebukes sinners, and therefore they hold him in contempt. Or perhaps the prophet himself stands at the gates and beginnings of virtues, and is hated by those whom he rebukes. It is not enough for sinners to hate the one who reproves or rebukes in the gates; they must also abhor the holy word that proceeds from his mouth. For whoever does not receive the prophet does not receive the one who sent him (Matthew 10).

But if they abhorred the holy word, or the one who spoke with integrity—moreover, the holy word is the Lord Jesus, concerning whom it is said, “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15:10)—then all Jews who say “Anathema to Jesus” abhor the word of God, which is perfect, holy, and undefiled.

For piety is an abomination to the sinner. Whatever we have said about the Jews can also be applied to pagans and heretics. Some of them abhor all the sacred Scriptures, in which the word of God is found; others, by perversely understanding what they read, place an abomination in the house of God.

### (Verses 11 and following)

“Therefore, because you plundered the poor and took choice spoil from him, you shall build houses of hewn stone, but you shall not dwell in them. You shall plant delightful vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine, because I know your many crimes and your mighty sins: enemies of the righteous, receiving gifts and oppressing the poor in the gate. Therefore the prudent person will be silent at that time, because it is an evil time.”

The Septuagint reads: “Therefore, because you struck the poor with your fist and accepted choice gifts from them, you built houses of hewn stones, but you shall not dwell in them. You planted desirable vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine, because I know your many impieties and your mighty sins: trampling the righteous, accepting exchanges, and turning aside the poor in the gates. Therefore the one who understands will be silent at that time, because it is an evil time.”

[Note: At this point the Cistercian manuscript also omits the word “with the fist.”]

So that Israel might not think that it was handed over to enemies for punishment solely because of idolatry, he adds the other crimes it had committed after abandoning the worship of truth.

“You plundered,” he says, “the poor,” so that you might take away from one who scarcely had what was necessary for subsistence; and whatever precious or beautiful thing you saw, you devoted to your own use. Thus, with the price of what you had robbed and taken from the poor, you built houses of hewn stone, clothing the walls with marble after stripping people bare.

Because you built these houses from robbery, and prepared them not merely for habitation and shelter, as human necessity requires, but also for beauty and luxury, you will be taken away by sudden captivity or death and will not dwell in them.

You also planted the most desirable vineyards, preparing them for future drinking, but you will not drink their wine, because I have known all your crimes and sins, and your mighty sins, which provoked my anger. You are enemies of righteousness, or of every righteous person; you accept gifts and oppress the poor in judgment.

Therefore, when the poor and prudent person sees the judge who has been bribed, he will be silent at that time, because it is an evil time.

[Note: For *redemptum*, “ransomed,” which we restored from the Palatine and Cistercian manuscripts, Martianus retained *furentem*, “raging.” Victor had previously noted that the words “enemies of the righteous, receiving gifts” are explained in this way: “Because a judge who accepts a gift is called ‘ransomed,’ we corrected *furentem* to *redemptum* with the aid of seven manuscripts from Florence. The correction is genuine, as is clear from Jerome himself, who writes below: ‘They also oppressed the poor, so that they might sell their judgment for a price against the truth of judgment.’”]

Or the passage may be understood as follows: What benefit is there now in enumerating your sins when your captivity is already at hand, no remedy remains, and a hostile army surrounds the walls of your cities?

We can also apply this to heretics, who plunder the poor or strike them sharply on the head—for this is what the Greek word κατεκονδύλιζον signifies—in accordance with what we read above: “striking the poor on the head.”

Heretics strike only the poor, those unable to withstand their threats, and they strike not the other members but the principal part of the heart and the truth of faith. I think that the poor are those who, content with a simple faith, are unable to answer the malice of heretics.

Moreover, whatever good work they have prepared as an offering to God, they will lose at the time of battle and conflict unless they resist their adversaries. These adversaries, by the composition and structure of their words, build houses for themselves so that they may remain safe and secure. But they will not dwell in them when ecclesiastical men have destroyed and overturned them.

They not only build houses; they also plant highly desirable and attractive vineyards, pretending to represent the mysteries of Christ. But they will not drink wine from them except the wine that is the incurable fury of dragons.

For the Lord waited for these vineyards to produce fruit, but they produced no grapes—only thorns or wild grapes—neither judgment but rather an outcry with which they blaspheme against their God through their maddened mouths.

They will not dwell in their houses or drink the wine of the vineyards they planted because the Lord has known their many impieties. Here “known” is not to be understood according to the passage we read elsewhere: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). Rather, it means that nothing is hidden from God and that he knows all the secrets of sinners.

“I have known,” he says, “many impieties,” which are not only many but also strong and oppressive, trampling upon righteousness itself or upon the one who is righteous.

“And you accept,” he says, “an exchange”—for which all the others alike translated ἐξίλασμα, “an expiation”; we have rendered it “a gift.”

[Note: This is how the Septuagint translators render it, although one Palatine manuscript omits the Greek word and reads, “we have rendered it a gift.”]

The word ἄλλαγμα, according to the idiom of the Scriptures, means “a price,” as we also read in the Gospel: “What exchange will a person give for his soul?” (Matthew 16:26).

They also turned aside the poor in the gates—or, as Symmachus translated it, “oppressed them”—so that, contrary to the truth of judgment, they might sell a verdict for a price, falling under what is written: “Gifts blind even the eyes of the wise” (Deuteronomy 16:19).

Heretics accept these gifts so that they may turn the severity of the Scriptures, which announce torments for sinners, into blessedness. While they promise every prosperity to the rich, they are especially savage and severe toward the poor.

When, therefore, an ecclesiastical, prudent, and discerning person recognizes that there are many impieties in what is called the house of God—and not only many but also strong enough to oppress righteousness—and when the rage of the teachers has progressed so far that they accept payment in judgment and do everything for gifts, while also avoiding the poor in the gates and refusing to listen to them, let him be silent at that time, lest he give what is holy to dogs and throw pearls before swine (Matthew 7), who, after turning around, may trample them.

Let him imitate Jeremiah, who said: “I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness” (Jeremiah 15:17), and the words of the Psalms: “I am alone until I pass over” (Psalm 140:10).

### (Verse 14, 15)

“Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you have said. Hate evil and love good, and establish judgment in the gates; perhaps the Lord God of hosts will have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.”

The Septuagint reads: “Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and thus the Lord God Almighty will be with you, as you have said: ‘We hated evil things and loved good things.’ And restore judgment in the gates, so that the Lord God may have mercy on those who remain of Joseph.”

You say that God is with you because you are children of Abraham. Hear what follows: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham your father” (John 8:39).

What are the works of your father Abraham? Love good and not evil.

It is a great sin not only to do evil but also to love it. Many people sin, and after the heat of pleasure has passed, their conscience torments them and they repent of their sin. But whoever not only does not grieve that he has done what is evil, but even glories in his crime, fulfills what is written: “When the sinner has come into the depth of impiety, he despises it” (Proverbs 18:3).

Seek, therefore, good and not evil. For if you seek good, by seeking good you immediately repel evil. You would never seek good unless you first repelled evil, fulfilling the words of the Psalmist: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27).

When you have sought good and avoided evil, then you will live in him who says, “I am life” (John 14:6). The one who believes in him who speaks in the Gospel seeks good: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). The one who flees from him concerning whom it is written, “The world lies in the evil one” (1 John 5:16), repels evil. And in the Lord’s Prayer he says: “Deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13).

“When you seek good and not evil,” he says, “and live, then the Lord God of hosts will be with you,” as you had said—that he was with you because you were born from Abraham.

Nor is it sufficient to seek good and not seek evil unless you have ἐπιείκησις in both matters,

[Note: Two Palatine manuscripts add “that is, piety.” Victor found these two words in all his copies as well. Thus the preceding Greek word ἐπιείκησις, which signifies piety and goodness, although it is not much used, has been preferred here to ἐπίτασις, which I found in the Cistercian manuscript and Victor in one Brixian manuscript. Moreover, Victor says that Jerome seems to explain himself in the first interpretation and to favor the reading concerning piety, since he immediately adds: “He hates evil who is not merely unconquered by pleasure but hates the works of pleasure. And he loves good who does not do what is good unwillingly, or from necessity, or from fear of the laws, but because it is good.” Nevertheless, I prefer ἐπίτασις, which means addition or increase and which Jerome often uses to indicate increase in action and intensity. Thus, in his commentary on Ezekiel 18, concerning the fifteenth statement—“he rendered true judgment between one man and another, or his neighbor”—he says: “This seems to mean the same as the first statement, where it is written: ‘If he is righteous and has rendered judgment.’ But when the truth of judgment is added, the judgment he renders between one man and another, or his neighbor, an *epitasis* of virtues is apparent.” Similar examples occur frequently elsewhere. The sense is much more coherent and more accurate: it is not sufficient to seek good and not seek evil unless we have *epitasis* in both matters, that is, order and increase with regard to each—first hating evil, since hatred is more than merely not seeking it, and then loving good. This is surely what he calls *epitasis*, and I have no doubt that readers will approve this interpretation rather than the former. For the moment, in the text we change *odiatis* to *oderitis* in accordance with the authority of the manuscripts.]

so that first you hate evil and then love good.

He hates evil who is not merely unconquered by pleasure but hates the works of pleasure. He loves good who does not do what is good unwillingly, or from necessity, or from fear of the laws, but because it is good, so that his conscience may possess the reward of the good work and of the love he has for goodness.

Thus the Apostle says: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). For not every almsgiving pleases God, but only that which is offered with cheerfulness.

When you hate evil and love good, establish judgment in the gates, concerning which we spoke above, so that, iniquity having been expelled, truth may return.

If you do this, perhaps the Lord God Almighty will have mercy on the remnant of Joseph, from the tribe of Ephraim and from the ten tribes, and they will be able to escape captivity.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript, joined by another Palatine manuscript, reads: “Joseph, who was from the tribe …”; shortly afterward it reads *potuerint*, “will have been able,” whereas other copies have *poterint*, “will be able.”]

All of this can also be applied to heretics: abandoning the error they invented, let them return to the Church; let them hate their former doctrines and love the truth in the Lord’s Church; let them exercise true judgment in the gates of vices and virtues, abandoning the former and passing over to the latter; and let those who have escaped from the jaws of the devil hope for mercy.

According to the Septuagint, however, with the order changed, the reading of the present chapter may be rendered more clearly as follows:

“As you have said, ‘We hated evil things and loved good things,’ so seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and as the Lord God Almighty is with you, restore judgment in the gates, so that the Lord God Almighty may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.”

### (Verses 16, 17)

“Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the Sovereign: In all the squares there shall be mourning, and in all the places outside it shall be said, ‘Alas, alas!’ They will call the farmer to mourning and those who know how to lament to wailing. In all the vineyards there shall be mourning, because I will pass through your midst, says the Lord.”

The Septuagint reads: “Therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty: In all the squares there shall be mourning, and in all the roads it shall be said, ‘Alas, alas!’ The farmer will be called to mourning, and those who know lamentation to wailing; and in all the roads there shall be mourning, because I will pass through your midst, says the Lord.”

I commanded you to seek good and not evil, so that you might live and the Lord might be with you. Again I warned you—so that you might not say that you had been instructed only once: “Hate evil, love good, and restore judgment in the gates,” you who hated the one who rebuked in the gate, so that the Lord might have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.

But because you were unwilling to do this, trampling my commandments and turning your shoulder away from me, therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty, who is the Lord of hosts: everywhere there shall be mourning, everywhere grief.

Farmers will be called to mourning, and those who know how, according to the custom of the province, to lead off a lament and stir up tears will be summoned. Thus there will no longer be mourning and wailing in all the squares, as was said above, but in the vineyards, where once there was the source of joy there will be the beginning of tears.

All this will happen because, he says, “I will pass through your midst.”

The Hebrew word “I will pass through,” which in their language is called *EEBOR* (), whenever it is used in the sacred Scriptures in the person of God, should be understood as punishment: he will not remain among them, but will pass through and leave them.

Therefore, in other passages, according to Aquila’s interpretation, when God is angry he calls his fury and anger ἀνυπερθεσίαν.

[Note: Victor says that this means “delay,” and that this meaning corresponds to the verb “I will pass through,” which signifies punishment because the anger of God does not remain in the one whom it touches but passes through and abandons him.]

All this can be referred to heretics: because they were unwilling to do the things that are just, there will be mourning in all their squares.

For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death (Matthew 7). Each heretic and pagan has his own squares in his fables and inventions, and the passage accordingly continues: “In all the places outside it will be said, ‘Alas, alas!’”

Those who are in the Church will not hear the “alas,” which is the final expression of punishment. But if they should happen to sin, lamentation will be taken up over them.

It will be said “alas, alas” outside or in all the roads because they do not have one way that leads to life and is the royal way. Instead, they have crooked and perverse ways, turning to the right and to the left, since they do not hear the Lord saying: “Do not be excessively righteous”; and: “Perverse are the ways that are on the left.”

They fall into a double “alas”: of flesh and spirit, of the present age and the age to come. By contrast, ecclesiastical people hear: “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4:4).

The farmer, too, is called to mourning—for heretics have their own farmers, in whose fields thistles and thorns grow—and those who know how to mourn are called to wailing, whether over their own sins or those of others.

We can also understand this positively, so that an ecclesiastical man, powerful in provoking repentance, may imitate his Lord, who said: “We lamented, and you did not mourn” (Luke 7:32), and may mourn for heretics, as Samuel once mourned for Saul, king of Israel (1 Samuel 15). The Apostle also says that he mourns over those who have not repented (2 Corinthians 12:21).

In all the vineyards, too, there will be mourning, because their vineyard is the vineyard of Sodom. In place of the wine of joy, which gladdens the human heart, they produced the wine of dragons and the incurable fury of asps.

They will suffer all these things because the Lord will pass through their midst, so that he may not dwell among them or say: “I will dwell in them and walk among them”; nor: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

### (Verses 18–20)

Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why [Vulgate: *ad*, “for what purpose”] do you desire the day of the Lord? That day of the Lord is darkness and not light: as when a man flees from the face of a lion, and a bear meets him; and he enters the house, leans his hand against the wall, and a serpent bites him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom and not brightness in it?

**The Septuagint:** Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you desire this day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light. As when a man flees from the face of a lion and a bear falls upon him; he enters the house and leans his hands against the wall, and a serpent bites him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom also, and without brightness?

Lest the prophet from Tekoa should seem entirely to neglect the people of his own tribe and direct his discourse only against the ten tribes, he now addresses both kingdoms—that is, Judah and Israel—in the prophetic utterance. [Note [Col. 1051D]: Three manuscripts read, “he directs a prophecy,” etc., and a little later, “the time of restoration also follows.”] This can be understood from many things, but especially from what follows: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria.” Thus the Jews and Israelites say: “Let the day come; let the foretold captivity come, provided that the time of restoration promised through the prophets also follows.” For there is not as much evil in the injury of captivity as there is good in what the Lord promises after the captivity. [Col. 1051B] To them the prophet replies that they are vainly awaiting, at the coming of the Son of God after the seventy years of Babylonian captivity, what was to occur only after a long period—although devastation, poverty, and innumerable miseries will overtake them.

“For those fleeing,” he says, “from the face of Nebuchadnezzar the lion, Ahasuerus will meet them” [Note [Col. 1051D]: Victorius inserts the word “bear,” judging it necessary here because the prophet’s words are being expounded: “As when a man flees from the face of a lion and a bear meets him.” The Brixian manuscripts supplied it to him; ours do not.], under whom the history of Esther is related; or, after the Assyrian and Chaldean empire has been destroyed, the Medes and Persians will arise. When, under Cyrus’s reign, you have returned, and, at Darius’s command, have begun to build the house of the Lord, and have placed all your confidence in the temple, so that you rest in it and lean your weary hands against the walls, then Alexander, king of the Macedonians—or Antiochus, surnamed Ἐπιφανής (*Epiphanes*)—will come, who will dwell in the temple and bite you like a serpent, [Col. 1051C] no longer outside, in Babylon and Susa, but within the boundaries of the Holy Land [variant: “your land”]. By these events it is proved that the day you desire is not one of light and joy, but of darkness and sorrow.

We have briefly said these things according to the historical sense, lest we leave the Jewish interpretation wholly untouched. Otherwise, there is no doubt that all our people understand the day of darkness to mean the day of judgment. Concerning it Zephaniah also writes: “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and coming very quickly: the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter and harsh” (Zeph. I, 14). And Isaiah says: “Behold, the day of the Lord comes, incurable, a day of fury and wrath, to make the world desolate and destroy sinners from it” (Isa. XIII, 9).

At the same time the confidence of the proud is struck down. In order to appear righteous before human beings, they are accustomed to await the day of judgment and say: “Would that the Lord would come! Would that we might be permitted to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I), imitating the Pharisee who spoke in the Gospel (Luke XVIII, 11–12): “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.” For by this very fact—that they desire the day of the Lord and do not fear it—they are judged worthy of punishment, because no human being is without sin, and the stars are unclean in his sight (Job XXV). And he has enclosed all things under sin, so that he may have mercy on all (variant: “may show mercy to all”) (Gal. III).

Since no one can pass judgment on God’s judgment, and since we shall give [variant: “we give”] an account even for an idle word (Matt. XII), and since Job offered sacrifices every day for his children, lest they might perhaps have conceived some perverse thought against the Lord (Job I), what audacity it is to hear the Corinthians saying: “You reign without us”—or, according to another reading, “You reigned”—“and would that you reigned, so that we also might reign with you” (I Cor. IV, 8).

Certainly, even if their own conscience did not reproach them, they ought to have imitated Paul, who says: “Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (II Cor. II, 29). They ought to be concerned for everyone, lest, as self-lovers desiring to reign themselves, they should desire [variant: “desire”] the torments of others—just as someone might wish his own country to be captured and his city overthrown, so that he alone might enjoy the friendship of the conquerors.

In our distress and tribulations we are accustomed to say: “Would that I might depart from the body and be freed from the miseries of this age,” not knowing that, as long as we remain in this flesh, we have a place for repentance. But if we depart, we shall hear the word of the prophet: “But in hell, who will confess you?” (Ps. VI, 6).

This is the sorrow of the world that leads to death. The Apostle does not wish the man who had fornicated with his father’s wife to perish through it (I Cor. V); and through it the unhappy Judas also perished, who, overcome by excessive sorrow, added murder to betrayal (Matt. XXVII)—a murder worse than all other murders. For where he thought he would find a remedy, and imagined the death of hanging to be the end of his evils, there he found the lion, the bear, and the serpent.

By these names, it seems to me, either various punishments are signified, or the devil himself, who is rightly called both lion, bear, and serpent. And when we suppose that we hear Isaiah saying: “Go, my people, enter your chambers; shut your doors; hide yourselves for a little while, until the wrath of the Lord passes” (Isa. XXVI, 20), and that we are, as it were, in our house, resting, as it were, in hell, then the serpent will bite us—the serpent called *Nahas* in the present passage and *Leviathan* in Job.

> **Note [Col. 1051D]:** A single letter caused Marianus to err, so that he thought Jerome had published *Commentaries on Job*, because he read here, “we have spoken more fully in that volume.” See our admonition in the exposition of the Book of Job, vol. III, in the appendix. We have restored the genuine reading, *discimus* (“we learn”), from two ancient manuscript codices; this strengthens our arguments against Marianus Victorius. —Martianay.

We learn more fully about its nature and manifold terror in that very volume.

> **Note [Col. 1052D]:** See the Admonition that we prefixed between the lines to the Exposition of Job in the Appendix, vol. III, p. 825.

In the gloom and darkness, which are contrary to light and brightness, the diversity of punishments is explained.

### (Verses 21–22)

“I hate and reject your festivals, and I will not accept the odor of your assemblies. If you bring me burnt offerings and your sacrifices, I will not accept them, and I will not regard the vows of your fattened animals” [Col. 1053A].

**The Septuagint:** “I hated and rejected your festivals” [variant: “solemnities”], “and I will not smell the odor of your gatherings. If you offer me burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not receive them, and I will not regard the propitiatory offering of your presence.”

This is properly said against the tribe of Judah and against those who had migrated from Israel to the ceremonies of God, yet did not withdraw from the high places; they worshiped idols and polluted the sacrifices of God with the enormity of their sins. I do not think he ever said concerning the offerings of calves that they made in Dan and Bethel: “If you offer me burnt offerings and your gifts, I will not receive them.”

God hates—and not only hates, but also rejects—the festivals of those who flee from the lion and encounter the bear, enter the house, and are bitten by the serpent, because they do not celebrate God’s festivals but their own, as the Lord says: “I hate and reject your festivals.” He neither receives the assembly and odor of such people nor regards it as a fragrance of good odor; he detests all their gifts and does not look upon their most lavish vows.

This will happen not only to the people of that time but also to us if we commit similar sins and suppose that we can offer God things obtained through robbery, perjury, and crimes, and thereby redeem our sins. We read that Zacchaeus restored fourfold whatever he had extorted and offered half of his possessions that had been honestly acquired (Luke XIX). For he could not offer what had been wickedly acquired into God’s treasury unless he first returned it to its rightful owners and then fulfilled what is written: “Honor the Lord from your just labors” (Prov. III, 9); and: “The wealth of a man is the redemption of his soul” (Prov. XIII, 8). God does not accept vows from the wages of prostitution (Deut. XXIII).

By contrast, the righteous person can say: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 2). For Judas the traitor, that prayer was turned into sin: he did not possess a good odor, but his deeds spoke: “My wounds have become putrid and corrupt, because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6).

All these things can also be said of heretics. While they flee from the lion, they encounter the bear; after entering the house that they suppose to be the Church of God, they lean against walls that they themselves have made, and are bitten by the serpent. Darkness and gloom snatch away their light and day, so that they are enveloped in palpable darkness and their firstborn are slain. God hates their sacrifices and rejects them from himself; whenever they gather under the name of the Lord, he detests their stench and closes his nostrils.

To hate, reject, and refuse to smell are expressions used by way of human likeness, so that we may understand God’s disposition through our own language. If they offer burnt offerings—or [Note [Col. 1053D]: Victorius, following the Brixian codices, retained “or they appear,” etc.; Martianay.] if they appear to fast, give alms, and promise chastity, which are true burnt offerings—the Lord does not receive them, nor does he deign to look upon their most lavish sacrifices.

For he does not judge the greatness of the sacrifices but the merits and motives of those who offer them. Thus the widow who put two small coins into the treasury in the Gospel (Luke XXI) is preferred by the Savior to all those who believed that they were offering the most lavish vows and sacrifices rich in marrow, giving little out of much, whereas she offered everything she possessed.

These words are stated more plainly and truly after the Lord’s coming concerning the Jewish people, who, although the temple and altar have been destroyed, believe that they are offering sacrifices. God hates and rejects their festivals, and does not accept the odor of their assembly when, gathered together, they say: “Crucify, crucify such a man!” (John XIX, 6); and: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25).

If they offer burnt offerings in the synagogues, gifts in the assemblies of Satan, and the most lavish vows, the Lord does not regard them, just as he did not regard Cain’s gifts (Gen. IV). They worship one God properly and offer correctly, but they are not regarded in this, because they do not divide their confession between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Our gifts, however—that is, those of the Church—which we offer from our firstfruits, God regards, just as he once regarded Abel’s sacrifices.

### 304 (Verse 23)

“Take away from me the tumult of your songs, and I will not hear the songs of your lyre.”

**The Septuagint:** “Remove from me the sound of your songs, and I will not hear the psalm of your instruments.”

He calls the beautiful songs of the Levites, with which they praised God, a tumult and confused sound, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner”; and they were also accustomed to offer these same things to idols (Ecclus. XV).

The prayer and psalms of the Jews, which they sing in the synagogues, and the contrived praise of heretics, are likewise a tumult to the Lord—or, so to speak, the grunting of swine and the braying of asses. The works of Israel are more aptly compared with such songs.

Understand “psalm,” “songs,” “lyre,” and “instruments,” according to the letter, as referring to the people of Israel, where such things were formerly done as an image of future realities; or understand them spiritually as referring to us and to the heretics. If we direct these things through good works, they are heard by the Lord; if through evil works, he closes his ears and does not deign to hear the songs of the impious.

### (Verse 24)

“Judgment shall be revealed like water, and righteousness like a mighty torrent.”

**The Septuagint:** “Judgment shall roll forth like water, and righteousness like an impassable torrent.”

Just as water, when it flows downward, uncovers what it had previously covered and exposes it to everyone’s eyes, so the judgment and righteousness of God, by which he once judged his own people, will be revealed to all and will be carried along like a very mighty torrent.

> **Note [Col. 1054D]:** Victorius reads: “like a very mighty torrent, which carries away whatever it seizes,” and so forth.

Whatever it seizes, it drags along with it and does not permit anything to resist it.

According to the Septuagint, however, the judgment of the wicked rolls forth like water because it does not remain in one sentence but is carried about by every wind of doctrine, rejecting what it had approved and considering worthless what it had previously praised. Their justifications are compared not with rivers and purest springs but with turbid and muddy torrents, which do not possess their own waters but gather them from rocks, cliffs, and thornbushes.

Whoever wishes to cross them will immediately be swept headlong; with his feet overturned, he will not be able to say: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. CXXIII, 5). For he treads upon sands without a foundation, and when he is endangered he will say, according to the Hebrews: “The torrent passed over my soul” (Ps. XXXIX, 3).

By contrast, we read concerning the righteous, whose judgment does not roll forth like water and whose righteousness is not carried along like an impassable torrent: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. XII, 5).

### (Verses 25 and following)

“Did you offer me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel? You carried the tabernacle of your Moloch and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves. And I will make you migrate beyond Damascus,” he said [Vulgate: “says”], the Lord; “God of hosts is his name” [Col. 1055B].

**The Septuagint:** “Did you offer me sacrifices and victims in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel? You took up the tabernacle of Melchom and the star of your god Repham, the figures that you made for yourselves. And I will transfer you beyond Damascus,” says the Lord; “Almighty is his name.”

> **Note [Col. 1055D]:** The words “in the wilderness,” which occur also in certain Greek copies, are absent from the Cistercian manuscript. The remainder reads as follows: “Did you offer me sacrifices and victims in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel, and did you take up the tabernacle of Melchom, the figure of Repham, and the star of your god, which you made,” and so forth.

> **Note [Col. 1055D]:** Martianay reads “all beasts” less correctly; this is certainly contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts.

From this passage we learn that all the sacrifices and offerings that Israel made in the wilderness were offered not to God but to its king Moloch. They carried his tabernacles and revered the image of their idols and statues.

What that image or idol itself was, he demonstrates in the following words: “The star of your god,” which in Hebrew is called *CHOCAB*, that is, “the Morning Star” (*Lucifer*), whom the Saracens still worship.

> **Note [Col. 1055D]:** Variant: “even to the present day.” And in *The Life of Saint Hilarion*, vol. II, col. 27: “Jerome taught that the nation of the Saracens was devoted to the worship of Lucifer.” See our observations at that passage concerning Abdala, emperor of the Saracens, who strove to increase the temples of Moloch and the worship of Lucifer. See Mill’s separate dissertation.

For this reason the Lord made them migrate beyond Damascus, that is, into Assyria and among the Chaldeans. His omnipotence is demonstrated by the fact that he is the Lord God of hosts.

We ask how they could have offered sacrifices and offerings not to God in the wilderness but to their own king, whom they call Lucifer. From the time when they transformed gold into the head of a calf, saying, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. III, 24), everything they did is shown to have been done not to God but to idols.

Although afterward we read that they offered certain things to the Lord, they did so not willingly but out of fear of punishments and of the slaughter of those who fell because of the idols. The Lord, however, regards not what is offered but the will of those who offer it.

Thus, whenever opportunity arose, they always turned [variant: “were occupied”] their hearts back to Egypt, desiring garlic, onions, cucumbers, and Egyptian meat, and scorning the manna given from heaven (Num. XI).

To understand this in that way, Stephen, the first martyr of the Gospel, worthy of his name, relates in the history of the Apostles: “They made a calf in those days and offered sacrifice to the idol, and they rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned and handed them over to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the Prophets: ‘Did you offer me victims or sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel? And did you take up the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of your god Remphan, the figures that you made in order to worship them? And I will transfer you beyond Babylon’” (Acts VII, 41 ff.).

Nor should the first martyr be thought to have erred because, in place of what is written in the prophet—“beyond Damascus”—he said, “beyond Babylon.” For he expressed the meaning rather than the wording: they were led beyond Damascus into Babylon, or beyond Babylon.

In the passage where Luke has Μολὸχ (*Moloch*), and where the Hebrew is written as **MELCHECHEM**, Aquila and the Septuagint translated it as Μολχὸμ (*Molchom*); Symmachus and Theodotion translated it as “your king.”

> **Note [Col. 1055D]:** We have restored this entire passage carefully and conscientiously with the help of many very ancient manuscript copies, because in the ancient editions we found much omitted and much incorrectly printed. Whoever compares the two will immediately perceive that the Septuagint edition read *Melchom* and *Remphan*, or *Rephan*, not Μωλὸχ and Ῥαιφὰν, according to the false edition of Erasmus and Marianus. —Martianay.

> The surviving copies of the Septuagint, however, have Μολὸχ; Aquila reads either Μελχὸν or Μαλχὸν. Perhaps for this reason Victorius does not name the Septuagint as the more accurate witness. The Cistercian manuscript prefers the Latin forms *Molchon* and *Raephan*.

Likewise, where the Septuagint reads *Rephan*, Aquila and Symmachus, transferring the Hebrew itself, have *CHION*; Theodotion has ἀμαύρωσιν (*amaurosis*), that is, “darkness.”

Again, in place of *SOCHOTH*, Aquila has συσκιασμοὺς (*syskiasmous*), that is—

> **Note [Col. 1056D]:** The reading seems more correct in the form preferred by Victorius, namely, “little shelters” (*umbracula*); but the manuscripts do not support it.

—“tabernacles”; Symmachus and the Septuagint have “tabernacle”; Theodotion translated it as “vision.”

This must also be observed throughout all the Holy Scriptures: the apostles and apostolic men, when setting forth testimonies from the Old Testament, consider not the words but the sense. Nor do they tread the same verbal path, provided that they do not depart from the meaning.

> **Note [Col. 1056D]:** The following examples, which Jerome notes in their respective places, provide evidence of this: Mark I and Matthew XI: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your face before you,” whereas in Malachi III, according to the Hebrew and Greek, it reads: “Behold, I send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face.” Likewise Matthew XXVI and Mark XIV: “I will strike the Shepherd”; from Zechariah XIII, according to the Hebrew and Greek, “Strike.” And I Corinthians II: “What eye has not seen nor ear heard,” and so forth; from Isaiah LXIV: “Eye has not seen, O God, besides you, what you have prepared for those who await you,” and so forth.

Whatever is said according to the letter against the Jewish people, apply entirely to those who, under the name of Christ, worship idols, invent perverse doctrines for themselves, and carry the tabernacle of their own king, the devil, together with the image of their statues and idols.

For they do not worship one idol but, according to the variety of their doctrines, adore different gods, as well as the star of their god (II Cor. XI). Although he is an angel of Satan, he transforms himself into an angel of light and falls from heaven like lightning (Luke X); and the Antichrist imitates Christ.

He aptly adds: “which you made for yourselves.” For they did not receive these things from God; they fashioned them from their own minds.

Therefore the Lord will make them migrate beyond Damascus, so that they may not drink the blood of the Lord but pass over into Babylon and hear through the prophet: “Babylon is a golden cup, intoxicating all the nations” (Jer. LI, 7).

For Damascus, as we have often said, is interpreted as “drinking blood,” or “the blood of sackcloth,” so that through repentance we may be summoned to drink the blood of the Lord.

### (Chapter VI, verse 1)

“Woe to those who are wealthy in Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria, the nobles, the leaders of the peoples, who enter pompously into the house of Israel.”

**The Septuagint:** “Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria. They have harvested the firstfruits of the nations and entered for themselves” [Note: The words “of the house of Israel,” which Jerome applies to the following verse, are immediately added here by the Cistercian manuscript.]

As we said above, the prophet’s discourse is directed toward Zion and the mountain of Samaria—that is, toward the two tribes called Judah and toward the ten called by the name of Israel—especially toward those who are nobles and rulers in both peoples.

> **Note [Col. 1057B]:** We have supplied the conjunction *et* (“and”), and, following the manuscripts, read *vacant* (“they indulge”) instead of *vacabant* (“they indulged”). We often silently correct such minor errors.

They indulge in luxury, after the example of that rich man dressed in purple who rejoiced at a banquet and was lifted up into such pride that he could not bear to see Lazarus, covered with sores, before his door, nor even grant him what would have fallen from the table (Luke XVI).

These are the leaders of the peoples who trust in riches, who are wealthy in Zion, and who place their confidence in the mountain of Samaria. They enter pompously into the house of Israel, so that the body may display the swelling of the spirit and they may seem like the elaborate vessels of a procession.

According to the laws of allegorical interpretation and the Septuagint translators, Zion refers to the Church, concerning which we read: “You who exalt me from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. IX, 15).

The mountain of Samaria, on account of pride and boastful confidence in the observance of God’s commandments, is understood of the heretics, who despise the Church, because God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and the foolish things to destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the understanding of the prudent (I Cor. I).

These have harvested the firstfruits of the nations in order to introduce them, under the Christian name, into their winepresses, where grapes are not trodden but destroyed; where must is not pressed out but poison.

“And they entered for themselves.” He said this aptly: “for themselves.” For they did not enter for God but entered for themselves. Otherwise, they have gone farther from God by withdrawing from the Church.

What follows—“house of Israel”—according to the Septuagint, must be read at the beginning of the following chapter; according to the Hebrews, at the end of this chapter, which we have expounded.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 1057]

### 309–310

In an inverted and disordered sequence, we both began and, with Christ’s help, will complete the work on the Twelve Prophets. For I have not discussed them from the first to the last according to the order in which they are read, but as I was able and as I was asked.

First, I addressed Nahum, Micah, Zephaniah, and Haggai to the most devoted students (*φιλοπονωτάταις*, “most industrious”) Paula and her daughter Eustochium (*προσεφώνησα*, “I addressed”); second, I dedicated two books on Habakkuk to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia; third, after a long silence, I explained Obadiah and Jonah to you, Pammachius, at your command.

In the present year, which received its designation from the fasti of the sixth consulship of Arcadius Augustus and of Anitius Probus, I interpreted the prophet Malachi for Exsuperius, bishop of the Church of Toulouse, and for Minervius and Alexander, monks of that same city.

> **Note [Col. 1057D]:** Martianay is mistaken, and Victorius earlier made the same mistake, assigning this consulship to the year 408 of Christ. It must, as is established by the sequence of the fasti and by ancient records, be referred to 406.

Immediately returning to the beginning of the volume, I could not refuse you the interpretation of Hosea, Joel, and Amos. After a very serious bodily illness, I displayed my rashness through the speed of dictation, committing to chance what others do not dare to write without repeatedly revising their style. Chance always follows those who dictate and tests their courage in matters of talent and learning.

For, as I have often testified, I cannot endure the labor of writing with my own hand. In an explanation of the Holy Scriptures, one seeks not carefully composed words adorned with rhetorical flowers, but learning and the simplicity of truth.

> **Note [Col. 1057D]:** Namely, the three-year period during which he refrained from explaining the Scriptures, as is learned from the preface to the Commentaries on Jonah.

> **Note [Col. 1057D]:** The Palatine manuscripts read *qui praedictam sequitur* (“which follows the aforesaid”), apparently referring to *temeritatem* (“rashness”).

### (Verses 2ff.)

“Cross over to Calneh and see; and from there go to great Hamath, and descend to Gath of the Philistines: to the best of these kingdoms, if their territory is broader than your territory. You who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the seat of iniquity. You who sleep on beds of ivory and live luxuriously on your couches; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery. Like David, they have thought that they possessed instruments for singing; they drink wine from bowls, anoint themselves with the finest ointment, and suffer nothing over the ruin of Joseph.”

[Col. 1058D] The Septuagint: “House of Israel, cross over all and see Calneh, and pass from there to great Hamath, and descend to Gath of the foreigners, the best of all these kingdoms, if their territories are larger than your territories; you who come to the evil day, who draw near and touch false sabbaths. You who sleep on beds of ivory, who overflow with luxuries on your couches, who eat kids from the flocks and suckling calves from the midst of the herds, who clap your hands to the sound of instruments—as though they were things standing firm, and not things fleeing; who drink strained wine and anoint yourselves with the first oils, and suffer nothing over the ruin of Joseph.”

[Note: The relative pronoun “who” was lacking; both the manuscripts and the Greek text supply it.]

[Note: The words “in Calneh” are absent from a Cistercian manuscript. They are also absent from the Greek text, except in one or two copies. Nevertheless, they are found in the Greek Fathers Theodoret and Justin, and should therefore be read.]

Cross over, all of you, to Calneh, which is now called Ctesiphon, and cross over, all of you. Who are these “all”? Both groups whom he mentioned above: “the nobles, the heads of the peoples,” and those “who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria.” You, therefore, cross over to the city of Persia, pay close attention, and from there [Col. 1059B] proceed to great Hamath, which is now called Antioch.

[Note: I fear that the holy Doctor has erred here through the haste of dictation. For Antioch, which acknowledges the kings of Syria as its founders, is immensely more recent than Amos. Indeed, Theodoret teaches in his commentary on Jeremiah 39 that Hamath, which because of its size was called “Great Hamath,” or “Hamath-Rabbah,” was not Antioch but Emesa—a famous city of Syria near the Orontes and close to Lebanon. The corrupted name Emas agrees with this, as does Hamath itself, which Jerome shortly notes; for among Eastern languages t and s are easily interchanged. Moreover, Riblah, which he names third, was situated in that region, as we learn from other passages of Scripture. Josephus also knows another Hamath, or “Lesser Hamath,” in Antiquities, book I, chapter 7; he reports that it is the same as Epiphany, as does Jerome. Compare the Hebrew Questions on Genesis, chapter 10.]

He calls it “great” in distinction from lesser Hamath, which is called Epiphany. Hence, even today, for those traveling toward Mesopotamia, the first station is called Emmas—a corrupted form of the name, but one retaining traces of its former designation. Its territory is called Riblah; there, in the presence of Nebuchadnezzar, the sons of Zedekiah, king of Judaea [variant: Judah], were killed, and his eyes were blinded. “And descend,” he says, “into Gath of the Philistines” (2 Kings 25).

You who dwell on Mount Zion and on Mount Samaria, descend to the Philistines, who live in the plains, and to the best of their kingdoms, which are subject to various cities—Gaza, Ashkelon, Azotus, Ekron, and Gath—and see whether their territory is broader than your territory, whether you or they possess the larger provinces. You, I say, you who are of the people of Israel, who are set apart for the evil day—that is, for the day of captivity—and draw near to the seat of iniquity, going to the unjust judge, the king of Babylon.

Although you are destined to suffer these things, you now sleep on beds of ivory and live luxuriously on soft couches, joining lust to sleep. You eat not to drive away hunger and sustain the human body, but for pleasure and luxury, preparing for your appetites whatever is tender and fat among the flocks and herds. The lust of your loins and throat, and of your stomach heated with food, is not enough for you unless you also soothe your ears with the songs of pipes, psaltery, and lyre. Thus what David did for the worship of God—discovering the orders of the Levites and the variety of instruments (1 Chronicles 23–26)—you turn toward pleasure and luxury.

You drink wine from bowls, not to satisfy thirst but to overwhelm the mind. You anoint yourselves, not with the purest oil to relieve the labors of the body, but with the most precious ointments. And while you abound in these things, if you see some of the people perishing, you are moved by no compassion over their destruction; rather, you despise them like brute animals, as though they were beasts dying in their own blood.

The prophet Ezekiel presents this same meaning under the example of shepherds: “They eat the milk of the sheep, clothe themselves with their wool, and devour whatever is first; but they do not heal the wounded, strengthen the broken, or seek the perishing” (Ezekiel 34:3–4).

Let us now transfer everything we have said according to the truth of the historical account, following the Septuagint interpreters, into the cloud of allegory. “House of Israel,” you who have withdrawn from me, who trust in Mount Samaria, who have harvested the first fruits of the nations: cross over, see, and proceed to the many walls—for this is the interpretation of Hamath-Rabbah—and from there descend gently into the winepress of those who fall while drinking. For Gath and Philistines have this meaning. Contemplate everything, especially the best kingdoms—or, as some read, “all the kingdoms”—or the best cities from all the kingdoms, and consider whether their territories are more extensive than yours.

For if we wish to examine this matter intellectually and investigate the philosophy of all the nations—Egyptians, Indians, and Persians—we shall find their boundaries narrower than those of the holy Scriptures: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world [variant: lands]” (Psalm 18).

To those whom he had previously addressed as “House of Israel, cross over all and see,” from what kinds of vices they are commanded to pass to better things, the following speech gives instruction. “Those who come to the evil day”—they prepare the evil day for themselves by their own vice. This does not mean that any day is evil in itself, but that each person prepares evil for himself, according to what we read in Ecclesiastes: “Do not say, ‘Why were the former days better than these?’ For you do not inquire wisely about this” (Ecclesiastes 7:11). It is foolish to attribute the matter to times, when it lies within our power either to make a good day for ourselves or an evil one.

These are the people who draw near and touch false sabbaths.

[Note: Our manuscripts read: “These draw near and touch [in order] to make false sabbaths”; for how then is the cutting-off of the flesh, and so forth?]

Just as circumcision of the flesh and circumcision of the heart are both so called, and there are Jews outwardly and Jews inwardly, one of which is rejected and the other approved, so there are holy Sabbaths of the Lord, founded upon truth, and other Sabbaths that are not holy and are false, following the leisure of the killing letter.

The following words—“who sleep on beds of ivory”—may be interpreted in this way. One who is the Lord’s athlete, trains for the contest, and prepares himself against hostile powers sleeps on the bare ground, imitating Jacob (Genesis 28). He places a stone beneath his head, the stone which the builders rejected and which became the cornerstone (Psalm 117; Acts 4).

But those who devote themselves to luxury and indulgence, doing everything for the sake of the belly, sleep on beds of ivory taken from dead animals and cling to unclean bones. Because vices appear beautiful and delight them with their present brilliance, they rest on their little beds and are weighed down by the deepest sleep.

These people do not eat solid and athletic food, by which the strength of combatants is increased, but soft, tender food belonging to the left side. Such are kids from the flocks and fattened, tender calves—indeed, calves still nourished by milk. This is what the Greek phrase μοσχάρια γαλαθηνά means, “suckling calves.”

They also clap their hands to the sound of instruments, so that all their actions may seek pleasure; they do nothing except provide for the belly and lust.

Let not the prudent reader immediately object: How then is it written, “The rivers clap their hands” (Psalm 97:8), and, “All nations, clap your hands” (Psalm 46:1), and, “Shout joyfully to God our helper” (Psalm 80:1)? In those passages they are not said to clap to the sound of instruments, but to have one harmony in the praise of God.

After the sound of the instruments he adds: “As though they were things standing firm, and not things fleeing.” The things of the world, and all bodies, according to Epicurus, flow and pass away from moment to moment. Nothing remains in its own condition; everything either increases or decreases, and, like rushing waters, slides headlong downward.

Hence we also read in secular literature (Virgil, Georgics 3):

> But meanwhile time flees, irretrievable time flees.

And elsewhere (Horace, Odes 2.14):

> Alas, the fleeting years, Postumus, Postumus,  
> Glide away.

Nothing is more fleeting than the age and the things of the age. What we hold, we lose even as we hold it; and through infancy, childhood, youth, manhood, advancing maturity, and the final years of old age—seven periods in which Philo describes human life—we are changed and hurry onward, reaching the boundaries of death without knowing it.

The words “those who drink strained wine” may properly be applied to heretics, who approve some Scriptures and reject others, desiring to drink wines that have been filtered. For in the holy Scriptures there is nothing muddy or foul, but everything is drawn from the upper spring in the purest form.

These are the people who anoint themselves with the first ointments. They possess no skill in preparing ointments and, without any knowledge of the Scriptures or of the traditions and teaching of the apostles, claim for themselves the dignity of the priesthood and say that they are the Lord’s anointed. They contaminate the purest oil with the dregs of their own understanding.

Although they do these things for the destruction of those whom they have deceived, they are tormented by no grief. Rather, they rejoice in the deaths of others and delight in the blood of the wretched.

This very fine interpretation—“as though they were things standing firm, and not things fleeing”—is not found in the Hebrew. Instead, it reads: “Like David, they thought that they possessed instruments for singing.” It therefore seems to me to have been added by the interpreters. In describing luxury, they put forward this sentence against such vices and pleasures, so that they did not translate what was written but added from themselves what seemed appropriate to them—or rather, altered it.

### (Verses 7ff.)

“Therefore now they shall go into captivity at the head of the captives, and the revelry of those who live luxuriously shall be taken away. The Lord God has sworn by his own life, says the Lord God of hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob and hate his houses, and I shall deliver the city with its inhabitants. If ten men remain in one house, even they shall die; and his relative shall take him up and burn him, to carry the bones out of the house. And he shall say to the one who is in the innermost parts of the house, ‘Is anyone still with you?’ He will answer, ‘It is finished.’ And he shall say to him, ‘Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord.’”

The Septuagint: “Therefore now they shall be captives from the beginning of the mighty, and the neighing of horses shall be taken away from Ephraim; for the Lord has sworn by himself, says the Lord God of powers: ‘For I shall abhor every insult of Jacob, and I hate his regions, and I shall remove the city with all its inhabitants.’ And it shall be that if ten men remain in one house and die, the members of his household shall take them up and attempt to carry their bones out of the house. They shall say to those who are in charge of the house, ‘Is anyone still with you?’ And he will say, ‘Certainly not.’ And he shall say, ‘Be silent, and do not mention the name of the Lord.’”

[Note: Victor has “the horses,” which is also the plural number in the Greek, ἵππων, “of horses.”]

Because of the earlier causes described by the prophetic speech—those who sleep on beds of ivory, live luxuriously on their couches, eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd, sing to the sound of the psaltery, drink from bowls, anoint themselves with the finest ointment, and, in addition, suffer nothing over the ruin of his people, who was descended from the stock of Joseph—the Lord now threatens and says: “Because they have done these and those things, now they shall go into captivity at the head of the captives.”

The meaning is this: Punishment is by no means being postponed for the future, nor is it being prophesied for some distant age. What is now pressing upon them, what is now about to come, my speech foretells: they will go at the head of the captives—that is, the princes and powerful men, of whom he had previously said: “Hear this word, you fat cows who are on Mount Samaria” (above, 4:1). And again: “Woe to those who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria, the nobles, the heads of the peoples, who enter pompously into the house of Israel.”

You who are first in wealth shall first bear the yoke of captivity, according to what is written in Ezekiel: “Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9:6). This does not mean from the holy people, as many think, but from the overthrow of the temple, which was holy. “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6), and “from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be demanded” (Luke 12).

“And the revelry of those who live luxuriously shall be taken away,” those who were united in the pursuit of pleasures and practiced banquets and common feasts. They shall be taken away together, so that those whose luxury was one may also have one punishment.

For this the Septuagint translated, “The neighing of the horse shall be taken away from Ephraim.” This is not found in the Hebrew and will be discussed at greater length when we begin to develop the tropological interpretation.

The Lord swore by himself—or, as we read in Hebrew, “by his life”—according to what is written in Isaiah: “Your new moons and your Sabbaths and your feast days my soul hates” (Isaiah 1:13). This does not mean that God has a soul, but that he speaks in terms of human emotions.

Nor is it surprising that he is said to have a soul, since he also testifies that he has other members—feet, hands, a belly, and other limbs—which are more lowly than the soul. If those who deny that Christ possessed a human soul object to us that Christ had a human body but that God was in him in place of a soul, let them hear that the substance of a soul is demonstrated in Christ, just as the members of his body possessed substance.

[Note: Perhaps the Cistercian manuscript reads more correctly: “In God the Father, as the other things that are said,” and so forth.]

In God the Father, however, the head, feet, and other things that are mentioned are not members; their names indicate instead a diversity of operations. So too the soul is not substantial, but is the affection of the inward mind and the seat of thoughts, through which God indicates his will.

The Lord therefore swore—the Lord, God of hosts, that is, Sabaoth, which the Septuagint translated as “of powers”—that he detests the pride of Jacob and hates his houses. Here “Jacob,” according to the preceding chapter, where it is written, “and they suffered nothing over the ruin of Joseph,” may mean either the ten tribes or, certainly, the whole house of the twelve tribes.

And he will deliver the city with its inhabitants—either Samaria or Jerusalem, or, in general, both.

We may refer this to the time of the Lord and Savior, after whose coming and passion God detested all the pride, or insult, of Jacob, by which [variant: because] they cried out that he was the son of a carpenter, a Samaritan, and one who had a demon (Matthew 13; John 8). Therefore Jerusalem was delivered, together with its inhabitants, to the Roman armies.

God’s anger raged against them to such an extent that even if ten men remained in one house, they too would die. A relative, or neighbor, would burn the corpses of the dead so that he could carry the bones out of his house, because, amid the crowds of the dying, intact bodies could not be carried out.

When he had already grown weary of carrying them away, he would ask the person in the innermost part of the house whether any survivors remained whom he should deliver to him. The other would answer: “It is finished; I have no one left to deliver to you for burial.” Before he could swear that he had no one, the one who had asked—the man who was outside and already knew that no one remained—would command him, saying: “Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord.”

He recalls this in order to show that they would not wish to confess the name of the Lord even when compelled by the weight and necessity of their misfortunes. The name of God had fallen into such complete oblivion among Israel that they did not consider it worthy to hear even in a simple oath.

We have drawn the faint lines of the historical account; let us now apply our hand to the allegory.

The leaders of the heretics, who for the sake of their pleasures devoured my people and suffered nothing over the ruin of Joseph, shall be led first to punishment. “And the neighing of the horse shall be taken away from Ephraim.” In the holy Scriptures the horse is understood in two ways: either as the pride and power of those who neigh, or as the greatness of lust.

It signifies pride and the agreement of the wicked in the passage: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses” (Psalm 19:8), and, “The horse is deceptive for salvation” (Psalm 32:17). The kings of Israel are commanded not to multiply horses for themselves (Deuteronomy 17). In the book of Job, the voice of the horse is compared with the sound of a trumpet (Job 39).

We read also in Zechariah—a passage confirmed by the testimony of the Gospel and referred to the presence of the Savior:

> “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saving; he is himself meek and rides upon a donkey and a young colt. And he shall destroy the chariots from Ephraim and the horses from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:9).

The horse also signifies the greatness of lust and an unrestrained desire for intercourse, as in Jeremiah, who describes luxurious and adulterous men and adds: “Each one neighs after his neighbor’s wife” (Jeremiah 5:8).

The coming of Christ and the wrath of God cripple such horses.

The Lord swears by himself—because he has no greater by whom he may swear—that he detests all the insults of the heretics and hates all their regions (Hebrews 6). Whatever they say is an insult and worthy of God’s hatred.

He will remove their city and their assemblies, together with those who dwell in them—that is, both the people and their teachers. Even if ten men remain—who, had they been found in Sodom and Gomorrah, would have prevented the fire from descending upon them (Genesis 19)—all will die by that death which leads to Tartarus. Of it Ezekiel writes: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20).

Their relatives and household members bury the bones of such people, of whom it is said: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Luke 9:60). The one who is outside and does not enter the house of the dead, but rather casts the dead outside, commands the one who burns the dead, dissolves them into ashes, and crushes their bones, to be silent and not defile the pure name of God with a dead mouth.

For God says to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your mouth?” (Psalm 49:16). Therefore we too must take care not to bury the dead, but rather, as living people, to bring forth those who are dead into life.

[Note: Victor preferred “lead [them] to life” (perducamus).]

If we do not do this, the command is given to us also, and it is said: “Be silent, for we are judged unworthy of the name of God.”

### (Verses 12ff.)

“For behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the great house with ruins and the small house with fissures. Do horses run on rocks, or can one plow with wild oxen? For you have turned judgment into bitterness and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood. You who rejoice in nothing, who say, ‘Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our own strength?’ For behold, I shall raise up against you, house of Israel, says the Lord God of hosts, a nation, and they shall crush you from the entrance of Hamath to the torrent of the wilderness.”

The Septuagint: “Therefore behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the great house with ruins and the small house with fissures. If horses pursue on rocks, will they be silent before women? For you have turned judgment into fury and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness. You who rejoice over no good word, who say, ‘Have we not possessed horns by our own strength?’ For behold, I shall raise up against you, house of Israel, says the Lord God of powers, a nation, and they shall crush you—not so that you may enter Hamath, but as far as the torrent of the West.”

[Note: The word “good” is added in a Cistercian manuscript; it is absent from the Greek text except in the Barberine and Aldine manuscripts.]

[Note: We restore “of powers” from the Cistercian manuscript. This is the proper translation by the Septuagint of τῶν δυνάμεων; previously the reading was “of hosts.” Victor preferred “so that you may not enter” instead of “not so that,” and so forth.]

Because you rushed into such madness that even at the time of death, when evils were imminent, you did not wish to name the Lord, therefore the Lord will command and will strike the great house with ruins and the small house with fissures.

If he commands, how does he strike? If he strikes, how does he command? But in commanding and ordering his ministers, he himself is seen to strike. Just as, when the Father commands and the Son acts, the one who commanded himself acts, fulfilling the verse: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148:5). For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (John 1:3).

[Note: Recall what we note on Ezekiel 37, col. 432 and following.]

And in Egypt, where the firstborn are said to have been struck down by the destroyer, the Lord testifies that he himself killed them (Exodus 12).

So also in the present passage the Lord commands, and he himself strikes through his ministers: the great house with ruins—that is, the ten tribes, which were called Israel—and the small house with fissures—that is, the two tribes, which were ruled by the stock of the house of David.

Observe the distinctive character of each house. Israel, because it had committed greater sins, is struck with ruins and handed over to eternal captivity. The house of Judah, in which the temple was located and which had sinned only in part, is held in a captivity of seventy years. It is not struck with ruins but with fissures. A split house can be repaired; ruins require not so much restoration as rebuilding.

He compares the ruins and fissures of both houses with horses and wild oxen. The former cannot run on rocks; the latter are so untamed that they do not accept a yoke on their necks, and, being wild cattle, refuse through their ferocity to split the earth with a plow.

Yet although horses and wild oxen cannot change their nature, you have changed the nature of God, making what was sweet bitter and turning the fruit of his righteousness into wormwood, the bitterest herb.

“You who rejoice in nothing”—or in idols and golden calves, which are nothing, as Esther says to the Lord: “Do not hand over your scepter to those who are not” (Esther 14:11)—or in nothingness and falsehood.
