You think that by your own strength you have taken horns for yourselves: kingship and power with which you may scatter your enemies.

Because you have done these things, behold, I shall raise up against you, great house and small house, which are to be struck with ruins and fissures—that is, house of Israel and all twelve tribes—a most savage nation of Assyrians and Chaldeans, which will crush and overthrow you from beginning to end, from head to tail, from the boundaries of your land that look toward the sun to the torrent of the wilderness—or, as the Septuagint translated it, of the West.

That is, from Hamath to Rhinocorura, between which and Pelusium the stream of the Nile, or the torrent coming from the desert, enters the sea.

We have said above that Hamath is Epiphany, which received its name from Antiochus, whose surname was Ἐπιφανής, “Epiphanes.”

Those who think that “house of Israel” here means the ten tribes will not be able to explain how the threat against the ten tribes says that they will be crushed from Epiphany to the boundaries of Egypt. Within those boundaries not the ten tribes alone but all twelve are enclosed, including Judah and Benjamin.

Some, following the anagogical interpretation, think that the great house and the small house signify the Jewish people and the Church gathered from the nations. The Jews are called great because of the patriarchs, the Law, and the prophets; we are called small because we were without the covenant and the commandments of God. Of us we read in the Song: “My sister is little, and she has no breasts” (Song of Songs 8:8).

That great and small house, gathered into one family of God, will be struck with ruins and fissures if it has no discipline and does not obey the commandments of God.

Whenever, therefore, the house of God, which is the Church, falls and is torn apart either in persecutions or in heresies and schisms, it shows the hand of God who strikes. If we wish to escape it, let us hear and follow the example supplied by the comparison.

Horses cannot pursue on rocks. “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4), who granted his apostles that they too should be called rocks: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

Whoever is found upon these rocks cannot be pursued by the hostile powers called horses, of whom we spoke above; their running is impeded, and they fall upon each successive rock.

Let us come also to another comparison, according to our custom, as we expound the edition of the Septuagint interpreters. If we cling entirely to the Hebrew, we might seem to have mocked the reader’s diligence and to have proposed the common edition in vain by remaining silent about it.

“Will they be silent,” he says, “before women”—clearly referring to the horses of whom he had spoken above.

[Note: Above, when he presented the text, he read “before women.” Although Victor says that the Greek reads ἐν θηλείαις, “among women,” the meaning is clearer as “before women,” which Saint Jerome himself also follows when he immediately adds: “These horses, that is, hostile powers, who rage after women,” and so forth. “Not to be silent before women” means that they cannot restrain themselves at the sight of women, as in Jeremiah: “Each one neighs after his neighbor’s wife.”]

“If horses pursue on rocks”: these horses—that is, hostile powers—rage after women. When they see a manly spirit strengthened by God’s power, they do not dare to approach. But when they see a weakened mind, enervated by ointments and pleasures and transformed into feminine softness, they immediately rage and cannot contain themselves; they leap toward lust.

It follows: “For you have turned judgment into fury.” The person who judges in anger turns judgment into fury, despite the Lord’s saying: “You shall not show partiality in judgment” (Deuteronomy 16:19), and elsewhere: “You shall not be partial to the poor in judgment, for the judgment is God’s” (Exodus 23:3).

Such a person descends to judge with an angry mind; indeed, although he does not know the case or understand the truth of judgment, he prejudges what sentence ought to be given. He also turns the fruit of righteousness, which is most sweet, into bitterness.

What we have said of one virtue should also be understood of the others—prudence, fortitude, and temperance. Whoever is angry will not be able to reap their fruits; and when he does reap them, they will be bitter. Hence it is said in Isaiah: “Woe to those who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet” (Isaiah 5:20).

Those who do this are the people who consider not the causes but the persons in judgment and turn the fruit of Christ’s righteousness, which is most sweet, into bitterness.

Therefore whoever is influenced in judgment either by kinship or friendship, or, conversely, by hostile hatred or enmity, perverts the judgment of Christ, who is righteousness, and turns its fruit into bitterness.

Those who do this “rejoice in no good word,” or, as Symmachus translated it, “without reason,” that is, ἀλόγως, “irrationally.” Lifted up in pride, they say: “Have we not possessed horns by our own strength?”

By contrast, the righteous person glories in the Lord and says: “Through you we shall scatter our enemies with the horn.” And elsewhere [variant: “in the same passage”]: “I shall not trust in my bow, nor shall my sword save me” (Psalm 43:6–7).

Hence in Exodus, according to the Hebrew and Aquila’s edition, we read: “Moses did not know that the appearance of his face was horned” [or: “that his face was horned”] (Exodus 34:29). He could truly say: “In you I scatter my enemies with the horn.”

We read elsewhere: “He shall exalt the horn of his people,” and, “He shall exalt the horn of his anointed” (Psalm 148:14; 1 Samuel 2:10), as well as of the altar and of clean, horned animals, which alone are offered to God. The interpretation of these matters does not belong to the present occasion.

Because of these great sins and this extreme pride, which speaks iniquity against God and sets its mouth on high, the Lord God Almighty says that he will raise up a most savage nation to crush and afflict them—or rather, to prevent them from entering Hamath and reaching the torrent of the West.

Hamath means “wall,” or “fortified.”

They will therefore be prevented by this most savage nation, to whom punishments have been assigned, from taking refuge in the fortified city, which is the heavenly Jerusalem, lest they enter and be saved. This is like the passage we read in Genesis, where God placed the cherubim and the flaming sword—which turns to guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24)—so that the one who had been expelled from paradise might not enter it while unworthy.

As for the following words, “as far as the torrent of the West,” we shall interpret them from Psalm 67, where it is written: “Sing to the Lord, sing praise to his name; make a way for him who rides upon the sunset; the Lord is his name” (Psalm 67:5).

Unless evil works have died within us, Christ will not ascend over us. When they have died and we have Christ as our charioteer, then, as we advance and proceed toward better things, the same psalm will command us: “Sing to God, sing praises to the Lord who rides upon the heaven of heaven toward the East” (Psalm 67:33–34).

Hence also in the mysteries we first renounce the one who is in the West, and who dies for us together with our sins; then, turning toward the East, we enter into a covenant with the sun of righteousness and promise that we shall serve him.

In place of “the torrent of the West,” Symmachus translated “the valley of the plain”; Theodotion, “the torrent of Arabia”; Aquila, “the torrent that is in the plain.”

[Note: I do not think this means “of Arabia,” but “of the Arabah,” rendered by Theodotion as τῆς Ἀραβά, a customary use of that word for a plain. We have discussed this matter several times in the book of Names, and it will have to be mentioned again below.]

These words show that, once excluded from the fortified city, their sins cannot die, nor can they reach the torrent that is level and plain, or the torrent of the wilderness, which is called the torrent of pleasure, according to what we read: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your pleasure” (Psalm 35:9).

[Note: Erasmus and Marianus introduce a false reading here, namely: “These words show that, once excluded from the fortified city, sins can in no way be fortified,” and so forth. I cannot understand what this is supposed to mean. MART. Two Palatine manuscripts read muniri, “be fortified,” instead of mori, “die,” as do the old editions of Erasmus and Victorius, which additionally insert contra peccata, “against sins.”]

## (Chapter VII—verses 1–3)

The Lord God showed me this: and behold, a maker of locusts at the beginning of the sprouting of the late rain; and behold, afterward, the shearing—or the shearer—of the king.

[Note: Martianay mistakenly retained *victor*, as did Victorius earlier and all the manuscripts; the matter itself clearly demands that it be corrected to *fictor*, “maker.”]

And it happened, when he had finished eating the grass of the land, that I said: “Lord God, have mercy, I beg you: who will raise up Jacob, for he is small?” The Lord had mercy concerning this. “It shall not be,” he said.

[Note: One Cistercian manuscript, agreeing almost with the Hebrew and the Vulgate, reads: “And behold, the late rain after the king’s shearer” (or “shearing”). The printed reading is better supported by Jerome’s exposition appended below.]

The Septuagint: Thus the Lord showed me: and behold, a brood of locusts was coming in the morning; and behold, one locust—the king Gog.

[Note: The same manuscript has *pro* (“instead of”) for *unus* (“one”); the Greek Complutensian edition prefers εἰς rather than εἷς.]

And it shall be, when he has finished devouring the grass of the land, that I said: “Lord God, have mercy: who will raise up Jacob, since he is small? Relent, Lord, concerning this; and this shall not be,” says the Lord.

The prophetic word foretells not only things that will occur after many ages, but also things near at hand, which immediately follow the prophecy. For we commonly think much more about ourselves than about our descendants, as Hezekiah says: “Let there be peace in my days” (2 Kings 20:19). Thus those who see that events have fulfilled what was previously announced may be converted to the worship of God, in whose prophets the truth of foretelling is found.

The Lord therefore shows that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, will come with an immeasurable multitude of troops, like a locust mowing down everything, at the beginning of the late rain, when Israel was in need of the final mercy of almighty God. The maker and creator of this locust is the Lord. This locust comes at the beginning of the late rain, when all things are green, every field is giving birth, and the blossoms of different trees burst into fruits of their own kinds. To state in a single phrase what I mean: they promise an abundance of all things—the blossoms of the trees and the grass of the crops.

These locusts, which flew about in the first spring, were followed by an innumerable *bruchus*—a “devourer”—which came after the late rain and was called the king’s shearer or shearing, because it laid everything waste and left absolutely nothing of the green grass upon the earth. Isaiah calls this shearer, or shearing, a sharp razor (Isaiah 7), which shaved all the hairs and locks from the body of Israel. And when he wondered what this razor was, he immediately added: the king of Assyria. The king’s razor and shearer, therefore, is the army of the Chaldaeans, which devastated everything like a *bruchus* and consumed not only crops but also wood, hay, and straw.

When the *bruchus* that had come after the locust had finished eating the grass of the land, and the prophet understood what he was seeing, he turned to prayer and said: “Lord God, have mercy, I beg you. I do not want my words fulfilled in the overthrow of my people; I do not want to have been chosen from among the shepherds for this purpose, that I should announce the ruin of the ten tribes. For who will be able to raise up Jacob, unless you alone can do so?” If he strikes him down, there is no one who can raise him up. Jacob is small, destroyed by the frequent incursions of his enemies.

While he was praying and pouring out the tears of his inner person, the Lord had mercy concerning this and answered: “I will not destroy the whole race of Israel; a remnant shall be saved.” Or certainly we should understand it in this way: he saw two future events together, first the locust and then the *bruchus*. He entreated the Lord on account of both, but is heard in only one respect, so that the *bruchus* does not lay waste everything to the point of annihilation. The flying locust, however, devours some things and leaves others intact.

It seems to me that the Septuagint interpreters understood the Hebrew word גֹּזִי (*GOZI*), which means “shearer” or “shearing,” as גּוֹג (*GOG*), supposing the Hebrew letter *zayin* to be *vav*, and comparing the innumerable multitude of the *bruchus* with the most savage nation of Gog, which is described as destined to devastate the land of Judaea.

[Note: Again the same manuscript has *GOI* instead of *GOG*, which may indeed seem more correct if, as Jerome says, they merely changed *zayin* into *vav*, letters quite similar in appearance. Yet it is clear that they read γώγ (*gog*). Therefore Victorius says: “If the Septuagint translated what is Hebrew *Gozi* as *Gog*, they must have taken not *vav* but *gimel* for *zayin*. But when they read *Goi*, they could have referred it to *Gog* in order to signify it.”]

But what Aquila intended by saying, “Behold, the late rain after the king of Gaza”—since Gaza is called *Aza* in Hebrew—I do not sufficiently understand, unless perhaps he himself wrote the word *GOZI*, and it gradually became *Gaza* through corruption.

Let us also speak spiritually. When people have committed grave sins after works of righteousness—of which it is said in the prophet, “Sow for yourselves righteousness and renew your fallow ground, and do not sow upon thorns” (Hosea 10; Jeremiah 4)—a brood, or generation, of locusts is brought upon them, coming in the morning, when, after the darkness of night has passed, they begin to recognize their sins. And because they have not performed repentance, the *bruchus* is brought upon them, which is called “Gog the king.”

[Note: Two manuscripts read δῶμα, “house” or “roof,” instead of “is translated.”]

For *Gog* is translated into our language as “roof”: a certain proud and arrogant strength. When it has consumed the grass and straw of our land, all who belong to the holy people will seek pardon and say: “Lord God, have mercy. For who else will be able to raise up Jacob” (Isaiah 10) except you alone? Who among physicians can heal the hemorrhaging woman—αἱμορροῦσα (*haimorrhousa*)—except you alone, at the touch of whose fringe health immediately returns (Luke 8:43–48)?

For Jacob is small, or of few in number, because no—or scarcely any—traces of virtue have remained in them. “Relent, Lord, concerning this,” which you threatened to do to your people.

We must understand God’s repentance in Scripture in the same way as his sleep and anger: not as though God repented or changed his decision—he who speaks through the prophet, “I am God, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6), and to whom we say, “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101:28)—but in the sense that, when we turn to better things, he too is said to repent of his sentence. Thus he neither gives the just the rewards he promised if they turn aside to wickedness, nor inflicts upon the sinner the punishments he threatened if the sinner turns toward salvation.

To the person who is about to repent it is said: “Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, that you may be delivered like a doe from snares and like a bird from traps” (Proverbs 6:4–5). If such a person first despises the Lord’s commandments and afterward, placed in distress, begins to awaken, he arouses the Lord who is sleeping for him and says: “Rise up; why do you sleep, Lord?” (Psalm 43:23). Conversely, whoever has stored up wrath for himself on the day of wrath will feel God as angry (Romans 2:5). But if he repents, wrath will be turned into mercy, and the Lord will change in either direction along with our disturbances and virtues, becoming either punishment or clemency.

## Verses 4 and following

The Lord God showed me this: and behold, the Lord God called for judgment by fire; and it devoured the great abyss and consumed the portion at the same time. And I said: “Lord God, cease, I beg you: who will raise up Jacob, since he is small?” The Lord had mercy concerning this. “But this also shall not be,” said the Lord God.

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts read *vocavit*, “called,” a reading almost matched by the Cistercian manuscript and the Vulgate. Previously the text had *vocabit*, “he will call.” Shortly afterward, one Cistercian manuscript, agreeing with the Vulgate, reads *comedit*, “consumed,” instead of *comedet*, “will consume.”]

The Septuagint: Thus the Lord God showed me, and behold, the Lord God called judgment in fire; and it devoured the great abyss and consumed the portion. And I said: “Lord God, stop! Who will raise up Jacob, since he is small? Relent, Lord, concerning this, and this shall not happen,” says the Lord God.

First the Lord showed the prophet the maker of the locusts at the beginning of the sprouting of the late rain, and after the late rain, the king’s shearer—or, to express the word literally, the king’s shearing—Sennacherib, who had shorn and devastated all the ten tribes. Now the same Lord shows Nabuchodonosor; indeed, he calls him and orders him to come against Judah and Jerusalem.

He calls him so that he may set the temple and Jerusalem on fire and execute judgment by fire upon the people who had once been his own. When the fire had come for judgment, to fulfill the Lord’s command, it devoured the great abyss and consumed the portion at the same time: all the cities of Judaea, and the Lord’s portion, which was called his temple.

When the prophet had seen this, he said to the Lord—not, as above, “Have mercy, I beg you,” but “Cease,” or “Stop”—so that he might obtain by his prayers that the one whom he already saw to have begun would cease. Especially since there is no one else who could raise up Jacob, lying prostrate, small, and humbled, except the Lord, who can bring back to the land of Judah those who have been captured and transferred to Chaldaea.

Because, in accordance with the prophet Hosea and the Psalmist, who says, “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle” (Psalm 77:9), we have referred the ten tribes, which were called Israel, to the person of the heretics, and the two tribes over which Judah ruled to the Church and the sinners within the Church—who indeed confess the true faith but, because of the filth of their vices, need purifying flames—therefore the Lord now shows that he calls judgment to the fire.

Thus the fire tests what each person’s work is (1 Corinthians 3:13), and what is written is fulfilled: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isaiah 50:11). Hence it is also said to Babylon: “You have coals of fire; you will sit upon them; they will be of help to you” (Isaiah 47:14, according to the Septuagint).

And in the psalm, the deceitful tongue, full of lies, is said to be purified by the fire of coals: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of desolation” (Psalm 119:3–4). From these coals of the altar, the desolating coal of the two Testaments is taken with tongs and purifies Isaiah’s unclean lips, so that he may prophesy the word of the Lord (Isaiah 6:6–7).

When the fire has been called for judgment, it first devours the abyss—that is, every kind of sin: wood, hay, and straw—and afterward consumes the portion; that is, it reaches the saints who are counted as the Lord’s possession and portion. For it is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord. And in Ezekiel those who are to inflict punishments are commanded: “Begin from my sanctuaries” (Ezekiel 9:6). In the Apostle also we read: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15).

When we have all been in sin and have lain under the truth of the sentence, the Lord will have mercy on us; and because we are small, he will raise us up at the time of the resurrection—or he will raise us up through virtues, though we had been lying in vices—while the Lord promises this and says: “But this also shall not be.”

He appropriately said “but this also,” because he had already said above: “This shall not be.” For he will not be angry forever, nor will he threaten eternally (Psalm 102:9). He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us. As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him.

## Verses 7 and following

He showed me this: and behold, the Lord was standing [the Vulgate reads “standing”] upon a wall of tin or plaster, and in his hand was a mason’s trowel. And the Lord said to me: “What do you see, Amos?” And I said: “A mason’s trowel.” And the Lord said: “Behold, I will place a trowel in the midst of my people Israel. I will no longer add to plaster over it. The high places of the idol shall be demolished, the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste, and I shall rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”

The Septuagint: Thus the Lord showed me: and behold, a man was standing upon a wall of adamant, and in his hand was adamant. And the Lord said to me: “What do you see, Amos?” And I said: “Adamant.” And the Lord said to me: “Behold, I will cast adamant into the midst of my people Israel. I shall no longer add to pass over it, and the altars of laughter shall be destroyed, the sacrifices of Israel shall be laid waste, and I shall rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”

[Note: As is customary, Erasmus and Marianus alter this Greek reading, introducing another fabricated reading, namely ἀλείψωσιν (*aleipsōsin*), which caused confusion among lexicographers, especially the physician Constantine, who, taking the word from Jerome, interprets it in Amos chapter 7 as follows: Ἀλείψωσις—εως, ἡ stagnatura, “the application of tin.” Thus Jerome, in chapter 9 of the prophet Amos. But γάνωσις (*ganōsis*), Aquila’s genuine word and Jerome’s reading, is translated by us as “brightness,” “illumination,” or “that which gives brightness,” which suits tin, or tin-plating, the subject discussed in this commentary. —MART.]

Before we discuss adamant, which Symmachus and the Septuagint translated for the Hebrew word אֲנָךְ (*ENACH*), we should briefly say that Aquila translated this word as γάνωσιν (*ganōsin*), and Theodotion as τηκόμενον (*tēkomenon*). The former signifies “tin-plating,” the latter “melting” or “being melted.” Thus that frying pan—which we read about in Ezekiel 4, where the frying or roasting of a people enclosed by siege is signified—may also be indicated among the ten tribes and in the kingdom of Jeroboam, who was Jehu’s grandson, under whom this prophecy is seen, by the term “tin-plating.”

The Lord, therefore, is seen standing above a wall of tin, or a plastered wall, and in his hand is a tin-plating implement, or a mason’s trowel, with which walls are customarily coated, receiving not only beauty but also strength against rain and frequent storms. We read in Ezekiel 13 that the Lord threatens that, when storm and hail arise, he will neither plaster nor cover the wall of Israel, but will abandon it to be broken apart by the rains.

Hence also now the one of whom it is written—“He shall be called the builder of the wall, himself the cornerstone, the builder of the house”—says that he will lay down the trowel in the midst of his people Israel, and cause it to cease and become idle, so that he will no longer plaster it or clothe and protect it with his aid.

When the Lord withdraws his protection and, so to speak, the clothing of the wall by making the trowel cease, then the high places of the idols, which in Hebrew are called בָּמוֹת (*BAMOTH*), shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of the ten tribes shall be laid waste, so that Dan and Bethel may be destroyed, in which the golden calves were worshiped.

We have explained, as best we could, what has been handed down to us by the Hebrews according to the truth of the historical account. Let us pass to the allegorical interpretation, concerning Xenocrates, who writes about the nature of stones and gems, setting down a few words:

[Note: Not that famous pupil of Plato whose life and writings Laertius reviewed, but another, younger Xenocrates of Aphrodisias, who practiced medicine and flourished in the time of Tiberius and is frequently praised by Pliny, Galen, Trallianus, and Aetius. Indeed, one may conclude that the book from which Jerome derives this material is the same one cited by Galen in Book 10 of *On Simple Medicines*, where he discusses the blood of bats—namely, *περὶ τῆς ἀπὸ τῶν ζώων ὠφελείας*, “On the benefit derived from animals.” The statements made here about softening adamant with the blood of a goat strongly support this identification.]

> “Adamant is the stone that bears its own name, which in Latin we may call *indomitum*, ‘unconquered,’ because it yields to no material, not even iron. For if it is placed upon an anvil and struck with a heavy blow of a hammer, the anvil and hammer receive damage before the adamant is crushed. And although fire subdues everything and consumes all metals, it makes adamant harder, so that not even a tiny corner of it is blunted by the force of excessive heat. I have seen adamant in gold, no larger than a millet seed; although the neighboring gold is consumed by long use and extreme age, the adamant alone is not worn away, and it cannot be diminished by any file. On the contrary, it wears down the file and furrows whatever it touches with lines.

> “This hardest and unconquerable stone is dissolved only by the blood of goats; when placed in warm blood, it loses its strength. It is small and unattractive, having the color of rust and the brilliance of crystal. Four kinds of adamant are described: the first Indian, the second Arabian, the third Macedonian, and the fourth Cyprian; according to the character of their regions they possess greater or lesser hardness. It is also said to detect poisons, like amber, and to resist magical arts.”

Such is the Lord and Savior. Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being made in the likeness of human beings; and being found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8).

Of him Isaiah writes: “He had no appearance” [another reading: “his appearance”] “nor beauty; we saw him, and there was no loveliness in him; despised and last of human beings, a man of sorrows and acquainted with suffering” (Isaiah 53:2–3).

He stands upon a wall of adamant—that is, upon his saints and apostles, to whom he granted that they too should be called adamants, unconquered by anyone, and should say: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” And again: “I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:35, 38–39).

Peter also, who was a most powerful adamant, was told: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against him” (Matthew 16:18).

This man and Lord, who stands upon a wall of adamant, has in his hand an adamant which, unless it is held by the hand of God and surrounded by his aid, loses all its strength. The Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can snatch anything from the hand of my Father” (John 10:29).

And he is so strong that it is said to him: “If you pass through fire, the flame shall not burn you” (Isaiah 43:2). The more he is struck by temptations, the stronger he becomes, and for the name of the Savior he rejoices amid blows.

Although it cannot be conquered by anyone, it is dissolved only by the heat of deadly lust. For this is said to be the nature of goats and of the blood of the goat itself: it is exceedingly hot with regard to lust, and what fire cannot subdue is dissolved by its blood alone.

The Lord therefore places such an adamant in the midst of his people Israel. He no longer passes over it, nor allows the altars—which deserve laughter and mockery—to be destroyed, nor permits all the mysteries of the heretics and the house of Jeroboam, who first divided God’s people, to escape being struck and overthrown by the sword.

## Verses 10 and following

Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam, king of Israel, saying: “Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land cannot endure all his words. For this is what Amos says: ‘Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall be led away captive from its land.’”

And Amaziah said to Amos: “You who see, go away [another reading: ‘depart’]; flee into the land of Judah, eat bread there, and there you shall prophesy. But in Bethel you shall no longer prophesy, because it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom.”

The Septuagint: Amaziah the priests of Bethel sent to Jeroboam, king of Israel, saying: “Amos is organizing assemblies against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land cannot endure all his words. For this is what Amos says: ‘Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall be led captive from its land.’”

And Amaziah said to Amos: “You who see, depart [another reading: ‘go away’]; withdraw into the land of Judah, and live there, and there you shall prophesy. But in Bethel you shall no longer prophesy, because it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom.”

Solomon’s proverb—or rather, command—is: “Do not rebuke the wicked, lest they hate you” (Proverbs 9:8). Conversely, concerning the good he commands: “Rebuke a wise person, and he will love you.” Elsewhere also he says: “Whoever rebukes a person’s ways will afterward find more favor than one who speaks what pleases” (Proverbs 28:23).

Thus Amos spoke to the people out of a desire for their correction and threatened them with terrors from the words of God, so that, by practicing repentance, they might return to God and abandon their idols.

Then the priest of Bethel—in which there was the golden calf established by Jeroboam son of Nebat (1 Kings 12), and by the others who succeeded him in the kingdom—sent to Jeroboam, the grandson of Jehu, to report to him: “Amos has rebelled against you,” or, “He is holding assemblies and gatherings in the midst of your kingdom, Israel. He speaks so much that the land of your kingdom cannot endure his words.”

He dares to send to the king of Israel as though he were a high priest, fearing that, if the people should turn to the worship of God, he would lose the glory of his priesthood.

When he heard the two statements—“The high places of the idols shall be demolished,” or “The altars of laughter shall be destroyed,” and “The sanctuaries,” or “ceremonies,” of Israel shall be laid waste, “and I shall rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword”—he reports only his own supposed injury, so that he appears to grieve solely over the king’s insult.

“For this is what Amos says,” he declares. You are mistaken, slanderer. In all his words the prophet does not speak as though they came from himself; he always places at the beginning: “Thus says the Lord.” Therefore Amaziah reports what the Lord spoke as though Amos the prophet had said it, in order to provoke the king more strongly to vengeance.

What does Amos say? “Jeroboam shall die by the sword.” Here too you lie. He did not say, “He shall die.” If he had said this, he would seem not to admit the possibility of repentance. Rather, he said: “The Lord shall rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword”—threatening punishment, not inflicting it.

Nor did he say, “Jeroboam shall die by the sword,” but “I shall rise with the sword against the house of Jeroboam.” Jeroboam himself did not die by the sword, but his house—that is, his son Zechariah—was destroyed when God struck him.

“And Israel,” he says, “shall be led captive from its land.” Add the rest: “if he does not repent.” But Jeroboam, scorning Amaziah’s utterly foolish message, did not wish to answer anything that he had reported. Therefore Amaziah himself assumes the authority of priestly eminence and says to Amos: “You who see, go away; flee into the land of Judah.”

As we have often said, prophets were formerly called “seers,” because they contemplated with the eyes of the heart the things they said would come. A careful reader may ask why Amaziah calls “seer”—using a prophetic title—the man whom he is forcing to leave the land of Israel.

We must answer either that he says it mockingly, by *κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν* (*kata antiphrasin*), “contrary to the expression,” because Amos is lying about everything; or because he saw that there were many among the people who gladly listened to him. For this reason he also reported to the king: “Amos is holding assemblies against you.” He does not dare to insult Amos openly, lest he injure those who were listening.

“Go,” he says, “into the land of Judah, where you were born, where madmen are gladly heard; eat your bread there, or live there—or perhaps practice your profession by which you obtain your food—and prophesy there, since you have many whom you are accustomed to lead astray.

“But in Bethel, where I am priest, you shall no longer prophesy, because it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom.”

He speaks as a false priest, flattering royal authority, so that he does not say, “It is the sanctuary of our God and the house of the idol,” but rather, “the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom.” This is customary among all who worship false gods: they attribute their own arrogance to kings, so that whatever they themselves do appears to have been done by the king.

Everything that we have interpreted concerning Amaziah, Jeroboam, Israel, and Amos must be referred *τροπολογικῶς* (*tropologikōs*), “figuratively” or “morally,” to the heretics. Their priest Amaziah sometimes sends to Jeroboam, the heretical king and patron of heretics, and accuses holy men and heralds of the faith before him, ordering teachers not to preach in Israel and not to act against the king’s will, because Bethel—that is, the house of God and the false Church—is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom.

For they commonly say: “The emperor is in communion with us.” And if anyone resists them, they immediately bring accusations: “So you are acting against the emperor? Do you despise the emperor’s commands?”

Yet let us consider that many Christian kings who persecuted the Church of God and attempted to establish Arian impiety throughout the world surpass King Jeroboam in wickedness. For he disregarded the commands of the false priest and did not wish to answer anything at his suggestion. These others, however, together with their many priestly Amaziahs, killed the prophet Amos and the priests of the Lord through hunger and deprivation, prisons, and exiles.

## Verses 14 and following

Amos answered and said to Amaziah: “I was not a prophet, nor was I a prophet’s son, but I was a shepherd, tending—or stripping—sycamores. And the Lord took me when I was following the flock, and said to me [the Vulgate adds: ‘the Lord said to me’]: ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’

“And now hear the word of the Lord. You say: ‘You shall not prophesy against Israel, and you shall not drip words against the house of the idol.’ Therefore this is what the Lord says: ‘Your wife shall commit fornication in the city, your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, your land shall be measured out by a measuring line, you yourself shall die in a polluted land, and Israel shall be led captive from its land.’”

[Note: Victorius placed *armentarius*, “cattle herder,” in the Vulgate edition instead of *opilio*, “shepherd”; Jerome’s following exposition supports this reading.]

The Septuagint: Amos answered and said to Amaziah: “I was not a prophet, nor was I a prophet’s son, but I was a shepherd tending sycamores [another reading: mulberry trees]. And the Lord took me from the sheep, and the Lord said to me: ‘Go, and prophesy against my people Israel.’

“And now hear the word of the Lord. You say: ‘Do not prophesy against Israel, and do not gather hearers against the house of Jacob.’ Therefore this is what the Lord says: ‘Your wife shall commit fornication in the city, your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, your land shall be divided by a measuring line, and you shall die in an unclean land; but Israel shall be led captive from its land.’”

We know that the prophet Amos also did what Scripture records the blessed apostles doing when the scribes and Pharisees warned them not to teach in the name of Jesus. They answered: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 4:16).

When the high priest of the idols ordered Amos not to prophesy in Bethel, Amos not only prophesied and showed that he feared more the God who sent him than the one who forbade him; he also boldly and freely announced punishment to the very man who had attempted to forbid him and obstruct the word of God.

“I was not,” he says, “a prophet—or, ‘I was not formerly,’ for one expression indicates humility and the other truth—nor a prophet’s son, nor descended from a prophetic line. Rather, when I was a cattle herder and was stripping the berries from thorn bushes, the Lord took me as I followed the flocks.”

For “cattle herder,” which in Hebrew is called בֹּקֵר (*BOCER*), Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition translated βουκόλος (*boukolos*), “one who pastures cattle,” not sheep. The Septuagint alone used αἰπόλος (*aipolos*), which properly means a goatherd, from αἰπόλιον (*aipolion*), which means “herd”—a herd that dwells in high places. This indicates that herds of goats always climb rocks, rugged crags, and elevated places.

But since the passage continues, “And the Lord took me from the sheep”—ἐκ τῶν προβάτων (*ek tōn probatōn*), “from the livestock”—it appears to signify sheep rather than goats, although at the beginning of Leviticus we read that both sheep and goats are designated by the name “livestock.” Thus the Lord speaks: “If he offers from the livestock”—ἀπὸ τῶν προβάτων (*apo tōn probatōn*)—“a lamb or a kid, a sheep or a goat, to the Lord” (Leviticus 1:10).

As for the expression “tending sycamores,” which Aquila translated as “examining sycamores” and Symmachus as “having sycamores,” some explain it by saying that *sycamina* denotes a kind of tree that grows in the plains of Palestine and produces wild figs. Unless they are stripped, these become exceedingly bitter little figs and are spoiled by gnats.

But to us—since the wilderness in which Amos lived produces no such tree—it seems more likely to refer to thorn bushes that produce berries and console the hunger and poverty of shepherds.

[Note: According to the Septuagint, Amos was an αἰπόλος (*aipolos*), and consequently the lowest among shepherds. For Donatus, in his *Life of Virgil*, says that αἰπόλοι are the least important among shepherds. An αἰπόλος is properly a shepherd of goats, that is, a goatherd, or ποιμὴν τῶν αἰγῶν (*poimēn tōn aigōn*), “a shepherd of goats,” and αἰγονόμος (*aigonοmos*), “a leader of goats.” I myself have often seen such shepherds in Vasconia stripping the berries from thorn bushes, because in our regions there is a great abundance of thorn bushes bearing black berries, which console the hunger and poverty of the poor. If they eat many of them, however, they immediately fall into dysenteric illness. —MART.]

Whatever interpretation the reader wishes to adopt, this much must be said: the Lord took a humble and rustic shepherd, sent him to his people Israel, and commanded him, leaving his own land, to go to Samaria and prophesy there the things that were to come.

“Since,” he says, “the Lord has commanded me to speak, you, Amaziah, say to me: ‘Do not prophesy against Israel, and do not drip words against the house of the idol.’ Hear, then, what the Lord threatens against you.”

In place of “the house of the idol,” the Hebrew has בֵּית יִצְחָק (*BETH ISAAC*), “the house of laughter,” for Isaac is interpreted as “laughter.” The Septuagint translated it “the house of Jacob,” substituting one name for another and failing to understand the matter itself.

Again, where we have placed “And you shall not drip words,” Symmachus translated it: “You shall not rebuke.” To “drip” as a prophet is an idiom of Scripture, because prophets do not pour out all God’s anger at once, but announce it through small drops of warning.

Because, therefore, you said to me, “You shall not prophesy,” your wife shall commit fornication in the city. Symmachus translated this more accurately as πορνευθήσεται (*porneuthēsetai*), “shall be subjected to fornication”: not that she herself will commit fornication, but that, in the passive voice, she will suffer violation by others.

The pain and disgrace are great when a husband, in the middle of the city and in the presence of everyone, cannot prevent his wife from being violated. “Your sons and your daughters,” he says, “shall fall by the sword.” The pain is not as great in a daughter who has been violated as in a wife who has been dishonored; nor is the pain as great in a wife who has been killed as in sons who have been slaughtered. A husband more readily hears that his wife has been killed than that she has been violated.

[Note: All our manuscripts have *audit*, “he hears,” instead of *habet*, “he has”; shortly afterward they consistently read *moriatur*, “may he die,” instead of *morietur*, “he shall die.” Finally, one Palatine manuscript reads: “until he sees the one who served idols,” and so forth.]

Nor is this injury sufficient unless his land too is divided by enemies with a measuring line and receives new inhabitants. Amaziah himself, who now boasts in the power of his priesthood, shall not die in his own land, but, led into captivity, shall die in a land polluted by idols. Nor shall he die before he sees the people whom he had deceived serving and held captive.

According to the moral interpretation, the priest Amaziah is interpreted as “strong and rigid” [another reading: “cold”], because, rebellious and fierce, he forbids an ecclesiastical man and true prophet to proclaim the words and teaching of God, and prevents him from correcting an erring people.

His wife, the false Church, shall be exposed to the fornication of all. His sons and daughters, whom he wrongly generated in error, shall be struck by the Lord’s sword. His land and entire possession shall also become the portion of demons. He himself shall die in a polluted land that has no God as its inhabitant but is contaminated by many errors of false religion. And the whole people that assumes for itself the false name of Israel shall be led captive from its land, so that it may not serve God but submit its neck to the yoke of heretics and demons.

### (Chapter VIII.—Verses 1 ff.) 

The Lord God showed me this: and behold, a hook for fruit. And he said: “What do you see, Amos?” And I said: “A hook for fruit.” And the Lord said to me: “The end has come upon my people Israel; I will no longer continue to pass them by, and the hinges of the temple will creak on that day, says the Lord God. Many will die; in every place silence will be cast down.”

The Septuagint: “Thus the Lord God showed me: and behold, a bird-catcher’s vessel. And he said: ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said: ‘A bird-catcher’s vessel.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘The end [another reading: ‘will come’] has come upon my people Israel; I will no longer continue to pass them by; and the ceilings of the temple will howl on that day, says the Lord God. There will be many falling; in every place I will impose silence.”

What Jeremiah sees under the form of a rod of watchfulness, or of an almond tree (Jeremiah 1)—because he has watched over the sins of his people, lest, as though their eyes were closed and blinking, he should fail to see their transgressions—Amos now likewise observes against Judah and Israel under the appearance of a hook, which in Hebrew is called *CHELUB* (כלוב), and which the Septuagint translates as “a bird-catcher’s vessel.” A bird-catcher, properly speaking, is called *MOCES* (מוקש), as we read above in this same prophet: “If a bird falls to the ground without a bird-catcher.”

The meaning is this: just as the branches of trees are pulled down by a hook in order to pluck their fruit, so I have drawn near the time of captivity. And so that we may know this to be what we are saying, God himself explains what the vision he had shown the prophet signifies: “The end has come upon my people Israel.”

What follows—“I will no longer continue to pass them by”—means that he will no longer overlook or neglect the iniquities of his people, nor permit their crimes to pass unpunished.

And lest he should seem to speak only about the ten tribes, he added: “The hinges of the temple, or the ceilings, will creak on that day, says the Lord.” This must be understood *hyperbolically* (ὑπερβολικῶς), meaning that so great a weight of evils will press upon them that even the hinges of the gates and the lofty ceilings will howl and feel the unbelievable devastation—when many die, and, after the inhabitants have been captured or killed, silence is cast down everywhere.

But if we wish to read “a bird-catcher’s vessel” instead of “a hook for fruit,” we should say that, just as bird-catchers use birdlime or nets to pull birds flying through the air and ranging in the heights down to the ground, so God, through Sennacherib or Nebuchadnezzar—whom we now understand as the bird-catchers—will seize, bind, deport, and kill his people, who had previously been free and exalted through observance of the Law. For nets are not unjustly spread for birds.

This must not be referred only to the time of the Babylonian captivity, but also to the coming of the Lord and Savior, when they said: “Take such a man away from the earth; crucify him, crucify him” (John 19:15), and they destroyed the wings of the dove. The end came upon them, and the final captivity; and thereafter the Lord did not spare them. The hinges of the temple, or the temple ceilings, howled as they fell upon the slain people. And silence was cast down everywhere: the Jews possessed Moses and the Prophets, yet did not possess the Word of God; they read the letter and lost the spirit. Their table became a snare, a retribution, and a ruin; their eyes were blinded so that they could not see, and their ears were stopped so that they could not hear; their back was bent so that they would not look toward heaven. Rather, together with that woman in the Gospel who had a spirit of infirmity (Mark 7), they remained forever bent toward the earth.

The wrath of God was poured out upon them, and the fury of his anger seized them, so that their dwelling became desolate and no inhabitant remained in their tents. Then was fulfilled: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord” (below, verse 11). This will be discussed more fully later, if we reach the end.

Let us therefore, seeing that God did not spare the natural branches, fear suffering the same things, and avoid the bird-catcher’s snares. Let us say to the Lord: “Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God; do not be silent toward me, and I shall become like those who go down into the pit” (Psalm 27:1).

Throughout the whole world the silence of the Jews has been cast down: wherever they are, they mutter rather than speak. Although their blasphemy against the Lord and Savior reaches even to heaven, every interpretation of the Scriptures is mute and silent and does not penetrate the ears of those who hear.

### (Verses 4 ff.)

“Hear this, you who crush the poor and cause the needy of the land to fail [Note: According to the Hebrew and the Vulgate of Victorius, *the impoverished*], saying: ‘When will the month pass, so that we may sell our merchandise, and the Sabbath, so that we may open the grain, to reduce the measure and increase the shekel, and set up deceitful scales, so that we may acquire the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals, and sell the refuse of the grain?’”

The Septuagint: “Hear these things, you who crush the poor in the morning and oppress the needy of the land, who say: ‘When will the month pass, so that we may trade, and the Sabbaths, so that we may open the granary, make the measure smaller and the weight larger, and make an unjust balance, so that we may possess the poor for money, and the needy for sandals, and trade in every kind of merchandise?’”

Lest the hook for fruit and the bird-catcher’s vessel seem to have been shown without purpose, and lest captivity seem to be impending without cause, the reasons for God’s anger are briefly described.

O Judah, O Israel, hear what crimes you have committed. You rise at night for prayer and hymns to God, yet your concern is to oppress, or crush, the poor, so that, exhausted by hunger and poverty, they may be removed from the land.

You wait for the new moons so that you may conduct business and increase interest upon interest, and for the Sabbaths so that you may open your granaries and give grain, expecting to receive more in return. For the sake of sordid profit you turn God’s festivals into opportunities for your own gain. When selling goods, you use a smaller measure, and when receiving them, larger weights, with an unjust balance, so that you may acquire the poor for money and regard human beings as so worthless that you fulfill what I said above about you: “Because you sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of sandals” (above, 2:6).

You leap into such a frenzy for profit that you sell the poor not grain—the eating of which sustains human bodies—but refuse and waste grain, mixing dust and chaff with wheat. We often see perverse teachers and rulers, who govern clergy without fear of God, doing the same. Jeremiah speaks of them: “Their clergy will not profit them” (Jeremiah 12:13, according to the Septuagint).

They think that godliness is a source of gain. Sitting in the temple like money-changers, they display doves—not in cages, but in chairs, as though they were teachers—selling the gifts of the Holy Spirit. They make the measure smaller and larger so that they speak to the poor either briefly or not at all, but address the rich and those from whom they pursue profit in the manner of public speakers, with very lengthy discourse. For money they crush and trample the heads of the poor, and instead of the Lord’s grain—which strengthens the human heart—they force refuse and the cheapest dust into hungry mouths. They even sell these things, which are without any value, although the Lord commanded the apostles: “You have received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10:8).

### (Verses 7–8)

“The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: ‘If I should ever forget all their works.’ Will not the earth be shaken because of this, and every inhabitant of it mourn? And the whole of it will rise like a river; it will be cast out and flow down like the river of Egypt.”

The Septuagint: “The Lord has sworn against the pride of Jacob: ‘If he will forget all your works forever.’ And because of these things shall not the earth be disturbed? And every inhabitant of it shall mourn, and its consummation shall rise like a river, and descend like the river of Egypt.”

Scripture often describes God as swearing. First, in Genesis: “The angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: ‘By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your beloved son, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore’” (Genesis 22:16–17).

And in Psalm 109: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:5). Whoever wrote the Epistle to the Hebrews, explaining this, says: “Since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself” (above, 4:2).

Above, in this same prophet, we read: “The Lord has sworn by his holiness,” or “by his holy ones”: “For behold, the days are coming upon you, and they will take you with weapons,” or “with spears,” and so forth.

He who had earlier sworn by his holiness, or by his holy ones, now swears against the pride of Jacob. If they do not believe him when he threatens, let them believe him when he swears, in human fashion—for people resort to an oath when their simple words are not believed.

Nor is it surprising if God is said to swear, since he sleeps with those who sleep and keeps watch with those who keep watch. He is also said to be angry with those who have stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath (Romans 2).

He swears that he will not forget their works to the end. For “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4); yet he keeps in memory everything they have committed, and brings it forward until the end and the time of judgment.

Hence penitents [another reading: *the suffering*] ask: “Do not remember our former iniquities” (Psalm 78:8), especially since the earth itself is moved, or troubled, against the proud and mourns—not the farmer or the immigrant, but its inhabitant. The consummation rises like a river and descends like the river of Egypt, so that whoever has repented may rise with the rising river, while whoever has persevered in his sins may descend like the river of Egypt and, entering the sea, be swallowed up.

By this he shows that the pride of Jacob, against which the Lord swears, is to be devoured by eternal punishments.

### (Verses 9–10)

“And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord [the Vulgate adds: *God*]: I will make the sun set at noon, and I will darken the earth in the daytime. I will turn your festivals into mourning and all your songs into lamentation. I will bring sackcloth upon every back and baldness upon every head. I will make it like the mourning for an only child, and its end like a bitter day.”

The Septuagint: “And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord God: the sun shall set at midday, and darkness shall come upon the earth in the daytime. I will turn your festivals into mourning and all your songs into lamentation. I will bring sackcloth upon every loins and baldness upon every head. I will make it like the mourning of a beloved one, and those who are with him like a day of sorrow.”

“That day” signifies the day of captivity, when both peoples will be led away to the Assyrians and Chaldeans. Because of the magnitude of their grief, the sun will set for them at noon, and, although the light is bright for all, darkness will fill everything. Their festivals and all their songs will then be turned into mourning and lamentation.

They will be girded with sackcloth over their entire backs, or loins, and, according to the custom of the mourners of old, they will have baldness upon their heads. We read that Job did this when his children died (Job 1). The magnitude of their mourning and grief will be so great that it will surpass the sorrow of a dying only child beloved by its mother; everything will be filled with lamentation and bitterness.

We can also understand this passage as referring to the Lord’s Passion, when at the sixth hour the sun withdrew its rays and did not dare look upon its Lord hanging on the cross (Luke 23). When darkness filled everything, their festivals and songs, after Vespasian and Titus had overcome them, were changed into lamentation and mourning. Everything was filled with tears, repentance, and sackcloth; and those heads became bald which previously, adorned with the hair of Nazirite vows, had nourished their locks for the Lord.

Then the firstborn son of God—the people of Israel, who had laid hands upon the Only-Begotten and true Son of God—was handed over to eternal mourning; and its end, or those who were with it, was filled with bitterness.

Now, therefore, while those who rejected the sun of righteousness have darkness, we who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death have seen a great light (Isaiah 9). Their entire festival has been transferred to the mysteries of the Church, so that while they weep, we sing praises to the Lord.

They gird themselves with ropes and sackcloth instead of a belt; to us, with the apostles, it is said: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). We are girded with the truth of Christ, fulfilling what is written: “Stand therefore, having your loins girded with truth” (Ephesians 6:14). They, however, have been surrounded instead by the devil’s falsehood.

Our head—of which the Savior says, “Even the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matthew 10:30)—has perpetual hair. In our head, which is Christ, we possess strength so that we may kill the lion. They slept upon the knees of the harlot synagogue (Judges 16), and, shorn by the devil, lost the power of their head; with their strength they also lost their eyes, of which it is written in Ecclesiastes: “The eyes of the wise are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness” (Ecclesiastes 2:14). Their companions are occupied in mourning; our companions are clothed in the garment of joy.

### (Verses 11–12)

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord. They will move from sea to sea and from the North to the East; they will go about seeking the word of the Lord, and will not find it. On that day the beautiful virgins and the young men will fail from thirst—those who swear by the sin of Samaria and say: ‘Your god, Dan, lives, and the way of Beersheba lives.’ And they will fall and will not rise again.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord God, and I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread nor a thirst of water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. The waters will be shaken from sea to sea; and from the North to the East they will go about seeking the word of the Lord, and will not find it. On that day the beautiful virgins and the young men will fail from thirst—those who swear by the propitiation of Samaria, who say: ‘Your god, Dan, lives, and your god, Beersheba, lives.’ And they will fall and will not rise again.”

The Hebrew does not have “waters.” And “propitiation,” which we translate as “sin” and which the Hebrews call *ASAMATH* (אשמת), signifies an idol, which is the beginning of sins.

Ancient history—both Latin and Greek and that of all barbarian peoples—records that nothing is more grievous than hunger. It often compels the besieged to eat human flesh and to rage against their own nature, so that parents do not spare their little children, and marital affection tears apart the limbs of a wife once loved.

If this is what bodily hunger does, what must be said about the hunger of souls? It oppressed the Jewish people on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, together with the most burning thirst: they had neither the bread that descended from heaven nor the waters that flowed from Jesus’ belly.

The Law was taken away from them, and the Prophets fell into eternal silence. They move from sea to sea, and from the British Ocean to the Atlantic Ocean—that is, from the West to the South—and from the North to the East. They wander throughout the whole world and are unable to find the word of God.

Here we shall ask the Jews what day they think is being signified, on which they endure a famine of hearing the word of God—especially since they read the Scriptures and follow the humility of the letter. We tell them that the predicted famine is a famine of spiritual understanding, in which Christ is seen and the Lord’s Passion and resurrection are found.

They go around the world and seek the word of the Lord, but do not find it, because they denied the Word of the Lord: the Word that came to be in the hands of all the prophets, that was in the beginning with the Father, that became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1).

At that time the beautiful virgins and the young men—or the elect and teachers—failed in thirst. This is what *BAURIM* (בחורים) signifies.

[Note: In accordance with the evidence of our manuscripts and of the Florentine manuscripts consulted by Victorius, we have corrected this passage as follows. Martianaeus retained it in a corrupt form, incomplete or without meaning, even after Victorius’ warning: “The beautiful virgins, whom they interpret as synagogues,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, from the same manuscripts and from the Brixian manuscripts cited by Victorius, we restored *they show* in place of *they say*: namely, they show that the curses of Deuteronomy have now been fulfilled, after the time came when the teachers of the chosen people failed—specifically, what is stated in chapter 28: that the Jewish people would be placed at the tail, would serve their enemies, and would be reduced to a small number.]

They interpret the beautiful virgins as synagogues, and the elect as the people’s teachers. When these have failed, they teach that the curses of Deuteronomy have been fulfilled in the Jewish people (Deuteronomy 27–29).

These elect and teachers swore by the idol of Samaria, namely the golden calves, and said: “Your god, Dan, lives”—at the borders of the Jewish land, where Paneas now is and where, at that time, the golden calf was worshiped—“and the way of Beersheba lives,” because, on account of the righteous and unrighteous kings of Judah alike, they traveled there by a long and infrequent route.

Because they did this, they will therefore fall and will not rise again—that is, they will not recover the condition they formerly possessed.

The Lord sends famine upon the land and upon those who set their minds on earthly things: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord, when, because of the sins of the people, teaching fails [another reading: *has failed*] in the churches.

They go from sea to sea—that is, from salty and bitter waves until they reach the sea—not encountering rivers or the sweetest and varied springs, but running back again toward bitter waters.

And they go from the North to the East, wishing to abandon the North—which is an exceedingly harsh wind and is called “right” by the ignorant—and reach the East, which they will not be able to find. They do not travel by a straight road, but go around by winding paths; they do not keep to the royal way, but are led through curved and twisting turns.

At that time the virginal souls will fail—those whom the Apostle calls undefiled and who desire to possess eternal chastity. He writes to the Corinthians: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2–3).

And if all virgins were beautiful or good, he would never have said, “The good virgins will fail.” Rather, to distinguish them from evil virgins, he called good those who are holy in body and spirit.

The evil virgins are the five foolish virgins who did not prepare oil for their lamps (Matthew 25). The good and beautiful virgins are those who possessed the light of virtues and entered the bridegroom’s chamber [another reading: *the bride’s chamber*].

The virgins will fail because they will not find the word of the Lord. From this we understand that when teaching is absent from the churches, modesty perishes, chastity dies, and every virtue departs, because they have not eaten the word of the Lord. Whoever eats it and is filled with its nourishment will hear Solomon say: “The righteous man, eating, satisfies his soul; but the souls of the wicked are hungry” (Proverbs 13:2).

[Note: The printed books and many manuscripts add here the name of Abraham: “And David, who had reached the old age of Abraham, freely sang,” and so forth. This is clearly false, because Abraham reached the age of 175 years (Genesis 25:7), whereas David died at the age of seventy, as is established from 2 Kings 5:4. Therefore the name of Abraham was inserted by the unlearned; the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Cygirannus does not read it.

Martianaeus: Manuscripts and printed books from before Martianaeus insert *Abraham* or *of Abraham*, a name which the Cistercian substituted for the following word, *freely*. That reading does indeed produce a somewhat more difficult sense, for David did not attain Abraham’s old age—Abraham lived 175 years, while David lived only seventy. Nevertheless, the ancient reading, which is found in all the books, is preferable to the one Martianaeus extracted from a single manuscript of Saint Cygirannus. The old age of the soul, that is, righteousness, can easily be understood *tropologically* according to the mind of the holy Doctor from the entire preceding context and from the subject of the cited psalm, not as referring to years. The meaning would then be that David, when he had reached Abraham’s righteousness, freely sang: “I was young, and now I am old; yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread.” The testimony just offered from Proverbs also agrees with this: “The righteous man, eating, satisfies his soul,” and so forth.]

And David, who had reached old age, freely sang: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Psalm 36:26).

How many martyrs perished from hunger during the persecutions and lacked grain and the other foods that nourish the body! Therefore he speaks of the bread that descended from heaven, and whoever eats it can neither hunger nor thirst.

When the virgins fail, the young men will also fail—those who had previously conquered the world. They will fail because they swear by the idol of Samaria, which we always understand as representing heretics, as this same prophet says: “Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in Mount Samaria” (above, 6:1).

Heretics despise the Church of God and trust in the falsity of their doctrines, raising themselves against the knowledge of God. With his people divided, they say: “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (1 Kings 12:16).

If anyone therefore swears by the sin of Samaria and says, “Your god, Dan, lives; the way of Beersheba lives,” he will fall and will not be able to rise again.

[Note: Previously, *your* was lacking. Concerning Beersheba, which is interpreted in various ways below, see the Questions on Genesis, column 337, and what we note there.]

The tribe of Dan could not find an inheritance at the farthest boundaries of the Jews, as is written in the Book of Judges (chapter 18); its name is interpreted as “judgment.”

Beersheba, according to variation of accent, is translated in our language as “the well of the oath,” or “the well of satiety,” and “of the seventh.” Thus heretics too will thirst at the farthest boundaries of the holy Scriptures, despising God’s judgment. They will desire the way of Beersheba, which was in the tribe of Judah, and, wishing to imitate many of the Church’s mysteries, will claim that they are satisfied and filled.

The Apostle Paul reproaches them: “Already you are filled; already you have become rich” (1 Corinthians 4:8). They swear in the name of the Lord, but, having fallen once—because they regard the gods of idols as their god—they will not rise again.

Those who wish to repent and do not say, “Your god, Dan, lives, and the way of Beersheba lives,” will hear through Jeremiah: “Shall one who falls not rise again? Or shall one who has turned away not return?” (Jeremiah 8:4).

### (Chapter IX.—Verse 1)

“I saw the Lord standing upon the altar, and he said: ‘Strike the hinge, and let the thresholds be shaken, for greed is at the head of them all, and I will kill their last one with the sword. There will be no flight for them: he shall flee [the Vulgate: “for them that flee”], and he who flees shall not be saved.’”

The Septuagint: “I saw the Lord standing upon the altar, and he said: ‘Strike the mercy seat, and the vestibules will be shaken; scatter them upon the heads of all, and I will kill their survivors with the sword. None of them who flees will escape, and none of those who are rescued will be saved.’”

Whoever, together with Ezekiel and John the Baptist, has seen the heavens opened (Ezekiel 1; Matthew 3), and whoever has had the veil that lay before Moses’ face removed from his eyes (Exodus 34), so that what is written may be fulfilled in him—“The commandment of God is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 18:9)—will see the Lord standing upon the altar and commanding the prophet, or, as many think, the angel who has been assigned to inflict punishments upon sinners, to strike the hinges of the temple, or the mercy seat, so that its thresholds, or vestibules, may be shaken.

“When,” he says, “the temple has been scattered and destroyed because of the wickedness of human beings, and my anger has begun from my sanctuary, let each one recognize that he cannot escape: greed possesses everything, his final destiny is death, and no protection can come to his aid in escaping God’s sentence.”

As for what we read according to the Septuagint—“to scatter upon the heads of all”—

[Note: Two Cistercian and Palatine manuscripts read: “so that he might cut them apart upon the heads of all,” and so forth.]

their heads are beautifully divided who of their own accord divided themselves from him who is the head of all and said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), crying out with impious voice: “Crucify, crucify such a man!” And: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

All this can also be referred to heretics, whose altar is struck and all whose sacrilegious initiations and mysteries are shaken. They have had greed in their heads, with the partridge crying out through them, gathering what it did not hatch, and making riches without judgment (Jeremiah 17).

Therefore the Lord will kill their last members, or their remnants, so that the chapter begun may be completed, and their final state may be foolishness.

When the Lord strikes the hinges and brings the sword upon them, no one will be able to escape or turn aside the Lord’s impending sword.

At the same time, this too must be noted: while the Lord stands upon the altar, first the mercy seat, or the hinges of the temple, is struck; then the vestibules are shaken; third, the heads of all are divided; fourth, those who remain are killed by the sword.

For unless the Lord crushes the pride of the heretics beneath his foot, strikes their perverse and wicked teaching with the spiritual sword, and divides among themselves their teachers—who are understood as the heads—and kills them for the sake of what is good, the disciples cannot be brought to life, according to what is written: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

The teachers are killed and struck so that the disciples may be brought to life; the heads are divided so that the remaining members may be healed.

### (Verses 2ff.)

“If they descend as far as Sheol, from there my hand will bring them up; and if they ascend as far as heaven, from there I will bring them down; and if they hide themselves on the summit of Carmel, from there I will search them out and take them away; and if they conceal themselves from my eyes in the depths of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it will bite them; and if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it will kill them. I will set my eyes upon them for evil and not for good.

“And the Lord God of hosts, who touches the earth and it melts [Vulgate: ‘will melt’], and all who dwell in it will mourn, and it will rise up like a stream and sink down like the river of Egypt.”

The Septuagint: “If they are dug down into Sheol, from there my hand will bring them out; and if they ascend into heaven, from there I will bring them down. If they are hidden on the summit of Carmel, from there [variant: ‘there’] I will search them out and take them away; and if they plunge themselves from my eyes into the depth of the sea, there I will command the dragon, and it will bite them; and if they go into captivity before the face of their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it will kill them; and I will fix my eyes upon them for evil and not for good.

“And the Lord God almighty, who touches the earth and shakes it, and all its inhabitants will mourn, and their consummation will rise up like a river and descend like the river of Egypt.”

The one who had said above, “There will be no escape for them: the fugitive will flee, and the one who flees will not be saved,” now divides that very flight into its parts and testifies hyperbolically that even if they do this and that, they will not be able to escape. “If they descend,” he says, “as far as Sheol, from there my hand will bring them up”—

[Note: Thus the Cluniac manuscript reads, and Marianus Victorius shows that this is how it ought to be read. Erasmus, however, and not a few manuscripts read it with another meaning—not that anyone is withdrawn from the underworld before the day of the resurrection. We understand this as referring to the resurrection of bodies. MART. — Thus all our manuscripts have it, and with the truth itself crying out, Victorius restored the reading, whereas previously the text had *nullus*, with an altogether contrary sense. Meanwhile, it is remarkable that Martianaeus retained the corrupt reading *nullus* in the text, yet approved in the Notes the true correction of the Cluniac manuscript and Victorius.]

—not that anyone is brought back from Sheol before the day of the resurrection, but that even those placed in Sheol are under his power. We recognize that this was fulfilled in the case of Dathan and Abiram, whom the opening of the earth swallowed alive (Num. XVI).

“And if they ascend,” he says, “as far as heaven, from there I will bring them down,” because Enoch and Elijah too, who were taken bodily into heaven (Gen. V; IV Kings II), are governed by God’s will. Observe also the propriety of the expressions: one descends to Sheol; one ascends to heaven. From Sheol we are brought up; from heaven we are brought down. In the one there is utter despair; in the other, the greatness of pride.

“If they are hidden on the summit of Carmel”—whether near the borders of Phoenicia in the northern region, or toward the south because of the wilderness’s vastness, where Nabal the Carmelite once lived (I Kings XXV)—“from there,” he says, “I will search them out and take them away.” And if they hide in the depth of the sea (Jonah I), and, to speak of the prophet, attempt to evade God’s eyes in Tarshish, there I will command the serpent—by which this passage signifies Leviathan or the whale, preserving the metaphor, so that through the serpent and the whale he may come upon his enemies. “And it will bite them,” that is, it will devour them with its jaws.

And lest, perhaps, from the things he said above, we should understand captivity from enemies in some other sense, Scripture, according to its custom, discloses what it had previously spoken in riddles: “And if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it will kill them.” Thus they are not to regard servitude as the final limit of their evils; even after being captured, the hostile sword will pierce them. And those who are able to survive and escape death will not evade God’s gaze; rather, he will set his eyes upon them for evil and not for good, so that he may continually visit them and compel them through torments to repentance.

He says that the omnipotent God will do these things—the God at whose touch and command the foundations of the earth are shaken, or melt away, and all its inhabitants are occupied with lamentation and mourning. He speaks thus to demonstrate the greatness of divine power, lest anyone should perhaps think that he wishes to do what he threatens but lacks the strength to carry out his will. But if the earth melts or is shaken, and even insensible nature perceives [variant: “senses deeply”] its Creator, how much more does man, a fragile creature whose soul’s treasure is enclosed in vessels of clay and in a bodily vessel?

And just as the river of Egypt flows into the sea and is swallowed up, so the land of Israel, of which he had said above, “He who touches the earth and it melts,” will go into captivity and be devoured by its enemies: *μετωνυμικῶς*—metonymically, that which possesses being signified by that which is possessed, through the divine utterance.

These things we have interpreted, as best we could, by following the sequence of the historical account—provided that our understanding did not fail us in certain matters. But David explains the whole *περιοχή*—the entire compass or scope—of this passage when he says: “Lord, you have examined me and known me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 1). Immediately he adds: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into Sheol, you are there. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (ibid., 7–9).

We read something similar also in Deuteronomy: “This commandment, which I command you today, is not above you, nor is it far away; it is not in heaven, so that you might say, ‘Who among us can ascend to heaven to bring it to us, that we may hear it and fulfill it in practice?’ Nor is it across the sea, so that you might make excuses and say, ‘Who among us can cross the sea and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do what has been commanded?’ Rather, the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you may do it” [variant: “that”] (Deut. XXX, 11–12).

For when the soul, released from bodily bonds, has obtained the freedom to fly wherever it wishes—or wherever it is compelled to go—because of the tenuity of its substance, it will either be led to the lower regions, concerning which it is written, “Let sinners be turned into Sheol, all the nations that forget God” (Ps. IX, 18), and, “In Sheol, who will confess to you?” (Ps. VI, 6), and, “Your glory descended into Sheol” (Ps.
