XLVIII, 18); or certainly it will be lifted to the heavenly places, where “the spiritual forces of wickedness” are in the heavenly realms. And if it wishes to claim for itself the knowledge of true circumcision—for this is what Carmel means—and, having rejected humility, to dwell in the mountains, it will not be able to escape the hand of God searching it out.

But if, despairing of salvation, it attempts to evade the Lord’s eyes and reaches the farthest boundaries of false waves, even there the Lord will command the crooked and ancient serpent (Apoc. XX), who is the enemy and avenger, and it will bite the soul. Once captured by vices and sins, it will be punished by the sword of the Lord—

[Note: A certain Medicean manuscript, according to Victorius, reads “will be struck.” He says that this reading agrees better with the Vulgate, which reads “he will kill,” and with the Septuagint, which has “he will destroy.” Let the reader choose whichever he prefers.]

—and he will set his eyes upon it for evil and not for good, so that through torments and punishments it may return to the Lord.

And when God almighty touches their earth, shakes it, and causes all earthly things to melt away, understanding their crimes, they will turn to mourning. The Lord himself will ascend and descend in two ways: he will ascend over the saints like the river of their consummation—that is, of the earth—in order to consume their earthly works; and he will descend over sinners like the river of Egypt, so that they may be thrust down by the Lord’s force into the bitterness of torments.

### (Verse 6)

“He who builds his ascent in heaven and establishes his bundle upon the earth; who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth—the Lord is his name.”

The Septuagint: “He who builds his ascent in heaven and establishes his promise upon the earth; who calls the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth—the Lord almighty is his name.”

The Lord God almighty, who looks upon—or touches—the earth and shakes it, is the one who daily builds his ascent in heaven [variant: “the heaven”]. He says in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17). He did not merely build Eve once from Adam’s rib as a type of the Church (Gen. II); daily he builds believers and the members of his body, and lifts them from earth to heaven, so that he himself may ascend in them.

The Lord ascended into heaven with Enoch (Gen. V); he ascended with Elijah (IV Kings II); he ascended with Moses—

[Note: He alludes to Moses’ *Anabasis*, or *Analēpsis*—“Ascension” or “Taking Up”—concerning which see *Pseudepigraphus Veteris Testamenti*, p. 839.]

—whose burial place could not be found on earth because he had ascended into heaven (Deut. XXXIV). He ascended with Paul, who, as a chosen vessel, was changed from a persecutor into an apostle (II Cor. XII), and, snatched from lowly things into the heights, ascended to the third heaven and, through the Holy Spirit and the Son, reached the Father and heard unspeakable words—the mysteries [variant: “mystery”] of the Trinity—which it is not lawful for human beings to hear.

This one, then, who daily ascends in the saints, established his bundle upon the earth. Concerning it he says in the Gospel: “Do not be afraid, little flock, because it has pleased my Father to dwell in you” (Luke XII, 32). This bundle is bound together by the one religion of the Lord. Hence religion itself received its name from *religare*, “to bind,” because it binds and fastens into the Lord’s bundle.

According to the Septuagint, however, he establishes his promise upon the earth [variant: “established it”], so that all the promises which the holy prophets proclaimed with their mouths may not be an empty sound and the hollow names of mere allegory—

[Note: Martianaeus has *crassa*, “gross,” incorrectly.]

—but may be established upon the earth. And when they have historical foundations, then let them receive the summit of spiritual understanding: so that Christ truly was born of a Virgin; truly raised Lazarus from the dead; truly healed the woman with the issue of blood (*αἱμοῤῥοῦσα*) at his touch; truly, at the Lord’s coming, the blind saw, the lame walked, withered hands were stretched out, and leprosy was cleansed.

Yet according to allegory, the divine word is born daily from a virginal soul; those dead through sin and bound by the cords of vices are daily commanded to come out from the tomb of their crimes; the discharge of blood is daily checked; the blind behold the light in the faith of Christ; those previously lame in faith run along the Lord’s way; dry hands, withered by greed, are stretched out toward almsgiving; and the leprosy of Miriam, which contaminates whatever it touches, recovers its former purity (Num. XII).

This Lord also calls the exceedingly bitter waters of the sea and pours them out over those who have turned their face toward the Lord. He calls the waters bitter in order to make them sweet. He brings forth the winds from his treasuries and, by his powerful command, suspends waters heavy with salt high in the air; then, melting and boiling them with ethereal heat, he distributes them as rain and sends them over the face of the earth, so that everything dry may be watered by showers, and where sin abounded, grace may abound all the more.

### (Verses 7–8)

“Are you not like the sons of the Ethiopians to me, O sons of Israel?” says the Lord. “Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Cyrene? Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the face of the earth; nevertheless, destroying, I will not destroy the house of Jacob,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “Are you not like the sons of the Ethiopians to me, O sons of Israel?” says the Lord. “Did I not bring Israel out of the land of Egypt, and the foreigners from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from the pit? Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the kingdom of sinners, and I will remove it from the face of the earth. Nevertheless, I will not remove the house of Jacob completely,” says the Lord.

In place of “Cyrene,” Aquila and the fifth edition placed the Hebrew word itself, **CIR** (), while the Septuagint has “pit,” that is, *βόθρος*; Theodotion has “wall”; Symmachus has “Cyrene.” We have followed the latter here.

I shall briefly conclude the understanding of the whole passage I have set forth, and of everything contained in this chapter, up to the place where it is written: “Those who say, ‘The evil will not approach, and it will not come upon us,’” so that we may understand the meaning of these words:

“I am the Lord God almighty. Nothing can be hidden from me. I touch the earth, and it is shaken. I build my ascent in heaven. I call the waters of the sea and pour them over the face of the earth. My name is the Lord; I am the creator of all things. I formed all nations from the same clay and gave them birth under an equal condition. Finally, I joined Ethiopians, Philistines, Syrians, and Jews—though differing in places and bodies—under the law of mortality. According to my will I transfer my servants here and there and move them into every province.

“Do not rise up in pride because I brought you out of Egypt and did not allow you, as my special people, to serve Pharaoh. I did the same for the Philistines, whom the Septuagint translated as ‘foreigners’ and who in Hebrew are called **CAPHTHORIM** (). I transferred them from Cappadocia and settled them in the regions of Palestine.

[Note: This passage is wholly dislocated and must be read in reverse order: “that I might transfer from Cappadocia those who are called **CAPHTHORIM** in Hebrew.” For who does not know that the Philistines are called **PHELESTHIM** in Hebrew, not **CAPHTHORIM**, which is the name of the Cappadocians? Victorius otherwise supplies his own correction: “who are called in Hebrew, that I might transfer them”—that is, from Cappadocia—which is less acceptable, since the passage can be restored, without inserting invented words, merely by changing the order of its clauses as indicated. But Martianaeus deserves no thanks from readers, since he concealed—or wholly failed to notice—the error which, as Victorius says, ought to be exploded with clapping hands.]

I transferred them from Cappadocia and settled them in the regions of Palestine. I also transferred the Syrians—that is, **ARAM** ()—from Cyrene. Since those who were made under an equal condition will be punished by an equal sentence of my judgment, I will overthrow all impious kingdoms without respect of persons.

“But you, O sons of Israel, of whom I said, ‘Israel is my firstborn son’ (Exod. IV, 22), and, ‘Out of Egypt I called my son’ (Hos. XII, 1), I will strike with the rod and visit your sins; yet I will not destroy you forever, and I will not remove my mercy from you” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

And, as those shaken and tossed in a sieve, I will cleanse and choose you, so that whoever is a little stone and has been strengthened through repentance will not fall out of my sieve. But whoever falls to the earth like dust will be struck by the sword, so that [variant: “and”] the sinners of my people may die—not because they sinned previously, but because they persisted in sins until death.

Every Israelite who first beholds God with the mind and is brought out of Egypt, if, longing for the vices of Egypt and the pleasures of the world, he returns not only to Egypt but to Ethiopia—where, according to Jeremiah (ch. XIII), the one who is there cannot change his skin—is saved [variant: “saves himself”] by the coming of Christ.

[Note: This is the reading of all the books, and it is sufficiently clear; nor do I see why Victorius changes it. In *eductus est*, he says, the sense otherwise does not hold together.]

In him is fulfilled what is written: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. LXVII, 32). And when he worships him, it will be said of him: “Before him the Ethiopians will fall” (Ps. LXXI, 9).

When they have fallen and have brought offerings to the Lord from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, they will be able to say: “I am black but beautiful, because the sun has discolored me” (Song I, 4). Bodies that languish in shade and idleness cannot endure the trials and heat of the world. But those prepared for struggle and contests, dried by the sun, overcome the injuries of the world and receive the blessing of the Holy Spirit, who says to the righteous: “By day the sun will not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. CXX, 6).

Thus Ethiopians become sons of God if they repent, and sons of God become Ethiopians if they plunge into the depths of sins. For the same God, creator of all, transforms Cappadocians into Philistines. Those who dwelt in the cold of faith and were subject to the harshest northern wind, he caused to fall as those who drink, and, having laid aside their pride, to experience the Lord’s judgment.

He also transferred the Syrians—that is, the exalted and lofty, who are called **ARAM**—from Cyrene, the weak wall, or the place that overhung the exceedingly bitter sea and lay near the Syrtes; according to the Septuagint, they were held in a pit. He changed them for the better, so that he might make them exalted.

For the eyes of the Lord are upon all sinful kingdoms, which the devil showed to the Lord (Matt. IV), and concerning which the Apostle says: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. VI, 12). Nevertheless, when he visits sinners with the rod, crushes and strikes those who persist in sin, he does not allow those souls called the house of Jacob—those who supplant sin, overcome in the contest, and seize the heel of their bloodstained brother—to perish forever.

### (Verses 9–10)

“For behold, I will command, and I will shake the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is shaken [the Vulgate adds: ‘wheat’] in a sieve, and not a little stone will fall to the earth. All the sinners of my people who say, ‘The evil will not approach, and it will not come upon us,’ will die by the sword.”

The Septuagint: “For behold, I command, and I will winnow the house of Israel among all the nations, as one winnows with a winnowing fan, and no crushed particle will fall to the earth. All the sinners of my people who say, ‘The evil will not approach, nor will evils come upon us,’ will die by the sword.”

The God who measured the waters in his hand, heaven with his span, and enclosed the whole earth in his fist (Isa. XL), in accordance with his greatness, will hold the edges of the earth with both hands and shake it back and forth like a sieve, so that the chaff and filth of sinners fall to the earth while the pure grain remains to be stored in the granaries.

Or, as the Septuagint translated it, he will hold a winnowing fan in his hand, cleanse his threshing floor, store the wheat in his granaries, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. Concerning them he speaks through Jeremiah: “What has straw to do with grain?” says the Lord (Jer. XXIII, 28).

The same thing is shown under the figure of another parable by that dragnet which is cast into the sea of this world and draws out fish of every kind; after the bad fish have been thrown away, only the good are kept (Matt. XIII). So also the Lord dispersed the wretched house of Israel throughout the whole world, shook it in a sieve, and winnowed it with a shovel. Since the little stones and pebbles do not fall upon the earth, those who are called the sinful people because of their filth and dust will die by the sword.

They will suffer this because they do not believe the prophecies of the prophets and do not think that what the Lord threatens through them will come to pass. While they promise themselves prosperity, they will afterward endure evils. This stands opposite to the saints who fear and do not sin, and who therefore do not die by the sword, because they said: “Evils will approach us, and punishments will come upon us, which our sins have deserved.”

God speaks more fully about this through Jeremiah: “I will take up and speak against a nation and a kingdom, to remove and destroy it; if that nation turns from its evils, I too will repent of the things I had thought to do to it” (Jer. XVIII, 7–8).

God therefore does not change, for he is always immutable; rather, we change him through our conversion. He rages, grows angry, threatens, and says that he will inflict punishments. If we repent, he too will repent of his sentence.

Again, according to the same Jeremiah (ch. XVII)—

[Note: In one Cistercian manuscript and another Palatine manuscript the reading is: “he promises prosperity, if we repent; but if we are dissolved through negligence, etc.”]

—he promises prosperity; if we are dissolved through negligence, he will also repent of his promise and change what he promised.

We may take the Ninevites and Jerusalem as examples of this: the former were delivered from impending punishments, while the latter lost what had been promised to their fathers.

### (Verses 11ff.)

“On that day I will raise up the fallen tent of David, and rebuild its openings [or breaches] in the walls; I will restore what had fallen down, and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations over whom my name has been invoked,” says the Lord who does these things.

The Septuagint: “On that day I will raise up the fallen tent of David, and rebuild what had fallen down; I will raise up what had been dug down and restore it as in the days of old, so that the remnant of humanity may seek me, and all the nations over whom my name has been invoked,” says the Lord who does all these things.

[Note: Previously it read *aedificabo*, “I will build,” less correctly in place of *reaedificabo*, “I will rebuild,” which is preferred by the manuscripts and the Greek *ἀνοικοδομήσω*.]

[Note: Martianaeus corruptly retained *suffusa*, “overflowing,” in place of *suffossa*, “dug down,” which our manuscripts and Victorius long ago restored from seven Florentine manuscripts according to the Greek *κατεσκαμμένα*. Shortly afterward, in place of *antiquos*, one Cistercian manuscript has *antiqui*. Finally, it omits the last word, *omnia*, “all,” which is also absent from the Alexandrian and Complutensian Greek copies.]

Where the authority of the apostles precedes—especially that of Peter and James, whom the chosen vessel calls pillars of the Church (Gal. II)—all suspicion of varied interpretation must be removed, and what such men explain must be followed.

When a question arose among the apostles in the Acts of the Apostles as to why Paul and Barnabas had received people from the nations without circumcision or observance of the Sabbath, Peter replied as he ought. James approved his judgment and said:

“Men, brothers, listen to me. Simon has related how God first visited the nations to take from them a people for his name; and with this the words of the prophets agree, as it is written: ‘After these things I will return, and I will rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will rebuild its ruins and raise it up, so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, and all the nations over whom my name has been invoked,’ says the Lord who does these things: his work is known to the Lord from eternity” (Acts XV, 13ff.).

This tent of David, then, had fallen—fallen in those who say, “The evil will not approach, and it will not come upon us,” whom the Lord had shaken in his sieve and tested, whose threshing floor he had cleansed with the winnowing fan of his majesty, and all of whom had been sinners he killed with the sword.

Now, according to the custom of Scripture, after torments and punishments, promising prosperity and joy, he says that he will raise it up and restore everything in the Lord’s resurrection, so that what had fallen in the synagogues may rise in the Churches. Believers will possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations, so that whatever remains of the bloody and earthly kingdom may be changed into heavenly kingdoms, and all the nations that have forgotten the Lord may be converted and return to him.

But if we wish to read according to the Septuagint—“so that the remnant of humanity may seek me, and all the nations over whom my name has been invoked”—

[Note: Three manuscripts read: “so that the remnant of Israel may seek me, and all …”]

—we should understand the remnant of humanity as those from the Jewish people who believed, and who, like a little stone, did not fall from the sieve, nor were cast away with the dust, chaff, and filth.

[Note: See pseudo-Rufinus, *Commentary on this Prophet*, p. 557ff., where he speaks of little stones placed in a sieve to moderate the sieve’s force.]

For remnants will be saved at the beginning of faith and at the end of the world, so that when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel may be saved [variant: “may be saved”—future] (Rom. XI).

The name of the Lord invoked over the remnant and over all the nations is the name concerning which the Savior says: “Father, I have revealed your name to the human beings” (John XVII, 6).

And, not to delay at length the rule governing the promises, the Jews promise themselves in vain expectation, and understand carnally as destined for fulfillment at the end of time, all the things proclaimed in this prophet and in the others concerning the rebuilding of Jerusalem [variant: “the walls of Jerusalem”], the Temple, and the blessedness of all things.

But we, who follow not the letter that kills but the Spirit that gives life, demonstrate that these things have already been fulfilled in the Church and are fulfilled daily in individuals who, falling through sin, are rebuilt through repentance.

### (Verses 14–15)

“Behold, days are coming,” says the Lord, “when the plowman will overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes the one who sows seed.

[Note: Again, Martianaeus incorrectly retained *comprehendit*.]

The mountains will drip sweetness, and all the hills will be cultivated. I will restore the captivity of my people Israel, and they will build the deserted cities and inhabit them; they will plant vineyards and drink their wine; they will make gardens and eat their fruits. I will plant them upon their own soil, and they will no longer be uprooted from their land, which I gave them,” says the Lord your God.

The Septuagint: “Behold, days are coming,” says the Lord, “when threshing will overtake the vintage, and the grape will vary in the seedtime. The mountains will drip sweetness, and all the hills will be planted. I will restore the captivity of my people Israel, and they will build the ruined cities and inhabit them; they will plant vineyards and drink their wine; they will make gardens and eat their fruit. They will be planted upon their own land, and they will no longer be uprooted from the land which I gave them,” says the Lord almighty.

After the fallen tent of David has been raised and the things that had collapsed and been overturned have been rebuilt, an abundance of all things is described. Those who previously went forth weeping, carrying their seeds, will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves (Ps. CXXV), so that the threshing of the sheaves may overtake the vintage, or the plowman the reaper, and the grape may take on its color at seedtime.

Or, as is more correct, the treader of grapes will overtake the sowing, and all things will succeed one another in such a way that no day will be without grain, wine, and joy.

At that time, with the winepresses full, grapes will be trodden, and must reddened with the blood of Christ and the martyrs will be poured forth—

[Note: See St. Zeno’s treatise 27ff., book II.]

—and such a treader of grapes will be a seedbed of the word of God, so that their blood may cry out in the world more loudly than the blood of righteous Abel cried out.

Whoever, by reason of his virtues, has climbed to the mountains will sweat honey—indeed, will drip the sweetness of the word of God—concerning which it is written: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. XXXIII, 9), and, “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 103).

Those who are below the mountains, or rather those who are second to the mountains, whom the Bridegroom leaps over in the Song of Songs (Song II) and calls hills, will be planted and will imitate God’s paradise, so that all kinds of doctrinal fruits may hang upon them.

Then, if anyone is captive through unbelief and has not yet believed in the Lord’s name, and is among the remnant of his former people Israel, he will return to the faith of Christ, so that the one whom he had heard in the Prophets he may hold in the Gospel.

These mountains that will drip sweetness and these hills that will be planted, after the Lord has restored the captivity of his people Israel, will build the cities that had previously been deserted and inhabit them. Thus each city that has been built may say: “I am a strong city, a city under siege” (Prov. according to the Septuagint), and concerning which the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V, 14). And in the Psalms it is said: “The river’s rushing stream makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 4).

[Note: Victorius prefers the plural, “make glad,” following the Greek *εὐφραίνουσι*.]

They will also plant vineyards with Noah (Gen. IX), drink their wine, and become drunk; and they will hear from the Lord Savior: “Drink, my friends, and become drunk” (Song V, 1). They will drink the wine which he promised that he would drink anew with his apostles in his Father’s kingdom (Mark XIV). This is the vineyard of Sorek, whose wine we drink daily in the mysteries.

Nor content with the happiness of these things, they will make gardens for their delight and irrigate them, so that no kind of virtue may be lacking in them, and they will eat their fruits. For the one who plants and waters will himself also eat.

And when the mountains and hills have done all these things—dripping sweetness, building cities and inhabiting them, planting vineyards and drinking their wine, making gardens and eating their fruits—then the Lord will plant those very planters upon his land, concerning which it is said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13), and in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the earth” (Matt. V, 4).

After he has planted them and firmly established them with a deep root [variant: “deep roots”], he will no longer uproot them from the land which he had given them [variant: “will give them”].

From this we understand that the Church will indeed be shaken by persecutions until the end of the world, but can never be overthrown: it may be tested, but not overcome. This will happen because the Lord God almighty—or “the Lord their God,” that is, the God of the Church—has promised that he himself will do it. His promise is the law of nature.

[Col. 1097]

## The One Book of the Commentaries of St. Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, on the Prophet Obadiah (C)

### Prologue

[Note: This too is entitled *Explanatio*—“Explanation”—and is addressed to Pammachius.]

[Col. 1097A] 359–360

“When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; when I became a man, I put away childish things” (1 Cor. 13). If the Apostle makes progress [Al. “made progress”], and, forgetting what lies behind each day, stretches himself toward what lies ahead, and, according to the command of the Lord and Savior, holds the plow and does not look back (Phil. 3; Luke 9), how much more should I, who have not yet reached the age of a perfect man and the measure of Christ (Eph. 4) [Note: [Col. 1097C] For *veneram*, apparently.], deserve pardon because, in my youth, provoked by the ardor and zeal for the Scriptures, I interpreted the prophet Obadiah allegorically [Al. “have interpreted”], although I did not know his historical meaning. My spirit burned with a desire for mystical knowledge; and because I had read that all things are possible for those who believe, I did not know that the gifts are diverse. [Col. 1097B] [Note: [Col. 1098C] In my opinion, two Palatine manuscripts more correctly read *litterulas* (“little letters”).] I knew the writings of the world and therefore supposed that I could read the sealed book. Fool that I was! The twenty-four elders, holding bowls and lyres in their hands, and the four living creatures full of eyes, rise from their throne, confess their ignorance, and sing glory to the Lamb (Rev. 5); and the rod from the root of Jesse, and supposed that I could do what I believed. Yet in my hand the word of God was not brought to pass, nor could I say, “From your commandments I gained understanding” (Ps. 118); nor did I remember that beatitude from the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). The coal had not yet been taken from the altar to cleanse my lips (Isa. 6:8). The error of my former ignorance had not yet been cut away by the fire of the Holy Spirit, 361–362 and I spoke boldly to the Lord: [Col. 1097C] “Here am I; send me.”

I hoped that what I had written lay hidden in little chests [Al. “lay there”], and I had consigned the first rash effort of my small talent to the flames, when suddenly a copy was brought from Italy by a certain young man who was as many years old as I had once been when I wrote it, and who praised my little work. I confess that I was amazed: however badly someone may have written, he finds a reader like himself. The other man praised it, while I blushed; he carried its supposed mystical interpretations to heaven, while I was prevented, with downcast head, from confessing my shame.

What then? Are we to condemn the things in which we played as boys? Certainly not. For we know that in the tabernacle of God both gold and goats’ hair were offered in the same way. We read in the Gospel (Mark 12) that the two small coins of the poor widow were approved more than the possessions of the rich [Al. “the possessions of the rich were approved”]. At that time we gave what we had; and now, if indeed we have made any progress, we return to the Lord what belongs to him. “By his grace I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15). Nor do I deny that during these thirty years [Note: [Col. 1098C] The words *in eius* are absent from the same manuscripts.] I have sweated in his work and labor.

The Father is merciful: he receives the son who returns quickly and does not wait until someone opens the door. He himself goes out to meet him; he prepares the ring and the robe. Although his brother envies him and calls him a fornicator and a wastrel, an angelic symphony of joy, together with that of all the heavenly virtues, resounds over his salvation (Luke 15). This is that time, my Pammachius, sweeter than light, when, after leaving the school of the rhetoricians, we were carried along by different pursuits, when Heliodorus—most dear to me—and I were striving to live together in the solitude of Chalcis in Syria [Al. “we wished to do so.”] What I thought was hidden has been made public.

I shall enter again upon the old tracks, correcting, if possible, the crooked strokes of the letters. I was an infant and did not yet know how to write; my hand faltered, my fingers trembled. Now, even if I have made no other progress, at least I possess that Socratic saying: “I know that I do not know.” Your Cicero likewise says that certain things begun and rough slipped from him when he was a young man. If he could say this of the books addressed to Herennius as well as of the *Rhetorica*, which I consider almost perfect, when comparing them with the expertise of old age, how much more freely may I acknowledge that the former belonged to youthful talent and the latter to mature old age!

In his books Against Marcion, Septimius Tertullian likewise admitted [Al. “confessed”] this; so did Origen in his commentary on the Song of Songs, and Quintilian in the twelve books of the *Institutes of Oratory*. [Col. 1099A] From these examples it is plainly shown that each age is perfect in its own sphere and ought to be judged according to the number of its years.

But now it is time to set forth the beginning of Obadiah [Col. 1100A] and, with the help of your prayers—you to whom this volume is written—to cross the broken sea and the winding whirlpools of the age.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1099]

[Col. 1099A] **(Verse 1.) “The vision of Obadiah.”** [Note: [Col. 1099D] Jerome—or Eusebius in the *Chronicle*—does not disagree with this, since under Jehoshaphat, king of the Jews, at the time when Ahab was king of Israel, Eusebius teaches that Obadiah prophesied. Yet Saint Augustine, *City of God* 18.31, says: “The three prophets among the Minor Prophets—Obadiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk—neither state their own times, nor is it found in the *Chronicles* of Eusebius or Jerome when they prophesied. On this matter we shall have more to say under the fifth year of Jehoshaphat in the *Chronicle*.]

The Hebrews say that this was the man who, under Ahab, king of Samaria, and the most impious Jezebel, fed one hundred prophets in caves—those who had not bent the knee to Baal—and that he was one of the seven thousand whom Elijah is accused of not knowing (1 Kings 18). His tomb is still venerated today, together with the mausoleum of the prophet Elisha and of John the Baptist, at Sebaste, which was formerly called Samaria. Herod, king of Judea and son of Antipater, later named it Augusta in honor of Augustus Caesar, using the Greek language.

Since this man had fed one hundred prophets, he received prophetic grace; from commander of an army he became commander of the Church. At that time he had fed a little flock in Samaria; now throughout the whole world he feeds the Churches of Christ. And *pherōnymōs* (φερωνύμως), that is, “appropriately to his name”—just as in the Acts of the Apostles Stephen was crowned by martyrdom (Acts 7)—so this man too was called the servant of the Lord.

Furthermore, the reason why, looking against Idumea, he sees not an “oracle,” that is, *lēmmā* (λῆμμα), nor the “burden” of Idumea, according to the rule and distinction that we set out in Nahum, is either that Edom—that is, Esau (Gen. 26)—is not counted among foreign nations, being the son of Isaac and the brother of Jacob. Hence his land is not given to Israel as a possession, Israel is not permitted to wage war against it, and Israel is forbidden to take up arms against its brother [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read *contra eum* (“against him”), and prohibit taking up arms against the brother.]; or else the title is “the vision,” not “of Idumea”—which, had it been written in that way, could have occasioned a question—but “of Obadiah,” that is, “of the servant of the Lord,” who sees the vision concerning the nations to which the Lord sent an envoy. And to them it is said: “Rise, and let us rise up against her for battle.”

For the destruction of Idumea is the vision of Nahum. [Note: [Col. 1100D] The reading *Nationum* (“of the nations”), which until now has prevailed in all the books instead of *Nahum*, is plainly an obvious error. Without it, both the context of Jerome’s writing and the sense and truth of sacred history would be impossible. It is surprising that none of the editors noticed this conspicuous mistake. It was easy to suppose that a copyist, deceived by the similarity of an abbreviated form, had made the error. We had already determined to restore the prophet’s name when, in one Palatine manuscript, we observed that the same correction had been entered by a later hand and that the word *Nationum* had been struck out.]

But if someone asks why the title says “The vision of Obadiah,” while nothing afterward is shown to have been seen, as in Isaiah: “I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (Isa. 6:1); and in Ezekiel: “The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God,” immediately followed by: “I looked, and behold, a storm wind was coming from the north, and a great cloud, with radiance around it” (Ezek. 1:1ff.); whereas after Obadiah’s vision it is immediately introduced: “Thus says the Lord concerning Edom”; and again: “Behold, I have made you small among the nations”—we shall take an example from Deuteronomy, in which not events but words are seen: “Pay attention to yourself,” it says, “and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the words that your eyes have seen” (Deut. 4:9).

And John says in his Epistle: “What we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon, and what our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). Moses likewise says that he saw the voice of the Lord speaking to him (Exod. 20). Therefore, if what has been said is introduced after the vision, and things ordinarily perceived by the ears are seen by the eyes of the mind, it is rightly called a “vision,” since prophets were formerly called “seers.”

**“Thus says the Lord God concerning Edom.”**

A small prophet in the reckoning of verses, not of meanings. Otherwise, as with Solomon’s three books, the shorter the Song of Songs is, the more difficult it is. We have expressed the meaning of the Epistle to Philemon. The Gospel saying too, though abbreviated, is narrower than the elaborate works of the Law.

So here too the prophet, like the servant of the Lord Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, like Moses the servant of God, and like the apostle, sees and hears the words of Christ—things worthy of prophetic service. Many think, following the interpretation of his name, that this servant is the servant of the Lord to whom it is said in Isaiah: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. 49:6, according to the Septuagint), the one who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7). But if we understand it in this way, we must seek another envoy who has been sent to the nations. While following the tropological interpretation, we lose the clearest prophecy.

We must therefore ask who this Edom, or Idumea, is to whom the Lord now speaks through Obadiah. In the book of Genesis we read very plainly that Esau, the son of Isaac, was called Edom because he sold his birthright for red lentil stew (Gen. 25). For Edom is interpreted as *pyrrhos* (πυρρός), that is, “red.” In the same volume we read that he was also called Seir, that is, “hairy,” because he was rough-haired and did not possess Jacob’s smoothness.

Thus one and the same man is called by three names—Esau, [Col. 1101A] Edom, and Seir—and he possessed the region now called Gebalene, which lies on the borders of Eleutheropolis. The Horrites had formerly inhabited it; their name is interpreted as “free,” and from this the city afterward received its name.

What is called EDOM in Hebrew (), and *Idoumaia* (Ἰδουμαία) in Greek, is now a village of Palestine, 365 named by its founder with this name. Both Latin and Greek history remember it.

This is the one to whom Amos says: “For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not revoke his punishment, because he pursued his brother with the sword, violated his compassion, maintained his anger continually, and kept his indignation forever” (Amos 1:11).

In Isaiah too, according to the Hebrew text, we read: “The oracle of Dumah. One cries to me from Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa. 21:11). Jeremiah also agrees with the same prophecy, saying: “Is wisdom no longer in Teman?” (Jer. 49:7), and the rest through the end of his prophecy, where it is said: “And the heart of the mighty men of Idumea shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in labor.”

Apart from a changed order and certain other details that appear to differ, a large portion of Obadiah is contained in Jeremiah’s book. These are the mountains of Seir against which Ezekiel’s face is strengthened, and he is told: “I will make Mount Seir desolate and deserted.” A little later: “You shall be devastated, Mount Seir, and all Idumea.”

It would be a lengthy task to examine all the Scriptures and bring forward everything concerning Mount Seir, especially the passages in Malachi, where it is written at the very beginning: “Was not Esau Jacob’s brother? says the Lord. Yet I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated. I made his mountains a desolation and his inheritance a dwelling-place of desert creatures. If Idumea says, ‘We have been destroyed, but we shall return and rebuild the desolate places,’ thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘They may build, but I shall demolish; and they shall be called the boundaries of wickedness, and the people with whom the Lord is angry forever’” (Mal. 1:2–4).

Since, therefore, we have learned that the land of the Idumeans is hostile to the land of promise; since we read that Esau is Jacob’s enemy and that he is a people with whom the Lord is angry forever, we must understand, according to the laws of tropology, either that this word was spoken against the Jews—who are rivals of Christians and persecute their brother Jacob, the supplanting people who snatched the birthright from them [Col. 1101D]—or certainly against all heresies and doctrines opposed to the truth. These doctrines seem close to us, but are more hostile; and they strive to expel the simple inhabitant of the house of Jacob from the paternal inheritance.

Since Idumea is interpreted as “earthly,” and because of its red color can also be understood as “bloodstained,” 366 therefore, when the Savior reports his victory over the world to the Father, while the angels cry out, “Lift up your gates, princes, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:7), and in Isaiah they ask in amazement: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with shining garments from Bosor, so beautiful in a white robe?” (Isa. 63:1–3), they speak directly to him: “Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one treading the winepress?”

He speaks in triumph, setting forth the victories of his cross: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me.”

Some refer Idumea to the flesh and think that the soul is provoked to fight against it, so that, by putting to death our members that are upon the earth—fornication, uncleanness, passion—we may attain eternal victory in Christ.

The Jews vainly dream that this prophecy is directed against the city of Rome and the Roman empire. They also claim that what is written in Isaiah, “The oracle of Dumah” (), can, by changing the shape of one letter slightly, be read with *res* instead of *daleth*, and can sound like “Rome” (). For in their language the letter *vau* is taken both for *u* and for *o*.

**“We have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy to the nations: Rise, and let us rise up against him for battle.”**

The Septuagint: “I heard a report from the Lord, and he sent a stronghold among the nations: Rise, and let us rise up against him for battle.”

As we said above, Edom and Idumea are the same, because in Hebrew the name is that of the one who founded it, while in Greek the city founded by him is named. Therefore either Obadiah heard, or all the prophets together heard—for they all write against Edom—that an envoy had been sent to the nations: the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. Of him the Father also speaks through Haggai: “I shall shake all the nations, and the Desired One of all the nations shall come” (Hag. 2:8). In Isaiah he is written as the Angel of great counsel and the Father of the age to come (Isa. 9).

Since, instead of “envoy,” that is, *sir* (), the Septuagint translated *periochē* (περιοχή), that is, “stronghold,” we can say that our envoy is himself also our stronghold. He says what the prophetic utterance has woven together: “Rise, and let us rise up against him,” or “against her,” for battle.

The envoy sent to the nations speaks these words: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Eph. 5:14).

And lest the battle seem perhaps difficult and unfamiliar to us, he says: “You have me first in the battle line. I shall be the *archistratēgos* (ἀρχιστράτηγος), the commander-in-chief of the battles. I am the one who appeared holding a sword to Joshua son of Nun; and, while Moses fought, I overcame Amalek under the banner of my cross” (Exod. 17).

[Note: [Col. 1101D] We supplied the word *meae* (“my”) from our manuscripts after *Victorium*, since these words are spoken in the person of Christ. The same manuscripts read *auditum* (“a report”) shortly afterward instead of *auditu* (“by a report”). Finally, as we also approve, our manuscripts read *missus est* (“has been sent”), in accordance with the Greek ἀπέστειλεν, whereas Martianay retained *missus sum* (“I have been sent”).]

Jeremiah, in his vision against Idumea, does not differ greatly from this: “I heard a report from the Lord, and an envoy was sent to the nations: Assemble yourselves and come against her, and let us rise up for battle” (Jer. 49:14).

It follows:

**(Verses 2ff.)** “Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are exceedingly contemptible. The arrogance of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock [Vulg. ‘of the rocks’], who raise up your throne [Vulg. ‘his throne’], who say in your heart, ‘Who will bring me down to the ground?’ If you are raised up like an eagle, and if you set your nest among the stars, from there I shall bring you down, says the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, I have made you least among the nations; you are greatly dishonored. The arrogance of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the holes of the rocks, who raise up your dwelling and say in your heart, ‘Who will bring me down to the ground?’ If you are raised up like an eagle, and if you set your nest among the stars, from there I shall bring you down, says the Lord.”

Jeremiah, whom we mentioned above, agrees almost word for word, saying: “Behold, I have made you small among the nations, contemptible among human beings. Your arrogance has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who dwell in the caves of the rock and strive to seize the height of the hill. When you raise your nest as high as an eagle, from there I shall bring you down, says the Lord.”

In prophetic interpretation we ought to follow our customary method: first laying the foundations of the historical meaning, and then, if we can, raising lofty towers and the summits of the roof.

“O Edom,” he says, “although you are small among all the surrounding nations and, in comparison with the other peoples, few in number, you lift yourself up with pride beyond your strength. Though you live in grottoes, indeed in caves of the rocks, humble and poor, possessing no lofty roofs of buildings, you are lifted up like an eagle into the heights. You swell so much in thought that you believe yourself to dwell among the stars. Even if you could penetrate the heights of heaven beyond the limits of nature, I would bring you down from there 368 and lead you to the earth, says the Lord God.”

The addition in Jeremiah—“and strive to seize the height of the hill”—has disclosed the riddle: it signifies Mount Zion and thereby intends either the city of Jerusalem itself or the temple built in it.

Those who discuss the nature of birds have also recorded that the eagle flies higher than all other birds. It is said to possess such keen sight that, while it is carried motionless over the seas on unmoving wings and is invisible to human eyes, from so great a height it sees little fish swimming below; and when they draw near the shore, it descends upon them like a missile, seizes its prey, and drags it to the shore on its wings.

If we have learned the history, let us follow the spiritual understanding. Although you may seem great to yourself, O heretic, and may despise the smallness of the Church, you are nevertheless small among the nations and contemptible—and not merely contemptible, but, with *epitasis* (ἐπίτασις), “exceedingly contemptible.”

“The arrogance of your heart has lifted you up.” For which heretic is not lifted up in pride, despising the simplicity of the Church and considering faith ignorance?

“You who dwell in the clefts of the rock and raise up your throne.” Although the rock is frequently understood either in the person of the Lord or as firmness—for the prophet says, “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. 39:5), and it is said to Peter, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16:18)—it is nevertheless also frequently understood in the opposite sense: “I shall take away,” he says, “the heart of stone, and I shall give you a heart of flesh” [Note: The Palatine manuscripts add “from your flesh”] (Ezek. 36:26). And: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9).

This is especially true here, where he did not say, “dwelling upon the rock,” on which the wise builder constructs his house, but “in the clefts of the rock,” signifying the divisions of heresies from Christ the Rock [Al. “of Christ”] and from the Church.

What follows—“raising up your throne,” and “who says in his heart, ‘Who will bring me down to the ground?’”—shows the swelling of the heretical mind, which trusts in its own mysteries and secrets and, as far as it is concerned—and we must understand this hyperbolically—promises itself the kingdoms of heaven.

Hence the Apostle writes to such people: “Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you have begun to reign without us—and I wish indeed that you had begun to reign, so that we too might reign with you” (1 Cor. 4:8). David likewise says something similar: “They have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has gone through the earth” (Ps. 72:9).

Therefore, if they are raised up like an eagle—for they too promise themselves the likeness of eagles, which are accustomed to gather around the Lord’s corpse—and if they set their nest among the stars, from there I shall bring them down, says the Lord.

For just as, while the master of the house was asleep, an enemy sowed weeds among the good seed (Matt. 13), so that great eagle “with great wings, long in the extension of its limbs, full of feathers and variegated,” which has a path into Lebanon, takes from the top of the cedar and plants it over many waters, so that the plants may sprout into a vineyard, is accustomed to set its nest among the stars of the Church, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “The righteous shall shine like the stars” (Matt. 13:43).

I said above that this can also be understood against the flesh: its strength has been diminished at the coming of Christ, it is contemptible, and it has been subjected to the authority of the soul. It raises itself in vain, dwelling in the caves of the rock—whether in the senses or in thoughts—and wishing to rule the soul, raising up its throne and believing that its works cannot be conquered.

It is told that although it raises itself up, imitates the heights of the eagle, and has deceived many of the saints, it has nevertheless been overcome and cast down by the Lord.

What we have understood concerning heretics and the flesh can also be understood against the Jews.

**(Verses 4ff.)** “If thieves had entered upon you, if robbers by night, how would you have kept silent? Would they not have stolen enough for themselves? If grape-gatherers had entered upon you, would they not at least have left you a cluster? How Esau has been searched out; his hidden things have been investigated!”

The Septuagint: “If thieves had entered upon you, or robbers by night, where would you have been cast down? Would they not have stolen enough for themselves? And if grape-gatherers had entered upon you, would they not have left a cluster? How Esau has been searched out, and his hidden things have been discovered!”

Jeremiah says something similar, though with the order changed: “If grape-gatherers had come upon you, would they not have left a cluster? If thieves by night, they would certainly have taken what was sufficient for them. But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hidden things, and they will not be able to hide themselves” [Note: All the manuscripts read *poterit* (“he will be able”); some also have *celari* (“to be hidden”). The Greek is κρυβῆναι οὐ μὴ δύνανται (“they shall certainly not be able to be hidden”).] (Jer. 49:9–10).

The meaning is this:

“If thieves and robbers, who customarily break into houses at night and carry off what is in them, had entered upon you, and, hidden by the darkness, had gone around the corners of your houses, they would certainly have taken what they thought could suffice for them, and through either satiety or ignorance would have left something in your buildings.

“If grape-gatherers had entered your vineyard and wished either to ravage it like enemies or to harvest it after being hired by you, even if their gathering had been thorough, they would still have left clusters hidden among the vines and leaves, between the branches.

“But all the enemies who came upon you at the Lord’s command—by whom the Babylonians and the army of Nebuchadnezzar are signified—searched out all your secrets and inspected the caves and openings of the grottoes in which you dwell.

“And in fact, to say something about the nature of the region, the whole southern territory of the Idumeans, from Eleutheropolis to Petra and Aila—for this is Esau’s possession—has dwellings in caves. Because of the excessive heat of the sun, since it is a southern province, it makes use of underground huts.

“‘I have stripped Esau bare,’ he says: that is, I brought into the midst what had been pressed down into the earth, and everything that you had closed up was opened. Since I was searching out your possessions together with the enemies, none of your secrets could remain hidden.”

Alternatively:

“I think that the thieves and robbers who enter by night, because they are children of night and darkness, are heretics who preach doctrines opposed to the truth. They steal what is sufficient for themselves and hasten daily to snatch from the flocks of the Church.

“These men enter the vineyard of our Lord (Ps. 79), which he transferred out of the Egypt of this age, and from whose produce he promises to drink wine in the kingdom of the Father. They wish to plunder everything so completely that they scarcely leave a cluster in it.

“But the Lord acts in the opposite way: through his holy and ecclesiastical men and teachers he brings into the open all their secrets, hidden mysteries, and the patriarchs of Esau—by whom I understand those who first devised the heresies. His first victory is that what had been concealed becomes visible.

“Therefore it is said with amazement: ‘How has Esau been searched out? His hidden things have been discovered!’

“Look at Marcion, Valentinus, and all the heretics: in the doctrines of demons they have a conscience seared, yet applaud themselves and deceive simple souls, initiating them, as it were, into divine mysteries through carefully composed speech.

“But when their thirty aeons, and their quadrads, and ogdoads and dodecads, and their double god, and their monstrous Abraxas have been brought into the open—[Note: Some manuscripts read *quadragenas* (“groups of forty”); others *quadrigas* (“four-horse chariots”). We discussed the name Abraxas shortly above in the commentary on Amos 3. Instead of *in medium* (“into the open”), Martianay retained *in medio* (“in the midst”).]—then the wisdom of Esau will be shown to be folly, and his secrets will be investigated.”

**(Verse 7.)** “All the men of your covenant have sent you to the borders; they have mocked you; the men of your peace have prevailed against you, those who eat with you; they will set an ambush beneath you. There is no wisdom in him.”

The Septuagint: “They have sent you away as far as the borders; all the men of your covenant have resisted you; the men of your peace have prevailed against you; they have set ambushes beneath you. There is no wisdom in him.”

Some distinguish the words we explained above—“How has Esau been searched out, and his hidden things discovered?”—all the way to the borders, so that the sense is: “Your hidden and secret things have been revealed as far as the borders.” But it seems better to us to connect them with what follows.

When Nebuchadnezzar came—of whom Jeremiah says against Idumea: “Behold, like a lion he shall come up from the pride of the Jordan against the fortified beauty, for I shall suddenly make him run against it” (Jer. 49:19); and afterward: “Behold, like an eagle he shall come up and fly, and spread his wings over Bosrah, and the heart of the mighty men of Idumea shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in labor” (ibid. 22)—all those who had formerly been allied with Edom and had served in the defense of the exceedingly proud city abandoned him and, joining the enemies, laid ambushes against him. They prevailed against him, and then it became clear that there was no wisdom in Edom, since he had placed his hope in those who were shown to be his adversaries.

Alternatively:

“When the hidden things of Esau, and the magnificent secrets by which the peoples had previously been entangled, have been brought into the open, so that an ecclesiastical man can say, ‘For we are not ignorant of his devices’ (2 Cor. 2:11), they will abandon the borders of Edom and leave him; and, migrating as far as the borders of the Church, they will bring forth their pernicious doctrines.

“Then they will mock and resist their former teacher, [Note: Victor writes *docentes* (“teaching”), and places the conjunction *et* before *praevalebunt*. No manuscripts known to us, nor, I think, any of those he consulted, support this.] saying that what they had learned was false. They will prevail against him, and, instructed in the faith of the Church, they will convict the false doctrine.

“Those who once ate with heretics—not the bread of the Eucharist, but the bread of mourning and the hearth-cake that does not return—will propose questions from the Scriptures. They will set ambushes for the Idumean and earthly man, and in every matter for the carnal teacher—for we read that heresies are numbered among the works of the flesh (Gal. 5). Then it will be shown that there is no wisdom in Edom.”

**(Verses 8–9.)** “Shall I not destroy the wise men from Idumea on that day, says the Lord, and wisdom from Mount Esau? And your mighty men shall fear from the south, so that the man from Mount Esau may perish.”

The Septuagint: “On that day, says the Lord, I shall destroy the wise men from Idumea and understanding from Mount Esau. And your fighters shall be afraid from Teman, so that the man from Mount Esau may be taken away.”

When the enemy has possessed your borders, and all the men of your covenant have mocked you and prevailed against you, then the wisdom of Idumea will perish, and its cunning will be shown to be folly.

The Lord himself will also remove wisdom from Mount Esau—that is, from the mountains of Seir—either because the Idumean city is situated on a mountain, or because the whole region, extending toward the south and bordering the desert, rises high among precipitous mountains.

Hence it is also said: “Your fighters shall fear from Teman,” which we have interpreted as “the south.” Just as I said above that Esau was called by three names, so the region of his kingdom that extends toward the south is called by three names: Darom, Teman, and Negeb (). According to Ezekiel, all of these signify the south, the southwest, and the south.

After the mighty men of his kingdom who dwelt [Al. “dwell”] in the south have feared, then the man from Mount Esau will perish—the man who was accustomed both to fight for the city and to give prudent counsel.

Alternatively:

“After those who had previously been deceived have turned to the Church, then, while the Lord himself fights, the wise men of Idumea will perish—the men who thought according to carnal and earthly things—and wisdom will be removed from Mount Esau, the wisdom that was raised up against the knowledge of God.

“Those who previously fought for Esau and Idumea with dialectical skill, and who held positions in Teman—which is interpreted as ‘completion’—will cease to fight for their former teachers.

“Or those who formerly promised themselves the light of knowledge and thought that they were in the south will fear and tremble, while an ecclesiastical man overcomes their sophistries, to such an extent that no one will remain who can fight either by the king’s counsel or by the strength of warriors for the pride and false doctrine of the heretics.”

## (Verses 10–11)

“Because of the slaughter and the iniquity against your brother Jacob, shame will cover you, and you will perish forever. On the day when you stood against him, when foreigners were capturing his army, and strangers were entering his gates and casting lots over Jerusalem, you too were like one of them.”

The Septuagint: “Because of the slaughter and the impiety against your brother Jacob, shame will cover you, and you will be removed forever. From the day when you resisted, on the day when foreigners captured his strength, and strangers entered his gates and cast lots over Jerusalem, you were also like one of them.”

[Note: Our manuscripts read “on the day when they captured”; the Greek has ἐν ἡμέραις αἰχμαλωτευόντων, “in the days of those taking captive,” and so forth.]

Therefore the man from Mount Esau will perish, and wisdom will perish from Edom, and prudence from Mount Esau, because you killed your kinsman and acted wickedly against your brother Jacob. When the Chaldeans and Babylonians were ravaging Jerusalem, besieging the city, entering its gates, and casting lots in the division of the spoils, you were their associate and were counted among the enemies.

Alternatively: “You will suffer all the things written above, O bloody, earthly, cruel Edom, because by false and deadly teaching, speaking impiously against the Lord, you killed your brother Jacob.” We read in Solomon: “There are those who speak and kill with the sword” (Prov. 25:18). And elsewhere: “The poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 139:4); and, “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5). Shame, therefore, will cover you, and you will say: “The shame of my face has covered me” (Ps. 68:8); and you will perish—not for a short time, but forever. For, so far as depended on you, you struck your brother with an eternal wound.

This too will be the cause of your punishment: when strangers were devastating Jacob’s army and entering through his gates into Jerusalem, once peaceful, and casting lots so that they might divide his spoils among themselves, you were one of the enemies. We have read, seen, and daily confirm that whenever persecution arises against the Church, Jews and heretics become far worse persecutors of Christians than pagans.

We can call the strangers entering the gates of Jerusalem λογισμοί, that is, evil thoughts; and we can interpret the gates of Jerusalem—that is, of the soul which rests and sees God—as the five senses, through which the enemies enter and divide Jerusalem’s spoils. If we see a woman in order to lust after her (Matt. 5), death has entered through our windows (Jer. 9). If we receive falsehood and the judgment of blood through our ears, the enemy has entered through another gate. Smell, taste, and touch likewise—if one is captivated by various perfumes, sweet foods, or delicate embraces—the adversaries have entered through the other gates and are dividing the spoils of wretched Jerusalem. Thus, whenever someone has fallen from the Church through the force of persecution and deadly pleasures, we see heretics exulting, the Jew rejoicing, such a one being among the persecutors, and them counted in the number of the pagans.

## (Verse 12)

“And you must not look with contempt on the day of your brother, on the day of his exile. You must not rejoice over the sons of Judah on the day of their destruction, nor enlarge your mouth on the day of distress. You must not enter the gate of my people on the day of their ruin.”

The Septuagint: “And you must not look with contempt on the day of your brother on the day of strangers. You must not rejoice over the sons of Judah on the day of their destruction; you must not speak arrogantly on the day of distress; nor must you enter the gates of the nations on the day of their troubles.”

[Note: Martianay retained “you must not despise,” although the manuscripts and the Hebrew and Vulgate texts cited by Victor contradict it.]

The meaning is the same as above. When the man from Mount Esau has perished because of the slaughter and impiety against his brother Jacob, and eternal shame has covered him, he will certainly no longer do what he previously did against his kinsman. He will not look with contempt or regard as insignificant his brother going into captivity, nor will he rejoice over the sons of Judah. Two tribes, apart from the Levitical tribe, ruled in Jerusalem and were called Judah; these were captured by the Chaldeans. Nor will he speak arrogantly, as though he were one of the victors, laughing at his brother’s distress. Nor, on the day of the devastation and ruin of my people, will you stride triumphantly through the gate of Jerusalem. You will not do these things because you too will suffer similar things.

Alternatively: when you see your brother captive through various persecutions and being led away in chains from the faith of the Church, following foreign things rather than his own city, you will not rejoice, because you too will suffer similar things. You rejoiced when Jacob was captured and exulted over the sons of Judah—whom we understand as Christ’s disciples—on the day of their destruction.

It is indicated that the soul is situated midway between vices and virtues and can turn toward either side at every passing moment. “You will not enlarge your mouth,” he says, “on the day of distress.” We must understand this according to a twofold meaning: bodily distress, in persecutions and sins; and spiritual distress, when the soul, captured by enemies and vices, has been led away into Babylon.

[Note: Our manuscripts, following Victor, correct the text to “when the soul has been captured and is led into Babylon.” Martianay heedlessly retained Erasmus’s corrupt reading, “has been captured.”]

Nor will you enter the gate of my people on the day of their ruin. For whenever denial has overwhelmed us, or pleasure, and an unhappy conscience has failed to preserve its former strictness, we easily slip into contrary doctrines that flatter our error and do not tend the wound but merely stroke it. It is a consolation in misery, however ruined one may be, to have something to hope for.

## (Verses 13–14)

“You must not look with contempt on his evils, on the day of his devastation, nor must you attack his army on the day of his devastation. You must not stand at the crossroads to kill those who have escaped, nor must you imprison his survivors on the day of distress.”

The Septuagint: “You must not look with contempt even upon their assembly on the day of their destruction; nor must you add yourself to their strength on the day of their destruction. You must not stand at their exits to kill those among them who have been saved; nor must you imprison their fugitives on the day of distress.”

[Note: In place of “their,” which occurs three times below, the Palatine manuscripts have “his,” in the singular. Soon afterward they do not recognize the words “from among them”; finally, they add “his” at the end, while the Greek differs in each place.]

Since you yourself will have been captured and destroyed when Babylon ravages you, among the other things you have done, do not do the following: Do not look with contempt upon or despise your brother Jacob on the day of his devastation. Do not join the Babylonian army, nor attack the army of Judah when, overcome by adversaries, it turns its back. When they begin to flee along roads known to them, through byways and paths leading into the wilderness, do not stand at the fork in the road, nor wait for them at the crossroads in order to kill those who have been rescued, seize others, shut them up, and either capture them yourself or hand them over to the enemy’s captivity.

We have said this according to the historical sense, for we must briefly select the clearer points and proceed to what is obscure. What heretic does not despise churchmen? Who does not exult in their misfortunes whenever, because of the people’s sins, they have been handed over to persecution, and many—either weak in faith or sown upon rocky ground—have fallen into denial? You may see them exulting and rejoicing, regarding our ruin as their victory, to such an extent that they join themselves to the nations and the persecution becomes more savage, whether it comes from Jews or from those who pretend to be our brothers and are counted under the same name.

When someone has escaped either by flight or by repentance, they stand at the byways, set forth sophisms, and produce testimonies as though from the Scriptures, so that they may offer stitched-together cushions to the weary and exhausted and place them under every elbow. Thus those who perhaps have overcome persecution by courage or escaped it through fear are deceived by corrupt doctrines and are again held captive in the prison of error; and this distress becomes far worse than that inflicted by the nations. For it is easier to free someone captured by pagans than one ensnared by the tricks of heretics.

## (Verses 15–16)

“For the day of the Lord is near upon all the nations. As you have done, so shall it be done to you. Your retribution will return upon your own head. For just as you drank upon my holy mountain, so all the nations will drink continually; they will drink and swallow, and they will be as though they had never been.”

The Septuagint: “For the day of the Lord is near upon all the nations. As you have done, so shall it be done to you. Your retribution will be repaid upon your head. For just as you drank upon my holy mountain, all the nations will drink wine; they will drink and swallow, and they will be as though they had never been.”

[Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read “but, as one drinking, you will drink,” and so forth.]

You will cease doing these things, O Edom, because the Lord’s vengeance will come upon you. For if, according to Jeremiah (Jer. 25), those who had no judgment requiring them to drink drank the cup, will you be left as though innocent? You will not be innocent, but “drinking, you will drink.” Further, when he says, “The day of the Lord is near upon all the nations,” let us read Jeremiah himself and see the Lord’s cup offered to all the nations. Hence it is said in the same prophet: “Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, intoxicating all the nations.”

The Assyrians and Babylonians held all the nations as far as the Propontis and the Scythian Sea, and the Ionian or Aegean Sea. Let us read Herodotus and Greek and barbarian histories, and we shall see how under the Babylonians and Assyrians this statement was fulfilled: “The day of the Lord is near upon all the nations.”

What follows—“As you have done, so shall it be done to you; your retribution will return upon your head”—has the meaning we read in the Psalm: “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who said, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations’” (Ps. 136:7 ff.). Hence the prophet also invokes a curse against Babylon: “Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is the one who repays you with the repayment with which you repaid us. Blessed is the one who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock.”

[Note: The same manuscripts here have “your repayment,” then the name “Zion,” and below omit the words “in the garrison”; instead they read “the Babylonian king,” “turned,” and so forth.]

For just as you drank upon my holy mountain, Zion, and rejoiced with the Babylonians, so all the nations whom the Babylonian had with him in his garrison will turn against you, drink, and rejoice. And they will not merely drink; they will swallow you up so completely that the Idumaeans will be as though they did not exist. Or certainly, when those nations have swallowed you, they themselves will be swallowed by the Medes, and vengeance will advance in this circle: you will consume Israel, the Babylonian will consume you, the Mede and Persian will consume Babylon.

Let us follow the order of interpretation. “The day of the Lord is near,” O heretic, “upon all the nations”: the time of judgment is near, in which all nations will be judged. As you have acted against churchmen, your grief will return upon your head, and your iniquity will descend upon your crown. For as you rejoiced over their death and celebrated a feast upon my holy mountain—that is, the Church—drinking not my cup but the devil’s, concerning which it is also said in Habakkuk, “Woe to him who gives his neighbor drink with turbulent ruin” (Hab. 2:15), so all the nations, whether hostile powers assigned to punishments or whatever opposing forces there may be, will drink and swallow your blood; and finally, when punishment comes upon all, they too will be as though they did not exist.

For whoever perishes in relation to Him who is, and who says to Moses, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14), is said, according to the rule of the Scriptures, not to exist. Hence we also read in Esther: “Do not hand over, Lord, your kingdom to those who do not exist” (Esth. 14:11).

We can interpret this passage in another way: “Because you rejoiced over the ruin of my servants, the same persecution will come upon you also, and you will suffer whatever you inflicted. And as you rejoiced against my people with the remaining nations, so all the nations will rejoice against you, devour you, drink, and crush you with a similar persecution.”

## (Verses 17–18)

“But on Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and it will be holy; and the house of Jacob will possess those who possessed them. The house of Jacob will be fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau straw. They will set them ablaze and devour them, and there will be no survivor of the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.”

The Septuagint: “On Mount Zion there will be deliverance; and it will be holy, and the house of Jacob will possess those who had possessed them. The house of Jacob will be fire, the house of Joseph a flame, but the house of Esau straw. They will be kindled against them and devour them, and there will be no grain-carrier for the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.”

[Note: Following Victor, from the manuscripts of Florence and Brescia, we have restored the word “there is,” whose absence made the sense difficult in the editions of Erasmus and Martianay. Other manuscripts read equally well: “For what the Septuagint translated πυροφόρον, we translate as ‘grain-carrier,’” and so forth. The learned, especially Salmasius, have been moved by the statement that Saint Jerome, according to the usage of ancient speech, called those “grain-carriers” who were then called agentes in rebus or veredarii. They acknowledge that the name and office of frumentarii existed in the regular army under the emperors: they were soldiers assigned in fixed numbers to the legions, who supervised transport, arranged for military grain and provisions to be brought into military granaries and from there into the camps, collected taxes, and compelled provincials to pay them. Later this became the office of the agentes in rebus and veredarii, as is clear from the title “On Exactions” in the Theodosian Code. But they maintain that the Greeks did not call them πυροφόροι in that sense, deriving the name not from ἀπὸ τοῦ πυροῦ, that is, “from grain,” but from ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρός, that is, “from carrying fire.” Thus it is more correct, and more frequent—as Jerome himself notes below—to write πυρφόροι rather than πυροφόροι. Moreover, the Hebrew word corresponding to πυροφόρος, Sarid, was interpreted by the ancients, as Jerome testifies, as “the remnant,” “the one escaping,” or “the survivor.” The Greeks commonly say of a great slaughter: οὐδὲ πυρφόρος ἐλείφθη, “not even a fire-carrier (πυρφόρος) was left,” or, according to the sense, “not even a messenger remained.” Whatever the truth of the Greek etymology—which Jerome himself does not press, indeed below explains it according to those who read πυρφόρον as the carrying of a firebrand—nothing prevents us from understanding “grain-carrier” in Latin in a sense closer to that of the ancient interpreters, namely, as signifying “the survivor,” “the fugitive,” “the messenger,” or something similar. For Salmasius himself cites the testimony of the grammarians: ἐχρῶντο κατὰ τὸ παλαιὸν ἐν τοῖς πολέμοις ἀντὶ σαλπιγκτῶν τοῖς πυρφόροις, “In ancient times, in war, they used a grain-carrier or courier (πυρφόρος) in place of a trumpeter.” Since such soldiers were inviolable and were not harmed by the enemy, the statement about a great slaughter may be understood to mean that not even a grain-carrier remained, that is, not even one survivor whom the enemy spared.]

With Idumaea overthrown and devoured by the enemy nations with which it had formerly made an alliance against Jacob, there will be remnants on Mount Zion, and there will be deliverance, and it will be holy. That is, either the Lord himself will return to the temple which he had abandoned because of sins, or it will be holy in the absolute sense—that is, the Holy of Holies. Under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, the house of Jacob will possess those who had possessed it as an inheritance. The house of Jacob, that is, Judah, will be fire, and the house of Joseph, that is, the ten tribes, a flame. For Ephraim, from whose tribe the rule of Samaria came, was born of Joseph. But the house of Esau, that is, the Idumaeans, who had proved so fierce and cruel against their brother, will be turned into straw. And as fire and flame quickly consume straw, so the two kingdoms, joined in the union of one rod according to Ezekiel (Ezek. 17), will lay waste and devour Idumaea; and no survivor of the people will remain who can report the overthrow of their enemies to the neighboring nations.

For there is the word which the Septuagint translated πυροφόρον, which we render “grain-carrier” according to the usage of ancient speech. Those whom they now call agentes in rebus or veredarii the ancients called frumentarii. But it is better to follow the Hebrew itself, namely SARID, which means either “the remnant,” according to Aquila; “the one escaping,” according to Symmachus; or, according to Theodotion and the fifth edition, “the survivor.”

All these things will happen because the Lord has spoken, and his command is his deed.

Alternatively: when the works of the flesh have been destroyed and earthly rule has been laid waste, there will be salvation in the Church for those who have not departed from their mother. The Holy One will dwell in it, of whom it is said in Isaiah: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3), because the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one source. The house of Jacob, the supplanter, will possess those who had possessed it as an inheritance, making Christians from the persecutors and receiving the Idumaeans themselves into the faith of the Church. The house of Esau, however, will be turned into straw.

And just as straw cannot endure the nearness of fire, so the house of Esau will not be able to withstand Jacob’s disputation, which has been set alight by the Lord’s word. “The sayings of the Lord are tested by fire” (Ps. 17:31). Nor will it withstand the flame of Joseph, whose name means “increase” (Gen. 37), and who, having been sold to his brothers, fed the people in Egypt. At their first encounter their sophisms will be turned into nothing.

They will be devoured for their salvation, according to what is said in Isaac’s blessing to Esau: “I have made him your lord, and I have subjected all your brothers to him as servants; and you shall serve your brother” (Gen. 27:37). No remnant of the house of Esau will remain when all things heavenly, earthly, and infernal bow the knee to Christ (Phil. 2), and everything is subjected to him, so that God may be all in all.

Because Esau had built hay, wood, and straw upon the foundation of Christ through his own fault (1 Cor. 3), the house of both Jacob and Joseph will therefore be turned into fire and flame, imitating their Lord, who says: “I am a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24), so that, when the sinners’ chaff has been devoured, pure grain may be gathered into the granaries.

All that we have said, and all that we are going to say, the Jews promise themselves for a future time, when instead of Christ they receive Antichrist, fulfilling the prophecy of the Lord and Savior: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5:43). Whatever we have interpreted against Edom, they dream against the Roman empire. What we say either has already been fulfilled historically under Zerubbabel, or certainly, according to prophecy and mystical meanings, is happening daily in the Church and is fulfilled in each person, in the kingdom of the soul against the flesh.
