According to the tropological sense, we say that the “grain-carrier” will cease to exist among heretics when there is no one among them who claims to possess the grain of wheat that died in the earth and the bread from heaven. Some think that the Septuagint translated not πυροφόρον, “grain-carrier” (from πυρός, “grain”), but πυρφόρον, “one able to carry a firebrand” (from πῦρ, “fire”). Therefore, accepting the different interpretations, we shall say according to the tropological sense that not only will the grain-carrier cease among heretics, but also the one who pretends to possess the light of Christ. For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11).

## (Verse 19)

“And those who are in the South will inherit the mountain of Esau, and those in the lowlands the Philistines. They will possess the region of Ephraim and the region of Samaria, and Benjamin will possess Gilead.”

The Septuagint: “Those who are in the Negeb will possess Mount Esau; those in the Shephelah, the foreigners; and they will possess Mount Ephraim, the plain of Samaria, Benjamin, and Gilead.”

When Judah, who dwelt in the South, has returned to his kingdom and possessed the whole region according to the division of Joshua son of Nun, which extends toward the Scorpion, that is, throughout Acrabithena—

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts read “toward the Scorpion,” that is, “all Acrabithena.” Although in one of them the word “Acrabithena” has been deleted and “Arabia” substituted in the margin, Victor’s reading, which we follow, gives the more coherent sense: after removing the unnecessary word, it joins the passage in a single sequence.]

—those who previously were confined within narrow boundaries will possess Mount Esau, that is, the mountains of Seir and the highlands formerly possessed by Edom. Those who lived in the Shephelah, that is, in the lowlands—signifying Lydda and Emmaus, namely Diospolis and Nicopolis—will possess the Philistines, the five cities of the Philistines: Gaza, Ashkelon, Azotus, Ekron, and Gath; or the whole region which, according to Acts of the Apostles, is called Saron.

Others think that the Shephelah, that is, the lowland region around Eleutheropolis, is being promised. This region extends to Rhinocorura and to the sea, so that those from the tribe of Judah will possess not only Eleutheropolis but reach as far as the coastal districts and subject the Philistines to their rule, whom they had not previously subdued.

The boundary of the sons of Judah will also be extended as far as Ephraim, where Neapolis now is, and as far as the region of Samaria, where Sebaste was founded. Benjamin, whose boundaries immediately north of Jerusalem extend outward, will possess all Arabia, which was formerly called Gilead and is now called Gerasa.

According to the Septuagint, however, those who are in the South will possess Mount Ephraim, the plains of Samaria, Benjamin, and Gilead. Whether this happened, God knows. It may have been partly fulfilled over the five hundred years up to Christ’s coming. But I know with complete certainty that it is fulfilled daily and confirmed in the kingdom of the Church.

Those who dwell in the South, that is, in the Negeb, and are in the true light, and those who occupy the lowlands and humble places—that is, his disciples, to whom he says, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 10:24)—will possess Mount Esau and the Philistines. We can understand them as representing the pagans because of the arrogance of their doctrines and their secular eloquence: teachers are represented by the mountain, and disciples, who are led by the authority of their teachers, by the Philistines and foreigners.

They will possess not only Mount Esau and the foreigners, but also the region of Ephraim and Samaria. We have often read of Ephraim and Samaria in Hosea, and we have interpreted them as the heresies that divide the Church under the Christian name. There too abundance is hoped for, and there they promise the preservation of faith.

Benjamin, the son of the right hand and of strength, where the temple of God is, will possess Gilead, which means “the migration of testimony,” signifying Israel according to the flesh. For the Lord’s testimony has migrated from them to us. According to the Septuagint, Benjamin himself and Gilead will also be possessed by those who are in the South.

## (Verses 20–21)

“And the migration of his army, the sons of Israel, will possess all the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath. And the migration of Jerusalem, which is in Bosphorus, will possess the cities of the South. And saviors will ascend Mount Zion to judge Mount Esau, and the kingdom will belong to the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “And this will be the beginning of the migration for the sons of Israel: the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and the migration of Jerusalem as far as Ephratha. They will possess the cities of the Negeb. And those who have been saved will ascend from Mount Zion to punish Mount Esau, and the kingdom will belong to the Lord.”

Our translation differs greatly in this passage from the Vulgate edition; therefore, in explaining the historical sense, we must follow the Hebrew truth. Those who had returned from Babylon to Judea according to the books of Ezra and Nehemiah were rightly called “the migration.”

[Note: Again, the Palatine manuscripts correctly read “the sons of the migration”; shortly afterward they read “possessed” instead of “will possess.”]

That entire army of the sons of Israel will possess the Edomites, the Philistines, Mount Ephraim, and Samaria—to the South, West, and North. Benjamin too, because it borders on the wilderness, will specially obtain Gilead. To the East they will rule over everything in the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath of the Sidonians, where once a widow fed Elijah (1 Kings 17).

Those who had been transferred from Jerusalem itself, the metropolitan city, to Sepharad—which we translate as Bosphorus—will possess the cities of the South, which are in the tribe of Judah. For, having returned to their own city, they will obtain what lies near it.

When these things have been fulfilled, just as in the Book of Judges the Lord sent saviors who saved the people from captivity, so they will ascend and come to Mount Zion to judge and distinguish Mount Esau, as though it were subject and enslaved to them—that is, the Idumaeans. When all have been subjected, the kingdom will belong to the Lord.

Where we have put “Bosphorus,” the Hebrew has SAPHARAD. I do not know why the Septuagint wished to translate it as Ephratha, or why they were able to do so, since Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion agree with the Hebrew truth. From the Hebrew teacher who instructed us in the Holy Scriptures, we learned that “Bosphorus” is what this place is called. And, as though he were a Jew, he said: “This is the region to which Hadrian transferred the captives.” Therefore, when our Christ comes, that captivity too will return to Judea.

We can understand it as any region of the Babylonian kingdom, although I have another opinion. It is customary for the prophets, when they speak against Babylon, the Ammonites, Moabites, the Philistines, and other nations, to make extensive use of their languages and preserve the idioms of their provinces. Since, therefore, the boundary called GEBUL in Hebrew is called SAPHARAD in the Assyrian language—

[Note: Learned critics have observed that in the Assyrian language the boundary is called Sephar, not Sepharad, although not strictly so. For grammarians explain it as the land of peoples near the land of Israel; at other times they explain it differently, saying that it is a city near the sea, that is, a coastal city. In Joshua, “the coast of the sea” is rendered by the Chaldean interpreter as Sephar iamma. Drusius consequently accuses Jerome of error because of the similarity of the two words.]

—I infer that this is the meaning: “The migration of Jerusalem, which has been divided throughout all the boundaries and regions, will receive the cities of the South,” that is, those belonging to its own tribe.

In place of what we translated “and saviors will ascend,” and what the Septuagint translated “those who have been saved,” the Hebrew has MOSIM—

[Note: The conjunction “and” was missing; the punctuation of what follows was also defective. For Mosim the Palatine manuscripts read Mosiim, with two i’s, which I do not reject.]

—which should not be understood passively, as Aquila, the Septuagint, and Theodotion render it, σεσωσμένοι or ἀνασωζόμενοι, “those who have been saved,” but actively, as Symmachus has it, σώζοντες, that is, “saviors.” For σεσωσμένοι, “those who have been saved,” are called PHELETIM in Hebrew.

[Note: The same manuscripts perhaps more correctly read Flettim.]

Since we have interpreted the historical sense as best we could and guided our little boat among rugged rocks, let us spread the sails of spiritual understanding, so that, with the Lord’s breath blowing and his mysteries being opened, we may happily reach the harbor.

At the time when Benjamin had possessed Gilead, the migration of the army of the sons of Israel—or certainly the beginning of the migration of Israel according to the flesh—will be this: it will reach the land of the Canaanites, and the prophetic word, which was endangered by famine in Judea, will pass to the dew of the nations, Israel’s fleece having dried up. There it will both feed and nourish, being received by believers and itself feeding believers.

[Note: In place of “the fields,” which had previously been printed, we substituted “the dew” from the manuscripts, since the correct sense required it. But the word “fields” had no place here and was not set in opposition to the dried fleece of the Jews; this was why we did not hesitate to correct the passage.]

Zarephath is either a compound of two words and means “the distress of bread,” or it is a single word and is translated “into a burning.” Canaan, however, is rendered in Greek as σάλος, that is, “movement”; or it is called “merchant” and “humble.”

Therefore the migration of the sons of Israel, when they have abandoned the letter that faces west and come to the life-giving Spirit, will move all that belongs to the Law. It will trade many pearls for one most precious pearl; and, laying aside Jewish arrogance, it will pursue Christian humility. It will reach the place where formerly there was distress of bread, where a widow, abandoned by her creator, scarcely fed her orphaned son, and where all her sins and vices are burned up.

The captivity or migration of Jerusalem, where once there was a vision of peace and which is now scattered throughout the whole world, will possess the cities of the South, that is, the Churches of true and perfect light, and will say with the repentant bride: “Where do you feed your flock, where do you make it rest at noon?” (Song 1:7). And, received with Joseph into the ancient brotherhood, it will be intoxicated with the blood of the shepherd and ruler.

If we read Ephratha according to the Septuagint, there can be no doubt that the faith of Christ is meant. For Ephratha means καρποφορία, that is, “fruitfulness,” and is δυώνυμος, “of two names”; it is also called Bethlehem, where the heavenly bread was born.

When these things have taken place, saviors—or those who have been saved—from the remnants of the Jewish people will ascend Mount Zion to judge and avenge themselves upon Mount Esau.

Just as the Lord calls the Apostles his light and says, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14), and granted Peter himself that he should be a rock; and just as the good shepherd bestowed upon them the names of shepherds; and whatever is said of him he grants to his servants so that it may be said of them, so the Savior himself wished his Apostles to be the saviors of the world. They ascended the watchtower of the mountain of the Church and, laying aside Jewish arrogance and all the mountains that were raised against the knowledge of God, prepared a kingdom for the Lord.

I have dictated this in two short night sessions, following the authority of the ancients and especially the Hebrew exposition, in hurried speech, and I have opened my mouth; but I do not know whether Christ has filled it. Therefore the discerning reader should seek more the coherence of the meanings than the elegance of the language. We do not dictate with the polish and arrangement of words with which we write.

[Note: Two manuscripts and Victor read levitate, “lightness.” I would rather read laevitate, with the diphthong, meaning “brightness” or “polish.”]

It is one thing, my Pammachius, to turn the style often and write things worthy of memory; it is another, with the shorthand writers’ signs prepared, to dictate whatever comes to one’s mouth out of embarrassment at remaining silent. In this prophet we have played like boys and presumed to act like old men. If someone says what is truer and better, pass over to his judgment.

Textual variants and omitted apparatus: In verses 10–11, the Vulgate adds *propter* (“because of”) before “iniquity”; the alternatives are *concupiscendam eam* (“to lust after her”) and *videas* (“you see”). In verse 12, Martianay retains *despicias*, against the manuscripts and the Hebrew and Vulgate text; two Palatine manuscripts read *impietatem fratris ejus* (“impiety against his brother”), and *laetaberis* is an alternative reading. In verses 15–16, the alternatives are *fecerit* for *fiet*, *juxta* for *eumdem*, and *suos* for *tuos*. In verses 17–18, the Vulgate reads *possederant*; two Palatine manuscripts read *quae signata est sermone* (“which is marked by the word”) in the discussion of Jacob’s disputation. In verse 19, *Saraptam* and *Gerara* are alternative readings. In verses 20–21, the alternatives are *possederit* for *possederat*, *potuerint* for *voluerint*, *quae* for *qui*, and *ut universae* for *et ubi universa*.

[Col. 1117]

## Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, One Book of Commentaries on the Prophet Jonah

### Prologue
[Col. 1117B] 387–388 Three years [Note: [Col. 1117C] Tillemont is troubled by this passage because of his preconceived opinion that the *Epitaphium Nepotiani*, judging from the works cited below, must be assigned at the earliest to the year 396; hence he wants *four years* read instead of *three years*. We, so that nothing may be rashly altered, have sufficiently shown in the chronological notes prefixed to Letter 60 in the preceding volume that this too is best understood as falling within the period of those three years.] passed, approximately, after I had interpreted five prophets—Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai—and, being occupied with another work, I was unable to complete what I had begun. For I wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, two volumes *Against Jovinian*, an apology, and *On the Best Kind of Interpretation* to Pammachius; also two books to Nepotianus, or *On Nepotianus*, and other works too numerous to list.

Therefore, after so long an interval, taking up the task of interpreting Jonah as though by a kind of restoration of rights, I beseech him who is a type of the Savior and who, having remained three days and nights in the belly of the sea-monster, prefigured the Lord’s resurrection, to grant us also our former ardor, so that we may deserve the coming of the Holy Spirit to us. For if Jonah is interpreted as “dove,” and the dove refers to the Holy Spirit, let us too interpret the dove from the coming of the dove to us.

I know that ancient ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin, have said much about this book, and that amid so many questions they have not so much disclosed as obscured its meanings, so that their very interpretation requires interpretation, and the reader departs much more uncertain than he was before reading. I do not say this to disparage great intellects or to taunt others by praising myself, but because it is the commentator’s duty to illuminate briefly and clearly what is obscure, and to explain not so much his own eloquence as the meaning of the author whom he expounds.

We therefore ask whether the prophet Jonah, apart from his own book and the Gospels—that is, apart from the Lord’s testimony concerning him—has been read elsewhere in the holy Scriptures. And, unless I am mistaken, it is written of him in the Book of Kings as follows:

“In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, reigned in Samaria for forty-one years. He did evil in the sight of the Lord and did not withdraw from all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin. He restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the Lord God of Israel, which he had spoken through his servant Jonah son of Amittai the prophet, who was from Gath, which is in Hepher” (2 Kings 14:25ff.).

The Hebrews, however, relate that he was the son of the widow of Zarephath [Al. Sarepta], whom the prophet Elijah raised from the dead, after his mother had said to him: “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of God in your mouth is truth” [Al. “of truth”]. For this reason, they say, the boy himself was also so called. For *Amittai* in our language means “truth”; and because Elijah spoke truthfully, the one who was raised is said to be the son of truth.

Moreover, Gath is a small village two miles beyond [or: at the second milestone from] Saphorim [Al. Sapphirim], today called Diocaesarea, on the road to Tiberias, where his tomb is also displayed. Others, however, want him to have been born and buried near Diospolis, that is, Lydda; they do not understand that the addition “in Hepher” distinguishes it from the other cities called Gath, which are still shown near Eleutheropolis or Diospolis.

The Book of Tobit too, although it is not held to be in the canon, nevertheless, because it is used by ecclesiastical writers, records something of this kind, when Tobit says to his son: “My son, behold, I am old, and I am at the point of departing from life. Take your children and go into Media, my son. For I know what the prophet Jonah said concerning Nineveh: that it will be overthrown” (Tobit 14).

And indeed, insofar as both Hebrew and Greek histories are concerned, especially Herodotus, we read that Nineveh was overthrown during the reign of Josiah among the Hebrews and of Astyages, king of the Medes. From this we understand that at first, when the Ninevites repented in response to Jonah’s preaching, they obtained pardon; but afterward, persisting in their former vices, they provoked God’s judgment against themselves.

The Hebrews also relate that Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, and Jonah prophesied at the same time. This concerns the foundations of the historical account.

[Note: [Col. 1119B] Thus read all the manuscript codices of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, of the monastery of Cluny, of Saint-Albinus of Angers, and of Saint-Cyran, etc.; the books published by Erasmus and Marianus likewise read it in the same way. Nevertheless, we know that this reading is false and that the name of Pammachius must be substituted for that of the venerable Pope Chromatius. For Jerome himself, in the preface to Book III of his Commentaries on the prophet Amos, expressly informs the reader that he published Commentaries on Obadiah and Jonah at Pammachius’s command—that is, at his request for an exposition of both those prophets. “Third,” he says, “after a long silence, I expounded Obadiah and Jonah for you at your command.” Therefore he expounded Obadiah and Jonah for the same Pammachius, not for Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, to whom he had assigned only two books on Habakkuk. We leave it to the reader’s divination to judge whence so persistent an error flowed into the printed and manuscript books. Unless perhaps he had also promised an exposition of Jonah to other holy men, as he did Commentaries on Amos and Hosea, though he dedicated those works to Pammachius. See the Commentary on Amos, chapter 1. If this occurred, we have a copy sent by Jerome not to Pammachius but to Chromatius. MART.—Although Martianaeus by no means denies that this is the reading of all the books, he nevertheless does not hesitate to declare it false through the fault of copyists, because, from Jerome’s testimony in Amos, which is about to be cited, this Commentary appears to have been inscribed by him to Pammachius, not Chromatius. I do not deny that the name of Chromatius could have been substituted by a scribal slip for that of Pammachius; but what conclusively proves that it was not substituted is the phrase “venerable Pope,” which could very properly be said of Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, but by no means of Pammachius. Therefore, when in that preface to Book III of the Commentary on Amos the holy Doctor says to Pammachius, “after a long silence I expounded Obadiah and Jonah for you at your command,” he must be thought to refer either only to Obadiah, which he dedicated to Pammachius; or, if to Jonah as well, to mean that he explained it at Pammachius’s prompting, not that he dedicated it in Pammachius’s name. The former opinion pleases us more, since Jerome has other examples of such expressions, in which, while enumerating several things together, he properly refers to one particular item. Thus, speaking of Eusebius in Book I of the Apology against Rufinus, he says: “I praised Eusebius in the Ecclesiastical History, in the arrangement of times, and in the description of the Holy Land; and, translating these same works into Latin, I gave them to the omens of my own language.” Yet it is certain that Jerome rendered only the latter two works into Latin, and by no means the Ecclesiastical History.]

Moreover, we are not unaware that, in the opinion of the venerable Pope Chromatius, it is the work of the greatest labor to refer the entire prophet to the understanding of the Savior: namely, that he fled, that he slept, that he was thrown into the sea, that he was received by the sea-monster, that after being cast onto the shore he preached repentance, that, grieved over the salvation of an innumerable city, he delighted in the shade of the gourd, that, reproved by God, he had shown greater concern for the green plant, which immediately became dry, than for so great a multitude of human beings, and the other matters which we shall strive to explain in the book itself.

Yet, to comprehend the prophet’s whole meaning in a brief preface, no one will be a better interpreter of his type than the one who himself inspired the prophets and beforehand marked out in his servants the lines of the truth that was to come.

Thus he speaks to the Jews, unbelieving in his preaching and ignorant of Christ the Son of God [Note: [Col. 1120D] The same Palatine manuscript adds “the Lord.”]: “The men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41).

The generation of the Jews is condemned while the world believes; and while Nineveh repents, unbelieving Israel perishes. They have the books; we have the Lord of the books (2 Corinthians 3). They possess the prophets; we possess the understanding of the prophets. The letter killed them; the Spirit gives us life (John 18). Among them the robber Barabbas is released; for us Christ, the Son of God, is set free.

# THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1119]

[Col. 1119D] 391 (Chapter 1.—Verse 1.) “And the word of the Lord came to Jonah, son of Amittai, saying: Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it, because its wickedness has risen before me.”

The Septuagint, except that they said, “the cry of its wickedness has risen to me,” translated the rest similarly.

Jonah is sent to the nations as a condemnation of Israel, because while Nineveh repents, they persist in wickedness. Moreover, what he says, “Its wickedness has risen before me,” or, “The cry of its wickedness has risen to me,” is the same as what is said in Genesis: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied” (Genesis 18:20); and to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Genesis 4:10).

According to the tropological interpretation, however, our Lord Jonah—that is, “dove,” or “grieving” (for both meanings are given), either because the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained in him (Luke 3), or because he himself grieved over our wounds, wept over Jerusalem, and by his bruising we were healed (Isaiah 53)—truly the son of truth, for God is truth, is sent to beautiful Nineveh, that is, to the world, than which we see nothing more beautiful with the eyes of the flesh [Al. “fleshy eyes”] (John 14). Hence among the Greeks it received its name from adornment, *kosmos* (κόσμος) [Note: [Col. 1121D] We have supplied the Greek word κόσμος from the manuscripts after Victorius; shortly afterward, for *de eo*, some read *a Deo*.]. And when each work had been completed, Scripture says of it: “God saw that it was good.”

To Nineveh, I say, the great city, so that, because Israel refused to listen, the entire world of the nations might hear. And this is because its wickedness has risen before God.

For when God had built something like a most beautiful house for the human being who was to serve him, humanity was corrupted by its own will; and from childhood its heart was carefully inclined toward evil (Genesis 8). It set its mouth against heaven, and, having built a tower of pride (Genesis 11), deserved that the Son of God, descending to it, should ascend to heaven through the ruin of repentance [Note: [Col. 1121D] Following Victorius, we have restored from the Brixian manuscripts *through the ruin of repentance*, instead of Martianaeus’s *through repentance of ruin*. Saint Jerome compares the tower’s erection with pride and its collapse with repentance.], since through the swelling of pride it could not ascend [Al. “undergo”].

“And Jonah arose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.” The Septuagint likewise.

The prophet knows, with the Holy Spirit suggesting it to him, that the repentance of the nations is the downfall of the Jews. Therefore, as a lover of his own country, he does not so much begrudge Nineveh its salvation as refuse to see his own people perish.

Otherwise, he had read that Moses, pleading for them, had said: “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if you do not, erase me from your book which you have written” (Exodus 32:31–32). Israel was preserved in response to his prayers, and Moses was not erased from the book; rather, the Lord took occasion through his servant to spare that servant’s fellow servants.

For when he says, “Forgive me,” he shows that he can be restrained. The Apostle likewise says something similar: “I could wish that I myself were accursed for my brothers, who are Israelites according to the flesh” (Romans 9:3). This does not mean that he desires to perish, for “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21); rather, he merits life all the more because he wishes to save others.

Furthermore, Jonah saw his fellow prophets being sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, to call the people to repentance; and Balaam too had prophesied divinely concerning the salvation of the people of Israel (Numbers 22). He therefore regards himself as the sole chosen one sent to the Assyrians, the enemies of Israel, and to the greatest city of its enemies, where there was idolatry and ignorance of God. And, greater than these things, he feared that, through the occasion of his preaching, if they were converted to repentance, Israel would be abandoned altogether.

For he knew, by the same Spirit through whom he was believed to proclaim the nations, that when the nations believed, then the house of Israel would perish. What was destined to happen at some time, he feared might happen in his own time.

Therefore Jonah imitated Cain (Genesis 4), and, departing from the presence of the Lord, wished to flee to Tarshish, which Josephus interprets as the city of Tarsus in Cilicia, with only the first letter changed [Note: [Col. 1122D] The Palatine manuscript has only the first letter. For the rest, see what we have observed on this subject in our commentary on Isaiah 2, and also in Letter 37 to Marcella in our recension.]. As far as can be understood from the Books of Chronicles, however, a place in India is so called.

The Hebrews, moreover, assert that *Tarshish* means “the sea” in general, according to: “By the violent wind you will break the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 47:8), that is, “of the sea.” And in Isaiah: “Howl, ships of Tarshish” (Isaiah 23:14).

Concerning this, I remember saying many years ago in a letter to Marcella: “The prophet therefore did not wish to flee to a definite place; but, entering the sea, he hastened wherever he was going. This is more fitting for a fugitive and a fearful man: not to choose a leisurely place of flight, but to seize the first opportunity for sailing.”

We can also say that he who had thought God known only in Judea and that his name was great in Israel (Psalm 75), after sensing him in the waves, confesses him and says: “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.” But if he himself made the sea and the dry land, why, leaving the dry land, do you suppose that you can evade the creator of the sea in the sea?

At the same time, through the salvation and conversion of the sailors, he is taught that even so great a multitude as Nineveh can be saved by a similar confession. Victorius, instead of “confession,” restores “conversion” from the Florentine manuscripts [Note: [Col. 1122D].]

Concerning our Lord and Savior we can say that he left his house and his homeland, and, having assumed flesh, in a certain sense fled from the heavenly regions and came to Tarshish, that is, into the sea of this world, according to what is said elsewhere:

“This is the great and spacious sea;
there are reptiles without number,
living creatures small and great.
There the ships will pass through [Al. “travel”].
That dragon whom you formed to mock him” (Psalm 103:25ff.).

For this reason, during his Passion he also said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Luke 22:42), lest, when the people cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” and “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), the fullness of the nations should enter and the branches of the olive tree be broken, to be replaced by shoots of the wild olive (Romans 11).

Such was his compassion and love for the people, because of the election of the fathers and the promise made to Abraham, that, hanging on the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Or certainly, since Tarshish is interpreted as “contemplation of joy,” the prophet, coming to Joppa—which itself means “beautiful”—hurries toward joy and the enjoyment of the blessedness of rest [Note: [Col. 1122D] The same is found in the Brixian manuscripts: “enjoying”]. He considers it better to devote himself entirely to contemplation and to enjoy the beauty and variety of knowledge than, through the occasion of the salvation of the other nations, to see perish the people from whom Christ was to be born in the flesh.

[Col. 1123A] (Verse 3.) “And he went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish; and he paid its fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “And he went up to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish; and he paid its fare and went up into it, to sail with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord.”

We read in the Books of Kings and Chronicles that Joppa was a port of Judea (2 Chronicles 2), to which King Hiram of Tyre also transported timber from Lebanon on rafts, to be carried overland to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1123D] Victorius says: “This history of Hiram is written in 1 Kings 5 and 2 Chronicles 2.” Yet I have not so far found Joppa mentioned in the Books of Kings. It is mentioned, however, in Joshua, Numbers, Ezra, Maccabees, and the Acts of the Apostles. Nevertheless, nothing has been changed, since, because the same history is treated there as well, it seems that not the matter but only the name has been omitted. Joppa is called Sappho today. Pliny reports that it was founded by the Phoenicians before the inundation of the lands. It is a town from which the port also received its name. In Hebrew, Joppa means “beautiful” or “lovely.” This is what the word [Hebrew term absent from supplied text] signifies. See what we note on this in Letter 108 to Eustochium, section 8.]

This is the place where, even to the present day, rocks are displayed on the shore, to which Andromeda was once bound and from which she was freed by the aid of Perseus.

The learned reader knows the story; but also, in accordance with the character of the region, since the prophet came from mountainous and steep country down to Joppa and the plains, he is rightly said to have descended and to have found a ship casting off its rope from the shore and entering the sea. He paid its fare, or the price of the ship—that is, of its transportation—according to the Hebrew, or, as the Septuagint translated it, “the fare for himself” [Al. “its fare”].

“And he went down into it,” as the Hebrew expressly has. For *yered* [Hebrew term present in source but not reproduced here] means “he descended,” so that the fugitive might anxiously seek hiding places.

Or “he went up,” as it is written in the Vulgate edition, so that he might arrive wherever the ship went, thinking that he had escaped if he left Judea.

Our Lord too, at the farthest shore of Judea—which, because it was in Judea, was called “the beautiful”—does not wish to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs (Matthew 15). But because he had come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, he gives the price to the passengers, so that, while wishing first to heal [Al. “save”] his own people, he might save the inhabitants of the sea; and, submerged amid whirlwinds and storms—that is, his Passion—and amid the insults of the cross, in the underworld, he might save those whom, as though sleeping in the ship, he had seemed to neglect (Matthew 8).

The prudent reader should be asked not to seek the same order in the tropological interpretation as in the historical account. The Apostle, for example, refers Hagar and Sarah to the two Testaments; yet we cannot interpret tropologically everything that is narrated in that history.

And, discussing Adam and Eve in the Letter to the Ephesians, he says: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh. This is a great mystery; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:31–32).

Can we therefore refer the whole beginning of Genesis, the making of the world, and the creation of humanity to Christ and the Church, simply because the Apostle used this testimony in that way?

Suppose that we refer what is written, “Therefore a man will leave his father,” to Christ, saying that he left God the Father in heaven so that the people of the nations might be joined to the Church [Note: [Col. 1124D] We have supplied the word *people*, which Martianaeus omitted, leaving the sense mutilated.]. How can we interpret what follows, “his mother,” unless perhaps we say that he left the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of the saints—and the other matters, much more difficult than these?

The same Apostle also writes: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). This certainly does not compel us to refer the whole Book of Exodus to Christ. For what can we say? That this rock was struck by Moses not once but twice (Exodus 17), and that waters flowed and torrents were filled? Shall we on this account force the entire history of this passage under the rule of allegory? Or will each passage, according to the diversity of its historical context, receive a different spiritual understanding?

Therefore, just as these testimonies have their own interpretations, and neither what precedes nor what follows requires the same allegory, so the prophet Jonah cannot, without danger to the interpreter, be referred entirely to the Lord.

Nor does the statement in the Gospel compel this: “An evil [Al. ‘wicked’] and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:39–40).

(Verses 4.) “But the Lord sent a great wind upon the sea, and a great storm arose on the sea, and the ship was in danger of being broken apart.”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord raised up a great spirit upon the sea, and a great storm arose on the sea, and the ship was in danger of being broken apart.”

The prophet’s flight can also be referred to the common condition of humanity: when a person despises God’s commands, departs from his presence, and gives himself over to the world, he is afterward compelled, amid the storm of evils and the shipwreck caused by the whole world raging against him, to recognize God and return to the one whom he had fled.

Hence we understand that even what people consider beneficial to themselves, when God does not will it [Al. “when God wills it”], is turned into destruction; and that assistance not only fails to benefit those to whom it is offered, but that those who offer it are themselves destroyed along with them.

So we read that Egypt was conquered by the Assyrians because it was helping Israel against the Lord’s will. The ship that had received the endangered man is itself endangered; the seas are stirred by the wind; in calm weather a storm arises. When God is opposed, nothing is secure.

(Verses 5.) “And the sailors were afraid, and the men cried out to their god, and they threw the vessels that were in the ship into the sea, so that it might become lighter for them.”

The Septuagint: “And those who were sailing were afraid, and each cried out to his god, and they threw the ship’s cargo into the sea, so that the ship might become lighter.”

They suppose that the ship was weighed down by its customary cargo and do not understand that the whole burden was the fugitive prophet. The sailors are afraid; each cries out to his own god. Though ignorant of the truth, they are not ignorant of providence, and beneath the error of religion they know that something must be venerated. They throw the cargo into the sea so that the lighter vessel might leap over the great waves.

Israel, by contrast, understands God neither in good things nor in evil ones; while Christ mourns over the people, Israel keeps its eyes dry.

“And Jonah went down into the inner part of the ship and slept in a deep sleep.”

The Septuagint: “Jonah went down into the belly of the ship, and slept and snored.”

As far as the historical account is concerned, the prophet’s mind is described as calm: he is not disturbed by the storm or by danger, maintaining the same disposition both in calm weather and when shipwreck threatens.

The others cry out to their gods, throw out the cargo, and each does what he can. This man is so quiet and secure, so tranquil in mind, that, descending into the ship’s interior, he enjoys peaceful sleep.

It can also be said that he was conscious of the flight and sin by which he had neglected the Lord’s commands; and he saw that the storm, unknown to the others, was raging against him. Therefore he went down into the inner part of the ship and hid himself in sadness, so that he would not see the waves of God’s vengeance swelling against him.

But the fact that he sleeps is not a sign of security, but of grief. For we also read that the Apostles, in the Lord’s Passion, were overcome by sleep because of the greatness of their sorrow (Matthew 26).

If, however, we interpret the passage typologically, the prophet’s sleep and deepest slumber signifies a human being numbed by the sleep of error, for whom it was not enough to flee from the presence of God: his mind also had to be overwhelmed by a kind of senselessness, so that he did not recognize God’s anger and, as though secure, slept and made the sound of deep sleep through his hoarse nostril [Note: [Col. 1125D] Elsewhere: “with a snoring nostril” and “with a snoring nose.” Victorius would have preferred *with the snoring of the nostril*, for *rhoncus* is the sound of one who snores.]

(Verses 6.) “And the helmsman approached him and said: Why are you overcome by sleep? Arise, call upon your God; perhaps God will take thought for us, and we will not perish.”

The Septuagint: “And the pilot approached him and said to him: Why are you snoring? Arise, call upon your God; perhaps God will save us somehow, and we will not perish” [Note: [Col. 1125D] The Palatine manuscripts add: “and he said to him, Why are you overcome by sleep? Arise,” and so forth.].

It is natural for each person, in his own danger, to hope more from another. Therefore the helmsman, or pilot, who ought to have comforted the frightened passengers, sees the magnitude of the danger, awakens the sleeper, reproves his thoughtless security, and urges him also, according to his own share, to entreat his god, so that, since the danger was shared, the prayer might also be shared.

According to the tropological interpretation, however, there are many who sail with Jonah and, possessing their own gods, hasten toward the contemplation of joy. But after Jonah has been discovered by the lot, and the storm has been calmed by his death and tranquility restored to the sea, then the one God will be worshiped, and spiritual sacrifices will be offered—sacrifices which, of course, according to the literal sense, they did not have in the midst of the waves.

(Verses 7.) “And each man said to his companion: Come, let us cast lots, and let us learn why this evil has come upon us. And they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.”

The Septuagint: “And each one said to his neighbor: Come, let us cast lots, and let us discover on whose account this evil has come upon us” [Note: [Col. 1126D] The same manuscripts read: “on whose account this wickedness is upon us,” omitting the rest that follows in this testimony.]. “And they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.”

They knew the nature of the sea; and, having sailed for so long, they understood the patterns of storms and winds. Certainly, if they had seen waves rising that were ordinary and such as they had sometimes experienced, they would never perhaps have sought the author of the shipwreck or, through an uncertain matter, tried to avoid a certain danger.

Nor should we immediately, on the basis of this example, put our faith in lots or join to this testimony the passage from the Acts of the Apostles in which Matthias is chosen for the apostolate by lot (Acts 1), since the privileges of individuals cannot establish a universal rule.

For just as the donkey speaks to Balaam in his condemnation (Numbers 22), and Pharaoh (Genesis 41) and Nebuchadnezzar, for their own judgment, learn future events through dreams (Daniel 2:4), yet do not understand God as the one revealing them; and Caiaphas prophesies without knowing that it was expedient for one man to perish for all (John 11 and 18); so here too the fugitive is discovered by lot, not through the power of lots—and especially not through the lots of pagans—but through the will of the one who governed the uncertain lots.

When it says, “Let us discover on whose account this evil has come upon us,” we must understand *evil* here as affliction and calamity, according to: “Sufficient for the day is its evil” (Matthew 6:34); and in the prophet Amos: “If there is evil in a city which the Lord has not made” (Amos 3:6); and in Isaiah: “I am the Lord, who makes peace and creates evil” (Isaiah 45:7).

In another passage, however, *evil* is understood as the opposite of virtue [Al. “truth”], according to what we read above in this same prophet: “The cry of its wickedness has risen to me.”

(Verses 8.) “And they said to him: Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your work? What is your land? And where are you going? Or from what people are you?”

The Septuagint: “And they said to him: Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your work? Where do you come from? Where are you going? What is your country, and from what people are you?”

The one whom the lot had identified they compel to confess with his own voice why the storm is so great, or why God’s anger is raging against them: “Tell us,” they say, “on whose account this evil has come upon us; what work you do, from what land and people you come, and where you are hastening to go.”

The brevity is also noteworthy, the kind we used to admire in Virgil:

> “Young men, what cause has driven you  
> to attempt unknown roads, and where are you bound?” he said.  
> “What is your lineage? Where is your home?  
> Do you bring peace here, or arms?”  
> (*Aeneid* 5)

The person, region, journey, and city are questioned, so that from these the cause of the danger may be discovered.

(Verses 9.) “And he said to them: I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

The Septuagint: “And he said to them: I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

He did not say, “I am a Jew,” for the division of the ten tribes from the two imposed that name upon the people; rather, he said, “I am a Hebrew,” that is, *peratēs* (περατὴς), “one who passes through,” like Abraham, who could have said: “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Psalm 38:13). Of him it is written in another psalm: “They passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people” (Psalm 104:13).

Moses says: “I will cross over and see this great vision” (Exodus 3:3).

“And I fear the Lord God of heaven”—not the gods whom you invoke, and who cannot save, but the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land. The sea, into which I am fleeing; the dry land, from which I am fleeing.

Elegantly, to distinguish it from the sea, the word used is not “land” but “dry land.” And in a brief statement the maker of the universe is revealed: he is Lord both of heaven and of earth and of the sea.

It is asked, however, how he can truly say, “I fear the Lord God of heaven,” when he does not obey his commands. Unless perhaps we answer that sinners too fear God, and that it belongs to servants not to love but to fear—although in this passage “fear” may be understood as worship, according to the sense of those who were listening and still did not know God.

(Verses 10.) “And the men feared with a great fear, and they said to him: What have you done? For the men knew [Vulgate: ‘had known’] that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.”

The Septuagint: “And the men feared with a great fear, and they said to him: What have you done? For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.”

The order of the historical narrative is reversed. Since it could have been said that there was no reason for fear, after he confessed to them, saying, “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land,” the text immediately adds that they feared for this reason: because he had told them that he was fleeing from the Lord’s presence and had not obeyed his command.

Finally, they complain and say: “What have you done?” That is: If you fear God, why do you flee? If you proclaim that the one whom you worship possesses such great power, how do you suppose that you can escape him?

They fear with a great fear because they understand that he is holy and a man of a holy nation—for, having cast off from Joppa, they knew the privilege of the Hebrew people—yet they cannot conceal the fugitive.

Great is the one who flees, but greater is the one who seeks him. They do not dare hand him over, yet they cannot conceal him. They reprove the fault and confess their fear; they ask the one who had been the author of the sin to provide the remedy.

Or certainly, when they say, “What have you done?” they are not reproving him but questioning him, wishing to know the cause of his flight—servants questioning the Lord, children their father, human beings their God.

“What,” they say, “is this great mystery, that the land should be abandoned, the seas sought out, one’s homeland left, and foreign places desired?”

[Col. 1128A] (Verses 11.) “And they said to him: What shall we do with you, and the sea will become calm for us? For the sea was growing more violent and swelling.”

The Septuagint: “And they said to him: What shall we do with you, and the sea will become calm for us? For the sea was growing more violent and raising up the waves.”

“Because of you,” they say, “the winds, the waves, the sea, and the depths have been stirred up? You have explained the cause of the sickness; indicate the means of healing. From the fact that the sea rises against us, we understand that the anger is caused by taking you aboard. If our fault is that we received you, what can we do so that the Lord may cease to be angry? What shall we do with you?” [Note: [Col. 1127] Victorius’s edition does not recognize the words “that is”; then, instead of *you are a worshiper*, it reads in one word *a worshiper*.]

“That is, shall we kill you? But you are a worshiper of the Lord. Shall we preserve you? But you are fleeing from God. It is our part to offer our hands; it is yours to command what should be done, by which the sea may become calm—the sea which now, by its swelling, testifies to the anger of the Creator.”

The historian immediately joins the cause of this question, saying that the sea was growing more violent and swelling. It was growing, as it had been ordered; it was growing in vengeance for its Lord; it was growing as it pursued the fugitive prophet. It was swelling with each passing moment, and, as though the sailors were delaying, it was raised into ever greater waves, to show that it could not postpone the Creator’s vengeance.

(Vers. 12.) And he said to them: “Take me up and throw me into the sea [the Vulgate omits “me”], and the sea will cease from you; for I know [the Vulgate adds “I”] that on my account this great storm has come [the Vulgate: “has arisen”] upon you.” The Septuagint: “And Jonah said to them: Take me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will become quiet for you; for I know that on my account these great waves are against you.”

The storm thunders against me, seeks me, threatens you with shipwreck, so that it may seize me; it will seize me so that you may live by my death. “I know,” he says, “that on my account this great storm has arisen.” I am not unaware that the elements are being thrown into disorder for my punishment, that the world is being thrown into confusion, that it is angry with me and that shipwreck is raging against you: the waves themselves command you to throw me into the sea. If I undergo the storm, you will recover calm.

At the same time we must observe the great courage of our fugitive: he does not evade, dissemble, or deny; rather, he who had confessed his flight willingly accepts the punishment, desiring to perish lest the others perish on his account and the guilt of another’s death be added to the sin of flight. This is the historical meaning. Otherwise, we do not fail to recognize in the winds that blow—winds which the Lord commanded in the Gospel to become quiet (Matt. VIII)—and in the little boat in danger, in which Jonah was sleeping, and in the swelling sea which he rebuked with the words, “Be silent and be still,” the Lord the Savior; nor do we fail to recognize the Church in danger, or the Apostles raising him up [variant: supporting him], who, when they abandoned him in his Passion, were in a certain sense casting him into the waves.

This Jonah says: “I know that on my account this great storm is upon you,” because the winds see me sailing with you toward Tarshish—that is, sailing toward the contemplation of joy, in order to lead you with me into gladness, so that where I am and the Father is, there you also may be (John XIV, 3). For this reason they rage; for this reason the world, which lies in the evil one, roars (I John [Col. 1129A] V, 19); for this reason the elements are disturbed. Death desires to devour me so that it may kill you as well, and it does not understand that it is taking the bait as on a hook, so that it may itself die through my death.

“Take me up and throw me into the sea.” For it is not our part to seize death, but willingly to receive death inflicted by others. Hence, even in persecutions, it is not permitted to perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is in danger; rather, one must submit one’s neck to the one who strikes. Thus, he says, appease the winds; thus pour libations into the seas: the storm that rages against you on my account will be calmed when I die.

[Note: Compare Book One Against Jovinianus, no. 41, where he discusses the Milesian virgins. Cicero praises something similar in his speech On the Consular Provinces; and an old epigram in the Anthology, Book III, under the heading “On Young Men”: “We are gone, O Milesian,” etc. There are also many examples of this courage among the ancients and throughout the Martyrologies.]

(Vers. 13.) And the men rowed in order to return to the dry land, but they could not, because the sea was moving and swelling against them. The Septuagint: “And the men tried to return to the land, but they could not, because the sea was moving and rising still more against them.”

The prophet had pronounced sentence against himself; but they, hearing that he worshiped God, did not dare to lay hands upon him. Therefore they strove to return to dry land and escape the danger, lest they shed blood, preferring to perish rather than to destroy.

What a great change of circumstances! A people that had served God says, “Crucify, crucify such a man!” (John XIX, 6). These men are commanded to kill; the sea rages, the storm gives the order, yet, neglecting their own danger, they are concerned for another’s salvation. Therefore the Septuagint also say παρεβιάζοντο—that is, “they desired to use force” and to overcome the order of nature, so as not to violate the prophet of God.

As for the statement that “the men rowed in order to return to dry land,” they thought that the ship could be rescued from danger without the sacrament of the one who was to suffer, although Jonah’s destruction was [variant: would be] the ship’s deliverance.

(Vers. 14.) And they cried out to the Lord and said: “We beseech you, Lord, let us not perish because of this man’s life, and do not place innocent blood upon us; for you, Lord, have done as you willed.” The Septuagint: “And they cried out to the Lord and said: By no means, Lord, let us not perish because of this man’s life, and do not place righteous blood upon us; for you, Lord, have done as you willed.”

Great was the faith of the sailors: they themselves are in danger, yet they pray for another’s life. For they know that the death of sin is worse than the death of the body. “And do not place innocent blood upon us,” they say. They call God to witness, so that whatever they are about to do may not be reckoned against them. In a certain sense they say: “We do not wish to kill your prophet, but your anger and he himself have confessed it, and the storm speaks, because you, Lord, have done as you willed; your will is being fulfilled through our hands.”

Do we not seem to hear in the sailors’ voice Pilate’s confession, when he washes his hands and says, “I am innocent of the blood of this man” (Matt. XXVII, 25)? The nations do not wish Christ to perish; they protest that his blood is innocent. And the Jews say, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Therefore, if they raise their hands, they will not be heard, because their hands are full of blood.

“For you, Lord, have done as you willed.” What we have undertaken, what the storm has risen up, what the winds rage, what the sea is raised into waves, what the fugitive is exposed by lot, what indicates what must be done—all this belongs to your will, Lord. For you have done as you willed. Hence the Savior also says in the psalm: “Lord, I desired to do your will” (Ps. XXXIX, 9).

(Vers. 15.) And they took Jonah and threw him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging. The Septuagint: “And they took Jonah and threw him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its agitation.”

He did not say “they seized him,” nor did he say “they attacked him,” but “they took him,” as though carrying him with obedience and honor. They threw him into the sea, not resisting but extending his hands to their will.

And the sea ceased, because it had found the one whom it was seeking. It is as though someone were pursuing a fugitive and hurrying along at a rapid pace; after overtaking him, he stops running, stands still, and holds the one he has captured. So also the sea, which had been angry while Jonah was absent, now holds within its depths the one it desired; it rejoices and cherishes him, and calm returns out of joy.

If we consider, before Christ’s Passion, the errors of the world, the contrary blasts of various doctrines, and the little boat—and the whole human race, that is, the Lord’s creation—in danger, but after his Passion the calm of faith, the peace of the world, security everywhere, and conversion to God, we shall see how, after Jonah’s casting down, the sea ceased from its raging [variant: fury].

[Col. 1130C] (Vers. 16.) And the men feared the Lord with great fear, and they sacrificed sacrifices to the Lord and made vows. The Septuagint likewise. [Note: These words are likewise found in the Septuagint; since they often occur elsewhere, here too we have supplied them from the manuscripts.]

Before the Lord’s Passion they cried out in fear to their gods; after his Passion they fear the Lord—that is, they venerate and worship him. And they do not fear simply, as we read at the beginning, but with great fear, in accordance with the saying: “With all your soul, and with all your heart, and with all your mind” (Matt. XXII, 37).

“And they sacrificed sacrifices,” which certainly, in the literal sense, they did not have amid the waves; but “the sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. L). And elsewhere it is said: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. XLIX, 14). And again: “We shall repay you the calves of our lips.” Therefore, at sea they sacrifice sacrifices and voluntarily make other vows, promising that they will never depart from the one whom they had begun to worship.

“For they feared with great fear,” because from the calm of the sea and the flight of the storm they perceived the prophet’s words to be true. Jonah, a fugitive in the sea, shipwrecked and dead, saves the tossing ship; he saves the Gentiles who had previously been driven about by the world’s conflicting opinions. And Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, and Joel, who were prophesying at the same time, could not correct the people in Judea. From this it is shown that the shipwreck cannot be calmed except through the death of the fugitive.

(Cap. II.—Vers. 1.) And the Lord prepared a great fish to swallow Jonah. The Septuagint: “And the Lord commanded a great sea-monster, and it swallowed Jonah.”

The Lord commanded death and hell to receive the prophet. The creature, which thought its prey had been placed before its greedy jaws, rejoiced as much in swallowing as it later mourned in vomiting him up. Then was fulfilled what is read in Hosea: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O hell” (Hosea XIII, 14).

In Hebrew, however, we read “a great fish,” for which the Septuagint translators, and the Lord in the Gospel, use “sea-monster,” explaining the matter more briefly. In Hebrew it says DAG GADOL, which is interpreted as “a great fish”; there is no doubt that it signifies a sea-monster.

It must also be observed that where destruction was expected, there was protection. As for the statement that he “prepared” it, this may mean either that he prepared it from the beginning, when he created it—as is also written in the psalm, “This dragon whom you formed to play with him” (Ps. CIII, 26)—or certainly that he caused it to come alongside the ship, so that it might receive Jonah, who had been thrown overboard, into its bosom and provide him a dwelling in place of death. Thus he who had experienced God as angry in the ship might experience him as merciful in death.

(Vers. 2.) And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights. The Septuagint: “And Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights.”

The Lord explains the mystery of this passage in the Gospel (Matt. XII), and it is superfluous to say either the same thing or something else when he himself, who suffered, has explained it. We ask only how he was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.

Some divide the time from Παρασκευή (paraskeuē), when, as the sun withdrew, from the sixth hour to the ninth hour night followed day, into two days and nights; then, adding the Sabbath, they reckon three days and three nights. We, however, should understand the whole by synecdoche (συνεκδοχικῶς), taking the part for the whole. Since he died on Παρασκευή, we count that as one day and one night, and the Sabbath as another; the third night, which belongs to the Lord’s Day, we refer to the beginning of the other day. For in Genesis the night does not belong to the preceding day (Gen. I), but to the following day—that is, it is the beginning of what is to come, not the end of what has passed.

To make this understandable, I shall put it more simply. Imagine someone leaving his lodging at the ninth hour and arriving at another lodging at the third hour of the following day. If I say that he traveled for two days, I shall not immediately be accused of falsehood, because the traveler did not spend all the hours of both days on the journey, but only part of them. This interpretation seems correct to me. If, however, someone does not accept it and can explain the mystery of this passage in a better sense, his opinion should rather be followed.

And Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the belly of the fish, and said: The Septuagint likewise, but with the order changed. [Note: The words that follow, which were likewise missing from the Septuagint, have been supplied from our manuscripts, although only their order was changed.]

If Jonah is referred to the Lord, and if by the fact that he was three days and nights in the belly of the sea-monster he signifies the Passion of the Savior, then his prayer must also be a type of the Lord’s prayer.

I know that some will find it incredible that a human being could be preserved for three days and nights in the belly of a sea-monster, in which shipwrecks were being driven along. Such people will be either believers or unbelievers. If they are believers, they will be compelled to believe much greater things: how the three young men, thrown into the furnace of blazing fire, remained so unharmed that not even the smell of fire touched their garments (Dan. III); how the sea withdrew and stood rigid like walls on either side, providing a path for the people who crossed (Exod. XIV); how, contrary to human expectation, the lions’ hunger increased, yet their ferocity, fearing its prey, looked upon it without touching it; and many similar examples.

But if they are unbelievers, let them read Ovid’s fifteen books of the Metamorphoses and all Greek and Latin history. There they will see Daphne changed into a laurel, or the sisters of Phaethon changed into poplar trees; how Jupiter, their supreme god, was changed into a swan, flowed as gold, carried off his victim as a bull, and other such things, in which the very obscenity of the myths denies the sanctity of divinity. They believe those stories and say that all things are possible for God; yet, while believing shameful tales and defending God’s universal power, they do not attribute the same power to what is honorable.

As for what is written—“And Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the belly of the fish, and said”—we understand that after he realized that he was safe in the sea-monster’s belly, he did not despair of the Lord’s mercy, but turned entirely to supplication. For God, who had said concerning the righteous, “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. XC, 15), and, “When he calls upon me, I will say, ‘Here I am,’” was with him. The one who was heard can say: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. IV, 1).

(Vers. 3.) “I cried to the Lord from my tribulation, and he heard me; from the belly of hell I cried, and you heard my voice.” The Septuagint likewise, with only this change: “From the belly of hell you heard my cry.” [Note: The words “you heard my voice,” which are likewise found in the Hebrew text, are absent here from the Palatine manuscripts.]

He did not say, “I cry,” but “I cried”; nor does he pray concerning the future, but he gives thanks for the past. He indicates that from the moment when, having been thrown into the sea, he saw the sea-monster, its enormous body, and its monstrous jaws swallowing him with open mouth, he remembered the Lord and cried out—either as the waters yielded and made room for his cry, or with the whole affection of his heart, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Crying in your hearts, Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 15).

He cried to the one who alone knows the hearts of human beings and who says to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV, 15), although Scripture records that Moses had cried out nothing before this utterance. This is what we read in the first of the Songs of Ascents: “To the Lord, when I was in tribulation, I cried, and he heard me” (Ps. CXIX, 1).

By “the belly of hell” we should understand the belly of the sea-monster, which was so large that it possessed the likeness of hell. But the passage may more appropriately be referred to the person of Christ, who, under the name of David, sings in the psalm: “You will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10). He was in hell alive, free among the dead.

(Vers. 4.) “And you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the sea, and the river surrounded me.” The Septuagint: “You cast me into the depth of the heart of the sea, and the rivers surrounded me.” [Note: The same Palatine manuscripts read, “into the deep and the heart of the sea.”]

With reference to Jonah, the interpretation is not difficult: enclosed in the sea-monster’s belly, he was in the deepest part and in the midst of the sea, surrounded by rivers.

With reference to the Lord the Savior, let us take as an example the sixty-eighth psalm, in which he says: “I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no solid ground. I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has submerged me.” Of him it is also said in another psalm: “Yet you have cast off and rejected; you have delayed your Christ. You have overturned the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary on the earth; you have destroyed all his walls” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 39–40), and what follows.

Compared with heavenly blessedness and that place of which it is written, “His place is in holy peace” (Ps. LVII, 2), every earthly dwelling is full of waves and full of storms. By “the heart of the sea” hell is signified, for in the Gospel we read, “in the heart of the earth” (Matt. XII, 14). Just as the heart of an animal is in its middle, so hell is said to be in the middle of the earth.

Or certainly, according to anagogical interpretation (ἀναγωγή), he recalls that he is in the heart of the sea—that is, in the midst of temptations. Yet, although he was among bitter waters and was tempted in every respect without sin, he did not experience bitter waters. Rather, he was surrounded by a river, of which we also read elsewhere: “The river’s flood makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 5). While others were drinking salty waves, I was drinking the sweetest streams amid temptations.

Nor should it seem impious to you if the Lord now says, “You cast me into the deep” (Ps. LXVIII, 27), since in the psalm he says: “For the one whom you struck, they themselves pursued,” in accordance with what is stated in Zechariah in the person of the Father: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. XIII, 7).

“All your torrents and your waves passed over me.” The Septuagint: “All your surges and your waves passed over me.” That swelling waves of the sea passed over Jonah and that a savage storm thundered is beyond doubt. We ask, however, how all God’s surges, torrents, and waves passed over the Savior.

“Life upon the earth is a temptation” (Job VII, 1), or, as it is found in Hebrew, “a warfare,” because here we wage war so that elsewhere we may be crowned. No human being can endure all temptations except the one who was tempted in every respect according to our likeness, without sin. Hence it is said to the Corinthians: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human. But God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (I Cor. X, 13).

And because all persecutions and everything that happens do not descend without God’s will, they are therefore called God’s torrents and waves. They did not overwhelm Jesus, but passed through him, threatening shipwreck without causing it. All the persecutions and storms by which the human race was afflicted, and by which all the little boats were broken, thundered over my head. I endured the storms and shattered the raging tempests so that others might sail more securely.

(Vers. 5.) “And I said: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” The Septuagint: “I said: I have been cast away from your eyes.”

Before I cried out from my tribulation and you heard me, because I had assumed the form of a servant and had also taken on its frailty, I said, “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” When I was with you and enjoyed your light, and in your light I was myself light, I did not say, “I have been cast away.” But after I came into the depth of the sea and was surrounded by human flesh, I imitate human feelings and say, “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.”

I spoke in this way as a human being. But as God—and as one who, although existing in your form, did not regard equality with you as something to be seized (Phil. II), since I wished to raise the human race to you, so that where I am and you are, there also may be all who have believed in me and you (John XVII, 24)—I say:

“Nevertheless, I shall again see your holy temple.” The Septuagint: “Will I perhaps again see your holy temple?” [Note: The Palatine manuscripts have, “For this the Septuagint translated.”]

The Greek word ἆρα (ara), which the Vulgate edition renders by “perhaps,” can also be interpreted as “therefore,” so that it forms the final conclusion of a proposition, assumption, confirmation, and syllogism—not the uncertain conclusion of one who doubts, but the confident conclusion of one who confirms. For this reason we translated it, “Nevertheless, I shall again see your holy temple,” in accordance with what is said in another psalm in his person: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory” (Ps. XXV, 8).

Also consider the Gospel reading in which it is written: “Father, glorify me with yourself with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII, 5). And the Father answered from heaven: “I have glorified, and I will glorify” (ibid., XII, 28). [Note: Most other books read, “I have glorified, and I will glorify.”]

Or certainly, because it is written, “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (ibid., XVII, 21), just as the Son is the temple of the Father, so the Father is the temple of the Son. For he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came” (ibid., XVI, 28); and, “The Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1).

Or the one and same Savior, as a human being, asks; as God, he promises; and, secure in possession of what he has always possessed, he says this. From the person of Jonah, however, whether as one who desires or as one who trusts, it can plainly be understood that, placed in the depth of the sea, he longed to see the Lord’s temple, and that in prophetic spirit he was elsewhere and contemplated something else [variant: elsewhere].

(Vers. 6.) “The waters surrounded me up to my soul; the abyss enclosed me.” The Septuagint: “Water was poured around me up to my soul; the abyss enclosed me at the last.”

These waters, which are near the abysses, which roll and flow upon the earth and drag much mud along with them, strive to kill not the body but the soul. They are friendly to bodies and are nourished by their pleasures. Therefore, in accordance with what we said above, the Lord speaks in the psalm: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered up to my soul” (Ps. LXVIII, 1). And elsewhere: “Our soul has passed through the torrent” (Ps. CXXIII, 3). And: “Let the pit not close its mouth over me, nor let hell shut me in” (ibid., LXVIII, 16). Let it not deny me an exit, since I descended willingly and shall ascend willingly; since I came as a voluntary captive, I must release the captives, so that the saying may be fulfilled: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII). For he captured for life those who had previously been held captive in death.

By the destructive and exceedingly evil powers of the abyss we should understand either powers devoted to tortures and punishments, or those to which the demons plead in the Gospel not to be sent (Luke VIII). [Note: The Palatine manuscripts read: “Hence comes the saying, ‘And darkness was over the abyss,’” etc.] Hence also, “Darkness was over the abyss” (Gen. I). At times “abyss” is understood of mysteries and very profound meanings, and of God’s judgments: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7); and, “Abyss calls to abyss at the sound of your cataracts” (Ps. XLI, 8).

“The sea covered my head; I descended to the ends of the mountains; the bars of the earth enclosed me forever.” The Septuagint: “My head entered into the clefts of the mountains; I descended into the earth, whose bars are everlasting restraints.”

That the sea covered Jonah’s head, that he descended to the ends of the mountains, and that he reached the depths of the earth, by which the globe of the earth is sustained by God’s will as though by bars and columns, is beyond doubt. Of these it is also said elsewhere: “I established its columns” (Ps. LXXIV, 4).

Concerning the Lord the Savior, according to both editions, it seems to me that the passage can be understood as follows: his principal part and head—that is, the soul which, together with the body, he graciously assumed for our salvation—descended into the clefts of the mountains, which were covered by waves; which had withdrawn themselves from heaven’s freedom; which the abyss surrounded; which had torn themselves away from God’s majesty; and afterward it penetrated even to the regions below.

To these places, as though into the extreme mire of sins, souls were dragged, as the Psalmist says: “They will enter into the lower parts of the earth; they will be portions of foxes” (Ps. LXII, 10–11). These are the bars of the earth, like the bolts of the outermost prison and punishments, unwilling to let captive souls leave the underworld. Therefore the Septuagint significantly translated κάτοχοι αἰώνιοι [variant: κατόχους αἰωνίους]—that is, “those desiring always to hold fast” those whom they had once seized.

But our Lord, of whom we read under the person of Cyrus in Isaiah, “I shall shatter bronze doors and break iron bars” (Isa. IV, 2), descended to the ends of the mountains and was enclosed by everlasting bars, in order to free all who had been shut in.

(Vers. 7.) “And you will raise my life from corruption, O Lord my God.” The Septuagint: “And let my life rise from corruption, O Lord my God.” [Note: We have restored the Septuagint’s wording almost word for word according to the evidence of our manuscripts, with the Greek text agreeing. Previously it was read quite differently: “My life will ascend from corruption to you, O Lord my God.” The Greek reads, καὶ ἀναβήτω ἐκ φθορᾶς ἡ ζωή μου, Κύριε ὁ Θεός μου. Hence, consistently, we restore “let it rise” shortly afterward in place of “it will ascend.”]

He said properly, “You will raise,” or, “Let my life rise from corruption,” because he had descended to corruption and to the underworld. This is what the Apostles interpret as prophesied in the fifteenth psalm concerning the Lord: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.” David, of course, died and was buried; the Savior’s flesh did not see corruption.

Others interpret it to mean that, compared with heavenly blessedness and the Word of God, the human body is corruption, since it is sown in corruption; and that in the hundred-second psalm it is signified in the person of the Just One: “He heals all your infirmities; he redeems your life from destruction.” [Note: Martianus reads “may be sanctified”; Victorius restores “redeems,” from the Vulgate, in place of “redeemed”; our manuscripts read “from corruption” in place of “from destruction.”] Hence the Apostle also says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII, 24).

And it is called the body of death, or the body of humiliation. Heretics use this as an occasion for their error, so that under Christ’s person they may falsely introduce the Antichrist; they occupy the churches in order to nourish their exceedingly fat belly, and while living carnally, they argue against the flesh [variant: they argue].

But we know that a body was assumed from the incorrupt Virgin: it was not Christ’s corruption, but his temple. If we are drawn to the Apostle’s statement to the Corinthians, in which the body is called spiritual (I Cor. XV), then, so as not to appear contentious, we shall say that the very same body and the same flesh will rise that was buried and placed in the earth, but that its glory will change, not its nature. For “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.”

When he says “this,” the body is in a certain way pointed out as though between two fingers: this in which we are born, this in which we die, this which those who are to be punished fear to receive, this which virginity awaits as its reward and adultery fears as its punishment.

Concerning Jonah, it may be understood as follows: he who, according to the nature of bodies, ought to have decayed in the belly of the sea-monster, to have become food for the beast, and to have been dispersed through its veins and limbs, remained safe and whole.

As for the words, “O Lord my God,” they express the affection of one who flatters, because he experienced the common God of all as his own and, as it were, his personal God through the greatness of the benefit.
