(Vers. 8.) “When my soul was distressed within me, I remembered the Lord.” The Septuagint: “When my soul failed within me, I remembered the Lord.”

“When,” he says, “I expected no other help, the remembrance of the Lord became my salvation,” in accordance with the words: “I remembered the Lord, and I rejoiced” (Ps. LXXVI, 4); and elsewhere: “I remembered the days of old, and I held eternal years in mind” (Ps. LXXVI, 6).

When I despaired of salvation, and the frailty of the flesh in the middle of the sea-monster’s belly allowed me to hope for nothing concerning life, whatever seemed impossible was overcome by remembrance of the Lord. I saw myself shut up in the belly of the sea-monster, and the Lord was my entire hope.

From this we learn, according to the Septuagint, that at the time when our soul fails and is torn away from the body’s structure, we ought to turn our thought to no one else except him who is our Lord both in the body and outside the body.

Concerning the person of the Savior, the interpretation is not difficult: he said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38–39); and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”; and, “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. XXX, 6); and other similar words.

“Let my prayer come to you, to your holy temple.” The Septuagint likewise. [Note: The words “the Septuagint likewise,” which were missing, have been supplied from the manuscripts here and in several other places.]

For this reason, in the Lord’s tribulation, I remembered him: so that my prayer might ascend from the farthest sea and the clefts of the mountains to the heavens, and come to your holy temple, in which you enjoy eternal blessedness.

It must be considered that, in a novel manner, “prayer” is made the subject of a prayer, and he prays that his prayer may ascend to God’s temple. He asks, as a priest, that the people may be freed in his body.

(Vers. 9.) “Those who keep empty things in vain will abandon their mercy.” [Note: Victorius, following the Vulgate, reads “they abandon”; he seems to prefer this reading himself in the exposition that follows.] The Septuagint: “Those who keep vain and false things have abandoned their mercy.”

God is merciful by nature and ready, through clemency, to save those whom he cannot save through justice. We, however, through our own fault, lose and abandon the mercy that is prepared and offers itself voluntarily.

He did not say, “Those who perform vanities”—for “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I, 2)—lest he seem to condemn everyone and deny mercy to the whole human race. Rather, he says, “those who keep vanities,” or “falsehood,” those who have passed into the affection of their heart; who not only perform vanities but guard them as though they loved them and thought they had found a treasure.

At the same time, observe the prophet’s courage: in the depth of the sea, in the belly of so great a beast, covered by eternal night, he does not think about his own danger but philosophizes about the nature of things in a universal judgment.

“They will abandon their mercy,” he says. Although mercy is offended—which we may understand as God himself, since “the Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and rich in mercy” (Ps. CXLIV, 8)—he does not abandon or detest those who keep vanities, but waits for them to return. They, however, voluntarily abandon mercy as it stands ready and offers itself freely.

This may also be prophesied concerning the Lord from the person of the Jews’ unbelief: while they imagine that they are observing human precepts and the commandments of the Pharisees, which are vanity and falsehood, they abandoned God, who had always shown them mercy.

(Vers. 10.) “But I shall sacrifice to you with the voice of praise; whatever I have vowed, I shall repay for salvation to the Lord.” The Septuagint: “But I shall sacrifice to you with the voice of praise and confession; whatever I have vowed, I shall repay to you, salvation to the Lord.”

“Those who keep vanities have abandoned their mercy; but I, who have been swallowed for the salvation of many, shall sacrifice to you with the voice of praise and confession,” offering myself, “because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V).

[Note: Here Victorius omits verus (“true”); below, ergo (“therefore”).] And as the true priest and sheep, he offered himself for us. “And I shall confess,” he says, “to you, as I confessed previously, saying: I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI, 15; John VI, 39). “And I shall repay the vows that I made to the Lord for the salvation of all, so that everything that you have given me may not perish forever.”

We see what the Savior promised in his Passion for our salvation. Let us not make Jesus a liar. Therefore let us be pure and separated from every stain of sin, so that he may offer us to God the Father as the victims he had vowed.

(Vers. 11.) And the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land. The Septuagint: “And he commanded the sea-monster, and it cast Jonah onto the dry ground.”

These are the words that we read above, which the Lord prayed in the belly of the sea-monster under the person of Jonah. Concerning this Job also speaks mystically: “Let him curse it who curses the day, he who is ready to capture the great sea-monster” (Job III, 8).

Therefore this great sea-monster, the abysses, and hell are commanded to restore the Savior to the earth. And he who had died in order to free those held by the bonds of death leads many out with him into life.

As for the word “vomited,” we should understand it in a more emphatic sense (ἐμφατικώτερον): life, victorious over death, emerged from the innermost vital organs of death.

### Chapter III

#### Verses 1–2

And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying: “Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it [Note: Victorius says: “The Septuagint translation corrupted this passage, for they translated it thus. Jerome, however, as is apparent from his Vulgate edition, rendered it as follows: ‘And preach in it the preaching that I speak to you.’ For the words ‘according to the former’ are not in the Hebrew, nor could they be, since otherwise it would be false that Jonah had previously preached in Nineveh, whereas up to this point only his flight from that city has been described. Those words were therefore deleted by him, and the passage restored in accordance with the Vulgate edition. We, on the contrary, judge that we have no right to act against the testimony of the manuscripts.”] according to the former preaching that I speak to you.”

The Septuagint: “And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying: ‘Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it according to the former preaching that I spoke to you.’”

The prophet is not told, “Why did you not do what had been commanded you?” The mere rebuke of shipwreck and being swallowed is sufficient, so that he who had not recognized the Lord when he commanded might understand him when he delivered him. Otherwise it is pointless, after beating a delinquent servant, to wish to charge him with what he did, since such a rebuke is not so much correction as reproach.

Our Lord, however, is sent a second time to Nineveh after the resurrection: he who had previously fled, as it were, saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39), and had been unwilling to give the children’s bread to the dogs (ibid. 15), now, because they had said, “Crucify him, crucify him! We have no king except Caesar” (John 19:15), proceeds willingly to Nineveh, so that after the resurrection he may preach what he had been commanded to preach even before the Passion.

Refer everything that he is commanded, that he obeys, that he does not wish, that he is compelled again to wish, and that he fulfills the Father’s will a second time, to the human being and to the form of a servant, to whom such words properly apply.

#### Verse 3

And Jonah arose and went to Nineveh according to the word of the Lord. Now Nineveh was a great city of God [the Vulgate omits “of God”], requiring a journey of three days; and Jonah began to enter the city, a journey of one day.

The Septuagint: “And Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, as the Lord had spoken to him. Now Nineveh was a great city to God, requiring a journey of three days’ travel; and Jonah began to enter the city, a journey of one day’s travel.” [Note: Our manuscripts supply the word *travel* (*viae*), which also appears in the Greek, ὁδοῦ.]

Jonah immediately accomplished by his action what had been commanded him. Nineveh, toward which the prophet was traveling, was a great city, and of such extent that it could scarcely be traversed in a journey of three days. But he, remembering both the command and his earlier shipwreck, completed the three-day route with the haste of a single day. Some, however, understand the matter more simply: that he preached only in the third part of the city, and that the word of his preaching quickly reached the rest.

Our Lord is properly said to rise after the dead and to preach the word of the Lord when he sends the apostles to baptize those who were in Nineveh in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—that is, over a journey of three days. This very mystery of human salvation is completed in the journey of one day [Note: Again, the word *travel* (*via*) was absent from Martianaeus’s edition, and the sense was consequently defective; our manuscripts, following Victorius, supply it], that is, in the confession of the one God—not so much by the apostles as by Jonah preaching in the apostles. For he himself says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

There can be no doubt why Nineveh is called a great city of God, since the world and everything in it was made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3). It should also be observed that he did not say “for three days and nights,” or “for one day and night,” but simply “for days” and “for a day,” in order to show that, in the mystery of the Trinity and the confession of the one God, nothing is dark.

#### Verse 4

And he cried out and said: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”

The Septuagint: “And he preached and said: ‘Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.’” [Note: Yet the Septuagint seems to have written not merely three, but forty-three. Indeed, in Justin’s *Dialogue with Trypho* occurs ὅτι μετὰ (ἐν ἄλλοις τρεῖς) τεσσαράκοντα τρεῖς, “because after (in other copies, three) forty days,” and so forth. The two words seem to have coalesced into one.]

The number three used by the Septuagint does not suit repentance. I am sufficiently astonished that it was translated in this way, since in Hebrew there is no correspondence of letters, syllables, accents, or word. For “three” is said *SALOS* (Hebrew not legible in the supplied text), and “forty,” *ARBAIM* (Hebrew not legible in the supplied text). Moreover, the prophet sent from Judea to the Assyrians on so long a journey demanded a repentance worthy of his preaching, so that ancient and festering wounds might be healed by an applied dressing of long duration.

The number forty, furthermore, is appropriate to sinners and to fasting, prayer, sackcloth, tears, and perseverance in supplication. Thus Moses fasted for forty days on Mount Sinai (Exod. 34), and Elijah, fleeing from Jezebel, when famine had been imposed on the land of Israel and God’s anger hung over it, is described as fasting for forty days (3 Kgs. 34).

The Lord himself, the true Jonah, sent to preach to the world, fasts for forty days; and, leaving us the inheritance of fasting, he prepares our souls under this number to eat his body. [Note: Victorius had previously written at this point: “Let heretics learn from these words, from the institution of Christ and the apostles, that the fast of Lent exists, and that by it we are prepared to eat the body of the true Christ, which is received on Thursday of Holy Week or at Easter itself.” That the fast of Lent derives from apostolic institution Jerome states even more clearly in his letter to Marcella against Montanus.]

The fact that he cried out fulfills that Gospel passage: “Standing, he cried out in the temple, saying: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.’” For every saying of the Savior, because he preached concerning great things, is called a cry.

#### Verse 5

And the men of Nineveh believed in God, and proclaimed a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. 417

The Septuagint likewise. [Note: The Septuagint’s words are supplied here by our manuscripts, as often elsewhere.]

Nineveh believed, while Israel persists in unbelief. The uncircumcision believed, while the circumcision remains faithless. And first the men of Nineveh believe—those who had reached the age of Christ. They proclaim a fast and clothe themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least.

The manner of repentance is worthy both in food and in clothing: those who had offended God by luxury and ambition seek to appease him through the condemnation of the very things by which they had previously offended him. Sackcloth and fasting are the weapons of repentance, the aids of sinners: first fasting, and then sackcloth; first what is hidden, and afterward what is public. The former is always offered to God, the latter sometimes also to human beings. And if one of these two necessities must be omitted, I would choose fasting without sackcloth rather than sackcloth without fasting.

Old age begins and extends down to the youngest (Job 25:5–6), for no one is without sin, even if his life should be only one day, and the years of his life are numbered (Job 14). [Note: Our manuscripts read, “not even if his life should be only one day.” Victorius says: “The passage is Job 14 according to the Septuagint, where it now reads, ἀριθμητοὶ δὲ μῆνες αὐτοῦ, ‘his months are numerable’; formerly, ‘innumerable.’ This testimony from Ezekiel 18 was read uncorrupted in Jerome as follows: ‘Therefore it is written: No human being is without sin, not even if his life should be only one day. But the years of his life are numbered.’ We have not altered the text except where it reads ‘innumerable.’”]

For if the stars are not clean in God’s sight, how much less are the worm and decay, and those who are held liable through the sin of offending Adam?

But the order is also most beautiful: God commands the prophet; the prophet preaches to the city; first the men believe, and when they proclaim the fast, every age puts on sackcloth. The men do not proclaim sackcloth, but only fasting. Those to whom repentance is commanded, however, appropriately join sackcloth to fasting, so that an empty stomach and mournful clothing may implore the Lord more earnestly.

#### Verses 6 and following

And the word reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, cast off his garment from himself, put on sackcloth, and sat in ashes. And he cried out and said in Nineveh, from the mouth of the king and his nobles:

“Let neither human beings nor animals, cattle nor sheep, taste anything; let them not feed, and let them not drink water. Let human beings and animals be covered with sackcloth, and let them cry out to the Lord with all their strength [the Vulgate: “to God”]. Let each person turn from his evil way and from the iniquity that is in his hands. Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and turn back from the fury of his anger, so that we shall not perish?”

The Septuagint: “And the word came near to the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, removed his robe from himself, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. And proclamation was made in Nineveh by the king and by all his great men, saying: ‘Let neither human beings nor animals, cattle nor sheep, taste anything; let them not feed, and let them not drink water. Let human beings and animals be covered with sackcloth, and let them cry out vehemently to the Lord. Let each one turn from his evil way and from the iniquity that was in their hands,’ saying: ‘Who knows whether God may turn, relent, and turn away from the anger of his fury, so that we may not perish?’” [Note: The same manuscripts read: “If God should repent and turn back from his anger,” in agreement with the Greek, εἰ μετανοήσει ὁ Θεὸς καὶ ἀποστρέψει ἐξ ὀργῆς, and so forth. The printed reading follows the Aldine exemplar.]

I know that many interpret the king of Nineveh—who is the last to hear the preaching, descends from his throne, casts off his former adornment, puts on sackcloth, and sits in ashes; and, not content with his own conversion, proclaims repentance to his fellow citizens as well, saying: “Let human beings, animals, cattle, and sheep be tormented by hunger, covered with sackcloth, and, having condemned their former vices, devote themselves entirely to repentance”—as referring to the devil. At the end of the world, they say, since no rational creature made by God is to perish, he will descend from his pride, perform repentance, and be restored to his former place.

To support this interpretation they also bring forward the example from Daniel, where Nebuchadnezzar, after performing repentance for seven years, is restored to his former kingdom (Dan. 4). But since Holy Scripture does not say this, and since it entirely overturns the fear of God by making people readily slide into vices, if they think that even the devil, who is the author of evil and the fountain of all sins, can be saved after repentance, let us cast this interpretation from our minds.

Let us know that sinners in the Gospel are sent into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25), and that it is said of them: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24).

We certainly know that God is merciful, and that, being sinners ourselves, we do not delight in his cruelty. But we read: “The Lord is merciful and just, and our God has mercy.” God’s justice is surrounded by mercy, and he proceeds to judgment with such a combination: he spares in such a way that he judges; he judges in such a way that he shows mercy. “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have kissed one another” (Ps. 48:8).

Otherwise, if all rational creatures are equal, and by their own free choice are either raised upward through virtues or plunged downward through vices; if, after a long cycle and innumerable ages, the restoration of all things will occur; and if there will be one rank among those who have served, what difference will there be between a virgin and a prostitute? What difference will there be between the mother of the Lord and—something wicked even to say—the victims of public lust? Will Gabriel and the devil be the same? The apostles and demons the same? Prophets and false prophets the same? Martyrs and persecutors the same?

Imagine whatever you wish; double the years and periods, and heap up innumerable ages of torments. If the end of all things is alike, the whole past is worthless, because we do not ask what we once were, but what we shall always be.

Nor am I unaware of what they customarily say against these arguments, preparing for themselves hope and salvation together with the devil. But it is not appropriate at this time to write at greater length against the perverse doctrine and the diabolical σύμφραγμα (“combination”) of those who teach in corners and deny publicly. [Note: The false reading that prevailed up to this point, deformed to suit the understanding of an ignorant glossator, was: “and the diabolical kingdom teaching, and openly denying the privilege to the angels,” and so forth. Nor is there any reason to note individually the defects from which it suffers, since, once adapted to the reading we have restored, its falsity immediately reveals itself. We have restored the text according to the evidence of the Palatine codices: “the diabolical σύμφραγμα, teaching in corners and denying publicly,” and so forth. This is Jerome’s customary condemnation of the Origenists: that they whispered insane doctrines secretly into the ears of their disciples, doctrines they were ashamed to teach openly, and denied what they had said.]

It is enough for us to have indicated what we think about this testimony and, as it were, briefly to intimate in our commentary who the king of Nineveh is, to whom the word of God reaches at the end.

What eloquence and secular wisdom are worth among the people of the world is shown by Demosthenes, Cicero, Plato, Xenophon, Theophrastus, Aristotle, and the other orators and philosophers, who are regarded as kings among human beings, and whose precepts are received not as the precepts of mortals but almost as oracles of the gods. Hence Plato also says: “States will be happy if either philosophers rule or rulers become philosophers.”

How difficult such people find it to believe in God—leaving aside daily examples and saying nothing of the ancient histories of the pagans—the testimony of the Apostle is sufficient for us. Writing to the Corinthians, he says: “Consider your calling, brothers: there are not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and the base things of the world, and the things that are despised, God chose” (1 Cor. 1:26), and so forth. [Note: The words “not many powerful,” which Victorius had previously restored from seven Florentine codices together with several Brixian and Roman manuscripts, Martianaeus nevertheless omitted; our manuscripts once again supply them.]

Again he says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent” (ibid. 1:19). And: “See that no one despoils you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Col. 2:8).

From this it is clear that the kings of the world hear Christ’s preaching last, and, laying aside the splendor of eloquence and the ornament and beauty of words, surrender themselves entirely to simplicity and rusticity. Reduced to the dress of common people, they sit in filth and destroy what they had previously preached.

Let us set before ourselves the blessed Cyprian, who had earlier been an advocate of idolatry and had attained such renown for eloquence that he even taught rhetoric at Carthage. [Note: It is better to hear Cyprian himself testify about this in Epistle 1 to Donatus, or in the book *On the Grace of God*: “When I lay in darkness and a blind night, and, wavering and doubtful on the sea of the tossing world, drifted with wandering steps, ignorant of my life and estranged from truth and light, I considered altogether difficult and hard, given my habits at that time, what divine favor promised for my salvation,” and so forth.] At last he heard Jonah’s word and was converted to repentance, and he attained such virtue that he publicly preached Christ and bent his neck to the sword for him.

Clearly, we understand that the king of Nineveh descended from his throne and exchanged purple for sackcloth, perfumes for mud, cleanliness for filth—not filth of thought, but of language. Hence concerning Babylon Jeremiah says: “Babylon was a golden cup, intoxicating the whole earth” (Jer. 51:7). Whom has secular eloquence not intoxicated? Whose minds has it not dazzled by the arrangement of its words and the brilliance of its eloquence? It is difficult for the powerful, noble, and wealthy to believe in God, and much more difficult for the eloquent. Their minds are blinded by riches, resources, and luxury; surrounded by vices, they cannot see the virtues and simplicity of Holy Scripture, judging not by the majesty of its meaning but by the lowliness of its words.

But when those who previously taught evil have turned to repentance and begun to teach good, then we shall see the peoples of Nineveh converted by one preaching, and what we read in Isaiah fulfilled: “Has a nation been born all at once?” [Note: Martianaeus retained the manifest error *sanata* for the two words *si nata*, which Victorius had earlier corrected from the Greek ἐτέθη. A second error, which Victorius himself did not notice, is *semel* (“once”) in place of *simul* (“together”); compelled by the same Greek text, εἰς ἅπαξ, we have corrected it from our manuscripts.]

Understand also, in the same sense, human beings and animals covered with sackcloth and crying out to the Lord: rational and irrational beings, the wise and the simple, repent at Jonah’s preaching, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “You will save human beings and animals, Lord” (Ps. 35:7).

We can also interpret the animals covered with sackcloth in another way, especially from those passages in which we read: “The sun and the moon shall be clothed in sackcloth” (Ezek. 32:7). And elsewhere: “I will clothe the heavens in sackcloth” (Isa. 50:3)—that is, with mournful clothing, grief, and sadness, which are metaphorically called sackcloth (*metaphorikōs*, μεταφορικῶς).

The statement “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive?” is deliberately expressed ambiguously and uncertainly, so that, while human beings are uncertain about their salvation, they may practice repentance more fervently and more strongly move God to mercy.

#### Verse 10

And God saw their works, because they had turned from their evil way; and God had mercy concerning the evil that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.

The Septuagint: “And God saw their works, because they had turned from their evil ways; and God repented concerning the evil that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.”

According to either interpretation—whether God was then threatening the Assyrian city, or whether every day he threatens the peoples of the world—God threatens them so that they may repent. If they turn, he too changes his sentence, and the conversion of the people changes it. Jeremiah and Ezekiel explain this more clearly: the Lord does not fulfill the good things he has promised if the good turn toward vices, nor the evils with which he threatens the wicked if they turn back to salvation.

Thus now also God saw their works, because they had turned from their most evil way. He did not listen to the words that Israel often used to promise: “Everything that the Lord has said, we shall do” (Exod. 24:3); he looked upon their works. And because he prefers the repentance of the sinner to death (Ezek. 18), he willingly changed his sentence, because he saw that their works had changed.

Indeed, God persisted in his original purpose, desiring from the beginning to show mercy. [Note: Another reading is *neminem* (“no one”). Victorius says that this reading too is not displeasing, so that the meaning would be: “God, desiring to punish no one, threatens what he is going to do.” But the earlier reading is better. Properly speaking, no one can be said to be going to do what he threatens in order not to do it.]

For no one who desires to punish threatens what he is going to do. Understand “evil,” as we said above, as punishment and torment—not as though God had contemplated doing anything evil.

### Chapter IV

#### Verse 1

And Jonah was afflicted with a great affliction, and he became angry; and he prayed to the Lord and said.

The Septuagint: “And Jonah was grieved with great grief, and he was confounded; and he prayed to the Lord and said.”

Seeing the fullness of the nations entering in, and what is said in Deuteronomy being fulfilled—“They provoked me with what is not God, and I will provoke them with what is not a people; I will stir them to anger against a foolish nation” (Deut. 32:31)—he despairs of Israel’s salvation and is shaken by great anguish. This breaks out into speech; he explains the reasons for his grief and, in a certain sense, says:

“I alone, chosen from so great a number of prophets, was the one who had to announce the ruin of my people through the salvation of others.”

He is therefore not grieved, as some think, because the multitude of the nations is saved, but because Israel perishes. Hence our Lord also wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19), and was unwilling to take the children’s bread and give it to the dogs (Mark 7). The apostles also preached first to Israel (Acts 13). And Paul desired to become anathema for his brothers, who are Israelites, whose are the adoption, the glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh (Rom. 9).

Beautifully, then, the one whose name means “grieving”—Jonah—is afflicted with grief, and his soul is sorrowful even unto death, because, insofar as it depended on him, he suffered many things so that the Jewish people would not perish.

The historical interpretation also suits the name of one who is grieving, signifying a laborious prophet weighed down by the miseries of travel and shipwreck.

#### Verses 2–3

I beseech you, Lord, is this not what I said while I was still in my own land? This is why I hastened to flee to Tarshish. For I know that you are a gracious and merciful God [the Vulgate adds “you are”], patient and of great mercy, forgiving evil; and now, Lord, please take my life from me, for death is better for me than life.

The Septuagint: “O Lord, are these not my words while I was still in my own land? Therefore I hastened to flee to Tarshish. For I know that you are merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy, and repenting concerning evils; and now, sovereign Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”

What we translated as “I beseech you,” and what the Septuagint rendered as “O indeed” (ὦ δὴ), is written in Hebrew as *ANNA* (Hebrew not legible in the supplied text). It seems to me to be an interjection of one who supplicates, expressing a conciliatory feeling. Since his prayer, in saying that he had justly wished to flee, in a certain sense accuses the Lord of injustice, he tempers his complaint by beginning with an entreaty.

“Is this not,” he says, “what I said while I was still in my own land? I knew that you would do this. I was not ignorant that you were merciful; therefore I did not wish to announce you as severe and savage. For this reason I wished to flee to Tarshish, to devote myself to contemplation, and to enjoy quiet and leisure on the sea of this world.

“I left my house, abandoned my inheritance, went out from your bosom, and came here. If I proclaimed you merciful, gracious, and forgiving of evil, no one would repent. If I announced you as cruel and merely a judge [another reading: “judgment”], I knew that this was not your nature. Placed, therefore, in this uncertainty, I preferred to flee rather than either deceive penitents through leniency or preach of you what you were not.

“Take my life, therefore, Lord, for death is better for me than life. Take my life, which was sorrowful even unto death. Take my life: ‘For into your hands I commend my spirit’ (Luke 15). Death is better for me than life. While alive I could not save one nation, Israel; let me die, and the world will be saved.” [Note: The three following verses, omitted by Victorius because he was misled by the recurrence of the same word *animam* (“life” or “soul”), are supplied by our manuscripts.]

The historical meaning is clear, and concerning the person of the prophet it can be understood as we have often said: he is grieved and wishes to die because, if the multitude of the nations is converted, Israel will perish forever. 424

#### Verse 4

And the Lord said: “Do you think that you are right to be angry?”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord said to Jonah: ‘If you are greatly grieved, are you?’” [Note: The Palatine manuscripts supply the missing particle, in agreement also with the Greek text, εἰ σφόδρα λελύπησαι σύ.]

The Hebrew word *ARA LAC* (Hebrew not legible in the supplied text), “you are angry” or “you are grieved,” can be translated in either way. Both meanings suit the person of the prophet and that of the Lord: he may be angry lest he appear to have lied to the Ninevites, or grieved because he understands that Israel is going to perish.

Reasonably, he does not say to him, “You are wrong to be angry” or “You are wrong to be grieved,” lest he seem to rebuke one who is grieving. Nor does he say, “You are right to be angry” or “You are right to be grieved,” lest he contradict his own judgment. [Note: The whole passage of these words had been omitted in the previously published books because its wording seemed to contradict the author’s position. Yet anyone attentive to the complete structure of the sentence will see that he questions the very one who is angry and grieved, especially because of the repeated occurrence of the word “grieved,” an omission frequently caused by scribal error. Since it was also absent from the books published up to now, we have supplied it according to the Palatine manuscripts and restored the passage to its original integrity.]

Rather, he questions the one who is angry and grieved, so that he may either state the reasons for his anger or explain his sorrow; or, if he remains silent, the true judgment of God may be confirmed by his silence.

#### Verse 5

And Jonah went out from the city and sat opposite the city, toward the east. He made himself a shelter there and sat beneath it in the shade, until he might see what would happen to the city.

The Septuagint likewise. [Note: The Septuagint’s words are supplied by our manuscripts, as so often elsewhere.]

The first fratricide and murderer, Cain, who dedicated the bloodstained world to the blood of his brother, built a city and called it by the name of his son [Note: Our manuscripts prefer *Cainan* to *Enoch*] Enoch (Gen. 4). Hence the prophet Hosea also says: “I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst; I will not enter the city” (Hos. 11:9). For, as the Psalmist says, “The exits of death belong to the Lord” (Ps. 67).

Therefore one of the cities of refuge is called Ramoth (Hebrew not legible in the supplied text), which is interpreted as “vision of death.” And rightly, whoever is a fugitive and, because of his sins, does not deserve to dwell in Jerusalem lives in the city of death, and it is beyond the streams of the Jordan, whose name expresses descent.

The dove, or the grieving one, therefore goes out from such a city and dwells opposite the east, where the sun rises. He is there in his shelter, contemplating all the passing times and awaiting what will happen to the city mentioned above: before Nineveh was saved and the gourd withered [another reading: “grew”]; before the Gospel of Christ shone forth and the prophecy of Zechariah was fulfilled: “Behold, the man whose name is East” (Zech. 6:12). Jonah was beneath the shelter.

For the truth had not yet come, concerning which the same evangelist and apostle speaks: “God is truth” (1 John 4:8). Elegantly it is added: “And he made himself a shelter there,” beside Nineveh. He made it for himself, for at that time no one from the Ninevites could dwell with the prophet. And he sat in the shade, either in the posture of a judge, or drawn together from his majesty and girded about the loins with strength, so that his garments would not fall all the way to his feet and to us who are below, but would be gathered about him by a tighter [another reading: “higher”] belt.

As for the statement “until he might see what would happen to the city,” Scripture uses its customary manner of joining human emotions to God.

(Vers. 6.) “And the Lord God prepared an ivy plant, and it grew up over Jonah’s head, to be a shade over his head and to protect him, for he had labored; and Jonah rejoiced over the ivy with great joy.”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord commanded a gourd, and it grew up over Jonah’s head, to be a shelter over his head and to protect him from his troubles; and Jonah rejoiced over the gourd with great gladness.”

At this point a certain Cantherus, of the very ancient family of the Cornelii—or, as he himself boasts, descended from the stock of Asinius Pollio—is said long ago to have accused me at Rome of sacrilege, because I translated “ivy” instead of “gourd.”

[Note: There are many corruptions of names and words in this passage, both in printed editions and in manuscript books. The printed editions read *Cantelius de*, etc.; the manuscripts, *Cornelius de*, etc.; one manuscript from Saint-Germain has *Cancherior de*, etc.; while others preserve what I think is the true reading, *Cantherus de*, etc. For Jerome here mocks a man who had formerly accused the holy Doctor at Rome of sacrilege because he had translated “ivy” for “gourd.” This accusation suits the proverbial expression *Canterius in porta*, or *Cantherius in fossa*—“a gelding at the gate,” or “a gelding in the ditch”—since that Cornelius was being dragged into a business in which he was entirely unable to contend with Jerome. Thus the name *Cantelius* was fabricated by the early editors; *Cantherius*, however, is not the proper name of the reviler but a word used by the mocker. This Cantherius may perhaps have been called Aemilius by his proper name, as may be inferred from the following words, where, instead of *Cornelii*, they are called “Aemilii,” and so forth. MART.

—The Palatine manuscripts have *Canterius*; others, *Cantelius*. Jerome’s letter 112 to Augustine, section 22, should also be compared, together with what we observe there.]

He was evidently afraid that, if ivy grew instead of gourds, he would no longer have anything from which to drink secretly and in darkness. And indeed, upon the very gourd-shaped vessels commonly called *saucomariae*, images of the apostles are customarily depicted; from these he too assumed for himself a name that was not his own.

[Note: Other manuscripts have *solet*, “usually,” and shortly afterward *adumbrari*, “to be shaded.”]

If names can be so readily exchanged that, instead of the seditious tribunes called Cornelii, consuls called Aemilii may be introduced, I am surprised that I should not be permitted to translate “ivy” instead of “gourd.”

[Note: All the manuscript codices read *pro quo*; Erasmus and Marianus, on their own authority, read *seria*. MART.

—On the authority of the manuscripts, and compelled by the very sense of the passage, we have restored *seria*, “serious matters,” in place of it; Martianus, however, relying on certainly corrupt books, wrote *seriem*.]

But let us come to serious matters. In Hebrew, instead of “gourd” or “ivy,” we read **CICEION** (), which is also called **CICEIA** in the Syriac and Punic languages.

[Note: From this word one may understand the rashness of the old editions, which retain, in Erasmus and Marianus, not Jerome’s genuine reading *CICEIA*, but the fabricated word *Elkeroa*. John Conon, who undertook to supply Hebrew words in Erasmus’s edition, apparently thought that the Punic language was identical with Arabic. Since he knew that the Hebrew *CICEION* was *alcerva*, or the *Elkeroa* of the Arabs of his own day, he dared—against all Jerome’s manuscript copies—to substitute *Elkeroa* incorrectly for *CICEIA*. From this false edition there spread a very serious error in Jerome’s explanation of Jonah, so much so that it entered even the excellent Pentaglot Lexicon of Valentin Schindler Oederanus. Under the root *cic* he cites the false reading of Erasmus’s edition and then adds: “The Punic language is the same as Arabic; it is not the time to discuss that matter. But the reader should be informed that in one manuscript of Saint-Germain *CICAESA* is written instead of *CICEIA*. If this were the genuine reading, it would have the Hebrew root *Cissa*, that is, ‘cucumber.’ Hence Jerome says below: ‘And let us say that, since we do not find the gourd elsewhere in Scripture, wherever the cucumber grows, there the gourd too is accustomed to grow.’ But the reading *Ciceia* appears more correct; in Greek it is **κίκι** (*kiki*), and in Latin, *ricinus*, “castor-oil plant.” MART.

—Our manuscripts have *Siceia*; Erasmus and Victorius have *Elkeroa* incorrectly. In the aforementioned letter of Jerome to Augustine it is said that *Ciceion* is written in the Hebrew volume, which the Syrians commonly call *Ciceia*. Recall what we noted on that passage, as well as Reinesius, *On the Punic Language*, chapter 13. Shortly afterward, the words *suo trunco se* (“supporting itself by its own trunk”) are absent from our manuscripts.]

It is a kind of shrub, or small tree, with broad leaves shaped like those of a vine, and with very dense shade; it supports itself by its own trunk. It grows especially abundantly in Palestine, and most of all in sandy places. In a remarkable way, if one casts its seed into the ground, it quickly rises as a tree; and within a few days one looks upon a small tree where previously one had seen only grass.

Therefore, at the same time when we were interpreting the prophets, we wished to express this very Hebrew name, because the Latin language had no word for this species of tree. But we feared the grammarians, lest they should find an opportunity for inventing explanations and fabricate either Indian beasts, or the mountains of Boeotia, or some other such monstrosities. We followed the ancient translators, who likewise translated it as “ivy,” which in Greek is called **κισσός** (*kissos*), since they had no other word to use.

Let us therefore examine the historical sense, and before considering mystical interpretations, let us discuss the literal meaning alone. Gourd and ivy are of such a nature that they creep along the ground and, without forks or supports against which they can lean, do not reach upward. How then could the gourd, rising in a single night without the prophet’s knowledge, provide a shelter, when by nature it cannot rise on high without trellises, reeds, or poles?

But the *Ciceion*, while suddenly producing a miracle at its growth and displaying God’s power in the protection afforded by the leafy shelter, also followed its own natural character. With reference to the person of the Lord and Savior, however, let us not abandon the gourd entirely because of our **φιλοκολύκυνθος**—our “love of gourds”—but let it be understood in this way, so that we may recall Isaiah’s words: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber field, like a city that is being besieged” (Isa. VIII).

And let us say that, since we do not find the gourd elsewhere in Scripture, wherever the cucumber grows, there the gourd too is accustomed to grow. Israel was compared with this species, because it once protected Jonah beneath its shade while he awaited the conversion of the nations, and gave him no small joy by making a shelter and tabernacle for him—rather a tent than a house, having the appearance of a roof but lacking the foundations of a house.

Moreover, our *CICEION*, a modest shrub that rises quickly and quickly withers, may in its order and life—or, as some read, “way”—be compared with Israel, which sends small roots into the earth and indeed strives to rise toward lofty places, but does not attain the height of God’s cedars and fir trees.

The locusts seem to signify the same thing: John ate them, and under the figure of Israel he says, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John III, 30). The locust is a small animal with weak wings; it rises from the earth but cannot fly very high, so that it is more than a creeping creature and yet does not equal the birds.

(Vers. 7 and 8.) “And the Lord prepared a worm at the rising of dawn on the following day, and it struck the ivy, and it withered. And when the sun had risen, the Lord commanded a hot and burning wind; and the sun struck Jonah’s head, and he was overcome by the heat. And he asked for his soul that he might die, and said: ‘It is better for me to die than to live.’”

The Septuagint: “And God commanded a worm in the morning on the following day, and it struck the gourd, and it dried up. And immediately when the sun had risen, the Lord commanded a burning, scorching wind; and the sun struck Jonah’s head, and he was distressed, and he became weary of his life, and said: ‘It is better for me to die than to live.’”

Before the Sun of righteousness rose, the shelter was green, and Israel did not wither. After he arose, and the darkness of Nineveh was dispelled by his light, a worm was prepared at the rising of dawn on the following day. Concerning this worm the twenty-first psalm is entitled, “For the taking-up of the morning”; it arises from the earth without any seed and says, “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI, 7). It struck the shelter, which, abandoned by God’s protection, lost all its greenness.

And the Lord commanded a hot and burning wind, of which it is prophesied in Hosea: “The Lord will bring a scorching wind rising from the desert; he will dry up its veins and make its spring desolate” (Hos. XIII, 15). Jonah began to be overcome by the heat and once again desired to die in baptism with Israel, so that in the washing he might receive the moisture which he had lost through denial.

Hence Peter also speaks to the parched Jews: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts II, 38).

Some understand the worm and the burning wind as Roman commanders, who, after Christ’s resurrection, completely destroyed Israel.

428 (Vers. 9.) “And the Lord said to Jonah: ‘Do you think that you are right to be angry over the ivy?’ And he said: ‘I am right to be angry, even unto death.’”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord God said to Jonah: ‘Are you exceedingly grieved over the gourd?’ And he said: ‘I am exceedingly grieved, even unto death.’”

[Note: Two manuscripts have *si valde*, in accordance with the Greek, apart from the Aldine edition and one copy, which have **εἰ σφόδρα**, “if exceedingly.”]

Earlier, when the Ninevites were doing penance and the city of the nations was saved, the prophet was asked the same question: “Do you think that you are right to be angry?” He answered nothing, but confirmed God’s question by his silence. For since he knew that God is gentle, merciful, patient, rich in compassion, and forgiving of evil, he did not grieve over the salvation of the nations.

Here, however, after the gourd had dried up and Israel had withered, when he was expressly asked, “Are you right to be angry over the ivy?” he confidently answered and said: “I am right to be angry,” or “to be grieved, even unto death.” For I did not wish to save some in such a way that others should perish; nor did I wish to win strangers in such a way that I should lose my own.

And truly, to the present day Christ mourns over Israel; and Jerusalem mourns even unto death—not his own death, but that of the Jews—so that those who deny may die, and those who confess the Son of God may rise again.

(Vers. 10 and 11.) “And the Lord said: ‘You grieve over the ivy, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow; it was born in a single night and perished in a single night. And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand human beings who do not know what is between their right hand and their left, and many beasts?’”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord said: ‘You spared the gourd, for which you did not labor, nor did you nourish it; it was born in the night and perished in the night. But shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than twelve myriads”—or, as some read, “thousands”—“of men who do not know their right hand from their left, and many cattle?’”

It is exceedingly difficult to explain, according to the allegorical sense, how this is said to the Son: “You grieve over the ivy, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow,” when all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John I, 3).

For this reason, someone who interpreted this passage and wished to resolve the difficulty that seemed to threaten him fell into blasphemy. Taking the Gospel saying, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God” (Mark X, 18), he interpreted the Father as “the Good,” while placing the Son at a lower level in comparison with the one who is perfectly and truly good.

429 In saying this, he did not consider that he had fallen rather into the heresy of Marcion—who introduces one God as entirely good and another as judge and creator—than into that of Arius. For although Arius proclaims the Father greater and the Son lesser, he nevertheless does not deny that the Son is the Creator.

Therefore, what we are about to say must be heard with indulgence, and our efforts must be encouraged by goodwill and prayers rather than scorned with a hostile ear. The ignorant can carp and disparage; but it belongs to learned people, and to those who know the sweat of laborers, either to extend a hand to the weary or to show the way to those who have gone astray.

[Note: From five Florentine manuscripts, as well as an equal number from Brescia and several Roman codices, Victorius restores: “our efforts ought rather to be encouraged and assisted by prayers”; formerly the reading was “to be heard and assisted by prayers.”]

Our Lord and Savior did not labor over Israel in the way that he labored over the people of the nations. Indeed, Israel speaks confidently: “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment; yet you have never given me a young goat, so that I might feast with my friends. But when this son of yours, who has devoured his substance with prostitutes, came, you killed for him the fattened calf” (Luke XV).

Yet the father does not refute him; rather, he says to him gently: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was necessary to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

For the people of the nations the fattened calf was sacrificed, and precious blood was poured out—concerning this Paul discusses the matter fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb. X). And David says in the psalm: “A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem” (Ps. XLVIII, 8).

430 Christ decreed that the one should increase; the other died so that the one might live. The latter descended to the underworld so that the former might ascend to heaven.

There was no labor of such magnitude in Israel. Hence the elder brother envies the younger, because after he has squandered his substance with prostitutes and pimps, he receives a ring and a robe and shines with his former dignity.

[Note: Martianus reads this with a faulty transposition after *quod*.]

When it says, “which was born in a single night,” it signifies the time before Christ’s coming, who was the light of the world. Of him it is said: “The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII, 12).

“And in a single night it perished,” when the Sun of righteousness set for them and they lost the word of God.

The great and beautiful city of Nineveh prefigures the Church, in which the number is greater than that of the ten—or, as some read, twelve—tribes of Israel. This is also signified by the fragments in the wilderness, namely the twelve baskets (Mark VI).

They do not know what is between the right hand and the left, either because of innocence and simplicity, so that an infant age may be indicated, leaving it to the understanding to determine how great the number of the other age must be when there are so many little ones; or certainly because, since it was a great city, and in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay (2 Tim. II), there was in it a very large multitude that, before doing penance, did not know what lay between good and evil, between the right hand and the left.

And there were also many beasts. For the number of beasts and irrational people in Nineveh is great—people who are compared to foolish beasts and made like them (Ps. XLVIII).

[Col. 1151]

## Two Books of Commentaries by Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, on the Prophet Micah. (C)

### Prologue

[Note: It is inscribed to the **φιλοπονώτατοι**—“most devoted to labor”—Paula and her daughter Eustochium, as is learned from the preface to the third book of the *Commentaries on Amos*.]

431–432 Micah, on whom I now wish to dictate commentaries, is, according to the Septuagint interpreters, third in the order of the twelve prophets; according to the Hebrew—or, as some read, according to the Hebrew truth—he is sixth. He follows the prophet Jonah, who comes after Obadiah, and thus Amos is third, while Joel is second after Hosea, who is first among all of them.

Therefore, since he has been placed, as it were, in the heart of the scroll, he ought to contain profound mysteries. The word of God, which always descends to the prophets, descended also to Micah (), whose name means “humility”: to Micah of Morasthi, which even today, near the city of Eleutheropolis in Palestine, is a small village.

Morasthi (), however, means “heir” in our language. Thus beautifully does humility—which among the virtues is perhaps the foremost—arise from the hope of the Lord’s inheritance.

Humility here is not that which proceeds from awareness of sins, but that which is counted among the virtues, in accordance with the saying: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (1 Pet. V, 6). And: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII, 14). And: “Before destruction a man’s heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. XVI, 18). Hence the Lord also says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

How, then, among us are names adopted as vows and as though in anticipation of a virtue—for example, Victor, Chaste, Pious, Upright—and among the Greeks one is called **σώφρων** (“self-controlled”) or **εὐσεβής** (“devout”), with appellative names turned into personal names; so among the Hebrews Micah, Obadiah, Zechariah, and others of this kind are bestowed by parents upon their children from the names of virtues.

## Book One

[Col. 1153]

[Cap. I—Vers. 1.] 433 “The word of the Lord that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.”

Or, according to the Septuagint: “The word of the Lord that came to Micah concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.”

The word of the Lord therefore came to Micah after Hosea, Amos, and Isaiah, who prophesied under Uzziah. From this we understand that Micah did not prophesy in the time of Uzziah, but in the days of his son Jotham. After Jotham, Ahaz reigned; Hezekiah then succeeded his father Ahaz, under whom the ten tribes were led away captive by the Assyrians (2 Kings XVIII).

Thus, as far as history is concerned and according to the order of the captivity—for Samaria, the capital of Israel, was captured first, and Jerusalem, the city of Judah, afterward—the title of the prophecy first concerns Samaria and second Jerusalem.

As for the mystical interpretations, since Samaria is always understood in relation to heresies and Jerusalem in relation to the Church, we say that the word of the Lord comes to the humble—or, as some read, to Jerusalem—and to Christ’s co-heir concerning perverse doctrines and concerning the Church, if perhaps it has committed sins, and that it establishes the order of the entire book.

That Samaria and the ten tribes, which were split from the house of David under King Jeroboam (1 Kings XII), are understood as representing heretics is attested by all Scripture, but especially by the prophet Hosea and by this very book, which calls heretics impious and members of the Church sinners.

For immediately it continues: “What is the impiety of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of the house of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?” This is according to the Septuagint translators. But how it is read in Hebrew we shall set forth shortly.

The fact that heretics always trust in what they regard as the exaltation of their doctrines and despise the simplicity of the Church is also expressed elsewhere: “Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria” (Amos VI, 1). For “the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II, 3).

Moreover, Samaria made golden calves for herself from her own understanding. They possessed beauty on the surface, but not the life-giving Spirit. She made them in the house of God, which is interpreted as Bethel. For the people of Israel could not receive gods unless they were made from the Scriptures and in the house of God.

Although they call their assemblies Bethel, after the manufacture of the idols Bethel ceased to be Bethel and is called Beth-aven, which means “house of an idol.” For this the Septuagint translated “house of On.”

This is enough concerning the title. Let us now come to the beginning of the prophecy, and while the Lernaean beast—the Hydra—is raging, let us invoke the coming of the Holy Spirit. You, Paula and Eustochium, pour out prayers to the Lord and Savior, so that envy may not harm me, but that my mind, freed from distraction, may think only about what it strives to explain and may not feel the blows of insults which the Lord despised in his Passion (Mark XIV; John XVI, XVIII).

(Vers. 2.) “Hear, all you peoples, and let the earth and its fullness attend; and let the Lord God be a witness to you, the Lord from his holy temple.”

The Septuagint: “Hear, all you peoples, and let the earth listen, and all who are in it; and let the Lord God be a testimony to you, the Lord from his holy house.”

[Note: Our manuscripts omit the final words, “the Lord from his holy temple,” and likewise at the Septuagint passage, “the Lord from his holy house.”]

Since the historical sense is clear, I leave its understanding to the reader’s judgment. According to the allegorical sense, however, he summons peoples to hear—that is, the Churches of the whole world—and the earth to listen, because earthly doctrines of heretics have been constructed in it.

That heresies are counted among the works of the flesh, which is always referred to the earth, the Apostle does not conceal in his Epistle to the Galatians (Gal. V). The Lord also indicates this plainly in the Gospel to the attentive hearer: “He who is of the earth is earthly and speaks of the earth.”

And in distinction from them he says again concerning those who belong to the Church: “He who comes from heaven is above all” (John III, 31). And: “What he has seen and heard, this he testifies.”

But if the words “Hear, all you peoples,” because of the Lord’s saying, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII, 8), convey something more than the words that follow, “Let the earth attend,” we shall apply “Hear, all you peoples” to the Church.

But to heretics who have adopted an earthly doctrine: “Let the earth attend, and all who are in it.” Thus, if the former hear and the latter attend, they will not suffer the things which the word of the Lord subsequently threatens.

“And let the Lord be a testimony to them”—or, as it is read in Hebrew, “a witness,” or, as Symmachus translated more explicitly, “testifying.” And he testifies from nowhere other than his own house, which is the Church; or certainly in the Son, that is, in our Lord Jesus Christ, who truly is the Father’s temple. From his mouth the Father speaks, penetrating the inward parts and marrow of those who are willing to attend and hear.

(Vers. 3 and following.) “For behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and he will descend and tread upon the heights of the earth; and the mountains beneath him will be consumed, and the valleys will be split like wax before fire, like waters pouring down a steep place. All this is for the transgression of Jacob and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what are the high places of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?”

The Septuagint: “For behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and he will descend and ascend upon the heights of the earth; and the mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire and like flowing water descending downward. All these things are because of the impiety of Jacob and because of the sin of the house of Israel. What is the impiety of the house of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of the house of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?”

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts have “What is the impiety of Jacob?” Most of the Greek copies likewise lack the word “house.”]

O Samaria and Jerusalem, hear and carefully attend to the Lord, who testifies to you from his temple and proclaims all that he is going to do.

“Behold, the Lord will go forth from his place.” He who is gentle and kind, whose nature is mercy, is compelled for your sake to assume the role of cruelty, which he does not possess.

“And he will descend and tread upon the heights of the earth.” God’s descent is the movement of his majesty toward lower things: to tread upon the earth and crush all the powerful.

“And the mountains,” he says, “will be consumed,” or “will melt,” and the valleys beneath him—by the mountains we should understand rulers, and by the valleys, peoples.

Just as wax cannot withstand the nearness of fire, and as waters are carried downward in a headlong course, so all the pride of the impious will be dissolved and flow away when the Lord comes.

All this will happen because of the crimes of the ten tribes, which he calls Jacob and Israel, and because of Judah’s transgression. For Samaria was the capital of the ten tribes, while in the kingdom of Judah Jerusalem built the idols of the high places. This is the literal sense.

According to the allegorical sense, however, the Lord will go forth from his place, which we may understand either as the Son or as all the saints. The Son himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10). And concerning the saints: “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Lev. XXVI, 12).

From these, therefore, he will go forth—not because he abandons them. The word of the Lord went forth from the apostles to their hearers, yet he did not abandon the apostles. Places of this kind—that is, those worthy to have God as their guest—are set on high, as though rising with Christ and seated with him in the heavenly places.

Hence he is said to descend to those who cannot hear his teaching on the mountain. And when he has descended, he will not ascend among the humble and those placed below, but among those who are called the heights of the earth, who, understanding the majesty of the coming Lord, will be shaken.

And although they are mountains, they will tremble at the presence of such a charioteer and rider.

The valleys, however—that is, souls inserted into earthly bodies, **χοϊκοῖς** [“earthly”], and not rising with the heavenly man—will not be able to endure his presence. Whatever is hard in them will be dissolved, and they will flow as waters do when they have no level course and are carried headlong into the depths.

The Lord will therefore come in terror to teach: to shake the mountains and dissolve the low places of the valleys, because Jacob has committed impiety and Israel has sinned.

The impiety of Jacob consists in the assemblies of heretics, which are called Samaria. The sin of Judah—that is, of the one who confesses the Lord—is none other than Jerusalem, in which many crimes are found.

That the house of Judah refers to Christ, whose Church it is, we have often said; let us now add this passage: “Judah, your brothers will praise you; your hand will be upon the neck of your enemies” (Gen. XLIX, 8).

It may also be understood in this way: because of the impieties of Samaria and the crimes of Judah, the Lord went forth from his former place and said to the Jews: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 38; Luke XIII, 35).

He descended from the heavens and ascended upon the heights of the earth—that is, upon those who, believing through the humility of the nations, were found worthy to become exalted.

The mountains were shaken: the doctrines of philosophers, exalted kingdoms, and those who remained humble were consumed and crushed by the Savior’s coming. As the Church increased and the mountains rose on high, the idols fell into the depths.

The Lord therefore went forth from his place, and a Church was built from the nations, so that the mountains might be shaken beneath his feet and the depths of the valleys dissolved, because Jacob acted impiously, Israel sinned, and all the tribes denied the Lord.

### (Verse 6 and following)

“And I shall make Samaria like a heap of stones in a field when a vineyard is planted; I shall drag her stones down into the valley, and I shall uncover her foundations. All her carved images shall be cut down, and all her wages shall be burned with fire; all her idols I shall consign to destruction, because they were gathered from the wages of a prostitute, and they shall return to the wages of a prostitute. Because of this I shall mourn and howl; I shall go stripped and naked; I shall make mourning like that of dragons and lamentation like that of ostriches, because her wound is incurable, because it has reached Judah and touched the gate of my people, even Jerusalem.”

The Septuagint: “And I shall make Samaria a place for guarding fruit in a field, and a plantation of a vineyard; I shall drag her stones into a ravine, and I shall uncover her foundations. All her carved images shall be cut down, and all her wages shall be burned with fire; I shall consign all her idols to destruction, because she gathered them from the wages of fornication, and from the wages of fornication she destroyed them. Therefore she shall mourn and lament; she shall go barefoot and naked; she shall make mourning like that of dragons and lamentation like that of the daughters of Sirens, because her wound has prevailed, because it has reached Judah and touched as far as the gate of my people, even Jerusalem.”

According to the order of sins, the order of punishments follows. Samaria sinned first: she made idols and worshiped calves instead of the Lord. Therefore she shall be the first to perish. I shall destroy her when the Assyrians come, and I shall make her like a heap of stones when a vineyard is planted, so that she may be reduced to mounds: “I shall drag her stones into the valley.” For she was situated in the mountains, where Sebaste now stands, in which the bones of Saint John the Baptist are also buried.

“And I shall uncover her foundations.” Such will be the ruin and such the overthrow of the city that not only will the walls and buildings collapse, but the foundations too will be uncovered down to the last stone. “All her carved images”—and all the riches that different kings had brought into her—shall be cut down, burned with fire, and reduced to nothing. For the wealth and varied furnishings that had been gathered from the supposed fornication of idols shall be carried to another prostitute, that is, to Nineveh. Just as they fornicated with the idols they had made in their own land, so they shall go to another land of idols and fornication, namely, to the Assyrians.

Thus far concerning Samaria. Since the same wound was to reach Jerusalem—for she too sinned through a similar error, abandoning her God and making idols—the prophet presents, as it were, a προσωποποιία [prosopopoeia, personification] of God and introduces, in his own person, the emotion of one who mourns. He says: “Because of this I shall mourn and howl; I shall go stripped and naked”—for I have lost the ten tribes—“and I shall make mourning like that of dragons and lamentation like that of ostriches.”

For just as dragons, according to the accounts of those who have written on natural science, resound with a terrible hiss at the time when they are conquered by elephants; and just as ostriches, forgetful of their eggs and as though they had not given birth, leave their offspring in the sand to be trampled under the feet of beasts (Job 39), about which more is written in Job—so I too shall walk stripped and naked, without children. I shall do this because her wound, that is, Samaria’s wound, is incurable. The same sin—or rather, the same punishment for sin—that overthrew Samaria shall reach Judah and the gate of my city, Jerusalem. For just as Samaria was overthrown by the Assyrians, so Judah and Jerusalem shall be overthrown by the Chaldeans.

Since we have understood Samaria once as the Church of heretics, which, having separated from God, became an assembly of the people, the Lord himself threatens that he will make her a place for guarding fruit, a field, and a plantation of vines. It is much better for an unprofitable city to be overthrown, for the stones with which it was built to be dragged headlong, and for it to be prepared as an orchard and vineyard, than for it to remain in a most evil construction.

When it has been destroyed and its foundations have been uncovered—foundations by which it seemed to conceal its mysteries and to possess firm doctrines on which it stood—and when all its idols, which seemed to possess an appearance and beauty fashioned by skillful speech, have been cut down by the ministers of God, that is, by ecclesiastical men, then, in place of the most evil building, various fruits of the Church shall grow. They shall not merely grow; they shall also be guarded. A vine of Sorek shall be planted, from which wine may be made—the wine that the Lord promised he would drink in the kingdom of the Father (Mark 14).

Not only shall its foundations, formerly pressed down beneath the earth, be opened and brought into the midst, and the idols they had fashioned for themselves be cut down; but its glory and riches, which it seemed to possess through fornication and through its error, shall also be consumed by my fire, concerning which I said in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled” (Luke 12:49). They shall be burned and reduced to nothing, because they were not acquired from the truth of doctrines, but gathered here and there from the fornication of the soul and from error.

Heretics do not possess riches that come from a paternal inheritance. Rather, each day they discover something to worship, and they fashion idols for themselves with skillful hands and a curious mind. Therefore, when their field has been turned into a place for guarding fruit and prepared for vineyards; when the stones with which the city had been built have been dragged into the depths; when their foundations have been uncovered; when all their carved images have been cut down and burned; and when the wages they had promised themselves in their vain hope, and everything they seemed to worship as God, has been reduced to nothing—for they had acquired all their price from the fornication of the soul—then, recognizing their former error, they shall return to themselves. They shall mourn over what they had formerly laughed at and lament over what, while committing fornication, they had in some fashion rejoiced in.

They shall remove from their feet whatever deadly thing they had possessed, and they shall be barefoot, because the earth on which they are to stand is a holy place. They shall cast away all the garments of their fornication and shall be naked, so that they may be clothed with Christ’s garment. They shall make mourning like that of dragons. For dragons too shall one day mourn when they see the great dragon captured and hanging on the fisherman’s hook, and the sea desolated.

They shall lament like the daughters of Sirens, for the songs of heretics are sweet and deceive peoples with a pleasant voice. Their songs cannot be passed by anyone who has not stopped his ears and become, as it were, deaf. Therefore this Samaria shall mourn and lament, because, wounded by the Lord’s arrow and receiving the wound of his word, she shall recognize her error.

Nor did she sin by herself alone: she also wished to introduce her iniquity and error through the gates of Judah. Hence it is said of her: “It has reached Judah and touched as far as the gates of my people, even Jerusalem.” He says that she touched the gates, by which we understand the ears. She could not enter the middle of the city; for if she had entered, she would have made Jerusalem into Samaria.

Whenever we see some members of the Church scandalized by the speeches of heretics, asking how they should answer their questions but nevertheless not withdrawing from the Church, let us say: Samaria—or Samaria’s wound—has come as far as the confessing people, as far as the ears of God’s people, as far as the ears of Jerusalem. This statement, “It touched as far as the gates of my people,” is to be understood ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [from a common construction], with the words “it touched as far as the gates of Jerusalem” also understood.

Thus far against Samaria and Jerusalem. Let us examine the other things that follow.

### (Verse 10 and following)

“In Gath do not announce it; do not weep with tears. In the house of dust sprinkle yourselves with dust. Pass over for yourselves, O habitation of Saphir [the Vulgate: ‘beautiful’], confounded with disgrace. She who dwells in Sennan has not gone out [the Vulgate: ‘at the exit’]. The house of Asel [the Vulgate: ‘neighboring’] shall receive mourning from you—the one that stood by itself, because she who dwells in Maroth [the Vulgate: ‘bitternesses’] has been weakened in what is good—for evil has descended from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem. The tumult of the chariot is for the inhabitant of Lachish; she is the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion, because in you the crimes of Israel were found. Therefore she shall send messengers against the inheritance of Gath, houses of deceit, for the deception of the kings of Israel. I shall yet bring an heir to you, O inhabitant of Mareshah; the glory of Israel shall come as far as Adullam.”

The Septuagint: “Those who are in Gath, do not exalt yourselves; those who are in Bachim, do not build houses of derision. Sprinkle earth upon your derision, O you who dwell in her cities in prosperity; the inhabitant of Sennan has not gone out. Mourn for the house beside her; she shall receive from you the wound of pain. Who has taken possession for good, she who dwells in pains? For evils have descended from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem. The sound of chariots and horsemen is the habitation of Lachish; she is the ruler of sin for the daughter of Zion, because in you the iniquities of Israel were found. Therefore she shall send messengers as far as the inheritance of Gath, empty houses; they were in vain for the kings of Israel, until I bring heirs to you, O inhabitant of Lachish; the inheritance shall come as far as Adullam.”

The Hebrew differs greatly from the interpretation of the Septuagint, and both my translation and theirs are entangled in such difficulties that, if ever we have needed the Spirit of God—and we always need his coming when we explain the holy Scriptures—we now desire his presence especially, so that he may disclose what he spoke in the prophets. Thus it may also be understood of us what he graciously promises elsewhere: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11).

Gath, as the history of the Books of Kings also testifies (1 Kings 17), is one of the five cities of Palestine, near the border of Judea. For those traveling from Eleutheropolis to Gaza, it is now still a very large village. It was the home of that Goliath the Gittite whom David killed in battle.

Since, therefore, the prophet—or rather, the Lord through the prophet—had said: “I shall mourn and howl; I shall go stripped and naked; I shall make mourning like that of dragons and lamentation like that of ostriches, because Samaria’s wound is incurable and beyond healing, and it has reached Judah and touched the gate of my people, Jerusalem,” I therefore still command in the voice of one who mourns: “Do not announce it in Gath,” lest the enemies hear and rejoice. “Do not weep with tears,” that is, do not even allow your grief to burst into sobs. Conceal your weeping, lest your adversaries rejoice; let your faces have no tears, although your breast has grief. Do not go outside, but in the house of dust, while the ashes of the ruins are falling, sprinkle yourselves with them.

“Pass over for yourselves, O habitation of Saphir”—which in the Syriac and Hebrew language is called “beautiful.” Samaria is situated in a most beautiful and fertile region of Judea, as it is still shown today. Therefore it is said to her: “O you who dwell in a most fertile region, because you have been confounded with disgrace, pass over in such a way, be led into captivity in such a way, that because of the greatness of your evils not even a neighboring Philistine hears your voice.”

As for what follows—“She who dwells in Sennan has not gone out,” which is interpreted as “exit,” or, as Symmachus translated it, “the abundant habitation has not gone out”—this too is said of Samaria, which stands at the very entrance of Assyria and, as soon as it is moved from its borders, enters hostile territory. “Abundant habitation” should be understood according to what we said above, namely, “beautiful habitation.” Therefore she who dwells in the exit, or in abundance, did not go out of her own will, but was led by force to the Assyrians.

Hence the neighboring house at her side, which is interpreted as Asel, namely the kingdom of Judah, shall receive mourning from you. For now, while Samaria has been captured, Judah stands firm and has God as its defender. Yet it received mourning, was struck with fear, and was weakened in its prosperity—she who dwells in Maroth, or Ramoth, that is, “in bitternesses,” or, as Symmachus translated it, “the habitation that provokes bitterness,” that is, ἡ κατοικία ἡ παραπικραίνουσα [the habitation that provokes bitterness]. In Hebrew this is called יושבת מרות, *Yoshevet Maroth* [“she who dwells in Maroth”], because of the captivity of the neighboring tribes.

“For evil has descended from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem.” After the Assyrian had devastated Samaria, he also came to Jerusalem, at the time when Rabshakeh was sent to insult it. The Fourth Book of Kings (2 Kings 18) and Isaiah (Isaiah 36) write more fully about this. There it is said that the king of Assyria sent from Lachish against Jerusalem; afterward, when Lachish had been captured, he moved on to attack Libnah.

Therefore the chariot and horsemen of the Assyrians shall come to you, O Lachish, a city devoted to idols, because the crimes of Israel were found in you, and you were the beginning of idolatry in Judah. Through you, as through a gate, the impiety of the ten tribes migrated into Jerusalem.

Nor shall tumult and chariots come only upon Lachish; they shall also come upon Gath, the metropolis of Palestine, concerning which I said above: “In Gath do not announce it.” For the Assyrian shall send his raiders, whom he calls messengers, and shall take possession of the house of idolatry and the city of deceit, which served as a snare for the kings of Israel.

As for what follows—“I shall yet bring an heir to you, O inhabitant of Mareshah”—the prophet aptly alluded to the name.
