Since *Mareshah* means “inheritance,” he called the arrival of enemies there the arrival of heirs. The *Mareshah* that is, the inheritance, shall come as far as Adullam, a city of Judah, which is glorious among the cities of Israel.

Symmachus therefore translated it as follows:

> “I shall yet bring an heir, and for you, O habitation of Mareshah, the glory of Israel shall come as far as Adullam,”

that is, “you who are glorious among the cities of Israel.”

Where the text says “of glory,” the word is the genitive singular—“of this glory”—not the nominative plural—“these glories.”

Or let us understand it in this way: The captivity of Israel, which came to Lachish, Gath, and Mareshah, shall also come as far as Adullam. The expression “the glory of Israel” should be read more precisely so that, by κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν [antiphrasis], disgrace or devastation may be understood.

As for the fact that above we interpreted the name of the prophet of Moresheth as “inheritance,” let the reader know that in the same verse we cited—“Therefore she shall send messengers against the inheritance of Gath”—the Hebrew has, in place of “the inheritance of Gath,” *Morasheth-Gath* [variant: *Morassheth*].

Thus far, according to the Hebrew, as we were able and as it seemed to us—certainly as we heard it from the Hebrews—we have steered our little boat among rocks and sharp reefs. Whether it has entered the harbor or is still tossed on the open sea, it will be for the reader’s prudence to judge. Now, with your prayers, let us proceed to other waves and, with shipwreck threatening the exposition here and there, escape if we can.

Gath is interpreted as “winepress.” Those, therefore, who are in Gath, that is, in the winepress, thinking that they have harvested the fruit of life and trodden the grape from the vine of Sorek, are lifted up in pride, unaware that the grape of the land of Judea is not found within the borders of the Philistines.

“Do not,” he says, “be lifted up, you who are in the winepresses. For your vine is from the vine of Sodom, and your branch from Gomorrah; your grape is a grape of bitterness, and your cluster is a cluster of gall; the wine of your dragons is the fury of dragons, and the fury of asps is incurable.”

Even if you produce fruit—for your vintage comes not only from Sodom and Gomorrah, but also from Egypt and the other hostile nations—the Lord will give your fruit to rust, your labors to locusts; he will kill your vineyards with hail and your mulberry trees with frost. Let the likeness of wine not deceive you, and do not call what is bitter sweet. Taste your wine carefully, and you will find that, instead of the wine of Sorek, it is the fury of dragons and the poison of asps.

Therefore do not be proud, but humble yourselves under the mighty hand of the Lord and pass over to that winepress of which the one who ascends from Edom and is red from Bosra speaks through the prophet Isaiah: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me.”

Again, since there are other foreigners—for the province of the Philistines contains many regions and cities—who speak against God through evil works and contrary opinions, saying, “We have been destroyed, but let us return and build what has been destroyed,” they are therefore called the boundaries of impiety and the people with whom the Lord is angry.

It is said to them: “Those who are in Bachim, do not build from the house of derision.” *Bachim* in our language signifies mourning and weeping. Accordingly, except for the Septuagint, all translators rendered it κλαυθμός, that is, “weeping.”

You, therefore, who are involved in such works and opinions—things worthy of weeping—do not restore your most evil building. Do not think your own opinion to be God’s construction, and do not build upon sand (Matthew 7), lest, when the storm comes and your house collapses, your vain labor give laughter to those who see it.

Rather, recognizing that your building deserves derision, sprinkle your heads with its ruins and dust, and do penance because you wished to build, without counsel, a house destined to fall.

The text continues: “She who dwells prosperously in her cities has not gone out, she who dwells in Sennan.”

This seems to me to have the following sense: You who are proud in Gath and in Bachim, who vainly attempt to build a house worthy of laughter, sprinkle yourselves with dust and do penance, because you wished to press detestable wine and construct a building contrary to God.

But the Church of Christ, which dwells prosperously and possesses Churches throughout the whole world, is joined by the unity of the Spirit. It possesses the cities of the Law, the prophets, the Gospel, and the apostles. It has not gone out from its boundaries, that is, from the holy Scriptures, but retains the possession it began, because it dwells in Sennan, which, as we said above, Symmachus interpreted as “abundance.” For it possesses the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, together with whom are all the riches of spiritual graces and virtues. Hence it is said to her: “Let there be peace within your strength and abundance in your towers” (Psalm 121:7).

But you who dwell beside Sennan, that is, beside the abundant Church—O heretics, O contrary doctrines—mourn for yourselves. You have built a house for yourselves in derision and pressed the winepress in pride. You have built your house not in the Scriptures but in the neighborhood of the Scriptures, a house now worthy not of laughter but of mourning and tears.

Hence it follows: “Mourn for the house that is beside her,” that is, beside Sennan. The added words—“she shall receive from you the wound of pain”—are also spoken to the same heretics. They are commanded to mourn the house near the Church, because the enemy and avenging devil, to whom they will be handed over for punishment, will himself inflict wounds upon them and exact from them the pain of wounds in return for their most evil building.

These wounds are inflicted so that, recognizing the sins they committed, they may do penance and so that the habitation of pains may become for them an occasion of good. Or else the statement is addressed to the Church, which mourns her former children and herself becomes the cause of the heretics’ salvation if they wish to return to their grieving mother.

As for what follows—“For evils have descended from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem”—Marcionites and Manichaeans also use this passage, on the grounds that the God of the Law is the creator of evils.

Let us say that evils descended from the Lord in the same way that the Savior speaks in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Just as Lucifer, who rose in the morning, fell there from heaven (Isaiah 14) and was crushed upon the earth, he who was being sent to the nations, so these evils that fell from the Lord and came to the gates of Jerusalem were not evils before they fell. But because they fell from the Lord, they became evils.

And so that we may understand the ambushes of evils: “They came,” he says, “to the gates of Jerusalem.” Since these gates are strong and adamantine, they are closed by the apostles, to whom the keys of Jerusalem were entrusted. The enemies linger before them, and they kill those whom they see going out.

Therefore, if someone belongs to Jerusalem, which dwells prosperously in its cities, he does not go out while he dwells in abundance. He always remains within and does not go out through its gates, for whoever goes out is killed—killed by those who exalt themselves in Gath, dwell in Bachim, and build a house for derision.

Finally, the evils that descended from the Lord to the gates of Jerusalem have only the din of chariots, the tumult of horses, and a confused sound before the gates of Jerusalem, so that with the spear of their mouth they may kill anyone whom they see wandering.

After this it is written: “O you who dwell in Lachish: she is the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion.”

Lachish is interpreted as πορεία ἐστίν, that is, “it is a journey” or “a going.” Those, therefore, who mounted their chariots, possessed horsemen, and had only empty tumult and sound are addressed by her who dwells prosperously in her cities: “These trust in chariots, and these in horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Psalm 19:8).

Because they moved their feet and were carried about by every wind of false doctrine (Ephesians 4), and wished to go out from the Church—which is interpreted as “watchtower,” that is, Zion—they became rulers of sin for the daughter of Zion. In her, that is, in the Latin peoples, the impieties of Israel were found, impieties that separated God’s people from its former kingdom.

She is therefore “the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion,” she who dwells in Lachish, that is, in a most evil journey, with a step continually wavering. The impiety of Israel is found in those who are always moving their feet and are said to dwell in Lachish.

“Messengers shall also be sent as far as the inheritance of Gath.” Gath is the most evil winepress, the winepress of poisons, built against the house of God. There are empty houses, built for derision. These empty houses were made in vain among the kings of Israel.

Historically, this refers to those kings whose sins are recorded in the Books of Kings and Chronicles. In the allegorical sense, however, it refers to the rulers of heretics and the leaders of perverse doctrines. For such men these houses are empty and built in vain. They shall continue until heirs arrive to possess them, heirs whom the Lord is to bring.

After this follows: “O you who dwell in Lachish, the inheritance shall come as far as Adullam.”

Adullam is interpreted as “the testimony of their drawing,” or “of their drinking,” which is expressed more significantly in Greek as μαρτυρία ἀντλήσεως αὐτῶν [“the testimony of their drawing”]. We read in Proverbs: “If you are evil, you alone shall draw up evils” (Proverbs 9:12).

She who therefore dwells in Lachish, that is, on a most evil road, shall come as far as the testimony of her exhaustion; she shall draw up and drink according to the measure of her works.

Or the passage should perhaps be divided in this way, so that “O you who dwell in Lachish” belongs to what precedes, and the order and sense are: “I shall bring heirs to you, O you who dwell in Lachish, from the Church, because you too shall belong to the inheritance of the Lord when you have drawn up and received what you deserve.”

I ask the reader, at the end of this chapter, not to regard necessity as willfulness, or to consider a lengthy exposition mere verbosity. Rather, let him marvel that in places so difficult I have found something to say, instead of blaming me for failing to omit any of the matters that had to be said.

### (Verse 16)

“Make yourself bald and cut your hair for the children of your delights; enlarge your baldness like an eagle, because they have been led away captive from you.”

The Septuagint: “Glory ÷ of the daughter ** of Israel: make yourself bald and cut your hair for your delicate children; enlarge your baldness like an eagle, because they have been led away captive from you.”

The words added by the Septuagint—“the glory of the daughter of Israel,” with “daughter” added—are read by the Hebrews at the end of the preceding chapter. But since you have chosen this arrangement and we have once undertaken it, necessity compels us to interpret the Scriptures as they are read in the Church, while nevertheless not omitting the Hebrew truth.

Accordingly, for the present the statement is addressed to Israel according to the literal sense, whether we understand the ten tribes in Samaria or Israel as a whole. Since the people have been led captive and all Judea has been devastated by the Assyrians and Babylonians, let them assume mourning and weep for their children.

Just as the eagle, which is queen of the birds, loses its feathers at a fixed season and remains featherless, so Israel too should lay aside all its former glory, with which it had previously been surrounded, and mourn its children, subjected to the power of its enemies.

That an eagle customarily loses its feathers at a fixed season is also written in the Psalter: “Your youth shall be renewed like that of the eagle” [the text here reads “your old age”] (Psalm 102:5).

The comic poet in the *Heautontimorumenos* says: “It has truly appeared, as the saying goes, the old age of an eagle” (Terence, Act 3, scene 2).

If we wish to understand this also of the present time of the Jewish destruction, we shall see that all the grace by which they once flourished before God has entirely departed from them. Where is the prophet? Where is the teacher of the Law? Where are the angelic defenses? Where is the unexpected victory of the few against the many?

Jerusalem has been made bald; she has lost all the hair of her former glory (Isaiah 33:18; 1 Corinthians 1). Her children, who cried out against the Lord, “Crucify him, crucify him!” (John 19:6), have been led into captivity.

I have read in the Commentary of a certain writer that the statement “make yourself bald and cut your hair for the children of your delights” may be understood of the human condition, so that the word of God is addressed to Adam or to the heavenly Jerusalem.

“O human soul! O city, once the mother of the saints, who were formerly in paradise and enjoyed the delights of various trees and possessed a most beautiful head of hair! Now, because you have been cast down from the heights and led away into Babylon, because you have come to the place of captivity and lost your hair, shave yourself and assume the clothing of a penitent. You who formerly flew like an eagle in the heights, mourn your children; mourn your offspring, who have been led captive from you.”

Editorial notes to the preceding text:

- [Col. 1155D] The Palatine manuscripts read: “all her wages shall be burned with fire,” in agreement with the Greek text. We correct less significant matters below.
- [Col. 1157] Elsewhere, and in one Palatine codex, the reading is *quem*. Compare what we said concerning the testimony of this reading in Homily 5 on Ezekiel, vol. V, col. 927.
- [Col. 1159D–1160D] The old reading was “She passes away from you,” undoubtedly false, as Victorius observed. He adds: “The Hebrew has, ‘Pass over for yourselves’; this too is an incongruous expression. Jerome acknowledges the word ‘Pass over’ when he says, ‘Pass in this way, be led into captivity in this way,’ but without the word ‘for yourselves.’ The Vulgate retained the better reading, which we too have followed, and Jerome does not appear to differ from it: ‘Pass over for yourselves, O habitation of Saphir,’ or ‘beautiful.’ Perhaps a corruption of the Hebrew word caused this error, one letter being changed into another. For *waw* is easily corrupted into *yod* through the injury of time or the carelessness of scribes. Otherwise the expression is improper and used nowhere else. The Vulgate edition, agreeing with itself in all manuscripts, was certain evidence to me. We have removed this error also from the Commentary, where ‘She passes away from you’ was read instead of ‘Pass over for yourselves.’ The Brescia codices and the Vulgate edition supplied the remedy.”
- [Col. 1160D] Martian reads “of the inhabitant”; then the manuscripts add the preposition “in.”
- [Col. 1160D] Two Palatine manuscripts read: “Do not build houses of derision; sprinkle earth upon your derision,” and so forth.
- [Col. 1160D] Victorius restores “which” from the Florentine codices.
- [Col. 1161D] The Palatine manuscripts omit “its own”; shortly afterward, in Symmachus’s translation, they read *Μαρήσα* for *Μαρέσει*, and *ὀδολλάμ*; Martian has *ὀδολάμ*. We often silently correct slight errors of this kind.
- [Col. 1162D] Compare the Book on the Site and Names of Places, under *Inachim*, from the Books of Kings.
- [Col. 1162D] One Palatine manuscript reads: “Christ possesses the Churches in unity,” and so forth.
- [Col. 1163D–1164D] Victorius says that “your youth,” not “your old age,” is the reading in all Hebrew, Greek, and Latin editions. We nevertheless changed nothing, since Jerome evidently intended to render the sense rather than the word, as is clear from his immediately following statement about the eagle’s old age from Terence. Moreover Matthew 24 gives us the correct reading when it says: “Eagles are the saints whose youth has been renewed like that of an eagle, and who, according to Isaiah, grow feathers and take wings in order to come to Christ’s passion.”
- [Col. 1164D–1165D] Terence wrote a comedy entitled *Heautontimorumenos*, that is, “The Self-Tormentor.” In Act III, scene 2, occur the words quoted by Jerome: “It has indeed appeared, as the saying goes, the old age of an eagle.” Do not be surprised that “your old age” is read here in Jerome instead of “your youth,” which occurs in all the hagiographical books: at this point the holy doctor attended to the sense of Scripture, not its words; nor could he have used the comic poet as a witness for his point unless he had used the word “old age” in quoting Psalm 102. — Martian.

### Chapter II (Verse 1 and following)

“Woe to those who devise futility and work evil upon their beds. In the morning light they do it, because their hand is against God. They coveted fields and seized them by violence; they plundered houses and falsely accused a man and his house, a man and his inheritance. Therefore the Lord says this: ‘Behold, I am devising evil against this family, from which you shall not remove your necks; you shall not walk proudly, for it is a most evil time. On that day a parable shall be taken up against you, and a song shall be sung with the sweetness of those saying: “We have been devastated by desolation; the portion of my people has been changed. How shall he depart from me, when one returns to divide our territories?” Therefore there shall be none for you casting the measuring-line by lot in the assembly of the Lord.’”

The Septuagint: “They became those who devise labors and work evils upon their beds, and together accomplish them by day, because they did not raise their hands to God. They desired fields and plundered orphans; they oppressed houses and seized a man and his house, a man and his inheritance. Therefore the Lord says this: ‘Behold, I am devising evils against this tribe, from which you shall not remove your necks, so that you may not walk upright ÷ suddenly **, because it is a most evil time. On that day a parable shall be taken up against you, and a lament shall be lamented in a song, saying: “Misery! We have been made wretched; the portion of my people has been measured out by a line, and there was no one to prevent him from turning away. Our fields have been divided.” Therefore there shall be none for you casting the measuring-line in the inheritance.’”

[Editorial note: Two manuscripts read here “they covet,” and shortly afterward “they falsely accuse.”]

What we placed at the end of the chapter according to the Hebrew, “in the assembly of the Lord,” for which the Septuagint translated “in the Church of the Lord,” is, according to the Vulgate edition, the beginning of the following chapter. Therefore, if the Lord commands, we shall discuss it there.

Woe, therefore, to you, assembly of the Jews, who both devise evil and bring it to completion in deed. You defile with debaucheries the beds given for rest; whatever iniquity you contrive by night, as though it were not possible to delay it, you hasten to carry out as soon as day has dawned, not considering that your hand is strong against the Lord.

To show what they devised by night and did by day, Scripture explains it in particulars. “They coveted,” it says, “fields and seized them by violence; and houses”—understand, “they coveted”—“and those which they coveted they plundered.” They not only falsely accused men and their houses, but with raging mouth also devastated their descendants, who, on account of their tender age, deserved compassion.

Because you did these things and devised futility, I, the Lord, shall devise evil against this family—not because what I devise is evil, but because what I inflict appears evil to those who suffer it. It shall oppress you so that you cannot lift up your necks or walk proudly, namely, you whom the time of captivity had crushed.

[Editorial note: The words “which I inflict” are absent from our manuscripts.]

Then [alternative: “at that time”] a parable will be spoken against you, and your miseries will be turned into a song:

“We have been devastated by devastation; the portion of my people.” That is, he says: “My temple, which alone among the other nations I possessed in greater measure, will be changed into a ruin. How will the Assyrian withdraw from me when he returns to distribute my fields among his own people by lot?”

Therefore, O house of Israel, against which I am devising calamity, you will have no share in the inheritance of the righteous. This same passage can also be understood of the final captivity: all these things befell them because they crucified the Lord, though the edition of the Seventy Translators must nevertheless be discussed.

For the glory of the daughter of Israel has been shaved and clipped, over her once most delicate sons; and if anything of her hair subsequently grew again, it was cut off by another shaving and clipping. Then all their plans were turned into labor, and the things they conceived, while their mind and soul were asleep, brought labors upon them; and whatever they had done was thrown into confusion as soon as the light of Christ and vengeance appeared.

For when they had read that Israel conquered Amalek when Moses raised his hands to the Lord, and that Amalek was overcome when Moses lowered his weary arms (Exod. XVII), they did not raise their hands to the Lord. Instead, while perpetrating every crime against the poor and the people of the Lord, they desired fields, plundered the houses of orphans, and laid waste to man, wife, children, and possessions alike.

Therefore the Lord devised [alternative: “was devising”] calamities against that tribe—not twelve tribes, but a tribe stained by wickedness and crime [Note: [Col. 1166D] Our manuscripts read “in the twelve tribes.” But, with Victorius, from seven Florentine and four Brescian manuscripts, we read “but a tribe defiled with wickedness and crime”; Martianus retained instead, “a tribe of wickedness, and confederated in crime.”] [Col. 1166C]—from which they were unable to lift their neck, nor to walk upright.

Indeed, to the present day they have been subjected to Roman rule, pressed beneath the yoke of captivity, and have not lifted their necks.

As for what follows—ἐξαίφνης, that is, “suddenly”—it is not found in the Hebrew volumes. Yet it can fit the present passage if we say: “Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I am suddenly devising calamities against this tribe, from which they will not be able [alternative: “are not able”] to lift their necks; and for that reason they will not be able to lift them, because the time is evil.”” For just as they did evil against the Lord Jesus, so they will endure the evils of perpetual captivity, and will come into such distress that all their songs and psalms will be turned into mourning.

And the people will know nothing else to say except this: “We have become misery, miserable as we are.”

For the promised land, which had first been divided by lot among two and a half tribes beyond the Jordan, when Moses stretched out the measuring cord, and which afterward was distributed by Joshua among the remaining tribes, has been divided among the nations by the Roman surveyor. Rather, since the Roman surveyor holds all the nations, no Jew possesses the ancient soil in its former liberty.

If we wish to follow a third interpretation, directing the whole discourse mentioned above toward the human soul—which, falling from paradise, has come into the captivity of this world—we shall see that all our thought is labor and pain, that our beds are full of evils, and that the very light which is seen is mixed with darkness; whatever we deliberate by night, we carry out in darkness.

For who among us raises holy hands to God without anger and inward thought? Who does not desire the estates of this age, having forgotten the possessions of paradise? You may see some joining fields to fields and boundaries to boundaries, while the countryside of cities is not enough for the small body of a single human being.

Therefore the Lord devises calamities against us from which we cannot lift our necks or walk upright, because the time is exceedingly evil, according to John’s words: “The world is set in wickedness” (I John V, 19).

The same is signified by that noble daughter of Abraham in the Gospel—the soul—which Satan had bound and bent down, and which, before the Lord’s coming, could neither be raised on high nor look upon [alternative: “receive”] its Creator. Hence the Savior says:

“This daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound, ought she not to be released from this bond on the sabbath day?” (Luke XIII, 16).

Since, therefore, all our glory has been shaved away, and we have extended our shaving—or [Note: [Col. 1167D] Two Palatine manuscripts prefer *viduitatem*, “widowhood”; in Greek, however, the word is γύμνωσιν, “nakedness.”] our nakedness—for this is how it is found in certain manuscripts, messengers have been sent to mourn us with Jeremiah, to take up a parable concerning us, and to say with the Apostle: “I shall mourn for many who have sinned and have not repented” (II Cor. XII, 21).

For who would not mourn upon seeing human souls, like varied household goods, possessed by demons and by different [Col. 1168A] vices? One demon casts out the cord of fornication, another that of avarice; one stretches the lines of murder, another those of perjury. The portion of the people of God has been divided by a cord, and the fields once belonging to holiness and paradise—whose fragrance Isaac delighted in through his son Jacob (Gen. XVII)—have been handed over to the Assyrians and the king of Babylon.

“And whereas foxes have holes and the birds of the air nests, the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII).

I have explained this according to the limited powers of my small intellect: first, the captivity of the people by the Assyrians and Babylonians; second, that inflicted by the Romans because they crucified the Lord; and third, the spiritual captivity by which each of us, together with Adam, fell from paradise and is entangled in the captivity of this world. From this captivity, when the Lord comes, “he will raise up the oppressed and release the fettered” (Ps. CXLIV); and those once held captive by the devil he will restore to their own possession. Then the Psalmist’s saying will be fulfilled: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII, 19).

According to this interpretation, a fourth captivity may also be understood as applying to the Church: each person leaves it through sin and is afterward brought back to Jerusalem by Ezra, whose name means “helper,” that is, by the word of God (I Esdras VII).

If anyone, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord, has possessed greater diligence, greater intellect, leisure, and grace, and can say something more plausible about the present chapter, I do not envy or disdain him; rather, I desire to learn from him what I do not know and shall gladly profess myself his disciple, provided that he teaches and does not disparage. For nothing is easier than for an idle and sleeping person to discuss the labor and vigils of others.

## (Verses 6–8)

“Do not speak, speaking; it will not drip upon these; confusion will not overtake them, says the house of Jacob. Has the spirit of the Lord been shortened, or are such his thoughts? Are not my words good toward one who walks uprightly? But, on the contrary, my people have risen up as an enemy: you have taken away the cloak from above the tunic, and you have turned those who passed by innocently into war.”

The Septuagint reads:

“In the Church of the Lord, do not weep with tears, nor let them weep over these things—for he will not cast away the reproaches which say: ‘The house of Jacob provoked the spirit of the Lord, if these are his inventions.’ Are not his words good toward him, and have not the upright walked?” [Note: [Col. 1167D] The same manuscripts insert the little word *jam*, “now,” here, and shortly afterward omit *spem*, “hope.” For *contritionem*, Victorius reads *contritionum*; the Greek has the singular συντριμμόν, “breaking” or “crushing.”]

“And previously my people resisted as an enemy against their own peace; they stripped off his skin, in order to remove the hope of the breaking of war.”

“Do not speak,” he says, “speaking.” Aquila translated this as: “Do not drip, dripping,” according to a Hebrew idiom, calling speech a “dripping” because it flows and reaches the ears of its hearers, like descending rain. 453

Do not deceive yourselves, O house of Jacob, and say to one another for consolation: “God is good; the captivity we fear will not come.” Will his abundant mercy and most compassionate spirit, which has arisen widely and abundantly for all, be shortened and become severe only against us? Or are his thoughts of such a kind as those we see in human beings, so that he holds on to ancient anger and is suddenly stirred to vengeance by fury?

To this the Lord replies: “I am indeed good, and my words sound of mercy—but toward those who walk on the straight path.”

But the one who—not merely long ago, but yesterday—venerated idols in insult to me and, insofar as it lay within him, seized tyrannical weapons against me; who stripped the unhappy people of God’s help and, as though from above a tunic, took away the cloak [Note: [Col. 1169D] Martianus retained *palliumque*, “and the cloak,” which Victorius had previously emended according to the manuscripts of Brescia, with the sacred text supporting his reading: “You took away the cloak from above the tunic.”]; who turned every simple believer and everyone acquiescing in the authority of his elders into war against me—will the Lord not drip upon him, and will confusion not overtake him?

The words which we have rendered, “And, on the contrary, my people have risen up as an enemy,” are so rendered because the word MUL () means both “contrary” and “yesterday.” Symmachus translated the passage more clearly, saying: “One day before, my people stood like an enemy,” thereby resolving the question: God was not charging the people with former vices, but with recent ones, which seemed to have been committed, as it were, yesterday.

This is according to the Hebrew understanding. In the present passage, however, the Seventy Translators do not agree with themselves at all. For after what has been set forth—“In the Church of the Lord, do not weep”—what connection is there with what follows: “For he will not cast away the reproaches which say: The house of Jacob provoked the spirit of the Lord”? And what of the next words: “If these are his inventions, are not his words good toward him, and have not the upright walked [or: will walk]?” How do these belong to what follows: “And previously my people resisted as an enemy against their own peace; they stripped off his skin, in order to remove the breaking of war”?

It seems to me that, in this extremely difficult passage, the sense can be restored or expressed as follows [Note: [Col. 1169D] We have deleted the particle *ut*, which Martianus intrudes here; shortly below, our manuscripts do not recognize the two words “or expressed.”], if the prudent reader will accept our reasoning.

The Church is commanded not to have sadness or anxiety over worldly affairs and the losses that ordinarily occur in this world. Its inhabitants are told: “You who are in the Church of the Lord, always rejoice, and whatever befalls you through his judgments, give thanks.”

I do not mean by this that you ought not to weep: “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh” (Luke VI, 21). Rather, I warn you not to mourn over things that belong to this age. If one of your relatives dies, if the treasury seizes your property, if the body is oppressed by gout or any other disease, do not weep or shed tears. Do not consider present things, but future ones; and be more distressed that you remain longer in this tabernacle of death. [Note: [Col. 1170D] Two Palatine manuscripts, with the opposite sense, read: “and rejoice more.”]

Rather, beware that you do not insult those who are falling and consider another’s ruin your own edification. Let each person measure himself by his own strength, not by another’s weakness.

Otherwise, what sort of justice is it to insult the branches of the wild olive against the branches of the olive tree, which were broken off because of their unbelief (Rom. XI), and to say: “The house of Jacob provoked the spirit of the Lord to anger, killing the prophets, worshiping idols, and crucifying the Son of God”?

Whoever does this will not be free from reproach, and by the measure with which he judged, judgment will be passed upon him. As he speaks of the sins of the fallen, so another will mock his fall.

The text continues: “If these are his inventions, are not his words good toward him, and have not the upright walked?”

What the Jewish people have offended in—that the fullness of the nations might enter—is God’s dispensation, so that afterward, when Israel believes, all may be saved and all may need God’s mercy. Hence, when the Apostle comes to the question of this passage (ibid.), he declares the depth of God’s wisdom, knowledge, and judgments to be an unfathomable abyss.

If, then, it is God’s invention and thought to break off the original branches of the olive tree and graft others from the wild olive, you must not insult them, but fear lest you fall. Nor should you think that you please God merely by reading his words—that is, the Scriptures. The Scriptures benefit the reader when what is read is fulfilled in practice.

If you can say, when speaking about the Scriptures: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3), then the Lord will give “a word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power” (Ps. LXVII, 12). And you, who proclaim Zion, ascend upon a high mountain, and you, who proclaim Jerusalem, raise your voice with strength (Isa. XL, 9).

In this way the words of God are good, if they are with him—that is, if God does not abandon the preacher, whose heart and lips are in agreement.

But one who confesses with his lips while his heart is far from God, who recounts his righteousness, takes up his covenant in his mouth, and is defiled by the filth of sins, does not have the good words of God with him.

This must be said not only of the sinner, but also of one who lacks spiritual grace—that is, the gifts of prophecy, teaching, interpretation, and the greater charisms. If such a person wishes to explain the causes of the elements and give an account of his faith, and to explain why God, who is good and the Creator of all things, came only to the Jews and called the nations only at the end of the age, he does not have the good words of God with him. Through his own ignorance he contaminates even those words of God that are good; and those words walk uprightly and require upright ears.

These things the Lord commands the succeeding people and the Church gathered from the nations: not to insult the former generation and not to be free from reproaches by insulting it. [Note: [Col. 1170D] Victorius omits the negative particle.] The true Judge himself, speaking without disturbance, relates how Israel opposed him in his Passion and did this not because it could harm its Creator, but because it did everything against its own peace.

Hence also the word addressed to Jerusalem: “If you had known the things that belong to your peace” (Luke XIX, 42).

Having lost peace, they stripped their own skin—that is, they took away from themselves the help of God, by which they were protected—and left themselves like naked flesh without skin or covering. Whatever had seemed beautiful while God’s mercy covered it from above, when that mercy withdrew, displayed its shame to those who saw it.

When peace and God’s help withdrew, because they had resisted the Lord—of whom it is said, “The Lord who crushes wars, the Lord is his name” (Judith XVI, 3)—they could not resist their adversaries. They were defeated in every conflict, and there was no one to crush the wars arising against them, 456 whether we understand their enemies as the human beings who led them into captivity or as the strength of the adversaries [Note: [Col. 1171D] From the Medicean and Fesulan manuscripts, Victorius rewrites this as: “the strength of the adversarial powers which daily slaughter their souls by blaspheming.”] who daily slaughtered their souls by blaspheming.

## (Verses 9–10)

“You have driven the women of my people from the house of their delights; from their little ones you have taken away my praise forever. Rise and go, for you have no rest here; because of its uncleanness, it will be corrupted with the worst decay.” [Vulgate: “because of his uncleanness.”]

The interpretation of the Seventy—if indeed it is the interpretation of the Seventy; for Josephus writes, and the Hebrews report, that only the five books of the Law of Moses were translated by them and delivered to King Ptolemy [or: “handed over to Ptolemy”]—differs so greatly in the present passage from the Hebrew truth that we cannot even set the sections out on equal terms, nor explain their meanings together. [Col. 1171C]

Therefore let us first discuss our translation, and afterward we shall come to theirs.

The discourse is still directed against the people of God, to whom he had already said above: “On the contrary, my people have risen up as an enemy; you have taken away the cloak from above the tunic.” They did not do only this, but also took captive women—that is, women who had once been delicate matrons—or, metaphorically, the cities of Judea, whom Isaiah likewise calls “daughters of Zion” (Isa. XXVI), since Zion had been the capital.

“You have also taken away,” he says, “from their little ones my praise forever.” No one remained among the people to sing my psalms, since all had either been killed or taken captive. Even the few who remained in Babylon testify that they cannot sing: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI, 4).

“Rise, therefore, and go into captivity, because you have no rest in this land. It has been polluted by your crimes and cannot be cleansed unless it first observes a long sabbath.”

I say to you that you have no rest here because your land has been polluted and will be corrupted by the worst decay—that is, by captivity, whether Babylonian or Roman, because it has drunk the blood of the Lord. The passage can be understood according to both historical interpretations.

### The Septuagint

“The leaders of my people will be cast out from the houses of their delights; because of their evil inventions [Col. 1172A] they have been cast out.” [Note: [Col. 1172D] The reading *electi*, “chosen,” was corrupt.]

This can be understood generally of the leaders of the Jewish people, the priests and Pharisees, who after the Lord’s Passion were cast out of the city of their delights, in which they had previously indulged because of their evil inventions. It can also be understood specifically of the line of David, because as soon as the Lord was born, “the ruler failed from Judah, and the leader from his thighs” (Gen. XLIX), when the one to whom it had been reserved came and the expectation of the nations appeared.

The prophetic word also describes the leaders of the Church who abound in delights and believe that they preserve chastity amid banquets and indulgence: they are to be cast out from spacious houses, luxurious feasts, and banquets procured with great labor, and cast out because of their evil thoughts and deeds.

If you want to know where they are to be cast, read the Gospel: into “the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXII, 13).

[Is it not confusion and disgrace to preach Jesus crucified, the teacher who was poor and hungry, while oneself is stuffed with food, proclaiming the doctrine of fasts with red cheeks and swollen face? If we occupy the place of the Apostles, let us imitate not only their speech but also embrace their way of life and abstinence.]

It is certainly holy to serve widows and the poor in the ministry of the Apostles (Acts VI, 2). “It is not right,” they say, “for us, having abandoned the word of God, to serve tables.”

But now the priest of Christ invites to dinner not merely the poor—not merely brothers and those who in turn cannot offer an invitation, from whom, apart from grace, the episcopal hand expects nothing—but soldiers and men girded with swords, judges, centurions standing guard before their doors, and companies of soldiers.

The clergy rush throughout the entire city, seeking to provide judges with things that those judges either cannot find in their praetoria or, having found them, do not purchase. Yet one should not think that this denunciation is directed generally against everyone. Rather, the prophetic word strikes those who are such and threatens them with punishments and eternal darkness, so that those who are not restrained by shame or modesty may at least repent through fear of punishment.

### The Septuagint

“Draw near to the eternal mountains.”

By the eternal mountains we may understand either angels or prophets, concerning whom it is also written in the Psalm: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1). And in another place: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me” (ibid. CXX, 1).

The person who is not separated by his sins from the fellowship of the blessed draws near to the eternal mountains, just as Moses drew near to God—not in bodily location, but in merit. To those who drew near to the eternal mountains the Lord himself was speaking: “I am God who draws near, and not a God who is far off” (Jer. XXIII, 23).

They are called eternal mountains in distinction from those that are not eternal—namely, the mountains of the dark beginning of this age. When these have been raised up like the cedar of Lebanon, they will pass away with the world, and their place will not be found.

### The Septuagint

“Rise and walk, for you have no rest here.”

We are commanded not to think that we have rest in any of the world’s affairs, but, as though rising from the dead, to strive toward what is above, to walk after the Lord our God, and to say: “My soul has clung to you” (Ps. LXII, 9).

If we neglect this and refuse to hear him who says, “Rise, you who sleep, and arise, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V, 14), we shall indeed doze, but we shall be deceived and shall not find rest. For where Christ does not enlighten the one who rises, what appears to be rest is tribulation.

### The Septuagint

“Because of uncleanness you have been consumed by corruption.”

In place of what we said, “you have been consumed,” the sense can sound in Latin, according to the Greek understanding, as “you have been corrupted,” so that the order is: “Because of uncleanness you have been corrupted by corruption.”

This is said of those who serve bodily pleasure and lust and corrupt not only their soul but also their body, being lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God.

It could also have said, “Because of uncleanness you have been corrupted,” and the sense would have been complete even without the word “corruption.” But because it says, “you have been corrupted by corruption,” it seems to me to have spoken in contrast with a salutary corruption, according to which the Apostle also says: “Although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV, 16).

The one who always carries the mortification of Jesus in his body, corrupts the outward man, and subjects the flesh to the authority of the soul—this person is indeed corrupted, but not by corruption, because his corruption is salutary.

## “You fled, with no one pursuing.”

This is said to those who, because of uncleanness, have been corrupted by corruption: the consciousness of their sins makes them unwilling even without punishment to resist their enemies and engage in battle.

Hence the fearful are expelled from the camp and driven from the battle line, lest they frighten the minds of their brothers in the battle of the saints (Deut. XX). In the curses of Leviticus the word is directed against such people: “The sound of a flying leaf will pursue you, and you will flee when no one pursues” (Lev. XXVI, 36).

I know that I once read in someone’s commentary on the opening of the Gospel according to John—“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”—that he referred the word “nothing” to wickedness. He further interpreted wickedness itself as the devil, and by this kind of step understood “what was made without Christ” to mean the devil.

If, then, wickedness—or the devil—is nothing, and those who were corrupted by corruption fled, with no one—that is, with nothing—pursuing them, the devil pursued them into nothingness.

If this seems to anyone excessively forced and explained more by rhetorical ingenuity than by a true interpretation contrary to the simplicity of Scripture, let him follow either the earlier explanation or whatever interpretation he himself may have discovered.

## (Verses 11–12)

“Would that I were not a man having the spirit, and that I might rather speak falsehood. I shall drip upon you into wine and drunkenness, and it shall be upon the one upon whom this people drips. Gathering, I shall gather Jacob, all of you; I shall bring together the remnant of Israel.”

[Note: [Col. 1173D] Following Victorius, from the Vulgate edition, the Hebrew manuscripts, and the manuscripts of Brescia, we read *quem*, “whom,” rather than *quae*, “which”; and shortly afterward *totum te*, “all of you,” rather than *totum in te*, “all in you.” Our own manuscripts also assisted us in this matter.]

[Note: [Col. 1173D] Our manuscripts add the remainder of the text: “I shall place him like a flock in the sheepfold, like a herd in the midst of the enclosures; they will make a tumult because of the multitude of people. For the one who ascends opens the way before them; they will divide, pass through the gate, and go out through it; their king will pass before them, and the Lord at their head.” And so forth.]

The Seventy Translators also differ greatly from the Hebrew in this chapter. Therefore let us first explain it according to what has been handed down to us by the Hebrews, and afterward, if the Lord wills, let us discuss their translation.

O Jewish people, to whom belong the promises, the covenants, and the law, and from whom Christ is descended according to the flesh (Rom. IX)—to you, when the Babylonians or Romans were threatening, I said: “Rise and go into captivity, for you have no rest in this land, which because of its uncleanness will be corrupted by the final devastation.” Do not think that I want to speak and take delight in proclaiming what I see is going to happen. I myself would wish to be accursed for my brothers, who are Israelites (Rom. IX, 3).

Would that I were speaking from my own feeling, and did not have the Holy Spirit; that I might rather be counted among the false prophets, perish alone, and what I say might not be true; that so great a multitude might believe in the Son of God and not be handed over to eternal captivity.

But because I am a prophet, speak by the Spirit of God, and have been sent by divinity [or: by truth], I proclaim the truth. Therefore I shall drip my word upon you like pure wine, which will intoxicate you and make you fall.

While I drip and sing of the evil of the coming captivity, this people will receive my showers—that is, willingly or unwillingly, it must endure what I say.

And do not think that I am only a prophet of evils [alternative: “of so many evils”]. The predicted captivity will indeed come now; but behold, the Word speaks in me—the Word who comes to all the prophets. When the prophet is silent, he does not speak; and now he says: “I shall come and assume a human body; I shall be born of a Virgin.”

Or understand it this way: “Because I came in the lowliness of the flesh and you did not believe in me, I shall come at the consummation of the world in my majesty, with the angels and the other powers. Then I shall gather you all together, Jacob; then I shall bring together the remnant of Israel and join you together with the people of the nations in my sheepfold. Then I shall enclose you with the strongest wall, and the multitude of believers and the tumult of the flock placed among the enclosures will be so great that the number of sheep will be surpassed by their abundance.”

And lest you perhaps think that, when I said, “I shall place him like a flock in the sheepfold and like a herd in the midst of the enclosures,” I was speaking of sheep, understand that these sheep are human beings. For the text continues: “They will make a tumult because of the multitude of people.”

A tumult is the voice of many, a cry emitted together by an immense multitude. We must not imagine that it is the voice of one person, but the common voice of all praising the good shepherd, who has leveled every difficult place and made it even with his foot; who is himself their guide on the journey, the gate of paradise, and says: “I am the gate.” With him dividing the way, going before them as the gate of the way, the believing flock will pass through him.

This shepherd is king and Lord. Hence the text continues: “Their king will pass before them, and the Lord at their head.”

If we wish to understand all these things as referring to his first coming, and refer “all of Jacob” and “the remnant of Israel” to the Apostles and to that multitude of Jews who were saved in the Acts of the Apostles, the interpreter’s exposition will not be contrary to the truth.

For the Lord truly gathered these people into his sheepfold, placed them in the midst of the enclosures, made a way before them, led them into the Church, and was their king before them; and he remains the Lord at their head forever.

### The Septuagint

“The spirit established falsehood. He dripped for you into wine and drunkenness, and it will be from the dripping of this people; Jacob will surely be gathered.”

[Note: [Col. 1175D] The words of the following section of the next chapter—“With all, receiving, I shall receive the remnant of Israel”—had been inserted here without reason and contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts in the printed editions.]

It must not be read, as many think, “the spirit stood as a liar,” but “the spirit established falsehood.” In Greek this is πνεῦμα ἔστησε ψευδὲς, that is, τὸ ψεῦδος, “the spirit established falsehood.”

For just as, in putrid wounds, so that cancer may not spread and dead flesh consume living flesh, physicians open [alternative: “cut”] and cauterize the wound with a cautery or with caustic (καυστικῷ) powder, so the Spirit of God put an end to falsehood, lest the people of God should thereafter be overthrown by the voices of false prophets.

We have often said—and now shall indicate in part—that whenever “spirit” is written in either the New or the Old Testament without an added qualification, it is to be understood in a good sense, so that no one may have doubts.

“The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” (Gal. V, 22). And: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (ibid. VI, 25). And elsewhere: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. VIII, 13).

In the Old Testament: “Giving breath to the people who are in it, and spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isa. XLII). There can be no doubt from what precedes that “it” signifies the earth. For those who tread upon earthly works and place them beneath their feet certainly deserve to receive not an evil but a good spirit.

By contrast, an evil spirit is always read with a qualification, as here: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man” (Matt. XII, 43); and elsewhere: “He rebuked the unclean spirit” (Luke IX, 43); and: “An evil spirit invaded Saul” (I Reg. XVI, 14), and other similar passages.

The Spirit of God, therefore, which put an end to falsehood among the false prophets, will drip for you into wine and drunkenness: the wine “which gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII), and the drunkenness with which Noah was drunk, and of which it is said: “Eat, my friends, and be drunk” (Song V, 1).

All this joy and drunkenness, compared with the wisdom of God—which, like a river, waters the heavenly Jerusalem—is only a drip and a very small drop.

Nor will those hesitate to call the wisdom of God a drop in human beings who have read of the stone cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. II), and that “the foolishness of God is wiser than men,” and that the Apostles themselves knew and prophesied only in part (I Cor. XIII, 9).

From this wisdom, therefore—that is, from the drip given to the Jewish people, for it came only to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel”—Jacob was gathered: everyone who supplants Esau, seizes his birthright and blessing, and, while still in the womb and not yet born, grasps the heel of his hairy brother.

### The Septuagint

“With all, receiving, I shall receive the remnant of Israel.”

When, he says, the people of the nations believe, when the whole world has been brought to my faith, and when the fullness of the nations has entered, then also the remnant of Israel will be saved.

This is not the remnant of which it is written in the Book of Kings: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal” (III Kings XIX, 18); nor that of which Paul says: “So also at this present time there is a remnant saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. XI, 15); nor that of which this prophet testifies above: “It will be from the dripping of this people; Jacob will surely be gathered.”

Rather, it is the remnant that will be received by God at the end, after all the others have been received. Concerning them it is now said: “With all, receiving, I shall receive the remnant of Israel,” so that what is written may be fulfilled: “God has shut up all under sin, that he might have mercy upon all” (Rom. XI, 32).

### The Septuagint

“I shall place their turning away like sheep in tribulation.”

The remnant of Israel, which I shall receive after I have received everyone else, I shall receive later. For now, because they have turned away from me, I shall place them in tribulation, constrain them, and make them sit without priest, altar, or prophet, so that they may understand through punishments the one whom they did not recognize through benefits.

### The Septuagint

“Like a flock in the midst of their fold.” [Note: [Col. 1176D] Here too we have restored, according to the testimony of the manuscripts, the words of the sacred text—“they will leap forth from human beings”—which had been omitted and which disrupted the sequence of Jerome’s exposition; they are set out below in their proper place.]

The word “I shall place” is understood.

“Not only,” he says, “will their turning away, by which they have turned away from me, be placed like a flock in tribulation; but after they have been afflicted and have completed the time of distress, they will be placed in rest—that is, in their fold.”

Then [alternative: “now”] they will depart from human beings and rise beyond the condition of human existence, fulfilling what follows: “They will leap forth from human beings.”

But not only will those people leap forth and depart. All to whom the word of God is addressed, who abandon human vices, imitate the conduct of divinity, and hear, “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High,” will leap forth from human beings and, as though carried upward, be borne [alternative: “are borne”] to heaven.

### LXX: “Go up through the breach.”

The present passage seems to have as its proper beginning and apostrophe of prophetic speech an address to the one who desires to be saved, to whom it is commanded that he go up through the breach. This will become clearer if we take an example from Genesis, where twins are born to Tamar, with whom the patriarch Judah had intercourse:

“It happened,” he says, “when she was giving birth and had twins in her womb, that during the birth one put out his hand. The midwife took it and tied scarlet thread on his hand, saying, ‘This one will come out first.’ But when he drew back his hand, immediately his brother came out, and she said, ‘Why has the wall been breached because of you?’ And she called his name Perez, which is interpreted as ‘breach.’ And after this his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread, and she called his name Zerah, who in our language is called ‘seed’ or ‘rising’” (Gen. XXXVIII, 27 ff.).

Thus the elder people, in whom there was “rising” and “seed” before the Church was born from the nations, put out its hand in its works, and afterward drew it back, hearing through Isaiah: “For your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I, 15). When it had drawn back [Al. “drew back”] its hand and ceased from works of righteousness, its brother, the people of the nations, came out. For his sake the hedge was breached, and the Lord and Savior destroyed the wall that was in the middle, the partition separating the two peoples; and he made one flock, creating the two in himself as one new man and making peace.

Therefore the midwife, speaking prophetically, says to Perez, the younger people: “Why has the wall been breached because of you?” If you have understood the example from Genesis, go up, you who desire to be saved—not through the old people, whose hand is drawn back, but through the new, in whom Christ is the way and Jesus is the gate, through whom we proceed to the Father. For he himself loosed the middle wall and partition, that is, the obscurity of the ancient prophets, and opened all the mysteries of the ancient Law; and, once the difficulty of proceeding had been dispersed, he revealed the way to the eyes of all, so that whoever wishes to proceed may be caught by no obstacle [Al. “hindered”] and may not be frightened by the darkness of obscurity.

### LXX: “Before their face they breached it and passed through the gate, and they went out through it. Their king went out before their face; but the Lord was their leader” [Al. “will be”].

For this reason I said to you: “Go up through the breach,” you who have risen with Christ and seek the things that are above. For the angels—or the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—breached what appeared to obstruct the way, and made a road for those wishing to enter. Because they invaded the path once the road had been opened, they not only entered the gate but also passed through it.

They entered because their king himself entered the same gate and opened the road for them, so that they might walk without any difficulty. For the Lord himself, both king and shepherd, is both the way and the gate, and he says: “I am the gate. Whoever enters through me will be saved; he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John X, 9). Concerning this gate it is also prophesied elsewhere: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. CXXVII, 20).

Whoever has entered must not remain in the condition in which he entered; rather, he must go out to the pastures, so that in entering there may be a beginning, but in going out and finding pasture, the perfection of virtues. The one who enters is still in the world and understands [Al. “will understand”] the Creator from created things. But the one who goes out transcends the whole of creation; counting as nothing all that can be seen, he will find pastures above the heavens, and feed upon the word of God, saying: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. XXII, 1).

This is said so that we may understand the Gospel testimony: “He will enter and go out and find pasture,” and what is now said through the Prophet: “They passed through the gate and went out through it.” Yet this passage and going out cannot be attributed apart from Christ our king, who is both king and Lord. For it is immediately connected: “But the Lord will be their leader.”

## Chapter III, verses 1 ff.

“And I said: Hear, princes of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel. Is it not yours to know judgment, you who hate the good and love evil, who violently strip their skins from them and their flesh from their bones, who have eaten the flesh of my people and stripped their skin from them, broken their bones, and cut them up as though in a cauldron and like flesh in the middle of a pot? Then they will cry out to the Lord, and he will not hear them; and he will hide his face from them at that time, just as they acted wickedly in their devices.”

The speech is plainly directed against the princes of Israel, and under the metaphor of lions or robbers their cruelty is described: they stripped the poor, killed them, crushed their flesh and bones, and afflicted the wretched people in the city of Jerusalem as though they were in the middle of a pot. For these things punishment is afterward inflicted upon them on the day of captivity, whether by Nebuchadnezzar or by Vespasian and Titus. They will cry out to the Lord, and he will not hear them and will hide his face from them, because they acted wickedly in their crimes.

### LXX: “And he will say: Hear these things, princes of the house of Jacob and remnant of the house of Israel.”

The sentence is joined to what precedes. Above he had said: “But the Lord will be their leader,” and he says: “Hear, princes of the house of Jacob and remnant of the house of Israel.”

In place of “remnant of the house of Israel,” all the translators, except the Septuagint, rendered “rulers of the house of Israel.” The Lord, therefore, who made a way for his people, went out before their face, and is himself the leader of the journey of the simpler people, whom he calls a flock. [Note: [Col. 1177D] Martianay, falsely and with the contrary sense: “those who wish.”] To those who do not wish to follow him as their guide, but are proud and, as judges of the people, do not follow his footsteps, he threatens and says: “Hear, princes of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel.”

But what is it that compels them to hear? “It is not yours,” he says, “to know judgment,” you who hate the good and seek evil. That is: you do not deserve to know the judgment of God, which is a great abyss, and the crooked mind does not discover the depth of his righteousness. Or how can you know the judgment of God, you who hate the good—

[The printed text repeats: “how can you know the judgment of God, you who hate the good”]

—and seek evil, who detest holy poor people and honor wealthy sinners?

At the same time, let us consider the force of the words. Not to love good things is sin; how much greater a crime is it even to hate them? And, conversely, not to flee evil is a fault; how great an impiety is it even diligently to seek it? After this the savagery of the judges and their cruelty toward their subjects are described.

### 466 — LXX: “Tearing their skins from them, and their flesh from their bones.”

“As they devoured the flesh of my people, stripped their skins from them, broke their bones, and cut them up like flesh in a cauldron and like flesh in a pot, so they will cry out to the Lord, and he will not hear them, and he will turn his face away from them at that time, because they acted most wickedly in their devices.”

It was not enough for them to strip the flock placed under them; they also afflicted their bodies with harsh rule and crushed their bones, so that they might break and shatter whatever strength there had been in them.

Just as they stripped my people and deprived them of every beauty and adornment of skin, and threw flesh and bones into the boiling pot that the Assyrian king kindled, handing my flock over to the devil and his angels, so they too, when the day of vengeance comes, will cry out to the Lord and will not be heard, because they themselves did not hear those who pleaded with them. They will stretch out their hands to the Lord, and God will turn his face away from them, because they too turned their faces away from those who prayed.

They will suffer all these things because they acted most wickedly in their pursuits and pleasures. They were not kings but tyrants; not overseers but lions; not teachers of disciples but wolves of sheep. They gorged themselves on flesh, grew fat, and were prepared for the punishments of the Lord like the fattest sacrificial victim destined for slaughter.

[Note: Victorius says that the reading itself will establish that *et* should be read as *sunt*; but the manuscripts do not support him.]

Thus far the speech has been directed against evil princes. The following speech, however, is against false prophets and the worst teachers, who overthrow the people of God by flattery, promising knowledge of the Scriptures.

## Verses 5 ff.

“Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and proclaim peace; and if someone does not put something into their mouths, they consecrate war against him. Therefore night shall be for you instead of a vision [Al. ‘division’], and darkness for you instead of divination; the sun shall set upon the prophets, and the day shall grow dark over them. Those who see visions shall be put to shame; the diviners shall be put to shame, and they shall all cover their faces, because there is no answer from God. Yet I am filled with the strength of the Spirit of the Lord, with judgment and power [Al. ‘truth’], to declare to Jacob his crime and to Israel his sin.”

### LXX

“Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and proclaim peace over them; and when nothing is put into their mouths, they consecrate war against him. Therefore night shall be for you instead of a vision [Al. ‘indivision’], and darkness shall be for you instead of divination; the sun shall set upon the prophets, and the day shall grow dark over them. Those who see dreams shall be put to shame, the diviners shall be mocked, and all these will speak against them, because there is no one who hears them, unless I am filled with strength in the Spirit of the Lord, with judgment and power, to declare to Jacob his impieties and to Israel his sins.”

We read that there were false prophets in Israel who, for gifts that had not been given to them, proclaimed peace; and if someone did not give presents, they announced that the wrath of God was coming upon him, even if he was holy. Hence it is now said to them that they speak lies, and that their speech is not prophecy but false divination; that they have not light but darkness and error. When the things they had promised have been turned into their opposite, they will then be covered with shame, because, he says, there was no answer from God.

Now [Al. “Then”] even the demons will not receive power to deceive them by their fraud. The oracles will be mute, the unclean spirit will be silent, and it will not dare to mock them.

This concerns the false prophets. Again, the speech of the prophet speaking about himself is introduced. While they prophesy falsely and are covered with shame and disgrace, I, instructed by the Holy Spirit, speak what I speak, and I speak the judgment of the Lord and his power [Al. “truth”]. While the false prophets bite with their teeth and proclaim peace, I announce without any fear Jacob’s crime and Israel’s sin, because they either worshiped idols instead of God or crucified the Son of God.

If, however, we wish to understand what is said according to the Septuagint as referring to heretics, who truly are false prophets and say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them, we will not be mistaken. They once deceive the people of God through error, and they do this in order to consume them, either simply by receiving their gifts or mystically by killing their souls. They promise them peace and heavenly kingdoms, and say: “It is not necessary for you to live continently and holily. Have the faith that we teach, and you will obtain all the Lord’s promises.” By saying these things they stir up the Lord’s wrath against them even more and consecrate war against them.

Therefore, O heretics, who think that you possess prophecy and imitate the Church of God, where you suppose that there is a vision, there will be night; and where you boast of prophetic utterance, there the unclean spirit will speak. For the sun of righteousness will set upon prophets of this kind, and they will see their own darkness and be put to shame. When they are proved to be diviners rather than prophets, they will be mocked for their dreams, and the peoples who had previously been deceived by them will speak against them.

Then those teachers themselves will also repent, and no one will hear them except I, whom they had offended. And because I am merciful and do not desire the death of the sinner (Ezek. XVIII), but desire that he turn back and live, when I have heard them I will give them the power of my Spirit and fill them with my judgment and strength, so that those who formerly deceived the people with flatteries may afterward, by proclaiming the truth, frighten them away from evil and recall them to the right path; and those who had caused the error may begin to heal the wounds they had inflicted and become an occasion of health.

Observe in the present passage that someone may teach after sin, provided that he has washed away his former vices through worthy repentance. Thus David, after adultery and murder, says in the psalm: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” Nor is he content with his own purification, but he adds: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit.” When you have done this, he says, “I will teach the transgressors your ways, and the ungodly will turn back to you” (Ps. L).

## Verses 9 ff.

“Hear these things, princes of the house of Jacob and judges of the house of Israel,

[Note: [Col. 1181D] The same authority says that *rulers* should be read, as at the beginning of the chapter, since the same word occurs in both places. But because the Vulgate edition reads *judges*, and Jerome likewise interprets it in that way, attending more to the sense than to the word, it seemed preferable to warn the reader rather than alter the reading.]

—you who abhor judgment and pervert everything that is right, who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity. Her princes judged for gifts, her priests taught for payment, and her prophets divined for money; yet they leaned upon the Lord, saying: ‘Is not the Lord in our midst? Evil will not come upon us.’ Therefore, because of you, Zion shall be plowed like a field, Jerusalem shall become like a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple shall be like the high places of a forest.”

### LXX

“Hear these things, rulers [Al. ‘judges’] of the house of Jacob and remnant of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert everything that is right; who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquities. Her rulers judged for gifts, her priests answered for payment, and her prophets divined for money; yet they leaned upon the Lord, saying: ‘Is not the Lord among us? Evil will not come upon us.’ Therefore, because of you, Zion shall be plowed like a field, Jerusalem shall be like a garden-watchtower, and the mountain of the Lord shall become a woodland grove.”

No one doubts that Jerusalem was overthrown because of the crimes described in this chapter. Above, a threat had been directed either against judges or against false prophets: “Hear, princes of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel.” And a few verses later: “Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray,” and the rest. Now the prophetic speech is woven generally against judges, false prophets, priests, and those who claimed for themselves knowledge of God. It accuses them because, on account of their crimes, Zion would be plowed like a field, Jerusalem would fall like a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple would become a high place covered with woodland.

We see that what was spoken has been fulfilled: the eyes confirm the utterance of the mouth; visible reality is the witness of prophecy. This same testimony is also written in the book of Jeremiah (Jer. XXVI), where mention is made of the prophet Micah and the devastation of Jerusalem is foretold.

The judges and princes of the house of Jacob and of the house of Israel—that is, of both the two tribes and the ten tribes—not only failed to administer judgment; they abhorred it and perverted everything that was right, so that not even a little justice might remain in the city. They built Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity: with the robbery of the poor, the slaughter of the innocent, and the killing of the holy.

If one of the princes appeared to judge what was right, he sold his decision instead and judged for gifts. The priests likewise did not teach the people unless they had received payment; and although it is said to the holy ones, “You received freely; give freely” (Matt. X, 8), they brought forth God’s response while accepting money and sold the Lord’s grace for greedy payment.

After these evils, not understanding their sin, and as though they could purchase God’s love with crimes, the judges, priests, and prophets remembered that they were God’s people and said according to their impenitent heart: “The Lord is in our midst, and evil will not come upon us.”

Because they did not repent, and the whole people followed the vices of its princes, priests, and prophets, Zion shall be plowed like a field, Jerusalem shall become like a heap of stones, and the temple that previously shone with gold and silver shall collapse into utter ruins.

This concerns the Jewish people, whose true captivity and final ruin were inflicted because of the crimes already mentioned, but above all because of the shedding of the Lord’s blood. Hence Zion was plowed like a field, Jerusalem was turned into mounds of stones, and that once noble and exalted temple was reduced to the final ashes.

If anyone transfers these things said about Jerusalem and Zion to the Church—for it is itself the house of Jacob and the house of Israel, according to what is written in Isaiah: “Jacob is my servant; I will receive him” (Isa. XLI, 8), and according to what is said to Timothy: “That you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church” (1 Tim. III, 15)—he will clearly perceive that the princes of the house of Jacob and the remnant of the house of Israel, or, as it is better written in Hebrew, the judges of the house of Israel, are none other than bishops, presbyters, and deacons.

Unless they guard their hearts with the utmost care, they abhor judgment and pervert everything that is right. For when they judge according to persons, and in the examination of a case the merit of the cause has no force but the power of the defendants does, do they not abhor judgment and pervert everything that is right?

It may also be understood in another way: the princes of the house of Jacob and the judges of the house of Israel abhor and detest judgment by avoiding the sentence of God the judge and corrupting every rule of the Scriptures through evil interpretations. These are the ones who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity.

When Scripture commands, “Do not bring the ungodly into the tabernacle of the righteous” (Ps. V),

[Note: Victorius notes that this is attested in Proverbs XXIV according to the Septuagint: μὴ προσάγαγε ἀσεβῆ νομῇ δικαίων, “Do not bring the ungodly into the pasture of the righteous.” At that place we do not have: “Do not seek impiety in the house of the righteous.”]

and when the Lord abhors a man of blood and deceit, these men appoint as clerics any of their followers, exposing their lives as a scandal to the peoples, and they are responsible for the unbelief of those who are scandalized (Matt. XVIII). Hence it is said that it is better for a man to have a millstone tied around his neck and be cast into the depths than to scandalize one of the least of the Church.

When the prophet Malachi calls priests angels (Mal. II), and their mouth is the oracle of the Lord (Deut. XIX, 19), they do not judge without accepting gifts, although they read: “Gifts blind even the wise and turn away rebuke like a bridle in the mouth” (Eccles. XX).

[Note: Victorius preferred *reproofs*, from the Greek ἐλεγμούς.]

And when it is said to the apostles, “Do not possess gold or silver, nor let bronze be in your belts” (Matt. X, 9), and even money acquired by the labor of a holy man is shaken from his hands, they sell the words of the Lord and trade in doves in the temple.

The prophets of Jerusalem also divined for money, not knowing that prophecy is one thing and divination another. For divination is never taken in the Scriptures in a good sense: “There shall be no omen in Jacob, nor divination in Israel” (Num. XXIII, 23).

[Note: [Col. 1183D] Victorius again substitutes *is* for *will be*.]

They seemed to themselves to be prophets, but because they accepted money their prophecy became divination. The apostle Peter says: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts III, 6). He certainly could have sold to Simon Magus what he was asking for; indeed, he could have pretended to sell it—for the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought—but he condemned the money offered together with the one offering it (ibid. VIII).

Now you see that the prophets of Jerusalem do not have prophecy in their mouths, yet lean upon the Lord and say: “Evil will not come upon us.” Because of them the watchtower of God is divided by the enemy’s plow; the place once belonging to peace becomes full of ruins; the temple of the Lord is turned into brambles and thorns and becomes a dwelling place of wild beasts.

No one should be troubled by what we read in the First Book of Kings: Saul, wishing to go to Samuel, told his servant that he could not go to him because he did not have the payment he could offer for the prophecy, and the servant replied: “Look, a quarter of a shekel of money has been found in my hand, and I will give it to the man of God, and he will announce our way to us” (1 Kings IX). For it is not written that Samuel accepted it or that they offered it to him; rather, they are fed by the prophet and invited to a meal.

But suppose that he did accept it: such contributions should be regarded more as offerings for the tabernacle than as payment for prophecy. A shekel contains twenty obols, and a quarter-shekel contains five obols.

### 472

Therefore, if our priests wish to sell prophecy and to display doves on their chairs, which the Lord overturned with a whip (John II), let them accept five obols, not the prices of estates.
