[Note: The printed editions read: “Would that they accepted not the prices of estates but five obols.” The excellent manuscript of Cluny reads: “And let them accept five obols for placing doves on their chairs, which the Lord overturned and scourged those asking for them, not the prices of estates.” MARTIANAY. Two Palatine manuscripts read: “for placing them on their chairs, which the Lord overturned and thoroughly scourged [read: ‘scourged them’], let them accept five obols, not the prices of estates.” Victorius: “Would that they accepted not the prices of estates but five obols.”]

The same point is made in the Third Book of Kings, where Jeroboam’s wife, when her son was ill, goes to Ahijah, the man of God, and brings him loaves, raisins, and a jar of honey (1 Kings XIV). It is said what she carried with her, yet the prophet is not said to have accepted it, since he rebuked her and foretold the coming mourning.

It is possible, of course, that those accustomed to going to diviners—for there were many diviners and soothsayers in Israel—may, out of bad custom, have thought the same about prophets and wished to offer holy men what they were accustomed to offer diviners. Scripture merely narrated what they wished to do, without stating that they dared either to offer it or that the prophet accepted it.

The apostle Paul says: “Those who serve at the altar share in the altar and live from the altar” (1 Cor. IX, 13). It is permitted to you, O priest, to live from the altar, not to live luxuriously. “The ox that treads out the grain is not muzzled” (ibid., 9).

We know these things, yet the Apostle does not abuse this permission. Though possessing food and clothing, he is content; night and day he works with his hands so as not to be a burden to anyone. In his Epistles he swears that he conducted himself holily and without greed in the Gospel of Christ, and he asserts the same not only concerning himself but also concerning his disciples: that he sent no one who would ask anything from the churches or wish to receive anything [Al. “who could receive anything”] (1 Thess. III).

If in certain Epistles he rejoices and calls the gifts of those who sent them the benevolence of God, he was not so much gathering for himself as for the poor of the saints who were in Jerusalem. These holy poor were those in Jerusalem who had first believed in Christ from among the Jews and, having been cast out by their parents, relatives, and kinsmen, had lost both their possessions and all their household goods, which were plundered by the priests of the temple and by the people.

If such are the poor, let them receive. But if under the pretext of the poor a few households grow rich, and we eat gold from glass and earthen vessels, or exchange our treasures and clothing, let the poor man in appearance not seek the wealth of senators.

What good is it not to have a little linen cloth around the neck to wipe away sweat? What benefit is there in being *monochitones* (μονοχίτωνες, “wearing a single tunic”) and displaying poverty in one’s clothing when the whole multitude of the poor sighs over our purse?

### 473

For this reason, because of us who are such people—who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity, who judge for gifts, answer for payments, and divine for money, while on top of this claiming a pretended holiness for ourselves and saying, “Evil will not come upon us”—let us hear the sentence of the Lord that follows:

Zion and Jerusalem, the watchtower and vision of peace, the temple of Christ at the consummation and at the end, when love has grown cold and faith has become rare, shall be plowed like a field, reduced to mounds, and become a high place of woodland or a garden-watchtower. Where once there were spacious houses and countless heaps of grain, there will scarcely be a small hut preserving the appearance of food, yet possessing no refreshment for the soul.

### (Chapter IV—verses 1ff.)

“And it shall come to pass in the last days [the Vulgate adds: *it shall be*]: the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall hasten, and they shall say:

‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he shall teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths. For from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many peoples, and shall rebuke strong nations even at a distance. And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruning-hooks. Nation shall not take up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any longer. And each man shall sit beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree, and there shall be none to terrify him; for the mouth of the Lord of hosts has spoken. For all peoples shall walk, each in the name of his god; but we shall walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and beyond.

“‘On that day,’ says the Lord, ‘I shall gather the lame, and I shall collect her whom I had driven out, and her whom I had afflicted; and I shall place the lame among the remnant, and her who had laboured into a strong nation. And the Lord reigned over them on Mount Zion, from this time forth and for ever.’”

> **Note:** One Palatine manuscript reads: “the lame, and her whom I had afflicted, who had laboured, into a nation,” etc.

The Seventy: “And it shall come to pass in the last days: the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, prepared upon the summit of the mountains; and it shall be raised above the hills. And peoples shall hasten to it, and many nations shall go and say:

“‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he shall show us his way, and we shall walk in his paths. For from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many peoples, and shall rebuke strong nations even at a distance. And they shall beat their swords into ploughs, and their spears into sickles; and nation shall no longer take up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any longer. And each shall rest beneath his vine, and each beneath his fig tree, and there shall be none to terrify him, because the mouth of the almighty Lord has spoken these things. For all peoples shall go, each in his own way; but we shall go in the name of the Lord our God for ever and beyond.’

“On that day,” says the Lord, “I shall gather her who has been crushed, and I shall receive her who had been cast out, and those whom I had rejected. And I shall place the crushed among the remnant, and the rejected into a strong nation; and the Lord shall reign over them on Mount Zion, from this time forth and for ever.”

Because the rulers of the Jews hated judgment and perverted everything that was right, and built Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity; and not only had they done these things, but they had also judged for bribes, the priests of Jerusalem had answered for a payment, and its prophets had divined for money. On their account Zion had become like a ploughed field, Jerusalem had collapsed into heaps of stones, and the mountain of the house of God had been desolated into the height of forests. Therefore now, when their house had been abandoned and deserted, when the Son of God, leaving the Temple, said, “Rise, let us go away from here” (John XIV, 31), and, “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII, 15), the angels also, according to Josephus, said:

> **Note:** Recall what we said concerning this testimony of Josephus in note b, at the end of no. 9 of Epistle 18 to Damasus.

“Let us depart from these dwellings. In place of Mount Zion, the Lord’s mountain has been raised up”—of which it is said to the prince of Tyre: “And you were wounded on the mountain of the Lord” (Ezek. XXVIII).

This mountain of the Lord was displayed in the last days, when the kingdom of heaven drew near. For at the consummation of the ages, for the rejection of sins, our Saviour appeared through his sacrifice,

> **Note:** The Palatine manuscripts read: “for the remission of sin.”

and he came at the eleventh hour to hire workers. When his Passion had been completed, John says: “It is the last hour” (1 John III, 18). For in six thousand years, if five hundred years are divided among the individual hours of a day, the last hour is consequently called the time of the faith of the nations.

> **Note:** Many held the opinion that this present age is confined within a cycle of six thousand years, after which the end of the world would come, corresponding to the number of days in which God created the world. Paul seems to hold this view in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 4; Barnabas teaches it in the Epistle attributed to him, page 54 of the Greek-Latin edition; Irenaeus, Book 5 *Against Heresies*, chapters 28 and 29; Origen, Book II *Against Celsus*; Saint Hilary on Matthew, chapter 20; and Saint Jerome in his Epistle to Cyprian. The curious reader may consult the notes and observations of the learned Hugh Menard on the Epistle of Saint Barnabas, pages 196ff., and, if he wishes, the two volumes of ours written in French in defence of Hebrew truth. —MART.

> **Note:** The matters which Martianus notes here concerning the ancients’ opinion that the age is confined within a cycle of six thousand years are not at all relevant. Much more pertinent, on the contrary, is what Saint Hilary teaches in his commentary on Matthew: that the first hour refers to Noah, the third to Abraham, the sixth to Moses, and the ninth to David and the Prophets; while in the eleventh hour the time of the Lord’s bodily coming is displayed. For, from the whole number constituting the span of the present age, his birth from Mary corresponds to the calculation by which the time of the eleventh hour is taken from the day. When the whole number is divided by five hundred, the time of his bodily birth is reckoned at the eleventh division of the entire calculation.

“And manifest,” he says, “shall be the mountain of the Lord, prepared above the summits of the mountains.” He shall be manifest who had previously been hidden; and he shall be prepared not merely among the mountains, but above the summits of the mountains—Moses and the Prophets, who prophesied concerning him. Although they wrote down all holy things, nevertheless, in comparison with the prophecy in which they foretold the coming of the Saviour, the other things are lowly and do not reach the summit of the mountains.

“And he shall be exalted,” he says, “above the hills” (Philippians II, 8–9). He appeared as a man and took the form of a servant; he humbled himself even unto death, and death on a cross. But the Father exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name. Compared with his way of life, the whole life of humanity is called plains and valleys.

To this mountain, therefore, which has been prepared above the summits of the mountains and exalted above the hills, all peoples shall hasten—or, as it is written in Hebrew, they shall flow—in the manner of rivers. That is, countless multitudes shall gather. Peoples shall hasten when Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those dwelling in Mesopotamia, Judaea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the regions of Libya near Cyrene, Roman visitors, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs shall all believe in him together (Acts II).

Do they not seem to you to have hastened to the mountain—those to whom it was said, “Follow me, and I shall make you fishers of men” (Matthew IV, 19–20), and who immediately followed the Saviour? Again, Scripture reports concerning James and John that, having left the boat and their father and the waves of this age, they hastened to the mountain. And Matthew the publican, hearing “Follow me” (Matthew IX), immediately ran.

The Gospel also proves that the peoples hastened when many crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judaea, and beyond the Jordan, and he healed them. As the peoples hastened, many nations also went to the mountain—that is, the whole world believing in him—and they said, challenging one another to approach the standard of the cross:

> **Note:** We have deleted the small words *ita* and *et*, in accordance with our manuscripts and seven others from Florence which Victorius consulted. Shortly afterward our manuscripts retain *quoque seu se patibulum* in place of *se patibuli*.

“Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.”

Ascent is necessary if one is to reach Christ, and to reach the house of the God of Jacob, the Church, which is the house of God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. We have already explained that Jacob signifies the Saviour: “Jacob is my servant; I shall receive him” (Isaiah II, 3).

They will also say this to those to whom they had spoken: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.” And they will add: “That he may show us his way”—whether one understands this as the way in the angels who preside over the churches, or in the Holy Scriptures, which show beforehand the way of the Lord and him who says, “I am the way” (John XIV).

“And let us walk in his paths”—that is, in the Apostles, through whom we have believed in Christ. For the spiritual law went forth from Zion, and the word of God passed to the nations from Jerusalem. He shall judge among many peoples (John V, 22), for the Father has given all judgment to the Son.

> **Note:** Victorius reads *transibit*; immediately afterward, on the authority of our manuscripts, we read *judicabit* in place of *judicavit*.

And he shall rebuke “many nations even at a distance” (Psalm XCIII, 11).

> **Note:** Victorius, again using both the Greek and Latin editions and the Florentine manuscripts, restores *strong* here in place of *many*.

For the Lord catches the wise in their craftiness and knows the thoughts of the wise, because they are futile. He judges among the peoples, determining who are worthy of salvation and who are unworthy; and at his coming every zeal for warfare shall be turned toward peace (Isaiah II, 4). Swords shall be changed into ploughs, spears shall be forged into sickles, and nation shall cease to wage war against nation. No one shall learn to fight, once the necessity of fighting has been removed.

There shall be such peace that each person will be secure not only in cities but also in villages and fields—and this will happen because the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

First, in the literal sense: before the child was born to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder, the whole world was filled with blood. Peoples fought against peoples, kings against kings, nations against nations. Finally, the Roman commonwealth itself was torn apart by civil wars: Cinna, Octavian, and Carbo fighting; Sulla and Marius; Antony and Catiline; Caesar and Gnaeus Pompey; Augustus and Brutus; and that same Augustus and Antony. In their battles all kingdoms poured out their blood.

After Rome received a single empire under the rule of Christ, the world became accessible to the journeys of the Apostles, the gates of the cities were opened to them, and a single empire was established for the preaching of the one God.

What is said—“They shall beat their swords into ploughs and their spears into sickles” (Joel III, 10)—may also be understood tropologically. We may say that, upon faith in Christ, anger and unrestrained abuse have been laid aside, so that each person may put his hand to the plough and not look back, and, breaking the darts and spears of insults, may desire to reap spiritual fruits. Thus, while others have laboured, we may enter into their labours, and it may be said of us: “They shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm CXXV, 8).

Now no one fights against another, because we read: “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew V, 9). No one learns to quarrel for the overthrow of those who hear; rather, he places silence upon his mouth and keeps quiet, because the time is evil (Psalm CIII).

“And each shall rest beneath his vine”: beneath that vine whose husbandman is the Father (John XV), so that he may press the wine which gladdens the human heart; and beneath his fig tree, plucking the sweet fruits of the Holy Spirit—love, joy, peace, and the rest.

All these things will happen according to both interpretations, because the Lord’s words are true, and for him to have spoken is to have accomplished.

“All peoples shall go, each in his own way; but we shall walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and beyond.”

“All the nations,” they say, “go according to their error; but we have hastened to the mountain of the Lord and have said, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob’ (Isaiah II, 3). And we shall walk in the name of Christ our Lord, because he is the mountain who is God.”

On that day, when the sun of righteousness shines, she who had previously been crushed shall be gathered, and she who had been expelled shall be received. The crushed one shall be gathered so that she may be placed among the remnant, and the abandoned one into a strong nation.

“For unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah” (Romans IX, 29).

But the Hebrew reads beautifully: “I shall gather,” he says, “the lame, and [or, ‘that is,’] her who had walked badly”—to whom Elijah said, “How long will you limp?” (3 Kings XVIII). Her foot, which had stumbled, had been cut off (Mark IX).

“Her whom I had driven out, and to whom I had given a bill of divorce, I shall gather; and her whom I had afflicted with various captivities, or handed over to the devil and his angels.”

And lest an attentive reader immediately object to us: “How do you assert that the lame woman is gathered and that she who had been expelled is collected, when the Jews remain in unbelief?” let him hear that this is said of the first Church of Christ, which believed from among the Jews. From it came the Apostles, and concerning it Luke records in the Acts of the Apostles that three thousand believed in one day, and elsewhere five thousand (Acts II). James also says to Paul concerning them: “You see, brother Paul, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law” (ibid., XXI, 20).

Consider also the prophetic significance. He did not say, “I shall place the whole lame woman in safety,” but, “I shall place the lame among the remnant,” so that the remnant and the election may be saved; and her who had laboured he shall place into a strong nation—that is, in the Christian name, which neither sword, nor fire, nor tortures will overcome. Look at the faith and suffering of the martyrs, and you will not doubt the strong nation.

“And the Lord shall reign over them”—that is, over many nations and over the lame remnant—on Mount Zion, in the Church, in the watchtower, in the contemplation of virtues, from the present age and into the future.

If someone wishes to understand what is said—“I shall gather her who was crushed, and I shall receive her who was expelled,” and the rest—as referring to the human soul, which before Christ’s coming had served various passions and vices and, like a wandering and diseased sheep, had been torn by the bites of wolves, he will not be mistaken, provided that he knows that she who had been crushed and afflicted will afterwards be under the Lord’s reign, will live in Zion, and will be carried back upon the shoulders of the good shepherd to the former mountain (Luke XV).

It should also be known that the chapter we have now interpreted, and the similar passage in Isaiah, are referred by the Jews and the heirs of their error to a thousand-year reign of Christ and the saints. They also interpret the statement, “All peoples shall walk, each in the name of the Lord his God,” to mean that every nation will be tortured together with its idol and sent into the fire of eternal punishment.

But the subsequent context demonstrates that this is not spoken of the end of the ages, but of Christ’s first coming, in which the lame remnant is gathered and the nations are saved beforehand.

Isaiah therefore presents a testimony of this kind:

“The word that came to Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem: For it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God upon the summit of the mountains; and it shall be exalted above the hills. And all nations shall come to it, and many peoples shall go and say:

“‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he shall announce to us our way, and we shall walk in it. For from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many nations, and shall rebuke a numerous people. And they shall beat their swords into ploughs and their javelins (*zibynas*) into sickles; and nation shall not take up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any longer’” (Isaiah II).

Significantly, it is said here [or, “of these things”] that the word of God, going forth from Jerusalem, judges among many nations and specifically rebukes the Jewish people. He will judge us as sinners according to the measure of our works; but them, as ungodly and deniers, he will not judge—he will rebuke them as condemned.

## BOOK TWO

### [Col. 1189]

We are always answering the envious, because envy does not cease; and the beginnings of our books refute the curses of our rivals. They commonly boast that I write certain sterile and barren absurdities of speech, and that, although I do not know how to speak, I cannot keep silent.

Therefore I beseech you, Paula and Eustochium, to close your ears to such barking, and, supporting my infancy—as they call it—with your prayers, obtain for me, according to the Apostle, an opening of my mouth, so that what can be applied to one speaking from the Scriptures may be fulfilled:

“The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power” (Psalm LXVII, 12).

I warn the fat bulls who have surrounded me (Psalm XXI) to be quiet and cease their abuse, lest they come to know their own evil deeds, which will be brought forth later if they continue [or, “are continuing”] to injure us.

For as to their saying that I compile the volumes of Origen and that it is unfitting to contaminate the writings of the ancients:

> **Note:** From Terence’s prologue to the *Andria*:
>
> “That plays ought not to be contaminated”; and from the prologue to the *Adelphoe*:
>
> “What they consider a vehement reproach,
>
> he regards as the greatest praise,
>
> when it pleases those who please you all and the people.”
>
> Finally, at the end, again from the prologue to the *Andria*:
>
> “Whose negligence he desires to imitate,
>
> rather than the obscure diligence of these men.”

What they consider a vehement reproach, I regard as the greatest praise, when I wish to imitate the man whom I do not doubt pleases all intelligent people—and you.

For if it is a crime to transfer the celebrated works of the Greeks, let Ennius and Virgil, Plautus, Caecilius and Terence, Cicero, and the other eloquent men be accused—those who transferred not merely verses but many chapters, the longest books, and entire plays.

Let our Hilary also be guilty of theft, because he rendered nearly forty thousand verses of the aforementioned Origen into Latin according to their sense in his commentary on the Psalms.

“I desire to imitate the negligence of all these men rather than the obscure diligence of those others.”

But now it is time to forge a second book on Micah and to crush the reborn heads of the hydra with the prophetic club—

> **Note:** That is, with a club. The manuscripts read *ropalo*; others have *palo* and *repagulo*.

—ῥοπάλῳ, “with a club.”

### (Verses 8–9)

“And you, tower of the flock, misty daughter of Zion, to you it shall come, and the former dominion shall come, the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem. Now why are you drawn together in grief? Is there no king for you, or has your counsellor perished? For pain has seized you like a woman in labour.”

The Seventy: “And you, tower of the flock, darkened daughter of Zion, to you it shall come, and the first principality shall enter, the kingdom [from Babylon] of the daughter of Jerusalem.”

> **Note:** The manuscripts read: “the first kingdom is from Babylon.”

“And now why have you known evils? Was there not a king for you, or has your counsel perished? For pains have taken hold of you like a woman in labour.”

We should understand the “misty” or “squalid tower of the flock”—which in Hebrew is called *Ophel*—as no other than the one of which Isaiah says: “And I built a tower in the middle of it,” that is, in the middle of the vineyard. The vineyard of the Lord is the house of Israel (Isaiah V, 2).

As long as this tower has a winepress—that is, an altar—and a wall around it, namely, the assistance of the angels, and the wild boar, the devil, does not enter the vineyard, it is neither squalid nor dark. Rather, because it has received its name from the Lord who shines, it is called a city set upon a mountain which cannot be hidden.

The tower, therefore, once belonging to the flock and people of God—for the wicked tenants killed the son of the householder (Luke XX)—is now squalid and abandoned. And under the name *Ariel*, it cries from the ground in Isaiah.

This is the tower of the daughter of Zion, or, as Symmachus translated it into Greek, “It is the daughter of Zion” (Isaiah XXIX).

> **Note:** Victorius reads, “and under the name Israel it cries,” etc. The Palatine codices read *est filiae*; I would rather read the nominative *filia* for *filiae*. Symmachus’s translation too may seem corrupt: instead of *ipsa est filia Sion*, one should read ἀπόκρυφος ἐστὶ θυγάτηρ Σιών, “the daughter of Zion is hidden.” Perhaps *ἀπόκρυφος* was changed into *ipsa* through a copyist’s error. Certainly the Barberini Greek Hexaplaric codex, cited by Montfaucon, gives Symmachus’s words as ἀπόκρυφος θυγάτηρ Σιών. In the commentaries on Isaiah, chapter 26: concerning Wisdom we read that, according to the Hebrew, she says in Proverbs, “God possessed me, the beginning of his ways,” although some manuscripts wrongly have “creature” in place of “possession.” Recall what we noted on that passage.

To this tower God will come, or the first power, which power is the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem.

The first Power comes to this tower—that is, the first Principality, the one who said: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last” (Revelation XXII, 13). And he who speaks in the person of the assumed human being says in Proverbs: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, for his works” (Proverbs VIII, 22), or, as it is written in Hebrew: “The Lord possessed me.”

> **Note:** Two Palatine manuscripts read: “She bore a posthumous child, the namesake of the captured ark of God and of the people.”

For *canani* does not mean “he created me,” but “he possessed me,” “he had me.”

The first Power comes, and the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem, so that after the first there may also be a second. For just as he himself confidently says, “I am the light of the world” (John VIII, 12), so he grants his disciples that they too may be called the light of the world, saying to them: “You are the light of the world” (John VI).

Calling himself the true vine in the Gospel, he speaks through Jeremiah concerning believers: “But I planted you as a completely fruitful, wholly true vine” (Jeremiah XXI).

And although he is the living bread descending from heaven, he gave it to the disciples so that they might be called bread. Hence the Apostle Paul also speaks confidently: “For we are all one bread” (1 Corinthians XVII).

In this manner, then, the first Power and the kingdom enter Jerusalem, so that he may make those who believe in it a power and a kingdom.

As for what is read in certain books—“And the first Principality shall enter [or, “may enter”], the kingdom of the daughter of Zion, and from [or, “is from”] Babylon”—we should know that this has been added, since it is found neither in the Hebrew nor among the other interpreters. It seems to me that the reference was to the Babylonian captivity, namely, that the people, coming out from there, came to Jerusalem.

It follows: “And now why are you drawn together in grief?” Or, as it is written in the Seventy: “And now why have you known evils?” To her, he says, the Lord is to come, together with the first Power and the kingdom.

Why now are you drawn together in grief, or why have you known evils? The answer immediately follows: “Because there is no king for you, and your counsellor has perished, because pain has seized you like a woman in labour.”

Or certainly, although you have all these things, through your fault you do not deserve the help either of a king or of a counsellor.

What he says, “Why have you known evils?” must be understood in the sense that everyone who deserves and suffers evils is said to know evils and to be ignorant of good. In accordance with what is also written in the First Book of Kings: “The sons of Heli, sons of pestilence, did not know God” (1 Kings II, 12). And elsewhere: “Whoever keeps the commandment will not know an evil word” (Ecclesiastes VIII, 5). And to sinners the Lord says: “Depart from me, you who work iniquity, for I do not know you” (Psalm VI, 9).

Conversely, concerning the Lord: “He who knew no sin was made sin for us” (1 Corinthians V, 21)—with “God the Father” understood.

The king and the Angel of the great counsel are understood to be the Saviour, who perished for the unbelieving people. Pains seized them like a woman in labour: for Israel, thinking that it would obtain sovereignty, was suddenly devastated. And just as a woman in labour cannot escape pain, so it could neither avoid nor delay the captivity that was approaching and the army surrounding the city.

Let us read the Scriptures, and we shall never find holy women giving birth in pain, except Rachel. Because she was on the road and at the hippodrome—that is, at the course of the horses sold in Egypt—she gave birth to a son of pain, whom the father later called “son of the right hand” (Genesis XXXV).

Eve, expelled from paradise and hearing, “In pains you shall give birth” (Genesis III, 16), is described as having given birth in pain. The wife of Phinehas, stricken and unable to rise, like the woman whom the devil bound in the Gospel (Luke XIII), gave birth after she had learned of the capture of the ark of God and the ruin of the people (1 Samuel IV).

But Sarah, because she was holy and her womanly functions had ceased, said when Isaac was born: “The Lord has made laughter for me; whoever hears will rejoice with me” (Genesis XXI, 6).

The pains, then, which seized the tower of the flock are the pains of the underworld and the pains of death. They surrounded and enclosed the Saviour also, but they could not seize him, as he himself says in the seventeenth Psalm:

“The pains of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me; the pains of hell encircled me.”

Some think that the squalid or dark tower and the daughter of Jerusalem refer to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of the saints. Concerning it the Apostle says: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews XII, 22). It is squalid as long as its children are not brought back to it, and as long as king and counsellor are not in it, and pains like those of a woman in labour have seized it because it has given birth in vain, seeing so many of its children killed.

### (Verse 10)

“Writhe and labour, daughter of Zion, like a woman in labour; for now you shall go out from the city and dwell in the region, and you shall come even to Babylon. There you shall be delivered; there the Lord shall redeem you from the hand of your enemies.”

The Seventy: “Writhe and act manfully, daughter of Zion, like a woman giving birth; for now you shall go out from the city and dwell in the plain, and you shall come even to Babylon. From there he shall deliver you, and from there the Lord your God shall redeem you from the hand of your enemies.”

She is commanded to grieve or give birth, and afterward it is added, “Act manfully.” This command is not given without reason: she must endure her pains patiently, go out from the city, dwell in the plain or region, and come as far as Babylon. When she has bravely borne the captivity inflicted on account of her sin, then the Lord will deliver her and her God will redeem her from the hand of her enemies.

After she has been delivered, she will say to those who insult her:

“Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise. Though I walk in darkness, the Lord is my light. I shall bear the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause and executes my judgment, and brings me out into the light; then I shall see his righteousness, and my enemy shall behold it and be covered with shame” (below, VIII, 9).

Hence this is sung with a fitting voice in the Psalms: “He will not be angry for ever, nor will the Lord threaten for eternity” (Psalm CII, 9).

That “Writhe and act manfully” pertains to the salvation of the one who grieves and acts manfully is also testified by Jesus son of Nave, to whom the Lord says: “Be strong and act manfully” (Joshua I, 1).

The daughter of Zion grieves and acts manfully because she has gone out of the city barefoot and naked, is to be led captive into the plain of Shinar, and is to remain in Babylon until Zerubbabel comes, and Ezra—whose name means “helper”—and delivers her from the hand of the Chaldaeans.

Although this is clear according to the literal sense, it seems to me that it can also be understood of the soul which, because of sin, has been expelled from the Church and handed over to the enemy and avenger for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved. It goes out from the city which the river’s rushing makes glad, and dwells not on the mountain where it had previously been, but in the plain through which the Assyrians’ army wanders. It remains amid the confusion of its vices; and after it has worn chains, turned the millstone, and ground flour for the Babylonians, it comes to itself and says:

“How many hired servants of my father have bread in abundance, while I perish here from hunger!” (Luke XV, 17).

Then, returning to its father’s house, it is received by the most merciful father and redeemed from the hand of the harshest master.

Let us set forth an example, so that what is commanded to the daughter of Zion—“Writhe and act manfully like a woman in labour”—may be understood as referring not to punishment but to her benefit.

Paul says to the Galatians: “My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV, 19). He grieved and was in labour for so long [or, “as long as”] until, through repentance, he gave birth again to those who had perished through sin.

Imagine a physician saying to someone feverish or wounded: “Grieve and act manfully; endure thirst; bear the cautery, so that more certain health may follow.”

### (Verses 11–13)

“And now many nations have been gathered against you, saying: ‘Let her be stoned, and let our eye look upon Zion.’ But they themselves did not know the thoughts of the Lord, nor did they understand his counsel, because he gathered them like hay on the threshing floor.

“Rise and thresh, daughter of Zion, for I shall make your horn iron, and I shall make your hoofs bronze, and you shall crush many peoples. And you shall slay—or, according to another reading, ‘I shall slay’—their spoils for the Lord, and their strength for the Lord of the whole earth.”

The Seventy: “And now many nations have been gathered against you, saying: ‘Let us insult her, and let our eyes look upon Zion.’ But they did not know the thoughts of the Lord, nor did they understand his counsel, because he gathered them like sheaves on the threshing floor.

“Rise and thresh them, daughter of Zion, for I shall make your horns iron, and I shall make your hoofs bronze, and you shall crush many peoples. And you shall vow their multitude to the Lord, and their strength to the Lord of the whole earth.”

O Jerusalem, O daughter of Zion, who will come as far as Babylon and there be delivered, and whom the Lord will redeem from the hand of your enemies: meanwhile [or, according to another reading, again] many nations have been gathered against you. They speak as though of an adulteress and say, “Let her be stoned, and let our eye look upon her.”

Or, as it is written in the Seventy: “Let us insult her and rejoice, and let our eyes despise Zion.” They did not know the Lord’s will and counsel, because the nations had been gathered against you for this purpose: that you might crush them like hay or straw on the threshing floor.

Rise, therefore, daughter of Zion, and with the iron horns which I promise to give you, and the bronze hoofs which you are to receive, winnow and crush the peoples, and kill them for the Lord of the whole earth. For he is pleased with such a victim and such a sacrifice.

The Jews, seeing that these things have not yet been fulfilled, promise themselves Christ’s coming in the future, and say that all nations will serve the Jewish people, and that the Roman empire—which they interpret under the name Edom—must be crushed by their hoofs and scattered by their horns. How foolish this is can easily be demonstrated from all the Scriptures; but that belongs to another occasion.

We, therefore, who follow not the letter that kills but the spirit that gives life, say that many nations of demons are gathered against the daughter of Zion, which is interpreted as the Church. In the present age, which is set in wickedness, they insult her and rejoice in the killing of her children, knowing neither the thoughts of the Lord nor recognizing his counsel.

“For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians II, 8).

He will therefore gather them like sheaves on the threshing floor, so that whatever seemed thorny, scattered, empty, and light may be crushed by her hoofs and winnowed by her horns, and the pure grain that remains may be offered as a gift to the Lord.

But what does he signify when he says: “You shall crush many peoples, and you shall consecrate their multitude to the Lord, and their strength to the Lord of the whole earth”?

Let us read Numbers, Joshua son of Nave, and the First Book of Kings, and we shall see how, among the nations that had been subjected, when all had perished by the sword, gold and silver—and from human beings as well as from beasts a fixed amount of spoil—was consecrated to the Lord.

Finally, Achan, who stole something from the ban devoted to destruction at Jericho, troubled the people; and from his sin a name was given to the valley, *Emek Achor*, that is, “valley of tumult” or “of disturbances” (Joshua VII).

> **Note:** We said in the notes on the *Book of Places* that the allusion must depend on the name.

To show that, according to the Seventy interpreters, who said, “You shall consecrate their multitude to the Lord, and their strength to the Lord of the whole earth,” this consecration should be understood in a good sense: Theodotion translated “multitude” as “gifts”; the Fifth Edition has “benefit,” that is, ὠφέλειαν; Symmachus has “profit,” that is, τὸ κέρδος αὐτῶν, “their gain.”

> **Note:** Victorius adds, “that is, δῶρα,” and immediately afterward, “their profit.”

[Col. 1195B] **(Chapter V.—Verse 1.)** Now you will be laid waste, daughter of the robber; they have laid siege against us; with a rod they will strike the cheek of the judge of Israel.

**The Septuagint:** Now the daughter will be obstructed with an obstruction; he has imposed distress upon us; with a rod they will strike the cheek of the tribe of Israel.

This does not mean that one tribe strikes the cheek of another, but that others strike the tribe of Israel on the cheek. I promised you, daughter of Zion, that a time would come when I would make your horn iron and your hoofs bronze, and, after crushing the multitude of demons, you would offer to the Lord whatever they had previously possessed (Rom. XI), the Lord of the whole earth. But since this will happen when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel has been saved, for the present, according to your merits, you are to be laid waste—or, as it is found in Hebrew, cut down. For, according to the Apostle (Phil. III), you are not called “Circumcision,” but “mutilation.” Nor do I call you my daughter, but the daughter of a robber, which in Hebrew is called BATH GEDUD (), that is, “the daughter of the devil, always girded for plunder.” For you made my house a den of robbers, resisted me, and your sons laid siege against me, against the Son, and against my Spirit.

[Note: Two manuscripts add, “and the Holy Spirit.”]

Is this not an insult to the Trinity, when, because of you, the Romans struck the head of the judge of Israel with a rod and a reed, saying, “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is the one who struck you?” (Matt. XXVI, 60); or when one of your servants struck him on the cheek, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?” (John XVIII, 22)? This is according to the Hebrew, to which Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition also agree.

According to the Septuagint, however, the meaning is much higher and seems to be understood as beginning from its proper source. “Now the synagogue is obstructed with an obstruction”; and those who will have been shut up within it will say, “He has imposed distress upon us”; and, subjected to Roman authorities, they will be struck on the cheek—the tribe of Israel. For the Lord has removed from Judea and Jerusalem “the strong and mighty man, the wise architect, and the discerning hearer” [another reading: “helper”], and its ways remain closed and blocked to this day; nor can it escape from captivity, but it is oppressed by an exceedingly harsh rule (Isa. III, 1–2).

If, however, we wish to understand this as spoken concerning the Church, “Now the daughter will be obstructed with an obstruction,” let us produce the example from Hosea in which the adulteress speaks: “I will go after my lovers, who gave me my bread and my water, my clothing and my linen, my oil, and everything that benefits me” (Hos. II, 5). Later, God, wishing to prevent this wicked intention, does not allow her to fulfill what she desires, but obstructs her roads so that she cannot reach her lovers and fornicate any longer. For he says:

“Therefore, behold, I will obstruct her roads with stakes, and I will block her paths; she will not find her way. She will pursue her lovers but will not overtake them; she will seek them but will not find them. And she will say: I will go and return to my former husband, because it was better for me then” (ibid., VI, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Instead of “higher” (*altior*), which is the true reading of our manuscripts, as the context itself makes clear, the other reading has hitherto prevailed.]

Observe the progress of the Lord’s work. The adulteress, finding no way and unable to proceed where she wished, constrained by necessity, returns to her former husband and confesses that it is better for her in the house of her former husband than it once was with her lovers; and through tribulations and blows Israel is instructed.

Hence, also, it is mystically said to David, under the figure of Christ:

“If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges. But I will not remove my mercy from him” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 31 ff.).

God therefore imposed tribulation upon the daughter of Israel, and angels appointed over punishments will strike her on the cheek. And lest you perhaps not know which daughter is obstructed with an obstruction and placed in distress, it immediately adds and says, “the tribe of Israel.” We are Israel, who perceive God with the mind; to distinguish us the Apostle says, “See Israel according to the flesh” (I Cor. XIX, 18). For he would never call Israel carnal unless he knew that there was also a spiritual Israel.

[Col. 1196D] **(Verse 2.)** And you, Bethlehem Ephratha, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, from you there will go forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his coming forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.

**The Septuagint:** And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephratha,

[Note: With the assistance of Palatine manuscripts we have removed the word “by no means,” which had been inserted here. The manuscripts at Brescia, likewise, which Victor consulted, do not have it; nor does the Greek text itself, whose wording Saint Jerome reports in the more accurate books as: ὀλιγοστὸς εἶ τοῦ εἶναι ἐν χιλιάσι Ἰούδα, “You are little, so as to be among the thousands of Judah.” Yet we do not deny that Theodoret read it with the negative particle, μὴ ὀλιγοστὸς, and thus preferred the Barberini manuscript, although at its margin it has ὀλιγοστὸς without μὴ. Finally, among the Latins Saint Cyprian, in Book II of the *Testimonies*, has “not insignificant.” Nor does it matter, as Victor says, that the Evangelist Matthew has a different wording, since Jerome clearly asserts here that the testimony cited by Matthew agrees neither with the Hebrew nor with the Septuagint interpreters. That the negative word was absent from the commonly received Septuagint edition Jerome plainly asserts to Pammachius in his book *On the Best Kind of Translation*, where he says at length: “Instead of ‘You are by no means the least among the rulers of Judah,’ the Septuagint reads, ‘You are small, to be among the thousands of Judah’; in Hebrew: ‘You are little among the thousands of Judah.’ I add one point worthy of notice: the Hebrew word [omitted in the supplied text] signifies not only ‘little’ but, conversely, ‘great’; this is also noted by Pochocchio in the miscellaneous notes to the *Gate of Moses*, chapter 2. Indeed, for Rabbi Tanchum, the learned Jew, it signifies not so much something small as something great in value.”]

you are least, to be among the thousands of Judah; from you there will go forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his coming forth is from the beginning, from the days of the age.

In the Gospel according to Matthew (Matt. II), when the magi had come from the East and Herod asked the scribes where the Lord Christ was to be born, they are reported to have answered: “In Bethlehem of the land of Judah.” Adding the prophet’s testimony, they said: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will go forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel.”

That this testimony agrees neither with the Hebrew nor with the Septuagint interpreters is evident even without my saying so. I think that Matthew, wishing to accuse the scribes and priests of negligence toward the reading of divine Scripture, set it down in this form because it was spoken by them.

There are some who maintain that almost all testimonies taken from the Old Testament contain this sort of error: either the order or the words are changed, and sometimes the meaning itself is different, because the apostles or evangelists did not extract the testimonies from the book but relied upon memory, which sometimes fails.

Let us therefore expound the Hebrew: “And you, Bethlehem”—that is, “house of bread”—“which are called Ephratha, are indeed little among the cities of Judah; compared with so many thousands, you are scarcely a small village. But from this small village Christ will go forth, who is ruler in Israel.”

And lest you think that he is only of the lineage of David, to whom I promised, saying, “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. CXXXI, 11),

[Note: Victor changes this to “your throne,” following the Vulgate, the Greek, and the Hebrew.]

the assumption of flesh does not hinder his divine majesty. For he was born from me before all the ages, and the creator of time is not confined within time. He is the one to whom I also said in another psalm, “Before Lucifer I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3). “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). He was in the beginning with God. And therefore his coming forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.

That Bethlehem itself is Ephratha is shown by the Book of Genesis, in which Scripture records: “Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephratha, that is, Bethlehem” (Gen. XXXV).

The two names signify a mystery. Bethlehem is called “house of bread” because of the living bread that came down from heaven (John VI). Ephratha, interpreted as “sees fury” (*furorem videt*),

[Note: The word *videt* (“he sees”), which is clearly the second part of the etymology of the name Ephratha, was lacking in the books hitherto published; our manuscripts supply it. I would nevertheless prefer *vides* (“you see”), both because the word itself has the sound of the second person and because the *Book of Names* on the Psalter likewise has: “Ephratha: you indeed see.”]

is so called because of Herod’s madness: deceived by the magi, he became exceedingly angry and sent men to kill all the infants in Bethlehem,

[Col. 1198A] and throughout all its borders, from two years old and under [another reading: “and below”], according to the time which he had carefully ascertained from the magi. Because of the immense quantity of blood, a voice was heard on high: “Rachel weeping and wailing for her children” (Jer. XXXI).

Let us read, at least according to the Septuagint interpreters, in Joshua, where the cities and towns of the tribe of Judah are described. Among other things, this too is written: “Tekoa and Ephratha, that is Bethlehem, and Phagor, and Aetham, and Culon, and Tami” [another reading: “Tatami”], “and Soris, and Caraem, and Gallim, and Baether, and Manocho, eleven cities and their villages” (Josh. XV).

[Note: In the Palatine manuscript: “Etham, and Chulon, and Dathan, and Sores, and Carem, and Galim, and Techer, and Manucho, twelve cities and their villages.” One manuscript of the Utrecht Library, cited by Reland, has: “Theco . . . Fagor, and Erhan, and Caulon, and Dathan, and Sores, and Corem, and Salim, and Tether, and Manacho,” etc.]

This is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any other interpreter. Whether it was erased from the ancient books through the malice of the Jews, lest Christ should appear to have arisen from the tribe of Judah, or whether it was added by the Septuagint, we do not know with certainty.

Nevertheless, we can also establish the same point from the Book of Judges, namely, that Bethlehem is in the tribe of Judah. For it is written: “There was a Levite dwelling on the sides of the house” [another reading: “the mountain”] “of Ephraim,” and he took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem of Judah. His concubine became angry with him and went away to her father’s house in Bethlehem of Judah” (Judg. XIX, 1).

It is appropriately said “in Bethlehem of Judah,” to distinguish it from the Bethlehem situated in Galilee, as I found in the same book of Joshua.

In our language Ephratha can signify καρποφόρον, “fruit-bearing,” “fertile,” and this too displays the same mystery as “house of bread.”

[Col. 1198C] **(Verse 3.)** Therefore he will give them up until the time when she who is in labor gives birth, and the remnant of his brothers will return to the sons of Israel.

**The Septuagint:** Therefore he will give them up until the time of her who is in labor; she will give birth [another reading: “those in labor will give birth”], and the remnant of his brothers will return to the sons of Israel.

Because Christ, who is ruler in Israel, went forth from Bethlehem, which is Ephratha, and because his coming forth occurred not only at the time when he was seen in the flesh but from the beginning of eternity, or from the beginning of the age—for he himself always spoke through the prophets, and the word of God came to be in their hand [another reading: “of the saints”]. Therefore he will give the Jews up and allow them to reign until the time of the woman in labor, when this will be fulfilled:

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. LIV, 1, according to the Septuagint).

When the barren woman has borne seven children, and she who had many children has become weak, and the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in place of the offense of the Jewish people,

[Col. 1199A] then all Israel will be saved, and the remnant of his brothers will return to the sons of Israel. And when the prophet Elijah comes—for his name is interpreted “The Lord is God”—he will turn the hearts of the fathers to the sons and the heart of the sons to their fathers (Luke I, 17). The last people will then be joined to the ancient people, so that they may truly be called sons of Abraham when they believe in the one whom Abraham saw and rejoiced to see (John VIII).

What, then, is the time in which the barren woman will give birth? In my judgment, it is the time of which Isaiah speaks: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. XLIX, 8). Understanding this as spoken of the time of Christ, Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 21).

I think that the same thing is mystically indicated by what is written in Ecclesiastes: “A time for giving birth, and a time for dying” (Eccl. III, 2). At the time when the people of the Gentiles was born from the barren woman, the synagogue lost its children.

It can also be understood in another way: The Lord will give up the temple, Jerusalem, and the Jews until the time when the virgin gives birth. After she has given birth, and the child has been born and has received the spoils of Samaria and the power of Damascus, when the people of the Jews have been slain, the remnant of Israel will be saved.

And the brothers of Christ—that is, the apostles—will return to the faith of the prophets and patriarchs who proclaimed the coming Christ, and the prophetic utterance of the psalm will be fulfilled: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you,” and the rest that follows (Ps. XLIV, 17).

[Col. 1199C] **(Verse 4.)** And he will stand and feed them in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God; and they will return, because now he will be magnified to the ends of the earth.

**The Septuagint:** And he will stand [and he will see], and the Lord will feed his flock in strength, and they will be in the glory of the name of the Lord their God, because now they will be magnified to the ends of the earth.

[Note: The words “and he will see,” which are also absent from the Greek copy at Complutum, are not recognized by the Palatine manuscripts; they likewise omit the word “his flock” shortly afterward.]

After the sun of righteousness has gone forth from the summit of the heavens and reached their limits, and the woman in labor has given birth, and the remnant of his brothers has returned to the sons of Israel, then the Lord himself, who previously walked and, while accompanying those who were on the road, did not yet have a fixed step, will stand and feed them in the strength of the Lord, so that they can say:

“The Lord is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing. He has placed me in a place of pasture; he has nourished me beside waters of refreshment; he has restored my soul” (Ps. XXII, 1).

He feeds them not only in the strength of the Lord but also in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God, when he says to the Father:

“Holy Father, preserve them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we also are. When I was with them, I preserved them in your name; those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished” (John XVII, 11).

“And they will return,” or, as Symmachus more aptly translated it, “they will dwell.” For the Hebrew verb JASUBU () has both meanings. They will dwell in the Church of the Lord, because Christ has been magnified to the ends of the earth.

Or, according to the Septuagint, because they themselves will be magnified together with their shepherd to the end of the earth, so that “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

[Col. 1199D] **(Verse 5.)** And this man will be peace: when the Assyrian comes into our land and when he treads upon our houses.

**The Septuagint:** And this will be peace: when the Assyrian comes upon your land and when he ascends over your region.

When the devil comes—for he is interpreted as εὐθύνων, that is, “one who reproves and corrects”—upon the land and region of believers, whom the Lord will feed in strength and in the majesty of the name of the Lord their God; when he tramples them with various tribulations and, like a proud man, ascends over and crushes the houses of our souls, that is, our bodies, yet nothing separates us from the love of Christ, then Christ’s peace, or Christ himself, will be in us. And it will be said of the holy person: “The enemy will profit nothing against him.”

Let us give an example, so that what we are saying may become clearer. The Assyrian came upon the land that once belonged to Paul and ascended over his region when he was in labors beyond measure, in wounds more abundantly, in prisons exceedingly, in deaths frequently; when from the Jews he received five times forty lashes less one, was beaten with rods three times, was stoned once,

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts supply the words absent from the printed books: “he suffered shipwreck three times.”]

suffered shipwreck three times, spent a day and a night in the depths of the sea, and endured dangers from robbers, dangers from false brothers, dangers from his own race, and dangers from the Gentiles. But in all these things he conquered because of him who loved him. And therefore he was filled with peace, because he had been filled with insults (I Cor. XI).

At the coming of Christ, which they pretend to await, the Jews insist that all these things will occur literally.

[Col. 1200A] **(Verse 6.)** And we will raise up over him seven shepherds and eight chief men; and they will feed the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod with his spears; and he will deliver from Assyria when he comes into our land and when he treads upon our borders.

**The Septuagint:** And seven shepherds and eight bites of men will arise against him; and they will feed Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod in its pit; and he will deliver from Assyria when it comes upon your land and when it ascends over your borders.

Where we have rendered “chief men,” and where the Hebrew reads NESICHE ADAM (), Symmachus translated “anointed men” (Christos hominum); Theodotion and the Fifth Edition, “rulers of men”; Aquila, “weighty” or “appointed men,” that is, καθισταμένους.

[Note: Martianay had read κατεσταμένους. We often silently correct this kind of matter elsewhere.]

Again, where I and Aquila translated “with his spears,” with “the land of Nimrod” understood, Symmachus renders “within its gates” (ἐντὸς πυλῶν αὐτῆς); Theodotion, “in their gates”; and the Fifth Edition, ἐν παραξίφησιν αὐτῶν, which we may render “with their short swords.” In Hebrew, however, BAPHETHEE () is written.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscript of Saint-Cyran and another of Saint-Benoît at Fleury. The Cluniac manuscript has *Baphethem*, which I think is a copyist’s error: instead of *Baphethee* he wrote *Baphetem*. It is possible that, from Theodotion and the Fifth Edition, *Baphetheem* could have been read in Hebrew, meaning “in their gates” or “with their short swords.” But the reading of the other manuscripts must be retained, since it is clear that Jerome read in Hebrew the feminine suffix of the third-person singular; for he translated, “with his spears,” with “the land of Nimrod” understood.

MART.—Our manuscripts have *Baphaethee*; in others Martianay found *Baphethem*.]

[Col. 1201A] Then there will be peace, when the remnant of Christ’s brothers has returned to the sons of Israel, and the Assyrian has come into our land, and, aided by the Lord, we have swiftly crushed beneath our feet the one who wanted to trample upon our houses.

For the Lord himself says: “We will raise up over him seven shepherds and eight chief men,” or “bites of men.” We will raise them up—I and my Son and the Holy Spirit—in accordance with what is written in Genesis: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). And at the beginning of Obadiah: “Rise, and let us go up against her in battle.”

I think that the seven shepherds are all the patriarchs, prophets, and holy men who served the hebdomad, that is, the Old Testament. The eight bites of men, or

[Col. 1201B] eight chief men, and, as Symmachus translated, “anointed men,” are all those of the New Testament who, from the apostles to the present age, have bitten the Assyrian and torn him with their teeth.

Hence Ecclesiastes also commands: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. XI). And in the temple of Ezekiel, which signifies the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem, one ascends by seven and eight steps (Ezek. XL). In the Psalter there are fifteen steps by which, through the hebdomad and the ogdoad, we ascend to sing praises to God. On the eighth day spiritual circumcision is celebrated; in the temple of the Jews the Sabbath is destroyed; and certain psalms are entitled “For the Eighth.”

These seven shepherds and eight bites of men, then, will feed Assyria with the sword. For the living and effective word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword (Heb. IV, 12), was sent by him who came to cast a sword upon the earth, so that two might be divided into three (Matt. X).

And they will feed the land of Nimrod—whose name is interpreted “descending temptation”—in its pit. For the land of the giant, hunter, and proud man who rebels against the Lord is not in the mountains but in pits. He fell like lightning from heaven and is always found among beasts. And because he is a hunter, he searches barren trees and forests.

[Note: Saint Ambrose agrees in his commentary on Psalm CXVIII: “We find no righteous hunter anywhere in the entire sequence of the divine writings.” And the author of the *Breviary on the Psalms*, under the name of our Jerome, says on Psalm XC: “Esau was a hunter because he was a sinner; and we find no holy hunter at all in the sacred Scriptures.”]

As far as I can recall from my memory, I have never read of a hunter in a favorable sense. Ishmael and Esau were hunters (Gen. XVI and XXVII), and they preceded the Jewish people as types. One of them was the son of an Egyptian woman, walking according to the flesh and living according to the flesh; the other lost his birthright for a dish of lentils and, envying his brother’s blessings, drove him away to Mesopotamia.

Therefore, once the land of Nimrod has been reduced to its pits: “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (Prov. XXVI, 7); and “he who opened a pit and dug it will fall into the pit he made, and his pain will return upon his own head, and upon his own crown his iniquity will descend” (Ps. VII, 16–17).

[Col. 1202A] And when the Assyrian has been pierced by the seven shepherds and the eight bites, Christ will have delivered us from the hand of Assyria, which had come upon our land and wished to trample upon the borders of Israel.

As for what Symmachus says, “And they will feed the land of Assyria with the sword, and the region of Nimrod within its gates,” this should be understood to mean that the strong man will be bound in his own house and the adversary wounded.

According to Aquila and the Fifth Edition, he will be pierced by the short swords and spears of the seven shepherds and the eight anointed men.

[Note: Martianay retained “the eight Christian men.”]

(Vers. 7 ff.) “And the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many peoples, like dew from the Lord and like drops upon the grass, which does not await a man and does not tarry for the children of men. And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forests and like a young lion among flocks of sheep; when it passes through, tramples, and seizes, there is no one to rescue. Your hand shall be exalted over your enemies, and all your foes shall perish.

“And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord, that I will remove your horses from your midst and destroy your chariots. I will destroy the cities of your land and demolish all your fortifications. I will remove sorceries from your hand, and there shall be no divinations among you. I will make your carved images perish, and your statues from your midst, and you shall no longer worship the works of your hands. I will tear out your sacred groves from your midst and destroy your cities, and I will execute vengeance in anger and indignation upon all the nations that have not listened.”

The Septuagint: “And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like dew falling from the Lord and like lambs upon the grass, so that no one may be gathered together or be among the children of men. And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among beasts in the forest, and like a young lion among flocks of sheep: as when it passes through, divides, and snatches away, with no one to rescue. Your hand shall be lifted up over those who trouble you, and all your enemies shall be destroyed.

“And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord, that I will kill your horses from your midst and destroy your chariots. I will overthrow the cities of your land and remove all your fortifications. I will remove your sorceries from your hands, and there shall be no speakers among you. I will destroy your carved images and your statues from your midst, and you shall no longer worship the works of your hands. I will cut down the sacred groves from your midst, demolish your cities, and execute vengeance in anger and fury upon the nations, because they did not listen.”

After we have been delivered from Assyria, when he comes upon our land and advances against our borders, and after we have been delivered by the Lord, who raised up against him seven shepherds and eight leaders of men, the remnant of Jacob—which we understand as the apostles and the first Church from the Jews—shall be in the midst of many peoples, like dew falling from the Lord. For the hearts of the peoples were burning with the devil’s fiery arrows, and all the nations, committing adultery against God, had hearts like a furnace kindled with fire (Hos. 7). Therefore the dew falling from the Lord became health for the sick.

What we read concerning Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael (Dan. 3)—that the spirit of whistling dew extinguished the fiery furnace—let us understand generally of all people: in the midst of all the nations, the apostles’ teaching was like dew from the Lord. [Note: Col. 1203D: Hitherto the reading “as though you were sprinkled by the Lord” was less correct. Our manuscripts correct it.]

The following words—“And like lambs upon the grass, so that no one may gather them together, nor may they be among the children of men”—let us understand of those among the nations who refused to believe: the apostles and the remnant of Jacob are over them like lambs cropping the grass and cutting down the herbage with their teeth. They will do this so that those who refused to be angels, receiving the spiritual dew, may not be gathered among human beings or counted among the rational portion, but that it may be said of them: “They are not in the labor of men, nor are they scourged with mankind” (Ps. 72:5).

“And the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of the nations like a lion among beasts in the forest and like a young lion among flocks of sheep.” For the Lord Jesus is the one of whom it is prophesied in Genesis: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you have arisen; lying down, you have slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub” (Gen. 49:9). And elsewhere: “He lay down and rested like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who will rouse him?” [Note: Victorius restores the wording in accordance with the Greek text: “who will rouse him?” Erasmus and Martianay, omitting the word “who,” read “he has roused him.”]

He also gave this command to his apostles, to whom he had said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), so that, just as no one can resist a lion among beasts or a lion’s cub among sheep, so they—delivered from the hand of the Assyrian and from the hand of the devil—might seize the beasts and the flocks. For “the Lord will save both men and beasts” (Ps. 35:7).

They would seize them, not in order to kill them, but in order to divide them—that is, to separate them from the unbelievers—and no one would be able to resist them. As the lion and the lion’s cub roam among the beasts and sheep, so the hand of God is exalted over those who had previously afflicted either God or the remnant of Israel.

“And all his enemies shall be destroyed”—not because the enemies perish and cease to exist, but because they perish insofar as they are enemies. Thus it is written to the Thessalonians: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:8). This killing does not signify annihilation, but the cessation of the wicked life in which they had previously lived badly. The text continues: “And he will destroy him by the manifestation of his coming.” He would never destroy him if “killing” meant annihilation, since he would already have ceased to exist. So here too the destruction of the enemies is understood according to the Proverbs of Solomon, in which it is written: “Destruction will lodge with the impious.” It will not be perpetual and will not reduce them to nothing; rather, it will lodge with them as long as the impiety within them is consumed. For God created human beings so that they would not perish, and he did not make death.

After this comes the passage: “And it shall come to pass on that day, when your hand, O Israel, has been lifted over your enemies and all your foes have perished, I will kill your horses from your midst”—that is, from the ruling faculty (ἡγεμονικόν) of your heart, the wanton impulses that burst forth after breaking their bonds like horses—and your chariots, in which you took pleasure amid your vices, joining sin to sin and riding as though triumphing in a chariot.

“And I will destroy the cities of your land.” For you did not build the city “which makes the river of God glad” (Ps. 46:4), which is situated upon the mountains, the heavenly Jerusalem (Matt. 5:14), but the city Cain had built (Gen. 4:17). Hence they are called “cities of the earth,” built by earthly works.

“And I will remove,” he says, “all your fortifications”—namely, the riches and pomp of the world, the eloquence of rhetoricians, and the snares of dialecticians, in which you trusted as though in fortifications.

“And I will remove sorceries from your hands,” by which either you yourself were deceived by others or, having been deceived, you deceived others; “and those who speak or proclaim shall no longer be yours.” Now the world is full of speakers and proclaimers: they speak what they do not know; they teach what they have not learned; they are teachers though they had not previously been disciples. When God has taught human beings knowledge, false presumption will cease and perverse teaching will be taken away.

“And I will destroy your carved images and your statues from your midst.” Our carved images are the things made by speakers, or the things we ourselves fashion for ourselves. Hence the Law commands us not to make a carved image for ourselves and not to set up statues in our land (Exod. 20; Lev. 26), and: “You shall no longer worship the works of your hands” (Deut. 5).

Wretched is the human condition, full of folly and error. It knows that doctrines have been composed from its own judgment; it does not fail to recognize that the idol has been fabricated by itself, yet it worships the work of its own hands in place of God. Human beings bow down so that, having been deceived, they may deceive others.

A promise is added, directed to the remnant—that is, to the ὑπόλειμμα, or remnant, of Jacob: “And I will cut down the sacred groves from your midst and destroy your cities,” so that he may destroy and consume all the trees of the forests and the sacred groves that were forbidden to be planted in God’s temple, as well as the cities badly built, which he had previously called “cities of the earth.”

After he has done this to the remnant of Jacob, he will then turn to the nations whom the apostles have devoured like lambs [or: “like fields”—an alternative reading] the grass. And because they refused to receive the dew of the word, he says: “I will execute vengeance in anger and fury upon the nations, because they refused to listen.” Hence the prophet also says: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Ps. 6:1).

This has been discussed according to the Septuagint interpreters, since it possesses a spiritual meaning and we ought to connect the sense with the preceding chapters. The Hebrews, however, dream up delirious interpretations of this kind:

After the seven whom they invent and whom they wish to be shepherds, together with eight princes of Assyrian men, have defeated the Assyrians and fed the land of Nimrod with their swords—and after this has happened when the Assyrian has previously come into the land of Judah—then, they say, when Christ comes, all the remnant of Jacob that may have survived among the nations will be blessed, like dew coming from the Lord and like rain upon the grass. They will no longer hope in human beings or in the children of men, but in God.

They will be bloodthirsty and cruel in the midst of the nations and peoples, taking vengeance upon their former masters, like a lion among the beasts of the forests and like a lion’s cub among flocks of sheep, and no one will be able to resist their strength.

Then your hand, O God—or O Israel—will be exalted over the Assyrians, and all your enemies and foes, who now possess you, will perish. On that day, when you have been delivered from the nations, I will remove your horses and chariots, which are in the midst of your cities. This does not mean that Israel will then have horses and chariots, but the horses and chariots of the Assyrians that are present in the midst of your cities.

I will destroy all your cities and the fortifications that you dedicated to idols. I will remove magicians and diviners from your land, and I will make all your carved images and statues perish; you will no longer worship the works of your hands. I will also tear out and overthrow all your sacred groves and your cities that you had dedicated to idols.

When I have done this for you and have become so appeased that whatever evil is in you has been removed, then I will also take vengeance in my anger and indignation upon all the nations that refused to listen to my word.

Let fleshly Israel answer at this point: does it say that these things have happened, or that they will happen? If it recalls things already done, let it produce the historical account and provide the authority of the ancient books. Let it show that all the nations and Assyria were once subject to Israel.

But if, playing with empty hope, it thinks that what is said refers to the future, then, when Christ comes, what idols will be removed from Israel, which it does not now worship? What sacred groves will be cut down, when it has none? What cities will be overthrown, when they were destroyed long ago? What diviners will be removed, when it has none and even boasts that it possesses none? Yet for so long the daughter of Zion has been abandoned and sits without an altar and without priests; while others eat their produce, they themselves, with parched throats, promise themselves future things of which they know nothing.

## Chapter 6

### Verses 1–2

“Listen to what the Lord says: Rise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Listen [the Vulgate: ‘Let the mountains hear’], mountains, to the judgment of the Lord, and you strong foundations of the earth; for the Lord’s judgment is with his people, and he will be judged with Israel.”

The Septuagint: “Listen to what the Lord has spoken: Rise, judge before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Listen, mountains, to the judgment of the Lord, and valleys, foundations of the earth; for the Lord’s judgment is against his people, and he will be judged with Israel.”

Instead of “strong foundations of the earth,” which the Septuagint translated as “valleys, foundations of the earth,” Symmachus and Theodotion rendered the phrase “the ancient foundations of the earth.” The fifth edition retained the Hebrew word itself, *ETHANIM*, “foundations of the earth.”

The prophet’s first words, therefore, are: “Listen to what the Lord says.” Then God speaks to the prophet: “Rise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.” Again the prophet speaks to the mountains, as he had been commanded—not only to the mountains, but also to the strong foundations of the earth—and says: “Listen, mountains, to the judgment of the Lord, and you strong foundations of the earth.” He gives the reason why he summons them to listen: “For the Lord’s judgment is with his people, and he will be judged with Israel.”

In place of the mountains to which the prophet speaks and the strong foundations of the earth, the Septuagint translated “hills and valleys,” understanding, as it seems to me, that the people had done nothing worthy of the hearing of mountains, but rather of hills, which are lower than the height of mountains, or of valleys sunk into the depths.

“Rise,” he says, “contend in judgment before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.” One who either sits, lies, sleeps, or is dead is commanded to rise [an alternative reading: “silent”], in accordance with the apostle’s statement: “Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). Rise from the dead, so that you may walk in newness of life; leave the earth and strive toward higher things.

“And contend in judgment against the mountains.” I think that these signify none other than the angels, to whom the administration of human affairs has been entrusted, in agreement with the Song of Deuteronomy: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the children of Adam, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. 32:8). These are ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation.
