[Note: Col. 1205D: Rufinus, especially in his Exposition of the Creed, will shed light on the meaning of this passage: “From the beginning,” he says, “when God had made the world, he appointed and set over it certain powers of the heavenly virtues, by whom the human race might be ruled and governed. Moses indicates that this was so in the passage of Deuteronomy also cited by Jerome: ‘But even some of these . . . did not govern by the laws in which they had received from God the power entrusted to them; nor did they teach the human race to obey the divine commandments, but to obey their own transgressions; and hence written bonds were made against us . . . By this written bond, therefore, each person was held by those most wicked rulers; Christ, when he came, took it away and stripped them of this power.’ See also St. Hilary, Tract on Psalm 61, no. 2.]

“And contend in judgment,” so that, whether mountains or hills are found not to have administered the peoples worthily, either the blame may appear to rest upon me, who appointed such rulers, or the fault may be removed from the people and referred to their princes. Let us read the Apocalypse of the apostle John, in which the angels of the churches are praised and accused according to the virtues and vices of those over whom they are said to preside.

For just as sometimes the fault belongs to a bishop and sometimes to the people; just as often the teacher sins and often the disciple, and sometimes the fault is the father’s and sometimes the son’s, according as they are instructed well or badly, so in God’s judgment the crime will be referred either to the angels, if they have not done everything belonging to their office, or to the people, if, while the angels did everything, the people themselves scorned to listen.

[Note: These ideas are plainly Origen’s; nearly the same words occur in Homily 24 on Numbers: “We have often said that the care and administration of the souls who are in the Church of God are entrusted to angels, and we have shown that they also come to judgment with human beings, so that through that divine examination it may be established whether human beings sinned through their own laziness or through the negligence of their guardians and monitors.” Jerome is speaking from Origen’s opinion, not his own. Recall what we said in the immediately preceding note.]

There are those who interpret the mountains, hills, and strong foundations of the earth as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the remaining patriarchs, before whom, as witnesses [or: “as authorities”] summoned to judgment, the case of the people of Israel is to be examined.

Others think that the mountains, hills, and valleys are angels, as we said above: some serve God in the heavenly places, others preside over human beings upon this earth, and others, established in the underworld, are called the foundations of those who became earthly through their own fault. Concerning these foundations of the earth we also read elsewhere: “A fire has been kindled in my anger; it shall burn as far as the underworld below; it shall consume the earth and its foundations” (Deut. 32:22).

The strong and ancient foundations of the earth—because of which the earth has not yet passed away and, suspended over emptiness, remains balanced—are the merits of the righteous, of whom the apostle speaks: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:20). Therefore, just as the apostles, the prophets, and the entire chorus of martyrs are the strong foundations of the earth, so, according to the Septuagint, the valleys and precipices—which are more significantly called in Greek φάραγγες, “ravines”—are the foundations of those who have received the image of the earthly (χοϊκός).

“Therefore the Lord’s judgment is with his people, and he will be judged with Israel.” He who, as God, could inflict punishments for the crimes of a sinful people does not wish to appear powerful but just, and he summons sinners to judgment, in accordance with the prophetic statement: “Come, and let us be judged, says the Lord” (Isa. 43:26). Even now he compels the people of Israel, in the presence of the angels and of all creation, to answer if they have anything to say, so that “God may be justified in his words and prevail when he is judged” (Ps. 50:6).

### Verses 3 ff.

“My people, what have I done to you, and how have I wearied you? Answer me. For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and delivered you from the house of bondage, and I sent before your face Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

“My people, remember, I ask, what Balak, king of Moab, plotted against you [the Vulgate omits ‘against you’] and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you might know the righteous acts of the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I grieved you, or in what have I wearied you? Answer me. For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery, and I sent before your face Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

“My people, remember what Balak, king of Moab, plotted against you and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim [alternative readings: “Schaenis,” “Seinis,” or “Scynis”] to Gilgal, so that the righteousness of the Lord might be known.”

Instead of “righteous acts,” or “righteousness,” Symmachus translated “mercies.” Where the Septuagint has “Schaenis,” all the translators rendered the Hebrew word itself, SETTIM [שִׁטִּים].

This is the place where Balak, king of the Moabites, gathered an army against Israel. It bears the same name as the trees that still grow in the wilderness of Mount Sinai. For wherever the Septuagint has “ark of the covenant,” “altar,” “tabernacle,” and the other objects that are reported to have been made from incorruptible wood, the Hebrew has *ligna Settim*, “wood of Settim,” which resembles the tree that we commonly call the white thorn. Hence I think that the Septuagint also translated it as σχῖνον, that is, “mastic tree”; but gradually, through the error of scribes, σχοῖνοι, “ropes,” came to be read for σχίνοις, “mastic trees.”

God therefore speaks to the people of Israel, summons them to judgment, and grants them permission to argue against him: “My people, what have I done to you that I ought not to have done? Or in what have I grieved you?” Although this is not found in the Hebrew, a father grieves his son when he is beaten, and “the iniquities of the sheep” are visited “with the shepherd’s rod” [or: “the shepherd’s rod”].

“How have I wearied you?” Or, as it is written more significantly in Hebrew, “With what labor have I burdened you?” Will you interpret my benefits as an insult? Will you, longing for the melons and Egyptian meats, regret that you were brought out of the land of Egypt and delivered from the house of bondage by my aid, because I gave you as leaders Moses, my friend, Aaron, my priest, and Miriam, my prophetess?

If this seems small to you, remember the time when Balak, king of Moab, hired Balaam the diviner for payment against you, and see how, against his own will, the seer blessed you while wishing to curse you (Num. 22): from Shittim to Gilgal, surveying the entire army of Israel with his eyes and changing places, as though I could not go with one who was proceeding and cross over with one who was passing over. I did this so that my mercies and righteousness might be known to you—so greatly did I love you that, although I am daily cursed by the mouths of blasphemers, I did not permit you to be cursed by your enemy.

The Hebrews interpret the passage “from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you might know the righteous acts of the Lord” (Num. 25) in this way: “From the time when you committed fornication in Midian until the time when Saul was anointed king at Gilgal (1 Sam. 10), recall what evils you committed, how many good things I did for you, and you will recognize my mercy toward you.”

This is what God spoke according to the historical sense to fleshly Israel. But we, who desire to contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face and truly have Abraham as our father, should hear God arguing against us when we have sinned and reproving us through the greatness of his benefits.

For we once served Pharaoh and the Egyptian people, making mud and bricks. But he redeemed us who gave himself as a ransom for all, so that we who had been redeemed might say: “Let those whom the Lord redeemed say, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the lands: For his mercy is forever” (Ps. 106:1).

He also sent before our face Moses, the spiritual law, and Aaron, the great priest—not bearing the typical ephod and truth, but having on his forehead the seal of holiness with which God the Father sealed him. [Note: The Cluniac manuscript reads: “not bearing a typical ephod and veil, but bearing the truth,” that is, “bearing the Urim and Thummim,” or the breastpiece in which there was the illumination of truth. MART.]

And he sent Miriam, the prophetic utterance. He did not merely grant us this, but also delivered us from the hands of our enemies.

Let us remember what the true Balak—the devil—planned against us, wishing to devour us and lick up our assembly. Balak is interpreted as ἐκλείχων, “one who licks away” or “one who devours,” the king of paternal water; for, according to another etymology, Moab means “paternal water.”

When Balak lay in wait for us, and lay in wait through his vain people, which is interpreted as Balaam, God did not permit us to be subjected to his curses. On the contrary, he blessed us, compelled by the truth of the matter itself: the vain people of the nations, born from him who is in the skin—for Beor is interpreted as “in the skin,” always devoted to the flesh and works of death—answered on our behalf.

The vain people, born from him who is wholly in the skin, continually changing places or standing upon thorns or upon ropes, answered for us, if we follow even the error of the Vulgate edition.

According to the word of the Savior, the thorns are the cares of this age, riches, and pleasures, among which the vain people live (Matt. 13; Mark 4). That it stands upon ropes means that it stands in the bonds of sins, for each person is bound by the ropes of his sins (Prov. 5). Isaiah also bears witness, saying: “Woe to those who draw their sins like a long rope, and their iniquities like the strap of a heifer’s yoke” (Isa. 5:18).

If it stands, then it stands only upon thorns and ropes. But if it wishes to go around, it has no firm step; always wavering and unstable, it reaches Gilgal, which is interpreted as κυλισμός, “rolling,” “whirling,” or “a wallow.” [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read “voluchrum” or “volucrum.”]

Whenever we see some people rise up against us and thirst for our blood with greedy mouths, and by God’s unexpected providence they become favorable to us who had come against us, let us say: Balaam came from the ropes as far as Gilgal, so that the righteousness of God might be known.

### Verses 6–7

“With what shall I come before the Lord? Shall I bend my knee before God on high? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with year-old calves? Can the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams or with many thousands of fattened goats? Shall I give my firstborn for my crime, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?”

The Septuagint: “With what shall I take hold of the Lord? Shall I receive my exalted God? Shall I take hold of him in burnt offerings, in year-old calves? Will the Lord receive thousands of rams or ten thousand fattened goats? Shall I give my firstborn for impiety, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?” [Note: We have removed the particle “if” here; it appears neither in our manuscripts nor in the Greek.]

God had summoned the people to judgment. Knowing his sin, the people do not wish to argue but to plead, yet they have no confidence even in their prayers. Nothing worthy can be offered to God for sin, and no humility can wash away the stains of transgressions, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and calves, marrow-filled burnt offerings, and the blood of rams and fattened goats to cleanse the stains of the soul (Heb. 10).

“Shall I give,” he says, “my firstborn for my crime,” as the king of Moab is described as having done (2 Kings 3), “or the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul,” as Jephthah did when, rashly fulfilling his vow, he offered his daughter (Judg. 11)?

We therefore, who are of God’s people, knowing that “no living person will be justified in his sight” (Ps. 143:2), and saying, “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. 72:22), repent for our sins and hesitate, saying: “With what shall I take hold of the Lord? How shall I receive my exalted God?”

How will I be able to hold him as he flees? With what purity will I be able to prepare lodging for the Trinity? Shall I take hold of him in burnt offerings, so that I may offer myself entirely as a burnt offering to him, or in year-old calves, so that, leaving milk and coming to solid food, I may become worthy of the acceptable year of the Lord?

If I offer a thousand rams, if ten thousand goats, and if, understanding all the Levitical sacrifices spiritually, I present them in myself; if a thousand fall at my side and ten thousand at my left hand (Ps. 91), still I shall be able to give nothing worthy by which I may take hold of or receive God.

If I give my firstborn for impiety and the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul, I shall indeed give whatever in me is first, but for my sin and impiety I shall offer nothing worthy to God. Hence David prays and says: “Wash me more and more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I know my iniquities, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 51:2–3).

For the sin of the soul, only blood is offered worthily; and it is not the blood of calves, rams, or goats, but one’s own blood that is offered worthily. The prophet says and asks: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” And afterward he answers: “I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 116:12–15).

Yet we do not give that blood itself; we repay it. And what comparison is there, when the righteous one died for sinners and the Son of God for human beings, while we sinners and human beings die for the confession of his name?

### Verse 8

“I will show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord seeks from you: namely, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God.”

The Septuagint: “It has been declared to you, O man, what is good, or what the Lord seeks from you, except to do justice, to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with your God.”

Because you hesitate, O people of Israel—or rather, the entire human race, for my speech does not address the Jewish people alone but runs generally to every human being—about how you can appease God for your sins, if you have no sacrifices by which your impiety may be compensated, I will answer you concerning what God seeks; indeed, I already showed it earlier in the Law.

For it is written in Deuteronomy: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God seek from you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, love him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord your God and his ordinances, which I command you today, so that it may be well with you?” (Deut. 10:12–13).

The Lord seeks this from us, and, desiring our salvation, he asks to receive what benefits the giver: that we do justice—that is, that we do nothing without reason and counsel, that the mind first judge what it is about to do and then complete it in action—and that we love mercy, not being merciful as though compelled or out of necessity, since “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7).

Let us not say, “Go today and return tomorrow, and I will give it to you.” Once we have done justice and loved mercy, what reward shall we receive? We shall walk with the Lord God, as Enoch, according to the testimony of the Hebrew books, walked with God and pleased him, and “he was not found, because God took him” (Gen. 5:24; Sir. 44:16).

You asked: “In what shall I attain the Lord, or in what shall I take hold of him?” I promise you something greater: do justice, love mercy, and you will walk with your God.

Or certainly, walking with God is not a reward but a command. Just as we are commanded to do justice and love mercy, so we are instructed to be prepared to walk with the Lord our God. We must sleep at no hour and be secure at no time, but always await the coming of the master of the household and fear the day of judgment; and in the night of this age say: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2).

[Note: Here, prudent reader, you have the restored genuine Hebrew reading *Esne*, which the printed editions alter to *Tsenea*, failing to read the letter *he* at the beginning of the word and following the present-day Masoretic pointing. You also have Theodotion’s complete reading, ending with the word Ἐλωαίχ, which Erasmus and, after him, Marianus changed into the Greek words Θεοῦ σου, because they did not pay sufficient attention to the reading of the manuscript copies. These teach us that Theodotion retained the Hebrew word itself, which he read *Eloaich*, so as to represent all the elements of the word more carefully. MART.]

Theodotion expressed the word ESNE ()—which the Septuagint translated as “to be ready” and which we rendered “to walk carefully”—more significantly as καὶ ἀσφαλίζου τοῦ πορεύεσθαι μετὰ Ἐλωαίχ, that is, “and take careful heed to walk with your God.” [Note: We restore ἀσφαλίζου, as Erasmus formerly did and as the Palatine manuscripts now prefer. Martianay’s ἀσφαλίζον is less correct.]

Or, as the fifth edition translated it, καὶ φροντίζειν, that is, “to act carefully and to take this concern upon yourself: to walk with your God.” For whoever says that he believes in Christ ought to walk as he walked (1 John 2:6). And the apostle Paul says: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1).

“The voice of the Lord cries out to the city, and salvation will be for those who fear your name” [an alternative reading: “his name”].

The Septuagint: “The voice of the Lord will cry out to the city, and he will save those who fear his name.”

In Hebrew this is the beginning of another chapter; among the Septuagint interpreters, however, it is the conclusion of the preceding one. Its meaning is: “Your God seeks nothing else from you, O man, except that you do justice, love mercy, and be ready to walk with your God.”

For the voice of the Lord is heard in his city, the Church, and it resounds daily in the holy Scriptures: not only those who love mercy, but also those who are lower and still fear the name of the Lord, are saved by his teaching and clemency.

But if this is the beginning of the following chapter, let us refer the words historically to Samaria, the metropolis of the ten tribes, which was captured when Micah prophesied, and say: The Lord rebukes Samaria and threatens it with the blows that are to come, so that when the people of Judah—or those who fear the name of the Lord—hear of others suffering punishments, they may themselves, struck by fear, attain salvation.

For when a pestilent person has been scourged, not only the wise but also the foolish will become wiser (Prov. 19:25). Apply this also generally to sinners and the righteous, so that the sufferings of some may become an example to the rest. The Lord himself interprets the same point in the Gospel concerning those upon whom the tower in Siloam fell (Luke 13): they were not the only sinners in the whole people, but their punishment was intended to summon the others to repentance.

### (Verses 10 ff.)

“Hear, O tribes, and who will approve it?” [Note: Our manuscripts add: “or, will testify to it.”] “Is there still fire in the house of the wicked, treasures of wickedness, and a diminished measure full of wrath? Shall I justify the wicked balance and the deceitful weights of the pouch? In these her rich men have been filled with iniquity; and those who dwell in her have spoken falsehood, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. Therefore I too have begun to strike you with destruction because of your sins. You shall eat, but you shall not be satisfied, and your humiliation shall be in your midst; you shall seize, but you shall not save; and those whom you save I shall deliver to the sword. You shall sow, but you shall not reap; you shall tread the olive, but you shall not anoint yourself with oil; and the must, but you shall not drink wine. You have kept the statutes of Omri and every work of the house of Ahab; you have walked in their desires, so that I might give you over to destruction, and those who dwell in her to hissing, and you shall bear the reproach of my people.” [Note: The same manuscripts read: “and your inhabitants to hissing, and you shall bear the reproach of my people.”]

The Septuagint: “Hear, O tribe [another reading: Hear, O tribes], and who will adorn the city?” Is there fire and a house of the wicked, storing up wicked treasures, and injustice with insult [another reading: iniquity]? Shall the wicked person be justified on the balance, and in the pouch deceitful weights, by which they filled themselves with the riches of their ungodliness [another reading: your ungodliness]? And those who dwell in her spoke iniquity [another reading: were speaking], and their tongue was exalted in their mouth. And I afflicted you with destruction because of your sins: you shall eat, but you shall not be satisfied; and I shall cast you back upon yourself; you shall seize, but you shall not save; and whoever is saved shall be delivered to the sword. You shall sow, but you shall not reap; you shall press the olive, but you shall not anoint yourself with oil; and the grape, but you shall not drink wine. The statutes of my people shall be destroyed, and all the works of the house of Ahab; you walked in their counsels, so that I might deliver you to destruction, and her inhabitants to hissing, and you shall receive the reproaches of the peoples.”

In this chapter the Septuagint diverges greatly from the Hebrew truth, especially at the beginning: “Hear, O tribes, and who will adorn the city?” and “The statutes of my people shall be destroyed.” In place of this we have put, in accordance with the sequence of the passage, “And you have kept the statutes of Omri,” although in Hebrew it is written, “And the statutes of Omri were kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab.” For if AMMI (עמי) had been written in Hebrew, the Septuagint would rightly have translated it “my people.” But since AMRI (עמרי) is written, with the letter RES added, it does not signify the name of a people but the father of Ahab; the history in Kings relates this [III Kings 16], and no one can doubt that this is an error. Finally, after the father’s name the son is placed, and it is said, “and all the works of the house of Ahab.”

Let us therefore return to the beginning of the chapter. First, while discussing it according to the letter, and while you pray, let us strive to grasp its spiritual meaning.

“Hear, O ten tribes of Samaria,” to whom the Lord bears witness: “There is still fire”—that is, iniquity—in the house of the wicked Omri, and the treasures of ungodliness remain in the royal house. Do you wish to hear individually with what evils your city is filled? Learn: a diminished measure provoking God’s wrath, a fraudulent balance, and differing weights—selling merchandise with one weight and buying it with another [Prov. 11; Deut. 25]. If the poor did this, poverty could perhaps defend the crime by necessity. But now her rich are filled not so much with riches as with iniquity, because all riches are generated through iniquity when they despoil others.

The accumulation of riches is followed by falsehood, and the hand accustomed to storing up treasures possesses a deceitful tongue. Truth produces poverty; falsehood produces riches. When your rulers were doing these things, I did not wish to overthrow you immediately; rather, I began gradually to strike you and to admonish you with various blows. I sent famine upon you, I sent thirst, I sent diseases, and devastation by the enemy all around: the grain crop produced no harvest, the pressed olive did not yield oil, and barren vineyards denied wine. Against your iniquities, fraudulent measures, and deceitful weights I brought these punishments.

But because you kept all the rites of idolatry that the wicked king Omri had established [III Kings 16 ff.], and every work of the house of Ahab and Jezebel, as though you were observing my law, I was driven by your crime to give you and your inhabitants over to hissing and to the reproach of my people, while, captured by the Assyrians, you are conquered like the people of God, and because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations [Rom. 2:24].

It should be noted in the present passage that where we read, “and you shall bear the reproach of my people,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “you shall receive the reproaches of the peoples,” AMMI (עמי), “my people,” is written in Hebrew. If, then, AMMI signifies “my people,” there is no doubt that above “my people” was wrongly translated in place of Amri. [Note: The same manuscripts consistently prefer Omri and Ommi.]

Thus far we have expressed what seemed to us appropriate according to the Hebrew. Now, returning to the translation of the Septuagint interpreters, let us discuss each point as we are able.

The Samaritan tribe is summoned to hear, though it has cut itself off from the people of God. It is told: “You labor in vain fashioning idols; you construct golden calves with the craftsman’s hand, and by imitation of Jerusalem you wish to build another metropolis. For who can adorn the city?” [Note: Victor says that the better reading is “in imitation,” as found in seven Florentine manuscripts.] Is it the fire kindled by the burning arrows of the devil? Or the house of the wicked, which, according to its hardness and impenitent heart, stores up wrath for itself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God [Rom. 2:5]?

And injustice increases insult, so that it not only robs from the house of God, which is the Church, but also devastates what belongs to others with pride and haughtiness. Can the person be justified who, without a balance or a weight, fraudulently amasses his riches from the testimonies of Scripture—riches that are treasures of iniquity? For when the Lord commands, “There shall not be in your bag a large weight and a small one” [Deut. 25], these people, for the sake of sordid gain, always show partiality in judgment; and in the same case they judge rich and poor differently, not according to the matter itself but according to the difference in their resources. The inhabitants of their city—which they think is adorned by them through corrupt doctrines and perverse teaching—speak falsehood, set their mouth on high, and despise the simplicity of the ecclesiastical people.

Therefore the most merciful God does not strike them all at once, but endeavors gradually to admonish them through blows, saying: “And I shall begin to strike you with destruction because of your sins.” The sense is: “O city that heretics wish to build, I shall strike you so that you may perish—not for your complete annihilation, but in accordance with what you are as a sinful city.”

It follows: “You shall eat, but you shall not be satisfied.” They read, but do not understand; and while feeding on the words of Scripture, they suffer the famine [another reading: poverty] of truth. “And I shall cast you out,” he says, “and you shall seize, but you shall not save; and whoever is saved shall be delivered to the sword.” “I shall abandon you,” he says, “to your own judgment; and after seeking many things and finding nothing, when you understand your error, you will see that you cannot be saved from any of your doctrines. But all who think themselves satisfied, who have not been cast out from themselves and have not grasped the truth, shall be delivered to the sword and instructed through punishments.”

“Therefore you shall sow, O tribe, and O most wicked city, which heretics construct with fire, iniquity, insults, a deceitful balance, and a fraudulent pouch, but you shall not reap; you shall press the olive, but you shall not anoint yourself with oil; and the grapes, but you shall not drink wine.” It benefits you, once you have recognized your error, not to have disciples; not to anoint your head with the oil of sins; not to become intoxicated by drinking the wine of the Sodomites.

“And the statutes of my people”—or of Omri—“shall be destroyed, and all the works of the house of Ahab,” those who became patriarchs and rulers among the heresies. We may refer them either to opposing virtues or to the founders of heresies, such as Marcion and Basilides, and more recently Arius and Eunomius.

“You walked in their desires,” namely, those of Omri and Ahab. He fittingly says, “in their desires.” For the teaching of wicked teachers is not the teaching of God but the inventions of their hearts. “And I shall deliver you to destruction,” so that you may perish according to what you are as a heretic. “And your inhabitants to hissing”—or, that you may follow the hissing of the good shepherd according to Zechariah: “I shall hiss for them and gather them, because I have redeemed them” [Zech. 10:8]. Or certainly to the hissing of the dragon, that is, to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved [I Cor. 5:5], and, once corrected, they may learn not to blaspheme [I Tim. 1:20]. They will suffer all this so that they may understand their error: that they have borne the reproaches and sins of all nations and of many peoples.

I know that some have referred to the Church what we have interpreted concerning the heresies. But I do not sufficiently understand how the names of Omri and Ahab, rulers of Samaria, can be referred to Jerusalem and Judah, under whose names the Church is interpreted.

### Chapter VII

#### (Verses 1 ff.)

“Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers clusters in autumn at the vintage: there is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the first-ripe figs.” [Note: The Hieronymian, or Vulgate, translation reads “early-ripe”; other books prefer “unripe,” a reading Jerome himself more approves in his Commentary.]

“Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers grapes in autumn after the vintage: there is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the first-ripe figs. The holy one has perished from the earth, and there is no upright person among human beings. All lie in wait for blood; each hunts his brother to death. They call the evil of their hands good; the ruler demands, and the judge is ready to repay, and the great man has spoken the desire of his soul, and they have troubled it. The one who is best among them is like a thornbush, and the upright one like a thorn from a hedge.”

The Septuagint: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest, and like one who gathers grapes at the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat of the firstfruits,” [Note: More correctly, remove the words “which my soul suffered” or, as Victor read, “desired”; they are found neither in our manuscripts nor in the Greek. Shortly afterward, in place of “revering,” Martianay reads “returning.”] “which my soul suffered. Woe is me, O soul, for the reverent one has perished from the earth, and there is no one who sets human beings right. All are judged in blood; each one afflicts his neighbor with affliction; they prepare their hands for evil. The ruler demands, and the judge speaks peaceful words; the desire of his soul is present. And I shall take away their good things like a moth devouring them, and walking upon the rule on the day of your visitation.”

After the captivity already foretold of both the ten tribes and the two—for the word of the Lord came to Micah the Morasthite concerning Samaria and Jerusalem—the prophet laments that no righteous person is found among the people on earth who can withstand God’s wrath and set himself in the middle like a wall.

“In vain,” he says, “I have spoken; in vain I wished to seek, in a city already harvested and destroyed, something like the last clusters. Since there is no cluster to eat, at least I sought immature figs, which the Hebrews call BECHCHORA (בכורה), or BECHURA, that is, large figs, for food.” It is as though he were saying: “Unable to find bread because of the greatness of the famine, I sought refuse and bran.”

“The holy one has perished from the earth, and there is no upright person among human beings”: everywhere ambushes, everywhere deceit; innocent blood is poured out. Through greed and lust, kinship is disregarded. They not only commit evil but also defend it, and, changing the names, call good what is evil.

The rulers themselves do not receive gifts from those who offer them; they compel their subjects to give and demand them. “And the judge is ready to repay,” judging another as he himself is judged by another, so that they may offer one another mutual support in their crimes and defend themselves through the crime of another.

Whoever is great and, as it were, most learned in the Law speaks not God’s will but his own. [Note: Victor inserted “as,” considering it superfluous and absent from all the Florentine manuscripts.] “And they have troubled it,” whether the city, the truth, or the land, of which it was said above, “The holy one has perished from the earth.”

For whoever is best among them is like a thornbush, pricking, catching, and wounding whoever approaches, and grasping him with its hooked tooth. And whoever is found upright is like a thorn from a hedge, so that pain may be found where assistance was expected. This is according to the Hebrew.

According to the Septuagint, however, who differ in several places and have translated the end of the chapter altogether differently, the sense seems to me to be as follows. The prophetic—or apostolic—word laments the human race in general, which has sown the seed of teachings in vain, and instead of crops and grain the late-coming reaper has scarcely found empty stubble and barren stalks; nor has he been able to find even small clusters in the vineyard, and so on to the end of the chapter.

For if blessed is the person who speaks into the ears of one who listens, and the listener’s ear is the wise person’s desire and the hearer who understands is the speaker’s joy, conversely the teacher’s grief is a bad disciple [Note: Martianay mistakenly reads “grief” (*doloris*) for “teacher” (*doctoris*)], in agreement also with Jeremiah’s words that suit this lament: “I have benefited no one, nor has anyone benefited me” [Jeremiah].

Some think that this is spoken in the person of the Savior, lamenting that among so great a multitude of believers and throughout the whole world of the human race he scarcely finds works worthy of his blood. In the twenty-ninth psalm he likewise says: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” [Ps. 29:10]. Others, however, assert that this does not at all suit his person, so that he should say, “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest,” when he said in the Gospel, “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest” [John 4:35], and elsewhere, “The harvest is indeed abundant, but the laborers are few” [Matt. 9:37].

Those who wish this to be understood as spoken in the person of the Savior say that it is not surprising if he says “Woe is me,” since he also wept over Jerusalem and shed tears at the death of Lazarus [Luke 19; John 11]. They refer the statement, “I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest,” to the consummation of the age, which they also interpret significantly as “harvest.” They say that this prophecy can be fulfilled at the time when, because iniquity has multiplied, the love of many has grown cold, and the Son of Man, when he comes, finds little faith on earth [Matt. 24:12; Luke 18:8]. Then, as stubble after the harvest and clusters after the vintage, scarcely any will be found among the devastation of all who have preserved their faith. They think that this voice is spoken in the person of the assumed human being, and that this is confirmed by what follows: “Woe is me, O soul,” concerning which he said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” [Matt. 26:38].

“The reverent one has perished”—another reading: “shall perish”—“from the earth,” either with the Antichrist killing the saints, or because all are falling through the magnitude of scandals. “And there is no one who sets right among human beings.” All are judged in blood, not in light and minor sins, but in the greatest sins, those involving blood. Neither kinship, friendship, nor family connection restrains crime. All will raise their hands to evil, so that even whoever cannot do evil will nevertheless sin in intention while preparing his hands.

The ruler himself asks, and the judge speaks peaceful words; he receives gifts, the desire of his soul. Since this is obvious, and since I avoid provoking the envy of rulers and judges, I leave it to the reader’s understanding, adding only this: “Gifts blind the eyes even of the wise” [Deut. 16:19]. They also give life to a soul that ought not to be given life, and kill the soul that lives by its deserts and virtues; and they do this for the sake of gifts that they shamelessly demand and still more shamefully receive.

Against them the Lord threatens, saying: “And I shall take away their good things”—the things they think good and that appear good to them. In the reality of the matter, however, those things will never be called good which both strip the giver and kill the receiver. Yet perhaps this is not so much a threat as a blessing: to take away their evils, and for the Lord and the divine word itself to enter their consciences and, like a moth, consume whatever is perverse; to devastate their predatory and evil thoughts; to walk upon the standard and rule of truth; and to lead back to what is straight those who were being guided by crooked opinions.

He does this in the light of truth, and on that day when the holy and chosen members of the Church ascend to the watchtower and, in the elevation of their doctrines and works, discuss heavenly matters.

### (Verses 5–7)

“The day of your watchtower, your visitation, has come; now their devastation will be. Do not believe a friend, and do not trust a leader. Guard the doors of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom; for the son dishonors his father, and the daughter rises against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the members of his household. But I shall look to the Lord; I shall wait for God my Savior; my God will hear me.”

The Septuagint: “Woe, woe! Your vengeance has come; now there shall be their weeping. Do not believe in friends, and do not hope in leaders. Beware of her who lies with you; do not trust her, for the son dishonors his father, and the daughter rises against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his household. But I shall contemplate the Lord; I shall wait for God my Savior; my God will hear me.”

Except for the beginning of the chapter, the two editions agree in the remaining parts. According to the historical sense, the day of the watchtower of Samaria or Jerusalem—which it had often expected and feared would come—and its visitation signify captivity. He says: “Your devastation has come; now there shall be the devastation of them,” that is, of the inhabitants, or the siege. For MABUCHA (מבוכה) in Hebrew signifies πολιορκία and φρούρησις—that is, “siege” and “guarding”—rather than “devastation.”

Therefore do not believe the voices of prophets, nor lend your ear to the deceiving flattery of diviners. For if faith is rare even among beloved names and the affection of blood relations, how much more so among those who flatter you and lie for the sake of their prey, and who, as though you were sick, prescribe not what is useful but what is delightful and pleasing!

“Do not believe a friend.” For Ahithophel also rose against David [II Kings 15], and the true Ahithophel, Judas, against Christ [Matt. 26]. “And do not trust a leader,” as the men of Shechem trusted Abimelech [Judg. 9]. They themselves made him king, and they were oppressed by him.

“Guard the doors of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom” [ibid., 16], so that you do not suffer what Samson suffered from Delilah [Judg. 16]. “For the son dishonors his father”: Absalom, namely, dishonored David; he polluted not only his kingdom but also his father’s concubines by incestuous intercourse.

“The daughter rises against her mother.” Although for this matter we do not meanwhile find testimony from the holy Scriptures, there are so many examples in daily life that we ought rather to mourn that they are so numerous than to seek them out.

“The daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law,” as Esau’s wife rose against Rebecca [Gen. 26]. “A man’s enemies are the members of his household.” Here I seek no examples, since there are more than we need to establish the point.

Since these things are so, do not believe, O Samaria [another reading: “O Samaria and Jerusalem”], the false prophets. But I, says the prophet, shall look to the Lord; I shall rejoice in God my Savior, or “my Jesus,” and my God will hear me.

The exposition of the Septuagint follows. They said: “Woe, woe! Your acts of vengeance have come,” that is, the punishments that must be inflicted for crimes. “Vengeance is mine, and I shall repay, says the Lord” [Rom. 12:19; Deut. 32:35]. And elsewhere: “The days of your retribution have come” [Hos. 9:7].

For the Lord executes vengeance on those who cry out to him day and night, saying: “How long, O holy and true Lord, do you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” [Rev. 6:10]. The acts of vengeance have therefore come, and now there will be their weeping—that is, the weeping caused by those acts of vengeance—so that those who previously laughed may mourn, and, departing immediately from this age, may endure the torments suffered in hell by that formerly purple-clad rich man who abounded in pleasures, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth [Luke 16; Matt. 8; 13].

As for what follows, “Now there shall be,” understand it either at the end of each person’s life or at the consummation of all things and the day of judgment, when universal acts of vengeance will come upon everyone.

Therefore do not believe friends, because every friend supplants by treachery; and one who is a friend for some reason is not so much the friend of the person whom he pretends to love as of the thing he loves. For a friend is called a friend from love. [Note: Martianay retained the corrupt reading “from loving” (*ab amare*) in place of “from love” (*ab amore*), as our manuscripts correct and Victor had earlier restored from the Florentine copies.] When someone was asked what a friend was, he replied: “Another self.”

If the example of the Pythagoreans is brought against us—those who gave themselves as sureties for one another to a tyrant—we reply that God’s judgment was not pronounced generally against all friends and every affection of love, nor against every age, but against the time of which the Apostle says: “In the last days difficult times will come. For people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, haughty, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, faithless to agreements, slanderers, uncontrolled, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, puffed up, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God” [II Tim. 3:1–4], and so forth.

Then “brother will deliver brother, and father son, and mother daughter, and a man’s enemies will be the members of his household” [Matt. 10:35–36].

Even now faith is rare, when one thing is on the lips and another in the heart, and the tongue’s honey conceals the poison of the mind. The friends of the rich are many, but even those who seem to be friends withdraw from the poor. Hence it is said: “If you have a friend, possess him in temptation” [Sir. 6:7].

I have read in someone’s *Controversy*: “A friend is long sought, scarcely found, and preserved with difficulty.” Theophrastus wrote three volumes on friendship, placing it above every affection and yet testifying that it is rare in human affairs. Cicero also wrote a book on friendship, which he entitled *Laelius*. In it, what is taught among our own writers—“Let him be our friend like old wine, and let us drink it in sweetness”—is expressed in almost the same words.

Friendship either accepts equals or makes them equal. Where there is inequality—one person’s superiority and the other’s subjection—there is not so much friendship as flattery. Hence we also read elsewhere: “Let a friend be of the same soul.” And the lyric poet, praying for a friend, says: “Preserve half of my soul” [Horace].

Therefore do not believe in friends, that is, in those people who pursue profits through friendships. If you wish to enjoy true friendship, be a friend of God, like Moses, who spoke with God as a friend with a friend [Exod. 33:11]. Be a friend like the Apostles, to whom the Savior says: “I shall no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing; but I shall call you friends, because you have remained with me in all my trials” [John 15:15].

That is a delicate friendship which follows the happiness and riches of friends. Such people do not seem to me to be friends but to love themselves.

Let us consider the Lord’s words more attentively: “But I shall call you friends,” he says. And he gives the reasons why he calls them friends: “Because you have remained with me in temptation,” and he did not stop there, but added, “in all my trials.” It sometimes happens that someone who has remained with us in one trial withdraws after being overcome in others.

The second commandment is: “Do not hope in leaders.” For “cursed is the person who places his hope in a human being” [Jer. 17:5]. Hope in a human being is vain; true hope is in God. Hence Paul says: “From among yourselves men will arise speaking perverse things” [Acts 20:30].

The Lord himself says through the prophet: “The leaders of my people did not know me; they are foolish children and without understanding. They are wise enough to do evil, but they did not know how to do good” [Jer. 4:22]. They were called leaders—leaders of my people—but because they did not know me and destroyed the name they bore by their conduct, they are therefore foolish children without understanding. They possess prudence only for subjecting the simple flock to themselves and trampling it under their feet; but they did not know how to do good or govern the people.

“Do not trust in leaders” [another reading: “judges”]: not in a bishop, not in a presbyter, not in a deacon, not in any human dignity. I do not say this because you ought not to be subject to such offices in the Church. For “whoever curses father or mother shall be put to death” [Lev. 20:9], and the Apostle teaches that those placed over the Church must be obeyed. Rather, I say that honoring leaders is one thing, and placing hope in leaders another [I Pet. 2].

Let us honor the bishop, show deference to the presbyter, and rise in respect for the deacon; yet let us not place our hope in them, because human hope is vain, while certain hope is in the Lord [I Thess. 4:13]. [Note: Our manuscripts add: “because there is one and certain hope.”]

The third commandment is: “Guard yourselves from her who lies with you; do not trust her.” Hence the Apostle calls women a weaker vessel and commands husbands to show them honor. For the man was not created on account of the woman, but the woman on account of the man [Eph. 5]. And he says: “Let the wife fear her husband” [I Pet. 3]. For a wife’s fear consists in loving her husband with fear; husbands are simply to love, because love belongs to the perfect. He says: “Husbands, love your wives” [Note: The same manuscripts add: “as Christ [loved] the Church.”] “and do not be bitter toward them” [Eph. 5:25]. This is so even if the wives provoke them to anger and do things by which they deserve to endure bitterness. For this is what παραπικραίνεσθαι signifies. Nevertheless, do not repay them with bitterness.

Solomon also says in Ecclesiastes: “I found one man among a thousand, but among all these I did not find one woman” [Eccl. 7:29]—perhaps taught by his own example not to trust women, through whom he had offended God [III Kings 11].

The lofty poet also says—not another Homer, as Lucillus [another reading: Lucilius] suspects concerning Ennius, but the first Homer among the Latins:

> Variable and ever-changing always—  
> [lacuna]  
> Woman.

Greek and Latin histories are full of examples of how many great men were deceived by their wives and had their lives betrayed.

The Scriptures testify concerning Delilah, whom we mentioned above, and concerning another woman before Delilah, who drew out Samson’s secret through seven days of tears and discovered what lay hidden by feigned love. Hence Samson later says: “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found my riddle” [Judg. 14:18].

Thus far we are instructed not readily to trust friends, leaders, or wives.

The reason given, however, does not seem fully to answer the proposition. For it says: “Because the son dishonors his father, the daughter rises against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies are the members of his household.” What does this have to do with a friend, a leader, or a wife, if son, daughter, and daughter-in-law rise against father, mother, and mother-in-law?

It seems to me, therefore, that the statement can be joined to what precedes in this way: “Do not trust friends, leaders, and wives,” who may change and exist only for a time, “when even son and daughter, forgetting their upbringing and infancy, rise against the authors of their life and bodies and insult those whom it is itself a crime to injure even with a look.”

But this explanation does not at all suit the daughter-in-law rising against her mother-in-law, or the statement that a man’s enemies are the members of his household.

Terence writes in the *Hecyra*:

> What is this? All mothers-in-law hate their daughters-in-law.

Although the statement is ambiguous, it is almost natural that a daughter-in-law should hate her mother-in-law and a mother-in-law her daughter-in-law.

This prophetic word describes, concerning the consummation and end of the world, what kind of generation will precede the coming of the Antichrist.

Now we must discuss it according to the interpretation given above, in which we spoke of heretics: “Hear, O tribes, and who adorned the city? Is there fire and the house of the wicked?” And again, concerning the Church: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest.” And again: “Woe is me, O soul; the reverent one [another reading: the returning one] has perished from the earth, and there is no one who sets right among human beings.” And thereafter: “The ruler demands, and the judge has spoken peaceful words; it is the desire of his soul.”

Hence a twofold curse follows: “Woe, woe! Your acts of vengeance have come; now there shall be their lamentations.” Let us say that what is written concerns heretics: “Do not believe in friends, O simple peoples, nor in wicked leaders who promise to be friends and rulers of heresies. For they seek not your salvation but their own profits, and they trample the deceived flock beneath their feet. And beware of her who sleeps with you; do not believe her in anything.” I can understand this as nothing other than the flesh, so that we should not readily believe the flatteries of the flesh, lest the hardness of the soul and manly steadfastness, once subdued, grow soft through its allurements.

“For the son who is born of God, neglecting his Creator, blasphemes him by whom he was created,” as Scripture says: “Have we not all one God? Has not one Father created us all?” [Mal. 2:10]. [Note: The order is reversed in the text: the second verse is presented first, and vice versa. Victor restored it to the text.] And the soul despises the heavenly Jerusalem and disdains the Church as its mother; whoever despises her shall die.

“And the daughter-in-law rises against her mother-in-law.” According to the tropological sense this appears difficult to understand. But whoever has read the *Song of Songs*, understood the bridegroom of the soul as the Word of God, and believed the Gospel that we recently translated in the edition according to the Hebrews—in which the Savior is said to say, “Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me by one of my hairs” [Matt. 10]—will not hesitate to say that the Word of God was born from the Spirit, and that the soul, which is the bride of the Word, has the Holy Spirit as its mother-in-law. Among the Hebrews the Spirit is feminine in gender and is called RUA (רוח).

Heretics, therefore, although they previously believed in the Scriptures written and published by the Holy Spirit, turn themselves toward new doctrines, the leaven of the Pharisees, and the commandments of human beings. While they despise the Word of God, they insult their mother-in-law.

And lest you doubt that the Word and Son of God is born from the Holy Spirit, consider Gabriel’s words to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” [Luke 1:35].

After this follows: “A man’s enemies are the members of his household.” According to the tropological sense, this seems to us to be explained as follows: “The head of every man is Christ, and Christ is the head of the Church” [I Cor. 11:3; Eph. 5:23]. His enemies are often those who are thought to be in his house, that is, in the Church. They do not depart from the head, but they think against their own head. Without a teacher and without the grace of the Lord, they promise themselves knowledge of the Scriptures by their own judgment; they are puffed up and know nothing, languish over questions, and engage in disputes and battles of words. Truly, while remaining in the house, they are enemies of the truth.

We must also know that almost the same words occur in the Gospel as those we now read in the Prophet. According to the context of that passage they have another meaning. Whether they were taken from the prophet or spoken by the Lord’s own authority is known by the Lord, who spoke both in the Prophets and in the Gospels.

There the Lord says: “I have come to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies will be the members of his household” [Matt. 10:35–36].

Having explained these matters—if indeed we have been able to touch upon the meaning of the Scriptures—the holy man, understanding that love has grown cold and that at the consummation of the world human beings will be lovers not of God but of themselves, while some trust friends, leaders, and wives, and son, daughter, and daughter-in-law rise against father, mother, and mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies are the members of his household—he himself believes in the Lord, and all his contemplation is in his God.

Although he is pressed by the tribulations and afflictions of the world, nevertheless, trusting in no one except him who says, “Do not fear; I have conquered the world” [John 16:33], he waits for God his Savior. Believing in him and always directing his eyes toward him, he hopes that he will be heard whenever he calls upon him.

### (Verses 8 and following)

Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise. When I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light. I shall bear the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him, until he judges my case and executes my judgment, brings me out into the light, and I shall see his righteousness. My enemy shall look upon me, and she who says to me, “Where is the Lord your God?” shall be covered with shame. My eyes shall see her [the Vulgate has “see into her”]. Now she shall be trampled underfoot like the mud of the streets. The day shall come for your walls to be built. On that day the law shall be far removed; on that day people shall come to you from Assyria, and to the fortified cities, and from the fortified cities to the River, and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain. And the land shall become a desolation because of its inhabitants and because of the fruit of their thoughts.

The Septuagint: Do not insult me, my enemy, because I have fallen and shall rise; for if I walk in darkness, the Lord will enlighten me. I shall endure the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my case and executes my judgment, brings me out into the light, and I shall see his righteousness. My enemy shall see me, and she who says to me, “Where is the Lord your God?” shall be covered with shame. My eyes shall see her. Now she shall be trampled underfoot like mud in the roads [Note: The Palatine manuscripts have “in his roads”; so too the Complutensian Greek exemplar, ὁδοῖς σου, “in your roads.”]. The day of the scraping away of the brick—your destruction—shall come; and on that day he shall reject your statutes. Your cities shall come to enclosure and division among the Assyrians, and your fortified cities shall be divided from Tyre to the River, and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain. And the land shall be scattered with its inhabitants because of the fruits of their inventions.

In the literal sense, it seems to me that Jerusalem is speaking against Babylon and the other nations that had insulted her: “Do not rejoice in my ruin, because through the Lord’s mercy I shall rise. After I have sat in captivity, he will bring me out of darkness, and he will be my light. I shall endure the Lord’s anger, because I know that I deserved what I have suffered, until I take vengeance on the nations and my judgment is carried out. For I know that he will bring me into the light, and I shall see his righteousness. My enemy Babylon, and the other surrounding nations, shall look upon me and be covered with shame—she who now mockingly says, ‘Where is the Lord your God?’ My eyes shall see her, and not after a long time, but now and in the present, trampled underfoot like the mud of the streets.”

Thus far Jerusalem—or the prophet speaking in the person of the people—has spoken. Now God is introduced as answering Jerusalem:

“O Jerusalem, the days have come for your walls to be built, walls that had been destroyed by the Babylonian devastation” [Note: Formerly, “which had been laid waste and destroyed”; Victorius has, “which had been destroyed by Babylonian devastation.”]. On that day the law shall be far removed—or, as Symmachus and Theodotion translated it, the command and decree, ἐπιταγὴν καὶ πρόσταγμα—and the meaning is this: “You will no longer be subject to Babylonian authority. On the day when your walls are built, people will come to you from Assyria and from the fortified cities—from the fortified cities, I say, as far as the Jordan, across which the people formerly passed; and from the Red Sea and all the nations as far as the Dead Sea, which is near your land; and to Mount Zion from the mountains of the Persians and Medes, to which they had previously been carried away. The remaining land of the Chaldeans and of those who laid you waste shall become a desolation, because of its inhabitants and because of their evil works.”

The Jews promise themselves this even to the present day. In the passage which we have interpreted, “On that day the law shall be far removed,” just as it has seemed to us and as their more learned men explain it, some frivolously assert and say: “On the day when the walls of Jerusalem have been built by Christ, the holy Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets, which are now held by us, will be taken from our hands and given to the Jewish people.”

As for what is said according to the Septuagint, “the day of the scraping of the wall, your destruction,” let us understand that this is said not of Jerusalem, as we explained according to the Hebrew, but still of Babylon: she too is to be destroyed and trampled like a brick. “And on that day he shall reject your statutes”—not God’s statutes, but those statutes which you, O Babylon, had ordered to be observed against the law of God [Note: Our manuscripts have sed alegitima, in one word. Although barbarous, it conveys something like “those which are by no means legitimate,” and perhaps is more accurate.]. “Your cities shall come to enclosure,” or to division, with the Assyrians attacking you—for Babylon was a city of the Chaldeans, not of the Assyrians. And your fortified cities shall become a division of the hostile army, from Tyre to the River Tigris, by which you are surrounded, and from the Great Sea to the Red Sea, which touches your regions on the side for those traveling toward India. “And from mountain to mountain”: that is, from the mountains of Judaea to the mountains of Media and Persia; all Mesopotamia and the entire region which is now held by you in between shall be subjected to the power of your adversaries. And the land shall become a desolation because of the exceedingly evil fruits of your endeavors.

Where the Septuagint translated “from Tyre,” we should know that the Hebrew has MASOR (מָצוֹר). If this word is divided into the preposition MA and the noun SOR, it means “from Tyre”; but if it is a single word, it means “fortification.” Accordingly, all the translators rendered περιοχὴν, καὶ περίφραγμα, καὶ πολιορκίαν—not “from Tyre,” as the Septuagint has it, but “fortification” and “the circuit of a walled city.”

This is according to the Hebrew and the expectations of carnal Israel and the people of the circumcision, as though an idle speech had introduced itself unnecessarily. Now let us come to the spiritual understanding, and, with the Holy Spirit himself explaining the things by whom they were written, let us labor over even the most difficult passages.

It seems to me that every soul is Jerusalem in which the Lord’s temple was built, the vision of peace, and the knowledge of the Scriptures. Afterward, having been overcome by sins, it was led into captivity and handed over to torments. It speaks against Babylon—that is, the confusion of this world—and against the opposing power that presides over this world:

“Do not insult me, my enemy, because I have fallen, and I shall rise.” For “the Lord raises up all who are falling” (Ps. CXLIV), and he speaks through the prophet: “Does one who falls not rise again?” (Jer. VIII, 4). And: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, only that he turn back and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

But if you despise me because I endure torments, learn through Ezekiel that punishments are first inflicted upon the holier, and that the Lord says: “Begin with my sanctuaries” (ibid., IX, 6).

“For if I walk in darkness, the Lord is my light.” Although the rulers of these darknesses deceived me, and I sit in darkness and the shadow of death, and my feet have stumbled against dark mountains, nevertheless “upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death light has dawned, and light shines in darkness” (Isa. IX, 2). And: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. XXVI, 1). And I shall speak to him and say: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Ps. CXVIII, 105). For he himself commanded me, established in the darkness of this age: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII, 35).

It follows: “I shall endure the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my case and executes my judgment, brings me into the light; and I shall see his righteousness.”

Every correction, at the present time, seems not to be a cause of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. Therefore the soul, recognizing that it has sinned, that it has the wounds of sins, that it is living among dead flesh, and that it needs cautery, says steadfastly to the physician:

“Burn my flesh, cut away my wounds, and bind all the humors and the harmful flux, ῥεῦμα, with a strong dose of hellebore. It was my fault that I was wounded; let it be my burden to endure such torments, so that afterward I may receive health.”

The true physician then shows the now healed and secure soul the reason for the treatment and teaches that he rightly did what he did. Finally, after torments and punishments, the soul, brought out of the outer darkness and having paid the final farthing, says: “I shall see his righteousness,” and speaks: “Your judgments, O God, have been justified.”

But if Christ “has become for us from God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (I Cor. I), then the one who says that after God’s anger he will see righteousness promises himself the sight of Christ.

These remarks concern penitents only. It is much better, however, not to have wounds and not to need a physician [Note: One Palatine manuscript has, “and not to need the treatment of a physician. Healing is not the blessedness,” etc.]. Treatment is not the blessedness of the healed, but consolation after pain. Therefore the one who has been healed must beware lest he sin again and something worse happen to him.

We read in Leviticus—provided that we read with open eyes and do not allow the veil placed over the Law to exclude the vision of the inner eye—that leprosy commonly develops in a burn’s welt and scar, that it changes the color of the hair, and that a fresh deformity is added to the former disfigurement of the scar.

This is said so that no one, secure because of repentance and thinking that after sin he can say, “I shall endure the anger of God, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my case,” may sin again, require cautery, and, after being healed, be wounded once more.

When the Lord has brought us into the light and we have seen his righteousness, then our enemy Babylon will see and be covered with shame—she who earlier said to us, “Where is your God?”—thinking that Jerusalem could not be healed after her wounds. Our eyes will look upon her, and she will be trampled underfoot like the mud of the streets.

And because the end of every punishment is the beginning of good things, and pain advances toward health, bricks will be made from her mud, and the making of bricks will be her erasure. On that day she will cast away her ancient errors, and her cities, which had been badly fortified, will come to enclosure, or division, and will be divided by the Assyrians.

From Tyre also, which is interpreted as συνοχὴ, that is, “confinement” or “distress,” other powers will arise, and there will be sedition as far as those who delight in the flux of this age and generate lusts in human beings. From sea to sea and from mountain to mountain wars will arise against one another, so that bitterness will fight against bitterness; exalted height, destined to be humbled, will fight against another height. Then this will truly be fulfilled: “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages, so that each may not hear the voice of his neighbor” (Gen. XI, 7). For it is beneficial that the worst powers should not agree among themselves.

And when Satan is divided against Satan, then at last his whole kingdom will be destroyed (Matt. XII). As often happens in great armies, when a tyrant has been killed and his attendants divide his kingdom among themselves, rise against one another, and civil war breaks out among them, so too this will happen at the consummation of the world. When Jerusalem’s walls have been built and Babylon has fallen, the Assyrians and Tyrians—from the river, the sea, and the mountains, that is, all the nations of demons—will fight among themselves. Their kingdom having been scattered, the kingdom will belong to the Lord Jesus, and every knee will bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue will confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. II).

So that you may know that the outcome of this sedition will be the advancement of the virtues, the Babylonian land will then be scattered with all its inhabitants, and Babylon will no longer produce fruit [alternative: “Babylonian fruit”].

### (Verses 14 and following)

Feed your people with your rod, the flock of your inheritance; those who dwell alone in the woodland, in the midst of Carmel, shall feed in Bashan and Gilead as in days of old. As in the days of your coming out from the land of Egypt, I shall show him wonders [alternative: “I showed him”]. The nations shall see and be ashamed because of all their strength [the Vulgate has “their own strength”]. They shall place their hands over their mouths; their ears shall be deaf. They shall lick the dust like serpents; like reptiles of the earth, they shall be shaken from their houses. They shall fear the Lord our God, and they shall fear you.

The Septuagint: Feed your people with your rod, the sheep of your inheritance, those dwelling alone in the woodland. In the midst of Carmel they shall feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in former days and as in the days of your coming out from the land of Egypt; I shall show them wonders. The nations shall see and be ashamed in all their strength. They shall place their hands over their mouths; their ears shall be deaf. They shall lick the ground like serpents that drag the earth; they shall be shaken in their enclosures [the Vulgate has “they shall be driven out”]. They shall fear the Lord our God, and they shall fear you.

When it says, “Feed your people with your rod,” God the Father is speaking to the Son, that is, to our Lord Jesus Christ: because he is the good shepherd and lays down his life for his sheep (John X), he should feed his people with his rod and the sheep of his inheritance.

And lest we think that the people and the sheep are the same, we read elsewhere: “But we are your people and the sheep of your pasture” (Ps. LXXVIII, 21). “People” refers to those who possess reason, while “sheep” refers to those who do not yet use reason, but are content simply with their simplicity, and are called part of God’s inheritance.

Both people and sheep need the shepherd’s rod, concerning which the Apostle also says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. IV, 21).

For this reason, I think, because the people of Israel were stiff-necked and always longed for Egyptian flesh, Moses used the legal rod, the striking rod, not only against the Egyptians, whom he struck with ten plagues, but also against the people in the wilderness—a rod that shattered all earthen and fragile vessels.

But from the Apostles of the Lord and Savior, who spoke wisdom among the mature (I Cor. II), the rod was shaken out of their hands, because perfect love casts out fear (I John IV).

If someone should object to us: “How is Christ now said to use a rod—that is, the good shepherd, who is certainly greater and better than the apostles—when it is a greater advance not to have a rod than to correct peoples and sheep with a rod?” we shall answer them according to what the Lord promises his apostles: that they will perform greater signs among the peoples than he himself did (John XIV).

Because the Lord was still speaking to carnal Israel, and not yet to the one who could perfectly know the mysteries, therefore it was said of him that he should feed his people and flock with a rod. But the rod was shaken out of the hands of the apostles, and the severity of the Law was tempered by the mercy of the Gospel.

These peoples and sheep, moreover, will be struck and fed with a rod because they had dwelt alone in the woodland. We can understand this both of those who separate themselves from the Church and give themselves over to the banquets and friendships of the Gentiles, and of those who, out of hatred for the human race, seek a solitary life, such as we read that Timon lived at Athens.

This does not mean that the solitary and prophetic life lived by Elijah (III Kings XVII and XIX) and John (Matt. III and XI) should be condemned. But if someone despises others, becomes proud, and dwells in the woodland of vices, he must be corrected with the rod.

The person who dwells alone but does not dwell in the woodland is praiseworthy for his virtues. But the person who is alone, does not perform works of righteousness, enjoys only the pleasure of leisure, does not labor in Christ’s work and toil, does not seek food with his own hands, as the Apostle commands (I Cor. IV), and is lifted up in pride—this person dwells in the woodland and moves among fruitless trees.

Nevertheless, because he is a good shepherd and strikes with his rod for the purpose of correction, the prophetic word promises better things and says: “In the midst of Carmel they shall feed in Bashan and Gilead, according to the days of eternity and according to the days of your coming out from Egypt.”

Carmel is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision”; Bashan as “confusion”; and Gilead as “the migration of testimony.” The people of God and the sheep of his pasture, who were formerly feeding without the Lord’s flock and wandering outside his Church in the woodland of errors, will afterward be transferred to knowledge of true circumcision. They will serve God in spirit, glory in the Lord, and place no confidence in the flesh. They will be the true circumcision, not merely mutilation.

When they have been fed by spiritual circumcision, understanding their former sins, they will be ashamed of their vices and blush; and they will be in the confusion that leads to life (Eccl. IV), because there is also another confusion that leads to death, in which Og, king of Bashan, once dwelt, since Bashan is interpreted as “confusion.”

From this most evil confusion the Lord also promises to deliver his people: “The Lord said, ‘From Bashan I will turn them back; I will turn them back from the depth of the sea’” (Ps. LXVII, 23).

When we have known true circumcision and have been confounded over our sins, then we shall be in Gilead, which is interpreted as “the migration of testimony,” in the Church of Christ, to which the testimonies of the Law and the sayings of the Prophets have passed.

This will happen to us according to the days of old, according to the days when we came out from the land of Egypt, concerning which Moses says: “Remember the days of eternity” (Deut. XXXII, 7)—not the days of this age, which are called evil, but everlasting days.

The one who does not look upon present things and has risen with Christ and sits with him in the heavenly places, already anticipating in mind that he has been freed from the days of the present age, remembers the days of eternity.

The divine word also promises that it will show wonders to his people and the sheep of his inheritance: “Then,” he says, “the nations shall see and be ashamed in all their strength,” because formerly they had laid waste to and prevailed against the people of God. Their shame will be beneficial when they understand their own evils.

They will place their hands over their mouths, and their evil deeds will take away from them all freedom of speech. Just as the hands of impious nations close their mouths, so the hands of the righteous will open their mouths, granting them the ability to speak with God through good works.

Their ears too will become deaf, because wickedness not only blinded the sight of their eyes but also made their ears deaf. They refused to hear “the voice of the enchanters and of the sorcerer who enchants skillfully.” And according to Isaiah: “They heard heavily with their ears” (Isa. XXXIII). Although “to hear heavily” is far less than not hearing at all and becoming deaf so as not to hear the word of truth.

After so many evils it is said of them that they shall lick the ground like serpents that drag the earth, walking on their bellies and eating earth all the days of their life (Gen. III). Performing works of the flesh—that is, earthly works—and dragging them along with themselves until the day of the Lord’s vengeance and visitation, they will not merely lick dust or small traces of earth, but the whole ground.

When they have done this, and have come to God’s judgment, and have been enclosed and disturbed, they will be disturbed and enclosed for as long as the earth they had dragged like serpents remains in them.

When that earthly element has failed, they will be stupefied and astonished—not in the Lord their God, for they will not yet deserve that he be called their Lord and God, but in the Lord our God.

Then there is suddenly an ἀποστροφὴ, a turning aside, and the words are addressed to Christ: “And they shall fear you.” For “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Prov. VII).

These things will happen so that the nations may see and be confounded in all their evil strength; that they may place their hands over their mouths and become deaf in their ears; that they may lick the earth like serpents that drag the ground; that they may first be enclosed, then, once enclosed, be disturbed; afterward, terrified, be struck with amazement before the Lord God of the saints; and finally themselves fear him.

This is according to the Septuagint. Since our edition does not differ greatly from theirs in the present passage, let us consider that what is said in one is also said in the other.

### (Verses 18–20)

Who is a God like you, who removes iniquity and passes over the sin of the remnant of your inheritance? He will no longer send forth his fury, because he delights in mercy. He will turn back and have mercy on us; he will cast away our iniquities and throw all our sins into the depths of the sea. You will give truth to Jacob and mercy to Abraham, which you swore to our fathers from days of old [the Vulgate has “which you swore to our fathers”].

The Septuagint: Who is God like you, removing iniquities and passing over injustices for those who remain of your inheritance? He did not retain his anger as a testimony, because he delights in mercies. He will turn back and have mercy on us; he will drown our sins, and all our sins will be thrown into the depths of the sea. He will give truth to Jacob and mercy to Abraham, as you swore to our fathers according to former days [alternative: “days of old”].

The prophet understands that the multitude of the nations has been disturbed in its enclosure so that it might be struck with amazement and fear God. For this reason, since the Lord rages in order to remove sins and grant salvation, he praises and marvels at the Lord and says: “Who is a God like you, removing iniquities and passing over injustices?” (Exod. XII).

Just as the destroyer in Egypt passed over the people of Israel and did not destroy them—hence the name “Passover,” φάση, that is, pascha, was derived from the passing over—so may you spare the nations, no longer imputing their iniquities to them.
