As for what follows, “for those who remain of his inheritance, he did not retain his anger as a testimony,” the meaning is this: If he spared the nations, which refused to believe in his Law, and did not wish to impute their iniquities to those who remain as superfluous remnants of the people, nor bring his anger against them as a testimony of their just punishment, what will he do with his flock, which is fed in the midst of Carmel, in Bashan, and in Gilead?

For he delights in mercy, and, turning back, he will have mercy on us. He himself will bear our serious sins and the iniquities that sit upon the talent of lead, and he will plunge them into the sea and prevent them from begetting (Zech. V).

He will give truth to Jacob and mercy to Abraham, so that he may restore his truth in Christ to the people who are Jacob, the supplanter, and the new people, who are always engaged in struggle; and so that he may grant mercy to the multitude of the nations—for Abraham is called the father of many nations—as he swore to those who became the fathers of our faith according to days of old: that from the whole multitude of human beings he would save some in truth and others in mercy.

Where we have translated, “He will no longer send forth his fury,” Symmachus translated “forever”; Theodotion, “to the end”; the Septuagint and the fifth edition, “as a testimony.” In Hebrew the word is LAED (לָעַד), which may be understood as “for ever,” “continually,” or “as a testimony.”

I too shall say at the end of this volume, sealing the labor of my little work with an invocation of the Lord:

“O God, who is like you? Take away the iniquity of your servant. Pass over the sin of my remnant soul. Do not bring your anger upon me, nor correct me in your wrath, for you are merciful and your mercies are many. Turn back and have mercy on me. Hurl down my iniquities and cast them into the depths of the sea, so that the saltiness and bitterness of my vices may perish in the false region.

“Give the truth that you promised to your servant Jacob, and the mercy that you pledged to your friend Abraham. Deliver my soul from the persecutors of your prophets, Ahab and Jezebel, as you swore to my fathers in days of old, saying: ‘As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, only that he turn back and live’” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

And elsewhere: “As soon as you have turned back and groaned, you shall be saved.”

Then my enemy will see and be covered with shame—the one who now says to me, “Where is the Lord your God?” (Ps. XLI, 4, 11). I shall see your vengeance upon her, and she will be like the mud of the streets and will be trampled underfoot, so that she may no longer build Egyptian cities from mud and straw.

---

## One Book of the Commentaries of Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, on the Prophet Nahum [Note: This exposition is also entitled “To Paula and her daughter Eustochium.”]

### Prologue

According to the Septuagint interpreters, in the order of the twelve prophets Nahum is placed after Jonah, because they appear to prophesy about the same city.

For it is written in Jonah: “The word of the Lord came to Jonah, son of Amittai, saying: ‘Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it’” (Jonah I, 1). In Nahum, however, the opening is: “The burden of Nineveh: the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.”

Thus both weave a prophecy concerning Nineveh, the metropolis of the Assyrians, which is now called Ninus.

In Hebrew, however, Micah is placed after Jonah, and Nahum follows Micah. Nahum is interpreted as “consoler.” For by the time of Hezekiah, king of Judah, the ten tribes had already been led away captive by the Assyrians. Under that same king, a vision against Nineveh is now seen for the consolation of the displaced people.

Nor was it a small consolation, both for those who were already serving the Assyrians and for the rest who, from the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, were being besieged by the same enemies under Hezekiah, to hear that the Assyrians too would be captured by the Chaldeans, as will be demonstrated in the continuation of this book.

It should also be understood—for Nineveh in our language, from Hebrew, means “beautiful,” and “beautiful” is what this world is called; hence among the Greeks κόσμος received its name from adornment—that whatever is now said against Nineveh is figuratively proclaimed against the world.

For this reason, the word “burden,” which the Septuagint translates as λῆμμα and Aquila as ἄρμα, is rendered in Hebrew MASSA, that is, “a heavy load,” because it weighs down the one against whom it is directed and does not allow her to lift her neck.

As for the addition “Nahum the Elkoshite,” some think that Elkosh was Nahum’s father and, according to Hebrew tradition, was himself a prophet. But Elcosi [alternative: “Elkoshite”] remains to this day a village in Galilee, small indeed and scarcely showing traces through the ruins of its ancient buildings, but nevertheless known to the Jews and shown also to me by my guide.

At the same time, we should observe that this very burden—or load or weight—is the prophet’s vision. He does not speak in ἐκστάσει, in a state of ecstasy, as Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla rave; rather, what he prophesies is a book of the vision of one who understands everything he says and makes the weight of the enemies into a vision among his own people.

Therefore, according to the ἀναγωγή, the spiritual sense, a prophecy concerning the consummation of the world is woven, O Paula and Eustochium, for the consolation of the saints, so that whatever they see in the world they may despise as passing and transitory and prepare themselves for the day of judgment, when the Lord will be an avenger against the true Assyrians [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts have: “against the men who will be Assyrians,” and so forth.].

## The Book Begins

### Chapter I—Verse 1

“God is jealous, and the Lord takes vengeance.”

This is the prophet’s voice praising God because he avenged the injury done to his people by the Assyrians. Or, according to the higher understanding, because he hears the groaning of his saints and, at the consummation of the world, makes their adversaries suffer punishments.

That zeal may be understood in a good sense, the Apostle Paul also shows when he says: “Be zealous for the greater spiritual gifts” (I Cor. XII) [Note: The same manuscripts have “better gifts”; the Greek likewise has τὰ κρείττονα.]. And in another passage: “I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God” (II Cor. XI). The Lord himself says in the Psalm: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII). And Elijah says: “With zeal I have been zealous for the Lord, the almighty God of Israel” (III Kings XIX).

We also read of the zeal of Phinehas and Mattathias (Num. XXV; I Macc. II), and of Simon the Zealot, an apostle of Jesus Christ, whom the evangelist Mark calls Simon the Cananaean (Acts I; Mark III).

The Lord is jealous for the salvation of those for whom he is jealous, so that those whom his clemency could not save, his jealousy may save. Hence God says to Jerusalem, which because of her excessive sins did not deserve the visitation of his zeal and fury, in Ezekiel: “My zeal has departed from you, and I will not be angry with you any longer” (Ezek. XVI, 42) [Alternative: “May my zeal depart,” and “it will depart,” in accordance with the Greek ἐξαρθήσεται.].

As long, therefore, as the world was practicing repentance, its consummation did not take place. But after iniquity multiplied and the love of many grew cold, so that even God’s elect were tested, then the jealous Lord comes for vengeance—not because he himself is an enemy and avenger, as is said of the devil, but because his vengeance is opposed to the enemy and, like fire, consumes wood, hay, and stubble, so that pure gold and silver may remain (Matt. XXIV).

“The Lord takes vengeance and possesses fury; the Lord takes vengeance on his enemies, and he himself is angry with his adversaries.”

The Septuagint: “The Lord takes vengeance with fury; the Lord takes vengeance on his adversaries, and he himself removes his enemies.”

According to both interpretations, because the Lord loves the one whom he corrects (Prov. III) and chastises every son whom he receives, he is angry in order to remove what is an adversary and enemy to him, and to remove it from among his enemies [alternative: “to remove enemies from among his enemies.”]. When contrary thoughts have been shattered and hostile words removed, they may return to their original state.

Accordingly, he says later: “The Lord is patient, and great is his strength.”

But because we have proposed to expound the historical sense once as well, let us understand the enemies and adversaries of God as the Assyrians, against whom, after he has been patient for a long time, he will afterward appear as an avenger with fury and anger.

### Verse 2

“The Lord is patient and great in strength, and cleansing he will not make innocent.”

This is expressed more distinctly in Greek: καὶ ἀθωῶν οὐκ ἀθωώσει [alternative: καὶ ἀθοῶν οὐκ ἀθοώσει].

The meaning is: He was long patient with the crime of the Assyrians, and in the strength of his great forbearance he endured their iniquities, urging them to repentance. But because, despising God’s goodness, they stored up wrath for themselves according to their impenitent heart on the day of wrath (Rom. II), the one who was previously patient will by no means allow them to depart unpunished as though they were pure and innocent.

Or certainly the passage may be understood in this way—for we wish at the same time to take what is said in a good sense: He is patient, sustaining all who fall and raising up the oppressed [alternative: “the fallen”] (Ps. CXLIV); he heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. And great is his power, dissolving hostility in the flesh [alternative: “hostilities”] and not making the guilty innocent, when even the one who takes excessive pleasure in himself is convicted, because he was saved not by his own merit but by the mercy of God [Note: If the manuscripts had added only the word animum, I would readily have restored “and not making the innocent innocent,” in place of “the guilty.” Such is Jerome’s meaning: no one, however innocent, will be innocent before God, both because he is not innocent by his own merit but is justified by God, and because he is convicted and receives pardon. This accords with what is written in Exodus XXXIV: “No one is innocent before you by himself.” Indeed, it also accords with the passage now under discussion: “cleansing he will not make innocent,” namely, that he will convict the innocent themselves, showing that they are saved not by their own strength but by God’s mercy. For the immediately following reading, we substituted “having been convicted” from the manuscripts; Martianus retained the corrupt two-word reading “because he was clever.” Victorius introduced only the word “because.”].

For although he says, “Behold, I have served you for so many years and have never transgressed your commandment” (Luke XV, 29), nevertheless, since the Lord is good to all and his mercies are over all his works (Ps. CXL, 6), and all have sinned and lack the glory of God (Rom. III, 23), the one justified by him freely will hear: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. XX, 15).

And so it will come about that, in the very act by which he convicts and forgives, he allows no one who is without fault to depart.

(Vers. 3.) The Lord is in the storm and in the tempest of his way, and clouds are the dust of his feet. Instead of “storm and tempest,” the Seventy translated “consummation [Note: [Col. 1234D] The words “and commotion,” which were lacking, are supplied by our manuscripts.] and commotion” [Col. 1234B], although where we have placed “in the storm,” the Hebrew *BASUPHA* () may also be understood to mean “in the commotion.” This signifies that at the end of the world all things will be shaken, according to what is written in Haggai: “Yet once more, and I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land” (Haggai II, 7). And when everything has been shaken—so that the ways of the Lord may be believed, who says in the Gospel, “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John XIV, 6); and also in Mark VII: “When the Son of Man comes in the clouds,” to which it is commanded in Isaiah (chapter V) that they should not rain upon the vineyard, and to which the truth of God has reached, as the Psalmist says, “Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm XXXV, 6)—then those very clouds, namely the Prophets and the souls of the saints, which had previously been weighed down by their union with the flesh, raised on high, will become of a more tenuous substance; and, made the footstool beneath God’s feet, they will minister in the lowest offices among the angels. For they will not be able to know the former and ancient things that pertain to the head.

Another will understand “clouds” in the opposite sense: that they always disturb what is clear, strive by their darkness to veil the bright light of the sun and stars, and, afterward subjected to the Lord’s power, are reduced to dust and nothingness; and that the earth in them, which is fertile, is dissolved.

(Vers. 4.) Rebuking the sea, drying it up, and reducing all the rivers to desert. In the literal sense, God’s power is described: he will take vengeance on Israel’s adversaries, since it is no great thing for him to destroy the Assyrians, whose majesty is such that he can even change the elements. Or, since we have said that the prophecy concerns the consummation of the world, understand it simply in this way: when the consummation of the world comes, and heaven and earth pass away, the sea and the rivers also will be dried up.

But as I read in the Psalms, “This is the great and wide sea, where are creeping things without number, small animals with great; there go the ships. This dragon whom you formed to mock him” (Psalm CIII, 25–26), it seems worthy of God’s goodness and mercy to destroy, by his threat, all the bitterness and saltiness of the sea; to humble the dragon reigning in the waters; and to dry up the pools of wickedness in which swim the small creeping things without number. For those who consort with the dragon are not worthy to be counted.

He also reduces the rivers to desert: all false-named knowledge, which rises up against God and uses the river of eloquence [Col. 1235B], the rolling abundance of words, twisting its swollen currents, and, amid the astonishment of its spectators, rushes headlong. Consider Plato, look at Demosthenes, and Tully, both philosopher and orator; look also upon the leaders of the heretics, among whom were Valentinus, Marcion, Bardesanes, and Tatian, and you will not doubt that these are rivers. But the Lord Jesus will consume all these with the breath of his mouth, destroy them by the brightness of his coming, and reduce them to deserts (II Thessalonians II). Observe at the same time that, according to the title inscribed “The Burden of Nineveh: the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite,” the world is rightly understood figuratively as Nineveh, and its sea—the rivers of its eloquence—will be dried up at the consummation.

Bashan has been weakened, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon [Col. 1235C] has languished. LXX: “Basanitis and Carmel have been diminished [Al. ‘Basanitis has been changed’], and the things that flourished in Lebanon have failed.”

Μεταφορικῶς—figuratively—through Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon, a fertile region and mountains planted with trees, the devastation of the Assyrians is shown: the one who was once powerful and flourishing and ruled over many nations will, when the Lord is angry, be laid waste. But we can also understand this of the consummation of the world: that all the powerful and noble, and those abounding in excessive wealth, will suddenly perish, and it will be said to them: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and the things that you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XX, 12).

Furthermore, according to the interpretation of the names—because *Bashan* signifies “confusion” and “shame”—we assert that at the consummation of the world everything deserving of disgrace and shame will be weakened when the Lord comes. Not only will sins be reduced to nothing, but Carmel also, which is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision,” and those who seem to themselves to be rich and flourishing in good works, will tremble when Christ comes; and what is said in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose [Al. ‘do you suppose that’] he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8). For as iniquity increases, the charity of many will grow cold, and because of this the wrath of God will come.

(Vers. 5.) The mountains are shaken by him, the hills are laid waste, and the earth trembles before his face, as do the world and all who dwell in it. LXX: “The mountains are shaken by him, the hills are convulsed, and the earth is contracted before his face, the universe and all who dwell in it.”

This may also be understood simply: at the consummation of the world, when the Savior comes in his majesty, the mountains and hills, the world and the earth, and all things will be shaken. For if at his passion the sun fled, the rocks were split, and the earth trembled (Matthew XXVII and Luke XXIII), much more will everything be disturbed at his glorification.

But figuratively, the mountains and hills are to be understood as the lofty and powerful, who at the Lord’s coming will be thrown prostrate upon the ground and, cast down from their thrones, will cling to the pavement. For “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth” (Psalm XXXIII, 17). Then the earth also will tremble, and the world and the universe will fear the face of the Lord. They will regard this as the greatest torture and punishment, because they will not dare to look upon his countenance.

[Col. 1236B] (Vers. 6.) Before the face of his indignation, who can stand? And who can resist the wrath of his fury? LXX: “Before the face of his anger, who can endure? And who can resist the wrath of his fury?”

For what we rendered, “And who can resist the wrath of his fury?” Symmachus translated more clearly: “And who can endure the anger of his fury?” Therefore either very few, or no one, will be found who is not deserving when anger corrects. Nor will there be any soul that does not tremble at God’s judgment, since even the stars are not clean in his sight (Job XXV, 5).

Moreover, let us transfer the Hebrew word *JACCUM* (), which Aquila and the Seventy translated as “will resist,” to the interpretation found in the Second Book of Kings and First Chronicles concerning the wrath of God, where the word is masculine. No one doubts that there the devil and the evil angels are understood as the wrath of God—those who are sent to punish those deserving of wrath. It will therefore be difficult to find anyone at the consummation of the world who is immaculate and pure enough to dare say, “The prince of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me” (John XIV, 30), and to stand before him with an untroubled face.

Concerning the Assyrians, however, the meaning is this: when the Lord comes in storm and tempest, drying up the empire of Babylon—which is interpreted as “sea”—and overthrowing all its kingdoms, which are understood as “rivers,” reducing its power and fertility to nothing—which are figuratively called Bashan, Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon—and shaking the breadth of its empire, which is called the world, then no power will be able to resist the God who is angry and takes vengeance on his people.

His indignation is poured out like fire, and the rocks are dissolved by him. LXX: “His fury consumes principalities, and the rocks are crushed by him.”

For what we rendered “is poured out,” Aquila translated συνεχωνεύθη, that is, “was fused”; Symmachus and Theodotion translated ἔσταξεν, that is, “dripped.” Whether, then, the indignation of God was fused like fire, or his fury dripped in the likeness of a conflagration, so that the hard hearts of human beings, which are called rocks, might be crushed and dissolved, God’s indignation is beneficial. For after sustaining our sins for a long time through patience, it has at last scarcely been fused; and yet it does not burst forth wholly into punishment [Col. 1237A], but will drip upon us with only a moderate heat.

If, however, a drop of his indignation consumes principalities against which we wage our battle and struggle, what would happen if God’s entire anger were poured out upon us? May Jesus grant that our heart of stone be taken away and a heart of flesh be changed within us, so that, our hardness softened, it may receive within itself the commandments of the Lord, which are written: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm L, 9). And so that you may know that what has been said expresses God’s mercy, not his severity, learn this from what follows.

(Vers. 7.) The Lord is good, and strengthens in the day of tribulation, and knows those who hope in him. LXX: “The Lord is gracious to those who await him in the day of tribulation, and knows those who fear him.”

When he begins to be angry with the nations [Col. 1237B] and to lay waste kingdoms once exceedingly powerful, he will know those who belong to him, and will not overwhelm those who are sailing in a single storm. According to ἀναγωγήν—the spiritual interpretation—let us understand “the day of tribulation” as the day of judgment, concerning which Isaiah wrote: “Behold, the day of the Lord comes, incurable, full of fury and wrath, to make the world desolate and destroy sinners from it” (Isaiah XIII, 9).

Let us hope in the Lord and await his coming with patience, so that when he comes we may experience him as good, not as judge, and so that he may know either those who hope in him or those who fear him (II Timothy II). For the Lord knows those who are his.

(Vers. 8.) And in the passing flood he will make an end of his place, and darkness will pursue his enemies. LXX [Note: [Col. 1237D] The Palatine manuscripts have the same reading as the LXX and omit altogether the words of their interpretation that follow.]: “And in the passing flood he will make an end: darkness will pursue those who rise up and his enemies” [Col. 1237C].

The Lord is patient and rich in mercy; he will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant eternally. But when wickedness has increased upon the earth and all flesh has corrupted its way, he will bring a flood that passes over, not one that remains forever. He will make an end, or a conclusion, of its place—that is, of the flood—so that, just as it is said of the impious, “I passed by, and behold, his place was not found” (Psalm XXXVI, 36), and, “The way of the impious will perish” (Psalm I, 6), so the way of the flood may perish after the Lord’s anger, with mercy alone appearing.

This can also be understood according to history: when he has devastated Israel and, as though by a flood, inundated the promised land, he will bring the captivity to an end by restoring Israel to its former dwellings. Conversely, darkness will pursue his enemies, the Assyrians, who led the people into captivity.

What we have said about Israel and the Assyrians can also be understood of the consummation of the world, of the saints and their persecutors, or of opposing powers: God will have mercy on the saints after his anger, while their persecutors and enemies, who chose darkness rather than light, will be overtaken by the very darkness they chose. For “they will be cast into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew VIII and XXII).

The word *MACOMA* (), which we translated as “his place,” was divided by all of them into two parts of speech, so that they rendered *MA* as the preposition “from,” that is, ἀπό; and interpreted *COMA* as “rising.” Accordingly, Aquila says ἀπὸ ἀνισταμένων, that is, “from those who rise”; the Seventy, “those who rise”; Theodotion, “from those rising against him”; and the fifth edition, “from those rising against him.” Symmachus alone, agreeing with our interpretation, says: “And in the passing flood he will make an end of his place.”

Some of our people interpret “those who rise and his enemies” as Marcion and all the ancient heretics who argue against the Creator.

(Vers. 9.) What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will make an end [Al. “that he will make an end”]; tribulation will not rise up twice. LXX: “What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will make an end; he will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in tribulation.” Symmachus more clearly: “They will not endure the assault of a second [Al. ‘of the second’] distress.” Theodotion: “A second tribulation will not rise up.”

He speaks according to tropology against Marcion, of whom we spoke above, and against all the ancient heretics who fabricate some unknown good God and say that he himself will bring about the consummation of the world. They accuse the God of the Law of cruelty because he punishes many and inflicts tortures for sins.

“What, then,” he says, “are you plotting against the Lord? He who created the world will also bring about its consummation.” And if he seems cruel, harsh, and bloody to you because he destroyed the human race in the flood, rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis VII), drowned the Egyptians in the waves (Exodus XIV), and struck down the corpses of the Israelites in the wilderness (Numbers XXXII) [Col. 1238C], know that he inflicted punishments in the present precisely so that he would not punish eternally.

Certainly, what the prophets say is either true or false. If what they appear to say about his severity is true, they themselves have said: “The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in tribulation” [Note: [Col. 1238D] Martianus retained here only: “He will not judge.”]. But if they are false, and this saying too is false—“A double tribulation will not rise up”—then his cruelty described in the Law is false as well.

But if it is true, as they will not be able to deny, since the prophet says, “The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in tribulation,” then those who have been punished will not afterward be punished. If they are afterward punished, Scripture lies—which it is impious to say.

Therefore those who perished in the flood, the Sodomites, the Egyptians, and the Israelites in the wilderness received their evils during their lifetime. Someone may ask here: if a believer is discovered in adultery and beheaded, what happens to him afterward? For either he will be punished, and this saying is false: “The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in tribulation”; or he will not be punished, and it ought to be desired by adulterers that, through a brief and immediate punishment in the present, they might escape eternal torments.

To this we shall reply that God knows the measures both of all things and of punishments; that the judge’s sentence is not anticipated; that the power to inflict punishment afterward upon the sinner cannot be taken away from him; and that a great sin may be washed away by great and prolonged torments.

But if someone has been punished, like the man in the Law who cursed the Israelites and the one who gathered wood on the Sabbath (Leviticus XXIV), such people are not punished afterward, because a light offense has been compensated by present punishment.

A Hebrew explained this passage as follows: “What do you think, O Assyrians, who are plotting iniquity against the Lord? Will he himself utterly destroy the people of Israel—that is, the twelve tribes? A double tribulation will not rise up”—that is, he will not hand over Judah and [Note: [Col. 1239] The manuscripts more correctly read thus. Previously “Jerusalem” was read; we restore similar minor readings below.] Israel to you, as he handed over the ten tribes and Samaria.

(Vers. 10.) For just as thorns embrace one another, so [Al. “so indeed”] their feast of those drinking together will be consumed like stubble full of dryness. LXX: “For they will be reduced to thorns as far as their foundations, and, like a bindweed entwined around them, they will be consumed [Col. 1239B], and like stubble full of dryness.”

The three kinds of ground that the Lord set forth in the parable of the seed (Matthew XIII), apart from the good soil that bears thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold fruit, seem to me to be repeated by the prophet: one that fell beside the way, another among stones, and a third among thorns. The Apostle also hints at this concerning those who do not build well upon Christ’s foundation (I Corinthians III), showing that some build with wood, hay, and stubble.

Let us therefore refer “wood” to what is now said: “For they will be reduced to thorns as far as their foundations.” “Hay” to what follows: “And like a bindweed that is entwined, it will be consumed.” “Stubble” clearly refers to the stubble of which it is now said: “And like stubble full of dryness.”

Therefore the Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing, because the wickedness that arose among the founders of heresy will be consumed as far as its foundation and roots. But if anyone among them seemed to possess a display of words—that is, empty leaves pleasing only to the eye, like bindweed, which in Greek is called σμίλαξ—it will be devoured and reduced to nothing.

Bindweed [Al. “vulvula”] is a plant resembling ivy, usually entwined around vines and shrubs and creeping at length. Whatever among them seems to display the magnificence of a crop but has neither ears nor grains of wheat, like stubble full of dryness, will be handed over to the fire.

This is according to the Seventy. But according to the Hebrew, truly the covenants and associations of heretics are like thorns embracing one another; and their feast and mysteries—for they too claim to have the Lord’s table—are a covenant of thorns, of people eating and drinking together. When, drunk from the vine of Sodom, they blaspheme the Creator with rabid mouths, is it not a feast of thorns? Yet it will be consumed along with its authors, like stubble full of dryness.

(Vers. 11.) For from you will go forth one who plots evil against the Lord, devising treachery in his mind. LXX: “From you will go forth a thought against the Lord, devising the worst things.”

Truly, from the heretics will go forth a hostile thought against the Lord. Is it not evil and treachery against God to say what Valentinus said: that the Creator was, as it were, the abortive offspring produced at the end by erring Wisdom? Is not Basilides’ licentiousness [Al. “shamelessness”] a thought against God, as well as the monstrous name ἄβραξας, which is preferred to the Lord the Creator?

Furthermore, because we wish to learn from the Hebrews and also follow their tradition, and to demonstrate to our own people—that is, to Christians—the explanation of the history, we must say: “A double tribulation will not rise up”—that is, not all the tribes will be captured by the Assyrians, as the ten were captured. For while the Assyrians are still in the land of Judah, and, as it were, embrace one another like thorns, rejoicing and celebrating, they will be consumed by the angel, when one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the enemy were slain in a single night (II Kings IX).

He also aptly compared the multitude of their army to a feast of drunkards, and said that the feast itself was not one of roses, lilies, or flowers, but like thorns embracing one another—thorns that are always handed over to the fire—and like stubble full of dryness, burned by a light flame.

What follows—“From you will go forth one who plots evil against the Lord, devising treachery in his mind” (Isaiah XXXVI)—they wish to understand of Rabshakeh: that, having gone forth from the Assyrians, he blasphemed the Lord and tried to persuade the people, despairing of the Lord’s aid, to surrender to the Assyrians and serve not God but idols (II Kings XVIII).

(Vers. 11, 13.) Thus says the Lord: Though they be complete, and likewise numerous, even so they will be shorn, and he will pass away. I have afflicted you, and I will afflict you no more; and now I will break his rod from your back, and I will burst your bonds. LXX: “Thus says the Lord, reigning over many waters: so they will be divided, and your hearing will no longer be heard; and now I will break his rod from you, and I will burst his bonds.”

According to the literal sense, the meaning is clear: “Although,” he says, “the Assyrians are strong, and their strength is increased by the number of all the nations, even so, when the angel lays them waste, they will be shorn.” For just as the number of hairs cannot resist a sharp pair of shears, so the number of God’s adversaries will be removed by easy cutting. Assyria will pass away, either ceasing to exist or, when its army has been destroyed, returning to its homeland and leaving you unharmed.

Again, the speech is directed to Judah and Jerusalem: “I have afflicted you, and I will afflict you no more”—not that he promises perpetual security, but security only for that period and from those enemies by whom it was then besieged.

He adds: “And now I will break his rod,” that is, the rod of the Assyrian, “from your back, and I will burst your bonds”: either signifying his power metaphorically, or the rod with which he was attempting to strike and the bonds that he was preparing for captives. Yet the siege of a confined multitude may also be understood as bonds.

According to the Seventy, however, the meaning is very different. He still appears to be speaking against those to whom he had said above: “What are you plotting against the Lord?” and, “From you will go forth a thought against the Lord, devising the worst things.” Thus the Lord says, reigning over many waters—or over the powers called the waters above the heavens—and commands them to praise the Lord; or else he speaks of the understandings, wisdom, and teachings of God.

For just as rivers will flow from the belly of the righteous, and abundant springs into eternal life, through the various and manifold sayings over which the word of the Lord rules (John VII), so the leaders of heresies also have their waters, over which they rule and which first flowed from their own fountain.

What follows—“And so they will be divided”—may be understood of the heavenly powers that serve God on high: each one is in its own office and ministry. Or it may refer to the manifold variety of wisdom. Since he had said, “reigning over many waters,” no confused and indistinguishable number of meanings should be supposed; rather, each saying has meanings divided among themselves, distinct subjects, and proper hypotheses.

When it is said, “Your hearing will no longer be heard,” this is a rebuke of those who had devised contrary things against God: once their sophistries and snares, by which God’s people were ensnared, have been exposed, their speech will no longer run on or be accepted by the peoples.

The statement that follows—“And now I will break his rod from you, and I will burst your bonds”—is said to those against whom the threat is made: that they should no longer be struck by the devil or subject to him, by whose authority they had devised and fabricated so many things. His dominion over them will therefore be broken, and the bonds by which the souls of sinners were tied will be burst by the word of God, which says to those who are in bonds: “Come out.”

(Vers. 14.) And the Lord will command concerning you [Vulg. “against you”]: no one from your name will be sown any longer. From the house of your god I will destroy the graven image and the molten image; I will make your grave, because you are dishonored. LXX: “And the Lord will command concerning you: no one from your name will be sown any longer. From the house of your god I will destroy the graven images and the molten images. I will make your grave, because they are swift. Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of the one who evangelizes and announces peace.”

I have included more from the Seventy interpreters because the second section could not be separated from the preceding one. For in the statement “because you are dishonored,” for which the fifth edition has ὅτι ὑβρίσθης (“because you have been insulted”), the Seventy translated, “because they are swift,” which in Hebrew is written *CHI CALLOTH* (). Unless “swift” is referred to the feet of the following section, the sentence remains suspended.

Therefore, according to my custom, I shall first examine the historical meaning and afterward the meaning of the Vulgate edition. “The Lord will command,” he says, “against you, O Assur, so that what you are about to suffer may not come by chance and without a judge, but that you may suffer it by God’s pronouncement.”

“No one from your name will be sown any longer.” For immediately after returning to Nineveh, Sennacherib was killed by his sons. Read Isaiah, and you will find that he was killed in the house of his god, which he had entered to worship. This is what is meant by, “From the house of your god I will destroy” (Isaiah XXXVII): you will be punished from the place from which you hoped for aid.

The graven and molten image will be your grave, so that your profane blood may be poured out among the altars and couches of those worshiping idols.

According to the Seventy interpreters, join what follows to the preceding words: “No one,” he says, “will be sown any longer from your name.” Never again, O heretics, will the souls of the deceived receive names from your doctrines—the names they had previously invoked over their lands, as is sung figuratively in the forty-eighth Psalm.

This cessation of sowing will benefit you, since the sowing first used to kill the soul of the sower and then the one in whom he sowed. Therefore the doctrines of error will die for you; and you, who previously seemed to yourself to live, will die to error. Having died in what is good for you, you will have the idols you worshiped as your grave. Thus all errors will be removed from your breast, which had previously been a temple of the god you had invented.

These things will happen to you, who once devised contrary things against the Lord, when the word of God—which always ascends the mountains, that is, lofty and exalted souls—comes swiftly to you, tramples upon the waves of former errors, reduces them to tranquility, and restores to you peace and the understanding of faith [Note: [Col. 1241D] Victorius restores *sensusque* from the Brixian manuscripts.].

Forgive my prolixity. Since I follow both the history and the tropology, I cannot briefly encompass both, especially when I am tormented by the variety of the translations and sometimes forced, against my conscience, to weave together the sequence of the Vulgate edition.

(Vers. 15.) Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of the one who evangelizes and announces peace. Celebrate your feasts, Judah, and fulfill your vows, because Belial will no longer continue to pass through you; he has utterly perished [Vulg. “has perished”].

I shall postpone the Seventy interpreters for a little while [Note: [Col. 1242D] Previously *disseram* was read incorrectly.], because among them the sections themselves are confused by the variety of the translation. After briefly explaining the history, I shall adapt their edition to my own expression.

It is written in the Book of Chronicles that, when Sennacherib was besieging Jerusalem, they could not celebrate the Passover in the first month (II Chronicles XXXII). But after his army had been slain by the angel and his flight and death had been announced, they celebrated the day of Passover with the greatest festivity in the second month.

Therefore what he says means this: “O Judah, who reigns in Jerusalem, do not be anxious, for your enemy has been killed in the temple of his god. Behold, a messenger is coming to you, running across mountains and hills, and announcing from a distant lofty watchtower, as it were, that Sennacherib is dead and that the city has been freed from his rule. Celebrate the festivals; fulfill the vows you promised to God for the death of the enemy. The transgressor and ἀποστάτης—for this is what Belial means—will never again pass through you. The whole of him has perished,” that is, his army, his king, and the empire of the Assyrians have utterly fallen.

This is according to the literal sense. But according to ἀναγωγήν, it is spoken to the Church and to souls confessing the Lord: the devil, who previously laid you waste and oppressed you with a most grievous yoke, has perished in the idols and together with the idols he had fashioned. Celebrate your festivals and fulfill your vows to God [Col. 1243A], continually singing with the angels: Belial will never again pass through you. Of him the Apostle also says, “What fellowship has Christ with Belial?” (II Corinthians VI, 15). For when Nineveh has been overthrown, he has utterly perished.

Whenever there is a most grievous persecution, such as under Valerian, Decius, and Maximian [Al. “Maximus”], and the Lord’s vengeance appears against his adversaries, let us say to the Church: “Celebrate your festivals, Judah, and fulfill your vows,” and so forth.

LXX: “Celebrate your festivals, Judah; fulfill your vows, because they will no longer continue to oppose you so as to pass into old age. It is completed; it is finished. He has ascended, breathing upon your face, rescuing you from tribulation.”

I have already said that, because of the variety of the translation, the sections themselves are also differently defined, and that the meaning of the Hebrew translation cannot be made to agree with the sections. What is now said is therefore of this kind:

“O Ecclesiastical one, because no one will any longer be sown from the name of your adversaries, their rod has been broken, their bonds have been shattered, and the one who would announce peace to you has come: celebrate your festivals—not in wine and feasts, as the carnal Jews imagine, but in spiritual delights and the pleasure of the torrent.

“O Judah, fulfill your vows, because your enemies will no longer pass through you to bring you into old age—that is, because they want you to bear the image of the old man. For what is old grows aged, and what grows aged is near destruction.

“The world has been completed; the adversary has been consumed. Christ has come to you, who previously breathed upon your face when he formed you from the clay; and after the resurrection, breathing upon the face of the apostles, he also said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX, 22). He is the one who rescues you from tribulation. For when Nineveh has been devastated and the world has passed away, tribulation too will pass away.”

(Cap. II.—Vers. 1, 2.) He has ascended who scatters [Note: [Col. 1243D] The Palatine manuscripts read, “He will ascend who scatters before you in your face,” etc. The Vulgate has “before you who keeps watch,” instead of “watching before your face.”] before your face, guarding the siege. Contemplate the way, strengthen your loins, greatly fortify your power [Note: [Col. 1244D] The Vulgate has, “because the Lord has restored the pride of Jacob, as the pride of Israel.” Compare the following exposition of Jerome.], because, just as the Lord restored the pride of Jacob, so he will restore the pride of Israel, because devastators have devastated them and ruined their branches.

Necessity compels me, as though between rocks and cliffs with shipwreck threatening, to turn the course of my speech between history and allegory, and to take care lest I suddenly run aground. For, according to the poets’ fables:

> On the right Scylla, on the left implacable Charybdis,
>
> Besets us: if we flee the rocks, we plunge into the deep; if we avoid the twisted whirlpools, we are carried onto the rocks.

The Lord is my witness that, in everything I discuss according to the Hebrew, I do not speak from my own judgment—which is condemned in the false prophets—but follow the exposition of the Hebrews. Having been instructed by them for no short time, I ought simply to report to my own people what I have learned. Certainly, it will be the reader’s judgment, after considering both interpretations, to decide which he ought to follow more closely.

The speech now turns to Nineveh—and this is especially why the prophets are obscure: while one matter is being discussed, the person suddenly changes to another—and it says to her: “Nebuchadnezzar has ascended against you to besiege you, to lay waste the fields before your face, pursue the farmers, ravage the countryside, and keep you yourself shut in.

“Since war threatens you, behold, I, the rejoicing prophet, now announce beforehand: contemplate and look carefully, and observe what is happening to you. Strengthen your loins,” that is, gird yourself; “greatly fortify your power,” that is, gather your armies. For just as the Lord avenged Judah for the pride of Sennacherib, when his army was slain in Judea and he himself was slaughtered by his sons, so he will avenge Israel—that is, the ten tribes possessed by Nineveh.

The Assyrians devastated and overthrew both Judah and Israel, and under the metaphor of a vine they ruined the branches of both [Al. “of both trees”].

LXX: “Observe the way, grasp the loins, strengthen yourself with great vigor [Alt. strengthen with vigor], because the Lord has turned away Jacob’s reproach, as Israel’s reproach; for those who shook them have thoroughly shaken them, and they have destroyed their branches.”

Three commands are given to Judah. First, that he should observe the way and carefully consider the path along which he is about to walk, in accordance with what is written in Jeremiah: “Stand in the ways, ask about the everlasting paths, and see which is the good way; and walk in it” (Jeremiah 6:16), so that, when we have stood at the many ways, we may come to that way which says: “I am the way” (John 14:6).

Next he is told to grasp the loins—that is, after choosing the way, to put his body to death and subject it to servitude, lest, like a king and teacher preaching to others, he himself should be found rejected (1 Corinthians 9). It would take too long now to say that the devil’s power lies especially in the loins, and that the promise is made to David: “From the fruit of your loins I will set upon your throne” (Psalm 131:11). And there is also the Apostle’s statement: “Levi was still in the loins of his father Abraham when Melchizedek met Abraham” (Hebrews 7:10). Likewise, John is girded with a leather belt (Matthew 3), and the Savior commands the disciples: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). The Apostle also says to the Ephesians: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth” (Ephesians 6:14). Although ἄσκησις, ascetic discipline, contributes greatly, and the restraint of life is superior to the mortification of the loins, nevertheless nothing mortifies them as does knowledge of the truth. Hence it is said: “Gird your loins with truth.” For if Christ is the truth, whoever has believed with his whole mind in Christ has mortified his loins in Christ.

Third, he is commanded: “Strengthen yourself exceedingly with vigor.” You have chosen the way, he says; you have grasped the loins; take up strength, so that you may be able to fight against your enemies.

And lest you perhaps lose confidence, you are given the reason why you should hope: “The Lord has turned away Jacob’s reproach, as Israel’s reproach.” This is ambiguous. Either he has turned away Jacob’s own reproach, by which he used to wrong others, or the reproach that Jacob suffered from others. But it seems to me better to understand that the reproach which Jacob used to inflict on others has been turned away by the Lord. For it does not show such great virtue to endure an injury inflicted by others as it shows the Lord’s abundant grace to be gentle, mild, and tranquil, unable to inflict injury.

The question arises how Jacob’s injury was turned away, just as Israel’s had been turned away. After Jacob wrestled with the angel, he deserved to receive the name Israel (Genesis 32); and because he saw God, he ceased to inflict injury. Therefore, just as Israel—the mind, or the man, who sees God and always thinks about God—does not know how to inflict injury, so every insolence and reproach has been turned away from Jacob, that is, from the supplanter, from him who is still engaged in the contest and supplants his enemies.

To show how “injury” is to be understood in a negative sense, Solomon is a witness when he says: “The eyes [Alt. eye] of the insolent, the tongue of iniquity” (Proverbs 6).

But how, according to both interpretations, the injury was turned away from Jacob, as it had previously been turned away from Israel, the following words make clear: “For those who shook them have thoroughly shaken them, and they have destroyed,” or “corrupted,” their branches. The angels of individuals, he says, who daily see the face of the Father (Matthew 18:10), shook off whatever dust had clung to Jacob and Israel. Hence Peter’s feet are washed (John 13). And through the prophet it is said: “Shake off the dust and arise, Jerusalem” (Isaiah 52:2). The Savior likewise commands the disciples: “Shake off the dust from your feet” (Matthew 10:14). And it is written in the Psalms: “As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of those who have been shaken off” (Psalm 126:4).

Thus the mind inclined to reproach has been turned away from the true Jacob and the true Israel, because whatever in them was earthly and formed from the dregs below was shaken off and cleansed by angelic ministers—or by admonishers and teachers. They not only shook them off but also scattered the vices which, for the present, soothe the senses with pleasure and resemble scourges, and the branches which are full of leaves but without fruit. The Lord says: “Every branch that remains in me and bears fruit, my Father cleanses, so that it may bear more fruit; but whatever does not remain in me and does not bear fruit, my Father will cut off and cast into the fire” (Matthew 15).

(Verses 3 ff.) “The shield of his mighty men is fiery; the men of the army are in scarlet. The reins of the chariots are fiery on the day of his preparation; and the drivers are stupefied; they are thrown into confusion on the roads; the chariots collide in the streets. Their appearance is like lamps, like darting lightning. He will remember his mighty men; they will stumble on their roads; they will quickly climb his walls, and the shelter will be prepared. The gates of the rivers are opened, and the temple is destroyed to its foundations, and the soldier is led away captive, and its maidservants were led away, moaning like doves and murmuring in their hearts.”

LXX: “The weapons of his might are men, strong men mocking in fire [Note: [Col. 1245D] Our manuscripts have ‘fiery reins’ instead of ‘in fire,’ and below Jerome himself seems to prefer that reading. Then, together with the Brixian manuscripts cited by Victorius, and the Greek text itself, our manuscripts supply their word. Shortly afterward, our manuscripts likewise substitute the same word for ‘his’; and in fact it is found in some Greek copies as ἑτοιμασίας αὐτῶν, ‘of their preparation,’ instead of αὐτοῦ, ‘of his.’]. Their chariot reins are for the day of his preparation, and the horsemen will be afraid at the exits; the chariots will be thrown into confusion and collide in the streets. Their appearance is like lamps of fire and like darting lightning; their nobles will be remembered, and they will flee by day; they will grow weak on their way, and they will hasten to the walls and prepare their defenses. The gates of the cities are opened, the royal palace has fallen, and the substance has been exposed; she herself was going up, and her maidservants were led like doves, speaking in their hearts.” [Note: [Col. 1246D] In Victorius: “Those who shook them shook them off,” that is, Jacob, etc.]”

According to the historical sense, the sequence concerning Nineveh continues, and the army of the Babylonians coming against it is described. When he says, “The reins of the chariots are fiery,” he signifies the speed of those preparing in burning reins; and a display of men preparing themselves for battle is described, as though by ἑπισκευή, preparation. Scripture now weaves together, in combination, what Israel once suffered, what Assyria did, and what the Babylonians inflicted upon the Assyrians.

Therefore, he says, it is not surprising that they come so swiftly to lay waste, since the drivers and warriors—whether of Israel before or of the Assyrians afterward—have been stupefied. Then, returning again to the order of the description: Such is the multitude of those coming, he says, that the massed army is confused along the road and cannot be distinguished. The chariots themselves, finding no road because of the multitude, collide with one another in the streets.

The appearance of the Babylonians is like lamps, like darting lightning, so that they terrify their adversaries by their appearance before striking them down with the sword. Then Assyria will remember its mighty men and seek those who have fallen along the roads. It will quickly climb the walls of Nineveh and, because of the very long siege [Note: [Col. 1246D] Martianus has “the longest”; but the manuscripts prefer “the most recent.”], will prepare shelters to ward off the heat (Psalm 126).

But what good is it to build a house unless the Lord has built it? What benefit is there in closing gates which the Lord opens? The gates of Nineveh are opened. It had possessed a multitude of citizens like the waters of rivers, and its temple—that is, its kingdom—has been destroyed, and the soldier has been led away captive; that is, everyone has been led to Babylon.

By “the maidservants of Nineveh,” understand metaphorically the smaller cities, villages, and fortified settlements. Or certainly, captive women will be led away before the faces of the victors; and such will be the terror that their grief will not even break out into sobs and wailing, but they will moan silently within themselves and swallow their tears with a muted murmur, like cooing doves.

This is according to the Hebrew tradition. Let us now come to the translators of the Septuagint.

“Those who shook them,” who shook Jacob and Israel, “and scattered their scourges,” also broke the weapons which they had been accustomed to possess when they were insolent, and with which they had oppressed the weak. They did not merely do this, but also destroyed in fire the strong men who mocked. Consider whether you can call “strong men mocking in fire” the opposing powers which serve the devil’s burning arrows—those who once possessed chariots and horses, strong and mocking men, with which they were driven into battle against Jacob and Israel on the day of their preparation.

Therefore the reins of these chariots and the horsemen will be thrown into confusion on the roads and collide in the streets when Jacob and Israel are enlightened [Note: [Col. 1247D] Both our manuscripts and the Florentine codices consulted by Victorius read “healed” instead of “enlightened.” It has perhaps been noted that there is an allusion to Hosea 7: “When I wished to heal Israel.”] by the Lord: both the demons and those who serve their will will be overthrown by the Lord.

We may understand this of his first coming, when the strong men, the drivers of the chariots, and the horsemen said: “What have we to do with you, Son of David? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8:29). But since we have once understood the prophecy against Nineveh as concerning the consummation of the world, it is better to say that at that time the weapons of the devil’s power will be taken away from human beings, together with his strong ministers who mocked human beings in fire.

“For all who commit adultery are like an oven; their hearts…” (Hosea 3). The chains by which captives were led into vices will also be loosened, together with the riders of the chariots. The horsemen will be afraid at the exits—that is, at the consummation of the world—and they will be thrown into confusion, and the chariots will collide in the streets. For although the road that leads to death is broad and spacious (Matthew 7), yet, constricted by the pressure of time, they will be unable to find a straight path; they will collide with one another, and nevertheless will breathe out their ancient fury, darting here and there like lightning.

“I was watching,” says the Lord, “Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:18).

When the devil and all his nobles understand this, they will remember the consummation that had once been foretold, and they will flee by day. They will no longer move about in nights; when day grows bright, the darkness will be driven away. They will grow weak on the way, making no progress and not accomplishing their efforts [Note: [Col. 1247D] Two manuscripts have “not accomplishing their thoughts.”], and they will hasten to the walls.

For such terror of the coming Lord will seize them, and they will be so weak for resistance that they will flee to the boundaries of the world, by which the world is enclosed and surrounded as by walls, and they will prepare themselves to resist. It is like someone fleeing from an enemy without daring to resist him: when he has reached a deserted place, if the enemy happens to pursue him, necessity compels him to fight.

But while they are considering these things, all the possessions that had been acquired and held by them will be brought into the open and exposed; the gates that they had closed will be opened, their kingdoms will fall, and their substance—that is, their riches—will be revealed.

But when the substance of the world itself and all its maidservants have subjected themselves to Christ and begun to serve him, they will be led away joyful and glad, believing from the heart of their confession, so that they may be compared with the purity of doves. They will murmur, or speak, in their hearts.

Then what is said in the sixty-seventh Psalm concerning the Savior’s victory will be fulfilled: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.”

(Verses 8–9.) “And Nineveh is like a pool of waters; its waters are hers. But they have fled. Stand, stand! And there is no one who turns back. Plunder the silver, plunder the gold! And there is no end of riches” [Note: [Col. 1247D] The Regina manuscript, together with the Palatine manuscripts, has “of all desirable vessels.”] “from all desirable vessels.”

LXX: “And Nineveh is like a pool of waters; its waters are hers. And those who were fleeing did not stand, and there was no one who looked back. They were plundering silver, they were plundering gold, and there was no end to her adornment; she was weighed down above all her vessels of desire.”

It is clear that, when the cities of Nineveh—which Scripture calls her daughters—have been led into captivity, Nineveh herself, which had nourished such great populations that she could be compared with the waters of pools, has a useless multitude, since no one is present to resist or withstand the assault of the invading Babylonians.

She had peoples whose only purpose was to flee. When their mother cried, “Stand, stand! Shut the gates, climb the walls, resist the enemies,” there was no one who would return [Note: [Col. 1247D] The same Regina manuscript has “who would resist” instead of “who would return.”], no one who would look back toward his mother. Instead, all turning their backs, they abandoned the city to the plunder of the enemies.

Hence it is said to the Babylonians: Since they have fled, plunder the silver, and seize in sudden devastation the wealth accumulated over so long a time. For there is no end of the riches, furniture, and vessels stored in Nineveh; you cannot carry off as much as she offers for plunder.

But because we have said once that beautiful Nineveh signifies the world, let us see what kind of pool the world is. Scripture does not say that the waters of Nineveh are like the waters of the sea, nor like the waters of rivers, nor like the waters of springs, nor like the waters of wells, but like the waters of a pool. Thus, just as in Jeremiah the people are reproved because they abandoned the fountain of living water and dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water (Jeremiah 2), so in Nineveh all those waters are waters that have fallen from heaven and, abandoning their former height, have descended into the depths.

For all the doctrines of this world that are outside the fountain of the Church and the enclosed garden cannot say: “The river’s rush makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45:4). Nor are they among those waters that praise the name of the Lord above the heavens. Although they appear great, they are nevertheless small and confined within a narrow limit.

Nor should anyone be disturbed because we understand “pool” in a negative sense [Note: [Col. 1248D] I understand this occurrence of the same word in such a way that what lies between the words was either entirely passed over or badly supplied. Martianus retained it without any intelligible sense: “because we have understood pool in a negative sense.” Victorius, by conjecture, placed two little words before “that pool,” and patched the passage as best he could. Now, with the help of the Regina manuscript, its original complete sense has been restored.], while that pool is understood in a positive sense—the one to which Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet is commanded to ascend.

There it is said with an added qualification: “the pool of the watercourse” and “the pool of the fuller” (Isaiah 7 and 36), which is accustomed to wash away dirt and remove stains from garments [Alt. filth]. Because it is set on high, the prophet is therefore commanded to ascend to it and, going to meet the king, to promise victory over the two smoking firebrands.

It follows: “Those who were fleeing did not stand,” namely, the inhabitants of Nineveh. First, they ought not to have fled from God; then, even if they had fled, they ought at some point to have stood. For there is a great difference between one who flees and stands and one who, fleeing, never stands. Whoever stands has ceased to flee; whoever does not stand is always advancing in flight.

Thus, amid so great a crowd of fugitives, there was no one who looked back, repented, and heard the Lord saying: “Return to me, returning children, and I will heal your breaches” (Jeremiah 3:22). Hence the holy man also says in the Psalms: “Flight has perished from me” (Psalm 141:5).

I think this also signifies the mystery of leprosy. Concerning it, Leviticus says: “When the leper has been separated by the priest outside the camp: if the leprosy stands still, the man is clean” (Leviticus 13–14). The one who had been cast out as a leper is cleansed, returns to the camp, and dwells among the people.

But if, he says, the leprosy has spread—that is, if it has not stood still but has grown, and has progressed in evil, and has changed the color of its former health—then the leprosy is most clearly confirmed by the one who possesses knowledge of examining and cleansing leprosy.

We too are commanded by the true Solomon to dwell in Jerusalem and never to leave it. If what had previously been subject to us flees from us and goes over to the Philistines, let us not leave the walls of our city, nor follow the footsteps of fugitives, lest, while wishing to save those who flee, we ourselves perish. Rather, let us leave the dead to bury their own dead (Matthew 8), and, while it is permitted, let us tear out and cut off from ourselves the eye, hand, and foot that causes scandal (Mark 9).

What is said—“They were plundering silver, they were plundering gold, and there was no end of her adornment; she was weighed down above all her vessels of desire”—is spoken of the waters of Nineveh and of those who fled and did not stand, nor was there anyone who looked back. Not content merely to have fled and not looked back, they also plundered silver, whatever eloquence appeared in the world; they plundered gold, whatever brilliant ideas existed in secular teaching, so as to adorn Nineveh and arrange their doctrines with every flower of thought and language.

Therefore Nineveh was weighed down above all her vessels of desire. For the more she possessed a great abundance of gold and silver, and varied furniture that was heavy, the more heavily she herself was weighed down, since she loved heavy things.

Hence in Zechariah iniquity sits upon a talent of lead (Zechariah 5); and the Egyptians, who were weighed down by sins, sank into the sea like lead (Exodus 14). And in the person of the sinner it is said in the Psalm: “Like a heavy burden they have been too heavy for me” (Psalm 37:5).

Peter, who earlier had trodden the waves with a light, swinging step, after being weighed down by unbelief and swallowed by the waves, was lifted up by the Lord’s hand (Matthew 14).

(Verses 10.) “She is devastated, torn apart, and mangled; the heart melts, the knees give way, there is weakness in all the loins, and the faces of all are like the blackness of a pot” [Note: [Col. 1249D] Victorius inserts “of them,” from the Vulgate edition and the Hebrew.].

LXX: “Shaking, renewed shaking, and boiling over, and breaking of heart, and dissolution of knees, and pains throughout every loin, and the faces of all like the scorching of a pot.”

Under the metaphor of a captive woman, devastated, torn apart, and mangled Nineveh is described: her heart melting, her knees giving way, her kidneys crushed, and the faces of all her inhabitants, because of the terror of the enemies and the greatness of their fear, appearing burned, wasted, and disfigured by pallor, like pots.

According to the Septuagint, however, we must understand more deeply what “shaking” and “renewed shaking” signify. What is said of the people of God? A human being at some point sins and returns to his former state; to one such person, as to Jerusalem, it is said: “Shake off the dust of your feet and rise, Jerusalem” (Isaiah 52:2) [Note: [Col. 1250D] One Regina manuscript has “your dust” instead of “the dust of your feet.” The Septuagint does not have “your” either, but only ἐκτίναξαι τὸν χοῦν, “shake off the dust.” The Vulgate edition and the Florentine manuscripts cited by Victorius agree with this; therefore he deleted “of your feet.”].

And of one who, after being shaken off, is deemed worthy to become one of God’s arrows and to be drawn by the Lord against his enemies, it is sung: “As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of those who have been shaken off” (Psalm 126:4).

When his footsteps, as of one walking upon the earth, have been sprinkled with dust, he will hear from the Savior: “Shake off the dust of your feet as a testimony against them” (Mark 6:11), unquestionably referring to those who refused to receive the preachers.

But the one who belongs to Nineveh, which has been weighed down above all the vessels of its desire, is not shaken off once but frequently. After he has again been shaken off and his surface cleansed, so that no dirt remains within, there is also a boiling over, which in Greek is more precisely called ἐκβρασμός, eruption. Properly speaking, ἐκβρασμός is used in such matters when what was hidden within bursts out onto the face. Hence the pustules that arise on the lips after an illness are also called ἐκβράσματα, and it seems to be a sign of health when the disease has erupted onto the surface.

This remedy is not applied to Nineveh only so that it may be shaken off repeatedly and the hidden sickness in its vital parts forced to emerge; the breaking of the heart and the dissolution of the knees [Alt. kidneys] are also proclaimed. Thus, just as Pharaoh’s hard, stony heart was broken—so long as he had it, he did not release God’s people (Exodus 7 ff.)—so Nineveh’s broken heart may be softened and changed into a heart of flesh, and [Alt. so that] its rigid knees, which previously did not bend before God, may be loosened and bent before God, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, and at whose name every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bends (Philippians 2:10).

After they have come to know their Creator, let them hear: “Strengthen yourselves, slack hands; and weak knees, [Note: [Col. 1251D] The Regina manuscript has “be strengthened,” which seems more correct according to the sense of the Septuagint, which translated the passage with passive force, as also in Zephaniah 2; “and weak knees, be made firm.” Otherwise Victorius’s “strengthen” appears superfluous, and all the Florentine manuscripts lacked it. The passage is from Isaiah 35: “Be strong, slack hands, and weak knees that have been paralyzed; be encouraged, fainthearted, or you who are fainthearted in mind.” The passage was altered from the Latin Vulgate, where it reads: “Strengthen the slack hands, and make firm the weak knees. Say to the fainthearted: Be strong, do not fear.” For this reason he deleted the word “strengthen.”] be strengthened” (Isaiah 35:3).

“And there will be pains,” he says, “throughout every loin.” We have already stated above that sexual intercourse is signified by the loin, and that all actions relating to intercourse are indicated by the term “loins.” Great pains, therefore, will be in the loins at the consummation, because all the dragon’s power is in the loins (Job 40:11). And for all those things because of which shaking, renewed shaking, boiling over, breaking of the heart, dissolution of the knees, and pains of the loins have preceded, the faces of all will be like the scorching of a pot: either close to fire and heat, or losing their brightness and darkening like coals, covered with eternal shame, from which the holy person is far removed when he says: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:7).

For with unveiled face he contemplates the glory of God (2 Corinthians 3). And I think that, just as one glory belongs to the sun, another to the moon, and another to the stars, and star differs from star in brightness (1 Corinthians 15:41), so at the resurrection of the dead there will be a great difference between the brightness of the saints and the blackness of sinners.

(Verses 11.) “Where is the dwelling place of the lions, and the pasture of the young lions, to which the lion went, and the lion’s cub entered, and there is no one to terrify? [Note: [Col. 1252D] We corrected “terrify” from the Regina manuscript after Victorius, with the agreement of the Vulgate and Jerome’s following exposition. Martianus retained “be terrified.”] The lion seized enough for his cubs and killed for his lionesses; he filled his caves with prey and his den with plunder.”

Instead of “caves” and “lionesses,” the Septuagint translated “nests” and “young lions”; in the rest, the sense is the same.

The statement still concerns Nineveh: it had been the dwelling place of kings and the court of nobles. To it the lion—the Babylonian king, that is, Nebuchadnezzar—went, together with the lion’s cub, his subordinate kings, and there was no one to resist them.

“The lion seized enough for his cubs and killed for his lionesses.” The same Nebuchadnezzar possessed everything by right of victory and handed captives over to slavery for his children and cities [Alt. cities], or certainly for his wives. He filled his caves—or, as it is in the Hebrew, his pits—with prey, and his den with plunder, filling his treasures and cities with gold, silver, clothing, and every kind of ornament, so that he might possess what Nineveh had possessed and what Babylon had conquered.

But because, according to the ἀναγωγή, the spiritual interpretation, we have interpreted Nineveh both in Jonah and in this prophet as this world, and according to John, “the whole world lies in the evil one” (1 John 5:18), after the world has passed through the dwelling place of beasts, in which lions fed, we will say in wonder and exultation: Where is the dwelling place of the lions to which the lion went?

The lion is the devil, of whom Peter also speaks: “Your [Alt. our] adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). The lion’s cub is the Antichrist, together with all perverse doctrines and contrary speech.

“You have heard,” John says, “that the Antichrist is coming; now many antichrists have appeared” (1 John 2). For there are as many antichrists as there are false doctrines.

Before Christ’s coming there was no one to terrify them. But after our Lord came into the world and entered Nineveh, he saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning (Luke 10), and Lucifer, who rose at dawn, fell from heaven (Isaiah 41).

For the true Samson came to the Philistines; and as he went to Timnah—which is interpreted as “his consummation”—in order to take Delilah, a poor woman from the nations, he killed the lion whose consummation had come; and after it had died, he ate the honey of sweetness.

The true David too, while guarding his father’s sheep, seized and killed the lion (1 Samuel 17). And Benaiah, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord is builder” (1 Chronicles 11), descended into the pit of this age, which used to cool its boiling waters, and killed the lion.

In Isaiah’s vision concerning the four-footed creatures, the distress of these beasts is described first: “In tribulation and distress, the lion and the lion’s cub” (Isaiah 35).

Before this lion was killed by Christ, he seized many as prey for his cubs and killed them for his little lions, his attendants—that is, the demons. Look at the gatherings of the heretics, and you will not search in vain for many captured by the lion. Consider the dead who have abandoned life, and you will not call their churches the sheepfold of a shepherd, but the caves of lions, which he has filled with the corpses and blood of the dead.

“You have appointed darkness,” David says, “and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. The young lions seek to seize and to seek their food from God” (Psalm 103:20) [Note: [Col. 1252D] Victorius adds “roaring” after the Vulgate model.].

The lion is rarely found by day, but it always prowls during the nights, so that it may snatch from Christ’s Church and, according to Habakkuk, be sated with choice foods (Habakkuk 1).

Finally, Judas belonged to Christ’s sheepfold, but, snatched away by the lion, he was strangled by hanging (Matthew 27). The prophet also, whom the Lord had commanded not to eat bread in the land where the golden calves and a false religion were found, because he ate, was struck by a lion (1 Kings 13).

Jeremiah likewise speaks of sinners: “The lion from the forest struck them, and the wolf destroyed them as far as their houses; and the leopard watched over their cities. All who go out from them will be captured” (Jeremiah 5:6). Notice in this that no one is captured except the one who has gone out from the cities of God.

In the Fourth Book of Kings (chapter 17), those who lived in the cities of Samaria and did not know the judgment of the God of the land were killed by lions, until they learned to worship God and were delivered from the lions.

For this reason, I think, whatever has been captured by beasts is not to be offered in God’s sacrifices (Leviticus 22:8), and the prophet says: “What was unclean and captured by a beast has not entered my mouth” (Ezekiel 4:14).

Therefore the lion was killed; and when false doctrines had been refuted, “food came out of the eater, and sweetness came out of the strong” (Judges 14).

(Verse 13.) “Behold, I am against you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will burn your chariots to smoke” [Note: [Col. 1253D] From the Regina manuscript we restore “your,” which Victorius had supplied from the Vulgate edition alone and the Hebrew. He also read “little lions” instead of “cubs,” though no manuscript supports it. Martianus retained “his” instead of “your.”] “and the sword will devour your young lions [Vulg. little lions]. I will destroy your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers will no longer be heard.”

LXX: “Behold, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will burn your multitude to smoke, and the sword will devour your lions, and I will remove your prey from the earth, and your works will no longer be heard.”

O Nineveh, you will suffer, with me as author, all the things that have been stated. I, the Lord, will burn your chariots to smoke and destruction, and I will cause all your nobles and subordinate kings to be devoured by the sword. You will no longer lay waste to lands, impose tribute, or send your envoys through the provinces; or else, I will no longer hear the angels who are your guardians pleading for you.

The same things are also said concerning the world, in which there is a multitude proceeding along the broad and spacious way that leads to death (Matthew 7). The Lord threatens to consume it with fire and suffocate it in the smoke of its excessive vanity [Alt. goodness].

The sword will also devour the lions: the living and sharp word of God, honed on every side. He further promises that he will remove its prey from the earth, so that no one will thereafter be captured in Nineveh; and, as though in mercy, he removes its evil works and restrains them, so that their voice and sound can no longer be heard. Hence he says: “And your works will no longer be heard.”

### (Chapter III.—Verses 1 ff.)

“Woe to the city of blood, wholly of deceit [Alt. “deceitful”], full of tearing apart; plunder will not depart from you: the sound of the whip, and the sound of the rushing wheel, and of the snorting horse, of the heated chariot, and of the mounted horseman, and of the flashing sword, and of the glittering spear, and of the multitude slain, and of the grievous ruin; there is no end of corpses. And they will fall upon their bodies, because of the multitude of the fornications of the beautiful and pleasing harlot, who possesses magical arts, who sold nations through her fornications and families through her magical arts.”

The Septuagint: “O city of blood, wholly deceitful, full of iniquity; the prey will not be handled. The sound of whips, and the sound of the shaking of wheels, and of the pursuing horse, and of the heated chariot, of the mounted horseman, and of the shining sword, and of the gleaming weapons, and of the multitude of the wounded, and of the grievous ruin; there will be no end of her nations, and they will grow weak in their bodies because of the multitude of fornication: the beautiful and pleasing harlot, leader of magical arts, who sells nations in her fornication and tribes through her magical arts.”

Where we have rendered “full of tearing apart,” the Hebrew has PHEREC MALEA [פֶרֶץ מָלְאָה], which Aquila translated as ἐξαυχενισμοῦ πλήρης, that is, “full of neck-breaking” [Note: The Royal manuscript has “full of neck-breaking”]. Symmachus, however, translated it as ἀποτομίας πλήρης, which we may render “full of cruelty” or “full of severity.” In another edition of his I found μελοκοπίας πλήρης, that is, “full of cuttings of flesh and pieces torn apart limb from limb.” Immediately afterward he added: “where there is unceasing prey.”
