The Hebrew PHEREC [פֶרֶץ], however, was not translated as “neck-breaking”—for which in Aquila’s edition we find ἐξαυχενισμόν [the manuscripts have αὐκενισμόν]—but as “steering,” that is, κυβερνισμόν, so that he might show both that the city was royal and that, as though in a ship, it held the helm of all the nations.

Her power is described—that is, the power of Nineveh—and under the lamentation of cruelty she is accused. “Woe to the city of blood,” in which there is no truth, but every kind of deceit; full of plunder and the tearing apart of spoils. “The sound of the whip”: the cruel sound of an ever-raging dominion; and “the sound of the rushing wheel.” Let us understand “sound” as “noise”: the heated wheel rushing in different directions; and the snorting horse and the heated chariot—“sound” being understood in every case.

The description of the army preparing for battle is so beautiful, according to the Hebrew, and so like a painting, that all my speech is inferior to it. For when he says, “and of the grievous ruin, and there is no end of corpses,” let us understand this of the adversaries who were killed by them. “And they will fall upon their bodies”: either they will fall because of their own multitude, as they are crowded together by one another; or they will fall upon the corpses of those whom they have killed. For αὐτῶν signifies both “their own” and “of them.”

“Because of the multitude,” he says, “of the fornications of the harlot”: because she fornicated with many nations and worshiped the idols of the whole world that she had subjected to herself. “Beautiful and pleasing, and possessing magical arts” signifies magicians. She “sold nations in her fornications and families in her magical arts,” that is, she exercised power over all nations.

These things have been said simply about Nineveh. But if, because of the name of beauty, we have rationally understood the world as Nineveh, then rightly the world—which is set in evil—is called “a city of blood” because of the multitude of its archers and of those who, as though with swords, kill human beings with their tongues. Hence also it follows: “wholly deceitful,” which refers to the perversity of doctrines, since it does not possess the word of God, where the head might recline, while it possesses every perverse doctrine.

“There is none who understands or seeks God; all have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:2–3). Although these things are now fulfilled in part [Note: The Codex Reginae has: “nevertheless they are fulfilled more fully in the transformation of the world”; and, a little later, with the older editions but without the negative particle: “whose prey will be handled”], they will be fulfilled more fully at the consummation, when, because iniquity has multiplied, the love of many will grow cold (Matt. 24).

How many are captured by Nimrod the giant and most savage hunter, because, growing proud against God, he has entangled many in his snares from his thicket! His prey, or his hunting, “will not be handled” by many. For he has many attendants and fellow hunters who rejoice in his hunting and stand beside him in the manner of captives [Note: We have restored this according to the authority of the Royal codex: “they stand beside him in the manner of captives.” Previously, it was apparently read less correctly as “boasting in the death of captives”].

But the sound of whips is also heard in the world, because “many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. 33:20). Those who are scourged by them cry out and testify to the greatness of their pain with mournful voices. One is seized by a demon, another by anger—which resembles madness—another by lust, hatred, envy, or pride: in them the scourge of the Assyrian king resounds.

But also in bodily afflictions we understand the devil’s scourge, concerning which it is said to the righteous: “And the scourge will not approach your tent” (Ps. 90:10) [Note: The same manuscript: “when we have seen this man,” etc.]. When we see one who has rotted away from jaundice (*morbus regius*, “the royal disease”) and remains upon his own corpse; another afflicted with dropsy and swimming in a swollen body, as his limbs increase and the form of the former human being diminishes; another afflicted with an *excetra* [Note: For *excetra*, printed editions read “in this land”; but Erasmus appears to have read the name *excetra* in the manuscripts; indeed, in the margin he noted, “recently in the *exedra*.” It is therefore clear that, on the authority of all the manuscript copies, *excetra* should be read, which signifies the hydra in Plautus. Jerome, moreover, repeatedly used this word against Rufinus, as in the preface to the books of Chronicles translated from Hebrew into Latin, in the preface to his Commentaries on Ezekiel, and in the prologue to Book II of the Commentaries on Habakkuk, as well as below, if we trust the manuscripts of Marianus. Thus we may know that Rufinus at some time suffered from dropsy, or intercutaneous water—a fact which, before our restoration, everyone had overlooked. To this may also be referred Jerome’s words that Grunnius would die in his own pus. MART.: What Martianus notes—that before him everyone had failed to know that Rufinus, who is mocked under the name *excetra*, had at some time suffered from dropsy or intercutaneous water—deserves to be condemned by everyone as boasting, since he learned from ancient records not merely that Rufinus had once suffered from it, but also that he had died from that disease]. We have seen him discharge certain pus-like fluids and the damage to a wounded lung; another feels his bodily fluid dry into stones [Note: The torment of stones was known to the ancients, as Jerome testifies. Therefore the opinion of those who thought that this stone-disease was unknown to the ancients and that it was instead regarded as leprosy is false. MART.: The Reginae manuscript has “with the fluid dried into stones”].

We should not hesitate to say that the sound of whips is Nineveh, although some suspect that these things arise either from corrupt air or from differences in foods and bodies. We who read that the fever was rebuked (Luke 4), and that the woman who for eighteen years had been bound by the devil was healed by the Lord (Luke 13), should know that all these are the scourges of Nineveh.

Hence it follows: “And the sound of the shaking of wheels,” while the human race is dragged here and there, and while, in uncertain wanderings throughout all things, we do not know where danger is or where safety [Note: “The Reginae codex omits ‘voices, where there is danger’”]. Concerning this wheel it is also written at the beginning of Ezekiel (Ezek. 1); and in the seventy-sixth Psalm we read: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 76:19).

Nineveh also has a pursuing horse, whose neighing, whose hoof digging into the earth, and whose heated breast always desire war, when the Lord speaks against the devil: “From afar he smells battle”; with a leap and a shout he spares no fugitives; he does not allow those who turn their backs to depart, but pursues them in order to overthrow, kill, trample, and crush them [Alt. “mock them”].

There is also in Nineveh “the sound of the heated chariot,” such as I think Pharaoh possessed, those chariots which were submerged by the Lord (Exod. 14). Four horses are yoked to this chariot, namely the four disturbances about which the philosophers also dispute and which Maro does not leave unmentioned when he says (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI):

> These desire, fear, grieve, and rejoice . . . .

With these horses and this chariot Nineveh disturbs everything.

There is also heard in her the sound of the mounted horseman, who, prepared for battle by a certain skill and maneuver, advances not without danger against the one fighting him. This horseman has the sword of speech, sharpened on the whetstone of dialectic and smoothed with the oil of rhetorical art. He has gleaming weapons, since Satan transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11), weapons that are opposed to the apostolic armor.

It is no wonder if there is in Nineveh a multitude of wounded, since there is a multitude of arrows. And just as the four things with which we fight and by which we are protected are the shields of the virtues—prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude—so, in contrast, there are four vices: folly, iniquity, luxury, and fear, by which we are struck by the enemy. Each of these contains within itself burgeoning and manifold kinds of arrows, by which wounds are inflicted. Unless medicine immediately heals them, there follows a grievous ruin. And would that as many in Nineveh were lightly falling and lightly wounded as are, because of the weight of the ruin, plunged down to the underworld!

“There is no end of its nations” [Alt. “of its groans”]: its wickedness has no end. And as there are many kinds of sins, so there are many nations of Nineveh, which “will grow weak in their bodies because of the multitude of fornication.”

Although this may also be understood of those who, because of sexual matters, have been weakened in body and, with the destruction of the soul, also break the flesh which they serve, nevertheless these nations of which we have spoken do not fall, according to the Hebrew, except “in their bodies,” and they do not stumble—as Symmachus translated—except “upon the corpses of the dead,” which have been cast down by the multiplication of fornication.

At this point the Septuagint interpreters, when we have rendered according to the Hebrew, “because of the multitude of the fornications of the harlot,” seem to have wished to make a new beginning, saying: “Because of the multitude of fornication.” With this sentence ended, they then begin: “Beautiful and pleasing harlot, leader of magical arts.” In place of “leader of magical arts,” Aquila and Symmachus translated “possessing magical arts.”

Nor will anyone be surprised that Nineveh is now the most pleasing of harlots [Note: The same manuscript: “that Nineveh is a most pleasing prostitute”], who sees such a multitude of human beings fornicating with her and nearly everyone being drawn to love her by her magical arts and certain incantations. She “sold nations in her fornications,” which remove the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot; and “tribes in her magical arts.” For she makes them love what they ought to have hated and hate what they ought to have loved, so that, once they have been deceived, they may, according to what is written, “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33), overthrow others also by her magical art.

I have read in the sacred Scriptures that *magicians* may also be understood in a good sense: “And the magician of the enchanter wisely” (Ps. 57). But such a magician enchants for this purpose: to draw back to sanity those who are bound by love of the harlot Nineveh.

### (Verses 5–6)

“Behold, I am against you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will uncover your private parts before your face, and I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to kingdoms. I will throw abominations upon you, I will treat you with contempt, and I will set you as an example.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will uncover your backside upon your face, and I will show your disgrace to the nations and your shame to kingdoms, and I will throw abomination upon you according to your uncleannesses, and I will set you as an example.”

Because you, O Nineveh, sold nations through your fornications and families through your magical arts, and, like a public prostitute, spread your legs before everyone, therefore I myself will come against you to overthrow you. I will not send an angel; I will not entrust your judgment to others.

“I will uncover your private parts before your face,” so that what you formerly did not see may be placed before your eyes. “I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to kingdoms,” so that those who fornicated with you may despise you, mock you, and treat you with contempt; and you will be an example to all who see you.

All these things are narrated under the metaphor of an adulterous woman who, when she has been discovered, is brought out into the midst and exposed before everyone’s eyes. Through a transference of meaning, prophetic speech describes the same thing most fully concerning Jerusalem in Ezekiel.

Yet these things are spoken more truly and more profitably of the world, for whose cutting and healing the true physician came from heaven. “Behold, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty”: because I am almighty, I can heal every disease; what is impossible for others is possible for me.

“I will uncover your backside before your face,” that is, your virtues, commandments, and words, which you threw behind your back. Although you do not deserve it, I will make you see them. For I had commanded you concerning my words that they should always move before your eyes, that they should be bound and hang before you. But you, having despised the command of the one who ordered you, left them behind your footsteps, so that you not only failed to do what I commanded, but did not even deign to see it.

Or certainly I will make you see and understand your errors, which formerly, while you were being carried along blind and headlong, you thought to be virtues. After this I will also show your nakedness to the nations whom you sold in your fornication, so that they may no longer be captured by love of you, but, seeing your filthy and shameful body within—though previously they had been led astray by its outward surface—they may cease to fornicate with you.

To kingdoms also, which are greater than nations, I will show your shame, which you yourself produced in order to possess it. “I will throw abomination upon you according to your uncleannesses,” so that, just as you are unclean, you may appear unclean, and may no longer deceive the many who previously clung to you and became one body with you.

“And I will set you as an example,” so that the likeness of a feared punishment may prevent the likeness of sinning (2 Cor. 5).

### (Verse 7)

“And it shall be: everyone who sees you will recoil from you and will say, ‘Nineveh has been devastated; who will shake his head over you? From where shall I seek a comforter for you?’”

The Hebrew does not contain “his head,” but we supplied it so that the sense might be clearer. Accordingly, Symmachus translated it thus: “And everyone who sees you will withdraw from you and will say, ‘Nineveh has been scattered; who will mourn with her?’”

The Septuagint, moreover: “And it shall be: everyone who sees you will descend from you and will say, ‘Wretched Nineveh, who will lament her? From where shall I seek consolation suitable for her—one who tunes a string?’” [Note: The Reginae manuscript has: “Who will groan over you? From where shall I seek consolation for you?”]

Whoever sees the ruins of Nineveh, with her set as an example for all, will be terrified and astonished, and will say: “Nineveh has been scattered; who will shake his head over you?” That is, who will grieve over you? Who can be your comforter? While you were powerful, like a cruel mistress, you did not pity the old man [Alt. “the old men”] or look upon the child; nor did you prepare a companion for your mourning, since you were unwilling to have a partner in your reign.

But whoever despises earthly things, and has scorned the magical arts of the sorceress Nineveh, and has not been ensnared by her false beauty, when he has seen all her ugliness within and has begun to hate what the others love, will flee and recoil from her—or, as the Septuagint says, will descend from her.

For as long as we honor earthly things and think them exalted, we are, as it were, upon the summit of pride, and we marvel at the beauty of Nineveh. But when we have considered her nature and despised all bodily goods as lowly, submitting ourselves to the power of God’s hand, then we will pity the Ninevites [Alt. “Nineveh”], judge all earthly goods worthy of lamentation, and say: “Wretched Nineveh! How many have been ensnared by your traps; how many do you hold bound by your chains! Who, do you suppose, will recoil from you and descend from your pride, and judge you wretched?”

What he says—“who?”—we should understand not so much as referring to something difficult as to something rare, as we have often said: “Who, do you suppose, is a faithful and wise steward?” (Matt. 24:45); and “Who is wise, and will understand these things?” (Hos. 14:10); and “Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps. 23:3).

Who, then, will groan over Nineveh? Who can be found who, burdened by this dwelling-place, will say with Paul: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:14)?

Every day we see that when death approaches someone and he understands that he is being taken from this world by fever, wound, or some other kind of disease, he fears and trembles, clinging with his whole trembling body to the embraces of Nineveh and scarcely being torn away from the body of the beautiful harlot.

What follows—“From where shall I seek consolation, or a comforter for you, who will tune a string?”—is still spoken in the person of the one who will recoil or descend from Nineveh and say: “Wretched Nineveh, who will lament her?” He is discussing the confused conduct of this age, in which nothing can please anyone permanently: what pleased displeases, and what had displeased pleases again.

Who, therefore, can be found as such a comforter—or, so to speak, as a lyric poet and harpist—who could draw her discordant strings into a single harmony and turn her vocal sound into a concert of praise to God?

What we have explained—“who will tune a string,” or “one who tunes a string”—which in Greek is ἁρμόσαι χορδήν, we find neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translators. In its place they have the beginning of another sentence: “Are you better than Amon, who dwells among the rivers?” Hence it seems to me that this should rather be joined with what follows.

### (Verses 8 ff.)

“Are you better than Amon [Vulgate: Alexandria of the peoples], which dwells among the rivers? Water surrounds it; its wealth is the sea; its walls are waters. Ethiopia was its strength, and Egypt, and there was no end; Africa and the Libyans were your helpers. Yet she herself is led away into exile. Her little ones are dashed to pieces at the head of every road; lots are cast over her nobles, and all her great men are fettered with chains. And you also will become drunk and will be despised; you too will seek help from the enemy. All your fortifications are like a fig tree with its early figs: if they are shaken, they will fall into the mouth of the eater.”

The Septuagint: “Tune a string, portion of Ammon, who dwell among the rivers; waters surround her, whose beginning is the sea, and her wall is water. Ethiopia is her strength, and Egypt, and there is no end of your flight. Phut and the Libyans became her helpers” [Note: According to the Greek text of the Vatican manuscript, omitting the name Phut, the Reginae manuscript reads: “and the Libyans became her consolers”]. “And she herself will go into captivity, and they will dash her little ones at the beginning of the roads, and they will cast lots over all her illustrious people, and all her nobles will be bound in chains. And you will become drunk and will be despised; and you will seek there to stand against your enemies” [Note: The Reginae manuscript rejects the word “your,” which certain copies do not know in the Greek]. “All your fortifications will be like a fig tree bearing early figs; if they are shaken, they will fall into the mouth of the eater.”

Where the Septuagint reads, “Tune a string, portion of Ammon,” the other interpreters translated: “Are you better than Amon?” The Hebrew who instructed me in the Scriptures said that it could be read in this way: “Are you better than No, Amon?” He said that NO in Hebrew means Alexandria, while AMON means multitude or peoples, and that the order of reading is: “Are you better than populous Alexandria, or Alexandria of the peoples, which dwells among the rivers, with water surrounding it?”

This is not because Alexandria was called by that name at that time—for it received its name from Alexander the Great, the Macedonian, long afterward—but because under its original name, that is, No, it had always been the metropolis of Egypt and exceedingly rich in peoples. Indeed, those who committed the deeds of Alexander to memory assert that it was the chief city of Egypt.

The prophet Jeremiah also, understanding Amon or No as Alexandria, in a vision against Egypt, to which he says, “Egypt is a beautiful heifer; a goad from the north will come upon her” (Jer. 46:20), adds more clearly: “The daughter of Egypt is confounded; she has been delivered into the hand of the people of the north, says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel. Behold, I will visit Amon of No [AMON MENNO, אמון מנא], that is, the tumult [Alt. “the mound”] of Alexandria” (Jer. 46:24 ff.). For AMON, as we have said, means “peoples”; MEN signifies the preposition “from”; and NO means Alexandria.

“And I will visit,” he says, “Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods” [Note: The words “and her kings,” according to Martianus, are absent]; “and her kings and Pharaoh and those who hope in him. And I will give them into the hands of those who seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of his servants.”

Thus it is said to Nineveh: “Are you more populous, or more powerful, than Alexandria?” The situation of Alexandria is described: it is situated upon the Nile and the sea, and is surrounded on every side by waters and rivers. “Water surrounds it, whose wealth is the sea; its walls are waters.” On one side it is enclosed by a branch of the Nile, on another by Lake Mareotis, and on another by the sea.

That Ethiopia and Egypt and Africa—for which the Hebrew has PHUT [פוּט]—and the Libyans are her protection is shown by the actual situation of the provinces and the city. “This city also,” says the prophet, “which my speech describes, will be captured by the Babylonian king, and the same destroyer will be yours and hers.” Josephus, the writer of Jewish history, also records this in his books.

“Her little ones will be dashed to pieces in the crossroads” [Alt. “in fetters”]; her nobles will be divided by lot among the victors, and her once most powerful rulers will be led captive in chains. Since Alexandria will suffer these things, you also, O Nineveh, will drink from the same cup: you will become drunk and, lying stupefied, will be despised. You will come into such need that you will ask help from the Babylonians—or, against the Babylonians—from your enemies.

All your strongholds and walls [Note: The Reginae manuscripts have: “and the walls which you stretched upward, the heights,” etc.] extended toward the heavens, the heights of your towers which you now think impregnable, and your strong and warlike men will be compared to early figs. If they are shaken by the slightest touch, they will fall into the mouth of the one devouring them.

For what the Septuagint reads—“Tune, or compose, a string”—is still addressed to Nineveh. The sense is: “Arrange and compose what is disordered in you, what is discordant in different directions, like strings; tune it, O Nineveh, because your beauty and greatness will profit you nothing, though you think yourself possessed of exceptional qualities, unless you tune yourself to sing.”

Consider, then, the whole portion of the sons of Ammon and whatever goods they are thought to possess: how these things did not protect them from going into captivity or prevent their little ones from being dashed to pieces on the roads. What benefit did the rivers provide Ammon, beside which her city was situated? What benefit, apart from the rivers, did the great multitude of wells and springs provide, beginning at the Dead Sea and surrounding her region? What protection did Ethiopia and Egypt, once her allies, offer her?

Therefore, just as the help of her allies did not save her, so there will be no end of your flight, O Nineveh; rather, you will be devastated here and there. What should I say of the Ethiopians and Egyptians who were protectors of the sons of Ammon, when even the Libyans were their allies?

She too will be led into captivity, and her little ones, because they will not be able to proceed, will be killed on the roads, thrown down before the eyes of their parents. All her wealth, perhaps, will be divided among the victors. None of her princes will escape, since they will be bound with iron and fetters.

And you too, O Nineveh, will become drunk, and you, once rich and beautiful and possessing so many lovers, will be despised by everyone. Pursued by enemies, you will seek rest and will not find it. All your warriors and all your auxiliary forces will be booty for the enemy, and will be captured without any effort, like early figs. When shaken, they will fall not upon the ground—so that at least there might be some small labor for those gathering them—but immediately into the mouth of the devourer.

Let these things be said *paraphrastically* according to the Septuagint interpreters. For we have once for all resolved to follow the Vulgate edition, so that we may not seem to have furnished [Note: Marianus Victorius adds, supported by the Brixian manuscripts: “so that we may not seem to have provided any occasion for criticizing *the hydra and Sardanapalus*.” Yet I have been unable to find the name *excetra* in our manuscript copies. It is nevertheless clear that by the name *excetra*, or hydra, and Sardanapalus, Rufinus is repeatedly attacked by Jerome. MART.: In precisely the same words by which Rufinus is commonly said to be attacked, Jerome writes below in the prologue to Book II on Habakkuk: “Let the hydra hiss, then, and let Sardanapalus insult, more shameful in his vices than in his name.” Yet no one among Jerome’s adversaries comes to mind except Rufinus, if that Rufinus is the one whose name signified shamefulness. In the meantime, we have restored the word *excetra* on the authority of our Brixian manuscripts and those of Victor] the hydra and Sardanapalus with an occasion for reproaching us.

Nevertheless, the example of the overthrow of Nineveh does not seem sufficiently to correspond with the sons of Lot, who are called Ammonites. First, the name is Ammon (Gen. 19), not Amman. Moreover, Ammana, which is now called Philadelphia, is not situated upon rivers, nor are its riches gathered from the sea, since it is inland. Its walls are not waters, nor does it have Ethiopia, Egypt, Africa, and the Libyans as allies. All these details correspond more suitably to Alexandria, both in power and in the example, as well as in the description of the place, the region, and the allied nations.

Nor would the most powerful city Nineveh ever hear from the prophet, when compared with the lesser Philadelphia, “Are you better?” For when someone is asked, “Are you better?” the one to whom the comparison is made is shown to be lesser than the one with whom it is compared. Nor should it take offense if it is captured, since a city greater, stronger, and more powerful—both by the nature of its location and by the strength of its men—was overcome by the same enemy.

Since we have interpreted Nineveh as this world, she is instructed to tune and compose her strings and prepare herself for a mournful song. For the portion of the sons of Amon, which had been much better than Nineveh and had dwelt among rivers, because it was caught in error, paid the penalties of its crime.

First, according to the historical interpretation concerning Alexandria, it must be said that “Ammon” means “peoples,” and that the sense according to the laws of allegory is this: “Consider the people of the Church, which dwells beside the streams” [Note: We have corrected this according to the Royal codex, instead of which Martianus incorrectly retained “all the prophets.” Victorius had already corrected it, at the prompting of the Brixian manuscripts, from “all” to “streams.” For he explains, he says, those words concerning that Alexandria mystically: “Are you better than Amon, which dwells among rivers? Waters surround it; its wealth is the sea; its walls are waters.” He asserts that Alexandria signifies the Church, and that its streams or rivers are the prophets and teachers]. “and has teachers around her, from whose belly rivers flow, whose beginning is the sea.”

From the reading of the Law, which without the wood of Christ is bitter, one reaches its mystery through the likeness of Marah [Note: We have corrected “Marah”; previously “myrrh” had been read corruptly. For just as the Hebrews could not approach the spring of Marah because of the bitterness of its waters until Moses had cast wood into the water, turning it into sweetness (Exod. 15:23 ff.), so the reading of the Law without the wood of the cross is bitter, like Marah. Jerome uses this comparison elsewhere as well, for example in Epistle 125 to Rusticus, where we have likewise corrected the passage; and in the Preface to the Epistle to Algasia, where he says: “Cast the wood of the Cross into Marah.” Saint Paulinus also writes, poem XVII:

> As in ancient times, by the prophet’s hands,  
> Through the mystery of the Cross, once wood was sent into the water,  
> He sweetened it and laid aside  
> The bitter waters of Marah.]

The Church has Ethiopia in her strength, for “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. 67); and Egypt, into which the Lord came upon a light cloud; and the Libyans, who formerly dwelt in arid places and afterward became her helpers.

If she does not attend to herself and guard her heart with all diligence, she too will be led captive and will mourn her children. Her little ones also, who are still at the beginnings of the roads and have not reached the middle of the journey, will be dashed to pieces at those very beginnings. Her fiercest enemies will hasten to divide among themselves whatever is most distinguished in her, casting lots; and her nobles, whom we may understand as rulers and governors, bound with chains and hindered by the heavy weight of fetters, will be dragged into captivity.

And you too, O Nineveh—that is, you unbelieving human beings, human beings wholly attached to the world—will feel punishments and will be made drunk with my cup, when those too have drunk who had belonged to my portion [Alt. “my lot”] but fell through their own fault. And you will be despised by me. You will seek an end amid the vices and disturbances that press upon you, but you will not be able to find either a resting-place or an end to your evils.

All your desires and pleasures, your worldly powers, and the doctrines which you seemed to possess as most secure will be devoured by the eater, concerning whom Samson says in a parable: “Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (Judg. 14:14). For then all your strong things, and those which promised sweet fruits to the eyes of those looking upon them, will fall at the first shaking of the tree into the mouth of the devouring devil, by whom Nineveh had always been tempted and possessed.

We passed over the phrase “and there is no end of your flight,” because it is addressed to Nineveh, yet is placed among the things written about Ammon and seems to have been inserted out of sequence in another place. Let us refer it to Nineveh by *hyperbaton*, so that the order is: “And you will become drunk, and there is no end of your flight, and you will be despised,” followed by the other things said to Nineveh.

We will interpret this as meaning that there is no end to Nineveh’s flight from God: she always makes progress in fleeing and never wishes to stand still, according to what we said above: “And the fugitives themselves did not stand, and there was none who looked back.”

And we will say that the sacred Scripture has been composed with these difficulties, and especially the prophets, who are full of riddles, so that the difficulty of the meanings may also be enveloped in the difficulty of the language; so that holy things may not easily be exposed to dogs, nor pearls to swine, nor the holy of holies to the profane.

But if we wish to interpret Ammon as referring to the sons of Lot, let us say that Lot had two sons by his two daughters, Moab and Ammon. The elder, Moab, is interpreted as “from the father” or “paternal water”; the younger, Ammon, as “son of my kindred” or “our people” (Gen. 19).

And I think that, just as the one who was born from Judah is called, because of his sin, “Seed of Canaan, and not Judah” (Dan. 13:56), and in Ezekiel Jerusalem, the sinful [Alt. “the harlot”], is addressed: “Your root and your generation are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite [Alt. “a Canaanite”], and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16:3), so those who came from the earlier people—that is, from the Jews—and those from the younger people—that is, from us—are figuratively called Moabites and Ammonites.

And because they turned aside from their father—for Lot is interpreted as “turning aside”—they are subjected to punishment and will suffer all the things we have explained above.

But if God’s severity begins with those who were once holy, and the one who dwelt among rivers will be cleansed by the fire of Gehenna, how much more will Nineveh, which formerly had no law and did not receive the yoke of God’s commandments, in the end fall, because of her pride, into the mouth of the devourer!

(Verse 13 and following.) “Behold, your people are like women in your midst; the gates of your land shall be thrown wide open to your enemies; fire shall devour your bars. Draw water for yourself because of the siege; build your fortifications, enter the mud, and trample it; take hold of the brick while kneading it. There fire shall consume you; you shall perish by the sword; it shall devour you like a *bruchus*. Gather together, therefore, like a *bruchus*; multiply like a locust. You have increased your merchants more than the stars of heaven. The *bruchus* spread itself out and flew away. Your guards are like locusts, and your little ones like swarms of locusts, which settle on hedges on a cold day.” [Col. 1263D] “The sun rose, and they flew away, and the place where they had been was not known.”

[Note: The manuscript of Regina omits the following verse, “The sun rose,” and so forth. Compare Jerome at the end of this section.]

The Septuagint: “Behold, your people are like women among you; by opening, your enemies shall open the gates of your land. Fire has devoured your bars. Draw for yourself the water of the siege. [Note: More correctly, as it seems, the Regius manuscript has *oppila*, meaning ‘shut,’ instead of *obtine*, ‘take possession of.’ Jerome likewise explains the following passage as referring to ‘the strongest bars with which they may shut and close the gates of the senses.’ The Greek, however, reads κατακράτησον, ‘take firm hold.’] Take possession of your fortifications; enter the mud and trample it in the straw; take hold above the brick. There fire shall consume you; the sword shall destroy you and eat you like a locust. You shall be weighed down like a *bruchus*; multiply like a *bruchus*. You have multiplied your merchants like the stars of heaven.”

The discourse continues to be addressed to Nineveh: “It is not surprising if your strong men and warriors immediately fall into the mouth of the devourer like early figs, since your people are effeminate and unable to resist. Your gates, therefore, shall be thrown open, and the city shall lie exposed to its enemies; fire shall consume the strongest bars by which the gates were closed. Draw water, then, and take care that drink does not fail the besieged fortification. [Note: Victorius says that the prophet’s words are explained as follows: “Draw water for yourself because of the siege; build your fortifications; enter the mud and trample it; knead and hold the brick.” From this it is beyond doubt that the old reading is false. Therefore, from all the manuscripts of Florence and Brescia, we restored *muni turres*, ‘fortify towers,’ in place of *munitio*, ‘fortification.’ This correction answers perfectly to the words, “Build your fortifications,” or, as the Septuagint translated them, “Take possession of your fortifications”; otherwise it would be an incongruous expression to speak of a besieged fortification. When he says “the besieged,” the city is understood from what precedes.] Make bricks, so that you may build up the breaches in the walls; for the siege is near. And when you have done all these things, you shall be devoured by the sword just as the earth is devoured by the *bruchus*.

“But even when you have multiplied like a grasshopper and, gathered together all at once like a locust, have collected your wealth like the stars of heaven—like locusts, grasshoppers, and the small offspring of locusts, called *attelabi* [variant: *adtelebi*], which, when warmed by the sun, fly away and are nowhere found—you likewise shall be scattered and flee. For this is the nature of locusts: when numbed by the cold, they fly about in the warmth.

[Note: The same writer says: ‘Jerome excellently explains the distinction between the locust, the *attelabus*, and the grasshopper, so that no one should suppose that the *bruchus* is the caterpillar that gnaws cabbages, as the people of Siena in Etruria call it. The *bruchus*, likewise called βροῦχος by the Septuagint, is among the Hebrews that small, wingless black locust, very like the chirping crickets, hiding in holes in the earth and emerging for food; the people of Rieti call it *morula*, from its dark color, like that of the Moors. This insect gnaws extraordinarily whatever green thing it finds. The *attelabus*, on the other hand, is that small locust which, after the harvest, jumps about in the fields and grain-plots; for it cannot fly like the locust. The people of Rieti call it *sallippulus*, from its jumping. Yet the Septuagint rendered by *attelabus* the Hebrew word [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], that is, “locust”; and both they and Jerome translated the other term as “locust,” as they also did in Ecclesiastes 12 for the word [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], as we explained there. Just as the *attelabus* is intermediate between the *bruchus* and the locust, so it appears that the prophet called “locusts” those larger creatures which, once they have taken flight, rush together in such a vast multitude to ravage the crops and every green thing that they darken the sky as though covered with clouds and take the sun’s rays away from the earth.’]

“Now the *attelabus*, which Aquila more significantly translated as ‘devourer,’ is a small locust between the locust and the *bruchus*. It crawls with tiny wings rather than flies, and is always jumping. For this reason, wherever it arises, it consumes everything down to the dust, because it cannot depart until its wings have grown.

“Following the Hebrew text, and treading in the footsteps of Scripture for the reader’s easier understanding, I have explained these matters more clearly. But I shall also follow the *tropologia* begun according to the Septuagint—first briefly, as in an epitome, and afterward discussing each point more fully:

“‘Your people, O Nineveh,’ that is, worldly people, who are properly called the people of the Assyrian city, have been so weakened by passions and enervated by vices that they are compared with the weakness of women. For they possess nothing strong, nothing robust or manly in their souls. Therefore their enemies, prevailing against them, have opened all their senses and entered through their bodily doors. The senses of the body are appropriately called the gates of the land of Nineveh.

“Yet even those who have enslaved themselves to vices possess, from the first creation by God, an opportunity to know God—like the strongest bars by which they might shut and close the gates of the senses. But fire itself shall consume them, [Note: The manuscript of Regina has ‘which is fortified by burning arrows.’] fire winged with burning arrows. Therefore it is said to Nineveh: ‘Draw water for yourself, and sprinkle yourself with speech, reason, and the opportunities for understanding God and practicing the virtues implanted within you; use these things in battle.’

“But you, with hands relaxed—that is, with works of pleasure—have lost whatever strength you possessed. Therefore turn back, repent, and once more take possession of your fortifications. And because you have once entered the mud and have been shut up in the body—which, like earth, straw, and water, is compacted of flesh, blood, veins, sinews, and bones—endure the body’s injuries and necessities. Let yourself be trampled by enemies, and endure everything that is worthy of repentance for the making of the flesh.

“For once you have taken up mud and straw and become entangled in the empty affairs of this age, you ought voluntarily to allow yourself to be trampled through injury. Yet do not despair utterly of salvation. Be confident, and bring your body—that is, your brick—into subjection because of the word you have received, as though it were water. [Note: Martianay’s manuscript omits the word ‘water.’] Subjugate it to yourself, so that you may rule your brick. Otherwise, if you do not do this, a living flame will afterward consume you—either raised up as punishment in Gehenna or kindled by the enemy’s burning arrows. You will be ravaged not only by fire; the sword also will eat you like the locust eats the green things of the earth.

“You will suffer this if you do not remain above the brick, but, weighed down by your own burden and losing all power of flight, are dragged wholly to the earth, just as the *bruchus* suddenly falls to the ground when, its flight exhausted, it can go no farther. Therefore possess virtues as innumerable as the *bruchus*, so that you may not be dragged to the ground by your own weight like the *bruchus*.

“You have suffered all these things because you multiplied for yourself the riches and commerce of various doctrines, supposing them brighter than the stars and more radiant than the constellations of heaven.”

[Col. 1265A] “I have said these things briefly, as I noted, in order to grasp the meaning. Now, returning to the beginning of the chapter, let us explain each point as we are able.

“Who would not say that beautiful Nineveh—the soul beautiful by nature—has been softened by the luxury and pleasures of this age, has reached womanly delights, and, having lost its manliness, has become weak as a woman? For if the soul of the righteous, coming to perfection as a mature man, preserving the rigor of its condition and cleaving to God, becomes one spirit with him, why should we not conversely say that the soul which loves the world becomes one with the world and, reduced to feminine softness, loses its manly vigor?

“I think that for this reason Pharaoh commanded in Exodus that every male child born to the Hebrews should be cast into the river, while every female should be kept alive (Exod. 1). For could the king of Egypt, who elsewhere says, ‘The rivers are mine, and I made them’ (Exod. 29:2), have commanded anything other than this: that whatever among the Hebrews—and among those who pass through this age—is strong and manly should be cast into the waters and carried by their currents into the sea? Conversely, whatever seemed feminine, soft, and beautiful in this age should be kept alive, grow, and produce offspring.

“Consider also that the Egyptian ruler could not kill the mature men of the Hebrews, nor those who had already emerged from infancy, but only those whose age was still tender, whose bodies were soft, and whose progress had just begun. He knew that the females could not be nourished unless the males had been killed. Therefore he wished to drown in the flood of his river whatever was strong and manly among the Hebrews, so that what was feminine might grow more freely by itself.

“As for what follows, ‘Your enemies shall open wide the gates of your land,’ you may understand it by taking a testimony from Jeremiah, where it is written: ‘Death has come up through your windows’ [variant: ‘our windows’] (Jer. 9:21). What Jeremiah asserts through windows is here shown through gates, and you may refer these gates to the senses.

“Knowing that the divine word speaks of two kinds of senses, Proverbs says, in distinction from evil senses: ‘You will find divine understanding.’ Here do not take ‘sense’ to mean the soul and mind, which is called νοῦς in Greek, but αἴσθησις, from which the five senses are named: sight, smell, taste, touch, and hearing.

“Thus the gates of the land of Nineveh are to be understood as the bodily senses; the gates of heavenly Jerusalem, however, are every divine sense that comes from above. The people of Nineveh open its gates through sight and hearing and all the remaining senses, seeking to seize bodily pleasures by the broad and spacious way that leads to death (Matt. 7). By contrast, people of God close their gates, stopping their ears so that they may not hear the judgment of blood; closing their eyes so that they may not see iniquity; blocking their nostrils so that they may not receive the first perfumes by smell for the feminization of their souls; closing the mouth of gluttony and the entrance to the greedy belly; and withdrawing their hands from soft touch, lest the belly, inflamed with desire, compel the soul, burning with feminine passion, to embraces.

“Those who are people of God open their senses—that is, the gates of heavenly Jerusalem—so that the word of God may enter them.

“An example of evil gates is: ‘You who lift me up from the gates of death.’ An example of good gates is: ‘That I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion’ (Ps. 9:15).

“When you see a lover of pleasure rather than a lover of God, devoted to luxury, say of him immediately: ‘He has opened the gates of his land to his enemies.’ For people do not open the gates of the land of Nineveh to the friends of their soul, but to its enemies.

“And if those who are considered leaders among the people have done the same, you will not be afraid to say of them also: ‘The leaders of my people have been expelled from the house of their delights.’ If you see them hindered by pleasures and luxury surrounding them on every side, showing no mercy to the poor and no concern for the people of God, you may apply to them what follows:

“‘Those who sleep upon beds of ivory and flow with pleasure upon their couches; who eat kids from the flocks and calves from the midst of the herd; who drink filtered wine and anoint themselves with the finest oils; yet they were not grieved over the ruin of Joseph’ (Amos 6:4).

“As for the statement, ‘Fire has devoured your bars,’ its meaning is this: If anything of natural goodness seemed to exist in your soul, something like bars that could prevent and repel the enemies attempting to break in through the gates of your senses, this has been set aflame by Babylonian fire.

“Likewise, ‘Draw the water of the fortification for yourself’ refers to the word of God, so that you may surround yourself with the teaching and reason of Scripture as with a most secure wall, preventing the enemy from breaking into your interior. ‘Take possession,’ he says, ‘of your fortifications.’ Whatever good you possess by nature, whatever beginning of the best Creator he has preserved in you, unhappy soul of Nineveh, hold it for your defense, and do not allow it to flow out from the ruling faculty (ἡγεμονικόν) of the heart.

“As for what is added afterward, ‘Walk [variant: ‘cut into’] in the mud and trample in the straw,’ someone may perhaps think that this is said of the soul which, fixed in the mud of the body and the straw of this world—empty and transient things—turns wholly within them [variant: ‘serves them’] and is trampled by demons.

“But I think it is said to the soul in this sense: ‘Endure the temptations and injuries to which you have been handed over, and the punishments you suffer according to your deserts. For if you tread upon the empty and fragile affairs of this world, know that you endure this as a remedy—provided that you have taken possession of the brick and subjected the flesh to the soul’s authority.’

“Finally it follows: ‘There fire shall consume you.’ If you are not above the brick, and do not rule the flesh, but remain in the brick, love straw, and live in the flesh according to the flesh, not only will the enemy’s burning arrows devour you; his sword also will kill you, and, like locusts, will consume with greedy tooth whatever green thing seemed to flourish in you and was spontaneously sprouting from nature’s goodness. [Variant: ‘will be consumed by a gnawing *bruchus*.] And just as the *bruchus*, having lost its power of flight and weighed down by its own burden, falls to the earth, so you, weighed down by the burden of sins, will be dragged to the ground.

“Therefore, lest you suffer such and so many things, multiply like the *bruchus*, and possess as many virtues as it possesses numbers. For since you have multiplied your commerce and gathered wealth of every kind—desiring, as it were, to possess heavenly things—by right and wrong alike, you must match the multitude of your sins with a multitude of virtues.

“Above, following the Hebrew text, I had reached the place where it says: ‘The sun rose, and they flew away, and the place where they had been was not known.’ I stated what seemed to me to be the meaning in the context of the discourse itself. [Col. 1268C] Now, since the Septuagint seem to have a beginning of their own distinct sense, I shall set down their testimony and follow the order of the explanation begun.”

581

The Septuagint: “The *bruchus* rushed forth and flew away; your mixed *attelabus* leapt forth, like a locust that climbs upon a hedge on the day of frost. The sun rose, and it leapt forth, and it did not know its place. Woe to them.”

“It seems to me that the multitude of Nineveh, without a ruler, without order, mixed together here and there, rushing wherever impulse carries it, may be compared with the *bruchus*, a small and innumerable animal that seems to raise itself only a little from the earth.

“Likewise the *attelabus*, called in Greek σύμμικτος and translated into Latin as *commixticius*, may be understood as an ignoble common people, a population gathered from diverse nations here and there—that is, not citizens but foreigners. Thus we are told that the people of Israel who went out from Egypt included a πολὺς σύμμικτος, a ‘great mixed multitude,’ consisting of Egyptians, Ethiopians, and various peoples.

“This mixed multitude of Nineveh, so to speak, is therefore compared with the leaping *attelabus* and the locust, which on a cold day, because it cannot fly away, settles on a hedge; afterward, when the sun has risen and it has been warmed by its heat, it leaps forth and flies to other regions, remembering nothing of the hedge on which it had sat during the cold.

“Let these things have been said *paraphrastically*, so that the prophet’s discourse may more easily be understood. In any case, you cannot doubt that the multitude of human beings which travels along the broad way and moves about in the world is called a *bruchus*, when you see them wholly devoted to the earth, running here and there in the fickleness of their judgment, and unable to fly toward higher things.

“Look at Rome, and at Constantinople, which, together with its former name, has changed its former poverty. Look at Alexandria, the head of Egypt, and, whenever the people rush into sedition either because of a shortage of grain or—something shameful and disgraceful—because of charioteers, mimes, and actors, see them rushing like a *bruchus*, wholly attached to vices, flying here and there in their fickleness and their moment-by-moment changes of opinion. Then you will truly be able to say: ‘The *bruchus* went off in a rush and flew away.’

“As for what follows, ‘The *attelabus* leapt forth, and your mixed multitude like a locust,’ I think that the *commixticius* differs from the *bruchus* in this respect: the *bruchus* is compared with an ignorant and innumerable crowd, whereas the *commixticius* is gathered here and there from all nations.

“Just as in cities some are citizens and others foreigners, who are content to live in a city that is not their own, so I think that the mixed multitude living in Nineveh consists of those who, according to their own opinion, seem to follow certain doctrines of truth and to be better than the *bruchus*. The *bruchus* does nothing except remain always upon the earth and, being without wings, serve food and the belly. The *attelabus*, however, at least takes small wings; and although it cannot fly into the heights, it nevertheless tries to leap from the ground. Finally, when it reaches the stage of the locust, it does indeed fly about, but its flight is not continuous: when its little wings fail and contract from the cold, even the locust settles down—not upon a fruit-bearing tree or green leaves, but upon a hedge woven from thorns and shrubs, or upon a wall fortuitously built from stones gathered here and there.

“Let us consider the sages of Greece, Egypt, and Persia, the Gymnosophists of India, the Samaritans, and the various opinions among them; and the Jews, their Pharisees, and Sadducees; and the many heresies of the Church. We shall see the *attelabus* raising itself a little from the earth, and the locust flying, but not with a full course. Because they do not possess the warmth of the sun of righteousness, and because their love toward God has grown cold, they sit upon thorny hedges.

“For all their doctrines, being cold and unable to fly, find for themselves a seat and resting-place amid the thickets of Aristotle and Chrysippus. From there Eunomius brings forth: ‘What has been born did not exist before it was born.’ From there Mani, in order to free God from the creation of evils, introduces another author of evil. From there Novatian withdraws forgiveness in order to abolish repentance.

“And, to sum up all of this briefly, all doctrines draw the streams of their arguments from those sources, so that they have even labeled the very places from which their arguments are taken *topica* (τοπικά), ‘topics.’

“This locust, therefore, which now sits upon hedges, when the time of judgment arrives and the world has grown warm at the rising of the sun, will leave its seat and the places to which it clung during the cold. Turning to better things, it will no longer remember its former seat.

“What we have said generally about the time of judgment can also be understood in part here: through learned and educated men, the light of the sun of righteousness may arise for such locusts; and, leaving their thorns, they may pass into pure and open flight.”

(Verse 18 and following.) “Your shepherds have slumbered, king of Assyria; your princes shall be buried. Your people are scattered upon the mountains [Vulgate: ‘your people have hidden in the mountains’], and there is no one to gather them. Your ruin is not obscure; your wound is exceedingly grievous. All who have heard the report concerning you have clapped their hands over you, for upon whom has your wickedness not continually fallen?”

[Col. 1270B] The Septuagint: “Your shepherds have slumbered; the king of Assyria has put your mighty men to sleep. Your people have gone upon the mountains, and there was no one to receive them. There is no healing for your ruin; your wound swells. All who have heard your report will clap their hands over you, for upon whom has your wickedness not continually rushed?”

“It is not surprising if your shepherds have slumbered, O king of Assyria, who ruled over Nineveh; and if your princes—your petty kings, that is, and the leaders of all the nations who formerly served you—are buried or wander about. Your people have become women in the midst of your city; its gates have been opened to your enemies; and the whole multitude sitting upon the wall has been compared with a locust which, as though warmed by the sun, has fled at the arrival of Nebuchadnezzar from the fortifications and turned its back upon its enemies, and whose place has not been found. [Note: Victorius says that all the Florentine copies have *illucescente*, ‘when it dawns,’ instead of *incalescente*, ‘when it grows warm.’ Both readings are good; but since, as Jerome says above, a locust is accustomed to be roused to flight when the sun’s heat arrives, he prefers that the old reading be retained.]

“Therefore, because God was angry with you, O Assyria, for devastating his people and raising your nest up to heaven, and because you are called ‘great in understanding,’ your city has been destroyed. All your princes who could have resisted your adversaries have been killed; and your remaining people, weak and ignoble, have been scattered among the mountains. None of your leaders can be found who might gather them and once more assemble an army from the scattered remnants.

“Your wound is not hidden, nor is it such a wound as a physician’s hand can heal. All who have heard that Nineveh has been overthrown, that the king of Assyria has been defeated, and that the once most powerful city and the king who was formerly ruler of the world have been wounded and lie half-dead, rolling in their own blood—whether they will be stunned by the magnitude of the event and the unexpected report and will press their hands together, or whether, rejoicing and mocking you because of the greatness of their joy, they will applaud with their hands and make a kind of joyful clamor.

“For no one can grieve over you and give tears to your overthrow and wound, because there is no one upon whom your wickedness has not continually fallen. And he says beautifully, ‘has passed over’: for the wickedness of the Assyrian king cannot remain continually in his enemies.”

Thus far let the order of the historical text extend.

“We must also, following the Hebrew text, before discussing the Septuagint edition—for in that edition the sense is altogether different—rise somewhat from history into the heights and show that, in the final prophecy of Nahum, a turning away (ἀποστροφή) is made toward the devil. [Note: Martianay has ‘with a great sense’; formerly the faulty reading was ‘and there is a sense,’ followed by ‘a great prince,’ and shortly afterward ‘strength’ instead of ‘fortitude,’ contrary to the Greek text.]

“This is the great prince of the Assyrians, who once boasted: ‘By my strength I shall act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I shall remove the boundaries of nations; I shall consume their resources, and I shall shake the inhabited cities’ (Isa. 10:13). To him it is said: ‘O Lucifer, who rose in the morning, how have you fallen to the earth and been crushed?’ (Isa. 14:12–13).

“Your city, Nineveh, once beautiful and powerful, has been destroyed. In it you presumed to exercise such authority that you dared even to say to the Son of God: ‘All these things have been handed over to me; if you fall down and worship me, I shall give them to you’ (Matt. 4:9).

“Your shepherds and petty kings have slumbered. They did not feed human beings unto salvation but nourished them for your slaughter, so that you might devour fatter victims. All your people and the multitude of peoples who once worshiped you have abandoned you and your city, fled to the mountains, and hidden themselves in the retreats of Christ’s apostles and teachers. Meanwhile, none of your leaders can be found who might recall your former multitude to himself.

“Your plague and wound have resounded throughout the whole world. All who were once deceived by your overthrowing have mocked you. Either no one, or scarcely anyone, exists whom you have not at some time deceived and through whom your wickedness has not passed.

“It should be noted that whoever has stood in the wickedness of the devil cannot mock his ruin and wound while remaining one of the shepherds and people of the king of Assyria. Rather, whoever has passed beyond it may mock him and clap, as it were, with good and upright deeds. [Variant: ‘with their hands.’]

“And appropriately, according to the Hebrew text, what has been said up to this point concerns the ruin of the world; finally it is spoken also of the devil himself, who was the prince of the world: ‘The world lies in the power of the evil one,’ and it is proclaimed as stricken and wounded.

“Among the Septuagint, however, the statement is still directed against the mixed multitude (σύμμικτος), that is, against the mixed multitude of the world: its shepherds have slumbered, and they have been put to sleep by the king of Assyria. Thus, while they describe among themselves what the Assyrian has done to others, and not what he himself suffers, the wound, plague, and death of the devil are left unmentioned.

“Woe, therefore, to those who are teachers of perverse doctrines in Nineveh. Appropriately it is said to them: ‘Your shepherds have slumbered’ (Ps. 131). For they have given sleep to their eyes and slumber to their eyelids. Therefore they did not find a place for the Lord, nor a dwelling for the God of Jacob. They did not hear of Ephrata, that is, the fruitful Church, nor find it among the densely wooded forests.

“Not only have the shepherds of this mixed multitude and of the locust—which, when frost threatens, sits upon hedges—slumbered; they have also been put to sleep by the king of the Assyrians. For the king of Assyria knows that he cannot deceive the sheep unless he has first put the shepherds to sleep.

“It is always the devil’s endeavor to lull wakeful souls to sleep. Indeed, even during the Lord’s Passion he presses the apostles’ eyes with heavy sleep. The Savior awakens them and says: ‘Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation’ (Mark 14:38). And again: ‘What I say to you I say to all: Watch’ (ibid. 13:37).

“And because he never ceases to lull the wakeful to sleep, whoever he has deceived and enticed to sleep with the sweet and deadly song of the Sirens, the divine word awakens and says: ‘Rise, you who sleep, and arise, and Christ will enlighten you’ (Eph. 5:14).

“Therefore, at the coming of Christ and of the word of God, of ecclesiastical teaching, and of the consummation of Nineveh—the once most beautiful prostitute—the people who had previously been put to sleep under their teachers will rise and hasten. They will go to the mountains of Scripture. There they will find the mountains Moses and Joshua the son of Nun; the mountains the prophets; the mountains of the New Testament, the apostles and evangelists.

“And when they have fled to such mountains and have devoted themselves to the reading of such mountains, if they do not find anyone to teach them—for ‘the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few’ (Matt. 9:37)—then their zeal will be commended because they fled to the mountains, and the teachers’ negligence will be condemned. For it adds: ‘And there was no one to receive them.’

“It follows: ‘There is no healing for your ruin; your wound swells.’ Therefore the mixed multitude of Nineveh cannot be healed because it does not lay aside its pride. Its wound is always fresh, and it is struck daily by the devil’s blows. After all these things there is no healing for its ruin. Although it may seem healthy to itself, its soul is broken and crushed, struck from above by the hammer of the whole earth; and it is not healed because it is always erect.

“But if it humbles itself and subjects itself to Christ, ‘God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart’ (Ps. 60:19); and: ‘A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God.’

“At the end it says: ‘All who have heard your report will clap their hands over you. For upon whom has your wickedness not continually rushed?’ When you, O mixed one (ὦ σύμμικτε), begin to suffer punishments, all who hear the report will mock you with harmonious clapping, with voice, and, so to speak, with the sound and concord of their deeds; they will rejoice over you.

“For there is no one, or at least scarcely anyone, upon whom your wickedness has not always rushed or come. If the city of Nineveh has mixed shepherds and strong men, and every false doctrine and deceitful opinion of knowledge comes from the mixed multitude, it must be feared that there is no one upon whom the wickedness of the mixed multitude (συμμίκτου) has not come.

“Observe carefully that he does not say, ‘Into whom your wickedness entered, O mixed one,’ but, ‘Upon whom it came.’ Often the arrows of false doctrines come upon us and desire, as it were, to enter the soul’s secret chamber. But when we close the gates, the mixed multitude (σύμμικτος) does indeed come upon us and, as far as lies in it, rushes upon us—and it always does so—but, with the Lord Christ helping us and our keeping our heart with all vigilance (Prov. 4), it rushes upon us but cannot enter.”

[Col. 1273]

THE TWO BOOKS OF THE COMMENTARIES OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, ON THE PROPHET HABAKKUK, TO CHROMATIUS. (C)

PROLOGUE.

[Col. 1273A] 587–588 First, Chromatius, most learned of bishops, we must understand that the name of the prophet is read corruptly among the Greeks and Latins as *Ambacum*, whereas among the Hebrews he is called *Abacuc*, and the name is interpreted as “embrace”; or, if we translate it into Greek more meaningfully, **περίληψις** (*perílēpsis*), that is, “embrace” or “embracing.” [Note: Another reading is *Ambachuch*. In Victor’s copy: Ἀββακούμ (*Abbakoum*).] [Note: The manuscript of Regina prefers **περίλημμα** (*perílēmma*), which has the same meaning.] Then, where the Seventy translators, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated **λῆμμα** (*lēμμα*), that is, “assumption” or “burden,” the Hebrew has *MASSA* (), which Aquila renders as “weight”; concerning this we have discussed more fully in the prophet Nahum. *Massa*, moreover, is never placed in a title except when what is presented is heavy and full of weight and toil. Hence the present prophecy must necessarily contain some severity, so that, just as in Nahum the burden that appeared to be directed against Nineveh, the city of the Assyrians, was heavy, so here too we must ask for whom the burden revealed to the prophet’s sight is intended.

There are four prophets in the volume of the Twelve Prophets among whom three have **λῆμμα**, that is, “burden,” as their title at the beginning: Nahum, Habakkuk, and Malachi. Zechariah, moreover, places two titles of this kind in the middle and near the end of his book, one of which is: “The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be its resting place” (Zech. 9:1); the other, at the end: “The burden of the word of the Lord concerning Israel” (ibid. 11:1). Concerning Nahum, a book has already been published in response to your prayers; concerning Zechariah and Malachi, if life permits, we shall speak. Now we have Habakkuk in hand. He is called “embrace” either because he is beloved of the Lord, or because he enters into contest and struggle and, so to speak, an embrace with God, and has received the name of one who embraces—that is, one who wrestles.

For no one has dared, in so bold a voice, to summon God to a dispute about justice and say to him: “Why, in human affairs and in the **πολιτεία** (*politeia*)—the civic order—of this world, does there prevail such great injustice? I cry out to you, suffering violence, and you do not save me? Why have you shown me iniquity and toil to behold? The law has been torn apart, and judgment does not reach its conclusion, because the wicked prevails against the righteous; therefore perverse judgment proceeds” (Hab. 1:2–4). [Note: Victor places the preceding verse first: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear?”]

You see that the voice is rash and, in a certain sense, blasphemous, since it summons its Creator to judgment in this way. It is as though a fragile vessel were to dispute with its potter (Isa. 45; Jer. 18; Rom. 9) why this or that had been made. We must also observe that the “assumption” or “burden”—which, as we have said, is heavy—is the prophet’s vision, and that the prophet understands what he sees as directed against the perverse doctrine of Montanus. He does not speak as a madman, nor, after the manner of deranged women, utter sounds without understanding. Therefore the apostle commands that, if something is revealed to another while some are prophesying, those who were speaking first should be silent (2 Cor. 14:33). And immediately he adds: “For God is not a God of dissension, but of peace.” From this it is understood that when someone keeps silent willingly and gives another room to speak, he can both speak and remain silent whenever he wishes. But one who speaks in ecstasy—that is, unwillingly—has no power either to keep silent or to speak.

Learn this also—for since you insist, you force me to interpret history for you as though I were supplying certain steps and ladders for one striving toward higher things: the prophecy is against Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans. Just as the earlier prophet Nahum, whom Habakkuk follows, delivered an oracle against Nineveh and the Assyrians, who devastated the ten tribes called Israel, so Habakkuk’s prophecy is directed against Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar, by whom Judah, Jerusalem, and the temple were overthrown.

And so that you may know that Habakkuk lived at the time when the two tribes called Judah had already been led into captivity, Daniel can instruct you: Habakkuk is sent to him in the lions’ den with a meal (Dan. 14 [in some traditions, 14:33–39]). Among the Hebrews, however, this story itself is not read. Therefore, whether someone accepts that Scripture or does not accept it, either position is favorable to us: either he accepts it, and the book of Habakkuk is written after the event has occurred; or he does not accept it, and the prophet writes, as it were, what he knows will happen. [Note: The manuscript of Regina reads with the opposite sense: “for either he does not accept it, and already … or he accepts it, and as though …”]

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1275A] (Chapter 1.—Verses 1, 2.) “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear? I shall cry out to you, suffering violence, and you will not save me? Why have you shown me iniquity and made me see plunder and injustice against me?” The Vulgate reads: “Why have you shown me iniquity and made me see toil.” The Septuagint reads: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear? I shall cry out to you, suffering violence, and you will not save me? Why have you shown me labors and pains, to see misery and impiety?”

For the present, according to the literal sense, the prophet complains against God: Why does Nebuchadnezzar devastate the temple and Judah? Why is Jerusalem, once the city of the Lord, destroyed? Why does the people cry and not receive an answer? Why does the oppressed man, crushed by the Chaldeans, cry out to the Lord and not get saved? Why has the prophet himself—or the people in whose person he now speaks—lived for this and been brought to this point, that he sees the iniquity of his enemies and his own suffering? Why does injustice prevail against him? He says this out of the anguish of his mind, not knowing that gold is refined in fire and that the three young men came out of the furnace purer than when they entered it (Dan. 3). [Note: The manuscript of Regina reads: “with anguish pressing upon him.”]

But we can also understand it more generally: the prophet, speaking in the person of human impatience, sees sinners multiplying and possessing riches in the world; their sons like a young plantation in their youth; their daughters adorned like the likeness of a temple; their storehouses full and overflowing from one place to another; their sheep fertile and multiplying in their paths; and the other things more fully written in Psalm 143. He breaks into a complaining and grief-filled cry:

“Why do you look upon contemptuous men and remain silent while the wicked tramples upon one more righteous than himself? Why do you make human beings like the fish of the sea and like reptiles that have no leader?” [Note: The manuscript of Regina records the remainder of the verse itself: “because I was jealous for the prosperity of sinners when I saw it”; and shortly afterward: “Therefore in vain have I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent.”]

We read something similar in Psalm 72: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out,” and what follows (Ps. 72:2). Again in the same psalm: “And if there is knowledge in the Most High. For behold, sinners and those who abound in the world have obtained riches,” and the remainder up to “my hands.” These things are spoken by those who do not know God’s judgments, which are unsearchable (Rom. 11), nor the depth of his riches, wisdom, and knowledge, nor that God sees in a way different from human beings. A human being looks only at present things; God knows things future and eternal (1 Sam. 18).

What if a sick man, burning with fever, asks for cold water and says to his physician: “I suffer violence, I am tormented, I burn, I am dying; how long, physician, shall I cry out and you will not hear?” And the wisest and most compassionate physician answers him: “I know when I ought to give you what you ask. I do not show mercy now, because this mercy is cruelty, and your desire is asking for something against yourself.” So also our Lord God, knowing the weights and measures of his compassion, sometimes does not hear the one who cries out, in order to test him, provoke him more strongly to ask, and make him, as though refined by fire, more righteous and pure.

Understanding this, the apostle says, according to the mercy he has received from the Lord: “Let us not grow weary in tribulations” (Eph. 3:13). [Note: Victor reads “We do not grow weary,” from the Vulgate edition at 2 Corinthians 4.] He blesses God at all times (Ps. 33), and knows that “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). He glories in toil and suffering. And with Jeremiah he says: “I shall call for tribulation and misery.” Thus, just as another person calls upon God, so the holy man and unconquered warrior desires tribulation and misery to come, in order to exercise and test himself. [Note: Victor, drawing from manuscripts at Brescia, has here: “to be rescued from the misery of the world.”]

[Col. 1276C] (Verses 3, 4.) “And judgment and contradiction became more powerful; therefore the law was torn apart, and judgment did not reach its end, because the wicked prevails against the righteous; therefore perverse judgment proceeds.” The Septuagint reads: “Judgment was made against me, and the judge receives; therefore the law was torn apart, and judgment did not reach its end, because the wicked prevails against the righteous; therefore perverse judgment proceeds.” [Note: Here as well as in the Septuagint, the manuscript of Regina consistently prefers “will proceed.”]

The prophet, or the people, still speaks to the Lord: judgment was made against them not by truth but by power, and nothing was upheld from the law and justice. Hence judgment itself did not reach its proper end. The end of judgment is to judge justly.

The following words show why he dares to speak in this way: “Because the wicked Nebuchadnezzar prevailed against the righteous Judah” (2 Kings 22), and this is why he said that judgment had not reached its end: it is unjust and perverse that the righteous king Josiah should be slaughtered by the king of Egypt (2 Kings 23), that Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah should serve (Dan. 3), that the Babylonian emperor should rule, and that Belshazzar should drink from God’s vessels among his prostitutes and concubines (Dan. 5).

This is what the prophet says concerning the condition of his own times—for we follow the historical sense because you once requested it, despite its lowliness. But according to the Septuagint, it is the common complaint of the saints to God: Why is unjust judgment made against them, and why is innocent blood shed in persecutions? And if at some time they stand before a secular tribunal, why does the judge, having accepted gifts, condemn the innocent and release the guilty? [Note: Another reading: “but if.”]

This can be said not only of the judges of the world but sometimes also of the rulers of the churches: because of gifts they tear apart the law and do not carry judgment through to its conclusion, and the wicked prevails against the righteous. In judgment, the sin of the rich is defended more readily than the truth of the poor. Hence the complaint is that perverse judgment proceeds.

Yet we ought not to be disturbed by this inequality of affairs, when we see that at the beginning of the world righteous Abel was killed by the wicked Cain (Gen. 4); later, while Jacob was an exile, Esau reigned in his father’s house (Gen. 28); the Egyptians afflicted the children of Israel with mud and brick; and the Lord, against whom the present complaint is directed, was crucified by the Jews (John 19), while the robber Barabbas was chosen (John 18). My days would fail if I wished to enumerate how, in this world, while the wicked prevail, the righteous are oppressed.

(Verses 5.) “Look among the nations and see; marvel and be astonished, because a work has been done in your days that no one will believe when it is told.”

The Septuagint reads: “Look at the contemptuous and behold; marvel at marvels and perish, because I am doing a work in your days that you will not believe if someone tells it.” [Note: We corrected the reading to *credetis* (“you will believe”), following the manuscript of Regina and the Greek **πιστεύσητε** (*pisteusēte*), a reading also approved by Victor. Martianay retained *credidistis* (“you believed”).]

Symmachus, instead of “because a work has been done in your days,” translated: “because a work will be done in your days”; the rest is similar.

Again, at the beginning of the chapter, where the Hebrew has *RAU BAGGOIM* (), and we translated it “look among the nations,” the Septuagint has “look at the contemptuous.” Apart from Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, who agree with our interpretation, I found in another edition, without an author’s name, **ἀνωνύμῃ**: “you will see slanderers”; and in another, likewise without an author’s title: “you will see those who turn aside.” [Note: In place of the words “**ἀνωνύμῃ** I found,” which our manuscripts after Victor also prefer, Martianay retained “in one word.”]

Accordingly, in response to the prophet’s earlier complaints, when he says, “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear?” and the rest up to the end of this opening section, the voice of the Lord responding is introduced, so that the prophet may see among the nations the iniquity that he thinks is being committed only in Israel. The Lord shows that not only Judah and Jerusalem, as the prophet supposed, have been handed over to the Chaldeans, but all the surrounding nations; and that the Chaldean will become so powerful and will later fall so completely that, if anyone foretold what would happen, the magnitude of the event would make him seem incredible.
