What the Septuagint and the other interpreters have rendered, “Look at the contemptuous,” or “you will see slanderers and those who turn aside,” also agrees with the meaning of this passage. They are convicted by the very language of audacity and contempt toward the Lord. Speaking in their person, the prophet had cried out: Why did they dare to despise God’s majesty, speak rashly, and, insofar as they could, slander God’s providence, turning away from the Lord while accusing him of injustice?

Therefore, “you will see the contemptuous,” and then you will marvel and count all your complaints as nothing when you see me working in your days. Do not perhaps say: “What does the future have to do with us?” The work will be so great and will overwhelm all your complaints, so that if someone now foretells that it will happen, you will not readily believe him. What this work is is demonstrated in what follows.

(Verses 6 and following.) “For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, advancing over the breadth of the earth to possess dwellings not its own. It is dreadful and terrible; from itself its judgment and its burden will proceed. Its horses are swifter than leopards and faster than evening wolves, and its horsemen will spread out. Its horsemen will come from afar; they will fly like an eagle hastening to devour. All of them will come for plunder; their faces are like a burning wind. He will gather captives like sand; he will triumph over kings, and tyrants will be a jest to him. He will laugh at every fortress, heap up a rampart, and capture it. Then his spirit will change, and he will pass through and fall. This is the strength of his god.”

The Septuagint reads: “For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, which travels over the breadth of the earth to possess dwellings not its own. It is terrible and illustrious; its judgment will be from itself, and its assumption will proceed from itself. Its horses will leap over leopards and will be swifter than the wolves of Arabia; its horsemen will ride, and they will come with force from afar. They will fly like an eagle ready to devour. Destruction will come upon the wicked who resist them face to face, and he will gather captives like sand. He will rejoice over kings, and tyrants will be his sport. He will mock every fortress, heap up a rampart, and seize it. Then he will change his spirit, pass through, and be reconciled. This is the strength of my God.”

What I had said to you—“Look among the nations and see; marvel and be astonished, because a work will be done in your days that no one will believe when it is told”—is what the following speech describes: “Behold, I am raising up Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, a most warlike and swift nation.” Almost all the Greeks who wrote barbarian histories bear witness to their strength and boldness in war.

This nation is not content with its own boundaries, but runs here and there and wanders throughout the breadth of the earth. This is its work—not to cultivate the land with the plow, but to live by plunder and the sword, and to possess cities that are not its own. Before it strikes, before it bursts into war, it carries terror on its face.

As for the words, “From itself its judgment and its burden will proceed,” Symmachus translated: “It will judge for itself, and it will proceed by its own decree.” They may be understood in this way: it will appoint rulers from its own nation, and its power and sword will have no auxiliaries from other nations; or, certainly, whatever it has done will be done to it, and it will be devastated just as it devastated others.

Its horses and horsemen, who will come from afar, will be so swift in pursuit and in laying everything waste that they will surpass leopards and evening wolves. Wolves are said to be fiercer when night is near, driven mad by hunger throughout the day. The horsemen will therefore fly—not to fight, since no one will resist, but to run everywhere like an eagle, to which all winged creatures are subject, hastening to devour. [Note: Martianay incorrectly reads *volatibus* (“flights”).]

And just as at the breath of a burning wind all green things wither, so at their appearance everything will be laid waste. The number of captives and the amount of plunder will be so great that, by **ὑπερβολή** (*hyperbolē*), exaggeration, it could even be compared with sand.

He himself, that is, Nebuchadnezzar, will reign throughout the whole world. Triumphing over kings before his chariot, he will hold them up to mockery and count them among his pleasures. He will possess such power and pride that he will strive to overcome nature and capture the most strongly fortified cities by the strength of his army.

For he will come against Tyre, and, having thrown up a rampart in the sea, will make a peninsula out of an island and provide an entrance through the waves of the sea into the city by land. Therefore he will laugh at every fortress, heap up a rampart, and capture it—that is, the fortress or Tyre. This is clearly demonstrated in Ezekiel, where it says: “Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, made his army perform great labor against Tyre. Every head was bald and every shoulder stripped of hair, yet no recompense was given to him or his army from Tyre for the labor by which he served against her” (Ezek. 29:19).

When he has heaped up the rampart and nothing has opposed his strength, then his spirit will be changed into pride. Thinking himself to be God, he will set up a golden image in Babylon and compel all nations to worship it. When he has done this, he will pass into the form of a beast and afterward fall. For this, Aquila and Symmachus translated **καὶ πλημμελήσει** (*kai plēmmelēsei*), “and he will transgress.” Holy Scripture has the custom of using *VASAM* ()—that is, “he will transgress”—for “he will cease to be what he had been.”

We have something similar in the idiom of our own language when we say, “The army has been beaten,” meaning that it has been killed and struck down; or, “The vineyard and field have sinned,” meaning that they have yielded no vintage or crops.

What is said at the end of the chapter—“This is the strength of his god”—must be read **εἰρωνικῶς** (*eirōnikōs*), ironically, so that the meaning is: “This is the strength given to him by Bel, his god.” By the fiercest exercise of authority, through a written decree and threats of death, he compelled all nations to worship Bel.

This is according to the Hebrew. Now let us come to the Septuagint, so that, after setting out each statement, we may fit it to an allegorical interpretation.

“Behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, which travels over the breadth of the earth to possess dwellings not its own.” God threatens the contemptuous and those who slander his providence that he will raise up the Chaldeans. The name “Chaldeans” is interpreted as meaning something like “demons,” or signifying exceedingly wicked angels who serve his fury and anger and the tribulation he inflicts upon sinners; or wicked human souls through whom God torments those who deserve punishment. [Note: Another reading: “whom.”]

These Chaldeans are a bitter and swift nation, sparing no one and quickly completing whatever has been commanded them. [Note: The manuscript of Regina reads: “what had quickly been [commanded].”] “They travel over the breadth of the earth.” The broad and spacious way is the one that leads to death (Matt. 7:13). On it walked the rich man in the Gospel, who shone in purple (Luke 16), and those of whom it is said: “They sleep upon beds of ivory and live in luxury upon their couches. They eat calves from the herd and drink filtered wine and anoint themselves with the finest oils” (Amos 6:4–6). Because they walk on the broad way, they are called “the breadth of the earth,” which is trampled under the footsteps of the Chaldeans.

They did not wish to walk along the narrow and constricted way that leads to life, along which Paul walked, glorifying God amid tribulation and distress (1 Cor. 6:12). [Note: Another reading: “boasting in God.”] The Chaldeans walk over the breadth of the earth in order to possess dwellings not their own. Every rational soul, even if through its own vice and fault it has become a lodging place of the Chaldeans, is nevertheless by nature a dwelling place of God.

And although the worst demon speaks in the Gospel: “I shall return to my house from which I came” (Matt. 12:44), we must not believe him, since no rational creature was made for the purpose of being a dwelling place of a demon.

It follows: “He is terrible and illustrious; his judgment will be from himself, and his assumption will proceed from him.” [Note: The same manuscript reads: “His assumption has proceeded from him.”]

The Chaldean is terrible because of the many and varied punishments he inflicts upon the contemptuous; he is illustrious because he assumes for himself the glory of divinity. Through his oracles, false answers, and cures of diseases that he himself had inflicted, he appears illustrious to the ignorant and to those who despise God.

The judgment and punishment of the contemptuous will be from him, that is, from himself or from the Chaldean. For, according to the apostle, they will be handed over to him for punishment, so that they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim. 1:20). Whoever repents of him and turns back to God will come out from him, having previously been held in his hands and having been subject to the Chaldean’s assumption.

Whenever we see someone who has served the devil for a long time and afterward turned back to God, let us say of him: “His assumption has proceeded from him.” For all who repent and abandon the demons—whose backs they had previously offered as horses for them to ride—and who, with the speed of leopards and evening wolves, cast off and shatter their riders, and come with empty and light backs to carry him who, gentle and poor, mounted the foal of a donkey (John 12), will hasten as though from afar. Not content with running and rushing, they will take flight and come like an eagle, so that they may feed upon the flesh of God’s word and satisfy the hunger of so long a time.

In the words **καὶ ἐξιππάζονται οἱ ἱππεῖς αὐτοῦ** (*kai exippazontai hoi hippeis autou*), which the Septuagint translated, “And his horsemen will ride,” Symmachus, according to the sense we have given above, translated: “His horsemen will be poured out,” that is, “they will fall and be dashed upon the ground.” [Note: In place of the words “and the Septuagint translated,” the manuscript of Regina and Victor, attributing this interpretation to Jerome himself, prefer “and we translated.”]

The wolves of Arabia—that is, of evening and the West—are rightly so called: their former wicked way of life has set, and they had previously been established in darkness. With their whole stride they abandon the evening. When they have left it and flown forth ready to eat the flesh of the word of God, then destruction will come upon the wicked, that is, upon the Chaldeans who resisted the faces of penitents so that they would not return to their Lord.

Therefore destruction will come upon the wicked who resist their faces from the opposite side. When those wicked have been destroyed and the captives have been snatched from their hands, then the divine word will gather, like sand, the captivity of the Chaldeans. It will rejoice in kings, and tyrants will become its sport, seeing that the once most powerful devil and his kingdoms—which he also showed to the Savior, saying, “All these I will give you if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9)—have been destroyed by his coming.

For wisdom delights, and knowledge takes pleasure, when folly is destroyed and the former power of tyrants, overcome and cast down, is turned into mockery. Nor was the dragon alone formed as a plaything for the Lord, being the beginning of His creation and made sport for the angels. [Note: Victor reads: “He was made a mockery for the angels,” and, on this point, praises the passage of Job 40 according to the Septuagint: **τοῦτ᾽ ἔστιν ἀρχὴ πλάσματος κυρίου πεποιημένος ἐγκαταπέζεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων**, “that is, the beginning of the Lord’s creation, made to be played with by the angels.” Shortly afterward, following the manuscript of Regina, we restored *parvulo* (“for a little one”) in place of *parvulum* (“a little one”).]

Nor will God give only him, like a sparrow, to a little one; if anyone else is cruel and tyrannical in mind, he too will be handed over to the word of God for mockery.

The text also says: “He will mock every fortress.” What other fortress is there than the one of which the apostle speaks: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of fortresses, destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. 10:4–5)?

If, therefore, there are fortresses either in teachings that promise to possess height and greatness contrary to the truth, or in all the glory, riches, and strength praised in this world, all will be destroyed, and the word of God will mock every fortress.

“And he will heap up a rampart and possess it through the rampart”—and through the earthly things he brings forth, he will convict it of its weakness in those matters in which it previously seemed to possess some strength. When this has been completed, then the spirit will be changed. He will no longer punish as he had punished before; rather, passing through sinners, he will plead for them and reconcile them to their former Lord. In all these things the strength of our God is displayed, the one who has accomplished such great deeds. [Note: Some read *qui* (“who”) instead of *quae* (“which”).]

You see how rugged these passages are and how contrary they are to the truth of the historical sense. What, according to the literal meaning, we interpreted concerning the Chaldeans now appears, according to the tropological sense, to signify the mercy and liberty of those who escaped from the hands of the Chaldeans.

The historical sense is strict and has no freedom to wander. The tropological sense is free, but is bounded by these laws alone: it must follow the piety of the interpretation and the continuity of the language, and it must not violently join together things that are greatly opposed to one another.

(Verses 12.) “Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One? And we shall not die? O Lord, you appointed him for judgment, and established him as strong for correction.”

The Septuagint reads: “Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One? And we shall not die? O Lord, you appointed him for judgment; and he formed me to reprove in his discipline.” [Note: Another reading is: “You appointed him in judgment.”]

Symmachus renders it more clearly: “Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One, so that we should not die? O Lord, you appointed him to judge; you established him as strong for correction.”

God had answered the prophet’s complaint: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear?” He said: “Look among the nations and see”; and after the preface he added: “Behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation.” After completing the whole description, whether of Nebuchadnezzar or of the devil, he mentions at the end: “Then his spirit will change, and he will pass through and fall; this is the strength of his god.”

When the prophet heard and understood that Nebuchadnezzar could receive power against Judah—or the devil against believers—in order to correct them, and that after the correction he himself would also be punished at the end, he answered the Lord:

“Then are you, O Lord my God, my Holy One”—he speaks in the affection of one who flatters and repents—“who created us from the beginning? By whose mercy we have continued to exist until now? I did not know that our adversaries could possess so much power; I did not know that Nebuchadnezzar, or the devil of this world, had received power over the world and all its nations. As far as his strength is concerned, none of us can resist him. But as far as your mercy is concerned, everything by which we live is yours, because we have not been killed by him and brought to the works of death.

“You, O Lord, appointed him for judgment, so that he might be the enemy and avenger, and so that through him you might correct whoever has sinned against you.”

But since we have interpreted the Chaldeans as demons and Nebuchadnezzar as their king, the devil, we must briefly touch upon the devil’s character and power, so that the prophet may justly say: “O Lord, you appointed him for judgment, and established him as strong for correction.”

A nation of demons is raised up against unbelievers and the contemptuous, bitter in punishment and present everywhere. It also walks wherever the breadth of the earth extends, so that it may possess human beings in whom Christ ought to have dwelt. It is dreadful and terrible, and difficult for anyone to overcome. It is not broken until, weighed down by the magnitude of its sins and by the burden of its iniquity, it reaches its end.

Its horses and horsemen, like leopards and wolves, will always thirst for blood and desire plunder. They will pretend to be absent, and when they are not expected, they will quickly come from afar. They will fly like an eagle, which raises its flight and wishes to place its nest among the stars of heaven, and it always hastens toward prey. In Ezekiel, under the figure of Nebuchadnezzar and the king of Egypt, he is also described in relation to the devil.

No demon spares anyone. All come hastening to plunder. Before their face is a burning wind; whatever they look upon, whatever meets their face, they desire to burn and destroy.

The king himself will be most powerful in the midst of the captives. He will receive their number from his attendants here and there, like the sand of the sea. He will triumph over kings, and tyrants will be his mockery. For by his overthrow he will deceive many saints; and those who seemed most powerful, who exercised tyranny against demons and expelled them from possessed bodies, he will subject to his slavery and assign to mockery.

He himself, exceedingly strong, with a mustered force and an army of the lost gathered together, will laugh at every fortress and strive to overthrow whatever is strong. For he will heap up a rampart—that is, surround them with earthly works—and when earth has been heaped up, he will easily seize every fortress. [Note: Martianay had read *aggravata* (“weighed down”) incorrectly here.]

After such a victory his spirit will be changed. His mouth will pass through to heaven, and, making himself a god, he will begin to blaspheme his Creator. When he has done this, he will fall. His ruin will show how strong his divinity truly was, and how false was the representation of the idols under whose images he subjected human beings to his worship.

When the prophet heard that the king of this world was so great and powerful that he gathered captives like the sand of the sea, triumphed over kings, made tyrants his mockery, laughed at every fortress, first heaped up a rampart and afterward captured it, and possessed such pride that he dared to resist his Creator and make himself like a god—although earlier he had spoken boldly to the Lord and had declared himself, or his people, or those in whose person he had complained, to be righteous—he now breaks into words of flattery and says:

“Then are you from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One?” That we do not die and are not captured by so great an enemy is due to your mercy. For you appointed him as a kind of executioner and made him strong, so that either no one or only a rare person can resist his strength.

According to the Septuagint, however, the words at the end—“And he formed me to reprove in his discipline”—may be referred to the person of the prophet, so that the meaning is: “For this reason I was inspired as a prophet: to reprove sinners and teach the discipline of the Lord.”

Some think that this is said of the Lord, who was formed by the Father and assumed a body for this reason: to instruct human beings in the teaching of God the Father. But how far this differs from the context of what precedes and from the whole content of the passage will be for the reader, rather than for my judgment, to determine.

[Col. 1284A] (Verses 13, 14.) “Your eyes are pure, so as not to see [elsewhere: may see] evil, and you cannot look upon iniquity. Why do you look upon those who act unjustly and remain silent while the impious man devours one more righteous than himself? And you make human beings like the fish of the sea and like a creeping thing that has no ruler?”

The Septuagint: “The eye is pure, so as not to see evils, and you cannot look upon affliction. Why do you look upon the contemptuous? Will you remain silent when the impious man devours one more righteous than himself? And you will make human beings like the fish of the sea and like reptiles that have no leader.”

[Note: [Col. 1283D] We have removed here the negative particle, which the printed books insert with the opposite sense; the manuscripts, and the Greek text itself, know only ἱνατὶ ἐπιβλέπεις or εἰς τὶ ἐπιβλέπεις, “Why do you look,” etc. It is also absent from the Hebrew: “Why do you look,” although there we did not dare to delete the negative particle, since the manuscripts provide no support.]

Jeremiah likewise speaks to God in much the same way: “You are righteous, O Lord, I acknowledge it; nevertheless I shall speak judgments to you. Why is it that the way of the wicked prospers, and that all who transgress and commit wrongdoing flourish? You planted them, and they took root; they have begotten children and produced fruit. You are near their mouth, but far from their inmost parts” (Jer. XII, 1, 2).

[Note: [Col. 1284D] The Florence manuscripts in Victorius’s possession read “flourish,” in agreement with the Greek εὐθύνουσαν.]

Thus Habakkuk too speaks in the same spirit: “Your eyes are pure, O Lord,” he says, “and I know that you do not willingly look upon evil and injustice, nor can anyone doubt your justice. Nevertheless, why do you allow the Babylonians to rage with such cruelty, and the righteous Israel to be oppressed by the impious Nebuchadnezzar—not because the one who is oppressed is perfectly righteous [elsewhere: perfect], but because he is more righteous than the one who oppresses him?”

And just as fish that have no ruler, irrational animals, and a multitude of reptiles without providential oversight are subject to the stronger, and whoever is more powerful in bodily strength dominates another, so among human beings—rational animals created in your likeness—reason and merit have no power, but bodily strength and irrational force prevail. If, however, we wish to understand the passage generally, as the prophet asks about providence—why the devil has so much power in the world, and why, while God rules, another exercises tyranny—the sense will be as follows, and this interpretation will be joined to what precedes:

“I know, O Lord my God, my Holy One, that through your providence and protection we do not die; and I know that you appointed the adversary for this reason: that, using him as an executioner, you might correct sinners without killing them. I know that nothing unjust pleases you, and that your eyes are pure from all iniquity, so that you cannot look upon the sufferings of those subjected to injustice. Nevertheless, I cannot discover why the unjust Cain kills the righteous Abel (Gen. IV), while you remain silent. Why, when the whale rages and devours everything, are not only the smaller fish, but even your own Jonah, devoured as well (Jonah II)? Why does the impious prevail, and the righteous suffer defeat? I do not say this because I suppose that anyone is justified in your sight and is without sin, or because I am ignorant of human frailty; but just as Sodom and Gomorrah are righteous in comparison with Jerusalem, and the tax collector in the Gospel is made more righteous in comparison with the Pharisee (Luke XVIII), so this man who is oppressed by the devil is indeed a sinner, but he is more righteous than the one who oppresses him.”

Why, then, is there no measure or standard, so that if the righteous is once oppressed and subjected, he may be subjected not to one who is impious, but to one more righteous than himself?

[Note: [Col. 1285B] The manuscript of Regina has: “Not that I should say.”]

“Am I to say that anything happens without you, and that the impious can accomplish so much against your will?” To think this is blasphemous. Since, then, you are the ruler and Lord of the universe, you necessarily bring about what cannot happen without you.

He says this, however, not because the prophet himself thinks in the manner I have stated above, but because he expresses human impatience in his own person. In the same way we frequently see the Apostle take upon himself various human opinions, and now say: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. VII, 23). And as though he were only beginning, he says: “Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended” and “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (Phil. III, 13; I Cor. XIII, 9). Again, as though he were perfect: “Let all of us, then, who are perfect, think this way” (I Cor. XIII, 9)—although it is obviously not one and the same thing to say that he knows in part and to say that he is perfect.

And lest you perhaps think that this is not characteristic of the Apostle’s practice but an argument of our own, he says to the Corinthians: “I have applied these things to myself and Apollo for your sake, so that in us you may learn” (I Cor. IV, 6).

[Note: [Col. 1285B] Martianaeus had falsely printed: “not of apostolic practice but of ours.” This is an argument that he himself is speaking. Victorius corrected it, with a less incongruous sense, to: “but of ours; this is an argument.” The manuscript of Regina has now restored the best reading.]

Otherwise, how can God hold human beings as though they were the fish of the sea and reptiles that have no ruler, when the angels of each individual continually behold the face of the Father who is in heaven (Matt. XVIII), and “the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him and delivers them” (Ps. XXXIII)?

Therefore, just as God’s providence extends even to individual human beings, so in the case of the other animals we may understand a general administration, order, and course of events: for example, how the multitude of fish is born and lives in the waters; how reptiles and four-footed animals arise on the earth; and what foods sustain them.

[Note: [Col. 1285C] No one who truly confesses God and believes as a matter of faith that his providence extends to every minutest thing either charges this passage of Jerome with error or does not strive charitably to interpret it in a sounder sense. Considering the whole context, we are persuaded that the holy Doctor can clear himself of suspicion of error in his own words; for he does not simply deny that God’s providence extends to every minutest thing, but denies that the providence governing rational beings is the same as that governing irrational beings.]

But it is absurd to reduce God’s majesty to the point of saying that he knows, moment by moment, how many gnats are born and how many die; how many bugs, fleas, and flies there are on the earth; how many fish swim in the water; and which of the smaller animals must become prey to the larger.

Let us not be such foolish flatterers of God that, while dragging his power down even to the lowest things, we wrong ourselves by saying that rational and irrational creatures are governed by one and the same providence.

For this reason that apocryphal book must be condemned as foolish in which it is written that a certain angel, named Tyri, rules over reptiles.

[Note: [Col. 1285C] I think that this name, Tyri, is corrupt through the fault of scribes. The manuscript of Regina reads Tygrin, which is somewhat better; perhaps Hegrin should be restored, for that is the name of the angel appointed over the beasts in the apocryphal book of Hermas. Or the word should be written in Greek letters as θηρίου or θηρίων, “of a beast” or “of beasts,” so that the name refers to the class of reptiles rather than to an angel. But a much more difficult question is which book Jerome is thought to be condemning as foolish. For although at first sight the reference seems to be to the book of Hermas, or of the Shepherd, there are substantial reasons that do not permit this conclusion.

First, it is contrary to all appearance that Jerome would utterly reject and condemn as foolish a book that elsewhere he often praises, regards as ecclesiastical, and considers worthy to be read for the benefit of the faithful. Second, that book does indeed mention, in the fourth vision, an angel who is over the beasts; but he is not there called Tyri or Tygrin, but Hegrin. This name they derive not from θηρίου, “of a beast,” but from ἐγρηγόρου, “watchful,” and they wish it to be formed from Daniel, where we read that Nebuchadnezzar, by the agency of an ἐγρήγορος, was reduced to the condition of the beasts.

Thus, in all copies of the Shepherd, whether printed or handwritten, according to P. Lenoury, we find: “The Lord sent an angel over the beasts, whose name is Hegrin,” etc. One manuscript of Colbert, cited by the same scholar, reads: “over the beast whose name is Hegrin,” so that the name is assigned not to the angel but to the beast, which may perhaps be called thus from the Greek ἄγριος, “wild, savage, beast.” Likewise in Ps. LXXIX, 14: μονὸς ἄγριος, “a solitary wild creature.” But the reliability of the Colbert manuscript is weak, since all the others contradict it; it is a more recent copy and bears the mark of a pedantic glossator.

Finally, the Shepherd cannot rightly be accused of foolishness for saying that an angel presides over reptiles, since this is the opinion of the ancient Fathers, as we shall demonstrate below. The scholastic doctors after St. Thomas likewise generally accepted it: “Every visible thing in this world has an angelic power appointed over it” (St. Thomas, II Part., q. 110, art. 1, ad 1).

Some therefore wish Jerome to be attacking here not the book of the Shepherd but the Recognitions attributed to Clement, since it is stated there, in Book I, chapter XLV, that God appointed rulers over every individual creature—“over trees also, mountains, springs, and rivers”; and that “among angels there is an angelic prince, among spirits a spirit, among stars a star, among demons a demon, among birds a bird, among beasts a beast, among serpents a serpent over serpents, among fish a fish over fish, and among human beings a human being, who is Christ Jesus.”

And if the name Tyri, however badly corrupted through the carelessness of scribes, is really Theri, the Greek θηρίον, this comes closest to the truth: it would then be more probable that Pseudo-Clement is being referred to, since he called the angelic power appointed over beasts “the beast.” Yet this conjecture is not entirely satisfactory, both for other reasons and especially because Pseudo-Clement taught that a beast, not an angel, was placed over the beasts.

It has therefore seemed more correct to others that Jerome is referring to an apocryphal book that no longer exists, and that he rightly condemns it as foolish because it assigned names and functions to individual angels. Some have suspected that it alludes to Origen’s Homily 13 on Ezekiel and Book I of On First Principles, chapter 5, and to Ezekiel’s own prophecies concerning Tyre.

The opinion that God appointed angels over animals and plants was commonly accepted among the ancients. It is explained above all by Origen, Homily 14 on Numbers, Homily 23 on Jonah, Homily 8 on Jeremiah, and Homily 4 on Ezekiel; by Athenagoras, in his Embassy for the Christians, p. 27, cited by Methodius in Epiphanius, heresy 64, no. 24; by Epiphanius himself, in his Book on Measures and Weights, chapter 22; and by Theodoret, Questions on Genesis, question 32, and elsewhere. It was also the opinion of the Platonists, as in Porphyry’s Περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων, Book II.]

—that an angel named Tyri presides over reptiles—

[Col. 1287A] and, by the same analogy, that particular angels have been assigned to fish, trees, and all beasts for their guardianship.

[Col. 1287A] (Verses 15 ff.) “He lifted everything up with the hook; he dragged it into his net and gathered it into his seine. Therefore he will rejoice and exult. For this reason he will sacrifice to his seine and offer incense to his net, because through them his portion has been fattened and his food made choice. Therefore he spreads his seine and never ceases to kill the nations” [the Vulgate: “will spare”].

The Septuagint: “He lifted up the end with the hook, drew him into his net, and gathered him into his seines. Therefore he will rejoice and be glad. Therefore he will sacrifice [elsewhere: sacrificed] to his seine and burn incense to his net, because through them he has fattened his portion and his chosen food. Therefore he spreads his net and never ceases to kill the nations.”

Because he had previously mentioned fish, saying, “You will make human beings like the fish of the sea and like the reptile”—which is expressed more precisely in Hebrew by REMES (), that is, κινούμενον, “everything that can move”—he therefore preserves the metaphor of fish in what follows. Just as a fisherman casts a hook, a net, and a seine, so that what the hook cannot catch the net may seize, and what escapes the net may be surrounded by the wider seines, so the Babylonian king ravaged everything and made the entire human race his prey (Dan. III).

When he says, “He will rejoice and be glad, and will sacrifice to his seine and offer incense to his net,” he signifies the idol that he made in the plain of Dura [elsewhere: Duram] and the statue of Bel, to which, as to a great seine, he sacrificed the fattest victims, compelling all the nations he had conquered to worship it.

For he believed that he had been fattened through them—that is, through his idols—and that his portion, namely all his wealth, was in them. As though they were great fish, he subjected even the leading men and kings to his rule; these are the choice foods that he calls them. And because he had once been filled by this most abundant fishing and had filled his seine—that is, his army—therefore he does not cease killing nations, that is, continually fighting and slaughtering them.

According to the Septuagint, however, the impious devil—who oppresses the righteous, holds human beings as the fish of the sea, and lays waste to everything like reptiles without a ruler—cast his hook, opposed to the hook by which the first fish was caught through the Apostle Peter and in whose mouth the stater was found (Matt. XVII). Adam fastened himself to his hook, and he dragged him out of paradise in his net; he covered him with his seines, with his varied and manifold deceits and frauds.

Therefore he rejoices and considers his snares greater than the commandment of the Lord. He sacrifices not to the hook—for this represents a perverse word, still at the beginning—but to his net, because in it he has caught the fattest victims. “Through one man the many were made sinners” (Rom. V, 19), and “in Adam all died” (I Cor. XV), and all the saints thereafter were expelled from paradise together with him.

Hence his foods are choice, so that, in the Psalmist’s words, “he may seek food for himself from God” (Ps. CIII, 21), wishing to overthrow the prophets and the apostles. And because he first deceived the human being, he does not cease each day to destroy the entire human race.

The passage may also be understood of the perverse and manifold teaching of heretics. They too catch many fish with their hook, their net, and their seines, and capture many reptiles. Therefore they rejoice, and they worship and honor as God the teaching by which they have been able to deceive and persuade; they despoil it and devote themselves to it with every art, since they know that by him they have slain so many victims and deceived so many powerful [and holy] persons.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] The manuscript of Regina reads: “so many powerful persons have been deceived by them.”]

[Col. 1288B] Scripture now calls these their fat portion and choice foods. Therefore, in imitation of beasts that, once they have tasted blood, always thirst for it, they spread their net, and all their effort is directed toward killing not a few, as at the beginning, but many.

Anyone who has seen such a multitude of heresies and perverse doctrines caught by the devil’s hook, net, and seines cannot doubt that this concerns the destruction of many nations. Yet the end of their catch is destruction.

(Cap. II.—Verse 1.) “I shall stand at my watch and fix my step upon the rampart; I shall keep watch to see what he will say to me and what I shall answer to the one who reproves me.”

The Septuagint: “I shall stand at my watch and climb upon the rock; I shall keep watch to see what he will speak in me [elsewhere: to me], and what I shall answer to my correction.”

Symmachus followed the sense more explicitly: “Like a watchman I shall stand upon the watchtower; I shall stand as one enclosed, and I shall keep watch to see what is said to me, and what I should answer and say in opposition to the one who reproves me.”

[Note: [Col. 1287D] “He followed the words”; the manuscript of Regina does not have this reading.]

For “rampart” and “rock,” in whose place Symmachus translated “enclosed,” the Hebrew has MASUR (), which Theodotion rendered “circle,” and Aquila and the fifth edition rendered “compass.”

[Note: [Col. 1287D] This is more correctly restored from the manuscript of Regina, following Victorius, after Martianaeus had read “circle” instead of “compass.” Jerome’s following exposition agrees with it, where he says: “And by this circle and compass, as by a wall, I shall enclose myself, lest,” etc.]

To the first complaint the Lord had answered: “Look among the nations, and see; wonder and be astonished.” To this the prophet, as though repenting of his earlier statement, had moderated his question, saying: “O Lord my God, my Holy One, we shall not die” (above, I, 12). Nevertheless, with reverence and praise of God, he had asked him: “Your eyes are pure, so that you do not see evil, and you cannot look upon iniquity” (ibid., 13). “Why do you look upon those who act unjustly and remain silent while the impious man devours one more righteous than himself?”

He then explained in detail what this devouring of the righteous was: that human beings should become like the fish of the sea and like reptiles; that all should be dragged to destruction by hook, seine, and net; and that there should be no end to their slaughter.

Therefore, because he is a prophet, and for that reason asks and says that he is in doubt, so that what is answered to him may be answered to everyone, he says: “I shall stand upon my watch,” that is, upon the height of my prophecy, “and I shall see what follows after the captivity of the people and the overthrow of the city and the temple.”

Or certainly the meaning is this: “I shall guard my heart with all diligence, and I shall stand upon Christ the rock. And by this circle and compass, as by a wall, I shall enclose myself, lest the roaring lion be able to break in upon me. I shall see what God will answer me after my second question; and after he has answered me and reproved me for complaining wrongly, I shall see what I too ought to answer him.”

He elegantly and wonderfully describes human impatience, which we are always accustomed to display in disputes: before anyone has answered us from the opposite side, and before we know in what respect he has reproved us, we prepare our reply.

This shows that the response is not a matter of reason but of contentiousness. If reason were involved, the answer ought to be awaited, and only then should one see whether one ought to reply or agree with a reasonable response.

It should also be noted from the words, “to see what he will speak in me,” that prophetic vision and the word of God do not come to the prophets externally, but internally, answering the inner person. Hence Zechariah says: “And the angel who spoke in me” (Zech. I, 9). And in the Psalms: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me” (Ps. LXXXIV, 9).

(Verses 2 ff.) “And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tablets, so that the one who reads it may run; for the vision is still for a distant time, and it will appear at the end, and it will not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and will not delay. Behold, the one who is unbelieving, his soul is not upright within him. But the righteous shall live by his faith.”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision, and make it clear upon boxwood [elsewhere: upon a boxwood tablet], so that the one who reads it may pursue it; for the vision [elsewhere: for the vision] is still for a time, and it will arise at the end, and it will not be in vain. If it fails, endure it, because it will surely come and will not delay. If he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him. But the righteous shall live by my faith.”

[Note: [Col. 1289D] The manuscript of Regina reads “so that it may run,” a reading properly attributed to Aquila and Symmachus, ὅπως τρέχῃ.]

For “tablets” and “boxwood,” which is called ALLUOTH [elsewhere: LUTH] () in Hebrew, Symmachus translated “pages.” And where the Septuagint has, “But the righteous shall live by my faith,” all the others translated, “He shall live by his faith.”

Finally, Symmachus, interpreting more significantly, says: “But the righteous shall live through his own faith,” which in Greek is ὁ δίκαιος τῇ ἑαυτοῦ πίστει ζήσει.

[Note: [Col. 1289D] This passage is corrupt in the ancient editions, both in the order of the Greek words and in the reading of the Hebrew text. Whoever wishes may compare them.]

[Note: [Col. 1290D] Martianaeus, attempting to correct this by transposing the Greek words, corrupts the sentence by reading πίστει τῇ ὁ δίκαιος ἑαυτοῦ ζήσει. We have restored the reading found in Eusebius and already in the edition of Erasmus.]

The word BAEMUNATHO () means “in his faith.” If it had JOD rather than VAU at the end, as the Septuagint supposed, and were read BAEMUNATHI (), they would rightly have translated, “in my faith.” But now the similarity between VAU and JOD, which differ from one another only in size, was the cause of the error. The following discussion explains why this has been said.

In accordance with the promise made to the holy man in Isaiah—“While you are still speaking, I shall say, ‘Behold, here I am’” (Isa. LXV, 24)—the Lord now answers the prophet as well and commands him to write the vision and arrange [elsewhere: set out] it upon tablets, that is, to write it more clearly.

I think that these are the tablets of which the Apostle also speaks to the Corinthians: “You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all human beings; you are manifestly a letter of Christ, ministered [elsewhere: made manifest] by us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (II Cor. III, 2, 3).

Solomon also signifies something similar in Proverbs, saying: “Describe it upon the breadth of your heart” (Prov. III, 3).

He is commanded to write more plainly so that the reader may run, and so that neither any obstacle may restrain his speed nor any desire to read be held back. He gives this command because the vision is still far off and appointed for a particular time. When the end of events arrives, then he too will come, and the prophecy will be proved true by its fulfillment in fact.

If, perhaps because of your eagerness, O reader, and your longing to see the vision, the promised event should seem to you to delay a little, do not despair that it will come; wait patiently. For you have me, who promise and say to you: “It will surely come, and it will not delay.”

But if anyone is incredulous concerning this promise of mine, and, when I say, “It will surely come, and it will not delay,” begins to doubt and silently waver within himself, thinking that what is delayed for a time will not come, he will displease my soul, in accordance with the saying: “My soul hates your new moons and your Sabbaths” (Isa. I, 13).

When God is said to have a soul, we must understand this as referring to his mind and thought, so that the meaning is: “He will displease my judgment.”

Just as the one who doubts, when I promise, that what I promise will come will displease me, so the righteous who believes my promise will live by his faith.

The picture of this chapter has been drawn, as it were, with these lines. What he says is of this kind, provided that we also combine the translation of the Septuagint:

“Write in your heart. Just as little children receiving their first lessons in letters train their curved strokes and trembling hand upon boxwood and become accustomed through practice to writing correctly, so you too, who have spoken in the person of the doubting people, write in the tablets of your heart and in the boxwood of your breast what I say.”

[Col. 1290D] The vision that is promised and commanded to be described is to be written more clearly, so that it may not be wrapped in any cloud or obscured by the obscurity of riddles. Let manifest hope have a manifest promise.

This I command you, O prophet, not because you do not know it—for you would not be a prophet if you were ignorant—but so that what you write more clearly the reader may be able to read and run through without impediment or difficulty.

The Septuagint translated this as ὅπως διώκῃ ὁ ἀναγινώσκων, that is, “so that the one who reads may pursue it,” in accordance with the passage written to Timothy: “Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, gentleness” (I Tim. VI, 11); and to the Romans: “Pursuing hospitality” (Rom. XII, 13); and to the Corinthians: “Pursue love” (I Cor. XIV, 1).

The vision itself of which I have spoken to you—“Write the vision and make it clear upon boxwood, so that the one who reads may pursue it”—is still appointed for a particular time, concerning which the Savior says: “At an acceptable [elsewhere: accepted] time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you” (Isa. XLIX, 8).

It will arise at the consummation of the world and in the final hour of the day, of which John also speaks: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18). And it will not come in vain: for it will save many and, together with the remnant of the Israelite people, gather a multitude of the nations.

If it should withdraw for a little while, and the vision that you, O reader, are commanded to read on boxwood and on the tablets described by the prophet should begin to come later than your wishes, wait for it; for it will surely come, and it will not delay.

But if your faith should doubt and you should think that what I promise will not happen, you will have as a great punishment the fact that you displease my soul.

The righteous, however, who believes my words and does not doubt what I promise will receive as his reward [Note: [Col. 1291D] In the manuscript of Regina: “will receive as his reward eternal life.” You should not immediately accuse or reject either yourself or him, etc.] eternal life.

You should not immediately argue, either by destroying yourself or by bringing him to life, that there is partiality with me, because he himself is the cause of his own being made alive, since he lives by his faith, just as you, because you withdrew and refused to believe, displeased my soul.

The prophecy concerning Christ is clearly contained in these words. Thus the proposed question is resolved: until he comes, iniquity will rule in the world and judgment will not reach its conclusion; and the true Nebuchadnezzar will catch human beings in his net and seine like little fish, and the rational [elsewhere: reasoning] animal like a reptile without a ruler.

As for the reason we have interpreted the word as “vision,” since the text says, “for the vision is still far off; and if it delays, wait for it”—that is, wait for the vision—let no one, deceived by error, suppose that I have used visus, a masculine noun, in place of visio, which is feminine, merely because the Latin usage is less common.

For HAZON (), which Aquila translates as ὁραματισμὸν, is called visus, “sight” or “vision,” in the masculine gender among the Hebrews, and to the end the masculine declension of the word for vision—that is, visus—is maintained.

The Septuagint, however, saying, “Write the vision,” and afterward, “If it fails, endure it, because it will surely come and will not delay; if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him,” first translated “vision” with the feminine gender, although among the Hebrews, as we have said, it is masculine.

Then, following the Hebrew gender, where the word is declined in the masculine, they too used the masculine in “endure him” and “my soul will not be pleased with him.”

[Col. 1292A] Since, according to what they had first translated—“vision”—they ought also in the rest to have used the feminine gender of vision, saying, “Wait for it, because it will surely come; and if it withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with it,” that is, with the vision, this point is noted lest we seem to keep silent about something we knew.

Otherwise, I am not unaware that, according to their translation, the passage may also be understood in this way:

“Write the vision in which Christ is promised, and weave into your prophecy, whether upon boxwood, tablets, or, as Symmachus translated, pages, this statement: at the appointed time and at the consummation of the world my Son will come, who will save the lost sheep of the house of Israel, join other sheep to the ancient sheep, and, making one flock, unite the two rods which Ezekiel—that is, the strength of God—holds joined and clinging to one another in his prophetic hand” (Ezek. VII).

“And if for a little while, O prophet—or you, O people, in whose person my prophet appears to have doubted—Christ withdraws and seems to delay, wait for him, for he will surely come, and he will not delay”; and the rest which we have already explained above.

As for the fact that the Apostle made greater use of the testimony of the Septuagint when writing to the Romans, “But the righteous shall live by my faith” (Rom. I, 17), rather than of the wording found in the Hebrew, the reason is clear.

[Note: [Col. 1291D] Victorius says: “Jerome testifies both here and in Galatians III that the Septuagint wrote, ‘But the righteous shall live by my faith.’ The most ancient Vatican manuscript retains this reading: for it has ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεώς μου ζήσεται, from which it appears that Romans I should likewise be read in this way. In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter X, we read: ‘But my righteous one shall live by faith,’ as though the word μου depended on what follows, just as it does in Numbers XXV: ἐν τῷ ζηλῶσαί μου τὸν ζῆλον. The similarity of JOD and VAU introduced a difference into the word.”]

He was writing to Romans who did not know the Hebrew Scriptures, and he was not concerned with the words so long as the meaning was secure and the present discussion suffered no loss because of it.

Otherwise, wherever the sense is different and the Hebrew reads one thing while the Septuagint reads another, note that he uses those testimonies which he had learned from Gamaliel, a teacher of the law.

### (Verse 5 and following)

And just as wine deceives the one drinking it, so it will be with the arrogant man, and he will not prosper—he who enlarges his soul like Sheol, and is himself like death, and is not satisfied. And he will gather all nations to himself and heap up all peoples for himself.

Will not all these take up a proverb against him, and a taunting saying about him, and say:

“Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own! How long will he burden himself with thick mud?”

Will not those who bite you suddenly rise up—613—and those who tear you apart be awakened? And you will become their spoil. Because you have plundered many nations, all the peoples who remain will plunder you, because of human bloodshed and the iniquity of the land, the city, and all who dwell in it.

**Note:** Victor emends this, in accordance with the Hebrew and the Vulgate edition, to “He gathered and heaped up.”

**The Septuagint:** But the arrogant and contemptuous man, the proud man, brings nothing to completion: he who enlarges his soul like Sheol, and is like death, is not satisfied. And he will gather all nations to himself and receive all peoples for himself. Will not all these take up a proverb against him, and an utterance for the telling of his story, and say:

“Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his own! How long will he burden his neck heavily”—[Col. 1293A]—because those who bite him will suddenly rise up, and your plotters will keep watch, and you will become their spoil?

Because you have stripped many nations, all the peoples who remain will strip you, because of human bloodshed and the impieties of the land, the city, and all its inhabitants.”

Since these promises concern the coming of Christ—or, as some prefer, the end of the vision and the completion of God’s aid—and since the one who believes that this will come to pass will live by his faith, whereas the unbeliever will be displeasing to the Lord’s soul, the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar will be deceived by his pride.

And just as wine acts against the one who drinks it, so that, after he has risen, neither his feet nor his mind retain their proper function, and all joy and mental exhilaration are turned into ruin, so the proud man will not prosper, nor will he bring his will to completion. According to Symmachus, **οὐκ εὐπορήσει**, that is, “he will have a lack of everything.”

**Note:** In the Regina manuscript: “He will bring his will to completion in nothing.” According to Symmachus, **οὐκ εὐκρατήσει**, which is preferable to **εὐπορήσει**.

Like death and Sheol, he is not satisfied with the slain; and, subjecting all nations and peoples to his rule, he did not consider an end to his greed. When he has been drunk with the Lord’s cup and lulled to sleep by the unmixed wine, will they not all speak about him by way of comparison—**πρόβλημα**, “a riddle” or “proverb”?

“Woe to him who, laying waste to the entire world, is not satisfied with plunder and does not cease stripping those already naked, and rages only so that he may devour and crush himself beneath the burden of iniquity and plunder like a very heavy necklace.”

At the same time, consider how elegantly he has called accumulated riches “thick mud.”

**Note:** The same Regina manuscript reads: “rages and is frantic, so that [he may devour] beneath the burden of iniquity and plunder,” etc.

Will not the Medes and Persians suddenly rise up—614—who, destroying the Babylonian empire, will first bite him and afterward tear him apart? Will Nebuchadnezzar become their spoil, and will the devastator of the whole world be plundered by the peoples who were able to escape his hand and cruelty?

This will happen to him because of human bloodshed—that is, the blood of the Jew—and because of the iniquity of the land, namely Israel, and of the city, undoubtedly Jerusalem, by which he generally signifies all who dwell in it.

Let us also examine the Septuagint. Everything that we have said about Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar can be referred to this world and to the devil, who, truly arrogant and proud, believing himself to be something, will bring nothing to completion.

**Alternative reading:** “brings nothing to completion.” For his efforts and all his labor will perish. Like Sheol and death, he is not satisfied with the slain, rejoices in the deception of all nations, and gathers peoples to himself.

When they see him cast into the Abyss and handed over to Tartarus, and see that the things they had read symbolically and **αἰνιγματωδῶς**, “enigmatically,” in the prophets have been fulfilled, they will interpret them concerning him and recall them with one voice:

“Woe to the devil, who multiplied for himself what was not his own! Woe to the partridge, which gathered what it did not hatch.”

“How long?” This may be the voice of those reproving him, or it may indicate the day of judgment. And he burdens his necklace with immeasurable weight. And fittingly, since he is arrogant and proud—for pride is especially displayed in the stretching out and raising of the neck and head—his necklace is made extremely heavy, so that it bends what had been erect.

And this will happen because those who bite him will suddenly rise up: either the angels, with whom the devil will be handed over for punishment, or those who had been held captive by him, who afterward repent and, turning to Christ’s standards, will bite him, according to what is said elsewhere:

**Note:** Again, the Regina manuscript lacks the particle *cum* (“with”). Immediately afterward, on its authority, together with that of seven Florence manuscripts and one Brescia manuscript in Victor’s possession, we restored *tradetur* (“will be handed over”) in place of *traditur* (“is handed over”), which Martianus wrongly retained after Victorius’s correction. It is clear that the discourse concerns the day of judgment and alludes to: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,” etc.

“Your peaceful men have laid an ambush for you” (Jeremiah 28 [XXVIII]).

Finally, it follows:

“And your plotters will awaken”—that is, those whom you had previously lulled to sleep and intoxicated. You will fall under the ambush of those who devastate your kingdom and restore those who had been captives to Christ’s ranks.

For you have plundered many nations, and you have stripped the Jewish people of the adornment and garments that I had given them. Therefore all the peoples who have not subjected their necks to your rule will strip you and make you naked. For you too have killed very many nations and shed their blood.

But also the impiety of the land—that is, of the Jewish land—and of the city, Jerusalem, and of all its inhabitants, who said against their Creator, “Crucify, crucify him! His blood be upon us and upon our children” (John 19:6), will return upon your head, and will be the cause of your despoiling.

This may also be interpreted concerning Antichrist, who will be so arrogant and proud that he will sit in the temple of God, making himself God. Like Sheol and death, he will kill so many and gather them to himself that, if possible, he will deceive even God’s elect (Mark 13).

He will also gather all nations to himself—[Col. 1294D]—and lead every people into his error.

**Note:** The word “nations” was lacking; we supplied it from our manuscripts. One Regina manuscript reads: “all nations, so that he may lead the whole people into his own way.”

When afterward they see him killed by the breath of Christ, they will understand that what had previously been foretold about him is true, and they will say everything that follows, with the same understanding with which we interpreted the passage concerning the devil.

When it says that “all the peoples who remain will strip you because of the bloodshed of human beings, the impiety of the land and of the city, and of all who dwell in it,” let us understand the remaining peoples as the holy ones who did not serve Antichrist. By them the impious man will be stripped because of the impiety that he exercised throughout the whole earth, the devastation of the city—that is, the Church—and the persecution of all who dwelt in it.

For such great devastation and such great impiety will rage in the final period, while Antichrist persecutes the Churches, and, as the iniquity of many increases, charity will grow cold to such an extent (Matthew 24) that the Lord, who knows the secrets of the heart and is not ignorant of what will happen, will say:

“When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

We may also, according to the apostle John—who writes, “You have heard that Antichrist is coming, and now many Antichrists have appeared; from this we know that it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18)—understand all heretics, and the entire perverse doctrine of those who arrogate knowledge to themselves and despise the simplicity of the Church; those who bring nothing to completion but delight in the deaths of many. We may call them arrogant and proud and apply the whole content of this chapter to their interpretation.

**Note:** In several manuscripts: “but delight in the bites of very many.”

They truly multiply for themselves what is not their own, and, gathering for themselves what will drag them to punishment like very heavy mud and a weighty necklace, they plunder many nations, shed human blood—616—and exercise impiety against the Church and against all its inhabitants.

**Note:** The Regina manuscript reads: “gather for themselves, or plunder many nations,” etc.

But the remaining peoples, namely ecclesiastical men who have not been deceived by their error, will suddenly rise up and awaken as if from a deep sleep. They will bite them, lie in wait for them, and hold them as spoil.

Some think that the passage, “Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his own,” and what follows, can be understood of the rich, who extend the boundaries of their possessions and, treating as human property what does not belong to man, gather it for themselves, only to be suddenly abandoned by it.

That earthly possession does not belong to man—that is, to a rational animal—the Lord also demonstrates when he says:

“If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16).

They expound the whole text of the chapter with reference to this person. But I do not know whether they can preserve the prophetic order of question and answer.

### (Verse 9)

“Woe to him who gathers wicked avarice for his house, so that he may set his nest on high and think to escape from the hand of evil! You have planned shame for your house; you have cut off many peoples, and your soul has sinned. For the stone will cry out from the wall, and the timber between the joints of the buildings will answer.”

**The Septuagint:** “O, he who multiplies wicked avarice for his house, so that he may place his nest on high and be rescued from the hand of evils! You have planned shame for your house; you have consumed many peoples, and your soul has sinned. Therefore the stone from the wall will cry out, and the scarab beetle will speak these things from the wood.”

The speech is still addressed to the same person, who heaps up evils for himself and does not understand that the abundance of riches is the cause of his house’s ruin. At the same time, by a metaphor of pride, he is accused of having placed his nest on high in the likeness of a bird and of having supposed that he would be rescued from the hand of evil—that is, that he would never fall into the power of enemies.

This plan of pride and arrogant thought ended in disgrace. You killed many peoples, and, in killing others, you raged against your own soul. You raged with such cruelty—or, according to another reading, “to such an extent”—that, if it may be said, the stones of the city and the timbers of the walls that you overturned cry out loudly against your savagery.

The Lord makes a similar point in the Gospel when the Pharisees reproached him for not rebuking the children who cried out to him, “Hosanna in the highest to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” He said:

“Have you not read that it is written” (Psalm 8:3), “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise?” And: “If these are silent, the stones will cry out” (Matthew 21:9, 16).

Although many think this should be understood as follows—“If the Jews are silent, a multitude of nations will confess me”—the more explicit and truer interpretation is this: even if human beings were silent, and an envious tongue did not proclaim the multitude of my signs, nevertheless the stones themselves, the foundations of the walls, and the construction of the buildings would be able to resound with my greatness.

To make this more significant, let us also provide examples from secular literature. Crispus—that is, Sallust—says in his Histories:

> “The Saguntines, renowned for their loyalty and sufferings, were illustrious among mortals through greater zeal than resources; for among them—even then, according to another reading, *queis* (“among whom”)—the half-ruined walls, roofless houses, and the scorched walls of the temples displayed the Punic hands.”

**Note:** As far as I know, Jerome records this passage of Sallust in Book 6 of the Fragments. We read in the Regina manuscript: “renowned among mortals through a greater zeal than resources.” Other printed books have: “renowned through the zeal of mortals, greater …”; Martianus has: “renowned through the zeal of death, greater …,” and so forth.

Cicero says something similar to Caesar in *For Marcellus*:

> “The walls of this senate house, by heaven, as it seems to me, are eager to give you thanks, because in a short time that authority will be present in these seats of your ancestors and of yourself.”

As for what we translated, “And the timber between the joints of the buildings will answer,” in place of which the Septuagint put, “And the scarab beetle will speak these things from the wood,” Symmachus translated more plainly, in his customary manner:

> **καὶ σύνδεσμος οἰκοδομῆς ξύλινος ἀποφθέγξεται αὐτά**

That is:

> “And the wooden joint of the building will speak these things.”

Theodotion likewise has:

> **καὶ σύνδεσμος ξύλου φθέγξεται αὐτά**

And the fifth edition also has:

> **καὶ σύνδεσμος ξύλου φθέγξεται αὐτά**

These interpretations agree with the translation of Symmachus and with ours. For what is called **CHAPHIS** in Hebrew—[the Hebrew term is unclear or corrupt in the supplied text]—signifies wood placed in the middle of a structure to hold the walls together; among the Greeks it is commonly called **ἱμάντωσις**, “a binding” or “bracing.”

This, then, is what the prophetic speech signifies according to the historical sense: the stones of the walls destroyed by you, and their burned timbers, will proclaim your cruelty.

Apart from the five editions—that is, those of Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the fifth edition—I found two other editions in the Twelve Prophets. In one it is written:

> “For the stone from the wall will cry out, like a worm speaking from the wood.”

In the other:

> “For the stone from the wall will shout, and the **σκώληξ**, ‘worm,’ will speak these things from the wood.”

**Note:** In the Regina manuscript, here and below, **κολεός**, “a capsule” or “sheath,” is read instead of **σκώληξ**, “worm.”

Aquila, too, gives something different from what we have said:

> **καὶ μάζα**

That is:

> “And a mass from the wood will answer.”

We shall explain what their interpretation means in the exposition of the Septuagint. In the Septuagint, **οἴ**, “O,” is placed instead of “woe,” and the speech is directed either against the devil, Antichrist, or the heretics who multiply wicked avarice for themselves.

Avarice is called wicked in contrast with good avarice: the good avarice of an ecclesiastical teacher, who is never satisfied with the multitude of his followers and, the more disciples he has, the more he is stirred to devotion to teaching.

Woe, therefore, to him who multiplies the worst kind of avarice for himself, so that he may gather perverse assemblies for his house and place his nest on high, in order to be rescued from the hand of evils.

For the devil, Antichrist, and the heretics promise that those who accept their doctrine will possess the kingdoms of heaven in the celestial regions and will not feel the fires of Gehenna. Yet when they have made these promises, their plan will not reach completion. Their plan will be one of confusion and disgrace for their house—or, according to another reading, “for their household”—after the final outcome of events has shown that what was promised was false, when it is proved to have been a plan of confusion rather than salvation.

This teacher of perversity, as we have said, consumed many peoples; and the more followers he had in his company, the more he sinned against his own soul.

Finally, the stones of his Church and the **κάνθαρος**, that is, the scarab beetle from the wood, will cry out against the avarice of the proud man, because by his persuasion he deceived all nations.

We may understand the stones as the dull hearts of believers in heretical doctrines, and the scarab beetle from the wood as the various perverse teachers who, for the sake of shameful profit, take up the preaching of the cross and speak from their belly. Their god is their belly, and they do everything for the sake of food; they are reduced to dung—for the scarab or beetle is a worm of dung—and they take up the cross only to teach, with a viper’s mouth, the avarice and pride of their master, the devil.

If you ever see one of the heretics speaking against the Church about supposedly hidden and secret mysteries, and preferring the devil’s house to Christ’s house, say:

“The stone from the wall cries out, and the beetle from the wood speaks.”

I have read in someone’s book that the scarab beetle is understood of heretics because they possess doctrines that should be compared to dung. Hence the Apostle says that he considered the error of the old teaching to be **σκύβαλα**, that is, “dung” (Philippians 3).

This does not mean that the old Law is counted as dung in comparison with the Gospel, as the Manichaeans suppose—for it is impious to say this, since both Testaments belong to one God—but that the doctrines of the Pharisees, the commandments of men, and the Jewish **δευτερώσεις**, “secondary traditions,” are called dung by the Apostle.

I know that one of the brothers understood the stone that cries out from the wall as the Lord and Savior, and the scarab beetle speaking from the wood as the thief who blasphemed the Lord. Although this may piously be understood in that way, I do not see how it can be fitted to the whole context of the prophecy.

There are some who think that the scarab beetle speaking from the wood can also be referred to the person of the Savior, but the very order of the speech shows that this is impious. For “the scarab beetle will speak these things from the wood” is not understood in a good sense but in a bad one: it will speak of the worst avarice of the one who multiplies it against his own house, and of the devil’s confusion, and of the other things previously spoken concerning his iniquity and crime.

As for Aquila’s statement, “And a mass from the wood will answer,” we refer “mass” to the sense that the Lord expressed in the Gospel:

“Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matthew 16:11).

When the apostles were uncertain and could not understand what this meant, the Evangelist explained, saying:

“He had spoken to them about the teaching of the Pharisees.”

Rightly, therefore, the teaching of the heretics speaks from the wood. For they cannot persuade in any other way unless they place the glory of the wood above their own perversity.

Nor should we omit what we had said:

“For the stone from the wall will cry out, like a worm speaking from the wood”—or, according to another reading, “speaks”—

or:

“The stone from the wall will shout, and the **σκώληξ**, ‘worm,’ will speak these things from the wood.”

Some of our people say that the worm speaking from the wood is the one who says in the psalm:

“But I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 21:7).

They also refer the vocal bird to the same person, who says:

“I have become like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Psalm 101:8),

and other similar passages.

### (Verse 12 and following)

“Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town in iniquity! Are not these things from the Lord of hosts? For peoples will labor in much fire, and nations will labor in vain and grow weary. For the earth will be filled so that they may know the glory of the Lord, as waters cover the sea.”

**The Septuagint:** “Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town in iniquities! Are not these things from the Lord Almighty? And many peoples failed in the fire, and many nations were hemmed in. For the earth will be filled so that it may know the glory of the Lord, as water covers the seas.”

There is no doubt that, according to the literal sense, the prophetic speech is still directed against Nebuchadnezzar. It laments that he builds Babylon with bloodshed and constructs its walls through the ruin and deaths of very many people.

Because he did this to the city that he had built with bloodshed, he afterward hears what will be brought upon him by the Lord. For it follows:

“Are not these things from the Lord of hosts?”—that is, the things that are being said.

“Peoples will labor in much fire, and nations in vain”: once Babylon has been burned, the peoples will labor and strive in vain, toward nothing, and the people of the Chaldaean nation will fail—[Col. 1298D]—because the earth will be filled so that it may know the glory of the Lord.

When Babylon has been overthrown, the power of God’s might will become manifest to everyone, like waters covering the sea. Thus the glory of the Lord will fill the whole earth, just as waters cover the channel and bed of the sea.

This is according to the literal sense, as we have said. Otherwise, it is clear that the devil, Antichrist, and the perverse doctrine of the heretics build a city with bloodshed—that is, their own Church through the destruction of those whom they have deceived—and establish a city in iniquities, speaking iniquity against God and setting their mouth on high.

When they have done this, it is openly shown that they build the city with bloodshed from themselves and establish it in iniquities. For it follows:

“Are not these things from the Lord Almighty?”—that is, such a building is not from the Lord Sabaoth, whom the Septuagint have now translated as “Almighty.”

Many peoples will fail, and although countless nations are led into their error, they will either grow weary—which is more strongly signified by **ὀλιγοψύχησαν**—or else they will be hemmed into a narrow place and will not be able to compare with the multitude of the Church.

When those people fail in the fire—whether this is understood as being consumed by the fire of the devil, their prince, or as being kindled by the fire of the Lord, of which he says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already burning” (Luke 12:49)—and when they withdraw from their former course, repent, and abandon the path they had begun, which is what **ὀλιγοψυχία**, “faintheartedness,” signifies, the whole earth will be filled with the glory of the Lord.

This will happen when their sound goes out into the whole world through the preaching of the apostles, “like waters covering the sea” (Psalm 18). That is, the waters of the Lord will cover all the saltiness and bitterness of the world that the earth had drunk, while the devil poured rain upon it from above, so that they will make the place of the sea and its former bitterness disappear.

Hence it is also said in the psalm:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1).

Although it does not agree with the order of the reading and does not fit the present text of Scripture, the passage can also be understood of Jerusalem, a city full of the blood of the prophets. Scripture records concerning it that the blood of the saints had overflowed in it from gate to gate (Matthew 23), and it says in the Lord’s passion:

“His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25).

God also says to it through Isaiah:

“When you lift up your hands to me, I will not hear you; for your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1:15).

This city was built in iniquities, and, according to the same prophet, justice slept within it. Its building was not from the Lord Sabaoth.

Therefore many peoples failed in the fire, and many nations grew weary at the time when the armies of Vespasian and Titus surrounded it. Those who came to the city for the solemn feast of Passover were shut up in it as in a prison—622—and they perished through hunger and want. The siege—or, according to another reading, “the besieging force”—brought them all the way to the final destruction under Hadrian.

After the city of bloodshed and the town of iniquities had been overthrown, after the peoples had been consumed by fire and the nations that had come to their aid had been scattered here and there and had let their weary hands fall, the whole earth was filled with the glory of Christ; and, as though by waters, the whole world was covered by his words and teaching.

### (Verses 15ff.)

“Woe to him who gives his friend drink, sending his gall and making him drunk, so that he may look upon his nakedness. He is filled with disgrace instead of glory. You also, drink and be stupefied. The cup of the Lord’s right hand will surround you, and a discharge of disgrace will come upon your glory, because the iniquity of Lebanon will cover you, and the devastation of beasts [Vulgate: animals] will terrify them, because of the blood of human beings and the iniquity of the land, the city, and all who dwell in it.”

[Note: Victor changes the text from *repletus est* (“he is filled”) to *repletus es* (“you are filled”), following the Hebrew and the Vulgate edition. In the exposition appended below, however, Jerome understands it differently.]

The Septuagint: “Woe to him who gives his neighbor a drink of turbid overthrow, making him drunk so that he may look upon their caves. Drink you also, to the fullness of disgrace, from glory; and be shaken. The cup of the Lord’s right hand has surrounded you, and disgrace has been gathered upon your glory, because the impiety of Lebanon will cover you, and the misery of beasts will terrify you, because of the blood of human beings and the impieties of the land and the city and all who dwell in it.”

[Note: The same editor writes *pro gloria* (“instead of glory”), although the Greek has ἐκ δόξης, “from glory,” and the Hebrew has [the corresponding Hebrew expression], “from glory.” Jerome says that, attending rather to the sense than to the force of the word, he translates it “instead of glory,” and retained it in the Commentary.]

For “turbid overthrow,” Symmachus translated καὶ ἀφιὼν ἀκρίτως τὸν θυμὸν ἑαυτοῦ—that is, “and releasing his fury without judgment.” Theodotion has ἀπὸ χύσεώς σου, which means “from your effusion.”

[Note: Martianus had read, as a single word and without sense, ἀποχύσεως; we correct it to ἀπὸ χύσεως. Perhaps Theodotion’s fuller reading was ἀπὸ χύσεως θυμοῦ σου, “from the effusion of your fury.” Victor has “from your diffusion.” Shortly afterward, instead of “unexpected,” the Regius manuscript has “sudden.”]
