The Fifth Edition has ἐξ ἀπροσδοκήτου ἀνατροπῆς τῆς ὀργῆς σου, meaning “from the unexpected overthrow of your anger.” Aquila has ἐξ ἐπιτρίψεως χόλου σου, which we may render, “from the sending forth of your fury.”

[Note: On the authority of the Regius manuscript we restore ἐπιτρίψεως; the Barberinian manuscript, cited by Montfaucon, agrees with this reading. Formerly the text had ἐκπέμψεως. We also correct ποτίζοντι, “giving drink,” where Martianus corruptly read ποτίζονται, “they are given drink.” We silently correct several other minor scribal errors.]

In another edition I found: οὐαὶ τῷ ποτίζοντι τὸν ἑταῖρον αὐτοῦ ἀέλλην πετομένην, which in our language means: “Woe to him who gives his friend a drink—a flying whirlwind.” Elsewhere I also read it translated: “Woe to him who gives his neighbor a drink, ἔκστασιν ὀχλουμένην,” that is, “a turbid madness.”

I have included this so that it may be known with what variety the Hebrew word *MASPHA* [Hebrew]—which the Septuagint translated as “overthrow”—differs among all the editions.

The attack against Nebuchadnezzar therefore still continues: he has forgotten his condition and, as though unaware that he is a human being, has given another human being gall and bitterness to drink. We may understand him either as the king of Judaea, or, more generally, as all those who made people drunk with evils, so that he might look upon the nakedness of Zedekiah and of all the captives. Symmachus and the Fifth Edition translated this as “so that he might look upon their disgraces.”

These words are spoken metaphorically of a drunken man disfigured by nakedness. Nebuchadnezzar made everyone drunk with the cup of his fury, and saw them all stripped and captive; those who had once been glorious were reduced to the lowest servitude. This is what follows: “He is filled with disgrace instead of glory,” with “friend,” “neighbor,” or “fellow participant in the kingdom” understood—the one who drank your cup, O Nebuchadnezzar.

Therefore, because you made many drunk, you too must drink from the Lord’s cup and be stupefied. You will be surrounded by the punishments of the Lord’s right hand, and, together with the disgrace of your vomiting, you will expel everything you had swallowed; from lofty glory you will be brought down to the lowest evils.

“For the iniquity of Lebanon will cover you.” Your pride, he says, and the overthrow of the Temple and the plunder of the sanctuary will strip and devastate you. Since he had once mentioned Mount Lebanon, under the same metaphor he compares the victims and sacrifices—or certainly the multitude of peoples who were killed in Jerusalem—to animals or beasts, saying: “And the devastation of animals will overwhelm you.”

You will suffer all this because you devastated Judah, overturned the land of promise, and destroyed the city of Jerusalem and all its inhabitants.

[Note: The Regius manuscript, together with Victor, reads: “I heard at Lydda a certain Jew,” and so forth.]

I heard at Lydda a certain Jew, who was considered wise among them and was called a δευτερωτής, “a secondary interpreter,” relating the following story:

“Zedekiah,” he said, “was blinded by King Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah—that is, at Antioch—and mocked in various ways; then he was led to Babylon” (2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 39). “There, one day, when Nebuchadnezzar was celebrating a banquet, he ordered a drink to be given to Zedekiah which, when swallowed, would loosen the drinker’s bowels into a discharge. Suddenly he had him brought before the faces of the banqueters and compelled by the force of his bowels to defile himself with excrement. This is what Scripture now says here: ‘Woe to him who gives his friend drink, sending his gall and making him drunk, so that he may look upon his nakedness, and disgrace instead of glory’—namely, that the man who had been a most powerful king was reduced by Nebuchadnezzar to such dishonor.

“Therefore God threatens Nebuchadnezzar that he too will drink such a potion and suffer everything that Zedekiah suffered.”

You recognize, without my saying so, how ridiculous this is. For if what follows—“You also, drink and be stupefied, and the cup of the Lord’s right hand will surround you, and a discharge of disgrace will come upon your glory”—is understood not of a cup but of the evils that Nebuchadnezzar is to drink, then the cup with which Zedekiah was supplied must likewise be understood as evils, not, as they wish, as a καθαρτικόν, “purgative.”

But if they say that it really happened and that the potion was prepared as I have related, then this cup which Nebuchadnezzar is to drink must also be judged full of a καθαρτικόν, so that the Lord of hosts and the almighty Lord, in great vengeance against Nebuchadnezzar, may give him a καθαρτικόν and make him be defiled by his own excrement.

This is directed against Jewish tradition.

Let us now come to the spiritual interpretation.

“Woe to you, devil, or Antichrist, or perverse doctrine of the heretics, who with your teachings and your turbid drink make the peoples of the deceived drunk [variant: making them drunk, overthrowing them, and giving them drink], and overturn their former faith, giving them a drink not from Shiloah, not from the Jordan, not from the springs of Israel, but from the torrent of Kidron and from the river of Egypt. Of this Jeremiah says: ‘What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon?’” (Jeremiah 2:18).

In Hebrew it is written *SIOR* [Hebrew], that is, “turbid and muddy.” Although the rivers of Egypt are believed to flow from the paradise of Scripture, nevertheless, because they are trampled under Pharaoh’s feet, they have lost their brightness; polluted with Egyptian mud, they have been turned into torrents. Of these the holy man rejoices that he has escaped, saying: “Our soul has passed through the torrent” (Psalm 123:5).

If someone objects that there is also the torrent of Cherith, from which Elijah drank (1 Kings 17), and another torrent from which the Lord drank on the way—for it is written, “He will drink from the torrent on the way” (Psalm 109:7)—the answer must be this: Whoever is in Egypt and on the way of this world, whether he be Moses or Aaron, Jeremiah or Elijah, must nevertheless drink from the temptations of Egypt and of the wilderness.

Therefore the Lord’s saying—who for this reason had assumed flesh, so that he might drink from the torrent—must also be considered. Reflecting on his majesty, he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). Then, seeing that he was in Egypt and that the waters could not be purified unless he himself drank from them, he said: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”

I have said this because the devil, through overthrow, a turbid cup, and every kind of perverse teaching, makes his neighbors drunk—that is, the rational creature—and causes those whom he has deceived to look toward his caves.

The doctrines of the Church are open; they rejoice in day and in light. Those who become drunk become drunk at night (1 Thessalonians 5:7), and those who make them drunk do not lead them into the courts of the Lord, which are oppressed by no shadow of roofs, but into caves. For they have made the Father’s house, which had been a house of prayer, into a den of thieves (Matthew 21), promising certain initiations and mysteries, hidden secrets known only to heretics. Isaiah also speaks of these: “And they will hide all the handmade things, entering into caves and clefts of the rocks and holes of the earth” (Isaiah 2:18–19).

Let us therefore not enter the caves of the heretics, nor hide ourselves there where the impious Saul was accustomed to discharge the excrement of his teachings (1 Samuel 24). Rather, let us ascend to the lofty cave of Mount Sinai, where Elijah saw the Lord (1 Kings 19), and Moses afterward saw his back (Exodus 33). And Isaiah, crying out about the Lord, says: “He will dwell in a lofty cave” (Isaiah 32:16).

But if someone does not possess a turbid cup and heretical teaching, and is a teacher in the Church, yet does everything for the sake of shameful profit, selling doves in the Temple—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—and strangling free birds in the priestly chair, he does not indeed make the house of prayer a den of thieves, but he makes the Father’s house a house of business.

After this comes: “Drink you also, to the fullness of disgrace instead of glory, and be shaken.” That is: O devil, O perverse doctrine, O heretic, who thought yourself to be a golden cup from which all the nations become drunk, so that they might see your caves and secrets—be filled, instead of the greatness of glory, with the fullness of disgrace, and regard the works of the potter’s hands as a clay vessel.

Drink also from the Lord’s cup, of which the psalm says: “The cup is in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine mixed with spices, and he poured from this into that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied” (Psalm 74:9).

And with regard to the preceding statement, “Be shaken”: do not think that the things on which you first wished to stand are firm and stable, because the cup of the Lord’s right hand has surrounded you.

Moreover, because you gave your neighbor a drink of turbid overthrow, disgrace will be gathered upon you and upon your glory, which you formerly believed you possessed. You will suffer this because the impiety of Lebanon will cover you, according to the saying: “Let his prayer become sin” (Psalm 108:7).

For Lebanon, according to the Greek, is a homonym of θυμίαμα, “incense.” Incense, however, is a σύμβολον, “symbol,” of spiritual incense, which is the worship of God. Therefore the perverse prayer of the heretics, not directed with evangelical simplicity, will be turned into sin for them, and the impiety of their worship of God will cover them.

Hence it follows: “And the misery of beasts will terrify you, because of the blood of human beings and the impieties of the land and of the city and of all who dwell in it.”

The sense is this: Those whom you deceived by your frauds and made your beasts instead of Christ’s sheep—when you see them in misery and suffering punishments for their error, then you will be terrified, then you will lie prostrate.

And lest you suppose, because I mentioned Lebanon and its beasts, that I am speaking of brute animals rather than of human beings, I tell you more plainly: You will suffer these things because you have shed the blood of many people whom you caused to perish for God. You exercised impiety in the land of the living, in the land of the gentle; and your impiety also raged in the city of the Lord, that is, in his Church. You made many who dwelt in it share in your impiety.

Let this be said concerning the person of the heretics.

But if we wish to understand it of the Antichrist—or of the devil who will work in the Antichrist—he too, with the cup by which he will seek to overthrow Christ’s discipline, will make many drunk, so that, drunk, they may enter his caves. But after the end has come, instead of the glory with which he had magnified himself, he will be filled with disgrace.

He will be filled with it because he will drink the cup of punishments and will be shaken: no longer firm in his wickedness, but trembling and repenting too late. The cup of the Lord’s right hand will surround him—the Lord and Savior—when he kills him with the breath of his mouth and destroys him by the brightness of his coming.

Then all the disgrace that he gathered for himself through thoughts, deeds, and words will come upon his glory, so that to the extent that he had previously been considered illustrious, he will afterward be full of disgrace.

For he blasphemed God, and the impiety he practiced in Lebanon will cover him. The fury of many people who raged against the Church of God will be charged to him. He will not be able to lift his neck, but will be pressed down to the earth by terror.

He killed many people and devastated the whole world—that is, the Church of Christ and its inhabitants—by his impiety.

It must therefore be understood that this chapter which we have now expounded—“Woe to him who gives his neighbor a drink of turbid overthrow”—and the preceding three chapters, in which it was said, “Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his”; “Woe to him who gathers evil greed for his house”; and “Woe to him who builds a city with blood,” can be taken equally, both according to the historical sense and according to the anagogical sense, whether against Nebuchadnezzar or against the devil, the Antichrist, and the heretics.

[Note: In Victor’s copy the words “and according to the historical sense” are missing.]

### (Verse 18)

“What profit is there in a carved image, since its maker has carved it; and in a molten image and a false likeness? For its maker has trusted in his creation, to make mute idols.”

The Septuagint: “What profit is there in a carved image, since they carved it; they formed a molten image, a false likeness? For its maker trusts in his creation, to make mute idols.”

[Note: The words “or, as it is written in Hebrew, Dora,” which were absent in Martianus, have been supplied from the Regius manuscript and other printed books; they were easily omitted through the customary scribal error caused by the recurrence of the same word. We correct several other minor matters.]

[Note: The Regius manuscripts read *quasi perfectus* (“as though perfect”), without the little word *pro* (“for”).]

Consequently, the preceding words are spoken about Nebuchadnezzar: he constructed the statue of the idol Bel and set it up in the plain of Dura—or, as it is written in Hebrew, Dora—about which we read more fully in Daniel (Daniel 3).

Scripture therefore marvels at the king’s madness and folly, because he himself ordered a golden statue to be made, while the maker trusts in the image he fashioned. This can also be understood generally against all worshipers of idols.

Let us not suppose that carving and casting are the same thing. “Carving” may properly be understood of stones and marbles; “casting” refers to those metals that can be melted and poured—for example, gold, silver, bronze, lead, and tin.

This has been said so that, according to the tropological interpretation, we may know the difference between a carved image and a molten image.

We read in Deuteronomy: “Cursed is everyone who makes a carved image or a molten image, the work of the hands of an artisan, and places it in secret” (Deuteronomy 27:15).

I think that the carved and molten images are perverse doctrines, which are worshiped by those who made them. See Arius carve for himself an idol of the creature and worship what he carved. Observe Eunomius cast a false likeness and bow his neck to his casting.

Scripture significantly says: “And he will place it in secret.” They too have their rites, and, as though for their more perfect disciples, they hand down secret sacraments which, if they come into the light, are immediately proved to be fabricated.

Their carving and casting will therefore profit them nothing.

The carving, which pertains to stones, is understood in those doctrines that display their folly at first sight. The casting is found where there appears to be some semblance of secular wisdom, and where, as though with gold, an idol has been cast from philosophical disciplines and the splendor of eloquence.

The creation will therefore profit its maker nothing. And the mute and deaf image will not be able to hear its worshiper.

When you see someone unwilling to believe the truth and, after the falsity of his doctrines has been exposed, persisting in the course he began, you may appropriately say: “He trusts in his creation and makes mute or deaf idols.” For κωφά among the Greeks signifies both “mute” and “deaf,” although Symmachus, translating it as ἄλαλα, seems to have understood “mute” more than “deaf.”

Nor should anyone be troubled by that idiom of Scripture about which we have often spoken: “Who, then, is the faithful and wise steward?” (Luke 12:42). And elsewhere: “Who is wise and will understand these things?” [variant: “understands”] (Psalm 106:43).

The word “who,” or “what,” can signify “rare,” whereas elsewhere the same expression can be understood as referring to impossibility: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation or distress?” (Romans 8:35), and so forth.

The same applies to the present passage: “What profit is there in a carved image, since its maker carved it?” In both places impossibility is demonstrated: no tribulation or distress can separate the Apostle’s love from Christ, and there is no profit whatsoever in idols.

### (Verses 19–20)

“Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’; ‘Rise!’ to a silent stone [variant: lying stone]. Can it itself teach? Behold, it is covered with gold and silver, and there is no spirit at all in its inner parts. But the Lord is in his holy Temple; let all the earth be silent before him.”

The Septuagint: “Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Wake up and arise’; and to a stone, ‘Be lifted up.’ And it is itself an image, and it is a production of gold and silver, and there is no spirit in it. But the Lord is in his holy Temple; let all the earth revere before him.”

[Note: We have corrected *operta*, “covered,” in place of *aperta*, “open,” and shortly afterward *quia vegetantur*, “because they are enlivened,” in place of *quibus*, “by which,” with Victor’s reading providing the better support.]

This too can be understood either against Nebuchadnezzar or against all who venerate idols. Human error is described: people judge silver, gold, gems, and silk—the materials with which idols are either wrapped or covered—to be gods because of the brilliance of the material, although an artisan may give them form but cannot give them the soul by which limbs are enlivened.

Conversely, the Lord is said to be in his holy Temple (Psalm 10): not in a temple made by human hands, but either in heaven or in each of the saints, according to the Apostle’s words: “Do you not know that you are God’s Temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). Elsewhere: “Your bodies are God’s Temple” (1 Corinthians 6:19). Or he is in the Son, as the Son himself says: “The Father, abiding in me, does his works” (John 14:10).

Or certainly, according to that passage in which it is said that the heavens, the earth, the seas, and the whole universe are sustained by the following power (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6):

> Within, the Spirit nourishes it; infused throughout its limbs,  
> Mind moves the mass and mingles with the great body.

The entire world—which consists of heaven and earth and is enclosed by the circles of the heavens—is declared to be God’s house. Hence the Apostle confidently says: “For in him we live and move and exist” (Acts 17:28).

If someone objects that the spirit is said not to be in idols although unclean spirits attend all images, let him learn the usage of Holy Scripture: it never names a perverse spirit absolutely, but always with some qualification, as in: “They were led astray by a spirit of fornication” (Hosea 4:12); and in the Gospel: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person” (Luke 11:24), and other similar passages.

Whenever “spirit” is read by itself and absolutely, without any qualification, it always refers to the good—in other words, to the Holy Spirit. Thus the Apostle says: “The one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Galatians 6:8). Elsewhere: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” (Galatians 5:22); and in another place: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16).

We do not say that the Holy Spirit is never named with a qualification. He is called the Holy Spirit, the principal Spirit, the upright Spirit, the Spirit of God, and by other similar names. Rather, our point is that the Holy Spirit is often named both with a qualification and by itself, whereas the perverse spirit is never read without a qualification.

One may also say—if someone stubbornly wishes to understand “spirit” here as a perverse spirit—that there is a difference between “There is no spirit at all in it” and “There is no spirit at all around it.” A spirit may sit beside images, but it cannot be inside them. Hence Aquila translated the Hebrew more pointedly: “And its spirit is not in its inner parts,” or “in its midst.”

It should also be known that in certain Hebrew volumes the word “all” is not added, but the text simply reads: “Spirit is not in it.”

If someone, overcome by reason, understands “spirit” in the good sense and asks why, if the passage refers to the Holy Spirit, it is written with the qualification, “There is no spirit at all in it,” let him know that “all spirit” can mean the various gifts of the Holy Spirit. The sense would then be: “It can possess no grace in itself, no power whatsoever.”

This is understood even more appropriately according to the tropological sense: in all the idols of the heretics and in the devil’s fabrications there is no grace of the Holy Spirit. They may seem to display an image of divinity and the beauty of doctrines, but nothing breathing or alive is present in them.

Let us also mention something lest we seem to have concealed what we know from the reader: among the Hebrews, “spirit” and “wind” are called by the same word, namely *RUA* [Hebrew]. According to the sense of the passage, it can mean either “spirit” or “wind.”

Thus here we may understand “spirit” as “wind,” because nothing blows within idols; or as “soul,” because the images are lifeless.

That “spirit” can mean “soul” is clearly shown by the Savior’s prayer: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Jesus could not have commended to the Father either a perverse spirit—which it would be impious even to imagine—or the Holy Spirit, who is himself God. Rather, he commended his soul, of which he had said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew 26:36; Mark 14:34).

He also said: “No one can take my soul from me; but by my will I lay down my soul, and of my own accord I take it up again” (John 10:17–18).

## BOOK TWO

### Preface

We are writing a second work on the book of Habakkuk, venerable Pope Chromatius, dedicating to you a little work on his Canticle and undertaking with all our strength an epic discourse composed in the manner of the Psalter—that is, in lyric style.

Let the hydra hiss, then, and let Sardanapalus mock—a man more disgraceful for his vices than for his name, as Cicero says. Let us continue the journey we have begun and, in response to your prayers—you who have overcome the flesh by virtue—discuss the clearest prophecy concerning Christ in the eighth prophet, that is, in the number associated with the Lord’s resurrection.

### The title of the Canticle

“Prayer of Habakkuk the prophet for ignorances.”

The Septuagint: “Prayer of Habakkuk the prophet with a song.”

Aquila, Symmachus, and the Fifth Edition, like us, translated “for ignorances.” Theodotion alone has ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐκουσιασμῶν, that is, “for voluntary acts,” or “for those who sin willingly.”

This is mentioned so that we may understand that, apart from the Septuagint, no one translated the phrase as “prayer with a song.” For in Hebrew it has *AL SEGIONOTH* [Hebrew], which is said to mean ἐπὶ ἀγνοημάτων, “concerning ignorances,” and which we translated “for ignorances.”

The sense is this: Earlier Habakkuk had spoken rashly: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear? I shall cry out to you, suffering violence, and you will not save?” Then, in his second complaint: “Why do you look upon those who act wickedly and remain silent while the impious person devours one more righteous than himself?”

In response to this he had heard: “Write the vision and make it plain upon tablets.” And afterward: “Behold, the one who is unbelieving, his soul will not be upright within him; but the righteous will live by his faith.”

He had learned that either Nebuchadnezzar, or the devil, or the Antichrist had been appointed for the judgment of sinners and made strong for chastising the nations. Now he does penance and laments that he had spoken rashly. He asks forgiveness so that he may obtain mercy, because he acted in ignorance.

Hence David also says: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Psalm 24:7).

Some think that the prayer is the prophet’s prayer that, at the coming of Christ, human error may be removed. Hence the prophet’s name is prefixed in the title: he prays in the prophetic Spirit that darkness may be taken away and light restored, that the image may be removed and the truth granted.

That this is prophecy is shown by the entire text of the Canticle, and especially by the words: “You will be known in the midst of the two animals”; “When the years draw near, you will be known”; and, concerning judgment: “When my soul is troubled in anger, you will remember mercy.”

Again, concerning Christ’s coming: “God will come from Teman, and the Holy One from the shadowy and dense mountain.” And concerning the future: “The tents of the land of Midian will tremble; you will mount upon your horses, and you will stretch your bow—yes, you will stretch it over kingdoms.”

If someone asks why Theodotion alone translated it “for the voluntary,” we can say either that it refers to the prophet’s confession—that he sinned willingly, not under compulsion, by forming a wrong judgment about God’s judgment—or certainly that the future faith of the nations is being indicated: they will voluntarily abandon their former error and believe in the one promised in the Canticle.

We read in the sixteenth psalm: “A prayer of David.” Similarly in another psalm: “A prayer of David.” In the eighty-ninth: “A prayer of Moses, the man of God.” In the hundred and first: “A prayer of the poor person when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before the Lord.”

And wherever else the word “prayer” occurs, nowhere is it read together with “a song.”

I do not know whether it is fitting to pray with a song, unless perhaps, according to the Septuagint, we say that the prophet prays for Christ’s coming and prophesies this very thing with delight, with psalms and a song: so that, insofar as it is a prayer, he may entreat the Father; and insofar as it is a song, praise may be offered to the Father who sent the Son and to the Son who came.

So much for the title of the Canticle. Let us now see what is said in the Canticle.

### Chapter 3, verse 1

“Lord, I have heard your report, and I was afraid. Lord, revive your work in the midst of the years.”

The Septuagint: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid. Lord, ÷ I considered ** your works, ÷ and I was astonished **; you will be known in the midst of the two animals.”

For the phrase which we, Aquila, and Theodotion translated “revive it,” Symmachus translated “make it live again.”

The words “I considered” and “I was astonished,” which the Septuagint has, are found neither in the Hebrew nor in any other interpreter. Once these words—which are not found in Hebrew—are removed, the Septuagint text can be read as follows: “Lord, your works will be known in the midst of the two animals.” Because this seemed unintelligible, the preceding words were joined to it.

In Hebrew we read *ADONAI*, “Lord”; *PHALACH*, “your work”; *BACEREB*, “in the midst”; *SANIM*, “of the years”; *HEIEU*, “revive it.”

[Note: Martianus has *HEINU*. Hence he conjectures that Jerome read in his Hebrew exemplar [Hebrew], *hhaijennu*, with the third-person singular suffix. But our manuscripts prefer *HEIEU*, and the Hebrew reading agrees with this; it is by no means right to suppose that the Masoretes corrupted it. In Hebrew the form is [Hebrew]; but in the manuscripts of this Commentary we clearly read *HEINU* in the final word. It is therefore certain that Jerome read in his Hebrew exemplar [Hebrew], *hhaijennu*, with the third-person singular suffix, not with the other [Hebrew], *hu*, which the Masoretic exemplars retain today.]

This is mentioned so that we may clearly recognize what has been superfluously added in the Septuagint.

The Hebrews explain this passage historically as follows:

“Lord, I have heard your report, and I was afraid.” I have heard, he says, the punishments that you have prepared for Nebuchadnezzar and for the devil, in which you said to him: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his” (above, 2:6); and secondly: “Woe to him who gathers evil greed for his house” (verse 9); and thirdly: “Woe to him who builds a city with blood and prepares a town in iniquity” (verse 12); and fourthly: “Woe to him who gives his friend a drink, sending his gall and making him drunk”; and fifthly: “Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ and to a silent stone, ‘Rise!’”

Just as I have been terrified at the thought that the great dragon must be pierced by so many wounds, so I beseech you, Lord, to fulfill what you promised and, when the appointed time has ended, to send back your Christ. For you said that the vision still waits at a distance and will appear at the end and will not lie.

Therefore revive what you promised; that is, fulfill your promise. Let your word not die fruitless, but let it be completed in deed.

According to us, this can also be understood of the Savior’s resurrection: let the one who died for us rise from the dead and be made alive.

According to the Septuagint, however, the sense is very different, and we must also give the explanation of the Vulgate edition.

“Lord, I heard your word in the Scriptures, and, when you gave me an ear”—according to what Isaiah says: “He added an ear to me for hearing” (Isaiah 50:5)—I heard in the manner in which you wish your word to be heard.

And, having contemplated your works more carefully—so that it might not be said to me, “They do not regard the works of the Lord, and they do not consider the works of his hands”—I understood the Creator from the creatures. Through each thing that you made, and through the works you carry out daily throughout the universe, I was wholly astonished. Losing the ordinary human mode of perception, I was transformed into a holy madness.

Or certainly, shaken by wonder, I burst forth trembling into your praises, saying: “You will be known in the midst of the two animals.”

Many think that this refers to the Son and the Holy Spirit, since the Father is understood through the Son and the Spirit. They interpret the two seraphim in Isaiah (chapter 6) and the two cherubim written of in Exodus (chapter 25) in the same way. These face one another [variant: “may face one another, and have…”] and have the oracle between them.

In Isaiah, they veil the Lord’s head and feet; in the present age they fly, and each cries out to the other the mystery of the Trinity. One of the seraphim—whose name means “burning”—is sent and comes to earth to cleanse the prophet’s lips, saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it would burn!” (Luke 12:49).

Some hold this view and support it with many testimonies from Scripture.

The simple interpretation, and the opinion of the common people, understands the passage of the Savior: he was recognized as crucified between two robbers (Mark 15; John 19).

Those who interpret it more carefully say that the Savior was understood and believed in the first Church, which was gathered both from the circumcision and from the uncircumcision, with two peoples surrounding him on either side.

Some understand the two animals as the two Testaments, the New and the Old. They are truly living and vital, breathing beings, and the Lord is known in their midst.

### “In the midst of the years you will make it known.”

The Septuagint: “When the years draw near, you will be known.”

“When the time comes,” he says, “and you have fulfilled your promises in deed, you will show that what you promised is true. Or, when the consummation draws near and your Son comes in the final hour to destroy sins, you will be known more clearly.”

It follows:

When the time comes, you will be made manifest, when my soul has been disturbed. This reading, apart from the Septuagint, is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any of the other translators. Its meaning is this: when the time comes of which it is said, “At an acceptable time I heard you,” the time of the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ (II Cor. VI, 2), then, O God the Father, your name will be known, a name that was previously hidden from human beings, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Father, I have revealed your name to human beings” (John XVII, 6).

What follows, “when my soul has been disturbed,” is joined in the edition of the Septuagint translators to what comes afterward, so that it may be read: “When my soul has been disturbed in anger,” with the division ending there; thereafter, “you will remember mercy.” The prophet’s punishment, that is, is sufficiently represented by disturbance alone: when his soul has been disturbed at God’s anger, punishment is not added, but mercy excludes anger.

The anger of God also has its measures: how much, for how long, for what reasons, and upon whom it is inflicted, in accordance with what is written: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink with tears in measure” (Ps. LXXIX, 6). If the prophet is disturbed at God’s anger, and the one who has been disturbed obtains mercy, what ought we to hope for—or rather, what ought we to fear—we whose deeds in their entirety deserve God’s anger?

What follows according to the Hebrew is:

“When you are angry, you will remember mercy.” We must not suppose that God forgets and, after his anger, remembers his mercy; rather, while we are placed under punishment, we suppose that he has forgotten us, in accordance with: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever?” (Ps. XII, 1). And whenever we are covered, as though by waves, by temptations, and the swift storm of demons rages against us, we speak as though to one sleeping: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?” At the same time, observe God’s clemency: he did not say, “When you have inflicted punishments, you will remember mercy,” but, “When you are angry.” Now one who is angry sometimes does not strike, but merely threatens. The apostle also perceived this when he said: “For the anger of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings” (Rom. I, 18). Where it is revealed, it is not inflicted; it does not strike. It is revealed in order to terrify, and so that it may not be inflicted upon those who have been terrified.

### (Verse 3)

“God will come from the South, and the Holy One from Mount Pharan.” The Septuagint: “God will come from Theman, and the Holy One from a shadowy and densely wooded mountain.” *Diapsalma.* Aquila, Symmachus, and the fifth edition retained the Hebrew itself, *THEMAN* (תימן, *Theman*); only Theodotion interpreted what *Theman* meant, saying:

[Note: [Col. 1310D] This is how the manuscript codices read: in Hebrew it is *Eloah*, which Theodotion read as *Eloim*. [Col. 1311D] The manuscript of Sancygirannus retains “God from the South,” etc., and does not have the word *Eloim*. MART.—In Hebrew it is not *Eloim* (אלהים), but *Eloah* (אלוה). Therefore Drusius writes, in Theodotion also, ἐλωᾶ or ἐλοᾶ (*Eloah*). The manuscript of Sancygirannus, cited by Martianus, has “God,” with which Eusebius also agrees, ὁ θεός (*ho theos*).]

“*ELOIM*, he will come from the South, and the Holy One from Mount Pharan, at the end.”

From this we understand that “from a shadowy and densely wooded mountain” was added by the Septuagint alone. Likewise, where the Septuagint translated *diapsalma*, and we have rendered it “always,” Symmachus translated “forever,” Theodotion “at the end,” and the fifth edition retained the Hebrew itself, *SELA* (סֶלָה).

[Note: [Col. 1311D] The words “from midday” are absent from the Reginensis manuscript; a little later, from the same manuscript, we restore “the bridegroom drives away the north,” in place of the erroneous “hesitates” found in Martianus.]

Thus “God will come from the South,” that is, from midday, from bright light, and from those who are called “sons of days.” Hence also in the Song of Songs the bridegroom drives away the north and calls the south, saying: “Rise up, O North, and come, O South; blow through my garden, and let my spices flow” (Song IV, 16).

God is always in the south: “Where,” he says, “do you feed your flock? Where do you lie down? At midday” (ibid., I, 6). And when Abraham was beneath the oak, God came to him only at midday (Gen. XVIII and XLIII). Joseph also, who preceded as a type of the Savior, prepares a banquet for his brothers at midday. Thus knowledge of God the Father comes to those who are worthy in full light. And knowledge of the Holy One, that is, of the Son of God, comes from a shadowy and densely wooded mountain.

A shadowy and densely wooded mountain may be understood either as the Father himself, full of virtues and every kind of wisdom, protecting all things with his majesty, spreading out his wings, and cherishing his young; or certainly as paradise and the heavenly places, full of angels, full of virtues, and full of exceedingly fruitful trees.

Would that it might also happen to me that, at my voice and exposition, God would come in clear light, and that his Son, concerning whom it is written, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. XX, 26), would come from the sublimity of speech that is shadowy and densely wooded, woven together with testimonies of Scripture here and there; and that, with the Father and Son coming together, the one who hears them might become their dwelling place, and the Scripture be fulfilled that says: “I and my Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

But since, in place of “shadowy and densely wooded mountain,” the Hebrew has “Mount Pharan,” and *Pharan* is interpreted as “the mouth of the seer,” in accordance with our interpretation it is beautifully said that knowledge of the Son comes from the speech of an educated man—not from just any speech, but from speech full of light, full of eyes, so that it may be conveyed manifestly and purely to the ears of its hearers. When he says “from the mountain,” understand lofty doctrines.

I heard a Hebrew explain this passage as follows: Bethlehem lies toward the South, and in it the Lord and Savior was born; it is itself the place meant by the present statement, “The Lord will come from the South,” that is, “He will be born in Bethlehem and will arise from there.” And because the one who was born in Bethlehem once gave the Law on Mount Sinai, he is the Holy One who comes from Mount Pharan; for Pharan is near Mount Sinai.

What follows, *diapsalma*, that is, “always,” has this meaning: the one who was born in Bethlehem and who gave the Law at Sinai—that is, at Mount Pharan—is always the author and giver of every benefit, past, present, and future.

Concerning the *diapsalma*, which is called *SELA* in Hebrew, the matter has been discussed more fully in the Psalter.

[Note: Jerome cites this passage in his letter to Marcella, where he discussed the word *Sela*, or the *diapsalma* of the Psalms, at greater length. Let the reader therefore beware the error of those who suppose that Jerome published complete commentaries on the Psalter, since it is established from Jerome himself—as we have often observed—that he published no such volume on all the Psalms of David. MART.—From several statements of his we gather that, when Paula, Eustochium, and Marcella were together at Rome, Jerome read the Psalter aloud to those holy women and subsequently explained it; this has also been noted in the general preface. At times he also explained in letters certain passages that seemed more obscure. Such is the letter to Marcella cited here, number XXVIII in our recension, concerning the *diapsalma*. It is therefore not necessary to suppose that Jerome expounded the entire Psalter in complete commentaries.]

At the same time, observe that, according to the Septuagint, *diapsalma* is used nowhere except in the Psalter and in the present passage. From this we understand that the Septuagint correctly prefixed “A Song” to the prayer.

### (Verse 4)

“His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. His brightness will be like light; horns are in his hands. There his strength is hidden.”

The Septuagint: “His power covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise, and his brightness will be like light; horns are in his hands, and he established the strong love of his power.”

For what the Septuagint translated, “and he established the strong love of his power,” we said, “there his strength is hidden.” Aquila translated, “and he established the hiding-place of his strength”; Symmachus, “and he established his hidden strength”; only Theodotion, agreeing with our translation, says, “and there is the hiding-place of his strength.”

The word *SAM* (שם), according to the character of the passage, is understood either as “he established” or as “there.” In the present passage, “there” should be read rather than “he established,” so that the meaning and order of the sentence are: “Horns are in his hands,” with “there” understood—that is, in the horns—“his strength is hidden.”

It is clear according to the Hebrew that, at Christ’s coming, everything was filled with glory, in accordance with what is said in the Gospel: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14). And elsewhere: “He made peace in the heavens and on earth through the blood of the cross, and he sat at the right hand of Majesty”; for his word runs swiftly. And elsewhere: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” (Ps. CXLVII, 1). Again, in the eighteenth Psalm: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” [or: “to the boundaries of the earth”] (Ps. XVIII, 5).

His brightness, like the sun of righteousness, also shone out in clear light; and the horns in his hands are the standards and trophies of the cross, and in those horns his strength was hidden. For although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II, 6 ff.).

On the cross, therefore, his strength was hidden for a little while, when he said to the Father: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38, 39), and: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Luke XXIII, 13). And on the cross itself: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”

According to the Septuagint, in the statement “His power covered the heavens,” we must understand that what is covered is lesser than that which covers—provided that what is covered is covered entirely and not merely in part. Therefore, since God’s power covers the heavens, his power is greater than the heavens that are covered by it.

We frequently read that the heavens are those who bear the image of the heavenly one and proclaim the glory of God. The apostle also proves that the power of God is the Lord and Savior: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 30).

This power is, as it were, the mother of all particular [or: spiritual] virtues. For example, he is called power, wisdom, strength, righteousness, temperance, truth, holiness, and redemption. “Christ,” however, “became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.”

These particular virtues, in which Christ is revealed according to the progress of those who receive him either as wisdom, or as strength, or as righteousness, and so forth, are contained in the general power of God, that is, in the Lord and Savior.

In the same way we understand the reference to the earth: those who were first called “earth” because they bore the image of the earthly one, and to whom it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. III, 19), are filled with the praise of the Lord at the Savior’s coming.

When the heavens have also been covered by God’s power—that is, protected and clothed on every side—and the whole earth has been filled with God’s praise, then his brightness will be like light.

The apostle does not conceal that the image of God and the brightness of his glory is God the Savior: “After the brightness of God’s glory appeared to us, he returned to his former majesty” (Heb. I). For although we knew Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him according to the flesh (II Cor. V, 16), but according to the spirit, because “what was made in him was life, and the life was the light of human beings” (John I, 3, 4).

The Savior also makes this clearer in the Gospel when he says: “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII, 5), so that after his ascension into heaven his brightness may be like light—that is, so that the Son may begin to be what the Father is.

As for what follows, “Horns are in his hands,” it is customary in Scripture always to use “horns” for kingdoms. Thus what Hannah says in the First Book of Kingdoms, “He exalted the horn of his Christ” (I Reg. II, 10), signifies the magnificence of the Savior’s kingdom. And in Daniel, the ten horns signify ten kingdoms (Dan. VII).

Thus it is now said, “Horns are in his hands,” just as elsewhere we read: “The heart of a king is in the hand of God” (Prov. XXI, 1). This means that the mind and governing principle of the heart of the holy man—who advances toward the kingdoms of heaven and, while still placed on earth, rules his body without sins—does not wander outwardly, but is situated under God’s protection.

Since neither the Hebrew nor the other editions have “horns are in his hands,” but “in his hand,” represented by the word *JADO* (ידו), let us understand the hand of God, strong and powerful, as his Son. Let us also say that all the kingdoms of heaven, and all those who strive to ascend to heaven, have been placed in this hand.

Isaiah likewise proclaims this when he says: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, in a fertile place” (Isa. V, 1), meaning “in a kingdom.”

For this reason, I think, no horned animal is listed among the unclean animals in Leviticus; and the same meaning is signified by the unicorn in the Psalms (XLIX and XCI), or *ῥινοκέρως* (*rhinokeros*); and by the statement: “Through you we will gore down our enemies with the horn” (Ps. XLIII, 7).

According to the Septuagint, we read: “And he established the love of his strong power.” This too must be understood of Christ: God the Father covered the heavens with his power, filled the earth with praise, made his brightness like light, and placed the kingdom in the hand of his Son in order to make his beloved loved by human beings—not lightly, but intensely and strongly—so that those who had loved him strongly and clung to his love might be taken from his hand by no one.

The devil, by contrast, makes us love the world and, in place of love of virtue, love vices—not lightly, but strongly, so that it may be said of us: “The devil established a strong love of his vices.”

### (Verse 5)

“Before his face death will go, and the devil will come forth before his feet.”

The Septuagint: “Before his face the word will go, and he will go forth into the plain after his feet.”

In place of the “death” that we translated, the Hebrew has three letters—DALETH, BETH, RES—without any vowel. If they are read *DABAR* (דבר), they signify “word”; if *DEBER* (דבר), “pestilence,” which is called λοιμός (*loimos*) in Greek.

Accordingly, Aquila also translated: “Before his face pestilence will go”; Symmachus: “Before his face death will precede”; the fifth edition: “Before his face death will walk.” Only the Septuagint and Theodotion translated the word as “word” rather than “death.”

Likewise, in the following verse, where we said, “The devil will come forth before his feet,” and the Septuagint translated differently—we shall discuss this later—Aquila translated “devil” as “flying creature”; Symmachus, Theodotion, and the fifth edition translated it as “winged creature,” which in Hebrew is called *RESEPH* (רשף).

[Note: In place of the fifth edition, the manuscript of Regina calls it the sixth.]

The Hebrews relate that just as in the Gospel the prince of demons is called Beelzebub (Matt. XII), so *Reseph* is the name of a demon who holds authority among the others and, because of his extreme speed and movement in different directions, is called a bird and a flying creature. They say that he is the one who spoke to the woman in paradise under the figure of a serpent and, because of the curse by which he was condemned by God, received this name; for *Reseph* is interpreted as “crawling on the belly.”

This, then, is what is meant: as soon as the Lord comes and is baptized in the Jordan, and the Father’s voice thunders at the descent of the dove—“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17)—the devil will meet him as he comes out of the waters. Death will stand before his feet, and the ancient serpent who tempted him for forty days in the desert.

But if, according to the Septuagint, we read, “Before his face the word will go, and he will come forth into the fields after his feet,” this signifies that the word of God precedes and prepares the hearts of believers before his visitation, which is now allegorically called his “face,” so that it may make crooked things straight and uneven things level, and so that the soul of the hearer, like a field that has been cut and prepared, may receive spiritual seed.

### (Verse 6)

“He stood and measured the earth; he looked, and dissolved the nations; the mountains of the age were crushed; the hills of the world bowed down before the paths of his eternity.”

The Septuagint: “He stood, and the earth was shaken; he looked [or: looked back], and the nations melted away; the mountains were crushed by violence; the hills of the age melted along the path of his everlastingness.”

The Savior stood, surveying everything and measuring the universe of the world with his eye, and dispersed the multitude of the nations. Once they had been dispersed and dissolved, the mountains of this age were crushed and the hills of this world bowed down.

There are also other mountains and hills, over which the bridegroom leaps and bounds in the Song of Songs (chap. 2). Concerning these the Psalm of Ascents also says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come” (Ps. CXX, 1).

The mountains of the age are the same as the dark mountains, concerning which Jeremiah commanded that our feet should not stumble over them (Jer. XXXI). These are the hills over which Saul ruled when he killed the priests of God (I Reg. XXII); for *Gabaa* is interpreted as “hill.”

He aptly says, “The hills of the world bowed down.” Before the Savior’s coming they walked with their necks erect, and no one could humble their pride. They were crushed and bowed down by the paths of his eternity, that is, of God, because his eternity deigned to come to us; or because from the beginning of the world until his incarnation he always came to the saints, became the word of God in the hand of each one, and conquered in all who overcame, bending his eternal path and crushing the hills and mountains.

Let this be understood metaphorically according to the Hebrew. According to the Septuagint, after the word has preceded the face of God and gone forth onto level ground, God the Father comes to the place where a region has been prepared for him by his word,[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “where a region has been prepared for him by his word,” etc.] and he comes after the feet of his word and stands—never preceding, but always waiting for it to prepare the way for him.

When he has stood beside the feet of his word, then immediately the earth—that is, the works of flesh and bodies, unable to endure God’s presence—is shaken. Once it has been shaken, the power of the word and the presence of God look upon all the nations of souls.[Note: Victorius restored “of souls” (*animarum*) from Florentine manuscripts; then, collating other witnesses, he read “many and diverse opinions.”]

By the nations of the soul we can understand the thoughts and the many opinions directed in different ways, which immediately dissolve and melt away. If anything on earth had raised itself against the knowledge of God and occupied the mind of the hearer, then, when the word precedes and God comes, it will be broken and crushed.[Note: Martianus read “and the coming and of God”; Victorius preferred “it is broken and crushed.”]

When the mountains have been broken and crushed at God’s appearance, the hills will plainly be consumed and reduced to nothing. They are not God’s mountains, but the mountains of the age. The everlasting path of God, looking toward those things that his word precedes, will consume and destroy them; the remaining phrase, *et fortius collibus saeculi*, is materially uncertain.[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads “looking toward those things which his word [precedes],” etc.; Victorius read “and those things in the hills” in place of “more strongly [than] the hills.”]

The mountains may also be understood as demons who operate among heretics and exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. The hills may likewise be understood as other demonic powers, which cause people to admire bodily beauty, dignities, riches, nobility of birth, and the other goods of the world.

One can see, after the coming of God’s word and the presence of God the Father, how human souls are shaken, how everything earthly is dissolved, and how former thoughts are reduced to nothing. Then demons are destroyed; then the heights of the age are brought to nothing; and all the learning of heretics, which had first swelled up, is humbled, crushed, and consumed at the coming of God’s word.[Note: Our manuscripts emend this after Victorius. Martianus retained the senseless reading, “and all heretics, whose learning …”; lesser points are corrected below.]

What previously seemed beautiful and great is cast away as contemptible and small. This happens because of God’s coming and Christ’s dwelling among us, in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Lev. XXVI, 12).

### (Verse 7)

“Because of iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia; the skins of the land of Madian will be disturbed.”

The Septuagint: “Because of labors I saw the tents of the Ethiopians; the tents of the land of Madian will tremble.”

The Ethiopians—dark [or: very dark], lovers of darkness, and alienated from every light, who feed on the flesh of the dragon, concerning which it is written, “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Ps. LXXIII, 14)—are understood as demons. Their dwelling becomes anyone who has labored in this world for honors and riches; this is significantly indicated by the single word “iniquity”: “For every rich person is either unjust or the heir of an unjust person.”

Observe people crossing seas, keeping watch before the doors of the powerful, enduring everything that the condition of slaves can scarcely endure, in order to amass riches and obtain some position of honor. After they have achieved this, they surrender themselves to luxury, pleasures, and every kind of iniquity, so that what greed gathered, luxury may consume.

These people, then, because of their labors, become a lodging-place of demons; and those who ought to have been the temple of God become the tent of the Ethiopians.

Likewise, when it follows, “The skins of the land of Madian will be disturbed,” or “the tents of the land of Madian will tremble,” understand the same tents as both the tents of the Ethiopians and the tents of the land of Madian.

After they have become rich and climbed to the highest rank by lawful and unlawful means, then their conscience of their sins will always fear death and judgment. At the slightest fever they will sigh over eternal punishments like prisoners—or robbers—in a jail.

*Madian* in our language sounds like “from judgment,” that is, condemnation. This shows that they are always in fear of judgment and eternal punishments, and that they endure with daily dread the torments they feel themselves [or: know themselves] to deserve.

### (Verses 8–9)

“Are you angry, O Lord, with the rivers, or is your wrath against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea? For you mounted [or: you who mounted] your horses, and your chariots are salvation. You will surely rouse your bow; the oaths sworn to the tribes that you spoke. Always.”

The Septuagint: “Are you angry, O Lord, with the rivers, or is your wrath against the rivers, or your onrush against the sea? He who [or: because he] mounted your horses, and your riding is salvation; drawing and stretching your bow over scepters, says the Lord. *Diapsalma.*”

Where the Septuagint has *diapsalma*, Aquila has “always”; the others translated it similarly to the versions given above. Since the discussion hastens toward the tropological interpretation, I shall briefly grasp the literal meaning of the passage and proceed to what follows.

Just as you dried up the Jordan and the Red Sea while fighting for us—for you were not angry with rivers and the sea, nor could insensible things incur any offense—so now, mounting your chariots and taking up your bow, you will give salvation to your people and fulfill forever the oaths that you swore to our fathers and tribes.

When it says, “Are you angry, O Lord, with the rivers, or is your wrath against the rivers, or your onrush against the sea?” it speaks ambiguously, more in the language of one asking a question than of one making an assertion.

There are good rivers and bad rivers. There is a very bad sea, and there is an excellent sea.

An example of good rivers is: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 4). And: “Whoever drinks of the water of the Lord, rivers of living water will flow from his belly into eternal life” (John IV).

An example of bad rivers is what Pharaoh says in Ezekiel: “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezek. XXIX, 9), in which the dragon dwells, along with many similar passages.

That the sea may also be understood in a favorable sense is shown by the twenty-third Psalm, in which the Church is discussed tropologically under οἰκουμένη (*oikoumene*), that is, “the inhabited world”:[Note: Victorius reads more aptly, “it is called ἡ οἰκουμένη,” that is, “the inhabited world.”] “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it. He founded it upon the sea and prepared it upon the rivers,” that is, the world. Since it is founded by the Lord upon rivers and prepared upon the sea, it is certainly understood in a favorable sense.

Likewise, in the passage about the vine that was transplanted from Egypt: “You stretched out its branches to the sea, and its shoots to the rivers” (Ps. LXXIX, 12), I think that “to the sea” can be understood in a favorable sense.

We say that the divine words that are clearer and offer drink, as it were, to the thirsty are called “rivers”; but those that are full of mysteries and placed in the deep—concerning which the apostle says, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. XI, 33), and the prophet agrees, “From the depths I cried to you, O Lord” (Ps. CXXIX)—are called “the sea” in Scripture.

This concerns the possibility that the sea may be understood in the better sense. There are many testimonies, however, that it is also understood in the opposite sense, including this passage in the Psalms: “This sea is great and spacious; there ships will pass, small animals with great ones. This dragon whom you formed to mock it” (Ps. CIII, 25, 26).

The same is shown in the Gospel, when the Savior rebuked the winds and the sea and said to it: “Be silent and be still” (Mark IV, 39). What is rebuked is evil, in accordance with Zechariah: “May the Lord rebuke you, devil” (Zech. III, 2), and with what is said to Timothy: “Reprove, console, and rebuke” (II Tim. IV, 2).

Therefore, when the prophet asks: “Are you angry, O Lord, with the rivers, or is your wrath against the rivers, or your onrush against the sea?” let us say this: if they are the rivers of Egypt and the Red Sea, red with blood, the Lord is angry with them and strikes them, and in his full onrush he rushes against the whirlpools that raise themselves against the knowledge of God.

Hence “the sea saw and fled” (Ps. CXIII), unable to endure God’s presence. And the Jordan turned backward, yielding to the glory of the people who were crossing, and it was divided both by Elijah and by Elisha.

To speak more plainly, understand as rivers the eloquence of heretics that flows against the truth and the Church; against these the Lord is angry. As the sea, understand the souls of those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, who are always tossed about by wickedness and overwhelmed by salty whirlpools.[Note: Martianus here too retained the erroneous *falsis* (“false”) for *salsis* (“salty”).] The Lord’s onrush comes upon this sea, so that it may feel his coming, know by what boundaries and barrier it is enclosed, and hear: “In you your waves will be crushed.”

If, however, the rivers are good and the sea is good, Jesus is washed in them and establishes his Church upon such a sea.

After this follows: “He who mounted his horses, and his riding is salvation.”

I ask what horses the Lord mounts, and I think there are none other than the souls of the saints, upon whom the divine word mounts, so that it may save both them and others through them.

Let us provide examples of horses. The bridegroom speaks in the Song of Songs: “To my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots I have compared you, my companion” (Song I, 8). This does not mean that Christ compares the Church, or that the word of God compares the soul whom he calls his bride, to Pharaoh’s chariots; rather, every soul, however holy and perfect it may be, is, when compared with God, like Pharaoh’s chariot and beast of burden.

Thus Moses also says to the Lord: “But I am ἄλογος (*alogos*), that is, irrational” (Exod. IV, 10). And David: “I became like a beast of burden before you” (Ps. LXXII, 23).

This does not mean that he is simply a beast of burden, but that before God he is a beast of burden.

Opposed to these horses are those possessed by Pharaoh, concerning which it is said: “Horse and rider he cast into the sea” (Exod. XV, 2). Such riding is not salvation, but destruction.

Let us seek other horses upon which the Lord mounts. In the Fourth Book of Kingdoms we read that Elisha’s servant rose early, went out, and saw an army surrounding the city walls, with horses and chariots (IV Reg. VI). After the prophet prayed and the servant’s eyes were opened, “he looked,” it says, “and behold, the mountain was full of horses and fiery chariots around Elisha.”

Pay close attention: horses and chariots are seen, yet among so many thousands of horses and chariots there is no rider. Their charioteer and ruler was the one of whom the Psalmist sings: “You who sit upon the cherubim, show yourself” (Ps. LXXIX, 2).

By such horses and such a chariot Elijah too was carried up into heaven (IV Reg. II).

If anyone wishes to learn from Zechariah who the red horses are, who the black, the dappled, and the white horses are, coming out from among the myrtles and from the mountains situated in the deep—or, as it is written in the Septuagint, from the mountains of bronze—we shall attempt to explain this in that prophet, if the Lord grants us length of life (Zech. I).

John also saw white horses and their riders (Rev. VI). I think that the horses are the bodies of those who will rise in glory, while the riders are the souls of the saints.

But if someone is a sinner and like me, he will sit upon a black horse, and it will be said of him: “All who mounted horses slumbered” (Ps. LXXV, 7).

Of such horses it is written: “The horse is deceitful for salvation” (Ps. XXXII, 14), for the flesh desires against the spirit, and its wisdom is hostile to God.

Let this be said about those who love their bodies and sit upon black horses. Let us instead prepare our souls as horses and chariots of the Lord, who mounted in Paul, mounted in Peter, and, riding in such chariots, traversed the entire world.

He also stretched his bow—or his arrows—against scepters, that is, against kingdoms, for which Jeremiah was sent, and uprooted, destroyed, and ruined them (Jer. XVIII). He made it so that sin would not reign in our mortal body.

By “scepters,” that is, “the kingdoms of the devil,” understand various sins: avarice, luxury, anger, slander, thefts, perjuries, and the rest. Against these the word of God, seated upon its horses and in its chariots, directs the twisted darts of his radiance.

[Note: Victorius preferred *fulguris* (“of lightning”), based on seven manuscripts from Florence.]

For the moment it does not release them, so that the one terrified by the drawn bow does not experience the discharge of the arrows. This is what it does “always,” as Aquila translated in place of *diapsalma*. For it always sits in his saints; it is always armed. Preparing sharp arrows in their tongues, it rides and moves here and there for the salvation of the world.

### (Verse 10)

**“You will cleave the rivers of the earth.”** The Septuagint: **“The earth will be cleft by rivers.”**

Because the Lord has raised up his bow in order to fulfill for the tribes the oaths that he spoke, it is consequently said: “You will cleave the rivers of the earth”—that is, you will divide and scatter the kings of the earth who fight against your people [Col. 1320A]. According to the Septuagint, however, which reads, “The earth will be cleft by rivers,” let us first set forth an example, so that by this as a kind of step we may ascend to higher things.

We read in the works of those who composed volumes on marvels and brought the Olympiads of Greece down to our own memory, explaining what new event occurred in the world in each individual year, that among other things rivers burst forth through earthquakes which had not existed before, while others in turn were swallowed up and perished. Evidently all the veins of the earth contain hidden waters within them, just as the human body contains blood; these waters are ruptured by the shaking of the earth and flow out into rivers.

If we understand this, let us see that the human soul naturally possesses waters and rivers within itself, but that through our negligence they are hidden and do not flow. When, however, it has been shaken by the preaching of the word of God and moved from its former condition, then what lay hidden bursts forth and flows out for the refreshment of those who drink [Al. *of the powerful*] [Col. 1320B].

I think that this also is signified by the wells dug by Isaac’s servants in Genesis, wells which the Philistines had filled with earth after Abraham had made them (Gen. XXVI). As long as Abraham lives, his wells are not closed; but when he dies and the wells are stopped up, if the servants dig, the Philistines resist and there is strife. If Isaac himself comes, however, digs the well, and finds water, the Philistines are unable to resist. Look at Peter and Paul, and you will have no doubt about the wells and rivers of Christ. Behold all the apostles, and you will understand that not four rivers but twelve rivers [Col. 1320C] issue from the paradise of the Scriptures.

Before the earth was shaken, these rivers lay hidden; although they were in the veins of the earth, they did not offer cups to the thirsty. But after, at the coming of Christ, the world and the whole earth had been shaken, they suddenly burst forth, and then this was fulfilled:

> “He made rivers in the desert,  
> and outlets of waters in a thirsty land,  
> a fruitful land into salt because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it”  
> (Ps. XXXIII).

And:

> “He made the desert into pools of water,  
> and a waterless land into springs of water;  
> and he made the hungry dwell there,  
> and they established a city for dwelling.”

For after the Lord came into the world, and what he said in the Gospel had been fulfilled—“For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX, 39)—then the land of Israel, from which rivers had formerly flowed and watered the whole Jewish people, dried up, and its springs were stopped. But the whole world, which had been desert and barren and did not possess the waters of the Lord’s preaching, was turned into pools of water; and as many teachers as it brought forth, so many springs did it possess. Nor is it enough for these springs and rivers to irrigate the peoples of the world; rather, in every province they gather those who hunger and suffer famine for the word of God into one people and build the Church, which is called a city for dwelling, and which the rushing of the river makes glad [Col. 1320D]. [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads, “Nor did it suffice for them, springs and rivers, etc.,” omitting *namely*.]

[Col. 1321A] **(Verses 11 and following.)** “They saw you, and the mountains were in pain; the torrent of waters passed by; the abyss gave its voice; the height lifted up its hands. The sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place; at the light of your arrows they will go, at the brightness of your flashing spear. In indignation you will trample the earth; in wrath you will stupefy the nations. You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ. You struck the head from the house of the wicked; you laid bare the foundation up to the neck. Selah.”

We have set down only our own edition, so that, following it—that is, following the Hebrew—we may weave together the continuity of the passage, and afterward discuss the Septuagint section by section.

“They saw you, O God, and the mountains were in pain”: that is, lofty kingdoms, the exalted powers of this age, and the four chariots in Zechariah that go forth from the bronze mountains (Zech. VI)—these saw you and trembled [Col. 1321B]. “And the torrent of waters passed by”: that is, all their violence and the persecution with which they harassed your people passed away after they saw you.

Then the abyss—that is, the underworld—praised you. Then also those above, namely the angels, clapped their hands in applause, so that by the gesture of their raised hands and a kind of dance they might display you as victor.

Your sun and moon, and all the splendor by which you had formerly illumined your people, but which afterward had been covered in the horror of darkness under the weight of evils, received their light again and regained their former brilliance. Your arrows and your flashing spear—that is, your scourges and your instruction—gave light to your people. Finally, in the light of your arrows and in the brilliance of your spear, which corrected them for this purpose [Col. 1321C], so that it might reform them, your people walked in your indignation.

Therefore, when you avenge the wrongs done to your people, you will trample earthly kingdoms and make all the nations marvel, because you went forth for the salvation of your people and came to them with your Christ. Although in Hebrew it is written, “You went forth for the salvation of your people with Jesus Christ, your Christ”—or, “with Christ, your Savior”—for Jesus is interpreted as “Savior.”

When Jesus Christ, your Son, came, you struck Antichrist from the house of the wicked, that is, from this age, which lies in the evil one. Or you struck the devil himself, who is the head of wickedness, and laid bare his foundation up to the neck—that is, you revealed what he had hidden, not for a brief time but forever. For this is what *Selah* means: “always” [Col. 1321D].

**The Septuagint:** [Note: [Col. 1321D] Our manuscripts supply the preceding words, “They will see you.”] “They will see you, and the peoples will grieve or travail”; for **ὠδινήσουσι** (*ōdinēsousi*) signifies both things. Consequently, when the earth has been ruptured and the rivers are flowing, the peoples who have drunk from the rivers of God will see God and will travail.

For by the very fact that they see God, they immediately conceive through the word of God and say:

> “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived in the womb,  
> and we travailed and gave birth;  
> we made the spirit of your salvation”  
> (Isa. XXVI, 17–18). [Note: Victorinus restores, from the Hebrew, the Vulgate, and Jerome’s own reading in his Commentary on Isaiah, “we shall make.” His claim that the Greek ὃ ἐποίησας (“which you made”) is read in a small number of copies rests on only one or two manuscripts; most, and the better ones, read ὃ ἐποιήσαμεν (“which we made”).]

[Col. 1322A] “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. V, 8). These peoples, therefore, washed by the rivers, have not yet seen God but will see him; and when they see him, they will conceive, so that they may bring forth the fruits of teachings.

But since the peoples are said to see, and it is not proper for peoples to see the face of God, although the statement is extended into the future—“they will see and give birth”—nevertheless, according to the tropological interpretation, the Hebrew should rather be followed, where it says: “They saw you, and the mountains gave birth.” For it belongs to the mountains to see God and give birth to children whom they have conceived from the word of God [Col. 1322B].

**The Septuagint:** [Note: [Col. 1322D] Here and below, in the Commentary, the Reginensis manuscript uses *disperdendi* (“scattering”) instead of *dispergendi* (“dispersing”); the Greek has **σκορπίζων**, “dispersing.”] “Disperse the waters of the way.”

There are different waters: some eternal, others brief. Of the eternal waters, those which flow from the springs of Israel, it was said: “The earth will be cleft by rivers.” Of the sudden waters that run for a time: “All the torrents go into the sea.” For the end of such waters is destruction.

Therefore God will disperse all the waters that have been trampled by perverse doctrines, when he has scattered the counsels of rulers and the wisdom of this world. If you ever see some heresy flourishing briefly and afterward dispersed by the grace of God, say that this has been fulfilled: “You will disperse the waters of the way” [652].

The word “way” may also be understood as “the devil’s way,” so that the sense is: The waters which the devil has trampled, and which have provided a way for many—that is, which have opened themselves to many errors—the Lord will divide and disperse.

Hence the other translators, wishing to describe heretical fury, rendered the passage: “The trampling, or rush, of the waters will pass by.” For they are carried headlong along the downward course of eloquence and rush precipitously, so that they may drag along with them anyone they find standing in their way and easily persuaded [Col. 1322C].

**The Septuagint:** “The abyss gave its voice, the height of its phantasy.” [Note: [Col. 1322D] The Reginensis manuscript adds *suae*, “of itself,” which is more faithful to the Greek **φαντασίας αὐτῆς**, “of its phantasy.”]

The abyss is often understood in a good sense, often in a bad sense, and sometimes indifferently. In a good sense:

> “Your judgments are a great abyss”  
> (Ps. XXXV, 7),

and:

> “Abyss calls to abyss”  
> (Ps. XLI, 8),

and what follows.

In a bad sense:

> “The waters saw you, O God”  
> (Ps. LXXVI, 17),

and what follows. The demons also plead not to be sent into the abyss (Luke VIII). In Genesis, however—“The abyss over which there was darkness” (Gen. I, 2)—I do not know whether it can be taken in a good sense.

It is used indifferently in the passage:

> “The springs of the abyss were broken open,  
> and the cataracts of heaven were opened”  
> (Gen. VII, 11).

And in the one hundred forty-eighth Psalm:

> “Dragons and all abysses;  
> fire and hail and stormy wind.”

Unless, perhaps, because it is placed among dragons, fire, and hail, it should be taken in a bad sense. I do not know whether one who has seen it clapping hands in praise of the Lord along with the others could say this.

If, then, we take “the abyss” in a good sense, let us say that, after the waters of the worst way [Al. *worst waters*] had been dispersed, your wise men saw you and, borrowing from your appearance the height of knowledge [Col. 1323A] that they possessed—for “they saw you and the mountains gave birth”—they brought forth in praises of their voice whatever they had previously thought about you.

And beautifully he calls the phantasy of opinion “height,” in accordance with Jesus son of Sirach, who says:

> “The abyss and wisdom—who will investigate them?”  
> (Ecclus. I, 2).

Hence, from the small mountain (Ps. XLI)—that is, from the assumption of a human body, which Daniel calls a stone cut from the mountain without hands, that is, without marital activity (Dan. II)—Christ, the abyss, calls upon the Father, another abyss, in the voice of his cataracts (Ps. XLI), so that he may give the evangelizers the word with great power.

Or certainly, the abyss of the New Testament, in testimony to the small mountain from which the prince of Tyre was wounded, calls upon the abyss of the Old Testament, so that through the cataracts of Christ—that is, through the apostles—the preaching may become stronger [Col. 1323B].

If anyone wishes to take the statement “The abyss gave its voice, the height of its phantasy” (Isa. XIV) in a bad sense, he will use the argument that, since the waters of the way—which are plainly understood in a bad sense—have been dispersed, this statement too should rightly be understood in the opposite sense.

At the same time observe that he did not say “its height,” but “the height of its phantasy,” that is, of its shadow and image. They seem to possess height and knowledge of the Scriptures; but all their height, compared with the truth, is phantasy, and they raise their voice in vain because the waters of the way have already been dispersed.

Let us search the Scriptures to see whether we can find *phantasy* anywhere in a good sense. Since it has been found rarely or never, we shall interpret the abyss and its phantasy more firmly in a bad sense [Col. 1323C].

**The Septuagint:** “The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order.”

If we follow a simple interpretation, the present words demonstrate the advancement of the sun and moon: according to Isaiah, in the future age the sun will shine sevenfold, and the moon will shine with the brightness of the sun (Isa. XXX, 26).

Because creation will be freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. VIII)—creation which is now subjected to vanity because of him who subjected it in hope of freedom—when, at the consummation of the world, all creation has been liberated, the sun and moon will also be liberated and will stand in their proper order.

But if we wish to understand Christ as the sun of righteousness, in whose wings there is healing, and the Church as the moon, which is illuminated by the splendor of this sun, it is not difficult to say that the true light, the light of human beings, the splendor of God’s glory, and the splendor of eternal light illumines her.
