At present, in this age, she grows and diminishes according to prosperity and oppression [Col. 1323D].

But when the sun has been raised up, and, according to the Apostle, God has exalted him and given him a name above every name (Phil. II), then the Church also, which in the present age cannot maintain her proper order, will return to the order that is due to her and will no longer be changed. Rather, standing firm in her fixed station [Col. 1324A], she will hear with Moses: “But stand here with me” (Exod. XXXIV, 2).

**The Septuagint:** “In the light of your darts they will go, in the brightness of the flashing of your weapons.” [Al. *in the brightness*]

The darts of God—that is, the arrows that go and advance—are not sent in order to destroy but in order to illumine. To distinguish these arrows and darts, Christ is called by Isaiah an elect dart, crying out:

> “He made me an elect dart,  
> and he hid me in his quiver;  
> and he said to me:  
> ‘It is a great thing for you to be called my servant’”  
> (Isa. XLIX, 2–3).

This arrow will have many arrows to send throughout the whole world. Hence the bride, wounded by the elect dart, says:

> “I am wounded by love”  
> (Song IV, 9).

In accordance with this, we too can say: “I am wounded by chastity; I am wounded by wisdom.” [Note: Here too the Reginensis manuscript prefers *by love*; shortly afterward, on its authority, the text was corrected to “in the true Solomon.” Victorinus reads “in the word of Solomon,” not inappropriately; Martianay incorrectly reads “in the man Solomon.”] Wounded by this dart of wisdom, the Queen of the South [Col. 1324B] was no longer herself, and, astonished, she found more in the true Solomon than fame had reported to her (III Kings X).

These arrows, then, which are sent into the light, also proceed in the brightness of the flashing of his weapons—that is, of God. For whoever has been armed so as to stand against the wiles of the devil, and girded with the Apostle’s armor (Eph. VI), will be approached by the darts of light, so that it may be said to him: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14).

But if someone is a sinner and groans that he dwells in the tents of Kedar, the sharp arrows of the Mighty One are sent to him, together with consuming coals (Ps. CXIX), so that he may first be pierced by the words of God and say:

> “I have been turned in misery,  
> while a thorn is driven into me”  
> (Ps. XXXI).

And after he has been pierced, then a consuming coal is sent to him through the Seraphim—that is, through the burning word of God—which will burn not only his lips, of which Isaiah alone had said that they were unclean (Isa. VI), but all the parts of his limbs as well, and reduce him to the solitude of sins [Col. 1324C].

**The Septuagint:** “In threatening you will diminish the earth, and in wrath you will bring down the nations.”

This may be understood as referring to the consummation of the world, when, after the multitude has been killed in frequent wars, few human beings will be found, and those who did not wish to belong to the people of God but remained nations and Gentiles will, in the Lord’s wrath, be led down to Tartarus.

But it is better to interpret the earth diminished by threatening as earthly works, and to understand by those who are established in the Church sinners who do not wait to be chastised by the Lord’s wrath. Rather, when they hear in the Scriptures what punishments await sinners, they do penance and gradually diminish their earth and advance toward heaven [Col. 1324D].

If one of us fears the Lord’s threatening, his earth is diminished. But whoever persists among the number of the nations and does not wish to be among those whose earth decreases, nor among the people of God, of whom it is said, “They will see you, and the peoples will give birth,” will be brought down with the nations for punishment.

**The Septuagint:** “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your christs.”

First let us see how many kinds of christs there are, and afterward we shall discuss how the Lord went forth for the salvation of his christs.

In the Old Testament, the patriarchs were also called christs, as it is written in the Psalms:

> “He reproved kings for their sake:  
> ‘Do not touch my christs,  
> and do not act wickedly against my prophets’”  
> (Ps. CIV, 14–15).

And in the First Book of Chronicles all those who came out of Egypt are called christs [Col. 1325A].

In Exodus also a priestly anointing oil is prepared (chap. XXX), with which the priests are afterward reported to have been anointed in Leviticus (chap. VIII).

There is another ointment with which kings are anointed in the kingdom, and it is divided into two kinds. If the person is David or Solomon—that is, “strong of hand” or “peaceful” (I Kings XVI)—he is anointed with a horn. But if he is Jehu or Hazael, he is poured over with a flask (IV Kings IX and XIX); the earthen vessel is so called, namely **φακός** (*phakos*).

Cyrus also, king of the Persians and Medes, who released the people from captivity—although many err and think that what is written refers to the Lord the Savior—hears through Isaiah:

> “Thus says the Lord to my christ, to Cyrus,  
> whose right hand I have grasped,  
> so that nations may obey before him”  
> (Isa. XLV, 1),

and so forth. At the end it is said: “But you did not know me,” which it is impious to understand of the Savior.

There is a prophetic ointment with which Elijah is commanded to anoint Elisha as prophet (III Kings XIX).

And above all kinds of ointment there is a spiritual ointment called the oil of gladness, with which the Savior is anointed, and to him it is said:

> “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you  
> with the oil of gladness above your companions”  
> (Ps. XLIV, 8).

I think that the companions are those to whom John speaks:

> “And you have an anointing from the Holy One”  
> (I John II, 20).

And shortly afterward:

> “I have written these things to you concerning those who deceive you. But the anointing that you received from him remains in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you; but his anointing teaches you about everything, and it is true and is not a lie. And just as it taught you, remain in him”  
> (ibid., 26–27).

And lest those who have lost the anointing of baptism should despair of having the chrism restored, it is written in Leviticus that when a leper, having been cast outside the camp, comes to the priest and his leprosy has been cleansed, the priest should place oil in his left hand, dip his finger into it, sprinkle the oil seven times before the Lord, touch with that same oil the ear of the one who had been a leper, his right hand, and his right foot, and put whatever remains of the ointment entirely upon his head (Lev. XIV).

When he has properly completed all these things, then he sacrifices a burnt offering for him, and he himself is called a christ of God [Col. 1325D].

I wish to say something, but I fear giving the negligent an occasion for ruin: the same person is frequently found to have been anointed in the Scriptures. Thus David was anointed three times (II Kings VI and XIX)—not, however, as though this referred to someone who has sinned and is anointed again—for it is sufficient for a leper, after losing the first ointment, to be anointed a second time—but rather to one who makes progress day by day, whose anointing always increases, who passes from the oil of the leper to the oil of the people and the saints, from the oil of the people reaches the oil of the priests, from the priests rises to the chrism of the high priest, from the high priest to the king, from the king [Note: [Col. 1325D] Martianay incorrectly omitted the words “to the patriarchs, and from”; reading “from the king and the patriarchs.” Our manuscripts and unpublished books supply the words “to the patriarchs, and from.”] to the patriarchs, from the patriarchs proceeds to Christ, and is anointed with the oil of gladness (Ps. XLIV, 8) [Col. 1326A].

Whoever has been smeared with this oil becomes one spirit with God, and where the Father and the Son are, there he also will be.

This, however, is rare, and it is the prayer of believers. I do not know whether the result follows. For it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions”—that is, with the oil which those who are your companions will scarcely ever be able to find.

For the salvation of these christs, then, God went forth from his place, just as Micah also says:

> “And he will go forth from his place to save”  
> (Mic. I, 3).

Because those who needed salvation did not wish to enter into him, he himself went forth from his majesty and from his place, in order to lead those who were outside into the land of the meek and the region of the living, from which Adam had been expelled, and from which Cain went forth and dwelt in the land of Naid (Gen. III and IV, according to the Septuagint) [Col. 1326B].

We should know, as we said above, that where the Septuagint has the plural, “to save your christs,” the Hebrew has **LAJESUA ETH MESSIACH ()**, which Aquila translated, “for salvation with your Christ.” This does not mean that God went forth to save the people and to save his Christ, but that he came for the salvation of the people with his Christ, in accordance with the Gospel passage:

> “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father;  
> and the Father, remaining in me, himself does his works”  
> (John XIV, 10).

The fifth edition likewise translated: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ.”

Theodotion, however, truly like a poor man and an Ebionite, and Symmachus, who held the same doctrine, following a poor interpretation, translated in a Jewish manner:

> “You went forth for the salvation of your people,  
> to save your Christ.”

And:

> “You went forth to save your people,  
> to save your Christ.”

I am about to say something incredible, but nevertheless true. These semi-Christians translated in a Jewish manner, while the Jew Aquila translated as a Christian.

The sixth edition, revealing the mystery most clearly, translated from the Hebrew as follows:

> “You went forth to save your people  
> through Jesus Christ, your Christ,”

which in Greek is:

> **ἐξῆλθες τοῦ σῶσαι τὸν λαόν σου διὰ Ἰησοῦν τὸν Χριστόν σου**

This meaning can be applied to the passage in which the Father went forth with the Son from the temple and the ceremonies of the Jews, saying:

> “Your house will be left to you desolate”  
> (Luke XIII, 35);

and came for the salvation of the Gentiles, in order to save believers through Jesus Christ, his Son [Col. 1326C].

**The Septuagint:** “You sent death upon the heads of the wicked.”

Let us not think that this refers to the common death by which we all die—Abraham died and was gathered to his fathers (Gen. XXV), as did the prophets, and Christ himself died (John XIX)—but that death was sent upon the wicked:

> “The Lord kills and makes alive”  
> (I Kings II, 6),

so that those who formerly lived in iniquity, having died to sin, might live for righteousness (I Pet. II).

Anna also signifies this in her prayer: “The Lord kills and makes alive.” He kills sinners by sending death upon the heads of the wicked, so that he may make them alive for righteousness.

I shall say something bolder: Christ came into the world for this purpose, to send death upon the heads of the wicked. And just as he himself died to sin once (I Pet. III), so they too might die to iniquity, and those who had become participants in this death might also become participants in life.

According to the Hebrew, where it is written, “You struck the head from the house of the wicked,” let us understand the head, as I said, as the prince of this world [Col. 1327A], and his house as the world and every sinful soul in which the devil had lodging.

The head is struck in the house of the wicked so that, once it has been struck and expelled, the house may become God’s house, righteousness may dwell there, and righteousness may walk in it.

This is also worthy to be understood of God, who went forth for the salvation of his people with his Christ: once such a head has been struck, he may become the head in us who is the head of every man and of his Church.

If, therefore, anyone still feels himself to be a house of the wicked, let him implore the coming of the Son of God, so that the head of the wicked may be crushed within him [Col. 1327B].

**The Septuagint:** “You raised up bonds as far as the neck, to the end.”

The Lord raised up bonds of love, so that, after laying aside our former burden and casting off the exceedingly heavy yoke by which we were oppressed, we might take upon ourselves Christ’s easy yoke; and, placed in his chariot, carry the best charioteer.

Theodotion also, understanding this in a good sense, says: “You adorned the foundation up to the neck” [Col. 1327C].

The fifth edition: “You laid bare,” or “emptied,” “the foundation up to the neck—*selah*, that is, forever.”

Because the foundation of Christ, which was in each person’s soul, had been buried by foreign peoples, the accumulated earth is removed, the excellent foundation is laid bare and adorned, so that what was hidden may appear and recover its splendor. This happens forever, which in Hebrew is called *selah*.

At the same time consider that the Septuagint themselves, compelled by the necessity of the subject, although they always interpreted *selah* as *diapsalma*, here translated it as “to the end” [Col. 1327D].

### (Verses 14 and following)

“You cursed his scepters, the head of his warriors, who came like a whirlwind to scatter me. Their exultation was like that of one who devours the poor in secret. You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters. I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the sound my lips trembled. Let rot enter my bones and swarm beneath me, so that I may rest on the day of my tribulation [Vulgate omits *my*], so that I may go up to our armed people.”

For the present we discuss only the Hebrew [Al. *we have set down*], so that we may discuss the Septuagint edition separately, for it differs greatly from all the other translations.

“You cursed,” he says, “the scepters”—that is, the kingdoms—“of him,” without doubt the wicked one, of whom he had said above: “You struck the head from the house of the wicked; you laid bare the foundation up to the neck.”

We understand the wicked one either as Nebuchadnezzar or as every adversary of the people of God. And not only his scepters, but also the head of his warriors whom you had struck, who came like a whirlwind to scatter me—that is, to overthrow Israel and lead it captive in different directions [Col. 1328A].

Thus they exulted while devouring the poor and Israel subjected to them, as though they were doing this in secret and devouring us while you were unaware.

You therefore came to battle for your people, and sending your chariots into the waters—that is, among the many nations—you made a way for them in the mud of many waters, so that you might trample them and crush them as the mud of your horses and chariots beneath their hooves and wheels.

As for what follows—“I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the sound [understand: your sound] my lips trembled; let rot enter my bones and swarm beneath me, so that I may rest on the day of tribulation, so that I may go up to our armed people”—the sense is this [Col. 1328B]:

Now we gladly endure every hardship, and at your threatening we tremble with all our innermost parts. Now my lips tremble, and the fear of my anxious mind is marked upon my mouth. And not only this, but I voluntarily seek and desire something else as well: “Let rot enter my bones [Al. *my bones*], and swarm beneath me.” That is, I gladly suffer what Job suffered. I desire not only my flesh but also the marrow of my bones to waste away, and my bed to swarm with bodily decay and innumerable worms, so that after I have endured these things here for my sins, I may rest on the bitter day, the day of tribulation, the day of necessity and distress.

And I shall go up to our armed people—that is, strong, warlike, and combative. Beautifully he says, “I shall go up,” for one always ascends to an armed people. And elegantly he says “our”: whoever has been afflicted, willingly endured hardships, and exchanged present evils for future rewards, confidently says “our,” so that, like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, he too may sleep in a good old age, full of days, and be gathered to his fathers [Col. 1328C].

If someone says, “Look: in expounding the historical sense, you have been enclosed, without realizing it, in the nets of allegory, and you have mingled tropology with history,” let him hear that metaphor does not always correspond to allegory in history. For history itself is frequently woven metaphorically, and under the image of a woman or of a single man it speaks of the whole people.

Here too, then, we can speak in the person of the people:

“I willingly undergo captivity; I endure hardships with equanimity; I am oppressed by the exceedingly heavy yoke of the Babylonians; and whatever belongs to the utmost and harshest necessity, I will endure gladly [Al. *I endure*]—provided that I may rest at the time when you curse the scepters of the wicked and your horses trample the mud of many waters, so that afterward, together with your saints Zerubbabel and Jesus son of Josedec, and Ezra the priest and Nehemiah, I may return to the promised land” [Col. 1328D].

Up to this point, lest we seem entirely to have omitted the historical sense, we have in a manner forced the interpretation and drawn the statements into captivity, without following their meaning. Let us now return to the Septuagint translators and to the tropological exposition [659].

**The Septuagint:** “You divided in astonishment the heads of the mighty.”

Just as Christ is the head of the Church and of every man (I Cor. XI), so Beelzebub, the prince of demons, is the head of all the demons who rage in this age; and each of their companies has its own heads and princes.

[Note: [Col. 1329D] From Origen, *Homilies on Joshua*, the following passage is taken almost word for word. The points most relevant to our subject are these: “I think rather that there is one prince of the spirit of fornication, but innumerable spirits who obey him in this office; and through each individual human being various spirits serving under that prince entice them to sins of this kind. Likewise, I think that there is one prince of the spirit of anger, but innumerable spirits acting under him, who kindle sins of this sort in each individual human being. Likewise, there is one prince of avarice, and so of pride and the other evils.”]

For example, the spirits of fornication have their own leader; the spirits of avarice have their own **ἄρχων** (*archon*, ruler); the spirits of vainglory, falsehood, and unbelief have overseers [Note: [Col. 1330D] The reading preferred by the Reginensis manuscript, *malitiae*, “of their wickedness,” is also acceptable; shortly afterward we read *dividet*, “he will divide,” instead of *dividit*, “he divides.”] of their wickedness.

Therefore the most merciful God, who had sent death upon the heads of the wicked and raised up bonds as far as the neck, to the end, also divides the heads of the mighty in astonishment, so that he may first separate the princes from their subjects, and, as it were, decapitate the body from the head; and where the worst head had been, there the best head may be placed.

Let us give an example, so that what we are saying may become clearer. Whenever a tyrant is beheaded, his images and statues are also taken down; and, with only the face changed, once his head has been removed, the face of the victor is placed above it. Thus, while the body remains and the heads are cut off, another head is substituted [Col. 1329B].

I am pleased to understand this concerning the assemblies of heretics: when the heads of the heresies have been separated from the other peoples, Christ begins to be head in their place.

At the same time consider the precision of Holy Scripture: it did not say, “You cut off” or “You severed the heads of the mighty,” but “You divided” them. For what is divided is not so much cut off and destroyed as separated into parts.

Thus, as in the construction of the tower (Gen. XI), the language that had been wrongly united was separated, and the worst compact was torn apart by a useful division, so these heads too, which seemed to have agreement among themselves and with their bodies—for there are many heads of heretics which, although they have different eyes, nevertheless bark against the Church with one, so to speak, blasphemous tongue—might be divided into parts and, separated from the bodies they had deceived, make room for the good head [Col. 1329C].

We can use this verse whenever we see kings and their leaders shedding Christian blood and afterward observe that the Lord’s vengeance has overtaken them. We saw this recently in Julian, and before him in Maximian, and earlier in Valerian, Decius, Domitian, and Nero. We can say to the Lord with exultation and prayer in the Canticle: “You divided in astonishment the heads of the mighty”—that is, in the astonishment of believers, or in the astonishment of all the nations that did not think they could fall so quickly.

When I was still a boy and was being trained in the school of grammar, while all the cities were being polluted with the blood of victims, and suddenly, in the very heat of the persecution, the death of Julian was announced, one of the pagans aptly said:

> “How,” he said, “do the Christians say that their God is patient and **ἀνεξίκακος** (*anexikakos*, not resentful)? Nothing is more wrathful, nothing more immediate than this present fury: he could not defer his indignation even for a brief interval.”

He may have said this jokingly. But the Church of Christ sang with exultation: “You divided in astonishment the heads of the mighty” [Col. 1330A].

Let me also say something similar to this: “Divide, Lord, in the astonishment of all, Ahab and Jezebel” (III Kings XXI and XVIII). I am not Elijah, certainly; yet that Ahab and Jezebel killed Naboth, took his vineyard, and made his garden a place of their luxury (IV Kings IX and X).

Let one of your servants, Obadiah, be found, feeding your poor and beggar; let the blood of the harlot be given to the dogs; let wicked and greedy Ahab be slaughtered by the Lord’s dart [661].

LXX: “They will be moved in it [Alt. in him], and they will open their bridles like a poor man eating in secret [Alt. in hiding].” When the heads have been severed from their bodies and divided in no other way than “in astonishment”—which in Greek is **ἐν ἐκστάσει**—the expression is declined accordingly, and it says **ἐν αὐτῇ**, that is, “in it.” They will also open their bridles, or “their” bridles—for either may be understood—so that, loosening that dominion by which they previously ruled the bodies subject to them, they may make way for a better horseman and a better charioteer.

They do this as though eating like poor men in secret, possessing neither freedom nor any abundance of food, but only scanty fare; and, eating it secretly, they would not want anyone to see what they are doing. It may also be interpreted another way: when the heads have been divided in astonishment, as though decapitated from the rest of the body, they will open their mouths—which had been bridled as though by the bit of condemnation—and, like those who eat, will gnash their teeth against one another, wanting to eat again but lacking the power to devour.

Understand how, after Christ’s coming, the heads of the demons, separated from the nations that had previously been subject to them, want to exercise their ancient power again. But because they have been cut off from their bodies, they do not possess full freedom to feed: they eat like poor men, and not merely poor men, but poor men in secret. They are poor because they have lost their former riches; they eat secretly because they are always lying in ambush, so that in hidden places they may kill the innocent.

These heads have the same teeth as arrows. And although he previously said, “I will ascend above the stars of heaven, I will set my nest on high, and I will hold the whole world as though it were eggs in my hand,” nevertheless they will be dragged down from the heights. Having lost their former possessions and all the substance of their household, they will scarcely attempt to eat and bite secretly, as poor men.

I know that the Hebrew differs greatly from what has been said; but what can I do, since I have once undertaken to interpret both the Hebrew itself and the Scriptures commonly used throughout the world?

[Col. 1331A] LXX: “And you brought your horses upon the sea, disturbing many waters.”

After God had sent death upon the heads of the wicked, had crushed the heads of the mighty in astonishment, and had broken them in the sea—for it is written in the Psalms, “You crushed the heads of the dragon” (Ps. LXXIII, 4)—with the rulers either killed or broken, and the strong man overcome, one comes to his house and plunders all his goods (Mark XIII). What else can we interpret as the goods, the house of the strong man, and the possessions of the ruler, except the sea of this world, in which the dragon dwells?

God therefore brings upon the sea of this world his horses—he himself being an excellent horseman and an outstanding charioteer—namely, the angels and the exalted powers, so that they may disturb the many waters, that is, the demons and hostile powers.

If we wish to interpret this of Christ’s coming, in accordance with what is written in the Apocalypse (chapter 19), namely, that the Word of God sits upon a white horse and that the entire army follows him on white horses, we shall see how Christ mounted upon his apostles, saying to them: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age”; and: “Go, baptize all nations,” and the rest (Matt. XXVIII).

Afterward he mounted upon one white horse, which I do not think to be anyone other than the apostle Paul. Riding upon him, he traveled throughout the whole world. The Word of God mounted upon his horses so that the many waters might be disturbed: either the many peoples who were previously in the sea and held subject to the dragon—for “broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (Matt. VII, 13)—and so that, after abandoning their former error, they might be disturbed and receive the approaching horseman; or certainly, as we said above, the hosts of demons would no longer exercise such dominion in the sea, but, disturbed, would yield and dread the wounds inflicted by the fighting horseman.

Would that the Word of God might also mount upon me and, by the spear of my mouth, kill him who rules over the many waters, so that, when the king has been destroyed, the disturbed waters that had been subject to him might offer their necks to my horseman; and, brought together into one chariot, may we become the Lord’s Cherubim—which is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge.” For never is a charioteer so arranged and so splendidly equipped as among those who are joined together by a multitude of knowledge and by the reins of wisdom.

LXX: “I kept watch, and my belly trembled at the voice of the prayer of my lips; trembling entered my bones, and beneath me my strength was disturbed.”

Or, as we find it written elsewhere, **ἡ ἕξις μου**, which we may render “my constitution” or “my condition”; different copies are indeed found.

These words may also be spoken in the person of the prophet, cohering with what precedes: “Because you sent death upon the heads of the wicked, raised the bonds up to the neck, divided the heads of the mighty in astonishment, and brought your horses upon the sea, disturbing many waters, therefore I guarded my heart with all vigilance; my inward parts trembled, and all of me—whether my strength or my condition—was disturbed, lest I should suffer similar things.”

They may also have a beginning of their own, with the prophet narrating his fear and how he was afraid that he might sin in some respect. At the voice of the prayer of his lips he was admonished, and he feared God so greatly that trembling entered his bones. Placed beneath the exalted hand of the Lord, he was disturbed with all the strength, or disposition, of his soul.

When he says, “Trembling entered my bones,” this should be understood **ἐμφατικώτερον**, that is, with particular force, so that we may perceive the greatness of the fear of God penetrating the whole soul and moving the entire person, lest he do anything displeasing to God.

And because Scripture also speaks allegorically of the members of the soul in accordance with the members of the body, let us understand the trembling belly as that power of the soul which receives spiritual foods; the lips as those by which the mind speaks with itself; and the strong, solid bones as doctrines by which the entire structure of the soul is made firm.

I have said these things briefly. If anyone finds explanations more perceptive and more truthful than these, give your assent rather to his interpretation.

LXX: “I will rest in the day of my tribulation” [Note: The word *meae* (“of my”)—which is not heard in the Greek—is absent from the Queen’s manuscript, as are also, shortly afterward, the words “or my condition.”] “so that I may go up to the people of my pilgrimage.”

Because I guarded my heart with all vigilance, my belly trembled at the voice of the prayer of my lips, trembling entered my bones, and my strength—or condition—beneath me was disturbed; and because of such vigilance I was made alien to sins. Therefore I now say confidently: “I will rest in the day of tribulation, so that I may go up to the people of my pilgrimage,” that is, to those who, like me, have been pilgrims in this world.

I will go upward although placed below, and, as though climbing from a valley toward higher places, I will strive with all eagerness, so that at the time when others are in tribulation and distress, my concern may be ascent: how I may rest with the people of my pilgrimage in higher places.

I think that the day of tribulation is the consummation of the world, concerning which Isaiah also says: “The day of the Lord is incurable, a day of wrath and anger, to make the whole world desolate and destroy sinners” (Isa. XIV).

### (Verse 17)

“For the fig tree will not blossom, and there will be no shoot on the vines; the work of the olive will prove false, and the fields will yield no food; the flock will be cut off from the fold, and there will be no herd in the stalls.”

LXX: “For the fig tree will not bear fruit, and there will be no shoots [Alt. plants] in the vines; the work of the olive will prove false, and the fields will produce no food; the sheep have failed because they had food to eat, and there are no cattle in the stalls.”

According to the Hebrew, concerning which we spoke above—“Let rottenness enter my bones and burst forth beneath me, so that I may rest in the day of tribulation, so that I may go up to the people of our [Alt. my] armed host”—the preceding words will be joined to what follows:

“Therefore I wished to endure tribulation for the present and afterward to go up to a strong people, because the day of tribulation and necessity will come; and while others are placed in distress, I will rejoice in your majesty: for the fig tree will not blossom, and there will be no shoot on the vines; the work of the olive will prove false, and the fields will yield no food,” and the rest.

Since these things do not differ greatly from the LXX, let us discuss them together with their interpretation.

When the day of tribulation comes, and I go up to the people who were once pilgrims with me—or certainly, when the day of the overthrow of the Jewish people and of the former people comes, and the daughter of Zion is left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber field, and like a city under siege [Note: Compare Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter XXVII, to whose testimony Victor here appeals.]—I, who have been chosen from the perishing people, concerning whom it was said, “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom, and we would have resembled Gomorrah” (Isa. I, 9), will join myself to the disciples of Christ.

Because he teaches them on the mountain, leaving the crowds and the weak below, I will climb to the mountains.

“For the fig tree did not give fruit”: the fig tree to which the hungry Lord came in the Gospel and found no fruit, and he cursed it, saying, “You shall not bear fruit forever” (Matt. XXI, 19).

Carefully consider what he said: “You shall not bear fruit forever.” He did not say, “forever and ever”; but when this age has passed and the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then this fig tree too will bear its fruits, and all Israel will be saved.

This is the fig tree to which the master of the household came for the third time and, finding that it was not producing fruit, wanted to cut it down. The gardener entrusted with it pleads on its behalf that he be given time, and says: “Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put manure on it; and if indeed it bears fruit—but if not, then you shall cut it down” (Luke XIII).

This gardener is either Gabriel or Michael, to whom the Jewish people have been entrusted. He pleads with the Lord on their behalf during the Passion and says: “Lord, give it time for repentance, and do not destroy them; and if indeed they bear fruit—but if not, then you shall destroy them.”

He says, “If they bear fruit,” but he did not say what they would suffer; nor did he say, “If they bear fruit, they will remain as they were.” Rather, with the judgment suspended, this is understood: “You will transfer them into the Church of the Gentiles and transplant them into another vineyard.”

The Lord came for the third time and found no fruit in them. First he gave the Law through Moses; second, he spoke through the prophets; third, he himself descended. And after the Passion, when forty-four years had been granted for repentance [Note: Again the same manuscript reads: “after the Passion, forty-two years, because …”], because they did not bear fruit, they were destroyed for the fourth time. This, however, is left to our own understanding.

For the parable does not say what the master of the household did afterward, but only what the gardener pleaded. From this we observe that those who produced fruit from this fig tree were transferred to the people of the Gentiles, to whom the prophet also ascended, saying: “I will rest in the day of tribulation, so that I may go up to the people of my pilgrimage.”

But those who did not produce fruit and remained in their hardness were overthrown. The same thing is signified by John’s saying in the Gospel: “Behold, the axe is laid at the roots of the trees [Alt. tree]. Every tree that does not produce fruit [Alt. produces good fruit] will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10; Luke III, 9).

We have spoken of the fig tree, showing that it is the Jewish people. Let us speak also of the vine—something that anyone who has read Isaiah will readily understand: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a hill, in a fertile place” (Isa. V, 1). And afterward: “I waited for it to produce fruit; but it produced thorns, and not judgment but a cry.”

And in Jeremiah: “But I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true; how have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. II, 21).

And more clearly in the Psalms: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Ps. LXXIX, 9).

This, then, is the vineyard to which the master of the household had often sent servants (Matt. XXI), to receive from it wine that gladdens the human heart. Because it had been turned into bitterness and, finally, dared even to kill the son of the master of the household, it produced not grapes but thorns, and not judgment but a cry: “Crucify him, crucify him!” and “We have no king except Caesar” (John XIX, 6, 15).

Therefore “the boar from the forest ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast devoured it” (Ps. LXXIX, 14).

The olive, too, will clearly be shown to represent the people of the synagogue by anyone who reads in the Apostle about the branches of the olive tree being broken off (Rom. XI), and about us being grafted in from the wild olive. Thus, in the branches we are to understand that the Jewish multitude was cut away, while in the roots the election of the apostles was preserved. We shall remain grafted into them if we bear fruit, and it will be said of us: “Your children are like shoots of olive trees around your table” (Ps. CXXVII, 4).

Many think that the fig tree, the vine, and the olive are understood mystically as the Trinity: the fig tree, because of the sweetness of its fruits, signifies the Holy Spirit; the vine is our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who says in the Gospel, “I am the vine” (John XV, 1); and the olive is God the almighty Father, by whom all things are illumined, from whom light proceeds, and to whom we may say: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10)—that is, “In the Son we shall see [Note: The same manuscript inserts here: “the light.”] the Holy Spirit.”

To these fruitful trees and to the most abundant vine, the fruitless trees come in the Book of Judges (chapter IX), asking that they reign over them. But the olive, the fig tree, and the vine never reign over the trees of the forest, which are destined for burning. Rather, the thorn-filled bramble rules over them, resembling the hedgehog that dwells in Babylon and always moves about in holes.

This shrub not only has thorns but also fire, wounding and burning whatever it touches. Finally, fire went out and consumed the trees of the forest.

To make clear the interpretation given above, in which we understood the statement about the synagogue—“The fig tree will not produce fruit, and there will be no shoots in the vines”—let us recognize that the reference is not to fruits but to good works.

In the olive the riddle is plainly disclosed, and it says: “The work of the olive will prove false.” For the fruits that they ought to have produced are demonstrated in works. But the work of the olive will prove false because it promises one thing and does another. They said to Moses, “Everything that the Lord has said we will do” (Exod. XXIV, 7), yet they were unwilling to believe in him who had been proclaimed by Moses.

The fields too will not produce fruit. Consider that Jerusalem, which once stood upon mountains, with mountains around it (Ps. CXXIV, 2), and whose foundations were in the holy mountains (Ps. LXXXVI, 1), is now called low-lying and level. It nourishes not only no human beings—that is, rational animals—but not even sheep or cattle, concerning which Solomon also speaks in Proverbs:

“Take care of the regions that are in the field, shear the grass, and gather hay, so that you may have sheep for [Note: Victor corrects this to *ad vestiendum* (“for clothing”); this is how it is read in the Greek of Prov. 27: **ἵνα ἔξῃς πρόβατα εἰς ἱματισμόν**. The Vulgate likewise says, “Let there be lambs for their clothing.” Our manuscripts agree with one another, differing from the printed reading only in reading *habeant* (“they may have”) instead of *habeas* (“you may have”): namely, “so that they may have sheep for food,” which is certainly a sound meaning.] food.”

There will be no cattle in the stalls, because “where the stalls are full, the strength of the ox is evident” (Prov. XIV, 4). The ox is a laborer; the ox sustains the Lord’s yoke; the ox in whose footsteps the one who sows will be blessed.

All these things will be taken away from the people because they acted wickedly toward their Creator God.

If you wish [Alt. do not wish] to understand the day of tribulation as the day of consummation, you will refer everything to those who say that they belong to the Church but do not possess works of righteousness.

The fig tree, the vine, and the olive—that is, the mystery of the Trinity—will not bear their fruit in them. They will have not only no grain or food for rational beings, but not even food in their fields for sheep and cattle; their stalls will be empty, and instead of lofty mountains they will dwell in flat and low-lying places.

### (Verses 18–19)

“But I will rejoice in the Lord and exult in God my Jesus. God the Lord is my strength, and he will set my feet like those of deer. And as victor he will lead me upon my heights, singing in the Psalms.”

LXX: “But I will exult in the Lord; I will rejoice over God my Savior [Alt. my Salvation]. The Lord God is my strength, and he will set my feet for consummation; upon the heights he will place me, so that I may conquer in his song.”

Since the fig tree, the vine, and the olive, according to what I have explained, do not produce their fruit; since the fields of the Jews yield no food; since the sheep are cut off from the fold and the cattle from the stalls; and since they heard from the Lord, “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 38); and since the people were handed over to captivity and scattered throughout the whole world—the prophet from the Jewish people, whose name means “embrace” because he loved the Lord, clung to him, and united himself to him, speaks in the person of the apostles and of the people who believe in Christ:

“But I will rejoice in the Lord and exult in God my Jesus.”

For this the LXX translated **τῷ Σωτῆρί μου**, that is, “my Savior” [Note: The Greek words **τῷ σωτῆρί μου**, and the words “that is,” are absent from the Queen’s manuscript.]

“God the Lord is my strength”: for I will have no other power except in Christ, and I will count all the righteousnesses of the Law as refuse.

“And he will set my feet like those of deer,” so that I may tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and, like a little child, put my hand into the hole, draw out the serpent, and play with the viper [Alt. Judas]. For “my beloved is like a young goat or a fawn of the deer” (Song II, 9).

And because he himself is a deer, he also granted me to be a deer: lofty with horns, splitting the hoof, chewing the cud, and driving away serpents by my scent. Of him it is said in the seventeenth Psalm: “He made my feet like those of deer, and he will set me upon the heights.” And in the twenty-eighth: “The voice of the Lord perfecting the deer.”

Therefore he will set my feet among his other deer and lead me to heavenly things, so that among the angels I may sing the glory of the Lord and announce peace on earth to people of good will.

I will sing his victory, triumph, and trophy of the cross.

Let us refer all this, according to the Hebrew and the fifth edition, to the time of the Jewish overthrow and to the Lord’s coming [Note: The Queen’s manuscript and one edition read: “so that, for a time …”].

But if we wish to understand it of the consummation of the world, it should be expounded as follows:

Just as in Exodus (chapter IX), when Egypt was struck, God struck their vines and their fig trees, killed the firstborn of humans and animals with hail, and the caterpillar and locust consumed the Egyptian crops; so the fig trees in Egypt produced no fruit, nor were there shoots in their vines; the work of the olive proved false—if anywhere it could be found in Egypt—and their fields yielded no food [Alt. fruit]. Their flocks failed because they had no food, and there were no cattle in their stalls.

But the people of Israel exulted in the Lord and rejoiced in their saving God.

So, at the consummation of the world, when iniquity has multiplied and love has grown cold (Matt. XXIV), when the fig tree has not produced fruit, the vines have had no grapes, the work of the olive has proved false, the fields have not brought forth food, and the other things that follow have occurred, then whoever is found righteous and worthy of God’s election will speak with exultation:

“But I will exult in the Lord; I will rejoice in my saving God. The Lord is my strength.”

And, as though placed by God upon the consummation of the age so that afterward he may ascend to higher things and be led by God to the summit, he will say:

“He will set my feet for consummation; upon the heights he will place me.”

When the prize has been set for those singing by Jesus the **ἀγωνοθέτης**, the judge and director of the contest, who was the first to conquer in the contest, “I will conquer in his song,” and my hands will fashion the lyre, the psaltery, and every kind of instrument; I will write a panegyric for the triumphant one.

And I, who at the beginning said, “How long shall I cry out, and you will not hear? I will cry aloud to you while suffering violence, and you will not save?” and who complained about his justice and judgment, will afterward praise his equity and surpass the other singers with my song.

[Col. 1337]

## THE ONE BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES OF THE PRIEST SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS OF STRIDON ON THE PROPHET ZEPHANIAH

### Prologue

Before I undertake Zephaniah, who is ninth in the order of the twelve prophets, it seems necessary to answer those who think that I deserve ridicule because, leaving men aside, I write especially to you, Paula and Eustochium.

If they knew that, while men were silent, Huldah prophesied, and that Deborah, at once judge and prophetess, overcame the enemies of Israel while Barak was afraid (Judg. IV); and that Judith and Esther, as types of the Church, both killed their adversaries and rescued Israel, which was about to perish, they would never bend their hand behind my back into the shape of a stork [Note: A similar expression is found in Persius, *Satire* 1: “whom no stork pecks from behind.” That is, no one laughs by bringing the fingers of the right hand together in the likeness of a stork’s beak. To curve the hand behind one’s back into a stork is, if I am not mistaken, the same as laughing at someone with a bent finger or hand shaped like a stork’s neck. In one manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés we read: “he would put his hand into a stork-shape.” MART.—The manner of ridicule is also noted in Letter 125 to Rusticus, section 18: “if you should suddenly look behind you, you would discover either the necks of storks bent behind you,” and so forth. From Persius, *Satire* I:

“O Janus, behind you, whom no stork pecks,” and so forth.] behind me.

I say nothing of Anna and Elizabeth, and the other holy women, whose star-like sparks the bright light of Mary conceals.

Let me turn to pagan women, so that among the philosophers of the world also they may see that differences of souls, not of bodies, are ordinarily investigated. Plato introduces Aspasia arguing. Sappho is mentioned together with Pindar and Alcaeus. Themista philosophizes among the wisest of Greece. Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi—that is, your Cornelia—is admired by the entire multitude of the Roman city.

Carneades, the most eloquent of philosophers and the sharpest of rhetoricians, who was accustomed to arouse applause among men of consular rank and in the Academy, was not ashamed to discuss philosophy in a private house while a married woman listened.

Why should I mention the daughter of Cato, the wife of Brutus, whose virtue ensures that we do not admire the steadfastness of her father and husband quite so much? History, both Greek and Latin, is full of the virtues of women, and these virtues would demand entire books [Alt. “would demand a whole book”].

For me, since another work presses upon me, it is enough to have said at the end of the prologue that the risen Lord first appeared to women (Matt. XXVIII and Luke), and that they became apostles to the apostles, so that men might blush not to seek the one whom the more fragile sex had already found.

### Chapter I

#### Verse 1

“The word of the Lord that came to Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah.”

The LXX likewise.

The Hebrews maintain that whenever a prophet’s father or grandfather is placed in the title, those ancestors too were prophets. Hence Amos, one of the twelve prophets, who said, “I am not a prophet, nor a prophet’s son, but a shepherd of goats, who gathers sycamore fruit” (Amos VII, 14), does not have his father’s name in the title [Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads: “Amos, one of the twelve prophets, and consequently does not have …” Instead of “I am not,” it also reads “I was not.”]

If this is true, the prophet Zephaniah, whom we now endeavor to explain, was born, so to speak, with a prophetic name and from a glorious line of ancestors [Note: The Queen’s manuscript rather more correctly reads *canone* (“lineage” or “rule”) instead of *nomine* (“name”); Martianus had read it very poorly as *cum addito, qui nomine* (“with the addition, who by name”).] For he had Cushi as his father, Gedaliah as his grandfather, Amariah as his great-grandfather, and Hezekiah as his great-great-grandfather. He himself, like the last charioteer, completed such a four-horse chariot.

Some have translated the name Zephaniah as “watchtower,” others as “the Lord’s secret.” Whether, therefore, it is interpreted as “watchtower” or “the Lord’s hidden thing,” either meaning suits the prophet.

For it is also said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III, 17). And elsewhere: “The Lord will do nothing unless he has revealed his instruction to his servants the prophets.” And the title of the ninth Psalm is interpreted as “concerning the hidden things of the Son.”

This prophet, therefore, who stood in a watchtower and in elevated places, and who knew the mysteries of the Lord, was the son of Cushi—which is interpreted as “humility” or “my Ethiopian,” concerning which we shall speak later. He also had Gedaliah as his grandfather, whose name means “the greatness of the Lord”; Amariah as his great-grandfather, whose name is likewise rendered “the word of the Lord”; and Hezekiah as his great-great-grandfather, whose name signifies “the strength of the Lord.”

Thus, from the strength of the Lord was born the word of the Lord; from the word of the Lord was born the greatness of the Lord; and from the greatness of the Lord was born humility, so that when someone has reached perfection he may say: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. IX). And in the Psalms: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. CXXX, 1).

Up to this point, as though sliding along an easy slope and running across level ground, we have stumbled over the fact that Cushi is also interpreted as “my Ethiopian.” For after such great virtues, how can the name “Ethiopian” sound as praise?

If Scripture had said *Cush*, that is, “Ethiopian,” the question would appear insoluble: for Cush was born from Ham. But in saying *Cushi*, that is, “my Ethiopian,” it seems to express a mystery: that the one who was once an Ethiopian, turned toward repentance—in accordance with the saying, “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. LXVII, 32), and in another place, “Before him the Ethiopians will fall” (Ps. LXXI, 9)—may say with the bride in the Song of Songs: “I am black but beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem” (Song I, 4).

We also read in Jeremiah that Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian eunuch, was pleasing to God (Jer. XXXVIII). And in the Acts of the Apostles, the Ethiopian eunuch of Queen Candace had such zeal for the Scriptures and the Law of God that he was reading in his chariot and came to Jerusalem to worship the Lord in his Temple (Acts VIII, 9).

Therefore such faith is crowned with a worthy reward: the evangelist Philip is sent to him, and he is immediately instructed; he believes, is baptized, and is saved.

And he is called not merely a eunuch, but, with the addition of “man,” “a male Ethiopian eunuch.” Because he was a eunuch of Christ and had made himself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, he had not thereby lost the designation “man.”

It is also fitting that Zephaniah, as the son of Cushi, that is, of “the Ethiopian,” writes in the books that follow about the repentance of the Ethiopians: “Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there they will bring offerings to me.”

This is what we have to say about the genealogy of Zephaniah, who prophesied in the days of Josiah.

Just as those who are illumined by Elijah are called the days of Elijah, so also the days of Josiah are those who raised themselves up toward the Lord—for Josiah is interpreted as “the elevation of the Lord.” He was a righteous man, and the history of Kings and Chronicles also writes about his praises (2 Kings XXIII; 2 Chron. XXXIV).

His father was Amon, and his grandfather Manasseh (2 Kings XXI). We read that Manasseh, after many crimes and after his captivity in Babylon, repented, turned toward better things, and obtained the Lord’s mercy.

Therefore, because of the faith by which he had believed in God, he gave his son a name derived from himself, **ἐπώνυμον**, that is, Amon. For **AMMON** (the Hebrew form is not supplied in the text) is interpreted as “faith.”

At the same time, consider that the title does not name the kings of the ten tribes—that is, the kings of Israel—but only the kings of Judah, as it did above. For the ten tribes had already been led into captivity by the Assyrians under Hezekiah, Manasseh’s father (2 Kings XVII).

This concludes the preface concerning the title, the genealogy, and the time of Zephaniah. Now let us see what the prophecy itself contains.

### (Verses 2–3)

“I will utterly gather everything from the face of the earth,” says the Lord; “I will gather human beings and cattle, I will gather the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea; and the ruins of the wicked shall be, and I will destroy human beings from the face of the earth,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “Let there be failing-away from the face of the earth,” says the Lord; “let human beings fail, and cattle; let the birds of the sky fail, and the fish of the sea—and the wicked shall be weakened—and I will remove the impious from the face of the earth,” says the Lord.

[Note: The same editors add from the Hebrew the text, “and the ruins of the wicked shall be.” Since this is found in no manuscript, and has also been added superfluously, the prudent reader will understand the matter. MART.]

The phrase that we have placed in the Septuagint, “and the wicked shall be weakened,” has been added from Theodotion’s translation. In its place Symmachus translated, “and the stumbling-blocks with the wicked,” so that “they shall be gathered,” or “they shall fail,” is understood.

[Note: The manuscript of Regina now corruptly reads, “and the wicked shall be in stumbling-blocks”; Symmachus wrote καὶ τὰ σκάνδαλα σὺν ἀσεβέσιν, “and the stumbling-blocks with the wicked.” The Barberini Hexaplar manuscript is the authority for this.] The Fifth Edition, however, has, “and weakness with the wicked shall perish.”

We must therefore, following our customary practice, first set forth the historical account and afterward discuss the higher meanings.

There can be no doubt that the final kingdom of the two tribes, which were called Judah and Benjamin, existed under Josiah. After he was killed, his sons who reigned afterward, and his grandsons, should be considered to have ruled less as kings than to have been made objects of derision by the Egyptian king and the Chaldaeans, and to have been tormented by various captivities and deaths.

Because the people could excuse themselves on account of wicked kings and say, “We wish to serve God, but we are prevented by the kings,” a righteous king is given. Since he zealously pursues the zeal of the Lord, while the people nevertheless persist in the worship of idols, the Lord brings forward a just cause for anger and prophesies the overthrow of Jerusalem, the captivity of Judah, and the victory of Nebuchadnezzar.

The Lord therefore says through the prophet: “I will by no means grant repentance any longer; but I will utterly consume everything from the face of the earth: neither human being, nor cattle, nor bird, nor fish of the sea shall remain.” Even brute animals feel the Lord’s anger; and when cities have been laid waste and human beings killed, Illyricum [manuscripts: Illyricus], Thrace, and the land in which I was born are witnesses that solitude and scarcity also come upon beasts, birds, and fish. Apart from sky and earth, growing brambles, and dense forests, everything has perished there.

[Note: All the manuscript codices retain the word *Illyricus*; but this is doubtless due to the ignorance of ancient copyists, who did not know that, when it is used for the province and region, *Illyris* is called *Illyricum*, in the neuter gender, not *Illyricus* in the masculine. MART.]

[Note: Stridon, a town on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia. We shall have much to say about Jerome’s homeland in his Life.]

“But this,” says the prophet, “will happen because the multitude of the wicked was excessive.” Thus the wicked will fall and human beings will be destroyed, and there will be solitude over the face of the earth.

We may also understand the same thing concerning the consummation of the world: human beings, cattle, birds, fish of the sea, and all things will fail; the wicked will be weakened, and iniquity will be removed from the face of the earth.

If we wish to understand something still higher—because the Septuagint says, “Let there be failing-away from the face of the earth”—

[Note: The manuscript of Regina adds, “we can”; but the more accurate sense, “we shall see,” depends on what follows below.]

—and to take “destruction” in a good sense, in accordance with the passage, “And Abraham failed and died in a good old age, old and full of days, and was gathered to his people” (Genesis 25:8), and with what Scripture reports about Isaac and Jacob, we see how they “fail away from the face of the earth,” and how they fulfill this command:

“Those who have their manner of life in heaven,” and who, although in the flesh, do not wage war according to the flesh, because they know that those who live in the flesh cannot please God, do everything within their power not to be in the flesh but in the spirit. Withdrawing from the earth, they say: “He raised us up and seated us together in the heavenly places in Christ” (Romans 8).

If someone objects to this interpretation—which we have taken in a good sense—of “Let there be failing-away from the face of the earth,” citing what is written concerning Ishmael:

“These are the years of Ishmael’s life: one hundred and thirty-seven years; and he failed and died, and was gathered to his people” (Genesis 25:17),

we shall answer him first that Ishmael too was a son of Abraham and received gifts and portions from his father according to his measure. Further, the text simply says, “He failed and died,” and does not add what is written concerning Abraham: “in a good old age, old and full of days, and he was gathered to his people.”

Or consider Isaac: “The days of Isaac which he lived were one hundred and eighty-five years. And Isaac failed and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days” (Genesis 35:28–29).

And likewise concerning Jacob: “Jacob ceased giving commands to his sons, and, lifting up his feet onto the bed, he failed, and was gathered to his people” (Genesis 49:32).

From this we understand that it is one thing simply to fail, and another to possess many virtues together with one’s failing.

What Scripture had first stated generally—“Let there be failing-away from the face of the earth”—it afterward divided into parts: “Let human beings fail, and cattle; let the birds of the sky fail, and the fish of the sea.”

Four things are commanded to fail: first, the rational human being; then the three things subject to humanity—cattle, birds, and fish—which I think are also mentioned in the eighth Psalm: “Moreover, the cattle of the field; the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (Psalm 8:8).

But what it had first called “all sheep and oxen,” separating them as the chief among cattle, it did not wish to count with the cattle that remained [variant: “were left behind”].

“Let human beings fail; let cattle fail; let the birds of the sky fail; let the fish fail.” It does not say, “Let the beasts fail; let the reptiles of the earth fail.” These ought not to fail, but to perish. Rather, let those fail who are capable of correction.

Thus Sarah’s womanly functions failed, and Abraham is commanded to listen to whatever Sarah ordered (Genesis 18, 21). Someone fails as a human being if he despises human things and no longer dies as a human being, and hears: “I said, You are gods” (Psalm 81:6).

Another fails as cattle when, ascending to higher things,

[Note: Through an erroneous interpretation—which Victorius had also noted—Martianus omits the negative particle. For if someone fails as a human being when he despises human things, and someone fails as cattle when he ascends to higher things, then he cannot be accused by the prophetic statement for ceasing to be cattle. The text is explaining mystically what it means to fail as a human being, cattle, bird, or fish. Our manuscripts, following Victorius, restore the particle.]

he is not accused by the prophetic word: “Human beings, when they were in honor, did not understand; they were compared with senseless cattle and became like them” (Psalm 48:21).

Someone fails as a bird of the sky when he makes himself the wings of an eagle and returns, rich, to the house of his teacher, abandoning all poverty (Proverbs 23).

Someone fails as a fish of the sea when, caught in the Lord’s nets, he is separated together with the good fish (Matthew 13).

When these things have been accomplished according to the Lord’s command, the wicked will be weakened, not having as much strength as before. But the impious will also be removed. He did not say, “They will be killed,” but “They will be removed,” so that, converted to better things, they may be transferred from impiety and iniquity to piety and righteousness, and may begin to be what previously they had not been.

This is according to the tropological interpretation. We must also set forth the interpretation of the elders. It will then be left to the reader’s judgment whether what has been said is intended to express severity or clemency.

### (Verses 4 and following)

“I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will destroy from this place the remnants of Baal, and the names of the temple-servants together with the priests; and those who worship upon the roofs the host of heaven, and worship and swear by the Lord, and swear by Milcom; and those who turn away from following the Lord, and those who have not sought the Lord or investigated him.”

The Septuagint: “I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over all who inhabit Jerusalem; and I will remove from this place the names of the Baals, and the names of the priests together with the priests; and those who worship upon the roofs the host of heaven; and those who swear by the Lord and swear by their king; and those who turn aside from the Lord; and those who do not seek the Lord and do not hold fast to the Lord.”

After the ruin of the wicked and the removal of the impious from the face of the earth, the following is consequently said against Judah and against Jerusalem in the person of the Lord: “I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” The stretching out of the hand indicates the act of one who strikes.

“And I will destroy from this place the remnants of Baal.” This does not mean, according to the Septuagint, that the names of the Baals are to be completely erased; rather, according to the Hebrew, he threatens to remove its worshipers from the people who, after the slaughter of their enemies, had remained few in Judah and Jerusalem.

[Note: The manuscript of Regina does not recognize these words according to the Hebrew.]

He also threatens to remove “the names of the temple-servants together with the priests,” because Judah and Benjamin had fallen into such great impiety that, in the Temple of the Lord—according to what Ezekiel writes and the Fourth Book of Kings shows—they had set up a statue of Baal, which the Lord calls the image of Zeal, and in that same sanctuary had worshiped idols and the Lord together (Ezekiel 8).

[Note: Earlier editors incompetently read “which the Lord calls the image of heaven.” This is entirely false, since the Lord never called the idol of Baal “the image of heaven,” but rather the idol or image of Zeal (Ezekiel 8:3, 5, 8). The manuscript codex of Saint Cygirannus also retains the word “idol” here: “which the Lord calls the idol of Zeal”; others read “image.” I know, however, that in Ezekiel 8 the phrase “image of heaven” was placed from Theodotion. MART. Compare what we observed in the note to our Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 8, col. 83.]

Therefore, pointedly, he called the priests of idols not priests but *temenitas*—that is, temple-servants or fanatics (2 Kings 10 and 17)—which in Hebrew is called *acchumarim*.

[Note: Erasmus did not permit himself to restore this passage; he conjectures that one should read *hierophantas* (ἱεροφάντας, “revealing sacred things”). Marianus, bolder than Erasmus but no more careful in reading the manuscripts, dared to overturn Jerome’s entire text and substitute Hebrew words for the Greek in this manner: “Therefore, pointedly, he called the priests of idols not [—], that is, priests, but temple-servants or fanatics.” He himself calls this corruption a restoration, despite the testimony of all the manuscript codices, which retain the reading we have printed. Further, the term *temenitos* or *temenites* in Suidas signifies a temple-servant, or one who dwells in a place sacred to the gods; for *temene* in Jerome’s commentary on Ezekiel 6 and in Suidas are temples, chapels, shrines, and sacred groves. *Temenoros* also means a temple-servant and guardian of a sacred place. MART. We restore from our manuscripts *temenitas*, correctly derived from *temenites*. For what Martianus reads, *temenitos*, from *temenitos*, is less satisfactory, since the Greek word does not seem to exist.]

Thus the Lord will remove from the place of Jerusalem, or destroy—and the phrase “and he will destroy” is understood throughout—the temple-servants and priests, those who worshiped on the roofs the host of heaven, the sun, moon, and remaining stars, and those who swore in the name of the Lord and in the name of the idol of the Ammonites, Milcom, which the Septuagint translated as “king.”

He will destroy from this place the remnants of Baal; he will destroy the names of the temple-servants together with the priests; he will destroy those who worship on the roofs the host of heaven; he will destroy those who worship and swear by the Lord and swear by Milcom; and he will destroy those who turn away—or turn aside—from following the Lord, and those who do not seek him—or do not hold fast to him.

The Israelites turn away from following the Lord when, abandoning his worship, they swear by Milcom, worship the host of heaven, and venerate Baal, the idol of the Sidonians.

Thus far the historical meaning has been explained. Let us now consider the anagogical meaning.

Because of the Lord, who arose from the tribe of Judah, and because of Jerusalem, in which Judah reigned—that is, the Lord and Savior—let us say that, when iniquity has multiplied, the love of many has grown cold, and the Lord has come, faith has appeared rarely on earth, to such an extent that even God’s elect are tested (Matthew 24; Luke 18), then the Lord stretches out his hand for the punishment of sinners over Judah, which seems to confess the Lord’s name, and over Jerusalem, the Church that received its name from peace.

He removes from the Church the names of the Baals, which is interpreted as “in higher places.” The Lord removes the names of empty glory and false admiration that circulate in the Church, where, according to James, the person wearing a golden ring is honored while the poor person is despised. When the judge and senator arrives, and the entire assembly rises together on behalf of all the rich, no place is granted to the holy poor man even to stand among their crowds and seats.

[Note: Earlier printed editions have “he venerates.” Shortly afterward, they retain *consessionis* instead of *consessiones*. The manuscript of Regina has “among the crowds and compressions.”]

He also removes the names of priests together with the priests who vainly applaud themselves in the title of bishop and the dignity of the presbyterate, but not in their work (James 2). Hence Scripture pointedly does not say, “the works of priests together with the priests,” but “the names”: those who merely bear false names of dignities and destroy their names by evil works.

He removes those who worship upon the roofs the host of heaven, those who are lifted up against the knowledge of God. They promise themselves a fictitious knowledge concerning everything that happens in the world, attributing it to the risings and settings of the stars, following the errors of astrologers.

He removes those who worship the Lord and Milcom, who think that they can serve the world and the Lord at the same time and satisfy two masters, God and Mammon. While serving as soldiers of Christ, they bind themselves to worldly affairs; they present the same image to God and Caesar; and although they claim to be priests of Christ, they consecrate their sons to Milcom, that is, to their king (2 Timothy 2).

They rightly have a human king, because they have lost the Lord as king. Those who turn away from the Lord through evil works and do not seek him retain their sins while he flees from them.

If someone wishes to understand this same thing concerning the soul of each individual, according to the interpretation of the names Judah and Jerusalem, he will not be mistaken. The Lord removes all the things we have mentioned, either at the consummation of the world or at the departure of individuals, when they hear: “Fool, this night your soul shall be required of you” (Luke 12).

He stretches out his hand over the one who does not confess the Lord,

[Note: The same manuscript of Regina omits the negative particle: “the one who confesses the Lord.”]

and over the one who boasts that he possesses a peaceful understanding, so that he may remove and destroy from such a Jerusalem every form of pride, false worship of God, the errors of various doctrines, slavery to God and the world at the same time, turning away from the Lord through daily sins, and neglect of God.

### (Verse 7)

“Be silent before the face of the Lord God, because the day of the Lord is near, because the Lord has prepared a sacrifice; he has sanctified his invited ones.”

The Septuagint: “Fear before the face of the Lord God, because the day of the Lord is near, because the Lord has prepared his victim; he has sanctified his invited ones.”

In place of what the Septuagint translated as “fear,” we have put “be silent.” In Hebrew this is an interjection commanding silence, which comedians also often use. But silence is also commanded absolutely, because the day of the Lord is coming.

[Note: All the codices read this way without the Hebrew word *has*, which Jerome says is an interjection commanding silence and often used by comic poets. Modern Hebrew grammarians think that it is the apocope of the verb *hissa*, meaning “he was silent” out of reverence, and that *has* has been placed for *hasseh*. Moreover, what the holy doctor says about the interjection commanding silence should not be understood as though *as* or *has* were an interjection among comic poets, but rather that they possess in their language similar interjections by which silence is commanded. MART.]

Let us understand the day of the Lord as the day of captivity and vengeance upon the sinful people; the victim as the overthrow of Jerusalem; and the sanctification of those whom he dedicated to slaughter, in accordance with what is said in Jeremiah: “Sanctify them for the day of their slaughter” (Jeremiah 12:3).

The sense is this: The captivity long ago foretold is coming against the wicked people; it is already near. The prophecy was composed under King Josiah. After he had been killed:

[Note: In Victorius’s edition: “after he had been killed, the devastation came.” Approximately four lines inserted here have been omitted.]

“Fear before the face of the Lord God, because the day of the Lord is near, because the Lord has prepared his victim; he has sanctified his invited ones.”

Complete devastation is coming, concerning which Ezekiel also says: “The end has come; the end has come” (Ezekiel 7:2), and so forth. “This victim pleases me; I have sanctified these victims for myself.”

This statement, “he has sanctified his invited ones,” can also be understood of the Babylonians, whom he calls even his servants for vengeance upon the people, to avenge his injury. “I have called Nebuchadnezzar my servant,” he says (Jeremiah 25:9). In the same book he calls him not only a servant but also a dove: “From before the sword of the dove” (ibid., 30).

According to the tropological interpretation, because the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, so that he may destroy their memory from the earth, and because the day of judgment is near—for compared with eternity, all the time of this age is short—or because the departure of individuals is near, let everyone fear and be silent, lest the face of the Lord, concerning which the saint says, “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:7), consume the hay, straw, and wood of sinners.

For the Lord has prepared his victim: the whole mystery of Leviticus, by which, through fire, the shedding of blood, and the true offering, those who are to be saved will be saved, and those who are called will be sanctified.

Some of our people understand the day of the Lord, his victim, and the sanctification of the invited ones as referring to the coming of the Savior, when the Lamb was sacrificed and the apostles and the others who were called through them were sanctified in his blood.

### (Verses 8–9)

“And it shall be on the day of the Lord’s sacrifice: I will visit the princes and the king’s sons, and all who are clothed in foreign clothing. And I will visit everyone who arrogantly steps over the threshold on that day, those who fill the house of the Lord their God with iniquity and deceit.”

The Septuagint: “And it shall be on the day of the Lord’s sacrifice, and I will take vengeance upon the princes, and upon the house of the king, and upon all who are clothed in foreign garments; and I will take vengeance upon all openly who are in the vestibules on that day, those who fill the house of the Lord their God with impiety and deceit.”

On the day of the Jewish captivity, when the whole people is to be sacrificed, the Lord will visit both the princes who drank strong drink in the morning and the king’s sons—or all those of royal descent, or specifically Josiah’s sons, whom we read were either killed or captured—and all who are clothed in foreign clothing, that is, those who, instead of worshiping God, venerated idols.

He will visit all who arrogantly step over the threshold on that day, that is, he will act against the proud, who with a certain arrogance and the haughtiness of rank ascend the steps of the temple and the threshold of the sanctuary.

Since in the place where we translated “those who arrogantly step over the threshold,” it can be understood according to the Hebrew as “those who leap over the threshold,” this too should be understood historically: “I will take vengeance upon those who,” according to the First Book of Kings, “do not tread upon the threshold of idols,” serving superstitions. They filled the house [variant: temple] of the Lord their God not only with the worship of idols but also with iniquity, crime, and every kind of falsehood, so that iniquity toward their subjects and falsehood toward their neighbors were added to their religious error.

[Note: Victorius has “let them step over the threshold”; then the manuscript of Regina: “it can be read.”]

But since we have begun to explain this tropologically as well, let us say that the Lord will visit, at the coming and passion of the Savior—that is, on the day of the sacrifice of his Son—the chief priests and priests of the Jewish people, and the royal house.

Until that time the kings of Judah from the line of David persisted, according to Jacob’s prophecy: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom it has been reserved, and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10).

After the Lord’s sacrifice, the kingdom was taken away from the Jews.

“And upon all,” he says, “who are clothed in foreign garments”—those who have withdrawn from God’s protection and clothing and have covered themselves with their own error.

“And I will take vengeance upon all openly who are in the vestibules,” that is, those who have gone out from the temple of God. Although they ought to be within, because of their sins they have gone outside and withdrawn from the Church of God, filling his temple with impiety and deceit.

Let this be understood of the Savior’s first coming.

Since we have already explained once concerning the consummation of the world and the day of judgment—which everyone interprets as the Lord’s day—

[Variant: “on the day.”]

we must know that at that time the Lord will visit the princes and the shepherds who eat the milk of the sheep and shear their wool, but do not care for the flock’s brokenness; and the king’s sons who boast that they are Christians and glory that they are sons of the king Christ; and all who are clothed in foreign garments.

The clothing of the king’s sons and princes is Christ, whom we receive as a garment in baptism, in accordance with: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14), and: “Put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (Colossians 3:12), and so forth.

In these passages we are commanded to put on the new heavenly person, according to our Creator, and to cast off the clothing of the old person together with his works (Ephesians 4).

Therefore, although we ought to be clothed in such garments, instead of compassion we put on cruelty; instead of patience, impatience; instead of righteousness, iniquity. In short, instead of virtues, vices—that is, instead of Christ, Antichrist.

Hence it is said of such a person: “He clothed himself with cursing as with a garment” (Psalm 108:18).

The Lord will also take vengeance most openly at his coming upon those who, although they ought to be in the Church with good works, have expelled themselves because of their thoroughly evil way of life and, delivered to Satan, linger in the vestibules—or rather not in the vestibules but before the vestibules—which is expressed more significantly in Greek as ἐπὶ τὰ πρόπυλα, “at the fore-gates.”

He will take vengeance upon all who fill the Church with various iniquities and sins, with impieties and deceit, and who mingle blood with blood.
