If we wish to understand this same passage concerning the souls of individuals, let us understand the princes and the house of the king as the *logismoi* (λογισμοί)—that is, thoughts and perceptions [variant adds: καὶ αἰσθήσεις, “and sensations”]—and the soul itself, which ought to be the dwelling of the king.

According to the preceding interpretation, let us also refer the foreign garments and everything that follows to each believer, who, although he ought to have been clothed with Christ and always to remain within, has covered himself with various garments of sins. Having gone out from the Church—that is, from the congregation of the saints—he has filled the temple of his body with iniquity and deceit.

### (Verse 10)

“And it shall be on that day,” says the Lord, “a voice of outcry from the Fish Gate, and a wailing from the Second Quarter, and great destruction from the hills.”

The Septuagint: “And it shall be on that day,” says the Lord, “a voice of outcry from the Gate of Those Who Are Pierced, and a wailing from the Second Quarter, and great destruction from the hills.”

On the day of the Lord’s sacrifice, when he stretches out his hand over Judah and over all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the hostile army besieges it, there will be a voice of outcry from the Fish Gate, a wailing from the Second Quarter, and great destruction from the hills.

They called it the Fish Gate because it led toward Diospolis and Joppa and was nearer to the sea than all the other roads of Jerusalem. Concerning it Ezra also reports: “The Fish Gate was built by the sons of Asnaa; they roofed it, and set up its doors, bolts, and bars” (2 Nehemiah 3:3).

When he says, “and a wailing from the Second,” he means the gate of the second wall in that same quarter. Concerning it we read in the Book of Kings: “And Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor [variant: Achobor], and Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the garments; and she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter” (2 Kings 22:14).

By “great destruction from the hills” he speaks of Mount Zion and the higher part of the city. For when the higher ground and the citadel of the city have been occupied, the descent down the slope is easier.

If we wish to understand the day threatened by the Lord as the day of judgment, at the time when the Ancient of Days will sit, the books will be opened, and the consciences of individuals revealed, then the “voice of outcry from the Gate of Those Who Are Pierced” will be fulfilled (Daniel 7).

The first gate will be that of the eyes, through which sins will be displayed before our eyes, and every spectacle and image of ancient crimes, vices, and lust will be brought into the open. Then what is written will truly occur: “Behold, the man and his works are before his face.”

Conscience will therefore torment him. After he has cried out in remorse from the first gate, that of the eyes, he will also wail from the second, which we can understand as the ears. Through these senses especially, through which vices had slipped in, their punishment will be felt, when we see what we have done and, instructed by speech and hearing the entire sequence of our sins, are driven into wailing.

Whatever had been lofty in us will be crushed, and because of blindness and deaf ears had been unknown to us.

Or else, when lofty words and learning coming from above crush and break us, what is written will be fulfilled: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Psalm 38:9), so that “a contrite spirit” may be a sacrifice to God (Psalm 50).

In us, who are human beings and have not committed sins so great that they can be compared with mountains, the hills are crushed. But in the devil and his angels, the heights of the mountains will be crushed.

Many think that, according to the history which we referred to the time of the Babylonians, this should be understood of the Savior’s first coming. At that time, because of the people’s immense sins and their resounding cry, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25), Jerusalem was surrounded by an army, and the crowd of mocking children was consumed by the two bears, namely Vespasian and Titus (2 Kings 2).

This interpretation certainly accords better with our faith, provided that we know that it can also fit the earlier history, or that the first captivity was a type of the second and complete overthrow of Jerusalem.

We must also observe the following: since *adagim* plainly means in Hebrew not “the Gate of Those Who Are Pierced” but “the Fish Gate,” allegorically the Fish Gate is in Jerusalem, through which the good fish are brought in after being separated from the bad, and they will mourn while the others enter who remained outside.

Or else, at the end of the world and at the consummation, those who did not preserve their baptism will mourn from the first gate, the Fish Gate; those who did not perform worthy repentance for their sins will mourn from the second. There will be great destruction upon the hills that were never bent down on account of their sins, so as to submit their necks and lament their crimes.

Through these two gates—baptism and repentance—there is either entrance into or return to Jerusalem, that is, to the Church of God.

### (Verse 11)

“Wail, inhabitants of the mortar, because the entire people of Canaan has fallen silent.”

[Note: On the authority of all the editions of Scripture, Victorius supplies “because.”]

The Septuagint: “Mourn, you who inhabit the cut-up place, because the entire people of Canaan has become like it.”

The mortar, which in Hebrew is called *makhthesh* (מכתש), and which Aquila translated as εἰς τὸν ὅλμον, “into the mortar,” must not be read with the first syllable short,

[Variant: “the first.”]

lest we think of a sphere, but with the syllable lengthened, so that we know it refers to a mortar in which grain is pounded: a hollow vessel also suited to medical use, in which specifically gruels are customarily pounded.

[Note: The manuscript of Regina has: “in which gruels are properly made.”]

Someone may say that he understands what the mortar signifies but wishes to know why it has been employed in the present passage.

Because the description of the captured city has already begun, and it says, “A voice of outcry from the Fish Gate, and a wailing from the Second, and great destruction from the hills,” the same order of description is now maintained, and the wailing of those who live in the valley of Siloam is mentioned.

The Scripture beautifully did not say, “you who live in the valley,” or “you who live in a hut,” but “you who live in the mortar.” Just as grain is pounded when a pestle strikes it from above, so the army rushing down upon you will descend from the Fish Gate, the Second Gate, and the hills.

It called the Jewish people the people of Canaan, in accordance with what we read in Daniel: “The seed of Canaan and not of Judah” (Daniel 13:56); and to Jerusalem: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezekiel 16:3); and in another place: “Canaan, in your hand is a balance of iniquity” (Hosea 12:7).

If we wish to construct the tropological interpretation according to both translations, those who dwell in the deepest dregs of sins and are submerged in the depths of their crimes are rightly driven to wailing and lamentation. They say: “I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance” (Psalm 68:2).

Hence it is added: “you who inhabit the cut-up place”—that is, the soul wounded by many iniquities, or the Church torn apart by schisms and heresies, lamenting children who have been killed at each wound.

When it says, “the entire people of Canaan has fallen silent,” or “has become like it,” it signifies that their blasphemy ceases on the day of judgment, and that the mouth which they raised on high and the tongue reaching down to the earth will fall silent in eternal silence.

Because Jerusalem sinned with sin, and therefore was made into a state of upheaval, the people are called Canaan, which is interpreted as “upheaval.”

Such a person cannot say, “He set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm 39:3), but is always uncertain, wavering, and in motion.

Therefore holy Noah, after awakening from sleep, imposed the name Canaan through a curse, saying: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be the servant of his brothers” (Genesis 9:25).

Sinners are not only made like Canaan; according to the quality and diversity of their sin, one is made like Pharaoh, another like the giant Nimrod.

Conversely, through good works and virtues—for the paths of the virtues are also diverse—one assumes the spirit of Abraham, another that of Moses, another that of Elijah. Hence the Apostle says: “Earnestly desire the better gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:31).

But the person who is perfect—according, nevertheless, to the perfection that human nature can receive—is marked by the likeness of God.

They all perished, wrapped in silver. The LXX: “All who were lifted up by silver perished.” He means those who placed their confidence in riches and possessed such great wealth that they considered themselves, as it were, wrapped and enclosed by their riches. Or, certainly, according to the LXX, those who had been lifted up into pride and despised the poor were, when wrath came, devastated. At the same time, consider that he did not say, “Those who are lifted up by silver will perish,” but that even now, before the day of punishment comes upon them, they have perished and collapsed in the very act of their pride, constantly thinking about their treasures and serving them. Whoever understands this, I think, will not greatly desire riches, in which such people will not perish, but have already perished because they were lifted up.

Nor should it be thought that only those have perished who were lifted up by silver; according to this definition, the one who boasts in the nobility of his family will also perish. The one who glories in dignities will perish; the one who is puffed up will perish; the one who glories in bodily strength will perish. The one who, softened by feminine languor, tends his hair, plucks out his hairs, smooths his skin, and adorns himself before a mirror will perish—this is properly the passion and madness of women.

But if anyone wishes to be lifted up and to glory in a holy pride, let him be lifted up with the apostles, when he is found worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus Christ; let him glory with the Apostle, who rejoiced in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance hope, and hope does not disappoint (Rom. V).

**(Verse 12.)** “And it shall come to pass at that time that I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will visit the men who are fixed in their dregs, who say in their hearts, ‘The Lord will do neither good nor evil.’” The LXX: “And it shall come to pass on that day that I will search Jerusalem with a lamp, and I will take vengeance on the men who despise their watches, and who say in their hearts, ‘The Lord will do neither good nor evil.’”

At the time and on the day of Jerusalem’s captivity, whether by the Babylonians or by the Romans—for she abandoned the law of the Lord and acted impiously against the Lord her Creator—the Lord will search all the hidden places of Jerusalem with a lamp, and will not allow anyone to escape unpunished. Let us read the histories of Josephus, and there we shall find it written that princes, kings, powerful men, and priests who had hidden themselves in fear of death were dragged even from sewers, caves, pits, and tombs.

“And I will visit,” he says, “upon those who trust in their bodies and in their strength,” which he calls διασυρτικῶς, that is, “dregs,” in a biting expression, or sins, in which they were completely fixed. They abolished providence and said that God was the author of neither good nor evil—that is, that he neither repaid good things to the good nor evil things to the wicked—but that everything was governed by the arbitrary power of fortune and carried along by uncertain chance.

At the consummation of the world, since the day of the Lord itself is understood here, the Lord will search Jerusalem—that is, his Church—with a lamp, and will take vengeance on contemptuous men who did not wish to keep their watches, that is, who despised the Lord’s commandments. Moreover, by rationalizing their sin, they blasphemed in their hearts, saying that doing good was of no benefit and doing evil was of no harm, because God would restore neither a reward for good works nor a punishment for evil ones.

Jerusalem, that is, the Church—which was formerly called Jebus, a name interpreted as “trampled”—was rightly called Jebus when she was trampled by the nations and was the sport of demons. But after the Lord’s peace began to dwell in her, and “his place was made in peace,” she received the name Jerusalem.

Since, therefore, in the final time, as we have often already said, iniquity will multiply, charity will grow cold, and the light of the sun will withdraw from Jerusalem, and such devastation will prevail that even God’s elect will scarcely be saved (Matt. XXIV), then the Lord will search out all vices in Jerusalem with the lamp of his word and reason, bring them into the open, and execute judgment and vengeance even for an idle word—not against sinners (for sin could also have obtained forgiveness), but against those who despise. Of them it is said in Habakkuk: “Look at the despisers, and behold” (Hab. I, 5); and elsewhere: “Why do you not look upon the despisers?” Then follows: “But the arrogant man and the despiser, a proud man,” and so forth.

Vengeance will be inflicted upon those who did not keep the Lord’s watches and say in their hearts: “The Lord will do neither good nor evil.” This does not mean that God does evil, but that the punishment seems evil to the one who suffers it. Otherwise the surgeon’s scalpel would also be evil because it cuts away wounds and amputates putrid flesh; and a father would be evil when he beats his son in order to correct him from his vices; and a teacher would be evil when he reproves a student in order to instruct him. For all discipline, in the present, does not seem to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it (Heb. XII, 11).

[Note: Martianay, with an awkward meaning, placed *alterum* before *veniat*; with the help of our manuscripts and the editors’ copies, we have expunged it. Soon afterward the Reginensis manuscript reads: “who always think about their treasures and preserve them; they have perished,” and so forth.]

[Note: For this it is given in the Reginensis manuscript: “The one who is puffed up by dignities will perish; the one who glories in strength,” and so forth.]

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “Vengeance shall be inflicted upon the proud.”]

**(Verses 13–14.)** “And their strength shall become plunder, and their houses shall become a desert. They shall build houses and shall not inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and shall not drink their wine. The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and exceedingly swift.” The LXX: “And their strength shall become booty, and their houses shall be destroyed. They shall build houses and shall not inhabit them, and they shall plant vineyards and shall not drink their wine, because the great day of the Lord is near—near and exceedingly swift.”

It is evident that, with respect to both captivities, their entire army was slaughtered, their houses demolished, and their fields and vineyards laid waste; nor did God’s patience delay any longer. But when they said to the prophets, “This will be for a later time, and for distant days,” the great day of the Lord came upon them, exceedingly near and swift.

According to the tropological interpretation, when the time of judgment comes, whether of each person’s death and departure from the world, then all their strength will become plunder, so that what had been strong in evil and had lifted itself up against the Lord may be turned, weakened and broken, toward what is better. It is as though someone were to plunder the strength of a robber, pirate, or thief and make them weak: their weakness benefits them, for their limbs, weakened after previously being misused, will cease from evil work.

As for what follows—“And their houses shall become a desert”—many in the Church build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity; it benefits such people for these houses to be destroyed. Let us read Leviticus, where a leprous house is ordered to be destroyed (Lev. XIV). Since the leprosy is persistent and spreads, its stones, timbers, and all its dust are ordered to be thrown outside the city into an unclean place.

Something similar is written at the beginning of Jeremiah: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms: to uproot, to dig under, to destroy, to build, and to plant” (Jer. I, 9–10). A very evil building is destroyed so that afterward a good building may be constructed; an iniquitous planting is uprooted so that another planting may be set in its place. Hence we read in Solomon: “It is better to dwell under the open sky than in a house of quarrels with iniquity, and in a new house” (Prov. XXI, 9).

Thus, like a good God, he destroys the houses of those who were fixed in their dregs and had said in their hearts, “The Lord will do neither good nor evil,” and he does not permit them to dwell in leprous and unclean houses. Nor does he allow them to drink wine from the vineyards they had planted. If they had planted the vineyard of Sorek, the whole choice and genuine vine, they would have drunk their wine and become drunk with the patriarch Noah and with Joseph at noon (Gen. IX and XLIII). But because they said, “The Lord will do neither good nor evil” (Deut. XXXII, 32–33), and their vine was from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot from Gomorrah—“their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them; the fury of dragons is their wine, and the incurable fury of asps” (Jer. IX, 23)—therefore they planted vineyards and shall not drink their wine.

Mystically, it is said of Sodom and Gomorrah that all their planting perished. If they had remained in what they had begun, so that they were like the paradise of God, and had not ended in evil so as to become like the land of Egypt, their planting would certainly have remained. Something similar is signified concerning the Egyptians in the Psalms: “He killed their vines with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost” (Ps. LXXVII, 47). As the most merciful God, he killed and overturned every Egyptian planting and all the little trees that, rooted in Egypt, bore bloody fruits, so that those who planted wrongly would not drink or eat their fruit.

The great and exceedingly swift day of the Lord is near, and no one can resist it. It is near either because of eternity, since nothing is long for him, or because of the greatness of the punishment, since for one who suffers, the punishment that must be inflicted never seems far away. Or it is near, as we said above, when we depart from the world and each person’s death brings about the consummation of the world; and it is not only near but also exceedingly swift, so that the swiftness of its coming is shown by the addition “exceedingly.”

[Note: Martianay’s text incorrectly had *longum*; our manuscripts, following Victorius, correct it.]

**(Verses 15–16.)** “The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man shall be afflicted there. That day is a day of wrath, that day a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and alarm against fortified cities and against the lofty corners.” The LXX: “The voice of the day of the Lord has been established as bitter and harsh; the strong man shall be afflicted. A day of wrath is that day, a day of tribulation and necessity, a day of misery and destruction, a day of darkness and whirlwind, a day of cloud and gloom, a day of trumpet and shouting against fortified cities and against the lofty corners.”

In accordance with what precedes, understand this either of the Babylonian captivity or of the final captivity they suffered at the hands of the Romans, over which the Lord also wept for Jerusalem, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you” (Matt. XXIII, 37), and so forth. Truly, the vengeance demanded from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar (II Chron. XXIV), and finally for the Son of God, when they said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” came upon them as a bitter day, because they had provoked the Lord to bitterness. It was a day established by the Lord, on which not any weak person but the strongest men would be crushed, and wrath would come upon them to the end. They had often endured the Lord’s wrath before, but that wrath had not been the wrath of consummation and the end (Matt. XXVII, 25).

Why is it necessary now to describe the calamities they endured in both captivities, how those who rejected the Lord’s light wandered in darkness and gloom, and how those who refused to hear the trumpets of the solemn days heard the shout—or, according to another reading, the blast—of warriors?

As for the fortified cities and lofty corners of Judaea that have been utterly destroyed, I think the judgment belongs more to the eyes than to the ears. Especially for us who now live in this province, it is possible to see and to verify what has been written. We scarcely see small traces of ruins in great cities that once existed.

At Shiloh, where the tabernacle and the ark of the Lord’s covenant stood, scarcely the foundations of the altar are pointed out. That city of Saul, Gibeah, has been destroyed down to its foundations (Josh. XVIII). Ramah, Beth-horon, and the other distinguished cities built by Solomon are shown as small villages.

Let us read Josephus and the prophecy of Zephaniah; we shall see the history of the former confirmed in the latter. This must be said not only of the captivity but also of the present day: after the killing of the servants and finally of the Son of God, the faithless inhabitants are forbidden, except for mourning, to enter Jerusalem. If they wish to weep over the ruin of their city, they buy the permission at a price, so that those who once bought Christ’s blood may buy their own tears; not even their weeping is free.

On the day when Jerusalem was captured and destroyed by the Romans, one may see a mourning people come, decrepit little women and old men covered with rags and years, displaying the Lord’s wrath in their bodies and attire. A crowd of wretched people gathers, and while the Lord’s gallows gleams, and his ἀνάστασις—“resurrection”—shines, and the banner of the cross flashes from the Mount of Olives, the miserable people mourn the ruins of their temple and yet are not objects of pity. Tears still run down their cheeks; their arms are livid; their hair is scattered; and the soldier demands payment so that they may be permitted to weep longer.

When one sees these things, can anyone doubt the day of tribulation and distress, the day of calamity and misery, the day of darkness and gloom, the day of cloud and whirlwind, the day of trumpet and alarm? For they even have trumpets in their mourning, and, according to the prophecy, the voice of festivity has been turned into lamentation. They howl over the ashes of the sanctuary, over the destroyed altar, and over the once-fortified cities and the lofty corners of the temple, from which they once threw James, the brother of the Lord.

Let this be said concerning the captivity of the Jews. But if, as above, we refer the day of the Lord to the consummation of the world or to each person’s departure from life, the interpretation will be clear: the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter, full of necessity and wrath, and the strong man will be afflicted there. Even those who are holy will indeed be saved, but only as through fire.

That day is a day of tribulation, distress, calamity, and misery, on which they will say, “Woe to us, for we have become miserable.” It is a day of darkness: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light” (John III, 20); and it is necessary that darkness follow the one who hates the light.

It will be a day of cloud and whirlwind, for the storm of the Lord will come upon him, together with the blast of the trumpet, which the Apostle signifies when he says, “At the last trumpet” (I Cor. XV, 52). It will be a day of trumpet and alarm against the fortified cities that they had built for themselves, like Cain, through the multitude of their sins; and against the lofty corners, that is, perverse works deviating from the straight way of the Lord.

Hence the Pharisees are also reproved by the Savior as ὑποκριταί, “hypocrites,” because they pray—or, according to another reading, worship—in the corners of the streets (Matt. VI). For the straight way leading to paradise is narrow and confined, the way that leads to life. But the broken, winding way, full of corners, broad and spacious, leads to death (Matt. VII).

At the same time, amid the Lord’s words of severity, observe his mercy: the day is bitter, a day of wrath, a day of tribulation, and a day of trumpet and alarm precisely so that the badly fortified cities and perverse corners may be destroyed.

**(Verses 17–18.)** “And I will afflict men, and they shall walk like blind men, because they have sinned against the Lord; and their blood shall be poured out like earth, and their bodies like dung. Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath, and in the fire of his jealousy the whole earth shall be devoured, because he will make a complete end, with haste, of all the inhabitants of the earth.” The LXX: “And I will afflict men, and they shall walk like blind men, because they have sinned against the Lord; and he will pour out their blood like dust, and their flesh like ox dung”—according to another reading, “buffalo dung”—“and their silver and their gold will not be able to rescue them on the day of the Lord’s wrath, and in the fire of his jealousy the whole earth shall be consumed; for he will make a complete and hasty end upon all the inhabitants of the earth.”

According to the preceding interpretation, it is not difficult to say that Jerusalem suffered these things because of the Lord’s cross. The Lord’s visitation withdrew from her, and all the people throughout Judaea were afflicted; because of the magnitude of the oppression, they walked like blind men, not knowing what to do. They suffered these things because they sinned against the Lord—that is, against the Son of God.

Since they shed the blood of the prophets and the blood of Christ, their blood was poured out like earth throughout the entire region, and their bodies remained unburied, like dung upon the face of the ground. Their wealthy men, too, who had amassed silver and gold through extreme iniquity, could not be delivered by their riches from the day of the Lord’s wrath. For the fire of the Lord’s jealousy, kindled against them, devoured the whole province.

The intervening time was not long. For forty-two years after the Lord’s crucifixion, Jerusalem was surrounded by an army, and her destruction was accomplished with haste—not only hers, but also that of all the inhabitants of the land of Judaea.

At the consummation, whether of the world or of each individual, all men will be afflicted who remained merely human and died like men. They will walk like blind men because they have lost the light of the virtues and will have no place for repentance. They will suffer these things because they sinned against the Lord. For if the Lord is justice, truth, holiness, and the other virtues, whoever acted unjustly, lied, and pursued prostitutes and vices sinned against the Lord.

But what follows—“And their blood shall be poured out like earth, and their bodies like ox dung”—seems absurd if we say that at the resurrection of the dead, at the consummation of the world and the judgment, blood will be poured out and bodies will lie like dung. Therefore the statement made to Noah must be understood differently: “And I will require your blood, the blood of your souls, from the hand of every beast, and from the hand of man; and I will require the soul of man from the hand of his brother. Whoever sheds man’s blood, his blood shall be shed in return” (Gen. IX, 5–6). It is ridiculous to believe that this refers to the resurrection, and it cannot stand as a statement about the present life.

[Note: This exposition of Jerome’s should be recalled by the Fathers of the Council of Trosle, who cite it in chapter 13.]

How many have shed blood, yet their blood was not poured out? Others killed a man by poison or by hanging, and yet, although the man died, his blood was not poured out. How, then, will the Lord pour out their blood in repayment, when the one who killed did not shed blood?

[Note: Erasmus and Marianus omit here the two Greek words τὸ and αἶτος [sic; presumably αἷμα], which the manuscript copies retain even in Greek characters, as Regius no. 3991, which reads: “The blood of man, τὸ ζωτικὸν αἶτος.” *Τὸ ζωτικὸν αἶτος* is the dwelling-place and seat of life, as Scripture says of blood: “For the soul of all flesh is in the blood” (Lev. XVII, 14).]

The blood of man, therefore, τὸ ζωτικὸν αἶτος [sic; presumably αἷμα]—that is, the vital principle by which he is animated, sustained, and lives—must be understood. Whoever pours it out, whether through scandal or through perverse teaching, will have it poured out from him on the day of judgment; that is, he will be compelled to lose what he seemed to possess as his vital element.

According to this understanding of blood, flesh is also to be understood. Isaiah says of it: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. XL, 6). And in Genesis the Lord says: “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3). The Apostle speaks of both: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption inherit the incorruption of God” (I Cor. XV, 50).

On the day of consummation, whether general or particular, all the blood that has been poured out will cry to the Lord and appear in the midst; and the works of blood and of earthly things will lie like dust and dung. The rich will not be able to deliver themselves by silver and gold from the day of wrath, while they hear the one who dies say: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20).

This does not mean that we deny that gold and silver can deliver the rich from death: “A man’s riches are the ransom of his soul” (Prov. XIII, 8). Rather, they cannot deliver them at that time, when necessity compels them to leave their riches behind.

For the whole earth and everything earthly will be devoured by the Lord’s jealousy. When he says “jealousy,” understand that the Lord still loves. For if he did not love the human soul, he would never be jealous over it; and, in the likeness of a husband, he would not avenge the sin of his wife if he did not love her, nor would he become angry over her adultery.

The Lord will do this with haste to all the inhabitants of the earth, to those who have given themselves entirely to the earth and have not been foreigners and pilgrims, like the righteous man who says: “I am a stranger in the earth, and a pilgrim like all my fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII, 13). Again, unwilling to dwell longer in the tabernacle of the flesh, he testifies in a tearful voice: “Woe is me, for my pilgrimage has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX, 5). For we who are in this bodily tabernacle groan and complain: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII, 24).

**(Chapter II—Verses 1–2.)** “Come together, gather yourselves, nation not beloved, before the decree brings forth the day that passes like dust; before the anger of the Lord’s fury comes upon you; before the day of the Lord’s indignation comes upon you.” The LXX: “Gather together and be joined together, uneducated nation, before you become like a flower that passes in a day; before the wrath of the Lord comes upon you; before the day of the wrath of the Lord’s fury rushes upon you.”

After the description of the evils that will come on the day of the Lord—in accordance with the twofold interpretation of the captivity that we mentioned above—the people are summoned to repentance. It is said to them: “Come together and gather yourselves,” or, as it is written in the LXX, “be joined together,” that is, in accordance with the Apostle, be bound together by the bond of charity. You are a nation not beloved, unworthy of God’s love; or, according to the LXX, an uneducated nation, of which it is said in Deuteronomy: “A foolish people and not wise” (Deut. XXXII, 6). And in Jeremiah: “In vain I struck your children; they did not receive discipline” (Jer. II, 30).

This is before what has been prophesied takes place, before the effect follows the command—an effect that will come as easily as dust passing by—before the Lord’s fury is completed against you.

At the same time, observe God’s mercy. It would have been enough for the wise to describe the attack of the coming evils. But because he does not wish to inflict punishments and only wishes to terrify those who will suffer them, he himself summons them to repentance, so that he may not do what he has threatened.

In general, the entire multitude of believers and those who are now called the people of God is gathered into the Church, and it is said to them: “Come together into the Church; join yourselves to one another in charity and peace, O uneducated nation, which does not wish to receive God’s discipline or possess knowledge of his commandments, but delights in riches, bodily health, the beauty of this world, and the pleasures of the flesh,” which passes like a flower that withers in a single day.

Therefore I say to you: “Come together; join yourselves to one another,” lest, when the time of judgment comes and all your glory has passed away, you wish to repent at a time when there will be no place for repentance but only for punishments.

Someone may ask how this can be understood of each person departing from the world. It is therefore said to each individual: “You who are occupied with the affairs of the world and run about in different directions, return to the Church of the saints. Join yourself to the life and assembly of those whom you see pleasing God. Gather the loosened members of your soul, which do not cohere with one another, into a single structure of wisdom; cling to its embrace; and hear, in a mystical sense: ‘Strengthen the weak hands; make firm the feeble knees’ (Isa. XL, 7). Do not glory in the good things of the flesh or in its flower, which passes away. ‘All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever.’”

We may also use this chapter for the present time. Whenever we see someone devoted to the honors of the world and occupied with gathering riches, coming to the Church rarely or never, we may say to him: “Gather yourself and join yourself to the people of God, you who do not hear the Lord’s commandments, before your glory passes away, before the day of the Lord’s fury comes upon you.”

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript has *gens non inerudita*, “an uneducated nation,” contrary to the Greek; shortly afterward it reads *pertransiens diei*, “passing of the day.”]

[Note: For *colligamini*, the same manuscript has *sociamini*, “join yourselves,” a reading that Jerome himself seems to approve in the Commentary.]

[Note: The manuscript adds *deditum*, “devoted,” after “honors of the world.”]

**(Verses 3–4.)** “Seek the Lord, all you meek of the earth, who have practiced his judgment. Seek righteousness; seek meekness, if somehow you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury. For Gaza shall be destroyed, and Ascalon shall become a desert. Azotus shall be expelled at noon, and Accaron shall be uprooted.” The LXX: “Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth; practice judgment, seek righteousness, and answer with it, so that you may be protected on the day of the Lord’s wrath, because Gaza shall be plundered, and Ascalon shall become a desert; Azotus shall be cast out at noon, and Accaron shall be uprooted.”

The “humble of the earth” are called humble not because of the humility that signifies virtue, but because they have been humbled by sins and cannot say with Christ: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.” And elsewhere the word is directed to the holy man: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find grace before God” (Eccl. III).

But the one who has been humbled by sins, weighed down by the consciousness of his offenses, and says, “My iniquities, like a heavy burden, have weighed me down” (Ps. XXXVII, 5), must hear: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28).

Let this be said at the beginning according to the LXX interpreters. But according to the Hebrew there is another meaning. For it is said to the saints: “You who keep my commandments, who are placed on earth and know that everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, who have imitated my meekness and have practiced judgment, seek the Lord in your meekness.”

And if you wish to know who this Lord is, “seek the righteous; seek the meek.” For the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John V, 22), who will judge justly. Since you are meek, therefore seek the meek one, so that whatever is lacking in your meekness may be supplied by him who is the source of meekness.

This, however, I say to you: “If somehow you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury”—that is, if perhaps, because you have sought the Lord and practiced his righteousness, you may be able to avoid the wrath of the coming day and escape the captivity that will be inflicted upon the Jewish people either by Nebuchadnezzar or by the Romans.

But if he doubts concerning those who have done his judgments, saying—or, according to another reading, “they say”—“If somehow you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury,” what will become of sinners? Such devastation will come upon the land of Judaea, and so exalted a Babylonian army will ascend here, that the same captivity will seize even the most powerful cities of the Philistines, which had always resisted you in equal contest.

Gaza will be destroyed, Ascalon will be reduced to solitude, and they will lead Azotus into captivity—not by theft but by war, that is, in broad daylight and through open victory. Accaron, whose name means “uprooting,” will suffer what its name signifies: it will be uprooted.

This is according to the literal sense and the Hebrew truth. According to the Septuagint, however, the humble of the earth, of whom we spoke above, are commanded to practice judgment and seek righteousness, which I think is none other than Christ. And because everyone who seeks will find (Matt. VII, 8), they are to answer to others what they have found—that is, they are to teach others. For “what benefit are hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure in either case?” (Eccl. XX, 32).

This, he says, I command you, so that you may be protected on the day of the Lord’s wrath, whether at the consummation of the world or at each person’s departure from the world. For Gaza, Ascalon, Azotus, and Accaron will suffer different punishments.

Gaza is interpreted as “his strength.” Therefore all who applaud themselves in bodily strength and worldly power, and say with the devil, “By strength I will act,” will be plundered on the day of the Lord’s wrath and reduced to nothing.

Ascalon, which is called “weighed” or “the fire that kills,” will, when the day of the Lord’s wrath comes, experience the measure of its crime and will be pressed down by the same weight with which it acted. Because it burned with the desire to shed blood, scandalized many souls, and fulfilled the words, “The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. V, 7), it will not be plundered like Gaza but, reduced to solitude, will be burned to ashes by the fires of Gehenna.

Azotus too, which in Hebrew is called ESDOD [Hebrew form not legible in the supplied text], and in our language means “the fire of generation,” will be laid waste in broad daylight. For it burned with lust and raged in the fire of generation.

Because all adulterers are like an oven, and their hearts are like one (Hos. VII), and they have been wounded by burning arrows, they will be cast out not in darkness or in a hidden judgment but at noon—that is, when the saints receive their full brightness—into darkness, and they will have no share in the company of the saints.

But Accaron, which is interpreted as “sterility” or “uprooting,” because it bore no fruits and uprooted many through the perversity of its teaching, will itself also be uprooted.

Understand all these variations in relation to the vices and sins of souls, and understand that on the day of judgment fire will test what each person’s work is (I Cor. III).

[Note: The printed editions read διασυρμικῶς; Marianus adduces διασυρμός in support of that reading, since it means “mockery.” But the reading of the manuscripts, which we have followed as preferable and more responsive to Jerome’s meaning, must be retained: διασυρτικῶς, that is, “in a biting expression,” is how he says that the bodies or strengths in which the proud trust were called “dregs.” Our manuscripts and Martianay’s likewise read διασυρτικῶς; Victorius preferred διασυρμικῶς.]

[Note: In Martianay the negative particle is lacking in the quotation, “Why do you not look upon the despisers?”]

[Note: At Jeremiah 1:10, another reading omits *this day*.]

[Note: At Zephaniah 1:15–16, alternative readings are “blast” for “shout,” “which” for “who,” and “we see” for “we shall see.”]

[Note: At Zephaniah 1:17, the Vulgate adds “their” after “gold”; the LXX alternative is “buffalo dung” for “ox dung”; another reading has “of the Lord” for “against the Lord”; and another omits “of God” in “the incorruption of God.”]

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads, “It will be poured out from him also, that which seemed to him …”]

[Note: Victorius supplies “of the Lord” after “jealousy,” and reads “loves” for “loved” and “becomes angry” for “would become angry.”]

[Note: In the LXX heading at Chapter II, the Reginensis manuscript reads “a nation not uneducated,” contrary to the Greek, and shortly afterward “passing of the day.” For “be joined together,” the same manuscript has “associate yourselves,” a reading Jerome himself seems to approve.]

[Note: At Chapter II, another reading has “to us” for “to one another”; and another adds “devoted” after “honors of the world.”]

[Note: At Zephaniah 2:3, Martianay omitted *justly*, restored from the manuscripts and previously by Victorius as necessary: the Son “will judge justly.” The Reginensis manuscript omits “you have practiced”; it then reads “of God” rather than “of the day.” Alternative readings have “who” for “because,” “they doubt” for “he doubts,” and “they say” for “saying.”]

[Note: At Zephaniah 1:16, an alternative reads “deviating from the straight way” for “deviating from the straight way of the Lord,” and “pray” for “worship.”]

[Note: Jerome himself condemns this interpretation in his Commentary on Amos I: “Azotus, that is, Asdod, the fire of the breast, or of the uncle.” Some, reading *Dor* incorrectly for *Dod*, think it means “the fire of generation.” In fact, “generation” among the Hebrews is called *Dor*, not *Dod*, and the shift of D to R is an easy error, since, as Jerome himself notes, the letters differ only by a stroke. See the Book of Names concerning Jesus in *Asdod* and *Asoth*. Victorius, conversely, notes that if this word signifies “the fire of generation,” the Hebrew manuscripts should be corrected, and the letter [the supplied text is lacunose here] should be substituted. Yet in Zechariah IX, when he explains the same word as “fire of a kind,” “fire of an uncle,” or “fire of the breast,” he shows that he had both readings, so that the word could be written both with [the supplied Hebrew letter is absent] and with [the supplied Hebrew letter is absent]. For generation is called [Hebrew term absent], uncle [Hebrew term absent], and breast [Hebrew term absent].]

## (Verses 5–7)

Woe to you who inhabit the seacoast, [Col. 1360A] nation of the destroyers: the word of the Lord is against you, Canaan, land of the Philistines; and I will destroy you, so that there will be no inhabitant [Vulgate: “no settler”]. And the seacoast shall become a resting-place for shepherds and sheepfolds for flocks. And the seacoast shall belong to the remnant of the house of Judah; there they shall pasture. In the houses of Ashkelon they shall lie down at evening, because the Lord their God will visit them and turn away their captivity.

**The Septuagint:** Woe to you who inhabit the seacoast, [Note: [Col. 1360D] In the Regina manuscript, “settlers of the Cretans,” here and below; the Greek has πάροικοι Κρητῶν, “settlers of the Cretans.” A little later it reads “pasture of shepherds” instead of “pasture of flocks,” corresponding to the Greek νομὴ ποιμνίων.] settlers of the Cretans: the word of the Lord is against you, Canaan, land of the foreigners, and I will destroy you from your habitation. And Crete shall become pasture for flocks and a sheepfold for sheep. And the seacoast shall belong to those who remain of the house of Judah; upon them they shall pasture, and in the houses of Ashkelon they shall lodge in the afternoon [Col. 1360B] from the presence of the sons of Judah, because the Lord their God will visit them and turn away their captivity.

As far as the historical interpretation is concerned, it is not difficult to explain, since above he had said: “Gaza shall be destroyed,” and “Ashkelon shall be a desert”; “Azotus they shall drive out at noon,” and “Ekron shall be uprooted.” Having named the four great cities of Palestine, he now shows that the word of the Lord is spoken generally against the province itself, and that this is foretold to it: “Woe to you who inhabit the seacoast,” when the Babylonian comes; for those who inhabit the region beside the sea will also perish and be removed. That the land of the Philistines is the land of Canaan is beyond doubt.

“And I will destroy you,” he says, “so that there will be no inhabitant.” You will come into such desolation—you who rejoiced in the overthrow of Judaea—that all your very strongly fortified cities will become sheepfolds for shepherds. And after the Lord has visited his people [Col. 1360C], caused them to return under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and they have built the temple and restored Jerusalem, you will be so uncultivated and so covered with thorns and nettles that shepherds from the remnants of the Jews will rest at afternoon in Ashkelon, and in the city once renowned they will make their flocks lie down. This will happen because the Lord will visit his people and turn away their captivity. Whether this has happened or not, God knows. For it is not now our purpose to weave together the truth of the historical account, but to make known to our people what we have received from the Hebrews.

According to the spiritual sense and the translation of the Septuagint, however, the passage is difficult to understand, especially since they also disagree in their interpretation. Where we translated “nation of the destroyers,” they said “settlers of the Cretans.” What is written in Hebrew, GOI [Col. 1360D] CHORETHIM (גוי כרתים), they read as GAR, that is, “settler,” in place of GOI, meaning “nation”; and for CHORETHIM, which means “of the destroyers,” they supposed the name of the island of Crete. Finally, Aquila and the Fifth Edition translated it as **a destructive nation**,

[Note: [Col. 1360D] The printed editions changed the threefold noun ἔθνος found in the manuscript copies to the noun γένος. Although the latter has the same meaning, the word placed by Jerome should not for any reason have been discarded. ἔθνος ὀλέθριον means “a pestilential nation” and “a pernicious people.” MART.—In place of ὀλέθριον, the Regina codex prefers ὀλεθριασθρυῶν; it is for the discerning reader to extract something sound from this word. In place of ἔθνος, γένος was consistently found elsewhere.]

ἔθνος ὀλέθριον, “a destructive nation.” Theodotion likewise has ἔθνος ὀλεθρίας, “a nation of destruction,” and Symmachus has ἔθνος ὀλεθρευόμενον, “a nation being destroyed”; all of these agree with our translation.

Again, where we said, “And the seacoast shall become a resting-place for shepherds,” and all the interpreters agree with this translation, the Septuagint reads: “And Crete shall become pasture for a flock, and a sheepfold for sheep.” Therefore, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, and holding to the path once begun in the Vulgate edition, we ask whether we have read the name of Crete elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures. And, if I am not mistaken, the answer is readily available: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies. This testimony is true” (Titus 1:12–13).

Those who waver and are carried about by every wind of doctrine, in the deception of men and the craftiness of error—when they ought to dwell in the land of confession, that is, in the land of Judaea—preferred to be settlers [Col. 1361B] of the Cretans, who are battered here and there by the different waves of the sea, [Note: [Col. 1361D] The Corybantes were priests of Rhea or Cybele who, seized by sacred frenzy, beat cymbals. They are said first to have occupied Mount Ida in Phrygia and afterward to have sailed to Crete. This now seems to be confirmed by Jerome, who also read aere Corybantio, “with Corybantian bronze,” not Corybantino, “Corybantine,” as the older editions retain. See “Corybantian bronze” in Virgil, Aeneid 3. MART.] and who sound with Corybantian bronze; and, according to the Apostle, they are “like a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1).

And because they are settlers of the Cretans, the word of God—that is, the threat—is directed against them. They are called the land of Canaan, always in fluctuation and always in motion, and the land of the foreigners: for, alienated from God, they move about on the seacoast and in the region of Crete.

The word of God, then, is made to them either at the consummation and end of the world, or daily through ecclesiastical men who can say with the Apostle, “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3). They are to be cast out of Crete and destroyed from their former habitations; and that region which previously contained a lost flock is to begin to be a sheepfold for the sheep of Christ. And Judah—that is, true confession—is to dwell on the seacoast.

When the world has already begun to be at evening, and when, of the many who are called, few are chosen, and those who are now called the remnant of the house of Judah have fed those who were previously pastured in the sea, in Crete, and in falsehood, they will turn aside into the houses of Ashkelon—that is, to the place from which previously the fire of the devil and the blood of the slain flowed. For Ashkelon is interpreted as “fire of the murderer.”

This will happen because the Lord will visit his people. Those who were previously easily captured by the sophistries of heretics, coming as if from captivity, will conquer their adversaries and dwell in their tents.

As for what is read in the Septuagint, “From the presence of the sons of Judah,” we marked it beforehand with an obelus. For it is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any of the interpreters, and it disturbs the context and the meaning of the chapter [Col. 1361D]—not because it would be difficult to construct a sense with this phrase inserted in some fashion, but because we once decided to follow the truth of the translation and the judgment of the more learned reader rather than that of the common crowd.

## (Verses 8 and following)

I have heard the reproach of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon, by which they reproached my people and magnified themselves against their borders. Therefore [Col. 1362A], as I live, says the Lord God [Vulgate omits “God”] of hosts, the God of Israel: Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah—dryness of thorns and heaps of salt, and a desert forever. The remnant of my people shall plunder them, and the survivors of my nation shall possess them. This shall happen to them because of their pride, because they blasphemed and magnified themselves against the people of the Lord of hosts. The Lord will be terrible against them; he will weaken all the gods of the earth, and men shall worship him, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations.

**The Septuagint:** I have heard the reproach of Moab and the insults of the sons of Ammon, by which they reproached my people and magnified themselves against my borders. Therefore, as I live, says the Lord [Alternative: “the Lord God”] of hosts, the God of Israel: Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah, [Col. 1362B] and Damascus shall be abandoned like a heap of a threshing-floor, and shall be destroyed forever. Those who remain of my people shall plunder them, and the survivors of my nation shall possess them. This shall happen to them because of their insult, because they reproached and magnified themselves against the Lord Almighty. The Lord shall be manifest against them, and he shall destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth; and each person shall worship him from his own place, all the islands of the nations.

With the exception of the prophet Daniel, who often sees visions of the four kingdoms and sets forth their differences under one image after another (Daniel 8), Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel follow this practice: after a vision concerning Judah against the other nations surrounding it, they turn the prophecy against those nations and announce what is to happen to them according to the distinctive characteristics of each, lingering for a longer time in their description [Col. 1362C]. The prophet Zephaniah now does the same, although briefly and in the same order.

After the Philistines—against whom a threat had already preceded—he says: “Gaza shall be destroyed, and Ashkelon shall be a desert; Azotus they shall drive out at noon, and Ekron shall be uprooted.” Now a prophecy is woven against Moab and the sons of Ammon, or, as the Septuagint adds, against Damascus, which is called Aram in Isaiah (chapter 17), because they had supplied assistance to Nebuchadnezzar, devastated Judah, trampled upon its sanctuary, overturned its temple, and, after subjugating the people of Israel, blasphemed the Lord.

For Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, after overthrowing the cities of the Jews, oppressed the other nations as well. Thus it happened that those who had insulted the people of God were themselves pressed by the same distress of evils and had Judah as a fellow slave—the people whom they had thought they held in subjection.

Therefore, before the captivity came, while Josiah was still king and Jerusalem and the temple had not yet been overthrown, the prophecy was directed against those who insulted, so that the former evils of the people of God might be lifted by the evil of the other nations [Alternative: “by evils”].

“I have heard,” he says, “the reproach of Moab”—which is now called Areopolis—and “the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon,” whose city is itself called Philadelphia, the second city of Arabia after Bosra. In these words they reproached my people and, after expelling the Jews, enlarged their borders in their land.

Therefore, because they blasphemed me and reproached my people, I, the Lord of hosts, who am able to accomplish what I threaten, and the God of Israel, who in my people myself suffer injury, will make Moab like Sodom and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah.

Let us read visions of this sort in Isaiah and Jeremiah, and we shall find there the same things that we now read here. “Dryness of thorns and heaps of salt, and a desert forever”—for which the Septuagint, I do not know with what intention, translated “Damascus uprooted and abandoned,” [Col. 1363B] unless, if I am not mistaken, they were deceived by the ambiguity of the word.

For “dryness,” which in Hebrew is called MAMASAC (ממשק), has, if the first letter MEM is changed and DALETH is taken in its place, the same remaining letters as “Damascus,” and it can be read for the preceding word as DAMASEC.

The question is how these cities—that is, Moab and the sons of Ammon—were reduced to the condition of Sodom and Gomorrah, and how, like the dryness of thorns and heaps of salt, they were not to be rebuilt forever [Col. 1363C].

That they were laid waste like Sodom and Gomorrah presents no difficulty to explain. But the statement that follows, “They shall be deserted forever,” may be interpreted either as the destruction of their kingdom—for afterward, being overthrown by the Chaldeans, they lost their kingdom, and subsequently were held first by the Antiochi and then by the Ptolemies, and finally bowed their necks to the Roman Empire—or else it must be understood as spoken hyperbolically, ὑπερβολικῶς.

[Note: [Col. 1363D] All manuscript codices read with an initial L, that is, Lolam, not olam as in the earlier printed books. From this we infer that there was a variant Hebrew reading at this place. For Jerome did not read ad olam in his Hebrew exemplar, but Leolam, with a prefixed Lamed. Unless we should say that the holy Doctor did not pay attention to the context but to the meaning of the word Leolam: he himself translated “forever,” which certainly indicates that he read ad olam in Hebrew, or perhaps ad lolam. Let impartial and learned readers judge these matters. MART.]

For LOLAM (לולם) signifies both eternity and an age; and from this it can be understood as one age, as a certain period of time, or as a single generation.

“Those who remain of the people of Israel shall lay them waste, and shall possess the Chaldeans who once blasphemed and supplied assistance.” This shall happen to them because of their pride, because they blasphemed and magnified themselves against the people of the Lord of hosts. The Lord of hosts will be terrible against them, and his terror will not kill the proud; he will not shed the blood of those who blasphemed, but he will destroy and weaken all their idols.

Thus those who were previously held by error and did not perceive the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 1364D] The Regina manuscript reads, “and did not perceive the Lord through his benefits.”] benefits, pressed by the necessity of evils, will know that idols are of no use, and all the islands of the nations will worship him, each from his own place.

Thus far according to the Hebrew.

Now let us return to the Septuagint interpreters and compel the Jews, who follow only the historical account, to explain to us when Moab and the sons of Ammon became like Sodom and Gomorrah, like heaps [Col. 1364A] of salt, and deserted forever. They ought to point out the sulfurous rains, [Note: [Col. 1364D] The same manuscript reads, “sulfurous rains, the earth turned into ash and embers,” without the word “vineyards.”] the earth turned into ashes and embers, and the sea overflowing above the wells formerly full of salt, which is now called the Dead Sea. They should also show when the Jews plundered them and when the remnants of the nations of Israel possessed them.

Or what kind of indignation of the Lord is it that, because of their blasphemy and insults, he should weaken and destroy them—not Moab and Ammon only, but the whole earth—so that all the islands of the nations may worship him, each from his own place? This would rather be granted to the blasphemers as a benefit, so that they might return from error to salvation.

If they wish to say that, after the return from Babylon, these nations were subjected to the people of Israel, we shall first demand the authority of the Scriptures by which they may prove that this happened. Then, when they are wholly unable to demonstrate it, we shall concede it to them for the sake of argument and say: “Granted that what you say happened. What justice would there be in blaspheming the grandfathers and reproaching the great-grandfathers, and then exacting punishment from their grandchildren?” For the sentence previously stated in the Law—that the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the sons to the third and fourth generation (Exodus 20)—has been dissolved by Ezekiel: “As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken; but the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20).

At the same time, observe that what was said is a proverb, and that it does not mean what the surface of the letter seems to express.

If it is unjust to repay grandchildren for what their grandfathers committed, how much more unjust is it, because of the stupidity of the Jews, to expect this very thing to happen at the consummation of the world, when not their Christ, as they suppose, but the Antichrist is to come.

Whenever they are pressed by the historical account to show that what was said has been fulfilled, they immediately leap forward to the future times of Christ. Everything they cannot explain they postpone for many ages, and they say that Moab, the sons of Ammon, Egypt, the Philistines, and Idumaea—who now insult the Jews—are to be punished at that time.

Let us therefore ask them why God punishes these particular nations and not the whole world, in which the Jews are scattered far and wide. If Moab deserves correction because it insults the Jews, and the sons of Ammon and the other surrounding nations likewise deserve it, why is Gaul not corrected? Why are the Britains not included in the threat? Why are the Spains exempt from punishment? For what reason is nothing said about Italy? Why is Africa passed over in silence? And, to say it once and for all: since the whole world holds the Jews captive, what so great crime have only the nations surrounding them committed that they alone should be named above all?

This is directed against the Jews and constitutes a general [Note: [Col. 1364D] Victor inserts “their.”] explanation wherever, in all the prophets, some prophecy is uttered against the nations.

Now we shall also establish from the very order of Scripture what we said above: that Damascus is not found in the Hebrew, nor in any other interpreter. [Col. 1365A]

After saying, “I have heard the reproach of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon,” he then added: “For Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah.” Therefore, what follows—“And Damascus shall be desolate, like a heap of a threshing-floor”—ought to have been preceded by some statement about Damascus, so that just as he had said of the two nations, “Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah,” after previously describing their sins, he might likewise have described the reproaches or blasphemies of Damascus, so that he might afterward appear properly to inflict punishment upon it.

Moreover, the very expression “like a heap of a threshing-floor,” which in Greek is said to be ὡς θιμωνία ἁλός, “like a heap of salt,” we think the Septuagint translated from ἁλός, that is, “salt.” But inexperienced people, thinking that θιμωνία meant a heap of grain or produce, added two letters, ω and ν, and, in accordance with the following idea of grain, placed ἅλωνος, that is, “of a threshing-floor,” in its place.

[Note: [Col. 1365D] On the authority of the Regina manuscript, we restore θιμωνία ἁλός, “a heap of salt,” in place of θημωνία ἅλωνος, “a heap of a threshing-floor.” The subsequent context of the sentence proves that ἁλός, not ἅλωνος, was placed here by Jerome; and we learn from the old Greek copies, too, especially from the Complutensian, that the former word prevailed over the latter. The same Regina manuscript prefers γράφεται, “is written,” in place of λέγεται, “is said.”]

Let this suffice concerning the variety and error of the translation, and concerning the difficulty of the historical account.

But the learned man who compares spiritual things with spiritual things, who does not seek the things below but those above, who rises with Christ from the dead and, putting off the old man, puts on the new, will refer the reproaches of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon to the teachers of doctrines opposed to the Church. They too seem to be of the race of Abraham, to have escaped the fire of Sodom and Gomorrah, and to dwell in little Segor.

But because their generation is in darkness and they cannot look upon the light of truth—for they have turned away from God the Father, which is signified by the names Lot and Moab—and because they have ceased to be sons of God, which is expressed by “my people,” and have remained conceived in an incestuous union in a dark cave, therefore, even to the present day, they insult the simplicity of the sons of Judah and desire to magnify their possession beyond its borders. Of them it is said in Proverbs: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established” (Proverbs 22:28).

Observe the heretics applauding themselves in dialectic, rhetoric, and the doctrines of every kind of sophistry; despising the rusticity of the Church as unworthy of their mysteries, which they have fashioned for themselves as idols, and regarding it as nothing [Col. 1365D]. and you will not ask what the reproaches of Moab and the insults of the sons of Ammon are, by which they reproached the people of God.

The Lord therefore swore by himself, saying: “As I live, says the Lord.” And beautifully, in contrast with the dead gods called idols, the God of Israel— that is, the God of the people who see God—calls himself living.

These nations, Moab and the sons of Ammon, of whom we said above, “Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah,” seem, because they are not Gentiles, to themselves to have escaped from Sodom and Gomorrah. But because they blaspheme the people of God and act against Israel, they will be counted as Sodom and Gomorrah, and will be destroyed as those cities were previously destroyed, leaving in themselves no trace of greenery or life [Alternative: “of strength”].

Nor is it surprising if we understand this of heretics, since even those who are called ecclesiastics, who have not observed God’s commandments and have departed from his precepts, are counted as Sodom and Gomorrah. Through Isaiah it is said to them: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; attend to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1:10).

And to the elders who, under the figure of Susanna, desire to corrupt the chastity of the Church, Daniel says: “This is God’s judgment: seed of Canaan, and not of Judah” (Daniel 13).

And so that you may know that whenever Sodom and Gomorrah and Egypt are named, the reference is not to those provinces which we see with our eyes, but to other spiritual realities against which the prophetic word threatens, read in the Apocalypse of John: “The place where their Lord was crucified is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt” (Revelation 11:8).

If Jerusalem, in which the Lord was crucified, is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, why should Egypt, Sodom, and Gomorrah not, conversely, if they have performed the works of Jerusalem and the land of Judah, be transferred into the land belonging to the Lord?

Finally, David was not a priest, nor was it lawful for him to eat the bread of the Presence (1 Samuel 21). But because his works increased one by one, and Saul’s persecution became an occasion for the growth of his virtues, therefore, while fleeing, he suddenly became a high priest without knowing it, received the bread of the Presence, and did not violate God’s commandment.

We have said all this because “Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah.”

Damascus also—which is interpreted as “drinking blood” or “the blood of a sack”—shall be abandoned by God’s mercy, like a heap of salt. For since its ruler is King Aretas, and the Damascenes seek to kill Paul, who is lowered through the wall in a basket (Acts 9), it is not said to Damascus, “You are the salt of the world.” Nor is that salt called the salt which is always offered in sacrifices, but rather the salt that has lost its savor, concerning which it is written in the Gospel: “If salt has lost its savor, with what will it be salted? It is useful for nothing, neither for the earth nor for the dunghill, but they throw it outside, so that it may be trampled upon by men” [Col. 1366D] (Matthew 5:13).

Moab, Ammon, and Damascus, therefore, who set themselves against the knowledge of the Lord and blasphemed the people of God, uttered many insults against them, and desired to enlarge their borders in the land of the Church and possess the people of God, shall be abandoned and destroyed [Alternative: “deserted”]. The remnants of the people of God—that is, ecclesiastical men instructed in the divine Scriptures—shall plunder them; and the survivors of the Lord’s nation shall possess them. This shall happen to them for their insult, because they reproached and magnified themselves against the Lord Almighty.

Observe the clemency; observe the mercy of the Lord. He suffers insult, he is blasphemed, and his borders are plundered. What does he do? He sends the remnants of his people, about whom we have spoken, to divide among themselves those who blasphemed him and lead them into his own possession.

For it is far better for a fool to serve a wise man, and for the Lord’s wisdom to correct his folly, than for him to be abandoned to his own foolishness.

The Lord Almighty will therefore come, and he will be manifest more clearly to them—to the one whom they now do not know and of whom they are ignorant. He will destroy all their doctrines, that is, their gods, and the idols of the various nations, so that, after the images they had fashioned for themselves from their own thinking have been overturned, the nations may turn to the Lord, and each in his own place may worship him whom he did not previously know.

(Verses 12ff.) “You Ethiopians also shall be slain by my sword; and he will stretch out his hand over the North and destroy Assyria. He will make the splendid city into a wasteland, an impassable place, and something like a desert. Flocks will lie down in its midst, all the beasts of the nations; the pelican and the hedgehog will dwell in its thresholds; the voice of one singing at the window, the raven on the lintel—for I will weaken its strength. This is the glorious city, dwelling in security, which said in her heart, ‘I am, and there is no other besides me any longer.’ How has she become a lair for beasts? Everyone who passes through her will hiss and shake his hand.”

**The Septuagint:** “You Ethiopians also shall be wounded by my sword; and I will stretch out my hand over the North and destroy the Assyrian, and I will make Nineveh a wasteland, waterless like a desert. Flocks and all the beasts of the earth will pasture in her midst; chameleons and hedgehogs will lie down in her mangers; beasts will cry out in their dens [variant: “in its dens”], and ravens at her gates; for her height is like a cedar. This is the city devoted to evil, which dwells in hope and says in her heart, ‘I am, and there is no one after me any longer.’ How has she become a wilderness, a pasture for beasts? Everyone who passes through her will hiss and shake his hands.”

The Jews refer this entire chapter, as well as the two preceding chapters concerning the Philistines, Moab, and the children of Ammon, to the coming of Christ. They think that he will come at the consummation of the world, build up Jerusalem, and free his people from the hand of the nations by which they are held captive. They understand the statement, “And men will worship him from their place, all the islands of the nations,” in this sense.

They maintain that not only the nations mentioned above, but also the Ethiopians, the Assyrians, and Nineveh, the city of the Assyrians, will at that time be made desolate, and that all the beasts of the earth—or, as it is written in Hebrew, “all the beasts of the nations”—will lie down in it. From this they think it is signified that Nineveh will be overthrown by all the nations. And because *Nineveh* is interpreted as “beautiful,” they refer “the beautiful city” in the present passage to Babylon. Everything that follows—“The pelican and the hedgehog will dwell in its thresholds,” and the rest—seems to them to apply more suitably to Babylon, whose desolation is also foretold in Isaiah.

Conversely, others affirm that the passage plainly concerns the Assyrian, of whom it had already been said: “He will stretch out his hand over the North and destroy Assyria, and he will make Nineveh a wasteland.” For by “the Assyrians” Nineveh is more properly understood than Babylon, which is a Chaldean city.

As for the statement, “The pelican and the hedgehog in its doorposts, and the raven on the lintel,” these are signs—or, according to another reading, judgments—of desolation. There are two kinds of pelicans: one aquatic and one belonging to the desert. When he says, “The voice of one singing at the window,” this may refer either to demons or to the cries of various birds, which commonly dwell in deserted cities.

Moreover, what both we and the Septuagint have translated similarly—“The raven on the lintel”—is written in Hebrew as *HAREB* (the Hebrew spelling is not supplied). According to variation in reading (the Hebrew form is not supplied), it may mean either “dryness,” “sword,” or “raven.” Hence Aquila translated it as “sword,” while others translated it as “dryness.”

[Note: Concerning this meaning of the word and the variation in its reading, we have spoken in Volume II against Richard Simon, who subverts Jerome’s works through a perverse interpretation. See below our marginal annotations on chapter 1 of Haggai. —MART.]

Bochart says in *Jerozoicon*, chapter V, that the same word is involved, whether written with *heth* or with *ayin*, a claim no one would have granted to Jerome. With *ayin* and *ḥolem*, it signifies “raven”; with *heth* and *ḥolem,” “dryness” and “desolation,” or “sword” if the vowel is *segol*. Yet Jerome did not write the word with Hebrew letters and a fixed Hebrew orthography, but in Latin as *Hareb*, a form that could represent either of the two Hebrew words. Thus Bochart, and the later offspring of the critics who follow him, accuse him without sufficient justification. Compare the holy Doctor himself below, in chapter 1 of Haggai, verse 11.

Then, as though mocking its ruin after its overthrow, the prophetic utterance says: “This is the glorious city, dwelling in security, which said in her heart, ‘I am, and there is no other besides me any longer.’ How has she become a lair for beasts? Everyone who passes through her will hiss and shake his hand.”

In accordance with what we said above, either beasts will truly dwell in the deserted city, or else, under the figure of beasts, the diversity of many nations is indicated.

If someone should ask how, according to the historical sense, this prophecy can be referred to the time of Nebuchadnezzar—since the Ethiopians and Assyrians are also named, and the Medes and Persians did nothing to them—let him read the histories. He will see that the Assyrians and Ethiopians too were subject to the Medes, as well as to the kingdom of Cambyses, the power of Cyrus, and all the events that followed.

This has been said according to the Jewish interpretation.

But if we observe that throughout the Scriptures those who are completely immersed in vices are called Ethiopians, in accordance with what we read in Jeremiah, “Can the Ethiopian change his skin?” (Jeremiah 13:23), then there is hope for Ethiopians who turn to better things: no one who wishes to repent will be excluded from salvation.

Thus the soul, formerly polluted and stained with the filth of sins, says, “I am black” (Song of Songs 1:4). Later, at the end of the Song of Songs, concerning that same soul, now cleansed and washed through repentance, it is written: “Who is this that ascends, made white?” (Song of Songs 8:5).

Moses also—that is, the spiritual Law of the Lord—took an Ethiopian woman from among the nations as his wife (Exodus 2). Mary—that is, the synagogue of the Jews—and Aaron—that is, the carnal priesthood, not the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek—murmur against the Law, but in vain. For immediately the synagogue is covered with leprosy; cast outside the camp, it is brought back into the camp after the appointed time, when Moses himself has prayed.

“For Ethiopia has already stretched out her hands to God” (Psalm 67). The divine utterance therefore now threatens those who cling to sins, who, forgetful amid the filth of their offenses, refuse to turn to better things and wash away their dark color. It threatens them with the sword—the sword of which I think it is also written in Genesis: “He stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword, which turns to guard the way to the tree of life.” And in Isaiah: “He will bring upon the dragon, the crooked serpent, a great and holy sword, and he will kill him on that day” (Isaiah 27:1, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Victorius inserts “and mighty,” following the Greek text of the Septuagint.]

It says that they will either be wounded or killed by the sword, so that, fearing punishment, they may imitate Nineveh and repent (Jonah 3), and not endure what the Lord threatens.

The prophecy of Jeremiah also expresses this: “I will speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to uproot and destroy them. And if they repent, I too will repent of all the evils that I said I would inflict upon them” (Jeremiah 18:7–8).

And so that you may know that the Lord now threatens the Ethiopians with the sword for the purpose of turning them to better things, shortly afterward in this same book he says concerning the Ethiopians: “Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, there my suppliants, the children of my dispersed ones, will bring me an offering” (below, 3:10).

[Note: The same manuscript corrects the reading to “daughter,” on the basis of the Hebrew and the Vulgate edition. In the Septuagint, instead of “daughter,” we read “I will receive.”]

Or, as it is found in the Septuagint: “From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive my dispersed ones, and they will offer sacrifices to me.”

After this the Lord does not speak as above, but the prophetic spirit speaks concerning him: “He will stretch out his hand over the North and destroy Assyria” (Jeremiah 1:14)—the North about which Jeremiah wrote: “From the North evils will be kindled against all the inhabitants of the earth”; and of which Solomon says: “The North is a harsh wind, but by name it is called ‘right’” (Proverbs 25:23).

Therefore God stretches out his hand as he brings punishment, so that the North too may feel its penalties, as may those who are in its land.
