Toward that land, according to Zechariah, the black horses go; concerning them it is said: “The black horses were going into the land of the North” (Zechariah 6:6).

Beautifully, whoever moves his feet and departs from the East—of which the same prophet says, “Behold, the man whose name is Dawn” (ibid., 6:12)—and looks toward the West immediately proceeds toward the North, which is not right but is called right by name.

[Note: In the Reginensis manuscript, the words “which is not right, but by name is called right” are absent.]

This can also be understood physically: whoever stands in the East and turns toward the West, facing it, has the North on his right. Those who have been chilled by its blast call it “right,” although it is right only in name; in reality and in its operation it belongs rather to the left.

After the Lord has stretched out his hand over the North, he will also destroy Assyria. *Assur* is interpreted as εὐθύνων (*euthynōn*). Many think this means “the one who directs,” but that is false. εὐθύνων means “the one who reproves” and “convicts.”

Since the devil himself is the enemy and avenger, and since he suggests sins and afterward convicts sinners on account of those sins, he is therefore called εὐθύνων. I think that he is the prince of the Assyrians, who dwells in the North and has Nineveh as his capital. He says in Isaiah: “By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of the nations and plunder their strength” (Isaiah 10, according to the Septuagint).

As for what follows concerning devastated Nineveh—“Flocks and all the beasts of the earth will pasture in it; chameleons and hedgehogs will lie down in its mangers; beasts will rest in its doorposts; ravens in its windows,” and the rest—it seems to me that it should be understood according to what is written either in the prophet Jonah or in Nahum.

In Jonah, we interpreted Nineveh—that is, “beautiful”—which repented at the preaching of Jonah, that is, of the dove, as the Church gathered from the nations.

[Note: Yet he had not yet begun to expound Jonah. Perhaps, by weaving threads and woof for himself, he had already prepared material for the work; these are the things he praises here.]

In Nahum, however, we moderated the interpretation concerning the world. It is not difficult to explain and say concerning the world that when the Ethiopians have been wounded by the sword of the Lord, and he has stretched out his hand over the North and destroyed the Assyrian, the prince of the world, then the world itself, together with its prince, will perish and be reduced to utter desolation. It will be pitiable to no one; everyone will hiss at its ruin and shake his hands.

At first sight, however, it seems blasphemous to say concerning the Church that it will become impassable and deserted, that beasts will dwell in it, and that afterward it will be addressed mockingly: “This is the city devoted to evil, which dwelt in hope and said in her heart, ‘I am, and there is no one besides me any longer.’ How has she become a wilderness, a pasture for beasts?”

But whoever considers the apostolic statement that “in the last times perilous times will come,” and that “people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, intemperate, savage, haters of good, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3:1ff.),

and also what is written in the Gospel—that because iniquity has multiplied, the love of many will grow cold—to such an extent that the saying will be fulfilled, “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on the earth?” (Matthew 24:12)—will not be surprised at the Church’s final desolation: under the reign of Antichrist, it will be reduced to a desert, handed over to beasts, and undergo everything the prophet now describes.

For if God did not spare the natural branches because of their unbelief, but broke them off, and turned rivers into desert, springs of water into thirst, and fruitful land into saltiness because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, why should he not, conversely, overthrow and return to the same thirst those concerning whom he had said, “He made the desert into pools of water, and the dry land into springs of water; he made the hungry dwell there,” and the rest—those whom he grafted from the wild olive into the root of the good olive—if, forgetful of his beneficence, they depart from their Creator and worship the Assyrian?

Although this may generally be understood of the coming of Antichrist or the end of the world, it can nevertheless be understood daily in those who pretend to belong to the Church of God but deny it by their works; who are hearers of the Law and not doers; who vainly boast that they are beautiful.

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “who vainly boast that they are beautiful.”]

Flocks dwell in such people—that is, a multitude of vices; brute animals that serve the body; and all the beasts of the earth, which devour their hearts. There are also chameleons, which have no single color but change continually among different sins: now greed, now luxury, now cruelty, now lust, now sadness, now exultation.

And there are hedgehogs in their mangers: a spiny animal, full of thorns, wounding whatever it touches. Beasts also lie in their openings—that is, in their hearts—and unclean ravens, in their gates, whether in their mouths or in their ears, so that they are always either speaking or hearing evil things.

After this it is added and said that the Church will suffer—or will have suffered—these things because it raised itself up in pride, lifted its summit like a cedar, devoted itself to evil works, and nevertheless promised itself future blessedness. In its heart it despised everyone else, thought that no one existed besides itself, and said, “I am, and there is no other besides me any longer.” How, then, has it become a wilderness, a pasture for beasts?

For where previously the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit dwelt, and where his angels presided over their ministries, beasts will then dwell—those of whom the prophet also laments, saying: “Do not give the soul that confesses you to the beasts” (Psalm 73:19).

“Everyone who passes through her will hiss and shake his hands.”

If we understand this of the angels, we shall interpret it as follows: when the angels have passed through her and have not remained in her, as they formerly used to do, they will be astonished and amazed. They will not support and sustain her as she falls with their hand, but will raise their hands and pass on. Or perhaps they will raise their hands with a hiss and, as mourners, clap them together in lamentation.

But if we wish to understand this of the devil and his angels, who also ravaged the vineyard that had been brought out of Egypt, we shall say that through the soul from which Christ has departed, and which had previously been the temple of God but has ceased to be so, the serpent passes and hisses. It pours out in her the poisons of its wickedness, and not only does this, but also moves its works, which are called “hands” metaphorically (*tropikōs*).

And lest you think that, because we have mentioned the serpent, we are violently interpreting the serpent’s hands as its works, receive Solomon’s testimony: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21).

We have said these things as best we could, serving the allegorical interpretation. But if anyone should discover interpretations more plausible and more rational than those we have set forth, let the reader be guided more by that person’s authority.

### Chapter III

**(Verses 1 ff.)** Woe to the rebellious and redeemed city! The dove did not hear the voice and did not accept correction; she did not trust in the Lord, nor draw near to the Lord [Vulgate: God] her God. Her princes are in her midst like roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves, leaving nothing for the morning. Her prophets are madmen, unfaithful men; her priests have polluted the sanctuary and acted unjustly against the law.

The Lord, who is righteous, is in her midst; he will not commit iniquity. Morning by morning he will bring his judgment to light, and it will not be hidden. But the unjust man did not know shame. “I destroyed the nations, and their corner-towers were laid waste; I made their roads desolate, because there was no one who passed by. Their cities were devastated, with no man remaining and no inhabitant.”

I said, “Yet you will fear me; you will accept correction, and her dwelling will not perish because of all the things for which I visited her.” Yet, rising early, they corrupted all their designs.

**The Septuagint:** “O illustrious and redeemed city, the dove did not hear the voice and did not accept correction; she did not trust in the Lord and will not draw near to the Lord her God. Her princes are in her like roaring lions; her judges are like the wolves of Arabia; they did not leave anything for the morning. Her prophets bear the spirit, men who despise. Her priests pollute the holy things and act impiously against the law.

“But the Lord is righteous in her midst, and he will not commit iniquity. Morning by morning he will bring his judgment to light; he is not hidden, and he does not know iniquity in exacting punishment, nor injustice forever. I removed the proud; their corner-towers were scattered. I destroyed their roads so that they would not pass through at all. Their cities failed, because no one remained standing or dwelt there.

“I said, ‘Nevertheless, you will fear me and accept correction, and you will not perish from his sight in all the things for which I took vengeance upon her.’”

[Note: This final verse, “Prepare yourself, rise early,” etc., is not found here in the Regin. manuscript.]

[Note: The same manuscript reads *elaam* and also omits the words “from before the sword of Jona.” Jerome himself approves the immediately preceding explanation of Nebuchadnezzar in his *Commentary on Jeremiah*, ch. XXV, at the end: “He will not be surprised,” he says, “to understand the dove of the Lord as Nebuchadnezzar, who has read above that he is called the Lord’s servant.”]

“Prepare yourself; rise early: all their clusters have been scattered.”

Many think that, because of the sequence of the passage, this is spoken against Nineveh, concerning which it was said above: “He will destroy Assyria and make Nineveh a desolation.” But Scripture would never call Nineveh a dove, although some think that in Jeremiah “from before the sword of the dove” refers to Nebuchadnezzar (Jer. XV). It should be known, however, that others argue conversely that in that passage, instead of “dove,” one may understand **Ἑλλάδα**, that is, Greece, so that the meaning is: “from before the sword of Jona,” that is, “from before the sword of Greece.” For *Jona* signifies both “dove” and “Greece.” Hence, even to this day the Greeks are called *Ionians*, the sea is called the Ionian Sea, and among the Hebrews their ancient name remains. Likewise, Roman princes retain their ancient title among barbarian nations and are called Caesars.

The whole passage, therefore, is spoken against Jerusalem: “Woe to the city, once a dove, always sinning, delivered into captivities and again redeemed by the Lord. Woe to the rebellious city”—which is expressed more significantly in Hebrew as **MARA** (), that is, **παραπικραίνουσα**, “making bitter.” We may say: “making God bitter,” that is, by your fault turning the sweet and merciful Lord into bitterness, so that he who wishes to show mercy is compelled to punish.

She did not hear the Lord’s command, and, when reproved, did not wish to accept correction. Nor, under the pressure of her evils, did she ever trust in the Lord her God; nor did she walk behind him; nor, when he said, “I am the Lord who draws near, and not one who is far away” (Jer. XXIII, 23), did she herself wish to draw near to him.

Her princes, judges, prophets, and priests are also described, so that in the city we may understand the people, and in the terms I have mentioned, the various ranks of office. Her princes, therefore, were always prowling like lions among their prey and seeking to shed the blood of their subjects. Her judges were rapacious, leaving to others nothing that they could seize.

Her prophets were raving—or, rather, stupefied—which in Hebrew is called **PHOEZIM**. Aquila translated it **θαμβευταί**. They spoke as though from the mouth of the Lord, yet proclaimed everything against the Lord.

[Note: The older editions impose upon us here a fabricated Greek reading: Erasmus and Marianus read **ἐνθουσιαζόμενοι**, but no trace of this word exists in the manuscript codices. These distinctly preserve Aquila’s reading, namely **θαμταί**, or **θαμπταί**, with *π* in the middle—a letter apparently omitted by ancient copyists entirely ignorant of the Greek language. **Θαμπταί**, “stupefied,” that is, “raving,” is applied because of the fury and madness of false prophets and similar false teachers. MART.]

[Note: At the suggestion of the Regin. manuscript, with Montfaucon’s Hexapla before us, we have restored this word as **Θαμβευταί**. We found it written thus: ΘaΜbΙΥΤΜ. In one or two places, as the actual strokes of the letters indicated, we readily corrected it by substituting **ΕΥΤΑΙ** at the end for **ΙΥΤΜ**. That this is the genuine reading, or interpretation, of Aquila is manifest from the fact that elsewhere, namely at Genesis XLIX, 3, he rendered the verb itself by **θαμβεύειν**; consequently no one will doubt that the noun derived from it was interpreted as **Θαμβευτάς**. This is also supported by the reading *caalbrutai*, which the aforementioned Montfaucon says he found in a ninth-century manuscript and which he quite suitably and ingeniously adapted to the orthography of the Greek letters as **Θαμβευταί**. In the books published hitherto there was **Θαμταί** or **Θαμπταί**; this plainly approached the true reading and spontaneously revealed itself as corrupted through the fault of the copyists.]

The priests committed sacrilege in the sanctuary, and, although they acted against the law, they offered victims according to the law. Because they acted unjustly, the Lord, who is righteous, will not act unjustly; rather, he will repay the evil city what it deserves.

“Morning by morning”—that is, openly and without any ambiguity—he will execute judgment upon it, and nothing will be able to be hidden from him. The Lord will do this so that the city, once reproved, may turn to better things. But unjust Israel did not recognize its shame, nor understand that the blows inflicted upon it were intended to lead it to repentance.

“I took vengeance on the nations,” he says later, “and destroyed their kingdoms, so that you who had not perceived me through punishments might at least recognize me through benefits.”

Or certainly it should be understood in this way: “I destroyed all your cities, O Judah, and all the villages and tribes subject to you, and your various borders; such a vast destruction of people occurred that no one remained to inhabit your cities. After I had done this, I sent my prophets, rising early and calling you to repentance, and I said: ‘I did these things to you, O Jerusalem, but I did them so that you would fear me and accept correction, and so that your dwelling—that is, the temple—would not perish because of all the crimes you had committed.’

“But, conversely, when I was calling the inhabitants of Jerusalem to repentance, they rose early, as though deliberately and defiantly, so that with the eagerness with which they ought to have returned to me they might complete all their designs and demonstrate by their deeds what they had conceived in their minds.”

This is according to the Hebrew.

But the illustrious and redeemed city, redeemed by Christ’s blood, clearly signifies the Church according to what precedes. She is also called a dove because of the simplicity of the multitude of believers within her. She did not hear the Lord’s voice, nor wish to accept correction; nor did she trust in the Lord, because she did not wish to draw near to the Lord her God and so obtain forgiveness of sins.

For a person says in vain that he hears the voice of the Lord his God and trusts in the Lord when by his works he destroys his faith, joins himself more closely to Mammon than to the Lord his God, approaches him with a double heart, and believes that he can serve two masters, the world and God.

Her princes are like roaring lions. We have no doubt about the roaring and prowling of lions when we see her princes thunder against subject peoples and crush the populace with tyrannical voices and raging insults, so that you would think you saw not a shepherd in the flock but a lion roaring among little sheep.

Her judges are also like the wolves of Arabia, killing in the evening and leaving nothing for the morning. They do not look toward sunrise but always remain in darkness, turning the little possessions of the Church and what is contributed to God’s treasury into their own profit, so that the poor have nothing to eat in the morning. Like wolves in the night, when no one sees them, they ravage everything; and, when they plunder all things like wolves, they do not even leave small portions of food for the needy.

Her prophets, too—that is, teachers who think they teach the peoples and speak from the Scriptures—are **πνευματοφόροι**, “spirit-bearers,” or “spiritual men” (and this should be read **εἰρωνικῶς**, ironically). They are “men who despise.” For in the Church it is fitting not merely to teach but to act, and not to destroy one’s words by one’s deeds. But when you teach another and do not act yourself, you should be called not so much a teacher as one who despises. Of such a person it is written in Habakkuk: “Look at the despisers and pay attention; marvel at the marvels and perish” (Hab. I, 5).

The priests, too, who serve the Eucharist and distribute the Lord’s blood to his people, act impiously against the law of Christ. They think that in making the **εὐχαριστία** they need only the words of the one who pronounces the invocation, not a virtuous life; they think that only the solemn prayer is necessary, and not the merits of the priests, concerning whom it is said: “The priest in whom there is any blemish shall not approach to offer sacrifices to the Lord” (Lev. XXI, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Compare Book 5 and following of *Against the Luciferians*. Be careful not to understand this as though the holy Doctor considered a virtuous life necessary in priests for them to confect the Eucharist validly. He is concerned only that, while priests flatter themselves because of their sacerdotal power, they do not abandon the proper rule of living and destroy by their example what they build by their authority.]

[Note: The Regin. manuscript reads: “in whatever blemish he may have.”]

Although the princes, judges, prophets, and priests of Jerusalem do these things, the Lord is nevertheless merciful and just. He is merciful because he does not depart from his Church; he is just because he gives each person what he deserves.

After morning has come and the night of this age has passed, he will bring his judgment to light, and neither he nor his judgment will be hidden. When he begins to demand from each person the money entrusted to him, he will not be unjust, nor will he allow injustice to prevail forever. Instead, he will pull down from their seats the proud princes whom God resists, and from the height they occupied.

Their corner-towers will be scattered—that is, their perverse intentions, turning aside from the straight path, in which the Pharisees had always been accustomed to pray, despising the corner-stone.

I think, however, that it is also beneficial for the proud to be pulled down from their arrogance and for their narrow lanes and corners to be scattered, so that afterward they may walk along the straight road.

Finally, it follows: “I will make their roads desolate, because there will be no one who passes through,” according to what is written in the first psalm: “The way of the wicked will perish” (Ps. I, 6).

Likewise in Hosea, where Jerusalem is described as committing fornication: “Behold, I will hedge up her ways with thorns, and I will block her paths; she shall not find her way. She shall pursue her lovers but shall not overtake them; she shall seek them but shall not find them. Then she will say, ‘I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better for me then than now’” (Hos. II, 6–7).

Observe that, unless the ways had been hedged up, the paths blocked, and unless the Lord had destroyed her roads, the fornicator-soul could never have said: “I will go and return to my former husband.”

Thus the roads of the proud and their corner-towers are scattered, so that they may not walk in arrogance and perversity; and their cities, which had been badly built in arrogance and pride, are destroyed, so that they may not remain standing and have wicked inhabitants.

And lest anyone think that we are forcing the meaning of Scripture, let him learn from what follows: “I did these things,” he says, “so that I might say to them: ‘Behold, the roads of wickedness have been destroyed. Henceforth fear me and learn [another reading: accept] correction, lest my correction also perish, finding no fruit of conversion in you; and all the means by which I wished to reprove you be rendered useless.’” To them the saying written in Jeremiah may be applied: “In vain I struck your children; they did not accept correction” (Jer. II, 30).

Or certainly: “Fear me and receive correction, so that all things may not perish from the sight of Jerusalem, nor may she be utterly brought to desolation because of the evils with which I threatened her” [another reading: “in which I threatened her”].

Let no one be disturbed—as I have often already said—because I interpret these things as spoken against the Church, since he knows that in the Holy Scriptures Jerusalem always bears the type of the Church. Whoever sins against her is either carried away into Babylon, or, if he wishes to descend there voluntarily, is wounded by robbers in Jericho.

For what is so illustrious as the Church, founded throughout the whole world? What is so redeemed by Christ’s blood, and a dove because of the grace of the Holy Spirit, as the Church gathered from the nations? In her, many who say that they believe in Christ have neither heard his voice, nor received correction, nor wished to be near him.

As for what is said, “Her princes are in her like roaring lions,” I know that I will offend many by interpreting this as referring to bishops and presbyters. Yet the wicked presbyters who wished to violate Susanna do not condemn the other presbyters who lived well. Nor are the wicked princes described by the prophetic word an insult to good princes: “When the fool is scourged, the foolish man will become wiser” (Prov. XIX, 15). If the foolish man becomes wiser, how much more will the one who is wise become so?

But those judges and princes who accept bribes and sell justice—are they not rightly called the wolves of Arabia, or evening wolves, as Symmachus translated? They do not deserve to be called the wolves of Benjamin, who “devour in the morning and give food in the evening” (Gen. XLIX), but evening wolves, who eat during the night and leave nothing in the morning.

As for what follows—“His prophets are **πνευματοφόροι**, spirit-bearers, men who despise”—let no one be troubled that, while interpreting this of teachers, we call them both prophets and despisers, since the Apostle also commands: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. IV, 30).

David likewise says in the fiftieth psalm: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L, 13). For unless the Holy Spirit, once grieved, had been accustomed to flee his former dwelling and leave his habitation, Paul would never have given the command I cited, and David, after his adultery, would not have feared losing what he had received.

Of this it is also written to the Hebrews: “How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified as unclean, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Heb. X, 29).

It is also written in the Third Book of Kings about the man of God—clearly a prophet—who had spoken at the altar in Samaria: “O altar, altar, thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, a son will be born to David’” (III Kings XIII, 2), and so forth. Because he despised the word of the Lord and ate with a false prophet—for Josephus interpreted this passage in that way—he was killed by a lion.

[Note: Formerly it read: “at the destroyed altar, after he had said.” Victorius retained *exstructum, postquam*—“at the altar that had been built, after he had said.” Soon afterward he also replaced “a son will be born to David” with “a son will be born to the house of Jacob.” Nothing similar is found in our manuscripts or in Martianay’s edition, and those two words, *exstructum postquam*, seemed moreover awkward in the context.]

And lest this be thought an accident rather than the Lord’s judgment, the false prophet who had deceived him foretold that this would happen, and the lion itself, punishing the despiser, spared the donkey.

It is therefore not astonishing if teachers who had been full of the Holy Spirit can become despisers, since among the negligent, who do not guard their hearts with complete vigilance, this very thing frequently becomes the cause of pride and contempt toward God: that they possess knowledge of God and know his abundant goodness, which he has hidden for those who fear him, yet despise the riches of his goodness and store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation.

The priests, too—those who administer baptism, invoke the Lord’s coming upon the Eucharist, make the chrism-oil, lay on hands, instruct catechumens, and appoint Levites and others as priests—should not be angry with us for explaining these things and with the prophets for prophesying them. Rather, they should entreat the Lord and take care lest they deserve to belong among the priests who violate the Lord’s holy things.

For it is not rank and the names of ranks, but the work proper to the rank, that ordinarily saves princes, judges, prophets, and priests. “Whoever desires the office of bishop,” he says, “desires a good work” (I Tim. III).

See what he said: “He desires a good work”—a work, not a rank.

[Note: Two of our manuscripts supply the word *opus*—“work”—with greater emphasis: **ἐμφατικωτέρως**.]

But if, disregarding the work, he looks only to the rank, the tower of Siloam quickly falls, the lofty cedars are struck by lightning, the raised neck is broken, and the swan, stretching out its neck and reaching toward the heights, is counted among unclean birds.

As for what we explained according to the Hebrew—“Nevertheless, rising early, they corrupted all their designs”—the Septuagint reads: “Prepare yourself, rise early; all their foliage has been scattered.” Since this differs greatly from the Hebrew and seems more in agreement with what follows according to the Septuagint, we shall explain it in the following section.

### (Verses 8–9)

“Therefore wait for me,” says the Lord, “for the day of my rising in the future; because my judgment is to gather nations and assemble kingdoms, in order to pour out upon them [Vulgate: upon them] my indignation, all the anger of my wrath. For in the fire of my jealousy the whole earth will be devoured. For then I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip, so that all may call upon the name [Vulgate: in the name] of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder.”

**The Septuagint:** “Therefore wait for me,” says the Lord, “for the day of my rising as a testimony; because my judgment is against the assemblies of the nations, to receive kings, to pour out upon them all my anger, the whole anger of my wrath. For in the fire of my jealousy the whole earth will be consumed. For then I will turn the tongue of the peoples toward its generation, so that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke.”

[Note: The verses “Prepare yourself, rise early,” etc., which we said in the preceding section are absent from the Regin. manuscript, are finally recorded here by the same manuscript.]

The Jews interpret these words as referring to Christ’s advent, which they expect to occur, and they say that, after all the nations have been gathered and the Lord’s fury poured out upon them, the earth will be devoured in the fire of his jealousy. And just as it was before the building of the tower, when all peoples spoke one language, so, when all have been converted to the worship of the true God, they will speak Hebrew and the whole world will serve the Lord.

We, however, who do not follow the killing letter but the life-giving spirit, nor Jewish fables, hear from the Lord: “Prepare yourself, rise early; all their clusters have been scattered.” We understand “prepare” as: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. LVI, 8).

We also hear the command in Proverbs: “Prepare your works at your going out” (Prov. XXIV, 27).

And we hear that which is solemnly prescribed in Leviticus (chapter XVI), where, in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, Aaron offers for the people a living scapegoat. Placing his hands upon its head, he invokes upon it all the sins of the people of Israel, hands it over to the care of a prepared man, and sends it into the wilderness—which we understand as referring to ourselves. By preparing ourselves according to the command of the true priest, we remove evil from the midst of the Church.

When we have done these things, the night passes and the day draws near; and, walking honorably as in the day, we say: “O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the light” (Ps. LXII, 1). Immediately we add: “In the morning you will hear my prayer; in the morning I will stand before you and will see” (Ps. V, 4–5).

For unless we have been prepared, the sun of righteousness will not rise for us. Once the sun has risen, all the clusters from the vineyard of Sodom are scattered and perish, so that not only the great bunches but also whatever seemed small within us may disappear as Christ’s lamp shines.

Promising us a reward for all these things, God says: “Wait for me on the day of my rising as a testimony.” For after vices and sins, God will rise within us.

And according to what he commands elsewhere: “You are my witnesses, and I am witness, says the Lord God, and the child whom I have chosen” (Isa. XLIII, 10). The Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, is witness for us, so that “in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand” (Deut. XVII).

It seems to me that the meaning stands more securely in this way, and that the truth is confirmed by these three witnesses, than according to the letter [another reading: “according to the second witness”]. There were two witnesses against Susanna (Dan. XIII) and against the Lord himself the Savior (Matt. XXVI), yet the word did not stand in their mouth.

Almost the entire city also testified against Naboth, but the agreement of the wicked witnesses did not establish the truth; it established a conspiracy in crime (III Kings XXI).

“For my judgment,” he says, “is against the assemblies of the nations, in order to receive kings”—that is, to bring them into the place of their punishments—“so that I may pour out upon them all the anger of my wrath.”

The one who is lesser quickly obtains forgiveness and is near to mercy; “but the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI, 6). Therefore the nations and the multitude of nations are gathered for judgment, while kings—that is, the leaders of perverse doctrines—are brought to punishment, so that all the anger of the Lord’s wrath may be poured out upon them.

This does not happen out of any cruelty, as the bloodthirsty Jews suppose, but out of mercy and according to the counsel of the physician.

For it follows: “In the fire of my jealousy the whole earth will be consumed.” When the nations have been gathered for judgment and the kings for punishment, so that wrath may be poured out upon them—not partially but wholly—and when anger has been joined with fury, everything earthly throughout the whole world, everything belonging to the works of earth—that is, of the flesh—will be consumed. The fire of my jealousy will devour all its brambles and thorny growth.

“Then I will turn the tongue of the peoples toward its generation,” so that each person, having laid aside error, may return to the ancient language of confession of the Lord. “At the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 10).

Having cast aside the bricks and bitumen that we used in place of stones and mortar, with which we built the pride of our error against the Lord, let us receive again the tongue that we formerly lost, and let us be under the yoke of Christ, who says: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 30).

It should be noted that where we translated, “I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip,” the Septuagint, instead of “chosen,” said “toward its generation,” with “earth” understood. From this the error arose: the Hebrew word **BARURA** (), which Aquila and Theodotion interpreted as “chosen” and Symmachus as “pure,” was read by the Septuagint as **BADURA** (). They considered the letter *resh* to be *daleth*, because of the great similarity between the two elements, distinguished only by a small stroke.

Likewise, where we translated, “on the day of my rising in the future,” all the others translated “as a testimony.” The Hebrew teacher who instructed me in the Scriptures asserted that in the present passage **LAED** () should be understood more as **εἰς ἔτι**, “for the future,” than as “for a testimony.” For **ED**, written with the letters *ayin* and *daleth*, can be understood as both **ἔτι** and **μαρτύριον**, that is, “future” and “testimony.”

We may also explain this passage as referring to Christ’s first advent, when, after all error had been removed, demons trampled down, and earthly works destroyed, the apostles spoke in all languages (Acts II), and, with the ancient error removed, one language of confession was restored.

The kings who are destroyed and consumed by divine fire should likewise be understood as the leaders of perverse doctrines.

### (Verses 10 ff.)

“Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there my suppliants, the children [another reading: daughter] of my dispersed ones, will bring me an offering. On that day you will not be ashamed of all your inventions with which you transgressed against me, because then I will remove from your midst those who boast arrogantly, and you will no longer continue to exalt yourself upon my holy mountain. I will leave in your midst a poor and needy people, and they will hope in the name of the Lord.

“The remnant of Israel will not commit iniquity, nor speak lies; a deceitful tongue will not be found in their mouth. For they themselves will feed and lie down, and there will be no one to frighten them.”

**The Septuagint:** “From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive my dispersed ones; they will bring me sacrifices. On that day you will not be ashamed of all your inventions with which you acted impiously against me, because then I will remove from you the insult of your reproach, and you will no longer continue to magnify yourself upon my holy mountain.

“I will leave in you a meek and humble people, and those who remain of Israel will fear the name of the Lord. They will not commit iniquity, nor speak empty words, and a deceitful tongue will not be found in their mouth. For they themselves will feed and lie down, and there will be no one to frighten them.”

When the Lord has restored to the peoples of believers a chosen lip, and all have called upon the name of the Lord and borne his yoke, then, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia—whence the queen of Sheba came to hear Solomon’s wisdom (III Kings X)—they too will bring sacrifices to the Lord: “And Ethiopia will be the first to stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. LXVII, 32).

The Ethiopian woman will be married to the true lawgiver, who struck Egypt with ten plagues (Exod. II), while the synagogue of the Hebrews looks on with envy.

As for what he says according to the Hebrew—“From there my suppliants, the daughter of my dispersed ones, will bring me an offering”—the meaning is as follows:

“O Israel, O former daughter of the synagogue, whom I scattered throughout the whole world: although you are envious, although you are tormented by jealousy, nevertheless victims will be brought to me from Ethiopia—that is, from the people of the nations.”

“On that day”—that is, when the multitude of the nations has believed—you also will not be utterly ashamed of all your errors with which you transgressed against me, choosing Barabbas and crucifying the Son of God (John VI).

Then I will remove from your midst the scribes, priests, and Pharisees, who boast arrogantly. You will no longer boast upon my holy mountain; instead, you will have a poor people, uneducated men and fishermen, who will hope in the name of the Lord.

“The remnant of Israel”—not the multitude that cried, “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX, 6), nor the chief priests and leaders, but the remnant—will no longer commit iniquity or speak lies concerning Christ, believing in the truth. A deceitful tongue will not be found in their mouth, since they know that every lie is from the devil (John VIII).

For they will feed and say: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing. He has placed me in a pasture of grass; he has led me beside the water of refreshment; he has restored my soul” (Ps. XXII, 1). There will be no one to frighten them, because the faith of believers will conquer the pride of their persecutors.

Let this be understood as referring to Christ’s first advent. The Jews promise and expect for themselves at the end that they will inhabit Jerusalem, be filled and fed, like animals, with material gifts and riches, with green grass, and that, after all nations have been destroyed and subjected to them, no one will remain who can frighten them.

[Note: The Regin. manuscript reads: “to be filled with material goods and works.” A little later, following the same manuscript and Victorius, the reading is *residere* (“to remain”) rather than *resistere* (“to resist”).]

We, however, taking from this fable an occasion for a true history, say [another reading: “we shall say”] that, once the chosen—or pure and bright—lip has been restored to us, as Symmachus interpreted it, we leave behind in the rivers of Ethiopia the teachers of perverse doctrines by whom we were formerly irrigated, together with all the blackness and sombre colour of the soul and the dragon’s venom with which we had been stained through vices and sins; and, with Israel once dispersed [another reading: “with the dispersed”], we shall bring gifts to Christ.

On the day when Christ’s light has risen for us, it will be said to each one of us: “You will not be ashamed of all your inventions”—that is, of your utterly evil thoughts—with which we acted impiously against the Lord.

All arrogance and reproach by which we raised ourselves against the Lord and against his holy mountain—our Lord and Savior—will be removed from us. In place of proud and empty names, there will remain in us a meek and humble people, so that we may think nothing arrogant, nothing swollen with pride, nothing displeasing to God.

Consider also that on the day of judgment and at the consummation of the world all names of rank will be removed, and one people will remain, one flock under the good shepherd, meek and humble.

Then the people of Israel, when the fullness of the nations has entered—for “God has confined all under sin, so that he may have mercy upon all” (Rom. XI, 32)—will fear the name of the Lord.

The remnant of Israel will no longer commit the iniquity by which they denied the Lord, nor speak empty words, promising themselves foolish fables. A deceitful tongue will not be found in their mouth, with Christ, who is the truth, speaking through them.

Then they will be fed, and together in one flock they will lie down in the Church, and they will not fear the attacks of the true Nebuchadnezzar.

Seeing and reading such great mysteries, let us cry out with the Apostle and say: “O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are your judgments and inscrutable your ways!” (Rom. XI, 33).

The prophet, sensing and pondering this as well, conjectures concerning God’s judgments:

“In the night I exercised myself with my heart; I searched my spirit and said: ‘Will God reject forever? Will he never again show mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in his anger?’ And I said: ‘Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High’” (Ps. LXXVI, 7 ff.).

The meaning is this: I had thought that the Lord would abandon sinners forever and restrain his mercies as anger succeeded them. But I understood that this happened so that, by the change of his right hand—the right hand of the Most High—he might change everything and have mercy upon those whom he had previously cast away.

Therefore, both we and the remnant of Israel, knowing that we shall give an account for every idle word (Matt. XII), and that the Lord will destroy all lying lips, should not speak vanity.

“For vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I, 2). And: “Every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII).

Let us not utter falsehood with our mouth. Rather, having received the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy (Luke X), let us fear no terror, nor dread the ambushes of wolves while Christ guards us. Instead, let us say: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. XXVI, 1), and the rest contained in the twenty-sixth psalm.

### (Verses 14 and following)

“Praise, daughter of Zion; shout for joy [Vulgate: ‘shout for joy!’], Israel; rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. The Lord has removed your judgment; he has turned away your enemies. The Lord, the King of Israel, is in your midst; you shall fear evil no longer.

“On that day it shall be said: ‘Jerusalem, do not fear; Zion, let not your hands grow weak. The Lord your God is in your midst; he is mighty—he himself will save you. He will rejoice over you with gladness; he will be silent in your love [Vulgate: ‘his love’]; he will exult over you with praise.’

“Nugas, those [Vulgate: ‘who’] who have departed from the law, I shall gather, because they were from you, so that you may no longer bear reproach because of them.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Rejoice, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem; exult and delight with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. The Lord has taken away your iniquities; he has redeemed you from the hand of your enemies. The Lord, the King of Israel, is in your midst; you shall see evil no longer.

“At that time, says the Lord, to Jerusalem: ‘Take courage; Zion, let not your hands grow weak. The Lord your God is in you; the Mighty One will save you. He will bring joy upon you and renew you in his love; he will rejoice over you with delight as on a solemn festival. I shall gather your broken ones.’”

[Note: This clause, “Woe to him who accepted,” etc., is not found in the Regina manuscript.]

“Woe to him who accepted reproach against her.”

It should not seem surprising—as we have often said—that Hebrew sections end in one way, while the Greek, and consequently the Latin, end in another. For wherever the translation differs in meaning, it is necessarily different either in its beginnings or in its endings.

The Jews promise all these things to themselves together with Christ, whom they think will come; whereas we who have received Christ have already obtained everything together with him. Therefore, if any Christian—and especially certain recent converts whose names I withhold lest I seem to injure anyone—thinks that the prophecy has not yet been fulfilled, let him know that he falsely bears the name of Christ and possesses a Jewish soul, lacking only bodily circumcision. For if these things have not yet happened but are still future, we have believed in the Savior’s coming in vain. Yet if, while not believing, we understand that the mystery which was hidden through eternal ages has been fulfilled in us and has now been revealed through the prophetic Scriptures and the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, we do not believe in vain (Colossians 1).

Let us finally consider the order of the reading, and we shall see that what is said concerns not the Jews but the Church of Christ. For after what preceded—“My judgment upon the assemblies of the nations, so that I may receive kings,” up to the place where it says, “so that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke,” and, “Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia I shall receive [Note: The same manuscript reads, “I shall receive from there my dispersed ones,” a reading supported by some Greek books.] my dispersed ones, who shall bring me sacrifices”—and after the remnant of the people of Israel who believe in Christ and have been saved, of whom it says, “They shall fear the name of the Lord who are the remnant of Israel, and there shall be none to terrify them”—the Holy Spirit, speaking of the consummation of the world as a whole, says:

“Rejoice, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem; rejoice and delight with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem.”

Every ecclesiastical soul, then, which has been set upon a watchtower and contemplates peace, rejoices and is glad that its iniquities have been removed and that it has been redeemed by him who redeemed all people with his precious blood. [Note: Two manuscripts read: “and that it has been redeemed by him.”] For Christ has become for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:30).

The King of Israel, who dwells in our midst, has redeemed us, saying: “I and the Father will come, and we shall make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23); and, “I shall dwell and walk among them” (Leviticus 26:12). We shall no longer see evil, thinking about and doing only virtues.

“On that day,” says the Lord, when we behold peace and have been placed on high, “let not your hands grow weak”—he who also said through Isaiah: “Strengthen the weak hands, and let your works be made strong” (Isaiah 35:3).

For the Lord is mighty, and no one can resist him; he is your Savior. He himself will restore to you the joy that you lost. Having cast off the old man, he will make you walk in the new, and he will do this in his love—not because of your merit, but because of his mercy.

“He will rejoice over you and delight in you,” as though receiving the richest sacrificial offering of your solemn festival, namely, your salvation. He himself will say to you: “I shall gather your broken ones.” For “God will not despise a broken and humbled heart” (Psalm 50:19), and, “He will not break a bruised reed” (Isaiah 42).

For the present, let us understand these words as referring to the Savior’s second coming. But because the prophet Zechariah exhorts Zion and Jerusalem to a similar joy, and Matthew says that this very prophecy was fulfilled at Christ’s first coming (Matthew 21), we are compelled—indeed, the very order of truth leads us—to understand what is said in Zephaniah not as something to be hoped for in the future, but as something already accomplished.

For it is written in Zechariah: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king is coming to you, righteous and saving; he is humble and rides upon a beast of burden [another reading: “under the yoke”] and upon a young foal” (Zechariah 9:9).

Let this suffice concerning the Septuagint.

According to the Hebrew, however, the Church is commanded to praise, and Israel—to see God in understanding—to shout for joy and rejoice. The place of peace is addressed in these words: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

At the end and consummation of the world, he has removed its judgment—not judging and rebuking it any longer, but saving it—and has turned away its enemies, the hosts of demons. The Lord, the King of Israel, will be in its midst; it will fear evil no longer.

“On that day it shall be said to free Jerusalem” [Note: Because the word “free” occurs again immediately afterward, these words seem to have fallen out of the commonly printed books. They are inserted here in the Regina manuscript: “You shall fear evil no longer. On that day it shall be said to free Jerusalem.” If one wishes to restore them to the text, I would not object.]—not to the Jerusalem that is enslaved with her children, but to the one who is the mother of the saints (Galatians 4): “Do not fear, Zion”—for she herself is also Jerusalem—“your works shall not be weakened, nor shall you do what you will later lament” [another reading: “what you will lament”].

The Lord your God, who will save you, mighty and powerful, will himself dwell in your midst. He will rejoice over you with exultation and gladness, and in his love [another reading: “in peace”] with which he has loved you, he will silence your sins. He will exult over you with praise, either because you are worthy of praise or because he sings together with your praises.

“Those who have departed from you”—or, as Aquila translated it, “those who have been transferred”—I shall gather, because they were from you. That is, those who had fled from your bosom through vices and sins and had come under the power of demons will come to you when the condition of all things has been restored, and you will no longer suffer reproach because of your lost children.

As for the word *nugas* [Note: Isidore likewise understands it this way in Book 10 of *The Origins*, under the letter N. He says: “*Nugas* is a Hebrew word, for it is explained thus in the prophets, where Zephaniah says, ‘Those who have departed from the law,’ and so forth,” which he evidently excerpted from the present testimony of Jerome. In my judgment, however, the word *nugas* does not reflect the character or origin of the Latin language, but seems to have been borrowed from another, more ancient language. Charisius almost indicates this in Book 1, where he says: “Although *nugas* is indeclinable, it is nevertheless common to all three genders: *hic*, *haec*, and *hoc nugas*.” We have said this in Jerome’s defense, since the sons of the critics, following Drusius, attack him everywhere, arguing that *NUGAE* does not have the same meaning in Latin and Hebrew, where they claim that it rather means “affected with grief.” We have discussed this elsewhere, and Martianaeus has separately collected considerable material in defense of the holy Doctor. A little later the Regina manuscript reads, “so that we may know,” instead of “so that we may be able to know.”], let us know that the word itself is Latin in Hebrew, and for that reason we have set it down as it stood in Hebrew. Thus we may recognize that the Hebrew language is the mother of all languages—a matter that cannot be discussed at present.

I wonder, however, that Aquila and the Septuagint, instead of what we translated as “they were”—in the passage where we said, “I shall gather them because they were from you”—wished to translate “woe,” or *οἴ*. Aquila always uses this not for lamentation but for calling and shouting aloud. For *HAJA* [the form of the verb “to be”]—whose beginning is the verb “I am”—in the plural past tense signifies “they were” or “they had been.”

I know that these matters are tedious for the reader. But if he notices that I am not writing controversies and declamations, nor exulting over commonplaces, but commentaries—and commentaries on the prophets—he will criticize me wherever I choose to play the rhetorician’s game rather than accuse me of failing, as I ought, to linger over such profound obscurities.

### (Verses 19–20)

“Behold, I shall destroy all those who afflicted you at that time. I shall save the lame and gather the one who had been cast out, and I shall make them a praise and a name throughout the whole land of their shame.

“At that time when I bring you back, and at the time when I gather you, I shall give you as a name and a praise among all the peoples of the earth, when I turn your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord” (Vulgate).

The Septuagint reads:

“Behold, I shall act in you and on your behalf at that time. I shall save the one who has been pressed down, and I shall receive the one who has been rejected. I shall place them in glory and make them renowned throughout the whole land. They shall be put to shame at that time when I do good to you, and at the time when I receive you, because I shall give you renown and glory among all the peoples of the earth, when I turn your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord.” [Note: The verse beginning “Woe to him who accepted …,” which, as we said, is not joined to the preceding chapter in the upper part of the Royal manuscript, is placed before this passage in the same manuscript.]

The synagogue, which does not limp but has been mutilated in both feet, promises this to itself at the coming of its Christ, whom it hopes will come. It thinks that all the nations which afflicted Israel will be destroyed by the Lord, that the synagogue will be saved, that she who had received a bill of repudiation will be gathered, and that they will be made a praise and a name throughout the whole land of their captivity, in which they had previously been put to shame.

It expects this to happen when Jerusalem’s captivity has been restored, the temple rebuilt, and the remaining order of ceremonies preserved. It makes this promise to itself, and therefore does not repent; while hoping for uncertain things, it loses certain salvation.

Nor do I wonder that the synagogue speaks in this way. Because it does not receive Christ, its eyes are painful; with Leah it is bleary-eyed, is not loved by Jacob, and is neglected when Rachel succeeds it (Genesis 29).

I am astonished—indeed, at Christians, or rather semi-Jews, who think themselves members of the Church, yet speak and profess things which, if true, make our faith in Christ vain. Our entire sacrament is abolished, and we are more pitiable than all other people, believing that he has come who has not come.

But because our hope is certain and the Jews’ desires are empty, let us now weave together the final part of the chapter according to the earlier interpretation, and bring forward the testimony of Jesus son of Sirach: “He who throws a stone on high throws it upon his own head” (Ecclesiasticus 23).

Because Zion and Jerusalem have been set on high, whoever insults Zion and Jerusalem and throws stones of abuse against her throws them upon his own head, and his reproach will return upon his own head: “His pain and his iniquity will descend upon his crown” (Psalm 7:17). [Note: The Royal manuscript reads, “his iniquity upon his crown,” and shortly afterward, “touching upon the mysteries of God,” instead of “pursuing.” At the end of the passage below, “what shall I say about the unbelievers?” appears in the manuscript, followed by “when some of the Churches …”]

How many people today reproach the soul which pursues the mysteries of God, wishes to see his peace, and say: “He is insane, drunk, and full of new wine. He avoids the gatherings of men; he scorns pleasures; he counts gold as dirt; he loves poverty alone.”

Those who are unbelievers even reproach it for the cross of Christ. And whenever they see it in distress and temptation, they say: “Where are your mercies and the acts of justice that you performed?”

What shall I say about unbelievers, when some leaders of the Churches reproach people of this kind, regard their way of life as madness, and do not praise their present conduct but reproach them for their former sins? They do not hear the command: “Do not reproach a person who turns away from his sins” (Ecclesiasticus 8).

Woe, therefore, to him who bore and accepted reproach and devoted himself to such a task as insulting Zion and the city of God. For the Lord is the avenger of this insult against his city, and he will say to Zion:

“Behold, I shall act in you and on your behalf”—that is, “I shall exact vengeance for you”—“and I shall save the afflicted one,” or, as the Greek says, “the one who has been pressed.”

The meaning is: “I shall save her who at present, like a grape and an olive, has been so tested by temptations and pressures that she has been pressed and afflicted in the winepress and beneath the beam, in order to produce wine and oil”—so that Jesus might drink the wine in his Father’s kingdom and be anointed with the oil above his companions.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “as though speaking to a grape and an olive,” and shortly afterward, “as pressed in the winepress and beneath the beam,” etc.]

I think that Job endured many sufferings because of the pressing of such wine and oil. But after he had produced wine and oil, he heard the Lord say: “Do you think that I answered you in any other way than that you might appear righteous?” (Job 40, according to the Septuagint). It is as though he were speaking to the grape and the olive: “Do you think that I pressed, afflicted, and crushed you for any other reason than to extract wine and oil from you?”

It follows: “And I shall receive the one who had been rejected.”

God seems to reject us when he leaves us to temptation. Hence Job says: “The visitation of the Lord has regarded me” [another reading: “has looked away from me”] (Job 10:12).

Nor do the righteous alone speak in this way, saying, “But now you have rejected and confounded us,” as it is written in the forty-third Psalm. The Lord and Savior himself, speaking in the person of the man whom he assumed, says: “But you have rejected and despised me; you have delayed your Christ; you have overthrown the covenant of your servant.”

That the person speaking in the forty-third Psalm is that of the righteous—“But now you have rejected and confounded us”—is proved by what follows: “All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor acted wickedly against your covenant; our heart has not turned back.”

The Lord, therefore, will receive at the end the one who appeared to be cast away amid temptations, and will place them in glory and make them renowned throughout the whole earth: namely, the children of the pressed and rejected one—that is, of the Church.

Whom else can we understand as the renowned children of the Church except the apostles? Look at Peter, Paul, Matthew, and John, and consider that which was promised to Abraham: “I shall make your name great.” This has been accomplished in them. Every day their names are spoken in the Church; every day their names are magnified—not because it benefits them that we name them in the Church, but because, by magnifying their names and continually reading what they wrote, we attain salvation.

“On that day,” he says, when the pressed and rejected one has been received and her children have been placed in glory—“for the Lord glories [another reading: “will glory”] in his athletes when he sees them crowned, just as he gloried against the devil because of Job”—those who had been your adversaries and had brought reproach against you will be put to shame. Then they will see that those whom they had considered wretched are happy, and that those whom they regarded as poor and cast down have become powerful and glorious.

Then they will see their captivity—the captivity by which they had been subjected in this world to harsh domination—being brought back to the heavenly Jerusalem, while they themselves rise to reproach and eternal confusion.

Grant us, Jesus Christ, who are pressed, afflicted, and rejected in this world, that you may receive us and place us in glory. May the *excetra* (water-serpent) [Note: The ancient editors, following their usual practice, corrupted this passage by inventing the reading “May that which is proud be confounded; let the hisses cease,” and so forth. They did not understand that Rufinus had written, “May the serpent be confounded in time,” so that temporary confusion might benefit it and bring about its salvation. This is also what we pray for our rivals, who today lie subject to confusion and contempt. *MART.*—Formerly the reading was, “May that which is proud be confounded; let the hisses cease,” and so forth. The Royal manuscript reads, “May the serpent and the hydra be confounded; let the hisses cease,” and so forth.] be confounded in time; let the hisses cease, let the poisons grow numb, and may its confusion contribute to its salvation.

This is according to the Septuagint.

According to the Hebrew, apart from the beginning, about which we spoke at the end of the preceding chapter, the text does not differ greatly from their translation and therefore, I think, does not require exposition.

---

## One Book of the Commentaries of Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, on the Prophet Haggai, addressed to Paula and Eustochium (C)

### Prologue

The prophet Zechariah also bears witness that, in the second year of Darius, king of the Persians and son of Hystaspes, the seventieth year of the temple’s desolation had been completed—the year which Jeremiah had foretold (chapter 25). After placing the title of his vision in the second year of the same king, in the eleventh month, Sebat, on the twenty-fourth day, he added:

“O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year” (Zechariah 1:7, 12).

Ezra likewise reports that, after the altar alone had been built and the foundations of the temple laid, the work was prohibited by a letter from King Artaxerxes:

“Then the work on the house of God in Jerusalem ceased, and it was not resumed until the second year of the reign of Darius, king of the Persians” (1 Esdras 4:24).

He immediately added:

“Then the prophet Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews who were in Judea and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel. Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to build the house of God in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, helping them” (1 Esdras 5:1–2).

At that time, among the Romans, Tarquinius Superbus was reigning as the seventh king after Romulus, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign. He was expelled eight years later by Brutus. Afterward the consuls administered the republic for four hundred and sixty-four years, down to Julius Caesar.

We have said this, Paula and Eustochium, so that from the title itself you may immediately recognize at what age the prophet Haggai prophesied.

For the present, it must be understood that both Haggai and Zechariah were prophets of great spiritual power, since they ordered the temple to be built despite the edict of King Artaxerxes and the Samaritans and all the surrounding peoples who were obstructing its construction. Zerubbabel and Jeshua son of Jozadak, together with the people who were with them, were no less faithful, since they obeyed the prophets’ commands more readily than the authority of the king who prohibited the work.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

### Chapter 1

#### Verse 1

“In the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet.”

Because the people who seemed to themselves to have returned from captivity had not yet built the temple, raised the city walls, or recovered the former glory of Jerusalem, but lived in hollow houses—and, as the Greek says more significantly, *κοιλοστάθμοις*, that is, in places situated below and sunk in a valley—the word of God is not addressed to them under King Hezekiah, or Amon, or Josiah, who had ruled the people of God as long as Jerusalem stood. It is addressed under Darius, king of the Persians, about whom Daniel also speaks mystically in his book.

In our language, Darius signifies “made generations” or “those who were”; in Greek, *γενεαὶ γενόμεναι* [Note: I cannot determine why the ancient editions retain, instead of *γενεαὶ γενόμεναι*, the other Greek expressions *γενέσεις γεγονόιαι* or *γεγονῆαι*. *MART.*—Against the character of the Greek language, Martianaeus writes *γιγνόμεναι*. The manuscripts, however, come closer to the old reading of Erasmus and Victorius, *γεγονόιαι* or *γεγονῆαι*. Only the Regina manuscript has *γεγονῖται*.].

A people without a temple, living below, did not deserve to have any other king except one who served generations, loved the flesh, and preserved the first commandment of the still-ignorant man cast out of paradise: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28; 9:1).

Therefore, because Darius was a lover of intercourse and a companion of the dragon, whose entire strength is in its loins (Job 40), the vision is seen by the people in the second year—in an impure number—and after the unity of virginity and the nakedness of paradise, the number signifies leather tunics.

Finally, in Genesis, after it is said on the first day, on the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth, following the completion of each work, “God saw that it was good,” this is not found concerning the second day according to the Hebrew, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. For the second day, which establishes the number that divides what was united, could not be approved by God’s judgment as good.

The sixth month is also specified. It does not possess God’s solemnities as the seventh month does, but is close to the six days in which the world was made. In this month one labors and eats bread in the sweat of one’s face; the earth produces thorns and thistles; and when it has received wheat-seed, it is more fertile in darnel and oats.

But because the altar had already been built, and they had wanted to build the temple against the hostile enemies who resisted them, but had not built it [Note: One Regina manuscript, in the opposite sense, reads: “had not wished”], “on the first day of the sixth month the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet,” so that the people might abandon the second year of King Darius, which divides what was united, and the sixth month which had passed, the number assigned to labor, and might return to God’s unity and follow an odd and solitary number—which even the pagan poet knew to be holy when he said (Virgil, *Eclogue* 8):

> “God delights in an odd number.”

The word of the Lord comes seeking to whom it should come and whom it should teach, by the hand of Haggai the prophet, who had good works and in whose deeds the word of God could rest.

But where hands are full of blood [Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “where hands are blood-stained”], where Jesus is killed, and the people dare to say, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27), there the word of God does not come.

To this day carnal Israel, possessing unclean hands, stretches them out toward the Lord; but because they are full of blood, the Lord speaks to them through the prophet:

“When you stretch out your hands, I shall turn my eyes away from you; for your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1:15).

The word of the Lord does not come into their hands because they are unclean; the word of God does not come to them because they have killed the word of God within themselves.

Nor should we think that the word of the Lord came only by the hand of the prophet Haggai. Since Haggai is interpreted as “festive” [Note: Instead of “festive,” the same manuscript prefers “solemnity.”], anyone who can celebrate festivals—not in the old leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:8)—can receive the word of God.

Let us also have clean hands, and let us be called *ἑορτάζοντες*, that is, “celebrating festivals,” and the word of God will come to us.

Let us set before our eyes the fact that the law is spiritual, and let us understand the spiritual solemnities about which it is written:

“Three times in the year you shall celebrate festivals for me. You shall keep the solemnity of unleavened bread: for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you at the time of the month of new grain, for in that month you came out of Egypt. You shall not appear before me empty-handed. And you shall keep the solemnity of the harvest of firstfruits from your works, whatever you have sown in the field; and the solemnity of completion at the end of the year, when you gather your works from the field” (Exodus 23:14 and following; Deuteronomy 16).

If we wish the word of God to come to pass in us, let us be Haggai—that is, let us celebrate festivals—and let us not appear empty before God (2 Corinthians 9). Sowing in the Spirit, let us reap eternal life from the Spirit, so that we may celebrate the solemnity of completion at the end of the year—that is, the gathering of our works from the field—the solemnity of the firstfruits from our works, whatever we may have sown in the field blessed by the Lord.

Let us also be Haggai, and throughout our entire life, until the completion of the year—that is, until our departure from this world—let us celebrate festivals in our works, which have arisen for us in our field.

Much can be said about the solemnity, but this is not the time. From these matters the diligent reader may adapt a spiritual understanding throughout the whole of Scripture. [Note: The repetition of the word “solemnity” deceived the ancient copyists. Believing that the passage between the two occurrences comprised a section of nearly three verses, they skipped it as their eyes hastened. Consequently, all printed books issued up to the present lack these necessary words from Jerome’s text: “of completion at the end of the year, that is, the gathering of our works from the field, the solemnity.” We now supply them for the first time from the Regina manuscript, with no doubt about their genuineness, which is established both by that manuscript’s authority and by the conspicuous error, frequently found in old books, which the omission itself reveals.]

“To Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, saying.” [Note: Let the ignorant cleric John now be ashamed of having reproached me and charged me with folly because the title of the book of Chronicles reads, “Here begins Jerome’s preface to Chronicles.” As though he were permitted to turn into a charge of ignorance against me what ought to be a matter of glory—namely, imitating Jerome and demonstrating faithfulness and diligence in reading manuscript codices. *MART.*]

We read in Chronicles that Jeconiah, who was led away to Babylon, was the father of Shealtiel, from whom Zerubbabel was born (1 Chronicles 3:6).

Matthew too, when he enumerates the Savior’s genealogy, says:

“After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah begot Shealtiel; Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel; Zerubbabel begot Abiud” (Matthew 1:12–13).

This Zerubbabel, descended from the tribe of Judah, that is, from David’s line, is a type of the Savior, who truly rebuilt the destroyed temple, namely, the Church, and led the people back from captivity.

From the stones of the old temple as well as from new stones that had previously been unworked, he built the Church; that is, from both the remnant of the Jewish people and the multitude of the nations, he erected a tabernacle for God the Father.

According to the various accents of the Hebrew language, his name is interpreted either as *ῥεῦσις παρακειμένη*, “an adjacent or exposed flow,” or “born in Babylon,” or “a prince from Babylon.”

The first interpretation is opposed by the flow signified in the name Jezebel, that is, “a vain flow” or “the flow of a menstruating woman,” which plainly signifies uncleanness. Zabulon is likewise interpreted as “the flow of night.”

Therefore, abandoning the vain, filthy, and dark flow of this world, let us follow the flow of Jesus, which has been set before us for drinking and offers itself from a most abundant spring, according to what is said in the Gospel:

“Jesus stood in the temple and cried out, saying: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink’” (John 7:37).

We shall be able to drink this flow when we ask it from God the Father, according to what we read: “Ask, and it shall be given to you” (Matthew 7:6).

For Shealtiel is interpreted as “petition of God.” And no one comes to Jesus unless the Father draws him (John 6:45).

A flow will therefore be born for us, set forth through supplication to God. It will be from the tribe of Judah—the royal tribe, which confesses or praises God—for Judah signifies both.

As a historical matter, “born in Babylon” is truly said of Zerubbabel because he was born there. But according to the deeper understanding, it signifies our Lord Jesus, because he too was born in the confusion of this world, was near the great river Chebar, and saw the great vision which Ezekiel, under his type, beholds at the beginning of his book (chapter 1).

When I said that Zerubbabel means “a prince from Babylon,” I did not mean that “prince” is literally part of the interpretation. Among the Hebrews his name is said to be composed of three complete elements: *zo* means “this”; *rob* means “teacher” or “greater”; and *Babel* properly means “Babylonian.” Thus the name Zerubbabel means “this teacher from Babylon.”

For the sake of brevity in interpretation, instead of the small details mentioned above, I wished to translate it as “prince from Babylon,” or “in Babylon.”

Just as Jesus son of Nun, who was himself also a type of the Savior, led the people from the wilderness into the promised land, so this man was born in Babylon in order to lead those who were in Babylon back to the promised land from which they had been carried away captive, and to say to those in chains, “Come out,” and to those sitting in darkness, “Be enlightened” (Isaiah 49).

The word of the Lord that came by the hand of Haggai is directed not only to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, about whom we have already spoken, but also to Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest.

Historically, Zerubbabel belongs to the royal tribe, while Jeshua belongs to the priestly tribe. In spiritual understanding, however, the two are one and the same: our Lord and Savior, king and great priest.

Zerubbabel bore his type insofar as he was king; insofar as he was high priest, his namesake Jeshua bore the type. Jeshua is interpreted as “Jao, salvation,” that is, “the Lord’s salvation” [Note: The number of restorations required in this passage can be learned only from the extremely corrupt and false text of the old editions, which reads: “But insofar as he was high priest, his namesake Jeshua bore him, who is interpreted as the salvation of God, that is, the Lord’s salvation; and he is the son of Josedec, which is likewise translated in our language as …, that is, God, …, that is, just.” Certainly I can now say confidently that scarcely anything in the present Commentary is Jerome’s, but that nearly all of it is Erasmian and Martianaean. If this is so, where before our age did there exist the true and genuine Jerome, truly pious, truly learned, and a faithful interpreter? *MART.*—Formerly the same sense read “his namesake”; Martianaeus writes *homonymus* without the aspirate, and severely criticizes the old editions for forcing Hebrew words into the text.], and he is the son of Josedec, which is also translated into our language as “the Lord’s just one.”

For God the Father and God the Son are just and holy, and there is no iniquity in him.

This is directed against Marcion and the other heretics who assert that the Lord and Savior is the son of another good god—some god or other—and not of the Creator, whom they call just.

And truly Jesus is the great High Priest, compared with whom all the priests of God are small and insignificant. For if he is called the great Priest, this is certainly said in distinction from those who are lesser. All who exist outside him and after him are lesser, just as he is the firstborn of all creation and the firstborn from the dead; so also he is chief and great among all priests.

### Verse 2

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: This people says, ‘The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built.’”

Pay close attention: it is not Zerubbabel or Jeshua who say, “The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built,” but the people, who were still subject to King Darius and had not yet shaken off the yoke of servitude.

Those who are held in captivity and have gone out from Jerusalem always delay and postpone building the temple of God, saying, “The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built.”

When you see someone who has come out of the Church—someone who had been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved (1 Corinthians 5)—thinking and intending to build through chastity the temple that he had previously destroyed through lust, yet continually putting off the day, say to him:

“Truly you too belong to the people of the captives, and you too say, ‘The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built.’”

For the one who has once decided to restore the temple of God, every time is suitable for building. Neither the devil as king, nor enemies on every side, nor the feigned piety of parents, relatives, or children can prevent him.

As soon as, having turned back, you cry out upon the name of the Lord, he will say: “Behold, I am here.”

### (Verse 3)

And the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai [Col. 1393A] the prophet, saying: “Is it time for you yourselves to dwell in paneled houses, while this house lies deserted?” Or, as the Seventy translated it, κοιλοστάθμοις, that is, “hollow” or “concave” houses.

On the same day mentioned above this vision again appears. As the prophet’s works advance, the gifts of prophecy also increase; and after a brief silence, in response to what the people had said—“The time has not yet come for the Lord’s house to be built”—the Lord’s almost deliberated response is brought forth and addressed to them: “Is it therefore time for you to dwell in houses situated below, and placed in a valley, while my house, which is on the mountain, remains deserted?” Or, as it is found in the Hebrew: “for you to dwell in paneled houses”—that is, decorated and furnished houses, intended less for use than for luxury—“while my dwelling, in which were the Holy of Holies, the cherubim, and the table of the Presence, is watered by the rains, made desolate, and scorched by the sun?”

Moreover, according to the allegorical interpretation: Every period in which the dwelling of the valley is chosen, or in which we serve pleasures, is inopportune.
