Hence the Stoics, who take care to define individual words, said that time is a time of correction or accomplishment; this is expressed more significantly in Greek as χρόνον εἶναι κατορθώσεως, “that time is the time of rectification.” For every period in which we serve not virtues but vices perishes and, as though it had never existed, is reckoned as nothing.

If, then, any one of us either dwells in a valley, or builds his house amid worldly pleasure and luxury, he does not build a temple for God, nor does the Lord have in him a place where he may rest his head; and he builds a house together with foxes, allowing the former dwelling of God to remain deserted.

[Col. 1393C] ### (Verse 4)

“And now thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways.”

Let the time of the one who speaks not be different from that of the one who acts; immediately turn my commands into deeds. For the Lord is omnipotent, and it is he who commands; certainly, the command of almighty God is not a light matter.

Until now you have had hearts serving your vices, without order and without a teacher, going wherever your desires dragged you. But now the Lord commands you to order your love toward him, and to set your hearts upon your ways, so that you do nothing without judgment and deliberation. Let the legal lamp always go before your feet, and let you say: “Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105).

Or certainly it may be understood in this way: Since you say, “The time has not come to build the Lord’s house,” while you yourselves dwell [Col. 1393D] in habitations sunk down in the lowest places, and my house lies deserted, “consider”—at the Lord’s command—and recall to yourselves what you have done and what you have suffered.

### (Verses 5–6)

“You sowed much, and brought in little; you ate, and were not satisfied; you drank, [744] and were not intoxicated; you clothed yourselves, and were not warmed. And he who gathered wages put them into a pierced purse.”

All your labor in building your houses and neglecting the house of God had no result. For you sowed more, and gathered far less than had been sown. Nor can you say that hunger followed because the farmer ceased from cultivating the land.

You also ate—lest perhaps one of you should say that the fasting was voluntary—and were not satisfied, because you had gathered only small harvests into your storehouses. You drank wine from the vineyards, but not enough for your heart to be glad, so that it might be said of you: “And wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103:15).

You had a cloak, but one that did not drive away the cold or preserve warmth. Whoever among you gathered wages, whether through commerce or by hired labor, worked in vain: his labor was expended without the reward of labor. For everyone’s money flowed away, as though someone were putting it into a pierced purse.

But according to the spiritual understanding, those who returned from Babylon and had not yet built the temple of God, continually postponing its construction and saying, “The time has not yet come for the Lord’s house to be built,” were neither captives nor yet endowed with complete freedom. Rather, placed as if in a kind of middle state, they sowed much and brought in little; they ate and were not satisfied; they drank and were not intoxicated; they clothed themselves and were not warmed; they gathered wages and, as though putting them into a pierced money-pouch, lost them.

If at some time you see someone, amid many works of sin, doing certain things that are just, God is not so unjust that, because of many evils, he forgets a few good deeds. He will make that person reap only what he has sown in good soil and gather it into his storehouses.

But whoever is utterly ἀποστάτης, an apostate, will not eat at all, but will perish from hunger. [Col. 1394C] Whoever sows much and brings in little eats little and not to satisfaction, in accordance with what the Lord threatens in the curses of Leviticus: “You shall eat and not be satisfied” (Lev. 26:26).

But the one who is holy will eat to satisfaction, and what is written will be fulfilled in him: “The righteous man, eating, fills his soul” (Prov. 13:25).

Likewise, whoever does not drink at all will perish from thirst, as also in Judith—if, that is, anyone wishes to accept the book of a woman: “And the little ones perished from thirst” (Judith 8). Whoever drinks little does indeed drink, but not to drunkenness.

But whoever can say to the Lord, “Your intoxicating cup, how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22:6), is intoxicated with Noah (Gen. 9); and although he is situated in Egypt, he is nevertheless drenched with wine at Joseph’s banquet with the patriarchs and his brothers (ibid. 43). He, overcome by the greatness of his joy and daily gladness, will be called, together with the apostles, who were transformed into ecstasy, “full of new wine” (Acts 2).

How the fact that the sons of Jonadab, son of Rechab, did not drink wine and are praised by the Lord in Jeremiah (chap. 35) is not contrary to this interpretation will be discussed more appropriately later.

[Note: Death intervening, however, he did not reach that chapter, but broke off the work at the thirty-second.]

After this it is said to those who neglected to build the temple of the Lord: “You clothed yourselves, and were not warmed.” We understand this from Psalm 103, where it is said of God: “The deep as a garment is his clothing.”

Although according to the Hebrew truth it refers to the earth, which is surrounded by the Ocean, nevertheless, according to the translators of the Seventy, who said τὸ περιβόλαιον αὐτοῦ, using the masculine gender and not αὐτῆς, the feminine, we are compelled to understand that this was said of God [alternative reading: “which”]:  his wisdom is unsearchable, and “the Lord makes darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. 17), nor are his mysteries disclosed to the unworthy.

Hence the righteous man rejoices and says: “In my heart I have hidden your sayings, that I might not sin against you” (Ps. 118:11).

This cloak, woven from the manifold meanings and words of wisdom, does not allow those who are fervent in spirit to be cooled, nor does it allow the warmth of love to grow cold when Boreas blows.

But the one who is intermediate, who has a cloak but is not completely covered by it—just as he brought little into his storehouses, ate but not to satisfaction, and drank but not to intoxication—will indeed be covered by the cloak of his thoughts and works, but will not be warmed.

The one who, because of the extreme poverty of his soul, has no cloak does not have one because, “since iniquity has abounded, love has grown cold in him” (Matt. 24:12).

Hence, concerning such a man, whose cloak is possessed by another, the Law commands: “You shall restore his garment to him before the sun sets, because he is poor and has placed his hope in it” (Deut. 24:15).

The same thing also happens to those who dwelt [alternative: dwell] in valleys or in paneled houses [746] and said, “The time has not yet come for the Lord’s house to be built,” so that they gathered their wages into a pierced purse (Isa. 40:10; 62:11).

If one of us does good works and works worthy of the reward that the Lord will repay us—for it is said of him, “Behold, the Lord, and his reward is in his hands, to repay each according to his works” (Matt. 16:27)—and the Apostle says elsewhere, “If anyone’s work remains which he has built upon it, he will receive a reward” (1 Cor. 3:13), that person gathers rewards to be preserved and to endure. Always adding virtues to virtues, he heaps up riches in an unpierced purse.

But whoever, after good works, sins not once or twice but frequently, and obscures and soils his former love by subsequent vices, gathers money into a pierced purse.

All these things happened to those who said, “The time has not yet come for the Lord’s house to be built,” while they themselves dwelt in valleys and allowed the Lord’s house to remain deserted.

[Col. 1395D] ### (Verses 17–18)

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways; go up to the mountain, bring wood [Vulgate: carry it], and build the house. Then it will be acceptable to me, and I will be glorified, says the Lord.”

The Seventy: “Thus says the Lord almighty: Set your hearts upon your ways; go up upon the mountain, and cut wood” (the rest is similar).

Again I, the Lord, command you—who had previously commanded you to set your hearts upon your ways and consider everything you do—to abandon your devotion to your lowly houses and ascend the mountain, where there is not wood for burning but wood useful for the work of my house. And so that you may do this more attentively, know that what you do will be pleasing to me.

The Hebrews say that wood was needed only for the roof-beams, since the walls of the temple remained standing after the fire. That is their view.

For us, however, the command is not to set our hearts outside our ways, but to set them again upon the ways where we had previously placed them; and after doing this, to ascend from concave houses to the mountain. When we have reached the height of the mountain—for which some copies read “the height of the discourse”—where the wood necessary for the building of God’s temple is found, let us cut it from the whole mountain of Holy Scripture, on which the various trees of virtues and of paradise have been planted, and let us build the temple of the Lord through good works and doctrines of truth. When it has been constructed, it will please the Lord, and he will be glorified [alternative: that he may be glorified] in it.

Therefore, since we have been commanded to set our hearts upon our ways, let us ascend the rational mountain. For each individual problem, let us seek appropriate wood from the testimonies of Scripture, cut it, and build within ourselves the house of wisdom. For once this house has been constructed, the end of its building will be that the Lord is glorified in us.

### (Verse 9)

“You looked for more, and behold, it became less; you brought it into the house, and I blew it away.”

The Seventy: “You looked toward many things, and they became few; you brought them into the house, and I blew them away.”

So that you may build my house more diligently, casting aside delay and putting away every ambiguity, I also tell you what happened to you who postponed building my house—not as above, “You sowed much, and, because the earth did not return the seed, you brought in little,” but this: when the crops were already whitening, the harvest season was approaching, and you thought that you held the grain in your hands, you reaped empty stalks and gathered barren straw without the fruit of ears.

The threshing-floors were full: hope was in your eyes, mourning in your hands. But even that which had scarcely been selected from the abundant harvest and countless heaps you brought into the house was scattered by my power. For I blew it away and reduced it to nothing, because the dead grain and empty husks, which are useful for food, had no flour or fine meal.

[Note: In the Reginensis manuscript: “which are not useful for food” (with “they possessed” supplied), “and they had neither flour nor fine meal.”]

It is also possible to understand the words, “You brought it into the house, and I blew it away,” of the offerings they presented on the altar, which God blew away. But since he said, “You brought it into the house,” if we understand what was brought in as offerings, we must say that they were offered in the temple. This does not fit the circumstances, since at that time the house of God had not yet been built.

This still happens to many who dwell in lowly buildings and, so far as they can, despise the desolate house of God. Although they are able to build it, they scorn to do so. As though they were already seeing ripe crops, they promise themselves the fruits of their works; but when hope deceives them, they scarcely find small results in place of great ones.

Even those small results which they had stored in the house and granary [Col. 1397A] of their mind are blown away by the word of God, as unworthy of his custody and protection.

How often have I seen great things hoped for, both in teaching and in conduct, from certain people; but when the harvest season arrived—that is, the time for teaching and for offering their life as an example to the peoples—they were thrown down from their height, and less was found in them than everyone’s opinion had promised itself.

Hence it happened that, little by little, as negligence crept in, they lost even the small thing which they seemed to possess.

They suffered this because they were secure in their former houses and did not ascend the mountain of the Scriptures to cut from it the wood of the Lord’s building. They did not construct the Lord’s house in themselves day by day; instead, despising its desolation, they lost even what they believed they possessed.

This, then, is assigned as the cause of the evils mentioned above.

### (Verse 10)

“Therefore, says the Lord of hosts, because my house is deserted while each of you hastens to his own house, for this reason the heavens have been restrained above you, so that they gave no dew, and the earth withheld [Vulgate: was prevented from giving] its produce.”

Not only, he says, did the heavens fail to give rain, by which watered soil produces crops; they did not even give the morning and nighttime dew, so that the dry fields might at least be tempered by a little moisture.

The earth also swallowed everything and, unwilling to return the seed to the farmers, held fast in its greedy bosom what it ordinarily produces spontaneously.

I think this is the dew of which it is said in the blessing given to Jacob: “May God give you of the dew of heaven” (Gen. 27:28), and “the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 132). It descends not from the air, in which a multitude of eagles, hawks, and vultures flies, but from heaven, so that if someone’s soul burns with disturbances and has been wounded by the devil’s dart, it may be cooled by this dew and moderate its fever.

When this dew is withheld, the earth also does not produce its crop. For no soul can produce grain without the dew of Christ.

### (Verse 11)

“And I called for drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the grain, and upon the wine, and upon the oil, and upon everything that the soil produces, and upon human beings, and upon animals, and upon every labor of human hands.”

Instead of “drought,” [Note: In this passage there is nothing Hieronymian in Erasmus and Marianus, who inserted the Greek words ῥομφαίαν and καῦμα, although these are found in no manuscript. They then similarly impose Hebrew forms according to their custom, whose reading and pointing are contrary to Jerome. For they read hhereb, where Saint Doctor read HAREB and interpreted it as “sword”; but where he read Hereb, or Oreb according to certain copies—that is, “drought”—they inserted hhoreb. Accordingly, in our present edition the passage in Zephaniah above, chapter 11, should be explained, and the critical writers corrected—Bochart, Simon, and in part John Drusius—whom I mentioned in volume II. MART.]

The Seventy translated μαχαίραν, that is, “sword.” In Hebrew also I found it written with three letters (), HETH, RES, BETH.

[Note: Recall what we observed above at Zephaniah chapter 2 concerning the varying pronunciation, and thus the meaning, of this word.] If we read it HAREB, it means “sword”; if OREB, καύσωμα (elsewhere καῦμα), “burning heat,” which we translated as “drought,” although it may more accurately be rendered “a scorching wind.”

And indeed, since the subject here is the earth and the barrenness of the fields, it seems to me that in the present passage a scorching wind should be understood rather than a sword, although every affliction inflicted upon human beings because of their sins may also be understood as a sword.

Drought, or a sword, was summoned upon the land and upon the mountains, so that they would not produce grain, wine, oil, or anything that the soil spontaneously generates. Since famine precedes, death consequently comes upon human beings and animals.

[Note: In the Reginensis manuscript: “death comes,” that is, “the sword or scorching wind,” and so forth. A little later it reads “a two-edged sword” instead of “a double sword.”]

That same sword or scorching wind consumes everything on which human hands have labored.

Thus the living and effective word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword (Heb. 4), is summoned or brought in, so that the negligent soul—which is interpreted as dry earth and desires rather to dwell in hollows than to build the house of God—may be struck by its edge and lose whatever fruits it thinks it possesses.

The sword is also brought upon the mountains that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God, and upon grain, wine, and oil, with which, as though with food, drink, and refreshment, the assemblies of heretics flatter deceived peoples.

Someone might appropriately say that their bread is “the bread of mourning,” that their wine is “the fury of dragons,” and “the incurable fury of asps”; and that their oil is the promise of heavenly things, with which they seem to anoint their disciples and promise rewards for their labors. The prophet detests this, saying: “May the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Ps. 140).

The sword of God also strikes the other things which they discover and fabricate spontaneously, as though by apostolic tradition, without the authority and testimonies of Scripture.

As for human beings and animals, let us understand them either as λογισμοὺς and αἰσθήσεις, that is, their thoughts and perceptions, or else as the rational and irrational elements in them—that is, the learned and the unlearned alike.

And it strikes every labor of their hands: their fasts, their various observances, and their chameunias.

[Note: This is a gloss, that is, “sleeping on the ground.” In the Reginensis manuscript we have restored ξηροφαγίαις from the manuscripts in place of ξηροφαγίοις.]

Those who fast through three Lents each year, humbling their souls with ξηροφαγίαις, “dry-food observances,” and who grow especially from the root of Tatian, hear concerning such labors: “You suffered so many things in vain.”

All these things which I have said can also be understood of the rulers of the Church who build a carnal house, provide for their children and possessions, and do not care either to build the temple of God in themselves or to restore the Lord’s Church, which is uncovered and ruined.

[Note: We restore “uncovered” (*intecta*) from the Reginensis manuscript; printed books read “unblemished” (*infecta*). The same manuscript, with equally good sense, reads: “whose life and word are fitting and scandalize,” etc.]

Their life and speech, often incongruous, scandalize many, drive them from the Church, and lead the house of God into solitude.

We do not say this in order to accuse everyone indiscriminately, but because in every office and rank there are some who build the temple of God and others who destroy it. Because of their vice, neither do the heavens give dew nor does the earth give its produce; the soil dries up, the mountains wither, and grain, wine, oil, and everything that the earth produces perish, as do human beings, animals, and every labor of human hands, cut down by the sword and destroyed by drought or scorching wind.

[Col. 1399A] ### (Verse 13)

“And Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and all the remnant of the people heard the voice of their God [Vulgate adds: ‘of the Lord’], and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him to them; and the people feared before the Lord.”

Pay close attention to the two understandings of the Savior represented in Zerubbabel the ruler and Joshua the priest—for he is both king and priest. It does not say that Zerubbabel and Joshua feared; rather, when Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people heard the words of Haggai the prophet, which are the words of the Lord, only the people feared before the Lord.

That is, it was only the multitude which had not yet come into the one perfect man and had not yet deserved to be joined to the spirit as that which is spirit.

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “and had not yet been joined to the spirit as that which the spirit was.”]

The people feared before the Lord, knowing that “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33).

### (Verse 13)

“And Haggai, the messenger of the Lord, one of the messengers of the Lord, spoke to the people, saying: ‘I am with you,’ says the Lord.”

[Note: Origen, in the second book of his Commentary on John, undoubtedly has this in mind. Jerome soon repeats almost the same argument, and we will cite it below in the preface to the Commentaries on Malachi. How far Saint Father Jerome recoiled from Origen is demonstrated by nearly the whole of his letter to Evangelus on Melchizedek, letter 73 in our recension, and also by letter 122 to Algasi[a], question 1. Thus those who think Jerome adhered to this error, whether from this passage of the Commentary, as Rufinus formerly did in Against Jerome I, or from the apocryphal work of commentaries on the Psalms, as Genebrard did, are plainly doing Jerome an injustice. More will be said on this matter below, at Malachi chapter 1.]

Some think that John the Baptist, Malachi—whose name means “Angel of the Lord”—and Haggai, whom we now have in hand, were angels, and that, for the sake of God’s dispensation and command, they assumed human bodies and lived among human beings.

Nor is it surprising that this should be believed of angels, since for our salvation the Son of God also assumed a human body. For this reason they also adduce testimony from apocryphal writings, where it is said that Jacob, who was afterward called Israel, was an angel and therefore supplanted his brother in his mother’s womb (Gen. 25 and 32).

They also say that John leapt in the womb of Elizabeth at the voice of Mary, the mother of the Lord (Luke 1), that all rational beings have one nature, and that for this reason human beings who have pleased God become equal to angels.

Let them hold this opinion.

For our part, let us simply accept “the messenger of the Lord”—that is, the angel, who in Hebrew is called MALACH ()—as referring to a prophet, because he announced the Lord’s will to the people.

Or, since in many places our Lord and Savior is called the Angel of God, as in “the Angel of Great Counsel” (Isa. 9:6), we may say that a type of the Savior went before him in Haggai.

The expression “the messenger of the Lord, one of the messengers of the Lord” is equivalent to saying “a prophet of the prophets.”

When it says, “the messenger of the Lord spoke to the people, saying, ‘I am with you,’ says the Lord,” he is not speaking to Zerubbabel and Joshua, with whom and in whom the Lord was always present. For, as we have said once already, according to different understandings they are accepted as representing the person of the Savior.

Rather, he is speaking to the people who had feared before the Lord. They were still a people who had not yet attained the love of God, which casts out fear.

Therefore the people receive a reward for the fear of God: that the Lord may be with them. The meaning is: “I will be your helper. Build my house, which has been destroyed in you. When I am established in your midst, no one will be able to prevent your building.”

### (Verse 14)

“And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel, [Col. 1400B] son of Shealtiel, ruler of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua, son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the entire people. And they entered and worked on the house of the Lord of hosts, their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius.”

Instead of “ruler of Judah,” the Seventy translated “of the tribe of Judah”; and instead of “work,” they translated “works.” The rest is similar.

Wherever we use “Lord of hosts,” they variously interpret it as “Lord almighty,” “Lord Sabaoth,” or “Lord of powers.”

The spirit of Zerubbabel and the spirit of Joshua are therefore stirred up, for the present according to the literal meaning, so that the kingdom and priesthood may build the temple of God.

The spirit of the people is also stirred up. It had previously been sleeping in them—not the body, not the soul, but, as we have said, the spirit, which knows better how to build the temple of God.

They entered—for they had been outside—and they performed works worthy of the inner chambers of the Lord’s house. It was in the same year of King Darius as above, and in the same month that was mentioned at the beginning, but not on the same day.

There one day of the month is given; here, however, the twenty-fourth, so that between the first day, on which the Lord spoke through Haggai, and the twenty-fourth, on which they entered and worked on the Lord’s house, there were twenty-two intervening days—the same number as the letters among the Hebrews.

They necessarily had to be taught what the elementary principles of the beginnings of God’s words were: principles that would prevent them from saying, “The time has not yet come for the Lord’s house to be built,” and from dwelling in concave houses and, as I said above, being sunk into the depths.

They were also to be urged to set their hearts upon their ways and remember how much they had suffered because of their negligence; to ascend the mountain, cut wood, build the Lord’s house, and no longer endure what they had previously endured.

Finally, during these twenty-two days, the people feared before the Lord. They entered on the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius, and worked on the house of the Lord of hosts, their God.

We are commanded to present ourselves in such a way that a spiritual house may be built into a holy priesthood for the offering of spiritual sacrifices pleasing to God. Thus the Holy Spirit may be stirred up in us, and we may enter the house of the Lord and perform the works of the Lord.

For Zerubbabel, of the lineage of David, and Jesus the priest, raised up eternally by the Father in power according to the Spirit of holiness through the resurrection of the dead, has already been raised up to preside over the work; we are to act with his help and direction.

Yet we cannot perform the works of God beforehand unless we fear before the Lord, believe, enter the temple of God, and carry out those things that are worthy of the house of God.

Since we are still in the world and the time of our building occurs under King Darius—a time in which people serve generation, marriage, and the flesh—we therefore enter the Lord’s house in the number six, in which the world was made, and in the second year, which divides unity. For the material from which the restoration of the world and the succession of offspring consist loves the binary number.

Thus, with both peoples gathered together, we enter the Lord’s house and construct the temple of God.

For the sum of the twenty-fourth number consists of two twelves, because the Church of Christ, which had first been overthrown, was built from both circumcision and the nations.

[Note: The better reading, also approved by Victorius, is: “for the twenty-fourth number consists of these two twelves.”]

We can also say that the eighth number, which is holy and is understood as a figure of true circumcision, when tripled produces the twenty-fourth number. Figuratively, we are taught to build the Lord’s house through the cutting away of the flesh, the circumcision of vices, and the belief that true purity is found in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Another person calculated the number as six times four and referred the four to the elements of the world, from which we subsist, and the six to the creation of the world in which those elements exist.

He says that because we are still in matter, enclosed in a heavy body, and subject to generation, we can indeed build the temple, enter the house of God, and, as though roused from deep sleep, stir up our spirit; yet we still do this on the twenty-fourth day.

## (Chapter II.—Verses 1 ff.)

In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the word of the Lord came through the hand of the prophet Haggai, saying:

“Speak to Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying: Who is there among you who is left who saw this house in its former glory? What do you see it as now? Is it not, in your eyes, as though it did not exist? And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord, and be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, high priest, and be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord of hosts, and act; for I am with you, says the Lord of hosts. The word that I covenanted with you when you came out of the land of Egypt, and my spirit shall be in your midst; do not fear. For thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet once more, after a little while, I will shake the heaven and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and I will shake all the nations. And the Desired One of all the nations shall come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts. The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, says the Lord of hosts. The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former, says the Lord of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, says the Lord of hosts.”

In the same year, but in the seventh month, in which God’s solemnities [Alternative reading: “the day”] are observed on the first and twenty-first day of the month—that is, when three weeks had been completed and the rest signified in the mystery of the Trinity had been perfected—the word of the Lord came for the third time through the hand of the prophet Haggai. He labored continually, sweating under his exertion, so that the word of God might always find access in him. [Note: In the Reginensis manuscript, “might have an ascent.”] “Forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians 3), he labored each day as though he had accomplished nothing in his earlier works.

Therefore it is said to him: “Speak to Zerubbabel, and to Joshua, and to the remaining people, who saw the ancient house of God and are now present at its restoration: in comparison with the former one, is not what is now seen such that it seems, in a certain sense, not to exist?” But do not despair, and do not let your weary hands fall. Rather, you, Zerubbabel, and you, Joshua, and all you people, take courage and do the work in my house. For I am with you, and my word which I covenanted with you when you came out of the land of Egypt. My spirit will not withdraw from you. Do not fear. I am the Lord Almighty who commands, and for whom to speak is to accomplish.

When I first gave the covenant, and appeared on Mount Sinai, I shook heaven and earth, the Red Sea, and the desert, in order to establish the Covenant with you. But now I promise you that once again I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land, so that, when these are shaken, all the nations may be shaken and—according to the Septuagint—the Lord’s chosen ones from all the nations may come; but according to the Hebrew, “the Desired One of all the nations,” our Lord and Savior, shall come.

Then I will fill this house with glory greater than the former, and I will continually add to it for you, says the Lord Almighty. And lest you perhaps think the guarantor weak, the gold is mine and the silver is mine, and all riches are mine. I will give gold and silver for the adornment of the temple, so that the glory of this house may become greater than that of the former. And because what I promise seems difficult, and human unbelief always hesitates before greater promises, I therefore say again—the one who promises is the Lord Almighty.

Moreover, because I know that nothing contributes so greatly to the building of the illustrious house, the house which is to surpass the former one, as peace, I therefore promise this also. “For I will give peace in this place,” says the Lord of hosts, so that the peace which surpasses all understanding may guard my house, and my place may be in peace.

For the present, I have drawn these lines of exposition παραφραστικῶς (“by paraphrase”), so that from them the prudent reader may rise, even without my saying more, to a higher understanding.

The word of God therefore comes to those who had begun to work in the house of the Lord Almighty, already in the time of rest—that is, in the seventh month—and in the fullest sacrament of the Trinity, on the twenty-first day of the month. It comes also to Haggai, who was celebrating God’s feast and had again prepared his hand for the Lord’s word, and it says to him:

“Speak to Zerubbabel of the tribe of Judah, and to Joshua the high priest, who for our sake deigned to become both man and priest, and to the remnant of the people.” For in comparison with the whole world, the number of believers was small at the beginning. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “what proportion it was,” and so forth.]

Let us therefore hear what he said.

There was once in Israel a house of God which is now so deserted that it is not even believed to have existed. From the time when what had been beloved became not beloved, and the one who was not the people of God began to be the people of God, that house—which had once been glorious—now appears before Zerubbabel and Joshua and the remnant of the people as though it did not exist.

We must understand this not only of the buildings of the temple, which we see to have fallen into ruin, but also of all the things that the Jews once possessed in splendor. Nevertheless, because the former house has become as though it did not exist, Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the priest are urged on, so that the kingdom of Christ and the priesthood may be strengthened, and so that his people—who were once the people of the earth—may perform works in the house of the Lord and know that God is present with them. Let them also perform the word that the Lord covenanted with them when they were coming out of the land of Egypt.

Would that we too might come out of Egypt, so that we may fulfill the covenant-word which we have received.

The Lord God also promises his spirit to those who perform works in his house and fulfill the word they have received, saying: “And my spirit shall be in your midst.” Behold the sacrament of the Trinity: “I am with you, and my spirit, and the Word in whom I established the covenant when you came out of Egypt.”

What he says, “in your midst,” should be understood in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “There stands among you one whom you do not know, who will come after me” (John 1:26).

Thus says the Lord of hosts to you who see the former house as though it did not exist:

“I shook heaven when my voice was heard from heaven. I shook the earth when I gave the Covenant to the former people; and at my coming, cloud, storm, and darkness were seen. I shook the Red Sea when I provided a way for the people crossing through it. I shook the dry land—either Egypt, emptied of the worship of God through the plagues, or the wilderness through which I led the people for forty years.” [Note: Again the same manuscript reads, “the people went around for forty years.”]

“These things I will shake once more.”

We see this fulfilled in the coming of the Lord and Savior. At the time of his passion, when the sun withdrew, heaven was shaken and darkness was made over the whole earth from the sixth hour to the ninth (Matthew 27 and Luke 23). The earth was shaken, rocks were split, and tombs were opened. The sea was shaken when the dragon that was in it was slain. The dry land also was shaken—the wilderness of the nations, once barren.

In this trembling of the universe, all the nations too were shaken, because the sound of the Lord’s apostles went out into all the earth, and their words reached to the ends of the world (Psalm 18). The nations were shaken for this reason: so that from their shaking there might come “the chosen of the nations,” [Note: The same manuscript is almost certainly more correct: “the chosen things of the nations might come, and those things that are distinguished wherever they are.”] the multitude of those who are chosen, together with whatever is distinguished and excellent anywhere.

For example, the chosen from Corinth, because there was a large people of God there; the chosen from Macedonia, because a great church of God had been gathered in Thessalonica and did not need to be taught about love (1 Thessalonians 4); the chosen from Ephesus, so that they might learn the mysteries of God, hidden and previously unrevealed.

Why say more? All the nations were shaken, to which the Savior had sent the apostles, saying: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28:19), and from the many who were called, the few who were chosen built the Church of the firstborn.

Hence the apostle Peter also says: “She who is elect in Babylon greets you, and so does Mark my son” (1 Peter 5:13); and John says: “The elder to the elect lady,” and afterward mentions the children of the elect lady.

When the nations had been shaken—we may also understand these as hostile powers, unable to endure the splendor of the Lord—the chosen things of all the nations came, and the house of the Lord was filled with glory: the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.

This is according to the Septuagint. In the Hebrew, however, the wording is better and more meaningful, as we have set it out above: “And I will shake all the nations, and the Desired One of all the nations shall come.” Truly, after he came, the glory of the house of the Lord was fulfilled.

And as far as the Lord is above the servant, so far is the house of the Lord—over which the Lord presides—better than the former house over which the servant presided. [Note: In the Reginensis manuscript, the word “Lord’s” is absent here.]

When he says, “The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, says the Lord of hosts,” I do not think anyone should suppose that he is speaking about the silver and gold possessed by the rich and kings. In that case, not only silver and gold would belong to God as Creator, but also the other metals: bronze, tin, lead, and iron, which subdues all things.

Rather, I understand the silver with which the house of God is adorned to be the sayings of Scripture, of which it is said: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, purified of earth, refined sevenfold” (Psalm 11:7). And the gold is what operates in the hidden understanding of the saints and in the secret place of the heart, shining with the true light of God. It is clear that the apostle also understood this of the saints who build upon the foundation of Christ: “gold, silver, precious stones” (1 Corinthians 3). Thus the hidden meaning is in the gold, a fitting word in the silver, [Note: Victorinus reads “a word that speaks”; the Reginensis manuscript is almost certainly more correct: “a fitting word.”] and works pleasing to God in the precious stone.

By these metals the Church of the Savior becomes more splendid than the synagogue once was. By these living stones the house of Christ is built, and eternal peace is granted to it.

But what follows in the Septuagint—“and peace for the soul, for the acquisition of every person who is created, to raise up this temple”—we have omitted as superfluous and scarcely coherent, since it is found neither among the Hebrews nor in any other interpreter.

## (Verses 11 ff.)

On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius [the Vulgate adds: “the king”], the word of the Lord came to the prophet Haggai, saying:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Ask the priests about the law, saying: If a man carries consecrated flesh in the fold of his garment, and with the edge of it touches bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food, will it become consecrated?”

The priests answered and said: “No.”

And Haggai said: “If one who is polluted in soul touches any of these, will it be defiled?”

The priests answered and said: “It will be defiled.”

And Haggai answered and said:

“So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord; and so is every work of their hands, and everything that they offer there: they shall be defiled.”

The Septuagint reads:

“On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to the prophet Haggai, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Ask the priests about the law, saying: If a man takes holy flesh in the edge of his garment, and the edge of his garment touches bread, or cooked food, or wine, or oil, or any food, will it be sanctified?”

The priests answered and said: “No.”

And Haggai said: “If one who is unclean in soul touches any of these, will it be defiled?”

The priests answered and said: “It will be defiled.”

And Haggai answered and said:

“So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord, and so are all the works of their hands. And whoever approaches there shall be defiled, because of their morning offerings. They shall grieve because of the face of their evil deeds, and hate those who rebuke at the gates.”

[Note: We have restored “there” (*ibi*) from the Reginensis manuscript in accordance with the Greek text, ἐγγίσῃ ἐκεῖ, “shall approach there”; Martianay instead reads “to you” (*tibi*).]

We have also included the edition of the Septuagint translators because it seemed to differ in certain expressions. What is said—“because of their morning offerings they shall grieve because of the face of their evil deeds, and, smelling them at the gates, they shall reproach them”—is found neither in the Hebrew nor among the other interpreters.

It should be noted that in this passage—“On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year”—it does not say, as it did above for the third time, “The word of the Lord came through the hand of Haggai the prophet,” but “to Haggai the prophet.” [Note: In the Reginensis manuscript: “Note, however, that in the fourth passage …,” which appears to be the more correct reading.]

There, because he was still making progress, [Note: The same manuscript reads, “because he still had prophecy.”] and only his works were pure while his mind had not yet received complete wisdom—or because he still lived among those who said, “The time has not yet come to build the house of the Lord”—the word of the Lord came to him only concerning his works.

Here, however, because the foundations of the temple have already been laid, and the people with their leaders have entered the house of God, and are doing work appropriate to the temple of God, and have heard the mystery, “I will shake all the nations, and the Desired One of all the nations shall come,” and he is full of prophecy, the whole word of the Lord is directed to Haggai. [Note: Victorinus reads, perhaps more correctly, “the word of the Lord is directed to the whole of Haggai.”]

We have already spoken of the twenty-fourth day and the second year. The number of the ninth month, which is added here, is never read in a favorable sense. The people sacrifice the Passover and celebrate other festivals; all its solemnity ends on the eighth day and does not reach the ninth. Those who prepare the Passover lamb begin to prepare it after the ninth day has passed. The Day of Atonement and Expiation in the seventh month is also celebrated after the ninth day. And in Jeremiah (chapters 19 and 52), as will be evident to readers, Jerusalem is attacked by the Babylonians in the ninth year.

Therefore, because the prophecy concerned the future uncleanness of the people, the ninth month is joined to the second year of Darius. Again, because an opportunity for repentance is given after the rebuke of uncleanness, on the twenty-fourth day the word of God comes to the prophet Haggai, so that, as though speaking in the person of the Lord, he might ask the priests a question arising from the law. He is told: “Ask the priests about the law, saying.”

At the same time, consider that it is the duty of priests to answer one who asks about the law. If he is a priest, let him know the law of the Lord; if he does not know the law, he himself proves that he is not the Lord’s priest. It is the priest’s duty to know the law and to answer questions about the law.

We read the same thing in Deuteronomy (chapter 17): if anywhere in the cities of Israel a question arises between blood and blood, between judgment and judgment, between leprosy and leprosy, or between dispute and dispute, they are to go to the priests and Levites, and to the high priest who is appointed in those days, and ask him about the law of the Lord. When they answer, they are to do what they are commanded. If they do not do so, they are to be exterminated from their people.

And lest these instructions seem to be found only in the Old Testament, the apostle also tells Timothy that a bishop must be not only irreproachable, the husband of one wife, wise, chaste, respectable, and hospitable, but also a teacher (1 Timothy 3).

And lest he seem to have said this by chance, the same care is observed in his instructions to Titus concerning the appointment of presbyters—whom he wishes to be understood also as bishops (Titus 1:5 ff.):

“For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what remained and appoint presbyters in each city, as I instructed you: if anyone is irreproachable, the husband of one wife, having believing children, not accused of debauchery or insubordination. [Note: Jerome here quotes the Old Vulgate, as the following expressions—“insubordinate,” “encourage in sound teaching,” and so forth—show; they occur in all manuscript codices, as we have printed them. MART.] For a bishop must be irreproachable, as God’s steward, not arrogant, not angry, not violent, not a striker, not greedy for shameful gain, but hospitable, chaste, kind, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the faithful word in accordance with doctrine, so that he may be able both to encourage in sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it.

“For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, whose mouths must be stopped.”

I have set this out at greater length so that we may know, from both the Old and the New Testament, that it is the duty of priests to know the law of God and to answer what they are asked.

Nor is simplicity and restraint in food sufficient in a teacher unless he can also instruct others in what he himself does. Certainly, because I think they will answer that this duty belongs to those who prepare themselves for teaching from adolescence, while simple men are frequently chosen for the priesthood by the judgment of the Lord and the vote of the people, let them at least possess this: after they have been ordained priests, let them learn the law of God, so that they may teach what they have learned. Let them increase their knowledge rather than their wealth, and not be ashamed to learn from laymen who know the things belonging to the priestly office. Let them spend more nights and days in the study of Scripture than in calculations and reckonings.

What is it, then, that Haggai asks the priests in the person of the Lord?

“If a man takes consecrated flesh in the fold, or edge, of his garment, and with its edge touches bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food, will it become consecrated?”

Before we discuss the question, we must for the moment understand according to the literal sense what consecrated flesh is, and what “unclean in soul” means.

The flesh of the victim sacrificed on the altar was holy, and among those consecrated meats there was great diversity. Some were eaten by the priests in the inner chambers of the temple; others by their relatives at home; others by those who appeared to be blemished among the priests; others by Israelites who had no uncleanness. The full rationale of this diversity is given in Leviticus.

A person was called unclean in soul who had touched the body of a dead human being. Here we should observe that, as long as the soul is in the body, the human body is not unclean. But as soon as the spirit that animates the limbs has departed, what is earthly becomes unclean, as is written in the same Leviticus:

“The Lord said to Moses, saying: Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them: They shall not defile themselves among their people by the dead, except for their relatives who are close to them: for their mother, their father, their sons and daughters, their brother, and their virgin sister who is close to him and has not been given to a husband. For these they shall not become unclean, nor shall they suddenly be polluted among their people” (Leviticus 21:1–2).

Consider that the priests are commanded not to approach just anyone who has died, except those relatives and close kin mentioned above. But the high priest, that is, the pontiff, had something more than the other priests, and neither piety nor affection could bend him so as to make him unclean even through the persons named above.

For Scripture says: “He shall not approach any dead soul; he shall not approach his father or his mother, and he shall not defile himself.”

Knowing, then, what consecrated flesh and uncleanness of soul are, let us see what the prophet asks.

“If any man”—the passage does not speak here of the pontiff, or of a priest, or of a Levite, but of any man; where no particular person is named, anyone at all is permitted to touch flesh—“takes consecrated flesh and binds it in the edge of his garment, and that edge of the garment touches bread, or any other cooked food, or wine, or oil, or anything besides these that a person can eat, can the bread, wine, oil, or any food be sanctified by contact with the garment in which the holy flesh has been bound?”

The priests answered and said: “It cannot”—that is, none of the things about which you ask will be sanctified; each will remain as it was.

Again another question is proposed to the priests, who had answered correctly above, and the likeness of the problem is adapted in such a way that an inexperienced person could easily slip. Suppose someone is ignorant of the law: just as he answered that bread, stew, wine, oil, or any food is not sanctified by consecrated flesh, he might answer this question in the same way and say that one who is unclean in soul does not defile the things which holy flesh could not sanctify.

Therefore he asks and says:

“If one who is unclean in soul touches any of these”—that is, one who has become unclean through contact with a dead body—“whether bread, stew, wine, oil, or the remaining foods, will these things that he touches be defiled through his contact?”

The priests answered, their leader being Jesus son of Jehozadak, and therefore knowing the law, and they said that through the contact of one who is unclean everything touched by him is defiled.

Haggai answered and said, leaving aside the previous matter—that consecrated flesh cannot sanctify the other foods—and weaving the occasion of his speech only from the second question:

“So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord. The one who is unclean in soul and has touched a corpse makes everything he touches, and everything he offers to me, unclean.”

The literal meaning is as follows:

“O people, who offer victims to me on an altar merely erected while my house lies in ruins, and who think that you are sanctified by its victims and their flesh, know that you are not so much sanctified by the offerings—which, with the temple destroyed, cannot benefit you—as all your works and everything you do are defiled because you neglect me and have tried to build your own house rather than mine.

“What is offered on the altar is indeed holy. But you are not so much sanctified by the victims as defiled because you live in valleys and are occupied with dead works.”

This is according to the historical sense, although we have traced within it the lines of a spiritual understanding.

According to ἀναγωγή (“higher, spiritual interpretation”), however, the ecclesiastical man who has sacrificed a spotless year-old lamb and has put on Christ—if he takes some of its flesh, binds it in the edge of his garment, and that edge touches the bread of Scripture, which strengthens the hearts of believers; or cooked food, the apostolic Epistles, which, like the flesh of the ancient Law, cut up and cook various things and serve them seasoned for eating; or wine, which gladdens the human heart; or oil, in which the face of the hearer is made cheerful; or any food—milk, by which the Corinthians are nourished (1 Corinthians 3), and vegetables, which the weak eat (Romans 14:3), and other things of this kind—does not thereby make those to whom these things have been given immediately eat them as sanctified.

For these things sanctify their hearers not because they are spoken, but because they are received. “For many are hearers of the law, and not doers.” [Note: Martianay’s text lacked “of the law”; we have restored it, as we have restored similar omissions elsewhere.]

I also think that all the things I have mentioned are not conveyed as sanctified from the garment’s contact to those who eat them because they are touched only by the edge of the cloak, while the consecrated flesh within does not know moisture, blood, veins, or sinews.

Therefore, just as the edge of the Lord’s garment and a light touch do not sanctify anyone except the one who eats the lamb’s flesh and drinks its blood, so, conversely, the person unclean in soul, and every perverse doctrine, must necessarily make whatever they touch unclean.

They have bread, wine, oil, and every food within their mysteries; but their mysteries are like bread of mourning, and all who touch them will be defiled. They too read the Scriptures and, as though from testimonies of Scripture, sprinkle their bread and bake it all night in the oven. But when it is given for eating, it drives those who eat it to madness.

They have stew and cooked food, attempting, according to the meaning of their perversity, to weave various mysteries from Scripture, as though to cook and season the lamb’s flesh; but that cooking is destruction.

They also have wine, but not from the vine of Sorek, which the Lord planted in Jeremiah, choice and wholly true (Jeremiah 2), but from the vine of Sodom.

They have oil, too, which they violently squeeze from testimonies of the Old and New Scripture and promise, as though for refreshment, to minds deceived and wearied. But the holy man rejects it and says: “But let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Psalm 140:5).

They also have various foods—namely, the many different hypotheses [ὑποθέσεις] and diverse treatises—which, because those who wrote them are unclean and they have been uttered by an unclean mouth, will make everyone who touches them unclean and draw him into their error.

Therefore Haggai, who knows the distinctions among solemnities and for this reason received the name associated with a feast, answered:

“So is this people, and so is this nation”—namely, of the Jews, the Gentiles, and all heretics—“before my face, says the Lord. Everything they do and everything they offer to me, whether vows for salvation, peace offerings, offerings for sin, offerings for guilt, or burnt offerings; whether almsgiving, fasting, or abstinence in food and chastity of body, shall be defiled before my face.”

For although the things offered by such people may appear holy in their outward form, nevertheless, because they have been touched by one who is unclean in soul, everything will be defiled.

(Verses 17ff.) 765 “And now set your hearts from this day onward, before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord. When you approached a heap of twenty measures, and there were ten; and when you entered the winepress to draw off fifty jars, and there were twenty. I struck you with scorching wind, blight, and hail—all the work of your hands—and there was none among you who returned to me, says the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “And now set your hearts upon this day and onward, before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord. What were you like when you put twenty measures of barley into the *cypselus*—a grain-measure—and there were ten measures of barley; and when you entered the winepress to draw fifty amphorae, and there were twenty? I struck you with barrenness, atmospheric corruption, and hail—all the work of your hands—and you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

Although everything that you offered me upon the altar was contaminated because you had not built the temple—for without the temple’s construction every gift is polluted—nevertheless I now exhort you, O people, to return in mind to the past and consider what happened: that is, from this twenty-fourth day of the ninth month in the second year of Darius, comprehend whatever has previously occurred, and for what reasons and how much you have endured, so that when prosperity subsequently comes to you, you may know why it has come.

Before you began to build the temple and to lay stone upon stone, when you approached a heap and thought that you had twenty measures, could you not scarcely gather half of it? [Note: [Col. 1410D] The Regina manuscript does not have the word *nonne* (“could you not?”), and thus lacks the interrogative marker.] Or, according to the Septuagint: when you put twenty measures of barley into a vessel called a *cypselus*, and thought that, although you had put in barley—the food of animals—you were at least secure concerning those twenty measures, did you not afterward return to the vessel and scarcely find ten measures?

Likewise, when you approached the winepress and saw the grapes, and your eyes promised you fifty amphorae—I do not say half, but could you scarcely press out twenty amphorae? I did these things by striking you with scorching wind, atmospheric corruption, dying crops, empty husks of grain, and clusters of vines, so that by the weight of your calamities you might be moved to seek my knowledge; 766 and even then there was none who returned to me.

The Hebrew has explained the entire passage from the words, “And now set your hearts from this day onward,” up to the place where it says, “the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have not blossomed; from this day I will bless,” as follows: “Certainly now the foundations of the temple have been laid. From this day, therefore, on which you laid the foundations—for in the past I punished you with barrenness, famine, hail, and drought, and none of you returned to me through these blows—set your hearts upon the future and what follows, and see that everything flows toward you in prosperity. This will happen because you have begun to build my temple and, rather than trusting in the altar alone, have not despised the building of my house.”

According to this interpretation, we may briefly say that some offer gifts to God in vain, and think that God can be appeased by alms and offerings, while they themselves have not built within them a temple for the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 1411; Col. 1114A] This note appears at the foot of column 1114, but its callout letter has not been printed in the text. In some manuscripts: “pertain to use”; in Victor: “come to food.”] Alms and gifts offered upon the altar are beneficial only when someone has built himself into a temple of God and, after building the temple, has offered gifts upon the altar.

Moreover, according to the spiritual interpretation, this is also said to us who now believe in Jesus Christ—provided that we truly believe and show the truth through the work of faith—so that we may return in mind to the time when we were Gentiles, serving vices daily and having not yet built within ourselves a temple for God.

Just as an architect and highly skilled mason joins stone to stone and binds the lower stone to the upper with lime and gypsum, so the architect—whom the apostle also declares himself to be: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (I Cor. III, 10), and whom the Lord threatens to remove from Jerusalem—knows how to join works to works and gradually build the temple of God.

The foundation of this temple is Jesus. Upon it let each person see what he builds: “One builds gold, silver, precious stones; another, wood, hay, stubble.” Three good things have three evils set against them.

These are the stones concerning which the Lord promises that he will build Jerusalem: “Behold, I will prepare your carbuncle as a stone, and your foundations of sapphire; I will make your battlements of jasper [Al. *jaspim*], your gates of crystal stone, and your wall of chosen stones” (Isa. LIV, 11–12).

We must not suppose, according to Jewish fables and foolish inventions, that God will build Jerusalem with gold and gems rather than with living stones, which now roll upon the earth and, according to the natures of stones, are either inflamed with faith, like the carbuncle; wholly heavenly and brought into the throne of God, like the sapphire; or shining with innocence and the simplicity of good works, like crystal.

We are therefore told to consider what we suffered previously, before we built the temple of God within us. “When you approached,” he says, “a heap of twenty measures, and there were ten”; or, according to the Septuagint, “when you put twenty measures of barley into the *cypselus*, and there were ten measures of barley.”

Whatever virtues and good works we seemed to possess before Christ was not wheat but barley. And that barley itself did not yield, according to our hope and desire, the hundredfold harvest that we read of in Isaac (Gen. XXVI); scarcely half of our labor could we find in it, and it was said to us: “Have you suffered so many things in vain?” (Gal. III, 4).

But when we entered the winepress and counted fifty amphorae of wine—a number which, when the seven weeks have been completed, contains the unity of divinity—and thought that we possessed wine that gladdens the human heart, the sacred number thirty was taken away from us. In that number the Lord is baptized; Ezekiel sees a vision at the beginning of his prophecy; and, according to the Hebrew text, priests approached the ministry of God. Twenty were left.

Esau loves this number; hence Jacob, knowing that he delighted in it, sends him certain animals as a gift, twenty and twenty. Observe also that Jacob himself, although holy—yet at the time when he was not with his father Isaac, that is, with laughter, nor with his mother Rebekah, that is, with patience, but had Assyrians as neighbors and dwelt in Mesopotamia, enclosed on either side by rivers—served Laban, the most cruel and greedy of men, for twenty years (Gen. XXXII).

Let no one be troubled if we say that some before faith in Christ and the construction of his temple can receive only half the fruit of their labor, since among unbelievers there is no fruit of good works. A person does not store up twenty and find twenty; rather, when he has stored up twenty, he finds ten—that is, half the fruit of his labor.

Jews, Gentiles, philosophers of this age, and all others who boast of wisdom receive the fruit and glory of their conduct and labor only in the present time, while all their hope and reward for the future age is taken away. This happens so that, by not falling into utter despair, they may not despise repentance, but may at some time turn, lay stone upon stone, and build the temple of God.

If they remain in unbelief, they will lose even the half that they seemed to possess. For it follows: “I struck you with scorching wind, blight, and hail—all the work of your hands.” Whatever is struck by blight, hail, and scorching wind is reduced to dust and ashes, and nothing useful for benefit or food is found in it.

The Lord did all these things because none among them was found who would return to him. But if they return and build the temple of the Lord, from the day on which they begin to build they will possess the things that the prophetic utterance adds.

(Verses 19, 20.) “Set your hearts from this day and into the future, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the foundations of the temple of the Lord were laid; set your hearts upon it. Is the seed yet in the granary, and have the fig tree, the vine, the pomegranate, and the olive tree not yet blossomed? From this day I will bless.”

The Septuagint: “Set your hearts from this day and into the future, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month and from the day on which the foundations of the temple of the Lord were laid; set it in your hearts. Is the threshing floor still known upon the earth? And have the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive trees that bear no fruit yet blossomed? From this day I will bless.”

“I have explained to you,” he says, “what you suffered before you began to build my temple. Now I will explain what prosperity is to come to you, because you have begun to build my temple.” From the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, on which the foundations of the temple were laid, consider how great an abundance of things will come.

The ninth month is what we call November or December. Nisan () is the first month among the Hebrews, called the month of new things. It is the season when they celebrate Passover, that is, at the beginning of spring, which, according to the course of the moon, often possesses part of the month of March and sometimes begins in April.

Therefore, if we understand Nisan as April, the ninth month according to the Hebrew reckoning will be December. Thus the tenth month [Al. December] is the season when the seeds lie hidden in the earth and future fertility cannot be inferred.

“Is the seed already in the bud?” he says. This is better expressed in Hebrew as “in the husk,” so that it signifies the sheath of the grain. “Have the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree given their blossom?”—so that from the blossom the fruit may also be understood.

Certainly not; for, as we said, in the month of December there are no signs of the future crops. [Note: [Col. 1413D] The reading of the Regina manuscript was preferred: “Certainly not; for, as we said, in the month …” Earlier printed books read: “certainly not in the ninth month, as we said.”] Do not therefore say that I infer this by rational calculation and conjecture future fertility from the blossoms of trees and the shoots of the crops. Behold, there are no signs; and yet I predict to you that, because you have begun to build my temple, there will be, unto my blessing, fertility of every kind of crop. This we have said according to the Hebrew text.

According to the Septuagint, however, the meaning is entirely different, and we must first explain it literally, after which the sequence of the spiritual interpretation will be treated.

“Set your hearts from this day, on which the temple was founded, into the future, and you will see that there will be such abundant crops, and so much grain will be brought from all the fields, that the threshing floor will not recognize its own crops—or rather, that there will not be separate threshing floors for individuals, but that, because of the abundance, threshing floor will be joined to threshing floor, and the separation of the threshing floors will not be discernible upon the earth.”

The vine, fig tree, pomegranate, and olive tree, which previously through your fault bore no fruit because you had not yet begun to build my temple, will bend under such abundance of grapes and fruit that evident fertility will reveal an evident blessing.

That the ninth month is not to be understood favorably is also related by the Fourth Book of Kings 770 and by the history of Jeremiah, in which Jerusalem is said to have been besieged (IV Kings XXV; Jer. XXX and XXXII). Nevertheless, since the foundations of the temple are laid at the end of the ninth month, we may understand that the temple of the Lord is not begun to be built unless evil works have first been brought to an end.

Therefore, on the twenty-fourth day of that month the foundation of the temple is laid. In this number there are two twelves (δύο δωδεκάδες), three eights (τρεῖς ὀγδοάδες), and four sixes (τέσσαρες ἑξάδες); this has already been discussed more fully above.

Whoever, therefore, devotes himself to the worship of God and despises the *rhathymus* (ῥᾴθυμος), that is, the negligent patron—who, according to the Septuagint interpreters in the Book of Ezra, forbids the temple of God to be built (I Esdr. IV)—does not know the measure of his harvest and his reward. [Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “he will not know the measure of his reward.”]

Or certainly, because it is said, “if the threshing floor is still known upon the earth,” let the one who sows in the Spirit and reaps eternal life from the Spirit (Gal. VI) not store up treasure for himself on earth, but let all his works and the rewards of his works be gathered in heaven.

The vine—that is, the word of God, whose cultivator is the Father in each person—and the fig tree, the sweetest gifts of the Holy Spirit; and the pomegranate, the doctrines of the Church and knowledge of the Scriptures, which is compared to the bride’s cheeks in the Song of Songs (Cant. VIII); and the olive trees will give refreshment and illumination of heart to the one who begins to build the temple of God.

That the vine, the fig tree, and the olive—setting aside the pomegranate for a little while—refer to the person of the Savior, God the Father, and the Holy Spirit is read more fully in the Book of Judges (ch. IX). There the fruitless trees go to establish a king over themselves, and they say in turn to the vine, the fig tree, and the olive tree that they should reign over them. Both the vine and the fig tree and the olive refuse such rule and do not deign to reign over fruitless trees.

Then those trees come to the thorny shrub, the king of their barrenness: the bramble, a bush woven with thorns and hooks, which holds whatever it touches, wounds what it holds, and delights in the blood of the wounded; moreover, it sends fire from itself and consumes the trees that have made it king.

We refer the bramble to the devil and, according to the nature of the shrub, interpret his nature. 771 The vine, the fig tree, and the olive, however, will be found where the pomegranate is, a tree that, because of the great multitude of its seeds and the geometric arrangement formed by the interwoven membranes—many separate chambers, yet all contained within one rind—is always set in the Scriptures as a representation of the Church.

(Verses 21ff.) “And the word of the Lord came a second time to Haggai, on the twenty-fourth [Note: The Hebrew text and Jerome’s Latin version do not have the word ‘day.’] day of the month, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying: I will shake heaven and earth together; I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms; I will destroy the strength of the kingdom of the nations; I will overthrow the chariot and its rider; and the horses and their riders shall come down, each man by the sword of his brother.

“On that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, says the Lord, and I will set you as a signet; for I have chosen you, says the Lord of hosts.”

The Septuagint adds “the sea and the dry land” after the words “heaven and earth,” and lacks “I will destroy the strength of the kingdom of the nations”; the fuller wording is known from its own reading. [Note: [Col. 1414D] That is, after the words “heaven and earth.” A little below, the word “our” is absent from the Royal manuscript.] It should be noted that on the same day—that is, on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month—the number of the month being omitted because they were prophesying the coming of Christ and his kingdom—the word of our Lord God comes a second time to Haggai, not “in his hand,” as previously, nor “to Haggai the prophet,” as in the fourth vision, but simply “to Haggai,” that is, to the one celebrating the Lord’s festivals, because he was to announce and behold not merely one who would come, but one who was coming.

Just as Abraham saw the day of Christ and rejoiced (John VIII), and John pointed out the Lamb of God with his finger (John I), so Haggai himself, seeing the kingdom of the Son of God, possessed within himself all the solemnities.

At this point many hold different opinions. Some suppose that the passage concerns his first coming; others, his second coming, when he will come in his majesty. We accept both, because he reigned when he came and will reign afterward.

Nevertheless, if we wish to understand it as referring to the end of the world, we shall say what the apostle writes to the Corinthians: “Every principality, every authority, and every power must be destroyed, so that God may be all in all” (I Cor. XV).

Because what is said is mystical and pertains to the end of things, the prophet is therefore commanded to speak to Zerubbabel alone, whom we have shown to have come forth as a type of Christ, through the assumption of a body, from the seed of David.

To him, therefore, are spoken the things that will occur at the end: that the form of this world will pass away, that there will be a new heaven and a new earth, [Note: In Victor’s edition this comma and the words “and the Lord will shake heaven and earth” are lacking.] and that the Lord will shake heaven and earth, destroy every principality, authority, and power, and overthrow the kings of kings—or, as it is found in Hebrew, the kingdoms—and destroy every hostile strength.

Then even those who formerly reigned and held nations under their authority will benefit from the destruction of their kingdoms; and when every impulse toward warfare has been dispersed, peace will follow. This is what he says: “I will overthrow the chariot,” or “the chariots,” “and their riders, and the horses and their riders shall come down.” [Note: With Victor, the Regina manuscript reads “and he will disperse the seats of kings.” Below it reads “and the riders who run,” instead of “the falling riders,” etc.]

To show you that what we have said is signified by the overthrow of chariots and the falling of riders, see how it is said concerning Christ in Zechariah that he comes as a meek king, riding upon a beast of burden and a young foal of a donkey, and destroys the chariots of Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd; and that both companies, from the Gentiles and from the Jews, may be held under the peaceful shepherd (Zech. 9).

In order that these perverse things may be destroyed, each person will rise against his brother with a sword—which I think signifies the exceedingly sharp word of doctrine, cutting away every perversion—and will cut off everything contrary.

The end of all these things is excellent. After the destruction of the thrones, the strengths of those who reign, the chariots, the horses, and the riders, “on that day,” says the Lord Almighty, “I will take you, Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, my servant.”

He is called a servant because of the human body, since then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him, and he himself will be seen as subject among all things that have been subjected.

When this has been fulfilled, God will set him as a signet upon his hand. “For God the Father sealed him” (John VI, 27); and he is “the image of the invisible God” and “the form of his substance.” Thus whoever believes in God will be sealed by him as though by a ring.

I ask you, reader, to forgive me for dictating in haste, and do not demand elegance of expression, which I have lost through long devotion to the study of the Hebrew language, although Alecto may always assert that I have been an infant and mute.

What shall I say to him? “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim it, with great power” (Ps. LXVII, 12).

[Note: The Regina manuscript seems to require that the text be read according to the person of the holy Doctor: “although I should assert that I have always been an infant and mute from the breast”; but what follows—“to whom shall I say,” etc.—does not allow this in any way. Jerome must have called Alecto his rival because he never ceased bringing insults. Concerning the final words, “great power” or “many powers”—for both readings are found—Victor observes: “The one who interprets Mark from the beginning, in the work attributed to Jerome, followed this reading, and of all the manuscripts in the Vatican Library only one codex retains it. The meaning of this reading is: ‘The Lord will give many powers, or great power, to the one proclaiming the word.’ We, however, corrected it to: ‘The Lord will give the word to the one proclaiming with great power.’ In all the commonly published Greek and Latin editions, both manuscript and printed, the reading is ‘to those proclaiming.’ Jerome himself not only consistently follows that reading elsewhere, but it is still preserved by a most ancient Greek Vatican codex, nearly a thousand years old, which reads δύναμει πολλῇ (‘with great power’); and forty-six very ancient manuscript copies of the Bible in my possession agree with it. The ambiguity of the Hebrew expression introduced the diversity.”]

[Col. 1415]

THE TWO BOOKS OF THE COMMENTARIES OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, ON THE PROPHET ZECHARIAH, ADDRESSED TO EXSUPERIUS, BISHOP OF TOULOUSE. (C)

Prologue

[Col. 1415C] 775–776 At the very end of autumn our brother, your son, the monk Sisinnius, delivered to me a letter expressing your esteem. After reading it, I rejoiced that you were safe and that you remembered me and all the brothers who serve the Lord in the holy places—among whose consolations you make friends for yourself from unrighteous mammon and prepare eternal dwellings—so that you may say with David: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII, 1).

For if the sparrow finds a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest in which to place its young (ibid.), why should you, who are a priest of the Lord and tread the winepresses at the end of the world so that you may give the wine of Christ’s blood to thirsty peoples, not freely proclaim and say: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God; blessed are those who dwell in your house” (Ps. LXXXIII, 3)?

I hear that in the valley of tears, in the place that God appointed for combat so that he might give a crown to the victorious, you arrange ascents in your heart, go from strength to strength, and imitate the poverty of the Lord, so that with him you may become rich, and that he may recline his head in you and be received, visited, nourished, clothed, and, above all, welcomed through the reading of the holy Scriptures on every day. [Note: The Regina manuscript does not have the word “days.” Perhaps it is more correct to omit it and understand “human beings” as implied instead of “days.”]
