Since I wished to offer you some little gift from my small talent, and my exposition of the twelve prophets was approaching its end, I did not wish to abandon the work I had undertaken. Rather, what I would have dictated even without you I consecrated especially to your name.

I rejoice that the extremely obscure book of the prophet Zechariah—and the longest among the Twelve—is to be explained at a time when, because of the haste of the one who is about to return, the interpretation allows no delay. Whether I wish it or not, I am compelled to dictate, at least during the profitable and stolen hours of the night, what I shall send to you.

Origen wrote two volumes on this prophet, reaching from the beginning to the third part of the book. Hippolytus also published commentaries, and Didymus, at my request, dictated books of explanations—three books on Hosea and five on Zechariah—for me. [Note: There is a notable error in the old editions, which read without any intelligible sense, “which he addressed with three others on Hosea and Micah.” Instead of *mihi* (“for me”), they impose the name Micah, which arose through the ignorance of ancient copyists and passed into certain more recent copies. The reading of other manuscript codices is plainly confirmed by the preface to the prophet Hosea, where it is written: “I saw Didymus … and asked him to write commentaries on Hosea; at my request he dictated three books, and also five others on Zechariah.” These words fit the present passage perfectly, as is clear to the discerning reader. Didymus therefore did not write on Micah, but on Hosea and Zechariah. MART. — Instead of *mihi*, two of our codices, one Palatine and one Royal, together with the old editions, prefer *Micha* or *Michaea*; this is nevertheless false, as Martianay has correctly noted. Jerome himself testifies in the prologue to Hosea that Didymus labored over commentaries on Hosea and Zechariah, which he says were dictated at his request. He does not say the same concerning Micah.]

But their entire interpretation was allegorical, and they touched upon the historical sense only briefly. Therefore, wishing to imitate that householder who brings forth from his treasure “new things and old” (Matt. XIII, 52), and the bride in the Song of Songs who says, “I have kept the new things with the old for you, my kinsman” (Cant. VII), I have mixed the spiritual interpretation of the Hebrews with that of our own writers, so that I might build upon rock and not upon sand (Matt. VII), and lay a firm foundation, which Paul the architect says that he established (I Cor. III).

It will be a mark of your benevolence to accept not our learning—for it is either nonexistent or small—but our willing devotion toward you, so that you may urge us on to the remaining books and encourage us to run across the broad field of the Scriptures.

If there are any to whom I previously promised interpretations of these or other books, let them forgive my extraordinary love for you and regard whatever I have written to you as written to them. “Love is patient; love does not envy; it does not seek its own.”

But now it is time, having set forth the words of Zechariah, to spread the sails of interpretation before the Holy Spirit.

BOOK ONE

[Col. 1417]

[Col. 1417D] (Chapter I.—Verse 1.) “In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius [Note: We have inserted the addition ‘king,’ which is not present in the Hebrew, on the authority of our manuscripts], the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, son of Barachiah, son of Addo, the prophet, saying.”

The Septuagint: “In the eighth month of the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, son of Barachiah, son of Addo the prophet, saying.”

Zechariah himself testifies that, in the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes, the seventieth year of the temple’s desolation that had been foretold by Jeremiah (chapters XXV and XXIX) was completed, saying: “O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year” (Zech. I, 12).

There is no doubt that Cyrus, king of the Persians, who destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans, in the first year of his reign sent approximately fifty thousand captives from Babylon back to Judea. He also returned the vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken and ordered the temple to be rebuilt in Jerusalem. He appointed as leaders of the people who returned Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, and Jesus, son of Jehozadak, the high priest.

After Cyrus, who reigned thirty years over the Persians, had been killed among the Massagetae by Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae, his son Cambyses succeeded him in the kingdom. After Cambyses had completed eight years, two brother Magi succeeded him. When the people had killed them, Darius, son of Hystaspes, was made king of the Persians by the decision of the seven families.

In the second year of his reign the word of the Lord came to Haggai the prophet and to Zechariah, son of Barachiah, son of Addo.

We have already spoken about Haggai; a few words must now be said about Zechariah’s title. Since he is the son of Barachiah, it is asked why he is called the son of Addo. There is no doubt, according to the Book of Chronicles, that this is the Addo who was sent to Jeroboam son of Nebat (II Chron. XII), under whom the altar was destroyed [Al. broken apart] and the king’s hand withered, and was restored again at his prayer (III Kings XIII).

Thus, from the first year of King Cyrus to the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes, forty years are counted, during which only the altar had been built and the foundations of the temple laid, because the surrounding nations obstructed the work, and because Cambyses, king of the Persians, had sent letters concerning this matter to the governors of Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, and Samaria. Ezra writes the history of this more fully.

Haggai, however, began to prophesy in the sixth month, on the first day of that month. Zechariah, in the same year but not in the same month, delivered his oracle two months later, in the eighth month. [Note: Victor reads “in the eighth month of the year.” Shortly afterward, all the printed books read “commotion” instead of “admonition.” We prefer the Regina manuscript’s *commonitionem*.]

Therefore, in keeping with the order of the Twelve Prophets, Haggai is rightly placed tenth and Zechariah eleventh. It shows great confidence—or rather, hope and faith in the Lord—that what had been neglected for so long, whether because the king or the nations prohibited it, should begin to be undertaken at the admonition of two men.

These matters we have prefaced according to the historical sense, as is our custom. Now we must briefly discuss them according to the *anagoge*, the higher or spiritual interpretation.

Among the Hebrews the eighth month, called Marḥeshvan () among them, Athyr among the Egyptians, and November among us, is the beginning of winter. When the heat of summer has been consumed, the whole earth is stripped of its greenness, and the bodies of mortals contract; and there is no solemnity prescribed by the Law.

For it is written that three times each year every male is to appear before the Lord our God (Exod. XXXIV). The first festival is that of Unleavened Bread, Passover, which in Greek and Latin we call *Pascha*. The second is Pentecost, after seven weeks, when the bread of the Presence is first offered from the new crops. The third is in the seventh month: the festival of trumpets, atonement, and booths—that is, σκηνοπηγία, the Feast of Tabernacles—whose final day is called the day of departure and the conclusion. [Note: Martianay’s text incorrectly had *turbarum*. Shortly afterward Victor correctly changes *egressionis* to *egressio*. The passage is Leviticus XXIII, where the Septuagint has ἔξοδιον.]

Therefore, a people living in captivity, still under the Persian king, with the temple not yet built and the walls and fortifications of the city not yet erected, does not see the prophecy in a time of rejoicing but after rejoicing.

Yet because he remembered the Lord, and because of remembrance possessed blessing, and because of blessing possessed testimony, 780 Zechariah, son of Barachiah, son of Addo, is sent to him.

Zechariah is interpreted as “the remembrance of the Lord”; Barachiah as “the blessing of the Lord”; Addo as “his testimony.” Let us therefore see what the Word of the Lord, who was in the beginning with God the Father, spoke through the prophet Zechariah to the people.

(Verses 2, 3.) “The Lord was angry with your fathers with anger, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Return to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will return to you, says the Lord of hosts. Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried out, saying—”

The Septuagint: “The Lord was angry with your fathers with great anger, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Return to me, says the Lord of powers, and I will return to you, says the Lord of powers. Do not become like your fathers, whom the prophets who came before rebuked, saying—”

The anger of the Lord does not signify a disturbance in the one who becomes angry, but the merits and sins of those against whom the anger of God rages. [Note: [Col. 1419D–1420D] We have removed the negative particle on the authority of the Regina manuscript and in accordance with the holy Doctor’s meaning. Victor likewise testifies that he did not find that negation in five Florentine and other Brescian codices. The sense is: in the Lord, anger does not signify a disturbance in God when he is angry, but the deserts and sins of those upon whom God’s anger rages.] Otherwise, the Lord never punishes in anger; rather, he reproves in order to correct. Hence the prophet prays in the Psalms: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Ps. VI, 1). And elsewhere we read: “Correct us, O Lord; nevertheless, not in your fury, but in your mercy” (Jer. X, 24).

The Lord was therefore angry with the fathers of those who are now being corrected—not, according to the Septuagint interpreters, with “great anger,” but simply with anger. For if he had been angry with great anger, he would never have summoned the captives to repentance through Daniel and Ezekiel.

Although he is angry with them, the Lord of hosts speaks to you. In Hebrew *Sabaoth* () is written in this place, which the Septuagint sometimes translates as “Almighty” and sometimes as “of powers.”

And he says: “Return to me, and I will return to you,” in accordance with what we read: “Draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you.” The contrary of this is: “You have departed from me, and I have departed from you.”

He commands those who have returned from Babylon to return to the Lord, so that the Lord may also return to them, lest the children begin to suffer what their fathers once suffered, to whom the prophets of that time likewise spoke.

It should be noted that in the few short verses and brief sentences of Haggai and Zechariah the phrase “says the Lord of hosts” is always added, so that they may know that it is the Lord who commands them in opposition to the king’s authority and the enemies raging around them; and so that, with this confidence, they may be stirred to build the temple.

(Vers. 4.) Thus says the Lord of hosts: “Turn back from your evil ways and from your most wicked thoughts.” But they did not listen, nor pay attention to me, says the Lord.

The Septuagint: [Note: [Col. 1420D] Instead of “Almighty,” the Regin. manuscript reads “of powers” (*virtutum*); the Complutensian Greek copy likewise reads τῶν δυνάμεων (“of powers”).] “Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn back from your most wicked ways and from your evil inventions; but they did not pay attention so as to hear me, says the Lord.”

The sentence depends on what precedes, and what follows must be joined to the earlier statements. For Zechariah is not speaking to the people, but showing what the earlier prophets said to their fathers, to whom they cried out, saying: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn back from your evil ways and from your most wicked thoughts.” Isaiah cried this; Hosea, Joel, Amos, and Jeremiah did likewise, urging them to abandon their evil ways and forsake their most wicked thoughts, by which they sinned both in deed and in mind. Nevertheless, they did not listen to the Lord admonishing them through the prophets, nor pay attention—not at all to the prophets who spoke to them, but to me, says the Lord.

[Note: One Regin. manuscript reads, “but they despised me, says the Lord.”]

For I was in those prophets, speaking and being despised. Hence also the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. 10:40).

(Vers. 5, 6.) “Where are your fathers, and the prophets? Will they live forever? Yet my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? And they turned and said: ‘As the Lord of hosts had determined to do to us [Al. with us], according to our ways and according to our inventions, so he did to us.’”

The Septuagint: “Where are your fathers, and the prophets? Will they live forever? Yet receive my words and my statutes, which I command through my Spirit to my servants the prophets, who overtook your fathers. And they answered and said: ‘As the Lord Almighty was prepared to do to us according to our ways and according to our inventions, so he did to us.’”

[Note: Here, with our manuscripts, the Hebrew, and the Vulgate agreeing, we have written “they will live” instead of “they live.” At the end, where it read *cum legeretur*, the same manuscripts and texts led us to make the change; accordingly, we have removed the adverb *ita*.]

“Where,” he says, “are your fathers, who neither listened nor paid attention to me? Where are your prophets?” The phrase must be understood *ἀπὸ κοινοῦ* [in common]: “Where are your fathers, and where are your prophets?” That is, your false prophets. For he would never say of the holy prophets, “Will they live forever?” Both those who sinned and refused to return [Al. turn back] to me, and those who, while sinning, deceived others through false promises, have been taken away by death. But my words, which I spoke through my prophets, remain forever; they overtook your fathers and showed that what I had said was true.

Those fathers of yours, confirming through the outcome of events the prophecies of my prophets, turned to repentance and said: “As the Lord of hosts foretold that he would do to us, so he repaid us according to our deeds and sins.” Let us read Daniel confessing to the Lord in his own person and on behalf of the people that they had refused to listen to him, and that everything they suffered had justly befallen them (Dan. 3).

(Vers. 7.) “On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son [Vulg. son] of Iddo, the prophet, saying.”

The Septuagint: “On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat, in the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo the prophet, saying.”

Some place the twelfth month instead of the eleventh, and, interpreting the twenty-fourth day of that same month by arithmetical reasoning, suppose it to be a firm and stable square number, wishing the things written to be certain and stable. We, however, may say that in the second year of King Darius, in the third month after the first vision—that is, in the eleventh month after the eighth, which among the Hebrews is called *SABAT* (), “Shebat”—the word of the Lord again came to Zechariah.

We have often taught that the number two is impure, relating both to the joining of flesh and to worldly affairs, and belonging to matter. The eleventh month, moreover, called *SABAT*, which in our language is rendered “rod,” signifies austerity and correction, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. 4:21), and the Psalmist’s: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:5).

It is in the harshest season of winter; among the Egyptians it is called Mechir, among the Macedonians Περίτιος, and among the Romans February. The twenty-fourth day of the month likewise signifies the bright shadow of night, as the moon wanes into darkness and the blind, perpetual terror of night increases. Accordingly, those who were still in captivity, and most of whom were exiles among the Medes, Chaldeans, and Assyrians, in the second year and the eleventh month, amid the severest cold, and on the twenty-fourth day of that month, see what follows concerning the Jewish people.

(Vers. 8 ff.) “I saw by night, and behold, a man mounted on a red horse; and he was standing among the myrtles that were in the deep. Behind him were red, sorrel, and white horses. And I said, ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the angel who spoke in me said to me, ‘I will show you what these are.’ Then the man who was standing among the myrtles answered and said, ‘These are the ones whom the Lord sent to patrol the earth.’ And they answered the angel of the Lord who was standing among the myrtles and said, ‘We have patrolled the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest.’ Then the angel of the Lord answered and said, ‘Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year.’ And the Lord answered the angel who spoke in me with good words and words of consolation.”

[Note: [Col. 1422D] The word “how long,” which is also present in the Hebrew and the Vulgate, was missing from Martianay’s text; we have supplied it from the Regin. manuscript.]

The Septuagint: “I saw in the night, and behold, a man mounted on a red horse, and he was standing between two shadowy mountains; behind him were red, sorrel, and white horses. And I said, ‘What are these, lord?’ And the angel who spoke in me said to me, ‘I will show you what these are.’ And the man who was standing between the mountains answered and said to me, ‘These are the ones whom the Lord sent to patrol the earth.’ And they answered the angel of the Lord who was standing between the mountains and said, ‘We have patrolled the whole earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest.’ And the angel of the Lord answered and said, ‘Lord Almighty, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year.’ And the Lord answered the angel who spoke in me with good words and consolatory statements.”

Let us first discuss the historical meaning. “I saw,” he says, “by night”—not in the daytime, as Moses did, who saw God face to face; nor as Isaiah, who said, “I saw the Lord seated upon a high and lofty throne” (Isa. 6:1), before the people were led into captivity, before Jerusalem was destroyed and the Temple. Rather, while the people were still established amid the evils of slavery, he sees in darkness the things that he sees on their behalf.

“And behold, a man mounted on a red horse.” The Hebrews think this is the angel Michael, who is the avenger of Israel’s iniquities and sins. They wish the myrtles among which he stood, and which were in the deep, to be understood as the prophets and saints who lived in the midst of the captive people and were themselves in the deep. The red, sorrel, and white horses followed the man—that is, Michael—in a changed order, as they suppose. The white horses signify the Medes and Persians, because under them the captivity was released and the Temple restored; the sorrel, the Macedonians, some of whom were friendly and others persecutors. Daniel’s final vision speaks most fully about this (chap. 8). The red horses signify the bloody and murderous Roman kingdom, which killed the people and overturned the Temple.

Others, preserving the order in which the text is written, interpret the man mounted on the red horse, together with the red, sorrel, and white horses, as four kingdoms. The first and second are bloody: the Assyrians and the Chaldeans. The former led the ten tribes into captivity under Shalmaneser; the latter burned Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple, carrying away Judah and Benjamin. They think the third and fourth, represented by the sorrel and white horses, signify the Medes and Persians. Some of these were merciful, such as Cyrus, Darius son of Hystaspes, and Ahasuerus, whom the Greeks call Artaxerxes, under whom the story of Esther took place; others were cruel, such as Cambyses and the rest.

Thus, when the prophet sees a man mounted on a red horse, followed by red, sorrel, and white horses, and does not understand what he has seen but desires to know the meaning of his vision, he says, “What are these, my lord?” The angel who spoke in him promises to explain. While that angel remains silent, the man standing among the myrtles gives the explanation. These are the kingdoms to which the Lord commanded that they patrol the earth and subject it to their power.

Finally, the angels who presided over the kingdoms and nations do not come to someone else, but to the man himself and the angel of the Lord who stood among the myrtles, and they say: “We have patrolled the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest.” The meaning is: All the kingdoms under us are safe and peaceful, and none is oppressed by distress.

From this answer the angel who interceded for Israel takes occasion to plead for the people and says to the Lord: Since the whole world is quiet and at peace, why, Lord, do you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah—especially since, according to your promises, the time of captivity has been completed? The Lord answered the angel who spoke in the prophet with good words and consolatory words: good words concerning the promise of future things, and consolatory words concerning present necessity.

This is the literal interpretation, so that we may not conceal from our people what we learned from teachers of a foreign language. The teachers of the churches, however, understand the night in which the vision is seen as the obscurity of mystical vision. For God has made darkness his hiding place (Ps. 17:12). According to the Septuagint, it is said of him: “The abyss is like a garment with which he is clothed” (Ps. 103:6).

The man who mounted the red horse, however, is the Lord and Savior, who, assuming the dispensation of our flesh, hears in Isaiah: “Why are your garments red?” (Isa. 63:2).

[Note: Victorius would have preferred that, since the old reading was once found, “who, assuming the dispensation of our flesh,” should be rewritten as “who, assuming the dispensation of assumed flesh.” He says that below, at Zechariah 9, the quiver in which the arrow is hidden is the dispensation of assumed flesh. And at Ephesians 4 he says: “Nor, when we say these things, do we immediately give place to another heresy which asserts that Christ’s dispensation was incomplete. Rather, we confess one Son, both God and man, lest, believing only in part the dispensation of the assumed man by which we were saved, we truncate it in part. For Christ assumed true flesh of ours, or, as it is more sacredly expressed, the true dispensation of our flesh—contrary to what the heretics Marcion, Manichaeus, and Valentinus blasphemed. For in this way it is shown that Christ’s body was true and not phantasmal, nor spiritual, airy, or heavenly, as the most learned Lord Jerome refutes this error in chapters 14 and 17 on Matthew; and after him the patron and champion of Catholic truth, the Lord Thomas, in the third part of the *Summa*, question 5, articles 1 and 2.”]

This one, who is now shown as red on account of the captive people, is described in the Apocalypse of John as seated in white garments and on a white horse (Apoc. 3 and 6).

[Note: The Regin. manuscript reads, “who is now shown red from the captive people.”]

As for the statement that he stood between two shadowy mountains—although the Hebrew does not contain “two”—they understand the New and Old Testament, which is said to be covered with very dense leaves, groves, and shadowy forests because it is enveloped in many obscurities. The myrtles that were in the deep, among which he is described as standing, they understand as the angelic powers that ministered to him even when he was present in the flesh.

Or, if we remove the word “two,” which is not written, we may understand the mountains simply, without number, as the many saints, apostles, and apostolic men who are remembered to have traversed the whole world—red, sorrel, and white. Some of them were crowned with martyrdom and are called red. Others are called sorrel because of their works, teaching, and variety of signs. Others received the rewards of virginity, integrity of doctrine, and a pure heart, which beholds God.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “by which they behold God.”]

Finally, the prophet asks the same man and angel who stood among the myrtles and says: “Who [Al. What] are these, my lord?” And the angel who spoke in him—that is, the prophetic understanding—promises to show what is seen [Al. what he sees]. Although he has made this promise, he himself does not answer; rather, the other who stood among the myrtles answers and says: “These are the ones whom the Lord sent to patrol the earth.”

For the apostles were sent by the Lord to fill the whole world with the preaching of the Gospel. After completing their work, they returned to the angel of the great counsel who stood among them, with whom they spoke in the words of the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Cor. 2:15), and among the peoples of both callings.

And they said to him: “We have patrolled the earth; we have completed the work that was entrusted to us; and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest. Previously it was deserted by God; now it is his dwelling. It rests from wars, from battles with vices and sins, because it has received the inheritance of the Lord who returned to the Father and said: ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you’” (John 14:27).

As for the fact that full mercy is requested, so that, as the seventieth year approaches, God may have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, they refer it to this interpretation: until true peace comes, and the sabbath-rest, and the number of seven decades—that is, the seventieth year—is fulfilled, neither Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace” and is the Church, receives complete freedom, nor the cities of Judah, which are souls confessing the Lord.

Finally, the Lord promises good words and consolatory words—what we now see in part and prophesy in part (1 Cor. 13:12). But when perfection has come, may the things that are partial be abolished; and, freed from the Babylon of this age, may we cry out: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted” (Ps. 125:1).

(Vers. 14 ff.) And the angel who spoke in me said to me: “Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy, and I am angry [Al. I will be angry] with great anger against the wealthy nations, because I was angry only a little, but they [Vulg. *ipsi*] helped toward evil.”

Therefore thus says the Lord: “I will return to Jerusalem with mercies, and my house shall be built in it, says the Lord of hosts, and the measuring line shall be stretched over Jerusalem.”

The Septuagint: “And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy, and I am angry with great anger against the nations that were imposed upon them, because, although I was angry only a little, they were imposed upon them for evil. Therefore thus says the Lord: I will turn back to Jerusalem in mercy, and my house shall be restored in it, says the Lord Almighty, and the measure shall be stretched over Jerusalem.”

These are still the good and consolatory words which the prophet is now commanded to proclaim: that the Lord has been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy. Whoever is jealous shows that he loves the one for whom he is jealous, rather than saying through Jeremiah: “As a woman despises her husband, so the house of Israel despised me” (Jer. 3:20). Through Ezekiel the Lord spoke to her: “When I am angry, I will no longer be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you” (Ezek. 16:42).

Therefore, he who has been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion—for they are one and the same city—is now angry with the wealthy nations whom he previously named under the red, white, and sorrel horses. He himself handed them over for correction, but they raged against those handed over: he wished the son to be corrected by a tutor, while they attempted to kill and punish an enemy.

The same idea appears in Isaiah: “I gave them into your hands, but you showed them no mercy. You made your yoke exceedingly heavy, and said, ‘I shall be mistress forever’” (Isa. 47:6).

[Note: Regin. reads: “But instead of *Senis*, other books have *you made the yoke exceedingly heavy*.”]

“Jealousy” is therefore understood *ἀνθρωποπάθως* [anthropopathically], in the manner of human passion, as anger. From this passage the heretics are refuted who disparage the Old Testament because the angry God does not desire to destroy those against whom he is angry, but to correct them.

“Because,” he says, “I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy, which their adversaries have depressed more than I wished, therefore thus says the Lord: I will return not with a single mercy, but with many mercies, to Jerusalem; and my house—that is, the Temple—shall be built in it under Zerubbabel and Joshua son of Josedech; and the builders’ measuring line shall be stretched over Jerusalem.”

Jerusalem and Zion—the vision of peace and the watchtower—which does not contemplate the wars of this age, nor lowly and earthly things, but peace and harmony and the heights of heaven, may be understood as the Church. Because of its vices and sins, and because its love grows cold each day, the angry Lord will hand it over to persecutions, so that, like pure gold and silver in a furnace, it may appear refined. Its adversaries, to whom it has been handed over and who strive to destroy it, fill Jerusalem with the blood of the slain from gate to gate.

Therefore the Lord, promising peace and mercy, says that he will build it again. And the measuring line, or cord, according to the measurements and ranks of each individual, is to be stretched out within it. What the cord is, the following chapter demonstrates, where the prophet says: “I lifted my eyes and saw; and behold, a man, and in his hand a measuring cord.”

The Temple of God, which the adversaries destroyed, may also be understood as the venerable body of the Lord, concerning which he himself said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). Destroyed in the Passion, it was raised in the resurrection and became the seed and beginning of all the temples concerning which the Apostle also speaks: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (2 Cor. 6:16).

(Vers. 17.) “Cry out again, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: My cities shall again overflow with good things; and the Lord shall again comfort Zion and shall again choose Jerusalem.”

The Septuagint:

[Note: This preceding clause, “And the angel who spoke in me said to me,” is not found in our manuscripts or in the Complutensian and Aldine Greek editions.]

“And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out again, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: The cities shall again overflow with good things, and the Lord shall again have mercy on Zion and shall again choose Jerusalem.”

The angel who earlier said to the prophet, “Cry out: Thus says the Lord of hosts,” now urges him again to cry out—not by raising his voice, but with his mind. This is what he commands him to proclaim: “My cities shall again overflow with good things.” The cities that you now see laid waste by the Babylonian fire shall again abound in every possession; and through their present goods the Lord shall comfort their former misery, and shall choose Jerusalem, which he had shortly before cast away.

If we refer this to the Church, to which he promises true and everlasting goods, those goods are to be understood of which we read: “May you see the good things of Jerusalem” (Ps. 127:5). And elsewhere: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. 1:19). And: “You shall trust in the Lord, and he will raise you above the good things of the land.” The wise man, to whom the Lord had revealed the uncertain and obscure things of his wisdom, promises these things to himself in hope of the future and says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

After the fires of the most savage persecution, which the Lord’s churches endured both from the Gentiles and from the Arian heretics, peace having been restored, we see the churches of the Lord overflowing with good things, Zion comforted, and Jerusalem chosen—those whom he had recently rejected. We can understand this same passage both of the Temple of the Lord and of each believer.

Some refer the comforted Zion, the chosen Jerusalem, and the other things proclaimed in this manner by all the prophets to the heavenly Jerusalem, which, having been destroyed through ruin, is to be rebuilt through virtues. Let the heretics suspect this. For our part, let us interpret Mount Zion and the mother of the firstborn and of the saints as the Church, which was built through the Passion and resurrection of the Lord and is built each day by him who knows the measurements and merits of each individual.

What we have said about the Church can also be understood of the souls of believers, who are built each day by the Lord and behold his peace, which was left to the apostles.

(Vers. 18, 19.) “And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns. And I said to the angel who spoke in [Al. to] me, ‘What are these?’ And he said to me, ‘These are the horns that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.’ And the Lord showed me four craftsmen. And I said, ‘What are these coming to do?’ He answered, saying: ‘These are the horns that scattered Judah, each man separately, and none of them lifted his head; but these have come to wear them down, to cast down the horns of the nations that lifted their horn over the land of Judah in order to scatter it.’”

The Septuagint: “And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns. And I said to the angel who spoke in me, ‘What are these, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘These are the horns that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.’ And the Lord showed me four craftsmen. And I said, ‘What are these coming to do?’ And he said: ‘These are the horns that scattered Judah and broke Israel; and none of them lifted his head. And these have gone out to sharpen them in their hands.’”

Four horns are the nations that lifted their horn over the land of the Lord in order to scatter it. The four horns that dispersed and scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem are four nations: the Babylonians, the Medes and Persians, the Macedonians, and the Romans. Now the Lord explains this when questioned by the prophet, and Daniel unfolds it most fully.

Daniel interpreted these four nations in his vision of the statue that had a golden head, a silver chest, a bronze belly, and iron and clay legs and feet (Dan. 2). Again, in another vision, he showed the same nations under the figure of four beasts—a lioness, a bear, a leopard, and another terrifying beast whose name he did not give.

Anyone who has read both secular and sacred writings will not doubt [Al. does not doubt] that the Medes and Persians became one kingdom after Cyrus’s victory. And Scripture very appropriately represents kingdoms by horns, following the sacred text’s custom of always interpreting a kingdom through horns, as in: “He has exalted the horn of his Christ” (Ps. 148:14), and elsewhere: “He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant” (Luke 1:69). The same prophet Daniel testifies that ten horns will reign at the end (Dan. 7).

At the time when this vision was seen, the Babylonian kingdom had already passed away; the kingdom of the Persians and Medes was present; that of the Greeks and Macedonians was to come, as was that of the Romans. What the Babylonians, the Medes and Persians, and the Greeks—that is, the Macedonians—did to Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem, an educated man recognizes, especially under Antiochus surnamed Ἐπιφανής [Epiphanes], under whom the history of the Maccabees was composed.

After the coming of the Lord and Savior, when Jerusalem was surrounded, what the Israelites endured is announced beforehand in the Gospel (Luke 19), and Josephus, the native historian of Jewish affairs, teaches at greatest length.

These horns scattered and dispersed Judah, almost each person individually, so that none of them, weighed down by the heavy burden of evils, could lift his head. The four craftsmen, or artisans, whom the Greeks call τέκτονες [craftsmen], are not seen by the prophet himself; the Lord shows them to him and explains who the craftsmen and artisans are. We understand them as angels obedient to the Lord’s authority, so that what the nations had destroyed, these might build.

What we have translated from the Hebrew as “These have come to wear them down”—namely, the kingdoms—the Septuagint translated as “These have come to sharpen them in their hands.” “To sharpen them” must be understood instead of “to wear them down.” Or “to wear them down” may mean that they submit every neck beneath Christ’s yoke, and not, as someone interpreted it, that once they have been sharpened they become worse.

For if the angels come for the purpose of making the wicked worse, they should not be called craftsmen—that is, destroyers of evil and builders of good—but should themselves be understood as evil-doers and destroyers.

It should also be noted that these four horns of the nations raised one horn against the people of God. They did not reign at the same time or oppress Israel simultaneously, but succeeded one another: the Medes and Persians succeeded the Babylonians; the Macedonian kingdom succeeded the Persian kingdom; and the Roman empire succeeded the Macedonian kingdom. We have said this according to the order of history.

The prophet’s statement that he lifted his eyes must be adapted spiritually to the meaning: “I lifted my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come” (Ps. 120:1); and: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvesting” (John 4:35); and what we read in Isaiah: “The Holy One said, Lift up your eyes and see who has shown all these things” (Isa. 51:6).

We therefore need the elevation of our eyes and spiritual understanding, so that we may see the opposing powers that have raised their horn against us, concerning which the Apostle speaks: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

Christ, when he came, overcame these four adversaries who were always fighting against the saints. Concerning them the Psalmist repeats: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90:13).

We can also understand the four horns that reigned against the people of God as the four πάθη [passions] which learned men, not translating the word-for-word expressions κακοζήλως [with misplaced zeal], interpret as disturbances: grief of spirit and joy, two concerning the present and two concerning the future—fear and desire. The distinguished poet also indicates these in the *Aeneid* (6):

“Here they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.”

Against these four craftsmen—or, so to speak, physicians and skilled artisans—are not seen by the prophet, since he could not yet see them without God’s showing them to him. Rather, the Lord shows him four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. Cicero discusses these most fully in his books *On Duties*, writing a separate book on the four virtues as well.

Those who destroy vices and build virtues, and all the saints who, possessing these remedies, continually restore the Church, are to be called craftsmen. Hence the Apostle also said: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (1 Cor. 3:10). And when angry, the Lord says in Isaiah that he will remove from Jerusalem the architect and the wise man (Isa. 3). The Lord himself, the Son of Almighty God and the Creator [Al. creator] of all things, is called the son of a craftsman.

I have read in someone’s commentaries that the four craftsmen are understood as the four Evangelists. They restore oppressed Israel—that is, the one who sees God—the Lord-confessing Judah, and Jerusalem, the vision of peace, to their former seat; and those whom the nations of vices had scattered from the Church, they drew back to salvation through the preaching of the Gospel.

(Cap. II.—Vers. 1, 2.) “And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand a measuring cord. And I said, ‘Where are you going?’ And he said to me, ‘To measure Jerusalem, and to see how great is its width and how great its length [Al. height].’”

The Septuagint: “And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand a geometer’s measuring cord. And I said to him, ‘Where are you going?’ And he said to me, ‘To measure Jerusalem, and to see how great is its width and how great its length.’”

The one who earlier, with his eyes lifted, had seen grievous things in the four horns now raises his eyes again to see the man concerning whom it is written: “Behold, a man; East is his name” (Zech. 6:12). Concerning him we also read above: “And behold, a man mounted on a red horse, and he stood among the myrtles that were in the deep,” or “among the shadowy mountains” (Zech. 1:8). And concerning him the Father speaks: “He built my city” (Heb. 11), whose architect and founder is God.

This same figure is seen by Ezekiel holding a cord in his hand and a reed for measuring according to a man’s cubit, in order to measure Jerusalem. The same prophet describes its dimensions—that is, its width and length—in mystical speech (Ezek. 40).

Some think this was partly fulfilled under Zerubbabel, Joshua, Ezra, Nehemiah, and the other leaders or kings who governed the people of Israel until the coming of the Lord and Savior. Others, especially the Jews, interpret it as referring to the thousand-year reign, seeking bodily things for bodily beings. Most of our people, however, refer it to the heavenly Jerusalem and say that it is to be rebuilt, having been laid waste by the ruin of sinful souls.

Let the heretics suppose this. For our part, let us interpret Mount Zion and the mother of the firstborn and of the saints as the Church, which was built through the Passion and resurrection of the Lord and is built each day by him who knows the measurements and merits of individuals.

What we have said about the Church can also be understood of the souls of believers, who are built each day by the Lord and behold his peace, which was left to the apostles.

[Col. 1430C] **(Verses 4 and following.)** And behold, the angel who was speaking in me was going out; and another angel was going out to meet him, and said to him: “Run, speak to that boy, saying: ‘Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall, because of the multitude of men and cattle within her. And I shall be for her, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and I shall be in her midst in glory.’”

The Septuagint: “And behold, the angel who was speaking in me was standing, and another angel was going out to meet him, and said to him: ‘Run and speak to that young man, saying: “Jerusalem shall be inhabited as a fruitful place by a multitude of men and cattle within her.” And I shall be for her, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and I shall be in her midst as glory.’”

The angel who was speaking in the prophet and was standing—or, as it is read in Hebrew, “was going out”—for this is what *JASA* signifies (יָצָא), the Hebrews consider to be Michael. And they suppose that the other angel who was going out and coming to meet him was Gabriel, who speaks to Michael so that he may speak to the prophet about the great abundance of all things, the multitude of men and cattle, and the strength of the walls that Jerusalem will possess—Jerusalem which at present seems to have been destroyed down to dust and ashes.

We, however, according to the spiritual meaning, interpret all these things in reference to the Church. She is inhabited without a wall—or, as the Septuagint translated it, *κατάκαρπος*, that is, “with an abundance of every kind of fruit”—and possesses a multitude of men and cattle; and the Lord is a fire around her, while he himself dwells in her midst in glory.

[Note: [Col. 1429D] Jerome did not read *Jotse* as a participle, according to the present Masoretic pointing, but *Jatsa* or *Jasa*, as is his custom, in the preterite, as has been established for us from the testimony of all manuscript copies. The printed editions read it with *ḥolem*, fully, or with *vav*, which the Masoretic exemplar does not express. MART.]

This is the city of which elsewhere we read: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI, 2). And again: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” (Ps. VII, 1). Whoever dwells in this city can say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. LI, 10). And: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has settled me. He has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. XXII, 1).

“And Jerusalem shall be inhabited,” he says, “because of the multitude of men and cattle, without a wall,” or “with an abundance of every kind of fruit.” Some interpret the men and cattle as two peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles. They say that those who, having lived in the Law, have come to faith in Christ are called “men”; but that we, who after idolatry were as though in the desert and wilderness of the Law and the Prophets, and received his passion, ought to be called “cattle.”

Others wish “men” to be understood as all rational persons learned in the Scriptures, and “cattle” as the simpler believers; and they apply to these the words: “You will save men and cattle, Lord” (Ps. XXXV, 7). These cattle and these living creatures hear the voice of the good shepherd, recognize him, and follow him. He is himself both the shepherd, because he rules us, and the door, because through him we enter into the Church and to the Father (John X). He is also a wall of fire all around, so that he may warm—or, according to another reading, “so that they may be warmed”—those who believe and dwell in the midst of it, who had previously grown lukewarm through the coldness of love and may become fervent in spirit.

But wolves and the fiercest beasts—of which it is written, “Do not hand over to the beasts the soul confessing you” (Ps. LXXIII, 19), and whose fruit is “hay, wood, stubble” (I Cor. III, 12), and which produce thorns and briars—he will consume with his own fire. And he who is fire to his adversaries will be glory in the midst of believers.

That the Lord is the wall of Jerusalem we also read in another place: “Mountains are around it, and the Lord is around his people” (Ps. CXXIV, 2).

[Note: [Col. 1431D] Very many manuscripts, leaving the Greek word, read as follows: “All these things the Jews think will come bodily under the *ἠλειμμένος* whom they promise themselves,” and so forth. The manuscript copy of the monastery of Saint Cygirannus adds after *Messia* a corrupt Greek word. See what has already been said about the name *ἠλειμμένος* in our notes on Isaiah, chapter XXVII. MART.]

All these things the Jews think will come bodily under the *ἠλειμμένος* whom they promise themselves in their vain hope. They think that Jerusalem will possess such great blessedness that, because of the multitude of men and all the cattle, she will be unable to have a wall; rather, the Lord’s own protection will be her wall, and she will enjoy the glory of him who dwells in her midst.

**(Verses 6 and following.)** “Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I have scattered you to the four winds of heaven, says the Lord. Ho, Zion! Rise up, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts: After glory he has sent me to the nations that plundered you; for whoever touches you touches the apple of his eye. For behold, I lift up my hand against them, and they shall become booty for those who had served them, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me.”

The Septuagint: “Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I shall gather you from the four winds of heaven, says the Lord. Be saved in Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the Lord Almighty: After glory he has sent me to the nations that plundered you, because whoever touches you is like one who touches the apple of his eye. Behold, I shall bring my hand against them, and they shall become booty for those who had served them, and you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me.”

[Note: [Col. 1432D] Earlier the text read “as though one touches”; we silently correct slight errors of this kind throughout.]

[Note: [Col. 1432D] In place of “rise up,” Jerome’s translation has “flee.” The Hebrew has [Hebrew term]. A little later, in place of “his eye,” Jerome’s Vulgate edition has “my eye,” although the Hebrew prefers [Hebrew term].]

The regions of the world, which the Greeks call *κλίματα*, are understood according to the position of Jerusalem and the Temple. The Assyrians, therefore, and the Babylonians, who devastated God’s people, dwell in the land of the north. Accordingly, in Jeremiah (chapter I), the pot which, according to Ezekiel (chapter XXIV), is full of meat—by which the city of Jerusalem is understood—is kindled from the face of the north.

Since, therefore, the angel who had met the angel prophesying in Zechariah had commanded him to speak to the boy—for, in comparison with the dignity of angels, the whole of human nature is called childhood, since the angels do not progress into us, but we progress into angels—and to say to him: “Jerusalem shall dwell without a wall,” and the rest, now the word of the Lord is addressed to those who dwell in the north: they are to be gathered from the four winds into which they had been scattered throughout the whole world, and those who dwelt in Babylon are to return to Zion.

Or certainly it may be understood in this way: “You who have been scattered in the four regions—or parts—of heaven, flee from the land of the north; and you, Zion, who now dwell in Babylon, flee and return to your former seat.”

The fact that the vocative “ho” is spoken three times is an exhortation to flee, so that they may know that they have been urged to flee not once but repeatedly.

It may also be said otherwise. The north wind is exceedingly harsh; it makes the hearts of its inhabitants exceedingly hard, and from it evils are kindled against all who dwell in the land. According to this same prophet Zechariah, black horses go out toward it, so that they may stand in their own region (Zech. I and VI).

The one who had said boastfully through Isaiah, “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will sit on the high mountain, above the lofty mountains in the north” (Isa. XIV, 13), boasts that he possesses his kingdom in the coldest region of the earth.

We read elsewhere: “Behold, smoke comes from the north” (ibid., 31). And concerning those who had departed far from the holy city it is said: “Behold, these come from far away, from the north and from the sea” (ibid., XLIX, 12). And through Jeremiah the Holy Spirit speaks, urging those who are in captivity to return to Jerusalem: “Go and read these words toward the north, and say: ‘Return to me, dwelling of Israel,’ says the Lord” (Jer. XLVI).

We are therefore commanded—we who have dwelt in the north and lost the warmth of the Lord’s fervor, who have been scattered throughout the world, and of whom the Gospel proclaims that the Lord sends his angels toward the four winds (Mark XIII), and gathers us, while we remain in the vices and confusion of this age—to flee into Zion, the Church of the Lord, and, leaving behind what is lowly, to stand in his watchtower and in the exaltedness of his doctrines.

What follows—“Thus says the Lord of hosts: After glory he has sent me,” and the rest—is introduced as the voice of the Savior speaking. He says that the omnipotent God sent him from the omnipotent Father, not according to that which he is omnipotent, but according to that in which he was sent after glory.

Although he was in the form of God, “he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. II, 6).

Nor is it surprising that Christ is called omnipotent. From his person we read in the Apocalypse of John: “Thus says the faithful witness, the beginning of God’s creation, who is and was and is to come, the Lord God Almighty” (Apoc. I, 4–5).

That passage also which we read in Psalm XXIII—“Lift up your gates, rulers, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (verse 7)—and the question again asked by other angels who do not know the mystery of the flesh—or, according to another reading, of the assumed incarnation—“Who is this King of glory?” is referred to Christ. “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.”

Where we read “Lord of hosts,” the Hebrew has written *SABAOTH* (צבאות), which the translators of the Septuagint render as “Almighty.” From this we understand that wherever “Lord of hosts” is said of Christ, he ought to be understood as omnipotent.

Nor is it surprising that Christ is called omnipotent: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him” (Matt. XXVIII, 18). And he says: “All things that belong to the Father are mine” (John XVII, 10). If “all things” means “God from God, Lord from Lord, light from light,” then he is also “omnipotent from Omnipotent.”

[Note: [Col. 1433D] It is commonly known, and noted by Victorius, that Jerome here uses the words of the Nicene Synod in the Creed.]

For it cannot happen that those who share one nature should possess different glory.

He was therefore sent after the glory of divine majesty to the nations that had plundered God’s people, so that those who had previously plundered them might become booty for those whom they had served, and that the whole former multitude of servants might know that the omnipotent God had sent him.

When he says, “Whoever touches you touches the apple of his eye,” understand “touching” as vexation and injury, according to what we read: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not harm my prophets” (Ps. CIV, 15). Whoever touches the Lord’s saints is like one who wishes to vex the apple of his eye and strives to deprive him of the clear light of which he speaks in the Gospel: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14).

God lifts up his hand in order to strike the hostile nations and to restore his people either to Jerusalem or to the Church. According to the tropological sense, understand the hostile nations as opposing powers, which daily subject sinners to their authority and compel them to serve them.

[Note: [Col. 1434D] In the manuscripts of Regin., “or restore Jerusalem to the Church.”]

**(Verses 10 and following.)** “Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming, and I shall dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations shall attach themselves to the Lord on that day, and they shall become my people; and I shall dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. And the Lord shall possess Judah as his portion in the sanctified land, and he shall again choose Jerusalem.”

The Septuagint: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I shall come, and I shall dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations shall flee for refuge to the Lord on that day, and they shall become his people; and they shall dwell in your midst. And you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you. And the Lord shall possess Judah as his portion in the holy land, and he shall again choose Jerusalem.”

These words are still to be understood as spoken by the Lord’s person: he urges his people, restored from captivity to their former dwelling, to rejoice and be glad because the Lord himself is coming and dwelling in their midst, and because many nations will believe in him. Of these nations it is said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II, 8).

And he dwells in their midst, saying to the disciples: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

And the Lord possesses Judah as his portion—the people confessing and believing in his name—and he possesses it nowhere except in the holy land, which is interpreted as the Church. And he again chooses Jerusalem, which he had abandoned to temptation during the persecutions.

Some Jews think that these things were partially fulfilled under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, Ezra and Nehemiah, especially since Jerusalem is chosen and Judah is possessed: namely, the two tribes that returned from Babylonian captivity and were called Judah, not Israel, because Israel remains among the Medes to this day.

Others postpone these things to the future, saying that at that time the nations will believe in him who is sent by the Lord, and that Jerusalem will be chosen—although all the nations have already believed in the Lord Savior, and she cannot be chosen who has been utterly destroyed.

It is rightly after the captivity that the daughter of Zion is summoned to joy, concerning whom it is also said in the psalm: “When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad” (Ps. LII, 7).

[Note: [Col. 1434D] The same, according to the Vulgate edition: “the captivity of his people.”]

[Col. 1434D] **(Verse 13.)** “Let all flesh be silent before the face of the Lord, because he has risen from his holy dwelling.”

The Septuagint: “Let all flesh fear before the face of the Lord, because he has risen from his holy clouds.”

Since these things are so, and the Lord is to possess Judah as his portion and to choose Jerusalem, let the whole human race fear the Lord’s coming, because he has risen from his holy dwelling.

The Lord is said to rise, and as it were to awaken from sleep, when he rises for vengeance on behalf of his people, according to what is written: “Awake; why do you sleep, Lord?” (Ps. XLIII, 23).

Or, according to the Septuagint, who said, “He has risen from his holy clouds,” understand the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, to whom the Lord entrusted the command not to rain upon Israel.

These are the clouds of which it is written: “And let the clouds rain righteousness” (Isa. XLV, 8). For these are not bodily clouds, into which denser air is gathered, that can rain righteousness.

In and with these clouds the Lord says in the Gospel that he will come (Luke XXI). And in Isaiah we read that the Lord came into Egypt upon a light cloud (Isa. XIX). Egypt is understood as the world, into which the Lord is remembered to have descended in the flesh—a flesh produced from the virgin womb and burdened by no weight of human seed or sins.

That “all flesh” is not to be understood absolutely as human beings, beasts, birds, and fish, but specifically as human beings, is shown by that Scripture which says: “Hear my prayer; to you all flesh shall come” (Ps. LXIV, 3). For not all flesh of irrational living creatures will come to the Lord, but that which is to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, concerning which it is said: “I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel II, 28).

**(Chapter III—verses 1 and following.)** And he showed me Jeshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord; and Satan was standing at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you. Is this man not a brand snatched from the fire?” And Jeshua was clothed in filthy garments and was standing before the face of the angel. He answered and said to those standing before him: “Take the filthy garments away from him.” And he said to him: “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I have clothed you in changing garments.” And he said: “Put a clean turban upon his head.” And they placed a clean turban upon his head and clothed him with garments.

The Septuagint: “And the Lord showed me the high priest Jeshua standing before the face of the angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, devil; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you. Is this man not like a brand snatched from the fire?’ And Jeshua was clothed in filthy garments and was standing before the face of the angel. He answered and said to those standing before his face: ‘Take the filthy garments away from him.’ And he said to him: ‘Behold, I have taken your iniquities away from you; clothe him in a long robe and put a clean turban upon his head.’ And they placed a clean turban upon his head and wrapped him in garments.”

[Note: [Col. 1435D] Jerome’s Vulgate edition inserts “the Lord.”]

Before we come to the spiritual understanding, we must briefly and concisely say how the Hebrews explain this passage.

They wish Jeshua the high priest—whom the Greeks call *ἀρχιερεύς* and the Latins *pontifex*—to be understood as the son of Jehozadak, who presided over the people together with Zerubbabel. An adversary stood at his right hand—this is what “Satan” means—in order to oppose him.

And rightly he stood at his right hand, not at his left, because the accusation was true: he too, together with the others, had taken a foreign wife. This is written at length in Ezra and in Malachi, who follows this prophet (I Esdras XII and Malachi II).

And the Lord said to Satan, to his accuser and adversary—for he is the enemy, avenger, and accuser of his brothers—“May the Lord rebuke you, Satan,” just as it is said, “The Lord rained from the Lord”; “and may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you.”

Since Jerusalem has now been chosen from all the cities of Judah, and the Lord does not impute to her the sins she committed, why do you try to overwhelm Jeshua like a brand—which is commonly called a burning log—who escaped from Babylonian captivity as though half-burned?

What follows—“Jeshua was clothed in filthy garments”—they interpret in three ways: either because of the unlawful marriage, or because of the people’s sins, or because of the squalor of captivity.

The angel before whose face Jeshua stood commanded the other angels, in the person of the Lord, to take away from him the filthy garments about which we spoke above. When they had fulfilled the command, the same angel again spoke to Jeshua: “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you.” These are the filthy garments. “And I have clothed you in changing garments,” that is, I have joined an Israelite wife to you. For this the Septuagint translated *ποδήρης*, which we may call a long robe, because it falls down to the ankles and feet—or, according to another reading, “to the feet and ankles.”

What follows—“Put a clean turban upon his head”—in Hebrew we read *SANIPH* (צָנִיף), which most call a *mitre*. In this they wish the dignity of the priesthood to be understood: after the filth of his sins had been removed, he possessed a pure priesthood.

Thus far the Jews.

Our own interpreters, however, reason as follows. The high priest is he to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4). Since he cannot be seen by himself, he is shown by the Lord to the prophet standing before the angel of the Lord. They wish this angel to be the angel of the great counsel—not because one is one person and another another, or because we admit two persons in the Son, but because the same and one person is shown both as a man who has been soiled and as an angel, the mediator between God and human beings.

They attempt to demonstrate that he is not Jeshua the son of Jehozadak from the fact that the present passage does not add “son of Jehozadak.” In other passages, wherever Jeshua the son of Jehozadak is genuinely meant, he is always designated by his father’s name.

Jeshua, therefore, is seen standing, established in a firm posture. And Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him. For he was tempted in every way, yet without sin. In the Gospel also the tempter approaches him, always seeking to oppose his right hand and his virtues.

What follows—“May the Lord rebuke you, Satan, and may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you”—they explain in this way: the Father and the Son are Lord, and in Psalm CIX we read: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’” The Lord speaks of another Lord—not because the Lord who speaks cannot himself rebuke, but because, through the unity of nature, when the one has rebuked, the one who speaks also rebukes.

“For whoever sees the Son sees the Father” (John XIV, 9). And this is he who chose Jerusalem, the Church that contemplates the Lord’s peace.

The brand snatched from the fire can most rightly be understood as one who, although he was in Babylon, was not consumed by the Babylonian fire and was not touched by the flame of this age. Hence Moses also sees in the wilderness a great vision in which the bush burned but was not consumed (Exod. III).

This Jeshua was clothed in filthy garments. Although he had committed no sin, he was made sin for us; he himself bears our weaknesses, and suffers for us, and we regarded him as being in pain, under a blow, and in anguish. Yet he was wounded for our sins (Isa. LIII, 4).

[Note: [Col. 1437D] The Regin. manuscript inserts: “for our iniquities and weaknesses, and for, etc.” More correctly, in Victor.: “for our iniquities, and he was weakened for sins, etc.”]

And in the Apostle we read: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us” (Gal. III, 13).

Here he speaks in Psalm XXI: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins” (Ps. XXI, 1). And in Psalm LXVIII: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you” (Ps. LXVIII, 6).

All these things are called filthy garments, and they will be taken away from him when he has erased our sins. Thus, because he was clothed in filthy garments, we, rising again in him, hear after baptism: “Let your garments always be white” (Eccl. IX, 8). And the whole Church of believers hears through Isaiah: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I, 16).

And concerning her it is prophesied in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” (Cant. III, 6).

Understand the *ποδήρης* as his incarnation, which is from the earth and is signified by the feet. Understand the clean turban upon his head as the splendor of divine majesty, so that the one and the same person may be seen adorned with the *ποδήρης* according to his humanity and with the turban according to his divinity.

**(Verses 6–7.)** And the angel of the Lord stood, and the angel of the Lord testified to Jeshua, saying: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: If you walk in my ways and observe my charge, you too shall judge my house and guard my courts, and I shall give you those who walk among these who now stand here.”

The Septuagint: “And the angel of the Lord stood, and the angel of the Lord testified to Jeshua, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: If you walk in my ways and observe my commandments, you too shall judge my house; and if you guard my court, I shall give you those who dwell among those standing here.’”

The Hebrews, continuing the order of their interpretation already begun, understand these words as being spoken by the angel of the Lord to Jeshua the son of Jehozadak. After the filthy garments have been removed and the dignity of the pure priesthood restored, he is commanded in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14).

A reward is promised to him if he walks in the Lord’s ways and keeps his commandments: he himself will be judge of his house—that is, he will continue as high priest in the Temple—and will guard its courts and vestibules. The Lord will also give him, from the number of the angels who at that time stood before his sight, those by whose assistance he will be surrounded and secure from every plot of his enemies.

According to our interpreters, who refer all these things to the Lord Savior, this appears difficult: Jeshua is told by the angel, “If he walks in the Lord’s ways and keeps his commandments, he too will judge his house and guard his courts, and the Lord will give him those who walk among those standing before him.”

This is easily resolved if we consider him who deigned to assume the form of a servant (Phil. II), and who, although he was rich, became poor for our sake (II Cor. VIII, 9).

Whatever, therefore, is said about the members is referred to the body. Our progress is the Lord’s victory. And when we have attained “to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV), he will judge the house of God, according to what the Apostle said: “But Christ is as a Son over his house, whose house we are” (Heb. III, 6).

And to Timothy: “If I am delayed, so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Tim. III, 15).

He will not only judge his house; he will also guard the Lord’s courts, concerning which it is written: “Worship the Lord in his holy court” (Ps. XXVIII, 2).

He will judge—or distinguish—his house according to the merits of each person, giving one ten cities and another five (Luke XIX), appointing some in the Church as prophets, others as apostles, others as teachers, and others as workers of signs (I Cor. XII); regarding some as eyes, others as hands, and others as feet, according to what we read: “God stood in the assembly of gods, but in the midst he distinguishes among gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 1).

He also gave him ministers from the number of the angels—those who, established in the flesh, are like angels, concerning whom the Apostle spoke: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

For if angels neither marry nor are given in marriage, and those who persevere in virginal continence are like angels (Matt. XXII), why should we not think that apostles and holy persons of angelic dignity were given to Jeshua, to stand beside him in the Church, never having feet that waver, but standing with the Lord who stands?

**(Verses 8–9.)** “Hear, Jeshua the high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, because they are men who are signs. For behold, I am bringing my servant, the Branch. For behold, the stone that I have set before Jeshua: upon one stone are seven eyes.”

The Septuagint: “Hear, therefore, Jeshua the high priest, and your neighbors who sit before your face, because they are men who are *τερατοσκόποι*, that is, observers of portents. For behold, I am bringing my servant, the Branch, because the stone that I have set before the face of Jeshua—upon the one stone are seven eyes.”

Our interpreters are pressed by the Jews at this point, since according to the sequence and wording of the passage they ought rather to understand Jeshua the priest as the son of Jehozadak than as the Lord Savior.

For if the speech is addressed to the Lord, and Christ is told, “Hear, Jeshua the high priest,” who is he concerning whom it follows: “Behold, I am bringing my servant, the Branch,” who is elsewhere called the stone and is set before Jeshua, and upon this stone are seven eyes?

Conversely, our interpreters strive to assert that the high priest Jeshua, the Branch, and the stone are all called Christ according to different interpretations. But it is extremely difficult to explain how this can be said of the same person to him as though of another.

Those, therefore, who wish Jeshua to be the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, interpret his friends who dwell or sit before him, and who are men of signs, as his disciples and prophets. For the prophets are appointed as signs of things to come.

What, then, does it mean that Jeshua and his friends are compelled to hear: “I shall bring my servant, the Branch,” and the rest?

Above, God had promised Jeshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, that if he walked in his ways and kept his commandments, he would judge his house and guard his courts, and that he would give him ministers of angelic dignity.

Now he tells him and his friends that complete happiness and perfect blessedness will come at the time when the Branch appears, concerning whom it is written: “Behold, a man whose name is the Branch” (Zech. VI, 12).

And in Malachi: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Mal. IV, 2).

And in Numbers: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man from Israel” (Num. XXIV, 17).

[Note: [Col. 1439D] The Regin. manuscript reads: “and a man shall rise,” etc.]

In the Gospel also we read most clearly concerning Christ: “In which the Branch from on high has visited us, to illumine those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace” (Luke I, 78).

The Branch himself is also called the cornerstone (Eph. II), because he joins the two peoples and unites the two walls into one house.

To unbelievers he is a stone of stumbling. Concerning him it is also said in the Psalms: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 22–23).

Upon this stone are seven eyes, concerning which Isaiah speaks: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root. And the Spirit of God shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of God shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 1 and following).

Those who wish the high priest Jeshua and his friends to be understood as the Lord Savior and his disciples, the men who are *τερατοσκόποι* and signs, interpret the passage as referring to the apostles—or, according to another reading, the disciples—who perceived his mystical signs and recognized future things from present events.

Thus, in the man who had been blind from birth (John IX), they interpret the restored eyes as referring to the people of the Gentiles; and in the woman suffering from an issue of blood (Matt. IX), they explain the Church as liberated from works of blood.

As for what follows—“For behold, the stone that I have set before Jeshua”—those who love the historical interpretation understand it of Christ in such a way that they say Christ will come after Jeshua the son of Jehozadak.

For “before Jeshua,” that is, “in his sight” and “before his face,” signifies what is future. He is called a stone because of the strength and power by which he has crushed all kingdoms; and we read of him also in Daniel as the stone cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. II).

**(Verse 10.)** “Behold, I shall engrave its engraving, says the Lord of hosts, and I shall remove the iniquity of that land in one day. On that day, says the Lord of hosts, each man shall call his neighbor beneath the vine and beneath the fig tree.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, I shall dig a pit, says the Lord Almighty, and I shall handle all the iniquity of that land in one day. On that day, says the Lord Almighty, each person shall call his neighbor beneath the vine and beneath the fig tree.”

Above he had said: “Behold, the stone that I have set before Jeshua; upon the one stone are seven eyes.” Now, consistently, he preserves the metaphor from the stone and says: “I shall engrave its engraving,” or “I shall carve its carving.”

What is written in Hebrew as *MAPHATE PHETHEE* (מַפְתֵּחַ פְּתָחָה), Aquila translated as *διαγλύψω ἄνοιγμα αὐτῆς*, that is, “I shall carve its opening.” Theodotion and Symmachus translated it: “I shall carve its engraving.”

[Note: [Col. 1439D–1440D] The same manuscript reads “Maphete phaetehaee”; then it gives Aquila’s Greek text and a word meaning “he passes over.”]

The meaning is this: “I shall cause this stone to be wounded by the nails of the cross and the soldier’s spear; and through his passion I shall remove the iniquity of the land in one day,” concerning which it is written: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII, 24).

On that day of Christ’s passion, the man who is perfect in Christ and who, together with the apostles, has ascended to the height of the Lord’s benevolence will call his neighbor—either believers from the Jews or, certainly, the people of the Gentiles—beneath the vine called Sorek, concerning which he says in the Gospel, “I am the vine” (John XV, 1), whose fruit gladdens the human heart; and beneath the fig tree, the sweetest fruits of the Holy Spirit, so that they may rest in eternal peace and, with the world’s sedition and the bloodshed of warriors—or, according to another reading, of wars—suppressed, may know that they are under the rule of the king whose name is mystically “peace” in Solomon.

The prophet Micah also recalls this same sitting beneath the vine and beneath the fig tree, saying: “On that day each person shall call his neighbor and his brother beneath his fig tree and beneath his vine, and there shall be none to frighten him” (Mic. IV, 4).

As for what is written according to the Septuagint—“Behold, I shall dig a pit”—we can understand a trench or pit in place of the engraving of the stone, for everything that is carved is also dug out.

Nevertheless, if someone more contentiously refuses to refer this to the stone, but wishes it to have its own beginning and its own meaning, let us say that the omnipotent God, on the day of the passion of his Son—or, as the Jews think, at the final end of the world, when he comes to judge—will dig out and bring into the midst the works of each person, and will handle the whole earth on the day of judgment.

For this is the one day. And on that day each of the saints will call his companions and friends, who are themselves saints, to rest and rejoice in the power of their works.

## (Chapter IV—verse 1)

And the angel who was speaking within me returned and roused me, as a man who is roused from his sleep.

The Septuagint: “And the angel who was speaking within me returned and roused me, as a man is accustomed to be roused from his sleep.”
