For where had he gone, so as to return—especially since he was speaking in the prophet and could not exist apart from the one in whom he was speaking? But whenever human frailty is left to its own weakness, we must believe that God and the help of his angels depart from us. Thus the prophet too, stunned by the astonishment of the great vision, was numb in his whole mind and could not see the clear light of truth. Therefore he is roused from the preceding vision to another vision, as though awakening from sleep, so that he may see what he did not see with closed eyes.

Let us speak in another way. The proverb of Solomon bears witness: “If you sit, you will be without fear; but if you sleep, you will sleep sweetly, and you will not fear the terror coming upon you, nor the assaults of the impious rushing upon you” (Prov. III, 23 ff.). Whoever has slept this sleep and has heard it said of him what we read written concerning Lazarus—“If he sleeps, he will be saved” (John XI, 12)—will be able to sing with the bride: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V, 2). Let us therefore see what the prophet rises to contemplate, as though from sleep.

## (Verses 2 ff.)

And he said to me, “What do you see?” And I said, “I saw, and behold, a golden lampstand entirely, and its lamp above it; and its seven lamps upon it; seven and seven vessels for the lamps that were above it. And there were two olive trees above it, one on the right of the lamp and one on its left.” And I answered and said to the angel who was speaking within me, “What are these, my lord?” And the angel who was speaking within me answered and said to me, “Do you not know what these are?” And I said, “No, my lord.” And he answered and said to me, “This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: ‘Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my spirit,’ says the Lord of hosts. ‘Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel? [You shall become] a plain; and he shall bring out the chief stone, and shall make its grace equal to grace.”

The Septuagint: “And he said to me, ‘What do you see?’ And I said, ‘I saw, and behold, a golden lampstand entirely, and a lamp above it; and seven lamps upon it, and seven vessels for the lamps that were above it. And behold, two olive trees above it, one on the right of the lamp and one on the left.’ And I asked and said to the angel who was speaking within me, ‘What are these, Lord?’ And the angel who was speaking within me answered and said to me, ‘Do you not know what these are?’ And I said, ‘No, lord.’ And he answered and said to me, ‘This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: “Not by great force, nor by strength, but by my spirit,” says the Lord almighty. “Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel, that you should be corrected?” And I will bring out the stone of inheritance: ‘Equality of grace, grace to it.’”

[Note: Victorius corrects “upon it,” that is, upon the lampstand. Then the Reginensis manuscript reads: “and seven lamps,” in the proper order.]

The angel who roused Zechariah as though he were a man rising from sleep asks him what he has seen, so that when he answers, confesses his ignorance, and inquires what he is looking at, saying, “What are these, my lord?”, we may hear from him: “This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: ‘Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my spirit,’ says the Lord.” Let us therefore go through the details, first explaining what seems correct to the Hebrews, from whom we have been instructed in the Old Testament, and then ascending by these steps, as it were, to the heights—or thresholds—of the Church.

They interpret the solid golden lampstand as the Law, that is, νόμος (*nomos*). The lamp, that is, the flame shining and gleaming at the summit of the lampstand, they interpret as Christ, who is the head of the Law and illumines the whole world. The seven lamps upon the lampstand are the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, about which we spoke above, that there are seven eyes upon the one stone. No one doubts that the Law was written under the dictation of the Holy Spirit. The seven vessels containing the oil poured into the lamps that shine upon the lampstand they understand in this way: these seven graces descend from heaven to human beings through the Law.

The two olive trees above the lampstand, on the right and left, between which the central lamp shines, they interpret as the Law and the Prophets. When the prophet had narrated his vision, not knowing what he was seeing, he questions the angel speaking within him—that is, his understanding illuminated by God. This angel is our angel, who wisely understands and makes God’s will known to us, and says: “What are these, my lord?” But the angel does not explain the prophet’s vision, as he had been asked; rather, he again questions the one who is asking: “Do you not know what these are?” When he answers, “I do not know,” the angel himself replies: “This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: ‘Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my spirit,’ says the Lord.”

The word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, who spoke not by an army nor by strength but by God’s spirit, is itself the interpretation of the vision: not by an army, nor by a multitude of warriors, but by the spirit of God the people were restored and are to be restored more fully, while their adversaries are to be devastated.

And what follows—“Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel, [you shall become] a plain”—they understand as spoken about the devil, who stood at the right hand of Jesus to oppose him and raised himself against Zerubbabel and the Jewish people. He was turned into a plain and humbled; he lies beneath Israel’s feet, because God will bring out the chief stone, Christ his Son, who has always been the help of the people of Israel. And his grace—that is, the grace of the stone—toward those whom he restored from captivity will make equal the grace that he has always exercised toward their fathers.

These are the things we have found stated by the Hebrews. Now let us discuss what ecclesiastical writers have written in their Commentaries.

The golden lampstand they understand as the Church, made of the purest gold, because in the holy Scriptures it seeks the meaning and understanding more than the words. That gold is understood figuratively is shown by the hindparts and shoulders of the dove in Psalm LXVII, which are said to radiate with the green or brilliance of gold.

They too understand the lamp as Christ, who shines in the Church and said of himself: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel” (Matt. V, 15)—that is, under the measure of the Law—but “upon a lampstand,” that is, the freedom of the Gospel, so that it may shine for all who are in the house.

They likewise understand the seven lamps and their vessels as the graces of the Holy Spirit, through which the Church receives the oil of God’s mercy and all the virtues.

The two olive trees above the lampstand they too understand as Moses and Elijah, who spoke with the Lord on the mountain and signified what he was going to suffer in Jerusalem (Matt. XVII). For the whole Law and the Prophets proclaim the passion of Christ.

Others interpret the two olive trees, one on the right and one on the left, as the Law and the Gospel, so that the Gospel is on the right and the Law on the left. Concerning the right and the left it is said in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me” (Song II, 6).

Most of our writers interpret the mountain as the devil and Antichrist, who would dare to stand before Zerubbabel—from whose lineage Christ was to be born—and to raise himself up, and to say in the Gospel: “All these things have been handed over to me, and I will give them to you if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. IV, 9). The Lord casts him down beneath his feet, makes the proud one humble and prostrate, and says: “Get behind me, Satan; for it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (ibid., 10; Deut. VI, 13).

They offer as an example in the Gospel the epileptic whom the apostles had been unable to heal. They ask why they had not been able to heal him, and they hear: “Amen I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you. But this kind is not driven out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII, 19–20). There the mountain is plainly understood as the devil.

Others, with considerable rashness, refer to Christ what is manifestly said about the devil, because Christ is frequently called a mountain in the holy Scriptures. There is no need to provide examples, since they are abundant. They are led into this error because the Septuagint reads: “Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel, that you should correct?” Evidently, they think that this mountain standing before Zerubbabel—that is, descending from Zerubbabel’s stock—wishes to correct the world himself, and that the following words refer to him: “I will bring out the stone of inheritance,” concerning which it is written: “You are he who will restore my inheritance to me” (Ps. XV, 5). And elsewhere: “He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved” (Ps. XLVI, 5). Again: “The portion of the Lord was made Jacob, the lot of his inheritance Israel” (Ps. CIV). And in the second Psalm: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance’” (Ps. II, 7–8).

The Lord will bring out the chief stone, concerning which we read: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” And: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1, 3).

But what he says—“He will make his grace equal to grace”—means this: “We have all received from his fullness, and grace for grace,” that is, in place of the grace of the Law, the grace of the Gospel, so that Israel’s believers and the people of the nations may receive equal grace and an equal gift. Hence Gabriel also says to Mary: “You have found grace with the Lord” (Luke I, 30). And the apostle Paul writes: “By grace you have been saved” (Eph. II, 8). And John the Evangelist says: “The Law was given through Moses; but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I, 17).

## (Verses 8 ff.)

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “The hands of Zerubbabel founded this house, and his hands shall complete it; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. For who has despised the days of small things? And they shall rejoice and shall see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel. These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which range throughout the whole earth.”

The Vulgate omits “are.”

The Septuagint: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘The hands of Zerubbabel founded this house, and his hands shall complete it. And you shall know that the Lord almighty has sent me to you. For who has despised the days of small things? And they shall rejoice and see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel. These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which look upon the whole earth.’”

The Hebrews and our own writers say many things. Following some of them and rejecting others, let us state what seems best to us, preserving the truth of the history, so that from it we may recognize the one who is prophetically announced through the historical account.

The hands of Zerubbabel, prince of the Jews who returned from Babylon, laid the foundations of the Temple, and his hands will reach to the Temple’s summit, completing what they had begun and building everything whose construction had been started. We read in Ezra that the Temple was begun and completed by Zerubbabel (I Esd. IV and VI).

And when, says the prophet Zechariah, you see the roof placed upon the Temple that you are now building, then you will understand that I was sent by the Lord and that I spoke what I said at his command.

“Who has despised the days of small things?” Here “who” is understood in the sense of “rare,” as in: “Who, do you suppose, is the faithful and wise steward?” (Luke XII, 42); and: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, and who shall ascend your holy mountain?” (Ps. XIV, 1). Rare, therefore, is the person who despises the small days of this age and considers royal power worthless.

When we see the powerful of this world shining in gold, gleaming with purple and sparkling gems, and surrounded by an army, let us say within ourselves: “Who, do you suppose, despises the days of small things?” Hence Jacob too, recognizing the brevity of human life, says: “The days of my life are few and evil” (Gen. XLVII, 9).

Those who despise the days of small things—and this refers to royal power, in order to admonish Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people building God’s Temple not to fear their adversaries, but to hear the Lord encouraging them—because they despise royal splendor, will rejoice and see the help of the Savior, who is promised from Zerubbabel’s lineage and is called a stone because of his strength, a tin stone.

In Hebrew it is written ABDIL [or Abdel], (—), because it is a wall, strength, and the power of believers.

For just as tin protects other metals from fire, and although bronze and iron are by nature extremely hard, without tin they are burned and consumed, so every strength of angels and human beings, if it does not have the Savior’s help, is shown to be weak and fragile.

This stone—that is, the mass—which among the Hebrews is written ABDIL, meaning “tin,” is etymologically explained by ἀποχωρίζων (*apochōrizōn*), that is, “separating” and “dividing.” Just as tin dissociates mixed and adulterated metals from one another through fire, so the Lord, the true assayer and χωνευτής (*chōneutēs*, “smelter”), separates the bronze of vices and the lead from the gold and silver of good works, so that pure gold and silver may remain.

In other words, this ἀποχωρίζων, or “separator,” is written of in the Gospel: “His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor and separate the chaff from the wheat” (Luke III, 17). He cries out through Jeremiah: “What has straw to do with grain?” says the Lord (Jer. XXIII, 28).

Many of our writers understand the hands of Zerubbabel, who founded the house and completed it, as Christ. If we accept this, we will be compelled to explain what the tin stone in Zerubbabel’s hand means. For surely another Christ is not to be approved in Christ’s hand? Some have understood the tin stone as the Lord’s body, which was stained by no spots of sin and is not called lead, but the purest tin.

We explained above that the seven eyes ranging throughout the whole earth and judging everything are the seven spirits; and that nothing is hidden from God, who knows the past, the present, and the future and repays each person according to his works—especially when he comes in the person of the one who separates the good from the evil and acts as a smelter.

## (Verses 11 ff.)

And I answered and said to him: “What are these two olive trees on the right of the lampstand and on its left?” And I answered a second time and said to him: “What are the two clusters of olives beside—or above—the two golden beaks, in which are the vessels made of gold?” And he said to me: “Do you not know what these are?” And I said, “No, my lord.” And he said: “These are the two sons of oil who stand beside the Ruler of the whole earth.”

The Septuagint: “And I answered and said to him: ‘What are these two olive trees on the right of the lampstand and on the left?’ And I asked a second time and said to him: ‘What are the two branches of olives that are in the hands of the two golden beaks, which pour out and draw back the golden vessels?’ And he said to me: ‘Do you not know what these are?’ And I said: ‘Certainly not, lord.’ And he said: ‘These are the two sons of fatness who stand beside the Lord of the whole earth.’”

When the prophet asked what the two olive trees signified, one of which stood at the right of the lampstand and the other at its left, the Lord—or the angel of the Lord—did not wish to answer. Understanding this, the prophet inquires a second time and says: “What are these two clusters of olives,” or “two branches,” asking about lesser things, since he was not worthy to hear about greater ones.

These two branches are in the hand of the two beaks, or above the two golden beaks, which in Hebrew are called SINTHOROTH [or Sinthuroth], (—), and in Greek μυξωτῆρες (*myxōtēres*), “nostrils” or “beaks.” These two μυξωτῆρες themselves, above which are the two clusters or two branches of olive, are made of the purest gold.

When the prophet also asked about the two branches and was again questioned by the angel whether he knew what the two branches signified, and he said, “No, Lord,” the angel of the Lord replied: “These are the two sons of oil,” as Symmachus rendered it; or of στιλπνότης (*stilpnótēs*), “splendor,” as Aquila translated it; or of ποιότητος (*poiótētos*), that is, “fatness,” as the Septuagint rendered it; or of λαμπρότης (*lamprótēs*), “brightness,” as Theodotion translated it—“who stand beside the Ruler of the whole earth.”

[Note: Compare Letter 57 to Pammachius, no. 11.]

Concerning the two olive trees that were at the right and left of the lamp, we read above. Therefore, when the prophet now asks about them, he is not worthy to receive an answer because he does not remember what came before; or because he wishes to hear more clearly here what was said obscurely there; or, certainly, the angel rebukes his persistence by silence, since he insists on knowing greater matters than he can understand. The Hebrews, however, affirm that the reason he heard nothing when asking about the olive trees was that he did not ask properly and did not inquire about everything he ought to have known.

Finally, afterward he asks more fully, adding the clusters or branches of olives, about which he had previously been silent. There he said, “What are these two olive trees?” Here he asks, “What are the two clusters of olives?” Μεταφορικῶς (*metaphorikōs*), the trees are straight in the manner of ears of grain, and, like ears with their awns, these trees are covered by a kind of enclosure of branches and leaves and rise upward.

[Note: Martianay retained: “the trees are covered.”]

Some of our writers interpret the two olive trees as the Son and the Holy Spirit, with the central lamp as God the Father. But I do not know how they can accept one as being on the right and the other on the left without blasphemy. They explain the branches, or clusters, of olives as the Savior’s incarnation and the likeness of the Holy Spirit to a dove, because we cannot see the whole olive trees, but only a certain part—so to speak, the small branches—of Christ’s incarnation and the manifestation of the Holy Spirit have been shown to us.

Others understand the two as the two Testaments: the Gospel on the right, the Law on the left, because in the one there is the spiritual sense and in the other the bodily sense; and because we cannot explain either the whole Gospel or the whole Law, but now know in part and prophesy in part (I Cor. XIII, 9), and cannot yet understand what is perfect.

There are those who interpret the two branches or two clusters of olives, and the sons of fatness or splendor, as the priesthood and the Law, which provide joy to the whole earth.

Others interpret them as Enoch and Elijah, one of whom pleased God in uncircumcision and the other in circumcision, and one of whom was taken up bodily into heaven (Gen. V and II Kings II).

For “splendor,” “oil,” “fatness,” and “brightness,” we read in Hebrew ISAAR (—), in accordance with what is written in the Psalms concerning the joy and happiness of the saints: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance—or fatness—of your house” (Ps. XXXV, 9). For πιότης (*piotēs*) more properly signifies “fatness” than “abundance.”

We have spoken of these matters as we were able and as the strength of our little talent permitted, briefly touching upon the various opinions of the Hebrews and of our own writers. If anyone says something better—or rather, truer—we willingly assent to what is better.

## (Chapter V—verses 1 ff.)

And I turned and lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a flying scroll. And he said to me: “What do you see?” And I said: “I see a flying scroll; its length is twenty cubits and its breadth ten cubits.” And he said to me: “This is the curse that goes forth over the face of the whole earth, because every thief, as it is written there, shall be judged, and everyone who swears shall likewise be judged. I will bring it forth,” says the Lord of hosts, “and it shall enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely by my name, and it shall remain in the midst of his house and consume it, its wood, and its stones.”

The Septuagint: “And I turned and lifted my eyes and saw a flying sickle. And he said to me: ‘What do you see?’ And I said: ‘I see a flying sickle, twenty cubits in length and ten cubits in breadth.’ And he said to me: ‘This is the curse that goes forth over the face of the whole earth, because every thief from this time until death shall be punished, and every perjurer from this time until death shall be tortured. And I will bring it forth,’ says the Lord almighty, ‘and it shall enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely by my name, and it shall rest in the midst of his house and consume him, his wood, and his stones.’”

The prophet, turning to another vision and raising his eyes from joyful and happy things to sadder ones, sees a flying scroll, which in Hebrew is called MEGELLA [or Gemell], (—), and which Aquila and Theodotion translated διφθέρα (*diphthera*), “parchment,” while Symmachus translated it κεφαλίς (*kephalis*), that is, “chapter,” in accordance with what we read in the Psalm: “In the scroll of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. XXXIX, 8); or, according to the Septuagint, δρέπανον πετόμενον (*drepanon petomenon*), that is, “a flying sickle.”

[Note: All the manuscripts I inspected transpose the first syllable here, reading Gemella for Magella. —Martianay.]

[Note: The words δρέπανον πετόμενον, “a flying sickle,” are absent from the Palatine and Reginensis manuscripts.]

Everything that he had seen above had announced the building of the Temple, the coming of the Lord and Savior, and the people’s freedom from Babylon. Therefore, lest his heart be lifted up with the Apostle—for whom an angel of Satan was given to buffet him (II Cor. XII), lest he become exalted—he too sees sad things, so that whatever arrogance had grown from the revelation of good things might diminish through the threat of sad things.

A flying scroll is shown, in which everyone’s sins are written down, so that each person may receive according to his works, whether good or evil, as Daniel says: “Thrones were set in place, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII, 10).

But if we accept the sickle, as the Septuagint translated it, let us take an example from John’s Apocalypse, in which it is written: “And the angel answered and said to him who sat upon the horse, ‘Send your sharp sickle and reap your vineyard, because its grapes are ripe’” (Apoc. XIV, 18).

In place of the sickle, we read of arrows and a sword in Deuteronomy: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. XXXII, 42). And because God did not spare the sinning angels, who through their own fault lost their heavenly dwelling, he himself says through Isaiah: “My sword is drunk in heaven” (Isa. XXXIV, 5).

All sinful peoples will perish by the sword—not, of course, by a bodily sword, since there are many different paths to death besides the sword—but by the spiritual sword, with which those who have not repented are to be struck. Concerning them the Psalmist proclaims: “Unless you convert, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it, and in it he has prepared instruments of death” (Ps. VII, 13–14).

And we read in Jeremiah: “How long will you cut, O sword—or blade—of the Lord? How long will you not be quiet? Return to your sheath” (Jer. XLVII, 6).

This sword is called not only a sickle, which cuts down hay, straw, and thorns, but also an axe of trees, which will cut down those who have not produced fruits worthy of repentance. Concerning them John the Baptist proclaimed: “Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10).

This scroll, in which everyone’s sins are written down, or the sickle that cuts down the offenses of all, is sent into the vineyard of the Sodomites, concerning which it is written: “Our enemies are foolish; for their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot is from Gomorrah. Their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them. The fury of dragons is their wine, and the incurable rage of asps” (Deut. XXXII, 31 ff.).

This sickle has a length of twenty cubits and a breadth of ten. In this number, joyful things are joined to sad things. For the Lord rebukes in order to correct. In twenty, which is made up of two decades, stern and sad things are announced; in ten, that is, one decade, better and prosperous things. For through every scourging and punishment Israel is instructed.

At the same time, let us warn those who think theft and perjury to be small crimes that the curse written in the scroll or sickle is brought upon the house of the thief and perjurer, remains in it, and consumes all its wood and stones. If there is so great a threat of punishment for things considered lesser—namely theft and perjury—what shall we say about fornication, adultery, murder, sacrilege, and all the crimes that the Apostle numbers among the works of the flesh (Gal. V)?

I have read that the twenty cubits of length and ten of breadth refer to the age of the Lord Savior, producing the number thirty; for “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,” and the world is to be judged by him (John V).

## (Verses 5 ff.)

And the angel who was speaking within me went out and said to me: “Lift up your eyes and see what this is that is going forth.” And I said: “What is it?” And he said: “This is the ephah going forth.” And he said: “This is their eye in the whole earth.” And behold, a talent of lead was being carried, and behold, one woman was sitting in the middle of the ephah. And he said: “This is impiety.” And he threw her into the middle of the ephah and cast the mass of lead into its opening.

The Septuagint: “And the angel who was speaking within me went out and said to me: ‘Look up with your eyes and see what is going forth.’ And I said: ‘What is it?’ And he said: ‘This is the measure that goes forth.’ And he said: ‘This is their iniquity in the whole earth.’ And behold, a talent of lead was lifted up; and behold, one woman was sitting in the middle of the measure. And he said: ‘This is iniquity.’ And he threw her into the middle of the measure and cast the leaden stone into its opening.”

The ephah, or measure, was going forth and was being carried through the air. And so that we might not doubt by what proper name it should be called, the angel himself who had shown the ephah, or measure, gives it a name and says, according to the Septuagint: “This is their iniquity in the whole earth”; according to the Hebrews: “This is the eye,” that is, the manifestation of all sins.

And behold, a woman was sitting in the middle of the ephah, or measure, which among the Hebrews is called EPHA (—), and is frequently translated by the Septuagint as οἴφι (*oiphi*, “ephah”). This woman herself was called impiety.

When he saw these things, behold, a talent of lead—that is, a mass like a stone—was being carried, either by its own force, by the Lord’s command, or by someone else whose name is not stated. The angel who was speaking in the prophet, going out from him and showing him everything, seized the woman called Impiety and threw her headlong into the middle of the ephah, which had previously been carried freely, with her sitting above the ephah and visible to all.

And lest she should again raise her head and rejoice in her iniquity and impiety, he throws the talent of lead, in the form of a very heavy stone, into the opening of the ephah, so as to crush and enclose Impiety in the middle and prevent her from escaping in any way.

We have sketched these things as shadows and outlines of the future image, so that we may fill out what remains with its proper colors.

The angel who was speaking in the prophet, having gone out from him and speaking, as it were, face to face, commands him to lift his eyes and see the sins of the people of Israel heaped up to a complete measure, with the transgressions of all filled to the brim. And this is called their eye, which in Hebrew is written ENAM (—), spelled with the letters *ayin*, *yod*, *nun*, and *mem*.

Or it means “their iniquity.” If it had been written with the letter *vav*, it would correctly be read ONAM [or UNAM] (—), as the Septuagint supposed. This error has frequently become established in the Vulgate edition, because the letters *vav* and *yod* have the same form but differ in size, and one is read in place of the other.

This ephah, or measure, is their eye in the whole earth—that is, the manifestation of their sins—so that the vices whose dispersion had kept them hidden might, being heaped together into one place, be exposed to everyone’s eyes, and so that Israel might go out from its place and show all the nations what sort of people it had been in its own land.

“And behold, a talent of lead was being carried.” In what follows we read “a leaden stone” in place of “a talent of lead.” A talent is called CHACHAR (—), and a stone ABEN (—). It is therefore the leaden stone that is also the talent of lead, which we have translated more clearly as a mass or sphere of lead, signifying the very heavy weight of sins.

And over this measure and ephah of all offenses, Impiety sat in the middle. We may call her by another name, idolatry, and denial of God. Hence the Savior says to the Jews: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matt. XXIII, 32).

This Impiety, who sat upon Israel’s sins and gloried in her crime, is afterward thrown into the middle of Babylon and oppressed by the evil of captivity. Or, according to Theodotion, she herself throws herself down and hides in the middle of the ephah, and draws upon herself the very heavy weight of lead, so that she has a sealed opening and can no longer boast of herself.

Or certainly she is crushed by the angel of God, so that she who previously rejoiced in crime may fall silent in eternal silence.

Where, and by whom, she is enclosed and carried, the following passage will show.

### (Verses 9 ff.)

“And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, two women were coming out, and there was a spirit in their wings; they had wings like the wings of a kite, and they lifted the ephah between earth and heaven. And I said to the angel who was speaking with me, ‘Where are these women carrying the ephah?’ And he said to me, ‘So that a house may be built for it in the land of Shinar, and it may be established and set there upon its base.’”

**The Septuagint:** “And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, two women were coming out, and there was a spirit in their wings; they had wings like the wings of a hoopoe. And they lifted the measure between earth and heaven. And I said to the angel who was speaking with me, ‘Where are these women carrying the measure?’ And he said to me, ‘So that they may build a house for it in the land of Babylon, prepare it, and set it there upon its seat.’” [Col. 1450C]

The Jews think that the two women who are coming out signify the kingdom of the Medes and the kingdom of the Macedonians, both of which afflicted the Babylonian people, and that impiety established its seat there. But they contrive this interpretation by artifice, so that what has been said about themselves may not be understood as applying to themselves.

For the two women who come out—there can be no doubt about this—are to be understood as the twelve tribes from the land of Judah: ten of whom were captured by the Assyrians, and two by the Chaldeans. “And there was a spirit in their wings,” that is, the power of the devil, concerning whom it is written in Ecclesiastes: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Eccles. 10:4). And in the Gospel we read of an unclean spirit which, after it has been driven out of its house, wanders through desert and arid places and, returning with seven other spirits more wicked than itself, comes back to its former house (Luke 11).

Thus, driven as if by wind and breath by this spirit, these women were carried swiftly in flight, and they had wings—according to the Hebrew, **ASIDA** (), which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as *herodion*; only the Septuagint translated it as *hoopoe*.

[Note: Compare Aelian, *History of Animals*, Book XIII, chapter 22. Some say that it means “stork”; Olympiodorus disagrees with them.] [Col. 1449D; Col. 1450D]

The Hebrews think that the *asida* is a kite, a most rapacious bird that is always lying in wait for domestic birds. Those who have written about the natures of birds, however, maintain that there are three kinds of *herodion*: one white, another speckled, and a third black. The latter is also the most savage and bloodthirsty, and in fighting it is so frenzied for mating that blood bursts from its eyes. As for the hoopoe, whose name we have adopted from the similarity of the Greek term—for the Greeks themselves call it *popa*, because it watches over human excrement [or: “settles upon human excrement”]—they say that it is an extremely filthy bird, always dwelling in tombs and always living in human dung. Indeed, it is said to make its nest from it and to feed its young on the worms of decaying excrement.

Whichever of the three birds you choose to understand by *asida*, it suits these women, Judah and Israel, who, because of their rotting sins, have been handed over to the power of demons and carried by them into captivity. [Col. 1451A]

They carried through the air, between earth and heaven, the ephah, or measure, in which impiety was confined, with a mass of lead placed on top so that it could not escape, and the extremely heavy weight of all sins.

[Note: Victorius supplies the word “lifting,” with the support of certain manuscripts.] [Col. 1451D]

Understanding this, the prophet did not ask what these women were—for that was evident to the prophetic spirit—nor what they were carrying, about which he had already been instructed above; rather, he asked where they were carrying it. Thus the text continues: “I said to the angel who was speaking with me, ‘Where are these women carrying the ephah?’” He answered: “So that a house may be built for it in the land of Shinar.” For the Septuagint, instead of this, translated “in the land of Babylon.”

Shinar is the plain of the Chaldeans, where those who had moved their feet from the East and could not stand in the service of God built the tower of pride (Gen. 11). Hence the city itself was called Babylon, that is, “confusion,” because there the languages of all peoples were confused and mingled together.

Impiety, therefore, is carried by these women into Babylon, so that its house may be built there, established, and set upon its base, and so that it may rest in an eternal dwelling. Truly, both according to the historical account and according to mystical interpretations, Babylon is the seat of impiety.

If you wish to understand the two women as the peoples of the heretics and the Jews—both of whom go out from the presence of God, are borne along by an uncertain spirit, and have the wings of a kite, a heron, and a hoopoe, since they continually act like the partridge, gathering wealth without judgment (Jer. 17), hastening to snatch things from the Church, delighting in disputes and quarrels, dragging to destruction whomever they deceive, and wallowing in the mire of lusts and everlasting filth—then these women lift the extremely heavy burden of impiety, build their house in confusion, and serve the Babylonian king, so that there the peoples of the heretics and the Jews may dwell, [820] where idolatry dwells, serving wood and stones.

## Chapter VI

“And I turned and lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots were coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze” [the Vulgate has “of brass”]. “In the first chariot were red horses, in the second chariot black horses, in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot dappled and powerful horses. And I answered and said to the angel who was speaking with me, ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the angel answered and said to me, ‘These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand before the Ruler of all the earth.’ The chariot in which the black horses were was going out toward the land of the north, and the white horses went out after them, and the dappled horses went out toward the land of the south. But the most powerful horses went out and sought to go and range throughout the whole earth. And he said, ‘Go, traverse the earth’; and they traversed the earth. And he called me and spoke to me, saying, ‘Behold, those going out toward the land of the north have caused my spirit to rest in the land of the north.’”

**The Septuagint:** “And I turned and lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots were coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses, in the second chariot black horses, in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot dappled, starling-colored horses. And I answered and said to the angel who was speaking with me, ‘What are these, Lord?’ And the angel who was speaking with me answered and said, ‘These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand before the Lord of all the earth.’ The chariot in which the black horses were was going out over the land of the north, and the white horses were going out after them, and the dappled horses went out toward the land of the south, and the starling-colored horses went out and watched in order to go around the earth. And he said, ‘Go and circle the earth’; and they circled the earth. And he cried out and spoke to me, saying, ‘Behold, those going out over the land of the north have caused my fury to rest in the land of the north.’” [Col. 1452B]

“I passed,” he says, “to another vision and lifted the eyes of my heart higher toward heaven. And I saw four chariots coming out from between two mountains which were of bronze—that is, unconquerable and extremely strong, incapable of being consumed by any age. The mountains which above he had called myrtle-covered, shady, and wooded, he now calls bronze.

“In the first chariot were red horses, bloody, bloodthirsty, and terrifying in Babylonian cruelty. In the second chariot were black horses: the kingdom of the Medes and Persians. Sitting in this chariot and going out by the decree of King Ahasuerus, it carried the death of all the Jews in its mournful message. In the third chariot were white horses: the Macedonians, under whose king Antiochus we read of the victory of the Maccabees. In the fourth chariot were dappled and powerful horses.

“For we know that some Roman rulers were merciful toward the Jewish people, such as Gaius Caesar, Augustus, and Claudius; while others were persecutors and terrifying, such as Gaius Caligula, Nero, Vespasian, and Hadrian.

“Instead of ‘powerful,’ Aquila translated **κρατερούς**; the Septuagint translated **ψαρούς**, while the Hebrew has **AMASIM** (). [Note: In some books Aquila may have written **κραταιούς**, which is more likely. Of the Septuagint manuscripts that offered **ψαρούς**, meaning “starling-colored,” none, so far as I know, now survives; all have **πυρρούς**, incorrectly, as Jerome notes.] Certain copies incorrectly have **πυρρούς**, confusing the distinctions of colors and kingdoms, since **πυρροί**, that is, ‘red,’ are not called **AMASIM**, but **ADAMIM** ().” [Col. 1452D; Col. 1453A]

When the prophet asked what the things he was seeing signified, the angel who was speaking in him answered and explained that there were four winds of heaven—that is, the four regions of the world, which the Greeks call **κλίματα**—which stand before and obey the Lord’s will. For none of the four kingdoms we have mentioned did anything apart from the Lord’s will.

“The chariot in which the black horses were,” he says, “was going out toward the land of the north.” How beautifully the first chariot, in which the red horses were, is passed over, while what the second, third, and fourth did is described! For by the time the prophet was reporting these things, the Babylonian kingdom had already passed away, and the Medes’ power possessed all Asia. Under their king Darius, in the second year of his reign, in the eleventh month [or, according to some copies, the tenth], which is called **SABAT** (), on the twenty-fourth day of the month, he contemplated all that we have explained above. [Col. 1453A]

“The chariot in which the black horses were was going out toward the land of the north,” so that Median power might overthrow the Chaldean kingdom.

This too should be noted: in the Holy Scriptures, **κλίματα**, that is, the regions of the globe and of the world, are named according to the position of Jerusalem and the Temple.

The white horses also went out after them, following the tracks of the Medes and Persians: the kings of the Macedonians, so that they might bring the Chaldeans and Babylon under their rule. But the fourth horses, that is, the starling-colored and dappled horses—for in Hebrew we read **BORODIM** (), and they are also called **AMASIM**, that is, “powerful” and “strong”—went out toward the southern region and swiftly traversed the whole earth.

And the angel who was speaking in the prophet cries out, commanding the Romans: “Go, traverse the earth; circle the world of the earth, and subject all kingdoms beneath your feet.” Then, turning to the prophet, he bears witness in a clear voice: “Behold, those going out toward the land of the north have caused my spirit to rest in the land to which they went.”

The Hebrews handed down to me, concerning this extremely difficult passage, that Alexander and all the Macedonians—that is, the white horses that went out after the Medes and Persians, who themselves had proceeded toward the land of the north—caused the prophetic spirit to rest in the land of the north, because they fulfilled God’s will against the Medes, and because in a short time the power of the Medes and Persians was destroyed by the Macedonians.

For those who are oppressed have great consolation if they know that their enemies will soon perish.

We hand these matters on to students of our language as best we can—or rather, as we have received them—following the truth of history. We do not hunt through the memory for the chariots of Pharaoh and the Babylonian vehicles as though this were an Egyptian-style explanation. For one must consider not what is written where, but in what manner it has been written.

According to the allegory, let us understand in the present passage whatever we said concerning the four horns and the four smiths.

I read in someone’s book that the four chariots, in which there are red, black, white, and dappled and powerful horses, are to be understood as the four Gospels, and the horses as the Apostles, possessing different graces through the diversity of their colors. Some are red in martyrdom; others are dark and black, knowing the mysteries of Christ, concerning whom it is said in the Psalms: “Darkness was under his feet” (Ps. 17:10), and, “He made darkness his hiding place” (ibid., 17:12). Others are white, through the grace of virginity; others are dappled and powerful, possessing the grace of healings and various virtues.

These four chariots, or vehicles, were sent to the four winds of heaven, that is, to the cardinal regions of the world and the whole globe, so that they might fulfill the Lord’s will. To them the angel later says: “Go and traverse the earth, and sow the Gospel throughout all the boundaries of the earth.” [Col. 1454C]

He also explained what follows—“Behold, those going out toward the land of the north have caused my spirit to rest in the land of the north”—by saying that the spirit of the Lord, or of the angel, rested when, in the land of the north, the most oppressive kingdoms of the devil were overthrown by apostolic preaching. These are the kingdoms which the devil showed to the Lord Savior on a high mountain and, displaying them, boasted that they had been handed over to him (Matt. 4).

# Book Two

[Col. 1453]

[Col. 1453D] [825–826]

“We pass from obscure matters to matters still more obscure [or: ‘to obscurities’], and with Moses we enter into the cloud and darkness” (Exod. 34). “Deep calls to deep at the voice of your cataracts” (Ps. 41:8); “and the spirit, turning and turning, goes on and returns to its circuits” (Eccles. 1:6). We suffer labyrinthine errors and guide Christ’s blind footsteps with a thread.

[Note: Some think that *petasatus* means one who is shod with a cothurnus or a soccus; but here it is more correctly understood as a *petasatus* bearer, one covered with a *petasus* or broad-brimmed hat. This signifies a man prepared for travel, as Sisinnius was when he was hastening to go to Egypt. MART.] [Col. 1453D]

The hat-wearing bearer of the book presses us toward this difficulty (Horace, Book I, Letter 2):

[Col. 1454D]

“Half the work is done by him who has begun it. . . .”

How much more, then, must we, who have already completed a third of the journey, sweat with the same labor over what remains, lest we lose what has gone before and the unfinished work increase the reader’s longing!

Therefore, venerable Pope Exuperius, be present through your prayers, though you are absent in body, and obtain from the Lord that the veil of Zechariah may be removed from before my face, the veil which was placed before Moses’ eyes (Exod. 31; 2 Cor. 3), because the common and lowly crowd could not bear the radiance of his face.

Then I too may be able to say with David: “The Lord will give the word to those who preach the Gospel with great power” (Ps. 67:12).

This is the beginning of the second book of the *Commentaries on Zechariah*, which we dictate with such haste that there is scarcely any opportunity for correction: Brother Sisinnius is hastening to go to Egypt, so that he may carry there as well the fragrance of the good odor which has been sent by you to the brothers; and so that the thirsty fields may be watered, not by the river of Ethiopia, but by the most abundant waters of Gaul.

### (Verses 9 ff.)

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Take from the exiles—from Holdai, Tobiah, and Jedaiah—and you will come on that day and enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who came from Babylon. And you will take silver and gold and make crowns, and place them on the head of Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest. And you will speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold the man whose name is Branch, and he will branch out beneath him, and he will build the Temple of the Lord. He himself will build the Temple of the Lord, and he himself will bear glory, and he will sit and rule upon his throne; and he will be a priest upon his throne, and there will be a counsel of peace between the two of them. And the crowns will belong to Helem, Tobiah, Jedaiah, and Hen son of Zephaniah, as a memorial in the Temple of the Lord. And those who are far away will come and build in the Temple of the Lord, and you will know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. And this will happen if you diligently hear the voice of the Lord your God.’”

**The Septuagint:** “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Take from the captivity, from the rulers, from its useful things, and from those who knew it; and you will enter on that day into the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who came from Babylon. And you will take silver and gold and make crowns, and place them upon the head of Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest. And you will say to him: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold the man, Branch is his name, and he will branch out beneath him, and he will build the house of the Lord. And he will receive power, and he will sit and rule upon his throne. And the priest will be at his right hand, and there will be a counsel of peace between the two. And the crown will be for those who wait, for its useful ones, for those who knew it, for the grace of the son of Zephaniah, and for a psalm in the house of the Lord. And those who are far from them will come and build in the house of the Lord. And you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you, and it will happen if you diligently hear the voice of the Lord your God.” [Col. 1455B–C]

I have once proposed to reveal to Latin ears the secrets of Hebrew learning and the hidden discipline of the teachers of the synagogue—at least insofar as it agrees with the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, in the most obscure passages, I must draw the lines of the historical account and then bring forward what I have received from ecclesiastical men, leaving it to the reader’s judgment which course should be followed more closely.

First, the order of the reading must be restored, so that what is said may become clear according to the literal sense.

“Take,” he says, “from Holdai, Tobiah, and Jedaiah, who came from the Babylonian captivity.” You will take from them the gifts that are offered—silver and gold—and you will enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah. There you will make crowns distinguished by the variety of gold and silver, not one crown but either two or several. For **ATAROTH** (), that is, **στέμματα**, indicates not one crown but either the dual or the plural number.

When you have made the crowns, you will place one of them upon the head of Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest, and you will speak to him:

“Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold the man whose name is Branch,” which in Hebrew is written **SEMA** (), with the letter **ṣade**, not **sin**. He is called Branch—that is, **ἀνατολή**, or **ἀναφύη**, or **βλάστημα**—that is, “sprout” or “shoot,” because he will suddenly grow up from himself and sprout from his root like a shoot. This man will build the Temple of the Lord.

[Note: The first interpretation, **ἀναφύη**, belongs to Aquila; the second, **βλάστημα**, to Symmachus, as we learn from the Barberini copy of the Hexapla.] [Col. 1455D]

When he has built it, he himself will also bear glory—that is, another crown, which in Hebrew is **HOD** (), and which one translator writes as **ἐπιδοξότης**, another as **εὐπρέπεια**, another as **ἀρετή**, and another as **δόξα**. These words signify renown, beauty, virtue, or glory.

They think that Zerubbabel is signified here: he suddenly rose from a lowly and captive condition to become leader of the Jewish people, built the Temple of the Lord, sat upon his throne, and ruled with princely authority. “And the priest,” he says, “Jesus son of Jehozadak will sit upon the priestly throne.” With their minds and counsels joined together, they will govern the people of God.

“And there will be peace between the two of them,” that is, between the one who belongs to the royal tribe and the one who descends from the Levitical line, so that priesthood and kingship together may rule the people of God. [827–828]

And the crowns which you make of gold and silver, after they have been placed upon the head of Jesus son of Jehozadak and upon the head of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, you will consecrate in the Temple under the names of those by whom they were offered—that is, Helem, Tobiah, Jedaiah, and Hen.

The second and third names are the same as above. The first has been changed: instead of Holdai, Helem is now given. The fourth, which had not been mentioned above, has been added: Hen. We shall speak about these names in what follows.

After the crowns have been restored to the Temple of the Lord and consecrated there as an everlasting memorial, he says, nations from the whole world, from far away, will come and build in my Temple, each according to his ability. Then, from the outcome of events and the prosperity of all things, you will know that the Lord sent me and that I foretold these things at his command. All this will happen if you obey the Lord’s commands and carry out his precepts.

**Holdai** means “the Lord’s supplication,” which is expressed more clearly in Greek as **λιτάνευσις Κυρίου**. **Tobiah** means “good of the Lord.” **Jedaiah** means “known to the Lord.”

In place of **HOLDAI** (), the text now puts **HELEM** () in the first position, which means “dream”; and in the fourth position it adds **HEN** (), that is, “grace.”

The crowns of these four men will be with the son of Zephaniah, whom above we read was called Josiah. He is the guardian and custodian of the Temple of the Lord, and there the crowns will rest in an eternal dwelling. [Col. 1456D–1457A]

The Hebrews report that Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, coming from captivity, brought gold and silver as offerings for the Temple, as well as crowns for the high priest and the leader. They also say that the one not previously mentioned, Hen—that is, “grace”—was Daniel, who came with an offering. Thus Helem is placed instead of Holdai so that, through the interpretation of the name “dream,” it may be shown that Daniel, while in captivity, and the three boys understood the mysteries of the royal dream. For after taking the three boys, Daniel prayed to the Lord and received the interpretation of the dream (Dan. 2).

The Circumcision attempts to explain these matters according to history. But we are obliged, according to the Septuagint translators, to say what our predecessors said.

“Take from the captivity, from its rulers, from its useful things, and from those who knew it, gold and silver. Enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who himself also came from Babylon, and make there golden and silver crowns, which you will place upon the head of Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest.”

The captivity of the Jews—that is, of the people who confess the Lord—means vices and sins. Whoever begins to repent and to desire the former Jerusalem, that is, the Church of Christ, abandons and leaves these things behind in Babylon. Gold and silver are offered by the rulers of the captives, by its useful ones—that is, by the useful ones of the captivity, who themselves have been handed over, for their own benefit, to the angel of Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved (1 Cor. 5)—and by those who know that captivity, namely, that after its punishments it is to be turned to the good.

Gold and silver are offered by those who confess the Lord both in understanding and in speech. From this gold and silver crowns are made in the house of Josiah, whose name means “saved,” and who is the son of the visitation of the Lord, that is, **ἐπισκοπῆς Κυρίου**. For he who was previously gravely ill is visited by the Lord.

Josiah is rightly called “saved,” because he too returned from Babylon. The crown, or crowns, are placed upon Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest, because as we advance and return to better things, the Lord is crowned through each of our virtues. Indeed, when we are crowned through the virtue of repentance, the Savior receives a crown in each of us, according to what Paul also says:

“From now on a crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me—not only to me, but also to all who love the appearing of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (1 Tim. 4:8).

Therefore the Father of the Lord Savior also received his name from the crown of righteousness. For **Josedec** means “Lord of righteousness,” because he renders to each according to his works.

James speaks of this crown in his Epistle: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him” (James 2).

The prophet is commanded, after he has placed the crown, or crowns, upon the head of Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest, to speak to him and say:

“Thus says the Lord: Behold the man, Branch is his name; and he will branch out beneath him,” and the rest.

We do not divide Jesus, nor can we make two persons into one person. The one who is called Jesus because he has saved the world is also called Branch, because in his days righteousness arose.

And it is sung in the Psalm: “Truth has arisen from the earth” (Ps. 84:12), because, having been born from a virginal womb at the consummation of the ages, he said: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). He came at the final hour, in accordance with what John says in his Epistle: “Little children, it is the final hour” (1 John 2:18). At that hour he hired for a denarius the people of the nations, who had been standing idle and doing nothing, and sent them into the vineyard (Matt. 20).

Otherwise, if he is made different according to the diversity of names, one will be the shepherd, another the ram, another the lamb, another the door, another the stone of stumbling, and another the rock of offense.

This one, therefore, who has been crowned through our virtues, will arise and be called Branch.

To him the Father spoke: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). And beneath him the multitude of believers will arise. It will build the house of the Lord, the Church, and he himself will receive the strength, beauty, progress, and glory of each person. He will sit and rule upon his throne, the throne of David, concerning which it is also written in the Gospel: “And the priest will be at his right hand” (Luke 1), or, according to the Hebrew, “upon his throne,” because he is both king and high priest.

He will sit upon both the royal and the priestly throne, and there will be peaceful counsel between the two, so that neither royal majesty may oppress priestly dignity, nor priestly dignity royal majesty, but that both may agree in the one glory of the Lord Jesus.

I read in someone’s book that what is said—“And peaceful counsel will be between the two” (Zech. 6:13)—refers to the Father and the Son, because he came not to do his own will but the Father’s, and because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father (John 14).

The crown—that is, the emblem of victory—is also promised, once Christ has been crowned, to those who await him, understand the benefit of their former captivity, and know all the mysteries of God, so that they may be in the grace of the son of Zephaniah, that is, in the visitation of the Lord.

Those who in Babylon said:

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. 136:1–2),

after they have returned to Jerusalem, may receive psalm and tambourine, and sing in the Church of the Lord.

Those who had been far from Judea because of greater sins may come through the truest confession, and through each of their advances build the house of the Lord. Then all, united in mind, may know that the Lord Almighty sent the prophet to them. Everything that has been promised will happen if they are willing to hear the Lord and, after practicing repentance, remain in good works.

## Chapter VII

### Verses 1ff.

And it came to pass in the fourth year of King Darius: the word of the Lord came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev.

> **Note:** Here there is a notable corruption of the text both in the Hebrew and among the LXX translators. For in the Hebrew one reads—according to Erasmus and Marianus—“And Regemmelech”; in the LXX, however, “And Arbath-Sager the king,” and so forth. These corruptions also occur below in the Commentaries, where the same names are found. —Martianaeus

And Sarasar and Rogommelech, together with the men who were with him, sent to the house of God to entreat the Lord, saying to the priests of the house of the Lord of hosts and to the prophets: “Must I weep in the fifth month, or must I consecrate myself, as I have already done for many years?”

And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: “Speak to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months during these seventy years, did you fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves? Are these not the words which the Lord spoke by the hand of the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem was still inhabited and prosperous, both it and its surrounding cities, and when the south and the plain were inhabited?”

### The Septuagint

And it came to pass in the fourth year under King Darius: the word of the Lord came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev. And he sent to Bethel Sarasar and Arabesser the king, and his men, to entreat the Lord, saying to the priests of the house of the Lord Almighty and to the prophets: “Has the consecration entered here in the fifth month, according to what they have already done for many years?”

And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: “Say to all the people of the land and to the priests: If you fast and mourn in the fifth and seventh months—and behold, seventy years—did you fast for me? And if you eat or drink, do you not eat yourselves and drink yourselves? Are these not my words, which the Lord spoke by the hand of the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, and its cities round about, and its hill-country and lowlands were inhabited?”

In the fourth year of King Darius, in the ninth month called Chislev, and on the fourth day of that same month, Sarasar and Rogommelech, together with the others who were with them, sent to the house of God—that is, to the temple which had already been restored by Zerubbabel and Jeshua—to ask the priests of the house of the Lord and the prophets whether, according to their former custom, they ought to weep and fast, or whether they should change mourning into joy.

The Hebrews believe that these men were Persian officers of King Darius who feared God. For, having heard that the temple had now been built, they wished to ask the priests of the house of the Lord and the prophets whether they ought to continue mourning and fasting, or to exchange sorrow for gladness.

The meaning of their inquiry was this: “In the fifth month—which among the Romans is called July—Jerusalem was overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar. For that reason, because of the desolation of the temple, we have fasted and mourned up to this time, consoling our grief with tears and fasts. But now, since it is said that the temple has been built, and since we see that the reason for mourning no longer remains, we ask whether we ought to continue doing this, or to exchange grief for joy.”

At the same time, it must be considered that weeping and fasting are called a consecration. Hence in Joel the priests are commanded to consecrate a fast and proclaim a healing (Joel V). Abstinence and fasting heal the wounds of the sinner, and sanctify those who have been healed.

After the Persian officers had sent their messengers, and the embassy of the inquirers to the priests and prophets had been completed, the word of the Lord came to the prophet, commanding him to tell the common people and the priests what answer they ought to give the envoys.

“When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month of Jerusalem’s captivity, and in the seventh month, when Gedaliah was killed by Ishmael, throughout the seventy years of the temple’s desolation and Jerusalem’s overthrow, did your fasting profit me?” (2 Kings XXV; Jer. XLI).

And conversely, whenever you eat and drink, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?

For God is not appeased by such things, but by good works, and by our doing his commandments, since food does not commend us to God. Neither shall we be lacking if we do not eat, nor shall we abound if we do eat.

Are these not my words, while Jerusalem and the cities of Judah still stood, which I spoke to you through the hands of my prophets, when Jerusalem and the cities of Judah still stood, when they abounded in all things, and both the hill-country and the plain overflowed with crops and enjoyed the most secure peace?

These, then, were the words of the Lord, as the following Scripture testifies: he desired true judgment and mercy; each person was to show compassion to his neighbor; no one was to oppress the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, or the poor; and no one was to devise evil in his heart.

“But they,” he says, “were unwilling to do these things. With deaf ears they despised my commands. Therefore great indignation came upon Jerusalem; and just as they were unwilling to hear me, so I also did not hear them.”

And now they inquire with such scrupulous concern when they ought to fast and mourn, although I previously said through Isaiah:

> “I have not chosen such a fast,” says the Lord, “nor that a man should humble his soul. But loose every bond of wickedness; undo the obligations of violent pledges; give your bread to the hungry from your heart. If you see someone naked, clothe him; and bring the poor and homeless into your tent. Then your timely light shall break forth, and your healings shall quickly arise” (Isa. LVIII, 5ff.).

As for what is written in the Septuagint—“Sarasar and Arabesser [or Arbath-Sager] the king sent from Bethel”—none of our writers has been able to explain it. For what has been badly translated from the Hebrew cannot be explained by any method.

Who, indeed, is this Sarasar, or Arabesser the king? The king of what province? To what place, or from what place, did he send Bethel? Or whose king could Arabesser be, since Bethel, which had formerly been associated with Judah, had by that time ceased entirely to be called Bethel, that is, “house of God,” and was instead called Beth-aven, that is, “house of the idol”?

They also attempt to explain what follows—“The consecration entered here in the fifth month, as they had done for many years”—in this way: that the consecration entered means that the temple vessels which had been taken away by Nebuchadnezzar were restored at that time.

As for the fast of the fifth and seventh months, they tried to refer it to the days of the week. But because the fast of the tenth month follows, they were compelled to refer these to months; and they remained entirely silent about what the fast of the fifth, seventh, and tenth months actually was.

Therefore let us remain content with our earlier explanation and not be drawn toward the false efforts of commentators, which arose from an error of translation.

### Verses 8ff.

And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Judge true judgment, and exercise mercy and compassion, each one toward his brother. Do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, or the poor; and let no man devise evil against his brother in his heart.

“But they were unwilling to pay attention. They turned a withdrawing shoulder; they made their ears heavy so that they would not hear; and they made their heart like adamant, so that they would not hear the law and the words which the Lord of hosts sent in his spirit by the hand of the earlier prophets. Therefore great indignation came from the Lord of hosts.

“And it came to pass just as he had spoken: they did not hear, and so they will cry out, but I will not hear, says the Lord of hosts. And I scattered them among all the kingdoms which they did not know; and the land was desolated because there was no one passing through it or returning to it; and they made the desirable land a desert.”

### The Septuagint

And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying:

“Thus says the Lord Almighty: Judge righteous judgment, and let each one show mercy and compassion toward his brother. Do not oppress the widow, the orphan, or the poor, and let no one remember the evil of his brother in his heart.

“But they were unwilling to pay attention. They gave a contemptuous back; they made their ears heavy so that they would not hear; and they made their heart disobedient, so that they would not hear my law and my words, which the Lord Almighty sent in his spirit by the hand of the earlier prophets.

“And great wrath came from the Lord Almighty. It will be as I said: they did not hear him. So they will cry out, and I will not hear them, says the Lord Almighty. And I will cast them among all the nations which they did not know. The land was desolated after them by whoever passed through and returned, and they made the chosen land a wilderness.”

> **Note:** The manuscript of Reginensis reads: “You were handed over to captivity and to desolation and death. Judge righteous judgment, lest…” Victorius nearly agrees, introducing the negative particle.

These are the things I wanted; these are the things I sought—not the fast of the fifth and seventh months, which signify desolation and death, since you failed to do them and were handed over to captivity.

Judge righteous judgment, lest you hear in the Psalms:

> “How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to sinners?  
> Judge the orphan and the widow; justify the humble and the poor” (Ps. LXXXI, 2–3).

And lest Isaiah also speak to you:

> “Those who justify the wicked for gifts,  
> and take away what is just from the righteous” (Isa. V, 23).

And lest Habakkuk, speaking on behalf of the oppressed, accuse God because of you:

> “Judgment has been brought against me,  
> and the judge accepts it.  
> Therefore the law is weakened,  
> and judgment does not reach its conclusion,  
> because the wicked oppresses the righteous” (Hab. I, 3–4).

Nor should we think that God’s command is new. Long ago he had commanded these things through Moses:

> “You shall judge the great as the small; you shall not show partiality, and you shall not pity the poor in judgment, because the judgment is God’s” (Deut. I, 17).

“Each one shall show mercy and compassion toward his brother.” After the severity of judgment, let kindness toward all follow, especially toward those whom we recognize as either related to us by blood or united with us in one faith.

Likewise, do not oppress the widow or the orphan, concerning whom we have been commanded:

> “Be a father to the orphans, and as a husband to their mother, judging the orphan and justifying the widow” (Eccl. IV, 10).

And do not oppress the foreigner or the poor, because exile makes one humble and poverty makes the other humble.

And let no man devise evil against his brother in his heart; or, as the Septuagint says:

> “Let no one remember the evil of his brother in his heart” (Luke X).

We ought to understand “brother” and “neighbor” either as the whole human race, since we were generated from one parent, or as those who are members of the household of faith, according to the Gospel parable, which wishes “neighbor” to be understood not as a blood relation but as every human being.

That anger must first be ended before the sun sets, and that the memory of all the wrongs we have suffered from others must be erased, we read in many places, especially in Jeremiah, who speaks in the person of God:

> “Let no one of you remember the evil of his neighbor in your hearts.”

> **Note:** In place of “Jeremiah,” which all the manuscript codices read, Marianus substituted the name “Zechariah,” because these words occur later in this same prophet and not in Jeremiah. We have wished to imitate the judgment of very learned men who did not dare to substitute the name Zechariah in the Gospels or to remove the name Jeremiah, although the latter entered the sacred text of the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter XXVII, verse 9, through the ignorance of ancient copyists. —Martianaeus  
>
> Since these words are not Jeremiah’s but rather Zechariah’s, which the holy Doctor repeats below in chapter 8, Victorius corrects the reading here to “Zechariah.” Although we do not follow his example against the testimony of the manuscripts, his liberty does not seem reprehensible.

When I commanded these things, they were unwilling to pay attention. They turned a withdrawing shoulder—or, as the Septuagint says, “a contemptuous back”—rejecting my commands by the posture of their body.

For when, with a wrinkled brow and contracted nostrils, we despise those who admonish us, we are accustomed to turn our back, according to what is written:

> “They turned their backs to me and not their faces” (Jer. II, 27).

“And they made their ears heavy,” he says, “so that they would not hear,” like a deaf asp stopping up its ears, which does not hear the voice of charmers or of the skillful enchanter.

They made their ears heavy so that they would not hear, and they set their heart so that they would not submit to the law of God. Hence Isaiah threatens them, saying:

> “The heart of this people has become gross;  
> they have heard heavily with their ears,  
> and they have closed their eyes,  
> lest they should see with their eyes,  
> hear with their ears,  
> understand with their heart,  
> and be converted, and I should heal them”  
> (Isa. VI; Acts XVIII, 27).

As for what is said according to the Hebrew—“They set their heart as adamant” [or “like adamant”]—it indicates hardness of heart, a heart of stone, because they were unwilling to receive the words of God.

Adamant is an exceedingly hard stone, called in Hebrew *samir* (Hebrew: [term omitted in the supplied text]). It is so hard that it breaks all metals, while it itself is broken by none. Hence the Greeks call it *adamas*, “the unconquerable.” Pharaoh’s heart was hardened by this adamant, so that he would not release the people of God (Exod. VIIff.).

And because they had—or rather, had set—their heart as adamant, willingly taking on hardness of heart so that they would not hear the words of the Lord, which he sent in his spirit—that is, in the Holy Spirit—by the hand of the earlier prophets, Isaiah, Hosea, and the others, who plainly lived before the captivity and had clean hands, great indignation arose because of their great sins.

Thus the Lord’s words were fulfilled, as he returned like for like: just as they had walked perversely toward him, so he also walked perversely against them and did not hear the words of those who cried out, because they too had rejected the words of the Lord with deaf ears.

Therefore he scattered them among all the kingdoms which they did not know: those of the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Medes, Persians, and the other nations subject to these empires, among whose lands they were dispersed.

All Judea was desolated, because it had no inhabitant, and there was no one passing through it or returning to it. And the land which had been a honeycomb among all lands, flowing with milk and honey because of its abundant fertility, they turned into a wilderness.

We can also refer these things to those who, sinning in the Church, have been cast out of the land of confession because they were unwilling to hear the Lord. They turned a withdrawing shoulder toward him, made their ears heavy, and set their heart as adamant.

Indignation from the Lord came upon them, and they were scattered among all the kingdoms of vices. Their land—whether soul or body—was desolated, having no Lord as inhabitant and no returning spirit within it.

The once-desirable land, which had been the dwelling place of the Trinity, was turned into a desert and a habitation of dragons.

Let us pass quickly over what is clear, so that there may be room for discussion of what is obscure. For we are not writing long and florid treatises in which eloquence plays for applause, but commentaries, whose task is to pass over what is evident and discuss what is obscure.

## Chapter VIII

### Verses 1ff.

And the word of the Lord of hosts came, saying:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been zealous for Zion with great zeal, and I have been zealous for her with great indignation.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have returned to Zion, and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. Jerusalem shall be called the city of truth, and the mountain of the Lord of hosts the holy mountain.”

### The Septuagint

And the word of the Lord Almighty came, saying:

“Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been zealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great zeal, and I have been zealous for her with exceedingly great fury.”

> **Note:** The manuscript of Reginensis reads “with great fury,” corresponding to the Greek *μεγάλῳ* (“great”); and shortly afterward it reads “I have returned” instead of “I will return.”

“Thus says the Lord Almighty: I will return to Zion, and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. Jerusalem shall be called the true city, and the mountain of the Lord Almighty the holy mountain.”

We learn more fully in Ezekiel (chapter XVI) how the Lord received Jerusalem—that is, the Israelite people—in the wilderness as a wife, covered her, lying in the blood of idolatry, with his cloak, and cherished her with marital love. Later, after eating fine flour, honey, and oil, adorned with beautiful garments and possessing, through the generosity of her husband, every ornament of jewels, she committed fornication with the Assyrians and Chaldeans and heard from the Lord:

> “As a wife despises her husband, so the house of Israel has despised me” (Jer. III).

Handed over to captivity and mocked by her lovers, stripped of her former beauty, she spread her legs to every passerby and was polluted to the crown of her head. Remembering her former happiness, she groaned:

> “I will return to my first husband,  
> for it was better for me then than now” (Hos. II, 7).

When he received her and again took her as his wife—although he had previously said to her, “I will not be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you” (Ezek. XVI)—he now says:

> “I have been zealous for Zion with great zeal,  
> and with great indignation I have been zealous for her.”

As great as was my former indignation, because she had been disfigured by many lovers and had stained my marriage bed—on account of which I handed her over to her lovers, not as an adulteress under a husband, but as a prostitute and worthless slave, publicly displayed in brothels—so much the more have I now returned to her, because she repented and built my temple, in which I shall dwell in her midst.

And she shall be called the city of truth, which was formerly called the city of falsehood. Of it Isaiah also wrote:

> “Truth slept in it” [or “was drowsy in it”],  
> “but now there are murderers” (Isa. II, 21).

It shall also be called the mountain of the Lord Almighty, the holy mountain, where, once the temple has been restored, victims are sacrificed and the order of the ceremonies is observed.

This is the historical interpretation.

Moreover, no one doubts that Zion and Jerusalem—“watchtower” and “vision of peace”—may be understood as the souls of the faithful. When they sin, the Lord becomes angry with them and hands them over to captivity, so that those who had not perceived God through good and prosperous things may perceive him through evil and adversity.
