When they have repented, the Lord will return to Zion and dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, which we understand to be one and the same city. Where the falsehoods of vices and sins formerly reigned, Christ, who is the truth, will afterward dwell.

And the mountain of the Lord of hosts shall be called the holy mountain, of which it is said:

> “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion” (Ps. CXLII, 1).

And:

> “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise  
> in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” (Ps. XLVII, 1).

Concerning this mountain Isaiah and Micah cry out:

> “In the last days the mountain of the Lord’s house shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills. All peoples shall flow to it; many nations shall hasten and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isa. II, 2–3; Mic. IV, 1–2).

Concerning this mountain and this city the apostle Paul, arguing in a sacred discourse—if, that is, in receiving the Epistle, he did not reject the authority of the Greeks in the Latin language—says:

> “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and countless thousands of angels, and the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven” (Heb. XII, 22).

### Verses 4–5

Thus says the Lord of hosts: “Old men and old women shall again dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, each man with his staff in his hand because of the multitude of his days. And the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets.”

> **Note:** One manuscript of Saint Albinus of Angers, cited by Martianaeus in his Notes on the Hieronymian Latin translation, reads *vir* (“man”) in the nominative, which he retained there and supports from the Hebrew idiom.

### The Septuagint

Thus says the Lord Almighty: “Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each one holding his staff in his hand because of the multitude of his days. And the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets.”

When I have returned to Zion and dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, he says, such will be the prosperity of all things, and such the cessation and tranquility of wars, that, with no enemy remaining, old age in both sexes will reach its furthest limit, and their trembling limbs will be supported by staffs.

The streets of the city will also be filled with boys and girls playing. This usually happens when cities enjoy security and profound peace, so that the joyful spirit of the cities celebrates itself in games and dances.

If we refer this to the Church, of which it is said:

> “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXIX, 2),

and:

> “The river’s streams gladden the city of God;  
> the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle.  
> God is in its midst; it shall not be shaken” (Ps. XLV, 4–5),

who could doubt that the streets of the Church are the virtues in which wisdom acts confidently and is proclaimed from the tops of the walls?

Hence the Psalmist cries out to the Lord:

> “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII, 96).

In these streets the bride seeks the Lord her Savior and speaks in the Song of Songs:

> “I will rise and go around the city, through the marketplace and its streets, until I find him whom my soul loves” (Song III, 2).

Thus old men and old women will dwell—or sit—there, concerning whom it is written, if one is willing to accept that book:

> “Old age is honorable, not measured by length of time nor reckoned by number of years” (Wis. IV, 8).

The gray hairs of human beings signify wisdom, and old age signifies an undefiled life. The Lord therefore says to Moses:

> “Appoint for yourself seventy elders, whom you yourself know to be elders” (Num. XI, 16).

For this reason no one before Abraham is called an old man. Of him we read:

> “Abraham, failing, died, nourished in a good old age, old and full of days” (Gen. XXV, 8).

For the glory of the old is their gray hair, concerning which it is said:

> “The wisdom of a man is his gray hair” (Wis. IV, 8).

Because of the multitude of their days, these men will hold staffs and rods in their hands and say to their disciples:

> “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with a spirit of gentleness and meekness?” (1 Cor. IV, 21).

For whoever brings forth wisdom from his lips strikes the foolish man with a rod.

> **Note:** In place of *excordem* (“one without heart”), Martianaeus retained, in one word, the manifestly erroneous two-word reading *ex corde* (“from the heart”), although Victorius had earlier restored *vecordem* (“the foolish”) with the help of the Brixian codices. He also noted that this testimony is found in Greek among the LXX, Proverbs X:  
> *Ὃς ἐκ χειλέων προφέρει σοφίαν, ῥάβδῳ τύπτει ἄνδρα ἀκάρδιον*—“Whoever brings forth wisdom from his lips strikes the heartless man with a rod.”  
> In the place of this, we read in the Vulgate edition: “Wisdom is found on the lips of the wise, and a rod on the back of one who lacks heart.”

And conversely:

> “Whoever spares his rod hates his son, but whoever carefully corrects him loves him” (Prov. XIII, 24).

Not only old men but also old women will sit in the streets of Jerusalem. Paul describes them with apostolic speech:

> “Honor widows who are truly widows.”

And elsewhere:

> “Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old, who was the wife of one man, who has testimony in good works: whether she has raised children, received strangers hospitably, washed the feet of the saints, assisted those in tribulation, and pursued every good work” (1 Tim. V, 3, 9–10).

Such old men and old women will sit in the streets of Jerusalem, holding staffs in their hands, and the streets of the city will be filled with boys and girls playing.

These are the boys and girls, the old and the young, whom the Psalmist urges to sing to the Lord, saying:

> “Young men and virgins, old men with the young, praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXLVII, 12).

And John the evangelist and apostle says:

> “I write to you, children, because your sins are forgiven for the sake of the Savior’s name. I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (1 John II, 12–13).

Solomon speaks of these in Proverbs:

> “He gives prudence to the innocent,  
> and to the young understanding and intelligence.”

And again:

> “Hear, children, the discipline of your father,  
> and attend, so that you may know understanding” (Prov. I, 4, 8).

Of these children, young maidens, and girls the forty-fourth Psalm also says:

> “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her.”

According to what is written:

> “The daughters of Judah rejoiced and were glad  
> because of all your judgments, O Lord” (Ps. XCVI, 8).

When they hear the Apostle say, “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV, 4), they will show the joy of their minds by the movement of their bodies and, dancing in celebration, will say with David:

> “I will dance and play before the Lord” (2 Sam. VI, 22).

### Verse 6

Thus says the Lord of hosts: “If it should seem difficult in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, will it also be difficult in my eyes?” says the Lord of hosts.

### The Septuagint

Thus says the Lord Almighty: “If it should be impossible before the remnant of this people in those days, will it also be impossible before me?” says the Lord Almighty.

In each of the words and sentences by which the prophet promises Israel prosperity—things almost unbelievable because of their magnitude—he introduces the statement:

“Thus says the Lord Almighty,” speaking in effect as follows: “Do not think that the things I promise are my own inventions, and do not believe them as though they came from a human being. The promises I repeat belong to God.”

He had said above that old women and old men would sit in the streets and, because of the length of time, hold staffs in their hands; that the streets would be narrowed by the multitude of people; that boys and girls would lead dances as on festival days; and that Jerusalem would be rebuilt and restored to its former state of happiness.

This seemed incredible to the remnant of the people who had returned from captivity, when they saw the city utterly abandoned, its walls in ruins and its burned walls displaying the hands of the Babylonians.

Therefore he joins these words: “If it seems difficult or impossible to you, who are the remnant of the captive people, that what I promise should happen—that in those days when Jerusalem is to be rebuilt there should be such happiness—will it be difficult or impossible in the sight of the Lord, who promises through my mouth that these things will happen?”

For:

> “What is impossible with human beings is possible with God” (Matt. XIX, 26).

We saw these things fulfilled in the churches of Christ during the time of persecution, when the savagery of the persecutors was aroused to such madness that they even destroyed our meeting places, handed the divine books over to the flames, and filled every island, mine, and prison with chained groups of confessors and martyrs.

Who at that time would have believed that churches would again be built by those very people who had previously destroyed them? Not because the same individuals were involved, but because the same imperial power which had formerly lurked in ambush with the rich (Ps. X) and, as though by decree of the senate, attempted to extinguish the name of Christ, now builds basilicas of the churches at public expense and raises their lofty summits—not merely decorating their ceilings and gleaming roofs with gold, but clothing their walls with veneers of various marble.

The divine books which it had previously consigned to the fire it now venerates, gilded and dyed purple and adorned with varied jewels, entrusting them to the protection of the Roman state.

### Verses 7–8

Thus says the Lord of hosts: “Behold, I will save my people from the land of the east and from the land of the setting of the sun. And I will bring them back, and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. They shall be my people, and I shall be their God, in truth and in righteousness.”

> **Note:** The missing words are likewise supplied by the LXX; our manuscripts provide them as well.

The LXX is similar.

Some Jews say that these things were fulfilled after Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, once the temple had been built, the walls of the city constructed, and the Jewish state restored by the Maccabees and the various rulers who governed Judea up to Herod.

Others say that they will be fulfilled at the end of the world under Christ, whom they await in vain.

We, however, say that they were partly fulfilled at that time—that is, after Zerubbabel and Nehemiah—and that they came beforehand in types and images, when the people were brought back from captivity, dwelt in Jerusalem, and were called God’s people, while the Lord was again called their God—not in falsehood and iniquity, but in truth and righteousness.

And now, under the Lord and Savior, we say that the promise is most fully fulfilled in the Church, that is, in the true Jerusalem, especially because it says:

> “Behold, I will save my people from the land of the east and from the land of the west.”

Concerning these places the Lord also spoke in the Gospel:

> “Many will come from the east and the west and recline in the kingdom of heaven with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Matt. VIII, 11).

Long before this the Psalmist had promised, saying:

> “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth.  
> From the rising of the sun to its setting,  
> from Zion comes the beauty of his splendor” (Ps. XLIX, 1–2).

For he will come from Zion who will deliver and turn away the iniquities of Jacob, when from east and west incense is offered to the name of the Lord in every place, and a pure sacrifice—not in the victims of the Old Testament, but in the holiness of evangelical purity.

Concerning this incense we also read elsewhere:

> “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 2–3).

And what this incense is, the following words show:

> “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.”

After the shoot from the root of Jesse had sprung up, one who would rule the nations, and in whom the nations hoped (Rom. XV), and after both the first people and the last—from east and west—believed in the Lord and became one flock, then all the nations were summoned to joy and stirred to gladness, as the prophet says:

> “Rejoice, O nations, with his people” (Ps. XXI, 28).

According to what is written elsewhere:

> “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord,  
> and all the families of the nations shall worship before him.”

And what follows—“in truth and righteousness”—signifies that the shadow of the old Law has departed and the truth of the Gospel has come, not in the righteousness of the Jews but in Christian righteousness. For the Lord himself is truth and righteousness, concerning whom we read:

> “Truth has risen from the earth,  
> and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV, 12).

Hence in the fourteenth Psalm righteousness and truth are mentioned together:

> “He who walks without blemish and practices righteousness,  
> and speaks truth in his heart.”

### Verse 9

Thus says the Lord of hosts: “Let your hands be strengthened, you who in these days hear those words from the mouth of the prophets, on the day when the house of the Lord of hosts was founded, so that the temple might be built.”

The Septuagint has translated “the Lord of hosts” as “the Lord Almighty”; otherwise it is similar.

After the temple had been built under Zerubbabel and Jeshua—for all these things are said in the fourth year of King Darius, on the fourth day of the ninth month called Chislev, when the temple had already been constructed—the same prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, who had encouraged both the leaders and the people to build it, now urge them to place faith in the things promised for the future on the basis of what had truly happened before.

They are to strengthen their hands, fearing neither the attack of the Medes nor the plots of the surrounding nations that sought to obstruct the work. They are to be strengthened by the mouth of the prophets from the day when the temple’s foundations were laid until the day when the temple was built, and they are to hear what follows.

We briefly explain the history, referring spiritually to the Church whatever is said about Jerusalem and the temple. In the Church hands are strengthened through good works, houses are founded when the foundations of faith are laid, and the temple is built when the multitude of believers is strengthened and lives in such a way as to be worthy of being the temple of God.

(Vers. 10.) For before those days there was no wage for human beings, nor was there any wage for animals; and for those entering and leaving there was no peace because of the tribulation. And I dismissed all people, each one against his neighbor.

**The Septuagint:** For before those days the wage of human beings will not be for profit, nor will the wage of animals endure; and for the one going out and the one coming in there will be no peace because of the tribulation. And I will send all people, each one against his neighbor.

The Septuagint referred everything to the future, but it is better referred to the past, as it stands in the Hebrew; and [Note: [Col. 1469D] Victorinus, and the truth of the exposition throughout, etc.] the truth of the exposition will confirm this. Before the house of the Lord was founded and the temple of the Lord was built, all your labor was fruitless. Human beings and animals alike, in agriculture, commerce, and various occupations, were frustrated by wasted efforts. Outside, adversaries; at home, sedition disturbed peace. Everywhere there was [Note: [Col. 1469D] In some books *justitia* (“justice”), in others, equally incorrectly, *jurgium* (“quarrel”). It is well known that *justitium* means a public mourning—an evil one—and the suspension of public legal business.] *justitium* because of the frequency of wars and domestic ambushes, since neither brother showed loyalty to brother, and every relationship was hostile.

The prophet Haggai, summing up this meaning in other words, says:

“And now set your hearts from this day onward: before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord. When you approached a heap of twenty measures, there were ten; and when you entered the winepress to draw out fifty jars, there were twenty. I struck you with scorching wind, mildew, and hail—all the work of your hands—and there was none among you who returned to me, says the Lord” (Hag. II, 16 ff.).

This too can be understood of the Church and of each individual believer. For before the house of God is founded in us, before we are built into a temple for God and hear from the Apostle, “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (II Cor. VI, 16), whatever good work we seem [Al. “may seem”] to possess—whether we are rational beings, who are called human beings, or simple creatures, who are called animals (for, he says, “You will save human beings and animals, Lord” [Ps. XXXV, 7])—has no reward with God. There are wars and dissensions within us, and everywhere tribulation and the absence of the peace of Christ, which, as he went to the Father, he left to the apostles (John XIV). The Lord’s sentence is fulfilled in us: “A man’s enemies are his household” (Mic. VII, 6). For every brother utterly supplants, every friend proceeds deceitfully, and a man mocks his brother and does not speak the truth; “they have taught their tongue to speak lies” (Jer. IX, 4). [Note: [Col. 1470D] The words “and a man mocks his brother” have been inserted on the authority of our manuscripts.]

But if we turn to Christ and become his temple, at once we shall hear the Apostle proclaiming: “Each one will receive his own reward according to his work” (I Cor. III, 8).

(Vers. 11, 12.) But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in the former days, says the Lord of hosts; but there shall be a seed of peace. The vine shall give its fruit, the earth shall give its produce, and the heavens shall give their dew; and I will cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things.

**The Septuagint:** And now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in the former days, says the Lord Almighty; but I will show peace. The vine shall give its fruit, the earth shall give its produce, and heaven shall give its dew; and I will cause the remnant of my people to possess all these things.

Before the foundations of God’s house were laid and the temple was built, there was no wage for human beings or for animals; and because of tribulation and distress there was no peace for those entering or leaving. All people were divided from one another by hostile hatred. But now, because the foundations of the Lord’s house have already been laid and the temple has been built, I will no longer deal as I did before with those who have returned from the Babylonian captivity. Everywhere there will be peace and joy, and future abundance will compensate for the former dryness and famine.

The vine will give its fruit, all the winepresses will be filled, the earth will be clothed with joyful crops, and everything will sprout through the rains that water it and the nighttime dew. All that I have said I will cause the remnant of my people to possess [Note: [Col. 1470D] Previously the text read, “I will cause the remnant of my people to possess.” Our manuscripts correct it.], because the foundations of the Lord’s house have been laid and the temple has been built.

The prophet Haggai speaks the same way at the same time. Above he had said: “I struck you with scorching wind, mildew, and hail—all the work of your hands,” after the foundations of the temple had been laid. “Set your hearts,” he says, “from this day and henceforth, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day when the foundations of the temple were laid; set your hearts upon it. Is the seed yet in the bud? Has the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree still not blossomed? From this day I will bless, and again I will shake heaven and earth together” (Hag. II, 18 ff.).

Let us speak also in another way, following the interpretation concerning the Church that we began above. Before anyone receives the faith of Christ and the foundations of the Holy Spirit are laid in him, no one can hear, “There is a reward for your work.” Whether he is a Jew, a heretic, or a gentile, whatever good work he may do, unless he does it in the name of Christ, he will not have the reward of his good work. We see the virgins of heretics, the austerity of philosophers, and the Jewish observance concerning varieties of food; yet, according to Haggai, we say [Al. “it is said”] that they eat and are not satisfied, drink and are not intoxicated, clothe themselves and are not warmed, and that whoever gathers wages puts them into a pierced purse (Hag. I).

But after they have received the faith of Christ—both those people and those who had been sinners in the Church, handed over to the captivity of this world because of the magnitude of their offenses, burned in the Babylonian fire—and after they have heard the Lord proclaiming, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to heal those who are brokenhearted” (Isa. LXI, 2), and after what is said through Amos has been fulfilled in them, “I will turn the captivity of my people Israel, and they shall build the ruined cities, and I will plant them” (Amos IX, 14), then in those days “righteousness and an abundance of peace shall arise” (Ps. LXXI).

The vine will give its fruit—the vine that says in the Gospel, “I am the vine, you are the branches. Every branch that remains in me the Father cleanses, so that it may bear greater fruit” (John XV, 8). When its branches—that is, its shoots and offshoots—have been cleansed, and, with budding eyes, have begun to promise the hope of future fruits, so that what is written may be fulfilled, “The flowering vines have given their fragrance” (Song II, 13), then the sun of righteousness will color the hanging clusters, so that, sent into the winepresses of the eighty-eighth and eighty-third Psalms, which are entitled “for the winepresses,” they may be trodden by the foot of the Lord, who ascends from Bosor [Note: [Col. 1471D] The manuscript of Reginensis reads “so that the clusters may pour,” namely, the grapes.], so that it may pour out the wine that gladdens the heart of man.

The earth too will give its produce—not dry, rocky earth full of thorns, but good earth that produces a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold (Matt. XIII), so that those who sow in tears may reap in joy (Ps. CXXV).

The heavens also will give their dew. Of these heavens it is written in the eighteenth Psalm (ver. 1): “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.” Of these heavens it is said in the song of Deuteronomy: “Rejoice, heavens, with him” (Deut. XXXII, 43)—that is, with the Lord and Savior; these are those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. VIII), who says with Moses: “Let my discourse be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. XXXII, 2).

Those who were dead in sins will rise, and those who lay in whitewashed tombs, which are full of the bones of the dead, will be raised; and those who dwell in the earth will rejoice. The following words show what will be the cause of their joy: “For the dew that is from you is their healing.”

The remnant of my people will possess all these things—peace, the fruit of the vines, and the abundance of the lands, which has grown through the dew of heaven. Concerning them Isaiah says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. I, 9). For “the remnant according to the election of grace has been saved,” not from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

(Vers. 13 ff.) And it shall be: just as you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you shall be a blessing. Do not fear; let your hands be strengthened. For thus says the Lord of hosts: Just as I resolved to afflict you when your fathers provoked me to anger, says the Lord, and I did not have compassion, so, having turned, I have resolved in these days to do good to Jerusalem and the house of Judah. Do not fear.

**The Septuagint:** And it shall be: just as you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you shall be a blessing. Trust and strengthen yourselves in your hearts [Note: [Col. 1471D] Victorinus restored “hands” in place of “hearts.” For, he says, not only do the Septuagint, whose translation this is, read ἐν ταῖς χερσίν ὑμῶν (“in your hands”), but so too does the Hebrew, the Latin edition, and Jerome himself in his Commentary. To be strengthened in one’s hands signifies completing the work begun.] because thus says the Lord Almighty: Just as I resolved to afflict you when your fathers provoked me to anger, says the Lord Almighty, and I did not repent, so I am prepared and have resolved in these days to do good to Jerusalem and the house of Judah. Trust.

He promises that these things will happen after the building of the temple, so that, just as the house of Judah and the house of Israel—namely, the two and the ten tribes—were a curse, a hiss, and an example among all the nations, so, when they have been saved and have returned to Judaea, they may become a blessing to all. “Do not fear,” he says, “the adversaries who rebel against you. Trust that what the Lord promises through me is true; let your hands be strengthened; complete the works you have begun.”

The cause of their strengthening is the Lord’s promise. For thus says the Lord Almighty, for whom nothing is impossible and who can fulfill what he promises: just as I resolved to afflict you and hand you over to captivity because your fathers provoked me to anger, and I did not have compassion—which the Septuagint translated οὐ μετενόησα, that is, “I did not repent,” whereas in Hebrew it is written ULO; NAAMATHI (), “but I did not have compassion”—not out of cruelty, but so that I might correct you through captivity and instruct you through every torment and scourging, so now, in the present time, I have resolved to do good to Jerusalem and the house of Judah.

It should be noted that when he is angry, the house of Judah and the house of Israel—that is, all twelve tribes that were handed over to captivity—are a curse among the nations. But after he resolved to do good, he does not do so for Judah and Israel, that is, for the two and the ten tribes—to Jerusalem and Samaria, Oholah and Oholibah. Rather, leaving Israel in captivity, he does good to Jerusalem and the house of Judah. At the end he adds, “Do not fear,” or “Trust,” in the sense we explained above. [Note: [Col. 1472D] Previously: “they are accursed.” Shortly afterward Victorinus reads “he does not do good” in place of “he does not do.”]

Concerning the Church and each believer, this can be understood as follows. During the time of persecution, Christians were a curse and an example to all the surrounding nations because they had offended their Lord. Later they become a blessing, when peace has been restored; and all this happens because the Lord, who was previously angry, later has compassion on Jerusalem—the vision of peace—and on Judah, which confesses the Lord’s faith.

Individual believers too, when they are expelled from the Church because of their vices and handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (I Cor. V), so that they may learn not to blaspheme (I Tim. I), will, when they have repented, return to their former state. They will see the peace of God and possess the glory of their confession.

Heretics slander the statement “I did not have compassion,” or “I did not repent,” as though God were either cruel or changeable if he either does or does not repent. If he repents, they say he is changeable; if he does not repent, they assert that he is cruel. Yet God repented that he had anointed Saul as king (I Sam. XV). And concerning the Ninevites, to whom he had announced through the prophet, “In three days Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III, 4), it is said that, when they repented, he himself changed his sentence—not through any defect of an unwise mind, but because of the variation in their conduct, whether evil or good.

For if they do evil, he threatens; if they lament their former sins, he has mercy [Note: [Col. 1473D] The word “has mercy,” without which the sense was incomplete or mutilated, has been supplied from the manuscript of Reginensis, which also reads “they have abandoned” in place of “they have lamented.”]. God does not change, for he is one and the same and cannot be changed; but when they are changed from evil to good works, he himself changes his decree concerning them.

He also says in Genesis: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sins are exceedingly great. Therefore, descending, I will see whether they are actually acting according to the cry that has come to me; and if not, I will know” (Gen. XVIII, 20–21). What he said means this: If they persist in their rage, punishment for sinners will not be lacking; but if they cease from their madness, they will become worthy of being known by me. “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19).

The Apostle writes to the Galatians: “But then, not knowing God” (Gal. IV, 8). Although God knows everyone and nothing, whether past, present, or future, is hidden from him, he says in the Gospel that he does not know the wicked: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke XIII, 27). Let us therefore understand God’s knowledge, repentance, anger, indignation, and all his affections not according to the weakness of human speech, but according to the meaning of the divine majesty.

(Vers. 16, 17.) These, then, are the words that you shall do: Speak truth, each one with his neighbor; judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates; and let none of you devise evil against his friend in your hearts. Do not love a false oath, for all these are things that I hate, says the Lord.

**The Septuagint:** These are the words that you shall do: Speak truth, each one with his neighbor; judge truth and a peaceful and just judgment in your gates; and let none of you devise evil against his neighbor in your hearts. Do not love a false oath, because all these things I hate, says the Lord Almighty.

I promised that I would not deal with the remnant of the captive people as in the former days. And just as I resolved to afflict them when their fathers provoked me to anger, and I did not have compassion, so now I have turned and resolved [Note: [Col. 1474D] The same manuscript reads, “I have turned to resolve in these matters.”] in these days to do good to Jerusalem and the house of Judah.

Therefore, so that my decision may remain firm and my promise not be void, do what I command: speak truth with your neighbors. Let us understand “neighbor” to mean the entire human race, because we were generated from one parent. Otherwise, if “neighbor” is understood as a relative, it would be permissible to lie to foreigners and strangers.

The Apostle says the same thing: “Putting away falsehood, speak truth, each one with his neighbor” (Eph. IV, 25). “Truth,” he says, “and the judgment of peace judge in your gates.” In judgment, truth and justice should come first; mercy follows afterward. For this is the judgment of peace: that the judge should intend to reconcile those who are at variance, according to the Gospel saying, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V, 9).

The following phrase, “in your gates,” agrees with the prophetic statement: “They hate the one who reproves in the gates, and they abhor the holy word” (Amos V, 10). Elsewhere: “They shall not be ashamed when they speak with their enemies in the gate” (Ps. CXXIX, 6). David too judged in the gates, when Absalom, promising to administer true judgment, was plotting against his father (II Sam. XIX).

It may be asked why among the Jews the place of judgment was at the gates. So that farmers would not be forced to enter the cities and suffer some expense, judges sat at the gates, so that they might hear both townspeople and country people as they entered and left the city; when the case was finished, each person could immediately return to his own dwelling.

“And,” he says, “do not devise evil against your friends in your hearts.” RAAH (), which everyone unanimously translated into Greek as κακίαν, that is, “wickedness,” can be understood in two ways: as affliction and as evil. In the sense of affliction: “Is there wickedness in a city that the Lord has not caused?” (Amos III, 6); and, “Sufficient for the day is its wickedness” (Matt. VI, 34). In the sense of evil, God says through the prophet Jonah: “The cry of their wickedness has risen to me” (Jonah I, 2). And in the Apostle we read: “Filled with all iniquity and wickedness” (Rom. I, 29).

Thus, in either sense, the holy person neither afflicts his friend nor devises evil against him in his heart.

“And do not love,” he says, “a false oath,” since the Lord commands in the Gospel: “But I say to you, do not swear at all; let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’” (Matt. V, 34). For one who does not swear can never commit perjury. Let the one who swears hear what is written: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. XX, 7).

“All these are things that I hate, says the Lord,” in accordance with the words of Malachi: “And you did all the things that I hated” (Mal. II, 13; according to the Septuagint). In commandments that pertain to life and are clear, we ought not to seek an allegory, lest, in the words of the comic poet, we look for a knot in a rush (*Plautus, Men.* II, 1).

(Vers. 18, 19.) And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid festivals. Only love truth and peace.

**The Septuagint:** And the word of the Lord Almighty came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and good festivals [Al. “solemnities”]—for this is expressed in Hebrew as TOBIM (), that is, ἀγαθὰς (“good”)—and rejoice, and love truth and peace. [Note: [Col. 1475D] The manuscript of Reginensis reads, “and you shall rejoice,” according to the Greek εὐφρανθήσεστε.]

In response to what Sarasar and Regommelech had asked through their messengers above—whether they ought to fast and mourn in the fifth month and the seventh month, as stated in the Septuagint, or whether, after the temple had been built, they should end the fast and lay aside mourning—the prophet answered in the person of the Lord, after setting forth many things in between that they should do and hope for: “The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth” (the word “month” is understood by common construction) shall be changed for the house of Judah and Jerusalem into feast days and joy. God seeks only truth and peace.

On this passage many of our people have said many things, and things that disagree with one another. Some, professing their ignorance by silence, have passed over it in their commentaries as though it were an exceedingly deep pit, judging it better to say nothing at all than very little. We are therefore compelled to return to the Hebrews and seek the truth of knowledge from the fountain rather than from the streams—especially since this is not some prophecy about Christ, where they usually evade the issue and conceal the truth with falsehood, but a historical sequence woven from what precedes and follows.

The fast of the fourth month, which among the Latins is called July, they think was established on the seventeenth day of that month [Note: It is observed on 17 Tammuz; the fast of the fifth month, discussed below, on the ninth day of Ab. Compare Philastrius, ch. 145, and Selden, *On the Civil Year of the Jews*, ch. 8.], when Moses, descending from Mount Sinai, threw down and broke the tablets of the Law (Exod. XXXII), and when, according to Jeremiah, the walls of the city were first breached (Jer. LII).

In the fifth month, which among the Latins is called August, when an uprising arose among the people because of the spies sent to explore the Holy Land, they were ordered not to ascend the mountain but to wander around the land for forty years, so that, with Caleb and Joshua excepted, all would fall in the wilderness (Num. XIV). In this month the temple at Jerusalem was burned and destroyed, both by Nebuchadnezzar (Jer. LII) and, many centuries later, by Titus and Vespasian; the city was captured [Note: [Col. 1475D] Up to now the printed and manuscript books alike have read *Bethel*, although that city was neither captured by Titus or Vespasian nor involved in the conquest of Jerusalem. It has therefore been restored by changing one letter to *Bether*, the city captured under Hadrian during the Jewish revolt led by Bar Kokhba. There is no doubt, if historical accuracy is considered, that Jerome wrote *Bether*, although he seems to confuse two wars—one under Hadrian and the other under Titus—into one, since more than sixty years elapsed between the conquest of Bether and the burning of Jerusalem.] and Bether, to which many thousands of Jews had fled, and the temple was plowed under, to the disgrace of the oppressed nation, by Turannius Rufus. [Note: [Col. 1476D] Another, no less serious error occurred in the previously published books, where *Titus Annius Rufus* was read instead of *Turannius Rufus*. We have not hesitated to restore the historical truth. His name was Turannius, not Titus Annius; he was the one who drove the plow over Jerusalem, and he is also mentioned by the most ancient Jewish authorities, such as *Sanhedrin*, chapter 7, and elsewhere: “Turannus Rufus plowed the temple.”]

In the seventh month, which among us is called October, as we said above, Gedaliah was killed, and the remnant of the tribe of Judah and of Jerusalem was scattered (IV Kings 25). Let us read Jeremiah (chapters XXXIX and XLI).

In the tenth month, which among us is called January because it is the gate and beginning of the year, Ezekiel, while in captivity, heard—and the entire captive people heard in the fifth month—that the temple had been overthrown. We learn this most fully in that same prophet.

This, then, is the entire meaning: You should know that the days of lamentation and fasting which you have hitherto observed in mourning are to be changed for you, because I have resolved to do good to Jerusalem and the house of Judah, into gladness, joy, and festivals—provided only that you love truth and peace.

According to the *anagoge*, we fast when the bridegroom is taken away from us (Luke V) and we are not worthy to have his presence. When the Lord returns to us and resolves to do good to us, all sadness will be turned into joy; and the former famine of the word of God will be balanced by the presence of his teachings and the abundance of heavenly bread.

(Vers. 21, 22.) Thus says the Lord of hosts: Until peoples come and dwell in many cities, and the inhabitants go one to another, saying, “Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord and seek the Lord of hosts.” “I too will go.” And many peoples and strong nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the face of the Lord.

**The Septuagint:** Thus says the Lord Almighty: Many peoples and the inhabitants of many cities shall still come; and those who dwell in the cities shall gather into one city, saying, “Let us go to entreat the face of the Lord and seek the face of the Lord Almighty.” “I too will go.” And many peoples and numerous nations shall come to seek the face of the Lord Almighty in Jerusalem and to entreat the face of the Lord.

The fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months will be changed into excellent festivals, to such an extent that the cities of Judaea, formerly deserted, will be filled with numerous inhabitants. One city will go to another, and they will encourage one another, saying:

“For these seventy years the roads of Zion have mourned, because no one went to the festival; all her gates were deserted, and her priests groaned. Now that peace has been restored, let us go to Jerusalem, where the Law commanded us to sacrifice victims and where every male among us is to appear before the Lord three times a year” (Exod. XXIII).

One city will say to another, “Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord and seek the Lord Almighty,” and the other city will answer, “I too will go.” At that time many peoples and innumerable and powerful nations will come to offer sacrifices to the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat his face.

“For the Lord is near to those who do not test him, and he shows his face to those who are not unbelieving” (Wis. I). “Whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father” (John XIV). The Lord and Savior is the image of the invisible God—not because the Son is visible and the Father invisible, but because, when the Son is named, the Father is understood. For the Father would not be the Father if he did not have a Son. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Father, I have manifested your name to the human beings” (John XVII, 6).

What we have said about Jerusalem and Zerubbabel, or about the time after Zerubbabel, is more correctly and fully referred to Christ and to Jerusalem, which is understood as the Church. Then peoples and nations from the whole world will hasten to offer sacrifices in the temple of the Lord.

During the time of persecution also, as we briefly indicated earlier, let the teachers and priests of the Church boldly promise captives and believers that the *paroikia* (παροικίᾳ, “sojourning community”) will again be built, tranquility will be restored, and the face of the Lord will be entreated in the churches.

We pass quickly over what is clear, so that we may dwell on what is more obscure.

(Vers. 23.) Thus says the Lord of hosts: In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations shall take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man, saying, “We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”

**The Septuagint:** Thus says the Lord Almighty: In those days, if ten men from all the languages of the nations take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man, saying, “We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”

Some Jews say that these things were fulfilled under Zerubbabel and after Zerubbabel. Others defer them to the future, when they expect Christ to come. We understand them more correctly and truly of the coming of the Lord and Savior, when he was born of the Virgin Mary.

For it is written, “Until peoples come” (Zech. VIII, 20). When “until” is said, it does not signify the present time, in which Zerubbabel and Joshua lived, but the future, when many peoples and strong nations will come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem and entreat the face of the Lord.

At that time and in those days ten men from all the languages of the nations will take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man, saying, “We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”

We also read in Isaiah: “Seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, ‘We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be called [Al. ‘invoked’] over us; take away our reproach’” (Isa. IV, 1).

Those women who are called seven there are the churches, whose number is also contained in the Apostle Paul: for he writes to seven churches—to the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Thessalonians. In the Apocalypse of John, too, in the midst of seven lampstands (Apoc. I), that is, churches—the Ephesians, Smyrnaeans, Pergamenes, Thyatirans, Sardians, Philadelphians, and Laodiceans—in their variety [Al. “truth”] and purest gold, the Lord enters girded.

Now in the prophet Zechariah ten are named. The Lord too sought ten, so that, if he had found them in Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, he might have rescued them from destruction.

The letter iota, from which the name of the Savior begins, signifies the number ten not only among the Greeks but also among the Hebrews. By this mystical expression it is shown that all who are counted under the Christian name—those whom the Lord says he left as seven thousand during the persecution of Jezebel and the flight of Elijah, who did not bend the knee before Baal (III Kings XIX)—and who have attained to the measure of a perfect man from all languages and nations, will take hold of the fringe of the Jewish man, that is, of the Lord and Savior. Of him it is said in the Psalms: “Judah is my king” (Ps. LIX, 9). And again: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” And again: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 8, 10). For “there shall be a root of Jesse; and he who rises to rule the nations—in him the nations shall hope” (Isa. XI, 10).

When they have taken hold of him, they will desire to cling to his footsteps, because God is with him.

Or certainly, all those from every language and nation who have believed will take hold of the Jewish man—the apostles, who are Jews—and say, “We will go with you, for through the prophets and through the voice of all the Scriptures we have learned that Christ, the Son of God, is God and Lord with you.”

Here the prophecy is most explicit, and it speaks of the coming of Christ and his apostles and of the faith of all the nations. We need seek nothing further.

As for our statement that the number seven thousand pertains to the Christian name, calculate in Greek ἑπτάκεις χιλίους and χριστειανοὺς, and you will find the same number and total, namely, one thousand nine hundred forty-one. [Note: [Col. 1477D] This passage greatly troubled Marianus Victorinus, as he himself admits in his annotations. When Erasmus had read ἑπτάκις χιλίους χριστιανοὺς (“seven times a thousand Christians”), Victorinus restored it as ἑπτάκεις χειλίους and χριστειανοὺς. I did not labor greatly over this restoration, because I found the true and genuine reading in our manuscript codices presented as follows: ΕΠΤΑΚΕΙϹ ΧΕΙΛΙΟΥϹ ΕΤ ΧΡΙϹΤΕΙΑΝΟΥϹ. This is precisely Victorinus’s restoration, apart from a few letters missing in the first and last words in Victorinus. The words Ἑπτάκεις χειλίους produce among the Greeks the number 1946, which is also produced by the word χριστειανοὺς, as it is written in the manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Cyran, in which all the Greek words are complete in their number of letters. In other copies I found χρειστιανοὺς, which likewise totals 1946. Victorinus therefore restored the passage incorrectly, wanting to calculate only 1941 instead of 1946. MART. — Victorinus and Martianus correctly observed that the same number must be rendered in Greek by the two words on one side, ἑπτάκεις χιλίους, which the word χριστιανοὺς renders on the other. They disagree only in this: Victorinus, so that the total on both sides would be 1946, reads ἑπτακεὶς and χριστειανοὺς; the other, calculating only 1941, writes ἑπτάκις and χριστιανοὺς. In reality, however, Jerome is not deliberately seeking either this or that number; rather, he is seeking conformity in the total of the Greek words. Victorinus’s reading should therefore be preferred, and our manuscripts also support it. Indeed, it was not necessary to write χειλίους, supposedly an Aeolic form, in place of χιλίους; still less satisfactory is χριστειανοὺς in place of χριστιανούς. For if the ε is removed from both words according to the rules of orthography, the same number, 1941, results—a number that two of our Latin manuscripts also prefer. This is the only point that the holy Father cleverly advances from the conformity of the number, to demonstrate that the seven thousand men who did not bend the knee before Baal signify Christians. Moreover, we are not unaware that in these games of numerical calculation people sometimes say even more, as in the teaching of Menasseh ben Israel: often a unit is added to the number formed by the letters of a word, and they call it [that is, “the whole”], because it stands for the entire word.]

They also refer to the mystery of this number the parable of the ten virgins in the Gospel (Matt. XXV), whom we interpret as the senses of flesh and spirit. If they prepare the oil of good works for their lamps and double the number five, they become holy, according to the Apostle, in body and spirit.

The ten cities too, which the person who has governed the senses of the body well will receive in the future after doubling the number, are related to this number’s sacramental meaning (Luke XVI).

## Chapter IX

### Verse 1

“The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Adrach, and Damascus is its resting-place; for the eye of man and of all the tribes of Israel belongs to the Lord.”

The Septuagint has: “The taking up of the word of the Lord in the land of Adrach [elsewhere Sedrach] and Damascus, its sacrifice, because the Lord regards men and all the tribes of Israel.”

All this vision—or “weight” and “burden” of the word of the Lord, as Aquila translated it—concerns the calling of the nations and the building of the Church. The order of the words is: “The taking up of the word of the Lord,” sharp toward sinners, gentle toward the righteous. For the name ADRACH () is composed of two complete words: AD, meaning “sharp,” and RACH, meaning “soft” and “tender.” It is not, as some incorrectly read it, Sedrach.

Some refer Adrach to the Jewish people and Damascus to the calling of the nations. Hence the people—or the taking up of the word of the Lord—comes upon the land of Adrach, over which the Lord exercised both his severity and his mercy (Isaiah 11:10, according to the Septuagint): severity toward those who refused to believe, mercy toward those who returned with the apostles.

Damascus, however, is called the Lord’s resting-place, in accordance with what is written in Isaiah: “And his resting-place shall be honor.” For before the child knew how to choose good or evil and to call his father and mother, “he received the strength of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria” (Isaiah 8:4). Hence Damascus is translated in our language as “drinking blood” or “the blood of sackcloth”: the first interpretation signifies a bloodstained people; the second, repentance joined to its cruelty.

What follows—“For the eye of man and of all the tribes of Israel belongs to the Lord”—they explain as follows: Therefore the temple of God must be built from both peoples, that is, from the land of Adrach and from Damascus, his resting-place, because whoever among the nations looks to God and hopes in him, as well as whoever is from all the tribes of Israel, belongs to the Lord. Or, according to the Septuagint: because the Lord regards all human beings equally, and all the tribes of Israel.

Let us also explain it another way. In the land of Adrach there is the burden and very heavy weight of the word of the Lord; but in Damascus there are his victims and sacrifice, because the Lord regards equally, without any acceptance of persons, both the faith of the nations and the faithlessness of Circumcision, and he is equally the God of all—placing upon some the heavy weight of his judgment, while resting in the habitation of others.

The Jews say that all these things will be fulfilled at the coming of Christ, which they expect at the end of time: that the land of Adrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, Azotus, and Philistia will bow their necks to the most powerful king and serve him as he dwells in Jerusalem; and that no one will dare raise a hand against Israel, when all the surrounding regions have been pacified. We, however, demonstrate that all these things have been accomplished spiritually at the coming of the Lord and in his Church.

### Verses 2 and following

“Hamath also shall be within its borders, and Tyre and Sidon; for they have acquired wisdom for themselves exceedingly. Tyre built its stronghold and heaped up silver like dust, and gold like the mud of the streets. Behold, the Lord shall possess her; he shall strike her power in the sea, and she herself shall be consumed by fire.”

The Septuagint has: “Hamath within its borders, Tyre and Sidon, because they were exceedingly wise; and Tyre built its stronghold and gathered silver like dust, and gold like the mud of the roads. Therefore the Lord shall possess her, and he shall strike her power in the sea, and she herself shall be burned up in fire.”

[Note: The name Hamath, which was missing although necessary to the context, has been supplied from the Queen’s manuscript.]

Hamath, which is interpreted as χόλος—that is, “indignation”—is the very city that received the name Epiphany from Antiochus Ἐπιφανής, Epiphanes; it is now a city of Coele-Syria.

This city, then, together with Tyre and Sidon, will be within the borders of Damascus—or within the borders of the land of Adrach—in order that they may believe in the Lord Savior, to whom the Father said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

The daughters of this Tyre—that is, the souls of those who believe in Christ—will bring gifts to the king, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts” (Psalm 44:13).

And when the city of God, the Church, has been built, of which the Psalmist sings, “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 86:2), the rest will immediately follow: “Behold, foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians—these were born there” (ibid., 86:4).

Of foreigners it is said in two psalms: “Foreigners shall serve me,” or “shall be subject to me.” Concerning the Ethiopians we read in the prophet Zephaniah: “From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia they shall bring offerings to me” (Zephaniah 3:10). And in the Psalm: “Ethiopia shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 67:32).

Concerning Tyre the Gospel says: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would perhaps long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11:21).

From the regions of Tyre and Sidon came that Canaanite Syrophoenician woman whose daughter was grievously afflicted by a demon; she met the Lord Savior (Mark 7). She consecrated the firstfruits of the faith of the Tyrians and Sidonians, so that those who had not believed in Christ’s time, because they had not yet seen signs and wonders, might afterward see them through the apostles and believe, and might share in that blessedness which the Lord promises when he says: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

Tyre and Sidon—of which one is interpreted as συνοχή, that is, “confinement” or “distress,” and the other as θήρευμα, that is, “a hunting-ground”—acquired such wisdom for themselves that, through their sophistries and the nets of dialecticians and the woven structures of sophists, which Scripture calls strongholds, Tyre proposed riddles to Solomon, the peaceful king, and gathered its silver—that is, the brilliance of eloquence—and its gold—that is, the cleverness of meanings—like dust and mud found in the streets and roads, so that it might possess the kingdom of idolatry that it had fortified.

[Note: Victor has “and the nets of dialectic and the σειρειτῶν [sic] weavings.”]

Against these strongholds the Apostle speaks: “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

And under the persona of Nineveh, which is interpreted as “adorned” or “beautiful”—for nothing is more adorned than the world—the word of God through the prophet is directed against the people of the world: “You also shall be drunk, and shall be despised, and shall seek help from the enemy. All your strongholds are like fig trees with their firstfruits; if they are shaken, they shall fall into the mouth of the eater.”

Thus the Lord will possess Tyre and Sidon when he has first struck their power in the most salt-laden and bitter sea of this age. And so that none of their former wisdom—that is, their swollen foolishness—may remain, by which they acquired weak strongholds and silver and gold resembling mud, he will refine them and cleanse them completely by fire. Of this the Savior speaks in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled!” (Luke 12:49), in accordance with what is written in Mark: “Everyone shall be salted with fire” (Mark 9:49).

### Verses 5 and following

“Ashkelon shall see and shall fear; Gaza also shall grieve exceedingly, and Ekron, because her hope has been put to shame. The king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited. A separator shall sit in Azotus, and I shall destroy the pride of the Philistines. I shall remove his blood from his mouth and his abominations from between his teeth; he too shall be left for our God, and shall be like a leader in Judah, and Ekron like a Jebusite. I shall encamp around my house with those who serve me, going and returning, and no oppressor shall pass over them again, because now I have seen with my own eyes.”

The Septuagint has: “Ashkelon shall see and shall fear; Gaza also shall grieve exceedingly, and Ekron, because she has been put to shame in her hope. The king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited. Foreigners shall dwell in Azotus, and I shall destroy the injury of the foreigners. I shall remove their blood from their mouths and their abominations from between their teeth; and these too shall remain for our God, and they shall be like a chiliarch, that is, a tribune, in Judah, and Ekron like a Jebusite. I shall establish an elevation in my house, so that no one may pass through or return, and no oppressor or one who drives them away shall ever again come upon them, because now I have seen with my own eyes.”

Ashkelon is interpreted as “ignoble fire,” or “weighed down” [elsewhere, “weights”]. Gaza means “strong” or “dominion.” Ekron means “barren” or “uprooted.” Azotus, called ESDOD () in Hebrew, means “fire producing,” or “the fire of an uncle,” or “the fire of a breast.” Jebusite means “trampled.”

We have expressed the etymologies of the names so that we may briefly trace the meaning.

When Ashkelon, Gaza, and Ekron saw that Hamath was within the borders of Damascus, and Tyre and Sidon, after being struck on every side and after all their hay, wood, and stubble had been consumed by fire, had been possessed by the Lord, they too, terrified by fear, grief, and shame, began to hope for better things.

Finally, Ashkelon, in which the devil had previously been present—ignoble fire—and which had reached the measure and weight of sins, trembled with fear because it had ceased to have inhabitants.

Gaza grieved exceedingly, repenting of its former crimes. It had once been strong, hard, and untamable, and had promised itself dominion over all; but its king and ruler—the contrary word and power of the enemy—had lost his authority.

Ekron too, being barren because it had no children apart from the Law and knowledge of God, was uprooted, so that it might hear the prophetic word: “Rejoice, barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1).

And when Ashkelon, Gaza, and Ekron had been terrified and grieved, whether because they no longer had inhabitants, or because they had lost their king, or because their former hope had failed them, foreigners would sit in Azotus, where fire gives birth—the fire which the Lord sent upon the earth and desired to burn (Luke 12).

For he himself baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3). There the relation of nephew and uncle is ἀδελφιδοῦς [elsewhere ἀδελφίδος] καὶ πατράδελφος, which the bride desires in the Song of Songs. There is also the fire of the breast and of the most abundant udder, concerning which we read in the same Song: “He shall lodge between my breasts” (Song of Songs 1:12). And the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

Where, according to the Septuagint, we said, “Foreigners shall dwell in Azotus,” the Hebrew reads: “MAMZER () shall dwell or sit in Azotus.” Instead of this we have rendered it, “A separator shall sit in Azotus.”

Understand the separator as the Lord, who separates the grain from the chaff (Matthew 3 and 13), and good fish from bad fish, and distinguishes silver and gold from dirt and dross.

When he has done this, he also makes the following promise: “I shall destroy the injury,” or “the pride,” “of the Philistines.” The Septuagint translated this as “foreigners.”

Philistines, in our language, are interpreted as “those falling from the cup”: they drank from Babylon’s cup and, becoming drunk, fell.

At the time, therefore, of the calling of the nations and the coming of Christ, they will no longer have pride, but will follow Jesus in humility and gentleness.

He will also remove blood from their mouths—that is, words of blasphemy—and abominations—the worship of idols and the eating of things sacrificed to idols—from between their teeth. Once these things have been removed, the Philistines, that is, the foreigners, will be left for the Lord, and he will be a leader in Judah, that is, among the people who confess the Lord. Thus the former people, which had been the head, will become the tail, and the later people, which had been the tail, will pass into the head.

Ekron, once barren and therefore uprooted, will be like Jebus, that is, like Jerusalem. For this city is called by three names: Jebus, Salem, and Jerusalem.

“And I shall encamp around my house,” he says—that is, around the Church—“with those who serve me”: those who serve me in various ministries and run here and there at my command, going and returning.

Or: “I shall encamp around my house with the protection of angels,” concerning whom it is written elsewhere: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33:8), so that there may be no one who goes and returns—that is, no one who plots against my people.

Nor shall an oppressor pass over them again. Of him Isaiah says: “The oppressor has ceased” (Isaiah 14:5). Or certainly, ἐξελαύνων, that is, “driving out,” carrying prisoners into captivity.

“For now I have seen with my own eyes”: with those eyes by which we may understand the prophets and all the saints, the Lord saw the calling of the nations and the security of the Church.

### Verses 9 and following

“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king shall come to you, righteous and saving; he is poor and riding upon a donkey, and upon a colt, the son of a she-ass. I shall destroy the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem; the bow of war shall be destroyed; he shall speak peace to the nations; and his dominion shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth.”

The Septuagint has: “Rejoice exceedingly, daughter of Zion; proclaim aloud, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king shall come to you, righteous and saving, himself gentle and riding upon a beast under the yoke and a new colt. He shall destroy the chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and he shall destroy the bows of the combatants and the multitude. He shall establish peace among the nations, and shall rule from the waters to the sea, and from the rivers to the outlets of the earth.”

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads, “He shall rule over the waters to the sea, and the rivers to the outlets of the earth,” in accordance with the Greek found in most copies: καὶ κατάρξει ὑδάτων ἕως θαλάσσης, καὶ ποταμῶν διεκβολὰς γῆς.]

The Evangelists write that this prophecy was fulfilled when the Lord entered Jerusalem, seated upon a donkey and a colt, and a crowd of children met him with palm branches, crying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest” (Matthew 21).

When the Pharisees rebuked him for not silencing the shouting children, he answered: “Have you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise’?” (Psalm 8:3).

Therefore Zion rejoices and Jerusalem shouts aloud—one and the same city, since Zion is the citadel of Jerusalem—because its king has come, the one promised in the prophecies of all the prophets: “Righteous, and himself the Savior,” that is, Jesus, as the angel interpreted the name when speaking to the Virgin: “He shall be called Jesus, because he himself will save his people from their sins” [elsewhere, “from their sin”] (Matthew 1:21).

He is also poor—or, as the Septuagint translated it, gentle—who, although he was rich, became poor for our sake; and he says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29).

He is “riding upon a donkey under the yoke,” or “upon a new colt,” signifying both peoples, that of Circumcision and that of the Foreskin. The former had borne the very heavy yoke of the Law, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Neither we nor our fathers were able to bear the heavy yoke of the Law” (Acts 15:10). Hence Paul also writes to the Galatians who wished to be circumcised: “Stand firm, and do not again submit to the yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1).

The new colt is the multitude of the nations, without the bridle of the Law and guided by no one, but always thrown down and broken in the precipices and chasms of idolatry. By the Lord’s sitting upon it, it learned to walk and to enter the straight way.

“And I shall destroy,” he says, “the chariot from Ephraim.” This is still spoken in the person of God the Father: let the chariot, or wagon, from Ephraim perish, and the horse from Jerusalem.

For the present, according to the literal meaning, this says that there will be no wars, since all things will have been pacified by Christ’s coming and birth.

According to the higher understanding, Ephraim refers to the multitude of heresies. Ephraim is interpreted as καρποφορία, that is, “fruitfulness” and “abundance of crops.” Concerning them it is written in the seventy-seventh Psalm: “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle.”

Of these chariots and wagons [elsewhere, “charioteers”] we read: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God. They are bound and have fallen, but we have risen and stand upright” (Psalm 19:8–9).

The horse that is destroyed from Jerusalem is the one of which we read: “A horse is deceptive for salvation” (Psalm 32:17). And in Jeremiah those who were devoted to luxury and lust hear: “They became to me like frenzied horses among females; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jeremiah 5:8).

Therefore they are recalled to repentance when the Psalmist says: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding” (Psalm 31:9).

When God has destroyed the chariot of Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, those who have been freed from such horses and chariots will be transferred into the Lord’s service, and they will become cherubim. Of them it will be said: “The chariot of God is multiplied ten thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice” (Psalm 67:18).

And: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song of Songs 1:8).

And: “Ride upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Habakkuk 3:8).

[Note: Victor refers this to the Greek text and the Latin edition: “You shall mount your horses,” and so forth.]

“The bow of war shall be destroyed,” so that fiery arrows may no longer be shot which could pierce the hearts of those devoted to pleasure.

“And he shall speak peace to the nations,” concerning whom it is written: “He himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10). And again: “The nations shall hope in him” (Isaiah 11).

“And his dominion shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71:8). This must not be weakened through allegory; rather, we must believe that it has truly been fulfilled, in accordance with what we read: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

Likewise, in the seventy-first Psalm, in the person of Solomon and of the true peaceful king, it is said: “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (verse 8).

### Verses 11 and 12

“And you also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent out your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water. Return to the stronghold, prisoners of hope; today also I declare that I shall repay you double.”

The Septuagint has: “And you, by the blood of the covenant, have sent out your prisoners from the pit which has no water. You shall sit in the stronghold, prisoners of the assembly; and for one day of your sojourning I shall repay you double.”

After the prophet’s discourse—or rather, after God the almighty Father himself—announced to Zion and Jerusalem that their king would come to them, gentle and riding upon a donkey under the yoke and a colt of a donkey, and that his power would extend from sea to sea and from the rivers to the ends of the earth, he turns directly to Christ himself, concerning whom the prophecy is made, and says:

“You also, by the blood of your covenant or pact, have sent out your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.”

This is understood as follows: by the blood of your passion, through your mercy you freed those who were held captive in the prison of hell, where there is no mercy.

Accordingly, after the Lord rose again, those who had been held by the sins of Adam—or, as some wish, by the ingrained error—and by the bonds of death rose with him and appeared in the holy city.

Concerning this blood of the covenant, and indicating his future passion, he himself spoke to the disciples: “Take and drink of this, all of you; for this is the cup of the new covenant in my blood” (Matthew 26:27–28).

As a foreshadowing of this, Joseph was sent by his brothers into a pit that had no water (Genesis 37); so too Daniel (Daniel 6) and Jeremiah, by the Chaldeans and by the Jewish people. Benaiah also, in a time of snow and cold, descended into a pit in order to kill a lion there (2 Samuel 23:20).

[Note: The words “into the pit” are absent from the Queen’s manuscript, which shortly afterward also reads “Eleanan” instead of “Benaiah.”]

Jeremiah, however, was not cast into the water of the pit but into the mud and mire of the pit, which could suffocate rather than refresh the thirsty (Jeremiah 37 and 38). Hence it is written in the Psalm: “I am sunk in deep mire, and there is no firm ground” (Psalm 68:3).

In this pit of hell once dwelt the rich man dressed in purple, whose boastful tongue was burned by the fires of punishment. He had no refreshment from any water, to such a degree that he asked for the tip of the poor man’s finger, dipped in water, to bring him relief (Luke 16).

Again, a word is addressed to those who were prisoners and were to be freed by Christ’s mercy: “Return to the stronghold, prisoners of hope.”

The sense is this: You who are now prisoners and are held in a harsh and terrifying hell, who hope for release from your bonds at Christ’s coming, return to the stronghold—or, “you shall sit in the stronghold”—of which it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the fortress of the holy”; so that you may learn to say: “Be to me a God who protects me and a fortified place, so that you may save me” (Psalm 70:3).

And the prophet may also speak of you: “Behold, a fortified city; our salvation shall establish a wall and a rampart” (Isaiah 26:1).

We must understand this stronghold to which God exhorts the prisoners of hope—or the prisoners who hope—as nothing other than the dwelling-place of paradise, into which the thief first entered with the Lord (Luke 23).

For this reason, through Zechariah they are summoned to the stronghold: because already then, and from that time onward, the Lord promised that, in place of brief tribulation, they would receive eternal rewards.

Or, as the Septuagint reads: “For one day of your sojourning I shall repay you double.”

Compared with eternity, everything we suffer in the world must be called one day—not a day of dwelling, but of sojourning—because we are strangers and pilgrims, as all our fathers were.

“For our present momentary and light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18). For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

### Verse 13

“For I have stretched Judah for myself like a bow; I have filled Ephraim, and I shall raise up your sons, Zion, against your sons, Greece, and I shall make you like the sword of warriors.”

The Septuagint has: “For I have stretched you, Judah, for myself like a bow; I have filled Ephraim, and I shall raise up your sons, Zion, against the sons of the Greeks, and I shall touch you like the sword of a warrior.”

The Jews refer this to the time of the Maccabees, who defeated the Macedonians and cleansed the temple, polluted by idolatry, after a period of three and a half years.

As for what follows—“I have filled Ephraim like a bow”—they think that those are signified who had come from the ten tribes called Israel under Hezekiah, among whom Josiah is also remembered to have reigned.

They interpret the preceding testimony differently from us and say: “O Christ, whom we hope [elsewhere, ‘hoped’] will come, and who will reign throughout all the regions of the earth: by the blood of your covenant, with which you found Jerusalem sprinkled in its own blood, according to Ezekiel (chapter 16), and with which you entered into a covenant with Abraham at the dividing of the calf, ram, and goat, you released your people Israel from captivity and from the furnace of the Chaldeans, in which there was no mercy (Genesis 15).

“Therefore you also, O Israelites, who were prisoners and hoped in the Lord, return to most strongly fortified Jerusalem; for today you have the Lord promising you that, in return for the brief injury of captivity, you will receive everything doubled, just as we read that Job received it” (chapter 42).

According to the tropological sense, this passage may be explained as follows.

Judah is stretched out in a bow when the Lord and Savior is sent by the Father into this world. He himself is the bow, the archer, and the arrow.

He is the bow, as in the present passage.

He is the archer, as in the forty-fourth Psalm: “Your arrows are sharp, exceedingly powerful” (Psalm 44:6), and when someone has been wounded by them he says: “I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs 2:5).

He is also the arrow, for he speaks through Isaiah: “He made me like a chosen arrow and hid me in his quiver” (Isaiah 49:2).

The chosen arrow is the word of God; the quiver in which the arrow is hidden is the dispensation of the flesh he assumed.

By this Ephraim is filled, so that when he has been armed and prepared for battle, he too may be wounded with the Lord’s arrows together with the nations. From Ephraim came Jeroboam, who first divided the people (1 Kings 12). That he is to be understood as representing the heretics is demonstrated more fully by the prophet Hosea (chapters 5 and 6), as is the statement made above: “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle” (Psalm 77:9).

When the Lord raises up the sons of Zion—that is, the sons of the Church—the teachers of contrary doctrines, every assertion of the philosophers, and the arguments of the nations will be destroyed, because the Lord himself is the sword of warriors. Of him it is said:

“Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one. In your appearance and your beauty, bend the bow, advance prosperously, and reign; because of truth and gentleness and righteousness, and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully” (Psalm 44:4 and following).

By this sword the Ethiopians are wounded, concerning whom it is written: “And you, Ethiopians, shall be wounded by my sword” (Zephaniah 2:12). After they have been wounded by Christ’s sword, they will lay aside their dark color and speak with joy: “The splendor of the Lord our God shall be upon us” (Psalm 89:17). David also promises this to himself after repentance: “You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 50:9).

This is the sword of which the Apostle writes: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit.”

### Verse 14

“And the Lord God shall appear over them, and his arrow shall go forth like lightning; and the Lord God shall sound the trumpet, and shall go in the whirlwind of the South. The Lord of hosts shall protect them.”

The Septuagint has: “And the Lord God shall appear over them; and his arrow shall go out like lightning. And the Lord God Almighty shall sound the trumpet, and shall go in the movement of his terror. The Lord Almighty shall protect them.”

[Note: In the Greek, “God” is absent; in the Queen’s manuscript, “Almighty” is absent.]

The Jews refer this passage to the time of the Maccabees. When they fought against Antiochus and conquered him, they say, the battle and victory belonged to the Lord, who went forth as a strong man to battle; his power appeared like lightning, and after the adversaries were defeated and scattered by death like a whirlwind, he protected the Jewish people.

We, however, refer everything to the understanding of the Savior, concerning whom it was said above: “I have stretched Judah for myself like a bow.”

When this bow has been stretched, and the heretics and the nations have been slain by the sons of Zion, the glory of the Lord will appear, and his arrow will go forth like lightning. Concerning this lightning we also read in Habakkuk: “They shall go in the light of your arrows, in the brightness of your flashing spear” (Habakkuk 3:11).

This lightning and brightness are also called, by another name, a trumpet and a blast, so that when the holy cry [elsewhere, “blast”] has sounded, the one who previously had deaf ears may say: “The discipline of the Lord has opened my ears and given me an ear for hearing.”
