As for what follows—“And he shall go in the whirlwind of the South,” or “he shall go in the movement of his threat”—he threatens and says that he will inflict punishments in order to have mercy on those who repent.

Accordingly, he joins the words: “The Lord Almighty shall protect them,” those whom he had previously terrified by his threat.

Let us read the history of the Ninevites.

### Verses 15 and 16

“And they shall devour and shall subject them with the stones of the sling; and drinking, they shall become drunk as with wine [the Vulgate: ‘from wine’], and they shall be filled like bowls and like the horns of an altar. And the Lord their God shall save them on that day as the flock of his people, because holy stones shall be lifted up over his land.”

The Septuagint has: “And they shall consume them, and shall bury them beneath sling-stones, and they shall drink their blood like wine, and they shall fill the altar like bowls, and the Lord shall save them on that day like sheep, his people, because holy stones shall roll over his land.”

Where we said “they shall be lifted up,” the Hebrew has METHNOSASOTH (), which may be interpreted as “wandering” or “fleeing.”

When the sons of Zion have been protected, and the Lord has sounded the trumpet and gone in a whirlwind against their adversaries, the ruin of the Greeks will be so great that they will be crushed not by swords, but by the throwing of stones and the rolling of sling-stones, so that they become prey and food for their enemies.

Then, “drinking, they shall become drunk as with wine.” It is not those who have been slain who will be drunk on their own blood; rather, those who have conquered will fight like drunk men in desperation, and they will please the Lord like the horns of an altar and its libation. This is understood in the bowls in which libations are poured upon the altar.

The Lord will also save them like sheep and the flock of his people. For they will not fight against the Macedonians as an armed army trained in the art of warfare; rather, they will come like a flock prepared for death and, with the Lord’s help, they will conquer.

And the holy stones that were oppressed—for he calls them stones because of the hardness of their tribulations and the strength of their spirit—will be lifted from their lowliness and will be glorious in his land.

Alternatively: His holy stones, belonging to the priestly order and fleeing in different directions, will obtain victory because he grants it.

Let us also speak according to the anagogical sense—or rather, let us explain a prophecy wrapped in many obscurities.

The sons of Zion, protected by their Lord, will devour their adversaries, whom we understand as the sons of Greece.

“And they shall subject them with the stones of the sling”: they will subject and humble their adversaries by the threats of Scripture. Nothing strikes so powerfully as an example drawn from the Holy Scriptures and a testimony sent forth by the turning of the mouth.

Where the Septuagint says, “They shall drink their blood like wine,” we do not read this in the Hebrew. Rather, it says, “Drinking, they shall become drunk as with wine,” so that they may hear the words of the Song of Songs: “Drink, friends, and become drunk” (Song of Songs 5:1).

Thus their drunkenness will please like a sacrifice of the altar, and like the horns—or the corners—of the altar.

The Lord will also save them like a flock, the people of his sheep, because the holy stones will roll over his land. They will be so light and will rise so high that they will not wait for the hands of the builders; rather, they will hasten to be placed upon Christ’s foundation and to be held together by the cornerstone.

Concerning them the Apostle Peter also speaks: “Like living stones, be built up into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God” (1 Peter 2:5).

These are the stones that will cry out if the Jewish people are silent (Luke 19). And they will roll upon the earth as long as they are in the body, because “an earthly dwelling burdens the mind that is occupied with many things” (Wisdom 9:15). And the Holy One, while situated in the flesh, says: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” (Psalm 54:7). As far as he is able, he strives, rolls, and rises toward the heights, but he is held back by the frailty of the flesh.

That land over which the stones roll is the land of which we read: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Psalm 95:1). And: “Let all the earth worship you and sing praise to you” (Psalm 65:4).

(Vers. 17.) For what is its goodness, and what is its beauty, except the grain of the chosen and the wine that makes virgins flourish? LXX: For if anything of it is excellent, and if anything good comes from it, it is grain for the young and wine of good fragrance for virgins.

Therefore, they say, the Maccabees, fleeing here and there, will prevail with the Lord’s help, so that, once the Macedonians have been expelled from the land of Israel, the temple may be cleansed, the precepts of the Law observed, and the instruction of the Scriptures may again make virgins flourish—that is, peoples believing in one God, who had previously been defiled by the practices of idolatry. By “the grain of the chosen,” that is, *BAURIM* (), they wish chosen and learned men to be understood, not young men, as the Septuagint translated it—men who deserve to eat grain, that is, the Law of God. For “wine,” which in Hebrew is called *THIROS* (), Aquila rendered it οἰνίαν (*oinian*); this too can be referred to the abundance of the vintage.

This is what the Jews think. For the rest, we understand “the grain of the chosen,” or “of the young,” and “the wine that makes virgins flourish,” or “the wine of good fragrance for virgins,” as the Lord the Savior, who says in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it produces greater fruits” (John XII, 24). From this wheat is made that bread which descended from heaven and “strengthens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII). Those who are strong in Christ eat this bread, and to them John the Evangelist says: “I write to you, young men, because the word of God remains in you [Al. us], and you are strong, and you have overcome the evil one” (I John II, 14).

He who is the grain of the chosen, or of the young, is himself also the wine that gladdens the heart of man, and it is drunk by those virgins who are holy both in body and in spirit, so that, made drunk and rejoicing, they may follow the Church, and it may be said of them: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her neighbors shall be brought to you; they shall be brought in gladness and exultation” (Ps. XLIV, 15–16). For how could those who, made drunk by the Savior’s cup, are born into virginity, fail to possess joy, and dare to say: “Bring me into the wine-cellar; strengthen me with perfumes” (Song II, 4)? This wine is of good fragrance, and therefore the same song says: “You will give me to drink of the wine of the perfumer, from the streams of your pomegranates [Al. pomegranates]” (ibid.). Those who follow the Lamb of God wherever he goes have been made drunk with this wine, clothed in white garments, because they have not defiled themselves with women: for they remained virgins (Rev. XIV).

## Chapter X

### Verses 1 and following

“Ask rain from the Lord in the season of the latter rain, and the Lord will make snow, and will give them rain, showers, to each one grass in the field. For the idols have spoken uselessly, and the diviners have seen a lie, and the dreamers have spoken in vain; they will console in vain. Therefore they have been led away [Al. brought] like a flock; they will be afflicted, because they have no shepherd.”

LXX: “Ask from the Lord suitable rain, early and latter rain. The Lord made phantasies, and will give them winter rain, to each one grass in the field; because those who spoke have spoken labors, and the diviners, false visions, and false dreams; they spoke, they consoled in vain. Therefore they have been dried up like sheep, and they have been afflicted, because there was no one to heal.”

Thus the prosperity promised for the time of the Maccabees—when the holy stones were raised above the earth, and the affairs of Israel increased so greatly that the peoples again fed upon the grain of the Law and your virgins were made drunk with the wine of the Holy Spirit—is promised in part. But because this is already the final age of the prophets, the world is declining toward its end, and all the things foretold await their appointed conclusion, “ask the Lord to give you the latter rain,” so that Christ who was promised may come and grant you dew and snow, for which the Hebrew has *AZIZIM* ().

I do not know why the LXX translated this as “phantasies,” unless perhaps they wished, under the name *phantasia*, to describe the greatness of grace and the wonder of the gifts. The Lord, therefore, who will make snow and dry up the whole earth, will irrigate it with the rains of evangelical preaching. He himself will give showers to believers, and everything will be filled with abundance, so that, after the nations have believed in Christ, they may understand that the things they formerly worshiped were vain.

Or let Israel itself understand—Israel, which was once held captive by the errors of idolatry—as recognizing that it worshiped idols in vain, listened to the lies of diviners, and yielded to dreams, which Scripture commands us not to believe (Deut. XIII). For this reason they were led away like a flock into captivity and afflicted without God as their shepherd, because they did not possess knowledge of the Law.

This entire passage is obscure and doubtful, and the reader ought to forgive us if, in matters that are ambiguous, we proceed with hesitant steps. According to the spiritual understanding, however, we can say that the Lord exhorts those who believe in Christ to ask for the latter rain at the consummation of the world, when the fullness of grace is to be granted and grass will grow for each person in his own field, so that they can say: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing. He has placed me in a place of pasture; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. XXII, 1–2).

For all idols, diviners, and dreamers spoke in vain and offered consolation vainly. He is speaking of heretics, who, under the Christian name, do not understand either what they say or what they affirm, but attend to deceitful spirits and teachers of demons who speak lies in hypocrisy and have a conscience branded as with a hot iron (I Tim. IV). Thus believers may not be led away by the consolations of those who make empty promises; and for this reason they have been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (I Cor. V), led away into the captivity of the king of Babylon, and afflicted because they do not possess Christ as their shepherd, although they falsely promise him to themselves under that name.

### Verses 3 and following

“Against the shepherds my wrath has been kindled, and against the he-goats I will visit. For the Lord of hosts has visited his flock, the house of Judah, and has made them like the horse of his glory in battle. From him comes the corner, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle; from him every exactor shall go forth together. And they shall be like mighty men trampling the mud of the roads in battle, and they shall fight, because the Lord is with them.”

LXX: “Against the shepherds my wrath has been stirred, and against the lambs I will visit. And the Lord God Almighty will visit his flock, the house of Judah, and will make them like his splendid horse in battle. From him he looked, and from him he established, and from him the bow in wrath [Note: In the Regin. manuscript: ‘who goes forth’; in the Greek there is ἐξελαύνων, or ἐλαύνων, and ἐξερευνῶν.]. Every one who leads forth together shall go out, and they shall be like warriors trampling the mud of the roads in battle, and they shall be prepared, because the Lord is with them.”

There is a twofold Jewish interpretation of this passage. Some think that everything is to be fulfilled at the coming of Christ; others that it has already been fulfilled under the Maccabees. Their explanation of what the Lord promises is as follows: The Lord was angry against the shepherds, rulers, and priests, and visited the he-goats and the people, according to what is written: “My people became a lost flock; their shepherds drove them away” (Jer. L, 6), so that the disciples might be punished for the fault of their teachers—not through the injustice of the judge, who repays the sins of the fathers upon the children, but because, while the teachers were sinning, the people applauded along with them.

At that time the Lord visited his he-goats, or his fattest lambs, and, according to the Septuagint, caused them to dry up through drought. Afterwards the almighty Lord visited his flock, the house of Judah: for he raised up Judas Maccabaeus and the others descended from him against the commanders of Antiochus, and made them like his horse of glory in battle—that is, those who were born from his stock. For a long time they oppressed the Macedonians.

What follows—“From him comes the corner, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle, from him every exactor shall go forth together”—they understand metaphorically, interpreting “corner” as royal power, because it holds the walls together [Al. “held them together”]. “And from him,” he says, “comes the peg,” that is, the priesthood. Read Isaiah, in which Eliakim is fixed in the temple of God like a peg (Isa. XXII). “From him comes the bow of battle”: strong men for fighting. “From him also every exactor together,” which in Hebrew is written *NOGES* (), and Aquila translated as εἰσπράσσων (*eispraxōn*), so that not only strong and good men, but also others unworthy of their lineage, came from them.

Judas Maccabaeus and all those of his lineage who were rulers among the people were both the corner, because they held the people together by royal power, and the peg, because they themselves were priests, and the bow of battle, because they proved to be exceedingly brave men—not merely arranging the army and battle line, but leaping first into combat.

Concerning what follows—“From him every exactor shall go forth together,” for which the LXX translated, “From him shall go forth every one who leads forth together”—we can also say this: No position of authority in the army will exist that is not arranged according to his judgment.

“And they shall be” men of the greatest courage, trampling the Macedonians like the mud of the roads in battle. They shall be exceedingly strong and shall fight, because the Lord is with them.

Our people refer these words to times of persecution: because of the fault of the priests, the people too are often handed over to adversaries. Yet afterwards the almighty Lord visits his flock, the house of Judah—those who confess God both in word and in heart—and makes them like the horse of his glory in battle. Concerning this horse the saints say: “Mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Hab. III, 8).

He will also be the bow of the Lord’s wrath, concerning which he says: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood” (Deut. XXXII, 42). And again: “My arrows shall consume them.” Concerning this bow and these arrows we read in the seventh Psalm (verses 13–14): “He bent his bow and prepared it; and in it he prepared the instruments of death; he made his arrows for those who burn.”

And they will trample their adversaries, he says, crowned in martyrdom, and will say: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble? When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh—those who trouble me, my enemies—they themselves have grown weak and have fallen. If armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear; if battle rises against me, in this I shall hope” (Ps. XXVI, 1 and following).

Then will be fulfilled that saying: “One of you shall pursue a thousand, and two shall put many thousands to flight” (Deut. XXXII) [Note: The same manuscript has “ten thousand.”]

### Verses 6–7

“They shall be put to shame, the riders of horses, and I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph. And I will turn them back, because I will have mercy on them; and they shall be as they were when I had not cast them away. For I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them. And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim; their heart shall rejoice as though from wine, and their children shall see and rejoice, and their heart shall exult in the Lord.”

LXX: “The riders of horses shall be put to shame. And I will strengthen the house of Judah and save the house of Joseph, and I will make them dwell, because I loved them. And they shall be as when I had not cast them away, because I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them. And they shall be like the warriors of Ephraim; their heart shall rejoice as though in wine, and their children shall see and rejoice, and their heart shall rejoice [Note: The Regin. manuscript adds, ‘and shall exult’] in the Lord.”

They explain these words in two ways according to the preceding interpretation, saying either that they were already accomplished under the Maccabees or that they are to be accomplished under Christ at the end of the age. The sense is this: When Judas has been made like a splendid horse in battle, has trampled his adversaries like mud, and has conquered while the Lord fought with him, then all the cavalry of Greece will fall, and the house of Judah and the house of Israel—for he calls the latter the house of Joseph, that is, the ten tribes—will be saved together. He will turn them back from the captivity in which they had been, and they will be as they were at the time when he had not cast them away. For he is the Lord their God, and he will hear them when they pray.

And Ephraim, who are now held captive, will later be released, and will attain such joy that you might think them drunk with wine. Their children too will see the triumphs of their fathers and will rejoice in the Lord, through whose aid they obtained victory.

Let us seek in history when Judas and Israel fought together against the Greeks, or at what time Ephraim returned from Assyrian captivity, when, according to Ezekiel (chapter XXXVII), the two rods—that is, Judah and Ephraim—were joined to one another and united into a single staff.

According to the tropological interpretation, this can be explained as follows. When the almighty Lord visits his flock, the house of Judah, then the riders of horses will be put to shame, concerning whom it is written: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. XV, 1). Concerning them the Psalmist also sings: “At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell asleep” (Ps. LXXV, 7).

And the chorus of the saints repeats: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of our God; they were bound and fell, but we have risen and stood upright” (Ps. XIX, 8–9).

The king of Egypt trusted in this cavalry; but, hurled into the sea, he was submerged like lead in the depths (Exod. XV), and by his example learned that what is written is true: “The horse is deceptive for salvation” (Ps. XXXII, 17). Above, in the four disturbances, we interpreted these chariots and four-horse teams: unless they are guided by a good charioteer with reins, they are carried headlong into ruin.

There is another charioteer, however, concerning whom Elisha speaks: “Father, father, chariot of Israel and its charioteer” (IV Kings II, 12).

Then God says that he will strengthen the house of Judah and the house of Joseph (III Kings XII, 16), so that those who were divided under the reign of Jeroboam may be joined together under Christ’s rule, and there may be one shepherd and one flock.

Judah and Joseph, although called by different names, are both referred to the one understanding of the Savior. Joseph gave grain to the peoples suffering hunger in Egypt (Gen. XLII and following), while the Lord satisfied the hunger of the world by his presence.

“And he will turn them back and have mercy on them,” and thus they will be one, as they were before he cast them away. Understand all these things in persecutions, when, after all hope had been abandoned, the Lord heard his servants.

“And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim.” At first they were weak and feeble; later they became strong and worthy of their name, for Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitfulness.”

“And their heart shall rejoice,” when they drink the wine pressed from the vine of Sorek. Their children are those to whom the apostle Paul says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19). And Peter, chief of the apostles, says: “As children of obedience, not conformed to your former way of life” (I Pet. I, 14). And in the Psalm we read: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII, 12).

These children, therefore, will exult and rejoice, and their heart will be glad in the Lord.

### Verses 8 and following

“I will whistle for them and gather them, because I have redeemed them, and I will multiply them as they had previously been multiplied. And I will sow them among the peoples, and from far away they will remember me, and they will live with their children, and they will return. And I will bring them back from the land of Egypt; I will gather them from Assyria, and I will bring them to the land of Gilead and Lebanon, and no place will be found for them.”

LXX: “I will signal to them and receive them, because I will redeem them, and they will be multiplied as they were formerly numerous. And I will sow them among the peoples, and those who were far away will remember me. They will nourish their children and turn back; and I will turn them back from the land of Egypt, and from Assyria I will receive them, and I will bring them into Gilead and Lebanon, and none of them will be missing.”

As we said previously, whether under the Macedonians or at the consummation of the world, they will have my signal as the sign of their gathering. “I will gather them,” he says, “by my whistle, so that I may show myself to be their shepherd.” For I redeemed them and delivered them from captivity with an outstretched arm. And I will multiply them, whom I had formerly multiplied, so that their dispersion among the peoples may not seem to be division, but the work of sowing. They will live with their sons, increased by a harvest of children and grandchildren.

And they will return not only from the land of Egypt but also from Assyria, and from both regions of the world they will return to Judaea, and to the land of Gilead and Lebanon, which the ten tribes formerly possessed—those called the house of Joseph and Ephraim. The number of those brought back will be so great that the land will not contain the multitude.

According to the higher interpretation (*anagōgē*), the Lord signifies and whistles for those who had previously been captives to sins, and says to them: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and you will find rest for your souls. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 29–30) [Note: Victorius restores, from Matthew’s text itself, “and I will refresh you” in place of “and you will find rest for your souls”; he adds these words before “and humble in heart,” etc.].

What could be more merciful than this signal and whistle, by which the scattered people are gathered? They are gathered because the Lord redeemed them—not with perishable silver and gold from their empty way of life, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb, the Lord Jesus (I Pet. I).

Therefore he says in the Psalm: “You are my exultation; rescue me from those who surround me” (Ps. XXXI, 7). And again: “You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth” (Ps. XXX, 6).

“And he will multiply them as they had formerly been multiplied,” so that what was promised to Abraham might be fulfilled: “I will multiply him and bless him, and he shall be blessed, so that he may become the father of many nations” (Gen. XVII, 9).

We must not understand Abraham’s children as those to whom the Lord says: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of your father” (John VIII, 39), but as those of whom the Apostle says: “All who are of faith are sons of Abraham” (Rom. VIII).

Isaiah bears mystical witness to this multiplication, saying: “The one who is small shall become thousands, and the one who is little shall become a great nation” (Isa. LX, 22).

We must not understand the multiplication and blessing of children carnally. Otherwise Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist—than whom no one among those born of women was greater (Matt. XI)—would have lacked this blessing. Rather, we must understand the multiplication by which multitudes of nations are called to faith.

Finally, the text continues: “I will sow them among the peoples, and from far away they will remember me.” They were sown among the peoples when they heard the Lord’s command: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). And elsewhere: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain forever” (John XV, 16).

When the apostles had been sown among the peoples, nations and peoples living far away would remember me, in accordance with the prophetic statement that fits this sentence: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Ps. XXI, 28–29).

What is said—“From far away they will remember me”—is similar to: “You who are far away, remember the Lord, and let Jerusalem rise into your heart” (Jer. XXXI). The whole multitude of the nations was far away, but it remembered God, because we are all descended from one parent.

And when, after the apostles had been sown among all the nations, the nations living far away remembered God, “they will live with their children,” so that those who had previously been dead through unbelief might begin to live by faith.

These are the children whom Paul nourished in the Gospel, writing to the Corinthians: “I gave you milk to drink” (I Cor. III, 2). And Peter writes in the Dispersion to believers who had been reborn: “Not from perishable seed but from imperishable, through the word of the living and abiding God, like newborn infants, so that you may desire rational milk and grow by it toward salvation” (I Pet. I).

To these children the evangelist John also wrote: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (I John V, 21).

“And I will bring them back,” he says, “from the land of Egypt, and from Assyria I will gather them.” From the land of Egypt, where King Pharaoh ruled, who once boastfully said: “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezek. XXIX, 3); and from the land of Assur, which was held by the Assyrian king, the great intellect, who also said: “I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13).

When the Lord has gathered the nations from the darkness of Egypt, from the tribulation of the world, and from the power of Assyria—which is interpreted as “rebuking and convicting,” for it is the enemy and avenger—he will bring them into the land of Gilead and Lebanon.

Gilead is translated in our language as “testimony of transmigration,” when we pass from carnal things to spiritual things, from a part to the whole; we leave earthly things and migrate to heavenly things. Lebanon, however, is interpreted as λευκασμός (*leukasmós*), that is, “whitening” or “making white.”

We are therefore brought out of the darkness of Egypt so that, after we have crossed over and migrated from the world, we may be made white in the Lord, and it may be said of us: “Who is this who ascends made white?” (Song VIII, 6).

Others, because of the ambiguity of the Greek expression—by which both the mountain of Phoenicia and frankincense are called Lebanon—now interpret Lebanon as frankincense, and think that God is signified by the frankincense. Thus, after we have passed from earth to heaven, the Savior’s prayer may be fulfilled in us: “Father, grant that they may be one in us, as you and I are one” (John XVII, 22).

Therefore the bride also says to the bridegroom in the Song: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon” (Song IV, 11).

And when he has brought us into the land of Gilead and Lebanon, no place will be found for us, so that we will no longer be confined by the narrowness of the earth but will enjoy the breadth [Al. height] of the heavens.

### Verses 11–12

“He will pass through the strait of the sea, and he will strike the waves in the sea; and all the depths of the river will be confounded. The pride of Assur will be humbled, and the scepter of Egypt will depart. I will strengthen them in the Lord, and they will walk in his name, says the Lord.”

LXX: “They will pass through the narrow sea, and they will strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the rivers will be dried up. All the injury of the Assyrians will be removed, and the scepter of Egypt will be taken away. I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, and they will glory in his name, says the Lord.”

The Hebrews relate that the captive people of the Jews were transferred not only into Media and Persia but also to the Bosporus and the northern region by the Assyrians and Chaldaeans. Afterwards some of them were brought back when the mercy of God turned toward them [Note: The Regin. manuscript reads: “when the mercy of God turned toward them.”]. This, they say, is what is now meant: “They will pass through the narrow sea”—the straits of the Propontis, which divide Chalcedon and formerly Byzantium by a narrow channel.

“And he will strike,” he says, “the waves of the sea,” the Lord going before his people, “and all the depths of the rivers will be confounded,” as once happened when the Jordan was dried up (Josh. III), and the people crossed the Red Sea in the wilderness (Exod. XXIV).

When they have been delivered from the depths of captivity and from the bitterness of evils, Assur will be humbled, and the rule of Egypt will withdraw from them. They will be strengthened in the Lord and will walk in his name in the land of Israel, says the Lord.

We have expressed these things in our language as they were handed down to us by the Hebrews, assigning the truth of the statements to those by whom they were spoken.

For the rest, we who are counted by the name of Christ leave behind the letter that kills and follow the life-giving spirit; indeed, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we seek not the Bosporus, nor the drying up of the sea again, nor the parched streams of the Jordan, which resemble fables, but the mercy of God worthy of his servants. With him going before us and opening the way, we cross the strait of the sea—or the narrow sea—which is very broad to sinners. “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to death; narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII, 13).

Concerning this sea we also read in the Psalms: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters, have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. CVI, 22).

The apostles descended into this sea of the world, in which the number of the saints is confined and held in tribulation; and the Lord descended first, so that he might free us from the bitter waves (Mark IV).

Into this sea the Gospel net is cast (Matt. XIII). It is woven from the testimonies of the Scriptures, so that it may draw many fish, buried in the whirlpools of this world, into the free air, enabling them to sing praises to God.

These are those who descended into the sea and perform many works in the ships of the churches, and behold the wonders of God in the depth of the riches of his wisdom and knowledge (I Cor. II), and in the Holy Spirit, who searches even the depths of God. To them the Lord says: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. IV, 19).

Concerning these fishermen who descend into the sea and are in ships, Isaiah also prophesies: “They shall fly in the ships of foreigners, and together they shall plunder the sea” (Isa. XI, 14).

For in the churches gathered from the number of the nations, the apostles flew throughout the whole world in order to plunder the sea and carry off the spoils of the dragon who ruled in the sea. Concerning him it is written: “This sea is great and spacious, with creatures too many to count; there are small animals with great ones; there the ships will pass. This dragon you formed to mock him” (Ps. CIII, 25–26).

The sea is broad and spacious for small and great creatures that move about with the dragon and whose number cannot be counted. But those who are upon the sea and fly over the sea in ships will hear the Savior say: “You rule the power of the sea; you calm the movement of its waves” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 10).

When they have crossed through the strait of the sea and trampled its waves beneath their feet, all the depths of the river will be confounded, concerning which it is written: “He turned the sea into dry land; they crossed the river on foot” (Ps. LXV, 6). Thus the injury, or pride, of Assur may be humbled, and the rule of Egypt may depart from the saints and believers. Those who have been delivered will be strengthened in the Lord and say: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Ps. CXVII, 14). And again: “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. XVII, 1). And with Jeremiah: “My strength, my help, and my refuge, Lord my God” (Jer. XVI, 19).

Therefore the Apostle, in whom Christ was speaking, said: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Phil. IV, 13).

And they will not only be strengthened in the Lord, but will also glory in him and say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14). And: “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31). And elsewhere: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: to understand and know the Lord, and to practice mercy and judgment in the midst of the earth” (Jer. IX, 23–24).

But because the Hebrew reads, “And they will walk in his name,” it should be understood in this way: Christians will walk in the name of Christ, and a new name will be written on their stones, and under the dignity of so great a name they will walk with the Lord, as Enoch walked, pleased God, and was translated (Gen. V).

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1497]

### 881–882

Brother Sisinius compels me to send out things untrimmed and unpolished, so that I have no opportunity—not to speak of correcting them, but even of rereading them. He hastens toward his own task, while we accomplish less in ours, since our learning turns out to be in vain; and whatever we conceive in our minds, we are not permitted to adorn with composed speech.

Receive, then, these books in their rough state—not through my fault, but because of the eagerness of the carrier—while he himself hastens to distribute your bronze coins to the saints and does not permit us to count out our own coins for you.

For although his talent is elegant and practiced, and his speech runs smoothly, worn by long use, unless it has been cared for and polished by the Author’s hand, it smells of the dirt of negligence; it either luxuriates in an excessive flowering of words, becomes gaping through its vowels, or grows harsh through its consonants.

Therefore it has also been handed down concerning Virgil that he composed his books with his tongue like a bear’s cubs, and by licking them made them better—books that would endure in everlasting memory and fulfill the demands of meter through unfettered prose.

We pass on to Lebanon, and to the two staffs and the three shepherds who were cut down in one month, and to the thirty pieces of silver for which the potter’s field was purchased as a burial place for foreigners (Matt. XXVII), and to the foolish shepherd’s vessels, and the remaining matters to the end of the volume. These things are woven together with such great mysteries that we need both the mercy of God and your prayers, lest our course be hindered by some error and those who are ill-disposed have a legitimate opportunity for slander—those who think they possess tongues for this one purpose: to tear their neighbors apart and console the hardness of their worn-out foreheads with a frenzy of words.

## Chapter XI

### Verse 1

“Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars. Howl, cypress, for the cedar has fallen, because the magnificent have been devastated. Howl, oaks of Bashan, because the fortified forest has been cut down.”

LXX: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars. Let the pine howl, because the cedar has fallen, because the nobles have been crushed. Howl, oaks of Basanitis, because the wooded forest has been laid low.”

Clearly Lebanon, to which the prophetic word is addressed when it says, “Open your gates, Lebanon,” signifies the temple of the Jews. It was restored—or rather built—by Zerubbabel, and is sung as destined to be overturned again by Vespasian and Titus.

And because he had metaphorically called the temple “Lebanon,” he preserves the metaphor in what follows, signifying through the cedars, cypresses, oaks of Bashan, and wooded forest the rulers, priests, and people of the Jews.

Lebanon opens its gates so that the Roman army may enter, and fire consumes its cedars, so that either everything may be devastated by burning or its leaders and rulers may be destroyed by the enemy’s assault.

The cypresses howl because the cedar has fallen, as priests and rulers mourn their mutual desolation. What he first stated obscurely he now sets forth more plainly: “because the magnificent have been devastated.”

I wish to know what the cedars of Lebanon are that have been burned; what the cypresses are for which the howl is commanded; what the pine is that has fallen. “The magnificent,” he says, “have been devastated.”

“Howl, oaks of Bashan,” that is, of confusion and disgrace, “because the most strongly fortified forest”—which in Hebrew is called *BESOR* and was translated by the LXX as “wooded”—has been cut down [Note: The printed editions read *Batsir*, from which we infer a variant reading in the Hebrew. Jerome therefore read as we do today in the Masoretic exemplar, namely *Batsor*, not *Batsir*, according to the corrections of the same [manuscripts], *Qere* and *Ketiv*. MART.].

The temple, which had grown in an impregnable strength and had been constructed by various kings and rulers, and later by Herod, was destroyed when the Romans attacked it.

Some who do not understand this passage refer Lebanon, the cypresses, pines, oaks of Bashan, and the wooded or fortified forest to hostile powers. Concerning such powers, they think that Ezekiel speaks under the name of Assur and Pharaoh: “Behold, Assur was a cypress in Lebanon, beautiful in branches, dense in shade, lofty in height, and its top was made to reach among the clouds; the waters nourished it, the deep exalted it” (Ezek. XXXI, 3–4). They think that the remaining words spoken about Assur and Pharaoh refer either to hostile powers or to the proud and to various rulers.

Of these we also read in the Psalm: “The voice of the Lord shatters the cedars, and the Lord will shatter the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII, 5). And elsewhere: “The day of the Lord of hosts is against every insolent and proud person, and against every lofty and exalted one” (Isa. XXII, 12–13). And shortly afterward: “Against every lofty cedar of Lebanon [Al. of the lofty ones], and against every oak tree of Bashan.”

They maintain that this is also prophesied concerning Lebanon: “Lebanon will fall with the lofty ones.”

But we shall follow the earlier interpretation, especially since what follows also agrees with this understanding.

(Vers. 3.) The sound of the shepherds’ wailing, because their magnificence has been laid waste; the sound of the lions’ roaring, because the pride of the Jordan has been laid waste.

The Septuagint: The sound of the shepherds’ mourning, because their magnificence has been made miserable. The sound of the lions’ roaring, because the roar of the Jordan has been afflicted.

The upper part of the chapter is contained in these verses as well. Those whom he had called cedars, firs, pines, and oaks of Bashan, and, explaining what these trees were, had introduced them by saying, “For the magnificent have been laid waste,” he now says by another *metaphor* (μεταφορά) that they are shepherds—that is, rulers and teachers, and those who were first among the people—who ought to weep and mourn, because their magnificence, beauty, and splendor have been laid waste and consumed: namely, the Temple in which they gloried.

“And,” he says, “the sound of the lions’ roaring”—those whom he had called lofty trees and, again, shepherds, he now calls the same men lions. And because he had spoken of lions, he preserves the metaphor and adds: “Because the pride of the Jordan has been laid waste,” or the roar and sound of the flowing water, which in Hebrew is called *GAON* (גאון). Just as he compared the height of the Temple, according to the character of the land of Judaea, with the height of Lebanon—for nothing in the Promised Land is loftier than Lebanon, nor more wooded or denser—so he joined the roar of lions to the river Jordan, which is the greatest river in Judaea and beside which lions dwell, on account of the heat of thirst, the proximity and breadth of the vast wilderness, and the reeds and marshes. Hence it is also said through the prophet: “A lion has gone up from the Jordan” (Jer. IV, 7), indicating that Nebuchadnezzar had gone out against Jerusalem from his seat, as a lion from its lair.

Alternatively: “The sound of the lions’ roaring, because the pride of the Jordan has been laid waste.” “The sound,” he says, “of the nobles,” because the Temple has been destroyed—the Temple from which they always hoped for help, and which once nourished the righteous, warriors, and powerful men as lions.

(Vers. 4, 5.) Thus says the Lord my God: Feed the flock destined for slaughter, which those who possessed them slaughtered and did not grieve, and those who sold them said, “Blessed be the Lord; we have become rich,” and their shepherds did not spare them.

The Septuagint: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Feed the sheep destined for slaughter, which those who possessed them slaughtered and did not repent, and those who sold them said, “Blessed be the Lord, and we have become rich,” and their shepherds suffered nothing on their account.

Where the prophecy is most evident and the true sequence of events is narrated through a figurative rendering of history, an allegorical interpretation is superfluous: we need not say that some shepherds are good and others bad, nor refer this both to the former people and to the new—that is, both to the priests and rulers of the Jews and to the bishops and presbyters of the Christians—and say that all negligent shepherds, whoever they may be, who cause one of the least to stumble are those who feed the flock destined for slaughter, suffer nothing on their account, feel no grief, and cannot say with the Apostle, “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (I Cor. XI). Nor need we say that they sell the peoples entrusted to them, of whom it is written, “Who devour my people as though eating bread” (Ps. LII, 5), and acquire riches from the deaths of others, praising those who plunder the wretched and blessing the wicked.

Let others interpret these things as they wish; we shall adhere to the order of explanation which we once undertook. “Because Lebanon has been opened, and its cedars and firs have been burned by consuming fire, and the wailing of the shepherds has been heard, and the roaring of the lions, because all the beauty and pride of the Jordan has been laid waste and consumed,” therefore the Lord my God said this to me:

“O prophet Zechariah, this word is addressed to you: Feed the flock destined for slaughter—that is, let it now be nourished and grow, although it is afterward to be slaughtered by enemies. These sheep and cattle were slaughtered by the Roman rulers who possessed and held them by the right of victory; they did not pity them, or rather, they sacrificed them and felt no pain—that is, they suffered no evil in return for such cruelty—and they sold those whom they had preserved, not out of mercy, but for the sake of profit.

“Let us read the ancient histories and the traditions of the mourning Jews: after the final overthrow which they endured under Hadrian, many thousands of people were sold in Abraham’s tabernacle—where now a very famous market is held every year—and those who could not be sold were transported to Egypt and were cut down by shipwreck and famine no less than by the slaughter of the nations.

“These victors, therefore, and avengers of the Lord, who slaughtered without grieving and sold the sheep, saying, ‘Blessed be the Lord; we have become rich,’ held this opinion: ‘The Jews offended by their sins; therefore we have oppressed them, and we have become rich from their price.’ Nor is it surprising,” he says, “that enemies, by the right of conquerors, slaughtered the sheep without grieving, sold them, and gloried in their crime, since their own shepherds and teachers did not spare them, and through their guilt the flock was handed over to wolves.”

[Col. 1501B] (Vers. 6, 7.) And I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. Behold, I will deliver human beings, each one into the hand of his neighbor and into the hand of his king; and they shall cut up the land, and I will not rescue them from their hand. And I will feed the flock destined for slaughter, on account of this, O poor of the flock.

The Septuagint: Therefore I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. And behold, I will deliver human beings, each one into the hands of his neighbor and into the hand of his kings; and they shall cut up the land, and I will not rescue them from their hands. And I will feed the sheep destined for slaughter in Chanaan.

What the Septuagint translated at the end of the chapter, “And I will feed the sheep destined for slaughter in the land of Chanaan,” is not in the Hebrew, and none of the other translators renders it. Since, therefore, their shepherds did not spare them, and they themselves first devoured my people, “therefore I also,” says the Lord, “will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land of Judaea.” For he is speaking of this land, concerning which the word was addressed to him, and not of the whole world, as the Jews, interpreting it wrongly, wish to distort God’s sentence in another direction.

After the destruction of the Temple—which happened to them because, after the Lord’s Passion, they were granted an interval of forty-two years but refused to repent—“I will let each one,” he says, “go against his neighbor, and they will cut one another down in mutual slaughter,” or during the very siege of the Temple, when a Roman army will surround Jerusalem. For there will be such wars and disagreements among the Jews themselves that the people will be divided into three factions. Let us read Josephus and the seven books of the Jewish captivity, and we shall see from the truth of history that this prophecy was fulfilled.

“And they shall cut up the land,” he says—without doubt the Romans destroyed the whole land and all the cities of the Jews. “And I will not rescue them from their hand.” Hear this, O Jew, who promises yourself the vainest hopes and do not hear the Lord speaking and affirming, “I will not rescue them from their hands”: your captivity among the Romans will be perpetual.

“And I will feed the flock destined for slaughter,” so that the Jews may continually be nourished for death, because this is God’s sentence. “O you who are poor of the flock”—that is, you righteous ones of Israel who have believed in the Lord Jesus and received the Son of God—hear what is said and learn the mysteries of the following chapter.

But as for what we read according to the Septuagint, “And I will feed the sheep destined for slaughter in the land of Chanaan,” we can understand it as follows: the Lord feeds and nourishes the Jewish people, which has been destined for death and dispersed throughout the whole world—that is, in the land of Chanaan and among the nations—in preparation for sacrifice.

(Vers. 8, 9.) And I took for myself two staffs: I called one “Beauty,” and I called the other “Bonds” [Vulg. “Bond”]; and I fed the flock. And I cut off three shepherds in one month, and my soul grew contracted toward them; for their soul also changed toward me. And I said, “I will not feed you. What is dying, let it die; what is being cut off, let it be cut off; and let those who remain devour each one the flesh of his neighbor.”

The Septuagint: And I will take for myself two staffs: I called one “Beauty,” and I called the other “Bond,” and I will feed the sheep. And I will remove three shepherds in one month, and my soul will grow heavy toward them; for their souls also roared against me. And I said, “I will not feed them. What is dying, let it die; what is failing, let it fail; and let those who remain devour each one the flesh of his neighbor.”

[Note: Victorius emends *irruebant* (“they rushed upon”) in place of *rugiebant* (“they roared”), in accordance with the Greek ἐπωροῦντο, or, as he himself prefers, ἐπορεύοντο.]

[Note: The manuscript of Regina reads *funiculum* (“bond”) here and below; but the Hebrew too has the plural number. It also reads, “he fed the flock with the two staffs joined together,” etc. A little later it likewise has, “his soul having grown heavy,” for “my soul will grow heavy.”]

Above he had said, “On account of this, O poor of the flock,” and, after an aposiopesis (ἀποσιώπησις), the following was understood: “Pay attention, because the gates of Lebanon have been opened, and the oak of Bashan, the firs, and the cedars have been cut down.” And he had added as a threat: “I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord.”

This appeared to refer to the one Jewish people, because, after killing the prophets, they had also laid hands on the Son of God and had shouted out with reckless voice, “His blood be upon us and upon our children!” (Matt. XXVII, 25). Now the Creator of the universe and Lord discloses the mysteries of his world and says that he had two staffs, calling one “Beauty” and the other “Bonds,” and that with the two staffs joined together he had fed the flock. He had also cut off three shepherds in one month, and his soul had become contracted—or indignant; or, as the Septuagint translated it, “my soul will grow heavy toward them.” There is no doubt that by the shepherds he means those whom he cut off.

And he gives the reason why he was so indignant at the shepherds that he cut them off in one month: “For,” he says, “their soul also changed toward me.” The meaning is: They did not love me with a wholehearted devotion, nor did the hireling shepherds love the true shepherd, because “the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John X, 11).

Therefore I too, in indignation, issued a sentence and spoke either to those shepherds whom I had cut off in my indignation, or, after cutting off the shepherds, to the flock that remained: “I will not feed you; but what has chosen death, let it die by its own will, and let them devour one another and tear one another apart in mutual slaughter.”

We have said these things *paraphrastically* (παραφραστικῶς), in order to prepare the path for the explanation that follows.

The Creator and shepherd whose sheep know his voice and follow him took for himself two staffs, or two *skytalai* (σκυτάλαι), that is, rods, which in Hebrew are called *MACALOTH* (מַקְלוֹת), in order to display the appearance of a shepherd. He called one staff “Beauty.” That is, under Noah he protected the whole human race with his blessing, when, after the world had been restored, sins had not yet become soiled upon it. For this reason the calling of all the nations is called beautiful and fair: nothing is more just than for the parent of the universe to call all alike, since he generated them under an equal condition.

And he called the other “Bonds.” For when the Most High divided the nations and scattered the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God (Deut. XXXII). “And the Lord’s portion became his people, Jacob; Israel became the bond of his inheritance.”

“And I fed,” he says, “the flock”—whether Israel itself, or the whole human race together with Israel.

“And I cut off,” he says, “three shepherds in one month.” I have read in the commentary of a certain writer that the shepherds cut off in the Lord’s indignation are to be understood as the priests, false prophets, and kings of the Jews, because after Christ’s Passion all of them were cut off at one time. Concerning them Jeremiah speaks: “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ Those who held my law did not know me. The shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal, and they followed idols” (Jer. II, 8).

Not satisfied with this explanation, he wishes the three shepherds cut off in one month to be understood as those who sinned against the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since all heretics sin either against one, or against two, or against all three persons.

Let him say what he wishes; for one must not detract from another’s interpretation. In our view, the three shepherds cut off in one month are Moses, Aaron, and Miriam (Num. 20). Miriam died in the first month, called Nisan (ניסן), in the wilderness of Zin; and in that same place, because of the water of contradiction, Moses and Aaron were condemned in the same month not to enter the Promised Land. Thus it happened that of the three shepherds one was cut off by present death, while the other two were cut off by a sentence of future death.

“And my soul,” he says, “became contracted toward them”—namely, toward the three shepherds whom I had appointed over my flock. “For their soul also changed toward me,” because they did not glorify me at the water of contradiction.

But if we refer this to the people, saying that the people’s soul changed toward God, it should be explained as follows: I was therefore indignant at them because, wavering between me and idols, they fought against me in various ways.

Therefore in anger I said to Moses, “Let me alone, and I will destroy them” (Exod. XXXII, 10).

[Note: Victorius observes that the words “I will not feed you” occur here in Zechariah, but Jerome interprets them as though they were spoken to Moses; similarly, in this same place, he explains Isaiah’s words, “If you listen, you shall eat the good things of the land,” as spoken to Israel in the wilderness.]

When he says, in anger, “Let me alone,” he invites supplication and shows that he can be restrained by him.

“What is dying,” he says, “let it die; what is being cut off, let it be cut off.” Let the bodies of all fall in the wilderness; let them, turned toward sedition, be torn by mutual bites like beasts; and let no one enter the Promised Land.

Some have understood two callings, of the Jews and of the nations, in the first and last Israel, under the name “Christians.” But they did not sufficiently consider how the Christian calling could have been cast aside first, while the Jews remained and were fed by God.

(Vers. 10, 11.) And I took my staff called “Beauty,” and cut it off, in order to annul my covenant which I had made with all the peoples. And it was annulled on that day, and the poor of the flock who kept watch for me knew that it was the word of the Lord.

The Septuagint: And I will take my beautiful staff and cast it away, in order to destroy my testament which I established with all the peoples. And it will be destroyed on that day, and the sheep of Chanaan, which are kept for me, will know that it is the word of the Lord.

[Note: Earlier, the word “my” was lacking.]

After the calling of Israel and the taking up of the second staff, which was called “Bonds,” the Lord took away the first staff, the nations of the whole world, which was called “Beauty,” and cut them off from his worship because they had revered idols; “all had turned aside, together they had become useless” (Ps. XIII).

Explaining more clearly what this staff was, he added: “In order to annul my covenant which I had made with all the peoples.” As soon as Israel was taken up, the multitude of the nations was cast aside. And as soon as the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was born—who is later narrated in the Gospel to have been twelve years old, sick, and dead—she began to bleed, *haemorrhousa* (αἱμορροοῦσα), and to be tormented by perpetual illness (Mark V; Matt. IX).

“And,” he says, “my covenant which I had made with all the nations was annulled.” And the poor of the flock understood—that is, the people of Israel who keep my commandments—that it is the word of the Lord: that is, that it is the Lord’s will to cast away the nations that deny him and to take up in Abraham the Israel that confesses him.

In place of what we translated as “and the poor of the flock understood,” the Septuagint translated, “and the sheep of Chanaan, which are kept for me, will know.” Some explain this as follows: the Jewish people will know, to whom it was said, “Seed of Chanaan, and not Judah” (Dan. XIII, 56), and which is now kept by my ceremonies. Or, because *Chananaei* is interpreted as “those prepared for humility,” those who were formerly prepared to be humbled by the Lord and abandoned will know.

The reason why, in place of what we translated as “the poor of the flock,” they said “the Chananaeans,” is clear. Among the Hebrews, “thus” is called *CHEN* (כן), and “poor” *ANIE* (עני). Joining these two words together, they interpreted “the poor of the flock,” that is, *CHEN ANIE* (כן עני), as the name of the nation of the Chananaeans.

(Vers. 12, 13.) And I said to them: “If it is good in your eyes, bring me my wages; and if not, refrain.” And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me, “Cast them to the statuary, the splendid price at which I was valued by them.” And I took the thirty pieces of silver and cast them into the house of the Lord, to the statuary.

The Septuagint: And I will say to them: “If it is good in your sight, give me my wages, assigning them; or refuse.” And they assigned my wages as thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: “Put them into the smelting furnace, and consider whether it is approved, just as I was approved for them.” And I took the thirty pieces of silver and put them into the house of the Lord, into the smelting furnace.

[Note: Martianus lacks the words “and I said to them”; in Victorinus they are missing: “that is.”]

When the poor of the flock of Israel, who keep my commandments, understood that the word I had spoken was the word of the Lord and that what I had said was true, he said to them—that is, to the poor of the flock:

“If it pleases you—for you are human beings, and I created you once for all with free will, and I also spoke to you in the wilderness: ‘If you listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land’ (Isa. I)—in return for this taking up by which I cast away the whole human race and chose you for myself as a special flock, and, as Creator of all, wished to have a small bond, give me my wages; that is, keep my commandments.

“But if you do not wish to give the wages, and it is not pleasing in your eyes to be reckoned under my name, openly refuse and do what you wish.”

At that time they answered Moses, “Everything whatever the Lord has said, we will do” (Exod. XXIV, 3). But at the end of the ages, in return for my choosing them from among the nations and rescuing them from Egypt’s iron furnace, “they weighed out my wages,” thirty pieces of silver, giving them to Judas the betrayer as the price of my blood (Matt. XXVI).

“And,” says the prophet, “the Lord said to me”—or the Savior himself, whose preceding words these are, testifying that the Father spoke to him—“Cast it to the statuary.” In place of this, the Hebrew reads *JOSER* (יוצר), that is, *ton plastēn* (τὸν πλαστήν), which we may call the maker or the potter.

The meaning is: “Cast my price to the potter, who is the Creator and maker of all.” He did not say “put it down,” but “cast it,” so that the Lord’s price might be weighed according to the judgment of the maker and potter.

And, ironically (*eirōnikōs*, εἰρωνικῶς), seeing that his price—that is, the price of the divine majesty—was set at thirty pieces of silver and that he had been betrayed for so cheap a payment, he says, “A splendid price at which I was valued by them.” This should be read with the irony and mockery of one saying:

“My people, and the poor who were once my flock and chosen by me as sons, judged that I should be bought and sold at such a price.”

“And I took,” says the Lord through the prophet, as God had commanded me, the thirty pieces of silver; I did not put them down, but cast them into the house of the Lord to the maker. In the house of the Lord I caused them to be returned by the betrayer to the priests and Pharisees, with the betrayer himself confessing, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matt. XXVII, 4).

But because it was the price of blood, they did not wish to put it into the *corbona*—that is, into the treasury—but bought with it the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners. For all of us who were foreigners and strangers to the Law, redeemed by his most precious blood, are buried and rest in the house of the potter and Creator of all.

For *plastē* (πλάστῃ), that is, “maker,” I formerly translated *statuarium*, compelled by the ambiguity of the word, since a single term signifies both a statuary and a maker.

[Note: Victorius says that Jerome retracts his rendering of the missing word as *statuarium*, although it more properly signifies “potter,” as Matthew the Evangelist translated it in chapter XXVII: “And they gave them for the potter’s field.” He does the same in Isaiah XIX with the missing word. In both places, however, he seems to have erred by attending only to the Greek words: here to *plastēn*, and there to *streblounta*, Aquila’s rendering, without at the same time considering the Hebrew word. Nevertheless, his first translation remains in both places. For his edition was disseminated throughout the whole world so quickly that later correction was insufficient. This did not happen in Isaiah XXXVIII, where he first translated the missing word as “ceased,” and later as “rest,” since the correction was accepted, although both versions were intermixed in Jerome himself.]

The Jews, maliciously interpreting this passage, say that the thirty pieces of silver signify the thirty commandments of the Law which they are ordered to perform, and again thirty-six others which are forbidden in the Law; and that they are told to return the silver of the commandments of the Lord to God, their maker and creator. Because they were unwilling to do this, they say that they themselves were cast away.

I wished briefly to indicate what they think; otherwise I am weary of reviewing their extremely elaborate explanation. Let us proceed to the remaining passages.

(Vers. 14.) And I cut off my second staff, which was called “Bonds,” in order to dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.

The Septuagint: And I cast away the second staff, which was called “Bonds,” in order to destroy the testament that existed between Judah and Israel.

[Note: We have removed the word “my,” which appears neither in the Greek nor in the manuscript of Regina.]

In this passage I know that I once read a long explanation—or rather, an inextricable tangle—by someone who brought the two staffs into a single association from the book of Ezekiel and adapted to this chapter everything that should be understood spiritually about the harmony of Judah and Ephraim.

Let us follow the order we began. After the Lord had been crucified by the Jews, after he had been valued at thirty pieces of silver, and after the price of his blood had been cast into the burial place of the nations that were foreign to the Law and the commandments of God, the Lord, no longer delaying his sentence, immediately said:

“I cut off my second staff, which was properly mine and clung to me in such a way that in Jeremiah it was called a loincloth, belt, and girdle—or, to use the customary word, a hip-cloth. This second staff, formerly called ‘Bonds’ and ‘my portion,’ was cast away by me so that I might dissolve the covenant, brotherhood, and harmony that had existed between Judah and Israel, and separate brothers from one another.

“Thus, in the number of the apostles and of those who repented, Judah would again be called ‘confessing,’ while Israel, Ephraim, and Joseph would be the names of those who remained in hardness of heart and said, ‘We have no king except Caesar’ (John XIX, 15).”

[Note: The manuscript of Regina reads, “they would be called Judah and confessing.”]

Therefore he did not add, “in order to annul the covenant or testament which I had with Judah and Israel”—for even to this day he extends his hand to those who repent—but rather, “in order to divide believers and unbelievers from one people,” saying:

“Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Matt. X, 34–35).

(Vers. 15 ff.) And the Lord said to me: “Take for yourself once more the implements of a foolish shepherd. For behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land who will not visit what has been abandoned, will not seek what has been scattered, and will not heal what has been broken; he will not nourish what stands, but will eat the flesh of the fat sheep and tear apart their hooves. O shepherd and idol who abandons the flock! A sword is upon his arm and upon his right eye; his arm shall dry up with dryness, and his right eye shall grow dark and be blinded.”

The Septuagint: And the Lord said to me: “Take for yourself once more the pastoral implements of an unskilled shepherd. For behold, I will raise up a shepherd over the land who will not visit what has been abandoned, nor seek what has been scattered, nor heal what has been broken, nor set straight what is whole; he will devour the flesh of the chosen sheep and pervert their ankles. O you who feed on vain things and who have abandoned the sheep! A sword is upon his arm and upon his right eye; his arm shall dry up with dryness, and his right eye shall be darkened with blindness.”

When he says, “Take for yourself once more the implements of a foolish shepherd,” he signifies that above he had taken for himself two staffs, one “Beauty” and the other “Bonds.” And because he cast them away because of their own fault and sin, and, after the brotherhood between Judah and Israel had been dissolved, we were grafted into the root of the good olive tree, while partial blindness came upon the house of Israel “until the fullness of the nations should enter” (Rom. XI), the prophet is now told to take up the very grave prophecy of the foolish or unskilled shepherd.

The foolish and unskilled shepherd is without doubt the Antichrist, who is said to come at the consummation of the world; and what kind of person he will be is indicated. By the shepherd’s implements we must understand his insignia and appearance: the shepherd’s bag, staff, pipe, and whistle.

Just as Isaiah, in order to indicate the captivity of the people, goes about naked (Isa. L); and Jeremiah goes to the potter’s house, so that through the destruction of the vessel that was being turned on the wheel and shaped by the craftsman’s hand he might show both the destruction of Israel and the power of God (Jer. XVIII); and Ezekiel, in order to demonstrate not only by his voice but also by his appearance the overthrow of Jerusalem, the flight of Zedekiah, and the burdens of the captives, breaks through the wall and is carried out upon his shoulders (Ezek. XII)—so Zechariah assumes the appearance of the foolish and unskilled shepherd in order to announce the one who is to come (Zech. XI).

This shepherd will arise in Israel because the true shepherd had said, “I will no longer feed you.” Under another name he is also prophesied in the prophet Daniel (chap. IX), in the Gospel (Mark XIII), and in Paul’s Epistle to the Thessalonians (II Thess. II) as “the abomination of desolation,” who will sit in the Temple of the Lord and make himself out to be God. He is also called “great understanding” through Isaiah (Isa. XXXII).

He comes not to heal but to destroy the flock of Israel. For the good shepherd visits sick sheep, searches for those who are scattered, brings back those who have been abandoned, and supports the weary. The evil shepherd does everything contrary: he devours the flesh of the fat sheep and tears apart and perverts the hooves of rams and sheep, so that they may not walk with a straight foot.

[Note: Victorius preferred *suscipiet* (“will receive”) because the subject is the Antichrist, whom the Jews will receive in place of Christ, as Christ said: “Another will come in his own name, and you will receive him.”]

The Jews received this shepherd, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming, so that those who did not believe the truth, in order not to be saved, may believe the lie and be judged because they consented to iniquity.

After the worst, foolish, and unskilled shepherd has been described, the prophetic word turns to the shepherd himself:

“O shepherd and idol.”

[Note: The manuscript of Regina adds “who abandons the flock,” which is not found in the other books.]

The shepherd is so criminal that he is called not a worshiper of idols but himself an idol, since he calls himself God and wishes to be worshiped by everyone. He has abandoned the flock to be devoured by wild beasts—the flock which the Lord had guarded for so long.

“A sword is upon his arm,” that is, upon his strength, “and upon his right eye,” with which he boasted that he saw the mysteries of God sharply and saw more than all the prophets before him, to such an extent that he called himself the Son of God.

That sword is the one of which we spoke above and will now discuss in part, the sword of which Isaiah also speaks: “My sword has become drunk in heaven” (Isa. XXXIV, 5).

The Lord’s sword will therefore be upon his arm and upon his eye, so that his strength and all his boast of power may be dried up by barrenness, and the knowledge that he falsely claimed for himself may be darkened by eternal shadows.

## Chapter XII

### Verse 1

**The burden of the word of the Lord concerning Israel:** The Lord says, who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundations of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within it: “Behold, I will make Jerusalem a threshold of drunkenness for all the peoples round about; but Judah also shall be under siege against Jerusalem. And on that day I will make Jerusalem a stone to be lifted by all the peoples; all who lift [Vulgate: “will lift”] it will be torn apart, and all the nations of the earth will gather against it” [Vulgate: “all the kingdoms”].

**The Septuagint:** “The lifting up of the word of the Lord concerning Israel,” says the Lord, “who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundations of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within it: Behold, I will make Jerusalem like thresholds that are shaken for all [alternative: “in all”] the peoples round about, and in Judea. And there shall be a siege around Jerusalem. And on that day I will make Jerusalem a stone trampled by all the nations; everyone who tramples it will mock it with mocking, and I will gather all the nations of the earth against it.”

There is a threefold interpretation from the place where we read, “Behold, I will make Jerusalem a threshold of drunkenness for all the peoples round about,” up to the place where it is written: “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man joined to me, says the Lord of hosts: Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (13:7). [Note: Martianay wrongly read *vim* (“force”) for *virum* (“man”).]

Some of the Jews think that these things have already been partly fulfilled, from Zerubbabel up to Gnaeus Pompey, who was the first of the Romans to capture Judea and the Temple—a history recorded by Josephus. Others, however, think that they are to be fulfilled at the end of the world, when Jerusalem has been restored; this is what the pitiable Jewish nation promises itself together with its *ἠλειμμένῳ*—its “anointed one”—whom above we read of as the foolish shepherd. Others—that is, we who are reckoned by the name of Christ—say that these things and others are fulfilled and will continue to be fulfilled daily in the Church until the end of the world. [Note: The Regin. manuscript reads, “that is, we who are reckoned by the name of Christ, say that these things and others are to be fulfilled daily until the end of the world.” This reading, especially in the words “these things and others,” instead of “in the Church,” appears more plausible.]

And lest we extend the length of the book by setting out each point—“This is what they say; thus others suppose; this is how we understand it”—we have set forth three interpretations, so that the prudent reader may understand, from the variety of interpretations, what is to be fitted to what.

The Lord, then, who stretches out the heavens like a skin, solidifies the earth with its lofty mass, and forms the spirit of man within it, is himself the Creator of all souls, so that from the two substances of soul and body he might join together one living being. For “spirit” is frequently understood as “soul,” as in the words: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). And: “You take away their spirit, and they fail, and return to their dust” (Ps. 103:29).

This Creator of the universe and Lord therefore testifies that he will set Jerusalem as a threshold of drunkenness for all the peoples round about, so that whoever touches its threshold may become drunk and fall—or that the threshold itself may fall upon the one who touches it. [Note: The Regin. manuscript does not have the word *crapulae* (“drunkenness”).] But Judah too, with Jerusalem under siege, has been captured by the nations and, having passed into their fellowship, will be compelled to besiege its own metropolis.

The Lord will not only set Jerusalem before all the peoples as a threshold of drunkenness; he will also set it as a stone to be lifted by all the peoples. Whoever wishes to lift it will be torn apart. For all the kingdoms of the earth will gather against Jerusalem.

It is customary in the cities of Palestine, and even to this day an ancient practice is preserved throughout Judea, that in villages, towns, and fortresses round stones of very great weight are placed. Young men are accustomed to exercise themselves with these and to lift them according to the variety of their strength: some as high as the knees, some as high as the navel, others to the shoulders and head; and some, with their hands straight and joined together, lift the weight above their heads, displaying the measure of their strength.

In the citadel of Athens, near the statue of Minerva, I saw a bronze sphere of very great weight, which, because of my weak little body, I could scarcely move. When I asked what its purpose was, the inhabitants of the city replied that the strength of athletes was tested by that mass, and that no one descended into the contest before it was known from lifting the weight whom he ought to be matched against.

The meaning, therefore, is this: “I will set Jerusalem before all the nations as a very heavy stone to be lifted.” They will indeed lift it, and according to the variety of their strength they will lay it waste; but, while it is being lifted, the very heavy stone must leave some tear or scrape upon the bodies of those who lift it. [Note: Two manuscripts read: “a tear, or an injury, upon the bodies of those who lift it,” and so forth.]

With regard to the Church, this may be interpreted as meaning that all persecutors who have fought against the house of the Lord will become drunk with the cup that Jeremiah offers to all the nations, so that they may drink, become drunk, fall, vomit, and go mad (Jer. 25).

I know that during the time of persecution many of our people were compelled to fight against the Church. But whoever wishes to lift this burden will indeed lift it, and because of the Lord’s anger by which he chastises sinners, he will support it with his own hands; nevertheless, he will not go unpunished, since God’s sword will fight against him.

In place of “a stone to be lifted,” which we have interpreted as best we could, the Seventy translated “a stone trampled by all the nations.” Everyone who tramples it—or “her,” that is, Jerusalem—will mock it with mocking. The meaning is plain: in either interpretation Jerusalem is to be trampled by hostile nations and persecutors, and it will be mocked according to the will of those who mock it. But the former interpretation is better and truer.

We explain each point briefly, so that at last we may come to the conclusion; for if we wrote at greater length, the reader’s mind might be confused both by the obscurity of the subject and by the length of the discourse.

### Verse 4

“On that day,” says the Lord, “I will strike every horse with terror and its rider with madness; but over the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and I will strike every horse of the peoples with blindness” [the Vulgate omits “with” before “blindness”].

**The Septuagint:** “On that day,” says the Lord Almighty, “I will strike every horse with bewilderment and its rider with madness; but over the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and I will strike all the horses of the peoples with blindness.”

At that time—for “day” signifies this—when Jerusalem has been besieged, so that Judah too is compelled to besiege it, the Lord will strike, both carnally and spiritually, all the horses of the adversaries with bewilderment, so that all who see them struck will be astonished; and their riders, oppressed by the magnitude of their evils, will be turned to madness. Over the house of Judah, however, which was compelled to do something against its own metropolis, the Lord will open his eyes, so that he may have mercy on them, make them worthy of his gaze, and illumine them with the light of his eyes. But he will strike all the horses of the peoples with eternal blindness.
