We have said above what the horses are to be understood spiritually as meaning: “A horse is deceptive for safety” (Ps. 32:17); and, “Some trust in chariots and some in horses” (Ps. 19:8), and other similar passages. We also said that their riders signify either demons or false teachers. All these will be turned to bewilderment and madness, so that they will be proved to understand nothing; but tangible darkness will overwhelm them, such as existed when the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck (Exod. 11).

Over the house of Judah—that is, the people who confess God—who, broken by the pressures of persecution and terrified by fear, seem to belong to the number of the persecutors, the Lord will open his eyes, so that he may look upon many of them who say to him: “Look upon me and have mercy on me” (Ps. 85:16), and so that they may deserve to hear: “The Lord will be your everlasting light” (Isa. 60).

This is the laceration inflicted by the very heavy stone with which the Lord threatens his adversaries who attempted to lift and harass Jerusalem.

### Verse 5

“And the leaders of Judah will say in their hearts: ‘May the inhabitants of Jerusalem be strengthened for me in the Lord of hosts, their God’” [another reading: “their own God”].

**The Septuagint:** “And the tribunes—that is, the *χιλίαρχοι* [‘commanders of a thousand’]—of Judah will say in their hearts: ‘We will find for ourselves those who inhabit Jerusalem, in the Lord Almighty, their God.’”

When the Lord has opened his eyes over Judah and struck all the horses of the nations with blindness, the leaders of Judah—of whom it was said above, “But Judah also shall be under siege against Jerusalem”—will make vows in their hearts, because they will not dare to speak openly, that Jerusalem may conquer and that Judah, conquered together with the enemies, may conquer together with its citizens.

Where we said, “May they be strengthened for me,” and the Seventy translated *εὑρήσομεν ἑαυτοῖς*—“we will find for ourselves”—the Hebrew reads **EMSA LI** [Hebrew text uncertain]. Aquila translated it *κάρτερησον μοι*, that is, “strengthen for me,” so that the meaning is: the chiliarchs, tribunes, and leaders of Judah will desire and make vows in the hidden sanctuary of the mind that God strengthen the inhabitants of Jerusalem in the Lord their God, and that they conquer their adversaries.

According to the tropological interpretation, the leaders and tribunes are the apostles and all apostolic men and teachers who presided over Christ’s army. They would wish to find no others for themselves except those who dwell in Jerusalem, the vision of peace, and who dwell in the Lord Almighty, their God.

Among these leaders was the apostle Paul, who found Titus, Timothy, Luke, and Silvanus; and Peter, who instructed Mark, the writer of the Gospel [another reading: “in the Gospel”]; and the other apostles, who filled the whole world with their teaching and instruction, so that they might have disciples who were inhabitants of Jerusalem.

### Verses 6–7

“On that day I will make the leaders of Judah like a furnace of fire among the wood, and like a torch of fire among the straw; and they will devour all the peoples round about, on the right and on the left. And Jerusalem shall again be inhabited in its own place, in Jerusalem. And the Lord will save the tents of Judah as at the beginning, so that the house of David may not boast greatly, nor the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem against Judah.”

**The Septuagint:** “On that day I will make the tribunes of Judah like a burning log among wood, and like fire among straw; and they will devour on the right and on the left all the peoples of the Lord round about. And Jerusalem shall still be inhabited in itself, and the Lord will save the tents of Judah as from the beginning, so that the glory of the house of David may not be magnified, nor the arrogance of the inhabitants of Jerusalem over Judah.”

When the leaders of Judah say in their hearts, “Strengthen for me, Lord, those besieged in Jerusalem, so that those who have been conquered by their own weakness may overcome through your help,” then I, the Lord Almighty, their God, will make the princes of Judah like a furnace of fire among wood and like a torch among straw, so that they may devour the adversaries with whom they had been joined by feigned friendship.

They will devour on the right and on the left, and kill all the peoples round about, so that Jerusalem may again be inhabited in its own place and no longer fear hostile attacks. They will also restore the cities, towns, villages, and hamlets of the tribe of Judah that had been plundered and devastated, just as they were before their destruction. And the royal house, the renowned and illustrious men of the tribe of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will not boast against the tribe of Judah that it is ruled by their authority and governed by their counsel; rather, they will know that victory in both belongs to the Lord.

Whether these things have happened or are to happen according to the historical interpretation, we leave the truth of the matter to the judgment of the Lord and to his saints, who have received from him the spirit of wisdom and truth.

Let us say that, at the time of the persecution of the Church, the leaders and tribunes of the Christian name, of whom we spoke above, when the Lord has restored peace to Jerusalem and destroyed the adversary by the breath of his mouth, will be like a furnace of fire among wood, devouring fruitless trees; and like torches among straw, so that whatever has no grain and is carried about by every wind of doctrine may be handed over to the fire.

“And they will devour,” he says, the leaders and tribunes of Judah, on the right and on the left, those who were unwilling—or do not know how—to walk in the middle way. They did not know the *ὑπερβολὰς κακίας*, the “excesses of wickedness.” Hence God’s people promise: “We will turn neither to the right nor to the left; we will walk along the straight way” (Num. 20).

The way on the right is frugality, which the Greeks call *φειδωλία*; the way on the left is extravagance; the middle and straight way is moderation. All, therefore, who are on the right-hand way, to whom it is said, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. 7:17), and those on the left, who hear, “The ways that are to the left are perverse” (Prov. 4:27), will be consumed by devouring flame.

When the adversaries have been deserted and removed, Jerusalem—that is, the Church—will again receive its former glory and remain in its proper state. The tents of Judah will be saved: the Christian communities scattered throughout the whole world, from which, as from tents and tabernacles, we desire to go to the house not made with hands and to the heavenly Jerusalem.

The tents of the common people and of all who are reckoned by the Christian name and counted among the multitude will therefore receive their former peace, once the leaders of the Churches have been besieged and put to flight, so that teachers and doctors may no longer think that peace has been restored to the Churches by their own teaching and wisdom, but by the help of the Lord.

### Verse 8

“On that day the Lord will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the one among them who stumbles on that day shall be like David; and the house of David shall be like God, like the angel of the Lord before them.”

**The Septuagint:** “And on that day the Lord will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and the one who is weak among them on that day shall be like the house of David; and the house of David shall be like the house of God, and like the angel of the Lord before them.”

When Judah has obtained victory and the Lord has restored its tents as they were at the beginning, so that the royal house may no longer boast against the people, then, on that day and at that time, the Lord—through whose help Judah will devour its adversaries on the right and on the left—will also protect those besieged in Jerusalem.

Everything will be transformed into such happiness and blessedness that the one who was considered most insignificant will be like a royal house, while the one who belonged to the royal house will be like one from the house of God—that is, like a messenger of the Lord and one of angelic dignity—in the sight of those who at that time have been saved.

According to the anagogical interpretation, the Lord will protect the inhabitants of the Church when, after the most severe persecution, peace has been restored to the Churches, and when Jerusalem will also be adorned by the meaning of its name—for Jerusalem means “vision of peace.”

Those who fought on behalf of the Church and confessed the Lord during the persecution will be so blessed that the one who was least and who, as a human being, stumbled in some sin of word or deed will be placed among the teachers. [Note: Martianay wrongly retained *hoc* (“this”) for *homo* (“human being”).] The teachers who have preserved their rank will be like the house of God and like the angel of the Lord, because with all our zeal we labor for this purpose, placed on earth and sweating through varied toil, that we may be transformed into angelic glory.

### Verse 9

“And on that day I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and prayers.”

**The Septuagint:** “And on that day I will seek to remove all the nations that come against Jerusalem, and I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and mercy.”

On that day, when the Lord protects the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the Lord will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. He will destroy them not for their ruin but for their correction, so that they may cease fighting against Jerusalem and begin to belong to Jerusalem.

For if he created all things from nothing, he did not create them in order to destroy what he had created, but so that what had been created might be saved by his mercy. Hence we also find written in the Wisdom that bears Solomon’s name—if anyone is willing to accept the book: “He created all things that they might exist, and the generations of the world are wholesome; and there is no deadly poison in them” (Wis. 1).

Just as the Lord came to seek what had perished and saved the human race, so he destroyed the nations in the sense that he destroyed them as hostile nations. Finally, the text continues: “I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and mercy.”

Paul also writes about this grace: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts” [another reading: “in your hearts”] “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). And in the aforementioned book it is written:

“Who can search out the things that are in heaven? And who has known your counsel, unless you gave wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from on high? And thus the paths of those who move upon the earth were corrected, and human beings were taught the things that please you” (Wis. 9:16). [Note: Victorius restores the sacred text as follows: “Who has searched out the things that are in heaven? And who has known your counsel, unless you gave wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from on high?” Shortly afterward, some manuscripts read *versabantur*—“were moving”—instead of *versantur*—“move.”]

And in Isaiah God says: “I have given my spirit upon you” (Isa. 42:1). Again, Scripture recalls concerning the same one: “I have given my spirit upon him” (ibid.).

The word “pouring out” indicates the sense of generosity, as is clear in what we have said: “The charity of God has been poured out in your hearts.” And elsewhere, in the person of God: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:29).

The apostle himself explains what the spirit of grace is when he says to the Hebrews: “How much worse punishments do you think he deserves who has trampled upon the Son of God, considered the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified to be common, and has insulted the spirit of grace?” (Heb. 10:29). Hence the various graces of the Holy Spirit are also spoken of.

The apostle’s greeting is: “Grace,” he says, “and peace be multiplied to you” (1 Tim. 1:1), so that after he has forgiven us our sins, peace may then follow through mercy.

The Jews say that these things have already been partly accomplished and will be fulfilled more fully at the consummation of the world. We, however, understand and affirm that they are fulfilled daily after the coming of Christ.

### Verse 10

“And they will look upon me whom they pierced, and they will mourn over him with a mourning as over an only-begotten one, and they will grieve over him as one grieves over the death of a firstborn.”

**The Septuagint:** “And they will look upon me, because they mocked, and they will mourn over him with mourning as over one most beloved, and they will grieve with grief as over a firstborn.”

The Hebrew letters **DALETH** and **RESH**, that is, D and R, are similar and are distinguished only by a small stroke. Thus it happened that those who read the same word differently translated it in different ways.

For the sake of understanding, let us give one example. “Samuel,” it says, “was clothed with an *ephod bad*” (1 Sam. 2:18), that is, with a linen garment, for *bad* means “linen”; hence *baddim* also means “linens.” In place of this Hebrew and Latin expression, some incorrectly read *ephod bar*, since *bar* may mean “son,” a sheaf of grain, “chosen,” or *οὖλος*, that is, “curly.”

What happened there through an error of interpretation, we discover has happened here as well. If it is read **DACARU** [Hebrew text uncertain], it is understood as *ἐξεκέντησαν*, “they pierced” or “they stabbed.” But if the letters are exchanged and placed in the opposite order, **RACADU** [Hebrew text uncertain], it is understood as *ὠρχήσαντο*, “they danced.” The error arose from the similarity of the letters.

John the evangelist, who drew wisdom from the Lord’s breast, a Hebrew of Hebrews whom the Savior loved most dearly (John 19), did not pay much attention to what the Greek letters contained. Rather, he translated word for word as he had read it in Hebrew, and he said that it had been fulfilled at the time of the Lord’s passion.

If anyone does not accept this, let him identify the passage of the sacred Scriptures from which John derived these words. When he cannot find it, he will be compelled, unwillingly, to accept the truth.

The Jews will mourn as over an only son and a firstborn, both of which are signified in the Lord and Savior. He is called “only-begotten” because of the uniqueness of his nature; “firstborn,” according to the Apostle, of those rising from the dead (Col. 1). [Note: In Martianay’s text, the word “firstborn” was missing or made meaningless.]

In place of “only-begotten,” the Seventy translated “most beloved,” concerning whom we read in the Gospel: “This is my most beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

Then they will grieve over the one whom they crucified when they see him reigning in glory. [Note: The Regin. manuscript reads “reigning in majesty”; shortly afterward it reads “from dancing” instead of “from leaping.”]

Among the Greeks, the word *κατωρχήσαντο* is composed not from mockery but from dancing; that is, they leaped as though playing against the Lord when they said, mocking and laughing: “Aha! You who destroy the Temple and build it in three days, save yourself, coming down from the cross” (Mark 15:29–30). They said these and other things in mockery, dancing in a kind of mad frenzy.

### Verses 11–12

“On that day there will be great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo. And the land will mourn, each family separately: the family of the house of David separately, and their women [or wives] separately” (for the Hebrew word **NESE**, that is, *γυναῖκες*, means both). “The family of the house of Nathan separately, and their women separately; the family of the house of Levi separately, and their women separately; the family of Shimei separately, and their women separately. All the remaining families, each family separately, and their women separately.” [Note: Martianay corruptly reads “whether it means.”]

**The Septuagint:** “On that day there will be great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of a pomegranate cut down in the plain; and the land will mourn by tribes, each tribe separately: the tribe of David separately, and their women separately; the tribe of the house of Judah separately, and their women separately; the tribe of the house of Nathan separately, and their women separately; the tribe of the house of Levi separately, and their women separately; the tribe of Simeon separately, and their women separately; all the remaining tribes separately, and their women separately.”

**ADAD-RIMMON** [Hebrew text uncertain], which the Seventy translated *ῥοῶνος*, was a city near Jezreel, formerly called by this name and now called Maximianopolis, in the plain of Megiddo. There Josiah, the righteous king, was wounded by Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23). Jeremiah composed Lamentations concerning him, which are read in the Church, and the book of Chronicles testifies that he wrote them (2 Chron. 35).

As at that time, after the sinful kings, all the people’s hope rested in Josiah, and when he was killed great mourning was stirred in the city, so we read in the Hebrew: “The breath of our nostrils, the Christ of the Lord, was captured in our sins; of him we said: ‘In his shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lam. 4:20)—although others, according to the spiritual interpretation, refer this to the Lord Jesus—so, when the Savior has been crucified, mourning will be renewed in Jerusalem, as it once was in the city of Hadad-rimmon, in the plain of Megiddo.

What follows—“They will mourn, each family separately, or each tribe separately; the family of the house of David separately, and their wives or women separately”—signifies that in a time of tribulation and mourning we must not devote ourselves to marriage and marital activity.

Hence in Joel, when captivity is near, it is said to the Jews: “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber [another reading: ‘bedchamber’], and the bride from her bridal room” (Joel 2:16). And when the Flood was imminent, Noah was commanded: “Enter the ark, you and your sons, your wife, and the wives of your sons” (Gen. 7:1). Later, after the Flood had ended, he was told: “Go out, you and your wife, your sons, and their wives” (Gen. 8:16), so that those who had been separated in the ark while danger threatened might, once the world had been restored, devote themselves to generation and children.

This is done not only in a time of distress but also in a time of prayer, when we wish to entreat the Lord. Thus the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5).

Thus now also the tribe of the house of David, the tribe of the house of Nathan, the tribe of the house of Levi, and the tribe of the house of Shimei are separated from their wives, so that they may mourn the only-begotten and firstborn Lord Jesus, concerning whom he had said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

In David the royal tribe is understood, that is, Judah. In Nathan the prophetic order is described. Levi refers to the priests, from whom the priesthood arose. In Shimei the teachers are understood, for from this tribe the ranks of teachers sprang up. He passed over the remaining tribes, which possess no special privilege of dignity. When he says, “All the remaining tribes, each tribe separately, and their wives separately,” he includes all the others without naming them.

Let us also say that, according to the Seventy, *ῥοῶν* does not mean one pomegranate tree, that is, one tree bearing pomegranates, but a place planted with such trees. According to the spiritual interpretation, the bridegroom says of this place in the Song of Songs: “I went down to see whether the vine had blossomed by the torrent’s growth, whether the pomegranates had blossomed” (Song 6:10).

The Savior descended to the torrent of this world and its troubled waters, of which Elijah is also described as having drunk in a figure of him (1 Kings 17), so that after the blossoms of the vine and of the pomegranate he might receive the fruit of both; and, giving his Church to drink, he would hear her say: “You will give me to drink of the wine of the perfumer, of the wine of my pomegranates” (Song 8:2). [Note: Victorius wishes *tuorum*—“your pomegranates”—to be restored. Although *meorum*—“my pomegranates”—is read in Song 8 and had accordingly been printed here, *tuorum* appears above at the end of chapter 9. Because the person changes, this word too must change. For the phrase is not, as Jerome cites it in the Vulgate and as the Seventy have it, “you will give me to drink,” but rather *ποτίσω σε*, “I will give you to drink.”]

Such a drink not only drives away the heat of the stomach but is also said to heal a diseased belly and benefit the remaining internal organs. Nothing is more beautiful than this fruit. In its redness it signifies the Church’s modesty; in the arrangement of its seeds, the ranks and members of the whole body distributed according to their several offices.

When the Savior finds no fruit in such a vineyard and among such fruits, he will say: “Every branch that does not bear fruit, the Father will take away; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse it, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2). And in another place John the Baptist cries out: “Already the axe has been laid to the roots of the trees” (Matt. 3:10). “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke 3:9).

At the cutting down of vices [another reading: “of evil things”; note: Martianay reads less well, “because on the day …”], when on the day of judgment all names of rank will be laid aside and what is written is fulfilled—“Behold the human being and his works” (Matt. 3; Luke 3)—and when the chaff has been separated from the wheat, there will be great mourning, not in another place but in Jerusalem.

For the wound and judgment will begin with the saints, and kings, priests, prophets, and teachers will beat their breasts when they see that the most beautiful things have been cut down and that the one whom they pierced reigns in the majesty of the Father and in his own majesty (1 Pet. 4).

## Chapter XIII

### Verse 1

“On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman.”

**The Septuagint:** “On that day every place in the house of David and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be opened, for transformation and for sprinkling.”

Concerning this fountain, which goes forth from the house of David, it is also written in the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. 47) that a fountain bursts forth in the house of the Lord and grows into a river called the water of remission and forgiveness. It proceeds to the wilderness and to the sea, which is now called the Dead Sea, and gives life to all the fish; and on both banks of the river trees of various kinds arise, abounding every month in fresh fruits.

And so that we may know that the house—that is, the Temple of God—is itself the house of David, which in Ezekiel is called the house of God and in Zechariah the house of David, this fountain proceeding from the house of God is referred to the Church and to knowledge of the Scriptures, so that we may all be reborn in Christ and that our sins may be forgiven us in the water of baptism.

Nothing is more unclean than a menstruating woman, who makes whatever she touches unclean; yet even these impurities will be washed away by Christ’s baptism.

In place of “for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman,” the Seventy translated “for transformation and for sprinkling.” This means that we pass from the Law to the Gospel, from the letter to the spirit, and from shadow to truth, so that future and eternal things may take the place of things brief and present.

The sprinkling signifies the Lord’s blood, of which the apostle Peter also speaks: “Grace to you, and peace be multiplied, in obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1:2). And again: “Knowing that you were redeemed not with perishable silver and gold, but with precious blood, as of an immaculate and most pure lamb” (ibid. 1:18). Whoever has been sprinkled and redeemed by this blood will be able to say with the prophet: “You will sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. 50:9).

### Verse 2

“And on that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will destroy the names of the idols from the land, and they will no longer be remembered; and I will remove the prophets [Vulgate: ‘false prophets’] and the unclean spirit from the land.”

**The Septuagint:** “And on that day, says the Lord Sabaoth, I will destroy the names of the idols from the land, and their memory will no longer exist; and I will remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.”

On that day, which he mentions so frequently, all idols will be removed from the land. This may refer to the idols of which the Psalmist says: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands” (Ps. 113:12), so that no religion may exist except that of the Christian name; and to those concerning which it is written in the prophet: “Howl, you carved images, in Jerusalem and in Samaria. As I have done to Samaria and its carved images, so will I do to Jerusalem and its idols” (Jer. 30).

Or it may refer to the idols of which the Apostle speaks: “The Spirit manifestly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared” (1 Tim. 4:1–2).

Just as idols are made by the hand of an artisan, so the perverse teaching of heretics turns whatever it fabricates into an idol and causes Antichrist to be worshiped in place of Christ.

In place of “false prophets,” the Hebrew reads simply “prophets,” that is, **NEBIM** [Hebrew text uncertain], who themselves signify false prophets; nevertheless, among the pagans too the priests of idols are called prophets.

### Verse 3

“And it shall be, when anyone prophesies again, that his father and his mother who begot him will say to him: ‘You shall not live, because you have spoken falsely in the name of the Lord’; and his father and his mother who begot him will pierce him when he prophesies” [the Vulgate: “his parents”; note: the Regin. manuscript inserts “they will mock,” which the sacred text rejects].

**The Septuagint:** “And it shall be, if a man prophesies again, his father and his mother who begot him will say to him: ‘You shall not live, because you have spoken falsely in the name of the Lord’; and his father and his mother who begot him will bind him in fetters when he prophesies.”

When the names of idols have been removed from the land, together with the false prophets and the unclean spirit that spoke through them, if anyone should again attempt to prophesy something in the person of the Lord, his father and mother will immediately forget their parental relationship in order to retain the service of God, and they will pronounce a sentence of death against their son.

So devoted to God will everyone’s minds be that no public judgment will be awaited; rather, such people will perish by the sentence of their relatives.

For the phrase “they will pierce him,” the Hebrew has the same word as above, **DACARU** [Hebrew text uncertain]. Why, then, did the translators of the Seventy there render it *κατωρχήσαντο*, “they insulted” or “mocked”—or, to express the word literally, “they danced against him”—and here wish to translate it *συμποδιοῦσιν*, “they will bind in fetters,” when Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it the same way in both places, “they pierced”?

It is rightly said that one who prophesies falsely is called a “man,” as the Apostle says: “Since there are rivalries and disputes among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man?” (1 Cor. 3:3). And in the Psalms: “But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81:7).

Those who are unworthy of the Spirit of God deserve to hear: “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). [Note: Other books read: “because they are flesh.”]

### (Verses 3 ff.)

“And it shall come to pass on that day that the prophets will be ashamed, each one of his vision when he prophesies; nor will they cover themselves with a sackcloth cloak in order to lie. But he will say, ‘I am not a prophet; I am a farmer, for Adam has been my example from my youth.’ And it shall be said to him, ‘What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?’ And he will say, ‘With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.’”

The Septuagint: “And it shall come to pass on that day that the prophets will be ashamed, each one of his vision when he prophesies; and they will put on a hairy skin in which they lied. And he will say, ‘I am not a prophet, because a man begot me from my youth.’ And I will say to him, ‘What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?’ And he will say, ‘With these I was struck in the house of him who loves me.’”

Whoever has attempted to prophesy, has been condemned by the judgment of his parents, and whose false prophecy has been demonstrated by an outcome contrary to his predictions, will be ashamed of his vision and will no longer cover himself with a hairy garment in order to lie. For this was the dress of the prophets: whenever they urged the people to repentance, they clothed themselves in sackcloth. Hence Isaiah too is commanded to remove the sackcloth from his loins and to walk naked (Isaiah 20), since the time was no longer one of repentance but of the captivity that was impending.

Therefore this false prophet too will not assume prophetic dress, lest, under another’s clothing and covering, he deceive the simple. Rather, he will cleave the earth with the plow, and, devoted to agriculture, will prove himself to be a man and subject to the sentence of God, who spoke to Adam:

“Cursed is the earth in your work; in labors you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the earth; and in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis 3:17–18).

And when he has shown himself to have been born for this purpose—that he may eat his bread in the sweat of his face—another will question him and say: “What do these blows and these wounds in the midst of your hands mean?” The sense is: “Why do you cling to the gallows? Why are your hands pierced with nails? What have you committed, that you should submit to this punishment and torment?”

And he will answer and say: “I received these wounds and suffered these blows, condemned by the judgment of my parents and of those who did not hate me but loved me.” And to such an extent will falsehood have been driven away and truth prevail that even the one who was punished for his own fault will rightly confess that he has suffered what was deserved.

**Note:** The Regin manuscript reads: “who was punished by his own judgment.”

The Hebrews explain what is written—“Nor will they cover themselves with a hairy cloak in order to lie”—as follows: “And they will not be filled with a demonic spirit.” In Isaiah we read of such men as *τριχιῶντες* (*trichiōntes*), that is, “hairy ones,” so that by means of this falsely assumed clothing they may not utter God’s words while pretending to speak for him, or deny the Lord. For *CHAESU* can be interpreted both as “they lie” and “they deny.”

### (Verses 7 ff.)

“‘Sword, awake against my shepherd and against the man who is joined to me,’ says the Lord of hosts. ‘Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered, and I will turn my hand toward the little ones. And it shall come to pass throughout all the land,’ says the Lord: ‘two parts in it will be scattered and will perish, and the third part will be left in it. And I will lead the third part through fire, and I will burn them as silver is burned, and I will test them as gold is tested. He himself will call upon my name, and I will answer him. I will say, “You are my people,” and he will say, “The Lord is my God.”’”

**Note:** Victorius, following the Vulgate edition, writes “will be destroyed” in place of “will be scattered”; he says that this emendation is supported both by the Hebrew word and by the Greek *ἐξολοτρευθήσεται*.

The Septuagint: “‘Sword, arise against my shepherd and against the man who is his fellow-citizen,’ says the Lord Almighty. ‘Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered, and I will bring my hand upon the shepherds. And it shall come to pass on that day,’ says the Lord, ‘that two parts will perish and fail, and the third part will be left in it. And I will lead the third part through fire, and I will burn them as silver is burned, and I will test them as gold is tested. He will call upon my name, and I will answer him, and I will say, “This is my people,” and he will say, “You are the Lord my God.”’”

For “sword,” which the Septuagint translated as *ῥομφαία* (*rhomphaia*), in Hebrew *AREB*, we find in Aquila and Symmachus *μάχαιρα* (*machaira*), that is, “sword” or “blade.”

For what we translated “against the man who is joined to me,” that is, *προσκεκολλημένον μοι* (“joined to me”), Aquila translated “against my fellow-tribal man,” that is, *σύμφυλόν μου* [another reading: *σύμφυλόν μοι*]; Symmachus has “against the man of my people,” which in Hebrew is called *AMITHI*; the Septuagint, “against his fellow-citizen”; Theodotion, “against his neighbor.” They read *VAU* at the end of the word in place of *JOD*, although these letters differ from one another only in size. If *JOD* is read, it means “my”; if *VAU*, “his.”

I am astonished that some wish to weaken this prophecy by allegorical interpretations. The evangelist Matthew referred it to the Lord and Savior after the disciples fled during his passion, and says that it was then fulfilled. They do this because they wish to appear more learned than others, while failing to hold to the rule of truth.

For the evangelist Matthew reports: “Then Jesus said to them: ‘You will all be scandalized because of me on this night. For it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’” And again: “But all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples, abandoning him, fled” (Matthew 26:31 ff.).

Nor should it be thought that the testimony was taken from another passage, since in the Gospel God says that the shepherd was struck by him, while in the present passage we read that a sword and blade were commanded: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” This sword, this *rhomphaia*, and this *framea* are the same sword of which the Lord also speaks to the Father in the twenty-first Psalm: “Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog” (Psalm 21:12).

Concerning this *rhomphaia* it is also written in the prophet Amos: “All the sinners of the earth will die by the sword” (Amos 9:10). This cannot stand literally at all, for many sinners perish in shipwreck, others by poison; some are suffocated by water, others consumed by fire. By this sword and this *rhomphaia* all sinners perish [another reading: “are punished”], including the Ethiopians of dark complexion, concerning whom Zephaniah bears sacred witness, saying: “You Ethiopians too will be slain by my sword” (Zephaniah 1:12).

After the good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:15), and who said to the Father, “Those whom you struck have persecuted, and they added to the pain of my wounds” (Psalm 68:27), had been struck by the Father’s will, and the man joined to God, who said, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 13:10), had hung upon the gallows and said, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46), immediately the sheep were scattered: the whole multitude of believers in Christ.

And the Lord turned his hand, as we read in the Septuagint, toward the shepherds, whom many wrongly interpret as the leaders of the Jews. But as it is written in Hebrew, he turned it toward the little ones, to whom the Lord had said in the Gospel: “Do not fear, little flock” (Luke 12:32). And in Isaiah: “Behold, I and the children, or little ones, whom God has given me” (Isaiah 8:18).

And two parts were made throughout all the land: the Jews and the Gentiles, who alike perished and failed. For in his passion the Psalmist’s voice was fulfilled, saying: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Psalm 11:1). And: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13:3).

When the Gentiles and the Jews had perished, the third part in the world—that is, the third people, the Christian people—suddenly grew. And beautifully he says: “The third part will be left in it,” that is, in the land, because of the Jews and Gentiles only those who confessed the Lord were reserved for life and habitation upon the earth.

This third part too, lest it become delicate and secure in its confession,

**Note:** The Regin manuscript reads: “and secure confession.”

is led and tested through fire like silver and gold. The Lord wishes this fire to burn in believers (Luke 12), and Paul desires them to be fervent (Romans 12). Hence the apostles, baptized in the Lord’s Spirit and fire (Acts 2), speak in the Psalm: “For you have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined” (Psalm 65:10–11). And shortly afterward: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment.” And elsewhere it is said to the believer: “If you pass through fire, the flame will not burn you, because I am with you” (Isaiah 43:2).

The fire does not therefore consume, nor does the flame devour, because it is the voice of the Lord who cuts through the flame of fire (Psalm 28:7).

When the little ones over whom the Lord turned his hand have thus been tested, and the whole multitude of the nations has believed through their calling, then the people of believers will call Christ by his name. When he says, “You are my people,” the people will answer: “You are the Lord my God.”

The Jews refer these things to Christ and insist that they are to be fulfilled at the end of time. But this is the difference between us and them: we say that they have already been fulfilled, while they speak of them as still to be fulfilled.

### (Chapter 14—Verses 1–2)

“Behold, the days of the Lord are coming [the Vulgate has: ‘will come’], and your spoils will be divided in your midst. And I will gather all the nations to Jerusalem for battle, and the city will be captured, the houses will be laid waste, and the women will be violated. Half of the city will go out into captivity, but the rest of the people will not be taken away from the city.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, the days of the Lord are coming, and your spoils will be divided within you, and I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem for battle. The city will be captured, the houses will be plundered, and the women will be defiled. Half of the city will go out into captivity, but the rest of my people will not perish from the city.”

**Note:** After Victorius, we have supplied “my” from the Regin manuscript, compelled by the Greek text itself, *τοῦ λαοῦ μου* (“of my people”).

The days that the Lord threatens will come, when Jerusalem’s spoils will be divided in its midst, together with the other events contained in the prophetic utterance, are those of which we also read in Isaiah: “The day of the Lord will come, incurable, of fury and wrath, to make the whole world a solitude and to remove sinners from it” (Isaiah 13:9).

But what necessity will there be for its spoils to be divided in its midst? It often happens that things seized suddenly in a city are divided outside, in the field or in the wilderness, lest the enemy perhaps arrive. Here, however, such a weight of evils will press upon the city that what has been plundered will be divided in the middle of the city, for the security of victory.

And not only will Jerusalem be captured, with all the nations aroused against it for battle; the houses of Jerusalem’s inhabitants will also be plundered, and the women violated, to the grief of their masters and husbands, who will be unable to prevent either the plundering of their houses or the defilement of their wives by the enemy. This accords with what we read elsewhere: “Those who have been gathered in your midst will fall by the sword; they will dash your children before your eyes, plunder your houses, and possess your wives” (Isaiah 13). Nothing more cruel or more miserable than this can be found: through fear of their own death, they will not dare defend either their children’s lives or their wives’ chastity.

The prophet Amos also speaks this very threat to Amaziah, the impious priest: “Your wife will fornicate in the city, your sons and daughters will fall by the sword, and your land will be measured by a measuring cord” (Amos 7:17).

And all these things will befall the Jewish people: “For the nations raged, and the peoples meditated on vain things. The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2:1–2). He mocked and derided them and troubled them in his fury, so much so that the Apostle, seeing that the years granted to them for repentance had already been completed, and that they nevertheless persisted in denial, though they had killed the Lord and persecuted the prophets and apostles, said: “Wrath has come upon them [another reading: ‘upon us’] to the end” (1 Thessalonians 2:16).

Josephus, who wrote a history of the Jews, records all these events in full, and says that they endured much greater calamities than those we read of in the prophets. Cornelius Tacitus likewise, who composed the Lives of the Caesars in thirty volumes, from Augustus to the death of Domitian.

But how half of the city was captured while the remaining people stayed in the city is demonstrated both by that period and by other occasions: the northern and lower part of the city was captured, while the Temple Mount and Zion, where the citadel was, remained intact.

The Jews say that these things are to be fulfilled under Gog; others say that they were partly fulfilled in the time of the Macedonians and Egyptians and of various nations. Leaving the truth of the time to the Lord’s knowledge,

**Note:** Victorius has “leaving the variation of the time”; then two manuscripts have “leaving it to the knowledge of the Lord.”

let us explain what has been written.

### (Verses 3–4)

“And the Lord will go forth and will fight against those nations, as he fought on the day of battle. And his feet will stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem to the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split from its middle toward the east and toward the west, with a very great chasm.”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord will go forth and will fight against those nations, as on the day of engagement and on the day of battle. And his feet will stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem on the eastern side. And the Mount of Olives will be split, half of it toward the east and half of it toward the sea, by a very great chasm.”

We must understand worthily of God the statements in the sacred Scriptures that speak of God’s going forth, fighting against the nations, standing with his feet upon the Mount of Olives, and the other things that are expressed and contained in Scripture *ἀνθρωποπαθῶς* (*anthrōpathōs*), that is, in humanly conditioned language and in bodily terms.

Otherwise, when the Apostle says, “who is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), and again, “to the King of the ages, incorruptible, invisible God” (1 Timothy 1:17), and when it is written in the Gospel, “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John 1:18), and again, “Not that anyone has seen God, except the one who is from the Father” (John 6:46), then just as we interpret his anger and repentance, soul, hands, feet, belly, eyes, and the other members of the body according to the variety of circumstances and the meaning of the interpretation, so too we must understand what is written here: “The Lord will go forth and will fight,” according to what we read in Habakkuk: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ” (Habakkuk 3:13).

And in Micah: “For behold, the Lord will go forth from his place; he will descend and tread upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains will be consumed beneath him, and the valleys will be split” (Micah 1:3–4).

**Note:** Martianay incorrectly retained “above”; Victorius had written: “we follow the Regin manuscript.”

And in Isaiah: “The Lord of hosts will go forth; he will crush the battle, stir up zeal, and cry out against his enemies with strength” (Isaiah 42:13).

God therefore goes forth from his place when he is compelled, for the correction of sinners, to break his quietness, gentleness, and mercy. Although by nature he is sweet, through our fault he is *παραπικραίνεται* (*parapikrainetai*), that is, “he becomes bitter”—not for himself, but for those who suffer, to whom the torments are bitter.

This is the one who elsewhere speaks through the prophet: “I am God, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6). And to him it is said: “But you are the same, and your years do not fail” (Psalm 101:28). And in the Epistle of James: “With whom there is no change” (James 1:17).

Now he goes forth and fights as on the day of battle, when he drowned Pharaoh in the Red Sea and fought on behalf of the Israelite people (Exodus 14). And his feet will stand upon those whom he has pitied, and they will not be moved, so that it may again be said of him: “And the Lord will sound the trumpet, and will walk in the tempest of his anger” (Zechariah 9).

**Note:** Victorius corrects the text from Zechariah itself to “in the tumult,” which in the Septuagint is *ἐν σάλῳ*. The Vulgate has “in the whirlwind.”

He will not walk when the sun has already declined and darkness is near after midday, as we read that he did in the case of Adam (Genesis 3).

And when he stands, he will not stand in a valley or in low places, but on a mountain—not one with barren trees and a sterile forest, but where olive trees grow, by which the eternal light is nourished, infirmities are dissolved, and rest is granted to the weary.

The Mount of Olives itself, on which the Lord’s feet stand, is opposite Jerusalem and toward the east, from which the sun of righteousness rises. It is planted with those olive trees of which it is said: “Your children are like young olive trees around your table” (Psalm 127:3).

Its middle part will be split toward the east, where the trees planted from the Gentiles are, of which one says: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Psalm 51:10).

The other middle part will be split toward the west and the sea. This is the people of circumcision, to whom God speaks through the prophet: “What has my beloved done in my house? She has committed abomination. Can vows and holy flesh remove your wickedness from you?” (Jeremiah 11:15), “or can you escape through these things?”

This beloved woman committed abomination in the house of God by crucifying the Son of God, and heard: “A shady and leafy olive tree, beautiful in appearance, the Lord called your name; your branches have become useless, and they have been broken from the good root, so that we might be grafted in their place.”

**Note:** The same editor maintains that “beautiful in appearance” should be read; the Septuagint has *εὔσκιον τῷ εἴδει* (“shady in appearance”).

And observe the mysteries of the Scriptures: when [another reading: “how”] the middle part that inclines toward the west and is struck by salty and bitter waves is said not simply to be in the sea, but in a very great and precipitous chasm of the sea. Of this Micah also speaks: “I will drag its stones down into the valley” — with no doubt that he means Jerusalem — “and I will uncover its foundations” (Micah 1:6).

We have said these things according to the weakness of our abilities, as in matters that are extremely difficult and obscure. The Jews, for their part, following the letter, attempt to show that the Lord will stand upon the Mount of Olives and that the mountain itself will be divided into two parts, so that the cleft begins toward the east in one part, while the other part extends its end toward the west; and that in the middle there will be a very steep ravine [another reading: “valley”], with one part divided toward the north and the other toward the south.

### (Verse 5)

“And the middle of the mountain will be separated toward the north, and its middle toward the south. And you will flee to the valley of my mountains, for the valley of the mountains will be joined as far as the nearest place. And you will flee as you fled from the face of the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. And the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.”

**Note:** In Jerome’s interpretation, *mons* (“mountain”) is read absolutely in place of “the middle of the mountain,” contrary to the Hebrew [reading not legible in the supplied text].

The Septuagint: “And the middle part of the mountain will incline toward the north, and its middle part toward the south. And the valley of my mountains will be stopped up, and the valley of the mountains will be joined as far as Asael. And it will be filled as it was filled by the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah.”

**Note:** The Regin manuscript has “will be filled” in place of “will be joined”; the Greek has *ἐγκολληθήσεται*.

“ And the Lord my God will be present, and all the holy ones with him.”

For what we said, “you will flee,” the Septuagint and the other interpreters translated *ἐμφραχθήσεται* (*emphrachthēsetai*), that is, “it will be stopped up” or “it will be filled.”

**Note:** In Martianaeus the form was defective: *ἐμφαχθήσεται*.

And for what we rendered, “for the valley of the mountains will be joined as far as the nearest place,” the Septuagint translated “as far as Asael” in place of “the nearest place.” Aquila retained the Hebrew word *ASEL*, with the short *e*, as *ἀζέλ*; Theodotion with the long vowel, *ἀζήλ*. Symmachus alone translated it as “the nearest place,” and we have followed him.

Let us paraphrase the passage so that what is written may become clear. When the Mount of Olives has been split by a great and precipitous chasm, so that one side of the chasm faces east and the other west, suddenly within that very chasm another ravine will break open, one toward the north and another toward the south. A precipitous quadrangle will be formed, so that the chasm extends in four directions: east and west, north and south.

“And you will flee,” he says, “to the valley that lies between the Temple and Zion.” These two mountains—the Temple and Zion—are called the mountains of God, because the valley of the Mount of Olives, enclosed on both sides by steep mountains, will draw its chasm as far as the mountain of the Temple, which is holy.

The earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah is traditionally assigned to the time when Uzziah, also called Azariah, attempted to claim for himself an unlawful priesthood and was struck with leprosy on his forehead (2 Chronicles 26). Of this earthquake we also read at the beginning of Amos: “The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake” (Amos 1:1).

Finally, after this wicked king died, at whose impiety the whole earth had been shaken, Isaiah saw the great vision that he wove into his book.

Let us pass to the spiritual understanding. After the Mount of Olives has been separated toward the east and the west by the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews, another division will again be made toward the north and the south. The north will be joined to the west, the south to the eastern region. Circumcision will stand on the left, and the Christian people on the right.

Concerning these two winds the Church speaks: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song of Songs 4:16), so that when the north wind, which is extremely cold and is interpreted as the devil, withdraws, the warm south wind may arrive. The bride seeks it and says: “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at noon?” (Song of Songs 1:16).

Of this Habakkuk also speaks mystically: “God will come from Teman” (Habakkuk 3:3), for which the Hebrew has: “God from the south,” that is, from the fullest light. Of this the Psalmist cries elsewhere: “You illuminate wondrously from the eternal mountains” (Psalm 76:5).

When the division of the two peoples throughout the whole world has become so great that some are separated toward the east and south—that is, toward the right—and others toward the north and west, namely toward the left, then whoever is holy will flee to the valley of God’s mountains, of which we spoke above: the Temple and Zion, that is, the two Testaments.

For that chasm which had previously been between the two mountains will extend as far as Asael, that is, as far as the house of God, which is near paradise and the heavenly Jerusalem and the holy mountain on which the Temple is situated.

And just as at the time when the most violent earthquake under Uzziah, the leprous king, terrified the hearts of mortals and scattered the terrified people in every direction, so the separation of the two peoples and, again, the fellowship of believers in one faith will rest in a peaceful dwelling between the two mountains, because the Old and New Instruments will be joined to one another.

What is said, “as far as Asael,” that is, “as far as the nearest place,” signifies that the two Instruments, of the Law and of the Gospel, are indeed joined to one another, but joined in such a way that they are nearer to one another than united. For we have lost much of the old Law and have received the grace of the new.

When this has been perfectly accomplished, then, he says, “the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.”

But if we wish, instead of “you will flee,” to follow what the other interpreters translated, “the valley of their mountains will be stopped up” or “filled,” we shall say this: the coming of the Lord Savior, after the two peoples have been separated from one another, will stop up and fill the chasm that divided them, so that they may proceed toward one another along a level road.

### (Verses 6–7)

“And it shall come to pass on that day: there will be no light, but cold and frost. And it shall be one day, known to the Lord—not day and not night—and at evening there will be light.”

The Septuagint: “On that day there will be no light, but cold and frost; it will be one day, and that day will be known to the Lord, neither day nor night; and toward evening there will be light.”

This plainly refers to the second coming of the Savior, concerning which John also speaks in his Apocalypse: “Behold, he will come with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Revelation 1:7). And the Lord declares in the Gospel that the Son of Man will come in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory (Matthew 24).

**Note:** Victorius found the reading: “He will come with power and great glory.”

He will come with clouds, that is, with angels, who are ministers of the spirit and are sent for various duties, and with the prophets and apostles, concerning whom it is written: “Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm 35:6).

When the day of his coming has been fulfilled, there will be no light, but cold and frost: the love of all will have grown cold, and because of the multitude of evils that will come upon them, everyone will grow cold and lose the warmth of his former faith.

After all sinners have contracted their cold and frost, there will be one day, perpetual and without succession of light and darkness, day and night. The Lord himself will be the light of all, concerning whom Isaiah says more fully: “The sun will no longer be your light by day, nor will the rising of the moon illuminate you by night; but the Lord will be your everlasting light, and your God your glory” (Isaiah 60:19).

And elsewhere he cries out to Jerusalem: “Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of your God has risen over you. For behold, darkness and gloom will cover the earth, over the nations; but the Lord will appear over you, and his glory will be seen in you. And kings will walk in your light, and nations in your splendor” (verses 1 ff.).

**Note:** We have restored the text according to the Regin manuscript, with the Greek agreeing word for word: *καὶ ἡ δόξα αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ σὲ ὀφθήσεται* (“and his glory will be seen upon you”). Previously the text read: “and the glory of your God has risen over you”; Victorius had restored “will rise.”

If darkness and shadows cover the earth over the nations, how will the nations again walk in the Lord’s splendor? Those nations will be in darkness that have contracted cold and frost; those will walk in the Lord’s light who have followed the kings, apostles, and prophets, concerning whom it is written: “The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord” (Proverbs 21:1).

Finally, in the evening—that is, in the time of darkness and sadness for all sinners—there will be light for the saints, and one eternal day. If this day will be known to the Lord—for he cannot be ignorant of what he created—we must consider how he says in the Gospel that no one knows that day, neither the angels nor the Son, but the Father alone (Matthew 24:36).

### (Verse 8)

“And it shall come to pass on that day that living waters will go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea and half of them toward the last sea. They will be there in summer and in winter. And the Lord will be king over all the earth.”

The Septuagint: “On that day living water will go out from Jerusalem, half of it toward the first sea and half toward the last sea; in summer and spring it will be so. And the Lord will be king over all the earth.”

At that time—for this is what is signified by the day known only to the Lord, in which light and darkness do not succeed one another but there will be perpetual brightness, according to what we read in the Apocalypse, “the city does not need the light of the sun, for the Lord God Almighty will be its light” (Revelation 21:23)—living waters will go forth from Jerusalem.

Concerning these waters we have argued above (chapter 13), setting forth the testimony of Ezekiel. Half of them will go toward the eastern sea, which the Greek books call *λίμνην Ἀσφαλτῖτιν* [the manuscripts have *Ἀσφαλτίτην*], and which is commonly called the Dead Sea because nothing can live in its waters.

Half will go toward the last sea, which leads toward Egypt and forms the shores of Palestine.

“In summer and winter,” he says, “it will be so”: these waters that go forth from Jerusalem will neither be frozen by the cold of winter nor dried up by the excessive heat of summer. The Septuagint, however, translated “spring” instead of “winter,” which does not correspond to the contrast with summer.

When the life-giving waters have entered both seas and have softened their bitter waters with a sweet stream, then the Lord will be king over all the earth.

The water that goes forth from Jerusalem—that is, from the Church—indicates the teaching of the Savior: “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3), according to what is written elsewhere: “The whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant waters cover the sea” (Isaiah 11:9).

Half of these waters will go toward the eastern sea, the people of circumcision, who were chosen in the apostles and through the apostles; and half toward the western sea, so that those may come from east and west who will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Or certainly we should understand the eastern sea and the last sea as the Old Instrument and the New. Unless it has been sweetened by the Savior’s stream and by his spiritual interpretation, the former is extremely bitter, with the letter killing and the spirit giving life (2 Corinthians 3:6).

What follows—“They will be there in summer and in winter”—is understood to refer to the living waters that go forth from Jerusalem, so that these living waters do not cease to flow either in peace or in persecutions.

Or, because the Septuagint translated, “In summer and spring it will be so,” let us say that at that time there will be no winter, but spring, and perpetual summer, when “the voice of the turtledove will be heard in our land,” when “the fig tree will put forth its green figs,” the vineyards will blossom, “winter will have passed,” and “the rain will have gone away” (Song of Songs 2:11–13).

At that [another reading: “that very”] time spring will be necessary because flowers will appear in our land, so that we may celebrate Passover and Pentecost, through which we pass from earthly things to heavenly things and offer all our fruits to God.

At Passover the end of winter and the beginning of spring are observed; at Pentecost, the beginning of summer, when we offer to God the work of our hands and our fruits.

Of this perpetual summer and spring the righteous speaks to the Lord: “You made the dawn and the sun; summer and spring you fashioned” (Psalm 73:16–17).

Then the Lord will be king over all the earth, when we say: “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice” (Psalm 96:1). And again: “Say among the nations, ‘The Lord reigns.’ For he established the inhabited world, which shall not be shaken” (Psalm 95:10).

He who has drunk will know that we have rightly interpreted the living water as the teaching of the Savior, as will the one who has heard the Savior preaching: “If anyone drinks from the water that I shall give him, it will become in him a fountain of living water, springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14).

And again: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

For just as the one who drinks from his teaching will have within himself a living fountain, so the one who believes in him, according to what is contained in the words of Scripture, will have rivers of living water flowing from his belly.

Many refer the living waters to baptism, which are to be given to those who thirst in spring and summer—that is, at Passover and Pentecost—when what is written will be fulfilled: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1:16).

### (Verse 9 and following)

“On that day the Lord will be one, and his name one. And all the land will return as far as the wilderness, from the hill of Rimmon to the south of Jerusalem. It will be exalted and inhabited in its place, from the Gate of Benjamin to the site of the former gate, as far as the Corner Gate; and from the tower of Hananel to the king’s winepresses. And they will inhabit it, and there will no longer be a ban; Jerusalem will sit secure.”

The Septuagint reads: “On that day the Lord will be one, and his name one, encircling all the land; and the wilderness from Geba to Rimmon, south of Jerusalem. But Ramah will remain in its place, from the Gate of Benjamin to the first gate, as far as the Corner Gate and as far as the tower of Anamael, to the king’s winepresses. They will inhabit it, and there will no longer be a ban, and Jerusalem will dwell in confidence.”

**Note:** Two manuscripts read *Ananeel*, here also in the Septuagint; other books read *Anameel*.

Jews and Christian Judaizers promise themselves the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem and the issuing of waters from its midst, flowing toward both seas, at the end of time, when circumcision will again be practiced, sacrifices offered, and all the precepts of the Law observed—so that they will become not Jewish Christians but Christian Jews.

“On that day,” they say, “when Christ sits reigning in Jerusalem, golden and adorned with jewels, there will be no idols and no differing worship of deity, but the Lord will be one, and all the land will return as far as the wilderness,” that is, to its former condition. He gives the names of the places, indicating from what place to what place Jerusalem is to be built: from the hill of Rimmon—for this is what Geba signifies, where there is a pomegranate tree—to the southern region of Jerusalem.

As for what follows, “But Ramah will remain in its place,” Aquila and the others translated it better, rendering it, “It will be exalted.” For *Ramah* means “exaltation,” according to that prophetic and Gospel passage: “A voice was heard in Ramah,” that is, “It sounded on high” (Matt. 2:18). Jerusalem, then, will be exalted and built in its former place, from the Gate of Benjamin to the gate called the Corner Gate, and from the tower of Hananel—not, as the Greeks and Latins incorrectly read, Anamael—to the king’s winepresses. This is written in Hebrew as *AMMELECH* [another reading: *Amalech*].

“And they will inhabit it,” he says, that is, Jerusalem; “and there will no longer be a ban”—no fear, namely, of hostile attack or any terror. Rather, Jerusalem will sit, or be inhabited, resting in eternal peace.

This is how the Jews dream of these things according to the letter, as do our chiliasts, who desire to hear again, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). In exchange for the continence and brief fasting of this life, they promise themselves bulbs, vulvas, and Phasis birds, and not the Ionian attagen, but the Jewish one, concerning which the Lord can truly say: “My spirit will not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). For “the flesh wars against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17).

**Note:** The manuscripts read *phasides*; but the reading of the printed books, *aves phasidis* (“birds of the Phasis”), should be retained, because *phasidis* is a substantive in the genitive case, not a plural accusative adjective. Let us add that in manuscript books the letter *I* is very often written for *E*, and conversely *E* for *I*, as I have frequently reminded readers, even before the *Notes on Jerome’s Questions* by Jean Le Clerc came to light. The birds of the Phasis are our pheasants, birds known from the river Phasis and brought to us by the Argonauts; for they are said to have been transported from that region to Greece. See Martial, book XIII, 72. — MART.

**Note:** The manuscripts read *Phasides* equally well, whatever may seem preferable to Martianus.

**Note:** He called it Ionian because the Ionian attagen is especially celebrated; consult Pliny, book X, chapter 48. The attagen is an Asiatic bird, which we call a francolin, *un francolin*: a species of pheasant, now also caught in Gaul and Spain and especially throughout the Alps. The attagen was formerly considered among rare birds, as can be gathered from this passage. — MART.

Nor do they oppose to us the Apocalypse of John (chapter 20), for that too must be expounded spiritually.

We, however, interpret the heavenly Jerusalem as the Church, which, while walking in the flesh, does not live according to the flesh, and whose citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3). For after the Lord Jesus has become king over all the earth—of whom the Holy Spirit speaks to the Father through the Prophet, “Give your judgments to the king, and your justice to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1)—then there will be one Lord, of whom it is written: “Know that the Lord himself is God” (Deut. 4:35).

“And his name one,” with every false religion trampled underfoot, according to what the Prophet sings: “Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” (Ps. 8:1). And again: “You have magnified your holy name above all things” (Ps. 137:3). Elsewhere: “As your name is, O God, so also is your praise throughout all the earth” (Ps. 47:11). Habakkuk likewise speaks of him: “The earth is full of his praise” (Hab. 3:5).

God himself speaks of the glory of this name: “Apart from me you will not know God, and besides my name, which has been magnified above all, there is none” (Isa. 44:8).

Then all the land in which the Jews dwelt will return as far as the wilderness, that is, as far as the people of the nations, which previously was deserted and had no knowledge of the Law—from Geba to Rimmon, that is, from the hill to the height. For from the earth and the wilderness we rise to the hills, and from the hills to the mountains. Thus the bridegroom in the Song of Songs leaps over the lesser hills and springs over the lofty mountains (Song 2), of which it is written: “The high mountains are for the deer” (Ps. 103).

But if we wish to understand *Rimmon* as “pomegranate”—for among the Hebrews it has both meanings—let us say that the boundaries of the Church begin from the hills, so that the entire ecclesiastical order may be built. We spoke above about this when we interpreted “the mourning of the only-begotten” and “the mourning like that of Hadad-rimmon.”

Nor is the Church content with this limit; it will reach as far as the south, in the fullest light. We explained this earlier and now remain silent on it, lest by repeating the same things too often we become tedious to the reader.

The Church, then, will be exalted: it began from the hills and reached the south. And it will inhabit its place, of which it is written: “There he placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22:1).

It will proceed from the Gate of Benjamin, whose name means “son of the right hand,” not “son of days,” as some mistakenly suppose. For it makes a difference whether the word ends with the letter *nun* or with *mem*.

And it will reach as far as the site of the eastern and former gate, as far as the Corner Gate. We begin from strength—for this is what “right hand” signifies—and we reach the former gate, so that through it we may enter the others. Immediately the Corner Gate meets us, where there is the cornerstone “which the builders rejected and which became the head of the corner” (Ps. 117:22).

This cornerstone joins the two walls and brings two peoples into one (Eph. 2). Of it God also speaks through Isaiah: “Behold, I will lay in Zion a cornerstone, chosen and precious, as a foundation; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isa. 28:16).

This cornerstone also desired the other cornerstones to be built upon it, so that the apostle Paul could freely say: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20).

Heretics do not imitate these stones. They do everything for the sake of glory and profit, and they pray in the corners of the streets, abandoning the straight path. For every corner breaks the straight line.

Therefore the prostitute in Proverbs (chapter 7), however we may wish to understand her—whose feet do not remain at home but wander outside and lie in wait at every corner of the streets—when she sees a foolish young man—for she does not invite one whom she perceives to be prudent and mature in old age, concerning whom it is written, “The wisdom of a man is his gray hair” (Wis. 4:8)—immediately seizes him, kisses and flatters him, leads him to the brothel, and invites him to intercourse.

Let us therefore leave the counterfeit corners and pass to the firm and solid corners of Christ. When we reach them, the tower of Hananel immediately meets us; its name means “most pleasing to God.”

For what is more pleasing than the tower of Solomon, concerning which it is said to the bride: “Your neck is like the tower of David, built at Thalpioth; a thousand shields hang upon it, all the weapons of the mighty” (Song 4:4)?

The Lord wishes this tower to be built in the Gospel (chapter 14), after the expenses and costs have first been calculated. And concerning it Jerusalem is told: “Let there be peace within your strength, and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 121:7). The holy man likewise speaks to the Lord concerning it: “You have led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Ps. 60:4).

From the tower of Hananel we reach the king’s winepresses, for which three psalms also bear a title. The Lord says in Isaiah: “I have trodden the winepress alone” (Isa. 63:3), so that our vintage may overflow in them, that we may press out the clusters and tread the red must made crimson with the blood of Christ, so that we may drink the wine that gladdens the human heart (Ps. 103).

The bride also speaks to the companions of the bridegroom in her desire: “Bring me into the wine cellar; place love over me” (Song 2:4).

If such winepresses intoxicate us, we shall dwell in Jerusalem, in which there will no longer be a ban—that is, a curse and abomination. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be accursed” (1 Cor. 16:22). And elsewhere: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus is accursed’” (1 Cor. 12:3).

**Note:** This exposition of Jerome should be noted because of the incompetence of modern critics, who maintain that Paul thought otherwise and, contrary to the unanimous agreement of the holy Fathers, teach many things that they do not know, thinking themselves learned if they utter unheard-of novelties. — MART.

For the salvation of his brothers he desires to be accursed, wishing to imitate his Lord, who, although he was not himself a curse, became a curse for us (Rom. 9).

When every ban has been removed, Jerusalem will dwell secure and confident, expressing in herself the words: “Blessed is the one who trusts in the Lord,” and, “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man” (Ps. 117:8). The prophet Jeremiah also speaks of this security and confidence: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord” (Jer. 17:7).

### (Verse 12)

“And this will be the plague with which the Lord will strike all the nations that fought against Jerusalem. The flesh of each one standing upon his feet will waste away, his eyes will waste away in their sockets, and their tongue will waste away in their mouth” [the Vulgate reads “their”].

The Septuagint reads: “And this will be the ruin with which the Lord will strike all the peoples who fought against Jerusalem. Their flesh will waste away while they stand upon their feet, their eyes will flow from their sockets, and their tongue will waste away in their mouth.”

The present Scripture testifies what the nations that will fight against the city of the Lord will suffer: “They will stand,” it says, “upon their feet, and their flesh will waste away and flow off; their eyes will rot and fall out of their sockets; and their tongue, which blasphemed the people of God, will dissolve into corruption and pus and rot within the enclosure of their teeth.”

It is clear to everyone that the Romans who overthrew Jerusalem did not suffer these things—unless perhaps the Jews assert that these are the nations destined to fight against the golden and jewel-adorned Jerusalem.

We, however, will say that all persecutors who afflicted the Church of the Lord have received, even in the present age, what they did, to say nothing of future torments. Let us read the ecclesiastical histories and see what Valerian, Decius, Diocletian, Maximian, the most savage of all Maximinus, and recently Julian suffered. Then by the facts we shall prove that, even according to the letter, the truth of the prophecy was fulfilled: their flesh rotted, their eyes wasted away, and their tongues dissolved into foulness and pus.

**Note:** The same manuscript inserts “Licinius,” who indeed raged most savagely against Christians and was eventually killed by soldiers. Jerome summarizes the others as follows: Maximian’s flesh rotted; Maximinus perished through wasting of the eyes; Diocletian through the foulness and pus of his tongue. He does not apply the prophet’s words to the first two, Valerian and Decius, or to the last, Julian, except insofar as the Lord’s vengeance appeared against his adversaries, as he himself says above in Nahum, chapter 1. Compare Lactantius’ excellent little book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. — MART.

But if heretics think that God’s cruelty is displayed in this statement, let them hear that all these things happen so that, when evils fail, good things may grow up. Whoever stands in the Lord and with the Lord will have his carnal things flow away, so that spiritual things may arise. His eyes, which saw badly, will fall from their sockets, so that others may be put in their place, capable of receiving the Lord, with the Prophet saying: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Ps. 122:1).

And the blaspheming tongue will therefore rot, so that another tongue may arise, one that glorifies God and can say: “My tongue will meditate on your justice; all day long, on your praise” (Ps. 70:15).

Hence Simeon, taking the Child into his arms and announcing what was to come, said: “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke 2:34), so that evil things may fall and the best things be raised up.

Hence also the Lord says: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

The people of the Gentiles did not see; but after faith in Christ they began to behold the light of truth, which speaks through the Prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me. He has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives, and sight to the blind, and to illuminate them with wisdom” (Isa. 61:1–2). Concerning this it is written: “The wisdom of a man illuminates his face” (Eccl. 8:1). And in the Psalms we read: “The Lord illuminates the blind,” or, “makes them wise” (Ps. 145).

For this is more exactly what the Greek word *σοφοῖ* signifies. The Jews saw; but because they refused to receive the light, they were covered with eternal blindness.

### (Verses 13–14)

“On that day there will be a great tumult from the Lord among them; and a man will seize the hand of his neighbor, and his hand will be joined to the hand of his neighbor. But Judah too will fight against Jerusalem, and the wealth of all the nations around will be gathered together: gold, silver, and very many garments.”

The Septuagint reads: “And on that day there will be great astonishment from the Lord upon them; and each one will seize the hand of his neighbor, and his hand will cling to the hand of his neighbor. And Judah will be prepared in Jerusalem, and will gather the strength of all the surrounding peoples: gold, silver, and very many garments.”
