When these miracles have been fulfilled—when the flesh of the enemies has flowed away, their eyes wasted, and their tongue rotted in the mouth of the blasphemers—then there will be great tumult, or astonishment, among them. For this is what the Greek term *ἔκστασις* means, which the Septuagint translated here.

“And each one will seize the hand of his neighbor, and his hand will be joined with the hand of the other,” because of the fear and burden of the evils that will descend upon them.

**Note:** The words “with the hand of the other” are absent in Victorius.

Judah too will fight against the capital city. We spoke of this above (chapter 12), along with the victory granted by the Lord. The riches of all the nations that fought against Jerusalem will be gathered together: gold and silver, and a great abundance of garments, which are among the most precious possessions.

Unhappy Judah promises these things to himself, hoping to receive the gold of the one whom he valued at thirty pieces of silver.

We, however, following the order we have begun, refer all these things to the blessedness of the Church: all who are in it will marvel at the subjection of the enemies and at their own happiness, and each person will seize the hand of his neighbor, so that they may join right hands and be united in mutual faith and fellowship.

But where the Hebrew reads, “And Judah will fight against Jerusalem,” the Septuagint translated, “And Judah will be prepared in Jerusalem.” Let us accept both senses. Judah, who once confessed the Lord’s name but, under persecution, persecuted Christ’s people, will himself be turned to joy. Or certainly, Judah—that is, every confessing and faithful person—will not fight against Jerusalem but will prepare himself in Jerusalem to wage war against its adversaries.

And this Judah will gather the riches of all the surrounding nations: gold, silver, and very many garments. We have often said that gold and silver are to be understood in terms of sense and speech. Accordingly, we must understand the garments in the same way, garments with which Christ’s Church is adorned, concerning which it is written:

**Note:** The Regius manuscript reads, nearly more correctly, “and we ought to understand those garments.” “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in varied adornment” (Ps. 44:10).

The crowd of believers rejoices that she is clothed in these garments and says: “I will rejoice in the Lord, because he has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a tunic of joy” (Isa. 61, according to the Septuagint).

For the Lord had said to her: “I clothed you with *τριχάπτοις* and fine linen” (Ezek. 16). By *τριχάπτοις* let us understand delicate garments, so beautiful and fine that they appear similar to hairs. The Church gathers these garments so that she may have clothing with which to dress her people, to whom the true preacher has given the command: “At all times let your garments be white” (Eccl. 9:8).

### (Verse 15)

“And such will be the ruin of the horse, the mule, the camel, the donkey, and all the beasts that are in those camps, like this ruin.”

The Septuagint reads: “And this will be the ruin of the horses and mules, camels and donkeys, and all the beasts that are in those camps, according to this ruin.”

The Jews insist that these things are to be fulfilled carnally in their own *ἠλειμμένος*—their anointed one. Truly, the Lord’s power will be great if the horses, mules, camels, donkeys, and all their beasts fall in the enemy camps just as the human beings have fallen. What a great triumph, what a glorious victory, for brute animals to be overcome when God fights!

Let us therefore speak according to the allegorical interpretation we have begun: all these evils fall for this reason, so that good things may suddenly arise.

**Note:** The same manuscript reads, “so that, in punishment, good things may suddenly arise,” etc.

Thus the one who was previously a horse neighing after his neighbor’s wife (Jer. 5), carried away by an uncontrolled lust and lying in the filth of pleasures—when he begins to pursue chastity—will hear: “Rise, let us go from here” (John 14:31), and, “Rise, come, my beloved” (Song 2:10), and in the Apostle: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illuminate you” (Eph. 5:14).

When the horses that had previously fallen rise again and offer their soft backs for the Lord to sit upon, they will say to God: “Mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Hab. 3:8).

In the same sense let us understand the mules, which are sterile and do not produce children but indulge in pleasure. The Psalmist refers to them: “Do not become like the horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

Just as those inclined toward lust are called horses, so we shall rightly call mules those who are virgins in the flesh but not in the spirit, who make themselves eunuchs not for the sake of the kingdom of heaven but for human pleasure [another reading: “human will”].

When these mules and eunuchs have been transformed into offspring and have produced spiritual children, they will hear through Isaiah: “Let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree.’ For thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I desire, and hold fast to my covenant: ‘I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that will not fail’” (Isa. 56:3 and following).

The kings of Israel had such male and female mules, especially David, who is referred to Christ (2 Sam. 13 and 1 Kings 1).

If we have understood who the falling and rising horses and mules are, let us pass to the camels, a ruminant animal that does not divide the hoof (Lev. 11). Let us say that the camel is all the sinners of the earth, who are weighed down by the heavy burden of their sins and appear to read the Holy Scriptures but do not divide the hoof: they ruminate on the divine words while neglecting what has been written.

More properly, however, the camel can be understood as the Jewish people, who meditate upon God’s Law and ruminate upon it, turning it over in their breast, but do not divide the hoof so as to believe in the Father and in the Son. They are unclean in that they do not separate the letter from the spirit, the shadow from the truth; they carry the burdens of the Law and hear through the Prophet: “Woe, sinful nation, a people full of iniquity” (Isa. 1:4).

Concerning such a camel, which ruminates but does not divide the hoof, it is said in Proverbs, as though to a son: “He who abandons the discipline of his father will meditate on evil words” (Prov. 21).

After the camel let us pass to the donkey, which once was driven without a bridle, was unclean, had many masters, and slipped down precipices, so that, falling, it might suddenly rise, carry the Lord Savior, enter holy Jerusalem, and be received by the crowd of believing children as he triumphed (Matt. 21 and John 12).

The Savior is said to have tied this donkey to the vine and the vineyard (Gen. 49:11), concerning which it is written in the Psalms: “You brought a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations, and planted it” (Ps. 79:9). To it the vinedresser himself speaks: “I planted you as a wholly true and fruitful vine” (Jer. 2:21).

All the beasts and animals that the Prophet includes under one name are to be interpreted according to the nature of each; and this accords with the Son of God more than with the things which the Jewish people presume upon through their foolish prophecy.

### (Verse 16)

“And all who remain from all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.”

The Septuagint reads: “And it will be that whoever remains from all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up every year to worship the King, the Lord Almighty, and to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.”

“All,” he says, “who remain from the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up every year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.”

The Jews also promise that these things will occur, through their vain hope, in the kingdom of a thousand years. The origin of this solemnity is as follows:

After the people of Israel had left Egypt and passed through the vast, terrible, and broad wilderness, in which there was no house, farm, town, or cave, they made themselves huts and tents—now called *papiliones*, “butterflies,” from their resemblance to a small bird—in which they could dwell with their wives and children, obtain food, and avoid during the day the heat of the sun, and during the night dampness, cold, and the adversity of dew.

It was commanded that on the fifteenth day of the seventh month the feast of Tabernacles should be celebrated. “And when your son asks you tomorrow,” he says, “‘What do these tabernacles mean?’ you will answer him: ‘For a long time we were sojourners in Egypt, from which the Lord brought us into the wilderness; and therefore we raise tabernacles, so that we may always remember God’s benefits when we begin to dwell in cities’” (Deut. 6:20–21 and Lev. 23:43).

He also commanded them to make tabernacles from the most beautiful wood, which the Jews call *citrus wood*, and from palm branches and foliage, as well as from very dense wood, willow, and poplar.

**Note:** We correct the text according to the Regius manuscript, reading *citrum* (“citrus wood”) instead of the erroneous reading *cedrum* (“cedar”). Citrus wood was indeed one of the four woods legally required for making the tabernacles, as those who have treated the Jewish *deuterōseis* clearly report. See *Menachot*, chapter 3, section 6; Maimonides, chapter 7, section 5.

**Note:** In Hebrew, Leviticus 23 reads [Hebrew term supplied in the source].

We have laid the foundations of the history so that from these we may pass to spiritual matters.

As long as we are progressing, running, and engaged in combat, we dwell in tabernacles, striving with our whole mind to pass from the tabernacles to a firm and stable dwelling, that is, the house of God.

Hence the holy man says in the Psalm: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5).

**Note:** The name “David” should more correctly be removed here, since our manuscripts also do not have it. And: “I am a stranger and a sojourner, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:31).

This is spoken by one who is in Egypt and still established in the world.

But the one who goes out from Egypt—which in Hebrew is called *MESRAIM* and means “tribulation”—and enters the wilderness of vices, travels on his way and says in the Psalm: “I will pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, as far as the house of God” (Ps. 41:5).

For it is wondrous to refuse to dwell with the Egyptians, but, after Pharaoh has been submerged, to desire to enter the promised land (Exod. 14).

Hence he speaks elsewhere: “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:1). And shortly afterward:

**Note:** Through an error in the printed editions this testimony has been sadly corrupted, as has also, a little above, *delicta* for *dilecta*, together with other errors of this kind that are often corrected.

 “Blessed are all who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (ibid., 5).

“For there is a voice of exultation and salvation in the tabernacles of the righteous” (Ps. 117:15). And in Proverbs we find written: “The houses of the righteous remain, and the tabernacles of those who act rightly will stand” (Prov. 2:21).

He promises permanence for the houses and stability for the tabernacles.

The holy man also says elsewhere: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, and behold the delight of the Lord, and visit his temple” (Ps. 26:4).

The one who dwells in such tabernacles and hastens to go from the tabernacles to the courts, from the courts to the house, and from the house to the temple of the Lord ought to celebrate the solemnity of Tabernacles in the most beautiful wood of wisdom, concerning which it is said in Proverbs: “It is a tree of life to all who draw near to it, and those who lean upon him, as upon a house of firmness” (Prov. 3:18).

**Note:** The phrase should unquestionably be restored in the inferior reading as *eam*, in accordance with the Greek *ἐπ’ αὐτήν*. Then, instead of *domum* (“house”), one should read *Dominum* (“Lord”), as the Greek has *Κύριον*. Victorius further substitutes *firmati sunt* for *firmitatis*, with five manuscript codices agreeing with his reading, although the Greek *ἀσφαλὴς* differs from it.

And in the branches of palms, which contain the sign of victory and the reward of courage; and in the foliage of the very dense tree that the Jews understand as the myrtle, on account of the mortification of flesh and lust.

**Note:** The Regius manuscript reads, “the mortification of vices and lusts.”

Hence myrrh is offered as a gift to the Lord Savior by the Magi (Matt. 2).

“And in the branches,” he says, “of willow and poplar,” which some call one tree. The very name of the wood, which in Greek is *ἁγνός*, indicates chastity.

Physicians, and those who have written about the natures of trees and herbs, say that if someone drinks willow blossom or poplar blossom mixed with water, every heat in him grows cold and the vein of lust dries up, so that thereafter he can no longer beget children.

Whoever is protected by the branches of such trees should celebrate the feast of Tabernacles, passing through the sixth month, which refers to the world, and observing a spiritual Sabbath in the seventh, on the fifteenth day of that month, when the moon of the night is completely full and all its darkness is dissolved in brilliant light.

We have said these things briefly, contemplating the vastness of the books long ago in our mind, so that we may proceed to what remains.

### (Verse 17)

“And it will be that whoever does not go up from the families of the earth to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, there will be no rain upon them.”

The Septuagint reads: “And it will be that whoever does not go up from the families of the earth to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord Almighty, these things will be added to them.”

For the Hebrew has, instead of what the Septuagint translated, “and these things will be added to them,” *ULO ALEHEM EJE GESEM*, which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion likewise translated as, “and there will be no rain upon them.”

**Note:** All our manuscripts read in this way; in Hebrew it is written [Hebrew text supplied in the source], which we now read: *Volo alehem jihjeh heggeschem*. How far this Hebrew reading differs from the reading of the ancients is now plain and certain to us. — MART. I would prefer *IJE*, which is the third-person ending; but the similarity of the words could have deceived the copyist.

The Church of the Lord Jesus is called the heavenly Jerusalem, concerning which the Apostle writes: “But the Jerusalem above is free, which is the mother of us all” (Gal. 4:26); and, “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Heb. 12:22).

This Jerusalem is not situated in low places but on a lofty mountain, concerning which the Savior says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14).

Therefore whoever is going to worship the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem must climb to the mountains.

But whoever belongs to the families and tribes of the earth, and for that reason cannot worship the Lord, will not have upon him the rain of the early and latter seasons, nor will his land be watered by the rains of heaven.

Or, according to the Septuagint, whoever does not go up from the families of the earth to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord Almighty, will be counted among those who fought against Jerusalem, whose flesh will waste away, whose eyes will flow out, and whose tongue will rot.

### (Verses 18–19)

“And if the family of Egypt does not go up and does not come, nothing will be upon them; rather, there will be the ruin with which the Lord will strike all the nations that did not go up to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles. This will be the sin of Egypt, and this will be the sin of all the nations that did not go up to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.”

The Septuagint reads: “But if the tribe of Egypt does not go up and does not come there, there will be upon them the ruin with which the Lord will strike all the nations that did not go up to celebrate the feast of Booths. This will be the sin of Egypt, and the sin of all the nations that did not go up to celebrate the feast of Booths.”

Whoever is Egyptian, or belongs to the other nations, so long as he remains Egyptian and pagan, will not ascend into Jerusalem. And because he cannot ascend or raise his step to the heights, the rain of the Lord’s blessing will not be upon him.

And this will be the greatest sin for the Egyptian, the Assyrian, the Chaldean, the Syrian, the Moabite, and the Ammonite, if they are unwilling to leave their lands and ascend to Jerusalem, so that through the tabernacles they may pass into Jerusalem and find the eternal house; if they cease to be people of other nations and become Israelites, “in whom there is no deceit” (John 1).

**Note:** The name “Assyrian,” which also seems superfluous, is omitted by Victorius.

All these things, which we touch upon in rapid speech, the Jews and our Judaizers—or rather, not ours, because they are Judaizers—expect to occur bodily. They promise themselves circumcision and marriages in the kingdom of a thousand years, lest the curse written against them be fulfilled: “Cursed is the barren woman who does not produce offspring in Israel”; and, “Blessed is the one who has offspring in Zion and household members in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9, according to the Septuagint).

But if this is true, all the virgins whom the kingdom of a thousand years finds will be subjected to perpetual curse and barrenness—or else they will have to marry in order to escape the curse.

(Verse 20.) On that day whatever is upon the horse’s bridle will be holy to the Lord; and the cauldrons in the house of the Lord will be like bowls before the altar. And every cauldron in Jerusalem and in Judah will be sanctified to the Lord of hosts.

The Septuagint: On that day whatever is upon the horse’s bridle will be holy to the almighty Lord; and the cauldrons that are in the house of the Lord will be like bowls before the altar-house; and every cauldron in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to the almighty Lord.

The Hebrew word *MESULOTH* (מצלות), Aquila and Theodotion translated as βυθόν (*bython*), that is, “depth”; Symmachus as περίπατον σύσκιον (*peripaton syskion*), that is, “a shady walk.” Only the Septuagint translated it as χάλινον (*chalinon*), that is, “bridle”; and we have followed them here, lest we seem to introduce something novel into a familiar question. When I asked a Hebrew what it meant, he said to me:

[Note: [Col. 1539D] If we read *Mesaloth*, or *Metsilloth*, it signifies the bells of horses, which they wear beneath the neck, or the ornament that they have between the eyes, from the root צלצל, *tsatsal*. But if *Mesuloth*, as Aquila and Theodotion read it, we interpret it as “depths” and “abysses,” from the root צול, *tsul*. MART. — In the Reginensis manuscript, *Maselloth*.]

We ought not to read *MESULOTH*, but *MESALOTH*, which signifies the trappings of horses and military ornamentation; and, apart from this passage, this word is found nowhere at all in the books of Holy Scripture. “Bridle,” however, is called *RESEN* (רסן) in Hebrew, not *MESULOTH*, as the Septuagint translated it.

The meaning, then, is this: at the time of perpetual solemnity and of Jerusalem’s kingdom, when all things have been pacified and made tranquil, cavalry will by no means be needed—that most powerful class of combatants—but all the ornament and beauty of the trappings will be devoted to the worship of the Lord. So much for what he said.

Let us refer the “depth” of horses and the shady—or dark—walk, *σύσκιον* (*syskion*), to mystical knowledge. David also boasted that he possessed this as an excellent horse, saying: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. 50:8). And the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways past finding out!” (Rom. 11:33).

Concerning this depth the prophet cried out to the Lord, and He heard him. In these depths and darknesses God placed his hiding place (Ps. 17). Moses entered these darknesses and divine mysteries in the gloom of Mount Sinai in order to see God (Exod. 19). Concerning these David also spoke in another psalm: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:9).

These hidden things and these mysteries are holy to the Lord. The evangelist John knew them, and dared to say what perhaps even the angels did not know: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). For this reason he is loved by the Lord, because he possessed an excellent depth; and he reclined upon Jesus’ breast, from which he also drew wisdom (John 21).

But if we wish to understand “bridle,” as the Septuagint translated it, as the word of God, let us understand by the bridle him who restrains horses raging with lust and sterile, wanton mules from vices, curbs them, and does not allow them to rush headlong. Of these it is said: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding. Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, of those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31:9–10).

James also speaks of this bridle: “We put bits into horses’ mouths, and we turn their whole bodies about” (James 3:3), so that they may walk along the straight path and be able to offer their gentle backs for the Lord to sit upon.

Such a bridle, and such a word, fashioned with the variety of gold and silver, prepares savage horses for the Savior to sit upon; and it makes them holy and specially consecrated to his worship.

I heard from someone a statement that was pious in sentiment, but ridiculous: that the nails of the Lord’s cross, from which the emperor Constantine had made bridles for his horse, should be called holy to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1539D] Indeed, Saint Ambrose spoke in this way in his *Oration on the Death of Theodosius*, no. 47, concerning these nails, which Constantine had used for bridles and for a diadem, and which were transmitted through faith to later kings: “Therefore the beginning of believing emperors is holy, that which is upon the bridle; from it came faith, so that persecution might cease and devotion take its place.” But those who infer from this that Ambrose himself is being censured here by Jerome, with his name suppressed, fail to observe that many others accepted the same interpretation, among them Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret, Sozomen, Paulinus of Aquileia, and Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 6. These writers certainly received it from earlier Fathers and show that the opinion had already become established before Ambrose. Indeed, Jerome himself, when he says that he heard this personally, exempts Ambrose—whom he never addressed—from this censure. Shortly afterward we supplied the adverb that was missing from the manuscripts.]

I leave it to the reader’s judgment whether this should be understood in that way. Let us pass on to the cauldrons, which will be in the house of the Lord like the bowls of the altar.

For every cauldron in Jerusalem and in Judah will be sanctified to the almighty Lord. Let those who have loved the Egyptian pots, the meat, the melons, the garlic, the onions [another reading: *onion bulbs*], and the cucumbers love bronze cauldrons as well (Num. 11).

Let us transform the Jewish cauldrons in which the flesh of sacrifices was boiled into bowls of spices before the Lord’s altar. Concerning these the bride says to the bridegroom: “My beloved has gone down into my garden, to the bowls of spices, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies” (Song 6:1).

The garden and paradise into which the bridegroom descends to the bride is the reading of the holy Scriptures. From these he gathers lilies, violets, roses, and various spices, so that he may fill the bowls of believing souls and pour out libations to the Lord from them.

When such cauldrons have been changed into the Lord’s bowls, and they are able to say, “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Cor. 2:15), and instead of the foul smell of flesh have begun to bear various flowers of virtues, then they will be sanctified to almighty God in Jerusalem and Judah. Of these we have often said that Jerusalem expresses “vision of peace,” and Judah “one who confesses.”

(Verse 21.) And all who sacrifice will come, and they will take from them and boil in them; and there will no longer be a merchant in the house of the Lord of hosts on that day.

The Septuagint: And all who sacrifice will come, and they will take from them and boil in them; and there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the almighty Lord on that day.

[Note: [Col. 1540D] So also our manuscripts and the Greek text have παντοκράτορος (*pantokratoros*, “almighty”). Previously it read *virtutum*, “of hosts.”]

In place of “Canaanite,” Aquila translated “merchant,” and we have followed him here.

When the cauldrons have been changed into bowls, all the surrounding nations—or those who have been left from all the nations—will come, sacrificing,

[Note: [Col. 1540D] In Victorius: “sacrificing to him.”]

and they will take the cauldrons and boil sacrificial flesh in them, so that they will not eat the lamb’s flesh raw, but, after all the moisture of the flesh has been boiled away, what has been prepared by the fire will remain for eating.

What the bowls before the Lord’s altar are, into which the Israelite cauldrons are changed, we have already stated, and we shall now say something further. The bride praises her bridegroom in the *Song of Songs*: “His cheeks are like bowls of spices” (Song 5).

By the cheeks is understood speech, which, when uttered by the Lord, brings forth various perfumes. Its fragrance of good odor will be so great that the Lord will make for himself a whip out of the testimonies of the scriptural text and drive from the temple those who sell and buy, saying to them: “It is written, ‘My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations’; but you have made it a house of trade” (Matt. 21:13).

Some apply to this passage what is written in Daniel, although it is not found in the Hebrew: “Seed of Canaan, and not Judah” (Dan. 13:56); and what the prophet Hosea says about Ephraim: “Ephraim is a participant in idols; he has set up stumbling-blocks for himself; he has provoked the Canaanites; they committed fornication” (Hos. 4:17–18).

[Note: [Col. 1541] The Reginensis manuscript reads: “they committed fornication and were built up,” although the sacred text rejects this.]

They wish every fornicator to be called a Canaanite and a foreigner, and assert that such a person must be removed from the house of God.

[Col. 1541]

THE ONE BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, ON THE PROPHET MALACHI, TO MINERVIUS AND ALEXANDER. (C)

Prologue

[Col. 1541B] 939–940

We intend to interpret Malachi, the last of the twelve prophets. The Septuagint translated his name as “His angel,” saying: “The assumption of the word of the Lord over Israel in the hand of his angel.” In Hebrew, however, it is written *MALACHI* (מלאכי), which is more correctly and precisely rendered “angel,” that is, “my messenger.”

We must not suppose, according to the opinion of certain Origenists, that an angel came down from heaven and assumed a human body in order to speak to Israel the commands that came from the Lord. For if names are to be interpreted, and from names not spiritual understanding but the order of history is to be constructed, then Hosea, whose name means “savior,” and Joel, which is interpreted “the Lord God,” or “beginning,” and the other prophets will not be human beings, but either angels or the Lord and Savior, because their names convey this meaning.

Finally, apart from the Septuagint, the other translators rendered the name *MALACHI* just as it is found in Hebrew. The Hebrews consider Malachi to be Ezra the priest, because this prophet also recalls everything contained in Ezra’s book, saying: “The priest’s lips shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7).

The time and the title also agree. We said the same thing in the Psalms:

[Note: [Col. 1541] On this subject he discussed the matter in our recension, Letter 140 to Cyprian, no. 4.]

Since titles that do not bear names are to be considered the property of those whose names are prefixed to the earlier psalms, Malachi—that is, Ezra—is therefore to be believed to have lived after Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied under Darius.

For this reason his book has no title, because the book itself serves as its title. In it we learn that, during the reign of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, Ezra son of Seraiah and of the others, up to the place where it says, “the son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest,” went up from Babylon at the beginning, and that the king granted him every request according to the hand of the Lord his God.

Those who went up with him from the Israelites included the sons of the priests, the sons of the Levites, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants, to Jerusalem in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king. They arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month. It was the seventh year of the king because Ezra began to go up from Babylon on the first day of the first month and arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month.

These matters, dear Minervius [another reading: *Minerveus*] and Alexander, united not so much by blood as by religion, I have briefly discussed in the Prologue, lest I abandon the work undertaken on the prophets and fail to labor for you with extraordinary effort. With your prayers supporting me, I shall explain what follows, setting forth Malachi’s words first according to the Hebrew truth and then according to the Septuagint translators.

Origen wrote three volumes on this book. But he did not touch the historical meaning at all; following his customary practice, he devoted himself entirely to allegorical interpretation and made no mention of Ezra.

[Col. 1544A]

[Note: [Col. 1543A] We stated above, in the first chapter of Haggai, that this was Origen’s doctrine: that certain human beings distinguished by holiness and more illustrious gifts existed by nature as angels. Since his commentaries on Malachi are lacking, this can be understood very clearly from volume 5 of his commentary on John 1:6, on the verse cited here as well, “Behold, I send my angel before your face,” and so forth. There he says: “Let us consider whether perhaps one of the holy angels, existing in the ministry, is sent down as the forerunner of our Savior; and certainly it is not surprising that, when the firstborn of all creation became incarnate out of love for humanity, some emulators and imitators of Christ came into being who loved to serve his kindness toward human beings through a similar embodiment.”]

He thought that the one who wrote the book was an angel, in accordance with what we read about John: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Matt. 11:10). We do not accept this at all, lest we be compelled to accept the fall of souls from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1543B] “Let us consider whether perhaps one of the holy angels, existing in the ministry, is sent down as the forerunner of our Savior. And certainly it is not surprising that some emulators and imitators of Christ, the firstborn of all creation, who became incarnate out of love for human beings, should have existed—those for whom it was pleasing to serve, through the same likeness of bodily form, the kindness that he had shown toward them.” Jerome, who here explicitly says that he does not accept this at all, elsewhere, in his letters to Evangelus concerning Melchizedek and to Avitus, chapter 1, and in the first book of his *Apology against Rufinus*, censures it at length.]

I do not know of having read other commentaries on this prophet, except for the brief treatise of Apollinaris, which should be called not so much an interpretation as points of interpretation.

[Note: [Col. 1544B] The Reginensis manuscript reads: “points of interpretation.”]

HERE BEGINS THE BOOK

[Col. 1543]

[Col. 1543B] (Chapter I.—Verse 1.) The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel, by the hand of Malachi.

The Septuagint: The assumption of the word of the Lord over Israel, by the hand of his angel.

What “burden” signifies—that is, weight—which in Hebrew is *MASSA* (משא), and which Aquila renders by ἅρμα (*harma*), or what λῆμμα (*lemma*), that is, “assumption,” means, which both the Septuagint and the other translators rendered in this way, we have discussed in other prophets.

For Nahum also writes: “The burden of Nineveh: the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite” (Nah. 2). And Habakkuk: “The burden that Habakkuk the prophet saw” (Hab. 1). And Zechariah: “The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus its resting place” (Zech. 9 and 12). And again later: “The burden of the word of the Lord over Israel.”

Let us therefore be content with that explanation, and let us now say only this: the weight of the word of the Lord to Israel—or, as the Septuagint says, over Israel—is indeed grievous, because it is called a burden, but it contains some consolation, because it is taken not against Israel but to Israel.

For it is one thing when, for example, we write to this or that person, and another when we write against this or that person. In the one case there is an open indication of friendship; in the other, an open confession of hostility.

It must also be understood that after Israel—that is, the ten tribes—had been led into captivity, the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin were likewise indiscriminately called by the former name, Israel.

When it says, “by the hand of his angel,” or Malachi, understand “hand” as referring to works. Thus the word of God also came by the hand of Haggai, by the hand of Jeremiah, and by the hand of Moses.

[Note: [Col. 1544D] Two manuscripts read: “and by the hand of Hosea it came.” From these manuscripts, together with Victorius, we supplied the words “and whose right hand is filled with gifts,” which were lacking in Martianaeus. We also correct lighter matters below.]

For in whose hands there is iniquity, and whose right hand is filled with gifts, and whose hands are full of blood, in them the word of God does not come. Rather, it comes in those who wash their hands among the innocent (Ps. 25). Pilate also tried to wash his hands with these waters, so as not to consent to the blasphemies of the Jews (Matt. 27). Concerning them the Psalmist rejoices, saying: “He led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. 22:2).

Through the prophet the Lord promises concerning this water: “I will sprinkle clean water upon you” (Ezek. 36). But the sinner becomes drunk from the Babylonian cup, and it is said of him: “Thorns grow in the hand of the drunkard” (Prov. 26:9).

The Septuagint: “Set these things upon your hearts.”

This is not found in the Hebrew, but I think it was added from Haggai, where we read: “And now set these things upon your hearts from this day and onward” (Hag. 2:16).

After the prophet’s title, or prologue, this must therefore be understood in two ways. “Set these things upon your hearts,” that is, pay attention to and consider what was said above: “The assumption of the word of the Lord over Israel by the hand of his angel.”

Or else: pay careful attention to what will be said afterward, so that you may know it not with the ears of the body but with the understanding of the mind and heart. Make for yourselves treasuries in which you may receive the riches of God’s words. Let wisdom act confidently when you have been enlarged and, with your heart filled with the words of God, have driven away the worst thoughts that proceed from the heart—murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts (Matt. 15), and the rest—and fulfill what the Savior said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8).

I have loved you, says the Lord. And you said, “In what way have you loved us?” Was not Esau Jacob’s brother, says the Lord? Yet I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau. And I made his mountains desolate and his inheritance into dragons of the wilderness.

But if Edom says, “We have been destroyed, but we shall return and rebuild the things that have been destroyed,” thus says the Lord of hosts: They will build, and I will destroy. And they will be called the boundaries of impiety, and the people with whom the Lord is angry forever.

Your eyes will see, and you will say, “Let the Lord be magnified over the boundary of Israel.”

The Septuagint: I have loved you, says the Lord. And you said, “In what way have you loved us?” Was not Esau Jacob’s brother, says the Lord? Yet I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau. And I made his boundaries desolation and his inheritance into dwellings of the wilderness.

Because Edom will say, “It has been destroyed; let us return and rebuild the desolate places,” thus says the almighty Lord: They will build, and I will destroy. And they will be called the boundaries of iniquity, and the people against whom the Lord has prepared himself forever.

Your eyes will see, and you will say, “The Lord has been magnified over the boundaries of Israel.”

Israel—that is, Judah—to whom the word of God and the vision of the Lord, its burden and the very heavy weight of punishments, used to come, is compelled to bear this burden so that it may lay aside its more grievous sins and learn through torments what it did not learn through benefits.

And lest the punishment inflicted upon his own people seem unjust, the Lord adds: “I have loved you.” For “the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

By saying “I have loved,” he denies the present while confessing the past. They respond to him with the recklessness by which they sin, having forgotten his benefits: “In what way have you loved us?”

The Lord answers them: “To say nothing of other things, and to deal with the fact that you have recently returned from the Babylonian captivity, I will consider your beginnings—before you were born, indeed before Rebecca brought Esau and Jacob forth from her womb (Gen. 25). I loved you in Jacob; I hated the Edomites in Esau.”

The apostle Paul, expounding this passage through a mystical argument, writes to the Romans, joining together two testimonies, one from Genesis and one from Malachi:

“But Rebecca also had conceived by one, even by our father Isaac. For when the children had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works, but from him who calls—it was said to her: ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. 9:10 and following).

The phrase “as it is written” refers both to the book of Genesis and to the prophet Malachi.

The Lord says not only, “I loved Jacob before he was born, and I hated Esau before he was brought forth from his mother’s womb,” but also: “I preserved my love and hatred toward their descendants. I showed hatred toward Esau, whose mountains, called Seir, I reduced to desolation; I made his cities deserted and gave them over to serpents and wild beasts.”

But if Edom—that is, Esau—says, “We have indeed been destroyed”:

[Note: [Col. 1545D] Other books read: “destroyed by the wrath of God.”]

“We shall again build cities,” know what the Lord foretells: while they build, I will destroy, and their eternal desolation will confirm my anger against them.

I therefore demonstrated my hatred toward Esau through events, but I shall demonstrate my love toward you—that is, toward Jacob—in what follows. When they have been destroyed and reduced to desolation, your eyes will see, and you will say: “Let the Lord be magnified over the boundary of Israel.” Through comparison with the evils suffered by your brother, you will perceive God’s benefits toward you.

The Jews falsely flatter themselves that Edom signifies the Romans and that Israel is prophesied to signify the Jews at the consummation of the world: when the Roman empire—that is, Edom—has been destroyed, the rule of the world will come to the Jews.

Having laid, as best we could, the foundations of the historical interpretation, we now come to spiritual understanding.

Israel means “a man” or “one who sees God”; or, as I think better, εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ (*euthytatos Theou*), “the most upright of God.” He is loved by the Lord and wishes to know the reason for the Lord’s love toward him.

The Lord responds that Esau and Jacob, born from one stock, signify vices and virtues proceeding from one source, the heart. From the freedom of the will we incline in either direction as we choose. But vices are born first, during infancy, boyhood, and youth; afterward a more mature age seizes and supplants them.

The elder brother is hairy and bloodstained (Gen. 25); he delights in hunting, forests, and wild beasts. The younger is gentle and simple, dwelling innocently at home.

God makes the boundaries of Edom—that is, of what is earthly and bloodstained—desolate; he allows nothing to grow from the earth or to remain permanently. If shameless wickedness tries to rebuild what has been destroyed by God’s word, the Lord declares himself the adversary of those things that are being rebuilt from vices.

When all the boundaries of the enemy have been overturned, then we shall be able to see the eyes of Israel, and every holy person will be able to say: “Let the Lord be magnified within the boundaries of those who behold God with the mind” (Wis. 11).

God’s love and hatred arise either from foreknowledge of future things or from works. Otherwise, we know that God loves all things and hates nothing that he has created. But he specially claims for his love those who are enemies and rebels against vices. Conversely, he hates those who desire to rebuild what God has destroyed.

God is said to hate ἀνθρωποπάθως (*anthropopathos*), that is, in human terms—as he is said to weep, grieve, and become angry—so that, when we hear of his hatred toward the wicked, we may flee those things that we understand God to hate.

(Vers. 6.) A son honors his father, and a servant his master. Therefore, if I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is my fear? says the Lord of hosts.

The Septuagint: A son glorifies his father, and a servant will fear his master. And if I am a father, where is my glory? And if I am a master, where is my fear? says the almighty Lord.

Although I began to love you as sons in Jacob before you were born, nevertheless choose by what name you wish to call me: either I am your father or your master.

If I am your father, render the honor owed to a father and offer the devotion due to a parent. If I am your master, why do you despise me? Why do you not fear your master?

He speaks to those who returned from the Babylonian captivity under Zerubbabel, Joshua son of Jehozadak, Ezra the priest, and Nehemiah (1 Esd. 3). They had built the altar, but had not yet built the temple or rebuilt the walls of the city; nevertheless, they continued in their former sins, venerating God neither with love nor with fear.

What we have called “glory” or “honor”—δόξα (*doxa*) among the Greeks and *CHABOD* (כבוד) among the Hebrews—is one word. But in keeping with the character of the Latin language, we have used “honor.”

For in the Gospel, when the Lord and Savior says, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1), the Greek reads δόξασον (*doxason*), that is, “glorify.” Many Latin writers have translated this as “honor.”

Let us also consider that in the Holy Scriptures a son and a servant come to be by will, not by necessity of nature. Whoever receives the spirit of adoption is changed into a son of God; whoever receives the spirit of servitude in fear becomes God’s servant (Rom. 8).

God therefore first wishes us to be his sons and to do good willingly. If we cannot attain this, he at least wishes to have us as servants and for us to withdraw from evil through fear of punishments.

We read of “sons” in a negative sense: “We were sons of wrath” and “sons of Gehenna” (Eph. 2:3), whom the Pharisees, traversing sea and land, made worthy of torments (Matt. 23).

Judas the traitor is called “the son of perdition” (John 17). And in Psalm 88 it is written concerning the Lord: “The son of iniquity shall not continue to harm him” (Ps. 88:23).

In Hosea also those born from a prostitute mother are called “sons of fornication,” concerning whom it is written: “Your mother has committed fornication” (Hos. 2:5).

In the Gospel the Jews are mocked as sons of the devil: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires” (John 8:44).

In a good sense we read of sons: “sons of God”—“as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12); “sons of wisdom,” as the Gospel proclaims: “Wisdom has been justified by her sons” (Matt. 11:19); “sons of Abraham”: “Truly I say to you, God is able from these stones to raise up sons for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9); and sons of the Apostle: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19), along with many similar passages.

Therefore a son honors, or glorifies, his father, in accordance with what is written: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

A servant also honors his master, though not with the same love as a son. But by a common construction—*ἀπὸ κοινοῦ*—we understand: “A son honors his father, and a servant his master.”

Nevertheless, almighty God, knowing the distinction between son and servant, seeks glory from the son and fear from the servant: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Eccl. 1:16), so that we may pass from the fear of servants to the glory of sons.

(Vers. 7.) To you, O priests, who despise my name, he says. And you said, “In what way have we despised your name?” You offer polluted bread upon my altar, and you say, “In what way have we polluted you?” In that you say, “The table of the Lord is despised.”

The Septuagint: You priests who despise my name, and you said, “In what way have we despised your name?” Offering polluted loaves upon my altar, you said, “In what way have we polluted them?” In that you say, “The table of the Lord is despised,” and “You have despised the things placed upon it.”

We have marked the words “and you have despised the things placed upon it” with an obelus because they are not found in the Hebrew and were added from what follows.

This word, therefore, is addressed to you, O priests, who despise my name. Having returned from Babylon, you ought, through fear of your former servitude, to have turned to the Lord with your whole mind. But not only do you fail to do this; imitating Cain, you answer God with proud words and question him whose hidden things cannot deceive him: “In what way have we despised your name?” (Gen. 4). Thus, through the shamelessness of dissimulation, you cover the wound of your conscience.

Do you wish to know in what way you have despised my name? You offer polluted bread upon my altar: namely, the bread of the Presence, which, according to Hebrew traditions, you yourselves ought to have sown, reaped, ground, and baked. Now you take whatever is available, and with reckless speech you respond: “In what way have we polluted them—or you?”

When the sacraments are violated, the one whose sacraments they are is himself violated.

The following words, “In that you say, ‘The table of the Lord is despised,’” can be interpreted in this way: after returning from Babylon, before the temple had been built, they lived in huts and amid the ruins of the old city. They had constructed only an altar, not one of the same glory as the former altar, and they thought that the holiness of religion was lacking because the splendor of construction was lacking.

We have drawn only faint lines with which the spiritual explanation must be impressed.

The divine word rebukes negligent bishops, presbyters, and deacons. Or, since we are a priestly and royal race, it rebukes all who, having been baptized in Christ, are reckoned—or, according to another reading, “we are reckoned”—by the name of Christ, asking why they despise the name of God.

When they ask in what way they have despised his name, he shows the causes of the offense: “You offer,” he says, “polluted bread upon my altar.”

We pollute the bread—that is, the body of Christ—when we approach the altar unworthily, and when, being filthy, we drink the pure blood. We say, “The table of the Lord is despised,” not because anyone dares to say this openly or to express with criminal speech what he impiously thinks, but because the works of sinners despise the table of God.

We can also say this in another way: the teacher of the Church who prepares spiritual bread and distributes it to the people, if he speaks among the people and flatters the rich on account of human glory or worldly profits that accompany glory, honors sinners, and, in accordance with James, receives those who come to him wearing gold rings (James 2), while driving away the poor saints, despises the name of God.

He pollutes the bread of doctrine and casts insults against God himself, considering God’s table of Scriptures to be common with the tables of idols and worldly doctrine.

(Vers. 8.) If you offer the blind for sacrifice, is it not evil? And if you offer the lame and the sick, is it not evil? Offer it to your governor, if he is pleased with it or receives your face, says the Lord of hosts.

The Septuagint: If you offer the blind for sacrifice, is it not evil? And if you offer the lame and the sick, is it not evil? Offer it to your governor, if he receives you, if he accepts your face, says the almighty Lord.

We learn more fully in Leviticus about the kinds of sacrifices that ought or ought not to be offered (Lev. 21 and 22).

The priests and Levites who returned from Babylon, together with the gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and servants of Solomon, whose *catalogue* Ezra records with the Greek term κατάλογος (*katalogos*), were offering unlawful sacrifices to God—blind animals, lame animals, and animals afflicted with various weaknesses (1 Esd. 2). This is what he means by “sick,” comprehending all such conditions in a single word.

“If you offer gifts of this kind to your governor,” he says, “would he not reject them? Would he not think that an insult had been done to him? And you dare to offer to God what you do not dare to give to human beings?”

It would take too long now to disclose the mysteries of all the sacrifices. I shall speak only of those contained in the present chapter.

The victim of the soul is blind when it is not illuminated by the light of Christ and does not possess an eye that gazes through the Gospel (Matt. 6).

A prayer is lame when the one praying approaches with a divided mind and hears, together with the Jewish people: “How long will you limp on both feet?” (1 Kings 18:21).

It is sick and covered with every infirmity when it does not possess the power of Christ God and the wisdom of God.

If prayers of this kind—without the light of truth, lacking the firm footprints of wisdom, and wasting away through various weaknesses—are offered to the head of the churches or to any learned and wise teacher, will they not be rejected and fall as an insult upon the one who dared to offer such things?

[Note: [Col. 1549D] Martianaeus corruptly retained *auferre*, “to remove.”]

### (Verse 9)

“And now entreat the face of God, that he may have mercy on you; for this has come from your hand. If somehow he will receive your faces, says the Lord of hosts. Who among you is there who would shut the doors and kindle my altar for nothing?”

The Septuagint: “And now entreat the face of your God, and implore him: these things have come about through your hands. If I receive faces from you, says the Lord Almighty; for even among you the doors will be shut, and my altar will not be kindled for nothing.”

In this passage the translators of the Septuagint differ greatly from the Hebrew truth, and where the translation differs, the meaning must also differ. Because you have offered lame, blind, and defective victims—for you have done all the things I have mentioned—repent, if somehow God may have mercy on you. For there is no one among you, down to the lowest ministry—not, I do not say, a high priest, priest, Levite, or cantor, but not even a doorkeeper, nor the man who puts fire beneath the altar to burn the holocausts—who does not receive payment from me for his labor. By saying this, he indicates the tithes of all the produce that is offered by the peoples. From this it is shown that the service more acceptable to the Lord is that which does not demand payment in the present.

Hence the Apostle preaches the Gospel freely (I Thessalonians 2), and labors with his own hands night and day so as not to burden anyone; and he testifies that this glory of his free preaching among the Gentiles must by no means be surrendered (II Thessalonians 3).

The Septuagint, however, suggests a very different meaning: “O priests who sacrifice defective victims, turn to repentance, and entreat and pray to the face of the Lord for the works of your hands.” But what follows—“If I receive your faces from you”—I do not know whether it suits an exhortation to repentance. No one says, “Pray to me, and I will not spare you.”

It continues: “Among you the doors will be shut,” namely, those of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Hence the Savior says: “I am the door” (John 10:9). Or otherwise: The doors of the Scriptures will not be opened to you; you will not be able to perceive the Holy of Holies or recognize the Lord’s mysteries, nor kindle his incense upon the altar, because your prayers will not reach him.

And this word, δωρεάν, which we have translated as “for nothing” or “freely”—those who follow the interpretation that we are now explaining translate as “grace,” so that they apparently do not have the grace to serve at the Lord’s altar.

### (Verses 10ff.)

“I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts. But you profane it by saying, ‘The table of the Lord is polluted,’ and, ‘What is placed upon it is contemptible, together with the fire that consumes it.’ And you have said, ‘Look, what weariness!’ and you have sniffed at it with contempt, says the Lord of hosts. You brought what had been taken by robbery, the lame and the sick, and you brought an offering. Shall I accept it from your hand? says the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “My will is not among you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept sacrifice from your hands, because from the rising of the sun to its setting my glorious name is among the nations; and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty. But you have profaned it by saying, ‘The table of the Lord is polluted,’ and, ‘Those things placed upon it are despised, his foods’; and you have said, ‘These things are from affliction,’ and you have sniffed at them with contempt, says the Lord Almighty. And you brought what had been taken by robbery, the lame and the defective, and you offered a sacrifice. If I accept them from your hands, says the Lord Almighty?”

[Note: Some manuscripts of the Reginensis read “Look” instead of “these things,” in agreement with the Greek Complutensian exemplar, which, as we know, more often adheres to the version praised by Jerome: ἰδού (“look”) instead of ταῦτα (“these things”).]

There is a rule of Scripture: When a very clear prophecy concerning future events is woven into the text, one must not weaken what is written through uncertain allegory. Therefore the Lord’s speech is now addressed literally to the priests of the Jews, who offer the blind, the lame, and the defective for sacrifice, so that they may know that spiritual victims will succeed carnal victims. They will offer the Lord not the blood of bulls and goats, but incense—that is, the prayers of the saints—and the offering will be made not in one province of the world, Judaea, nor in one city of Judaea, Jerusalem, but in every place: not an unclean offering, as among the people of Israel, but a pure one, as in the ceremonies of Christians.

[Note: Victor says that Jerome calls the Christian ceremonies the Mass, which the Greeks call λειτουργία (“liturgy”): “While they were ministering—or, more properly, sacrificing—and fasting to the Lord, the Holy Spirit said …” (Acts 13:2). Clement the Martyr, Basil, and Chrysostom also give the Mass this name. That it is a sacrifice you can learn not only here from Jerome’s learned discussion, but more fully and clearly in his exposition of Ezekiel 46. I cannot therefore help but marvel at the madness of the new heretics, who, contrary to Christ’s own institution and the perpetual practice and consensus of the whole Church, remove from the faithful the sacrifice of which the whole world has never been deprived. I could refute this falsehood at length if others before us had not already done so learnedly and abundantly, or if we were now composing disputations rather than scholia.]

“For from the rising of the sun to its setting the Lord’s name is great among the nations,” as the Savior says: “Father, I have manifested your name to human beings” (John 17:6). And since, he says, my name will be great among the nations, O rulers of the Jews, you have profaned and are profaning it.

For this reason, O priests and rulers of the Jews, “in every place an offering is made to me,” and my name is great among the nations, because you say, “The table of the Lord is polluted, and what is placed upon it is contemptible, together with the fire that consumes it.”

After returning from Babylon, the people built only an altar of rough and unworked stones, according to the Book of Ezra (I Ezra 6), without a temple, without the buildings of the city, and without the construction of walls. They supposed that the worship of religion was inferior because the temple’s adornment was lacking.

The Lord speaks to them: You consider the altar polluted, and the holocausts and victims placed upon it polluted; you also consider the fire that consumes the victims polluted. You do not understand that almighty God seeks not gold, gems, and a multitude of victims, but the intentions of those who offer them.

Those who think that not the altar but the table should be understood—on which the loaves were placed—cannot, I do not see how, interpret what follows, “together with the fire that consumes it.” For the fire does not consume the loaves of the Presence, which they always exchanged, new ones for old, and the removed loaves passed into the use of the priests (Leviticus 2:4).

Or certainly it should be understood in this way: “You have profaned my name by saying, ‘What benefit is there if we offer the best things? Whatever may be offered must be consumed by fire.’” The fruit of the altar is fire, and the food of the fire is the victim or the holocaust.

Nor was the impiety of the earlier statement enough; you also said: “Look, it is from weariness,” and you sniffed at it with contempt, says the Lord of hosts. The meaning of this statement is: You said, “We have returned from captivity; we were the spoil of our enemies; we labored greatly on the long journey; we are poor; whatever we have been able to possess has been consumed by the hardship of the road. Whatever we have, we offer.” By saying this, you have sniffed at your sacrifices with contempt—that is, you have made them worthy of my contempt.

Or, as it can be read in Hebrew: “And you sniffed at me by saying these things.” You have not wronged the sacrifice, but me, to whom you were sacrificing. Therefore I will certainly not accept it from your hand, says the Lord Almighty.

Some think that this passage, which is spoken specifically about the Jews because their victims are unclean and polluted and the sacrifice is transferred to the Gentiles, should be understood as referring to the priests of the Church who negligently offer victims to the Lord. If we accept this, then the victims must once again be transferred from the Church to another religion.

[Note: Some manuscripts read differently and preserve another sense: “And how do we read the Gospel, if in turn things that are not to come will succeed the Gospel?”—MART.]

“And just as the Gospel succeeds the Law, so in turn things that are not to come will succeed the Gospel.” They also refer the polluted table of the Lord to the holy Scriptures, if they are understood otherwise than they were written.

### (Chapter II, verses 1–2)

“Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male in his flock, but, when making a vow, sacrifices a defective animal to the Lord. For I am a great king, says the Lord of hosts, and my name is fearsome among the nations.”

[The Vulgate omits “I am.”]

[Note: Beginning of chapter II according to the Septuagint.]

“And now this command is for you, O priests: If you will not listen, and if you will not take it to heart, so as to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send poverty upon you, and I will curse your blessings; indeed, I will curse them, because you have not taken it to heart.”

The Septuagint: “And cursed is the powerful man who had a male in his flock, and his vow was upon it, yet he sacrificed a defective animal to the Lord; because I am a great king, says the Lord Almighty, and my name is illustrious among the nations. And now this command is for you, O priests: If you will not listen, and if you will not take it to heart, so as to give glory to my name, says the Lord Almighty, I will send a curse upon you, and I will curse your blessing, and I will curse it—”

[The text contains signs indicating a corruption or interpolation here.]

“—and I will scatter your blessing, and it will not be yours, because you do not take it to heart.”

The words “and I will scatter your blessing” were added by the Septuagint and are not found in the Hebrew.

Whatever the human mind can discover as an excuse for its sin, and whatever false defense it can use to justify itself, the divine word, foreseeing this, rebukes and condemns. The meaning is this: You offer the blind, the lame, and the defective, and not from what belongs to you, but from what you have taken by robbery and plunder and from the tears of the wretched; and in addition you say, “From weariness and poverty we offer what we have.” Therefore I speak generally, so that your own conscience may accuse you.

Certainly you plead poverty, the injustice of captivity, and the smallness of your possessions. Hear what I add: “Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male in his flock, but, when making a vow, sacrifices a defective animal to the Lord.” If you have no male, the curse does you no harm. By saying this, he shows that they have what is best but offer what is bad.

Therefore this command is addressed to you, O priests: You have done what is impious, in contempt of me. But because I prefer the sinner’s repentance to his death, I say even now: If you will not listen to me or understand, so as to give glory to my name, which is fearsome among the nations, I will truly send poverty upon you, so that you will no longer lie but, compelled by want of everything, will say that you do not have the best things to offer.

“And I will curse your blessings,” he says—that is, those things that you now possess through my blessings. Or whatever is blessed by you will be cursed by me. “And I will curse them”—the blessings, that is—because you were unwilling to understand what is said. This is what is meant by “you have not taken it to heart.”

We can understand “the cursed and deceitful man” as the people of the Jews. Although they had in their flock the male, the Lord and Savior, and the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1), and although they had been admonished by the prophecies of all the prophets to sacrifice and receive the ram caught by its horns in the thicket of Sabec (Genesis 22), they refused to do this. Instead they sacrificed a defective victim to the Lord by crucifying the Savior and choosing Barabbas, the instigator of robbery and sedition (John 18), who according to mystical interpretations refers to the devil.

When they despised and preferred the devil to the Savior, the name of Christ became fearsome among the nations, which accepted the Lord’s Passion and worship him with reverent honor.

This can also be said of us: If, having been created by God as intelligent and possessing a nature suited to sacred disciplines, we neglect our understanding and surrender ourselves to vices and sensuality, then, although we have a male, we sacrifice a defective victim to the Lord.

Our prayer is defective and polluted when it is corrupted by anger, envy, hostility, or another disturbance of the soul; when, bringing our gift to the altar and remembering that our brother has something against us, we do not first go and make peace with him (Matthew 5:23).

Hence the Apostle also commands: “I desire, therefore, that men pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger or dispute” (I Timothy 2:8).

The shepherd of our thoughts and virtues is the mind, of which it is said in the hundred-and-second Psalm: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name.” If he has ruled his flock well, that blessing is fulfilled in him: “Blessed are the herds of your oxen and the flocks of your sheep” (Deuteronomy 28:4).

But if, naturally possessing a male—that is, something strong, firm, and robust—he sacrifices something weak, excessively soft, feminine, and wanton, or something weakened and corrupted by various disturbances of the soul, he will find fulfilled in himself what is written: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6:7). And: “To whom more has been given, more will be demanded of him” (Luke 8).

Therefore it is said specifically to the priests that, if they will not listen and retain in their hearts so as to give glory to the Lord’s name by good conduct (Romans 2)—while, on the contrary, his name is blasphemed among the nations because of them—he will send poverty upon them in every good thing and turn their blessings into a curse.

Those who abuse health for lust, turn wealth into sensuality, and defile a good reputation by filthy conduct change God’s blessings into a curse.

Or certainly, because the command is addressed specifically to priests, their blessings are turned into a curse when they do not bless holy people with a true affection of the heart, as Isaac blessed Jacob, Jacob blessed the patriarchs, and Moses blessed the twelve tribes (Genesis 27 and 49; Deuteronomy 33). Instead, through flattering words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent (Romans 16), bless those who act unjustly, flatter sinners provided they are rich, and indulge their vices. Of such people it is said: “My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and pervert the paths of your feet” (Isaiah 3:11).

### (Verses 3–4)

“Behold, I will cast the arm at you, and I will scatter upon your faces the dung of your festivals, and it will carry you away with it. And you will know that I sent this command to you, so that my covenant might be with Levi, says the Lord of hosts.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, I will separate the shoulder for you, and I will scatter the stomach upon your face—the stomach of your festivals—and I will receive you together. And you will know that I sent this command to you, so that my covenant might be with the Levites, says the Lord Almighty.”

Because he is speaking to the priests, he says: “I will throw upon your faces the things that you consider holiest in the Law and that were granted to you by God from the victims as a reward for your virtues”: the shoulder-blade, which the Septuagint translated as “shoulder,” that is, the animal’s right foreleg.

“And I will scatter,” he says, the ἔνυστρον—that is, the stomach—or, according to the Hebrews, the dung, namely PHARES (), using metonymy: calling the container by the name of what it contains. For the priests received from the victims the foreleg, the breast, the tongue, the stomach, and the other portions described in Leviticus (chapters 7 and 9).

He declares that he will cast all these away from himself because of their sins and throw them into the faces of the priests (Numbers 18; Deuteronomy 18), so that those who offer may be such as the things offered are.

“And it will carry you away with it,” he says—that is, the dung of your festivals—so that your foul faces may be disfigured by a filthy mixture of dung. From the fact that I cast you away, you will understand that I am the same one who once chose your father Levi, and through Levi, Aaron, and granted you the glory of the priesthood, so that my covenant—or testament—might be with Levi and he might minister to me in an everlasting priesthood.

It should be noted that the Hebrew word BRITH (), “covenant,” is translated by Aquila as συνθήκη, that is, “agreement” or “covenant.” The Septuagint always has διαθήκη, that is, “testament.” In many passages of Scripture, however, “testament” does not mean the will of the dead but the covenant of the living.

God desired all human beings, but especially priests, to be without blemish, and to adorn either the shoulder or the arm with good works. The breast signifies a good conscience; the tongue, holy confession, so that what we believe in the heart for righteousness we may confess with the mouth for salvation (Romans 10).

The stomach, too, should contain nothing deadly, but only what sustains and nourishes our life. For unless food is digested in the stomach and the body is irrigated by its nourishment, the body becomes weakened, loses its strength, and moves toward death.

We, however, turn everything in the opposite direction. The Lord throws away our arm, or separates our works from the works of the saints; and although we have been commanded, while fasting, to anoint our head and wash our face from the filth of sins, and with unveiled face to contemplate the Lord’s glory (II Corinthians 3), we now say: “The confusion of my face has covered me” (Psalm 43:16). Like Cain, our face has fallen (Genesis 4), and we cannot fulfill what was commanded: “Lift up your eyes and see” (Jeremiah 13:20).

Instead, our faces are smeared and polluted with the dung of vices, and we say: “My wounds have become foul and festering, because of my foolishness” (Psalm 37:6).

Therefore all these things have been turned into dung, as Scripture says: “And the dung will carry you away with it”—the dung with which our faces are smeared, although we ought to come to God’s festivals full and clean: either to eat the flesh of the lamb with our sandals on (Exodus 12), or, after completing seven weeks, to offer God the fruits of our works (Leviticus 23), or to live as travelers in the tabernacles of this world and say: “I am a sojourner with you and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Psalm 38).

Because we have translated the phrase as “the dung will carry you away with it,” whereas the Septuagint translated it, “I will receive you together,” the Septuagint wording introduces the interpretation that, after the priests have been covered with disgrace and shame, understood their sin, and repented, they will then be received by the Lord. This interpretation suits what follows: “And you will know that I sent this command to you.”

Nevertheless, the former interpretation seems truer to me, lest words of one who flatters should be placed amid words of threat, especially since what follows also expresses God’s anger.

### (Verses 5ff.)

“My covenant with him was one of life and peace, and I gave him fear, and he feared me, and he was afraid before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found upon his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many away from iniquity. For the lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the Law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

The Septuagint: “My testament with him was one of life and peace, and I gave him fear, so that he might fear me, and he was afraid before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found upon his lips. Walking in peace and directing others, he walked with me, and he turned many away from iniquity. For the lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and the law will be sought from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord Almighty.”

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript, following the Greek, has “so that he might fear me with fear,” ἐν φόβῳ φοβεῖσθαί με.]

The perfect duty of a priest is described here in the person of God: what he ought to be and what the one who commanded him to exist in that form wished him to be.

Earlier he had said: “So that my covenant might be with Levi, says the Lord of hosts.” Through the patriarch Levi it reached his descendants—Aaron and Eleazar, Phinehas, and the others born from his line. Now at the end he says: “You have invalidated the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts.”

From this it is clear that everything said concerning Levi refers to the priests, and specifically to the high priest.

We read in Numbers about Phinehas, who struck Zimri with a dagger together with the Midianite woman:

“Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, turned away my wrath from the children of Israel, because he was jealous with my jealousy against them, and I did not destroy the children of Israel in my jealousy,” and he says: “Behold, I give him my covenant of peace, and it shall be for him and for his offspring after him a covenant of everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and made atonement for the children of Israel” (Numbers 25:11).

We should not understand the “covenant of life,” or covenant, as referring to the life that we share with beasts and all living creatures, but to the life that says: “I am life” (John 14:6). For our life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3). Of him we can say that he himself is also our peace, as the Apostle confirms: “For he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

Therefore the Lord gave Levi, and through him his descendants, the command to fear him. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110:10). They were to be afraid before his face, or to withdraw and draw back, indicating the fear of the mind by the trembling of the body, according to what is written: “Upon whom will I look, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

“The law of truth was in his mouth”—that is, the teaching of the peoples, which in a priest must not be corrupted by any lie but must proceed entirely from the fountain of truth.

“And iniquity was not found upon his lips,” so that he might imitate his Lord, of whom it is said: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Peter 2:22).

“He walked with me in peace and uprightness,” so that he might possess peace within himself and make peace for others, show partiality toward no one in judgment, and therefore walk with God, as Enoch walked, who was transferred to the Lord and was not found (Genesis 5).

“And he turned many away from iniquity.” Whoever is a priest and does not rebuke those who sin neglects the priestly office.

“The lips of a priest will guard knowledge.” He did not say “will proclaim,” but “will guard,” so that they may speak at the proper time and give their fellow servants their food at the proper time.

“And they will seek the law from his mouth.” The same thing is written in Haggai: “Ask the priests about the law of the Lord” (Haggai 2:12).

It belongs to the discipline of a priest to answer questions about the Law. If, while diligently displaying knowledge in other matters, he shows negligence in the holy Scriptures, he boasts in vain of a dignity whose works he does not perform.

This is what the Apostle Paul writes to Titus: “So that he may be able to exhort with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1:9). And to Timothy: “Since childhood you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation, so that you may rebuke sinners publicly” (II Timothy 3:15, 13).

It follows: “Because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

Ezra, priest of God, explains the name Malachi, which means “angel of the Lord.” An angel, that is, a messenger, is most truly called a priest of God, because he is the mediator between God and human beings and announces his will to the people.

For this reason there is a breastpiece on the priest’s chest (Exodus 29), and doctrine and truth are placed in the breastpiece, so that we may learn that a priest must be learned and must proclaim the Lord’s truth.

Some falsely think that what is said about Levi, and through Levi about the priests, should be understood as referring to Christ, without considering what follows, which is contrary to the person of Christ.

### (Verses 8–9)

“But you have departed from the way and caused many to stumble in the Law. You have invalidated the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts. Therefore I have made you contemptible and lowly before all the peoples, just as you have not kept my ways and have shown partiality in the Law.”

The Septuagint: “But you have turned aside from my way and weakened many in the Law; you have corrupted the testament of Levi, says the Lord Almighty. And I have made you contemptible and dissolved among all the nations, because you did not keep my ways but showed partiality in the Law.”

A prudent reader understands, even without my saying so, that this does not pertain to the person of Christ or to those dedicated to his worship.

The meaning is this: I wanted you to do what is contained in the preceding chapter and what I spoke through Moses in Deuteronomy: “Give Levi his instruction and truth to the righteous man” (Deuteronomy 33:8, according to the Septuagint), and what follows.

But you have departed from the straight way, or turned aside, although I said: “You shall not turn aside either to the right or to the left” (Deuteronomy 5:32). You have weakened many in the Law, or caused many to stumble, as Aquila and Symmachus translated it.

To turn aside to the right is to abstain from foods that God created to be used, to condemn marriage, and to fall into what is written elsewhere: “Do not be overly righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7:17).
