To turn aside to the left is for someone to give himself over to luxury and lust and to cause many to stumble in the Law. For such a person it would be better for a millstone to be hung around his neck and for him to be thrown into the sea than for him to cause one of the little ones to stumble.

Those who weaken many are those who, after believers in Christ have received the strength of faith, weaken them through the negligence of their own conduct. To them it is rightly said: “You have invalidated the covenant of Levi, the covenant of life and peace,” and the rest of what we said pertains to the priestly office.

“For this reason,” he says, “I have made you contemptible and lowly before all the peoples,” so that they would despise you and, instead of honoring and glorifying you, trample you as rejected and abject people.

“Just as you have not kept my ways and have shown partiality in the Law.”

Among all the sins of Levi—or of those descended from Levi, the priests of God—this is placed last and regarded as the greatest: that they show partiality in the Law, considering not causes but persons, despising the just poor and receiving and honoring the unjust rich.

To them it is said in the eighty-first Psalm: “How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to sinners?” (Psalm 81:2). And Paul says to the Galatians: “God does not show partiality to a human being” (Galatians 2:6).

The Apostle James argues against and condemns this sin more fully (James 2).

Whatever is said to the people of the former covenant, let us consider said also to us, so that we may withdraw more cautiously from vices, show no partiality in the Law, and, although we are worshipers of God, prefer no falsehood to the truth.

### (Verses 10 ff.)

“Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Why, then, does each of us despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers? Judah has transgressed, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah has profaned the sanctuary of the Lord, which he loved, and has taken the daughter of a foreign god. May the Lord destroy the man who does this, master and disciple, from the tents of Jacob, and the one who offers an offering to the Lord of hosts.”

The Septuagint reads: “Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created you? Why have you each abandoned your brother, so as to profane the covenant of your fathers? Judah has been abandoned, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah has profaned the holy things of the Lord, in which he delighted, and has found for himself foreign gods. May the Lord destroy the man who does these things, until he is expelled from the tents of Jacob, and from among those who offer sacrifice to the Lord Almighty.”

Before we discuss the present chapter, the tradition of the Hebrews must be set forth—or rather, the truth of Scripture must be explained. We read in the book that bears the title of Ezra, spoken in the person of Ezra himself:

“The princes came to me, saying: The people of Israel, and the priests and Levites, have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands, but from their abominations, namely, from the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites. For they have taken daughters from among them for themselves and for their sons, and have mingled the holy seed with the peoples of the lands. The hand of the princes and magistrates was also foremost in this transgression. When I heard this report, I tore my cloak and tunic, pulled out the hair of my head and beard, and sat mourning” (I Esdras 9:1 ff.).

And again, later:

“Among the sons of the priests were found those who had taken foreign wives: among the sons of Jeshua son of Jozadak, and his brothers, Maaseiah, Eleazar, Jarib, and Gedaliah. They pledged themselves to put away their wives, and for their guilt they offered a ram from the flock” (I Esdras 10:18–19).

At the end of the chapter, after listing those who had taken foreign wives, Scripture also records:

“All these had taken foreign wives, and among them were women who had borne children.”

After their return from the Babylonian captivity, therefore, the princes, priests, Levites, and the rest of the people put away their Israelite wives, who, worn down by poverty, the hardships of the long journey, and the weakness of their sex, had not been able to endure the labor and had acquired bodily weakness and deformity. [Note: One manuscript reads: “had been broken by the toil.”] They entered into marriages with foreign women who were either in the flower of youth, more beautiful in bodily appearance, or daughters of the powerful and wealthy.

The prophet Ezra therefore rebukes them and urges them to repudiate their new wives, so that they may take back the wives whom they had dismissed:

“Is not one father,” he says, “Abraham, the father of us all? Concerning him it is written in Isaiah: ‘Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you, because he was one, and I called him’” (Isaiah 51:2). “Has not one God created us, who chose our race from Abraham? Why, then, do we despise our former wives and cast away the daughters of our brothers, abandoning the covenant of our fathers and failing to take wives according to the Law?”

“Judah has transgressed”—for this was the tribe that returned from Babylon with the priests and Levites—“and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem.” This does not refer to the ten tribes, which were held by the Assyrians, but to those who returned from Babylon at the command of King Cyrus, under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah. [Note: One manuscript, supported by the Reginensis manuscript and Victorius, reads “those [cities] of Cyrus”; consequently, “have returned” follows.]

“Because Judah has profaned the sanctuary of the Lord, which he loved, and has taken the daughter of a foreign god”: that is, by mingling the seed of Israel with that of foreigners and taking as wives the daughters of the nations—that is, of the pagans—who served idols.

Because they did this, the prophetic word is directed against them, and they are recalled from their sin by curses:

“May the Lord destroy the man who does this.”

How beautifully he does not cut off forgiveness from error, nor say, “May the Lord curse the one who has done this,” but rather, “the one who will do this,” directing the curse toward the future, so that he may call sinners to repentance.

“Master and disciple,” he says, “from the tents of Jacob”—whether he is a priest or a layman, they will be struck by one and the same curse. There will be no difference in punishment among those whose sins are equal.

“And the one who offers an offering to the Lord of hosts”: this means that the Lord should also destroy the one who wishes to offer an offering at the altar on behalf of such men. Their only remedy is not to do what those men have done.

Some, not understanding this passage and not knowing the truth of its history, interpret the words, “Have we not all one father?” as referring to Abraham, and even call Abraham the father of the nations, according to what is written: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:9).

Others, however, affirm that the one Father is the one God, in accordance with what we read in Deuteronomy: “Is he not himself your Father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?” (Deuteronomy 32:6). And again: “You have forgotten the God who created you” (ibid., 18). Elsewhere: “I have begotten and raised children, but they have abandoned me” (Isaiah 1:2). And in the book of Psalms: “The children of strangers have lied to me; the children of strangers have grown old and have limped from their paths” (Psalm 17:46).

And by departing from this one Father, those who sinned made many fathers for their vices: “For everyone who commits sin is born of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

They interpreted the following words—“Why does each of us despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers?”—in this way: We were all begotten by one father and ought to be one, possessing one language of confession; but afterward, through pride and the building of the tower against God, we were divided into many languages and opinions (Genesis 11).

They also refer the passage to almsgiving, saying that we despise our brothers when we do not share with them the things we have received from God for the support of life.

They proceed further and assert that, according to Scripture, our brother is called “the Lord.” Thus the Lord commanded Mary Magdalene to announce to his brothers that the Lord had risen (John 20), and he says in the Psalm: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing to you” (Psalm 21:23).

The Jews, therefore, abandoned their brother and profaned the covenant of their fathers, which God had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so that in their seed—which is interpreted as Christ—all the nations might be blessed.

They conjecture these things in various ways because they do not find a certain path. Finally, they also explain the words that follow according to the Septuagint—“Judah has been abandoned, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem”—as follows: The Jews have been abandoned because they blasphemed the Lord Savior, and they have endured what is written: “According to the multitude of their ungodliness, drive them out, for they have provoked you, O Lord” (Psalm 5:11), so that they would be scattered as wanderers and exiles throughout all the provinces.

“For they have profaned the holy things of the Lord,” loving foreign gods instead of the Son of God and finding gods for themselves. “For whoever does not receive the Son does not receive the Father who sent him” (Luke 9:43).

And because they did this, they would perish until they were humbled, either by the hardship of captivity or by consciousness of their sins, and would be cast out from the tents of Jacob, so that, after the temple and altar had been destroyed, sacrifices—or, according to another reading, beasts—would no longer be offered among them.

Not content with this explanation—for Judah is interpreted as “confession of the Lord”—they transfer the meaning to the penitent person. After confessing the Lord, if he sins, he commits an abomination in Israel and in Jerusalem, in the understanding that sees God and in the vision of peace.

For he pollutes the mysteries of Christ by receiving his body and blood unworthily (1 Corinthians 11), because he has loved vices and found foreign gods for himself, possessing as many gods as he has sins.

According to the apostle Paul, “their god is the belly” (Philippians 3:19), and according to Peter—or, in another reading, James—“by whatever anyone is conquered, by that he is subjected” (2 Peter 2:19).

Whoever does this will be exterminated—or, according to another reading, is exterminated—from the Church and from the tents of Jacob, which overthrows vices and sins, until he is humbled for his own good and a victim is offered for him to the Lord Almighty.

### (Verses 13 ff.)

“And this you have done again: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping and groaning—or, according to the Vulgate, with howling—so that I will no longer look upon the sacrifice or accept anything favorable from your hand. And you said: ‘For what reason?’ Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have despised. She is your companion and the wife of your covenant. Did not one make them, and is there not the remnant of his spirit? And what does the one seek except the seed of God? Guard your spirit, therefore, and do not despise the wife of your youth. When you hate her, send her away, says the Lord God of Israel; but iniquity will cover his garment, says the Lord of hosts. Guard your spirit and do not despise her.”

The Septuagint reads:

“And again you have done these things that I hate: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, lamentation, and groaning, so as no longer to look upon the sacrifice or receive anything acceptable from your hands. And you said: ‘For what reason?’ Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you abandoned, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make one, and is there not the remnant of your spirit? And you said: ‘What else does God seek except seed?’ Guard your spirit, therefore, and do not abandon the wife of your youth. But if, because you hate her, you send her away, says the Lord God of Israel, impiety will cover your thoughts, says the Lord Almighty. Guard your spirit and do not abandon her.”

Let us interpret the history and, fitting brief explanations to each verse, discuss what has been handed down to us by the Hebrews.

The Israelite wives who had been abandoned, seeing foreign women in the beds of their husbands, fled to the help of the one God. Day and night they lay prostrate before the altar of the Lord, making his providence the object of reproach with their tears, groaning, and wailing, because he did not regard human affairs and did not assist the wretched.

Therefore God says that he cannot receive sacrifice and offering from the hands of the priests who committed these things, being hindered by the tears and lamentations of their wives. He also asks them why he does not accept sacrifice from their hands, and immediately adds:

“Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have despised,” saying: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).

For this reason she is called a companion, a wife of union, and a wife of the covenant: she was made by God from the man’s rib.

“And the remnant of his spirit”—whether of God, as some think, or of the husband, as others suppose—means that, because of their affection, one soul seems somehow to exist in two, joined in spirit and united in mind.

Since one made both, man and woman, their union was made by God for the purpose of producing children. For the one God seeks nothing except the seed of God—that is, children begotten from the Israelite stock.

Since, then, you have fertile wives and rejoice in children, why do you seek the beauty of wives, which is appropriate to prostitutes, not to wives?

Through the prophet, therefore, God commands and says: “Guard your spirit”; do not be led away by lust, and do not be conquered by love of foreign women.

“And do not despise the wife of your youth,” so that she who was first joined to you in virginal marriage may remain with you into old age.

But it could happen that the princes, priests, Levites, and people would reply: God commanded through Moses that when we hate our wives, we should send them away.

The reading should therefore be understood as follows: “You say to me: ‘It is written, When you hate your wife, send her away,’ says the Lord God of Israel” (Deuteronomy 24).

He immediately replies: This was indeed commanded in the Law, but because of the hardness of your hearts. The Lord develops this more fully in the Gospel: “Whoever unjustly sends away his wife, except on account of fornication” (Matthew 5:32), “his iniquity will cover his garment”—that is, the body with which the soul is clothed—says the Lord of hosts, so that he may be punished in the very thing in which he sinned.

Therefore, after resolving this little question, he repeats and reinforces what he had said above: “Guard your spirit and do not despise her”—whether this means guarding your spirit, or the wife herself, if she is poor or deformed.

What we have explained specifically, following the book of Ezra, concerning abandoned wives, others believe was spoken generally against those who seize what belongs to others and, gathering riches unjustly, dare to offer gifts to God—gifts that he says he cannot receive, being prevented by the tears, weeping, and groaning of those who have been despoiled.

They appropriately connect this passage with the saying: “Honor God from your just labors” (Proverbs 3:9).

They also introduce the following interpretation: those who, because of the loss of their property, the death of their children, shipwreck, and other things belonging to worldly loss, are turned to tears and give themselves entirely to lamentation and groaning, without despising all things through strength of mind, hope in God, and the rewards of the future—even if they direct a prayer to God, it is not received by him, because they disfigure themselves with lamentations that are unseemly and inappropriate for a man.

They interpret the following words—“Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your youth, or adolescence, whom you have despised; she is your companion and the wife of your covenant or testament; and no other made her, and she is the remnant of your spirit”—in this way: They call the natural understanding “the wife of youth,” and the law written in the heart, which has been implanted in all human beings.

Hence even the nations that do not have the law of God do the things of the Law.

This wife is also praised in Proverbs: “A wife is joined to a man by God” (Proverbs 19:14). We are commanded to drink from our own waters and springs; no one else is to share in drinking, and we are to rejoice with the wife of our youth.

This wife even prompts unbelievers to say: “Let God judge, and let God see” (Judges 7:13). To her I entrust the judgment of everything between me and you.

Ecclesiastes also speaks of her: “Live life with the wife whom you have loved all the days of your vain life” (Ecclesiastes 9:9). [Note: The former reading was “of your birth,” nearly echoed by the Aldine Greek exemplar, νεότητος (“youth”). But nearly all manuscripts read “of your vanity,” as does the more correct Greek text, ματαιότητος (“vanity”); finally, the Hebrew and the Vulgate support the printed reading.]

This wife is the remnant of our spirit, because she is always joined to our understanding. If she departs from us, we immediately offend God, and our own impiety covers us.

Thus the command is repeated: “Guard your spirit” (Galatians 6)—not the flesh, since those who are in the flesh cannot please God; not the soul, since “the natural person does not receive the things that belong to the Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:14); but the spirit, because “the Spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Romans 8:26).

### (Verse 17)

“You have wearied the Lord with your words, and you said: ‘How have we wearied him?’ By saying: ‘Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him’; or else: ‘Where is the God of judgment?’”

The Septuagint reads:

“You have provoked the Lord with your words, and you said: ‘How have we provoked you?’ By saying: ‘Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he delights in such people’; and: ‘Where is the God of justice?’”

One manuscript reads *provocavimus eum* (“we have provoked him”), in accordance with the Greek *παρωξύναμεν αὐτὸν* (“we provoked him”), whereas the Aldine codex has *σε* (“you”) instead.

The seventy-second Psalm develops this passage more fully. It begins:

“How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart! But my feet almost stumbled; my steps nearly slipped, because I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners. For they have no regard for their death, and there is no firmness in their affliction. They are not in the troubles of mortals, nor are they scourged with other people” (Psalm 72:1 ff.).

And afterward:

“I said, then, ‘In vain I have justified my heart, and washed my hands among the innocent.’”

The people, therefore, returning from Babylon and seeing all the surrounding nations—including the Babylonians, who served idols—abounding in wealth, flourishing in bodily strength, and possessing everything that is considered good in this world, while they themselves, though possessing knowledge of God, were covered with squalor, hunger, and servitude, were scandalized and said:

“There is no providence in human affairs. Everything is driven by uncertain chance and is not governed by God’s judgment. Rather, evil pleases him and good displeases him. Or, if God judges everything, where is his fair and just judgment?”

The unbelieving mind raises this kind of question against God every day when it sees the wicked powerful and the saints humble; when it sees the former overflowing with every possession, while the latter do not even have the necessities of life; and when it sees them sometimes deaf in their ears, blind in their eyes, covered in ulcers over every part of their bodies, and weighed down by illness, like Lazarus, who is read of in the Gospel (Luke 16) as desiring to sustain his needy soul with the crumbs thrown away from the remains of the tables before the gate of the purple-clad rich man.

The rich man was of such ferocity and cruelty that one human being did not pity another, though even the tongues of dogs had pity on the latter. Not understanding the time of judgment, nor that true goods are those which are everlasting, they say: “Evil pleases him, and where is the God of judgment?”

### (Chapter 3, verse 1)

“Behold, I send—or, according to another reading, ‘I shall send’—my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face. And immediately the ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Behold, I shall send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face. And suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of justice whom you desire.”

The Lord interpreted this passage in the Gospel concerning John the Baptist, saying:

“This is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I shall send my angel before your face, and he will prepare your way before me’” (Matthew 11:10).

He did not use the same words that the Septuagint translators rendered. [Note: Victorius changes “I shall send” to “I send,” “and he will prepare” to “and he prepared,” and “before me” to “before you,” from Matthew’s text; otherwise, he says, the Evangelist would have used almost the same words as the Septuagint. Jerome’s manuscripts, however, do not differ here from the printed reading, which already differs sufficiently from the Septuagint.]

Mark the evangelist, also joining together two testimonies, from Malachi and Isaiah, under the words of one prophet, began as follows:

“The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way’” (Mark 1:1–2).

Although these words are found in Malachi in a different form, what follows—“The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isaiah 40:3)—is spoken by the prophet Isaiah.

Immediately explaining of whom both testimonies are spoken, he says: “John was in the wilderness, baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (Mark 1:4).

The evangelists also interpreted the prophecy of the prophets as referring to John. Although they agree in meaning, they differ in wording. For what the Septuagint translated as “Make straight the paths of our God,” Mark and Luke said, “Make straight his paths.” John, however, says: “Make straight the way of the Lord.”

From this it is clear that the apostles, the evangelists, and the Lord and Savior himself do not follow the authority of the Septuagint translators, since they possess knowledge of the Hebrew language and have no need of them. Rather, they translate from the Hebrew what they read, without concern for the syllables and points of the words, provided that the truth of the meaning is conveyed.

We have shown that they did this in many passages, and especially in the book entitled by us *On the Best Kind of Interpretation*, where the matter has been established by many testimonies brought together at once.

The words, therefore, “Behold, I send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face,” are spoken in the person of Christ: he sent John into the wilderness of Judea to preach a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.

The words that follow—“And immediately the ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire”—speak of him as though of another, according to the customary usage of Scripture.

There is no doubt that this ruler is the Savior, who is the Creator of all things and is called the angel of the covenant and the Angel of the great counsel.

Others, however, think that the words, “Behold, I send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face,” were spoken in the person of the Father; and they understand what follows—“Immediately the ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire”—as spoken by him concerning the Lord Savior.

John prepares the way and makes straight the paths of our God in the hearts of believers, in which, because of their crookedness and unbelief, God previously could not walk.

They interpret the temple either as the Church or as each individual believer in the Church: “You are being built into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5).

And concerning those who have believed: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

The Jews understand the words, “Behold, I send my angel,” as spoken concerning the prophet Elijah. What follows—“Immediately the ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire”—they refer to *ἠλειμμένον*, that is, “their Christ,” whom they say will come at the end of time.

But I am astonished that the outcome of events does not teach them the truth. What temple will the ruler find as his own, when it has been destroyed to its foundations? Or, if it must be rebuilt by another before Christ comes, what more will their Christ do, when everything has been restored by another?

In the Gospel, our Lord, interpreting the prophet Elijah as John the Baptist, says: “If you are willing to accept it, he himself is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14).

This same prophet, whom we are now discussing, also writes at the end: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the Lord” (below, 4:5).

He also gave us the means of understanding how Elijah is John, by saying that John came in the power and spirit of Elijah.

### (Verses 2 ff.)

“Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts, and who will be able to consider the day of his coming? And who will stand to behold him? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fuller’s herb. He will sit refining and cleansing as silver [the Vulgate omits “as”], and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver. They will be offering sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness.

“Then the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the Lord, as in the days of old and as in former years.

“And I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers; against those who defraud the hired worker of his wages, oppress widows and orphans, and oppress the foreigner; and they have not feared me, says the Lord of hosts.

“For I am the Lord, and I do not change.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Behold, he will come—or, according to another reading, ‘he comes’—says the Lord Almighty. And who will endure the day of his entrance? Or who will be able to bear seeing him? For he enters like the fire of a refiner and like the herb of those who wash. He will sit refining and cleansing like silver and like gold, and he will cleanse the sons of Levi and melt them like gold and silver. They will be offering sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness, and the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the Lord as in former days and as in previous years.

“And I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and those who swear falsely in my name; against those who defraud hired workers of their wages, oppress widows by force, strike orphans, pervert the judgment of the foreigner, and do not fear me, says the Lord Almighty.

“For I am the Lord your God, and I do not change.”

Above we read of the question raised against the Lord by those who say: “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him”; or else, “If they displease him, where is the God of judgment?”—that is, “Where is the truth of justice?”

To resolve this question, the word of the Lord replies: “I will send my angel, who will prepare my way, and the ruler whom you seek will come to his temple.” He is the judge of truth, concerning whom it is said in the Psalm: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Psalm 72:1).

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

He is the angel of the covenant whom you seek, to whom evil is not pleasing, who does not show partiality in judgment (Colossians 3:25), and who is changed by neither mercy nor severity:

“For in the hand of the Lord there is a cup of unmixed wine full of mixture, and he poured from this into that” (Psalm 75:9); that is, mercy tempers justice, and justice mercy.

This one, therefore, will come immediately and swiftly to his temple—that is, to the Church.

“And who will be able to consider the day of his coming?” If no one can consider it because of the power of his majesty, who will be able to bear it?

“And who will stand to behold him?” That is, who will be able to see him in his glory with eyes that are bleary and blinking? [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “with bleary eyes and blind minds in one brightness,” etc.] He is the sun of righteousness, and healing is in his wings.

He will come “like a refiner’s fire and like fuller’s herb” (below, 3:2). “For fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will rage around him” (Psalm 50:3).

Then he will call heaven above and earth, in order to judge his people. Rivers of fire will be drawn forth before him, rolling along all the sinners. [Note: One manuscript reads “will be drawn.” Victorius thinks Jerome alludes to Daniel 7: “His throne was a flame of fire; its wheels were burning fire; a river of fire was drawing forth, going out before him.” Jerome says that it drew every sinner, enveloping them in flames.]

The Lord is called fire, and a consuming fire (Deuteronomy 4:24), so that he may burn up our wood, hay, and stubble.

He is not only fire but also fuller’s herb, called in Hebrew *BORITH* (the supplied text prints no Hebrew letters), which the Septuagint translates as *πόα*, that is, “fuller’s herb.”

To those who commit grave sins he is a refining and consuming fire; but to those who commit lighter sins he is fuller’s herb, restoring purity through washing, according to what is written in Isaiah:

“The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning” (Isaiah 4:4).

Those who have filth need the spirit of judgment, so that they may be washed; those who are full of blood need the spirit of burning, so that the blood externally smeared upon them may be removed.

“And he will sit refining and cleansing like silver,” so that, according to Ezekiel (chapter 22), whatever has been mixed into our gold and silver—that is, into our understanding and speech—namely bronze, tin, iron, and lead, may be boiled away in the Lord’s furnace, so that pure gold and silver may remain.

Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already burning!” (Luke 12:49).

“And he will purify the sons of Levi.” For it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God (1 Peter 4:17). Elsewhere it is written: “Begin with my sanctuaries” (Ezekiel 9:6).

By the sons of Levi understand the entire priestly dignity.

If the priests are to be purified and refined so that pure gold and silver remain, what must be said about the rest?

When they have been cleansed and refined, they will offer just sacrifices to the Lord. Their sacrifice, offered for Judah and Jerusalem—that is, for those who confess the Lord and perceive his peace with the mind—will then be pleasing, as in the days of old and as in former years.

Thus, just as they pleased God in the beginning, so after sin and repentance they will begin to please him again, once they have been cleansed of every filth of sin.

“And I will draw near,” he says, “to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness.”

How great is the dread of judgment, when he himself is both witness and judge!

He is a witness against all sorcerers and adulterers. These crimes are committed secretly, and therefore they are brought into the open, so that they may not remain hidden for long.

After sorcerers are placed adulterers; after adulterers, perjurers; after perjurers, those who defraud hired workers of their wages and refuse to pay what they owe for their labor.

The words “widows and orphans” are to be understood with “defraud,” and “oppress the foreigner and stranger”—or perhaps the catechumen, who has not yet become a citizen in the city of Christ.

Even if they had committed none of these things, the single crime sufficient for their punishment would be that they did not fear the Lord.

We must therefore not consider perjury, failing to pay the laborer his wages, defrauding the widow and orphan, and oppressing the foreigner and stranger to be trivial sins. They are compared with sorcery, magic, and adultery.

We understand these words both according to history and according to tropology, so that what was said at that time to the princes of the Jews may now be said to the princes of the Churches.

The words that follow—“I am the Lord, and I do not change”—are included because he had previously said, “He is like a refining fire and like fuller’s herb,” so that we should not suppose that he changes the nature of his divinity when he is called, for our sake, an angel, a fire, or *BORITH*.

### (Verse 6)

“And you, sons of Jacob, have not been consumed. For from the days of your fathers you have departed from my statutes and have not kept them.”

The Septuagint reads:

“And you, sons of Jacob, have not departed from the sins of your fathers; you have turned aside from my statutes and have not kept them.”

Above he had said: “I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, those who defraud hired workers of their wages, widows and orphans, and those who oppress the foreigner, and they have not feared me, says the Lord of hosts.”

Declaring himself to be a just judge, because he does not show partiality in judgment, he added: “I am the Lord, and I do not change.”

The meaning is: You are continually changed by sorceries, adulteries, perjuries, frauds, and violence; but in judgment I am changed by no variation of persons.

Although I confess that I am a severe and just judge, O sons of Jacob, nevertheless you have not been consumed by the diversity of punishments, according to what is written in Jeremiah: “In vain I struck your children; they did not accept correction” (Jeremiah 2:30).

Nor have you done this only recently or once, so as to deserve forgiveness for an error. Rather, you possess an inherited impiety, since from the days of your fathers you have departed from my statutes and have not kept what I commanded.

According to *anagogy*, however, we should understand the sons of Jacob—the supplanter and the twin who seized the birthright—as those who do not depart from the sins of their fathers, who turn aside from the statutes and do not keep what has been commanded, namely, those established in the Church who do not depart from vices and assume for themselves the false name of Christian religion.

(Vv. 7 ff.) “Return to me, and I will return to you,” says the Lord of hosts. And you said, “In what way shall we return?” If a man afflicts God, because you afflict me? And you said, “In what way have we pierced you?” In tithes and firstfruits. In [Vulgate: “And in”] scarcity you are accursed, and you have pierced me, the whole nation. Bring the entire tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in my house; and test me in this, says the Lord: whether I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out a blessing upon you to overflowing. And on your behalf I will rebuke the devourer, and it shall not destroy the fruit of your land [another reading: “vineyard”], nor shall your vineyard be barren in the field, says the Lord of hosts. And all nations shall call you blessed; for you shall be a desirable land, says the Lord of hosts.

LXX: “Return to me, and I will return to you,” says the Lord Almighty. And you said, “In what way shall we return?” If a man supplants God, because you have supplanted me? And you said, “In what way have we supplanted you?” “Because the tithes and firstfruits are with you, and although you see, you look away, and you supplant me” [another reading: “you have supplanted me”]. The year has been completed, and you have brought the produce into the treasuries, and there shall be plunder in your houses. Return, therefore, in this matter, says the Lord Almighty. Unless I open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out my blessing upon you until it suffices, and divide food for you, and do not destroy the fruit of your land, and your vine shall not be weakened in the field, says the Lord Almighty; and all nations shall call you blessed, because you shall be a willing land, says the Lord Almighty.

[Note: Here too we have removed the little word “so that,” supported by the same manuscript and by the Greek text.]

[Note: Formerly the text read “we pierce,” “and firstfruits,” and “you pierce.” The Reginensis manuscript, in accordance with the Vulgate, corrects these to “we have pierced,” “and first offerings,” and “you have pierced.” Immediately afterward it also read “into my storehouse,” whereas the Reginensis manuscript has only “into the storehouses.” We have inserted “my” after Victorius, although that word occurs neither in that manuscript nor in the Hebrew or the Vulgate edition.]

At the beginning we said that by the prophet Malachi Ezra the priest ought to be understood, and that everything written in his history is also contained in this book. Now we say that in his and Nehemiah’s time—for it is clear that they lived at the same time—there was a very severe famine; and because of the famine there was an uprising, and the poor, compelled by necessity, sold their sons and daughters, all their property, and their entire possessions. Finally they say: “Our sons and our daughters are very numerous; let us receive grain in payment for them, and let us eat and live.” And there were others who said: “Let us pledge our fields, vineyards, and houses, and receive grain during the famine.” And Ezra says: “I became exceedingly angry when I heard their outcry and these words; my heart deliberated within me, and I rebuked the nobles and the magistrates” (Num. 5:2 ff.), and so forth.

Therefore, at a time of famine, when grain was extremely expensive, so that people were compelled to sell their own children, both those who possessed little and those who had stored abundant crops in their storehouses, out of necessity or because of the high price, were unwilling to pay tithes to the Levites, who had no share in the inheritance of Judah; rather, the firstfruits and tithes were their inheritance.

Lest this be thought to be our own assertion, let us set forth Ezra’s testimony: “And I learned,” he says, “that the portions of the Levites had not been given, and that each one of the Levites and singers and ministers had fled to his own region. And I brought the matter before the magistrates and said: ‘Why have we abandoned the house of God?’ And I gathered them together and stationed them at their posts. And all Judah brought the tithes of grain, wine, and oil into the storehouses. And we appointed over the storehouses Shelemiah the priest and Zadok the scribe” (Neh. 13:10 ff.), and so on.

We have heard Ezra’s history; now let us repeat the prophet’s words, examining more carefully whether the prophecy and the history agree. When it is said, “Return to me, and I will return to you,” says the Lord Almighty, it is evident that those whom he urges to return have departed from the Lord. And observe the Lord’s clemency: he promises like for like, so that in the measure with which they have measured, it may be measured back to them (Matt. 7:1). And as it is written in Leviticus: “If you walk perversely against me, I too will walk against you with perverse fury” (Lev. 26:27–28). So now also he exhorts the people to return, so that he too may return to them.

But because they do not understand that they have departed from the Lord, they shamelessly ask: “In what way shall we return?” They say: “When did we depart, so that we should rightly be compelled to return?” The Lord replies: “If a man afflicts God, because you afflict me?” [Note: Victorius is silent concerning the words “which is written.”]

The Hebrew word written as HAJECBA [Hebrew term not supplied in the text] the LXX translated, “if he supplants”; Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion instead rendered it, “if he defrauds,” so that the sense is: “If a man defrauds God, because you have defrauded me?” [another reading: “because you defraud me?”]

And in truth, according to the historical sense, because the people were not paying tithes and firstfruits to the Levites, the Lord says that he himself was suffering the fraud, since his ministers, driven daily by hunger and want, had abandoned the Temple. [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads, “driven daily by hunger and want,” etc.] For if he is visited in others when they are in prison, if the sick person is received, and if the hungry and thirsty person receives food and drink, why should he not himself receive tithes in his ministers, and, if they are not given, himself be deprived of his portion?

[Note: You will find the same thing in the Pentaglot Lexicon, where the root Caba, or Ceba, means “he fixed, inserted, fastened, affixed.” Among the Syrians, too, in Colossians 2, Vecabeh means “and he affixed it to his cross.” From this it is evident that Jerome was skilled in the Chaldean and Syriac languages, whatever the unlearned author of the recent Questions on Jerome may wish. MART.]

This word HAJECBA is interpreted in the Syriac and Chaldean languages as “if he affixes.” Hence, many years ago, we translated it in this way, with greater reference to the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, in which men crucified God, than to tithes and firstfruits (referring to the written words: “he is visited in prison, the sick person is received, and the hungry and thirsty person receives food and drink”).

[Note: I would prefer, following the same manuscript, to remove the three lines enclosed in parentheses, since they disturb the proper sequence of the discourse and seem altogether to have been repeated by scribal error from the immediately preceding context. The reading would then continue directly: “with reference to tithes and firstfruits,” to which the written words refer.]

Let the prudent reader ask how our interpretation agrees with what follows: “In tithes and firstfruits,” and let him see whether we can say this: “To affix me to the cross, to lay criminal hands upon your God, you first prepared yourselves through much previous reflection by withholding tithes and firstfruits—not, I say, from my priests and Levites, but from me, who commanded through Moses that they be given [another reading: “to give”]” (Exod. 23).

Let this much be said by us concerning a single word, leaving the judgment of its meaning to the reader’s discretion. Now let us follow the order of the prophecy. Because you have not paid me tithes and firstfruits, therefore you are accursed in hunger and want, and you supplant me, or defraud and deprive me, the whole nation.

In place of “nation,” which is written in Hebrew as AGGOI [Hebrew term not supplied in the text], the Septuagint translated ἔτος (“year”) instead of ἔθνος (“nation”).

[Note: It is clear from the similarity of the Greek words ἔθνος and ἔτος that the LXX translators themselves were not mistaken in translating, having read one for the other—even though the two words differ enormously—but rather that copyists of the Greek manuscript incorrectly wrote ἔθνος for ἔτος.]

And the sense is: “Behold, the year has been completed, and you have carried nothing into my treasuries, but have brought it into your own storehouses. And in place of the tithes and firstfruits—which would have been small things if you had given them—you have lost the fertility of your possessions and the abundance of all your crops.”

But so that you may know that this was accomplished while I was angry, because you defrauded me of my portion, I urge and admonish you to bring tithes into the storehouses—that is, into the treasuries of the Temple—and let the priests and Levites who minister to me have food. And test me, whether I will not pour out such abundant rains that the floodgates of heaven may be believed to have been opened. And I will pour out blessing upon you to overflowing. The word “pouring out” indicates the name of generosity.

It may happen, however, that the fields are fertile because they are watered by the rains, but that either locust, bruchus, blight, or caterpillar destroys them, and human labor perishes. [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads more neatly and briefly: “or locust may come, or bruchus, or caterpillar, and the labors of human beings,” etc.] Therefore he adds and says: “And I will rebuke the devourer on your behalf”—namely, the locust and the other creatures we have mentioned—and “it shall not destroy the fruit of your land.”

Your vineyard also will fill the winepresses, and all the nations round about will marvel at the fertility of your land, to such an extent that everyone will desire to dwell in it, and you will be an example of the abundance of all things to all nations.

What we have said about tithes and firstfruits, which were formerly given by the people to priests and Levites, understand also of the peoples of the Church. They have been commanded not only to give tithes and firstfruits, but also to sell everything they possess, give it to the poor, and follow the Lord the Savior (Matt. 19; Mark 10).

If we do not wish to do this, let us at least imitate the beginnings of the Jews, so that we give a portion of everything to the poor and render due honor to priests and Levites. Hence the Apostle also says: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3), and that the presbyter is to be honored with double honor, especially one who labors in the word and teaching of God.

Whoever does not do this is convicted of defrauding and supplanting God, and is cursed in the want of all things, so that “the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, while the one who sows in blessing will gather fruits abundantly in blessings” (2 Cor. 9:6).

Whenever famine, scarcity, and want of every kind oppress the world, let us know that this descends from God’s anger. He says that, in the poor, if they do not receive alms, he himself is defrauded and deprived of his portion [another reading: “possession”].

We can also interpret tithes and firstfruits in this way: If someone learned and instructed in the Law [another reading: “instructed in the law”] of God is able to teach others, he ought not to attribute what he possesses to his own wisdom and ingenuity. Rather, let him first give thanks to God, who bestows all things; then to his priests and teachers, from whom he was taught. If he does not give thanks, but claims the knowledge for himself, he will be cursed in want.

But if, recognizing God as the giver and giving thanks to those through whom he was instructed by God, he humbles himself and brings food into God’s storehouse—that is, ministers the nourishment of Holy Scripture to the peoples in the Church—then immediately the floodgates of heaven will be opened over him, spiritual rain will be poured out, and God will command his clouds to rain upon him. He will enjoy abundance in all things, and on his behalf he will rebuke the devourer—namely, hostile powers. His labor will bear fruit, and he will attain what is written: “Blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of those who hear” (Eccles. 25).

He will also lift up his eyes and see the regions, because they are already white for harvest (John 4), and he will gather fruits for eternal life. His vineyard will not be barren in the field—he who says in the Gospel: “I am the vine” (John 15:1), and who speaks through the prophet: “I planted you as a fruitful vineyard, wholly true” (Jer. 2:21).

And through such humility of confession and thanksgiving to God and to the teachers of his Church, he will attain such blessedness that all nations will call him blessed and will desire to dwell in his land and teaching—those who have heard him disputing in the Church.

(Vv. 13 ff.) “Your words have prevailed against me,” says the Lord, “and you said: ‘What have we spoken against you?’ You said: ‘He who serves God is useless, and what profit is there, because we have kept his precepts and because we have walked mournfully before the Lord of hosts?’ Therefore now we call the arrogant blessed, since those who commit impiety have been built up; they have tested God, and they have been saved.”

LXX: “You have made your words heavy against me,” says the Lord. And you said, “In what way have we spoken against you?” And you said, “He who serves God is useless; and what more is there, because we have kept his commandments and because we have walked as suppliants before the face of the Lord Almighty?” And now we call strangers blessed, and all who commit iniquity are built up; they resisted God, and they have been saved.

Earlier he had said: “You have wearied the Lord with your words,” and you said, “In what way have we wearied him?” In this: when you said, “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him”; or certainly, “Where is the God of judgment?”

Now he repeats the same point more fully. The people who seemed to have returned from Babylon, to possess knowledge of God, observe the Law, understand their sin, offer sacrifices for sin, pay tithes, observe the Sabbath, and fulfill the other commandments prescribed by God’s Law, saw all the surrounding nations abounding in every possession while they themselves were placed in want, famine, and misery. They were scandalized at every turn and said: “What profit is it to me that I worship the one true God, abhor idols, and, pierced by the consciousness of my sins, walk sorrowfully before God?” This passage, as we said above, is treated more fully and extensively in the seventy-second Psalm.

Therefore the prophet, who is a spiritual physician, heals all the wounds and declares that the words of blasphemy recoil upon the Creator. Speaking in God’s person, he says: “Your words have prevailed against me,” or, “have become heavy.” For, according to Zechariah, iniquity sits upon a talent of lead (Zech. 5); and what is spoken against God is weighed down by the great mass of blasphemies.

Not understanding their extremely weighty words and their blasphemy, they ask: “What have we spoken against you?” The Lord answers them: “You said: ‘He who serves God is useless, and what profit is there, because we have kept his precepts?’” They demand payment for serving God in the present age; therefore they do not receive it. And because “we have walked sorrowfully before the Lord,” in accordance with what is written in the Psalms: “All day long I walked sorrowfully” (Ps. 37:7).

“Therefore we call the arrogant blessed”—those who grow proud against God and hurl impious words of blasphemy. For they have been built up, and after their crimes and blasphemies they enjoy every prosperity. “They tested God,” or “resisted God,” and they have been saved. They consider the salvation and happiness of the present age to be salvation; and for this reason they are deceived by their errors.

We can understand this also of the heretics Marcion, Valentinus, and the others who do not accept the Old Testament and speak against the Creator of the world: they advance in their impiety and have many companions in crime. Those who remain in the Church are scandalized by them and, ignorant of the reasons for God’s judgment, continue the prophet’s words. [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads, “by whom they are scandalized”; shortly afterward, “the prophet continues his words.”]

(V. 16.) “Then those who feared God [Vulgate: “the Lord”] spoke, each one with his neighbor.”

LXX: “These things those who feared the Lord spoke, each one to his neighbor.”

According to the Hebrews, it should be understood in this way: while those who blasphemed the judgment of God were speaking, those who feared God spoke among themselves, saying that the recompense of good and evil is not in the present and brief age, but in the future and eternal one; that a human being cannot know God’s judgments or dispute his equity and justice; and the other things which a righteous person ought to say to another righteous person.

He did not say what they spoke; but from what he adds—“Then those who feared God spoke, each one with his neighbor”—we should understand that those who feared God spoke the things contained in the words of all the Scriptures.

According to the LXX, however, ἐξαίρετον (“distinctive” or “excellent”) should be read, and with emphatic delivery, so that we say: “These are the things those who fear the Lord spoke, each one to his neighbor”—that is, those who vainly boast and say: “What profit is there, because we have kept his precepts and walked sorrowfully before the Lord?” For if they feared the Lord, they would not say such things.

(Vv. 17–18.) “And the Lord paid attention and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the Lord and think upon his name. And they shall be mine,” says the Lord of hosts, “on the day when I act, as my treasured possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him. And you shall return and see what difference there is between the righteous and the impious, and between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.”

LXX: “And the Lord paid attention and heard, and wrote a book of remembrance in his presence for those who fear the Lord and reverence [another reading: “fear”] his name. And they shall be mine,” says the Lord Almighty, “on the day when I act, as a possession; and I will choose them as a man chooses his son who serves him. And you shall return and see what difference there is between the righteous and the iniquitous, and between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.”

[Note: Our manuscripts and the Greek archetype likewise have ἐπιστραφήσεσθε (“you shall return”). Formerly the reading was “I will return.” In the Hebrew also, Martianus had read “return” instead of “you shall return.”]

While the righteous were speaking and those who feared God were speaking individually with their neighbors, refusing either to hear or to utter words of blasphemy, the Lord paid attention and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who feared him and thought upon his name, so that when the day of judgment comes he may repay both penalties to the blasphemers and rewards to those who fear him.

The book that was written is the one of which we read in Daniel: “Thrones were set in place, and the books were opened” (Dan. 7:10). On the day when the time of judgment arrives, those who fear the Lord will be the treasured possession of the Lord of hosts.

In place of “treasured possession,” the Hebrew has SGOLLA [Hebrew term not supplied in the text], which Aquila translated as περιούσιον (“special possession”), and the others as περιποίησιν (“acquisition” or “possession”).

[Note: Our manuscripts have Sogolla here and elsewhere. Jerome himself should also be consulted in his commentary on Matthew 6, at the verse “our supersubstantial bread.” There he says: “We examined the Hebrew, and wherever the LXX expressed περιούσιον, we found Sgolla (the manuscripts: Sogolla), which Symmachus translated as ἐξαίρετον, that is, ‘special’ or ‘excellent,’ although in one place he translated it as ‘peculiar,’ and so forth.”]

Therefore those who fear the Lord, who spoke with their neighbor and answered the words of blasphemy, will be his treasured possession on the day of judgment, and he will spare them, because every human being is under sin. Or he will choose them, as a man is accustomed to choose his son who serves him. In this there is a twofold affection: both the affection of a father for his son and the relationship of a master toward a servant.

Then you who now blaspheme and say, “What profit is there, because we have kept his precepts and walked sorrowfully before the Lord?” will recognize their election and blessedness, and your own misery [another reading: “and your misery”]; and, turned toward repentance, you will see what difference there is between the righteous and the impious, and between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.

[Col. 1574C] (Chapter 4.—Vv. 1 ff.) “For behold, the day will come, burning like a furnace, and all the proud and all who commit impiety will be stubble; and the coming day will set them aflame,” says the Lord of hosts, “which will leave them neither root nor shoot. And for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing will be in its wings; and you shall go forth and leap like calves from the herd. And you shall trample the impious when they have become ashes beneath the soles of your feet, on the day when I act,” says the Lord of hosts.

LXX: “For behold, the day is coming, burning like a furnace, and it will burn them, and all the foreigners and all who commit iniquity will be stubble. The coming day will set them ablaze,” says the Lord Almighty, “and no root or branch will be left in them. And for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing will be in its wings; and you shall go forth and leap like calves released from their bonds, and you shall trample the wicked, and they shall be ashes beneath [another reading: “between”] your feet, on the day when I act,” says the Lord Almighty.

Because the impious wearied me with their words and said: “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him”; and, “He who serves God is useless; and what profit is there, because we have kept his precepts and walked sorrowfully before the Lord of hosts?” (cf. Wisdom 2, at the end).

And those who feared God spoke against their rash words, and each one conferred with his neighbor about the things pertaining to the fear of God. The Lord paid attention and heard, and a book of remembrance was written for those who fear the Lord and think upon his name. And when the day comes, he promises that he will have them as his treasured possession and spare them as a man spares his son who serves him.

He makes the point still more emphatically and says: “Behold, the day will come”—that is, the day of judgment—which will be light for the saints and darkness for sinners. That day itself will be kindled like a furnace or oven, so that all the impious may be turned into stubble and burned in the furnace’s flames. When it has set them aflame and burned them, it will leave in them no root or shoot of wickedness. This concerns what the impious will suffer on the day of judgment.

By contrast, it is said what will happen to those who fear the name of God: “And for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise,” [another reading: “because”] he who will judge all things truly and will allow neither good nor evil, neither virtues nor vices, to remain hidden. “And there will be healing in his wings,” so that, having healed them through repentance, he may carry them upon his shoulders, in accordance with what is written in Deuteronomy: “Spreading out his wings, he received them and carried them upon his shoulders” (Deut. 22:11).

Then those who are now confined in the world as in a prison will go forth, and they will leap like calves from the herd, or like calves released from their bonds. Hence the Apostle says: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23), so that he may go forth and leap like a calf released from its bonds and like a victim of the Lord.

Nor is he content with this conclusion of joy; he also says that they will trample the impious when they have become ashes. Hence an imprecation is also directed toward the righteous: “But may God crush [another reading: “will crush”] Satan under your feet swiftly” (Rom. 16:20).

Abraham, speaking to the Lord and recognizing himself, in comparison with the divine majesty, to be ashes, said: “I am earth and ashes” (Gen. 18:27). Therefore he will see the sun of righteousness, rest among its allotted portions, and, carried by it, be lifted up to heavenly things.

But he who proudly said, “I will set my throne above the stars; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13), will be brought down to the earth and will be like ashes beneath the feet of the saints when the day of the Lord, the Judge, arrives.

(V. 4.) “Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded him at Horeb, with precepts and judgments for all Israel.”

[Note: The words of the LXX are the same. Here, as elsewhere, we have supplied them from the support of the manuscript codices, since they are necessary.]

The LXX likewise. There will be a just recompense according to merits in the future, when the flame, consuming and devouring the root and shoot of the proud, will destroy and burn them, and the sun of righteousness will rise for those who fear the Lord, with healing in its wings.

Therefore: “Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I gave him on Mount Horeb”—that is, Sinai—“with precepts and judgments for all Israel.”

The Apostle says: “We know that the law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14), and blessed David says: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18). Since spiritually all were eating the heavenly manna, and the entire people of Israel were drinking from the same spiritual rock that followed them—and the rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:3–4)—those who believe in Christ ought spiritually to observe the precepts of the Law, which he gave at OREB [Hebrew term not supplied in the text], interpreted as “dryness,” through which the moisture of all vices is boiled away and the rheum of lust is dried by the rays of the sun of righteousness.

The Lord spoke to all Israel, which perceives God with understanding, of whom it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

(Vv. 5–6.) “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. And he will turn the heart of the fathers toward the children, and the heart of the children toward their fathers, lest perhaps I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

LXX: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and illustrious day of the Lord comes. He will turn the heart of the father toward the son and the heart of a man toward his neighbor, lest, coming, I strike the earth completely.”

[Note: Gerohus, a twelfth-century writer, in his book On the Corrupt State of the Church, edited by Baluzius in the Miscellanea, uses this testimony of Jerome, which he quotes to the end of the book, to place the holy Doctor among the principal proponents of the view that Moses and Elijah are the two appointed witnesses who will appear on the day of the Lord and fight against Antichrist. It is known, however, that most of the other Fathers understand Elijah and Enoch. Here, however, he has read “specifically,” and not well, in place of “spiritually.”]

After Moses—whose commandments we have taught must be observed spiritually—he says that Elijah is to be sent, signifying the Law by Moses and prophecy by Elijah, as Abraham says to a certain rich man dressed in purple: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luke 16:29).

And when the Lord and Savior was transfigured on the mountain, he had Moses and Elijah speaking with him in white garments; they were telling him what he would suffer in Jerusalem (Mark 9). For the Law and the entire chorus of the prophets proclaim Christ’s Passion.

Therefore, before the day of judgment comes and the Lord strikes the earth with a curse—or entirely, or suddenly, as the LXX translated it—for this is what ἀρδὴν signifies, the Lord will send in Elijah—whose name means “my God” and who is from the town of Thesbe, a name signifying conversion and repentance—the entire chorus of the prophets, so that he may turn the heart of the fathers toward the children: namely, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the patriarchs, so that their descendants may believe in the Lord the Savior, in whom they too believed. For Abraham “saw the day of the Lord and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

Or “the heart of the father toward the son” means the heart of God toward everyone who has received the spirit of adoption; and “the heart of the children toward their fathers” means that Jews and Christians, who now disagree among themselves, may agree in a shared devotion to Christ.

Hence it is said to the apostles, who proclaimed the seed of the Gospel throughout the whole world: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. 44:17).

For if Elijah does not first turn the heart of the fathers toward the children and the heart of the children toward their fathers, when the great and terrible day comes—great for the saints, terrible for sinners—the true and just Judge will strike not heaven, nor those who dwell in heaven, but the earth with a curse, because they perform earthly works.

The Jews and the Judaizing heretics think that their anointed [text reads: ἠλειμμένρν] Elijah will come and restore everything. Hence a question is also put to Christ in the Gospel: “What of the fact that the Pharisees say that Elijah is to come?” He answered them: “Elijah will indeed come; and, if you believe, he has already come” (Mark 9:10, 12), understanding John in Elijah.

# DEFENSE OF HIERONYMUS’S LEARNING AGAINST J. CLERICUS, COMPOSED BY THE REVEREND JEAN MARTIANAY AND APPENDED TO THE COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHETS

## Prefatory Notice

[Col. 1577B]

As the distinguished orator says, the defense of innocence, often obstructed by the wickedness of many, breathes only with difficulty; nor can truth prevail among the majority when, rejected by force and influence from every quarter, it cannot find a place in which to stand.

I have by no means feared these difficulties, now that I am about to plead the cause of the greatest teacher against John Clericus, an open enemy of the Catholic Church, a despiser of the holy Fathers, a hidden enemy of Christ God, and hostile to all learned men.

For what learned person, and especially what faithful one, would not be moved by the insults in his Questions on Jerome, in which that most ignorant man, swollen with heretical error, has attacked the saint and that immortal intellect? Who could any longer tolerate a great man’s being injured with impunity by a lowly cleric, and the interpreter of the sacred Scriptures, complete in all respects, being insolently scorned by a shameless, verbose sophist?

This is surely no more bearable for me than it would be for Cato’s spirit or Cicero’s stomach, since nothing is more important to me than that Jerome’s name should always be held in the highest honor, and that it should not suffer the stigma of any ignorance because of a man who ineptly teaches Minerva.

I therefore undertake so great a cause with the greatest eagerness, and at the expectation of many colleagues and all good men—not to increase the hatred directed against a heretical writer already condemned in everyone’s judgment by his life and books, but to come to the aid of Jerome’s reputation and esteem, which that loquacious critic has attempted to violate and corrupt in every way.

To confess the truth about myself: although John Clericus has directed many calumnies and snares against me, never has the expectation of my own accusation or the judgment of learned men been able to move me so deeply as the wicked complaints, quarrels, calumnies, and snares that he is attempting at one and the same time to direct against Jerome and against our new edition of his works.

Yet this turns out very conveniently for us: his incredible boldness is joined to singular stupidity. For just as he has been outspoken in attacking the reputation of the greatest men—I mean Origen and Jerome—so he has made his intentions and efforts plain to everyone in the hope of performing a miracle of himself and winning admiration.

Nor, content with treating the studies and learning of the ancients as worthless, does he even dare to appoint himself emperor for the defense of public liberty in the republic of letters.

“I seem to myself,” he says, “to be pleading not my own cause, nor that of others who have been expressly attacked, but that of no small or contemptible part of the human race. For here the rights of human nature are at stake; here the common liberty of the entire republic of letters is at stake. These rights and this liberty are violated and oppressed by those who for several centuries have maintained that students of literature can in no way call into question what the consensus and authority of earlier ages have decreed,” and so forth. *Questions*, 3, p. 46.

To cut down, therefore, the boastfulness and arrogance of this self-appointed champion of liberty, I bring his lies and ignorance into the open. For although he may never repent of his state of mind, I shall at least overturn his arguments by this defense and destroy the false reputation for learning that he has acquired among many ignorant people through his abundance of published books.

Once Jerome’s title as a wise and learned man has been established, I shall again cross swords with our critic, to demonstrate that in attacking our Paris edition of the works of the holy Doctor he was entirely destitute of judgment, good faith, diligence, and knowledge.

## CHAPTER ONE. On Jerome’s Complete Learning and John Clericus’s Singular Ignorance

What was most desirable for confirming in every way Saint Jerome’s knowledge of the Greek, Latin, and Hebrew languages seems to us to have been granted and offered at this time not by human planning but almost by divine providence.

For there has long taken root, among certain simple Catholics and among those who are ignorant and unskilled in the Oriental languages, a pernicious opinion in the Church of God: that Jerome did not by himself possess sufficient command of Greek or Hebrew, but always made the closest use of Greek and Jewish interpreters, with whose help he had partly learned their dialects, and by whose assistance he took care to transmit to us, his present friends and to posterity, the things found in his commentaries.

I had attempted to uproot this ignorant opinion and unjust suspicion from people’s minds through very numerous annotations and a separate commentary on the book of Hebrew Names. But now John Clericus—a man unpleasant in speech and entirely lacking in moderation—has disrupted my task and in some way even broken my zeal more forcefully. For he has stripped our discussion of its dignity and hoped to weaken it by daring stubbornly to deny that Jerome possessed perfect knowledge of the languages.

I therefore bring forward this man with his Questions on Jerome, in order, if possible, to restore Jerome’s reputation, should it have suffered loss; to regain the goodwill of scholarly friends; and to satisfy both rivals and well-wishers.

If prudent readers judge the matter severely and conscientiously, the authority of Jerome’s complete learning, which ought to remain in him, will endure; while the proofs and indications of ignorance will remain permanently fixed upon our Clericus.

### § 1. On Saint Jerome’s Greek Learning
John Clericus begrudges Jerome his knowledge of Greek speech on account of certain passages in the *Chronicle* and in Eusebius’s book *On the Places*, passages which, although by no means obscure, Jerome overturned by his interpretation and did not render into Latin. If we grant this to the nauseated stomach of clerics, and to Joseph Scaliger, who insolently and indecorously attacks all other writers, let us proceed to the arguments by which those eminent men assail Jerome and contend that his knowledge of the Greek language was mediocre or nonexistent.

I. “Lest these matters should seem incredible to those who would not investigate them, or lest they should seem to those who do investigate them to require proof,” says Clericus, “we shall here set down a few examples, for it would take too long to collect them all. But we shall select those from which it will plainly be evident that one must not rashly trust Jerome when he translates Greek. Certainly,” says Scaliger, “if anyone today translated Greek as Jerome did, he would be torn limb from limb not by strangers but, like Actaeon, by his own dogs.” We shall produce separately several sentences from the preface of Eusebius to the *Chronological Canon*, with Scaliger’s translation, followed by Jerome’s, so that they may be compared with one another:

> Μωῦσέα γένος Ἑβραῖον προφητῶν ἁπάντων πρῶτον ἀμφὶ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν . . . ἀμφί τε τῆς τῶν ἐθνῶν δι’ αὐτοῦ θεοθεογνωσίας χρησμοὺς καὶ λόγια θεῖα γραφῇ παραδεδωκότα etc.

That is, according to Scaliger:

> Moses, a Hebrew by race, who, first of all the prophets, concerning our Savior—that is, Christ—and concerning the knowledge of God which the nations acquired through him, committed prophecies and divine oracles to writing, etc.

Now let us hear Jerome:

> Moses of the Hebrew nation, who, first of all the prophets, explained the divine laws in the sacred Scriptures before the coming of the Lord and Savior. The most learned men have reported that he lived in the time of Inachus, etc.

There was no reason for Jerome to alter the sense of the words ἀμφὶ τοῦ etc. παραδεδωκότα except that he did not sufficiently understand them; for Eusebius’s meaning is much better and could easily have been elegantly expressed in Latin, so that no excuse remains for Jerome based on the difference between the languages. Nor does Jerome offer a paraphrase of Eusebius’s words, but another sense, one which, as I have said, cannot at all be compared with Eusebius’s. Thus writes John Clericus, *Questions*, question 3, pp. 52 ff.

What John Clericus observes here, following Scaliger, both critics unwittingly brought upon themselves; for they are the ones who tear Jerome limb from limb, like Actaeon by his own dogs—Jerome who calls his unjust reprovers his dogs: “Therefore let them hear, my dogs,” he says, in the preface to Job. And in the preface to his Latin translation of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*:

> Nor am I unaware that there will be many who, in their customary desire to disparage everything—a vice avoided only by the man who has written nothing at all—will sink their tooth into this volume, etc.

Scaliger and Clericus therefore slander Jerome the translator of Eusebius’s preface to the *Chronological Canon* and criticize his translation because they do not attend to the fact that Eusebius’s wording was altered here for the sake of a better meaning, and that either a contradiction or an ambiguity in the Greek words was removed—an ambiguity that would have been evident and certain to us had the Latin translation been purely literal.

Eusebius says that Moses was the first of all the prophets to deliver divine oracles concerning Christ and the calling of the nations. This statement certainly seems contrary to what is said of Abraham and the patriarch Jacob both in the first and in the later book of the *Chronicle*. For we read of Abraham:

> To him, first of all the prophets, the word of God, when it had appeared in human form, promised the calling of the nations; this promise the word of Christ brought to completion in our own time through the preaching of the Gospel to all nations.

Of Jacob, Eusebius likewise says:

> Jacob died in the one hundred forty-seventh year of his life, prophesying about Christ and the calling of the nations.

If Abraham was the first of all the prophets, and Jacob prophesied before Moses—or published divine oracles concerning the Lord Christ and the calling of the nations through him—how is Eusebius consistent with himself when he teaches that Moses was the first of all the prophets to deliver oracles and prophecies concerning the Savior and the preaching of the Gospel?

We can indeed excuse Eusebius by making this qualification: he said that these things had been handed down in writing by Moses. But a simple reader, unaware that such a qualification must be made, will detect many statements in the testimonies quoted above that contradict one another and do not sufficiently cohere.

Jerome therefore more conveniently altered the passage, acting not as a translator but as an author, so that he might call Moses the Jewish lawgiver by his proper designation. He says:

> Moses of the Hebrew nation, who, first of all the prophets, explained the divine laws in the sacred Scriptures before the coming of the Lord and Savior, is reported by the most learned men to have lived in the time of Inachus.

John Clericus ought to have weighed these matters according to judgment, not in a spirit of rivalry or on the presumption of hatred, lest it be said to him:

> From the point at which I thought I was rendering good service to my Latins and encouraging our people to study, from that same point I am summoned to account.

But, to come to a brief answer: Jerome had a very necessary reason for altering the sense of the words ἀμφὶ τοῦ etc.; because he understood them perfectly, he did not wish to translate them into Latin. Hence no room remains for Clericus’s slander, based on the difference between Eusebius’s Greek words and Jerome’s Latin, since it is clear to a prudent reader that the Greek was altered so that a suitable and clearer sense might be found in the Latin translation—a sense that was obscure and ambiguous in the Greek original.

II. “The following words occur in Eusebius,” says John Clericus:

> In the present work, having brought the times together and set the years of each nation opposite one another in corresponding columns, I composed the work of the *Chronological Canon*, Χρονικοῦ Κανόνος σύνταξιν ἐποιησάμην.

“Let us now read Jerome, who, in translating these words, is much more obscure and less Latin, and does not even render their meaning:

> In the present writing, placing the same periods opposite one another and counting the years of the individual nations, I joined them together in such a carefully ordered arrangement that what was contemporary with what might be perceived.
