“He seems to have believed that σύνταξιν meant ‘order,’ although it is the same as σύνταγμα and signifies ‘this work.’ If he had understood the Greek words, he would never have preferred to say ‘carefully ordered arrangement’ as the title of the work; but certainly, as Scaliger says in his note on this passage, he did not understand it.”

Our critic could not have displayed his ignorance more plainly than when he attached himself to that of Scaliger as though he were its attendant. They claim that Jerome did not understand Eusebius because they themselves made no effort to understand either Eusebius’s Greek or Jerome’s Latin.

For what else can Eusebius’s *Chronological Canon* be, among learned and studious readers, than a series of periods set opposite one another, and a carefully ordered arrangement of kingdoms correspondingly opposed to each other, so that what was contemporary with what may be perceived at a glance? Jerome therefore translates perfectly and gives Eusebius’s Greek words pure Latin, saying:

> In the present writing, placing the same periods opposite one another . . . I joined them together in a carefully ordered arrangement.

[Note: [Col. 1579D] Nevertheless, *stylis* in the plural would be more correct. Thus, a little later, no one who compares Jerome with himself will doubt that σύνταξιν means a book in Eusebius: where Eusebius had previously said, ἐν μὲν τῇ πρὸ πάντος σύνταξει, Jerome translated, “in the earlier little book.” [Col. 1580D]]

He calls the *Chronological Canon* a “writing” because the book is arranged by writings—that is, columns—and joined together in a carefully ordered arrangement, or described through a suitable disposition of periods. He did not therefore intend “carefully ordered arrangement” as the title of the *Chronological Canon*, as the slanderer Clericus falsely alleges; rather, he interprets the σύνταξις of the *Chronological Canon* as a carefully arranged sequence and order of periods set opposite one another in columns.

Let the attendant of Scaliger therefore be ashamed of both foreign and personal ignorance: he allowed himself to be persuaded that σύνταξις and σύνταγμα do not signify a series of things brought together, an order, a composition, or even a distribution into classes. This is just as if I were to say “canon”—something those who know Greek and Latin will readily grant me.

III. So that I may omit nothing of what Clericus objects, it is useful to recall a question of this sort, numbered 6, p. 54:

> “But why, I ask, since I have resolved to investigate the matter more carefully, being one who puts nothing before truth, why did he translate these words as: ‘Since these things stand thus, I deemed it necessary to pursue the truth more diligently’? For it is false that Eusebius concedes to Porphyry that the matter stands thus, etc.”

If Clericus had awaited an explanation of this question from some studious reader of Jerome, he could never have displayed such manifest folly as to suppose that Eusebius, in Latin, conceded to Porphyry that Semiramis lived after Moses, and that the same Moses must be regarded as almost 850 years older than the Trojan War.

The words “since these things stand thus” do not refer to Porphyry’s opinion, but to the discordant views of Christians and pagans concerning the age and antiquity of Moses, so that the sense is: “Since these things stand thus, and their opinions differ, I deemed it necessary to pursue the truth more diligently,” or “I resolved to investigate the matter more carefully.”

This is the sense Eusebius has both in his own work and in Jerome, his translator; but among Jerome’s critical sycophants, Scaliger and Clericus, it is treated as something alien and utterly absurd.

IV. Clericus contends that the following words are no less corrupted:

> “But when I observed among the Hebrews differing versions of the chronological periods, one excessive, the other deficient, I followed the latter. Nevertheless, even according to this reckoning I found Israel, the progenitor of the Hebrews, from whom the twelve tribes of the Jewish people are counted under the name of Israel, to have been contemporary with Inachus, whom the Greeks report to have first ruled at Argos.”

“For this Jerome has the following, alien to Eusebius’s meaning and deserving no praise for clarity, elegance, or even accuracy:

> Nor did I fail to notice that differing numbers of years are found in the Hebrew books, and that more or fewer are read according as it seemed to the translators; and that what the multitude of copies has drawn into acceptance ought rather to be followed. But however one may wish to calculate it, one will find that in the time of Inachus, whom they say first ruled at Argos, the patriarch Israel lived, from whom the twelve tribes of the Jews took the name of Israel.

“Scaliger rightly observes that nothing of the sort was written by Eusebius and that this was not his meaning. The Caesarean bishop surely intended to say that in the sacred books of the Jews there are two systems of reckoning the years: the longer, which is that of the Septuagint translators, and the shorter, which belonged to the Hebrew manuscripts of his own age and which Eusebius was able to know especially through Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. He himself followed the latter, and yet it does not follow from this that Inachus was older than Israel. This is indeed a paralogism, as Scaliger observes; but Jerome’s reasoning is worse, since he wishes the same conclusion to remain valid whichever reckoning we follow. Besides, everything else is empty.”

I see no paralogism in Eusebius; nor do I see, nor can I see if I am sane, how Jerome’s reasoning is worse. Eusebius wished it to be understood that differing numbers of years are found in the sacred books of the Hebrews: a longer reckoning among the Septuagint translators, a shorter one in the Hebrew source. He himself followed the lesser total; yet even according to this shorter reckoning Inachus was not older than Israel, from whom the twelve tribes of the Jews took the name of Israel.

I utterly fail to understand what in Jerome’s Latin words could be found alien to, or contrary to, this meaning of Eusebius. Although Jerome did not translate the Greek word for word and added several things of his own, he nevertheless wrote nothing against Eusebius’s meaning. For he acknowledges that differing totals and numbers of years are found in the sacred books of the Hebrews, and he does not reject the shorter reckoning followed by Eusebius; rather, in accordance with Eusebius’s meaning, he makes the patriarch Jacob contemporary with Inachus.

Clericus could easily have noticed these things had he not been obstructed by gross stupidity and had he not wished to heap slander upon slander.

V. They add from the same preface, persistently reproving Jerome because he said that it was manifest that Semiramis and Abraham were contemporaries. They suppose that this argument proves their point:

> “It is wrongly called manifest when no one before Eusebius had reported it, no one had believed it, it had not yet been proved, and it had not yet been conceded.”

As though things denied by no one required proof, and as though many matters in the records of history were not manifest in themselves and accepted on the authority of reading alone. It was therefore manifest on historical evidence and by comparison of the various historical records—both Hebrew and those of other nations—that Semiramis and Abraham, who was Chaldaean by race, lived at the same time and became famous.

VI. “These things would be more than sufficient,” says Clericus, “if we were dealing with men who were as severe judges of the long-dead as they are unjust judges of the living. But for their sake we shall add one further passage from the *Chronicle*, at number 1250, in which Jerome’s translation has rightly been corrected by two supreme critics. It concerns a poet who no longer survives:

> ‘Arctinus,’ he says, ‘who composed the *Aethiopis* and the *Ilii Persis*.’

“In Greek it is Ἰλίου Πέρσιν, that is, ‘the destruction of Troy,’ as Joseph Scaliger shows. It should therefore have been translated in that way; but Jerome did not understand the rarer word Πέρσιν. See also Claudius Salmasius, p. 600 of the Utrecht edition of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*.”

What is slander and folly, if this is not? Clericus asserts that Jerome’s translation, namely *Ilii Persin*, was rightly corrected by the supreme critic Joseph Scaliger at number 1250. Yet when I review the passage cited, I read only this in Scaliger:

> “Et Ilii Persin. Ἰλίου Πέρσις is the same as Ἰλίου ἅλωσις.”

In the rest of what is said at number 1250 there is profound silence concerning Jerome and his translation. Here, then, we catch the slanderer Clericus in an absolutely manifest falsehood, and thereafter in threefold ignorance—an ignorance that deserves no pardon even from those most willing to spare him.

First, he dreamed that the word Πέρσις, which signifies destruction and overthrow, was a rare word, although that very word is found in Scapula’s lexicon, worn smooth in boys’ hands and accepted by ordinary usage.

Second, our Clericus was ignorant of the custom of ancient writers, who frequently used Greek words in the titles of their little works, as Varro does in the second book of *On Agriculture*:

> “But be of good cheer,” he says, “for I shall satisfy you no less than he who wrote the *Bougonia*.”

The very learned Varro undoubtedly knew that bees were called Βουγόνους and Βουγενεῖς by the poets. Nevertheless, he did not render *Bougonia* into Latin, because among learned men Greek proper names were more customary in book titles than Latin translations.

Following this custom, Jerome inscribes Greek works with their proper names: *Ilii Persin*; Origen’s *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*; *On the Vision of Quadrupeds*, τετραπόδων; and six hundred similar examples which no one but Clericus could have been ignorant of or could have slandered.

Finally, the third argument for Clerican ignorance is taken from the same preface of Eusebius, from which John Clericus himself took the beginning of his slander. It is manifest and certain to us that Jerome understood the Greek word Πέρσιν and supplied a corresponding Latin translation, since he translated it in this way in the Eusebian preface to the *Chronological Canon*:

> After these events came the overthrow of the Trojan city, which Homer follows after a long interval.

Here, therefore, by Ἰλίου he understands the destruction or overthrow of Troy, just as above he had rendered Πέρσις μέχρι τῆς Ἰλίου ἁλώσεως in our language as “up to the capture of Troy.”

Let every friend and admirer of our critic Clericus therefore be ashamed that he failed to detect such great ignorance in him and did not bravely undertake to defend the cause of Doctor Jerome against the same heretic.

Besides what has already been reported and refuted, Clericus could produce nothing else from Eusebius’s two books of the *Chronicle* to show that Jerome was ignorant of the Greek language. From this we may infer that the holy Doctor possessed the highest mastery of this language, since his reprovers detected no error in him.

As for the rest, from page 59 through page 63, since they consist of nothing but the slanders of Clericus, whose words pour forth without restraint, we meet them with laughter. Nothing is more childish than his statement on page 62:

> “There are those who might suspect that he wished, by a clever excuse, to attribute the faults of ignorance to haste. Certainly, if we wish to speak the truth, such a device is not foreign to Jerome’s character, which was wholly composed for boasting and concealment.”

Because Clericus wrote this in an angry and insolent manner, it will seem unworthy to some and ridiculous to others. Ridiculous to those who had thought that his criticism consisted in the defense of truth, the reliability of testimonies, and the proof of difficulties—not in perpetual slander; unworthy to those who see more deeply and do not hesitate to believe that the *Questions Concerning Jerome* aim at corrupting the faith of the Church.

But let us proceed to the remaining matters which Clericus wished to complete by his own unaided effort.

VII. “But if anyone should nevertheless think that Jerome perhaps slipped through haste while translating that book, let him undertake the labor of comparing with the Greek the Latin translation of another work by the same Eusebius, *On the Situation and Names of Hebrew Places*. He will see that the Bethlehemite Solitary has everywhere displayed no examples of greater skill or diligence in that work.

“1. At the first word, *Ararat*, Eusebius had said that remnants of the ark are still shown in the mountains of Armenia, δείκνυσθαι λείψανα τῆς κιβωτοῦ—that is, ‘remnants of the wood,’ as is plainly clear from the middle and final words of the paragraph. Why, then, did Jerome translate it as *vestigia*, ‘traces,’ an unsuitable and obscure word? Why later as *monumenta*, ‘memorials,’ and finally simply as *ligna*, ‘wood’? What reason was there for speaking more obscurely when a clear word was available?

“2. Martianaeus himself noted that συνευωχεῖσθαι is shortly afterward badly translated as *gaudere*, ‘to rejoice,’ although it means ‘to feast with someone.’ Jerome, however, had regard to the etymology from εὖ and ἔχειν, ‘to be well’; this is a most deceptive method of interpretation and not that of a particularly learned man.

“3. In the same place, ἀποβατήριον is badly translated as *exitus* or *egressus*, ‘exit’ or ‘departure,’ as though it were ἀπόβασις. It is actually a place at which one ascends, or a place of ascent, if one may speak so. Otherwise ἀποβατηρία is κλίμαξ νεὼς, as Hesychius teaches—that is, a ladder by which one disembarks from a ship.

“4. In the words of Nicolaus of Damascus, where he mentions Mount Baris, why is the word μέγα, which precedes ὄρος, omitted, and the place simply called a mountain, although the word is necessary? This is not ignorance but negligence.

“5. After the same writer had said that the report was that many had fled to Mount Baris at the time of the flood, he adds: ‘and that someone, carried by the ark, came to rest upon the ridge, and that remnants of the wood were preserved for a long time.’ Perhaps this was the man of whom Moses, the lawgiver of the Jews, wrote. It is manifestly a reference to Noah, whose family is not excluded, although he alone is mentioned. But Jerome, understanding this very poorly, makes Nicolaus speak in the plural: ‘others floating upon the ark’s hull,’ etc.”

If we answered Clericus’s minute questions one by one, we would draw out the thread of controversy at excessive length. I shall therefore settle the matter and the questions briefly.

1. He asks why Jerome translated the Greek word λείψανα into Latin as *vestigia* and *monumenta*, rather than as “remnants of the ark.” He could have raised this doubt only through his own ignorance. Let him therefore consult Marius Nizolius in his notes on Cicero, col. 1652, from whom he will learn that *vestigia*, *monumenta*, and *reliquiae* have the same meaning among the Latins:

> *Vestigium, -ii*: remnants, sign, mark, memorial.

2. Clericus fabricates a double falsehood. I never at all thought that συνευωχεῖτο τοῖς οἰκείοις had been badly translated as “he rejoiced with his children.” Nor did Jerome have regard to an etymology from εὖ and ἔχειν; he elegantly expressed the sense of the words: “and rejoicing with his children.” For Noah, after leaving the ark with his offspring and offering sacrifices to God, could not have feasted in a holy manner except while rejoicing with his children and members of his household.

3. Here one must say to the ignorant Clericus: Why do you stand so awkwardly? [Note: [Col. 1581] Compare what we annotated on this passage, vol. III, cols. 125 and 127.] He wishes ἀποβατήριον to mean a place at which one disembarks or descends, and at the same time denies that Jerome translated it elegantly as *exitus* or *egressus*, as though ἀποβατήριον were the same as ἀπόβασις.

Thus, according to our critic, descending from a ship and exiting or going forth from a ship are utterly different things; so too are ascent and departure. Let us therefore teach him what ἀπόβασις means, so that he may learn not to slander a translation he does not understand:

> Ἀπόβασις, say the most learned authorities in the Greek language, means exit, departure, descent; in Pliny, a leap; in Plautus, an outcome; in Thucydides, ἀπόβασις τῆς γῆς, “going forth onto land” (in Livy, “after the ascent from the ships onto land”).

The Armenians therefore called the place where Noah came ashore ἀπόβασις, an exit or departure—what we would say in French, *la descente*, *le débarquement*.

4. Jerome would have translated the Greek name μέγα into Latin superfluously, since he later adds concerning Mount Baris:

> To which, they assert, many fled during the flood and were saved there.

Those who were saved on the mountain at the time of the flood could have fled only to a very high mountain, as Nicolaus of Damascus reports.

5. Clericus, the critic of Jerome’s translation, behaves foolishly when he objects to the plural expression:

> Others, however, floating upon the ark’s hull, etc.

Yet he himself has conceded that Noah’s family is not excluded by the mention of Noah alone in Eusebius. Jerome therefore more correctly translates in the plural than if, with pedantic zeal, he had named Noah alone.

VIII. “In the entry *Astaroth Carnaim*, ὑπὲρ τὴν Σοδομῖτιν—that is, ‘above the Sodomite territory’—is translated as *in supercilio Sodomorum*, ‘on the brow of the Sodomites.’ This cannot be tolerated unless Sodom were a mountain on whose brow that city had been built, which everyone knows to be false.”

Do you not marvel, prudent reader, at the learning of this observation and the keenness of our Clericus’s intellect? “It cannot be tolerated,” he says, “as *on the brow of the Sodomites*, unless Sodom were a mountain,” and so forth. It would indeed be intolerable if he knew nothing of the fact that *supercilium* means the same as a higher and more elevated place, and that here *on the brow of the Sodomites* signifies what the entry *Save* signifies: “above the region of Sodom.”

Let us therefore understand both passages as referring to the higher and more elevated parts that belonged to the territory of Sodom, and we shall laugh at Clericus’s sheer nonsense.

IX. “At *Arbo*, or rather *Arbe*, Hebron is said to have been βασίλειον Davidis, that is, οἴκημα, ‘the royal dwelling, the seat of David,’ but it is badly translated as *regnum*, ‘kingdom.’ It is just as if someone should say in Greek of Versailles, where the palace of Louis XIV is located, Βερσαλίαν βασίλειον εἶναι Βασιλέως Κελτῶν, and another should translate it as, ‘Versailles is the kingdom of the king of the Celts.’”

There you have a man writing in Greek and Latin. But what will you say if I call him ignorant and foolish? He is certainly ignorant, for he did not know that βασίλειον in the sacred Scriptures signifies “kingdom,” as in Proverbs 18:19:

> ἰσχύει δὲ ὥσπερ τεθεμελιωμένον βασίλειον  
> “But it grows strong like a kingdom firmly founded.”

The *Epitome of the Treasury of the Greek Language* by Henri Estienne acknowledges this meaning, so that we must greatly marvel that a critical scholar was ignorant of what is even found in grammarians.

[Note: [Col. 1583D] Clericus replies: even if βασίλειον were found in the Scriptures in the sense of “kingdom,” Hebron would still be wrongly translated as David’s kingdom rather than David’s palace or royal seat, since his kingdom is known to have extended over the whole tribe of Judah. The passage Martianaeus adduces here does not properly signify a kingdom founded, but a palace founded; for in the Hebrew there is [term omitted], *armon*, which means “palace.” [Col. 1584D]]

Moreover, it is an indication of a foolish writer to call Louis the Great “the king of the Celts,” as though he ruled only the Celts and not the people of France, or the entire nation of the Franks. I have said more about this unlearned difficulty at the end of the book on the Canon of the Sacred Volumes, written in French; therefore I shall now pass over the difficulty.

X. After John Clericus had thus ignorantly reproved Jerome, he immediately turned to criticize Bonfrerius and Martianaeus, adding the following:

> “We have notable examples of this matter in the book *On Hebrew Places*. Since neither Jacobus Bonfrerius nor John Martianaeus remembered that in Greek manuscripts Η and Ι are frequently confused . . . they left, in the entry *Astaroth*, Σοδομίτην instead of Σοδομῖτιν. Why, you will ask, do you prove a matter known to boys? Because Bonfrerius and Martianaeus erred in it—or rather, if we stand by their editions, Jerome himself, deceived by faulty Greek writing. Thus Eusebius speaks concerning Amalecitis: Ἀμαλεκῖτις, χώρα ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ. But it was printed as Ἀμαληκίτης, which is a mere solecism; and likewise in Jerome: *Amalecites, a region in the desert*, etc.”

Those who have never read Bonfrerius and Martianaeus will think Clericus reliable in this paragraph. But those who have carefully examined both editions of the book *On Hebrew Places* will scarcely be able to tolerate the critic’s perverse reliability, ignorance, and inconsistency.

The learned Bonfrerius observed that in the entries *Astaroth Carnaim* and *Lasan*, instead of Σοδομίτην one should read Σοδομὰν or Σοδόμην. In the entries *Save* and *Seboim* he also printed Eusebius’s correct reading, namely Σοδομῖτιν, not Σοδομίτην.

Then, under the entry *Amalecites*, instead of *Amalecitis*, he writes:

> “*Amalecites* is rather a patronymic name derived from the region than the name of the region itself: the region and people are called Amalec.”

Thus writes Jacobus Bonfrerius. But Clericus wickedly attacks him as though the most expert editor of Eusebius had written none of these things.

As for me, I had no hesitation in taking an example from the learned and prudent Bonfrerius. I therefore wished to remind the reader of that man’s observations when I wrote under the entry *Lasan*:

> “Bonfrerius thinks that τὴν Σοδομὰν should be read, and that this is more correct than what is found concerning Sidon in Jerome.”

Previously, under the entry *Bethsaida*, I read Γενησαρίτιδι in the Greek text; but in the notes, together with Bonfrerius, I read Γενησαρίτῃ, adding ex tempore:

> “We leave readings of this sort to the judgment of the learned.”

Moreover, to make Clericus’s slander manifest, let readers remember that in my notes on the third Greek fragment of the book *Hebrew Names*, col. 560, I wrote the following:

> “There are no lack of scribal errors in the Greek manuscript, nor corruptions of names. I generally correct manifest and acknowledged faults without notes; the rest I transcribe carefully, just as they are read in the Greek codex—for example, Σὶθ instead of Σὴθ, etc.”

Who would believe that, after I had expressed such an observation in these precise words, Clericus the critic could charge me with failing to remember that Η and Ι are frequently confused in Greek manuscripts?

Unless I were dealing with a man ignorant of this business and of the reading of manuscripts, both Greek and Latin, I would challenge him to collate and dispute the Greek manuscript that I used, so that he himself might reluctantly testify that in the new edition I changed hundreds of instances of Ι into Η because I knew that inexperienced copyists had written iota for eta in very ancient exemplars.

But I suppose this will pass without consequence for you, Clericus, who rejoiced at finding a mere solecism in the word *Amalecites*. Reread what you wished to teach from Cassiodorus in the *Questions Concerning Jerome*, p. 66, and then pp. 378 ff. See how little consistent you are when condemning the reading *Amalecites* instead of *Amalecitis*, while at the same time warning that the ancients often wrote *omnis* for *omnes* and *omnes* for *omnis*—that is, that plural accusatives were indiscriminately terminated in ES, EIS, and IS.

Learn, therefore, that the ancients wrote *Amalecites* and *Amalecitis* indiscriminately, just as they wrote *Joannis* for *Joannes* in the nominative case. Since these things are so, I produce you yourself as a witness to your own ignorance and inconsistency—qualities you ought to have concealed, had your customary desire to disparage everyone else and that critical art of yours, by which you do not blush to place yourself above all other writers, permitted it.

XI. Finally, our Clericus objects to Jerome’s Greek learning as follows:

> “I shall add here a small matter, indeed, but one that will show that nothing is truer than what I have said. Eusebius wrote: Ἰτουραία ἢ καὶ Τραχωυῖτις, ‘Ituraea, which is also Trachonitis.’ Why, then, did Jerome translate it: *Ituraea and Trachonitis, a region*? etc. The reader may suspect that these are the names of two districts of the region that constituted the tetrarchy of Philip.

> “You are being pedantic, you will say, if you cut such matters down to the bone. On the contrary, it is pedantic negligence in the man who did not translate more conveniently. I do not know whether he thought that the particle ἢ, ‘which,’ should be deleted because he supposed it meant ἢ, ‘or.’

> “The reason for suspicion is this: he stumbled similarly in the entry Τραχωνῖτις: Τραχωνῖτις χώρα, ἣ καὶ Ἰτουραία—that is, ‘Trachonitis, a region which is also Ituraea.’ Yet he translated: ‘Trachonitis, a region, or Ituraea.’ If I had translated in this way, Martianaeus would never have forgiven me, even if I said that I was the founder of a new work. He would have shouted that this was a device by which I was trying to conceal my ignorance so as not to be accused of a bad translation, etc.”

As long as our Cleric’s insatiable eagerness to speak and criticize Jerome continues, so long will he reveal himself to be foolish and imprudent. For whoever does not see what the occasion requires; or speaks too much; or puts himself on display; or fails to consider the persons with whom he argues; or has no regard for the dignity of the matters themselves; or, finally, is in some respect inelegant, wordy, or excessive—that person is called foolish.

“He would have shouted,” he says, “Martianaeus, if I had translated with Jerome: ‘the region of Trachonitis, or Ituraea.’” On the contrary, Martianaeus would have loudly praised you if you had been skilled in critical scholarship and had not displayed your ignorance so openly. Who would not now marvel at the observations of childish boasting which no prudent person would deign to write against so great a man, even if those observations were true? But since they are extremely ignorant and utterly false, there is nothing in them for which we can grant Cleric any indulgence.

1. Cleric foolishly criticizes Jerome, unaware that the holy Doctor was imitating the style of Luke the Evangelist, who [Col. 1584D], in chapter 3, verse 1, said that Philip was tetrarch “of Ituraea and Trachonitis” (τῆς Ἰτουραίας καὶ Τραχωνίτιδος), that is, *Ituraeae et Trachonitidis*. Let the holy Evangelist, then, be accused—and not Jerome—because, by omitting the particle ἣ, “which,” he gave readers occasion to suspect that Ituraea and Trachonitis were the names of two districts of the region that constituted Philip’s tetrarchy. It was therefore neither ignorance nor negligence that caused the Greek particle to be omitted in Jerome’s translation. Rather, he wished to follow the Evangelist’s footsteps instead of torturing himself with a vile interpretation.

2. Very learned men suspect that Ituraea and Trachonitis were different regions—Strabo, Andrichomius, and Bonfrerius among them. A critical writer speaking about a geographical matter ought not to have been wholly unaware of their opinions.

3. Cleric is ignorant of a matter known even to children: namely, that Jerome’s rendering, “Ituraea, or Trachonitis,” signifies the same thing as Cleric’s rendering, “Ituraea, which is also Trachonitis.” In both expressions we understand [Col. 1585A] one region, which is called either Ituraea or Trachonitis.

4. Our critic deserves no confidence, since he concealed the fact that Jerome expressed the Greek particle ἣ a hundred times by the relative pronoun *quae*, “which,” very appropriately in the book *On Places*. For example:

- Column 141: Ἀμᾶν, ἣ νῦν Φιλαδελφία—“Aman, which is now Philadelphia”;
- column 163: Βαβὲλ, ἣ Βαβυλὼν—“Babel, which is also Babylon”;
- column 185: Καριαθιαρεὶμ, ἣ καὶ Καριαθβὰδ—“Cariathiarim, which is also Cariatbaal”;
- column 203: Ἐγλὼμ, ἣ καὶ Ὀδολλὰμ—“Eglom, which is also Odollam.”

In the same place:

- Ἐσὼρ, ἣ καὶ Ἀσὼρ—“Esor, which is also Asor.”

Likewise, columns 268 and 275:

- Σοφειρὰ, ἣ καὶ Σουφὴρ—“Sophera, which is also Sophir.”

Let learned and prudent readers now judge how highly the criticism of John Cleric ought to be valued: in it there is no judgment, no reliability, and no learning, although judgment, reliability, and learning are precisely the duties and functions of authors in this kind of writing.

§ 2. On the Hebrew Learning of Saint Jerome

Now that we have dismissed the Greek difficulties raised by John Cleric—which he had hoped would pave the way for him to pass a somewhat bolder and freer judgment concerning Jerome’s Hebrew learning—we shall demonstrate by several more notable examples from the *Jerome Questions* that their author was utterly ignorant of the Hebrew language and an utterly foolish critic in his criticism of the holy Doctor. Jerome’s virtue and knowledge [Col. 1585B] shine in the Church of God like a most brilliant light, by which, as a coin is obscured amid the riches of Croesus, all Clerican learning and his judgment—bolder even than calumny—are thrown into darkness.

At the advice of my friends—especially the most illustrious Lord de Camgrand, archdeacon of the Church of the Saints, and Lord Bellet, a most studious and learned canon—I pass over Cleric’s trifles and silly old-womanish absurdities in the *Jerome Questions*, since they judge them worthy of laughter and guffaws, not of my response. Moreover, the very wise superiors of our Congregation, together with many of my most devoted colleagues, order me to devote my time and labor to publishing the works of Saint Jerome, rather than to refuting a heretic who knows no end either to speaking or to publishing books. I shall therefore offer fewer examples, from which a learned and intelligent judge will be able to form an opinion about the ignorance displayed in the questions I have omitted.

I. Our critic wished to prove by arguments of the following kind that Jerome possessed no grammatical knowledge:

> “Since these things,” he says, “are clearer than midday, our Benedictine monk—who ought to have learned from this, at least, that nothing outstanding in Hebrew grammar could fruitfully be expected from Jerome—offers us this passage and similar ones, so that we may accept from Jerome precisely what we do not know. It is worthwhile to hear the man disclose a great secret, one which has until now escaped all Hebrew grammarians. He says [Col. 1585C]:
>
> ‘The four names here listed by Jerome or Philo are written among the Hebrews with a diphthong, as follows: Hiram, Histob, Hira, Hisboseth. Nor were the letters aleph, heth, and ain used among the ancient Hebrews as consonants, but as vowels, as Jerome’s present annotation plainly declares. It states that aleph, heth, and ain form a diphthong with the following *jod* in the four names just mentioned. Hence the opinions of certain modern grammarians disappear—those who have thought that every diphthong is excluded from the Hebrew language and that Hebrew words always begin with a consonant, never with a vowel.
>
> ‘1. It was not merely certain grammarians, but absolutely all ancient and modern Hebrew grammarians, who held that no word begins with a vowel, except for a few whom it is unnecessary to name.
>
> ‘2. Almost all of them also held that diphthongs exist, with the principal exception of the German Jews. On this matter, see Johann Buxtorf’s *Thesaurus*, chapters 3 [Col. 1585D] and 4, and other grammarians.
>
> ‘3. The opinion of the grammarians who deny that a Hebrew syllable can begin with a vowel is not a conjecture but the most certain truth; no one has opposed it except a drowsy man, such as Jerome here, and his hoarse echo, Martianaeus. The matter can be demonstrated in three words. Every vowel has a definite sound—A, E, I, O, U—and is not pronounced indiscriminately with all five of those sounds, as is evident from aleph, heth, and ain, by the proper names in which they occur. This is also clear from the way the ancient translators pronounced them, so that no one may think we rely solely on the authority of the Masoretes.
>
> ‘4. The first index of names that falls into one’s hands will demonstrate the point, but it will already be evident from the four names cited. I ask: if alpha is a vowel, which of the five vowels is it? Without doubt, A. Therefore one ought to read AISTOB and AISBOSETH, not Histob and Hisboseth—without a diphthong—or Eistob and Eisboseth. Next, what vowels were Hheth and Hain? Was the former the Greek eta (ἦτα) and the latter O? How do these form a diphthong for us, if we believe Jerome—a diphthong such as the Greek ΕΙ? It ought to have been written Ηἰρὰμ and Οἰρὰ, which the Seventy Translators nevertheless did not do, although the pronunciation of those names was well known to them; nor did Jerome himself do so. Will three vowels joined with [Col. 1586A] *jod* form one and the same diphthong? No one will believe it. What, then, shall we conclude from this? Neither the Bethlehem monk nor the Parisian monk—whom I would certainly not equate with each other, lest Martianaeus misunderstand me—paid sufficient attention to what they were saying. If they had written with greater care, they would no more have said that Aleph, Heth, and Ain are vowels and form diphthongs among the Hebrews than they would have said that the Latin H is a vowel in the Latin language.
>
> ‘I had almost omitted Martianaeus, who, to defend this fiction about Hebrew words beginning with a vowel, adduces the example of the Arabs. They pronounce Vau, with which many words begin, as W, which the French express by *ou*: thus *ouaheb*, which the Arabs pronounce *Waheb*, while modern grammarians of Hebrew write *vaheb*. But he ought to have known that no Arab treats Vau as a consonant, any more than the European peoples who use the letter W do; for that letter has no sound by itself and must necessarily be joined with a vowel, both in the European languages and in Arabic. If Martianaeus still prefers what sleepy Jerome carelessly uttered to the evident usage and certain analogy of the Hebrew language, let him do so. Let him feed his mind on his own dreams, and continue to admire in Jerome above all what most requires our indulgence. We shall never be ashamed that we have failed to please such a man.’” [Col. 1586B]

*Questions*, no. 4, pp. 85 ff.

I ask forgiveness from all students for having transcribed so many absurdities and such worn-out grammatical quibbles from our contentious opponent. Necessity compelled me to do so, so that I might answer the fool according to his folly, lest he should appear wise to himself and lest John Cleric—son of Apollo, father of the Muses, champion of literary freedom—should laugh at us as drowsy, yawning, dreaming, and hoarse-voiced.

But come: let us reproduce here the entire passage from Jerome and the uncorrupted integrity of our annotation, so that from it Cleric’s ignorance, dishonesty, and perversity of opinion may be clearer than midday. He wishes to coat a pure vessel with incrustation in every respect. Jerome’s context is therefore as follows:

> Hiram, living in exaltation.
>
> Histob, a good man.
>
> Hiras, watchful.
>
> Hisboseth, a man of confusion.
>
> **THEREFORE WE HAVE WRITTEN THESE NAMES WITH ASPIRATION, BECAUSE AMONG BOTH THE GREEKS AND THE HEBREWS THEY ARE WRITTEN WITH A DIPHTHONG.**

### Our Annotation

[Col. 1586C]

The four names listed here by Jerome or Philo are read as written with a diphthong among the Hebrews, as follows: Hiram, Histob, Hira, Hisboseth. Nor were the letters aleph, heth, and ain used among the ancient Hebrews as consonants, but as vowels, as Jerome’s present annotation plainly declares. In it he states that aleph, heth, and ain form a diphthong with the following *jod* in the four Hebrew names just mentioned. Hence the opinions of certain modern grammarians disappear—those who have thought that every diphthong is excluded from the Hebrew language and that Hebrew words always begin with a consonant, never with a vowel.

As for the Greek diphthongs in the four names given above, it is not readily apparent that the matter is exactly as Jerome testifies, except perhaps in the name Hiram, which is written Χειρὰμ among the Greeks. The other names are written in Greek without diphthongs: Ἰεβοσθὲ, Ἰστὼβ, Ἴρας. But after carefully examining the Septuagint translators, we show that the name Hisboseth was written with a diphthong in the Alexandrian manuscript at 2 Kings 2:10: Εἰεβοσθαὶ, *Eiebosthai*. From this it is sufficiently clear that the other Hebrew names were likewise written in ancient times among the Greeks with the diphthong εἰ. This is confirmed even more convincingly by the name Jabes, which is commonly written Ἰαβὶς but is found in the same Alexandrian manuscript with the diphthong Εἰαβεῖς.

Finally, it is well known to the learned that the vowel Ι and the diphthong εἰ were used indifferently among both Greeks and Latins; and, in accordance with that usage, Ἰστὼβ and Εἰστὼβ, Ἴρας and Εἴρας were written indiscriminately.

All this was belched forth by the yawning and drowsy Jerome and his hoarse Echo, Martianaeus; their belching jaws are considered a dream by Cleric, who, if we believe one who boasts and displays himself so magnificently, scarcely seems to have disputed with Apollo over the Tripod. Yet I catch him dreaming when he says that I bring forward the example of the Arabs in order to defend my fiction—as he calls it—from the initial *vau*. Let him reread my annotation on the diphthongs noted by Jerome among the Hebrews; if I happened by chance to mention *vau*, I confess myself a dreamer. If not, then we may regard it as certain and established that our Cleric feeds his mind on false dreams and insults.

But let us speak cautiously and step by step, and take up the critic’s difficulties individually from the beginning, so that we may inspect more attentively [Col. 1587A] the man snoring in deep sleep.

1. “Not merely certain men,” he says, “but all Hebrew grammarians, ancient and modern, except for a few, have held that no word begins with a vowel.” Certainly, if a few are excepted, only some remain—not many, and not all. Yet the number of grammarians is smaller than that of fools and critics, which is unlimited. I was therefore right and precise when I spoke of “certain” men. Moreover, I had read only a few Hebrew grammarians, and, among the books of that kind that I had examined, I ought to have said “certain,” lest, like Cleric, I boast of knowing what I do not know at all.

2. “Almost all,” he says, “held that diphthongs exist.” This is not so, since our Latin writers of Hebrew grammatical works do not teach us diphthongs at all. See Bellarmine, Mair, our Thomas Dufour, Pagninus, and others.

3. The grammarians’ opinion that syllables do not begin with a vowel is so far from the truth that the contrary position is more evident and more truthful among all sane people who are not infected with rabbinic frenzy. The proper names of men, regions, and mountains found among the Septuagint translators—followed by Origen and the other Greek writers in their lexicons of Hebrew names—demonstrate our Jeromean position with complete clarity.

4. The very ancient index of names will teach that Cleric is foolish when he maintains that the vowel Aleph must always be read [Col. 1587B] as A, since it is often read as I, E, O, or U. As for how aleph, heth, and ain formed a diphthong among the ancients, enough has already been said in our annotation, which no one has opposed except a drowsy and snoring critic, Cleric.

From all this it is plainly evident that our glorious champion may be beaten by everyone’s words, since he dares to set himself above Jerome in Hebrew grammar.

II. “Now let us come,” says the same critic, “to the construction of nouns, of which the two principal rules are these: an adjective must agree in gender with its substantive, and the adjective is placed after it. It is also established by constant usage that numeral nouns, which are called ordinal, form the feminine in *-ith*, except the first. Thus from *hhamesch*, ‘five,’ are formed *hhamischi*, ‘fifth’ masculine, and *hhamischith*, ‘fifth’ feminine. If Martianaeus is unaware of this, let him read Johann Buxtorf’s *Thesaurus*, book 2, chapter 1, and T. Erpenius’s *Grammar*, book 3, chapter 7. The matter is so well known that anyone who undertakes to prove it after the grammarians is merely wasting time.

“Nevertheless, if we believe Martianaeus’s manuscript codices, Jerome thought that ‘the fifth generation’ could be said in Hebrew as *hhamischa dor*, although *dor* is [Col. 1587C] masculine and it is necessary to say *dor hhamischi*, as the Concordance will show, if consultation of it is needed in so clear a matter. For Jerome says in his letter to Damasus: ‘If it were the fifth generation, it would be read in their language *AMESA DOR*.’ In the margin the editor added *hhamischa dor*. This is the same as if I were to say in Latin *quinta annus*, or something worse.

“The Amerbach brothers, who had added words written in Hebrew characters to the Erasmian editions, printed this passage according to the norms of Hebrew grammar. But Martianaeus corrects them as follows: ‘This passage was entirely corrupted in the books previously published. For instead of *amesa dor*, as Jerome wrote it, they changed the gender and the order of the words, reading *dor amisi* in the masculine gender, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscript codices of the letter to Damasus.’ They evidently wished to protect Jerome’s reputation, which Martianaeus imprudently betrays here. For if he carefully examined the manuscript codices, he teaches us that Jerome committed the threefold error I have described; and if children committed such an error in Latin at school, they would not escape the rod.

“Nevertheless, I think that the manuscript codices here contain what Jerome intended to write, and that Martianaeus cited them in good faith as evidence. This is suggested by the error of the same kind that immediately precedes it. For, speaking of the word *hhamuschim*, which occurs at Exodus 13:8, he says [Col. 1587D]:

“‘In the remainder, the interpretations do not differ; the whole dispute concerns the word *AMUSIM*, which is written with these letters: heth, mem, sin, jod, mem—whether it means “five” or “armed.” And indeed we cannot deny that “five” is said in this language, though not “fifth,” as they translated it, in the singular. But we emphatically deny that [Hebrew form], whatever vowel-points are attached to it, means “five”; and all who are not ignorant of the elements of the Hebrew language know that *hhamesch* means “five,” whereas *hhamischim* means either “fifths” or “fifty.”’”

To break briefly the inflated spirit of our Cleric, we remind present and future students that this enemy of Jerome was so ignorant that, even as an old man, he did not know what boys and infants could have taught him. He criticizes and harshly chastises Jerome as though Jerome had not known the construction of nouns or the gender of the Hebrew word *dor*, because Cleric himself still did not know that the Hebrew noun [Col. 1588A] *amesa* is masculine, not feminine. Yet here he writes this explicitly and strives to teach it against Jerome and against our edition, in which I printed *AMESA DOR*. To Doctor Cleric this is the same as saying in Latin *quinta annus*, or something worse.

Let the first barbarous and solecistic disgrace, then, be removed from Jerome and cling entirely to Cleric, who is ignorant of the construction and gender of Hebrew nouns.

The second unforgivable error of this writer—one which, if committed by boys in Latin at school, would be punished—is his enormous ignorance in supposing that, by constant usage, ordinal numerals form the feminine in *-ith*, except *rischona*, “first.” For all the other feminine ordinal nouns from first through tenth have a double form at the end: namely, *-ith* and *-iia* or *-ija*. For example, *scheni*, “second,” has *schenith* and *schenijach*. If Cleric is still unaware of this, let him read Pagninus’s *Thesaurus* under *schēni*, and the grammatical work of our T. Dufour, p. 191.

Or, if it is necessary to refute him in grammatical matters by the authority of the prophets, let him read the eloquent Isaiah, chapter 15:5 and 19:24, who uses the feminine form *schelischia*, that is, “third,” or “three-year-old,” “tertiary.” The same [Col. 1588B] usage occurs in Jeremiah, chapter 48:34. I am very surprised that a critical writer, amid such a heap of his books, should be ignorant of grammatical rules and should regard the prophetic style of a new interpreter of the Bible as a solecism.

We take the third argument from Clerican ignorance from the order of the words *amesa dor*, or, as he himself reads it, *hhamischa dor*. He judged this construction to be inverted, because he did not know that in the sacred books the nouns *ames* and *amesa*, or *hhamesch* and *hhamischa*, are not placed after but before the substantive. For example, Genesis 5:6: “And Seth lived *AMES SCHANIM*, five years”; and 47:2: “He took *HHAMISCHA ANASCHIN*, five men.”

Let him therefore learn that masculine ordinal nouns ending in *-i* are placed after their substantive, as in *jom hhamischi*, “the fifth day.” Other numeral nouns, although masculine in gender, have a feminine termination and precede their substantive, as in Leviticus 23:6: *ubahhamischa asarjom*, “and on the fifteenth day.” See also the book of Numbers, chapter 28:17, and chapter 29:12.

These are unmistakable errors of ignorance, which do not allow Doctor Cleric to withdraw his hand from the rod. But what shall I say of the same dishonest praiser and defender of Jerome’s false editors? He praises the Amerbachs [Col. 1588C] because they printed *dor hhamischi* according to the norms of Hebrew grammar and removed Jerome’s words *amesa dor*, allegedly to protect the reputation of the holy Doctor by this corruption. But he calls Martianaeus imprudent for restoring the genuine words in the context of the letter to Damasus.

Yet since falsehood has no rewards and falsity possesses little strength, what is the reason that he adorns falsifiers with praise and that iniquitous corruption has such power over him, while he does not especially love the sincere editor? Do you wish to know the reason? He does not praise the faithful integrity of writings because he himself is not upright in mind; rather, his entire breast is composed for concealment and falsehood. He is a false Christian, a false interpreter of the sacred Scriptures, a false writer on critical scholarship, a false champion of freedom of thought, and a false editor of many volumes. He is nothing but a critical sycophant and a most ignorant cleric.

I can prove both charges from his ensuing words: “Nevertheless, I think …” For he emphatically denies that *Amusim* can mean “five,” because, with brazen effrontery, he quotes Jerome’s statement in mutilated and corrupted form as follows:

> “And indeed we cannot deny that ‘five’ is said in this language, not ‘fifth,’ as they translated it, in the singular.”

Jerome did not say this, nor is anything of the kind found in our edition. Jerome’s true statement is:

> “And indeed we cannot deny that ‘five’ is said in this language; but ‘five’ in the plural number, not ‘fifth,’ as they translated it in the singular. Therefore *AMUSIM*, however it is supplied with vowel-points, signifies ‘five’ in the plural number—that is, fivefold, in groups of five, fifths, and fifty”—

as Cleric himself, in his ignorance, admits, affirming what he had previously denied and teaching what he had attacked after corrupting it.

III. After twisting the weapons of his own ignorance, our Cleric seeks foreign assistance against Jerome, with the following preface:

> “But lest I seem to be alone in holding this opinion about Jerome’s grammatical learning, I shall bring forward several relevant passages from the *Biblical Exercises* of John Morin. He wrote them with another purpose, certainly, but they confirm our opinion no less, although we do not approve everything he says.”

He subsequently brings forward seven or eight observations by Morin, two of which he rejects as false. He illustrates the first rejected observation in the following manner:

> “Morin explains this at greater length, but he is mistaken. For in place of the word [Hebrew form], improperly added here by the Amerbachs, there ought to have been added [Hebrew form], which Jerome read as *Eloe*, as Jean Martianay correctly observed after John Drusius.”

Finally, at the end of all Morin’s observations, John Cleric adds:

> “These are the words of a most learned man, which those who have read Jerome’s works or carefully compared his translation with the Hebrew codex know to be utterly true; nevertheless, Martianaeus did not even attempt to refute them, any more than the other similar statements.”

It is true, Cleric—most kindly disposed to becoming an object of laughter—that I did not wish to provoke the guffaws of the learned by attempting to refute Morin’s observations. For what wise man could restrain his laughter on hearing that Morin had rebuked Jerome over an absolute case, allegedly not distinguished from the construct case, or because he had failed to distinguish between the absolute and construct forms in *nasiche adam*, Micah 5:4? Jerome translated it “chief men,” not “chiefs of men.”

But how could the holy Doctor have read *nasiche adam*, or *nesiche adam*, if he did not distinguish between the absolute and construct forms? Let Cleric now say whether he thinks *nesiche* is an absolute form. If he says that it is construct, then Jerome did distinguish the construct form from the absolute form, *nesichim*. And if the Latin translation does not preserve the construct form—“chiefs of men”—then Morin and Cleric should not vent their anger against Jerome the translator, provided that the euphony of the Latin language into which he was translating has been preserved intact.

They should then accuse Aquila as well and declare him ignorant of Hebrew grammar for failing, like Jerome, to distinguish between the absolute and construct forms; for he wrote “constituted men,” not “constituted of men.”

Cleric would have passed over such trivial observations, unworthy even of so learned a man, along with me, had he not been oppressed by envy and hatred and attempted in every respect to suppress Jerome’s little works. But if he is not ashamed of his own ignorance, because of Morin’s grammatical trifles that somewhat diminish Jerome’s learning, let him at least be ashamed to hear the most learned writers of his own kind—that is, heterodox writers—praising Jerome’s learning to the skies.

Those men possessed the modern lexicons and many Hebrew grammars, but they did not wish to be so foolish with our Cleric as to set themselves above Jerome in Hebrew matters on that account. Those learned Protestant teachers knew that no later generation receives nothing from its predecessors, and that whatever has been transferred into lexicons or grammars was received and borrowed from the ancient Jews and translators, not fabricated and disseminated by modern writers.

But now let us hear those very interpreters praising Jerome.

From the critical notes [Col. 1589C] of Louis Cappel on the book of Esther, p. 570, new edition:

> “Since it is therefore established that these headings belong to Jerome, for what purpose or with what intention would passages from another translation have been placed beneath them? Third, if the Latin translation of these passages is compared with the Greek, Jerome’s judgment, intelligence, learning, and learned and candid freedom in translating will be discovered in it; and consequently the purity and elegance of the style, or language, and the character of the expression are the same as in the rest of the body of the book. For those passages were not translated barbarously or crudely word for word from the Greek, but Jerome faithfully expressed the meaning of the Greek context learnedly and elegantly, insofar as this could conveniently be done while preserving the phraseology and elegance and purity of the Latin language.”

From the tenth prolegomenon [Col. 1589D] of Brian Walton:

> “We therefore conclude that the authority of the Vulgate is no different from that of other versions which faithfully render the original texts, since what the more celebrated doctors of the Roman Church have written about it and its authority can be applied to the other versions. Although we do not acknowledge it as divine, it must nevertheless be held in high esteem and not rashly attacked, both because of its antiquity and its general use throughout the West for a thousand years, and because of the learning and fidelity of its translator, whom we recognize for the most part as Jerome. The most learned Protestants freely proclaim that he rendered a great service to the Church.
>
> “A learned man says: ‘I have never doubted that the Christian Church owes much to its author for having made intelligible to Latin ears the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, written in so foreign a language.’ Certainly Theodore Beza, in the preface to the New Testament of 1559, declares that it ought to be preferred to all other Latin versions, and reproves Erasmus for rejecting the ancient translator because he differed from the modern Greek codices, whereas he appears to have followed a more accurate exemplar. Beza therefore defends the Vulgate against Erasmus, while the most learned John Boys, in a justly proportioned volume, often defends the same translator against Beza’s frequently unjust censures.
>
> “Paul Fagius, in chapter 4 of his Latin version of the Chaldean Paraphrase, says the following against those who, because the Vulgate does not correspond in every respect word for word [Col. 1590A] to the Hebrew text, hiss at it, condemn it, and reject it:
>
> “‘They do not consider whom or what the Vulgate author followed. For whenever he seems to differ from the Hebrew truth, I almost always discover that he followed either the Septuagint, the Chaldean paraphrast, or one of the rabbis. The Vulgate edition was therefore not born arbitrarily, as certain half-learned men foolishly and imprudently proclaim.’
>
> “Ludovicus de Dieu, a man distinguished for his knowledge of languages, writes the following in the preface to his notes on the Gospels, where he compares the Syriac, Arabic, and other versions with the Vulgate and with the versions of Erasmus, and especially of Beza, speaking of the author of the Vulgate:
>
> “‘If I assert that the Vulgate translator, whoever he may finally have been, was a learned, indeed a most learned man, I shall not judge that I have erred. I admit that he has his blemishes and his barbarisms, but I cannot deny that I admire his faithfulness and judgment throughout, even where he appears barbarous.’
>
> “For this reason he often prefers the Vulgate among variant readings and defends it against Beza.
>
> “Finally, the most illustrious Grotius, explaining in the preface to his notes on the Old Testament why he refers his notes to the Vulgate as though to the text, says that he has always held the Vulgate translator in the highest esteem, not only because it contains no unsound doctrines, but also because it contains a great deal of learning, although its style of expression is sufficiently rough.
>
> “From these testimonies it is sufficiently clear that the most learned Protestants, although they do not place the Vulgate [Col. 1590B] upon the throne of authenticity, do not equate it with the sources, and do not regard it as free from every error, nevertheless do not despise it but render it the honor that is due to it, for the reasons we have already explained.”

Thus far Brian Walton, whom we know to have been a learned and prudent man. Let Cleric therefore shout with the ignorant and half-learned, foolishly and imprudently criticize and reject the translator of the Vulgate—that is, Jerome—and his translation. For my part, it is enough that I admire, praise, and defend Jerome’s judgment, fidelity, intelligence, and learning together with the most learned writers of every age.

# CHAPTER II. On the Integrity and Usefulness of the New Edition of the Works of Saint Jerome, and on the Ignorance and Malice of John Cleric’s *Jerome Questions*

For some time, quite a few critical and miscellaneous works by John Cleric had emerged from darkness into the light, in which debates insulting to learned men, and burdensome and irritating to the wise reader, frequently occurred. At the beginning of the present century, however, the same author’s *Jerome Questions* appeared, in which he poured out the entire venom of his breast—namely, his anger and hatred—against us and our new edition of Saint Jerome [Col. 1590C].

Nor did our Cleric merely follow the custom of other critics by airing trivial objections or slandering the details of our edition. Rather, if he could, he wished to overthrow it completely and remove the author’s memory from among the living. How eagerly he worked to disturb Martianaeus through his writings is shown by the admonition prefixed to the *Jerome Questions*. In it he hoped to stir up the envy of all literary men, indeed the particular hatred of my dearest colleagues against me. He even tried, through flattering appeals, to enlist the prudence and authority of my superiors, so that I might finally be prohibited from producing the Jerome edition. And indeed, if they had granted Cleric’s request, nothing would have remained to prevent me from becoming the most wretched of all editors and writers of the present age.

As I investigate the cause of such great anger, I suspect none other than my having undertaken the defense of Jerome and erected a trophy to his learning. Nor am I a great speculator in this matter, since Cleric himself agrees with me. He begins his seventh Question [Col. 1590D] as follows:

> “We have already said that we would have had no controversy with Martianaeus if he had bestowed moderate praise upon Jerome.”

The cause of my condemnation, then, is that I have raised Jerome to heaven with praise and taken pleasure in defending his little works against abusive Clerics. But let us hear the defendant-orator himself set forth the arguments for my crime.

## John Cleric’s Greetings to the Reader

> “Everyone has praised the industry and learning of the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, who in France have produced excellent editions of several Latin and Greek Fathers; everyone has wished that they would continue, in accordance with their admirable undertaking, to enrich our libraries. It especially pleased all good and learned men that those Fathers had been so illustrated by them with prefaces and notes that the editors abstained from every insult toward recent writers.
>
> “This continued until Jean Martianaeus, far from imitating the fairness and prudence of his colleagues, began to publish Jerome and, in his prefaces and notes, to tear apart the reputation of the most learned men devoted to the Roman Church—not even excluding his Benedictine colleagues—and of those who had separated from that Church. Then almost everyone [Col. 1591A], both experts and nonexperts in these matters, complained competitively about the excessive bitterness that he poured out upon learned men in a wholly inappropriate place. He was so delighted by it that, although the insults had been removed from the prolegomena of the first volume—apparently at the command of the superiors of the learned order—he restored them several years later, with his anger in no way appeased, at the beginning of the second volume. I hear that this also greatly displeases those superiors.
>
> “As for me, against whom he attacked by name—and most bitterly, and in more than one place—I began to examine what novelty this edition was introducing. I noticed that the man had entirely failed to consider what his shoulders could refuse to carry and what they could bear. I wished to warn both the literary republic and the Benedictine order about this in the present little work, so that they might see to it that their reputation suffer no harm if they allow such a man any longer to contaminate Jerome’s writings with those insulting and insufficiently learned additions.
>
> “At the same time I have said much about Jerome himself, from which it will be clear that those people act wrongly who hold recent critics in such contempt in comparison with him that they regard them as though they were blind when placed beside him. If these remarks contribute to confirming and increasing the study of good and sacred letters, I shall have reason to rejoice. Certainly I wrote them with that intention. If not, I shall at least never regret this intention of mine. Farewell.”

Clericus, our man, did not wish to attack his Martianaeus without any preliminary defensive preparation [Col. 1591B], whom he bitterly regrets to have been the editor of Jerome, one who showed no mercy to the heretics who were always most hostile to the holy Doctor. But, setting aside everything that does not concern Clericus or the republic of letters—matters of which the malicious man makes no mention except to stir up pressure against my bonds—let us examine more carefully what he has to complain of on his own behalf. “I,” he says, “against whom he has inveighed by name, and indeed most fiercely,” etc. I confess, Clericus, that I did not wish to speak with greater consideration of you than you have spoken in more than one place against Jerome. The excessive harshness of my words is yours, since I received it from your Mosaic Pentateuch, as I warned the reader in my annotations, which you strive to call insufficiently learned because they prove you ignorant in every respect.

Turn, then, to my Commentary on the book of Hebrew Names, volume II of our edition, where these same things are written about you. “From these things,” I said, “it plainly appears how different Jerome’s diligence was, how different his talent and zeal in sacred matters, from that which the critics of our own time now display.” But when I have said this, they immediately accuse me of envy, or ignorant men brand me with the reputation of a bitter writer, as though a fault changed with the person; and as though what Clericus may do with impunity against Jerome, I may not do on behalf of Jerome against Clericus, an advocate of novel opinions and doctrines.

If this accusation should ever arise, I have nothing to oppose in this Apology [Col. 1591C] except the words of the holy Doctor, on whose account I undertook it: “Truth,” he says, “is bitter, wrinkled of brow and sad, and it gives offense to those who have been corrected . . . . Let truth and sincerity be in us, and bitterness will immediately follow.” Thus he speaks in Book I *Against the Pelagians*.

Hence come my “insulting and insufficiently learned notes and additions,” by which I have supposedly contaminated Jerome’s writings; hence the “excessive harshness” of which Clericus and his ignorant associates complain. But if those who have been corrected feel such bitterness toward truth, how much bitterness shall we feel toward the lies and insults of John Clericus? Falsehood has always been more bitter to me than gall, and more intolerable than every harshness. Yet falsehood frequently dominates our critic; nor do I know another writer who takes pleasure in so many and such great lies.

“I began,” he says, “to weigh what this edition brought forth that was new, and I noticed that the man had given no thought to what his shoulders could refuse to bear, or to what they were capable of bearing.”

But how do you say that you examined my edition, when you have not yet read the preface prefixed to volume I? Or, if you read it while examining the work, why do you pretend that I had given no thought to what my shoulders could refuse to bear, or to what they were capable of bearing? Examine and weigh, then, these words of my preface more carefully:

> “But when we undertook to prepare for the public benefit the divine Library of St. Jerome, previously unpublished, so many and such weighty matters of the greatest importance rested upon us [Col. 1591D] that the magnitude of the work imposed upon us not only presses upon our necks, but requires us to fall beneath the burden before it can be lifted. For who would not be afraid,” etc.

Now see how many lies there are at the very threshold of your *Hieronymian Questions*, since it is clear that I had considered what my shoulders could bear, while you neither noticed nor examined this, although you do not hesitate to present that very thing falsely to the reader.

But now observe what I said not about you, but about the prudent and fair-minded reader:

> “Yet this great hope sustains us in the case of the fair-minded reader: namely, that he will more readily grant us pardon if, in matters obscure in themselves and not previously attempted by anyone, we have not entirely satisfied his desire; or at least if something should occasionally have escaped us while writing that would not have escaped keener and more diligent eyes. Moved especially by this expectation, we publish certain Prolegomena,” etc.

After making this and similar preliminary statements, I had reason to expect that you would pardon my faults, if I could obtain anything fair or good from John Clericus. In truth, I had no hope of obtaining pardon from an ignorant man, because I had long heard that you were excessively angry with those who criticize you and savage toward every opponent.

Let us proceed at last, so that from the latter part of our preface we may show that the attacker of the edition is both a liar and ignorant. For, when examining what new things this edition brought forth, he found nothing worthy of notice—apart from my rashness and unlearned additions—about which he wished to warn the entire republic of letters and the Benedictine Order.

But our preface comes before John Clericus’s warning, because the antidote comes before the poison. For we explicitly indicate what our edition brings forth, addressing both the republic of letters and the Benedictine Order in these words:

> “Moved especially by this expectation, we publish certain Prolegomena toward the elucidation of this divine Library of St. Jerome, which will open up many things that, before our age, had been closed and unknown; remove from minds the errors of writers and books; and enrich the Church of Christ with the sacred Volumes translated into Latin by Eusebius Jerome, both from Greek and from Hebrew.”

Our Clericus considers such gifts worthless [Col. 1592B], because he has nothing else occupying his mind except my rashness and the bitterness poured out against him. Yet among the many curses he has scattered against me, finally overcome by truth, he was compelled to write the following in Question 9, page 291:

> “I cannot but praise Martianaeus’s plan of publishing Jerome’s translations as they exist in the most ancient books, without the alterations later made in them, and in the order in which they are found in those same books, without omitting the ancient divisions that appear in them. For we seem to see these translations as they came from Jerome’s hand, or at least altered as little as possible.”

Here we have the accused confessing. He must be prosecuted, so that at last he may be expelled from the sacred republic of letters and may become a disgrace even to his own associates, together with his ignorant book of *Hieronymian Questions*.

## § ONE. On the extraordinary ignorance displayed in John Clericus’s First Question

John Clericus devotes his entire First Hieronymian Question to disparaging my learning, in order to prove that Martianaeus lacked sufficient knowledge of Latin, Greek, and Hebrew to publish Jerome successfully. How far he has departed from his purpose, however, the following replies will show. For he could not establish by arguments what he wished to prove [Col. 1592C], but showed himself unequal to judging our new edition and highly suited to exposing his own bitterness and ignorance: he repays proper work with insults instead of thanks, and whatever I have explained in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew in accordance with the truth, he himself ignorantly distorts in order to heap contempt upon me.

He therefore introduces his first question under this title and heading: “What is required in one who undertakes to publish and elucidate Jerome?” He then adds:

> “To satisfy this question, first of all a distinction must be made between two kinds of assistance with which the man who wishes to publish and elucidate Jerome with credit must be equipped. The first may be called external: it consists in an abundance of manuscript codices with which earlier editions are to be compared and weighed. John Martianaeus repeatedly claims that he was most excellently equipped in this respect; he began to publish at Paris the works of Jerome, the first volume of which saw the light in 1693. In this matter I do not wish to detract from his credibility. But I have not decided to discuss this kind of assistance here, since I cannot visit the libraries in which those manuscript codices of Jerome are preserved.
>
> “The second kind of assistance may be called internal, and may chiefly be reduced to six points. First, the editor must be a lover not so much of Jerome as of truth [Col. 1592D] in his works. Second, he must be sufficiently learned in Latin and sufficiently practiced in reading the ancients to understand that writer properly. Third, he must be learned in Greek, so that he can easily grasp the Greek passages interspersed throughout Jerome’s works and, when necessary, compare what Jerome translated from that language with the Greek exemplars. Fourth, he must know the Hebrew language, without which knowledge he can form no judgment about the many things Jerome says concerning that language. Fifth, he must have carefully compared his translation, as well as the Septuagint and fragments of the other more recent Greek versions, with the Hebrew text. Sixth and finally, he must be accustomed to handling manuscripts and, through long practice, thoroughly trained in all the duties of a skilled critic.
>
> “If a Benedictine monk who edits Jerome is equipped with these six qualities and uses them as he ought, all who henceforth read that writer will have reason to thank him and give him thanks for wishing to devote himself to reprinting him. But if he lacks them, not even the entire Benedictine Order—although it now contains many learned men—will be able to prevent scholars from saying that it is regrettable that so many manuscript codices are in the hands of a man who does not know how to use them properly, and that the leaders of the Order are acting wrongly by not transferring the responsibility for publishing Jerome to someone more competent.”

Everyone agrees with Clericus concerning these six qualities, which are absolutely necessary in an editor of the works of St. Jerome. But the critic of a new edition must be equipped with them no less than the editor himself. If such aids can be lacking in our attacker, it will be plain and evident to all students that it was not Martianaeus the editor, but Clericus, the most ignorant man, who was the critic of his edition. This requires no lengthy discussion, since a few examples in each point will suffice.

### I.

Clericus is so entangled and inexperienced in carrying out the duties of a skilled critic that, in the present matter, he does not know what assistance is external and what is internal and inherent. He calls “external assistance” what, in an edition of the works of St. Jerome, he ought to have called the principal and internal assistance: namely, an abundance of manuscript codices, which a skilled editor must compare and collate with printed books, or earlier editions [Col. 1593B].

For who does not know that, in restoring ancient books and textual records, the principal and virtually internal assistance must be sought from the authority and reliability of the older manuscript codices, whereas the editor’s expertise is a necessary aid, but an external and less important one? I should like our Clericus to be persuaded of this: that the restoration of ancient books can often be achieved solely by comparing manuscript codices with printed books; and that, without this first assistance, the entire chorus of critics could not produce or attain it by conjecture. Let Clericus, therefore, the critic of the edition of Jerome, learn from Jerome’s editor what assistance is internal and what external in restoring a writer of such great antiquity.

### II.

> “It is a customary fault,” says the Critic, “of those who undertake to publish ancient writers to praise the writers they publish to an extraordinary degree, so that at the same time they may persuade the reader that they have undertaken a most useful labor and that they deserve thanks for it.”

He later admits that not only ordinary people but also the eminent Desiderius Erasmus preceded the Benedictine monk in this practice and lavished excessive praise upon Jerome [Col. 1593C].

If it is a customary fault among editors who do not love truth and justice to exalt the writers they publish, then it is certainly a more customary fault among rivals and slanderers to detract from the praises of writers whose reputation for wisdom gives them no pleasure. But this discussion of Clericus is confused and aimless. Elsewhere I have shown that he heaped immoderate abuse upon Jerome, whereas I have not yet added praises equal to Jerome’s virtues. But let us return to the individual points and hear what John Clericus says about Martianaeus.

> “If someone looks for the second quality of an editor of Jerome’s works in Martianaeus’s style—that is, knowledge of the Latin language—he will easily notice that the good man has had little practice in reading ancient writers, since his prose, teeming with barbarisms, shows plainly that he possesses no taste whatever for better Latin speech. He does not even imitate Jerome himself, except in those things that ought rather to be avoided, as pupils usually imitate the faults of their teachers rather than their virtues.
>
> “These things are so evident that they immediately force themselves upon everyone who is not utterly ignorant of the Latin language and who reads Martianaeus’s Prolegomena, Commentaries, and Notes even casually. Perhaps someone might say that in such writings elegance of language, or purity measured by the standard of the Augustan age, is not strictly required. I myself do not deny this; but no one would say that barbarism is required or pleasing, especially where matters are not being treated that can be expressed only in ecclesiastical language . . . . . .
>
> “Nor should you say that the good man disdained a more elegant style and pursued nothing except clarity. For if you read any page, you will understand that the man strains every effort to imitate, if not Cicero, at least Jerome—but in vain. You read only the style of a breviary, occasionally encrusted with Hieronymian expressions forcibly inserted into the prose; yet in that structure there is much more mud than marble. Moreover, you repeatedly notice the unfortunate Critic, which is a necessary consequence of his insufficient understanding of the Latin language.”

To finish an entire chapter of critical discussion without any argument or examples is not the work of a skilled critic, but of a loquacious and foolish abuser. A general and vague discussion of my ignorance of Latin is merely the polished little speech of malicious men; it is not a demonstration of barbarous language or of the style of a breviary. I could therefore justly have used my right and dismissed, with a loud voice and no other proof, the accusation of a hostile spirit as wholly unworthy of belief. But let us return Clericus to the company of those ignorant of Latin and mark his prose, teeming with barbarisms, with several examples [Col. 1594A].

In Question 10, pages 350–351, the dull Critic laughs at us and wished to insult my Latin in these words:

> “Who would not begin to favor that outstanding Scholiast who silences such men? For what it means to silence a tongue I do not know, unless perhaps our Benedictine, when he speaks, is accustomed to thrust his tongue out of his mouth, then withdraw and close it inside his lips when he is silent. But, leaving aside the joke, which is unsuitable for a tragedy, let us hear what follows:”

That clownish wit of our boastful soldier displays great ignorance of Latin. He does not know what it means to “silence a tongue”; and while staging tragedies over trifles, he admits that he has not read Plautus, whose words these are in the *Miles Gloriosus*, act III, scene 10:

> For if your enemies discovered your plan,  
> by your own plan they would silence your tongue and bind your hands,  
> and they would do to you the very things you wished to do to them.

[Col. 1594B] Here is my prose teeming with barbarisms; here is the style of my Plautine Breviary, Clericus, who have utterly fallen into the trap of jesting, since you provide an opportunity for your ignorance to be noted forever, as well as for the cultivated care of my Latin. For if the Muses spoke Latin, they would speak in the language of Plautus. Thus, whether you wish it or not, it is now established that Martianaeus, your “good man,” has had more practice in reading ancient writers than Clericus, the enemy and slanderous critic of that same Martianaeus.

The same Question 10, page 380, supplies another argument for his ignorance, when he says:

> “In chapter 11:28 of Numbers, the Latin translator, after recounting the inspiration of Eldad and Medad, introduces Joshua speaking: ‘My lord Moses, stop them.’ The Anonymous Scholiast has in the margin: ‘Hebrew: Shut them in.’ Concerning this little annotation Martianaeus writes: ‘Hebrew *chelaem*, which the Chaldee translates *esarinun*,’ etc. Thus nothing prevents that Scholion from truly being Hieronymian. The single word *recludere*, in the sense of shutting, ought to have taught our Monk that the Scholion was not Jerome’s, since Jerome did not speak so barbarously and knew that *recludere* means ‘to open’ among purer speakers. Nevertheless, he used that word in the translation of Scripture because he did not correct everywhere the barbarism of the older version [Col. 1594C]. But he would not have spoken that way in a scholion, especially since the word more frequently signifies ‘to prohibit’ than ‘to shut.’”
