I said that this chapter supplies another argument for Clerican ignorance; but I mean an argument containing many kinds and indications of ignorance. For there is extraordinary ignorance in every sentence of this difficult passage.

1. It is evident from his saying that the single word *recludere*, in the sense of shutting, ought to have taught his monk that the Scholion was not Jerome’s. For that verb, in the sense of shutting, is genuinely Hieronymian and particularly characteristic of Jerome.

2. This can be proved from copies of the older Latin version and from other translations.

3. It most clearly demonstrates that our critic has no judgment when he asserts that Jerome would have spoken more purely in some scholion or little annotation than in the Latin translation of the divine Scriptures.

I now make these three kinds of lies and ignorance evident from the facts themselves.

That Jerome used the word *recludere* in the sense of shutting not only in his translation of Scripture but also in his prefaces and Commentaries is proved by the following testimonies.

In the preface to his translation of the prophet Daniel from Hebrew, Jerome writes:

> “Finally, when I was still a young man, after reading Quintilian and Cicero and the flowers of rhetoric, when I had shut myself up in the mill of this language, and with much sweat,” etc.

In Book VI of his Commentaries, on Jeremiah 29:

> “His duty is to distinguish between prophets who speak by the Holy Spirit and those who speak by a contrary spirit; and he is to be shut up in prison, so that he may pay the penalty for his lie and cease to deceive the people any longer.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Why did the prophet dare to write the truth, and why does he want him shut up in prison so that he may not speak?”

Then, on chapter 32:

> “He ordered him to be shut up not in the prison itself, but in the vestibule of the prison.”

Likewise, in Book I of his Commentaries on the prophet Habakkuk, chapter 1:

> “And many nations were exhausted at the time when the city was surrounded by the armies of Vespasian and Titus; coming for the solemn day of Passover, they were shut up in the city as though in a prison, and they perished from hunger and want.”

Let our Clericus now decide whether the word *recludere* ought to have taught me that the Scholion cited above was not Jerome’s. And if he is capable of feeling shame in literary matters, let him be ashamed of his own ignorance, since he was so inexperienced in reading ancient writers that he did not know that the verb *recludere* is also used by Justinus, Book I:

[Col. 1595A]

> “Orthanes,” he says, “through messengers asks his daughter, who was among the king’s royal concubines, whether the son of King Cyrus was king. But she says that she herself does not know and cannot learn from another, because each of them is shut up separately.”

A second great and reckless lie of his ignorance occurs in Clericus’s assertion that Jerome used the word *recludere* in the sense of shutting in his translation of Scripture because he did not everywhere correct the barbarism of the older version. But how does our Critic dare to assert that the supposedly prejudicial barbarism of the word *recludere*, left uncorrected, remained in the ancient Latin version through some other older translation, when he neither possessed any copy of such an older version nor could see and examine one anywhere?

What I have said is too mild. He was so much a liar and so ignorant that he did not compare or test the expressions of Jerome’s translation from Hebrew against the older Latin version derived from the Seventy Translators.

Anyone who reads even the single thirteenth chapter of Leviticus—for this is neither burdensome nor the work of an exceptionally diligent man—will immediately be convinced that the word *recludere* does not belong to the Anonymous and older Latin Translator but to St. Jerome translating from Hebrew.

For wherever our version retains the verb *recludet* (“he will shut up”), [Col. 1595B] the Septuagint translation retains the Greek word ἀφοριεῖ, that is, “he will separate.” This is so in verse 4 of the chapter just mentioned, and likewise in verses 5, 11, 21, 26, 31, 50, and 54. Since the Greek word ἀφοριεῖ cannot be rendered in Latin as *recludet* even by the most ignorant clerics, it follows that the word could never have appeared in the older Latin version translated from the Greek words and then have been corrected by Jerome—if that is how ignorant men prefer to understand the matter.

Moreover, many Latin translators, together with Jerome, use the word *recludere* in the sense of shutting. These include Pagninus, Arias Montanus, the Latin translator of the Chaldee, and sometimes the Latin translator of the Syriac as well. If Clericus wishes to call all of them ignorant of the Latin language, I shall not be surprised that he has so often called the Scholiast of the Hebrew Canon foul and barbarous. For the present, this is enough concerning the supposedly barbarous word *recludere* in Clericus, although it is customary and used among the historiographer Justinus, Jerome, and other translators who speak pure Latin.

We take the third argument for the same abuser’s ignorance from the final part of the preceding difficulty, where he tries to teach us that Jerome used the word *recludere* in his translation but would not have used it in a scholion or little marginal annotation. [Col. 1595C] From this we learn how refined is the judgment of our critic, who demands elegance of Latin speech in marginal scholia but does not require the same elegance in a finished translation.

How contrary this is to the practice of learned men, and how much it conflicts with the duty of an excellent translator, Jerome himself could have taught Clericus if he had read his little works more attentively.

Let all students therefore hear, not a critic without judgment, but this holy Doctor giving the following instructions concerning the Latin translation in his letter to Sunnia and Fretella:

> “In the same place, ‘in the Valley of Tears.’ For this you say that the Greek has κλαυθμῶνος, that is, ‘of weeping.’ But whether we say ‘lamentation,’ ‘mourning,’ ‘weeping,’ or ‘tears,’ the sense is one and the same. And we follow this practice: where there is no change in meaning, we preserve the elegance of the Latin language.”

And below, in the same letter:

> “The same rule of interpretation must therefore be followed, as we have often said: where there is no loss of meaning, the *euphonia* [εὐφωνία] and propriety of the language into which we translate should be preserved.”

Had our critic Clericus obeyed this rule, he would not have sinned absurdly and childishly by warning that Jerome’s translation of Scripture teemed with barbarisms, while he preserved the elegance of Latin speech in scholia and annotations [Col. 1595D].

He forged another feeble argument against my Latin, which I reproduce here out of order, since it appears on pages 379–380 before the matter just refuted. I preferred first to refute the alleged barbarisms of my style before becoming entangled in grammatical quibbling.

Clericus therefore brings forward Cassiodorus’s warning to those who copy the books of the ancients, and joins warning to warning while exulting against us at length in these words:

> “If our Benedictine monk, or that foul Scholiast whom at the beginning he tried to foist upon us as Jerome, had obeyed that rule, neither would have sinned childishly at Numbers 6:8. Jerome had written: ‘All the days of his separation shall be holy to the Lord.’ But the barbarous Scholiast, who did not know that *omnis* is an accusative case, just like *dies*, noted in the margin that the Hebrew has ‘on all days,’ as though the words ‘every day’ signified something else!
>
> “The most polished monk here publishes a similar specimen of his learning, when at the bottom of the page he writes: ‘The manuscript books read this verse in two or three ways. More have it thus: “All the days of his separation,” etc. Others, however: “[Col. 1596A] Every day of his separation,” etc. Finally, the Royal manuscript reads, with the Latin Vulgate: “On all the days of his separation,” etc. The Canon of Hebrew Truth contains these variant readings.’
>
> “As though these were variant readings, when the last is a mere corruption and the second and first are entirely the same! Let the Editor of Jerome consult the man whom Rome has not clothed in a more learned purple for many years—I mean Henry Noris, Dissertation 4, on the Pisan Cenotaphs, chapter 3—from whom he will learn that plural accusatives of the third declension, whose plural genitive ends in *-ium*, are indiscriminately terminated in *-es*, *-eis*, and *-is*.”

These are the words of a writer extravagantly insolent, in which he displays many examples of his ignorance. He calls us foul and barbarous because we noted variant readings that truly are varied and different in verse 8 of chapter 6 of Numbers.

But, so that our refutation may proceed in its proper order according to the evidence of the books, let the attentive reader remember my annotations on the divine Library of St. Jerome, especially on Joshua 1:14:

> “But you shall pass over armed before your brothers, all strong-handed men,” etc.

Many years ago I warned the prudent and curious reader about a variation of this kind and said:

> “The Septuagint reads in the singular, ‘every strong-handed man’; the Canon of Hebrew Truth, the Royal manuscript of the Bible, and one Corbeiensis manuscript follow this reading, although in manuscripts *omnis* and *fortis* could easily have been written for *omnes* and *fortes* [Col. 1596B], since the ancients frequently wrote I for E.”

What I wrote there was read seven years before the publication of the book *Hieronymian Questions*. Thus this recollection is like a reproach directed against Clericus, who has forgotten the benefit he received. For I had taught him both the variant readings of Scripture and the orthography of the ancients, which I had learned not from Cassiodorus’s warning but from daily reading and continual use of the oldest manuscript codices.

He therefore orders us, ignorantly and childishly, to approach the purple-clad master of grammar, although in this matter we had been ahead of every wise and foolish man even before that master’s warning.

What shall I say about the variant reading of the verse in Numbers? I am more learned than our comic figure in the republic of letters, who is ignorant of the agreement of all editions of Sacred Scripture. Let the critic Clericus consult Brian Walton’s Polyglot Bible on this matter; let him consult Thomas James’s *Papal War*, from which he will learn that *all the days*, *every day*, and *on all days* are variant readings, and indeed of greater importance than many of those collected by the learned Walton from the Alexandrian manuscript [Col. 1596C].

Nor is it necessary that a reading always vary in meaning merely because it varies in wording, provided that it is expressed and formulated in different words. Thus, in the Polyglots, the following Greek variant is noted at Genesis 1:14: εἰς φαῦσιν ἑπὶ τῆς γῆς, and in the Alexandrian manuscript εἰς φαῦσιν τῆς γῆς—“for illumination upon the earth” and “for illumination of the earth.” Likewise, in chapter 3, verse 9, ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παραδείσου in the Alexandrian manuscript and ἐν μέσῳ τῷ παραδείσῳ: “in the middle of the paradise” and “in the middle of paradise.”

Let Clericus now shout that the Scholiast was foul and the Critic unfortunate for having noted such variant readings in Greek; or, if he ever wishes to come to his senses, let him ask pardon for his extraordinary rashness, his own ignorance, and his inborn desire to censure all other writers.

But who would not be astonished at the fury of our critic, who asserts that “on all the days of his separation he shall be holy to the Lord” is a mere corruption of verse 7 of chapter 6 of the book of Numbers? John Clericus’s word was never safe; but now he proves himself faithless in the matter of faith before everyone, when he dares with excessive confidence to assert that the purest and most unimpaired reading is a mere corruption.

Let the prudent and religious reader therefore consult this verse of Scripture in the authentic books, and he will find a marvelous harmony in the sacred text and in all the sacred translators. [Col. 1596D] For the Hebrew reads as follows:

> “On all the days of his Nazirite state, he himself shall be holy to the Lord.”

The Septuagint Translators:

> “On all the days of his vow he shall be holy to the Lord.”

The Chaldee:

> “On all the days during which he shall be a Nazirite,” etc.

The Samaritan text and translation:

> “On all the days of his Nazirite state,” etc.

The Syriac translator:

> “On all the days of his abstinence he is holy to the Lord.”

The Arabic is similar. Finally, the Vulgate, together with the others:

> “On all the days of his separation,” etc.

John Clericus calls this harmony of Scripture and all the translators a mere corruption. Let the judgment of this matter therefore rest with the eyes of learned and Christian men.

Now, if I wished to bite back at John Clericus’s Latin in kind, how much ignorance of that language could I justly expose from his works? But the role I might have assumed has already been taken by the critical reply of a learned writer, who gathered a rich harvest of barbarisms and solecisms—that is, the errors and faults—of our critic from the dust of his *Harmony of the Gospels*.

I therefore send John Clericus to Father Lepineul, so that he may draw a taste of Latin speech from the best grammarian rather than [Col. 1597A] continue, as usual, to pursue a style full of barbarism. And, asking pardon for the past, let him especially ask this one question: Can the following Latin phrase have escaped a man who speaks purely—“You read only the style of a breviary”? By this expression he wished to procure praise for himself and brand Martianaeus with a reputation for ignorance.

### III.

After the ignorant critic attempted to overcome my diligence in Latin, he likewise persuaded himself, and tries to persuade everyone, that whatever Greek competence I may possess is nonexistent. He does so in the following sequence of words:

> “Third, in publishing Jerome, assistance must be sought from the Greek language, since he scattered many Greek passages throughout his works and also translated many things from it. These cannot be sufficiently understood, nor marked with the censor’s stroke where necessary, except by a man so skilled in that language that he does not repeatedly need the help of a lexicon.
>
> “Those who translated ἀντὶ φοινίκων τὰ βαΐα σύρουσι as *coram palmis ramos palmae trahunt*—‘before the palms they drag the branches of a palm’—certainly seem not to have attained this knowledge of the language, as we briefly noted in the *Critical Art*, part III, section 1, chapter 13, no. 25. But we shall later bring to light many other and clearer indications of the matter.
>
> “Jerome himself, as we shall demonstrate when we come to that question, was not skilled in the Greek language. But his errors cannot be detected except by someone more skilled; this, however, his editor must necessarily do. To be sure, in some of the more obvious faults, so that I conceal nothing, Martianaeus has occasionally done this, but he ought to have done so much more frequently.
>
> “From knowledge both of Latin and Greek, and from reading the best writers, which we insist must be required of the editor and elucidator of Jerome, comes that philological learning which Erasmus judged absolutely necessary for him. He therefore rightly thought he had to excuse himself for having undertaken to elucidate Jerome’s letters before he was sufficiently prepared in the humane letters . . . .
>
> “Martianaeus ought to have weighed these things carefully. For although, through Erasmus’s efforts—not to mention Mariano Vittorio—he received Jerome purged of countless faults, nevertheless, since he undertook to test the labor of both against the ancient codices and to sit in judgment upon both, he ought to have been equipped with scarcely less critical learning than Erasmus before undertaking the task. Few, I think, will persuade themselves of this once they have read the man’s prefaces, commentaries, and notes.”

At this point Clericus brings forward no example of my ignorance except the Greek words ἀντὶ φοινίκων, etc., which do not seem to him to have been interpreted with sufficient learning. [Col. 1597B] Concerning this unlearned interpretation, he again warns us in Question 9, page 318:

> “Shortly afterward,” he says, “Martianaeus observes that these Greek words were inserted into Jerome’s text: ἀντὶ φοινίκων τὰ βαΐα σύρουσι. He translates them most absurdly as ‘before the palms they drag the branches of a palm,’ whereas they ought to be translated ‘dragging palm branches instead of dates,’ as we demonstrated long ago in the *Critical Art*, part III, section 1, chapter 13.”

I could scarcely have known what that *Ars Critica* of the acrimonious Reciter Clericus was, had I not read through the *Paris Journal of the Learned* a few months ago, and in it the dissertation of Monsieur Carel, who attempts to restore the Greek words of our manuscripts as a third party—but solely by his own conjectures, not on the faith and authority of ancient books. Concerning the exceedingly absurd translation of the Greek words in Clericus’s *Ars Critica*, D. Carel writes as follows in the French journal:

> “One agrees with M. le Clerc that the Greek word φοῖνιξ signifies equally the palm tree and the dates that are its fruit; but the same is not true of the verb σύρειν, which never means “to pluck” or “to gather,” as M. le Clerc translates it, but always “to draw.” Moreover, the continuation of St. Jerome’s discourse does not permit these words to be given the sense assigned to them by M. le Clerc. St. Jerome wishes to dissuade his friend Sophronius from translating into Greek, and for the Greeks, the Latin version of the Psalms that he had just made from the Hebrew, because that would be doing something useless; it would be carrying wood into the forest, *in silvam ligna ferre*; it would be giving the Greeks a Greek version when they already had several others which they rightly valued. In short, St. Jerome says, it would be making my ignorance known to the learned men of that nation, by giving them the opportunity to compare my version with those they already possess: *Et doctissimos quoque viros testes imperitiae meae facere volueris*. St. Jerome therefore cannot here be comparing his own version with fruits and those of the Greeks with barren branches; that would be saying the very opposite of what he intends and falling into an evident contradiction.”

If I had written this about the *Ars Critica* of John Clericus, not all learned men—at least not my rivals—would immediately have assented to my words. But who would not trust a learned man who has examined and weighed the Greek words and Clericus’s translation of them? It is therefore clear from his observation that John Clericus is ignorant of the Greek language, since he translated the verb σύρειν as *vellere* and *decerpere*. Furthermore, it is certain and evident from the same observation of Monsieur Carel that Clericus is so blind in mind that he not only absurdly interprets the words inserted into Jerome’s text, but also makes Jerome himself utterly absurd and inconsistent.

Let us now come to the objection of our critic, who wished to brand me with the reputation of ignorance and folly in translating these same Greek words. The judgment in this matter must be based on the words of my annotation, not on those of an ignorant writer who is indulging in hostility. Here, then, is the context of Jerome’s preface to his Sophronius, vol. I, cols. 837–838:

> “If you translate this little work of mine into Greek (as you promise), and wish to make even the most learned men witnesses to my ignorance, I shall say to you that Horatian saying: ‘Do not carry wood into the forest,’ etc.”

Our annotation:

[Col. 1598B] “At this point the older exemplars add certain Greek words from which I have been unable to extract any meaning: ΑΝΤΙΦΑΟΝΙΚΩΝ ΤΟΒΑΙΑ ϹΥΡΟΥϹΙΝ, unless one should read ἀντὶ φοινίκων τὰ βαΐα σύρουσι, that is, *before the palms they drag palm branches*. The sense is: if you translate my little work into Greek and wish to make the most learned men witnesses to my ignorance, you will do no differently from those who bring little branches before trees; hence I may rightly say to you that Horatian saying: ‘Do not carry wood into the forest.’ However much these words may seem to cohere with one another, they do not greatly appeal to me: first, because the sentence is complete without these Greek words, and secondly, because manuscript codices are found in which such words are absent. The Sorbonicus is one such, as is Vaticanus no. 344. Finally, neither Erasmus nor Marianus remembers this Greek proverb in his editions. I do not know whether they were overcome by the difficulty of the matter, or rather whether this resulted from the lack of the older manuscript exemplars with which we are abundantly supplied, by a sufficiently evident dispensation of Providence.”

I ask the fair-minded and prudent reader to weigh these words of mine according to the principles of the *Ars Critica*, and to see whether our Clericus is a subtle and skilful judge of ancient and modern writers. Certainly I shall say confidently, and shall cite all the rules of the grammarians and all the Greek lexica, in proof of my translation: *before the palms they drag palm branches*. For ἀντί, or ἄντα in Greek, is in Latin *coram*, *contra*, *e regione*: ἄντα ἰδὼν means “having looked directly before one’s eyes,” “looking back opposite”; ἀντία δέσποινης φάσθαι means “to address someone before the mistress.” Thus ἀντὶ φοινίκων in Latin will mean “opposite,” “before,” “against,” “on the other side.” Τὰ βαΐα means “palm branches,” as the Gospel also teaches. Finally, σύρουσι, according to all the grammarians, is the third-person plural of σύρω, “I drag”; it may also be a dative plural: σύρουσι, “for those dragging.”

Where, then, is the ignorance of the Greek language with which Clericus charged me? Now, if we attend to the sense of Jerome’s context, what accords more closely with that Horatian saying, “Do not carry wood into the forest,” than this: “before the palms, do not drag little branches”?

[Note: [Col. 1597D] Martianaeus, Clericus, and Carelius are mistaken and torment themselves miserably throughout this entire dispute. We shall show in its proper place how the reading ought to be restored, replacing it with ἀντιφιλονεικῶν τοῖς κατασύρουσιν, which means “to refute those who disparage, after initiating a controversy.”]

It remains, then, for me to answer our critic: “As you are, so you think everyone is.” For a fool walking along the road considers all others foolish and ignorant.

Thus also, on page 460, he attacks our edition, saying:

> “The second epistle is to the monk Evangelus, not Evangelium; for the name is not *Evangelius*, but *Evangelus*, as analogy requires, and usage likewise . . . . Yet Martianaeus, with his customary grammatical acumen and expertise, preferred the unusual form to the usual one, and the form contrary to analogy to its corresponding form, in the title of this epistle, although both were read in the manuscripts. In this matter he sinned no less than those who invent Greek names contrary to the analogy of the language, since the choice depended on his judgment . . . . In interpreting the word φιλεγκλήμων, which Jerome uses at the beginning of this epistle, he is no more successful. He translates it as ‘a lover of complaints,’ or ‘complaining,’ because it provides an occasion for complaints and controversy, whereas ἐγκαλεῖν means ‘to accuse,’ and φιλεγκλήμων means ‘a lover of accusations.’ Indeed, Jerome, speaking of a dangerous treatise, as he calls it, names its author φιλεγκλήμων, although rather harshly—for the word is used only of a man afflicted by an excessive eagerness to find fault—as though it were a question whose solution might easily incur a charge of error.”

In this dispute, even if we do not have an analogy of Clericus’s word and name, we nevertheless have from him an exact likeness and sudden image of his character. For in his own sense he is truly φιλεγκλήμων, “a lover of accusations”—and of false accusations, as is clear from the present chapter. When he ought to have given thanks to the new edition for restoring the genuine word and the name *Evangelus* or *Evangelium*, and for removing the name *Evagrius* from the older editions, he suddenly forgot the benefit and descended to insults and accusations against me, as though I had preferred the unusual name *Evangelius* to the customary *Evangelus*. Our later prolegomenon in vol. II of the new edition refutes that accusation, where these words are written:

“Epistle to Evangelus, or Evangelium, by the same holy Doctor, etc.” Therefore Jerome was writing an epistle to Evangelus at that time. In the margin also it bears this title: “Epistle to Evangelus.” Finally, in the chronological order of the epistles in vol. II, I entitled it under no. 17: “Epistle to Evangelus, on Melchizedek.”

Is this to prefer the unusual name *Evangelius* to the customary *Evangelus*? Clericus complained here too! Our φιλεγκλήμων certainly complains that I have translated his name as “complaining,” or “a lover of complaints.” “A lover of accusations” pleases him more, both because of his own character and because of his ignorance of the Greek language. He must remove that ignorance from Scapula’s Lexicon, p. 730:

> “Φιλεγκλήμων: a lover of complaints, complaining; also an informer, an accuser.”

Let me be as ignorant as such lexicographers in interpreting Greek words. Let Clericus alone be wise in his own eyes and appear to himself supremely learned. But enough concerning Greek questions; let us come to the Hebrew.

IV. “Fourthly, it is necessary that the editor and interpreter of Jerome be skilled in the Hebrew language; and this must be acquired by a twofold labor. The first consists in an accurate knowledge of contemporary grammar and of the method by which both the rabbis and other recent interpreters customarily explain the Old Testament. The second consists in examining that same language in comparison with the languages of the neighboring Syrians, Chaldeans, and Arabs, and even of the more distant Ethiopians. From this comparison, unmistakable light shines upon many passages of Sacred Scripture . . . . Without this twofold labor, we cannot judge sufficiently correctly of the ancient translations, and therefore of Jerome’s. Erasmus was deprived of both these aids; indeed, he did not even think about the latter. Nor did any of his contemporaries. The former, however, he supplied through the work of others, as he candidly acknowledges in his letter to the Archbishop of Canterbury:

> ‘The Greek passages that had either been omitted or incorrectly added we restored, and we did the same with the Hebrew. But in this area, since we could accomplish less by our own efforts, we achieved it with the assistance of others, especially the brothers Amerbach, whose help I willingly used, since I had rather scraped at the letters of the Hebrews than learned them.’

“Through their work, however, everything was rashly forced into conformity with the Massoretic manner of reading, and whatever Jerome had written differently in Latin was written in Hebrew characters, as though everything that differed from the Massoretic reading were erroneous. Martianaeus has rightly noted and corrected this error throughout, which I acknowledge just as readily as I point out what seems to me to have been less correctly done by him. Yet he is so imbued with a knowledge of Hebrew grammar that, through Jerome’s less precise expressions, he is led into errors scarcely pardonable—as when he thinks that Hebrew words begin with vowels and diphthongs, on the basis of a passage of Jerome that he has misunderstood (*On Hebrew Names*, col. 40). He also attacks more than once, in his commentary on the same book, those who think that meanings now unknown to us were once signified by Hebrew words; and consequently he does not regard the ancient interpreters as deserving condemnation when they translate words differently from the way we now customarily do. Yet this is so true, and has been so demonstrated by learned men, that it can no longer be called into question by anyone skilled in these matters.

“For example, the Septuagint interpreters frequently have ἀλλοφύλους for Philistines; this is also found in the Greek lexicon of *Hebrew Names*. Since those by whom the Hebrew names were translated—whether they were earlier than Jerome or Jerome himself—did not understand the reason for this translation, they resorted to various forced and twisted etymologies, translating the word as ‘falling,’ or ‘the fall of a cup,’ or ‘falling by drinking,’ or ‘two have fallen,’ as though it had to be derived from *naphal*, ‘he fell,’ and *schathah*, ‘he drank,’ or *schthajim*, ‘two.’ But elsewhere we have shown that the reason for the translation must be sought in the Ethiopian language. We shall also produce other examples of this matter later.”

Here, as elsewhere, our Clericus wanders amid manifold errors. First, he thinks that an accurate knowledge of contemporary Hebrew grammar is absolutely necessary for restoring the Hebrew words that Jerome frequently inserts; yet shortly afterward he candidly admits that the Hebrew words in Jerome’s works were thoroughly corrupted because the brothers Amerbach, together with the others whose services Erasmus used, rashly forced everything into conformity with the Massoretic manner of reading—that is, with an accurate knowledge of contemporary Hebrew grammar, which depends entirely upon vowel points, changes of points, and the critical signs of those same Massoretes. Let the learned reader therefore see what confidence he ought to place in a critic so inconsistent with himself that he overturns with his own hand, in the same observation, what he is attempting to establish.

Second, he confesses that the errors of the Erasmian edition were repeatedly noted and corrected by Martianaeus, when he ought to have said “always and everywhere.” For there is no Hebrew word in all the works of St. Jerome that I have not corrected and restored according to the testimony of very many ancient manuscript codices. Although in this matter the threats of critics hung over me, I nevertheless came to the rescue and undertook the task. I therefore give thanks to myself for having been able to procure so great a restoration in the works of St. Jerome, amid the gratitude of my rivals and of many ignorant men.

Third, our Clericus charges me with errors scarcely pardonable, into which I am led by Jerome’s less precise expressions—that is, when I think that Hebrew words begin with vowels and diphthongs because of a passage of Jerome wrongly understood at vol. II, col. 40. This passage has already been discussed above, where we debated Jerome’s Hebrew learning. But I am astonished that our critic is still ignorant of the rules of ancient as well as modern grammarians, by which we can demonstrate most clearly that many Hebrew words begin with vowels.

Among the ancient Hebrew grammarians, the following is found in Jerome, *On Hebrew Names*, under the name Gomorrah:

> “It must be known that Hebrew has no letter G, but that it is written with the vowel *ain*.”

[Note: [Col. 1599] It is improper to say that among the Hebrews vowels are letters, as we have shown from the passages of Jerome cited above.]

This name therefore began with a vowel, not with a consonantal letter: Omorrha. There is no less agreement between the Greeks and Jerome concerning diphthongs in the four words Hiram, Histob, Hiras, and Hisboseth, concerning which Jerome writes:

> “For this reason we have written these names with aspiration, because among both the Greeks and the Hebrews they are written with a diphthong.”

Do not more recent grammarians frequently write *vav scourec*, that is, the vowel or diphthong *u* or *ou*? For example, Genesis 1:10, *oulmicveh*, “and the gathering of the waters, namely, he called seas.” And to teach Clericus many principles of contemporary grammar, let him hear Thomas Dufour, chap. 2, *On Reading*, p. 14:

> “Finally, *sheva* is read after a long movement; except initially, after which it is not read, as in *oüvno*, a word of two syllables, etc.”

[Col. 1600C] Thus *vav* is initial in the word, a vowel or long movement, which many read as *ou*, as though it were a diphthong, while others read it as the simple vowel *u*. According to the rules of that same grammar, the final syllables in the trisyllabic words *Eloah*, *Jeschonah*, and *Maschiahh* begin with the vowel *a*, or *patahh*, which skilled grammarians call “assumed,” because its sound is heard before the consonantal letter written above it.

In the same way, the proper name of God—which must never be read as it is written and which has foreign points—is frequently to be read in the sacred Hebrew text as *Elohe*, *Elohim*, and *Adonai*, although ignorant Clerici here read *Jehove*, *Jehovi*, and *Jehova*. Finally, the proper names of persons, cities, and mountains frequently begin with a vowel letter, and are seen read in this way by the Septuagint interpreters and Jerome: Adam, Eve, Abel, Abraham, Ada, Our or Ur, and so forth. By these examples we most decisively prove the ignorance of our Clericus and the accurate knowledge of contemporary grammar possessed by Martianaeus, the editor of Jerome.

Fourth, with an impudent lie Clericus dares to write that I attacked those who think that meanings now unknown to us were once signified by Hebrew words, and he cites my commentary on the book of *Hebrew Names*. To refute the slander of this wicked writer, I believe it sufficient to transcribe what is found in vol. II of our edition, cols. 311–312. This, then, is what I wrote five or six years ago.

“Besides these matters, the modern Hebrew critics and the hangers-on of critics—although completely unskilled and ignorant of Hebrew—bring many charges against Jerome. Their arguments were collected by the most distinguished Louis Ferrandus, a man who deserved exceedingly well of Sacred Scripture and of Jerome. When he undertook the task of defending Jerome’s Hebrew learning, he proposed, in a praiseworthy effort, to satisfy the objections by gathering from every side the arguments with which the learning of the holy Doctor is attacked. In chapter 3, section 4 of the *Disputationes Prolegomenorum* to the *Biblical Summary*, he began to fight against those who are always finding something to criticize in Jerome’s etymologies or interpretations.

“But many do not wish that the whole defense of the greatest interpreter of Scripture should depend upon the responses of this distinguished man, since they scarcely accept half of his replies. For who, say many, can patiently endure such vague and frivolous responses in defense of Jerome as these, found on p. 140 of the *Biblical Summary*?

> ‘The interpretations of the remaining sixth objection can easily be defended or excused by resorting to unknown meanings, or by laying the blame upon careless writers. One might perhaps also add variation in the reading, which may have been responsible for the ancients producing interpretations alien to our usage.’

> ‘The sound of the word, which is nearly the same in the names Hereb and [illegible]; Cades and [illegible], may have deceived Jerome, who was intent upon higher matters and perhaps in haste, just as even the most learned men daily make mistakes in such matters.’”

Certainly the matter is settled if we bring forward nothing else in defense of Jerome’s Hebrew learning. For whether the holy Doctor was mistaken through haste or through attending to higher matters, the learned will consistently judge that Jerome frequently went astray in his interpretations and etymologies of names. Moreover, there is no error so obvious, no kind of corruption so evident, that it cannot be defended, provided we flee to those hiding places of ignorance—to unknown meanings of Hebrew names or to the careless ignorance of ancient writers.

It is therefore preferable to supply new and particular answers rather than cling to these general assertions, with which even moderately learned men, as it seems to me, have not been sufficiently satisfied.

These, candid reader, are the things that I wrote and have now transcribed in full concerning meanings—or significations—of Hebrew words that are now unknown. It is for you to recognize my sincerity and avoid Clericus’s slander, or to strip this vainglorious soldier in the republic of letters of his office. For that soldier, a false champion of public liberty, partly through confidence in victory and partly through the pain of disgrace, proceeded to every kind of audacity and insult in his *Hebrew Questions*, attributing to us his own ignorance and the singular envy with which he attacks everyone so bitterly.

For the rest, lest anything deceive him, I believe that many, indeed almost all, meanings of Hebrew words were unknown to our Clericus, who, inspired by a slight breeze of Greek and Hebrew learning, holds the most learned ancient writers in contempt and never ceases to lay traps for their editors.

V. “Fifthly,” he says, “one who undertakes to edit Jerome ought to have carefully read the Septuagint interpreters and the fragments of the others, and to have compared them with the Hebrew text, so that he may judge correctly of the comparison that Jerome so often undertook. For this ability is not acquired by reading the Breviary, nor suddenly supplied by fleeing to concordances and lexica, but by prolonged and attentive reading of the Hebrew text and the ancient interpreters. Since this was lacking in John Martianaeus, he consequently admitted many errors, as will later become clear, etc.”

I do not know what harm the Breviary may have done to John Clericus. Yet he is often distressed that I perform this task diligently and conscientiously. With what audacity, then, does he now dare to assert that I lacked the ability to read the Hebrew text and the ancient interpreters through long and attentive study? There is scarcely a page in the three volumes of the works of St. Jerome already published from which his shameless mouth could not be silenced.

Indeed, if it did not smell of self-glorification, I would recall to the mind of the learned reader the whole little work in vol. II, which contains no small part of Origen’s *Hexapla*. Nor could I have collected, copied out with my own hand, and prepared so many fragments of the Hebrew text and of the ancient Greek interpreters without attentive and prolonged reading of all these materials.

Therefore either no one is learned, or this foolish sycophant Clericus is an ignorant man, who has neither seen nor understood my labor, set against his slanders.

But let us come to the cause of our Clericus’s distress, which one annotation pricked so sharply that it robbed him of sleep and made him represent Martianaeus and Bonfrerius as dreamers.

He thus defends his own ignorance:

> “But John Clericus could not have noticed what Martianaeus was about to dream: that *elon* had ever been read as *aulon* by the Septuagint interpreters—not merely in Numbers and Deuteronomy. Nowhere is *elon* translated by the Septuagint interpreters as αὐλών, but not even in the entire Old Testament. Martianaeus was deceived, it seems, by an inattentive reading of Jacques Bonfrerius’s notes on the book *On Places*, where he conjectures that αὐλών had been deformed from [illegible]. Our writer understood this as though the Septuagint interpreters had done it, and in this matter he was seriously mistaken. For the Septuagint interpreters either took that word appellatively, as the name of a tree, or translated it as Ἥλων, as in Judges 9:37, etc. Martianaeus ought to have noticed these things before accusing me of ignorance. He ought also—let me mention this in passing—to have reprinted the book *On Hebrew Places* more accurately, instead of reproducing throughout for the reader the errors of Bonfrerius’s edition, as he has done here. For both editions incorrectly have Αὐλῶν instead of Αὐλὼν, and ἐπίμηκος instead of ἐπιμήκης; anyone not wholly ignorant of Greek will immediately understand this.”

Our dispute here concerns the word Αὐλὼν or Αὐλῶν, and ἐπίμηκος instead of ἐπιμήκης.

First, I can demonstrate most clearly, both from the Septuagint interpreters themselves and from Eusebius and Jerome, that Αὐλῶν is a Hebrew name, not a Greek one, as some thought in the time of St. Jerome. For we read in Deuteronomy 1:1:

> “These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness toward the west, near the Red Sea, between Pharan, Tophol, Lobon, Aulon, and the gold mines”: ἀναμέσων Φαρὰν, Τοφὸλ, καὶ Λοβὸν, καὶ Αὐλὼν, καὶ καταχρύσεα.

Here Aulon is no less a proper name of a place set down by the Septuagint interpreters than Pharan, Tophol, and Lobon, among which places Moses addressed the whole people of Israel in the wilderness.

Therefore, just as someone would be foolish to deny that Pharan, Tophol, Laban, and Haseroth are specifically Hebrew names and proper names of places, so too must one be called foolish who stubbornly denies to Jerome that Aulon, used by the Septuagint for Haseroth, is the proper name of this place and a Hebrew name.

The same can be proved from the book *On Hebrew Places*. For Eusebius’s purpose is to explain proper names of places—and indeed Hebrew names, not Greek appellatives. It follows that Αὐλῶν in the book *On Hebrew Places* is a proper and purely Hebrew name.

Eusebius himself teaches this in these words:

> “Αὐλῶν, a great, extended plain, is still called so today”: Αὐλῶν, πεδιὰς μεγάλη ἐπίμηκος εἰς ἔτι καὶ νῦν καλεῖται, etc.

“Aulon, a great valley, is called [so] to this day.” Or, as Jerome translates it:

> “It is called a great and level valley, extending to an immense length, surrounded on both sides by mountains succeeding and joined to one another. These mountains begin at Lebanon and beyond and reach as far as the wilderness of Pharan. In Aulon itself—that is, in the level valley—are the distinguished cities Scythopolis and Tiberias, and the lake beside it; also Jericho, etc.”

From these words it is easy to conclude that our Clericus, by asserting that Αὐλῶν is a Greek appellative, would at the same time persuade the reader that this name is surrounded by mountains succeeding one another and that distinguished cities are situated in it, as well as the regions through which the middle Jordan flows. Since such claims can be made only by a madman, it remains for us to say that Aulon is the proper name of a certain place, a Hebrew name set down in its proper order and explained by Eusebius in the book *On Hebrew Places*.

I have said more than enough about Jerome in the proper places, namely vol. II, cols. 342, 344, and 345, and afterward col. 394, in the notes. Let whoever wishes consult them; I do not wish to repeat what has already been done.

But what is to be made of the editions of Bonfrerius and Martianaeus, which write Αὐλῶν with a circumflex and ἐπίμηκος instead of ἐπιμήκης? Those who are not wholly ignorant of Greek will say that the matter is correctly presented in this way, because Αὐλῶν is written in ancient books to distinguish the proper Hebrew name from the Greek appellative αὐλὼν.

Furthermore, among Greek writers certain adjectives frequently end both in *-os* and in *-es*: thus ὀμβρηρὸς and ὀμβρήρης, “rainy”; ἐπίμηκος and ἐπιμήκης, “extended in length,” and so forth. I am no longer surprised that our critic Clericus is ignorant of this, since he is ignorant that Aulon is a proper name among the Hebrews just as it is among the Greeks and Latins: Aulon, a spring, valley, and mountain of Greater Phrygia; Aulon, a town of Magna Graecia; Aulon, a city on the coast of Macedonia; and so forth.

VI. “Sixthly,” says Clericus, “we stated that the editor and interpreter of Jerome ought to be accustomed to handling manuscript codices and to undertaking all the duties of a skilled critic. We do not see sufficiently clear specimens of these abilities in Martianaeus, although he speaks of nothing but manuscript codices.”

He then produces a single example to prove that my restoration of the preface to all the books of the Old Testament—“you anoint the head of the Lord reclining at table with the most precious myrrh of faith”—is the work of an ignorant and unfortunate critic. For, contrary even to Erasmus’s interpretation, he wishes Jerome to have alluded not to the woman who poured the precious ointment from the alabaster jar upon the head of the Lord reclining at table, but to the women who carried myrrh to the tomb.

This explanation, or rather song, of our critic is so charming that it deserves to be committed to perpetual monuments. I therefore transcribe it in full, as it appears after Erasmus’s annotation:

> “But if we read Jerome’s words attentively, we shall see that he looks much more directly, so to speak, toward the women who carried myrrh to Christ’s tomb than toward the woman, or women, who poured ointment upon his head as he reclined at table. For he speaks as though he were saying: ‘You are by no means seeking the Savior in the tomb, whom you might anoint with myrrh after his death, as the women in the Gospel did; rather, with your myrrh you anoint the head of him who is alive.’”

[Note: [Col. 1603B] We discuss this reading more fully in the relevant preface of Jerome, where we show both that Clericus is deceived by his desire to disparage and that he himself deceives. Writers of that age not infrequently use *myrum* for ointment. One example among many is St. Gaudentius of Brescia, Sermon 20, shortly after the middle, in nearly the same words as Jerome: “Upon one is founded the Church; another bears the precious myrrh of faith among the people.”]

Bravo, Clericus! Jerome’s restoration belongs to you: all the manuscript codices are eager to thank you; you alone, as a writer of the *Ars Critica*, can change the most precious ointment of faith into the myrrh of a scabrous man. There is only one thing you ought greatly to fear: namely, that the context of Jerome’s preface be placed before the eyes of the reader. For if it appears, you will immediately be judged not a skilled critic but a delirious paraphrast.

Therefore, I beg you, spare the editor’s freedom—you who are yourself the champion of freedom of thought in the republic of letters—and read again what you did not understand, or certainly did not wish to understand, in Jerome’s preface:

> “But I also ask you, handmaids of Christ, who anoint the head of the Lord reclining at table with the most precious myrrh of faith, who by no means seek the Savior in the tomb, since Christ has already ascended to the Father for you, to set the shields of your prayers against the barking dogs who rage against me with rabid mouths and go about the city, thinking themselves learned if they disparage others. I, knowing my own humility, shall always remember that saying: ‘I said, I will guard my ways,’ etc.”

[Col. 1604A] How could it enter the mind of anyone attentively reading Jerome’s words that Jerome here looks much more directly toward the women who carried myrrh to Christ’s tomb than toward the sinful woman who poured the most precious ointment upon the head of the Lord reclining at table in the Gospel narrative?

Jerome expressly teaches that Paula and Eustochium anoint the head of the Lord reclining at table, because they frequently ministered at table to the members of Christ—that is, to the poor—and filled the whole Church of Christ with the fragrance of their virtues, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.”

Then the holy Doctor asserts that these same handmaids of Christ by no means seek Christ in the tomb, to anoint him with myrrh, because Christ had already ascended to the Father for them. What Jerome affirms, John Clericus denies; and what Jerome denies, Clericus affirms.

Jerome therefore alludes to the woman who poured the alabaster jar of precious ointment upon the head of the Lord reclining at table, and, delighted—as Erasmus notes—with the Gospel expression, preferred to say μύρῳ rather than *unguentum*. This is what Jerome says, and what his editor Erasmus says; I have willingly agreed with both.

But at the end of this defense of Jerome, alluding in my customary manner to Clericus, I say that Jerome looked more directly toward the author of the *Hieronymian Questions* than toward those whom he rebuked in these words:

> “That you may set the shields of your prayers against the barking dogs who rage against me with rabid mouths and think themselves learned if they disparage others, etc.”

INDEX OF SOME OF THE MORE NOTABLE LIES AND DECEPTIVE LITTLE CONCLUSIONS OF JOHN CLERICUS

[Col. 1603]

[Col. 1603B] Lest we draw out the rope of contention with Clericus any longer, and lest that ignorant critic, having been punished for his learning in the first *Question*, enjoy impunity to chatter in the rest, I have thought it necessary to bring forward here several of the more celebrated passages of the little book of the *Hieronymian Questions*, so that the perverse faith, ignorance, and stupidity of this writer may become increasingly evident and he may be held in disgrace by all wise men.

Here, therefore, rather by an index than by a careful disputation, we shall expose Clericus as plainly a liar and an ignoramus.

A
To perform an act merely to insult one’s opponent is the mark of a dishonest and incompetent writer. *Hieronymian Questions*, pp. 362 and 377, where Clericus writes:

> “Thus Martianaeus showed himself an incompetent critic, substituting the Scholiast’s correction for Jerome’s words; and these will certainly have to be restored by those who hereafter publish Jerome, etc. Nearly all the manuscripts have: ‘And when the Lord had descended through the cloud, Moses stood with him, invoking the name of the Lord; and when he passed before him, he said: “Sovereign Lord God,” etc.’ . . . But Martianaeus’s edition has been rewritten by I know not whom, in conformity with the Hebrew manuscript: ‘He stood there with him’—that is, with Moses, as appears in the margin—‘and as the Lord passed before him, he said.’ This is a sheer corruption of Jerome’s version, as we have already said.”

The *Additions and Changes* printed at the end of Volume I of our edition, however, recommend that this reading be restored in the following words:

> “Column 100, chapter XXXIV of Exodus, verses 5 and 6: this reading of the Vulgate seems to us to be restored: ‘And when the Lord had descended through the cloud, Moses stood with him, invoking the name of the Lord. And when he passed before him, he said: “Sovereign Lord,” etc.’ First, the Memmian Canon of the Hebrew Truth reads in this way, together with all the other manuscript codices, except the Canon of Saint-Germain. Second, the critical marginal notes in the Canon of Saint-Germain are so formulated that we can easily understand that the text of Jerome’s version was altered at this point, either by the Scholiast himself or by another writer who added marginal scholia. Nevertheless, this too should honestly be credited to the Hebrew scholiast’s credit: namely, that the sense of Scripture is that which he himself restored. For from Numbers, chapter XIV, verses 17 and 18, it is evident that God spoke the words already cited from Exodus: ‘Sovereign Lord God,’ etc. Let anyone who wishes compare the two passages.”

From this it is clear that our critic Clericus is a dishonest and incompetent adviser, for after ten years he now advises us to restore the reading of Jerome’s version which we ourselves had advised should be restored so long ago.

## [Col. 1604] **AMOR**

A keen love of slander, p. 298, *Hieronymian Questions*.

> “In the same prologue to Genesis,” says the critic, “Jerome rightly mocks those who thought that the Seventy translators were inspired; for it is one thing to be a prophet and another to be a translator, as he correctly says. But Martianaeus should either have corrected this passage or reconciled it with himself, since in the preface to Chronicles, according to the Septuagint translators, he says that the Septuagint translators, filled with the Holy Spirit, translated what was true.”

This slanderer did not read my notice placed in columns 1415 and 1416, in which I reconcile Jerome’s statements in the following manner:

> “Next, this should be considered: although Jerome gathered testimonies from all his little prefaces in order to blunt Rufinus’s criticism, by which that slanderer accused the holy Doctor of envy toward the Septuagint translators, nevertheless he does not reproduce any of this Prologue—in the book on Chronicles—in the later book of his *Apology*, at the end of which all the prefaces to the Old Testament are recited. Why this happened we do not yet know, unless we may conjecture, to some extent with Erasmus, that Jerome did not speak according to his own opinion when he said that the Septuagint translators had been filled with the Holy Spirit and had added many things to the sacred books on the authority of the Holy Spirit. Rather, he attributed this to the opinion of his friends Domnio and Rogatianus, among whom copies of the Septuagint translators perhaps carried such great weight.

> “Whatever may be thought of Erasmus’s conjecture, it is certain that in six hundred other passages Saint Jerome denies that the Greek version of the Septuagint translators was produced under the impulse of the Holy Spirit. ‘For it is one thing,’ he says in the Prologue to Genesis, ‘to be a prophet and another to be a translator,’ etc. When he cites these words against Rufinus in the second book of his *Apology*, he could not have repeated there the words of the subsequent preface to Chronicles in his own defense without immediately being convicted of folly in the matter of the Septuagint translators, concerning whom he would have written such mutually contradictory statements. He therefore wisely keeps silent about what he had formerly attributed to the opinion and expression of Domnio, for whom the Septuagint edition perhaps possessed the highest authority, etc.”

Let the incompetent craftsman of slander now see whether I have reconciled Jerome’s prologues.

## C

### **CORRUPTOR**

He is a corrupter of books, p. 320. For he corrupts whatever he wishes to correct, reading in Jerome’s preface to his Latin translation of the prophet Daniel:

> “Finally, I too, as a young man . . . when I had shut myself into the mill of this language, and with much . . .”

when, according to the authority of all editions and manuscript codices, he should have read:

> “when I had shut myself up in the mill of this language, and with much . . .”

[Col. 1605]

### **CORRUPTIONIS absurdissimus patronus**

He is the most absurd defender of corruption, p. 297.

> “I have often been amazed that in the editions of Erasmus and Victorius this prologue is read more correctly in the second *Apology against Rufinus*, where it is inserted, than at the beginning of Volume III, where it stands separately. Martianaeus should have taken care not to commit anything similar. Since he did not, I shall point out from the aforementioned *Apology* an additional error which I have detected in the words quoted by me: where, instead of *illucescere* [to make shine], one should read *illustria* [illustrious things], as it is in that *Apology*, and as the following words show: ‘He makes illustrious those things which had previously been less so.’”

The very words of the Prologue to Genesis refute this delirium:

> “Origen’s diligence moved me to dare this. He mixed Theodotion’s translation with the ancient edition, distinguishing the whole work by an asterisk (*) and an obelus (÷), that is, by a star and a spit, while either illuminating (*illucescere*) the things that had previously been lacking, or slaughtering and piercing whatever was superfluous.”

Tell us, illustrious Clericus, what do your *illustria* contribute here? Will you deny that stars shine in the heavens and illuminate the earth? If you can deny this, likewise deny that the asterisks, or stars, shone in Origen’s work, in which he distinguished the text by an asterisk and an obelus, illuminating what the Septuagint had omitted and supplying it himself from Theodotion’s edition.

If I were not weary of contending with delirium, I would say much in response here to the incompetent Clericus’s admonition. But since this is an index, it briefly indicates all the criticisms of our critic.

### **CRITICUS**

He is an impious critic, and not a Christian, who attempts to remove from sacred Scripture the mystery of Christ the Redeemer and God. Pages 365 and 366.

> “In the fifteenth verse of the same chapter, instead of *ipsa conteret* [‘she shall crush it’], as nearly all the Latin manuscript codices have, as our monk admits, and as many Fathers read—including Augustine—he himself published *ipse* [‘he’], from a single codex which he mentions. Why does he not also commend the other codices mentioned in the Louvain Collection? Perhaps the passage ought to have been printed according to the reading of the majority of codices rather than altered on the basis of a few codices.

> “For what Jerome has in the *Hebrew Questions* contributes nothing to the matter, since in the Version he often follows not his own opinion but ecclesiastical usage, especially in the more important passages (see Genesis IV, 8). The Septuagint translators have here: ‘He himself will preserve your head.’ In these words *αὐτός* [‘he himself’] seems to have been used because the Septuagint translators, although they used the neuter word *σπέρμα* [‘seed’], had in mind the masculine noun *γόνος* [‘offspring’], which has the same meaning. Likewise, the ancient Latin Translator, although he used the word *semen* [‘seed’], nevertheless added *ipsa* [‘she herself’], because he was thinking of offspring or progeny. It would be easy to produce many examples of this kind of construction from the best authors.

> “I know that later the pronoun *ipsa* was referred to the Church, as though she were described under the name of a woman, or even to the Virgin Mary. But these faulty interpretations would not prevent me from representing the ancient reading, for which a reasonable explanation can be given.”

I do not wish to enumerate the dreams of incompetence contained in this *Question* of Clericus, since that would take too long. Let the diligent reader merely beware of what I have noted elsewhere: namely, the impiety of our Socinian critic, who, going beyond even the expressions of his own fathers, denies that one should read, “He himself will crush your head,” lest he be compelled to believe that Christ the Lord, by his own power, crushed the head of the ancient serpent and freed the human race from its power.

How shamelessly he lies when he asserts that what Jerome has in the *Hebrew Questions* contributes nothing to our restoration of *ipse conteret caput tuum*—“he himself will crush your head”—will become perfectly clear from Jerome’s own reading. The statement of the holy Doctor in the *Hebrew Questions* is therefore as follows:

> “He himself will preserve your head, and you will preserve his heel. It is better in Hebrew,” he says, “as follows: ‘He himself will crush your head, and you will crush his heel’; because our steps too are hindered by the serpent, and the Lord will crush Satan beneath our feet swiftly.”

Here, Christian reader, you have the mystery of your redemption in Christ; you also have a reliable witness for my restoration of *ipse conteret*—“he himself will crush”—which John Clericus would not oppose if he had not been shipwrecked in faith in Christ God and in the heritage of religion.

[Note: [Col. 1605] Nevertheless, the word *ipsa*, which the Vulgate also has, should not be rejected; it can also be defended by sound arguments.]

## F

### **FIDES**

There is no faith in the critic who urges Jerome’s editor to corrupt the letter F, which appears in the books *On Hebrew Names* and *On Hebrew Places*. He urges this contrary to the authority of all editions and manuscript codices, pp. 397 and 398.

> “This also,” says Clericus after Richard Simon, “cannot be tolerated in these etymologies: that names beginning with the Hebrew letter *Pe* should be written with the Latin F, as though the two were identical, whereas Jerome otherwise habitually renders it by PH, both in his translation and in his commentaries. It is absurd that P should be omitted, or PH, and F put in its place, although F does not exist in the Hebrew language. And, to reveal what I suspect, this book was perhaps rewritten by some monk who transferred names beginning with PH to the letter F. The same thing was done in the book *On the Situation and Names of Places*.”

Who would not be astonished at critics so stupidly fierce that they still do not know that the Hebrew letter is represented by the Greek Φ, and that both have the sound of the Latin F? Let them therefore recall the Latin alphabet, whose order and sequence Jerome followed in both books, *On Hebrew Names* and *On Hebrew Places*. If these first rudiments of grammatical art are insufficient, let them at least learn that I could not, without enormous recklessness and audacity, have altered in Jerome’s books what all printed and manuscript books throughout the world preserve.

Finally, what benefit would such a corruption of the letter F in the books of Jerome have brought, when the crime would have been exposed by Jerome himself? For he himself warns the reader concerning the letter F placed in the book *On Hebrew Names* as follows:

> “But it should be known,” he says, “that among the Hebrews there is no letter P, nor is there any name that expresses this element. It must therefore be taken abusively, as though it had been written with the letter F.”

Simon and Clericus ought to have noticed this before accusing me of incompetence for retaining the letter F in its proper places. If I had dared to alter it, I have no doubt that both critics would immediately have shouted that I was a falsifier; such is the hostility they exercise against Martianaeus.

## S

### **SYCOPHANTA**

He is not a skilled critic who teaches not what is true but incites the ignorant crowd against his opponents. Such is our Clericus, *Question* 13, pp. 449–450.

> “The Hebrews place what follows—‘And he did not know when he slept with her, nor when he rose from her’—above the text as something incredible and as something that nature cannot accept, etc.”

These are Jerome’s words concerning verse 33 of chapter XIX of Genesis. But in the note printed beneath the page, the Benedictine Editor says:

> “I examined more carefully several manuscript codices, but I could find nothing in them that helped clarify this passage.”

He then gives a note by Erasmus, complains that Marianus Victorius remained silent here, and, after observing that other codices have *adjungunt* or *opponunt* in place of *appungunt*, adds:

> “Whether, therefore, we understand that points were placed above these words of Scripture, or that the words themselves were added in the upper part of the sacred text, outside the sequence of the remaining words—in whatever manner one believes this was done—the Hebrews intended to signify something incredible, both by the points and by the position of the words.”

Who would not laugh at the outburst of our monk, who with such arrogance attacks the reputation of learned men in a matter known to every beginner? Before consulting Hebrew manuscript codices, he ought to have examined editions supplied with vowel points. All of them have an unusual point placed upon the letter in the word *bkoumah* when she rose; the Masorah gives the marginal note *nakoud hal vau*: “the vau is pointed,” that is, a point is placed above the vau. Innumerable interpreters have treated this subject, including Johann Buxtorf in his *Commentary on the Masoretic Treatise*, chapter XVII, where he shows that the Talmudists mentioned the matter.

Let our author read more carefully the printed Bibles and the critical commentaries of learned men before he turns to handwritten books. Those who have never devoted diligent attention to the readings of printed editions do not know how to use manuscripts. It is exceedingly foolish to boast of manuscript Bibles when one has not read the printed ones.

No one will deny that our heretic is here raving in his assault upon me, hoping that through my incompetence he would win a trophy worthy of a triumphal statue throughout the whole republic of letters. But lower your brow, sycophantic critic, so that you may not doubt that I have devoted diligent attention to the readings of printed books.

You say that all editions supplied with vowel points have an unusual point placed upon the letter vau in the word *bkoumah*. Then you have not read the Hebrew Bibles of Münster and Elijah Hutter; you have not read the Complutensian Polyglot, nor the Paris edition of D. Le Jay, in which no point is placed upon that letter. You have not read the Hebrew Bibles of Sanctes Pagninus and Arias Montanus, which in the Geneva edition retain no point upon the letter vau, whereas in the Antwerp edition they have two points, not one, placed upon that same letter.

Now see, unjust slanderer, whether I read the printed books before boasting of manuscript codices. Yet you are not ashamed of such a great slander and such arrogance, calling a simple and candid observation—without injury to anyone’s name—arrogance and an outburst by which I attack the reputation of learned men.

I advise you henceforth not to infect the simple words of your enemies with your own poison, lest we always have to say of you, the critic Clericus:

> “Innocence would have perished if power had always been joined to wickedness, and if everything that slander desires were to prevail.”

Jerome, Book III of the *Apology against Rufinus*.

If we wished to examine everything in this Index of Clerican incompetence and to measure it strictly against the most exact standard of a *Response and Defense*, this would not be a place where we could bring this little work to an end, but where we would have to begin a second apologetic volume. Yet this is neither necessary nor would it be anything but tedious, since what we have observed may serve as a specimen from which it is sufficiently clear that what we have already said about the incompetence of Clericus’s *Questions* is altogether true, even though we leave further statements unmade.

Certainly, our freedom in rebuking an incompetent and insufficiently modest critic cannot be denied us without the greatest incompetence or injustice.

# Volume back matter

[Col. 1607]
